<meta>This is the title page of the first volume of Luis de Molina’s influential work on law and economics. It establishes the author's credentials and the scope of the legal theory contained within.</meta>

# LUIS DE MOLINA
## OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS, <note>original: "E Societate Iesu," the Jesuit Order</note>
### FORMERLY THE PRIMARY PROFESSOR
### Of Sacred Theology at the University of Évora, <note>original: "Eborensi Academia," a prestigious Portuguese university where Molina taught</note>
# A TREATISE ON JUSTICE AND LAW,
-> *Which is* <-
### CONCERNING COMMUTATIVE JUSTICE REGARDING <term>Commutative justice: The branch of justice governing private interactions, exchanges, and the fulfillment of promises between individuals.</term>
-> *External Goods: Otherwise titled "On Contracts."* <-

-> IN WHICH THE QUESTIONS AND DIFFICULTIES <-
-> pertaining to this subject are examined no less concisely and learnedly than they are <-
-> seen to be decided forcefully and accurately from the infallible foundations of HOLY JUSTICE; <-
-> so that nothing further is left to be desired or added by anyone. <-

-> *A work not only for Students, Theologians, and Canon Lawyers; but also truly for Doctors of Civil Law practicing in both courts,* <note>original: "vtroque foro," referring to the separate legal systems of the Church and the State</note> <-
-> *the Ecclesiastical as well as the Secular, being especially useful and necessary.* <-

-> WITH A TRIPLE INDEX: ONE OF DISPUTATIONS, <-
-> another of passages from Holy Scripture, and a final subject index, most ample and rich. <-

<meta>The previous page served as the title page for Johannes Busaeus's "The Garden of Christian Virtues" (1610). However, the current page begins a dedication for a different, yet contemporary, Jesuit work: Luis de Molina’s influential treatise on Justice and Law. # TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS,

->AND<-

# MOST WISE

## SENATOR,

## ANDREA MOROSINI. <note>Andrea Morosini (1558–1618) was a prominent Venetian historian, statesman, and senator known for his dedication to the Republic of Venice.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece featuring a central mask or face flanked by scrolling foliage and two bird-like figures at the outer edges.</image-desc>

->*Ascanio Colofino sends his fondest greetings.*<- <note>original: "S. P. D." (Salutem Plurimam Dicit), a standard Latin formal greeting.</note>

<image-desc>Large historiated initial 'V' set within a square frame, depicting a winged putto or angel amidst dense foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

Just as the Sun, with its preeminent light, Most Illustrious Sir, is the governor of the other spheres and the Leader in the Heavens—for if it were removed from the world, universal darkness would take hold, and the brilliance of the other spheres could in no way retain or protect their light—so too among the Virtues stands Justice itself and Law. <term>Iustitia & Ius: Justice (the moral virtue) and Law (the legal framework).</term> Without these, all other virtues must necessarily collapse, and human society would be unable to stand firm. When Justice is snatched away from human affairs, it is as if the Sun were removed from the world. Therefore, those authors who have written on this subject have chosen for themselves the most excellent theme for their writing. Those who exercise its daily duties through the administration of justice, the punishing of human errors, the restraint of wrongdoing, and the curbing of desires, have always been held in the highest honor by all. Such men are judged the Leaders of Republics and Kings. To perform these duties even better at times, it is not out of place to shape and, as it were, polish the edge of the mind—even if it is already quite capable and suited by its own nature or other studies—by reading the writings of distinguished men. Indeed, among all those who have written about Justice and Law within our memory and that of our fathers, by the weightiest consensus of learned men, no one has recorded these questions in literary monuments better, more accurately, or more appropriately for Christian Philosophy and justice than **LUIS DE MOLINA**. <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600) was a Spanish Jesuit whose work "De Iustitia et Iure" fundamentally shaped modern economic and legal thought.</note> He was a most learned and upright man from that celebrated Society of Jesus, emerging into the light as if from a "Trojan Horse"—a nursery, so to speak, of the most learned men. <note>original: "equo Troiano," used here as a positive metaphor for a group that produces a sudden, powerful abundance of talent.</note> Since this man’s disputations on contracts <note>original: "contractibus," referring to the section of Molina's work dealing with the ethics of trade, prices, and loans.</note> were being published with such exquisite and learned treatment, I decided that I must choose a Patron whose name, inscribed as it were upon the front of the book, would provide protection for both the author and myself. Thus, some honor might be summoned for you from the public gaze of the lettered world, as if upon a Theater of honor and glory. You, Most Illustrious Sir, were the primary person who occurred to me, to whom this honor—and this duty—is owed, because...

<summary>This page contains a formal dedication by Ascanio Colofino to the Venetian Senator Andrea Morosini, prefacing Luis de Molina's famous work on Law and Justice. It uses the metaphor of the Sun to describe Justice as the essential foundation of human society.</summary>

<keywords>Luis de Molina, Andrea Morosini, Justice, Law, Society of Jesus, Jesuit scholarship, Ascanio Colofino, contracts, legal philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>The previous page established the book's subject: a treatise on Justice and Law (likely by Luis de Molina), dedicated to the Venetian polymath and statesman Andrea Morosini. It began by comparing Justice to the Sun, without which human society would fall into darkness. The current page continues this dedication by enumerating Morosini’s personal virtues, his family’s prestigious history, and his rapid political ascent in the Venetian Republic.</meta>

...as you are the one who could best provide and undertake this patronage. For who among the Venetian nobility is to be preferred above you, if we weigh all the qualities in you—both your own and those of your family's honors and praises? 

For if we seek authority, you possess it to the greatest degree possible for your age. You have acquired it not only through a steady course of all virtues, omitting nothing required of an excellent Senator, but also by the most distinguished judgments of the Republic <term>R. P.</term> <note>original: Res Publica; referring here specifically to the Republic of Venice.</note> concerning you, which has heaped every dignity and honor upon you. 

If we consider learning and erudition, there is no storehouse in human hearts more polished or adorned than yours, who since childhood seem to have been nourished by the very milk of the Muses. In those first studies by which minds are imbued with humanity, you made rapid progress through great deeds, entering the fields of Philosophy as a youth and almost as a boy. In that arena and wrestling ground, you proved yourself so well that no one of such tender age was considered a more excellent Venetian philosopher. 

With your feet firmly planted in this spring—or rather, this ocean—you then tasted all the streams of other sciences. You left nothing untried, nothing unexamined. From this, a brilliant reputation and fame for your learning spread abroad, such that the most distinguished Council of Ten <term>Xvirorum Collegium</term> <note>The "Council of Ten" was a powerful governing body in Venice; they oversaw state security and, as noted here, the appointment of official historians.</note> by unanimous vote appointed you to the most honorable and weighty task of writing the History of Venice.

If, indeed, we look at the splendor of your family: who does not know the praises of the Morosini <note>original: MAVROCOENAE, the Latinized form of the Venetian Morosini family name.</note> clan? How many Princes <note>In the Venetian context, "Princes" refers to the Doges.</note>, how many Senators, how many Bishops and Cardinals has it produced? History is full of the illustrious deeds of the Morosinis. If I wished to recount them briefly, I would have to weave a volume and a history rather than a letter. 

But if I omit all else, I cannot pass over your household praise in silence. For who in the City does not admire and revere your father, a most distinguished Senator of the highest prudence and proven integrity? Such humanity, kindness, and approachability shine in his very face and manners that he wins the goodwill of all. You follow in his footsteps at an equal pace, together with your brothers, **NICCOLÒ** and **PAOLO**, who are most adorned with every kind of virtue and public splendor. Thus, one can easily recognize in you three living images of your parent.

Finally, if we desire the honors bestowed by the Republic, who has performed greater ones at your age? You have flown through every rank of honors with great speed; the path has been open to you for every magistracy and court—to the office of Advocate or Tribune, to the College, and to the Senate. Nothing has been denied to you that could be sought or expected at your age, so that now, by the anticipated judgment of all, there is no doubt what you will soon become.

Since you shine like a most brilliant light in the Republic through your erudition, family splendor, and dignities, I judged that I should rightly seek your patronage. Receive, therefore, into your protection both the work itself—namely the author's book, which deals with **Justice and Law**—and me, the Bookseller <term>Bibliopola</term>, who for a long time has been most bound to you by many duties and a certain devoted impulse of mind and respect. Expect even better things daily (if you do not despise these) for the common benefit of students.

->*Farewell.*<-

The text offers the book on Justice and Law to Morosini as a patron of learning and the Republic.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded the formal dedication to the Venetian statesman Andrea Morosini, highlighting his reputation for learning and his prestigious role within the Republic's Council of Ten. This page begins a new section: the printer's address to the reader, justifying the publication of these scholarly works.</meta>

# THE PRINTER
## TO THE DILIGENT READER.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a central figure, possibly a cherub or classical youth, surrounded by ornate foliate scrolls and floral motifs.</image-desc>That famous and widely repeated maxim of the divine Plato comes to mind, learned Reader: that man is not born for himself alone, but that his birth is claimed partly by his country, partly by his parents, and partly by his friends. Reminded of this Platonic principle, and being very eager to satisfy my old practice and long-standing custom—striving to vigorously promote the efforts of students—I judged that I should spare no constant labor, nor avoid any expenses, however heavy, even for myself. I have done this especially in printing those authors whom either the excellence of their outstanding talent or their distinguished learning combined with piety has rendered recommended to all who follow and presented to posterity.

Among these authors, the very Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus <term>Societatis IESV</term> <note>The Jesuits, a Catholic religious order known for their rigorous education and scholarship.</note> easily hold—in the judgment of many right-thinking people—not the last but indeed the primary role. Consequently, we have been entirely focused on this: that certain selected works of theirs, which were not so long ago presented for the inspection of learned minds, might be studied and explored both at home and abroad through our effort, which we believe is not without merit. 

Hence, we recently published the commentaries of Suarez <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617), a Spanish Jesuit priest and a giant of late Scholasticism.</note> on the first part of the philosophy of Aristotle the Stagirite <note>original: "Aristotelis Stagiritæ"; referring to Aristotle of Stagira.</note>. Furthermore, we have published the first volume of studies by Vasquez <note>Gabriel Vásquez (1549–1604), a prominent Spanish Jesuit theologian often compared to Suarez.</note>—who is equal in piety and not dissimilar in talent—on the First Part of Saint Thomas Aquinas. We intend to bring forth the second volume not much later, just as we promise to give soon the first commentary on the second part. 

Nor did we think we should omit the *Paraphrases of Gospel History* by the Reverend Father Salmeron <note>Alfonso Salmerón (1515–1585), a founding member of the Jesuits and a renowned biblical scholar.</note>. Having already released the first volume <term>Tomo</term>, as it is commonly called, we will (God willing) offer others as quickly as possible to be studied and handled by the hands of the learned, who have long been eagerly waiting for them. 

To these has been added the treatise *On Contracts* <note>original: "de Contractibus"</note> by Father Molina <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600), a Jesuit whose work on law and economics remains highly influential.</note>, a man truly famous for the reputation of his most solid learning. This work, subjected to the most exact scrutiny of scholars and most diligently corrected, and newly adorned by our effort with summaries prefixed to each Disputation, we have recently published from the printing press. Just as we expect many other monuments of his fertile talent very soon...

<summary>In this preface, the printer addresses the reader, citing Plato to justify his laborious and expensive work in publishing great scholars. He lists several prestigious Jesuit authors he has recently published or plans to publish, including Suarez, Vasquez, Salmeron, and Luis de Molina.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Francisco Suárez, Gabriel Vásquez, Thomas Aquinas, Alfonso Salmerón, Luis de Molina, Society of Jesus, Jesuits, book trade, printing history, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the printer's address to the reader, following his explanation of why he chose to publish the works of Jesuit scholars. The previous page ended with a mention of Francisco Suárez’s commentaries.</meta>

Therefore, with an equal spirit—and as a testament to the goodwill with which we have provided these prior works for the benefit of scholars—we wish to serve you both sincerely and constantly, as far as our resources and abilities allow. We shall soon bring these works into the public light, fully aware of the great and remarkable benefit that will come to all learned men—and especially to the followers, lovers, and admirers of divine wisdom—from their diligent reading, yielding a high return for scholarship and a most abundant fruit. 

For your part, in keeping with your characteristic kindness, please receive our efforts with gratitude. By favoring us with your kind support <note>original: "applausū"</note> as you use these works for your own advancement, you will spur us on as we race forward to serve you. You will undoubtedly see it proven, by the work itself and by this lived experience, that nothing has been in the past, nor is at present, more important <note>The Latin "antiquius" literally means "older," but in this context, it is a classical idiom meaning "of greater importance" or "more dear."</note> to us than your own advantage.

In the meantime, farewell; live long and happily. And if it please you, offer a prayer from the heart for one who wishes you well, as a kind of repayment in kind.

->From our Venetian Print Shop <term>Calcographia</term> <note>While "Calcographia" often refers specifically to copper-plate engraving, it was frequently used by Renaissance printers to refer to the printing house or the art of printing as a whole.</note> in the year of the reborn century <note>original: "renascentis seculi." This refers to the turn of the new century, the 1600s.</note> 1601, on the Ides of March <note>March 15th.</note>.<--

# INDEX OF DISPUTATIONS,
## which are contained in this second volume on Justice.

<image-desc>An ornate historiated initial 'P' depicting a scholar or clerk seated at a desk within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

Agreements and contracts: what they are, and on civil and natural obligation. Disputation 252
On named and unnamed contracts. 253
Which contracts are completed by consent alone, which by word alone, which by writing, and which by action <note>original: "opere"</note>. 254
On bare and "clothed" agreements <term>pactum nudum</term> <note>In Roman law, a "bare agreement" was a simple promise that lacked the legal formalities (the "clothing") required to be enforceable in a civil court.</note>, and when a civil obligation arises or does not arise from a bare agreement or an unnamed contract. 255
If a bare agreement is confirmed by an oath, whether a civil obligation arises from it, and whether an action is granted for it in canon and civil law. 256
Whether a natural obligation, binding in the court of conscience, arises from a bare agreement; and whether this holds true in canon law and in the Kingdom of Castile. 257
To what extent there is a right to withdraw <term>poenitentiae</term> <note>Literally "repentance," referring to the legal right to back out of a contract before it has been executed.</note> in bare agreements and unnamed contracts under civil law, and whether it has a place in canon law and in the Kingdom of Castile. 258
Contracts which are of "good faith" <note>bona fides</note> and those of "strict law," and on other divisions of contracts. 259
A contract is to be judged as celebrated according to the customs and laws of the place, and for which contracts a public document is necessary for proof under Portuguese law. 260
Who may enter into contracts. 261
A promise differs from a purpose: on the two types of promises, and at the same time on the virtues of truthfulness and faithfulness. 262
Whether a promise can be freely revoked before it is accepted, and whether this is a feature of its nature or of positive law. 263
By whom a promise may be accepted, and to what extent one made to an absent person is valid. 264
Whether a condition or a burden <note>original: "modus, & gravamen"</note> can be attached to a gift in favor of a third party; and whether it can be removed or revoked before it is accepted by them. 265
Whether an internal promise made to a person has the power to obligate. 266
A promise or a formal agreement <term>stipulatio</term>: how much deliberation and spontaneity it must have to be binding. 267
Whether a promise or formal agreement is valid regarding an uncertain thing, the action of another, a sacred or public thing, or a free person. 268
Whether a promise of something that exists only in hope is valid; and to whom a promised thing belongs if it perishes <note>This refers to the legal question of who bears the loss if the item is destroyed before delivery.</note>. 269
On the promise to pay another's debt, or to pay one's own on another day or in another place; and on promises made disjunctively ("this or that"), cumulatively ("this and that"), or for an uncertain thing from several options. 270
On the promise of an impossible or illicit thing, or one that is contrary to good morals because it would provide an occasion for ruin; and what if this last one is confirmed by an oath. 271
For what reasons it is lawful not to fulfill an accepted promise before it is carried out. 272
The difference between a promise and a completed gift <term>donatio</term>. 273
Who can give gifts. And specifically on alms and gifts made by a wife. 274

<column-break/>

On gifts made by a husband, and on those spent on concubines; and similarly on a gift made to a concubine by a soldier or a cleric. 275
To what extent a member of a religious order can give gifts or alms. 276
To what extent a minor son <note>under paternal authority</note>, a spendthrift <term>prodigus</term>, or an enslaved person <term>mancipium</term> can give gifts. 277
A gift which requires formal registration <term>insinuatio</term> <note>A public recording of a gift to prevent fraud or excessive generosity.</note> to be valid, and what if it is confirmed by an oath. 278
A gift which does not require formal registration to be valid. 279
Whether a gift of all the donor's goods is valid, and what if it is confirmed by an oath. 280
On the revocation of a gift due to the ingratitude of the recipient. 281
On the revocation of a gift because a child is born to the donor. 282

The various types of gifts, formal agreements, or promises; and on unconditional ones and those set for a specific day. 284
On conditional gifts, formal agreements, or promises. 285
On gifts with a condition <term>sub modo</term>; and whether things given to induce a woman to give wrongful consent, or for other ends, are subject to restitution if the end is not achieved; and on alms and other gifts made for feigned reasons, or those involving a false description. 286

On gifts between spouses. 289
On betrothal gifts, and gifts made before marriage or because of marriage. 290
On a gift from a father to a son. 291
On remunerative gifts <note>Gifts given as a reward for past service.</note>, and generally on gifts made for a specific cause. 292
Deceit <term>dolus</term>, legal fault <term>culpa</term>, and accidental occurrence: what they are, and how many types of legal fault there are. 293
On a loan for use <term>commodato</term>, and its difference from a "precarium" <note>A loan held only at the will of the lender.</note>, and when a thing lent for use can be reclaimed. 294
To what extent the borrower <term>commodatarius</term> is held liable if the thing perishes or is damaged. 295
Whether things lent for use should be preferred over one's own when both cannot be saved; and for whom they perish if they are sent through a third person. 296
To what extent the borrower is held liable if they are in delay <term>mora</term> in returning the item; on expenses incurred with it; and whether a set-off <term>compensatio</term> can be made. 297
On a loan held by request/at will <term>precario</term>. 298
On a loan for consumption <term>mutuo</term> <note>A loan of things that are consumed by use, like money or grain, where the borrower is expected to return an equal amount of the same kind.</note>. 299
On a loan made to the Church, a city, or a minor. 300
On a loan made to a son under paternal authority. 301
On the legal defense <term>exceptio</term> of money not actually received regarding a loan. 302
What usury is, and how many types there are. 303

# INDEX.

Whether usury is unlawful. 304
On mental usury. 305 <note>Mental usury refers to the internal intention or expectation of receiving a profit from a loan, even if it is not explicitly stated in a contract.</note>
To what extent things received through mental usury must be restored. 306
Whether it is usury in a loan <term>mutuum</term> with an agreement that a woman grant sexual access to herself, or that the borrower forgive an injury. 307
Whether it is usury to give a loan with an agreement that the borrower must lend an equal amount in return. 308
Whether it is usury to lend with an agreement that the borrower perform or pay for something they are otherwise bound to do, or be bound to care for, defend, harvest crops, till fields, grind in a mill, or buy from the lender's shop at a fair price. 309
Whether it is usury to lend with an agreement that the borrower be bound to hire, buy, or sell something, receive part of the loan in goods or debt, pay in another location, or provide a service of the tongue <note>original: "a lingua" — likely meaning legal advocacy or praise</note>, of service, or of the hand <note>physical labor</note>, or to free from taxes or other burdens, or to confer an office or a benefice. 310
Whether it is usury to lend wheat or something else so that the same amount is returned when it is worth more: or to give it when it is worth more so that an equal value is returned in wheat, or to give old wheat so that new is returned. 311
If the value of money increases by a decree <term>pragmatica</term>, whether it is usury to receive as much money as was given in the loan; and generally, what should be judged concerning the increase or decrease of coins and measures. 312
Concerning the King's ministers who receive something to wait for debtors or to pay creditors. And concerning those leasing Royal revenues with an agreement that the King take several thousand gold pieces of the price in debts owed by the King. 313
Emerging loss <term>damnum emergens</term> and ceasing profit <term>lucrum cessans</term>: what they are. And whether it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note> by reason of emerging loss. Or for one who received a loan under usury to lend part to another under the same usury. 314 <note>These terms are the two standard legal justifications for charging interest: actual loss incurred by the lender or the loss of a certain profit they could have made elsewhere.</note>
Whether it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of profit that ceases because of the loan. 315
When, and to what extent, profit is judged to cease. 316
Whether an agreement that the borrower, if they do not pay at the fixed time, pays a certain penalty, is usurious. 317
Whether it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of the risk to the loaned property which the lender undergoes. 318
Whether it is usury for a guarantor <term>fideiussor</term> to receive something to act as a guarantor for another. 319
Whether it is usury to receive the fruits <note>revenue or produce</note> of a pledge <term>pignus</term> beyond the principal. And whether it is avoided by buying the same thing instead with an agreement for resale. 320
Whether a son-in-law is free from usury who, while the dowry is not yet paid to him, receives a pledge to be enjoyed, without counting the fruits toward the principal. 321

**The Macedonian defense** <note>original: "Macedoniani exceptio"; a Roman legal rule that barred creditors from suing for the recovery of money lent to a son who was still under his father's legal power</note> is available to a son under paternal authority, even in the court of conscience <note>the "forum of conscience" refers to moral and religious standing rather than just civil legality</note>, and the reason why. **The establishment of a Majorat** <note>original: "Maioratus"; an entailed estate that must be passed down intact to a single heir, usually the eldest son</note> of all present and future goods: when it is valid, even according to the law of Castile, and when it is not. disp. 280. nu. 13.

**The possessor of a Majorat** can grant someone the benefit of a usufruct or another service for the duration of their life, but only as a personal obligation, not a real <note>property-binding</note> one. disp. 470. nu. 4.
**The possessor of a Majorat** cannot newly grant the assets of the Majorat under a long-term lease <note>original: "emphyteutica"; a lease where the tenant improves the land for a fixed rent</note> without the permission of the founder or the King. disp. 470. nu. 11.

### What a Covenant and a Contract are, and on Civil and Natural Obligation.
->DISPUTATION 252.<-

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *From where the word "covenant" <note>original: "pactum"</note> is derived.*
2 *What a covenant is.*
3 *What a contract is.*
4 *A promise, even when accepted, is not strictly a contract.*
5 *Obligation from justice is twofold: natural only, or natural and civil together.*
6 *What a contract is in a broader sense.*
7 *When a gift <note>original: "donatio"</note> is a contract in the broad sense, and when it is not.*
8 *A generous promise that has been accepted is a contract in a broad sense, and an obligation can arise from it on the part of the promisor.*
9 *Whether and when a donor is held liable for eviction <note>term: "eviction" (evictio) refers to the legal recovery of property by a person with a superior title, forcing the current possessor to give it up</note>.*
10 *What a contract is in an even broader and less strict sense.*
11 *An accepted gift is a contract in the broadest sense.*
12 *What "acceptance" is, and that it is a contract in the broadest sense.*

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
In Disputation 114 of this second treatise on justice, we began to speak of the Transfer of ownership by the prior owner's own will, and from there until now we have dealt with last wills and testaments. Now, however, we must discuss Contracts, so that it may be understood to what extent ownership is transferred (or not) by the will of the contracting parties, and how much legal right is acquired from each contract or quasi-contract. But first, we will speak of Contracts in general, taking the word "Contract" in its broadest sense; then we will descend to specific ones.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate scrolling leaf and vine motifs.</image-desc> Because a Covenant <note>original: "pactum"</note>, if the word is taken strictly, has a broader meaning than a Contract, we must begin with the Covenant. Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD) whose writings make up a large part of the Digest of Justinian</note> in the first book of the Digest, under the heading "On Covenants," says that the word *pactum* is derived from *pactio* (agreement), and from *pactum* the word for "peace" (*pax*) was derived, as if the effect took its name from the cause. However, it is generally preferred—as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), an influential scholar and archbishop</note> says in the fifth book of his *Etymologies* and as referenced in the chapter "On the Signification of Words"—that *pactum* is derived from "peace" (*pax*). From *pactum*, the gloss on the aforementioned first book says that *pactio* was derived.

2 A Covenant, or agreement (*pactio*), as Ulpian says in the same cited book, is the consensus and agreement of two or more people on the same point. This definition and another by the same Ulpian (Digest, book 3, "On Promises") explain each other: A Covenant is the consensus and convention of two. From this it is established that a "pollicitation" <note>term: "pollicitatio" refers to a unilateral promise or offer made by one party that has not yet been accepted by another</note> or a promise, as long as it has not been accepted, is not a covenant, because it is not the agreement of two on the same point, but only the promise of the one offering, as Ulpian adds in that same book. However, once it has been accepted, it truly takes on the nature of a covenant, as Paul <note>Julius Paulus, another prominent Roman jurist</note> rightly affirms in the same place along with Bartolus; this is because there is now a consensus and agreement of two on the same thing. By this same reasoning, a gift, which is a thing handed over to someone for free, has the nature of a covenant by the very fact that it is accepted; for it is likewise the consensus of two on the same point.

<column-break/>

3 A Contract properly and strictly speaking, as Ulpian reports from Labeo <note>Marcus Antistius Labeo, a Roman jurist of the early Empire</note> in the Digest "On the Meaning of Words," is a mutual obligation. That is, it is a covenant from which an obligation arises on both sides <note>original: "vltro, citroque"</note>. Thus, Labeo’s formal statement should be explained by its effect, understanding the cause from which that effect arises in the abstract, through which he defines a contract. Buying and selling is therefore a contract in the proper sense: because it is a covenant—and not just any kind—but one from which an obligation arises as soon as it is celebrated, both on the part of the buyer and the seller. The buyer, by the rule of justice, is bound to hand over the price to the seller, and the seller is bound to hand over the merchandise (the thing sold) to the buyer. Indeed, the seller, after handing over the merchandise, is bound to the buyer for "eviction"; that is, to pay the buyer as much as it concerns them that the thing was not taken from their power, if it is recovered by another person as being theirs or belonging to them.

4 However, an accepted promise is not strictly a contract: for although an obligation of justice arises on the part of the promisor to hand over the promised thing, no obligation of justice arises on the part of the person to whom the promise was made—and it is only of this [mutual] obligation that Labeo speaks in his definition. Indeed, that definition, according to the mind of Labeo and Ulpian, seems only to be understood regarding a "civil obligation," which is one for which a legal action is granted under civil law and in the external courts.

5 For a twofold obligation of justice is distinguished. One is natural only; that is, it arises from the nature of the thing itself and is not hindered by the statutes of positive law, yet it is not supported by civil law because the law does not wish to grant a legal action for it. Such is the obligation that arises in one who has sold a thing for more than its just price, but not beyond half [of the just price]...

<summary>This page introduces the second volume of Molina's work on justice, specifically defining the legal and moral differences between a "pact" (agreement) and a "contract" (mutual obligation). It establishes that while all contracts are pacts, not all pacts are contracts, and it begins to distinguish between natural obligations and those enforceable by civil law.</summary>
<keywords>Luis de Molina, contract law, pactum, mutual obligation, civil obligation, natural obligation, Ulpian, Labeo, Roman law, eviction, sale and purchase</keywords>

--- Page 58 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 252. The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a point about the "just price" and the distinction between legal liability and moral obligation (the forum of conscience).</meta>

[...half] of the just price: for here, by the very nature of the case and in the forum of conscience, he is bound by justice to restore what he received beyond the just price; yet, so that lawsuits are not multiplied, no action is granted against him under either civil or canon law. Another natural obligation is distinguished as being both natural and civil; namely, that which arises either from the nature of the case alone or from a concurrent statute of political law, and is supported by civil law granting a legal action against the person so bound. An obligation of this kind is one where a person who has sold grain above the price fixed by a just law is bound to restore the excess price; there are almost infinite other examples which frequently arise from just contracts and various other sources.

<margin>6</margin>
Secondly, the term <term>contract</term> <note>original: "contractus"</note> is used more broadly, though less strictly, for every pact from which an obligation arises, at least on one side, as is gathered from the **law "If of donation," in the Code, title on pacts**, from the **law "If anyone of purchase," at the beginning of the Code, title on the formal words of annual legacies**, and from the **law "Contract," in the Code, title on the good faith of instruments**; this is also affirmed by the **gloss on the "Sacred Authentica regarding minors" in the Code, title "If against a sale," on the word "contracts."**

<margin>7</margin>
In this sense of <term>contract</term>, a gift <note>original: "donatio"</note> that begins with the delivery <note>original: "traditione"</note> of the thing being given is not a contract. This is because, once the thing is handed over, no obligation of justice remains—neither on the part of the recipient who accepted it, nor on the part of the giver, who is thereafter bound to nothing else. This is especially true since one who has given in this way is not held liable for <term>eviction</term> <note>original: "evictio"; the legal recovery of property by a third party with a superior title</note>, as is clear from the **law of Aristo, the last paragraph, in the Digest, title on gifts**, and as is affirmed by the **gloss on the paragraph "Others," on the word "of sale," in the Institutes, title on gifts**, as well as by **Antonio Gomez, volume 2, Various Resolutions, chapter 2, number 5, and chapter 4, number 1, and the doctors of law commonly.** An exception is made if the recipient had incurred expenses on the thing given to him, and the giver was aware that what he gave belonged to someone else; for then he is held liable for the subsequent expenses and damages, but not for the value of the thing he gave, as is clear from the **law of Aristo, the last paragraph, cited above.** And in this sense, **Conrad [Summenhart], "On Contracts," question 16**, is to be understood. That obligation follows the gift "by accident" <note>incidentally</note>, but it arises "by itself" from the fraud and the giver's knowledge that the thing belonged to another; by reason of that knowledge, he is considered to have been the unjust cause of the damages that followed accidentally from that gift.

<margin>8</margin>
But when a gift begins with a promise, it is a <term>contract</term> in this second sense. For although no obligation arises on the part of the recipient from an accepted promise (notwithstanding what **Soto, book 6, "On Justice," question 2, article 1**, might have said to the contrary), it undoubtedly arises on the part of the giver. For even though that promise proceeded from the giver's <term>liberality</term> <note>generosity or free-will</note>, and was therefore an act of the promisor's liberality and not of justice, nevertheless an obligation of justice resulted from it. By this obligation, the promisor remained bound by justice to fulfill what he promised, led solely by liberality, as will be explained more fully in its proper place below. Indeed, the **final gloss on the law of Aristo, last paragraph, cited above, and the gloss on the paragraph "Others," on the word "of sale," in the Institutes, title on gifts, and Antonio Gomez, volume 2, Various Resolutions, chapter 2**,

<margin>9</margin>
number 35, and the common opinion of the doctors which he cites, affirms that when an accepted promise has preceded and the delivery of the promised thing follows, the giver is held liable for <term>eviction</term>. They give this reason: that the giver, through the preceding promise, remained obligated to transfer the ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the promised thing; but he did not fulfill this in practice when the thing delivered belonged to someone else, and for that reason

<column-break/>

it is recovered by law. They confirm the same opinion from the **first law of the Code, title on the law of dowries**, where, when a thing given as a dowry is recovered by a third party, the giver is liable to the son-in-law for eviction. I believe this opinion is true when what was promised was not a specific, individual thing, but was defined by its kind or class, such as two hundred gold coins, so many bushels of wheat, so many oxen, or something similar. For then, because the promise did not regard this specific item more than that one, the promisor is not released from his obligation by paying with something belonging to another, even if he pays it through ignorance. However, when the promised thing was a specific individual item—for example, *this* house, *this* horse, *that* particular slave, or something similar—I judge that if it is recovered by law after being delivered, the giver is not held liable for eviction, unless, when he made the promise, his intention was to bind himself to give another similar thing or its value in the event that the thing was not his own. Such an intention is generally not to be presumed in those making promises. The reason for our opinion is that the promise had its origin only in liberality, and it binds the promisor no further in conscience or in the external court than he intended to promise and bind himself. Therefore, since the promise only had this specific, determined item as its object, the promisor would certainly be held only to that by virtue of the promise. And if it should perish by chance before delivery, or be found to belong to another and recovered after delivery, he is held to nothing else, unless it is clear that his intention was otherwise. We can confirm this opinion of ours: First, because in a case of doubt, the condition of the possessor is better; and he who promised and delivered a specific item is in possession of his other property. Therefore, unless it is certain that his intention was to deliver the value again in the event of eviction, he is held to nothing else. Secondly, because one who promises a specific item might perhaps not have promised another if he had known that one was not his. Since a gift binds the giver to nothing other than what he intended to bind himself to, it follows that unless the contrary intention of the promisor is clear, he should not be forced to pay another in its place in that event. Thirdly, because

<margin>10</margin>
when a gift begins with delivery, the giver is certainly not held for eviction for any other reason than that he intended to give nothing else than precisely what he delivered. Therefore, since he who promised a specific item intended to promise or give nothing else than that specific thing he promised, he should certainly be forced to pay nothing else, even if it is recovered by law. To this is added that the **law of Aristo, last paragraph, in the Digest, title on gifts**, speaks universally of the gift of a specific thing, making no distinction as to whether it began with delivery or with a promise. Regarding the **first law of the Code, title on the law of dowries**, on which the contrary opinion relies, it must be said: that passage is speaking of a promise of a class of things as a dowry, and thus for an "onerous cause" <note>a context involving a burden or exchange, like a marriage contract</note>, and that is a different reasoning than for a purely gratuitous promise, which we are now debating. Finally, it should be noted regarding this matter that when the donor expressly wishes to be held liable for eviction, then, even if the gift began with delivery, he would be held for eviction, as...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal and moral definitions of contracts and gifts, specifically examining whether a donor is liable if the gift is legally seized by a third party (eviction). He distinguishes between specific gifts (where the donor is usually not liable) and generic gifts like money or grain (where the donor must fulfill the promise even if the first attempt failed).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal definition of a "contract." The previous page concluded by explaining that a gift given upon delivery might not strictly be a contract because no future obligation remains. This page expands that definition to its broadest possible legal sense.</meta>

Treatise Two. Disputation 253.
A 2
<meta>catchword: Con-</meta>

as found in book 2 of the **Code, title on eviction**.
<margin>10.</margin> Thirdly, <term>contract</term> <note>original: "contractus"</note> is understood even more broadly, and less strictly, for any agreement whatsoever, whether an obligation <margin>11</margin> arises from it or not. And in this way, a gift—whether it begins from a promise or from the actual delivery of the item—is called a contract by the very fact that it has been accepted. This is gathered from the **law "If of donation" in the Code, title on the grounds of fear**, from the **law "If anyone of purchase" at the beginning of the Code, title on thirty-year prescription**, and from the **law "Contract" in the Code, title on the good faith of instruments**. This is also affirmed by the **glosses on the "Sacred Authentica regarding minors," on the word "contracts," in the Code, title "If against a sale,"** and by **Molina, book 4 on primogeniture, chapter 2, number 61.** Although no obligation arises from an accepted gift that begins with delivery (neither on the part of the giver nor the receiver), insofar as ownership is transferred by the meeting of minds—both the giver's intent to give and the receiver's intent to accept—it is truly a pact and a contract in this widest sense of the word, which we are discussing now.

In this same sense, a <term>release of debt</term> <note>original: "acceptilatio"</note> is considered a contract. This is an act where a debtor asks their creditor if they have received or settled the debt and wish to let it go, and the creditor responds, "I have received it," or "I release it," thereby extinguishing the previous debt. Although no new obligation arises from such a release—rather, the past obligation by which the debtor was bound is dissolved—it is called a "distraction" <note>original: "distractus," a legal term for the unbinding of a contract</note> or the dissolution of a contract in the first two strict senses of the word. Because it occurs through the meeting of minds between the creditor pardoning the debt and the debtor requesting and accepting that pardon, it takes on the nature of a contract in this third sense. These three senses of contract are handed down by **Conrado on contracts, question 16**, **Sylvester on the word "contract," question 1**, and **Soto**; they generally agree with **Bartolus** both elsewhere and in the **law "Labeo" in the Digest, title on the meaning of words**, and are gathered from the three laws cited above along with the glosses there. Nor does this last sense clash with the word "contract" itself: for a "drawing together" <note>original: "tractus"</note> of different wills or consents toward the same end—whether to transfer ownership, create an obligation, or dissolve one—is not unworthily called a "contract" <note>The author is playing on the Latin *con-trahere*, meaning to draw together</note> in the broad sense. Therefore, there is no reason for Soto to criticize these three definitions of contract against the laws and the learned doctors.

# On Named and Unnamed Contracts.
## DISPVTATIO CCLIII.
### SUMMARY.

1 *What a named contract is.*
2 *What purchase and sale are, and number 6.*
3 *What an unnamed contract is.*
4 *Which contracts are reciprocal and which are not.*
5 *An unnamed contract, clothed in the form of a stipulation, passes into a named contract.*
6 *The four kinds of unnamed contracts.*
7 *Negative unnamed contracts are reduced to affirmative ones; those composed of many parts are resolved into the simple parts of which they consist.*
8 *In a case of doubt as to whether a contract is named or unnamed, it is considered unnamed.*
9 *Unnamed contracts are to be regulated and judged according to those named contracts which they most closely resemble.*
10 *Exchange is an unnamed contract.*

<column-break/>

Contract, taken in its widest sense, is divided into the <term>named</term> <note>standardized contracts with specific legal titles</note> and the <term>unnamed</term> <note>custom agreements without a specific legal title</note>, as is clearly gathered from **law 1, the last paragraph, joined with the second-to-last paragraph preceding it, and from the law "Of the law of nations" at the beginning of the Digest, title on pacts.** <margin>1</margin> A † **unnamed contract**, as Ulpian says in the cited law "Of the law of nations," is one that does not remain under the general name of an agreement or contract, but passes into a proper and specific name of a contract. Understand this whether such a contract belongs to the law of nations and claims a name peculiar to itself, or whether it was introduced by civil law with a specific name and form.

<margin>2</margin> To the first † kind belongs **sale**, which is a pact of goods for a price, such as wheat for money. For when two things that are not "price" are exchanged for one another—such as wine for oil, or wheat for wool—or even when things that are "prices" are similarly exchanged—such as a gold coin for several silver ones, or a silver coin for several copper ones—it is not a "purchase and sale," but rather an **exchange** <note>original: "permutatio"</note> or **currency swap** <note>original: "cambium"</note>. To the same kind belong **leasing**, **partnership**, **loans of specific items** <note>original: "commodatum"</note>, **loans of fungible goods** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, and other similar types, among which you may count **betrothals** and **marriage**. However, since these last two contracts do not deal with external goods, but with the mutual power over bodies for the act of generation, they are outside this second treatise on justice.

To the latter kind belong **long-term leases** <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note>, **feudal grants**, the **stipulation**, and the **release of debt**, which were invented and introduced by civil law. These last two were introduced under a specific form of words; if this form is observed, a civil obligation results from them, and consequently, a legal action is granted against those who refuse to stand by them.

<margin>3</margin> Truly, **unnamed contracts** are those that lack a proper and specific name of a contract. Examples will be provided shortly.

<margin>4</margin> Among contracts, whether named or unnamed, some † are **reciprocal** <note>original: "respectiui"</note>. Namely, those in which one party is bound so that the other may be bound in turn, and therefore they produce an obligation on both sides; these are contracts in the first and most proper sense explained in the preceding disputation. Such are sale, leasing, partnership, and the like. Others, however, are **not reciprocal**; specifically, those that do not produce an obligation on both sides of the contracting parties, and therefore are only contained in the two latter senses of contract explained in the preceding disputation. A release of debt is of this sort, according to what was said there.

<margin>5</margin> There is also the **stipulation**, which is applied when a promise is made by only one side. For † the form of a stipulation was invented and introduced by civil law so that unnamed contracts might pass into named contracts, and so that a civil obligation might arise from them. Therefore, if the form of a stipulation is added to a promise made by only one side, it causes it to pass into a **named non-reciprocal contract**. If, however, it is added to a mutual promise on both sides—as if it were said, "Do you promise to give me a measure of wheat so that I may till your field?" and the other says in turn, "I promise to till your field for a measure of wheat"—then, with both promising, a **named reciprocal contract** results by reason of the added stipulation. This matter will be discussed more extensively in the two following disputations.

<summary>This page defines the broad legal category of "contracts," including those that dissolve obligations (like debt release) or transfer property without future duty (like gifts). It introduces the distinction between "named" contracts (standardized legal forms like sales and leases) and "unnamed" contracts (custom agreements).</summary>
<keywords>named contracts, unnamed contracts, sale and purchase, exchange, debt release, stipulation, reciprocal contracts, legal obligation, Roman law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Molina's legal and theological analysis of the nature of contracts. Following the previous page's discussion on the broadest definitions of "contract," he now moves into the categorization of "innominate" (unnamed) contracts, distinguishing them from standard "nominate" (named) contracts like sales or leases.</meta>

->### Luis de Molina | On Contracts<-

9 All reciprocal <term>innominate contracts</term> <note>original: "contractus innominati"; these are agreements that do not have a specific traditional legal name or a standard pre-set form in Roman law</note> are reduced to one of four types, as held in the law *Naturalis* at the beginning of the **Digest, title "On Prescribed Words"** and in **Law 5, title 6, part 5** <note>This refers to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish legal code</note>. Namely: **I give that you may give** <note>original: "do ut des"</note>, **I give that you may do** <note>original: "do ut facias"</note>, **I do that you may give** <note>original: "facio ut des"</note>, and **I do that you may do** <note>original: "facio ut facias"</note>. For when a thing that is not a price (money) is given in exchange for a price, it is a **purchase and sale** <note>original: "emptio & venditio"</note>, as found in the cited law *Naturalis* in the section "And if indeed," and thus it is a <term>nominate contract</term> <note>A contract with a specific legal name and established rules</note>. However, when two things are given or promised for one another, and neither is a price—or perhaps both could be considered a price—it is the innominate contract **I give that you may give**. Likewise, when a person’s labor or action is of a hirable nature and a price is given or promised for it, it is a **letting and hiring** <note>original: "locatio & conductio"</note>, and thus it is a nominate contract, as held in the same law *Naturalis* in the section "But when." But when a thing is given or promised that is not a price, it is an innominate contract. On the part of the one promising the action, it is the contract **I do that you may give**; on the part of the one promising a thing for that action, it is the contract **I give that you may do**, as the same law adds: for example, if one person agrees with another, "I will give you my horse so that you will free your slave." The same applies if a price is given for an action that is not hirable, as if someone says, "I give you a hundred [coins], and you free your slave." This is held in the cited section along with the **Gloss of Accursius** <note>A famous 13th-century legal commentator</note> there. Furthermore, the common opinion, which **Padilla** refers to and follows regarding the law *Naturalis* in the section "But if I do," number 5, affirms along with **Bartolus** <note>A highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> that those two contracts, **I give that you may do** and **I do that you may give**, should be distinguished in this way. When, however, an action is promised or exchanged for an action, it is the contract **I do that you may do**; for example, if one person agrees with another, "I will repair your houses, and you will cultivate my field."

7 Several things must be observed. First: A negative is reduced to an affirmation; indeed, a "non-action" is included under the broad term "action" <note>original: "factum"</note>. Hence, if someone bargains thus, "I give you my horse so that you cease your lawsuit with Peter," or so that you do not do some other thing, such a contract is included under the species **I give that you may do**.

Second, compound contracts made up of the simple ones mentioned above must be broken down into the simple parts of which they consist, and thus compound contracts are to be numbered along with the simple ones they contain. Both points are affirmed by **Padilla** on the law *Naturalis* at the beginning, number 22, by **Bartolus**, and others whom Padilla cites.

8 Third, in case of doubt as to whether a contract is nominate or innominate, it should be considered innominate. This is proven by **Laws 1 and 2 of the Digest, title "On Prescribed Words,"** and **Law 1 of the Digest, title "On the Estimatory Action,"** and is affirmed by Bartolus and the more common opinion of the doctors, which **Alva[rez]** and **Valaf[asco]** cite and follow in **"On the Right of Emphyteusis," question 6, number 4.** However, when a thing is given for both a price and another thing—such as a farm for a thousand gold coins and a horse—if the price (money) exceeds the value of the other thing, as it does in this example, it is considered a sale. This is the common opinion of the doctors and Bartolus, cited by **Padilla** above at number 2, and is proven by the law *Tenetur*, section 1 of the **Digest, title "On the Action of Purchase,"** the law of *Aristotle* at the beginning of the **Digest, title "On Donations,"** and much more clearly in the chapter *Ad quaestiones* in the **Decretals, title "On the Exchange of Things."**

Fourth: Since nominate reciprocal contracts also have their origin in those four headings that encompass all innominate contracts, 

<column-break/>

it follows that certain innominate contracts are more similar to some nominate contracts than others. Innominate contracts are to be regulated and judged according to those nominate contracts to which they are most similar. For instance, the contract **I give that you may give** must be regulated according to **purchase and sale**; for in a purchase and sale, a thing that is a price (money) is given for a thing that is not a price. The contract **I give that you may do**, however, must be regulated according to **hiring**, in which a thing that is a price is given for the use or a hirable labor.

<margin>Question</margin>
There remains the same difficulty arising from what has been said so far. For if you weigh what was said regarding the innominate contract **I give that you may give**, it seems to follow that **barter** <note>original: "permutatio"</note> and **exchange** <note>original: "cambium"</note> are innominate contracts; yet, if you look at the definition of a nominate contract, they clearly seem to be included among them. For barter is a contract introduced by the <term>law of nations</term> <note>original: "ius gentium"; laws common to all people, often contrasted with civil law</note>, older than purchase and sale, and accepted universally among all nations, which does not apply to purchase and sale; furthermore, it enjoys the specific name of "barter" or "exchange."

<margin>Argument</margin>
10 The common opinion affirms that barter is an innominate contract. This is stated by the **Gloss on the title of the Code, "On the Exchange of Things,"** and the final gloss on **Law 1 of the same title**, as well as by Bartolus and the doctors whom **Padilla** refers to and follows on the law *Naturalis* at the beginning, number 13. This is so even though the last-cited gloss and many others (whom Padilla cites at section "And if indeed," number 9, and whom **Antonio Gomez** follows in his **"Various Resolutions," volume 2, chapter 8** at the end) incorrectly affirm that barter only exists when specific, individual things are exchanged for other specific, individual things. They think it is not included in the contract **I give that you may give**, which they believe only includes cases where, at least on one side, the thing exchanged is certain in its kind or species but uncertain as an individual item. **Padilla**, **Pinellus** (in the **Code, "On the Rescission of Sale," part 2, chapter 1, number 10**), and the doctors they cite rightly disagree with them. These authors show clearly enough that the exchange of things that are specific individuals on both sides is included under the contract **I give that you may give**, and that barter extends as widely as the contract **I give that you may give**. The common opinion of both glosses, Bartolus, and the doctors—namely, that barter is an innominate contract—is gathered clearly enough from the law *Iuris gentium* at the beginning of the **Digest, title "On Pacts,"** from the law *Naturalis* in the section "If indeed" of the **Digest, title "On Prescribed Words,"** from **Law 5, title 6, part 5**, and from other laws.

<margin>Response to the argument</margin>
To the contrary argument, the Gloss on the **Code, title "On the Exchange of Things,"** Bartolus on the law *Iuris gentium*, and others respond that the name "exchange" <note>original: "permutatio"</note> is by its nature common to all reciprocal contracts, even purchase and sale. For a contract to be "nominate," it is not enough for it to retain a name of some general or sub-category; rather, it is necessary that it claim for itself a peculiar and specific name, as was said in the definition of a nominate contract. This does not apply to barter. Everything said in this dispute, and what could be added to it, will be made manifest from the following discussions.

<summary>This page categorizes innominate contracts into four types based on the exchange of goods and actions, distinguishing them from nominate contracts like sales and leases. It specifically debates whether barter and currency exchange should be classified as innominate or nominate contracts under Roman and Spanish law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of contract law by Luis de Molina. Having previously categorized contracts as nominate or innominate, he now focuses on the "perfection" of contracts—the specific moment or method by which an agreement becomes legally binding. This page introduces the distinction between contracts formed by consent, by words, by writing, and by the delivery of a thing.</meta>

### Which Contracts are completed by consent alone, which by word alone, which by writing, and which by performance.

->DISPUTATION 254.<-

->S U M M A R Y<-

1 *Contracts which are perfected by consent, by writing, and by words; see also number 3.*
2 *Betrothal and marriage are perfected by consent alone; and what they are.*
3 *The <term>stipulation</term> <note>original: "stipulatio"; a formal Roman law contract consisting of a question and an answer</note>, and by what form of words it is perfected.*
4 *Anyone can stipulate through a representative, a notary, or another person.*
5 *A response must follow a stipulation immediately, and not after an interval.*
6 *Contracts perfected by consent alone are validly perfected even if consent follows after an interval.*
7 *Stipulation is not necessary for the validity of a contract in the Kingdom of Castile.*
8 *Acceptance is perfected by words, and its purpose.*
9 *What the <term>Aquilian stipulation</term> <note>A legal formula used to release a person from all obligations under a contract</note> is, and how it extinguishes an obligation.*
10 *If the form of acceptance is not observed, a natural obligation is at least removed by a bare pact.*
11 *Acceptance and bare remission under the law of Castile extinguish any civil obligation.*
12 *If contracts are suspended until a writing is completed, they are not perfected before then; and when a deposit is lost.*
13 *Contracts perfected by a thing (performance), and what must be attended to in them.*

---

<margin>1</margin> Of contracts, some are perfected by **consent**, which is understood as a mutual expression of will that is clear and manifest. Such are **purchase and sale**; **letting and hiring**; **partnership**, and **mandate** <note>original: "emptio & venditio; locatio & conductio; societas, & mandatum"</note>, as found in the **Institutes of Justinian, "On obligations from consent," single section**. For names of this sort were established to signify these very agreements, decisions, and mutual consents. Thus, if the contracting parties do not suspend such contracts until a writing is completed, they are perfected by the very fact that they mutually consent, and they give rise to a civil obligation and a legal action, even if no delivery, formal words, or writing has occurred. This is true even if the contracting parties, for greater stability or so that the contract may be better proven, intend for a public document to be drafted afterward. Furthermore, such contracts can be perfected between absent parties through a letter, by which they express their mutual consent to one another, and 

<margin>2</margin> through messengers, as the cited section adds. These same rules apply to **betrothals** and **marriage**, because they are made and perfected by mutual consent alone expressed to one another. Indeed, the name "betrothal" <note>original: "sponsalia"</note> signifies a mutual consent and a promise of contracting a marriage later; the name "marriage" <note>original: "matrimonium"</note>, however, signifies a granting of power over their bodies for the act of generation, through mutual consent for that grant.

<margin>3</margin> Other contracts are perfected by **words**, that is, by a certain form of words or voices. Of this kind is the **stipulation**, which is perfected when one person's question precedes—in which he asks of the other: "Do you promise?" or "Do you bind yourself to give me this thing?" or "to do this or that?" or "to give or do this in exchange for that?"—and is followed by the response and promise of the other, by which he promises or grants that he will do it. So it is held in the **Institutes, "On verbal obligations"** at the beginning, in **Law 1 of the Digest, same title**, and in **Law 1, title 11, Partida 5**. The person, moreover,

<column-break/>

who asks and requests the promise is said to **stipulate** for himself from the other, and is therefore called the **stipulator**; but the one from whom he stipulates is called the **promissor**. Sometimes "to stipulate" is also used passively, in which case the one who is asked and promises is said to stipulate and to have been stipulated, as is clear in the Law *Si non forte* in the **Digest, "On the recovery of what was not due"**, and in the **Authentica "On the equality of the dowry"** <note>The "Authentica" refers to a collection of Justinian's later laws, or "Novels"</note> along with the gloss there on the word "stipulate," and in the section "Furthermore by novation" in the **Institutes, "In what ways an obligation is ended"**. Formerly, certain forms of words were prescribed for asking and answering, without which the contract was not valid; today, however, it is enough that someone sufficiently expresses their request to another in any meaningful language, and the other expresses their consent. So it is held in the **Institutes, "On verbal obligations," section 1**, in the **Code, "On contracting and committing stipulations," Law *Omnes***, and in **Law 2, title 11, Partida 5**. Hence it is enough if the promissor, when asked, responds "even so" or "why not" or something similar, as the gloss on the cited law *Omnes* affirms. It is also enough if he says "why not?" or "certainly," as held in **Law 1, section *Si quis* of the Digest, "On verbal obligations"** and the cited **Law 2 of Castile**; which adds that if he responds "it is good" or "if it is done so, it will be done well," the stipulation is not considered perfected, and thus no obligation arises from it, because words of that sort do not signify consent and a promise being made at that moment. I said a little earlier: "in any meaningful language," because, as the final gloss on **section 1 of the Institutes, "On verbal obligations"** affirms—and as the common opinion follows, which Antonio Gómez refers to in **volume 2 of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 9, number 3**—it is not enough if it signifies something only because the stipulator and promissor decided it should. Observe, however, that a stipulation made between people of different languages is valid, even if the question is asked in one language and the promise is made in another, provided they understand one another, at least through an **interpreter**. So it is held in **Law 1, final section of the Digest, "On verbal obligations"**, and **section 1 of the Institutes, same title**, and **Law 2, title 11, Partida 5**. Because the contract of which we speak is perfected by words—that is, by the voices of both the stipulator and the promissor—neither letters nor nods are sufficient to perfect it. From this it follows that it cannot be perfected between absent parties—that is, between those so far apart that one cannot perceive the sound of the other's voice. So it is held in the **Institutes, "On useless stipulations," section *Item verborum***, in the beginning of **Law 1 of the Digest, "On verbal obligations"**, and in **Law 1, title 11, Partida 5**. If, however, it is stated in a public instrument <note>A legal document drafted by a notary</note> that the stipulator and promissor were present, the instrument is upheld unless the one who promised provides the most sufficient proof to the contrary. From the same principle, it follows that a stipulation cannot be contracted with a **mute** person, or a **deaf** person who cannot hear voices; for a mute can neither ask nor promise by voice, and the deaf person of whom we speak can neither hear the question nor the promise. So it is held in the **Institutes, "On useless stipulations," section *Mutum***, at the beginning of **Law 1 of the Digest, "On verbal obligations"**, and in other laws.

<margin>4</margin> Because, however, contracts that are not perfected by words can be made by a mute or a deaf person through signs or writing, as held in the **Digest, "On actions and obligations," Law *In quibuscunque***, surely the deaf and mute can stipulate and promise through a representative <note>original: "procuratorem"</note> assigned for that purpose by signs or writing, or through a public notary <note>original: "tabellionem"</note>. Likewise, they can stipulate through a servant or a son, and the same applies to absent persons. This is held in **Law 1 at the beginning of the Digest, "On verbal obligations"**.

Observe this: for a stipulation to be valid, it is necessary...

<meta>This page continues Disputation 254 regarding the "perfection" of contracts. On the previous page, the author began defining contracts perfected by consent alone versus those requiring specific words or forms. Here, he examines the strict requirements of Roman "stipulation" and how they contrast with the more flexible laws of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina / On Contracts

<margin>6</margin>
It is required that not only the one stipulating and the one promising be present in the manner explained, but also that the response follows immediately after the interrogation. This means there should be no interval of time such that the promisor has first turned his attention to other matters. For if he responds after turning to other things, and the question is not put to him again, the <term>stipulation</term> <note>A formal verbal contract consisting of a specific question and answer.</note> is invalid. However, if the person questioned steps away but returns and makes the promise before turning to other business, the stipulation is valid. This is according to the Digest (Law 1, section "Which is present," and Law "Continuous," at the beginning, regarding verbal obligations) and the <term>Siete Partidas</term> <note>The fundamental law code of Castile (Law 2, Title 11, Partida 5).</note>. In other contracts, however, which are perfected by **consent**, the contract is completed even if the consent of the other party follows after an interval, as held in the Law "If I stipulate," final section, with the commentary there.

<margin>7</margin>
Finally, observe this concerning the law of the Kingdom of Castile (Law 1, 3, Title 8, Book 3 of the *Ordenamiento de Alcalá*, which is today Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación*): a promise and a contract are valid by the very fact that it is understood that one intended to obligate themselves to another, whether that person is absent or present. This holds true whether a formal stipulation was made and its legal form observed, or not—as long as the consent by which one intended to bind oneself was expressed. From this, a civil obligation arises, and a legal action is granted against the one who intended to bind themselves in that manner. Because many controversies will be brought up in the following sections on the occasion of that law, it is useful to quote it here. It reads as follows:

> <note>original Spanish: "Pareciédo que alguna se quiso obligar..."</note> It appearing that someone wished to obligate themselves to another by promise, or by some contract, or in another manner, they shall be bound to fulfill that which they obligated themselves to do. They may not raise an exception claiming that no stipulation was made (which is to say, a promise made with certain legal solemnity), or that the contract and obligation were made between absent parties, or that it was not made before a public notary, or that it was made to another private person in the name of others between absent parties, or that someone obligated themselves that another would give or do something. We command that the said obligation and contract shall always be valid in whatever way it appears that one wished to obligate themselves to another.

From this it is clear that in the Kingdom of Castile, even if the stipulation was made by letters or by gestures—and thus by a mute or deaf person—and between absent parties and after an interval, or even if no question preceded it but a "naked promise" was made by gestures or letters (which therefore does not qualify as a formal stipulation), it is valid. This is noted by Gregorio López and others. For in that kingdom, all the subtleties, solemnities, and "legal thickets" of civil law—which provide handles for litigation and do not allow the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>The internal, moral judgment of an individual (forum conscientiae), as opposed to the external legal court.</note> to agree with the external court—have been rightly abolished. The remaining things that could be said about stipulation in this place will be more conveniently explained in the following sections, where it will be examined whether the acceptance of a promise is nevertheless necessary in the Kingdom of Castile for an obligation to arise.

<margin>8</margin>
**A**cceptance <note>original: "Acceptilatio"; the formal verbal release from a debt.</note> is also a contract, or rather a "de-tract" <note>A "distractus" is the undoing or dissolution of a contract.</note>, which is perfected by words. And as held in the Institutes (on the modes by which an obligation is removed, section "likewise by acceptilation"), it only dissolves a civil obligation contracted by words—that is, through a stipulation—but not civil obligations arising from other sources. For just as it was introduced into civil law that a stipulation, which is perfected by words, should induce a civil obligation, it was judged consistent with reason that such an obligation should also be dissolved by other words, namely, those of acceptance.

<column-break/>

Acceptance is performed, as held in the same place and in the Digest (on acceptilation), by the debtor asking the creditor: <gloss>That which I promised you, do you hold as received?</gloss> <note>original Latin: "quae tibi promisi, habesne acceptum?"</note> and the creditor responding <gloss>(meaning immediately, as was said regarding stipulation): I do,</gloss> <note>original Latin: "habeo"</note> or by other equivalent words. Because a civil obligation produced by stipulation is extinguished by acceptance just as if that which was owed from the stipulation had been paid, it is called an "imaginary" or virtual payment.

<margin>9</margin>
**F**urthermore, in the cited place and the Digest, a method is handed down by which civil obligations arising from a source other than stipulation may finally be extinguished through acceptance. Specifically, if the † debt from any other source is first converted into a debt from a stipulation, and then acceptance is performed. For instance, the creditor first stipulates from the debtor in this manner: <gloss>Whatever you owe me from such and such a title, or whatever such and such a thing is valued at for which you are held to me, do you promise to give?</gloss> and the debtor responds: <gloss>I promise.</gloss> In this way, they have converted † the debt from other sources into a debt from a stipulation of the kind called **Aquilian**, because it was invented by Gallus Aquilius for the purpose we are now discussing. If the debtor then further asks the creditor: <gloss>Whatever I promised you today through the Aquilian stipulation, do you hold it all as received?</gloss> and the creditor responds: <gloss>I do;</gloss> then by such an acceptance, the entire debt and civil obligation is extinguished. Paulo de Castro (who summarized the law in the Digest) says: If † the form of acceptance is not observed, but there is only a naked pact or a promise of the creditor accepted by the debtor which remits the debt contracted by stipulation, the creditor would be wrong to sue. For although the civil obligation is not then extinguished, it nevertheless extinguishes the **natural obligation**, according to what must be said in the following disputation. Therefore, because in that event the civil obligation remains, a legal action is granted to the creditor against the debtor; however, because the natural obligation was extinguished by that naked pact, the creditor is bound naturally and in the court of conscience not to seek it. Thus, an "exception" <note>A legal defense or plea.</note> is granted to the debtor against the creditor, on the grounds that the creditor agreed not to seek the debt or had remitted it. By this exception, the civil action is shattered and the debtor is defended, who at that point is bound to nothing by natural obligation or in the court of conscience. This is clear from the Institutes (on exceptions). In the same summary, Paulo de Castro adds that if the civil obligation was not born from a stipulation but from a contract perfected by consent alone or by a "thing" (performance), and the debt was remitted by the creditor through acceptance, then even if the civil obligation was not extinguished, the natural obligation was nonetheless extinguished by that acceptance (which functioned as a pact of remission), and the debtor is granted an exception to shatter that civil obligation.

<margin>11</margin>
Would that these subtleties had never been introduced by civil law! They provide fuel for litigation and are difficult to understand, nor do they allow the external court to agree with the court of conscience. By that law of Castile cited above, they have been abolished, since from a naked pact, not only an exception but also a civil action is granted.

<summary>This page analyzes the formal requirements of "stipulation" and "acceptilation" in Roman law, contrasting them with the laws of Castile which prioritize intent over ceremony. Molina argues that strict legal formalities often create a rift between legal reality and moral conscience.</summary>
<keywords>stipulation, acceptilation, Aquilian stipulation, Kingdom of Castile, contract law, natural obligation, civil obligation, court of conscience, legal formalities, debt remission</keywords>
