<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "perfection" of contracts—the point at which an agreement becomes legally binding. The author is transitioning from contracts perfected by specific words (stipulations) to those requiring written documents or the physical delivery of goods.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 255.

<insert>d.</insert> is given, and therefore there arises not <insert>only a natural obligation, but a contrary obligation</insert> even a civil obligation, by which a civil obligation is entirely removed and extinguished, just as a civil obligation contracted by formal promise is extinguished through a formal release <note>original: "acceptilationem" — a Roman law procedure for the formal discharge of a debt without payment.</note>.

<margin>12</margin>
**Other contracts are perfected by writing.** First, for instance, when the contracting parties suspend the contract until it is completed in writing, then—even if by its own nature it would be perfected by consent alone, such as a sale or a lease—the contract so suspended is not perfected until the writing is fully finished and signed; rather, it is lawful for any of the contracting parties to withdraw from that contract. If, however, one of the parties has received <term>earnest money</term> <note>original: "arrham" — a deposit or "hand-penny" given to seal a bargain.</note> and one of the parties withdraws from such a contract without the other's consent, then, if it is the one who gave the earnest money, he loses it; if it is the one who received it, he returns double the amount. This is held in the Law "Contractus" of the Code <note>The Code of Justinian, C. de fide inst.</note> and Book 4 of the Institutes, Title 36. There it is simultaneously explained when people are to be judged, or not judged, to have wished to suspend a contract until a public document is completed. Maranta, in *The Order of Judgments* (part 4, dist. 9, n. 88 and disp. 4 n. 4), along with Baldus and others, asserts that by the very fact that the parties, while celebrating the contract, said, "let a notary be sought for us to draft the instrument," they are deemed to have wished to suspend the contract until the writing is finished, unless the contrary is evident from elsewhere.

Furthermore, when by civil or canon law a writing is required as a matter of form for a certain contract, or for its validity, it is not perfected until the writing is executed, as held in the cited Title 36. An example used there is an <term>emphyteutic contract</term> <note>A long-term or permanent lease of land, common in Church property management.</note> regarding Church property, and in a contract which needs it for validity, as will be said in its place regarding donations exceeding a certain amount.

<margin>13</margin>
**Finally, there are other contracts** which are perfected by the thing itself, or by delivery <note>original: "traditioneve" — the physical handing over of an object.</note>, and are not considered consummated before then. Of this kind are donations, <term>loans for consumption</term> <note>original: "mutuum" — a loan of fungible goods like money or grain where the same value is returned.</note>, <term>loans for use</term> <note>original: "commodatum" — a loan of a specific item to be returned intact.</note>, deposits, pledges, and the like. Indeed, so that you may distinguish them, take the excellent rule of Bartolus on the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentium" — Law 2 in the Digest on Pacts.</note>: One must look to the name of the contract, and if it signifies the thing itself or an external act, then the contract is not perfected before that act is put into execution. For example, because "donation" signifies the giving of a thing out of liberality, the contract of donation is not considered perfected before the delivery of the thing. Similarly, because a "loan for consumption" signifies the giving of a thing not out of liberality, but so that the same kind and value may be returned—by which reason ownership is transferred through the loan—the contract of loan is certainly not considered perfected before the delivery of the thing being loaned. By the same reasoning, since a "loan for use" signifies the delivery of a thing out of liberality regarding its use, so that the exact same item is returned, that contract is not considered perfected before the liberal delivery of such a thing for use. Similarly, because a "deposit" signifies the placing of a thing with someone for safekeeping, and a "pledge" with a creditor for the security of a debt, these contracts are not considered perfected before the delivery of the thing. However, because a <term>mortgage</term> <note>original: "hypotheca" — a security interest where the debtor keeps possession of the property.</note> signifies only the obligation of a thing for the security of a debt, without any delivery of such a thing, it is perfected by consent alone; just like a sale and a lease, which signify acts of agreement alone in those contracts, and like a partnership, which signifies an agreement among people for a business venture,

<column-break/>

to be carried out further for their common profit and loss. Finally, because an "exchange" signifies the mutual delivery of one thing for another, it is not considered entirely perfected before the delivery on both sides. And it is the same for other respective <term>innominate contracts</term> <note>original: "contractib. innominatis" — agreements that do not fall under a specific standard Roman legal name but are still binding if one party has performed.</note>. Nonetheless, when all these innominate contracts are fulfilled by one side, a civil obligation arises, as will be said in the following disputation.

## On the Naked and Clothed Pact, and when a Civil Obligation arises, or does not arise, from an Innominate Pact and Contract.

### DISPUTATION 255.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *When contracts and pacts produce a civil obligation and action.*
2 *What a naked pact is.*
3 *A naked pact is clothed in various ways.*
4 *The five kinds of "clothing" with which naked pacts are clothed.*
5 *In what ways a naked pact differs from a clothed pact.*
6 *A donation is called a clothed pact by privilege of law.*
7 *The promise of a dowry and certain others are clothed by privilege of law.*

<margin>1</margin>
According to the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentium" — Digest, book on pacts.</note>, pacts or agreements sometimes produce a civil obligation, and thus an action is granted from them; but sometimes they do not produce one. For when they pass into a named pact or contract, they produce a civil action and obligation; but when they do not pass into a named contract, they produce neither a civil obligation nor an action. An exception is made unless either an act or a cause situated in the nature of things intervenes, on account of which something is already owed beyond the agreement, or unless pacts of this kind are contained within and cohere without an interval, being joined with some named contract, or with a contract in which an act or cause has intervened. Add to this—following the commentary on the law of nations <note>original: "gl. l. iuris gentium"</note>—unless it has been peculiarly granted by privilege of law to some pact in which none of these things are found, that it produce a civil obligation and action. All these things are found in the Law "of the Law of Nations" cited at the beginning and in the two sections cited.

So that these things may be better understood, and that we may proceed to explain those things proposed in the title of this disputation, it must be known: These three things are distinguished in law: a <term>pollicitation</term> <note>An offer made by one party that has not yet been accepted by the other.</note> (or a simple promise not yet accepted), a **naked pact**, and a **clothed pact**. Because such a pollicitation is not a pact, as was shown in Disputation 212, let us omit it for now, with only this reminder: Under common civil law, no civil obligation arises from it, nor is an action granted, as will be shown later when we speak of promises and donations; in which place we will also examine whether at least a natural obligation arises from it, and whether under Canon Law and in the Kingdom of Castile an action is granted from it.

# Ludwig Molina: On Contracts

### Section 255 (Continued)

<margin>2</margin> A **naked pact** <note>original: "pactum nudum" — an agreement that is not legally enforceable because it lacks specific legal formalities.</note>, as held in the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentium"</note> and the cited locations, especially the paragraph "but when there is none," is an agreement that neither transforms into a **named contract** <note>original: "contractum nominatum" — a contract with a specific legal name and established rules, such as a sale or a loan.</note>, nor involves a performance or a cause on the part of one of the parties. Therefore, beyond the agreement itself, the other party remains uncommitted. Nor does it align with such a pact or a named contract in a way that creates a bond. 

For example: if you promised to give Peter a loan of one hundred, and he accepted the promise, but you have not yet delivered the money to him, and no **stipulation** <note>original: "stipulatio" — a formal verbal exchange of "Do you promise?" and "I promise."</note> took place in that promise (where Peter would first ask, "Do you promise to give me a loan of one hundred?" and you would reply, "I promise"), such an agreement is "naked." This is because it lacks the character of a stipulation, nor does it function as a loan; as explained in the preceding discussion, a contract for a loan is only completed by the actual performance or delivery of the money or a similar thing. Similarly, it does not take the form of any other named contract, nor is it linked with another contract or agreement. 

In the same way, it is a naked pact if you agreed with someone to deliver twenty sheep in exchange for one ox, but no stipulation occurred, no delivery was made, and the agreement was not linked to any other contract. The reason is that this is an **innominate contract** <note>original: "contractus innominatus" — a contract that does not fit into standard categories like "sale" or "hire."</note> of the type "I give so that you may give" <note>original: "do vt des"</note>. It does not fall under any named contract category, and neither side has performed a delivery, act, or cause that would bind one to the other beyond the simple agreement. Consequently, according to what was said at the start of this discussion, no civil obligation arises from such pacts, nor is a legal action granted.

<margin>3</margin> However, if any of these agreements were made with an intervening stipulation, then—because it would thereby take on the character of a named contract—it would be called a **clothed pact** <note>original: "pactum vestitum"</note>, and a civil obligation would arise from it. For instance, if a stipulation were added to that agreement to exchange twenty sheep for one ox: if you asked whether he promised to give one ox for twenty sheep, and he replied, "I promise"; and he in turn asked if you promised to give twenty sheep for one ox, and you replied, "I promise." Then, even if no delivery were made by either side, it would be a pact "clothed" by stipulation. A civil obligation would arise, and a legal action would be granted—an action that would never be granted for the same agreement if it remained a "naked pact." This is expressly held in the Law *ex placito* regarding the exchange of things. 

However, because today contracts that are otherwise "innominate" are usually committed to writing and performed before a **notary** <note>original: "tabellione"</note> or public scribe, they are typically celebrated with a mutual stipulation. The public official asks each party on behalf of the other, and they promise each other. In public instruments, it is customary to attest that such a mutual stipulation took place. Bartolus and others, whom Antonio Gómez refers to and follows, affirm this. Thus, today, "innominate" contracts are rarely given as "naked," especially if they are celebrated before a notary or public scribe. 

In the same way, if—in that same naked pact regarding the exchange of twenty sheep for one ox—a delivery occurred from one side instead of a stipulation,

<column-break/>

for instance, if you delivered twenty sheep to the other person, or the other delivered an ox to you, the pact would immediately become "clothed" by that delivery and cause. Because of this, the party who has not yet fulfilled their part of the contract remains civilly obligated to the one who did perform. Consequently, the one who performed is granted a legal action, which the law calls an **action for prescribed words** <note>original: "actio praescriptis verbis"</note> or an **action on the facts** <note>original: "in factum"</note>. 

By this action, if the other party does not fulfill their part in the due time, they can be compelled either to pay "interest" (that is, to pay what they promised or the value of what the performance was worth to the claimant) or to provide a **restoration** <note>original: "condictio"</note> so that the claimant receives back what they gave—since it was given for a cause that did not follow through. The choice lies with the person who performed to sue in whichever of these two ways they prefer. This is gathered from the Laws and is expressly stated in the Digest, where Padilla explains why the "action for prescribed words" is so named and how it differs from an "action on the facts." Read the same author and Antonio Gómez on this point. 

The laws of the *Partidas* <note>original: "l. 5. ti. 6. par. 5." — referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous Spanish statutory code.</note> agree with this, adding that a sworn statement of the value of the suit is granted against the one who did not perform, so that the damages are settled based on the oath of the one who fulfilled their part, provided the judge also arbitrates whether the estimate is fair. This is also established so that when the person who performed seeks the return of what they gave, they can simultaneously sue for the interest or damages resulting from the other's failure to perform. Gregorio Lopez attempts to explain that law in a way that does not disagree with what has been said so far. 

It should also be noted that in a contract of the type "I do so that you may give" <note>original: "facio vt des"</note>, the law affirms that a specific **action for fraud** <note>original: "actionem de dolo"</note> is granted to the one who performed the act against the one who did not return what was promised, rather than the "action for prescribed words." This has caused much trouble for legal experts, and they find it difficult to give a reason for this diversity—why such a peculiar rule was established for that specific contract. Read Padilla on this point among others.

A naked pact is also "clothed" by its **coherence** with another named contract, or one already clothed by performance. Indeed, by the very fact that it is joined immediately <note>original: "incontinenti"</note> to one of those, it is considered clothed by that connection. A specific civil obligation arises from it, and an action for prescribed words for interest is granted against the one who is in default of fulfilling such a pact. 

For example: if someone sold or leased their houses to another, and at the same time entered into an agreement to exchange an ox for a horse, or that for an ox he would cultivate the lessor's field, such an agreement is "clothed" by its connection to the other contract of sale or lease. A civil obligation arises from it immediately. The same applies if someone delivered ten sheep to another so that they would cultivate his field in the future, and at the same time entered into an agreement that, for a ram given upon his return, he would complete a certain journey. Because this second agreement is connected to the first—which, though innominate, was "clothed" by the delivery of the sheep—it is considered clothed itself, and a civil obligation arises from it just as from the first. The same would be true in the two examples proposed if those first contracts were made first, and **afterwards**,

# Second Treatise, Disputation 255 (Continued)

<margin>
...before they turned to other matters; for in the meantime, while they do not turn away, they are considered to have added the later agreements immediately. It would be otherwise if they added them after turning to other things, for then they are considered added after an interval.
</margin>

...afterwards, before they finalized the contract, they might turn to other things; for in the meantime, as long as the contracting parties do not turn to other matters, they are considered to add the later agreements immediately <note>original: "incontinenti" — a legal term meaning without an intervening act that breaks the continuity of the negotiation</note>. It would be different if they added those terms after they had turned to other business; for then they are considered to have been added after an interval <note>original: "ex intervallo"</note>.

<margin>4</margin>
From what has been said, it is clear that there are certain pacts which, by the very fact that they are made, are produced "clothed." Specifically, these are contracts perfected by consent alone, such as sale, hiring/leasing, etc. For agreements of this kind immediately obtain a peculiar and specific name of "contract" and do not need any other "clothing." Others, however, are clothed by the use of a certain fixed form of words, such as pacts—otherwise naked—that transition into a **stipulation** <note>original: "stipulatio" — a formal verbal exchange of question and answer</note> or an **acceptilation** <note>original: "acceptilatio" — a formal oral release from an obligation</note>. And these, by that very fact, are also considered "named contracts." Furthermore, there are others which are perfected and clothed by an action <note>original: "in facto"</note>, so that they transition into named contracts; these are types like a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, a **gratuitous loan** <note>original: "commodatum"</note>, and a **deposit**. There are also others which are clothed by an action resulting from an external cause, from which, beyond the pact, an obligation results, yet they do not transition into named contracts. These are **innominate** <note>unnamed</note> contracts followed by performance, at least on one side, as was explained. Finally, there are others which are considered clothed simply by being attached immediately to some of the other clothed contracts, as was explained just a moment ago. These five modes by which pacts are "clothed" are enumerated in the Gloss, by Bartolus, and others on the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentium §. quinimò. ff. de pact." — referring to the Digests of Roman Law</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
The distinction between † naked pacts and pacts clothed in any manner, as is easily understood from what has been said, is this: from a clothed pact, a civil obligation arises and therefore a legal **action** <note>original: "actio" — the right to sue in court</note> is granted. From a naked pact, however, no civil obligation arises; hence the legal expert in the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentium, §. sed cum nulla"</note> concludes thus: "Therefore, a naked agreement does not produce a civil obligation." Understand this to mean a *civil* obligation. Covarrubias <note>a famous Spanish legal scholar</note> gives the reason in the chapter "any pact" <note>original: "c. quòuis pactum, de pact. p. 2. §. 4. a nu. 12."</note>: it is to prevent lawsuits from multiplying, which would increase greatly if an action were granted from a naked pact. He also challenges the reasoning given by others.

<margin>6</margin>
When you hear that a civil obligation does not arise from a naked pact, understand it (as we said above) unless a civil obligation is granted to some naked pact by a **legal privilege**, so that an action is provided. By this reasoning, although under ancient law—if a gift began with a promise that was accepted—a civil obligation did not arise from a purely gratuitous promise before delivery was made, because a formal stipulation had not occurred. This was because it was a naked pact, since before delivery it was neither completed as a gift nor had it transitioned into a named contract, as explained in the preceding discussion. Today, however, † by the law of the **Code** <note>original: "de iure Codicis" — referring to the Code of Justinian</note>, a civil obligation arises from a naked pact of gift, and an action is granted which passes to the heirs of the recipient and against the heirs of the promisor. This is held in the law "if anyone [promises] silver" <note>original: "l. si quis argentum, præsertim, §. vlt. C. de donationib."</note>, where it is expressed that the action granted from such a naked pact of gift is based on that very law. The same is held in the Institutes and in the 4th book of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "lib. 4. Lusit. ord. tit. 55."</note>.

<margin>7</margin>
By the same † legal privilege, a civil obligation arises from a naked pact of a promised **dowry**, and an action is granted. For a contract of dowry, as is clear from the name itself, is neither considered perfected nor does it obtain the status of a named contract before delivery—just like a gift,

<column-break/>

a loan, and a gratuitous loan—as explained in the preceding discussion. Thus, a promise of a dowry that has been accepted would otherwise be counted among naked pacts. However, in favor of marriages, it was granted that a civil obligation should arise from it and an action be given, as is clear from the law "for the collection" <note>original: "l. ad exactionem. C. de dot. promiss."</note>. The same legal privilege is granted to a promise by which someone promises another that they will pay a debt which someone else owed to them, or that they will pay a debt on another day or at another place which the promisor himself owed. This will be discussed in Disputation 270. Bartolus, on the law of nations <note>original: "l. iuris gentiū"</note>, says that by **Praetorian law** <note>law issued by the Roman judges or Praetors</note>, the same privilege was granted to a naked pact of a **pledge** <note>original: "pignoris"</note>, namely that a civil obligation and an action arise from it. However, since a pact of a pledge is usually attached to the contract for whose security the pledge is promised, a truly "naked" pact of a pledge will rarely occur. The Gloss counts various other instances in which an action is given from a naked pact by legal privilege. The doctors <note>legal scholars</note> doubt whether such a legal privilege should be called a "clothing" of the pact, so that even in these cases, one should not say that a civil obligation arises from a "naked" pact. The Gloss affirms that such a privilege should be called a clothing of the pact; but Bartolus rejects this. Although the question seems to be about the choice of words, Bartolus’s opinion is preferred, as it agrees with the common way of speaking and the law. Read the foundation on which he relies in Bartolus.

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...is not expressed, it is held that no civil obligation arises from a naked pact confirmed by a bare oath, nor is a legal action granted. Indeed, the law <note>original: "l. si-quis pro eo" — referring to a specific passage in the Roman Digest</note> seems to decide clearly that when a person is not a freedman <note>original: "libertus" — a former slave</note> but a freeborn citizen <note>original: "ingenuus"</note> who has promised services under oath, no legal action is granted against the one making the promise based on such a pact confirmed by oath. And this is the more common opinion, especially among the interpreters of Roman Civil Law <note>original: "iuris Cæsarei"</note>, as affirmed by Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century expert in Church law</note> and Covarruvias.

Regarding Canon Law <note>Church law</note>, however, Innocent and others cited by Panormitanus and Covarruvias have asserted that no action is granted from a naked pact confirmed by oath. Instead, they argue that only an ecclesiastical judge, by virtue of his office and by reason of the sin <note>original: "ratione peccati"</note> in which a person persists by refusing to keep a sworn promise, can compel that person to fulfill the pact. These authors argue this because, since under Civil Law no civil obligation or action arises from such a pact, the same should hold for Canon Law. They reason that there is no specific text in Canon Law changing this, and where there is no specific rule in Canon Law, one must follow Civil Law.

<margin>1</margin>
However, two conclusions must be established to resolve this dispute. The first is against Innocent and those who follow him: namely, that **under Canon Law, a legal action is indeed granted from a naked pact confirmed by oath.** This is the view of Bartolus, Panormitanus, and Felinus, and it is the common opinion as reported by Covarruvias. It can be proved, first, because a legal action is granted for a naked pact under Canon Law even without an oath, as shown in the title "On Pacts" <note>original: "c. 1 de pactis"</note>. Therefore, it follows with even greater reason that an action would be granted for the same pact when it is confirmed by an oath. Second, even in contracts that are technically void under Civil or Canon Law—provided they are not immoral—if they are confirmed by an oath, a legal action is granted. Examples include the sale of a dowry property or a sale made by a minor. Since a naked pact naturally creates a "natural obligation" <term>Natural obligation: a moral debt that is recognized by conscience but might lack a formal legal mechanism for enforcement</term> in the court of conscience (which a void contract does not), and since the oath creates a legitimate right for the person to whom it was sworn, a legal action is granted by both Canon and Civil law.

<margin>2</margin>
The second conclusion: **Under Civil Law, a legal action is granted from a naked pact confirmed by oath.** This is affirmed by Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and others. To me, this is beyond doubt based on what was explained in Disputations 149 and 150. In my judgment, the same arguments used for the previous conclusion sufficiently prove this one as well.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, even those who hold the opposite opinion admit that in certain specific cases of naked pacts confirmed by oath, a civil action is granted. There is no reason why it should not be granted for other naked pacts confirmed by oath, unless the pact itself is prohibited by Civil Law and thus void. As Covarruvias excellently demonstrates, those laws cited by opponents do not speak of services in general, but specifically of services that freedmen <note>former slaves</note> were accustomed to performing for a certain time as a condition of their freedom. It was forbidden for freeborn citizens to be bound to such servile obligations, whether by formal stipulation or oath. Therefore, if a freeborn person tried to bind themselves to such services, the act was declared void and useless. This is why those laws state that if a freeborn man promises such services under oath, it is void and no natural obligation arises. However, if a freeborn man promises services not as a freedman but as a tailor or a shoemaker, an action would be granted against him—even if he promised them through a naked pact under oath. This holds unless the pact was reciprocal and the other party refused to do their part; in that case, the promisor is not bound, as the promise and oath were made under the implied condition that the other party would also uphold the agreement.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 255 and 256 regarding whether "naked pacts"—simple agreements made without the formal legal "clothing" of specific rituals or categories—create a binding obligation. ### Treatise 2, Disputation 257

<margin>1</margin> The **D**octors of law <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established legal and theological authorities of the medieval and early modern periods.</note> commonly agree—followed by Covarruvias, Antonio Gómez, and Padilla—that a **natural obligation** <note>original: "naturalem obligationem"</note> arises from a "naked pact" <term>naked pact (pactum nudum): a simple agreement that lacks the specific legal formalities required by Roman law to be enforceable in a secular court</term>. By this obligation, the parties are bound in the **court of conscience** <term>court of conscience (forum conscientiae): the internal moral realm where one is answerable to God, rather than an external human judge</term> to keep their word, under the threat of mortal sin, provided the matter to which they are bound is significant enough to warrant such a serious fault. The reason is that, if we look only at **natural law** and the **law of nations** <note>original: "ius naturale ac gentium" — the universal principles of justice shared by all peoples</note> before civil laws were introduced, there was no distinction between "named" and "unnamed" <note>named contracts (like "sale") had specific legal protections; unnamed ones (like "I give so that you give") were harder to enforce</note> contracts.

<margin>2</margin> Nor, as Fortunius and others testify, was there any difference between **naked** and **clothed** pacts. Therefore, in the court of conscience, and considering the very nature of the matter, an obligation arose from all such agreements. We call this a "natural" obligation to distinguish it from a "civil" obligation, from which a legal action is granted by civil law. To avoid a surplus of lawsuits, the **civil law** chose not to grant a civil obligation or legal action based on naked pacts (with a few exceptions shown in Disputation 255). Nevertheless, the law did not take away the power these pacts had under natural law to bind a person naturally; rather, because of that natural power, the civil law introduced various legal effects for them.

<margin>3</margin> Specifically, if someone was owed something **based on a naked pact**, although they could not demand it in an external court, if it were paid to them once, they could **retain** it in that same court and could not be forced to return it. Likewise, if the person owed something to the same creditor, they could perform a "set-off" <note>original: "compensationem"</note> for what the creditor owed them from the naked pact, and could not be forced in court to pay more than the difference. Furthermore—and this amounts to nearly the same thing—one could offer a **defense** <term>defense (exceptio): a legal shield used by a defendant to block a plaintiff’s claim</term> against a claimant, arguing that the debt was either only owed or had been remitted via a naked pact, and thus they were not bound to pay. This is found in the law <note>original: "l. iuris gentium" — a reference to the Digest of Justinian</note> where Ulpian, dividing agreements generally (which have force by the law of nations), says: *“Some agreements of the law of nations produce actions* <note>meaning, in civil law</note> *and some produce defenses.”* He immediately adds that only "named" contracts and "clothed" pacts produce a legal action, while naked ones produce only a defense. From this, he concludes: *“Therefore, a naked agreement does not produce an obligation [in civil law], but it produces a defense.”* This must be understood as applying to civil law and the external court. Likewise, because of the natural obligation remaining from a naked pact, although a civil action is not granted against the person who made the agreement, it is granted against a **guarantor** <note>original: "fideiussor"</note> if one was provided for the fulfillment of the pact. For the same reason, a **pledge** <note>original: "pignus"</note> can be retained if it was given to fulfill a naked pact.

<margin>4</margin> These authors confirm that a natural obligation results from a naked pact and that the aforementioned effects are granted by civil law because of it, as cited in the Institutes and the Digest.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding the second point of the proposal: the common opinion of the Doctors is that **by Canon Law** <note>Church law</note>, a legal action **is** granted based on a **naked pact**, according to the chapter *c. 1 de pact.* in the Decretals. This is affirmed by Panormitanus, Felinus, and others, as well as Gómez and Covarruvias. Since a natural obligation arises from a naked pact, and men are bound to stand by them in the court of conscience, the salvation and good of souls required that an action be granted in Canon Law, which is exactly what happened. Felinus and others excellently observe that the action granted by Canon Law for a naked pact only takes place in cases belonging to the **Church tribunal** <note>original: "tribunal Ecclesiae"</note> either because of the persons involved or the subject matter. It also applies to cases involving laypeople living in Church lands or territories subject to the temporal rule of the Pope; however, it is different in the temporal cases of other laypeople. Nevertheless, a "denunciation" <note>original: "denunciatio"</note>—midway between a brotherly correction and a judicial one—can be used against them. We have discussed this regarding brotherly correction and will do so in Treatise 5. By this path, they can be compelled by Church prelates to stand by their naked pacts, insofar as they are bound in the court of conscience, to rescue them from mortal sin. This is the view of Felinus, Bartolus, and many others. Felinus, Panormitanus, and Covarruvias also observe that for an action to be granted in Canon Law from a naked pact to compel someone to fulfill it, an **expression of the cause** is necessary.

<column-break/>

Otherwise, the defendant will not be compelled to pay unless the plaintiff sufficiently proves the **cause** <term>cause (causa): the underlying reason or consideration for an agreement, such as a loan, a sale, or a gift</term>. 

<margin>6</margin> For example, suppose a document is found stating that *“Peter agreed with John that he would give John something on such a day,”* say an ox or a hundred gold coins. If the **cause** for which Peter was to give this is not contained in the document, he will not be forced to give it unless John proves the cause sufficiently or Peter confesses it. But if the cause is expressed in the writing, Peter is immediately compelled to pay unless it is proved most clearly that the cause did not actually exist. Since he confessed the cause (whether in the writing or outside it), the burden of proof shifts to him to show it did not exist. Take another example: If a writing says Peter binds himself to give John a hundred coins on Michaelmas, and the reason given is that Peter promised it for a service John was going to perform, but John did not perform it; or as compensation for another thing that John did not provide—then John must prove the cause existed, otherwise Peter is not forced to pay. But if the writing says he will give it in compensation for a service or another thing that John *has already* provided or is *currently* providing, Peter will be forced to pay unless he himself proves the cause did not truly exist. In this context, observe that a **title of donation** <note>i.e., making a gift</note> is considered a "sufficient cause" for a person to be compelled to pay. Thus, if the writing says (or it is proved he said), "I promise I will give to John as a gift," or "as alms," or in any other way for free and out of liberality, he will be compelled to pay both in the secular and the ecclesiastical court.

<margin>7</margin> This is because a **naked pact of donation** creates a civil obligation today, even under civil law, as shown in Disputation 255. <margin>Objection</margin>

<margin>8</margin> But if someone objects that a person who promises without expressing a cause is **presumed to have wanted to make a gift**...

<summary>This page explains that while "naked pacts" (simple agreements) lack full enforcement in Roman Civil Law, they create a "natural obligation" binding in conscience. In Canon Law, these agreements are legally actionable to ensure the soul's salvation, provided a specific reason (cause) for the promise is stated or proven.</summary>
<keywords>naked pact, natural obligation, civil obligation, court of conscience, Canon Law, cause of contract, donation, legal defense, Ulpian, Felinus, Covarruvias</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 257, specifically investigating when a person is legally or morally bound by a "naked pact" (a simple agreement without formal rituals) if the underlying reason or "cause" for the agreement is not explicitly stated or performed.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

<margin>Resolved.</margin>
According to the law *Campanus* in the Digest <note>original: "l. Campanus, ff. de lib." — referring to a specific section of the Roman Digest regarding the status of persons</note>, when a debt is recorded in writing but no cause is expressed, it is to be presumed that it was a gift. Therefore, the person who promised is compelled to pay, unless they can prove the contrary. However, it must be said that this is understood to apply when it is established, or sufficiently proven, that the person making the promise knew at the time that no other reason existed for making the promise; in that case, a gift is presumed. If, however, it is clear that the promiser believed there was a underlying reason which did not actually exist, or if we are in doubt whether they were perhaps led by a reason that did not hold or did not take effect, then the intent to give a gift is not so strongly presumed that they should be forced to stand by a **naked pact** <term>naked pact (pactum nudum): a simple agreement that lacks the specific legal formalities required by Roman law to be enforceable in a secular court</term>.

The cited Doctors confirm that when the cause is not expressed, or not sufficiently proven from elsewhere, **Canon Law** does not grant a legal action based on a naked pact to force a defendant to fulfill it. This is because Canon Law does not grant more power to a naked pact than Civil Law grants to a **stipulation** <term>stipulation (stipulatio): a formal, oral contract in Roman law that was legally binding because of its specific wording</term>. Yet in Civil Law, a stipulation does not grant a right to sue to force someone to keep a promise unless the cause of that promise is expressed—whether that cause was the title of a gift or something else. This is clear from the law *circa* in the Digest <note>original: "l. 2. §. circa, ff. de doli except." — Digest 44.4.2.3 concerning the "exception of fraud"</note>. Although the stipulation and subsequent promise may be established, if the cause of such a promise was not expressed, the promiser can raise a defense against the one suing them, claiming they are acting in bad faith by demanding fulfillment when the cause for the promise was never met. For instance, they might say they promised to give one hundred on a certain day in exchange for an equal amount they were supposed to receive as a loan, but they never received it. In that case, it falls to the plaintiff to prove that the cause was fulfilled or that the promise was made as a gift. By the same reasoning, Canon Law would not grant a legal action based on a naked pact unless the cause for the promise is established.

**9** Nevertheless, observe this: in a **loan** <term>loan (mutuum): specifically a loan of "fungible" items like money or grain that are consumed and replaced by an equal amount</term>, even if someone confesses in writing to have received money, wheat, or anything else, they are still granted an **exception** <term>exception (exceptio): a legal defense used by a defendant to block a plaintiff’s claim</term> within two years from the date of that written confession. They may claim they did not receive the items, but made the confession in the hope of a future payment or delivery. If they raise this exception within two years, then it is up to the opponent to prove that they actually counted out the money or delivered the goods; otherwise, the opponent will lose the case. If, however, two years pass before the defense is raised, then it falls to the borrower to prove that the money was not counted out or the goods were not delivered; otherwise, they will be forced to pay. This is held in the Code <note>original: "l. in contractib. C. de non nu. pec." — Codex Justinianus 4.30.5 regarding the defense of "money not counted"</note> and other laws, as we shall discuss more extensively in the section on loans.

**10** Furthermore, regarding a **dowry**, even if a husband confesses to have received it, as long as the marriage continues, he is allowed to raise the exception that the dowry was never actually paid, but that the confession was made in hope of receiving it. Once that defense is raised, it falls to the person who promised the dowry to prove it was paid. If the marriage is dissolved—either by the death of a spouse or by divorce—and the marriage did not last for a full two years, the husband, his father, or his heirs have one year from the dissolution of the marriage to raise the same defense. In that case, the burden of proof lies with the one who promised the dowry; otherwise, they will be forced to pay it. If, however, the marriage—

<column-break/>

—lasted beyond two years, but was dissolved before ten years were completed, he is only allowed to raise this defense within three months from the day the marriage ended. If the marriage lasted more than ten years, then upon its dissolution, such an exception is not granted. Instead, the person who made the confession (or their heirs) must prove that the dowry was *not* delivered; otherwise, they will lose the case. All of this is found in the final law and the following authentic text in the Code <note>original: "C. de dote cauta non numerata" — Codex 4.30 concerning dowries promised but not paid</note>. Generally, when something was owed for any reason—whether money or something else—if a creditor made a written confession that they received it, or if you promised because of that reason to return the legal instrument in which the debt was contained, those creditors are allowed within thirty days of making that confession or promise to raise the defense that they did so in hope of a future payment or delivery which never took place. Then it falls to the debtor to prove they paid the debt; otherwise, they will be forced to pay again. After those thirty days have passed, such a defense is not admitted, and the burden shifts to the creditor to prove the debt was not paid. This is held in the Code section *super* <note>original: "l. in contractib. §. super, C. de non num. pec." — Codex 4.30.5.1</note>.

**12** Finally, regarding this second part of the disputation, one must observe that there is a very wide distinction between **Civil Law** and **Canon Law**. We say that in Civil Law, no action is granted for a naked pact unless it is "clothed" by the subsequent performance of the cause, as was shown in Disputation 255. Yet in this disputation, we say that for an action to be granted in Canon Law (whereby an opponent is compelled to stand by a naked pact), it is necessary for the cause to be expressed or proven. In the former case (Civil Law), we are speaking of a cause already put into execution, which therefore "clothes" the pact and takes it out of the category of a naked pact. In the latter case (Canon Law), we are speaking of a cause expressed within the pact itself, or proven elsewhere, or confessed by the defendant, whether it has been executed or not.

For example: if Peter agrees with John to give him a loan of one hundred, but has not yet delivered it, since a loan implies a **burdensome cause** <note>original: "causam onerosam" — a reason involving an exchange or obligation rather than a pure gift</note> (namely, that John must later repay the same amount), John is granted a legal action against Peter in Canon Law to force him to provide the loan. In Civil Law, however, the action would be denied because it is a naked pact and no delivery or fulfillment has occurred on either side—fulfillment of the cause being what "clothes" a naked pact. Similarly, if Peter and John, by public instrument but without a formal stipulation, agreed to exchange an ox for ten sheep on a certain day, and neither side has made a delivery, each is granted an action against the other in Canon Law if the other refuses. This is because the cause was expressed (the exchange for another thing). However, in Civil Law, no action would be granted, because it is a naked pact not yet "clothed" by the fulfillment of the cause by either of the contracting parties. Covarruvias elucidates this matter, which is quite clear in itself, with many more examples. He speaks much better on this than Antonio Gómez, Padilla, and many other legal experts, who do not pay attention to these different meanings of "cause."

**13** Regarding the third of the points proposed in this disputation, it must be said here,

<summary>Molina explains that under Canon Law, a "naked pact" can be legally enforceable if a clear "cause" (reason for the agreement) is stated, unlike in Civil Law which usually requires formal rituals or actual performance. He also details the specific time limits and burdens of proof for defending against claims of debt or unpaid dowries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 257 regarding the enforceability of simple agreements. It transitions into Disputation 258, which examines the legal right to withdraw from a contract (the right of "repentance") under Civil Law, Canon Law, and the specific laws of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 258.

In the same way that it was explained concerning **Canon Law** <term>Canon Law: the body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership for the government of the Christian organization and its members</term> that a legal action is granted based on a **naked pact** <term>naked pact (pactum nudum): an agreement made without the formal legal rituals required by ancient Roman law</term>, it must be affirmed that such an action is also granted for the same naked pact in the secular courts of the Kingdom of Castile. This is according to Law 3, Title 8, Book 3 of the *Ordenamiento* <note>original: "ord." refers to the *Ordenamiento de Alcalá*, a set of laws promulgated in 1348</note>, which is Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collect." refers to the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish laws</note>, the words of which we recorded in Disputation 254. We can confirm this because, if a **stipulation** <term>stipulation (stipulatio): a formal oral contract requiring specific wording to be legally binding</term> is added to a naked pact, Civil Law commonly grants an action from it, as shown in Disputation 255. This is because it transforms, by that very fact, not only into a "clothed pact" but even into a "named contract" <term>named contract (contractus nominatus): a standard contract recognized by law, such as a sale, lease, or partnership, which carries specific legal protections</term>. However, as the cited law of Castile holds, in that kingdom, an action is granted in the same way for any pact or promise that has been accepted, whether the form of a stipulation was added or not. Therefore, in that kingdom, a legal action is granted for a naked pact just as it is in Canon Law. All Spanish doctors seem to agree on this doctrine, including, among others, Gregorio López <note>A famous Spanish jurist and commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> on Law 3, Title 6, regarding the phrase <term>Qualquier de las partes</term> <gloss>Either of the parties</gloss>, and Law 1, Title 11, on the phrase *gran pro*, and Law 4, Title 4, Gloss 1, Part 5. Also Molina, Book 4, *On Primogeniture*, Chapter 2, number 62; Covarrubias, Book 1, *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 14, number 15; and Antonio Gómez, Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, Chapters 8 and 9. Nevertheless, some of them and several others do not speak as accurately as they should, failing to attend to those various definitions of "cause" <note>original: "causæ" — the legal reason or consideration behind a contract</note> explained just a little earlier. What has been said so far will be made clearer by the things we will add in the following disputation.

### To what extent, in a naked pact and in innominate contracts, there is a place for withdrawal according to Civil Law, and whether it has a place in Canon Law and in the Kingdom of Castile.

->D I S P U T A T I O CCLVIII.<-

->S U M M A R Y<-

1 *Withdrawal <note>original: "pænitentia" — the legal right to change one's mind and back out of a contract before it is completed</note> has no place, even in Civil Law, in an **innominate contract** <term>innominate contract (contractus innominatus): an agreement that does not have a specific legal name but is based on mutual performance, such as "I give so that you may give" (barter)</term>, as long as it has been satisfied by both parties according to common opinion.*
2 *There is a place for withdrawal even in a contract strengthened by a stipulation, where one of the parties does not wish to fulfill the contract on their side.*
3 *When there is a place for withdrawal in an innominate contract, both on the part of the one fulfilling it and the one not fulfilling it, and when there is not.*
4 *There is no place for withdrawal in an innominate contract if the other contracting party wishes to stand by the contract.*
5 *Withdrawal is not admitted from an innominate contract under the law of Castile.*
6 *There is no place for withdrawal in "named" contracts and others that are equivalent to them.*
7 *Withdrawal has a place in a simple promise <note>original: "pollicitatione"</note> when it has not yet been revoked.*

<margin>1st conclusion.</margin>
For the sake of clarity, this disputation must be addressed with several conclusions. The first is:
**1** When an innominate contract has been satisfied by both sides, there is no place for withdrawal for either of the contracting parties, even under common Civil Law. This is because they are instead mutually bound to one another regarding **eviction** <term>eviction: a guarantee that the property transferred will not be taken away by a third party with a better legal claim</term>, as gathered from the final gloss on the law *Ex Placito* in the Code, regarding the exchange of things. The common opinion of the doctors affirms this, which Antonio Gómez follows in Volume 2, Chapter 8. This conclusion is clear: because against one who has fulfilled their part, there is no place for withdrawal for the other, as we shall see; therefore, when both have fulfilled their part, there is no place for withdrawal for either. The second conclusion: Even if
<margin>2nd conclusion. ✝</margin> a pact were strengthened by a stipulation, if one of the contracting parties did not wish to fulfill the contract on their part, it would be within the right of the other to "repent" <note>withdraw</note> and dissolve

<column-break/>

the contract, both in the external court <note>the secular or ecclesiastical legal system</note> and in the court of conscience. Indeed, it would be within their right to reclaim what they gave on their part. They gather this by reasoning from the opposite sense of Law 3, Title 6, Part 5; and Gregorio López affirms it there in Glosses 1 and 3, along with others whom he cites. He confirms this from the Digest <note>original: "ff. de cond. cau. data causa non fequuta" — referring to the legal action to recover something given for a purpose that was not realized</note>. It can also be proven because in reciprocal pacts, there is a tacit condition of keeping the pact if the other party also keeps it. Therefore, if one breaks faith or does not keep the pact, the other is not bound to keep it either; rather, they can
**3** demand back what they gave. The third conclusion †: under common Civil Law, in innominate contracts, while the matter is still "whole" <note>original: "re integra" — meaning before any part of the contract has been performed</note> on the part of both contractors (so that neither has fulfilled the pact on their side), there is a place for withdrawal for each of them. But if only one has fulfilled their part, there is a place for withdrawal on the part of the one who fulfilled it; they can, therefore, reclaim what they gave, even if the other party is neither in delay nor at fault, but is ready to fulfill their part. On the part of the one who has not yet fulfilled their side, however, there is no place for withdrawal in comparison to the one who has fulfilled it. Instead, a legal action is granted to the one who fulfilled it against the other, to compel them to fulfill the contract, or—if they cannot fulfill it—to compel them to pay the "interest" <note>compensation for damages</note> or to restore what they received, whichever the one who fulfilled it prefers, according to what was explained more fully in Disputation 255. However, if the one who had not yet fulfilled their part had incurred any expenses in preparing to fulfill it, or if damages emerged in their own property for any other reason due to the other's withdrawal, then the one who fulfilled the part is bound either not to withdraw (by standing by the contract) or to keep the other harmless by repairing the damages that followed from it. I believe the same holds even if neither had fulfilled their part, if similar damages arose for one because the other withdrew. This entire conclusion is established from Law 9, especially in the beginning and first paragraph, and much more clearly from the law *Si Pecunia* in the Digest, and the Gloss and Bartolus affirm it there, as do Antonio Gómez and the doctors commonly. You might object that while a "civil obligation" <term>civil obligation: a debt or duty that can be enforced in a court of law</term> might not arise from innominate contracts on the part of the one who fulfilled it compared to the one who did not, a **natural obligation** <term>natural obligation: a moral duty that cannot be sued upon in court but has some legal effects, like preventing the recovery of a payment voluntarily made</term> does arise. From this natural obligation, Civil Law admits "set-off" <note>compensation</note> for what is owed, and an exception, as all these things were shown in the preceding disputation. Therefore, you might argue, there is no place for withdrawal in the secular court for the one who fulfilled it when the one who did not fulfill it is ready on their side to do so. The logic of this follows: because when the one who fulfilled the part wants to reclaim what they gave in court on the grounds of withdrawal, the one who hasn't fulfilled yet will "except" <note>object</note> that the thing is naturally owed to them and they are not bound to return it. To this objection, it must be said that Civil Law only grants set-off and exception from a natural obligation when the obligation is "simple"—that is, not involving a corresponding similar obligation on the part of the other. But in the case proposed, there was a corresponding similar obligation; for the one who gave was similarly naturally bound, both to give and also to not reclaim after they gave. Because, therefore, no civil obligation arose on the part of the one who gave compared to the one who received but did not fulfill, and by the very fact that the one who gave withdraws, the civil obligation to fulfill on the part of the other (who had not yet fulfilled) is extinguished, the Civil Law dissolves the mutual obligation...

<summary>This page discusses the enforceability of simple agreements in Spanish law and examines the legal right of "pænitentia" (withdrawal) from contracts. It concludes that while Roman Civil Law often allowed parties to back out of incomplete agreements, Spanish law and Canon Law are stricter, prioritizing the fulfillment of promises once accepted.</summary>
<keywords>naked pact, innominate contract, withdrawal, pænitentia, Kingdom of Castile, Canon Law, Civil Law, natural obligation, stipulation, contract performance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether a party can legally withdraw from a contract—a concept known as "the right of repentance"—after an agreement has been made but before it is fully executed. Molina is comparing Roman Civil Law, which often allowed such withdrawal in "innominate" (unnamed) contracts, with Canon Law and the laws of Spain, which tend to uphold the binding nature of a simple promise.</meta>

natural obligation remaining on both sides, if it were not for the withdrawal <note>original: "pœnitentia," refers to the legal right to change one's mind and revoke a contract</note>, a compensation and an exception should be granted. As far as **Canon Law** is concerned, whether withdrawal should be admitted in **innominate contracts** <term>innominate contracts: agreements that do not fall into standard legal categories like "sale" or "lease" but are based on "I give so that you give" or "I do so that you do"</term> according to that law, just as it is permitted in **Civil Law** <term>Civil Law: specifically the Roman Law codified by Justinian</term>, **Baldus** in certain places and several others—whom **Felinus** (in chapter 1, number 13, *on pacts*) and **Gregorio López** (on Law 3, Title 6, Part 5) cite—affirm that it should be granted. They are led to this because it is so arranged in Civil Law, and nothing contrary is found sanctioned in Canon Law; and in the **Ecclesiastical Court**, one must stand by the dispositions of Civil Law when nothing to the contrary is established in Canon Law. From this they conclude that, although an action is granted from a **naked pact** <term>naked pact: a simple agreement made without formal legal ceremonies</term> in Canon Law, it is nonetheless denied in an innominate contract to the person who has not yet fulfilled their part against the one who *has* fulfilled theirs, to force them to stand by the contract by not withdrawing from it through "repentance."

<margin>4th Conclusion</margin> Nevertheless, we propose this **fourth conclusion**: Although when the one who has not yet fulfilled is in **default** <term>default (mora): a legal delay or failure to perform an obligation on time</term>, or has a deliberate intention of not fulfilling at the due time, it is lawful for the one who has fulfilled to dissolve the contract and reclaim what they gave—and this is true in Canon and Civil Law as well as in the **court of conscience** <term>court of conscience (forum conscientiae): the moral or spiritual judgment of an action, often handled in confession, as opposed to a legal court</term>, according to what was said in the second conclusion—nevertheless, as long as the other party is not in default and is ready to fulfill their part, it is not lawful, neither in Canon Law nor in the court of conscience, for the one who fulfilled to reclaim what they gave on the grounds of "repentance." If they do reclaim it and it is awarded to them in a secular court, they are bound to restore it and stand by the contract. But if they have become unable to do so because the thing is no longer in their power, they are bound to restore as much as it mattered to the other party that they did not depart from the contract. Baldus later followed this conclusion in his commentary on the Code, *on the exchange of things*, departing from his earlier opinion; Felinus and Gregorio López (in the places cited) and others embrace the same. The reason for this is that from an innominate contract, a **natural obligation** <term>natural obligation: a debt or duty that is morally binding even if it cannot be enforced by a specific legal action</term> arises on both sides, even before anything is fulfilled. By reason of this, each of them is bound in the court of conscience to stand by the contract, so long as the other has not failed nor is in default of fulfilling, as shown in the preceding dispute. And by reason of this obligation, an action is granted in Canon Law from a naked pact, and thus "repentance" is not admitted even when the matter is untouched <note>original: "re integra," meaning before any performance has begun</note>, as explained there. Therefore, "repentance" shall not be granted on the part of the one who fulfilled while the other is not in default and is ready to fulfill; for in this event, nothing is excepted in Canon Law, and Civil Law would equally admit "repentance" when the matter is untouched on both sides as it admits it on the part of the one who alone has fulfilled. This conclusion is confirmed because, if a **stipulation** <term>stipulation: a formal legal promise</term> had intervened and neither were in default, certainly "repentance" would not be admitted even in Civil Law, whether the matter were untouched or on the part of the one who fulfilled, as is clear from the law *ex placito* in the Code, *on the exchange of things*. But Canon Law and the court of conscience care nothing for the solemnity of a stipulation; rather, Canon Law grants an action from a naked pact just as if a stipulation had intervened (which, beyond the pact, adds only a preceding formal questioning). Therefore, neither in Canon Law nor in the court of conscience is "repentance" permitted when neither of the contracting parties is in default.

<margin>5th Conclusion</margin> **Fifth conclusion**: In the **Kingdom of Castile**, there is no place for "repentance" in innominate contracts, just as there is not in Canon Law or the court of conscience. This is clear from Law 3, Title 8, Book 3 of the *Ordenamiento*, which is Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Collection*. For as was proved in the preceding dispute, it grants an action from a naked pact and likewise denies "repentance." This is affirmed by Gregorio 

<column-break/>

López (Law 3, gloss 3, Title 6, Part 5) and Antonio Gómez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 8, numbers 4 and 5). According to what has been said so far, the Supreme Pontiff could, and should, abrogate those Civil Laws that admit "repentance" in innominate contracts and grant the recovery of what was rightly paid by the other party. For, as is clear from what has been said, they foster sins and multiply lawsuits, rather than diminishing them. Indeed, all those things concerning naked and "clothed" pacts, and "innominate" and "named" contracts—which were invented and introduced in Civil Law by pagan men more with subtlety than with utility—ought to be abolished, just as was done in the Kingdom of Castile by that cited Law 3, either entirely or for the most part, in accordance with Canon Law. The external court ought to be made equal to the court of conscience. I have no doubt that by this reasoning, lawsuits would be diminished rather than increased, and men would be freed from the very difficult investigation of these matters as they have been handed down so far in a scattered and entangled way in Civil Law.

<margin>6th Conclusion</margin> **Sixth conclusion**: In **named contracts** <note>original: "contractibus nominatis," such as sale, hire, or partnership</note>, and in others that enjoy the privilege of Civil Law or the bond of justice—such as the promise of a dowry, or gifts accepted before they are fulfilled by work—there is no place for "repentance." This is established by the law *Sicut* and other laws which the final gloss cites there, in the Code, *on actions and obligations*; these laws are certainly to be understood as referring to contracts of this kind. Observe, however, that some contracts are "named" which by their nature allow for dissolution by one or either of the contracting parties whenever they wish, even against the will of the other; in these, "repentance" has a place in this sense: that it is permissible to dissolve them so they have no further force, yet those effects which they have achieved up to that moment retain their force from those same contracts. Such are **partnerships** <term>partnership (societas): a contract where two or more people agree to share resources for a common goal</term> when not contracted for a specific time (for it can be dissolved whenever any of the partners is unwilling); likewise **precarium** (that is, a loan granted at the pleasure of the lender), **mandates**, **deposits**, and if there are any others like these, as the cited gloss and another law, *If money*, in the Digest, *on the cause given*, affirm according to various laws.

<margin>7th Conclusion</margin> **Final conclusion**: In a **pollicitation** <term>pollicitation: a promise made by one party that has not yet been accepted by the other</term>, before it is accepted, "repentance" is permitted by Civil Law, Canon Law, and in the court of conscience, as we shall see in its proper place. That is, in any pact where for a reasonable cause the power of revoking it is granted, as in donations when causes are present for which the power to revoke them is given, as we shall see in their proper places.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the classification of contracts, moving from the "right of repentance" to the fundamental distinction in Roman Law between "good faith" and "strict law" agreements.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 254

<margin>1</margin> Other divisions of contracts must be added. And first, some are called **good faith** <note>original: "bonæ fidei"</note>, and others are of **strict law** <note>original: "stricti iuris"</note>. The same division applies to legal actions, as is clear from the *Institutes*, in the section "on actions," paragraph "of actions," and the two following. However, this division is more broadly applicable because actions sometimes arise from a contract, and sometimes from a **quasi-contract** <term>quasi-contract: an obligation that arises from circumstances rather than an explicit agreement, such as returning money paid by mistake</term>, or some other title. Furthermore, from those actions which are called "good faith" and arise from contracts, you will understand which contracts are called "good faith"; for other contracts, which do not produce good faith actions, are of strict law. Following the *Institutes* in the place cited, the following actions are called **good faith**: from buying, selling, leasing, hiring, **management of affairs** <note>original: "negotiorum gestorum," where someone acts for another without a prior agreement</note>, mandate, deposit, partnership, tutelage, loan for use, pledge, **division of an estate** <note>original: "familiæ erciscundæ," an action given between co-heirs regarding the division of a deceased person's property</note>, **division of common property** <note>original: "communi dividundo," an action given between those who have something in common to be divided between them</note>, and from **appraisal** <note>original: "de æstimato," which arises when I hand over an appraised item to you, so that you either return the item or its appraised value; if you sell it for a higher price, the profit is yours</note>. Likewise, an action of good faith exists in **exchange** <note>original: "permutatione," understood as a specific type of contract distinct from other "unnamed" contracts</note>; likewise, the action for claiming an inheritance, and the action for demanding or recovering a **dowry** <note>original: "dotis"</note> after a marriage has ended; and likewise that action for a dowry which is today called **by stipulation** <note>original: "ex stipulatu"</note>, as noted in the *Institutes* in the place cited.
<margin>2 †</margin> Other actions, however, which are not listed there, and the contracts or quasi-contracts from which they arise (among which you should count a **stipulation** <term>stipulation: a formal verbal promise</term> within the limits of a stipulation, that is, when a good faith contract is not employed) are called **strict law**. This is affirmed by the glosses of **Accursius** and other doctors in that place, according to those three paragraphs. The glosses of **Panormitanus** and others say the same in the chapter "Since the venerable," under "exceptions." See also **Conrado Reggio**, *On the Possessor*, part 2, section 6, from number 4; **Sylvester** under the word "contract," question 21; **Alvaro Valasco** on the law of **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis: a long-term lease of land</term>, question 5, number 1; and other doctors whom they cite.

<margin>3</margin> Beyond other distinctions, these two are passed down between contracts (or actions) of good faith and those of strict law: First, that † in good faith contracts, the judge has the power to judge from what is **good and equitable** <note>original: "ex bono & æquo"</note>, whatever seems right to him, even if it was not expressly stated or said in the agreement. In strict law contracts, however, he cannot judge except according to what was expressed in the agreement, unless it has been otherwise specifically established by law regarding a certain contract or action. This is gathered clearly from the paragraph "in good faith" in the *Institutes* on actions, and the doctors teach it there and in other cited places. 
<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, † "good faith" in the matter we are discussing is taken not as it is distinguished against bad faith, malice, fraud, and craftiness; for that kind of good faith ought to be in all contracts, as noted in the law "good faith," in the Code "on actions and obligations." Rather, it stands for **equity**, or the judge's discretion according to what equity and the nature of the thing require. Hence, in this context, "good faith contracts" are those in which the judge's discretion and arrangement, according to what equity and the nature of the thing require, has the greatest power. For that reason, the opposite branch is "strict law contracts," in which the judge's discretion does not have such power, but he is bound to judge according to what was said and agreed upon. In this matter, observe two things. One is that, just as

<column-break/>

within just prices there are contained the lowest, the middle, and the rigorous; so too a judgment—whether it be stricter according to exactly what the parties agreed (as in strict law contracts), or whether it be more kindly according to what equity requires more than the rigor of the law (as in good faith contracts)—is always contained within the limits of a **just judgment**, which in its scope encompasses both the "kind just" and the "rigorous just."

The second thing is that the "good faith" or equity left to the judge's discretion (which has a place in good faith contracts but not in strict law contracts) is not the same thing as **Epicheia** <term>Epicheia: the interpretation of a law or contract based on the perceived intent of the author rather than the literal words</term>. Through Epicheia, just as we judge regarding laws that certain events are not considered included in them—because if the lawmaker had been asked about them in particular when making the law, he would have replied that it was not his intention for them to be included—so in contracts we judge that it was the intention of neither party that certain cases be included, unless there was fraud or malice in one of them, which should not be protected. Therefore, because it conflicts with justice for such events to be included in pacts, it certainly has no place even in strict law contracts. And it is about this kind of judgment that the well-worn proverb is understood: **"The highest law is the highest injury"** <note>original: "Summum ius, summa iniuria," meaning that the law, when applied too strictly without equity, can be the greatest source of injustice</note>. **Tullius** <note>Cicero</note> provides an example in the first book of *On Duties* regarding a general who, when he had entered into a pact with the enemy to abstain from fighting for three days, himself fought against them during the nights.

Therefore, the difference between good faith and strict law contracts is that in the former, the judge can extend his judgment more toward what equity demands between the contracting parties; in the latter, however, he can do so far less, but must adhere to the words and arrangement of the contracting parties as far as justice allows; and for that reason, they are called strict law contracts. **Covarrubias** and **Alvaro Valasco** explain the origin of this division and the naming of both branches in the places cited, excluding the false opinion of some. Read them. As to why privileges were granted to the former rather than the latter, the doctors commonly say it was because the former are more frequent and more necessary for human society; however, when the facts of the matter are clear, one should not care much from where the legislators were led.

<margin>5 †</margin> The second difference is that, according to Civil Law, when † **fraud** <note>original: "dolus"</note> gave cause to a good faith contract—meaning that the other person would not have celebrated such a contract unless they had been induced by fraud to celebrate it—the contract is **void by the law itself** <note>original: "ipso iure nullus"</note>. This applies even if the one who was misled by fraud nonetheless wants it to be valid, because it is void by law out of hatred for the fraudulent person, not out of hatred for the one who suffered the fraud. When, however, fraud gave cause to a strict law contract, the contract is not void by the law itself, but it must be rescinded by an **exception** <term>exception: a legal defense raised by the defendant to stop an action</term> or opposition by the one who suffered the fraud and was induced to contract in that way. If, however, the fraud did not *give cause* to the contract (suppose that even if fraud had not intervened, the contract would have been celebrated, but one of the parties was nonetheless induced by fraud to give more or receive less than they otherwise would have), the contract is indeed valid whether it is of good faith or strict law. But an action is brought to compensate for the damage that one of the contracting parties received because of the fraud. All these things are clear from the law "If by fraud" in the Code *on the rescinding of a sale*, from law 3, final paragraph, in the Digest *on partnership*, and "fraud or fear" in the Code *on useless stipulations*, with the glosses on those laws; and the glosses, **Bartolus**, and others affirm this elegantly at the beginning.
