# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

Digest, on fraud; gloss on the Code, on the rescinding of a sale; the gloss and Panormitanus on the chapter "with the beloved," number 6 and following, on buying and selling; Conrad on contracts in the summary of the whole work, at question 17, statement 14, together with statements 1 and 2 joined there; Covarruvias on the rule "possessor," part 2, section 6, number 6; Alvarus Valascus on the law of long-term leases <note>original: "emphyteusis"</note>, question 5, number 9; and the doctors of law commonly. For this reason, the opinion of a few must be rejected—whom Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and Conrad mention—who assert that even when fraud <note>original: "dolus"</note> gives cause to a **good faith contract**, it is not void **by the law itself** <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>, but must be rescinded by a **defense of fraud** <note>original: "doli exceptione"</note>, no differently than a contract of **strict law** is rescinded by a defense of fraud.

I should advise, along with Conrad and Covarruvias in the places cited and with others, that in the **forum of conscience** <note>the internal moral judgment of an individual before God, as opposed to a legal court</note>, when fraud has given cause to a contract, even if it is one of strict law, it is void. The reason is that consent to a contract through fraud—which would not have been drawn out had the fraud been removed—is insufficient by the very nature of the thing for an obligation to result from it by reason of such a contract, because it is not as voluntary as is necessary for that purpose. Thus, this second distinction only has force in the **outward forum** <note>the public legal system</note>, in which the law wished to provide a greater and more immediate remedy in good faith contracts than in those of a stricter nature. Perhaps, however, it would be expedient if, according to the nature of the thing itself, the outward forum were made equal to the forum of conscience in this part, and therefore a contract of strict law to which fraud had given cause would be void by the law itself, just as a good faith contract is. Read what we say more extensively on this matter in Disputation 352. Finally, I should advise that we are not speaking here of the contract of marriage, in which it is a peculiar rule that, even if fraud gave cause to it, it is nonetheless valid, both in the forum of conscience and in the outward forum, and it can be rescinded by no defense, because of its very nature and the indissolubility which it claims for itself by **natural law**. Regarding this matter, there will be a discussion in the section on marriage; something will also be added in the progress of this work. Those things which have been said about fraud—whether giving or not giving cause to a contract—will become clearer in the section on buying and selling, where we will also explain what fraud is.

<margin>6</margin> Furthermore, of contracts, some are those by which **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> is transferred, both full and direct, as usually happens in a gift, sale, exchange, loan, and others; some are those by which only **useful ownership** <term>useful ownership: "dominium utile," the right to use and profit from property, often held by a tenant or vassal while another holds the legal title</term> is transferred, such as a fief and a **long-term lease** <note>original: "emphyteusis"</note>, whether in perpetuity or for a time exceeding ten years; some are those by which only the **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the fruits/profits of another's property</note> is granted, as are many types of leases; some are those by which only the **use** is granted, such as a **loan for use** <note>original: "commodatum"</note> and the leasing of some things for use only, like pack animals for a journey; and some are those by which none of these are granted, such as a **deposit**, a **pledge**, and a **mortgage**; for it is not permitted for a depositary, or for one to whom something has been given as a pledge, to use the things deposited or given in pledge, but only to guard them or hold them for security.

Likewise, in a comparison of contracts regarding the person who received something from them, or to whom something is owed or remitted: some are called **lucrative**. These are namely those by which, without any burden or compensation, something is granted or promised out of pure 

<column-break/>

liberality, such as a gift (whether it begins from a promise or from the delivery of the thing); a **release of debt** <note>original: "acceptilatio"</note>, by which something is remitted to someone out of pure liberality; and a **loan for use** <note>original: "commodatum"</note> or a **grant at will** <note>original: "precarium"</note>, regarding the use of the thing which is granted through such a contract; for the thing is received by the borrower with the burden that it be restored and that the most diligent care be applied to it, as we shall say in its proper place. Other contracts are called **onerous**, namely those upon which a burden is imposed in return, such as buying, selling, leasing, and other similar ones.

### DISPUTATION 260.

-> S U M M A R Y <-

<margin>1</margin> 1 *Any contract is considered celebrated according to the laws and custom of the place.*
<margin>2</margin> 2 *What kind of proof a contract celebrated in Portugal requires.*
<margin>3</margin> 3 *What a plaintiff can do if they lack sufficient proof by witnesses, or other proof which would suffice by common law.*

<margin>1</margin> Regarding contracts in general, it must be observed first that each one is considered celebrated and is to be interpreted according to the laws and custom of the place in which it is made. This is proven by the law "If he should be unwilling," the paragraph "Because constant," in the Digest on the **aedilitian edict** <note>rules regarding the sale of slaves and livestock</note>, and it is affirmed by Bartolus on the law "No one is," in the Digest on two defendants; Panormitanus on the chapter "With M," number 5, on constitutions; Sylvester under the word "contract," question 8; and the doctors of law commonly.

<margin>2</margin> It must then be observed that, although the things said so far—namely when a civil obligation arises, and an action is given from some contract, and when a contract is considered perfected and when not—have a place in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, there is nonetheless this peculiar feature there: when a contract, or its dissolution, or the payment of a debt, concerns an **immovable thing** <note>real estate or land</note> which exceeds the value of six hundred **reais** <note>the Portuguese currency</note>, or a **movable thing** (or things) which exceed the value of thirty thousand reais, proof by witnesses is not admitted, nor by the private writing of the person with whom the contract was celebrated (even if five or more witnesses are employed in it), but only by a **public instrument** <note>original: "scripturam publicam"</note> drawn up by a **notary** <note>original: "tabellionem"</note> or a public scribe, or by a ship's scribe if it was celebrated on some ship while they are sailing or staying on the sea or in the rivers of the **Conquest** <note>original: "conquisitionis," referring to the Portuguese overseas territories</note> and the navigation of that kingdom, or in a place or town of the same Conquest—provided, however, that there is no notary or public scribe there. And upon the return, the ship's scribe is bound to hand over such writings made on the ship or in such a place to one of the notaries or public scribes of the place to which the ship has returned or in which it has deposited its cargo. If, however, a contract is celebrated in another kingdom, that proof by witnesses which would be valid according to **common law** <note>the *jus commune*, based on Roman and Canon law</note>, or according to the law or custom of such a kingdom, is admitted in Portugal regarding such contracts.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal proof in contracts, specifically focusing on the laws of Portugal (Lusitania) regarding when public deeds are required versus when witness testimony or personal oaths are sufficient.</meta>

### Treatise Two, Disputation 261. Page 17

...was sufficient. However, when a contract concerning movable goods—which do not exceed the value of thirty thousand reais <note>The "real" (plural *reais*) was the standard currency of the Kingdom of Portugal.</note>—is celebrated in Portugal through a public deed <note>original: "scripturam publicam"; a formal legal document drafted by a public official or notary</note>, then proof of payment of the debt arising from such a contract is not permitted through witnesses, but only through a public deed. All these points are found in Book 3 of the *Ordinances*, Title 45, at the beginning and in sections 1, 2, and 3.

<margin>3</margin> At this point, observe that if the immovable property <note>such as land or buildings</note> involved in the contract did not exceed the value of six hundred reais at the time the contract was celebrated, or if the movable goods did not exceed thirty thousand reais, witness testimony or private writing is admitted as proof—even if the value increases before payment is made. This is because the law considers the value at the time the contract was made, which is all the law provides for; it does not account for the accidental increase or decrease in value that happens afterward.

When someone lacks a public deed to prove such contracts or debts where a public deed is required, they are permitted to summon the person with whom they contracted (or whoever owes the debt) to court, so that the matter may be decided by that person’s oath. Indeed, if the defendant swears that they made no such contract, or owe nothing—or even if they admit to the contract but swear they owe nothing because they have paid or for some other legitimate reason—they are immediately acquitted by the judge. The plaintiff is then condemned to pay all the expenses the defendant incurred by appearing in court, or any loss suffered for that cause. However, if the defendant is unwilling to swear, the matter rests on the plaintiff's oath, and the defendant is compelled to pay what the plaintiff swears is owed.

These rules apply when both the plaintiff and the defendant are the principal parties—the one who owes and the one to whom it is owed—who ought to know the facts of the debt. For if an heir (or someone similar) is the one from whom a debt of the deceased is demanded, or something deposited with the deceased is claimed, it is enough if the heir swears they do not know of such a debt or object, or what became of it; they are then acquitted, and the plaintiff's oath will not be taken. Yet, if the heir refuses to swear this, the plaintiff's oath will be taken. If the plaintiff also refuses to swear, the defendant is acquitted. Similarly, if an heir or an executor of a will demands a debt due to the deceased from someone else, leaving it to the debtor's oath: if the debtor swears they owe nothing, they are acquitted. If they refuse to swear, they are compelled to pay, and the matter is not left to the plaintiff's oath; this is because in that event, only the debtor, and not the plaintiff, would reasonably be expected to know about the debt. All these rules also apply when the debt is of such a nature that proof by witnesses or private writing would be admitted according to what has been said, but the plaintiff lacks even this proof. These are explicitly found in Title 45, cited from section 4 to 9, joined with Title 8 and the penultimate and last sections of Title 36, Book 4 of the *Ordinances*.

Although a defendant might swear falsely to be acquitted, and this could be proven by witnesses or a public instrument, such proof is not admitted—not even for the sole purpose of punishing them for perjury—except when a private 

<column-break/>

writing of their own has been shown to them and they have sworn it was not theirs. In that case, proof to the contrary is admitted only for the purpose of punishing them for perjury. This is found in the cited Title 45, section 9, and Title 8, section 3. It is added in the following section 4 that when it is clear from a public deed that the defendant committed perjury, the King should be informed so he may judge what must be done to close the door to future perjuries.

<margin>†</margin> Observe that what † has been said also applies in common law <note>original: "iure communi"; the body of Roman and Canon law used across Europe</note> when a plaintiff lacks sufficient proof by witnesses or other means sufficient under common law. This is clear from the law *Manifestae* in the Digest, on oaths; the laws *In bonae fidei*, *Delata*, and *Generaliter* in the Code, under the same title; and the final chapter, at the beginning, under the same title. It is also affirmed by Maranta in *On the Order of Trials*, part 6, in the chapter on the oath and its distinction and use, numbers 11 and 12.

Although clerics are prohibited from swearing before a secular judge without the license of their prelate (whether in testifying or for any other reason), when they seek something in a civil case before a secular judge and the matter is left to their oath, they are granted permission in the Archdiocese of Évora to swear before him without any other license. This is found in the *Constitutions*, Title 10, chapter 12.

<margin>†</margin> In Portugal, many circumstances are excepted in which contracts, debts, and payments can be proven by witnesses, even if they concern immovable property exceeding six hundred reais or movables exceeding thirty thousand reais.

The first exception is when agreements were made between parents and children—not adopted children, but natural ones—or between a father-in-law or mother-in-law and a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, while the marriage lasts. For promises of dowries <note>original: "Dotum"</note> and agreements made before a marriage contract require a public deed for their proof, as was declared later in the sixth part of the *Extravagant Laws*, Title 1, Law 2. The same applies to contracts celebrated between the same parties after a marriage is dissolved. Likewise, contracts celebrated between brothers (whether sharing both parents or only one), between first cousins, and between a cousin and an uncle (either the father’s brother or the mother’s) can be proven by witnesses, even by their successors in property after their deaths.

However, if a contract between any of the aforementioned persons had been celebrated by a public deed, then proof by witnesses is not admitted to show the dissolution of such a contract or the payment of debts resulting from it; it can only be proven by public deed. All these are found in Book 3 of the *Ordinances*, Title 45, sections 10, 11, and 19, joined with Law 2, Title 1, part 6 of the *Extravagant Laws*.

The second exception is when a partnership <note>original: "societas"</note> among certain merchants <note>original: "mercatores"</note> regarding contracts, leases, or merchandise was celebrated by public deed or any other legitimate proof sufficient under common law. Any doubts arising between them or their heirs regarding such a partnership, or things depending on or pertaining to it, may be proven by witnesses. This is found in the cited Title 45, section 12.

Third, payments of pensions for emphyteusis <note>A long-term land lease where the tenant has the right to use and improve the land in exchange for a fee</note>, ground rents, or the leasing of a house or any other thing—provided they do not exceed the amount of thirty thousand reais <note>The "real" (plural *reais*) was the currency of Portugal</note> (understanding this of each payment individually, even if many taken together exceed that sum)—can be proven by witnesses. There is no hindrance even if the contracts from which the debts arise were celebrated by a public deed. This is held in the cited title, section 13.

Fourth, *Alvarás* <note>original: "Aluaras"; private warrants, vouchers, or signed documents</note>, as they are called in that kingdom, provide legitimate proof against those by whom they were written and signed, provided they are written and signed by Archbishops, Bishops, ordained Abbots, noblemen of ancestral manors, Knights confirmed by the King, Doctors of Sacred Theology, or of Canon or Civil Law (provided they were created in some university through examination), or by ministers of justice of the High Court <note>original: "do desembargo"</note>. If, however, they belong to Archbishops, Bishops, Royal Princes <note>original: "dos Infantes"</note>, Dukes, Masters, Marquises, or Counts, it is sufficient if they are signed by them, provided they were drawn up by their scribes, for them to effect full proof. This is held in the same place, section 14.

Fifth, the loan <note>original: "Commodatum"; a loan for use where the specific item is to be returned</note> of clothing, weapons, pack animals, silver and gold vessels for food and drink, and other household furniture can be proven by witnesses, even if they exceed the amount of thirty thousand reais. This is held in the same place, section 15.

Sixth, a public deed is not necessary to prove payments of *sisas* <note>original: "sysis"; a traditional Portuguese tax on the sale of goods</note> and other taxes, nor to prove purchases and sales made through brokers between foreigners and natives, nor between natives, if they are done through brokers specially deputized for that purpose. In these two cases, however, two witnesses and the broker himself are necessary for proof. Neither is a public deed necessary to prove those things which are handed over to be sold by town criers or by the women whom they call *adelas* <note>original: "adelas"; female second-hand dealers or resellers of small goods</note> in that kingdom; or things handed over to agents or other craftsmen to be sold. This is held in the same place, sections 16, 17, and 18.

Seventh, a public deed is not necessary to prove those things which are owed from a quasi-contract <note>An obligation that arises from an act that is not a formal agreement, but is treated like a contract by law</note>, such as when Peter owes Paul something because Paul usefully managed Peter’s business without any prior agreement between them. Likewise, it is not needed in the leasing and hiring of immovable property for a year, provided the price does not exceed the value of thirty thousand reais. This is held in the same place, sections 20 and 21.

When a contract cannot be proven according to what has been said so far except by a public deed, proof by witnesses is not admitted, even if a smaller sum is sought in court than the total amount which it was not permitted to seek. For example, if a movable item was sold for forty thousand reais, it is not permitted to seek thirty thousand or less by offering proof of the contract through witnesses. This is held in the cited place, the penultimate section.

If a simulated contract <note>A "sham" contract intended to hide the true nature of a deal</note> was celebrated by a public deed—for example, one in which usury was contained but hidden under the form of the document—then the simulation can be proven by witnesses. This is held in the same place, the last section.

Observe this last point regarding all these matters of Portuguese law mentioned so far: In cases where it was said that proof is not admitted except by public deed, it is very common to appeal to the King to grant permission that, notwithstanding that ordi-

<column-break/>

-nance, the matter may be proven by witnesses; and once that faculty is obtained, proof by witnesses is admitted. Read a long discussion concerning this entire Portuguese disposition in Álvaro Valasco's *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 7.

## Who May Enter Into Contracts.

# DISPUTATION 161.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A contract cannot be celebrated by one who lacks the use of reason.*
2 *When a minor and a spendthrift may contract, and when they may not.*
3 *A son under paternal authority who has reached puberty can contract regarding military property, or property treated as such.*
4 *Whether the alienation of adventitious property <note>Property a child acquires from someone other than the father, such as through a maternal inheritance</note> made by a son of age with the father's consent is valid. And what is the case in the Kingdom of Castile. number 6.*
5 *A son under paternal authority who has reached puberty is bound by every contract made by himself, even without the father's consent, except in a loan.*
7 *When religious <note>Members of religious orders under vows</note> are bound by their contracts, and when they are not.*
8 *When slaves are obligated by their contracts, and when they are not.*
9 *When a supreme Prince contracting with his subject remains obligated to him.*

1 We have explained contracts in general; it seems relevant now to speak in general about those who can celebrate them. Since the celebration of contracts is a human act, it is known that all those who lack the use of reason cannot celebrate them by themselves; such as an infant, a sleeping person, a drunkard, a madman, a frantic person, and others like them. Therefore, for a gift made to them to be valid, it must be accepted by another in their name.

2 Among the rest, those who are not prohibited can celebrate contracts. To what extent minors and spendthrifts <note>original: "prodigi"; people legally restricted from handling their own money due to extreme wastefulness</note> can or cannot celebrate them was stated in Disputation 224, in conjunction with what was said from Disputation 220.

3 A son under paternal authority <note>original: "filius familias"</note>, if he has reached puberty, can celebrate contracts regarding military property <note>original: "bona castrensia"; property or wages earned through military service</note>, or property treated as such; this is because he has free administration of those goods, no differently than if he were entirely his own master; but not if he is below the age of puberty, as we showed in both Disputation 230 and 231.

4 <margin>Question.</margin> Regarding adventitious property <note>Property coming to the son from outside the father’s estate</note>, when the father has the administration and the use of the profits of it, the doctors of law agree that if the son is over twenty-five years old, the sale he makes of those goods with the father's consent is valid, and invalid if he does it without that consent, as was said in Disputation 228 regarding the fourth effect of paternal power. They doubt, however, <margin>The opinion of some.</margin> whether if he has reached puberty but is not yet twenty-five, the sale of the same goods made with the father's consent is valid.

<meta>This page continues a legal and theological discussion regarding the capacity of individuals to enter into contracts, specifically focusing on the rights of a "son under paternal power" (filius familias) to manage and sell property with or without his father's consent.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 261

<margin>Their argument.</margin>
Antonio da Butrio, Johannes de Imola, and many other interpreters of Canon Law—citing the chapter *Constitutus* regarding the legal restoration of rights—argue from that text that such a contract is not valid. For in that text, it is recorded that a father, who held certain property in common with his two sons (who were minors still under his legal authority), sold that property. To ensure the contract was firm, he emancipated the sons <note>Legal release from the father's absolute authority, known as *patria potestas*</note> and had them consent to the contract after their emancipation. This was done as if their consent would have been insufficient unless they were first emancipated and left paternal power, even if the father’s authority and will were present. Faber <note>Johannes Faber, a 14th-century jurist</note> holds the same opinion in his commentary on the *Institutes* regarding useless stipulations, as do several other interpreters of Civil Law <note>original: "iuris Caesarei"</note> regarding the laws on property belonging to children.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
Although this text clearly suggests—by arguing from the opposite sense—that sons under paternal power *can* alienate <note>To transfer ownership of property</note> their <term>adventitious property</term> <note>Property acquired by the son from sources other than the father, such as a mother's inheritance</note> with the will and consent of the father, the cited authors respond that this should only be understood to apply to sons who are over twenty-five years of age. They confirm this opinion from the end of the section on "the ward" in the *Institutes*, where it is held that a child near the age of puberty cannot bind himself to anyone, nor even less alienate his property, even with the authority and consent of his father. The same reasoning applies to a youth who has reached puberty but is still under paternal power and has not yet completed his twenty-fifth year.

<margin>The true contrary opinion.</margin>
The common interpretation of the Civil Law maintains the contrary opinion, both elsewhere and in the laws regarding children's property. This is the view of the "Gloss" <note>The standard medieval commentary on Roman law</note>, Paulus de Castro, and Bartolus, who approves of that same gloss. This is the view we must undoubtedly embrace. It is clearly gathered from the text that permits a son under paternal power to alienate adventitious property with his father's consent, let alone bind himself to others regarding it. To restrict that text only to sons over twenty-five years of age is an arbitrary interpretation; the text itself clearly suggests the opposite. It states that sons are prohibited from alienating adventitious property (of which the father has the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</note>) without the father's consent in order to "restrain youthful heat," lest they later suffer a sad outcome. Such a justification does not aptly apply to those over twenty-five.

Regarding children under the age of puberty, however, it is expressly held that they cannot alienate any of their property or bind themselves to another even with the father’s consent and authority. Although a child under puberty can bind himself civilly to another with the authority of a <term>curator</term> <note>A court-appointed guardian for a minor</note>, he is denied the ability to do so by his father’s authority. As the Gloss says, this is because a tutor is legally liable to the ward if he provides authority poorly; however, because of "paternal reverence," a father is not held liable to his young son even if he provides authority poorly.

Observe, however, that when we say a son who has reached puberty can alienate and bind his adventitious property with his father's consent, this must be understood with the condition that if the property is "immovable" (such as land or buildings), a judge's decree must be added. Generally, the alienation or binding

<column-break/>

of a minor's immovable property without a judge's decree is invalid, as is clear from the laws concerning the estates of minors and the common opinion of the doctors of law. Furthermore, a son under paternal power cannot give away even his "legitimate portion" <note>The minimum share of an inheritance guaranteed by law to a child</note>, even with the father's consent and authority; specific laws render such an act void, as was said in Disputation 149. If a minor son were found to be harmed by the alienation or binding of his property done with his father's consent, he would be granted the benefit of <term>restitutio in integrum</term> <note>A legal remedy where a contract is cancelled and the parties are restored to their original positions</note>.

<margin>To the argument.</margin>
Regarding the chapter *Constitutus*, it must be said that perhaps one of the sons was under the age of puberty. His consent was therefore void while he was under paternal power, even if the father's authority were added. For that reason, he was emancipated so that the father could remain his tutor and provide authority, which, combined with a judge's decree, would make the contract valid. This is why the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> commands in that same text to check whether the full solemnity required by law was observed for the contract to be valid; if it was not, the contract should be declared void. If it was observed, the minors should be helped through the benefit of legal restoration.

It should then be said that if both sons were past puberty at the time of the contract, the father emancipated them because of the conflicting legal opinions on whether a contract made by a son under paternal power (but who is still a minor) is valid with the father's consent. Since a judge must more easily consent to the alienation of immovable property when a curator is involved, and the property sold by the father in that chapter was immovable, emancipation was the safer path.

The confirmation from the section on "the ward" is of no weight. For in that case, the restriction is made to a child under puberty because, due to their weak age, it is not expedient to allow them to be bound even with the father's consent.

Just as a son is granted the right to alienate and manage adventitious property (where the father usually has the usufruct and administration) with the father's consent, so too is he granted the right to alienate and bind property without express consent when he has "free administration" of it. This occurs either because he lives far from his father, or because the father has left him the usufruct and total management of the goods. The same would apply to <term>profectitious property</term> <note>Property given to the son by the father specifically for business or trade</note> if he were set up by the father to trade with it; by that very act, the father is deemed to consent and grant him the faculty to do business with such goods. Read what we have said about all these matters in Disputation 228 regarding the first and fourth effects of paternal power, and Disputations 230, 231, and 232. To these, add what we said in Disputation 138 regarding a son who is a member of the clergy. Finally, observe that although alienations made by a son outside these scenarios are not valid unless they depend on the father's consent, a son who has reached puberty is nevertheless generally held liable for the contracts he makes, even if the father's implicit consent was not present. An action can be brought against the son, as is established in the *Institutes* and the laws on actions and obligations.

It concludes that while children under puberty are strictly limited, older sons can alienate property with paternal consent and a judge's decree for land, though they are generally personally liable for their contracts.</summary>

obligations, as found in the law *tam ex contractibus* (regarding jurisdictions) and the law *filiorum* (regarding deposits). Nevertheless, if the son is a minor and is found to have been harmed by the contract, he is granted the benefit of <term>restitution in integrum</term> <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum"; a legal remedy restoring a person to their original position before a contract or loss</note>, just like other minors who are not under paternal power, as is clear from the law *sed utrum* (regarding minors). Therefore, what was said in Disputation 224 regarding contracts entered into by youths who have reached puberty but lack parents and guardians should be understood similarly for those who remain under paternal power.

Regarding <term>loans</term> <note>original: "mutuo"</note>, however, if a loan is made to a son under power without his father’s consent, legal action is generally not granted against him. This will be discussed in the section on loans, and it arises from the benefit of the <term>Macedonian Senate Decree</term> <note>original: "senatus consulti Maced."; a Roman law that prohibited lending money to sons under paternal power to protect fathers and discourage sons from wishing for their fathers' deaths</note>.

<margin>6</margin> In the **Kingdom of Castile**, under Law 22, Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, it is prohibited for a son under power (whether an adult or a minor) and any minor under a tutor or curator to buy anything on credit by themselves or through an intermediary without the authority of their father or guardian. It is also forbidden for anyone to sell to them on credit. Otherwise, the contract is rendered null and ineffective, even if confirmed by an oath, so that nothing can be demanded from it at any time, even from the guarantors. Heavy penalties are also established for those who enter into such contracts using an oath. Because these rules are established for the common good and as a just penalty for the sellers, I believe that in the **court of conscience**, nothing is owed from such contracts—even by the guarantors. One may, in good conscience and in the secular courts, defend oneself against creditors using the exception provided by that law, which established this as a just punishment for the sellers. Indeed, the legislator was able to establish this justly in the sense explained earlier; one must not think he intended otherwise, or else that law would provide an occasion for sin, which is not to be presumed of a Christian legislator in this instance.

<margin>7</margin> Concerning **religious persons** <note>members of religious orders, such as monks or friars</note> and the extent to which they can enter into contracts—whether they live under obedience, dwell far from their superiors, or are present with them, and whether they are deputized for the task or not, as well as when they have been expelled from their order or live in the secular world with a dispensation—this was discussed in Disputation 140.

<margin>8</margin> Regarding the **contracts of slaves** (as was partly stated in Disputation 140), whether they contract with their masters or with others, no **civil obligation** arises. Consequently, no legal action is granted to them or against them in the secular courts, even after they have attained the state of freedom. This is held in the law *in personam* and the law *quod attinet* (on the rules of law).

An exception is made when a slave has promised money to his master in exchange for freedom. In that case, once freedom is granted, legal action is allowed against the freed person to pay the money promised while he was still a slave. This is held in the law *promissa* (on whether a slave's own act counts).

In the same way, if there was an agreement between a master and slave that the master would manumit him for a certain sum of money, and the master accepted the money from the slave, 

<column-break/>

the slave is granted legal action against the master to compel his manumission, as was stated at the end of Disputation 38.

Furthermore, although a civil obligation does not arise from a slave's contract, a **natural obligation** <note>A moral or conscientious duty that may not be enforceable by a lawsuit but has other legal effects</note> does arise. By this obligation, the slave is bound in the court of conscience to stand by the contract, fulfilling it as much as he can, either while he remains a slave or after he becomes free. Likewise, the master or anyone else who entered into a contract with him is bound to stand by and fulfill it, provided the slave also wishes to fulfill his part, if the contract is <term>onerous</term> <note>A contract where both parties provide something of value to the other</note>.

This is held in the laws *quod attinet* and *si quod dominus* (on the recovery of undue payments). From this natural obligation, it follows that if a master owed a slave something and paid it after the slave was freed, the master is not granted the right to sue for its return, because he paid what he owed by natural obligation. Likewise, if someone pays on behalf of a slave, or if the slave himself pays after being freed, the money cannot be reclaimed. Furthermore, a guarantor for a slave is bound to pay, and a pledge given for him remains obligated, whether someone else gave it or the slave gave it from his <term>peculium</term> <note>original: "peculio"; the personal property or savings a slave or son was allowed to manage as their own</note> which he was administering. See all these points in the law *naturaliter*. See also our discussion in Disputation 38 and Antonio Gómez in *Various Resolutions*.

<margin>9</margin> Whether, however, if a **supreme prince** enters into a contract with his subject, he remains obligated to him. All agree that he remains obligated. But the question is whether that obligation is only **natural** or also **civil**. The more common opinion asserts it is only natural, though it has the force of a civil one. They are led to this because civil obligation originates from positive civil law, from which such a prince is exempt.

However, I believe it must be said, along with Antonio Gómez and a few others cited by him and Padilla, that the prince is also **civilly obligated**. Firstly, because by the very fact that the prince enters into a contract with his subject, he is deemed to submit and obligate himself so that a civil action can be brought against him and he can be judged in the secular court. Just as the subject, by virtue of the same contract, remains obligated to him; otherwise, no one would wish to contract with the prince.

Furthermore, although his own ministers cannot coerce and compel him to fulfill the contract if he resists, if he were to resist against justice, he would be a tyrant in that matter. The entire commonwealth could then coerce and compel him to stand by his contracts—provided, however, that far greater evils are not feared from such coercion; for in that case, it would be better to endure that tyranny.

Regarding the extent to which a **wife** can or cannot enter into contracts without her husband’s consent, this will be more conveniently noted in Disputations 257 and 343, and when the contract of partnership between spouses is discussed.

Molina argues that even a supreme ruler is civilly bound by his contracts to maintain the integrity of commerce and avoid tyranny.</summary>

### A promise differs from a resolution: regarding the two types of promises, and also the virtues of truth and fidelity.

->DISPUTATION 262<-

->SUMMARY<-

1. How a resolution is distinguished from a promise.
2. Two types of promises.
3. The virtue of truth, or what truthfulness is.
4. Fidelity, which is the virtue and foundation of justice; from where it gets its name.
5. Obligation from fidelity is broader than obligation from justice.
6. Fidelity is a distinct virtue from the virtue of Truth.
7. How the obligation from the virtue of fidelity differs from the obligation to tell the truth.
8. When the violation of a promise is not by its nature a mortal sin, such that the one who promised cannot be compelled.
9. A promise binding only by moral decency, if confirmed by an oath, produces a legal action even in civil law.
10. A promise binding only by moral decency, if its violation is destructive to the other party, binds under pain of mortal sin.
11. A simple promise based on justice does not always bind under pain of mortal sin.
12. An accepted promise, in the case where it is a <term>naked pact</term> <note>original: "pactum nudum"; an agreement that is not legally enforceable because it lacks specific formalities or consideration</note>, which by privilege of law is granted to produce a civil obligation.

---

<margin>1</margin> We must next discuss contracts in particular, and we should begin with <term>donation</term> <note>original: "donatione"; the act of giving a gift</note>, which is a lucrative contract. Because a donation usually begins with a promise, and before the delivery of the item it is neither considered perfect nor categorized as a named contract (as explained in Disputation 152 and the two following), we must begin with the gratuitous promise, including under that category the promise that arises from gratitude. Although the order of origins required that, before the external promise, we should consider whether an obligation arises from a purely internal promise, this will be done more conveniently if we first examine how much force an external promise has to create an obligation before it is accepted; after this has been explained, we will provide the former.

<margin>1</margin> Above all, it must be observed that it is one thing to have a <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "propositum"</note>—that is, a deliberate and firm will to do something for the benefit of another—and to express this with a future-tense verb by saying, "I will do this," or "I will give you this or that"; and quite another for someone, out of their own liberality, to bind themselves by their own will to do something, and to express this with a future-tense verb by saying, "I promise I will do," or "I will give this to you," or "on such a day I will give you this," or "for your sake I will do this or that." For the first is not a promise properly speaking, nor does it induce any obligation to fulfill it, as is manifest of itself and established from the chapter <italic>literaturam</italic> regarding vows and the redemption of vows. **St. Thomas [Aquinas]** affirms this in **2.2. question 88, article 1**, distinguishing a resolution from a

<column-break/>

vow—that is, from a promise made to God—as something pre-required for a vow. Navarro in his <italic>Manual</italic>, chapter 12, number 26, and others generally agree. However, the <term>gloss</term> <note>a standard legal commentary written in the margins of law books</note> there in the chapter <italic>literaturam</italic> wrongly explains that text as if it were talking about a "naked pact"; whereas the text only speaks about a resolution to enter a religious order, which is defined as inducing no obligation because it did not reach the level of a promise. The second, however, is a promise, and if it is accepted and the other necessary circumstances are present (which will be discussed in their place), it always induces an obligation. Therefore, when words are ambiguous—whether they signify only a resolution or truly a promise—one must refer to the mind of the speaker to see what they intended to signify. This is especially true in these gratuitous matters, since no one is bound further than they intended to bind themselves.

<margin>2</margin> Next, it must be observed that there are certain promises that only induce an obligation to fulfill what was promised out of a certain <term>moral decency</term> <note>original: "honestate morali"; acting according to what is virtuous and fitting for a person of integrity</note>, but not out of justice; while others induce an obligation out of justice as well. To understand this better, observe: just as eating moderately is an external act of the moral virtue of temperance,

<margin>3</margin> so too is uttering words consistent with the mind an external act of moral Truth, the opposite vice of which is lying. For right reason prescribes that words uttered should be consistent with the mind, and that the will is held to command those words that are not dissonant with the mind. Furthermore, the virtue of this kind that resides in the will is called "Truth" by **Aristotle in the 2nd book of Ethics, chapter 7**, and by **St. Thomas** below in **question 109**, taking the name of the virtue from the truth of the act commanded by it. Thus, the word "truth" is used equivocally for the moral virtue explained here, and for the truth that ought to be in the act commanded by it (or believed to be in it by the speaker), so that it is an external act of that moral virtue. **St. Thomas, in the place cited**, says this virtue can also be called "Veracity." Just as uttering words consistent with the mind is an act of moral virtue, so also is matching deeds to promises, or to agreements made with someone, an act of moral virtue, since right reason similarly requires this.

<margin>4</margin> The virtue that commands such an act is called "Fidelity" <note>original: "fides"</note> by **Cicero in the 1st book of On Duties**; and as he says, it is named from <italic>fit</italic> [it is done] and <italic>dicitur</italic> [it is said], as if through it, what was said is done <note>original: "quasi per eam fiat quod dictum est"; a traditional Latin etymology linking 'fides' (faith/fidelity) to 'fiat' (let it be done) and 'dictum' (what is said)</note>. This seems to be the primary use of this word among many that we explained at the beginning of this section. **Cicero** defines it there as the "constancy and truth of things said and agreed upon." For it is established as true and rendered constant when what was said and agreed upon is actually done. **Cicero** adds that this fidelity is the "foundation of justice." Note here that he did not say it <italic>is</italic> justice itself, but the base and foundation of justice.

<margin>5</margin> For obligation from fidelity extends more widely than obligation from justice. And when justice is overturned because fidelity is not kept, and pacts and agreements are not fulfilled, two vices are committed: one of injustice, which is by its nature a mortal sin, insofar as one does not render to a neighbor what is owed to them by justice given the pact and agreement; the other of infidelity, which is by its nature a venial sin (as we shall say), insofar as what was honorably said and agreed upon is not fulfilled in deed, but is made false. Therefore, the opinion of **Cajetan** (on question 13, article 1) must be rejected, where he asserts that when someone is bound by contract to something out of justice that was promised and agreed upon, justice...

<meta>This page continues Disputation 262, specifically addressing the distinction between the virtue of truthfulness (telling the truth in the moment) and the virtue of fidelity (fulfilling a promise over time). # Luis de Molina, On Contracts

justice itself is the virtue of fidelity <note>original: "fidei virtutem"</note>, by which one stands by their words and agreements. However, the formal reason for the virtue of fidelity exists only when someone is bound solely by moral decency, in the manner already explained. Regarding the lack of fidelity, we should understand that passage from **Ecclesiastes 5: If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it: for an unfaithful promise (that is, one not fulfilled in action) and a foolish one is displeasing to God.** <note>original: "Si quid vouisti Deo, ne moreris reddere: displicet. n. Deo infidelis (quæ scilicet opere non impletur) & stulta promissio."</note>

**Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> below, in Question 113, Article 1, considers in a point of doubt whether the specific virtue of fidelity is distinct in kind from the moral virtue of truth, or truthfulness, even when fully explained. He judges them to be of the same kind; for, he says, it seems to be of the same character for a person to speak the truth and to make those words, promises, and agreements come true by fulfilling them in action.

<margin>6</margin>
I think, however, that these are distinct virtues in kind. First, because it is one thing to speak the truth—to which one is bound in all assertions, promises, and agreements at the moment they are uttered—and it is another thing to fulfill in action what was promised or agreed upon with one's neighbor. Moral virtues are distinguished into kinds based on their objects. Furthermore, the obligations arising from these two explained virtues are of different characters.

<margin>7</margin>
The obligation arising from the virtue of fidelity to fulfill a promise and to make good on a word or agreement is in relation to the person to whom the promise was made or with whom the agreement was struck. For that reason, if that person releases the promisor, the promisor is no longer bound to fulfill the promise or agreement. But the obligation to speak the truth—that is, to speak according to what is in one's mind, both in assertions and in promises or agreements—cannot be removed by the person to whom we are speaking.

If, while someone is promising, they have no intention of fulfilling it, they sin in two ways. First, because they are lying by saying the opposite of what is in their mind, which is a common fault in both false assertions and false promises. Second, because they have a purpose of not fulfilling the promise in the future, even though they are bound by the virtue of fidelity by the very fact that they intended to promise, despite the simultaneous hidden purpose of not fulfilling it. Our opinion is confirmed by the fact that someone who merely intends to give Peter a hundred [coins] and asserts he will give them, is bound to speak the truth—that is, to actually have the intention of giving at that time—but he is not later bound to make his word true by fulfilling the purpose. This is because a mere purpose does not give rise to that other distinct obligation of a different character toward another person which results from a promise.

<margin>8</margin>
When someone intends only to promise and bind themselves out of moral and political decency, as explained—which is what happens most often—infidelity or the violation of a promise without any reasonable cause is not, by its nature, a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>a grave sin that severs one's relationship with God</note>, but a <term>venial sin</term> <note>a lesser sin that does not sever the relationship with God</note>, as Cajetan rightly affirms below in Question 113, Article 1. Nor can the one who promised be compelled by public authority to fulfill what he promised, as Cajetan also rightly adds in the same place. Much less is anyone bound to fulfill a mere resolution to do something,

<column-break/>

which he signified with words about the future in the manner explained above. For these reasons, Cajetan in Question 88, Article 1, rightly asserts that the simple promises of men are little esteemed today, according to the proverb: *Anyone can be rich in promises.* <note>original: "Pollicitis diues quilibet esse potest"; a quote from Ovid's Ars Amatoria.</note>

<margin>9</margin>
Note, however, that if someone confirms a promise with an oath—even one binding only by moral decency—then the person to whom it was made acquires a corresponding true right that it be fulfilled for him. From such a promise, a civil legal action is granted, not only by canon law but also by civil law, according to what was said in Disputation 150 and what will be said at the end of the following disputation.

It has been said that a promise based on moral decency alone does not bind, by its nature, under pain of mortal sin. Just as a lie is by its nature only a venial sin, yet if it is destructive to one's neighbor it becomes a mortal sin when the harm it inflicts is not slight, so too is the "infidelity" we are discussing. If it is notably destructive to the one to whom something was promised, it will be a mortal sin, even if the one who promised did not intend to bind himself out of strict justice.

<margin>10</margin>
For instance, if someone promised they would bring reinforcements to another in war, and for that reason the other person did not make other arrangements for their affairs, the promisor would sin mortally if he lied while promising and did not intend to help, because that lie would be destructive. Likewise, if after making the same promise with the intention of fulfilling it, he failed to keep his word through his own fault, he would sin mortally, because that infidelity would similarly be very destructive to the person to whom the promise was made. The same applies if a doctor or a lawyer promised their labor to someone whose life or goods were in danger unless they helped; or regarding someone to whom a secret of some importance was committed after they gave their word not to reveal it. All of these are examples from Cajetan, Question 113.

Finally, observe regarding a promise by which someone intends to bind themselves only out of political and moral decency: since the resulting obligation is toward another, but is not based on justice but only on moral decency, it follows that the virtue of fidelity by which one is bound is a virtue annexed to justice (insofar as it is toward another), yet it falls short of the perfect definition of justice (insofar as what is owed is owed only out of moral decency).

Cajetan, in the places cited where he speaks of a simple promise—that is, one confirmed neither by oath nor by formal <term>stipulation</term> <note>a formal legal contract in Roman law</note>, nor made in exchange for something else—seems to describe no simple promise that binds out of justice. Hence he says absolutely that it binds only out of moral decency and under pain of venial sin by its nature. On the contrary, **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), another influential Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> in Book 7 *On Justice*, Question 2, Article 1, asserts without distinction against Cajetan that a simple promise binds out of justice, and for that reason, not fulfilling it is by its nature a mortal sin.

<margin>11</margin>
We, however, walk a middle path. For we judge it to be false that every simple promise binds out of justice, and therefore we think it must be conceded with Cajetan that there are promises...

Molina mediates between Cajetan and Soto, discussing when breaking a promise constitutes a mortal versus a venial sin based on the potential harm caused.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the virtue of fidelity and how it transitions into the realm of legal and moral obligation. It specifically concludes the discussion on whether a "simple promise" creates a debt of justice or merely a moral duty, then moves into Disputation 263 regarding the revocation of promises.</meta>

obligation, which binds only out of moral and political decency, and that this type is more frequent among men than the kind which binds out of justice.

Nevertheless, we believe that there is such a thing as a simple promise <note>A promise made without the formal legal ceremonies usually required to make it enforceable in a court of law.</note> that binds out of justice, and thus, by its very nature, carries the weight of a mortal sin <note>original: "sub culpa lethali"; a serious moral failing that separates the soul from God.</note>; indeed, its transgression creates an obligation to make restitution, not only for any subsequent damages but for the promised item itself. This is because the item is owed out of justice by the very fact that it was promised. Furthermore, in the external forum <note>The public legal system or "civil court," as opposed to the "internal forum" of private conscience.</note>, a legal action is granted based on such a promise once it has been accepted. The first part of our opinion, in which we agree with **Cajetan** and disagree with **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican theologian who argued that simple promises do not create a strict debt of justice.</note>, is clear from what has been said so far.

<margin>12</margin>
The second part, however, in which we agree with **Soto**, is proven by the fact that—as shown in Disputation 255—a promise of this kind, once accepted, is a "bare pact" <note>term: <term>pactum nudum</term>—A legal agreement that lacks the specific formalities or "clothing" of a contract, which under older Roman law would not have been enforceable.</note> to which the privilege of law has been granted so that a civil obligation arises from it. Thus, a legal action is granted both to the recipient and to their heirs against the one who made the gratuitous promise and their heirs. <note>original: "l. si quis argentum. §. vltimo. C. de donatio." — refers to the Code of Justinian, book on donations.</note> This is also supported by the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, at the beginning.

Both parts of our opinion are confirmed because, since a gratuitous promise proceeds solely from the liberality of the promiser, it is certainly within their power to bind themselves either only out of moral decency or to entirely of their own will constitute themselves a debtor of the promised thing. Just as the liberal delivery of a thing is a sufficient title for transferring ownership, so too a liberal promise of a thing can be a sufficient title for it to be owed out of justice—if the promiser intends to bind themselves that far. For pacts and contracts are free while they are being made; but after they are made, they bind out of justice, either from the nature of the thing itself or from the intention of the promiser, especially if the contract is entirely gratuitous and beneficial to the recipient.

Therefore, when someone intends to make themselves a debtor to another person through a gratuitous promise—just as one who vows chastity, poverty, obedience, or anything else to God intends to make themselves a debtor to God—they are deemed to have intended to bind themselves to that person out of justice. However, when they do not intend to take such a heavy burden upon themselves, they should only be thought to have intended to bind themselves out of moral decency.

Furthermore, in the forum of conscience <note>The internal moral realm where a person stands before God.</note>, one must abide by the intention of the one who promised, because it depends solely on their will how far they wished to make themselves a debtor. But in the external forum <note>The public court of law.</note>, this must be judged by conjectures, considering all the surrounding circumstances. If someone says in a public document or a signed handwritten note, "I promise I will give this or that," or "I bind myself to pay this," they are deemed to have intended to bind themselves out of justice, and not out of moral decency alone.

### Whether a promise can be freely revoked before acceptance, and whether this arises from its nature or from positive law.

16 *The three types of acceptance of a promise.*
17 *How a promise is distinguished from a mere "intent to promise," gathered from the form of the words.*
18 *Whether an unaccepted donation to pious causes <note>Charitable or religious works.</note> is valid.*
19 *An action under Canon and Civil Law is granted from an unaccepted promise if it was confirmed by an oath.*
*And what in Portugal and the Kingdom of Castile? number 20.*

The doctors <note>Learned legal and theological scholars.</note> agree that a promise, before it is accepted and thus before it passes into a pact, regularly produces neither a civil obligation nor a legal action in the secular court. This is evident from various laws, including the law on pacts and "bare promises" <note>original: "nuda pollicitatio"; a promise without a formal agreement.</note> in the Digests of Roman Law. The law does not always permit someone to be urged to fulfill what they merely promised. From this arises the rule that a promise or donation can be revoked at the donor's whim before it is accepted, as held in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, and gathered from other legal authorities.

<margin>3</margin>
From this, it also follows that if someone sent a thing as a gift through their servant or someone else to a third party, and before that third party accepted the donation—either because they were unaware of it or for any other reason—the person who was sending the gift died, the donation is rendered void. Consequently, that item must be restored to the heirs of the donor, rather than to the intended recipient. This is expressly held in Law 2, section "but, and if someone," joined with the glossary there in the Digest, *On Donations* <note>original: "ff. de don."; refers to the *Digest* or *Pandects* of Roman Law</note>. The common opinion of the doctors affirms this, which among others, Antonio Gómez records and follows (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 3). The reason is that since a mandate <note>term: <term>mandatum</term>—A legal instruction or authorization given to another to act on one's behalf.</note> regularly expires upon the death of the mandator <note>original: "morte mandantis"; the person giving the instruction.</note>, as is clear from the Law on Mandates in the Code and the section "rightly also" in the Institutes under the same title, that donation is considered tacitly revoked by that very fact before it is accepted by the recipient. Labeo <note>A famous Roman jurist.</note> agrees in the Digest, *On Donations*, adding that the same applies even if the item is sent to the recipient through the recipient's own servant; unless it is delivered to the servant with the intent that it immediately belongs to the recipient. For if the servant receives it in the name of the master and is among those types of persons who can accept in the place of the recipient (as will be discussed in the following disputation) and acquires it for the master, then such a donation cannot be expressly revoked, let alone revoked by the death of the donor. This is especially true since in that event, the servant does not take on the role of a mere messenger for the sender. This further follows from the law "If I," in the Digest, *On Donations*. From this, we must reject the opinion of Gregorio López (Law 23, title part 3, word "dying"), where he says, following Bartolus, that if money has already been counted out to a messenger, the mandate does not expire upon the death of the sender, but the messenger can deliver it to the one to whom it was sent by the deceased. This is contrary to the cited laws and the common opinion of the doctors, unless they understand it to refer to a messenger of the recipient who receives it in the sender's name.

<margin>4</margin>
I said that a mandate regularly expires upon the death of the mandator because this is understood in certain ways. First, if the matter is "entire" <note>Meaning the task has not yet begun or been significantly acted upon.</note>, or if the mandate is specifically about such a matter. Secondly, because if the mandate is for something the agent is to execute *after* the death of the mandator, it does not expire upon death, as the glossary on the cited Law on Mandates says and is held in the law "If I forbid," the final section in the Digest, *On Mandates*. Furthermore, if the mandate is for pious causes <note>term: <term>pias causas</term>—Charitable works, religious foundations, or aid to the poor.</note>, although the mandator may lawfully revoke it while they live, it is not considered revoked by their death. This is affirmed by Covarruvias (Volume 1, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 14, number 16), following the common opinion of the doctors. The same is more clearly proven in the law "If a father," at the beginning, in the Digest, *On Manumissions by Rod*; where a mandate in favor of liberty <note>The legal process of freeing a slave.</note> does not expire upon the death of the mandator. Therefore, if someone gave something to another to be delivered as alms, or to be spent on another pious cause, such a donation and mandate are not considered revoked by the death of the mandator, but must be spent on the very things for which they were delivered.

<margin>5</margin>
Antonio Gómez, at the cited number 3, along with the common opinion he records, says: If someone were appointed as a proxy <note>term: <term>procurator</term>—A person authorized to represent another in legal or business matters, possessing more formal authority than a simple messenger.</note> by another with the power of donating, and

<column-break/>

donated something before he and the recipient who had accepted the donation were aware that such power had been revoked—either expressly or tacitly by the death of the one who appointed the proxy—then a donation of this kind is valid. The reason is that there is a distinction between a simple messenger and a proxy: acts performed by a simple messenger are regularly invalid after the mandate has been revoked (even tacitly by the mandator's death), even if the messenger and the one with whom they are dealing are ignorant of the revocation. However, acts performed by a proxy before the revocation of power is known are valid. An exception is made in the final chapter, *On Proxies*, Book 6 <note>Refers to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a collection of canon law.</note>, when a marriage is celebrated by proxy. Because the essence of marriage is the consent of the principal party, if at the time the proxy celebrates the marriage the principal has revoked the power or changed their mind, such a marriage will be invalid, even if the revocation was unknown to the proxy and the other contracting party.

<margin>6</margin>
That acts performed by a proxy are valid while the revocation of power is unknown is held in the law "If I had mandated" and "Among the causes" in the Digest, *On Mandates*; and the law "Indeed to a proxy" at the beginning and section 1, in the Digest, *On Payments*; and many other laws which Antonio Gómez cites in that same place, and which the glossary on the final chapter *On Proxies*, Book 6, affirms. Observe, however, that when the execution by a simple messenger is not a donation but an "onerous contract" <note>A contract where both parties give and receive something of value, like a sale, rather than a gift.</note> with a third party, or if the messenger themselves has incurred expenses (even in delivering a donation), then even if the mandate was revoked by death or otherwise, if the messenger was ignorant of this while executing the mandate, they would have a legal action of mandate to be kept entirely harmless and to be reimbursed for expenses. This is held in the section "rightly also" in the Institutes, *On Mandates*, and at the end of the discussed number 58, section 2. Therefore, there is almost no difference between a proxy and a simple messenger, except in the case of a donation.

<margin>7</margin>
According to what has been said so far, I think it must be stated that if someone gave something to a servant or someone else to deliver as a gift to another, and that person unjustly usurped it for themselves, or unjustly delayed the delivery or the announcement of the donation to the recipient so they could accept it, and it happens that the sender dies in the meantime: then such a servant or intermediary is bound to a double restitution of that thing when the donation was not for pious causes. First, to the heirs of the giver, because the mandate was not fulfilled and expired with the death of the mandator; therefore, that item now belongs not to the recipient, but to the heirs of the donor. Second, to the intended recipient, whom the servant unjustly deprived of that benefit through usurpation or detention, which the recipient would have otherwise obtained.

This event is actually quite frequent in confessions and has been explained by no one. Certainly, I would advise Christian princes to pass a law decreeing that in donations, the mandate does not expire with the death of the mandator. For equity demands that the will of the deceased, which was meant to be put into execution...

At the beginning of this disputation, it was therefore said that a promise, before it is accepted, does not regularly produce either a civil obligation or a legal action, because occasionally a civil obligation and action do arise from a mere promise alone. This occurs, for example, when a promise is made to a city for repairs needed due to fire, earthquake, or some other disaster (Law: *Pactum*, Law: *Propter incendium*, and Law: *Ob causam* in the Digest, *On Promises* <note>original: "ff. de pollic."; referring to the *Digest* of Roman Law, Book 50, Title 12.</note>). Likewise, when it is made out of gratitude for an honor granted to the promisor by a city or the state. Likewise, when a work promised to a city has begun to be built, the promisor is compelled to finish it. Likewise, if someone promised a thing to a city and delivered it to the townspeople, even if it has not yet been accepted by the city, he is not allowed to reclaim it or revoke the promise; indeed, if he should seize it and take possession of it, the city is granted a legal action to reclaim it against him (Law: *Pactum*, and Law 1 in the Digest, *On Promises*). However, if someone delivers a thing to a third party to be given as a gift to another person who has not yet accepted it, he remains free to reclaim it from the one to whom he delivered it and to revoke the donation (as is clear in Law: *Absenti* in the Digest, *On Donations*, and Law: *Hunc ergo* in the Digest, *On Unauthorized Management*). <margin>The commentaries on the chapter *Scimus*, under the word *pollicitationem* (Question 12, Case 2), agree on these points, as does Covarrubias (Chapter *Quamuis pactum*, part 2, § 4, number 17) and Antonio Gómez (Volume: *Various Resolutions*, chapter 9, number 3), who says this is the common opinion.</margin>

Whether, under the law of the Kingdom of Castile, a civil obligation and legal action arise from a promise made to private individuals before it is accepted by them—and whether the promisor is free to revoke it and render it void—is a matter of debate † among the Castilian doctors. This is due to Law 3, title 8, book 3 of the *Ordenamiento*, which is Law 2, title 16, book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* (1567) was a major consolidation of Spanish laws.</note>, the words of which we recorded in Disputation 255. **Column 2:**

...rendered void in the meantime, while it has not been accepted by the recipient or another in his place, and that this is the practice in the courts. This is because it was not the intent of that law to revoke the common law insofar as it establishes that while a donation is not accepted, it can be revoked by the donor. Gregorio López is of this same opinion (Law 4, title 4, glossary 1, and Law 1, title 11, on the word <margin>*Gran pro.* part 5. He adds then that if it is clear from the words of the donation that the donor intended to bind himself—for example, because he promised not to revoke the gift, or because he confirmed it with an oath—then, by virtue of that law of Castile, it is irrevocable even before it is accepted. Law 1, title 11 seems to say the same if the document states that he "binds himself to deliver" this or that.</margin> "Great promise," part 5). Molina also embraces this same opinion (Book 4, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, number 6), and besides Covarrubias and Gregorio López, he cites Avendaño in its favor.

He proves it first: because that law speaks only of a "stipulation" <note>term: <term>stipulatio</term>—A formal verbal contract in Roman law involving a specific question and answer.</note> and a contract, and it should not be extended to a donation, which is not properly a contract.

Setting aside other things that could be answered, it is certain that the law speaks even of a "naked" or informal promise. For it says (as we recorded in Disputation 255): *It appearing that someone wished to bind himself to another by promise, or by contract, or in another manner, etc.* Here it mentions a "promise" in addition to a "contract," and adds universally, *or in another manner.*

Second, he proves it because the law says: *It appearing that someone wished to bind himself to another.* However, he who gives a gift does not intend to bind himself before the recipient is informed and accepts, according to certain laws that Molina cites.

One could respond that perhaps this is true when a donation begins with a delivery through a messenger—as when a donor sends or orders something to be given to a recipient without a preceding promise. It is different, however, when it begins with a promise, because a promise signifies an obligation to perform. Under the common law, an obligation does not arise from acceptance except as a condition; without that condition, by the arrangement of the common law, an obligation does not arise from a promise. But an obligation *does* arise from the promise itself, which by its nature signifies an obligation and by its own power produces one. Furthermore, although what Molina asserts might be true under the common law (which took away the binding force of a promise before it was accepted, for people do not intend to bind themselves more than the laws and customs of the place allow), it is not true given that law of Castile. That law both restored to a promise its full binding force and abolished the common law in many other respects. Finally, despite Molina’s arguments, the limitations that Gregorio López added to his opinion must undoubtedly be admitted.

Third, he proves it because, even if we say that the said law rejected the formality of the stipulation and reduced the matter to "canonical equity" (whereby a legal action arose from an informal agreement), it still cannot be said that the law excluded acceptance. Even in canon law, acceptance is necessary, and before it occurs, the donor can freely revoke the donation.

It must be said that since canon law has established nothing to the contrary regarding the necessity of acceptance...
