# Louis Molina, On Contracts #

**Column 1:**

...prescribed, in the ecclesiastical forum <note>The Church's legal jurisdiction, which dealt with matters of sin, sacraments, and clerical property.</note>, regarding the necessity of acceptance, one must abide by the arrangement of civil law, as we shall soon say. However, the law of Castile has clearly corrected the common law <note>original: "ius commune"; the traditional body of Roman and Canon law used across Europe.</note> in that area. For that reason, a certain promise is valid in the Kingdom of Castile which is not valid under civil or canon law. This is something Gregory Lopez must admit within a certain limitation he adds.

The two other reasons Molina adds have no force, and for that reason, I neither report nor resolve them.

Based on this, although I once leaned toward the opinion of Covarruvias, I now incline more toward the opinion of others, even if the promise—whether made in writing or by word—is not confirmed by an oath or a promise not to revoke it. I am led to this because that law clearly signifies it; whenever it mentions a "contract," the words *or obligation* <note>original: "o obligacion"; Spanish legal terminology embedded in the Latin text.</note> are added, which also includes the obligation arising from a similar promise or any other source, all of which are discussed at the beginning of that law. As for what Covarruvias reports about practice, others do not teach it; rather, the others, like Covarruvias himself, debate the question as a matter that is very much in doubt in the courts. At the very least, nothing was so accepted and firm that it would be wrong to embrace the contrary. Furthermore, legal experts can not unfairly be faulted for trying to drag the laws of particular kingdoms more than is just toward the arrangements of the common law.

<margin>Question</margin>
**10** It is a matter of doubt whether † under canon law a legal action <note>The right to sue or demand performance in court.</note> is granted based on a promise before it is accepted.
<margin>Panormitanus's basis.</margin>
Panormitanus, in the chapter "Qualiter," in the section on Agreements, thinks it is granted. He is led by the words of that same chapter, which state: *Great care must be taken to ensure that what is promised is fulfilled in practice.* <note>original: "Studiosè agendũ est, vt ea, quæ promittuntur, opere compleantur."</note>
<margin>It is confirmed.</margin>
Fortunius is of the same opinion in the first law of the Digest, on Agreements; he confirms it from the chapter "Si tibi absenti," on Prebends, in the Sixth Book. There it is held that the grant of a benefice <note>An ecclesiastical office or position that provides an income, such as a parish or a cathedral post.</note> made by a Bishop to an absent person is valid, even if that person has not yet accepted it—indeed, even if he does not know it was made. The Bishop cannot revoke it or grant the benefice to another before the person to whom it was made refuses it. Furthermore, even if he does refuse it, if he repents of this refusal and accepts the grant before the Bishop grants it to someone else, the benefice belongs to him and not to the other to whom it was later granted.
<margin>Decision.</margin>
The contrary opinion—namely, that under canon law no action is granted from a promise before it is accepted—is affirmed by the same Panormitanus (contradicting himself) in the chapter "Cum inter universas," on Elections. Felinus also holds this in the first chapter on Agreements, and it is the common opinion of the doctors, which is followed by Covarruvias in the chapter "Quamvis pactum," Antonio Gomez in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, and Molina in book 4, *On Primogeniture*.

It will be worthwhile, however, to weigh at the same time whether a natural obligation <note>A moral or conscientious duty that binds the soul even if it cannot be strictly enforced in a civil court.</note> arises from a promise before it is accepted, such that the promisor is bound to fulfill the promise in the court of conscience and cannot lawfully revoke it. For the answer to the preceding doubt depends in large part on the definition of this doubt.

<column-break/>

Panormitanus and Felinus, in the places cited, think it does arise, and that the promisor cannot revoke such a promise in the court of conscience. The contrary is affirmed by Bartolus on the law "Si unus," on Agreements, with a certain annotation there; Covarruvias; and Antonio Gomez. Namely, they believe that a natural obligation (specifically a complete one) does not arise, and the promisor can revoke the promise before it is accepted with a safe conscience. This opinion is pleasing, as it is entirely linked to the view that under canon law no legal action is granted from a promise before it is accepted, as the common opinion of the legal experts affirms. The reason for both opinions is this: the civil law, for the benefit of the state and to remove moral scrupulosity and reduce lawsuits, was able to establish that a promise and a gift, before it was accepted, would have no force at all to bind the giver. Instead, it would be entirely up to him to revoke the promise and gift at his whim. It clearly established this in the laws cited above. Therefore, since nothing is found enacted to the contrary in canon law—and civil laws have force in the Church’s forum when nothing to the contrary is defined in canon law—it follows that under canon law, one should neither say that a legal action is granted, nor that a natural obligation arises from a promise or gift before it is accepted. Rather, the giver can freely revoke it.

<margin>To Panormitanus's basis.</margin>
Regarding the chapter "Qualiter," on Agreements, on which Panormitanus relied, it must be said that the discussion there concerns an *accepted* promise; this is more evident from the 8th book of the Letters of Blessed Gregory, Letter 38, from which that chapter was taken.
<margin>To the condition.</margin>
Regarding the chapter "Si tibi absenti," it must be said with Covarruvias that the grant of a benefice is not a gift, but the execution of a duty which a Bishop is bound to perform by his office. Therefore, this specific arrangement of canon law has immediate force and cannot be revoked by the Bishop. Just as canon law rightly established this regarding grants of benefices, it could have established the opposite for some reasonable cause—namely, that when a Bishop grants a benefice at his discretion, he could revoke it while the grant was not yet accepted, and grant it to someone who appeared more worthy and fit. The fact that the benefice is not the property of the Bishop, but of the Church, and that the Bishop acts only as a minister and dispenser, would be no obstacle.

<margin>Question</margin>
**12** There is a doubt whether † the fact that a promise does not produce a natural obligation before it is accepted—meaning the promisor is free to revoke it—stems from the very nature of the matter (because a promise, under natural law <note>The universal moral principles perceived by reason, independent of man-made statutes.</note> alone and excluding all man-made law, does not bind), or whether it arises from positive law <note>original: "iure positivo"; specific laws enacted by human authorities like the state or church.</note>, which established this for the common good and granted free revocation to the promisor without first asking the recipient if he wished to accept.

There are few who speak of this matter, because Sotus's opinion on the practice does not make it very important to know this. Sotus, in book 3, On...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 263. Page 27 #

**Column 1:**

...on justice, question 5, article 3. Regarding a donation made to an absent person before he knows of it or has accepted it, after he had previously argued that it creates an obligation before acceptance, he added: It is responded, however, that since a gift <note>original: "datio"</note> implies a relationship to the recipient, an obligation does not seem to arise before the other party accepts it; and therefore it can perhaps be revoked, even without any just cause.

However, if a donation is made solemnly before witnesses to an absent person, then one must abide by civil law. For I judge that without the consent of the recipient <note>original: "donatarius"</note> or a legitimate cause, the laws do not permit revocation; and if this is the case, conscience does not permit it either. Thus far Soto. Here you see him hesitant, judging that an obligation does not arise from a promise or donation before it is accepted, and therefore it can be revoked. He seems to speak from the very nature of a donation or promise that has not been accepted, since he is led by the reasoning that a donation implies a relationship to the recipient.

<margin>It is challenged.</margin>
However, although a donation, to be perfect and to pass into a "named contract" <note>A specific category of contracts in Roman law that have defined names and standard legal remedies.</note>, requires not only someone agreeing to it but also someone physically receiving it—as was shown in Disputation 254—it nevertheless does not imply a relationship to the recipient except <term>in name only</term> <note>original: "secundum dici"; a Scholastic logic term referring to something that is defined by its relation to another thing but does not necessarily require that other thing to exist or be present yet.</note>, as the practitioners of logic call it. Similarly, although a promise requires the acceptance of the person to whom it is made to take on the character of a formal pact, it does not imply a relationship to that person except in name only. Whether a promise or donation has been accepted or not, it always involves a relation in name to the one to whom it is made. For even a promise that has not been accepted is still made *to* someone, and a donation not yet accepted is likewise made *to* someone, just like those that have been accepted.

Furthermore, this matters little to the matter we are debating: namely, whether the promisor—having on his part the internal intent and the external word—remains obligated by the nature of the thing itself to hand over the object if the recipient (to whom he has obligated himself on his part) wishes to accept it. Because of this, is he bound to inform the person of the promise or donation made to him, so the person can see if he wishes to accept it?

Item: Soto seems to contradict himself in the words he subjoins. For from the fact that a donation or promise is made to an absent person before witnesses, surely neither a receiver nor an accepter is provided. Therefore, if the reasoning he relied on in his earlier words had any weight, even if the donation or promise were made before witnesses, it could be revoked before the absent person knew of it and accepted it.

Furthermore, if he is speaking of common law <note>original: "ius commune"</note>, it is clear from what has been said that witnesses do nothing to prevent a promisor or a donor from freely revoking the donation; but if he is speaking of the law of Castile because of the cited Law 3, and according to the opinion of Antonio Gomez and others whom we mentioned above, surely witnesses only serve as proof. In the same way, in that kingdom, he would be forced to fulfill the promise and donation in practice, even if witnesses were not present, provided he confessed the donation or promise with the intent of obligating himself. Therefore, Soto’s foundation and doctrine fall apart.

<margin>13th Decision, Question.</margin>
Nevertheless, the view that it is only from positive law <note>Law created by human legislators, as opposed to natural law.</note> that a promise, before it is accepted, does not

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

produce a natural obligation—rather than from the nature of the promise itself—is affirmed primarily by Covarruvias in the chapter "Although a Pact" <note>original: "quāuis pactum"</note>, part 2, paragraph 4, number 16, in the final words. Then, in the same opinion, are Panormitanus and Felinus, who, as we reported above, teach that even if civil law poses no obstacle, a natural obligation arises from a promise before it is accepted. Much more so Fortunius, who even grants a legal action <note>The right to sue in court.</note> based on it under Canon Law. In the same opinion are those who think that a natural obligation and an obligation in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>original: "forum conscientiae"; a person's moral standing before God rather than their standing in a human court of law.</note> arise from a purely internal promise, whom we shall mention in Disputation 265; for they will assert this much more strongly regarding a promise that has already been made external.

This opinion is first persuaded by what we showed above: namely, that under civil law, a legal action is granted for a promise made to a city or a republic, even if it has not been accepted. For if that promise, looking only at its nature, did not have the power to obligate, surely civil law would never have attributed that power to it above its own nature and force. For although the law has sometimes been accustomed, for the common good, to take away the binding force that certain contracts or acts have by their nature—such as from sales made by minors, or by Churches without the established formalities, or from the sale of dowry lands, or from donations made without <term>registration</term> <note>original: "insinuatio"; the official recording of a gift in public records, often required for gifts over a certain value.</note> beyond a certain sum, and many other cases—it has not, however, been accustomed to attribute to acts of alienation a force beyond their own nature.

This is especially true when the transfer is purely a gift <note>original: "gratuita"</note>, which is what we are now debating. For it is not fair that the state should despoil me of my goods by attributing a force beyond their nature to purely voluntary acts proceeding from me, so as to transfer the ownership or right of my goods to others. Nor perhaps can it do so, especially when no reasonable cause exists for it to happen.

<margin>14</margin>
Secondly, this view is persuaded by the cited Law 3 of Castile, which established that many promises are valid without acceptance. Neither Gregory Lopez nor Covarruvias denies this when it is clear from the promises that the promisor intended to obligate himself without acceptance. For it must not be said that the law intended to attribute force to such promises beyond their nature, nor perhaps could it achieve that, as was just said.

Thirdly, the same is persuaded by this: those who judge that an external promise, before it is accepted, does not have the power to obligate by its own nature, are led by the idea that before acceptance it does not have the character of a "pact," and before it takes on the character of a pact, it cannot have the power to obligate. But this foundation is easily overturned by the fact that when it is accepted by another on his behalf (because no representative <note>original: "procurator"</note> was appointed by the recipient for that purpose), it certainly does not take on the character of a pact until the consent and acceptance of the recipient are added. And yet, if a promise is accepted by a public notary, or by the son or servant of the recipient, without the recipient knowing or having previously given authority for it, by that very fact under civil law it begins to obligate the promisor—contingent upon the future acceptance and consent of the recipient—such that the promisor cannot revoke the promise...

# Ludovico Molina | On Contracts #

**Column 1:**

...for in that intermediate time, during which the recipient is not asked whether they hold the gift as ratified, as will be discussed in the following dispute: therefore, the fact that an external promise does not have the nature of a **pact** <note>In legal terms, a "pact" usually requires the consent of two parties, whereas a promise can be one-sided.</note> before it is accepted does not prevent it from having the power of obligating by its very nature at that time.

Fourthly, the same point is persuaded by the reasoning for which Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> in the cited place is more lenient. Namely, that in accepted gratuitous promises, the obligation of the promisor does not arise, from the nature of the thing, from the acceptance, but from the promise itself, by which out of liberality they wish to promise and obligate themselves to the recipient without any compensation or mutual obligation on the part of the recipient. Therefore, setting aside **positive law** <note>Human-made law, such as the statutes of a kingdom or the Roman legal tradition.</note>, which introduced acceptance for the common good as a condition without which it generally does not want the promisor to be obligated, the promise itself binds the giver under **natural law** <note>The moral law believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>. Just as positive law introduced the recipient's acceptance as a condition without which the promise would not bind, so in some cases it was able to waive it entirely, as in promises made to a city; in others, it was able to relax it in part, namely so that the acceptance of a public notary and others (whom we shall explain in the following dispute) would suffice; which it indeed did.

<margin>15</margin> And in the same way, the law of Castile was able to loosen the reins even further, namely so that no one's acceptance would be necessary whenever it was clear that the promisor intended to obligate himself. Indeed, a promise and a gift always depend on the recipient's acceptance from the nature of the thing to the extent that, if they do not accept it, the obligation which arose from their nature will be dissolved—just as, after a gift or promise has been accepted, the obligation contracted from it is dissolved whenever the recipient releases the obligation.

Nevertheless, what we contend is that the promise itself, by its own nature and setting aside whatever positive law may decree, has the power to obligate the promisor on their part before it is accepted. Thus, they are held to manifest the promise to the recipient so that, if the recipient wishes to accept it, the promisor may fulfill it, just as they were held to do on their part before the acceptance.

For that distinction which Soto <note>Dominic de Soto, mentioned on the previous page.</note> provides in the cited place and elsewhere between a gratuitous promise and a non-gratuitous or "respective" one (such as is seen in contracts) is greatly to be noted. A respective promise of a price in a sale, or of marrying someone in a betrothal, is by its own nature conditional—"if you also give back and promise in return." For that reason, before the promise of both is complete, neither binds, but it is lawful for either to freely withdraw from it. But a gratuitous promise is absolute, and therefore immediately obligates on the part of the promisor as far as the nature of the thing goes. Acceptance is not necessary by the nature of the thing, except so that it may be known that the recipient wishes to hold the promisor obligated, as the promisor is already obligated to them by the force of the spontaneous and gratuitous promise alone.

<margin>16</margin> There have not been wanting in these our times those who, in order to maintain that a promise before acceptance does not bind in any way by the nature of the thing, devised a triple

<column-break/>

kind of acceptance. One, by which the recipient himself would accept. A second, by which another would accept in his place and name. And a third, by which, with no specific human accepting, the acceptance would be made by the prince or legislator through the law itself, by the very fact that the law decrees that a certain promise has the force of obliging without anyone’s acceptance.

It is, however, a fiction to assert that legislators thought a promise does not have the power of obligating by its nature without acceptance, and that when they decreed that certain promises should bind without acceptance, they intended to accept those promises through that law in place of the recipients, and thus attributed the power of obliging to them. For there is no trace of this matter either in the laws or among any Doctor, Theologian, or Jurist.

Furthermore, those who affirm that a promise by its nature does not have the power of obliging without acceptance are led to this because without acceptance they do not achieve the status of a **pact**. But truly, from the fact that the law wants them to bind without acceptance, they certainly do not achieve the status of a pact until they are accepted by the recipient himself. Therefore, it is a fiction to recur to that triple kind of acceptance to maintain that, by the nature of the thing and without acceptance, a promise has no power to obligate.

<margin>17</margin> Lastly, I should advise that it is a far different thing for someone to promise something to another, or to resolve within himself in this manner and express it outwardly—"I give this thing to Peter"—and, from the will of giving, to send it to Peter or command that it be given to him. For the first two signify an obligation to give; but this third signifies only a purpose and a will to give, and a command that it be put into execution. Therefore, in this third event, by the nature of the thing and setting aside the disposition of common civil law, it seems within the donor's power to revoke the gift before the thing is delivered to Peter, because they have not yet bound themselves to complete the work, but all those things emanated from the will to give. Thus it happens that, with nothing in the law of Castile preventing it, it is within one's power in that kingdom to revoke a mandate, since there is nothing from which it appears that they wished to obligate themselves; for that law requires, so that one may be compelled to fulfill something, that it be clear they intended to obligate themselves. By the same reasoning, if in that kingdom such a donor dies before the agent completes the gift, then, since that mandate expires with the death of the mandator, that thing must be delivered to the heirs of the mandator, not to the recipient, according to the laws cited above.

<margin>18 Question</margin> A further doubt is whether a donation for **pious causes** <note>Donations intended for religious or charitable purposes.</note> that has not been accepted is valid. The *Gloss* <note>The standard medieval commentary on Roman law.</note> on the law *illud*, under the word *alia causa* (Code, *On the Most Holy Churches*), affirms that it is invalid. Molina follows this in Book 4 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, number 58; as do Julius Clarus (section *Donatio*, question 12, last verse), Covarruvias (1 *Resolutions*, chapter 14, number 16; and in the *Rubric on Testaments*, part 3, number 13), and Antonio da Gama (Decision 383, number 3); and they say it is commonly approved.

Julius Clarus adds that this must be noted because one might easily respond to the contrary. For this opinion, I see no other reason than, according to...

Second Treatise. Dispute 264.

According to civil laws <note>The Roman legal tradition used in secular courts.</note> alone, this must undoubtedly be said: and nothing to the contrary is found to be established in canon law <note>The internal legal system of the Catholic Church.</note>.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Felinus <note>Felinus Sandeus (1444–1503), an influential Italian canon lawyer.</note> in chapter 1, on pacts, number 7, along with Bartolus, Baldus, Panormitanus, and others whom he cites, asserted that a natural obligation arises from it, and a legal action is granted, and therefore it is valid. And this opinion is entirely pleasing to me. For just as civil laws, which render those wills invalid that lack a certain formality, have no force in dispositions for **pious causes** <term>charitable donations for religious or social welfare purposes</term>, because regarding those causes, nothing that detracts from their validity—as they are viewed in natural law alone—has force without the approval of the Supreme Pontiff: so too, civil laws that annul unaccepted promises have no force in promises regarding pious causes, since no such thing is found to be approved by canon law. By this same reasoning, we shall say below that donations to pious causes are valid without **insinuation** <term>the formal public registration of a large gift before a judge</term> beyond the sum prescribed by civil law, with nothing hindering the fact that civil law intends to include donations even to pious causes, as is clear in the law *Illud* in the Code *de sacrosanctis Ecclesiis* <note>original: "C. de sacrof. Eccl." - referencing the Code of Justinian.</note>. Accursius seems to have known this, as he asserted in the cited gloss that promises to pious causes without acceptance are invalid.

And from what has been said in this doubt, it is established that Bartolus and Baldus are also of the opinion that from an unaccepted promise, an obligation arises standing on natural law alone: for they cannot otherwise affirm that from a promise made to pious causes, a natural obligation arises and an action is given.

<margin>Query.</margin>
The final doubt in this matter is whether from a promise not yet accepted, but confirmed by an **oath** by the promisor, an action is granted by canon and civil law. Bartolus and the more common opinion of the interpreters of **Caesarean Law** <note>The Roman Law of the Emperors.</note>, just as they deny that an action is granted under civil law from a "naked pact" <note>An informal agreement that lack specific legal requirements.</note> confirmed by an oath, they nevertheless affirm it is granted by canon law, as we reported in dispute 256: so too, they deny that an action is granted from that promise under civil law. Bartolus, in the law *si quis pro eo*, on guarantors, affirms that not even a natural obligation proceeds from it, but only an obligation in relation to God, whom the swearer is bound not to have summoned as a witness to a false or unfaithful promise. Just as Innocent and others deny that an action is granted in canon law from a naked pact confirmed by an oath, as was reported in the same place: so too, they deny it is granted from the promise of which we are treating.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
19 It must † nonetheless be said, with Panormitanus on the chapter *cum venissent*, on constitutions, number 26 and 27, and Covarruvias in the chapter *quamvis pactum*, part 1, section 2, number 2 and 4, and part 2, section 4, number 16, and others whom he cites, that under both canon and civil law, an action is granted from it; not indeed that the power to obligate (which a promise not confirmed by an oath would have had before it is accepted, standing in natural law alone, as we showed in dispute 150) is "revived," but because, as we proved extensively there, from an oath that is confirmed—when the promise itself is not about an illicit thing, and when both the promise and the oath were emitted purely spontaneously—there arises not only an obligation in relation to God to perform so as not to bring Him as a witness to an unfaithful promise, but also a specific obligation to the person to whom it was made under oath,

<column-break/>

granting a right to that person, so that it may even be sought by their heirs; by reason of which the promised thing is owed to them simply, and by reason of which an action is given under canon and civil law, even when the promise or contract confirmed by such an oath is void and null under human law, as is clear in the chapter *cum contingat*, on oaths, and the chapter *cum mulieres* in the same title of book 6, and the chapter *quamvis pactum*, on pacts, book 6, and in the authentic *sacramenta puberum* in the Code *si adversus venditionem*. Since indeed these things are clear enough from what was said in dispute 256 and dispute 150, joined with those things we premised in dispute 149, it is not necessary to add more on this matter.

20 I would † however advise that, since under **Portuguese Law** <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> such an oath would be void unless it were emitted with a specific license from the King—nay, even the promise, though otherwise valid, would be void for that reason, as shown in dispute 149—certainly, an action from such a promise confirmed by oath would not be granted in Portugal.

In **Castile** <note>A kingdom in modern-day Spain.</note>, however, if the opinion of Molina and others were true, who affirm that an action is not given in that kingdom from an unaccepted promise, surely, since it is lawful in that kingdom to confirm by oath those things which would not be valid without an oath (as said in dispute 149), it must be admitted that an action is granted in that kingdom from a promise confirmed by an oath.

According to our own opinion, however, the same must be said—not indeed because that promise, stripped of the oath, is not valid in that kingdom, but <unclear>through</unclear> law 12, title 1, book 4 of the **New Compilation** <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* (1567), a major collection of Spanish laws.</note>, it is expressly granted in that kingdom that perpetual donations can be confirmed by oath, as we reported in dispute 149. If, however, a promise of that kind were not perpetual, but for something to be granted for a time, then, if confirmed by oath, it would be invalid in that kingdom: because it would be void by the very fact that it was confirmed by oath, unless it were made for a dowry or **earnest money** <term>arrhas; a deposit paid to confirm a contract</term>, as shown in dispute 149.

<margin>1</margin> **A** promise, by the very fact that it is accepted by the one to whom it was made, even if it remains within the limits of a "naked pact" <term>pactum nudum; an informal agreement that originally didn't grant a right to sue</term>, nevertheless by a legal privilege today—following the law *si quis argentum* <note>original: "l. si quis argentum. C. de donat." — a specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding donations.</note>—gives rise to a civil obligation and a legal action, as was shown in Dispute 255 and the preceding dispute. From this it follows that although before this law, a civil obligation did not arise from an accepted promise, nor was a legal action granted unless a formal verbal agreement <term>stipulatio</term> intervened or delivery <term>traditio</term> followed (by which that "naked pact" would be "clothed" and pass into a named contract of donation), today, however, neither of these is necessary for that purpose.

<margin>2</margin> From this, another distinction arises: namely, that since a formal verbal agreement <note>original: "stipulatio"</note> cannot be made between absent parties via letter or messenger, but only between those present (as seen in Dispute 254), formerly a donation that began with a promise could not be perfected via letter or messenger while delivery was pending, in such a way that a civil obligation would arise. Today, however, because it is perfected by the mere mutual consent of the promisor and the acceptor expressed outwardly, it can be perfectly performed and completed via letter or messenger, through which one promises and the other accepts. This is no different from other contracts perfected by consent, as mentioned in the cited Dispute 254. This is according to the law *si quis argentum* and other laws that grant this privilege to an accepted promise, and it is the common opinion of the doctors <note>Legal scholars.</note>, which among others, Antonio Gomez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4) and Julius Clarus <note>An influential Italian jurist (1525–1575).</note> (section *testamentum*, question 12) report and follow. There, with the same gloss and common opinion, he warns that it is absolutely necessary that the messenger be specifically appointed for that purpose; otherwise, the donation will be invalid.

<margin>4</margin> I said above: "that donation which begins from a promise, while delivery was not yet following," because a donation perfected by delivery—even before the law *si quis argentum*—could be made between

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

absent parties via letter or messenger. Through these means, one could signify to another that he was sending such a thing as a gift, which the other would receive, or that he was giving as a gift something the recipient already had in his possession. Or, the recipient could ask through a messenger for a certain thing to be given to him, or for a thing he already had to be formally gifted to him. This is held in the law *absenti* <note>original: "l. etiam l. absenti. ff. de donat." — Digest of Justinian.</note> and the law *nec ambigi* in the Code, and is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez cites and follows in the place mentioned.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>The Question:</margin> The question is: if someone should promise something as a gift to an absent person, but did not send a messenger to signify this to them, and instead someone who heard the promise reported it to the recipient on their own initiative, and the recipient then accepted the promise—is the donation considered perfected under common law <note>The shared Roman-Canon legal tradition of Europe.</note>, such that the promisor could not thereafter revoke it? <margin>Decision.</margin> The scholars cited and followed by Julius Clarus and Menchaca <note>Vázquez de Menchaca (1512–1569), a Spanish jurist.</note> (Book 2, *On Controversies*, chapter 15) deny that it remains perfected.

Their reasoning seems to be that under common law, for an acceptance to perfect a donation, it is necessary that the promise reaches the acceptor through the promisor himself, or through his own instrument—namely, through his agent, his own letter, or a messenger specifically appointed by him for that purpose. They judge the same to be true in reciprocal contracts: for them to be perfected, it is necessary that mutual consent reaches from one to the other through the consenting party himself or his instrument; otherwise, the contract is not considered so perfect that either side cannot freely withdraw from it. And this opinion, being common and received in practice, seems right to embrace.

<margin>6</margin> <margin>The Question:</margin> Next, it is questioned: if a free promise is made to someone who is present but remains silent, should it be considered complete so that it cannot thereafter be revoked? <margin>Decision.</margin> The common opinion, reported and followed by Julius Clarus, Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a famous Spanish canonist often called the "Spanish Bartolus."</note>, and Molina (Book 4, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2), affirms that it is considered perfected. For although in "onerous" contracts <note>Contracts where both parties give something, like a sale.</note> he who is silent is not considered to consent, in "gratuitous" things <note>Gifts or favors.</note> which benefit the silent party, he is presumed to consent according to the rule "he who suffers [allows] it" and the rule "he who is silent [consents]" <note>original: "qui tacet, de reg. iur. l. br. 6." — a standard legal maxim.</note>. Therefore, since the donation is expressed and the consent or acceptance is presumed by law, the donation must be considered perfected so that it cannot be revoked later. Antonio Gomez does not disagree, but rather agrees with this common opinion, only denying that silence presumes consent in onerous contracts.

Furthermore, if the person to whom the promise was made accepted it in such a way that its execution was left to the judgment of the promisor (saying, for example, "if you wish" or "if it pleases you"), then the promisor is not bound—at least not under pain of mortal sin—to fulfill the promise, because it was not fully and completely accepted.

The law also allows that certain specific people can enter into agreements <term>stipulari</term> on behalf of others, and thus accept promises and donations with effects for those others.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 264.

7 And although this occurs so that the donor, after that acceptance, cannot revoke the donation, it always depends on the ratification and consent of the recipient <term>donatarius; the person receiving the gift</term> for the donation to be absolutely firm. This is primarily granted to those who are under the power of others, in comparison to those under whose power they are, as held in the Institutes <note>original: "§. si quis alij, Inst. de inut. stipul."</note> and the law of the Partidas <note>original: "l. 7. tit. 11. par. 5."; referring to the Siete Partidas, the famous Spanish legal code.</note>

8 Such a person is first of all a slave <term>mancipium</term> in relation to his master. For whether he enters a formal agreement <term>stipuletur</term> or accepts for himself or for his master, the master can demand it for himself just as if he himself had made the agreement and accepted it. This is held in the Digests <note>original: "l. 2. ff. rem pupilla sal. fore"</note> and affirmed by the Gloss. It is also agreed that this applies to those who acquire for us. The cited Gloss, following the Institutes, adds that even a formal agreement or acceptance made by a slave to a master who only has the right of "use and profit" <term>vsum fructú; usufruct</term>, or simply the right of use, is valid. This also applies to an acceptance made through a slave who was possessed in good faith, whether that slave actually belonged to someone else or was a free man <note>In Roman law, if you believed in good faith that a free person was your slave, you could still acquire certain rights through their actions.</note>. The same is affirmed by the Gloss on the Sixth Book of Decretals regarding usury.

A son is also such a person, during the time he is under his father's legal power, as held in the cited law and affirmed by the cited glosses.

A member of a religious order <term>religiosus</term> is similarly such a person in relation to the abbot or the monastery. For a religious person, regarding the acquisition of goods for the monastery, is compared to a slave, according to the laws on monks. As Bartolus and Innocentius affirm, so does Gregorio Lopez in his commentary on the cited law.

Others, however, who are simply independent <term>sui iuris; of their own right</term>, cannot enter into agreements or accept in the place of those to whom they are partially subject—such as a servant in place of a master, the son of a madman in place of his father or mother, a student in place of a teacher, and other similar cases.

Furthermore, this power is granted to judges when they enter into agreements in the name of an absent party, whether that party is a ward <term>pupillus; an orphaned minor</term> or someone else. It is also granted to public scribes or notaries. All agree without controversy that when a scribe or notary acts in judicial proceedings for an absent person who belongs to that court, he may enter agreements or accept from others pertaining to that court. This is expressly arranged regarding the judge and such a notary in the fifth Partida.

<margin>Question.</margin>
9 But what if a scribe or notary, acting as a public official, were to enter an agreement or accept a gift *outside* of a court proceeding? There is a massive controversy among the learned doctors on this point, which Molina relates more clearly than others in his work on primogeniture.

Molina himself thinks it should not be doubted that a "useful action" <term>utilis actio; a legal right to sue for enforcement</term> is acquired for the absent person from such an acceptance by a notary, so that it is not necessary for the notary to formally transfer that right to the person. He affirms this is the common opinion of Bartolus and others. He also argues that the notary’s acceptance works so that, once ratification

<column-break/>

or acceptance by the recipient follows, the donation is entirely confirmed, and the recipient has a legal right to sue the donor and the donor's heirs. However, he says the whole doubt is whether—during the interval before the recipient's ratification and acceptance occurs—the donor is free to revoke the donation accepted by the notary, thereby making it void and extinguishing that legal right which the recipient held dependent on his own future ratification.

The common opinion of the doctors—which, among others, Covarrubias and Julius Clarus follow—asserts that the donor *cannot* revoke the donation in that intermediate time. This is because, once acceptance by a public official has occurred, it is considered no less firm and complete than an acceptance by a son under a father's power, a slave, or another person legally permitted to accept in the name of an absent party. Therefore, since a donor cannot revoke a gift in the time between the acceptance by these people and the recipient's ratification, it follows that he cannot revoke it in the time between the notary's acceptance and the recipient's ratification.

Decius and many others, whom Molina cites and follows, embrace the contrary opinion: namely, that the donor is free to revoke it in that intermediate time. Among the authors of this opinion, there are those who even claim *this* is the common view. They are led to this because no specific text is found that grants a donation accepted by a notary such force that the donor cannot revoke it before the recipient’s ratification.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
10 The following points will reveal what I think about this matter. First, the opinion of Covarrubias and Julius Clarus seems much more common. And in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, it seems it should be entirely embraced, not only because it is more common and is the opinion of Bartolus, but also because it seems sanctioned in the <insert>4th Book of the Ordinances, Title 75</insert> at the beginning, in these words:

> *Pure and simple donations made without any condition or cause—past, present, or future—as soon as they are made by the grant of those who make them and accepted by those to whom they are made, or by a notary or person who by law can accept in their name, are immediately firm and perfect in such a way that they can never be revoked at any time.* <note>original: "As doaçoẽs puras e simpresmente feitas..." in Portuguese.</note>

Observe that the law specifically mentions the person of the notary; as for other persons who can legally accept on behalf of an absent person, it covers them with general words. Furthermore, the acceptance of a donation by a notary is customarily done outside of court, not just within it.

Secondly, looking only at the "Common Law" <note>The *Ius Commune*, based on Roman and Canon law.</note>, I do not see an open text that grants a scribe or notary the power of entering agreements and accepting outside of court in the name of an absent person; for all the texts, if examined, seem to speak of court proceedings and the judge's orders.

Thirdly, the opinion of Molina cited above is entirely unpleasing to me, insofar as he affirms on one hand that a donation accepted by a notary produces a legal right for the absent person, yet once ratification follows...

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding the role of a notary (tabellio) in making a gift binding. The previous page discussed whether an acceptance by a public official on behalf of an absent person prevents the giver from changing their mind. Here, Molina explores the specifics of when a gift becomes "irrevocable" and what happens if one of the parties dies before the final confirmation.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...of the absent person, the donation remains entirely firm; and on the other hand, he asserts that in that intermediate period between the notary’s acceptance and the recipient's <term>donatarius; the person receiving the gift</term> ratification, the donor can revoke it and extinguish the <term>vtilem actionem; "useful action," a legal right to claim the property in court</term>.

For there is no express text that grants more power to a notary's acceptance made outside of court—either for that first effect or any other—than if it were done by any other private individual. Therefore, if Molina denies on that basis that an acceptance made outside of court makes a donation irrevocable, he must also deny that the acceptance has the power to result in a "useful action" for the absent person, or that the donation is entirely firm once ratification follows. It would be as if a donation made to an absent person through a private individual's acceptance gained no legal force at all; a foundation upon which Cynus <note>Cynus de Pistoia (c. 1270–1336), a famous Italian jurist and poet.</note> and others, whom Molina cites above at number 70, also seem to deny it.

Fourth, as it is the common opinion, sanctioned by Portuguese law, and more widely accepted in practice everywhere, we should embrace the opinion of Covarrubias and Julius Clarus. (Along with Bartolus, Innocent, and the Gloss of Accursius <note>original: "§. si quis alij, Instit. de inutilib. stipul."</note>). For the doctors of law commonly understand the statutes such that a clerk or notary has the faculty of formal agreement <term>stipulandi</term> and accepting in the name of the absent person, whenever he accepts as a public person. Furthermore, because he accepts in a public document, he is deemed to accept as a public person unless the contrary is established elsewhere. However, when he accepts by word in private conversations, he would not be deemed to accept as a public person unless it were explicitly stated. Therefore, it is not necessary that he always accepts, or is presumed to accept, as a public person—though Molina contends otherwise in the place cited.

Fifth, because the acceptance might not concern a pure gift, but one with a condition or burden <term>cum modo, & grauamine</term> placed on the recipient, there would be doubt as to whether the recipient would wish to accept it with that specific burden. This is even more true in reciprocal contracts <note>Contracts where both parties owe something to each other.</note>. By the mere acceptance of the notary in the name of the absent person, the donation or contract would gain no firmness before the ratification and consent of the absent party. This consent must, in turn, be made manifest to the other contracting party. In that intermediate time, it would be entirely possible for the other party to withdraw from the donation or contract, as Molina rightly affirms in the cited place. The reason is that since such contracts are reciprocal, the consent of each individual has this implicit condition: "if you, in turn, consent to the burden or the repayment." Truly, just as the one in whose name the notary accepted could withdraw from the contract before he personally consented and made it known to the other party, so too could the one who first gave consent withdraw and revoke it. For such contracts are not considered perfected before the mutually accepted consent of both.

Observe that when a donation is massive, and the condition or burden is so small in comparison to the gift that it is believed no one would refuse to accept it with that burden—

<column-break/>

—as usually happens in the establishments of <term>maioratuum; entailed estates or "majoratus," where property is kept within a family line</term>, then certainly the same must be said of such establishments and the "vocations" to them as is said of other pure donations. When (according to what will be said in the proper place) they are established as irrevocable, it is clear enough of itself, as the reasoning is exactly the same.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
11 According to what has been said so far, it is clear what should be said regarding the following doubt. Peter donated one hundred gold coins to John, who was absent, and a notary accepted in John’s place. But before the news of the donation reached John's ears and he could ratify it, John departed this life. The question is whether the "useful action," which John was entitled to from the notary's acceptance, passes to John’s heirs, and whether they can ratify and accept the donation. To this, without a doubt, following the opinion of Covarrubias and Julius Clarus which we embraced shortly before, we must answer affirmatively, just as they themselves answer affirmatively.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Indeed, from the notary's acceptance, John had acquired a full and perfect right to the promised thing, as if from a full and perfect donation that could no longer be revoked by Peter. For that reason, that already perfectly acquired right passes to John’s heirs.

The exact same thing must be said if Peter were to die before John’s acceptance. In that case, because a perfect right had been acquired for John from the notary's acceptance, and no mandate intervened which would expire upon the death of the one giving it (which through a silent revocation would make the donation void), Peter's heirs are the debtors to John and to John’s heirs for the things donated by Peter to John. Molina also agrees with this in Book 4 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, number 77, although he is led by other fundamental reasons which you may read there.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
12 From the same points, it is clear what should be said to this other doubt. Peter donated a horse to John, who was absent, and a notary accepted the donation in John’s name. But before John ratified it, Peter donated the same horse to Francis, who accepted the donation in person. The question is: which of these donations is to be preferred?

<margin>Decision.</margin>
It must be said without a doubt that if delivery <term>traditio; the physical hand-over of the item</term> has been made to neither, John—to whom the donation was first made and who first acquired the perfect right—must be preferred. If, however, delivery was made to Francis, then because he obtained ownership <term>dominium</term> by that very act, whereas John only had a right to the thing and a personal action <note>A legal claim against Peter personally, rather than a direct claim on the horse itself.</note>, it must be said that Francis is to be preferred. Nevertheless, Peter is bound to pay John the full value of the horse by reason of the injustice committed against him, by delivering to Francis a thing that was owed to John out of justice. Covarrubias and Julius Clarus agree on this, whatever others may have said to the contrary.

13 A Parish Priest, although according to the chapter *quanquam* <note>original: "cap. quanquam, de vsuris lib. 6."</note> regarding usury he is counted among those who can acquire a "useful action" for the absent, this only takes place in the specific case of that chapter. This is manifest from the text itself: namely, that when a guarantee is provided to him regarding the restitution of gains wrongly acquired through usury, he acquires a "useful action" for those to whom the restitution is owed.

It also addresses conflicting gifts, noting that while a physical delivery to a second person may transfer ownership, the original recipient is still owed the value of the gift in justice.</summary>

# Second Treatise.
## Disputation 265.

<margin>14</margin> A **legal representative** <term>procurator; an agent authorized to act for another</term> of a city, town, or any other community, can formally contract and accept in their name, and by that very act, he acquires a **useful action** <term>vtilem actionem; a legal right to sue or claim property</term> for them. <margin>15</margin> The same is true for the **guardian** <term>tutor; a protector of a minor's person and property</term> of a ward, and the **curator** of a minor, an insane person, and for the same reason, a spendthrift, in relation to those for whom he is guardian or curator. This is held in the law *eum qui*, the last paragraph, in the Digest *regarding agreed-upon money*, and law 8, title 11, part 5 <note>original: "l. eum qui. §. vlt. ff. de constituta pec. & l. 8. tit. 11. par. 5." This refers to the Siete Partidas, a foundational Spanish law code.</note>.

<margin>16</margin> A **representative** of any other person, although he acquires possession and ownership of a thing in the name of his principal even if the principal is unaware of it—as stated in the law *possessio quoque*, the last paragraph, in the Digest *on acquiring possession*—nevertheless, if he contracts or accepts something in that person's name, the right to legal action does not immediately belong to the principal. Instead, it is necessary that the representative first **cede** <term>cessio; the formal transfer of a legal right from one person to another</term> that right to him. However, if he refuses to cede it, he shall be compelled by the authority of a judge and by an **action on the mandate** <term>mandati actione; a lawsuit based on a contract of representation</term> to cede it, as held in the last paragraph cited, and law 1 at the end of the Digest *on actions against managers*.

Or certainly, so much is handed over from the goods of the representative to the principal as that legal action was valued at, according to the laws cited in law 8, title 11, part 5. However, when the representative does not have sufficient goods, and because of death, absence, or another similar cause, the principal (or the one whose business was managed) cannot be sufficiently helped otherwise, then a **useful action** is granted to him without any formal transfer, as held in law 2 of the Digest *on actions against managers*, and as gathered from the next-to-last law, last paragraph, of the Code *on the Trebellian Decree*, and from the last law of the Code *on actions and obligations*. All these matters are arranged in the cited law 8. Read the other laws which Gregorio Lopez cites there.

In the following events, however, a "useful action" is granted to the principals without any transfer based on the contract or acceptance of such representatives. First, if the principal is **present** while the contract or acceptance is made, as in the Digest *on verbal obligations* and law 9, title 11, part 5. Next, if the contract or acceptance was made concerning the payment of a **pension**, fruits, or other rents from the principal's own property, such as from the leasing of a house or another thing, in the Digest *on representatives* and the cited law 9. Likewise, when the contract was made **in court**, as in the Digest *on praetorian stipulations* and law 9 cited above.

When it is in the interest of the one contracting or accepting that something be given or done for another absent person, the contract by which he stipulates this for that other person is valid. For example, if a guardian transfers the guardianship to another, the contract is valid by which he stipulates that the ward's property will be kept safe by that other person. Likewise, if someone contracts for something to be given to his own representative, the contract is valid because it results in the benefit of the contracting party himself.

<margin>17</margin> Likewise, if someone **contracts** with John for a hundred to be given to Peter, which the contracting party himself owes to Peter, the contract is valid. However, the right to sue John does not belong to Peter by that contract, but to the contracting party himself, who can compel John to pay Peter what he promised, and furthermore, to satisfy him if any damages followed for him because he did not pay Peter at the appointed time. So it is held in the Institutes *on useless stipulations* <note>original: "institut. de inutilibus stipulationib. §. sed & si quis."</note> and the Digest *on verbal obligations*.

<column-break/>

and law 10, title 1, part 5.
All the explained events, and certain others in which a contract or acceptance made for an absent person or in the name of an absent person is valid, are placed in the second gloss on the section "if anyone to another" in the Institutes *on useless stipulations*. Read that.

<margin>18</margin> Finally, it must be observed, according to the third law of **Castile**, title 8, book 3 of the *Ordinamiento* (which is law 2, title 16, book 5 of the *New Collection*), that sometimes a person promising a **legal right** <term>Ius intenti; a specific legal claim or intent</term> regarding an absent person cannot revoke the promise. This is our opinion based on the preceding discussion, even if no one had accepted that promise in their name at all. Indeed, it is everyone's opinion that it is irrevocable when it has been accepted at least by some private person in their name, as Gregorio Lopez, Covarrubias, and other doctors who agree with them affirm. Much more so will he not be able to revoke it in that kingdom when it has been accepted by any of the persons explained so far.

### Whether a "burden" or "condition" can be attached to a gift in favor of a third party. And whether, before it is accepted by him, it can be removed and revoked.

### D I S P V T A T I O N  CCLXV.

### S V M M A R Y

<margin>1</margin> *A fixed condition or burden cannot be attached to a **perfected gift**; it is otherwise if it is not perfected, number 2.*
<margin>3</margin> *If a recipient is bound to restore the gift to a certain third party after a set time, a "useful action" to demand that thing is acquired by that third party and his heirs.*
*Indeed, even a **real action** <term>actio realis; a claim based on ownership of the thing itself rather than a personal debt</term> according to some, number 4.*
*However, the contrary is held in number 5.*
*It is otherwise, however, regarding the **law of Castile**, number 7.*
<margin>6</margin> *Understanding of law 1 and the law "whenever" in the Code "on gifts."*
<margin>8</margin> *Whether a condition or burden attached to a gift in favor of a third party can be canceled by the giver before it is accepted by that third party; where it is held with Bartolus and the more common opinion.*
*And what if that third party were the **Church** or a **pious place**, number 9.*
*Likewise, what about the law of Castile, number 10.*

<margin>1</margin> This disputation, as far as its later part is concerned, is joined with the preceding disputation and therefore must be examined in this place. A **gift** is perfected by the very fact that it can no longer be revoked, either because it has been accepted or for other reasons according to what has been explained so far. Neither a condition nor any other **burden** <term>grauamen; a requirement or duty attached to a property or gift</term> can be attached to it without the free will of the recipient. This is expressly held in the law *perfecta* in the Code *on gifts which are under a burden*, and Covarrubias affirms it.
<margin>2</margin> Meanwhile, however, while it **can be revoked**, a condition or another burden can be attached to it, both in favor of the giver himself and in favor of a third party. For instance, that after such a time, or after the death of the giver, he should restore the whole thing or a part to such and such a person, or to a Church or Hospital; or that every year he should pay so much for this or that purpose, or do this or that. This is held by an argument from the contrary sense in the cited law *perfecta*, and expressly

<meta>This page continues Disputation 265, moving from the general principles of representation to the specific legal mechanics of "burdens" or conditions placed on gifts intended to benefit a third party. It references the earlier discussion on how ownership is transferred.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, *On Contracts*

<margin>Law 1, 2, 3 in the same title; and law 7, title 4, part 5; as affirmed by Covarruvias in the same place, and the doctors of law commonly.</margin>
The reasoning, however, is that since a **donation** <term>donatio; a gift</term> arises from the pure generosity of the donor, and the recipient is not forced to accept it, the donor is certainly free to give what is his own under whatever conditions and **burdens** <term>gravamina; legal obligations or restrictions</term> he chooses, provided they are not inherently unfair or forbidden by positive law.

3 If a recipient is **burdened** to restore the thing given to him to a third party after a certain time, then—even if that third party did not specifically request it from the donor or formally accept the gift—when the time comes for the thing to be restored, he and his heirs have the right to a **useful action** <term>utilis actio; a legal right to claim the property</term> to demand that thing. This is expressly held in the law *Quoties* in the Code *on donations under a condition*, and is the consensus of the common opinion of the legal scholars.

<margin>Question 4</margin>
Decius and others, whom Covarruvias mentions in the third section above, were of the opinion that such an **action** is not only **personal** <term>actio personalis; a claim against a specific person</term> but also **real** <term>actio realis; a claim against the object itself, regardless of who holds it</term>. Therefore, they argue the third party could **claim it** <term>vendicare; to legally recover property</term> from whoever might possess it. From this, it is further inferred that because that burden was placed on the thing by the donor, the recipient not only cannot sell or transfer it, but if he attempts to do so, the sale is null and void.

<margin>Argument</margin>
They are led to this opinion because, as stated in the cited law *Quoties*, in ancient times when the third party had neither stipulated with the donor for the thing to be restored nor accepted the gift, if the recipient did not restore it when the time came, the right to sue was granted not to the third party, but to the donor himself to demand it. However, by that same law *Quoties*, a **useful action** is granted to the third party—namely, the same action that was once granted to the donor. But the action granted to a donor when a pact or burden placed on the recipient is not observed is a **claim for the thing** <term>rei vendicatio</term>, as is clear from the first law of the Code *on donations under a condition*; therefore, this same right belongs to the third party.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
This opinion is confirmed by law 7, title 4, part 5 <note>This refers to the *Siete Partidas*, a famous Spanish law code</note>, which establishes that when a recipient is burdened to restore a gift to either the donor or a third party after a certain time, the **ownership and possession** <term>dominium et possessio</term> of that thing passes by the law itself, without any formal delivery, to the person to whom it was to be restored when that time arrives.

<margin>Decision 5</margin>
The contrary opinion—namely, that the **action** belonging to the third party is only **personal**—is the common view of the scholars. Thus, if that thing has been sold and delivered by the recipient to someone else, or transferred under another title, the sale is valid; the third party can only sue the original recipient for **damages** <term>id quod interest; the value of the loss</term>. This is affirmed by Covarruvias (cited in section 3) and Antonio Gómez (on the Laws of Toro, number 25).

And this is the view we must undoubtedly embrace. For as held in the law *Traditionibus* in the Code *on pacts*, and as we have explained at length in Disputations 2 and 3, it is a general rule that ownership is not transferred without **delivery** <term>traditio; the physical or legal handover of an item</term>, except in cases expressly stated by law. The case we are discussing is not among those exceptions, as will become clear from the resolution of the argument on which the contrary opinion relies. However, if the third party to whom the **restitution**

<column-break/>

of the donated thing was to be made were the Church, or another holy place, or a city, or if the gift were to be used for the ransom of captives, then a **real action** to claim it would be available, according to the second-to-last law of the Code *on most holy Churches*, as was said more fully in Disputation 3. For other reasons and laws, read Covarruvias and Antonio Gómez in the places cited.

<margin>To argument 6</margin>
Regarding the argument for the contrary opinion: while the first premise is granted, the second must be denied. That which is arranged in law 1 only applies to the specific case of that text—namely, when someone has donated something with the burden that they be provided with food and support. When such support is not provided, a **real action** is granted to the donor to claim back the thing he gave, and this is by a special privilege regarding maintenance. Indeed, from that same law joined with the law *Quoties*, the opposite of what we are discussing is actually inferred.

<margin>To the confirmation</margin>
For in the law *Quoties*, both the donor and the third party (to whom the thing was to be restored) are only granted a **claim for the return of the thing** <term>condictio; a personal action to recover something specific</term>. A *condictio*, however, as held in that first law, is a personal action and not a real one; for so we read it written in that law: "For not only does a *condictio*—that is, an action against the person—proceed for you by law in this case, but the divine princes have also decreed that a **claim for the thing** <term>vendicatio</term> should be given in this case." <note>The "divine princes" refers to the Roman Emperors who issued the decree.</note>

7 As for the confirmation, Covarruvias (at the cited place, number 5) attempts by a rather forced interpretation to bring the discussion of that law back within the boundaries of the common law. However, even if unwillingly, he confesses that he does not satisfy himself, and he admits that under the law of Castile <note>original: "iure Castellae"</note> a **real action** is available. Moreover, he admits that ownership and possession of the thing are acquired by the third party the moment the time for restoration arrives. Antonio Gómez also applies other no less forced interpretations to that law in order to reduce it to common law terms, and finally adds: "I say that by the law of the Kingdom of Castile, ownership and possession can be acquired in that event without any delivery." And this was entirely pleasing to us in the cited Disputation 3, along with Gregorio López (in his notes on that law), Molina, and Rodrigo Juárez, whom we cited. For that law is express, and it is corroborated by the preceding law 6; when it speaks of a donation of a thing with a burden to provide maintenance, it equates other donations made with other burdens to it in the same law, which Gregorio López noted in his comments. This pertains to the first part of the proposed dispute.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
Regarding the latter part, there is a doubt whether—when a **donation** is made with a burden placed in favor of a third party—the donor can remit or revoke that burden before it has been accepted by the third party.

Indeed, as is clear from what was said in the first part of this dispute, that third party has a right to demand the fulfillment when the time for performance arrives, even if he did not stipulate it with the donor nor accept it; and he holds this action such that it is not necessary for anyone to transfer it to him.

### Tractate Two, Disputation 265.

...so that, due to a lack of acceptance, it would henceforth be forbidden to revoke the **majorat** <term>maioratus; a legal arrangement, often called an entail, where property is kept within a family line and cannot be sold</term>. So says Molina in Book 6, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, number 75, a matter which will be discussed in its proper place.

When, however, a **burden** <term>gravamen; a legal obligation or condition imposed on a gift</term> is imposed in any other way for the benefit of one or more persons who would succeed in a certain order, the doctors of law also agree that if it was accepted by that third party, it cannot be revoked by the donor in respect to that person. If, however, it were accepted by a **notary** <term>tabellio; a public official who drafted legal documents and often acted as a legal witness</term> in that person's name, Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions* (chapter 14, number 11), Iulius Clarus (section on donations, question 13), and generally all those whom we mentioned in the preceding disputation, assert that a donation made to an absent person and accepted by a notary is sufficient to prevent revocation. Molina, however, in the place cited (number 74), following the opinion we reported from him in the previous disputation, judges that it *can* be revoked. Some, with whom Covarruvias (in the same place, number 13) seems to agree, believe that a **stipulation** <term>stipulatio; a formal legal promise</term> made by the donor himself in the name of an absent third party—whereby he requires the recipient to give a certain thing or amount to that absent person at a certain time—is equivalent to a stipulation made in the name of that absent person by a notary. I see no solid foundation for this assertion, however, because no text is brought forward to prove that the recipient has the power to formally stipulate a burden in the name of an absent person that the donor is imposing on that same recipient for the third party’s benefit.

Likewise, when a donor has confirmed a burden with an **oath**, revocation would be invalid. This is because a promise confirmed by an oath, even if not accepted by the recipient, grants a legal action; the promised thing is simply and entirely owed to the recipient, as was shown in Disputation 263. In the present matter, Covarruvias (number 10) affirms this along with Gulielmus Benedictus and others.

When the matter is no longer "whole"—meaning the burden has already been paid to the absent third party—the doctors commonly agree that it cannot be revoked. So say Iulius Clarus (section on donations, question 13) and Covarruvias (at the end of numbers 13 and 14). On this point, there can be no doubt, since by the act of receiving it, that third party is considered to have accepted the donation. Iulius Clarus also maintains that once the appointed time for the payment of the burden arrives—even if it has not yet been delivered or accepted by the third party—it can no longer be revoked by the donor. Many others, cited by Covarruvias, affirm the same.

They are led to this because from that specific moment <margin>9</margin> a right is perfectly acquired by that third party. However, if one reads Covarruvias carefully, he does not actually agree with them unless that third party is the **Church**, a **pious place** <term>pius locus; a charitable foundation or religious institution</term>, or a **captive** whose ransom is being paid. In those cases, because a legal action is available to the third party from that moment (according to the cited law *Quoties*), and because a right and action for a donation to the Church or the others listed grants a "right in the thing" <note>original: "ius in re"</note> and even ownership of the thing owed (according to the second-to-last law in the Code *On the Most Holy Churches*), it follows that the burden cannot thereafter be revoked.

Regarding a third party who does not fall into

<column-break/>

the categories just listed, Covarruvias clearly feels—along with **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a titan of medieval Roman law whose opinions often carried the force of law</note> and according to what we shall soon say—that it *can* be revoked. He argues that just as the third party acquired a right to the thing as soon as the donation with the burden was made (but a revocable one), so too when the time for restitution arrives, he has only a right to the thing and a **personal action** <term>actio personalis; a claim against a specific person rather than the object itself</term>, not a **real action** <term>actio realis; a claim that follows the property regardless of who holds it</term>. This depends on the donor persevering in that same will, and therefore the right remains similarly revocable. I believe, however, that we should not depart from the opinion of the others.

For the law *Quoties* does not grant an action to the donor and the third party against the recipient to demand the burden until the time for restitution arrives and the recipient fails to keep the promise. Therefore, since that action has already begun for the third party at that point, he is deemed to have a "perfected right" by the disposition of the law *Quoties*, so that it is simply and perfectly owed to him. Consequently, because it is already entirely owed to him—such that the recipient is at fault if he does not hand it over—the donor cannot revoke it.

When the donor who imposed the burden dies before the time for restitution arrives, and before the burden has been accepted by the third party for whom it was left, Bartolus and the common opinion (which Covarruvias and Iulius Clarus follow) affirm that the donation remains confirmed by the burden. It cannot be revoked by the donor's heirs, because the power and right to revoke that was in the donor does not pass to his heirs. This is proven by Law 3 of the Digest *On Exported Slaves*, and Law 1 in the Code *If a Slave is Alienated in This Manner*, and Law 3 of the Digest *On Those Set Free Without Manumission*.

Except for all these specific events, Bartolus and a much more common opinion of the doctors (followed by Covarruvias, Iulius Clarus, Navarro in his *Apology on Church Revenues*, and Molina) affirm that it is entirely within the donor's power to **change his mind** <note>original: "poenitere"</note> and revoke a burden imposed for a third party. They prove this first from Law 3 of the Digest *On Exported Slaves* and the Code *If a Slave is Alienated in This Manner*. There, it is held that if a slave is sold or given under the condition and burden that he be freed after a certain time, it is within the owner's power to change his mind before that time and revoke the burden of **manumission** <term>manumissio; the legal act of freeing a slave</term>. Therefore, the same applies to any burden imposed for any other third party before it is accepted by them. Second, they argue from the Law *Aristo* in the Digest *On Donations*, which proves that a donation, insofar as it contains another pact, is an "innominate contract." For that reason, regarding that pact, a change of heart is allowed. For example, if someone gives his slave to Socrates on the condition that he be freed after five years, a change of heart is allowed within those five years; once the five years have passed, he can separate him from Socrates and return him to slavery, as Bartolus, **Paulus de Castro** <note>A famous 15th-century legal commentator</note>, and many others interpret that text.

<summary>This page discusses the legal limits of revoking conditions (burdens) placed on gifts for third parties. It concludes that while donors generally have the right to change their minds before acceptance, this right is lost if the donor dies, if the condition is confirmed by an oath, or if the beneficiary is a privileged entity like the Church.</summary>
