### Luis de Molina / On Contracts

Section 1 of the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the Digest is a massive 6th-century collection of Roman legal opinions</note> concerning the recovery of property given for a cause that was not fulfilled, and according to the first section of the law "pecuniam" in the same title, where this is expressly stated.

Thirdly, Molina argues that when something is given to someone with a burden <term>gravamen; a legal condition or obligation imposed on a recipient</term> in favor of a third party, it is considered as two separate donations: one of the property itself being given, and the other in relation to the third party regarding the burden established for their benefit. Therefore, just as the first donation can be revoked before it is accepted, so too can the second, so long as that burden has not yet been accepted by that third party. This reasoning, however, does not have as much strength as it might seem to have at first glance.

First, because exceptions must be made for the privileges granted by the law "quoties" in the Code <note>original: "C."; refers to the Code of Justinian, a collection of imperial laws</note> regarding conditional donations; these privileges are granted to this second type of donation and not to the first. Second, because Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note> and nearly all who follow him believe their opinion holds true even if the third party for whom the burden was placed were the Church or another "pious cause" <term>pia causa; a charitable or religious foundation</term>. Furthermore, a donation made to a city is valid without formal acceptance, as was shown in Disputation 263. And perhaps, following what was said there by Bartolus, Felinus, and Baldus regarding donations to pious causes before they are accepted, we should deviate from Bartolus and the common / opinion of those who follow him when the burden is imposed for the benefit of a charitable cause.

The contrary opinion—namely, that by the very fact that a donation with a burden has been made and accepted, it is forbidden for the donor to revoke that burden, even if it has not yet been accepted by the person for whose benefit it was placed—is followed by Paulus Castrensis in various places, Guillaume Benedicti, Rodrigo Juárez, Dueñas, and others whom Antonio Gómez cites and follows in his commentary on Law 40 of Toro, number 29. And although Rodrigo Juárez asserts that the common opinion of the doctors is against Bartolus, Antonio Gómez rightly admits that Bartolus's opinion is much more common.

<margin>Argument.</margin> These authors prove their opinion as follows: First, from the law "quoties" in the Code regarding conditional donations. For that law grants a right and a legal action to the third party even before the burden is accepted. However, a donation that has not been accepted usually grants neither a right nor a legal action, as is clear from what was said in the preceding disputations. Therefore, since a right and action acquired by someone cannot be revoked, it follows that such a burden cannot be revoked.

<margin>Resolved.</margin> It must be said, however, that this only proves it cannot be revoked after the time has passed when it ought to have been fulfilled, according to what was said above with the authors of the contrary opinion. For it is only from that time that the third party has a full right and action to demand the fulfillment of the burden, as stated above, and this depends on the fact that it was not previously revoked by the donor, as shown by other cited laws.

<margin>Argument.</margin> Next, he proves the same opinion from the first law of the Digest regarding those who are freed without manumission <term>manumissio; the legal act of freeing a slave</term>, where the jurist Paulus says that if a slave is sold on the condition that they be freed after a certain time, even if the seller changes his mind, the slave remains free.

<margin>Resolved.</margin> However, the Gloss of Accursius <note>a 13th-century commentary on Roman law that became standard in legal practice</note> responds there that this refers to the seller changing his mind after that time has passed, and thus after the slave was meant to have obtained freedom, in which case it cannot be revoked, as stated above. Therefore, I believe we should adhere to Bartolus's opinion as the more common one, which relies on later legal principles.

Note well Covarruvias in the place cited at the end of number 8: when a burden is imposed for the benefit of the donor's heir, the revocation is valid according to everyone's opinion, even if the time for fulfillment has passed and even if the heir has accepted the burden. This is clear enough from what we said in Disputation 196.

<margin>The Law of Castile.</margin> Finally, it should be observed that in the Kingdom of Castile <note>Spain</note>, according to Law 3 of the Ordinance frequently cited, by the well-known opinion of all, a burden imposed cannot be revoked once it has been accepted by any private person in the name of the third party for whom it was placed. However, according to our opinion and that of those we cited in Disputation 263, by the very fact that a burden is imposed by a donor with the intention of binding themselves, it cannot be revoked, even if it has been accepted by no one and the time for fulfillment has not yet arrived, as is clear from what was said / in that same disputation.

# Whether an internal promise made by a person has the power to bind them.

-> DISPVTATIO CCLXVI. <-

-> SUMMARY <-

> 1 *Ownership is not transferred by a purely mental act or promise, and the reason why. num. 2.*
> 2 *This also holds true in the Kingdom of Castile. num. 4.*
> 3 *Exceptions applicable under civil law are all called "external," even if they apply under the law of Castile.*
> 4 *Whether an internal donation, according to natural law, binds the donor in the "court of conscience" <term>forum conscientiae; the moral standing of a person before God, as opposed to a legal court</term> to reveal and deliver the gift to the recipient, where it / seems Ledesma holds this view. num. 8.*
> 6 *Possession is lost by the simple will to no longer possess. Indeed, ownership is also lost when possession is abandoned at the same time.*
> 7 *An internal promise regarding a lawful matter, confirmed even by an internal oath, binds the promisor under penalty of mortal sin.*

To clear the way with a point that contains no difficulty: Jacques Almain in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2) and Thomas of Argentina in the matter of marriage (Question 1) rightly affirm that ownership <term>dominium; the legal right to possess and use property</term> is not transferred by a purely internal act. Thus, they rightly judge that even if someone says internally, "I give this thing of mine to Peter," ownership of that thing does not pass to Peter. However, they rely on weak foundations.

<margin>Argument.</margin> They argue as follows: First, the internal consent of both spouses is not sufficient to contract a marriage, and consequently, for the spouses to receive mutual power over each other's bodies; therefore, neither is the internal giving of any other thing sufficient to transfer ownership.

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, donations and contracts depend on civil laws to be valid; but civil laws only concern themselves with external works; therefore, a purely internal donation is insufficient to transfer ownership.

It also introduces a new discussion on whether a purely internal or mental promise has the power to transfer ownership or create a moral obligation.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 266
C 3

1 The legitimate reason why ownership <term>dominium; the legal right of possession and control</term> is not transferred by a purely internal act is this: as shown in Disputations 2 and 3, and as is established by the law "Traditionibus" <note>original: "l. traditionibus"; a specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding the delivery of goods</note> in the Code <note>original: "C."; the Code of Justinian, a 6th-century collection of Roman laws</note> regarding pacts, and from the law "Quoties" regarding the sale of property, as well as from other laws, the delivery of the item <term>traditio; the physical or symbolic transfer of possession</term> is regularly necessary for the transfer of ownership. Consequently, ownership is not usually transferred by an internal donation or contract, nor even by external ones, unless delivery occurs.

<margin>To the 1st argument:</margin>
The conclusion of the first argument of Almainus <note>Jacques Almain (c. 1480–1515), a French theologian</note> and Argentinatis <note>likely a reference to a commentator from the school of Strasbourg</note> is invalid. This is because marriage is a reciprocal contract, and for that reason, the consent of each party carries a silent condition: "if the other also consents in turn." Therefore, it is not considered an absolute contract until after the mutual expression of consent and their mutual acceptance. Each party is free to withdraw from the contract before that mutual expression and acceptance occurs, which is a feature common to all reciprocal contracts.

However, if someone bound themselves by a purely internal act to take a woman as his wife—meaning he wished to take upon himself the obligation of marrying her out of his own free will, provided she did not stand in the way—then the question proposed in the title of this disputation would apply. This would not be a reciprocal contract, but a bare promise arising solely from his own generosity.

<margin>To the 2nd:</margin>
The second argument of those same authors truly has no force. Donations and contracts depend on civil laws in the sense that civil laws can, for a just cause, render contracts and donations invalid which would have been valid under natural law alone. It is not, however, as if no contract or donation could be valid unless the civil law first establishes something about them or makes them valid. For if all civil law were set aside and one stood on natural law alone, promises, sales, purchases, exchanges, and other contracts would be valid, as is well known in itself and agreed upon by the common opinion of the learned.

<margin>3</margin>
To approach the question proposed in the title: certainly, this question has little practical utility. For since the civil law, for the common good of the state, has granted the power to revoke promises and donations before they are accepted—even if they were made in word or writing, and thus even if they were manifested externally (as is clear from what was said in Disputation 263 and following)—it will certainly be much more permissible, following that provision of civil law, to revoke purely internal promises and donations. This is true regardless of whether they would have had the power to bind someone under natural law alone. Indeed, since the power to revoke donations before they are accepted is universal, the exceptions found in civil law (namely, when a promise or donation is made to a city, and so on) are to be understood as applying when such promises or donations are made externally. Otherwise, if they were purely internal, they should still be considered as included in that universal grant of revocation.

<margin>4</margin>
The same applies to that very broad exception made in the Kingdom of Castile, in Law 3, Title 8, Book 3 of the *Ordenamiento* <note>The *Ordenamiento de Alcalá*, a set of Spanish laws promulgated in 1348</note>,

<column-break/>

which is Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish laws updated in 1567</note>, the words of which we quoted in Disputation 254. This is clear both from the law as a whole and especially from its words: *Appearing that someone wished to bind himself to another by a promise* <note>original: "Pareciendo que alguno se quiso obligar a otro por promission"</note>. For a promise cannot "appear" unless it has been made externally.

It follows that in that kingdom, the common provision of civil law still holds regarding a purely internal promise. Therefore, if the proposed controversy has any place in practice today, it is only when a purely internal promise is made for some "pious cause" <term>pia causa; a charitable or religious purpose</term> and is not a vow <note>a promise made directly to God</note>, but was made solely with the intention of binding oneself to a private person. This follows the opinion we embraced in Disputation 263: namely, that in promises and donations for pious causes, the civil law provision (which allows promises and donations to be revoked before they are accepted) does not apply.

<margin>Question</margin>
What we primarily intend to dispute in this section is whether—setting aside the provisions of civil law and remaining only within the limits of natural law—a purely internal donation (in which someone says to himself: "I give this thing of mine to Peter," or "I promise Peter I will give him this thing") binds the donor or promisor in the court of conscience <term>forum conscientiae; the internal moral realm of the soul as judged by God</term>. Does it oblige them to reveal the donation to Peter and to hand the thing over to him if he wishes to receive and accept it? Furthermore, does Peter, by the force of such an internal donation or promise made to him, acquire a right to that thing? This would be similar to the right an heir acquires to the property of the deceased—whether by will or by intestacy—the very moment the person departs from life. For although the heir remains free to enter into (that is, to accept) or to repudiate that inheritance, in the meantime, as long as he does not repudiate it, he has acquired a right to it; it must be revealed and offered to him so that he may see whether he wishes to accept it or rather to repudiate it.

Many who have not paid attention to the civil law provision cited above, or who were ignorant of it, argue absolutely whether a purely internal donation or promise binds in the court of conscience. Among their number are Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican theologian</note> and Ledesma <note>Pedro de Ledesma (1544–1616), a Spanish theologian</note> in the places to be cited. However, the controversy is only to be called into question in the sense explained by us.

<margin>The affirmative side is argued 1.</margin>
The side that affirms this can be persuaded. First, because words and writings are signs of concepts; they have no power to bind except from the internal act they express and from the intention of the will to bind and promise. For this reason, in the *Institutes* <note>A textbook of Roman law</note> regarding the division of things, in the section "By Delivery" (*per traditionem*), and elsewhere, it is held that nothing is so agreeable to natural equity as to uphold the will of an owner who wishes to transfer his property to another. Clearly, if you take away the will and the internal intention to bind oneself from an external promise or donation, you remove the obligation in the court of conscience. Therefore, a purely internal donation or promise (when it exists in itself) has the power to bind in the court of conscience, not only if it is made to God, but also if it is made to a human being.

<margin>Second</margin>
Second, looking at natural law alone, acceptance is not necessary for a promise or donation to be valid and irrevocable; but by positive law...

<summary>This page explores whether a purely mental promise, never spoken or written, creates a moral obligation under natural law to fulfill it. Molina distinguishes between civil laws, which require formal delivery or external expression for a gift to be legally binding, and the internal "court of conscience" where the donor's intent is the primary factor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological investigation into whether a purely internal (mental) promise or donation is binding under natural law, specifically addressing arguments 2 through 7 of the disputation.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...good was introduced so that it might regularly be a condition required for that purpose. For positive law <note>Human-made law, as opposed to natural law.</note> does not grant this to those donations and promises that are valid and irrevocable without acceptance beyond their own nature, nor perhaps could it, as was shown at length in Disputation 263. But if external signs are necessary so that an internal promise or donation might be binding, this is only because it could not otherwise be accepted by the person to whom it was made—unless that person is God, who gazes upon the heart. Therefore, a purely internal promise or donation, based on natural law alone, is valid and irrevocable, not only if made to God, but also if made to a human.

The consequence is clear, because acceptance is not necessary—based on natural law alone—for an internal donation and promise to be binding; and external signs are not necessary except for the sake of acceptance. Accordingly, both are conditions introduced by human law so that an internal donation may be binding.

<margin>Thirdly.</margin>
Thirdly, if by a purely internal act you promised or donated something to someone, and today—with no new promise or donation made, nor the past one confirmed—you signify to them in words: "Yesterday I promised or donated this to you; see if you want it, and consider the promise or donation ratified?" Certainly, if they accept, you remain bound. Therefore, the internal promise, by its very nature and based on natural law alone, binds you.

The consequence is clear: because that signification made in words was not the promise or donation itself, and therefore did not create the obligation; rather, it was only the instrument by which the internal promise or donation was manifested. This was necessary so that it could be accepted by the recipient <term>donatarius; the person receiving a gift</term>. Acceptance, however, is only a condition introduced by civil law for a donation to be binding; if that is set aside, the donation binds based on natural law alone, as has been said and shown.

<margin>Fourthly. 6</margin>
Fourthly, possession is lost by the mere † <note>Molina often uses this mark to signal a specific legal reference or traditional point of debate.</note> will not to possess, as is clear from the Digest, book 1, paragraph "if a man," book 3, paragraph "on losing," and the law "if anyone," book 2, final paragraph, regarding the acquisition of possession <note>original: "ff. de acquirenda possess."; refers to the Digest of Justinian, a massive compilation of Roman law</note>; and as we have said in the section on possession. Indeed, even ownership <term>dominium</term> is lost by the mere will to relinquish it when possession is simultaneously abandoned—though not when possession is retained—as held in the cited law "if anyone," final paragraph, along with the gloss there. For that reason, as soon as something is internally intended by its owner to be abandoned <term>pro derelicto; a thing thrown away or abandoned</term>, ownership of it is lost, and it belongs to the first person to take it. In fact, even without an internal act of desertion, ownership is lost through a sort of habitual intention of deserting it, because the owner is clearly of such a disposition that, if asked, they would respond that they leave the thing free for any occupant. For this reason, we say that pieces of wood of small value, which flooding rivers carry away over a very long distance—so that it is presumed the owners will not seek them, even if they knew who had them—are considered abandoned and become the property of the first occupant. And anchors left in ports by their owners because they depart unwillingly to spend money or effort in extracting or searching for them—we say these are considered abandoned and become the property of the first occupant and the one who extracts them. Therefore, by the same reasoning, a purely internal donation or promise will be sufficient, based on natural law alone, for the recipient to acquire the right (which we explained above) to the thing thus donated or promised to them.

<column-break/>

Fifthly, although in an internal promise (whatever anyone may say) a lie is not found—because a lie consists in something being signified outwardly other than what is held in the mind—nevertheless, by comparison to that faithlessness, it occurs by not fulfilling what was promised. This is clear in a vow or internal promise made to God, according to that passage in Ecclesiastes 5: *If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases Him.* Since, therefore, faithlessness is evil in itself (unless a legitimate cause exists to excuse one from fulfilling what was promised), it certainly follows that from an internal promise, based on natural law alone, an obligation arises to fulfill what was so promised.

<margin>Sixthly.</margin>
7 Lastly, an internal † promise regarding a thing that is not illicit, made to a human, if it is confirmed by an oath—even a purely internal one—binds under penalty of mortal sin to the fulfillment of what was promised. And this is not only in relation to God (lest He be brought in as a witness to a false or unfaithful promise), but also in relation to the human to whom such a promise was made. That person acquires a true right to that thing, and it is truly owed to them, even to the point that the right transfers to their heirs. Indeed, they can remit the entire obligation and, by that means, completely free the one who had so bound themselves from every burden of such a promise confirmed by oath, as all these things were shown at length in Disputations 149 and 150. Therefore, by a purely internal act, a human can bind themselves to another human, based on natural law alone and in the court of conscience <term>forum conscientiae; the internal moral realm where a person is judged by God</term>. Thus, the entire foundation is overturned upon which those rely who affirm that a purely internal promise cannot bind, even based on natural law alone and in the court of conscience alone.

St. Thomas [Aquinas] below, in Question 88, Article 1, seems to have inclined toward the contrary opinion. For he says that a promise from one human cannot be made to another human except through words or any other external signs; to God, however, it can be made through internal thought alone. This is because, as held in 1 Kings 16 <note>original: "1. Reg. 16"; in modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 16:7.</note>: *Humans see those things that appear; God, however, gazes upon the heart.* And in Book 4 of the *Sentences*, Distinction 38, Question 1, Article 1, sub-question 1, he says that no one can be bound by the will except to Him alone who is the knower of the will—who is God alone. And this is the more common opinion.

Ledesma <note>Pedro de Ledesma (1544–1616), a Spanish Dominican theologian.</note>, however, explains St. Thomas by saying he understands that a promise cannot be made to a human by a purely internal act in such a way that the promisor could be **compelled** to fulfill the promise, because knowledge of the promise is necessary for that. It could also be said that St. Thomas is speaking assuming the arrangement of positive law, which took away the power of binding from it. This is the way many of those who hold the same opinion seem to understand it.

Among those who began to discuss this matter more accurately is Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a major figure in the School of Salamanca.</note>. In Book 4 of *On Justice*, Question 5, Article 1, in response to the first objection, and more fully in Book 7, Question 2, Article 1, in response to the first objection—having proposed several of the arguments we constructed a little while ago (though not with as much force as we applied to them)—he asserts that this question is doubtful and can be defended on either side. But he rather inclines to the view that a purely internal promise and donation [have]
<meta>catchword: force</meta>

<summary>Molina argues that internal promises and donations are binding under natural law and in the court of conscience, even without external signs or acceptance, using analogies from abandoned property and internal oaths. He contrasts this with the common opinion of Thomas Aquinas, which he and other theologians like Ledesma and Soto seek to reconcile or challenge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the debate over whether an internal promise—one made in the mind without being spoken or written—is morally binding under natural law. It specifically addresses the views of prominent theologians like Victoria and Ledesma regarding charitable promises.</meta>

...it has no power to bind in the court of conscience <term>foro conscientiæ: the internal "court" of a person's moral standing before God, distinct from a legal court</term> or under natural law alone, unless an external manifestation is added as a necessary condition. And Victoria <note>Francisco de Vitoria (c. 1483–1546), a foundational Spanish philosopher and theologian.</note> seems to have held this same opinion in his lectures on the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica.</note>. They are led by no other reason than this: since it is natural for a human to signify their thoughts to others through words or external signs, no obligation can arise from an internal promise before it is shown externally.

<margin>8 † Ledesma on 2. 2. question 18, article 1, doubt 13.</margin>
Ledesma finds it more pleasing to say that purely internal promises and donations *do* bind in the court of conscience under natural law alone. It seems to me that the six arguments we constructed in support of that view are very persuasive. According to those arguments, one should say that not only purely internal vows—that is, promises of a "greater good" made to God—are binding (which everyone agrees on), but also purely internal promises made for pious causes <note>Charitable or religious purposes, such as helping the poor.</note>, even when made to humans rather than God. For example, if someone promised within themselves to give ten gold coins in alms to a specific poor person, or promised a hundred gold coins as a dowry to a specific orphan because of her poverty.

However, this would have to be asserted regarding purely internal promises for pious causes only if the opinion we followed in Disputation 263 is true: namely, that even external donations made to pious causes cannot be revoked, even if they have not yet been accepted. For if, as others affirm, they could be revoked, there would be even greater reason to revoke those that were purely internal before they were accepted.

<margin>Regarding the first three arguments.</margin>
For someone who prefers the opposite opinion—due to the authority of St. Thomas Aquinas and the reason that a promise or donation, to bind in relation to someone, must by its nature be capable of being known by the person to whom it is made (which does not apply to a purely internal donation regarding another human)—let them say the following to the first three arguments: Although in an external promise the power to bind comes from the internal promise, in a purely internal one, the condition required for an obligation to arise is missing—namely, the external manifestation. Because of the lack of this condition, it does not bind.

<margin>Regarding the 4th.</margin>
To the fourth argument, let them say: although an internal act is enough for the person performing it to lose something within themselves, it is not enough to transfer a right to another person unless the necessary condition is added—that is, the external manifestation of that same act.

<margin>Regarding the 5th.</margin>
To the fifth, let them say: "unfaithfulness" in the context of an internal promise assumes there was already an obligation to fulfill what was promised. Because such an obligation exists in the case of an internal vow (because God sees it), but not in the case of an internal promise made to a human (due to the lack of the external manifestation), it follows that no "unfaithfulness" is seen in not fulfilling such a promise.

<margin>Regarding the 6th.</margin>
To the sixth, I do not see what else can be said except that the obligation toward the person to whom a promise (confirmed by an oath) was made arises from the oath itself, which binds in relation to God. For that reason—as something attached to the oath and accompanying it—an obligation results from a purely internal act regarding another human.

# How much deliberation and spontaneity a promise or stipulation must have to be binding.

## DISPUTATION CCLXVII.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Ownership is not transferred by a purely internal act or promise, and why. Number 2.*
*This also holds true in the Kingdom of Castile. Number 4.*
3 *Defenses available under civil law are all called "external," even if they apply under the law of Castile.*
5 *Whether an internal donation, according to natural law, binds the donor in the court of conscience to manifest and hand it over to the recipient.*
*Where the author seems to agree with Ledesma. Number 8.*
6 *Possession is lost by the mere will to no longer possess. Indeed, even ownership is lost when possession is abandoned at the same time.*
7 *An internal promise regarding a lawful matter, and confirmed even by an internal oath, binds the promisor under pain of mortal sin.*

1. For a promise or stipulation to be valid (and this applies to a completed donation as well), it is necessary first of all that it be a fully deliberate human act. For this reason <note>original: "Quā ratione"</note>, the promises and stipulations of those who do not have the use of reason are entirely invalid, as is clear from the sections "On the Insane" (*furiosus*) and "On the Ward" (*pupillus*) in the *Institutes* <note>The *Institutes* of Justinian, a fundamental Roman law textbook.</note> regarding useless stipulations, and Law 4, Title 11, Part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note>, and it is very well known in itself.

2. Likewise, if the act proceeds from someone who has the use of reason but is not fully deliberate, it is similarly invalid, as the doctors of law commonly and rightly affirm, because such acts are not "fully human" acts.

3. Observe, however, that the level of full deliberation that would be enough to make a sin "mortal" <term>lethal fault (lethalis culpa): a serious sin that separates the soul from God</term>—for instance, if someone moved by sudden anger, yet aware of what they were doing, struck another person severely—is also enough for a promise made to God or man to be binding. I do not believe a better rule can be given for judging when a vow or promise made to a human is binding based on the degree of deliberation.

4. Consequently, it is very rare for external promises to fail to bind due to a lack of full deliberation. Navarro <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canon lawyer and economist.</note> agrees in Chapter *Non dicatis*, number 67, section "I add thirteenthly," and in his *Manual*, Chapter 12, number 24, where he proves this learnedly.

5. Likewise, for a promise or stipulation to be valid (and the same for a completed donation), it is necessary that it arises neither through fear, nor through force, nor through fraud—whether on the part of the one to whom the promise is made, or someone else intending the promise to be made. This is established in Law 28, Title 11, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and the law *Dolo* in the Code <note>The Code of Justinian.</note> regarding useless stipulations. St. Thomas Aquinas agrees in 2. 2. question 89, article 7, response to the 3rd. As for what is added in the cited Law 28...

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...is joined, namely, even if a promise extorted by force, fear, or fraud is confirmed by an oath, the claim that the promisor is not bound to fulfill it is undoubtedly false. This is according to the arguments in Disputation 149 and according to what St. Thomas <note original: "D. Tho.">Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian</note> affirms in the cited response to the third point, unless the oath is first relaxed or the obligation to fulfill it is waived by the one to whom the promise was made. Read Gregorio López <note original: "Greg. Lopez">A famous Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the Siete Partidas</note> on that law.

<margin>6</margin> Indeed, regarding what is added in that law—namely, that if the fear, fraud, or force later ceases and the promisor fulfills the promise, the receiver is not bound to restore what was received—this is true in the **external court** <term>foro exteriori: the public legal system or civil court</term>. This is because the person is presumed to be giving of their own accord and wishing to confirm the past promise. The law "if by force" <note original: "l. si per vim. C. de ijs quæ vi, metusue causa fiunt">A reference to the Justinian Code regarding acts performed under duress</note> agrees with this. The same holds true in the **court of conscience** <term>foro conscientiæ: the internal moral judgment of a person before God</term>, if it is clear that they fulfilled the promise with that intent. However, if they fulfilled it involuntarily—perhaps because they were led by error to believe they were bound to fulfill the old promise, or for some other similar reason—then the receiver is bound in the court of conscience to restore what was received.

The reason for these things is twofold. First, because equity does not allow anyone to report a benefit from their own wickedness, whether for themselves or for another to whom they intended it; yet they would report such a benefit if someone who promised involuntarily were bound to fulfill that promise. Second, because that which is **mixed voluntary** <term>voluntarium mixtè: an action done under pressure where one chooses the lesser of two evils; it is voluntary because you chose it, but involuntary because you didn't want the circumstances</term> found in such a promise is caused by the injustice of the one intending the unjust effect. Such a "mixed voluntary" act is not sufficient for someone to transfer ownership or the right to their property to another, especially in acts of pure generosity, as is very well known.

If, however, the mixed voluntary act—by which something is promised to someone—only took its occasion from the wickedness of *another* person (who did not intend that specific effect), then the promise would be valid. For example, if someone, while their death is unjustly threatened by another, vows something to God so that He might snatch them from that danger, the promise is valid. Although they vow out of fear, the voluntary element seen in that vow only took its occasion from the unjust death that was threatening them.

Similarly, a promise would be valid by which someone promised something to another person to free them from such a danger <note>i.e., paying a third party for protection against a threat the third party did not create</note>. This is because the voluntary element in that promise was not the intent of the attacker, but only took its occasion from the wickedness of another. Likewise, when fear is justly inflicted, a promise arising from such fear would be valid, even if made to the one from whom the fear proceeds. For instance, if someone promised something to another so that they would remit a just punishment for themselves or another, the promise would be valid, provided the one remitting the punishment had the power to release it for that price or reward.

<margin>7</margin> Two things must be observed here. One is that

<column-break/>

**reverential fear** <note>The fear of upsetting a parent, superior, or someone in authority</note> is equal in this regard to fear struck through threats. Thus Sylvester <note original: "Sylv.">Sylvester Prierias, a 15th-century theologian</note> under the word "restitution," point 2, pronouncement 7. Navarrus <note original: "Nauar.">Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canon lawyer</note> agrees in all these things in his *Manual*, chapter 12, number 52, and chapter *non d’catis* number 67, at the section "I add thirteenthly," read the laws and doctors he cites.

<margin>8</margin> The second point is that in the **court of conscience**, even if the fear is not of the sort that would "overcome a steady man" <note original: "metus nō sit cadens in constantem virum">A legal standard in Roman law: fear must be significant enough to affect a reasonable, brave person, not just a fearful person</note>, if it truly makes the promise "mixed involuntary," it renders it null. Sylvester well notes this in the cited pronouncement 7 and the two following, and Navarrus agrees in the cited section. This is because fear renders a promise null precisely because it makes it mixed involuntary. In the **external court**, however, since the fear would be considered "light" (not affecting a steady man given the quality of the persons involved), help will not be given to the one who promised from such fear. This is because it is not presumed that such light fear made the promise mixed involuntary, as Navarrus rightly says in the cited place.

If, however, Peter promises Francis that he will **take care** or **see to it** that John gives him this or that, or that he performs this or that for him, such a promise is valid; because then he is promising his own act—that is, that he will take care or work it out with John. ...those who follow him, affirms that the promisor is held to nothing, based on the argument of the final law, the penultimate paragraph of the Digest *On the Rhodian Law of Jettison* <note original: "l. vlt. §. penult. ff. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu maris">Digest 14.2.10.1, regarding maritime loss</note>, and other legal principles. Indeed, in such a case, if he promised a penalty, he does not owe it, because he has not transgressed that which he bound himself to under that penalty.

However, when he has promised not only that he would **take care** <note original: "se curaturum">To use one's best efforts</note> but also that he would **bring it about** or **achieve it** <note original: "se effecturum, aut consequuturum">To guarantee a specific result</note> that another person would give or do something, I am pleased by the opinion of Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist known as the "Spanish Bartolus"</note> in the cited number 3, and others whom he cites (regardless of what many say to the contrary). Namely, that the promisor is held to damages <term>interesse<gloss>the difference between the current state and the state if the promise had been fulfilled</gloss></term>, or to a penalty if he imposed one upon himself, should the result not be achieved. For in that case, he is deemed to promise the penalty if he does not succeed, rather than the damages themselves. This is clearly what the cited law of Castile <note>A reference to the *Leyes de Toro* or the *Nueva Recopilación*</note> establishes. Yet understand this: unless it is clear from the circumstances that he did not wish to bind himself to anything if he did not succeed, but was only affirming, based on his own prayers and industry, that the other would do it, and saying so to signify with what great effort and diligence he would take care of it; and that the person to whom he promised this understood it so.

In the **court of conscience**, however, one must stand by the intention of the promisor. Unless, perhaps, he knew that he would not obtain the result, or he doubted it, and in that way deceived the person to whom he promised it, so that the person entered into a burdensome contract because of that promise which he otherwise would not have made. For example, if he brought it about that a man married a certain woman because he promised he would obtain some office for him from the King, and persuaded him of this as a certainty when he knew it was uncertain; for then he is bound to pay that man as much as the value of what he promised to obtain. On all these matters, read Maranta in his 7th disputation, in which he does not differ much from us.

<margin>9</margin>
According to **common law**, there are several instances in which a promise is binding, even if the act of another is promised. First, when the one who promised the act of another bound himself to a penalty unless that other performed it. For although he is not then held for damages (unless he promised it as an alternative with the penalty), he is nonetheless held to pay the penalty. This is found in the law "that stipulation" <note original: "l. stipulatio ista">Digest 45.1.38</note>, at the beginning of the final verse, *On Verbal Obligations*, and in the section "conversely" in the title *On Useless Stipulations* <note original: "tit. de inutilib. stipulat.">Institutes 3.19.21</note>; and the gloss on the section "if anyone another" affirms this in the same title of the Institutes. The reason is, as Covarruvias well notes in the cited place, that the promise then becomes his own obligation in the event of a default—that the other did not perform what was within the promisor's power to influence. Nor does that payment strictly have the nature of a penalty, but rather of compensation for the fact that the other was unwilling to act. Therefore, even if no fault occurred on the part of the promisor, he is held to pay that penalty.

Second, when someone promises that **his own heirs** will do something; for then they are held, as found in law 11, title 11, Part 5 <note>The Siete Partidas</note> and the final law of the Code *On Contracting Stipulations*. There it is simultaneously established that if someone promises that when he dies, he will build a house for someone, the promise is valid, and the heirs are held to fulfill it. The same is found in the section "thus however" in the title *On Useless Stipulations*.

Third, if someone in a **legal proceeding** promises that another will appear, or that another will ratify something; for then the promise is valid, and unless the other appears or

<column-break/>

ratifies what he promised in court would be ratified, the promisor is held for damages. This is found in that 13th law of Castile, and the law "as often as anything" <note original: "l. quoties quid">Digest 45.1.137.pr.</note> *On Verbal Obligations*, and law 2 *On Ratification*. The reason, according to Covarruvias in the cited place, number 7, is that in stipulations of this kind, by legal interpretation, the one who promises the act of another is deemed to promise damages unless the other performs it.

Fourth, in a promise or stipulation that the **property of a ward** will be safe, as found in the cited law 11 and the law "praetorian" <note original: "l. prætoriæ">Digest 46.5.1</note> *On Praetorian Stipulations*.

Fifth, when someone has promised the act of another **under oath**; for then, because he must not be presumed to intend to commit perjury, he is deemed to have intended to promise what was placed within his power—namely, that he would take care of it. This is the addition to the gloss on the section "if anyone another" in the title *On Useless Stipulations*. Panormitanus, Felinus, and the common opinion which they cite, follow Covarruvias in the chapter "Although a pact," part 2, section 5, number 2, and Gregorio Lopez on the cited law 11. Read the cited gloss for these and several other instances.

Regarding the remaining points we proposed:
<margin>10</margin>
A promise concerning a **sacred or religious thing**, and likewise concerning a public thing designated for the common use of all—which, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 12 and Disputation 79, cannot be possessed by the person to whom it is promised—is entirely invalid.

<margin>11</margin>
The same applies to a promise by which a **free man** is promised as a slave <term>mancipium<gloss>a person held as legal property</gloss></term>. This is found in section 1 of the Institutes *On Useless Stipulations*, in the law "between the stipulating parties," the section "sacred," *On Verbal Obligations*, and law 22, title 11, Part 5.

<margin>12</margin>
However, should a thing that was uselessly promised for that reason **change its status**—for instance, if a public thing becomes private, or a free man becomes a slave—the promise does not become valid because of that, but remains useless and void. But if, when the thing was promised, it was in such a condition that the promise was valid, and yet it later changes status—as if a slave obtains freedom, or if a thing that was private and secular becomes public or sacred—the promise is rendered useless. These points are found in the section "neither in suspense" and the section "likewise on the contrary" in the title *On Useless Stipulations*, and in the cited law 22. Concerning the promise of certain other things that cannot be possessed by the one to whom the promise was made, whether such a promise is valid, the same must be said as we said regarding the legacy of those same things at the end of Disputation 196.

<margin>13</margin>
Observe several things concerning these matters. First, if by the **act of the promisor** a slave obtained freedom, or a private thing became public or sacred, and for that reason rendered the promise useless, then he is held for damages, as is most well-known of itself and hinted at in the cited section "likewise on the contrary."

Second, if a thing is **partly sacred** and partly not—such as a chalice in regard to its silver, and similar things—then the promise made about the thing is valid in regard to that which is not sacred in the thing. Thus the gloss on section 1 at the word "religious" in the Institutes *On Useless Stipulations*.

Third, although a promise of a **grave** is invalid because a grave is a sacred thing, nevertheless a promise or gift of the **right of the grave**, or the right of bringing a dead person into the grave, would be valid; just as a legacy concerning rights of this kind is valid. Indeed, rights of this kind can be possessed by a layman, as in disputation...
<margin>14</margin>

Although either the right of a tomb, or the right of bringing a dead person into a tomb, may be granted, promised, given, and bequeathed, they cannot, however, be sold. This is because they are counted among sacred things <term>res sacrae<gloss>objects or rights dedicated to God or religious purposes</term>, and thus selling them would be the sin of simony <note original: "simoniae">The act of selling sacred or spiritual things</note>, as is clear from the Canon law <note original: "c. quaestia. & c. postquam. 13. q. 2.">References to the Decretum Gratiani</note> and the Laws of Castile <note original: "l. tit. 13. par. 2.">Reference to the Siete Partidas, the 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>. The fourth point is that, although a promise concerning a free man, a sacred thing, or a public thing is useless <note original: "inutilis">In a legal sense, meaning void or unenforceable</note>; nevertheless, if it was promised under an onerous title <term>oneroso titulo<gloss>a contract where both parties give and receive something of value</gloss></term> in compensation for another thing, then the promisor is held to damages <term>interesse<gloss>the financial difference the promisee suffers because the promise was not kept</gloss></term>. Specifically, they are liable for as much as it would matter to the other person if that thing were a slave or private property. In that case, they are held in the same way as if the promised thing belonged to someone else—they would be liable for eviction <note original: "de euictione">The legal liability of a seller if the buyer is deprived of the property by a third party with a better legal claim</note>. This is according to the Gloss on the section *On Useless Stipulations* <note original: "In tit. de inutilib. stip.">Digest 45.1</note>, Gregorio Lopez on the cited Law 22, and the doctors of law commonly. However, if it were promised under a lucrative title <note original: "titulo lucrativo">As a gift or without compensation</note>, the promisor would be held to nothing at all, unless they made the promise through fraud <term>dolus<gloss>intentional deceit or bad faith</gloss></term> and damage resulted from it.

### Whether a promise of a thing that exists only in hope is valid. And for whom the promised thing perishes.

## DISPUTATION CCLXIX.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A promise of a thing which is in hope is said to have a tacit condition—"if it should come to exist" or "if it is gathered"—and for that reason, it is valid.*
2 *Fraud and gross negligence are considered in the promise of a thing which is in hope.*
3 *When a promised thing has perished, at whose risk is it understood to have been destroyed.*

<margin>1</margin>
Regarding the first point, it must be said that a promise of those things which are still "in hope" is valid. Namely, fruits that will be born from some field, the offspring of a female slave <note original: "partus ancillae">Under the laws of the time, the children of enslaved women were considered property that could be contracted for before birth</note>, or of other animals, and similar things. However, such a promise has a tacit condition: *if* they are born, or *if* they are gathered from there. Otherwise, they are not owed, unless it happened through the fault of the one who promised that they were not born or gathered. Understand this to mean gross negligence <term>lata culpa<gloss>extreme carelessness or failure to exercise even slight care</gloss></term>, if the promise was
<margin>2</margin>
gratuitous. This is sufficiently expressed by the cited law of Castile, which says only that the promisor is held for fraud <note original: "de dolo">Deceit</note> and thus also for gross negligence, which is counted alongside fraud. We taught all these things in Disputation 200 regarding the legacy of similar things. And regarding the promise, this is found in Law 20, Title 11, Part 5, and the laws *Interdum* and *Inter stipulantem* in the Digest *On Verbal Obligations*.

Furthermore, fruits promised in this way must be paid when they have reached the state in which they can be handed over, as held in the cited Law 20. However, Gregorio Lopez rightly says there that fruits must be paid out according to their quality and the custom of when they are usually gathered. And the offspring of animals are not to be separated from their mothers and paid out before this can be done without danger to them.

Because, indeed, the offspring of a female slave can be nursed by another wo-

<column-break/>

-man, the child should certainly be nursed by its own mother in the meantime until another can be found. Afterward, however, it must be nursed and raised at the expense of the recipient <note original: "donatarij">The person receiving the gift</note>, which the recipient shall pay to the master of the slave woman, if another nurse cannot be conveniently found and it is necessary that the child be nursed by its own mother.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the second point: when a promised thing is a specific, individual item <term>in individuo<gloss>a unique, identified object, not just a general category</gloss></term> and must be paid on a certain day, if it should perish before that day arrives without the fault of the debtor (understand "fault" broadly, if it is owed from a gratuitous promise, according to what was said just before), the loss falls to the creditor <note original: "perit creditori">A legal maxim meaning the buyer/receiver bears the loss of a specific item if it is destroyed by chance</note>, and the promisor is held to nothing. So it is held in the penultimate law of the Digest *On Payments* <note original: "ff. de solutionib.">Digest 46.3</note>, and in Laws 18 and 9 of the Siete Partidas. Other laws agree, and manifest reason supports it, since only that specific thing was owed.

If, however, something remained of it that retains the same nature as it had in the whole—for example, if the promised thing was a ship or a house, and planks, wood, or stones remained—then that is owed to the creditor, according to what was said in Disputation 194 regarding the legacy of a similar thing. If, however, something remained of it which is of a different nature than it was in the whole—for example, if the meat of a promised animal remained—I believe it is not owed to the creditor, according to what was said in the same place, but belongs to the promisor.

All these same things are to be said similarly if no day was appointed on which that specific promised thing was to be paid and it perished before it was requested, without gross negligence by the promisor. But if the specific thing promised for a certain day perished after that day, or if a thing not promised for a certain day perished after the creditor rightly demanded it; then, if the promisor was not legitimately hindered, and thus was at fault in not paying it, the loss is his, and he is held to pay its value.

All these things are handed down in the cited Law 18, and other laws agree. If, however, he was legitimately hindered, so that he was not at fault in not paying it, the loss falls to the creditor, as is hinted in the same law and is established from the Digest <note original: "l. quod te mihi. ff. si cert. pet.">Digest 12.1.5</note> and the Digest on the *Rhodian Law of Jettison*. This is also consistent with the law *Cum res* and is affirmed by Bartolus and others whom Gregorio Lopez and Covarruvias follow.

These same principles similarly apply when some indeterminate part of a whole was promised, and that whole from which it was to be paid perished. For example, if from the wheat which is being carried for someone in a certain ship, he promises a measure <note original: "modium">A Roman unit of dry volume, roughly 9 liters</note>, and the entire wheat of the ship perishes, he is held to nothing. This is gathered from the law *In naui Saufeii* in the Digest *On Hiring*. And the reasoning is exactly the same as when a specific individual thing was promised.

When the promised thing was a specific slave, and before the promisor was in default <term>in mora<gloss>legal delay or failure to perform an obligation on time</gloss></term> in delivering him, the slave is killed by the promisor; then, if he kills the slave because of a crime committed against the promisor that was worthy of that punishment, he is held to nothing at all—for example, if he killed him because he found him committing adultery with his wife, or sleeping with his daughter. This is held in Law 19, Title 11, Part 6.

This is beyond doubt if it were done by public authori-

Nor is this lacking in probability: for, if it were another person's slave, he would not be bound to pay the value of that slave; since he would rightfully show that the slave was worthy of such a punishment, regardless of whose it was, so that the entire loss he caused by killing it is forgiven by public authority as compensation for the most serious injury he received from such a slave, and so that other men might henceforth abstain from such a shameful act. C. si cert. petat.">A reference to the Justinian Code regarding lawsuits for specific things</note>. Except, unless the promisor had fallen into such poverty because of that cause that it must be judged that he did not intend to bind himself in that event, according to what will be said below in Disputation 272 regarding the lawful revocation of a promise.

Observe this last point: when someone has bound themselves under a certain penalty to pay something by a certain time—whether it was determined as an individual, or certain in species or genus—then, if they could not pay it without their own fault, either because an impediment arose or because (according to what has been said so far) the thing promised perished, the promisor is certainly not held to the penalty. For a debtor is excused from even a conventional penalty when it was not their fault that the payment was not made, as Covarruvias <note original: "Cou. c. quāuis pactū">Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a major Spanish legal scholar</note> shows in part 2, paragraph 5, from number 4, regardless of what certain others may argue to the contrary.

Except, unless it was expressly stated in the agreement that he would be held to that penalty in any event, so that it no longer has the character of a penalty, but only the name, and is as it were an obligation for damages <term>interesse<gloss>the financial loss or "interest" one has in a contract being fulfilled</gloss></term>, even if he does not pay without his own fault. It must be seen, however, whether if the obligation to pay the principal debt remains, such a penalty takes on the character of usury <note original: "rationem induat usurae">Interest charged on a loan that is considered excessive or morally wrong</note>, and is therefore illicit: because it cannot be accepted as a true penalty, nor as compensation for emerging loss or ceasing profit <term>lucrum cessans<gloss>the loss of expected profit due to a breach of contract</gloss></term>, nor by any other just title. For if there were some just title by reason of which it was imposed, then it could rightly be demanded and received.

# On the promise of paying the debt of another, or of paying one's own on another day or at another place, and on promises made disjunctively, or cumulatively, and concerning an uncertain thing from among several.

## DISPUTATION 270.

->SUMMARY<-

1 A promise to pay the debt of another, even if it is only an informal agreement <term>pactum nudum<gloss>literally a "naked pact," an agreement that lacked the formal legal solemnities required by old Roman law but was increasingly recognized in later European law</gloss></term>, creates a civil obligation.

2 The same applies to the promisor's own debt. Clarify this, however, as in number 2.

The same applies to the promisor's own debt. Clarify this, however, as in number 2.

3 A promise to pay made disjunctively <note original: "disiunctiuè">Using "or," e.g., "I or Francis will pay"</note> or cumulatively <note original: "copulatiuè">Using "and," e.g., "I and Francis will pay"</note>: when it binds everyone to pay the whole amount <term>in solidum<gloss>a legal term meaning each person is responsible for the entire debt, not just a portion</gloss></term>, and when for a part.

4 How a promise of two or more things under a disjunctive name is to be fulfilled: and at whose risk the promised thing perishes. Clarify this as in the following number.

5 What a disjunctive clause placed in someone’s favor effects.

When someone promises another that they will pay a debt which a certain third party owes them—even if the promise is made between absent parties, whether by letter or by messenger, or by any other means, and even if no formal stipulation <margin>1</margin> intervenes but only an informal agreement—they contract a civil † obligation, and a legal action is granted against them. This is true even if the debt of the other person was only a "natural" debt <note original: "naturale">A debt that is morally owed but might not be legally enforceable in court</note>, for which an action would not be granted in the external court. The same is true if he promised that he would pay his own debt, but on another day or in another place. This is held in the section on established money in the *Institutes* and the *Digest*, and in Law 3, Title 11, Part 5 <note original: "l. 3. tit. 11 part. 5">A reference to the Siete Partidas</note>. And we also counted this outcome in Disputation 255 among those in which, by common law, an action is granted from an informal agreement by privilege of the law.

<margin>2</margin> Note, however, that for an action to be granted from such a promise in the external court, it is necessary that it be sufficiently understood from the words of the promisor themselves that they intended to bind themselves. For if they only said, "The debt which Peter owes you will be paid in full," or something similar which is ambiguous as to whether they intended to bind themselves personally, they will not be compelled to pay in the external court because of such words. This is expressly held in the authentic text "if ever" in the Code and in Law 3, Title 11, Part 5.

<margin>3</margin> But if he who † makes himself a debtor for another says this: "I promise you that I, or Francis, will pay you Peter's debt"; then, if Francis consents, both are held to pay the debt, but each of them for only half. If, however, Francis does not consent, then the one who promised under that form is held to pay the entire debt. But if the promise is made cumulatively in this form: "I promise you that I and Francis will pay you Peter's debt," then whether Francis consents or not, the one who promised in that form is only held to pay half. All these things are expressly established by the three laws cited.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis from page 44 regarding indeterminate obligations and the destruction of promised items. It focuses on Disputation 270, which examines "disjunctive obligations"—promises to provide one thing or another—and how the law handles ambiguity or disagreement between the parties.</meta>

->Second Treatise. Disputation 270.<-

the person making the promise has the power to pay whichever of those things he prefers, as is very well known from the law itself; this is gathered from the law <note original: "l. stipulatus sum Damam. ff. de verborum obl.">"I stipulated for Dama," Digest, on verbal obligations</note> and is held in the law <note original: "l. 2. §. Scæuola. ff. de eo quod certo loco">Digest, concerning what is [to be given] in a certain place</note> and in the <term>Siete Partidas</term> <note original: "l. 23. tit. 11. par. 5.">The fifth Partida, title 11, law 23 of the medieval Spanish legal code</note>.

If, however, before the promise is fulfilled, one of those things should perish, the <term>promisor</term> <note>the person who made the promise</note> is bound to pay the remaining one. This is held in the law <note original: "l. Stichum. §. 1. ff. de solutionib.">Digest, on payments, regarding the slave Stichus</note> and several other passages in the Digest and the <term>Siete Partidas</term>. Furthermore, if the item that perished was of less value, or if the promisor began to have a greater need for it or a greater affection for it, he may satisfy the debt by offering the value of the item that perished, provided that he himself had the right to choose which one to pay.

To me, the side that affirms this seems true when that thing did not perish through the fault of the promisor, as the gloss on the aforementioned section "Scævola" correctly estimates in the word *only*, according to the marginal addition. This is proved by the law <note original: "l. cum res. §. sed si Stichus. ff. de leg. 1.">Digest, on legacies, book 1</note> and is embraced by Gregorio López in his commentary on the cited law 23. However, when that thing perishes through the fault of the promisor, the creditor might not be satisfied with the price, but may wish to receive the thing that remains safe, as is expressly held in the law regarding the slave <term>Stichus</term>. But if, after the promisor had chosen that specific thing to pay, it were to perish without his fault, he would not be bound to pay the one that remains, nor the price of the one that perished; instead, the loss falls upon the person to whom the promise was made, as is self-evident and agreed upon in the cited section "Scævola."

**5** Observe this: if someone should say, "I grant you one or two carts of wood from my forest," or something similar, or should say, "I permit you to extract them," then the choice belongs to the <term>donatary</term> <note>the person receiving the gift</note>. This is because the "either/or" choice was clearly added for their benefit. Therefore, after they have extracted one cart, the owner of the forest cannot prohibit them from extracting another. This is the opinion of Maranta, along with many others whom he cites.

**6** When a single specific thing was promised in the singular, yet it is ambiguous which of two or more things it might be—for example, if the promisor had two slaves of the same name, let us say, <term>Pamphilus</term>, and said, "I promise you my slave Pamphilus"—and it cannot be determined from the surrounding circumstances which one he meant; then the choice belongs to the promisor or his heirs, according to the Digest and the <term>Siete Partidas</term>.

In this event, however, if one of those things should perish, I do not believe he is bound to pay the other. Instead, one must rely on the oath of the promisor as to which one he intended. But if he is deceased, and it is entirely unknown whether it was the one that remains or the one that perished, then certainly the one that remains must be divided between the one to whom the promise was made and the heirs of the promisor.

The reason is that the obligation of the promisor did not fall upon both things (as in a promise of two things under an "either/or" condition), but only upon one of them; yet it is unknown which one was intended. In the <term>internal forum</term> <note original: "foro conscientiæ">The "court of conscience," referring to moral and religious obligation rather than civil law</note>, when the promisor is certain which one he intended: if he intended the one that perished, he is bound to nothing; but if he intended the other, he is bound to pay it in full, as is self-evident.

<column-break/>

**7** Observe this: when the promisor intended one thing, but the person who requested the thing intended another and <term>stipulated</term> for it, the <term>stipulation</term> <note>a formal verbal contract</note> or promise is invalid. This is held in the Institutes <note original: "§. si de alia, Instit. de inutilib. stipulat.">Institutes of Justinian, on useless stipulations</note> and the Digest, as well as the <term>Siete Partidas</term>.

The reason is that for a stipulation to be valid, it is necessary that the person stipulating and the person promising agree on one and the same thing. Otherwise, the contract is perfected regarding nothing; indeed, not even a simple pact is completed by the promise of one thing and the acceptance of another. Hence, if one asks for Pamphilus, and the other responds, "No, but I will give you Stichus," the promise and stipulation are invalid, unless the stipulator immediately accepts Stichus.

By this same reasoning, if someone stipulates absolutely, saying, "Do you promise to give me ten?" and the other responds under a condition, "I promise, if the ships from India arrive this year," then unless the stipulator accepts that conditional promise immediately, such a promise or stipulation is useless. The same is true if someone stipulates for one thing specifically, such as Pamphilus, and the other responds, "I will give you Pamphilus or Stichus." This stipulation and promise are also invalid unless the one stipulating immediately accepts that "either/or" promise. Furthermore, it is the same if a stipulation for several things under an "either/or" condition comes first, followed by a grant of only one of them specifically; even if it is accepted immediately, it is invalid, as Antonio Gómez affirms.

**8** Nevertheless, if someone stipulated for a hundred, and the other responds, "I will give you fifty," even if a new acceptance does not occur, the promise is valid specifically for fifty. This is because it is a promise of a part that was contained within the original stipulation. The same applies if one requested a horse and a mule, and the other responded, "I will give you a horse"; for the promise is valid regarding the horse, since the horse was included in the request.

But if, to a person stipulating for a hundred, the response is "I will give you a hundred and fifty," unless the extra fifty are accepted immediately, the promise for the extra fifty is invalid; it is valid only for the hundred requested and promised. This is found in the Digest, the Institutes, and the <term>Siete Partidas</term>.

Furthermore, when the Institutes say that a stipulation is invalid if you ask for ten and the answer is "I will give five," or if you ask for five and the answer is "I will give ten," this must be understood as follows: it is not invalid regarding the five included in the ten (on which both parties agree), but regarding the other five where they disagree.

**9** In the <term>internal forum</term>, however, I consider that if the person who was asking accepted the terms in that sense because he was pleased with it, even if he said nothing—and the promisor understood this, as is always to be presumed when it is beneficial to the one being promised—then according to the rule...

It establishes that while the debtor usually chooses which item to pay, mutual consent and specific intent are required for a contract to be valid in both civil law and moral conscience.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

the rule <note original: "qui tacet, de reg. iu. in 6.">"he who is silent [is seen to agree]," from the Rules of Law in the Sixth Book of Decretals</note>, which is to be understood as applying to the silent party in matters that are favorable to them, the promisor is held to be bound to give that thing according to what was stated in Disputation 264.

<margin>10</margin> I believe the same is true here in the **Kingdom of Castile** in the civil courts, on account of the third law of this kingdom, which is frequently cited, and according to **Canon Law**, where the formal solemnity of a <term>stipulation</term><note>A formal verbal contract in Roman law that required specific matching words between the parties to be valid.</note> is not necessary. Antonio Gómez agreed with us on this <note original: "2. tom. var. resol. c. 9. nu. 4. conclus. 1. & 4.">in his *Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 9</note>, regardless of what Gregorio López says in his commentary on the cited law 26. I believe the same would apply when one party asks for something under a condition and the other grants it absolutely, or if one asks for a longer period for payment and the other grants a shorter one—notwithstanding what Antonio Gómez says to the contrary in conclusion 2 of the cited section. This is because the promisor intends to bind himself, as we suppose; and since what is promised is more favorable to the petitioner than what he originally asked for, there is no doubt that he has tacitly accepted the promise. Indeed, I believe the same would hold when he asks absolutely and it is granted under a condition, or if he asks for a shorter time and a longer one is granted, provided the circumstances entirely persuade us that the petitioner tacitly accepted what was granted to him, even though it was not granted in the exact way he requested. This is true regardless of the subtleties of **Imperial Law** <note original: "iuris Cæsarei">Roman Civil Law, often contrasted with local or church law.</note>.

And I believe the same applies when the stipulation is phrased as a choice between two things (a disjunction) and the response is for one specific thing; or conversely, the stipulation is for one specific thing and the grant is phrased as a choice between that thing and another. Note that even if these would not be valid as a formal stipulation unless an immediate acceptance of the response followed, they would still be valid as a **simple promise** that was at least tacitly accepted.

Finally, observe that if the person asking and the person promising agree on the thing promised, but the name of the place designated for payment was ambiguous, and one understood one place while the other understood another, the promise is still valid. If there are clues as to which place was likely being discussed, the promisor should be forced to pay in that place—unless the promisor acted with deceit, which should not benefit him. This follows the law <note original: "l. quoties in stipulationibus... ff. de ve. b. obl.">"As often as in stipulations," from the Digest on verbal obligations</note> and the *Siete Partidas* <note original: "l. 25. tit. 11. par. 5.">The fifth Partida, title 11, law 25</note>. If, however, the matter is entirely doubtful, the place that is more favorable to the promisor must be chosen, according to the rule <note original: "l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. de regul. iuris.">"In stipulations, the interpretation should always be..." from the Rules of Law in the Digest.</note>.

### On the promise of an impossible or illicit
### thing, or that which is against good morals
### because it provides an occasion for ruin;
### and what if the latter is
### confirmed by an oath.

### DISPUTATION 271.

->SUMMARY<-

1 A promise of a thing that is simply impossible is void, even if it is a legal impossibility; see number 2. However, limit and clarify this in many ways, as in numbers 2 and 4.

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> A promise concerning an evil thing—whether evil in itself or because it is prohibited—is void. Clarify this, however, so that the promise remains valid for the part that is licit or possible; number 4.
<margin>5</margin> A promise or agreement against **good morals**, or one that leads to sin, is void by the law itself. Clarify fully in the following numbers.
<margin>7</margin> When the remission <note>forgiveness or waiving of a claim</note> of fraud or theft is valid. Clarify in number 10.
<margin>8</margin> When promises or agreements that are void only by human law are valid if confirmed by an oath.
<margin>9</margin> The multiple types of promises against good morals.
<margin>11</margin> What is included under the term "promise" when someone remits something in the past or the future.
<margin>12</margin> A release from being held to give an account of administration does not prevent one from being held to return those things which, if such a remission had not been made, one would be bound to return by a real action.

<margin>1</margin> For a promise to be binding, it is necessary that what is promised be possible; for **no one is bound to the impossible** <note original: "l. impossibilium. ff. de regul. iur.">Law "Of impossible things," Digest, Rules of Law</note>, and the rule "No one can" <note original: "regula nemo potest, de regul. iur. in 6.">Rules of Law in the Sixth Book of Decretals</note>. For this reason, if someone promises a specific, individual thing that had already perished when the promise was made, or which perished before the time for payment arrived, such a promise is void because it is impossible to fulfill what was promised. This is held in the section on useless stipulations and the *Siete Partidas*.

<margin>2</margin> An exception is made when the thing was taken by theft and then perished. After it has perished, if the person to whom the thief owed the item stipulates for it, the stipulation and promise are valid to the effect that the thief is held to pay the value to the stipulator. This is because the thief was in <term>mora</term><note>A legal state of "delay" or default where the debtor bears the risk of the object's loss regardless of how it happens.</note> and owed the item due to the unjust taking. The same applies whenever a debtor of a thing was in *mora* for any other reason when the item perished. However, if the owner stipulated for the item from the thief *before* it perished, or if the thief promised to hand it over on a certain day with the other party consenting, and the item perished in the meantime, it perishes for the owner. In that case, the thief is held to nothing, because by the intervention of that stipulation or accepted promise, the thief ceases to be in *mora* for the delivery. This is expressly held in the law <note original: "l. scire. §. vlt. ff. de ver. obl.">Digest, on verbal obligations.</note>

Just as physical impossibility makes a promise void, so too does **legal impossibility**, whether it arises from divine law or human law.

<margin>3</margin> For this reason, a promise concerning an evil thing—whether it is evil in itself or prohibited by positive law—is void by that very fact. <note original: "§. quod turpi. Instit. de inutilib. stipulationib.">"That which is for a shameful cause," Institutes, on useless stipulations</note>. The reasoning is supported by the fact that it implies a contradiction for anyone to be bound to do what is illicit.

<summary>This page discusses legal nuances of contract acceptance through silence or partial agreement and introduces the principle that promises of impossible, illegal, or immoral acts are legally void. It specifically addresses how the destruction of a promised item or the "legal delay" (mora) of a thief affects the validity of an obligation.</summary>
