<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 271.</header>

holds: for then he would call it illicit, and a perplexity would be created in which we would sin both by doing it and, similarly, by not doing it; both of which are clearly very absurd. Regarding this entire matter, much has been said in Disputation 95.

<margin>4</margin> Observe this: where a promise is partly licit and partly illicit, or partly possible and partly impossible, then the one who promised is held to fulfill the licit and possible part. For "the useful is not vitiated by the useless," as the rule <note original: "utile per inutile non vitiatur, de reg. iu. lib. 6.">A legal maxim meaning that a valid part of a document is not made void by an invalid part.</note> regarding the rules of law states in the Sixth Book of Decretals.

Some apply this example to a **prodigal promise** <note>A "prodigal" promise is one where the giver is recklessly or excessively generous, often beyond their means or social standing.</note>, saying that the promisor is held to fulfill the promise only regarding an amount in which there is no prodigality, but not regarding the excess. I believe, however, that this example is false. For although a promise may arise from liberality (that is, not from a prior debt), once the promise is made, its fulfillment and execution are not an act of liberality but of debt—either out of justice, if the promise was such that it bound out of justice, or out of moral honesty, if the promise bound only out of moral honesty and transferred a right based on that honesty, according to the principles handed down in the previous sections. 

Therefore, since there is no prodigality in the execution, but rather the fulfillment of a debt already contracted through justice or moral equity, once the promise is made, the promisor is certainly held to fulfill the entire promise in the court of conscience and the external court. It is no hindrance that the promise was prodigal and involved a <term>venial sin</term><note>A "venial" sin is a lesser sin that does not completely break one's relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" or deadly sin.</note>; the promisor must blame his own imprudence and fault for promising such an amount. This cannot prejudice the right that the recipient acquired from such a promise. Just as it would not be prejudiced if that prodigal gift began with the actual delivery of the item, or if delivery took place after the prodigal promise was made; for the recipient is not held to restore what was received simply because it was given to him prodigally. 

Indeed, if the example we reject were true, it would follow that a rich noble girl—who did wrong by entering into an engagement against the will of her father with a man of low birth and no wealth—would not be held to fulfill what she promised, on the grounds that it was promised with sin and prodigality, and because the execution could not happen without causing scandal to others and disgrace to the girl herself. But no one can affirm that, especially since it is against the practice of the Church. For although that girl was prodigal and did wrong in making that promise, the other person nevertheless acquired a right of justice for himself through that promise. The girl, once the promise is made, does not do wrong by fulfilling it; rather, she does good—indeed, she does what she is bound to do by justice, and if she were to fail in it, she would sin mortally.

<margin>5</margin> Not only is a promise void if the promisor would transgress some right and thus sin venially or mortally by carrying it out, but those promises or pacts are also null which are against **good morals** because they either provide a manifest occasion for sin or bring prejudice to the morals that it is expedient to maintain in a well-ordered republic.

From the first heading, promises and pacts are null and void by the law itself <note original: "ipso iure">A legal term meaning the law invalidates the act automatically, without needing a specific court ruling.</note>

<column-break/>

by which one person grants to another that he should not be held liable for theft or fraud <note original: "dolo">Fraud or intentional deceit.</note> that he might commit, or that such restitution cannot be demanded from him. For example, if someone hired another as a manager, buyer, or agent of his affairs, having entered into a pact with him that he would not be held liable for fraud or theft committed in that administration: such a pact or promise is null by the law itself because it is against good morals. It would provide <margin>7</margin> a manifest occasion for ruin for such a manager, and this ought not to be permitted for any reason in any well-ordered republic. 

If, however, after the theft or fraud has been committed in the course of administration, the person to whom those goods or rights belonged chooses to forgive them, then such a remission is valid; since it does not provide an occasion for future ruin, but only pardons debts or offenses already committed. Similarly, it is invalid if someone makes a pact or grants to another that he not be held liable for an injury or violence that he might inflict in the future; it is otherwise, however, if the injury or violence already inflicted is pardoned. Likewise, it is invalid if a person making a will grants to a guardian or curator that they shall not be held liable for fraud committed in the administration of his children's property. These rules are found in the Digest and Code of law <note original: "l. si vunus... ff. de pactis... C. de pactis.">References to the Corpus Iuris Civilis, the foundation of Roman law.</note> and the laws of the *Siete Partidas* <note>The landmark 13th-century statutory code of Castile.</note>. The same applies if someone, inciting another to theft or another crime, promises before the crime is committed that he will pay the penalty in the other's place if he is condemned for it in the future.

From the second heading, the following pacts and promises are null: 
1. If someone promises that he will not revoke a will, or that he will die without a will (intestate), as was said in Disputation 151. 
2. If someone makes a deal with another saying, "Do you promise to give me this much only if you do not appoint me your heir?" Such a promise is null because it takes away the power of freely making a will. 
3. A donation of all present and future goods is similarly null, because it takes away the power of making a will, as will be discussed later. 
4. A pact concerning the inheritance of someone who is still living—under the condition that the goods might come to them—is null unless the person whose goods they are consents to the pact. 
5. A pact involving a penalty for someone who breaks off a marriage engagement is also null, because marriages ought to be free, and such a penalty detracts from that freedom. 

All similar pacts and promises are void, as prejudice to good morals and the common good of a well-ordered republic can easily arise from them. For this reason, they are invalidated by human law.

Observe this, however: since the things that fall under these pacts and promises are not evil in themselves, nor are such pacts and promises null of their own nature but only by the disposition of human law, this rule must not be extended further...

48 Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...how they are rendered void by human law. This argument does not hold: that there is as much, or greater, reason for this to be rendered void as for that, nor that no fewer inconveniences are born from this than from that; therefore, just as that is void by such human law, so this should be judged void. For, in order for something to be rendered void or prohibited by human law, it is not enough for there to be sufficient causes for it to be prohibited or rendered void; rather, it is further required that, by a disposition of the law on account of those or other causes, it is actually prohibited or voided. In the meantime, as long as that disposition of the law is not added, it is to be judged as neither void nor prohibited.

<margin>Quest. 8</margin>
The doubt is whether pacts and promises, which are void and null by human law based on the two points explained, bind to their observation by the force of an oath if they are confirmed by one. Many, led by the fact that such pacts and promises are often said in law to be **against good morals** <note original: "contra bonos mores">A legal term referring to actions that conflict with the established ethical standards or public policy of a society.</note>, commonly judge that even if they are confirmed by an oath, they nevertheless do not bind, as we reported in part in Disputation 151. For an oath performed against good morals is not obligatory, as held in the law *non est obligatorium*, regarding the rules of law, book 6.

<margin>Argu- ment.</margin>
<margin>Decis.</margin>
In this place, this universal rule must be established, by which we shall resolve the questions occurring in these matters in the following sections. If a promise or pact is made to a human and confirmed by an oath, they bind, even if they are void by human law according to the two points explained—provided, however, that the oath by which they are confirmed is not also found to be void by human law. Therefore, when the oath is not also void by human law, then, for a promise or pact confirmed by an oath to not bind to its fulfillment when made to a human, it is necessary that they concern an evil thing—that is, something prohibited by divine or human law. Nor would it be enough if the promise itself or the pact were prohibited from being made, but it would be necessary that the execution itself, or the object of the promise or pact, be prohibited, as we showed in Disputation 151. This rule will be found sufficiently proven if what we said in the cited Disputation 151 is weighed, joining the two preceding ones, where we most strongly confirmed it regarding a promise not to revoke a will, and in several other events. It is exactly the same in the rest of the matters included therein, and where we laid the foundations, it is quite clear. Indeed, we can confirm it because a promise by which we promise interest to a **usurer** <note>A person who lends money at interest, which was often legally or morally restricted in this period.</note>, or a hundred to a **highwayman** <note original: "grassatori">A bandit or violent thief who accosts travelers.</note> so that he does not unjustly kill us, is no less against good morals; these people cannot receive such things without lethal fault and the burden of restitution. Nor is such a promise any less void than other promises which, based on the two mentioned points, are against good morals. But that promise made to the usurer or highwayman binds if it is confirmed by an oath, as shown in Disputation 149. Therefore, these others also bind when they are made to a human, and when the oath by which they are confirmed is not void by human law.

We said that such promises and pacts confirmed by an oath bind if they are made to a human; because if they are made to God, so that they take on the character of a vow confirmed by an oath, and either they are not regarding a good thing, or even if

<column-break/>

they are regarding a good thing, they impede some greater good, then they do not bind. This is because God does not want indifferent things promised to Him, nor likewise does He want a greater good to be hindered by promises made to Him, as was shown in the three cited disputations.

We added, moreover: "provided the oath by which they are confirmed is not also void by human law." For if it is made void by human law, even if such pacts and promises are made to a human, they do not assume strength from the oath, as explained in Disputation 149, using an example from the **Council of Trent** <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Reformation.</note>, session 25, chapter 16. There, renunciations and obligations—even for pious causes—made by novices before their profession are rendered void, even if confirmed by an oath, unless they are made with the license of the Bishop or his vicar within only two months before the profession, etc. An example is also used from **Portuguese law and the law of the Kingdom of Castile** <note>Molina was a Jesuit theologian who lived and taught in both Portugal and Spain (Castile).</note>, where obligations and contracts are void if an oath is attached to them, and this is so that secular cases are not called away from the secular to the **ecclesiastical court** <note original: "Ecclesiasticum forum">Church courts, which had jurisdiction over cases involving oaths.</note> for that reason.

<margin>9</margin>
<margin>To the argum.</margin>
Regarding that from which many are said to depart from our rule, it must be said that something is called "against good morals" in two ways. One is narrow and proper: because it is clearly at least a venial sin against divine or human law. The other is broad: because although it is not a sin in itself, it can easily bring prejudice to the good morals that ought to be preserved in a well-ordered republic, as explained in Disputation 151. When, however, the laws affirm that the pacts and promises of which our rule speaks are against good morals, they take "being something against good morals" in the broad sense. But the rule of law which holds that an oath performed against good morals is not obligatory takes "being something against good morals" in the narrow sense—namely, for that which is contrary to good morals, which is sin alone.

<margin>10</margin>
It was said above that if, after **theft or fraud** <note original: "furti, aut dolus">Theft or deceit/fraudulent dealing.</note> have been committed in administration or in any other matter, they are forgiven, the forgiveness is valid. This is because it does not provide an occasion for ruin, as it would if someone forgave fraud or theft before they were committed; rather, it only pardons a debt contracted and a crime committed, as is expressly held in the law *si unus*, paragraph *illud*, joined with the gloss there, and the paragraph *pacta* in the Digest *de pactis*. It must be observed, however, that when someone has had the administration of another, or conducted their business, or shared something with them, or had a partnership or any other business: from the fact that they are freed from the duty of rendering an account of the administration, or that they receive a release from the one who could provide it after a division is made or an account of any other thing rendered—indeed, from the fact that the one who delivers the release promises that they will require nothing further from them regarding that matter—they are not for that reason judged to be forgiving if the person took anything by theft from there, or if they committed any fraud in that administration or business. Rather, they can demand it, unless they have expressly forgiven the fraud or theft committed, or they effect the release or forgiveness with such words that it is sufficiently understood that they intended to remit the fraud or theft as well. Thus it is held in the law *tres fratres*, in the Digest *de pactis*; the law *quidam decedens* (otherwise the law *ita autem*, paragraph *Iulianus*), in the Digest *de administ. tut.*; and the law *Aurelio*, paragraph *Gaius*, in the Digest *de liber.*

For that is what such a remission signifies; and certainly, such a release is not rendered void by any law, even for the future.

<margin>12</margin>

Indeed, if he owed something else beyond that for which the accounting was remitted to the person who remitted it, he can still be compelled to pay. This is gathered from the law *Aurelio*, paragraph *Caius*, law *Aurelius*, paragraph *Maevia*, and the law *creditor debitori*, paragraph *Titia*, in the Digest, on the legacy of releases. ## On the causes for which it is lawful not to 
## fulfill a promise that has been accepted 
## before it is carried out.

### DISPUTATION CCLXXII.

### S U M M A R Y

1. For what reasons it is lawful for a promise not to be fulfilled before it is perfected by delivery.
2. What is necessary for someone to be bound to fulfill a promise.
3. A general promise does not bind the promisor except to those things to which, if asked, he would likely have responded that he intended to bind himself.
**Expand on this in many ways, as in number 6.**
**Likewise, understand this much more strongly in the "court of conscience" <note original: "in foro conscientiae">Refers to moral/religious obligation before God, as opposed to civil law.</note>, under number 3.**
**Clarify this, however, as in numbers 7, 8, 9, and 10.**
4. One promising to take a certain woman as his wife is not bound to marry her if she commits fornication before the marriage is contracted.
**Expand this to include if she becomes leprous or paralyzed before the marriage, or if something more shameful should happen to her, number 5.**
**Clarify as stated there.**
11. A mutual promise: if it is not fulfilled by one side, it can lawfully not be fulfilled by the other.
12. What kind of ingratitude suffices to revoke even a perfected donation.

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
In Disputation 263, it was shown that it is lawful to revoke a promise before it is accepted, except in certain cases explained there. In its proper place below, we will also explain the causes for which it is universally lawful to revoke a donation, even if it has been fully completed by delivery. Now, however, we are only disputing for what causes it is lawful not to fulfill a promise before it is perfected by delivery: both when it has been accepted, and also in those events in which we said in Disputation 263 that it binds before it is accepted.

<margin>2</margin>
St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 110, article 3, in the fifth response—along with Seneca and Tully <note>Cicero</note>—says that for one to be bound to fulfill his own promise (which would otherwise be obligatory), it is necessary that the status of the persons, things, or business does not change. Cajetan, Soto (in *On Justice and Right*, book 7, question 2, article 1), Navarrus (in his *Manual*, chapter 18), and the doctors of law commonly subscribe to this. However, not just any change suffices. Nevertheless, a change would suffice if it rendered fulfillment impossible in fact, or even in law—that is, if fulfillment became illicit, according to what was said in the preceding disputations.

For example, if I promised to give a certain slave or horse on a certain day, and they died before that day, you are bound to nothing by that very fact.

Likewise, if you promised to give a sword, and before delivery the one to whom it was promised falls into a rage or madness, you are not bound to give it to him; indeed, you would rather sin by delivering it to him. You are bound, however, either to keep it for him until another time or to deliver it (or its value) to his guardian.

<margin>3</margin>
Furthermore, a change releases the promisor from fulfilling the promise if, had the change occurred to him when he made the promise, he would have made an exception for it; or if, had he been asked then, he would have answered that his mind was not to bind himself in such an event. The reason for this is that a liberal or gratuitous promise does not bind more than the promisor intended to bind himself; and the promisor did not intend to bind himself in that event. For just as in a general grant those things are not included which the person would likely not have granted in a specific case (as held in the rule *in generali*, on the rules of law, book 6), so in a promise those events are not included which the promisor would have excepted when he made the promise, had they been proposed to him specifically with these or those circumstances. For just as *epicheia* <note>The principle of equity: interpreting a law or promise according to the spirit and intention of the maker rather than the strict literal wording.</note> has a place in laws to except events which the legislator would have excepted had they occurred to him (and which are therefore not considered included in such laws, even if the legislator thought nothing of them when he passed the law), so it is also in a promise. A promise is like a law that the promisor imposes upon himself; therefore, events are not considered included which the promisor would have excepted then, had they occurred to him or been proposed. Nor can there be any better interpreter of his own promise than the promisor himself, even if he promised absolutely and thought nothing of events that were then unforeseen.

For when such events arise, he is to be asked whether, if they had occurred to him or been proposed by another while he was promising, he would have said that his intention was not to bind himself in those cases. If he responds that he would not have, they are to be judged as not having been included.

<meta>This page continues Disputation 272 of Louis de Molina’s work on contracts. Having established the general principle that promises are subject to "tacit conditions," Molina now provides specific practical examples involving religious vows, marriage contracts, and financial obligations, focusing on how a significant change in circumstances—or facts unknown at the time of the promise—can release a person from their debt or duty.</meta>

# Louis de Molina, On Contracts

<column-break/>

Here are some examples. First, if you vowed to God to fast every Friday of the year, and in that year the Feast of the Nativity of the Lord <note>Christmas</note> falls on a Friday, on which day all the faithful eat meat; to judge whether on that day, with nothing hindering your vow, you may eat meat and not fast, you must be asked: if, when you made the vow, it had occurred to you that the feast of the Nativity would fall on a Friday that year, would you have excluded that day? If you answer affirmatively, you are certainly not bound to fast.

But if you are hesitant, and possess a conscience that is more scrupulous and fearful than is just, it must be judged by the decision of a prudent person that you are not bound to fast. For it is not to be believed that you intended both to abstain from meat on that day and to be an outlier in your household, with the burden of fish being prepared for you alone.

<margin>4</margin>
Next, if you promised a woman that you would take her as your wife, and, before the marriage is contracted, she commits fornication, you are not bound to marry her: because you did not intend to bind yourself to marry her in that event, should such a circumstance arise; furthermore, because she is unworthy of you keeping the faith you pledged to her. This is held in the chapter *Quemadmodum*, on the law of oaths <note original: "cap. quemadmodum, de iureiur.">A reference to Canon Law, specifically the Decretals of Gregory IX, Book 2, Title 24, Chapter 21.</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
Where it is added that the same applies if, after such a promise, she were to become leprous, paralyzed, or lose her eyes or nose, or if something else more shameful or equally shameful should happen to her: for all these events, through <term>equity (epicheia)</term> <note>The principle of interpreting a law or promise according to its spirit and the intention of the maker rather than its strict literal wording.</note>, are judged not to be included in that absolute promise made without any limitation. Such a promise always contains a tacit condition: "provided the state of things is not changed in these ways." The same would apply if you promised to marry someone you believed to be a virgin.

For if, before the marriage is contracted, you learn for certain—either through your own experience or the report of others—that she was not then a virgin, you are not bound to marry her, since if you had known this, you would never have promised to marry her. However, when the cited chapter *Quemadmodum* says that he who promised under oath to marry a woman cannot raise the objection of *prior* fornication, but only *subsequent* fornication, this must be understood as referring to prior fornication known to him at the time of the promise. It is otherwise regarding unknown fornication through which she lost her virginity, or which rendered her notably more infamous than she was known to him before. For if at the time of the promise she was already infamous for fornications and he knew it, and nevertheless promised to marry her, the fact that other fornications are discovered later which make her only slightly more infamous is not a sufficient cause to make it lawful to not fulfill the promise.

<margin>6</margin>
Similarly, if you promised something and later fell into such great poverty that, if you had foreseen it, you would never have promised such a thing, you are not bound to fulfill the promise. Likewise, if you promised your labor to someone to manage their business or for anything else, and your son falls into a serious illness such that he greatly needs your labor and presence, and you are not sufficient for both tasks, you are not bound to fulfill the promise: because you did not intend to obligate yourself in that event.

The same applies in other similar events, which must be judged by the decision of a prudent person, considering the quality and quantity of the change in circumstances, compared with

<column-break/>

the thing promised, and weighing all other concurrent circumstances. For one must always follow what right reason prescribes or what a prudent person's judgment determines, as <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), an influential Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> rightly noted in Question 113, and no more convenient or certain rule can be established. However, the proposed examples should be kept before the mind’s eye, by which anyone may easily be guided to judge other events that may occur.

<margin>7</margin>
There are, however, several things to be observed. The first is that if a person has been in <term>default (mora)</term> <note>A legal term for an unjustifiable delay in fulfilling an obligation.</note> of fulfilling what they promised, and an impediment later arises which would have fully released them had it occurred before the delay, they do not remain fully released. For although they are not then bound to fulfill what they promised, they are nevertheless bound for the <term>damages (interesse)</term> <note>The loss suffered or profit lost due to the non-fulfillment of the contract.</note> and losses following from the fact that they did not fulfill it at the time when they could and should have. Hence, if you promised to pay a hundred this month, etc., and when you were able and there was no cause to excuse you, you neglected to do so, and by chance you later fell into the greatest poverty, this certainly does not excuse you from the burden of paying it, no differently than other debts to which you were bound by crime or an onerous contract before that poverty; because from the time of the delay, you are bound by the unjust detention to pay damages and subsequent losses, and thus by way of a fault.

<margin>8</margin>
Second, if the impediment excusing one from the fulfillment of a promise is temporary, the promise must be fulfilled after the impediment is removed. For example, if you promised to enter a religious order and an event occurred which, had you foreseen it, you would not have bound yourself to enter in that circumstance, you are certainly bound to enter the religious order when things return to their original state. This observation, however, must be judged by the decision of a prudent person; for it is not universal. For if, while you were rich, you promised a hundred to Peter out of generosity—because, among other things, your status and abundance of goods invited it—and before you were in default you suddenly fell into the greatest poverty, you are surely entirely excused from fulfilling the promise. Nor are you bound to fulfill the promise if later, by some chance or your own industry, you come into a rich fortune; because you did not intend to obligate yourself except in the state of things in which you were when you promised.

<margin>9</margin>
Third, when someone is released from the fulfillment of a promise due to a change in the state of things, they are released from fulfilling it even if it was confirmed by an oath; this is proved by the chapter *Quemadmodum* on the law of oaths, cited above. For there the discussion was about a promise confirmed by an oath. Reason also supports this. For when a promise admits a tacit condition when it is not confirmed by an oath, it also admits it when an oath is added to it. For we do not promise anything else under oath than what is contained in the promise itself, which we confirm by the oath.

<margin>10</margin>
Fourth, and it must be carefully noted, there is a great difference between a promisor not having fully grasped what they promised—in the sense that if they had fully grasped or experienced what was contained in the promise, they would have restrained themselves from making it—and the state of things being so changed that if that change had occurred while they were promising, they would not have wanted to promise or obligate themselves in that event. From these...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 272 regarding when a person is released from a promise. It specifically addresses the "two points" mentioned at the end of the previous section, moving from the psychological intent of the promisor to the legal definition of a gift (donatio) as opposed to a mere promise.</meta>

Of these two points, this is the second, which we have been discussing until now, and which we affirm—along with the common opinion of the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to established legal and theological scholars like the Doctors of the Church or university professors of law.</note>—concerning the obligation to fulfill a promise.

That first point, however, by no means releases one from fulfilling a promise. This is because those things which the promisor did not fully grasp, or which they had not experienced in detail, are nevertheless contained within or attached to the thing promised. Therefore, they promised all of those things, even if—had they experienced or understood them—they would never have issued such a promise. One must blame themselves for promising something without having sufficiently weighed and understood the matter.

For this reason, a person is not released from entering a **religious order** <note>Latin: *religione*. In the 16th century, this specifically referred to joining a monastic order like the Jesuits, Dominicans, or Franciscans.</note> simply because they did not grasp the penances and difficulties of that order when they vowed to join it. It is not then permitted for them to leave on those grounds, claiming that if they had understood and experienced the hardships, they would never have made the vow. Rather, if they leave, they are a transgressor of their vow and **sin mortally** <note>Latin: *lethaliter peccat*. A "mortal sin" is a grave offense in Catholic theology that severs the person's relationship with God.</note>, as everyone admits and as the practice of the Church maintains.

Indeed, a vow binds a person even if it was made not only without enough maturity, but even if it was made **rashly** through lightheadedness. However, such lightheadedness in making a vow may make it easier to obtain a **dispensation** <note>A formal release from a religious obligation granted by a church authority.</note> when other causes are present—namely, if the person does not have the character or nature suited to that state of life, or lacks the strength for the labors of the religious order, or other similar reasons.

<margin>11</margin>
The question arises: if two people make mutual promises to each other, but neither promise was made specifically in view of or as compensation for the other, is it lawful for one person to fail to fulfill their promise because the other does not fulfill theirs? **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canon lawyer known as "Doctor Navarrus."</note> in chapter 18, number 7, cited above, says no.

However, I consider it far more probable that it is lawful. For just as **compensation** <note>The legal principle where two debts cancel each other out.</note> takes place in other types of debts, it also applies to debts arising from a free promise. Furthermore, by the very fact that the other party does not wish to fulfill their part, they become unworthy of having the promise fulfilled to them, and they are shown to be ungrateful.

<margin>12</margin>
If such **ingratitude** is sufficient to revoke a **gift** <note>Latin: *donatio*.</note> even after the promised item has been physically handed over, it is much more sufficient to justify not fulfilling a promise in the first place. What specific ingratitude suffices to revoke a gift will be discussed in its proper place below.

When a promise is made for a cause that does not exist, we will discuss below in its proper place when such a promise does not bind.

->The distinction between a promise and a completed gift.<-

## DISPUTATION 273.

### SUMMARY.

1 *Where the word "Gift" comes from.*
2 *What a gift is.*
3 *When a gift is said to be "perfected."*
4 *How a perfected gift differs from an accepted promise that binds one to fulfillment.*
5 *What things are necessary for a gift to be valid.*

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
A **gift**, as the legal consultant **Paulus** <note>Julius Paulus, a prominent 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note> says in the law *Senatus* in the Digest regarding gifts made in anticipation of death, is named after the word *dono* <note>meaning "I give"</note>, as if it were a "giving of a gift." From this, it follows that it only occurs when the giving proceeds from **liberality** <note>Generosity or free will, without legal compulsion.</note>.

For only then does what is given have the character of a gift. As gathered from **Saint Thomas Aquinas** in the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 18, question 1, article 2, and from **Aristotle** in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 2, it can be defined in this way:

<margin>2</margin>
It is a **liberal giving**, or, as Saint Thomas and Aristotle say, an **irrevocable** one; that is, it is not given in exchange for another thing to be returned. This should be understood as meaning that if one thing is owed out of justice as compensation for another, it is not a pure gift. We include here "remunerative gifts," which are truly gifts proceeding from liberality, and the thing given is truly a gift, even if it also proceeds from gratitude; this does not prevent it from being a gift. Furthermore, the person to whom the gift is made is called the **donee** <note>Latin: *donatarius*.</note>.

As was stated in Disputations 252, 254, and 255, <margin>3</margin> a gift is **perfected** <note>Legally finalized and binding.</note> and takes on the character of a "named contract" when the **delivery** <note>Latin: *traditio*.</note> of the thing being given occurs and is accepted. This is true whether the delivery is an actual physical handover or a "fictional" one <note>A legal handover where the physical object doesn't move, such as handing over the keys to a house.</note>, according to what was said in the section on possession.

<margin>4</margin>
Therefore, a gift understood in this way differs from an accepted promise that binds one to fulfillment. In a gift, **ownership** <note>Latin: *dominium*.</note> is transferred to the donee because delivery has occurred. In an accepted promise, however, ownership is not transferred; rather, the donee only acquires a **right to the thing** <note>Latin: *ius ad rem*. This means you have a legal claim to get the item, but you don't own it yet.</note> promised to them, according to what was said in Disputations 2 and 3.

Because of this, if the person who made the promise delivers the promised item to someone else instead—whether for free or for a price—that second person acquires ownership of it. The first person, to whom it was originally promised, can only bring a **personal action** <note>A lawsuit against a specific person rather than a claim to recover the object itself.</note> for damages against the one who promised it. This is because they did not have a **right in the thing** <note>Latin: *ius in re*. Full legal ownership/property right.</note>, but only a right *to* the thing, as was stated there.

<margin>5</margin>
For a gift, strictly speaking, to be **valid**, all those things are necessary which we explained were necessary for a valid promise in the preceding disputations. Sometimes "gift" is used broadly to include even a free promise before it is fulfilled. However, just as we mixed in many points about gifts in the broad sense while explaining promises, in the following sections we will speak much about the same "gift" in the broad sense.

<margin>Disputation 261.</margin>
1 Therefore, regarding those of whom it was said in **Disputation 261** that they are able to enter into contracts, they are also able to give gifts—whether by bestowing alms for pious causes or for non-pious ones—unless they are prohibited for some specific reason, as will be explained.

2 It can be said † universally concerning those who are subject to the power of another: regarding the administration of certain goods, they can give gifts from them, both as alms and in any other way, with the consent (either expressed, tacit, or presumed) of the one to whom they are subject, as far as they understand it to be that person’s will. This is the common view of the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to established legal and theological scholars.</note> and, among others, **St. Thomas [Aquinas]** in the *Summa Theologica* (2. 2. question 32, article 8), although he deals only with alms in that passage, and the matter is very well known in itself.

<margin>Marriages in Portugal are celebrated in two ways.</margin>
3 To truly examine † to what extent wives who are under the power of their husbands may give gifts, one must observe that marriages in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> are celebrated in two ways, as we shall discuss more extensively below when we speak of the contract of partnership.

<margin>1. By the contract of half-shares.</margin>
4 One way † is by the **contract of half-shares** <note>This refers to community property, where assets are pooled and split equally.</note>, of which no mention is made in **Common Law** <note>The *ius commune*, the shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law.</note>, and by which all marriages are deemed contracted in that kingdom unless something else was expressed at the time of the wedding. For by the very fact that the marriage is consummated by physical union, the goods of both spouses become common regarding ownership; once the marriage is dissolved by the death of one, or by a divorce between them, all goods are divided into two equal parts, one of which is handed to one spouse and the other to the other, or to their heirs. The other way [marriage] is celebrated is by the **contract of earnest money and dowry** <note>original: "arrharum & dotis"</note>, as they call it, which is the only one mentioned in Common Law.

<margin>2. By the contract of dowry and earnest money.</margin>
5 Truly, there is a † very wide difference, which must be especially observed

<column-break/>

regarding the matter we are now discussing, between this [second type of] marriage as it was celebrated under **Common Law** and as it is celebrated under the law of the **Kingdom of Castile** and the custom of **Portugal**. Under Common Law, a certain amount was given to the husband as the wife's **dowry** <note>Latin: *dos*. This was property brought by the bride to support the costs of the household.</note> to sustain the burdens of marriage, so that he might provide the wife with suitable maintenance. However, the administration of the dowry and all its fruits and profits throughout the duration of the marriage belonged to the husband alone; but when the marriage was dissolved, he had to restore only the dowry to the wife or her heirs. Besides the dowry, the wife was bound to manage the household in those matters proper to a wife, and thus she was bound to provide the industry and labor befitting her status and the family, as the management of the household required. If she earned anything beyond this through her own industry, work, and labor, it was hers and not her husband’s. Furthermore, all other goods that remained to the wife after the dowry was paid, and which she later acquired through gift, legacy, inheritance, or any other means, belonged to her—not only in ownership but also in free administration and disposal—although she could commit their administration to her husband if she wished. All these goods are called **paraphernalia** <note>From the Greek *para* (beside) and *pherna* (dowry). In legal history, this refers to property a woman owned in her own right, separate from her dowry.</note>. But under the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal, the administration of all goods and the wife's paraphernalia, as well as the work and industry of the wife acquired during the marriage, belong to the husband alone. The wife has absolutely no administration of the goods, unless perhaps, when they contracted the marriage, she reserved some for her own use and free administration and disposal—which happens very rarely. When the marriage is dissolved, the wife first withdraws whatever she brought, even if nothing remains for the husband or his heirs; then the husband withdraws whatever he brought. If any goods remain, such an increase is called **gained goods** <note>original: "bona lucrata"; essentially the profit or community property earned during the marriage.</note>, and half belongs to the husband and the other half to the wife or her heirs.

<margin>Having established this, let us approach the matter. Palude on the 4th, distinction 15, q. 3, art. 6, conclusion 2. Gabriel, ibid. d. 16, q. 4, concl. 4.</margin>
6 Having † established this, let us approach the matter. **Palude** and **Gabriel**, the authors of the *Summae* under the entry "alms," and the Doctors generally affirm that a wife can give alms and other gifts as she wishes from her **paraphernal goods**, even against her husband's will, because the ownership and administration of those goods belong to her, and she is not subject to her husband in that regard. This very point is suggested by **St. Thomas** (2. 2. q. 32, art. 8). This is true under **Common Law**, according to what we just reported, which is what these authors are speaking about. **Navarrus** <note>original: "Nau." referring to Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canonist.</note> (in the *Manual*, ch. 17, no. 54) restricts this: except where the custom and statutes of the province decree otherwise. He seems to have added this because of the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal, in which the administration of paraphernal goods belongs to the husband alone. Hence, he judges that in these kingdoms, wives cannot give alms from paraphernal goods without at least the tacit consent of the husband; just as he immediately adds regarding common "gained goods" that she cannot give alms from them in these same kingdoms without the husband's consent, because the administration of those goods belongs not to the wife but to the husband alone. <meta>This page continues the discussion of property rights within marriage, specifically focusing on whether a wife has the authority to give alms or gifts from the household's assets or her own earnings under the laws of Castile and Portugal.</meta>

## Second Treatise, Disputation 274.

Petrus de Palude and Gabriel Biel, in the places cited, along with Silvester Prierias and Angelus de Clavasio under the entry "alms," Richard of Middleton in the 4th book, distinction 15, article 2, question 6, St. Thomas Aquinas in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 32, article 8, reply 2, and others, assert that if a wife is hardworking and industrious, she may give alms and gifts even against her husband's will. This applies if she earns something extra through sewing <note>original: "acu", literally "by the needle"</note> or any other labor and industry without taking away anything necessary for the proper management of her family. They argue this because such profit is hers regarding both ownership and administration. These Doctors, however, are speaking of Common Law <note>The "ius commune," a mix of Roman and Canon law used across Europe.</note>, according to which things acquired in this way belong to her and are under her administration. 

However, Martin de Azpilcueta <note>referred to as "Navarrus," a highly influential 16th-century Spanish canonist</note> in citation 154, affirms that the opposite is true in the kingdoms of Portugal and Castile. In these realms, such earnings—along with everything else—are held in common between husbands and wives, but the administration belongs entirely to the husband alone. Therefore, by law, she cannot give gifts from such earnings without her husband's permission any more than she could from her paraphernal property <note>Property a bride brings into a marriage beyond her dowry which she typically retains control over.</note>. The Doctors generally seem to agree, if you weigh their words correctly, that wives cannot give alms—and much less other gifts—from goods whose administration belongs to the husband without his express or presumed consent. 

Therefore, since in these two kingdoms the administration of all goods universally belongs to the husband, it seems to follow from the words of these same Doctors that wives generally cannot give alms or gifts without the husband's consent (at least his presumed consent). If they do so, they sin and are bound to restore what they gave—at least by counting it as part of the goods that would fall to them in a settlement, if they think or doubt the husband would want it that way, unless they obtain forgiveness from their husbands. And this appears to be the opinion of Navarrus.

Nevertheless, the Doctors commonly affirm that wives, without the express permission and consent of the husband, can give the kind of alms that women of the same status and condition are commonly accustomed to giving, relative to the size of their wealth and the needs of their children and family. They hold the same for other gifts and transfers that women of the same status and condition are accustomed to making. The reason is that they can presume this to be the husband's will. St. Thomas, Navarrus, Alonso Tostado <note>referred to as "Abulensis," the Bishop of Avila</note>, Silvester, and Angelus add that even if a husband forbids his wife from doing such things, she can persuade herself that his prohibition was only intended to keep her from giving alms and the like beyond the *customary* measure, but not to prevent her from giving the usual amount.

However, in the event that a woman convinces herself that her husband’s will is that she should give nothing at all in alms, Petrus de Palude says in the cited place that she can still distribute from the common goods an amount that would belong to her or her children upon the dissolution of the marriage, taking it as part of her share at that time. According to this opinion, she could give larger alms than usual with that intention.

This opinion is nonetheless false. Since the administration of all goods belongs to the husband while the marriage lasts, the wife cannot, against his will,

<column-break/>

deprive him of a portion of that administration. This is especially true since it results in a loss to his marital rights. Furthermore, his own daughters whom he has by her would have a smaller legal inheritance portion from the woman's estate at the time of the marriage's dissolution. Also, with the goods the wife spends in this way, the husband could have traded and earned other profits. Finally, common goods might be diminished so that upon the dissolution of the marriage, the wife's portion would not be as large; the woman also exposes herself to the danger of becoming so used to such largesse that she eventually gives away the husband's goods as well. Navarrus, Alonso Tostado, Silvester, and others judge that if it were clear to the wife that her husband's will was that she give or spend nothing at all, she would sin if she gave anything even in alms, and she would be bound to restore it to her husband, at least by taking it as part of the goods that belong to her. Indeed, Navarrus says the same if she spends anything against her husband's will on games, makeup <note>original: "pigmentis", referring to cosmetics or dyes</note>, and other similar things.

<margin>Decision 7</margin>
For my part, just as I consider the opinion of Petrus de Palude to be entirely false, I also judge the opinion of these other doctors to be too harsh and not at all to be embraced, insofar as they deny that a wife—even against her husband's will—can make moderate alms and other gifts and transfers which women of the same status and condition are accustomed to making, given the quality of the wealth of both spouses, the dowry, the goods she brought, and other concurring circumstances. This is especially true in Spain and particularly in Portugal, when the marriage was celebrated with a contract of "half of the goods" <note>The community property system where assets are shared equally between spouses.</note>.

**First**, because a wife is not a slave of the husband, but a partner <note>original: "socia"</note>. She is not excluded from the administration of the family and its goods, but is a co-partner <note>original: "compar"</note>, even if she is subject to the husband in that regard as the head of the family, so that nothing is done in a disorderly or superfluous way.

**Second**, because a husband does not owe a wife food and support in the same way he does a son—merely enough to be whatever the husband wants. Rather, he owes her, as a partner and mother of the family, a decent support according to the quality of their status, the amount of their wealth, and other circumstances. In exchange for this, the wife gave him a dowry and, moreover, provides her help and labor as far as the proper administration of the family requires from her side. To the decent support of a wife belong all those things which women of her status and condition are accustomed to have and do.

For a father would not be said to provide decent support to a son in his studies or at court unless he supplied the necessities not only for food and clothing, but also for the expenses which young men of the same condition and status are accustomed to make there. In the same way, a husband would not be said to provide competent support to his wife unless he permitted her to have and to do what women of the same condition and status commonly have and do. On the contrary, if a certain portion were legally adjudicated to her for her competent support, the calculation for that judgment would take into account not only food, clothing, adornment, and service, according to the quality of her person and other circumstances—

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

<column-break/>

but it pertains to almsgiving, honorable recreation, and donations which right reason would require her to make, considering the circumstances. Therefore, because a husband would be acting irrationally if he forbade her from all such expenditures, the wife is not bound to obey such a prohibition, as it is irrational and injurious to her—unless a specific reason intervenes why such things should be forbidden to her more than to others of the same status and condition. For instance, if they had fallen into greater poverty than others of their rank, or had more children than them: for then equity would require that both spouses temper their spending, and the wife would be bound to obey her husband as long as he does not exceed the limits of equity; and in a case of doubt, she is bound to stand by the husband's command. According to these principles, then, as long as a wife makes no expenditures on food, clothing, adornment, alms, honorable recreation, and moderate gifts beyond what is customary for other women of moderate means in her social station, it must be said that she does not sin, even if she does so against her husband’s will.

Indeed, even if she were to sin by doing something against her husband’s will beyond what is regularly customary among those of moderate means in her station, if she still does not exceed the breadth of expenditures that women of her status are accustomed to make, I judge that she is not bound to make restitution <note>restitution: the legal and moral obligation to pay back or restore property to its rightful owner.</note>. This is because those expenses were not beyond those which she "purchased," as it were, when she entered the marriage contract; and consequently, she would not be sinning so much against justice as against the obedience she owes her husband in that regard. Nevertheless, confessors should always restrain wives so that, as far as possible, they obey their husbands and maintain peace with them. This is especially true since no danger of sin threatens them if they abstain from spending, whereas they could easily fall into sin through excess if they transgress the will of their husbands.

However, when wives notoriously exceed their husband's will, they would not only sin but would also be bound to restore the excess, if they understood that their husbands wished to obligate them to restitution, or if they were in doubt about it. Richard <note>Richard of Middleton</note> in the place cited, Viguier in his *Institutes* chapter 12, section 2, verse 5, and Juan Medina in the code *On Alms* in the question "from what goods alms should be made," section "from the things said," seem to agree with this explained opinion of ours.

I said above that this opinion of ours holds place especially in the Spanish lands: because in them, wives reserve no goods for themselves whose disposal belongs to them, as wives used to reserve <term>paraphernalia</term> <note>Paraphernalia: In Roman and Common Law, property that a bride brought into a marriage that remained her own and was not part of her dowry.</note> for themselves under the common law, from which they could freely give alms and other donations and make expenditures at their pleasure in any amount. It would be very harsh and irrational for a wretched woman who fell into the hands of a harsh and greedy husband to be able to alienate nothing at all for her decent adornment, competent alms, and honorable recreation—nor even those things which moderate women of her status are accustomed to alienate—without his permission. Such a partnership of goods between husband and wife would be judged to have been entered into very irrationally and unjustly.

I added: "especially in Portugal," when the marriage is celebrated with a contract for half of the goods <note>medietas bonorum: a community property arrangement where assets are split 50/50.</note>. For although in the kingdoms of Portugal and Castile, when a marriage is celebrated with a contract of <term>arrhae</term> <note>Arrhae: Earnest money or a "bride price" given by the husband to the wife as a form of security.</note>

<column-break/>

and <term>dowry</term> <note>dos: the property brought by a wife to her husband at marriage.</note>, the administration of all goods belongs to the husbands, nevertheless the dowry, paraphernal goods, and *arrhae* always remain safe for the wife. She or her heirs receive all of it when the marriage is dissolved, even if nothing remains for the husband or his heirs. Nor is she held liable for debts contracted by the husband during the marriage; rather, she is preferred over other creditors. However, when a marriage is celebrated with a contract for half of the goods, the matter does not stand thus. Instead, half of all the expenditures the husband makes is lost to the wife. Furthermore, if after all the goods of the husband and wife are consumed, any debts remain when the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death, the wife is bound to pay half. It is much harsher for such a wife, by entering into a partnership of goods with her husband, to be able to alienate nothing at all without his permission. If he is harsh and greedy and denies her permission for everything, it would be harsh if she were bound to restore to him what she moderately alienated according to the custom of others of her status, while he remains free to alienate whatever he pleases from the common goods of both.

<margin>8 *Objection* 33. q. 5.</margin>
But if someone should object against us with the chapter *Quod Deo* [33. q. 5], where Augustine says to a certain married woman:
> *You ought to have done nothing regarding your clothing, nothing regarding your gold or silver, or any of your money or any of your earthly things, without his* (namely, the husband’s) *judgment.*

It must be said that Augustine is speaking there of immoderate alms and gifts, such as those were. For she had given away all her goods while her husband was still living and, having put on a monastic habit, wished to live in a private house like a nun.

Therefore, because a wife can give moderate alms and donations for the quality of her status, even without her husband's permission, as has been said, she certainly can set them aside not only for needy parents but also for brothers or other blood relatives, and grant them to them without the husband's permission—provided, however, that she does not make other alms and gifts which, when taken together with these, exceed the sum she can spend without her husband's permission.

And in the same way, the husband can set aside and distribute to his needy blood relatives what he can distribute to other poor people or bestow upon others.

We can prove this because the order of charity requires that poor blood relatives or relatives by marriage be preferred to other poor people, all other things being equal. It certainly follows that gifts can be lawfully given, or even donated, to needy blood relatives rather than to those who are not in need. Indeed, equity requires that one be a little more kind toward blood relatives than toward others, and that the other spouse should not take this poorly, provided the excess is not great. For one of the circumstances that must be weighed to judge how much a wife can spend without the husband's consent (or even a husband without the wife's consent) is the occurring need of their own relatives.

Second Treatise, Dispute 275.

[The resources] should be turned into alms for the relatives of the other spouse. The reason why this should be observed is as follows: First, because such compensatory donations can be larger, based on the quantity of merit, than others.

Second, because this is a debt owed by both spouses and contributes to the splendor and honor of both; one spouse cannot deprive the other of that benefit by giving it only to their own needy relatives. Second, unless the need of the relatives is extreme, some ordinary alms should nevertheless be given to others, as an example to neighbors and for the honor of the family, and so it does not cause a scandal to others who do not know the reason why the customary alms are being omitted. Third, in Dispute 218 regarding the fifth effect of parental power, it was explained to what extent not only sons but also daughters, even if they are married, are bound to provide support <note>original: "alimenta," referring to the legal obligation to provide food and necessities.</note> to their parents when they are in need; and that they are able and bound to pay this debt even against the husband's will. Read what was said there. Indeed, I believe such a debt should be paid from the common property of both spouses if the marriage was celebrated under a contract of equal sharing <note>original: "contractu medietatis," a legal arrangement where property is shared 50/50.</note>. If, however, it was under a contract of earnest-money and dowry <note>original: "arrharum & dotis."</note>, I think it should be paid from the surplus profits <note>original: "superlucratis," assets gained during the marriage beyond the original dowry.</note>, if there are any at the time. But if there are no surplus profits and the resources are given to the wife's parents, the wife must take what was thus spent from the portion that falls to her when the marriage is dissolved.

<margin>Question 10</margin>
From what has been said, we can decide the question which Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canon lawyer known as "Navarrus."</note> answers in the cited place (number 155): namely, whether a woman who brought a very large dowry can give forty gold coins to the woman who nursed her as an infant, against her husband's presumed will. Navarro says no, even if she gave them to her in parts over a period of time, when from the beginning she intended to reach that sum through installments.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I believe, however, that first, consideration must be given to the wife’s status, and reason requires that she make such a gift, provided it is not immoderate, considering the quality of such a wife. For indeed, the wife "purchased" with her dowry and her own property the ability to make the expenditures that pertain to her; therefore, if the husband, considering the wealth of both, could make such a donation to his own wet nurse, perhaps the wife could also make the same to hers—especially if the marriage was celebrated under a contract of equal sharing, or (even if celebrated by contract of earnest-money and dowry) if there are surplus common goods for both spouses, she can make it in Spain from those common goods.

Finally, although I think the reins should not be loosened more than is just for wives, but rather should be tightened in this regard, certainly if the wife restrained herself from other donations and expenses otherwise permitted to her so that she might give that sum to her nurse when equity demands it; and if she could bring such a large dowry and so much property, and the resources of both spouses were so abundant, I would not hesitate to affirm that it is lawful to give that sum, either all at once or certainly in parts. Indeed, I do not believe that having the intention from the start to reach that sum in parts is a sufficient reason for it to be unlawful, when it would be lawful without that intention

<column-break/>

to achieve the same result over the course of time.

Regarding what follows, the doctors of law admit that it is permitted to a wife secretly, even against her husband's will: First, to avoid notable harm to the husband or the family, the wife may bestow or spend what she judges to be necessary for that purpose.

Thus Abigail, contrary to what her husband had done and without consulting him at all, offered gifts to David (1 Kings 25) <note>A biblical reference to Abigail providing food to David's army to prevent him from attacking her husband Nabal's household.</note>, by which she appeased him. This is affirmed by Palude, Gabriel, Navarro, and many others in the cited places. The reason is that the temporal harm of the husband or the family also overflows onto the wife herself and her property; and for that reason, whether it is imminent because of the husband's malice or from elsewhere, and whether it is from inadvertence, ignorance, powerlessness, malice, or another reason, if the husband does not meet the danger, it is lawful for the wife to meet it and make the necessary expenses for it, looking out for herself and her family.

12 For this same reason, as Navarro (number 154) and others rightly affirm, if a husband is a spendthrift <note>original: "prodigat ac dilapidet," squandering or wasting assets.</note> and wastes the property, it is permitted for the wife to hide and save it against his pleasure, providing for the future of herself and the family; for in that regard, she is not bound to obey her husband to the common detriment of herself and her husband. However, that which Navarro and others affirm there—namely, that it is permitted for a wife to give moderate alms against her husband’s pleasure to avoid his spiritual harm, so that by this path God might enlighten him and lead him to true repentance—is certainly not approved by us, because that would not result in temporal harm to the wife. Since the husband's spiritual evil does not so overflow onto the wife that she cannot avoid any sin herself; and just as a stranger could not take his property and make alms from it so that he might be rescued from sin, so the wife cannot bestow the husband's goods in alms against his will to rescue him from sin.

13 Furthermore, since the administration of property belongs to the wife when the husband is absent, or a spendthrift, or mentally incapacitated <note>original: "mente captus."</note>, or for any other reason, then the wife can bestow alms, and give and spend those things which the husband was accustomed to. Palude, Navarro, and others in the cited places agree. It is fair, however, that the wife be somewhat more frugal than the husband was, especially when she understands that such would have been the husband’s will if he were present or of sound mind.

14 Likewise, when a husband prescribes a certain amount to the wife for food or for her other expenses, if she, by living more sparingly, saves something, she can make alms and other donations from that, as the doctors commonly affirm. These things concern the wife.

<margin>1</margin>**U**nder Portuguese law, it is a crime for husbands not only to give away but even to transfer ownership of immovable property <note>original: "bona immobilia," such as land or buildings</note> in any other way without the express consent of the wife, whether they married under a contract of shared assets <note>original: "contractu medietatis bonorum," a 50/50 split</note> or one of earnest-money and dowry, as stated in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 6, and as will be discussed more fully below. Regarding money and other movable goods, if a husband gives any away without his wife's consent, then upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of one spouse, the man or his heirs are required to count that gift as part of his own share of the estate. An exception is made if the gift is a reward for service or given as charity; a man can make these without his wife's consent. Provided, however, they are not "immense"; for then the wife or her heirs can sue to have the gift annulled. Understand this to mean: insofar as it prejudiced her rights—specifically, by ensuring the excess is deducted from the husband's share, and if his assets are insufficient, the recipient must restore half of the increase that belongs to the wife. This is found in the cited Title 6, last paragraph. However, this ordinance should be understood practically and as it is accepted in common usage. For a man, as the administrator of the property, can make gifts of minor importance without consulting his wife—gifts which the management of the estate requires based on the total wealth of both—so that he is not later required to count them against his share of the assets. This is especially true since it was said in the preceding dispute that a wife can also make moderate gifts without consulting her husband, such as other wives of similar status and wealth are accustomed to making,

<column-break/>

considering all other circumstances. Indeed, just as a son living away from his parents at court or at university, who has the administration of the funds sent to him for his support, can make the kind of gifts that others of his status usually make (when the father does not restrict him more than other parents commonly do); and if he makes some small, useless, or bad gift or expenditure, he is not required to account for it later when dividing the inheritance with his brothers. Thus, with much greater reason, it should be said of a husband: even if he makes a small bad gift or expenditure relative to the size of his wealth, he is not later required to take it out of his share; for the administration of property in this fluid and fleeting life should not be managed with such extreme rigor. By the same logic, if a wife makes a small bad gift or expenditure from the common property, she is not required to take it from her own share.

If, however, a husband were to give a large sum as a dowry for his sister, or make other large and extraordinary gifts without the free consent of his wife, or if a wife did so without the husband's consent, then they would be required to count those against their respective shares. Indeed, Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canon lawyer</note> says in his Manual, chapter 17, number 155, that if a husband does not count such a large gift made without consent against his share, the recipient is bound to warn the wife, so that she may either receive compensation or force the husband (or his heirs) to take it out of his portion. Note, however, if it were the wife who made the gift without the husband's knowledge: because a wife does not have the administration of those goods and thus sins against justice toward her husband, not only she but also the recipient would be at fault. In that case, it would not be enough (if the woman did not take it from her share) to simply warn the husband or his heirs; the recipient would be bound to restore to the husband or his heirs that portion of the gift which belonged to the husband.

<margin>2</margin>Regarding the same Portuguese law, if a husband has given anything to a concubine or another person with whom he is carnally involved—whether that property is movable or immovable—the wife can, without her husband's consent, reclaim it during the husband's entire lifetime and for four years after his death. During this entire time, it shall be adjudicated to her so that it remains her whole and private property, and she may dispose of it as she wishes, even while the husband is still alive.

If the wife should die before the husband, her heirs (provided they are her descendants or ancestors) can reclaim it within four years of her death. The same rule applies to property that was sold, pledged, or transferred to such a concubine by the husband through any other contract; the wife or her heirs shall not be forced to pay any price for its return. This is because fraud is presumed, and it is assumed the husband received no real price. Because the law is based on this presumption, if it were clear to the wife that the husband truly did receive a price, she would be bound in the court of conscience to return the price or whatever else the husband received in exchange. This is found in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 8, and Book 5, Title 28, last paragraph.
