# Second Treatise, Disputation 275.

<margin>3</margin> Antonio da Gama, in decision 226, reports a case where a certain wife sought to reclaim money from her husband’s mistress <note>original: "concubina"</note> which the husband had gifted to her. A lower judge had ruled in favor of the wife according to Portuguese laws. However, upon appeal, that decision was later revoked by the judgment of certain senators. They were led to revoke it for several reasons. First, because they argued that the legal ordinance only refers to things where ownership did not actually pass to the mistress, and which the wife could therefore legally "vindicare" <note>a legal term meaning to claim back property one still owns</note>. They argued that even if the husband had given money to the mistress, she had already spent it or used it to buy other goods; since one who buys something with another's money truly acquires ownership of the item bought, the mistress now owned those items. Secondly, they argued that just as a husband can sell or transfer movable goods without his wife’s consent, he can also give them as gifts. They claimed a wife cannot revoke a gift made by the husband unless it is "immense" <note>excessively large</note> and there are not enough assets left for her to receive her rightful half or the goods that belong to her, according to the final section cited previously.

I do not doubt, however—concurring with Gama in that same passage—that the lower judge’s sentence was correctly delivered and should not have been revoked. The revocation was contrary to a sound understanding of the ordinances. For the ordinances speak universally of *anything* given to a mistress by a husband, whether it be movable or immovable property. They do not only speak of cases where the item can be reclaimed because the wife still holds ownership, but also if it has been consumed. Since the mistress accepted it against the prescription of the law, she did so at her own peril, knowing she would be held liable to pay it back if the wife, according to that ordinance, reclaimed it. Indeed, the wife would not have been sufficiently protected—as the laws intended to protect her in that regard—unless the laws applied to the entire estate. Furthermore, while a husband generally transfers ownership of a movable object when he gives it to a mistress, and she is not bound to return it or its value to the wife before a court sentence is passed (provided the husband keeps the wife "indemnified" or compensated), if he does *not* keep her compensated, then the mistress is bound to restore it. She is not bound for the full value of the item, but for that portion which belonged to the wife—that is, half, if the marriage was celebrated under a contract for half of the goods <note>a "communal property" arrangement</note>. Or, if the item was part of the profits belonging to both, it would apply if the marriage was held under a contract of dowry and arras <note>earnest money or a bride-price given by the groom</note>. However, nothing is owed if there were no surplus profits and nothing prevented the wife from receiving her full dowry and other property belonging to her. Therefore, if the mistress had sold the item, the wife could not reclaim it from a third party who now possessed it, but she would have a personal legal action against the mistress for the value of that item. Thus, the Portuguese law, which grants the wife the entire item through reclamation from the husband’s mistress, is a "penal" law and does not have force before a court sentence is issued. From this, the first argument used by those senators is overturned. Their second argument is of no weight: for although the ordinances allow a husband to alienate movable goods without his wife’s consent under any other title, they expressly state that if he gives anything as a gift without her consent, he is required to count that against his own portion of the estate—unless the gifts are for services rendered or are acts of charity. 

<column-break/>

That exception—regarding "immense" gifts—should only be understood as applying to charitable alms and gifts given in gratitude for services. All these points are clearly evident in Title 6, the last section cited.

<margin>4</margin> From what has been said, it is clear that in Portugal, when a woman receives something from a married man as payment for a "venereal act" <note>sex work or illicit sexual favors</note> or as a gift, such that it harms the wife’s interests, she is not bound to restore it in full to the wife before a court sentence is passed. However, since that property was held in common by the husband and wife, and the mistress cooperated in the injustice the husband committed against the wife by spending it, she acquires ownership but remains morally liable. If the husband (as he is bound to do) either obtains a release from his wife or satisfies her by taking that item out of his own share of the property, the mistress is not bound to restore anything. But because the mistress believes the husband will not restore it, and knows the wife wants it restored, she herself is bound to restore to the wife the portion that the wife held in that property. The same should be said of what a male lover receives from another man's wife in a similar manner. Only in the absence of such a wife is he bound to restore to the husband the portion that would have come to the husband from those things, as well as any damages—at least for lost profit—that resulted from it.

<margin>5 Question.</margin> In the Kingdom of Castile, however, where the contract for "half of all goods" is not in use in marriage, there is doubt as to how much a man may give from the "surplus gains" <note>original: "superlucratis," referring to wealth acquired during the marriage, known as *gananciales* in Spanish law</note> and spend them without his wife’s consent; and whether he is bound to any restitution to the wife if he gives those goods away superfluously or spends them badly. First, it is established in that kingdom that the husband has free disposal of all these goods without the wife’s consent, even if they are immovable property, and every contract by which he alienates them is valid—unless it is proven that it was done with the intent to defraud the wife of her portion. For Law 5 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "noue. collect." referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish laws</note> states:
> <note>original Spanish: "Otro si, que los bienes, que fueren gana los y mejorados y multiplicados durante el matrimonio entre el marido y la muger, los pueda enagenar el marido durante el matrimonio, si quisiere sin licentia ni otorgamiēto de su muger. Y que el cōtrato denagenamiēto vala : saluo si fuere probado quelo hizo cautelosamēte por defraudar o damnificar ala muger."</note>
> "Furthermore, regarding the goods that were gained, improved, and multiplied during the marriage between the husband and the wife: the husband may alienate them during the marriage if he wishes, without the license or grant of his wife. And the contract of alienation shall be valid, unless it is proven that he did so cautiously to defraud or harm the wife."

<margin>6</margin> Palacios Rubios, in his commentary on the chapter *Per vestras* regarding gifts, section 66, says that it is not permitted for a husband to give gifts from common goods without his wife’s consent; for this reason, if he gives any of them without such consent, he is required to take it from the portion that belongs to him. He holds the same view regarding assets he spends to free himself from a crime committed by his own fault. With even greater reason, he holds the same for what a husband spends on harlots, or otherwise squanders and destroys.

Navarrus, in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 155—though he agrees with Juan Lopez in the commentary on gifts between husband and wife—says that a husband is not bound to restore to the wife what he spends, well or badly, from the common gains. Because, he says, only those things found to be "gained" at the time of the dissolution of the marriage are considered profits. The rest, although they would have been profits for the wife's half, were nevertheless "revocably" gained, so that the husband, who held the free administration of them, could harm both himself and his wife by administering them well or badly.

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

<columns>

...[to do]; nevertheless, at the end of that section, he holds the opposite view regarding donations. Namely, if the husband makes them without the consent of his wife, he is required to count them as part of his own share of the estate. If the husband does not take the gift out of his own share, the recipient <note>the "donatary," or person receiving the gift</note> is required to disclose the matter to the wife, so that she may either receive compensation or compel the husband, or his heirs, to count it toward his portion.

Antonio Gómez, however, in his commentary on Law 50 of Toro (number 75), and Gregorio López on Law 13, Title 10, Part 5, as well as Juan López (cited by Navarro) and others, assert that the husband is permitted full and total administration of the common gains in this sense: whether he spends them through donations, or to be released from a penalty for a crime <note>original: "delicto"</note>, or by wasting them on mistresses or in any other prodigal way, he is not held to any restitution toward the wife, nor must he take what he consumed out of his own portion. This holds true as long as he does not spend the money specifically to defraud the wife—that is, with the intent to deprive her of her share of those goods. Such fraud would be presumed if he were to make an excessively large <note>original: "immodicam"</note> donation. This is how they understand the established law of Castile, which seems to imply this; they argue that this is the accepted style and practice in that kingdom.

The following arguments suggest that this could be established and accepted in practice without injustice to the wife. First, a wife contracting marriage in that kingdom always keeps her own capital <note>original: "capitale," referring to her dowry and private assets</note> safe, even if nothing remains for the husband or his heirs; thus, the entire loss of the capital of both parties falls solely upon the husband. Second, it is the husband who primarily earns the profit; and under common law, all gains belonged to the husband alone, just as the losses did. Therefore, it is not contrary to equity that, although the wife in that kingdom is granted half of the gains found at the time the marriage is dissolved, the husband is nonetheless freely granted the power to alienate all goods, both movable and immovable (always saving the wife's capital) during the entire time the marriage lasts. He would not be bound to any restitution to the wife, even if he spent and lost those goods prodigally and inordinately, provided he did nothing to defraud the wife with the intention of diminishing the portion she ought to have in the profits.

<margin>7</margin> However, we must embrace a certain middle opinion † along with Molina (*On Primogeniture*, Book 2, Chapter 10, from number 65), who explains this matter learnedly, as is his custom, and with Gutiérrez (*Practical Questions*, Book 2, Question 121). Navarro and others whom he cites seem to have intended the same. Namely, regarding donations, the husband in Castile has somewhat "looser reins" <note>original: "laxas habenas," a metaphor for having more freedom or control</note> over the profits earned during marriage than he does in Portugal. He can exercise a slightly more generous liberality in those gifts that are usually connected to and permitted in the administration of assets. However, he cannot make excessive gifts that would result in a notable loss to the wife regarding the earned profits, whether he gives them to his own blood relatives, in-laws, or others. For any such excess, he would be held liable both in conscience and in the civil court to take those amounts from his own half of the goods. The reason is that under the name of the power

<margin>8</margin> to † alienate <note>the legal right to sell or transfer property</note>, the power to give gifts is not considered granted, especially excessive ones. This follows the argument of the law *creditor* (paragraph *Lucius*) in the Digest on mandates: where a mandate to dispose of a thing as one's own is given, the

<column-break/>

power to give it away is not understood to be granted, even though one might otherwise alienate it. Likewise, through equity <note>original: "epicheiam," a legal principle of interpreting the spirit of the law over the letter to ensure fairness</note>, these excessive donations to the prejudice of the wife are not considered granted to the husband by that law of Castile. Indeed, such a law would be irrational and hardly equitable, which should not be presumed of legislators, especially Christian ones. Nor does a law include something which, if the legislator were asked about it specifically, he would answer in the negative. Add to this that such excessive donations are presumed to be made with the intent of defrauding the wife, even if they are made out of affection for relatives or strangers. Under the law we are discussing, donations made—even presumptively—to defraud the wife are understood to be prohibited, as Molina rightly judges that law should be interpreted.

Furthermore, I judge it should be understood that if something is spent because of a crime or fault <note>original: "delicto"</note> of the woman, and this is the only reason the common gains are diminished, she is not required to restore anything to the husband from her own capital for that reason. It would be otherwise, however, if such expenses diminished the husband's capital; for then the wife would be required to keep the husband harmless regarding his capital due to her own fault.

<margin>9</margin> In Portugal, † however, since no such law has been enacted, and setting aside that provision of Castilian positive law for the reasons we have explained, and standing only on the nature of the matter, the husband would do an injury to the wife by dilapidating what are certainly common goods. It must be said that if a husband who married under a contract of *arras* <note>a marriage contract involving a specific dower or pledge</note> has spent common profits—either by giving excessively, or to free himself from a penalty for a crime committed by his own fault, or on mistresses, or in any other way that injures the wife—he is required to take that amount from his own share. This is especially true since no greater administration of goods is granted to him in that kingdom when the marriage was celebrated with a contract of *arras* than when it was celebrated with a contract of "half of the goods," as is clear from Law 4, Title 6, and other places cited.

<margin>10</margin> On the occasion † of what has been said regarding donations made to concubines <note>mistresses</note>, I should point out that Law 2 of the Code (*On donations between husband and wife*) was granted in favor of soldiers. It stipulates that donations made by soldiers to their mistresses are void to the extent that they can revoke them and reclaim what they gave as a gift. Thus, if they promised them anything for free, they would not be bound to pay it either in conscience or in court. For whenever a law grants someone the right to reclaim something, it is considered, with far greater reason, to grant them the right to withhold it and a legal defense if they are sued for it. However, if they had given them something as a "just price" <note>original: "precium iustum"</note> for the use of their bodies, they could not reclaim it; for that would not be a donation, which is the only thing discussed in that law. Likewise, if they had given something in compensation for services performed or other benefits received from them, they could not reclaim it, even if it were a "remuneratory" donation <note>a gift given as a reward for a specific service</note>; for that passage only discusses other purely gratuitous donations, as the final gloss well notes in that place.

<margin>11</margin> On the occasion † of that law, when a certain clergyman had given some estates to his mistress, the cleric's heirs in Portugal wanted to reclaim what had been donated to the mistress in the deceased's place. They argued that the cleric, as a "soldier of Christ" <note>original: "miles Christi"</note> according to the doctrine of Bartolus (which the addition to the cited gloss follows),

# To what extent a religious person may donate or give alms.

## DISPUTATION 276.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *Religious superiors of a monastery must give appropriate alms.*
*They may also make moderate donations according to the nature of their administration. Number 2.*
*Regarding what applies to inferior ministers, see number 3.*
<margin>4</margin> *A religious person expelled from a monastery may, while he lives, give alms and make donations that are not for evil purposes.*
*But what about in a final will?*
<margin>5</margin> *When a religious person holding a benefice, or the use of certain goods, may give alms and make donations.*
<margin>6</margin> *Whether annual incomes that are not ecclesiastical benefices can be granted to religious persons after the Council of Trent.*
<margin>7</margin> *Religious persons living in monasteries cannot give alms or make donations except by the permission of their superior, at least a presumed one.*

---

<margin>1</margin> Saint Thomas (in the *Sentences* 4, d. 15, q. 2, art. 5, final question), Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado, a prolific 15th-century Spanish theologian</note> (on Matthew chapter 6, q. 60), and others rightly affirm that those superiors of convents who have the supreme administration of goods and have no prescription from a higher power to follow in that regard, can and ought to give alms from the surplus of the convent. Indeed, even from the "necessary" goods—meaning those that are not strictly surplus but are appropriate for maintaining the status of the convent—they can and should give alms that are appropriate in the judgment of a prudent person. They can also
<margin>2</margin> give moderately according to the nature of their administration, in the manner we will add below, as Medina (in his treatise *On Alms*, the chapter on what goods alms should be made from, section "Abbots") and others rightly affirm. However, Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palud, a 14th-century Dominican theologian</note> (in the *Sentences* 4, d. 15, q. 3, conclusion 5) well observes that although they can give alms and donate some things during their life, they can leave nothing in a legacy at death without the express faculty of the Supreme Pontiff. This is because they are not the owners <note>original: "domini"</note> of those goods, but the dispensers; and because their administration expires along with their life.

<column-break/>

This, indeed, must be said generally of prelates. According to the resources of the monastery or convent, and having considered all other concurrent circumstances and observed any regulations—if any exist in that convent by the decree of the whole order, province, or any higher superiors regarding the amount, manner, or dependence on the majority of the chapter or the vote of certain deputies—they can make not only appropriate alms, but also remuneratory donations <note>Donations given as a reward or payment for services rendered.</note> and others which the good of the convent, decency, and the right administration of those goods and the convent shall judge to demand and permit. Read Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canonist</note> (chapter *Non dicatis*, number 11). Since he is a dispenser and not the owner of those goods, certainly if he gives anything that is clearly a dissipation rather than a dispensation <note>Molina plays on the words "dissipatio" (waste/scattering) and "dispensatio" (stewardship/distribution).</note> of those goods, he not only sins, but the donation is also invalid. The recipient is bound to restore it to the convent, and the prelate himself is bound if there is any way he can restore it. Among these cases, count it if (God forbid) he should live luxuriously and give to a mistress, as Abulensis rightly says (on Matthew chapter 6, q. 37). Likewise, if he should give anything inordinately—that is, without a reasonable cause—to his relatives from the goods of the monastery.

<margin>3</margin> Inferior ministers or officials who administer goods within the order and rank of the monastery, such as procurators and those who have care of the monastery, and other similar persons (all of whom, as decreed in the Council of Trent, Session 25, chapter 2, ought to be removable at will), can give appropriate alms according to the rules or customs of each religious order or monastery in that regard, or according to the prescription and will of the prelate of that same monastery, or at least his undoubtedly presumed will. Read, among others, Navarro (chapter *Non dicatis*, numbers 8 and 9). In our Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits), of which Molina was a member.</note>, however, this depends in all things on the prescription and will, at least presumed, of the superior to whom they are subject.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding other religious persons: First, a professed religious person who has been expelled from a monastery—as was said at the end of Disputation 140—although he is still a religious person in truth and has ownership of nothing, he is nevertheless seen as having been tacitly granted the right not to live under the obedience and rule of the religion, as well as the convenience and use of all the things he might acquire. However, whatever of those goods remains after his death belongs to the monastery from which he was expelled, as we showed in that same place. Regarding such a religious person, there is no doubt that in the meantime, while he lives, he can give alms and make donations that are not for evil purposes as he wishes, and these are valid. This is proven because the entire convenience, use, and disposition of those goods belongs to him while he lives, just as if he were not a religious person. He no longer has anyone whom he is bound to follow in that regard; instead, as far as administration, acquisition, and alienation of goods are concerned, he conducts himself as if he held ownership and were entirely his own master <note>original: "sui juris," meaning legally independent.</note>. For this reason, I believe that if he spends anything on harlots, or gives and spends perversely for some other reason, the act holds. Nor are the recipients bound to restore those things any more than if he were not a religious person, but the true owner of those goods.

<meta>catchword: minus.</meta>

...less. However, through a final will, he cannot dispose of those goods without the express permission of the Supreme Pontiff <note>original: "Summi Pontificis"</note>, as stated in the cited place: since he is not the owner of them, and only their use and benefit are granted to him for as long as he lives.

<margin>5</margin>
A religious person living lawfully either within or outside a monastery who holds an ecclesiastical benefice, or who has been granted the convenience, free use, and disposal of certain goods—such as a cathedral stipend or another office he administers, or a specific portion of the monastery's goods granted annually for his support so that he might seek nothing more—or one to whom certain annual revenues have been granted for his expenses and use (which they call a <term>tença<note>original: "tença"; a Portuguese term for a pension or grant, often provided by the crown or family for the support of an individual.</note></term> in the Kingdom of Portugal) by his parents, relatives, or someone else, with the consent of the monastery or by a dispensation from the Supreme Pontiff; or finally, one to whom other goods have been granted for his use and disposal with the superior's consent; provided that, if there is any restriction on their use and disposal (namely that he must spend them on these things and not others, or that he must return to the superior for permission or inform him of the things on which he wishes to spend, and not consume them except with his approval), provided, I say, that he observes whatever restriction was made, he may make alms from those same goods and give them for purposes that are not unlawful. For regarding unlawful purposes—such as if he gives something to a concubine, or in some other similarly perverse way—he certainly cannot do this; if he attempts to do so, the act is not valid, and the recipient is bound to restore it, either to the monastery or to the Church to which those goods belonged. For neither should the superior be thought to have granted permission for such alienations <note>legal transfer of property</note> when he granted the use of those goods to the religious person; this is because in a general grant, those things are not thought to be included which would be denied if they had been proposed in specific detail. Nor, if the superior had intended to grant such permission, would he have granted it validly: because his power, which was granted not for destruction but for building up, does not extend to that. Surely such an alienation is null by law itself, and therefore the recipient is bound to restore what he received in this way, as <margin>Abulensis on Matthew chapter 6, question 17, article 3.</margin> Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish theologian known as "El Tostado."</note> rightly notes on Matthew chapter 6. However, when a donation by the religious person of whom we speak is made to relatives from the goods of an ecclesiastical benefice that he administers, since he is not the owner of those goods (as are other beneficiaries mentioned above when the conversation was held regarding the wills of beneficiaries), it has been stated to what extent such a donation is valid or not. Observe further that a religious beneficiary has the free disposal of the revenues of the benefice for all things that are pious and which pertain to his own competent support, and no restriction can be placed on him in any part regarding these. On all these matters read, among <margin>Navarrus, chapter "non dicatis" from number 9 to 12.</margin> others, Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), an influential Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note>.

<margin>6</margin>
Whether it is lawful, after the decree of the Council of Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) initiated major reforms in the Catholic Church; Session 25 dealt with the reform of religious orders.</note>, Session 25, chapter 2, to grant religious persons such annual revenues that are not ecclesiastical benefices. <margin>Navarrus discusses the matter in chapter "non dicatis" from number 14 and 18, and chapter "nulla" from number 24 to 36.</margin> Navarrus discusses the matter. Although he thinks they cannot be permitted to have them as their own personal property—indeed, not even as properties of the mona-

<column-break/>

-stery and in the name of the monastery, but granted to themselves for any uses whatsoever, even secular ones—nor even that they should have them for pious uses alone without just cause; he nevertheless judges that it is not against that decree for them to be granted to him for a just cause, not for any uses at all, but only for pious and honest ones, and subject to removal at the will of the superiors. Read him. However, where such grants have not been introduced, or if they have already been introduced and could be extinguished without scandal, it would certainly be expedient for them to be abolished entirely and permitted by no means anew; and this is much more in harmony with the decree of the Council of Trent.

<margin>7</margin>
As for the remaining religious, everyone agrees that while they stay in the monastery, they can give nothing, either in alms or in any other way, except by the good pleasure (at least undoubtedly presumed) of their superior, as held in the law chapter *non dicatis*, question 1, and the chapter *cum ad monasterium*, on the status of monks. However, when they travel with the permission of their superiors, or reside in schools, they also agree that they can give the alms that honest students or travelers are accustomed to give. For that is seen as the presumed will of the superior, who provides them with the necessities for traveling or residing in schools. Thus, among others, Navarrus, chapter *non dicatis* number 8. But if a superior should grant a certain amount of money to someone residing in schools or elsewhere for his support, then, however much he wished to subtract from his own support, he could bestow it in alms or other honest donations, or otherwise spend it decently. If, however, he spent anything on harlots or in other disgraceful acts, he would not only sin by alienating the monastery's goods in such a way, but he would also not transfer ownership, and the recipient would be bound to restore it to the monastery. For, as Abulensis well notes on Matthew chapter 6, what he would spend in such a way—even if he had subtracted it from his own support—is not the property of the religious person, but of the monastery; nor could the superior grant him the power to alienate anything of the monastery for that use, even if the religious person subtracted it from his own lawful support.

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of property rights, moving from religious individuals to those under the authority of others, such as sons under paternal power (filius familias) and minors under guardianship.</meta>

# Second Treatise. Disputation 277.

<margin>1</margin>
A **son under paternal power** <note>original: "filius familias"; in Roman law, a son who remains under the legal authority of his father regardless of his actual age.</note>, if he has reached the **age of puberty** <note>original: "pubes"; the legal age of discretion, usually 14 for boys.</note> and possesses **military property** <note>original: "bona castrensia"; property a son acquired through military service, which he was allowed to own independently of his father.</note>, or quasi-military property <note>original: "quasi castrensia"; property acquired through public office or professional practice.</note>, may donate from these goods freely, just as he may enter into other contracts, as was stated in Disputations 230, 231, and 261.

When the **use-fruit** <term>usufruct; the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</term> and the administration of a son’s **external property** <note>original: "bonorum adventitiorum"; property coming to the son from outside sources, like an inheritance from his mother, rather than from his father.</note> belongs to the son—perhaps because he lives far from his father and holds some external property there, or because the father has left him the free administration of certain external goods (for which it is enough that the father does not demand those goods from the son regarding their administration and profits)—then a donation made by the son from such goods is valid and lawful. This follows what was said in Disputations 8, 138, and 228 concerning the first and fourth effects of paternal power, as well as Disputations 232 and 261. However, even if the father holds the use-fruit and administration of the son's external property, a donation made by the son with the father's consent is valid, provided the son has reached puberty, whether or not he has exceeded twenty-five years of age, as shown in Disputation 261. If, however, in all the cases explained, the son was **under twenty-five years old** when he made the donation and finds himself disadvantaged by it (even if he made it from military or quasi-military goods), he is granted the benefit of **total restitution** <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy where a person is restored to their original position as if a contract had never happened, typically granted to minors who were cheated or made poor decisions.</note> up until his twenty-ninth year, as stated in Disputation 261.

Regarding goods that are **paternal property** <note>original: "profectitia"; property derived directly from the father's estate.</note> (as discussed in Disputations 233 and 234) such that the ownership and profits belong to the parents, and likewise regarding external goods of which the father claims the use-fruit and administration: the son cannot make a donation from these, not even for **alms** <note>original: "eleemosynam"</note>, except according to the father's prescribed will or at least his presumed will. If he makes a donation against his father's will, he commits a sin. As **Saint Thomas** says in the *Sentences* (Book 4, Dist. 15, Q. 2, Art. 5), although a son has a right to be supported by his father's goods when he has none of his own, he does not have the right to give them away without the father's will, at least as it is presumed.

When a son is traveling, or residing at school or at court at his father’s expense, it is regularly presumed to be the father’s will that the son gives alms or similar gifts that others of the same condition and status are accustomed to giving in those places. However, depending on whether the son recognizes his father’s will as more or less inclined toward this, and considering other current circumstances, he may give the same as others, or more, or less, according to what he presumes of his father’s will.

But when he exceeds this, and wastefully consumes property on **games, with prostitutes, or in other vain ways**, the extent to which he is bound to make restitution and bring that amount to the division of inheritance with his brothers—and the extent to which the recipient is also bound to return it—was discussed in Disputation 248. However, when he wastefully consumes his own external property against the will of his father (who holds the use-fruit and administration), although he sins, he would rarely be bound to make restitution. This is because he consumes what is his own in terms of ownership, and he would only rarely defraud the father of the use-fruit; furthermore, a father would rarely be so

<sig>ii</sig>

<column-break/>

harsh as to demand restitution for being defrauded of that use-fruit. Read what we said in Disputation 234 regarding what a son spends from what he earns in his father’s house through his own craft or industry.

<margin>2</margin>
**Minors** who are not under paternal power, even if they have **guardians or tutors** <note>original: "curatores, aut tutores"</note>, may donate as much as is permitted to them by those guardians. How much guardians can and should permit them is explained in Disputation 224 in the section *Furthermore, regarding support.* Hence, donations are lawful and valid if they are made from the funds provided by guardians or tutors for their personal expenses, whether they live in the guardian's house or far away at school, court, or elsewhere—provided they do not exceed the sum prescribed by the guardians. Indeed, if guardians do not permit them alms, donations, and honest recreations in the manner explained in the cited section, minors could make them even against the guardians' will; for such expenses are owed to them by the guardians, as shown there. In cases of doubt, however, one must stand by the judgment of the guardians. But if they spend something badly beyond the sum that ought to be granted for their support, although they may not be bound to make restitution (since they spend what is their own), they nonetheless sin by exceeding the guardian's instructions, and the guardians may recover what was wrongly alienated against their orders. The minors themselves may also recover such items through the benefit of **total restitution** if they were significantly harmed. Meanwhile, as long as it is not recovered, I would not dare to obligate the recipient to make restitution if they received it without force, fraud, or deceit, following what was said at the end of Disputations 224 and 261. It also belongs to the tutors and guardians of minors to give those alms and donations on behalf of the minors which we explained in the cited section, but not larger or unusual ones, as shown there. This is agreed upon by **Juan Med.** in his *Treatise on Alms*, **Paludanus** on the *Sentences*, and **Armilla** under the entry *Alms*.

When such a minor has reached puberty and has either obtained a **grant of age** <note>original: "veniam aetatis"; a legal decree allowing a minor to act as an adult before the usual age.</note> or lacks a guardian, the things he alienates—even by donation—are valid, according to what was said in Disputation 224. However, if he should alienate any **immovable property** (real estate), a judge's decree must intervene; otherwise, such alienation of immovable property is void. Nevertheless, if he finds himself harmed and had not obtained a grant of age when he alienated **movable property**, he would be granted the benefit of total restitution.

Furthermore, a youth of age, even if he has a guardian and has not obtained a grant of age, can donate what he wishes from **military or quasi-military property**. This is because the free administration of those goods belongs to him independently of the guardian, just as was said regarding the son under paternal power.

A **spendthrift** <note>original: "prodigus"; someone legally declared incapable of managing their affairs due to wasting money.</note>, if he has a guardian, cannot make alms or donations other than those permitted by the guardian. Read what we said in Disputation 120 regarding all these matters. Also, those who lack the **use of reason** cannot donate, but only their guardians and tutors can provide for this in their place,

as was said in the same place and in Disputation 261.
<margin>4</margin> A **slave** <note>original: "mancipium"; referring here to a person in a state of legal servitude or bond-service.</note>, if they possess any goods—for instance, because they entered into an agreement with their master to pay a certain amount daily or at fixed times from their labor and keep the remainder for themselves, or from other sources as described in Disputation 38, or if the master allows them some property and the free disposal of it (among which you may count if the master gives a certain daily portion for their sustenance and leaves it to the slave’s discretion to set aside and sell some of it for themselves)—if, I say, in any of these ways, the slave has goods, they may give **alms** from them, and donate or alienate them in other ways. However, from the master's goods, they can donate nothing, even as alms, without the master's express or presumed approval. Indeed, not only do they sin if they do so, but they are also bound to **restitution**, unless the master is of such a mind that, although he is displeased that his goods are given away by the slave (even as alms), he does not wish for restitution, especially from his own slave, who would normally be excused from it due to his poverty. Furthermore, if the person who received the gift believes or suspects it is given against the master’s will, they not only sin against justice by receiving it but are also bound to restore it, unless it is certain that the master’s will is that it not be restored. In a case of doubt as to whether it would please the master, the slave can donate nothing. But if they donated something in **good faith**, thinking it would please their master, even if they later learn the master’s will was contrary and that he wants it restored, the slave is not bound to restore it. This is because there is no obligation arising from the thing received (which they no longer have), nor from an unjust taking, since they did not sin by bestowing it in good faith. However, the slave is bound to warn the recipient that it is the master’s will that it be restored. If the recipient also received and consumed it in good faith and was not made wealthier by it, they are bound to no restitution. But if they have not consumed it, or were made wealthier by it, they are bound to restore it, or as much as they were enriched by it.

### SUMMARY.

1. How large a donation is valid without **insinuation** <term>insinuation; the formal public registration of a deed of gift before a judge or magistrate</term> under Common Law and the law of Castile. And what the law of Portugal says regarding men and women.

4. Registration does not require a judicial inquiry into the cause, nor a judge's decree, even under the law of Castile.
5. Why registration was introduced.

7. The donor cannot renounce the requirement for registration or the law that introduced it. And what if it is done with an oath? (Number 8).
8. If a donation is confirmed by an oath, is it valid without registration regarding the excess? Yes, under Common Law and the law of Castile. However, see the clarification in number 10. Under Portuguese law, it is otherwise (Number 9).
10. What an oath added to a contract of donation effects.

17. The remission of a debt exceeding five hundred *solidi*, or exceeding the sum established in Portugal, is invalid without registration, according to common opinion. Understand and clarify this as in numbers 19 and 20.
18. The remission of a debt is counted among donations.

Next, we must explain how much one may donate without registration, which donations require registration regarding the excess value, and which do not.
<margin>1</margin> Under **Common Law** <note>original: "ius commune"; the combined Roman and Canon law that formed the basis of European legal systems.</note> in the law beginning *Sancimus* at the start of the title "On Donations" in the Code, it was decreed that a donation made without registration was valid up to the value of three hundred *solidi*. If it exceeded that sum, it would be invalid regarding the excess, but valid for the three hundred *solidi* included within that larger sum. For the law intends that what is useful should not be spoiled by what is useless in that event. Later, however, in the second to last law, final paragraph of the same title in the Code, this was extended so that a donation without registration was valid up to the value of five hundred *solidi*, but not for the excess. This same law has force in the **Kingdom of Castile**, where it is established in Law 9, Title 4, of the Fifth *Partida* <note>The "Siete Partidas" was the foundational statutory code of Castile.</note>.
Under **Portuguese Law**, however, if a donation is made by a male, it is only valid without registration up to the value of three hundred gold coins, which we call **cruzados** <note>a Portuguese gold coin</note>; otherwise, it is invalid for the excess. If it is made by a woman capable of donating, it is only valid up to the value of one hundred and fifty gold coins, but not for the excess. This is found in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 54, at the beginning.
<margin>2</margin> There is, however, a doubt as to what should be understood by the name "solidi" under Common Law and the law of Castile. Legal experts—among whom Julius Clarus (Book 4, Sentences, section "Donation," question 15) and the prolific Ioannes Guterrius (Treatise on the Confirmatory Oath, part 1, chapter 7) refer to others—vary greatly indeed. Setting aside other opinions, Covarruvias (in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 11, number 3; and *On the Collation of Ancient Coins*, chapter 3, numbers 3 and 4; and chapter 6, from number 5) and Gregorio Lopez (on Law 9, Title 4, of the Fifth *Partida*) are satisfied that a **solidus** was of the weight and value of the gold coin we call the **Castellano**. And Covarruvias and others report that this is the accepted practice in the courts of the Kingdom of Castile. Furthermore, as to what value should be assigned to this coin today, so that it may be understood how great a sum a donation...

Second Treatise. Disputation 278.

->Whether a donation in the Kingdom of Castile requires registration, and how much is required, is not entirely agreed upon by everyone.<-

I think it should be established as certain that a minimum donation of five hundred **solidi** <note>original: "solidorum"; an ancient gold coin used as a legal benchmark.</note>—each valued at four hundred eighty-five **maravedis** <note>original: "marauedinorum"; the primary unit of account in Spain at the time.</note> in our time, which is fourteen silver **reals** and nine maravedis—does not require **registration** <term>insinuatio</term> <note>The formal recording of a large gift before a magistrate to make it legally binding and prevent fraud.</note> in the Kingdom of Castile. For in the year 1550, **Charles V** passed a law (Law 6, Title 18, Book 6 of the New Compilation) in which he declared the value of the Castillian coin to be four hundred eighty-five maravedis, and under heavy penalties, he forbade anyone from accepting more for it. **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a famous Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> also assigns this same value to that number in the places cited, having examined and demonstrated the matter learnedly. Nor do we know of any time in Spain when it had a lower price since the use of maravedis began.

**Gabriel Monterroso**, in his *Practica* (Treatise 7, folio 117), records a sentence passed in the year 1546 in the **Chancery of Valladolid** <note>original: "Pinciano praetorio"; the high court of the Spanish crown.</note>, which was later confirmed in the same court after both parties petitioned for the matter to be reconsidered. It was pronounced that each of the five hundred *solidi* should be valued at five hundred maravedis, so that a donation is valid in this kingdom without registration up to the value of two hundred fifty thousand maravedis. However, since the value of the Castillian coin had not risen to the price of four hundred eighty-five maravedis until that year, I do not see by what reasoning fifteen maravedis—which makes up the difference to five hundred—were added to each *solidus* in that sentence.

Perhaps someone might say that already by the order of **Charles V**, the cause was that gold shields <note>original: "scuta"; the Spanish *escudo* coin.</note> of twenty-two **carats** <note>original: "caractorum"; we call these *quilates* in Spanish.</note> and the mark of twenty-two carat gold remained at the value of twenty-four thousand maravedis, as it was before in the time of the Sovereigns **Ferdinand and Isabella**. At that time, gold coins were minted at twenty-three and three-quarter carats, so that they lacked only a quarter-carat of being the purest gold (about which there will be more extensive discussion below when dealing with currency exchange). Those judges, then, added that increase to each *solidus* because in **common law** <note>The *Ius Commune*, the Roman-canonical legal system used throughout Europe.</note> the discussion concerned *solidi* of the purest gold, and the **Law of the Partidas** <note>original: "lex partita"; referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational law code of Castile.</note> speaks in accordance with common law. By the very fact that a mark of twenty-two carat gold was valued in this kingdom at twenty-four thousand maravedis, the value of coins made of pure gold increased by one-twelfth of their value. Nor, at the time that sentence was passed, had the law of Charles V mentioned above been issued; if that law is correctly inspected, it forbade accepting a higher price even for the coins minted by Ferdinand and Isabella than what they were valued at previously, when a mark of gold at twenty-three and three-quarter carats was sold for twenty-four thousand maravedis. This certainly seemed somewhat unfair and led to this kingdom being stripped of the older, purer gold coins more quickly than they would have remained in it; yet it was intended to meet that evil with that law, as is manifest from the law itself.

<column-break/>

If anyone argues this way, setting aside other points that will be mentioned to the contrary below, let them note that a much higher value would have to be added to each *solidus* for that reason. For an increase of one-twelfth part over four hundred eighty-five maravedis is far more than fifteen maravedis; it is, in fact, a little more than forty-four maravedis.

Later, in the year 1566, **King Philip** <note>Philip II of Spain.</note>, through Law 13, Part 2, Title 21, Book 5 of the New Compilation, raised the gold shield of twenty-two carats (which in the time of Charles V was valued at three hundred fifty maravedis) to the value of four hundred maravedis. By the same law, he established that the **Castellano** <note>A specific gold coin of Castile.</note> of twenty-two carats was worth five hundred forty-four maravedis, increasing the price of the *Castellano* in the same proportion as he had increased the price of the shield. Furthermore, by setting that price only for the *Castellano* of twenty-two carats, he clearly implied that he left it open for more to be accepted for a *Castellano* of more carats, according to the greater quantity of gold it contained—especially since no *Castellano* of only twenty-two carats is known to have ever been minted in this kingdom.

The question arises whether, now that the price of the *Castellano* has been increased today by King Philip to five hundred forty-four maravedis, a donation is valid in this kingdom without registration if it is valued at five hundred *solidi*, where each is valued at the price of five hundred forty-four maravedis. Or even, whether each should be valued at an even higher price by a twelfth part, because of the two carats of gold (or one and three-quarters) that are missing from today’s twenty-two carat *Castellano* (valued at five hundred forty-four maravedis) to reach the standard of the ancient *solidus* or *Castellano* of pure gold, or one of twenty-three and three-quarter carats. For indeed, both common law and the *Law of the Partidas* with it were speaking of the ancient *solidi*, which had more than twenty-two carats of gold.

Despite this reasoning, I believe it should be said that today, for the purpose of judging which donation requires registration and which does not, the *solidi* should be valued at the ancient price of four hundred eighty-five maravedis. This is despite both the increase in the price of the *solidi* or *Castellanos* and the decrease in the carats of the same coin, which is the reason why ancient *solidi* are worth more today by their very nature than the price of five hundred forty-four maravedis. The reason that leads me to this is that whenever a value has been established by law, contract, or any other means through the expression of a specific currency—such as that a certain number of *solidi*, shields, or ducats should be paid, or something should be valued or sold for so many *solidi*, shields, or ducats—surely the variation in the price of that currency that occurs later changes nothing regarding the ancient value and price established by law, contract, or other means. This holds whether the price of the coin is increased or decreased without the coin itself being changed, or whether the price is kept the same but the coin itself is changed in terms of carats or weight, as is everywhere accepted in practice when the price of money is taxed by the law and the will of the prince, as is done in Spain. For example, regarding the price of the shield...

### Ludovico Molina, *On Contracts* ###

...the value of the ducat <note>original: "ducati"; a common gold coin.</note> being increased by King Philip, it changes nothing of the ancient value expressed by law, contract, or any other such reason regarding that currency. For if it was established by law that whoever committed a certain crime should pay a penalty of so many ducats, the penalty must be paid in the ancient value of the ducat—three hundred seventy-five **maravedis**—and not in the increased value of the ducat—four hundred twenty-nine maravedis—as is the accepted practice. The same applies when, by contract or other means, so many ducats were to be paid, as is similarly the accepted practice in this kingdom. Portuguese practice holds the same. For although the gold **crusado** <note>original: "cruciatus"; a Portuguese gold coin.</note>, once valued at four hundred copper coins (which they call **reais** <note>original: "reais"; the unit of currency in Portugal.</note>), is today of much greater price—both because of the greater gold carats it contains compared to other gold coins minted today, and because the price of a mark of gold with fewer carats has been increased in Portugal above the ancient price of purer gold; and finally, because with the price of the silver **real** <note>original: "regalis argentei"</note> increased by King Sebastian to forty copper coins, the crusado is paid with ten silver reals, which was once paid with eleven—from all these causes, I say, because the gold crusado is of much greater price today than it once was, a value of a crusado expressed and established by law, contract, or other means is not paid in today’s value of the crusado, but in the ancient value, as is received by use and custom. And for this reason today in Portugal, a donation made by a husband that exceeds three hundred crusados of the ancient value requires **registration** <term>insinuatio</term> <note>The formal act of recording a gift in public records before a judge to prevent fraud or impulsive poverty.</note>, as is the accepted practice, regardless of the fact that it is paid today with a smaller quantity of gold and silver than in the past. The same must be said in this Kingdom of Castile regarding a donation that exceeds the value of five hundred **solidi** <note>original: "solidorum"; an ancient gold unit used for legal thresholds.</note>, or **Castellanos**, of the ancient price, regardless of the fact that today it is paid with a smaller quantity of gold and fewer solidi of today’s value. 

As for that sentence passed by the senators in the **High Court of Valladolid** <note>original: "Pinciano praetorio"</note>: it must be said that since those senators relied on no solid foundation to establish the estimation of five hundred maravedis to define the sum that could be donated without registration, and since we have shown quite clearly that the estimation was four hundred eighty-five maravedis (which **Charles V** declared, forbidding any departure from it as the ancient standard), and which **Covarruvias** and others showed by deducing it from their principles—that sentence [of the Valladolid court] ought not to be followed. I suspect, however, that those Senators established that estimation because it produced a certain number of thousands of maravedis, and was a middle ground between the estimation of the Castillano then and the opinion of **Paulus de Castro**, **Jason**, and others, which was more common at that time, as **Gutierrez** and others report in the place cited.

<margin>5</margin> **Registration** <note>original: "Insinuatio"</note> in the matter proposed is the manifestation of a donation before a judge, with the donor appearing before him and declaring that he is making, or has made, such a donation to such a person, and with a notary recording it in the acts. Nor is it necessary for the judge to be in the place of judgment at that time, as **Julius Clarus** affirms along with **Johannes Andreae**, **Imola**, and others, and says is the accepted practice. It can also be done by the donor appearing through his proxy <column-break/> before the judge, or even through the recipient of the gift, to whom he grants the mandate and faculty in the instrument of donation to appear before the judge and register that donation, as **Gutierrez** says. For it is open to anyone who cannot or does not wish to be present for his own business to conduct it through others, as is held in the law. Without a judge, however, a notary and witnesses are not sufficient for a donation exceeding the sum to be considered registered and valid regarding the excess, as the common opinion of the doctors affirms; and **Gregorio Lopez** says this has always been observed in the courts of Castile. Moreover, the cited law of Castile declares that registration ought to be done before the "supreme judge of the place." Therefore, if it is done before local petty judges, the registration will be invalid, as Gutierrez says; rather, the judge ought to be the head of the jurisdiction, or one who constitutes a single tribunal with him, such as the <term>Alcaldes</term> <note>original: "Alcades"; Spanish municipal magistrates.</note>, whom they call the **High Mayors** of the city or town in the Kingdom of Castile, who form one tribunal with the governors <note>original: "correctoribus"</note>, as will be said in Treatise 5. Regarding which judges this should be done before under common law, see the law *In hac* in the Code *on donations*.

<margin>4</margin> Whether formal **judicial inquiry** <note>original: "causae cognitio"</note> and a decree of the judge are necessary for registration, and whether he must interpose his authority for that donation: the common opinion of the doctors with **Bartolus** affirms that none of these are necessary by common law or in the Kingdom of Castile, but it is enough that the donation was made known to the judge. So say **Julius Clarus**, **Gutierrez**, and **Gregorio Lopez** in the places cited; and **Antonio Gomez** and many others whom they cite. And this is clearly signified by the cited Law 9; which, having said that a donation exceeding five hundred solidi was null regarding the excess, added: *Unless he does it by deed, and with the knowledge of the High Judge of that place where he makes the donation.* <note>original: "Fueras ende, si lo hiziere con carta, e cō sabiduria del mayor Iulgador de aquel logar, do hiziere la donacion."</note> Here it requires only the "knowledge" of the judge, which the word "registration" signifies. The reasons are that registration is not a contentious matter, but of purely voluntary jurisdiction, and for that reason does not require a formal trial.

<margin>5</margin> Indeed, it was introduced not to take away from men the freedom to give according to their own judgment—and therefore the judge cannot prohibit or hinder such a donation if the free will of the donor is evident—but it was introduced, first, so that men might perform donations of such greater importance more maturely by first going before a judge, lest they be easily impoverished by **fickleness of mind** <note>original: "animi leuitate"</note>; and second, lest fraud and deceit intervene in them, and lest they be made by force or fear. The presumption of these things ceases if they are first manifested to a judge and recorded in the acts, as is clearly hinted in the Code *on donations*. But because this last reason was the chief one for which registration was introduced, surely when any suspicion arose from the circumstances that fraud, force, or fear intervened in the donation, the judge would be bound not to consider it registered until he had interrogated the donor under oath as to whether he was induced to give by force, fear, or fraud, and similarly interrogated the recipients whether they had induced him to give by themselves or through others, and performed whatever other greater inquiry he judged expedient.

<summary>This page explains the legal requirements for registering large gifts (insinuation) in Spain and Portugal, arguing that such registration exists to prevent impulsive poverty and fraud rather than to restrict personal freedom. Molina clarifies that registration requires a high-level judge's "knowledge" but not necessarily a formal trial.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 278 ###

Because, therefore, such an investigation is necessary in this event; and because it is the duty of a prudent judge to at least examine the donor to see if they were induced to give by force, fear, or fraud; and finally, because there have been those who asserted that it is always necessary for this to be done; for the sake of greater caution, a practice has prevailed in this **Kingdom of Castile**, as reported by Gutierrez in the place cited and Gabriel Monterroso in *Practice*, tract 7, folio 119. This practice requires the judge to question the donor on whether the donation was fake or simulated; and upon the donor replying that it was not, the judge would approve it, interpose his decree and authority, and record everything in the official acts. Gutierrez adds that this is done for greater caution, but it is not strictly necessary for the donation to be valid and considered <term>insinuated</term> <note>Insinuation was the Roman law requirement to publicly register gifts exceeding 500 gold coins (solidi) to prevent secret transfers that might defraud heirs or creditors.</note>.

<margin>Portuguese Law. 6</margin>
Regarding **Portuguese law**, the insinuation must be performed before the King or before the senators appointed for this purpose, and the donation must be approved by them. The insinuation is made after the King or senators first order an investigation. In this inquiry, the donor is primarily to be questioned: were they led by anyone through some cleverness, fraud, or fear? Or are they being held in chains, or facing some similar cause for making the gift? And is it truly their will that it be confirmed and approved by the King? Furthermore, some of the donor's neighbors should be questioned—those presumed to know the situation better than others—regarding how the donation was made. When this entire investigation has been reported to the King or the senators, if it is established that the donation was made properly and that it is the donor’s will for it to be confirmed, an instrument of confirmation is granted to the recipient. Only then is the donation considered insinuated, confirmed, and valid regarding the excess amount, and not otherwise. These matters are found in *Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 54*, at the beginning and in section 1.

7 The requirement for insinuation, or the law that demands it for a donation to be valid, cannot be waived by the donor. Even if a waiver is included in the deed of the gift, the donation remains invalid regarding the excess amount. So affirms Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 7 (with no one objecting, as far as I know). Gabriel Monterroso affirms the same in tract 7, folio 16, column 2. Those who debate whether the addition of an oath makes it valid—a topic to be discussed shortly—concur with this. For if a simple waiver alone could make the gift valid, that entire question would be superfluous. Antonio Gomez proves his assertion: First, because a law that introduces a <term>solemnity</term> <note>A "solemnity" refers to a formal legal ceremony or requirement necessary for an act to have legal force.</note> as a required form for an act to be valid cannot be waived, based on the legal principle "no one can" <note>original: "l. nemo pot." referring to a specific law in the Digest of Roman Law.</note>; such is the law we are discussing. Second, because the same fraud, fear, or force used to drive someone to give could also be used to force them to waive the insinuation. Thus, the law would be of no significance and would not address the harm it intended to remedy—an intention that should not be presumed of the law.

8 It is also a matter of doubt whether, if a donation is confirmed by an **oath**, it is valid without insinuation regarding the excess amount; that is, whether the oath supplies the defect of insinuation. Although many interpreters of the Civil Law <note>original: "iuris Caesarei"; referring to the Roman law tradition as used in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, following Baldus, once asserted it was invalid, the more common opinion of the exponents of Canon Law—which today the doctors of both schools commonly embrace—affirms that it is valid, following the legal principle "when it happens" <note>original: "c. cum contingat de iureiu."</note>. Among others, Julius Clarus reports and follows this most clearly in *Sentences*, Book 4, section on Donations, question 18, as does Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*,

<column-break/>

chapter 4, number 8; Gutierrez in his repetition of the law "no one can" and on "confirmatory oaths," part 1, chapter 7; and Sylvester under the word "donation," questions 4 and 6. Indeed, from what was said by us in Disputations 149, 150, and 151, this is quite manifest when joined with what we said in Disputation 256 and at the end of Disputation 263. For to give more than five hundred **shillings** <note>original: "quingentos solidos"</note> is not evil in itself, nor is it prohibited by Roman or Castilian law; it is merely rendered void for the common good of the state if it is done without insinuation. It is no different from the alienation of <term>dowry land</term> <note>Land brought into a marriage as part of a woman's dowry, which was protected by law from being sold or given away by the husband.</note>, which is not evil in itself or prohibited by Roman law, but merely void; yet if it is confirmed by the wife's oath, it is valid, as held in the chapters "when it happens" and "although of the woman" in the sixth book of the Decretals. The same applies to the alienation of a minor's property without the formalities established by civil law; if it is confirmed by the minor's oath, it is valid, as is clear from the law regarding the "oath of youths." The same is true of a pact where a father agrees with a daughter or son that they should be content with a certain portion of goods and waive the rest of their legal inheritance; if confirmed by the child's oath, it is valid, as is clear from the chapter "Who a pact" <note>original: "cap. Quis pactum"</note>. All these things were explained in the cited Disputation 146. Therefore, in a similar way, if a donation exceeding the sum of five hundred shillings is made without insinuation but is confirmed by an oath, it will be valid, with nothing in Roman or Castilian law standing in the way.

9 <margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
I deliberately made no mention of a gift made in **Portugal** exceeding the sum permitted without insinuation. For in that kingdom, not only would an oath confirming such a donation be void, but the mere inclusion of an oath would be enough to make the entire donation null by that very fact, according to what we reported in Disputation 146 from the law of that kingdom. Certainly, in that kingdom, even if a donation made without insinuation is confirmed by an oath, it is invalid regarding the excess, and even regarding the sum below the excess, unless such an oath is used by royal permission. In the **Kingdom of Castile**, however, as we reported in the same disputation, the opposite holds; for there it is permitted not only to confirm with an oath those things which would otherwise lack force, but even all otherwise valid perpetual donations.

10 Julius Clarus, in the cited question, number 2, refers to the opinion of certain legal experts (which he claims is common) asserting that a donation made without insinuation, if confirmed by an oath, is only valid regarding the excess when the insinuation was specifically waived and that waiver was confirmed by the oath. For they say that if the insinuation was not specifically waived, the donation is invalid regarding the excess, even if it is confirmed by an oath. Julius Clarus adds that although one should perhaps not depart from this opinion when advising or judging, in a point of law it does not pass without difficulty. For the same "favor of the soul" <note>A legal concept where the spiritual obligation of an oath (to avoid perjury) takes precedence over technical legal formalities.</note> seems to apply, upon which the doctors cited above principally base themselves. Thus far Julius Clarus, who tremulously inclines toward that same opinion. Gutierrez attributes the same to him in the cited number 2 and seems to subscribe to it. Nevertheless, Antonio Gomez rightly affirms the contrary in the cited number 8: namely, that a gift confirmed by an oath is valid regarding the excess, even if the insinuation is not waived. -> **Ludovico Molina on Contracts** <-

The previous opinion has no probability, especially if one weighs what we said in Disputation 151 and the two preceding it. Indeed, if someone promises under oath that they will give one thousand **solidi** <note>The *solidus* was a gold coin; under Roman law, gifts exceeding 500 solidi had to be officially registered to be valid.</note> to someone for free, since that which he promises is not evil or prohibited by natural or positive law, he remains bound by the force of the oath alone. The **recipient** acquires a true right, not only in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>Internal moral accountability to God.</note> but also in the **external forum** <note>The public legal system.</note>, even if he does not renounce the requirement for registration. This is clear enough from what was said in the cited disputations. And this is surely a solid foundation for everyone as to why a gift that has not been registered, if confirmed by an oath, is valid regarding the excess amount.

Julio Claro, along with Federico of Siena, adds a qualification: that a gift confirmed by oath is valid without registration regarding the excess only when the registration, by the form of the law or statute, ought to have occurred during the very act of giving. However, this does not apply where the law or statute requires the gift to be registered within a certain time, such as within a month from the day the gift was celebrated, or within another similar timeframe. In that case, the oath attached to the gift does not confirm it in the event that it is not registered within the time prescribed by the statute. The reason is that an oath is regulated according to the time of the contract; for that reason, if a cause later arises by which the contract is rendered null, the power of the oath cannot be extended to its confirmation. He also mentions that Curtius the Younger affirms this to be the common opinion.

However, I am entirely persuaded that this is false. For the oath by which such a promise or gift is confirmed bestows strength upon the gift by itself and supplies the place of registration, so that after the oath, registration becomes superfluous. Therefore, it could not be rendered null due to a lack of registration, as the opinion we are attacking supposes. Furthermore, registration depends on the donor himself, in whose name the gift must be manifested to a judge. By the very fact that the judge finds the gift to be voluntary on the part of the donor, he cannot but hold it as registered and firm regarding the excess, as was said above. Moreover, he who binds himself to something by oath is considered by that same oath to be bound to all things necessary for it to take effect. Thus, in the matter we are debating, the donor himself would be bound to register the gift to fulfill his oath, if registration were necessary for the gift to be valid. He ought to blame himself if he omitted it; this would certainly by no means excuse him from the obligation he took upon himself by oath to fulfill the gift.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
A doubt arises: if someone, without registration and without an oath, gives someone more than five hundred **solidi**, but includes a clause in the document of the gift (as <term>notaries</term> <note>Latin: *tabelliones*; public officials authorized to draw up legal documents.</note> frequently are accustomed to do) stating that he is making as many gifts as there are sums under five hundred solidi—is that gift valid regarding the excess? 

<margin>Decision 11</margin>
The common opinion of the doctors affirms that such a clause achieves nothing, as it is seen as being applied in <term>fraud of the law</term> <note>original: *in fraudem legis*; an attempt to bypass the spirit of a law by technically following its letter.</note>. This is the view of Bartolus, Antonio Gomez, Julio Claro, Gutierrez, and many others cited by Gabriel Monterroso, who says it was so judged in the court of Valladolid.

<column-break/>

This can be confirmed by the <term>Authentica</term> <note>A collection of Justinian's legal updates.</note> regarding non-alienation. There, if Church property is handed over in <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A long-term land lease similar to a freehold.</note> with a pact that, when the lives for which it is granted end, it should begin again for other lives based on a new contract made at the same time from the beginning, that new contract is rendered void as a machination introduced in fraud of the law. The same reasoning applies to the prolongation of time, the multiplication of contracts, and the multiplication of sums through feigned distinct gifts made at the same time.

<margin>12</margin>
Bartolus, Antonio Gomez, Gutierrez, Gama, and others whom they cite affirm that this holds true even when several things are given at one and the same time, none of which exceed the value of five hundred solidi, but all of them together do exceed it. For although, due to the diversity of the things given, they may be considered multiple gifts or stipulations, for the purpose of requiring registration when they exceed the sum of five hundred solidi, they are regarded as one when they are made to the same person at the same time.

<margin>13</margin>
The same is said by Gama, following Romano and others, when a certain sum is given to several people at once which exceeds five hundred solidi, even if the portion that belongs to each individual recipient from that sum does not reach five hundred solidi. The reason is that in requiring registration when a sum exceeds five hundred solidi, the law does not consider the recipients, but the donor, lest he be impoverished rashly through force, fear, or fraud. For that reason, when the body of the gift is one and the act of giving is one, registration is required, even if there are many recipients and the gift is multiplex on their part.

<margin>14</margin>
Gama thinks the same applies when several things are given by the same donor to many people at the same time, which together exceed the sum allowed without registration, even though the items given to individuals do not reach that sum. He says this was so judged by the senators in **Portugal**.

<margin>15</margin>
When someone at different times, without registration, gives many things to one and the same person—even if all taken together exceed the sum not permitted without registration—if the things given in individual acts of donation do not exceed that sum, all the gifts are valid. This is defined in the Code of Justinian and is supported by the common opinion of the legal experts.

<margin>16</margin>
When someone has given someone an annual amount that does not exceed the allowed sum in any single year, but over two or more years it does exceed it, a distinction must be made. For if it is given such that upon the death of either the donor or the recipient the gift expires, the entire gift is valid without registration. But if it is given so that it passes to the heirs of either—that is, the heirs of the donor are bound to pay it, or it must be paid to the heirs of the recipient—it is invalid regarding the amount exceeding five hundred solidi. This is defined in the law and is supported by common opinion.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
Whether, however, the <term>remission of a debt</term> <note>Canceling a debt as a form of gift.</note> made without registration...
