<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the "insinuation" (formal registration) of large gifts. It specifically addresses whether the forgiveness of a debt or the renunciation of a legal claim counts as a gift that must be registered if it exceeds the 500 solidi limit.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 278 ###

Whether a gift—if it exceeds five hundred **solidi** <note>The *solidus* was a gold coin; Roman law required gifts over 500 solidi to be officially registered.</note>—is valid regarding the excess, or in Portugal, whether a gift for that sum is valid without registration.
<margin>17 Decision.</margin>
The common opinion of the legal experts affirms that such a gift is invalid when the debt is certain. This is the view of the "Gloss" on the law *si quis obligatione* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de reg. iuris"</note>, as well as Bartolus, Panormitanus, and others whom Covarruvias cites and follows (Book 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 8). It is also held by Julius Clarus (Book 4, *Sentences*, section "Donation," question 16, number 2) and Antonio Gómez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 9). 
<margin>18</margin>
Indeed, the law *in aedibus* at the beginning of the Digest title "On Donations" <note>original: "ff. de donationib."</note> counts the **forgiving of a debt** <note>original: "Remissionem debiti"</note> among donations; see also the law *si mulier* and the law *peculium* (with Bartolus's commentary). The same must be said regarding the pardoning of a legal right when it is certain, as well as an **agreement not to sue** <note>original: "pacto de non petendo"</note> and a legal assignment, as Julius Clarus affirms in the cited place (numbers 3 and 4) along with others.
<margin>19</margin>
This must be understood to apply when it is done in the manner of a gift, purely out of generosity. For when it is done as a recompense for another thing, or for the forgiveness or assignment of another right—as occurs in legal settlements—then no registration is necessary. 

When something is sold for more than half of its **fair price** <note>original: "iusti pretij"</note>, and the portion exceeding half the fair price also exceeds five hundred solidi, and this amount is later pardoned by the buyer or returned to the seller, there is no doubt that registration is necessary for the amount exceeding five hundred solidi. This is because it would be a forgiveness of a true and undisputed debt, and thus a gift, according to what was just said. 

Likewise, when a thing is sold for less than half its fair price, and the seller renounces the claim for **legal injury** <note>original: "læsioni renunciaret"; referring to *laesio enormis*, where a seller could rescind a contract if the price was less than half the value</note>, if he does this with a purely generous intent so that the buyer remains safe both in the public courts and in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "conscientiæ foro"</note>, then surely, if the amount remitted below half the fair price exceeds five hundred solidi, registration would be necessary for the remission of the excess to be valid. This is because it is a true gift of that quantity or right which would remain with the seller unless he purely and freely renounced that injury. At the very least, it cannot be denied that this is a **tacit or presumed gift** <note>original: "donationem tacitam, seu præsumptã"</note>, regarding which Julius Clarus says (in the place cited, number 1) that registration is necessary; he notes that this specific decision once brought him great honor in his legal practice. 

If Covarruvias (at number 8 cited above) intends anything contrary to this doctrine, his opinion is certainly not pleasing. Bartolus, on the law *Modestinus* (number 1), and with him Silvestrus (under the word "donation," question 7), and Baldus, make a distinction: 
<margin>20 Opinion.</margin>
Either a sum exceeding five hundred solidi is owed from several different causes—such that the amount owed from each individual cause does not exceed five hundred solidi—or it is owed from one single cause. In the first case, they say the forgiveness of the total debt does not require registration; in the latter case, however, it does. Their reasoning is simply that the forgiveness of a debt arising from several causes is considered multiple remissions, and thus multiple gifts; but a forgiveness from only one cause is considered only a single gift and remission. 
<margin>It is refuted.</margin>
However, since it was defined in the Code of Justinian <note>original: "C. de donationib."</note> (law *sancimus*, section *si quis aut per*) that gifts of different things (which are otherwise considered multiple) are considered a single gift if they are made at the same time—specifically for the purpose of requiring registration—the same must undoubtedly be said of a forgiveness of debt made at one time, even if that debt

<column-break/>

arose from several causes. Antonio Gómez affirms this along with Imola (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 9).

<margin>21 Question.</margin>
The question arises whether a recipient to whom something exceeding five hundred solidi has been given without registration can retain the excess with a **safe conscience** <note>original: "tuta conscientia"</note> before the giver asks for it back. 

The side that says "no" can be argued as follows: because the law that introduced the requirement for registration is not a **penal law** <note>A law that imposes a punishment for a crime</note>, we cannot say that a court sentence must be awaited before the excess must be restored to the giver, both in the public courts and in the court of conscience. This is especially true since the giver is no less—in fact, more—at fault for omitting the registration than the recipient. Laws do not usually adjudge a penalty to the one who was at fault, but to the treasury, when both contracting parties were at fault, which is not seen in the present case. 

Neither can we say that the law is based on a **presumption** that such a huge gift was extorted by fraud, force, fear, or deceit. First, because in that case, not only would the excess be void, but the entire gift would be, yet the law decrees the opposite. This confirms that the law was not introduced as a punishment for the recipient; for then it would have rendered the whole gift void, not just the excess. Second, if the law were based on that presumption, then as soon as it became clear in the public court from the giver's confession that no fraud, force, fear, or deceit occurred, the entire gift would be pronounced valid. For against a law based solely on a presumption, the confession of the person in whose favor it was introduced is valid—even if it is a "presumption of law and by law" <note>original: "praesumptio iuris & de iure"; a legal presumption that cannot be rebutted by evidence</note>. 

However, legal practice holds the opposite. For even if it is clear from the giver's confession that none of those things occurred, the gift is nonetheless pronounced void regarding the excess, and the excess is awarded to the giver or his heirs. Furthermore, if that law were based on such a presumption, then—since a law based solely on a presumption has no force in the court of conscience—the giver would be bound to restore the excess awarded to him for lack of registration, and he would sin mortally by seeking it. No one would affirm this, nor does it agree with practice in any way. 

It remains, therefore, that the law has rendered any gift exceeding the limit void for the common good if it is made without registration. This being the case, since the recipient possesses that excess by no legal title and has not made it his own, it follows that in the court of conscience, without waiting for any sentence or demand, he is bound to restore it to the giver, or to the heirs if the giver is deceased.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Nevertheless, I believe it must be said: First, as long as the giver (or his heirs) are not considered unwilling, the recipient can retain the excess with a safe conscience. For no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting. 

Secondly, that one can simply retain such an excess with a safe conscience as long as it is not demanded back. For since—if that law were set aside—the entire gift would be valid and would transfer ownership, that law today surely has no more force than what has been accepted by custom. No one, however, no matter how God-fearing, ever restores the excess to the giver or his heirs unless he is first sued on the grounds that the gift was not registered. Therefore, since custom interprets that law and prescribes against it, even if the original intention of the legislators was different, the law has no other force today than that the recipient is bound to restore the excess if it is demanded.

To grant more than a recovery of the gift on those grounds would be to ensnare men’s consciences without any benefit to the state. Such a thing is neither consistent with a just law, nor with the mature judgment and integrity of legislators, which must always be presumed in the law. Rather, in accordance with these laws, they should be interpreted and understood piously through **epicheia** <note>From the Greek "epieikeia," meaning equity or fairness—the principle of interpreting the spirit of a law when the literal application would be unjust.</note>.

## A gift which does not require registration to be valid.
# DISPUTATION 279.
### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *A gift for the redemption of captives, the repair of houses, the construction of a church, a hospital, or another pious place is valid in any amount without registration.*
<margin>2</margin> *A gift for pious causes, of whatever sum or quantity, is valid without registration, notwithstanding any civil law or statute.*
<margin>3</margin> *A gift from a Prince who recognizes no superior, or a gift made to a Prince, does not require registration, regardless of the amount.*
<margin>4</margin> *The same applies to a gift made by a military commander. Number 4.*
<margin>5</margin> *A remuneratory gift, or one given for a specific cause—even if that cause is in the future—does not require registration to be valid.*
<margin>6</margin> *A remuneratory gift, or one given for a specific cause, is not strictly a "gift."*
<margin>7</margin> *A gift given as a dowry, or for a wedding, or because of a marriage, is valid without registration.*
<margin>8</margin> *A gift made to a father by a son at the time of his emancipation, though it may seem to be for a cause, still requires registration.*
<margin>9</margin> *When a remuneratory gift or one given for a cause requires registration.*
<margin>10</margin> *When a reciprocal gift requires registration.*
<margin>11</margin> *When the establishment of a **mayorazgo** <note>An entailed estate that passes to a specific heir, common in Spanish and Portuguese law.</note> requires registration.*
<margin>12</margin> *A gift made in anticipation of death does not require registration.*
<margin>13</margin> *The renunciation of a future right that depends on acceptance does not require registration.*
<margin>14</margin> *When a gift under Portuguese law requires registration, and when it does not.*

<margin>1</margin> By the law *Illud* <note>found in the Codex of Justinian, title "On Sacred Churches"</note>, it was decreed that while a gift made to others would not be valid without registration unless it was under two hundred **solidi** <note>The "solidus" was a standard gold coin of the late Roman Empire; 500 solidi was a significant fortune.</note>, a gift made to churches, hospitals, the poor, or a city would be valid without registration up to five hundred solidi. The "Gloss" <note>Standard medieval legal commentary</note> on that passage understands this to apply to gifts made to other similar **pious causes** <note>Acts of charity or religious devotion.</note>. Later, in the law *Sancimus* and the section *Alias vero* <note>Codex, title "On Donations"</note>, it was established that other gifts made without registration were valid only up to three hundred solidi, while those made to the aforementioned pious causes were valid up to five hundred without registration. Most recently, however, by the penultimate law in the same title, the power was granted to give up to five hundred solidi universally without registration. No specific limit, however, was set for the **redemption of captives** <note>A vital charitable activity in this era, used to buy back Christians captured by Barbary pirates or Ottoman forces.</note>, nor for the repair of houses ruined by collapse or fire—provided the gifted item is not used for something else, and provided that if any value remains after 

<column-break/>

the houses are repaired that was not registered and exceeds five hundred solidi, the gift is invalid regarding that excess. The law 9, title 4, part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Spanish legal code</note> establishes the same, adding that a gift can also be made for the construction of a church without registration and without any limit, and likewise for a hospital, a church, or another pious place, just as for repairing ruined buildings.

Certain authors cited in the "Gloss" on the laws *Illud* and *Sancimus* asserted that today, for all pious causes mentioned in these two legal sections, a gift can be made up to eight hundred solidi. They argue that since the law *Illud* allowed gifts to pious causes up to five hundred solidi when other gifts were only permitted up to two hundred, it follows that when the law *Ultima* <note>The final law in that section of the Codex</note> extended the general limit to five hundred solidi, it implicitly granted pious causes a further increase of three hundred solidi (the same "bonus" amount pious causes previously held over standard gifts). However, the cited Gloss, Antonio Gómez (in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 10), and the legal experts generally reject this. For when the law *Sancimus* extended standard gifts to three hundred solidi, no increase was added to pious causes; rather, it was expressly stated that they were only permitted up to five hundred solidi, as before. Therefore, one cannot infer an equal increase for pious causes based on an increase for non-pious gifts unless a specific law states so, and no such law is found.

For this reason, the cited Glosses, Antonio Gómez, and many others affirm that—except for gifts for the redemption of captives, the repair of ruined houses, and (under the law of Castile) the building of a church—a gift for pious causes made without registration in excess of five hundred solidi is invalid today, as that is what the civil law we have cited establishes.

<margin>2</margin> Nevertheless, it must be said that gifts for **pious causes** require no registration at all. Consequently, regardless of the amount, they are valid without registration, not only in the court of conscience <note>Refers to moral or religious standing before God.</note> but also in the external secular courts. This is the view of Panormitanus, Felinus, Bartolus, Silvester (under the word "donation"), Julius Clarus, and many others cited by Felinus and Clarus; though not all are inspired by the same reasoning. The strongest reason is that which Panormitanus provides based on the text, which we also gave above in Disputation 134. Specifically, in those matters pertaining to pious causes and generally to the **supernatural end of the salvation of souls**, no constitution of secular princes has power, nor can it prejudice a spiritual good, except insofar as it has been approved by the Supreme Pontiff. For this reason, legacies and other final dispositions for pious causes are valid even if the formalities required by civil law were not observed. Therefore, since the civil laws which establish that gifts to pious causes...

**2.** A gift made by a prince who recognizes no superior, given to any private person, even if it is not for a pious cause, does not require registration, regardless of how great the quantity is, as is clear from the law *Sancimus*, section *Exceptis* <note>Code of Justinian, book on donations</note>. The same applies to a gift made by a private person to such a prince, as is held in the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's legal updates</note> titled "also from private persons," and in the section "so that pledges are not made," and in the cited law 9.

**4.** A gift from a Master of Soldiers (that is, a commander) made to soldiers regarding movable property or self-moving property <note>original: "rebus mobilibus aut se moventibus" - referring to goods like furniture vs. livestock or slaves</note>, whether it consists of the goods of such a commander or the spoils of enemies, and whether it occurs during the occupation of war or while they reside elsewhere, is valid without registration regardless of its quantity. So it is held in the second-to-last law of the Code, *On Donations*.

**5.** Likewise, a remuneratory gift <note>A gift given as a reward for a service already performed</note>, and generally a gift given for a cause—even if the cause is in the future (as almost all the cited doctors affirm)—does not require registration to be valid. So it is with the gloss on the law *Aquilius* (otherwise *Atilius*) *Regulus* on the words "not a pure [gift]," in the Digest *On Donations*; and Bartolus there. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which they report and follow: Molina, book 2 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 8; Julius Clarus, book 4, section *Donation*; Antonio Gomez; and Gama. This is proved primarily by the cited law of *Aquilius Regulus*, where Aquilius had given and promised the residence of a certain garret to a teacher of his—both because he had lived in his father's house and because he had taught Aquilius himself—and after Regulus's death, the heirs of Regulus wanted to

Likewise, registration would be required if it exceeded the legal limit, which is not required here. Thus far the gloss. > *If someone has rescued another captured by bandits or enemies, and receives something for it from him, this gift is irrevocable. For it must be called the reward for extraordinary labor, which, in contemplation of safety, cannot be estimated in a certain way.*
This is found there, where Bartolus's summary has it thus: When a gift is made for the sake of remuneration, it does not need registration. Thirdly, it is proved by the law "By this right," where we read:
> *But also these stipulations, which are made for a cause, do not constitute a gift. Finally, Pegasius thought that if I promised you a hundred on this condition, that you would swear to take my name, it is not a gift: because it was done for a purpose, and the purpose followed.*
Thus far that section. Because therefore a gift for a cause is not simply a gift, it certainly

<column-break/>

**7** does not require registration. Fourthly, † it proves this because a gift for a dowry, because it is for a cause, never required registration in comparison to the husband, because in comparison to him it did not have the nature of a gift. Today, indeed, it does not require registration even in comparison to the wife, as held in the last law of the Code *On the Law of Dowries*. Likewise, a gift for marriage, or on account of marriage, today does not require registration, as held in the *Authenticum* titled "that betrothal generosity," and Gama affirms this. In this place, observe that a gift for marriage, in relation to the spouse who contracts with such a recipient, does not have the nature of a gift, but of an onerous contract <term>Onerous contract: A legal agreement where both parties give and receive something of value, unlike a "gratuitous" gift which is one-sided.</term>.

Arias Pinel, in his commentary on the Code, thinks—though others agree that a remuneratory gift does not need registration—that a 
**8** † gift made to a father by a son at the time of emancipation <term>Emancipation: The legal process of releasing a child from parental authority (patria potestas)</term> does require registration, if it exceeds the sum permitted to be given without registration. He argues that nothing prevents this, even though it seems remuneratory for the benefit of emancipation received from the father. This is argued: first, because if a cause-based gift did not require registration, fathers would easily be exposed to the frauds of sons, being easily enticed and deceived by the love of emancipation; especially since by common law parents have a reward established for the benefit of emancipation (half the use of the son's separate property). Also because of the law which requires registration for a gift made by sons to parents no less than (indeed more than) those made to others, because fraud and deception can more easily intervene between parents. And although the law says paternal power is "inestimable" for the good of the father, this rather seems to suggest that no reward can equal the benefit of emancipation, rather than suggesting a gift made in recompense for that benefit should require registration.

**9** The doctors observe that when † something is given in remuneration, or for another cause, if what is given exceeds the limits of the reward or the cause, then, as to the excess, it does not have the nature of a gift for a cause, but of a simple gift. And so, if that excess exceeds five hundred solidi, the gift is invalid regarding that which exceeded five hundred solidi, if the gift was not registered. So says Molina in the cited place, and Gama, and others. This accords with the decree "Related 2" on wills, with those words: > *some things may be conferred according to the merit of the service.*

**10** In a † reciprocal gift, if it is made simultaneously on both sides—as if they mutually agree: "I give you such an estate, and you in turn give me such a thing"—registration is not necessary. For gifts of this kind are both made for a cause, and rather have the nature of an onerous contract than a gift. And the gloss on the law regarding "agreements at the point of death" speaks of this kind of reciprocal gift, and with it Julius Clarus and others whom he cites. If, however, a gift of a lesser

<margin>11</margin>
In the case of remuneratory gifts <note>gifts given as a reward or in thanks for a service</note> made without a prior agreement for payment, if a larger gift follows, it is considered remuneratory up to the value of the preceding merit. However, regarding the excess amount, it is not; therefore, if such an excess exceeds five hundred solidi <note>original: "quingentos solidos" — a standard gold coin unit for legal limits</note>, it will require registration for that portion which exceeds the limit.

Regarding whether an <term>entailed estate</term> <note>original: "maioratus" — a legal arrangement where property is tied to a family line and cannot be sold</note>, when established by a contract between living persons, rightfully requires registration: First, when it is established as part of a dowry or a wedding gift, it would not require it, as is clear from what has been said. Similarly, when it is established by royal permission, registration would not be necessary, because the royal permission has the force of registration, as Molina well observes in Book 2, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 8, number 19. Finally, when it is established without royal permission, Molina also excellently shows in the same place from number 15 that Spanish entailed estates do not require it. This is because, for the most part, the successors are burdened with carrying the name and coat of arms of the founder, and other burdens are usually imposed on them, because of which the institution of the estate should be considered a "gift for a cause" <note>a gift given with specific conditions or duties attached, rather than a pure gift</note>. Furthermore, and most importantly, an entailed estate is usually established for the memory of the founder and the splendor of their family, and therefore for that purpose, it is for the benefit of both the individual and the family, of which the founder remains the head. Finally, because those goods are left to successors without the power to sell them, and with the requirement that they pass to a successor called by the first founder himself; and since the establishment of such entailed estates serves the splendor and benefit of the commonwealth, and is permitted by law for 그hat reason, it must be judged through <term>equity</term> <note>original: "epicheia" — the principle of interpreting the spirit of the law rather than just the literal text</note> that such an institution is not at all included under the law of registration. Additionally, this is the accepted practice.

Molina, in the cited place at number 20, thinks that if the annual income of an entailed estate does not exceed five hundred solidi, then by the provision of the law *Sancimus* <note>a specific decree in the Code of Justinian</note> it does not require registration. I think, however, that this is false. First, because that provision only speaks of when an annual sum is what is given; but when an entailed estate is established, what is given is not an annual sum, but the property itself, which produces that sum annually. Furthermore, that property is of much greater value than the income of individual years. Secondly, because that provision only applies when a gift expires upon the death of either the donor or the recipient (but an entailed estate and its income pass to heirs), being called first to the estate, and then to the heirs of heirs, without any end date.

<margin>12</margin>
Finally, a <term>gift in anticipation of death</term> <note>original: "donatio causa mortis" — a gift given by someone who believes they are about to die</note>, even if it exceeds the value of five hundred solidi, does not require registration. This is held in the final law of the Code, *On gifts in anticipation of death*.

Antonio Gomez, in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 10, adds:
<margin>13</margin>
When that which is given does not belong to the donor at present, but in the future, registration is not necessary. From this, he infers many corollaries. But I would rather say: when the laws grant someone something dependent on their acceptance, then the renunciation of the right which would come to them by that agreement does not require registration. Therefore, if one does not accept a legacy, or if one does not enter into an inheritance already passed to them—even if the right being renounced exceeds the value of five hundred solidi—the renunciation is valid. For this same

<column-break/>

reason, if a parent grants a son or daughter the power to decide concerning goods of which the parent would have been the heir (whether the child wished it or not), such a power is valid, even if those goods exceed the value of five hundred solidi. For the same reason, if a father leaves to a son still under his authority the <term>usufruct</term> <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> of the son’s "adventitious" goods <note>property acquired from sources other than the father, like a mother's inheritance</note>—because the laws grant the father that usufruct only if he chooses to claim it, as shown elsewhere—such a grant of the usufruct is valid, although it exceeds the value of five hundred solidi. Regarding the renunciation by which a son or daughter legally renounces their share, or, being content with one part, renounces the rest: since such a renunciation is invalid without an oath, and the oath supplies the defect of registration, the question of whether the renunciation is valid without registration when it exceeds five hundred solidi ceases to be an issue. On the same basis, Antonio Gomez (cited above) affirms that a renunciation by which a wife renounces half of the property gained during the marriage to her husband is valid without registration. I believe this, however, to be false: because it concerns a thing owed to her by virtue of the preceding marriage contract, no differently than if goods were owed to her from any other contract. The release or surrender of such a right, if the value exceeds five hundred solidi, would be invalid without registration regarding the excess, as was said in the preceding disputation.

<margin>14</margin>
<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The doubt regarding almost everything said in this disputation is whether these rules have force in Portugal. In Book 4 of the *Ordinances* <note>the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the laws of Portugal</note>, title 54, at the beginning, without any exception for any gift, it says: <note>original: "Todas as doações assi de beens moueis como de raiz, como de huns e outros juntamente que passarem de trecentos cruzados dourou sua verdadeira ualia, serã insinuadas e aprouadas per uos, ou por os desembargadores que pera ella forē deputados: e nõ sendo insinuadas, nõ ualeraã, saluo atee adita contia."</note> "All gifts, whether of movable goods or real estate, or of both together, that exceed three hundred gold cruzados <note>Portuguese currency</note> of their true value, shall be registered and approved by you, or by the judges appointed for it; and if not registered, they shall not be valid, except up to the said amount." By these words, it seems that everything said so far is excluded by the law of that kingdom. Nevertheless, despite these words, the contrary must be said. Not only because, as Gama (decisions 219 and 302) rightly says regarding remuneratory gifts and gifts for a cause, that ordinance ought to be explained through the older common laws; but also because that universality is not to be understood regarding the *types* and *modes* of giving, but regarding the *material*, as the ordinance immediately explains itself by saying: "whether of movable goods or real estate or both together." Nor is it to be believed that the ordinance intended to overturn so many common laws and opinions of the learned doctors as have been explained in this whole disputation.
<margin>Decision.</margin>

### Whether a gift of all the donor’s goods is valid, and what if it is confirmed by oath.

## DISPUTATION CCLXXIX.

### SUMMARY.

> 1 *A gift of all present and future goods is invalid, according to the common opinion.*
> *Indeed, by the law of Castile, a gift of even all present goods only is invalid, number 2.*

### Second Treatise, Disputation 279.

3. A gift of all goods, both present and future, confirmed by an oath is valid, contrary to the common opinion.
4. A gift of all goods, present and future, made to the Church is valid, according to the common opinion.
5. A gift of all goods, even future ones, under the law of Castile and confirmed by an oath, is valid.
6. A gift of all goods, present and future, and under the law of Castile regarding present goods, when it can be reduced to the sum permitted by law without formal registration <note>original: "insinuatione" — the legal requirement to register large gifts with a magistrate</note>, so that it may be valid.
7. A gift of all goods, present and future, does not include legal rights and actions <note>such as the right to sue or pending legal claims</note>.
8. A gift of all goods, present and future, with the right of use <note>original: "usufructu"</note> reserved, and when it might not be valid.
9. And what is to be said concerning the law of Castile. Number 9.
10. Whether a gift is valid if someone gives their entire inheritance to another.
11. A gift in anticipation of death <note>original: "Donatio causa mortis"</note> of all goods, present and future, is valid.
12. A gift of all goods, present and future, made in a marriage contract or a settlement—and thus mixed with a burdensome cause <note>an "onerous cause" implies a gift given in exchange for something else, like a marriage agreement</note>—is valid. See the declaration there.
13. The establishment of an <term>entailed estate</term> <note>original: "maioratus" — property tied to a family lineage that cannot be sold</note> of all goods, present and future; when it is valid, even under the law of Castile, and when it is not.

---

This dispute, along with the two preceding ones, concerns the quantity that one may validly give away, or not; for that reason, it is connected to them.

1. A gift† of all of a donor's goods, both present and future, is invalid; this is because, through such a gift, the donor strips themselves of all power to make a will <note>original: "facultate omnem testandi"</note>; this is something granted to no one under civil law <note>Roman law</note>, according to what was said in Disputation 151. This is gathered from the law regarding "stipulations conceived in this manner" <note>referring to Digest 45.1.61</note>, the law regarding "if brothers," the response regarding "partnership," and the law "from that" regarding "useless stipulations," as well as laws regarding "inheritance," "agreed pacts," and "with the gift" at the end, and the final law on pacts. And with Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous 14th-century jurist</note> at the first cited place, the common opinion of the doctors affirms this, which is recorded and followed by Corneas in *Various Resolutions*, Molina in Book 2 *On Primogeniture*, Antonio Gomez on the Laws of Toro, Julius Clarus, Gutierrez on *Confirmation by Oath*, and Gama in his *Decisions*.

2. <margin>Law of Castile.</margin> However, regarding the law of † Castile, Law 69 of Toro (which is Law 9, Title 10, Book 5 of the *New Collection*) states that even a gift of all *present* goods is invalid, and all Castilian doctors agree on this in the places cited.

3. <margin>Question.</margin> Before we examine the matter more broadly, the doubt is whether a gift of all goods, present and future, is valid if it is confirmed by an oath. The common † opinion of the doctors affirms that it is invalid. Their entire foundation is that by such a gift, the liberty to make a will is taken away, which is considered contrary to "good morals" <note>original: "bonos mores" — public policy or legal ethics</note> according to the law on stipulations and other cited laws. Indeed, that which opposes good morals is invalid, even if confirmed by an oath, because an oath should not be a "bond of iniquity" <note>a legal principle that an oath cannot force someone to do something illegal or immoral</note>. Thus Molina, Antonio Gomez, and Julius Clarus affirm this alongside Bartolus, Panormitanus, and many others whom they cite.

<column-break/>

Clarus, question 20; Gutierrez, chapter 11; and Gama, Decision 386. Those who established the Portuguese Ordinances were of the same opinion, as we noted in Disputation 151. Indeed, they explicitly decreed this in Book 4, Title 4. However, in that same Disputation 151, we showed quite effectively (if we are not mistaken) that for someone to surrender the power to make a will, and thus donate all their present and future goods, is not so contrary to good morals as to constitute a fault—neither a mortal nor a venial sin. Therefore, if both are confirmed by an oath, the gift is valid. We deduced this from its own principles, which truly pertains more to theologians than to legal experts, as was said there. Fortunius Garcia and others, whom Covarruvias cites and follows, agree with us. Therefore, the points discussed extensively in that dispute relieve us of the burden of examining the matter at length here. In that place, we explained in what sense the laws affirm that stripping oneself of the power to make a will is "contrary to good morals."

4. Our opinion and that of Covarruvias is confirmed because not only those who agree with us, but even the common opinion of the authors of the contrary view, affirm that a gift of all goods, present and future, made to the Church is valid. If it is valid, then it certainly contains no sin; otherwise, the civil laws, which render it absolutely invalid, would still have force even when the gift is made to the Church. For it is not to be believed that the Supreme Pontiffs would encourage sins, or wish for something that is inherently illicit and void under civil law to have force just because it is given to the Church. If a gift of all goods is not illicit in itself, it is undoubtedly valid if confirmed by an oath, with nothing preventing it, even if civil law has rendered it null; and this holds even if it is made to a private person. Furthermore, among the authors who believe a gift of all goods is invalid even with an oath, the following affirm that such a gift made to the Church *without* an oath is valid: Bartolus, Panormitanus, and many others followed by Julius Clarus, Antonio Gomez, Gutierrez, and Gama. Read also those cited by Covarruvias. They confirm this from the law "We command no one" <note>Codex 1.2.14</note>, where a gift of an entire patrimony made to the Church is declared valid. However, in my judgment, the strongest foundation is that civil law does not prejudice gifts or last wills made for "pious causes" <note>charitable or religious purposes</note>. For the same reason, it was said in Disputation 178 that a gift to a pious cause, no matter how large, does not require formal registration. Antonio Gomez and others, along with Panormitanus, affirm that if someone gives all their present and future goods to the Church, the Church is bound to support them from those same goods. This is understood to cover whatever the donor lacks, provided the donor applies their own industry and labor according to their social standing.

5. Regarding the gift † of all present goods, which is null under the law of Castile, many of the doctors agree; however, they deny that a gift of *future* goods is valid in that kingdom even if confirmed by an oath. Since it is valid under common law <note>the *Ius Commune*, based on Roman and Canon law</note>, as we shall say, and does not take away the power to make a will, it is established that it is not contrary to good morals. Thus Antonio Gomez, Law 69 of Toro.

It concludes that while civil law often restricts these gifts, they are valid when confirmed by oath or made to the Church for pious causes.</summary>

### Luis de Molina on Contracts

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
The question is whether a donation of all present and future goods—or, in Castile, a donation of all present goods—that is invalid as a whole because it was not made for a pious cause, might at least be valid for the portion included within the whole. This is similar to what is said regarding a donation exceeding five hundred <term>solidi</term> <note>The *solidus* was a gold coin; Roman law required gifts above 500 to be officially registered</note> made without <term>insinuation</term> <note>original: "insinuatione" — the formal registration of a gift before a public official or judge</note>, which is 

<margin>Decision 6</margin>
valid up to the five hundred solidi limit. The common opinion of the doctors is that such a gift is not valid even for a part; this is reported and followed by Antonio Gómez on Law 69 of Toro, number 2; Guterrez, chapter 11, cited at number 3; and Julius Clarus, § donation, question 20, number 2. Although Clarus adds that the contrary could be defended in a debate. The reasoning is not the same as the donation exceeding five hundred solidi without registration. For in a donation without registration, a certain limit is prescribed up to which it is valid, and it is only annulled regarding the excess. However, in a donation of "all goods," no limit is prescribed up to which it might be valid or beyond which it is not. Therefore, if a donation of all present and future goods (or in Castile, of all present goods) were only invalid as to the total sum and not as to the parts included within it, then the gift would be valid if even a single <term>obol</term> <note>A coin of very small value</note> were deducted, and thus the law would be useless or would certainly cause the greatest confusion.

Antonio Gómez at the cited place, number 1, and Guterrez, number 13, along with others they cite, assert that a donation of all present and future goods is void, even if it is a reciprocal gift by which spouses or brothers mutually give all their goods to whichever one is found to be the survivor. However, I judge this to be true if the donation is <term>inter vivos</term> <note>original: "inter vivos" — a gift made between living persons that takes effect immediately</note> and irrevocable. It is otherwise if it is a <term>causa mortis</term> gift <note>original: "causa mortis" — a gift made in anticipation of death</note>, or for some other reason is revocable, as is usually the case; for then it is valid, because it does not take away the power to make a will. Julius Clarus seems to speak only of this latter kind of reciprocal donation of all goods in question 20, cited at the final number, where he affirms the opinion contrary to Antonio Gómez; understood in this way, his opinion is true.

If someone were to donate only all their present goods, the donation would be valid under <term>Common Law</term> <note>original: "iure communi" — the shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</note>. For he would not be stripping himself of the power to make a will, since he would remain free to make a will regarding those goods he might acquire in the future. This is proven by Law *Omnes*, § *Lucius*, Digest: *On things done to defraud creditors*, and Law *Si quis argentum*, § *Sed et si quis*, Code: *On donations*. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus, § donation, question 19, number 2; Antonio Gómez, Law 69 of Toro, number 1; Covarrubias, *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 12, number 4; Guterrez, cited chapter 11, number 1; Molina, book 2 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10; and Gama, decision 26, number 3.

The same holds under Common Law if someone gives "their own," or even "all their own goods." For under that phrasing, only present goods are understood by the name of "goods" or "all goods." This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus, cited question 19, numbers 3 and 4; Gama, decision 206, number 3; Aries Pinellus agrees in his commentary on the Code: *On maternal goods*, part 1, number 3. This is proven by the final law of the Code: *Which things can be pledged*, in those words: "for it is just to look at the intentions of the contracting parties rather than the phrasing of the words." The discussion there concerned the form of words we are debating, and 

<column-break/>

the jurist confesses that the term signifies only present goods. The same is proven more clearly by Law *Si ita*, Digest: *On the legacy of gold and silver*, and Law *Omnes*, § *Lucius*, Digest: *On things done to defraud creditors*. However, when it is established from elsewhere that the donor, by the name of "all goods," also intended future ones, then the donation would be invalid; for one must stand by the mind and will of the contracting parties rather than the words, as related from the final law of the Code: *Which things can be pledged*.

7. It is asked whether a donation is valid if someone says: "I give you all my present and future goods, movable and immovable," or in Castile, "all my present goods, movable and immovable." The common opinion, followed by Julius Clarus, cited question 19, number 5, and Guterrez, cited chapter 11, number 16 (with which Pinellus agrees in *Maternal Goods*, part 1, from number 24), affirms that it is valid. This is because under the name of "movable and immovable goods," <term>rights and actions</term> <note>original: "iura, & actiones" — legal claims, debts owed to the person, or the right to sue</note> are not included, but are distinguished as a third kind of goods, according to Law *A Divo Pio*, § *In venditione*, Digest: *On things judged*, and Law *Quamvis*, § *In peculio*, Digest: *On the peculium*. Therefore, that third category remains with the donor, through which he may make a will. Add to this that a donation based on consent should be interpreted favorably so as to be valid, provided the words allow it and the contrary intent of the donor is not established, following the argument in Law *Quoties*, at the beginning, Digest: *On doubtful matters*. Guterrez and Aries Pinellus (above, from number 10) judge the aforementioned opinion to be especially true if it is said: "movable and immovable goods existing in such a place," since rights and actions are not contained by a place, as is clear from Law *Caius*, Digest: *On legacies*, book 2, and Law *Si fideicommissum*, § *Tractatum*, Digest: *On judgments*. Understand this, however, provided that the person making such a donation in the Kingdom of Castile actually possesses some rights and actions at the time of the donation; otherwise, under that phrasing, he would in reality be donating all his present goods universally, and therefore the donation would be invalid in that kingdom. Understand further, provided it is not established from elsewhere that the donor, by "movable and immovable goods," intended to include rights and actions as well; for then one must stand by his intent rather than the words, according to the final law of the Code: *Which things can be pledged*. Guterrez and Pinellus agree. Regarding what has been said in this whole section, read what we have discussed extensively in Disputation 202.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
The question arises whether a donation is valid under Common Law if someone gives all their present and future goods, excepting the <term>usufruct</term> <note>original: "usufructu" — the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another without destroying it</note> of those same goods. Paolo di Castro, on the final law of the Code: *On pacts*, and elsewhere, Decius and others whom Covarrubias cites (book 3, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 12, number 1), are of the opinion that it is invalid. They are moved by the fact that, if that donation stands, nothing is left to the donor from which he might make a will. Not the usufruct itself, because that right of enjoyment which the donor reserved for himself expires with his death; nor the perception of fruits, which are counted among his future goods, which he also donated. Therefore, the donation is invalid and introduced in fraud of the law. And indeed, if the sense of that donation were that even the fruits to be perceived that remained (or could remain) at the time of death were included in "future goods," and the donor could not make a will regarding them, then the opinion of Paolo di Castro, Decius, and others would be most true. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis from Disputation 280 regarding the validity of a "donation of all goods." It specifically examines whether reserving a "usufruct" (the right to use and profit from property) allows a person to legally give away their entire estate while still technically retaining the "power to make a will," which was a requirement for such gifts to be valid under Common Law.</meta>

### Treatise Two, Disputation 280.

...and others cited by Covarruvias, interpreting the opinion of Paulus Castrensis, say that if a donor says: "I give you all my present and future goods, except for the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> and the fruits to be gathered from it," the donation is valid. This is because the donor can still make a will regarding those excepted fruits. Bartolus also responds in his 76th Counsel that for a donation of all present and future goods to be valid, it is not enough for the donor to reserve the usufruct for disposal during their lifetime; rather, unless they can dispose of it through a last will and testament, they do not truly retain the power to make a will. Covarruvias (chapter 12), Molina (chapter 10, number 2), Julius Clarus (question 19, last number), and the doctors generally agree. However, Covarruvias (at the end of number 3) doubts whether those words actually take away the power to bequeath them. You should read his work.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Nevertheless, it must be said that a donation of all present and future goods is valid if the usufruct is reserved. So says Paulus Castrensis, contradicting his earlier view, in the law <note>original: "l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta"</note> *A stipulation conceived in this manner* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de verborum oblig." — the section of the Roman Digest concerning verbal obligations</note>. This is also held by Bartolus in Counsel 76, Panormitanus in Counsel 102, Alexander, and the more common opinion followed by Molina (*On Primogeniture*, book 2, chapter 10, number 19), Covarruvias (chapter 12, number 1), Antonio Gómez (Law 69 of Toro, number 3), Julius Clarus (book 4, question 19), and Guterrez (chapter 11, number 14). The strongest reason is that in the reservation of a usufruct, the "fruits" (income or produce) are understood to be excepted by reason of that right. Thus, they are not considered part of the gift, but rather excluded from it. The donor can freely dispose of these fruits and their value, both while alive and through a last will, and the donation of "all goods" is no obstacle when this reservation is included.

Indeed, if the donor dies <term>intestate</term> <note>without a legal will</note>, such fruits belong to the legal heirs and not to the recipient of the gift, unless that recipient is also the legal heir. Read other reasons in Covarruvias at the cited number 1.

When, however, the reserved usufruct is so small that it is insufficient even for the donor's decent maintenance, or if so little remains of the fruits after maintenance that it should be considered as nothing in relation to the donor's estate: then, because the power to make a will would not be considered to remain with them, the donation would be invalid. So say Covarruvias (number 3), Guterrez (number 14), and Molina (number 25).

<margin>1</margin>
In general, although a donation of all present and future goods is considered valid when the donor reserves something for themselves (beyond basic food/alimony) that they can freely bequeath, the doctors rightly interpret this to mean it must be a "competent" and sufficient amount relative to the donor's total estate. A tiny amount should be treated as nothing, and thus not count as retaining the power to make a will. This is the view of Paulus Castrensis, Alexander, Aretinus, and others followed by Molina, Julius Clarus, Covarruvias, Guterrez, Antonio Gómez, and Gama (Decision 348, number 3). Julius Clarus argued that 

<column-break/>

for such a donation to be valid, the reserved part must at the very least exceed one-twentieth of the donor's estate.

However, Molina (number 25), Gama, and others do not approve of this fixed rule, but believe the matter should be left to the judgment of a prudent judge. Gama, in a certain case discussed in his work, judged that a sum of four thousand copper coins—which are called *reais* in Portugal and <term>maravedis</term> <note>A small Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account</note> in Castile—was sufficient, given the status of the persons involved, for the donation of all present and future goods to be considered valid. He further mentions that the younger Alexander judged an even smaller sum to be sufficient in another case.

<margin>Question.</margin>
The question is whether in Castile—where a donation of all present goods is invalid—if a donor reserves the usufruct of them, the donation becomes valid. Covarruvias (chapter 12, number 4), although he admits that such donations are declared valid in the courts of that kingdom, personally considers them invalid. He is led to this because he believes such a reservation of usufruct does not stop the gift from being a "donation of all present goods."

<margin>First Argument.</margin>
He proves this: First, because the fruits to be gathered in the future do not belong to the donor's "present goods," but to their "future goods." The right of enjoyment itself, which the donor reserves, cannot be counted among the donor's "present goods." Furthermore, the usufruct that belongs to the donor at the time of the gift is "causal" (tied to ownership); but the one they reserve for themselves is "formal," which cannot arise until after the ownership of the goods has passed to the recipient by virtue of the gift. Thus, such a usufruct does not belong to the goods the donor *has* when they give, but to goods they will have *after* the donation is made.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, because the doctors who departed from the opinion of Paulus Castrensis and others while standing on Common Law alone, admit that in a donation of all present and future goods with reserved usufruct, all "present" goods are indeed given. They believe the right of usufruct does not prevent it from being a gift of all present goods because the donor cannot bequeath that right itself; they only defend the gift because the *future* fruits (excepted by the usufruct) can be bequeathed.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, because the Law of Castile intends for a donation of all present goods to be null because it requires something to be reserved from the "present goods" that the donor can bequeath at the very moment of the gift. The law effectively wants to ensure the donor does not lose their freedom to make a will, even if they were to face death immediately after the gift. Consequently, even if we say the formal right of usufruct is part of "present goods," such a reservation is not enough, because this right ends at death and cannot be bequeathed by the donor.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Molina (chapter 10, from number 22) rightly rejects this opinion as "novel" and "hardly probable." Guterrez follows him, as does Antonio Gómez. Because, truly, from the resolution of the argu-

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of whether a donation of all one's goods is valid if the donor reserves a "usufruct" (the right to use and profit from the property). Molina is specifically refuting the arguments of the jurist Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, who questioned whether such a reservation truly preserves the donor's legal "power to make a will."</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...of the arguments on which Covarruvias relies; once that is sufficiently clear, let us proceed to dismantle them.

<margin>To the 1st argument.</margin>
To the first reason of Covarruvias, therefore, it must be denied that the right of enjoyment—which the donor reserves for himself—cannot be counted among the donor's present goods. Indeed, Covarruvias himself confesses that the points by which he attempts to prove this have weak force. For it is one and the same usufruct <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> in number; while it is joined with the <term>direct ownership</term> <note>Dominium directum: the legal title to property, as opposed to the right to use it</note>, it is called "causal," and while it is separated from it (because the usufruct belongs to one person and the direct ownership to another), it is called "formal." It differs from itself only accidentally, in terms of being joined to or separated from the direct ownership regarding the person to whom it belongs. Therefore, the fact that—once the direct ownership is transferred to the recipient through donation—that usufruct which before the transfer was called "causal" is now called "formal," does not prevent the donor from having reserved for himself the very same usufruct in number which he held before the donation was made. It is simply true that he reserved that same usufruct for himself from his present goods at the time of the donation, as a part of those same goods.

Add to this that through donation alone, unless <term>delivery</term> <note>Traditio: the formal physical or symbolic transfer of property</note> occurs, ownership is not transferred to the recipient but remains with the donor. Therefore, since the reservation of the usufruct happens at the same time as the donation, and both precede the delivery of the goods (even through a <term>constitutum clause</term> <note>A legal fiction where the donor agrees to hold the property on behalf of the new owner while keeping possession</note>, as is regularly done because the goods must remain with the donor so he may enjoy them for as long as he lives), it follows that at the time of reservation, that usufruct is still "causal." Only later, once delivery is made, does it begin to take on the nature of a "formal" usufruct.

From this it follows that it is simply false to say he does not reserve a usufruct for himself that is "causal" at the time of reservation, and even for a little while after the reservation, even though it may take on a "formal" character after delivery is later performed. Finally, it is added that the donation—as Covarruvias himself concedes—is made in a single act along with the reservation, at which time the usufruct being reserved is among the present goods of the donor himself.

<margin>To the 2nd.</margin>
To the second reason, it must be denied that those doctors admitted such a thing. And certainly, if they had thought so, they would have erred shamefully, since it is most manifest that such a usufruct is part of the goods which belonged to the donor at the time of the donation. Furthermore, the fact that a donor cannot bequeath a usufruct of this kind in a will does not mean it is not part of those goods; rather, it is because the usufruct expires with the life of the donor himself. If, however, the donor sells it, he will be able to make a will concerning the price—either at the very time he gives the gift and reserves it for himself, or later as time progresses.

<margin>To the 3rd.</margin>
Because, in truth, to maintain that a donation of all present and future goods with a reserved usufruct was valid under <term>Common Law</term> <note>Ius commune: the subsidary legal system based on Roman and Canon law used across Europe</note>, it was enough that the donor could make a will concerning the *fruits* (profits) by reason of the right of enjoyment reserved to himself, even if he could not make a will concerning the *right* of enjoyment itself. For that reason, they defended the donation on that ground; they did not, however, judge that the right of enjoyment itself was not part of the goods the donor had at the time of donation.

To the third argument, it must be said that perhaps those legislators were not led by the reason that it would render a donation

<column-break/>

of all present goods void, but rather so that subjects would not remain despoiled of all their goods at any time.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
It must then be said that a donor who reserves the usufruct for himself—at the same time he reserves it and effects the donation—can sell the right he reserves and make a will concerning the price. Add that the laws do not presume he will die immediately before he can perceive any fruits concerning which he might make a will, but rather presume the contrary. Add also that the laws do not so much intend in family dispositions that a donor must, in every eventual outcome, be able to make a will with effect (as if a fortuitous event could not occur to prevent the making of that will), as they intend that the donor does not absolutely and entirely strip himself of the faculty of making a will.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
10 There is a doubt whether, under common law, if someone gives their entire **inheritance** to another, the donation is valid. Bartolus (on the last law, *Code: concerning pacts*) and the more common opinion of the doctors (followed by Julius Clarus, book 4, *Sentences*, section on donation, question 19, number 6; and Gutierrez, chapter 11, cited number 4) assert that it is invalid. Since an inheritance includes all goods found to be his at the time of the donor's death, the donor thereby strips himself of the power to make a will. This opinion is approved by me. However, the same Bartolus—contradicting himself in the law *it was asked* <note>original: "l. quæsitum est."</note> (penultimate section, *Digest: on legacies I*)—asserts it is valid, because by such a gift only "all present goods" are deemed donated. Purpuratus held the same on the last law of the Code, *concerning pacts*. However, the first view seems truer. And even if this second view were true, such a donation would be invalid under the law of Castile <note>The dominant kingdom of Spain</note>, as is clear from what has been said so far.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
11 There is also a doubt whether not only a donation *between the living* <note>inter vivos</note> of all present and future goods (or in Castile, of present goods only) is invalid, but also a **donation in view of death** <note>donatio causa mortis</note>. Antonio Gomez (on law 69 of Toro, number 5) argues on rather weak grounds that it is invalid; indeed, in his *Various Resolutions* (volume 2, chapter 4, at the end of number 22) he seems to contradict himself. It must be said, however, with the common opinion of the doctors (which Julius Clarus refers to and follows in the cited question 19, number 7; and Molina <note>The author, referring to his own work *On Primogeniture*</note> in book 2, chapter 10, number 14) that it is undoubtedly valid. For since a donation in view of death can be revoked at the mere whim of the donor, he certainly does not strip himself of the power to make a will, even if it is of all present and future goods; and therefore the reason why a similar donation between the living is invalid does not apply to it.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
12 Finally, there is a doubt whether—although a donation of all present and future goods (and in Castile, of present goods only) is not valid while it remains within the limits of a gift—it might be valid if it is made for an **onerous cause** <note>A legal obligation involving a trade-off or burden, like a dowry or a settlement, rather than a free gift</note>, such as for a marriage, a settlement, or something similar. <margin>Decision.</margin> Molina (in book 2 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10, number 17) affirms that it is valid. Although under civil law a free donation of all present and future goods is rendered null, no law is found that prohibits anyone, for an onerous cause, from alienating and abdicating all their goods, even future ones. This opinion is pleasing to me, and I see no one opposing it; it is supported by Menchaca (*On Created Successions*, book 1, section 1, number 32) regarding the institution of a <term>mayorazgo</term> <note>An entailed estate that passes to a single heir to keep a family's wealth intact</note> of all goods.

<summary>This page discusses the legal mechanics of usufruct and why reserving it allows a donor to legally give away their entire estate without losing the "power to make a will." Molina also clarifies that while free donations of all goods are generally restricted, gifts made in anticipation of death or for "onerous" reasons (like marriage settlements) remain valid.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 280.

At this point, observe: if a donation of all present and future goods made for a **dowry** was of such a small amount in comparison to the woman to whom it was made, and she was so situated that, by comparison, that entire donation could be counted among donations for <term>pious causes</term> <note>Donatio ad pias causas: gifts for religious or charitable purposes, which often enjoyed special legal protections</note>, then there is no doubt that it is valid. This is because a donation for pious causes is valid even if it consists of all present and future goods, as we have shown above.

Likewise, if a donation of all present and future goods—whether as a dowry or as a <term>gift in anticipation of marriage</term> <note>Propter nuptias: a gift from the groom or his family to the bride</note>—is made at the same time as a marriage agreement with the other spouse, it is valid. Specifically, when such a donation is joined with an <term>onerous contract</term> <note>A contract where both parties give and receive something of value, rather than a mere gift</note>, or rather is strengthened by it in relation to the other spouse, then we have recently said, along with Molina, that it is valid; for it does not remain solely within the limits of a purely free gift. I believe the same would be true if it were made under a condition, such as "if such-and-such a person wishes to contract marriage with this woman," because then it would be linked to an onerous contract through that condition. This holds as long as the dowry or marriage gift is not so excessive in comparison to the other spouse that the addition of such a condition, or the connection with such an onerous contract, should rightly be judged as being made in fraud—simply to make a donation of all present and future goods valid. In that case, it should be considered invalid.

Finally, since a donation in a dowry or for a marriage is a free gift in relation to the recipient, it follows that if it is not to be judged as a donation for a pious cause based on the circumstances, nor is it joined with an onerous contract (by comparison to which the whole dowry or marriage gift is appropriate and not excessively large), and it is not made under the condition of a contract with specific designated persons but is given absolutely as a dowry or marriage gift of all one's goods without expressing with whom or with what woman—then such a donation will be invalid. And in this way, you will reconcile what Molina teaches in the cited passage with what Gutierrez and the doctors he cites affirm in chapter 11, numbers 9 and 10.

<margin>13</margin>
From everything that has been said in this entire dispute, you will understand when the institution of a <term>maioratus</term> <note>An entail: a legal arrangement keeping an estate intact by passing it to a single heir, usually the eldest son</note> from all present and future goods (or in Castile, from all present goods) is valid and when it is not. For an entail is either established so that it can be revoked, or so that it cannot be revoked, according to the principles to be handed down elsewhere.

If it is established in the first way (revocable), then, since the power of making a will is not taken away by that institution, the fact that it was established from all goods does not invalidate the institution. So says Molina, book 2, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10, number 13.

If, however, it is established in the second way (irrevocable), and the King’s authorization is present to establish it from all present and future goods, then such an institution is valid. This is because, through that authorization, the Prince is deemed to grant a dispensation from the legal rule that renders a donation of all goods invalid. So says Molina in the same place, number 15.

However, if it is established without the King’s authorization, then the institution will be invalid because the person strips themselves of the power to make a will. So says Molina in the same place, number 16.

An exception is made unless it is confirmed in the Kingdom of Castile by an oath.

<column-break/>

In that kingdom, the addition of an oath to donations is valid and lawful, even when the contract would be invalid without the oath, as held in laws 11 and 12, title 1, book 4 of the *New Collection*, and as we have often said. In our opinion, just as a donation of all present and future goods confirmed by an oath would be valid, so too would be the creation of an entail from all present and future goods. And according to the opinion of others, this is also true when in this Kingdom of Castile it is created from all present goods alone and confirmed by an oath, as was said above. In the Kingdom of Portugal, however, an entail established from all present and future goods would be invalid even if confirmed by an oath, unless such an oath was added with the intervening express authorization of the King. This is because, as we related from book 4 of the *Ordinances*, title 3, above in dispute 149, the law itself would be void, and the institution would be null by the mere addition of the oath. But if the oath were added by the King’s authorization, then, by the force of the oath, in our opinion, the institution would be valid—and also because such an institution is then deemed to have been made by the King’s authorization.

Observe that the fact that the institution of an entail from all present and future goods is valid if done by the King’s authorization, as Molina admits, clearly confirms that the act, viewed in itself, is not against <term>good morals</term> <note>Contra bonos mores: acts that are inherently unethical or harmful to the public interest</note>. Otherwise, Kings would not provide authorization for it, nor would it be made valid by such authorization. Therefore, if it is confirmed by an oath in a kingdom where the addition of an oath is not void, it will undoubtedly be valid. This is contrary to what the common opinion of the Doctors (including Molina) affirms regarding a donation of all present and future goods confirmed by an oath.

Furthermore, an exception is made unless the person who established the entail from all present and future goods without royal authorization and without confirmation by oath did so as part of an onerous contract of marriage, a settlement, or something similar in the manner explained above; or unless he reserved a sufficient quantity of goods for himself from which he could freely make a will, also in the manner explained above, as Molina rightly affirms in book 2, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10, number 17.

# Luis de Molina | On Contracts

...whether a donation can be revoked for any cause of ingratitude; it is generally held to be of no value. 
And what of the law of Castile?
6 **Whether a donation confirmed by an oath can be revoked due to ingratitude, and when.**
7 **A donation made for a specific cause <note>donatio ob causam: a gift given in exchange for a specific action or service</note> cannot be revoked due to the ingratitude of the recipient.**
8 **By what reasoning a dowry given to a husband cannot be revoked because of the ingratitude of the wife.**
9 **The same applies to a marriage gift made to a husband.**

In **Disputation 272**, we explained certain chapters regarding when it is permitted not to fulfill a donation while it is still within the limits of an accepted promise or is otherwise binding. Now, however, here and in the two following disputations, several other points must be handed down regarding the circumstances under which it is lawful to revoke a donation, not only while it is within those limits, but even when it has been entirely completed and perfected by delivery, and has already acquired the nature of a <term>named contract</term> <note>contractus nominatus: a category of contracts specifically recognized and named under Roman law, carrying specific legal obligations</note>.

In the final law of the Code *On Revoking Donations* <note>original: "Lege vlt. C. de reuocandis donationib."</note>, in the section "It should be known" of the *Institutes*, and in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, five causes are listed for which a donation can be revoked due to the ingratitude of the recipient. Of these, only the first four are mentioned in the final chapter of the Decretals and in Law 10, Title 4, of the fifth *Partida* <note>The Siete Partidas: the famous 13th-century Castilian statutory code</note>. This is because, as Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note> says in the cited chapter, the last cause pertains not so much to the vice of ingratitude as to a <term>conditional donation</term> <note>donatio sub modo: a gift given with a specific "mode" or burden attached, like a requirement to perform a task</note>, which will be discussed below.

**The First** cause is if the recipient pours out "atrocious injuries" against the donor. It is sufficient to pour out such an injury even once for the law to apply, as Gregory Lopez <note>A renowned 16th-century Spanish jurist and commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> says regarding the cited Law 10, specifically on the phrase *by word* <note>original Spanish: "de palabra"</note>. And there is no one who doubts that this should be understood to include injuries committed through speech. Indeed, the Portuguese Ordinances in Title 55, section 1, clarify that it is not necessary for these to occur in the donor's presence; it is enough if they occur in his absence. However, what should be judged as "atrocious" is left to the judgment of a prudent judge, looking at the circumstances: the status of the person to whom they are said, the place (such as in a court or the marketplace), whether before many people or few, and other factors, as we discussed in Disputation 176 regarding the second cause of disinheritance. Many rightly think the same applies if the injury is physical (provided it does not involve "laying hands," as that pertains to the second cause explained soon). Examples include if the recipient were to hang horns before the donor's doors <note>A symbolic public insult common in the era, often implying the person was a cuckold or otherwise dishonored</note>, or do something similar, or if he were to chase him away or keep him imprisoned to his great disgrace, as Panormitanus, Gregory Lopez, Giovanni d'Andrea, and Albericus maintain. Law 10 of Castile clarifies that the same applies if the recipient accuses the donor of a crime for which he might be killed, mutilated, lose the majority of his goods, or incur notable infamy. Gregory Lopez notes this is worth remembering because it was not so explicitly stated in the <term>Common Law</term> <note>Ius Commune: the combination of Roman and Canon law that formed the basis of European legal practice</note>.

This should be understood, however—as we said in Disputation 176 regarding the third cause of disinheritance—provided that the recipient was not legally bound to accuse or reveal such a crime, such as the crime of heresy, or a crime against the Prince 

<column-break/>

or the Republic. We said the same would apply if such a recipient, without being forced, acted as a witness, advocate, procurator, or informer for such a crime against the donor. Read what was said there. In all these matters, Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> agrees and affirms the same applies if he accuses the donor while seeking redress for an injury to himself or his kin. For even in this event, he is not considered ungrateful; it would be otherwise if he were not pursuing an injury to himself or his own people.

<margin>Second</margin>
**The Second** cause is if the recipient "lays impious hands" upon the donor. Furthermore, hands are not considered "impious" if they are laid without mortal fault—for instance, in defense of the Republic, or in defense of oneself or a neighbor, or for another just cause. By the term "hands," it is understood even if he strikes the donor injuriously with a stone, a piece of wood, or another object, according to what will be said in Treatise 3 regarding the violent laying of hands on an ecclesiastical person. Even a probable ignorance—that the person he was injuriously striking was the donor—would excuse him from this penalty. Read the things said in Disputation 176 regarding the first cause of disinheritance.

<margin>Third</margin>
**The Third** cause is if he inflicts notable damage on the donor's external goods. Understand this to mean "unjustly," with no just cause excusing him. Hence, this includes if he accuses him of a crime because of which the donor would incur a significant loss of his property, as Law 10 of Castile affirmed regarding the second cause. However, what loss should be judged "grave" is left to the discretion of the judge, considering all concurrent circumstances. Nor is it necessary, for it to be grave, that the damage reaches half of the donor's goods, as Panormitanus and Gregory Lopez affirm. The Portuguese law (Title 55, section 3) decrees that it is enough to revoke the donation if the recipient *attempts* to inflict such damage on the donor's property, even if he does not succeed. However, the contrary is clearly hinted at in the final law of the Code, Law 10 of Castile, and the final chapter of the Decretals; therefore, outside of Portugal, the opposite must be asserted.

<margin>Fourth</margin>
**The Fourth** cause is if the recipient brings danger to the life of the donor. Understand this to mean by himself or through another, without a reasonable cause that excuses him from fault (as he would be excused if he accused him of the crime of heresy or <term>treason</term> <note>laesae maiestatis: an offense against the dignity of the ruler or state</note>). Furthermore, since attempting or arranging for his death is bringing danger to the life of the donor, even if death does not follow, it is certainly not necessary in this fourth cause for the effect of death to follow; the cited laws clearly indicate this. The Portuguese law, however, extends this to danger of the donor's body or status. For it says: <note>original Portuguese: "quando o donatario palguna maneira insidiou accerca de alguun perigo e danno da pessoa do doador: assi como se el le per si, ou por otrem lhe procurasse a morte, ou perigo de seu corpo, ou estado"</note> "when the recipient in any way plots concerning some danger and harm to the person of the donor: as if he by himself, or through another, should procure his death, or danger to his body, or status." Since penalties should not be extended <note>A legal principle that punitive laws should be interpreted strictly and not broadened by analogy</note>, certainly under Common Law and the law of Castile, no other danger would be sufficient except that of life.

<margin>Fifth</margin>
**The Fifth** cause is when the donation was made "with a mode" or burden <note>sub modo: as previously defined, a gift with strings attached</note> to which the recipient bound himself in writing or by word, but failed to fulfill it. For then, by reason of the unfulfilled burden...
