<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the revocation of donations due to ingratitude. Having introduced the five general legal grounds for revocation in the previous page, Molina now examines specific exceptions for remarrying mothers, the rights of heirs to pursue or defend such actions, and whether the law allows for revocation based on causes of ingratitude not explicitly listed in the statutes.</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 281.

...if the conditions are not fulfilled, a donation can be revoked; this is held in the final law of the Code *On Donations* <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de donationib."</note> and in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, § 6.

Formerly, under the law of the Code in the law *his solis* <note>Code 8.55.1</note>, women who passed into a second marriage were not permitted to revoke a donation made to their children on the grounds of their children's ingratitude. Much less was this permitted if the children were disreputable <note>original: "meretrices"</note>, as is added in that same law.

<margin>2</margin> Today, however, by the law of the *Authentica* <note>The "Authenticum" is a medieval collection of the *Novels* (New Laws) of Emperor Justinian</note>, mothers who transition to a second marriage are permitted to revoke donations made to their children before that transition in only three specific events. The first is if the son plots against the mother's life. In this event, it is not necessary for the mother's death to actually follow. The second is if he lays impious hands upon his mother <note>i.e., commits physical assault</note>. The third is if he plots the total loss of all his mother’s property. Hence, in this event, it is also not necessary for the effect to follow; it suffices if the attempt is made. This is held in the *Authentica* "If a mother" <note>original: "si mater"</note> in the Code *On Revoking Donations*, in the *Authentica* "On Marriages" § "A mother," in Law 10, Title 4, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and in Law 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, § 6.

If, in the events explained throughout this entire dispute, the donor himself did not revoke the donation while he lived, nor did he begin legal action for revocation, then his heirs cannot revoke it. Furthermore, if the donor did not revoke it while the ungrateful recipient was still alive, nor began action to revoke it, he cannot later bring an action against the recipient’s heirs to return the gifted items. Since these rules were established as a penalty for the recipient's crime of ingratitude, the legal action expires with the death of the recipient. It also expires with the death of the donor if the matter was still untouched <note>original: "res integra," meaning no legal steps had yet been taken</note> and, while both were still living, action for revocation had not begun.

This is held in the final law of the Code *On Revoking Donations*, the final chapter *On Donations* [in the Decretals], Law 10, Title 4, Part 5, and Law 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 55, the penultimate paragraph. This is also gathered from other laws cited by Gregorio Lopez in the final gloss; Antonio Gómez, Volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 4, Number 14; and Molina, Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, Chapter 9, Number 36.

However, Panormitanus, along with Giovanni d'Andrea, Silvester, Antonio Gómez, Gregorio Lopez, Molina, and many others limit this rule when the donor knew of the ingratitude and remained silent. In such a case, he is judged to have forgiven the offense through his silence. It is otherwise if he did not remain silent, but was preparing to execute the revocation and was prevented by death, following the argument in the law *posthumus* § the last, in the Digest *On Inofficious Wills*, and the law *sancimus* at the end of the Code under the same title.

The situation is also different if he was ignorant of the ingratitude, or even if he knew of it, he did not have enough time to revoke the donation. In those cases, the right to take action passes to the donor's heirs against the recipient's heirs. This is sufficiently implied by the contrary sense of the cited laws, as a condition is placed on all of them that the donor "remained silent." One cannot be said to have remained silent if they were ignorant or lacked the time to act.

This is confirmed by the gloss on the law *fideicommissum* in the Code *On Trusts*, which states: if a testator who left a trust or a legacy did not change his will, yet the legatee committed such a crime against the testator that, had the testator known, he would have revoked the legacy, then the legacy is not owed based on the unspoken or pre-

<column-break/>

sumed will of the testator in that event. The final gloss on the law *sororem* in the Code *On those who are unworthy* agrees with this.

From both glosses, Panormitanus concludes: If a recipient of a gift slept with the donor's wife without the donor's knowledge, the donor's heirs can revoke the donation on that ground. For that is an atrocious injury, and is counted among those we commemorated in the first cause of ingratitude. Unless, perhaps, someone argues that this injury is "accidental," whereas only "direct" injuries are contained in the second cause, according to what we said in Disputation 176, § 1. Note, however, that above in Disputation 176, we did not admit a similar limitation when there was a legitimate cause for a father to disinherit a son, or a son a father; for the reasoning is not equal, as we said there with Antonio Gómez and Molina. Read what was said there.

Regarding the fifth cause of ingratitude handed down in the final law of the Code *On Revoking Donations*—namely, when the recipient did not fulfill the "mode" <note><term>modus</term>: a specific obligation or purpose attached to a gift, such as "I give you this land so that you build a chapel"</note>—observe the following. Although the faculty to revoke the donation does not pass to the heirs except according to what was just explained, the donor's heirs *can* compel the recipient and his heirs to fulfill the "mode" and the agreed-upon pacts. For in this regard, no penalty is seen, only in the matter of revoking the donation itself. Therefore, the right to revoke only expires with the death of the recipient or donor, in the manner explained so far for all five causes of ingratitude.

Also observe that since the revocation of donations for these five causes is established as a penalty, the recipient—even if he was ungrateful—is not bound to restore the gifts until one of those causes has been sufficiently proven against him in court, according to what is sanctioned in the final law § "From these" in the Code *On Revoking Donations*, and a sentence has been passed by a judge. Covarruvias agrees with us in his *Epitome*, Part 2, Chapter 6, § 8, though he is somewhat hesitant. Read what we said in Disputation 176, § "It is doubtful, what if a son," etc.

When a cause is sufficiently proven and a sentence is passed, and the donation is revoked for ingratitude, Antonio Gómez, Gutierrez, and many others observe that it is revoked along with the fruits <note>the profits or yields from the property</note> gathered from the start of the legal proceedings <note>original: "a lite contestata"</note>, but not with the fruits gathered before that. For these belong to the recipient, as the gloss says on the law *generaliter* § "accordingly" in the Digest *On Testamentary Freedoms*.

Whether it is lawful to revoke a donation for other causes of ingratitude beyond the five numbered in the final law of the Code *On Revoking Donations*.

<margin>3</margin> The common opinion of the Doctors, along with the gloss on the cited final law, affirms that it is permitted, provided the causes are more serious than, or equally serious as, those listed. Panormitanus, Antonio Gómez, Molina, Giulio Claro, and Navarro follow this opinion. Finally, this is the opinion of everyone we cited in Disputation 176 who affirms that parents may disinherit children for other similar causes beyond the fourteen listed there. Nor are they led by any other arguments than those we dissolved there.

Hence...

It concludes that while only five causes are explicitly listed in Roman law, legal consensus allows for revocation in cases of equally or more severe offenses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding whether a gift can be revoked if the recipient proves ungrateful. The previous page established that there are five specific statutory reasons for revocation; here, Molina addresses whether other reasons—like failing to support a destitute donor—count, and whether legal agreements or religious oaths can prevent a donor from taking back a gift.</meta>

### Page 78
->### Luis de Molina: On Contracts<-

Hence, as the previously cited Glossator, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous expert in canon law</note>, and certain others argue, if a recipient of a gift <term>donatarius; the person receiving the gift</term> does not support a donor who has become destitute, the donation can be revoked for ingratitude. Some of these thinkers limit this rule to cases where the donation was of a large amount and the recipient can easily afford to help, given the donor’s poverty.

To us, however, the opposite opinion is more pleasing, consistent with what we taught in the cited disputation. We are guided, first, because in the final law cited <note>original: "lege vltima citata," referring to the Code of Justinian 8.55.10</note>, after listing those five causes explained above, it adds: *From these causes only* <note>original: "Ex his tantummodo causis"</note>, *if they have been proven in court by clear arguments, do we allow donations made to them to be overturned.* Notice that by using the exclusive word "only," the law excludes all other causes of ingratitude whatsoever.

<margin>Decision.</margin> Second, because that law is "penal" <note>meaning it imposes a penalty or loss of rights</note>. It is a violation of legal principle to extend a penalty to other cases by an argument of parity or "greater reason" <note>original: "maioritate rationis"</note> beyond those cases for which the penalty was expressly established. The authors of the contrary opinion are led by no other argument than that it is an equal or greater reason to revoke a donation if an equal or greater cause of ingratitude occurs. Read what we have written extensively on this in the place cited.

Molina admits in Book 1, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 9, number 35, that a "perfect" donation <note>a gift that is legally complete and finalized</note>—which is inherently irrevocable—cannot be revoked due to enmities, even capital ones <note>deadly feuds</note>, provided they do not make the recipient ungrateful in the specific ways explained in the final law of the Code *On the Revocation of Donations*. For the same reason, a <term>maioratus; a family inheritance or entail</term> established through an irrevocable donation cannot be revoked. However, as he adds in number 42, it is different for a "revocable" donation or an entail established by such a gift. Since these are treated the same as a "revocable legacy" <note>a gift in a will that can be changed</note>, they expire if capital enmities arise between the donor and recipient, or between the founder of the entail and the person called to it, as was stated in Disputation 212.

<margin>4</margin> And regarding such revocable donations, *Gregorio López* <note>a 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in Law 10, Title 4, Part 5, affirms that the right to revoke them passes to the heirs if the ingratitude was not forgiven by the donor.

<margin>Doubt.</margin> It is a matter of doubt whether a pact is valid if a donation is made with a clause or agreement stating that "even if the recipient is ungrateful, the donation cannot be revoked" (as is often added by notaries in Castile), and whether the donation could then still be revoked for ingratitude.

<margin>Decision 5</margin> The legal doctors commonly cited, followed by *Antonio Gómez* in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 14; *Gregorio López* in Law 67, Title 18, Part 3; and *Gutiérrez* in the cited chapter 19, number 5, affirm that it can nevertheless be revoked. This is because such a pact and the renunciation of the right to revoke for ingratitude are void; they offer an "occasion for delinquency" <note>original: "occasionem delinquendi," meaning they encourage bad behavior by removing the consequences</note>, according to the laws in the Digest *On Pacts* and *On Dowry Pacts*. The same was decreed on this foundation in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 55, last paragraph. Although the cited laws of Castile seem to suggest the opposite—since the law includes that clause when teaching the form for drafting a gift instrument—various solutions are provided by Gregorio López and

<column-break/>

Gutiérrez in the places cited. Thus, despite that law, the common opinion should be held, especially when that clause is not confirmed by an oath.

<margin>6</margin><margin>Doubt</margin> A further doubt is: what if the donation is confirmed by an oath? Is it then lawful to revoke it for ingratitude? <margin>Decision.</margin> It must be said that if only the donation itself is confirmed by oath, and it is not expressly stated that it cannot be revoked for ingratitude, it can undoubtedly be revoked. This is because it carries a "tacit condition" established by law: "unless the recipient is ungrateful." Adding an oath does not exclude the silent conditions that a promise (or the law it rests upon) naturally contains. If, however, the donor expressly stated that they would not revoke the gift even for ingratitude, and confirms that with an oath, then indeed, following *Johannes Andreae* and others cited by *Gregorio López* and *Gutiérrez*, we must say it is wrong <note>original: "nefas," a moral or religious prohibition</note> to revoke the donation, regardless of what Ripa and others have said to the contrary.

The reason is manifest: the donor does not sin by failing to revoke the gift when ingratitude occurs, just as a victim of usury does not sin by paying interest, nor does someone who promised a hundred coins to a highwayman to save their life sin by paying him. This is clear in itself and is implied in the laws of the Code and the Decretals. An oath that can be kept without sinning must be observed under pain of mortal sin. It does not matter if the person for whom it is fulfilled takes from it an "occasion for ruin" (like the usurer keeping the interest or the highwayman not returning the money). Therefore, in the scenario we are discussing, it is wrong to revoke the donation despite the recipient's ingratitude.

This is confirmed by the canon law chapter *Quemadmodum*, section *illud*, regarding oaths. There it is determined that if a husband promised his wife under oath that he would not accuse her even if she fell into adultery, he cannot accuse her of that crime to obtain a divorce. Since he can refrain from accusing her without sinning (by forgiving her), the added oath obliges him to keep what can be kept without sin. The same reason applies here. Note, however, that since the recipient makes himself unworthy of the oath being kept through his ingratitude, I believe that authorities—not only ecclesiastical but also secular (as discussed in Disputation 149)—can release the donor from that oath as a punishment for such ingratitude. Once that release is granted, the donor can lawfully act to revoke the gift, regardless of what Gutiérrez says in number 6.

<margin>7</margin> It should be observed that a "donation for a cause" <note>original: "donatio ob causam," a gift given in exchange for something or as a reward</note> is not revoked for ingratitude. This is because such a gift does not truly have the character of a simple donation, but is rather a "recompensation" or a debt, according to the law of the Digest *On Donations*. This is affirmed by the Gloss on the Code, Panormitanus, Giulio Claro, Gama, *Gregorio López*, and others. They gather this from the law *si pater* in the Digest...

<meta>catchword: ...in the Digest</meta>

<summary>Molina argues that donations can only be revoked for the five specific legal reasons listed in the Code of Justinian, excluding other forms of ingratitude. He also discusses how oaths and specific contracts interact with the right to revoke a gift, noting that while an oath not to revoke is generally binding, authorities may release a donor from it as a punishment for the recipient's behavior.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether certain types of gifts can be revoked for ingratitude. The previous page explored the general rule that gifts can only be revoked for five specific legal reasons. Here, Molina examines special cases: remunerative gifts, dowries, and church appointments.</meta>

### Second Treatise. Disputation 282.

Regarding donations. Arias Pinellus <note>Arias Piñel (1512–1563), a prominent Spanish jurist</note> however (in Book 1, part 3, number 62, corollary 14 of the Code *concerning the goods of the mother*) argues that this rule does not apply to those "remunerative" gifts which—though it is fitting they be made—are nonetheless acts of generosity. For example, when a fixed salary was established for a famous person, and because he performed his duty strenuously and rightly, he is rewarded with something extra. Similarly, when a prince rewards services rendered: although it is fitting for the prince to reward them, he is not strictly bound to do so. This opinion is pleasing to me.

8. Thus far, for the same reason, a dowry <term>dos; property brought by a wife to her husband to support the costs of marriage</term> given to a husband is not revoked due to the ingratitude of the wife, as is clear from the law *si dotem* <note>original: "l. si dotem, C. de iure dotium," referring to the Code of Justinian 5.12.10</note>. Other laws agree—such as the final law of the Code *concerning the promise of a dowry*, with those words: *let the generosity remain true and irrevocable*—as does the law *if a father on behalf of a daughter* <note>original: "l. si pater pro filia, ff. de colla. dotis"</note>. This is affirmed by Gutierrez (in the cited chapter 10, number 4), Gama (Decision 163, number 4), Gregorio López <note>A famous 16th-century commentator on Spanish law</note> (on the cited law 10, gloss 1), and others whom they cite.

However, Gregorio López considers this to be true regarding a daughter only if it was the father who provided her dowry; this is because he is legally bound to provide a dowry, and thus he is not exercising generosity toward her, but fulfilling a debt. He thinks differently if a stranger provided the gift. For although a stranger cannot revoke a donation due to the ingratitude of the woman who received the dowry by reclaiming it from the husband (as is clear from the law *si dotem*), López thinks the stranger can reclaim the dowry from the wife once the marriage is dissolved.

Yet, I believe this is false, especially if the woman has children remaining from that marriage. Because of the children, such a revocation would result in a loss for the husband, in whose eyes the dowry was not a "gift" but an "onerous contract" <term>contractus onerosus; a legal agreement where both parties give and receive something of value</term>, as was shown in Disputation 279.

Furthermore, I am inclined to think that López’s opinion is simply false, and one must say, in agreement with the other cited doctors, that a dowry cannot be reclaimed even from the woman on account of ingratitude. This is because it was given for an "onerous" reason <note>i.e., the maintenance of the marriage and children</note>. If it could be reclaimed for any reason, the husband might never have been willing to accept the marriage in the first place—especially since he might hope, even if he has no children, to become his wife's heir, either by her will or by law if she leaves no relatives within the tenth degree.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin> 9. And for these same reasons, I believe the same must be said regarding a gift made to a husband for the wedding <note>original: "donatione ad nuptias," a pre-nuptial gift from the bride's side</note>, which similarly takes on the nature of an "onerous contract" in relation to the wife; the final law of the Code *concerning the promise of a dowry* also speaks of these donations.

<margin>Decision.</margin> Whether, if an ecclesiastical benefit <term>beneficium Ecclesiasticum; a church office that provides an income</term> is conferred on someone, and he is ungrateful to the person who granted it in any of the ways explained, the grantor can revoke the grant. Johannes Andreae, Panormitanus, and Julius Clarus (Question 21, number 6) along with the doctors generally say no. This is because that grant is not strictly a "donation" (a gift), but is the execution of a duty the grantor is bound to perform—even though some generosity is seen in the fact that it was granted to this person rather than another.

Regarding the revocation of a slave's freedom due to the ingratitude of the freedman, this was discussed in Disputation 228.

<column-break/>

### On the revocation of a gift because children are born to the donor.

## DISPUTATION CCLXXXII.

### SUMMARY.

1. *A gift made to a stranger by one who has no children is revoked if children are subsequently born, and why.*
2. *A general disposition does not include those things which the person making the arrangement would likely have excluded.*
3. *The revocation of a gift due to the arrival of children is supported not only by the presumed intent of the donor but also by law and statute.*
4. *A gift made to a stranger is rendered entirely void by the arrival of children.*
5. *When a gift is revoked in its entirety due to the arrival of children, and when it is not, according to the laws of Portugal and Castile.*
6. *A gift cannot be revoked through the law "If ever" (si unquam) when it is established that the father had thought about having children.*
7. *When a gift falling under the law "If ever" is valid if it is confirmed by an oath.*
8. *When a gift extinguished by the birth of children might come back to life if the children later die while the father is still living.*
9. *When a gift is revoked by the law "If ever" by a legitimate child born later.*
10. *A gift made to the Church is not revoked in its entirety by the arrival of children.*
11. *In which cases a remunerative gift, or one given for a specific cause, is revoked in its entirety by the arrival of children.*

When someone who has no children makes a gift, if children are later born to him, the gift is revoked by the law itself and becomes void. This is held in the law *If ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam," the famous law in Code of Justinian 8.55.8</note> and Law 8, Title 4, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish legal code</note>, as well as by Johannes Andreae and Panormitanus. This is the common opinion of the Doctors, which Covarrubias, Antonio Gómez, Julius Clarus, Gregorio López, and Gutierrez all follow.

1. Although † the cited law *If ever* only speaks of a gift made to a "freedman" <note>a former slave</note>, the Glossator there judges that the same applies when the gift was made to any other "stranger"—that is, anyone who is not among the donor's children or descendants. The doctors commonly agree and the cited law of Castile <note>Spain</note> so decrees.

The reason is that the donor is presumed at that time to have not thought about children; had he thought of them, he either would not have given the gift or would have given it on the condition that children were not born to him. No one is presumed to have wanted to prefer strangers over his own posterity, according to the legal arguments found in the Code <note>original: "l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideic." and "l. generaliter, §. cum autem, C. de instit. & substi."</note> and other laws.

2. And † because in grants and arrangements, that which the person...
<meta>The text cuts off at the catchword "conce-" (likely "concessisset" or "concederet"), indicating the discussion continues on the next page regarding what the donor would have granted had they known the future.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses why dowries and church appointments cannot usually be revoked for ingratitude and introduces the major legal rule that gifts to strangers are automatically voided if the donor later has children. Molina explains that the law presumes a parent would always prioritize their own future children over a stranger.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological discussion regarding the revocation of gifts. While the previous page focused on ingratitude, this page shifts to the revocation of a gift because of the subsequent birth of children to the donor—a concept known in Roman and Civil law as "revocation for the supervenience of children."</meta>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts #

granting or disposing of property, were he to be asked about a specific case, he would make an exception for it. This is supported by the general rule in the *Rules of Law* <note>Referring to the *Regulae Iuris* in Book 6 of the Decretals, a standard collection of legal principles</note>, and is consistent with the law *tale pactum* <note>original: "l. tale pactum, §. vlt. ff. de pactis"</note> in the Digest, as the final gloss and doctors of law commonly note. Therefore, a person who gives a gift in the situation we are discussing is presumed to give it under a silent condition: "provided that no children are born to me."

3. At this point, † observe that the revocation of a gift in this event does not derive its power solely from the presumed intent of the donor. It is also greatly supported by statute and by positive law itself. The law establishes this revocation both because of that presumed condition and for the benefit of the children, regardless of what the donor’s actual mind might have been. This was correctly noted by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish canonist and "the Spanish Bartolus"</note> in his *Epitome* (part 2, chapter 6). This is especially true because such a gift would be **inofficious** <term>inofficious; a legal term for a gift or will that fails in its moral duty toward family, specifically by depriving children of their rightful inheritance</term>. In such a case, the donor was not fulfilling the duty of a father, as he was depriving his children of their **legitimate portion** <term>legitima portio; the minimum share of an estate that must, by law, be reserved for the children</term>, which the children ought to inherit from the father by law, whether the father willed it or not.

Because this law is neither a penalty nor based solely on a guess of intent, but rather derives its power primarily from the legislator's decree for the benefit of the children and the common good of the state, Covarruvias rightly states (in the cited number 17) that this revocation has power in the **court of conscience** <term>forum conscientiae; the internal realm of moral and spiritual standing before God, as opposed to a secular court</term>. It happens by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> as soon as children are born to the donor, without waiting for a court sentence.

4. When † a gift made to a stranger is revoked because of the birth of children to the donor, the entire gift is then rendered null, and everything that was given must be restored in full. This is held in the law *if ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam, C. de revocan. donationibus"</note> in the Code, with those words: *let everything, whatever he had bestowed, return to be under the will and power of the donor.* The same is decreed in Law 8, Title 4, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous Spanish law code</note> with the words: *And it ought not to be valid in any way*. This is affirmed by Gregorio López and the common opinion of the doctors, including Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential medieval jurist</note>, Panormitanus, Antonio Gómez, Julio Claro, and Gutierrez.

<margin>The Question</margin>
The question is: how large must a gift be for the whole thing to be revoked upon the birth of children?

<margin>The Decision</margin>
5. We say † first of all that gifts which right reason and the proper administration of property require—given the donor’s status and means—are not "inofficious." A father is not required to count these against the "third" of his goods in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> or the "fifth" in Castile <note>These refer to the "available portions" of an estate that a parent could freely give away without infringing on the children's mandatory inheritance</note>, even if he has children. Rather, these belong to ordinary expenses and the management of one's estate. Therefore, even if children are born later, these gifts are not revoked.

And observe: one can give more in this manner to different people over time than one could give all at once. We are debating, therefore, only the excess beyond such reasonable gifts. The cited Law 8 of Castile says a gift must be revoked if it consists of all the goods, or a **large part** <margin>Status of the doubt.</margin> of the father's goods. Antonio Gómez said it must be the majority of the goods. Baldus and others cited by Covarruvias claimed it must be at least half the goods. Bartolus, however, judged that it was enough if he had given a 

<column-break/>

specific item, and it was not necessary that he give a specific fraction of his total goods.

The more common opinion, followed by Covarruvias, Gregorio López, and Julio Claro, agrees with Bartolus: it is enough if the gift is a **notable part**, even if it is less than half of the donor's goods. This clearly agrees with the law *if ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam"</note> in the Code, which uses the words: *All goods, or some part of his resources, bestowed by gift.*

Nor does the cited Law of Castile contradict this; for under the name of a "large part" of the donor's goods, a part that is notably large—even if less than half—is included. Some, whom Gregorio López mentions, said it should be at least a fourth part of the donor's goods. It is better stated by López and Julio Claro that this should be left to the judge's discretion, looking at all the circumstances. The judge should weigh whether the donor, if he had been thinking of children at the time, would have given such an amount or not. One might say that if the gift is "inofficious" to the child—because in Portugal it exceeds a third of the goods, or in the kingdom of Castile a fifth—the gift should be revoked in its entirety. But when it is not inofficious (for instance, if in Portugal it did not exceed a third), it should be left to the judge’s discretion. Certainly, if it exceeded a fifth in Portugal, it should be revoked no less than in Castile, even if it were not technically "inofficious" in Portugal.

<margin>The Question</margin>
Since the law *if ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam"</note> arose from the presumption that if the donor had thought of children, he would have given under a silent condition, the more common opinion of the doctors (including Gregorio López, Julio Claro, and Gutierrez) concludes:

6. When † it is clearly established that the donor gave the gift while specifically thinking about having children, the gift is valid. It cannot be revoked in its entirety, nor while the donor is still living. The words of the cited Law 8 are in agreement with this.

Furthermore, they judge this to be much more true (following Bartolus and Antonio Gómez) when the donor has **expressly renounced** the law *if ever*. Others, whom the same authors mention, believe the opposite: they argue that the law was established in favor of the children, and while the donor could renounce a favor to himself, he cannot renounce a favor intended for his children.

<margin>The Decision</margin>
I prefer the opinion of Bartolus and the common view, provided that—as Gregorio López and Gutierrez affirm against Bernardo Díaz, Bishop of Calahorra—it is understood as follows: Although the gift is not automatically null, nor can it be revoked in its entirety while the father is alive, nevertheless, **after the father's death**, the children can revoke it to the extent that it was inofficious—that is, to the extent that it touches upon their "legitimate portions."

Indeed, this distinct privilege of the children (which will be the subject of the following disputation) always remains safe for the children. A father cannot renounce it, nor can he bring any prejudice against it; even though,

<summary>This page discusses the legal revocation of gifts when a donor unexpectedly has children. It concludes that while reasonable gifts are upheld, "inofficious" gifts that deplete a child's mandatory inheritance (the legitimate portion) are subject to revocation based on both presumed intent and statutory law in Spain and Portugal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the revocation of gifts (donations) when a donor, previously childless, subsequently has children. It specifically addresses how oaths and the death of those children affect the legal status of the gift.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 282 ###

...even though, while he lacks children, he can freely give in the same way he could if he had them. Furthermore, the donation of a father who has children is valid, even if it is of great value and "inofficious" <term>inofficious; a gift that violates the moral duty to provide for one's children</term> toward them; it is only revoked after the father's death to the extent that it is found to be inofficious to the children, as I shall discuss in the following dispute. However, as Gregorius Lopez <note>Gregorio López de Tovar (1496–1560), a major commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> correctly affirms in the cited place: if the children were to lack maintenance while the father is alive—the father having made such an inofficious donation—the recipient of the gift could be compelled either to provide them with maintenance or to restore the gifted property to the extent of the children's **legitimate portions** <term>legitima; the minimum portion of an estate guaranteed to heirs by law</term>.

<margin>Doubt 7 Decision</margin>
The doubt is: what if the donation—of which the law *If ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam"; referring to the Code of Justinian 8.55.8, which governs the revocation of gifts upon the birth of children</note> speaks—is confirmed by an **oath** from the donor? Will it then be valid? It must first be said † that if the donation itself is confirmed by an oath after the children are born, it is entirely void by the law itself, just as if the oath had not been sworn. This is proven because, as was said in the preceding dispute, an oath is understood according to the nature of the promise or act upon which it falls; it does not exclude the silent conditions which the act has of itself or by the disposition of the law, even without the oath. Therefore, that donation is rendered void by the birth of children just as if it had not been confirmed by an oath.

This is the view of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential medieval jurist</note> at the cited section *Imperator*, and it is the common opinion of the doctors of law, which Iulius Clarus <note>Giulio Claro (1525–1575), an Italian jurist known for his "Sententiae Receptae"</note> reports and follows in his fourth book of *Sentences* (section on donation, question 23, number 1), as does Antonio Gomez (number 11, cited), Covarruvias (chapter *quamvis pactum*, part 1, section 4, number 3), and Gutierrez (chapter 9, cited, numbers 8, 9, 10). It must then be said that if the donor renounced the law *If ever* and confirmed that renunciation with an oath—or when he gave simply and confirmed the gift with an oath, his intention was not to revoke it even if children were born to him—the donation is valid by consent. In this case, it is not void by the law itself, nor can it be revoked in its entirety while he is alive (as was said regarding when a donor expressly renounces the law *If ever* but without an oath). However, despite the father’s oath, the children will still be able to bring a **complaint of an inofficious donation** <note>original: "querela inofficiosae donationis"</note> against it and revoke it to the extent that it affects their legitimate portions.

Indeed, I believe that if a parent promised an inofficious gift under oath, the oath does not prevent him from being excused from fulfilling the promise to the extent that it would be inofficious to the children's legitimate portions. Gutierrez agrees with this (number 10, cited). The first of these points is proven because the whole matter has the same force as if no oath had been added, as was said a little before; therefore, it will have all the more force when the confirmation of an oath is added.

Furthermore, because none of those things contain anything evil, if they are confirmed by an oath, they will have force from that oath, and the donor will be bound in conscience and in the external court to stand by them. The second point is proven because that right—of the complaint of an inofficious donation and of revoking that donation to the extent it affects the children's legitimate portions—is the children's own right. Therefore, the father could not bring any prejudice to them by his own oath; rather, the children can bring a complaint of an inofficious donation and revoke it just as if the parent's oath had not intervened. Finally, the third point is proven because a father does wrong by promising inofficiously; he transgresses the law by which he is prohibited from diminishing the children's legitimate portions through a gift or a last will. Therefore, even if he has bound himself by oath to carry it out, he is not bound to stand by his promises to the prejudice of his children. For **an oath is not a bond of iniquity** <note>original: "iuramentum non est vinculum iniquitatis"; a standard legal maxim meaning an oath cannot be used to justify a sinful or illegal act</note>, such that it could obligate one to that which is evil and prohibited to a father.

<margin>Doubt Decision</margin>
The next doubt is: what if, after the donation mentioned in the law *If ever*, children are born to the donor, but while the donor is still living, the children depart from this life? Does the donation, once extinguished and void by the law itself, revive? Bartolus (at the law *Titia*, section *Imperator*) and certain others denied that it revives. The contrary is affirmed by the common opinion, which Iulius Clarus (question 23, cited, number 9) and Antonio Gomez (volume 2 of *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 4, number 12) report and follow. I think, † however, it should be said that if the donor, after the birth and subsequent death of the children, allows the recipient to enjoy the donated goods and does not seek them back, the gift revives. This is based on the presumed will of the donor, who by that very act is judged not to want to revoke the donation, but rather to confirm it.

<margin>8</margin>
And this is what Iulius Clarus and Antonio Gomez seem to mean in the cited places. Hence, in this event, the heirs of the donor, after his death, will not be able to recover those goods from the recipient. But if the donor, knowingly and deliberately, did not allow the recipient to enjoy those goods even after the death of the children—either because he was reclaiming them, or intended to reclaim them, or did not have time to reclaim them after the children's death—then it certainly does not revive. Instead, the donor will be able to claim those goods for himself, and after his death, his heirs can do the same.

The reason is that, as held in the cited law *If ever*, by the very fact that children are born, everything that had been donated reverts to remain at the donor's disposal and control. Since, therefore, what was donated belongs and reverts to the donor by the law itself, it certainly cannot thereafter belong to the recipient except by the presumed or express will of the donor, and thus by a new right and title. And this is clearly what Iulius Clarus and Antonio Gomez seem to mean in the cited places; in this, they do not disagree with the opinion of Bartolus. Rather, Bartolus's opinion is to be judged true in the strict and proper sense of the words: for that is not a "revival" of the donation through the death of the children, but rather a silent gift of the goods made again to the same recipient by the original donor. In this event, Bartolus does not deny that a second silent or presumed donation is valid.

<margin>9</margin>
There is † furthermore a doubt: if after the donation mentioned in the law *If ever*, a **spurious** <note>A child born of a relationship prohibited by law (e.g., adultery or incest)</note> or even a **natural** <note>A child born of unmarried parents who were legally capable of marrying each other at the time of conception</note> son is born and is legitimized by the Prince, whether such a preceding donation is revoked. Iulius Clarus (book 4, *Sentences*, section on donation, question 23, number 6) thinks it is revoked if a natural son is legitimized by a rescript of the Prince; he cites Johannes Andreae in his additions to the *Speculator*, and reports from Paris de Puteo that this is the common opinion. Ripa was of the same opinion in his commentary on the law *If ever*.

However, according to the same Paris de Puteo, Julius says the opposite...

He also concludes that if such children die, the gift only "revives" if the donor specifically intends to treat it as a new gift.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the revocation of gifts upon the birth of subsequent children, moving from general rules to specific cases involving legitimized children, gifts to the Church, and remunerative donations.</meta>

# Luis de Molina #

[Julius] Clarus states that if such a son were born before the gift was made but is legitimized afterward, then the donation is not revoked. Tiraqueau, Salicetus, and others affirm the opposite in the first instance, as Gregorius Lopez <note>Gregorio López de Tovar (1496–1560), the preeminent commentator on Spanish law</note> records and follows in his commentary on Law 8, under the phrase "of his legitimate wife" <note>original: "de su muger legitima"</note>; Alvarus Valascus also agrees with this in his 94th consultation, number 6. This opinion is most clearly supported by the cited Law 8, which states:
> that if afterward he should have a son or daughter by his legitimate wife whom he married later, as soon as he has them, the donation is therefore revoked and must not be valid in any way. <note>Original Old Spanish: "que si despues huiese hijo o hija de su muger legitima con que casase despues, que luego que lo a, es reuocada por ende la donacion, e no deue valer en ninguna manera"</note>
From these words, you see that everyone who is not born from a legitimate marriage is excluded.

And indeed, I believe it is false that the contrary is the common opinion, as Julius Clarus affirms along with Paria and Puteo; nor is there a text or reason that would persuade one of it. Hence, although by Portuguese law the **natural son** <term>natural son; a child born of parents who were not married but were free to marry at the time of conception</term> of a commoner succeeds to the father's goods equally with other legitimate sons (as was said in Dispute 166), Alvarus Valascus nevertheless contends in the cited consultation that a donation previously made by the father is not revoked by the birth of such a son. This is because things granted in favor of such children should not be extended further than they are found to have been granted. Furthermore, the rule of the law *If ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam"; the Roman law rule that gifts are revoked if children are later born</note>—which many claim is an exceptional rule—takes precedence, especially since it should not be presumed that the father was donating under a tacit condition that the gift would be void if a natural son were born. The law *If ever* is founded on such a presumption specifically regarding **legitimate** children.

For this reason, Gregorius Lopez, in the cited gloss, concludes insufficiently that a natural son annuls a donation made by the mother before his birth, based on the fact that a natural son born from a non-condemned union <note>A union not considered incestuous or adulterous by the law</note> to a woman who is not of high rank is permitted to challenge the mother's will as **inofficious** <term>inofficious; a legal term for a will or gift that unfairly excludes one's natural heirs</term>. However, it must be added that the birth of such a son, if he is legitimized by a subsequent marriage, renders a donation made before his birth and legitimation null; for children legitimized by a subsequent marriage are held as legitimate and are equal to those born after a legitimate marriage. Although the words we just related from Law 8 might seem to sound to the contrary at first glance, it is nonetheless to be believed that the legislator did not intend that; especially since such children are truly said to be born of a legitimate wife with whom he contracted marriage after the gift, even if they were not born of her after the marriage was contracted, but before.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
The further doubt is: if a donation, as described in the law *If ever* (Codex, On the revocation of donations), is made to the **Church**, and children are later born to the donor, is it revoked in its
<margin>Decision 10</margin>
entirety? It must be said—following Bartolus, Panormitanus, and the common opinion related and followed by Julius Clarus, Antonius Gomez, Gama, and Covarruvias—that it is not revoked in its entirety, but only up to the **legitimate portions** <term>legitima; the portion of an estate that the law requires be left to the children</term> of the children born afterward. This ensures the gift is not "inofficious" toward them, according to what will be said in the following dispute regarding when a donation is made to one son and others are born later to whom it is inofficious. In that case,

<column-break/>

# On Contracts #

the prior donation is not revoked in its entirety, but only up to the legitimate portions of the children.

The reason why a donation made to the Church is not revoked in its entirety is because the Church is held in the place of a child, and therefore it should not be revoked more than if it had been made to a son. Furthermore, it is not to be believed that one who donated to the Church did so under a tacit or presumed condition that if children were born, it should be revoked in its entirety by his will. Moreover, one must lean in favor of a **pious cause** <term>pia causa; a legal category for charitable or religious donations</term>. This agrees with the words of Augustine (Question 4, final chapter) from his sermon on the life of clerics: "Whoever wishes," he says, "to disinherit his son and make the Church his heir, let him look for someone else to receive it, not Augustine. Indeed, by God’s grace, he will find no one." How praiseworthy was the deed of Saint Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage! For a certain man, since he had no children and expected none, donated all his property to the Church (retaining the **usufruct** <term>usufruct; the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term> for himself). Children were born to him unexpectedly. The bishop returned the things he had donated. The bishop had the power not to return them by the **law of the forum**, but not by the **law of heaven**. <note>original: "iure fori... iure poli"; human law versus divine/moral law</note> Thus far Augustine. When he says the bishop had the power not to return them by the law of the forum, it is understood regarding the amount beyond the legitimate portions, as we said just now with Bartolus and others; for no one doubts that the legitimate portions had to be returned even in the external forum (according to the law *If all*, Codex, On inofficious donations), as will be said in the following dispute. Truly, when he adds "not by the law of heaven," he does not mean that the bishop was bound by justice or under pain of sin in the forum of conscience to return the excess; but only out of a certain moral equity, and because it was more pleasing to God and served the edification of the people, as the glosses, Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and others explain in the cited places.

Hence Augustine says in the same sermon that this deed filled all who heard it with the praises of God. And certainly, since it was a donation of all one's goods (as that one was, which Aurelius revoked in its entirety), reason and thus the "law of heaven" demand that it be revoked by the ministers of the Church not just for the legitimate portions, but entirely, so that the donor might have the means to freely make a will and increase his children's inheritance from his own patrimony. What has been said about a donation made to the Church is to be understood as applying to a donation made to any other pious cause. Antonius Gomez wishes to extend this to a donation made to **ancestors** <term>ascendentes; parents, grandparents, etc.</term>; but since ancestors are not regarded in the place of children as the Church is, I would not dare extend this to a donation made to them.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
The final doubt is: if a donation is **remuneratory** <term>remuneratory donation; a gift given as a reward or payment for services rendered</term>, or otherwise given for a cause, and children are later born to the donor, is the donation revoked in its entirety according to the law *If ever*, or at least up to the children's legitimate portions? Gregorius Lopez and Gutierrez distinguish this
<margin>Decision 11</margin>
excellently, along with Tiraqueau and many others whom they cite.

They argue that such a donation is not purely an act of generosity on the part of the donor, but has a cause by which he is bound to perform it—whether out of his own gratitude or another similar cause. In such a case, the donation is revoked neither in its entirety nor in part. In this, Julius Clarus and the common opinion which he cites agree.

The reason is that, since this is something owed, it certainly pertains to the proper administration of goods to give it, whether the donor has children or not. Nor is the donor required to count this toward the **third** <term>the "third" (terço); the portion of an estate in Portuguese law that a person could freely give away without affecting the children's inheritance</term> of his goods in Portugal, nor the **fifth** <term>the "fifth" (quinto); the equivalent freely disposable portion in Castilian law</term> in Castile. However, if the donation is so liberal on the part of the donor that there is no cause for which he is bound to give it, then—even if there is a cause on the part of the recipient for which it is done—the donation will be revoked, at least up to the **legitimate shares** <term>legitima; the portion of an estate that must by law be reserved for the children</term> of the children. For example, if someone gives a **dowry** <note>money or property brought by a woman to her husband at marriage</note> to an outside woman, and later children are born to the donor, then although that donation is for an **onerous cause** <note>original: "causam onerosam"; a legal exchange involving a burden or obligation rather than a pure gift</note> in relation to the husband to whom she is dowered, the donation will certainly be revoked—at least insofar as it was **inofficious** <term>inofficious; a legal term for a gift that ignores the donor's moral and legal duty to provide for their own children</term> to his own children. This is because the donor was not bound by any debt to grant it as a dowry but did so out of his mere liberality.

This is confirmed because if someone endows his own daughter, yet that dowry is inofficious toward the other children (either those already born or those born later), it is revoked to the extent it was inofficious to the other children, as was shown above in the material on the partition of goods. This holds even if the father is bound to endow his own daughter, and even if the dowry is a donation for an onerous cause in relation to the son-in-law. Therefore, it will be revoked much more so if the dowry was conferred upon an outside woman; for the father could not, to the prejudice of his children, give that to an outsider out of his mere liberality. I said that a donation of this kind made as a dowry is revoked at least insofar as it is not inofficious to his own children: since it was given for an onerous cause in relation to the husband of the recipient, certainly the increase will not be revoked, but the father will be considered to take it from the "third" of his goods in Portugal and the "fifth" in Castile.

Unless, however, the dowry in this Kingdom of Castile was conferred upon a granddaughter: for then, even if the grandfather has other children and the father of such a granddaughter is still living, he will be considered to have "improved" that granddaughter in the third and fifth of his goods, regarding such an increase beyond the legitimate shares of the children.

### Regarding the revocation of a gift made to one of the children when others are born later. And regarding a gift made to a stranger by one who has children. And whether a donation may be declared inofficious in relation to **ascendants** <note>parents or grandparents</note>.

# DISPUTE CCLXXXIII.

### SUMMARY.

1 **A donation made to one of the children, if other children are born later, may be revoked as inofficious up to the required amount of the legitimate share.**
**The same also applies if other children had already been born.** *number 2.*
**Indeed, even if such a donation were inofficious in deed and intent,** *number 3.*
**And even if it had been confirmed by an oath.** *number 4.*
**And what should be said concerning the law of Castile? extensively,** *numbers 5.*
6 **A donation made by a parent to a grandson from a son, improving**

<column-break/>

him in the third of his goods, cannot be rescinded by the son as inofficious.
7 **A donation that is merely inofficious, made to a stranger, is revoked up to the legitimate share of the child.**
8 **A donation inofficious in deed and intent, made to a stranger: when it may be revoked in its entirety by the children.**
**And the same is to be said regarding ascendants, just as with children.** *number 9.*

In the preceding dispute, we spoke only of the revocation of a donation made by one not having children (whether he be married or not) when children are born to him afterward. Now, however, three proposed matters remain to be discussed.

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the first point, when someone who has children gives something to one or more people which diminishes the legitimate portions of those who are born after those donations were made, then the donations are revoked up to the necessary support of the goods—that is, insofar as they are inofficious to the legitimate shares of the others—but not in their entirety, or regarding the increase.

<margin>2</margin> This is held in the law *si totas* in the Code *De inofficiosis donationibus* <note>On Inofficious Donations</note>, and Law 8, title 4, part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*] and Law 3, title 8, book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación* agree. It is exactly the same if someone, having many children already born, gives something to one or some of them which diminishes the legitimate shares of the others: for the donations are revoked insofar as they are found to be inofficious to the rest, as is clear from the *Authentica* <note>a collection of Justinian's legal updates</note> regarding immense donations, from laws 1, 2, 3, the law *cum donationibus*, the law *si mater*, and the final law in the Code *De inofficiosis donationibus*, as well as from the two cited laws of Castile which speak universally, and from book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 77, § 4.

<margin>3</margin> Moreover, both points are true even if those donations were inofficious in deed and intent <note>original: "re, & consilio"</note>—that is, even if they were made with the intention of defrauding the legitimate portions of the other children—as is expressly held in the law *si liqueat* in the Code *De inofficiosis donationibus*.

Indeed, all these things are affirmed by **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note> on the law *Titia*, section *imperator*, in the Digest *De legatis secundo*; by **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer</note> in the last chapter on donations, number 5; and by the common opinion of the doctors, which **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist</note> reports and follows in the first book of his *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 19, numbers 1 and 12; **Antonius Gomez** in the second volume of his *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 4, numbers 11 and 13; **Julius Clarus** in the 4th book of his *Sententiae*, section *donatio*, question 21, number 3, and question 24, numbers 1 and 2; and **Guterrius** in *De iuramento confirmato* <note>On Confirmed Oaths</note>, part 1, chapter 9, number 11. Although **Emmanuel Acosta**, in the chapter *si pater*, third part, on the phrase "he cannot deprive," from number three, admits that this is the common opinion and wishes to dissent from it in part, he later agrees with it entirely, led by the *Authentica* on immense donations as the most recent law, which established that such donations should only be revoked up to the legitimate shares due to the other children.

<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, what has been said remains true even if the parent had confirmed the donation with an oath, and by the same oath had bound himself not to revoke it. Since, as was said in the preceding dispute, a father could not, by his own oath, prejudice his children regarding their legitimate portions.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "inofficious" donations—gifts that are legally voidable because they unfairly reduce the inheritance (the "legitimate portion") guaranteed to the donor's children. Molina is specifically examining how these laws apply in the kingdoms of Castile and Portugal when children are born after a gift has already been made.</meta>

-># Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts<-

And since he sins by giving inofficiously <note>original: "peccat inofficiose donando"; meaning he fails in his moral and legal duty to his heirs</note>: for an unjust bond is not a bond of iniquity. This is the view of Giulio Claro, question 24, cited at number 3, and the doctors of law whom we cited in the preceding disputation. Remember, however, as was said in the previous disputation, that we should not take into account those donations which a father rightly makes according to the size of his estate and his lawful administration of it when judging whether he has given inofficiously; rather, we judge only by the increase above such rightly made donations.

<margin>§</margin> The question is: if a father, having only one son, makes a large donation to him, and afterwards other sons are born to him, is that donation revoked in this kingdom of Castile to provide the **legitimate portions** <term>legitima; the portion of an estate that must by law be reserved for the children</term> of the other sons? Furthermore, should the **third** and the **fifth** be deducted first <note>In Castilian law, the "third" (tercio) could be used to favor one child over others, and the "fifth" (quinto) could be given to anyone</note>—in which that first son would be considered **favored** <term>melioratus; "improved," or given a larger share than his siblings</term> according to Law 26 of Toro (which today is Law 5, Title 6, Book 5 of the *New Collection*)—or is it revoked to the level of the legitimate portions without deducting the third, but only the fifth? Or is it even revoked to the level of the legitimate portions with neither the third nor the fifth deducted, but dividing the donor's entire estate into unequal or equal shares?

There have been those who thought that not even the **fifth** of the goods should be deducted in this event. They were led by the reasoning that perhaps, if the father had thought about the children yet to be born, he would have given nothing to that first son (following the law *si unquam* in the Code regarding the revocation of donations), but would have instead maintained equality among them.

But this opinion is improbable and openly against the law *si totas* in the Code regarding **inofficious donations** <note>original: "de inofficios. donat."; a gift that violates the legal rights of heirs</note>. That law establishes that, in this event, the donation is revoked only as far as necessary to provide the legitimate portions owed to the other sons, but not regarding the "increase," as was said a little while ago. Therefore, since the fifth of the donor's goods does not belong to the legitimate portions owed to the sons in this kingdom—just as the **third** <term>terço; the Portuguese equivalent of the disposable portion</term> does not belong to them in Portugal—certainly those portions must be set aside in those kingdoms in which that son (to whom the gift was made) would be considered "favored," as has been said elsewhere. Nor does the law presume in this case that the father would have given nothing if he had thought of the children to be born. Nor does it presume the father wished to maintain absolute equality among the children, especially since the firstborn is usually the one to whom the donation was made; he is typically more beloved, and parents usually prefer him over others in property so that the memory of the family may be preserved especially in him.

Bernardo Díaz, Bishop of Calahorra—whom Gregorio López refers to and follows—thinks that the donation should be revoked to provide the legitimate portions after deducting only the **fifth**. Thus, the legitimate portions of the sons in that event would be the remainder of the donor's estate divided into equal parts, without deducting the **third**, which would be a special gift to the one to whom the donation was made. Besides the reasoning similar to that just mentioned regarding the third and fifth—which is dismissed in the same way—these authors are chiefly led by the following reasoning:

Since in this kingdom [Castile] everything except the **fifth** is the "legitimate portion" in comparison to descendants—because a parent can only dispose of the fifth among outsiders—therefore, at the time of that donation, since the father had no other descendant

<column-break/>

besides that one son, everything except the fifth was his legitimate portion, owed entirely to him.

Nor could the father at that time impose any burden <note>a legal restriction or condition on the property</note> on the **third** of those goods for that son; for a burden cannot be imposed on the third of the goods (according to Law 26 of Toro, which is Law 11, Title 6 of the *New Collection*) except when one of the descendants is being "favored" <term>melioratio; the act of giving a larger share to one heir from the disposable portion</term> in it. In the event we are discussing, "favoring" has no place. For just as there can be no "choice" except by taking one from many and preferring him to the others (as is proven by many laws), so there is no "favoring" except when one is preferred over many in that which he is said to be favored.

Therefore, because the entire estate of the donor, except for the **fifth**, was the legitimate portion in relation to that son to whom the donation was made, surely when other sons are born, that whole amount must be divided into equal parts to establish the legitimate portions of the sons, and the donation must be revoked accordingly. Consequently, the donation is revoked down to the equal shares of that whole which are the legitimate portions of the other sons, with the **third** not being reserved for the one to whom the donation was made. Thus, regarding Law 26 of Toro, which establishes that if a parent gives something to one of the descendants, he is understood by that very act to be "favored" in the third and the fifth (even if the parents do not express it), these aforementioned authors respond: that law is only to be understood in comparison to sons or descendants who were born at the time the donation was made. It does not apply when, at the time of the donation, there was no other descendant except the one to whom the donation was made, because in that event, "favoring" in the third has no place, as has been proven.

Covarrubias, Gutierrez, and others whom they cite, confess that when there was only one descendant to whom an excessive donation was made, he is not considered to be favored in the **third**, nor could any burden be imposed on him in the third by the donor, for the reason just given.

Nevertheless, along with Castillo, Antonio Gómez, Baeza, and Palacios Rubios, they rightly judge that the donation should only be revoked to provide the legitimate portions after deducting from the donor's estate not only the **fifth** but also the **third**. This son to whom the donation was made should have these as a special privilege, if all of it is necessary so that the donation remains entirely his.

They are chiefly led by this: the law *si totas* in the Code regarding inofficious donations establishes that such a donation is only to be revoked regarding the legitimate portions absolutely owed by a parent to children born later. But by the very fact that other children are born, a father in this kingdom owes them nothing for their legitimate portions out of the **fifth** and the **third**; because, unless the third and fifth are entirely [used] by reason of the dona-

This is according to Laws 17 and 18 of Toro, which are Laws 1 and 2, Title 6 in the *New Collection*. Thus, such a donation should only be revoked up to the amount of the legitimate portions, after first deducting the **third** and the **fifth** <note>In Spanish law, the "tercio" (third) could be used to favor one child, and the "quinto" (fifth) could be given to anyone</note> which the son who received the donation holds as a special privilege. <margin>An older opinion.</margin> Perhaps more clearly, and in harmony with the mindset of these legal experts, we might say: When a parent has only one descendant—whether they give a gift to them or otherwise dispose of goods in their favor—this is done absolutely. In such a case, neither the "improvement" of the third share <term>melioratio; the legal act of giving one heir more than the others</term> has a place, nor can any burden be placed upon that third. This is because, as the reasoning provided above proves, as long as there is only one descendant, that parent's entire estate (after deducting only the fifth) constitutes that single descendant's legitimate portion.

7 However, this is under the condition that if another descendant is born, the "improvement" of the third takes effect, and a burden can be imposed on it under that same condition. This burden will indeed take effect if the condition is met—that is, if another descendant is born later. If, however, the donation or irrevocable disposition toward that descendant was made without such a condition, then even if another descendant were born later, a burden could not be imposed on what was irrevocably granted to him. This is because once a donation is perfected, neither a condition nor a burden can be imposed on it, as was stated in Disputation 265.

Furthermore, the interpretation they attempt is a "violence" <note>original: "violentia"; a legal term for a forced or strained interpretation</note> to the same law: first, because the law speaks universally; second, because it similarly holds weight in comparison to heirs born after the donation as it does for those who were already born at the time of the donation when several existed. Therefore, we must deny their conclusion: that because the whole estate (except the fifth) was the legitimate portion of that single descendant before other descendants were born, the legitimate portions owed to those born later from other brothers must be equal shares of that *entire* original estate. 7 Regarding the second point—namely, when an excessive donation is made to a **stranger** <term>extraneus; someone outside the immediate family/heirs</term> by someone who had a son or sons at the time of the donation—we must say: If the matter is found to be "inofficious" <note>original: "inofficiosa"; a gift that violates the legal duty to provide for one's children</note> to the sons (because it diminishes the legitimate portions owed to them, though it was not made with the specific intent to defraud them), it should be revoked only up to the required support of the estate. That is, it is revoked only until the children's legitimate portions remain whole. Any increase or growth, however, belongs to the recipient of the gift. This is gathered from the first and last laws of the *Code of Justinian* on inofficious donations, and from Law 18, Title 6, Part 5. What has been explained so far regarding inofficious donations made to one of the sons applies even more strongly if the inofficious donation was made to a stranger—namely, that it is revoked only so far as it is no longer inofficious to the sons. This is agreed upon by Bartolus, Panormitanus (in the last chapter on donations, number five), and the common opinion cited and followed by Covarrubias (Chapter 19, number twelve), Antonio Gómez, and Julius Clarus. This holds true even if the parent who made the donation had confirmed it with an oath, for the reasons stated above regarding donations to a son. Generally, however, an action to revoke an inofficious donation lasts only five years, as is clear from the final law in the *Code of Justinian*. ### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

And this opinion seems to be established in Law 8, Title 1, Part 5, as Gregorius Lopez asserted in his final gloss there. Emmanuel Acosta also agrees in the place cited, number 16. Others, however, have judged that such gifts should be revoked in their entirety; among their number are Bartolus, the Emperor <note>original: "S. imperator"</note> in the cited text, and Panormitanus, number 5. They argue based on the law concerning the rights of patrons <note>original: "l. si libertus. ff. de iurepatronatus"</note>, which establishes that things alienated in fraud of the law are null by the law itself. Emmanuel Acosta says this is the common opinion. Indeed, Antonio Gomez and Julius Clarus affirm this universally in the places just cited. However, Bartolus and Panormitanus make an exception when a gift was made in fraud of the children but something was nevertheless left to them. In that case, they hold that the donation is not revoked, even if it is intentionally undutiful <term>inofficiosam; a gift that ignores the legal duty to provide for one's heirs</term>, except to the extent of the children's **legitimate portions** <term>legitimas; the portion of an estate that must by law be reserved for the heirs</term>, according to the law *omnimodo* <note>Justinian Code, C. de inoffic. test.</note>. Emmanuel Acosta shows that this is the common view and follows it himself where he discusses this at length. Read him there. For this reason, Covarruvias said that the matter, as distinguished by the doctors of both civil and canon law, generally tends toward this: that an undutiful donation, even one made to a stranger, should be revoked only as far as the legal share is concerned. Choose whichever view you prefer. Certainly, in such a variety and uncertainty of opinions, the condition of the recipient currently in possession should be judged better, so that he is not forced to return the gift unless he fails to leave the children their full legal shares—which he is bound to do without waiting for a court sentence.

And since he would be bound to return the remainder only as a penalty for the wicked plan of the donor and recipient, surely, even if one were to embrace the opinion of those who assert that a donation that is undutiful in both deed and intent should be revoked in its entirety, this would not take place until after a sentence has been passed.

<margin>9</margin> Finally, regarding the third point, it must be said that an undutiful donation occurs in relation to **ascendants** <note>parents or grandparents</note> just as it does in relation to **descendants** <note>children or grandchildren</note>. In the same way, it is revoked up to the portion owed to the ascendants from the goods of the descendants, such as the shares in the children's goods when the children have no descendants of their own. This is clearly gathered from the law *si filius* <note>C. de inoffic. donationib.</note>, and is affirmed by the glosses and by Bartolus and Emmanuel Acosta. For since parents have no less right than children to complain against an undutiful will, and since the complaint against an undutiful donation was introduced following the pattern of the complaint against an undutiful will, the second right is certainly granted to parents regarding their children’s goods no less than the first.

### How many types of donations, stipulations, or promises there are. And concerning those that are "pure" or for a specific day.

# DISPUTATION 284.

## SUMMARY.

*1. When a donation, stipulation, or promise is called "pure."*

<column-break/>

*2. A promise for a certain day creates an obligation, even if it is uncertain when that day will occur, and it passes to the heirs.*
*3. How a promise and a stipulation for a certain day differ from a legacy for a certain day.*
*4. In what case a conditional donation is understood as pure and must be paid immediately.*
*5. In what case a day and time constitute a "condition" properly speaking, and when they do not.*
*6. How the word "immediately" is to be understood.*
*7. A promise made for a certain day, when there are many days of the same name: how it is to be understood.*
*8. A promise to pay something in a certain year or every year: when it is understood to be made at the beginning or at the end of the time.*

Just as in Disputation 205 we divided **legacies** <term>legatum; a gift of property or money left in a will</term> into those that are pure, for a certain day, under a condition, with a "mode" <note>a specific purpose or requirement</note>, with a demonstration, or for a cause; so also a donation, stipulation, or promise can be divided into the same members. Therefore, what was said in that disputation regarding all those types of legacies will greatly lighten our burden here. For, so that the same things are not uselessly repeated, it will be necessary for the reader to refer back to what was said there concerning legacies, insofar as they share common ground with donations, stipulations, or promises.

<margin>1</margin> A stipulation, donation, or promise is called **pure** when neither a day nor a future time is set for its fulfillment, nor is a condition, mode, demonstration, or cause added. Nevertheless, it is sometimes understood more broadly to include both those stipulations and promises made for a future day, and those made under a condition that is not pending in the future—and therefore do not suspend the obligation of the stipulation or promise, as was said in the cited disputation regarding a "pure" legacy. This is evident from the laws on novations and verbal obligations. In the cited disputation, we also said that when it is not certain that a legacy is non-pure, it should be considered pure; the same is to be affirmed regarding a stipulation and a promise. Read what was said there.

<margin>2</margin> When something is promised for a **certain day**—at least because it is certain that the day will come, even if it is unknown and uncertain *when* it will be—by that very fact an obligation arises from the stipulation or promise. The obligation passes to the heirs of the person to whom the promise was made, and against the heirs of the person who promised. In this, a stipulation or promise for a certain day differs greatly from a legacy for a certain day.

<margin>3</margin> For if a legatee dies before the person making the will, the legacy for a certain day expires, and the legatee does not transmit it to his heirs, as was shown in Disputation 205. However, the person to whom a promise is made, even if he departs this life before the promisor, transmits the obligation to his heirs so that the promised thing may be paid to them. Hence, if someone says, "I promise you one hundred on the day of my death," or "to be paid in ten or twenty years after my death," because that day is certain to come (even if it is uncertain when it will be), the promise is valid, even if the one to whom it was made...
