<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal obligations following a promise or contract, specifically focusing on when a debt becomes due if it is tied to an event like death or marriage. It explores the distinction between a "deadline" and a "condition" in legal agreements.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 284

...has been made, and [the recipient] should die before the promisor, the heirs of the promisor are still bound to pay it, either to the person to whom the promise was made or to that person's heirs. That is, if someone says, "I promise you a hundred on the day of your death, or ten years after your death," these sums are indeed owed to the heirs of the person to whom the promise was made. However, although an obligation arises from such promises as soon as they are made, it does not mean the promised thing must be paid immediately; rather, it must be paid on the day established in the promise.

Therefore, if the promised item is requested before that day, the promisor or their heirs have a defense <term>exceptio; a legal plea used to delay or defeat a claim</term> that the day destined for payment has not yet arrived. All these points are evident from the section "Every stipulation," at the verse "on a day," in the *Institutes* on verbal obligations <note>original: "Instit. de verb. oblig."</note>; from the law "to yield the day" in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. de verb. sign."</note>; from the law "claim for a certain sum," and the gloss there; from the *Institutes* on exceptions; from the single law in the *Code* titled "That actions begin from and against the heir" <note>original: "C. vt actiones ab hæredes & contra hæredem incipi"</note>; from the law "scrupulosam" in the *Code* on contracting a stipulation; from the section "after death" in the *Institutes* on useless stipulations; and from laws 12 and 14, title 11, of the fifth *Partida* <note>A famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>.

<margin>4</margin> Observe this: it would be far different if someone were to say, "I promise you a hundred *when* I die," compared to if they said, "I promise you a hundred *if* I die," or "if the sun rises six months from now." Although an obligation arises in the first case as soon as the promise is made (as just shown), it also arises in the second. This is because that future condition is determined to a single outcome <note>meaning it is an inevitable event</note>, and thus it does not suspend the promise or the obligation arising from it. This is why in both cases the promise is counted among the "pure" <term>puras; unconditional or straightforward</term> promises, using that term broadly to distinguish it from a promise made under a condition that is still pending in the future. Both types of promises are considered the same for this effect. Nevertheless, I say that while these two types of promises agree in this respect, they differ in another.

In the first case, the promised thing is not owed except on the day of the promisor's death, because the promise was truly made for that day. Therefore, if the action is brought before then, it is struck down by the defense that the fixed day for fulfillment has not yet arrived. In the second case, however, the promised thing is owed immediately and is to be paid immediately. No defense is available to strike down the legal action if the thing is requested, because it is not a promise made *for* the day of death or *for* the day the sun rises after six months, but rather a promise made *under the condition* that death will happen or the sun will rise. Since both are certain to happen, such conditions do not suspend the obligation. Instead, they are treated as if the promise were made under a "present or past" condition, which is necessary and does not suspend the obligation of the promise at all, or as if the thing had been promised entirely unconditionally. This is held in the law "if a ward," in the *Digest* on donations; the law "but if under it" on the recovery of undue payments; the law "when at present" and the two following in the *Digest*; the section on conditions in the *Institutes*; and laws 12 and 17, title 11, of the fifth *Partida*, as well as many other laws we cited in Dispute 206.

<column-break/>

However, Gregorius Lopez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>, commenting on the cited law 12 at the words "the day I shall die" <note>original: "el dia que yo finare"</note>, does not seem to have noticed this clear distinction between these two types of promises, nor does the gloss on the section "which under condition" seem to have noticed it.

<margin>5</margin> When something is promised on a day or at a time that is uncertain whether it will actually occur, then that day or time has the force of a "pending future condition." Consequently, it makes the stipulation or promise "conditional" in the strict and proper sense, as was said in Dispute 205 regarding legacies left for an uncertain day. Therefore, the discussion of such stipulations and promises belongs to the following dispute.

Examples include: "Do you promise me a hundred on the day you are created a bishop?" "On the day the ships arrive from India?" "When you reach puberty?" "On the day you contract a marriage?" and similar promises. Just as it is uncertain whether you will be made a bishop, whether ships will come from India, whether a child will reach puberty, or whether someone not yet married will ever marry, it is entirely uncertain whether the day or time in which these things might happen will ever come.

For this reason, such promises or stipulations are regarded the same whether they are made in the form of an "uncertain day" or under a "condition" in this other form: "Do you promise me a hundred *if* you are made a bishop?" "*if* the ships arrive from India?" "*if* you reach puberty?" etc. This is found in the *Digest* in the laws "he who promised" and "whatever."

An exception must be made to this entire rule when something is promised for an uncertain day, but that day was specified solely for the benefit of the person to whom it was promised, following what was said in Dispute 205 regarding similar legacies. For example, if someone promised a female cousin two hundred gold coins for the sole or primary reason that they be given when she marries, so that she might not waste them and be left without a dowry. Or when someone, on account of services rendered that were worth such a price (or a little less), promised someone four hundred on the day they contract marriage, and had not otherwise compensated the services provided. In that case, since it is not believable that the promisor intended for the services to go unpaid if the recipient did not marry, we must judge that the uncertain day was added only for the benefit of the recipient. Therefore, if the person to whom the promise was made for that reason dies, they certainly transmit what was promised to their heirs, and it must be paid to them immediately. Likewise, if it is certain that the person will not marry—either because they enter a religious order, take holy orders, are already old, are unfit for marriage for another reason, or because there is a certain and safe hope that they wish to maintain perpetual celibacy—the promised four hundred must be handed over to them, especially with the authority of a prelate. They must be handed over either by the person who promised them, by their heirs, or by whoever was charged with executing the promise in the event of a marriage.

<summary>This page discusses the legal distinction between promises tied to a specific future time (like death) and those tied to uncertain conditions (like marriage). It argues that if an event is certain to happen, the obligation is immediate, whereas truly uncertain events create conditional obligations that may pass to heirs under specific circumstances of fairness.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the legal analysis of when debts and obligations become due, moving from promises tied to death (discussed on page 87) to the technical differences between "certain days," "uncertain days," and specific calendar dates like the Kalends or feast days.</meta>

## Ludovicus Molina on Contracts
### Page 88

Because the promise we are discussing throughout this section, made for an uncertain day, does not take the form of a conditional promise so much as a promise "with a mode" <term>sub modo; a qualification added to a gift or contract that imposes a duty on the recipient without stopping the contract from taking effect immediately</term>, we have dealt with it extensively in Dispute 208. Read what was said there at length.

When something has been promised for a certain day in the manner explained above, an obligation arises from that very promise. It is a true debt, even if it is not to be paid immediately but at the time pre-fixed in the promise itself, as was also said above. From this it follows that if it is paid before the pre-fixed day, recovery of the payment <note>original: "repetitio"; the legal right to demand back money paid by mistake</note> will not be granted. However, if it were promised for an uncertain day, or otherwise under a condition pending in the future, and the condition had not been fulfilled, then because the condition was not yet met, it would simply not be a debt. Yet if the condition had been fulfilled, recovery would not be granted because it would then simply be a debt. All these points are found in the law *Sub ea conditione* and the law *Qui promisit* in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the Digest of Justinian</note> regarding the recovery of undue payments. We shall return to this subject in Dispute 567.

When a stipulation or promise is "pure"—meaning that neither a condition nor a specific time is added for when the thing should be paid—then it must be paid immediately. See the law *Eum qui calendis*, paragraph *Quotiens*, in the Digest, title "On Verbal Obligations," and the section "Every stipulation" in the *Institutes* under the same title. However, regarding obligations for "fixed money" <term>constituta pecunia; a formal promise to pay an existing debt</term>, something was said in Dispute 270: a space of ten days is granted for payment when a certain day has not been pre-fixed between the contracting parties, according to the law *Promissor*, paragraph 1, "On fixed money."

When it is established by the two laws cited first that payment must be made immediately, this should be understood morally—that is, with some tempering of the time. <margin>6</margin> This is because a creditor ought not to arrive immediately with a sack to receive the debt. † With these words, which I have just written, the law *Quod dicimus* in the Digest, "On payments," explains the word "immediately" as it applies to the matter we are discussing. Indeed, it is pleasing to transcribe that explanation word-for-word from that law. Hence, this is rightly left to the judgment of a judge, as per the law *Continuus*, paragraph *Cum ita*, in the Digest, "On verbal obligations," and Law 1, paragraph 2, Title 11 of the 5th *Partida*. The final paragraph of the *Institutes* on "Useless stipulations" also agrees. 

Furthermore, the time for payment must be judged by the nature of the thing promised: for example, if future fruits are promised, or if a house is promised to be built, or if something is to be paid in a distant place, or if something existing in a distant place is promised, and so on for other things. This is found in the law *Interdum*, and the law *Continuus*, paragraph *Cum ita* and following, in the Digest, "On verbal obligations," the section "Places" in the *Institutes* under the same title, and Law 2, paragraph *Si quis ita*, in the Digest regarding things promised in a certain place.

<margin>7</margin> However, when a stipulation or promise is for a "certain day" and there are many such days, and it is not expressed which of them is meant—such as when it is said, "I will pay on the Kalends," or "on the Ides," or "at Easter," or some such thing—it is understood to mean the next such day that occurs, such as the Kalends, Ides, or Easter coming up most soon. But if a contract is made on the day of the Kalends itself, in which it is said, "I will pay or do this on the Kalends," it is understood not to mean the Kalends on which the contract is made, but the next future Kalends. These points are found in the law *Eum qui calendis* at the beginning, in the Digest, "On verbal obligations," and Law 15, Title 11, of the 5th *Partida*.

If it is said, "I will pay you by such a day," for example, "by St. John's Day," the promisor can pay immediately if he wishes, and can compel the creditor to receive it. This is because that delay of time was established solely for the favor of the debtor. This is held in the law

<column-break/>

*Quod in diem* in the Digest, "On payments." However, when a day has been pre-fixed for the benefit of the creditor, the creditor cannot be compelled to receive the debt before that day, as held in the law *Si ita relictum*, paragraph *Pegasius*, in the Digest, "On legacies," Book 2, and other laws cited in the gloss on the law *Quod in diem* mentioned above. 

Furthermore, when it is said, "I will pay by such a day," the promisor is not compelled to pay on that very day, but on the following day; this is because that entire day ought to be granted to the discretion of the one paying, nor can it be certain that he failed to pay on that day until the whole day has passed. This is held in the section "Every stipulation" at the end, in the *Institutes*, "On verbal obligations." If, however, it is said, for example, "I will pay you *on* St. John's Day," then he can be compelled to pay on St. John's Day itself, because that form of words seems to signify that the matter must be paid before that day has passed. This is found in the law *Liber homo*, Book 2, paragraph *Decem hodie*, in the Digest, "On verbal obligations."

<margin>8</margin> When someone † has promised that he will give a certain thing to another "in such a year," or "each year" (understand the same for months or other periods of time), then it must be paid at the end of the year, according to the law *Qui hoc anno* in the Digest, "On verbal obligations," and other laws. But when he has promised it as a quantity, such as an annual alms of a hundred gold coins, they must be paid at the beginning of each year, as held in Law 1 of the Code, "When the day for a legacy yields," Law *Nec semel* in the same title of the Digest, and the law *In singulos* in the Digest regarding annual legacies. Accursius <note>A famous 13th-century legal glossator</note> affirms the same regarding the cited laws, and in the *Institutes* under "Verbal obligations," the section "But if so," gloss 1; and it is defined in Law 13, Title 11, of the 5th *Partida*. The matter is nevertheless controversial when standing on Common Law <term>ius commune; the shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</term> alone. Read what Gregorius Lopez <note>The primary commentator on the Spanish *Siete Partidas*</note> reports on this matter in the cited Law 15.

When someone has promised something under a certain penalty, or on a certain established day, or with no such term pre-fixed for fulfillment, look to the laws arranged in the cited Law 15 and following, and the laws that Gregorius Lopez cites there.

## DISPUTE 285.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 285

<margin>
A negative potestative condition <term>potestative; a condition whose fulfillment depends entirely on the will of one of the parties, such as "if you choose not to go to Rome"</term> and how the form of a promise is understood under it.
10. A condition added for the benefit of another is not considered fulfilled in contracts, though it is treated differently in last wills. Note and understand this as explained there.
11. A condition stating that someone who has never married should not marry in the future voids the contract to which it is attached.
</margin>

What a condition is, and its many types, was explained at length in Disputation 206. However, the following conclusions must be laid down.

<margin>
1
</margin>
**First conclusion.** Conditions that are not impossible, which concern the present or the past—or even the future if restricted to a single certain outcome—do not suspend gifts, stipulations, or promises when they are attached to them. Instead, if such conditions are actually true, the legal arrangements made under them are valid, even if the parties are unaware of the facts at the time. However, if the conditions are not true in reality, the arrangements made under them are void by that very fact. This conclusion is established from what was said in the preceding disputation and was shown at length in Disputation 206; for that reason, there is no need to dwell on it further.

<margin>
2
</margin>
**Second conclusion.** An impossible condition <note>original: "conditio impossibilis"</note> is **not** treated as if it were never added in gifts, stipulations, or promises, provided they are irrevocable. On the contrary, if the conditions cannot be met, then the irrevocable stipulations, gifts, and promises are invalid. This is proven in the Institutes <note>original: "Instit. de inutilib. stipul."; a section of the primary Roman law textbook regarding useless or void verbal contracts</note> and the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the standard abbreviation for the Digest of Justinian, the massive collection of Roman legal opinions</note>. The law states that our conclusion applies not only to formal stipulations but also to other contracts such as sales, leases, etc. Regarding what is added at the end of that same law—namely, that a stipulation is valid under the condition "if you do not touch the sky with your finger"—this does not contradict the preceding doctrine, nor does it limit it. This is because such a condition is not truly "impossible" in a legal sense, but rather "necessary" <note>because it is a certainty that a human will not touch the sky, the condition is treated as a settled fact</note>. This is supported by Accursius, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors, which is followed by Emmanuel Acosta and Molina.

<margin>
3
</margin>
Molina <note>Luis de Molina, the 16th-century author of this work</note> rightly observes that in the case of *mayorazgos* <term>majoratus; an entailed estate that passes to a single heir and cannot be sold or divided</term> established by an irrevocable gift or contract, one must consider whether the thing added is truly a "condition" or rather a "mode" <term>modus; a qualification or duty attached to a gift that does not stop the gift from taking effect immediately</term>, as is often the case. If it is a mode, it does not void the establishment of the estate, nor is there a legal obligation to fulfill that mode, as was stated in Disputation 208.

<margin>
4
</margin>
In the conclusion above, we said "provided they are irrevocable." This is because if an impossible condition is added to a "gift in view of death" <note>original: "donationi causa mortis"; a gift given by someone who believes they are dying, which can be taken back if they survive</note>, it is treated as if it were never added. This is the same way impossible conditions are treated in other "last wills" <note>wills and testaments</note>. Consequently, such a gift is valid, as noted in Disputation 209, because it is revocable and therefore counted alongside last wills for that purpose. This is proven by the law

<column-break/>

concerning conditions in the Digest. It is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Emmanuel Acosta, Antonio Gómez, and Molina. Molina says the same applies to other revocable gifts, and even to *mayorazgos* established through such revocable gifts or contracts. However, since these are not technically "last wills" (unlike a deathbed gift), and an impossible condition by its very nature voids the arrangement under natural law, the fact that it does **not** void a last will is a specific rule of human (civil) law. We showed both of these points in Disputation 208. Regarding the idea that an impossible condition voids a contract from its beginning and creation, rather than just its final outcome: I am not entirely certain of this opinion. Unless you argue that because last wills are revocable and only confirmed by the death of the person making them, they were granted this special privilege; and since revocable contracts share those two traits, the same privilege should rightly be extended to them.

<margin>
5
</margin>
**Third conclusion.** If a gift, stipulation, or promise is made under a future condition that is not yet determined, then the obligation and the debt are indeed suspended in reality. They do not arise until the condition is fulfilled, and only if it is fulfilled. Nevertheless, from the moment of such a promise, there arises a "hope" <term>spes; a legal expectation of a future right</term> of a future debt, and thus a "qualified" obligation. If the person to whom the promise was made dies before the condition is met, they pass this hope or qualified debt to their heirs. In this regard, a conditional gift or promise differs greatly from a legacy <term>legatum; a specific item left to someone in a will</term>. A person receiving a legacy does not pass the "hope" of that legacy to their heirs if they die before the condition is met; instead, the legacy expires entirely. This is stated in Disputations 205 and 206 and is proven by Covarruvias. These points are explicitly found in the Institutes and are accepted by everyone without controversy.

Although the doctors agree that a stipulation, promise, or contract made under a condition passes to and against the heirs of the promisor while the condition is pending, and although they agree that if the condition is "casual" <note>dependent on chance</note> or "mixed" <note>dependent on both chance and will</note>, the right to fulfill it passes to the heirs, there is

<margin>
6
</margin>
nonetheless a great debate regarding "potestative" conditions. If the condition is not personal (meaning it doesn't strictly adhere to one specific person's actions), the debate is whether the right to fulfill that condition passes to the

<meta>catchword: heirs- (haere-)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal conditions within contracts and gifts, specifically focusing on whether these conditions and obligations pass to heirs if the original parties die before fulfillment.</meta>

## Louis Molina / On Contracts

The heirs of the person who was bound to fulfill a condition should be considered, as if it were sufficient for the condition to be fulfilled by the heirs, or even that it could be fulfilled for the heirs of the person to whom it was owed. Bartolus and the common opinion, which Covarruvias reports in *Practical Questions*, chapter 38, hold that the right to fulfill such a proactive condition does not pass to the heirs of the person bound to it, nor is it sufficient if it is fulfilled for the heirs of the person to whom it was owed. Instead, they believe that the moment either party dies, the condition is considered to have failed, and therefore the contract or promise made under that condition vanishes. However, I am much more in agreement with Covarruvias in the same place, and the two glosses <note>interpretive comments by medieval legal scholars</note> he cites: the right to fulfill that condition both passes to the heirs of the person who owed it, and it is sufficient if it is fulfilled for the heirs of the person to whom it was owed. For equity demands this, and natural reason itself teaches it. Furthermore, besides other laws cited by Covarruvias, this is proven by Law 2 of the Code *on agreements between buyer and seller*, which agrees with Law 42, Title 5, Part 5. There, the right to fulfill a <term>potestative condition; a condition within the power of a person to fulfill</term> passes to the heirs of the seller and can be fulfilled for the heirs of the buyer. And although it was specifically provided there that the seller's heirs could fulfill that condition, the second gloss there says the same holds true even if no such provision was made. Moreover, nothing was provided there regarding the buyer's heirs. The same is proven by analogy in the Law *Veteris* of the Code *on contracting stipulations*, which contains these words:

> *Settling the disputes of the ancient law, we generally decree that every stipulation—whether it consists in giving, in doing, or is mixed of both—shall be transmitted both to heirs and against heirs, whether specific mention of heirs is made or not. For why should that which is just between the principal parties not be transmitted to and against their heirs?* <note>original: "Veteris iuris altercationes decidentes... trasmitti, siue specialis hæredum fiat mentio, siue non."</note>

And thus, such stipulations are regarded as if they were conceived only "in giving," since heirs can just as well fulfill the "doing." That subtle and unnecessary scrupulousness is exploded, through which people used to think it was impossible for an act imposed on one person to be fulfilled by another. And why, since the nature of all men is nearly similar, can they not all fulfill the same acts, or at least a little more or less, so that human intentions do not fail due to such technicalities? Thus far the law. Read in Covarruvias at the cited place a long dispute on this matter, and how he addresses the laws relied upon by Bartolus and others.

<margin>7</margin>
At the same time, observe that conditions—whether they are proactive, casual <note>dependent on chance</note>, or mixed—must always be fulfilled according to the expressed form, whether they are fulfilled by those they were enjoined upon, or by their heirs, or by others. It is not enough if they are fulfilled in an "equivalent" manner <note>original: "æquipollenter"</note>, as proven by the laws *Qui hæredi* and *Mæuius* in the Digest *on conditions and demonstrations*, and affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion, which Covarruvias refers to and follows.

<margin>8</margin>
**Fourth conclusion.** A gift, stipulation, or promise—by the fact that they were made under a condition pending in the future and the condition is not yet fulfilled—cannot be revoked or have a burden or restriction added to them any more than if they had been made unconditionally, according to what was said in Disputation 265. So says Silvester under the word "gift," question 15, number 19, with no one disagreeing; it is also gathered from the law *Potior* in the Digest *on those who are prior in pledge*. It can also be confirmed

<column-break/>

because from such stipulations and promises made under condition, by the very fact that they have been accepted and are perfect in their own order and grade, there arises an obligation and "debt in hope" <term>debitum in spe; a legal expectation of a future right</term> no less than a "debt in fact" arises from unconditional ones. Nor is the promisor any less bound by a promise made under condition, in the event that the condition is fulfilled, than if it were made unconditionally. Therefore, by the very fact that the stipulation or promise made under condition is perfect in its own order and grade, neither a burden nor a limitation can be placed upon it.

<margin>9</margin>
When a stipulation or promise is made under a negative potestative condition <note>a requirement that someone *not* do something</note> which would only be considered fulfilled upon the death of the person to whom the promise was made—such as "I promise you a hundred if you do not climb the Capitol" or "if you remain a widow"—the Institutes *on verbal obligations* state that this is the same as if the promise were made in this form: "I promise you a hundred when you die." Here the gloss rightly affirms that these promises are not similar in all respects. For this second one is a "promise for a certain day," as seen in the preceding disputation; but the first is purely conditional, and would cease to have force if the person climbed the Capitol or entered a marriage. However, it is similar to the second insofar as the promised thing would not be simply owed unless the condition were kept until the time of death. Furthermore, Emmanuel Acosta says that in stipulations, promises, and contracts made under such negative conditions, it is commonly accepted that the **Mucian Caution** <term>cautio Mutiana; a legal bond where a beneficiary receives their inheritance immediately by promising to return it if they break a negative condition, such as remarrying</term> does not apply, unlike in last wills made under the same conditions, as shown in Disputation 209. Molina also affirms this with Bartolus and the common opinion. The same Mucian Caution does apply in a "gift in anticipation of death" <term>donatio causa mortis</term> made under the same potestative condition, as is expressly held in the Novels *on marriage*. This was asserted by Emmanuel Acosta, Antonio Gomez, Molina, and many others they cite. This clearly confirms that a gift in anticipation of death follows the rule of last wills (even regarding impossible conditions), rather than the rules of stipulations, promises, and other contracts. Molina thinks the Mucian Caution also applies in other revocable gifts because they follow the rule of last wills in the matters discussed.

<margin>10</margin>
This must be added: Although in last wills, if something is left under a condition that benefits another person, and that person prevents the condition from being fulfilled, the condition is held as fulfilled <note>original: "habeatur talis conditio pro impleta"</note> and the legacy is valid (as shown with examples in Disputation 206); however, in stipulations, promises, and contracts, the matter is the opposite. Namely, the promise or contract is invalid if the condition is not fulfilled, even for that reason. So affirms the common opinion of the doctors, which according to Gregory...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of conditions in contracts and estates, moving from the rights of heirs to the specific nature of "modes" or purposes attached to gifts and inheritances.</meta>

Second Treatise, Dispute 286.

Gregorio Lopez <note>original: "Greg. Lopez"</note> on Book 14, Title 4, Part 7, and Emmanuel Acosta <note>original: "Emman. Acost."</note> at the section "if anyone by judgment," Limitation 3, report and follow the view of Luis de Molina <note>original: "Molina"</note>, Book 2, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 13, number 16. However, regarding <term>entailed estates; an inheritance (maioratus) that must stay within a family line</term> established through an irrevocable contract, he rightly says that one must observe whether what was arranged as a condition is truly a "condition" or rather a "mode." For if it is a "mode" <note>a requirement or purpose attached to a gift, rather than a strict 'if-then' condition</note>, and the successor to the estate was not the one responsible for failing to fulfill it, he ought not be deprived of the estate for that reason.

<margin>I</margin>
Furthermore, he considers it right to limit the provided rule when there are indications that the intent of the founder of the estate was that the person called to inherit should not be excluded if the condition went unfulfilled through no fault of their own. For example, if he called someone to the estate under the condition that they marry a certain woman, and it was not the heir's fault—perhaps he would have gladly married her, but it was prevented by her, or by a third party, or by the course of nature because she died—it is certainly not to be believed that the founder wished him to be excluded from the estate in such an event. This is especially true since the founder usually calls someone to the estate based on their closeness in kinship; it is not believable that he wished to exclude the closer relative in favor of a more distant one when the failure was without any fault. Read Molina in the cited place, who pursues this matter learnedly.

<margin>II</margin>
Finally, it must be added that a condition stating that someone who has never married should not take a spouse in the future—which, when added to last wills, is held as if it were not written and thus does not spoil the will, as said in dispute 207—if it is added to a formal promise or contract, it is *not* held as if it were not written. Rather, it spoils the contract unless such a condition is fulfilled, as is clear from what has been said so far. For it is counted among those conditions that are "impossible by law," which spoil promises and contracts. However, what was said in that same dispute regarding things common to donations, promises, and other contracts as well as last wills, need not be repeated here. At the same time, the things added in dispute 208 should be selected, as a fuller understanding of what has been said depends on them.

### On donation with a requirement. And whether things
### given to induce a woman to a
### wicked consent, or for other
### ends, are subject to restitution if the
### end does not follow. And on
### alms and other donations given for
### false reasons, and in which a
### false description occurs.

->DISPUTE 286.<-
->SUMMARY.<-

1. Things given with the intent of drawing someone to a certain end cannot be reclaimed, even if that end is not achieved.

<column-break/>

Explain, however, and understand, as stated there.

Regarding "donation under a mode" <note>donatio sub modo; a gift given for a specific purpose</note>, much was said in dispute 208, explaining last wills made under such requirements. Now, however, only what remains in the title we proposed needs to be explained, as these are certain examples we reserved from the cited dispute, to be more conveniently explained in this place.

<margin>1</margin>
Briefly, it must be said that things given to women with a certain agreement—even if they would not have been given if the donor knew the woman could not be swayed that way, and even if the woman knows they are sent with that wicked intent and accepts them with the intent of not consenting—as well as things given with the intent of enticing someone to change their mind or something similar—even if they would not have been given if the donor knew the recipient could not be led to that end—are not subject to <term>restitution; the legal obligation to return a gift</term>, even if the end for which they are given does not follow. This is true when they were not given under a strict condition or contract for that end, but only with the hope and intent of leading the recipient to that end, as usually happens. This is clearly gathered from the Law "on reclaiming" in the Code *on conditions for a cause* <note>original Latin reference: "l. si repetendi. C. de condit. ob causam."</note>. There, when someone had given gifts to another's wife with the intent of swaying her to go away with him, and he did not achieve that end and wished to reclaim the gifts, he is barred from reclaiming them because he did not express that he was giving them under the condition of that goal. In that place, observe that when the recipient has accepted the thing in good faith and consented, not believing it was given to her under the condition of that end, she is held to no restitution when she has not been <term>enriched; made wealthier (locupletior) by the gift</term> by it; because she is not bound either by the thing received or by any injustice in accepting it.

<margin>2</margin>
Observe then, that if a man who sent gifts to a woman for a wicked purpose sees himself frustrated in his goal and asserts that he only sent those gifts under the condition of her "wicked consent," this is not a sufficient reason for the woman to be bound to return them, even what she has not yet consumed or by which she has been enriched. The reason is that such donations are not customarily made with that formal legal intent, and the woman can presume that he is lying out of a desire for revenge because she refused to consent, asserting this to pressure her into consenting just to free herself from the burden of returning the gifts. This is further supported by the cited law, which denies the right to reclaim to a donor asserting he gave under a "tacit condition," because such a thing is not to be presumed when he did not express it at the time of the donation. Read regarding all these matters what we say at the end of dispute 170.

In dispute 209 and the two following, we spoke at length about alms given because of feigned poverty or feigned holiness, and about other donations, particularly those conferred by kings because of services or other false reasons, and to what extent all these are subject to restitution. And regarding donations in which a "false description" <note>falsa demonstratio; providing an incorrect reason or description for a gift</note> occurs. We explained all these together with last wills made in a similar way; therefore, there will be no need to repeat them.

<summary>This page discusses the legal distinction between a "condition" and a "mode" in inheritance and gifts, ruling that heirs should not lose their estates for failing to meet requirements beyond their control, and that gifts given for seduction or specific intents cannot generally be reclaimed if the goal fails.</summary>

### On gifts made in anticipation of death.

-> DISPUTATION 278 <-

-> *S U M M A R Y* <-

1. *What a gift made in anticipation of death is.*
2. *When a thing given in anticipation of death is delivered, ownership is revocable in as many ways as the gift itself can be revoked.*
3. *How ownership of the thing given is understood to remain with the recipient.*
4. *A gift made in anticipation of death, followed by delivery, is a suitable title for transferring ownership, albeit revocably.*
5. *A gift made in anticipation of death can even be made between absent parties via letter or messenger, but the recipient's acceptance is required.*
6. *A gift made in anticipation of death that is not accepted, if it possesses the required solemnity of a codicil or a will, would be valid as a legacy.*
7. *A gift made in anticipation of death is judged "perfected" in two ways.*
8. *A gift made in anticipation of death can be made under two methods or conditions.*
9. *What constitutes an absolute gift under the condition of death.*
10. *A gift made in anticipation of death is considered revoked if the recipient dies before the donor.*
11. *The donor may revoke the gift at any time before their death.*
12. *If a gift between the living is revoked for ingratitude, the fruits (profits) gathered before the legal contest are not reclaimed.*
14. *When a gift made in anticipation of death is not considered revoked.*
15. *When a gift made in anticipation of death transitions into a gift between the living.*
16. *Where in a legal document a promise or clause of "non-revocation" can be added to make the gift irrevocable.*
17. *Cases where an oath added to the gift does not make it irrevocable.*
18. *Cases where a gift confirmed by oath does not transition into a gift between the living, and when it does; also number 19.*
*And regarding Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitan."</note>, number 19.*

Gifts in general (as held in the *Institutes* <note>original: "Instit. de don. §. 1."; a fundamental textbook of Roman law</note>) are divided into what are called gifts "between the living" <term>inter vivos; gifts given during one's lifetime without the expectation of imminent death</term> and gifts "on account of death" <term>donatio causa mortis; a gift made by someone who believes they are about to die</term>. Having explained the difference between the two, and joining those things which have been said about gifts so far with what will be said in the following pages, the nature of gifts between the living will be sufficiently clear; therefore, this section will deal solely with gifts made in anticipation of death.

1. A † gift in anticipation of death occurs when something is delivered or promised for free, so that—provided the donor's death follows (whether death in a general sense or specifically from a current danger) before the recipient's

<column-break/>

death—the thing becomes the recipient’s irrevocably. This is because the donor retains a "walking" <note>original: "ambulatoria"; meaning changeable or fluid</note> power to revoke the gift right up until the moment of their death. For this reason, in Law 1 and the Law of the Senate in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. de mortis causa donationib."; the Digest was the primary collection of Roman legal opinions</note> and the *Institutes* at the beginning of the section on gifts, this distinction is established: in a gift made in anticipation of death, the donor prefers to have the thing himself rather than the recipient having it, but he prefers the recipient to have it rather than his own heir. In a gift between the living, however, the donor prefers the recipient to have the thing rather than himself.

In the explanation proposed, it was first said, "when something is given for free, etc." Because a gift in anticipation of death is truly a gift, it must be made freely, and it must take on the character of such a gift according to what was discussed in Disputation 273.

2. It was added: "is delivered or promised." Just as other gifts sometimes begin from a promise alone and sometimes from physical delivery, so it is with gifts made in anticipation of death. When the delivery <term>traditio; the physical handing over of property</term> of the gifted item occurs, the recipient acquires <term>dominium; legal ownership or lordship over a thing</term> of the gifted item. However, when † a thing is delivered as a gift in anticipation of death, the recipient acquires a "revocable ownership" in as many ways as the gift itself can be revoked, as will be explained below. This is affirmed in Law 2 and Law "if a thing in anticipation of death" <note>original: "l. si mortis causa res"</note> and the Glosses there in the *Digest*. This is also asserted by Covarrubias <note>original: "Cou. in rub. de test. p. 3. nu. 16."</note>, Antonio Gomez, and Molina in Book 1 of *On Primogeniture*.

3. When you hear that the recipient acquires "ownership" of the thing given in anticipation of death upon delivery, understand this: if the delivery is made so that it becomes the recipient's *immediately*, then they hold ownership, as stated expressly in the laws cited above. This is always presumed unless otherwise stated. But † when a thing is delivered with the express statement that it should only belong to the recipient *when* the donor's death follows, then the ownership of the thing so delivered remains with the donor until his death.

<margin>Objection</margin>
What if you object to this doctrine, citing the principle <note>original: "ff. de acq. rerum dom."</note> that ownership does not pass to a recipient by mere delivery unless a "title" and a suitable "cause" for acquiring it precede it?

<margin>Refutation</margin>
4. It must be said that † the gift in anticipation of death itself, followed by delivery, is a "suitable title" for transferring ownership—though revocably. This is similar to when a husband delivers dowry items before a marriage with the agreement that they become his immediately; it is a suitable title for him to acquire ownership, even though he loses it if the marriage does not actually take place.

5. When † a gift in anticipation of death begins with a promise and no delivery follows, it used to be that this could only be done between parties who were both present and through a formal verbal contract <term>stipulatio; a strict formal agreement in Roman law</term>, so that upon the donor's death, a legal action could be taken to obtain the thing. This was the common opinion. Today, however, just as a gift 

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "donatio" as noted by the catchword "natio" for the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page defines "donatio causa mortis" (gifts made in anticipation of death) and explains how ownership is transferred to the recipient, noting that such ownership remains revocable until the donor's death. It distinguishes these gifts from standard lifetime gifts by the donor's intent to prioritize their own use of the item until death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "gifts made in anticipation of death" (donatio causa mortis), specifically focusing on how they are perfected, how they can be revoked, and how they differ from standard gifts between the living.</meta>

## Treatise II, Disputation 287

A gift between the living <note>Latin: *donatio inter vivos*</note> can be validly made by a bare pact <term>bare pact (pactum nudum): a simple agreement that might not meet all the formal requirements of a contract but is still recognized under certain legal conditions</term>, not only between those present—provided the recipient <note>Latin: *donatarius*</note> accepts it, at least tacitly by remaining silent—but even between those who are absent, via a letter or a messenger appointed for that purpose. It is valid once accepted, even by persons who are not the intended recipient, provided they are among those legally designated for that role, according to what was extensively discussed in Disputation 264, together with what was explained in Disputations 254, 255, and 263. In the same way, a gift made in anticipation of death <note>Latin: *donatio causa mortis*</note> can be made in a similar manner and will gain legal force if it is confirmed by the death of the donor. This is the view held by the Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on Roman law</note> on the law *When a father*, section *To Menius* in the Digest <note>The *Digest* (ff.) is a major part of the Body of Civil Law</note>, book 2 on legacies, and the final Gloss on law 2 in the Code <note>The *Codex* (C.) is another part of the Body of Civil Law</note> regarding the law of dowries. This is also the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> and the common consensus, which Antonio Gómez (number 16) and Covarrubias (number 14) cite and follow. This remains true even if it is done in a will or a codicil <term>codicil: a legal document used to make additions or changes to an existing will</term> using any of the aforementioned methods; for pacts and contracts can be validly made within a will or codicil, as Covarrubias affirms (number 17) along with Bartolus and the common opinion of the Doctors of Law.

<margin>6</margin> However, if a gift in anticipation of death were made—whether in a will, a codicil, a letter, or even orally—without anyone accepting it, it would not hold the legal status of a contract or even a bare pact. In that case, if the formal presence of witnesses (which will be discussed below) was observed, the arrangement would still be valid—not as a gift in anticipation of death, but as a legacy or (which is the same thing) as a specific trust <term>fideicommissum: a request in a will for an heir to transfer specific property to someone else</term>. This follows the law *A soldier to his sister*, at the beginning, joined with the first Gloss, and the law *When a father*, section *Of the gift* in the Digest, book 2 on legacies, and the law *If a gift* in the Code on gifts. Antonio Gómez agrees with this (number 18, at the end), as does Covarrubias in his section on wills (part 3, number 17). It is also affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the Doctors, which Julio Claro (question 5, number 18) refers to and follows. Nevertheless, he rightly judges that this must be limited to those who are legally capable of making a will. For since it then has the nature of a legacy rather than a gift in anticipation of death, it will certainly be invalid if made by someone who cannot make a will, even if they were capable of making a gift in anticipation of death (as will soon be said regarding a son under his father's authority).

In that same explanation of gifts in anticipation of death, we added those words: "so that by the death of the donor—either absolutely, or by that specific death which is feared in the immediate future—the gift is made, and the property becomes irrevocably the recipient's, provided it follows before the death of the recipient." To understand these words, observe: as Molina <note>Luis de Molina, the Jesuit author of this work</note> in Book 1 on Primogeniture (chapter 12, number 15) rightly noted—along with the first Gloss on the law *It does not seem* in the Digest on gifts in anticipation of death, which the doctors commonly follow—

<margin>7</margin> † a gift in anticipation of death can be considered "perfected" <term>perfected: a legal term meaning the act is fully completed and legally binding</term> in two ways. First, so that it gains the character of a gift in anticipation of death. It achieves this perfection the moment it is fully executed, before the donor's death follows. This perfection is sufficient for the recipient to obtain not only a right to the item given but even ownership, if the donor delivers the item to them, as shown above. However, they obtain both of these revocably, so long as the gift remains in place and the donor’s death has not yet occurred. In the second way, a gift in anticipation of death can be considered perfected so that it can no longer be revoked. It does not achieve this perfection unless the donor's death occurs while the gift is still in effect. Regarding this second type of perfection,

<column-break/>

the law *No, if not* in the Digest on gifts in anticipation of death states: "A gift made in anticipation of death does not seem perfected until death follows." Understand this to mean the death of the donor.

<margin>8</margin> Next, observe that a gift † in anticipation of death can be made in two modes. One is under a condition, specifically if the death that is immediately feared should follow. In this case, if the donor escapes that immediate danger or fear of death—perhaps because they decided not to undertake a dangerous task—the gift is considered revoked immediately. This is how it is usually done by one suffering from a disease from which they fear they might die, making a gift in anticipation of death. Likewise by someone who, either heading into war, or undertaking a dangerous or long sea voyage or pilgrimage, makes such a gift; and in other similar events explained in laws 3, 4, 5, and 6 of the Digest on gifts in anticipation of death. Indeed, they are considered to give in this way unless they state otherwise, as is clear from laws 2 and 3, and the section *If a thing in anticipation of death*, and the section *The Senate*, under *In anticipation of death* in the Digest. Also in the Institutes <note>The *Institutiones* (Inst.), an introductory legal textbook by Emperor Justinian</note> on gifts, at the beginning; and the law *Not every* at the beginning of the Digest; and the last law of title 4, part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>. Covarrubias (number 23), Antonio Gómez (volume 2, chapter 4, number 19), and the common opinion they cite all agree.

<margin>9</margin> In the second † mode, a gift in anticipation of death is made under the condition of the donor’s death in an absolute sense. Such a gift is considered to be one made by someone who, moved by no immediate danger or fear of death, nonetheless gives in anticipation of death. It is also of this type when someone, even if moved by immediate danger, sufficiently expresses that they are giving in anticipation of any death, whether near or distant. This is held in laws 2 and *The Senate* in the Digest on gifts in anticipation of death.

<margin>10</margin> Thirdly, † observe that a gift in anticipation of death is considered revoked by the very fact that the recipient dies before the donor, as held in the law *Not every* in the Digest, and the law *If a thing in anticipation of death* at the end, and the section *The Senate* near the end. This also appears in the Institutes and the last law of title 3, part 5. In this respect, a gift in anticipation of death is similar to a legacy, which is rendered void by the very fact that the legatee <term>legatee: the person receiving a legacy or inheritance</term> dies before the testator <term>testator: the person who made the will</term>, as was said in its proper place. From all these points, you will now easily understand those words added in the explanation of the gift in anticipation of death, which gave occasion for all that has been said.

<margin>11</margin> Finally, in that same explanation, we added: "with the † donor's ambulatory <note>original: *deambulatoria*</note> power to revoke that gift entirely until the moment of their death." For, just as in other final wills it is always within the testator's power to revoke them while they are still alive, so too it is always within the power of a donor in anticipation of death to revoke the gift while they live (according to the law *Who, in anticipation of death* in the Digest and the last law of title 4, part 5). This is true, as Oldradus and others affirm, and as Gama (decision 258, number 2) confirms, even if the gift was made by two people; for any one of them can revoke it, even if the other has already died. In this, too, a gift in anticipation of death matches legacies, and for that reason, it is numbered among final wills in its own way, as it has more in common with legacies than with gifts between the living. This is stated in the Institutes at the cited location, and in the law of Marcellus, section *Paulus* in the Digest. Alvaro Valasco (consultation 61, number 7) says that when a gift...

Read, among others, Molina, book 4 on primogeniture <note>The right of the firstborn to inherit the entire estate</note>, chapter 11, from number 1 to 22.

Furthermore, in the explanation of the gift in anticipation of death, it was said that it is made with the power of revoking the same gift entirely. For although the delivery of the gifted thing had been made, and the recipient had acquired ownership of that thing according to what was said above, nevertheless, by the very fact that the gift is revoked—either because of a change of heart or for any other reason explained—the gifted thing must be restored. It must be returned not only with all its fruits currently attached to it, but also with all those gathered from it, and a valuation of those consumed, from the day on which the gift and delivery of that thing were made. So says the law *cum quis* in the Digest, "regarding the reason given when the cause does not follow," of which these are the words:
> *When someone has made a gift in anticipation of death, and the donor has recovered, he may sue for the fruits of the gifted things as well, and the offspring, and he can seek back whatever has been added to the gifted thing.* <note>original: "Cum quis mortis causa donationem fecisset, cum conualuisset donator, condicit fructus quoque donatarum rerum, & partus, & quod accreuit rei donate, repetere potest."</note>
And the law *videamus*, 2, the section "and the same is," joined with the preceding

<column-break/>

words in the Digest regarding interest; and other laws agree, and Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a primary authority on Roman law</note> affirms this as the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez (volume 2, Various Resolutions, chapter 4, number 21) and Aries Pinel (law 2, part 2, number 11) follow. The reason is that both the thing itself and its fruits are given under the condition that the gift is confirmed by the donor's death. Therefore, by the very fact that it is not confirmed but revoked, the thing must be restored with all the fruits gathered from it; and the recipient is to blame if he consumed any. If, however, the donor had expressed in some words that it was not his intention to claim back the gathered fruits, then it would be enough to restore the thing with the fruits still attached to it. For example, if the donor had said: "Use this estate of mine for your support, and I give it to you after my death."

This is because the gift was absolute, and the gifted thing is only claimed back as a penalty. Antonio Gómez (at the cited number 21) thinks the same should apply if a gift is revoked due to the birth of children (according to what was said in Disputations 282 and 283): namely, that it is not revoked regarding fruits gathered before such a birth. This is because the gift was absolute, even though by legal provision it is revoked by the birth of children. I consider this opinion to be certain regarding fruits gathered and consumed in good faith, from which the recipient has not been made wealthier. Regarding the remaining fruits, although it seems probable to me, it is not without difficulty. Firstly, because the revocation of that gift is based on the presumed will of the donor—who is not considered to wish to give in the event that children are born—and simultaneously on legal provision, as explained in Disputation 281; and thus it seems to be made under a condition pending in the future: "if children are not born." Secondly, because that gift, even regarding the fruits, can be "inofficious" <term>inofficious (inofficio): a legal term for a gift or will that unfairly excludes natural heirs, like children</term> to children born later; and insofar as it was inofficious to them, they seem to have the right to revoke it, even regarding gathered fruits, if they exist or if the recipient was made wealthier by them.

14 When someone gives in anticipation of death in such a way that the thing would be returned in no other event except if the donor changed his mind and revoked the gift by his own will, then it would not be considered revoked by recovery from illness, or escape from danger, nor if the recipient died before the donor. Likewise, when he gives in such a way that it could be revoked in no other event except if the recipient died before the donor; then it could not be revoked by the donor's change of heart, nor by recovery from illness or danger. Likewise, when he gives in such a way that the thing would be restored in no other event than if the donor escaped from that illness or danger, then it cannot be revoked by a change of heart, nor by the death of the recipient before the donor. This is found in the law *senatus*, the section "in anticipation of death," and the law *si alienam*, the section "Marcellus," in the Digest regarding gifts in anticipation of death; Covarrubias agrees in his chapter on testaments, part 3, number 23 at the end, and part 2, number 1 at the end, and 12 and 13.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 287

...can never be revoked, or if the donor promises that they will never revoke it, then it passes into a **gift between the living** <term>donatio inter vivos: a legal gift made during the donor's lifetime that is generally irrevocable</term> and is rendered irrevocable. This is expressly held in the law *where it is so given* <note>original Latin: "l. vbi ita donatur"</note>; it is further agreed upon in the law *if another's*, in the section *Marcellus* at the end, and the law *the senate*, in the section *by reason of death* at the end, in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de mortis causa dona." referring to the Pandects of Roman Law</note> regarding gifts in anticipation of death. Against a commonly rejected gloss <note>An explanatory note in a legal margin</note> on the law *where it is so given*, this is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the scholars, which they report and follow: Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 22; Molina in book 4 of *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, numbers 40 and 45; Julius Clarus in the section on *gifts*, question 4, last number; and Covarrubias in the commentary on testaments, part 2, number 11. As held in the cited law *where it is so given*, in that event, the mention of "death" signifies the impulsive cause for giving—that is, death is the reason—or that the execution of the gift is suspended until the donor's death, so that the recipient only begins to possess the gifted item from the time of the donor's death. This is preferred over it being a **gift in anticipation of death** <term>donatio causa mortis: a gift made in expectation of approaching death, which can usually be revoked if the donor survives</term>, as if the donor did not intend the gift to be firm and irrevocable unless their death followed before revocation. Therefore, from a favorable interpretation of the law—by which it must be believed that the donor did not intend their act to be void and useless—such a gift must be understood in this way: it should be said that it is not a gift in anticipation of death (since that would be repugnant to its added substance), but is a gift between the living.

Antonio Gómez in the place cited; Covarrubias in the section on testaments, part 2, numbers 13 and 14, with the common opinion of the scholars, which they report and rightly subjoin:

16. A promise not to revoke that gift—which, viewed in itself, clearly sounds like a gift in anticipation of death—can be added either in that part of the legal instrument where the gift itself is made (that is, in the "dispositive" words of the instrument in which the substance of the contract is contained), or afterwards in the part of the instrument where the execution and confirmation of the contract are contained. If it is placed in that first part of the instrument, they say it passes into a gift between the living, according to what has been said so far. If, however, it is placed in the latter part, they judge that it does not pass into a gift between the living but remains a gift in anticipation of death, as if that promise should be considered as if it had not been added. This is because things added in the "execution" <note>The concluding or formulaic part of a legal document</note> do not increase the disposition, as held in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of Canon Law</note> 1, regarding prebends. Furthermore, and most importantly, it is believed that such words were added rather by the will and custom of the **notaries** <note>original: "tabellionum"</note> than by the pleasure and consent of the contracting parties; indeed, it should not be thought that the parties intended to contradict the main disposition in the execution phase. Molina, in book 4 on primogeniture, chapter 2, number 46, dissents from this doctrine. However, what has been said pleases us. Yet we must admit that if it were clear that the aforementioned clause in the execution was added from the mind of the donor, it would be sufficient to make the gift in anticipation of death pass into a gift between the living. For as Molina rightly affirms, the cited *Clementine* must be understood as referring to words placed incidentally in the execution, which do not so manifestly restrict, interpret, or increase the disposition.

By the best law, however, Covarrubias judges that the preceding doctrine should be limited, unless that promise placed in the

<column-break/>

execution was confirmed by an **oath**. Since it is just, and it should not be presumed to have been added rashly, nor is it usually or possibly added except by the consent and will of the contracting parties, then it should be judged that such a promise emanated from the donor, and therefore they caused the prior gift to transition into a gift between the living.

17. When someone has not only promised not to revoke a gift made in the form of a gift in anticipation of death, but has also confirmed this by an oath, it should be said all the more that a gift of this kind passes into a gift between the living, as Covarrubias affirms from the cited number 11 with the common opinion of the scholars, and Molina affirms above at number 46. At the end of number 14, however, Covarrubias rightly adds: if someone were to give in anticipation of death and confirm that gift with an oath, only affirming under oath that they *wish to give in this way*, then it remains within their power to revoke the gift, and a gift of this kind does not pass into a gift between the living. Primarily, this is because such an oath would be "assertory" rather than "confirmatory." Secondly, because an oath is understood according to the nature of the act upon which it falls, and that gift is revocable by its very nature. These points agree with what we said in Disputation 155, in the response to the fourth point, concerning a will confirmed in a similar way by an oath.

Molina, at the cited number 46 and the following, concedes:

<margin>A doubt</margin>
18. If the donor promised by oath that they would never "contravene" <note>To act against or cancel</note> the gift made by them in the form of a gift in anticipation of death, that gift does not pass into a gift between the living, but remains "on account of death," and they can revoke it, with such a promise and oath posing no impediment. The reasoning is that to revoke is not to "contravene" a gift which is, by its own nature, revocable. I think, then, that this doctrine is false, not only because in the common use of speakers a promise not to contravene such a gift signifies not revoking it, but also because through revocation that gift is destroyed and rendered null, as is very well known. And thus, one who revokes it is certainly judged to contravene it, and should consequently be regarded as a breaker of a promise and a perjurer.

In **this kingdom** <note>Likely referring to Castile/Spain, the author's jurisdiction</note>, however, such a confirmation would be valid: since an oath is permissible in all things which, excluding the oath, would not be valid, as was said in the cited disputation and elsewhere.

It should be noted, however, that when words and circumstances suggest they intended to give between the living, they may still defer the execution of such a gift until the time after their death...

Luis de Molina, *On Contracts*

...so that someone might say then that they give those goods for the period after their life, or that the recipient should not obtain them until the donor departs from this life, or something similar. This does not make that gift a **gift in anticipation of death** <term>donatio causa mortis: a gift made in expectation of approaching death, which can usually be revoked</term>, but rather it remains a **gift between the living** <term>donatio inter vivos: a gift made during life that is generally irrevocable</term>. Thus, if at the time of a marriage contract for a female relative with another person, someone says, "I give such estates to her as a dowry after my death," or "I give her such estates as a dowry, which she may obtain after my death," it is certainly a gift between the living. Only the execution of the gift and the delivery of those goods is deferred until after the donor's death. This is the view held by Gama <note>Portuguese jurist Antonio de Gama (1520–1595)</note> in Decision 103, numbers 3 and 4, and Decision 143, along with others he cites. When a gift is made absolutely without any mention of death—not only if it is made by a healthy person and by someone who faces no danger of death, but even if it is made by a person who is seriously ill or who fears some other danger of death, and for whom it is likely to be believed that they were led to give by the fear of death—it is still to be considered a gift between the living. This is proved by the Law *Scia*, final section, at the end, in the Digest regarding gifts in anticipation of death <note>original Latin: "l. Scia. §. vlt. in fi. ff. de mor. caus. donat." - 'ff.' refers to the Digest of Justinian</note>, whose words are these: *“He who gives absolutely gives not so much by reason of death, but as one who is dying.”* <note>original: "Eum qui absolute donaret, nō tam mortis causa, quam morientem donare."</note> This is agreed upon by the Law *Scia* joined with the gloss there, in the Digest regarding dowries; and it is affirmed by the gloss on the Law *at Celsus*, section *Julianus*, on the word *had promised*, in the Digest regarding the exception of fraud. This is also the opinion of Bartolus and the common consensus of scholars, which Julius Clarus reports and follows in the section on gifts, question 4, numbers 1, 2, and 3; Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 15; Gregorio López on the final law, title 4, part 5, on the words *of death*; and Gutiérrez in *On the Confirmatory Oath*, chapter 11, number 18. However, Julius Clarus rightly considers this doctrine should be limited (in the cited number 3) unless the gift was made in a testament or a codicil <note>An addition or supplement to a will</note>, and neither the recipient nor anyone else defined by law to stipulate and accept on behalf of others accepted it; for then such a gift would have the force of a legacy and could therefore be revoked. However, when mention of death is made in the gift—because, for instance, the donor said, "after my death," or "when I die, I give you this or that," or "if I depart this life from this disease, or in this war, or on this journey, I give you this or that," or something similar—then it is a gift in anticipation of death. So say the cited Doctors of Law. And in a case of doubt, when mention of death has been made, the inclination should be that the gift is in anticipation of death rather than between the living. Emmanuel Acosta, in book 1 of *Selected Interpretations*, chapter 18, number 1, says along with Alexander and many others whom he cites, that if such a gift were made in the presence of only two witnesses, it should be considered a gift between the living, and only the execution delayed until the time of death. Since for a gift in anticipation of death to be valid it must be made in the presence of five witnesses (as will be said in the following disputation), lest we call it invalid, it is to be presumed in that event that the time of death was not added to suspend the confirmation of the gift until death, but only to suspend its execution. Regarding what has been said in this entire section, read Covarrubias in the commentary on testaments, part 3, number 23.

# To what extent gifts in anticipation of death agree with contracts, and to what extent with last wills.

## DISPUTATION 288.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A gift in anticipation of death agrees with contracts regarding its beginning, but with last wills regarding its effect.*
2 *For a gift in anticipation of death to be valid, five witnesses are required; however, it is otherwise under the law of Castile.*

### Second Treatise, Disputation 288.

**G**

---

Since (as reported by Julius Clarus in his *Book of Sentences*, section on gifts, question 5) there has been a great debate among the doctors of law as to whether a **gift in anticipation of death** <term>donatio causa mortis: a gift given by someone who expects to die soon, which can be revoked if they survive</term> leans more toward the nature of **contracts** or toward **last wills**: some contend absolutely that it leans more toward contracts, while others argue for last wills.

<margin>1</margin> Today, however, the common conclusion is this: If a gift in anticipation of death is viewed in terms of its beginning, its arrangement, or its production, it leans more toward contracts than toward last wills. But if it is viewed in terms of its effect and stability—so that it can no longer be revoked—it leans more toward last wills than toward contracts. And from this, the doctors wish that regarding the beginning and production, the gift in anticipation of death should be confirmed according to the laws of contracts; but regarding its effect and stability, it should follow the laws of last wills, unless something specific has been legally decreed otherwise for both. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Covarruvias in his commentary on testaments, part 3, number 21; Antonio Gomez in his *Various Resolutions*, volume 1, chapter 4, number 16; Julius Clarus in the cited question 5; and Molina in book 1 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 12, number 18, and especially number 16.

<margin>2</margin> It was said: "unless something specific has been decreed regarding both." For, according to the first part of the proposed rule, the formality that suffices for other contracts to be valid ought to suffice for a gift in anticipation of death to be valid. However, the matter is quite the opposite: for, as seen in the final law of the Code *On gifts in anticipation of death* and the final law of title 4, part 5, if the thing is to be valid, it is necessary that it be done before **five witnesses**. This is the formality required by common law for codicils. It is not, however, necessary that they be formally requested or that they be male, as was stated in Disputation 131. Yet, those who are permitted to make a testament before fewer than five witnesses are, by that very fact, considered permitted to give in anticipation of death before fewer than five witnesses. This is because whatever formality is waived in a testament is also considered waived in a gift in anticipation of death and a codicil, as in the law *Marcellus* at the beginning of the Digest *On gifts in anticipation of death*. Covarruvias observes (in the same part 3, number 21, following Bartolus and others) that because some law might waive a requirement in a testament regarding the number of witnesses, it does not necessarily follow that the same proportional amount is waived in a gift in anticipation of death. For example, if in a certain event two of the necessary witnesses for a testament were waived for someone, it does not mean he could give in anticipation of death before only three; rather, it only means that when it is lawful for someone to testify before fewer than five witnesses, it is lawful for that same person to make a codicil or a gift in anticipation of death with that same number of witnesses.

However, because the number of witnesses or some other

<column-break/>

formality might be increased in a testament, it does not mean that anything is considered increased in a gift in anticipation of death, as Covarruvias says in the same place. From the teaching handed down, Covarruvias (in the cited place) and Antonio Gomez (*Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 4, number 16) infer that today in this kingdom, if a **notary** <note>original Latin: "bellio," likely a shortened form of "tabellio," a public scribe or notary</note> is present, three witnesses from the neighborhood where the gift is made suffice for a gift in anticipation of death. <margin>The Law of Castile.</margin> This is because that formality today in this kingdom suffices for both a codicil and an **oral testament** <term>testamentum nuncupativum: a will declared aloud rather than written</term>, according to what was said in Disputations 127 and 131.

<margin>3</margin> Molina (*On Primogeniture*, book 1, chapter 12, number 17) correctly observes that although five witnesses are necessary for a gift in anticipation of death according to the final law of the Code, it does not follow that just as many are necessary for other gifts that are confirmed by the death of the donors. Therefore, it is not necessary for the validity of a **majoratus** <term>majoratus: an entailed estate that passes to the eldest son</term> established by such gifts; rather, the witnesses required for the validity of other contracts suffice. The reason is that, although all such gifts are categorized with last wills regarding their effect and stability, they follow the rules of contracts regarding their beginning and production. Furthermore, from the fact that the cited final law specifically requires five witnesses, it does not follow that this must be extended to other gifts confirmed by death, unless the same is specifically decreed for them or they are similarly excepted from the rules of other contracts in that regard.

<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, concerning a gift in anticipation of death, it is specifically decreed in the final law of the Code *On gifts in anticipation of death* that **public registration** <term>insinuatio: the formal recording of a gift in public records to make it legally binding</term> is not necessary, even if it exceeds the sum of five hundred **gold coins** <term>solidi: late Roman/medieval gold coins used as a standard for legal limits on gifts</term>, just as registration is not required for legacies. Since registration is necessary in the very production of a gift for it to be valid regarding the excess amount, one would certainly have to say the same for a gift in anticipation of death if the contrary had not been specifically decreed for it due to its similarity to legacies. This confirms that this is an exception for a gift in anticipation of death, because in other gifts that are only confirmed by the death of the donor, registration is regularly required.

Hence, in the law *Gifts which parents* in the Code *On gifts between husband and wife*, it is clearly held that in those gifts from parents to children, and from one spouse to another—which are not confirmed except by the donor's death—public registration is necessary for the amount exceeding five hundred gold coins. If, however, they are confirmed in a last will by the donors, they are indeed valid regarding the excess, but in the nature of a legacy. The common opinion of the doctors affirms this same thing, which Antonio Gomez (*Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 4, number 18) reports and follows, regardless of what a few others (whom Gomez also mentions) say to the contrary against that cited law.

From this, you will first understand that Antonio Gomez, in the place cited, did not correctly infer that registration is unnecessary in a gift in anticipation of death simply because such a gift is compared to a last will regarding its confirmation and effect. For that is not the origin or the reason for the matter; rather, it is because it was excepted from other gifts by a specific privilege of the law in that regard, as was stated. Because he erred in this origin, it is no wonder that he was also misguided in giving the reason why, in a gift from a parent to a child or a husband to a wife, it is necessa-
