# Luis de Molina
# On Contracts
### Page 98

...registration <term>insinuatio: the formal public recording of a legal document</term> is necessary; however, in a gift made in anticipation of death, it is not.
Secondly, you will understand that Molina was not correct in his second book on primogeniture, chapter 8, number 21, where he asserted that registration is not necessary in a **majorat** <term>maioratus: an entailed estate that passes to the eldest son</term> established by a revocable contract on the grounds that it is compared to a last will. For it is not compared to a last will in any way other than how the gifts of parents to children, or one spouse to another, are compared to last wills, in which it has nonetheless been shown that registration is necessary. Therefore, the legitimate reasons why registration is not necessary in those cases are the other reasons we discussed with the same author in Disputation 279, where we said that majorats established by an irrevocable contract do not require registration. For whatever causes persuade us that a majorat established by an irrevocable contract does not need registration, they convince us of the same with far greater reason regarding a majorat established by a revocable contract.

<margin>5</margin> In a † gift made in anticipation of death, the **Falcidian Law** <term>Lex Falcidia: a Roman law requiring that at least one-fourth of an estate remain with the designated heir</term> has a place, just as it does in legacies <note>original: "l. cum pater. §. eorum, ff. de lega. 2."</note>. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion which Antonio Gomez relates and follows in his *Various Resolutions*. Covarruvias, however, in his commentary on testaments, believes this should be limited (along with Juan Anibal) to when the gift in anticipation of death is made in a testament or codicil, but otherwise when it is made outside of a testament and codicil. Yet the laws and other Doctors speak universally; therefore, I judge that this limitation should be rejected.

<margin>6</margin> In a † similar way, concerning a gift between husband and wife which is confirmed by the death of the donor, the Falcidian portion is deducted, as held in the law *in donationibus*. The same is true for other gifts confirmed by death, as is clear from the reasoning given in the cited law, and as affirmed by the glosses and Bartolus, and the common opinion of the Doctors, which Molina relates and follows in his first book on primogeniture.

<margin>7</margin> Furthermore, in a † gift in anticipation of death, when something is given to two people, the **right of accrual** <term>ius accrescendi: the right of a beneficiary to take the portion of another beneficiary who cannot or will not receive it</term> applies, just as when something is similarly bequeathed to two people as a legacy. Both are held in the law *unica* in the Code regarding the removal of lapses. Antonio Gomez affirms this in the passage cited.

<margin>8</margin> Likewise, in a gift † in anticipation of death and in other revocable gifts, an **impossible condition** is held as if it were not written <note>original: "pro non apposita"</note>, just as in last wills, as was shown in Disputation 285.

<margin>9</margin> Furthermore, the **Mutian bond** <term>cautio Mutiana: a security or promise given by a beneficiary to ensure they will not perform a prohibited act</term> applies † when a gift in anticipation of death or other revocable gifts are made under a negative condition within one's power, as was proven in the same place.

<margin>10</margin> Moreover, in a † gift in anticipation of death, the capacity or incapacity of the recipient <note>original: "donatarii"</note> is considered at the time of the donor's death, not at the time of the gift, as held in the law *in mortis causa* and affirmed by the gloss there. The same is true for legacies, as is clear from various laws. In the same way,

<column-break/>

the legal requirements for making a gift in anticipation of death or a legacy on the part of the donor are looked for at the time of the death of the one so giving or bequeathing—provided, however, that the legacy is made by a codicil and not by a testament, as is clear regarding legacies; and the same is true of a gift in anticipation of death, as the cited gloss says by way of argument.

Therefore, because in almost all the things mentioned so far, and in certain others, a gift in anticipation of death is made similar to legacies by a specific provision of law, it is not without merit that in the final law of the Code on gifts in anticipation of death, it is said:
<margin>11</margin> In these cases of death, † gifts made in anticipation of death have been reduced almost in all respects to the example of legacies. Thus, by the provision of the law, they approach legacies more than they do contracts, even though they hold a middle ground between legacies and gifts between living persons <note>original: "inter vivos"</note>. Therefore, if the authors mentioned at the beginning of this disputation intended it in this sense—that gifts in anticipation of death approach last wills more than contracts because they are made similar to them in far more things by specific provisions of law—then their opinion is very true, and the two laws cited openly support them.

<margin>12</margin> As for the second part of the rule proposed above, this distinction is established by a specific law: that legacies are not confirmed until the heir left in the testament enters into the inheritance. Thus, if none of the heirs appointed in the testament enter the inheritance, the legacies perish, as shown in Disputation 181 (except for certain outcomes explained there, and except for the law of Castile, where this is not necessary). But † indeed, a gift in anticipation of death is considered entirely confirmed immediately upon the death of the donor. So much so that, even if no one enters the inheritance, the recipient of the gift can ask that a curator be appointed for the deceased's goods and demand from them the thing given, if it was not delivered while the donor lived. If, however, the heirs **by intestacy** <term>ab intestato: inheriting when there is no valid will</term> take possession of those goods, they are bound to pay the gifted item to him. This is the opinion of the gloss, Bartolus, and the common consensus of the Doctors, which Covarruvias, Julius Clarus, Molina, and Antonio Gomez follow. This distinction, however, is to be understood as applying when the gift was accepted, at least by someone who could accept it in place of the legatee; it is otherwise if it was made without such acceptance in a testament or codicil, for then it assumes the nature of a legacy entirely.

<margin>13</margin> Linked with the † distinction just established is this other one: that if a specific thing was designated and given, and its delivery was not made while the donor was living (such that ownership of that thing would have passed to the recipient while the donor lived), then immediately as the donor departs from life, the **ownership** <term>dominium: legal title and right of control</term> of that thing passes to the recipient without any dependence on the entry into the inheritance.

<summary>This page analyzes the legal similarities between gifts made in anticipation of death and legacies, concluding that they are treated almost identically regarding capacity, conditions, and the Falcidian portion. A key distinction remains that these gifts, unlike legacies, become valid immediately upon death regardless of whether an heir accepts the inheritance.</summary>

...at the end of the law <term>ff. de publiciana: a reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding the Publician action for recovering property</term>, and the common opinion of the learned doctors affirms this, which is recorded and followed by Antonio Gomez in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 17, at the beginning; and by Covarrubias in the commentary on testaments, part 3, number 15. The ownership of a legacy <note>original: "Dominium autem legati"</note>, however, does pass, but it depends on the acceptance of the inheritance; and so, once the inheritance is accepted, it is imagined by a legal fiction to have passed from the moment of the testator's death, as was explained in Disputation 181 and elsewhere.

<margin>14</margin> † From this, it will be easier to explain which legal action is available regarding a gift in anticipation of death. For if, during the life of the donor, the delivery of the gifted item was made to the recipient, so that ownership and possession of that thing passed to them, it is clear that no further action is necessary for them, as Antonio Gomez well says in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 16. But if delivery was not made, and a specific individual thing was gifted to them, then—since ownership of that thing passes to the recipient immediately upon the death of the donor, as was just said—certainly the action of **vindication** <term>rei vindicatio: a legal action by which a plaintiff proves they are the owner of a specific item and requires the possessor to return it</term> is available to them, along with the actions we shall mention shortly. If, however, the gift was something designated by its type or category, but not a specific individual item, then, if a **stipulation** <term>stipulatio: a formal verbal contract in Roman law</term> took place, or if such a gift was made in a will or a codicil, an action arises from the stipulation or a claim for recovery based on the law <note>original: "l. si quis argentum. C. de donationib."</note>. If no formal stipulation took place, but only a "naked pact" <term>pactum nudum: an agreement that is not legally binding under strict Roman law because it lacks a specific form</term> was agreed upon, they only have a claim for recovery under the same law. In these events, however, a **hypothecary action** <term>actio hypothecaria: an action to enforce a mortgage or lien</term>, which is granted for legacies, does not apply; for as Covarrubias says in the place cited, nothing in the law has established that. But if the gift was made in a will or codicil, even without a stipulation and by a naked pact, then, because it has the character of a legacy, the actions specific to legacies are available. On this matter, read Covarrubias in his commentary on testaments, part 3, numbers 16 and 17.

<margin>15</margin> † Lest we return to this second part of the proposed rule later, it must be stated that a gift † in anticipation of death comprising all present and future goods is valid. This is because, since a gift of this kind can be revoked at the will of the donor, they do not deprive themselves of the power to make a will through it, as we especially showed with the common opinion of the doctors in Disputation 280, in the section "it is also doubted."

<margin>16</margin> † To return to the first part of the proposed rule, several points are gathered from it. The first is that, although under common law wives could enter into contracts regarding **paraphernalia** <term>paraphernalia: property belonging to a married woman beyond her dowry, which she historically managed herself</term>, the administration of which belonged to them; nevertheless, in these kingdoms of Portugal and Castile, they have no administration of goods, unless by chance they had reserved ownership and administration for themselves by a specific peculiar pact (which rarely happens). Instead, the entire administration belongs to the husbands. Therefore, just as wives in these kingdoms cannot enter into contracts except by the authority of the husband—as is clear from the **Laws of Toro** <note>original: "l. 54. & 55. Tauri"</note>, which are laws 8 and 2, title 3, book 5 of the *New Collection*, and which the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 6, assume and custom observes—so also they cannot make gifts in anticipation of death. This is because a gift in anticipation of death, regarding its production and beginning, follows the rules of contracts rather than those of last wills. This is affirmed, following Panormitanus and the common opinion of the doctors, in places where wives are prohibited from entering contracts without the husband's authority, by Covarrubias, Antonio Gomez, and Molina in his second book on

<column-break/>

primogeniture, chapter 9, number 4, and Gutierrez. Whatever Navarrus may have asserted to the contrary in his third book of *Consilia* was not correct.

<margin>17</margin> † It is doubted whether † a gift in anticipation of death is valid <margin>Doubt</margin> between spouses. Covarrubias speaks obscurely on this matter. I believe it should be stated briefly with Emmanuel Costa. First, a gift <margin>Decision</margin> made between living spouses is regularly not confirmed before the death of the donor, as will be seen in the following disputation. It is then confirmed and made valid by the death of the donor when delivery of the gifted thing preceded it; for if no delivery preceded it, it is entirely null, and therefore not even confirmed by the donor's death. But a gift in anticipation of death made between spouses—whether delivery preceded it or not, and even if made by a mere promise—is valid and is confirmed by the death of the donor in the same way we have discussed regarding other gifts in anticipation of death made between others. This is affirmed by Antonio Gomez and the common opinion of the Doctors. Therefore, if one spouse gifts a specific determined thing to the other in anticipation of death, the ownership of that thing passes to the recipient by the very fact that the gift was confirmed by the donor's death. Read the doctors whom Emmanuel Costa cites for this opinion. However, even if one spouse delivers the thing to the other as a gift in anticipation of death, ownership of it does not pass to the recipient but remains with the donor while they live. As for the law in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de mort. ual. donationib."</note> which asserts that a gift having the form of a gift in anticipation of death is invalid if made by one spouse to the other with a pact that it cannot be revoked, it must be said either that the law was passed at a time when a gift between living spouses was not confirmed even by death, or certainly that it must be understood regarding the added pact. Since it is against the substance of a gift between spouses—whether made between the living or in anticipation of death—such a pact is undoubtedly null; therefore, it is held as if it were not added. If someone objects to us using the law which declares a gift in anticipation of death made by a father-in-law to a son-in-law or daughter-in-law to be invalid—because even if the father-in-law dies, the marriage still continues between the recipient and the donor's child—the answer is that the text itself gave the reason: since the father-in-law is regarded as if the gift were for the child through the son-in-law or daughter-in-law, the law did not want such a gift to be confirmed by death while the marriage endured. # Luis de Molina on Contracts

...of one of the spouses giving to the other: since the marriage is dissolved by death. Emmanuel Acosta, in the place cited at number 8, affirms that this was the only meaning intended by the famous <term>gloss: an interpretive comment in the margins of medieval legal texts</term> on Law 2, at the beginning, on the word "legacy" in the <term>Digest: a major part of the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Iuris Civilis) regarding doweries</term>.

<margin>18</margin>
A † **gift made in anticipation of death** <note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note> made to the other spouse is rendered void if the donor is deported or afflicted with a more severe penalty such that their goods are surrendered to the <term>fiscus: the royal or state treasury</term>. This is evident from the law *si aliquis* in the Digest regarding gifts in anticipation of death, and is affirmed by Molina, among others, in book 4 on primogeniture, chapter 11, number 22. He correctly adds, however, that <term>majoratus: entailed estates passed to the eldest son</term> established through a revocable gift between living persons do not expire upon the deportation of the donor. Although gifts made in anticipation of death to others expire upon the deportation or more severe punishment of the donor, a special provision is made in favor of

<margin>19</margin>
† the **wife**. It is established that in the case of deportation or a more severe penalty for the husband, a gift made between living persons from the husband to the wife remains valid if delivery of the item had already occurred, provided the gift or delivery was not made out of fear of the impending penalty. In such a case, the donated property belongs to the wife according to the agreement and not to the treasury. However, the husband retains the power to revoke that gift as long as he remains naturally alive, just as he could if he had not been condemned. This is held in the law *res uxoris* in the <term>Codex: the Code of Justinian</term> regarding gifts between husband and wife. It is further established that a gift made in anticipation of death to the same wife, made without suspicion of avoiding penalty, is valid and is not revoked by deportation or a more severe penalty. The husband retains the right to revoke it while he naturally lives, as was said regarding gifts between the living. This is found in the law *sed si mors* at the beginning of the Digest regarding gifts between husband and wife. Emmanuel Acosta thinks it is necessary for delivery to have occurred so that a gift made in anticipation of death does not expire upon the husband's deportation. However, I believe this is not necessary, because the law *sed si mors* speaks generally about gifts made in anticipation of death to a wife; and where the law does not restrict, we ought not to restrict, since a gift in anticipation of death between spouses is valid without delivery. Note here that the cited law says the gift is confirmed by the husband's deportation, where the law implies and Covarruvias affirms that ownership of the donated thing passes to the wife at that very moment, even though such ownership is revocable because the husband can revoke it while he lives. Hence, the law adds that the "fullest confirmation" of such a gift occurs upon the natural death of the deported man. The words of that law are these:
> *It is humane that a gift, which was made from the beginning in anticipation of death, be confirmed by the aid of what follows, as if it were ratified upon the husband's death: provided, however, that the husband is not deprived of the liberty to revoke it; because his death must be awaited so that the gift may then have its fullest firmness, when he is taken from this light, whether he has returned or is still serving his punishment.* <note>original Latin: "Humanum est, donationem, quæ mortis causa ab initio facta est..."</note>
So far the law. I observe two things:

<margin>20</margin>
One is that in † cases where it was said in Disputation 9—especially regarding the law of **Portugal and Castile**—that the goods of those so condemned are not surrendered to the treasury and that such condemned persons can make a will, a gift made in anticipation of death to a stranger does not expire through deportation or another more severe penalty. The other

<margin>21</margin>
† point is that when one spouse has given and delivered a donated thing to the other, whether the gift was

<column-break/>

between living persons or in anticipation of death, then, upon the death of the donor, the gift is traced back to the time of delivery. This is not in regards to ownership (since this only belongs to the recipient spouse from the time of the donor's death, as was said), but in regards to the **fruits** <note>the profits, rents, or produce of the property</note>, which belong to the recipient from the moment of delivery. This is found in the law *donationes quæ parentes* and the gloss there, and the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarruvias records and follows.

<margin>22</margin>
From the same † first rule proposed, it is concluded, secondly, that a gift made in anticipation of death is valid when it is left to the **will of another**. For example: "If Peter wishes it, I give you one hundred after my death." Indeed, since contracts that depend on another's will as a condition are valid, and since a gift follows the rules and laws of contracts between living persons regarding its creation and arrangement (when nothing to the contrary is disposed by law), such a gift made under that condition will certainly be valid. So says Emmanuel Acosta in his *Selected Interpretations*, book 1, chapter 1, number 6.

<margin>23</margin>
From the † first part of the rule, many have wanted to explain why a **son under paternal authority** <term>filiusfamilias: a son who remains under the legal power of his father, regardless of age</term>—although he cannot make a will regarding <term>adventitious goods: property a son acquires from sources other than his father, such as an inheritance from his mother</term>, even those for which he has the right of use and administration—can nevertheless make a gift in anticipation of death with his father's consent. However, Covarruvias and others rightly reject this. As was shown, a son can enter into contracts regarding such goods without his father's consent when the use and administration belong to him. The extent to which a father's consent is required, and the extent to which a son can be bound by contracts, was explained in the cited disputation. Therefore, the fact that he can give in anticipation of death with only his father's consent (since he cannot make a will even with that same consent under common law) proceeds from a specific provision of the law, not from the general doctrine of the rule.

<margin>24</margin>
What † should be said on this matter, I will briefly add. In Disputation 138, we said that a son under paternal authority, if he is of age, can make a will regarding his <term>peculium castrense: property a son acquired through military service</term> without any father's consent, and therefore he can freely give from that same property in anticipation of death. This is because he who can make a will can also make a gift in anticipation of death. Therefore, since today under the law of this **Kingdom of Castile**, a son of age can freely make a will regarding a **third** of his adventitious goods, he can similarly give that same third in this kingdom in anticipation of death without any father's consent. Molina rightly affirms this along with others.

Although under common law and in **Portugal**, a son of age cannot make a will even with his father's consent, nor with his adventitious goods, even if the use...

This was stated in the most recently cited Disputation, and at the start of Disputation 236. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Covarruvias (from number 6) and Julius Clarus (Book 4, Opinions, section on "Gifts," question 6, numbers 3 and 4) follow. However, this cannot be done without the express consent of the father, as the more common opinion of the doctors asserts, which the same authors record and follow in that place.

<margin>
A Doubt
From Decius
</margin>
25 There is a **doubt** whether the father’s consent is necessary for a son’s **gift in anticipation of death** <note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note> because it involves a loss to the father, to whom the <term>usufruct: the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</term> belongs—and for that reason his consent is required—or whether it is required by a provision of law as a necessary formality to give the agreement authority. Although some have affirmed it is necessary for the first reason, the more common and truer opinion (along with the <term>gloss: a standard legal commentary</term> on Law 1, section "by necessity," in the Code on goods of children) is that it is necessary for the latter reason. Covarruvias (numbers 6 and 7) and Julius Clarus (number 5) record and follow this. This can even be confirmed by the fact that even when the usufruct and administration of those goods belong to the son, the father’s consent is no less necessary, even though in that case there is no loss to the father.

26 For this reason, the cited authors (both at number 7) conclude, along with the final gloss on Law 1 at the beginning of the Digest regarding the authority and consent of tutors, and the more common opinion of the doctors, that a gift in anticipation of death made by a son **to his father** is invalid if it relies solely on the father's consent. This is because no one can provide legal authority for their own personal benefit, as held in Law 1 and the law regarding a ward <note>original: "l. pupillus"</note> in the Digest. Therefore, for such a gift to be valid, the authority of a **judge** must intervene.
From the same foundation, Julius Clarus (number 6), with others he cites, concludes that for a son's gift in anticipation of death to be valid, the **express consent** of the father is necessary, and silent consent is not sufficient. This is because when someone’s consent is required as a necessary legal formality, it must be express.

27 There is a doubt: what if a son under paternal authority makes a gift in anticipation of death within a **will** with his father’s consent, and adds a clause stating that "if it does not hold as a will, let it hold as a <term>codicil: an informal supplement to a will</term>, or as a gift in anticipation of death"? Julius Clarus (question 5, number 8), from whom Covarruvias (number 10) does not seem to differ, makes an excellent distinction. Either such a gift was made with a formal <term>stipulation: a verbal contract in Roman law</term> by the recipient, or at least with an acceptance—perhaps through another who could accept on his behalf—so that it turned into a simple agreement through the silent consent of the recipient who was present and heard the gift but remained silent; or else neither a stipulation nor an acceptance occurred. In the first case, they say such a gift is valid when that clause is used which expressly mentions a gift in anticipation of death. They affirm the same if he had used the clause: "if it does not hold as a will, let it hold as any other final wish." This is because, for the act to be upheld, the words must be understood broadly, and a gift in anticipation of death is included under

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

"final wish" in a broad sense.
I would say that even if no such clause were added, such a gift would be valid, because it is a true contract inserted into a will and legitimately performed. Therefore, although the will itself is worth nothing (because a son under paternal authority cannot make a will even with his father’s consent), that contract—legitimately performed and inserted into a void will—remains valid. In the second case, however, since it is not truly a gift in anticipation of death but a mere **legacy** <note>original: "legatum"; a specific bequest in a will as opposed to a contract between parties</note> inserted into a useless will, I believe it gains no firmness at all, even if those clauses are used. This is because a son under authority cannot make a will or a legacy, even with his father’s consent.

28 From the first part of the rule, it follows that although a young person under twenty-five who is not under paternal authority can make a will even against his **guardian’s** <note>original: "curator"</note> will, a gift in anticipation of death made by him without the guardian's authority is void. Indeed, if it involves immovable property (like land) or other things that cannot be sold without a judge’s decree (according to what was said in Disputation 224), it is invalid unless a judge’s decree is also added. But if he lacks a guardian, or has been granted "the benefit of age" <note>original: "veniam aetatis"; a legal exception allowing a minor to act as an adult</note>, and the gift is of movable goods, such a gift will be valid, just as any other contract made by the same minor regarding the same property is valid.
The more common opinion of the doctors affirms the first part of this assertion, which Guterriez (on confirmed rights, part 1, chapter 13) and Molina (Book 2 on primogeniture, chapter 9, number 9) record and follow at length. They confirm it by noting that a gift in anticipation of death, regarding its creation and validity, follows the nature of **contracts**. Therefore, one who cannot validly enter into contracts without a guardian's authority cannot validly make a gift in anticipation of death without that same authority. Thus, the rule "he who can make a will can give in anticipation of death" must be understood as "unless he has been rendered unable to enter into contracts," either entirely or unless he follows a specific legal formality.
However, in a will or codicil, there is no doubt that such a minor can give in anticipation of death without the guardian's authority or a judge’s decree, provided there is no stipulation or acceptance by the recipient. This is because such a gift is a legacy rather than a contract, as said above. Furthermore, through <term>epicheia: a reasonable or equitable interpretation of the law that looks to the intent of the legislator</term>, I believe that a gift made in a will or codicil with a stipulation or acceptance is valid even without delivery of the item. For if the legislators were asked about this matter when they established the laws and granted the power of making wills to such minors, I do not doubt they would have answered affirmatively.
It must also be observed that if such minors give in anticipation of death outside of a will, or even deliver the item and confirm the gift with an **oath**, promising they will always hold it as settled and firm and will never revoke it, they not only give validly, but such a gift transforms into a valid **gift between the living** <note>original: "donatio inter vivos"</note>. This is according to what was said in the preceding Disputation: because contracts by minors, otherwise invalid due to a lack of formality, are made valid...

## On Gifts Between Spouses.

### DISPUTATION 289.

### SUMMARY.

1 *Gifts between spouses were regularly invalid under ancient law; today, however, if they are not revoked, they are confirmed by the death of the giver.*
2 *A gift made between spouses after the marriage contract but before it is consummated requires confirmation by the giver's death. It is different, however, under the law of Castile (see number 3).*
4 *What is required for a gift between spouses to be confirmed by the giver's death.*
5 *For a gift between spouses to be confirmed by death, it is sufficient that the thing given was delivered through a "constitutum" clause <note>a legal agreement where a seller agrees to hold the property on behalf of the buyer</note> or another legal fiction through which civil possession is acquired.*
6 *A gift between spouses is confirmed even by the **civil death** <note>the loss of all legal rights, such as through certain criminal convictions or entering a monastery</note> of the giver, excluding the treasury; it is conditional, however, unless revoked before natural death.*
7 *A gift between spouses made without formal registration <note>original: "insinuatio"</note> is confirmed by the giver's death only up to the amount permitted by law without registration. This fails unless it was confirmed by the giver in a will or codicil.*
8 *A gift between spouses confirmed by death is retroactive to the time it was delivered regarding the profits or "fruits" of the property.*
9 *A gift between spouses transfers ownership to the recipient immediately upon the giver's death, without waiting for the inheritance to be accepted, according to whether registration was made or not.*
10 *The **Falcidian portion** <term>Falcidian portion: a Roman law rule ensuring that an heir receives at least one-fourth of the estate after all legacies are paid</term> is deducted from a gift between husband and wife just as it is from legacies.*
11 *A gift in anticipation of death between spouses is not confirmed by the giver's death in two specific cases.*
12 *The various ways a gift between spouses is considered tacitly revoked (also see number 13).*
14 *Regarding the law of Portugal and Castile.*
15 *In which cases a gift between husband and wife is valid immediately.*

<column-break/>

16 *When a giver is said to be "made poorer" or not.*
17 *Whether a renunciation made by a wife to her husband while the marriage lasts—by which she gives up profits from the goods of both—is valid immediately.*
18 *Cases in which the recipient is not "made richer," even if the giver is "made poorer."
19 *Whether a gift between spouses that is confirmed by death becomes irrevocable if it is confirmed by an oath.*

We must next discuss certain gifts for which specific laws have been established. We shall begin with **gifts between spouses**. In the preceding Disputation, we explained how far a **gift in anticipation of death** <note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note> has force between them. Now, however, we must discuss only **gifts between the living** <note>original: "donatio inter vivos"; gifts given while both parties are alive, intended to take effect immediately</note>.

Since under common law wives had ownership and administration of **paraphernal goods** <term>paraphernal goods: property brought into a marriage by a wife that is not part of her formal dowry</term>, gifts between spouses used to be more frequent than they are today in these kingdoms of Castile and Portugal. In these kingdoms, the administration of all the wife's property usually stays with the husband; either the goods of both spouses become common property (as in Portugal), or the appraised dowry is usually handed over to the husband so that ownership of it passes to him. First, we will explain in which events such a gift is confirmed by the death of the giver; then, in which cases it remains firm immediately, without needing to wait for the giver's death.

<margin>1</margin> At this point, it should be noted that formerly **gifts between spouses** were regularly void. This was to prevent spouses from stripping themselves of their property out of mutual love, and for other reasons (as stated in the Digest, Book 24, Title 1). Later, however, the Emperor Antoninus <note>likely referring to Caracalla</note>, in a speech given in the Senate regarding this matter, obtained the rule that while it remained entirely within the power of the giving spouse to revoke the gift while they lived, if they did not revoke it during their lifetime, it would be confirmed by their death, and the heirs could not revoke it. For this differs little from a legacy or a gift in anticipation of death. Therefore, just as these two are granted to each spouse in relation to the other, so this other type should not be denied to them. This law is in force today, as is clear from the Code (Title on gifts between husband and wife) and the laws of the Partidas (Part 4, Title 11) and the Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, Title 9). This is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, followed by Antonio Gómez, Julio Claro, and Gutiérrez. See also Covarruvias.

<margin>2</margin> Although Azo and certain others wanted to except from this rule a **gift made by one spouse to the other** after the marriage was celebrated by words of present consent <note>original: "per verba de praesenti"; a legally binding marriage contract</note> but before it was consummated by sexual union—as if that gift were entirely valid immediately and did not need confirmation by the giver's death—nevertheless, the contrary is quite clearly laid down in the Digest (Book 24). Namely, by the very fact that the gift is ma... <note>text cuts off</note>

Navarrus says the same if the gift was made before a marriage celebrated through **words of the present** <note>original: "per verba de præsenti"; a legal term for a marriage contract where the parties agree to be married immediately, as opposed to a promise to marry in the future</note>, but intended for the time when the marriage would be celebrated. This is expressly found in the law *cum hic status*, paragraph *si sponsus* in the Digest regarding gifts between husband and wife, and the law *quod sponsa* in the Code regarding gifts before marriage. Note, however, that today under the law of **Castile** <note>original: "iure Castell."</note>, specifically Law 52 of **Toro** <note>original: "Tauri"; referring to the Laws of Toro (1505), which standardized Spanish law</note>, gifts made
<margin>In Castile</margin>
to a bride in the present before the marriage is consummated are valid immediately, in the same way that wedding gifts made before a marriage contract between a future bride and groom are valid immediately, by the agreement which will be explained in the following disputation.

<margin>4</margin>
Observe this: for a **gift** <note>original: "donatio"</note> between spouses to be confirmed by the death of the donor, it is necessary that the gifted item be delivered to the recipient—at least by **symbolic delivery** <note>original: "ficta traditione"; a legal fiction where the item isn't physically handed over, but legal possession is transferred</note>—before the death of the donor. Otherwise, it is entirely void. This is held in the law of Papinian in the Digest regarding gifts between husband and wife, which, since it mentions the decree of the **Divine Severus** <note>The Roman Emperor Septimius Severus</note>, is later than the decision in the law *cum hic status*. This is consistent with the law *res uxores* in the Code under the same title, in these words: *or even if it had come to her by the gift of the husband by law before the crime.* And below: a marital gift bestowed upon a wife before the time of the crime and accusation, which certainly signifies delivery. The same is proven in Law 2 of the Code, *si quis alteri, vel sibi*, which requires delivery so that a gift from a father to a son may be confirmed by the father's death; moreover, the same reasoning applies to a gift made from one spouse to another. This is affirmed, following Bartolus, by the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Antonio Gómez in his commentary on Law 50 of Toro, number 65, and in the second volume of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 23 at the end; Julius Clarus, question 9, number 6; Covarruvias in the section on wills, part 3, number 3; and Gregorio López <note>An influential commentator on Spanish law</note> on the cited Law 4 at the word *in his life* <note>original: "en su vida"</note>. This is true regardless of what Azo may have said to the contrary.

<margin>7</margin>
Therefore, it was said "at least by symbolic delivery" because, for a gift to be confirmed by the donor's death, it will suffice if the gifted item is delivered through a **transfer clause** <note>original: "clausulam constituti"; a legal clause where a seller/donor agrees to hold the property on behalf of the new owner</note>, or through another symbolic act by which **civil possession** <note>legal recognition of ownership</note> is acquired. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus and Gregorio López in the places cited, following the final gloss on Law 2 of the Code regarding a dowry promised but not paid. From this law, as that same gloss and the cited doctors affirm—along with the common opinion cited by Covarruvias—it is clearly gathered that a symbolic or virtual delivery is deemed to have occurred if the husband, with the intent of giving an **increase** <note>original: "incrementum"; an additional gift beyond the standard dowry</note> (which is presumed in case of doubt), has confessed that he received a larger dowry than he actually received. For since the husband possesses the dowry the entire time the marriage continues as if it were delivered to him by his wife, he is similarly deemed to possess that "increase" as if it were received from the wife. Thus, it is considered delivered by the wife's power and received from her hand. From this, it follows that unless the husband revokes such a gift while he lives, it is confirmed by his death, and the wife can claim such an increase from the husband's heirs, as is expressly held in the cited Law 2.

<margin>6</margin>
In the preceding disputation, it was said that a gift—

<column-break/>

<margin>I</margin>
—made between the living by a husband to his wife is confirmed by the **civil death** <note>original: "morte ciuili"; the loss of all legal rights and status, usually due to banishment or life imprisonment, which the law treats as if the person had died</note> of the husband, and that property does not belong to the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscum"</note> but to the wife. However, it is confirmed in such a way that if the husband does not naturally die at that time, it remains within his power to revoke the gift. Both points are expressly held in the law *res uxoris* in the Code regarding gifts between husband and wife. Gregorio López, in the cited gloss along with others he mentions, says that if after the confiscation of the husband's goods and the awarding of the gifted item to the wife, the husband revokes the gift, that item does not belong to the treasury; this is because at the time of confiscation, the treasury had no right to it. Gregorio López also seems to add that a gift made by a wife to her husband is confirmed by the civil death of the wife, and the gifted item does not belong to the treasury but to the husband. However, I strongly doubt this matter, because that rule seems to have been introduced only in favor of wives, of whom alone the cited law *res uxoris* speaks. Nor does the reasoning for that constitution, which the text itself provides, apply to husbands. For the text says: *And a marital gift bestowed upon a wife before the time of the crime and accusation, because it served as a **reward for modesty** <note>original: "pudicitiæ præmio"</note>, must be observed just as if nature, not punishment, had taken her husband away.* Furthermore, a **gift in anticipation of death** <note>original: "causa mortis"</note> made to a husband expires upon the civil death of the wife, just as other gifts in anticipation of death made by others expire upon the death of the donor; only a gift in anticipation of death made by a husband to a wife does not expire upon the husband's civil death, as it is a specific privilege of wives, as was said in the preceding disputation. Therefore, the same should seemingly be said regarding a gift between living persons made by a wife to her husband.

<margin>7</margin>
Since, however, no **registration** <note>original: "insinuatio"; the formal recording of a gift in public records, required for gifts exceeding a certain value</note> preceded it, a gift between the living made by one spouse to another is confirmed by the death of the donor only up to the amount that is legal to give without registration, but not regarding the "increase," as was said in the preceding disputation. This is expressly found in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 9, paragraph 1, and the law *donationes quas parentes* in the Code regarding gifts between husband and wife. Julius Clarus affirms this in Book 4 of his *Opinions*, question 17, number 3, as does the common opinion of the doctors. If, however, it is confirmed in a last will, such as a testament or a codicil, then it is indeed valid regarding the excess—not as a gift, but as a **legacy** <note>original: "legati"</note> and a last will, which does not require registration. Consequently, for the purpose we will join next and other similar effects, that gift (regarding the excess) is not retroactive to the time of delivery, but only has force from the time it was confirmed by death, as is expressly held in the cited law *donationes quas parentes*, and as the gloss there affirms on the word *referatur*.

<margin>8</margin>
As was said in the preceding disputation, since a gift between the living made by one spouse to another is confirmed by the death of the donor, it is then retroactive to the time when the delivery of the gifted item was made. This is not retroactive regarding **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note>—because although delivery was made, ownership never passes to the recipient until the gift is confirmed by the donor's death, as is clear from the laws *etiam* and *a marito* in the Code regarding gifts between spouses—but only regarding the **fruits** <note>original: "fructus"; the profits, crops, or income generated by the property</note>. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors (following the gloss on the word *referatur* in the law *donationes quas parentes*), which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in his commentary on Law 50 of Toro, number 65, and in the second volume of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 23; Julius Clarus, question 9, number 7; Gregorio López in his cited gloss; and Covarruvias in...

As a result, a thing given in this way does not begin to be acquired through <term>usucapion</term><note>The legal process of gaining ownership of property through long-term undisturbed possession</note> until the gift is confirmed by the death of the donor, as Gregorio Lopez correctly observes in the passage cited. Furthermore, as was stated in the preceding paragraph, if the gift was not <term>registered</term><note>original: "insinuata"; the formal public recording of a gift, usually required for large amounts</note> but was nonetheless confirmed by the donor's last will, then regarding the portion that exceeds the legal limit allowed without registration, the gift does not apply retroactively to the time of delivery. Instead, the profits from that portion would only belong to the recipient from the moment of the donor's death.

<margin>9</margin>
It must also be observed that in such gifts between the living made by one spouse to another—if they were either registered or do not exceed the amount allowed without registration—the ownership of the gift passes to the recipient immediately upon the donor's death. This happens without having to wait for the <term>acceptance of the inheritance</term><note>original: "aditione hæreditatis"; the formal act by which an heir accepts the rights and obligations of the deceased</note> by the heir. In this respect, these gifts differ from legacies, as was discussed in previous sections regarding death-bed gifts. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the Doctors, which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in his *Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 4, number 23. However, if such a gift was not registered and it exceeds the legal limit, then for the excess amount, ownership does not pass to the recipient unless the heir has first accepted the inheritance. This is because, regarding the excess, the gift has the legal force of a legacy. If the excess was small, then by <term>concomitance</term><note>the principle that a small incidental part follows the legal status of the main part</note> (according to what was said in Disputation 57), ownership of the excess would pass to the recipient along with the rest of the item, because it is mixed together and one cannot easily designate which part of the item constitutes the excess and which does not. On the other hand, if the value of five hundred <term>solidi</term><note>gold coins used as a standard for the registration limit</note> was small compared to the excess, then ownership would certainly not be acquired by the recipient before the heir accepts the inheritance.

<margin>10</margin>
From a gift between husband and wife, the <term>Falcidian portion</term><note>original: "falcidia"; a Roman law rule ensuring that a legal heir receives at least one-quarter of the estate</note> is deducted just as it is from legacies. This is established in the Code under the Falcidian Law and in the Digest regarding gifts between spouses. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the legal scholars, as stated in the preceding disputation.

<margin>11</margin>
A <term>death-bed gift</term><note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note> between spouses is not confirmed by the death of the donor in two specific events. The first is if the recipient dies before the donor; in that case, the gift is rendered void. This is clear from the Digest and the Code under the relevant titles. However, if both spouses die in the same shipwreck, house collapse, fire, or similar event, and it is not clearly established who died first, then the gift is confirmed. If such spouses had made reciprocal gifts to each other, the gifts of both would remain confirmed and valid. This is expressly stated in the Digest regarding "Doubtful Matters," and the common opinion follows this, as cited by Antonio Gómez, Emmanuel Acosta, and Covarruvias. The reason is that, since the gift was already made and the item delivered to the recipient who possessed it, and since it is confirmed by the death of the

<column-break/>

donor, and it is not certain that the recipient died before the donor, the gift is considered valid in favor of the recipient who is in possession. This is especially true since the decree of Emperor Antoninus only requires two things for the gift to hold: that the donor did not revoke it while alive, and that the recipient did not die before the donor—and in this case, the latter cannot be proven. Thus, Covarruvias rightly affirms, along with Bartolus and others, that even if both spouses died in different places from different causes, so long as it is not proven that the recipient died first, the gift should be deemed valid. It is up to the donor's heirs to prove that the recipient died first. Emmanuel Acosta correctly notes that if the spouses had given to each other mutually on the condition that "whoever dies last gets the goods," then if both died simultaneously in a shipwreck or collapse, and it was unclear who died last, the gift would be entirely void. This is because the gift was made under a positive condition ("if one survives the other"), and that condition was not met, but rather failed.

<margin>12</margin>
The second event in which a gift between spouses is not confirmed by the donor's death is if the donor <insert>either implicitly or expressly</insert> revokes the gift. The donor has the full legal right to do this. This is found in the Digest, the Code, and the **Portuguese Ordinances**, Book 4, Title 9. It is not even necessary for the donor to physically take back the item or the possession; it is enough if there is evidence that the donor "changed their mind" <note>original: "pænitentia"; legal regret or withdrawal of intent</note> and persisted in that state until death without re-confirming the gift.

<margin>13</margin>
A gift is considered implicitly revoked if a divorce occurs between the spouses in the meantime, as noted in the Digest and Code—unless the divorce was by mutual consent and goodwill, or if it is clear the donor intended the gift to persist nonetheless. Similarly, a gift is considered implicitly revoked if the donor sells, exchanges, bequeaths, or gives the same item to someone else. Indeed, even if they give it to another as a pledge or subject it to a specific mortgage, it is revoked unless the donor's intent to let the gift stand is clear.
<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Furthermore, in **Portuguese Law** <note>original: "Ius Lusitanú"</note>, it is established that if one spouse gives a gift to the other at a time when they had no children, and later children are born to the donor, the gift is automatically revoked. When the marriage is dissolved by death, that property must be divided between the survivor and the heirs of the deceased. The same applies if the gift was made before the marriage contract; if children are born and the property becomes communal according to the custom of the kingdom, then upon dissolution, the gift is divided equally. This is prescribed for similar cases. Since all these matters are arranged in a single line of legal reasoning, the first part of this rule might seem unreasonable if it were understood as applying once the marriage was celebrated...

->### Second Treatise, Disputation 289<-

In a contract involving <term>earnest money</term><note>original: "artharum"; refers to 'arras,' a sum of money or property pledged by the husband to the wife at the start of a marriage</note> and dowry, equity does not allow for a specific outcome: namely, that if a wife gave her husband something from her dowry or her <term>paraphernal goods</term><note>Property belonging to a married woman that she owned independently of her dowry</note>, or if a husband gave his own goods to his wife, and children were subsequently born, the donated item would be divided equally between the surviving spouse and the heirs of the deceased. I understand the first part of this provision to apply only when the marriage was celebrated under a contract of "half-shares" <note>A system where spouses shared ownership of all property acquired during the marriage</note>, as the rest of that regulation speaks only of that case. However, when a marriage is celebrated under a contract of earnest money and dowry, one must abide by the provision of the <term>common law</term><note>The Roman Law used as a standard across Europe</note> (Law 4, *Code: On the revocation of gifts*), as discussed in Disputation 281. Consequently, the entire gift would belong to the heirs of the deceased if the donor died without a will. But if the donor had made a will, they could dispose of a third of that property as they pleased, just as they could with a third of their other remaining assets. Guterrius, in *On the Confirmation of Oaths* (part 1, chapter 3, number 16), refers to Law 3, title 12, book 3 of the *Fuero* <note>The *Fuero Real*, a 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>, which states: <note>original Spanish: "**Si el marido quisiere dar algo a muger, o la muger a el marido... fuera quanto en su quinto.**"</note> **"If the husband should wish to give anything to his wife, or the wife to her husband, provided there are no children, they may do so after one year has passed since they were married, and not before. And if after this gift children are born, the gift shall not be valid, except for up to one-fifth of the value."**

<margin>Castilian Law.</margin>
Here, first of all, you see that the common law is modified: a gift between spouses is valid immediately and does not require confirmation by the death of the donor, provided it is made after one year of marriage and they have no children. It is further modified in that the gift is not entirely revoked by the birth of children, but remains valid up to a <term>fifth</term><note>The "quinto" was the portion of an estate that a person with children could freely give away under Spanish law; the rest was reserved for heirs</note> of the donor's goods. Although Antonio Gómez (on Law 5 of Toro, number 66) considers this a unique rule and, along with Palacios Rubios, believes it only applies in the Kingdom of Castile, he thinks the common law applies regarding the first year of marriage. He suggests that gifts made within the first year are confirmed simply by the passing of that year, much like gifts are confirmed by the death of the donor in common law. However, the same Guterrius (at the cited location, number 25), along with Rodrigo Suárez, Gregorio Lopez, and others, says that one should not judge according to the laws of the *Fuero* unless it is proven they have been accepted by custom. Indeed, they argue it is not established that the cited law was accepted by custom, but rather the opposite seems true—especially since that law was not included in the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish laws compiled in 1567</note>.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Returning to Portuguese law, in the cited Title 9, first paragraph, it is established that when a gift is confirmed by the death of the donor, if that donor leaves behind heirs in the ascending line (parents/grandparents) or descending line (children/grandchildren), and that gift encroaches upon their <term>legitimate portions</term><note>The "legitima," the legally protected portion of an estate that must go to direct heirs</note>, the heirs can revoke the gift to the extent that it touches their portions. The gift itself is calculated among the assets from which the legitimate portion is drawn, and the remainder belongs to the recipient of the gift. This confirms that gifts can be declared <term>undutiful</term><note>original: "inofficiosas"; a legal term for gifts that unfairly reduce the inheritance of forced heirs</note> not only in relation to descendants but also to ancestors, as was stated in Disputation 283. In the same paragraph, joined with the second paragraph, it is added: if the donor disposed of a <term>third</term><note>In Portugal, the "terço" or third was the portion of the estate one could freely give away, regardless of having children</note> of their goods through a gift, the donated items are calculated with the rest of the deceased's assets, and the legitimate portions are drawn from the whole pile. The gift is then treated as a legacy

<column-break/>

so that the third of the deceased's goods is divided proportionally between that gift and any other legacies. In this way, the gift and the other legacies are reduced proportionally as much as necessary so that the heirs' legitimate portions remain intact. All of this should be done similarly in the Kingdom of Castile if the donor leaves only ancestors as heirs. However, if the donor leaves descendants, the same should be done, but in relation to a **fifth** of the goods, which is the only portion a person leaving descendants can dispose of in this kingdom.

<margin>Castilian Law.</margin>
For the entire Portuguese provision contained in the cited paragraphs 1 and 2 is consistent with common law, assuming that in Portugal it is lawful to dispose of a third of one's goods, whether the testator has ancestors or descendants.

Antonio Gómez observes (on Law 50 of Toro, number 67) that in cases where a gift between spouses is revoked, if the recipient had consumed the donated item, they are only liable for the amount by which they were enriched. However, I believe this is only true if the item perished without the recipient's fault, or if it was spent usefully on expenses that the husband was otherwise bound to pay, or which he was satisfied for the wife to pay. It is different if the recipient gave the item away or consumed it uselessly. For as long as they saw that the gift was not yet confirmed by the donor's death, it was not lawful for them to spend it uselessly or squander it. The laws cited by Antonio Gómez do not prove more than this. I understand the law regarding the <term>Falcidian portion</term><note>A Roman law rule ensuring an heir received at least one-fourth of the inheritance after legacies were paid</note> in the same way.

<margin>15</margin>
In the following circumstances, a gift between husband and wife is valid immediately: First, if it is made by an Emperor, King, or other prince who recognizes no superior, to an Empress, Queen, or similar wife—or conversely, from such wives to their husbands. This is held in the second-to-last law of the Code, *On gifts between husband and wife*.

Second, if a husband gives to a wife, or a wife to a husband, for the restoration of buildings destroyed by fire, but only for the amount required for the construction of the building.

Third, if the gift is made for the sake of compensation or <term>remuneration</term><note>A "remuneratory gift" is one given in return for a service or benefit, rather than out of pure's generosity</note>. For example, if a husband and wife give something to each other mutually: in that case, even if one consumes the thing given to them while the other keeps theirs, the gift is valid immediately. This is affirmed by Gama (Decision 231, number 2). By this reasoning, if an old or low-born husband gives to a young or noble wife as a reward for her nobility or youth, or conversely if an old or low-born wife gives to a young or noble husband in recompense for his nobility or youth, the gift is valid immediately. This is the common opinion of the Doctors, cited by Bartolus, Panormitanus, Covarrubias, and Antonio Gómez.

However, Giulio Claro (Question 9, cited above, number 5) believes this should be limited so that it only has force when it occurs in the very act of establishing the dowry, not...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Disputation 289 regarding the validity of gifts (donations) between spouses under Roman civil law, Spanish law (the Partidas), and Portuguese law. It specifically addresses exceptions where gifts are immediately valid rather than being suspended until the death of the donor.</meta>

->### Disputation 289 continued<-

...but after the dowry has been established and the marriage has been contracted; however, the <term>doctors of law</term><note>The "doctores" refers to the established legal commentators and authorities of the time.</note> generally affirm the contrary.

Fourth, when one of the spouses gives to the other so that they may attain some <term>dignity</term><note>A rank, public office, or title of honor.</note>: the gift is indeed immediately valid up to the amount necessary for that purpose (Law *quod adipiscendæ*, and the two following, <note>original: "ff. de don. inter vir. & vxor."; referring to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman law</note>).

Fifth, when the donor does not become poorer by giving, even if the recipient becomes richer. Likewise, when the recipient does not become richer, even if the donor becomes poorer. This is held in the chapter *vir.* on gifts between husband and wife, Law 4, 5, and 6, title 11, part 4 [of the *Partidas*], and book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 9, paragraph 2, and in the laws to be cited immediately.

<margin>16</margin> At this point, observe that in the case proposed, a donor is not said to become "poorer" by the fact that they do not acquire something to which they had a right that depended on their own acceptance; therefore, they are not said to become poorer if they renounce that right in favor of the recipient spouse. However, they are considered to become poorer if, after having accepted it, they then gave it to the other spouse; in that case, such a gift would not be valid unless it were confirmed by death. Thus, if something is given to a husband, and by the husband's order it is given to the wife—and the wife only receives it after the husband has accepted it—that gift is not confirmed except by the death of the husband (as held in Law 3, final paragraph, of the Digest).

An example of when a donor does not become poorer by giving: if someone were to appoint one spouse as an heir, or leave them a legacy, and name the other spouse as a <term>substitute</term><note>A person designated to receive an inheritance if the primary heir cannot or will not take it.</note>. If the first spouse renounces the inheritance or legacy in the form of a gift in favor of the substitute, not accepting it themselves, the gift would be valid. This is because, in the sense explained, the donor does not become poorer, even though the recipient becomes richer (as held in Law *si sponsus* and the following sections of the Digest, and Law 5, title 11, part 4). Another example is if one spouse gives the other a property belonging to someone else: because the donor does not become poorer (since they are not giving their own property), the gift is valid for the purpose of starting <term>usucaption</term><note>The legal process by which ownership of a thing is acquired by long-continued possession.</note> from the moment of delivery.

<margin>17</margin> From this doctrine and these examples, Antonio Gomez and others infer that a <term>renunciation</term><note>A formal rejection of a right or claim.</note> is immediately valid whereby a wife, while the marriage is still standing, renounces to her husband the profits gained from the assets of both. However, I believe with Gregorio Lopez that this is false. Because in this kingdom (or in Portugal, assuming the custom of that kingdom regarding the contract of <term>earnest money</term> and dowry), once the marriage is celebrated, half of the profits are owed to the wife by the power of the contract alone, independent of any new acceptance. Thus, she transmits this right to any of her heirs. Since a gift—and even a remission of debt—between spouses is invalid unless confirmed by death, it follows that such a renunciation is invalid unless confirmed by death, and unless it is formally recorded if it exceeds the sum allowed to be given without such a record. Read more in Gregorio Lopez, who confirms this same point in the cited place.

<column-break/>

<margin>18</margin> Examples of when the recipient does not become richer, even if the donor becomes poorer, are as follows: If a wife buys perfumes for her own adornment from things given by her husband. Likewise, if one spouse gives the other a burial plot, or something that the recipient then gives to a monastery, a Church, or for divine worship. For besides the fact that these things are given to become religious or for the service of God, the recipient does not become richer from them while they live, even though perhaps, if they had not been given, the recipient would have spent money to acquire them and thus would have become poorer.

This is held in Law *si sponsus* of the Digest and Law 6, title 11, part 4. Furthermore, if a wife gives to her husband so that he may give it as a dowry for the daughter of both, or if after she gave it, she allowed it to be given as a daughter's dowry, the gift is valid on the same grounds (as held in the Law *si ue uxor* of the Digest).

Observe this: in cases where a gift between spouses is immediately valid, if after calculating such gifts the <term>descendants</term><note>Children or grandchildren.</note> or <term>ascendants</term><note>Parents or grandparents.</note> do not have their full <term>legitimate portions</term><note>The minimum share of an estate that must by law be left to certain heirs.</note>, the amount missing to complete those shares must be taken from the donor's <term>third</term><note>The "tercio," or one-third of the estate which a person could freely give away in their will under Spanish law.</note>, not from the gift made to the spouse. But if the "third" is not enough, then the missing amount must be supplied from the gift. This is held in book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances. I believe the same should be said according to the common law and the nature of the matter: this holds true even if the gift were confirmed by an oath (as we will discuss next), because an oath cannot prejudice the legitimate portions owed to descendants or ascendants from the donor's assets.

<margin>19 A Doubt</margin> The final doubt in this disputation is whether a gift made by one spouse to another—which normally is not confirmed except by the donor's death—becomes irrevocable if it is confirmed by an oath, and thus becomes valid by that very fact. To this, following the common opinion of the doctors (including Panormitanus, Bartolus, Covarruvias, and others), it must be said that it is undoubtedly confirmed and valid. It is no less valid than a sale made by a minor or the sale of dowry land, which are valid if confirmed by an oath, even though they would be void or legally null without the oath. This is clear from what was said in Disputation 149 and the two following.

The reason is that such a gift is not against natural good morals, nor is it prohibited by <term>positive law</term><note>Laws created by human authorities rather than natural or divine law.</note>, nor even rendered null; rather, by human law alone, it is made dependent on the death of the donor occurring before the death of the recipient, with the donor granted the power to freely revoke it while they live. Both of these conditions cease the moment an oath is taken...

<meta>catchword: ...oath</meta>

<summary>Molina discusses exceptions to the rule that gifts between spouses are only valid upon death, such as when the gift is for a public office, when the donor doesn't become poorer (like renouncing a legacy), or when the gift is for religious purposes. He also addresses the power of an oath to make such gifts irrevocable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of donations between spouses, specifically focusing on gifts confirmed by oath and the legal category of betrothal gifts known as "sponsalitia largitas."</meta>

...and confirmed by an oath, not only because an oath regarding a lawful matter must be kept under penalty of <term>mortal sin</term><note>A grave sin that, in Catholic theology, severs the relationship with God.</note>, but also because when it concerns a lawful matter, and the thing is not received unjustly by the recipient, it transfers a true right to them, by which it is henceforth owed to them. Indeed, it transfers <term>ownership</term><note>original: "dominium"; the full legal right to a property</note> if <term>delivery</term><note>original: "traditio"; the physical or symbolic handing over of an item</note> follows: all of which are found in the matter we are discussing. Thus, such a donation is not only valid and irrevocable if delivery follows, but even if only a promise confirmed by an oath occurs without delivery.

However, it must be observed that under <term>Portuguese Law</term><note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, far from an oath making the donation irrevocable, it is by that very fact null and void, unless such an oath was applied with the King's license, according to what was said in Disputation 149.

## Concerning betrothal gifts, and donations before or on account of marriage.

### DISPUTATION 290.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *What betrothal bounty is.*
2 *Betrothal bounty, if nothing else is specified, is always understood to be under the condition of a future marriage.*
3 *In which cases betrothal bounty is valid, even if marriage does not follow.*
*And regarding the laws of Castile and Portugal, numbers 4, 5.*
6 *When things given as betrothal bounty are considered lost by the groom to the bride.*
7 *Betrothal bounty does not require formal registration, regardless of the amount.*
8 *What pre-nuptial and marriage-related donations are under common law.*
9 *What a marriage donation is in the Spanish territories.*

1 That which one future spouse gives to the other before a marriage contracted through <term>vows in the present</term><note>original: "verba de praesenti"; words that create a legally binding marriage immediately, such as "I take you as my wife," as opposed to "I will take you."</note> is called <term>betrothal bounty</term><note>original: "sponsalitia largitas"; a legal term for gifts given during the engagement period.</note>. Although formerly, before the time of <term>Constantine</term><note>The Roman Emperor (r. 306–337 AD); his laws heavily influenced later European marriage law.</note>, what one gave to the other became the absolute property of the recipient immediately unless it was specified that it was given under the condition of a future marriage—so that even if marriage did not follow, neither the recipient nor their heirs were bound to restore it, as is clear in the Law "If daughters" in the Code on pre-nuptial donations and other laws—2 from the time of Constantine it was decreed that such a donation, when nothing else is specified, is always understood to be made under the condition of a future marriage. If the marriage is completed, the entire thing given becomes the recipient's property by that agreement.

3 If, however, it is not completed, a distinction must be made. For it is either not completed through the fault of the donor; in which case, the entire thing similarly becomes the recipient's property. But if the one through whose fault the marriage is not completed had conversely received some gift from the other spouse, they nonetheless restore it in full to the giver. If, however, the marriage is not completed through the fault of the recipient, then they restore everything they received as a gift to the donor. All these things are established in the Law "Since the ancients" in the Code on pre-nuptial donations, and Law 3, title 11, part 4 [of the *Partidas*].

<column-break/>

See the Law on this matter by Antonio Gomez on Law 52 of Toro, number 1 and following.

When, however, the marriage is not completed without any fault of the spouses—such as by the death of one of the donors, or because one enters a <term>religious order</term><note>Becoming a monk or nun before the marriage is consummated.</note> before it is contracted or consummated, or for another similar reason—then a distinction must be made. For if the donation was made by the groom to the bride, and neither <term>intercourse</term><note>original: "copula"</note> nor a <term>kiss</term><note>original: "osculum"; in Roman and Medieval law, a formal kiss during betrothal had specific legal consequences for property rights.</note> occurred, then the groom or his heirs recover everything that was given. If, however, a kiss occurred, they only recover half; the other half belongs to the bride or her heirs.

If intercourse occurred before the decree of the <term>Council of Trent</term><note>A major church council (1545–1563) that refined marriage laws, requiring a priest and witnesses for a marriage to be valid.</note>, everything belonged to the bride or her heirs because by that very act the marriage was considered celebrated and consummated. Today, however, since by intercourse following only betrothal, the marriage is considered neither consummated nor celebrated, the bride gains no more through intercourse than through a kiss alone.

When the donation was made to the groom by the bride, then whether a kiss or intercourse occurred or not, the bride or her heirs recover everything that had been given. All these things are found in the Law "If by the groom" in the Code on pre-nuptial donations and Law 3, title 11, part 4.

These rules also apply when the marriage is either not completed or not consummated due to one of the spouses entering a religious order. For since they do this without any fault of their own, the bride would gain half of the things given to her through a kiss, just as if the betrothal were dissolved by the other's death, as the <term>gloss</term><note>A marginal or interlinear commentary on a legal text.</note> affirms on the chapter "Legal decrees," question 2, on the word "gift," and the Law "God is with us" in the Code on bishops and clerics agrees; and the doctors commonly affirm this, whom Antonio Gomez cites and follows on Law 52 of Toro, number 8.

<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>
4 Observe several things regarding what has been said so far. First, regarding the law of the <term>Kingdom of Castile</term><note>A major kingdom in what is now Spain.</note> after Law 52 of Toro, among betrothal bounties are also counted those things which spouses give to one another through vows in the present before the marriage is consummated by intercourse; nor do these have the status of "donations between husband and wife" in this kingdom as they do under <term>Common Law</term><note>original: "iure communi"; referring to the shared Roman and Canon law of Europe.</note> and in Portugal, as was said in the preceding disputation. Therefore, what was said a little earlier regarding the profit of half of these donations when a kiss occurs and the betrothal is dissolved by death or entry into religion, similarly applies in this kingdom when a marriage by vows in the present is dissolved in any of those ways before it is consummated by intercourse.

<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>
Second, regarding the law of Castile, when a marriage is dissolved and the wife gains the <term>arrhas</term><note>original: "arrhas"; a pledge or earnest money, often a specific portion of the groom's property (up to 1/10th in Spanish law) given to the bride.</note>, and some betrothal bounty or bounties made by the groom to the bride preceded it, then the wife does not gain both, but only one of them. It is granted to her, or her heirs if she has died, that within twenty days of the dissolution of the marriage, they may choose either the *arrhas* or the betrothal bounty or bounties. If they have not chosen within that time, then it falls to the husband or his heirs to give whichever of those they prefer—namely, either the *arrhas* alone or only the betrothal bounty or bounties.
