<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of marriage gifts, specifically addressing how Portuguese law differs from general civil law regarding the timing of property sharing and the registration of high-value gifts between spouses.</meta>

<header>Ludwig Molina on Contracts.</header>

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
The third point is that in Portugal, when a marriage is celebrated under the contract of <term>half of goods</term><note>original: "medietatis bonorum"; a legal arrangement where each spouse owns half of the combined household assets.</note>, the rules stated regarding <term>betrothal bounty</term><note>original: "sponsalitia largitas"; gifts given during the engagement period.</note> only apply before the marriage is consummated through physical union. Indeed, until that point, the assets of the contracting parties are not held in common. However, once the marriage is consummated, since the assets of the spouses become common property—as is clear from Book 2, Title 47 of the Ordinances—it follows that assets bestowed by one spouse on the other through betrothal bounty (and indeed gifts from any third party) become common to both spouses. Upon the dissolution of the marriage, these must be divided between the husband and wife, unless at the time of the donation it was specifically granted under the condition that, should the marriage end, the assets would remain the private property of the recipient. This, however, rarely if ever happens. Furthermore, in this event, Book 4, Title 9 of the Ordinances seems to establish in its introduction that if they have children at the time the marriage is dissolved, the matter should be divided between both spouses.

<margin>Doubt 6 Decision.</margin>
The fourth point is that there is a significant doubt: whether the things a groom sends to a bride before the marriage is contracted through <term>words of the present</term><note>original: "per verba de praesenti"; the formal exchange of vows that created a legal marriage before the Council of Trent.</note>, or in this kingdom before it is consummated, should be considered gifts via betrothal bounty (so that they become the wife’s property), or whether they should merely be considered "sent" so that the bride may come to the husband more elegantly adorned. In this latter view, the items are for her honor and to show the affection with which she is to be treated during the marriage, but <term>ownership</term><note>original: "dominium"</note> of these items does not pass to her. 
Regarding this doubt, regardless of what Antonio Gomez said to the contrary in his commentary on Law 52 of Toro, it must undoubtedly be said that unless it is clearly evident that the groom sent them with the intent of donating them, it must be judged that they were sent only for the latter purposes we explained. Therefore, neither does ownership pass to her, nor does she claim these as her own special property when the marriage is dissolved. Likewise, she does not gain half of them through the <term>kiss</term><note>A legal custom where a betrothal kiss entitled the woman to half the engagement gifts if the man died or broke the engagement.</note> if the betrothal is dissolved before the marriage is contracted or, in this kingdom, before the marriage is consummated. This is the common opinion of the doctors following Bartolus, which Julius Clarus and Gama (Decision 71) cite and follow; it was according to this opinion that the decision was made in Portugal. For as the <term>gloss</term><note>Standard medieval commentary on legal texts.</note> on the law "When anything" (Digest: *Si certum petatur*) argues: a donation should never be assumed when there is a suspicion that something was bestowed for a reason other than pure gift-giving.

<margin>7</margin>
The fifth point is that in the case of such betrothal bounty, when it is a true donation, it does not seem that <term>registration</term><note>original: "insinuatio"; the formal recording of a gift in public records, usually required for gifts exceeding 500 gold coins (solidi).</note> is necessary for it to be valid and for ownership to transfer, even if it exceeds the value of five hundred <term>solidi</term><note>A traditional unit of currency in Roman and medieval law.</note>. Just as registration is not necessary in the gathering of <term>earnest money</term><note>original: "arrhatũ"; often referred to in Spanish law as "arras," a pledge of assets given by the groom.</note>. This is clearly hinted at in Law 52 of Toro, where the whole amount (without any distinction) is said to belong to the bride, or half if only a kiss occurred. I hear this is the accepted practice in Portugal; the <term>Authentic</term><note>A later supplement to the Justinian Code.</note> "regarding betrothal bounty" agrees in its introduction, even if the gloss in that same place rightly says that "betrothal bounty" is understood in a far different sense in that context.

<margin>8</margin>
A "donation before marriage" or "on account of marriage," of which the law speaks, was a specific kind of gift that

<column-break/>

a husband, or the husband's father, grandfather, or another in the husband's place, made to the wife on account of the marriage as a compensation for the <term>dowry</term><note>The assets brought by the bride to the marriage.</note>, and for the greater security and protection of that dowry. It belonged to the wife while the marriage lasted, although the administration and the profits from it belonged to the husband. When the marriage was dissolved, however, a gift of this kind returned to the husband and became his property.
And since this donation was formerly only made before the wedding, it was called a "donation before marriage." But later, because it was permitted that both the gift and the dowry could be made, established, or increased after the wedding was celebrated, it was called a "donation on account of marriage," as found in the *Institutes* regarding donations. All of these points, besides the law just cited, are evident from the final law and the Authentic "dowry given," and throughout the whole title of the Code "On donations before marriage," and from Law 1, Title 11, Part 4.
Today, however, "donation on account of marriage" in that specific sense is not in use, especially in the Spains. In its place in the Spains, <term>arras</term><note>original: "archae"; a Spanish legal custom where the groom pledges a portion of his current and future property to the wife.</note> have succeeded in the sense that they are customarily given by husbands to wives. Nevertheless, a "donation on account of marriage," as discussed in <term>Imperial Law</term><note>original: "Cęsareo iure"; Roman civil law.</note>, differs greatly from *arras* in this sense, as will be said in another place. Antonio Gomez, Julius Clarus, Gregorio Lopez, Alvarez Valasco, and Covarrubias all agree on these points.

<margin>9</margin>
By some today, and even by the Laws of Toro (as mentioned in Disputation 238), a "donation on account of marriage" refers to what is given by parents or others to a male so that he may take a wife. This meaning, however, is far different from the one used in Imperial Law. It would be more appropriate to call that donation a "donation *for* the wedding," primarily because that would remove ambiguity and distinguish this donation from the "donation *on account of* marriage" which was used in ancient times and of which the laws speak.

Regarding a simple donation from a father to a son, almost everything that could be said here was stated in Disputation 243. Namely, regarding <term>common law</term><note>original: "iure communi"; here referring to the general body of Roman and Civil law.</note>, if from a father...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 21

...to the son—or to a child of either sex who is under the father’s <term>legal power</term><note>original: "potestas"; the Roman legal concept of patria potestas, where a father held significant legal control over his children’s property and person.</note>—is invalid unless the <term>delivery</term><note>original: "traditio"; the physical or symbolic transfer of possession of an item.</note> was performed by the father. Furthermore, even if delivery was made, the father retains the right to revoke the gift at any time during his life. If he does not revoke it, the gift is confirmed upon the father's death and becomes entirely valid. This validity is retroactive to the time of the original delivery, so that any profits or "fruits" gathered from the gifted property belong to the son. This applies provided that a formal <term>registration</term><note>original: "insinuatio"; the public recording of a gift, which was legally required for donations exceeding a certain value (usually 500 gold coins).</note> was made, if the value exceeds the amount permitted to be given without such registration. Otherwise, the gift is not confirmed by the father’s death alone regarding the excess value, unless the father expressly confirms it at the time of death. In that case, the excess value will be valid not as a standard gift, but as a <term>legacy</term><note>original: "legati"; a gift left in a will, which did not require the same public registration as a lifetime gift.</note>, which does not require registration. However, the profits and use of the property gained through delivery up until the father's death will not be applied retroactively to the son; these matters follow the same rules as donations between spouses, as explained in Disputation 289. This is also clear from the laws regarding gifts from parents, as noted in the <term>Ordinary Gloss</term><note>original: "glo. ibi"; the standard medieval legal commentary on Roman law.</note> on the Code regarding donations between husband and wife, and in the laws cited by Antonio Gómez, Covarruvias, and other common authorities.

<margin>2</margin> The following cases are excepted, in which a gift made by a father to a son under his power is valid immediately:

The first is if it is confirmed by law, as mentioned in Disputation 243. This is proven in the same way we showed for gifts between spouses in Disputation 289, a view followed by Julius Clarus, Covarruvias, and Gutierrez. **Note an exception in Portugal:** an oath of this kind is not valid unless it includes an express license from the King, as stated in Disputations 240, 243, and 289.

The second is if a father gives his son (who is under his power) the <term>usufruct</term><note>original: "usufructum"; the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another.</note> of "adventitious" assets—those assets the son acquired from a source other than the father—following what was said in Disputation 8.

The third is if he gives movable goods to a son under his power who is setting out for war or to the royal court. In such a case, the gift is valid immediately and the items become <term>military property</term><note>original: "bona castrensia"; property a son could own and control independently of his father's power, traditionally earned through military service.</note>, as stated in Disputation 23. However, in Portugal, the son is bound to return to the father whatever remains upon his return. Similarly, a gift of books from a father to a son under his power who is preparing to practice a profession he has studied is confirmed immediately. The same applies to anything else given for the exercise of that profession. The reason is that all such goods are treated as "quasi-military property" of the son. However, all these gifts discussed in this third case should perhaps be viewed as <term>remuneratory gifts</term><note>original: "donationes ob causam"; gifts given for a specific reason or service rendered, rather than pure generosity.</note> rather than simple gifts.

<column-break/>

The fourth case, added by many, is when the father's gift to the son under his power is a reward for services rendered. However, this is a remuneratory gift rather than the simple gift we are currently discussing. We discussed whether such a gift is valid immediately and whether it must be accounted for in an inheritance in Disputation 244.

Navarrus, following Azor, adds that generally in all circumstances where gifts between spouses are valid immediately (as discussed in Disputation 289), they are also valid if made by a father to a son under his power, because these two types of donations are legally equivalent. Thus, he holds that if a father gives something to a son to help him obtain a dignity or office, or in other cases explained in the cited disputation, the gift is valid immediately. However, this requires greater evidence than just Azor's opinion. Since these matters depend on <term>positive law</term><note>original: "iuris positiui"; laws enacted by a government or ruler rather than natural or divine law.</note>, one would need to produce a specific text proving that rules established for one of these types of gifts must be understood to apply to the other.

Furthermore, in Disputation 243, it was stated that under <term>Common Law</term><note>original: "iure communi"; the shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law.</note>, a simple gift made by a father to an <term>emancipated</term><note>original: "emancipato"; a child legally freed from the father's power.</note> son or daughter, or by a mother or maternal grandparents (and today in Portugal, by a paternal grandfather) to a child—whether emancipated or not—is valid immediately, even if delivery has not taken place.

Consequently, in Portugal, a gift to a married son is valid because he is considered emancipated by the very fact of his marriage. This is supported by the Code under the titles on donations and confirmed by Antonio Gómez and other common doctors.

<margin>3</margin> It has also been said regarding the Law of Castile, following the Laws of Toro (specifically Law 17 and Law 26), that every simple gift made to a son—whether he is under paternal power or <term>independent</term><note>original: "sui iuris"; legally independent.</note>—is entirely valid without the need for delivery, whether the gift comes from the father, mother, or other ancestors.

<margin>Castilian Law.</margin> Nevertheless, such a gift can be revoked at will until the death of the giver if delivery was not made. But if delivery was made, even through a "constitutum" clause (a legal phrasing acknowledging the transfer), the gift is entirely firm and irrevocable.

Thus, the Common Law is corrected in three ways: First, because a gift from a father to a son under his power without delivery is valid and confirmed by the father's death (the opposite of Common Law). Second, because a gift to that same son, if accompanied by delivery, is immediately firm and irrevocable (the opposite of Common Law).

Third, because a gift made by a father to an emancipated son, or by a mother or other ancestors to even a dependent son, was firm and irrevocable under Common Law even without delivery; but under Castilian Law, it is always revocable until the death of the giver if delivery has not occurred.

Regarding the points made in this third section, Gregorius and others agree.

# On remuneratory donations, and generally on donations for a cause.

## DISPUTATION 292.

### SUMMARY.

1. Remuneratory donation is of three kinds.

Finally, donation in general can be divided into donation for a cause <note>original: "ob causam"; a gift given for a specific reason or expected action.</note> and simple donation, or one not for a cause. What each type of gift is was explained in Disputations 238 and 243. Furthermore, donation for a cause can be divided into a remuneratory donation—such as one made because of services or a benefit received—and a donation made for any other reasons. However, so much has been said so far in various places about both remuneratory donations and those for other causes, that this dispute might rightly be judged as overflowing. Nevertheless, we thought it worthy to mention them under a specific title and dispute, adding a few points regarding remuneratory donation.

In my judgment, three types of remuneratory donation can be distinguished. The first is that by which services received are compensated to the point of equality, so that if it were not done, not only would great ingratitude be committed, but an action—either for <term>unauthorized management</term><note>original: "negociorum gestorum"; a legal claim for expenses incurred by someone acting on another's behalf without prior authorization.</note> or another similar claim—could be brought, because the services are not considered to have been provided purely for free. Concerning such donations, the law is discussed in the <term>Digest</term><note>original: "ff."; an abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Justinian’s Roman law.</note> under the laws *Aquilius regulus* and *hoc iure*, the final section, joined with the preceding ones, and the law *si pater*, final section, on donations. It was said of these same donations in Disputation 279, following the common opinion of the doctors, that they do not require <term>registration</term><note>original: "insinuatione"; the formal public recording of a gift to make it legally binding.</note>, and in Disputation 281, that they cannot be revoked on account of ingratitude.

Furthermore, regarding these same donations, a person who is otherwise prohibited from giving—provided they have the administration of the goods—is not considered prohibited from making remuneratory donations. As Panormitanus notes with Bartolus in the rubric on donations, and the chapter *per tuas*, number 6, under the same title; Sylvester under the word "donation," question 3; and other doctors. This is gathered from the laws cited, because this is not, strictly speaking, "giving." It is also gathered from chapter *si quos*, 12, question 2, where it is defined that a prelate <note>A high-ranking church official.</note>, who cannot alienate property without formal ceremony, may nevertheless make appropriate remunerations of this kind without such ceremony.

The second type is that by which a benefit or service provided is compensated out of gratitude to the point of equality, yet it could be omitted without fault; for in such a remunerator, gratitude and liberality are seen rather than a debt. For example, when something is given out of gratitude to a servant who has served energetically for his salary, because he is worthy of the reward, even though it could be omitted without fault; and in other similar events. Such remunerations can be made by a prelate who administers the goods of a monastery, and even a <term>guardian</term><note>original: "tutor"; someone legally responsible for a minor's property.</note> from the goods of a <term>ward</term><note>original: "pupilli".</note>, and others like them.

<column-break/>

A secular bishop can do far more regarding the goods of his bishopric, as can the head of a household regarding his own goods. Nor do I believe the head of a household in Portugal is bound to count these gifts against the <term>one-third</term><note>original: "tertio"; under Portuguese law, a person could only freely give away one-third of their estate away from their heirs.</note> of his goods, or in Castile against the <term>one-fifth</term><note>original: "quinto"; the equivalent limit in Spanish law.</note>, if he made them while he was still living. For such donations pertain to the proper administration of goods, even if they were of no small amount, considering the quantity of services or benefits they had received.

You might say, "provided that he made them while he was still living." Since the administration of the goods of a monastic prelate, a secular bishop, and the head of a household ends with their lives, it is clear that neither the prelate through a last will—nor indeed the secular bishop regarding the goods of the bishopric, which he cannot bequeath—can validly command that such remuneratory donations be made after their death. Nevertheless, even a monastic prelate could and should advise that remunerations of the first type be paid by successors as true debts or liabilities.

I also judge that if a head of a household commands through a last will that remunerations of the second type be made, he is bound to take them from the third or fifth of his goods, which he can freely dispose of for that time. They are not to be ordered from the general mass of the estate, because they do not take on the character of a liability or a true debt, nor does the administration of the goods belong to him for that time [after death].

The third type of remuneratory donation is that by which debts and services, of which we spoke in the second type, are compensated more than equally, yet moderately, as far as it belongs to a truly grateful soul not to be content with equality, but to compensate something more; and all of this does not exceed the boundaries of the virtue of gratitude. This type of gratitude is permitted to the heads of households regarding their own property.

And, if the donation is made between living persons within the limits of right reason—considering his resources, the needs of his children, and other concurrent circumstances—I judge that he is not bound to take it from the third or fifth of his goods. It is otherwise if it is done through a last will, as was said regarding the second type of donation.

Navarrus rightly attributes this very type of donation not only to other beneficiaries and secular bishops (whom he wrongly denies are masters of the income of their benefices) but also to bishops and regular <note>Members of a religious order living under a "rule" (*regula*).</note> beneficiaries, as was related when discussing the wills of ecclesiastics. For this pertains to the lawful and proper administration of those goods and to their appropriate expenses.

# On Guile, Legal Fault, and Fortuitous Events; also, how many types of Legal Fault exist.

## DISPUTATION 293.

### SUMMARY.

1 *Loan for use and gratuitous grants are numbered among lucrative contracts.*
2 *Deceit in the broad sense.*
3 *Good deceit.*
4 *Bad deceit (fraud), and number 9.*
5 *Craftiness.*
6 *Fallacy.*
7 *In what fraud consists.*
8 *Machination, and what it encompasses.*
10 *Theological fault.*
11 *In how many ways legal fault is understood.*

14 *The types of gross negligence, and number 20.*
15 *When fault is called deceit.*
16 *Fault is distinguished from deceit.*
17 *True deceit and presumed deceit.*
18 *Gross negligence, and number 21; also slight and very slight negligence.*
19 *What deceit requires to be distinguished from fault.*
22 *When a horse lent for a specific use is said to perish at the risk of the borrower, and when at the risk of the lender.*
23 *A borrower is held liable for the slightest negligence if they do not apply the most exact diligence in guarding the borrowed thing.*
*Otherwise in a deposit, a lease, and similar cases, in which that diligence which is commonly used suffices. number 24.*
25 *In how many ways a fortuitous event is understood.*

1 **W**e have read thus far concerning donations. Next, we must speak of <term>commodatum</term> <note>original: "commodato"; a loan for use where the specific item must be returned.</note> and <term>precarium</term> <note>original: "precario"; a grant of use that can be revoked at any time by the owner.</note>, which are calculated among lucrative contracts, as was already said above in Disputation 259, and thus they come closer to a donation than other contracts do. 
However, so that these and other contracts, as well as many other matters, may be explained more conveniently in the following sections—namely, to what extent one is held liable or not held liable based on legal fault—those things proposed in the title of this disputation must first be explained.
2 **Guile** <note>original: "Dolus"; deceit or craftiness.</note>, taken broadly, is the execution of cleverness or astuteness, by saying, doing, or omitting something, by which 

<column-break/>

rightly or wrongly another is deceived in some matter, whether it results in loss for that person or not. Thus it happens that guile is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense, as Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> says with Labeo in Law 1, Paragraph 1 of the Digest *On Deceit* <note>original: "ff. de dolo"; "ff" is a standard abbreviation for the Digest of Justinian.</note>; and when taken in the bad sense, it is called "evil guile" <note>original: "dolus malus"; fraud or malicious intent.</note>, as the same Ulpian adds in the following paragraph, to differentiate it from guile taken in the good sense.
3 If † indeed the execution of cleverness—by saying, doing, or omitting something by which another is deceived—is done rightly (that is, in accordance with right reason), it is **good guile** <note>original: "dolus in bonam partem".</note>. Paul professes to have used this kind in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 12, saying: *being crafty, I caught you with guile* <note>original: "cum essem astutus dolo vos cepi".</note>. Solomon used the same kind of guile in the third book of Kings, chapter 3, when the women were contending before him regarding the infant, as to whose son it was: he ordered the boy to be divided in half so that the truth might be revealed by the women themselves. Commanders in a just war often use the same kind of guile, feigning many things by which they deceive and capture the enemy.
4 When † however the execution of cleverness is done perversely to deceive someone, then it is **evil guile**. This is defined by Ulpian, citing Labeo in the aforementioned paragraph: **It is every kind of craftiness, fallacy, and machination employed to circumvent, trick, and deceive another.**
5 Here, † the gloss understands by the name of **craftiness** <note>original: "calliditatis".</note> when someone circumvents by the mind, omitting outwardly what they were bound to do or reveal: such as when one sells a thing, suppressing a defect that they were bound to reveal, and it remains hidden from the buyer.
6 By the name of † **fallacy**, it is understood when one deceives with words. For fallacy, according to St. Thomas (part 2, question 118, article 8), differs from fraud in that fallacy consists in words,
7 while **fraud** † consists in deeds. **Machination** † 
8 seems to be the attempting to deceive or circumvent someone by words or deeds. Thus it follows that machination encompasses fallacy and fraud within itself, while guile extends even more broadly. We can, however, define **evil guile** more clearly and briefly in this manner:
9 **It is the † perverse execution of cleverness by saying, doing, or omitting something by which another is deceived.**
**Fault** <note>original: "Culpa"; negligence or blame.</note>, however, is understood far differently by theologians 
10 than by legal experts. For among † theologians, it is a voluntary deviation from right reason and the law of God. Because of this, it is always an offense against God worthy of punishment; it is divided into mortal and venial.
11 Among † legal experts, it is understood in two ways. First, broadly, such that it encompasses evil guile—both true and presumed—as well as other species of legal fault within its scope. In the other way, strictly, such that it encompasses the remaining species of fault, excluding deceit.
For deceit is a true legal fault. Hence Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist.</note>, on Law *Quod Nerva* in the Digest *On Deposits*, says: he who promised to keep a master harmless when receiving someone as a servant is held liable if any loss comes to the master through the servant's fault—such as if the servant takes something from him by theft—because deceit is truly a fault.
12 Bartolus, in the cited law *Quod Nerva*, number 7, defines **legal fault** † taken broadly as: **A deviation from that which is good, and which could have been foreseen through human diligence.**

It introduces the legal standards for liability in contracts like loans and deposits based on the degree of negligence or intent involved.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 293, which examines the legal categories of fault, deceit, and accidental loss. Having previously defined the broad types of contracts, Molina now delves into the specific degrees of negligence (gross, slight, and very slight) and the distinction between accidental loss and legal liability.</meta>

<header>Ludovico Molina</header>

<margin>13</margin> For that which happens so unexpectedly and contrary to hope that even the most diligent could not foresee or avoid it, is called a <term>fortuitous event</term> <note>original: "casus fortuitus"; an "act of God" or an unavoidable accident</note>. Because a deviation from the good—in which legal fault is situated—sometimes consists in doing something and sometimes in failing to do something, it follows that legal fault may consist sometimes in an act of commission and sometimes in an act of omission. If, for instance, you took a thing lent to you through dangerous places, and it was not lent to you so that you might expose it to those dangers, then, if it should perish on that account, it is rightly said to be your fault, which was situated in the act of commission.

But if you were negligent regarding its preservation because you did not apply the guardianship that any most diligent person could have applied, and it perished on that account, it is rightly said to be your fault, situated in an act of omission. If, however (considering the purpose for which the thing was lent to you), you neither committed nor omitted anything that any diligent person would not have likewise done, then if it should perish by robbery or some other means, it is said to have perished, in comparison to you, by a fortuitous event without your fault. This explanation of fault in the broad sense, and of fortuitous events, is commonly embraced following <term>Bartolus</term> <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note> by both legal experts and theologians, among whose number are Panormitanus, Sylvester, Navarrus, Gabriel, and others.

<margin>14</margin> Bartolus, in the cited law (with whom Panormitanus and many † of the cited authors agree), distinguishes five species of fault in the broadest sense. Namely: the very slightest, <margin>15</margin> slight, gross, greater, and broadest. For if, they say, a fault is committed knowingly and industriously, then it is <term>deceit</term> <note>original: "dolus"; intentional fraud or malice</note>. If, however, it is not done industriously and <margin>16</margin> knowingly, but † out of thoughtlessness, it is fault in the strict sense, which is distinguished from deceit. Because one cannot otherwise know externally whether someone fell into fault knowingly and industriously except either through the confession of the one sinning or through indications; <margin>17</margin> † it follows that when deceit is established through the confession of the sinner or through manifest indications, it is called "true deceit." This is what is called "broadest fault" by Bartolus. When, however, the signs of deceit are indeed pressing but are not so manifest, it is called "presumed deceit," which Bartolus calls "greater fault." But if † the fault arises from lack of consideration, then, if it is because he did or omitted what most men in that situation would not do or omit, it is called <term>gross fault</term> <note>original: "culpa lata"; gross negligence</note>. For example, if someone who had a borrowed book left it on a bench outside the house where it was obvious it would be stolen, that borrower is said to have lost it through gross fault. If, however, the fault is because he did or omitted what diligent people in that matter would not do or omit, it is called <term>slight fault</term> <note>original: "culpa leuis"</note>: as if the borrower left the same book inside a room, but with the door open, from where it could be stolen. Finally, if the fault is because he did or omitted what only the most diligent would not do or omit, it is called <term>very slight fault</term> <note>original: "culpa leuissima"</note>. Navarrus, in the place cited above, gives an example of someone who left the same book in a room that was indeed locked, yet did not test with his hand or finger whether it

<column-break/>

<header>On Contracts</header>

remained locked. However, I would not dare to condemn for "very slight fault" one who did not test it with a finger or hand, unless he had experienced that the key was unreliable; rather, I would count this among fortuitous events. For men are not to be bound to excessive and scrupulous diligences in human commerce and moral affairs.

Therefore, these things are to be judged by the judgment of a prudent person, considering the concurrent circumstances. Examples of gross, slight, and very slight fault can also be applied to craftsmen and others who exercise some office. For if any of them, in attending to their duty, omits what most others are not accustomed to omit, and for that reason errs, he will be said to err from gross fault. If, however, he omits what only the diligent are accustomed not to omit, he will be said to err from slight fault. But if he omits what only the most diligent are accustomed not to omit, he will be said to err from very slight fault.

Nevertheless, some things must be observed regarding all these matters. The first is that I agree with what <term>Sylvester</term> <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian</note> says: namely, that fault in the strict sense is not correctly distinguished from deceit on the grounds that fault is from lack of consideration while deceit is when knowledge is present. For <margin>19</margin> † something more than knowledge is required for deceit: namely, the intent of inflicting damage by that route. Hence, if consideration and knowledge are present without the intent of inflicting damage, it will be fault and not deceit. For example, if someone considers that by not applying such and such diligence, or by undertaking such a thing, a thing borrowed by him is being exposed to danger, and nevertheless out of laziness and sluggishness he does not care to apply diligence, or out of rashness he undertakes a dangerous thing—not intending the neighbor's loss—he is certainly not said to commit deceit, but gross, slight, or very slight fault, according to the nature of what he omits or the danger to which he exposes another's property against the owner's will.

<margin>20</margin> Furthermore, † it is more pleasing that we divide fault in the broad sense into deceit and into fault in the strict sense; and the latter into gross, slight, and very slight, which is more consistent with the laws. Moreover, presumed deceit, if it is in reality what it is presumed to be, will be true deceit in itself; if, however, it is not in reality what it is presumed to be, it will be fault, falsely presumed to be deceit.

<margin>21</margin> Second, † perhaps fault in the broad sense can be better defined this way: It is a deviation, by committing or omitting, from that to which one is in some way bound, and which could have been foreseen at least by the most diligent. I said: "it is a deviation from that to which one is in some way bound," because a deviation from that to which one is in no way bound is surely not a fault. Therefore, because he who received a horse on loan for war, or for a journey through places that the lender himself understood to be dangerous, is not bound to avoid the dangers that war or passage through those <margin>22</margin> places entails; it follows certainly that if the horse perishes because the borrower exposed it to those dangers, it is not said to perish by the fault of the borrower, nor does it perish to him, but to the lender, as held in the laws of the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff. commodati"; references to Roman civil law regarding loans for use</note>.

It is otherwise, however, if he exposed it to greater dangers than those

He argues for a standard of "reasonable diligence" rather than scrupulous perfection, using practical examples like a borrowed book or a horse used in war.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 293, moving from the definition of a fortuitous event to the specific legal meaning of "liability" and the various degrees of negligence required in different types of contracts. Molina distinguishes between "theological fault" (sin) and "legal fault" (contractual liability).</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 293, Page 113 ###

to which the thing was lent, when he explains it, or exceeds those very limits, as is established from those same laws.

The word, however, <term>is held</term> <note>original: "tenetur"; meaning to be legally bound or liable</note>; as placed in that part of the definition, does not signify an obligation under theological guilt <note>sin</note>, but being held by reason of the contract. This is because otherwise the risk of the object will pertain to him, or because he will otherwise lose something or incur some detriment, in the same way that we say someone is "held" to know the law. If not—if through ignorance of the law he pays out legacies without deducting the <term>Falcidian portion</term> <note>a Roman law rule where a horizontal cut of 25% of an estate was reserved for the heir before legacies were paid</note> from them—he loses that portion and cannot reclaim it, as was said in its proper place.

I added to the definition, <gloss>and at least could have been foreseen by the most diligent;</gloss> and I did not say, <gloss>by himself:</gloss> because although, for someone to incur what is properly established as a penalty, or to be held to make restitution by reason of unjust acceptance, it is necessary that it could have been foreseen and done by himself, or by a person he put in place, what he was held to do and did not do, or what he was held to avoid and did not avoid: because, without a voluntary act on the part of the sinner, theological guilt cannot exist. Nevertheless, when someone is held by contract to some degree of diligence, such that if he does not apply it, the thing perishes to his own loss and not the owner's, certainly then one does not care so much about the diligence that he himself could actually apply, as about the diligence which good men (sometimes the most diligent) are accustomed to apply in a similar matter, considering the concurrent circumstances.

<margin>23</margin> For human justice, consistent with natural equity, was established so that men might be more ready to enter into those contracts which lead to human commerce and society—such as a <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodatum"</note>, a <term>deposit for safekeeping</term> <note>original: "depositum"</note>, a <term>lease or hire</term> <note>original: "locatum"</note>, and other similar ones—and so that lawsuits and difficulties regarding occurring events might be removed from the midst. It is established in contracts which are made for the benefit of the receiver alone, such as a loan for use, that the receiver is regularly held to that diligence regarding the preservation of another's property which the most diligent are accustomed to apply. He, however, who receives it as a loan for use, should see whether he wishes to undergo such a burden, and whether he is fit to undergo it; for it is not equitable that the person who provides the thing as a loan should suffer detriment because of the receiver's unfitness. This is sufficiently clear from the law <note>Molina cites specific passages of the Roman Digest and Institutes regarding actions and obligations</note>. To be held to the diligence which the most diligent are accustomed to apply is to be held for <term>very slight fault</term> <note>original: "culpa leuissima"; the highest standard of care</note>.

<margin>24</margin> In other contracts, however, which are not made solely for the benefit of the receiver—such as a deposit, a lease, and the like—the law did not intend for the receiver to be held to such great diligence. Instead, regularly, if the contract was for the benefit of both the giver and the receiver, he would be held only to the diligence which diligent people are accustomed to apply, and thus would be held only for <term>slight fault</term> <note>original: "leui culpa"</note>. If, however, it were only for the benefit of the giver, he would be held to the diligence which men commonly apply, and therefore only for <term>gross fault</term> <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>, as will be seen in the progression of the text. From what has been said, that which Major, Covarruvias, Adrian, and others have noted is clear: namely, that fault taken in a legal sense does not always have theological guilt joined to it, but rather is sometimes without any sin,

<column-break/>

whether mortal or venial. This is especially true when someone is held to some diligence if he wishes to obtain, or not lose, some profit, and when he is held by some contract to diligence in the manner explained. Therefore, if someone should receive a thing as a loan, and because he is naturally forgetful, he leaves it in a place frequented by thieves; and if on that occasion it perishes, while it perishes by his fault, he is held—both in the external court of law and in the court of conscience—to restore the value of it to the owner. This holds even if, when he so left it, it was not in his power to do otherwise because he was forgetful, and thus even if he committed no theological guilt in that matter.

<margin>Objection.</margin> Against the first part of the definition, you will perhaps object as follows: A depositary <note>one who holds property for another</note>, who receives a thing for no benefit of his own but only for that of the depositor, is not held for slight or very slight fault, but only for gross fault or fraud, as will be seen in its place. Therefore, not every fault requires that he who falls into it be held in some way to the opposite; otherwise, slight and very slight fault would have no place in comparison to the depositary, and therefore it would not be rightly said that he is not held for them. For he who says a depositary is not held for such fault supposes that he might fall into it, yet is not held to restore the thing which perished from that fault.

<margin>Satisfaction.</margin> To this argument, the premise being granted, the conclusion must be denied. For in order for a depositary to be truly said not to be held for slight or very slight fault, it is not necessary that he fall into them and, after falling, not be held for them. It is enough if he cannot fall into them, because in comparison to him, not applying the diligence which the most diligent or diligent people apply cannot have the nature of "fault," because by the force of the contract of deposit he is not held to those diligences. Therefore, a depositary who did not apply the diligence which only the diligent or most diligent are accustomed to apply to things delivered to them—if the deposited thing perishes for that reason—can rightly and truly say that the thing deposited with him perished by no fault of his, because he was not held to that diligence. From which it follows that it is false that he who says a depositary is not held for slight or very slight fault supposes that the depositary falls into those faults and is not held to restore the deposited thing because of them; and therefore all the points added in proof of the conclusion in the proposed argument collapse. We can also say that when the laws and doctors say a depositary is not held for slight and very slight fault, they intend only this: he is not held for the negligence which, in comparison to a borrower, for example, would be slight or very slight fault.

<margin>25</margin> The third point is that although that is properly said to happen by a <term>fortuitous event</term> which happens beyond hope and without fault, yet in the matter of which we treat, it can and ought to be taken more broadly. Namely, for that which happens without fault, even if it does not happen beyond hope, but rather is believed likely to happen.

In this way, we can say that a horse lent for war, or for a journey through dangerous places, perished by a fortuitous event—that is, without the borrower's fault—when it perished in the war or was captured by robbers.

<summary>Molina explains that legal liability (tenetur) in contracts differs from moral sin (theological guilt), as one can be legally required to pay for a loss even if they were not morally at fault. He outlines the three levels of negligence—gross, slight, and very slight—and how the required level of care depends on who benefits from the contract.</summary>

->Louis de Molina, On Contracts<-

# On the loan for use, the distinction between it and a precarious loan, and when a lent item can be reclaimed.

## DISPUTATION 294.

### SUMMARY.

1. Definition and etymology of the <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodatum"; a contract where a thing is lent for a specific purpose and the exact same item must be returned</note>.
2. What constitutes the subject matter of a loan for use.
3. The various ways a loan for use is undertaken.
4. What a loan for use is as distinguished from a <term>precarious loan</term> <note>original: "precarium"; a loan granted as a favor that can be recalled at any time</note>.
5. What a precarious loan is.
6. A loan for use cannot properly be reclaimed before the time—either stated or implied—for which it was granted has expired.
7. When the lender is held liable for damages following the borrower's use.
8. When a loan for use can be revoked before the time granted for its use.
9. A loss occurring to the lender regarding the lent item is a sufficient cause to revoke the loan.
10. How a loan for use and a gift differ.

A loan for use, as stated in the *Institutes* <note>original: "Instit. quib. mod. re contrab. oblig. §. item hi"; referring to Justinian’s Institutes, a foundational Roman law textbook</note>, is the gratuitous granting of someone else's property for use alone. It is called *commodatum*, as if "given for convenience" <note>original: "commodo datum"</note>, as the gloss on the single chapter regarding the loan for use states. Moreover, the one who receives the thing as a loan is called the borrower <note>original: "commodatarius"</note>.

In the definition, it says "for use alone," because when a horse, a garment, or anything else is lent, the property is not granted in terms of ownership—nor even in terms of possession. Rather, the lender is said to possess the item, even naturally, through the borrower, as held in the law *rei commodatæ* and the following law in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. commodati"; 'ff' is the standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Roman law</note>. Because it is granted only for use, while the ownership remains with the lender, the exact same item must be returned. Thus, if it perishes without any fault on the part of the borrower, it does not perish for him, but for the lender to whom it belongs, as is held in the *Institutes* and other sections of the law. A further addition to the definition is "gratuitous granting": for if the thing is granted for use in exchange for some interest or payment, it will not be a loan for use, but either a rental <note>original: "locatio"</note>, if the interest paid is money, or an "unnamed contract" if it is something else.

<margin>2</margin> The subject matter of a loan for use includes both movable and immovable things, as held in the *Digest*. These are primarily things that are not consumed by their use. For things that are consumed by use, such as money and other similar items, cannot be lent for use unless it is for "pomp and show" <note>original: "ad pompum, & ostentationem"</note>, as the law states. Sylvester, under the word "commodatum," understands the term "pomp" to mean any use that is not the consumption of the thing. I would say that when the laws provide a distinction between a loan for use (*commodatum*) and a <term>loan for consumption</term> <note>original: "mutuum"; a loan where the borrower consumes the item (like grain or money) and returns an equivalent amount, not the same item</note>, the matter of the loan for consumption consists of things that are weighed, numbered, and measured, such as money, wheat, wine, oil, etc.; whereas the matter of the loan for use consists of things that

<column-break/>

are not consumed by use. This should be understood because it is generally and for the most part how it happens. Therefore, in a case of doubt as to whether a contract is a loan for use or a loan for consumption, if the matter is a thing consumed by use, we judge it to be a loan for consumption; otherwise, we deem it a loan for use.

It should be observed that someone who has the right to use a thing—perhaps because they rented it or for another reason—even if that thing belongs to another, can lend it for use. This is asserted in the *Digest* with the words: "Julius further says that even a dwelling can be lent for use."

If something is given as a loan for use to a <term>ward</term> <note>original: "pupillus"; a minor under the care of a guardian</note> for a specific use or time, the contract binds the lender so that he cannot revoke it before that time or before the use is completed. However, if the ward himself gives something as a loan without the authority of a <term>guardian</term> <note>original: "tutor"</note>, the contract does not bind him, and it can be revoked. This is because although a ward can bind another to himself without a guardian’s authority, he cannot be bound to another without that same authority. This is held in the law *Iulianus* and other legal sources.

Neither is a ward, to whom something has been lent, held liable except for fraud <note>original: "dolus"</note>. But if fraud is not involved, and the lent item perishes or is made worse, he is only held liable to the extent that he was made wealthier by it. All these points similarly apply to a <term>prodigal</term> <note>original: "prodigo"; a person legally declared incapable of managing their own affairs due to wasteful spending</note>, and to a ward who has reached puberty but is still under twenty-five years of age and has a curator. Read what was copiously disputed regarding all these matters in Disputation 224.

<margin>3</margin> The term "loan for use" is frequently used broadly to include the precarious loan as well; however, it is more properly used in a strict sense as distinct from the precarious loan. It is in this second way that it is usually understood in law. For when something is lent for a certain time, or for a certain use—such that it is understood to be for a certain time to be determined by the judgment of a prudent person—it is called a loan for use in the strict sense. Such is the case if someone lends something for a month, or ten days, or some other determined time.

It is also such a case if one lends a book to be transcribed, or a horse for making a journey from Seville to Lisbon. By that very act, he is understood to have lent it for exactly as much time as is judged necessary for it to be transcribed (unless otherwise expressed in the contract), and the horse for exactly as much time as is necessary to go to Lisbon and return. But when something is lent "at the pleasure of the lender" <note>original: "vsq; ad beneplacitū"</note>—either because it was expressed that way in the contract, or because neither a time nor a specific use was expressed—then it is called a "precarious loan" <note>original: "precarium"</note>. The name is applied because it is usually granted at the "prayers" (*preces*) of the person requesting it. This distinction between the loan for use and the precarious loan is held in the *Digest* and is clearly gathered from the chapter on precarious loans. The doctors of law commonly agree on this. In this disputation and the following ones, our discussion will only concern the loan for use in the strict sense; we will discuss the precarious loan in Disputation 298.

<summary>Molina defines the 'loan for use' (commodatum) as a free loan of property where the specific item must be returned, distinguishing it from 'loans for consumption' (mutuum) and 'precarious loans' (precarium) which are revocable at will.</summary>
<keywords>loan for use, commodatum, precarium, precarious loan, contract law, Roman law, liability, wards, guardianship, property rights</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 294, expanding on the legal and moral obligations of the lender and borrower in a loan for use. It specifically addresses the conditions under which a lender might or might not be able to reclaim an item early.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 294. 135
H 2
<meta>catchword: Especially</meta>

6. In a <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodato"</note> strictly defined, the item cannot be reclaimed before the completion of the specific task or the expiration of the time for which it was granted. To do so would be an injustice, and the borrower is not bound to return it before that time has elapsed, even if the lender demands it. Rather, if the item is taken from the borrower without their free consent, the person taking it is held liable for <term>interest and restitution of damages</term> <note>original: "interesse, damnorumque restitutionem"</note>, both in conscience <note>the internal moral forum</note> and in the external court <note>the legal system</note>, as seen in the law regarding loans for use <note>original: "l. incommodato. §. sicut. ff. cõmod. & c. vnic. eodem tit."</note>. For just as a gift is an act of liberty and a benefit when it is made or when a thing is promised, it nevertheless binds the giver once it is done; the thing given cannot be reclaimed without injustice. A loan for use—which is a kind of gift regarding the *use* of the thing being lent—is an act of liberty and a benefit while it is being made or promised. However, after it has been granted for a certain time or use, it cannot be reclaimed without injustice before that time or use is completed. Added to this is the principle that a person should be helped, not deceived, by a benefit conferred upon them. If the lender were to reclaim the item lent for a specific use or time before that use or time was finished, the borrower would be deceived and would suffer a loss from the loan. If the borrower had known the item would be reclaimed prematurely, they either would not have undertaken the task for which they accepted the item, or they would have provided for themselves from elsewhere, thus avoiding the damage that follows from this untimely reclamation. This is the reasoning established and rendered by the two laws cited above.

7. Here, before I raise a doubt regarding what was just said, observe: from this same legal foundation, one who knowingly and prudently lends an item that is useless or harmful for the purpose for which it was requested—whereby the borrower suffers a loss—is held liable for the subsequent damages. An example is if one lent <term>defective vessels</term> <note>original: "vitiosa vasa"</note> for pouring wine into them. It is otherwise, however, if the lender did this out of ignorance. This is found in the cited section "Sicut," and in the penultimate law of the Digest on loans for use.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
8. A doubt arises concerning the doctrine just handed down: whether, if the lender unexpectedly suffers an equal or greater loss resulting from *not* revoking the loan than the borrower would suffer from its revocation, the lender can lawfully revoke it before the time or use is completed. We say "if it follows unexpectedly" because if the lender, when they lent the item or promised to lend it, foresaw or feared that such a loss would occur and lent it anyway, then there can be no doubt—neither in conscience nor in the external court—that they cannot revoke the loan against the borrower's will. By that very act, the lender is judged to have wished, out of generosity, not only to lend the item but also to undergo that inconvenience for the sake of the recipient.

<term>Angelus</term> <note>Angelus de Clavasio, a 15th-century canon lawyer</note> (under the word *commodatum*, no. 4) and <term>Sylvester</term> <note>Sylvester Prierias, a 16th-century theologian</note> (in the same place, question 4) judge that when a borrower could not have provided for themselves from elsewhere except by accepting the item from that lender, the lender can, in the forum of conscience, revoke the loan before the use or time is finished. This is because a lender ought to provide for themselves from their own property rather than

<column-break/>

for the borrower. Nor in that event can the borrower justly complain about the lender, either that they suffered a loss from the lender’s benefit or that they were deceived by them; for this occurred beyond the lender's intention, and when the lender lent the item, they did not intend to bind themselves to not revoking the loan in such a circumstance.

<term>Navarrus</term> <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century Spanish canonist</note> (in the *Manual*, chapter 17, no. 182) affirms that the reasoning is exactly the same in conscience and in the external court. For that reason, the lender cannot revoke the loan even in the forum of conscience at that time. Regarding the point that moves Angelus and Sylvester, he responds: although the lender, before they granted the use of their property to the borrower out of generosity, ought to have provided for themselves from that thing rather than for another, they cannot do so after the grant has been made. This is because a <margin>Decision</margin> right to that use—indeed, *in* that use—has already been acquired by the other party, and the lender is bound to keep faith with them.

Briefly, I will set down what I think about this matter. First, I agree with Navarrus that this matter should not be judged differently in conscience than in the external court—unless there were probable conjectures in the external court that the lender's intent was one thing (at least a sort of habitual intent), while in reality it was another internally.

For if the lender was in such a disposition when they lent or promised to lend the item that, even if they understood that loss would befall them, they would still have lent it or promised to lend it for the same use or time, then surely in the forum of conscience they are bound to fulfill a promise not yet completed and cannot revoke a loan already made, regardless of what might be said in the external court according to what we will add below. The reason is that they then had the intention of lending even with such great loss to themselves; therefore, after they once bound themselves to it, they cannot in the forum of conscience revoke the loan before the use or time is finished, nor fail to fulfill the promise.

Furthermore, when the promisor was in a sort of habitual disposition such that, if they had foreseen an equal or greater loss to themselves, they not only would not have promised to lend but would have replied that they did not intend to bind themselves to lending in that event; then, if they have not yet fulfilled the promise and an equal or greater loss befalls them if they do lend, they are certainly not bound to lend, neither in conscience nor in the external court. Indeed, if the loss has not yet arrived but they fear it is about to, they are not bound to fulfill the promise unless the other party is satisfied that the loan may be revoked if the loss occurs. This doctrine is clear from what was said extensively in Disputation 272. For a generous and gratuitous promise, before it is fulfilled by delivery, does not bind the promisor more than they intended to bind themselves; and a promisor of the sort we are now discussing did not intend to bind themselves in such an event and with the circumstances of things so changed. Nor does it matter if someone else would have promised the same to the borrower at that time, unless this lender had promised to help them, and consequently the borrower had provided for themselves from elsewhere and that opportunity has passed; for that is not a reason why this person should be more bound by their gratuitous promise than they intended to be.

It also explores whether a lender can revoke a loan if they suffer an unexpected personal loss, contrasting the views of several prominent legal and theological scholars.</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

Especially since it was no hindrance to the borrower in seeking a promise from someone else, and since something similar could have happened with another person. It must be added that even if the lender had bound himself by an oath to lend the item, if he remained in the aforementioned state of mind, he is not bound to lend it, as was shown in the cited disputation. This is because a promise confirmed by an oath contains a tacit condition: "unless the circumstances of the matter change so much that the <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodatum," a gratuitous loan of a specific object to be used and returned</note> becomes harmful to the lender." An added oath does not exclude this inherent condition. Read what has been said there.

<margin>Objection 9</margin>
Furthermore, a forceful argument for the scholar Navarro arises: if, after the item has been delivered as a loan, a loss occurs to the lender unless he revokes the loan. Since the borrower, through the delivery of the item, has acquired a <term>right in the thing</term> <note>original: "ius in re"</note> to use it for the entire time for which it was lent, it follows that—just as in a free gift, where ownership is transferred the moment delivery is made and cannot be revoked due to a later need of the giver (except for specific causes expressed in the law, explained in Disputation 281 and following)—so too a loan for use should not be revocable due to a later need or loss of the lender if he does not reclaim it before the time is up.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
Nevertheless, the contrary view seems more probable to me, and this is not only in the forum of conscience but also in the external <note>legal</note> court. First, because of the presumed will of lenders, who would not intend to bind themselves to not reclaiming the loan in such an event before the use or time is completed. The nature of the matter itself teaches that this should be presumed of everyone. In <term>gratuitous contracts</term> <note>contracts where only one party benefits, like a free loan</note>, such as a loan for use, the lender is no more bound not to revoke the contract than he intended to obligate himself not to revoke it, as is self-evident. Therefore, the laws cited above, which teach that a lender cannot revoke a loan before the use or time is finished, must be understood through <term>equity</term> <note>original: "epicheia," the principle of interpreting the spirit of the law rather than its strict letter to avoid injustice</note>. This applies as a general rule, excluding circumstances where, from the nature of the thing itself, it is presumed that the person did not intend to obligate himself to not revoke the contract in such an event.

<margin>10</margin>
Next, the reasoning is far different in a gift compared to a loan for use. For in a gift, once the delivery of the thing is made, the recipient acquires full <term>ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium"</note>, and the item no longer belongs to the giver. It is no wonder then that even if the giver later suffers a grave need for it, he cannot revoke the gift. But in a loan for use, ownership remains with the lender, and the thing is owed back to him after its use. Therefore, since it should not be presumed that he wished to lend it in such a way that, if a grave and unforeseen loss resulted for him, he could not reclaim it, it is manifest that the reasoning is not equal in both cases. From this and the preceding reason, it is clear enough that he is not being unfaithful if he revokes the loan in such an event, since he truly did not intend to bind himself to that extent.

Thirdly, because if children are later born to a donor, a gift made to a stranger is revoked in its entirety (as stated in Disputation 282). This is due to the presumed will of the giver, who would not have intended to give in that event.

<column-break/>

Therefore, much more so in a loan for use, where ownership is not transferred, it will be lawful to revoke the loan. Since a notable loss to the lender is established, it is clear he did not intend to lend in that circumstance. This is the only case in which we say a loan for use can be reclaimed before the use or time has expired.

<margin>Objection</margin>
Fourthly, because if a person who has leased out a house finds it necessary to live in his own house, he can expel the tenant from it, despite the inconvenience and loss to the tenant (according to the law *aede* in the Code regarding leases, and other laws we shall see in their proper place). Therefore, much more so—not only in conscience but also in the external court—it will be permitted to revoke a purely gratuitous contract of a loan for use when, by not reclaiming it, an equal or more serious unforeseen loss threatens the lender.

<margin>Response</margin>
This opinion holds true even if the borrower, at the time the contract was made, had someone else who could lend to him but later lacked that option. For the person who gave the loan left the borrower free to seek a loan from anyone else; by providing the loan, he did not intend to strip himself of the freedom to reclaim it if he himself came to be in grave need of his own property. The same thing could have happened to the borrower if he had accepted a loan from someone else—namely, that if that other person had a grave need for his property, he would similarly have reclaimed the loan. The current lender would not have reclaimed it if he had not been in grave need himself.

And if anyone objects to our opinion using the legal rule from the *Sixth Book of Decretals* which states: *"No one can change his plan to the detriment of another"* <note>original: "Mutare consilium quis non potest in alterius detrimentum"</note>, the answer is that this must be understood as being without a reasonable cause and as intending the detriment of the other person specifically. It is different when there is a reasonable cause, and the detriment to the other occurs by accident: not intending that loss at all, but only intending to avoid one's own loss, from which the other's loss follows incidentally. All these factors are seen in the matter proposed.

<margin>Objection</margin>
If someone again objects with Rule 61, which states: *"What is granted as a favor to someone should not be turned into their loss,"* we must similarly say this is understood as being without reasonable cause and as intending the loss of the other person specifically.
<margin>Resolution</margin>

1 <margin>But there are exceptions, as noted there.</margin> <margin>Also, in which case the borrower may retain it without being said to have sinned. (See number 6)</margin> When † something is lent for the sake or benefit of the borrower alone—as is usually the case—then, if the thing is lost or returned in a worse condition, the borrower is held liable even for <term>slightest negligence</term> <note>original: "culpa levissima," the highest standard of care where even the smallest oversight results in liability</note>. This is held in the <note>references to the Body of Civil Law, including the Digest and Institutes</note> single chapter on loans, Law 3, and throughout the titles on actions and obligations.

2 However, when something is lent for the benefit of both the borrower and the lender—for example, if items are lent to host a mutual friend whom the lender is also visiting in the borrower's home—then the borrower is only held liable for <term>ordinary negligence</term> <note>original: "levis culpa," the standard of care a reasonable person takes with their own property</note> and anything greater, but not for the slightest negligence.

But if the item is given solely for the benefit of the lender, then the borrower is held liable only for <term>deceit</term> <note>original: "dolus," intentional harm or fraud</note>. <margin>Add also "gross negligence," which in contractual obligations is equated to deceit. (See Law of Nerva, on deposits)</margin>

Examples of when a thing is granted solely for the benefit of the lender are sometimes cited as follows: if a man lends jewelry to his bride so that she may come to him more beautifully adorned; or if someone who is to provide stage plays to the people gives theatrical equipment to those he has hired for the performance. This applies when they receive no payment for the performance, or when they receive payment only to perform, while the one exhibiting the games is responsible for providing all materials at his own expense. In that case, the items necessary for the performance benefit only the one providing the show.

This same rule is generally observed in contracts: when what is given benefits only the receiver, the receiver is held liable even for the slightest negligence. When it benefits both, he is held for ordinary negligence (but not the slightest), as in a <term>pledge</term> <note>original: "pignus," collateral for a debt</note> or a <term>rental</term> <note>original: "locato"</note>. And when it benefits only the giver—as is usually the case in a <term>gratuitous deposit</term> <note>original: "deposito," leaving an item for safekeeping without pay</note>—the receiver is held liable only for deceit and <term>gross negligence</term> <note>original: "lata culpa," extreme carelessness</note>. This rule is gathered from the Laws on the Rules of Law and the common opinion of the doctors of law.

3 Therefore, † the word "generally" was used in that rule:

<column-break/>

because the proposed rule fails in the case of a <term>permissive loan</term> <note>original: "precarium," a loan granted by request that can be revoked at the lender's will</note>. For although the thing is given in such a case for the sole benefit of the receiver, because the lender is free to demand back what he gave whenever he wishes, the laws have determined that the receiver is held liable only for deceit or gross negligence. This exception also appears occasionally in other contracts, as will be seen in the progress of this work.

4 As for a <term>fortuitous event</term> <note>original: "casus fortuitus," an accidental act of God or chance that cannot be foreseen, such as a lightning strike or a sudden robbery</note>, the borrower is generally not held liable. It is said "generally" for several reasons. First, he is liable for an accident if that was specifically included in the <term>agreement</term> <note>original: "pactum"</note>. Second, if the borrower used the lent item in a different way or for a different purpose than that for which it was granted, or if he was in <term>default</term> <note>original: "mora," a legal delay in returning the item</note> in restoring it, and any of these factors provided the occasion for the thing to perish or be worsened (which the law calls the borrower being "at fault for the fortuitous event"), then he is held liable for the accident. 

Examples include: if I lent you a horse to go to one place, and you took it to another, and by that reason you encountered bandits or some other misfortune befell it. Or if I lent you dishes so that you might hold a feast in your house, and you carried them far away or across the sea, and on that occasion they were lost to theft, shipwreck, or another misfortune. Or if, because you were late in returning the item to me, it perished.

5 It must then be observed † that if the lent thing would have perished in the same way even if it were with the owner—supposing the borrower had not been late in returning it, or had not used it differently than agreed—then the borrower is not bound to restore the thing itself. He is only bound to pay the value of the use of the item beyond what was agreed, or for "lost profit" if that profit is valued at more than the use itself. This is the opinion of many doctors of law, although the commentary on the Law of Loans asserts the contrary. Our reason and that of the aforementioned doctors is that, in such an event, the borrower is not liable to the owner for more than what he caused or the loss he occasioned by his delay or unauthorized use. When the thing was going to perish even with its own owner, he was truly neither the cause nor the occasion of its destruction.

6 It must also be observed † that if the borrower believed that the owner of the thing would be content for him to retain it, or to use it differently or for another purpose than what was requested, and this was indeed the case, then he has not sinned by retaining it or by that agreement...
