### Ludovici Molinæ on Contracts

...by using it, he is not held to any restitution in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>the "internal forum" or moral standing before God</note>, even if this use was the occasion for the item's destruction. Indeed, he is not even held liable in the external court, if the lender's intent to allow such use was evident in that court. The reason is that, in truth, he did not transgress the owner’s will.

If, however, it were evident that the borrower had been deceptive, and that the delay and use of the lent item were against the owner’s will, then—if that was the occasion for the item perishing—even if he did not sin (his <term>good faith</term> <note>believing he was acting rightly</note> excusing him), he would nevertheless be held to restore its value in both the external court and the court of conscience. This is because it would be unlawful for him to breach the loan contract in that way, except under the condition that, if the owner were not satisfied, the borrower would be held liable for the <term>interest</term> <note>the legal compensation for loss or damage</note>.

<margin>7</margin>
Furthermore, it must be observed that when a borrower uses a lent item against the lender's will for a purpose other than that for which it was lent, or exceeds the specific and prescribed limits of its use, he is then said to commit **theft**. Consequently, the lender is given a "theft action" against him. This is supported by the law *qui iumenta* in the Digest <note>Digest 47.2.55</note>, the section *furtum est* and *furtum autem fit* in the Institutes <note>Institutes 4.1.6-7</note>, and other laws cited by Covarruvias in his *Various Resolutions* <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a major Spanish jurist</note>. However, he rightly states, alongside others he cites, that when it is not certain that such use should be believed to be against the owner's will, the borrower should not be condemned as a thief for that reason.

But when it is clear that the use was against the owner's will, the borrower should not necessarily be judged <term>infamous</term> <note>legally disgraced</note> for being so condemned; nor, in this Kingdom of Castile, should a judge regularly impose the sevenfold penalty. All these points made regarding <term>fortuitous events</term> <note>accidents or acts of God beyond human control</note> concerning the loan contract are to be understood similarly in cases of <term>precarium</term> <note>a loan granted by request and revocable at will</note>, deposits, pledges, leases, and other similar contracts.

<margin>8</margin>
Observe also this regarding loans and the other contracts I just mentioned: if it is specifically agreed in a pact that the receiver shall not be held liable for <term>gross negligence</term> <note>original: "lata culpa," extreme carelessness</note> or any lesser fault, then, even if the item perishes through the receiver's fault, he is not held to restore it. This is because "no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting." However, a pact stating that the receiver is not held liable for **fraud** is void by the law itself, as it is against good morals, as held in the law *in commodato* and the law *illud non est* regarding deposits. Read what was said in Disputation 271.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note> and indeed others, whom Antonio Gómez refers to and follows, affirm that when an item is delivered with a **valuation** <note>a specific price set at the time of the loan</note> in these kinds of contracts, that valuation has a specific effect. Specifically, if the receiver was otherwise liable for <term>slightest negligence</term> (as in a loan for use), he becomes liable even for accidents. If he was only liable for <term>ordinary negligence</term> (as in a pledge or lease), he becomes liable for the slightest negligence, but not for accidents. Thus, a valuation always means the receiver is held to one degree higher of liability than he would otherwise be by the nature of the contract.

They are led to this by the law *si ut certo* in the Digest, where we read: "And if by chance an estimated item is given, every risk must be provided for by him who receives the valuation he is to provide." The <term>Gloss</term> <note>the standard legal commentary</note> explains this according to Bartolus’s opinion, and a similar gloss is found in other sections of the Digest.

<column-break/>

Item: they are led by the final section of the law on "action of estimation" <note>Digest 19.5.17.1</note>, which states that if an item is delivered for sale with a valuation, on the condition that either the price or the item itself be returned, then the risk belongs to the one to whom it is delivered.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Johannes Andreae, Panormitanus, Silvester (under the word *commodatum*, question 7), and others assert the contrary opinion. Namely, that the valuation only ensures that it is certain what must be paid back in the event that the item itself is not restored—because it has perished or been returned in worse condition through the receiver's fault—according to the nature of the contract. Truly, the opinion of the Gloss, Bartolus, and those who follow them displeases me.

For I do not see the law from which it can be gathered that a valuation in every contract operates to add exactly one degree of liability beyond those which the receiver would otherwise be held to by the nature of the contract; nor does this agree with right reason or the nature of the thing itself. Therefore, I believe it should be said that the laws relied upon by authors of the contrary opinion are to be understood as follows: when, from the manner of delivering the valued item and binding the receiver to restore either that price or the item itself in every event, it is sufficiently understood that the *entire risk* is cast upon the receiver. In that case, not just one degree of risk is added, but the entire risk. Therefore, when this is not sufficiently expressed, or not sufficiently understood from the custom of the country, the valuation will only effect what Panormitanus and the others affirm <note>i.e., it just sets the price for standard liability</note>.

From what has been said, both in this entire disputation and in Disputation 183, it is clear enough that the opinion of Soto <note>Domingo de Soto, a contemporary Dominican theologian</note> is false and contrary to the law on loans and other cited laws, as well as the common opinion of the doctors. Soto argues that in loans and other contracts where ownership is not transferred—such as for borrowers, depositaries, hirers, etc.—one is not held to restitution for the whole thing for a fault less than a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>original: "culpa lethali," a grave moral failing</note>. He claims for lighter faults, one is only held to restore a part of the thing according to the quantity of the fault.

Ledesma partly subscribes to this same opinion, saying that in the court of conscience, such receivers are not obliged to such a great penalty for a fault lighter than a mortal one.

They seem to have fallen into this opinion because they thought that such receivers are obliged to restitution as a punishment for an unjust taking or damage unjustly inflicted. They failed to notice that this obligation arises from the **very nature of the contract**, given the disposition of civil and canon law, not only in the external court but also in the court of conscience. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canonist</note> correctly noted this against Soto in his *Manual*.

Second Treatise. Disputation 296.

# Should lent items be preferred over one's own property when both cannot be saved? And who bears the loss if they are sent through a third party?

### DISPUTATION 296.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *A borrower is held liable for <term>deceit</term> <note>original: "dolus"; intentional or gross negligence</note> if, in a common danger, he saves all his own property and abandons the items lent to him. The same applies to a <term>precarium</term> <note>original: "precarium"; a loan granted by request that can be revoked at any time</note> and a loan for use made for the sole benefit of the lender.*
2 *A borrower is required to prefer a more valuable lent item over his own property of lesser value.*
3 *In which cases a borrower is required to compensate for his own cheaper property if he sacrifices it for a more valuable lent item.*
4 *One receiving a more valuable lent item by a <term>precarium</term> grant, and when he may compensate his own cheaper property with it.*
5 *A borrower may prefer his own more valuable property over cheaper items lent to him.*
6 *A borrower is required to prefer lent items over his own if they are of equal value.*
7 *In a loan for use, an item delivered to a messenger appointed for that purpose perishes at the risk of the creditor; otherwise, it is the reverse.*
8 *If a lent item is delivered to a messenger before the creditor notifies the debtor to hand it over to him, it perishes at the risk of the debtor.*
9 *When a lent item is sent to the lender through a person other than the one designated, who bears the risk if it perishes?*
10 *If a creditor agrees with a debtor that the debt should be sent via someone who brings a specific sign <note>a token or password for identification</note>, and another person comes bringing that sign, at whose risk does the debt perish?*

**T**wo doubts remain regarding the custody of a lent item. First, if a borrower in a shipwreck, fire, or other similar event cannot save both his own property and the items accepted as a <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodatum"</note>, is he held to any restitution if he saves his own property and abandons the borrowed items?
1 In the first place, † I respond that if he saves all his own property and leaves behind the lent or <term>deposited</term> <note>original: "depositam"</note> item, deceit is presumed in the <term>external court</term> <note>the public legal court, as opposed to the court of conscience</note> unless the contrary is established elsewhere. He will, therefore, be compelled to restore it, as is clear from the law *Good Faith* regarding deposits, and the law *What Nerva* in the Digest <note>Digest 16.3.32</note>, joined with the law *If for a certain purpose*, the section *Now it must be seen*, at the phrase *But that* in the Digest title on Loans for Use <note>Digest 13.6.5.2</note>. This holds true even in a *precarium* grant and in a loan for use made for the benefit of the lender alone; for all these parties are held to no less a standard of custody for the item received than a <term>depositary</term> <note>one who holds an item for safekeeping</note>, of whom the laws cited in the first place speak.
2 Secondly, † I respond that if the lent item is more valuable than the borrower’s own, the borrower is bound to prefer the lent item over his own, even if the loan was accepted for the benefit of both parties or for the lender alone. Whether he can then seek compensation from the lent item for the loss of his own cheaper property, which he abandoned to save the more valuable property of another, I will discuss shortly.
This second point is proved in this manner: Since even when an item is accepted for the sole benefit of the lender, the borrower is bound to exercise that same custody which any person would provide for their own property. Any person, however, if they could save only one of two items, would abandon the cheaper and save the more valuable; therefore, the borrower in question must also set aside his own cheaper item to save the more valuable item of the lender.

<column-break/>

3 Whether † he can be compensated for his own cheaper item? A distinction must be made. If the <term>loan for use</term> was made for the sake and benefit of the borrower alone, he cannot claim compensation. This is proven because, by the force of the contract and the benefit received, he is bound at his own expense to provide that level of custody for the lent item which the most diligent person would apply to their own property. Therefore, he could not seek compensation not only for his own cheaper property but even for property of equal value which he might lose in order to keep the lent item of another safe. Nor does it matter that—as will be said below—the lender is held liable for extraordinary expenses made regarding the lent item; for that is not understood to include those expenses to which he is bound by reason of the contract regarding its custody, but rather other extraordinary costs, such as if a lent slave fell ill, or took flight through no fault of the borrower, and it was necessary to spend something to provide medical aid or to bring him back from flight. If, however, the item—which was destined to perish by fire, shipwreck, or other similar misfortune unless preserved by the borrower's industry—would have perished in the same way while in the owner's possession, then I judge it probable that the borrower can compensate for his own cheaper item. This is because the danger is then considered common to both parties' property and did not arise by occasion of the loan; and in such an event, everyone ought to aid their own property more than another's. Likewise, if after another's property was snatched from a shipwreck or fire, it were necessary to incur some expenses for its preservation (because it suffered some damage from water or fire and needed to be helped by certain costs or applied industry), then the owner of that item would be bound to pay these expenses and the value of the applied industry; this is because such efforts no longer pertain to the custody of the item to which the borrower is bound by the force of the contract.
But if the item was lent for the benefit of both, or the lender alone, then he can seek compensation for his own cheaper item, nor is he bound to hand over the more valuable item to the lender until the lender pays the value of the loss incurred in its preservation. I am led to assert this for two reasons: First, because no one seems obligated to preserve another's property at their own loss when the contract is celebrated for the benefit of both—and much less when for the sole benefit of the other; in such a case, one ought to look after oneself more than the other. Second, because to suffer a loss in one's own goods to save another's is to incur expenses on behalf of another's property; and since the contract is celebrated for the benefit of both or of the giver alone, surely the giver is bound to pay the expenses necessary for the preservation of the item received, just as is a <term>depositor</term> <note>one who leaves an item for safekeeping</note>, a <term>lessor</term> <note>one who rents out property</note>, and—

<sig>H 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: -one handing over [tradens]</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the ethical and legal obligations of a borrower during a disaster, concluding that while a borrower should prioritize saving more valuable lent items, they may be entitled to compensation for their own sacrificed property depending on who benefited from the loan.</summary>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...placed as a <term>pledge</term> <note>original: "pignus"; property held as security for a debt</note>, and by the same reasoning, accommodating it for the benefit of both parties, or for the benefit of the giver alone.

4 Regarding the person who has received something by <term>precarium</term> <note>original: "precario"; a type of loan where the item is held at the will of the lender and must be returned on demand</note>, there may be a doubt as to whether he can offset <note>original: "compensare"; to seek reimbursement or credit</note> the loss of his own more valuable property. For since he is only held liable for <term>gross negligence</term> <note>original: "lata culpa"; a failure to exercise even the most basic care</note>, one might think he could seek compensation, just like one who received a <term>loan for use</term> <note>original: "commodato"; a gratuitous loan of a specific object to be returned</note> for the benefit of both parties, or like one who has hired an item, or received it as a pledge. This would also apply to a <term>depositary</term> <note>original: "depositarius"; someone entrusted with another's property for safekeeping</note> or someone receiving a loan solely for the benefit of the giver. However, I believe that since a *precarium* does not typically serve the benefit of the giver, but is solely a favor to the receiver, such compensation has no place.

The reason is that when a contract is for the sole benefit of the receiver, he is bound to guard it at his own expense by reason of the benefit received. Right reason and the nature of the thing itself require this. Although human law has "loosened the reins" in this contract—stating that the one who receives by *precarium* is liable only for gross negligence—this certainly does not grant him the freedom to seek compensation for what was necessary to spend or lose of his own property to provide the guardianship required to avoid that level of fault.

5 Thirdly, I respond that if the lent items are of less value, the borrower may prefer his own more valuable items. This is because equity does not allow one to suffer a far greater loss in his own property to avoid a smaller loss to another's, and because a borrower is only held to the <term>utmost diligence</term> <note>original: "exactissimam diligentiam"</note> that any person would apply to his own affairs. No one, in order to preserve his cheaper belongings, would allow his more precious ones to perish.

However, if the loan was made for the sole benefit of the borrower, even if it were granted as a *precarium*, the borrower is bound to restore the value of the lent items to the lender if they perished so that he could save his own. This is proved because, as stated above, such a borrower is bound—even at the cost of equal loss to his own property—to exercise that diligence in preserving the lent items to which he is bound by the contract. Therefore, if in the situation described he is permitted to prefer his more precious property over the cheaper lent items, it is not so that the lender should suffer the loss of his property, but only so that the borrower does not suffer the loss of the greater value which his own property has over the lent items. If, therefore, he chooses to preserve his own more precious things, it must be with the burden and under the condition that he keeps the lender harmless by restoring the value of the lent items to him. If, however, the loan had been made for the benefit of both, or for the sole benefit of the lender, then the borrower would not be held to any restitution, just as a tenant is not held to the landlord, or a person holding a pledge to the one who gave the pledge, or a depositary to the depositor. This is because, as stated above, if expenses are incurred in preserving such things, those who retain the ownership of those things are bound to pay them.

6 Finally, I respond that if the loan for use, or the *precarium*, was made for the sole benefit of the borrower, and the items thus lent are equally precious as the borrower’s own property, the borrower is bound to prefer the lent items over his own. If he

<column-break/>

does not do so, he is bound to restore their estimated value. This is proven from what has been said, since such a borrower is bound to preserve the items lent to him even at the cost of an equal loss of his own. If, however, the loan was made for the benefit of both, or for the sole benefit of the lender, then the borrower may prefer his own property of equal value to the lent items, and is not bound to any restitution of the loan. The same applies to a pledge, a lease, and a deposit, because these are done for the benefit of the depositor or both parties. For the same reason, Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century canonist</note> on the chapter *bona fides* (cited, number 2), Angelo de Clavasio, Silvester Prierias, and the author of the *Armilla* under the words "loan" and "deposit," Gabriel Biel (in Book 4, distinction 15, question 10, last doubt), and certain others define these matters differently; but what has been said by us presents itself as far more consistent with reason and resting on more solid foundations.

<margin>Question.</margin>
The second doubt is whether, if a borrower sends the lent item back to the lender through a servant or another messenger, and it perishes or disappears—either because the messenger ran away with it, or because it perished by chance or for any other reason—it perishes to the loss of the lender, or rather to the borrower, such that he is bound to restore it again.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
7 Regarding this, it must first be said that if the lender, or anyone else to whom a specific item (either uniquely identified or determined by type and quantity) is owed by any other contract or title, designates a specific person through whom it should be sent to him, then generally, if after it has been delivered to the person designated by him, that thing perishes through the fault of the messenger or for any other reason, it perishes to the creditor and not the debtor. This holds true even if the obligation to restore it had arisen from the debtor's unjust acceptance or retention of it. The reason is that by the very fact that he designated the person to whom it should be delivered, he ratified the payment; indeed, by that very act, the delivery to him is considered completed through that person, and the debt is paid to him. These points are clear from the law *eum qui* (§ last) and the law *si mei* (under the word "si dominus") in the Digest on loans, and from Law 4, Title 2, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and law *vlt.* in the beginning of the Digest on sailors, innkeepers, and stablekeepers; and the doctors to be cited and others commonly affirm this.

8 Observe, however, that if the creditor sent a messenger to the debtor to tell him to send the lent item (or whatever else is owed), but the creditor did not specifically indicate to him that he should send it *by that messenger*, then if the debtor delivers it to him and it does not reach the creditor, the payment is not considered made. It no more perishes to the creditor than if the debtor had sent it through someone else, according to what remains to be said. The reason is that the messenger was only intended to remind the debtor about the payment, not to have the payment delivered to him. This is held in the law *si mei* (§ *commodatam*) in the Digest on loans, and Law 4 cited above, and the doctors commonly affirm this.

9 Next, it must be said that when something was lent for the sole benefit of the borrower, and it is sent through a person not at all designated by the lender, if the borrower was not in <term>default</term> <note>original: "mora"; a legal delay in performing an obligation</note> in restoring it, nor at fault (even the slightest) in delivering it to such a person, nor had he taken the risk of accidents upon himself, or if his unjust delay provided the occasion for it to perish (because if he had not been in default, perhaps it would not have perished), then it perishes to the borrower.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 120 regarding the liability of a borrower when returning an item. It specifically addresses the risks involved when using a messenger or servant to return property and begins a new Disputation on the consequences of being in "mora" (legal default or delay) in returning a borrowed item.</meta>

An example of the first part is when you sent the item through a servant whom you had often found to be faithful, and he ran away with it or it was lost by some other means. In such a case, if none of the circumstances mentioned in the latter part occurred, the loss falls on the <term>lender</term><note>original: "commodanti"; the person who lent the item for use</note>, to whom the item belonged. Consequently, the borrower is held to no restitution. This is because, since even the most prudent person would not have applied any greater diligence, morally speaking, the borrower was certainly not even in the <term>slightest fault</term><note>original: "levissima culpa"; the highest standard of care in Roman law, where even a tiny mistake creates liability</note>. The second part is evident from itself and from what has been said above. Both parts are established by the law <italic>eum qui</italic>, the final paragraph, by the two following laws, and by the law <italic>argentum</italic> in the <term>Digest</term><note>original: "ff."; a shorthand for the Pandects or Digest of Justinian, the primary source of Roman law</note> regarding <term>loans for use</term><note>original: "commodatum"</note>, as well as from law 4, title 2, part 5. Both parts are affirmed by Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 185; Angelus under the word *commodatum*, number 15; Sylvester in the same place, question 10; Panormitanus on the chapter *significante* regarding pledges, number 8; Bartolus; and the common opinion, which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in the second volume of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7, number 3.

The same must be said when the loan was for the benefit of both parties, or for the benefit of the lender alone, such as in a <term>pledge</term><note>original: "pignore"; property held as security</note>, a <term>hired thing</term><note>original: "re conducta"</note>, a <term>deposit</term><note>original: "re deposita"</note>, and in a <term>precarium</term><note>original: "precario"; a loan held at the will of the lender</note>. Likewise, it applies as a rule when a <term>specific, unique item</term><note>original: "res in individuo determinata"</note> is owed and is sent to the creditor, even if ownership of it does not yet belong to him. This holds unless there is negligence (<term>culpa</term>), for which the debtor is held liable according to the nature of each contract, and unless he was in <term>default</term><note>original: "mora"; a legal delay in performing an obligation</note> in restoring that thing, such that the delay provided the occasion for its loss. It also holds unless he has taken responsibility for the <term>slightest fault</term> or for <term>unforeseeable accidents</term><note>original: "casu fortuito"</note>; in these cases, the loss falls on the creditor, not the debtor who sent it. Therefore, if someone who received something as a loan for the benefit of both parties sent that item, or a pledge, or a hired thing back to the creditor through someone who was considered a good man—but whose faithfulness he himself had tested only once or never at all—and the messenger runs off with it, the item is lost to the creditor, to whom it belonged. This is because the debtor was not in <term>slight negligence</term><note>original: "leuis culpa"; a failure to exercise the care that a reasonable person would</note> by sending it in that manner, nor is he liable for a lesser degree of fault by the force of the contracts through which he owed that item. If, however, someone who received a thing by *precarium*, or as a loan for the sole benefit of the lender, or who holds it as a deposit, sends it to the creditor through someone whom he never knew before, but who told him that the creditor said to send it to him, and the debtor had no sinister suspicion about the man—even if that man lied about being a messenger—if he runs off with the item, the loss is the creditor's. The reason is that the debtor was not in <term>gross negligence</term><note>original: "lata culpa"; extreme neglect or lack of basic care</note> by handing the item to such a messenger, but only in slight negligence; and by the force of those contracts, he is not liable for any fault lighter than gross negligence or <term>fraud</term><note>original: "dolus"</note>. What has been said in this paragraph is clear from the laws cited in the preceding paragraph, joined with the law *apud Labeonem*, final paragraph, of the Digest regarding the meaning of words, and the doctors cited in the preceding paragraph agree.

However, when that which was owed was not a specific item, but was certain in its general type and quantity—such as what is owed from a <term>monetary loan</term><note>original: "mutuo"</note> and various other titles—then, unless it is sent through a person designated by the creditor for that purpose, if it is lost before being delivered to the creditor, the loss falls entirely on the debtor. This is true even if there was no fault on his part at all, but it was lost through robbery or an unforeseeable accident. The reason is that <term>the loss falls on the owner</term><note>original: "res domino perit"</note> when no fault occurs on the part of the other person (who is not the owner), and no agreement was made that the loss should be his, nor was the item owed to the creditor as a specific, unique thing. In the case

<column-break/>

proposed, the ownership of the thing thus owed belongs to the debtor, and no fault or agreement has occurred on the part of the creditor for the loss to be his, nor was it owed to him as a specific thing. Furthermore, when an <term>indefinite thing</term><note>original: "res indeterminata"; such as a certain amount of grain or money rather than a specific gold ring</note> is owed, the debtor is not released from the obligation of paying it until he delivers it to the creditor, or the creditor ratifies the payment, or remits the debt. None of these are seen in the case proposed. All these points are clearly gathered from the chapter *significante* on pledges and from the law *incendium* in the Code, and they are affirmed by the cited doctors; Navarrus agrees in the same place, number 67, as does Juan Medina in *On Restitution*, question 2, in the 4th place of the section "to that which," etc.

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>A Doubt</margin>
There is a **doubt** regarding what happens if the creditor and debtor agree that the debt should be handed over to whoever brings a certain "sign" or token, and a third party, knowing this, took that sign, requested the debt, and fled with it: does the loss then fall on the creditor, or rather on the debtor?
<margin>Decision</margin>
Indeed, it must be said that if the thing owed was a specifically determined item, it undoubtedly is lost to the creditor, according to what has been said. And on this, everyone agrees. However, when it was owed as an indefinite thing, Antonio Gómez (in the place cited, number 3) judges that it is lost to the debtor. I think, however, a distinction must be made. For if the debtor revealed the sign, and from that it arose that another person deceived them both, then the loss is the debtor's. But if the creditor revealed it—or while they both were agreeing, someone else passing by or standing there heard it and either took the sign himself or revealed it to another who took it—then the loss is the creditor's. This is because by such a pact, the creditor himself consented and was the cause for the item being given to the one presenting that sign. Bartolus and others, whom Antonio Gómez refers to in the cited place while interpreting their words against the common opinion, affirm this very clearly.

## To what extent a borrower is held liable if he is in default of restoring the borrowed item. And concerning the expenses made for it. And whether compensation can be made for it.

### DISPUTATION CCXCVII.

->SUMMARY<-

1. When a borrower is considered to be in default for not restoring the borrowed item.
2. A borrower placed in <term>default</term><note>original: "mora"</note> is not only bound to restore the thing but also its value.
3. A borrower placed in default, even by the <term>slightest fault</term>, is held liable for all damages, even for <term>lost profit</term><note>original: "lucri cessantis"; the gain that the lender could have made if the item had been returned on time</note>.
4. In what cases a borrower placed in default due to inability to fulfill the contract is held liable for interest.
5. To what expenses of the borrowed item a borrower is held.
6. In what things <term>compensation</term><note>original: "compensatio"; the legal offsetting of one debt against another</note> is said to take place.
7. When compensation can take place in a loan for use.
8. If a thing is lent to two people, when each is held for the whole amount <note>original: "in solidum"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the legal and ethical analysis of "commodatum" (a loan for use). Having previously discussed the risks of returning items via messengers, Molina now transitions to the consequences of "mora" (legal delay or default) and the responsibility for expenses incurred during the loan period.</meta>

# Louis de Molina, On Contracts

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the first point, it must be established that if a specific time was prearranged for which the thing was lent, the <term>borrower</term><note>original: "commodatarius"; the person who receives the item for use</note> is in <term>default</term><note>original: "mora"; a legal state of delay that triggers liability</note> by that very fact once the time expires, unless they restore the thing or the contrary will of the lender is evident. Nor is it necessary that, once the time has passed, the <term>lender</term><note>original: "commodans"</note> must first demand his property before the borrower is said to be in default. For *the set date makes the demand on behalf of the master or creditor, as held in the final chapter of "On Leases," the law "magnam" in the Code "On Contracting Stipulations," and law 2 of the Code "On the Law of Emphyteusis."* Likewise, if the thing was lent for a certain use, once that use is finished, or the time has elapsed in which it could have been conveniently finished, the borrower is similarly in default, unless the contrary will of the lender (at least presumed) is evident. However, when something was lent for use indefinitely, with neither a time nor a particular use expressed, then, as long as the contrary will of the lender is not evident, the borrower is not to be judged as being in default.

<margin>2</margin> With this established, it must first be said that if the borrower (the same applies to one who took a thing on lease) stubbornly retains it until a condemnatory sentence is passed against him, then he is held not only to restore the item, but also its value in addition, as a penalty for his <term>contumacy</term><note>stubborn refusal to obey a court order</note>. This is found in *the law "non abs re" in the Code "On Where by Force," law 12, title 10, part 7, and book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 59, at the beginning*, and in other laws which we shall cite in *Disputation 498*, where we demonstrate this matter more broadly regarding leases.

<margin>3</margin> Next, it must be said that if the borrower was in default of restoring the lent item due to even his <term>slightest fault</term><note>original: "levissima culpa"; the highest standard of care where even the smallest negligence creates liability</note>, he is held to the lender for all subsequent damages, even for <term>lost profit</term><note>original: "lucri cessantis"; the gain the lender would have made had the item been returned on time</note>. All agree on this. For since this contract was celebrated for the benefit of the borrower alone, certainly if he fails to fulfill it even by the slightest fault, he is held for all damages or <term>interest</term><note>original: "interesse"; legal compensation for loss</note> to the lender. Especially since this is a <term>good faith contract</term><note>original: "bonæ fidei"; a type of contract where the judge assesses what is fair and equitable rather than following strict, literal formulas</note>, as seen in *Disputation 259*, in which the judge’s discretion has more place than in contracts of strict law; so that even if these things were not included in the formal agreement, the judge can weigh them and pass a sentence based on what is good and equitable, just as the nature of the matter itself demands.

<margin>4</margin> The entire difficulty, however, is whether a borrower is held for "interest" to the lender when he was in default of fulfilling the contract entirely due to inability, and did not fall into that state even by the slightest fault. A few things must be said first. If the lender included in the agreement that the borrower would be held for interest if he were in default, he is indeed held; and this is true even if the lender did not specify it, and even if that default happened without the borrower's fault or by a <term>fortuitous event</term><note>original: "casu fortuito"; an accident that could not be foreseen or prevented, like a storm or sudden illness</note>. This is because it is understood to be so by the very fact that such an agreement was added. This is both because, by the nature of the thing (setting aside that agreement), he was held for interest if he fell into default by his own fault, and the agreement was added to effect something further. It is also chiefly because, by that very act, the lender wished to sustain no damage—even of lost profit—from the loan, and intended to signal this to the borrower. Moreover, just as an agreement is valid by which the risk of the lent item itself from a fortuitous event is shifted to the borrower (as seen in *Disputation 295*), so too is an agreement valid by which the risk of <term>emergent damage</term><note>original: "damni emergentis"; actual loss incurred</note> or

<column-break/>

lost profit resulting from a default caused by a fortuitous event is shifted to the same borrower. For it is entirely within the lender's right to be unwilling to lend except on the condition that he be rendered completely harmless, even regarding lost profit, if such should happen to him from such a favor, even without the borrower's fault.

Next, it must be said that if the lender did not include this in the agreement, the borrower is not held for interest regarding lost profit and emergent damage that happened to the lender from a default into which the borrower fell without any fault of his own. This is proven because, if the contrary is not included in the agreement, the borrower is not held for the loss of the item itself that happens by fortuitous event and without his fault, even if the loan provided the occasion for the loss (namely, because the item would not have perished if it had not been lent), as was said in *Disputation 295*. Therefore, he is much less held for the interest of lost profit and emergent damage which comes to the lender from a delay in restoring the item, when the borrower was in no fault for such delay. For by the very fact that someone gives something as a loan for use, if he does not include the contrary in the agreement, he is judged to expose himself to the risk of his own property if it happens without the borrower's fault, and consequently to the risk of the interest he hoped for from it. Note, however, that if the borrower, while he was in default, had used the lent item, he is held to restore to the lender the value of that use, if the lender wishes it; for when the use and time of the borrower ceased, the value of the use belongs to the owner, just like the loss of the item would.

It must be added that when a loan for use is for the benefit of both parties, and the inability to restore the lent item at the stated time arose only from the borrower's <term>slight fault</term><note>original: "culpa leuissima"; here meaning a middle degree of negligence</note>, he would not be held for interest to the lender unless the contrary was included in the agreement. The same must be said of a thing received as a pledge or a lease. The reason is that in contracts of this kind, the receiver is only held for "slight fault" and any other greater fault. By this same reasoning, if the loan was for the sole benefit of the lender, and the delay arose only from the slight or slightest fault of the borrower, he would not be held for interest to the lender. The same must be said in a <term>precarium</term><note>a loan granted by request and revocable at will</note> and a deposit. The reason is that in these contracts the receiver is only held for fraud and <term>gross negligence</term><note>original: "lata culpa"</note>. The law "quod te mihi" in the Digest "On things credited" agrees with all this, and the law "Celsus," paragraph 1, in the Digest "On receiving arbitrators" supports it. This concerns the first of the points proposed.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding the second point, a distinction must briefly be made. For if the expenses made on the lent item are ordinary—such as those regarding the food or housing of a lent slave or beast of burden—the borrower is held for them, and therefore cannot demand them from the lender. But if they are extraordinary—such as those regarding the health or the flight of a slave—he can demand them from the lender, unless they are light and small, for the borrower is held even for these. All these are found in the law "in rebus," the paragraph "possunt," in the Digest "On Loans for Use."

<margin>6</margin> Regarding the third point, observe: <term>Set-off</term><note>original: "compensatio"; a legal mechanism where mutual debts cancel each other out</note>, as will be said more copiously in *Disputation 560*, does not properly have a place unless the things are of the same nature and kind, and consist of weight, number, or measure; as when the debt is money, and the thing in which the set-off ought to be made is similarly money;

<summary>Molina explains that a borrower is in legal default (mora) as soon as a loan's term expires. He clarifies that while borrowers are usually liable for damages caused by their negligence, they are not liable for accidental delays unless a specific prior agreement was made.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal obligations following a loan for use (commodatum). Having previously addressed the delivery and risks of the borrowed item, Molina now explores the legal concept of "compensation" (set-off)—whether a borrower can refuse to return an item because the lender owes them a separate debt.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 298.

money; or when the debt is wheat, wine, oil, or something similar, and the thing in which the <term>compensation</term><note>original: "compensatio"; a legal "set-off" where two mutual debts cancel each other out</note> must be made is of the same kind. However, when they are of different kinds—as when one is money and the other is a horse, wine, or oil, or when one is wheat and the other is wine or oil—it is not strictly compensation. Nor is it properly compensation when they are of the same kind but do not consist of weight, number, or measure; for instance, when one <term>slave</term><note>original: "mancipium"</note> is owed and compensation is intended with another, or when one horse is owed and compensation is intended with another horse. This is noted by Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in his commentary on the chapter "Ad nostram" regarding oaths, and in the final chapter "On Deposits," and is affirmed by the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 56. In cases where compensation would otherwise take place but is blocked because the debt and the object are not of the same nature or kind, the <term>withholding of the object</term><note>original: "detentio rei"</note> succeeds in place of compensation until the debt is paid. Panormitanus calls this "indirect compensation."

<margin>Question 7. The opinion of many. Their arguments.</margin>
Having laid this foundation, the question arises whether compensation has a place in a <term>loan for use</term><note>original: "commodatum"; a loan where the specific item must be returned</note>. Panormitanus, in the cited passage, says the common opinion of the doctors is that compensation does apply in a loan for use, and thus the borrowed item can be withheld for a debt, provided that debt is <term>liquid</term><note>original: "liquidum"; a debt that is clear, undisputed, and fixed in amount</note>. Sylvester, Navarro, and others affirm and embrace this. They confirm it from the final law of the Code "On Compensation" and the final chapter "On Deposits," where compensation is admitted in other contracts, with "deposits" being the only exception. The Portuguese Ordinances also agree; the argument being that an exception in only one contract confirms the rule in all other contracts.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
However, the contrary is expressly held in the final law of the Code "On Loans," where compensation or withholding of a borrowed item for another debt is forbidden. Nor do I see how the authors of the contrary opinion can satisfactorily answer this text. The same is very clearly laid out in Law 67, Title 2, Part 5, which was drawn from the cited Code law. The same is affirmed by the <term>Gloss</term><note>the standard medieval commentary on the law</note> and by Gregorio Lopez <note>a prominent Spanish jurist</note>, and others whom he cites.

The cited Gloss makes an exception when two things occur together. First, when the borrowed item is not to be restored in itself, but in money, because it perished while with the borrower or for some other reason. Second, that the debt to be set off is liquid. Because in that case, it is not the borrowed item itself that is being restored, but a debt in its place, it is not surprising if a set-off of the monetary debt arising from the loan applies against another monetary debt, or that it can be withheld until any other debt is paid.

The same Gloss and the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 59, Paragraph 1, make a second exception: when the debt for which the borrowed item is withheld arose from **expenses made on the borrowed item itself**. For such a debt, the item can be withheld; this is laid out in the legal digests.

<column-break/>

However, the cited Law 9 limits this: provided the expenses were made **while** the item was being borrowed. If they had been made previously, it could not be withheld for them.

Regarding the arguments used by the authors of the contrary opinion: one must say that the argument from the "contrary sense"—that an exception in one case confirms the rule for the rest—only applies when there is no express text stating otherwise, as there is in the matter we are discussing. Because the matter of formal compensation does not regularly apply to a loan for use as it does to a deposit (since money and things consisting of weight, number, or measure are usually "deposited" or "mutuated" [lent as a commodity] rather than "borrowed for use"), and because an exception is made for expenses incurred on the item, the law did not feel the need to explicitly except the loan for use in the same way it excepted the deposit.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The question is: if an indivisible thing, such as a wagon, a beast of burden, or something similar, was lent to **two people**, will each be liable for the **whole amount** <note>original: "in solidum"; meaning either person can be sued for the full value</note>, or only for half? This applies to leases and deposits as well.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
It must be said that if it was not stipulated in the contract that each should be held for the whole, and the item perishes without fault of the recipients, each is only held for half of the fee (if the item was rented) or half the value (if they agreed to be liable for accidents). This is affirmed in Law 5, Title 2, Part 5, and in the Digest regarding vehicles lent to two people. However, when the item perishes through **fault**, then each is held for the whole in this sense: if it perishes through the fault of both, each is liable to the owner for the whole, though if one restores the whole, the other must reimburse him for half. This is clearly held in the laws on deposits. But if the item perishes through the fault of **only one** of them, then he alone is liable for the whole to the owner, and the other owes nothing, as is clear in the cited passages. Law 5 of Castile, which speaks obscurely and concisely, should be interpreted according to this.

## On Precarious Loans.

### DISPUTATION CCXCVIII.

#### SUMMARY.

1. What a precarious loan is, and how it differs from a standard loan for use.
2. A precarious loan cannot be revoked immediately, except for some reasonable cause.
3. Something can be granted as a precarious loan for a fixed time.
4. A precarious loan cannot be granted with a pact that it not be reclaimed until the full time has passed.
5. One receiving a thing as a precarious loan is said to possess it naturally; otherwise for a standard borrower.
6. Rights of way or legal easements can be granted as a precarious loan.
7. One holding a thing as a precarious loan is liable only for fraud and gross negligence.

### Ludovico Molina On Contracts

<margin>8</margin> *In how many ways a <term>precarious loan</term><note>original: "precarium"; a legal arrangement where property is granted to someone upon their request, but remains revocable at the owner's will at any time</note> is ended.*
<margin>9</margin> *How a precarious loan is considered revoked; in which cases a contrary act is necessary, and in which not.*
<margin>10</margin> *Graces and privileges: under what form they do not expire with the death of the grantor but instead require revocation, and under what form they do expire.*
*And what is observed in Portugal.*
<margin>11</margin> *A grace or privilege granted "until the good pleasure of the Apostolic See" does not expire with the death of the grantor.*
<margin>12</margin> *Whether a grace granted "until the pleasure of the Pope or the King" expires with the death of the person who granted it, or not.*
<margin>13</margin> *What precarious loans are, and in how many ways they are made (see also number 14).*
<margin>15</margin> *For what purpose precarious loans are renewed every five years.*

<margin>1</margin> According to the legal authority Ulpian <note>a famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> in the first law of the Digest "On Precarious Loans," a <term>precarious loan</term> is that which is granted for use to a petitioner for as long as the grantor allows—that is, as long as the grantor has not revoked it. The distinction between a precarious loan and a <term>loan for use</term><note>original: "commodatum"; a loan for a specific purpose or time that cannot usually be revoked early without cause</note> was previously explained in Disputation 294.

<margin>2</margin> Although a precarious loan may be revoked and reclaimed at the grantor’s discretion according to its definition, legal experts such as Panormitanus, Navarrus, and Angelus de Clavasio observe that it cannot be revoked *immediately* after it has been granted unless some reasonable cause arises for doing so. <margin>3</margin> The reason is that such a sudden revocation suggests bad faith on the part of the grantor; specifically, it suggests they intended to harm the recipient by granting something and then snatching it back instantly. Since a grant is a benefit, it ought to help the recipient, not deceive them. Therefore, a grantor who seeks to revoke a precarious loan without a new, reasonable cause will be blocked by a legal plea of bad faith. A prudent judge will grant the recipient a certain amount of time to use the item they received.

<margin>Doubts</margin> A doubt arises as to whether something can be requested and granted precariously for a fixed period, such as for a month or another certain time. <margin>3</margin> It must be said that without doubt this can be requested and granted. However, <margin>Decision</margin> the meaning in such a case is that the precarious loan ends when that time is up, and the item must be returned unless the arrangement is extended. Furthermore, the item can still be reclaimed and revoked during that fixed time at the grantor’s discretion. This is why we commonly say: "Lend me your book for a month, and if you want it back before then, I shall return it."

<margin>Doubt 4</margin> Another doubt is whether something can be granted precariously with an agreement that it will not be reclaimed until the full time for which it is granted has passed. The answer is no. Such an agreement is null and void because <margin>Decision</margin> it goes against the very nature of a precarious contract. This is affirmed by Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and Antonio Gómez.

<column-break/>

Bartolus and others argue that no force can be given to such an agreement, as a person cannot possess another's property against the owner's will. This discussion concerns situations where something was granted precariously for a fixed time. Silvester and Angelus de Clavasio affirm that if such a pact were added as part of the precarious contract—namely, that the item is accepted for a certain time such that it cannot be revoked during that period—the entire contract would be void, as it contains a condition that destroys the nature of the contract itself. This does not contradict the law; when something is granted for a fixed time, and the grantor asks for it back before the time is up, the user cannot block the request by claiming the time hasn't expired. Instead, the fixed term simply means that once the time is over, the contract ceases and the item must be returned without waiting for a formal revocation.

<margin>5</margin> Although a person in a <term>loan for use</term> does not "possess" the item in a legal or natural sense (rather, it is the lender who possesses it through them), the person who receives a <term>precarious loan</term> is said to possess it naturally. This is affirmed by the standard legal glosses and Antonio Gómez.

<margin>6</margin> <term>Servitudes</term><note>original: "servitutes"; legal rights to use another's land, such as a right of way</note> and rights can also be granted precariously. For instance, the right to cross another's field or to have a beam resting on a neighbor's wall can be granted "until the pleasure of the grantor." Indeed, whenever such a thing is granted at someone’s request, it is considered a precarious grant and can be revoked by the grantor.

<margin>7</margin> The person who holds a precarious loan is only liable for <term>bad faith</term><note>original: "dolus"</note> and <term>gross negligence</term><note>original: "lata culpa"</note>. However, if a different standard was agreed upon in a pact, one must abide by that pact, as discussed in Disputation 295.

<margin>8</margin> A precarious loan ends with the death of the person to whom it was granted. This is because it is considered a personal privilege for the recipient, and thus expires with their life. However, it does not end with the death of the grantor; rather, it continues in relation to the grantor's heirs until they choose to revoke it. This is the common opinion of the doctors of law, followed by Covarruvias and Valasco, despite what some older commentaries might suggest to the contrary.

<margin>9</margin> It is greatly to be observed in this place that when a precarious loan is granted without a pre-defined time...

Molina explains that while the owner can generally revoke it at will, they must not act in bad faith, and the loan’s legal status changes depending on whether the grantor or the recipient dies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion from the previous page regarding the termination of precarious loans. He transitions from general property loans to the legal status of "graces" and "privileges" granted by sovereigns and the Church, focusing on whether these expire when the grantor dies.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 298.

is granted by way of a loan, it is considered granted until it is revoked, or until the grantor changes their mind, as stated in the second law, first section, "On Precarious Loans" <note>original: "l.2.§.1. de precar."</note>. Therefore, for it to cease and end on the part of the grantor, it is necessary for it to be revoked by a contrary act of the grantor or their heirs. Even when something is granted precariously for a fixed time, a similar contrary act is necessary for it to cease before that time. And regarding such a <term>precarious loan</term><note>A grant of property or rights that can be taken back at any time</note>, we said just recently that it is not ended by the death of the grantor until it is revoked by the heirs.

However, it is a far different matter when someone grants something "until their good pleasure," or "meanwhile, so long as it shall be their will," or—what is the same thing—"meanwhile, as long as they wish," or "while it pleases them," or "at the whim of their will." In these instances, because the language refers to the will or "good pleasure" of a person living in this world, and such a will or pleasure ceases at death, it follows that such a grant or precarious loan expires with the life of the one who granted it. No contrary act of revocation is necessary. This is expressly held in the fourth law of the Digest "On Leasing" <note>original: "l. 4. ff. locati"</note> and in the chapter "If Graciously" <note>original: "c. si gratiose"</note> regarding rescripts in the Sixth Book of Decretals. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, whom Molina, Alvarus Valascus, Covarruvias, Bartolus, and others follow and cite.

<margin>10</margin>
Therefore, if a grace or privilege is granted by the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> or a supreme temporal prince absolutely, or under the form "until it be revoked," or "meanwhile, so long as it shall not be revoked," or "meanwhile, so long as we have not revoked it," it does not expire upon the death of the grantor. This is because it requires a revocation to cease. This is clearly handed down in the law "With a Precarious Loan" <note>original: "l. cum precario"</note> and the chapter "If a Delegate" <note>original: "c. si delegatus"</note>. However, if it is granted under this other form: "meanwhile, so long as this shall be our will," "until our good pleasure," "at our whim," or "while we so wish," it expires upon the death of the grantor, as is clear from the law and the cited doctors.

From this, Alvarus Valascus draws a point for legal practice: when a prince grants donations or privileges under the clause *so long as it be our grace* <note>original: "en quanto for nossa merce"; a Portuguese legal formula</note>, it expires upon the death of the grantor. However, if there is further added: *and we do not command the contrary* <note>original: "e nan mandar o contrario"</note>, as he says is the custom in <term>Lusitania</term><note>Portugal</note> to add to royal provisions for offices, jurisdictions, and similar things, then it does not end with the death of the grantor. This is because, by reason of what is added, a new revocation of will is required.

<margin>11</margin>
It must be observed in this place that when something is granted "until the good pleasure of the <term>Apostolic See</term><note>The office of the Papacy, rather than the individual person of the Pope</note>," or "meanwhile, so long as the Apostolic See shall wish," then it does not expire upon the death of the grantor. To expire, it requires revocation by a contrary act. This is expressly held in the chapter "If Graciously" in the Sixth Book, where we read: *If a grace is granted until the good pleasure of the Apostolic See,* then, because the See itself does not die, the grace shall endure perpetually unless it is revoked by a successor. The common opinion of the doctors agrees with this.

<margin>Question 12.</margin>
The doctors, however, dispute this: if something

<column-break/>

is granted "until the pleasure of the Pope" or "the Supreme Pontiff" or "the King," does it expire upon the death of that Pope or King who was living when it was granted? Many assert it does not expire, because the *dignity* <note>The legal office or status</note> does not expire; nor is the Apostolic See something different from the dignity of the Supreme Pontiff. Likewise, when someone is appointed as a judge or executor and mention is made not of the person, but of the dignity (the office), then surely—unless the grantor's intent appears otherwise—both the person living at the time of the grant and the successors in that same office are considered to be appointed, as we shall see in Treatise 5.

<margin>Opinion of some.</margin>
The opinion of others, toward which Covarruvias and Alvarus Valascus incline, affirms the contrary. They are led by the chapter "If Graciously," which states: *If it is graciously granted to you by the Roman Pontiff that you may retain the benefits you held at the time of your promotion "until the good pleasure of his will," such a grace expires by his death (by which his good pleasure is entirely extinguished).* 
To these words, however, the authors of the contrary opinion could very well respond that the text there is speaking about the specific *person* holding the Roman Pontificate who had graciously granted the right to retain those benefits "until *his* pleasure"; this is clearly the natural sense of those words.

Two things please me regarding this matter. First, as Covarruvias says, one must weigh the matter using conjectures from the surrounding circumstances to see whether the "good pleasure" was reserved to the *person* established in that office, or rather to the *office* itself (that is, whoever holds that dignity in general). In the first case, the grant expires with the person; in the second, it does not. Furthermore, in case of doubt, one should rather incline toward the grant being made in the first sense (the person) rather than the second, and therefore it expires. This is what Covarruvias and Valascus affirm, both because the cited chapter favors it and because such favors are not to be extended beyond their terms.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
The second point is that such grants—where this ambiguity exists—are rarely made except by a third party who has the power of granting things in the name of princes, such as by <term>viceroys</term><note>Governors acting in the name of the King</note> and other governors of provinces. For example, when the viceroys of the Indies grant an office or something else under this form: *so long as it be the grace of the King, or his Highness, or as he shall see fit* <note>original: "em quanto for merce del Roy, ou su alteza ou ouuer por bem"</note>. In this event, Alvarus Valascus thinks the grant expires with the specific King in whose time it was made. Since the one who granted it is not considered to have thought about future Kings from whom he received no power, but only about the one from whom he holds it and in whose name he acts. Furthermore, a general naming is restricted to the person in whom alone it is verified. I believe, however, even in such grants made by viceroys, the words and circumstances must be weighed to see if they intended to grant at the good pleasure of the King for the time being. The laws Valascus cites do not prove his point if they are carefully weighed. However, if it were said, "I grant this at the pleasure of the Kings of Portugal..."

Molina concludes that grants made at a person's "good pleasure" usually expire at death, whereas those tied to an office (like the Papacy) or granted "until revoked" remain valid until a successor takes formal action.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 298.

of Portugal, or of the King for the time being, then the grant would not expire upon the death of the first king, but would be perpetual until a contrary agreement was revoked.

There are, however, several points to be observed regarding what has been said so far. **First**, although the will and "good pleasure" of someone granting something is judged to cease upon their death, it does not cease during sleep, drunkenness, madness, or insanity. This is clearly gathered from the chapter "Greater" <note>original: "ca. maiores. §. vlti. de bapt."</note> regarding baptism and its effects, and from various laws in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de acquiren. poſſeſ." and "ff. de vſucapi."</note>. In these states, the person is still considered potentially capable of willing by their nature in this life. Indeed, they are considered to remain in the same state of will as they were before they were deprived of the use of reason, as is clear from the cited laws and affirmed by Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a Spanish jurist</note> in the cited location, numbers 4 and 5.

**Second**, there is this distinction between ordinary and delegated jurisdiction (as we shall see in Treatise 5): ordinary jurisdiction does not expire upon the death of the grantor, even if the matter is still <term>untouched</term><note>Latin: "res integra"; a legal state where no significant action has yet been taken on a case</note>. Delegated jurisdiction, however, if the matter is untouched, expires immediately upon the death of the grantor, or when the grantor’s own jurisdiction ceases for any other reason. It is different if the matter is no longer "untouched": for then it does not expire, unless it was granted only until the "good pleasure" of the grantor. From this, you will understand the chapter "If a delegate" <note>original: "ca. ſi delegatus. §. 1. de offic. deleg. lib. 6."</note>, where it is established that if a delegate of the Apostolic See <note>The Pope or the Vatican</note> has sub-delegated a task for as long as he himself judges it should be held: then, if the delegate dies before the matter is finished, the jurisdiction does not expire in the sub-delegate. It would have expired, however, if he had sub-delegated only until his "good pleasure"; for in that case, the "good pleasure" would have expired with his life.

**Third**, the things I have said here regarding jurisdictions or "graces" <note>Special favors or privileges granted by a superior</note> granted by a supreme prince or by inferiors—concerning when they expire at the death of the grantor and when they do not—will have a more convenient place in the fifth treatise. For that reason, I defer them until then. In the meantime, you may read Molina <note>The author referring to his own work</note>, Book 1, *On Primogeniture*, chapter 25.

If someone has handed over their property to another as a <term>pledge</term><note>Collateral for a debt</note>, and then obtained the use of that property back from the creditor as a <term>precarious loan</term><note>A loan held only by the permission of the lender</note>, then as soon as the debt is paid, the loan ends. This is very well known and is found in the law "If a debtor" <note>original: "l. ſi debitor. ff. de precario"</note>.

If someone who has granted another thing precariously sells it or otherwise transfers it, then the one who buys it (or to whom it passes by another title) can revoke the loan whenever they wish. This is held in the Digest and the Decretals, and is affirmed by Alvaro Valasco in the cited question 24, number 8.

Finally, one must observe in this dispute that <term>precarium</term> (the neuter form), which we have discussed so far, is one thing; and <term>precaria</term> (the feminine form, plural *precariae*), discussed in Canon Law under the title "On Precaria," is another.

<margin>13</margin> Indeed, *precariae* are grants made in perpetuity, or for the life of the receiver, or for a certain fixed time (whether short or long). Such a contract cannot be revoked before that time has elapsed. The exception is if it involves the property of the Church and was granted unreasonably by a minister of the Church; in that case, the successor is not bound to stand by the predecessor’s contract, but

<column-break/>

can, and should, reclaim the Church property that was so poorly alienated, as is held in chapter 2 of "On Precaria."

<margin>14</margin> These kinds of *precariae* are made in many ways. Sometimes something is granted for a certain annual payment (<term>pension</term>) in perpetuity, or for life, or for another time; in this case, it does not differ from an <term>emphyteusis</term><note>A long-term or perpetual lease of land in exchange for a rent and improvement of the land</note>, unless the time for which it is granted is less than ten years; for then it would be a simple lease, according to what is said elsewhere. Sometimes something is granted regarding its <term>usufruct</term><note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of a property without owning it</note> in exchange for other possessions that the receiver gives, or agrees to give to the Church after their death. Sometimes, however, something is granted freely, either because of merits, or to a poor person or a pilgrim, and this for a fixed time, or for life, or for several lives. The name "precarious" was given to this contract because all these things are usually granted at the "prayers" (*preces*) of the receivers. These points are clear from chapters 1, 2, and 3 of "On Precaria" and other cited legal sources. Read Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note> and Alvaro Valasco.

<margin>15</margin> In chapter 1 of "On Precaria," it was decreed that *precariae* should be renewed every five years. This is not so that a new contract begins—as if the contract ended after five years—as Alvaro Valasco rightly observes (against the gloss and others), but rather lest the property be lost to the Church through forgetfulness. These contracts are usually made with an express clause that the receiver is bound to renew the contract every five years, otherwise they lose the grant. Where this custom flourishes and the cited Canon Law is in active use, the clause is considered present even if omitted, because the contract is assumed to be entered into according to the custom of the place and the disposition of the law. However, Panormitanus says such renewal is not necessary where it has been abolished by custom, which is obvious in itself and no one can deny.

This is done so that the differences and similarities between these contracts may be understood. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property transfer, transitioning from the previous page's discussion on the expiration of grants to the formal definition and obligations of a loan for consumption (mutuum).</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 299.

...if he wishes to help, by depriving himself of his own property: with the expectation that he may later receive just as much from the other.

<margin>1</margin> A **loan for consumption** (*mutuum*) † is the delivery of a thing for use, such that it immediately becomes the property of the recipient, and he later restores just as much of the same kind and quality. From this it is called a "loan" (*mutuum*), because it is given from me to you in such a way that what was mine becomes yours <note>This is a classic etymological wordplay common in Roman law: *mutuum* derived from *ex meo tuum* ("from mine to thine").</note>, as held in the *Institutes, "In what ways an obligation is contracted by a thing," at the beginning, and in the Digest, "If a certain thing is sought," law 2, paragraph "it is called."*

<margin>2</margin> It is stated in the definition that a loan is the delivery of a thing: because a loan, just like a loan for use (*commodatum*), belongs to the class of contracts that are perfected by the thing or the delivery itself <term>real contracts</term><note>A "real contract" is one where the legal obligation is not created by a mere promise, but only when the physical object is handed over.</note>, as was said in *disputation 254.* It agrees with the *commodatum* in what is immediately added in the definition, namely, "for use." However, it differs from it in the addition "so that it immediately becomes the property of the recipient." For the thing loaned passes into the ownership of the borrower (*mutuatarius*), that is, the one to whom it is given as a loan. And for that reason, even if it perishes by a chance occurrence and without any fault of the borrower, it perishes for him [the borrower], not for the lender (*mutuans*). <note>This is the legal principle of *res perit domino*: the risk of loss lies with the owner. Since the borrower becomes the owner of the specific grains or coins, he bears the risk if they are destroyed.</note>

<margin>3</margin> In the definition it is added, "that he restore just as much later": because it is of the nature of a loan that restoration is not made immediately, otherwise it would be an exchange [barter]. Furthermore, "of the same kind and quality" is added because the nature of the contract of a loan demands it. Thus, even if it is not explicitly stated when the contract is made, the borrower is bound to restore just as much of the same species and quality, or goodness. Therefore, if someone who received old wine as a loan restores new wine, he does not satisfy the debt, because he does not restore wine equally as good as that which he had received. Observe in this place that it is not essential to a loan that the *exact same* physical items are not returned, but rather that the borrower is *not bound* to restore the exact same items. Since the borrower is only bound to restore an equivalent of the same kind, he fully satisfies the debt by returning the very same thing he received, provided it has not been made worse.

<margin>4</margin> The laws † and elsewhere determine that the subject matter of a loan consists of things that are weighed, numbered, and measured, and which are consumed by use, such as money, wheat, wine, oil, and other things of that kind. Under the name of "consumption," they also include the legal transfer (*alienation*) of the thing through its use; in this way money, while it is used to pay for something, or is exchanged for another thing, or is given away or loaned, is said to be "consumed" in relation to the giver, insofar as ownership of it is transferred to another by such use. In this place, note in passing that since in a loan of money the primary consideration is the value it has as money, it is deemed to be returned in the same kind and quality or goodness if money of the same value is restored, even if it is not of the same material. For example, if someone receives two hundred gold coins as a loan, the payment of the loan is satisfied if he restores an 

<column-break/>

equal value in silver or copper coins, or vice versa. This is true unless it was specifically agreed in the contract that the money be paid in the same material, or unless there were a law or custom that a certain part of debts should be paid in silver or gold, as in Portugal. However, since the cited laws affirm that those things are the subject matter of a loan, I think it should be understood (as we said in *disputation 294*) as a general rule, and for the most part, to distinguish whether a contract is a loan for consumption (*mutuum*) or a loan for use (*commodatum*), as the matter can be doubtful. Indeed, since a thing is given so that it immediately becomes the property of the recipient, and another of the same kind and goodness is restored later, it is surely a loan, even if what is given is not consumed by use, nor strictly consists in weight, number, or measure. For instance, if someone asks for an ox or a ram from a friend, intending to restore another similar one to him later, it is a loan. The same applies if a craftsman asks for a certain weight of gold or silver from a friend to make an artifact, intending to restore equal weights of the same material; or if someone asks for stones or wood which he needs to build a house, intending to restore an equal quantity of the same material and of equal quality later.

<margin>5</margin> A loan † can be given by the owner of the thing being loaned. Another can also give it in the owner's name, and then the person in whose name it is given acquires the right of action [to sue for recovery].

<margin>6</margin> If a certain deadline † was agreed upon in which the borrower is bound to pay the loan, he is bound to return it within that time (and not before, even if the lender asks for it). Otherwise, he will be liable for all damages and for "lost profit" (*lucrum cessans*) <note>Lost profit refers to the money the lender could have made had the debt been paid on time.</note> which followed from the lender's delay (*mora*). If the lender spent anything in the recovery of such a debt, the borrower is also bound to pay that to him. The reason is that the borrower, through the unjust delay of payment, is the cause of all these damages to the lender. Consequently, in the "court of conscience" <note>This refers to moral or religious obligation, distinct from civil court judgments.</note>, without waiting for a legal sentence, he is bound to repair all those things. In that place, Gregorius Lopez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note> says that if the loan is of something other than money, only the "intrinsic interest" of the thing to be paid is due, not the "extrinsic interest" of the profit that could have been acquired by trading with that thing. However, that legal limitation only speaks of sales. Furthermore, Gregorius Lopez limits this by saying that if the lender was a merchant, then even extrinsic interest is owed. Therefore, from the delay (*mora*) of any loan, extrinsic interest is also owed, if such interest would truly have existed for the lender. I would advise in passing that the limitation by Gregorius Lopez and Bartolus is surely of no weight if that law were to be extended to a loan. For in that law, extrinsic interest is openly excluded, even if the person is a merchant who ought to have traded and profited from the purchased thing.

<margin>7</margin> When no deadline has been fixed for the payment of the loan, then the borrower is bound to pay it whenever the lender asks for it. Provided, however, that he does not ask for it immediately...
