### On a Loan Made to the Church, a City, or a Minor.

### DISPUTATION 300.

### SUMMARY.

1. *Under the name of "City," towns are also understood to be included.*
2. *In order for the Church and the city to be held liable for a loan, what must be proven by the lender, in which cases, and why. Number 7.*
3. *When a loan is said to be "turned to the utility" of the Church or City, such that they are held liable for it.*
4. *When a Church or City is considered to be made wealthier, so that it is held liable for a loan.*
5. *When an administrator of the Church has a legal action for "business managed" against the Church.* <note>original: *negociorum gestorum*; an action to recover expenses for work done on behalf of another without their prior consent.</note>
6. *When a lender is granted an action against the Church to have the loan paid to him.*
7. *Why a lender is bound to prove that the loan was converted to the utility of the Church or city.*
8. *A minor enjoys the same privilege as the Church and the City regarding a loan, so that the lender is bound to prove the loan was converted to his benefit.*

<margin>1</margin> Under the name of "Church" in this place, pious places and locations such as hospitals are understood. Under the name † of "City," other towns are also understood, as held in Law 3, Title 11, Part 5, and affirmed by the first gloss on the law *Ciuitas* in the Digest <note>original: *ff. si cert. petat.*; referencing a specific section of the Roman Digest.</note>. The same law also includes Kings when they receive a loan through their ministers in the name of the King, but without their specific mandate. For as Gregorio López noted in the same place on the word "of the King," since the King's property is managed through administrators, the King enjoys the privilege of minors, according to the final law of the final title of Part 6; there you may see what the same Gregorio teaches in this part regarding Kings and other towns that are not cities.

<margin>2</margin> When † the Church or a city has received something as a loan, in order for them to be bound to pay it back, the lender must first prove that what was received was converted to the benefit <term>utility</term> of the Church or city. This is held regarding the city in the law *Ciuitas* and in Law 1 of the Code *On the payments and releases of city debts,*

<column-break/>

Book 11, and Law 3, Title 1, Part 5. Regarding the Church, it is found in the Authentic text *Hoc ius porrectum* <note>A medieval legal update to the Roman Code regarding sacred churches.</note> and the Law 3 cited above. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a major Spanish jurist.</note> records and follows in his *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 17, number 3. Otherwise, neither the city nor the Church is bound to pay it; instead, the person who received it in the name of the Church or city is liable. The creditor must bring an action against that person and his heirs for those amounts that are not proven to have been converted to the benefit of the Church.

Regarding this matter, the view of Panormitanus <note>A famous canon lawyer.</note> following Innocent is preferred. He teaches that we must distinguish between whether the prelate <note>A high-ranking church official like a bishop or abbot.</note> and the chapter <note>The governing council of a cathedral or monastery.</note> together received the loan for the Church, or if the prelate alone did, or if some other individual assigned to the administration of the Church did so. In the first case, a further distinction is made: either the sale <term>alienation</term> of the Church's immovable property (or precious movable property that can be preserved) is necessary to pay the debt, or the Church's revenues and other movable goods are sufficient.

If the sale of the first kind of property <note>i.e., land or precious items.</note> is necessary, then—since these cannot be sold by the prelate and chapter without evident benefit or necessity to the Church, and any sale made otherwise is invalid (as will be discussed below regarding long-term leases)—it follows that they cannot be sold indirectly due to a loan unless there is manifest benefit or necessity to the Church. Therefore, when it is not clear that the loan was undertaken and spent for the Church's benefit, even if the authority of both the prelate and the chapter intervened to take it, such property cannot be sold to pay the loan. And in this event, the Authentic text *Hoc ius porrectum* establishes that the creditor is bound to prove it was converted to the benefit of the Church in order for the Church to be held liable. From this, other laws are derived that establish the same regarding the Church.

However, this reasoning does not hold for a city council. This is because the sale of the city's immovable property made by the council is valid even without evident benefit to the city. Thus, Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist.</note>, with whom Panormitanus agrees, rightly affirms that if such a council takes a loan for the city, the lender is not bound to prove it was converted to the city's benefit for the city to be bound to pay him back, even if it were necessary for the city to sell its immovable property to do so. Indeed, Bartolus adds that if someone else, by mandate of the assembly or the city, takes a loan for the city, the lender is not bound to prove it was converted to the city's benefit; for the city itself, or the assembly, is seen to have taken the loan.

When, however, it is not necessary to sell property of the first kind to pay a loan taken by both the prelate and the chapter, but revenues and other movable goods are sufficient, then the lender is not bound to prove it was converted to the Church's benefit. The reason is that the prelate and the chapter have the free administration of those goods, and for their sale, it is not necessary to establish...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "stare," which likely continues into "constare" (to establish/be clear) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legal requirements for a loan to be valid against corporate entities like the Church or a city. It establishes that while individual administrators may borrow, the institution itself is generally only liable if the lender can prove the funds were used for the institution's benefit, particularly when land or valuable property is at stake.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from Disputation 300 regarding the obligations of the Church and cities to repay loans, focusing on who bears the burden of proof regarding whether the borrowed funds were actually used for the institution's benefit.</meta>

->Tractate Two, Disputation 300.<-

...stands, that this is done for the evident benefit of the Church. This doctrine can be confirmed from the chapter *Quod quibusdam* <note>original: "c. quod quibusdam, de fideiuss."; a reference to Canon Law regarding sureties or guarantors.</note>, where, by arguing from the opposite sense, it is clearly gathered that when an individual member of a religious order accepts a loan of money with the consent of the prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as an abbot or bishop.</note> and the majority of the chapter <note>The governing body of a religious community.</note>, the monastery must repay it, even if it was not converted to its benefit. Therefore, speaking with even greater reason, when the loan has been accepted by the prelate and the chapter together, it must likewise be repaid.

In the same way, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in Canon Law.</note> says that when the prelate alone accepts a loan that can be repaid from goods of the latter kind <note>Likely referring to movable goods or liquid assets discussed on the previous page.</note>, it is not necessary for the lender to prove it was converted to the benefit of the Church, provided the prelate has universal administration. Since the prelate has free administration of those movable goods—as we showed in the place cited above—this also agrees with the cited chapter *Quod quibusdam*.

Panormitanus says it is different for a city administrator, because he does not have such free administration of the city's goods. Therefore, he says, the city council could block the payment of such a loan unless it were proven that what the administrator had borrowed in the city's name was converted to the city's benefit; this is clearly taught in the law *Ciuitas* <note>original: "l. ciuitas. ff. si cert. pet."; a reference to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman civil law.</note>.

However, after the death of the prelate—since a prelate cannot bind the Church for the time after his life except out of necessity and for the benefit of that Church, as is clear from chapter 1, *De solutionibus* <note>On payments.</note>—there is a greater probability that the lender is then bound to prove that the loan was converted to the Church's benefit. Nevertheless, Panormitanus, in the place cited with Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), another highly influential canonist.</note>, affirms that in that event it is enough to prove that when he gave the loan, the Church was in manifest need of that money, which he gave to relieve that necessity. He argues there is no need to prove that it was actually converted to the benefit of the Church, because that would impose a heavy burden on those lending to prelates, which would result in harm to the Church, as they would find no one to provide loans to assist in its times of need. Chapter 1, *De solutionibus*, agrees, as it only requires that the debts were contracted for the necessity of the Church for a successor prelate to be bound to pay his predecessor’s debts. Furthermore, the chapter *Quod quibusdam* agrees, as Panormitanus brings it forward. Regarding the *Authentica* <note>A collection of Justinian's legal "Novels" or new laws.</note> that extends this right and requires proof through the condition that what was given to the Church was converted to its benefit, they respond that this is to be understood when it would be necessary to alienate <note>To sell or transfer ownership of.</note> immovable property or precious movable goods of the Church to pay the debt; but not when the income and other movable goods would suffice. In the same way (regarding what pertains to the Church in this event), Law 3, Title 1, Part 5 <note>original: "l. 3. tit. 1. par. 5."; a reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish law code.</note> is to be understood, which simultaneously requires the creditor to prove that the Church lacked the thing at that time and that it was converted to the Church's benefit. Yet in a loan that the rector of a city had accepted in its name, it would not be enough to prove it was given to relieve the city's necessity, but it would also be necessary to prove it was converted to the city's benefit, as is established from the law *Ciuitas* and Law 1 of the Code *De solutionibus* <note>On payments and the liberation of city debts.</note>; Law 3, Title 1, Part 6 also harmonizes with this.

Finally, when some particular person, deputed 

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> for the administration of the Church, accepts something as a loan in the Church's name, a distinction must be made: either a certain sum was fixed for him by the Church that he could borrow, or it was not. In the first case, if he does not borrow beyond that sum, the Church is bound to pay it, even if it is not converted to its benefit, as is clearly gathered from the chapter *Quod quibusdam*. <margin>2</margin> However, I understand this to be the case when it would not be necessary to alienate the Church's immovable goods or precious movables to pay it. For then, even if the Church itself (that is, the prelate and chapter) had accepted that loan directly, the creditor is bound to prove the loan was converted to the Church's benefit, as was said above—much more so when it was accepted through the intervention of an administrator. But when no limit was fixed for him, or if he exceeds the fixed sum, then the Church is not bound regarding the excess, except insofar as it is found to have been converted to its benefit, as is decreed in the aforementioned chapter *Quod quibusdam*; it falls to the creditor to prove it was converted to the Church's benefit. Exactly the same is to be said of an individual to whom some care of a city has been entrusted.

<margin>3</margin> In the matter proposed, however, something is said to be "converted to the benefit of the Church or city" if it was spent on that which the Church or city was bound to do, or on that in which the city or Church would have spent just as much of its own goods. <margin>4</margin> Indeed, then the Church or city is deemed to have been made **wealthier** <note>original: *locupletior*; a legal term meaning "unjustly enriched" or having their financial position improved.</note> by that whole amount: since it would have spent just as much from its other goods, as is clearly gathered from the law *In pupillo* <note>Regarding payments to minors.</note>. But when what was borrowed is spent on something in which the city or Church would have spent nothing, a distinction must be made: If it was spent reasonably and prudently, even if by some unexpected circumstance or event it did not result in the advantage of the city or Church, then the city or Church is bound to pay the whole amount—especially if the person who so accepted and spent it had the power to borrow, but without a fixed limit. This is clearly gathered from the law *Quod si ultro* <note>From the section on "unauthorized management of affairs" (*negotiorum gestorum*).</note>. <margin>5</margin> Moreover, it can be confirmed because the administrator of the Church in that event is entitled to an action for **management of affairs** <note>original: *actio negotiorum gestorum*; a legal claim for expenses incurred while managing someone else's business without their explicit request.</note> against the Church, so that what he prudently spent in that matter may be paid back to him. <margin>6</margin> Therefore, by the same reasoning, an action will be granted to the lender against the Church to pay him the loan that its minister prudently accepted in the Church's name. But if what was borrowed was spent imprudently and irrationally, then the city or Church is only bound to pay as much as it was made wealthier thereby. If the Church or city received more benefit from it than the amount of the loan, it is only bound to pay the amount of the loan. Read Panormitanus in the cited places regarding all these things; Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist.</note> and Gregorio López also hand down some points in the cited passages.

<margin>7</margin> Why Innocentius <note>Pope Innocent IV, a famous canonist.</note> and Panormitanus (in chapter 1, *De deposito*, number 9) observe very well: In a loan of money, the laws establish that the lender is bound to prove that what he gave as a loan was converted to the benefit of the Church or city; but this is not the case in other contracts made in the name of the city or Church by those having the power...

<summary>This page discusses the legal burden of proof for loans made to the Church or city administrators, concluding that while utility must often be proven, exceptions exist for prudent administration and loans made during times of manifest necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal obligations of corporate bodies (Churches and cities) regarding loans, transitioning into the specific legal protections afforded to minors and adult sons living under their father’s authority.</meta>

->Luis de Molina, On Contracts.<-

...performed. The reason, however, is that since prelates, administrators, and others who manage the goods of Churches and cities are usually prone to accepting loans, and usurers <note>Moneylenders charging interest.</note> to giving them, unless the matter was handled for the benefit of Churches and cities in the manner explained, their goods would easily be alienated and perish in relation to the loan. In other contracts, therefore, those who contract with a Church or city are not held to prove that what they gave on their part was converted to the benefit of the Church or city in order for there to be an obligation on the part of the Church or city to fulfill the contract.

<margin>2</margin> A minor <note>A person under the legal age of majority, usually 25 in Roman law.</note> having a tutor or guardian enjoys the privilege of the Church and city; namely, if the tutor or guardian accepts anything as a loan in the minor's name, the minor is not held to pay it unless the creditor proves it was converted to the minor’s benefit. This is clearly gathered from the Code <note>original: "l. 3. C. qñ ex facto tutoris"; referring to the Justinian Code.</note>, and from the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. 5. tit. 1. par. 5."; a 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note>, as Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential legal commentator.</note> affirms and the doctors of law commonly agree. 

When a minor accepts a loan himself without the authority of a tutor or guardian and is found to be harmed by it—because the money was lost or consumed through his own easygoing nature or fault—he is granted **restitution to his original state** <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy restoring a person to their position before a contract was made.</note>. Thus, he is not held to restore it insofar as he is found to be harmed, but only insofar as he is found to be enriched by it. But if the one who gave the loan was a usurer who gave it at interest, out of hatred for such a person, it has been decreed that the burden of proof lies on him to show that the minor was actually made wealthier and to what extent he was made wealthier. This is how they understand the laws concerning such lenders. 

However, when the one who gave the loan was not a usurer, it is up to the minor seeking restitution to prove that he was harmed by such a loan; otherwise, he will be compelled to pay the loan in full, according to the common opinion of the doctors cited by Antonio Gómez. In this place, observe that in the **forum of conscience** <note>The internal realm of moral and religious duty, as opposed to the external legal court.</note>, a minor is held to pay as much as he was made wealthier from the usurer's loan, even if the usurer cannot prove it. Read what was said regarding the contracts of minors in Disputation 224.

### On a Loan made to a Son under Paternal Power.

### DISPUTATION 301.

#### *SUMMARY.*

> 1 *A son under paternal power <term>filiofamilias</term> <note>A son, regardless of age, who is still under the legal authority of his father.</note> is entitled to the Macedonian exception against one lending to him.*
> *Even if he holds a dignity by which he would leave paternal power. num. 6.*
2 *The Macedonian exception is available to the son even in the forum of conscience, and why.*
> *And how it stands in Castile and Lusitania <note>Portugal.</note>.*
3 *To which persons the Macedonian exception and privilege may be extended.*
4 *The Macedonian exception or privilege cannot be waived, according to the common opinion.*
5 *The Macedonian exception can be raised even after*

<column-break/>

*a judgment, but before payment.*
7 *A son under paternal power having military property <note>original: "bona castrensia"; property acquired by a son through military service, which he could control independently.</note> today is not entitled to the Macedonian exception.*
8 *A son under paternal power who pays a debt contracted from a loan is not entitled to reclaim the payment.*
> *Understand this, however, and declare it as stated there.*
9 *In which cases the Macedonian exception does not apply.*

<margin>1</margin> IF a loan is made to a son under paternal power, even if he has then exceeded the twenty-fifth year of his age, in effect he is not held to pay it. For although he may be bound by that and other contracts, both civilly and naturally, according to what was said in Disputation 261, he is nonetheless granted by civil law an **exception** <note>A legal defense or objection.</note> or opposition against someone demanding payment—whether privately or in court—stating that he is not held to pay it by the privilege of the **Macedonian Decree** <note>original: "Senatusconsulti Macedoniani"; a Roman Senate decree from the 1st century AD.</note>. This was granted to remove the evils that were accustomed to arise from such loans, among which were the deaths of parents, so that the sons might have the means to pay debts contracted from such loans. And because a certain usurer named **Macedo**, whose loans had been followed by the deaths of many parents in Rome, was the occasion for this privilege being granted, it was named "Macedonian." This privilege is established in the Digest and Code and the Institutes.

<margin>2</margin> This has a place not only in the external court but also in the **forum of conscience**, as Innocent, Panormitanus, and many others commonly affirm. The reason is that public power could introduce this for the common good, and a just law has force in the forum of conscience. Panormitanus says that since among Christians such danger of parental death from loans made to sons does not loom, that law ought to be abolished. He does not, however, deny that in the meantime, while it is not abolished, it has force. Furthermore, if it were abolished, perhaps experience would show many evils and sometimes the deaths of parents. 

Since in **Castile and Lusitania** <note>Spain and Portugal.</note> sons leave paternal power by the very fact that they are married, and thus the Macedonian Decree does not have a place for those sons, it is good that for the others, such a privilege should persist with the limitations applied by civil law and explained below. Another similar rule, more broadly extended for this purpose, was granted in Castile to sons and minors who buy something on credit by themselves or through an intermediary without the consent of parents or guardians; which was discussed in Disputation 261. No fewer inconveniences have followed in these kingdoms from loans to sons under paternal power than from purchases on credit.

<margin>3</margin> This privilege is extended not only to sons after the death of their parents—so that they are not held to pay even then, when they have ceased to be sons under paternal power, the loan they accepted while they were sons—but also to the parents, even if they hold the sons' private property, and to the guarantors.

<summary>This page discusses legal protections for minors and adult sons under paternal power, specifically the "Macedonian Decree" which allows sons to refuse repayment of loans to prevent the incentive for parricide. It also addresses how these laws apply in the "forum of conscience" and in the kingdoms of Spain and Portugal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of loans, specifically focusing on the "Macedonian Decree," a Roman law that prohibited lending money to sons who were still under their father's legal authority (filiifamilias), regardless of their actual age.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 301. ###

...those who, unless they bound themselves as guarantors with the intention of making a gift to such sons under paternal authority <note>original: "filijsfa milias"; an adult son still legally subject to his father's power in Roman and Spanish law</note>, are not held to pay the loan in their place, as is held in the law "But if the father" <note>original: "l. sed si pater"</note>, section "not only," in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree <note>original: "ff. ad Maced."</note>. And all these points are held in law 4, title 1, part 5 <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish law code</note>.

<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, even if the sons and their guarantors renounce this privilege, such a renunciation is invalid: because this privilege was introduced not so much for their own favor as for the favor of the parents and out of hatred for those who give loans <note>to discourage predatory lending to heirs</note>. So affirm the final gloss on the final law of the Code regarding the Macedonian Decree <note>original: "C. ad Maced."</note>, and the first gloss on the first law "Although" <note>original: "tametsi"</note> in the Digest on the same title; Antonio Gomez <margin>5</margin> where cited above, and the doctors of law commonly. Indeed, if someone is summoned to court for <margin>5</margin> such a debt and does not raise the "Macedonian exception" <note>the legal defense based on this decree</note>, and is condemned, he can still raise it after the sentence is passed but before he pays, and he shall be acquitted, as is expressly held in the law "Although" <margin>6</margin> cited. Likewise, a son obtaining a dignity <note>a high office or title</note> by which he leaves his father's power—according to those things said in Disputation 229 regarding the 6th and 8th outcomes by which one is freed from paternal power—does not take away the fact that he can use the <margin>7</margin> Macedonian exception, as held in law 1, final section, of the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree. Today, <margin>7</margin> since the military property <note>original: "bona castrensia"; property earned through military or professional service</note> of these men exists, they normally cannot use that privilege, according to the things added in the final section cited.

<margin>8</margin> If a son under paternal authority pays a debt of this kind, or another pays in his place (understand the same for a guarantor), the payment is valid and cannot be reclaimed <note>original: "repeti"</note> once it has been so paid. The reason is that it was truly a debt, even if, while it was being demanded, the exception would have applied. What we have said about the son paying must be understood as applying if the payment is made from property of which he can dispose. And then the father cannot prohibit the son from paying such a debt. If, however, the son pays from the father's money without the father's consent, then the father can reclaim what was so paid: unless the one who received it consumed it in good faith and was not made wealthier by it; for then he is not held liable to the father for a thing consumed in good faith. All these things are clear from the law "If the son" <note>original: "l. si filius"</note> in the Digest on "seeking a certain sum," joined with the law "But also if" <note>original: "l. sed & si"</note>, section "if from another," in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree; and they are held in laws 4 and 6, title 1, part 5.

In the following outcomes, the Macedonian Decree of the Senate does not apply. *First*, when the son under paternal authority was believed to be independent <note>original: "sui iuris"; his own master, not under a father's power</note>; or if he affirmed himself to be independent, and the lender was not deceived by a light or empty persuasion. So it is held in the law "If anyone [believed] the father" <note>original: "l. si quis patrem"</note> and the penultimate law of the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree; laws 1 and 2 of the Code on the same title; and law 4, title 1, part 5. To this outcome belong the examples used in the law "If anyone [believed] the father" and law 4 of Castillo, as cited. Namely, when someone exercised a public office, or another ministry, or trade, as if he were a father of a family <note>head of a household</note>. For besides the fact that those giving them loans could easily be deceived, believing them to be independent, certainly today after the laws of the Code, they possess either military property, or quasi-military property, or certainly "adventitious" property <note>original: "adventitia"; property coming from outside sources like a mother's inheritance</note>, of which the use and administration belong to them, at least by the father's tacit consent. Such men are held to pay from those goods for what is given to them as a loan, as we shall soon add.

*Second* is if the son, when he received the loan, has military or quasi-military property: for then he is held to pay the loan, as held in law 1, final section, and law 2 of the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree. I believe the same is true when he has adventitious property, the use and administration of which belong to him at least by the father's tacit 

<column-break/>

consent. For since, after the laws of the Code, he has no less free administration of these goods than of military property, he will certainly be held to pay from them a loan received after he had the administration of those goods. Indeed, the Macedonian Decree of the Senate was introduced to prevent loans when a son does not have his own property from which to pay it, and this was because of the evils that followed from taking such a loan <note>such as sons wishing for their father's death to pay off debts</note>.

*Third*, if the son is a soldier when he took the loan. Then it is held in the final law of the Code regarding the Macedonian Decree and law 4, title 1, part 5. For then there is not only a legal presumption that it was taken for expenses in war, but it was also decreed in favor of war so that it might be paid, in order that soldiers might more easily find a loan in time of war.

*Fourth*, when the loan was not in money, but in some other thing, such as wheat, wine, oil, etc. For the Decree of the Senate speaks only of money given as a loan. An exception is made if, in fraud <note>to bypass the law</note>, the loan is given in a thing that is not money so that, by selling that thing, money might be obtained from it: for then the Macedonian Decree of the Senate applies. Both are held expressly in the law "But Julian," section "of a loan" <note>original: "§. mutui"</note>, in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree.

*Fifth*, if the money was owed by the son under another title, such as from a purchase or a lease, and the son agrees with the creditor to have it henceforth as a loan. An exception is made unless, in fraud of the Decree, a sale or another title preceded it first, and the loan followed afterward. Both are held in law 4 of the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree.

*Sixth*, if the son is a guarantor for that money which another person who is independent <note>original: "sui iuris"</note> received as a loan: for then, if the other does not pay the loan, the son is compelled to pay it. An exception is made unless, in fraud of the Decree, it was done so that under that color <note>pretense</note> the money would come to the son, with the other person binding himself as the principal debtor. If, however, the lender was aware of this fraud, the legal exception is available against him. So it is held in the law "But Julian" at the beginning, in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree.

*Seventh*, if the son received the loan by the command or consent of the father, or with the father's knowledge and without his contradiction; or if the father was prepared to pay the son's loan, or if the father approved it after the contract was made, or paid part of the loan; or if the son himself, after he was made independent, approved or confirmed the contract, or began to pay part of the loan. For in all these outcomes the father while he lives, or the son after he is made independent, is held to pay the loan in full, and they cannot raise the Macedonian exception. So it is held in law 1 "if permitting," the law "Macedonian," and the final law of the Code regarding the Macedonian Decree; in the law "If however," and others in the Digest on the same title; and law 6, title 1, part 5.

*Eight*, if the son, living for study or in another place far from the father, received a loan for those things which it was incumbent upon the father to spend on him, or for which paternal piety would not refuse to make expenditures on him, such a loan must be paid without any exception: provided it does not exceed what the father was going to spend on that son. So it is held in law 2 and the law "Macedonian" in the Code regarding the Macedonian Decree; and in "But Julian," section "which is said" and the following section, in the Digest on the same title; and in the cited law 6.

It transitions into a new discussion (Disputation 302) regarding the legal defense used when a person signs a loan agreement but never actually receives the money.</meta>

Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous expert in Canon Law</note>, in the chapter "Because to certain people" regarding guarantors, note 3, says in the same way, a member of a religious order sent from a monastery to study or for another purpose, who receives a loan there for necessary expenses: the monastery is held to pay that back.

Ninth, when what a son under paternal authority <note>original: "filius familias"; an adult son still legally subject to his father's power in Roman and Spanish law</note> received as a loan is found to have been converted to the father's use: then the father is held to pay what was used for his benefit, according to the law "But Julian," section "accordingly," in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree <note>original: "ff. ad Maced."; Roman law prohibiting loans to sons under their father's authority</note>.

Tenth, if a son under authority was put in charge of some business by the father and received a loan for that business, the father is held to pay it. The same if he was put in charge by another; for he who appointed him is held to pay the loan, unless he had forbidden taking the loan. This is found in the law "But Julian," section "sometimes," in the Digest regarding the Macedonian Decree. Read what Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 6, note 2, verse "ninth," and Gregorio Lopez on law 7, title 1, Partida 6, gloss 2, teach.

# On the defense of money not received regarding a loan.

## DISPUTATION 302.

### SUMMARY.

1. The defense of money not received <term>defense of money not received (exceptio non numeratæ pecuniæ): a legal protection for someone who signs a debt document before actually receiving the funds</term> in a loan can be raised within a two-year period, and in two ways.
2. It fails in Portuguese law, in which only sixty days are granted. note 2.
3. The defense of money not received has a place in whatever thing is promised as a loan.
4. The defense of money not received does not have a place in other contracts, except in a dowry.
5. The defense of a thing not delivered applies within thirty days to one confessing to have received it in hope of future delivery; otherwise, he is held to prove that the thing was not delivered. note 5.
6. A borrower renouncing the defense of money not received: for what purpose can he not object that the money was not counted out?
7. For the renunciation of money not received to be valid, is it enough to be done in the same instrument of confession of the loan, or is another instrument required? And what about the law of Castile and Portugal, and what penalty are notaries and public officials punished with? note 8.
8. Notaries and other public officials making instruments of renunciation of money not received: by what penalty are they punished under Portuguese law?
9. If the lender proves the money was counted, to what is the borrower who objected compelled? And if he does not prove it, what is he compelled to return to the borrower?
10. In what case is the defense of money not received not admitted, even if raised within the two-year period? note 13.
11. An extrajudicial defense of money not received works so that it is considered a perpetual defense, and the burden of proving the contrary is thrown back on the creditor.
12. The defense of money not received belonging to a debtor passes to his heirs and guarantors, both active and passive.
14. Does the defense of money not received even under Portuguese law apply to a debtor for another cause, yet not arising from a loan?
15. The defense of money not received under Portuguese law is admitted even after the established time, for the purpose,

<column-break/>

that the debtor takes the burden of proof upon himself.
16. Can the defense of money not received be raised by a debtor through a guaranteed instrument? <note>original: "instrumentum guarentigiatum"; a document with an executive clause allowing immediate enforcement</note>
17. The defense of money not received can be raised by a debtor notwithstanding an oath, even in the forum of conscience <note>the "internal forum" or moral judgment of the Church, as opposed to a civil court</note>.
18. Only a civil obligation arises from a confession of a loan under the hope of future payment.

IN a loan <term>loan (mutuum): specifically a loan of fungible goods like money or grain, where the borrower is expected to return the same amount and quality</term>, it is established that if someone, in hope of (for example) the counting out of money promised to him as a loan, has confessed in a signed note <note>original: "chirographo"</note> or another public instrument, or before witnesses, that he owes so much money given to him as a loan, he can, within a two-year period <note>original: "biennium"</note> from the day such a confession was made, object or raise the defense that the money was not counted out <note>original: "pecuniam non fuisse numeratam"</note>. And then the burden of proof lies with the creditor to prove it was counted out. But if the creditor does not prove it, he who had confessed it in the instrument or before witnesses is acquitted.

He can, however, raise the defense either by initiating a lawsuit within that two-year period against the creditor so that he returns the instrument of that confession, since the money was not counted out; or so that he confesses the money was not counted out, if the confession was made before witnesses; or, when the creditor demands the debt within the two-year period, by objecting that the money was not counted out. But if he raises the defense in neither way within the two-year period, he is compelled to pay the loan, unless he himself proves that the money was not counted out. These things are clear in the Institutes on literal obligations, single section; in the laws "Six caution," "If within," "Assertion," and "In contracts" in the Code regarding money not received; and law 9, title 1, part 5 <note>of the Spanish *Siete Partidas*</note>. But according to Portuguese law, only sixty days are granted for raising the defense from the day the confession was made, as is clear in the 4th book of the Ordinances, title 47, in the beginning and following sections.

<margin>Portuguese law.</margin>
I said above: "in hope of, for example, the counting out of money": because although this defense is called "of money not received" in the law, it nevertheless has a place in whatever thing is promised as a loan which someone has confessed he owes in the hope of delivery <note>original: "traditionis"</note>, as is clear in the law "In contracts" at the beginning, in the Code regarding money not received, law 9, title 1, part 5, and book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 47, at the beginning. But does this defense also have a place in other contracts? It must be answered in the negative along with the gloss on the law "In contracts" at the beginning, in the Code regarding money not received, and with Baldus and others whom Gregorio Lopez cites and follows in the quoted law 9, gloss 1—provided however you except the confession of gifts received, about which there will be discussion in its own place. For in other contracts, a confession of a thing received immediately prejudices the one confessing to the effect that, even if he objects that it was confessed in hope of delivery, unless he sufficiently proves that he did not receive it, he is reputed to have received it, and the burden of proving it does not belong to the other, according to the law "Generally" in the Code regarding money not received. If, however, someone confesses he has received what another owed him in hope of delivery, so that the confession is to free the other from the debt, then the one confessing is granted to object within thirty days from such a confession that the thing was not delivered; and if that defense is made within that time, it belongs to the debtor to prove that he delivered it; but if the creditor does not object within that time, it belongs to him to prove that the thing was not delivered. So it is held in the law "In contracts," section "On the rest" in the Code regarding money not received, and as Paulus Castrensis and Baldus affirm...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from Disputation 302 concerning the "defense of money not received." It explores whether a borrower can waive their right to claim they never received the cash and how different legal systems—specifically Roman Common Law, Castilian law, and Portuguese law—treat such waivers and the burden of proof.</meta>

Gregorio Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*</note> affirms this as cited above, as does Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 6, at the final note.

<margin>6</margin>
Whether a borrower <term>borrower (mutuarius): the person receiving a loan of fungible goods, like money, which must be repaid in kind</term> who has confessed to having received the loan and has renounced the **defense of money not received**, can nevertheless raise the exception that the money was not actually paid. According to the Common Law <note>The *Ius Commune*, the Roman-canonical legal system used across Europe</note> and the law of Castile, it must be said that he cannot raise the defense to the effect of shifting the burden of proof <term>burden of proof (onus probandi): the obligation to provide evidence for a claim</term> back onto the lender. This is according to the gloss on the law "if from a caution" in the Code *on money not counted* <note>original: "C. de non num. pec."; refers to the Code of Justinian</note> and the common opinion of the doctors; it is also established in law 9, title 1, of the 5th *Partida*. However, the defense will be admitted to the effect that, if the borrower himself proves the money was not paid, he shall be released from payment. This is the view of Gregorio Lopez on the aforementioned law 9, in the second-to-last and last glosses, and others whom he cites.

<margin>7</margin>
Whether, however, for the renunciation to be valid and have the aforementioned effect, it must be made in the same legal instrument in which the confession of debt was made. Gregorio Lopez in his last cited gloss, and Antonio Gomez on law 30 of the Laws of Toro, note 52, say that the common opinion is that it is not enough for it to be in the same document, but it must be done in another. This is because the same ease, hope, and desire for the loan that would lead someone to confess to the loan would also lead them to renounce such a defense. However, the cited law of Castile establishes that it is sufficient if it is done in the same instrument; this was also the opinion of Fabri and others whom Gregorio Lopez cites there, and whom Hernando Acosta on law 6 regarding "if from a caution," on the word "is compelled," cites more copiously and follows.

<margin>8</margin>
Rightly, however, in Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> under the title cited at the beginning, it was decreed that if a renunciation of this kind of defense is made, it is void by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>. Furthermore, the penalty of loss of office is decreed for notaries <term>notary (tabellio): a public official authorized to draw up and attest to legal documents</term> and other public ministers who prepare instruments in which such a renunciation is included. Alvaro Valasco, however, in his *Consultation* 5, notes 12 and 13, understands that ordinance to apply when the renunciation is made at the time of the contract in the very instrument by which the contract is celebrated. It is otherwise if it is made later after an interval of time. For he judges that it is then valid in Portugal, just as it is valid by the common opinion of all under Common Law if it is made after an interval. This opinion is not without probability because of those words of the ordinance: *at the time of the contract* <note>original: "que ao tempo do contracto"</note>.

<margin>9</margin>
When a borrower has raised the defense in a timely manner that the money was not paid, the burden of proving that it was paid—according to what has been said—falls on the creditor. Then, if the creditor sufficiently proves it was paid, the borrower is compelled not only to pay the entire debt but also all expenses tripled. No other testimony is required against him thereafter beyond his own past confession. If, however, the creditor does not prove the money was paid, he is compelled to return the document of confession to the debtor and release him from that confession. These points are found in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 47, section 1. The same should be said standing on Common Law alone, except for that triple penalty of expenses, which I do not immediately find in Common Law.

<margin>10</margin>
When, in the instrument of confession of a debt from a loan, the notary testifies that in his presence and that of witnesses the money was counted out, then the defense of money not received is not admitted to the effect of requiring the creditor to prove it was paid. Rather, by that testimony of the notary alone, the debtor is compelled to pay the loan. This is held in the cited section 1;

<column-break/>

and the second-to-last gloss on the law "if from a caution" agrees, as does the second gloss on the law "in contracts" at the beginning of the Code *on money not counted*, and the *Authentica* "if indeed they die" regarding legal instruments, cautions, and trusts.

<margin>11</margin>
In the Portuguese Ordinances, the following section 2 states that if someone who confessed to a debt in the hope of money being paid <note>original: "numerandæ"</note> raises an exception outside of court before the creditor within the time prescribed by law, saying they did not receive what they confessed to owe, or did not receive such a large sum, this is sufficient for the defense to be considered perpetuated. The burden of proving the contrary is then shifted to the creditor. This agrees with the law "in contracts," section "in all," in the Code *on money not counted*, and the gloss on the law "if within" on the word "complaint" in the same title. Gregorio Lopez and others whom he cites agree on law 9, title 1, Partida 5, on the words *or any of the others*. Although they seem to require that it be ordered by a judicial decree <note>original: "rescripto"</note>, the Portuguese law only advises this so that it can be properly proven in the future. When the creditor is absent or cannot be reached, it is enough if the defense is made before a judge. This is found in the law "in contracts," section "in all," in the Code *on money not counted*, and in the cited title 47, section 2.

<margin>12</margin>
If a debtor dies before the time prescribed by law for raising the defense, his heirs can raise the defense within the same timeframe, even against the heirs of the creditor, if the creditor also died before that time elapsed. However, once that time has passed, the heirs cannot raise the defense, even if they are minors, nor is "restoration to the original state" <term>restoration to the original state (restitutio in integrum): a legal remedy allowing a person to be returned to their previous legal position, often used to protect minors from errors</term> granted to them in this matter. And just as heirs can, so also can guarantors <note>original: "fideiussores"</note> raise the defense, according to the law "if within" in the Code *on money not counted* and the cited title 47, section 3.

<margin>13</margin>
But if the debtor, after making the confession, pays part of the debt or acknowledges the debt, the defense of money not received is not granted to him thereafter. This is held in the cited title 47, section 4.

<margin>14</margin>
When a debtor, before his confession, was already obligated to the creditor under some other title—for instance, sale, lease, or something similar—and by an agreement entered into with the creditor, confessed that he henceforth owed that same amount as a loan, does the defense of money not received then apply to him?
<margin>Question.</margin>
Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 6, note 4, affirms that it does apply. Others, however, whom he cites, rightly deny it. This was settled in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 47, section 5, and the law "generally" in the Code *on money not counted* agrees. The same is true if the confession is that he owes it from an *old* loan which he received before that confession. In that case, he is not confessing to a loan in hope of payment, but to money already counted out to him. If someone, however, through their last will <note>i.e., a testament</note> confesses that they received such or such an amount as a loan from another, then the defense of money not received does not apply to the heirs, as Antonio Gomez and others whom he refers to rightly prove.

<margin>15</margin>
By the same Portuguese law, in the second-to-last and last sections, it is decreed: <margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> even if the debtor has not raised the defense within the time granted by law that the money was not paid, he is admitted to raise the defense provided he takes upon himself the burden of proving that it was not paid. And provided that in those instances where proof is not admitted in that kingdom except through a public document (according to what was said in Disputation 260), he proves it by a public document. When, however, the creditor must prove the debtor's confession;

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

<margin>Question</margin>
16 The doubt is whether, if a debtor has **confessed** to having received the money and has promised to pay it by a guaranteed instrument <note>original: "instrumento guarentigio"; a legal document that allows for immediate debt collection (execution) without waiting for a full trial or court sentence</note>—which, without waiting for any sentence, is ready for execution—can he nevertheless raise the **defense of money not received**, either within the two-year period before he is sued, or after he is sued according to the form of the instrument? This must be done within the ten days included in that same two-year period, which are granted only in this kingdom of Castile to raise an exception after the debtor opposes the execution, which was initiated by virtue of such an instrument's contract, according to laws 1, 2, and 3, title 21, book 4 of the New Collection <note>original: "nouæ collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of 1567, a compilation of Spanish laws</note>. This is particularly relevant since in this kingdom, based on the cited laws, not just any exceptions are permitted to debtors within those ten days, but only certain prescribed ones, among which this one is not listed. Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous Italian jurist</note> denied that this exception could be raised. Antonio Gómez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>, however, in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 6, number 3, along with many others whom he cites, rightly affirmed that it *can* be raised within that time, and by that very act, the burden of proving that the money was actually paid is thrown back onto the lender. First, because that confession of money received, and the obligation to pay it back, always carries that tacit condition: "if it is actually paid." Furthermore, a period is prescribed by the disposition of the law <margin>Decision</margin> within which the debtor can raise the exception that the condition was not fulfilled, and thereby shift the burden of proof to the lender. Therefore, the defense against the debtor, no matter how many clauses of the guaranteed instrument fortify it, always has that same tacit condition, unless the debtor fails to object within the time given by law that the money was not paid. This reasoning is confirmed because the clauses of a guaranteed instrument do not have greater power to prevent this defense than an oath would have, by which a debtor who made such a confession bound himself to pay the money he confessed to receiving. Yet, provided there is a just cause, the debtor can in good conscience and in the external court <note>The public legal system, as opposed to the internal "court of conscience"</note> raise the defense that the money was not counted/paid, as seen in the final law of the Code *on money not counted*.
17 [The nature of the execution] follows the nature of the promise upon which it falls. Since that promise was made in the hope of payment, it carries the tacit condition: "if the money is paid." Therefore, despite the clauses of the guaranteed instrument by which the debtor granted free execution without waiting for a judge’s sentence, he can object that the money was not paid; for he similarly granted that right under the hope of payment, and consequently under the condition that the money would be paid. Note in passing, however, that if the document were an "assertory" one, in which the borrower <term>borrower (mutuatarius): the recipient of a loan of fungible goods</term> had affirmed as a matter of fact that he had received that money as a loan, then the defense of money not received would not be granted to the effect of shifting the burden of proof onto the lender, as we explain more fully in Disputation 349 regarding the defense of an unpaid dowry. Second, because it must first be established that a thing is actually owed—an obligation one took upon oneself via a guaranteed instrument—before execution can be made against him. Surely a guaranteed instrument does not prevent an exception that arises from the very nature of the thing and the disposition of the law, such as the one we are now discussing;

<column-break/>

and this is what Junior de Antonio Gómez, as cited, intended. Furthermore, Antonio Gómez adds in the same place that the cited laws of Castile, when an instrument is "guaranteed," exclude exceptions other than those listed there *only if* the lender's claim is well-founded by the nature of the contract. In the case proposed, however, the debtor's claim—to raise an exception and shift the burden of proof—is well-founded by the nature of the contract and the disposition of the law. Once that exception is made, it is up to the lender to prove that the money was actually paid, both by legal disposition and by the nature of the contract itself.

18 Finally, I should add that when someone confesses to a loan in the hope of payment, but the money was not actually paid, a **civil obligation** to pay the debt arises without a **natural obligation**; and thus an obligation arises only in the external court, not in the court of conscience. Meanwhile, as long as the two-year period granted for raising the defense has not expired, that obligation is not so firm, because it can be struck down by the defense and the burden of proof thrown onto the lender. After the two years have passed without the exception being raised, the obligation remains firmer; yet it never has a natural obligation <note>A moral/natural law requirement to pay, as opposed to a purely legal requirement</note> joined to it, regardless of what some legal experts (whom Antonio Gómez cites in volume 2, chapter 6, number 6) have argued to the contrary. This holds true even if that confession was fortified by an oath to pay such a loan, as was said before and is held in the final law of the Code *on money not counted*. And this is the civil obligation without a natural one which is discussed in the single paragraph of the Institutes *on literal obligations* and the Code *on money not counted*.

Since the loan <term>loan (mutuum): the lending of fungible items where the same amount and quality must be returned</term> (as will be seen) is as it were the seat and foundation of usury, the order of this discipline requires that we discuss usury at this point. To begin with the name, **usury** [usura] seems first to have signified "use" [usus]. Hence Cicero in *Against Verres*: *Why, for the sake of the lawsuit, did you give such long-lasting usury (that is, use)?* And in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: *Nature gave the usury of life (that is, the use), just as she gave money.*

<meta>This page transitions from the legal defenses against debt collection in Castile to a fundamental theological and legal investigation into the nature of usury. It begins Disputation 303, which defines the terms and moral boundaries of profit derived from loans.</meta>

->### Second Treatise<-

2 <margin>Cicero, book 2, On Old Age.</margin> **J**ust as the word "culture" <note>original: "cultura"</note> is derived from "cultivation" <note>original: "cultus"</note>, so "usury" <note>original: "usura"</note> is derived from "use" <note>original: "vsus"</note>. From there, the name was transferred to signify that which grows from the use of some thing, like a fruit. This is according to that passage of Cicero in his book *On Old Age*: *The earth never returns what it receives without usury* <note>original: "Terrā nunquam sine vsura reddit"; here Cicero uses "usury" in its original sense of "interest" or "increase" in a positive, agricultural way</note>. In this context, Cicero calls "usury" the increase of fruit over the seed—the profit, as it were—which the earth returns from the seed entrusted to it.
According to these meanings of the word, "usury" is not a name specifically for a vice, its material, or its object. However, by adaptation, the term has been taken to signify profit from a loan <note>original: "lucrum ex mutuo"</note>; that is, an increase intended or received above that which was given in the loan, by virtue of the loan itself. Since, as we shall see, this increase is an evil due to the very nature of the thing—an objective malice—it follows that it is an object of vice and sin. Because the name of an object is sometimes stretched to signify an act or a habit (just as, conversely, the name of an act or habit is often stretched to signify its object), the name "usury" has also come to signify the vice and sin by which profit from a loan is intended or received. Thus, just as "heresy" is an equivocal term referring both to the crime of heresy and to its object, and "theft" refers both to the crime and the thing stolen, so also "usury" in this discussion is equivocal, referring both to the profit from a loan and to the vice that has that profit as its matter and object. We are speaking of usury in these two senses in this section.

3 <margin>Ambrose, book 4, question 4, last chapter, where he says: *You shall demand usury from him whom you rightly desire to harm... To whom arms are rightly brought, to him usury is lawfully brought. From him whom you cannot conquer in war, demand usury, for it is no crime to kill him. He fights without steel who demands usury. He strikes without a sword, and takes vengeance on his enemy, who is a usurious pursuer of his foe.*</margin> **T**hat name must be carefully observed: teachers sometimes take the name of profit more broadly when, speaking less strictly of this matter, they occasionally call usury "licit." This occurs when they have called "licit usury" a benefit estimable in price which a lender sometimes lawfully receives beyond the thing loaned—not indeed by virtue of the loan itself, but on some other basis. In this way, according to the more common and truer sense, Ambrose understood usury in book 4, question 4, last chapter, when he said: *You shall demand usury from him whom you rightly desire to harm, etc. To whom arms are rightly brought, to him usury is lawfully brought. From him whom you cannot conquer in war, demand usury, for it is no crime to kill him. He fights without steel who demands usury. He strikes without a sword, and takes vengeance on his enemy, who is a usurious pursuer of his foe.* <note>Molina is quoting St. Ambrose's *De Tobia*, a classic text used in the Middle Ages to justify taking interest from non-Christians or enemies in times of war</note> Therefore, where there is a right of war, there is a right of usury. Thus far Ambrose. By these words, he means that when we can lawfully kill someone by the right of war and seize their goods, we can then also lawfully receive something beyond the thing loaned from them—not as a debt arising from the loan, but on another basis, by which we can seize all their goods in a just war. However, Ambrose must be read with the understanding that this is only when it can be received without causing scandal.

4 **U**sury is also called *foenus* <note>the standard Latin term for interest on a loan</note>, from *foetus* [offspring], as if it were the birth and fruit of money or another thing given in a loan. Since, however, a thing given in a loan is by itself unfruitful and sterile <note>A core Aristotelian and Scholastic argument: money does not "breed" like animals, so charging for its "offspring" is unnatural</note>, such that more is owed than the thing itself, it follows that such "offspring" and fruit is illicit. Sometimes, however, *foenus* and "to lend at interest" <note>original: "fœnerari"</note> are taken more broadly, meaning the same as to give a loan and to share. In this sense, it is used not only in Holy Scripture, as we shall see, but also among secular authors. For Pliny, in book 2, chapter 6, says: *The sun lends <note>original: "Fœnerat"</note> its light to the other*

<column-break/>

->### Disputation 303. I<-
->135<-

*stars*, that is, it imparts and communicates it. As for the fact that usury is called *Onzena* in Portugal <note>Portuguese: *onzenice*</note>, it seems to have originated from the fact that usurers used to receive one for every ten they gave in a loan—and thus eleven [*onze*] for ten—according to the example of the Council of Agde, 14, question 3, last chapter.

5 **U**sury, considered as the object and matter of use, is sufficiently defined by Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note> in his *Summa* under the word "usury," and by others, as follows: **It is profit from a loan.** <note>original: "Est lucrum ex mutuo"</note> Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose (book 4, question 3, chapter 1 and following) all agree. By the name of "profit" in this context is understood money or any other temporal thing estimable by a price, as those three Fathers, the Council of Agde in the cited chapters, and the teachers commonly affirm—whether it be a service, or any other burden estimable by a price, or something else. However, the grace and glory to be obtained from God, even if intended as the reason for the loan, are not included under the name of "profit" here. This is partly because they are not temporal goods estimable by a price, and partly because God Himself, by His own spontaneous and full freedom through the merits of Christ, imparts them to us as earned rewards, as if they were a prize for the loan made out of love for Him and our other merits. Likewise, the internal friendship and benevolence of the person to whom the loan is given, or of another, even if intended by the loan, is not understood under the name of "profit from a loan," as St. Thomas (2.2, question 78, article 2) and the teachers have commonly noted. Primarily, this is because through the loan, such things are intended as the cause and object whereby the borrower is moved to it by his own gratitude and moral honesty, which is purely spontaneous and free. Furthermore, it is lawful to intend the benevolence and friendship of one's neighbor through any good work, nor is any injury done to him in this. Moreover, although benevolence and friendship may sometimes be valued more highly by someone than money, of themselves they are not among those things that are estimated and sold by a price, and by comparison of which a civil obligation could arise, because they lie hidden within and are bestowed or not bestowed spontaneously and freely. We call "estimable by price" those things that can be sold or exchanged in human commerce for another thing, and regarding which a civil obligation can arise. Add to this that money or another thing estimable by price can be lawfully intended and received through a loan, provided it is given out of the gratitude and liberality of the borrower, as we shall see—let alone intending friendship and benevolence. For usury is only illicit and unjust to the extent that it is received as something owed—since it cannot be owed on account of the loan—or as something not fully given voluntarily. In the effect of gratitude and liberality, even if it arises from the loan as a motivating cause, usury is not perceived, because that act is purely free and voluntary; for that reason, it can be lawfully intended and received when it is given by the borrower in that spirit. Finally, for something to be called "profit from a loan," it must be an interest above that which was given in the loan, and otherwise not owed, nor should the lender have a right to receive it from any other source. For if it can be lawfully received from a basis other than the loan, as in...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Luis de Molina continues his technical definition of usury, moving from the etymology of the word to the specific legal and moral conditions that constitute a usurious contract.</meta>

->### Luis de Molina, On Contracts<-

...compensation for a loss incurred, or for profit lost <note>original: "damno emergente, aut lucro cessante"; these were the two standard legal justifications for charging interest on a loan without it being considered usury</note>, or for any other reason, it will not be called profit from a loan, but rather "interest" <note>original: "interesse"</note> obtained through another heading.

<margin>6</margin>
Regarding that other part of the definition, "from a loan" <note>original: "ex mutuo"</note>, it should be observed that the term is used broadly here to include not only a true and formal loan, but also a <term>virtual loan</term> <note>original: "mutuū virtute"; a transaction that isn't a loan in name but functions as one in practice</note>. For if someone sells on credit at a price higher than the strict "just price," and receives that increase because he expects delayed payment (as it is always presumed that this is the reason for the increase), the contract is usurious. This is because selling on credit is, in effect, leaving the price in the hands of the buyer as a "virtual loan"—a sum he was otherwise supposed to pay immediately. Therefore, taking an increase for that reason beyond the just price is taking profit from a virtual loan, and thus it is usury. Similarly, if someone buys at a price lower than the lowest just price because he pays in advance, he commits usury. This is because paying in advance is, in effect, giving a loan until the time the goods are delivered. Thus, subtracting something from the just price for that reason is to gain profit from a virtual loan, which is usury.

<margin>7</margin>
By this second part of the definition, any profit that does not arise from a loan is excluded from the category of usury, whether that profit is just or unjust. Therefore, if someone sells something for more than the strict just price in a cash sale <note>original: "pecuniā numeratā"</note>, although that price increase is unjust and subject to restitution in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal moral judgment of the Church</note>, it does not technically pertain to usury, because it does not proceed from either a formal or a virtual loan, but from a purely unjust sale. Likewise, if someone leases his gold coins for the sake of display or recreation, or so that they might be boiled with food for a sick person <note>original: "vt cibi cum ea concoquantur ægroto"; a historical medicinal practice where gold was thought to impart healing properties to broth</note>, or for some other use, and receives a moderate fee for that use, such a fee and profit is not usury. Rather, it is just profit, as St. Thomas Aquinas and other doctors commonly affirm. For that profit is not from a loan, but from the *leasing* of money, since the ownership of that money remains with the person leasing it out. Therefore, if the money is lost then without even the slightest fault of the person hiring it, the loss falls on the owner (the lessor), and not on the person hiring it—whereas, if it were a loan, the loss would fall on the borrower and not on the person who gave the loan.

<margin>8</margin>
To judge whether any contract is usurious, one must use this rule, which suffers no exception: one must see whether a formal or virtual loan intervenes in that contract. If it does, and profit is intended from it, the contract is usurious and such profit is usury. If not, it cannot be usurious, whether it be just or unjust in other respects.

<margin>9</margin>
It should be noted that the thing given in a loan, or the equal amount owed by reason of the loan, is called the <term>principal</term> <note>original: "fortem" or "sors"</note>. As Domingo de Soto rightly says, this name was derived from partnership contracts and applied to others. In a partnership contract, each partner puts his "lot" (his portion) into the common pile, and at the time of distribution, he first withdraws it if it remains intact; only then does he receive the portion of the profit which falls to him beyond the principal. In this sense, Ambrose calls the loan, or the equal amount owed by reason of the loan, the "principal," whereas the profit taken above it by reason of the loan

<column-break/>

he calls usury, saying: *Whatever is added to the principal is usury.* <note>original: "Quodcunque accedit sorti, vsura est"</note> It is used in the same way frequently in law and by the doctors. The principal is also called "capital" and "the main sum" both in partnership contracts and in the matter at hand, when we distinguish usury from the principal, capital, or main sum owed by reason of a loan.

<margin>10</margin>
Usury, as a vice and a sin, is nothing other than the taking of, or the will to take, profit from a loan. From this definition, both in this sense and the preceding one, the contract in which usury is intended or intervenes is called "usurious." However, when usury in the first sense is in a contract but has not yet been received, it is called "agreements" <note>original: "pactionibus"</note> by some, and the obligation to make restitution does not yet arise from it. But when it has already been received, it is called "exactions" <note>original: "exactionibus"</note>, as if it were demanded and received. And then the obligation to restore it arises.

<margin>11</margin>
Received usury, which is now subject to restitution, is also divided into "mental" and "real" usury, and again into "open" and "palliated" usury. **Real usury** occurs when there is a tacit or express agreement regarding profit from a loan. It is real usury not only when someone openly bargains for profit, but also when he hints at it while giving the loan—for instance, if he says to the borrower, "You know the custom," or "I trust this money will not come back to me empty," or "Remember that I am deprived of the use of this money and have children," or something similar.

<margin>12</margin>
**Mental usury** occurs when no agreement (neither tacit nor express) regarding profit from a loan intervenes, yet the one who gives the loan does so with the intention and hope of receiving profit. This is because he knows the borrower will give it, not out of liberality or gratitude, but out of fear that a loan might be denied to him another day, or for some other reason. He who gives a loan with this intention commits the sin of usury, and by later accepting such profit, he not only sins but is also bound to restore it. However, a specific discussion is reserved for mental usury.

From this you will easily understand that mental usury is not distinguished from real usury in the same way that a sin of the mind is distinguished from an external sin. For in both mental and real usury, there is a sin of the mind and an external sin. If someone has the will to lend for the sake of profit and puts this into an external agreement, but has not yet executed it or expressed it further, he has sinned only by a sin of the mind of real usury. But when he later executes it, he sins with the external sin of real usury. Similarly, if someone intends to lend for profit without any external agreement (even a tacit one) because he knows the other will pay profit to avoid being denied a loan later, then if that will has not yet resulted in an external act, it is a sin of the mind of mental usury. But when it results in an external act because he gives the loan with that intention, it is the external sin of mental usury.

<margin>13</margin>
**Open usury** is when the loan is formal and profit is taken or intended from it. **Palliated usury** <note>literally "cloaked" or "disguised" usury</note> is when the loan is virtual, as in the case of one who sells on credit or buys with advance money, and profit is intended or taken from it. Sometimes palliated usury is used by some to mean both mental usury...
