### Whether Usury is Illicit.

### DISPUTATION 304.

#### SUMMARY.

1 *Whether usury is licit or not, throughout the disputation.*
2 *Usury is illicit by natural, divine, and human law; also at number 7.*
3 *That which is paid by borrowers for the wages and labor of workers is not usury, but a salary.*
4 *Likewise for what is paid for the action of giving a loan; also at number 4.*
5 *Compensation of one action for another is permitted, just as it is for one object for another.*
6 *In what case an injury is done to one who is willing and consenting.*
7 *Usury is illicit by the nature of the thing against commutative justice.*
8 *Usury is illicit according to the Old Testament.*
9 *Likewise from the New Testament and Canon Law; numbers 9, 10.*
11 *Usuries which were granted by Imperial Law.*
12 *The "usury of usury" <note>compound interest</note> prohibited by Imperial Law.*
13 *Imperial laws permitting usury were abrogated by Canon Law.*
14 *An action to reclaim paid usury is permitted today, even under Portuguese and Castilian law.*
15 *Usury is illicit in itself even in Deuteronomy, though permitted there against foreigners.*
16 *Whether a loan can be given as a debt arising from another contract, so that something may be perceived from it.*
17 *What "interest" <note>original: "faenus"</note> can signify.*
18 *Usuries can be permitted to avoid greater evils.*

<margin>1</margin>
**T**he side that denies [that usury is illicit] argues as follows. First, because usury is permitted to the children of Israel regarding foreigners in Deuteronomy 23. For so the text has it: "You shall not charge interest to your brother, but to a stranger." And in chapter 28 following, among the rewards proposed to that people if they keep the law, one is: "You shall lend to many nations, and you yourself shall receive interest from none." And Christ in Luke 19 says to the "wicked servant" because he kept his money in a cloth: "Why did you not give my money to the bank, so that I might have exacted it with usury?" Therefore, usury viewed in itself is not illicit; otherwise, it would neither be permitted by God, nor promised as a reward, nor would Christ have uttered those words.

Second, civil laws permit usuries, as is evident in the <term>Digest</term> and the <term>Code</term> <note>the foundational texts of Roman Civil Law</note> regarding usury. Since laws of this kind do not seem to be condemned as iniquitous, it follows that usury is not illicit in itself.

<margin>2</margin>
**T**hat usury is, however, illicit is so certain that the contrary, as we shall see, most clearly conflicts with the Catholic faith. Because it must be shown that usury is illicit by natural, divine, and human law, I have decided that one must begin from the very nature of the thing.

I should first advise that it is an insufficient reason for proving that usury is illicit from the nature of the

<column-break/>

thing if one argues: "It is against the nature of a loan <note>original: "mutui"</note> to receive anything beyond the principal; therefore usury is illicit."

For it is also against the nature of a <term>gratuitous loan</term> <note>original: "commodati"; a loan of a specific item to be returned intact</note> to receive anything for the use of the thing lent, and yet it does not follow from this that it is illicit to receive it. It only follows that the nature of the "commodatum" is destroyed, and it passes into a just contract of "leasing" <note>original: "locati"</note> if the price received is moderate; or it passes into a just "unnamed contract" if what is received is not a price. I should also advise that, just as receiving a price for a thing lent for use destroys the nature of the "commodatum" and makes the contract pass into another species, so in a <term>loan for consumption</term> <note>original: "mutuo"</note>, receiving something beyond the principal does not destroy the nature of the loan. The reason is that a loan <note>mutuum</note> consists in this: that something is given for use which immediately becomes the property of the receiver, and he later restores just as much in kind and quality. But the fact that a pact is made so that something further is returned does not destroy that other part in which the nature of the loan consists. However, since a "commodatum" consists in something being granted for use for free, while the ownership of the thing remains with the giver, if a pact intervenes that something be returned for that use, the nature of the "commodatum" is destroyed by that very fact, and the contract passes into a distinct species. It remains, therefore, to be shown more clearly why usury is illicit by the nature of the thing; which is indeed done by the following reasoning.

From the nature of the thing, it is illicit and against <term>commutative justice</term> <note>the justice governing private exchanges between individuals</note> to exact or receive more than the value of the thing given in the exchange of one thing for another, unless something else intervenes by reason of which that extra amount is justly received. But to receive something beyond the principal for a loan is to receive more than it is worth for the exchange of the thing given in the loan, unless something else intervenes by reason of which it may be justly received. Therefore, if it is a matter of the loan alone, it is a sin by the nature of the thing and against commutative justice to receive anything beyond the principal, and consequently usury is illicit, contrary to commutative justice, and subject to restitution.

The consequence is evident, and the "major premise" is clear from the nature of commutative justice itself, whose role is to establish equality in exchanges. Moreover, this same premise is most widely accepted in other exchanges, such as in a sale, in which it is not permitted to receive a higher price than the goods are worth, and in a lease, in which it is similarly a sin to receive a higher price than the use of the thing being leased is worth, and in permutations and other unnamed contracts which must be made according to equality to be just.

The "minor premise," however, is manifest from the terms themselves. For to receive beyond the principal is nothing other than to receive beyond the value of the thing given in the loan. For it is always licit to receive the full value of the thing given in a loan, even if more in quantity must be received, nor does any usury occur in that. For example, if at a time when wheat is worth more, you give some measures as a loan to be restored at the time of harvest when it is expected to be worth less, it is lawful for you to bargain that the borrower then restores as much more as is sufficient so that the prices of the wheat at both times are made equal; because then nothing is received beyond the principal value agreed upon.

However, this is more a matter of selling wheat on credit at the current price and buying nearby wheat at the price it will be worth at the time of delivery, rather than giving a loan.

<summary>Molina begins investigating whether usury is illicit, weighing arguments from Scripture and Roman law before concluding that it violates commutative justice by demanding more value in return than was originally lent.</summary>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts
## Disputation 304 (Continued)

<column-break/>

...we would argue that today [the Old Testament prohibitions] would have no force. They would not pertain to moral precepts, but rather to the judicial or ceremonial precepts of the Old Law, which ceased with the death of Christ—as we have shown at length in the section on the Old Law (1. 2.). Therefore, since there are not such blatant testimonies in the New Law prohibiting usury, the Church Fathers would certainly never have defined the illegality of usury as a matter of faith today if it were not such by the very nature of the thing. Indeed, the passages of the Old Testament clearly enough imply that usury is evil and illicit by its very nature; for they do not bear any mark of being merely judicial or ceremonial precepts.

<margin>Objection</margin>
We can also be confirmed in the view that usury is illicit by the nature of the thing because Aristotle, guided by natural light, further condemns it in the fourth book of the *Ethics* (near the end of chapter 1). He condemns usurers as a vice, specifically those who give small amounts in exchange for large returns, calling it a "shameful way of making profit." Additionally, in the first book of the *Politics* (chapter 7), he appears to condemn interest <note>original: "fœnus"</note>. Furthermore, Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says at the end of the second book of *On Duties* <note>original: "De officiis"</note> that to give money at interest is the same as "killing a man." Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a famous Spanish jurist</note> also refers to others in the cited location who, following the light of nature, condemn usury.

<margin>Satisfied. 8.</margin>
From the testimony of the Sovereign Guide [God], it is more clearly established that usury is illicit. In Ezekiel 18, "to give at usury and to receive more than was given" is counted three times among the lethal sins by which justice and grace are lost. In Psalm 14, among the requirements for "dwelling in the tabernacle of the Lord and resting on His holy mountain," it lists "he who has not given his money at usury." In Psalm 54, it is listed among other vices: "usury and deceit do not depart from its streets." In Psalm 71, it is said of the Messiah that "He will redeem their souls from usury and iniquity."

9. From the New Testament, that passage from Luke 6 is even clearer: "Lend, hoping for nothing from it." <note>original: "Mutuum date nihil inde sperantes"</note> This is the testimony cited by Pope Urban III in the chapter *Consuluit* (under the title "On Usuries"), as if usury were prohibited in that place. Pope Alexander III seems to imply the same in the chapters *Quia in omnibus* and *Super eo*, saying that usuries are condemned by the pages of both Testaments—even though no other place in the New Testament appears where usury is so openly condemned. On the contrary, it is objected that in that passage, Christ seems to be offering "counsel" <note>An optional path to perfection rather than a strict command</note> that a loan be made without looking for a similar return, so that it might be more pleasing and meritorious before God, as seems manifest from the context itself. Just as Soto (in book 6 of *On Justice and Right*, question 1, article 4) thinks that those words of Christ contain only counsel. He adds, however, that usury is sufficiently prohibited by the sacred pages of the New Testament insofar as "theft" (broadly defined) is prohibited, under which usury is included.

He also adds, by an *a fortiori* argument <note>an argument that if a lesser thing is true, a greater thing must be even more true</note>, that it can be gathered from there that usuries are illicit. For if a Christian is encouraged to abstain even from the expectation of a return of a similar favor, how much more must we judge that usuries are prohibited? I would say that although that passage alone might not be entirely convicting, it nevertheless favors the view; and it should not be doubted that Christ intended both meanings in that place, since Urban III used that testimony in that sense. However, I do not believe those Supreme Pontiffs intended to define that this is the literal sense of that passage.

Nor do I believe they would have defined usury as illicit based on that passage alone. 

<column-break/>

However, when it is established from elsewhere that usury is illicit by natural and divine law, they rightly use that passage to defend the same point. For although the definitions of the Supreme Pontiffs and the Church are most certain, it is not necessary that everything they use to confirm those definitions be equally certain, as we have said regarding matters of faith. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta</note>, in his commentary on usury (question 3, chapter 1, number 10), cites the Bull of Leo X from the Council of Lateran as if, with the Council's approval, the same testimony of Luke 6 were cited as containing a precept against lending for usury. However, it is not introduced there as an assertion of the Council or of Leo X, but rather as the reasoning used by some to condemn the <term>Mount of Piety</term> <note>original: "montem pietatis"; a charitable pawnshop that charged low interest to cover costs</note> which was being discussed. Later in that same Bull, their opinion is rejected, and the contrary is defined. Thus, it cannot be gathered from that Bull that such is the indubitable literal sense of that testimony.

10. Now, regarding human law—that is, the sacred canons—it is established that usury is illicit and prohibited under heavy penalties throughout the entire title "On Usuries" in the *Decretals* and the *Sixth Book*, as well as in *Distinction 47* and *14, questions 3 and 4* across many chapters. Among these laws, many are from the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Pope Martin, the Council of Lateran, and the Council of Lyons; and all of these are General Councils. Most recently, in the decree of the Council of Vienne <note>the *Clementina*</note>, it was defined: "If anyone falls into such error as to presume to affirm pertinaciously that practicing usury is not a sin, we decree that he is to be punished as a heretic." Furthermore, it strictly enjoins local authorities and inquisitors of heretical depravity not to fail to proceed against those found defamed or suspected of such error as they would against those suspected of heresy.

11. As for Imperial <note>Roman/Civil</note> Law, it not only permitted usuries in the sense that it did not punish the crime (in the same way that <term>prostitution</term> <note>original: "meretricium"</note> is permitted among Christians to avoid greater evils), but also in that it did not allow for the reclaiming of certain usuries once paid. Moreover, it granted a legal action for demanding usuries permitted by certain laws, as is clear in the *Digest* and *Code* under the title "On Usuries." Consequently, the opinion of Soto (book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 1) must be rejected, as he affirms the contrary. I said that Imperial Law granted an action for certain usuries permitted by law because the civil laws did not permit usury in just any amount. The maximum usury that civil law permitted was the <term>centesima</term> <note>meaning "one-hundredth"</note>, which is one percent per month. This means that for someone who loaned one hundred gold coins, one gold coin would be paid each month beyond the principal, totaling twelve gold coins a year. They permitted this usury only for <term>maritime loans</term> <note>original: "pecunia traiectitia"</note>, where the money was loaned to be carried across the sea, and the risk of the money belonged to the lender rather than the borrower. In other cases, if the lender was a nobleman, the rate permitted was only...

# Second Treatise. Disputation 304. Page 141

...it was permitted for him to receive a third part of a hundredth <note>original: "tertiam partem centesimæ"</note>—that is, a third of one gold piece each month for every hundred he had given as a loan, or (which is the same thing) four gold pieces per year. If, however, he were a merchant, he was permitted to receive two parts of a hundredth—that is, two-thirds of a gold piece each month for the same hundred given as a loan, and thus he was permitted to receive eight gold pieces every year. But for all other people, it was only lawful to receive half of a hundredth—that is, half a gold piece each month, or six gold pieces annually, for every hundred lent. All other forms of usury were prohibited. These points are contained in the law *eos qui* <note>A reference to the Roman Code</note>, and Soto <note>Domingo de Soto, a Spanish scholastic theologian</note> explains them better than others in the place cited above. Furthermore, compound interest <note>original: "vsuræ vsurarum", or interest on interest</note> was prohibited under Imperial Law. For example, if six gold pieces were owed annually as interest, it was unlawful to take future interest on those six, even if an agreement intervened stating that if they were not paid, they should be added to the principal and interest paid on them. This is held in the final law of the Code *On Usury*. From this you will understand that the more heavy and wicked forms of "cloaked" or hidden usury sometimes paid in our own times are more severe than those that were once allowed by the civil laws.

<margin>13</margin>
At that time, however, there were laws of this kind permitting true usury contrary to natural law, as has been shown. For this reason, among many other points of Canon Law, they were rightly abolished along with many others in the Council of Vienne <note>Held in 1311–1312</note>, in the decree *Clementina vnica de usuris*. At the same time, it was decreed that if any public official presumed to judge that usury should be paid, or that when found to have been paid it should not be restored, he would be excommunicated by the law itself. In this regard, Canon Law prevails over Civil Law, because the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> has full power over lay authorities in those matters which concern the salvation of souls and the supernatural end, as was shown in Disputation 29. Consequently, today—

<margin>14</margin>
—a legal action is granted in the secular court to reclaim usury already paid. This is granted under Portuguese law, as is evident in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 14. Read also what is arranged in Title 27, the penultimate and final sections, and in Book 1, Title 67, section 19. The same is granted under the law of Castile in Book 8 of the *New Collection*, Title 6, throughout. Regarding the penalties for usurers, it will be discussed below in its proper place.

Scholars dispute whether the Emperor Justinian abolished the Imperial laws that permitted usury. A gloss on the *Authentica* to the Code *On Usury* and certain other parts of Canon Law affirm this. They convince themselves of this because the same Emperor accepted the faith of the Council of Nicaea and commanded it to be observed; and in the Council of Nicaea, usury was condemned. This is the more common opinion among legal experts. However, in my judgment, the contrary is sufficiently proven by Conradus in *On Contracts*, question 23, and Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 6. Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis, a famous canonist</note> and the cited Covarruvias were of the same opinion.

<margin>15</margin>
It remains to satisfy the arguments proposed at the beginning of this disputation. Regarding the testimony from Deuteronomy 23 cited in the margin <note>"You shall not charge interest to your brother... to a foreigner you may charge interest."</note>, it must be said: from that passage, it is sufficiently gathered that usury is illicit in itself. For that very reason, it was prohibited regarding brothers—that is, the children of Israel—and the other testimonies from the Old Testament we cited confirm the same. But that word, "but to the stranger," is understood by Saint Thomas, Cajetan,

<column-break/>

Soto, Alphonso de Castro, Alexander of Hales, and others whom Covarruvias refers to, as follows: it was not as if usury was permitted to the children of Israel toward foreigners as something *lawful*, but only as something *unpunished* to avoid greater evils. Specifically, it was to prevent them from oppressing their own brothers with usury out of greed, a vice to which that people was very prone. Just as, in the opinion of the same doctors, a bill of divorce was permitted to them because of the hardness of their hearts, according to the word of Christ. And just as among us, prostitution is permitted—which conflicts with natural law—to avoid greater evils. Indeed, it is in the same way that it says slightly earlier in that same chapter: "There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel." That permission for foreign prostitutes, which is gathered there by an argument from the contrary sense, is not to be understood as something lawful, but as something unpunished to avoid greater evils. Others understand the testimony cited in the argument differently: namely, that usury was permitted to the children of Israel toward foreigners as something lawful, but only toward their *enemies* who inhabited the Promised Land which God had granted them, and toward any others with whom they might carry on a just war in the course of time. For by the very fact that it is lawful to despoil true enemies of their goods, it is also lawful to give them a loan with a contract that they might perhaps return something extra.

<margin>16</margin>
For when something is otherwise lawfully owed, in the opinion of the scholars, it is lawful to give a loan with a contract that it should also be paid back. Alexander clearly agrees with this in his commentary on the Council of Tours, as does the final gloss there, because that is not "receiving profit from a loan," but rather using the occasion of a loan to recover a debt owed from elsewhere, in which case usury is not properly found. This is how Conradus and Juan Medina understand that passage. Gabriel, Major, and others whom Covarruvias cites above also approach this view, rejecting neither opinion.

Ambrose was clearly of the same opinion in the passage we cited in the previous disputation. It is even more evident in Ambrose’s book *On Tobit*, chapter 15, from which that text was taken. In that place, he puts forward this opinion and adds the words of that text as confirmation. Thus, the first gloss on that same text—suggesting that Ambrose meant that just as no one should be harmed, so usury should be demanded from no one—actually conflicts with the text and with Ambrose’s mind, regardless of what Soto says. Nor does the opinion of Conradus and others have as little probability as Soto claims, provided it is understood that there is no scandal. Certainly, at that time, there was no less scandal in the children of Israel taking usury from those people (in the manner explained) than in their seizing their lands and goods. Especially since it is not so entirely clear that usury is illicit by its very nature until it is diligently investigated and a legitimate reason for the matter is found; thus, it is not something that can be known by almost all peoples. This can be confirmed by the fact that it escaped the notice of the most wise founders of the Imperial Law. Thus, this matter seemed unknown to the nations from whom the children of Israel were permitted to take usury in that chapter. Provided also that it is understood as lawful...

...we would argue that today they would have no force, for they would not pertain to moral precepts but to the judicial or ceremonial laws of the Old Covenant, which ceased with the death of Christ—as we have already shown when we discussed the Old Law. Therefore, since there are not such explicit testimonies in the New Law prohibiting usury, the Church Fathers surely would never have defined it as a matter of faith that usury is illicit today if it were not so by the very nature of the thing. Indeed, the passages of the Old Testament themselves clearly enough imply that usury is evil and illicit by its very nature; for they bear no resemblance to either judicial or ceremonial precepts.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
We can also confirm that usury is illicit by the nature of the thing: Aristotle, guided by natural light <note>The "light of nature" refers to human reason unaided by divine revelation</note>, condemns it as illicit in the 4th book of the *Ethics* at the end of chapter 1. There he certainly condemns moneylenders and those who "give little to receive much," calling it a shameful way of acquiring gain. Also, in the 1st book of the *Politics*, chapter 7, he seems to condemn interest <note>original: "fœnus"</note>. Furthermore, Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> at the end of the 2nd book of *On Duties* says that to lend at usury is the same as killing a man. Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva, a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> also mentions others in the cited place who, following the light of nature, condemn usury.

<margin>Satisfaction 8</margin>
From the Old Testament, it is clearer than light that usury is illicit. In Ezekiel 18, among the deadly sins by which justice and grace are lost, it is counted three times: "to give at usury and to receive more." Psalm 14, among the things necessary to dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle and rest on His holy mountain, lists the one "who has not given his money at usury." Likewise, in Psalm 54 <note>The text says Psalm 14 again, but refers to the contents of Psalm 54/55</note>, many other things are recounted: "usury and deceit have not departed from its streets." In Psalm 71, it is said of the Messiah: "He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity."

<margin>9</margin>
From the New Testament, there is that even clearer passage in Luke 6: "Give a loan, hoping for nothing in return." This testimony is brought forward by Pope Urban III in the chapter *consuluit* under the title *On Usury*, as if usury were prohibited in that place. And Alexander III seems to imply this in the chapters *quia in omnibus* and *super eo* under the same title, when he says that usury is condemned by the pages of both Testaments—though no other place in the New Testament appears in which usury is so openly condemned. On the contrary, it is objected that in that place Christ seems to be giving a counsel <note>A "counsel of perfection" is a spiritual recommendation for those seeking higher holiness, whereas a "precept" is a mandatory command for all</note> that a loan be made without looking for any return, so that in this way it might be more pleasing and meritorious before God, as seems manifest from the sequence of the context itself. Soto <note>Domingo de Soto, a Dominican theologian</note> in book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 2, thinks that those words of Christ contain only a counsel. But he adds that usury is sufficiently prohibited by the sacred pages of the New Testament insofar as theft—broadly understood, under which usury is included—is prohibited there.

He also adds, by an argument from the stronger reason <note>original: "argumento a fortiori"</note>, that it can be gathered from there that usuries are illicit. For if a Christian is instructed to abstain even from the expectation of a similar favor in return, how much more must it be judged that usury is prohibited. I would say that although that passage alone might not be entirely convincing on its own, it nevertheless favors the view, and it should not be doubted that Christ intended both meanings in that place, since that testimony has been used in the common consensus. This was the view of Urban III. Although I do not think those Supreme Pontiffs intended to define that this is the strictly literal sense of that passage.

Nor do I believe they would have defined from that passage alone

<column-break/>

that usury is illicit. However, when it is established from other sources that it is illicit by natural and divine law, they use that passage as well to defend the same point. For although the definitions of the Supreme Pontiffs and the Church are most certain, it is not necessary that every argument by which they are confirmed be most certain, as we have said in the matter of faith and as is handed down by many. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer</note> in his commentary on usury, question 14, chapter 3, number 10, cites the bull of Leo X in the Lateran Council, as if in it—the council having approved the act—the same testimony from Luke is cited as a precept against lending under usury. However, it is not brought forward there as an assertion of the Council or of Leo X, but rather as the reason why some were doubting so that they might condemn the *Mount of Piety* <note>term: Mount of Piety (mons pietatis) — a charitable pawn shop run by the Church to provide low-interest loans to the poor to protect them from usurers</note>, which is what was being discussed there. Later in the same bull, that opinion is rejected and the contrary is defined. Thus, it is not gathered from that bull that this is the undisputed literal sense of that testimony.

<margin>10</margin>
Now † indeed, it is established that usury is illicit by human law—that is, by the sacred canons—and prohibited under heavy penalties throughout the title *On Usury* in the Decretals and in Book 6; specifically, in Distinction 47 and question 14, cases 3 and 4, through many chapters. Among these laws: the chapter *quoniam multi* (Distinction 47) is from the Council of Nicaea; *si quis* (question 14, case 4) is from the Council of Pope Martin; the chapter *quia in omnibus* regarding usury is from the Lateran Council; the chapter *usurarum* on usury in Book 6 is from the Council of Lyons—and all these are general councils. Most recently, however, in the single *Clementina* decree on usury, at the final paragraph, it was defined: "If anyone falls into that error so as to presume to stubbornly affirm that practicing usury is not a sin, we decree that he be punished as a heretic." Furthermore, it strictly enjoins local authorities and inquisitors of heretical depravity not to fail to proceed against those whom they find rumored or suspected of such error, just as they would against those suspected of heresy.

<margin>11</margin>
As far as Imperial Law <note>original: "ius Cæsareum," referring to the Roman Civil Law of the Emperors</note> is concerned, it not only permitted usury in the sense that it did not punish the crime (in the same way that prostitution is permitted among Christians to avoid greater evils), but also in this: that it did not allow the reclaiming of certain interest once paid, and further, it granted a legal action for demanding certain interest permitted by the laws, as is established in the Digest and Code *On Usury*. Thus, the opinion of Soto (book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 2), who affirms the contrary, must be rejected. I said that Imperial Law granted a legal action for certain interest permitted by law: because civil laws did not grant usury in just any amount, as is clear from the law *eos* and the two following in the Code *On Usury*. For the maximum usury that civil law allowed was the *centesima* <note>The "hundredth part," meaning 1% per month or 12% per year</note>; it required that a hundredth part be paid each month, so that he who lent a hundred gold coins would be paid one gold coin each month beyond the principal, and twelve gold coins would be paid each year. And they allowed this usury only in "bottomry" <note>original: "pecunia traiectitia," loans for maritime trade where the lender assumed the risk of the ship sinking</note>, which is money lent so that it may be carried by the borrower by sea, and the risk of it pertains to the lender, not to the borrower, as is clear in the cited law *eos* and in the Code *On Maritime Interest*. In other events, if the person who gave the loan was a nobleman, only...

<column-break/>

it was permitted for him to receive a third part of a hundredth <note>The *centesima* was the standard Roman interest rate of 1% per month, or 12% annually. A third of this is 4% annually.</note>, that is, a third of one gold piece every month for every hundred he had given as a loan, or (which is the same thing) four gold pieces every year. If, however, he were a merchant, he was permitted to receive two parts of a hundredth, that is, two-thirds of a gold piece every month for those same hundred lent, and thus he was permitted to receive eight gold pieces every year. But for all other men, it was only lawful to receive half of a hundredth, that is, half a gold piece every month, or six gold pieces annually, for every hundred lent. All other types of interest <note>original: "usuræ"</note> were prohibited. This is found in the law *Those who*, and Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic philosopher</note> explains this better than others in the place cited above. Furthermore, compound interest <note>original: "usuræ usurarum," literally "usury of usuries"</note> was prohibited by Imperial law. For example, if six gold pieces were owed annually for a hundred, it was a crime to take interest on those six in the future, even if a contract intervened stating that if they were not paid, they would be added to the principal and interest paid on them. This is held in the final law of the Code *On Usury*. From this you will understand that the hidden or cloaked usuries of our own times are sometimes more heavy and wicked <unclear>gracholui</unclear> than those that were formerly conceded by civil laws.

<margin>13</margin> Indeed, such laws permitting true usury were so unjust and contrary to natural law, as has been shown, that they were rightly abolished—along with many others—by the Canon laws, specifically the decree *The Only One* <note>original: "clem. vnic." referring to a decree in the Clementines collection of Canon law</note> regarding usury in the Council of Vienne. At the same time, it was decreed that if any public official presumed to judge that usury should be paid, or that it should not be restored once found to have been paid, he would be excommunicated by the law itself. And in this matter, Canon law prevails over Civil law, because the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> holds full power over secular authorities in those matters which concern the salvation of souls and the supernatural end, as was shown in Dispute 29. As a result, today

<margin>14</margin> a legal action is granted in the secular court to reclaim usury already paid. This is granted by Portuguese law, as is clear in Book 4, Title 14 of the Ordinances. Read also what is arranged in Title 27, the second to last and last paragraphs, and Book 1, Title 47, paragraph 19. The same is granted by the law of Castile in Law 8 of the New Collection, Title 6, throughout. Concerning the punishments of usurers, it will be discussed below in its proper place.

The Doctors <note>Scholarly authorities in law and theology</note> disagree as to whether the Emperor Justinian abolished the Imperial laws that permitted usury. The Gloss <note>Standard marginal commentary on legal texts</note> on the passage *To these* in the Code *On Usury* and certain other parts of Canon law affirm that he did. They convince themselves of this because the same Emperor accepted the faith of the Council of Nicaea and commanded it to be observed; and in the Council of Nicaea, usury was condemned. This seems to be the more common opinion of legal experts. However, in my judgment, the contrary is sufficiently proven by Conrad <note>Conradus Summenhart (1450–1502)</note> in his *On Contracts*, question 22, conclusion 10, and Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577)</note> in *Various Matters*, Book 3, number 6; and Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canonist</note> and the cited Covarruvias were of the same opinion.

It remains to satisfy the arguments proposed at the beginning of this dispute. <margin>15</margin> Regarding the testimony from Deuteronomy 23 cited in the first argument, it must be said that it is sufficiently gathered from that text that usury is illicit in itself, for it was prohibited for that very reason among "brothers"—that is, the children of Israel. This is confirmed by the other testimonies from the Old Testament we have cited. But as for that word "unto a stranger" <note>original: "alieno," referring to the permission in Deuteronomy 23:20 to lend to foreigners at interest</note>, it is understood by St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> in his work *On Evil*, question 12, article 7, and in his *Summa*, 2nd part of the 2nd part, question 78, article 1; and by Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, a major commentator on Aquinas</note> 

<column-break/>

in his commentary there; Soto in his 6th book *On Justice*, question 1, article 1; Alfonso de Castro in *Against Heresies* under the entry "Usury"; Alexander of Hales, and others whom Covarruvias cites in his *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 1, number 7. They argue that usury was not permitted to the children of Israel toward strangers as if it were lawful, but only as something that would go unpunished to avoid greater evils. Specifically, it was to prevent them—because that people was very prone to greed—from oppressing their own brothers with usury. Just as, in the opinion of the same Doctors, a "bill of divorce" <note>The biblical allowance for a husband to divorce his wife</note> was permitted to them because of the hardness of their hearts, according to the word of Christ. And just as among us prostitution <note>original: "meretricium"</note> is permitted (even though it conflicts with natural law) to avoid greater evils. Indeed, in the same way that it is said a little earlier in that same chapter: "There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel." For that permission of foreign prostitutes, which is inferred by the opposite sense, is not to be understood as if it were lawful, but as something unpunished to avoid greater evils. Others understand the cited testimony differently: namely, that usury was permitted to the children of Israel as a lawful thing toward strangers—that is, toward their enemies who inhabited the Promised Land which God had granted them, and toward any others with whom they might wage a just war in the future. For by the very fact that it is lawful to despoil true enemies of their goods, it is also lawful to give them a loan with a contract that they return something beyond the principal. <margin>16</margin> For since it is somewhat doubtful among the Doctors whether it is lawful to give a loan with a contract that something additional be returned, Alexander III clearly agrees in chapter 1 *On Usury* in the Council of Tours, and the final Gloss there, because that is not "receiving profit from a loan," but rather recovering a debt from another source by occasion of the loan—in which case usury is not properly found. This is how Conrad understands that passage in *On Contracts*, question 24, and Juan Medina in *On Things Acquired by Usury*, question 2. Gabriel Biel agrees in his commentary on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, question 11, and John Major <note>John Mair (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher/theologian</note> in the same place. Covarruvias cites these authors without rejecting either opinion. Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan</note> was clearly of the same opinion in the final chapter of question 4, whose words we cited in the preceding dispute; it is even more evident in the same Ambrose’s *On Tobit*, chapter 8, from where that text was taken. In that place, he puts forward this opinion and joins the words of that text as confirmation. Thus, the first Gloss on that same text—claiming Ambrose meant that just as no one should be harmed, so interest should be demanded from no one—plainly conflicts with the text and the mind of Ambrose, regardless of what Soto says in the cited place. Nor does the opinion of Conrad and the others have as little probability as Soto claims there, provided it is understood that no scandal arises. Certainly, at that time, there was no greater scandal in the children of Israel taking usury (explained in this way) than there was in them usurping the lands and goods of those people. Especially since usury being illicit by the very nature of the thing is not so clear until it is diligently investigated and a legitimate reason for it is found, such that it cannot be ignored by almost all peoples. ### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

Today, these [prohibitions] would have no force if they did not pertain to moral precepts, but rather to the judicial or ceremonial laws of the Old Law, which ceased with the death of Christ—as we showed extensively when we discussed the Old Law <note>Referring to the "Prima Secundae" (1. 2.) of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica, which Molina is commenting upon.</note>. Therefore, since there are not such clear testimonies in the New Law prohibiting usury, the Church Fathers would surely never have defined it as a matter of faith that usury is illicit today if it were not so by its very nature. The passages of the Old Testament themselves clearly enough indicate that usury is evil and illicit by its very nature; nor do they have any <unclear>likeness</unclear> <note>original: "imagiê"</note> of either judicial or ceremonial precepts.

<margin>Objection</margin>
We can also confirm that usury is illicit by the nature of the thing. Aristotle, led by natural light, condemns it as illicit in the 4th book of the *Ethics* toward the end of chapter 1. He condemns usurers as having a vice and calls those who give little to get much "shameful profit-seekers" <note>Aristotle argued that money was "sterile" and should not "breed" more money.</note>. In the 1st book of the *Politics*, chapter 7, he also seems to condemn usury. Furthermore, Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says at the end of the 2nd book of *On Duties* that to give money at usury is the same as "killing a man." Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and theologian.</note> also cites others who, following the light of nature, condemn usury.

<margin>Proof 8</margin>
From the Old Testament it is even more clearly established that usury is illicit. In Ezekiel 18, among the deadly sins by which justice and grace are lost, "giving at usury and receiving more" is counted three times. Psalm 14, among the requirements for dwelling in the Lord's tabernacle and resting on His holy mountain, lists "he who has not given his money at usury." In another passage <note>The text says "Psalm 14" again, but the quote "non defecit de plateis eius usura & dolus" is actually Psalm 54:11 in the Vulgate (Psalm 55 in modern Bibles).</note>, it is mentioned: "usury and deceit have not departed from its streets." In Psalm 71, it is said of the Messiah: "He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity."

<margin>9</margin>
From the New Testament, there is clearly that passage in Luke 6: "Lend, hoping for nothing in return" <note>original: "Mutuum date nihil inde sperantes"</note>. Pope Urban III cites this testimony... as if usury were prohibited in that place. Pope Alexander III seems to favor this as well... when he says usury is condemned by the pages of both Testaments, since no other place in the New Testament appears where usury is so openly condemned. To the contrary, however, it is objected that in that passage Christ seems to be offering a counsel <note>A "counsel" is a spiritual recommendation for the perfect, whereas a "precept" is a binding law for all Christians.</note>, suggesting that a loan should be made without looking for a similar return, so that it might be more pleasing and meritorious before God. Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a key figure in the School of Salamanca.</note> in book 6 of *On Justice*, question 1, article 1, judges that those words of Christ contain only a counsel. But he adds that usury is sufficiently prohibited by the New Testament because vice <note>original: "suetum," likely a transcription error for "vitium"</note> taken broadly, under which usury is included, is prohibited.

He also adds, by an "argument from the stronger reason" <note>term: a fortiori — a method of reasoning that suggests if a lesser fact is true, a greater one must certainly be true.</note>, that usury is collected as illicit from that passage. For if a Christian is taught to abstain from even the hope of a similar favor in return, how much more must it be judged that usury is prohibited? I would say that although that passage alone might not be entirely convincing, one should not doubt that Christ intended both meanings in that place, since Urban III used that testimony as a consensus. Nonetheless, I do not believe those Supreme Pontiffs intended to define that as the only literal sense of that passage.

Nor do I believe they would have defined

<column-break/>

usuries as illicit from that passage alone. However, when it is established from elsewhere that they are illicit by natural and divine law, they rightfully use that passage to support the same view. Although the definitions of the Supreme Pontiffs and the Church are most certain, it is not necessary that all the arguments by which they are confirmed be equally certain, as we have said in the matter of faith... Navarrus <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist.</note> cites a bull of Leo X from the Lateran Council, as if it approves that same testimony from Luke 6 as containing a commandment against lending at usury. However, it is not presented there as an assertion of the Council or Leo X, but rather as the argument used by those who were led to condemn the "Mount of Piety" <note>term: Mount of Piety (original: "montem pietatis") — a charitable institution that provided low-interest loans to the poor to protect them from usurers.</note>, which is the subject of that discussion. Later in the same bull, their opinion is rejected and the contrary is defined. Thus, it follows from that bull that the literal sense of that testimony is not an undisputed matter.

<margin>10</margin>
Now, it is established that usury is illicit by human law—that is, by the sacred canons—and prohibited under grave penalties throughout the entire title "On Usury" in the Decretals... Among these laws, there is a decree from the Council of Nicaea, one from Pope Martin, one from the Lateran Council, and one from the Council of Lyons; all of which are general councils. Most recently, in the *Clementines* <note>term: Clementines (original: "Clementina") — a collection of Church laws from the 14th century.</note> it was defined thus:
> *If anyone falls into the error of presuming to stubbornly affirm that practicing usury is not a sin, we decree that he be punished as a heretic. We strictly enjoin the local Ordinaries and inquisitors of heretical depravity not to fail to proceed against those found defamed or suspected of such error as they would against those defamed or suspected of heresy.*

<margin>11</margin>
As for Caesarean Law <note>term: Caesarean Law — Roman Civil Law as codified by the emperors.</note>, it did not only permit usury in the sense that it did not punish the crime (in the same way that prostitution is permitted among Christians to avoid greater evils), but also in that it did not allow the recovery <note>original: "repetitionem" — the legal right to sue to get back money already paid.</note> of certain usuries once paid. It even allowed legal action to demand usury in certain cases... Therefore, the opinion of Soto, who affirms the contrary, must be rejected. I said that Caesarean law granted usury by a specific law: for civil laws did not permit usury in any amount... The maximum usury the civil law permitted was the "hundredth part" <note>term: hundredth part (original: "centesima") — a monthly interest rate of 1%, totaling 12% per year.</note>; that is, that the hundredth part be paid every month; so that he who gave a hundred gold pieces as a loan would be paid one gold piece every month beyond the principal, and twelve gold pieces every year. They permitted this usury only in "maritime money" <note>term: maritime money (original: "pecunia traiectitia") — high-risk loans for sea trade where the lender assumed the risk of the cargo's safety.</note>, that is, money lent to be carried across the sea by the borrower where the risk belonged to the lender and not the borrower... as is clear in the cited laws. In other events, if the lender were a nobleman, he was only permitted...

## Second Treatise, Disputation 304

...it was granted to him to receive a third part of the *centesima* <note>The *centesima* was the standard Roman interest rate of 1% per month, totaling 12% per year.</note>, that is, a third part of one gold coin every month for every hundred he had given as a loan—which is the same as four gold coins per year. If, however, he were a merchant, he was permitted to receive two parts of the *centesima*, that is, two-thirds of a gold coin every month for those same hundred lent, and thus he was permitted to receive eight gold coins per year. For other men, it was not lawful to receive more than half of a *centesima*, that is, half a gold coin each month, or six gold coins annually, for a hundred lent. All other forms of usury were prohibited. This law is cited and explained better than others by Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic theologian.</note> in the place mentioned above. Furthermore, compound interest <note>original: "vsuræ vsurarū"</note>—the charging of interest upon interest—was prohibited by Caesarean law. For example, if six coins were owed annually for a hundred gold coins, it was a sin to take further interest on those six coins in the future, even if a contract intervened stating that if they were not paid, they would be added to the principal and interest paid on them. This is found in the final law of the Code, *On Usury* <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de vsur." referring to the Codex Justinianus.</note>. From this, you will understand that many "clothed" or hidden forms of usury—which are more severe and wicked—are sometimes paid out of the favor of the debtor, even though they were at one time permitted by certain civil laws.

<margin>13</margin>
In truth, such laws permitting actual usury were contrary to natural law, as has been shown. For this reason, besides other canonical laws, they were rightly abolished along with many others in the Decree of the Council of Vienne <note>The Council of Vienne (1311–1312) took a hard line against usury, declaring that anyone who maintained that usury was not a sin should be punished as a heretic.</note>. At the same time, it was decreed that if any public authority presumed to judge that usury should be paid, or that usury already paid should not be restored when discovered, they would be excommunicated by the law itself. In this matter, Canon Law prevails over Civil Law, because the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> holds full power over secular powers in those things which concern the salvation of souls and supernatural ends, as was shown in Disputation 29. Consequently, today <margin>14</margin> a legal action is granted in the secular court to reclaim usury that has already been paid. This is granted under Portuguese law, as is evident in the Ordinances, Book 4, Title 14. Read also what is arranged in Title 27, the second-to-last and last sections, and Book 1, Title 47, section 19. The law of Castile grants the same in the New Collection, Book 18, Title 6, throughout. Regarding the penalties for usurers, this will be discussed in its proper place below.

The learned Doctors dispute whether the Emperor Justinian abolished the Caesarean laws that permitted usury. The Gloss on the *Authentica* <note>A collection of Justinian's new laws (Novels).</note> and certain other authorities of Canon Law affirm this. They convince themselves of this because the same Emperor accepted the faith of the Council of Nicaea and commanded it to be observed; and in the Council of Nicaea, usury was condemned. This seems to be the more common opinion of legal experts. However, in my judgment, the contrary is sufficiently proven by Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502).</note> on contracts, question 22, and Covarrubias in his *Various Resolutions*, book 1, number 6; Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> and the cited Covarrubias were of the same opinion.

<margin>15</margin> It remains to satisfy the arguments proposed at the beginning of this disputation. Regarding the testimony from Deuteronomy 23 <note>Deuteronomy 23:19-20 says: "You shall not charge interest on loans to another Israelite... On loans to a foreigner you may charge interest."</note> mentioned in the argument, this must be said: from that passage, it is sufficiently gathered that usury is illicit in itself. Indeed, for that reason, it was prohibited among "brothers"—that is, the children of Israel—and the same is confirmed by the other testimonies from the Old Testament cited by us. Regarding that word "but to a stranger," St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, Cajetan, 

<column-break/>

Soto, Alfonso de Castro <note>A Franciscan theologian and jurist (1495–1558).</note>, Alexander of Hales, and others cited by Covarrubias understand it thus: it was not as if usury was permitted to the children of Israel toward foreigners as something *licit* (morally right), but only as something *unpunished* to avoid greater evils. Specifically, it was to prevent them from oppressing their own brothers with usury out of greed, to which that people were very prone. Just as, in the opinion of these same Doctors, a bill of divorce <note>original: "libellus repudij"</note> was permitted to them because of the hardness of their hearts, according to the words of Christ. And just as among us, prostitution <note>original: "meretricium"</note> is permitted—even though it conflicts with natural law—to avoid greater evils. Indeed, in the same way, a little earlier in that same chapter, it says "there shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel"; for that permission of foreign prostitutes, which is gathered there by the argument from the contrary sense, is not to be understood as something licit, but as something unpunished to avoid greater evils. 

Others understand the testimony cited in the argument differently: namely, that usury was permitted to the children of Israel as something *licit* toward foreigners—that is, their enemies who inhabited the Land of Promise which God had granted them, and toward any others with whom they would wage a just war. For by the very fact that it is lawful to despoil true enemies of their goods, it is also lawful to give them a loan with a contract that they return something beyond the principal. <margin>16</margin> For when something is lawfully owed from another source, in the opinion of the Doctors, it is lawful to give a loan with a contract that it be returned along with that debt; Alexander III agrees with this in the Council of Tours, as does the final gloss there, because that is not taking a profit from a loan, but recovering a debt from another source by occasion of a loan, in which usury is not properly found. This is how Conrad and Juan Medina <note>Spanish theologian (1490–1547).</note> understand that passage. Gabriel Biel and John Major agree with this, as do others cited by Covarrubias, who rejects neither opinion. 

Ambrose was clearly of the same opinion <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note>, whose words we cited in the preceding disputation, and it is even more evident in the same Ambrose's book *On Tobias*, chapter 8, from which that text was taken; in that place, he puts forward this opinion and subjoins the words of that text as confirmation. Consequently, the first gloss on that text—as if Ambrose meant that just as no one should be harmed, so interest should be demanded from no one—surely conflicts with the text and Ambrose's mind, whatever Soto may say above. Nor does the opinion of Conrad and others have as little probability as Soto affirms in that same place, provided it is understood that scandal is avoided. Truly, there was no greater scandal at that time in the children of Israel taking usury from them in the manner explained, than in them usurping their lands and goods. Especially since the fact that usury is illicit by the very reason of nature is not so clear—until it is diligently investigated and its legitimate reasoning discovered—that it could not be ignored by almost all peoples. This can even be confirmed by the fact that it was hidden from the wisest creators of Caesarean law. Thus, this thing seems unknown to the nations from whom the children of Israel were permitted to take usury. Provided also it is understood to be lawful...

<margin>Objection</margin> ...we would argue that today these [prohibitions] would have no force, on the grounds that they did not pertain to moral precepts, but to the judicial or ceremonial laws of the Old Law, which ceased with the death of Christ. We demonstrated this at length in <term>volume 2</term> while discussing the Old Law. Therefore, since there are no such clear testimonies in the New Law prohibiting usury, the Church Fathers would certainly never have defined the illegality of usury today as a matter of faith if such a thing were not illegal by the very nature of the matter. Indeed, the passages of the Old Testament themselves suggest clearly enough that usury is evil and illicit by its very nature; for they do not bear any likeness to either judicial or ceremonial precepts.

It is further confirmed: we can prove usury is illicit by the nature of the matter. <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, guided by natural light, condemns it as illicit in the <term>4th book of Ethics</term> at the end of <term>chapter 1</term>. In the same place, he rebukes "usurers"—those who give small amounts in exchange for large returns—and calls it a "shameful acquisition of gain." In the <term>1st book of Politics, chapter 7</term>, he also appears to condemn interest. Furthermore, <term>Tullius</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> says at the end of the <term>2nd book of On Duties</term> that "to give at interest is the same as killing a man." <term>Covarrubias</term> <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> also cites others in the place mentioned who, following the light of nature, condemn usury.

<margin>The answer.</margin> <margin>8.</margin> It is established even more clearly from the Old Testament that usury is illicit. In <term>Ezekiel 18</term>, among the deadly sins by which justice and grace are lost, "giving at usury and taking more in return" is counted. <term>Psalm 14</term> <note>Psalm 15 in modern Bibles.</note>, listing what is necessary to dwell in the tabernacle of the Lord and rest on His holy mountain, includes "he who has not given his money at interest." In <term>Psalm 54</term> <note>Psalm 55.</note>, likewise, other evils are recounted: "usury and deceit have not departed from its streets." In <term>Psalm 71</term> <note>Psalm 72.</note>, it is said of the Messiah: "He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity."

<margin>9.</margin> From the New Testament, there is that clear passage in <term>Luke 6</term>: "Lend, hoping for nothing therefrom" <note>original: "Mutuum date nihil inde sperantes."</note>. This testimony is cited by Pope <term>Urban III</term> in the chapter *Consuluit* (under the title "On Usurers"), as if usury were prohibited in that place. And Pope <term>Alexander III</term> seems to suggest the same in the chapters *Quia in omnibus* and *Super eo* under the same title, when he says that usury is "condemned by the pages of both Testaments," even though no other place in the New Testament appears where usury is so openly condemned. On the contrary, it is objected that in this passage Christ seems to be offering "counsel" <note>In Catholic theology, a 'counsel' is a recommendation for higher perfection, whereas a 'precept' is a mandatory command.</note>—that a loan should be made without looking for a similar return, so that for that reason it becomes more pleasing and meritorious before God, as seems manifest from the context of the passage itself. <term>Soto</term> in <term>Book 6, On Justice, Question 4, Article 2</term>, judged that those words of Christ contain only a counsel. He adds, however, that usury is sufficiently prohibited by the sacred pages of the New Testament insofar as theft—taken in a broad sense, under which usury is included—is prohibited therein.

He also adds, by an "argument from the stronger reason," that it can be gathered from this that usury is illicit. For if a Christian is taught in that place to abstain even from looking for a return of a similar favor, how much more must it be judged that usury is prohibited? I would say that although that passage alone might not be entirely convincing, there should be no doubt that Christ intended both meanings in that place, especially since <term>Urban III</term> used that testimony in that sense. However, I do not believe those Supreme Pontiffs intended to define that this is the *literal* sense of that passage.

Nor do I believe they would have defined

<column-break/>

usury as illicit based on that single passage. Nevertheless, since it is established from elsewhere that usury is illicit by natural and divine law, they rightly use that passage to define the same thing. For although the definitions of the Supreme Pontiffs and the Church are most certain, it is not necessary that all the arguments by which they are confirmed be equally certain, as we have said regarding the matter of faith, and as is handed down by many. <term>Navarrus</term> <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist.</note> in his commentary *On Usury* (14, question 3, chapter 1, number 10) cites a bull of <term>Leo X</term> from the <term>Lateran Council</term> <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517).</note>, as if in it—with the Council's approval—the same testimony from Luke 6 was cited as containing a "precept" against lending at interest. However, it is not cited there as an assertion of the Council or of Leo X, but as the reason why some people were led to condemn the <term>Montes Pietatis</term> <note>Institutional "mountains of mercy" or charitable pawn shops that charged a small fee to cover expenses, which some argued was a form of usury.</note>, which is the subject of discussion there. Later in the same bull, their opinion is rejected, and the contrary is defined. Thus, it follows that one cannot gather from that bull that this is the undisputed literal sense of that testimony.

<margin>10</margin> Now, however, it is established that usury is illicit by human law—that is, by the sacred canons—and is prohibited under heavy penalties throughout the entire title "On Usury" in the <term>Decretals</term>, and in <term>Book 6</term> of the same title, as well as in various chapters of the <term>Decretum</term>. Among these laws, many are from the <term>Council of Nicaea</term>, others from the council of <term>Pope Martin</term>, and the chapter *Quia in omnibus* is from the <term>Lateran Council</term>. The chapter *Usurarum* is from the <term>Council of Lyons</term>, and all these are general councils. Most recently, however, in the <term>Clementina</term> <note>A collection of canon laws issued by Pope Clement V.</note> under the single chapter "On Usury," it was defined thus: "If anyone falls into that error that they presume to stubbornly affirm that practicing usury is not a sin, we decree that they are to be punished as a heretic." Nevertheless, we strictly enjoin the local Ordinaries and the inquisitors of heretical depravity not to fail to proceed against those whom they find defamed or suspected of such error as they would against those defamed or suspected of heresy.

<margin>11</margin> Regarding <term>Caesarean Law</term> <note>Roman Civil Law, specifically the Justinian Code.</note>, it used to permit usury not only in the sense that it did not punish the crime (in the same way that prostitution is permitted among Christians to avoid greater evils), but also in that it did not allow for the recovery of certain usuries once paid, and further in that it granted a legal action for demanding certain permitted interest, as is established in the <term>Digest and Code on Usury</term>. From this, the opinion of <term>Soto</term> (Book 6, On Justice, Question 1, Article 2), who affirms the contrary, must be rejected. I said that Caesarean law granted a legal action for interest permitted by a specific law: for the civil laws did not permit usury in just any amount. The maximum usury allowed by civil law was the <term>centesima</term> <note>Literally "the hundredth part"—a 1% monthly interest rate, equaling 12% per year.</note>, that is, that the hundredth part be paid every month. Thus, for someone who lent a hundred gold coins, one gold coin would be paid each month beyond the principal, and twelve gold coins would be paid each year. And they permitted this usury only in "maritime loans" <note>original: "pecunia traiecticia" or "nautico foenore."</note>—that is, money lent to be transported by sea, where the risk of the money belonged to the lender rather than the borrower. In other cases, if the lender was a nobleman, only [a lower rate] was permitted...

<summary>Molina argues that the prohibition of usury is a universal moral law rooted in nature and Scripture, rather than a temporary Jewish legal code. He contrasts the strict prohibitions of Canon Law, which eventually declared the defense of usury to be heresy, with the regulated tolerances of Roman (Caesarean) civil law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical legal and moral definition of usury. While the previous page discussed historical interest rates allowed under Roman law, Molina here focuses on the strict definition of usury according to Scholastic theology, distinguishing between "formal" loans and "virtual" loans found in trade practices.</meta>

-># Luis de Molina on Contracts<-

### Page 136

...compensation for a loss occurring <note>original: "damno emergente"</note> or for profit ceasing <note>original: "lucro cessante"</note>, or from any other source, it will not be called profit from a loan, but interest obtained from another title.

<margin>6</margin> Regarding that other part of the definition, **from a loan**, it must be observed that it is taken broadly here, as it includes not only a true and formal loan, but also a virtual loan <note>original: "mutuum virtute." A virtual loan is an exchange that functions like a loan even if not called one.</note>. For if someone sells something for more than the strict just price on credit, and receives that increase because they are waiting for payment (as is always presumed to be the cause), the contract is usurious. This is because to sell on credit is, in effect, to leave the price with the buyer as a virtual loan—money that was supposed to be paid immediately. Therefore, to receive an increase for that reason, beyond the just price, is to receive profit from a virtual loan, and is thus usury. Similarly, if someone, because of an advance payment, buys something for less than the lowest just price, they commit usury. This is because to pay in advance is virtually the same as giving that money as a loan until the time the goods are delivered; therefore, to subtract something from the just price for that reason is to carry away profit from a virtual loan, which is usury.

<margin>7</margin> Through this second part of the definition, any profit that is not from a loan—whether that profit be just or unjust—is rejected from the category of usury. Therefore, if someone sells something for more than the strict just price for cash, although that increase in price is unjust and requires restitution in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal forum of the soul and confession</note>, it nevertheless does not pertain to usury, because it proceeds neither from a formal nor a virtual loan, but from a simple unjust sale. If someone leases their gold coins so they can be used for display or recreation, or so that a sick person might be comforted by them, or for some other use, and receives a moderate price for that use, such a price and profit is not usury. It is a just profit, as **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for these legal theories.</note> and the doctors commonly affirm. For that profit is not from a loan, but from the **leasing** of money, where the ownership of that money remains with the person leasing it. Therefore, if the money is lost then without even the slightest fault of the person hiring it, the loss falls on the owner (the lessor), and not the one hiring it. In a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, however, the loss would fall on the borrower, and not the lender.

<margin>8</margin> To judge any contract to see if it is usurious, one must use this rule, which suffers no exception: One must look to see whether a loan, either formal or virtual, intervenes in that contract. If it does, and profit is intended from it, the contract is usurious, and such profit is usury. If not, it cannot be usurious, whether it is otherwise just or unjust.

<margin>9</margin> It must be observed that what is given in a loan, or the equivalent amount owed by reason of the loan, is called the **principal** <note>original: "sortem," literally "the lot" or "the share."</note>. As **Soto** rightly says in his sixth book *On Justice*, this name was derived from the contract of partnership <note>original: "societatis"</note> and passed to others. For in a partnership contract, each partner puts his "principal"—that is, his portion—into the common pile; at the time of division, he first draws that out if it remains intact, and then receives the part of the profit that falls to him beyond the principal. In this sense, **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> calls the loan, or the equal amount owed by reason of the loan, the "principal," while the profit received above it by reason of the loan

<column-break/>

he calls usury, saying: *Whatever is added to the principal is usury.* It is used in the same way frequently in law and by the doctors. The principal is also called the "capital" and "the main sum" both in the partnership contract and in the matter at hand, when we distinguish usury from the principal, capital, and main sum which is owed by reason of the loan.

<margin>10</margin> Usury, considered as a vice and a sin, is nothing other than the acceptance of, or the will to accept, profit from a loan. From this, and from the preceding definition, the contract in which such profit is intended or intervenes is called usurious. However, when usury exists in the agreement but has not yet been accepted, it is called "usury of the pact" by some, and an obligation to restore it does not yet arise from it. But when it has already been received, it is called "usury of the extraction," as it has been exacted and received. Then, an obligation arises to restore it.

<margin>11</margin> Even received usury, which is already subject to restitution, is divided into **mental** and **real**. And again, into **open** and **cloaked**. It is **real** usury when a tacit or express pact regarding profit from a loan intervenes. Indeed, it is real usury not only when someone openly bargains for profit from a loan, but also when they hint at it while giving the loan. For example, if the lender says, "You know the custom," or "I trust this money will not return to me empty," or "Remember that I am deprived of the use of my money and I have children," or something similar.

<margin>12</margin> **Mental** usury, however, is when neither a tacit nor an express pact regarding profit from a loan intervenes, but the person who gives the loan does so with the intention and hope of receiving profit from it. They know the borrower will give it, not out of liberality or gratitude, but out of fear that the loan will be denied them another day, or for some other reason. He who gives a loan with this intention commits the sin of usury, and by later accepting such profit, he not only sins but is also bound to restore it. However, a specific dispute regarding mental usury will be set aside for later.

From this, you will easily understand that mental usury is not distinguished from real usury in the way a sin of the mind is distinguished from an external sin. For in both mental and real usury, there is a sin of the mind and an external sin. If someone has the will to lend for the sake of profit and puts that into an external pact, but has not yet executed it or expressed it further, they have sinned only with the mental sin of real usury. When they later execute it, they commit the external sin of real usury. Similarly, if someone has the will to lend for profit with no external pact (even a tacit one), because they know the other person will pay profit so the loan isn't denied later, then if that will has not yet come forth into an external act, it is a mental sin of mental usury. When it does come forth into an external act because they give the loan with that intention, it is the external sin of mental usury.

<margin>13</margin> **Open** usury is when the loan is formal and the profit is taken or intended from it. **Cloaked** usury <note>original: "palliata," literally "cloaked" or "veiled."</note> is when the loan is virtual, as in one who sells on credit or buys with advance money, and profit is intended or taken from it. Sometimes mental usury is also called cloaked usury by some.

<summary>Molina defines the technical differences between formal and virtual loans, and distinguishes between "real" usury (based on a pact) and "mental" usury (based on intent), emphasizing that usury occurs whenever profit is sought specifically from the act of lending.</summary>
<keywords>usury, mutuum, principal, virtual loan, mental usury, cloaked usury, just price, credit sales, restitution, Luis de Molina</keywords>

...real, in which a tacit pact intervenes. We, however, following the common usage of speakers, will call "cloaked usury" <note>original: "palliatam usuram"; this refers to interest hidden within other types of contracts, like inflated sales prices on credit</note> only that which is intended or received as profit from a virtual loan.
