## Is Usury Illicit?

### DISPUTATION 304.

### SUMMARY.

1. Whether usury is licit or not, discussed throughout the disputation.
2. Usury is illicit by natural, divine, and human law; see also number 7.
3. Usury is not what is paid to a borrower for the wages and labor of workers, but a stipend. Likewise for what is paid for the action of giving a loan; see also number 4.
5. Compensation of one action for another is permitted, just as one object for another.
6. In what case an injury is done to one who is willing and consenting.
7. Usury is illicit by the nature of the thing against commutative justice <note>term: commutative justice (the virtue governing fair exchange between individuals, requiring that what is given is equal in value to what is received)</note>.
8. Usury is illicit according to the Old Testament. Likewise from the New, and by Canon law; see numbers 9 and 10.
11. Usury which was granted by Imperial law <note>original: "iure Cæsareo"; referring to Roman civil law</note>.
12. Compound interest <note>original: "usura usurarum"</note> is prohibited by Imperial law.
13. Imperial laws permitting usury were abrogated by Canon law.
14. The legal action to recover paid usury is permitted today, even by Portuguese and Castilian law.
15. Usury in itself is illicit even in Deuteronomy, although it was permitted there against foreigners.
16. Whether a loan can be given as a debt arising from another contract, so that something may be perceived from it.
17. What "interest" <note>original: "fænus"</note> can signify.
18. Usury can be permitted to avoid greater evils.

<margin>1</margin>
**T**he side that argues it is not illicit pleads first: because usury is permitted to the sons of Israel regarding foreigners in Deuteronomy 23. For that text says: *You shall not charge interest to your brother, but to a stranger.* etc. In the following chapter 28, among the rewards proposed to that people if they keep the law, one is: *You shall lend to many nations, and you shall not receive interest from any.* And Christ in Luke 19 says that he will say to the wicked servant who kept the money in a handkerchief: *Why did you not put my money in the bank, so that I might have collected it with interest?* Therefore usury, viewed in itself, is not illicit; otherwise it would not be permitted by God, nor promised as a reward, nor would Christ have uttered those words.

Second, civil laws permit usury, as is established in the Digest and the Code <note>references to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman law</note> regarding usury. Since such laws should not be seen as condemnable or unjust, it follows that usury is not illicit in itself.

<margin>2</margin>
That usury † is nevertheless illicit is so certain that the contrary most clearly conflicts with the Catholic faith, as we shall see. Because it must be shown that usury is illicit by natural, divine, and human law, I have decided to begin with the nature of the thing itself.
I would first warn that it is an insufficient reason for proving usury is illicit by the nature

<column-break/>

of the thing, if someone argues: It is against the nature of a loan <note>original: "mutui"</note> to receive anything beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note>; therefore usury is illicit.
For it is also against the nature of a loan for use <note>term: commodatum (a loan where the specific object, like a tool or a book, must be returned for free)</note> to receive anything for the use of the thing lent, and yet it does not follow from this that receiving something is illicit; it only follows that the nature of the "commodatum" is destroyed and it transitions into a just contract of hiring <note>original: "locati"</note> if what is received is a moderate price, or it transitions into a just unnamed contract if what is received is not a price. I would also warn that, just as taking a price for a thing lent for use destroys the nature of the "commodatum" and makes the contract pass into another species, it is not the case in a loan <note>term: mutuum (a loan of fungible goods like money or grain where ownership passes to the borrower and they return an equivalent amount later)</note> that receiving something beyond the principal destroys the nature of the loan. The reason is that a loan consists of this: that something is given for use which immediately becomes the property of the receiver, and he later restores the same amount in kind and quality. The fact that a pact is made so that something is returned in addition does not destroy that other part in which the nature of the loan consists. But since a "commodatum" consists of something being granted for use for free, while the ownership of the thing remains with the giver, certainly if a pact intervenes so that something is returned for that use, the nature of the "commodatum" is destroyed by that very fact, and the contract passes into a distinct species. It remains, therefore, to show more clearly why usury is illicit by nature; which is done by the following reasoning.

It is illicit by the nature of the thing, and against commutative justice, in the exchange of one thing for another, to demand or receive more than the thing given is worth, unless something else intervenes by reason of which that extra amount is justly received. But to receive something beyond the principal for a loan is to receive more for the exchange of the thing lent than it is worth, unless something else intervenes by reason of which that extra is justly received. Therefore, by the force of the loan alone, it is a crime by the nature of the thing and against commutative justice to receive anything beyond the principal, and consequently usury is illicit against commutative justice and subject to restitution.

The consequence is evident, and the major premise is clear from the nature of commutative justice itself, whose role is to establish equality in exchanges. Moreover, the same major premise is most widely accepted in other exchanges, such as in a sale, in which it is not permitted to receive a higher price than the merchandise is worth; and in hiring, in which it is likewise a crime to receive a higher price than the use of the thing hired is worth; and in permutations and other unnamed contracts, which must be made according to equality to be just.

The minor premise is manifest from the terms themselves: for to receive beyond the principal is nothing other than to receive beyond the value of the thing given in the loan. For it is always said that one receives the full value of the thing given in the loan, even if more in quantity must be received, and in that no usury intervenes. For example, if at a time when wheat is worth more, you lend some measures to be restored at harvest time, when it is expected to be worth less, it is lawful for you to bargain that the borrower then restores as many more measures as are sufficient to equalize the prices of the wheat at both times; because you then bargain to receive nothing beyond the principal. However, this is rather to be seen as a debt of the current price of the wheat, and buying wheat at the price it will be worth at the time of delivery, rather than a loan...

<summary>Molina begins Disputation 304 by defining usury and outlining why it is considered illicit under natural, divine, and human law, specifically arguing that it violates the principle of equality in commutative justice.</summary>

# Louis Molina on Contracts

### On Loans and Equality of Value

...to give. Regarding the same, observe a minor point: if you exclude cases where, by reason of different value—which the same thing in kind, quality, and goodness is expected to have at different times—something must be added or subtracted from the quantity of the thing to be restored, so that equality in value (in the manner explained) is achieved between what was given as a loan and what is to be restored. (Indeed, since in a loan, as stated in Disputation 299, it is understood that an equal amount must be returned—not only in kind, weight, number, or measure, but also in quality and goodness—it follows that the equality seen between the thing given and the thing returned consists in something **indivisible** <note>In scholastic terms, "indivisible" means a fixed, exact point of value, rather than a flexible range.</note>, especially when the loan is in money, whose value is fixed by law. This fixed equality exists both in the money given and in that returned in compensation. Consequently, equality in a loan does not usually behave the same way as equality in other exchanges, where one thing is traded for another of a different kind.)

...For indeed, when things are of different kinds and are not price-controlled by law, not only does the value of each not consist in a fixed point, but neither does their comparison to one another regarding value. Thus, the equality between them is not "indivisible," but has a certain **latitude** <note>term: latitude (a range of "just prices" within which a buyer and seller can negotiate without committing a sin of injustice)</note>. For example, if you wish to balance wheat with wine, oil with honey, a horse with an ox, or linen with wool according to their value, certainly the "just and equal" price has a certain range in the exchange of such things.

...But truly, when things are of the same kind and consist of weight, number, or measure—provided they are of the same quality and goodness, as wheat or oil usually are—even if the value of a bushel of wheat or a jar of oil does not sit at a single fixed point, the equality in value of one bushel of wheat compared to another, or one jar of oil to another (which are permitted in a loan), consists in a fixed point. This is even more true for the equality in value between a hundred gold coins given as a loan and the same amount returned for them.

...To make the strength of the proposed reasoning shine more brightly, let us clear away some objections that might be raised against it.

**First objection:** You might object that while the reasoning proves that nothing beyond the principal can be lawfully received for the *thing* given in a loan, it does not prove that nothing can be lawfully received for the **use** of it, which is estimable in money and of which the lender is deprived for a time.

<margin>Objection</margin>
...To clear away this objection, one must observe that two types of "use" for a thing given in a loan can be distinguished. One is for **business and profit**: selling it for gain, bartering it, transferring it to another location, or saving it for a time when it might be worth more; or, if it is money, buying it for the same purpose, transferring it elsewhere, or giving it in currency exchange.

...The other use is not business, but the **mere consumption** of the thing accepted in the loan. If it is money, this means buying necessities, or even luxuries and superfluities, paying a debt, giving it away, or spending it vainly on a prostitute and other similar things. If it is wheat, wine, or oil, it means consuming it in daily use or in any other way.

...Having explained this, I say in response to the objection, first:

<column-break/>

If the person who gives the loan is deprived of some profit because of the loan—profit they were going to perceive through the use of that thing—or if they incur some loss, we do not deny that by reason of such **lost profit** or **emerging loss** <note>term: lost profit and emerging loss (Latin: *lucrum cessans* and *damnum emergens*; these are the two standard legal justifications for charging interest to compensate the lender for their own losses)</note>, they may lawfully receive a fitting compensation beyond the principal. Indeed, because of this and other things that may be joined with a loan, we added those words to the major premise of our argument: *unless something else intervenes by reason of which that additional amount is justly received*; and we strengthened the minor premise with similar words.

...Next, I say to the objection that for a thing given in a loan, an equal amount is paid back not only regarding ownership, but also regarding use. Indeed, a thing of the same use is paid back for a thing that was to be consumed by the person who gave the loan, had they wished to use it before the time of repayment. Thus, unless "lost profit" or "emerging loss" intervenes due to the loan, they are paying back an equal value even regarding the use for the time during which the lender is deprived of it. For this reason, if the lender accepts anything beyond the principal, they sin against **commutative justice** <note>term: commutative justice (the moral requirement that exchanges must be strictly equal in value)</note>.

...Add to this that when lost profit or emerging loss does not intervene, the loan actually works to the advantage of the giver: for if the thing were to perish by theft, rot, or other misfortune, the loss falls not on the lender, but on the borrower. Regarding lost profit and emerging loss, more will be said later in its proper place.

<margin>Objection</margin>
...You will object secondly: Although the proposed reasoning proves that one cannot accept more than the principal for the thing given in a loan, it does not prove that one cannot justly receive something for the **labor of counting the money** (both when it is given and when it is received), or for measuring, weighing, delivering, and receiving other things, or for the costs of drafting documents, or for the **risk** to which the loaned thing is exposed (lest it perhaps not be restored, or not without difficulty and labor in demanding it).

<margin>Response</margin>
...The response is that no one denies that a competent compensation can be lawfully received for these factors. The costs of documents, if any are made, should be paid by the borrower, for whose benefit the loan is made; this is admitted by Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 209; and John Major <note>A Scottish philosopher and theologian</note> on the *Sentences*; Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, an Italian theologian</note> under the word "usury"; Juan Medina on exchange; and others.

...All these things can indeed be estimated at a price. Thus, if a just wage is accepted for them, it is not profit from the loan, and therefore not usury, but a just stipend from other sources. Likewise, no one denies that if what is given is exposed to risk or to the troubles of the lender, it is right to accept a price for that risk and the troubles to which the lender exposes themselves.

...For a thing given in a loan, while it is subject to a moral or likely risk of this kind, is worth as much less as that risk is greater or more likely. To accept a price for that reason is not profit from the loan, but from another lawful source joined with such a loan. Nevertheless, human law could very well prohibit anything being accepted for these reasons, as men could easily find an excuse...

<summary>Molina argues that loans (mutuum) require strict equality in value because they involve fungible goods. He clarifies that while charging interest for the loan itself is usury, lenders can be compensated for administrative labor, document costs, actual financial losses (lost profit/emerging loss), and risk.</summary>
<keywords>usury, mutuum, commutative justice, lost profit, emerging loss, lucrum cessans, damnum emergens, Martin de Azpilcueta, risk compensation, scholastic economics</keywords>

--- Page 205 ---
<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on whether charging interest for a loan can be justified by viewing the "act of lending" as a separate service or by the borrower’s consent. He argues against these justifications to maintain the strict prohibition of usury.</meta>

...taking it as a kind of veil for cloaking and practicing usury.

<margin>Objection 4</margin>
Thirdly, you will object: Even if the same reasoning proves that nothing can be taken beyond the **principal** <note>original: "sorte" — the original amount of the loan, excluding interest.</note> for the thing being lent, it nonetheless does not prove that something cannot be justly taken for the *act* of providing the loan. For, as we showed in Disputation 93, for a good action that one is not bound to perform, one can accept a price. The act of lending is such an action; therefore, for that act, something can be licitly accepted beyond the value of the thing lent. This is especially true since that profit would not be "from the loan"—that is, from the thing lent—but from another heading, namely from the action itself, which is worthy of a price in its own right.

Perhaps someone, led by this reasoning, might try to grant what is inferred from it, responding that it does not follow that usury is licit. This is because what is accepted for the action is not usury, nor is it an illicit price, provided it is moderate in view of the value of the action. They might add that human law can nevertheless rightly prohibit a price being taken for that action, so that a path to usury is not introduced by taking more than the action is worth. However, I do not doubt that the contrary must be affirmed: that Holy Scripture, Canon Law, and the very nature of the matter require this. For usury is **any profit from a loan**, not only if you understand "loan" to mean the object or thing given, but also if you understand it as the action itself.

<margin>To Objection 5</margin>
To this objection, it must be said that when a good-faith action occurs in an exchange for an equal value, the act of giving is sufficiently compensated within the limits of **commutative justice** <note>term: commutative justice (the virtue governing fair exchange between individuals, requiring that what is given and what is received are of equal value)</note> by the action of returning the same amount. For just as a recompense is made to reach equality of object to object, so a compensation is made of action to action. Therefore, just as it would be usury and injustice to take something extra for the object, so it is to take it for the action; our principal reason, if rightly considered, proves both.

We have a fitting example in sales, hiring, and other exchanges. For although a sale is a "good action," nothing can be taken as a price for it beyond the price owed for the thing sold and beyond the action by which that price is paid. The same applies to other similar actions of justice in exchange. I said that the action of lending is sufficiently compensated, within the limits of commutative justice, by the action of returning the same amount. This is because, while the lender has looked to the benefit of the borrower (even while keeping himself harmless by asking for an equal amount back), the borrower—though bound by justice to nothing more—is nonetheless bound by moral honesty and gratitude to show gratitude toward him. This, however, does neither create an obligation of justice nor grant any legal claim to the lender. Therefore, what was said in the cited Disputation 93 must be understood as referring to good actions that are not performed as an exchange for something else of equal value.

<margin>Objection</margin>
Fourthly, you will object: "To one who is willing and consenting, no injury is done." <note>original: "volenti, & consentienti non fit iniuria" — a fundamental legal maxim suggesting that if someone agrees to an arrangement, they cannot later claim they were wronged by it.</note> Therefore, even if a loan is not worth more than its equivalent, when someone contracts that they will give something beyond the principal for the loan and then gives it, no injury is done if it is accepted, and thus

<column-break/>

the one receiving it is not bound to restore it to him.

6. It must be said that, although no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting with *full liberty*, and thus if a borrower, out of purely his own liberality and gratitude for the benefit received, were to give something beyond the principal, he would transfer **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> and the lender would not be bound to restore anything to him (since that would be a true gift); nevertheless, an injury *is* done to one who is willing and consenting not with full liberty, but with a **mixed involuntary** <note>term: mixed involuntary (a choice made under pressure or necessity, like a sailor throwing cargo overboard during a storm; the act is "voluntary" because it is chosen, but "involuntary" because it is not what the person would want in an ideal situation)</note> state. This occurs when something is taken from him when there is no other title by which it is owed. Such a will and consent is ineffective without another title for transferring ownership or a right to the thing given. In the case proposed, the borrower would not want to give anything beyond the principal if the lender were willing to lend without that increase; therefore, he gives it with a mixed involuntary will. So says St. Thomas in *On Evil*, question 13, article 4.

Fifthly, you will object: Sometimes the borrower gains a far greater benefit from the loan than the amount he agrees to pay beyond the principal. It will then be lawful for the lender to "sell" that great benefit which the borrower derives from the borrowed money by taking something extra from him.

<margin>Objection</margin>
To this objection, while granting the premise (that the borrower benefits), the conclusion must be denied. First, because that benefit does not come from the money itself, except as it is subject to the **industry** and risk of the borrower. It is wrong for a lender to take a price for the fruit of another person's hard work.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
Secondly (and this response confirms the preceding one), because through a loan, the ownership of the money given is transferred to the borrower. Thus, from that moment, it does not "bear fruit" as the lender's money, but as the borrower's money. Nor is it exposed to risk for the lender, but for the borrower. It is wrong for anyone to take a price for the benefit and fruit of a thing that already belongs to another, and which bears fruit precisely because it is subject to the industry and risk of that other person. Just as it is wrong for a seller to take a price for the fruit of the thing he sold (which now belongs to the buyer) beyond the price of the thing itself. If the ownership of the money remained with the lender, and only the use, or the business and fruit, were granted while the money remained at the lender's risk, then—even if it produced profit as the lender's property—he could "rent out" that use for a competent price. He could also contract with the receiver so that the fruit and profit were divided between them in some fair proportion, as usually happens in a **contract of partnership** <note>original: "contractu societatis"</note>, which is what that would be, rather than a loan, as we shall see in its proper place.

7. The principal reason proposed by us, and explained by the solutions to these objections, sufficiently proves (in my judgment) that usury is illicit from the **very nature of the thing** <note>original: "ipsa rei natura"</note>. Thus, based on **natural law** <note>original: "iure solo naturali"</note> alone, it is illicit, contrary to commutative justice, and subject to the obligation of **restitution** <note>term: restitution (the requirement to return stolen or unjustly gained goods to their rightful owner to restore the balance of justice)</note>. Other reasons are formulated by Conrad on Contracts (q. 22 and 23), Covarruvias (3. var. ref. c. 1. nu. 5), Gabriel (in 4. distin. 15. q. 11), Major (q. 29), Scotus (q. 2), and others, which certainly do not seem to persuade the matter as effectively.

We can further confirm that usury is illicit by natural law because, if it were not illicit by natural law, then the very clear prohibitions concerning it in the Old Testament (which we will soon cite)...

<summary>This page refutes the idea that charging interest is justified by calling it a "fee for the act of lending" or by citing the borrower's consent. Molina argues that because ownership of money transfers to the borrower, any profit made from it belongs to the borrower's effort, not the lender's capital.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal and theological analysis of usury. Having previously discussed the theoretical nature of lending, he now moves into specific scriptural and legal authorities (Aristotle, Cicero, the Bible, and Canon Law) to prove that charging interest is inherently wrong under both natural and divine law.</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

### Page 140

...we would argue, today they would have no legal force because they would not pertain to moral precepts, but rather to the judicial or ceremonial laws of the Old Covenant, which ceased with the death of Christ. We have already demonstrated this at length in our discussion on the Old Law in the *Prima Secundae* <note>original: "1. 2." — referring to the second part of Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae</note>. Therefore, since the New Law does not contain such explicit testimonies prohibiting usury, the Church Fathers would certainly never have defined the illegality of usury as a matter of faith today if it were not already illicit by the very nature of the thing. Indeed, the passages of the Old Testament clearly enough suggest that usury is evil and illicit by its very nature, as these prohibitions do not bear the character of merely temporary judicial or ceremonial rules.

<margin>Objection</margin>
We can further confirm that usury is illicit by the nature of the thing: for **Aristotle**, guided by the light of natural reason, condemns it as illicit in the *Ethics*, Book 4, at the end of Chapter 1. There, he condemns moneylenders and those who give small amounts to receive large ones, calling it a "foul way of acquiring gain." Furthermore, in the *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 7, he appears to condemn interest. **Cicero** also, at the end of Book 2 of *On Duties*, states that to lend at interest is the same as "killing a man." **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a famous Spanish jurist</note> also cites others who, following the light of nature, condemn usury.

<margin>The Answer</margin>
**8** It is established even more clearly from the Old Testament that usury is illicit. In **Ezekiel 18**, among the lethal sins by which justice and grace are lost, it is counted three times: "to give at interest and to receive more." In **Psalm 14**, among the requirements for dwelling in the Lord’s tabernacle and resting on His holy mountain, it lists "he who has not given his money at interest." In **Psalm 54**, among other evils recounted, it says "interest and deceit do not depart from its streets." In **Psalm 71**, it is said of the Messiah: "He shall redeem their souls from interest and iniquity."

**9** From the New Testament, there is that clearer passage in **Luke 6**: "Lend, hoping for nothing in return." This testimony was cited by Pope **Urban III** in the chapter *Consuluit* under the title of usury, as if usury were prohibited in that very place. Pope **Alexander III** seems to suggest the same in the chapters *Quia in omnibus* and *Super eo* under the same title, when he says that usury is condemned by the pages of "both Testaments," even though no other place in the New Testament appears where usury is so explicitly condemned. On the contrary, it is objected that in that passage, Christ seems to be offering a *counsel* <note>In Catholic theology, a "counsel" is a recommendation for perfection, whereas a "precept" is a mandatory command.</note> rather than a command, suggesting that a loan be made without looking for a similar return so that it might be more pleasing and meritorious before God, as seems manifest from the context. **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto, a contemporary theologian</note> (in Book 6, *On Justice*, question 1, article 3) is alone in thinking that those words of Christ contain only a counsel. However, he adds that the New Testament prohibits usury elsewhere, as it prohibits theft in a broad sense, under which usury is included.

He also adds, by an *a fortiori* <note>An argument from the stronger reason: "if a lesser thing is true, then a greater thing must also be true."</note> argument, that usury is shown to be illicit from this. For if a Christian is commanded to abstain even from the hope of a similar favor in return for a benefit, how much more must it be thought that usury is prohibited? I would say that although that passage alone might not be entirely convincing, one should not doubt that Christ intended both meanings in that place, especially since Urban III used that testimony in his consensus. However, I do not believe those Supreme Pontiffs intended to define that as the *only* literal sense of that passage.

Nor do I believe they would have defined 

<column-break/>

usury as illicit based on that single passage alone. However, when it is established from other sources that it is illicit by natural and divine law, they rightly use that passage to defend the same point. For although the definitions of the Popes and the Church are most certain, it is not necessary that every scriptural proof they use to confirm them be equally certain, as we have said regarding matters of faith. **Navarro** <note>The famous canonist Martín de Azpilcueta</note>, in his commentary on usury, cites the Bull of **Leo X** from the Lateran Council as if it used that same testimony from Luke 6 to establish a mandatory precept against lending at interest. However, it is not cited there as an assertion of the Council or of Leo X, but as a reason used by those who were led to condemn the *Mons Pietatis* <note>A "Mount of Piety" was a charitable institution that offered low-interest loans to the poor to protect them from usurers.</note>, which is the subject being discussed there. Later in that same Bull, the opinion of those people is rejected and the contrary is defined. Thus, it cannot be concluded from that Bull that such is the undisputed literal meaning of that testimony.

**10** † But truly, that usury is illicit by **human law**—that is, by the sacred canons—and prohibited under heavy penalties, is clear throughout the entire title "On Usury" in the Decretals and Book 6 of the same. It is also found in several chapters of Distinction 47 and Case 14, questions 3 and 4. Among these laws, the chapter *Quoniam multi* is from the **Council of Nicaea**; *Si quis* is from the Council of **Pope Martin**; *Quia in omnibus* is from the **Lateran Council**; and *Usurarum* is from the **Council of Lyon**—all of which were general councils. Most recently, in the single *Clementina* <note>A collection of canon laws</note> on usury, it is defined that: "If anyone falls into the error of presuming to stubbornly affirm that practicing usury is not a sin, we decree that he be punished as a heretic." Furthermore, it strictly enjoins local bishops and inquisitors of heretical depravity not to fail to proceed against those defamed or suspected of such error as they would against those suspected of heresy.

**11** † As far as **Caesarean Law** <note>Roman/Civil Law as opposed to Church Law</note> is concerned, it did not only "permit" usury in the sense that it did not punish the crime (in the same way that prostitution is permitted among Christians to avoid greater evils), but also in that it did not allow for the recovery of certain interest once paid. Furthermore, it even granted a legal action to demand interest permitted by certain laws, as is clear from the Digest and the Code. For this reason, the opinion of Soto, who affirms the contrary, must be rejected. I said that Civil Law granted a legal action for interest "permitted by certain laws," because the civil laws did not allow interest in just any amount. The maximum interest allowed by civil law was the **centesima** <note>1% per month, or 12% per year</note>. This meant that for every hundred gold coins lent, one coin was paid each month beyond the principal, totaling twelve coins a year. This interest was only allowed in cases of **money in transit** <note>original: "pecunia traiectitia" — a risky loan for maritime trade, also known as bottomry.</note>, which was money lent to be carried from sea to sea, where the risk belonged to the lender rather than the borrower. In other cases, if the lender was a nobleman, the law only permitted...

He also notes that Roman Civil Law historically permitted limited interest (the centesima) for high-risk maritime loans, though he maintains its moral illegitimacy.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 304

Column 1:
...it was allowed for him to receive a third part of a **centesima** <note>The *centesima* was the standard Roman interest rate of 1% per month, or 12% per year. Here, Molina describes a lower rate of 4% per year.</note>, that is, a third of one gold piece each month for every hundred lent, or (which is the same thing) four gold pieces per year. If, however, he were a merchant, he was permitted to take two parts of a **centesima**, that is, two-thirds of a gold piece each month for those same hundred lent, and thus he was allowed to take eight gold pieces per year. For other men, it was only lawful to receive half a **centesima**, that is, half a gold piece monthly, or six gold pieces annually, for every hundred lent. All other forms of usury were prohibited.

<margin>12 Soto cites these laws, and explains them better than others in the place cited above. Furthermore, **compound interest** <note>original: "usura usurarum" — charging interest upon interest already owed</note> was prohibited under Imperial Law. For instance, if six gold pieces were owed annually for a hundred, it was a crime to take interest on those six in the future, even if an agreement was made that if they were not paid, they would be added to the principal and interest paid on them. Thus it is in the final law of the Code on Usury. From this, you will understand that more grievous and wicked forms of **cloaked usury** <note>original: "usura palliatus" — hidden or disguised interest charges</note>, or secret usury, are sometimes paid out of "favor" in our times than those which were once granted by the ancient civil laws.</margin>
<margin>13</margin>
Ultimately, these laws permitting true usury were contrary to **natural law** <term>Natural Law: A philosophy suggesting that certain rights or values are inherent by virtue of human nature and universally cognizable through human reason.</term>, as has been shown. Therefore, along with many other laws, they were rightly abolished by the single decree on usury in the Council of Vienne <note>The Council of Vienne (1311–1312) was a major church council that declared any ruler who passed laws permitting usury to be a heretic.</note>. At the same time, it was decreed that if any public authority presumed to judge that usury should be paid, or that paid usury should not be restored when discovered, they should be excommunicated by the law itself. In this matter, Canon Law <note>Church law</note> prevails over Civil Law, because the Supreme Pontiff has full power over secular powers in matters concerning the salvation of souls and the supernatural end, as was shown in Disputation 29.
<margin>14 †</margin>
As a result, today a legal action is granted in the secular court to reclaim usury that has already been paid. This is granted under Portuguese law, as is evident in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 14. See also the laws in Title 27 and Book 1. The same is granted under the law of Castile in the New Collection, Book 8, Title 6. Regarding the penalties for usurers, this will be discussed later in its proper place.

Scholars debate whether the Emperor Justinian abolished the Imperial laws that permitted usury. The commentary on the Code and certain other parts of Canon law affirm this. They would persuade you of this because the same Emperor accepted the faith of the Council of Nicaea and ordered it to be observed; and in the Council of Nicaea, usury was condemned. However, in my judgment, Conrad <note>Conradus Summenhart, a German theologian</note> and Covarruvias prove sufficiently that this was not the case, and Panormitanus and the cited Covarruvias were of the same opinion.

<margin>15</margin>

Regarding the testimony from Deuteronomy 23 <note>"You may charge a foreigner interest, but you may not charge your brother interest."</note>, it must be said that from that passage, it is sufficiently gathered that usury is illicit in itself. Indeed, for that reason, it was prohibited among "brothers"—that is, the children of Israel—and the other testimonies from the Old Testament we have cited confirm the same. Regarding that word, "but to a stranger," St. Thomas understands it as follows...

<column-break/>

...there, Soto, Alfonso de Castro, Alexander of Hales, and others whom Covarruvias refers to, argue that usury was not permitted to the children of Israel toward foreigners as if it were **lawful**, but only as something **unpunished** to avoid greater evils. Specifically, it was to prevent them from oppressing their own brothers with usury out of greed, a vice to which that people was quite prone. This is similar to the opinion of the same doctors regarding the "bill of divorce," which was permitted to them because of the hardness of their hearts, according to the word of Christ. It is also like how among us, the existence of prostitutes is permitted—which conflicts with natural law—to avoid greater evils. Indeed, in that same chapter a little earlier, it is said: "there shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel." That permission for foreign prostitutes, which is gathered there by an argument of contrast, should not be understood as something lawful, but as something unpunished to avoid worse outcomes.

Others understand the cited testimony differently: namely, that usury was permitted to the children of Israel as a lawful thing toward "strangers"—that is, their enemies who inhabited the Land of Promise which God had granted them, and toward any others with whom they might wage a **just war** in the course of time. For by the very fact that it is lawful to spoil true enemies of their goods, it is also lawful to give them a loan with a contract that they return something beyond the principal. 
<margin>16</margin>
For when † something else is lawfully owed, it is the opinion of the doctors that one may give a loan with a contract that the debt be paid back through the loan. Alexander [of Hales] openly agrees with this regarding the Council of Tours, as does the gloss there, since that is not "receiving profit from a loan," but rather recovering a debt from elsewhere by occasion of the loan—in which case "usury" is not strictly found. This is how Conrad and Juan Medina understand that passage. Gabriel, John Major, and others whom Covarruvias cites also agree, though he rejects neither opinion.

Ambrose was clearly of this same opinion in the passage we cited in the previous disputation. It is even more evident in Ambrose’s book *On Tobit*, Chapter 18, from which that text was taken. In that place, he puts forward this opinion and adds the words of that text as confirmation. Thus, the first gloss on that text—suggesting Ambrose meant that just as no one should be harmed, so usury should be demanded from no one—actually conflicts with the text and Ambrose’s mind, regardless of what Soto says. Nor does the opinion of Conrad and others affirm it there, provided it is understood that there is no scandal. Certainly, the scandal was no greater in that time for the children of Israel to take usury from them in the manner explained, than for them to seize their lands and goods. This is especially true since the fact that usury is illicit by the very nature of the thing is not so clear until it is diligently investigated and its legitimate reasoning found; it is not something that could be known by almost all peoples. This is confirmed by the fact that it escaped even the wisest compilers of the Imperial Law. Thus, this matter seemed unknown to the nations from whom the children of Israel were permitted to take usury. Provided it is also understood that it is lawful...

# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...that it is lawful to receive interest from enemies and to plunder their goods, provided there is an express or presumed will of the public authorities to whom this is permitted. For without at least such a presumed faculty, neither can war be waged against enemies, nor can their goods be plundered and seized, as was said above when we discussed the subject of war.

<margin>17</margin> Regarding the second testimony brought forward in that first argument, it must be said: "To lend" <note>original: "fœnerari"</note> in that passage means the same thing as "to give a loan," according to what was said in the preceding disputation regarding the meaning of this word. For in those words, such an abundance of goods is promised as a reward that they themselves might be able to give loans to other nations, and would not need to receive loans from them. Moreover, that the word is used in that sense there can be confirmed from those other words in the same chapter: *You shall not lend to your brother at interest* <note>original: "Non fœneraberis fratri tuo ad usuram"</note>. Here it is clearly evident that it means the same as "to give a loan"; otherwise, the addition of "at interest" would be not only superfluous but even nonsensical. The same is confirmed by that passage in Ecclesiasticus 29: *Lend to your neighbor in his time of necessity.* In the same way, we showed in the preceding disputation that this term is used by secular authors.

Regarding the third testimony from Luke, it must be said: the discourse is metaphorical. For Christ wishes that we cooperate with the natural and supernatural goods bestowed upon us—with the help of His aid and grace—and that by this means we should multiply merits, which redound to His glory in such a way that the benefit is ours, both in terms of merits and the reward.

Furthermore, it can be added that the metaphor might be explained as "giving to the table" <note>original: "dare ad mensam" — referring to depositing money with bankers or changers</note> in terms of legitimate business, so that the money remains the property of the one putting it forward, and he earns profit while the money remains at his own risk; thus, by the name of "usury," legitimate profit from it is understood, according to what was said in the preceding disputation.

Regarding the second argument, the solution is clear from what has been said.

At the conclusion of this disputation, it must be added that since usury is prohibited by **natural law** <note>The set of universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of specific religious revelation</note>, and since it results in detriment to the commonwealth and its parts, public authorities are bound by their office to prohibit it—not only for Christians, but also for the non-believers <note>original: "infidelibus"</note> subject to them. They sin mortally by permitting it to Jews or other non-believers within their commonwealth in exchange for taxes they pay, or for any other convenience.

In the same way, they sin mortally by admitting Jews or other non-believers to live in their lands under a pact that allows them to practice usury, even if they promise fat taxes for such residency. The Supreme Pontiff, however, by the fullness of power which he holds over all Christian Princes for the salvation of souls and for spiritual ends, may prohibit and impede this by censures or whatever other ways he judges expedient.

Moreover, in this kingdom, in Book 8 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collectionis" — referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, the 1567 compilation of Spanish laws</note>, title 6, laws 1, 2, and 3, usury is prohibited under heavy penalties for Jews, Saracens <note>A common early modern term for Muslims</note>, and other non-believers. Note this: although it is always a mortal sin by its nature to cooperate so that usury is paid, or to approve of usury, or to directly consent

<column-break/>

to it by giving approval for it to be practiced toward others—and no dispensation for these things can be granted even by the Supreme Pontiff, as Alexander III affirms in the chapter *super eos, de usuris*, supported by manifest reason because usury is against natural law, in which the Supreme Pontiff has no power to dispense—<margin>18</margin> nevertheless, to **permit** usury, not only to non-believers but even to the faithful, to avoid greater evils and scandals which would arise if the public power tried to prevent them in some rare event, would not be a sin, but licit. This is because doing so is not consenting to the sin of usury, but permitting it to avoid greater evils or for some greater public good; for the same reason, heretics might be tolerated in some particular event.

Regarding the penalties established against public authorities who establish laws or statutes by which they grant that usury be exacted, or order it to be paid, or prohibit the recovery of what has been paid—likewise for judges who hand down a sentence that usury be paid, or that it not be restored when the borrower seeks its return—we shall see below when we discuss the penalties of usurers.

On these matters, Conrad [Summenhart] discusses extensively in *On Contracts*, question 25 and the three following; and others whom Covarruvias refers to in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 1, number 8. You may also read Driedo in *On Christian Liberty*, book 2, chapter 1; and Cajetan on the *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 78, article 1, reply to objection 3.

# On Mental Usury.
## DISPUTATION 305.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *Whether every hope and intention of obtaining some profit from a loan constitutes mental usury.*
2 *Which hope and intention constitute mental usury, and in the following number.*
3 *He is made a "mental usurer" who principally intends to obtain something beyond the principal.*
4 *The questions of confessors regarding usury, according to which rules they should be made: following number.*
5 *Whether or not the reason for the usurer's intention exists in the lender, and how it can be discerned.*
6 *Whether a lender is a usurer if he prompts the borrower to remunerate the benefit of the loan.*
7 *The chapter "consuluit, de usuris" — regarding which hope it should be understood.*

<margin>1</margin> **SO THAT** we may first clear ourselves of **mental usury** <note>original: "mentali usura" — interest that is not explicitly contracted but is expected or hoped for in the mind of the lender</note>. Having set down those things which were said about it at the end of disputation 303, the question is: whether every hope and intention of obtaining some profit from a loan constitutes mental usury.

<margin>Question</margin> Many distinguish that there are two kinds of intention for profit from a loan. One is primary and principal, the other is less principal and secondary. They call it "principal" when a person is either moved to give a loan solely for the sake of the profit he hopes for from the loan, or even if he is simultaneously moved by something else—such as goodwill toward the borrower, or to assist his necessity—he is nonetheless chiefly moved for the sake of profit; such that, if he did not hope for profit, [he would not lend].

<summary>Molina argues that biblical mentions of "usury" are often metaphors for spiritual merit and asserts that civil rulers must prohibit usury even among non-Christians, though they may "permit" it only to avoid greater social evils. He also introduces the concept of "mental usury," where the sin lies in the lender's internal expectation of profit rather than an explicit contract.</summary>
<keywords>natural law, mental usury, biblical interpretation, public authority, Jewish and Muslim subjects, Nueva Recopilación, papal authority, lending to enemies</keywords>

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on the biblical and legal definitions of lending, specifically refuting the idea that charging interest is permitted by certain scriptural passages. This page transitions into the concept of "mental usury"—the internal intention of the lender—and distinguishes between legitimate hopes for gratitude and sinful intentions for profit.</meta>

### Second Treatise. Disputation 305. 143

...would not give the loan if they did not hope for it. However, they call it "less principal" and "secondary" when, although one hopes for and intends profit from the loan, they lend primarily out of benevolence or another end, such that even if they did not hope for profit, they would still lend.

Having established this distinction, they teach that a "principal" hope and intention of profit from a loan constitutes mental usury; it is otherwise if the intention is "less principal" or "secondary." Hence, they define usury as profit from a loan where there is an express or tacit pact, or a principal intention of profit. This is the common view among the interpreters of canon law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority for the government of the Christian organization and its members.</note> regarding the chapter *Consuluit* on usury, consistent with the gloss on the words "those hoping" <note>original: "sperantes"</note>, Sylvester in the word *Usura* 1 at the beginning, and others.

Conrad, however, in his work *On Contracts*, question 29, conclusion 2, says that although intending to gain someone’s benevolence does not make the person who lends with that intention usurious; yet if he does not stop there, but directs that benevolence further toward temporal things, such that he intends a retribution beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem" — the original amount lent</note> from the borrower's benevolence, he falls into mental usury.

Johannes Medina, in *On Things Acquired through Usury*, question 1, differs little from this opinion, affirming that when profit or temporal advantage is intended as the "end" <note>the ultimate goal or purpose</note>—whether that end be the principal one or less principal, and whether it is intended to happen through the benevolence and liberality of the recipient or not—such an intention makes the lender a mental usurer. If, however, he says, profit is not intended as the *end* of the loan, but only exists as a "motive and impulsive cause" for lending—because, for instance, seeing that the borrower will be grateful, one is enticed and invited to lend out of benevolence or another honorable end, whereas if he saw the person would be ungrateful, he would be withdrawn from giving the loan—then, even if such profit is the motivating cause without which he would not lend, the hope of obtaining such profit does not make him a mental usurer.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Hence he says that the hope and gaze upon profit and advantage as the *end* of the loan—whether it be the whole end or a part, whether it be the principal or less principal end, and whether it be intended immediately or through the intervention of the borrower’s benevolence—makes the lender a mental usurer. He affirms that this is the hope that the doctors, following the chapter *Consuluit*, call "principal." But the hope of profit and advantage, not as an "end" but as a "motive and impulsive cause," he says, does not make the lender a mental usurer, even if it is such that he would not lend without it; and he says the doctors call this a "less principal" hope.

Nevertheless, I believe this dispute should be settled with two conclusions. The first is:

<margin>2</margin>
The hope and intention <note>original: "Spes, ac intentio"</note> of obtaining some profit or advantage through a loan beyond the principal, which arises from the benevolence, gratitude, and liberality of the borrower, does not make the lender a mental usurer, even if it is intended as the principal end to which the loan is directed, and even if the lender would not have lent unless he hoped for such profit or advantage. Therefore, what is received in this way is not subject to restitution <note>The legal and moral obligation to give back ill-gotten gains.</note>.

Soto affirms this in *On Justice*, book 6, question 1, article 2.

<column-break/>

Cajetan 2.2.q.88. art. 2. ad 4. and in his *Summary* under the word *Usura*, in the chapter on mental usury, and in volume 2 of his *Opuscula*, treatise 8, chapters 2 and 3. Almain in 4. dist. 15. q. 2. Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 208, and in his *Commentary on Usury* 14. q. 3. ch. 1. no. 20. And as it was expressed by Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century theologian.</note> in question 13 *On Evil*, article 4, reply 13, it matches question 2. 2. q. 78. art. 2. It can be proved: First, because as all concede, usury is not located in the fact that something is received from the gratitude and liberality of a borrower wishing to show favor for the benefit of the loan—which the borrower not only can do lawfully but is even bound to do out of a certain moral honesty—but it is only located in the fact that something is received for the loan as if it were a price. This is signified by those words in the definition of usury, "profit from a loan," as was said in the two preceding disputations. Therefore, the intention of a loan involving profit or advantage that comes from the benevolence, gratitude, and liberality of the borrower is not usury.

The consequence is manifest from the fact that an intention takes its species and nature from the "end" intended by it. Second, it is lawful by any other benefit to intend the benevolence of someone so that, moved by these benefits, they might be grateful and liberal toward the giver; at least by intending this through other benefits, there is no sin against justice, nor is any injury done to the one upon whom they are conferred. Therefore, it will similarly be lawful to intend the same through the benefit of a loan; and at least he who does this neither sins against justice nor causes injury to the borrower, as a usurer does.

Third, usury is illicit because it is "mixed involuntary" on the part of the one paying it <note>This refers to a choice made under pressure, like a merchant throwing goods overboard in a storm; the borrower pays interest not because they want to, but because they need the loan.</note>, as was explained in the preceding disputation. But he who intends some profit or advantage through a loan out of the gratitude and liberality of the borrower intends nothing "mixed involuntary." Therefore, he does not intend usury, and thus he is not a mental usurer.

From this I gather that if someone, seeing a King in need of money and hoping that he will be grateful and liberal toward the one who helps him with a loan, offers him a large sum of money—hoping for and intending Royal liberality in that way, and otherwise not intending to lend—he is neither a usurer, nor is he bound to make restitution if the King bestows something upon him beyond the principal. Whether that be an office, a commendam <note>A type of ecclesiastical benefice or property grant.</note>, or a dignity, or money, or something else: provided, however, it is sufficiently presumed that the King bestows it out of gratitude and a liberal mind (as is generally to be presumed of Kings), and provided that the one who gave the loan hopes for and intends it from Royal gratitude and liberality.

<margin>3</margin>
The second conclusion: To intend something beyond the principal, not out of the borrower's liberality, but as a price and non-gratuitous recompense for the loan, makes the lender a mental usurer—whether that intention is principal or less principal, such that he would nonetheless lend without it or for some other reason. The doctors whom we cited for the preceding conclusion agree on this.

And although Navarrus in the cited places may criticize it, if he is read attentively, it will be found that he is purely consistent with himself there. Moreover, the conclusion can be proved because usury is located in the fact that...

Molina concludes that seeking a borrower's favor or royal rewards through a loan is not usurious if the eventual reward is given freely out of gratitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 143 regarding "mental usury." Molina is specifically addressing the nuances of a lender's intent—distinguishing between a sinful expectation of profit as a "price" for a loan and a permissible hope for a gift motivated by the borrower's gratitude.</meta>

# 144 Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

...if there is profit from a loan—that is, as compensation for the loan, and not out of gratitude and liberality—then because that intention for profit (whether it is the primary or secondary motive) is directed toward such an object, it always takes on the character of the sin of usury. This is because moral acts derive their specific nature and their evil from their object. This is confirmed by the fact that when an object is evil in itself and intrinsically—as usury is—whether the intention is the primary or secondary motive makes the sin greater or lesser, but it does not make it *not* a sin. This is different from theft: whether intended primarily or secondarily, it always taints the intention; that intention makes it a sin. Since an intention to steal joined with some other primary intention does not stop the intent to steal from being a sin. Therefore, if Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> contends that profit can be lawfully intended through a loan as if from the gratitude and liberality of the borrower, while simultaneously being intended secondarily as the price of the loan, his opinion is false on both counts, as the points just mentioned clearly prove. However, if he means that it can lawfully be intended as a secondary goal from the liberality of the borrower, but as an end toward which the loan is directed (so that the borrower is moved to give liberally in the manner explained in the first conclusion), then it can be lawfully intended not only as a secondary goal, but even as a primary goal, as was shown in that same place.

Nor does Navarrus clearly seem to intend anything else (even if he does not explain himself sufficiently) than that profit can be lawfully intended partially out of the borrower's liberality. For this reason, he ought rather to have corrected Medina <note>Johannes Medina (1490–1546), a theologian who wrote extensively on restitution and usury.</note> and Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who analyzed the legality of various contracts.</note>, who deny this, rather than Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), an influential Dominican theologian at the University of Salamanca.</note>, who concedes that it can be intended as a primary goal in that way without the sin of usury.

<margin>4</margin>
Confessors <note>Priests who hear confessions and provide moral guidance.</note> ought to examine the intentions of both the giver and the receiver of a loan according to the doctrine of these two conclusions, especially in cases where such matters are being resolved. Indeed, no one can better know their own intention in hoping for and receiving something from a borrower than the lender himself, who has received something beyond the principal <note>original: "vltra sortem" — the original amount lent.</note>. Thus, if he hoped for and received it solely from the gratitude and liberality of the borrower, and is personally persuaded (removing all doubt) that the borrower gave with that same spirit, then he is neither to be condemned for the sin of usury nor compelled to make restitution—unless it later becomes clear that the borrower gave back something beyond the principal involuntarily or as a "price" for the loan. However, if he intended or accepted something as a price for the loan, he is to be condemned for the sin of usury. Furthermore, if he is in doubt about the borrower's spirit—whether he gave out of gratitude and liberality (and thus fully voluntarily) or rather involuntarily and with mixed motives, such as out of shame or fear that the loan would be denied another day—then he is to be condemned for the sin of usury. This is because he either wished to practice injustice or exposed himself to the danger of practicing it by intending to receive or by receiving something beyond the principal with the intent of keeping it. When it is not clear what the giver's spirit was, it must be judged from his character—whether he is rich or poor, liberal or stingy, or greedy—and from other circumstances. Often a confessor or any other 

<column-break/>

prudent man will be better able to judge this than the penitent or the one asking the question, especially if that person is scrupulous, lacks good judgment, or is not experienced in practical affairs. If a doubt persists in the mind of the receiver as to whether the gift was given fully voluntarily or not, he must reveal it to the one from whom it was received, until the full freedom and liberality of the giver is established, or until the giver freely waives his right to it. This applies whether the gift was accepted with doubt and sin, or in good faith and the doubt arose later.

<margin>5</margin>
An appropriate example to distinguish a usurious intention from a non-usurious one in a lender is found in the case of a Canon <note>A member of a cathedral chapter who is required to attend daily prayer services.</note> who goes to the divine office intending to receive the daily distributions <note>Payments or stipends given to clergy who were physically present at church services.</note>. For just as such a Canon is guilty of simony <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things or spiritual offices.</note> if he intends those distributions as a price for the divine office; but if he intends them not as a price, but as a debt ordered for the maintenance of the Church's ministers (which is given by the Church from what the people provide only to those present at the office, and thus becomes their due), he is not guilty of simony—even if his primary intention is to obtain what is owed to him in that way. So too, if someone who gives a loan intends something beyond the principal as a price for the loan, he is a usurer. But if he intends it on another basis—namely, from the liberality of the borrower and as a debt of gratitude and moral honesty—and it is given with that same spirit, he is not a usurer, even if he would not have given the loan unless he hoped it would be so.

<margin>6</margin>
You may ask whether a lender who prompts a borrower to remunerate the benefit of the loan—for example, by saying it is fair to reward it or that he hopes for a reward—is a usurer and bound to return what he receives if the borrower, so prompted, sends something beyond the principal. It must be said that if the lender, by that path, only intends to receive that profit from the liberality and gratitude of the borrower, and if he likely persuades the good man that the borrower, so prompted, will give beyond the principal from liberality and fully voluntarily, then he is neither a usurer nor bound to return what he received. This is the view of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> on the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 78, article 1. Nor do I think this outcome is morally impossible if the borrower is liberal and generous and other circumstances align. Although it is dangerous to prompt a borrower in that way, and confessors ought to discourage it, confessors should be instructed in this doctrine of ours and Cajetan’s so that they may be prudent and not command restitution for something that is not subject to restitution.

<margin>Decision on a Doubt</margin>
Regarding the objection from Luke 6: "Lend, hoping for nothing in return" <note>original: "Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes."</note>, and the fact that Pope Urban III defined, based on this testimony in the chapter *Consuluit* regarding usury, that when a loan was given with hope of profit and something was received, the lender is to be judged a usurer and compelled in the court of the soul <note>The "internal forum" or the realm of conscience and confession.</note> to restore what he received.

<margin>Objection</margin>

<margin>7</margin>
It must be said that if that testimony is taken as having the force of a command, it is to be understood as referring to the profit discussed in our second conclusion—namely, profit as a price—but not to what the first conclusion discusses, which is profit from the liberality and gratitude of the borrower. Urban III understood it in the same way. Indeed, he had been asked at the beginning of the chapter about that kind of hope, and he answers the question at the end.

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of "mental usury"—a situation where a lender hopes for or intends to receive extra profit from a loan without explicitly contracting for it. # Items received through mental usury: to what extent they must be restored.

## DISPUTATION 306.

## SUMMARY

1. *When a lender is bound to restore items accepted through usury.*
2. *The various ways lenders and borrowers are said to give and receive something beyond the principal.*
3. *Whether a "mental usurer" is bound to restore profit from a loan in the same way a "real usurer" is.*
4. *Another interpretation of the chapter "Consuluit" regarding usury.*

---

<margin>1</margin> Although this matter is debated by many others, we shall resolve it briefly, as it was stated under the title regarding "items accepted through mental usury" <note>Mental usury refers to the internal desire or intention to gain profit from a loan, even if no formal agreement for interest was made.</note>. While the intention to receive usury is enough to constitute the sin of usury, as long as the result does not follow, no obligation of restitution arises, as is well known. This principle is common to any other intention to receive something unjustly or to cause harm. Indeed, if an intention to receive usury preceded the act, but at the time of receiving the item the intention changes—because the lender believes it is being given out of the borrower's pure generosity and accepts it as such—then, even if it is later discovered that it was given "mixed-involuntarily" <note>A legal term for an action done with some reluctance or under pressure, but technically chosen.</note>, an obligation to restore does not arise from the act of "unjust taking," but only from the nature of the thing received. This is because, at that moment, the taking itself was not unjust.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the matter at hand, there are four ways it can happen that something is given and received beyond the principal <note>The "principal" is the original amount of the loan.</note>. The first is when the borrower gives out of pure gratitude and generosity, and the lender accepts it as something given in that manner. In this event, it is clear that neither the sin of usury occurs, nor does any obligation to restore arise.

The second is when the borrower gives it involuntarily as the "price" of the loan, and the lender accepts it in the same way. In this case, it is also clear that the sin of usury occurs on the part of the lender, and they are bound to restore what was accepted.

The third is when the borrower gives it involuntarily as the price of the loan, but the lender accepts it in good faith, believing it is being given out of gratitude and pure generosity. In that case, since such a gift is "mixed-involuntary," it is insufficient to transfer ownership by way of a donation. Since no other legal title exists by which the receiver might gain ownership or a right to the thing, they are certainly bound to restore it as soon as they realize and know it was given in that manner. However, if they consumed it while still in good faith, they are only bound to restore it if any of it remains, or if they became wealthier because of it. This is because the obligation to restore then arises not from an unjust taking (since good faith excuses the receiver from the sin of usury), but only from the fact that they possess the item.

<margin>4.</margin> The fourth way is when the borrower gives out of gratitude

<column-break/>

and generosity, but the lender accepts it with a usurious intention, as if it were a reward for the loan. Richard of Middleton <note>original: "Richardus in 4. dist. 15. art. 5. q. 5."</note> and Duns Scotus teach that when the usurer has not manifested his intention to the borrower through any external pact or other means of demanding profit, he certainly sins by accepting the profit with that intention, but he is not bound to restore it. It is otherwise when he has manifested his intention in the aforementioned way. Although they do not explain themselves fully, they seem led to assert this because, when he hasn't manifested his intention, it must be presumed that the borrower is giving it purely out of generosity.

<margin>3 Rebuttal.</margin> However, this opinion is false and goes against the chapter *Consuluit* regarding usury <note>A specific decree in Canon Law (Decretals of Gregory IX) addressing mental usury.</note>, as Domingo de Soto and Juan Medina have rightly noted. Indeed, if that opinion were accepted, one would have to affirm that a "mental usurer" is never bound to make restitution. For whenever an expression of usurious intention has preceded the act by some pact or any other means, and the acceptance of profit from the loan follows, then it is "real usury," as is clear from what was said in Disputation 305. The chapter *Consuluit*, however, defines that a *mental* usurer is bound to make restitution.

Furthermore, it is unreasonable—and contrary to what often happens in reality—to provide a general rule that whenever a lender has not expressed their usurious intention, the borrower is giving purely out of generosity if they provide something beyond the principal. This is especially true since usurers are not usually deceived in their usurious intentions; rather, the borrower regularly gives with the same mindset that the usurer presumes.

Moreover, Panormitanus and others on the cited chapter *Consuluit*, as well as Almain and many others cited by Covarruvias, hold an opposite view: namely, that whenever a person accepts anything with a usurious intention, they are bound to restore it, even if the borrower gave it generously, and even if this fact later becomes known to the usurer. They are persuaded by this for several reasons.

First, because the cited chapter *Consuluit* states that items accepted with a usurious intention are subject to restitution in the "court of conscience" <note>The internal moral judgement of a person before God, often handled in confession.</note>.

Second, because an unjust taking alone is sufficient to bind the receiver to restoration. Therefore, since he who accepts with a usurious intention accepts unjustly, it follows that he is bound to restore it.

Third, because a donation is neither completed nor is ownership of the thing transferred until it is accepted by the recipient, as explained in its proper place. But one who accepts something with a usurious intention does not accept it as a gift, but as profit from a loan. Therefore, he does not acquire ownership of it, and consequently, he is bound to restore it.

The authors of this opinion, however, do not agree on to *whom* the restoration should be made. Almain and some others think it should be given to the poor, and Thomas Cajetan agrees with this opinion—namely, that there is an obligation to restore what is accepted in this way. These authors are led to this because the borrower, by the very fact that he gave it generously, renounced his own ownership of it...

Molina argues against the more lenient view of Scotus, asserting that unjust intent taints the transaction and necessitates restitution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on "mental usury," specifically addressing whether a lender who internally intends to profit from a loan—but receives a gift that the borrower gave freely—is required to return that gift. It transitions into Disputation 307, which explores non-monetary forms of usury, such as services or personal favors.</meta>

# Louis de Molina on Contracts

can happen by the sole will of the giver, as is evident in the case of someone who leaves what was his as abandoned <note>original: *pro derelicto*; a legal term for property intentionally cast aside by an owner</note>. Therefore, if the receiver did not acquire ownership of it but is bound to restore it, it follows that restitution should be made not to the giver, but to the poor. Others, however, believe that restitution must be made to the one who gave it.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I shall express our opinion in two conclusions. The first is: as long as such a usurer is unaware that the borrower gave freely, he is bound to make restitution to him—if not from the very nature of the thing, then certainly for the sake of conscience. All agree on this. It can be proven because he believes he has received it unjustly and that the borrower gave it involuntarily, without renouncing his ownership. Therefore, he is bound under pain of mortal sin to restore it to the borrower, provided the matter is significant enough to constitute a mortal sin.

The second conclusion: As soon as he knows that the borrower gave freely, he can lawfully retain what he received with usurious intent, and he is its legitimate owner <term>dominus<gloss>the legal owner or master of a property</gloss></term>, even if he sinned in the act of receiving it. In this, Soto (Book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 4), Lope de Medina (question 4, cited), Cajetan (on 2.2, in the place cited, and under the word "usury," chapter on mental usury, and volume 2 of his *Opuscula*, treatise 8, chapter 3), Covarruvias (on the rule *Peccatum*, part 2, at the beginning, number 4), and many others whom he cites, all agree. It can be proven because the free grant of the borrower was sufficient to transfer ownership, at least when the acceptance of the one to whom it was granted was added. He seems to have had sufficient acceptance—if not formally, then certainly in effect—by the very fact that he received it, since he intended to acquire ownership of it in the best way he could. Furthermore, even if that virtual acceptance were insufficient to acquire ownership of the thing so received, there would nevertheless be another acceptance which he would elicit by the very fact that he understood it was being freely granted to him. This would be enough to establish him as the owner of that thing, because the prior gift made to him had not yet been revoked. Therefore, it would free him from the burden of restitution, as Cajetan rightly noted. Read other reasons, if you please, in Soto and others.

4. Regarding the first argument of the opposing opinion, it must be said that the chapter <note>A reference to Canon Law</note> *Consuluit* speaks of cases where it is not later established to the usurer that the borrower’s grant was free.

Regarding the second argument, it must be said that an unjust taking only obligates one to restitution when actual damage is given by it, and thus when it is simultaneously "materially" unjust <note>Material injustice refers to an actual loss of property or rights, whereas "formal" injustice refers to the sinful intent of the actor.</note>. It is not so when it is only "formally" unjust—that is, from the intention and estimation of the receiver. For then, an obligation of restitution does not arise from it except by accident—that is, because of conscience—while the erroneous conscience persists. A fitting example is found in one who, believing he is taking or destroying someone else's property, takes or destroys what was actually his own.

Regarding the third argument, it must be said that a formal acceptance of the thing occurs there, which he thinks he is receiving usuriously, and that this is, in effect, an acceptance of the same thing as a gift to himself, as has been explained. It must then be said that, at least after it is established that the thing was given to him freely, a formal acceptance of the same gifted thing occurs, and that is enough.

That point against Almainus <note>Jacques Almain (c. 1480–1515), a French theologian</note>

<column-break/>

and others must be added. If a usurious intention were enough to bind the receiver to restitution, then restitution would have to be made to the one who gave it, not to the poor. The reason is that the borrower has a presumed and, as it were, habitual will that, if he does not transfer ownership to the receiver, it remains with himself. But if he had renounced ownership, as the opponents believe (like those who hold a thing as abandoned), then it would certainly belong to the first person to occupy it; and thus, a mental usurer of this kind could lawfully retain it for himself. Additionally, the poor do not succeed except in the absence of a true owner to whom the thing can be restored, or unless human law decrees it in some event. We know of no provision of human law that commands that what is received in this manner be restored to the poor.
