# Second Treatise, Disputation 312.

the value it later had in the hands of the borrower; otherwise, the lender would suffer a loss from the benefit he provided, which does not seem consistent with reason. It must be said that even in that event, the increase in value is not owed to him. For just as he would avoid the loss of a decrease in value by reason of the <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutui"; specifically a "mutuum," a loan where the borrower returns the same amount and quality of a fungible item.</note>, so too must he bear the loss of that increase which comes to him accidentally by reason of the loan. For as we shall say below, nothing can be accepted for <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucro cessante"</note> or <term>emerging loss</term> <note>original: "damno emergente"</note> unless it has been formally or effectively included in the agreement.

<margin>
It is resolved.
</margin>
The chapters *Cum olim* and *Cum Canonici* concerning taxes agree with this conclusion of ours. In the first of these, when a certain currency had previously been accustomed to be paid, and later another of lesser value had succeeded it—which a certain Bishop had received from those who owed the former for several years, and those years were not as many as were necessary to prescribe against that Bishop—the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope, acting as the supreme legal authority in Canon Law.</note> decreed that the former currency must be paid, or as many of the later coins as would equal the former value. In the latter chapter, however, when a pension was previously paid in a certain amount of money, and later another of greater value succeeded it, and certain Canons to whom that pension was owed contended that it should be paid in a quantity equal to the number of those coins which had preceded, the Supreme Pontiff defined that it must be paid either in the former, cheaper money, or if that is no longer in use, it must be paid only according to the valuation of the former money.

Furthermore, the universal practice of the **Spains** <note>Molina refers to the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula, including Castile, Aragon, and Portugal, collectively as "The Spains."</note> confirms our conclusion. For neither in **Portugal**, nor in **Castile**, nor in any other Spanish kingdom that I know of, is there any currency today that is worth a **ducat**—that is, eleven silver **reals** and one **maravedi** in Castile, or four hundred **reais** in Portugal. This is because the old gold ducat has increased in value in the Spains (as will be explained in the section on exchange), and yet old debts of so many ducats—whether they are <term>annuities</term> <note>original: "census"; a common historical financial instrument where a person paid a sum in exchange for an annual return.</note> or any other annual rents, or whatever else—are paid according to the ancient value of the ducats. Since today there is no coin that has that exact value, it follows that in contracts and universally in paying off debts, account is taken only of the ancient value of the currencies, so that debts are paid to the equality of that value, and not according to the number of the coins themselves or the increase or decrease in value they have over time. The same conclusion is confirmed by what was said in Disputation 278.

In this same way, if by a loan or by any other contract or title a measure of wheat (for example) is owed, and afterwards the measures are changed—whether they increase or decrease—the measure of wheat must be paid in the quantity it was before the measures were changed. And in this, **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian often called Doctor Navarrus.</note> and all the doctors agree. Since the quantity owed was neither greater nor lesser than it was before that variation, that is what must be paid. This was observed in Portugal in past years and was sanctioned by public law. For when **King Sebastian** decreed that the measures of wheat, wine, oil, etc., which were unequal in different parts of his kingdom,

<column-break/>

should be reduced to equality so that the whole kingdom would use the same equal measures, he simultaneously announced in the same law that older debts and rents of grain, wine, oil, and other such things were to be paid in neither a smaller nor a larger quantity than they were paid before that change. Instead, it was to be established in each place how much wheat (for example) in the old measure would correspond to the new measures, so that it might be paid to equality; and so also for the measures of other things.

<margin>5</margin>
**The second conclusion.** Even if it were expressed in a contract of loan, or in any other, that a debt in money of a certain material and shape should be paid—for instance, that a loan should be returned in coins of the same type as those given—I believe that if they increased or decreased in value, the payment should be made to equal the ancient value in coins of that type, subtracting or adding from them as much as necessary so that the value is paid to equality. Exception is made when the contrary is understood from the words of the contract or the disposition—namely, that in any event of variation, that specific number of coins of that type must be paid, neither more nor less. This is sometimes done for fear of the variation of currencies in value. And I understand the latter part of this conclusion of ours according to what **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canon lawyer.</note> and **Covarrubias** teach in the cited passages. I am persuaded of the former part because in loans and other contracts and dispositions, the greatest consideration is given to the quantity of value; the stipulation that money of such quality be paid is usually made so that the debt is not paid in a cheaper currency that places a heavy burden on the creditor.

<margin>6</margin>
**Observe two things.** One is: although it is not <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender.</note> to give a loan with the condition that money of the same type be paid as that which is given, it is rare in practice to give a loan with the burden that the borrower be bound to return money of a better type in human estimation. For example, giving a loan in copper coins when there is a great abundance of them, with the burden that it be returned in gold or silver. That burden is perhaps unjustly imposed beyond the principal. However, if the borrower did this voluntarily out of gratitude for the benefit of the loan, or because he can easily do it by saving gold and silver coins from his income while spending the borrowed copper, no usury would occur. When, however, it is done involuntarily or with mixed will, it would be the sin of usury on the part of the lender because he gave the loan with that burden, and he would be bound to remit it before payment. But after payment, restitution would only need to be made to the borrower if he incurred any expenses in searching for that specific money or suffered some other loss. When he has reported no damage from it, I do not see that restitution must be made to him; because that burden, if there was any, seems rather to have the character of an insult than of damage given. For an insult alone without damage, restitution is not owed, as will be shown later when we discuss restitution.

The second is: if, because the borrower or any other debtor is in <term>default</term> <note>original: "in mora"; a legal delay in performing an obligation.</note> of paying the debt, the creditor incurs some loss, either because of the variation in the value of the money or other similar...

## Concerning the King's ministers; those who receive something to wait for debtors, or to pay creditors. And concerning those leasing royal revenues with a pact that the King takes some thousands of gold coins in price for debts the King owes.

### DISPUTATION 313.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *Public officials receiving a gift from debtors so that they might wait for them commit usury. And in how many ways they commit usury throughout.*
2 *To wait for payment is called a <term>loan in effect</term> <note>original: "mutuum virtute"; meaning that while not a formal loan contract, the act of delaying a debt functions economically as a loan.</note>.*
3 *Early payment is a loan in effect; and therefore usury is committed in it.*

Concerning the gifts that public officials receive, and how far they sin, or are held to restore what they have taken, it was discussed in the aforementioned Disputation 83, especially Disputation 86. Assuming those points, we will only speak in this place of what pertains to <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of making an unethical or immoral monetary profit from a loan.</note>.

<margin>1</margin>
**1** Those who receive taxes, other revenues, and generally debts owed to the King, sometimes tend to receive something so that they might wait for the debtors. This is clearly usury, subject to <term>restitution</term> <note>The legal and moral obligation to return ill-gotten gains to the original owner.</note> to the giver. For indeed, to wait for payment is a loan in effect: therefore, it is usury to receive anything for that reason. This also usually results in a loss for those to whom the King is a debtor, to whom payment should be made by these same public officials from those goods: they are therefore held to the restitution of damages incurred for that reason.

They are often unjust in many other ways to the King's creditors, to whom they are held to pay debts from the King's goods by royal decree. Sometimes they receive something so that they may make an **early payment** to them. In this, usury clearly intervenes, as Martín de Azpilcueta (Navarrus) in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 245, and the doctors commonly affirm; and this applies whether what they receive is a remission of part of the debt which the creditors leave to them, or anything else. For indeed <margin>2 3</margin> that early payment is a loan in effect; therefore, to receive anything estimable in price for that reason is usury, with the burden of restoring it to the giver. Sometimes, however, so that they do not delay a payment already due, or so that in payment they might prefer these creditors over others, they receive a part of the debt or something else, which the creditors themselves usually offer freely so that they may enjoy the money owed to them and its payment not be delayed. In both cases they commit injustice with the burden of restoring what they so receive. For it is not in their power to delay payment if they have royal goods from which to pay, or if it stands through them

<column-break/>

that they do not have them: nor is it a just title to receive something so that they do not unjustly delay payment. Likewise, if there are not enough goods for everyone to be paid immediately, it is an injustice to make "saleable" the choice of whom they should prefer in payment; they have no right to this, and it results in public detriment, as well as in a burden and prejudice to others who—because they do not grant as much or more—are placed behind others. Just as the King himself cannot for that reason receive a remission of part of the debt, and is held to restore it if he receives it for that reason: so those who pay in the King's place cannot receive it for themselves; and if they do receive it, they are held to restore it. Therefore, when there are not sufficient goods for everyone to be paid immediately, those who have a right of preference should be preferred, either because of a mortgage or for any other reason. But if no one has a right of preference, the goods should be divided in a certain proportion among the creditors, and so payment should be made to everyone in parts, so that no one is burdened. Furthermore, such ministers often (though rarely) make an agreement with a certain third party, that he should buy such debts with ready money immediately from the King's creditors at a lower price than what is owed to them, pretending that this can be done lawfully because those debts are worth less to the creditors themselves due to the difficulty and trouble of recovering them. And since, if another merchant did not buy them at the same price, he would not be condemned for injustice, because considering the circumstances of that debt in comparison to the creditor, it is not worth more. However, since in these times there are many in the city of **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olysiponensi"</note> who would gladly sell such debts for a third less than what is owed to them, sellers are easily found. And since this certain middleman knows that he will be paid immediately because the King's minister usually chooses whom to pay first, he pays them sometimes with the King's own money, and afterwards a bonus is paid to him by the King's minister, to be divided with that same minister according to the pact entered between them. Thus the capital for such unjust business grows in a wondrous way, while the King pays the debts in full, and the creditors rightly complain that because of difficult and delayed payments, they are defrauded of the money owed to them, and such public ministers and middlemen, against justice, usurp those things for themselves by that art and fraud. No one of sound mind can doubt that all these things are subject to restitution to the creditors themselves, and that the public ministers or such middlemen have no right to keep them for themselves. Likewise, such ministers are accustomed to keep the King's money occupied in their own business dealings, and for that reason delay payments; this is also usually the cause for creditors to sell those debts at a much lower price to others so they can enjoy their money. Surely, because they are the cause for payments being delayed in that way, they are held to restore to the creditors the losses that occur for that reason. Moreover, they are held to restore to the King the losses that follow for him; for because payments are not made at the proper time, everything is sold and leased to him at a higher price. By the King's command, through faithful and suitable ministers, all these things ought to be diligently investigated and severely punished, and such ministers should be compelled to restore everything.

<summary>Molina discusses the corruption of royal officials who accept bribes to expedite or delay payments, categorizing such acts as usury and demanding full restitution. He specifically highlights a fraudulent scheme in Lisbon involving middlemen who buy government debts at a discount using the King's own money.</summary>

Treatise Second. Disputation 314.

...wealth, which they had unjustly seized in the ways explained.

Another such abuse began to be introduced in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> a few years ago, rising along with greed. Merchants lease from the King a portion of the trade of the Indian ships, or something similar, for a large sum of thousands of gold coins. They do so, however, under the condition that they receive—as part of the price—five hundred or one hundred thousand gold coins in payment for the same number of thousands of gold coins that the King himself owes to others. But then, since many things are owed by the King, and cannot be paid to everyone at the established time (especially in these calamitous times), they buy such debts from many people at a third—and sometimes more than a half—less than the actual debt is worth. By this trick, when the King pays the debts in full, they themselves profit by a large portion of those debts. This is the reason why many nobles are reduced to poverty in this way. Likewise, so they do not delay the payment of the debts which the King orders to be paid by them from the remaining price owed to the King, they are accustomed to receive a pardon through certain agreements. All these things are most unjust, and the King ought to provide relief by ordering that what they have unjustly seized by this trick be returned to those to whom it was owed, by publishing a public edict so that those to whom it was owed might reclaim it, and by prohibiting in the future that the leasing of his revenues be done by paying part of the price in debts that the King himself owes to others. Let what has been said by me in this disputation not be taken as if I think all the King's ministers, or all the lessees of royal revenues, commit the aforementioned outrages: for I know that many are God-fearing and abstain from such unjust and filthy ways of profiting.

Whether, however, it is sometimes lawful to buy those debts at a lower price, the payment of which the creditor will only obtain with difficulty, will be discussed in the material on buying and selling.

## What is emergent loss and lost profit? And whether it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of emergent loss. Or whether he, who has received a loan under usury, may give a portion to another as a loan under those same usuries.

# DISPUTATION 314.

### SUMMARY.

1. What is emergent loss <note>original: "damnum emergens"</note>.
2. What is lost profit <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note>.
3. Emergent loss is twofold.
4. An agreement for paying a suitable price beyond the principal for emergent loss is licit.
5. Emergent loss is estimable in money, and for that reason something beyond the principal can be demanded without usury.
6. A borrower is not bound to pay the lender before the time because of a loss occurring to himself from the loan.
7. Whether one receiving a loan under usury can give the whole of what he received, or a part, to another as a loan under those same usuries.

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
Licit interest—the loss of which someone suffers so that he may grant a loan or something else to another, or so that he may do or omit something—is called <term>emergent loss</term> <note>original: "damnum emergens"; a loss that "emerges" directly from an action, like a repair cost incurred because money was lent away.</note> or <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; literally "ceasing gain," referring to an opportunity cost or potential profit that was missed.</note>. For if the loss of interest is in acquired goods—falsely because in the future, concerning the goods he then had, he will be compelled for that reason to spend something more than he would have otherwise spent, or if something of his goods is made worse or entirely destroyed—it is called emergent loss.

<margin>2</margin>
If, however, the loss is of interest that was to be acquired but is omitted, it is called lost profit. For that which someone newly acquires by his own industry is called profit <note>original: "lucrum"</note>; when he stops acquiring it, it is said to "cease." Let us illustrate both emergent loss and lost profit with examples. If someone has money to repair his houses and gives it as a loan, and suffers the ruin or detriment of one of the houses, this loss of the houses is called an emergent loss in his goods. Likewise, if he has money to buy wheat at harvest time for the maintenance of his family, and because he gives it as a loan he must later buy it at a much higher price, that increase which he later pays out of his goods is called emergent loss from the loan. But if he has money to trade with, and because he gives it as a loan he is prevented from acquiring the increase which he hoped for from that trade, and he does not compensate for it from elsewhere by his industry, such an increase is called lost profit: because it is not a loss in goods already acquired, but of a profit which he hoped for and which he gives up by reason of the loan.

<margin>3</margin>
In which † place, observe that lost profit can also be called emergent loss, taking the word "loss" broadly; just as not obtaining a profit which one lawfully could, and which one gives up, can by the best right be called a loss in the goods which he otherwise would have had. In this disputation we will speak only of emergent loss taken strictly; but in the two following, we will speak of lost profit, so that the discourse may be clearer.

When the loss emerges from the fact that the borrower is in delay of paying—because he clearly oversteps the term established for paying the loan—it will be discussed in the following disputation, while we examine the same regarding lost profit. Now the discourse is only concerning emergent loss from the loan up to the term destined for payment; as, for example, regarding the loss which someone suffers from the fact that he gives money as a loan for a year, which he had ready to buy wheat for his family's maintenance, or to repair houses, or something similar.

<margin>4 Conclusion</margin>
The following conclusion must be established: An agreement for a suitable price beyond the <term>principal</term> <note>original: "fortem"; the base amount of the loan.</note> for such emergent loss is licit. Soto agrees in this conclusion in Book 6 *On Justice*, Question 1, Article 3, although he says undeservedly that there is not as much certainty in it as there is in others of which the following disputation will speak. It is, however, expressed by <term>St. Thomas</term> <note>original: "D. Thom."; St. Thomas Aquinas</note> in the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 78, Article 2, in the first response, and it is the common opinion of the Doctors.

<margin>5</margin>
It can be proven, because such † emergent loss is estimable in money, and equity does not allow that the lender—beyond the benefit of the loan, by which he deprives himself of the use of his money for a time by granting it to another—should suffer that other expense in his goods for free. Therefore, he may demand...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological analysis of lending, moving from the specific abuses by Portuguese merchants to a theoretical discussion on "emergent loss" (damnum emergens) and "lost profit" (lucrum cessans) in contracts. It builds on the idea of indemnity—the right of a lender to be protected from loss caused by the act of lending.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

...to receive, beyond the principal of the loan, a competent compensation for that loss, and he can do so lawfully without any stain of usury or any other vice. This is confirmed because, as Saint Thomas <note>original: "D. Thom," referring to Thomas Aquinas in Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 78, a. 2, ad 1</note> rightly observes in the place cited, it can happen that the loss which the neighbor avoids by having that money, or the profit which he hopes for, is far greater than the loss the lender incurs by lending it. Therefore, charity and equity demand that he who has the money ready to avoid his own loss should grant it as a loan to the one who needs it more; and, in turn, the borrower should restore the loss which the lender incurred for that reason. Thus, an agreement <note>original: "pactum"</note> regarding a competent price for the loss emerging from the loan is lawful. This opinion of ours will be further strengthened by what will be said in the following disputation regarding lost profit <term>lucrum cessans: profit that one fails to make because their capital is tied up in a loan</term>.

<margin>Question 6</margin>
You will ask: What if some loss emerges for the lender from the loan before the borrower is in default <note>original: "in mora," a legal state of being late on a payment</note> of paying, yet the lender did not include a clause in the agreement that this should be paid to him? Is the borrower bound to pay? Major <note>John Major, the Scottish theologian</note>, in book 4, distinction 15, question 30, seems to affirm this, saying that although he cannot be forced to pay it in an external court, he is nevertheless bound to pay it in the court of conscience; this is because the lender incurred the loss for the borrower's sake, and the borrower was the occasion of it by seeking and receiving the loan.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The contrary, however, must undoubtedly be affirmed along with Saint Thomas, question 13 *On Evil*, article 4, reply 14; Soto, article 3, conclusion 3; and Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer</note> in his *Commentary on Usury*, question 4, number 46, who also agrees in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 211, and others. The reason is that although a borrower is tacitly bound by the contract of the loan to cover the loss that comes to the lender from the borrower's delay in paying at the appointed time (as will be said in the next disputation), he is not bound to the loss that occurs within the appointed term—and thus with no delay occurring on his part. The lender should blame himself for not being cautious and for not including that in the agreement. This can be further confirmed by the fact that perhaps the borrower would not have wanted to accept the loan with such a burden, nor would it perhaps have been expedient for him. Therefore, if the lender intended for the borrower to be held responsible for any loss that might emerge, he ought to have warned him of that fact and included it in the agreement. The same should be said, with even greater reason, regarding profit that ceases by reason of the loan <note>lost profit</note> when it was not included in the agreement.

<margin>Question 7</margin>
Connected to the loss emerging by reason of the loan, let us examine what was proposed in the last place in the title of this disputation. Namely: if someone takes a loan under usury <note>borrowing money at interest</note>, and another person asks him for a loan, can he lawfully grant him the whole or part of that loan with the same burden he himself accepted? That is, can he require the second borrower to pay a proportionate share of the interest beyond the principal that he himself was going to pay to the original lender? Almain <note>Jacques Almain</note> seems to deny this. Angelo and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias</note> affirm it along with Ancharano. Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart</note> disputes this same matter. And although he defines the matter differently, I believe a distinction must be made. For if the cause for which the first person took the loan under interest still persists—so that he does not yet

<column-break/>

regret having accepted it for that reason—the matter can be answered: it can be lawfully demanded, if you wish to grant the loan with the same burden. That is, I may say: "I will grant it to you on the condition that you are bound to pay the proportional interest beyond the principal to the usurer, which I was going to pay to him."

For in this, usury is not seen on the part of this lender, but only the act of keeping himself harmless <note>original: "indemne," meaning avoiding a loss</note> by letting another share the burden of the usurer, and by depriving himself of the loan (or part of it) despite the reason for which he took it still persisting. Therefore, it is as if he were selling the loss emerging to himself because he gave the money to the second borrower. But if the cause only partially persists, or he finds it less useful, so that he regrets having taken the loan under usury, then—according to the extent of the persisting cause and the benefit or profit of which he deprives himself by lending that money—he can pass on part of the burden of paying the usurer, but not the whole of it, according to what will be said in the next disputation regarding lost profit.

Finally, if the cause has entirely ceased—either because he does not need that money at all, or because he took the loan for a vain purpose and regrets having taken it—then it is usury to give that loan to another with that burden. This and the preceding assertion are proven together: because that money is no longer the usurer’s, but belongs to the one who took it from him as a loan. Nor, in this third case, is there any cause on his part why he could justly place that burden on the shoulders of another, or why he could lawfully "sell" it to him by shifting the burden onto him. In the first scenario, he is preserving the loan for an end that still entirely persists; in the second, he deprives himself of the same loan for an end that still partially persists, by reason of which he can only partially, and not entirely, shift the burden onto the new borrower. Therefore, it is a sin and usury to shift any of that burden in the third scenario, and in the second scenario, to shift more of the burden than is proportionate to the cause that still persists or the profit which ceases for him because of such a second loan.

L

...the judge regarding lost profit, just as regarding emergent loss, according to what seems right to the judgment of a prudent man.
<margin>6</margin> Lost profit <note>original: "Lucrum cessans," the potential profit a person misses out on because their capital is tied up elsewhere</note> can be sold by a lender as something that can be valued at a price.
<margin>7</margin> Money that is subject to a merchant’s industry is worth more than if it were in the hands of another.

<margin>12</margin> A merchant, just like a fisherman, can rightly sell the "interest" <note>original: "interesse," meaning the legal compensation for a loss or missed opportunity</note> that he hopes for from his money.

---

<margin>1</margin> The Doctors <note>Scholastic theologians and legal experts</note> whom we shall cite below, and others commonly, agree on the following conclusions. The first is: When someone gives a loan unwillingly <note>original: "inuitus"</note>, he can lawfully demand compensation for the profit ceasing for him before the term destined for payment, and he may contract for it. Indeed, if he is forced into such a loan, even if no agreement is made, the one who forces him is bound to pay that full profit to him. Examples include if someone threatens a merchant—who has money ready for trading—with death or some other serious evil unless he gives it as a loan; or if a vassal gives a loan to a King or another temporal lord because he rightly fears he will be harassed by him or suffer serious troubles unless he gives the loan. This is proven because he who gives a loan unwillingly under such an agreement truly suffers the loss of such profit unjustly; therefore, not only can he lawfully contract for it, but the one who is the cause of that injustice is bound to restore it to him, even if it was not included in the agreement. This is no different from one who steals money from a merchant which the merchant had ready for trading; he is bound to restore not only the money itself but also the profit of which he unjustly deprived him by the theft of the money. Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> agrees in *Summa Theologiae* 2. 2. question 62, article 4, in the main body and in the responses to the first and second points. Soto <note>Domingo de Soto, a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic philosopher</note> in *De Iustitia et Iure* book 6, question 1, article 3, conclusion 3, rightly adds that this holds true not only when one is unjustly forced to give a loan, but even when he is forced *justly*. For instance, if a King, at the onset of war and with the public good absolutely demanding it, should take money as a loan from unwilling merchants because he could not otherwise assist the state <note>original: "reipublicæ"</note>: for then, the merchants could contract for the lost profit and emergent loss, and the King himself, even if no agreement had intervened, would be bound to restore it to them beyond their money. Indeed, if the King were unable to pay, he would be bound to compel the other parts of the state to contribute to the payment. Since that money was taken from the merchants for the good of the state—to which all parts are bound to assist in a certain proportion—and because the urgent necessity of the state did not allow time for it to be demanded and taken from all parts then,

<column-break/>

the King took it. For if the necessity allowed time for it, it would surely be an inequity to burden certain parts of the state more than others by taking the entire sum from them alone, notwithstanding that it was taken with the intention of restoring it to them.

<margin>2</margin> The second conclusion: He who of his own accord gives a loan for a certain term or day can lawfully contract not only for emergent loss but also for lost profit, if any profit ceases for him because the borrower does not pay the loan at the prefixed term. In this, Soto agrees with the other doctors in the cited article 3; and he gives the reason: because the lender can signify to the borrower that he is unwilling for him to retain the loan beyond that term. Therefore, since he suffers the detriment of emergent loss or lost profit unwillingly beyond that term, he can lawfully demand it. Hence, some suggest that a prior agreement is necessary so that the emergent loss or lost profit from such a delay <note>original: "mora," a legal term for default or delay in performance</note> is owed to the lender. It must be said, however, that by the very fact that something is given as a loan for a certain term, the borrower is held liable for the emergent loss and the profit ceasing for the lender because payment was not made at the prefixed term. This holds even if the payment is not made through no fault of the borrower, or if he is unable to pay, or for some other similar cause, provided it does not arise from the lender's side. The reason is:
<margin>3</margin> because by the very fact that a term is prefixed for the payment of the loan, an agreement is understood to intervene—tacitly and by virtue of the act—that the borrower is held to the compensation <note>original: "interesse"</note> of which the lender is deprived by the failure of payment at 그 term. As was said in Disputation 299 when discussing loans, and as is proved by clear laws: since that obligation arises from the contract, it follows that even if the omission of payment is without legal fault on the borrower's part, he is held to such interest without waiting for a judicial sentence, as was said there. Johannes Medina <note>Juan Medina, a Spanish theologian</note> in *On things acquired through usury* question 3, and finally Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI, writing as a theologian</note> on restitution agree, because the matter of "interest" was touched upon. Also Saint Thomas, question 13 *On Evil*, article 4, response 14, and 2. 2. question 62, article 4, response 2; the Gloss on the chapter *Conquestus* under usury; Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note> in the same place and in chapter 1 under usury, number 6; and other laws which the Gloss, Panormitanus, and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Mazzolini da Prierio</note> under the word "usury" 1, question 26, and others cite. This is confirmed by the chapter *Pervenit* concerning guarantors <note>original: "fideiussoribus"</note>, where, when a guarantor pays the creditor because the principal debtor did not pay at the prefixed term, it is commanded that the principal debtor keep him entirely harmless by satisfying him, not only for what he paid for him, but also for the entire interest, the detriment of which he suffered because of that payment. The reason given there (namely, so that he does not suffer loss from where he seems to have deserved a reward) also applies when someone has lent for a term and incurs the detriment of emergent loss or lost profit because payment was not made at the prefixed term. Nor does it matter if someone objects based on the law *Si sterilis*, paragraph *cum per venditorem* in the Digest *On actions of purchase*, which states that when a seller was in delay of delivering the thing sold, he is indeed held for the interest of lost profit and emergent loss if they are intrinsic to the thing sold, but otherwise if they are extrinsic to such a thing.

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...in the contract of sale, which is most frequent in human commerce; however, the laws are clear and establish the contrary in the case of a loan <note>original: "mutuo"</note>, as was seen in the cited disputation.

<margin>4</margin>
It must be observed that when a lender, because a loan was not repaid to him at the appointed time, takes a loan under usury <note>interest-bearing debt</note> from someone else, the borrower is bound to pay the lender for the loss of that usury which he incurred because of the delay in the payment that was owed to him. Understand this not only when he was compelled by necessity to pay other debts or to provide himself with absolutely necessary things through a loan under usury, but also when he took a loan under usury for a business transaction advantageous to him, which he was going to perform with the money that was to be paid to him. However, that interest will regularly be less than the profit that would be lost to him from the money not paid at the appointed time, if he did not undertake that business which he otherwise would have; the borrower is liable for all of this because of the delay, as has been said. Therefore, taking a loan under usury for that business turns to the benefit of the borrower, who was in default <note>original: "in mora," a legal state of delay</note> in repaying the loan. 

But when he takes a loan under usury for a thing that is not necessary, or from which less profit was to be hoped for than the amount of the usury, then the borrower is not bound to restore it, except for what was reasonably taken under usury, or the lost profit resulting from the delay of payment, as the borrower prefers. Likewise, when it was believed that the borrower, if warned, would have paid the money with less expense to himself, the lender would be bound to warn him that he wished to take a loan under usury unless the loan was repaid to him—provided, however, that he could conveniently warn him. Likewise, when the lender can help himself with less loss to the borrower than by taking a loan under usury, he is bound to do so; nor will the borrower then be bound to pay him the increase that was spent more by taking a loan under usury. These same things are to be understood similarly concerning a guarantor <note>original: "fideiussore"</note>, who was either forced to take a loan under usury to pay for the principal debtor, or later took a loan under usury because the debtor was in default of paying him what he himself was forced to pay in the debtor's place. On all these points, Cajetan (on 2.2, q. 78, art. 2, ad 1), Angelus (under the word *usura*, 1, no. 19 & 20), Sylvester (in the same place, question 26), Gabriel (on book 4, dist. 15, q. 11, art. 1, note 2), and the doctors commonly agree.

<margin>Question</margin>
What the Doctors chiefly dispute in this matter of lost profit is this: Whether, because no one compels him, but he gives a loan to someone voluntarily at their request, he can lawfully contract with them for the profit that for that reason is lost to him within the term for which the loan is requested and granted, and before the borrower is in default of paying it. For example, if someone has a certain amount of money destined for business this year, from which he hopes for a profit of one hundred gold coins, and another asks for it as a loan to be repaid after a year, can the lender then contract so that the borrower, beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem," the original sum</note>, gives back to him as much as that profit is estimated to be while it is still in hope, according to those things which must be said in the following disputation? A similar example is if someone has

<column-break/>

money ready for buying annual rents <note>original: "annuos redditus," similar to an annuity or investment in land revenue</note>, and another asks for it as a loan and prevents him from buying them; can he contract with him for the profit of those annual rents which is lost to him because of the loan, according to how much it will be estimated based on the probability of finding them and other concurrent circumstances?

Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV</note> (final chapter on usury) denies that it is right in these events to contract for lost profit, and affirms that it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of it. St. Thomas seems to suggest the same opinion (q. 13 *On Evil*, art. 4, ad 14, and 2.2, q. 78, art. 2, ad 1) where, while conceding that a lender can lawfully contract for a loss emerging from the loan <note>original: "damno emergente"</note>, he adds that one cannot contract for lost profit. He gives the reason that he does not yet have it, and it can be hindered in many ways; and that which is of such a nature, he says, cannot be sold. Soto (Book 6 *On Justice*, q. 1, art. 3, conclusion 4) strongly inclines toward the opinion of Innocent, although he does not dare to reject the contrary opinion, which is more common among the doctors.

It is argued, first: that for profit to "cease" <note>to be lost</note> is nothing other than for the lender to be restrained from profit; but when someone gives a loan of his own accord, he cannot be said to be restrained from profit; therefore he can receive nothing for profit which properly and truly does not cease for him.

Second, because by the contrary opinion a great door is opened to usury; for anyone will easily pretend that profit is lost to him because of the loan, and under that cloak, as it were, will receive something beyond the principal. And this second argument moved Innocent to embrace that opinion.

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
The contrary opinion, however, is the common one of the doctors, and is undoubtedly to be embraced by us: namely, that in similar events, a lender can lawfully contract for lost profit <note>original: "lucro cessante"</note>, just as for emergent loss <note>original: "damno emergente"</note>, and receive beyond the principal as much as shall be estimated by the judgment of a prudent man, according to those things to be said in the following disputation. Thus affirm Conrad (on contracts, q. 30), Cajetan (2.2, q. 78, art. 2, ad 1), Major (on book 4, dist. 15, q. 30), Gabriel (ibid, q. 11, art. 1, note 2), Almain (ibid, q. 2), Juan Medina (on things acquired through usury, q. 3, cause 2), Adrian (on restitution, the question "because it was done regarding interest"), Angelus (under *usura*, 1, no. 15), Sylvester (ibid, q. 19), Navarro (in his Manual, ch. 17, no. 211, and in his Commentary on Usury, 14th question, 4, no. 47), Covarruvias (3 *Various Resolutions*, ch. 4, no. 5), Scotus (on book 4, dist. 15, q. 2), Panormitanus, and others whom Covarruvias and others cite. 

Moreover, it can be proved: first, because profit lost by reason of a loan is no less estimable in money than loss emerging from a loan. For a prudent merchant, who has some money ready for business from which he hopes to gain one hundred, will not estimate that profit so hoped for as less than suffering a loss of twenty with equal probability—indeed, far more. Therefore, just as it is right for him to contract for that emerging loss and receive something beyond the principal by reason of it, so it will be lawful for the same person to contract in a similar way for lost profit.

Nor is the response of Soto sufficient—namely, that lost profit depends on the lender's industry, while emergent loss is a mere suffering <note>an external event happening to the person</note>. In the first place...

While some early authorities like Pope Innocent IV viewed this as usury, Molina aligns with the "common opinion" of modern scholars, arguing that potential profit has real economic value and can be lawfully contracted for if reasonably estimated.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 315

...since it depends on the lender's industry <note>Skillful application to business or trade</note> to avoid an emerging loss <note>original: "damnum emergens"</note>—for instance, by repairing houses with the money he lends, or by buying wheat with it when he expects the price to rise—just as it depends on that same industry whether he loses a profit by lending. Furthermore, one undergoes an emerging loss as voluntarily as one loses a potential profit; however, the response of Soto assumes the opposite as the foundation upon which he relies, as will be manifest to anyone examining Soto’s words. Secondly, our assertion is proved because when someone lends involuntarily, and for that reason loses a profit, he can either lawfully contract for that lost profit <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note> and receive something beyond the principal <note>original: "vltra sortem"</note> solely by reason of the injury done to him by being forced to lend, and consequently being forced to be deprived of profit; or also because lost profit is something estimable in money, and therefore he can lawfully receive something by reason of it. If Soto grants the first point, he then wrongly adds that if the King, upon the outbreak of war and the demands of the public good, lawfully takes a loan from unwilling merchants, the merchants can then lawfully contract for the lost profit and receive a competent estimation beyond the principal: for in that case, no injury is done to them.

<margin>6</margin> If, however, he grants the second point, then lost profit can be sold by the lender as something estimable in price, even if he is not forced to lend.

<margin>7</margin> Thirdly, although money in itself is not worth more than its face value, yet when it is subject to the industry of a merchant who has destined it for trade and hopes for profit from it, it is worth more to him. For this reason, if someone 
<margin>8</margin> † unjustly takes it from a merchant, he is bound to compensate him for the lost profit, as St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, 2. 2. q. 62. ar. 4. ad 2.</note> asserts. This is because he has not only caused him loss in the money itself, but also in the profit he hoped for from it: therefore, a lender can lawfully receive a price beyond the principal for lost profit. The logic is clear. This is both because he suffers a loss beyond the principal of that profit for the benefit of the borrower, so that he may help him through the loan, and also because everyone concedes that when a thing being sold was worth more to the seller than to others, the seller can receive a price beyond the common market price equal to how much more it was worth to him, even 
<margin>9</margin> if it is worth less to the buyer. Fourthly, if someone † asks a laborer not to hire out his services to others but to accompany him for some recreation, the laborer can lawfully demand from him the price of the profit lost by omitting to hire out his services. If someone 
<margin>10</margin> likewise † asks to borrow a craftsman’s tools, and this causes the craftsman to stop working and his profit from his labor and industry to cease, he can surely lawfully demand not only the value of the use of the tools, but also, in addition, as much as he 
<margin>11</margin> was going to earn through his labor and industry. Therefore, † by the same reasoning, a merchant who had money destined for trading—and hoped for a certain profit from it as if from a tool subject to his industry—will be able to lawfully demand the estimation of the profit lost to him because he gives it as a loan to the one requesting it.

<margin>12</margin> Fifthly, a fisherman can lawfully sell the fish he hopes to catch in a cast of the net, as is established in the law "si iactum" <note>A reference to Roman Law regarding the sale of an "expectation" or a "chance" (emptio spei).</note>. Therefore, † by the same reasoning, a merchant can sell to a borrower the "interest" <note>The difference between his current state and where he would have been (inter-esse).</note> which he hopes for from the money he had destined for trade. Such a contract is of the "innominate" type <note>A category of contracts in Roman law that do not have a specific name but are binding based on mutual performance.</note>: "I will do—or rather, I will desist from—this

<column-break/>

trade for your benefit, if you give me a certain amount to desist." Just as a fisherman can not only sell the uncertain fish he hopes to catch in a cast of the net, but can also be paid to desist from casting the net for the sake of someone who requests it of him. Other arguments not to be despised may be read in Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer.</note> in the commentary cited at number 49.

To Soto's first argument, the premise must be denied. For it is not of the nature of lost profit that it must be involuntary on the part of the one losing it—as if, in order for a price to be lawfully demanded and received for it, it were necessary for the lender to be forced to suffer it. For even if he suffers it of his own accord, either by lending at the request of the borrower, or even sometimes by offering it to him out of charity—because he sees that a far greater benefit will come to the borrower from that loan than the profit he himself loses and the price the borrower will pay for it—it does not therefore cease to retain the character of lost profit, nor to be estimable in price, as has been shown at length.

To the second, it must be said first of all that the truth should not be hidden because some people, by their own fault, wish to use it as a cloak to hide their crimes, pretending that profit is ceasing for them when in reality none is. It must be said next that this argument only proves that confessors and those consulted on matters of conscience ought to be cautious. According to what will be said in the following disputation, they must diligently examine whether profit truly would have ceased or not, and to what extent, lest usury be practiced under such a cloak. Likewise, it proves that public authorities ought to be cautious so that, when they understand that profit did not cease (or not as much as those receiving more than the principal claim), they do not fail to pronounce the contracts usurious and punish the men who celebrated them as usurers. It also proves that when it is not openly clear that profit is lost, or not as much as is claimed, such contracts should be discouraged before they are made. These points, however, do not take away from the fact that it is most expedient for the truth in this matter to be known and manifested—both so that those who lawfully made such contracts and justly received the price of true lost profit are not condemned for sin or ordered to make restitution, and also so that just contracts that are beneficial to both parties are neither prohibited nor condemned.

As for St. Thomas, in the two places cited earlier, he does not oppose this common opinion of the doctors. For † hope for profit is 
<margin>13</margin> twofold. One kind is in "proximate potential," because the money was already destined for trade, and the trade is hindered by the loan and not compensated for elsewhere. The other is in "remote potential," namely, when the money or other thing given in a loan was not destined for trade, but could have been destined; and then, if it were given as a loan, it would happen that the profit which *could* have come from such trade was hindered. In those two cited places, St. Thomas is speaking of lost profit that was in hope in this latter [remote] way, which therefore could have been hindered in many ways, or rather...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 315 regarding the conditions under which a lender may justly charge a fee for a loan based on the profit they lose by not using that money for their own business—a concept known as "lucrum cessans" (lost profit).</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

### When and to what extent profit is to be considered lost.

#### DISPUTATION 316.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *What is required for profit to be considered lost.*
2 *Profit merely in potential is not considered lost unless it would have been realized in action.*
3 *Profit from a loan does not "cease" if the loaned money was not destined for trade.*
4 *What constitutes "lost profit" that a lender can lawfully sell to a borrower.*
5 *Lost profit can be claimed from a loan, even if the money is drawn from a larger pool destined for trade.*
6 *How lost profit should be estimated within the limits of justice.*
7 *Profit in hope should not be valued the same as profit in hand.*
8 *Lost profit can be included in a contract in two ways.*
9 *Losses of property are estimated in the same way as lost profit.*
10 *What conditions must be observed so that a price for lost profit can be accepted without it being considered usury.*

---

<margin>1</margin>
For profit to be said to "cease" <note>original: "lucrum cessare"; this refers to the business profit a lender gives up by lending their capital to another</note> by reason of a loan, and therefore for a just price to be received on that account, it is first required that the profit truly be hindered by the loan itself and not compensated for from another source. To the extent that it is compensated elsewhere, it is not considered to be "lost," and therefore a price cannot be lawfully accepted in proportion to that which is not actually lost.

<margin>2</margin>
From this it follows that if the profit exists only in hope or remote potential—in the manner explained at the end of the previous disputation—specifically because the money or other thing given in the loan was not already destined or decreed for trade, then no profit is considered lost. This remains true even if the money *could* be so destined in the future or might have been applied to trade had it not been loaned. Such profit is so uncertain, and in such a remote state of potential and hope, that it does not provide a grounds for lawfully accepting a price. This was excellently taught by St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> in the passages cited in the previous disputation, and other Doctors <note>learned theologians and legal scholars</note> agree. Likewise, if the money given in the loan was indeed destined for trade, but not so firmly or certainly that it might not have ended up otherwise, something must be deducted from the value of the "lost profit." This deduction depends on how likely it was that the money would not have been applied to trade—perhaps because an opportunity for the intended trade might not arise, or because it could be hindered in various other ways. For the more uncertain a profit is, the less it is worth,

<column-break/>

regardless of where that uncertainty originates.

<margin>3</margin>
It also follows that if the money was indeed destined for trade, yet the lender gives it as a loan without the trade and profit being diminished—perhaps because he uses other funds he had intended to save, or borrows money from others, or finds support elsewhere so that he has the same profit at the time the loan is repaid as he would have had if he hadn't lent it—then no profit has "ceased" for him. Consequently, he cannot lawfully receive any price for it. However, if only a *portion* of his profit is lost because of the loan, while the rest is compensated for in the ways described, he may lawfully receive a price for that specific part which truly ceased due to the loan, but not for the part that did not. Furthermore, if he completely stops trading because of the loan, but compensates for all or part of the profit he hoped for through his office or some other industry <note>personal work or business activity</note>—which he would not have undertaken if he had continued his trade—then his lost profit from the loan is reduced by the amount he gained through that other industry. In such a case, it would be a sin for him to accept a price for the portion already compensated. If, however, this other industry is more troublesome and laborious, he may lawfully accept some increase in price as a consideration for the fact that, for the borrower’s sake, he gave up a less laborious trade to engage in a more difficult one. Merchants who claim they are losing profit because of a loan and therefore contract to receive something beyond the principal <note>original: "vltra sortem"; the initial amount lent</note> must be carefully examined according to these principles. It will often be found that either no profit is lost to them, or not as much as they claim, if they are judged by how much profit actually ceased because of the loan.

The same must be observed regarding those who effectively give a loan by selling on credit. They often claim they have lawfully sold on credit for a price higher than the "rigorous" price <note>the highest end of the fair market value for an immediate cash sale</note> of the item. They argue that as merchants, they always have their money exposed to trade, and they lose much more profit because they are not paid immediately than the small amount they add to the price for selling on credit. There are some who, led by this reasoning, wrongly permit this. Yet, in truth, it is usury <note>the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender</note>, because no profit truly ceases for them, and thus they have no just title to demand that increase. If the matter is examined closely: if these men only sold for immediate cash, they certainly would not have sold as many goods by the end of the year as they do by selling on credit, because they would find far fewer buyers. Nor does selling on credit to many people prevent them from selling for immediate cash to anyone who wishes to buy that way. Thus, by selling on credit, they lose no profit they would have had by only trading in cash. Rather, their profit increases, provided they sell on credit within the limits of a just price to those who lack present money; for they sell to these people in addition to the others, whereas they would not have sold to them at all if they did not offer credit.

<summary>Molina argues that a lender can only charge for "lost profit" if they truly lose a business opportunity because of the loan. He critiques merchants who use "lost profit" as a pretext for usury, particularly when selling goods on credit.</summary>
<keywords>lost profit, lucrum cessans, usury, just price, credit sales, lending, contracts, Roman Catholic moral theology, Scholastic economics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 317, focusing on the specific conditions and ethical boundaries for determining "lost profit" (lucrum cessans) when a lender provides a loan. It addresses whether a lender can claim compensation for profit they might have made if they had invested the money themselves.</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 317. Page 165

<margin>4</margin> to sell to them. In this place, observe that the **lost profit** <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note> which one can lawfully sell to a borrower is that which, for that reason, ceases to come to him from others, because he wishes to give the money to the borrower either formally or effectively as a loan. However, if profit ceases for him regarding the borrower because he would have preferred to buy with cash immediately—thereby having a greater supply of money with which he could trade and profit with others—this is not truly "lost profit." That is to say, the profit does not cease because he would have had it elsewhere were it not for the loan; rather, it is simply that he does not obtain as much or as high a quality of profit from the borrower as he would like if the borrower had paid in cash instead of buying on credit. Therefore, he cannot lawfully sell to the borrower on the grounds that the borrower "owes" him profit, or because the borrower does not give him immediate money for his goods (which he could then use to profit with others). He can only sell the profit that truly ceases for the lender regarding his own affairs with *other* people—people who were ready to buy those goods—because he chose to give the goods to this borrower on credit, setting aside and postponing those other opportunities.

<margin>5</margin> The question arises: what if someone, possessing many thousands of gold coins, had destined only four thousand for trade, from which he hoped for five hundred coins in profit, and another person asks him for a loan of either a part of those or the entire four thousand? Can the lender accept the valuation of that lost profit, provided he does not wish to replace that trade with his other gold coins, but abandons the trade because of that loan and does not compensate for that profit from elsewhere? It must be answered—along with **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 212—in the affirmative. For truly, that profit ceases for him because of such a loan; he can prudently reserve his other money for other necessities or choose not to expose it to trade, just as he had previously and lawfully decreed not to expose it. Even if he does this out of greed or faint-heartedness, it remains within the limits of justice. By the very fact that he does not wish to expose his other money to trade, that profit truly ceases for him because of the loan; he can, therefore, lawfully seek and receive compensation for it.

<margin>6</margin> It is a great sin <note>original: "nefas"</note> to receive more for **lost profit** than it is worth according to the judgment of prudent men, after considering all concurrent circumstances, as is very well known. If he accepts anything beyond a strict just price, then if you look at it in terms of the loan itself (the reason for the payment), it is **usury**; if you look at it in terms of the "interest" <note>original: "interesse"; legal compensation for loss</note> of the lost profit being sold, although it may not be usury under that heading, it is still an unjust sale and an excessive, unjust price. On both counts, however, he is liable for **restitution** <note>the obligation to return the ill-gotten gain</note> in the court of conscience in a similar way. If the lender, in the business or the opportunity for business from which he desists due to the loan, was going to incur greater expenses than he does by desisting from that business, that increase in expenses must be deducted from the lost profit. Indeed, all expenses that were to be made in that trade must be calculated along with the capital, and only the remainder—what is left over and above the expenses and the capital—is called profit. Furthermore, if the capital in that business was subject to any risk, such as maritime navigation or something similar, or because it could happen that by intending to profit, not only would no profit be gained, but even some of the capital

<column-break/>

might be lost, then something must be deducted from the estimation of the profit that was hoped for and which ceases due to the loan. This deduction should be more or less, according to whether the risk was greater or smaller, regardless of what **Soto** <note>Dominic de Soto (1494–1560), a Dominican theologian</note> says to the contrary in Article 3, cited above. For the labor as well, which the lender was going to undergo by trading, the learned doctors say that something should be deducted from the estimation of the lost profit. However, **Soto** correctly observes (where mentioned above) that this is not universally true. For someone might rightly—especially if he had no other way to seek a living—prefer to expend his labor rather than lose any of the profit he hoped for for the sake of leisure. From this it happens that a hired laborer, who is asked to cease from labor to give attention to an honest recreation, can justly demand the full price he would have earned by working to satisfy the one asking; for he is entirely free to prefer acquiring the full price with labor rather than losing any of it by ceasing from labor.

From this it is now clear that the doctrine of **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent commentator on Aquinas</note> (on the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 78, Article 2, response to the first objection) is true, which others commonly approve. Namely, that <margin>7</margin> it is a sin to accept as much in price for lost profit as the profit that was probably hoped for. For besides the reasons already mentioned for which something must be deducted, there is also this other reason: the profit itself exists only in "hope." Something in hope is worth less than if it were already a "thing" <note>original: "in re"; in reality</note>, by as much as that hope can be frustrated and such profit can be diminished. Therefore, by the judgment of a prudent man, considering the recurring circumstances, it must be judged how much it is worth. Its just price does not consist in an indivisible point but will have a certain range <note>original: "latitudinem"; a margin of error or flexibility</note>, just as the prices of other things usually have. And just as when someone destroys another's potential crops <note>original: "fata"; likely referring to 'foetus' or future fruits</note>, he is not bound to restore to him as much as he hoped for from them (after deducting expenses), but as much as those potential crops are valued by the judgment of a prudent person—weighing the greater or lesser distance of the fruits from the reality, and weighing the risks to which they were subject, along with other concurrent circumstances—so the matter stands regarding the value of lost profit.

**Johannes Medina** <note>Juan Medina (1490–1546), a Spanish theologian</note>, in his work *On things acquired through usury*, Question 3 and the last, correctly <margin>8</margin> observes that **lost profit** can be brought into a contract in two ways. One way is so that, just as it is uncertain how much the profit will be, so the price is uncertain and dependent on what the outcome of the matter proves to be in another similar venture (after deducting expenses and other things that must be deducted according to what has been said so far). For example, if someone has a thousand gold coins destined for trade and gives five hundred of them as a loan with the agreement that the borrower will give him as much for the lost profit as he gained with the other five hundred coins—after deducting any greater expenses he would have had trading with a thousand coins rather than only five hundred, and subtracting something for the risk to the capital, if it was exposed to any risk in trade. Or, including in the contract that if he gained nothing with the other five hundred gold coins but lost some of them, the borrower should restore no profit and even retain as much for himself from the five hundred coins. Or, if he gives the entire thousand gold coins as a loan with the agreement that the borrower will pay as much as it is found that some other person gained in a similar trade with another thousand coins, after deducting the expen...

<summary>This page discusses the ethical and legal limits of charging a borrower for "lost profit." It emphasizes that such a charge must be based on a realistic, prudent estimation that accounts for business risks and labor costs, rather than charging the maximum potential profit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "lost profit" (lucrum cessans) from the previous page, specifically regarding how to estimate its value in a loan agreement. It then transitions into Disputation 317, which investigates the legality of late-payment penalties in loan contracts.</meta>

<margin>9</margin>
In these cases, one may restore or retain something from the capital if the other party has lost any portion of that capital. This type of contract is licit because equality is maintained; the uncertainty regarding the **lost profit** <note>original: "lucro cessante"; this refers to profit a lender misses out on because their money is tied up in a loan</note> is reflected in the price. This is approved by Angelo <note>Angelo da Chivasso, a 15th-century canon lawyer</note> under the entry for "usury," and by Gabriel <note>Gabriel Biel, a late scholastic philosopher</note>. This is not unlike a contract where someone who has destroyed another’s crops agrees to restore as much as is found to have been harvested by a neighbor from a similar field, minus expenses. In another way, lost profit can be included in an agreement so that an amount is paid for it based on its current estimated value while it is still a "hope" of profit, regardless of whether the actual outcome later proves to be more, less, or nothing at all. Regarding lost profit estimated in this way, what Cardinal Cajetan says is true, and the doctors of law commonly speak of it. In this same way, it is customary to estimate damages to things that were still only "in hope," such as when crops are destroyed or money is stolen from a merchant.

<margin>10</margin>
Leaving aside other conditions that Conradus <note>Conradus Summenhart</note> and others require for a price to be accepted for lost profit without it being considered **usury** <note>the practice of charging unethical or illegal interest on a loan</note>—conditions which are clearly not all necessary based on what was said above—they also add this condition, which Johannes Medina admits: namely, that the price for the lost profit should not be taken immediately at the time the loan is handed over, but later, when the loan is to be repaid. However, for this to be true, it must be understood that if such a price is deducted immediately, the "lost profit" is technically reduced, and if the price is not adjusted for the fact that less profit is now "ceasing," the lender would receive more than the actual lost profit. For example: if you give me a loan of five hundred gold coins out of a thousand you had intended for trade, and the lost profit is estimated at thirty, but you take those thirty at the moment you give the loan, you are actually only handing over four hundred and seventy to me. Because you have kept some back, you lose less profit than the full thirty; therefore, you should not receive the full thirty but should subtract a portion relative to the money you are still able to trade with yourself.

# Whether a Contractual Agreement for a Penalty is Usurious if the Borrower Fails to Pay on Time.

## DISPUTATION 317.

### SUMMARY.

*1. The various types of penalties.*
*2. Contracting parties may establish penalties and bind themselves to them.*
*3. How a conventional penalty differs from a legal or judicial one.*
*4. A moderate penalty may be set for a borrower if they do not pay by the fixed deadline.*
*5. The conditions that must be observed so that a penalty in a loan contract can be justly established and exacted.*

**H**aving examined whether a lender may licitly receive anything from a borrower by reason of lost profit or **emergent loss** <note>original: "damni emergentis"; actual financial loss incurred by the lender because of the loan</note>, let us now consider whether it is licit to agree that, if the loan is not restored by the fixed deadline, the borrower shall pay something extra as a penalty.

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
Regarding the matter at hand, a penalty is usually distinguished as being of three types: legal, judicial, and conventional. A **legal penalty** is one imposed by a law or statute. For example, if there is a law in a city stating that a guardian is required to use a minor's money to buy property or engage in licit trade from which profit is hoped—and if they fail to do so through their own fault, they are compelled to pay five percent to the minor; such a penalty is "legal" because it is set by law. A **judicial penalty** is one a judge imposes if something is not done or paid within a certain time. For instance, if a borrower is summoned before a judge when the payment is due, and the borrower confesses the debt, the judge may order that it be paid within a certain time under a specific penalty. A **conventional penalty** is one established by an agreement or covenant by the consent of the parties, to be applied if the contract is not upheld or if payment is not made within a certain time.

<margin>2</margin>
This being established, no one doubts that it is right to establish not only legal or judicial penalties against a delayed debtor—who by their own fault and against the creditor's will fails to pay at the fixed time—but also a conventional one. This is provided the penalty is reasonable and moderate relative to the amount to be restored and the degree of fault involved. Indeed, if it were immoderate or irrational, it would be unjust by that very fact and would not be binding. Although the contracting parties do not possess public power (which would allow them to establish just penalties by public authority as legislators and judges do), because the practice is inherently fair and useful, the disposition of the law grants them the right to establish these penalties by mutual consent and to bind themselves to them, just as they do for other contents of the same contracts. This is evident from various laws <note>Molina cites specific sections of the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman law, such as the Code and the Digest</note>, provided that custom is observed.

<margin>3</margin>
Because a conventional penalty is owed based on the contract, a distinction is made between it and legal or judicial penalties. Legal and judicial penalties are generally not owed until a sentence is passed; however, a conventional penalty, looking at the nature of the matter alone, is owed without waiting for a sentence, as was argued in Disputation 97 with Covarruvias and Navarro.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding legal and judicial penalties, as it pertains to the present matter, I only wish to warn about the example given concerning guardians: it is a sin to hand over the money of wards for usury. Since usury is illicit by natural law, it is never licit to practice it, no matter how pious the cause. To what extent guardians and curators are bound by common law and the law of Portugal to use a minor’s money to buy property or annual rents, or to trade with it, was discussed in Disputation 224. Most of what could be said here about conventional penalties was explained in Disputation 97. As for what specifically belongs to this disputation, the Doctors of Law agree that a moderate penalty can be set for a **borrower** <note>original: "mutuario"</note> if they do not pay by the fixed deadline. This is the view of Duns Scotus, Gabriel Biel, John Major, Jacques Almain, Conradus Summenhart, Johannes Medina, Navarro, and Angelo.
