<meta>This page continues the discussion on penalties for late payments in loan contracts, specifically focusing on the conditions required for such penalties to be considered morally licit and not usurious. It then transitions into Disputation 318, which examines whether a lender can charge extra if they take on the physical risk of the goods or money being transported.</meta>

Tractate Two, Disputation 318. Page 167

...usury. See number 31. Sylvester <note>Sylvester Mazzolini da Prierio, an influential 16th-century theologian</note> in the same place, question 28, and others. Nevertheless, they establish several 
<margin>5</margin> conditions so that such a penalty can be imposed and demanded justly, without the vice of usury.

The first condition is that it must not be imposed in fraud of usury. This means that the loan should not be given specifically because of the penalty—viewing it as a type of profit expected from the loan. Rather, it should be imposed either because it is in the lender's interest for the loan to be repaid by the fixed time, or because the lender simply wishes to have what is owed to him at that term, whether it truly matters if he has it then or not. For by the very fact that a borrower detains the money beyond the fixed term against the lender's will, he commits an injury against the lender and falls into fault; therefore, a moderate penalty can be established by mutual consent, which the borrower pays because of that fault. According to this doctrine, it must be examined in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal moral judgment of the individual before God</note> whether the penalty was imposed in fraud of usury or not. However, I do not agree with Navarrus, Conradus, and certain others who argue in the cited places that usury exists simply because someone lent to a person they knew would fail to pay on time through their own fault, or because the lender secretly hopes the borrower misses the deadline so the penalty applies. Although it must be admitted that these are strong signs that the penalty was intended as a fraudulent way to gain profit from a loan—and such intentions are joined with the sin of greed and a sin against charity toward one's neighbor (since it is not lawful to hope for a neighbor’s fault for one's own gain)—nevertheless, these intentions do not contain inherent injustice. Therefore, they do not constitute the sin of usury, nor do they obligate the lender to restore the penalty money they received. Nevertheless, a law would be just and holy if, to avoid these and other evils, it altogether prohibited receiving such a penalty from a borrower. Regarding the **Portuguese law** <note>original: "lege Lusitana"; likely referring to the strict anti-usury statutes in the Portuguese *Ordenações*</note> on this matter, we spoke in Disputation 97; we judged that it is founded on a presumption of usury and does not hold force in the court of conscience when usury is not truly present.

The second condition they add is that no scandal should arise from the imposition and demand of such a penalty. This, however, does not pertain to avoiding the sin of usury or injustice, but rather to avoiding the sin of scandal against charity toward one's neighbor.

The third condition is that there must truly be fault on the part of the borrower. For if he does not pay at the fixed term through no fault of his own—either because he was unable to, or for some other just cause—then nothing can be lawfully taken from him as a penalty. This is because a penalty presupposes and requires a fault. This is agreed upon in the canon *Significante*, under the title "On Pledges," and elsewhere. Conradus, Medina, Navarrus, and others in the cited places affirm this. However, the matter is quite different when something is owed by virtue of a contract due to **lost profit** <note>original: "lucri cessantis"</note> or **emerging loss** <note>original: "damnis emergentis"</note>, as was said in Disputation 314. Observe here that, in my judgment (whatever others may say), if a borrower has made himself unable to pay by the fixed term through his own fault—either by squandering his goods or by some other reason he could have avoided and should have looked out for—he is truly in fault if he does not pay at the term, and thus remains subject to the penalty.

The fourth condition is that if he pays part of the debt, the entire penalty should not be demanded, but only a part in propor-

<column-break/>

tion to the part that remains to be paid. This applies unless the obligation is indivisible, according to the sense explained in Disputation 97; for then the entire penalty would be owed, as was said there. The canon *Suam*, "On Penalties," agrees with this condition.

# Whether it is usury to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of the risk to the thing lent, which the lender undergoes.

## DISPUTATION CCCXVIII.

### *SUMMARY*

<margin>1</margin> 1. *It is usury to refuse to lend unless the lender retains the risk of the thing, so that the lender may receive something beyond the principal from the borrower.*
2. *Limit this, however, as in number 2.*
3. *If an insurance contract is not demanded as a condition without which the lender will not lend, but the borrower enters into it of his own accord, no usury occurs in it.*
4. *If a lender, for the risk he has taken upon himself, receives no more than a just price, he is not bound to restore any of that price.*
5. *The true and more common understanding of the chapter "Naviganti" regarding usury.*

<margin>I</margin> An example of the proposed question is if someone, formally or in effect, lends one hundred to someone to be transported by sea or through other dangerous places, and takes upon himself the risk of that money until it arrives in the Indies or another place where it is sent. Is it usury to demand and receive something beyond the **principal** <note>original: "sortem"</note> by reason of the risk he undertakes? For if the money perishes before it arrives at its destination, it is lost to the lender and not the borrower. This contract is frequent in **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olyssipone"</note> and other similar places. On this matter, let this be the first conclusion: It is regularly unlawful and usurious to be unwilling to lend except on the condition that the risk of the thing lent remains with the lender, so that for that reason he may receive something beyond the principal from the borrower—even if it is only a just price that would be judged fair by a prudent person for taking on such a risk. On this, the Doctors commonly agree: Conradus, *On Contracts*, question 39; Cajetan on the *Secunda Secundae*, question 78, article 2; Joannes Medina; Covarruvias; Navarrus; Soto; and others. The reason is that the burden imposed on the borrower—to celebrate a **contract of insurance** <note>original: "contractum assecurationis"</note> with the lender regarding the thing he receives as a loan, and to pay him a price (even a just one) for the risk undertaken—is certainly a cost that can be valued in money. It is no less a burden than requiring someone to grind at the lender's mill, or other burdens discussed in Disputations 309 and 310. Indeed, it is far greater; for in some of those cases, only the burden is imposed that the borrower do at the lender's mill for the same price what he would have done elsewhere anyway.

# Luis de Molina
## On Contracts

<columns>
...the lender’s [risk], but in the matter we are discussing, a burden is imposed on the borrower to absolutely enter into an insurance contract and pay its price, something he might have otherwise chosen not to do, either with this lender or any other. Therefore, just as imposing those other burdens on a borrower is considered usury <note>charging interest on a loan, which was traditionally forbidden by the Church</note>—as shown in the cited disputations—so too it will be illicit and usurious to impose this specific burden on him. Regarding those other outcomes, we noted that Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI, a noted theologian before his papacy</note> holds a unique view; so too in the matter of restitution in the question beginning "Occurrunt circa prius," etc., he is unique on this point. He claims that the lender practices neither usury nor anything illicit because he asks for no more than a just price in exchange for the risk he undertakes. However, Adrian does not account for the fact that while that insurance contract might be just in itself, it is unjust to obligate the borrower to enter into it by reason of the loan. This is because taking on such an obligation is a burden that can be valued in money, as we stated regarding those other cases in the cited locations.

<margin>2</margin>
I stated in the conclusion that this is regularly illicit and usury because whenever the lender's profit would cease <note>original: "lucrum cessans," a legal concept where a lender is compensated for the profit they lose by not investing the money elsewhere</note> unless another person simultaneously entered into that insurance contract with him, it would be neither illicit nor usury for him to refuse to give a **maritime loan** <term>traiectitia pecunia: money lent for sea voyages where the lender bears the risk of loss</term> unless that other contract was made at the same time. For example, if there were a merchant who does not want his money to sit idle, but wants to send it to the Indies exposed to his own risk for trade there, and he does not want to lose that hope of great profit, even though it is joined with a probable risk to his capital: then, if another person requested that money from him (either formally or effectively) to trade in India and bring back goods bought with it, the lender could refuse to lend it unless the borrower pays him the amount of his lost profit and simultaneously enters into an insurance contract, so that the lender receives no less profit from that money than if he had traded it himself. We certainly saw and approved of such a contract in Lisbon, even though the person receiving the loan did not refuse the insurance contract at all—in fact, he would not have taken the money without it. Since he was among those who held the rights to the returns of the Indian ships leased from the King, this entire contract was beneficial to him, made with the same lender who provided the maritime loan, which amounted to many thousands of gold coins.

<margin>3</margin>
**Second conclusion.** When the insurance contract is not demanded as a condition without which the lender refuses to lend, but the borrower enters into it of his own accord with the lender, then no usury occurs in it, even if the lender receives something beyond the **principal** <term>sors: the original amount lent</term> by reason of the risk. This holds even if the lender invites the borrower to the contract, provided he receives precisely what is due for the risk he undertakes and not by reason of the loan itself. Indeed, no sin is committed if the price is moderate and there is no scandal, as there regularly will not be. The cited Doctors and many others affirm this. It can be proved because taking on that risk has a monetary value; any third party who entered into the same insurance contract with the borrower could receive a competent price for undergoing that risk. Since, therefore, the

<column-break/>

lender—by the fact that he provides the benefit of a loan to the borrower—is not in a worse condition toward him than any stranger would be, it follows that if he enters into an insurance contract with him at the same time, he can receive a competent price beyond the principal by reason of the risk he undertakes. In that case, two contracts occur. One is a loan, by reason of which he can lawfully receive nothing beyond the principal. The other is an **innominate contract** <term>a contract that does not fall under a specific legal name but is binding</term>: "I will act, or I will take upon myself the risk of the money I lend you, so that you give, or if you give, to me so much or so much." This is a just contract, by reason of which it is not unjust to receive something beyond the principal. For this contract, because it renders the person who pays the price secure from risk, common usage has applied a specific name and called it an "insurance contract." It is practiced not only regarding loans but very frequently in many other matters. We shall speak of these below in their proper place.

<margin>†</margin>
**Third conclusion.** He who is a usurer according to the first conclusion, if he did not receive more for the risk he undertook than a moderate and just price, is not bound to restore the price itself. Instead, he is bound to restore only what is estimated by a prudent judgment to be the value of the burden he imposed on the borrower by forcing him to enter that insurance contract. However, if he received anything beyond a just price, he is also bound to restore that. Finally, everything we said in Disputation 309 regarding similar outcomes should be applied here and confirmed in the same way; for that reason, I will not dwell further on this conclusion.

In this matter, a particular difficulty regarding the second conclusion is posed by the section *Naviganti* under "On Usuries," which reads as follows:
> One who lends a certain quantity of money to someone sailing or going to a fair, and because he takes the risk upon himself, receives something beyond the principal, is to be considered a usurer. <note>This refers to a decree by Pope Gregory IX in the Decretals, which initially seemed to forbid any extra charge on maritime loans</note>

There are various interpretations of this text. The Gloss there, and certain others, understand it as if it truly is usury for a lender to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of risk. However, this interpretation is deservedly rejected by almost everyone. The more common interpretation among the Doctors is that the text must be understood in the case of our first conclusion: namely, when the lender gives the loan on the condition that the borrower enters into an insurance contract with him. Almost all the Doctors we cited regarding the first conclusion, and many others, understand the text this way. This interpretation is not improbable, regardless of what Navarrus <note>Martín de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canonist</note> says to the contrary in the cited places. Adrian and Navarrus, however, explain that text by saying that Gregory IX proceeded based on a legal presumption; thus, it is to be understood in the "external court" <note>the public legal system</note> but not in the "court of conscience." For they say that since many people used to cloak usury in this way—only lending to those who sought maritime loans with an insurance contract—and since some among them did not actually intend to transport the money elsewhere, or they demanded more for the insurance than was a just price so they could receive something by reason of the loan, Gregory IX, to remove these frauds and injustices, wished to introduce a "presumption of law and by law" against those receiving anything beyond the principal by reason of maritime risk. He decreed that by that very fact, they should be considered usurers...

<summary>This page discusses the morality of combining loans with insurance contracts, concluding that while forcing a borrower to buy insurance is usurious, a voluntary insurance agreement at a fair price for the risk taken is licit. Molina reconciles this with medieval canon law by interpreting old prohibitions as measures against fraud rather than a total ban on risk-based fees.</summary>

...should be considered usurers in the external forum <note>the "external forum" refers to the public courts of law or the Church's public judgment, as opposed to the "internal forum" of private confession</note>; and Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canon lawyer</note> says, with some hesitation, that he did not say one who accepts more than the principal is a usurer, but rather should be *considered* a usurer—that is, judged as such in the external forum. Perhaps Gregory IX intended to declare in that chapter that maritime interest <note>original: "nauticum fœnus," an ancient form of marine insurance/loan where the lender bore the risk of the ship sinking</note>, as permitted by civil laws, is usury; it does not matter that the lender takes upon himself the risk of the lent money. Indeed, the civil laws (as mentioned in Disputation 34) permitted maritime interest at a rate of one percent <note>original: "vsuram centesimæ"</note> because of the risk the lender assumed. However, they did not grant it solely because of the risk, but also because of the loan itself. Therefore, because that interest was taken partly because of the loan, Gregory IX rightly declared in that chapter that those who received it should be considered usurers, despite the fact that they were simultaneously receiving it because of the risk. To understand this, one must realize that the civil laws regarding maritime interest (found in the Code and the Digest) are today abrogated <note>repealed or no longer in force</note>, not insofar as they allowed something to be received for risk, but insofar as they allowed an increase because of the loan itself. From these three explanations, choose whichever you prefer.

# Whether it is usury for a guarantor to receive something to act as a guarantor for another.

## DISPUTATION 319.

### SUMMARY

1 *A guarantor may lawfully receive something for providing a guarantee for another, by reason of the risk and the obligation undertaken, according to common opinion.*
2 *To give a loan to someone on the condition that they act as a guarantor for the lender is to commit usury.*
3 *A creditor may accept a moderate price from a guarantor to release that guarantor from their obligation.*
4 *The obligation of paying on behalf of someone else can be estimated at a price.*
5 *What must be considered regarding a "just price" when someone acts as a guarantor.*

Connected to the dispute over whether it is lawful for a lender to receive something beyond the principal due to risk, let us examine whether it is lawful for a guarantor <note>original: "fideiussor," a person who promises to pay a debt if the original borrower defaults</note> to receive something for acting as a guarantor for another. This payment would be by reason of the risk and the obligation he takes upon himself, so that if the principal debtor does not pay, he himself satisfies the debt in their place.

<margin>1</margin>
The common opinion of the doctors affirms that one can lawfully receive something. Among their number are Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, a major commentator on Aquinas</note>, Soto, St. Thomas, Conradus on Contracts, Navarrus in his *Manual*, and in his *Commentary on Exchange*, Juan Medina, Covarrubias, and others whom he cites, agreeing with the laws on donations.

The reason is that the obligation he undertakes is estimable at a price—not only when he likely fears he will be forced to pay for the

<column-break/>

debtor, but even when he fears no such thing. This is no different than how the obligation to grind grain in a lender’s mill at a customary and just wage can be valued at a price, even if the borrower might have ground it at another mill for the same wage and it was no more difficult to go to the lender’s mill than any other. From this you will understand that † to give a loan to someone with a contract that they must be a guarantor for the lender is usury—just as it is usury to lend with a contract that the borrower must grind grain in the lender’s mill.

<margin>2</margin>
However, it is not unlawful to refuse to give a loan if someone who was asked to be a guarantor refused to return that favor. Note this: a moderate price for acting as a guarantor is not lawful because it is "just compensation" above the principal for money that the guarantor *might* pay (as if he were giving a loan to the debtor); that would clearly be usury, as it would be profit coming from a loan. Rather, it is lawful because it is just compensation for the *obligation* the guarantor takes on to pay that money in the event that the debtor fails.

<margin>3</margin>
For although money given as a loan (or a "quasi-loan") is not worth more than itself, the *obligation* to provide that quasi-loan in the event the principal debtor defaults is estimable in money—especially since the money must be given to a debtor who has already failed in his credit regarding the principal debt. For that reason, a guarantor can sell the undertaking of that burden for the sake of the debtor. For the same reason, a creditor can accept a moderate price from a guarantor to release him from that obligation.

Covarrubias, in the place cited, says that when it is likely the guarantor will pay nothing for the debtor, it is a sin to accept anything for acting as guarantor; he says it is only lawful when there is a risk of paying. In the same way, he claims it is a sin for a creditor to accept anything to release a guarantor from the obligation when there is no risk of the debtor failing.

I prefer the common opinion, which affirms what has been said universally—though it is admittedly very little that is lawful to accept when no risk is feared.

<margin>4</margin>
Indeed, if the obligation to pay for someone is estimable at a price even if the hope of needing to pay is slim, that price is simply lower as the risk is less to be feared.

<margin>5</margin>
In † judging the price that is strictly lawful to receive for being a guarantor, one must consider the size of the debt, the greater or lesser risk that the guarantor will have to pay for the debtor, and the greater or lesser hope that the debtor—in the event the guarantor pays for him—will reimburse what was paid, as he is bound and compelled to do in both conscience and the external forum. But if anything more is accepted for being a guarantor, that excess must be restored.

It must also be observed that if anything is accepted as a fraud to hide usury, it is subject to restitution. For instance, if the owner of money gives it to another to lend out, but only on the condition that the owner of the money acts as the "guarantor" <note>This describes a "straw man" setup where the lender pretends to be a guarantor to charge an extra fee on their own money</note>: for if the owner of the money then accepts...

<summary>This page explores the ethics of guarantees, concluding that while charging interest on a loan is usury, charging a fee to act as a financial guarantor is lawful because the guarantor is selling a service (taking on a risky obligation) rather than just lending money.</summary>
<keywords>guarantor, usury, maritime interest, risk, obligation, just price, restitution, contract law, debt, legal forum</keywords>

### Whether it is usury to receive the fruits of a pledge beyond the principal. And whether this is avoided by instead purchasing the same thing with a pact of resale.

### DISPUTATION 320.

#### SUMMARY.

1. In which cases one may receive the fruits of a pledge beyond the principal, and in which cases one may not.
2. A creditor is liable even for slight fault <term>levis culpa: a legal standard of negligence where one fails to exercise the care a reasonable person would take</term> if fruits are not gathered from the pledge.
3. Fruits of a thing purchased with a pact of resale <term>pactum de retrovendendo: a contract where the seller has the right to buy the item back at the same price</term> at the same price are not counted toward the principal.
4. If a thing purchased with a pact of resale perishes, the loss falls on the buyer and not the seller.

<margin>1</margin> It is not to be doubted that a creditor is bound to count toward the principal—or return to the debtor—the fruits <note>In legal terms, "fruits" (fructus) refers to the produce, rent, or profit generated by a property, such as crops from a field or rent from a house</note> of a pledge received from him, after deducting the expenses incurred in collecting them. For if he should receive them beyond the principal, and not by reason of lost profit <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note> or emergent loss <note>original: "damnum emergens"</note>, or from the free donation of the debtor, or as a just penalty, or for some other just cause, he commits usury. This usury is "open" if he receives them specifically because of a loan, and "cloaked" <note>original: "palliatam"</note> if he receives them while expecting payment under any other title. This is found in Chapters 1 and 2 *On Usury* and the chapter *Significante* regarding pledges, and is clearly gathered from the definition of usury.

Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican theologian and key figure in the School of Salamanca</note> in *On Justice and Right*, Book 6, Question 1, Article 2, says: If a debtor gives a sterile field to a creditor as a pledge, which he did not intend to cultivate, and the creditor by his own industry and labor gathers modest fruits from it, then perhaps the creditor is not bound to count those toward the principal. Because, Soto says, he perceived them without detriment to the creditor, nor is he bound to count the fruits of his own industry toward the principal. He adds, however, that if the fruits are of any significance, and were perceived from a field that was not considered sterile but was simply not cultivated due to the owner’s laziness, they must be counted toward the principal. Navarrus <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canonist</note> in his *Manual*, Chapter 17, number 216, rightly disapproves of this assertion by Soto, saying that both small and large fruits are to be counted toward the principal when they exceed expenses, including the value of the cultivator's labor and industry. Since they are truly the fruits of that field, they belong to the owner of the field, once expenses are deducted—unless it is understood to be the free will of the field's owner that the cultivator may keep them for himself.

<margin>2</margin> Observe that when a pledge is fruit-bearing, and by the fault of the creditor—even a slight fault—fruits are not perceived from it, the creditor is bound to count the value <note>original: "interesse"</note> of those fruits toward the principal. For example, if the pledge were a house and he did not rent it out through his own negligence, or if it were a field usually sown and seeds were not committed to it through the creditor's negligence. I said "even a slight fault":

<column-break/>

since if the contract of pledge was celebrated for the benefit of both parties, as is regularly the custom, he is liable even for slight fault—though not for the slightest fault <note>original: "culpa leuissima"</note>—according to what was said in Disputation 293 and those following, and what will be said below in its proper place when we discuss pledges. On this matter, among others, read Conradus <note>Conradus Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian</note> *On Contracts*, Question 32.

<margin>3</margin> Observe also this: when something is received not as a pledge, but as a purchase for the money which the one offering the pledge was seeking, yet purchased with a "pact of resale"—that is, that whenever the one who owned the thing should restore the price, he would receive it back purchased for the same price, and thus the prior sale would end; or with a pact that if he restored the price within a certain time, the prior sale would be dissolved, otherwise the thing would become entirely unredeemable—then, without the vice of usury, the first buyer would receive the fruits without them being counted toward the principal.

<margin>4</margin> The reason is that, in that case, those fruits are not perceived from another’s property, but from one's own, during the interval while the price is not restored to him. Therefore, if the thing perishes during that time, it perishes to the buyer and not to the one who owned it before. This is affirmed by the Portuguese Ordinances <note>Refers to the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the legal codes of Portugal, where Molina taught</note>, Book 4, Title 14, Paragraph 2, and by the common consensus of the learned doctors. Hence Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Catholic theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note> in his commentary on the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 78, Article 2, rightly warns those who receive certain cities from princes as a pledge for money which the princes need: if they wish to make the fruits of those cities their own without the vice of usury or the burden of restitution (not counting them toward the principal), they ought to buy those cities for that same money with a pact of resale. In this way, they lawfully make those fruits their own. Observe, however, that the price must be equal to the thing, so that it at least reaches the "lowest just price," considering that a thing bought with the burden of having to sell it back is worth far less than if it were sold free from that burden.

But if the price falls far short of the lowest just price, in the external forum <note>the public legal court</note> the contract will be presumed usurious (as "cloaked usury") and therefore null; the buyer will be subject to the penalties for usurers, as the Portuguese Ordinances state in the cited place. However, in the forum of conscience <note>the internal forum of the soul and confession</note>, if usurious intent was absent, whether the price falls short by a little or a lot from the lowest just price, the contract will only be "unjust," carrying the burden of restoring what was lacking to reach the lowest just price.

### Whether a son-in-law is immune from usury who, while the dowry is not yet paid to him, receives a pledge to be enjoyed without counting the fruits toward the principal sum.

### DISPUTATION 321.

#### SUMMARY.

1. A son-in-law is not bound to count toward the principal the fruits of pledges which he received for a promised dowry during the time it was not paid to him.

It distinguishes between actual usury and legal contracts used by princes and commoners to manage debt and property.</summary>

Second Treatise, Disputation 32. 171

**3. Various interpretations and understandings of the chapter *Salubriter* concerning usury, along with the author’s true opinion.**
**4. Those entering into marriage are accustomed to celebrating two contracts.**
**5. The provision of the chapter *Salubriter*, regarding usury, applies to a son-in-law not only in relation to a father-in-law, but also to anyone else whose daughter he has married. Furthermore, it applies in Portugal when parties marry under a contract of "half of the goods." num. 6.**
**7. A son-in-law, on the grounds of lost profit, can receive just compensation for a delay in the payment of a dowry.**
**8. Whether a son-in-law is called a usurer if he enjoys the father-in-law’s property until the remainder of the dowry is paid, even when no profit is lost to him by the delay of the dowry payment.**
**9. Whether a son-in-law can bargain with a father-in-law to be paid a certain amount of money every year until the dowry is paid.**
**10. Whether a statute is valid which requires a father-in-law to pay a son-in-law a certain amount of money to support the burdens of marriage until the dowry is paid.**

On this matter, we must first cite the definition of Pope Innocent III in the chapter *Salubriter* <note>original: "c. salubriter, de vsuris"</note> regarding usury, which states:
> Truly, we do not believe that a son-in-law should be compelled to count toward the principal the fruits of properties pledged to him by his father-in-law for a promised <note>original: "pro numerata," literally "counted out" or promised</note> dowry; since often the fruits of the dowry are not sufficient to support the burdens of marriage.

These are the words of the Supreme Pontiff. In them, he clearly defines that a son-in-law is not bound to deduct from the debt the profits of the pledges he received for a promised dowry during the time it remained unpaid. On this subject, there are quite varied opinions among the learned doctors, which you may read in part in Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish canon lawyer</note> (Various Resolutions, Book 3, chapter 1, number 3) and in Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), also known as Doctor Navarrus, a prominent canonist</note> (Commentary on Usury, question 4, number 71).

2. Certain legal experts <unclear>†</unclear> have asserted that this was granted to the son-in-law as a privilege out of favor for the marriage, so that he might bear its burdens—as if, by a grant of law, something were licit for the son-in-law which, setting aside the privilege, would truly be usury and illicit. Those who considered the Portuguese Ordinances <term>ordinationes Lusitanas: the national legal code of Portugal</term> seem to have followed this opinion; in Book 4, Title 14, § 1, they say: *“And although usuries are generally reproved and forbidden, as has been said, in some cases, however, by both canon and civil law, usury is permitted and licit,”* and they immediately subjoin the example of the son-in-law according to the chapter *Salubriter*.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
However, this opinion is entirely improbable, as theologians commonly observe. Since usury is illicit in itself by both natural and divine law, human law certainly cannot grant a privilege making it licit for someone. Thus, it follows that Innocent III, in the chapter *Salubriter*, was not creating new law, but was only declaring what the nature of the matter itself entails in this event.

The more common opinion of the doctors affirms that this is licit for the son-in-law by reason of lost profit <term>lucrum cessans: profit that is lost because one does not have the capital to invest</term> and emergent loss <term>damnum emergens: a loss that actually occurs because of a breach or delay</term>, and that Innocent III was only declaring this in the chapter *Salubriter*. This is the view of Hadrian <note>Pope Hadrian VI, writing as a theologian</note> (on Restitution, regarding usury), Covarruvias (on Contracts, question 9), John Major <note>Scottish philosopher and theologian (1467–1550)</note>, and many others,

<column-break/>

whom Covarruvias cites. Covarruvias himself follows this same opinion in part, as does Juan Medina <note>Spanish theologian (1490–1547)</note> (on Things Acquired through Usury). However, just as this opinion displeases many others, it is also not approved by me.

Firstly, because that text does not give such a reason, but a far different one: namely, that it is licitly accepted beyond the principal for "supporting the burdens of marriage." To support these, says the text, the profits of a dowry paid immediately are often insufficient. Therefore, when the dowry is delayed (as if the Supreme Pontiff were saying), the profits of a pledge are licitly accepted to support the burdens of marriage, as they do not usually exceed the profits of a dowry paid immediately. Secondly, the Supreme Pontiff in that chapter intended to declare something peculiar regarding the son-in-law by reason of the burdens of marriage <term>onera matrimonii: the financial obligations of maintaining a household and family</term>, rather than providing a general principle for the son-in-law (and everyone else) to licitly accept something beyond the principal due to lost profit or emergent loss.

Thirdly, if it were licit for the son-in-law to take the fruits of the pledge beyond the principal only by reason of lost profit or emergent loss, then, if the dowry were to be paid in money and the son-in-law was not going to trade with it but intended to support himself and his wife from the income of his own inheritance, he could take nothing beyond the principal. Indeed, no profit would be lost to him, nor would any loss emerge from the delayed dowry. Nor would it matter if he then spent more with his wife than the profits of the pledge were worth (as some authors of the contrary opinion respond); for when he was not going to compensate for that from the income of a dowry paid immediately, no loss would emerge for him, nor would profit be lost from the delay of the dowry, and thus he could not take the profits of the pledge on those grounds.

Fourthly, because if it were lawful for the son-in-law to take the profits of the pledge only by reason of lost profit or emergent loss, then, if those profits exceeded the lost profit or emergent loss, it would surely be wicked for him to take the profits in full (as authors of the contrary opinion confess). Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff would not have said absolutely that it is lawful for the son-in-law to take them beyond the principal, but would have added, "provided that the lost profit and emergent loss are not exceeded." Thus, it follows that the Supreme Pontiff intended something else by that definition.

Fifthly, if that son-in-law were an industrious man who expected far greater profits from a dowry paid immediately than those necessary for him to support the burdens of marriage, then surely, by reason of lost profit, he could licitly accept greater profits than those he needed to support the marriage burdens. Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff was not moved to define this based on the grounds of lost profit or emergent loss; otherwise, he would have declared that it is lawful for the son-in-law to take sometimes more, sometimes less, than those profits.

Juan Medina, in the place cited above, while not entirely repudiating the common opinion, leans instead toward the idea that Innocent III relies on a presumption: that the father-in-law intended to *gift* the profits of the pledge to the son-in-law in the meantime while the dowry was not yet paid, in order to support the burdens of marriage.

Navarrus seems to feel this same way in his *Manual*, chapter...

...edition. But truly, that Supreme Pontiff, in that chapter, did not think at all of a "presumption of donation," as is clear enough to anyone looking at the words of that text and the reasoning behind the definition he gave. Indeed, that definition would seem reckless if it relied on such a presumption, nor would the Supreme Pontiff have safely settled men’s consciences in that matter. Furthermore, that decision would not apply when someone other than the father provided a dowry for the bride; yet universal practice understands that text to apply generally, which is why Medina’s opinion must be rejected.

**Fortunius**, in the place cited above, after a long dispute, embraces the opinion of those asserting that the chapter *Salubriter* <note>original: "caput salubriter," a reference to a specific section of Canon Law</note> only applies to a son-in-law in relation to a father-in-law, and not in relation to anyone else who might have provided a dowry for his wife. He convinces himself of this because a father is bound to provide a dowry or to nourish his daughter; for that reason, while the father has not yet paid the dowry, the son-in-law can licitly receive the fruits of a pledge from him without counting them toward the principal, in order to support the daughter during that time. He says this is the reasoning given in the chapter *Salubriter*: namely, that for a son-in-law to receive the fruits of a pledge for the support of his own wife in place of the father is to receive those same fruits to support the <term>burdens of marriage</term> <note>Latin: "onera matrimonij," the legal and financial obligations of maintaining a household and family</note>. This opinion does not satisfy me. Firstly, because, as will be clear from what follows, it does not touch the heart of the matter. Secondly, because, as **Navarrus** <note>The famous canonist Martin de Azpilcueta</note> rightly says in the cited place, number 72, it unworthily restricts the chapter *Salubriter* to a son-in-law in relation to the father-in-law alone; for the opinion of all the <term>doctors</term> <note>Scholarly authorities in law and theology</note> understands it in relation to anyone who has promised a dowry.

**Soto**, in Book 6 on Justice, Question 1, Article 2, in the response to the last point, says that the son-in-law can receive the fruits of a pledge without counting them toward the principal because, in this sense, he is bound to support the burdens of marriage. He argues that since the husband is bound to return the dowry in its entirety to the wife or her heirs when the marriage is dissolved, he is meanwhile bound to nourish the wife; for that reason, the law presumes that something was bought with that dowry from which, while keeping the dowry intact, he might nourish the wife. This opinion also does not please me.

<margin>3</margin>
First, because, as Navarrus rightly says in the cited place, it would follow that in Portugal—where men regularly contract under the <term>contract of half of the goods</term> <note>Latin: "contractu medietatis bonorum," a community property arrangement where assets are shared equally</note> and are not bound to keep the wife's dowry intact—the chapter *Salubriter* would not apply. However, custom holds the contrary, and the regulations in Book 4 of the cited place establish this.

Second, because if, as Soto affirms, it were based on that presumption, it would surely be based on a presumption of <term>lost profit</term> <note>Latin: "lucrum cessans," a legal justification for interest when a lender loses out on other investment opportunities</note>, and thus Soto falls back into the common opinion which he himself attacks. Third, because when it is clear that the son-in-law was not going to buy or trade anything with that money, he surely could not receive the fruits of the pledge without counting them toward the principal; for a law based on a presumption has no force in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>Internal moral judgment before God, as opposed to a legal court</note> when the opposite of the presumption is evident—especially when what the law establishes would be inequitable and unjust if that presumption were removed.

**Cajetan**, in his commentary on the *Summa*, 2.2, Question 78, Article 2, response 6, says that by reason of the burdens of marriage, a son-in-law can receive the fruits of pledges without counting them toward the principal. He says it is "accidental" whether the son-in-law would have profited from the dowry

<column-break/>

or not, and for that reason, he says one should not worry about what is accidental, since the fruits are *per se* <note>essentially or by their nature</note> designated for supporting the burdens of marriage. This doctrine needs a greater explanation to be satisfactory.

<margin>3</margin>
To provide the legitimate cause of this matter and the intent of Innocent III in the chapter *Salubriter*, we must observe the following: The decision of that chapter concerns a very common occurrence in which someone establishes that he will give a son-in-law a certain amount of dowry. Because he cannot pay it immediately, at least in the form he intends and promises to pay it, he meanwhile hands over some properties to the son-in-law as a <term>pledge</term> <note>Latin: "pignus," collateral</note> to be enjoyed until the dowry is paid in full. This happens whether the father-in-law sets a certain deadline to pay the dowry and receive back his pledges, or whether he simply says he will pay the dowry, and in the meantime, while he has not paid, the son-in-law may enjoy those pledges.

In this situation, Innocent III was consulted as to whether the son-in-law was being a usurer by not counting the fruits of such pledges toward the principal debt, and whether he should be compelled to count them toward the principal. He responded in the negative, leaning on this reason: that those fruits are not received as compensation for waiting for the payment of the dowry—for that would indeed be <term>palliated usury</term> <note>Disguised or hidden usury</note>—but as compensation for the burdens of marriage during the time the dowry is not paid, which those burdens are worth. And this is what the reasoning concisely proves, which Innocent gave at the end of the chapter, saying:
> "Since frequently the fruits of the dowry are not sufficient to support the burdens of marriage;"
as if he were saying: the burdens of marriage are worth the fruits of the entire dowry paid immediately. Even if the entire dowry were given in those fruitful properties to be enjoyed for the whole time the marriage lasts, the fruits of the pledges are not greater than the fruits of the entire dowry would be if it were paid in properties or if the son-in-law bought properties with the dowry money. Therefore, the burdens of marriage, which the son-in-law supports until the payment of the dowry, are worth the fruits of the pledges; and consequently, he is not bound to count them toward the principal.

<margin>4</margin>
So that you may understand this better, observe that two contracts are usually involved when people celebrate a marriage. One is that by which the spouses hand over mutual power of their bodies to one another; and in this consists the essence of marriage. The other is that by which the husband takes upon himself the burden of supporting the wife in exchange for the dowry. This is an <term>innominate contract</term> <note>A contract that does not fall under a specific name like "sale" or "lease" but is "I will do if you give"</note>. According to common law (which the chapter *Salubriter* addresses), the dowry was given to the man to be enjoyed for the entire time the marriage lasted to undergo the burdens of marriage, which he would return in full upon the dissolution of the marriage. Just as the burdens of marriage for the entire time the marriage lasts are worth the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property</note> of the dowry for that entire time, so the burdens for half the time are worth the usufruct for half the time, and the burdens for a quarter of the time are worth the usufruct for a quarter of the time, and so on. From this it follows: if the father-in-law does not wish to give the dowry to be enjoyed except after a certain time has elapsed—during which the son-in-law must first support the burdens of marriage—the son-in-law can licitly and justly demand, in compensation for those burdens, the enjoyment of property equal in value to the dowry. This is because he does not receive it as compensation for the delay...

It specifically addresses the "burdens of marriage" (onera matrimonij) as a justification for a son-in-law to keep such income without it being subtracted from the principal debt.</meta>

...delay of the payment of the dowry, but for the burdens he sustains during that period of delay. And this is the reason why he is not bound to count the income of the pledge toward the principal, not only when this was expressly written into the contract, but even when productive pledges were simply handed over to him while the dowry remained unpaid: because they are then considered to have been given to him according to the disposition and declaration of the law in the chapter *Salubriter* <note>original: "ca. salubriter," a reference to a specific section of Canon Law</note>, especially since there is a most sufficient reason for receiving them and not counting them toward the principal.

<margin>He solves the issue.</margin> 

<margin>5</margin> From this, I first conclude that the rule of the chapter *Salubriter* has force for the son-in-law, not only in comparison with the father-in-law, but also in comparison with any other person who provided the wife's dowry. For a son-in-law can no less licitly receive a suitable price for sustaining the burdens of marriage from any stranger than from a father-in-law while the dowry remains unpaid.

<margin>6</margin> I conclude, secondly, that the rule of the same chapter applies even when couples marry under a contract of "half of the goods" <note>This refers to community property or *medietas bonorum*</note>, as is the custom in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>. For although the husband is not bound to keep the wife's dowry whole <note>Since it is mixed with his own assets in community property</note>, that does not change the fact that he sustains the burdens of marriage and spends his own patrimony, its fruits, and his own industry on supporting his wife while the dowry is not paid. Therefore, in compensation for this and the other burdens of marriage, he may licitly receive the income from a pledge, provided it yields annually as much as the dowry would have yielded if paid immediately in the form of property.

<margin>7</margin> Third, I conclude that it is irrelevant to the matter at hand whether a son-in-law loses some profit or not due to the dowry not being paid immediately, so that he may well receive the income of the pledge without counting it toward the principal while the dowry remains unpaid. Since he receives those incomes as a just compensation for the burdens he sustains at that time, and not as compensation for the wait for payment, then even if no profit were lost to him from the delay (as if the dowry were to be paid in cash that he would have just kept in a chest), he could still justly receive them on that other ground. In this place, observe <note>original: "obserua"</note> that we do not deny that a son-in-law, on the basis of <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>literally "profit ceasing"—a legal concept where one is compensated for the profit they *would* have made if they had the money in hand</note>, can receive just compensation for the delay, just like anyone else who loses profit of an equal amount due to a delay in payment. Therefore, if a son-in-law were very industrious, and more profit was lost to him by the delay of a cash dowry than the income from the pledges given to him, he could licitly demand the additional profit beyond those fruits.

**Fourth, I conclude,** if the son-in-law does not sustain the burdens of marriage while the dowry is unpaid—for instance, if the wife stays in her father's house after the wedding and is fed by the father, so that the son-in-law bears no greater burden for her than he would otherwise—then he certainly could not receive the income of the pledges without counting it toward the principal, because that just title ceases to exist.

**Fifth, I conclude,** if the father-in-law agreed with the son-in-law on a certain dowry to be paid not immediately but at a fixed time, and the father-in-law handed over pledges only as security for payment at that deadline; then, even if the son-in-law...

<column-break/>

...sustained the burdens of marriage before that deadline, he could not receive the income of the pledges without counting it toward the principal. The reason is that for the burdens of the entire time the marriage exists, he agreed with the father-in-law for the dowry to be paid at that term. Thus, in the dowry to be paid then, he receives compensation both for the burdens he sustains before the payment, and this is by the agreement between both parties; therefore, he cannot receive another price for them.

<margin>8</margin> You will perhaps ask: <margin>A Doubt</margin> **What if the father-in-law, at the beginning,** decided he would give the son-in-law two thousand gold pieces for his daughter's dowry, but after the marriage is celebrated, seeing that he cannot pay immediately, he asks for a year's delay with the agreement that meanwhile the son-in-law may enjoy the father's property? Will the son-in-law then be a usurer, assuming no profit is lost to him by the delay? The side that argues "yes" can be persuaded thus: For the son-in-law to grant a delay is effectively to lend those two thousand gold pieces; but to receive anything above the principal for a loan is usury. This is confirmed because if the son-in-law had already received that money and the father-in-law asked to borrow it back for a year, it would be usury to take the income of that property beyond the principal to grant the loan. Therefore, it is usury to take them for a delay in paying money already owed by a previous agreement. I believe it must be said <margin>Decision</margin> that it is indeed usury if the son-in-law receives the income from that property from the father-in-law specifically for the delay or the loan of those gold pieces, regardless of the fact that he sustains the burdens of marriage. However, if he says to the father-in-law: "When you ask for a delay, let us treat the things you promised or gave me to support the burdens of marriage as null, or let us dissolve the previous contract; and let us enter this other just one anew, so that for sustaining the burdens of marriage while you do not hand over that money, you give me the income of this property; then, when you have delivered the money, let it from then on be the price for the subsequent burdens of marriage." Then I believe this contract is just and not at all usurious, even if the son-in-law loses no profit from the delay of the payment.

**You might object by the same reasoning:** <margin>Objection</margin> if a stranger asks him for that money which he receives to support the marriage burdens, could he make a similar contract with him and receive something above the principal for sustaining the marriage burdens while the money is unpaid, even if no profit is lost to him? This conclusion must be denied: because it is not the business of a stranger to compensate for the burdens of marriage, in the way it pertains to a father-in-law or another who gives a dowry. For that reason, in comparison to someone who does not provide the dowry, he has no other title than that of a loan, by reason of which he can receive nothing above the principal.

**Hence you will understand,** if a son-in-law, after licitly receiving property from the father-in-law to enjoy in place of an unpaid dowry, needs as much money as the dowry is worth and asks for it as a loan from some stranger, it is a sin for such a stranger to take the income of that property for the money he lends the son-in-law, even if an agreement is made between them that the lender receives payment from the father-in-law from the dowry owed to the son-in-law...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal exceptions to usury regarding dowries, arguing that a son-in-law may keep the income from a pledge to cover the 'burdens of marriage' without reducing the principal debt. He clarifies that this applies only if the income is intended for marital support and not as a fee for a loan or delay in payment.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...tains. The reason is that, assuming a stranger loses no profit from the loan, he has no other legal title for receiving the fruits of that possession beyond the principal, except for the loan itself. For that reason, he would commit the sin of usury if he were to accept them. However, a son-in-law, who possesses another just title <note>i.e., the "burdens of marriage" such as supporting the household</note>, commits no usury.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
The doubt is whether, just as a son-in-law can bargain with a father-in-law to receive the income of a possession (without it being counted against the principal) until the dowry is paid in full, he might also bargain to receive a certain fixed sum of money instead. 

<margin>Decision</margin>
Joannes Andreas <note>A famous 14th-century expert in Canon Law</note> and certain others whom Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a leading Spanish jurist</note> cites in the aforementioned place, deny this. They argue that the law <note>Specifically the chapter *Salubriter*</note> only grants this exception for the "fruits" of a pledge, which depend on fortune <note>Meaning they are variable based on harvests and weather</note>. However, this opinion is rightly rejected by the common body of legal scholars. Since those fruits—while they still depend on fortune—could be sold every year for a determined price, there is certainly no reason why a son-in-law, just as he may lawfully bargain for the fruits themselves, may not also bargain for a sum of money equivalent to that price. Furthermore, since a son-in-law lawfully receives the income of a possession as just compensation for the burdens of marriage he sustains, there is no reason why he cannot similarly bargain for a yearly sum of money. This sum would be a just price for the burdens he supports, equal to what the dowry itself would have yielded if it had been delivered in the form of landed property.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
10. The doctors <note>Legal and theological scholars</note> dispute whether a statute would be lawful if it decreed that, as long as a dowry remains unpaid to a son-in-law, the father-in-law is bound to pay him a certain sum of money every year to support the marriage burdens—for example, a fourteenth of the total estimated value of the promised dowry. 

<margin>Decision</margin>
From what has been said, it is easily established that such a statute is lawful. This is true not only by reason of "lost profit" <note>term: <term>lucrum cessans</term> — the profit a person misses out on because their capital is tied up or unpaid</note> (especially in places where annual rents are easily purchased with money, as Covarruvias argues), but also because it represents a just price for sustaining the burdens of marriage, as is clear enough from the preceding discussion.

---

### Whether, after the marriage is dissolved, the son-in-law can still receive the income of the pledge without it being counted against the principal. And what about the children of a deceased wife? Likewise, what of a wife after her husband's death, and concerning the wife and heirs who do not descend from the wife in comparison to the husband or his heirs?

## DISPUTATION 322

#### SUMMARY

1. Whether a son-in-law, after the marriage is dissolved, can receive the income of a pledge (without counting it against the principal) as the guardian of the children until the dowry is paid to him.
2. How the husband's heirs are bound to restore the dowry to the wife or her heirs. And what is observed in Portugal.

<column-break/>

3. How the income of dotal property belongs to the wife after the marriage is dissolved, and what of its use.
4. How the wife, until her dowry is restored, ought to be maintained from her husband's estate.
5. What the law is in Portugal and Castile.
6. If the husband's heirs are in delay of paying the dowry, they are bound only to compensate for "lost profit."
7. Whether a statute is lawful which binds the husband's heirs to pay a certain sum of money to the wife until they pay her the dowry.

---

<margin>Doubt</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
1. **T**he doubt is: if a son-in-law was receiving the income of a pledge while the dowry remained unpaid, and the wife dies leaving a son before the dowry is paid, can the husband (who is the guardian or curator of the son and the usufructuary <note>One who has the right to the income/use of property owned by another</note> of his goods) continue to receive that same income without counting it against the principal until the dowry is paid? The Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Ordinationes Lusitanæ," the national legal code of Portugal</note> (Book 4, Title 14, § 1) deny that this can be done without the vice of usury. And this must undoubtedly be the case. For that just title for receiving income beyond the principal—namely, sustaining the burdens of marriage by supporting a wife—has ceased to exist.

Note, however, that the husband can then demand the dowry immediately from the father of the deceased woman or whoever else provided or owes the dowry, which the son of the deceased now inherits. If it is not paid immediately, he can demand the entirety of the "lost profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note>. This is not limited only to what the dowry could return if it were paid in land, but also includes the estimated profit he might have expected from it through his own industry, seeing as he stands in place of the son as the usufructuary of all those goods. The son can seek this same "lost profit" after the father's death, or his guardian/curator can do so. However, if the son-in-law dies and the wife survives (to whom the promised dowry then belongs), since the burdens of marriage have ceased, the woman cannot seek anything beyond the principal from her father or the debtor, except only for the lost profit caused by the fact that the dowry was not paid immediately.

2. Regarding the † wife after the husband's death (who had already received the dowry), and regarding the heirs of a wife who dies without children, to whom the husband or his heirs are bound to pay the dowry, it must be noted: By Common Law <note>i.e., *Ius Commune*, the Roman-Canonical legal tradition</note>, not only does the husband remain in possession of all goods as head of the family when the marriage is dissolved by the wife's death, and her heirs must receive the dowry and other goods belonging to her from him; but also when the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death, his heirs remain as the head of the family, and the wife must receive what belongs to her from them. Nevertheless, until the dowry is restored to her, the wife can retain the house in which she lived with her husband and all the goods found within it. In Portugal, however, when a marriage was celebrated under a contract of "half of the goods" <note>original: "medietatis bonorum," referring to community property</note>, the wife remains in possession of all common goods or those obligated in any way as the head of the family, and the husband's heirs must receive half of all the goods from her, while she retains the other half.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of financial obligations following the dissolution of a marriage, specifically focusing on the timeline for returning a dowry and the widow's right to maintenance from her late husband's estate.</meta>

### Treatise Two, Disputation 322

When a marriage has been celebrated with a contract involving <term>earnest money</term> <note>original: *arrhae*; a small payment or gift given at the time of a contract to seal the agreement</note> and a <term>dowry</term> <note>original: *dos*; the property or money brought by a bride to her husband</note>, the goods that were the husband's private property pass immediately to his heirs. The wife may not remain in possession of them. However, for all other goods—those that are the wife’s own property or those to be divided between her and the husband's heirs—the wife remains in possession. From her, the husband’s heirs must receive what belongs to them. This is established in the 4th Ordinary Law, Title 7, Paragraph 1, and the three following paragraphs. Furthermore, in Portugal, when a marriage is celebrated with such a contract, it is customary to include a clause in the legal instruments stating that if the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death, the wife shall remain the "head of the family" <note>original: *caput familiae*</note>, and the heirs must receive the husband's portion from her. Such an agreement must be upheld.

Next, it should be observed that in cases where—under common law or the laws of Portugal—the wife or her heirs are entitled to receive the dowry and her other property from the hand of the husband or his heirs, common law once dictated a specific timeline. The husband or heirs were required to restore the dowry over three years: one-third in the first year, one-third in the second, and one-third in the third. Recently, however, it was decreed that when a dowry consists of certain <term>immovable goods</term> <note>i.e., real estate like land or houses</note> that were not appraised at the start of the marriage, they must be returned immediately without any delay.

<margin>3</margin>
If the dowry consists of <term>movable goods</term> <note>e.g., furniture, jewelry</note>, "self-moving" things <note>i.e., livestock or slaves</note>, or <term>incorporeal rights</term> <note>e.g., debts owed or legal claims</note> that were not appraised—or if the total sum must be returned based solely on a prior valuation—then the dowry must be restored within one year from the day the marriage ended. This is expressly stated in the Code of Justinian and the laws of the Siete Partidas. However, the jurist Antonio Gómez notes that in this kingdom <note>likely referring to Castile/Spain</note>, it is now customary to include a clause in dowry documents requiring payment within thirty days, and such an agreement must be honored. Similarly, in Portugal, if a specific agreement is made in the dowry documents regarding this matter, it must be followed.

<margin>4</margin>
From the day the marriage is dissolved, the <term>fruits</term> <note>i.e., the income, crops, or offspring</note> of immovable dotal property (if delivered unvalued) belong to the wife or her heirs. The same applies to the fruits of unvalued movable property, such as the offspring of livestock, the freight charges of a rented ship, or the wages from rented pack animals or servants. However, the *use* of all these things, and the use of a dowry that consists of a cash sum (which the husband owes as a debt rather than as specific physical items), belongs to the husband or his heirs for the entire duration of the time granted to them for the dowry's restoration. This is affirmed by Antonio Gómez, Covarruvias, and others.

In the meantime, so long as the dowry has not been handed over to the wife within the time permitted by law, she must be provided with <term>maintenance</term> <note>original: *alimenta*; basic living expenses like food, clothing, and shelter</note> from the husband's estate. This is the consensus of legal scholars. It should be understood, however, that she must actually request this support and have no other means of sustaining herself. Therefore, if someone else provides her with maintenance, the husband's heirs are not required to pay—unless they had refused to provide for her when asked, forcing her to seek help elsewhere. In that case, the heirs must reimburse what she spent. Covarruvias notes that if she remarries during that time and is poor, and her dowry has still not been returned, she must still be provided with maintenance. It is different, however, if she is wealthy or if her second husband supports her.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, if the income from her dotal property or her other goods belongs to her during that time (according to what has been said), she must support herself from those. Only if those funds are insufficient for her full support must the remainder be paid from the deceased husband's estate. Moreover, Covarruvias includes "mourning clothes" <note>original: *vestes lugubres*</note> among the maintenance to be provided. The woman is also expected to work during this time according to the custom of the country and her social status. As soon as the dowry is paid to her, maintenance is no longer owed, even if it is paid immediately after the husband’s death.

Because this right to maintenance arises from the fact that support is owed to the wife in lieu of the dowry while it remains unpaid, this is a personal privilege of the wife. Consequently, if the wife dies, her heirs are not entitled to maintenance during the period before the dowry is returned to them.

<margin>5</margin>
I believe, however, that in these kingdoms of Portugal and Castile—where either all property is held in common or at least the profits gained during the marriage are shared—the custom is for the wife to be supported from the common goods until the partition of property is finished and her dowry is returned.

One should also note that if the wife remains pregnant, maintenance must be provided to her from the common property even if the dowry is returned to her immediately.

<margin>6</margin>
With these points established, we must agree with Covarruvias and Cajetan. During the time when the husband's heirs are in <term>default</term> <note>original: *mora*; a legal delay in fulfilling an obligation</note> of paying the dowry to the wife (or the husband's heirs are late paying the wife's heirs), the wife or her heirs can only demand "lost profit" <note>original: *lucrum cessans*; the financial gain they would have made if they had the money on time</note> resulting from the non-payment. They cannot demand anything else beyond the principal, despite what some might say, because they have no other just legal title to demand more. Before any legal default occurs, they can only claim the "fruits" of the dowry if those belong to the wife from the day the marriage ended, and the wife can additionally demand what is necessary for her adequate maintenance during that time.

<margin>7</margin>
<margin>A Doubt</margin>
Scholars debate whether a statute would be licit if it decreed that, as long as the dowry remains unpaid to widows, the husband's heirs should be bound to pay them a certain annual sum of money—for example, at a rate of one for every fourteen <note>approximately 7.14%</note> of the dowry's valuation. As was determined at the end of the previous disputation, such a statute is considered licit for a son-in-law while a promised dowry remains unpaid.

<summary>This page details the legal timelines and requirements for returning a dowry to a widow, emphasizing her right to financial maintenance from her late husband's estate until the assets are restored.</summary>
<keywords>dowry, maintenance, inheritance law, Portugal, Castile, restitution, marriage contracts, widow's rights, legal default</keywords>

--- Page 242 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding the financial rights of widows and transitions into a new disputation concerning feudal and emphyteutic contracts, specifically whether certain arrangements between a lord and a tenant constitute usury.</meta>

Many authors, whom Covarruvias cites in his *Variarum Resolutionum*, book 3, chapter 1, number 3, corollary 7, affirm that this is illicit and goes against the canon law <note>original: "clemetin. 1. de vsuris"; referring to the Clementine Constitutions, a collection of Church laws</note>. Their reasoning is that such an arrangement would introduce usury. I certainly do not dislike this opinion. For, as established from what has been said, in the first year widows are only owed certain fruits of the dowry, and furthermore, if they lack sufficient maintenance from elsewhere, they are owed what is necessary for their station. Thereafter, however, they are only owed for "lost profit" <note>original: <term>lucrum cessans</term>; a legal concept where one is compensated for the profit they would have made if they had possession of their capital</note>. If she receives anything more, she commits usury. Therefore, a statute that granted them more would be unjust. Indeed, even if such a statute were to estimate a fixed amount to be paid to her annually based on the aforementioned points, it would have no force in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal moral judgment of a person before God, as opposed to a legal court</note> unless those fruits of the dowry and maintenance, or the lost profit, were truly worth that total amount, considering all circumstances affecting each individual widow. For this reason, I would not advise the creation of such a statute.

Unless, perhaps, it were enacted as a just penalty against the husband's heirs when the dowry is withheld against the widow's will beyond the time prescribed by law, and where true fault exists on the part of those withholding it. This is the view of Cajetan in his response to the sixth point cited earlier. For where fault is lacking, or if the widow does not resist the delay, nothing can be taken as a penalty; where there is no fault, a penalty has no place. Thus, such a statute would be neither prudent nor safe even as a penalty.

### **Whether it is usury for a property owner not to count the income of a pledge toward the principal for a loan received from a feudal tenant or an emphyteuta.**

### DISPUTATION 323.

->*SUMMARY.*<-

<margin>1</margin> *How a property owner may not be bound to count the income of a pledge toward the principal for a loan received from a feudal or emphyteutic tenant, and why. num. 3.*
<margin>2</margin> *How Chapter 1 "On Feuds" and the chapter "Conquestus" on usury are to be understood.*
<margin>4</margin> *Under what conditions contracts of fiefs and emphyteusis can be established.*

<margin>1</margin> **I**n Chapter 1 "On Feuds" and the chapter *Conquestus* "On Usury," it is held that when a feudal tenant <note>original: <term>feudatarius</term>; one who holds land from a lord in exchange for service</note> gives the property owner <note>original: <term>proprietarius</term>; the lord or "direct owner" of the land</note> a pledge for a loan consisting of the very property he held as a fief, that owner is not bound to count the income <note>original: <term>fructus</term>; the produce or profits from the land</note> he receives from that property toward the principal of the loan. This applies provided that in the meantime, while he holds the pledge and receives its income, he exempts the tenant from the service that the tenant owed him for the "useful ownership" <note>original: <term>utile dominium</term>; the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to "direct" ownership</note> of that property. However, if the owner either demands the service or accepts it when offered without declaring that he does not wish to receive it as a debt for the use or ownership of that property, then he is bound to count the income from that pledge toward the principal or return it to the tenant.

<margin>2</margin> The Doctors <note>learned legal and theological scholars</note> add that the teaching of those chapters is to be understood as applying when the tenant had not made improvements to the feudal property. For if the property yields 

<column-break/>

greater income by reason of those improvements, then the owner is bound to count that excess toward the principal or return it to the tenant. They also add that this should be understood as applying when the tenant gave no price for the fief (and you may add: nor was it given to him in compensation for some services or merits), but only in exchange for service or a pension to be provided in the future.
For if, by reason of a price or preceding merits, a smaller pension or lesser subsequent service was imposed on him from the beginning—such that he receives part of the income because of the price or preceding merits, and another part because of the pension or subsequent service—then it will be usury not to count the portion of the income corresponding to the price or preceding merits toward the principal, or not to deliver it to the tenant. Martin de Azpilcueta <note>referred to as "Nauarrus"</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 218, and others whom he cites, agree. Azpilcueta says the same regarding emphyteutic property <note>original: <term>emphyteusis</term>; a long-term lease where the tenant must improve the land and pay a small rent</note> in relation to the owner, and others he cites concur. Indeed, this is enacted in the 4th book of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, title 14, paragraph 4.

<margin>3</margin> There is, however, no small difficulty regarding the reason why usury does not occur in such a contract. The Gloss on the chapter *Conquestus* says this was granted as a privilege of the Church. Yet this is rightly rejected by the common opinion. For if usury occurs by the very nature of the thing, a privilege surely cannot make it lawful, as was said in Disputation 321. Therefore, the common opinion of the doctors affirms that this is lawful even when the property owner is not the Church but any layperson.
Soto in *De Iustitia*, book 6, question 1, article 2; Juan Medina in *De rebus per usuram acquisitis*, question 2; Conradus on contracts, question 32; and several others argue that this arises from the nature of the fief. It belongs to that nature that when the property is given as a pledge to the owner (who already holds the direct ownership), he can take its income without counting it toward the principal, while meanwhile remitting the burden the tenant owed by reason of the useful ownership.
Yet this, unless more is added, is surely not sufficient. For the tenant to concede the useful ownership for a time, being deprived of the income while the owner receives it, is something estimable in price. Thus, for the lender to receive that income without counting it toward the principal—or to impose that burden on the borrower by virtue of the loan (namely, that he must hand over a pledge and be deprived of its fruits)—seems by the very nature of the thing to contain the vice of usury. Covarruvias, after Adrian, says these two chapters are to be understood as applying when the income does not exceed the value of the service that is remitted to the tenant. Nevertheless, even this does not fully satisfy. For to force the tenant, because of a loan, to exchange those fruits for the remission of service is a burden estimable in money; and thus, the stain of usury is not avoided in that way either.

<margin>4</margin> Therefore, in this difficult matter, nothing more convenient occurs to me than what is said by John Major, Gabriel Biel, Jacques Almain, and certain others. Namely, that just as sometimes contracts of fiefs and emphyteusis...

<meta>catchword: first</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the morality of widow maintenance and whether certain feudal arrangements—where a lord receives land income instead of service during a loan—constitute usury. Molina argues that such swaps are generally lawful but must be balanced to avoid exploitation or hidden interest.</summary>
