<meta>This page continues a discussion on the financial arrangements between lords and tenants in feudal or long-term lease (emphyteutic) contracts, specifically addressing whether a lord can keep the profits of a pledged property without it being considered usury.</meta>

...initially instituted, they were instituted with certain conditions. If these were violated, the "useful ownership" <note>original: <term>dominium utile</term>; the right to use and profit from land owned by another</note> would be lost and would return to the owner. Thus, they could also be instituted with the condition that if a feudal or leased property were given as a pledge to the owner, the profits from it would belong to him, and he would not be bound to count those profits toward the principal debt, provided he remits the service or the pension <note>the annual rent or obligation</note>. It seems they were indeed instituted this way in practice, as is evident from the usage and declaration of those two types of rights.

The result is that it is not necessary to explicitly state this in a pact when the feudal or lease contract is first made (as Gabriel and Almainus seem to suggest in the cited passages), nor when the feudal or leased property is later handed over as a pledge to the owner.

Therefore, it must be said that the owner does not receive the profits (without counting them toward the principal) by virtue of a loan—for that would be usury—but by virtue of the nature of the feudal and lease contracts. Perhaps Sotus and Medina intended nothing else.

## Whether the Forfeiture Clause applies to pledges, and whether it is usurious.

# DISPUTATION 324.

### SUMMARY

1 **What is the "forfeiture clause" in sales? And what is it in pledges?** <note>original: <term>Pactum legis commissoriæ</term>; a clause providing that if a condition is not met, the property is forfeited</note>
3 **The forfeiture clause, when prohibited in pledges, is void.**
4 **A pact stating that if the debtor does not pay within the term, the pledge is sold at a fair price by the judgment of an honest man, is valid, even under the laws of Castile and Portugal.**
5 **Is it usury to lend with a pact that, if the debt is not paid within a certain time, the pledge remains sold at a fair price?**
6 **Whether a guarantor may lawfully agree with a debtor that if the debt is not paid within a fixed term, a pledge remains sold to him at a certain price.**

<margin>1</margin>
A "forfeiture clause" in sales occurs when something is sold with a pact or condition that if the buyer does not provide the price within a set term—such as within a month, a year, or another period fixed by the contracting parties—the item is considered "unsold."

In that case, if the buyer does not pay the price within that term, it is in the power of the seller, once the term has passed, either to keep or reclaim the item he sold (thereby dissolving the sale) or to compel the buyer to pay the price. This is because that pact was added solely for the benefit of the seller; hence, such a pact is valid in sales.

<margin>Digest, "on the forfeiture clause"</margin>
This is held in the first law and throughout the entire title of the Digest <note>original: <term>ff. de lege commissoria</term>; referring to Justinian’s Digest, Book 18, Title 3</note>, and all the Doctors [of law] agree.

<column-break/>

Thence, it was called a "forfeiture clause" because the item is sold under that law and condition so that, if the price is not paid within the prescribed time, the buyer falls into "forfeiture" <note>original: <term>commissum</term></note> and for that reason loses the item as if it had not been sold to him. This is similar to how a long-term tenant is said to fall into forfeiture and lose his lease when he fails to observe certain conditions, as will be discussed in its proper place.

<margin>2</margin>
In pledges, however, the forfeiture clause occurs when someone receives a pledge for a loan (or any other debt) under the law and condition that, if the debtor does not pay the debt within a certain time, the pledge becomes the property of the creditor for that debt, or is considered bought at some other fixed and determined price—as if the debtor, by the very fact that he did not pay within the fixed time, falls into forfeiture and thus loses the pledge.

<margin>3</margin>
This pact is condemned and rendered void in pledges by the final and first laws of the Code <note>original: <term>C. de pactis pignorum</term>; Code of Justinian, Book 8, Title 34</note>, by the chapter *Significante* on pledges, by Law 41, Title 5 and Law 12, Title 13 of the Fifth Part <note>The *Siete Partidas* of Spain</note>, and in the beginning of Title 26 of Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances. Indeed, if the pledge were worth more than that price, and that pact were added as a profit from the loan or from the delay of payment, it would be usury, regardless of any positive law prohibiting such a pact.

<margin>4</margin>
To avoid this and other evils, such a pact in pledges has been rightly prohibited and made void by the cited laws. Consequently, even if a debtor oversteps the fixed term, he can reclaim his pledge once the debt is paid. [However, if the creditor suffered any "lost profit" or "emergent loss" <note>original: <term>lucrum cessans</term> or <term>damnum emergens</term></note> because of the delay, the debtor is bound to compensate him for it, as was stated in Disputations 315 and 299.]

Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis, a famous canonist</note> observes in the cited chapter *Significante*, number 6, that if the pact is that—should the debtor fail to pay within the term—the pledge is sold, not at some fixed and determined price, but at a "fair price" according to the judgment of an honest man, then such a pact is valid.

<margin>5</margin>
This is now defined today by the cited laws of Castile and in the Portuguese Ordinances, in the cited title, paragraph 1: let the pledge be appraised by two honest men. In this process, it is established that once the term has passed, the creditor chooses one man and the debtor the other, and an oath is administered to them that they will appraise the price sincerely. In the same place, paragraph 2, it is added: if the pact is that the pledge is sold for a fair price to be appraised at the *discretion of the creditor*, such a pact is automatically null, even if they agreed that an oath would be taken before the price was appraised. Baco a Pagor, cited there and by others, says that if the pact was that the pledge, once the term passed, would "remain sold," it is valid; for the meaning would be that it remains sold at a fair price to be appraised by the judgment of an honest man. This opinion is pleasing; it is the common view and is approved by Covarruvias among others in his *Variarum Resolutionum*, Book 3, Chapter 2, at the end of number 7.

There has been no lack of those who argued against what has been said so far in this manner: It is usury (they say) to obligate a debtor to sell a pledge because of a loan or a delay in payment, even at a fair price, just as it is usury to obligate someone to enter into...

It notes that such clauses are only valid in pledges if the property is sold at a fair market value determined by impartial appraisers.</summary>

...as an insurance contract <note>original: "contractum assecutationis"</note>, as was shown in Disputation 318. Therefore, it is usury to lend with an agreement that, if the debt is not paid within a certain time, the pledge remains sold at a fair price.

To this, Covarruvias responds in the place cited, §. It would be usury if this were done as a burden for the loan, and imposed as a profit from the loan. If, however, it is done so that the creditor keeps himself free from loss <note>original: "indemnem servet"</note>, and by that path receives compensation at the deadline for the thing owed to him, there is no usury. He adds that such a burden can even be lawfully enjoined upon the debtor as a just penalty if he does not pay the debt at the appointed time, as Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer</note> well noted in his *Manual*, chapter 17, numbers 203 and 217.

<margin>Question 6</margin> The question is whether at least a guarantor <note>original: <term>fideiussor</term>; someone who guarantees another's debt</note> can lawfully agree with the debtor that, if the debt is not paid within the fixed term, the pledge shall remain sold to him at a certain price. Whatever <margin>Satisfaction</margin> Covarruvias says in the cited place, certainly this type of contract is not disapproved, but rather permitted and approved by civil law (the last law of the Code on contracting a sale). I would inquire: if the price is fair, or if it is joined to the debtor who <unclear>desires it</unclear> as a just penalty—so that the pledge would truly be his at that lower price—or if the guarantee were worthy of such compensation, I would not dare to disapprove of such a pact, according to what was said in the preceding disputations. Nevertheless, it is always advised that men abstain from such pacts. Regarding the contract of a pledge, it will be discussed below in its proper place.

->### DISPUTATION 325.<-

->### SUMMARY.<-

1 What a Mount of Piety <note>original: <term>mons pietatis</term>; a charitable pawnshop that lent money at low interest to the poor</note> is, and what its laws are.
2 Whether a Mount of Piety can lawfully receive anything beyond the principal.
3 The penalty of excommunication "already passed" <note>original: <term>latae sententiae</term>; a penalty that follows automatically upon the commission of an act</note> decreed by Leo X against those who argue or preach against the Mounts of Piety.

<margin>1</margin> Lastly, we must dispute concerning the Mount of Piety: whether it is usurious, or rather lawful and holy. The Mount of Piety is in use especially among the Italians. For when those in need of money were being oppressed by the usury of the Hebrews, and others were forced to sell clothes and other things they had bought at a great price for very little to meet their needs for a short time; to avoid these and many other evils, the so-called Mounts of Piety were erected at the persuasion of preachers and other pious men. They are <sig>M</sig> <column-break/> nothing other than a certain sum of money publicly set aside to help those in need through a loan, so that by this means greater evils and losses might be avoided.

Moreover, that money was usually gathered from the contributions of private individuals, each according to their devotion, whether by a gift among the living or by a last will; sometimes even the republic designated it from the common goods for that purpose.

The laws of these Mounts were that, from that money, a loan would be given to individual needy persons up to a certain sum, to be repaid within a year or two, with pledges left that were worth that amount.

But if they did not return the money within the prescribed term, the pledges were immediately sold, and the loan was paid from the price and replaced in the Mount; the increase in price <note>the profit from the sale over the loan amount</note>, however, was returned to the owners of the pledges.

Because, however, ministers were necessary to have care of this money, and to give and receive it in loan, and to guard the pledges, and to return them to the owners or sell them and receive the payment of the loan—who certainly needed a competent salary; and because expenses were also necessary for renting a house in which the money and pledges would be kept, and where those needing a loan would come; and also for buying account books, a chest for keeping the money, and other instruments for carrying out that business: lest the money of the Mount gradually decrease and finally be consumed by all these expenses, it was ordained that each borrower should contribute a small amount each month beyond the principal <note>original: <term>sortem</term>; the principal sum of the loan</note> in proportion to the sum they received in loan—precisely as much as, by a prudent judgment, would suffice for all those expenses. Thus, neither would the money of the Mount increase from the loan, nor would it decrease, but it would be preserved perpetually in the same state for the benefit of the needy.

<margin>2</margin> And regarding this last law alone, there was once a controversy: whether such an acceptance of that small amount beyond the principal for those expenses and ends was lawful, or whether it was truly unlawful and usurious. This controversy has persisted among some even to our own times, despite the fact that Leo X, in the Lateran Council <note>The Fifth Lateran Council, 1515</note> with the approval of the same sacred Council, defined and declared that Mounts of Piety erected and instituted under the explained form are lawful. <unclear>And in the second volume, opuscule tract 6.</unclear> Therefore, Cajetan in his second volume, tract 6, and Soto in his sixth book *On Justice*, question 1, article 6, contend that usury intervenes in that reception beyond the principal for those expenses. They argue those expenses—at least insofar as they are ordained toward the preservation of that money (as in the opinion of Cajetan and Soto)—ought to be made from the Mount itself or from elsewhere, and not by the borrowers contributing to it, because to receive an increase for that reason is usury.

They prove this because if some wealthy man had set aside some money in that way for several years, retaining ownership of it, he would certainly be a usurer if he received any increase from the borrowers for those expenses; since the expenses for preserving his own money belong not to the borrowers but to himself, even if he has it set aside for a loan for their sake. Therefore, although he has abdicated ownership of it...

...[had grant]ed it; and he transferred it to the state, which granted it specifically for that use: so that it will pertain to the state itself to make those expenditures from that same money, or from elsewhere, rather than to the borrowers. For that reason, if the state receives anything from them beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note>, it commits usury. But if, says Sotus <note>Domingo de Soto, a 16th-century Spanish Dominican theologian</note>, that money belongs to no one, it will fall to the fund itself to preserve itself; and thus it will belong to the administrators to make the necessary expenditures from it, with nothing hindering the fact that, while the purpose for which it was left is being carried out, it is gradually consumed.

Johannes Medina (in *On things acquired through usury*, question 10) and Navarrus (in his commentary *On Usury*, from number 64) affirm the contrary opinion, which Navarrus also touches upon in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 213; and this view is undoubtedly to be embraced. For just as it is lawful to receive something from borrowers by reason of lost profit <note>original: <term>lucrum cessans</term></note> or emerging loss <note>original: <term>damnum emergens</term></note>, as was shown in the preceding disputations, and no usury is seen in that—because it is not received "for the loan," but on the "occasion of the loan" from a far different title—so it is right for the lender to wish to lend on no other condition than by entering into a tacit or express agreement that he be kept free from loss. For that reason, he can lawfully receive from them the loss that arises for him, or the profit that ceases for him, because of the loan.

In the same way, it is right to receive from borrowers all the expenses that are incurred so that a loan may always be kept ready in their favor and given to them when they wish. For he who provides the benefit of a loan is not bound to undergo those expenses; rather, it is right for him to bring those expenses into an agreement with the borrowers, so that if they wish to receive a loan prepared out of charity solely for their own convenience, they should pay them; otherwise, they should refrain from taking the loan. Thus it happens that, by commutative justice <note>justice regarding private exchanges and contracts</note> in that event, the borrowers are bound to pay them—not indeed by the power of the loan itself (as if, excluding every other contract, they were bound to them from the loan alone), but by the power of another just contract. By this contract, according to natural law, a loan is prepared for their benefit if they are willing to contribute proportionately to the expenses made for that same benefit. It is no less worthy to bargain for these expenses than for lost profit or emerging loss by reason of the loan.

In this place, observe: just as one who keeps a loan for a longer time usually pays more for lost profit (because a greater profit usually ceases for the lender over a longer time), so also equity demands that one who keeps an equal quantity of money as a loan from a <term>Monte di Pietà</term> <note>literally "Mount of Piety," a charitable pawnshop that provided low-interest loans to the poor to protect them from usurers</note> for more months should contribute more, at a rate based on the time, toward those same common expenses of the Mount. This is because he acts as an impediment, preventing those who would contribute to those same expenses from receiving that money during those months.

And from this, the objection of the adversaries ceases, by which they say it should not be enjoined that those who keep money as a loan for a longer time should contribute more.

Add that, since in these matters—due to the variety of circumstances—a perfect equality cannot be reached, it is enough to establish reasonable laws

<column-break/>

which, as much as the nature of the thing allows, preserve equality.

Nor is there any reason for the borrowers to complain about them, especially since none of them is forced to enter into such a contract, and since all these things are organized so that the borrowers themselves may be freed by that means from far greater burdens and costs.

In confirmation of this opinion, it is added that, with the approval of the sacred Lateran Council <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517)</note>, it was defined by Leo X in session 10, with the established penalty of a sentence of excommunication <note>original: "excommunicationis latae sententiae"</note> for those who dared to preach or dispute anything to the contrary, whether by word or in writing. There, Leo X also affirms that the Mounts of Piety were approved by his predecessors—Paul II, Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII, Alexander VI, and Julius II—with indulgences granted in their favor.

And indeed, Cajetan and Sotus (which I say with all due respect to such most learned men who have deserved well of Theology and the Christian religion) speak with too little reverence and too much boldness regarding the definition of the Supreme Pontiff and a General Council pertaining to morals. They restrict more than is just the power that exists in the Church for defining and declaring what pertains to faith and morals; nor is their opinion safe. Furthermore, what Sotus says—namely, that many things of that Council were not accepted—is frivolous.

For although statutes which are of human law cease to have force if they are not accepted, nevertheless the definitions and declarations of those things which pertain to faith and morals, if they are of a Council and the Supreme Pontiff, do not depend on "acceptance" to be most certain in themselves.

Moreover, the other evasions of Cajetan and Sotus—namely, that the intention of the Supreme Pontiff and the Council was not to approve the laws and chapters of the Mount of Piety except with the limitation "insofar as they were not contrary to the sacred canons"—are surely of no weight.

For in that session, the controversy is expressly disputed for both sides: whether it be right to receive anything from borrowers beyond the principal for those expenses; and the affirmative was defined. Add, however, that it is better if those who erect such Mounts of Piety would leave some revenues to pay those expenditures.

Finally, that which is clear enough from what has been said must be observed: it is not lawful to bargain for and demand anything beyond the principal to *increase* the Mount of Piety, or for anything else other than precisely for necessary expenses. For in that which would be received above that, manifest usury would intervene.

To the argument to the contrary: although some attempt to deny the premise, it is clear enough from the reasoning we have constructed that it must be denied fearlessly.

For although it pertains to the owner of the money to make the expenditures necessary for the conservation of his money, and he cannot bring them into an agreement to be paid by the borrowers when he has not directed them toward the loan and the convenience of the borrowers; nevertheless, when they are precisely made...

### Whether the usurer acquires ownership of those things which he acquires through usury.

<column-break/>

1 Consequently, we must examine whether the usurer acquires ownership <note>original: <term>dominium</term></note> of those things which he acquires through usury. The Gloss on the chapter *si quis usuram*, fourteenth, fourth question; Scotus in the fourth, distinction fifteen, second question, third article; Paludanus in the same distinction and question, fifth article; Hadrian on restitution in the matter of usury; and many other interpreters of Canon Law affirm that he does acquire ownership.

2 This can be argued for. First, because (as in the *Institutes* on the division of things, paragraph "through delivery") the ownership of a thing is acquired through delivery <note>original: <term>traditio</term>, the legal transfer of a physical item</note>, and this reason is given there: because nothing is so agreeable to natural equity as to hold as valid the will of an owner who wishes to transfer his property to another. Therefore, since the borrower, by his own will, delivers the usurious profit to the lender (which belonged to the borrower), it follows that the lender acquires ownership of it.

Nor does it stand in the way that such a delivery is "mixed involuntary" <note>An action done under duress, such as throwing cargo overboard to save a ship; it is "involuntary" in spirit but "voluntary" in the moment of choice</note>. For as Aristotle says in the third book of the *Ethics*, chapter one, such an act is simply voluntary, and only involuntary in a certain respect; not unlike the will of one who, compelled by a storm, throws his goods into the sea, which is simply voluntary.

3 Second, one who gives or delivers a thing out of fear—even the kind of fear that would affect a steadfast man—transfers ownership of it to the recipient. This is gathered from the chapter *Abbas*, concerning things done through force or fear, and is noted there by the Gloss and the Doctors generally. For the text says: those things done through force or fear ought by law to be revoked as void; as if by the law itself they were not void and null, but must be made void and revoked by the authority of a judge. However, the Gloss there excepts certain events in which things done through force or fear are null by the law itself.

From this, the argument is constructed: it is seen to be no less involuntary and against one's will when something is extorted through fear than when something is received on account of a loan; but ownership is acquired of that which is extorted through fear, with nothing preventing it from being subject to restitution; therefore, the same applies to that which is received on account of a loan.

7 Third, if on account of the "mixed involuntary" nature seen in the payment of usury, ownership were not transferred to the recipient, it would follow that it is also not transferred when something is sold in a "mixed involuntary" manner—such as when someone, pressed by the necessity of money, sells a thing which he otherwise would in no way have sold. But the consequence is manifestly false, and against common usage and the common opinion of the learned; therefore, so is the premise. The logic is proven because there is no greater reason why a mixed involuntary act should impede the transfer of ownership in one case than in the other.

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate regarding the acquisition of property. On the previous page, the author was laying out arguments for why a usurer might be considered the legal owner of property gained through interest. This page concludes those arguments and then shifts to the contrary—and preferred—opinion that usury never transfers true ownership.</meta>

-> Second Treatise, Disputation 326 <-

...the law prohibits receiving it, and therefore resists the acquisition. However, for a law to prohibit a thing or resist it does not always prevent the transfer of ownership <term>dominium; the legal right to possess and use property</term>, even if the thing is handed over in a manner contrary to the law. This is evident because a person who has taken a vow of chastity, although they sin against divine law by contracting a marriage, nevertheless remains in a valid marriage, and the other spouse acquires power over their body. It is also evident because if someone sells a thing to one person but has not yet delivered it, and then—though sinning against natural law—sells and delivers that same thing to a second person, the second buyer nonetheless acquires ownership through that delivery, as was stated in Disputation 2. Therefore, the usurer acquires ownership of the thing acquired through usury.

Fifth, if the usurer did not acquire ownership of the things he acquires through usury, it would follow that all subsequent contracts he celebrated regarding those things with others would be void and null. Thus, if a usurer sold bread or wine for money he had acquired through usury, he would be bound to restore that money to the person from whom he had originally taken it as usury. This is because the ownership would still reside with that original person—just as the ownership of a stolen thing remains with its original owner no matter whose hands it falls into or by what title it was passed, and must therefore be restored to him. Such a consequence, however, seems most absurd.

<margin>4</margin> The **contrary opinion**—namely, that the usurer does *not* acquire ownership of the thing acquired through usury, but that it remains with the giver—is held by St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian</note> in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, question 78, article 3. There, he says the usurer is bound to restore the fruits <note>original: "fructus"; the profits or products derived from an asset, such as crops from a field or rent from a house</note> of a thing acquired through usury that is not consumed by use, because they are the fruits of a thing whose ownership remains with the person from whom it was taken through usury.

The reasoning is exactly the same regarding the ownership of things that *are* consumed by use—such as money, wheat, wine, oil, etc.—which are acquired through usury. St. Thomas implied this in the same place in his response to the third point. And although in the *Commentary on the Sentences* (Book 4, distinction 15, question 2, article 4) he seems to say that the usurer acquires ownership of things gained through usury, he is not speaking there from his own settled opinion, as is clear from his addition of the phrase, "as some say." Later, in the *Summa* cited above, he expressed his own definitive view.

Alexander of Hales, William of Auxerre, Cajetan, Soto, Juan Medina, Covarruvias, Gabriel Biel, John Major, Jacques Almain, Angelus de Clavasio, Silvester Prierias, and many others are of this same opinion.

Accessing this same view are seen to be 

<column-break/>

St. Bonaventure and Richard of Middleton. And this is, without a doubt, the view we must embrace.

It can be proved, first, because—as stated in the law *Nunquam* in the Digest <note>A reference to Roman Civil Law: Digest 41.1.31</note>—a bare delivery never transfers ownership unless a sale or some other **just cause** (that is, another just title) has preceded it. But the title by which something is received due to a loan or a usurious agreement is **unjust and null** by natural, divine, and human law (both canon law and the specific civil laws of Christian kingdoms), as was seen in Disputation 304. Therefore, the usurer does not acquire ownership of the thing acquired through usury. I know that the Gloss <note>Standard legal commentary</note> and Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous medieval jurist</note> explain that law as referring to a cause that is truly just or *thought* to be so; for they say that when a non-existent debt is paid, ownership is transferred even if a true just cause did not intervene, provided it was believed to be such.

However, in the matter proposed, it is now well-established that a usurious title is unjust and null; therefore, in a usurious acceptance, a cause *thought* to be just cannot intervene. Thus, the doctrine of the Gloss and Bartolus does not conflict with our opinion.

<margin>2</margin> Furthermore, it seems improbable to me that—by the very nature of the thing and in the "court of conscience" <note>An internal moral judgment before God, rather than a legal court</note>—when someone pays a non-existent debt believing they owe it, ownership is transferred to the receiver, regardless of what the external court says. Thus, before prescription <note>Acquiring a right through the passage of time</note> occurs, the person to whom a non-existent debt was paid (believing it was owed) does not acquire ownership.

<margin>1</margin> Second, if a usurer acquires some productive thing through usury, such as a field, he is bound to restore not only the field itself but also the fruits gathered from it (minus expenses), as even the authors of the contrary opinion admit. But there is no other reason why he should be bound to restore the **fruits** except for that which St. Thomas gives in the cited article: namely, because the ownership of the field does not belong to the usurer, but to the person who gave it to him for the loan. This is because the fruits of a thing belong to its owner. Therefore, the usurer does not acquire ownership of the thing he gets through usury.

If you were to say that the usurer is bound to restore those fruits by reason of the **delay** <note>original: "mora"; a legal term for a failure to perform an obligation on time</note> in restoring the thing to which the fruits belong, because he prevents the borrower from gathering the fruits...

...then it would follow that if the borrower had not intended to cultivate that field or would not have gathered so many fruits from it, the usurer would not be bound to restore more to him than he would have gathered. For a delay in restoring a thing—where ownership belongs to the one bound to restore it—only induces an obligation to restore the *damage* following from that delay to the person to whom the thing was to be restored.

<margin>3</margin> Third, no less is required to transfer the ownership of a thing to another than to renounce one's own right and grant it to the other regarding that thing; for ownership...

<sig>M 3</sig>

### Luis Molina on Contracts

...is more than a mere right, as is established from the stated Disputations 2 and 3. However, the payment of usury is not sufficient for the borrower <term>mutuatarius; the person receiving a loan</term> to be considered to have renounced his right in the thing <note>original: "ius in rem"</note> which he pays, or for that right to be considered transferred to the usurer. Otherwise, the usurer would not be bound to restore that specific thing to the borrower. Therefore, it is even less sufficient for transferring ownership <term>dominium; the full legal right to a property</term> over it.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
Furthermore, if the usurer were to acquire ownership of a thing acquired through usury, and the borrower were to lose it, the usurer would not be bound to restore the *exact same thing* <note>original: "eandem numero rem"</note> which he received on account of the loan, but only its value. Yet, no one would grant this conclusion.

Finally, if the usurer were the owner of the money or other property he had acquired through usury, then surely if he had certain privileged creditors—or those who held a general mortgage <term>hypotheca; a legal claim against property as security for a debt</term> on his goods—those creditors would have to be preferred. Thus, they would be paid from the money or other goods acquired through usury before the borrowers to whom those goods originally belonged. However, no one would grant this either.

<margin>An Answer</margin>
This consequence is proven because, as we shall see in Disputation 86, when dealing with assets belonging to a debtor, privileged creditors or those holding a mortgage must be preferred over others. If those who paid usury do not retain ownership of the things they paid, we certainly know of no privilege granted to them by law whereby they should be preferred over other creditors in the distribution of those assets.

<margin>6</margin>
However, it must be observed in this place that sometimes a usurer becomes the owner of usurious money "by accident," because of the mixing <note>original: "commixtionem"</note> of that money with other legitimate money. For example, if one hundred units were owed to him—which he had given as a loan with a pact that one hundred and ten be restored—and the borrower sends him one hundred and ten without specifying which are for the principal and which are for the interest, then by receiving them, he becomes the owner of both the principal and the interest. This is because one cannot be distinguished from the other; in such an instance, the larger quantity prevails and causes the ownership of the whole to belong to him who acquires ownership of the greater part of it.

The same would apply if a usurer mixes a quantity of usurious money with a large amount of his own other money so that it cannot be distinguished. In that case, he becomes the owner of what he acquired through usury, as is gathered from the section "Furthermore, what by alluvion" <note>original: "§. præterea quod per alluionem," referring to Roman law on property accretion</note> and the following sections of the *Institutes on the Division of Things*. This was also discussed in Disputation 57.

I believe, however, that if the "pile" <term>aceruus; a collective sum or physical heap of coins</term> of money remains, the borrower then has a right in the thing so that he may be repaid from it—before all other creditors—the amount he paid beyond the principal. It is treated as something belonging to another mixed in there, which can be separated from the whole by a judge’s decree without detriment to the entire pile. Note that when two people mix money or something else by mutual consent, both remain owners of the resulting pile, to be divided between them at the proper time; any loss to the pile then affects both. All this is gathered from the section "But if the grain" <note>original: "§. quod si frumentum"</note> in the *Institutes on the Division of Things*. Read what was said in the cited Disputation.

<column-break/>

From this, it is clear that if a usurer spends money from an entire pile in which usurious money is mixed—and of which the usurer holds ownership—by buying, donating, or some other similar means, he transfers ownership of the money he thus spends to the recipients. This is because he is giving what was legally his. I think, however, that as long as the pile of money from which he spends remains "the same in number" as it was when the usurious money was mixed into it, the borrower retains a right to compensation from that pile. Even if the pile is slightly changed by adding or taking away money (in the same way that a fire, which is continuously fueled by logs, is said to be the "same fire" even though parts are successively destroyed and others generated), the borrower retains a right in that pile of assets, wherever it may be and into whomever's power it comes, so that the usury he paid may be returned to him before all other creditors.

The situation would be different if that pile were gradually consumed, so that the pile in no one's possession was the "same in number" as the one that existed when the usurious money was mixed in. In that case, the right in the thing <note>original: "ius in re"</note> would cease, and the borrower would only have a "personal action" <term>personalis actio; a lawsuit against a specific person rather than a claim on a specific object</term> against the usurer and his heirs to be restored what he paid as usury. He would have no right of preference to be paid from the usurer’s goods before other creditors. These points are quite useful for understanding when people celebrating contracts—whether for profit or exchange—with usurers are bound to restore to the borrowers what they received from the usurers.

To the first argument of the opposing opinion, one must deny that delivery <term>traditio</term> is sufficient for the transfer of ownership unless a "just title" <term>iustus titulus; a valid legal reason like a sale or gift</term> is present at the same time, as has been shown. Regarding the cited testimony, it must be said that it speaks of the "will" of an owner delivering his property under a just or sufficient title for transferring ownership. For if someone delivers his property as a price for something not worth that price, surely that "will" is not held as valid. Nor can the authors of the contrary opinion assert that the borrower's will is valid in the matter we are discussing; indeed, they admit that the usury paid is still owed to the borrower and that he can reclaim it from the usurer. This arises only because the "will" with which he paid it was not ratified or sufficient to renounce his right to the thing and transfer it to the lender.

As for the point added regarding "involuntary mixing," it must be said that although it may be "voluntary in a certain respect" <note>original: "secundum quid"</note>, if it is nonetheless unjustly extorted—because one is forced to give through fear, or because one gives a price for a thing not worth it because he cannot obtain it otherwise—such an "involuntary" act is not sufficient to transfer ownership, even if it is simply "voluntary" at the moment. The reason is that it cannot create a "just title." In this place, observe that if a title is partly just and partly unjust, ownership is transferred by delivery, but with an obligation on the part of the recipient to restore enough so that the title is made entirely just.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 326

For example, if someone buys something below the **just price**, whether in terms of the money paid or the value of the item, ownership <term>dominium; legal title and right of possession</term> is indeed transferred. However, in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "in conscientiæ foro"; the internal moral judgment of a person, usually in the context of confession, rather than a civil court</note>, the buyer is bound to increase the price until it reaches at least the lowest level of what is considered "just."

If, however, something were sold for *more* than the just price, and the money were paid in installments such that the full rigorous just price was reached first, and only afterward was the "surplus" paid—then certainly the ownership of that surplus would no more pass to the seller than the ownership of interest passes to a usurer.

The reason is that after the final just price has been reached, there is no longer any **just title** <note>a legal basis for ownership</note> on the part of the seller to receive that surplus. But when the entire price is paid at once, such that it cannot be distinguished what was paid toward the just price and what was paid as a surplus above the just price, then the same must be said as we stated above regarding when a loan and its interest are paid to a usurer at the same time.

To the second point, it must be denied that a donor or a person delivering property through fear unjustly inflicted transfers ownership. As for the chapter titled *Abbas* <note>Referring to the famous canonist Panormitanus, often called "The Abbot"</note>, it should be said that his words are as follows: *those things which are done through fear and force ought, by right, to be revoked as void* (interpret this as being hollow in themselves). This does not mean the contract was "invalid" in the sense that it would be valid if a judge didn't interfere; rather, the judge pronounces it void and commands that it be possessed such that it is immediately restored, as the same text adds immediately after. Thus, it follows from that text that ownership was not considered transferred in that event.

It would indeed be a wonder if ownership were transferred in a "mixed" involuntary act <note>an act where one chooses the lesser of two evils, like throwing cargo overboard in a storm</note>, while the law clearly teaches the opposite. See the law on fear <note>original: "l. metum, §. uolenti, & multo aperte §. licet, ff. quod metus causa"</note>, where it is taught that a thing given through force remains among the goods of the one who suffered the violence. For that reason, the victim is granted not only a **personal action** <note>a lawsuit against a specific person</note> but also a **real action** <note>original: "realis actio"; a lawsuit to reclaim the specific physical object itself</note> to claim the thing as his own property. Another thing can be said, which is perhaps more accommodated to the laws:

<margin>7</margin> According to **civil law**, by a fiction of that same law, ownership of a thing given and delivered through force or fear is deemed to have been transferred. For that reason, civil law does not grant a real action, but a personal one; nor is that contract considered invalid "by the law itself" <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>, but rather it must be annulled by a judge's sentence after the quality and quantity of the fear have been examined. This is because not just any fear is sufficient to pronounce a contract invalid; a greater degree of fear is required to invalidate one contract than another—especially to pronounce a **marriage** invalid, which by its nature is irrevocable and indissoluble. Indeed, looking only at the nature of the thing itself and standing only on **natural law**, no amount of fear would make a marriage null; rather, it was **positive law** <note>human-made law, like Church or state law</note> that made it invalid "by the law itself" when it was celebrated through "fear that might overcome a steadfast man" <note>original: "metum cadentem in constantem uirum"; a standard legal test for whether coercion was severe enough to void a contract</note>. This matter is to be disputed in its proper place.

Although ownership is transferred in the manner explained under civil law when something is delivered through force, and a contract celebrated through force or fear is not null by the law itself but must be revoked by a judge's authority, later in **Praetorian law** <note>laws established by Roman magistrates (Praetors) to supplement or correct the rigid civil law</note>, in accordance with the nature of the thing and equity,

<column-break/>

it was introduced that a contract celebrated through force or sufficient fear would be null by the law itself, and it was pronounced that ownership of the thing thus given remained with the giver. A real action was granted to reclaim it, as is clear from the two cited sections of the Digest on the cause of fear. This is the view of Bartolus and, after him, Panormitanus, which is consistent with the text there. According to these views, Panormitanus says that the teachings in the cited chapter *Abbas* must be understood and limited.

I believe that the Supreme Pontiff, in the chapter *Abbas*, intended nothing other than what we explained just above: because he spoke after Praetorian law was introduced and in accordance with it.

<margin>8</margin> Therefore, by the nature of the thing and in the **court of conscience**—and even externally according to Praetorian law—ownership is not considered transferred when something is given and delivered through force or sufficient fear. It was only formerly deemed transferred by a fiction of civil law, as the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous canonist</note> noted, whom Angelus and Sylvester follow and cite in the mentioned places.

Therefore, **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto, a prominent 16th-century Spanish theologian</note> undeservedly departed from our opinion (which he had followed in his earlier work *On Justice and Right*). He claimed that donation and other contracts celebrated through "fear that might overcome a steadfast man" are valid, but are to be annulled by a judge's sentence, according to the cited chapter *Abbas*.

<margin>11</margin> He affirmed this opinion in order to defend the idea that a marriage celebrated through such fear is valid under natural law alone, and is only invalid because of positive law. Although we are not entirely inclined toward that opinion, the contrary view has always pleased me and many others; this will be examined in the section on marriage.

Even if in marriage—because of its indissolubility and other privileges it has by its nature above all other contracts—the opinion Soto devised were proven, I would never consider it preferable in a **donation**. A donation, to be valid, requires more liberty and voluntary will than other contracts, because it is a purely lucrative contract and an act of liberality, entirely without any mixture of justice between the giver and the recipient.

<margin>9</margin> To the third point, it must be said that not just *any* "mixed" involuntary act vitiates a contract. For instance, a "mixed" involuntary act is seen in one who gives a gift to entice someone to his own ends—such as a woman to fornication, or a rich man to provide a loan—where he would not give if he knew they could not be moved by that path. Such a motive neither vitiates the donation nor prevents the transfer of ownership, as was said in Disputation 286. This is because the person simply wills to give, having considered all the concurrent circumstances, and is not deceived in anything that would support the giving. But if he knew that force was present, his "habitual will" would not be to give. On this basis, the donation can be considered void by itself, as was said in Disputation 209 and the two following, and in Disputation 286; and likewise to...

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...is induced to give through force or fear unjustly applied, for which reason the donation could be voided; in this way, the **involuntary nature** observed in one who, pressed by necessity, sells a thing which he otherwise would not have sold, does not void the sale. This is because, simply speaking, having weighed all the circumstances that actually occur, he *wills* to sell. Furthermore, he is not ignorant of any aspect of the object (which would otherwise undermine the sale), nor is he induced to sell by fear or force unjustly applied in a way that would void the contract. Moreover, from the perspective of the object, there is an equality between the payment and the price.

<margin>8</margin> Therefore, regarding the formal argument, the logical consequence must be denied if that consequence is understood to refer to what is explicitly "involuntary." However, to better understand why that consequence is invalid, observe that a **usurious payment** does not transfer ownership <term>dominium; legal title and right of possession</term> for this reason: because that which is paid as usury <note>original: "in usuram"; interest on a loan</note> is a price given for a thing that is worth no price at all. For this reason, the acceptance is unjust across the entire breadth of what is given, regardless of how much "voluntary" intent might intervene on the part of the giver in that specific manner or view.

<margin>9</margin> But if the usurer contends that a **donation** is occurring there—since the borrower voluntarily gives what he sees is not owed—then we say: the promise and payment of usury is "involuntary" in the sense of a donation. It is unjustly extorted as a price and compensation for the loan, even if it is demanded by the usurer under the name of a "donation" and granted by the borrower under that same name. This holds as long as the act itself does not proceed from the gratitude and pure liberality of the borrower. We say that this kind of **mixed involuntary** action <note>A philosophical concept where an action is willed only to avoid a worse evil, like throwing cargo overboard during a storm</note>, which is unjustly extorted and accepted by the usurer, is incapable of transferring ownership. Taking the premise in this sense, if the proposed argument were valid, it could similarly be proved that usury is not illicit, and that what was received as usury would not be subject to restitution. One could argue that if usury were illicit because of this "mixed involuntary" state, then that other sale [out of necessity] would also be illicit, and what was received from it would be subject to restitution. Since the doctors of the contrary opinion are bound to concede that the argument lacks the power to prove these latter two points, they must necessarily admit that it also lacks the power to prove that ownership is transferred by the payment of usury. Whatever they would answer to the argument as formulated in the latter case can be used as an answer when it is formulated to prove that usury transfers ownership.

<margin>10</margin> To the fourth point, it must be said that **natural law** <note>original: "ius naturale"; universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature</note> resists an action or acceptance in two ways. First, because that action is by its very nature void under natural law for the purpose of transferring ownership. Second, because although the act is inherently capable of transferring a right and ownership to another, it nevertheless results in injury to another or is rendered evil for some other reason. Now, natural law resists the payment and reception of usury in the **first way**, as is clear from what has been said, and for that reason, ownership is not transferred.

However, natural law resists in the **second way** in those two other scenarios proposed in the argument, which is why it is no surprise that a right and ownership are transferred in those cases. For through the sale of a thing, unless delivery follows or the thing is subjected to a mortgage

<insert>M</insert> <note>This "M" is a signature mark for the printer to keep track of the gathering of pages</note>

<column-break/>

for the buyer, the buyer only acquires a **right to the thing** <note>original: "ius ad rem"; a personal claim against the seller</note> but not a **right in the thing** <note>original: "ius in re"; a property right that holds against everyone</note>, as was shown in Disputation 2. Therefore, the thing itself does not remain obligated to the buyer, but only the person of the seller is obligated to deliver it to him and to transfer ownership of it, provided it is within the seller's power. Because the thing remains the property of the seller and is "free" in itself, and because the sale of a free thing by its owner—accompanied by delivery—is capable of transferring ownership, it follows that even if the seller sins against natural law by selling it to a **second buyer**, he nevertheless transfers ownership to him. This is because natural law and positive law <note>man-made laws, like civil or canon law</note> do not resist the second sale by stripping it of the power to transfer ownership (which it has by its nature), but only through the resulting guilt, insofar as it is done to the injury of the first buyer. In the same way, a commandment against selling in a sacred place or on a feast day does not resist a sale in such a place or time as if to prevent the transfer of ownership, but only so that guilt results from that sale.

In the same way, because a **simple vow** of chastity does not involve a delivery [of oneself] to God in the same way a **solemn vow** does—since a simple vow of chastity has not yet been accepted by the Church in the way a solemn one has—it follows that a simple vow of chastity does not render a marriage contract void (through which the mutual delivery of bodies between spouses occurs), whereas a solemn vow of chastity does render it void, as will be discussed in its proper place.

<margin>11</margin> Note, however, that the power exists in the **Supreme Pontiff** to invalidate a marriage after a certain simple vow of chastity. For example, **Gregory XIII** <note>Pope from 1572–1585</note> invalidated marriages following the simple vow of chastity taken by those in the **Society of Jesus** <note>The Jesuits, Molina's own order</note> who have not yet made their profession, after two years of probation. Just as the **Council of Trent** <note>1545–1563; a major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church</note> invalidated clandestine marriages because it was expedient for the Church to avoid the grave evils arising from them, so too, because it was judged useful for the Church, Gregory XIII invalidated any marriage that might be attempted after such a simple vow of chastity was issued in the Society of Jesus.

What should be said regarding the fifth argument will be made clear from the following disputations.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 327.

<margin>5</margin>
**Concerning things acquired through usury which are not consumed by use.**
† If a usurer, by trading with things consumed by use that were acquired through usury, acquires something further, he gains legal ownership of it; however, he is bound to restore to the borrower all "emerging loss" and "lost profit" <note>original: "damnum emergens & lucrum cessans"; these are the two standard categories of legal damages: actual loss incurred and the profit one was prevented from making</note> because he did not restore the usurious interest. The same must be said of a depositary <note>one who holds property for another</note>. (number 6). Indeed, the same applies even to a thief. (number 7).
<margin>8</margin>
A thief selling a stolen item acquires the price for himself, even though he does not transfer ownership to the buyer, and the contract is valid.
This fails if, at the time of the contract, both the buyer and the seller know the item is stolen. (number 9).
And this is also true according to Portuguese and Castilian law.

William of Auxerre <note>original: "Altisiodorensis"; a 13th-century theologian</note>, and a few other theologians and legal experts after him, judge that whatever a usurer gains further with usurious money, or with any other thing acquired through usury, is subject to restitution. They prove this in several ways:

<margin>1</margin>
First, because, as held in Romans 11: "if the root is holy, so are the branches" <note>original: "si radix sancta, & rami"</note>: therefore, on the contrary, if the root is harmful and deadly, so are the branches. Since a usurious thing is acquired unjustly and is subject to restitution, so also is that which is further acquired by it.

<margin>2</margin>
Second, because fraud and deceit ought to protect no one, and no one should report a benefit from their own iniquity. Therefore, just as a thief is bound to restore not only the money he stole but also whatever he further obtains with that money, so the usurer is bound to restore whatever he gained further with the money or other thing acquired through usury and unjustly detained. They say that if a usurer returns to his heart and consults his conscience, he will find it dictates this to him; to state the contrary of what conscience dictates is certainly a sin.

<margin>3</margin>
Third, because a thing bought with usurious money takes the place of the money, just as, conversely, the price acquired from a usurious thing takes the place of the thing. For it is an axiom of the legal experts that "the price succeeds in the place of the thing" <note>original: "pretium succedere loco rei"</note>, which is gathered from the law *si rem, & pretium* in the Digest on the petition of inheritance, and from the law *imperator* in the Digest on legacies. Therefore, the usurer has no more right to that which is acquired from the usurious asset than to the asset itself from which it is acquired, and consequently, he is bound to restore it.

St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> (Summa Theologica 2.2, Question 78, Article 3) and the doctors commonly observe that among † things acquired through usury, some are consumed by use, such as money, wheat, wine, oil, and the like. These are said by legal experts to "perform a function in their kind" <note>original: "functionem suscipere in genere suo"; this refers to fungible goods which are interchangeable</note> because, in the payment of such things, one is usually substituted for another of the same kind. This is because a debt is sufficiently paid by returning another thing of the same kind, since they are usually of the same nature, goodness, and quality. For this reason, they are the specific and proper material of a loan <term>mutuum; a loan of fungible goods to be returned in kind</term>, as was said in Disputation 299.

Others, however, are not consumed by use and are said in the same legal place not to perform a function in their kind, because in payments

<column-break/>

they must be returned in the exact same number <note>meaning the specific individual item must be returned, not just a similar one</note> because of the disparity in value, goodness, and other qualities that usually exist in such things—such as lands, slaves, horses, and the like. For that reason, they are usually the material not of a loan <term>mutuum</term>, but of a commodatum <term>a loan of a specific thing to be returned itself</term> and other contracts, as was said in Disputation 194 and Disputation 299.

<margin>4</margin>
This being established, the first † conclusion is: The usurer does not acquire ownership of the "fruits" <note>profits or produce</note> of those things acquired through usury which are not consumed by use, and which are properly said to have fruits; rather, the ownership of them belongs to the borrower, just as the ownership of the thing itself immediately acquired through usury belongs to him. From this, it follows that the usurer is bound to restore them to the borrower, after deducting expenses. Indeed, if through the usurer's negligence the thing did not produce fruits which it would have produced in the borrower's possession, he is bound to restore those to him as well. The first part—that the ownership of those fruits belongs to the borrower—is the opinion of St. Thomas in the place cited, and of all those whom we mentioned in the preceding disputation who affirm that the usurer does not acquire ownership of the use. Indeed, this follows from the truth of that opinion: since the ownership of the fruits belongs to the one who has the "beneficial ownership" <term>dominium utile</term> of the thing that produces them, unless by some specific title (such as a lease, donation, or similar) the fruits separately belong to another. Therefore, there is no reason to dwell further on this part. The second part—namely, that the usurer is bound to restore them to the borrower after deducting expenses—is the common opinion of all those who assert that the usurer acquires ownership of the thing acquired through usury and subsequently the fruits; for, just as he unjustly detains the usury, so he unjustly perceives and retains the fruits from it, and therefore he is bound to restore both to the borrower. The final point is proved because by detaining the usury, he unjustly prevents the borrower from perceiving those fruits which he would have perceived if the asset were in his own power; for that reason, he is bound to restore the whole of the damage inflicted. If, however, the borrower was not going to perceive fruits from it, then the usurer is not bound to restore the fruits which he himself did not perceive through negligence. The reason is that he is not liable on account of the thing received (since the borrower would have perceived none from it), nor on account of the unjust taking or the damage from unjust detention, since the borrower himself was not going to perceive any.

<margin>5</margin>
The second conclusion: if the usurer, † by trading with things consumed by use acquired through usury, acquires something further, he gains ownership of it and is not bound to restore that specific gain. Nonetheless, he is bound to restore to the borrower not only what he received from him as usury, but also the entire lost profit or emerging damage resulting from the fact that the usurious things were not restored to him. This conclusion is held by St. Thomas in the place cited; Soto (Book 6 *On Justice*, Question 4, Article 4, Conclusion 2); Juan Medina (*On things acquired through usury*, Question 4); Adrian (*On Restitution*); and many others.
<meta>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "Ratio" (Reason), indicating the start of the explanation for the second conclusion on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses whether a usurer must restore profits made from assets acquired through usury, distinguishing between consumable (fungible) goods like money and non-consumable goods like land. Molina concludes that while a usurer may gain legal title to profits from trading usurious money, they are still morally and legally bound to compensate the victim for all lost potential earnings.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

The reason, moreover, is that such things are not productive in themselves, but only insofar as they are subject to the **industry** <note>original: "industriæ"; refers to the human labor, skill, and effort applied to a task</note> of the person trading. Thus, what is acquired from trading is the fruit of that industry and therefore belongs to the trader, who also bears the risk of those items. Furthermore, he is bound to restore to the borrower whatever "emerging loss" or "lost profit" <note>original: "damnum emergens, aut lucrum ei cessans"; legal terms for actual financial loss and the loss of potential gain</note> arose from the unjust detention of those same things. For the same
<margin>6</margin> reason, the same must be said of a **depositary** <note>someone entrusted with another's property for safekeeping</note> who similarly gains something using the property of others which he holds in deposit.
<margin>7</margin> Indeed, for the same reason, the same must be said of a **thief** who gains something by trading with stolen property, as affirmed by Soto, Medina, and Mairon <note>original: "Sotus, Medina, & Maio."; prominent 16th-century Spanish theologians and jurists</note> in the cited places, and by the doctors of law commonly. This harmonizes with the law *si pecunia* <note>original: "l. si pecunia. C. de rei vendicatione"; a specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding the recovery of property</note>, which states that if a depositary buys possessions with another’s money which he held in deposit, and those possessions are delivered to him, they become the possessions of the depositary. He is not bound to give those possessions to the owner of the money, even as a compensation for the money; it is enough if he pays him back with his own money and, moreover, if any losses—including lost profit—followed for the depositor because of the delay in paying it back. Law 10 of the Code *si quis alteri vel sibi* <note>original: "l. x. C. si quis alteri vel sibi"; "if someone [contracts] for another or for himself"</note> also agrees; it states that if a wife, using the money of her deceased husband which belonged to him, buys something for herself and not for her son, she legally acquires ownership of it. The son can only take action against the mother to have the money restored to him. Likewise, the penultimate law of the same title in the Code says: He who buys with another’s money acquires the action of purchase and ownership for himself—not for the one whose coins they were—if possession was delivered to him. Other laws cited in the *Gloss* <note>the standard medieval legal commentary on Roman law</note> for the three aforementioned laws confirm this. Likewise, Law 49, Title 5, of the Fifth *Partida* <note>original: "l. 49. tit. 5. part. 5."; referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> establishes the same as the cited laws. Finally, the same is confirmed by the law
<margin>8</margin> *qui vas*, the last paragraph, in the Digest *de furtis* <note>original: "ff. de furtis"; the section of the Digest dealing with theft</note>, which states: If a thief sells a thing he took by theft—for example, a horse—the price belongs to the thief and not to the owner of the horse, and the thief has acquired ownership of that price. For that reason, if the owner of the horse takes the price away from the thief by force, he commits theft or robbery. The reason is that the contract by which a seller distracts <note>sells or transfers</note> another's property through sale, exchange, or another method is valid, as is clear from the law *rem alienam* in the Digest *de contrah. emptio* <note>original: "ff. de contrah. emptio"; regarding the contraction of a purchase</note>. However, if the seller does not transfer ownership of the sold item to the buyer through such a contract—as held in the law *ex empto* in the Digest regarding actions of purchase—it is because, since he was not the owner of that item, he could not transfer ownership of it to the buyer against the will of the true owner. Instead, ownership persists with the ancient owner, who can reclaim it wherever he finds his property, and whoever has it is bound to hand it over to him. Nevertheless, the contract is valid: because the seller is bound to the buyer for **eviction** <note>original: "euictione"; a legal guarantee where the seller must compensate the buyer if the item is reclaimed by a third party with a better title</note>, and thus for the value that item had when it was with the buyer, and for all damages following from the eviction. He is not, however, bound for the price the buyer gave for it. Law 19, Title 5, of the Fifth *Partida* agrees with these points: since the contract was valid, and the buyer was the owner of the price he gave for it, the seller acquired ownership of it, with nothing hindering the fact that it was given in compensation for another's property. From this it follows that if the thief, with that price, buys something

<column-break/>

further, he acquires ownership of the thing purchased and transfers that ownership entirely to the seller. Nor is such a seller bound to restore that price to the person from whom the thief had received it for the stolen item; for the buyer of a stolen item only has a personal action against the thief to pay him for the evicted item and all damages following from that cause. He does not have a "real action" <note>an action "in rem" against the specific object rather than the person</note> for the price he gave for it, as if that price, wherever it might end up, were obligated to him for the stolen item he bought with that price—which was either evicted or must be restored to its proper owner. In all these things said regarding the sale of another's property, Conradus <note>original: "Cont."; referring to Conradus Summenhart, a theologian</note> agrees in *On Contracts*, question 70.
<margin>9</margin> It must be observed, however, that if the item being sold is stolen, and at the time of the contract both the buyer and the seller know this, the contract is invalid, and therefore the seller does not acquire ownership of the price. Similarly, if only the buyer knows it—who bought it, for instance, from the one to whom the thief had sold it—then the seller is not bound to stand by the contract, nor is he bound to the buyer for eviction. What has been said so far must therefore be understood as applying when only the seller knew the item was stolen, and also when both the buyer and the seller were ignorant of it. All these points are found in the law *si in emptione*, in the paragraph *item si emptor*, in the Digest *de contrahen. emptioe*. The Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 30, paragraph 4, agree and further dispose that when the seller also knew the item belonged to another, the price is to be applied to the **redemption of captives** <note>a common charitable use for fines or confiscated goods in the Mediterranean world</note> and is not to be returned to the buyer. That Ordinance seems to extend this even when the item was not stolen, but the buyer knew it belonged to another. However, the *Gloss* on the cited paragraph *item si emptor* only affirms that the contract is invalid when the item was stolen and the buyer knew it. This should be affirmed when standing on common law alone, because in that law an exception is only made when the item was stolen; and, besides the laws cited above, the law *rem alienam* in the Digest speaks universally, affirming that the sale of another's property is valid in the case we explained above. Gregory Lopez <note>original: "Greg. Lop."; a famous commentator on the Spanish *Partidas*</note> agrees on Law 19, Title 5, of the Fifth *Partida*, gloss 1. He observes, however, that looking jointly at common law and the law of Castile, if the buyer knew the item belonged to another, the seller is not bound to return the price to him, nor is he bound for eviction, unless an express pact to the contrary was drawn up; thus Law 19 cited, and the law *si fundum* in the Code *de euictionibus*. Yet in either event—namely when the price is not taken as a penalty for the crime from one who buys while knowing—according to the more probable opinion with certain glosses which Gregory Lopez refers to and follows. In Portugal, however, it is applied to the redemption of captives, as was said. Since this is a penalty, however, I, having been asked, am consoled by this opinion. Regarding this matter, however, speech will return at the end of Disputation 340.
From what has been said, it is easily understood that although a usurer does not acquire ownership of a thing acquired through usury which is not consumed by use, nor of the fruits he received from it for himself as owner, yet if he sells it or its fruits, he acquires ownership of the price...

<summary>Molina argues that while a person (like a usurer or thief) might not rightfully own an item, the "industry" they put into trading it can grant them legal ownership of the resulting profit or price, provided the contract is valid and the buyer is acting in good faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral resolution of whether a person (such as a usurer or thief) who trades with property that is not rightfully theirs becomes the legal owner of the resulting profits. It concludes the responses to objections from the previous disputation and transitions into a new topic regarding the fraudulent transfer of assets to avoid paying creditors.</meta>

& of the things which he has further acquired with that price, even if he did not transfer ownership to the buyers of a thing that is not consumed by use, nor similarly of the fruits of that thing.

In response to the first argument to the contrary, it must be said that a thing acquired through use does not relate [to the gain] as a root from which a branch efficiently proceeds, but rather as the material which the usurer uses for trading, which, insofar as it is subject to his own **industry** <note>original: "industriae"; refers to the person's labor, skill, and entrepreneurial effort</note>, produces profit. Or, it is like another person’s tool, which a craftsman uses to create his own manufactured object. Therefore, just as a craftsman acquires ownership of the artifact he made with someone else's tool—even if he used it against the owner's will and for that reason sins and is bound to restore the value of that use, and furthermore any other damage that happened to the owner of the tool due to its absence—so too the usurer acquires full right and ownership of the profit which he perceives through his own industry by using the usurious property. This remains true even if he sins by using it against the owner's will, and he is bound to restore to that owner, not indeed the price of the use, but the price of the thing itself, because when a thing is consumed by use, no price is owed for such use distinct from the price of the thing itself which is consumed by that use. Furthermore, he is bound to restore to the owner any other damage that happened for that reason, or any profit that ceased for the owner.

In response to the second, it must be said that there is no absurdity if someone sometimes attains a temporal gain from a wicked act. For a prostitute justly receives the price of the act of fornication, in which she sins mortally. In the case proposed, the usurer attains profit from his own industry, even if through the intervention of another's property unjustly detained. It should also be added regarding what is included in the same argument, that conscience—if it does not err through a false appearance of things or vain fear—dictates no such thing. Meanwhile, however, while an **erring conscience** <note>a theological term for a conscience that sincerely but mistakenly believes a neutral or good act is sinful</note> might dictate this, it would be a sin to act against conscience; yet the sin would not arise from the nature of the thing which he performed while thus erring, but from the fact that he operated against a conscience, even one so erring.

In response to the third, the premise must be denied. Regarding that axiom of the legal experts gathered from those laws, it must be said with **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> on the laws *qui vas* and *si rem, & pretium* cited above, that it must be understood in "universals," as the legal experts call them, such as an inheritance, a universal trust, and a dowry. For if someone, in good or bad faith, has received an inheritance belonging to another and sold something from it, the price he received for it is added to the inheritance in place of the thing sold. Thus, if before the inheritance is sought from him, he buys the same specific thing again at a lower price, that increase in price accrues to the inheritance and belongs, along with it, to the legitimate heir. And this is what the laws from which that axiom is gathered provide.

# What things are said to be alienated in fraud of creditors, and to what extent that alienation can be rescinded, and when the thing so alienated becomes subject to restitution by the receiver.

### DISPUTATION 328.

#### SUMMARY.

1. *When an alienation is considered made in fraud of creditors.*
2. *In how many ways something is said to be alienated in fraud of creditors, and by what action it may be revoked.*
3. *If a father-in-law alienates a dowry in fraud of creditors without the son-in-law's knowledge, an action is not given against the son-in-law, but against the daughter after the husband's death, unless children survive.*
4. *The same regarding a donation made to a son for a marriage.*
5. *Property alienated through a last will in fraud of creditors is revoked, even if it was alienated in good faith.*
6. *If an alienation does not make the alienator unable to pay debts, it is valid regardless of the title by which it was made, even in the **forum of conscience** <note>the "internal forum" or the realm of moral and religious judgment, as opposed to a civil court</note>.*
7. *By an alienation made under any title, ownership is transferred to the receiver, even in the forum of conscience, if he was not aware that the alienation was made in fraud of creditors. Declared, however, as stated there.*
8. *A receiver of an alienation, if he knows the thing alienated to him was another’s, and the alienator similarly knows, is bound to restore it or its value, even in the forum of conscience.*
9. *The receiver of an alienation, even in the forum of conscience, is not bound to restore what was alienated to him in fraud of creditors if it is not sought by the creditors, or if it is sought after a year has passed from the day of knowledge of such alienation.*
10. *Whether one who knowingly receives an alienation in fraud of creditors sins against justice, just as the alienator does.*
11. *A second buyer who knowingly buys a thing sold to another and incites the seller to sell it to him, is bound even in the forum of conscience to restore it to the first buyer, even if it is not sought by him.*

In order that we may more conveniently pursue those things which we began to examine in the two preceding disputations, the proposed disputation must be inserted here, which will shed light on many other things in the progress of this work.

As is established in the **Code** and the **Digest** <note>the foundational texts of Roman Law compiled under Emperor Justinian</note> under the titles "On things done in fraud of creditors," "On what grounds manumission is not permitted," at the beginning and the section "in fraud," and also in the **Institutes** "On actions," the section "likewise if anyone in fraud": something is then considered alienated in fraud of creditors when a debtor alienates something, seeing that through that alienation sufficient goods do not remain for him to pay his debts. Indeed, such an alienation—to the extent that he remains unable to pay his debts—is considered made in fraud of creditors. From this rule is excepted when liberty is granted to someone in favor [of the slave], for the use of liberty has prevailed so that even if the master of the slave is made unable to pay his debts through that alienation, it is not considered made in fraud of creditors, provided that the mind and intention to defraud the creditors in that way were not present.

### Ludovicus Molina. On Contracts.
