<margin>From this exception, it is established that for an alienation to be considered as made in fraud of creditors, a specific intention and mind to defraud those creditors is not regularly necessary; rather, simple knowledge is sufficient.</margin>
This is gathered from the cited section and from other laws; for the laws call such knowledge the "plan to defraud creditors," and thus fraud itself, as the legal expert sufficiently suggests in the law **"if anyone when he had"** <note>original: "l. siquis cum haberet. ff. quae in fraud. credit."; 'ff' refers to the Digest of Justinian</note>. This is what Bartolus seems to have intended in that place, and after him Jason, whom Gregorio López refers to in law 7, title 15, part 5, penultimate gloss.

<margin>3</margin> When $\dagger$ anything has been alienated in fraud of creditors in the manner explained, the laws make a distinction. This is because it is either alienated by an **onerous title** <note>original: "titulo oneroso"; a transfer involving an exchange of value, like a sale</note> or a **lucrative title** <note>original: "titulo lucrativo"; a transfer where the receiver gives nothing in return, like a gift</note>. If it is by an **onerous title**, then if the person who received it was aware that the one alienating it did so in fraud of creditors, a **rescissory action** <note>an "actio rescissoria" is a lawsuit to undo a contract</note> is granted to the creditors against him to compel him to return what he received so that the debts may be satisfied from it. No price is restored to him unless it is found among the debtor's assets, or in some other way the debtor was made wealthier by that price. Such an action is only granted to creditors within a year from the day they knew such an alienation was made in their fraud. All these things are held in the penultimate law of the Code <note>original: "l. pen. C. quae in fraudē credit."</note>, in the first law, and in the law **"if a debtor"** with the following law, and the final law of the Digest on the same title. However, for someone to be said to have been "aware" that an alienation was being made in fraud of creditors, it is not enough for him to know the alienator has creditors; it is further required that he understands the debtor's assets are not sufficient to satisfy the debts. But if someone is warned by the creditors not to buy a person's property because the transfer is in their fraud, and he nevertheless buys it, he is judged to buy it as one aware of the fraud, and an action is granted to the creditors against him. These things are established from the law **"the praetor says"** in the sections **"what he says"** and **"if anyone."** If an alienation was made in fraud of prior creditors, and afterwards other debts are added, then the subsequent creditors are not given an action to rescind that alienation, unless the prior creditors were satisfied out of their assets. If the person against whom the creditors are given an action to rescind the alienation has already alienated that thing and transferred it to another who received it in **good faith**, then no action is given against this second person, but only against the first one to restore the value of that thing. He can be compelled to restore the same value if he consumed the thing or caused it to no longer exist in another way. This is held in the law **"he who from a debtor."**

<margin>4</margin> However, when something has been alienated in fraud of creditors by a **lucrative title**—such as by a donation or something similar—then whether the receiver was aware of the fraud or not (receiving it in good faith), an action is similarly granted to the creditors against him to return it to satisfy the debts. There is this distinction: if he was aware of the fraud, he is bound to return the thing or its value if he alienated or consumed it; but if he was not aware of the fraud, he is only bound

<column-break/>

to return it if it is still in his possession; otherwise, he is bound to return nothing except insofar as he was made wealthier by it. This is held in the law **"he who however"** in the section **"in a similar way"** and the penultimate law of the Code agrees. From this it arises that, since a **dowry** <note>original: "dos"</note> passes to a son-in-law by an **onerous title** <note>because the husband takes on the financial "burdens of marriage"</note> but to a daughter by a **lucrative title**, if the son-in-law was not aware that the transfer was in fraud of creditors, an action is not granted against the son-in-law—even if the father-in-law alienated that dowry in fraud of creditors.
<margin>3</margin> However, an action is granted against the daughter after the death of her husband, as noted by Bartolus and others. They make an exception: unless that daughter had surviving children from such a deceased husband; while they are living, revoking the dowry (which was made in fraud of creditors) would result in a detriment to them, and thus to the deceased husband who received that dowry by an **onerous title**.
<margin>4</margin> What $\dagger$ has been said regarding a dowry should be understood similarly regarding a **donation for marriage** <note>original: "donatione ad nuptias"</note> made to a son; for it is considered to be made by an **onerous title** in comparison to his wife.
When something must be returned through such a rescissory action because it was alienated in fraud of creditors, it must be returned with the **fruits** <note>original: "fructibus"; products of the property like crops, rents, or interest</note> which it had pending at the time it was alienated, even if they were not then ripe; for the person to whom it was alienated is judged to have received those fruits also from the alienator. Furthermore, it must be returned with the fruits which he had from the moment of the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "contestatae litis"; the formal start of a lawsuit</note> by which that rescissory action is sought. However, fruits gathered in the intervening time do not have to be restored but belong to the possessor of that thing during that middle period.

<margin>5</margin> It should be observed that when $\dagger$ something was alienated through a **last will** and by **legacy**, or a **donation in view of death** <note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note>, if that alienation results in detriment to the creditors, an action is given to the creditors to revoke it—even if it was alienated in good faith on the part of both the alienator and the receivers. Indeed, the receivers are bound in the **court of conscience** <note>the "forum conscientiae" refers to moral/religious obligation rather than just legal enforcement</note> to restore it, even if it is not requested, when they see it is necessary to pay the debts of the deceased. The reason is that the property of the deceased represents the person himself, and from those assets all debt must be deducted before everything else, as was said above regarding the partition of the property of the deceased. Nor could the deceased dispose of these assets for the time after his death in any other way, since he did not remain in a state of acquiring other assets with which he might pay the debts. Consequently, creditors are first given an action against the **heirs** of the deceased, who represent his person. But if the **inheritance** is not sufficient for this, an action is also given against the **legatees** and those receiving **donations in view of death**. All these things are clear from the law **"we know"** and from the law **"he who however"** in the penultimate verse.
These things having been established, the following conclusions must be added, which only take place when the assets of the alienator were not subject to creditors by title of a **mortgage** <note>original: "hypothecae"</note>, nor had a **real burden** <note>an obligation attached to the physical property itself</note> by which the debts were owed, but the creditors only held a **personal action** against the alienator.

### Second Treatise. Disputation 3. Question 2. Article 8.

**Left Column:**

which was made, it did not render the one transferring the property <note>original: "alienantem"</note> unable to pay the debts that they then had, by whatever title that transfer was made—whether **onerous** <note>a transfer involving payment or exchange, like a sale</note> or **lucrative** <note>a transfer without payment, like a gift</note>, and whether by granting it to a daughter as a dowry or in any other way—not only did the receiver acquire ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of what they so received, but also, if later the one who so transferred it becomes unable to pay debts even contracted before that transfer, the receiver is held to no restitution to the creditors, neither in **conscience** <note>moral or religious obligation</note> nor in the **external court** <note>civil or legal court</note>. In this conclusion everyone agrees, and it is most evident in itself.

<margin>7</margin> **The second conclusion.** If the one who received the property was not aware that the transfer was made in fraud of the creditors, then by whatever title they received the thing—whether onerous or lucrative—they not only acquired ownership of the thing so received, but also are not held to restitution to the creditors in conscience or in the external court. An exception is made: unless the transfer was made by a **lucrative title** <note>as a gift</note> and the one transferring it was aware of the fraud against the creditors; for then the receiver is held in the external and internal courts to restore the thing received, or the amount by which they were made wealthier from it; provided, however, that it is sought by the creditors within a year from the day they had knowledge of the transfer made in their fraud. It is otherwise, however, if the thing is not sought, or is sought after the year has elapsed; for then they are held to no restitution in either the external court or the court of conscience.

The first part—namely, that they have acquired ownership of the thing so received—is manifest from what has been said. It can be proven: first, because that thing belonged neither to the creditors, nor did it have any **real burden** <note>original: "onus reale"; a legal claim or lien attached directly to the property</note> in relation to them, as if they had a **right in the thing** <note>original: "ius in re"</note>, as we suppose in all these conclusions; and it belonged to the one transferring it, as we also suppose. Since, therefore, the title by which it was transferred was sufficient to transfer ownership to the receiver, it follows surely that the receiver acquired ownership of it. Second, because if someone sells a thing to one person and neither delivers it nor subjects it to a mortgage, and later sells and delivers the same thing to another, the second buyer acquires ownership of it because the first only had a **personal action** <note>a right to sue the person, rather than a right to the specific object</note> and a right to the thing, and the second title, along with delivery, was sufficient to transfer ownership to the second buyer (as was explained in Disputation 2). Since, therefore, similar things are seen in the matter proposed, it follows that the receiver acquired ownership of it. This part will be made clearer when we show below that even if the receiver had been aware that the transfer was in fraud of creditors, they would still acquire ownership of it.

The second part—namely, that they are held to restitution neither in the court of conscience nor in the external court—is clear regarding the external court from the laws cited above, which in that event do not grant a lawsuit <note>original: "actionem"</note>, except in the exception added in the third part of this same conclusion. Regarding the court of conscience, it is proven: because, first, they are not bound by reason of an unjust taking, because they received it in **good faith** <note>original: "bona fide"</note>, being ignorant that the transferor was becoming unable to pay their debts. Nor are those who receive something from others held to inquire whether the transferors have debts, and whether there remains to them suf-

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

ficient goods to pay them. Indeed, that would be to place a most heavy yoke upon the necks of those entering into contracts. Furthermore, they are not bound by reason of the thing received, because that thing (as we suppose) belonged neither to the creditors nor had a real burden in relation to them, but belonged to the transferor; and through the title—whether it was onerous or lucrative—ownership of it passed to the receiver, as was proven in the first part of the conclusion. Therefore, in the court of conscience, they are not held to restitution, especially since **positive law** <note>man-made statutes or regulations</note> not only does not oppose this, but rather supports it. We can confirm this because someone who in good faith receives and buys a house that was previously sold to another is held neither in conscience nor in the external court to deliver it to the first buyer, as all admit; otherwise, the laws would be most unjust if they approved the second purchase, for they would be approving and defending sins. But a creditor who first bought a thing has a greater right to it—since they have a **right to the thing** <note>original: "ius ad rem"</note> in particular, which was owed to them—than other creditors have to things not owed to them in particular, which are transferred in their fraud. Therefore, when they have been received in good faith from the hand of those who transferred them, they are not liable to restitution.

Regarding the third part: when the one who transferred it by a lucrative title <note>gift</note> was aware that the transfer was in fraud of creditors, the receiver is held in the external court and the court of conscience to restore the thing received, or the amount by which they were made wealthier, provided it is sought by the creditors within a year of knowing of the fraud. Otherwise, if the thing is not sought or is sought after a year, the obligation is proven. For as is clear from what was said above, the laws in that event grant a **rescissory action** <note>original: "actionem rescissoriam"; a legal power to void a contract and return to the previous state</note>, yet with the limitation that the thing be sought within a year from the day of knowledge. Since, therefore, the law is just, expedient for the public good (lest creditors be defrauded of their debts), and rests upon equity, it follows that it has force in the court of conscience. Nevertheless, since, excluding that positive law, there would be no obligation of restitution in that event (as is clear from the proofs of the two preceding parts), and since that law does not make the transfer null and void, but only grants a lawsuit so that it may be rescinded (which will be further explained immediately), it follows surely that if the thing is not sought, or is sought after a year has passed from the day of knowledge, no obligation of restitution arises, not only in the external court but also in the court of conscience. Agreeing with us in this conclusion is Covarrubias <note>original: "Conar. var. res. c. 3."</note> toward the end of number 6, where he rejects the opinion of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> (of which there will be talk in the following disputation), if Cajetan understands it to apply when the one receiving something from a usurer was ignorant that sufficient goods did not remain for him to pay his debts.

<margin>8</margin> **The third conclusion.** When the person to whom $\dagger$ the transfer was made was aware that the transfer was in fraud of creditors, and the transferor likewise, and what was so transferred is sought by the creditors within a year from the day of knowledge, the receiver is held to restore it, or its value if it no longer exists or is no longer in their possession; and this applies both in the external court and in the court of conscience. This is consistent with what has been said...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of "alienation in fraud of creditors"—the act of a debtor transferring property to someone else to prevent creditors from seizing it. The previous page established that if a receiver is unaware of the fraud, they generally keep the property, except in certain cases of gifts.</meta>

### Louis de Molina, On Contracts: Disputation 3

...before all these conclusions. For the laws in that event grant a **rescissory action** <note>a legal procedure to cancel or "rescind" a contract and return the parties to their original state</note> so that what was thus received may be fully restored, unless something of the price, or of that which was given in exchange, is found among the assets of the principal debtor. Therefore, since those laws are just, they certainly have force even in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "forum conscientiæ"; the internal moral or religious judgment of an individual, as opposed to a legal court</note>.

<margin>9</margin>
**Fourth Conclusion.** In the event of the preceding conclusion, the receiver is bound to restore what they received in fraud of creditors neither in the **external court** <note>the civil or secular legal system</note> nor in the court of conscience, if it is either not sought by the creditors, or if it is sought after a year has passed from the day they became aware of such a transfer <note>original: "alienationis"</note>. As far as the external court is concerned, this conclusion is clear: since the laws in that event only grant a rescissory action within a year from the day of awareness of such a transfer; therefore, if the thing is not sought, or if it is sought after a year has already passed from the day of awareness, the one who received the thing shall not be compelled to restore it in the external court.

As for what pertains to the court of conscience, it is proven thus. First, because that transfer was valid in itself, and the receiver acquired **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the thing so received, as is sufficiently proven by those two reasons with which we confirmed the first part of the second conclusion. Since, therefore, positive law <note>man-made law as opposed to natural law</note> only grants a rescissory action to creditors against the receiver within a year from the day of awareness, it follows that if the creditors do not seek the thing, or seek it after the year has passed, the receiver is not bound to return it, but is safe even in the court of conscience. Second, because as held in the *Institutes* on actions <note>original: "Inst. de actionib. § item si quis in fraudem"</note>, in that event a rescissory action is granted, that is, for the purpose of rescinding the transfer. Therefore, the laws hold that the transfer was valid in itself and that ownership was transferred by it to the receiver; otherwise, that transfer would not be said to be "rescinded," but would be judged to have been void by the law itself. Hence the penultimate **gloss** <note>an interpretive commentary written in the margins of legal texts</note> in that place affirms that ownership was transferred. Indeed, there is an express text on this matter in the *Digest* <note>original: "l. si sciens, ff. de contrahen. empt."</note> where it is held: a buyer who purchases from a debtor while knowing that the creditor would be defrauded by that transfer becomes the owner of the thing so bought. However, the gloss correctly adds there that a rescissory action is given against that purchase. And that other gloss in the *Institutes* on actions says that the action is **personal** <note>directed against a specific person</note> against the person who so bought and received the thing in fraud of the creditor, but it is not **real** <note>original: "realem"; an action directed at the "thing" (res) itself regardless of who holds it</note> against the received thing, and the Doctors commonly agree on this. Third, because as held in the *Digest* <note>original: "l. vlt. § si procurator, ver. non solum, ff. quæ in fraud. creditoris"</note> a receiver compelled by a rescissory action to restore a thing is bound to restore it with the **fruits** <note>profits, produce, or rent derived from the property</note> it had at the time they received it, as well as those perceived after the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "a lite contestata"; the point in a trial where the issues are formally defined</note>, but not with the fruits of the intervening time. Therefore, the laws judge that the transfer was valid and that ownership was transferred by it; for by no other title are those fruits of the intervening time granted to the receiver except that the transfer was truly valid and they were the owner of the thing during that time. They are ordered, however, to restore the fruits that the thing had when the transfer was made because, since they already existed, they are never considered separately from the thing; both those,

<column-break/>

as well as the thing itself, are considered to have been received in fraud of the creditors. They are also ordered to restore the fruits perceived after the joinder of issue, because from that day they were at fault and in delay of restoring the thing, and for that reason, they unjustly deprived the creditor of those fruits. And certainly, the laws cited in this part rely on the nature of things, as is manifest to one examining it, and only out of a certain equity do they grant a rescissory action, which has force only from positive law: which means that in such laws one must abide by them in the court of conscience.

<margin>Objection</margin>
But you will object against this conclusion: Anyone who, knowingly and deliberately, transfers property in fraud of creditors, sins against justice toward those same creditors, insofar as through that transfer they render themselves unable to pay the debts which they owe them out of justice. Therefore, anyone who, knowing this, receives something from them, also sins against justice toward those same creditors by cooperating in the sin of transfer, and thus is held to restitution to them—if not on account of the thing received, then certainly on account of the unjust reception.

<margin>10 Response</margin>
To this argument, having granted the premise regarding the sin of injustice **incidentally** <note>original: "per accidens"; indirectly or as a side effect</note>—that is, not by reason of the work itself that they do, but insofar as they incidentally render themselves unable to pay by that work—the conclusion must be denied. This is because the receiver uses their own right within the limits of justice by receiving and making their own a thing that is in itself free—that is, obligated to no other—and by using the sin of the giver for their own advantage; no differently than one who lawfully receives a loan under **usury** <note>charging interest on a loan, which was historically debated as a sin</note> uses the sin of the giver for their own advantage. And perhaps, one who receives by **lucrative title** <note>as a gift</note> from one transferring in fraud of creditors would not even sin against **charity** <note>the Christian duty of love toward others</note> toward the creditors, because the order of charity does not require that one postpone their own advantage so much as to keep the creditor immune from an equal loss. Regarding the one transferring, they do not sin against charity when they offer the gift themselves, because through that offering their sin is completed, and the acceptance is only the use of another's sin already completed, for one's own advantage—as we said above regarding the matter of **almsgiving** <note>Question 32, Article 7</note> concerning a poor person who receives money offered to them in alms by such a debtor. On the contrary, the opinion of **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Catholic theologian</note> would hold place if the receiver, knowingly and deliberately, incited the debtor to transfer in fraud of the creditors; for then they would be the cause of that sin of injustice toward the creditors, and thus would be held to restitution to them. This is no different than how one would be held to restitution if they persuaded a debtor not to satisfy the creditors, and for that reason were the cause of the loss against justice that followed for them. Furthermore, if someone incited a debtor to transfer, being ignorant that the transfer was in fraud of creditors, or without sin not attending to it, they would certainly be held to no restitution, even if the debtor knew they were transferring in fraud of the creditors. The reason is that, by so inciting them, they did not sin against justice, ignorance excusing them from that fault; and thus they would not be held to restitution on account of the unjust reception, nor on account of the thing received, as shown above.

<margin>11</margin>
Hence I infer that if a second buyer knows that the thing they are buying has been sold to another, and incites the seller...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 329.

...so that [the seller] might sell and hand it over to them; in such a case, not only is an action granted in the **external court** <note>original: "exteriori foro"; the public legal system</note> to the first buyer against that person within a year from the day they learned of the sale made to defraud them—as Baldus notes regarding the code on fraudulent creditors—but also in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "conscientiae foro"; the internal moral judgment before God</note> that person is bound to restore the thing to the prior buyer, even if it is not requested. This is because they were the cause of the injustice committed against the buyer. Indeed, I believe that even in the external court, an action should be granted beyond the year on this basis. For the laws that only grant an action within a year against a buyer (or one receiving the thing by another title) who knew it was being alienated to defraud creditors, speak only of cases where the receiver was not the **unjust cause** of such a transfer. To punish such a crime and compel the repair of the injustice which the receiver committed against the creditors by that pact, the laws have never denied an action; nor was **positive law** <note>man-made laws as opposed to natural or divine law</note> necessary for such an action to be valid, as it was in cases where the receiver was not the unjust cause but was merely aware that the transfer was fraudulent.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
On the other hand, you might perhaps object to this same conclusion: Creditors, in whose fraud the transfer was made, were prior in time; therefore, they are prior in right. For "he who is first in time is stronger in law" <note>original: "qui prior est tempore potior est iure"; a foundational legal maxim</note>. Therefore, whoever accepted a transfer knowing it was made to defraud creditors is bound in the court of conscience to restore it to the creditors.

<margin>Response.</margin>
This argument, if it had any force, would prove that the thing must be restored to the creditors in the external court. To the argument, therefore, it must be said that the rule "the creditor prior in time is stronger in law" must be understood as referring to creditors who hold a **real right** <note>original: "ius reale"; a right directly over a physical object (like a mortgage), rather than just a claim against a person</note>. It is otherwise for those who only have a **personal action** <note>a claim against a specific person to do or pay something</note>, which are the only types we are discussing in the proposed conclusions. How this is to be understood will become clear in the following disputation.

## Whether the mortgaged goods of a usurer are by the law itself for the payment of interest, and the goods of a thief for the payment of thefts.

### DISPUTATION 329.

-> SUMMARY <-

1. Whether the goods of a **usurer** <note>one who lends money at interest, which was historically considered a sin or crime</note> are tacitly **hypothecated** <note>pledged as security or mortgaged</note> for the payment of interest. Decided in number 3 and number 6 to the end.
2. And what about the goods of a thief? Number 2 and following.
4. The chapter *Cum tu*, regarding usury: its true exposition and understanding.
5. Understanding of the law *Si et me, et Titium* regarding the claiming of certain things <insert>newly provided.</insert>

<margin>1</margin>
From what was said in the preceding disputation, this will be more clearly defined. Certain **Glossaries** <note>standard legal commentaries</note> on the chapters *Cum tu* and *Tua nos* (regarding usury) and the chapter *Quanquam* (regarding usury in Book 6) suggest that a usurer’s goods are tacitly mortgaged for the payment of interest. Thus, by whatever title they pass to anyone else, they pass with that burden, so that the interest must be paid from them.

<column-break/>

Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> affirms in the first two chapters cited that this was the common opinion of the ancient interpreters of canon law.

However, Panormitanus—along with Johannes Andreae, Hostiensis, Federico, and more recent authors—embraces the contrary opinion, and that is the common view today: Cajetan (volume 2, work 8, chapter 4), Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 1, article 4, reply 3), Covarruvias (3 *Variarum Resolutionum*, chapter 3, number 6), Navarrus (in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 265), Silvester (under the word "usury" 6, number 5), and many others. Therefore, Cajetan and Soto say that although a borrower has a **real action** <note>a legal right to claim a specific physical item</note> for the goods they paid beyond the principal (if those same items still exist and are owed to them, no matter whose hands they fall into), they do not have such a claim in comparison to the usurer's other goods—even if they were bought with usury money. Instead, they only have a **personal action** against the usurer to restore what was accepted beyond the principal. By reason of the person, they also have an action against the usurer's goods as long as they remain in the usurer's possession. However, once those goods are transferred, the action does not pass to the person who receives them, unless they come to that person through the usurer's last will (as in an inheritance), according to what was said in the previous disputation and elsewhere.

They prove this opinion: first, because such a mortgage and obligation does not arise from the nature of the thing itself in the usurer’s goods. Second, because such a rule is found nowhere in the law. Finally, because it would **ensnare the consciences** <note>original: "illaqueare conscientias"; a common theological phrase meaning to create an impossible moral burden or legal trap</note> of people conducting business with usurers. Even if the usurers were very wealthy from their own inheritance, and even if people contracted with them in good faith, they would be held liable for whatever they received from them—whether by gift or by a paid contract—as it would remain obligated for the payment of interest, no matter whose hands it reached. 
<margin>2</margin>
They affirm that all these same points hold place regarding the goods of a thief; for they are not mortgaged for the payment of thefts, even if they were bought with stolen money.

Johannes Medina (on things acquired through usury, question 4, near the end) and certain others whom Covarruvias and others cite, assert that although the other goods of a usurer are not mortgaged for interest, nevertheless, properties bought with usury money *are* mortgaged for those payments. Thus, they pass with that burden to the ownership of whoever receives them, at least when they receive them by a **lucrative title** <note>a title acquired without payment, such as a gift or inheritance</note>. They are led by the chapter *Cum tu* on usury, where it is established that properties of this kind are to be sold, and the borrowers are to be satisfied from their price; these words also suggest that if anything remains, it belongs to the usurer.

Panormitanus and many others, although they affirm that properties of this kind are not mortgaged for paying interest (for if they were mortgaged, they would pass with that burden regardless of the title by which they were transferred), they nevertheless assert that when they are transferred by a lucrative title, they must be taken from the power of those who received them and be sold. The interest should be paid from their price when there is no other source to pay them from; if any of the price remains, it should be left to the one to whom it passed by that title. And they say this was established in the cited chapter *Cum tu*, while it is commanded therein that properties can be sold...

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...possessions bought with usurious money; and he adds that the usury should be paid from the price. Indeed, he adds that this was established out of a certain **equity** <note>original: "æquitate"; fairness or justice beyond the strict letter of the law</note>, because possessions of this kind take the place of the usurious money that was used to buy them. This is based on the argument of the law *Si et me, et Titium* <note>A reference to Digest 12.1.32</note>, where it is established by a certain equity that since my property, or something owed to me, has come to you, you are bound to restore it to me. **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canonist</note> is in agreement with **Navarrus** <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish theologian and lawyer</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 266, although he adds that this should be understood to apply when the property was accepted with the knowledge, or the likelihood, that it was being alienated to defraud a creditor.

**Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian</note> in the place cited, and many others, believe that no distinction should be made in this regard between property bought with usurious money and any other property of a usurer. Furthermore, they believe no distinction should be made as to whether the property passed to another by an **onerous title** <note>original: "titulo oneroso"; a transfer involving payment or exchange, like a sale</note> or a **lucrative title** <note>original: "lucratiuo"; a transfer involving no payment, like a gift or inheritance</note>. Instead, one must only distinguish the time, or rather the status of the usurer, when he alienated the property. If, Cajetan says, at the time the usurer alienated the goods, he retained sufficient assets from which he could restore the usury, then no matter the title by which they were alienated, the receiver is not bound to any restoration, even if the usurer later becomes unable to pay them back. But if the usurer did not retain sufficient goods, but rather became unable to restore the usury through that very alienation, then—no matter what title the alienation was made under—the receiver remains obligated to restore that portion of the usury for which the usurer was rendered unable to pay. The receiver should blame himself for buying from, or receiving a dowry with a wife from, or receiving by any other title from a person who was so bound by debts that his debts equaled or exceeded his assets. Cajetan would say the same regarding someone receiving from a thief, or from any other debtor. Many others embrace this opinion, though many rightly restrict it to cases where the receiver was aware, or should have noticed, that through that alienation the usurer would become unable to restore the usury. Some of those further restrict it to when the alienation was made by a lucrative title. Among others, this is embraced by Adrianus on the subject of restitution, the last question on usury; **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560)</note>, *De Iustitia et Iure*, book 6, question 1, article 4; Gabriel; Paludanus; Navarrus; Angelus; Sylvester; **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist</note>; and Medina in the cited response, although he is not very firm on it. However, I am surprised that these Doctors remembered nothing of the legal arrangements explained by us in the preceding disputation regarding **alienation in fraud of creditors** <note>original: "alienationem in fraudem creditorum"; selling or giving away assets specifically to avoid paying debts</note>, according to which, as we shall say, this matter was to be defined.

To add in a few words what I think: first, 
<margin>Decision 3</margin> I do not approve of Medina's opinion. For among other reasons, as Panormitanus well says, if goods bought with usurious money were **hypothecated** <note>pledged as collateral for a debt</note> or had a **real burden** <note>original: "onus reale"; a legal obligation attached to the physical property itself, regardless of who owns it</note> so that the usury should be paid from them, then to whomever they came, by whatever title, they would pass with that burden. However, Medina and those who embrace the same opinion deny this when they have passed by an onerous title. Furthermore, nothing of the sort is gathered from the chapter *Cum tu* regarding usury, as I will soon add, upon which the chapter itself rests. Whence St. Thomas [Aquinas], in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, question 78, article 3, reply to the second objection, 

<column-break/>

established no distinction in this regard between goods bought with usurious money and other goods of the usurer. Next, I would ask Medina: if he who received those goods from a usurer by a lucrative title alienates them by an onerous title, do they pass to this last possessor with that real burden, and do they remain subject to restoration for usury, or not? If he says they remain so: On the contrary, because the usurer transferred as much right as he had to the one to whom he alienated those goods. But if the usurer himself had alienated them by an onerous title to the last possessor, they would not remain subject to restoration, as Medina himself affirms; therefore, they do not remain subject to restoration when alienated in a similar way by one who received them immediately from the usurer by a lucrative title. But if he says they do not pass to the last possessor with a real burden, then it follows that they did not have that burden even in the hands of the one who received them immediately from the usurer by a lucrative title. For if they already had it, by whatever title they might later pass to another, they would retain that which they had once taken upon themselves.

<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, the opinion of Panormitanus is also not approved. For nothing of the sort is established by that text [the canon law], nor is any distinction made in that text as to whether those goods were alienated by a lucrative or an onerous title, as is clear to anyone consulting that text. Indeed, that text does not even speak of those goods after they have been alienated by the usurer, but while they are still in his own ownership and power. This is clear because it decrees that those goods are to be sold, and from them the usury is to be paid, so that the usurer may be absolved from the penalty and from the sin he committed in receiving them. *It is manifest, however,* <note>original: "manifestum autem est"</note> that the remission of the usurer's sin does not depend on the fact that things bought with usurious money are sold when they are already in the right and power of another so that usury may be paid from them. Rather, it depends on it while they are in his own power. For unless he restores it then—either from elsewhere or by selling those things when he can—he continues in sin, and therefore it cannot be forgiven him. Rightly, however, the Supreme Pontiff [the Pope] commands there that the execution of the restoration of usury by the authority of a judge should begin rather from the sale of things which the usurer bought with usurious money, than from the sale of other goods of the same usurer.

<margin>5</margin> The text in the law *Si et me et Titium*, which Panormitanus and Navarrus cite for the same opinion, has nothing to do with the matter. For the *case* <note>original: "Casus"</note> of that law was this: Someone asked me and Titius to give him a loan of money. I ordered my debtor to promise it to him. He promised and gave it, the borrower thinking that he was not my debtor, but Titius's. It was asked whether he remained obligated to me. The *jurist responds* <note>original: "Respondetq; iurisconsultus"</note> that although the matter is doubtful—because that person entered into no contract with me, but with my debtor—nevertheless, it is more consonant with reason that he remains obligated to me out of a certain equity, insofar as my money, or money owed to me, reached him. Behold, the case of that law is far different from the matter we are discussing. For he who received money as a loan is bound to restore it because he has no title to keep it for himself (as the gloss notes there), and the only doubt was whether he was bound to restore it to *me*. The jurist responds that he is bound to me out of a certain equity, insofar as he received money owed to me, with my command intervening. In the matter

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into whether property acquired with usurious gains (interest charged on loans) must be restored to victims. however, in the case we are discussing, a person who receives an item from a usurer that was bought with usurious money actually acquires ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of it. They have a just title to keep it for themselves, and the item does not pass to them with any real burden <note>original: "onere reali"; a legal claim or encumbrance that follows the physical object regardless of who owns it</note>, as **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a 15th-century legal authority</note> himself affirms. Thus, the legal reasoning is quite different in each event.

Because the personal property of a usurer or a thief does not carry a mortgage or a real burden—even if bought with usurious or stolen money—it does not automatically provide the funds to pay back those usuries or thefts. Indeed, if those goods have been transferred <note>original: "alienata"; sold or given away</note> by the usurer or thief, the extent to which they are subject to restitution for the stolen items or interest must be determined by the rules discussed in the preceding section. This matter should be judged by the laws established regarding transfers made to defraud creditors; for those who lent money, or those from whom things were stolen, are considered creditors in relation to the usurer and the thief.

<margin>6.</margin> It must be said, † first of all, that if such goods are transferred by a usurer or thief through a last will and testament—including by a legacy or a gift made in anticipation of death—they are entirely subject to restitution until the usury and stolen goods are fully paid.

Secondly, it must be said that if such goods are transferred under a different title at a time when that transfer did not make the usurer or thief unable to pay the usury or stolen goods, they are not subject to restitution at all.

Thirdly, it must be said that if the receiver was not aware that the transfer was being made to defraud creditors, then they are not bound to restitution, regardless of the title under which they received the goods. An exception is made if the usurer or thief, aware that the transfer was fraudulent, gave the goods away under a **lucrative title** <note>original: "titulo lucratiuo"; a transfer like a gift where the receiver pays nothing</note>. In that case, the receiver is bound, both in the external legal court and in the court of conscience, to restore the item received, or the amount by which they were made wealthier, provided that the creditors make a claim within one year from the day they learned of the fraudulent transfer. If it is not claimed, or if it is claimed after the year has passed, then the receiver is not bound to any restitution, even in the court of conscience.

Fourthly, it must be said that if the receiver *was* aware that such goods were being transferred to defraud creditors, the goods are subject to the restitution of usury and stolen things. If the goods are no longer with the receiver, they are bound to restore their value, provided the creditors claim the goods or their value within a year of discovering the fraud. Otherwise, if not claimed within a year, they are not bound to restitution.

Finally, it must be said that if the person who knew of the fraud actually persuaded the transferor to make that transfer, then they are bound to restore to the creditors—even after the year has passed—whatever is necessary from the value of the items received to pay back the usury or stolen goods. This is true even if no claim is made. All these points were shown in the preceding dispute.

<column-break/>

->**Those who enter into contracts with usurers, thieves, and others of this kind, and to what extent they are bound to make restitution.**<-

### DISPUTATION 330.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *The goods of a usurer, a thief, and other similar people are of two different kinds.*
2 *The ownership of things sold by a usurer or thief remains always with the original owners.*
3 *A person contracting with usurers and others, and knowingly receiving another's property from them, is bound to restore it to the rightful owners if the debtor does not. If they received it unknowingly, they are bound to restore it if they still have it, or otherwise as much as they were made wealthier by it.*
4 *When someone buying their own property from a usurer or thief, or receiving it by another title, is bound to restore it (and from number 12 to the end).*
5 *Whether those selling food and clothing to usurers and similar people are bound to restore what they receive from them in exchange.*
6 *Those providing services to usurers and similar people are bound to restore what they received from them as wages for their duties.*
7 *Whether servants serving debtors who are unable to pay their debts are bound to restore what they received as their wages.*
8 *Whether the wife of an insolvent debtor is bound to restore whatever she spends.*
*And what applies to children (number 9).*
10 *And what also applies to the son-in-law and the daughter with a dowry (number 10).*
11 *Whether someone lending to an insolvent debtor is bound to restore to the creditor whatever profit they received from the loan.*

This dispute depends for the most part on what was said in the four preceding disputes. One must remember, however, † that of the goods of a usurer, thief, or any other similar debtor, some are those to which ownership belongs to them, and some are those whose ownership belongs to others. Furthermore, of these, some are **consumable** by use <note>original: "consumptibilia vsu"; items like food or money that are used up when used</note>, which are replaceable in kind <note>original: "functionem in suo gñe recipiunt"; fungible items</note>, and some are not consumed by use, nor replaceable in kind. Let us begin with things whose ownership does not belong to the debtors themselves. **Medina** <note>Bartolomé de Medina (1527–1581), a Spanish Dominican theologian</note> is unique in this part (in his work *On Restitution*, question 10, and *On Things Acquired through Usury*, question 4). He affirms that when a usurer, thief, or similar debtor is known to have goods remaining to restore their debts, if someone makes a contract with one of them regarding a thing consumed by use, and they know the ownership belongs to someone else, not only is the contract valid, but they even acquire ownership of that thing. They are not bound to restore it to the original owner, even if the debtor fails to make restitution. This is argued because, since such a thing is replaceable in kind—that is, it is sufficiently restored if another of the same type and quality is returned—it follows that while the debtor remains able to restore it, ownership transfers to the one who receives it. Therefore, the receiver is not bound to restitution by reason of the thing received.

<sig>N</sig>
<meta>catchword: Con-</meta>

It also begins a new section on contracts with "tainted" individuals, distinguishing between consumable (fungible) and non-consumable goods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the restitution of property. The previous page established that while some goods bought with usury can be legally transferred, others are still subject to claims by the original owners. # 194 Luis Molina: On Contracts

<margin>2</margin>
The contrary position, however, must undoubtedly be asserted. The reason is that when a transfer of such items is made by a thief, a usurer, or a similar debtor, the true owners of those things certainly do not lose their **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note>. Therefore, into whichever hands they pass, and by whatever title, the ownership of those things always remains with the original owners. This is self-evident and is clearly gathered from the laws <note>Molina refers here to the Digest of Roman Law: *l. rogasti* and *l. si etsi fur*</note>. Consequently, those who receive such items are always bound to restore them by reason of the thing received. Furthermore, they are bound by reason of an unjust reception if they were aware that the items belonged to someone else, either when they received them or when they consumed them. See, among others, **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> on the rule *peccatum*, part 3.

Observe, however, that because such things are treated as <term>fungibles</term> <note>items like money or grain that can be replaced by an equal amount of the same kind</note>, and are sufficiently restored by handing over others of the same type and quality, contracts celebrated regarding them are not only valid, but such items can also be lawfully accepted from the hand of usurers, thieves, or <term>depositaries</term> <note>people entrusted to hold property for another</note> when there is no doubt that these men will restore them to the true owners. However, they should be accepted with the intent and the burden that, if they are not paid back by those men, the receivers themselves must restore them; otherwise, they sin in accepting them. It follows that those who receive items knowing they belong to another are always held to their restitution—not only because they hold the items, but because of the act of receiving them. This is because they either receive them unjustly, or, if they were received justly, it was done with the intent and under the law that they themselves should pay in the event the primary debtors default.

By that same reasoning—namely, because such things are sufficiently repaid with others of the same type and quality—it must be said that when no loss follows from a delay, and no malice toward the owners results, those holding the items can wait for the primary debtors to pay. Indeed, equity demands that the owners then seek payment from the primary debtors rather than from those holding the items, especially when they were not at fault in holding them. The same reasoning applies to depositaries, usurers, and even thieves: when they are certain they will restore such things at the proper time, they may take from them for alms and other titles, as **Medina** <note>Bartolomé de Medina, a Scholastic theologian</note> and others affirm. At the very least, they do not sin mortally if they are certain they will restore them without any loss to the owners, even if they transfer them.

<margin>3</margin>
Let us therefore establish this general conclusion regarding things that are <term>consumable</term> by use as well as those that are not, where the ownership does not belong to the usurers, thieves, depositaries, or any other debtors. Anyone who receives such items from them by any title, if they receive them knowing they belong to another, or if this becomes clear to them before they transfer or consume them, is bound to restore them to the proper owners in the event that the primary debtor does not restore them. If, however, they receive, transfer, or consume them while ignorant that they belong to another, they are bound to restitution if they still possess them; otherwise, they are only bound to the extent that they have been made wealthier by them. This is the common opinion of the doctors. The reason for the first part is that he who knowingly receives, transfers, or consumes such things is bound not only because of the thing received, but also because of the act of receiving or the damage caused by knowingly consuming or transferring those

<column-break/>

items; therefore, whether he still possesses them or not, he is bound to full restitution when the primary debtor has not restored them. Nevertheless, that debtor will remain bound to satisfy him for what he restored in the debtor's place. The reason for the second part is that such a person is only bound by reason of the thing received: therefore, he is only bound to restore them if he has them, or to the extent that he has been made wealthier from them.

<margin>4</margin>
As † pertains to the property of the usurer and other debtors where the ownership *does* belong to them, the doctors (whom we said in the preceding dispute agree with **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note>) for the most part affirm that as long as the debtor is not rendered unable to restore his debts by the contract he celebrates—either because sufficient goods remain for him to restore, or because he gains as much for his estate through that contract as he transfers away (such as if he buys a farm at a just price, or sells a farm to get money for useful trade)—the contract celebrated with him is so valid and lawful that anyone receiving something from him in that way is bound to no restitution in the eyes of the law or in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>the internal moral judgment of an individual before God</note>.

But if, they say, he is rendered unable to restore, or more unable than he was before, the receiver is bound to restore as much as the debtor was made more unable through that contract, whether the contract was for profit or a burden. Some, however, understand this to mean that when one receives it knowingly, he is bound to restore it in full; but if he was ignorant, he is only bound to restore as much of the thing received through that contract as is found with him after he gains knowledge, or as much as he was made wealthier by that thing. So says **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prieras</note>, **Angelus** <note>Angelus de Clavasio</note> when discussing usury, and others. And according to these principles, they define many questions.

<margin>5</margin>
The first is whether † those who sell things pertaining to food, clothing, and other daily uses to such debtors are bound to restore what they receive from them in payment. They respond that if they sell them things without which they cannot preserve life, they are not bound to restore what they receive in compensation; but if they sell them things that they could do without, they are bound to restore. So **Sylvester**, **Gabriel**, **Angelus**, **Soto**, and others seem to teach.

<margin>6</margin>
Similarly, † they affirm that barbers, teachers of children, and others like them are bound to restore what they receive from them as wages for the services they provide. **Medina**, however, and others judge that in these and other similar events, he who in good faith hired out his labor to a usurer or other debtor, not knowing him to be unable to pay his debts, can later lawfully receive the wage for his labors, even if he then understands that the man is unable to pay his debts. The excellent reason for this assertion is that he has by then become a creditor to this man just like the other creditors: therefore, he can receive and demand the price owed to him, just as other creditors can demand and receive what is owed to them.

<margin>7</margin>
As for servants † who serve debtors who are unable to pay their debts, they make a distinction...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the obligation of restitution, specifically focusing on the household and associates of a debtor—servants, wives, children, and lenders—and whether they are required to pay back creditors if the debtor becomes insolvent.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 330

...they are distinguished. For, either such servants are of the kind who, by their services, bring as much benefit to the goods of the debtors as the debtors spend on them for food, clothing, and wages, or they are not. In the former case, the servants are bound to no **restitution**; because the debtors are not rendered <term>insolvent</term> <note>original: "impotentes," meaning lacking the power or means to pay</note> toward paying their debts because of the servants, nor do the debtors sin by keeping them and spending the aforementioned things on them. In the latter case, however, both the debtors sin by keeping them, and the servants themselves are bound to restore to the creditors as much as the debtors were rendered insolvent for that reason. So says **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prieras, a 16th-century theologian</note> in the place cited above, question 6; **Angelus** <note>Angelus de Clavasio</note> at number 21; **Gabriel** <note>Gabriel Biel</note> at conclusion 1; **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto</note> in the place cited; and **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 270.

<margin>8</margin>
Regarding the **wife** of such a debtor, **Sylvester** says in the same place that she is bound to restore whatever she consumes. However, **Navarrus** speaks better at number 268, agreeing with what we reported a little earlier from **Medina** and **Hadrian** <note>Juan Medina and Pope Hadrian VI</note>. He affirms that since a husband is no less a debtor to her for suitable maintenance—according to the quality of her person and the size of her <term>dowry</term>—than he is a debtor to his other creditors, she is bound to no restitution, provided she consumes only from those things whose ownership belongs to the husband, and she does not consume more than is due to her from the husband. Observe, however, that these things only apply when the marriage was celebrated with a contract of <term>earnest-money</term> <note>original: "artharum," or *arras*, a traditional gift from husband to wife</note> and dowry. For when it is celebrated with a contract of **community of goods** <note>original: "medietatis bonorum"</note>, as in **Portugal**, then, since all debts contracted after the marriage was celebrated and consummated pertain equally to both spouses, the wife, upon the dissolution of the marriage, shall be held liable for half of the debts then remaining. This is especially true when she contributed to the consumption of those goods from which the debts resulted; and this holds regardless of whether the husband alone gave cause to such debts through his own crime—for instance, through a theft which the husband committed alone without the wife's consent. Furthermore, observe that in whatever way the marriage was celebrated, if the wife knowingly consumed something whose ownership did not belong to the husband, she is bound to restore to the owner the whole of what she consumed therefrom, if the husband does not restore it. The reason is that she is then held by reason of the thing received, and of the reception or consumption, insofar as she either consumed it in bad faith, or if, without sin (and therefore not unjustly because she could not excuse it), she was bound to consume it with the intention of restoring it when she could, according to what was said at the beginning of this dispute.

<margin>9</margin>
Regarding **children**, if by their own labor and industry they acquire as much for the parent as they consume, they are bound to no restitution. If, however, they do not acquire as much, **Sylvester** says in the same place (with whom **Armilla** <note>Bartolomeo Fumo, author of the *Aurea Armilla*</note> agrees under the word *restitution*, number 35, and *usury*, number 39) that they are bound to restore as much as the parent was rendered insolvent for that reason. But **Navarrus**, at number 269, distinguishes thus: If such children were able to support themselves by their own labor, or by serving others, or by some other means, they are bound to restore; for in that event the parent was not bound to provide them with nourishment. If, however, they were not able to support themselves, they are bound to no restitution; because the parent in that event was bound to support them, and there-

<column-break/>

-fore they are regarded as **creditors** in comparison to such a parent. If, however, they should consume more than was due to them from the parent for support, then they would be bound to restore the excess.

<margin>10</margin>
Regarding the **dowry** which a son-in-law or daughter received from such debtors, **Sylvester** (q. 4), **Angelus** (n. 19), **Navarrus** (ch. 17, n. 271), and others respond that the son-in-law and daughter are bound to restore to the creditors as much as the one who gave it was rendered insolvent for that reason. They add that if the one who gave it has other sufficient goods to pay certain debts, and the dowry was only necessary to pay <term>uncertain debts</term> <note>debts where the specific creditor is unknown, often satisfied by giving to the poor</note> (which consequently should be restored to the poor), they can petition the **Bishop** to apply it to them as if they were the poor, for the purpose of living their lives and sustaining the burdens of marriage.

<margin>11</margin>
Regarding one who gave a **loan** to such debtors, **Sylvester** and **Angelus** respond: If he knew, or likely presumed, that they wanted to receive the loan to spend it uselessly on games, luxuries, or other useless things, he cannot accept payment from them. If he does accept it, he is bound to restore to their creditors as much as they were rendered insolvent by the occasion of that loan and its repayment. It is otherwise, however, when he gave the loan to them in good faith, not believing they would be rendered insolvent by that occasion. These authors respond the same way when someone buys something from them knowing or presuming they want the price for useless things, or when he has celebrated any other contract with them in a similar way. These and similar points are what are usually said regarding the matters we are disputing.

<margin>12</margin>
The following points must be added by us, consistent with what was said in the two preceding disputes. First, he who in good faith and without sin received anything from such debtors out of the goods whose ownership belonged to them, because he was ignorant that the <term>alienation</term> <note>the transfer of property</note> was in **fraud of creditors**, is bound to no restitution—not only when it has been consumed, but even if he still possesses it. An exception is made if he received it by <term>lucrative title</term> <note>a gift or inheritance rather than a purchase</note> and the one who gave it to him alienated it in fraud of creditors; for then, if it is sought by the creditors within a year from the day they knew of the alienation done in fraud of them, he is bound to restore it in the external court and in the forum of conscience. But it is otherwise if it is not sought, or if it is sought after a year has elapsed from such knowledge; then he is bound to no restitution. These points are clear from the two preceding disputes. From them, it is established that what we reported above from **Medina** and **Hadrian** is true: namely, when someone, being ignorant that another is rendered insolvent, has hired out his services to him or celebrated another <term>onerous contract</term> <note>a contract where both parties give something, like a sale or lease</note> with him (by which he made that person his debtor), he can demand and receive such debt just like other creditors. Nothing prevents this, even if he realizes before the payment the insolvency which the debtor had before such a contract, or that the debtor was rendered more insolvent by the occasion of the contract entered into with him.

...whether they are lucrative <note>referring to gifts or benefits received for free</note>, or if they receive something from them, they were aware that the <term>alienation</term> <note>original: "alienationem," the legal transfer of property to another</note> was done to defraud creditors because such debtors were rendered unable to pay their debts. In such cases, they are bound to no restitution, neither in the <term>external court</term> <note>original: "exteriori foro," referring to public law and human judges</note> nor in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>original: "conscientiae foro," referring to one's moral standing before God</note>, if those goods are either not sought by the creditors, or if they are sought after a year has passed from the day they knew the transfer was made to defraud them. If, however, the goods are sought within that year, they are bound to restore them, both in conscience and in the external court, to the extent that the debtors were made unable to pay their debts by that transfer. They are bound to the same restitution even if the creditors do not seek it, when, knowing that the transfer was for the purpose of defrauding creditors, they incited the debtors to celebrate those contracts and effect those transfers. All these points are clear from what was said in the two preceding disputations.

Following these points, it must be said that when the servants of certain nobles—who are so weighed down by debt that they are unable to pay it—have begun to serve them in <term>good faith</term> <note>original: "bona fide," believing the situation to be legal and honest</note>, or were received into their service with the masters helping them, they are not only not to be ordered to restore what they received from them for food, clothing, and wages (even if such servants eventually realized that the transfer was in fraud of creditors), but they are not even to be forced to leave their service. This is especially true when, if they were to leave, others would not be lacking who would similarly serve the same masters. For besides the fact that by the law of charity one is perhaps not bound to avoid loss to creditors at such great personal inconvenience, they do not avoid that loss by leaving. However, <term>confessors</term> <note>priests hearing confessions</note> must be careful that by admonishing such men (who usually act in good faith) and ordering them to leave the service of their masters, they do not become the cause of them serving thereafter in <term>bad faith</term> <note>original: "mala fide"</note> and with sin.

I should give two warnings. One is that what was said above regarding a woman who entered a marriage contract with a community of property and consumed it to the detriment of creditors remains in effect, with nothing we have just added standing in its way. The other is that in the case of a daughter’s <term>dowry</term> <note>original: "dote"</note> and a gift to a son for a wedding, there is more difficulty than in other transfers, despite what we have said. The reason is that all debt must first be deducted from the paternal goods, whether the one who received it wishes to bring the dowry or wedding gift into the <term>collation</term> <note>original: "collationem," the legal process of bringing gifts back into a common estate to ensure fair distribution among heirs</note> upon the parents' death or not. Indeed, the goods the parent had when they gave them must be calculated; and after deducting all the debt the parent had at that time which the son or daughter chose, the dowry or wedding gift is to be deducted from there, as was said in its place regarding the matter of the collation of goods. From this it follows that in the court of conscience, that son or daughter is bound to pay the debts the parent had when they gave the dowry or gift, if sufficient goods did not then remain with the parent to pay those debts. And at the very least, this applies when there are also other co-heirs of the same parent, and that dowry or gift would be <term>inofficious</term> <note>original: "inofficioque," a legal term for a gift that unfairly reduces the inheritance of other legal heirs</note> to them for that time, unless a contribution were made from it to pay those debts.

# On those cooperating in usury, whether they sin and are bound to restitution.

## DISPUTATION 321.

### SUMMARY.

1 *In how many ways one is said to cooperate in usury.*
2 *One cooperating with the party receiving a usurious loan is bound to no restitution.*
3 *Usurers who persuade others to give at usury are bound to restitution.*
4 *A person depositing money with a usurer: in what case they are bound to restitution.*
5 *Princes and others who help usurers are bound to restitution.*
6 *Notaries who draw up instruments for a usurious contract: in what cases they are bound to restitution. The same must be said for witnesses, number 7.*
8 *Managers of business, or factors, and others who give at usury or demand it in the name of others: in what case they are bound to restitution.*
9 *When the servants of usurers are bound to restitution.*
10 *Whether and when the brokers of usurers are bound to restitution.*

One can cooperate in <term>usury</term> <note>the practice of lending money at interest, which was historically considered a sin</note> in two ways. First, by acting on behalf of the usurer; second, by acting on behalf of the one who takes the loan at usury. Regarding this second way of cooperating, the following rule is to be established: He who cooperates in this way is bound to no restitution, even if he persuades the usurer to grant the loan at usury, and even if he persuades the borrower to pay the usury so that the usurer does not deny the loan on another day, and even if, with the consent of the borrower, he draws up the document by which the borrower is later forced to pay the usury. The reason is that just as the borrower does not commit an injustice by asking for a loan at usury, so neither does he who acts on his behalf with the usurer to grant it commit an injustice against the borrower. This is true even though he might incur the mortal sin of <term>scandal</term> <note>the sin of leading another person into sin</note> by advising usury and inciting the usurer to it—just as the borrower himself can incur the mortal sin of scandal by inciting the usurer to grant the usury. Also, in the case where someone, without fraud or deceit, persuades the borrower to pay the usury while acting on his behalf and not the usurer's, no injury is done to him; nor does he share in the sin of the one giving at usury, but rather holds himself on the side of the one receiving. In all these points, the <term>doctors</term> <note>learned theologians and legal scholars</note> commonly agree. Therefore, let us speak only of those cooperating in usury in the first way.

<margin>Question</margin>
As for those who persuade usurers to lend at usury, and who give money to them so that they may practice usury with it, **Gabriel** <note>Gabriel Biel</note> in Book 4, distinction 15, question 11, article 2, conclusion 3; **Juan Medina** on matters acquired through usury, question 4; **Sylvester** under the word "usury," question 9, number 2; and others whom he cites, contend: If these people do nothing more—that is, they neither demand nor later receive the usury, but the usurers themselves demand and receive it—they are bound to no restitution, even if they sinned mortally by advising it or by providing money so that it would be done. They are led to this because neither of those...
