->Second Treatise, Disputation 331.<-

...then the effective occasion or cause of the loss to the borrowers belongs to both: for indeed, even the usurers themselves, although they go further and give loans at interest, do not provide the effective cause of that loss until they demand and receive the interest; especially since the borrowers themselves can defend themselves against the <term>usurious contract</term> <note original: "usurarium pactum">An agreement involving the charging of interest on a loan, which was generally prohibited or strictly regulated under Canon Law at this time.</note> and refuse to pay the interest.

<margin>3</margin> The contrary opinion, however, is to be entirely embraced following Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic theologian.</note> in *On Justice*, Book 6, question 1, article 4, near the end; Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canonist known as "Navarrus."</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 265; Palude, and others. The reason is that, for someone to be bound to <term>restitution</term> <note original: "restituere">The act of returning ill-gotten gains or compensating for a loss to restore justice.</note> as a cooperator in an injustice, it is enough if the effect follows from their partial cause, even if the effect depends on other intermediate free causes that cooperate with it. This is manifest in the case of one who advises a theft or a murder. Therefore, to the extent that those who advise usury, or provide money for its exercise, were partial causes of the unjust and usurious effect, they are bound to make full restitution—but only in the default of those to whom the usurious profit actually went, who are themselves bound to repay the advisor if the advisor pays in their place.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding one who † deposited money with a usurer—not indeed so that he might practice usury with it, but nevertheless suspecting he would use the money for that purpose—the doctors of the law make a distinction. If the <term>depositary</term> <note original: "depositarius">The person receiving the money for safekeeping.</note> already had, or could easily have obtained, other funds with which he would have practiced usury in the same way, then the one who made the deposit is neither bound to restitution nor has he sinned. This is because he merely used a sinful man for the deposit and custody of his money, offering him what, due to the man's own malice, would become the material for sin, though similar material would not have been lacking from elsewhere. If, however, the depositary would not have had money from elsewhere to practice usury, or to practice it in such a large quantity, then it was a sin to deposit money with him without an urgent necessity, because one is bound to avoid the sin of another and the harm to one’s neighbors. So says St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, 1225–1274.</note> in the *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 78, article 4, at the end, and others. I believe, however, that in that event, the depositor is not bound to restore the interest which the depositary acquired with that money; because the depositor was bound to avoid the sin of that depositary and the harm to other neighbors only out of charity, and not out of justice. Furthermore, it was within the power of all those involved to avoid these things if they had wished. The same would be entirely true if he had given the same money to the same usurer by a loan or any other just contract, not intending that he should practice usury by that means.

<margin>5</margin> Temporal † lords, judges, advocates, and any others who, by statute, precept, patronage, or any other means, assist usurers in demanding interest from borrowers and in compelling them to pay it, not only sin mortally, but are also bound to make restitution. Each is responsible for all the interest for which he was a co-cause of the payment, provided that those to whom the interest went do not restore it themselves. For if, in their default, these officials make restitution, those who received the interest are bound to reimburse them. Judges and temporal lords, whose duty it is to administer the law by virtue of their office, are bound to restore to borrowers the interest that has been paid if the borrowers seek it back from the usurers in their presence, yet they do not order and compel the usurers to pay it back as they are bound to do by office; just as they are bound to restore

<column-break/>

it if they have hindered its restitution. So says Sylvester <note>Sylvester Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), author of the *Summa Sylvestrina*.</note> under the word "usury," 7, at question 10; Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, from number 275; Soto and Medina in the places cited, and the doctors of law commonly. This is because all these people are truly the cause of the injustice and the loss suffered by the borrowers.

<margin>6</margin> Concerning † the <term>scrivener</term> <note original: "tabellione">A public official who drafted legal documents, similar to a modern notary.</note> and notary who draws up the instrument of a usurious contract, the doctors commonly distinguish. If they draw up a <term>simulated instrument</term> <note original: "simulatum instrum.">A legal document designed to hide the true nature of a transaction—in this case, to hide the fact that interest is being charged.</note> in which usury does not appear, and by which the borrower is forced to pay interest, then in the default of the usurer, each of them is bound to restore whatever interest the borrower is forced to pay because of it. It does not matter that the borrower consented to the creation of that instrument. Unless, however, he drew it up at the petition of the borrower and acting as his representative; for although he sins in drawing it up in this latter case, he is not bound to restitution, as was said at the beginning of this disputation. In whatever way he draws up the instrument, he may receive a competent fee, which he is not later bound to restore; just as a murderer is not bound to restore the price he received to kill someone unjustly once he has completed the deed, as was said in its proper place. But if the instrument was not "veiled" (not hidden), the scrivener is not bound to restore the interest the borrower paid; because, by the power of that instrument, the borrower cannot be forced to pay it; rather, by its very power, he can defend himself using that same instrument, showing that what is being sought is usury and that he is not bound to pay it. An exception is made if he draws up the instrument where the payment of usury is unjustly commanded: for then, because the borrower will be forced to pay interest by the power of such an instrument, the scrivener who drew it up is bound to restore it. This is according to Sylvester in the cited place, question 7, and Navarrus and Medina above, and the doctors commonly.

<margin>7</margin> Regarding † witnesses who are present at the drawing up of the instrument, they are to be judged just as the scrivener who draws it up; namely, they are bound when the scrivener is bound: so the cited doctors affirm. Concerning these, however, and any other cooperators who are bound only by reason of unjust acceptance or damage inflicted, observe this: if they concur in the contract or act in <term>good faith</term> <note original: "bona fide">Acting honestly without intention to deceive or knowledge of wrongdoing.</note>, being probably and invincibly ignorant that it is usurious and unjust, they are bound to no restitution. This is because it is not by reason of the thing received (which I assume did not come to them), nor by reason of unjust taking, since they did not sin in concurring in that agreement, being excused by <term>invincible ignorance</term> <note original: "ignorantia invincibili">A legal and moral concept referring to ignorance that a person could not have overcome by reasonable diligence, thus removing culpability.</note>. So say Soto and Navarrus in the places cited. Add that it is often to be presumed regarding the borrowers that they do not wish these people to be held to restitution, but only the usurers to whom they paid the interest.

<margin>8</margin> Business † managers, or "factors" as they are called, <term>tutors</term> <note original: "tutores">Legal guardians of minors.</note>, and <term>curators</term> <note original: "curatores">Legal guardians for those unable to manage their own affairs.</note>, and universally all who give [money] for usury in the name of others, and who demand and receive it, are bound to restitution in the default of those whose business they managed and to whom the interest went. So says Sylvester above at question 4, Navarrus number 267, Soto, and

<margin>9</margin> Medina in the places cited. Concerning † other servants of usurers, who only carry the loan, knowing it is for usury, or only receive the interest when sent by their own masters—which the borrowers would have paid regardless—Scotus and Sylvester wish to say in the places cited...

# Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

...and others, whom Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian and critic of Luther.</note> refers to, are not held to restitution. Navarrus, however, and Medina, as cited above, affirm the contrary; their opinion seems safer and more probable, because those who receive the interest are truly co-causes of the usurious effect. However, one who neither demands interest nor gives money at interest, but only writes a record for the giver’s memory of how much was given to each person as usury, does not seem to be held to restitution, since they cooperate very little, if at all. 

<margin>10</margin> Brokers—whom the Castilians call *corredores* and the Portuguese *corretores*—if they play the part of usurers by seeking out people to take loans at interest and persuading them to do so, are held to restitution, as Soto and Navarrus affirm in the places cited; this is because they cooperate toward an unjust effect. Sylvester, in the place cited above, question 3, contends the opposite along with others he cites, arguing that they only cooperate so that a loan is given at interest, but not so that the interest is later demanded and paid. This opinion, however, was rejected above when we dealt with those who persuade others to give at interest. 

One thing must be observed universally concerning cooperators, as we said a little while ago regarding witnesses: if it is likely believed that the borrower does not wish to bind that person to restitution—as in the case of servants who carry the loan for usury or receive the interest when sent by their masters—it should be believed that such a person is excused from the burden of restitution. And regularly, many of the cooperators discussed in this disputation will easily obtain a pardon from the obligation of restitution from the borrowers if they ask for it. This is because the nature of the matter requires it, no part of the usury came to them, and the usurers themselves are held to full restitution, which the borrowers can demand from them in the <term>external forum</term> <note original: "foro exteriori">The public legal or ecclesiastical court system, as opposed to the private "court of conscience" in confession.</note>.

### To what extent the heirs of usurers are 
### held to restore usury.

->DISPUTATION 322.<-

->SUMMARY<-

1 *The heirs of usurers are held to restore usury and can be compelled to do so.*
2 *If the heirs of usurers have prepared an <term>inventory</term> <note original: "inventarium">A legal list of the deceased's assets used to limit an heir's liability for the deceased's debts.</note>, they are not held in the external forum beyond the value of the inheritance; it is otherwise, however, in the court of conscience.*
3 *If there are multiple heirs of usurers, whether they are held for the portion of an heir who does not restore.*

<margin>1</margin>
**T**o what extent usurers, and those cooperating with them, are held to restore usury has been explained in the preceding disputations. At the same time, they are held to restore to the borrowers <term>lost profits</term> <note original: "lucra cessantia">Profit that the victim could have made if they had not been deprived of their money.</note> and <term>emerging losses</term> <note original: "damna emergentia">Actual losses or expenses incurred by the victim due to the injustice.</note> resulting from the fact that they took usury from them or delayed restoring what was taken. If the borrowers are no longer alive, these must be restored to their heirs; if they lack heirs, they must be restored to the poor, as is held in the chapter *Cum tu* under the title *On Usury*. Understand this to mean they should be spent on other pious works for the benefit of the souls of the borrowers.

<column-break/>

...the heirs themselves, if they were alive, as in the cited chapter *Cum tu*. Nor is this rule peculiar to debt arising from usury; rather, it similarly has a place in every loss to temporal goods unjustly inflicted on neighbors, and universally in every debt of the deceased. For just as <term>actions</term> <note original: "actiones">Legal claims or rights to sue.</note> in favor of the deceased pass to the heirs, so also do <term>passive actions</term> <note original: "passivae actiones">Legal liabilities or debts.</note> pass against them—though not to the point of paying a penalty for the crime of the deceased, since the crime expires with the death of the deceased, as will be said in Treatise 3 (meanwhile, see Covarruvias, *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 3, number 7).

<margin>2</margin>
The question is whether heirs are held beyond the value of the inheritance. All agree they are not held if they have prepared an inventory. When they have not done so, although a more cautious opinion holds that in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note original: "foro conscientiae">The internal moral realm of the soul and God, often addressed in the sacrament of Penance (confession).</note> heirs are not held for the debts of the deceased beyond the value of the inheritance (even if they are held in the external court), we nevertheless showed in Disputation 217, along with Covarruvias, that they are held in the court of conscience as well. Covarruvias, however, in his *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 3, number 8, exempts the heirs of a usurer regarding the payment of usury. This is drawn from the chapter *Quia quoniam* on usury in Book 6 <note original: "in Sexto">Refers to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a collection of canon law promulgated in 1298.</note>, which commanded that satisfaction for usury be made insofar as the strength of the inheritance allows. In my judgment, however, these words do not sufficiently prove this exception. Firstly, because the text does not speak of the event where the heirs had not prepared an inventory, which is very rare. Secondly, because if that text had intended to exempt the heirs of usurers, they should undoubtedly be considered exempt such that they would not even be compelled in the external forum to restore the full usury if they had not made an inventory, since the text there is discussing the external forum. It is incredible, however, that the text intended to grant them a privilege in the external forum only in comparison to a usurious debt, and not in comparison to other debts.

<margin>3 Question</margin>
If there are many heirs, they are held to restore usury, as with any other debts, each according to their portion, following the share of the inheritance that falls to them. The <gloss>Question</gloss> truly is: if one of them becomes unable to pay, or does not restore for another reason, are the remaining heirs held to restore that portion, at least until their own shares are exhausted? The older interpreters of canon law, thinking that all the goods of a usurer were subject to a <term>mortgage</term> <note original: "hypothecae">A legal pledge or lien on property to ensure the payment of a debt.</note> for the payment of usury, answered in the affirmative. More recent authors, among whose number is Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canonist.</note> on the cited chapter *Tua nos*, and others, affirm that the same opinion should be followed and practiced so that the soul of the deceased, having achieved full satisfaction, may be more quickly freed from punishments. Nevertheless, they add that the remaining heirs are not held to this by the rigor of the law, because the goods of the deceased were not mortgaged for that purpose, and passive actions that were against the deceased are divided among the heirs by the disposition of the law according to their share, as is clear from the Code, title *On Hereditary Actions*, law 2, and from the Code, title *On Pacts*, law *Pacto successorum*, and as was said in Disputation 155 and elsewhere. Navarrus, in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 278, absolutely affirms that the rest are held to restore in place of that one, and brings no other foundation for this than the chapter *Tua nos* on usury. However, the contrary must be asserted with Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican philosopher and cardinal.</note>, Medina, and Soto: namely, that they are simply not held. Sylvester also moves toward this opinion. The reason is that which we gave with Panormitanus and others, why they are not held by the rigor of law. Nor is the contrary gathered from the chapter *Tua nos*...

<summary>This page discusses whether intermediaries (like brokers and servants) and heirs are responsible for restoring money gained through usury. It establishes that while heirs are generally liable for the deceased's debts, their legal obligation is usually limited to the value of the inheritance they received.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 333

...it is said in that place; heirs are to be compelled to pay usury with the same severity by which the deceased would have been compelled if he were alive. This signifies that all heirs taken together—each according to the portion that falls to them, in which alone they represent the deceased—are to be compelled by that same severity by which the deceased would have been compelled. From this you will understand that if the estate, after paying the legacies and donations made in anticipation of death, was sufficient to pay the usury so that the payment of usury and other debts of the deceased did not touch the legal shares <note>original: "legitimas"; the "legitim" is the portion of an estate that laws reserve for certain heirs, which cannot be given away via a will.</note> due to the heirs, and it was not necessary for the legatees to contribute to the Falcidian fourth <note>The "Lex Falcidia" was a Roman law ensuring that an heir received at least one-quarter of the estate after legacies were paid.</note>, then the legatees and those receiving donations in anticipation of death are not held to pay usury in default of the heirs who have become unable to pay them, or for some other reason do not pay them. However, when any usurious item has come to one of the heirs, legatees, or donees, it would always be subject to restitution to the borrower who gave it, or to his heirs, as is manifest from the preceding disputations.

## To know concerning the crime of usurers, to which tribunal it belongs; and who are called notorious or manifest usurers.

### DISPUTATION CCCXXXIII.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> 1 The punishment of usurers belongs to the secular judge, but the recognition and declaration of usury belongs to the ecclesiastical judge.
<margin>2</margin> 2 In how many ways usurers are said to be notorious and manifest.
<margin>3</margin> 3 Two or three singular witnesses <note>A "singular witness" is one who testifies to a unique event; in law, two people witnessing two different acts of the same crime were often treated differently than two people witnessing the same act.</note> of the highest integrity are admitted in Spain to prove "veiled" usury.
<margin>4</margin> 4 Whether it suffices for a usurer to be called "notorious" if it is proved through clues and arguments.

<margin>1</margin> To speak of the punishments of usurers, two points that were posited must first be expedited. As for the first, setting aside other opinions, it is settled that this crime is, in itself, secular; and therefore, to judge it belongs to the secular judge. Indeed, it is simply against the law of nature and justice, no differently than homicide, adultery, and other similar crimes, the judgment of which belongs to secular judges. So says Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 3, number 11. <margin>Sylvester under the word "usury," 9, at the beginning, with Panormitanus and many others whom they cite: Clearly, however, whether usury is a sin, and whether the sin of usury occurs in any particular contract, belongs to the judgment of the Church, and one must stand by its definitions in that regard.</margin> Sylvester, under the word "usury," 9, at the beginning, with Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as Panormitanus.</note> and many others whom they cite: Clearly, however, whether usury is a sin, and whether the sin of usury occurs in any particular contract, belongs to the judgment of the Church, and one must stand by its definitions in that regard. To restrain the vice of usury through ecclesiastical penalties—and even some temporal ones, as shall be judged expedient for the health of souls—belongs to the Church. Furthermore, as Covarruvias well observes in the place cited, since formerly civil laws did not prohibit all usury, it was the Church that began to restrain and punish this vice entirely with its own laws, looking out for the salvation of souls; and from there the canons forbidding usury took their origin, committing their punishment, with various established penalties, to ecclesiastical judges.

<column-break/>

Indeed, since for many centuries, in the absence of civil laws and to supplement the negligence of secular princes, the Church has been accustomed to judge and punish this crime, ecclesiastical judges in each province can and ought to involve themselves in the punishment and prohibition of this crime to the extent that it has been received by custom in that place, not hindering the fact that the crime, in itself, belongs to the secular tribunal. In this place, remember that the restraint of all sins through fatherly and pastoral correction belongs to the prelates of the Church, according to what was said regarding fraternal correction in Question 33, and which will be added a hundred times, both to rescue the delinquents themselves from sins and to keep them in their duty thereafter, and also to repair the scandal caused to others.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the second point, it must be said that those are primarily called "notorious" or "manifest" usurers who are such by notoriety of the fact. These are people who practice usury in the sight of the people, with so many seeing it that it cannot be hidden by any evasion, according to those things that are to be explained in another place. For this, it is not necessary that they perform many usurious acts, as some have thought; it is enough if they perform one publicly in that manner, as Navarrus affirms in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 280, with Panormitanus and others. Nor is it necessary that they practice usury through a formal loan; it is enough if they execute it through a "virtual" loan, by selling a thing for more than its strict just price because of a delayed payment, as Navarrus says in the same place and Sylvester under the word "usury," question 9, 2, with Panormitanus and others, consistent with the text there. Secondly, "notorious" or "manifest" usurers are those who are such by notoriety of the law. These are they who have been condemned for that crime by a manifest sentence of a judge, or who have confessed that crime about themselves before a judge in the proper legal order, or about whom it has been fully proved by suitable witnesses before a judge, as is to be shown elsewhere, and as Covarruvias, Sylvester, Navarrus, and the doctors generally affirm. However, if someone suffers from a bad reputation (*infamia*) for being a usurer because many upright men hold that opinion of him, he is not yet called a "notorious" or "manifest" usurer as we are speaking now, unless he is simultaneously notorious in one of the ways we have explained. Indeed, even if the infamy is proved before a judge, and along with it there is one witness (or many who are not above all exception), and these together with the infamy do not create full proof, he is not called a notorious usurer. On the contrary, even if he is condemned by a judge to some extraordinary and arbitrary penalty for that reason, he will not be called a notorious usurer, according to what is to be said elsewhere; and Covarruvias agrees. Also, many "singular" witnesses—that is, those who are not co-witnesses to the exact same usurious act, but where one testifies to one act and another to another—are not considered full proof so that someone may be called a notorious usurer and be punished with the "ordinary" <note>The "ordinary" penalty is the standard punishment set by law for a proven crime.</note> penalty, unless they are so many that, in the judgment of a prudent judge, they are equivalent to full proof, especially when infamy concurs and other occurring circumstances are considered. Meanwhile, on this matter, read among others Covarruvias and Angelus under "usury," 2, number 19.

<margin>3 Law 4, Title 6, Law 8 of the New Collection.</margin> In this kingdom <note>Referring to Spain.</note>, however, there are admitted two or three singular witnesses, of the highest integrity <note>original: "omni exceptione maiores"; literally "greater than every exception," meaning witnesses whose credibility cannot be challenged.</note>, to pro-

...proving hidden usury <note>original: "usuram palliatam"; this refers to "palliated" or disguised usury, where interest was hidden behind other types of contracts to evade the ban on usury.</note>.
You will perhaps ask whether arguments, or clues that someone practices usury, combined with their general bad reputation, are sufficient for them to be called a manifest or notorious usurer. <margin>4</margin> It must be said that nothing else suffices except those things which evidently show that he practices usury. And the chapter *Cum in dioecesi* (On Usury) speaks of such judgments, where the discussion concerns a notorious usurer by the notoriety of the fact <note>A legal status where the crime is so public and evident that it requires no further proof.</note>, as is clear to anyone looking at that chapter, whatever Sylvester, Angelus (in the places cited), and others might say to the contrary. However, by the law of Castile, the aforementioned proof through manifest clues is admitted in the crime of usury. The *Gloss* on chapter 2 of *On Usury*, book 6, says that he who has confessed before a priest and witnesses that he is a usurer, and has ordered usury to be restored by handing over his account books, should be considered a manifest usurer for the purpose of being subject to the punishments established by law for manifest usurers; many approve this gloss, whom Sylvester (in the cited place) and others refer to and follow. But I, for my part, find no other modes of being a notorious usurer in the law except those explained a little earlier; nor do I believe that any confession made outside of court makes the confessor a notorious sinner. Navarrus seems to agree with us in the cited place, not numbering this among the other modes of a notorious usurer.

### On the punishments of usurers, and of certain people who favor them.

<margin>1</margin> 1 Notorious usurers, even before a sentence is passed, are "infamous" <note>original: "infames"; in Roman and Canon law, *infamia* was a legal status involving the loss of certain rights, such as the ability to testify in court or hold public office.</note> under common civil law.

<margin>1</margin> By civil law, usurers are "infamous" by that very fact <note>original: "eo ipso"; automatically, without needing a judge's ruling.</note>, even before a sentence is passed. This penalty is found in the law *Improbum Faenus* <note>original: "wicked interest"</note>, under the title *On those who are branded with infamy*, and in Gratian’s Decree, case 3, question 7, chapter *Infames*; the chapter *Inter dilectos* (On the Excesses of Prelates) agrees, and Bartolus reports that someone in reality rendered his brother’s will null (in which the brother passed him over and instituted a certain usurer as heir) for the reason that, by passing him over, the brother had instituted an infamous person, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 159. Read Sylvester under the word "Usury," 8, question 4.

<margin>2</margin> Because † this penalty was established by common civil law, which (as was said in Disputation 304) used to permit some forms of usury, the Doctors doubt whether that penalty still has a place today even against those practicing usury that was permitted by that old law. The more common and true opinion, which Covarruvias refers to and follows, is that it does apply even to them. For by the very fact that all usuries are now prohibited, that penalty is extended to those practicing any usury whatsoever: especially since it was established not for those practicing this or 그 usury, but generally against "usurers."

But if, after this condemnation, they fall back into the same crime, they lose half of all their goods, to be divided in a similar way; and if they fall back again after this second penalty, they lose all their goods, to be divided similarly. So it is held in law 4, joined with law 5 following, title 6, book 8 of the *New Collection*. In Portugal, however, by Law 4, Ordinance title 14, in the beginning, the usurer loses to the King's treasury...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 334

According to royal law <note>original: "Regis"; likely referring to the laws of the Kingdom of Castile</note>, the penalty is double the amount lent at usury, and furthermore, double the interest itself if it had been received at the time of sentencing. Additionally, the offender is sent into exile for two years to regions in Africa; this is for the first offense. For the second offense, both penalties are doubled for him, and for the third, they are tripled. However, the person who accepts the loan at usury is punished for each instance by the loss of an amount equal to what he borrowed, which is paid to the royal treasury <note>original: "fisco regis"</note>. If he has paid any interest, that amount is credited toward the portion he is compelled to pay to the treasury. And in the final paragraph, it is established that if any of those who celebrated a usurious contract exposes the other before he himself is accused, and before the King has granted the penalty to anyone else <note>likely referring to a "denunciator" or bounty hunter receiving a portion of the fine</note>, he shall not be subject to the aforementioned penalties. Even if he cannot fully prove what he disclosed, his own confession shall not harm him or lead to the penalty established by that ordinance for those celebrating a usurious contract. Read also the provisions in the same book, title 27, in the second-to-last and last paragraphs, and book 1, title 67, paragraph 19.

<margin>5</margin>
A cleric <note>A member of the clergy, such as a priest or deacon.</note> who is a usurer is also legally infamous <note>original: "infamis"; a legal status involving the loss of certain rights and social standing</note> under canon law, as cited in the chapter *Inter dilectos*. He is to be suspended from his office and his benefice <note>A church office that provides a living or income.</note> on account of the usurious act, as is clear in the chapter *Praeterea* (On Usury). Indeed, he is even to be deposed <note>Permanently removed from his rank and office.</note> from his office and any benefice already obtained, as is established in chapter 1 of *On Usury*, as well as the chapters *Si quis oblitus* and *Quoniam multi* (14, question 1) and chapter 1 (distinction 47). Furthermore, he is to be barred from obtaining any new office, according to the cited chapter *Inter dilectos* and the chapter *De Petro* (distinction 47). And there is a rule regarding the infamous in the Rules of Law, book 6, which states: "The gates of dignity should not open for the infamous." <note>original: "Infamibus portæ non pateant dignitatum."</note> Covarruvias (3 *Variarum Resolutionum*, chapter 3, number 3), along with Hostiensis, says that a usurious cleric should first be suspended; then, if he is stubborn and persists, he should be deposed. Panormitanus, however, in the cited chapter *Praeterea*, seems to suggest that either penalty can be imposed indifferently, since both are found established in law. Indeed, the laws do not explicitly state that suspension must be imposed first and deposition later, although it is equitable that such an order be followed. Both penalties can be imposed, according to the *Gloss* on the chapter

<margin>6</margin>
*Praeterea* (On Usury). It says that a Bishop can grant a dispensation <note>A legal exemption from a church rule.</note> after penance and satisfaction <note>Making amends or repayment.</note> so that a usurious cleric may be eligible for ecclesiastical benefices. Covarruvias affirms in the cited place that this view is commonly accepted. Later, however, citing another *Gloss* on the chapter *Inter dilectos*, he restricts this to mean it applies to benefices already held, but not to those yet to be obtained. I believe, however, that the *Gloss* on the chapter *Inter dilectos* does not deny that a bishop can make a usurious cleric eligible to obtain new benefices that become vacant after penance and satisfaction, and to which he acquires a right anew after such penance—which is how the *Gloss* on *Praeterea* should be understood. Rather, it only asserts that he cannot be made eligible by the Bishop to obtain those benefices to which he was elected and had a right *before* penance and satisfaction; from those he must be entirely barred, and they must be conferred upon another. Nevertheless, the Bishop can grant a dispensation so that he remains in those already held. For although the Bishop could depose him from them, he also has the power not to depose him, but to suspend him for a time (as held in the cited chapter *Praeterea*), and after penance and satisfaction, he can leave him in his own already-held benefice.

<margin>7</margin>
In the chapter *Quia in omnibus* (On Usury), which is from the Lateran Council, it is decreed that manifest usu-

<column-break/>

rers shall not be admitted to the communion <note>original: "cōionē"; fellowship or participation in the sacraments</note> of others. Although Panormitanus, Angelus (under the word "Usura," 2, number 5), and others understood this to mean they should not be allowed to be present at the sacrifice of the altar <note>The Mass.</note>—so that they might be shamed, in the same way that excommunicated persons are not permitted to attend—the text nevertheless does not say this. Rather, it means they are not to be admitted to the reception of the Eucharist, as Sylvester (in the cited question 4) and others affirm. Furthermore, it is decreed that offerings in the Church shall not be received from them; a matter we discussed in question 32, article 7. It is further established that if they depart from this life while in that sin, Christian burial <note>original: "ecclesiastica sepultura"</note> shall not be granted to them. Moreover, if anyone accepts an offering from them or grants them Christian burial, he shall be compelled to return what he received and shall remain suspended until he has made satisfaction at the Bishop's discretion; doctors of law understand this suspension to happen automatically <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>. Gregory X, in the Council of Lyon (Clementine 1, *On Usury*), commanded that this decree be observed inviolably under the threat of divine malediction. Later,

<margin>8</margin>
in the Clementine decree *On Burials* (1), it was decreed that whoever presumes to knowingly bury manifest usurers shall be excommunicated automatically, and shall not be absolved until he has made satisfaction at the Bishop's discretion.

In the chapter *Quanquam* (On Usury, book 6), it was also decreed that even if manifest usurers, in their will or any other last testament, command that the usury they received be restored—whether they specify the amount or not—they are still not to be granted Christian burial until full satisfaction has been made for the usury, as far as their assets allow. Alternatively, sufficient security must be provided through pledges or guarantors <note>original: "fideiussoribus"</note>. This security should be given either to those to whom restitution is owed, if they are present, or to others who can legally receive it on their behalf (such as children or other persons specified by law). If all these are absent, it should be given to the local Ordinary <note>The Bishop or his equivalent.</note>, his Vicar, or the Rector of the parish in which the deceased lived, in the presence of some trustworthy people of the parish, or a public notary, by mandate of the Ordinary. Furthermore, it is commanded that if the amount of usury is certain, that exact amount must be stated in the security. If it is not certain, a probable amount should be stated according to the judgment of the one receiving the security. If the receiver knowingly sets an amount lower than what is probable, he is held liable for restitution up to the probable amount. It is added there that if any member of a religious order admits manifest usurers to Christian burial in any other way, he incurs the penalty of suspension established in the cited chapter *Quia in omnibus*. It is also commanded that no one shall be present at the making of their wills. Likewise, no one shall admit them to confession or absolve them before they either restore the usury or provide security in the aforementioned manner. Furthermore, it is established that the wills of manifest usurers made in any other way (that is, without the usury being satisfied or security provided as explained) shall be void and null by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>.

Regarding the aforementioned points, observe several things. First, these rules only apply to notorious usurers, not to others. Burial and the Eucharist are not to be denied to the latter if they seek them publicly, though they are not to be absolved in the forum of conscience <note>During private confession.</note> unless they have made restitution or are prepared to do so; just as is customarily done with secret thieves and other debtors.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 334

[9] ...is not said [by the law] that security <term>caution: (cautio) a legal guarantee, such as a deposit or a co-signer, to ensure an obligation is met.</term> must be provided with pledges or sureties; it only says that **suitable security** must be provided. However, under the name of "suitable security," as the gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval commentary on legal texts.</note> notes there and as the legal scholars agree, nothing else is understood than security provided with pledges or sureties, according to the law *si mandato Titii*, paragraph *ultimo*, in the Digest under the title *Mandati*.

[10] But if someone is unable to give either pledges or sureties, he must swear an oath that he is unable to provide them, and also that he will fulfill his obligation as much as lies within his power; and that shall be sufficient, as noted by that same gloss, as well as Angelo <note>Angelo de Clavasio, author of the *Summa Angelica*.</note> under the word "Usury" 2, number 8; Sylvester, question 4, cited; and Navarro in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 279; following the chapter *Alma mater*, paragraph *illis*, regarding the sentence of excommunication in Book 6 <note>The *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law.</note>. If someone is in danger of death and wishes to provide all these things but cannot because he is in a desert, or at sea, or has been pierced by a sword, or is otherwise so affected that such a swift death is feared that there is no time to provide them, he must be absolved by any priest whatsoever. This is provided that, if time permits, he swears that he will perform what he can of the aforementioned requirements. If, however, others are present, he should protest before them that he owes these things, and he should command that they be restored from his goods. Furthermore, the confessor should obtain from him the power to manifest all the aforesaid to the Ordinary <term>Ordinary: a church official, usually a bishop, who holds regular jurisdiction over a territory.</term>, so that if the person recovers, the Ordinary may take care to compel him to fulfill all those things; but if he does not recover, he may compel the heirs to fulfill them. So says Navarro in the place cited, number 280, with Sylvester on the word "Restitution" 6, question 1.

[11] Third, under the name of "Ordinary," anyone is understood who has episcopal jurisdiction, such as a Cathedral Chapter while the see is vacant, and its Vicar, and Abbots, and other superiors in certain places, and their Vicars.

[12] Fourth, if there is a public notary in this event, he may, by mandate of the Ordinary and in the name of those to whom the restitution of usury is owed, stipulate [the terms]; this acquires for them a right in the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to the public, legal court of the Church, as opposed to the internal forum of the individual's conscience.</note>. It is otherwise, however, if he does not do this by mandate of the Ordinary, as noted by the cited gloss and the doctors commonly.

Fifth, those who bury a notorious usurer—even one who commanded usury to be restored—before the requirements of the chapter *quamquam* <note>A specific decree in Canon Law regarding the burial of usurers.</note> are carried out, are excommunicated by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, according to the Clementine decree 1, *de sepulturis*, which was established after that chapter.

Covarruvias, in *Various Resolutions* 3, chapter 3, number 5, says that although it is enough for someone to be a notorious usurer in any of the ways explained in the preceding disputation to incur the penalties of the chapter *quia in omnibus*, nevertheless, to fall into the penalties of the chapter *quamquam*—and especially for his testament to be null—it is required that he be a notorious usurer by notoriety of fact. He seems to wish to say that it is not enough for one of his acts to be notorious in that way, but that it is required that he have practiced it with more notoriety. This opinion is not approved by me. First, because it is not gathered from that text; and where the law does not distinguish, we ought not to distinguish. Second, because other scholars do not affirm it. Finally, because that text also speaks of the penalties of the chapter *quia in omnibus*, such as the prohibition of ecclesiastical burial, and it presupposes that other chapter. I would freely grant that the testament of a usurer

<column-break/>

is valid if he was not notorious before death, even if after death it is sufficiently proved that he practiced usury, and for that reason he is condemned and his heirs are ordered to restore it, and thus the crime becomes notorious. The reason is that, since a testament is confirmed by the death of the testator, and that testator before death and at the time of death had no impediment why that testament should not be valid, it will surely remain valid after death. If, however, that testator had been condemned before death, and died without satisfaction or suitable security, then the testament would be null by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>.

[14] Just as the testament of a notorious usurer is null by the law itself, so also is a codicil <note>An addition or supplement to a will.</note> and any other final will of his. Thus says the last gloss on the chapter *quamquam*, commonly received, as Covarruvias, Sylvester, and Angelo report and follow. The reason is that such is the intent of that law; otherwise, it could easily be evaded. As for legacies for "pious causes" <term>pious causes: (pias causas) bequests to the Church, hospitals, or the poor.</term> left in them, the scholars agree that they are not valid when they are left by a notorious usurer who died impenitent. But when signs of repentance have appeared, certain scholars, whom Sylvester and Covarruvias refer to and follow, affirm they are valid, even though the same final disposition is not valid as to the rest, if he did not restore or provide suitable security before death.

[15] Regarding the testament of a notorious usurer who is an infidel <note>A non-Christian, such as a Jew or Muslim, living under Christian law.</note>, subject to the laws and jurisdiction of a Christian Prince: although some judge it to be valid, it pleases us to say, with Covarruvias and others, that it is invalid. For although spiritual punishment, such as the denial of ecclesiastical burial, has no place for those infidels, the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> can nevertheless annul their testament insofar as they are subject to Christian Commonwealths. And by *epicheia* <term>epicheia: a principle of legal interpretation that looks at the spirit of the law rather than the strict letter in specific cases.</term> it must be judged that such was the mind of the cited chapter *quamquam*, even though it thought nothing of them at the time; for it is to be believed that if the legislator were asked then whether he wished to include them in that law regarding the penalty of the nullity of the testament, he would have answered in the affirmative.

[16] The testament of a notorious usurer who once was such, and ceased from that practice, is null if he did not restore or provide suitable security before death. So says Felinus and others whom Covarruvias refers to and follows.

[17] Does a testament made by a notorious usurer before providing security take on strength and become valid if the usurer provides suitable security before death? It must be answered in the affirmative, along with the gloss on chapter *quamquam*, Bartolus, and others whom Sylvester and Covarruvias refer to and follow. The reason is that a testament is made firm by the death of the testator; and such a testament had all the necessary elements to be valid before the testator's death. Furthermore, because we should incline in favor of testaments.

[18] But if a notorious usurer, after making a testament, indeed provided suitable security, but after the security he secretly practiced usury, should such a testament be judged valid? It must be answered in the negative...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 334

...must be responded to: because it must be presumed that the penance and the security <term>caution: (cautio) a legal guarantee or pledge</term> were fictitious. This is the view of Covarruvias in the place cited, and others; Panormitanus, however, in chapter *si quia* on all points, number 10, suggests it is valid. I believe this is true in the forum of conscience <note>The "forum of conscience" refers to the internal moral standing of a person before God, as opposed to the "external forum" of legal courts.</note>, when it is plausibly believed that the security was provided without fiction and with the intent of making restitution: for the fact that he later practiced usury does not render the previous act invalid.

19 But what if someone who was not a usurer composed a will <term>testamentum: a last will and testament</term>, but later became a notorious usurer—is that will rendered void? The answer must be in the affirmative: because a will is confirmed by the death of the testator. Yet at the time of death, he did not possess the conditions necessary for it to be valid. This is the view of Covarruvias, as above, and others whom he cites.

20 In Chapter 1 regarding usury, book 9, it is decreed that neither a college nor a university, nor any other individual person of whatever status or dignity, should rent houses to foreigners or anyone else not originating from the same republic who publicly practice usury or wish to do so, so that they may practice usury in them; nor should they allow them to keep rented houses or live in their lands. Instead, they must expel them within three months, never to admit them again, and furthermore, they must not grant them houses under any other title. Those who do otherwise—if they are Patriarchs, Archbishops, or Bishops—incur the penalty of suspension <note>A "suspension" is a church penalty that prevents a cleric from exercising his office or receiving its income.</note> by that very fact (*ipso facto*). If they are lesser individual ecclesiastical persons, they incur the penalty of excommunication by that very fact. If it is a college or another ecclesiastical university, it incurs the penalty of interdict <note>An "interdict" is a collective penalty that bars a community from certain religious services and sacraments.</note> by that very fact; if they remain stubborn for a month, the ecclesiastical lands themselves shall be subject to the interdict until they expel the aforementioned usurers. These penalties are imposed only on ecclesiastics. Regarding laypeople, it is commanded that, regardless of any privilege, they be restrained by the local bishops <term>ordinaries: the resident bishops or authorities of a diocese</term> through ecclesiastical censures. Thus, by the power of this chapter, laypeople do not incur excommunication automatically (*ipso facto*).

21 In the single Clementine decree <note>A reference to the "Clementines," a collection of Canon Law issued by Pope Clement V.</note> regarding usury, it is decreed that communities, their rulers, judges, or any other officials who have established, written, or dictated statutes by which usuries are permitted, or by which payment is compelled, or by which reclaiming them is prohibited after they have been paid, are by that very fact excommunicated. A similar penalty applies to those who knowingly presume to judge that usuries be paid, or that they not be restored when they are reclaimed after being paid.
Likewise, unless the aforementioned statutes are deleted within three months by those who have the power to delete them, they are by that very fact excommunicated; and those who observe either those statutes or a similar custom incur the same penalty. In the same place, it was also decreed that when someone is presumed to have committed usury, they shall be compelled by censures to show their account books <note>original: "codices suarum rationum"</note> so that the matter may be better understood from them.

22 Finally, it must be observed that if a usurer has received something as usury and paid usury himself, the right of reclamation <term>repetition: (repetitio) the legal right to demand back money paid by mistake or illegally</term> is granted neither to him nor to his heirs until they themselves pay back the usuries they received from others. Thus Michael on usury. If, however, someone received usury and paid it in the name of the Church or someone else, reclamation is granted, even if the person who paid it in another's name

<column-break/>

is a usurer and has usuries that must be restored. So says Panormitanus in that place, and Sylvester under the word "usury," question 9, number 4.

### Whether it is lawful to take a loan at interest; and whether one may persuade a lesser evil to avoid a greater.

## DISPUTATION 335.

### SUMMARY.

1 In which cases it is lawful to take a loan at interest, and when it can be advised to avoid a greater evil.
2 Whether it is lawful to take money on loan at interest to spend it on tournaments and games.
3 Whether it is lawful for someone to induce a lender to lend to him so that he may avoid a greater evil; and thus generally, whether it is lawful to induce someone to a lesser evil so that he may avoid a greater one.

An end must be placed on this entire treatment of usury with the proposed disputation. Because, however, the things that could be said copiously in this place were explained above in Question 42 while disputing about scandal, I shall finish this matter in a few words.

1 Therefore, the first conclusion is: By taking a loan at interest <term>mutuum: a loan of things that are consumed by use, like money</term>, an injustice is not committed against the usurer. This is very well known, since no injury is done to him in it, but rather it is the borrower who suffers injury from the usurer.

Second conclusion: A borrower can commit an injustice against his wife, children, and creditors by taking a loan at interest. For example, if he contracts a great debt to their prejudice, especially by practicing what are called *mohatras* <note>A "mohatra" was a sham contract used to hide interest: a person buys an item on credit at a high price and immediately sells it back to the lender for a lower price in cash.</note> and wasting his goods. This is clear in itself, and it is affirmed by Soto, *On Justice*, book 6, question 1, article 5; and Navarro in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 263.

Third conclusion: It is never lawful to induce a usurer to lend at interest. This is evident, because since he cannot practice it without sin, it would be inducing him to sin, which is not permitted.

Fourth conclusion: It is a sin, without some necessity, to offer someone the occasion for a new mortal fault by demanding a loan from him when you know he will seek interest, even if he is habitually ready to lend under that agreement. The reason is that, under the guilt of mortal sin, you are bound by the law of charity to avoid his mortal sin if you can do so without inconvenience or grave trouble to yourself—even if the scandal on his part is not that of the "little ones," but of the "Pharisees." <note>The "scandal of the Pharisees" refers to those who are not led into sin by weakness but take offense out of malice or pride.</note>

Fifth conclusion: If someone is in need of money, even moderately, or because of a notable profit that he hopes for, or to sustain his life through trade, or because he is under some pressure of necessity and cannot easily have the money from elsewhere, he may lawfully ask for a loan, and nothing prevents him from doing so even if he understands that the person from whom he asks will demand interest.

Indeed, if he understands that the other person will not give the loan unless he himself offers interest, he may say to him: "Lend me a hundred, and I will restore a hundred and ten to you," or "Lend me a hundred, and see..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page concerning the morality of usury and the specific circumstances under which one might offer more than the principal amount in a loan. It transitions into a broader ethical debate about the 'lesser of two evils.'</meta>

->Luis de Molina, *On Contracts*<-

# Page 204

...of however much you wish, I will restore to you further. The reason for these things is that this is not cooperating with his sin for one’s own benefit, but rather offering it to him for a reasonable cause, even though one knows that from his own malice it will become an occasion for sin and a "scandal of the Pharisees" <note>A theological term referring to when someone takes offense or is led into sin not because of the act itself, but because of their own preconceived malice or legalism.</note>, all of which are permitted. In the case where he says, "lend me a hundred, and I will restore a hundred and ten to you," or "see how much more you want me to restore," he is not seeking a loan for the sake of usury <term>usury: the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender</term>, but only offers him an occasion for that sin; and he shows himself ready to receive it in that way if the other is unwilling to give it otherwise. All these conclusions are explained at length in the place cited, especially in article 7, and for that reason I will not dwell on them further now.

<margin>a</margin> Whether, however, in the case of someone who wants money for a venial end <note>A "venial" end refers to a minor or pardonable motive, as opposed to a "mortal" or grave sin.</note>, such as for some superfluous things like tournaments, other games, or spectacles, our fifth conclusion holds. Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 262; Cajetan under the word "usury," last chapter; Soto in Book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 5; and others, affirm this, saying that in such an event one sins venially at most. I would not dare to condemn it when others of the same social status concur in putting on those same displays, and it would be in a way unseemly for the one demanding money for usury not to follow them. Otherwise, when he could conveniently avoid that for which he wants the money, and it would be more reasonable to avoid it: I would not dare to say that he does not sin lethally <note>Molina uses "lethally" to mean a mortal sin—one that, in Catholic theology, severs the relationship with God.</note>, and Conrad Summenhart in his *On Contracts*, question 47, affirms that he sins lethally.

<margin>3</margin> On the occasion of the fifth conclusion, it is usually asked in this place whether it is permitted to induce someone to a lesser evil so that he may avoid a greater one. For example, whether it is permitted to induce one who is unwilling to help a person in extreme need to at least help him by giving him a loan at interest—which is a lesser evil—or whether it is permitted to induce one who has decided to take revenge on someone by killing him to take a milder revenge instead, when he cannot otherwise be moved; or one who wants to commit adultery or a more serious theft, to instead commit simple fornication or a lesser theft.

The side denying this can be argued for: First, because evils are not to be done so that good may come, as Paul says in Romans 3. But to advise a lesser evil is to cooperate in it, and consequently to bring it about; therefore it is illicit, even if it is done with a view to such a great good as avoiding a greater evil.

Second, it is a crime for him to do a lesser evil to avoid a greater one to whom that is proposed; therefore it will also be a crime to advise it to him.

Third, to advise a lesser evil to avoid a greater is to advise evil and to induce someone toward it, which is certainly never permitted.

Fourth, it is a crime to ask from someone, or to advise him, that which he cannot perform without sin. But if he to whom it is advised performs the lesser evil to avoid the greater, he sins; therefore it is a crime to ask it of him or advise it to him.

However, this latter part of the dispute must be satisfied by this conclusion: Although it is a crime to persuade someone to a lesser evil whom we can deter from the greater by some other means; and although it is also a crime, solely to prevent the execution of someone’s wicked habit toward a greater evil (such as sodomy), to persuade him to begin practicing another

<column-break/>

lesser evil, such as simple fornication; it is nevertheless lawful, when we cannot otherwise move someone from the execution of a greater evil, to persuade him to instead carry out another lesser evil, provided that this does not result in the harm of some third party in particular.

We applied examples at the beginning of the second part of this dispute. Soto, Book 6 *On Justice*, question 1, article 5; Angelus under the word "usury" 2, number 2; Sylvester under the word "usury" 7, question 1; Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 263; Innocent on the chapter *Super eo* regarding usury; Cajetan in his *Summa* under the word "tyranny," and in his second volume of works, tract 31, chapter 13, in the solution to the third doubt, agree in this conclusion. In that place, Cajetan reconciles what he had said in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 78, article 4, with those things which he taught in the same *Secunda Secundae*, question 95, article 9, where he inclined toward this same opinion; therefore there is no reason for Soto to doubt Cajetan's opinion in this matter.

The last part of this conclusion, in which alone there can be difficulty, can be proven when understood with the limitation we applied. Because he who cannot otherwise withdraw a person from committing a greater evil, and advises him to execute a lesser one instead, or asks this of him, does not advise or ask that he do that which is a lesser evil, but rather asks for the exchange of a lesser for a greater, or the preference of the lesser, given that in his wickedness he was going to do one or the other. This object, however, is not an evil, but a good, according to that rule of logic: "of two evils, the lesser is to be chosen" <note>original: "ex duobus malis, minus est eligendū"</note>, which Saint Gregory also approves and advises in the chapter *Nervi*, distinction 13; therefore, that advice and petition is not evil, but good in its object.

Secondly, one who is perplexed by invincible ignorance between two things, one of which he is necessarily going to do, and thinks both are sins, certainly does not sin by choosing that which seems lesser to him for the sake of avoiding the greater, as all concede and as Saint Gregory agrees in the cited chapter *Nervi*. He would sin, however, if he chose what seemed greater to him. Therefore, the choice of a lesser evil to avoid a greater is not evil in itself, but rather good, given that the evil was going to happen; and thus the advice and petition for that choice will be good, given that by the malice of the person being advised, one of those evils was going to happen.

Thirdly, if such advice were evil, it would be because the neighbor was being induced to sin. The consequence, however, is false, because since he has already decided to sin, he is not induced to sin by that advice, but rather to diminish his fault—and to desist from a portion of the fault is a good thing; therefore, that advice is good. Augustine is clearly of this same opinion in the chapter *Si quod verius*, case 33, question 2, where he says: "If he is going to do what is not permitted, such as either killing his wife or dismissing her, let him now commit adultery so that he does not commit homicide."

To the first argument to the contrary, therefore, the minor premise must be denied: for it is not cooperating with it as it is an evil in itself, but it is lawful to cooperate in the preference for the lesser evil, given that the one being advised does not wish to desist from evil; and that preference is good.

To the second, having granted the antecedent, the consequence must be denied, because it is within the power of the one being advised to avoid even the lesser evil, and...

<summary>Molina discusses the ethics of 'harm reduction,' arguing that it is morally permissible to suggest a lesser sin to someone who is determined to commit a greater one, provided no other means can stop them.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the previous discussion on the morality of advising someone to choose a "lesser evil" to prevent a greater sin. It then transitions into a new major section (Disputation 336) regarding the legal and ethical foundations of buying and selling.</meta>

and therefore he sins in doing that, even if less so than if he committed a greater evil; but truly, it is not in the power of the one who gives the advice to keep the one he advises from sinning entirely. For that reason, it is lawful for him to offer advice, so that at least a part of the guilt might be avoided in that way.

To the third point, the antecedent is to be denied: it has been shown that to advise a good thing is to lead toward a good thing.

To the fourth, the major premise is to be denied when it is not sought absolutely, but given the fact that the one from whom it is sought is unwilling to desist from sin, it is requested as a preference for a lesser sin and a reduction of the guilt he had intended.

Regarding the excuse of Lot from guilt when, in Genesis 19, he offered his daughters to the Sodomites <note>In the biblical narrative, Lot offers his daughters to a mob to protect two angelic guests; theologians debated whether this was a sin or a strategic "lesser evil."</note>—a matter which Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Catholic theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> and Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic philosopher.</note> weave into a long dispute in the places cited above—certainly much more than what they affirm there, we are pleased with what the same Cajetan says in his commentaries on that same passage. Namely, that this offer of prostitution was hyperbolic—not with the intent that the thing should actually happen, but to show how troublesome and hard it was for him to have that injury inflicted upon the guests he had received. It is used in the same sense as when someone, to show how reluctantly they tolerate something being done, is accustomed to say, "Kill me rather than do this." And certainly, although Lot would not sin by suggesting that lesser evil if you only look at the guilt of the Sodomites, he would nonetheless sin against justice and paternal duty toward his own daughters by offering them up even to avoid the greater sin of the Sodomites, according to the limitation we added to the final part of our conclusion.

# Buying and Selling: What it is.
## DISPUTATION 336.
### SUMMARY.

1 *The contract of permutation <note>Barter or exchange of goods.</note> is older than buying and selling.*
2 *For what purpose money was introduced.*
3 *The contract of buying and selling originated simultaneously with money.*
4 *Buying and selling is a contract distinct from permutation, leasing, and emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis: a long-term or perpetual lease of land where the tenant must improve the property in exchange for a low rent</term>.*
5 *What is properly called a "sale," and in what things it consists.*
6 *Which things come under the name of a sale (and in number 9).*
7 *What is a sale.*
8 *Whether it is buying and selling if a price and another thing are given for a certain item.*
9 *When it should be considered a sale rather than a permutation.*
10 *What the Alcavala or Sisa <note>Historical sales taxes in the Iberian Peninsula.</note> is in Portugal and Castile.*
11 *How buying and selling is known to be distinct from leasing and hiring.*

Hitherto we have dealt with lucrative contracts and those that accompany them; and on the occasion of our discussion on loans, we have disputed at length regarding usury. Now let us proceed to the remaining contracts, taking our beginning from the most frequent and excellent of them: that is, from buying and selling.
In this place, it must be observed, as the Jurist

<column-break/>

says in Book 1 of the *Digest* <note>The *Digest*, or *Pandects*, was a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions commissioned by Emperor Justinian I.</note> "On contracting a sale," and as we read written in the *Institutes* <note>The *Institutes of Justinian*, a legal textbook for students of Roman law.</note> "On buying and selling," that from the beginning
<margin>1</margin> there was only the use of **permutation** <note>Barter.</note> among men, by which they exchanged wine for wheat, oil for honey, an ox for a horse, a shoe for a house, and so on with other things—everyone exchanging a thing they did not need as much for another they lacked. In that permutation, one thing did not have the character of a price or merchandise more than the other, and for that reason, the contract was of the same nature on both sides, nor did the contracting parties receive different names. But afterward, because of the inequality of things—such as shoes compared to a house, or an ox to a horse—and because many often did not need what was offered, money was invented and introduced to make exchanges easier for the sustenance of life and for human society (which are necessary because no one is self-sufficient but needs the things and labor of others). Money was to have a certain value by public authority and be a price and, as it were, a measure of other things; and as Aristotle says in *Ethics* book 5, chapter 5, it is like a surety <note>Latin: *fideiussor*; a guarantor.</note> for future exchanges that anyone might need. This is because when someone offers that money in the future which they received for a thing they did not need, they may receive those things which they do need for it.

<margin>2</margin> Because money was introduced for the commerce of things by public law and authority, it was called *nummus* in Greek, from *nomos*, that is, "law," as Aristotle says in the cited chapter. It was called *pecunia* in Latin, from *pecude* <note>original: "a pecude"</note> [cattle]: because, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author.</note> in book 33, chapter 3, money among the Romans was once stamped with the mark of a beast.
<margin>3</margin> From this, the origin of the contract of buying and selling is also easily clear (as the Jurist says in the cited places): for it began at the same time as money. Indeed, by the very fact that money was introduced, it began to have the character of a price in comparison to other things, and other things began to have the character of merchandise in comparison to it. Simultaneously, a contract resulted, coalescing from two parts of different natures and names: one is the exchange or agreement of merchandise for a price, called **selling**, and the exchanger is called the **seller**; the other truly is the exchange or agreement of price for merchandise, called **buying**, and the exchanger is the **buyer**. And this contract, according to the Jurist in the cited places, is distinct in kind from permutation, even if that matter was once doubted, as explained in Book 1 of the *Digest* "On the permutation of things."
<margin>4</margin> From what has been said, it is clear that neither the exchange of a thing that is not a price for another thing that is not a price (such as an ox for a horse), nor the exchange of a thing that is a price for another thing that is a price (such as gold money for silver money), is called buying and selling. Rather, those contracts are distinct: the first is called **permutation**, and the second is called **exchange** <note>Latin: *cambium*.</note>, about which we will speak in their proper places. Note this: not every exchange or agreement of that which is not a price for a price is a sale. For if a thing is granted only for its use, or for the fruits to be gathered from it in exchange for a price, it is not called a sale, but a **lease** <note>Latin: *locatio*.</note>; and if it is granted only for the usufruct <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it.</note> and beneficial ownership for a certain annual or monthly payment, it is called **emphyteusis**.

<summary>This page concludes a theological debate on the 'lesser of two evils' using the story of Lot, before beginning a legal analysis of the origins of 'Buying and Selling,' specifically focusing on how the invention of money transformed simple barter into modern commerce.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal and ethical analysis of contracts, specifically transitioning from the general theory of exchange to the formal definitions of buying and selling.
