->### Ludouicus Molina on Contracts<-

<margin>5</margin> Therefore, when a thing is granted in terms of **direct ownership** <note>original: "directum dominium" — the ultimate legal title to a property, as opposed to the right to simply use it.</note> for a price—whether it is simultaneously granted in terms of its use or not—it is properly called the **sale** of a thing, even if it is only granted in part, such as when half a field or a house is sold. Furthermore, when someone holds a certain right in the property of another and grants that right to someone else for a price, it is called a sale; for example, if a **tenant-farmer** <term>emphyteuta: someone holding a long-term, inheritable lease on land belonging to another</term> grants their **leasehold right** <note>original: "ius emphyteuticum"</note> for a price, they are said to be
<margin>6</margin> selling it, whether they grant it to the property owner or to someone else. **Servitudes** <term>easements: legal rights to use someone else's land for a specific purpose</term> can also be sold, just as I can sell you the right of passage through my field into your field, or the right to set a beam into my wall, or a servitude agreeing not to build my wall or house any higher. Similarly, the **surface rights** <note>original: "superficies"</note> of a plot of land upon which you may build a house can be sold (*Law 1, § 1, Digest on Surface Rights*). It is considered a sale if the surface rights are granted for a single, one-time price. If, however, they are granted for an annual or monthly price, it is considered a **lease** or a "surface-rights contract." One may also sell the right to receive annual income from me or from my field; this is called an **annuity contract** <note>original: "contractus censualis"</note> and is a certain type of buying and selling. These and similar things can be sold.

Therefore, if **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a prominent Spanish Scholastic philosopher often cited by Molina.</note> (*On Justice, Book 6, Question 2, Article 1*) understands by the name of "thing" all and only those things explained above, his definition of buying and selling can be accepted. Namely: *selling is the alienation of a thing for a price*, that is, a contract by which a thing is transferred for a price; and *buying is the acquisition of a thing for a price*, that is, a contract by which ownership or quasi-ownership is obtained (in the ways explained) for a price. However, to tell the truth, the contract of buying and selling is more easily understood and explained than it is fully and exactly defined.

One thing must be observed regarding Soto's definition: it is not essential to the nature of a sale that the thing is actually alienated or that ownership is transferred. For if the thing does not belong to the seller, even if the sale is valid (according to what was said extensively in Disputation 327), ownership is nonetheless not transferred, even if delivery follows. Therefore, it is only essential to a sale that, by its own nature, it is **intended to transfer ownership** or quasi-ownership for a price upon delivery, even if this is hindered by something else. This is all that can be gathered from the law *cum manu sata* (*Digest on the Contract of Purchase*), the words of which are:

> No one can be seen to have sold a thing if the arrangement regarding ownership is such that it does not pass to the buyer; instead, this is either a lease or another type of contract.

That is the passage. The sense of these words is this: it is essential to a sale that the ownership of what is sold is intended to be transferred by the power of the contract. Read, among others, Alvaro Valasco (*On the Law of Emphyteusis, Q. 19*), Pinelo (*On the Code, Rescinding Sales, Part 2*), and Lassarte (*On the Tithe of Sale, Chapter 1*).

<margin>7</margin> Perhaps we can better define **selling** in this way: *It is a contract, perfected by consent, of merchandise for a price.* The word "contract" serves as the general category; by the phrase "perfected by consent alone," those contracts are excluded which are not finished by consent, such as a loan for use, a loan for consumption, a barter exchange, and others. By the phrase "merchandise for a price," we exclude **leasing and hiring**, because although they are also

<column-break/>

perfected by consent and involve a price, one does not find "merchandise" in them. Indeed, by the name "merchandise," we only mean those things explained just above as being the subject matter of a sale. **Buying**, then, will be: *a contract, perfected by consent, of a price for merchandise.*

<margin>8</margin> A doubt arises when a price and another object (such as a horse) are given for something (such as a house), or when labor and a certain amount of money are given. Is this a **sale and purchase**, or rather a **barter exchange** <note>original: "permutatio"</note> or an **unnamed contract**? The common opinion of the doctors (following Bartolus and Panormitanus, and followed by Antonio Gomez, Arias Pinelo, and Lassarte) is that when there is not a great difference in value between the price and the thing given along with it for another thing, one must look to the words of the contracting parties (*Digest, On the Rules of Law*). If their words sound like buying and selling, the contract should be judged as such; then, not only the price but also the horse promised with it may be demanded by an "action on the sale." If, however, the words sound like a barter or an unnamed contract, it should be judged as a barter, and then the price can be demanded by an "action on the prescribed words."

It was said: "when there is not a great difference in value." For if there is a **great excess in the price**, then, regardless of the words used, it is judged a sale and purchase. If there is a **great excess in the value of the thing** given with the money, it will be a barter or an unnamed contract, even if the words sound like buying and selling. Gomez, Cavallos, and Lassarte agree on this, as do Panormitanus and Bartolus. The reason is that such a notable excess in either the price or the thing makes one element the primary part and the other merely an "annexed" or secondary part. Thus, by its very nature, the contract is a sale or a barter depending on which part has the much greater value. When the nature of a contract is clear, it should not be judged solely by the words or the intent of the parties.

<margin>9</margin> Lassarte, following Tiraquellus and the common opinion, says: what was said at the beginning from the common opinion should be understood as applying when it does not involve prejudice to the **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note> or a third party. For if a tax is owed on a sale but not on a barter (or vice versa), or if a **right of retraction** <term>the legal right for a relative or neighbor to step in and buy a property at the same price</term> applies to a sale but not a barter (as is the case in this kingdom), then, if the value of the price exceeds the thing (even by a little), the contract will be judged a sale. Conversely, if the thing given with the price is more valuable, it is a barter, regardless of what the parties said.

<margin>10</margin> Observe that in this kingdom, according to the laws of the *New Collection*, and in Portugal, a tribute called the **Alcabala** or **Sisa** <note>These were significant sales taxes in the Spanish and Portuguese empires; the Alcabala was usually 10%.</note>—which is a tenth part of the price—is owed on sales and also on barters. However, in this kingdom, only the seller is held to pay the full amount based on the value of the price, as held in Law 1...

Molina also discusses how mixed payments (money plus goods) are categorized for tax purposes, specifically mentioning the Alcabala tax in Spain and Portugal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal analysis of contracts, specifically looking at how taxes apply to sales and exchanges in the kingdoms of Spain and Portugal. It transitions from discussing specific tax exemptions to a more general legal theory on how to distinguish a "sale" from "labor" or "barter."</meta>

Tractate 2, Disputation 337.

An exception is made when oil is sold in Seville <note>original: "Hispalis"</note>; for then, the seller pays half and the buyer pays half, as is held in the cited Title 17, Law 3, and Title 18, Law 2. However, if the King’s oil is sold, because the King is exempt from paying this tribute, the buyer alone pays half of the **Alcavala** <term>Alcavala: A heavy sales tax historically common in Spain and its colonies</term>, as is added in Law 4 and held in Title 18, Law 3. In Portugal, however, it is the rule that one half falls to the seller to pay, and the other half to the buyer.

In both kingdoms, however, a double tribute is paid upon an exchange <note>barter</note>. This is because, according to the laws *sciendum* and *sed si quis permutauerit* in the Digest and the Code regarding the exchange of things, each person in an exchange acts as both seller and buyer in relation to the other. For this reason, every exchange is considered a double buying and selling. In this kingdom <note>Spain</note>, Law 2 expressly decrees that if any price intervenes in an exchange of one thing for another—whatever that price may be, whether it is greater or lesser than the value of the thing being exchanged—the Alcavala must be paid on both items being exchanged. Thus, in this kingdom, a person who receives one hundred gold coins and an ox in exchange for a house must pay a tenth part of the price (that is, ten gold coins) and, in addition, a tenth part of the value of the ox as it shall be appraised. On the other hand, the person who receives the house is bound to pay, not indeed a tenth part of the value of the whole house, since he owes nothing on that part of the house that corresponds to the hundred gold coins he gave for it, but only a tenth part of the value of that portion of the house which, in the judgment of a prudent person, corresponds to the ox. So says Laffarte, in the cited chapter 17, number 1, according to the cited Law 2 and other statutes.

The situation would be different if we set aside that particular provision of the law, even though the Alcavala would still be due in this kingdom upon sale and exchange. Indeed, when the hundred gold coins paid along with the ox for the house far exceed the value of the ox, the entire contract is judged to be merely a purchase and sale. In that case, only a single Alcavala would be owed based on the combined value of the ox and the hundred gold coins, as the same Laffarte rightly noted according to common opinion and the principles of common law. Perhaps the same rule should be stated for Portugal as for this kingdom; however, since I am currently far from there, do not have the legal articles of that kingdom with me, and am ignorant of their practice, I can define nothing certain on this matter.

To return to the point from which we digressed: When the words of the contracting parties do not make it clear which contract they intended, then, if the price clearly exceeds the value of the thing given along with it, the contract is judged to be a purchase and sale. If, however, the value of the thing given with the price exceeds the price itself, it is considered an exchange <note>barter</note>, following the argument of the text in the Digest on the acquisition of ownership.

Finally, when the thing and the price are of the same value, and it is not clear from the words of the parties which contract they intended to celebrate, Baldus and certain others have judged that the contract should be considered one of purchase and sale. However, the more common opinion of Bartolus, Tiraquellus, and others—whom Antonio Gomez refers to and follows—asserts that it is an exchange, based on the argument of the text in

<column-break/>

the beginning of the Digest on the *actio aestimatoria* <note>a legal action regarding valued goods</note>. Nevertheless, it is more pleasing to say with Alciato, Covarrubias, and Pinellus in the cited places, and Laffarte in chapter 17, number 22, that it is a sale as to one part and an exchange as to the other, especially when it concerns the prejudice of a third party (as in the case of a **retraction** <term>retractu: the right to buy back a property or preempt a sale</term>) or when deciding whether a double or single tribute is to be paid from that contract.

Furthermore, observe how to distinguish when a contract is for purchase and sale versus when it is for letting and hiring <note>labor/lease</note>. If someone creates a work for another for a price using material that the other person provides—such as making rulers from wood provided by the owner, or rings from gold or silver provided to him—it is a contract of **letting and hiring** <note>original: "locatio et conductio"</note> and not a purchase and sale. Consequently, in these events, the tax which they call the Alcavala or the **Sisa** <term>Sisa: An excise tax on food or essential goods</term> in Castile and Portugal is not owed.

This is defined in the Digest and the Institutes regarding hiring. If, however, he creates the work for a price using material that the craftsman himself provides, it is a purchase and sale, and therefore the aforementioned tribute is owed. This is the case if someone makes rulers for a price, or shoes, or rings, from material provided by the craftsman himself. This is expressly held in the three cited laws and confirmed by Laffarte.

Note, however, that in the Kingdom of Castile, the Alcavala is not paid in the same amount for gold and silver as for other things, as is arranged in Law 18, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Collection*.

Note further an exception to the latter part of the proposed rule: if someone builds a house for another for a price on the land of the person paying the price. For even if the agreement is such that the craftsman provides the building materials and the labor for that price, the contract is one of letting and hiring, not of sale and purchase, and therefore the Alcavala is not owed on that contract. The reason is that since the buyer provides the site for building the house, the ownership of the materials passes into the ownership of the soil <note>a legal principle where what is built on land becomes part of the land</note>. Thus, the material is viewed as something accessory to the construction for that price; it is a contract of hiring, as is expressly held in the Digest, and as Laffarte affirms, where he disputes many similar cases.

<margin>6</margin> When a purchase and sale is suspended until a document is completed, what is owed in Spain.

<margin>14</margin> A sale made regarding pledges—stating that if the debtor has not paid by a certain day, the pledge is considered sold at a fair price to be judged by a specific person—is valid.

<margin>16</margin> A purchase and sale is valid when a certain price is established by reference to something else.
<margin>17</margin> In how many ways a hiring and leasing agreement is valid.
<margin>18</margin> A sale made by an absent person with a guarantee of ratification: when it is considered perfected once it has later been ratified.
<margin>19</margin> The **Alcavala** <term>Alcavala: A common sales tax in the Spanish kingdoms</term> is not owed if the sale is not ratified.
<margin>20</margin> Ratification is retroactive to the time the contract was celebrated.

<margin>1</margin> Purchase and sale, since it is among those contracts perfected by mutual expressed consent (as explained in Disputation 254), can be perfected by that very fact without writing, provided the contracting parties agree on the thing and the price. Indeed, it can be perfected not only in the presence of the object, but also between absent parties through letters or a messenger, as shown in the cited disputation. Furthermore, as soon as the contract has been perfected in that manner, it is not lawful for either of the contracting parties to withdraw from it against the will of the other. All these points are established in the title "On Obligations from Consent" at the beginning of the *Institutes* regarding purchase and sale; and in the *Institutes* "On Donations" <note>original: "Institu. de donationibus"</note> at the section *aliæ autem*, in the phrase *perficiuntur*, joined with the following phrase; and in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff." refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> under "On Contracting a Purchase," law 2; and law 1 of the *Digest* "On the Exchange of Things"; and laws 6 and 8, Title 5, Part 5; and law 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "l. Lusit. ord."</note>, Title 23 at the beginning, and Title 24 at the beginning. In these latter sources it is added that if the seller, after the price has been paid, does not deliver the item within the established term, he is held liable to the buyer for "interest" <note>original: "interesse"</note>, both for the loss of profit and the actual damage arising. This must be understood as referring to the intrinsic profit and damage of the thing itself, and not indeed to the extrinsic, according to the law *si sterilis* in the section *cum per venditorem* of the *Digest* "On Actions for Purchase," as was said in Disputation 299. However, when a purchase and sale has been perfected in the aforementioned way, either of the contracting parties may compel the other to commit the contract to writing for greater stability and easier proof; for everyone is compelled to do that which does not harm themselves and benefits another. So says Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 27, although

<column-break/>

the glosses <note>Glosses were marginal comments or explanations in medieval and early modern legal texts</note> he cites contribute little to the point. Certain parts of the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 36, penult section, favor this. I would, however, advise that if Antonio Gómez’s opinion is true, the public instrument must be prepared at the expense of the one who compels the other to do it, when he demands it be committed to writing some time after the contract was celebrated.

<margin>4</margin> Because a purchase and sale is perfected by consent alone, without any delivery of either the price or the goods, Lassatte (in "On the Tithe of Sale," chapter 3, number 1) and others whom he cites, most excellently judge that the **Alcavala** <note>original: "alcaualam"</note> is owed in this kingdom from the moment the contract is perfected in the manner explained, even if neither the thing nor the price has been delivered. This is proven by Law 1 in those words, *Of the whole price for which they shall sell* <note>original Spanish: "De todo el precio porque vendieren"</note>, and Law 10 by the words, *Because the payment is not finished* <note>original Spanish: "Por no ser acabada la paga"</note>, Title 17; and Law 31 by those words, *After the granting and the sale is made* <note>original Spanish: "Despues del otorgamiento y hecha la uenta"</note>, Title 19, Book 9 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collectionis," referring to the Nueva Recopilación of Spanish law</note>. The reason is that this tribute is established in the contract of sale itself as a burden regarding its substance. Castillo and Montalvo, however, who asserted that the Alcavala is not owed before the delivery of the goods and the price, relied on the false foundation that the contract is not perfected before delivery. Even Baldus, who judged that the tax <note>original: "gabellam"</note> on a sold item is not owed before delivery, was speaking of a statute from whose words and disposition it was gathered that the tax was not imposed unless the sale was consummated by delivery.

From this definition it follows that the five days given in Castile to declare or pay the Alcavala to a public official under penalty of a double payment must be counted, not from the moment of delivery of the goods and price, but from the moment the sale is finalized in the manner explained, as Law 31 (cited above) clearly holds. This same point is to be similarly understood regarding the time given in the same kingdom for the redemption <note>original: "retractum," the right to buy back family land</note> of a sold item by right of blood. Lassatte affirms both points in the place cited above, number 4, and Montalvo and Matienzo (whom Lassatte mentions) agree on this second point.

From the same definition it follows that not only can a tax collector <note>original: "gabellariũ"</note> act to obtain the Alcavala from the moment the sale is finalized in the predicted way, but even if the goods are never delivered—indeed, even if the parties repent of the contract before delivery—it is still owed, and he can act to obtain it. It also follows that if the lord of the place where the sale was celebrated had the right to the taxes and died before the delivery of the goods and price in that same place, the Alcavala is owed to the heirs of the deceased, and not to the successor of the entailed estate <note>original: "maioratu"</note> in whose time the goods and price were delivered, unless he himself is the heir. Furthermore, by the same reasoning, if one tax collector had contracted for the taxes at the time the contract was celebrated, and another at the time of delivery, the Alcavala would be owed to the first collector, not the second; Book 12, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Collection* agrees. It follows further that if a sale is made in a place and time in which the tribute is owed, and the goods and price are delivered in a place and time immune from the tribute, the Alcavala is still owed. Conversely, it is not owed if the sale is celebrated in a place and time immune from the tribute, and the delivery happens at a time when it is not immune there. Similarly, it follows that if someone celebrated a sale at a time when he himself was not immune from the tribute, and delivered the item...

<summary>Molina defines a sale as legally binding ("perfected") at the moment of mutual consent regarding item and price, rather than at delivery. This legal distinction determines exactly when sales taxes (Alcavala) are triggered and which tax collector or heir has the right to the revenue.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 33

...delivered it at a time when he was exempt, then he owes the <term>alcabala</term> <note>original: "alcaualam"; a common sales tax in Spain and its territories</note>. Conversely, he does not owe it if he was exempt at the time he sold it, even if that immunity had ceased by the time of delivery. All of this is handed down by Lassarte in the place cited above, at number 9 and the three following sections.

<margin>5</margin> What has been said—that purchase and sale are perfected by the mere consent of both contracting parties expressed to each other, without the need for writing—must be understood to apply unless the contracting parties agree or intend for the contract to be made and perfected through a written document. In that case, before the writing is fully completed, either by the contracting parties themselves or by some third party (whether he be a public official or someone else) and signed by the parties, the contract is not considered perfected. This remains true even if mutual consent regarding the item and the price, expressed in words, preceded it; rather, it remains within the power of either party to withdraw from that contract. This is found in the <note>references to Roman and Iberian law follow</note> Institutes, "On Purchase and Sale," § 1; the Code, "On the Trust of Instruments"; the Digest, "On Contracting a Purchase"; the *Partidas*, Part 5, Title 3, Law 6; and the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Chapter 36, at the beginning and § 1. When, however, the contracting parties mention that a document should be made regarding the matter, either before the contract or at the time of the contract itself, they are considered to have suspended the contract until the writing is perfected. This was decreed in the *Partidas*, Part 5, Title 5, Law 6; and it was the opinion of Azon and the glosses on the two laws cited first, as well as several others. Nevertheless, Bartolus, Baldus, and many others asserted the opposite: namely, that it is not enough for the contract to be considered suspended until the writing is made unless the contracting parties expressly state so. The Portuguese Ordinances, in the cited § 1, either require an express will that the contract otherwise not be valid, or certainly that it be understood in some way from the manner of contracting, which is explained with two examples. Therefore, they seem to choose a middle path, or certainly the opinion of Bartolus explained a little more fully. However, all agree that when, after a purchase and sale has been celebrated by mutual consent, the parties discuss or agree on making a document for that matter, this does not suspend the contract, but they act regarding the document only for greater firmness and easier proof. Thus, it follows that before such a writing, it is not lawful for either party to withdraw from that contract perfected by mutual consent.

Although that Law 6 is received in practice in this kingdom, and judgment must be made according to it, as the Spanish doctors—including Covarruvias in chapter *Relatum* 1, "On Witnesses," number 9—affirm; nevertheless, Gregorio Lopez in the same place, Lassarte (as above, number 14), and many others whom they cite, believe it should be limited when it is understood from the circumstances that mention of the writing was made only for proof and greater security, and they did not intend to suspend the contract. For instance, if the delivery of the price or the item sold was made during the very celebration of the contract without waiting for any writing. In this event, Lassarte reports that he judged thus in a certain case, and the sentence was confirmed by higher judges, confirming the same matter with several laws.

<margin>6</margin> Since, according to the doctrine handed down, a purchase and sale is suspended so that a document may perfect it, the <term>alcabala</term> from such a contract is not owed earlier, nor do the days for declaring the contract or paying the tax begin to run until the writing is finished and perfected. Consequently, this tax is owed to whichever <term>gabellarius</term> <note>a tax collector or tax farmer</note> or lord holds the right at the time the writing is perfected, and not

<column-break/>

to the one who held it at the time of the agreement and mutual consent, as affirmed by Antonio Gomez (Book 2, *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 1, number 17) and Lassarte (as above, number 15). It also follows that if the seller was exempt from that tax at the time the writing was completed, he does not owe it, even if he was not exempt at the time of the agreement.

<margin>7</margin> For a purchase and sale to be valid, and thus considered perfected, it is necessary that a certain price be established; otherwise, it will be null. Thus it is in the Institutes, "On Purchase and Sale," § *Pretium*; the *Partidas*, Part 5, Title 5, Laws 1 and 9; and the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 23, § 1, Law 4. From this it follows that if a contract is celebrated in this manner—"I sell you this thing for whatever price you wish," or "for what you judge it to be worth," or "I buy this thing from you for whatever price you wish," or "for what you have judged"—such a contract is invalid, as in the Digest, "On Contracting a Purchase," law *Quia sæpe*, § *Illud*; the Code, "On Contracting a Purchase," law *In vendentis*; and the cited Partida 5, Law 9, § 1. The same applies if it is said, "I sell you this thing," or "I buy it from you for a <term>just price</term>," <note>original: "pretio iusto"</note> according to what it shall be judged to be worth. If, however,

<margin>8</margin> a specific person is determined and it is said, "for as much as such a person shall judge," the contract is valid, as held in the Code, "On Contracting a Purchase," last law; the Institutes, "On Purchase and Sale," § *Pretium*; and the cited Partida 5, Law 9, § 1. But if that person does not judge the price, either because he died, was otherwise hindered, or because he was unwilling, the sale is rendered null. There is no need to resort to the judgment of another, as held in those four laws. However, by the very fact that he has judged the price, the contract is perfected. Yet, if he judged a price that is greatly excessive or deficient, recourse is had to a judge so that prudent men may reduce it to equality by their judgment, as in the cited Law 9 and § 1; this is agreed upon in the Digest, "On Partnerships," law *Societate*, § *Arbitrorum*, and law *Unde si*, and affirmed by the Gloss on the last law of the Code, "On Contracting a Purchase." In the Portuguese Ordinances, in the cited § 1, it is added that if two arbitrators chosen by a judge agree, their judgment must stand; but if they disagree and the judge agrees with one of them, that must be followed.

<margin>9</margin> There are several things to be observed regarding these matters. The first is that a sale in which the price is left to the judgment of a designated third person is not properly "conditional"—as if the contract were perfected but dependent on the fulfillment of a condition—but is simply an absolute contract, not yet completed and perfected, because there is no price until it is defined by that third person. From this it follows not only that the <term>alcabala</term> is not owed before the price is established, but also that, once the price is established, the debt of that tax is not retroactive to the time in which the agreement was made, but only begins from the time the price was established. Therefore, if at the time the price was established, there was already another <term>gabellarius</term> or another lord of the tax, the tax is owed to the later collector or lord, not to the prior one. Likewise, if at the time the price was established, the tax was not owed (either by reason of the seller's privilege or some other reason), that sale is exempt from such tax, even if at the time the agreement was made in that manner, the sale would have been subject to the same tax. Therefore, attention must be paid to the time of the consummated contract by the establishment of the price, and not to the time of the agreement made in that manner. Thus Lassarte, in the cited Chapter 3 from number 19, where he pursues this matter extensively and learnedly.

->Luis de Molina, On Contracts<-

<column-break/>

<margin>10</margin> When, however, a sale is conditional, the tax is first and foremost not owed until the condition has been fulfilled. This is the common affirmation of the <term>Doctors</term> <note>The "Doctors" refers to established legal scholars and authorities of the time</note>, whom Antonio Gomez [citing various sources] and Lassarte [as cited above] refer to and follow. The reason is that the contract is still "pending," and if the condition fails to be met, the contract could be rendered null. Furthermore, while a condition is pending, neither of the contracting parties is permitted to withdraw from the agreement against the will of the other—as Lassarte affirms with various commentaries and the common opinion—and the treasury thus acquires a "hopeful right" to that tax. 

Nonetheless, if the parties dissolve the contract by mutual consent before the condition is fulfilled, the tax is not owed, as Lassarte rightly affirms. The reason is that in the Spanish kingdoms, this tax is neither granted nor owed except in cases of a "pure and perfect" sale or exchange. A sale that is dissolved by mutual consent while the condition is still pending was never "pure and perfect." Consequently, even if the delivery of the sold item had occurred while the condition was pending (and thus ownership had technically transferred to the buyer, as Bartolus teaches), if the contract is dissolved by mutual consent during that same period, the tax is not owed for that same reason: namely, that the sale was never pure and perfected. 

This same rule does not apply to a "modal" sale <note>original: "venditione sub modo"; a sale where a specific duty or burden is attached to the transfer</note>, as Lassarte rightly observes. This is because a "mode" does not suspend the sale; rather, the sale is considered complete and perfect immediately, as is clear from what we have said regarding modes in their proper place above. Therefore, the tax is owed immediately upon such a sale. Although this is how things stand regarding conditional sales;

<margin>11</margin> because it is the nature of a conditional contract that, once the condition is fulfilled, its legal force is "pulled back" <note>original: "retrotrahatur"; the legal doctrine of retroactivity</note> to the time it was celebrated, as if it had been entered into purely and unconditionally at that time. This is gathered from various laws in the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff."; the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> and other legal sources. It follows that if the contract is not dissolved and the condition is fulfilled, the tax is considered owed from the moment the conditional sale was celebrated, not from the moment the condition was fulfilled. Therefore, the tax is owed to the lord and the tax collector <note>original: "gabellario"</note> who were in office at the time the contract was celebrated, not those in office when the condition was met. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, Antonio Gomez, and Lassarte. 

Following the scholar Baldus, Lassarte rightly adds that if the tax was not owed at the time the conditional contract was celebrated—perhaps because it was entered into at a fair where such taxes were exempt, or for some other reason—the tax is not owed even if the condition is fulfilled at a time when that exemption no longer exists. This is because one must look to the time of the contract's creation, not the time the condition was met.

<margin>12</margin> Bartolus and the common opinion of the Doctors (whom Gomez and Covarrubias follow) limit this doctrine of retroactivity in conditional contracts. It should be under-

<column-break/>

stood to apply when the condition is "causal" or "mixed," but it is different when the condition is "potestative" <note>A causal condition depends on chance or a third party; a potestative condition depends entirely on the will of one of the parties</note>. The latter does not pull the contract back in time; therefore, if a sale is celebrated under a potestative condition, the tax will be owed to the tax collector and the lord who are in office at the time the condition is fulfilled. 

Covarrubias restricts this limitation, explaining that it applies when the condition is so "potestative" that it cannot be fulfilled against the will of the other contracting party. By arguing from the opposite sense, when a potestative condition can be fulfilled even against the will of the other party, it *does* pull the contract back to the time of celebration. Lassarte rejects the common limitation of the doctors, even in the restricted form used by Covarrubias. Although he attempts to address the laws cited by Bartolus and others, he does not sufficiently satisfy the legal arguments from which Covarrubias’s restriction is clearly gathered. 

I should advise, however, that when a condition is such that, if it had existed at the time of the contract's celebration, it would have made the seller immune from the tax, it also renders him immune even if he was not immune at the actual time of the sale. For example, if someone celebrates a contract saying: "I sell you this thing for a thousand gold coins, provided I enter into Holy Orders." Certainly, once the condition is met, the <term>alcabala</term> tax is not owed. The reason is that although one must look at the time the sale was celebrated rather than when the condition was met, the fulfillment of the condition pulls the contract back to its inception. It is as if the sale were celebrated purely and unconditionally at that time while he was already in the state described by the condition. Thus, the condition is viewed as being present then, making him immune from the tax as if he had already been initiated into Holy Orders. This is proven by the final law in the Digest "On the Stipulation of Slaves" and other laws which Lassarte cites and learnedly examines.

<margin>13</margin> This must be understood, however, provided that such a condition was not added in <term>fraud</term> to avoid paying the tax, as that same law proves and the same doctor rightly affirms. For a fourth reason: if someone sells the future fruits of a field, since it is a conditional sale (contingent on the fruits actually growing), once the condition is met, the contract is pulled back to the time it was celebrated. The tax is owed to the tax collector and lord who were in office then, unless this was done to defraud a later tax collector or lord by making an agreement with the previous one to be satisfied with a smaller tax. This is according to Lassarte and the laws of the <note>original: "nouæ collectionis"; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish law</note> New Collection. This concludes the first of the points we said should be observed.

<margin>14</margin> The second point is that in matters of <term>pledges</term> <note>original: "pignoribus"; collateral or pawned items</note>, a sale is valid if it is made in this manner: "if you have not paid the debt by such a day, the pledge shall remain sold for a fair price," specifically as judged by the arbitrament of prudent men. This is held in the Digest and the Portuguese Ordinances.

<margin>15</margin> Third: although no contract is valid in which the price is left to the judgment and will of one of the contracting parties, it is nevertheless valid if the thing is sold under the law and condition that it is given...

#### O 2

...the sale is granted if it pleases the buyer. If, however, a certain time period is prescribed to him within which he may withdraw from the contract if he says it does not please him, then if that term arrives and he has not signaled to the seller that he is displeased or unwilling to buy it, the contract shall be confirmed. It shall not be lawful for him to withdraw from it thereafter. This is held in the **fourth book of the Lusitanian Ordinances** <note>original: "l. Lusitan. ord."; refers to the Portuguese legal code</note>, **title 23, last paragraph**, and the **paragraph "Purchase"** in the **Institutes on Buying and Selling**. Antonio Gomez affirms this in the **second volume of Various Resolutions, chapter 2, number 19**.

<margin>16</margin> The fourth point is that a purchase and sale are valid when a certain price is established by reference to something else. For example, if it is said: "I buy this thing from you for the amount you paid for it," or "for the amount he who sold or gave it to you bought it," or "for the money I have in my purse," or "in such a place." For then the sale is valid, provided it was indeed bought by the seller (or by the one from whom the seller bought it or who gave it to him), or provided the buyer actually has money in his purse or in that other place. If these conditions did not exist, the contract would be null, because then no price would have been established. This is held in the **law "This sale," paragraph "Of this sort"** and the **law "If anyone a field"** in the **Digest on Contracting Purchases**, and **law 10, title 5, part 5**, as well as other laws cited by Antonio Gomez in the **second volume of Various Resolutions, chapter 2, number 9**. 

From this, he concludes that a sale is valid if someone says: "I sell to you," or "I buy from you, this thing at the price for which it is commonly sold in the market," or "at the price for which it will be sold at such and such a time," or "at the price which shall then be fixed by public law." In the same way, when a thing is understood to be sold at a certain price—namely, one fixed by law or the common price at the time—the sale would be valid even if no mention of the price was made. <margin>17</margin> In the same way also, a lease <note>original: "locatio"</note> would be valid by which something is leased without any mention of price, provided it was customary for it to be leased at a certain price; for it would be understood to be leased at that price. Furthermore, a lease is valid with no price established in places where, after houses are leased, the price is customarily fixed by public officials—as happens in Salamanca regarding houses leased to students. Gomez, in the place cited, and in **chapter 3, number 4**, observes with Accursius <note>original: "Azone"</note> and others that in cases where a contract of purchase and sale, or of lease and hiring, is invalid because a certain price was not established, if it happens that the things so sold or leased are delivered and consumed, or fruits are gathered from them, or they are used for the purpose for which they were leased, the seller or lessor can then sue for the thing, the fruits, and the use, according to how much these shall be valued. This is not done through an action on the sale or lease (since those contracts were null), but by an **action on the prescribed words** <note>original: "actione præscriptis verbis"; a legal remedy used when a specific contract type does not apply but equity requires a solution</note> or an **action on the facts** <note>original: "in factum"</note>, according to the **law "As often as"** in the **Digest on Prescribed Words**. In what has been said so far, Alvaro Valasco agrees in **On the Law of Emphyteusis, question 11, from number 5**, whom you may consult, as well as Pinellus in his commentary on the **Code, On the Rescinding of a Sale, in the Rubric, part 2, chapter 1, from number 1**. Moreover, regarding this last point, Alvaro Valasco rightly says there, against Pinellus at number 19, that when the things which had been delivered still exist, a **claim for the recovery of the thing** <note>original: "rei vendicationem"</note> is available to the one who delivered them, because the contract was null; there is no action to have the price fixed and the sale perfected. In this, Antonio Gomez does not disagree with Alvaro Valasco, even though Valasco cites him for the contrary opinion; nor do the things we have just said disagree.

<margin>18</margin> A doubt arises: if someone, believing his friend wishes to 

<column-break/>

sell something, and seeing an opportunity, sells it in the friend’s name and by managing his business, while promising or binding himself that the friend will ratify it—and later the friend does ratify it—when is the sale considered perfected? It must be said that the sale is not considered perfected until the **ratification** <note>original: "ratū habitio"</note> occurs, because the sale depends upon it. Nevertheless, it is the nature of ratification that it **acts retrospectively** <note>original: "retrotrahit"</note> by a legal fiction to the time in which the act was done, as if it had been perfected then. This is clear from the **law "It is permitted"** in the **Digest on Judgments**, **law 6 "A field," paragraph 1** in the **Digest on Pledges**, the **law "Donations which parents," last paragraph** in the **Code on Donations between Husband and Wife**, the **last law** in the **Code on the Macedoniano Decree**, and from other laws.

<margin>19</margin> From this, as far as the **alcabala** <note>original: "alcauala"; the Spanish sales tax</note> is concerned, a question arises: if at the time of ratification the owner of that thing is immune from the tax, yet was not immune at the time the contract was celebrated, does he owe this tax? Likewise, if at the time of ratification there was already a different **tax farmer** <note>original: "gabellarius"; the official or private contractor authorized to collect the gabelle/tax</note> or lord, to which tax farmer or lord is the tax owed? To this one, or to the one who was in place at the time the contract was celebrated? Lassarte, in the place cited above, **chapter 3, from number 24**, says rightly in the first place that the tax is not owed before the ratification has followed, because the sale is not perfect but depends on the ratification. Likewise, the days granted for paying the tax or declaring the contract to the tax farmer run from the moment of ratification, not from the moment the pact was initiated. Then he answers the proposed questions: If the one ratifying the sale made in his name is not immune from the tax at the time of ratification, then the tax is owed to the later tax farmer, and not the earlier one. The reason, he says, is that a legal fiction cannot bring prejudice to the later tax farmer to whom (setting aside the fiction and looking at the truth of the matter) the tax would be owed. He cites Baldus, Tiraquellus, and Aretinus for this opinion. But if, he says, at the time of ratification he was immune from the tax, the tax is owed to the earlier tax farmer. He gives the reason that then the tax was not owed to the later tax farmer, because he was already immune by then; however, by his own ratification, he was able to bring prejudice upon himself by pulling the contract back to the time in which it was celebrated in his name, at which time the tax was owed to the earlier tax farmer, because at that time he himself was not immune.

<margin>20</margin> This doctrine is certainly not approved by me. For indeed, ratification—by the disposition of civil law, in accordance with right reason and natural equity—pulls back that which is ratified to the time it was done, so that it is considered perfected then. Thus, it is the civil law itself which, by this disposition, before such ratification and before such a favored contract, just as it brought prejudice to the very person who ratifies the past contract (so that nothing prevents him from owing the tax due to the retrospective effect, even if he is immune at the time of ratification), so also it could bring prejudice—and in the thing itself has brought prejudice—to the later tax farmer, so that by reason of the retrospective effect the tax should be owed to the earlier one, even if at the time of the retrospective effect there was no immunity from the tax. Nor do I see by what logic the fulfillment of a condition (by reason of retrospective effect, fiction, and the disposition of law) should bring prejudice to the later tax farmer in one event, so that it is not to him, but...

->What earnest money effects in a contract of purchase and sale. And when the ownership of the sold thing is acquired. And regarding another perfection of the same contract.<-

## DISPUTE 338.

### S U M M A R Y.

1. *What earnest money is.*
2. *Under the name of earnest money given before a sale is perfected, the buyer loses it if he withdraws; if the seller withdraws, he is bound to restore the earnest money and give an equal amount from his own goods. The same applies after a sale is perfected under Portuguese and Castilian law, with two limitations in number 4.*
3. *Once a sale is perfected, under common law, neither of the contracting parties can withdraw from the contract; otherwise, the earnest money is lost, and they are held liable for total damages.*
4. *The law of earnest money established in purchase and sale also takes place in hiring and leasing.*
5. *Whether the sales tax is owed when the contract is rescinded by losing the earnest money.*
6. *What is necessary for a buyer to acquire ownership of the purchased thing, even under Portuguese law.*

1 **Earnest money**† <term>Arrha: a deposit or "down payment" given to confirm a contract</term> in a contract of purchase and sale is that which is given as a sign and proof of a celebrated contract, and as a kind of pledge that the contract will be upheld. Hence Gaius the jurisconsult <note>Gaius was a celebrated 2nd-century Roman jurist</note> says in the beginning of the **Digest on the contract of sale**: <quote>What is often given under the name of earnest money for a purchase does not mean that a convention without earnest money does nothing, but so that it can be more clearly proved that the price was agreed upon.</quote>

2 Note, however, if before† the sale is perfected (in the manner explained in the preceding dispute), anything is given under the name of earnest money—the buyer promising he will buy for such a price and giving earnest money for it, or the buyer and seller suspending the contract until a writing is completed—and the buyer gives earnest money after mutual consent and agreement concerning the thing and the price, then that earnest money provides such security that if the buyer withdraws from the contract (as he can, since the contract is not yet perfected), he loses the earnest money to the seller. If the seller withdraws, he loses double to the buyer—that is, the earnest money he received and an equal amount from his own goods. This holds even if nothing of the sort was said when the earnest money was delivered. This is held in the **Institutes on Purchase and Sale, paragraph 1, at the words "however,"** and the **Code on the faith of instruments, the last paragraph of the law "Contracts."**

When, however, the contract is already perfected in the manner explained in the preceding dispute, and the earnest money is given by the buyer to the seller, the more common opinion (standing † on common law) is that neither of the contracting parties is allowed to with-

<column-break/>

-draw from the contract. Some assert that the one withdrawing is liable for total damages beyond the earnest money; however, Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century legal commentator</note> and many others affirm that the earnest money should be deducted from the total damages, as reported by the glosses on the two cited laws, and Antonio Gomez in **Various Resolutions, volume 2, chapter 2, number 18**; Villalobos in **Antinomia, letter V, number 8**; and Gregorio Lopez in **gloss 1 on law 7, title 5, part 5**. Furthermore, regarding Portuguese law (**Book 4 of the Ordinances, title 4, paragraph 1**) and Castilian law (**law 7**, cited above), the opinion of Azo in the **Code on Contracting Purchases** is approved, which Salycetus followed, affirming † it to be common in practice: namely, that it is lawful for either of the contracting parties to withdraw from the contract by losing the earnest money or double its value, in the manner explained. Thus it happens that earnest money in these kingdoms, and according to the opinion of Azo and Salycetus, renders a contract already perfected and finished weaker; for in the meantime, while the delivery of the sold thing has not been made, it is lawful for either party to withdraw from the contract under that penalty. Two events are excepted in Portugal, however, in which even if earnest money is given, neither party may withdraw. The first is when the contract is celebrated through middlemen or **Brokers** <note>original: "Corretores"</note>, as they are called, concerning certain goods between merchants, whether they are natives of the Kingdom of Portugal or foreigners; for then neither party may withdraw against the will of the other, even by losing the earnest money or its double. The Ordinances give the reason that this has always been maintained by custom in that Kingdom. The second is when it is expressed that the earnest money is given or received solely as part of the price, or simultaneously as part of the price and a sign of the contract. Thus it is held in **title 24, paragraph 2 and 3**. In this kingdom <note>referring to Castile/Spain</note>, **law 7** cited above excepts when the earnest money is given at the same time as part of the price, or "by granting" <note>original: "por otorgamiento"</note>—that is, not as earnest money, but only as a sign of a perfected contract. In these events, neither can withdraw against the will of the other, even by losing the earnest money or its double. And I believe this last point—namely, when it is expressed as not being given as earnest money but only as a sign of a perfected contract—holds place in Portugal. All the aforesaid are to be considered as having weight in the forum of conscience, since the laws are just and equal for all contracting parties and are not based on mere presumption.

5 These † are likewise to be understood in a contract of leasing. In this place, observe that since the loss of earnest money is established as a kind of penalty (even in Portugal and Castile, while it is permitted for contracting parties to withdraw from an otherwise perfected contract with that disadvantage), it is not owed until it is demanded.

6 It is a matter of doubt whether † in the event where it is lawful for either party to withdraw from a perfected purchase and sale by losing the earnest money, the **sales tax** <note>original: "alcauala"</note> is owed. Lassarte, in **On the Tenth of the Sale, chapter 3, number 18**, affirms it is owed, because the sale was truly perfected and the right to that tribute was acquired by the treasury. Nor is the sale dissolved for the past by a withdrawal from the contract, but only so that it is not valid for the future; which is what **law 7 of Castile** signifies when it says: <quote>and the sale shall not be valid thereafter</quote> <note>original: "e no valdra despues la vendida"</note>, and the Portuguese law in the cited **paragraph 1**, which says: <quote>This penalty is given to the said buyer and seller, so that...</quote>

# Second Treatise. Dispute 339.
# O 3

...that they might trust in the perfection of the said contract; and they wished to use another new provision, namely, to give and receive the said earnest money <note>original: "sinal" in Portuguese; "arrha" in Latin. This refers to a down payment that secures a contract.</note>, as has been said.

This opinion is not truly approved by me. Since by the very fact that earnest money is delivered, it is permitted by legal disposition to withdraw from a contract, the sale seems to be suspended, such that it is not considered "perfected" until delivery is made. Instead, it is lawful for both contracting parties not to stand by the agreement, provided they lose the value of the earnest money. Nor is this truly "rescinding" or "revoking" a contract, but rather not standing by it, as it is still too weak to be binding; this is clearly what the words of the cited Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lufitaniarum ordinationũ"</note> mean. Furthermore, against the seller's will, the buyer can refuse to stand by the contract, and conversely, against the buyer's will, the seller can refuse. Consider also that, by the law of this kingdom, the seller is held to pay the full sales tax <note>original: "alcaualæ"; a common tax on transactions in the Iberian peninsula</note>. It would be harsh if, when the buyer does not stand by the contract (as the law permits him to do against the seller's will), the seller were nevertheless held to pay the full tax, which could be far more than the earnest money the buyer loses. These are the points regarding the first of those matters proposed.

<margin>7</margin>
Regarding the second point, it must be observed that for a buyer to obtain ownership <note>original: "dñium" (dominium)</note> of the thing bought, it is not enough for the sale to be perfected in the manner explained in the preceding dispute. Instead, the delivery <note>original: "traditionẽ"</note> of that item is further necessary, according to what was said in disputes 2 and 3, and which will be repeated in the following sections. Nor is that sufficient; it is further required that the buyer pays the price, or offers it, or provides guarantors or pledges for its payment, or certainly, that the seller considers it as paid, trusting the buyer for it. If none of these things happen—even if the thing is sold and delivered to the buyer for a certain price to be paid immediately or on a specific day—ownership of the thing so bought does not pass to the buyer but remains with the seller. Thus, even if the buyer sells it to another and delivers it, having received a price for it or transferred it under any other title, the first seller, as its true owner, can claim and recover it wherever it may be found, unless the price is paid to him. This is expressly held in the Institutes <note>original: "§. vẽditæ inft. de rerũ diuif."</note> and the Digest, as well as the Portuguese Ordinances. We shall return to this in Dispute 536. Indeed, if the price is not paid within the term fixed for payment, the seller can either demand the price or, if he does not want the price, demand his property back instead, even if the price is then offered to him. This is held in the cited Portuguese Ordinance. If the property belongs to the Royal Treasury <note>original: "fifci"</note>, a minor, or the Church, and is sold by an administrator, ownership is not considered to pass to the buyer until the price is paid. This is gathered from the law and noted by Bartolus. Furthermore, the Portuguese Ordinances observe that the seller is bound to deliver the thing before the buyer renders the price. If, however, neither of the contracting parties trusts the other, then the item and the price should be placed in the hands of a third party, from whose hand the buyer receives the item and the seller receives the price. Observe finally that sometimes purchase and sale are said to be perfected in two

<column-break/>

other ways by the law and the doctors, a matter which will be discussed in Dispute 366.

### Threefold purchase and sale. Which of these is peculiarly called trading. And whether it is licit.

## DISPUTE CCCXXXIX.

-> S U M M A R Y <-

1. *The origin of the word "Business" and its many types.*
2. *Who are "factors" or "agents".*
3. *The three types of purchase and sale.*
4. *What "trading" is in the most proper sense.*
5. *Trading, in its most proper sense, is not a work of virtue nor of vice, but is indifferent.*
6. *Whether, and when, trading is licit.*
7. *On what grounds trading may be rendered evil and illicit.*
8. *That "trading" is signified by the name "literature" mentioned in Psalm 70.*

<margin>1</margin>
"Business" <note>original: "Negotiũ"</note>, according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar famous for his etymologies</note> in his book *Etymologies*, was so named as if to say "without leisure" <note>original: "fine otio"</note>. Therefore, it generally signifies any act concerning practical and external affairs that prevents leisure. Among "businesses" taken generally in this way, some are called public and some private. However, the present term "business," as Isidore says there, is used in two ways. One is for a cause or a lawsuit. The other is for exchange to prepare a profit by buying, or by acquiring something through another kind of exchange and selling it at a higher price without changing the item, or by exchanging it with profit in some other way. This twofold peculiar use of "business" took its origin from the fact that both of these activities are the ones that chiefly prevent leisure, occupy us most, and fill the soul with the greatest anxieties. Of these two, it is the latter usage that serves our purpose. Although Augustine uses the word "business" <note>original: "negocium"</note> to signify this matter, Isidore in the cited place thinks that a lawsuit or cause should rather be called "business," while exchange for profit—of which we speak—should be called "trading" <note>original: "negotiationẽ"</note>. Those who practice it are called "traders" by a specific name, and they are also commonly called "merchants." Those, however, who are put in charge of such trading by others, whom

<margin>2</margin>
in Spanish we call *factores*, are called "agents" <note>original: "inftitores"</note> because they "press upon" <note>original: "inftent"</note> the business, as Ulpian says. Nevertheless, this word is also applied to principal merchants in Holy Scripture, according to that passage in Proverbs 31: *“She is like the merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.”* Nor does the origin and derivation of the word differ from what Ulpian handed down.

<margin>3</margin>
Having explained these things, it is customary to distinguish three types of purchase and sale. Understand the same for "exchange" broadly taken. For there is a certain kind of purchase and sale by which someone buys those things which are necessary for the support of himself and his family, and sells what is superfluous. And this is, as it were, natural, and is in itself good and licit, as St. Thomas and the doctors commonly hold, along with Aristotle in the first book of the *Politics*...

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts
# Page 214

...practitioners, they affirm. For the order of nature looks not to profit, but to fitting sustenance, and concerns heads of households and politicians, rather than "businessmen" strictly speaking. There is another kind of exchange where something is bought so that, after being changed by industry <note>original: "industria"; referring here to labor or processing</note>, it may be sold. This, as Chrysostom says in the chapter *Ejiciens* (88th Distinction) <note>This refers to a passage in the "Decretum Gratiani," the foundation of medieval Canon Law, often attributed to John Chrysostom, which was traditionally very critical of merchants.</note>, is not "pure" business. This is because the item bought is made better through industry and art. This category can also include the sale of things previously made, which are sold by their own craftsmen (distinguishing this from the first kind of sale). Saint Thomas Aquinas appears to have included this under the first kind of buying and selling. To this kind of buying and selling belongs not only one who buys wool to make cloth to sell, or iron to make swords to sell, but also one who buys birds or horses so that, after training them and getting them accustomed to something, he may sell them. Finally, there is the kind of buying and selling where something is bought so that, unchanged, it may be sold at a higher price to acquire a profit. 

<margin>4.</margin> And this † is what is most properly called "business" <note>original: "negotiatio"</note>, and regarding this, there is doubt as to whether it is lawful. For Chrysostom, in the cited chapter *Ejiciens*, seems to condemn it.

Regarding this matter, this first conclusion must be established:

<margin>5</margin> This business, strictly and most properly understood, is in itself a work of neither virtue nor vice, but is indifferent to either. Thus, if it is done dutifully and directed toward a good end, it is lawful and morally good, and it is 

<margin>6</margin> useful and necessary to the Commonwealth. The first part—namely, that it is "indifferent" whether it be a work of virtue or vice—is from Augustine in the chapters *Fornicari* and *Quoniam* in the 88th Distinction. In the former, he says: *“It is never lawful for men to commit fornication; but it is sometimes not lawful to trade.”* <note>original: "Fornicari hominibus semper non licet: negotiari verò aliquando non licet."</note> In the latter, he teaches that the vices that intervene in trading belong to the traders, not to the art or the business itself, as if it could not be exercised without vice. This same part will be corroborated and made more clear by what I shall add. The second part—namely, that if it is done properly and directed toward a good end, it is lawful and morally good—is clear enough if taken in the conditional sense in which it was uttered. Furthermore, it is proved that this condition can be put into action. First, on the part of the "end": since one can intend profit from business for the sustenance of one's own life and that of one's family; this end is morally good, belonging to the virtues of self-care and justice. Likewise, it can be intended for performing works of mercy, liberality, and other virtues with one's wealth, both in the state in which one currently is, and in a higher one, if, by multiplying wealth, one happens to rise to it. Therefore, business and the profit from it can be referred to a morally good end. Next, it is proved that business can be done "properly," even if profit is intended by selling for more than was bought. For lies, perjuries, deceptions, and whatever other such vices are accustomed to intervene in buying and selling, are the vices of the traders, not of the trade itself, as Augustine says in the chapter *Quoniam* (88th Distinction), and as is manifest in itself; wherefore they can be avoided while trading. Moreover, profit from this kind of business and the increase in price can be lawful and just for many reasons. First, as a reward for labor, industry, and risk, by buying in a distant place and transporting to the Commonwealth things that are necessary for it, at the risk of losing one's own goods. Second, because of the diversity of times, in which just prices 

<column-break/>

undergo variation due to the abundance or scarcity of things, the multitude or fewness of buyers, and because of other circumstances. Thus it happens that if, in a time of abundance and without prejudice to others, someone buys a store of goods to keep for a time of scarcity, he can lawfully and justly sell it for more than it was bought, due to the variation of the "just price." Third, because the "just price" does not consist in a single indivisible point <note>A key Scholastic economic concept: the "just price" was seen as a range (latitude) rather than a single fixed number.</note>; wherefore, a person could sell for more than they bought within the "latitude" of the just price, even if no factors of place, time, or other circumstances had changed to increase the price. These and similar reasons are the grounds upon which one may lawfully and justly sell for more than one bought. From this, it has been explained and shown that business is not only not an evil work in itself, but can even be exercised in a morally good way.

The third part—namely, that business is useful and necessary to Commonwealths—is proved: since no province abounds in all things, but it is necessary that many things be transported from one to another—indeed, it is often necessary that many things be carried from one part of a province to other parts of the same province. Individual citizens cannot achieve this, partly because of poverty, partly because they are intent on other matters, and partly because they lack the proper leisure for it; and finally because if everyone were to transport necessities only for themselves, they would incur far greater expenses in procuring them than are incurred when necessary things are brought in by various men. Surely, it is useful and necessary for Commonwealths that there be "businessmen" who transport those things and have them ready for sale whenever anyone needs them. Furthermore, when foreigners bring goods by sea or land, it is useful and necessary that they bring them in great quantities so they suffice for the State and can be sold more cheaply. Since they cannot wait for individuals to buy from them what they will need as time goes on, it is surely useful and necessary for Commonwealths that there be "merchants" <note>original: "mercatores"</note> who buy them more cheaply then, and keep them to be sold at a higher price to individuals when they have need of them. Likewise, in a time of abundance, farmers and others who have an abundance of things often need money to gather their harvests and for other necessities, and they cannot keep their merchandise until a time of scarcity. It is therefore not useless to Commonwealths for there are merchants who then buy such merchandise and keep it to be sold at a higher price in a time of scarcity. Provided, however, they buy them at a just price in the time of abundance, and do not hinder individuals of the Commonwealth from buying necessities for themselves at that time; nor later use frauds and tricks to increase the prices of things and vex the Commonwealth.

<margin>7</margin> Second conclusion. Business can be rendered bad not † only from perjuries, lies, excessive price, and from other circumstances arising from the wickedness of the traders, but also from many other factors, such as the status of the person (if the one who trades is a cleric or a religious, whom business misbecomes), from circumstances of time, place, or the person to whom something is sold, and from others, as will become manifest in the following disputes. Finally, business, because of the desire for profit, is a thing which—given human fragility—is inherently...

Now we must run through several chapters by which a sale can be rendered illicit or even null. And beginning from the object and the things themselves, it must simultaneously be explained which things can or cannot be sold.

<margin>1</margin> In the † first place, however, the following can be sold: all goods taken together, even future ones, provided that under the name of "future things" the price is not understood to be given for that sale as it will remain in the future, so that the seller remains "intestable" <note>unable to make a will or leave an inheritance</note> by that sale; for in that case, the contract would be null. When, however, the price (which is received in place of the other things) is preserved, and that which will be acquired in the future by that price is also preserved, the seller is not rendered "intestable" by that contract—just as one is who donates all his present and future goods. Therefore, the laws which we cited in Disputations 280 and 151, by which a donation of all present and future goods is rendered null, do not have a place in the matter proposed. Add that, since it was said in Disputation 280 that a donation of all goods made under an <term>onerous title</term> <note>A contract where both parties give something of value.</note> (such as to a daughter for contracting a marriage) is valid, it is far more valid in the sale of which we speak, which is an onerous contract in which the price succeeds in the place of the merchandise. This very thing is confirmed by the law *mulierem* <note>original: "l. mulierem. ff. de iure dotium"; a reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding dowry rights.</note> and is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonius Gomez in volume 1...
