### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

<margin>3</margin> ...as recorded and followed by [the jurist Antonio Gomez] in resolution number 4. Observe, however, that when † all goods are said to be sold, and nothing else is expressed nor clear from other sources, it is understood that present goods are sold, but not future ones. We showed this regarding the donation of all goods in Disputation 280, and it is confirmed by the law *Last* in the Code, title *On things pledged*; law *If so* in the Digest, title *On the legacy of gold and silver*; and law *All*, paragraph *Lucius*, in the Digest, title *On things done to defraud creditors*. Besides the doctors <note>The "doctors" refers to the "Doctors of Law," the recognized legal authorities and commentators of the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> whom we cited in Disputation 280, Antonio Gomez asserts this same view above, following the opinion of Bartolus and the common consensus of the doctors, confirming it with various other legal points.

<margin>4</margin> An entire inheritance, or a part of it, † can also be sold by an heir; provided, however, that it has already been granted by the death of the person to whom the seller exists as heir. This is gathered from law 1, by an argument from the contrary sense, and more clearly from the following laws in the Digest, title *On a sold inheritance or action*. The same is gathered <margin>5</margin> from law 1 and the following in the Code under the same title. Once an inheritance † is sold, all "useful actions" <term>Useful actions (actiones utiles): Legal claims or rights to sue that are granted by a judge based on equity, even if the strict letter of the law doesn't provide for them.</term>—both active and all rights and benefits that pertained to the heir by reason of that inheritance—pass to the buyer, and this happens without any formal legal assignment being made. However, if a formal assignment is made, "direct actions" <note>original: "actiones directae"; these are standard legal claims based on the strict letter of civil law.</note> also pass. This is expressly stated in the law *The buyer of an inheritance* in the Code, title *On a sold inheritance or action*, and is affirmed by the Gloss <note>The "Gloss" refers to the standard marginal commentary on Roman law, usually the Glossa Ordinaria of Accursius.</note> there, by Bartolus, and by the common opinion of the doctors which Antonio Gomez records and follows in number 5 above. The final Gloss on the cited law observes that if someone who buys an inheritance sells it to another, the "useful actions" belong to the final buyer even before a legal assignment by the heir, but not to the first buyer. 

However, "passive actions" <term>Passive actions (actiones passivae): The liabilities or debts of the deceased that creditors can sue to recover.</term>, by which the deceased was bound (and thus the heir by reason of him), do not pass against the buyer. Instead, they remain with the creditors of the deceased against the heir, regardless of the fact that he sold the inheritance. Nevertheless, if the heir pays such debts, he may recover them from the buyer by an action for "business conducted" <note>original: "actione negotiorum gestorum"; a legal claim for reimbursement when one person manages the affairs of another.</note>. Indeed, under the name of "inheritance," only the goods of the deceased are understood, after deducting legacies and the entire debt; only that net amount is understood to be sold to the buyer. All these points are held and clearly gathered from law 2 of the Code, title *On a sold inheritance or action*, and are affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez records and follows in the cited number 5. 

The reason why passive actions apply against the heir, and he cannot transfer them to the buyer of the inheritance—even though he can transfer the active ones—is this: since the active claims are his own, he can therefore cede and confer them to another. The passive actions (the debts), however, are not his own, but belong to the creditors of the deceased against him; therefore, without the creditors' consent, he cannot transfer them to someone else. Indeed, unless that other person expressly consents, he is not understood to take them up, as gathered from the cited laws 1 and 2. This doctrine fails, however, when the Treasury <note>original: "fiscus"; the public or royal treasury.</note> has sold to someone an inheritance granted to another. In that case, by the privilege of the Treasury, the passive actions that were against the heir pass to the buyer of the inheritance, as seen in law 1 of the Code, title *On the sale of inheritance actions*. 

Note also that in the case of a *fideicommissum* <term>Fideicommissum: A legal arrangement where a testator asks an heir to transfer the inheritance (or part of it) to another person (the fideicommissary) at a later time.</term>, whether it be the first, second, or further beneficiary, the actions pass—not only the active ones, but also the passive ones—by the very fact that the inheritance has come to him. Or, it may be divided between him and the preceding heir according to the proportion of the goods of the inheritance, if the entire inheritance does not come to the beneficiary, as was said and shown in Disputation 186. This, however, arises from the fact that the inheritance does not pass to the beneficiary by the authority of the heir, nor 

<column-break/>

by a contract entered into between living persons by the heir with the beneficiary, but it passes through the last will of the testator, who left one heir and another as a substituted beneficiary. By that very fact, because the inheritance passes to the substitute by the command of the testator, he himself is the heir representing the deceased; therefore, the actions that were against the deceased descend to him according to the portion of the inheritance that belongs to him, and they cease to apply against the prior heir. Thus Antonio Gomez states in the cited number 5, along with Baldus and others.

<margin>6</margin> Furthermore, † observe that if an heir sells an inheritance but does not deliver it, ownership of it does not pass to the buyer, just as it passed to the heir by the very fact that he entered into the inheritance—even if it had not been delivered to him, nor had he taken possession of it. Consequently, if the heir, after that first sale, sells and delivers the same inheritance to another, the ownership of the inheritance's assets passes to the second buyer, who is therefore preferred over the first. The first buyer only has a claim for damages <note>original: "actio ad interesse"; a legal action for the loss of interest or potential profit.</note> against the heir. All these points are found in the law *He who to you* in the Code, title *On a sold inheritance*, and are affirmed by Antonio Gomez in the cited number 5.

<margin>7</margin> It was said above that an inheritance † can be sold by an heir, provided it has already been granted. For if it is sold while the person to be succeeded is still living, the sale is null, as it is against good morals due to the danger that could threaten the person to be succeeded. <note>The law feared that selling a living person's inheritance might tempt the buyer to hasten that person's death.</note> So it is held in law 1 of the Digest, title *On a sold inheritance*, and law 13, title 5, Partida 5. <note>Molina here cites the "Siete Partidas," the famous 13th-century statutory code of Castile.</note> 

<margin>8</margin> The same † is true if an inheritance not yet granted is donated, or granted under another title, or if agreements are made among heirs concerning it without the knowledge or consent of the owner of those goods. For if the owner were aware and consented, and persisted in that agreement throughout his whole life, such a sale or grant would be valid, as in the last law of the Code, title *On agreements*, and the law *From that* in the Code, title *On useless stipulations*, and the cited law 13.

<margin>9</margin> However, † what has been said remains true even if the person selling the inheritance was a "pupillary substitute" <term>Pupillary substitute: An heir appointed by a father to take over his child's inheritance if the child dies before reaching the age of puberty (legal maturity).</term>, who, after the death of the child's father, might sell the hope he then had for the child's inheritance. So it is in law 2, paragraph *That*, of the Digest, title *On a sold inheritance*. 

<margin>10</margin> Not † only is the sale or grant null, but also the one who sells or grants it is deprived of the inheritance if it should be granted to him, and it is assigned to the Treasury. See law 2 at the end of the Digest, title *On those who are unworthy*, and law *A certain person in law*, the last paragraph, and the following law in the Digest, title *On donations*. 

If anyone objects to the text in law 3, the paragraphs *When specially* and *That*, and the law *If a universal partnership*, in the Digest, title *On partnerships*, where it is held that a partnership can be entered into even concerning inheritances to be granted to the partners, the answer is: this must be understood as a contract concerning *uncertain* inheritances and in general (if any should be granted to the partners), which the cited law 13 states expressly. It does not apply to a contract concerning the inheritance of some *certain* and determined living person; for such a contract would be invalid. On all these points, the common opinion of the doctors agrees, which Antonio Gomez records and follows in the cited number 5.

<margin>11</margin> A person † can also sell not only a whole thing, or a certain and designated part of it, but also his share of something held in common (undivided), and likewise a right of easement, as was said in Disputation 336. The law *If in a purchase*, paragraph *Of all*, in the Digest, title *On entering a purchase*, and law *As often as* 2, in the Digest, title *On easements*, agree, and Antonio Gomez affirms this in number 4 above.

<summary>This page discusses the legalities of selling inheritances under Roman and Spanish law, clarifying that an inheritance can only be sold after the owner's death and detailing how rights and debts are transferred. It emphasizes that selling the inheritance of a living person is void and immoral, as it creates a dangerous incentive for the buyer to desire the owner's death.</summary>

->Tractate Two, Disputation 340.<-

**12** A debt can also be sold, as can a legal action <note>In Roman and Civil law, an "action" (*actio*) is the right to pursue a claim in court.</note> that one person holds against another. This is true whether the debt is "pure" <note>A "pure" debt is one due immediately without conditions.</note>, or deferred to a specific day, or subject to a condition. It can be sold whether the debtor knows about the sale or remains ignorant of it. By the very act of sale, the "useful action" <term>Useful action (*actio utilis*): A legal claim granted by a judge based on fairness or equity when the strict, formal letter of the law might not provide a remedy.</term> passes to the buyer even without a formal assignment; however, if a formal assignment (*cessio*) is added, the "direct action" <note>The formal, original legal right.</note> also passes. Not only does the claim to the owed item pass, but also any security interest such as a pledge, a mortgage, or a personal guarantor (*fideiussor*) if any of these were provided to secure the debt. Furthermore, if a pledge, mortgage, or guarantor is given to the seller *after* such a sale has been completed, the buyer still has the right to claim these, as stated in the law *to the buyer of a name* <note>original: "l. emptori nominis"</note> in the Digest, title *On the sale of an inheritance or action*. All of this, besides the cited law, is established by the laws *those who are sons of a family*, *names*, and *the seller of an action* in the Digest under the same title, as well as the law *the sale of a name* in the Code. However, because a person has sold another’s debt, they are not held liable if the debtor turns out to be insolvent, provided they ensure that the person truly is a debtor. But when one sells a specific sum of a debt, they are bound to ensure that the debtor actually owes that entire sum. This is held in the law *if a name*, joined with the following law, in the Digest, title *On the sale of an inheritance or action*.

**13** Similarly, a debt can be given as a gift, and in the same way, the legal actions pass to the recipient as if the debt had been sold to them (Code, title *On donations*). It can also be given as a dowry (Code, title *On actions and obligations*), or given in payment of another debt (Code, same title), or as a pledge (Digest, title *On the action of a pledge*, and Code, title *Which things can be pledged*). It can even be left as a legacy in a will (Code, title *On legacies*). By the same reasoning, it can be granted through exchange (*permutatio*) or other legal titles.

<margin>Antonio Gomez agrees on these points, as cited above, number 6.</margin>
**14** These matters must be understood with a qualification: a legal action may not be sold, entrusted, or transferred to another who is "more powerful" (*potentior*). In such a case, the assignment or transfer is not only invalid, but the person who transfers it loses the right they had to that debt as a penalty, as held in law 2 of the Code, title *That it may not be permitted to transfer to a more powerful person*. The commentators and Antonio Gomez (cited at number 6) affirm that this is especially true when the person to whom it is transferred is more powerful by reason of their public office. The Portuguese Ordinances <note>The *Ordenações*, the primary legal code of Portugal at this time.</note> (Book 3, title 45, at the beginning) dispose of this by leaving no right to either the person transferring or the one receiving it in that event; rather, they further threaten such a public official with punishment. The same is established in the same place, paragraph 1, when someone who possesses a thing, fearing a legal action will be brought against it, transfers it to someone more powerful by reason of office who can better defend it: by that very act, they lose all rights they had to that thing, and it belongs to their adversary.

**15** One might ask, however, if the transfer of an action is made to a more powerful person not by reason of their office, but because of their social rank or some other quality, does the transferor incur the same penalty? Indeed, the cited law 2 regarding the "more powerful" speaks without distinction, not restricting it to those powerful by office. Therefore, standing by the common law, when it is clear a transfer was made with the intent that the defendant should have a more powerful adversary, the judge would be bound to fine the transferor with that penalty. However, the Portuguese Ordinances (paragraph 2 of the cited place) only establish as a penalty in that event that the transfer be void, and that the transferor cannot act through any other person, such as a proxy, but must act only by themselves. When—

<column-break/>

—on the other hand, a thing about which a lawsuit is feared is transferred to someone more powerful *not* by reason of office so that they might defend it, the law there only establishes that the transfer is void, and the one who transferred the thing is bound to defend it.

**16** In the fourth part of those same Ordinances, title 45, it is first explained when a thing is considered to have become "litigious" <term>Litigious (*litigiosum*): A legal term for a property or right that is currently the subject of an ongoing lawsuit.</term> in various circumstances. Then, it is prohibited for such a thing—while a lawsuit is pending and before a final judgment—to be sold, exchanged, or granted to another by the defendant, or for the plaintiff to transfer the legal action to another. If the defendant sells or exchanges such a thing, and the buyer (or the person in the exchange) knows it is litigious, the contract is void. They must restore it to the defendant and lose the price paid (or whatever else was given in exchange) to the state treasury (*fiscus*); the defendant also pays the same amount to the treasury. If, however, the buyer did not know the item was litigious, the contract is still void, but the buyer recovers the price and an additional third of its value. The seller then pays to the treasury an amount equal to the price.

When a litigious thing is sold, exchanged, or given to someone more powerful by reason of rank or office, the defendant pays the plaintiff double what they received in exchange for it, and pays the same amount to the treasury. The plaintiff of a litigious thing incurs the same penalty if they sell, exchange, or give the legal action to a more powerful person.

If a litigious thing is given as a gift and the recipient knows it is litigious, the donation is void and must be restored to the donor; furthermore, the recipient pays its estimated value to the treasury, and the donor pays the same amount to the treasury. When the recipient was unaware the thing was litigious, the same rules apply, except the recipient pays nothing to the treasury, and the donor pays the recipient a third of the value of that thing.

The plaintiff who sells, exchanges, or gives away a legal action for a litigious thing to a more powerful person incurs all these same penalties.

If, after the sale, exchange, or donation of a litigious thing, a sentence is passed in favor of the plaintiff, that sentence is executed against whoever received the thing under any of the stated titles. It is not necessary to summon them if they knew it was litigious; otherwise, if they were ignorant of it, they must be summoned and heard in a summary proceeding.

However, the aforesaid rules do not apply to a donation given as a dowry or for a wedding, nor to a contract between the litigants themselves concerning the litigious thing, nor to a contract of partition among heirs concerning goods they were disputing, nor to a nomination regarding succession in a thing under dispute, nor finally to a legacy of a litigious thing in a will. In that final event, the heir is bound to pursue the lawsuit and deliver the thing to the legatee if they win. The legatee, however, may join the lawsuit and pursue it if they judge it expedient, to prevent any trickery against them. All of this is held in the cited title 45.

**17** Although a sale is void if there is no "thing" to be sold, nevertheless, if a thing is "in hope" <note>This refers to *emptio spei*, the sale of an expectation.</note>, it can be sold before it exists. On this basis, the offspring of a slave-woman or of livestock, and the fruits of the fields, can be sold while they are still just a hope. Likewise, one can sell the "cast of a net" <note>Buying the catch of a fisherman before he pulls his net up.</note>, or whatever might be caught in a day's hunting, or the "missiles" <note>In Roman festivals, small tokens or coins (*missilia*) were thrown to the crowds; one could contract to buy whatever a person managed to catch.</note> if any should come to hand...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the second column, continuing onto the next page.</meta>

# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...come into someone's possession, while they are being sent, and similar cases, as found in the law *nor is a sale* <note>Latin: "l. nec emptio." This refers to the Digest (Pandects), book 18, title 1.</note> in the Digest under the title *On the Contract of Sale*, the law *in the meantime* <note>Latin: "l. inter dū."</note> in the title *On Verbal Obligations*, and the law 11, title 5 of the fifth *Partida* <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the foundational medieval Spanish law code.</note>. There is, however, this difference:
<margin>18</margin> that when offspring or fruits are sold while they are still just a hope, the sale is conditional—it only takes effect if they are born or harvested—according to the cited law *nor is a sale*, the first law, the last verse, in the title *On Conditions and Demonstrations*, and law 11, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*.
<margin>19</margin> If, however, a seller deceives a buyer because he sells something for which there was no hope, or if the seller was the reason it was not born or harvested, he is liable to the buyer for the amount that the "hope" was valued at, according to the law *if a cast* <note>Latin: "l. si iactum." This refers to the "cast of a net" in fishing.</note> in the Digest under *On Actions for the Buyer*, and for any subsequent damages the buyer suffered. This is based on the law *nor is a sale* and law 12, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. But when the "cast of a net" is sold, or whatever might be caught in a hunt, or something similar, it is understood that the "hope" alone is sold. For that reason, whether something is caught or not, the agreed price is owed, as per the law *nor is a sale*, the law *the buyer* in the final paragraph, and law 11 as cited.
<margin>20</margin> But if the fisherman refuses to cast his net, or the hunter refuses to hunt on that day, he is liable to the buyer for the estimated value of that "hope" and for subsequent damages, as per the law *if a cast* and law 12. If, however, something was caught but he did not deliver it to the buyer, he will be liable for the value of what was caught, as stated in the law *if a cast*. This distinction between offspring or fruit on one hand, and the cast of a net or hunt on the other, is to be understood when the words of the contracting parties do not suggest otherwise. For if someone stated they were buying the *hope* of a slave woman's offspring, it would not be a conditional sale, but a "pure" <note>A "pure" contract is one not subject to conditions; it is binding immediately.</note> one; thus, the price would be owed even if nothing were born. Likewise, if someone said to a person casting a net, "For every pound of fish you catch, I will give you this much," or to a hunter, "For the first thing you catch, I will give you this much," it is clear that these are conditional sales that depend on something being caught. This is found in law 11, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. Finally, observe that if "missiles" <note>In Roman tradition, "missilia" were small tokens or gifts thrown into a crowd by officials; people could buy the "hope" of what they might catch.</note> are sold in the manner explained above, and something is caught that later turns out not to have belonged to the thrower and is reclaimed by its owner, the seller is not liable in that event; as held in the law *nor is a sale*. The reason is that the "hope" was sold—whatever might be caught, of whatever nature it might be.
<margin>21</margin> If the buyer and seller do not agree on the price—for instance, if the seller says it was higher and the buyer says it was lower—the sale is void, unless the price agreed upon by both can be established by other means, according to the law *in sales* in the Digest and law 20, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. However, if the seller claims it was lower and the buyer claims it was higher, the sale would be valid, and they should stand by the lower price. The same applies to leases in the law *if ten* in the title *On Hiring and Leasing* and law 20, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. Likewise, if the buyer and seller do not agree on the thing being sold—because during the contract one understood one estate, or slave, or whatever other thing, and the other understood something else—the contract is similarly invalid, both in the external court <note>Civil or secular law.</note> and in the court of conscience <note>Moral or religious law.</note>, unless there are clear signs that both understood the same thing. This is according to the law *in sales* and law 20, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. The same is true if there was an error in the "substance" of the thing sold, even if they agree on the object itself—for example, if brass <term>Brass (*auricalcum*): A golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc, often mistaken for gold in antiquity.</term> was sold as gold, or tin as silver, per the law *in sales*.

<column-break/>

and law 21, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. When vinegar is sold as wine, Ulpian says in the cited law *in sales* that the sale is valid because, he says, the "essence" of both is nearly the same. However, he immediately restricts this: if the vinegar was made from wine, it stands; but if it was vinegar from the beginning, he judges in this second case that the sale is not valid. The Gloss <note>The standard medieval commentary on Roman law.</note> interprets this in two ways. First, that in Ulpian's view, the sale is only invalid when the vinegar was not generated from wine but was vinegar from its very origin and was sold as wine. And this seems to reflect Ulpian's words better than what I will add next. Second, that the sale is invalid when it was vinegar at the beginning—that is, at the time the contract was made—but valid if the wine soured and turned to vinegar after the contract was concluded. This second interpretation seems true to me, whatever Ulpian may have felt. For vinegar, if it is truly vinegar, is of the same species whether it was generated from wine or not. Therefore, if it was vinegar when it was sold, it is irrelevant to the invalidity of the sale whether its origin was from wine or not. Furthermore, the "essences" of things consist of an indivisible point, as is clear from Metaphysics <note>A reference to Aristotelian philosophy: a thing either has an essence or it does not; there is no "near" essence.</note>. Therefore, even if they are close, it does not stop them from being different essences. Add to this that it is neither expedient for human commerce that such a sale be valid, nor does it agree with right reason; therefore, one must lean toward it being invalid. Especially since that law is not "positive law" <note>Man-made law enacted by a ruler.</note> intending to establish a rule, regardless of the nature of the thing, but is merely the opinion of Ulpian stating what he thinks about the nature of the thing, in which he could easily have been mistaken.

Although I will discuss errors in quality later when we speak of defects in sold goods, observe this: If someone sells a slave who was thought to be male, and it is later discovered to be female, the sale is void, even if the seller was ignorant of it. This is based on the law *otherwise* in the Digest and law 21, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. If, however, one sells a woman as a virgin who is found to have been "corrupted," the sale is valid, as is added in the cited laws. An exception is made unless the seller, knowing she was not a virgin, sells her to someone who believes she is and who otherwise would not have bought her. In that case, an action is granted to the buyer to rescind the sale, according to the law *from the purchase*, the paragraph *if anyone [sells] a virgin*, and law 21, title 5 of the fifth *Partida*. Likewise, when the parties agree on the object being sold, an error in the name does not make the sale invalid, as held in the law *in sales*. However, if someone who has two slaves with different jobs sells one in their absence, using the name of one but the job description of the other: if the seller knew their names, he is deemed to have sold the one he named, even if it does not have the job he described. But if he was ignorant of which name belonged to which slave, he is deemed to have sold the one who held the job he described. This is the interpretation of the Gloss on the law *in sales* at the word *absent*, and it is decreed in law 21 as cited.

<margin>22</margin> When the thing being sold was destroyed or had perished at the time of the sale, I believe a distinction must be made. For either it was an estate that was being bought...

Molina critiques traditional Roman legal opinions on whether selling vinegar as wine is valid, using metaphysical arguments to assert that a mistake in essence voids a contract.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 34 of the Second Treatise, focusing on the validity of sales contracts when the object of the sale is destroyed or if there is a fundamental error regarding what is being sold. It specifically addresses how knowledge or ignorance of these facts by the buyer or seller affects the legality of the transaction.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 34.

...considered by reason of a building, such as a house, a mill, or another similar structure, or by reason of the plants that were upon it, such as an olive grove or a vineyard, or if it was something else that one bought for a single price as a whole. In the first scenario, if both the buyer and seller were ignorant that the entire building or all the plants had perished, the sale is rendered null, even if the land itself remains. If, however, a major part of the building or plants had perished, the buyer may choose not to stand by the contract and may reclaim the price, if any was given; or he may choose to stand by the contract, requesting that the price be reduced in proportion to the part destroyed. But if half of the building or plants, or some other minor part, had perished, the contract is valid, but the price is reduced for the buyer by as much as the estate is worth less because of the destroyed part. This is held in the laws *the house* <note>Latin: "l. domum." Referring to Digest 18.1.57.</note> and *the trees* <note>Latin: "l. arbōtib." (l. arboribus). Referring to Digest 18.1.58.</note> in the Digest under the title *On the Contract of Sale*, and in Law 14, Title 5 of the Fifth *Partida* <note>The *Siete Partidas* was a foundational Spanish law code.</note>.

If, however, the seller was aware but the buyer was ignorant that the building or all the plants had perished, the sale is null, as held in the cited laws, because a sale is invalid without the thing itself. Yet, the cited Law 14 rightly adds that the buyer may then sue for his "interest" <note>The term "interest" (*interesse*) here refers to the legal claim for damages or the value the buyer lost because the sale was not valid.</note> to the extent that it was in his interest for the sale to be valid. But if some part of the building or plants remained, however small it might be, the contract is valid, but the seller is liable to the buyer for his interest—that is, the value of what was destroyed—as held in the cited laws. And the cited Law 14 adds that the buyer is permitted to "swear to the loss in court" <note>Latin: "iurare in litem." A legal procedure where a party provides an oath regarding the value of the damages.</note>, which is deduced and sanctioned from the principles of common law.

But if the buyer was aware, but the seller was ignorant, that a part of the building or plants was destroyed, then the contract is valid, and the buyer is compelled to pay the full price; for "no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting" <note>Latin: "volenti, & consentienti nulla facta est iniuria." A famous legal maxim meaning a person cannot claim legal injury if they voluntarily consented to the situation.</note> in the celebration of that contract. This is held in the cited laws. If, however, at the time of the contract the seller was aware of the destruction but informed the buyer, who nevertheless entered into the contract, the contract is valid, and he pays the full price established. This is held in the cited Law 14.

Furthermore, when there was knowledge on both sides of how much of the part had perished, but the seller did not know that the buyer knew, then the contract is valid, and there is a "compensation of fraud" <note>Latin: "doli compensatio." A legal concept where the wrongdoings of both parties cancel each other out.</note>, but a deduction is made from the price if the property is worth less than the established price by reason of the part that perished. This is held in the cited laws.

---

These same things must be said similarly in the second scenario: namely, when what was sold was not an estate bought by reason of a building or plants, but something else bought together for a single price. The only exception is that when half has perished, while the buyer and seller were ignorant, the sale is rendered invalid, as the text proves in the law *if two* <note>Latin: "l. si duo." Referring to Digest 18.1.44.</note> in the title *On the Contract of Sale*, the words of which are:
> If someone has bought two slaves together for a single price, and one of them died before the sale, the purchase of neither stands. <note>original: "Si duos quis seruos emerit pariter vno pretio, quorum alter ante venditionē mortuus est, neq; in uno constat emptio."</note>

The reason for the distinction between this second scenario and the first, as established by law, is this: in the first, the land of the estate remains, which is the principal part of the building, olive grove, or vineyard; and therefore it is sufficient if half of the building or plants survived for the sale to be valid, because in truth the greater part of the estate or the thing bought remains. In the second scenario, however, since this is not seen, it is always necessary for the greater part of the thing bought to remain for the sale to be valid.

<column-break/>

<margin>23</margin> This same rule is observed when there is an error in the substance of the thing being sold. If the error is in a minor part, the sale is valid, but the price is reduced by as much as the thing is worth less because that minor part is of a different substance. If, however, there is an error in the majority or in half the part, the sale is invalid. Julian affirms this in the law *from him* <note>Latin: "l. cū ab eo" (l. cum ab eo). Referring to Digest 18.1.41.1.</note>, the final paragraph, in the title *On the Contract of Sale*, whose words are:
> You, being unaware, sold to me, who was also ignorant, a table covered in silver as if it were solid: the purchase is null, and the money given on that account may be reclaimed. <note>original: "Mensam, argento coopertam, mihi ignoranti, pro solida vendidisti imprudēs: nulla est emptio, pecuniaq; eo nomine data cōdicitur."</note>

Therefore, the contrary decision of Ulpian in the law *what in* <note>Latin: "l. quid in." Referring to Digest 18.1.41.pr.</note> in the same title must be rejected, where he openly defines that even if there is an error in the greater part, if there is no error in some part, the sale is valid. I know that among other explanations of the glosses, one is that this should be understood in the sale of an inherited thing made to one of the heirs by the other co-heirs in a partition. Yet Ulpian speaks universally, although he uses an example of a sale made to an heir; nor is there any reason why this should be particularly admitted in a sale made to an heir. Nor does that seem to be positive law, but rather Ulpian's personal opinion on how it should be judged given the nature of the thing. In this, the opinion of Julian should rather be embraced, as it is consistent both with the nature of the thing itself and with other laws, especially the opinion of Marcellus in the cited law *if two*.

<margin>24</margin> A free person cannot be sold; if a sale is made, it is null, even if it is made while he is free to take effect at a time when he might be a slave. See the law *if in a purchase* <note>Latin: "l. si in emptione." Referring to Digest 18.1.5.</note> in the paragraph *of all things* <note>Latin: "§. oium rerū."</note> at the verse *free* in the Digest under *On the Contract of Sale*; the first paragraph of the Institutes *On Useless Stipulations*; and Law 15, Title 5 of the Fifth *Partida*. This has a place only where Roman laws are in force; regarding this matter, read what we said in Disputation 32, Title 3, on how someone can be reduced to slavery. However, when it is asserted in the law *and of a free man* <note>Latin: "l. & liberi hominis." Referring to Digest 18.1.4.</note> in the Digest under *On the Contract of Sale* that the purchase of a free person made by one ignorant of his freedom is valid, it is to be understood as having the effect that the seller, who knew he was free and sold him as a slave, is liable to the buyer for his interest. So it is held in the final paragraph of the Institutes *On Purchase and Sale*. If, however, the seller sold him ignorantly, the buyer reclaims the price. So says Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Explanations*, chapter 2, number 50. Read what we said at the end of Disputation 268.

---

Likewise, sacred things such as churches, and public things such as plazas, public roads, and all things of a city or town—namely those set aside for the common use of those who live there—cannot be sold without the consent of the supreme Prince.
<margin>25</margin> If they are sold, the sale is null, even if such things are sold to take effect at a time when they would no longer be such. See the law *if in a purchase*, the paragraph *of all things*, in the Digest under *On the Contract of Sale*; the first paragraph of the Institutes *On Useless Stipulations*; the final paragraph of the Institutes *On Purchase and Sale*; and Law 15, Title 5 of the Fifth *Partida*. When, however, it is affirmed in the law *of a free man* in the Digest under *On the Contract of Sale* that such a purchase is valid, it is to be understood as having the effect that the seller, who knew they were sacred or public while the buyer was ignorant, is liable to him for his interest, as in the final paragraph of the Institutes *On Purchase and Sale*. But if the seller was ignorant, while the buyer knew the things were sacred or religious, the buyer only reclaims the price. See the final paragraph of the Institutes *On Purchase and Sale* joined with the law *the buyer*, final paragraph, in the Digest *On Actions for the Buyer*, and Antonio Gomez affirms this with Bartolus in the cited number 50. Read what we have said more extensively regarding this at the end of Disputation 268.

**31** The sale of another’s property is prohibited in this sense: if the buyer knew at the time of the contract that it was stolen, the contract is invalid. He is also punished there who, in the city of Lisbon <note>Latin: "Olysipponensi ciuitate."</note> or in a place where the King is staying, buys anything exceeding the value of fifty of those gold coins which they call <term>reais</term> <note>The *real* (plural *reais*) was the historical currency of Portugal.</note> from anyone other than the ministers of either sex appointed to sell things publicly, or from the craftsmen who make and sell them, provided it is similarly discovered later that it was taken by theft.

In Castile and the realm, in Book 6 of the *New Collection*, Title 22, this Law 5 was decreed: *We command that no person dare to buy, nor let them buy, from a female or male servant who serves another, items of food or drink, nor barley, nor straw, nor firewood, nor other household items and furnishings; and that he who buys them in whatever manner shall be banished as a concealer of theft, and shall be proceeded against as such: and we command our justices to punish it with all diligence and rigor.* <note>Original in Spanish: "Mãdamos, que ninguna psona sea osada de cõprar..."</note>

**32** The sale † of one's own property to oneself is also null. However, if the seller had some interest in it, even if it be any right whatsoever, the sale is valid to that extent. (Law *suæ rei*, joined with the law *si in emptione* § *rei suæ* in the Digest on the contract of sale).

**33** Furthermore, the sale † of that which is not saleable in itself is not only illicit but also null. Of this sort are all those things in whose sale simony intervenes, such as an ecclesiastical <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provides an income.</note>, a sacrament, and other things which will be discussed in the subject of simony. Of this sort also are those things to which one is bound without any price being demanded, according to what was explained extensively in Disputation 93.

**34** When something is indeed saleable in itself, but nevertheless cannot be sold without sin, nor can it be fulfilled after the contract is celebrated without sin, then the contract of sale does not bind; rather, it must be departed from both in conscience and in the external court. If, however, it has been fulfilled on both sides, it is valid by the nature of the thing, provided it has not been rendered void by positive law. For example, if someone sells to an infidel something that serves precisely an act of infidelity, such as an idol or something similar, the sale is a sin, and similarly the fulfillment of the contract already celebrated by handing over the thing sold is a sin; for that reason, that contract does not bind one to its fulfillment. However, after it has been fulfilled on both sides, the seller is not bound to restore the price. Indeed, if the seller has handed over the thing, which he cannot recover, he can demand the price. A similar example can be applied to one who sold poison or a sword with which someone was to be unjustly killed. These points are established from what was said in Disputation 94, and therefore I do not dwell on them further.

Second Treatise, Disputation 341. 221

...as has been said, observe that under <term>Common Law</term> <note>Latin: *ius commune*, referring to the combined Roman and Canon law used across continental Europe.</note> in the law *quod saepe*, section *veni*, in the Digests on contracting a sale, and in Law 17, Title 1, Part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the legal code of Castile.</note>, the purchase and sale of poison is prohibited if it cannot serve human use or benefit even when mixed with another substance. Such a sale is so strictly prohibited that the contract is considered null. I understand this to mean it does not bind the parties to its completion. However, after it has been fully carried out by both sides, the seller is not held to restore the price unless he is condemned to do so—especially if the item sold no longer exists, or exists without danger of any evil to the possessor. For if an evil were feared, he would be bound to rescind the sale and recover the poison. Observe also that if the poison serves for hunting, or for creating certain colors <note>For dyes or pigments.</note>, or for other similar uses necessary to the Commonwealth, it can indeed be sold—but only to those who, by their office or other circumstances, are clearly established to want it for such purposes.

Several other things were also prohibited from being sold under Common Law, as seen in the chapters on things that cannot be sold and things that should not be exported. Many things are also prohibited from being sold by private laws <note>Local or municipal statutes.</note>, which must be learned in each individual place.

## Whether someone can be compelled to sell their own property.

# DISPUTATION 341.

### SUMMARY.

1 *As a rule, no one can be compelled to sell their own property. However, this fails in many ways, number 2.*
3 *Separation between spouses regarding their bed and habitation must be made due to the excessive cruelty of the husband.*

This disputation is partly joined with the preceding one, and therefore we connect it to that.

1 Although, as a rule, no one should be forced to buy anything or sell their own property—according to the law *iniquum* in the Code on contracts of sale, the law *nec emere* on the right of deliberation, and Law 3, Title 5, Part 5, as well as other laws cited by Panormitanus, Covarruvias, Alvares Valasco, and Antonio Gómez—nevertheless, because both the subjects themselves and their goods are subject to public powers, when the common good demands it (while maintaining equity), those same powers can first set a just price for those putting things up for sale or lease, especially when the things are necessary for daily use and the preservation of life.

2 Furthermore, they can † compel someone to sell a house, or any other of their estates, at a just price if the public good requires it. For instance, if it serves the favor of religion or public utility—such as when it is necessary to pave a road to a public or religious place—based on the argument of the text in the law *si locus*, final section, on how services are lost, and in the law *si quis sepulchrum* on religious matters and funeral expenses.

Because of this, for the purpose of enlarging a monastery, a church, or a hospital (when it is expedient), or for erecting or building one anew, someone can be compelled to sell their own house or other estate. Similarly, this applies to public schools, or a King’s palace, or

<column-break/>

any other similar thing being enlarged or built. So says Antonio Gómez in the place cited above, and Gregorio López on the cited Law 3, gloss 1. This is the common opinion which Covarruvias reports and confirms in the cited place from number 7, and examines. Finally, at the end of the chapter, he concludes that although a Supreme Prince <note>A monarch or sovereign ruler.</note> can compel this for a common utility that is not strictly a necessity, other lower public powers regularily could not compel it unless there were some degree of necessity involved. (Indeed, Alvares Valasco in the cited consultation says that in Portugal, in all these matters, one always recurs to the Supreme Prince.) However, Covarruvias admits that the common opinion is the contrary of this latter part. At number 8, following Saliceto and others according to the handed-down doctrine, he reports that while anyone has the right to build their own building higher, this can nevertheless be prohibited when it would result in monks or nuns being seen within their own homes. By the same reasoning, the opening of new windows from which they could similarly be seen can be prohibited; he inclines toward this opinion a little further down when a new building is being made from which that inconvenience would follow.

Furthermore, if two people own a slave in common, and one wants to grant him freedom, the other is compelled to sell his share if there is someone to offer the price; this is done in favor of liberty. This is stated in the Code on common manumission and Law 3, Title 5, Part 5. And in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 25, final section, it is decreed that if anyone has a Moorish male or female captive <note>A reference to the practice of enslaved captives from North Africa/the Ottoman Empire.</note> and that person is necessary to ransom a Christian captive in their place, the owner must be compelled to sell them, with an appraisal made in the manner prescribed there.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Likewise, in a case of scarcity and in a time of necessity, the public power—even if it is an ordinary judge—can and ought to compel subjects to sell grain and other necessities at a just price. By the same reasoning, they can prohibit anyone from buying more than is necessary for themselves and their family, so that the food supply suffices for others. This is agreed upon in the Digests on the office of the City Prefect and the gloss on the text in the chapter *sicut*, distinction 47, as well as other laws and doctors cited and followed by Panormitanus, Antonio Gómez, Covarruvias, and Silvester under the word "purchase," question 4.

When, likewise, a master treats a slave with great harshness and cruelty, he must be compelled by the public authority of a judge to sell that slave. The same applies if he forces the slave to shameful or illicit acts. These are found in the final section of the Institutes on those who are under their own or another's power, and Law 3, Title 5, Part 5.

From this, Antonio Gómez (in the cited place, along with Baldus and others) gathers that if any temporal lord were to be cruel and treat his subjects with excessive austerity, they could be deprived of their jurisdiction over them, or he could be compelled to sell it, when it is judged that the subjects would not otherwise be sufficiently protected.

But if the jurisdiction belonged to an <term>entail</term> <note>Latin: *maioratum*, a form of inheritance where property cannot be sold or divided but passes to the eldest heir.</note>, or its alienation was prohibited, he should at least be deprived of the use of it for the duration of his life, or be forced to sell that use to another.

3 All these things are proven by the argument of the single law in the Code on those endowed with any power, and the chapter *literas* at the end, on the restitution of those despoiled, where † it is held that on account of the maximum cruelty of a husband, a separation is to be made between...

### To what extent buying and selling is lawful or unlawful for clerics and religious.

### DISPUTATION 342.

#### ->SUMMARY<-

1 *Business for mere profit, where something is bought to be sold dearer, is forbidden to clerics who perform it themselves; however, the contract is not void. Number 6.*
2 *The punishment against clerics practicing trade is manifold.*
*And what regarding the law of Portugal and Castile. Number 3.*
4 *How many things are necessary for a cleric or ecclesiastic to lose his privilege due to trading.*
5 *Trading clerics are not exempt from taxes.*
6 *The <term>alcabala</term> <note>A significant sales tax in Spain and its colonies.</note> is exacted from ecclesiastics without the prior three-fold warning regarding things they sell through trading.*
7 *Which businesses are said to be forbidden to clerics, and which are not.*
8 *To which clerics business is permitted so that no tax is owed, and what kind.*
9 *In which lowlier offices a cleric loses his privilege if he practices them, and in which he does not.*
10 *Whether clerics and religious may conduct mere profit-seeking business through others.*
11 *Clerics can buy necessities and sell surplus from their revenues.*
*Indeed, if they have bought something cheaper, not with the intention of reselling it dearer, they may sell it dearer when the price increases and make a profit.*
12 *Political trade <note>Business conducted for the sake of the state or civil administration.</note> is not lawful for clerics.*
13 *Clerics may use some craft to sustain their life, unless the craft is shameful, sordid, or indecent.*
14 *Clerics or ecclesiastics can lawfully buy certain things to exchange for others and sell dearer.*
15 *Clerics can lease estates for their sustenance, but not to make a profit.*

Consequently, we must examine to what extent, by reason of the seller or the one to whom something is sold, a purchase and sale may be unlawful or null; and we must begin with the ecclesiastics.

<margin>1</margin>
1 Regarding this matter, the first conclusion is: <term>Negotiatio</term> <note>Latin: *negotiatio*. In this context, it refers specifically to "mercantile trade" or "business for profit" rather than simple transactions.</note> for mere profit, where something is bought so that, unchanged, it may be sold dearer, is unlawful and forbidden to clerics if they practice it themselves; however, it is not invalid. The reason for the prohibition is the extreme indecency regarding their status, for the reasons stated in Disputation 339. This conclusion is proposed by *Augustine in the chapter "Fornicari," distinction 88; Gelasius in the chapter "Consequens," and Jerome in the chapter "Negotiationem," in the same distinction; and it is held in the final chapter of "On the life and honesty of clerics," Clementines 1, and chapter 1, "Lest clerics or monks [engage in secular business]," and in other laws.*

<margin>2</margin>
2 The punishment established for clerics practicing such trade is excommunication, as is established in *chapter 2, under "Lest clerics or monks..."* although 

<column-break/>

it is not a <term>latae sententiae</term> penalty <note>A penalty that follows automatically upon the commission of an offense.</note>, but <term>ferendae sententiae</term> <note>A penalty that must be formally pronounced by a judge or superior.</note>. There is likewise the penalty of suspension and deposition <note>Removal from office or status.</note>, as is clear in *chapter "Consequens," distinction 88; the penultimate chapter of distinction 91; and the chapter "Sed nec" under "Lest clerics or monks."* There it is added that the religious <note>Referring to members of religious orders, such as monks or friars.</note> are to be punished even more severely. Furthermore, these punishments are not automatic, but must be pronounced, as will be manifest to those consulting those texts. Since such punishments are not imposed except for a mortal sin, the doctors commonly agree that it is a mortal sin for clerics or monks to practice such trade by themselves. So hold *Conrad on Contracts, question 52, conclusion 4; Juan Medina on Restitution, question 30, at the end of article 2; Navarro in the Manual, chapter 25, number 111, section 34; Silvester under the word "Clerics" 3, question 3; Angelus under the word "Clerics" 9, number 3; and others, despite whatever Cajetan may have written to the contrary in his "Summa" under the word "Cleric."*

At this point, observe that today the Council of Trent *Session 22, chapter 1, "On Reform"* has renewed the ancient punishments and laws in this matter, commanding Bishops to restrain clerics in that regard by using those punishments and others added to them. These points are understood, however, to apply to clerics established in Holy Orders <note>Deacons, priests, and bishops.</note>, as *Conrad, Medina, Silvester, Angelus, and others* assert in the cited places. For clerics established in minor orders do not sin mortally. Regarding beneficiaries who are not established in Holy Orders, *Silvester* is uncertain in the cited place, and the other cited doctors seem to incline toward the view that they do not sin mortally. Regarding the religious, *Angelus, Conrad, and Silvester* judge that they sin mortally, even if they are not established in Holy Orders, and their opinion is not displeasing.

Likewise, it is established as a punishment for trading clerics that if, having been warned three times by the Bishop or another who has quasi-episcopal jurisdiction over them, they do not abstain, they lose their clerical privilege. This does not refer to the privilege of the canon <note>Protection from physical violence.</note>, as if one who struck them would not incur excommunication, nor to the privilege of the forum <note>The right to be tried in an ecclesiastical court.</note>, as if they could be punished or sued before a secular judge; but rather that they and their goods are no longer exempt from taxes and other burdens. If, however, they later repent and amend their ways, they begin to enjoy the same privilege again. So it is held in the *final chapter of "On the life and honesty of clerics."*

<margin>3</margin>
Fourthly, in the Portuguese Ordinances, book 1, title 32, in the beginning, secular judges are commanded † not to allow clerics, nor beneficiaries, nor even knights of the golden spurs, or <term>Fidalgos de solar</term> <note>Portuguese/Spanish: Nobles of an ancestral house or established lineage.</note> as they call them, who live as such, to practice this kind of trade, as it is prohibited to them by law. This agrees with *law "vlt." of the Code on rescinding sales*, which prohibits this to palace officials. And in a few words, the "Extravagant" laws, title 3, law 12, although ecclesiastics are pronounced immune from the payment of customs duties both for those things they need for their habitation and also for those they have sold from their own rents or as things not necessary to them; they are nevertheless commanded to pay for those things which they have bought and sold by trading.

Likewise, in the Kingdom of Castile, although in *law 6, title 18, book 9 of the New Collection*, the Church and ecclesiastics are pronounced immune from the payment of the <term>alcabala</term> on things they sell, law 7 nevertheless adds: <note>original Spanish: "Lo contenido en la ley ante desta, mandamos que no aya lugar, en lo que los clerigos y Iglesias vendieren por via de mercaduria, trato y negociacion..."</note> *“The contents of the law preceding this, we command shall not apply in what clerics and Churches sell by way of merchandise, dealing, and business,”*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether ecclesiastics (clergy and members of religious orders) are subject to secular taxes, specifically the alcabala, when they engage in commercial trade rather than simple management of their own property.</meta>

...of such things, we command that they pay the **alcabala sales tax** <note>Original: *alcauala*. A common sales tax in the Spanish Empire.</note>, just as if they were **laypeople** <note>Original: *legos*. Non-clergy members of society.</note>. *Indeed, several things must be observed in this place. The first is that an ecclesiastic, on account of trading, loses that ecclesiastical privilege by which both he and his goods are not subject to burdens and tributes. It is established from the final chapter of "On the life and honesty of clerics" <note>Latin: *c. vlt. de vita & honest. cleric.* A reference to the Decretals, a collection of Canon Law.</note> that a threefold warning is necessary for this loss of privilege to occur. However, regarding the tribute or tax owed specifically on the item he sells or exchanges through trade, that warning is not necessary, as Gregory Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> rightly noted regarding Law 49, Title 6, Part 1, and others agree.*

<margin>5</margin> For neither the Church nor secular Princes intended to exempt them from tribute in the case of **trading** <note>Original: *negotiatione*. Specifically referring to business conducted for profit.</note> that is forbidden to them by canon law; thus, they were never immune from this tribute. Nor does the Church protect them in that regard, as is clear both from the very nature of the matter and from the present **Clementine** <note>A collection of canon law issued by Pope Clement V.</note> decree regarding assessments. There, while those who demand tributes from ecclesiastics are ordered to be restrained by excommunications, this is limited to things *which they do not carry or have carried for the sake of trading*. By these words, using an argument from the contrary sense (as the gloss noted in the same place), it is openly signified that tribute can be demanded from them for things they carry for the sake of trading, without any other warning. Finally, the final chapter of "On the life and honesty of clerics" not only fails to defend them from paying tribute on things they alienate through trade, but furthermore imposes a penalty: if, having been warned three times by their **Ordinary** <note>A bishop or other high-ranking church official with jurisdictional power.</note>, they do not cease trading, they lose their clerical privilege entirely regarding tributes and the burdens of the rest of their goods and persons. This point does not seem to have been sufficiently attended to by Lassarte <note>An author on tax law.</note>, where he thinks that by a prescribed custom against that chapter, the **alcabala** is exacted...

<margin>6</margin> ...from ecclesiastics without a previous threefold warning for things they sell or exchange through trade, as if that warning were necessary according to that chapter.

Second, although when something is bought to be sold for exchange, it does not simply belong to the "third type" of buying and selling explained in Disputation 339 (which is the subject of our discourse here), but rather to the "second type" (which is not regularly forbidden to ecclesiastics, as we shall say, nor is it strictly called "trade"); nevertheless, there are certain things belonging to that second type which closely approach the third type. For that reason, they are least becoming of ecclesiastics and should be judged as forbidden trades through **equity** <note>Original: *epicheiam*. A legal concept referring to the spirit of the law rather than the strict letter.</note>.

<margin>7</margin> Of such a kind is if an ecclesiastic buys grapes so that, through servants or ministers hired for that purpose, he may make wine from them to sell later. Likewise, if he buys wool so that, through hired workers and artisans, he may make cloth from it to sell. I would say the same if an ecclesiastic made cloth to sell from the wool of the revenues of his own **benefice** <note>A church office that provides an income.</note> or from his own flocks, using hired workers and artisans. Thus, when these things are sold, a **gabella** <note>A general term for a tax or excise duty.</note> is owed, no differently than if laypeople were selling them, as Lassarte affirms. This is despite the fact that these trades simply belong to the second type of buying and selling explained in Disputation 339...

<column-break/>

...and should only be judged as forbidden to ecclesiastics through equity—a point which he himself did not sufficiently notice.

I would say the same if an ecclesiastic rented others' fields, which he cultivated through workers, so that he might sell the fruits gathered from there; indeed, he would owe the tax on the fruits sold. For although the fruits are born from his own seed, and by the very fact that they are received they belong to him and not to the lord of the field regarding ownership; nevertheless, because it is not becoming for a cleric to rent others' fields, cultivate them through workers, and gather fruits to sell them for profit—but rather this is specifically forbidden to him among other things—this must surely be counted among the trades forbidden to him. Consequently, he owes the tax on the sale or exchange of such fruits, just as when he rents the revenues of someone else's benefice to sell them for profit, which is likewise forbidden to him.

However, it would not be "trade" if he cultivated his own fields through servants or ministers hired for that purpose and sold the fruits, or if he sold grapes from his own vineyards, or made wine from them to sell, or if he sold the fruits of his own benefice. For this reason, he would not owe tribute on things sold in this way. Lassarte agrees on these points.

In a similar way, it must be said that if he rented someone else's saltworks to sell the salt made from there, it is trade and he therefore owes the tax. If, however, he produced and sold it from his own saltworks through ministers, it is not trade, but the sale of the fruits (or quasi-fruits) of his own estate, for which an ecclesiastic does not owe tribute. In the same way, if he rented someone else's flocks and sold the offspring, milk, cheese, and wool, it would be trade; otherwise if he sold these same things from his own flocks, since it would be the sale of the fruits of his own property. So says Lassarte.

Silvester <note>Silvester Prierias, a 15th-century theologian.</note> and Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a prominent 16th-century canonist.</note>, whom Lassarte and others follow, affirm: If a monastery has a vein of iron and produces iron from the material through hired ministers and sells it, they do not owe tax. They say the same if they buy the same vein, but the monks themselves produce the iron from the material to sell; because similarly, this is not "trading" but buying material so that, having been transformed into something else through the ministry of the ecclesiastics, they may sell a finished product made by the ecclesiastics themselves.

But they add that if a monastery buys a vein so that they may produce iron from it through lay administrators to sell, it is trade, and the tax is owed from the iron sold in this way. Yet Navarrus rightly speaks cautiously, saying: *if they buy the vein alone*. As if to say, it would be different if they bought the estate in which the vein is located. For if they bought only the vein, they would be judged to be buying the material alone from which to make iron through hired ministers to sell; that, however, would be trading, no differently than it is trading to buy grapes from which to similarly make wine and sell it. If, however, they bought the estate, the material of the vein would be counted among the fruits of such an estate, the ownership of which was acquired by purchase, and the iron would be similarly produced there by the ministry of others, and therefore...

<meta>This page continues Molina's legal and moral analysis of whether the clergy and religious orders should pay secular sales taxes (the alcabala). He is specifically defining the boundary between "management of property" (exempt) and "commercial trade" (taxable/forbidden).</meta>

### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

therefore, that would no more be considered **commercial trade**, nor would a tax be owed from it, than if that same estate or mine were not purchased, but were the monastery's own property. In that event, the very authors with whom we are disputing have asserted that it is not commercial trade, nor is a tax owed; this is something that **Federico de Senis** <note>Federico Petrucci of Siena, a 14th-century canon lawyer.</note>, whom they themselves cite, had asserted before them.

And certainly, since by the name of a **"vein"** <note>Original: *venæ*. Refers to a vein of ore in a mine.</note>, it is common to understand not just the raw material, but the source from which it is extracted and of which it is the "fruit" (or quasi-fruit), I believe it should simply be asserted along with Federico de Senis that no more tax is owed from the **iron** made from it than would be owed from the material itself if it were sold so that others might make iron from it. This is the same as the tax that would be owed from the **salt** of a salt-works which a monastery bought outright, so that it might produce, extract, and sell salt from that water through the labor of laypeople. In such an event, no one would claim that commercial trade is taking place or that a tax is owed.

That opinion of **Lassarte** <note>Gundissalvus de Villadiego Lassarte, a Spanish jurist.</note> should also be rejected, where he asserted (in number 60) that if a monastery or a cleric buys an estate full of **ripe fruits** and later sells the surplus, he owes tax on the fruits he sold. His reasoning is that those fruits are parts of the thing purchased; therefore, if he buys the estate with the intention of selling the surplus, Lassarte says commercial trade is involved, and tax is owed on the fruits so sold. I believe the contrary must be said. For he who buys such an estate buys it for itself, so that he may enjoy the fruits of both this year and the years following, and sell the excess. It is merely **accidental** <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality—here, the fact that the fruit happened to be ripe at the moment of purchase.</note> whether the fruits are ripe or not; nor does he later sell them as parts of a purchased thing that he bought to resell, but as fruits perceived and gathered from a field that has now become his own. Therefore, it cannot be called commercial trade, and consequently, the cleric does not owe tax on the fruits sold in this way. This is confirmed by a very strong **argument against the man** <note>Latin: *argumento ad hominem*. Using the opponent's own logic against them.</note>. Since the same author often correctly affirms in the same chapter that a cleric does not owe tax on trade that is not forbidden to him by canon law; who, then, does not see that it is **not forbidden** for clerics to buy estates with ripe fruits, even with the intention of selling the surplus—both from those currently hanging and ripe, and from those he gathers in subsequent years? Therefore, no tax is owed from them.

<margin>8</margin> Thirdly, it must be observed that just as through **equity** <note>Original: *epicheiam*. A legal principle allowing for the relaxation of the letter of the law in favor of its spirit.</note> certain things from the second kind of buying and selling (explained in Dispute 339) are counted among the trades forbidden to clerics, so too certain things, which would otherwise belong to the trades forbidden to those same clerics, are **exempted** from the number of those trades because of some intervening circumstance that makes them lawful for those clerics. Let the first example be what Lassarte brings forward (number 78), based on the chapter *Dilecti* and its glosses. If a certain cleric is so **poor** that he cannot otherwise be suitably supported except by renting someone else's field, and he supports himself partly by eating the fruits and partly by selling them, that kind of renting is not counted among the illicit trades for clerics. Because from that

<column-break/>

circumstance—that the cleric cannot otherwise be supported—it is not illicit for him.
The cited chapter *Dilecti* and those two glosses speak of a **monastery** that held rented fields from others because it could not otherwise be suitably supported. In that event, Lassarte rightly notes in the cited place that tax is not owed on the fruits sold: because if a particular trade is **not prohibited** to a cleric by the sacred canons, he does not owe tax on it. 

The second example is this: There are **religious** <note>Members of religious orders, such as Jesuits or Dominicans.</note> in the regions of **Brazil** and the **East Indies** who diligently labor for the expansion and preservation of the Church. To sustain themselves appropriately, they need many things sent to them from **Spain**, but they do not have money in Spain. Since there is a great scarcity of money in Brazil, and money is worth a great deal in the East Indies, they need to send certain **merchandise** that is bought cheaply there and is worth much more in **Portugal** <note>Original: *Lusitania*.</note>. Once delivered to Portuguese merchants, the proceeds are used to send them the things they need. In this way, they avoid the enormous costs of transporting necessities to themselves from Portugal, and they do so without being occupied or distracted by business. By this reasoning, if not as many people as are necessary for the **salvation of souls** are supported there, certainly more are supported than otherwise would be. Surely, there is no one who can rightly condemn this prudent and **economic management** <note>Molina uses "economic" in the original sense of household or institutional management (*oeconomica*).</note> of providing necessities for such a great good of the Church, or assert that it is contrary to the sacred canons—provided that no more merchandise is sent than is needed to buy necessities in Portugal. Therefore, since tax is not owed on trade that is not illicit for clerics, no tax is owed on the goods so sent, nor on their price. Other similar examples could be brought forward, which are easily understood from these two. Now, having observed these things, let us return to the point from which we digressed.

<margin>9</margin> In the **Clementine decree** <note>A collection of canon laws.</note> *De vita et honestate clericorum*, it is ordained that if a cleric—whether he is in holy orders or not—publicly and in his own person exercises the office of a **butcher**, a meat-seller, or a **tavern-keeper**, he should be specifically warned three times by the bishop to desist from that office within a set time. If he does not desist, or if he takes it up again later, he **loses his clerical privilege** automatically if he is married. If he is not married, he loses the privilege regarding his property (in the sense explained above), provided he does not dress entirely as a layman. But if he dresses entirely as a layman, he loses his clerical privilege in every way until he repents. Since this is a **penal law**, it is necessary that all the aforementioned conditions occur for him to incur the penalty. Furthermore, even if a cleric performs other lowlier offices, he does not incur that penalty. Read, among others, **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent theologian.</note> and **Angelus** <note>Angelus de Clavasio, author of the *Summa Angelica*.</note> on this topic.

<margin>10</margin> However, it is asked whether it is lawful for clerics and religious to engage in **lucrative trade** through others by giving money to a relative, so that he may trade in their
