<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on whether clerics and religious orders are permitted to engage in trade and the resulting tax implications. It specifically addresses the distinction between "business for profit" (forbidden) and "management for sustenance" (permitted).</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 347.

...it will be [allowed], either by entering into a partnership with one or more others, or by leasing the revenues of a benefice, or some other arrangement with others, provided that the partners apply all the labor and industry. **Juan Medina** <note>Juan Medina (1490–1546), a Spanish theologian at Alcalá known for his work on restitution and contracts.</note> excuses such men. Firstly, because the reason for the prohibition ceases to apply, since trade conducted through another person neither distracts the cleric nor occupies his mind; and, provided the money is handed over for lawful trade, any sins committed by the person through whom the trade is done are not imputed to the cleric. Secondly, because the laws seem only to forbid an ecclesiastic from trading in his own person, as is clear from the **Clementine decree** *de vita & honestate clericorum* <note>Original: "clem. 1. de vita & honest. cler." A section of Canon Law concerning the conduct of the clergy.</note>, which only punishes a cleric when he exercises the office of a butcher or a tavern-keeper by himself. Furthermore, the chapter *Significante* <note>A specific chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding appeals.</note> mentions as a lawful thing that certain canons possessed public stalls in which meat was cut. Also, the Clementine decree on the state of monks, although it forbids monks from hunting by themselves, does not forbid them from doing it through others. For my part, while I do not think it is a mortal sin to trade through others in this way, I do judge that some degree of foulness and indecency is involved in such trade by reason of their status, when no circumstance is present to excuse it; therefore, I judge it should be disapproved of for its own sake. Note this: it is lawful for clerics and religious to own public buildings which they lease to others either for selling meat or for conducting other businesses, and from which they receive rent; such were the "stalls" discussed in the cited chapter *Significante*.

<margin>Decision</margin>
**11** The second conclusion. It is lawful for clerics to buy necessities for their own use and that of their household, and to sell surplus goods, whether from the fruits of their own fields, from the revenues of their own benefice, or from wherever else they obtained them. Indeed, even if they bought something at a lower price without the intention of selling it dearer, it is lawful for them—if the price later increases—to sell it for more and make a profit, and they owe no tax on it. This is the common opinion of everyone, and there is no difficulty in it, even if an ecclesiastic is drawn to sell by the high price, intending to buy similar things cheaper later. This conclusion is confirmed because these matters pertain to **economic governance** <note>In the Aristotelian sense: the management of a household (oikonomia).</note>, which ought to be evident in clerics and Bishops, according to Paul in **1 Timothy 3 and 5**. If, however, anything should come to an ecclesiastic from a dissolved partnership entered into with another, or from any other trade he might exercise through another, and he were to sell those things, he would owe tax on them just as if he were a layman.

**12** The third conclusion. **Political trade**—that which is necessary for the supply of an army or citizens—does not befit clerics, because they ought to be strangers to secular government and business, according to **2 Timothy 2**: *No man being a soldier to God entangleth himself with secular business.* This accords with the chapter *Episcopus* <note>Distinction 88 of the Decretum Gratiani.</note>, which is taken from the Apostolic Canons; it commands that neither Bishops, nor priests, nor deacons should undertake secular cares, otherwise they should be deposed. This is further supported by chapter 1 and following in the 21st case, question 3. However, it could be of such importance to the commonwealth and the common good that an ecclesiastic might devote himself to such things as charity demands, in which case a dispensation should be granted to him. Indeed, to see to it that the poor are helped in times of famine, and for a cleric or religious to labor in that cause—ensuring that goods are bought elsewhere and necessities are imported—is both permitted by the laws and demanded by charity,

<column-break/>

especially when these things cannot be sufficiently accomplished by laypeople alone.

**13** The fourth conclusion. It is lawful for clerics to practice some **craft** <note>Original: *artificio*. Refers to manual trades or skills.</note> from which they may earn something and sustain their lives, provided they do not, for that reason, neglect the duties they are bound to by their clerical office, and provided the craft is not shameful, base, or unbecoming of a cleric. This conclusion is expressed in many laws, such as the chapters *Clericus* 1 and 2, distinction 91, where it is stated: *A cleric may provide food and clothing for himself by a small craft or by agriculture, without detriment to his office.* And again: *All able-bodied clerics should learn both crafts and letters.* The chapter *Presbyteri* in the same distinction and the first chapter *De celebratione missarum* agree, where rural work is permitted to clerics. This conclusion is further confirmed by the example of **Paul**, who, although he was a Bishop, worked with his hands and practiced the craft of **tent-making**, as is clear from **Acts 18**. And **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century Church Father.</note>, following the example of the Apostles, advised monks to weave baskets or hampers, cultivate gardens, build beehives, weave nets, and write books, both to procure food and to banish idleness. As was said: provided the craft is not shameful or base. For just as clerics are forbidden from exercising the office of a tavern-keeper or a butcher because of the indecency and lowliness of the office, so too are similar base and "dirty" crafts considered forbidden to them, such as that of a **tanner** (that is, one who prepares hides into leather), and others of that kind. Similarly, they are forbidden from exercising offices unbecoming to clerics, such as making playing cards, dice, or weapons of war. Likewise, in practicing crafts, **avarice** must be far removed, although this is not a mortal sin unless joined with injury to one's neighbors.

**14** The fifth conclusion. Ecclesiastics can lawfully buy certain things to transform into something else and sell for more—for example, raw material from which they make finished goods to sell. Likewise, they may buy animals to nourish in their own fields so that, when they have grown or given birth, they may sell them and their offspring. Likewise, a mule or other beast of burden, so that when it has grown and served them for a time, they may sell it for more. Furthermore, they can lease out their own estates and beasts. However, to buy beasts solely to lease them out would be a form of trade and thus unlawful for them.

**15** They may also lease estates for the sustenance of themselves and their household, which they cultivate by paying a certain portion of the fruits or money. However, for the sake of profit, to lease larger estates in order to sell the fruits and make a gain is forbidden to them, as was stated above.

<margin>1</margin> Judges, their officials, and ministers—and sometimes even their domestic servants—are prohibited by common law from building new houses, constructing ships, or buying anything except necessities for food and clothing within the place where they exercise jurisdiction. This applies even if they act through a middleman <note>Original: "per interpositam personam."</note>. They are also forbidden from exchanging goods, taking loans from subjects, or accepting any gifts. None of these actions are valid, even if the person who gave or sold the item consents after the official's term of office has ended. This is established in the Code <note>The *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman law.</note> in the law "The Only One" on the contracts of judges, joined with the law "To the Principals" and the law "To the Governors." Indeed, in the law "It is not permitted," the buyer is punished with a fourfold penalty. These same rules and others like them are prohibited under heavy penalties in the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, titles 38 and 39.

<margin>The Law of Castile.</margin> In the Kingdom of Castile as well, in book 3 of the *New Compilation* <note>Original: "nouæ collect." referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century collection of Spanish laws.</note>, title 6, law 2, it is forbidden for assistants, governors, magistrates <note>Original: "correctoribus."</note>, and their ministers—including those called *Alcaldes mayores* <note>Senior municipal judges or governors.</note> and other lower officials—to build houses, engage in trade, or graze animals in the place of their jurisdiction during their term of office, whether by themselves or through a middleman, under the penalty of forfeiting what was built, bought, or contracted to the royal treasury.

Furthermore, in law 33, title 4, those called *Alcaldes mayores* are commanded not to allow their ministers, called *Alguaziles* <note>Bailiffs or constables responsible for executing court orders.</note>, to buy—personally or through a middleman—the items sold during the execution of court sentences, under a fourfold penalty. Likewise, in law 47, title 2, book 9 of the same collection, those ministers called *Contadores* <note>Accountants or auditors of the royal treasury.</note>

<column-break/>

and officials of the accounting office are forbidden, directly or indirectly, through themselves or a middleman, from buying *juros* <note>State-funded annuities or bonds.</note>, assignments of revenue, or making any contract or agreement regarding these things, under the penalty of forfeiting all such assets to the Royal Treasury.

<margin>2</margin> It has been explained in Disputation 224, in the section "Property of a Minor," that guardians, curators, and persons subject to them—as well as, in Portugal, the judges of orphans, the scribes of those same judges, and the "auditors of remainders" <note>Original: "contadores dos residuos," officials who audited the remaining assets of estates or charitable foundations.</note>—cannot buy the property of minors in their care, and what penalties they incur under common law as well as the laws of Castile and Portugal.

<margin>3</margin> It was stated in Disputation 248 under what penalties executors of wills in Portugal are forbidden from buying anything for themselves or others, even through a middleman, from the assets of the deceased. Common law agrees in the law "In Purchase," the last paragraph, and the law "It is not permitted," which generally forbid those who manage others' affairs from buying the property involved in those affairs, even through a middleman, under a fourfold penalty.

In Disputation 26, we discussed in general who can or cannot enter into contracts. From that, it is easily understood whose purchase or sale is valid based on whether they have the legal capacity to contract.

Regarding the wife, it was explained in Disputation 275 to what extent the administration of property belongs solely to the husband under the common law of Castile and Portugal, and in what matters it depends on the wife's consent. It was noted that under the laws of these kingdoms, a wife has no administration of property unless she perhaps reserved some for herself when they contracted the marriage, which rarely happens in these kingdoms.

<margin>4</margin> Therefore, if a wife enters into a purchase, sale, or any other contract regarding assets she does not manage without at least the tacit consent of her husband—or if the husband does not later ratify the contract—it is undoubtedly null and void. This is true even if the contract is confirmed by an oath, as noted by Covarrubias and Antonio Gómez, because it results in prejudice against the husband, which is why it is forbidden to the wife. This is confirmed by the Laws of Toro <note>The *Leyes de Toro* (1505) were a landmark set of 83 laws regulating Castilian civil law.</note>, specifically Law 54 and the five following it. In the first of these, it is decreed that a wife, during the marriage, cannot refuse an inheritance (whether from a will or if someone dies without one) without the husband's permission; however, she may accept it without his permission through the "benefit of inventory" <note>A legal protection allowing an heir to accept an inheritance without becoming liable for the deceased's debts beyond the value of the assets received.</note>. In the second, it is decreed that the wife cannot enter a contract, withdraw from an existing contract, release anyone from an obligation, or sue/defend in court without the husband's permission. Even if she attempts this through herself or a representative, it is null and void. In the third law, the husband may grant her general permission for all these things. In the fourth, a judge can, for legitimate and necessary cause, compel the husband...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of contracts, specifically focusing on the requirements for marital consent in Portugal and Castile, the restrictions on sales between family members, and the prohibition of trade with enemies of the faith.</meta>

Therefore, the husband should grant his wife the power to perform all those acts which she could not do without such authorization. If the husband is compelled by law but refuses to grant it, a judge may grant it to her instead. In the fifth point, a husband can ratify all actions his wife performed without his prior authorization, and a general ratification is sufficient. In the sixth point, when a husband is absent and his return is not expected soon, if there is danger in delay, a judge—having recognized a legitimate, necessary, or useful cause for the wife—can grant her the power for those things to which a husband would have consented; such authorization is legally valid.

All these rules also have force in Portugal <note>Original: "Lusitania"</note>, because the same reasoning applies to contracts regarding earnest money <note>term: "arrharum" (earnest money), a down payment to solidify a contract</note> and dowry <note>term: "dotis" (dowry)</note> when nothing else is specified. By the custom of that Kingdom, it is understood in the same way as in Castile. These rules have much more force when there is a contract for a "partnership of goods" <note>This refers to a community property arrangement between spouses.</note>, because then all property becomes common to both spouses, and the administration belongs to the husband alone, though he remains dependent in some matters on the wife’s consent. Furthermore, by common law, a wife can enter into contracts, as well as take legal action and defend herself in court (at least through a legal representative), regarding property which she manages by that same right. I would say the same for these Kingdoms if the wife had reserved any property for herself, the administration of which belonged to her alone.

<margin>5</margin> If a wife and husband enter into a contract with a third party, the husband is considered by that very act to provide her the authorization to enter into it; this is self-evident and proven in the law *Titius* <note>Original: "l. Titius, in princ. ff. quibus modis pign. vel hypo." referencing the Digest of Roman Law.</note> and affirmed by Antonio Gomez and others.

He is also considered to grant her authorization if he assigns her to some trade or administration, or if she enters into a contract in the husband’s presence and he remains silent. This is the opinion of Antonio Gomez, supported by various laws <note>Citing the Digest regarding the actions of masters and business managers.</note>.

If a contract made by a wife without her husband’s authorization is beneficial to her, and the husband’s ratification does not follow because he is deceased or absent, the contract is valid. This is no different from a contract made by a minor without the authority of a guardian or curator; it is valid for the purpose of obligating the other party to the minor's benefit, though it is not valid when it does not result in the minor’s benefit, as shown in Disputation 224 and elsewhere. This opinion is favorable, especially since it is likely the husband would have ratified it if he were able.

<margin>6</margin> Furthermore, under Portuguese law, the sale of immovable property <note>term: "rei immobilis" (real estate or land)</note>—or property treated as immovable—made by a husband without the wife’s consent is invalid. This will be discussed further below when we speak of the contract of partnership between spouses. However, a husband can sell or resign a public office without the wife’s consent, as will also be added there.

<margin>7</margin> Under the same Portuguese law, a father or any other ancestor cannot sell anything to one of their descendants, nor exchange anything with them, without the authorization of the co-heirs, or, if the co-heirs are unwilling to grant it, without judicial consent.

If they should sell or exchange anything without both authorizations,

<column-break/>

the contract is invalid, and the item must be brought to the partition of the estate. The person who bought it or exchanged something for it loses what they gave for it. This is stated in the *Ordinances* <note>Original: "l. ordin. titu. 82." referring to the Ordenações do Reino de Portugal.</note>. Observe, however, that since this law is penal regarding the loss of the price paid, and a penalty is not owed before a sentence is passed, if the descendant had obtained it at a just price, they are not bound to bring it to partition unless it is demanded. If, however, they had purchased it at an unjust price, it would be sufficient to bring to partition the amount up to a competent price.

Furthermore, if someone were to buy something in this manner through invincible ignorance of the law, they are not bound in the "court of conscience" <note>The "forum of conscience" refers to moral/religious standing rather than civil law.</note> to pay the penalty, because a penalty has no place where there is no fault. If, however, the co-heirs were to demand it then, the buyer could make a secret compensation <note>term: "clam compensationem" (a private deduction of what is owed to offset a loss)</note>, provided it could be done without scandal, even if the co-heirs believed there was a fault when in truth there was none.

<margin>8</margin> Between a father and a son, while the son is under the father's power, there can be no buying and selling except regarding military or quasi-military property <note>term: "bona castrensia, aut quasi castrensia," property a son acquired through his own service in the military or public office, which was legally his own.</note>. Regarding "adventitious" property <note>term: "bona aduentitia," property coming to the son from outside sources like a mother's inheritance.</note>, since the father is the administrator of those goods, the contract is invalid, just as it is for a guardian or curator with a minor regarding the goods they manage.

<margin>9</margin> Next, it is prohibited to sell to Saracens, Turks, and other enemies of the Christian name: horses, arms, iron, iron wire, wool, steel, and all other types of metals, as well as instruments of war, bindings, hemp, and ropes—whether made of hemp or any other material—and the material itself, and other such things; and with far greater reason, galleys and ships. This is established in the *Bulla Coenae* <note>A famous papal bull listing various excommunications.</note> and other church laws. In these chapters, it is also prohibited to carry or sell to Saracens in time of war, or even during a truce, victuals and any other merchandise. These matters and the penalties established for them must be discussed in another place. Certain things are also prohibited from being sold or exported to Saracens and enemies under Portuguese law, under heavy penalties, consistent with Canon law and Civil law.

***

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological examination of contracts by Luis de Molina. Having previously discussed the capacity of persons (specifically spouses) to contract, he now moves to the "circumstances" of the contract—specifically the location (sacred spaces) and the nature of the market (monopolies).</meta>

Louis de Molina: On Contracts

**A**s far as the circumstance of location is concerned, there is no doubt that buying and selling can be rendered illicit by the sacred nature of the place. It is unbecoming for a matter so profane—which distracts so much from divine things and provides an occasion for so many risks to conscience and offenses against God—to be carried out in a sacred place. This is especially true if the goods for sale are actually carried into that place and sold there as if in a public marketplace. *Consequently, this acts against the virtue of religion, whose purpose is to offer worship and honor to God, and it constitutes the vice of sacrilege.* <note>original: "sacrilegij vitium"</note>

<margin>2</margin> The doctors <note>referring to established legal and theological scholars</note> generally agree that it appears to be a mortal sin <note>term: "lethale" (lethal/mortal), a grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace</note> of sacrilege to bring goods into a sacred place and sell them there as if in a public market. This is suggested, first, by the example of Christ in *Matthew 21*, who, having made a whip of cords, cast the buyers and sellers out of the Temple and overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. Our most mild Lord would by no means have done this for a mere venial sin <note>term: "veniale" (venial), a lesser sin that does not break one's relationship with God</note>. Second, it is against the precepts of the Church. Indeed, in the chapter *Decet* regarding the immunity of Churches, book 6, it states: *Let negotiations, and especially fairs, cease in Churches and their cemeteries.* Furthermore, in the chapter *Reliqui* regarding the custody of the Eucharist, when certain clerics were placing furniture in churches and allowing others to do the same—so that the churches looked more like lay houses than the dwelling of God—the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> added: *We firmly forbid furniture of this kind to be admitted into Churches, unless because of hostile incursions, sudden fires, or other urgent necessities it is necessary to take refuge in them; provided, however, that once the necessity ceases, the items are returned to their original places.* The Council of Trent also, in Session 22, in the decree on things to be observed in the celebration of Masses, commands prelates <note>high-ranking Church officials like bishops</note>, among other things, to bar all secular actions, vain and profane conversations, walking about, noise, and shouting, so that the house of God may truly be seen to be, and be called, a house of prayer.

<margin>3</margin> However, when only the agreements <note>original: "pacta"</note> for buying and selling or other contracts are made in a church, while the goods to be sold are in other locations, this would not be a mortal sin, as affirmed by Conradus on contracts, Johannes Medina, Soto, Angelus, and Sylvester. The same would apply when someone buys something in a church that was found there by chance, which another person was carrying through the city to sell. This is because the matter is small, and also because the church itself does not become a place for merchandise. Nevertheless, all these things are not free from venial sin. Furthermore, selling candles and other small items for divine worship in churches, without noise and with almost no "business" atmosphere, could even be free from venial sin if done with a view toward divine worship; yet it is better that these things be kept outside the church. So say Sylvester and others under the word "negotiation." Nor does it matter that Christ the Lord cast those out of the Temple who were selling things that served divine worship. For they made the Temple like a marketplace by the multitude of goods sold and the crowd of sellers, which was not without great noise and disturbance. Moreover, there were also the tables of the money-changers, who practiced exchange in the Temple, not only by swapping currency but also by giving credit under usury <note>term: "vsura" (usury), the practice of charging interest on loans, which was strictly regulated or forbidden by Church law</note>; for this reason, they truly

<column-break/>

made the house of God a "den of thieves" because of the injustices they practiced therein, as Christ added. Furthermore, the things that served divine worship then were of a far different nature—namely animals—than those used in the Christian church.

In addition, I would offer several warnings. First, in those things that pertain to the worship of God—in which the purpose of faith and internal religion is displayed outwardly as a sort of reward, not only for the honor of God and the edification of the faithful but also as an example to non-believers—much smaller sins should not be tolerated than in other matters that do not pertain to faith and religion.

Second, not everything that the Supreme Pontiffs forbid or command is forbidden or commanded under the guilt of mortal sin, even if they establish precepts that bind to guilt and say, out of an affection for divine honor, that they "firmly forbid" them. Consequently, to discern whether a precept binds under mortal or venial sin, one must look at the gravity of the matter being commanded and the penalty established by the law. For the Supreme Pontiffs ought not only to command those things they wish to be observed under mortal sin, but also those they wish to be kept under venial sin; nor does charity demand that all things be commanded under mortal sin, or that laws which bind to such guilt be multiplied. Hence I conclude that a mortal sin is not easily to be judged from the fact that something unbecoming regarding business is done in a church, or because some furniture is unbecomingly placed in it—especially since the circumstance of a mortal sin being committed in a church does not, according to the common opinion of doctors, necessarily have to be confessed, because it does not reach the limits of a "lethal circumstance." I do not know what, by its very nature, could be more unbecoming in a church (aside from the scandal of one's neighbors) than a mortal sin itself. Moreover, the necessity of those who would otherwise do unbecoming things in a church provides no small excuse from guilt if they occur in a church, as is clear from the chapter *Reliqui* on the custody of the Eucharist.

<margin>4</margin> Third, when doing something unbecoming in a sacred place is a mortal sin, the prelates and those who by office have the care of the Church sin mortally if they do not forbid and prevent it, provided they are able to do so.

Regarding the circumstance of the time when an act is performed, we shall speak more conveniently when the discussion turns to the observation of feast days.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the ethics of commerce. Having just addressed the location of trade, he now turns to the controversial topic of monopolies and price-fixing, examining when exclusive trading rights are a sin against the public good and when they might be permitted by a King.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 3

*4 Whether merchants, if they agree among themselves that none of them shall sell below a certain price, or buy above a certain price, are bound to make restitution for the damages subsequently caused to private individuals.*

*5 Whether those who buy a great abundance of goods at harvest time or another time and store them so that a high price is induced in the city, and others are forced to buy much more dearly from their hands, are bound to restitution. And what is the law of Portugal and Castile regarding this.*

<margin>1</margin> **A** monopoly is named from the Greek words *monos*, meaning "one," and *polium* <note>original Greek: *polein*</note>, meaning "sale," as if it were the "sale by only one" in some province, city, or town. He who practices a monopoly is called a "monopolist," that is, a "lone seller."

<margin>2</margin> Properly speaking, a monopoly exists when someone, or a group of people, obtains the exclusive right to sell certain goods. This is generally unfair and injurious to the State <note>original: *Respublica*, referring to the organized political community</note>, because citizens are forced to buy goods more dearly from their hands, while others in the State are prevented from trading justly and conveniently, and from being more generous in price to their fellow citizens. This results in harm to the citizens, even if the monopolists sell at a "just price" <note>term: *iusto pretio*; the price determined by common estimation in a fair market</note>. For this reason, it is rightly forbidden by the legal experts in the Code of Justinian <note>original: *unica. C. de monopoliis*</note> under penalty of the loss of all goods and perpetual exile.

By the same law, it is forbidden for merchants to agree among themselves not to sell a certain commodity below a certain price, or not to buy it above a certain price. Likewise, it is forbidden for craftsmen to agree that a task begun by one of them shall not be continued or finished by another, or for other similar pacts to be made. This is because it is established that such agreements are generally unfair and to the detriment of the State. Although these pacts are also called "monopolies" by many, they are prohibited in that law as distinct pacts, as is clear from the heading, the text, and even from the penalty established there, which is distinct from the penalty decreed for monopolies. Indeed, those practicing these illegal pacts are only punished by a fine of forty pounds of gold; and judges who turn a blind eye or are negligent in punishing these crimes, as well as monopolies, are afflicted with a penalty of fifty pounds. However, because we must speak as the majority do, we shall include these under the name of monopolies as well.

<margin>3</margin> I said that monopolies are generally unfair and injurious to the State, because sometimes they are not unfair—namely, when they are created by public authority, with the common good demanding it. For if the State should need certain goods, and there is no one who wishes to bring them in (because perhaps that trade would involve maximum labor and the risk of loss) unless a privilege were granted that no one else could bring or sell those goods, then it will surely be lawful to grant such a privilege. This must be done at a taxed, moderate price, considering all the concurrent circumstances, so that those who use the privilege do not burden the State more than is just. Likewise, if there is no one willing to undertake a certain office beneficial to the State, such as selling certain goods or transporting foreigners, it may then be granted to one or several people that they alone may perform such a duty, with a moderate price set for them, lest there be a fear that they might exceed the just price.

<column-break/>

Because it is likewise beneficial to the common good that books be composed and printed, and no one would easily be found willing to print them unless a privilege were granted that no one else should print them within a certain time, or bring those printed elsewhere to sell, we see daily that such a privilege is justly granted with a set price, so that it does not exceed what is reasonable and just to the detriment of the State. In a similar way, because the King of Portugal opened the navigation to India at his own expense and subdued the places of those regions, he was able to establish for his own benefit (which also results in a benefit to the State, since it provides the means by which he may defend it without burdening it with new taxes) that no one besides himself, or those to whom he has granted that trade for a certain price, may bring certain goods from India, or carry them from Portugal to India, or sell them there. Juan Medina <note>a Spanish theologian, 1490–1546</note> adds that it should not be condemned if a King, placed in some public necessity, grants to certain merchants or craftsmen for a certain sum of money the right to be the sole sellers of something in his Kingdom, provided a moderate price is set for them so they do not burden the State more than is just. Indeed, the public necessity in which the King finds himself excuses him from sin, and the merchants are excused by the privilege granted to them by the King for that reason. For just as the King could demand from his subjects that they contribute to relieve that public necessity, so he can subject them to this burden, provided it is moderate and involves less trouble and loss for them.

In this matter, observe that no better rule can be given than this: it is permitted to grant such privileges when right reason and the common good demand it, having weighed all circumstances on the part of the subjects, the King, and those to whom they are granted. At the same time, care must be taken that in helping the common good, certain parts of the State are not burdened more than others, as far as possible, since it belongs to the King to help all equally. However, those who would grant such privileges irrationally and to the prejudice of the subjects—both the King (or the State) who grants them and those who obtain or use them—would sin mortally <note>term: *lethaliter*; a grave sin</note>. All these would be held to the restitution of all damages to the subjects that followed from this against their will.

<margin>4 <br/> Question</margin> The doubt is whether merchants who agree among themselves that none of them shall sell below a certain price, or buy above a certain price—and generally, those who unfairly practice such agreements and monopolies to the prejudice of the State and their neighbors—are bound to restore the damages to private individuals of the State that followed for that reason. Domingo de Soto <note>influential Dominican theologian, 1494–1560</note> and Juan Medina answer in the affirmative. Francisco de Vitoria <note>original: *Cont.* likely referring to the school of Francisco de Vitoria or his commentators</note> also seems to agree when he says they sin against justice. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, 1491–1586, a famous canon lawyer</note>, Sylvester Prierias, and John Major only affirm that they sin mortally, but do not discuss whether they are bound to make restitution.

<margin>Decision</margin> Our first conclusion is this: When the agreement causes private individuals to buy above the "rigorous just price" <note>term: *pretium iustum rigorosum*; the highest point of the fair price range</note> that would otherwise have existed, or to sell below the "lowest just price"...

### Louis de Molina, On Contracts
#### Page 230

...should sell <note>The text begins mid-word, likely continuing 'venderent' (should sell) from the previous page.</note>, there is no doubt that they are bound to make restitution, at least up to the limits of the **just price**. This is proven because they sin against justice and are, therefore, the unjust cause of this subsequent loss to private individuals.

**The second conclusion.** When merchants agree among themselves on a price which, even without that agreement, would be just but "rigorous" <note>term: *pretio rigoroso*; the highest possible price within the range of fairness, as opposed to a 'pious' or 'moderate' price</note>, they certainly sin against the charity owed to their neighbors. They would deserve to be punished with a very heavy fine by the public authorities as men who are harmful to the Commonwealth <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note>. However, I do not see that they sin against **justice**, and therefore they are not bound to restitution, provided that none of them used fraud, force, or fear to prevent others from selling more cheaply.

This conclusion is proven because someone who, without force, fear, or fraud, persuades another who wanted to sell more cheaply to sell at a "rigorous" but still just price, would certainly not sin against justice. Similarly, someone who, through advice alone, turns someone away from making a donation or a legacy they intended to make does not sin against justice. Therefore, by the same reasoning, neither do those merchants sin against justice when they agree among themselves in that manner.

If, however, they were to induce others to sell in that way through fraud, force, or fear, they would sin against justice toward the buyers. This is no different than how someone sins against justice toward a recipient of a gift or legacy if they use force, fear, or fraud to prevent someone from giving or bequeathing something to that person. Indeed, this is done against the right that everyone has to receive from anyone whatever that person wishes to give them of their own accord; this right is unjustly harmed when the donor is barred from giving or bequeathing by force, fear, or fraud. From this, it is clear that if a Prince <note>term: *Princeps*; the sovereign or head of state</note> grants a privilege of monopoly without a reasonable cause, both he and the one who obtains the monopoly sin against justice, even if the price of the monopoly is set at a just level. This is because it is against justice to prohibit others from selling at that time, as it results in injury to the buyers who could buy from them at a cheaper price, and it results in injury to those who would have been sellers. Certainly, for whatever loss results from this, both to those who would have bought and those who would have sold, the Prince and those who obtained and used the privilege would be bound to make restitution. In the aforementioned events, restitution should be made to private individuals if it is clear who they are and how much damage they suffered. If not, something must be done that results, more or less equally, in the benefit of those same private individuals—such as by selling something in that community at a price lower by as much as is needed to compensate for the damage, or by doing something similar. If it cannot be satisfied in any of these ways, it should be restored to the poor or spent on other pious works for the souls of those to whom it was owed.

**5** Whether those who, at the time of harvest or vintage <note>the grape harvest</note>, or any other time when there is an abundance of certain things, buy such a great quantity of them with the intention of keeping them for a time when they will be sold more dearly—so that they are the cause of a high price <note>term: *carustiam*; a state of dearness or scarcity</note> being induced in the Commonwealth—are bound to restitution. This happens either because they prevent citizens from buying what they need for their family's sustenance at that time (and which they truly would have 

<column-break/>

bought if such storers had not anticipated them), thus forcing them to buy much more dearly later from their hands; or because by buying such a large quantity they are the cause of prices increasing at that time, making citizens buy more dearly. Whether, I ask, those who buy in this way sin mortally and are bound to make restitution for the damage brought upon the Commonwealth and the citizens by that means.

In the first place, the doctors <note>learned authorities/theologians</note> agree that such people sin mortally. This is the view of Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 23, number 91; Johannes Medina on *Restitution*, question 36; John Major on the *Sentences*; Gabriel Biel; Sylvester Prieras; Angelus de Clavasio; Domingo de Soto, and others. As far as restitution is concerned, those doctors who bring this into debate commonly assert that they are bound to make restitution for the damage to the Commonwealth and to private individuals thus inflicted. Restitution should be made in the same way explained just above for monopolists. This is the assertion of Major, Medina, Gabriel, Sylvester, and Angelus in the places cited.

What I think about this matter will be revealed by the following conclusions. **The first conclusion.** Men who buy things to store them until a time of scarcity, with the intention of selling them more dearly and making a profit, do not sin if they buy at the current just price and later sell at the current just price. <margin>Decision</margin> This is provided they do not prevent individuals in the Commonwealth from buying necessities at the time of abundance, and that the large quantity they buy does not increase the prices at that time. Rather, they are useful to the Commonwealth; all agree on this, as is manifest from what was said in Disputation 339.

**The second conclusion.** If they are harmful to the Commonwealth by inducing a high price for things, increasing their prices, and preventing citizens from buying necessities for themselves at a suitable time, they sin by buying in that way. They ought to be prohibited and punished by the Commonwealth as harmful people. Indeed, in a time of scarcity, they can even be forced as a penalty to sell more cheaply than they bought to the prejudice of the Commonwealth. On this conclusion, too, all agree.

And the same must be said of those called *regatones* <note>term: *regatones*; hucksters or retailers who buy goods to resell them immediately for a profit without adding value</note>, <margin>Portuguese Law</margin> if they are an obstacle to private individuals buying necessities from those who bring them. The prohibitions of Portugal against buying wheat, barley, flour, millet, rye (which the Spanish call *centeno*), and oil for the purpose of reselling them, and the penalties established for this, are found in the fourth book of the *Ordinances*, title 32, from the first paragraph, and more extensively in the fourth part of the *Extravagant Laws*, title 9. The prohibition of this Kingdom <note>referring to Castile/Spain</note> against similarly buying wheat, barley, oats, or rye, and the established penalties, are found in Law 19, title 11, book 5 of the *New Collection*.

**The third conclusion.** I do not see how men, by inducing a high price in the manner explained by buying, <margin>Castilian Law</margin> are bound to restore the damage caused to the Commonwealth. I am led to this because I do not see that they sin against **justice** toward the Commonwealth or its parts by inducing a high price for things as a side effect. Rather, they only sin against the love of neighbor. For they are using their own right within the limits of justice, buying things in a time of abundance with their own money at a just price; and the things they buy are not owed by justice to others in the Commonwealth so that they should be sold to them instead. Otherwise, those selling them to such hoarders and keepers...

# Sales are rendered illicit because things are sold more dearly to foreigners, and from perjury, lies, and an affection for profit.

## DISPUTATION CCCXLVI.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A sale is rendered illicit if things are sold more dearly to outsiders than to natives.*
2 *Understand this, however, and declare it as in number 2.*
3 *In what cases a sale is rendered illicit on the part of the contracting parties.*
4 *Buying and selling from an inordinate affection, when it is a lethal fault.*

1 A sale is also rendered illicit if things are sold more dearly to outsiders and travelers than to natives, as gathered from chapter 1 on buying and selling. This is understood by Conradus <note>Conrad Summenhart, a German theologian</note> on contracts, question 51 at the end, Johannes Medina on restitution question 30 article 4, and others, when the limits of the **just price** are exceeded.
2 Observe that if many outsiders arrive at some place, especially wealthy ones eager to buy, then, with such buyers multiplied, the prices of things increase. It is not wrong to sell to them more dearly than was previously sold to natives, or than it is sold in that place after those same outsiders have departed. Nor is there any harm if then, when goods in that place are sufficient for both outsiders and natives, they are sold more dearly to foreigners eager to buy than to natives who do not wish to give anything but the customary price. Examples include if the King, in transit with his people, arrives at some place intending to depart the next day or after a few days. Likewise, when the Spanish fleet <note>original: "classis Hispanica"</note> from the New World <note>the Americas</note> reaches the islands called the Terceiras <note>the Azores</note>, the price of all things they wish to buy suddenly increases greatly, both for consumption there and on the journey, and also to carry away to Seville <note>original: "Hispalim"</note> and other parts. Meanwhile, prices in comparison to the natives remain as they were before, because the goods of the place are sufficient for everyone, and the natives do not wish to give anything but the customary price. This has been accepted by custom, and I do not dare to condemn it; for that thing, in comparison to the many buyers who arrive very wealthy from the New World and are most eager to buy, is worth more than in comparison to the natives.
But if things were not sufficient even for the natives, surely

<column-break/>

the price would increase in comparison to everyone, nor would sellers neglect to rejoice with the newcomers so that they might sell to the natives more cheaply.
3 Buying and selling is rendered illicit by perjury, lies, and other similar crimes which arise from the wickedness of the buying and selling, but not from the buying and selling itself, as is well enough established. Regarding lies, and even perjury, I would only warn that if they are done with the intention of deceiving the buyer so that he buys beyond the **just price**, they are **lethal sins** <note>mortal sins</note> of injustice, if the excess beyond the just price is so great that it suffices for a lethal fault. For whatever is ordered toward a lethal end is a lethal sin, even if it is not numerically distinct from the end itself, but forms one sin numerically with it when there is no sufficient interruption for a numerical distinction of sins in the category of death. Therefore, that lie is in itself a **venial fault** <note>a minor sin</note> in the category of lying, and perjury is lethal; yet both are lethal faults of injustice from their relation to the lethal end of taking a notable amount from one's neighbor beyond the just price: it is then numerically the same as the intention of the end itself.
4 Buying and selling from an inordinate affection for profit is a lethal fault when someone, for the sake of profit, transgresses some precept binding under lethal fault, or is equally prepared to transgress it. Nor are there two species-distinct lethal sins—the appetite for profit and the transgression of such a precept, or the will to transgress it—because an inordinate appetite for profit is in itself only a venial fault. Thus, it is enough to confess the transgression of the precept, or the will to transgress it, and it is not necessary to confess the inordinate appetite for profit from which the transgression took its origin.

It then introduces Disputation 348 regarding how these prices are determined for both common and newly imported goods.</meta>

...placed by law. It consists of an **indivisible point** <note>original: "consistit verò in indiuisibili"; meaning it is a single fixed value rather than a range</note>, such that if anything more is accepted for the item, the sale becomes unjust and the excess is subject to restitution—provided, however, that the law which established it is just and equitable. All of this will become clearer in the following sections.

<margin>2</margin> There is another kind of price which the thing itself possesses, set apart from any human law or public decree. This is called the **natural price** by Aristotle in the place cited, and by others. This is not because it does not depend heavily on human estimation (by which people choose to value a thing more or less, such as a gemstone sometimes being valued at more than twenty thousand gold pieces, even though many other things are by their nature more excellent and useful for human needs). Nor is it called "natural" because such a price is not highly inconsistent and variable, as will be seen. Rather, it is called natural because it arises from the things themselves, set apart from any human law or decree, though it still depends on many circumstances by which it varies, as well as on human affection and estimation, the comparison of various uses, and sometimes solely on human pleasure and whim.

Therefore, because this kind of price does not arise purely from the natures of things, but depends on the circumstances by which it varies—and what is more, on human affection and the estimation of things according to their own pleasure—it follows that it does not consist of an **indivisible point**. Instead, it has a certain **latitude** <note>original: "latitudinem"; a range or span of acceptable prices</note> of what is just and measured for the merchandise, considering all the circumstances that actually concur here and now in human commerce. You should not understand this to happen solely because human judgment is uncertain in itself and varies among different men (as if the price actually consisted of an indivisible point by the nature of the thing, but human judgment simply failed to reach it). Rather, it is also because the estimations of things and the affections toward them—upon which the variation of price depends—are themselves varied.

<margin>3</margin> At the very least, it must be established that a certain latitude of just price is given by the nature of the thing, within which justice is not violated. Perhaps within that latitude there is one indivisible point in which justice is most perfectly preserved regarding the object, or the price in comparison to the goods.

From this, it is easily established that the Doctors <note>Academic and theological authorities</note> rightly distinguish a **threefold just price** for things: namely, the **highest** (or rigorous), the **medium** (or moderate), and the **lowest** (or pious). This distinction only takes place in the natural price, not in the legal price. Furthermore, the latitude of the natural just price is sometimes larger and sometimes smaller. For the more precious a thing is, or the higher its estimation, the larger the latitude in the just price typically is.

For example, if the **medium price** of some item is one hundred, the **rigorous price** would be, for instance, one hundred and five, while the **pious price** would be ninety-five. Thus, the total latitude of the just price in that event is ten. Sometimes it will be much larger, and sometimes smaller, according to the quality of the things sold and the common usage surrounding them. But if the medium price of a thing is ten, the rigorous will be eleven, or eleven and a half, and the pious nine, or eight and a half—sometimes more or less, depending on the quality of the goods and their common estimation. It follows that those three prices which are

<column-break/>

within the latitude of the just also have their own ranges. For that which is only a little distance from the middle of the latitude—whether toward the rigorous price or toward the pious price—is compared with the middle and called the **medium** or **moderate price**; the remaining parts constitute the latitudes of the extremes.

Now, as long as the total latitude of the just price is not exceeded, **commutative justice** <note>The justice governing private exchanges between individuals</note> is not violated. Therefore, the Doctors conclude that without a violation of commutative justice, someone can sell the exact same thing to one person at a different price than to another at the same time. Thus, without the vice of **usury**, a merchant can sell on credit <note>original: "vendetotarius creditum"; likely a typo for "vendere operarius" or "vendere ad creditum"</note> for more than for cash, provided he sells to one at the rigorous price and to the other at the medium or lowest price—a point we have often made regarding the matter of usury. This is affirmed by Cajetan, Johannes Medina on restitution, Soto, Covarruvias, and the Doctors generally.

<margin>4</margin> By the nature of things, the **legal price** comes after the natural price and, in a certain way, presupposes it. Indeed, human law—by the power of the Prince or Ruler to establish what they judge to be expedient for the Commonwealth and to compel the citizens to it—determines a fixed price within the range of the natural just price. This is done so that sellers do not exceed it, thus looking out for the good of the Commonwealth and avoiding other evils. Since, therefore, the legal price presupposes the natural and comes after it, we will first clear up those matters regarding the natural price, and afterward we will speak of the legal price.

## From where the natural price is to be judged just or unjust.

## DISPUTATION CCCXLVIII.

### SUMMARY.

1 *The natural price is twofold.*
2 *The just price depends not on the nature of things, but on human use and estimation.*
3 *Many circumstances increase and decrease the price (continued in the following numbers).*
4 *The just price varies according to the mode of selling.*
5 *The just price should not vary because of the poverty of the buyer or the seller.*
6 *From what factors the just price increases.*
7 *By what things the prices of items are to be measured.*

The natural price is further divided into two types. One is for a thing commonly sold in a province, but whose just price varies as circumstances change, such as the price of wheat, cloth, wine, shoes, and similar things. The other is for a thing newly brought into a province where it was not customarily sold. Such was the price at which that wood with which things are dyed <note>Brazilwood, used for red dye</note> first began to be sold when it was first brought from the region of **Brazil** to **Spain**. Such also is the price at which many things brought from **India** <note>Referring to the East Indies/Asia</note> began to be sold in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, which were not previously accustomed to being sold in Portugal. We will first attempt to treat the source for judging whether that first kind of price is just or unjust; then we shall speak of the second kind of price.

<summary>Molina defines the "natural price" as a range (latitude) based on human estimation and circumstances, rather than a fixed point. He categorizes this range into rigorous, moderate, and pious prices and distinguishes between prices for common goods and newly imported colonial goods like Brazilwood.</summary>
<keywords>just price, natural price, legal price, market latitude, commutative justice, rigorous price, pious price, Brazilwood, imports, economic ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "natural price," specifically how it is determined not by the essential nature of things, but by their utility to humans and common social estimation. It transitions from the definition of price types to the practical circumstances—such as scarcity, demand, and the manner of sale—that cause prices to fluctuate justly.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 3

**2** First, it must be observed that the **just price** is not to be judged based on the "nature" of things in themselves—that is, according to their biological nobility or perfection—but rather according to how they serve human needs. For it is in this way that they are valued by men and possess a price in human commerce and exchange. Indeed, God granted these things to humans for this purpose: that men might hold private ownership over those things which serve their needs, even though at the first creation all things were common to all.

From this it follows that although mice are more "noble" according to their living nature than grain is, they have no price among men because they are useless for human needs. <note>The author uses a classic scholastic argument: a living mouse is biologically "higher" than a dead seed of grain, yet the grain is more valuable because it sustains human life.</note> From this it also follows that a house is usually justly sold for a higher price than a horse, or even a <term>mancipium</term> <note>original: "mancipium"; referring to an enslaved person. In the legal and economic framework of the time, human beings were tragically categorized alongside livestock in discussions of property and price.</note>, even though a horse and a human are of a far more excellent nature than a building.

Next, it must be observed that the just price of things is not considered solely based on the things themselves as they serve human use—as if the quantity of the price were taken absolutely from the necessity of the use the thing serves (all other things being equal). Rather, the quantity of the price depends largely on the **estimation** <note>original: "aestimatione"; the subjective or social value placed on an item.</note> by which men choose to value something more or less for its use.

And this is why the just price of a single gemstone, used only for ornament, may be greater than the just price of a vast quantity of grain, wine, meat, bread, and horses—even though the use of these latter things is more useful and better for the nature of the thing than the use of a gemstone. Therefore, that quantity of the just price for a gemstone depends on the fact that men have chosen to value it so for that specific use.

This is also why the just price of a hawk for fowling <note>hunting birds</note> is higher among the nobility (who have chosen to value hawks highly for the pleasure of their souls) than the price of other things that are far more useful. Furthermore, this is why among the **Japanese**, certain iron and earthenware items, corroded by age and of no value among us, are of immense price because of their antiquity. It is clear that the just price among them does not arise from the nature of the objects, nor from their convenience for use, but from the fact that they have chosen to be so affected toward them and to value them so much.

Finally, this is why trinkets and cheap items from among us, when they are carried to the **Ethiopians**, are of far greater price among them than the gold they exchange for them; whereas, on the contrary, gold is of far greater price among us. In all these cases and many others like them, it is only the estimation by which men in various places have chosen to value this or 그 (that). Exchanges made in those regions according to the common estimation of things there are not to be condemned—even if some may seem laughable due to the lack of sophistication <note>original: "ingenii ruditatem"</note> or the customs of the people where they occur (a subject we discussed at length when speaking of enslaved people).

Thus, the just price of things depends greatly on the **common estimation** of men in each region. Therefore, when a thing is commonly accustomed to be sold at a certain price in some region or place—without fraud, monopolies, or other deceits—that price must be held as the measure and rule for judging the just price of that thing in that region, as long as the circumstances do not change which would cause the price to rightly increase or decrease. This is consistent with the law <term>pretia rerum</term> <note>A reference to the Roman Digest (ad legem Falcidiam), stating that prices are not based on individual utility but common value.</note> and the common consensus of the learned doctors.

**3** Third, it must be observed that there are many circumstances that increase or decrease the prices of things. A **scarcity** of goods due to a poor harvest or similar causes makes the just price increase; **abundance**, however, makes it decrease. A multitude of buyers gathering at one time more than another, and with greater eagerness, makes the price increase; a rarity of buyers makes it decrease.

Likewise, a greater need among many people for certain things for some use at one time more than another (given the same quantity of goods) makes the price increase; for example, horses are worth more when war is imminent than in a time of peace. Similarly, a **lack of money** in a certain place makes the price of other things decrease, and an abundance of money makes it increase. For the smaller the supply of money in a place, the more its value increases, and therefore more things are bought with a certain amount of money, all else being equal. For example, if the fruits of the earth are equal in proportion in two provinces, and one has a greater supply of money than the other, those fruits will be sold for a lower price in the province with less money, and laborers will be hired for a lower price than in the other.

**4** Fourth, it must be observed that the **manner of selling** things also varies their just price. For instance, if something is sold "under the spear" <note>original: "sub hasta"; an ancient term for a public auction.</note>, or through brokers, heralds, or women who have the task of selling another's property; or if a student sells his books, or a person leaving a place sells the furniture he had bought for his own use—all these things are usually sold much more cheaply than they are sold by merchants. If they are sold at the price accustomed for that manner of selling, the price is not to be judged unjust.

The reason is partly because things sold in that manner are customarily valued that way, as common usage testifies; and also because, when they are sold in that way, there is considered to be a lack of buyers compared to when they are in the hands of merchants, who wait for buyers and have their money tied up in those goods in order to make a profit. For this reason, it is commonly said that **fragile or slow-moving goods** <note>original: "vitroneas merces"; literally "glass-like goods," referring to items that lose value if they do not find a buyer quickly.</note> for which a buyer must be sought, lose a third of their price. Thus, in these and similar events, as long as the accustomed price for that mode of buying and selling is followed, the price should not be judged unjust, even if it differs from the price at which merchants sell or the price at which it would be bought at another time. This is correctly taught by **Cajetan**, **Medina**, **Soto**, **Navarrus**, **Covarrubias**, and others.

**5** Note, however, that the manner of selling based on a particular buyer's need for the item—when that need is not shared by others—or based on the fact that the buyer hopes for a great profit from it, does **not** increase the common price of that thing. Likewise, the fact that a seller does not need the item he is selling does not decrease the price. Otherwise, it would be lawful to sell more dearly to a poor man than to a rich man, or to one in extreme necessity than to one who is not.

<summary>This page explains that the "just price" of a good is determined by social utility and common estimation rather than biological complexity. It outlines how factors like scarcity, money supply, and the specific context of a sale (such as an auction) legitimately influence market value.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the determination of the "just price" in commerce. The previous page established that value is based on human utility rather than the biological "nobility" of an object. Here, Molina addresses whether a seller can charge more based on the buyer's specific needs or the seller's own losses.</meta>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...necessity. Regarding the point that a higher price cannot be accepted simply because of the buyer’s convenience or potential profit, it is proved thus: that convenience does not belong to the seller, but to the buyer. Therefore, the seller cannot charge a price for it; otherwise, he would be selling what is not his own. This is the view of **Saint Thomas** <note>original: "Diuus Thom. 2. 2. q. 77. ar. 1."; referring to Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologica, where he discusses the ethics of buying and selling.</note> and the doctors of the church commonly agree with him. We can confirm this by noting that otherwise, a lender—if the borrower expected a great profit from a loan—could sell that profit to the borrower and thus receive something beyond the principal. Everyone denies this, and in the section on **usury** <note>Interest charged on a loan, which was heavily regulated and often forbidden by Church law during this period.</note>, it was shown to be usurious.

However, if the seller were to suffer a loss from the sale of a thing—either through **lost profit** <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>A legal concept where one is compensated for the profit they would have made if they had not entered the current contract.</note> or **emergent damage** <term>damnum emergens</term> <note>Direct loss or expenses incurred by the seller because of the transaction.</note>, or because that item was very useful to him for building or something else, or if he were deeply attached to it and felt pain in selling it—then he could sell that loss. Indeed, he could even charge for the loss of pleasure he takes in possessing it, accepting something beyond the common price based on how these things would be valued by a **prudent judgment** <note>The "prudent man" (vir prudens) was a standard legal fiction used to determine what a reasonable, moral person would decide in a given situation.</note>. The reason is that all these things belong to the seller himself, and he is not required to suffer a heavy loss or the destruction of his own interests; therefore, he can sell those interests to the buyer along with the thing he sells. This is rightly affirmed by Saint Thomas, **Scotus**, **Navarrus**, and the doctors generally. Observe, however, that for a price to be justly accepted for these things, it must be included in the agreement so that the buyer buys them knowingly and deliberately. For perhaps the buyer would not want to pay a price for those personal factors, but only for the item he needs, as **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto, a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian and contemporary of Molina.</note> rightly affirms.

<margin>6</margin>
The transport of merchandise from a place where it is in great abundance to a place where there is a scarcity is a reason for its just price to increase. Similarly, the improvement of a thing—whether through human industry or by nature (such as if an animal has grown to its proper age while in the hands of the buyer)—makes its price increase. Likewise, selling things in small quantities or parts, in the way that those we call "retailers" are accustomed to sell, causes their price to increase; for things are generally sold more cheaply when a large multitude of them are sold together than when the same things are sold piece by piece. These and others are the circumstances by which the common price of things varies. On these matters, read among others **Conrad** and **Johannes Medina**. How much the price ought to increase or decrease when a circumstance changes must be judged by a prudent person’s estimation.

From what has been said so far, it is clearly evident that the rule of **Scotus** is false. He and **Major** claim that the just price of goods in a merchant's hand is this: they must calculate all expenses they incurred in buying, transporting, or preserving such things, and in addition, a just wage for the industry, labors applied, and risks to which they exposed themselves—no differently than if they had been hired for a wage to store those things for the Commonwealth. They argue that if they sell the goods at a price corresponding more or less to all these factors, it will be a just price; but if it notably exceeds this, it will be unjust. From this they infer that if a merchant's ship is accidentally sunk or

<column-break/>

captured by enemies while carrying merchandise, or if a house where he stored goods is burned down, he can compensate for this by selling his other merchandise at a higher price to the Commonwealth.

This rule, with its corollary, is clearly false based on what has been said, and it is commonly rejected by the doctors, including **Soto**, **Medina**, **Covarruvias**, and **Conrad**. Indeed, the prices of things are not to be measured by the profit or loss of merchants, but by the **common estimation** <note>The market value determined by the community, rather than the personal costs of the individual seller.</note> in the place where they are sold, taking into account all present circumstances. This holds true whether the merchants earn little (due to bad luck or lack of skill) or even suffer a loss, or whether they earn a great deal through good fortune or diligent effort. For goods perish, lose value, or increase in price for their owners, not for the Commonwealth to which they are carried or for which they are preserved.

When something is newly imported into a province, its just price must be established by prudent judgment, considering the quality, utility, and the abundance or scarcity of the item, as well as the expenses, risks, and difficulties in bringing it there. Even the novelty of an item makes it more precious. Once these and other circumstances are weighed, the just price of that thing must be established either by the governors of the Commonwealth or by the buyers and sellers themselves. A price is not to be condemned as unjust simply because the profit is high, provided the thing is considered precious due to its rarity and novelty and has many buyers. No other fixed rule can be established regarding this matter.

# On Buying and Selling Below or Above Half the Just Price.

## DISPUTATION 349.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *One who sells for more than half the just price, or buys for less than half, sins and is bound to make restitution, even in the civil courts.*
2 *How buying for less than half the just price or selling for more than half is to be considered.*
3 *The time at which the just price of a sold thing must be considered.*
4 *A legal action is granted to the seller against the first buyer, but not against a third-party possessor. There are, however, exceptions.*
5 *To what a seller of a thing for more than half the just price is bound, even in the court of conscience.*
6 *If a sold thing perishes by chance, no legal action is available to either the buyer or the seller.*
7 *If a sale is rescinded by legal remedy, whether a tax is owed. And what is observed in **Portugal**.*
9 *If the seller has been harmed and the buyer chooses to return the item and take back the price, what must be done.*
10 *When a purchased thing must be returned due to excessive loss, whether it must be returned with the fruits gathered from it. And whether the same applies in a public auction.*

<summary>Molina argues that the "just price" is determined by the common market value rather than a merchant's personal expenses or losses, refuting the idea that merchants can hike prices to recover from disasters like shipwrecks. He also introduces the legal and moral implications of "enormous loss," where a price deviates by more than half its true value.</summary>
