<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral and legal ethics of contracts, moving from how a "just price" is determined to the legal consequences of departing from it by more than half its value—a concept known in legal history as "enormous loss" or *laesio enormis*.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 349

<margin>3. Whether the same should be said for leases, exchanges, currency exchanges, and other good-faith contracts (no. 12). And what of the law of Castile? (ibid.)</margin>
<margin>13. Whether the action arising from Law 2 of the Code on Rescinding Sales is valid, even with an oath (no. 15). And what of the law of Portugal and Castile?</margin>

To consequently examine whether something can be sold for a higher price or bought for a lower price than it is worth, we must begin with the proposed disputation, in which the external court <note>The "external court" refers to civil or ecclesiastical law courts, as opposed to the "internal court" of conscience or the confessional.</note> agrees with the internal court of conscience.

<margin>1</margin> The doctors of law agree that if someone sells for more than half the just price, or buys for less than half the just price, they commit a sin. They are held to make satisfaction not only in conscience but also in the external court. Indeed, if no fraud was involved in the contract—even if someone knowingly and prudently bought something for less than half the just price, or knowingly sold it for more than half—the injured party is granted an action in the external court to compel one of two things, at the choice of the one who caused the injury: either to bring the price to its just level, or to rescind the contract. 

Thus, when someone buys for less than half the just price, they are compelled either to increase the price up to the just level or to rescind the contract by returning the goods and receiving back the price paid. Conversely, when someone has sold for more than half the just price, they are compelled either to restore the excess over the just price or to return the full price and take back the goods, as they prefer. This is established in Law 2 of the Code on Rescinding Sales <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescin. vend."; referring to the Codex of Justinian, a cornerstone of Roman Law.</note>, the chapters "with beloved" and "with cause" regarding buying and selling, Law 56 of Title 5 of the Fifth Partida <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the foundational statutory code of Castile (Spain).</note>, and the Fourth Law of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 30. That this action is granted even when the buyer and seller were fully aware of the item's true value is proven by Arias Pinellus and followed by Covarruvias, who retracted an earlier contrary opinion. That this same obligation exists in the court of conscience will be made manifest in the following disputation. I specified "if fraud was not involved" because if fraud on the part of the injuring party occurred, they would not have such liberty regarding the method of satisfaction, as will become clear in Disputation 352.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding buying for less than half the just price, the doctors agree that if a thing is worth ten in just price, and it is bought for four or four and a half, the purchase is "below half" because it is less than five, which is half of ten. However, regarding selling for more than half the just price, some argued that this only occurs when something is sold for more than double; for instance, if a thing is worth ten at a strict just price, they argued it is not a sale "above half" unless it sells for more than twenty. 

Nevertheless, the contrary opinion is common and should be embraced: it is sufficient if it is sold for more than half *above* the just price. In the given example, this would be more than fifteen—say, fifteen and a half or any higher price. This is affirmed by the glosses on Law 2 of the Code and the chapter "with cause," which Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> approves, even if some earlier texts leaned toward the contrary view. This same opinion is embraced by Soto, Antonio Gomez, Covarruvias, Gutierrez, and many others. It is today the defined law in this Kingdom of Castile (Law 56 cited above, and Law 1, Title 11, Law 5 of the New Collection) and in Portugal. This opinion is further strengthened because, as the gloss rightly says, according to the contrary view, the sale would not be "above half" the just price, but "above double."

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, the just price of a sold item must be considered at the time the contract was celebrated, not before or after. This is proven by the law "if by will" at the end of the Code on Rescinding Sales and the other cited laws. Because the just price does not consist of a single indivisible point <note>Molina refers to the legal concept that the "just price" is a range (lowest, middle, highest) rather than a single fixed number.</note>, it follows that to prove something was bought for less than half the just price, it is not enough for witnesses to state that the just price at the time was "X." Instead, it is necessary to testify that the price paid was less than half of the *lowest* just price of the item at that time. A buyer is not bound to buy at the strict or middle price; it is enough if they buy at the lowest just price. Similarly, to prove a sale was "above half," witnesses must affirm that the price received exceeded the range of half above the *highest* strict price of the item at the time. Read Covarruvias on this.

<margin>4</margin> If a thing is bought for less than half the just price and the buyer has alienated it (sold or given it away) under any title, the seller is granted an action against the first buyer. If the buyer cannot restore the item—either because they cannot or will not recover it—they must at least increase the price to the just range. However, an action is not typically granted against a third-party possessor <note>The person who now owns the item after the first buyer sold it.</note>. This is the argument of the gloss on Law 2 and is agreed upon by Antonio Gomez and the Portuguese Ordinances. 

I believe the same holds true when a buyer has voluntarily consumed or destroyed the item. As the cited gloss rightly notes, it was the buyer's own doing that the item is no longer in their possession to be returned to rescind the contract; therefore, they are bound to increase the price to the just level. However, if the primary buyer cannot pay, Covarruvias and many others affirm that an action is granted against a third-party possessor if that third party acquired the item through a "lucrative title" <term>lucrativo titulo</term> <note>Meaning they received it as a gift or inheritance rather than paying for it.</note>. In such a case, they must either restore the item or increase the price to the just range. Or, if they consumed or sold it in good faith, unaware the original seller was defrauded, they must return as much as they were enriched by it. An action is also granted against a third possessor if they also bought it for less than half the just price, or if they acquired it (whether by gift or purchase) knowing that it had originally been bought for less than half the just price. This is consistent with what was said in Disputation 328 regarding assets alienated to defraud creditors.

<summary>This page discusses the legal and moral rules regarding "enormous loss" (laesio enormis), which allows a contract to be rescinded if the price is more than 50% above or below the fair market value. It outlines the rights of the injured party to either adjust the price or cancel the sale, and discusses how this applies if the goods have been passed on to a third party.</summary>
<keywords>just price, enormous loss, rescission of contract, laesio enormis, buyer's rights, seller's rights, Castilian law, Portuguese law, third-party possessor, court of conscience</keywords>

--- Page 302 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of contracts where a party has been "injured" by a price that is more than 50% above or below the fair market value (the "just price"). This legal principle, often called *laesio enormis*, allows for the rescinding of a contract or a price adjustment. Here, Molina addresses what happens when the physical object no longer exists or when taxes have already been paid on the transaction.</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts

<margin>5</margin> When a thing has been sold for **more than half the just price**, if the buyer has since transferred it to another person so that he can no longer retrieve it, or if he has consumed it, he is not granted an action against the seller in the **external court** <note>The civil or public legal system.</note>. The reason is that the seller is only bound to either rescind the contract or restore the excess price, whichever he prefers. However, the contract cannot be rescinded because the buyer is unable to return the item purchased. This is the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Antonio Gomez (number 22 as cited) and Gutierrez (book 2 of *Practicae Quaestiones*, question 137) report and follow. This view is supported by Law 56, title 5, part 5. Nevertheless, Covarruvias (book 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 4, at the end of number 14) and Aries Pinel (on Law 2 of the Code *On Rescinding Sales*, part 2, chapter 1, number 59) hold the opposite view. However, in the **court of conscience** <note>The internal moral judgment or the confessional.</note>, the seller is still bound to restore the excess price, at least down to the highest or "rigorous" just price.

<margin>6</margin> If the item has perished by **accidental misfortune**, or has been notably worsened—whether it was bought for less than half the just price or sold for more than half—no action is granted to the defrauded buyer or seller. The reason is the same: the thing perished through no fault of the opponent, and because it has perished, the contract cannot be rescinded (a choice the opponent is entitled to make). This is the gloss on Law 2 of the Code *On Rescinding Sales* and the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Gomez, Covarruvias, Pinel, and Gutierrez as cited above; it is also defined in Law 56 of this Kingdom <note>Referring to the laws of Castile.</note>. Therefore, we should not worry that Panormitanus (on the chapter *Eum dilecti* regarding buying and selling, last number) asserted the contrary and claimed it was the common view of the interpreters of Canon Law. 

Covarruvias, in the place cited, says that if a buyer who had bought a thing for less than half its just price then sold it at a just price, and the thing subsequently perished, an action is granted against that first buyer to restore the increase in price up to the lowest just price (or as much as he was made wealthier by it). His reasoning is that the thing "remains" with the first buyer in the form of the price he received for it. Therefore, since he has the excess he received, he is compelled to complete the just price. We find this opinion pleasing, and it is shared by others whom Covarruvias cites. Furthermore, he adds that an action should be given against one who sold a thing for more than half its just price, even if the thing sold has since perished, because the excess of the unjust price remains with him. The laws seem to speak clearly to the contrary (especially Law 56), as does the common opinion of the doctors; therefore, in the external court, an action will not be granted. In the court of conscience, however, both he and the one who defrauded by buying for less than half the just price will be bound to restore the excess, regardless of the fact that the item has perished.

<margin>7</margin> There is a doubt as to whether, if a sale is **rescinded** by the remedy of Law 2 of the Code *On Rescinding Sales*, a **gabella** <note>A sales tax or excise duty.</note> is owed, and who ought to pay it. Indeed, everyone agrees that it is owed, because the sale was not conditional but absolute; nor was it void by law, but valid, and only later rescinded by the personal 

<column-break/>

action of the injured party. Therefore, since the right to the tax was established for the treasury at the moment of sale, a later rescission in favor of the injured party cannot take away that pre-existing right. This is the view of Aries Pinel (part 2, chapter 3, number 35) and Lassarte (on *Decima Venditionis*, chapter 14, number 13).

Regarding who must pay and how much, putting aside other opinions reported by Lassarte, I believe we should say: if the seller was the injured party and the buyer chooses to bring the contract to equity <note>To balance the contract by paying the fair value.</note> by paying the amount missing to reach the lowest just price, then because the price of the sale increases, the tax to be paid to the treasury also increases. And because this is not a "new" sale but an adjustment to equity, the increase in tax is owed to the lord and the tax-collector who were in place at the time of the *first* sale, not to those in place when the price is adjusted. Furthermore, because the buyer's only "fault" was defrauding a portion of the just price (which he has now restored), in this Kingdom <note>Castile</note>, the seller pays the whole tax according to the local laws. However, in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, just as the buyer had paid half the tax and the seller the other half, each will pay half of the tax increase.

<margin>8</margin> But if the buyer was the injured party because he bought the thing for more than half the just price, and the seller wishes to adjust the contract to equity by restoring the excess above the highest rigorous just price, Lassarte says (at number 17) that the treasury ought to keep the **entire tax** based on the unjust price set in the first contract. He cites Law 1, title 17, and Law 9 of the *New Collection*, which state that a tenth of the *entire price* for which a thing was sold must be paid, because that first sale was perfected and the treasury thereby acquired the right to the whole amount. 

However, I believe this is false. We should not cling so tightly to the words of the law when they would dictate something harsh and dissonant with **right reason**—especially when a more suitable interpretation exists. Lassarte himself confesses that the law, as he understands it, contains something "hard." Therefore, since the law does not explicitly say that the tax must be paid on the whole amount even if the price is declared unjust by a judge's sentence, it is not likely that the legislators intended this. They likely intended it to apply only to prices not proven to be unjust. Otherwise, they would have created a truly harsh and iniquitous law, which we should not presume. We must say, through **epicheia** <note>A principle of legal interpretation where one follows the spirit/intent of the law rather than the strict literal wording to ensure justice.</note>, that the law is not to be understood as applying to a price declared unjust by a judge. Consequently, the tax paid on that portion unjustly taken above the rigorous price should be restored (if the tax-collector had already received it). This applies not only when the contract is adjusted to equity but also when the contract is dissolved, the seller restores the full price, and takes back the item. I hear that this is indeed the practice in Portugal.

<margin>9</margin> If the seller was injured and the buyer chooses to return the item and receive back his money, a distinction must be made. Either he knew the item was worth more and let it go...

### Second Treatise | Disputation 349

...at such a meager price, or if he purchased it while being ignorant of the true value. In this latter event, since he was not at fault—neither in the purchase nor in later rescinding the contract according to the law's prescription—and because in this kingdom <note>Referring to Castile/Spain.</note> the seller is liable for the loss of the sales tax <term>gabella: a state tax on the sale of goods</term> which he paid; whereas in Portugal, since the buyer pays half and the seller pays half, each of them shall bear the loss of the portion they paid. In the first case, however, because the buyer was at fault by purchasing at such a vile price and by personally defrauding his brother <note>A common legal metaphor for a fellow citizen or party to a contract.</note>, he shall pay the seller the tax that the seller had paid, in addition to the price. This is based on the argument in the law *Debet* in the Digest <note>The *Pandects* or Digest of Roman Law</note> under the section on the Edicts of the Aediles; it states that when a contract is rescinded because a seller, knowing a thing was defective, sold it anyway, he is held to restore more than just the price to the buyer—he must also return the tax the buyer paid because of that purchase. The same reasoning applies to the matter we are discussing here.

<margin>Question</margin>
If, however, the buyer was the one harmed <note>Meaning he paid significantly more than the fair price.</note>, and the seller chooses to restore the price and take back the item, and if the seller knew the item was worth less when he sold it, the seller alone shall bear the loss of the sales tax for the reasons just mentioned. But if he sold it in ignorance of the value, then in the Kingdom of Castile he alone shall bear the loss of the entire tax, because according to the laws of that kingdom, he alone paid it; furthermore, he chose to rescind the contract, and the buyer was not at fault. In Portugal, however, each shall bear the loss of the part they paid: the seller for the reasons just stated regarding Castilian law, and the buyer because the seller was in no way at fault toward him such that the seller should be held to pay the buyer's portion of the tax.

<margin>10</margin>
Furthermore, when a thing must be restored because the price was either below or above half of the just price, should the buyer return it along with the fruits <note>fructibus: profits, crops, or rents produced by the property.</note> gathered from it? Antonio Gomez (volume 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 2, number 24), Gutierrez (book 2 of *Practicae Quaestiones*, question 14), and many others—whom Gutierrez and Covarruvias (book 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 3, number 9) also cite—answer in the negative. Covarruvias admits in the cited passage that this opinion is the one accepted in legal practice. The reason is that the buyer acquired ownership of the thing so purchased, and that ownership persists as long as the rescission of the contract is pending. Therefore, in the meantime, while the contract is not yet rescinded, he makes the fruits his own.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Moreover, because the seller was in possession of the price during that entire time, and is not today held to restore that price with interest (as Covarruvias himself admits), equity in compensation demands that the buyer retain the fruits gathered from the thing so purchased for himself. However, Covarruvias, along with certain others and Gregorio Lopez (at the cited Law 56, on the words "to abandon the thing"), inclines toward the view that the fruits ought also to be restored. To me, however, the opinion of Antonio Gomez and Gutierrez is more proven, especially when the item was sold for more than half the just price and the contract is to be rescinded by the seller's choice. Beyond the reasons already proposed, equity surely does not allow a buyer to have possessed such an excessive price for all that time without being held to return the interest on it, while the seller nonetheless receives the item back with all the fruits gathered from it, or has their value deducted from the price. I also find the same opinion very probable when the item was bought for less than half the just price and the contract is to be rescinded at the buyer's choice—at least that he should not be held to restore all fruits, but at most a proportional share, according to

<column-break/>

the amount of the price deficiency relative to the range of the just price. For equity demands no more, nor does human law decree anything to the contrary. This same sentiment is confirmed by the fact that it is accepted in practice, as Covarruvias admits, and because interest on the price is not today required to be restored in compensation. Furthermore, in cases of doubt, the condition of the one currently possessing the fruits is better. This pleases me more than the idea that the buyer should be restored the "interest of the price" or the lost profit from it, as Gutierrez argues in question 135. However, whether expenses made by the buyer for improvements on the purchased item must be paid to him if the contract is rescinded, and whether the fruits he gathered should be deducted from those expenses, will be discussed more conveniently in Disputation 463.

<margin>11 | Portuguese Law</margin>
Even if a thing was sold in a public auction <term>subhastatio: a judicial sale or public auction</term> for less than half the just price, what has been said so far still applies. So Antonio Gomez (number 8) and the doctors commonly agree regarding the law *Si quos* in the Code *On Rescinding a Sale*. It is also defined in this Kingdom <note>Spain/Castile</note> in Law 13, Title 1, and Law 5 of the New Collection, and in Portuguese Law, Book 3, the final Title. There it is added that if, by order of a judge, a thing has been announced at auction for the entire time established by the ordinances, and by the judge's mandate the price found for it is signaled to the owner of the thing so he may see if he wishes to pay the debt—if, after waiting eight more days, the owner does not pay the debt and the thing is sold, no action is granted afterward to either the owner or the buyer on the grounds that the thing was bought or sold for less or more than half the just price. Remember, however, that the just price of a thing sold in a public auction is to be estimated by the agreement explained in the preceding disputation.

<margin>12</margin>
The aforementioned rules apply not only to buying and selling, but also to leases, exchanges, currency trades, and all other "good faith" contracts. This is proven by the law *Maioribus* in the Code, and the common opinion affirms it, as cited by Antonio Gomez (number 22) and Aries Pinel (on the law *On Rescinding a Sale*, part 1, chapter 3, number 17). It is defined in this Kingdom in Law 1, Title 1, Book 5 of the New Collection, and in Portuguese Law at Title 30, paragraph 2. From this doctrine in this Kingdom <note>Castile</note>, leases and rentals of the King’s revenues are excepted. In these contracts, it is decreed that neither on the part of the King’s ministers who lease them out, nor on the part of those who rent them, shall the remedy of the law *On Rescinding a Sale* have any place. This is found in Laws 14 and 15, Title 9, Book 9 of the New Collection. Also excepted is when a craftsman leases himself <note>Contracts his services</note> to build or finish something for a certain price; he is not heard afterward even if he says he was deceived by less than half the just price. This is held in Law 3, Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection. There is doubt, however, whether this remedy applies once the lease time has passed and the fruits are no longer in the hands of the tenant. Alvaro Valasco (*On Emphyteutic Law*, question 28), along with others, denies it; for, he says, there is no longer a place for the defendant to choose the rescission of the contract, and the option is given to him to either choose that or bring the contract to equality. He says he has seen this judged more than once, although they add that it is commonly judged to the contrary.

All of this is contained in book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 30, the penultimate paragraph.

<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>
As far as the law of Castile is concerned, this matter is not so clear. However, Law 56, Title 5, Part 5 seems to suggest the same thing, while establishing that if an oath is made by the buyer or seller who is over fourteen years of age, by which he binds himself—regardless of whether the thing is worth more or less—never to attempt the aforementioned action, that oath is valid and the action cannot be attempted. By these words, it is implied that a lower level of confirmation than an oath is not sufficient for this purpose. Regarding common law, Antonio Gómez in the cited chapter 2, number 26, affirms that the same rule as Portuguese law has force.

<margin>Common law.</margin>
14 † First, because with the same ease that someone could be led to sell below half of the fair price, or to buy at more than half of the fair price, they could also be led to renounce the benefit of Law 2 of the Code, *On the Rescission of Sale*, and to say that they are donating the increase or decrease up to the fair price. Therefore, Law 2 would have provided insufficient protection. This is confirmed by an argument from similarity from the law *Si mulier* in the Code regarding the Velleianum Decree and from the law *Doli*, the section *Diversum*, in the Digest under "Donations." Furthermore, in the final law, the section *Item quaesitum* in the Digest under "Recovery of things not owed," Scaevola says:

> It was likewise asked whether a pact, which is usually written into agreements in this manner—that "from this contract there shall be no further controversy between them"—prevents a recovery. He responded: Nothing is proposed that would prevent it.

From these words, it is clear that such renunciations do nothing to prevent the action from being attempted, just as if they had never been made. Aries Pinel, against the common opinion, holds the same view regarding Law 2 of the Code, *On the Rescission of Sale*, part 1, chapter 2, from number 10. Covarruvias, however, in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 4, from number 1, disputes this at length. First, he holds that a 

<column-break/>

renunciation in general terms does not block the action from Law 2 of the Code: this is one of the interpretations he applies to the section *Quaesitum est*, namely that it follows regarding renunciations in general, but it is different regarding a specific renunciation of Law 2, or even "donations" of the excess or deficit of the price up to the fair amount. He shows that in such specific cases the action is blocked, and he shows this to be the common opinion of Bartolus and other doctors, which Aries Pinel does not deny in the cited place. Indeed, the authors of the Portuguese Ordinances thought this same point should be asserted when standing on common law; in the penultimate paragraph, after the stated disposition, they add: "even if in these events something else is disposed by common law." Covarruvias thinks this opinion should be limited: when the excess is notable or enormous—below or above half the fair price—a specific renunciation or donation does not block the action from Law 2, and he reports that it has been so judged in practice in this Kingdom and elsewhere. Choose which you prefer. I would advise that in the "forum of conscience" <note>The realm of moral and religious judgment, as opposed to a legal court</note>, even in Portugal, if it is clear that there was a true intent of donating the excess or deficit of the price, the action has no place. In the "external forum" <note>A public court of law</note>, however, because such renunciations or donations are presumed not to be free, but involuntary or forced, they are declared null in Portugal. Under common law the matter is controversial, as has been related; and when there are conjectures that the donation was involuntary, the action is granted, even by Covarruvias and other authors of the common opinion, relying on common law alone.

15 If someone had sworn an oath not to attempt the action from Law 2, or not to go against the contract: if indeed he did it with a true intent of donating, he would be bound entirely by the oath, and he could not be released from it, as it was justly made. Exception is made in Portugal, where it would be void by that very fact, unless it was done by Royal faculty, as said elsewhere. But if it was not applied with a true intent of donating, it would still have to be kept for as long as a relaxation of the oath was not obtained, because it concerned a licit matter on the part of the one swearing. Nevertheless, a relaxation could be sought, just as when someone has sworn he would pay interest. Exception is made in this Kingdom of Castile, if the oath was performed by one older than fourteen years, according to the cited Law 56; because then the action is not given in the external forum, because he is deemed to have renounced with an oath the remedy of Law 2, and for that reason the action is denied. The same is true in common law, according to the gloss on Law 2 of the Code, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarruvias refers to and follows in the cited chapter 4, number 5. However, Aries Pinel, Gutierrez, Molina (book 2, *On Primogeniture*), and others except these cases, as does Gregorio López in the final gloss on Law 56, and many others they cite, unless the harm is "most enormous" <term>laesio enormissima: a legal concept where the price is so wildly unfair (e.g., less than half or more than double) that the law intervenes more aggressively</term>; although Aries Pinel does not approve of the distinction between "most enormous" and "not enormous" harm beyond half the fair price. However, we shall return to this subject in Disputation 374.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the fairness of prices in contracts. While the previous page focused on the time limits for rescinding a contract due to "enormous loss" (over half the value), this page examines whether it is a sin—requiring restitution in one's private conscience—to buy or sell at an unfair price even if the difference is less than the legal threshold for a lawsuit.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 350. 239

# Whether it is permissible for something to be sold for a higher price than it is worth, or bought for a lower price, when the difference is not more or less than half of the just price.

### DISPUTATION 350.

#### SUMMARY.

1. *Whether a person selling a thing for more than it is worth, or buying for less, commits a sin such that they are bound in the court of conscience <note>The "court of conscience" (forum conscientiae) refers to a person's private spiritual standing before God, as opposed to a public legal court.</note> to restore or make up the difference to the just price. It is argued "yes" in number 3, following the common opinion.*
2. *Buyers and sellers may lawfully outmaneuver one another.*
4. *Buying, selling, and similar contracts were introduced for the common benefit.*
5. *One who sells in good faith, with probable ignorance, a thing beyond the just price, although they may not sin, is nonetheless bound to restore the difference as soon as they become aware. This is clarified and explained there.*
6. *Why civil and canon law permit buyers and sellers to deceive themselves above or below the just price.*
7. *Restoration of full rights <note>A legal remedy called "restitutio in integrum," which returns parties to their original state.</note> is granted to minors and the Church when they are harmed above or below the just price.*

---

<margin>Question 1</margin>
Regarding the proposed dispute, the doctors agree that when fraud <note>original: "dolus"</note> does not intervene in a contract, no legal action is granted in the external court—whether secular or ecclesiastical—according to the canon and civil laws cited in the preceding dispute, which only grant such action when the harm is more or less than half of the just price. It is, however, a matter of controversy whether a sin is nonetheless committed, carrying the burden of restitution in the court of conscience, up to the limits of the just price.

Durandus of the Order of Friars Minor, as cited in *On Contracts* question 17, and St. Antoninus in part 2, title 1, chapter 16, last section, asserted that those buying or selling in this manner neither sin nor are held to restitution. Certain legal experts, whom Covarruvias cites in *Various Resolutions* book 2, chapter 4, number 11, held the same opinion.

We can argue for this opinion as follows. First, because it is permitted by both civil and canon law, as established in Law 2 and the law *If by will* <note>original: "l. 2. & l. si voluntate"</note> in the Code *On the Rescission of Sale*, and the chapters *With the beloved* and *With cause* <note>original: "c. cum dilecti, & c. cum causa"</note> in the section on buying and selling. It is permitted to such an extent that if a person so defrauding another is summoned to court, they will be acquitted. Since, therefore, what is done by the authority of the law is done justly and lawfully, it follows that no sin intervenes in it, nor does any obligation of restitution arise from it.

This reasoning is confirmed because human law could justly decree—as a penalty and to avoid lawsuits and the peril of souls—that one who defrauds another in this manner would not be held to restitution. This is similar to the law of prescription <note>A "statute of limitations" where a right is lost or gained over time.</note>, which has force even in the court of conscience.

Second, because Law *In causes*, paragraph *The same Pomponius* <note>original: "l. in causae. §. idē Pōponius"</note> in the Digest *On Minors*, and Law *Likewise if for a price*, paragraph *In the same way* <note>original: "l. item si pretio, §. quēadmodū"</note> in the Digest on

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin>
leasing, hold that it is naturally permitted for buyers and sellers to outmaneuver <note>original: "circumuenire"</note> each other: both to buy for less what is worth more, and to sell for more what is worth less. Therefore, he who in buying or selling departs from the range of the just price neither sins nor is bound to restitution.

This is confirmed by that common proverb of the legal experts: "A thing is worth as much as it can be sold for." The doctors note this from the Law *Prices of things* in the Digest *On the Falcidian Law*, both there and frequently elsewhere. Likewise, from the Law *In a matter* in the Code *On Mandates*, which holds:

> In his own matter, every man is the moderator and arbiter.

Therefore, for his own property, a person may lawfully seek and accept an excessive price.

Gerson, in *On Contracts* and in his *Flowers*, asserted that such a buyer or seller indeed sins, but is not bound to make restitution. He persuaded himself of this because the person does not sin against justice, since no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting <note>original: "volenti, ac consentienti iniuria non fiat"</note>. Furthermore, such a contract is not void by civil or canon law, as it is when something is bought for less than half the just price, or sold for more than half the just price.

However, the common opinion of theologians and legal experts rightly asserts the contrary. Namely, <margin>3 Decision</margin> that whoever departs from the limits of the just price or the value of the thing—whether by buying, selling, leasing, exchanging, or celebrating any other contract—commits a sin and is bound to restitution up to the range of the just price or value of the thing, even if the departure was not more or less than half the just price. It will be either a mortal or venial sin, depending on the magnitude of the departure from the just price. Thus hold St. Thomas in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, question 77, article 1; Cajetan in *Opuscula* 17, response chapter 12, doubt 3; and more extensively and better in the *Summa* of the whole work, in the addition after question 57; Juan Medina *On Restitution* question 32; Soto in book 9 *On Justice* question 13, article 1; Navarrus in his *Manual* chapter 23, from number 77; Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions* book 2, chapter 4, number 11; and many others whom Covarruvias and Navarrus cite.

This can be proven first by the reasoning of St. Thomas: Because <margin>4</margin> buying and selling and other similar contracts were introduced for the common benefit, as Aristotle is the authority in book 1 of the *Politics*, insofar as one person needs the thing of another and vice versa. However, what is introduced for the common benefit ought not to be a burden to one rather than the other, as natural law demands, which prescribes: "That which you would not reasonably wish to be done to yourself, do not do to another." But it would be a burden to one rather than the other unless equality is preserved between the thing and the price, or between whatever other things are exchanged. This would be against commutative justice <note>Justice governing private exchanges between individuals.</note> for both parties, the purpose of which is to establish equality in exchanges. From this it follows that any departure from the entire range of the just price is a sin against commutative justice, and thus what is so defrauded is subject to restitution.

Second, it is proven from 1 Thessalonians 4:

> That no man overreach, nor circumvent his brother in business: because the Lord is the avenger of all such things.

Paul says "overreach," specifically by selling a thing for more than it is worth, or by exchanging a thing with another unequally by excess in any other way. And Augustine says in book 13 *On the Trinity*, chapter 3:

> It is common, either by looking at oneself or by observing others, to wish to buy cheap and sell...

<summary>This page explores the moral obligation of "just price" in contracts, arguing that while civil law only intervenes when a price is off by more than 50%, the "court of conscience" requires full restitution for any unfair pricing as a matter of commutative justice.</summary>

...to sell dearly, he believes is common to all. But since this is in truth a vice, anyone can achieve the kind of justice by which he may resist it. See how **Augustine** condemns this as a vice contrary to justice. Furthermore, he adds that he knew a man who paid a much higher price for a certain book <note>original: "codice"</note> than the seller, who was ignorant of its value, had requested from him. Many believe this man was Augustine himself. Thirdly, the same point is proven because—as the authors of the contrary opinion admit, and as is held by the provisions of civil and canon law—if someone sells for sixteen something that was worth ten at the highest rigorous price, he is bound to restore the entire range that is beyond ten, because he sold it for more than half the just price <note>This refers to the legal doctrine of "laesio enormis" (enormous loss), where a contract could be rescinded if the price was off by more than 50%.</note>. Therefore, he sinned against justice regarding that entire range. Otherwise, if he had not sinned against justice regarding that entire range, but only regarding the excess beyond half the just price, he would only be bound to restore one. Thus, whatever is received for that item beyond ten is entirely received against justice and is subject to restitution. It would indeed be strange if someone who received sixteen for a thing worth only ten were bound to restore six, but if he only received fifteen, he were bound to no restitution at all.

<margin>5</margin> The doctors of the common opinion rightly advise this: if someone in good faith <note>original: "bona fide"</note>, through probable ignorance, has exceeded the range of the just price, although he did not sin (his ignorance excusing him), he is nonetheless bound afterward, when he discovers the truth, to restore that which he exceeded. This is the view of Conradus, Covarrubias, Navarrus, and Medina in the cited places. Note, however, that if he had consumed the excess in good faith, he is only bound to restore as much as he was made wealthier by it; for he would not be bound on account of the unjust taking, but only on account of the thing received. They add this: if someone receives something while in doubt as to whether he is exceeding the limits of the just price, he sins by so receiving it and is bound afterward to restore it, unless it turns out he did not exceed the limits. However, I would say he does not sin if he receives it with a firm and certain intention both to examine later whether it was an exceeding of the limits of the just price, and also to restore it if he finds that anything was exceeded.

<margin>6</margin> Regarding the first argument for the contrary opinion, it must be said that neither canon nor civil law permits this as something licit <note>In legal philosophy, "licit" means morally permissible, while "permitted" often means the law chooses not to punish it to avoid a greater evil.</note>. Rather, solely to avoid lawsuits and greater evils, the law does not impede it, nor does it grant a legal action to repair the loss, in the same way that brothels <note>original: "lupanaria"</note> are permitted—not as being licit, but to avoid greater evils. Thus, it cannot be asserted that this is done by the authority of the law; for the law does not approve of it, but only, for a just cause, neither punishes nor prevents it. In the same sense, a person who is defrauded, but not beyond or below half the just price, is acquitted in court; because, to avoid greater evils, he is neither punished nor compelled either to rescind the contract or to provide satisfaction up to the limits of the just price. This is not, however, as if his deed were approved in court, or pronounced just or licit.

In response to the confirmation, the antecedent must be denied when the fraud was committed in bad faith. In that case,

<column-break/>

the law would be fostering sins and would be iniquitous. Similarly, those civil laws which were pointed out—which granted the right of ownership through long-term possession <note>original: "præscriptionem"</note> even with bad faith—were abolished by canon law. Finally, whatever the case may be regarding whether human law could grant this when the fraud was in good faith (which would rarely happen and could not be sufficiently established), nothing has been decreed on that matter to this day; therefore, one must stand by natural law, as explained a little earlier.

To the second, Covarrubias responds (Variarum resolutionum, book 2, chapter 3, number 2) that those legal experts in the laws are speaking about "circumvention" within the limits of the just price. However, that is ineptly called "circumvention," as is clear in itself; nor do I believe that is the meaning of those words, even though many interpret those laws in that way. It is more pleasing to say that "natural law" is taken there to mean the same as the "law of nations" <note>original: "gentium iure"</note>. In that sense, it is said to be "licit" because it is permitted and left unpunished; for there was never any nation that granted a legal action for every single fraud of price or value. And Covarrubias does not reject this exposition in his latest edition. But if those legal experts judged that this was licit by natural law in itself and strictly speaking, they were surely shamefully mistaken, and their opinion should not be followed—just as they also erred by admitting prescription with bad faith as if it were licit.

To the first part of the confirmation, it must be said that the proverb—"a thing is worth as much as it can be sold for"—is true if it is understood as meaning as much as it can be sold for *within* the range of the just price. For they only intend to show that the just price does not consist in a single indivisible point. To the second part, it must be said that in that law it is only held that an owner of his own property is a "moderator and arbiter" in the sense that he can dispose of it to his own prejudice as he wishes; a proxy <note>original: "mandatarius"</note>, however, cannot, but is held liable for fault. From this, it is wrongly concluded that an owner can licitly and justly sell his property beyond the just price.

To the first point, by which Gerson was led, it must be said that although an injury is not done to one who is willing and consenting, this applies when he wills it entirely voluntarily. It still happens, however, when he wills it with a "mixed" voluntariness <note>A scholastic concept where one "chooses" something they don't want (like paying too much) because the alternative is worse.</note>, and the discussion concerns the excess which is given for free in that involuntary manner, as is clear from the things often said regarding the matter of usury.

To the second, it must be said that a contract in which someone is deceived beyond or below half the just price is not void <note>original: "irritum"</note> in law, but a legal action is granted so that the one who caused the harm may either rescind it or reduce it to equality. Furthermore, whether an unjust contract is void in itself or not is irrelevant to whether the obligation to restore arises, especially in the court of conscience.

<margin>7</margin> Note this: for a minor or for the Church, when they are defrauded but not beyond or below half the just price, although the benefit of the law <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescind. vendit" (referring to the Code of Justinian on rescinding sales)</note> mentioned in the preceding disputation is not granted, the benefit of "restoration to the original state" <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum"</note> is nonetheless granted if they have been notably harmed.

<summary>Molina argues that any price outside the "just range" requires restitution in conscience, even if civil law does not provide a legal remedy for small discrepancies. He refutes the idea that "a thing is worth what it can be sold for" applies to prices that exploit a buyer's necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 351 of Molina’s "Second Treatise." The previous page discussed the general obligations of restitution when a price is set unfairly. Here, Molina explores specific exceptions where a price might deviate from the "common just price" due to the specific circumstances of the buyer or seller, such as personal attachment to an item or a lack of need on the buyer’s part.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 351.

Events in which, without injustice or the burden of restitution, a transgression of the price occurs which would otherwise be just. Also, whether a merchant who sold at the lowest price but withheld part of the goods because they did not reach the rigorous price <note>The "rigorous price" refers to the highest extreme of the fair market range.</note> is bound to restore them.

### DISPUTATION 351.

#### SUMMARY.

1 **Buying and hiring**, *in which cases it may be lawful at a lower price than what is just.*
2 **Selling and leasing** *when it may be lawful beyond the just price.*
3 **A seller**, *whether by reason of a particular affection they have for the item, they may accept something beyond the just price.*
4 **Gifting** *of the excess or deficit in buying and selling, and other similar contracts, when it may be presumed.*
5 **A merchant** *selling his goods at the lowest price and retaining part of the goods up to the rigorous price, whether he sins and is bound to make restitution.*

<margin>1</margin>
When buying or hiring would be useful to the seller or lessor, but less useful or even troublesome to the buyer or hirer—and the latter, led by charity or the requests of the seller or lessor, should buy or hire—then it would be lawful for him to buy or hire at a lower price than what would otherwise be just. This is because the price would be considered just in relation to him, after considering all the concurrent circumstances. According to these circumstances, it must be judged by the judgment of a prudent person how much may be subtracted from the otherwise just price. An example is found in one who, being asked, hires the labor of a poor person for his sustenance, or for some other modest price, so that the person has the means to support himself. So says Medina <note>Juan Medina (1489–1545), a Spanish theologian.</note> on restitution, question 3, part 2, near the end; Conrado <note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts.</note> on contracts, questions 57 and 58; Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), author of the "Summa Sylvestrina."</note> under the word "buying," question 7; Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), also known as Navarrus, a famous canon lawyer.</note> in his Manual, chapter 23, number 84; and Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a key figure in the School of Salamanca.</note> in book 6 on justice, question 3, article 1.

The reason for this is, first, because the price—which would otherwise be just—decreases because the buyer or hirer does not need the thing, or it is troublesome for them to buy or hire it at that time, as the first four authors cited affirm. Secondly, it is because when there is an abundant supply of sellers or lessors offering themselves to sell or lease, and there are no others who wish to buy or hire, the price drops, as Soto says. However, Soto wrongly denies that the price also decreases for that other reason affirmed by the other doctors.

<margin>2</margin>
Conversely, if the thing being sold or leased is worth more to the seller or lessor than the common just price—for instance, because if he gives it up, a profit ceases for him or a loss emerges—the price can be increased by as much as these things are valued. This is provided, however, that he signals this to the buyer or hirer: namely, that he is asking for that increase in price for the sake of the "lost profit" <note>original: "lucri cessantis"</note> or the "emerging loss" <note>original: "damni emergentis"</note>. If the buyer or hirer consents, the price is valid.

<column-break/>

For perhaps the buyer or hirer only wishes to buy the thing itself, or its use, and not that lost profit or emerging loss, from which no benefit comes to him and which he is not bound to buy, even if he intends to buy or hire the item. Furthermore, for the price to be increased and accepted for this reason, it is necessary that the sale or lease be done for the sake of the buyer or hirer, to assist them or to do them a favor. If the seller or lessor exposes the thing for sale or lease because he himself needs the money, then because he sells for his own sake, he cannot accept a higher price on account of the profit that ceases or the loss that emerges. Read what has been said on this matter in Disputation 315.

<margin>3</margin>
Whether, however, by reason of a particular affection <note>That is, sentimental value.</note> that the seller has for the thing being sold, he may accept something beyond what is otherwise a just price. Navarrus, in the cited number 84, whom many have followed since, affirms it: because it is estimable in price to deprive oneself of a thing to which one is so greatly attached. This opinion is to be understood as applying when the seller is not merely lightly attached to the thing he sells, and furthermore, when he is not equally attached to the rigorous just price for it, but much less so. For if he were equally attached to the price, the deprivation of the thing he loved would be compensated by the equal pleasure from the fair and just price. Likewise, it is to be understood as applying when he would not have exposed that item for sale himself, but having been offered a purchase at the rigorous just price, he was unwilling to sell, and only consented to the sale when asked as a favor to the buyer. Furthermore, it is to be understood provided the buyer understands that, beyond the thing itself at its rigorous price, he is also buying the seller's affection for that thing. For perhaps he does not wish to buy that, but only the thing, and it cannot be justly sold to someone who is ignorant that they are buying it. Because all these conditions rarely occur, one should be advised not to exceed the rigorous price for this reason, especially since it has the appearance of injustice and can generate scandal.

<margin>4</margin>
It should be observed that although, as a rule, in buying and selling, leasing, and other "onerous" <note>Contracts where both parties provide something of value.</note> contracts, a gift of the excess or deficit from the range of the just price is not to be presumed; nevertheless, if the contracting parties know the value of the things and neither contracts with the other out of some necessity, nor does force, fear, fraud, or anything similar intervene, then a gift can be presumed if some deficit or excess from the range of the just price occurs. So says Navarrus in "It Became Known" <note>original: "c. nouit." referring to a chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note> on judgments, notable 6, number 61, following Conrado on contracts, questions 57 and 58, and Medina on restitution at the end of question 31, regardless of what others have said, whom Navarrus cites. It would be different, however, if someone, pressed by necessity, should sell—even if the other buys at the seller's instigation and even if the buyer tells him the thing is worth more but he is unwilling to buy at a higher price—unless perhaps the thing sold in that manner was not worth more than the lowest price, or there were clear conjectures of a true intent to give a gift.

<margin>5</margin>
As for what was proposed in the second part of the dispute: there was no lack of those who tended toward the view that in such an event, no sin against justice occurs, but only against faithfulness, and thus no obligation of restitution arises. He proposes, however...

<summary>This page explores nuances of the 'just price' in commerce, arguing that prices can be legitimately adjusted based on a buyer's lack of need, a seller's sentimental attachment, or as a presumed gift between informed parties. Molina emphasizes that these deviations are only moral if they are transparent and free from coercion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 351, where Molina examines whether a seller can secretly charge more after a price has been agreed upon, provided the higher price is still within the legally or morally "fair" range. He is debating a specific case involving cloth sales and the moral obligations of contracts.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

### Column 1

the case of a man who—while a yard of cloth was sold at a lowest price of twenty-four silver coins, a middle price of twenty-five, and a rigorous <note>The "rigorous price" (*pretium rigorosum*) was the highest price a merchant could charge while still remaining within the bounds of "just price" according to market standards.</note> price of twenty-six—having sold six yards at twenty-four coins, only delivered five and a half yards, or otherwise made a secret compensation <note>original: "occulta compensationem." In moral theology, this refers to the act of a person taking what they believe they are rightfully owed from someone who will not pay, without the use of a court.</note> for twelve reals. Arguments are brought forward to support this opinion. First, because the doctors commonly say it is lawful to sell at a higher price within the range of the just price, provided that equality and a just price are maintained. The fact that an express agreement to sell for less preceded this, they argue, only proves that he sinned against fidelity due to deceit, but not against justice. Nor is the buyer "reasonably unwilling" regarding the excess price, because, since he wants to buy, no injury is done to him by the fact that the item is sold at a just price.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Second, because if someone, being ignorant of the just price, were to give twenty-six reals for a yard, the seller is not bound to restore anything to him; and this is for no other reason than that he sold it at a just price, albeit the highest one.

Third, because if someone, compelled by necessity but knowing and being prudent, were to give twenty-six reals for a yard, the seller would be safe in his conscience. However, if it were not a just price, the seller would not be excused by the fact that the other gave it knowingly and willingly, because he gave it compelled by necessity. If therefore, this author adds, the seller in these events is immune from restitution because he did not sell at an unjust price; therefore it is similar when a pact has preceded, provided he receives that much and no more. For the fact that an express pact preceded does not affect the justice of what was given and received, but only relates to fidelity and truthfulness; for which reason the seller sins by breaking his word and not making his word solid. But after all this, the same author adds: "Think about it."

I have no doubt that this opinion is false, and that it paves a road for sins and injustices. Therefore, lest it deceive the confessor and the penitents, I have chosen to report it at length and respond to each point. First of all, this author does not consider that buying and selling are perfected by the mutual consent of the buyer and seller. This does not happen only when the goods are delivered and the price is received, but the contract was consummated before that by mutual consent. Such is the nature of a contract that, after it is rightly consummated, it binds both contracting parties out of justice. This applies not only to "onerous" contracts <note>Contracts where both parties give something, like a sale.</note> but also to "lucrative" ones <note>Contracts involving a gift or benefit to one party.</note>. For by the very fact that someone, out of liberality and intending to bind himself, has promised, if the recipient has accepted, the promisor is bound by justice to fulfill the promised contract, as has been shown in the matter of promises and donations. Therefore, by the very fact that a yard of cloth was sold for twenty-four silver coins—just as the buyer is bound by justice to stand by the contract by paying twenty-four silver coins for the yard—so the seller is bound by justice to stand by the contract by delivering the yard for only those silver coins, even if the lowest just price for the yard is that amount. Therefore, if he defrauds anything, either regarding the agreed merchandise or by secretly taking from the goods of the buyer, he sins against commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs the fairness of exchanges between individuals, requiring that one person gives a fair equivalent for what they receive.</note> and is bound to make restitution. No one has ever existed who asserted the contrary, or could truly affirm it. Furthermore, this author does not consider that when someone does not stand by a pact or contract that binds out of justice, such as buying and selling,

<column-break/>

### Column 2

he sins in a twofold way, as was explained in Disputation 262. Namely, against justice, while he does not fulfill the contract as he is bound by justice to do, or transgresses it (which in its nature is a mortal sin, as said there); and against the faith or fidelity given, which is the foundation of justice and extends more widely than justice.

Indeed, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas and authority on economic ethics.</note> judged that when faith is given in such a contract, it is not distinct from the justice by which one is bound by that contract, and similarly, infidelity is not distinct from the injustice of not standing by that same contract. Moreover, the same author does not notice that it is one thing for both contracting parties to be free, while the contract is being celebrated, to not want to agree with the other except at the price he prefers within the range of the just price; but it is quite another thing after the contract has been celebrated and they have agreed by mutual consent on a certain price within the range of the just price. In the latter case, justice is violated if something extra is secretly taken for the goods; for that is undoubtedly an injustice, and even a theft. For if the setting of a price by public authority has so much force that the taking of a higher price for goods is an injustice requiring restitution, how much more will this be achieved by a contract of buying and selling, consummated and perfected by the mutual consent of both parties at a certain and determined price within the range of the fair price.

Next, one may argue thus: Everyone has the right to refuse to buy from a private person except at the price they wish, even within the range of the fair price. Therefore, anyone who would force him to buy at the middle or rigorous price, when the common good does not demand it, would certainly do him an injury and sin against justice, with the burden of restitution for as much as it was in his interest not to buy in that way. Much more, then, does he do him an injury, sin against justice, and remain bound to restitution who, after the buyer has used his right and bought at the lowest price by mutual consent, secretly takes from him up to the rigorous price. Add that, if this opinion (or rather pernicious error) were granted, one would have to concede that someone who sold a house, a horse, or any other thing, if he finds he did not receive the rigorous price, could—without the vice of injustice and the burden of restitution—secretly compensate himself up to the rigorous price. Who can fail to see how false this is, and how many doors to evil it opens in the Republic and the Church?

Therefore, to the first argument of the contrary opinion: even if the major premise is granted (if it is understood to apply *while* the contract is being celebrated), the minor premise must be denied. Namely, that from an express preceding agreement to sell at a lower price—or rather from a contract of sale at a lower price consummated by mutual consent—it can be concluded that there is only a sin against fidelity and not against justice. For it has been shown that the contrary is true.

As for what he adds, that the buyer is "not reasonably unwilling" regarding the excess price, etc., this is undoubtedly false. This is true not only if understood after the contract is perfected at a lower price, but even if, without his consent, he were secretly made to buy at a higher price—though it would not be so if the seller were unwilling to celebrate the contract with him except at the higher price.

To the second point, it must be said that everything assumed is true while the contract is being celebrated; conse...

<summary>Molina refutes the idea that a seller can secretly take extra money or withhold goods to reach the "rigorous" (highest fair) price after agreeing to a lower one. He argues that once a contract is mutually agreed upon, its terms are bound by commutative justice, and any secret deviation constitutes theft.</summary>

# Whether a purchase and sale in which deceit intervenes is valid.

### DISPUTATION 352.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *Multiple types of deception.*
2 *When someone is said to be deceived by fraud.*
3 *In how many ways fraud can intervene in a contract.*
4 *When fraud is said to give cause to the contract.*
5 *When fraud is said to be incidental to the contract.*
6 *In how many ways fraud is said to intervene in a contract.*
7 *Fraud giving cause to a good-faith contract renders the contract void by the law itself on the part of the deceived, not the deceiver.*
*Limit this in marriage, number 9.*
*Clarify and understand, as in number 11.*
8 *If the deceived person wishes to stand by the contract, the deceiver is also bound to stand by it, but not vice versa, even though the contract is void.*
10 *When fraud gives cause to the contract, the deceiver is bound to the deceived for all damages, both for lost profit and for emerging loss.*
11 *Fraud giving cause to the contract when applied by a third party does not render the contract void, but the deceived is given an action against the third party.*
*Understand as in the following number.*
12 *Involuntary error, in which case it does not vitiate the contract by the nature of the matter.*
13 *Incidental fraud in a contract does not render the contract void, but an action is given to the deceived to recover what they paid in excess.*
14 *When fraud is incidental to a contract, whether the deceiver is given the option to reduce it to equality.*
15 *If a seller knows the value of a thing and sells it for more than it is worth, whether they are bound to restitution.*
16 *Fraud giving cause to a contract of strict law rescinds the contract by means of an exception, or by an action for fraud; otherwise in the court of conscience, in which it is void by the law itself.*
17 *When fraud is incidental to a contract of strict law, to what the fraudulent person is bound in the court of conscience, and to what in the external court.*
18 *The practice to be observed in the court of conscience regarding contracts entered into through fraud.*

<margin>1</margin> What was said in Disputations 349 and 350 is to be understood as applying when fraud properly so called, or deceit <term>dolus: a legal and moral term for intentional deception or trickery</term>, does not intervene in the contract. Now, however, we must examine whether a purchase and sale in which deceit intervenes is valid. It must be observed,

<column-break/>

as noted learnedly, among others, by Conrad <note>original: "Conr. de contractibus." Refers to Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian whose work "On Contracts" was a standard reference.</note> in the summary of the whole work, in the addition after summary question 57, that deception can arise in many ways. One way is through the ignorance of the deceiver. For example, if someone, thinking they are selling a thing at a just price, sells it for more than it is worth. This deception is said to intervene "in the matter itself" <note>original: "re ipsa"</note> and not "by purpose" <note>original: "a proposito"</note>. Another way is with the knowledge that the other is being deceived; this deception is said to be "by purpose." For example, if someone, knowing a thing is worth less, sells it for more than it is worth. This, moreover, can happen in many ways. For
<margin>2</margin> it either happens with deceit intervening—as when, by proposing something false, someone is led to buy something, or led to buy it for more than it is worth; or if something is done so that the buyer is deceived, such as putting quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," i.e., mercury. This was a common trick to make a horse or mule appear energetic or to hide ear-related ailments.</note> into the ears of a beast for sale so that it appears less sluggish for that reason, or covering up its defects so they are not recognized by the buyer; or finally, if by deed or words an occasion for deception is offered to the buyer, or if something is not disclosed to them which the seller is bound to disclose as if by duty, according to what will be said in the following disputation. If, however, none of these intervene, but the item is sold for more than it is worth solely with the knowledge that it is worth less, while the seller affirms that they will not give it for a lower price, then it is indeed said to be sold "by purpose" for more than it is worth, but not with deceit <note>original: "cum dolo"</note> according to what was said in Disputation 293, and as we will add shortly below.
<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, deceit can intervene in a contract in two ways. One, such that it gives cause to the contract. The other, such that it does not give cause to the contract, but
<margin>4</margin> is incidental to the contract. Deceit is said to give cause to a contract of purchase, for example, when the buyer would not have bought the thing unless they had been led to buy it by deceit. As when they buy something because they were falsely told it was useful for a purpose for which it was not useful, which they would not have bought if that had not been said. Or if they buy wine because they were lied to that it was of a certain age or from a certain place, which they would not have bought if they knew it was not of that age
<margin>5</margin> or was from another place. In contrast, deceit is said to be incidental <note>original: "incidere." This refers to fraud that affects the terms (like price) but not the existence of the deal itself.</note> to the contract when the buyer was indeed going to buy that same thing, but not at such a high price, unless they had been so induced by deceit.
<margin>6</margin> Moreover, deceit is said to intervene in a contract of purchase in two ways. One, through the seller themselves, or with the seller participating in it. The other, through some third party, such as a broker or anyone else, without the seller participating in it.
<margin>7</margin> These things having been established, the first conclusion is: when deceit gives cause to a purchase, sale, or any other good-faith contract <term>bonae fidei: contracts based on mutual trust where the parties are expected to act honestly, rather than just following the letter of the law</term>, and the other contracting party participates in the deceit, the contract is valid neither in the court of conscience nor in the external court. Instead, in favor of the deceived person, let it be void by the law itself <term>ipso iure</term>, even if the deceived was not cheated beyond or below half of the just price; indeed, even if the contract was otherwise equal on both sides. But if the deceived person nevertheless wishes to stand by the contract, the deceiver cannot dissolve it, but is compelled to stand by it. We established this conclusion universally regarding every good-faith contract in Disputation 259, and we proved it from the law "If by Deceit" in the Code on Rescinding Sales.

<summary>This page introduces the moral and legal implications of fraud (dolus) in contracts, distinguishing between fraud that causes a contract to happen and fraud that merely influences the terms. Molina concludes that a contract born of the seller's fraud is void in both moral and civil law to protect the victim.</summary>

<keywords>deceit, fraud, contract law, good faith, just price, Conrad Summenhart, rescission, court of conscience, incidental fraud, horse-trading tricks</keywords>

<meta>Continuing the analysis of fraud in contracts from Disputation 352, specifically focusing on the validity of agreements when a third party is the source of the deception, and distinguishing between fraud that causes a contract versus fraud that is merely incidental to it.</meta>

### Treatise Two, Disputation 352.

<margin>11</margin> **The third conclusion.** When <note>Latin: "dolus"</note> deceit indeed provides the cause for a contract, but is employed by a third party without the other contracting party participating in the fraud, the contract is valid. However, the deceived person is granted a legal action against the third party who employed the deceit, as is expressly stated in the Digest, Book 2, regarding brokers <note>original: "l. 2. ff. de proxenetis"</note>. This is the commentary on the law and the elegantly cited passages, consistent with the text there and the commentaries on the chapter regarding buyers and sellers <note>original: "c. cum dilecti. de empti. & vend."</note>. Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart, a 15th-century theologian</note> and Medina <note>Juan Medina, a 16th-century Spanish theologian</note> agree on this, at least regarding the external court <note>the public legal system</note>. However, in the court of conscience <note>the moral/spiritual realm</note>, standing solely on natural law, they believe the contract is void. They are convinced of this because, since error removes the voluntary nature of an act, and the deceived person truly would not have given consent unless led to it by deceit, that consent does not have enough "will" to be considered necessary to bind the contracting party. Furthermore, they believe that human law has attributed force to such a contract for the sake of the public good so that it might be valid, despite the lack of full voluntary consent. Therefore, they ask whether that contract truly has force in the court of conscience such that the other party can, with a clear conscience, take action against the deceived person—even if they know about the third party's deceit. This depends on the intent of human law in that matter. If, they say, the intent of the lawmakers was only to deny both parties the ability to dissolve the contract, and to permit action against the deceived to make them stand by it—only to the extent that one is permitted to act when the price is not more or less than half the <term>just price<gloss>the fair market value determined by common estimation rather than individual greed</gloss></term>—then the other party cannot in good conscience compel the deceived person to stand by the contract, because the contract is actually void in the court of conscience. If, however, the intent of the lawmakers was to grant full validity to the contract, then one can act in good conscience and compel the person to stand by it, because it is truly valid in the court of conscience. Conrad does not dare to define what the intent of human law was on this matter. Medina, however, thinks the intent was to grant it power so that it would be valid in the court of conscience, and thus the deceived person can safely be compelled to stand by it.

<margin>12</margin> To offer my own view: I believe that such a contract, standing solely on natural law, is valid, and the foundation upon which Conrad and Medina lean is false. They claim that the lack of "voluntariness" is sufficient to make the contract void by the nature of the thing. For this reason, in proving our first conclusion, we did not rely solely on the lack of voluntariness as they do, but primarily on the injury and deceit by which the contracting party—through whom the obligation must arise—extracts consent. At this point, observe that while the "involuntary" nature arising from an error regarding the motive (which a donor relies upon to give) might make a donation invalid, in <term>onerous contracts<gloss>contracts where both parties give and receive something of value, like a sale</gloss></term>, the involuntary nature arising from an error regarding the motive—whereby someone is induced to contract with another, such as to buy, exchange, or hire—does not invalidate the contract by the very nature of the thing. Much less does it invalidate it when the involuntary nature arises from ignorance of other circum-

<column-break/>

-stances which, if known, would have prevented the contract from being celebrated. The reason is that no contracting party would accept such a rule if proposed by the other, nor is such a rule beneficial to the common good; therefore, by the nature of the thing, contracts are not considered to be celebrated under such a rule. For this reason, I believe human laws in this matter have established and explained what the nature of the thing itself holds. Therefore, when in commerce and human contracts an inequality does not result from an error, I believe not only that contracts are not rendered invalid by an error in motive, but also that there is no obligation to alter or moderate them. And from this, other doubts raised by Juan Medina cease—namely, whether a contract is valid when a buyer deceives himself through vincible or invincible ignorance, believing the thing he was buying was suitable for a purpose for which it was not. It must be said that it is valid. If, however, an inequality results from the error because more than the strict <term>just price<gloss>the highest acceptable price in a fair market</gloss></term> was given, then the contract must be reduced to equality. Whether ignorance of a defect in a sold item renders a contract invalid, and whether a seller is bound to disclose it, will be discussed in the following disputation.

You may ask whether a <term>gabella<gloss>a sales or excise tax</gloss></term> is owed on contracts that are void on the part of the buyers in the manner explained, so that if the tax collector has received it, he is bound to restore it to the seller. I believe it must be answered that it is owed: because on the part of the seller they are valid and bind him, which is enough for the treasury to have acquired a right that, once sought, it does not lose. In that event, only the seller who was at fault is bound to pay it in full, even in Portugal according to the law "he owes" <note>original: "l. debet"</note> at the end of the Digest regarding the edict of the aediles, and those things said in Disputation 349. Lassarte seems to agree in his work on the tithes of sales <note>original: "de decim. vend. c. 14. nu. 10"</note>.

<margin>13</margin> **The fourth conclusion.** When deceit was indeed committed by a contracting party, but it was only **incidental** to the contract <note>original: "incidit in contractu"</note>—for example, the other person was already going to buy the item, but not at such a high price—then both in the court of conscience and in the external court, the contract is valid. However, a legal action is granted to the deceived person (even if they were not deceived beyond half the just price) to recover what they paid in excess because of the deceit. This was also asserted in Disputation 259 and is found in the elegant commentary at the beginning of the Digest regarding deceit, and the commentary on the chapter regarding buyers and sellers, according to the text of the law of Julianus <note>original: "l. Iulianus, §. si venditor"</note> and the law "if anyone affirms" <note>original: "l. si quis affirmaverit"</note> regarding deceit, and here in the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. 57. tit. 5. p. 5"</note>. Conrad, Medina, Angelus, Sylvester, and the doctors of law commonly agree on this. The reason the contract is valid in both courts is this: because the deceit was not the *cause* of the contract, since the contract would have happened even if deceit had not intervened; however, it was the cause of the excess in price, and therefore it is only invalid regarding that which the deceit caused. For "a useful thing is not vitiated by an intermediate useless thing," as held in the legal rule <note>original: "reg. utile, de reg. iur. lib. 6"</note>. Regarding the second part of the conclusion, observe that when deceit is incidental to a contract, restitution must be made not only for what was taken beyond the strict just price, but also for whatever was taken through deceit above the price the buyer would have actually and justly accepted. Indeed, all such...
