# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...the increase was unjustly extorted through deceit.

You may ask whether, in the event of this fourth conclusion, the <term>tax collector<gloss>original: "gabellarius"; an official responsible for collecting the "gabella," a common excise tax on goods</gloss></term> is bound to remit or restore the tax due based on the first contract. The answer must be in the negative: indeed, the seller must be punished because of the deceit in the payment of that full amount, according to the law "he ought" <note>original: "l. debet. ff. de ædil. edict." — a reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding the Edicts of the Curule Aediles</note>; and in Portugal, he is bound to restore to the buyer, along with the part of the price that he received in excess, that part of the tax which the buyer paid relative to that portion of the price.

<margin>Doubt 14</margin>
14 **The doubt is whether, when deceit occurs in a contract,** the deceiver is given the option to either rescind the contract or reduce it to equality as he prefers—just as the option is given when someone has defrauded another without deceit by more or less than half of the just price.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Angelus and Sylvester, in the places cited, respond in the affirmative. The contrary opinion is preferred, following Conrad and Medina in the places cited, and Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, a prominent Spanish jurist and bishop</note> in "Various Resolutions," Book 2, Chapter 4, Number 11, which is more consistent with the laws. For the laws establish nothing in favor of the deceitful person; indeed, it would be a great favor if he were to report a non-slight advantage from his own deceit. Therefore, it must be said that when deceit occurs in a contract, just as the deceived party cannot rescind it without the deceiver's consent, so the deceiver cannot rescind it without the deceived party's consent; instead, he is bound to the excess price which he received through deceit.

Covarruvias, in the same place, asserted that when someone,

<margin>Decision</margin>
15 **knowing a thing to be worth less, sells it for more,** he is considered to have sold it through deceit, even if he did not use lies or other persuasion, but sold it for that amount solely by reason of his knowledge of the fact. On account of this, he says, an action will be granted against him in the <term>external court<gloss>the public legal system or civil law</gloss></term>, even if he did not defraud more or less than half of the just price. Conrad affirms the contrary opinion in the cited addition, and it is more common and more consistent with the laws, and should be embraced. Martin de Azpilcueta (Navarrus), however, in the chapter "He Knew" regarding judgments <note>original: "c. nouit. de iudi. notab. 6"</note>, and Panormitanus and others whom Covarruvias cites there, do not intend what Covarruvias thinks they affirm. Rather, they only say that through "evangelical denunciation" and a correction intermediate between "fraternal correction" and judicial correction—which will be discussed in Treatise 5 and was mentioned above regarding the matter of fraternal correction—a prelate can compel the one who defrauded in this way to make satisfaction, whether he defrauded knowingly or unknowingly, so that he may cease from sin. Nevertheless, the same Navarrus affirms elsewhere that such a process through that intermediate correction is not commonly permitted to ecclesiastics today by secular princes. But certainly, even against the will of secular princes, they could use that process and power, as it is incumbent upon prelates by virtue of their office and descends from divine law; provided that neither they nor their ministers abuse it by extending it further than is proper, but use it sincerely.

16 **The fifth conclusion. When deceit provided the cause** for a <term>contract of strict law<gloss>contractus stricti iuris; a formal contract where the literal terms are strictly enforced, as opposed to "good faith" contracts</gloss></term>, the contract is valid in the external court. However, the deceived person is granted a "defense of deceit" <note>original: "exceptio doli"</note>, on the grounds that deceit gave cause to the contract, so that by means of such a defense, he may not be compelled to fulfill it if any part of the contract remains to be fulfilled. Likewise, if after the contract has been fulfilled, the deceived person suffers any loss, an "action for deceit" <note>original: "actio de dolo"</note> is granted to him against the deceiver to repair the damage. So says the Gloss on the law "and elegantly," at the beginning <note>original: "l. & eleganter, in princip. ff. de dolo"</note>, and the Gloss on the chapter "with the beloved" regarding buying and selling.

<column-break/>

Conrad, in the cited addition to Question 14 and the two following, and Angelus and Sylvester in the cited places, agree according to the law "if anyone with another" <note>original: "l. ſiquis cum aliter, ff. de verb. oblig."</note>. We also established this conclusion in part in Disputation 259. There, with Conrad, Covarruvias, and others, we said that in the <term>court of conscience<gloss>the moral/spiritual standing of the individual before God</gloss></term>, the contract is void by the law itself, and the deceitful person is bound to rescind it if the deceived person so wishes, because consent extracted through deceit and injury is not sufficient to bind the deceived person; and it is expedient that the same be decreed in the external court.

17 **The sixth conclusion. When deceit occurs** in a contract of strict law <note>meaning the fraud was incidental to the deal, rather than the primary reason for it</note>, it is valid in the court of conscience and the external court, according to those things said similarly in the fourth conclusion regarding good faith contracts. Furthermore, although in the court of conscience the deceitful person is bound to reduce the contract to equality, in the external court he will not be compelled to do so. Instead, only a defense of deceit will be admitted if the contract has not yet been fully performed by the deceived party. If, however, it has been performed, the deceived party will be granted an action for deceit against the deceiver to repair the damage caused, according to those things said and shown in the preceding conclusion. Read Conrad in the cited place and the laws he cites. Regarding the tax (gabelle), the same must be said about this and the preceding conclusion as was said regarding the fourth.

18 **To better adapt what has been said so far to practice,** distinguish this: either someone is deceived while the other contracting party is ignorant of it; and then, if no inequality arises in the contract because no transgression of the limits of the just value was made, the contract is valid and firm in both courts, and no change is necessary. If, however, an inequality arises—either more was received than the rigorous just price, or less was given than the lowest pious price—then in the court of conscience it ought to be reduced to equality, but only to the limits of what is just. This is also true in the external court if the transgression was more or less than half of the just price. But if the deception occurs with the other party knowing but without deceit, and without concealing things that he was bound to manifest (according to what will be said in the following disputation), then exactly the same things must be said as we just said regarding when someone was deceived while the other party was ignorant.

But if lies or deceit intervened, a distinction must be made. Either the other person was induced by them to contract, or to increase the price or compensation; or not, because he did not give them credit, knowing that such is the custom of those celebrating similar contracts; or even if those lies had not been employed, he would have contracted similarly. And then exactly the same must be said as in the two cases above: because the deceit employed was neither the cause of the contract nor of increasing the compensation or decreasing it. And hence, merchants who lie and affirm with an oath that a thing is worth more, or that they bought it for more, and many other fabrications—both to sell, or to sell for more, or to buy, or to buy for less—will often be excused both from the burden of rescinding such contracts and from the restitution of that part of what they received. When someone was induced by lies or other deceits to contract, or to increase the price or compensation, deceit is said to intervene in the contract...

Second Treatise, Disputation 353.

...in the sense in which we have spoken more extensively so far in this disputation. If, at that time, deceit was the cause of the contract, it is invalid in the <term>court of conscience<gloss>the internal moral judgment of an individual, often in the context of confession</gloss></term>, if the deceived person so wishes; and even in the external court <note>the public, secular, or ecclesiastical legal system</note>, if the contract was made in <term>good faith<gloss>original: "bonae fidei"; a legal standard requiring honesty and fairness</gloss></term>, even if no inequality in value arose from it, as was stated in the first conclusion. Observe, however, that when there is no inequality, it is regularly not a <term>mortal sin<gloss>original: "culpam lethalem"; a grave sin that separates a person from God's grace</gloss></term> to not rescind that contract, or not to offer its rescission to the deceived party. Nor, when the matter is still <term>fresh<gloss>original: "re integra"; a legal state where the contract has not yet been fully executed or can still be undone</gloss></term> so that the contract could be dissolved, does an obligation regularly arise to restore anything under the penalty of mortal sin. And from here, those who lie about an item being older than it is, or being from a certain place, will be excused from mortal sin and the burden of restitution under mortal sin, if they sold it to someone who would not have bought it at all—or not at such a price—had he known its true age or origin, provided the item in itself (all circumstances considered) was equally good and of equal value. Likewise, they are excused when the buyer would not have bought it for so much, but the increase in price was not so great as to be required for a mortal sin <note>Molina refers to the theological concept that for a theft or fraud to be a mortal sin, it must involve a "significant" amount of money</note>. However, while the matter is fresh, there is always an obligation under <term>venial sin<gloss>a lesser sin that does not break one's relationship with God</gloss></term> to rescind the contract, or to offer to do so to the deceived party, or to restore to him what he would have paid less—at least when he would have bought it from another at a lower price, if he had not been thus deceived by this seller, even if he bought it from this seller within the limits of the <term>rigorous just price<gloss>the highest possible price that is still considered fair in the market</gloss></term>. For when he could have bought no better wine from anyone else, or at a cheaper price, then, although an injustice was done to him by selling it in that way, since no loss followed (including <term>lost profit<gloss>original: "lucri cessantis"</gloss></term>), no obligation of restitution would arise. I said that "regularly" a mortal sin does not intervene by not rescinding similar contracts or not restoring; because if the thing were of great value, and especially if the buyer would otherwise have bought it for a lower price from someone else, such that this decrease in price would suffice for a mortal sin, then it would indeed be a mortal sin: both to enter into that contract with deceit, and (while the matter is fresh) not to rescind it, and finally (when the matter is no longer fresh) to omit the restitution of the damage resulting from that contract to the person thus deceived.

Sometimes it is in **quantity**, as when the measure or weight is diminished. Sometimes it is in **quality**; for example, if a horse or a slave suffers from some disease or other defect by which it is rendered notably useless for the purpose for which it is bought; or if a herb or medicine is sold as being useful for a purpose for which it has no power. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the moral obligations of sellers when a contract involves deceit or hidden defects. It moves from general principles of fraud to the specific legal and moral duties of a seller to disclose significant faults in the goods being sold.</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...regarding defects, if the item was notably purchased for that purpose, a distinction must be made. For either the defect is obvious—for example, if a horse is one-eyed, that is, having only one eye, or if a house being sold is in ruins—or it is hidden. Having established these points, and keeping in view what was said in Disputation 340 regarding defects (especially those concerning the substance of the item), as well as what was said in the preceding discussion, the proposed dispute must be addressed with the following conclusions.

<margin>2</margin> **First Conclusion:** If the defect was not obvious, and the buyer was unaware of it, while the seller knew of it and did not reveal it despite it being significant, the seller is liable to the buyer for all damages that followed as a result. For instance, if he sold a diseased sheep that infected others, or a slave whom he knew to be a thief, he is liable for the thefts and other subsequent damages, including <term>lost profit<gloss>original: "lucri cessantis"; the income the buyer would have earned had the item been as described</gloss></term>. This is expressly stated in the law *Julianus* at the beginning of the <term>Digest<gloss>original: "ff."; the Digest of Justinian, a massive collection of Roman legal opinions</gloss></term> on actions of purchase; in the law *si vinum*, second section, under the word *planè*, in the Digest on the risks and benefits of the thing sold; and in the first law of the <term>Code<gloss>original: "C."; the Codex of Justinian, a collection of imperial constitutions</gloss></term> on the <term>Aedilian actions<gloss>original: "aedilitijs actionibus"; legal remedies established by the Aediles, Roman officials who oversaw market fairness</gloss></term>. The same is affirmed by <note>Saint</note> Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, question 77, article 3, and commonly by the doctors <note>of law and theology</note>. The reason is provided by Thomas in the same place and is proposed more fully and clearly by L. Medina in his discussion of the same question. Specifically, the seller, by the very act of offering his property for sale, is held, as if by a duty of his office, to manifest the notable defects of the item so that the buyer is not deceived. Since the seller has a greater knowledge of his own property than the buyer, and since he himself offers the item for sale to receive a just price for it, it belongs to him to ensure everything regarding the item is handled so that the sale is sincere and without deception. Just as it belongs to the buyer to handle what concerns the price, it belongs to the seller—almost as a professional duty—to provide a proper knowledge of the item by disclosing its hidden notable defects so the buyer is not deceived. This is especially true after it was enjoined by human law, as seen in the <term>Aedilian Edict<gloss>a set of rules in Roman law protecting buyers from hidden defects in livestock and slaves</gloss></term>. Hence, <margin>Ambrose, Book 1 of *On Duties*</margin> *Ambrose, in Book 1 of "On Duties,"* says: *"In contracts, it is commanded that the defects of those things which are sold be brought forward; and unless the seller has disclosed them, even if the goods have passed into the buyer's right, the contracts are voided by an action of fraud."*

<margin>7</margin> Because, therefore, the seller is held as if by duty to manifest defects, he is judged to be deceitful not only if he positively hides defects by doing something to keep them from the buyer, but also if he behaves negatively by not bringing them forward and manifesting them. He is bound to this by duty and by justice if he knows of them. For this reason, one who knows of defects and does not manifest them is said to sell by <term>fraud<gloss>original: "dolo"; intentional deceit or trickery</gloss></term> in the Code on Aedilian actions, and Ambrose implies the same in the words cited. From this, it is clear that a seller who does not manifest hidden defects of an item he sells to a buyer acts against justice and against that which he is held to do by duty; therefore, he is bound to make <term>restitution<gloss>the act of making right a wrong or compensating for a loss</gloss></term> for all damages that followed for that reason. He is no different than one who is bound by his office to prevent damages to citizens; such a person is bound to restore all things he could have prevented but did not due to his negligence. From what has been said, you may gather that one who knowingly sells <term>litigious property<gloss>original: "rem litigiosam"; property that is currently the subject of a lawsuit</gloss></term> to one ignorant of such a defect is bound to restore all subsequent damages, including lost profit.

<margin>4</margin> **Second Conclusion:** In the event of the first conclusion, if the buyer would not have purchased the item had he known of the defect, the contract is null in the <term>court of conscience<gloss>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the internal moral judgment of an individual, often in the context of confession</gloss></term>.

<column-break/>

In the external court, however, he is granted what is called a **redhibitory action**—that is, an action to recover his price and return the item. But if he would have purchased the item anyway, though at a lower price, the contract is valid in both courts; however, the seller is bound to restore to the buyer the amount by which he would have paid less for the item. Consequently, in the external court, the buyer is granted an **action for the lesser amount** (as they call it, *quanto minoris*) to reclaim from the seller the difference in value. The first part of this is clear from what was said in the first conclusion of the preceding disputation. For he who knowingly sells a defective item to someone ignorant of the defect is judged to commit fraud against the buyer and sins against justice, as is established from the explanation of fraud given at the beginning of the preceding disputation and from what was just said. Therefore, if such fraud gave cause to the contract—meaning the buyer would not have bought the item if the defect had been disclosed—the contract is null in conscience and in the external court, as shown in the first conclusion there. But if he would have bought it, yet for a lower price, and thus fraud occurred *within* the contract, the contract is valid in both courts, but the seller is bound to restore to the buyer only as much as he would have paid less, as seen in the fourth conclusion of the same disputation. And so, the third part, along with the first, remains proven because of their similarity.

<margin>3 5</margin> The second and fourth parts—namely, that in the first scenario, the buyer is granted a **redhibitory action** in the external court (which under common law and the law of Castile lasts for six months from the day the contract was celebrated), and in the third scenario, an **action for the lesser amount** is granted (which lasts for one year from the day the contract was celebrated)—are established from the laws in the Digest on the Aedilian Edict, from the Code on Aedilian actions, and from Law 65 of the Laws of the Siete Partidas <note>the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>. Furthermore, from the fact that civil law grants a redhibitory action and orders the contract to be rescinded, you should not conclude (as *Contra* concludes in his 34th statement) that the contract was valid in the external court but merely subject to being rescinded.

<margin>6</margin> **Rescission**, as the gloss on the Digest concerning fraud notes excellently and elegantly at the beginning, does not always look to annul a contract as if it were valid by law before the rescission. Instead, it is sometimes for the purpose of revoking a fact—that is, to compel the seller to restore the price he received and take back the item he gave—precisely because the contract was null by law from the start. This is greatly to be observed: one should not always conclude that because the law orders a contract to be rescinded, the contract was valid by law before that rescission. As the gloss on the Code notes, if there is ignorance on the part of the buyer, the time limit for both actions begins to run from the day he discovers the defect, according to the Digest on the Aedilian Edict. This is affirmed by Gregorio López in his notes on the aforementioned Law 65, and by Antonio Gómez in his *Various Resolutions*, and others whom he cites. These types of actions are called "Aedilian" because they were introduced by the Aediles. However, once the six months granted for the redhibitory action have passed, anyone who has not used it may, for the following six months, initiate the action for the lesser amount, as is clear from the Digest and the Partidas. Once these times have passed, neither of the predicted actions has a place, because they are prescribed <note>expired</note> by that time, nor can they be further...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of the "Aedilian actions"—legal remedies for buyers who discover defects in purchased goods. The previous page established that a seller who knowingly hides a significant defect is liable for all resulting damages. This page discusses the time limits for these legal actions, how they apply in the "forum of conscience" (moral duty), specific variations in Portuguese law (particularly regarding the slave trade and livestock), and the rules for when a seller is genuinely ignorant of a defect.</meta>

...to be attempted, as is expressly held in the law *cum proponas* <note>original: "l. cum proponas"; a specific law within the Roman Code</note> of the <term>Code on Aedilian actions<gloss>Roman laws overseen by officials called Aediles, regulating markets and sales</gloss></term>. Diego de Covarruvias <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist and bishop</note> observes very well in his work on the rule *possessor* (part 2, section 11, number 5), along with many others whom he cites, that such legal actions are <term>prescribed<gloss>legally expired due to the passage of time</gloss></term> even when the seller acted in bad faith. The reason for this is that the law did not grant these actions for a long duration. In the **forum of conscience**, however, the seller remains bound—even after the legal action has expired—to return the price when fraud gave cause to the contract, and to reduce the price when fraud occurred during the contract. This is because he is bound to this in the court of conscience by the very nature of the matter, and these duties cannot be "prescribed" or expire when bad faith is involved. Indeed, they cannot even be prescribed with good faith in such a short time, according to what has been said regarding the matter of prescription.

The <term>Gloss<gloss>standard medieval commentary on Roman law</gloss></term> on the law *Julianus* and the jurist Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century lawyer</note> (on the <term>Digest<gloss>original: "ff."; the primary collection of Roman legal opinions</gloss></term> regarding actions of purchase) and the Gloss on the law *cum proponas* (in the Code on Aedilian actions) affirm that while the aforementioned actions, which are <term>Praetorian<gloss>laws introduced by Roman judges (Praetors) rather than formal statutes</gloss></term> by right, are prescribed within the stated time, there remains an "action of the thing sold." This latter action arises from <term>civil law<gloss>formal statutory law (ius civile)</gloss></term> and is perpetual. Covarruvias also noted, citing Panormitanus and others, that an action for fraud also remains; however, let the legal experts examine these matters more diligently. All these things said regarding the contract of buying and selling where a defect is not disclosed, and those that follow, are similarly to be understood for <term>barter<gloss>original: "permutatione"; the exchange of goods</gloss></term> and other contracts. This is clear from the law *sciendum* (second to last section of the Digest on the Aedilian edict), where it is added that both parties in a barter hold the place of both buyer and seller.

<margin>Portuguese Law. 7</margin> According to **Portuguese Law**, however, when someone buys, barters, or acquires through another <term>onerous contract<gloss>a contract where both parties give and receive something of value</gloss></term> a <term>slave from Guinea<gloss>original: "mancipium ex Guinea"; referring to the historical Trans-Atlantic slave trade which was a major part of the Portuguese economy during Molina's time</gloss></term> from the hands of those who transport them from there, or those who conduct that trade, or those who bought them from any of these for resale: a legal action is granted only within one month, counted from the day of the slave's delivery, when the dispute concerns a disease that the slave had at the time the contract was celebrated, or regarding a limp or similar defect of the arms or hands. However, if the person who sold the slave is not in the same location, as long as the buyer protests the aforementioned defects before a judge within that month and shows the slave to two doctors who can testify to the defects, another month is granted in which he may also take action.

If the person who sold the slave is a foreigner, a month is granted to bring action against him, counted from the day the seller arrives in the kingdom. The same rule applies to any <term>beasts of burden<gloss>original: "iumenta"; pack animals like mules or horses</gloss></term> acquired by purchase, barter, or similar contract. Regarding other slaves and all other things—and even slaves from Guinea when they are not purchased from the hands of the specific merchants mentioned—or when the dispute involves any defect other than disease, limping, or issues with the arms and hands, the common law is followed in Portugal. All these things are decreed in the fourth book of the <term>Ordinances<gloss>original: "Lord. tit. 16"; referring to the Ordinances of the Kingdom of Portugal (Ordenações do Reino)</gloss></term>, title 16.

As for the <term>tax<gloss>original: "gabellam"</gloss></term>, when a <term>redhibitory action<gloss>an action to cancel the sale and return the item</gloss></term> or an action for a price reduction (*quanto minoris*) is granted in the circumstances of the preceding conclusion, the same must be said as was stated at the end of the third conclusion and after the fourth in the preceding discussion. Lassarte (in his work on sales, chapter 14, number 10) and others whom he cites agree. And it is in

<column-break/>

the events of this conclusion that the law *debet* (in the Digest on the Aedilian edict) speaks.

**8** **Third Conclusion.** The things said in the two preceding conclusions also apply when the seller was ignorant of the defect of the item, just as the buyer was—with two exceptions. First, the seller is not liable for damages, because he was not the cause of them, as his ignorance excuses him. Second, the contract remains valid, and only an action for a price reduction (*quanto minoris*) is granted against the seller. This is expressly held in the law *Julianus* at the beginning of the Digest on actions of purchase and in the <term>Siete Partidas<gloss>original: "l. 64. tit. 5. p. 5."; the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</gloss></term>. St. Thomas agrees (Summa Theologica, 2nd part of the 2nd part, question 77, article 2), as do Covarruvias, Juan Medina, Panormitanus, Domingo de Soto, Conradus, Sylvester, Martín de Azpilcueta (Navarrus), and the doctors of law commonly. The reason is, primarily, the nature of the thing itself: it is wrong to receive as much for a thing with a hidden defect as if it lacked that defect, since by its nature it is not worth as much. Secondly, positive law rightly decrees this.

**9** If the thing sold was a field for grazing that contained grass harmful to cattle, then a redhibitory action (to cancel the sale) is granted even if the seller was ignorant of the defect, as is held in the Code and the Partidas. The law *Julianus* adds that if someone, not knowing his slave was a <term>runaway<gloss>original: "fugitivum"</gloss></term> or a thief, sold him, although he is not liable for any subsequent damages in either case, he is nonetheless bound—when the slave was a runaway—to return however much less the slave was worth with that defect. But when the slave was a thief, the seller is liable for nothing.

The text gives the reason: although both are defects of the "soul" (character) and not the body, we can nonetheless keep a thief as a slave, but not a runaway. For that reason, in the case of a runaway, the seller is bound to refund the difference in value as if it were a matter of <term>eviction<gloss>the loss of a property right due to a legal claim</gloss></term>. However, the text says that if someone, not knowing the slave was a thief, sold him while assuring the buyer he was faithful, then he is bound to return the difference in value, because he should not have lightly affirmed what he did not know and deceived the buyer with his claim. Observe in this place, as held in the law *ob quae vitia*, that this is the distinction between defects of the soul and of the body.

**10** Thus, while the seller is liable to the buyer for a physical defect, he is not liable for a defect of the soul (character) unless it is specifically included in the agreement, and the seller promises that if the beast or slave is found to have such a character defect, he will rescind the sale or restore the amount by which the value is judged to have decreased. Defects of the soul include a horse being timid, or a beast being malicious, kicking, and similar things. Nevertheless, the same law excepts these two defects of the soul in slaves for which the seller is liable: being a thief or a runaway. And the law *Julianus* explains that if the seller knew of those character defects, he is liable not only for them but for all subsequent damages, just as if they were physical defects; but if he was ignorant of them, he is only liable for an action for a price reduction (*quanto minoris*).

<meta>This page continues Molina’s examination of the "Aedilian actions"—legal remedies for defects in purchased goods. The previous page discussed the expiration of these actions in civil law versus their persistence in the "court of conscience" (moral duty). This page moves into specific cases: defects like theft or flight in slaves, the impact of sales taxes (gabella) when a price is adjusted, and the moral obligations of a buyer who discovers an item is more valuable than the seller realized.</meta>

### On the Defects of Fugitives and Thieves

**10** Regarding the known defect of being a fugitive: one is generally not held liable for the defect of being a thief, unless the seller has specifically vouched that the slave is faithful <note>original: "assueuerit illum fidelem eſſe"</note>. However, the Law of Castile (64, title 5, part 5) seems to treat these as equal; it suggests that a seller who is ignorant that a slave is a thief and does not disclose it, or does not disclose the defect of being a fugitive, allows for the <term>action for price reduction<gloss>Latin: "actio quanto minoris"; a legal claim to recover the difference between the price paid and the actual value of the defective item</gloss></term> in both cases. This is unless you argue that the Castilian law should be interpreted according to the <term>common law<gloss>The standard Roman-Canonical legal tradition used across Europe</gloss></term>.

### On the Sales Tax (Gabella)

**11** Regarding the <term>sales tax<gloss>Latin: "gabella"; a common excise or contract tax</gloss></term> concerning the outcomes explained in this conclusion, I would say this: when the "action for price reduction" is granted without the fault of either party, the tax collector ought to remit and restore a portion of the tax. This follows what was discussed in Dispute 399: when a sale is reduced to equality <note>i.e., the price is made fair</note> without the fault of the contractors. However, when a <term>rescission of sale<gloss>Latin: "redhibitoria"; an action to cancel the sale entirely due to a hidden defect</gloss></term> is granted without fault, in Castile the seller shall bear the entire loss of the tax, while in Portugal, both contracting parties shall bear it equally. But when the action is granted because the seller promised a rescission if the sold item had a defect, then the seller alone shall bear the entire loss of the tax, even in Portugal, because he bound himself to that by his own word.

### Fourth Conclusion: When the Seller Errs in Value

**12** In a similar way, if someone—thinking a thing is defective—sells it at a lower price than it is worth (for example, if he sells a healthy slave believing him to be diseased, or a precious gem thinking it is glass or some other cheap material), the buyer is bound to increase the price up to the limits of the <term>lowest just price<gloss>The minimum fair market value for an item</gloss></term>. This is true whether the buyer bought it knowing the truth or being ignorant of it, and it follows the same reasoning we provided in the preceding conclusion. This is the view of St. Thomas [Aquinas], Conradus [Summenhart] on contracts, Medina, Soto, Silvester, Nauarrus, and the doctors of law generally.

However, when there is only an error in the *value* of the thing, and not in its substance, quantity, or some hidden quality, a legal action would not be granted in the external court <note>the public legal system</note> unless the seller was defrauded by more than half of the just price (according to what was said in Disputes 349 and 350). In that case, the tax to be paid would increase accordingly.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note>, in his *Summa* under the word "purchase" (2), says that if someone knows the value of a gem and buys it from a <term>rustic<gloss>A simple, uneducated country person or farmer</gloss></term> who is ignorant of its value, the buyer might tell the rustic that he wants to have the item with a completely clear conscience and without any scruples—and therefore, the rustic should see if he wishes to "gift" him any extra value the item might have. Cajetan argues that the buyer can then, with a healthy conscience, buy it for far less than it is worth without explaining its true value, provided the rustic agrees to the "gift." However, this opinion is improbable. One must undoubtedly say that the buyer is bound to make restitution to the rustic up to the full minimum value of the item. That "veiled" obtaining of a "gift" regarding the extra value does not have enough of a voluntary nature (due to the rustic’s ignorance) to make the donation valid.

However, I agree with what Cajetan teaches in the same place: namely, if both the buyer and the seller are ignorant of the value of the item, and they effectively entrust themselves to fortune, bargaining for a price so that—whether the thing is worth more or less—the sale remains firm and valid, then the sale is indeed valid. Neither of them is bound to any restitution if the item is later found to be worth much more or much less. The reason is the risk to which both exposed themselves. 

<column-break/>

Observe, however: if the buyer were shrewd and the seller simple, and the buyer bought the thing at a very cheap price because he saw he was exposing himself to almost no risk of loss but had a high probability of huge gain, then he is not safe in conscience. He is bound to restore at least as much as that "hope of gain" <note>original: "lucrādi ſpes"</note> was worth, which he bought from that simple person at such a low price.

Furthermore, if the sale was not truly a matter of both parties committing themselves to fortune in the way explained, but the rustic sold the item believing it was not worth more, the purchase would certainly be unjust—even if the other party, keeping silent, had intended to expose himself to some risk. It would be unjust by a much greater margin if the buyer intended to buy the thing in the common way other things are bought: namely, that if he found himself defrauded by a defect in the item, he would intend to reduce the contract to equality.

Note this: someone who buys a field in which he knows there is a treasure, or a vein of metal or precious stone (such as jasper or similar), is not bound to disclose this to the seller, nor to give a higher price for that field than it would be worth without the treasure or vein. The reason is either because—as Soto says (Book 6 on Justice, question 3, art. 2)—only the surface of the field is valued and sold; or because (as we said in Dispute 56) although the owner of the field could prohibit digging in it, just as he can prohibit hunting, nevertheless according to the <term>law of nations<gloss>Latin: "ius gentium"; laws considered common to all mankind</gloss></term>, the treasure does not belong to the owner of the field, but to the finder. This reasoning, as is clear from Dispute 54, does not apply to veins of metals, the ownership of which belongs to the owners of the fields. Nevertheless, the same must be said of them because of Soto's reasoning and because of what we add below. (The extent to which treasures and metal veins belong to the King under Castilian and Portuguese law was discussed in the cited disputes). This doctrine is confirmed by the fact that it is accepted by the law of nations that such a field, bought at a price otherwise just, is considered justly bought. This agrees with the words of Christ in Matthew 13: *The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid; and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.* We will add another, perhaps better reason, in the following doubt.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
**13** There is a doubt: if herbs are brought to be sold as fodder <note>original: "pabulũ"; animal feed</note> for beasts of burden, and a pharmacist <note>original: "pharmacopola"</note> is either able to buy them for that purpose, or discovers before he buys them that among them is an herb (or herbs) of great price for making medicines—is he safe in conscience by buying them at the price at which herbs are commonly sold for animal fodder, without disclosing the value of some of them to the seller? Or is he bound to restore to the seller the lowest just value they would have if it were understood what purpose they served? And although, according to what has been said so far, it might seem that he is not safe in conscience but bound to make restitution, I believe the contract should be upheld.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
First, because the intellect seems to lean toward this as the truth, and the contrary seems harsh. Second, because those herbs in that "mode of selling"—that is, as fodder for beasts—neither are worth more, nor are they commonly valued more by anyone in that place...

### Second Treatise

For this reason, since the pharmacist buys them at the common current price, and the price of the herb itself—insofar as it serves another use in his art and ministry—is the fruit of his own expertise and skill; he is certainly no more bound to restore the increase in price (because they are worth more for this other use) than the seller himself would be. If that seller had harvested those same herbs from the middle of someone’s crops as useless and harmful to the harvest, he would not be bound to restore the price to the owner of the field to whom they belonged as property before they were gathered. Nor would the same pharmacist be bound to restore anything if, while searching for herbs through the fields, he had found them among someone’s crops or in a field designated for animal pasture and gathered them from there.

This same principle confirms that one who knows a treasure or a vein of gold or silver lies hidden in someone's field is not bound to disclose it. Instead, he may buy the field at the common price at which it is valued for the use for which it is commonly sold. This kind of value is, in itself, the value of that field. However, the value by reason of the hidden treasure or vein is an **accidental value** of the same field. One who wishes to buy that field by reason of the common and inherent value of fields is not bound to disclose this accidental value.

<margin>14</margin> **Fifth conclusion.** If a defect—which was otherwise hidden—was known by the buyer at the time of the contract (either because the seller revealed it to him or because he recognized it by some other means), then neither an <term>action for rescission<gloss>Latin: "redhibitoria"; a legal action to cancel a sale due to a defect</gloss></term> nor any other action is granted to him in the **external court** <note>The civil or legal court system, as opposed to the internal court of conscience.</note>, unless he has been cheated beyond half of the <term>just price<gloss>Latin: "iustum pretium"; the fair market value determined by common estimation</gloss></term>. In that event, the remedy of Law 2 of the Code on Rescinding Sales is granted to him. Likewise, in the **court of conscience**, the contract is valid; but if the price is not equal to the thing's value, the seller is bound to bring the contract back to equality by restoring the excess he received beyond the <term>rigorous price<gloss>Latin: "pretium rigorosum"; the highest acceptable fair market price</gloss></term>. This conclusion is the common opinion of the doctors. <term>As for the first part, it is expressed in Law 1, paragraph "if it is understood," Law "if however," paragraph "to him who" of the Digest on the Aedilian Edict; Law 66, title 5, part 5; and other laws cited by Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of "Various Resolutions," chapter 2, number 48.</term> The remaining points are clear from what was said in Dispute 349 and those following.

<margin>15</margin> **Sixth conclusion.** If the seller, during the making of the contract, states that he does not wish to be held liable for any hidden defect, but that the buyer must purchase the item at his own risk, and the seller was truly ignorant of the defect, then he is not liable for the hidden defect. Indeed, if the price at the time of the contract was fair—considering the circumstances, the appearance of the thing, and the fact that the seller was shifting the risk of a hidden defect away from himself—then even if a defect were discovered later that made the price excessive, the seller would be bound to nothing, either in the external court or in the court of conscience. This is because the buyer bought the item at a just price, given the circumstances at the time of the contract, and took the risk of a hidden defect upon himself.

I rightly said in this conclusion, "and the seller was truly ignorant of the defect." For if he knew of any defect, even if he said in a general sense that he did not want to be held liable for the hidden defects of the thing, he will nonetheless be held liable in both the court of conscience and the external court, just as if he had said no such thing. This is established in the Law "I ask" <note>original: "l. quæro"</note> in the Digest on actions for purchase, where it is held: if someone sold a field and said, "I sell you this field, and if it has any

<column-break/>

### Dispute 353.
### 351

servitudes <note>Legal obligations or rights of way attached to a property.</note>, you will be bound by them," then if the seller was ignorant that the field had servitudes and some are later discovered, the seller is held to nothing. But if he knew it had a specific servitude and did not disclose it, an action is granted against him by reason of such a hidden defect which he did not express. It does not matter that he said in general that he did not wish to be held liable for servitudes, if there were any. In the same way, if someone says he is selling a thing with a specific defect, but mentions it as if it were hidden while listing other defects that the thing clearly does not have, it is the same as if he did not reveal the defect at all. An "action for rescission" or an <term>action for price reduction<gloss>Latin: "quanto minoris"; a claim to recover the difference in value caused by a defect</gloss></term> is granted against him. For example, if someone has a horse that is secretly lame and says: "I am selling you this horse as if it were lame, blind, and deaf, and as a horse having all other defects," such a disclosure is invalid. All these things are held in Law 66, title 5, part 5; and Panormitanus, Soto, Navarrus, and Antonio Gómez agree in the places cited, as do the doctors commonly.

<margin>16</margin> **Seventh conclusion.** If a defect is **open and manifest**, no action is granted against the seller in the external court, unless the buyer has been defrauded of more than half the just price. This is common opinion and is clear from Law 1, paragraph "if it is understood," and Law "if however," paragraph "to him who" of the Digest on the Aedilian Edict, and other laws cited by Antonio Gómez. In the court of conscience, the contract is also valid, and if it is equal, the seller is held to nothing. However, this is understood to mean: unless at the time of the contract it was clearly evident to the seller that the buyer was ignorant of a notable defect that was otherwise open. In that case, in the court of conscience, he would be bound to warn him if the item, with that defect, were notably useless for the purpose for which he bought it, as the doctors commonly affirm.

<margin>17</margin> <margin>Doubt</margin> There is a **doubt** as to whether it is universally lawful for a seller not to disclose a defect in a thing, provided he reduces the price by as much as the thing is worth less because of that defect.
<margin>Decision</margin> The doctors commonly agree with **St. Thomas** (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 77, article 3) that this is lawful when the defect is manifest in itself. For then, if he mentions the defect, he could easily prejudice himself by giving the buyer an occasion to reduce the just price; thus, when the defect is manifest in itself, he is not bound to disclose it.

<margin>Question</margin> When the defect is **hidden**, St. Thomas in the same place (and in his commentary on the Sentences, Book 4, distinction 15, question 2, article 1, as he seems to affirm) suggests that when no danger threatens the buyer from the defect, considering the purpose for which he bought the thing, the seller can choose not to reveal the defect to him. This is provided he decreases the price enough so that the price does not exceed the value of the thing. St. Thomas relies on the fact that since no harm follows for the buyer from the defect and the contract is equal, the seller is using his right by not disclosing a hidden defect; if he did disclose it, he might prejudice himself by providing an occasion for something to be taken away from the just price. **Gerson** held this same opinion, as do **Cajetan** (on the cited article 3) and **Soto** (De Iustitia et Iure, book 6, question 3, article 2). They add, however, that if the buyer is of a kind who can be presumed to be going to resell the same thing, the seller is bound—after the thing has been delivered—to warn him of the hidden defect, so that the buyer himself does not deceive another purchaser in the same amount that was deducted for him.

Conrado de Summenhart on Contracts, question 54; Juan Medina on Restitution.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal and moral analysis of the "Contract of Sale," specifically focusing on the seller's obligation to disclose hidden defects in the goods being sold. ### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

<note>original: "restit. q. 34." refers to questions on restitution.</note> Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in the chapter *Iniustum* regarding the exchange of things; Gabriel Biel <note>a German scholastic philosopher</note> in his commentary on the 4th book, distinction 15; Sylvester Prierias under the word *emptio* <note>purchase</note>, question 20; and Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 23, number 89, all hold a specific opinion. They believe that when it is likely presumed that a buyer would still purchase an item even if they knew of a defect (though perhaps not as willingly), it is lawful for the seller not to disclose that **hidden defect**, provided they subtract from the price as much as the item is worth less because of that defect.

However, they say that when it is likely believed the buyer would *not* have bought the item at all if they had known the defect, then failing to disclose it is a sin, and the contract is considered null and void. Bartholomaeus de Medina says the same applies when it is doubtful whether the buyer would have purchased it with the defect revealed. They are led to this conclusion because they believe such a contract is **involuntary** on the part of the buyer; ignorance causes an involuntary consent, and for that reason, the contract is null.

<margin>Decision</margin> I believe a middle path should be walked. First, it must be observed that not every hidden defect renders a contract invalid in the **external forum** <note>the public law courts, as opposed to the internal "court of conscience"</note>, nor does every defect grant grounds for a <term>redhibitory action</term> <note>a legal action to cancel a sale and get a refund due to a defect</note> or an action for a <term>price reduction</term> <note>original: "actione quanto minoris," a legal claim to get back the difference between the price paid and the actual value</note>. Rather, this only applies to defects that make the item **notably less useful** for the purpose for which it is customarily bought. This is established in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de ædi. edict." referring to the Edict of the Curule Aediles in Roman Law</note>, where it is explained at length which defects are significant enough to help a buyer via a refund or price reduction, and which are not. Gregorius Lopez observes the same regarding the laws of the *Siete Partidas* <note>the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> regarding "bad illness." For this reason, at the start of this discussion, when we mentioned defects in quality, we deliberately said: "whether it is a notable defect in quality compared to the use for which the thing is bought, such that it is notably less useful for that purpose."

<margin>19</margin> Next, it must be observed that the foundation of the previous argument—that the contract is "involuntary due to ignorance"—is **false**. This is the foundation upon which Conradus and others lean, as we partly discussed in the previous dispute. If that foundation were universally true, then whenever a buyer was ignorant of even a minor quality—which, if known, would have stopped the purchase—the contract would be null by the law itself, whether the seller knew of it or not. Consequently, as soon as the buyer learned of it after the contract was finished, they could dissolve it. Indeed, it would be null in the **forum of conscience** <note>the moral standing before God</note> for lack of voluntary will. But no one would concede this; no one would admit such a rule into the practice of contracting, nor is it beneficial for the **common good**. Contracts are not understood to be celebrated under such a rule, even in the forum of conscience alone.

Furthermore, as Domingo de Soto rightly argues, just as a buyer can be "involuntary" about a purchase when a hidden defect is ignored, they can also be "involuntary" regarding the **quantity of the price** they give within the "range of the just price" <note>Scholastics believed the "just price" wasn't a single number but a range: "lowest," "mid," and "rigorous/highest."</note>. If the buyer knew of the defect, they wouldn't want to buy it at that price, but at a lower one. Therefore, if the foundation of those other doctors were true, it would be illicit not to reveal a defect even to a buyer who would still buy the item, just at a lower price. The seller would be bound to restore whatever they received above what the buyer *would* have given. However, the authors whose foundation we are overturning actually deny this.

<column-break/>

<margin>20</margin> Having established these points, I believe it should be said: When **defects do not render the thing notably less useful** for its intended purpose, the seller is not bound to disclose them, even if they presume the buyer would not purchase it if they knew.

The seller is, however, bound to lower the price so that it does not exceed the "rigorous" <note>highest</note> just price, considering all the concurrent circumstances. But if the defects **notably render the item less useful** for its customary use, the seller is bound to disclose them, even if they presume the buyer would still buy it, though at a lower price.

For example: if someone sells a slave who is healthy, not a runaway, not a thief, not a drunkard, and not afflicted with any other notable defect, the seller is **not bound to disclose** that the slave has a harsh personality, is slow at work, is a "friend of wine" <note>original: "vini amicum," meaning someone who drinks a bit too much but isn't a functional alcoholic</note>, or has some other similar common vice of slaves.

Furthermore, if a shoemaker makes shoes from a weaker part of the leather, he is certainly not bound to warn the buyer about this. Firstly, because the defect is somewhat manifest. Secondly, because the item is useful in its own way according to the quality of the leather; for not all shoes can be made from the firmest leather. It will be enough, therefore, if he moderates the price according to the quality of the shoes. However, if the leather were "burnt" <note>chemically damaged or brittle</note> and for that reason the shoes were likely to break quickly, and the defect was hidden from a buyer who isn't an expert in leather quality, the seller would be bound not only to match the price to the quality but also to **warn the buyer**. He should say that the shoes would otherwise be worth more, but because the leather is somewhat burnt and will last less time, he is reducing the price accordingly.

The reason is that such a quality causes the shoes to break much sooner, making them **notably less useful** for their intended use than shoes usually are by their nature. In the same way, a merchant who sells cloth that is badly burnt and will soon tear is bound not only to reduce the price but also to warn the buyer of the damage. Likewise, with hats <note>original: "galeti" or "galeri"</note>, not all turn out with the same weave or utility. When a defect is not very notable—perhaps the hat will last, but not as long as others, or won't keep its shine as long—the craftsman is not bound to reveal the defect, but only to moderate the price.

But if the defect were very notable, rendering the hat largely useless for its purpose, he would be bound not only to set a price according to quality but also to say: "I am selling this so cheaply because it will not last long," etc. The conclusions proposed in this arrangement should be understood according to this doctrine.

I am led to assert this for two reasons. First, because this matter must be understood **morally**. Second, if craftsmen were bound to disclose every single defect in the things they put up for sale, it would result in a notable loss for them, as the price would be dragged down by deterred buyers. It would impose an **extremely heavy yoke** upon human commerce, which even god-fearing people could not bear; indeed, it would be very harmful to those who...

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "dete-" (likely "detegunt" or "deterrentur"), continuing the argument about the practical burdens on trade.</meta>

<summary>Molina argues for a balanced approach to commercial transparency, stating that sellers must disclose "notable" defects that significantly impair an item's utility, but for minor flaws, a simple price adjustment is sufficient to maintain a "just price." He rejects the idea that any hidden flaw automatically voids a contract, arguing that such a strict rule would destroy human commerce.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 3.

...by revealing defects, they would find very few buyers, and much would be deducted from their price; whereas, on the contrary, those who are less God-fearing would find many buyers by remaining silent about such flaws.

Secondly, although the obligation to reveal defects is rooted in the very nature of things, this must be understood gently and according to what human commerce and our shared human frailty require. It also depends greatly on the arrangement and moderation of human law. For the civil law does not intend to place such a heavy burden on the necks of men that they are bound to manifest every single defect of a thing universally, but only the **serious** ones which render the thing notably less useful, as is evident from the entire title in the *Digest on the Edict of the Aediles* <note>original: "ff. de ædil. edict." refers to Roman law regarding the responsibilities of sellers for defective goods</note>.

I would advise that, in both the **external forum** <note>the public courts of law</note> and the **forum of conscience** <note>the internal moral standing before God</note>, one should not consider whether the thing is useless specifically to the person who bought it, but rather whether it is useful or useless in itself for the purpose for which it is normally bought. For example, if a slightly lame horse is sold to a "gentle doctor" <note>likely meaning a doctor who only needs a horse for light travel rather than heavy labor or war</note> without the defect being revealed: even if the horse is not particularly useless for the specific purpose the doctor bought it for, since it is nonetheless notably less useful in itself for the general use of a horse, a **redhibitory action** <term>an action to cancel a sale and return the price</term> or an action for **a reduction in price** <term>original: "quanto minoris"; a legal claim to recover the difference between the price paid and the actual value</term> will be granted to him in the external forum. The obligation is the same in the forum of conscience, regardless of what Domingo de Soto and a few others might say to the contrary.

When a thing is found to be notably less useful because of a **hidden defect**, and the contract is to be rescinded, the seller returns the price, but receives back the item along with any "fruits" <note>profits or offspring, such as a foal from a horse or rent from a building</note> perceived from it, after deducting the buyer's expenses and the effort they applied.

When a buyer asks about the defects of a thing, the seller is bound to reveal them, even if they do not render it notably less useful. If they are not revealed, it constitutes true **fraud** <term>original: "dolus"; intentional deception</term> on the part of the seller. Consequently, if the buyer would not have bought the item had they known of the defects, the fraud is the "cause" of the contract, and the contract is therefore null in both the forum of conscience and the external forum. If, however, the buyer would still have bought it but at a lower price, the fraud "incidental" to the contract requires restitution in conscience and the external forum only for the amount by which the buyer would have paid less. But if the buyer would have bought it at the same price anyway (because the seller would not have given it for less, and the buyer could not find another seller at a lower price), then, since the lie was only used to complete the contract more quickly or smoothly, the seller is bound to no restitution. In this specific event, the lie is not "pernicious" <note>meaning it does not cause harm or loss of property</note>. In other cases, however, the lie is pernicious, and if the matter is grave, it is a **mortal sin** <note>original: "culpa lethalis"; a serious sin that separates the soul from God</note>, whatever Soto says to the contrary in the place cited above.

When, according to what has been said so far, a seller is bound to manifest a defect, or a buyer is bound to warn a seller of the greater value of a thing, if this is not done knowingly, it must be judged as either a mortal or venial sin based on the amount of harm to which the other party is exposed. Because a notable loss threatens one who buys from a **heretic** or someone else who has by law lost their property due to a crime—since there is a risk the crime will be brought to judgment and the person condemned to the loss of goods they owned from the moment the crime was committed—the fact that those goods are subject to such danger is a major defect. Consequently, it is a mortal sin for such a criminal to sell their goods at that time or to dispose of 

<column-break/>

notably valuable property through another burdensome contract without manifesting that "defect" of legal risk, as Martin de Azpilcueta <note>referred to as "Navarrus"</note> concludes in the cited number 89, and as we have said in Disputation 93.

When, however, someone fails to manifest a defect they were bound to reveal due to **vincible ignorance** <term>ignorance that could have been overcome through reasonable effort</term>, then a mortal sin could still occur if a notable harm results for the neighbor. Especially if the thing being sold were harmful, the seller would be bound not only to restore the amount the thing was worth less because of the defect, or to dissolve the contract, but also to restore any subsequent damages, since they followed from their own fault—vincible ignorance by no means excuses one from blame.

It must also be observed that when a contract is null because a hidden defect was not revealed, if the purchased thing perishes, it perishes for the seller; they are nonetheless bound to return what they received for it. They will only receive back whatever remains of the item, along with the profits the buyer gained from it, after deducting expenses and the value of the labor applied. The reason is that a thing normally perishes for its owner; but through a contract that is null by law, the ownership of the purchased thing never actually passed to the buyer.

<margin>22</margin> It must furthermore be observed that if many things are bought together and only one is defective enough to be returned, and the contract for that item is null according to what has been said: if the remaining items are so connected to it that separating them is difficult—for instance, if many servants were bought together for a specific service and the remaining ones cannot perform it without the one who is defective—then the contract is dissolved for all of them, even if the individual items were bought at distinct prices. But if they do not have such a connection, then only the defective one is to be returned and its price restored (if it was sold for a specific price, or based on an estimation by a judge's order if the parties do not agree). This is the view of Antonio Gómez in his *Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 2, number 48, following various laws and doctors whom he cites.

<margin>23</margin> Regarding what was said in conclusions 5 and 7—namely, that when a buyer recognizes a defect, no legal action is granted to them—observe this: if the defect is in **quantity** (for example, in weight or measure) and the item is regulated by public authority (such as bread of a certain weight or wine of a certain measure for a set price), then even if the buyer recognizes the shortfall and consents because they cannot find another way to buy, an obligation still arises for the seller in the forum of conscience to restore the missing amount. Likewise, a legal action is granted in the external forum.

The reason is that in things taxed by public authority, the **just price** in comparison to a thing of a certain weight or measure consists in an indivisible point. For that reason, whatever is subtracted from the substance of the thing regarding weight or measure by one receiving the full price taxed by law, justice is violated to that extent and restitution is owed. Nor does the fact that the buyer knew of the defect and bought it anyway prevent this obligation; for that "tacit consent" to being defrauded of part of the goods was not fully voluntary, but mixed with the involuntary. For a "donation" of that sort to be...

<margin>24</margin> Observe: if a price is established by public authority for bread of a specific weight—for example—it would be unjust if it were too low. This is because, when considering the actual value at which wheat is commonly bought by those who make and sell such bread, and considering the labor and expenses involved in the baking, no just or moderate <term>stipend</term> <note>compensation or profit for labor</note> remains for their work and the money they have rightly invested at the risk of loss. In such a case, they neither sin nor are they bound to <term>restitution</term> <note>the legal and moral obligation to pay back a debt or repair a wrong</note> if they reduce the weight of the bread by as much as is necessary for a just and moderate compensation to remain for them.
The reason is that they are not bound to abandon these services which are necessary to the Commonwealth. Since the price taxed by public authority is found to be unjust in practice, the public law does not bind the conscience in this matter, because it is found to be unjust, at least <term>materially</term> <note>meaning that while the law was intended to be fair, its physical result in the real world is unfair due to circumstances like high grain prices</note>. What has been said regarding bread is to be understood in a similar way for all other things whose prices are fixed by public authority. In confessions, the consciences of those who claim the price is unjust due to its smallness should be burdened; it must be diligently examined whether this is truly the case. One should ask about the price at which they buy a measure of wheat, the additional expenses they incur, the labor they apply, the number of loaves they produce for sale, the value of the bran and lesser flour that remains, and finally, after computing everything, it must be weighed whether the situation is as they say. They should not be allowed to subtract more from the weight than is necessary for a moderate compensation—which should lean toward the lower rather than the rigorous end of the scale.
<margin>25</margin> When the price is not fixed by law, and something is mixed into the things being sold—such as water into wine, or some unusual substance into medicines—a distinction must be made. If the mixtures can cause harm, then those selling the goods mixed in that way are bound to all subsequent damages, and likewise to the restitution of the amount by which those goods are worth less to the buyer than what he gave for them. If, however, they do not cause harm but are nevertheless less useful for the purpose for which they are bought, then the sellers are bound to restore how much less they are worth to the buyers for that purpose. Therefore, if they are of no use for that purpose, they are bound to restore the entire price; for example, if a medicine is rendered useless for its intended purpose because of the mixture.
But if the goods mixed in that way are still useful for the purpose for which they are bought, and as much is taken off the price as is fair for the mixture, then the sellers are not bound to restitution, because they have not exceeded the just price. Nevertheless, they sin unless they do this compelled by necessity—for instance, because they cannot otherwise extract a just price for the item (such as wine) unless they mix a little water into it, or unless the item with that mixture is truly worth what is given for it, and the buyer would not have bought a better version for that same price.
However, sellers must be restrained from such fallacies and deceptions. On these points, Conrad <note>original: "Conrad. de contractibus" refers to Conrad Summenhart, a 15th-century theologian</note> in his questions 54 and 55, and Juan Medina <note>original: "Ioan. Medin." refers to Juan de Medina, a Spanish theologian</note> in his

<column-break/>

treatise on restitution, question 34, the penultimate section, and Sylvester <note>original: "Sylu." refers to Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio</note> under the word "buying," question 19, and others agree. Soto <note>original: "Sotus" refers to Domingo de Soto, a major figure in the School of Salamanca</note> also approaches this in his work *On Justice and Law*, book 6, question 3, article 2.

## Whether a sale is just at the current price when made by someone who knew that goods of the same kind would soon arrive in great abundance, or that a decree <note>original: "pragmaticam," a royal legal ordinance</note> by which the price would be reduced was soon to be promulgated.

# DISPUTATION 354.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> 1. *One who sells goods at the current price, knowing that others of the same kind will soon arrive in great abundance, does not sin against justice, nor is he bound to restitution.*
<margin>2</margin> 2. *Indeed, he does not even sin against charity. (Number 2).*
<margin>3</margin> 3. *He does sin, however, if he knows a decree or law is about to be published regarding the reduction of the price. (Number 3).*
<margin>4</margin> 4. *A Prince sins against justice, with the burden of restoring damages, if he does not see to it that laws regarding the reduction of the price of things are published as soon as possible.*
<margin>5</margin> 5. *If a seller knows a law is about to be published regarding the value of goods, can he put them up for sale in a large quantity, especially knowing that buyers, ignorant of the law, would buy just as much from others at the same price?*
<margin>6</margin> 6. *A merchant who knows a siege is being prepared for a city in which he had goods, and quickly sells them: is he bound to restore the price to the buyers if the goods are plundered by the enemies or if they suffer loss for them in some other way?*
<margin>7</margin> 7. *One who has a house in a court city <note>where the royal court resides</note> which he knew would soon depart, and rents it out at the then-current price: does he sin, and is he bound to restitution?*

<margin>1</margin> Conrad Summenhart in his *On Contracts*, questions 62 and 63, and Juan Medina in his *On Restitution*, question 35—following Cicero and Antipater in the third book of *On Duties* <note>original: "de officijs"</note>—assert that he who sells his goods at the current price, knowing that others of the same kind will soon arrive in great abundance while the buyers are ignorant of this, sins against justice and is bound to restitution.
They are led to this first because that abundance soon to arrive truly decreases the price; it is as if the goods were already present. Since, if it were known, the price would immediately decrease in reality before those goods arrived, therefore, he who sells at the current price while knowing this sells beyond the just price, and thus sins against justice and is bound to restore the difference.
Secondly, they argue that the common estimation that the then-current price is just is based on error and ignorance of the fact that so many goods are arriving. Therefore, the just price at that time should not be considered according to that common estimation, but according to...
