### Second Treatise, Dispute 35.

the truth of the matter, and therefore the just price will be that which would exist if the knowledge currently missing were present to the buyer.

Third, because a seller is bound to reveal a hidden defect of a thing to the buyer that makes it less valuable, as is clear from the points discussed in the previous dispute. However, the fact that similar goods are about to arrive in great abundance makes the current goods no less "devalued" in reality. Therefore, in a similar way, he is bound to reveal this to the buyer, and not accept a price higher than he would receive if the buyers possessed the same knowledge that he has.

<margin>1st Decision.</margin>
The opposite opinion is embraced by Saint Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologica 2.2. question 77, article 3, reply 4), Cajetan in the same place, Domingo de Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 3, article 2, reply 3), Gabriel Biel, Sylvester Prierias, Covarruvias, Arias Pinel, and others whom they cite. This was also the opinion of Diogenes, whom Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> mentions in his favor. We should also embrace this view: namely, that he who sells goods in this manner neither sins against justice nor is bound to any <term>restitution</term> <note>the moral obligation to return ill-gotten gains or compensate for a loss</note>. Nevertheless, they add that it is a "fullness of virtue" <note>an act of exceptional merit beyond what is strictly required</note> if he discloses the matter or lowers the price.

This is proved, first, because if he were sinning against justice and were bound to restitution, then surely those who sold their goods at the current price while being *ignorant* that more goods were arriving would also be bound to restitution. Even if they did not sin (due to their excusable ignorance), they would still be selling items at an excessive price. Since no one admits this consequence—indeed, even the authors of the opposing view deny it—it follows that the person with knowledge does not sin against justice nor is he bound to restitution. The logic holds because the goods themselves are not worth more in the hand of an ignorant man than in the hand of one who knows more goods are coming; therefore, if the latter is bound to restitution because of an "excess" over the just price, the others would be too.

Second, the <term>just price</term> <note>the fair market value determined by the community rather than an individual</note> of a thing is what items of that type or similar ones are worth *here and now* according to common estimation in that place—whether certain circumstances are commonly known or commonly unknown—provided those circumstances do not make the thing defective in itself. Since the private knowledge of a few individuals does not remove the common estimation, nor make the thing defective in itself, it follows that it does not decrease the price of the items.

Third, because if such commonly unknown circumstances were to decrease the price, it would follow that someone who sold grain at the high current price during a drought would be bound to return part of the price if rain suddenly fell due to natural causes; but no one says this. The logic is clear because the circumstance—that rain was about to fall by natural causes—is of such a nature that it would have decreased the price if it had been known by the buyers and sellers.

Fourth, because if a specific individual's knowledge of a future abundance decreased the just price of what he sells, then likewise a specific individual's knowledge of a future shortage would increase the price of items he might buy to save for that time of need, since the reasoning is the same. Thus, Joseph would have sinned,

<column-break/>

and would have been unjust (with the burden of restitution) when, in Genesis 41, he bought and stored grain at the current price during the time of abundance, knowing by private knowledge of the great shortage soon to follow. If the Egyptians had perceived this in the same way, they would by no means have sold their grain at a low price; rather, each would have kept it for themselves for the time of famine, so they wouldn't have to surrender all their possessions later to feed themselves, as they did.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
The doubt remains whether, even if such a person does not sin against justice nor is bound to restitution, he nonetheless sins mortally against <term>charity</term> <note>the Christian duty to love and care for one's neighbor</note>. There are those who say he does.

<margin>2nd Decision.</margin>
Saint Thomas clearly suggests the contrary when he says it is only a "fullness of virtue" to reveal a future abundance or lower the price. By these words, he clearly teaches that doing so is a work of <term>supererogation</term> <note>an act that is good to do but not a sin to omit</note>, and therefore the opposite is not a sin. This must undoubtedly be affirmed: since he is using his own right and selling his goods at a just price. <margin>3</margin> However, in this specific event, I believe a sin against justice *is* found, carrying the burden of restitution: if someone knows a law has been established by which the price of grain or the value of money is to be decreased (as in Portugal, where the value of copper coins was rightly decreased by public law to almost half in recent years). If, because of such knowledge of a law not yet <term>promulgated</term> <note>officially announced to the public</note>, he sells more grain at the expense of others who were ignorant of it than he would have otherwise sold, or spends more of that money than he would have otherwise distributed. I am led to assert this because a public law should be equal and common to all subjects. A prince would sin against justice if, before it was announced to everyone, he revealed it to certain people who, anticipating the announcement, became rich at the expense of others. By the same logic, whoever uses knowledge of that law to the prejudice of others—no matter how that knowledge reached him—sins against justice and is burdened with restoring the losses that happened to his neighbors in that way.

<margin>4</margin>
Thus, a prince sins against justice, with the burden of restoring damages, unless he carefully ensures that such laws are kept as secret as possible and are promulgated across the whole kingdom simultaneously, so that some are not enriched through the injury and detriment of others due to knowing such laws early. Bartolus clearly agrees with this opinion of ours, as cited by Covarruvias. Covarruvias suggests this is the practice in the <term>external forum</term> <note>the public legal court system</note>; though, not noticing that the reasoning is different in this case compared to when one knows goods are arriving, he adds that in the <term>forum of conscience</term> <note>the internal moral judgment of the soul and God</note>, the opposite should be asserted following Saint Thomas. Arias Pinel agrees with us much more clearly, providing the distinction between the two scenarios.

<margin>5</margin>
For he who uses knowledge of a law before it is announced to enrich himself at the loss of others is using knowledge of something that ought to be common to all, to the detriment of others; and therefore he does them an injury. But he who uses knowledge that goods are arriving to the same effect does not...
<meta>catchword: ...use</meta>

<summary>Molina argues that while market-driven "insider information" (like knowing a shipment is coming) doesn't require price adjustments, using "insider information" about upcoming government laws or currency devaluations is a sin against justice requiring restitution.</summary>

### Ludovico Molina 
### On Contracts

He uses knowledge of a matter that ought to be common to all; rather, this pertains to the industry, skill, and the luck of merchants. Alvarius Valerius agrees with this opinion of ours in his 64th consultation, at the end of number 8, where he refers to several others as well.

However, I spoke carefully a little while ago when I said: "if, having knowledge of a law of this kind that has not yet been promulgated, he sells more grain than he otherwise would have sold, or spends more money than he otherwise would have distributed." This is because, on account of that knowledge, his condition does not remain worse than that of others, nor worse than his own condition would have been if he did not have that knowledge. Therefore, he can perform all those actions with a clear <term>conscience</term> <note>inner moral sense of right and wrong</note> that he would have done even without that knowledge; it does not matter that a loss to others follows incidentally. This is because, like everyone else, he sells grain and distributes money at the current price, which is what they are truly worth at that time.

<margin>Question 5</margin> 
You may ask: can he use this knowledge to sell *more* grain than he otherwise would have sold if it does not result in a loss for the buyers? For example, if they were going to buy just as much from others at the same price—others who were also ignorant of the law. Similarly, can he use that knowledge to spend more money than he otherwise would have spent if it does not result in a detriment to the recipients? For example, if he buys things with that money from people who will spend it immediately, or gives it as a loan to someone who will use it right away.

<margin>Decision</margin> 
The answer must be in the negative. This is because, although it does not result in a detriment to the recipients immediately, it nevertheless results in a detriment to other citizens in whose hands that money will be at the time the law is promulgated. And because it results in a detriment to other citizens who would otherwise have sold their goods at the current price, had he not sold so much to them because of his knowledge that the price was about to be reduced.

There are, however, several points to observe regarding the more common opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, which we embrace. The first is that while it is permitted for someone who knows a massive supply of goods is coming to not only sell his goods at the current price but even to put *more* of them up for sale than he otherwise would, it is nonetheless a sin—carrying the burden of <term>restitution</term> <note>the requirement to pay back the victim for their loss</note>—to use fraud, lies, and deceit to induce people to buy them who will suffer a loss as a result. This is because they clearly would not have bought so much before the arrival of the other goods unless they had been led to it by fraud. For, although it is permitted to put one's goods up for sale regardless of that knowledge, and to allow the loss of others for one's own profit and advantage by selling at the just price then current, it is nonetheless a sin and contrary to justice to induce anyone through lies, fraud, and deceit to undergo a loss in that manner. Neither Saint Thomas nor the other authors of the same opinion assert the contrary, nor is this what they call into controversy.

<margin>Case</margin> 
The second point is this: just as in other moral matters, when one circumstance is varied, the case is easily changed—whence it often happens that someone who does not attend to that circumstance gives an answer contrary to what he otherwise would have given—so the same can easily happen in the matter proposed here. I shall clarify the matter with an example, from which many other things can be easily understood. There was a rumor that those who had obtained a license from the King in this city of Cuenca <note>original: "Conchensi"</note> to mint copper coins had greatly exceeded that license,

<column-break/>

or their authority. The matter was reported to the King, and he secretly ordered the city governor to suddenly close the mint, forbidding any more coins to be minted or anything to be removed from that building. Before this order was executed, it came to the knowledge of a certain individual who had a massive quantity of copper mixed with silver in that building, already flattened into plates (which they call *rieles*) so that coins might be made from them. He sold that mass for six thousand gold pieces to someone who was completely ignorant of the situation, making many excuses (as the buyer claimed) for why he was selling, by which the buyer was induced to purchase. Shortly thereafter, the mint was suddenly closed, and doubts began to arise as to whether the contract was just and valid, and whether the buyer was bound to undergo that risk and pay the price for which he had bought the mass. Many responded in the affirmative,

<margin>Decision</margin> 
guided by the opinion of Saint Thomas explained thus far. I, however, always consistently said that the contract was null and that the buyer was not bound to pay the price. In this matter, I often found the seller to be quite God-fearing and entirely ready to clear his conscience, and willing to stand by my judgment, whatever others might affirm to the contrary. I argued: First, because the seller had used his knowledge of a secret royal decree before it was executed to sell the item and cast his own loss and risk onto the buyer. This does not have the same weight in the case proposed as it does in a public law regarding the taxation of goods or the value of money, which ought to be equal and common to all. Second, because, as the buyer presented the case, the seller did not lead the buyer to purchase merely by putting the goods up for sale, but by many fabrications by which he induced him to buy, so that he might shift the loss and risk hanging over him onto the buyer. We explained just a moment ago that this is not permitted and pertains to fraud and deceit. Third, and especially, because by the very fact that such a huge transgression of the King's licenses had been made, and that the material (beyond the license obtained) was prepared in a public building for minting coins, the material was "tainted" <note>legally defective or "vitiosa"</note> in that it was liable to be seized by the King as a penalty, as indeed happened later by a judge's sentence. Therefore, just as the goods of heretics and others who have incurred the loss of their property by the law itself are considered "tainted," and the seller is bound to reveal the defect to the buyer (otherwise deceit gives cause to the contract, if the buyer would not have bought it had he known the defect, as was said in the preceding dispute), so that material under those circumstances was tainted. Consequently, since it was sold without the taint and the risk it already faced being disclosed, and the buyer would by no means have bought it if he had known, the contract was certainly null, as deceit gave cause to it, according to what was said in the previous dispute.

From what has been said so far, it will be easy to understand what should be said in the following event. <margin>6</margin> A certain merchant knew that a siege was being prepared for the city in which he had goods, while others were generally ignorant of it. He quickly sold them and took the payment. The question is: is he bound to make restitution to the buyers if the goods are later plundered by enemies, or if they suffered a loss on account of them for some other reason?

-> Response <-

<meta>The catchword "Respon-" indicates the next page begins with "Respondeo" (I respond).</meta>

<summary>Molina clarifies that while selling with secret market knowledge is generally allowed, using lies or fraud to induce a sale is a sin requiring restitution. He uses a local case from Cuenca involving an illegal minting operation to demonstrate that selling "tainted" goods liable to royal seizure without disclosure renders a contract void.</summary>
<keywords>just price, market ethics, fraud, Cuenca, minting, royal decree, tainted goods, restitution, contracts, siege</keywords>

--- Page 322 ---
<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of whether a merchant with private knowledge of future market shifts must disclose it. He is concluding his refutation of stricter views (like those of Summenhart and Medina) and beginning a new discussion on credit sales and usury.</meta>

Second Treatise. Dispute 355.

The answer is that if that merchant merely put his goods out for sale and sold them at the current price—without lies or other frauds and deceits—he is neither bound to make restitution nor has he sinned; rather, he has exercised his own right. For the fact that a siege was being prepared <note>original: "obsidio pararetur"</note> is not to be considered a defect in the goods themselves, in the same way that goods are considered defective if they are liable to be seized as a just penalty for the seller's crime. That is a different kind of danger, which looms from an external cause; it is not a quality of the thing itself, even when compared to the external cause. Therefore, just as when wine or wheat is destined to be spoiled by an external cause, but does not have an internal quality that makes it easily susceptible to corruption, it is not considered a defect of the wheat or wine; so too, the fact that a siege is being prepared against a city is not considered a defect in the things that are inside it.

<margin>Question 7</margin>
In the following case as well, there is neither an obligation to make restitution nor a sin. A man who had a house near the court <note>The "curia" or traveling royal court, which brought immense business to a city</note> knew that the court would soon depart from there. He rented out his house at the price then current; when the court actually left, the price of the lease—both for that house and for others—was greatly reduced. Truly, he exercised his own right by leasing the house at the price current at that time, without lies, fraud, or deceit. It is no obstacle that if the person renting it had known the court was going to depart, he would not have rented the house at such a price, or perhaps not at all.

Regarding the first argument for the opinion of Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart, a German theologian</note> and Medina <note>Bartholomew de Medina, a Spanish Scholastic</note>, the premise must be denied. As has been said, the **just price** is determined according to the common estimation of men, regardless of circumstances that are unknown. Therefore, it must be denied that an abundance of goods which is unknown should have the same effect on lowering the price as if it were present or known. Indeed, even if the goods had already arrived, as long as the fact was not commonly known, the just price of the goods would be what they were commonly estimated at by those who were commonly ignorant of the arrival of the others.

Regarding the second argument: even if the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied. The fact that the common estimation is founded on ignorance does not prevent the price, as commonly estimated, from being truly just.

Regarding the third argument: once the major premise is granted, the minor must be denied while the fact remains unknown, as is clear from what has been said.

# Whether it is lawful to sell a thing more dearly in expectation of payment, or to buy it more cheaply with advanced payment, especially on account of lost profit or emergent loss.

## DISPUTATION 355.

->### S U M M A R Y<-

*1. When it is lawful to sell a thing on credit more dearly while waiting for payment, and to buy more cheaply with advanced payment.*

<column-break/>

*2. A person who sells a thing for a term beyond the "rigorous" just price, or buys below the "lowest" just price because of advanced payment, commits usury. Clarify this, however, and understand it as in number 4.*

*3. Merchants commit usury if, at the end of a trade fair when the price of goods usually decreases, they sell their goods on credit for the price that was current at the beginning of the fair.*

*5. When a person selling goods on credit at a higher price than they are worth at the time of the contract is excused from usury, and when they are not.*

*6. How the price of "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>Profit a seller misses out on because they don't have the cash in hand to reinvest</note> is to be calculated.*

*7. If a seller is about to sell his goods immediately, but it is believed they will be worth more in three months, whether he can sell them on credit to be paid at that time for the price they are expected to be worth then.*

*8. Goods that will be worth more in the future are not worth more at the present time to one who is compelled to sell them.*

This matter is for the most part clear from what was said regarding **usury**. However, as a supplement to both that matter and this one, a few things should be added here.

1. Everyone agrees that since the **just price** of a thing (when not fixed by law) does not consist of a single point <note>meaning there is a range of acceptable prices</note>, it is lawful to sell a thing on credit for more than if the money were paid immediately, provided it stays within the range of the just price—that is, up to the **rigorous** <note>highest</note> just price. Similarly, it is lawful to buy a thing more cheaply with advanced money within the range of the just price—that is, down to the **lowest** just price.

The reason is manifest: in these cases, there is no transgression of the limits of the just price. Thus, to judge whether injustice or "cloaked usury" <note>hidden interest</note> is involved in sales or purchases where something is sold for more because payment is expected later, or bought cheaper because of advanced payment, one must look at whether the price exceeds the rigorous just price or fails to reach the lowest just price. If it is found not to go outside these limits, it must be judged that neither injustice nor usury is involved.

2. Furthermore, everyone agrees that injustice is committed and usury is involved if a seller exceeds the rigorous just price (what the thing is worth in cash right now) for the specific reason of delaying payment into the future. Similarly, if a buyer, for that same reason, buys below the lowest just price because he pays in advance. So says **St. Thomas [Aquinas]** in the *Summa Theologiae*, 2nd part of the 2nd part, question 78, article 2, reply 7, and the doctors generally; this is in harmony with the chapter *Consuluit* regarding usury. The reason is clear: in both outcomes, profit is seen to arise from the nature of a loan, which is cloaked usury, as was explained in Dispute 303. In the first case, it is just as if the just price, which the buyer was to pay immediately, were left to him as a loan by the seller until the time of payment, and for that reason the seller receives that increase in price at the time of payment. In the latter case, it is no different than if the advanced price were given as a loan to the seller until the time the goods are delivered, with the agreement that he should then return more than it was worth...

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of market knowledge and the boundaries of the "just price" in credit sales. Molina argues that merchants can profit from private information if no fraud is involved and defines "cloaked usury" as charging outside the standard price range specifically for the passage of time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina's discussion on the ethics of pricing and sales. The previous page concluded a section on whether a merchant must disclose secret knowledge of future market shifts (like a coming siege or the departure of a royal court). Here, Molina moves into the specific conditions under which selling on credit at a higher price constitutes usury versus a legitimate compensation for the seller's lost opportunities.</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts #

...goods are worth more than the price; these two are profit from a loan in substance, and thus **veiled usury** <note>original: "usura palliata"; this refers to interest hidden within a contract that looks like a normal sale but functions as a loan</note>.

<margin>3</margin>
From this, Soto <note>Dominic de Soto (1494–1560), a major Spanish scholastic theologian</note> (Book 6, *On Justice*, Question 2, Article 3, before the fourth conclusion, and Question 4, Article 1) infers that merchants commit **usury** and are bound to make restitution when, at the close of fairs <note>original: "nundinarum"; these were major international trading events</note>—at which time, due to a lack of buyers, the price of goods usually decreases and is far lower than at the beginning or middle—they sell their goods on credit at the price they were worth at the start of the fair. In the same way, they commit usury with the burden of restitution if, when the price of wheat decreases because of a sudden arrival of a huge supply by sea or because of rain on which the year's fertility depended, they sell on credit at the price it was sold for immediately before, which was higher than the current rigorous price <note>original: "pretio rigoroso"; the strict market value at that exact moment</note> for which it is commonly sold for cash. The same must be said of any other goods in similar events; it is no obstacle that the merchants themselves might have bought them at a higher price and will lose money unless the price rises, as was said in Disputation 348.

<margin>4</margin>
Although it is not lawful to receive more than the rigorous **just price** solely because one expects payment later, nor to buy below the lowest just price solely because one pays in advance; nevertheless, on the grounds of **lost profit** <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; profit that a seller misses out on because their capital or goods are tied up</note> or **emergent loss** <note>original: "damnum emergens"; an actual loss or expense incurred by the seller due to the transaction</note>, it is lawful to increase or decrease the price beyond the limits of the just price, according to what a prudent judgment estimates these are worth, as was shown extensively in Disputation 314 and the two following. Observe, however, that the seller needs to signify to the buyer that this departure from the normally just price limits is being made by reason of lost profit or emergent loss, especially when it is not clear that the buyer intended to "buy" that lost profit or emergent loss along with the goods. If the buyer only intended to buy the thing at a just price, and did not simultaneously wish to compensate for lost profit or emergent loss, an injury would certainly be done to him, with a burden of restitution, if he were unknowingly charged for them. When a profit is considered to be "lost" or a loss "emergent" was explained at length in the cited disputations, especially 316.

<margin>5</margin>
On the grounds of lost profit, the final case discussed in the chapter *Naviganti* <note>A famous decree by Pope Gregory IX in the "Decretals" concerning sea-loans and usury</note> regarding usury is licit. In that place, Gregory IX defines that a person is excused from the sin and vice of usury who sells his goods on credit at a price higher than they are worth at the time of the contract, provided there is a likely doubt whether the thing sold will be worth more or less at the time of payment, and provided the seller was not going to sell those goods at the time of the contract but was going to keep them to be sold at the time set for payment. For example, if a measure of wheat is sold in December for eight silver pieces, but it is expected to be sold in the beginning of May for a much higher price, then a person who had firmly intended to sell his wheat in May can, without sin or the vice of usury, sell it on credit in December when requested, at the price it was expected to be worth (more or less) in May. The reason is that when it is morally certain it will be worth more in May, and it is unknown how much the price will rise,

<column-break/>

the just price for the **lost profit**, appraised at the time of the contract, will certainly be reached if the price is increased to the midpoint between the highest and lowest price expected in May. By that reasoning, the profit the seller loses by not keeping his wheat until the time he expected it to be worth more is both appraised and sufficiently paid for; and both the buyer and the seller expose themselves to equal risk. For even if the wheat is worth more in May, the seller is content with that set price; and even if it is worth less, the buyer nevertheless pays that same price. This is what Gregory IX intended to define in that chapter. Observe, however, if the seller was not going to keep his wheat until the day set for payment, but for a shorter time—in which it was going to be worth more than at the time of the contract, but less than at the fixed term of payment—then he cannot bargain for the price it will be worth at the time of payment. This is because he does not lose that much profit by selling now; he can only bargain for the price it would have been worth at the time he had actually intended to sell it. Similarly, if he had intended to sell it at a time when it was expected to be worth more than at the deadline given for payment, then he can bargain for the price it would have worth at the time he intended to sell it, whether the deadline for payment is before or after that time. The reason is that he loses all that profit by selling in the present. Observe, however, that a deduction must always be made from the price for whatever the seller would have spent on storing and preserving that wheat. Likewise, if the wheat or any other merchandise was going to suffer some deterioration due to dryness or any other cause, a deduction must also be made from the price according to its estimation. Add this: if it was not morally certain that the seller would have kept the merchandise until the time it was going to be worth more, he cannot take the full price increase that he could have licitly taken if it had been morally certain. Finally, the seller is bound to decrease the price by as much as, all circumstances considered, he might lose less profit by selling at the fixed term of payment, according to what was said in Disputation 316. Thus say Mair, Sylvester, Soto, Covarruvias, and the doctors commonly.

<margin>6</margin>
Although the price of lost profit can be appraised at the time of the contract in the manner explained according to the chapter *Naviganti*, a sale can also be made another way. Namely, that as much price be paid as the goods are commonly worth at the time the seller had intended to sell them. The reason is that, in truth, the seller loses that much profit, and in this way he exposes himself to the risk that, if for some reason it is worth less then, less will be given to him. However, he is always bound to deduct from the price if he loses less profit because of the expenses of storing that merchandise and because of the other things just mentioned. But if anyone sells wheat or any other merchandise with a pact that he be given the **highest price** <note>original: "supremum pretium"</note> it reaches from the day the contract is made until the time he had intended to keep it, that contract is **usurious**.

<summary>Molina discusses when selling goods on credit at higher-than-market prices is considered usury. He explains that sellers may charge more to compensate for "lost profit" (lucrum cessans) if they had intended to hold the goods until a future date when prices would be higher, provided they account for storage costs and risks.</summary>
<keywords>usury, credit sales, lost profit, emergent loss, just price, wheat trade, market fluctuations, Dominic de Soto, Gregory IX, restitution</keywords>

--- Page 324 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 336 regarding the ethics of credit sales. It addresses whether a seller can peg a future price to the highest point in a given timeframe and then transitions into Disputation 356, which examines how the risk of non-payment affects the "just price" of a contract.</meta>

Furthermore, even if a seller determines a specific month or week, and adds a clause to the agreement that he should be paid the highest price that the goods reached during that month or week, the contract is **usurious** <note>original: "usurarius"; charging interest or gaining an unfair advantage from a loan or credit sale</note>. The reason for this is that the seller himself would have chosen only one day—or even one hour—in which to sell, and he would not have received more than the value of the goods at that time. By choosing the supreme price of the entire month or week, he exposes the buyer to the risk that if the goods are worth more at any point in that time, the buyer is bound to pay it. Meanwhile, the seller secures himself, ensuring he receives no less than what the goods would have been worth at the time he chose to sell. Who does not see that imposing this burden (which is undoubtedly worth a specific price) in exchange for waiting for payment is **veiled usury**?

However, if it were agreed that the buyer would pay neither the highest price nor the lowest reached in that time, but rather a middle price between the two, then there would be no usury. This is because the contract would be balanced, removing the risk equally from both the buyer and the seller. In this, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan philosopher</note>, Gabriel Biel, Covarruvias, Juan Medina, and the doctors of law generally agree.

<margin>7</margin>
The doubt is: if a seller is about to sell his goods immediately, but it is likely believed that those goods will be worth more in three months, can he licitly sell them on credit to be paid at that time, but at the price he hopes they will be worth then? Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note> affirms this and responds that the expectation of payment can be considered in two ways. First, as an action distinct from the buying and selling; in this way, because the payment is delayed, nothing more can be accepted than what the thing is worth in the present, as it would be usury to take more.

Second, it can be seen as an action that completes the contract of sale. For a contract is completed not by the agreement alone, but by the **delivery** <note>original: "traditione"; the physical handing over of the goods or payment</note> of the goods by the seller and the payment by the buyer. Therefore, Cajetan says, because the goods will be worth more at the time the contract is to be completed by the payment of the price, such a contract is licit. It does not matter that the goods are worth less at the time they are handed over, nor that the seller would not have kept them until that future time.

Conrad Summenhart <note>original: "Cont."; a 15th-century German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts</note> seems to approach the same opinion. Cajetan confirms his view from the chapter *In Civitate* on usury, where Pope Alexander III—making no mention of whether the seller would have kept the goods for future sale—responds that pepper or cinnamon, which sells for five when paid in cash, can without sin be sold for six on credit, provided it is believed they will be worth about that much at the time of payment.

However, Cajetan criticizes the glosses <note>standard legal commentaries</note> on the chapters *In Civitate* and *Naviganti*, which claim the case is the same for both. Those glosses argue that the ruling in *In Civitate* must be understood to apply only when the seller was planning to keep his goods until the time fixed for payment, as is stated in the chapter *Naviganti*.

Nevertheless, the contrary must undoubtedly be maintained:

<column-break/>

namely, that such a contract is illicit and usurious. Pope Gregory IX clearly expressed this in the chapter *Naviganti*. Therefore, it must be said that the case is the same for both chapters, and that Gregory IX further explained what Alexander III had said. This is affirmed by the doctors generally, in addition to the glosses on both chapters, including Juan Medina, Soto, Covarruvias, and many others whom he cites. Major, Gabriel Biel, and Silvester Prierias also agree.

Our opinion can be confirmed as follows. First, because a contract of sale is perfected by consent, as shown in Disputations 254, 336, and 337. The value of the thing ought to be considered according to what it is worth at the time of its delivery, as is clear in itself, because it is then handed over for use and consumption. This is gathered openly from the chapter *Naviganti*. Furthermore, the payment of the price is not the completion of the contract, except regarding the obligation that had already arisen from the perfected contract itself. Thus, the just price of a thing sold on credit should not be measured by the time of payment, but by the time of the sale and the delivery of the goods.

<margin>8</margin>
Second, because a thing that will be worth more in the future is not worth more to someone who is going to sell and deliver it immediately than it is worth in the present. This is because ownership of it does not stay with him, and it can be consumed immediately by the buyer. Therefore, if he sells and delivers it in the present, he cannot sell it for a higher price just because he delays payment until a time when it will be worth more, any more than if he were selling it for immediate cash.

Third, because if it is consumed immediately, it cannot increase in value. Therefore, at the time of payment, the price owed is not what it would have been worth then if it had been kept by the seller until that time. You may read other reasons in Medina and Soto in the places cited. From these reasons just given, Cajetan's foundations are so clearly overturned that there is no need to respond to them further.

# Whether by reason of the danger of losing the capital, or the difficulty and trouble of recovering it, it is licit to sell on credit above the rigorous just price, or to buy with advanced payment below the lowest just price. #

## DISPUTATION CCCLVI. ##

### S U M M A R Y ###

1. Whether it is licit to sell on credit for a time above the just price, or to buy below the lowest price with advanced payment, by reason of the danger of losing the **capital** <note>original: "capitale"; the principal amount of money or value invested</note>, or because of the difficulty of recovering it due to the location or the quality of the persons involved.
2. The danger of losing capital, the quality of the place and person, and the fear of expenses and labor in recovering the debt are all things that can be appraised in the price.

<summary>Molina argues against the theologian Cajetan, stating that selling goods on credit at a future expected higher price is usurious because the value of a sale is fixed at the moment of delivery. He then introduces a new discussion on whether the risk of a buyer defaulting justifies increasing the price.</summary>

<keywords>usury, just price, credit sales, contract law, Cajetan, delivery of goods, risk of loss, market value, restitution, Luis de Molina</keywords>

--- Page 325 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 356 concerning whether a seller can increase the price of goods sold on credit to compensate for the risk of non-payment or the difficulty of debt recovery. It contrasts the views of major Scholastic thinkers like Juan Medina, Domingo de Soto, and Martin de Azpilcueta (Navarrus).</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

<margin>Juan Medina, *On Penitence*, question 38, case 3 and 4, judges that...</margin>
By reason of the danger of **losing the capital**, or a portion of it, when—judging by the quality of the person and the concurrent circumstances—some such danger is likely to occur in moral terms, it is licit to increase the price beyond the **just price** <note>original: "pretium iustum"; the standard market value determined by common estimation</note>. This increase should be as much as that danger is valued by a prudent judgment. Conversely, one may decrease the price from the lowest just price when buying with an advance payment. Likewise, an increase is permitted by reason of the expenses, labor, and anxiety to be undergone in recovering that debt. Although Medina provides other significant arguments to prove this, the primary one is that all these factors are estimable in money; nor is anyone bound to undergo them, or to subject themselves and their property to them, for free. Thus, as we said in Disputation 319 according to the common opinion of the doctors, a **guarantor** <note>original: "fideiussorem"; someone who guarantees a debt</note> can accept a competent price for the obligation he takes upon himself to pay for a debtor if the debtor fails, based on the size of the obligation and the risk he subjects himself to. Therefore, says Medina, provided the seller does not indiscriminately raise the price for everyone to whom he sells on credit, but only for those where the aforementioned risks are likely feared—and he does not raise it equally for all, but according to the quantity of the risk and likelihood—and provided no **scandal** <note>a moral stumbling block or public outcry</note> arises, he may strictly speaking increase the price as much as those factors are valued by a prudent judgment. If, at the time of the contract, he sets a certain and moderate price with the buyer according to the risk then feared, whatever happens later, he is neither bound to restore that increase nor can he take more. This is because it was established as a just price by the agreement of both parties in exchange for the risk he was undergoing, regardless of how the matter later turned out.

<margin>Soto, book 6, *On Justice*, question 4, article 1, reply 2...</margin>
Although Soto admits that regarding expenses and labor that are likely feared, someone can bargain with a buyer or a borrower for a certain just and moderate price—so that whatever happens later to either party, he can neither take more nor be bound to restore it—he nevertheless denies that anything can be accepted for other reasons without the vice of **usury** <note>original: "vsuræ vitio"; charging interest on a loan, which was traditionally forbidden</note>. He is quite annoyed <note>original: "stomachatur"; literally "his stomach is turned"</note> with Medina for introducing such an opinion. One may read the reasons Soto relies upon in his own work. In this second point, **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canon lawyer</note> agrees with Soto in his *Manual*, chapter 23, number 81.

<margin>Conradus, *On Contracts*, question 59, corollary 1 and 2...</margin>
After the third conclusion and argument 2, after the 4th, he denies that the price can be increased for the risk of losing the capital or part of it. Regarding expenses, however, he says it can indeed be increased, but with the condition that if no expenses are later incurred, only the just price of the thing should be kept. On this second point, several others agree:
<margin>Sylvester Prierias in *Rosa Aurea*, case 6; John Major in book 4, distinction 15, question 40, argument 7; Navarrus in *Manual*, chapter 23, number 84...</margin>
Though Navarrus adds that this is dangerous, because at the time of payment the seller might change his mind or forget, and thus take the whole price. Likewise, he might die before payment, and then his heirs would receive the whole price. However, Navarrus says a precaution can be used by handing a note to the debtor stating that if he pays in full at the appointed time, that amount will be deducted from the price.

<column-break/>

Conradus says that the price can nonetheless be increased for the fear of expenses and similar things. If, however, the price is increased specifically for the "strike of fear" <note>the psychological burden of risk</note>, he believes the creditor is not bound to restore anything, even if none of the things he feared later come to pass.

I will state what I think about this matter in two conclusions. **First:** Besides the fact that increasing the price for the reasons proposed is a matter full of danger in itself and prone to generating scandal—and for that reason should in no way be advised—I believe it is also illicit in itself and induces an obligation to restore the excess price. This is unless, at the time of the contract, it is made manifest to the buyer that the price is being increased beyond the otherwise just price for those reasons, and the buyer consents to such a pact—especially when it is not clear that the buyer wishes to "buy" those risks and losses alongside the goods. The proof is that, as we said in the preceding Disputation 314 regarding **lost profit** and **emergent loss** <note>original: "lucro cessante ac damno emergente"; the two standard justifications for interest in Medieval law</note>, if the buyer only intended to buy the thing at a just price and not the risks the seller thinks he is undergoing, an injury would surely be done to him if such risks were sold to him without his knowledge. Therefore, a sin would occur, along with the obligation to restore such a price.

**Second conclusion:** Although it seems no one should be advised to increase the price for these reasons—due to the danger of cloaking and introducing usury, and due to scandal and damage to the Commonwealth (especially since the seller could refuse to sell without a secure guarantor, or could even impose a **conventional penalty** <note>a late fee agreed upon in advance</note> if something he fears happens through the buyer's fault)—nonetheless, if that increment of price is drawn into the agreement and manifested to the buyer at the time of the contract as being accepted by reason of the expenses, risks, and labor the seller undergoes, and if it is moderate for the quantity of those factors (considering the quality of the buyer so that the fear arises from the nature of the matter and not from the greed or cowardice of the seller who trembles with fear where there is no fear), I do not see why the contract would not be licit. The proof is that, besides the fact that all those things are estimable by a price and thus can be justly sold, a right to receive one hundred on a certain day—which the seller acquires by selling his merchandise for one hundred to be paid on that day—is worth less in itself (as Soto admits in his third response) the more that hundred is subject to danger and requires greater labor and expenses to recover. This is so true that a right to recover one hundred is justly bought by others for ninety or eighty. Therefore, a seller can now increase the price until, by a certain proportion, the right to recover more than the otherwise just price is made equal in value to the just price that would be paid at the time of the contract. This is done by increasing the price for a certain day by as much as the right to it is worth less due to the risks, labor, and expenses that are justly feared, compared to if the price were paid immediately.

<summary>This page discusses the morality of raising prices in credit sales to compensate for the risk of non-payment or the costs of debt recovery. Molina concludes that while risky and potentially scandalous, such increases are licit if openly negotiated, moderate, and based on objective risks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the pricing of goods sold on credit. Second Treatise. Disputation 357.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
You might object that if the argument proves anything, it proves that a thing can be sold at a higher price for those same reasons without specifically deducting that increase for those causes in the contract. Indeed, the right to that price, which is acquired at the time of the contract when the thing is sold on credit, does not in truth exceed the value of the merchandise. However, it must be denied that this follows. For when a thing is sold on credit, the price for which it is bought is not a right that the seller acquires in the present, but rather money to be paid by the buyer at a set term, in comparison to which the seller acquires a right. By raising the price, however, the buyer is unknowingly forced to "buy" the risk of the price, the labor, and the expenses. The seller, by acting in this way, causes the buyer to consent to a higher price and subsequently to a right to a higher price; this is not permitted when the buyer is unaware.

I have deemed it unnecessary to report and resolve the arguments of <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560) and Martin de Azpilcueta, known as Navarrus (1491–1586), were leading Spanish scholastics and jurists who wrote extensively on economics and morality.</note> Soto and Navarrus, as it will be easily understood from what has been said how little weight they carry.

## Whether the manner of selling goods on credit causes their **just price** to increase. And concerning goods that are brought to fairs in vast quantities or transported by sea.

### DISPUTATION 357.

-> S V M M A R Y <-

1 *Whether the manner of selling goods on credit causes their just price to increase.*
2 *Whether merchants at fairs, where it is customary to sell goods on credit, commit a sin and are bound to **restitution** <note>Restitution is the moral obligation to return ill-gotten gains or compensate for a loss caused to another.</note> if they sell more dearly on credit than for cash.*
3 *When a delay in payment may be a circumstance that increases the **just price** of merchandise.*

<margin>1</margin>
Certain authors have asserted on this basis that goods can be justly and lawfully sold on credit beyond the usual **just price** <note>original: "pretium iustum"; the fair market value determined by common estimation</note> of those same things. They argue that goods are worth more under that mode of selling than when sold for immediate cash; as if that higher price were the proper and peculiar just price for those goods under that specific mode of sale. This would be no different than when goods are sold at **auction** <note>original: "subhastæ"; literally "under the spear," referring to the Roman practice of marking an auction with a spear</note>, which have their own peculiar just value, or when goods offered voluntarily lose value and decrease in price—even if their just price is otherwise higher—while sold in that manner, as explained in Disputation 348. They confirm this by noting that an abundance of buyers causes the price to increase, as shown in the same disputation; and when goods are sold on credit, there are more buyers. This † cause is rightly rejected by all; on this matter, among others, one should read Juan Medina’s *On Restitution*, question 38, cause 6. The primary reason is that the laws openly state the contrary: they teach that it is not permitted to sell more dearly on credit than for cash, except for a peculiar reason, such as **lost profit** <note>original: "lucri cessantis"; a legal concept where a seller is compensated for the profit they could have made elsewhere if they had received the cash immediately</note> or something similar. If the reason provided above were legitimate, it would be universally lawful

<column-break/>

to sell more dearly on credit than for cash. Furthermore, that increase in price from selling in that manner arises because the price is waited for, and thus it arises from a **virtual loan** <note>original: "virtuali mutuo"</note>, which is **veiled usury** <note>original: "palliata vsura"; a term for a contract that hides an interest-bearing loan (usury) under the guise of a different transaction, like a sale</note>, illicit by both divine and natural law. Therefore, since that abundance of buyers does not simultaneously cause the cash price to increase, but is only an occasion for sellers to illicitly sell more dearly from the very nature of the thing, it follows that this cause is not among those that cause the price of things to increase by their nature—as would be the case with an abundance of cash buyers. We shall provide some qualification to this doctrine, which is true in itself, shortly.

<margin>2 Question</margin>
Certain people, whom Covarruvias refers to in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 3, number 6, have asserted that those † merchants who sell goods at fairs—where it is very common to sell on credit—more dearly on credit than for cash, do not sin and are not bound to restitution. They argue that human society and the public good demand this mode of selling because it is not easy to find as many cash buyers as such a vast quantity of merchandise requires. Soto also affirms the same in *On Justice*, book 6, question 4, article 1, reply 4; not indeed regarding the aforementioned goods, but regarding those which are transported by sea in vast quantities, which cannot be sold all at once for immediate cash. He judges that the price then is not what they are worth in cash, but what they are worth with a future payment term granted. Covarruvias leans toward the opposite of the first opinion, while Navarrus, in his *Manual*, chapter 23, number 82, rebukes and attacks the latter.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
I believe, however, that a distinction must be made. If goods are brought to fairs or by sea (as in the **Indies ships** <note>original: "Indicis nauibus"; referring to the Spanish fleets returning from the Americas and Asia</note>) in vast quantities, and considering the multitude of buyers who gather to buy them—either to carry them elsewhere for resale or to resell them gradually in the same city or region—they are truly worth that price. But because the buyers lack such a vast quantity of cash to pay immediately, the goods are sold on credit as is necessary for common use for such a quantity of merchandise. In that case, I judge that no injustice occurs by selling them more dearly on credit than they would be sold for cash if they were put up for sale *only* for cash. Because of their sheer quantity and the scarcity of cash, it would be necessary for the just price to decrease significantly; yet there is no lack of buyers or need for the goods, only a lack of the faculty to buy such a large quantity for cash as would be expedient to purchase.

Indeed, if they were sold only for cash, it would result in those buying the goods becoming very wealthy and carrying off an enormous profit. They would buy at a very low price due to the multitude of goods and the thin resources of many to buy for cash, and they would sell at a high price because of the scarcity of those goods once they were transported to individual locations. Therefore, regarding such merchandise, Soto most truly affirms that they are not imported to be sold for immediate cash, but that their just price is what is customarily given for them when sold on credit.

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

But if the aforementioned goods—considering the quantity of buyers and other circumstances—are not worth as much because they are actually sold for a lower price at the same time by those very merchants (or by others) without any urgent need for immediate cash forcing them to lower the price they would otherwise seek for cash payment; then, since selling all at once is a circumstance that usually decreases rather than increases the **just price** <note>The 'just price' (pretium iustum) was a central concept in Scholastic economics, referring to the fair market value determined by common estimation, rather than just the seller's whim.</note>, as explained in Disputation <margin>348.</margin> 348: it certainly follows that if they are sold on credit at a higher price (whether all at once or in parts) than they would be sold for in parts for cash, then **usury** <note>Usury, in this period, was the sin of charging any certain profit on a loan. Scholastics like Molina were trying to distinguish between sinful interest and legitimate market fluctuations.</note> is present, carrying an obligation to restore that increase in price as something unjust.

At this point, observe that the doctrine handed down in the first place by <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560) was a Dominican theologian whose work on justice and law influenced Molina.</note> Soto and others (whom Covarruvias refers to) does not regularly apply unless merchants buy on credit in that manner for the purpose of reselling and transporting those goods to other places for the common needs of men. For there are many merchants who cannot trade at all, or only very poorly, unless they buy on credit and the price is deferred until such time as those goods are sold, either entirely or in part. Others, though they are wealthy, cannot take on a vast quantity of goods to be transported and sold in various places unless some delay in payment is granted to them. However, when a crowd of both types of these merchants comes to buy, it is clear from the very nature of the matter that the price of goods bought on credit increases beyond what those same goods would be worth if they were sold for cash only. And in this sense, and by reason of this and similar outcomes, it is true that goods sold on credit, under that manner of selling, are sometimes worth more than if those same goods were sold only for cash—even though the contrary should be asserted as a general and regular rule. And this is the balance with which we promised a little while ago to season this doctrine, which is true when speaking of the matter in itself and regularly.

<margin>3</margin> Indeed, so that these points may be more strongly supported and better understood, observe: although a delay in payment of the price is "virtually" a loan, since the price (when not fixed by law) does not consist in an indivisible point but can increase from various circumstances (as explained in Disp. 338), it follows that the granting of a delay in payment can sometimes be the occasion and circumstance for the **just price** of a commodity to increase. This happens because the number of buyers is multiplied, as they wish to buy in a far greater quantity than they would or could if that delay were not granted to them.

Therefore, when the price is not fixed by law, it can increase in two ways by reason of the delay in payment. One way is as a sort of retribution and compensation for the delay. And in this way, it is **usury**, because it is a profit coming from what is virtually a loan. The other way is as an increase in the **just price** of the commodity occasioned by the delay, which was the cause for the buyers to multiply, and thus the just price increased (or rather, did not decrease) because of that method of selling. And in this way, since it is not a profit from a loan either formally or virtually, it is not usury, but part of the just price. I 

<column-break/>

said "when the price is not fixed by law": for if it is fixed by law, since the payment for the good consists in an indivisible value (just like the payment for a formal loan), then certainly a delay in payment cannot be the occasion for a higher value of that thing which is to be compensated, and therefore cannot justify a higher compensation.

### DISPUTATION 359.

#### SUMMARY

1 *When usury intervenes in a purchase with anticipated payment, and when it does not.*
2 *The price of a thing must be considered at the time the thing is delivered, and not at the time of the contract.*
3 *Money paid in advance can be used to buy in two ways that which is believed will be worth less at the time of delivery.*
*Indeed, even without money paid in advance, by earnest money alone, or by the contract intervening. No. 4.*
5 *Whether a buyer with anticipated payment can lawfully buy a house to be delivered to him after a certain time, or after the death of the seller, which was then believed to be worth the same price as now at the time of the contract.*

<margin>1 2</margin> We must now speak of purchase with an anticipated price <note>This refers to "forward contracts" or "pre-payment," where a buyer pays now for goods to be delivered later, often at a discount.</note>. And since the price of a thing is to be considered at the time of its delivery, and not at the time the contract is celebrated, it follows that if a thing is bought now to be delivered after two months—when it will likely be worth much less—it is justly bought now at the price it is believed it will be worth, more or less, at that time. For example, if wheat is sold two months before the harvest for twelve silver pieces <note>original: "argenteis"</note>, but it is believed that at the time of the harvest it will be worth eight silver pieces, it can be bought two months before the harvest with anticipated payment, to be delivered at the time of harvest, for eight silver pieces.

The same must be said of oil, wine, and other things which are usually worth less at the time of the new harvest. And this is the second case defined by <note>Pope Gregory IX (reigned 1227–1241) issued the Decretals, a major collection of canon law. The chapter "Naviganti" discussed the risks of maritime trade and interest.</note> Gregory IX in the chapter *Naviganti*, regarding usury. Conversely, if a thing is worth eight silver pieces now, but it is believed it will be worth twelve silver pieces after three months, and it is bought now with anticipated payment for eight silver pieces to be delivered after three months, "cloaked usury" <note>original: "usura palliata" - a contract designed to look like a sale but functioning as a high-interest loan.</note> is committed, with the burden of restoring whatever more the thing is likely believed to be worth at the time of delivery.

<margin>3</margin> Observe what <note>Juan Medina (1490–1547) was a Spanish theologian who wrote on restitution and contracts.</note> Medina notes excellently on restitution, question 38: after the fifth cause, there are two ways to buy with anticipated money that which is believed will be worth less at the time of delivery. One way is by determining the price at the time the contract is celebrated according to what it is believed it will be worth at the time of delivery; and the chapter *Naviganti* on usury speaks of this kind of price. For example, if wheat, which is believed will be worth more or less eight silver pieces at the time of the new harvest, is bought three months earlier with anticipated money for those same eight silver pieces.

Second Treatise, Disputation 61.

And then, whether by some chance it happens to be worth more, and beyond half of the **just price** <note>original: "iusti pretij." Under Roman and Canon law, a contract could be overturned for "laesio enormis" (huge loss) if the price was less than half or more than double the fair market value.</note>, or less, and below half of the just price; the contract is nonetheless just, and it must be upheld. There is no ground to object that a fraud has occurred beyond or below half of the just price. The reason for this is as follows: because that was not the price of the thing as a finished result, as it already existed in reality, but as it existed under that **hope** <note>original: "spe." This refers to speculative value or the "price of a chance."</note>, and as it could turn out either prosperously or adversely for either party. For that thing, as it existed in that state of hope, that was the just price according to common estimation, whatever might later follow in effect. It is just like when the **cast of a net** <note>original: "iactus retis." A classic legal example where one pays for whatever a fisherman catches in one throw; the contract is valid even if the net comes up empty.</note> is bought for a price which, before that cast, was estimated to be just; the contract is just and must be upheld, whatever happens afterward—even if that was not the price of the actual outcome, but of the outcome as it existed under that hope.

The same must be said when a purchase is made with an **anticipated payment** <note>paying upfront for goods to be delivered later.</note> at a fixed price, which was believed would be worth more or less at the time of delivery. Likewise, when a debt is sold at a fixed price, which the seller was going to keep for sale at the time appointed for payment, according to what was said in Disputation 355.

In another way, something can be bought with anticipated money, not indeed by determining the price at the time of the contract, but by buying at the price at which the thing will commonly be worth at the time of delivery. In that case, one must stand by that price, and all things are to be understood according to what was said regarding sales on credit in a similar manner in the cited disputation.

<note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560) was a key figure in the School of Salamanca, which pioneered modern economic theory.</note> Soto excellently observes in *On Justice*, book 6, question 4, article 1, first conclusion, that all things said regarding purchase with anticipated money have a place in a similar way even if the payment is not anticipated, but only the contract is celebrated before the time of delivery, with **earnest money** <note>original: "arrha." A down payment or deposit given to bind a contract.</note> given or accepted between the contracting parties, or even without earnest money intervening.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
A doubt arises: what if someone desires to hold the property of another and its fruits, but the owner does not wish to sell unless he first enjoys them for ten years, or for his entire life? Will the contract be licit if the price is sold by anticipated payment at what will probably be the value at the time of delivery—for instance, if it is a field or a house which is likely believed to be worth the same then as it is now? It must be said that if the seller does not take upon himself the risk of the thing 

<margin>The Decision</margin>
being sold until the time of delivery—so that, if it perishes or is damaged by some accidental chance, it perishes or is damaged for him—this contract is unjust. For since, just as the risk of a purchased thing belongs to the buyer, so also do the fruits; surely, when the seller reserves for himself the right of enjoying the thing sold for some time, he ought to subtract as much from the price of the thing (at least by a rigorous estimation) as that right he reserves for himself is valued, or the risk he throws onto the other. Or certainly, he should rather take the damage of the thing upon himself during that time. And according to this doctrine, I understand Conrad <note>likely Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts.</note> in *On Contracts*, question 59, at the end of the third conclusion. But if the seller takes the risk of the sold thing upon himself for that whole time, it is exactly as if a harvest or any other thing were bought with anticipated money at the price at which it would be valued at the time of delivery—a contract which surely no one would condemn.

->Practice regarding the purchase and sale of wool in some places in Castile.<-

### DISPUTATIO CCCLIX.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Whether the purchase of wool with anticipated money, as is customary in some places in Castile, is licit.*
2 *Wool in the kingdom of Castile is counted among its chief natural riches.*
3 *There are three types of wool in the kingdom of Castile.*
4 *Wool prices in the kingdom of Castile depend heavily on commissions sent from Genoa.*
5 *Why the purchase of wool in Castile is made with anticipated payment.*
6 *At what time wool sales in Castile are made with anticipated payment.*
7 *Which circumstances increase or decrease the price of wool.*

The question of whether the purchase of wool with anticipated money, as occurs in some places in Castile, is licit, is highly controversial and very necessary to define exactly.
However, because its accurate decision depends much on the knowledge of the manner in which this business is accustomed to be carried out, and the circumstances because of which it is necessary that a large part of the money be paid in advance, we will first elucidate this in this disputation; then we will approach the question in the following disputation. We will speak of the manner in which it is done in this city of **Cuenca** <note>original: "Cochensi." Cuenca was a major center for the textile industry in 16th-century Spain.</note> and in its neighboring towns, where we have been able to investigate by diligent inquiry. If, however, there are different circumstances elsewhere—as perhaps in the **Segovian** district, where I hear that the **Genoese** <note>Genoese bankers and merchants were the primary financiers of the Spanish Crown and international trade at this time.</note> and other foreigners do not come to buy wool, but that there a huge quantity of high-value cloths are made from the wool of that city and the neighboring towns, which are carried to all the Spains and various other places—if, I say, there are other circumstances in that city or elsewhere, it will be for those who know them to define this question according to them. It is our task, however, to speak according to the information handed down to us regarding this matter.

Among the chief natural riches of Castile, wool is not undeservedly counted, along with the flocks of which wool is the fruit. For since, because of the excellence of the wools, many thousands of weights are exported annually, both to Italy (and from there to Constantinople and other parts) and to Flanders and other places; the result is that they nourish as many ewes as possible in Castile, and many rams, because of the profit they bring back from the wool, cheese, and meat.
From this it has further resulted that the kingdom of Castile abounds much in mutton; which is more tender, healthier, and better to the degree that the wool is more excellent. For thin wool and the best wool do not arise except from delicate flesh, which is sweeter and healthier than the rest.

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

### Page 264

Although it sometimes happens that from grazing on salty land, and where the waters are salty, the meat of livestock whose wool is less precious and less delicate tends to be sweeter, healthier, and better. Indeed, salt contributes much to making the meat of rams <note>original: "arietum." Molina distinguishes between the meat and wool quality of male rams versus female sheep.</note> better, because it consumes the superfluous moisture of the rams and preserves them from diseases. And from this it arises that where places are more saline and salty, there are more sheep and rams with black wool: for 그 color arises from the heat and scorching of the ram. It also follows that black rams are more robust and more patient of labor than white ones, and their meat is sweeter, healthier, and better. Therefore, the quality of meat and wool depends for the most part on the grazing and the waters.

There are, however, even in the same region, three kinds of wool: namely, the lowest, the middle, and <margin>3</margin> the highest, in terms of excellence. These different grades are said to arise partly from grazing—because the better and more abundant the feed the livestock are nourished with throughout the year, the more and better meat they have, and they produce more abundant and better wool—and partly from care, ensuring that in the flocks there are only sheep and rams of the best meat and wool, from which similar livestock are procreated. Furthermore, the more livestock an individual raises for this trade, the better wool he usually has; since he is accustomed to provide them with the best grazing in other regions during the winter time, and he takes greater care that the rams and sheep are selected and of the best quality. It is also added that such livestock, which are cherished with better and more abundant grazing and hydration, tend to have longer wool, yet they are never so affected by the "scab" <note>original: "scabie." A skin disease (mange) common in sheep that ruins wool quality.</note> or by the rot; which they call *roante* <note>original: "rorantem... qua roantē vocāt." Likely a local Spanish term for a type of wool decay or "rot."</note>, two things which contribute not a little to the excellence of the wool. There is, however, a far greater supply of middle and top-grade wool than of the lowest, which is modest in comparison to the others. Merchants, however, usually buy both the supreme and the middle grades, although sometimes they buy something of the lowest, especially to fulfill their "commissions," as they call them, of which we shall speak shortly.

<margin>4</margin> Not only does the price of each of these three kinds of wool not consist in an indivisible point <note>A legal and economic concept: the "just price" is not a single fixed number but a range (latitude) within which a price is considered fair.</note>—having its own range of a low, middle, and rigorous just price, and being inconstant and varied by the diversity of concurring circumstances, as we shall explain—but also all of them do not have the same price at one and the same moment in time. Instead, they have widely different prices, with an excess of three or four silver reals <note>original: "regalium argenteorum." The real was a standard Spanish silver coin.</note> for each weight <note>original: "pondere." Referring to the *arroba*.</note>. For if a weight of the lowest grade wool is sold for eleven or twelve silver reals with anticipated payment, a weight of the middle wool is sold for fourteen, fifteen, or sixteen silver reals, solely due to the difference of the soil from which one is purer than another, and according as the seller has more select livestock, or more ewes than rams. Indeed, the wool of ewes is more excellent than that of rams, other things being equal, because it is less dirty, and for that reason yields more weight when washed than that of rams, and because it is finer. And a weight of the highest grade is sold for seventeen, eighteen, or nineteen silver reals; and in the same proportion, the prices of these same three kinds of wool usually increase or decrease.

The Genoese, and sometimes the Florentines, although sometimes they buy more and sometimes less, nevertheless usually buy...

<column-break/>

...they are accustomed to buy so much in this city of Cuenca <note>original: "Conchensi ciuitate." Cuenca was a major center for the Spanish wool industry.</note>, and in the neighboring towns, especially in the mountains (they call them *de la sierra* <note>Spanish: "of the mountain range."</note>) which begin from here toward the north, and in which the wool is better: sixty or eighty thousand weights of wool, which we call *arrobas* <note>An *arroba* is a traditional Spanish unit of weight, roughly 25 pounds or 11.5 kilograms.</note>, each of twenty-five pounds. In buying these, and transporting them into this city, they look to various kinds, but from the same source, which is the principal thing. In these places they are washed and packed into sacks; likewise they are carried in carts to the seaports. In taxes, which are paid from them, and in various officials necessary for all these things, the Genoese spend annually about two hundred thousand gold pieces. The same is done by these Genoese in certain other places in Castile from which wools are conveniently carried to the Mediterranean Sea, so that they may be taken from there to Italy; and it is done by various other merchants in other places from where they are more easily transported to the ocean, to be sent from there to Flanders. That the Genoese buy more weights of wool in one year than another depends on the "commissions" <note>original: "commissionib." These are purchase orders or contracts sent from headquarters in Italy.</note> which are sent to them from Genoa by the principal traders. Indeed, in this city of Cuenca there are usually business managers of those who reside in Genoa, and sometimes commissions are sent to certain citizens of this city to manage the business of those staying in Genoa. However, that the commissions are more numerous or larger in one year than another usually happens because of a greater or lesser dispatch of wool in Italy, and in the places to which they are exported from there in the preceding year, and likewise from the shipwrecks of the vessels by which they were carried, and from various other circumstances. Because there is a far greater supply of wool carried from this city and from other places in Castile to foreign nations than what is used in making cloth in the same places, it is more clearly seen that the prices of wool <margin>see</margin> in this city and elsewhere depend on the commissions sent from Genoa. If they are many, the price of wool increases greatly; but if they are few and less extensive, the price decreases, as the principal buyers are lacking and the merchandise is abundant. And this is the principal cause of the increase and decrease of the price of wool in this city. <margin>Year 1592</margin> Thus, in this year 1592, it was found by experience that wools of the third kind, which in other years were accustomed to be sold for twenty-one or twenty-two reals, were sold after the sheep were shorn for sixteen reals, because few commissions sent here from Genoa were said to have reached only thirty-six thousand or forty thousand weights. From this it further resulted that those who, in hope of commissions, had bought many weights with anticipated money, did not even find the full price which they had given for them. From the same source it follows that the price of wool in this city depends much on the will of the Genoese. For since this merchandise loses value unless they themselves buy it, and since commissions are sent to only three or four, or at most to five, six, or seven people, it is almost in their power to set the price. For if they do not wish to increase the price, the owners of the wool are forced to sell it there, especially...
