...especially since wool contracts are made over a long period of time and are largely carried out with **money paid in advance** <note>original: "pecunia anticipata." This refers to the practice of credit or forward-funding, where the buyer pays before the product is ready.</note>. None of these buyers would dare to purchase via a contract and advance payment at a higher price, but instead, they follow the lead of the **Genoese** <note>Genoese merchants were the primary international financiers and wool traders in 16th-century Spain.</note>. Nevertheless, it is no less true that the Genoese—because of the scarcity of these wools among foreign nations and the many large commissions they receive—customarily increase the price so they can preempt each other in buying and complete their business more quickly, especially when the owners of the wool refuse to sell at a low price. Furthermore, because those to whom the commissions are sent are few, they more easily reach an agreement among themselves so that none of them exceeds the **common price** <term>common price: the "just price" established by the market rather than by legal decree</term>, whereas the sellers are many, and many of them are pressed by poverty. Thus, it is harder for the sellers to agree that none should sell below a certain price, even though some occasionally try to persuade others to do so.

5 The reason why the sale of wool, more than other goods, is customary and even necessary to be conducted largely through contracts and advance payments—aside from the desire for profit on the part of the buyers—is primarily this: such a vast quantity of wool requires so many animals to be raised by so many people, for the great good of the owners and the entire kingdom. This requires massive expenses for the nourishment and wages of the servants, for the leasing of pastures, especially in the **winter time** in very distant places, and for many other things. Truly, unless many were assisted by some money paid in advance, they could not sustain it. At the loss of both the common good and their own, they would neither nourish so many animals nor report as much profit as they do by selling with advance payment. Added to this are various other necessities of the many sellers which, along with the preceding reasons, compel them to sell either part or all of their wool for advance money—provided they do not pay a price for the advance itself as a vice <note>Molina is warning against usury, where the advance payment might be used as a pretext for an illegal interest-bearing loan.</note>. Certainly, this is done so that some part or parts are paid at various times when they most need the money—either to move the livestock to distant pastures, to bring them back, or to meet other expenses in other affairs. This is usually the reason why they do not sell grain and many other things in advance in the following season.

There is also another cause on the part of the owners of the livestock and wool why it is necessary for wool contracts to be made in advance. If the wool were not already sold at the time of **shearing** <note>original: "tonsionis."</note>, and if there were not people present to receive it at that time, the owners of the wool would be heavily burdened and suffer loss. Since there is so much wool and it occupies much space, and since those who raise the largest flocks shear them away from their own homes in neighboring towns, they would be forced to spend a great deal on transporting it or guarding it outside their own homes if the wool were not received immediately. If it had to be kept in sacks, expenses would be incurred in buying the sacks and packing the wool in them. If it were kept outside of sacks, it would require a massive house or houses, with the risk that from the heat of the floors and the moisture of the frames, the wool would rot and be ruined. These and other reasons on the part of the sellers are what compel the contracts to be made in advance.

Furthermore, on the part of the Genoese, it is because livestock in this region—due to its coldness—are not 

<column-break/>

shorn until the month of June. Often, if the contracts were not made in advance but were only celebrated after the shearing was done, the merchants would not have enough time in so many places to complete the deals, receive the wool, bring it to this city, and do everything else necessary so that the wool, finished at the proper time, could be transported to Italy from the ports in that same year. They would suffer a massive loss from a one-year delay in that business, as they would be forced to have their money tied up for that entire time and would be hindered from other great profits. Indeed, even when contracts are made in advance, they often do not have time to wash all the wools before the arrival of winter, and some are carried over into the following year.

You might say: "Let the contracts be made in advance, but let the price not be determined; rather, let it be established as whatever the price happens to be at the time of the wool's delivery." Aside from other things that will be clear from what is to be said, this does not apply in the matter proposed. For since the Genoese are the ones on whom the setting of the price depends—since they buy the vast majority of the wool and others follow them in price, as was said a little before—surely, without their contract with the owners of the wool, it could not be established what the price would be at the time of delivery. To be sure, when there are many people who buy a commodity in small amounts at the time of delivery—as usually happens with grain, wine, and oil during the harvest—then if some buy with advance money, they can very well determine from the common purchases of others what the common price is at the time of delivery. But truly, when there are so few buyers that they buy almost the entire commodity of the region (leaving only a small amount to be bought by others), they are the ones who, through their contracts, cause the commodity to be cheap or to increase in price. Since they are the ones who effectively establish the price, it is not possible for their advance contracts to be made in reference to a price that would "run" at the time of delivery <note>Molina argues that there is no "market price" independent of these large-scale advance contracts.</note>.

For these reasons, therefore, the buying and selling of wool has largely been accustomed to be done with money paid in advance. Sometimes the owners of the livestock sell only a certain part of the future wool in this way, reserving the rest to be sold at another time; sometimes, however, they sell the whole lot. Sometimes they receive only a part of the money in advance at one or more times and the rest at the time of delivery; sometimes they receive the total in advance, according to each person's need and as the buyers and sellers agree among themselves. Those who are not so pressed by necessity usually keep their wool for a more opportune time for sale, which is usually the time of shearing or thereabouts. It is also said that when the money is paid in advance, it is most frequent to pay six or eight **reals** <note>original: "regales." A Spanish silver coin.</note> for each weight, and of the remaining price, half is given to some at the time the livestock are moved at the beginning of spring, and the other half at the time the wool is delivered.

6 These advance sales happen throughout the entire year, from the shearing of one year until the shearing of the next, and they regularly begin in the month of July. This is done at a price even lower than what was paid the previous year with advanced money <note>original: "pecunia anticipata." This refers to credit or forward-funding where the buyer pays months before the product is ready.</note>. The Genoese merchant contends that he loses far more profit because the wool was not delivered at the time established this year—meaning he is forced to keep that capital outside of the exchange market <note>original: "extra cambium." Capital "in exchange" refers to money active in international banking and currency markets, which generated consistent interest.</note> for so long—than the actual decrease in the price at which he buys the following year’s wool. Therefore, the agreements for the following year’s wool usually begin from July of one year. Sometimes the sellers invite the "shearers" <note>original: "carptores." Agents or merchants who contracted for the clip.</note> to make contracts, and at other times the buyers invite the sellers, depending on whether the sellers find themselves in greater, lesser, or no need of advanced money, and according to whether there are more and larger, or fewer, commissions being made. These deals are made at the feast of Saint Bartholomew and at the feast of Saint Michael—at what they call the *Mesta* <note>The Honored Council of the Mesta was the powerful guild of sheep owners in Spain.</note>, which are like certain fairs for livestock and wool where other matters pertaining to livestock are handled. The Genoese flock there through their business agents, along with other wool merchants and the owners of the flocks and wool, and many purchases and sales of wool are customarily celebrated there. Since the primary circumstance that varies the price of wool is, as stated above, the commissions for wool that already exist or are expected in the future, the prices of wool are established according to those, while considering other circumstances as well. The prices may increase or decrease from the time the agreements begin until the flocks are shorn and the wool is received; the buyers always take care to buy at the lowest price possible, and the sellers strive to sell at the highest price possible.

<margin>30</margin> Under these same circumstances, the sooner the Genoese buy with advanced money, the more they take care to decrease the price, saying that they always have their money in exchange or in other business, and for that reason, the sooner they pay it out, the more their profit ceases; this loss is offset by the decrease in the price of the wool due to the advance payment. <margin>31</margin> A sign that this is the case is that the Genoese themselves willingly raise the price by one or two reales per weight <note>The "weight" or *arroba* was roughly 25 lbs.</note>, provided the whole price is paid at the time of receiving the wool—especially if they are expected to wait three months after the receipt, at least for half of the price. For not only would their money have earned as much or more profit during that time, but they also hold it more safely than if they buy it with advanced payment. <margin>32</margin> They also usually increase the price by a half or one real per weight if they contract with advanced money with someone from whom they hope the delivery of wool will be of the best and most sincere quality—namely, because he will deliver it without being sprinkled with dust or otherwise unclean, or because he will deliver more wool per sheep than others. It is also said that the more wool a seller has, the more the Genoese usually

<column-break/>

increase the price of that wool, even if it is of no better quality. It is said, likewise, that the more wool someone has, the better they usually stand by the contract to deliver the whole lot; from the buyer's perspective, this results in less expense for the agents who receive it and arrange for it to be transported away. This does not happen when wool is bought from many different people, each in a small quantity. Therefore, in this type of contract, that common circumstance is lacking—namely, the rule that the more of a certain merchandise is bought at once from someone, the cheaper it is usually bought. Excluding other circumstances that might cause the price of wool to rise or fall, from the time the advanced purchases begin until the delivery of the wool, there is usually a gradual increase in the price of one silver real per weight. However, due to the circumstances of the commissions—because new ones arrive unexpectedly, or they fail to receive wool to complete those already accepted, or previously granted commissions are restricted or withdrawn (which happens more rarely)—the price of wool usually undergoes a large increase or decrease. Thus, what was expected to be worth eighteen reales sometimes reaches twenty-one or twenty-two, or even more; and sometimes it decreases to sixteen reales, as happened this year in [15]92. This is the reason why those who bought with advanced money, if they later wish to sell their wool to the Genoese or other locals for cash at the time of delivery, they scarcely find—or don't find at all—the price they originally gave for it. In which event, those who are less God-fearing resort to selling on credit, either to those who buy via <term>Mohatras</term> <note>A "Mohatra" was a fraudulent contract used to hide usury, where a seller sells an item on credit at a high price and immediately buys it back for a lower cash price.</note>, or to those who want to manufacture cloth from the wool but lack the money for it; and to keep themselves from loss and make some profit, they exceed the just price, which is manifest usury. 

In these wool purchases with advanced money, many of the natives of this region follow the Genoese, buying at the price the Genoese buy, even though they do not buy in such vast quantities as the Genoese do. Profit remains for them from such advanced payments because it is rare to find someone who does not trade with their own money. For if they do not buy wool with it, they will buy wheat, oil, or something else, or spend it on manufacturing cloth, or buy estates or an annual rent, from which they might always gain something to sustain their family. Furthermore, some of them buy wool in that manner to make cloth from it; others to resell it, either to the Genoese if they need it, or to others for making cloth; others, finally, buy indifferently to resell it if a favorable price occurs, or to make cloth from it, as they judge will be more useful and better for them as time progresses. For a long time, there was a law in this Kingdom that the natives should have the right of <term>retractus</term> <note>The right of first refusal or "withdrawal," allowing a local to step into a foreigner's contract.</note> regarding the wool that foreigners bought. For foreigners were not admitted to buy wool in this Kingdom by any other rule than with this...

### DISPUTATION 360

#### SUMMARY

1 *How the purchase of wool in the kingdom of Castile with advanced money is lawful.*
2 *At what time the just price of a thing should be considered.*
3 *Under what circumstances the purchase of wool in Castile with advanced payment is permitted, and see number 5.*
4 *Why sales made with advanced money can be called valid.*
5 *The circumstances from which a contract is judged just, and according to what state they must be observed.*
6 *How a price not fixed by law may decrease in two ways by reason of advanced payment.*

**Juan Medina** <note>Juan de Medina (1489–1545), a Spanish theologian who wrote extensively on restitution and contracts.</note> on restitution, question 38, penultimate doubt; **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), also known as Doctor Navarrus, a famous canonist and early economist of the School of Salamanca.</note> in his Manual, chapter 23, number 82; and others—noting nothing † about the peculiar practice of this contract—condemn it as usurious. They claim there is a burden of restoring the increase in price beyond the supreme rigorous just price <note>term: "supremum rigorosum iustum." In Scholastic economics, the "just price" was a range; the "supreme" was the highest morally acceptable price, while the "infimum" was the lowest.</note> at the time of delivery. Not a few of those who wrote after them follow these doctors. Indeed, there are certain strong arguments for this opinion.

2 First and most importantly, we can argue as follows: the † just price of a thing is not what it is worth at the time of the agreement, but at the time of delivery. If it is unknown how much it will be worth then, and a price must be justly established at the time of the agreement for the time of delivery, it must be established in one of two ways. Namely: either by reference to the price that is commonly found to be valid at the time of delivery, by stipulating that such an amount be paid then; or by establishing a "middle price" between the supreme and the lowest just price at which it is hoped it will then be worth, so that the seller and the buyer undergo an equal risk. All these things are clear from the preceding disputations and are confirmed by the chapters *In ciuitate* and *Nauiganti* (in the second and third cases) in the Decretals *De usuris* <note>These are specific chapters in Canon Law used to determine what constitutes usury in maritime and commercial loans.</note>. Since, therefore, in this purchase of wool with advanced money, neither is the price established by reference to what the wool will be worth at the time of delivery, nor is a middle price con-

<column-break/>

-stituted between the highest and lowest expected values, but rather a price is set that does not even reach the lowest just price <note>original: "infimum iustum."</note> estimated for that time—and this is done because of the payment of all or part of the price with advanced money—it surely follows that the contract is unjust. It would be **palliated usury** <note>term: "palliata usura." Disguised usury, where interest is hidden under the guise of a different type of contract, like a sale.</note>, with the burden of restoring up to the lowest just price that the wool will have at the time of delivery.

Second (and the strength of this is contained in the preceding), to buy wool for seventeen silver pieces by advancing part of the payment in the month of September or January—when the wool is believed to be worth twenty or twenty-one silver pieces at the time of delivery—is effectively the same as giving seventeen silver pieces in order to have twenty returned at the time of the wool's delivery. But this is manifest usury, with the burden of restoring the excess; therefore, that contract is usurious.

Third, such wools are not bought with advanced payment as they exist "in potential" or in an imperfect state, in the way that by buying a crop in the blade <note>original: "sata." Specifically, crops still growing in the field.</note>, one buys the fruits that are in them potentially; or as, by buying a "cast of the net," one buys the fish as they are potentially in it. This is clear from the fact that the buyers of such wool do not undergo the risk of loss, whereas those who buy the growing crops or the cast of the net undergo the risk of the fruits or the fish. Therefore, they buy them according to the "perfected state" they will have at the time of delivery, and dependently upon them having that state. Hence, if by chance they perish before delivery, the price is restored to the buyers. Therefore, just as they are bought according to their perfected state and for the time in which they will have it, so their just price is what they will have at that time. From this it follows that if, because of the advanced agreement and the delivery of money, something is subtracted from the lowest just price that will then exist, palliated usury is committed.

**Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a key figure in the School of Salamanca. The reference is to his work "De iustitia et iure."</note> in book 6 *On Justice*, question 4, article 1, in the latter part of his response to the last point, does not condemn such purchases of wool with advanced money at a lower price than the wool is worth at the time of delivery. He says this is acceptable provided they are only done two or three months before the shearing of the wool, at a time when the owners of the flocks need money to pay for pasture and to bring back the flocks—or at least provided they are only done within a year before delivery. The reason is that this business now requires that it be done with advanced money, and that is the just price of the wool, insofar as it is sold in advance according to the necessity of the matter. It is also said that the most wise and prudent **Vitoria** <note>Francisco de Vitoria (c. 1483–1546), the founder of the School of Salamanca.</note> approved this contract, and that the merchants of **Burgos** consulted the doctors of Paris, and the same contract was approved by them. Certain others who wrote after Soto also defend the same contract, and among others **Córdoba** <note>Antonio de Córdoba (1485–1578), a Franciscan theologian.</note> in his Spanish *Summa*, question 85, where he lays out the practice of this business.

Regarding this matter, submitting to the judgment of others, I will add what I think. First of all, when the wools are not of the kind that are carried to foreign nations, as with many...

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

In many places in Spain where these conditions do not exist, the same must be judged concerning purchases made with advanced money at a lower price than what is expected at the time of delivery. Like other similar purchases of wheat and other goods, these are to be considered usurious—unless some particular reason, such as lost profit <note>original: "lucri cessantis." A legal concept where a merchant is compensated for the potential profit they lose by tying up their capital in a specific venture.</note> or some other factor, as explained in the preceding sections, provides an excuse. I affirm the same regarding wools of the same kind as those exported from this kingdom, but which are bought in places where there are no merchants who buy for export, but rather for making cloth or hats within this Kingdom. This applies even if they are taken to Portugal or other places that are not overseas to make hats, or even if they are taken to some overseas province in a very small quantity. 

An exception might be made if perhaps in the city of **Segovia** and neighboring towns there is some circumstance which prevents those contracts from being condemned. Such a case might be if no wool were bought there in advance, the price of wool bought at the time of shearing would be no higher than the price currently paid in advance. On this matter, those who are experienced, learned, and god-fearing (who have been mentioned to me) will judge better than I. For merchants must always be heard, and their proposals must be weighed to judge whether a contract should be condemned or not; otherwise, by its nature, it is unjust and usurious, as is the case we are now disputing. I am led to assert the doctrine handed down a little earlier because, in truth, the three arguments proposed evidently conclude that such contracts, by their nature, are usurious unless some circumstance or circumstances are present to excuse them. 

The mere need of the flock and wool owners for money to send their livestock to winter pastures <note>This refers to the "Mesta" system in Spain, where sheep were moved long distances between summer and winter grazing lands.</note> and bring them back—and thus the requirement from this head that many wool agreements be made with money paid in advance, either in whole or in part—is certainly not enough to make contracts lawful and free from usury that are otherwise usurious by nature. This is despite what **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a prominent Spanish theologian of the School of Salamanca.</note> seems to suggest; hence, he relies on a rather weak foundation for establishing his opinion.

<margin>3</margin>
But since in moral matters a change of some circumstance or circumstances is often the reason why a case varies, so that what is otherwise one way by its nature is not so due to the circumstances, I believe something else must be said. Where the circumstances are present that were explained in the preceding discussion regarding this city of **Cuenca** <note>original: "Conchensi ciuitate."</note> and neighboring towns, such contracts are not to be condemned as either usurious or unjust. This is provided that, despite the concurrent circumstances, the price for the advanced money is not reduced below the lowest just price <term>Just Price: The "iustum pretium," a medieval economic theory stating that there is a morally "fair" price for goods, often determined by common estimation rather than just supply and demand.</term> which then runs for that method of selling, and provided that the need of one's neighbors does not cause their blood to be sucked by monopolies or unfair agreements more than right reason would then prescribe.

The circumstances are, first, that wool agreements at a fixed price ought to be made in advance for the good of both the sellers and the foreign buyers. Furthermore, it is not practical to base the price on what they would commonly have at the time of delivery; this is because that price would depend heavily on the agreements made by those very foreign

<column-break/>

buyers at the time of delivery—indeed, it would depend more on them than on the sellers, and far more than on the other buyers. This is because a few foreigners buy a far greater quantity of wool than all the natives of that province combined. Therefore, it is almost within their power to set the price, both at the time of the agreement and at the time of delivery, as was explained in the preceding disputation.

Secondly, the future price at the time of delivery depends heavily on the quantity of wool bought in advance. So much so that many prudent men experienced in business are convinced that if advanced purchases were not made by foreigners, wool at the time of shearing or the start of delivery would be worth far less than it is now when bought with advanced money. The reason is that if no wool had been sold, very many owners—pressed by necessity to sell and gasping for a price—would sell much more cheaply at the time of delivery than they do now when selling with partially advanced money.

Among others whom I consulted, I found one who excelled in judgment and experience. Although he was not a man of letters, he proposed in his own judgment that this business was usurious and unjust. When I asked him whether the wool would be sold at a higher price at that time than it is now with advanced money if no advanced purchases were made (but if it were forbidden by public law for everyone to make an agreement before the day of delivery), he first replied: "If the resources of the owners of the flocks and wool were so great that they could all wait without receiving any advanced money to make their agreements at the time of delivery, I have no doubt they would sell them for more than they do now with advanced money. For it is necessity," he said, "that forces them to sell more cheaply for advanced money." 

But when I went further in my questioning and said: "Imagine that the owners of the flocks and wool had exactly the same resources they have now, and a law were passed prohibiting wool from being bought and sold in advance. I ask then: if the wool owners sought elsewhere for a way to meet their needs until that time, would the wool then be sold at a higher price at the time of shearing and delivery than it is now in an advanced purchase, or not?" He replied that they would then be sold more cheaply at the time of delivery than they are now in advance, so that the men could quickly meet their many and most serious needs. Nor, if purchases and sales were made in that way, could as many livestock be maintained as are maintained now.

<margin>4</margin>
From this, therefore, I gathered that the sales which are now made with advanced money are neither unjust nor usurious. For <margin>5</margin> the circumstances from which the just price of a thing is to be weighed, and from which it must be judged whether a contract is just or unjust, must be considered according to the present state of things, not according to an imagined state. Given the existing needs of the owners of flocks and wool, and other things as they are now, the wool would be sold at the time of shearing at a cheaper price—or certainly not at a higher just price—than it is now bought for with advanced money, if up to that time no sales of wool were made (either because a public law prohibited them or because buyers were unwilling to buy until then). Therefore...

<summary>Molina examines the wool trade in Castile, arguing that advanced payments are not usurious if they reflect the actual market reality where sellers' desperate need would otherwise drive prices even lower at harvest time. He emphasizes that moral judgment of contracts must be based on real-world economic conditions rather than theoretical ideals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of whether advance payments for wool are usurious. Molina argues that market conditions, rather than a hidden interest rate, often determine the lower price paid for wool when purchased months before delivery.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 360

Advance purchases, such as those made now, are not usurious or unjust because they are not made at a lower price than what would be considered a just price at the time of the wool shearing, provided such advance purchases had not occurred. Indeed, if they are regularly made at a lower price than what the wool is worth at the time of delivery, this is because—once these advance purchases are partially eliminated—the needs of the owners of the wool and sheep are diminished. Since the quantity of wool that would otherwise have to be sold all at once at the time of delivery is reduced by these same purchases, they are themselves the cause for the price of the remaining wool to increase at the time of delivery. Therefore, the vast quantity of wool exposed for sale, the multitude of sellers, and their many heavy needs would be the circumstances that, taken together, would make the wool worth far less at the time of delivery if no advance purchases preceded it than it is worth now at the time of delivery, or at the price for which it is now bought with advanced money.

To understand this better, imagine that the wool is shorn around the **Feast of Saint Michael** <note>September 29th; a traditional date for settling accounts and agricultural cycles.</note> but cannot be removed or sent to Italy or Flanders until the month of June. In that case, there would be no need for the wool owners to make sales with advanced money. Since they would start selling their wool at the time of shearing, they could use the proceeds to send their flocks to winter pastures and bring them back. Likewise, the foreigners would have sufficient time from the end of September until June or July to buy the wool and transport it to the place where it is washed.

But who would doubt that when foreigners had so much time to buy the wool, and so much wool was offered for sale by so many owners starting from the end of September, they would be so pressed by their needs—the cost of supporting the sheep for the entire previous year and the immediate need to send the sheep to winter—that the wool would be sold at the time of delivery for a price as low as it is currently sold with advanced money? Who would also doubt that later, as time progressed and the supply of wool remaining for sale grew smaller, and as that wool came into the hands of sellers with greater resources who were not pressed by such necessity, and as it became more necessary to fulfill the commissions of foreigners for that year, the price would increase? This regularly happens with wheat, wine, and oil, which are worth less at harvest time because of their abundance, the crowd of sellers, and their poverty, than they are later as time goes on.

Therefore, in the purchase of wool made with advanced money, the reason why the wool is bought at a cheaper price is not so much the anticipation of payment as it is the beginning of the wool-selling season. At that time, there are more sellers pressed by greater necessity, and there is less need for foreigners to buy immediately to fulfill their commissions compared to later in the season. All these factors cause the merchandise to lose value and consequently decrease the **just price** <note>The "just price" (pretium iustum) in Scholastic thought was the market price reached without fraud or monopoly, reflecting common estimation and local conditions.</note>. You would find the same thing if you imagined that the wool was shorn at the usual time, but there was no time remaining in that summer or autumn to prepare and ship it to Italy or Flan-

<column-break/>

-ders, and one had to wait for the following summer. Indeed, if you imagine that foreigners do not want to buy one year’s wool except to ship it the following year, then purchases would not be made with advanced money, nor would they be made at a higher price at the time of delivery than they are now with advanced money, for the reasons just stated.

There is also another circumstance: the **commissions** <note>Orders or contracts sent by principal merchants to their local agents.</note> sent from Italy and Flanders by the leading merchants or heads of companies to their agents residing here are usually sent with a limit on a certain price for each weight of wool, which they must not exceed. For they are not bound to buy at the price the Spaniards want, but at the price they themselves choose. Since these agents are primarily the ones who establish the price, and they do so depending on the commissions they receive (not increasing the price unless they first consult and receive approval from the principal merchants whose business they conduct), the price limit in the commissions has as much power to prevent the price from rising if the agreement is made at the time of delivery as it does if it is an advance purchase. Consequently, if wool is regularly bought at a lower price with advanced money than by an agreement made at the time of delivery, it does not arise so much from the anticipation of payment as from the fact that these are the first purchases, when there are more sellers pressed by greater needs and there is a larger supply of wool to be sold to fulfill the commissions—all of which cause the goods to be cheaper.

To this, we add what was said at the end of Dispute 357 regarding the increase in price when a thing is sold on credit; it can be adapted here regarding the decrease in price for advanced money. Truly, although an advance payment is a **loan in effect** <note>original: "mutuum virtute." While legally a sale, the early payment functions like a loan because the buyer loses use of the cash for a period.</note>, since the price is not fixed by law and does not consist in a single point, it can decrease based on various circumstances. From this, it follows that an advance payment can sometimes be the occasion or circumstance for the just price of the goods to decrease, because it increases the number of sellers who are pressed by necessity and 

<margin>6</margin>

offering many goods. Therefore, when the price is not fixed by law, it can decrease in two ways by reason of advance payment. First, as if the lower price received is a reward or compensation for the advance payment. In this way, it is **usury**, because it is a profit from a loan in effect. In the second way, although the price decreases (or rather, does not increase) on the occasion of the advance payment, it is because the advance payment was the cause for sellers to multiply, and thus the just price decreased, or rather did not exceed what it would have been if such advance purchases had not preceded it. In this way, since it is not profit from a loan, it is not usury.

Finally, this must be observed regarding such foreign buyers: since the just price of wool with advance payment does not consist in a single point but has a certain range within the limits of what is just, one must always check whether the lower price given in an advance purchase—compared to what the wool is expected to be worth at the time of delivery—is nonetheless at least the lowest just price commonly prevailing for that wool under that method of selling.

<summary>Molina argues that paying a lower price for wool in advance is not necessarily usury, as the lower price is often driven by market forces—such as high supply and seller desperation at the start of the season—rather than being a fee for the "loan" of the money.</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

in the same way, regarding the decrease in price, it is permissible for the buyer to subtract from it the amount of "lost profit" <note>original: *lucrum cessans*; a legal concept where a party is compensated for the profit they missed out on by choosing one investment over another.</note> they truly incur. If the price reduction does not exceed the total decrease in value and the lost profit, there is no reason to condemn the contract as unjust. Nevertheless, such buyers should always be advised not to be cruel toward their neighbors who are sellers, whom they see pressed by necessity; they would lessen the severity of God's just judgment by showing mercy. However, if the discount is greater than those two factors combined, the contract is both unjust and usurious, carrying the obligation to restore whatever was taken in excess.

As for the other local buyers in the area, if they likewise buy at a just price (following the method of buying already established by foreigners, or likely to be established), there is no reason for them to be condemned. This is because they are buying at the current just price, and they should not be in a worse position in that regard than the foreigners, even if they profit from that business. Thus, having justly purchased wool with advanced money, they may later resell it to those same foreigners or any other buyers within the limits of the current just price.

I should warn that both these locals and the foreigners must keep in mind that they profit in this business through advanced money. Therefore, it is unlawful for them—under the pretext of lost profit—to take as much as that money would have earned them if they had *not* paid it in advance. Indeed, they must subtract from their claim of lost profit whatever amount they gain by buying in advance, since their lost profit is reduced by that much. Therefore, if their lost profit does not exceed what they gain by making the purchase in advance, then truly they have no "lost profit" at all; consequently, they can subtract nothing from the price (which would otherwise be just) on the grounds of lost profit. If, however, they lose more than they gain, they may only subtract that specific difference.

Finally, I should warn that because wool is purchased two or three years before the shearing, it is unlawful to decrease the price more than one would for a single year's advance—as Soto <note>referring to Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a highly influential Spanish Dominican scholastic and contemporary of Molina.</note> rightly stated—unless it is specifically for the reason of lost profit and included in the contract. Otherwise, usury is committed, and there is an obligation to pay it back. For as far as the price increase at the time of delivery is concerned, it makes no difference whether the wool was bought two years in advance or merely three months.

It remains for us to respond to the arguments of the opposing opinion. To the first, it must be said that the "major premise" is generally true in itself; however, it is not true when, due to the accidental circumstances of these advance purchases, the price of the remaining goods must necessarily increase. Since the price the goods will have at the time of delivery depends largely on a few buyers—whether they buy in advance or pay at the time of delivery—the circumstances we explained apply. To the "minor premise," it should be said that although a price is set which normally does not reach the lowest price the wool will have at delivery (assuming these advance purchases), it is still a price that would be considered the lowest the wool would have had if no advance 

<column-break/>

purchases had occurred. Therefore, one must deny that less is being paid due to the advance payment than would be paid at the time of delivery if no advance purchases had taken place; this is sufficient for the contract to be neither unjust nor usurious.

To the second argument, it must be said that the "major premise" would be true if that specific wool would have been worth that much at the time of delivery even if no advance purchases had occurred. But it is different if, because of so many existing advance purchases, it is not the wool itself but the *remaining* wool that increases in price because of those prior sales. Finally, it must be said that the "major premise" is generally true when the explained circumstances do not intervene; otherwise, it is false. Therefore, while the "minor premise" is admitted, the conclusion must be denied.

To the third argument: if the premise is granted, the conclusion would follow if we were talking about the price the wool *would have had* if no advance purchases had preceded it. But the conclusion must be denied regarding the price the remaining wool will have at the time of delivery *because* of those advance purchases. The conclusion is also denied because the explained circumstances are present. Finally, regarding the three reasons proposed, it must be said that they are indeed very firm—almost like demonstrations in moral matters—if they are understood in themselves, isolated from circumstances. But if they are understood as being unaffected by any intervening accidental circumstances, they become "false drawings" <note>original: *pseudographos*; a logical term for a fallacious or deceptive argument.</note> of a syllogism.

# Whether a debt due in the future may be justly bought for a lower advance price than the amount owed.

## DISPUTATION 390

### SUMMARY

1. *A debt or right which a creditor holds for future payment can be understood in two ways.*
2. *When a debtor can justly buy back the debt from a creditor at a lower price through advance payment.*
3. *Whether it is a just contract when a third party buys the debt from a creditor via advance payment.*
4. *Whether the same applies to a current or past debt that has not yet been paid.*
5. *When a debt that can be collected without labor or expense may be bought at a lower price via advance payment.*

---

### This disputation also concerns purchases at a lower price through advanced money; therefore, it is to be examined in this place.

<margin>Question 1</margin>
I. A debt, or the right that a creditor holds to have something paid to him in the future, can be understood as being bought in two ways. One way is by the debtor himself. For example, if someone owes a hundred to be paid a year from now, and he now buys from the creditor the right to receive those hundred at the end of the year, for ninety-five paid immediately, or for some other amount.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 361, Page 271

<margin>2</margin>
...at another price below one hundred. In the second case, it is purchased by a third party. For example, if Peter, for ninety paid immediately, buys from Paul the one hundred that John owes Paul, which is to be paid in a year. Navarrus, in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 232, asserts that even in the first case proposed, that contract is licit, even if no "lost profit" <note>original: *lucrum cessans*; the profit one gives up by choosing one investment over another.</note> occurs, or even if no "emergent loss" <note>original: *damnum emergens*; a direct financial loss resulting from an action.</note> arises for the debtor from the early payment. This is true even if the debt is certain and it is morally believed that it will be paid at its proper time without any labor or expense on the part of the creditor.

The reason given is that in that contract, no loan <note>original: *mutuum*; specifically a loan of fungible goods like money where the same amount must be returned.</note> takes place, but rather a purchase—not of the money that is owed, but of the *right* to receive it. This right to a future debt is worth less than the thing itself would be if it were present, because such a right is "sterile" <note>Molina uses "sterile" here to mean that the money cannot produce further profit while the holder is waiting for the due date.</note> for that entire time. Therefore, he says, as long as it is not done as a fraud to hide usury, and as long as the higher amount owed is not forgiven as a "price" for the early payment, but instead the right to one hundred to be paid after a year is bought for, say, ninety-five present coins, the contract is licit, and the price is equal to the value of the right being bought. However, Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> criticizes him for this, because while Cajetan allows the contract to be licit in the second case (as we will mention shortly), he denies it is licit in the first.

This opinion of Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous Spanish canon lawyer.</note> is singular and, in my judgment, entirely improbable. Therefore, against it, we establish this first conclusion: Excluding "lost profit" or "emergent loss" arising from the debtor paying that smaller price early, that contract is illicit and usurious—unless the creditor, out of sheer generosity and without any "mixed involuntary" <note>original: *involuntariè mixtè*; an Aristotelian term for an action done under pressure, like throwing cargo overboard during a storm to save a ship.</note> pressure, forgives the debtor the remainder of the debt. I hold this to be true even if it is likely that the creditor would only recover the debt with difficulty, expense, and labor, and even if some third party would justly buy that same debt for that same price (or even less) because of those same troubles and difficulties in recovering it, as we will explain in the second case.

I said "excluding lost profit or emergent loss" because, even if the debt resulted from a loan and the creditor’s kindness, the debtor would not be bound to pay early. If, however, the creditor demanded early payment and thereby lost profit, he could sell that right to the debtor for a just price according to the strict rigor of justice, regardless of what Angelus <note>Angelus Carletus de Clavasio, author of the *Summa Angelica*.</note> said to the contrary. I also added "unless the creditor out of sheer generosity," etc., because when it is clear the creditor is forgiving part of the debt out of pure kindness—even if he does so to entice the debtor to pay early—no one can doubt the contract is licit and the forgiveness is valid.

The rest of the conclusion is proven by the distinction between a debtor buying back their own debt and a third party buying that same debt. In comparison to a third party, that debt is worth no more than the creditor’s right, given the debtor's bad disposition toward paying (even if that arises from the debtor's own wickedness). Therefore, because the debt is expected to be recovered with greater difficulty, labor, and expense, even if caused by the debtor's malice, the debt and the right are worth less to a third-party

<column-break/>

buyer. But the debtor himself is bound to pay it in full and to fulfill the obligation he has completely, by removing all malice and doing everything in his power. If, after doing everything in his power, he cannot pay the debt, he is fully bound to pay as much as he can and remains obligated to fulfill the rest in the future as soon and as well as he is able. Thus, whatever he gives in an early payment, if it is less than the full debt, the creditor’s right and the obligation the debtor holds still represent a greater value than that payment; therefore, he cannot buy it back at a "discounted" price. Indeed, since his early payment acts as a loan in relation to the creditor (as is clear from the preceding disputations), it follows that if the full debt is forgiven because of that smaller payment—not out of generosity, but through a "mixed involuntary" choice—it is a profit from a loan, and thus "palliated" <note>original: *palliata*; disguised or hidden usury.</note> usury. On this point, the Doctors commonly agree, even if they have not fully grasped the distinction we have provided between the debtor himself and a third-party buyer. These matters will become clearer in what follows, where we will also address the foundations of Navarrus’s argument.

<margin>3 Question</margin>
As for the second case proposed, Cajetan, in his *Summa* under the word "usury," although he agrees with us on the first case regarding disguised usury, nevertheless in the final chapter (following Innocent and John de Ripa, whom Cajetan cites), is of the opinion that when a third party buys a debt with advanced money, the contract is licit. This is supposedly true even if no lost profit or emergent loss arises for the buyer from that early payment, and even if the debt is such that it will be recovered at its proper time without expense or labor. Navarrus holds the same opinion in the place cited.

Cajetan proves this because the creditor in this case does not sell what is owed to him, but the *right* that he has to it. Once the contract is entered, the creditor is no longer entitled to the debt; instead, for that price, he grants the buyer the right he had against the debtor. Therefore, if the debtor later fails to pay—whether due to poverty or some other reason—the creditor is not held liable for anything, and he can licitly keep the price he received for the right he transferred to the buyer. Now, in such a contract, no loan is seen, but a mere purchase and sale of that right. Where a loan is seen (at least in essence), and usury is suspected, the one receiving the loan is bound to something in the future because of it. However, that does not apply here, because the creditor who sold the debt for advanced money is bound to nothing in the future. Thus, usury does not intervene in such a contract. Cajetan further proves that there is no injustice here because the right being sold is worth less than the thing itself would be if it were present. Indeed, that right is "sterile" until the time the debt is paid. Just as land that is sterile for several years is worth less and is bought for a lower price than if it were immediately fruitful, so a right can be justly bought with present money for a lower price than the value of the debt itself. Indeed, Cajetan says the just price is whatever is commonly offered for such a right...

<summary>Molina debates whether selling a debt at a discount is usury. He concludes that while a debtor cannot "buy back" their own debt for less than its value (which would be disguised usury), a third party may justly buy a debt at a discount because they are purchasing a "sterile" future right rather than making a loan.</summary>

# Luis de Molina
## On Contracts

At this point, observe that in the payment of such debts (which they call *pagas* <note>Spanish for "payments" or "promissory notes."</note>), when they are far from the time for which they are owed, they are called "green" or "bitter"; however, when the time for which they are owed arrives, they are called "ripe." This metaphor is taken from fruits which, when they are distant from the time of harvest, are called green and bitter, but when they are harvested, they are ripe. And from this, the cited authors construct another argument: that just as fruit is worth less and is bought more cheaply the further it is from the time of harvest, so too these payments—or rather, the rights to them—are worth less and are sold more cheaply when they are far from the time they are due than when the time of payment is already present.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
The contrary opinion—namely, that such a contract is unjust and imposes an obligation to make restitution up to the full amount that was owed and which is thus "bought" with early money—is the common opinion of the doctors: Conrad [Summenhart] *on Contracts*, question 67 and the two following; Johannes Medina *on Restitution*, question 38, last doubt; [Domingo de] Soto, book 6 *on Justice*, question 4, article 1, reply 3; John Major on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, question 40, argument 7; Gabriel [Biel] in the same place, question 11, article 3, doubt 4; Angelus [de Clavasio] under the word "usury," part 1, numbers 63 and 64; Sylvester [Prierias] under "usury," part 2, question 14; and many others. Therefore, against Cajetan, Navarrus, Innocent [IV], and Joannes de Ripa, the second conclusion is established.

<margin>4</margin>
When a debt, speaking morally, will be paid in full at its proper time without labor or expense, the contract is illicit and induces an obligation of restitution when such a debt is bought from a third party with early money at a lower price than that which the debtor is bound to pay in the future—provided, however, that the buyer does not lose as much profit <note>original: *lucrum cessans*; a common justification for interest where the lender loses the chance to profit elsewhere.</note> or incur as much emerging loss <note>original: *damnum emergens*; a direct financial loss caused by the transaction.</note> from that early payment as the excess of the debt over that early payment. When, however, there is a danger that the debt might not be paid in full, or that it might not be paid without labor and expense, then it can be bought at a lower price than what is owed, by as much as it is judged by a prudent person's judgment to be worth less because of the feared labor, expenses, or any other risk.

The first and primary part of this conclusion is proven: First, because the right to receive one hundred a year or two years from now is in truth worth no less in itself than one hundred when it is morally certain that it will be paid then in full and without labor or expense. Otherwise, no iniquity would surely be seen in a loan <note>original: *mutuum*; a loan of fungible goods like money where the same amount must be returned.</note> from the fact that something beyond the principal was required to be paid, on the grounds that the right to payment remaining with the lender was of less value in itself than the thing given in the loan. Such a consequence, however, is heretical, as is clear from what has been said in the matter of usury. It follows, then, that the contract is unequal in the case we are discussing if something less is returned by early payment for the hundred that are owed in the future in that manner. Bartolus [de Saxoferrato] on the law *per diversas* in the Code, title *on Mandate*, and Baldus [de Ubaldis] on law 2 in the Code, title *lest while a suit is pending*, agree with us, teaching that an "action" <note>A legal claim or right to sue for property.</note> for some thing is worth as much as the thing itself, deducting labor and expenses. Understand this also to mean deducting something by reason of risk if, before any expenses are made or labor undertaken, there is a risk that the thing will not be paid, or not paid in full.

<column-break/>

Second, the same part is proven because if the right to receive one hundred a year from now were not worth one hundred now, it would follow that I could say without injustice to someone asking me for a loan of one hundred a year from now: "I do not wish to lend, but I will buy from you the action <note>The legal right to collect.</note> by which you are bound to pay me one hundred a year from now," and that I could rightly buy it for ninety or ninety-five paid immediately. Since indeed that action would be worth no more, the consequence would be manifest usury. Third, if an obligation to pay one hundred after a year were not worth one hundred now, it would follow that if someone had given one hundred as a loan to someone else to be paid after a year, he could not justly receive one hundred from him in the present in exchange for the obligation which that other person holds toward him from the loan—than which nothing can be said to be more absurd. Fourth, if the obligation to pay one hundred after a year were not worth one hundred in the present when the debt will morally be paid without labor and expense and in full at its proper time, it would follow that it would be permitted to sell more dearly on credit than for cash, even when the seller was not going to keep the merchandise and when no profit would cease for him or loss emerge from selling on credit. But the consequence is against the chapters *In civitate* and *Naviganti* regarding usury; therefore so is the antecedent. The logical sequence is proven because the right and obligation which results in the present from someone selling on credit is not worth as much as the debt itself paid in the present, as the authors of the opinion we are impugning affirm.

The second part of the conclusion—namely, that if the buyer loses as much profit or incurs as much loss from the early payment as the excess of the debt over that early payment, the contract is licit, especially if it is signaled to the creditor that the increase is accepted because of that lost profit or emerging loss—that part is conceded by all and is sufficiently clear from the preceding disputations.

The third part—namely, when there is risk that the debt may not be paid in full, or not without labor and expense, it can be licitly bought at a lower price by as much as it is judged by prudent judgment to be worth less for that reason—is also conceded by all. And so it is if the debt is litigious <note>Subject to a lawsuit.</note> or not entirely certain. Nor does this part of the conclusion need any other proof. In this context, observe that one hundred thus owed is sometimes worth ninety, more or less; sometimes eighty, sometimes seventy, sixty, or fifty; and sometimes much less, according to the magnitude of the things that are feared.

Observe also this: if a debt is of little value to a creditor—for example, if something is owed to him by the King, concerning which there is little hope that it will be recovered—and someone, by his own industry or through the favor <note>Influence or high standing.</note> that he has with the King or his ministers, hopes that he will easily recover it; then, if he gives the creditor for that debt as much as it is worth in reality to that same creditor, the contract will be valid and just by the nature of the thing, without any burden of restitution, even if the buyer easily recovers the whole debt and gains a great advantage. The reason is that the just price of a thing bought is not how much it is worth to the buyer (especially because of his own industry or favor with someone), but how much the thing is worth in itself and to the seller himself, as is established from what was said in the sections above.

In Disputation 313, it was said that those upon whom falls the duty to pay...

However, he allows for discounts if the buyer suffers a loss of potential profit or if the debt is risky and difficult to collect, such as debts owed by the Crown.</summary>

Nor can they, by themselves or through an intermediary, buy the debts they are supposed to pay on the King's behalf at a lower price than what is actually owed; just as the King himself cannot do this, as was shown in the first part of this disputation. Many other things have been said on this matter in the cited discussion.

<margin>5</margin> Note finally that not only can future debts be bought from a third party at a lower price for the reasons explained, but also debts that should be paid in the present, or those that remain from the past but have not yet been paid.

Regarding the resolution of those points relied upon by Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian.</note> and Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist.</note>, observe the following: Many admit to the contract in the second conclusion—which we rejected—where a debt is bought at a lower price from a third party with no intervention, and they use those authors' reasons. Consequently, they affirm that those buying debts in that manner with advanced money are indeed performing an unjust contract due to inequality, and are held to restitution, but they do not incur the penalties of <term>usurers</term> <note>Usury was the sinful practice of charging interest on a loan. Scholastics debated whether specific complex contracts were hidden loans.</note>. To me, the opinion of Medina <note>Johannes Medina (1490–1546), a Spanish theologian.</note> in the cited place is far more proven: that the contract is usurious because it is seen as a virtual loan.

Thus, in response to the foundation of Cajetan and Navarrus, it must be said that in such a contract, not only is the right to another's debt being sold, but the debt itself; thus, it is at the buyer's risk. This is just as one who sells the "cast of a net" <note>Latin: *iactum retis*, a legal term for buying the hope of a catch.</note> also sells the fish he might catch, so that the profit or the risk belongs to the buyer. Next, it must be said that although formally only a purchase and sale are seen in that contract, a loan is seen virtually, along with an obligation for something beyond the principal because the money was advanced. Regarding the proof to the contrary, it must be said that for a virtual loan to be seen, it is enough that the one acting as the borrower is held to something in the future, either by himself or through someone else he has appointed in his place. The creditor, however, who sells a debt at a lower price for advanced money, appoints his own debtor in his place, who is then held to something beyond the principal to the buyer in the future. 

As for what Cajetan tries to prove—that no injustice intervenes in that contract—it has been clearly shown that a right to one hundred, when it is morally certain it will be paid in full without labor or expense, is worth one hundred; and therefore injustice does intervene in that contract. Regarding the example of barren land brought forward by Cajetan, it must be said that land is fruitful by its nature, and its value is estimated from the fruit it can bear when cultivated. Money, however, and the right to it, are entirely unfruitful by nature; for that reason, money does not have value based on a remote potential to produce the fruit of profit, as it is subject to the use and industry of another who can trade with it, as was shown extensively in Disputation 304. From this it follows that nothing else can be estimated in price from it, except only <term>lost profit</term> <note>Latin: *lucrum cessans*, a legal justification for interest when a lender misses another investment opportunity.</note> or <term>accruing loss</term> <note>Latin: *damnum emergens*, loss actually incurred by the lender.</note>.

As for the argument Cajetan constructs from the metaphor of fruits while they are green and when they are ripe, it must be said: Fruits are worth more when they are ripe than when they are green because they have become 

<column-break/>

better; money, however, whether it is owed for a longer or shorter time, does not become better in itself, and therefore does not have a greater value. Add to this that green fruits are worth less because of the risks they are subject to until they ripen, and because of the labor and expenses to be spent on them. If a debt were subject to similar risks, its value would also decrease for that reason, as has been said.

### On the purchase of sheep, shifting the risk and the care to the seller for a certain time. And on goods to be delivered at a time when they are worth less, when they will later be worth more. And on the purchase of oxen which the seller does not have, by leasing them to him.

## DISPUTATION CCCLXII.

<margin>1</margin> The purchase of sheep at the common price, but with a pact that they be kept by the seller at his risk until a certain time, and that their "fruits" belong to the buyer, is an unjust contract with an obligation to make restitution.

<margin>2</margin> If someone buys something at the common price at the time of the contract, but it is to be delivered at a time when it is hoped it will be worth more, is he held to restore the increase in value that was expected at the time of delivery, even if it did not happen?

<margin>3</margin> Regarding one who buys oxen which the seller does not possess, and leases the same back to the seller: how he is held to restitution.

In this and the following disputation, several cases must be settled before we move on to the price fixed by law.

<margin>1</margin> The first case is if someone buys a thousand sheep in the autumn—for example, at the common price of that time—but with a pact that they be kept by the seller until June, and the "fruits" (namely the milk, cheese, wool, and offspring) belong to the buyer, while the risk to the sheep remains with the seller. This contract is unjust with an obligation to restore the estimated value of the risk, and further, the estimated value of the care and other expenses incurred by the seller for those sheep up to that time. It is likewise usurious if it is hoped that, by reason of the advanced payment, all those benefits are received and those burdens are shifted to the seller. If, in that contract, a pact were added that, once the fruits were gathered, the seller would be held to buy those sheep back at the same price he sold them for, the contract would be openly usurious: because it would be exactly as if the buyer gave that price as a loan to the seller and demanded the fruits of the sheep over all that time in addition to the principal. Therefore, the contract would be void by law, nor would the seller be held to pay the buyer anything other than the price he received for the sheep in the autumn. And he should subtract from that price as much as the fruits the buyer received were estimated to be worth. Likewise, if someone at a time when sheep, lambs, and rams are worth less, buys a thousand indefinitely—not designating which specific ones—at the common price then, but to be delivered at a time when

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

will be worth more, the contract is unjust and usurious; because the risk is cast back upon the seller, and in exchange for an advance payment, something more is received than what the goods are worth—or are expected to be worth—at the time of delivery. Therefore, that entire increase, or whatever that increase was estimated to be at the time the sale was made, must be restored, regardless of how the event actually turns out afterward. All these points are clear from the preceding discussions and require no further proof.

<margin>2</margin>
The second case, linked with the last part of the preceding one, is as follows: If someone sells wheat, or anything else, at the common price at the time the contract is celebrated, but to be delivered at a time when it is morally expected to be worth more, then, even if at the time of delivery it is not worth more than at the time of the contract, the buyer is bound to restore as much of that increase as was expected to occur at the time of delivery, valued at the time the contract was celebrated according to that hope. This is because, in truth, the buyer bought the whole thing at the time the contract was celebrated for a lower price than it was worth then. So says Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian.</note> with others, under the word "usury," question 8. He adds the same in question 9: if someone sells something for twenty, to be delivered in the future when it was expected to be worth only fifteen; for although at the time of delivery it happens by some chance to be worth twenty or more, the seller is nevertheless bound, for the same reason, to restore to the buyer what he received in excess of what was estimated, more or less, at the time of the contract to be the value at the time of delivery; because at the time the contract was celebrated, it was not worth more for the time of delivery.

<margin>3</margin>
The third case is if someone buys oxen from another which the seller does not actually possess, and then leases those same oxen back to the seller; the doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established academic authorities in theology and law.</note> commonly distinguish the following. If the buyer knew, or presumed, that the seller did not have them, then the contract is a fraud to hide usury <note>A "dry exchange" or fictitious lease used to bypass the prohibition on charging interest on a loan.</note> and must be restored; the buyer is bound to return the lease payment, as if it came from a thing that did not exist, following the argument in the Digest <term>on the condition of having no cause</term> <note>Original: "de conditione sine ca[usa]"—a legal principle regarding enrichment without a valid basis.</note> throughout. If, however, the buyer bought in good faith, believing the seller possessed the oxen, then, provided the price for the oxen and for their lease was a just one, he is not bound to restore the payment which he received and consumed in good faith, except to the extent that he was made wealthier by it. Indeed, he is not even bound to restore that by which he was made wealthier, but could recover it if any part of the payment remained to be paid, when, by having bought and leased the oxen in that way, an equal amount of profit would have ceased for the buyer. So says Sylvester under "usury," 2, question 7; Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a leading canonist.</note> in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 230; and others whom they cite, with whom Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a key figure in the School of Salamanca.</note> agrees, book 6 *On Justice*, question 4, article 2, response 3; and the same is to be understood regarding other similar things.

There are, however, several things to be observed. The first is: if someone had bought two or more oxen indefinitely—meaning that because no specific individuals were bought, the risk for them did not pertain to the buyer but to the seller—then it would be wicked to receive a price from their lease. This is because they would not perish for the lessor, nor would there be any specific oxen that belonged to him, and consequently from which he could justly receive the fruit of a lease.

The second is: if in good faith he had bought two specific oxen from someone, whom he believed possessed 

<column-break/>

them, and had leased those same oxen to him, then, even if the seller did not have those oxen, and even if the buyer was not going to trade with that money, he could nonetheless lawfully receive the lease payment. The reason is that on the part of the buyer and lessor, the contract would have been valid and would have taken effect by the payment of the price for the oxen. Fraud should not protect the seller and lessee; therefore, in the court of conscience and in the external court, he is bound to pay the buyer and lessor as much as it concerns him that those oxen belonged to the seller. But note this: if the buyer did not see the oxen, the contract is suspect, because no one usually buys oxen at a certain price which he does not see for himself, or through another, to know what they are like; therefore, the contract is judged to have been celebrated in fraud of usury in that manner. If, however, he saw them, but the seller lied about them being his when they belonged to another, then, if while the lease contract entered into in good faith persisted, the oxen perish without anyone's fault, they perish for the buyer and lessor; and the seller will only be bound to him for the price of the lease up until they perished, and also for as much as it concerns the buyer that those oxen belonged to the seller. That a thing can lawfully be sold with an agreement that it be leased back to the seller is proven by Gomez, Decision 39, and Aluarus Valascus, *On Emphyteutic Law*, question 1, number 18.

### DISPUTATION CCCLXIII.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *Whether a broker, or other intermediary, selling a thing for a higher price than was set for him to sell it, can retain that increase for himself.*
2 *Whether a mediator, finding a thing to be bought from one person for a certain price, and buying it from another for a lower price, can retain for himself the difference by which he could have bought it more dearly.*
3 *The cunning and shrewdness of tailors, who buy cloth to make clothes for someone; how these are to be explained and resolved.*

<margin>1</margin>
These cases are frequent in confessions. What is asked in the first place is: If someone gives something to a broker, or to anyone else, to be sold for ten (for example), and he sells it for twelve, is that mediator bound to deliver the full twelve to the owner of the thing, or can he retain for himself that increase in price above ten? Regardless of what Angelus <note>Angelus de Clavasio (1411–1495), author of the *Summa Angelica*.</note> said under "sale," number 28, a distinction must certainly be made. For if those two units received above ten are beyond the <term>rigorous price</term> <note>The highest point of the "just price" range or a legally fixed price.</note> or the price fixed by law, they must be restored to the buyer; because they were unjustly received from him beyond the just price. If, however, they were not received beyond the just price, a further distinction is required. Because if there was a tacit or express agreement that he should only return ten to the owner of the thing, and if the mediator found anything more, he should take it for himself, then it is clear that those two belong to the mediator.
