## Second Treatise, Disputation 364.

to retain the surplus. If, however, such an agreement was not made, the money must certainly be restored to the owner of the property. First, because these funds are the price of the object itself, and consequently belong to the owner, whose presumed will was that if more than ten <note>The text uses "ten" as a placeholder for a specific currency amount or value.</note> could be found, they should receive more and have it delivered to them. Second, because that mediator was conducting the business and acting in the place of the owner; therefore, the profit or loss ought to belong to the owner of the property. This holds true whether the mediator received a wage from the owner to sell it, or did so for free out of friendship at the owner's request. Nor does it matter if the mediator says: "I could have sold it for ten to a certain person who offered me ten, but I did not want to give that person the item, and instead sought out another buyer." It does not matter, I say, because whatever moral diligence they apply, the profit—for the reasons already given—belongs to the owner. Such mediators, who sell someone's property without being paid a wage, often claim that they have secretly taken the surplus for themselves as a price for their labor, which they were not bound to provide for free. This is not to be easily permitted. First, because the owners perhaps assumed it was being done for free as a favor and would not have wanted to use their services for a wage, since they could have found others to do it for free, or would have preferred to sell the item themselves. Equity does not require that the owner be forced to pay a wage in that event, and much less that the seller should secretly take whatever amount seemed right to them. Second, because while it is taken secretly, the owner believes they have received a favor from the mediator, which they are bound by gratitude to compensate with either services or other favors; equity does not allow the mediator to receive both benefits without the owner's knowledge. Third, because <term>occult compensation</term> <note>original: "occulta compensatio"; a theological concept where a person secretly takes what is owed to them if they cannot obtain it through legal means.</note> has no place except when a debt cannot be obtained by any other way. In this case, however, the mediator can seek a just wage from the owner through an <term>action for services rendered</term> <note>original: "actione negotiorum gestorum"; a legal claim for managing someone else's affairs without an express contract.</note> if they did not intend to provide their labor for free. Shyness in asking for payment does not make it licit for them to perform occult compensation at such expense to the owner, who has a right to know whether the labor was provided for a price, whether they have paid it (and how much), or whether they have instead received a favor. It must be observed, however, that if the mediator was ordered to sell in a specific place, such as in this city, and could not find more than ten there after applying moral diligence, but then carried the item to a very distant place where they found more for it, they could keep that increase for themselves, since it would be the fruit of their own industry. On these points, Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a 16th-century theologian.</note> (under the word "purchase," question 25), Gabriel <note>Gabriel Biel, a late scholastic philosopher.</note> (in book 4, distinction 15, question 11, article 3, doubt 4), and Navarro <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist.</note> (in his Manual, chapter 23, number 97) generally agree.

<margin>Question</margin>
What we ask in the second place is this: If someone asked another person to buy a certain thing for them, and the person so asked could have bought it from someone for twelve, but sought out another who sold it to him for ten, the question is whether the mediator can retain for himself that <margin>decision</margin> difference by which he was able to buy the item cheaper? The answer is that he cannot retain it. First, because all of that is included in the diligence that the other person requested of him. Second, because he was conducting the business of another; and just as the loss would

<column-break/>

belong to the one whose business he was conducting if he later could not find anyone to sell the item at that higher price, so too the benefit ought to belong to the same person. If, however, after spending time and effort in the place where he was asked to buy, he could only find the item at a certain high price, but by traveling to a very distant location he bought it at a lower price, he could then retain the difference for himself as the fruit of his own industry and labor. <note>The following section discusses tailors or garment-makers (fartores).</note> Tailors, when they are commissioned to buy cloth or silk to make clothes for someone, are accustomed—beyond the profits explained at the beginning of this second question, which we said should not be allowed—to receive a portion of the price from the merchants. For example, the merchants might say they would not have given the goods to anyone else for less than twenty silver pieces per yard, but for the tailor's sake, they are willing to remit half a silver piece for every yard for the agents to take for themselves, because they came to them rather than other merchants to buy. Or, once a price is set (for example, twenty silver pieces per yard) and paid to the merchants, the merchants might grant the tailor two or three silver pieces to entice them to buy from their shops in the future. Furthermore, the tailors argue that they can receive this as a reward for their labor and industry, and to compensate for the profit they could have made working while they were going to other people's houses to buy these things. These practices are full of <term>scruples</term> <note>In a theological sense, "scruples" refers to deep moral concerns or doubts about the sinfulness of an action.</note> and should be discouraged before they happen. Because of that profit, they do not conduct the business of those for whom they buy the cloth or silk faithfully; instead, they pay a higher price than they would if they were conducting their own business, nor do they test whether they could buy the goods more cheaply from other merchants. Also, after it is done, such tailors must be diligently examined to see if they acted unfaithfully—specifically, whether they could have bought the merchandise more cheaply elsewhere or by persisting more, and whether, because of the profit and reward they expected from the merchants, they neither persisted nor went to others. If they are found to have acted unfaithfully, I would be inclined to say the burden of restitution must be imposed, and these perverse and secret ways of making a profit are not to be tolerated against the will of those whose business they are conducting.

## On the legal price—that is, the price fixed by law or public authority—especially concerning grain.

### DISPUTATION CCCLXIV.

### SUMMARY.

1. Fixing the legal price of things belongs to public powers and governments.
2. Any transgression of a fixed price is against justice.
3. A transgressor of a fixed price falls into mortal sin.
4. The increase over a fixed price is subject to restitution.
5. A transgressor of the law is bound not only to pay the penalty but also to make restitution to the person who suffered the loss.
6. What is required for a law fixing a price to bind in the court of conscience.
7. A price fixed in a time of abundance is not presumed to last in a time of scarcity.

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

<margin>8</margin> Whether a law that is reasonable and just in a civil court <note>original: "in foro fori"</note> should be presumed to be equally just in the Court of Heaven <note>original: "in foro Poli," referring to God's judgment/conscience</note>.
<margin>9</margin> A legislator who does not repeal a law that was once just but has become unjust is bound to restore all damages to their subjects. This is explained further in the text.
<margin>10</margin> The conditions under which a law taxing the price of grain becomes unjust.
<margin>11</margin> If grain of a better quality than what is usually sold is provided, can a price higher than the legally taxed price be accepted? Or, if it is of worse quality, is the seller bound to lower the price?
<margin>12</margin> Whether foreigners who bring grain from a place where it is taxed to a place where no tax is imposed on them, and sell it for more, commit a sin and are bound to restitution.
And what if they are residents who bring it in? See number 13.
<margin>14</margin> Whether clergy are bound to sell grain at the legally taxed price.
<margin>15</margin> Whether it is lawful to sell grain above the legally taxed price if it is to be transported at the seller's expense to a place where it is sold more dearly.

<margin>1</margin> **W**e must consequently speak of the **legal price**. All authorities agree † that it belongs to the public powers not only to establish just laws concerning other matters as they judge expedient for the common good, but also to set and define the prices of goods, as they see fit for that same common good within the limits of equity. For if a price were to exceed the limits of equity, considering all concurring circumstances, the law would be unjust and thus would not have the power to bind, at least in the forum of conscience. This kind of power resides primarily in the supreme prince, and in other governors of the commonwealth derived from and dependent on him, to the extent that it has been granted by laws, custom, or a specific faculty for that purpose. In the Kingdom of Portugal, <note>Portuguese legal reference</note> the **town councilors and officials of the chambers** <note>original: "os uereadores, e officiaes das camaras"</note> are prohibited from taxing the price of grain, wine, and oil, as held in law 8, title 1, part 6 of the *Extravagant Laws*.

The legal or taxed price—since it is limited and restricted by the determination of public authority to a certain point within the limits of equity, having considered all circumstances—requires, for example, that a measure of wheat not exceed a certain price. It follows, therefore, that this price consists in an **indivisible point** <note>In Scholastic economics, a "natural price" is usually a range (pious, moderate, rigorous), but a "legal price" is a fixed number that cannot be exceeded.</note>. The public authority, by the power it has to bind its subjects in order to serve the common good, narrows the broad range of the otherwise natural just price of that item to that determined and indivisible value.

<margin>2</margin> From this it follows that any transgression of a price so taxed is against justice, as it exceeds the breadth of what is just. Therefore, in that excess, the seller is said to "overreach his brother," contrary to the words of **Paul** in 1 Thessalonians 4: *That no man overreach or circumvent his brother in business.* <note>Molina is using Biblical authority to argue that price-gouging above a legal limit is a sin requiring repayment.</note> Consequently, he is bound to restore that excess, according to the common opinion of the learned doctors. This is the view of **Johannes Medina** on restitution, question 31 and more extensively in 36; **Soto** in *On Justice*, book 6, question 2; **Castrus**; **Covarruvias**; **Navarrus**; and others.

<margin>3</margin> For this reason, they say, when † the law defines the price of a thing (such as grain) and simultaneously imposes a penalty

<column-break/>

on those who transgress the law, even if the penalty is so light that we would not judge it a mortal sin in the transgression of other laws, in this case it is different. If the transgressor accepts a price beyond the legal tax which, in the matter of theft, would suffice for a mortal sin, he must be judged to have fallen into mortal sin. This is not because of the imposed penalty, but because he has notably violated justice. Therefore, he would have sinned mortally through the transgression even if no penalty had been established by that law.

<margin>4</margin> From this it is also easily understood that any increase in price beyond the legal tax is subject to **restitution**, without waiting for a court sentence, because it was unjustly received. However, the penalty established by that law is not owed until a sentence is passed. Furthermore, it should be understood that even if a transgressor † is condemned by a judge to pay a penalty far greater than the amount they accepted above the taxed price, they are not thereby freed from the obligation of restoring to the buyer what was paid in excess. This excess must be restored to the buyer not as a penalty, but as something unjustly taken from them. It does not matter that a much larger sum has already been paid as a penalty for the crime. **Covarruvias**, in the place cited, excellently warns judges that when they punish such transgressions, they ought to command the transgressors to restore what they took above the taxed price, even if it is not beyond half the just price <note>Under older Roman law (the principle of *laesio enormis*), a contract could often only be rescinded if the price was off by more than half; Molina argues that for legally regulated goods, *any* excess is illegal.</note>. For in those things taxed by law, an action is granted in the external court for any excess whatsoever. And if the judges do not command this restitution, the obligation to restore remains nonetheless in the forum of conscience. It does not matter if the seller says the buyer offered the whole price freely, because it is not to be presumed that the buyer wanted to make a gift, but rather that they offered it "involuntarily-mixed" <note>A technical term meaning the buyer consented only because they had no other choice to get the needed goods.</note>, because they could not find the goods at a lower price.

<margin>6</margin> The cited † doctors agree that for a price-taxing law to bind in the forum of conscience, it is necessary that it be **reasonable and equitable**, not departing from the limits of a just price. For although the prince has the power to restrain human greed and to moderate the prices of things as the common good demands within the limits of equity, he does not have the power to reduce them irrationally or outside those limits. He must consider the actual circumstances which, by the nature of the situation, increase the price. The prince's power does not extend to the irrational or the unjust. Thus, if a massive famine <note>original: "sterilitate," meaning a crop failure or period of scarcity</note> occurs and the prince wants grain to be sold at the same price it was reasonably sold during a time of abundance, the law would be **irrational and unjust**. It is certainly not a sufficient excuse to say that it serves the common good for grain to be sold at the abundance price during a famine so that the poor are not burdened. This is not sufficient, I say. First, because if equity and justice—from the very nature of the thing—demand that the price rise so that the owners of the grain do not suffer injury, we must not allow the owners to be wronged just because the poor might suffer difficulty. The poor should be helped through **alms** rather than through an unjust sale. Second, because one should not establish a law that injures all sellers just for the sake of the poor...

Molina argues that while the state has the right to set prices for the common good, these prices must be equitable; if a price ceiling is set too low during a famine, it becomes an unjust law that does not bind the conscience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "legal price" (pretium legitimum) for grain. It explores the ethical limits of government price controls, arguing that laws must adapt to changing circumstances like famine to remain morally binding.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 364

If grain is sold at a specific price: especially during times of scarcity and famine, when the poor are rarely able to buy at the price fixed by law—since only the powerful and public officials, whom the grain owners cannot resist, tend to secure it. Third, because for the sake of providing for the Republic <note>original: "Re-pub." referring to the common good of the state</note> and the common good, equity does not allow certain individuals to be burdened more than others. Rather, everyone in the commonwealth, according to their means and status, should be burdened in a certain proportion to contribute what equity demands. Therefore, it is unjust to burden only the owners of grain by forcing them to sell their grain below the lowest just price <note>original: "infra pretium infimum"</note> that equity requires based on the very nature of the thing. Fourth, because many of those who possess grain are farmers; in a year of sterility, once all their expenses, labor, and industry are calculated, a measure of grain costs them a far higher price than the one they are ordered to sell it for. Truly, no equity allows this. Furthermore, an injury is done to farmers if the prices of all other goods increase during a time of rarity and a surplus of buyers, while grain—which they produce with such great labor and expense for the high utility of the Republic—is not allowed to be sold at the price that its rarity and the abundance of buyers naturally demand. These points confirm what will be said in the following disputation; likewise, they will be greatly strengthened by what follows, where we shall overturn the contrary assertion held by certain legal experts who seem to have sworn by the poorly understood words of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note>.

<margin>7</margin>
From what has been said, I conclude that if grain was previously taxed by law at a reasonable and moderate price, but in the months of March or April a great sterility for the following year is discovered—whether due to a lack of rain or some other reason—men are not thereafter bound to sell their grain at the price fixed during the time of abundance. This is because † it must be presumed that the will of the prince <note>The ruler or sovereign authority</note> is not that a law passed in a time of plenty should still hold force when such great sterility occurs. Nor, even if the prince willed it, would the law then be reasonable and just, and consequently, it would not be binding in the court of conscience <note>original: "in conscientiæ foro"</note>. This is what Navarrus <note>original: "Nau." referring to Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canonist</note> intended when he said at the end of the cited number 88 that when the greatest necessity arises, the price tax is entirely removed. Lope de Medina <note>original: "lo. Med."</note> agrees in Question 36, and much more clearly in Question 31. However, when the sterility is not so great as to make the law manifestly unreasonable and unjust if it were to persist, one must abide by the law while it is not revoked, and one should appeal to the prince and petition him to remove or change it.

<margin>8</margin>
Furthermore, doctors <note>Theologians and legal scholars</note> agree that in a case of doubt as to whether a law † is reasonable and just, it must be presumed to be so, and it must be followed in the court of conscience. In cases of doubt, one must obey superiors; their prudence and judgment are to be relied upon rather than the private judgment of subjects. However, when the injustice is manifest—whether this arises from the corruption and wickedness of the King's advisors, or from ignorance or negligence in failing to see the obligation to repeal, moderate, or change the law due to new circumstances, or because they did not sufficiently attend to or weigh

<column-break/>

the factors that must be considered in fixing a just price—which is not difficult to happen, especially since they are often far from the place where the grain is being sold and must rely on the suggestions and judgment of others—then buyers who purchase according to that law below the lowest just price of that commodity are bound to make restitution <note>term: restitution — the act of restoring something to its rightful owner or paying its fair value</note> up to the range of the just price. This is self-evident and Medina agrees in Question 36. This is understood even if they bought in good faith, though in that case, if they had consumed the item in the same good faith, they would only be bound to restore the amount by which

<margin>9</margin>
they were made wealthier. Those † who passed such a law, or failed to repeal or change it after it became unjust, would be bound to restore all damages that followed for the subjects because of that law, unless ignorance excuses them from fault in passing or failing to repeal the law. I say "unless ignorance excuses them from fault" because, since these officials are not bound to restitution based on the thing received (unless they were also among the buyers), if ignorance excuses them from fault, they remain entirely free from the burden of restitution. In a similar way, those judges sin and are bound to restitution who subsequently punish those who sold grain above a price fixed by an unreasonable and openly unjust law. For they are bound to restore the penalties they collected for this reason, as well as all damages they inflicted by harassing them. I will offer one example. While I was teaching these matters at the University of Évora during the reign of King Sebastian <note>Sebastian I of Portugal, reigned 1557–1578</note>, it happened that although the tax for a measure of grain (which in that Kingdom is called an *Alqueire* <note>A Portuguese unit of volume, roughly 13–17 liters</note>) had been justly set the previous year at six *vinténs* <note>original: "vigenorum," small silver or copper coins</note>, a massive famine caused the price in the public market to rise to fifteen or sixteen *vinténs*, at which price it was sold by foreigners to whom the tax in that Kingdom did not apply. A judge arrived who, as was the custom, had been sent to investigate certain crimes, and he began to punish the local people who had sold grain of equal quality for more than six *vinténs*. Surely this was unjust, carrying the burden of restoring both the penalties and whatever other damages the judge had caused for that reason. Once he was warned, he immediately ceased, as he was bound to do.

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>Doubt</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
There is a doubt whether a law † fixing the price of grain becomes unjust because other things that farmers need—such as shoes, wine, oil, the wages of laborers, etc.—are not also taxed. The answer is negative, provided that the price at which the grain is taxed is reasonable and proportionate, considering the abundance or scarcity of the grain, the number of buyers, and other circumstances from which the value of things must be estimated, according to what was said in Disputation 348. The reason is that the price of grain only depends accidentally on the other things the farmer needs. And since it is more beneficial to the Republic for grain to be taxed than other things, and it would be extremely difficult to tax everything else. Furthermore, when a just price is established for grain, given all current circumstances, no injury is done to its owners if, for the good of the Republic, only grain is taxed. If, however, shoes were taxed but the leather from which they are made was not, and this caused the shoemakers, given the price at which they buy leather, to lose...

# Louis Molina on Contracts

...they would not be able to receive a just and moderate price for their labor, then the law would be unjust and would not be binding in conscience. The same would apply if the price of baked bread were fixed without a corresponding price limit on the wheat, and this caused the female bakers <note>original: "pistrices"; in this period, professional baking was often a female-dominated trade in certain regions</note> to not receive a just and moderate wage. The same should be said for other things which inherently depend on other non-taxed goods, alongside the things already stated at the end of Disputation 355.

<margin>Question 11</margin>
Assuming the price-fixing law is just, it is asked: if a better quality of wheat is offered than what is commonly sold, can a price higher than the legal limit be lawfully accepted? Or, if a worse quality is offered, is the seller obliged to lower the price below the legal limit?

<margin>Decision</margin>
The answer is no, if the difference in quality—better or worse—is minor. Such a minor difference is to be considered as nothing; otherwise, there would be almost no grain that could be sold at the legally established price. Indeed, among those grains commonly sold, there is none which, when compared to another, is not found to be slightly better or worse. I believe that it is rarely possible to lawfully rise above the legal price due to superior quality. However, regarding a defect in quality—such as if the wheat is rotten or worm-eaten, so that it is notably worse than the wheat usually sold—the seller is indeed bound to lower the price by a proportional amount of its lower value, because the law is intended to apply to common wheat. If in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> distinct prices have not been established for the varieties called *Galego* and *Anafil*, I believe the price for *Galego* wheat should be lowered. For as I hear, it is commonly valued at a quarter less because fewer and far inferior loaves of bread in value are made from an equal measure of that wheat compared to the other. Thus, a law that established an equal price for both types of wheat would be unjust.

If the price of wheat is fixed, the flour made from it is considered fixed by that very fact, so that it cannot be sold more dearly. To do so is an evasion of the law <term>fraud of the law (fraus legis): acting against the spirit or intent of a law while technically following its words</term> and against the mind of the legislator. Even if flour was not specifically mentioned when wheat was taxed, reducing wheat to flour and selling it at will is an evasion. As stated in the legal code <note>original: "L. contra legem, ff. de legibus"</note>, he acts in fraud of the law who, while observing the words of the law, circumvents its meaning. Therefore, those who sell it this way are bound to make restitution for the excess price. By the same logic, if someone gave their wheat to male or female bakers under a contract where they returned a price higher than the legal limit for each measure, and kept the remainder for themselves as the reward for their labor, they would be acting in fraud of the law. They would be bound to restore the excess price to the bakers if they shifted the entire risk onto the bakers, for it would be the same as if they sold them the wheat at that higher price. If, however, the owner took upon themselves the risk of the wheat, flour, and bread—such that if they perished or if less money was made from them than the set price, the loss fell to the owner—but if more was made, the bakers took the increase as their wage, I do not see that such a contract is illicit by its nature. This is provided the profit the bakers hoped for was commensurate with the labor, expense, and industry they applied. I say "by its nature," because in this Kingdom, this

<column-break/>

seems to be prohibited, for the reason that the owners would in truth be the bakers themselves, though using the service of public bakers, which is prohibited by law.

Anyone who sells wheat at the legal price, but with a pact that the buyer pays in oil, wine, or any other merchandise which the buyer provides at a lower price than its usual selling value, certainly acts in fraud of the law. They are bound to restore however much more that merchandise was worth. Indeed, if the seller imposes a burden on the buyer that has a measurable value—such as requiring the buyer to simultaneously purchase wine, oil, or anything else from them at a higher price than the buyer would have otherwise paid—the seller is bound to restore the value of that burden. This is because that value is considered part of the price received beyond the legal limit for the wheat. This is the opinion of Medina (Question 36) and Navarro (Manual, Chapter 23, Number 88), and the matter is clear enough in itself.

<margin>Question</margin>
12 It is a question whether foreigners <note>original: "alienigenæ"</note> bringing wheat into Portugal from Castile or elsewhere—who are not subject to the price tax in Portugal so that they may be encouraged to bring it—sin or are bound to make restitution if they sell their wheat above the price fixed for the inhabitants of that Kingdom. The reason for the doubt is whether the price fixed by law for the inhabitants is the "true just price" of grain in that Kingdom by its nature, or not. If it is the just price, it follows that what the foreigners accept above it is beyond the natural just price, and thus subject to restitution. If it is not just, it follows that the law taxing that price for inhabitants is unjust, and thus inhabitants could take just as much for their own wheat of equal quality. There are those who answer this doubt by saying the Commonwealth and the King can grant that price increase to foreigners as a reward for their labor and expenses, to invite them to import wheat for the benefit of the Kingdom. They argue that by this grant, foreigners can lawfully accept the increase and are not bound to restore it. Nor, they say, is any injury done to the buyers, since they are not forced to buy; and to one who is willing and consenting, no injury is done. I certainly would not dare to declare the consciences of the sellers safe on this ground. The King perhaps thought nothing of a "gift," but only permitted them to sell at the price they wished and could, exempting them from the legal tax to attract the supply of wheat. Also, what the buyers give them above the legal price is given with a "mixed" involuntary intent <note>meaning they only agree to the high price because of necessity, not true free will</note>. Nor is the foreigners' wheat worth more than other common wheat of equal quality in that place simply because of the expenses they incurred in transporting it or the labor they undertook. Therefore, since the King proposes nothing from his own or from common goods as a reward to them, I do not see how their consciences can be made safe on that ground. I believe they are safe only on this ground: because they are exempt from the price-fixing law, they can safely sell within the "latitude of the just price" <note>the range of prices considered fair by the market when not restricted by law</note> which the grain has by its nature, excluding the price-fixing law, and considering the concurrent circumstances of that place.

## Second Treatise, Disputation 364.

<margin>Decision</margin>
...it holds: that either there is a greater supply of money for wheat than is being sold, and more buyers approach them, so that by the nature of the situation the value of their wheat increases; or it happens that the more the local residents are squeezed by the law of price-fixing <note>original: "taxationis"; referring to a legally mandated price ceiling</note> and are commanded to sell at a cheaper price, the more the value of the foreigners' wheat increases by the nature of the situation. This is because the foreigners become the sole sellers, as the locals are unwilling to sell at such a low price as the law has fixed for them. If there were no price cap, there would certainly be no increase in price beyond the natural rate that the foreigners would receive; indeed, a person would be insane to want to buy wheat of equal quality from foreigners at a higher price than from locals. On the contrary, the price of the foreigners' wheat would decrease if there were no cap, as locals and foreigners would compete for preference from the buyers in the sale. I say, therefore, whether a price-fixing law is imposed on locals or not, if foreigners sell beyond the rigorous just price which grain in that place then possesses by the nature of the case—all concurrent circumstances being considered—they both sin against justice and are bound to restore the excess. Since, however, there is no reason why foreigners should be condemned in the forum of conscience, let those who were in the Alentejo region <note>original: "transtagna Lusitania regione"; literally the region "across the Tagus" in Portugal</note> in the year I was there consider the following: they maintained a price cap of six vintens <note>original: "vigenorum"; the vintém was a Portuguese coin worth 20 réis</note> from the previous year. Does the fact that wheat was sold publicly by foreigners in the market for sixteen vintens not sufficiently prove that the cap was more than "lenient"—not to say openly unjust? And was it fair for a judge to come later to investigate and punish those locals who sold wheat that year for more than six vintens? I have already recounted a little earlier how the judge, having been admonished by religious and learned men, finally ceased his investigation.

<margin>Question 13</margin>
You ask whether, if the Portuguese import wheat from another kingdom, they may sell it above the legally fixed price, just as foreigners sell it. It must be answered in the affirmative, at least in the forum of conscience, provided that scandal is avoided.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The same applies in the external forum <note>the civil or public legal system</note>, if it is established there that the wheat was brought in from another kingdom. For the intent of the legislator is not to make the condition of the local citizens worse than that of foreigners in this matter, especially since the utility to the Kingdom is equal whether the wheat is brought from another kingdom by a Portuguese man or by a foreigner. Indeed, this very point is openly conceded in Law 5, final paragraph, title 9, part 4, of the *Extravagantes* laws <note>supplementary laws outside the main legal codes</note>, regarding when wheat is imported from the Kingdom of Castile. This is permitted provided that in the first town of Portugal, those importing it receive a sworn certificate from the judge of that town stating that it was imported from Castile.

<margin>Question 14</margin>
The question is whether clerics <note>members of the clergy</note> are bound to sell at the legally fixed price, such that if they exceed it, they are bound to restore the excess just like laypeople. The reason for doubting this is that since they are not subject to the laws and jurisdiction of secular princes, and consequently cannot be punished by them, it follows that even if they sell above the price fixed by the prince's law, they neither sin nor are bound to restitution, provided they do not exceed the natural just price (in the same manner we discussed regarding foreigners in Portugal).

<margin>Decision</margin>
Nevertheless, it must be affirmed according to the common opinion of the doctors that if they receive anything beyond the price fixed by a just law, they are bound to restore it. And although Navarrus <note>Martín de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canon lawyer</note> in his *Spanish Manual*, chapter 23, number 84, expressed doubt and made an exception for places where foreigners are exempt from the price-fixing law (as in Portugal)—led by the reasoning that since clerics 

<column-break/>

are no more subject to that law than foreigners, they ought to be able to sell their wheat of equal quality at the same price foreigners sell theirs—he rightly changed his opinion in the Latin edition, number 88. To the reason for the doubt, Medina <note>Juan de Medina, another prominent theologian</note> in Question 36 (cited) and Navarrus (where mentioned above) respond: although they are not bound by the power of the price-fixing law as if they were subjects of it, they are nonetheless bound insofar as, once the law is enacted, the common price in that place is the one fixed by the law. Indeed, by divine and natural law, both they and foreigners cannot receive more for their wheat in the place where they sell than the common price of that place. This is because only that price is just, whether it is "common" because the law is absent, or "common" because a law has been enacted and everyone sells accordingly. However, this foundation of theirs is quite weak, as is clear enough from what we said a little earlier regarding foreigners in Portugal. For if they are exempt from the law, then in relation to them there remains only the range of the natural price, which does not consist of a single indivisible point. If the fixed price is too low, and for that reason sellers are lacking, the natural price of the wheat increases in relation to them, as was said regarding the foreigners in Portugal; therefore, they could licitly sell within that entire range of the price. Thus, it should be said—as we stated with Vitoria, Soto, Sylvester, and others in Disputation 31, final conclusion—that clerics are subject to such laws and to the other laws of the secular princes of the Republic of which they are members, provided they do not conflict with clerical liberty. Although they cannot be judged according to those laws nor punished except before and by ecclesiastical judges, as was said in the same place, it follows that just as laypeople sin and are bound to restitution if they sell beyond the just price fixed by law, so also ecclesiastics sin and are bound to restitution. Foreigners, too, are bound by the laws of the Republic in which they conduct business, regarding matters pertaining to that business—just as they are also bound to pay taxes justly imposed by the laws of that place. For they are admitted to trade on the condition that they are bound by all those laws. Therefore, just as they are bound to restore taxes to the King if they do not pay those imposed by just laws, so also they are bound to restitution if they receive anything beyond the price fixed by law. It follows that in Portugal, it is a specific privilege, expressed in the Portuguese law itself, that foreigners are not bound by the grain price-fixing law.

<margin>Question 15</margin>
The question further is: if different prices for grain are fixed for different parts of the Kingdom—for instance, if it is fixed at a lower price in Évora than in Lisbon, or if it is fixed in Évora but not in Lisbon where it is sold for more—is it lawful to sell wheat in Évora at the price for which it is sold in Lisbon, provided it is to be transported to Lisbon at the seller’s expense?

<margin>Decision</margin>
The answer is: if the wheat being sold is not a specific designated lot, but rather a certain number of measures to be delivered in Lisbon—so that the entire risk of the wheat until it is delivered in Lisbon belongs to the seller, along with the transportation and costs—then there is no doubt that the contract is valid and licit. For although the agreement is made in Évora, the contract is suspended and then perfected in Lisbon. The same would apply if a specific designated amount of wheat were sold in Évora, but the seller took the costs upon himself...

...and the risk, until he delivers it to Lisbon. Because by taking on that risk—which otherwise would belong to the buyer, as we will see in the following—the contract is suspended by virtue of the delivery to Lisbon, and it is the same as if the wheat were sold in Lisbon. But if the seller does not take the risk, and it belongs immediately to the buyer, then it cannot be sold except at the price fixed for Evora <note>original: "pretio Euorae taxato"</note>. This is because the contract is completed at Evora. Therefore, any increase beyond the fixed price of Evora would have to be restored, minus the expenses the seller incurred in transporting the wheat. If those expenses were equal to the price increase, he would be bound to no restitution. 

Observe this: if a seller was determined to transport his wheat for sale in Lisbon, but at the request of a buyer (who wanted to transport it at his own expense) he desisted from that transport and delivered it to the buyer immediately, then in the forum of conscience <note>the "internal forum" or the person's standing before God, rather than a legal court</note>, provided no scandal occurs, he could take as much beyond the fixed price of Evora as would be estimated by a prudent judgment to be the <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; a legal and moral concept where one is compensated for the profit they *would* have made had they not entered a specific agreement</note> occurring because he did not bring his wheat to Lisbon for sale. For that increase would not be part of the price of the wheat itself, but compensation for the lost profit, which he could then lawfully sell. Regarding all these matters, among others, read Juan de Medina, question 36, cited from the section "another doubt."

The fact that a price is fixed in one part of the kingdom and not in another—because that part does not seem to be in such need—does not make the law inequitable. However, if in the same part of the kingdom some were allowed to sell beyond the fixed price while others were not, and this without a specific cause (such as allowing those to sell sooner who brought wheat from another kingdom, or from the same kingdom but permitted due to the cost of transport, or some other cause expedient to the common good), then that law could not be excused from the charge of injustice because of that inequality, and it would lose its power to bind the conscience. However, just because public officials overlook the enforcement of the penalty for some and not for others, the law does not cease to retain its binding force. Therefore, both the officials sin, and the transgressors similarly, and they are bound to restore whatever they receive beyond the price fixed by law. But if, with the knowledge of the ruler, either everyone or the majority were to sell with impunity beyond the price fixed by law, it would then be presumed that the law had lost its binding force by the will of the prince. These points are from Medina, in the response to the 3rd and 4th points.

# Whether it is expedient, especially in the Kingdom of Portugal, for grain to be price-fixed in the manner it usually is.

## DISPUTATION 365.

### SUMMARY.

1 When the price of grain is fixed, two periods must be considered.
2 Under what circumstances one is forced to sell their property for less than the just price.
3 The governors of locales ought to ensure that necessities are sold at a just price.
4 When the common good is to be preferred to the individual.

<column-break/>

5 A law fixing a price below the <term>lowest just price</term> <note>original: "iustum infimum pretium"; the bottom end of the range of fair market value</note> which a thing has by its nature is called inequitable and unjust.
6 A price-fixing law which establishes the lowest just price rather than the highest or middle is called just; but it is unjust when it fixes it below the lowest point.
7 If a Prince fixes a price below the lowest just price which the thing has by its nature, he sins and is bound to restore the damages to the owners that follow from it.
8 The custom of fixing the price at a certain time: which is to be approved and which is not.
9 How and when grain is to be fixed, and what must be observed for the fix to be called just.
10 The price of grain is very rarely to be fixed, because of great difficulties.
11 Merchants are not to be allowed to sell their wares at whatever price they want.
12 Why the price-fixing of grain is necessary.
13 What those who fix grain prices should beware of.

While I was explaining these matters at Evora, it happened by chance that, without my knowledge, someone offered certain arguments to Cardinal Henry <note>Henry I of Portugal (1512–1580), known as the "Cardinal-King," who reigned from 1578 to 1580</note>, who was not yet King. These arguments contended that the price-fixing of grain in that Kingdom was not expedient; rather, that many evils arose from them. I neither saw the arguments, nor could I know whose they were. But when Cardinal Henry had sent them to the supreme senators, the responses came into my hands by chance. And, since from long experience of many years, I also judged those price-fixes to be least expedient—led rather by the very grave dangers to souls which I detected than by temporal advantages or disadvantages—I took care to respond to those reasons. I hoped perhaps to bring some light to the government and the public good, and to help ensure that those price-fixes would not be made thereafter, just as they were not made up until my departure from Portugal in the year 1591, nor, as I believe, up to this day. What I then dictated from the pulpit, I will now also add for the same reasons. In those responses, to address the objection that the price fixed for grain in the year immediately preceding had been notoriously unjust, it was argued as follows:

> "Regarding the price-fixing of grain, two periods are to be considered. One, when there is an abundance of grain, or at least a moderate supply. The other, when there is sterility and a rarity of it. In the former period, the just price of grain is to be fixed by attending to its quantity and all other circumstances from which a just price is derived, as the laws dispose. But in the latter period, one should not attend to the quantity of grain nor the other concurrent circumstances which would demand that the price increase; rather, a certain moderate price is to be fixed, which buyers can conveniently reach."

It is worthwhile, however, for us to examine whether this last point is true—the point upon which the entire judgment depends: whether a price-fix issued according to that doctrine in a time of sterility and rarity of grain is just or unjust. We must ask what causes unjust prices to be continued at such times, to the injury of many. From this it further happens that the owners of grain, seeing such diminished prices have been established, transgress the law with the gravest harm to their own...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s argument regarding the justice of price-fixing laws for grain. On the previous page, he discussed the specific conditions under which a merchant might be required to restore funds if they sold above a legally set price. Here, he begins to challenge the legal and theological authorities commonly cited to justify forcing sellers to trade below the "just price" during times of scarcity.</meta>

**Second Treatise, Disputation 385.**

...danger to their souls, believing they are committing a mortal sin, and with their confessors ordering them to make restitution. This is because it is quite difficult for private individuals to condemn a public law as unjust, and in cases of doubt, one must abide by the law in the **forum of conscience** <note>The internal moral standing of a person before God, as opposed to an external legal court.</note>.

<margin>1</margin> First, I am surprised that Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> is cited in support of that opinion, because he very clearly refutes and attacks it there, instead embracing the contrary view, which he confirms with various legal arguments. I am also surprised that Angelo <note>Angelus Carletti di Chivasso, author of a famous handbook for confessors.</note> and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras, a Dominican theologian.</note> are cited for the same opinion, as they say no such thing. They only state that when someone is forced by necessity to buy a thing for more than it is worth, an injustice is committed with the obligation to restore the excess. For example, if a medicine necessary to save a life is sold to someone for more than it is worth, the excess must be restored.

And Sylvester, in the same place, expressly says that in a time of necessity, those who have an abundance of goods not needed for their own survival can be compelled to sell them to others at a **just price** <note>A central concept in Scholastic economics: a price that reflects the true value of a good based on common estimation and utility, rather than exploitation.</note> so that they may sustain their lives. He says this is how it is observed in times of famine. He transcribed all of this from Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note>. In these writings, you can see no mention is made of a reduction from the just price that the item would naturally have at that time. Indeed, no theologian who speaks of a price fixed by law affirms the opinion we are attacking. Rather, Juan Medina <note>A Spanish theologian known for his detailed work on restitution.</note>, who discussed this matter more extensively and accurately than others, if read carefully, only grants public authorities the power to moderate the price and curb the greed of sellers within the limits of the just price—that is, what the grain would naturally be worth considering all concurrent circumstances.

Furthermore, Castro, Soto, Navarrus, and Covarruvias, while affirming in the places cited in the previous dispute that those selling above the legally fixed price are bound to restore the excess, add that the legally fixed price is only just because the law would otherwise be unjust and would not bind in the forum of conscience. Thus, they certainly hold the same view. For, as I shall soon show, even if the opinion we are attacking were true—that a prince could, for the good of the Republic, command that during a famine grain be sold for less than its natural value—anyone who broke that law might sin, but would not be bound to make **restitution** <note>The act of paying back money obtained through an unjust transaction.</note>.

Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential medieval jurist.</note>, in his commentary on the "care of the flesh" <note>original: "cura carnis"; referring to the Roman law regarding the oversight of food supplies.</note>, provided the opening for some legal experts to hold this inhibitory opinion, which I do not doubt is entirely false. For <margin>2</margin> there, in asking whether someone is ever compelled to sell his property for less than the just price, he answers that one is compelled in times of barrenness and scarcity, following the **Rhodian Law of Jettison** <note>original: "l. 2. §. cum in eadem. ff. ad l. Rhodiam de iactu maris"; an ancient maritime law principle regarding goods thrown overboard during a storm to save a ship.</note>. He brings forward no other foundation. Yet the same Bartolus later sufficiently explains himself in the same passage.

Specifically, he means this is understood to apply when the necessity is **extreme** <note>A technical legal term for life-or-death situations where property rights may be suspended.</note>. For just as one should be helped for free if they are in extreme necessity and have no money, so too should they be helped for a lower price than the thing is worth if they cannot pay more. Indeed, Bartolus would be ridiculous, and those who follow him would be ridiculous, if they wanted to gather anything else from that law. For the case of that law is this:

<column-break/>

When many were sailing in someone else’s ship and carrying their goods in it, they were compelled by a storm to throw many of the goods into the sea so that by this lightening of the load, they might preserve both their own lives and the remaining goods. The question was asked whether those who saved their lives and goods by this means were bound to contribute to paying for the goods that were thrown overboard for their benefit and good. The legal expert responds that the owners of the goods that were saved are bound to contribute according to the value of the goods saved for each; however, the persons whose lives were saved in this way are not bound to contribute. From this, Bartolus and certain others conclude that in a time of necessity, all things are common by both divine and human law. But if they understand this to apply to any necessity other than *extreme* necessity, they are surely ridiculous and speak against the common opinion of the doctors, as is quite clear from what we have said extensively regarding almsgiving. Nor does that text speak of any necessity other than the saving of lives. Indeed, as we showed at length in the same matter, that text does not even prove what Bartolus concluded from it—namely, that in a time of necessity, someone can consume another’s property for free. For those who were sailing in that ship were wealthy, as is clear since they were transporting merchandise, and they are ordered to contribute to the payment for the goods thrown overboard in proportion to the goods saved for each. The common and most true opinion of the doctors is that if a wealthy person in extreme necessity consumes someone else's property, he is bound to pay for it at a just price. Therefore, the decision of that text is not based on the idea that all things are common in time of necessity or that it is lawful to consume others' goods for free; rather, what that text defines was established out of a certain equity. This is because humans in a storm are usually helpful, both by assisting in unloading the ship and through other services to preserve the ship and the other goods. Therefore, there is no reason why humans should be ordered to contribute, even though the shipowner and the others whose goods were saved are ordered to contribute to the payment for the jettisoned goods. Many other reasons could have moved the legislators to establish this out of equity.

I ask you, prudent reader, to weigh how remote and how weak—not to say inept—are the consequences used to prove from that text that it is lawful in times of grain scarcity to tax it below the just price it naturally has. If anything is gathered from that text, it is only that in extreme necessity someone can be compelled to sell what another needs to escape that necessity for a lower price than the thing is worth, if the other cannot pay more. And even that, as shown, is not proven by that text. To conclude further that a prince can, in times of famine and high prices, tax grain below what it is worth is surely a non-sequitur—unless one were making a comparison to those in extreme necessity who would perish unless helped in this way, which happens very rarely and only to a very few during a general shortage. Unless another foundation is brought forward, it is certainly not proven that such a law is just.

<summary>Molina argues against the legal practice of fixing grain prices below their natural market value during shortages, refuting the misapplication of medieval maritime law and theological authorities who are often cited to justify such controls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s refutation of the idea that rulers can arbitrarily lower the price of grain during a famine. He is specifically addressing arguments that claim "all property becomes common" during times of need, arguing instead that such claims are often based on a misunderstanding of Roman law and the nature of the common good.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

...in comparison with others, who, at least by selling their inheritance—as the Egyptians did in the time of Joseph <note>A reference to Genesis 47, where the Egyptians sold their land to Pharaoh in exchange for grain during a famine.</note>—can pay the **just price** <note>The "just price" (*iustum pretium*) is the fair market value of a good, determined by common estimation rather than the seller's greed.</note>. It is even less acceptable to claim it is just that poor farmers should be compelled to sell their wheat to the rich and powerful at such a price. Why, then, do the teachers of this opinion cry out that the justice of this law holds that in times of famine, all things are common and another’s property may be taken without theft? It is as if they believe that by the mere fact of there being a famine, there is immediately an "extreme necessity" for everyone—whereas experience often teaches the opposite.

This same opinion is usually supported by the law *si pendentes* in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff. de usufruct." refers to the *Digest* of Justinian, specifically the section on usufruct (the right to use and enjoy someone else's property).</note>. However, that text proves nothing at all. 

<margin>4</margin>
The case described there is this: If the use and enjoyment of a certain field is bequeathed to someone, all the burdens of that field belong to them. For example, if something must be paid from that field for the repair of public sewers, or because of an aqueduct passing through that field, or for the passage of an army, or if a certain portion of the harvest must be provided to the municipality at a price lower than the common market rate—all these burdens belong to the person enjoying the use of the land. This is the law. From this last point, the authors we are disputing believe their opinion is confirmed. However, as is clearer than daylight, the text does not speak of a "time of necessity," but of any time whatsoever, based on a specific burden that the land itself carries. And even if it did speak of a time of necessity because of a burden that the land had only for that time, nothing could be concluded from it that would have any force to confirm the opinion they intend.

At this point, observe that when many goods are exported from a place, the ruler of that place could prohibit their export so that the people might have a plentiful supply of necessities. Likewise, he could permit the export on the condition that a certain portion be sold to the people at a lower price to suffice for them. In the same way, when buyers come from another kingdom, just as a prince could prohibit foreigners from taking those goods out of his kingdom (lest they run out or be sold too dearly), he could also grant permission to export them on the condition that a portion be taken and sold to the inhabitants at a lower price. This is rightly the case regarding salt in these years in this **Kingdom of Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitaniæ Regno." Molina spent much of his career teaching at the University of Coimbra in Portugal.</note>. And this is what the cited law, *si pendentes*, seems to intend.

The laws are much clearer in favor of <margin>3</margin> our opinion, which states without distinction that rulers ought to ensure that necessities are sold at a **just price**. Among these is the first law, the section "on the care of meats" in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff. de offic. praefect. urb." refers to the office of the Urban Prefect, responsible for the city's food supply.</note>, and many others cited by Covarruvias. Now, the **just price** is that which is equal and proportionate to the value of the thing. And **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Scholastic theologians like Molina.</note> in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 77, says that equality must be maintained in buying and selling between the thing and the price so that justice is preserved; otherwise, either mercy or liberality will be mixed in on the part of one of the contracting parties, or injustice will intervene in the contract.

Indeed, I would warn that this matter is not to be judged solely by the arrangement of human law. For this is the very thing in controversy: whether the power exists in a prince to decree that, in a time of famine, goods must be sold at a lower price than they are worth by their very nature at that time. Rather, it must be judged from the very **nature of things**.

<column-break/>

As a result, the examination and decision of this matter belongs to theologians and moral philosophers rather than to legal experts.

You might say: From the nature of things themselves, or by **natural law**, it is sufficiently proven that a law is fair which, in a time of famine, reduces the "lowest just price" <note>The Scholastics recognized a range for the just price: the "highest," "middle," and "lowest."</note> (which would otherwise be naturally just), and thus the prince has the power to establish such a law. For the **common good** of the Republic must be preferred to the private good of individuals. Therefore, since the common good of the Republic demands it, this can be lawfully decreed, and it is no obstacle that it results in a loss for some individuals.

To this, however, it must be said: if something were so necessary for the common good of the Republic that without it the Republic—as a body viewed in its entirety—would suffer a notable detriment, then the common good should be preferred to the private. In this sense, Covarruvias rightly concedes that if something were so necessary to the public good that the Republic not only lacked it but was in desperate need of it, such that it had to be given at a lower price than its natural value, then the prince could compel a subject to sell it for less than it is worth. However, this happens very rarely, because the Republic can usually pay the just price through a contribution from other parts of the Republic.

Furthermore, to assist the common good, it is not fair that one part of the Republic be burdened more than others who are able to contribute in their own degree and proportion. Moreover, when the Republic can continue to exist as a Republic without a certain thing, and the only result of a lack of that thing is a variation among the parts of the Republic—meaning some people become richer and more powerful while others decrease in wealth and power, even though all parts remain safe in their existence as members of the Republic—then that thing is not said to be "necessary for the common good." This is because the good of the Republic remains whole in all its parts, even if the parts suffer some change regarding wealth and power. Indeed, it matters little to the good of the Republic that parts which were previously richer are made poorer, provided that others in the same Republic grow in wealth and power. Rather, this belongs to the "roll of the dice" of fortune; all parts of the Republic have the right to rise to a higher level if their luck allows, and no one is owed a certain fixed status; they may descend or ascend.

From this it follows that, just as a prince cannot take from the rich to give to the poor (who are not suffering extreme or near-extreme necessity) simply so that there are no beggars or notably poor people in his kingdom; and just as he cannot take from the wealthiest merchants who acquired their riches by a just title to give to the poor; so too he cannot compel things to be sold at a lower price than they are worth by their nature, given the concurrent circumstances. To compel someone to sell for **four** something that is actually worth a minimum just price of **six** is the same as compelling someone to give away **two** of their own goods for free to another.

<summary>Molina argues that rulers cannot force sellers to trade below the natural market price during a famine unless the state's very existence is at stake. He maintains that shifts in wealth between social classes do not constitute a "common good" crisis that justifies violating private property rights.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s argument regarding grain price controls (taxas). Having previously argued that rulers cannot arbitrarily set prices, he now examines the specific injustices that arise when the state fixes grain prices below their "just minimum" value during a famine, particularly within the Kingdom of Portugal.</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 365.

In a pragmatic law <note>A civil decree or royal ordinance.</note>, however, by which grain might be priced lower during a time of scarcity than it is actually worth, not only would the rich be compelled to give from their own resources to the poor for free, but even many poor people—and those who have gathered wheat with great labor and expense—would be compelled to give for free to the rich. This is especially true since the King, in this **Kingdom of Portugal**, is accustomed to seizing wheat for himself at that fixed price to prepare his fleets and for many other purposes. He is also accustomed to granting permissions to nobles and powerful figures so that wheat may be sold to them at the fixed price, even against the will of the owners. This is further aggravated because judges and other public officials—who are not typically poor—often take wheat at the fixed price not only for themselves, but for their relatives, friends, and even others who transport it elsewhere for profit after entering into a partnership with them. They do this against the owners' will, to say nothing of the other abuses and harassments inflicted upon the owners of the wheat.

To speak summarily, the **Commonwealth** <note>The "Respublica" or the state/civil society.</note> can only compel the rich to sell grain to the poor at a lower price than its natural value in those specific circumstances where it could also compel them to give **alms** <note>Charitable donations (eleemosyna).</note> in that same amount. As we have stated following Soto and Covarruvias in the matter of almsgiving, this only occurs when people are in **extreme necessity** <note>A technical term in moral theology meaning a life-or-death situation where property laws may be suspended to save a life.</note> of such help, or if extreme necessity is justly feared unless they are assisted.

In such a case, it is not only the owners of the wheat who should be compelled to help the poor; rather, other wealthy people should simultaneously be compelled to contribute alms so that the entire Commonwealth is burdened equally and proportionally. In any other circumstances, just as the rich cannot be forced to give alms, they cannot be forced to sell their goods at a lower price than they are worth. To do so would be the same as forcing them to give alms in the amount of that price reduction. As for the poor, just as they are never bound to give alms to the rich, they can never be forced to sell things to them for less than their value. If the rich buy these things at a lower price, even with the authority of the prince intervening, they are bound to restore the difference in price to the sellers.

From these points, and from five other reasons we established in the preceding disputation to prove the same thing, I believe it has been sufficiently shown <margin>5</margin> that a law is unjust if it fixes the price of grain or any other merchandise below the "just minimum" <note>The lowest price a good can be sold for while still being considered fair based on market conditions.</note> that the merchandise naturally possesses, considering all concurrent circumstances. Therefore, in the **court of conscience** <note>The internal moral judgment of a person before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note>, such a law does not bind a person to obedience. I will add one point which I promised above to explain.

Namely: even if the prince had the power to establish such a law for the public good, and that law had the force of obligation, those who broke it—though they might sin—would still not be bound to **restitution** <note>The moral obligation to pay back or compensate for a loss caused by an injustice.</note>. The reason is that such a law would not establish "commutative justice" (which consists of equality in value between the thing and its price), but would merely forbid grain from being sold at that price for the sake of the common good. Therefore, those who transgressed the law would indeed sin against obedience to the prince and perhaps against charity toward their country and neighbors, but not against justice itself; and for that reason, they would not be bound to

<column-break/>

restitution. For just as if a prince commanded the rich to give alms to the poor in the situations we mentioned earlier, no one would claim the rich are bound to restitution if they disobeyed the prince's command. This is because they did not sin against justice, but only against obedience to the prince and against charity toward their country and neighbors. The same would hold in the case proposed here.

From what has been said so far, it clearly follows that even if a law fixing the price of grain was justly enacted, if it does not set the just minimum price that the grain naturally holds under the current circumstances, the prince is bound to repeal or change that law when circumstances change significantly, causing the natural price of grain to rise.

<margin>6</margin> Since laws of this kind are usually intended to establish the "just minimum" price of grain rather than a maximum or a middle price, and since a law is unjust if it sets a price below that natural just minimum (as <margin>7</margin> has been shown), it follows that when circumstances change significantly to increase the natural price, the King and his council are bound—under the guilt of **mortal sin** <note>A grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> and the burden of restoring the damages that followed for the grain owners—to repeal or change the law by increasing the price of grain (unless the King and his council are excused by probable ignorance).

<margin>8</margin> From this, you will understand that the custom of fixing grain prices from one September to the next is not to be approved, unless the legislators are vigilant in removing or changing the law if circumstances change significantly during the year. This is difficult to achieve in remote parts of the kingdom unless they entrust the task to judges, though that does not seem expedient. You will further understand that the opinion of those who argue that the price fixed during a time of abundance or moderate supply should persist during a time of scarcity (on the grounds that frequent changes in laws are not expedient) is even less acceptable.

For although frequent changes in other laws may be harmful, in the case of grain pricing—where the price must be equal to the merchandise for the law to be just—the law must be changed as often as the change in circumstances requires (which is very frequent), or else a fixed price should not be set at all. Instead, it should be left to men to sell as the circumstances and the nature of the thing itself require, under the penalty of mortal sin and the burden of restitution.

<margin>9</margin> Finally, to offer our judgment on whether it is expedient to fix the price of grain, I will add a few things. First, although no injury is done to those who rent church revenues, or to other powerful people and churchmen themselves, if grain is priced within the limits of its natural just price, an injury is nevertheless done to them if it is priced below the minimum just price. It injures the renters because the ownership of the grain belongs to them and they are forced to sell it for less than it is worth; it injures the churchmen and the powerful because the renters, knowing they will be harassed by the price-fixing law, pay less...

<summary>Molina argues that fixing grain prices below their "just minimum" is morally and legally unjust, as it effectively forces the poor to subsidize the rich and powerful. He asserts that rulers commit a mortal sin and owe restitution if they fail to adjust these prices as market conditions change.</summary>
