they lease their revenues at a high price from Ecclesiastics and the powerful.

The second point is that it belongs to the legislator (especially a Christian one) to look to and attend not only to the temporal advantages or disadvantages that follow from his law, but also to the spiritual welfare of his subjects. Since the political end of the state is further ordered toward the supernatural end of eternal life, the legislator must certainly attend to the spiritual good and the salvation of the souls of his subjects when making laws; he must not stop at the sole temporal advantage of the **Commonwealth** <note>The "Respublica" or the state.</note>.

And for that reason, if he sees that a grave spiritual detriment to many arises from any of his laws—whether due to the frailty or even the malice of his subjects—he is bound by the precept of charity to abstain from passing that law. This is especially true if his intent and the goal of the law can be achieved just as well by another path. In the matter at hand, there is a vast number of people who transgress the law of price fixing <note>The "taxa," a government-mandated maximum price.</note>, even a just one, at the gravest risk to their souls. They not only commit a mortal sin but are also bound to **restitution** <note>The theological requirement to pay back illegal profits to avoid eternal punishment.</note> under penalty of eternal destruction; once this bond is contracted, many are never freed from it because of the difficulty of paying it back and because they do not fear God very much. And this is what moves me most to argue against the law of price fixing for grain. 

For grain is not a thing sold by only one or two people, but by many in every town, and by almost all farmers in large or small quantities. Furthermore, it is not something sold only in the public market, but secretly in private houses and without witnesses, by which means the law is violated more freely according to one’s greed. Moreover, diminished prices are usually set, even though grain is sold publicly by foreigners at a much higher price. In this **Kingdom of Portugal**, a fixed price is usually neither set nor expedient in the city of **Lisbon**, toward which grain usually flows from the rest of the Kingdom—especially from the region across the Tagus <note>The Alentejo or Ribatejo regions.</note>. This causes merchants to voluntarily offer a price beyond the legal limit because of the greater profit they gain by transporting and selling it in Lisbon. Certainly, this is a matter that entangles the consciences of many in this Kingdom of Portugal with the burden of restitution, from which few extricate themselves.

Nor should the councilors <note>The "senatores," high-ranking judges or state officials.</note> say that only those who lease ecclesiastic and noble revenues transgress the price law, based on the fact that almost only they come to them to seek pardon from the penalty, or are the ones who usually defend themselves in court claiming they should not pay the fine. No, I say, the councilors should not say this, but should rather believe the confessors and professors of theology who are consulted daily on this matter. If only those powerful men approach them for that reason, it is because the farmers, when caught, pay the penalty immediately, while it is overlooked with the powerful; furthermore, not even a tenth of those who break the law come to the notice of those who investigate such things for punishment. There are very many who easily expose themselves to the risk of paying forty gold coins if caught, certain that they will gain two hundred if they sell beyond the legally fixed price. Meanwhile, I will omit the perjuries that occur daily when people are questioned about this, partly through malice and partly through ignorance and false

<column-break/>

mercy on the part of those being questioned.

<margin>10</margin> From these points, it will be easy to understand our judgment on this matter. **Martin de Azpilcueta** <note>original: "Nauarrus," a famous 16th-century Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 23, number 88, judged that the price of grain should very rarely be fixed for various reasons he provides, and because it is usually an occasion for many sins. I am of the same opinion, especially in the Kingdom of Portugal. First, because a price should not be fixed—nor can it be licitly, justly, or validly fixed—except within the range of **natural justice** <note>The "just price" determined by common estimation and market forces rather than decree.</note>, as has been shown copiously and, unless I am mistaken, effectively. However, it is difficult to hit upon that price immediately after the harvest when the reality hasn't yet been proven by the experience of time. This is even more difficult when the effort for the common good is directed toward ensuring the price does not exceed the lowest just level. 

Second, because the parts of the Kingdom of Portugal are so varied in their abundance or scarcity of grain, in the quantity of money, and in prices and other circumstances, it is very difficult to establish a just price for each one; and since the price is at its minimum, it will be difficult to maintain equality at their borders. Third, because, as has been proven, it is necessary to vary the law as circumstances change during the course of the year; but this is difficult for councilors occupied with other matters who do not attend to it. Thus, many are first oppressed by the injustice of the law, and what is worse, are later unjustly punished before the law is corrected, as experience itself testifies. 

Fourth, because a fixed price is not imposed on foreigners; but a fixed price imposed only on natives causes foreigners to raise their prices much higher and strip Portugal of its money, as explained above. Add to this the well-founded fear—and even the affirmation—that foreigners often buy wheat from natives above the legal price and resell it for even more than they paid. Fifth, because since there is no fixed price for Lisboners and foreigners, this causes everyone else not to restrain themselves but to sell above the legal price, especially to Lisbon merchants who offer more than the legal limit. Additionally, in such a great inequality between the price at which foreigners sell and the price at which natives are ordered to sell, it is difficult to defend the law as being just. Understand the same when, in the **Kingdom of Castile**, the fixed price is fourteen silver reals per measure, yet grain is so rare and must be brought from so far away that, counting transport costs, those who bring it are allowed to sell it for twenty-five or thirty silver pieces. Sixth, leaving aside what is feared and said concerning public officials, I am moved most by the maximum danger to souls, which I explained just before.

<margin>11</margin> You will say: "What then? Are all to be permitted to sell at whatever price they want?" From that, surely, would follow the ruin of the Commonwealth. Since nine out of ten parts of the grain sold in Portugal belong to those who lease the revenues of the Church and the nobles, and since these people try as much as they can to raise the price by whatever ways they can, surely, if they are allowed to sell for whatever price they want, they will sell beyond what is just and suck the blood of the poor. From this, it will happen that in a short time they will acquire <margin>12</margin> all the goods and estates of others. I see that this is the most powerful reason why the councilors claim that a fixed price for grain is absolutely necessary for the Kingdom of Portugal. Regarding which, it must be said...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s argument against the "taxa" (fixed price law) for grain in Portugal. He is proposing an alternative administrative method to ensure supply and fair pricing without the negative spiritual and economic consequences of a universal price ceiling.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 366.

it must be said that this evil (if it is not spoken of with hyperbole) is in no way to be tolerated. It can, however, be easily addressed without a price-fixing law <note>original: "taxationis lege"; referring to the *taxa*, a government-mandated maximum price.</note>, which involves the whole kingdom and produces as many evils as we have recounted above.

For since such men, if they do this, are unjust and harmful to the **Commonwealth** <note>The "Respublica" or the state.</note>, they can certainly be compelled to give an account of the grain they hold in each town from their commendams, ecclesiastical revenues, and the holdings of the nobility—which is not difficult to know in every town. At that point, they can be forced to sell it at a moderate price, as the nature of the thing and the concurrent circumstances demand, and as it is commonly sold by others in the same place. Indeed, it could be sold and distributed by public authority as the common good of that people requires, provided a just price is returned to the owners, and leaving them all the grain that would not be necessary for the common good and the needs of the people in the place where they hold it.

And by that method, without a price-fixing law, it would come to pass in Portugal that everyone would sell grain at a just and moderate price, and an opportunity would be provided for foreigners to come into the ports, and the evils mentioned above would be avoided. In the same way, other natives who abound in grain and are unwilling to sell it at a moderate price when the people need it should be compelled to sell in each town, so that equality might be preserved among all. This means is much more effective—that the people buy grain at a just price—than establishing a price-fixing law and, neglecting this diligence (which alone suffices), permitting everyone to sell at whatever price they please, and then investigating transgressors to punish them. For it is easy: to acquire two hundred [units of profit] by selling beyond the price fixed by law, they expose themselves to the risk of paying a much smaller penalty than the law prescribes. This is especially true since judges only care to exact the penalty and are not at all concerned that the excess price be returned to the buyers.

<margin>13</margin> I should advise that the greatest care must be taken lest those to whom the distribution of grain is committed take it for themselves, their friends, and other public ministers. Instead, they should distribute it to poor farmers for sowing, and to bakers for selling publicly baked bread of a just weight and moderate price, according to the price at which they buy the grain. Care must also be taken lest the poor spend more in obtaining a measure of wheat from those to whom its distribution is committed than the amount the owners of the wheat could exact from them in addition. Furthermore, care must be taken lest the owners of the wheat be unjustly harassed by being detained for more days and travel expenses to ensure the grain is sold, or by selling it at a lower price than is fair, or by not leaving them as much as is right for the support of their own family or for other needs, or by making public instruments at their expense, or by forcing them into it. Among other abuses of those judging, this is accustomed to occur: they are used to taking all the grain to be distributed from everyone, leaving no individual the necessary amount for the support of their own family or for other things; and then, after petitions in writing have been made by their servants or ministers at no small cost,

<column-break/>

and offerings and bribes have been presented either to the judges themselves or to their servants and ministers to intercede, they are accustomed to grant them a portion of their own wheat. In other ways they harass them (especially the farmers), and the cry of the miserable ascends into the ears of the **Lord of Sabaoth** <note>The Lord of Hosts; a biblical reference to God hearing the cries of the oppressed.</note>. These are sins against justice, carrying the burden of **restitution** <note>The theological obligation to pay back ill-gotten gains to be absolved of sin.</note>.

For judges are bound by their office and by justice to see that this is done without unnecessary expenses, and that the people and the poor are not harassed by their arrival. If all the abuses that are <unclear>committed</unclear> in this matter reached the ears of the senators, along with the quantity of grain that they report as distributed in their responses according to the price fixed by law, perhaps they would not value that distribution so highly. I would also hope that, in place of the inquiry made every year regarding those who sold grain above the price fixed by law, an inquiry would be made into those who sold grain and other things on credit above the rigorous just price. This inquiry should be made not only by lay powers but also by ecclesiastical authorities during <unclear>visitations</unclear>. Where **disguised usury** <note>original: "palliata vsura"; lending at interest hidden within a sales contract.</note> is discovered, the sellers should be compelled to restore what they received beyond the just price, and the penalties for usurers, both civil and ecclesiastical, should be executed against them. For in this way, great spiritual disadvantages would be avoided, and buyers would not be oppressed as poor people by usury. These things are said under the judgment of others, out of zeal for the honor of God and the common good.

### Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

<margin>
14. In which case the seller may cast out or expel the buyer against their will, or sell to another.
15. When the risk of goods sold by measure belongs to the seller alone.
16. A purchase and sale is said to be "perfected" in three ways.
</margin>

<margin>7</margin>
1. Consequently, we must examine whether, if a purchased item perishes or is rendered worse before **delivery** <note>original: "traditionem"; the formal transfer of physical possession</note>, it perishes for or is a loss to the buyer, or rather the seller. I say "if it perishes or is rendered worse before delivery," because if the item perishes or is degraded after **actual or fictional delivery** <note>Molina refers to "fictional delivery" (traditio ficta), a legal concept where ownership is transferred by words or keys without moving the physical object</note> is made to the buyer (according to what was said in Disputation 13), it is clear that the loss or deterioration belongs to the buyer. 2. This is not only because **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> is transferred to the buyer through delivery—provided the price is paid or considered paid—and because a thing normally perishes for its owner; but also because, through that delivery, the seller has paid his debt and entirely fulfilled the contract on his part.

3. Furthermore, delivery only applies to a specific thing determined as an individual item. When a specific, individual thing is sold, the risk of that thing immediately pertains to the buyer, even if it has not yet been delivered, as we shall see shortly. Thus, it follows by even greater reason that it perishes for him or is worsened if it has already been delivered to him. This is agreed upon in the laws *Lectos* and *Si neque* in the Digest <note>Molina cites "ff. de periculo, & commod. rei vend.," referring to the Roman Digest section on the risk and benefit of sold items</note>.

However, before delivery, if the contract of purchase and sale is "perfected" in the manner explained in Disputations 337 and 338 (such that it is not lawful for the contracting parties to withdraw from the contract), a distinction must be made. Either something is sold as a specific individual item—such as this particular slave, or this house, etc. (which legal experts call a sale of a **specific item** <note>original: "speciem"</note>)—or something is sold as an **undetermined item** <note>original: "indeterminatum in individuo"</note>, such as so many measures of grain or wine without determining which ones specifically, or ten sheep without designating which ones; this, legal experts call a sale of **goods in general** <note>original: "in genere"</note>. This latter case can happen in two ways: either by designating the source (such as wine from such a vat, or grain from such a heap, or fruits I shall gather this year, or from my flock, or similar things) or by designating nothing at all.

4. This being established, it must be said: If that which is sold is so undetermined as an individual that the sellers are only bound to deliver an individual or individuals of some **type** <note>original: "speciei"</note>, but no more from those in one place than others, nor more from those you possess than others—for example, if one sold ten sheep or ten measures of grain without designating from where—then if those from which he intended to pay should perish or be rendered worse (so they no longer maintain the quality they were understood to be bought as), they perish for and are a loss not to the buyer, but to the seller himself. The reason is that the buyer, by that contract, acquired a right to no specific thing, but only a right that things of such a type and quality be delivered to him. The seller is not bound to deliver any one thing in particular, but some thing indefinitely. Hence, whatever thing of that type and quality perishes while with the seller, it perishes for the one to whom it belongs—the seller—and not the

<column-break/>

5. buyer. And this is what legal experts intend when they say that **a general category cannot perish** <note>original: "genus perire non posse"</note>, based on the argument of the text in the law *In ratione* and the law *Incendium*.

6. For they mean to say that when an individual of some type is owed indefinitely, the obligation always remains, even if whatever individuals were held by the creditor are destroyed; because the type itself cannot perish, and the obligation was only toward something indefinite of that type. This is the view of Baldus, Gregorius Lopez, and Antonio Gomez.

7. Observe, however: if that which is owed in general or indefinitely varies in its value, the benefit or the loss of that change pertains to the buyer. This is manifest of itself and is gathered from the chapter *Naviganti* regarding usury. For example, if I bought six bushels of grain to be delivered after four months, any increase or decrease regarding the market value they then have certainly pertains to me.

8. Observe further: when a sale was celebrated in the aforementioned way, the fact that all those things from which the seller intended to provide the goods and fulfill the contract perish does not free the seller from fulfilling the contract. Instead, he is bound to buy or by another means seek out the goods to deliver, unless the buyer wishes to be content with the price being returned and withdraw from the contract. The reason is that the sold goods were entirely undetermined within the breadth of that type by the agreement of the parties. Therefore, even if all things of that type which the seller then had (and from which he intended to pay) perish, he is not freed from fulfilling the contract regarding the delivery of the goods. If, however, the determination was made formally or effectively by the agreement or intention of the parties from some certain things—so that the undetermined thing was to be delivered from *those*—as if someone sold ten sheep "from his flock" (not determining which ones), or so much weight of wool "from his flock," or so many bushels of grain "from such a heap," or "from his crops," or so many jars of wine "from such a vat"; then, if all those things perished without the seller's fault, he would be freed from fulfilling the contract, and would only be bound to return the price, if he had received any.

Next, it must be said: if something determined is sold from a specific thing or from certain things—for instance, twenty sheep are sold "from a flock of a thousand," or ten bushels "from a heap of grain," or four jars of wine "from some vat," etc.—or if a whole thing determined as an individual is sold **by measure** (for example, if I say "I sell you this vat of wine for four silver pieces for each jar," or "I sell you this heap of grain at such a price for every measure," or "I sell you this field at such a price for every acre," or "I sell you my flock at such a price for every head of cattle or herd"); then the risk of the purchased thing, before it is delivered, weighed, numbered, or measured, pertains to the seller. However, once delivery is made, or once the sold thing is weighed, numbered, or measured, the risk begins to pertain to the buyer. The text is fundamental and express on this point in the Digest.

<summary>Molina explains the legal principle of "risk of loss" in sales, arguing that for generic goods (like "ten sheep"), the seller bears the loss if their stock dies, but for specific items or measured goods, the risk shifts to the buyer only after delivery or measurement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the "Contract of Sale," specifically focusing on the moment "risk" (periculum) transfers from the seller to the buyer. The previous page established that for specific, individual items, risk usually passes to the buyer immediately upon agreement. This page examines exceptions, particularly regarding goods sold by weight, measure, or count.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 366

**Concerning the contracting of a sale:** The first part of this entire assertion is found in the section "but even if from a wine-cellar" <note>original: "sed etsi ex dolario"</note>, where the jurist Gaius says that when an indeterminate amount is sold from a determinate thing—for example, a certain number of measures <note>original: "metretæ"; an ancient Greek/Roman unit of liquid volume</note> from a specific wine-cellar—the risk remains with the seller until they are measured out. This holds true whether they were sold for a fixed price per unit or all together for a single price.

The second part of the argument is found throughout the cited paragraph, where Gaius establishes a distinction between when a determinate thing that consists of weight, number, or measure is sold as a whole for a single price (which is called **selling "as a body"** <note>original: "vendi ad corpus"; selling a specific bulk lot regardless of the exact quantity</note>, a subject we will discuss more extensively in the following disputation) and when it is sold at a fixed price for each unit of weight, measure, or count (which is called **selling "by measure"** <note>original: "vendi ad mensuram"</note>). When it is sold "as a body," the entire risk pertains immediately to the buyer, as we shall discuss shortly; however, when it is sold "by measure," the risk does not fall to the buyer until the item has been measured, weighed, or counted.

He provides this elegant reasoning for the matter: when a thing is sold by measure, each individual jar, weight, or acre—or each individual animal—is considered to have been bought under an **implied condition** <note>original: "tacita conditione"</note> that the measuring, weighing, or counting actually takes place. When a thing is sold under an implied condition that is pending in the future, even if the thing being sold is a specific, individual object, the risk does not pass to the buyer until the condition is fulfilled, as we shall say below. These same points are held in the Code, Title on the risk and benefit of a sold thing, Law 2 <note>original: "l. 2. C. de peric. & commod. rei vend."</note>, where it is expressed that the same applies when a determinate thing is sold in that manner. Likewise in the *Siete Partidas* <note>The foundational legal code of Castile</note>, Law 24 and 25, Title 5, Part 5; and in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 31, Laws 5 and 6. Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> agrees in his *Practical Questions*, Chapter 3, and this is the common opinion which he reports.

<margin>Doubt 9</margin>
However, it is asked whether, when one sells (for example) an entire vat for a price calculated at so much for each measure, the sale should be called "as a body" or "by measure," as we just described. Baldus and Paul of Castro <note>Influential medieval commentators on Roman law</note> judged it to be "as a body," and therefore the risk before measuring would belong to the buyer; they argued a sale is only called "by measure" when specific jars are sold, and not the entire batch of wine. However, Saliceto and others, including Covarrubias (cited above) and Lassarte, rightly affirm the contrary. This view is also favored by Gregorio López in his commentary on the laws cited earlier. Indeed, it is expressly stated in the cited laws, so there is no reason to doubt the matter.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Therefore, because in a sale—both when an indeterminate amount is sold from specific things, and when a whole determinate thing is sold by measure—there is an **implied condition pending in the future** <note>original: "tacita conditio pendens in futurum"</note> regarding whether it will be delivered, measured, weighed, or counted. If the condition is not met, the contract is rendered null. It follows that if the entire thing perishes before the condition is fulfilled, the contract is null, and consequently the **sales tax** <note>original: "alcauala"; a common Spanish tax on transactions</note> is not owed, and the seller is bound to return the price to the buyer if they had received it. But if the condition is fulfilled, first of all, any benefit or

<column-break/>

disadvantage regarding a higher price of the thing sold at the time of delivery belongs to the buyer. This is very well known and is gathered from the Canon Law <note>original: "c. nauiganti, de vsur."</note> and is explicitly stated in Law 24, Title 5, Part 5. Furthermore, since the contract is retroactive once the condition is fulfilled—meaning it is considered to have been celebrated at the time it was first entered into—it follows that the **tax** <note>original: "gabella"</note> is owed to the lord and the tax collector who held office when the contract was initiated, not to those who are in office when the condition is fulfilled, should they be different people. So says Lassarte in the place cited above.

11. Among things that consist of weight, number, or measure, some are customary to **taste** <note>original: "gustari"</note>, such as wine, honey, cinnamon, etc.; others are not affected by tasting, such as wheat or a mass of gold or silver. In those things customary to be tasted, Law 24 of Title 5 says that for the risk to pass to the buyer, it is enough—disjunctively—that they either be tasted, or weighed, or measured. This was the opinion of Azo, as Gregorio López notes in Gloss 3, and Antonio Gómez is of the same opinion. Thus, this must be asserted in the Kingdom of Castile because of that law.

12. However, the Gloss on the law "What is often" <note>original: "l. Quod sæpe"</note> in the Digest regarding the contracting of a sale, and certain other glosses, affirm the contrary. In confirmation of this, they cite the law "If anyone [buys] wine" <note>original: "l. si quis vina"</note> in the section "if by aversion" <note>original: "si aduersione"</note>. Specifically, when such a thing is sold "as a body" and mention was made of tasting (either formally or by implication, because it was bought under the condition that it would please once tasted), the risk does not belong to the buyer until it has been tasted. However, when it is sold "by measure" under that same implied or express condition of tasting, both are required cumulatively for the risk to pass to the buyer: the tasting AND the weighing or measuring. Gregorio López, in the cited gloss, admits this is the common opinion of the doctors, which certainly should be followed outside the Kingdom of Castile; it is also defined in the Portuguese Ordinances in the cited place, paragraph 5.

Note: If a deadline was established between the buyer and seller by which the sold item was to be measured, weighed, counted, or tasted, and the buyer was the cause of the task not being completed, then the risk pertains to the buyer from that moment forward. The seller is then only held liable for **fraud** <note>original: "dolo"</note> or **gross negligence** <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>. If, however, no deadline was established, but the seller warns the buyer in front of witnesses to come and execute the task within a certain time, and the buyer does not come, the risk pertains to the buyer in a similar way thereafter. This is found in the Digest and the *Siete Partidas*.

Note further: if someone sells, as an "either/or" choice <note>original: "sub disiunctione"</note>, the slaves **Stichus or Pamphilus** <note>These are traditional "placeholder" names used in Roman legal examples, like "Person A or Person B."</note>, then whichever of them dies first before delivery is the seller's loss. But if the last one dies before delivery, it is the buyer's loss. The same applies if both die at the same time; in both events, the buyer pays the price. This is held in the Digest and affirmed by the Gloss on the Institutes.

The same applies to any other things in a similar manner...

# Luis de Molina
## On Contracts

in the manner of items sold under a choice: for only the last one to remain perishes for the buyer, while the others perish for the seller. The choice belongs to the seller when the buyer has not chosen the option for himself or included it in the agreement to pay for whichever he wishes, as is held in the paragraph "if a purchase" <note>original: "§. si emptio"</note> previously cited.

<margin>12</margin>
In the third place, we must discuss when something, or certain things, are sold as specific individuals: such as this slave, this house, these two oxen, this jar, or these jars of wine, this field, etc. and they are not sold by measure, but "as a body" <note>original: "ad corpus"; meaning the specific physical object regardless of its exact measurements</note>, nor under any other condition pending in the future. In such a case, by the very fact that the sale is celebrated, the entire risk pertains to the buyer. Therefore, if the things sold deteriorate or perish entirely before delivery <note>original: "traditionem"</note> without the fault of the seller, it is the buyer’s loss, and he is nevertheless bound to pay the full price if he has not yet paid it. This is held in the paragraph "when however" <note>original: "§. cum autem"</note> joined with the gloss there, in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale; and in the Law "that which often" <note>original: "l. quod saepe"</note>, the paragraph "in those," in the Digest on Contracting a Purchase; and Law 1 and following in the Code on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing; and Law 1 and following in the Digest on the same title; and Law 23, title 5, part 5; and Law 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 1, at the beginning. This is affirmed by Covarruvias, Lassatte, Antonio Gomez, and the common opinion of the doctors which they cite in the mentioned places, especially Covarruvias. 

The reason for this rule is not that ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the sold thing passes to the buyer before delivery—and thus it perishes for him as the owner, as Sylvester seems to suggest under the word "purchase" <note>original: "emptio"</note>, question 2, pronouncement 4, and as certain others suggest. For the contrary is established from the paragraph "when however" at the end, in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale, where it is expressly held; from the Law "by deliveries" <note>original: "l. traditionibus"</note> in the Code on Agreements; and from other laws and those things discussed in Disputation 2 and chapter 3, and elsewhere in the previous sections, as the common opinion of the doctors affirms. The legitimate reason, therefore, is because the laws have so disposed, in accordance with right reason. Since the said seller, by that contract, is strictly constituted as a debtor of a specific and singular thing, and the buyer acquires a right to that thing alone in exchange for the price, it is rightly decreed that if, by some accident, it is rendered worse or perishes entirely, the whole risk is the buyer's, and the seller remains free from the debt. Just as the risk and loss then regard the buyer, so too does the benefit. Whence, if anything should be added to the property by alluvion <note>alluvion: land gradually added to a riverbank by the flow of water</note> before delivery, or it is rendered better by any other means, that whole benefit falls to the buyer's advantage. This is held in the paragraph "when however" in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale; and the Law "that which," at the beginning, in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing; and Law 23, title 5, part 5.

<margin>13</margin>
In the following events, however, the risk pertains to the seller. The first is if the thing perishes or is rendered worse by the fault of the seller, because he did not apply the due diligence regarding its custody and preservation. For the seller is, by the disposition of the law, like a guardian and manager of the thing; wherefore he is held liable for fraud <note>original: "dolo"</note>, gross negligence <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>, and light negligence <note>original: "leui"</note>, because the contract is celebrated for the benefit of both the buyer and the seller; but he is not held liable for the slightest negligence <note>original: "leuissima"</note>. This is held in the Law "that which often," the paragraph "if the thing," in the Digest on Contracting a Purchase; the paragraph "when however," at the phrase "but if it shall have fled," joined with the gloss there at the word "fault," in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale; the Law "if sold," in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing; and the Law "the seller of a house," in the Digest on Actions of Purchase. 

It does not matter that in the Law "custody" in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, it is said that the seller is held to that diligence to which a borrower <note>original: "commodatarius"</note> is held regarding a borrowed thing; while a borrower, as

<column-break/>

was said in Disputation 295, is held even for the slightest negligence. This does not matter: because, as the gloss in the same place explains consistently with the cited laws, either that law understands the situation when the thing was lent for the benefit of both the lender and the borrower (in which event the borrower is only held for light negligence, as was seen in the cited disputation), or it understands that he is held to a *similar* diligence as that which a borrower maintains, even if not to *as great* a degree. Antonio Gomez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 32, and Sylvester under the word "purchase," question 2, pronouncements 7 and 8, seem to agree on this matter.

The second case is when the seller was in delay <note>original: "mora"; a legal term for default or failure to perform an obligation on time</note> in delivering the sold thing: for then, even if it should perish by a chance accident or become worse, it would perish or become worse for the seller. This is gathered from Law 1, "that," in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing. Sylvester, under the word "purchase," question 2, pronouncement 9, says that when the thing would have perished in the same way even if it were with the buyer, it perishes for the buyer and not for the seller in the "court of conscience" <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the moral or religious judgment of one's soul</note>, even if he was in delay in delivering it. This is consistent with what we said in Disputation 295, and with the doctors whom we cited there, regarding when a borrowed thing perishes with the borrower in a similar way after his delay. Sylvester adds that in the "external court" <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public, secular court of law</note>, even if the thing would have perished in the same way with the buyer, it will be judged to have perished for the seller. He cites in confirmation of this the Law "if when the thing," the final paragraph, in the Digest on Legacies, book 1. The gloss, however, on the paragraph "when however" in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale, mentions both this and the contrary opinion, and seems to lean toward the view that even in the external court it is not then considered to perish for the seller. This is consistent with the Law "likewise if beaten," the final paragraph, in the Digest on the Sale of a Thing; nor does the text Sylvester cites contradict this, but rather supports it. For in that text, it only says that if a bequeathed estate perishes before it is delivered to the legatee, with a delay in delivering it intervening, it perishes for the heir. The text gives the reason: because the legatee could have sold it before it perished, if it had been delivered to him. From which words, by the opposite sense, it is gathered that when it is entirely certain that the thing would have perished in the same way with the legatee or the buyer, it is considered in the external court to have perished for him; in doubt, however, it is considered to have perished for the seller or the heir; and this is our opinion. In this place, observe that if after the seller's delay the buyer were in delay in receiving the bought thing—because the seller offered it to him and the buyer did not accept it—then it would perish for the buyer. For a thing always perishes for the one who is last in culpable delay, as is held in the Law "that" in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, and the Law "if through the buyer" in the Digest on Actions of Purchase.

The third case is when it was expressed in the contract that the risk pertained to the seller: for then it regards him by that very agreement, as much as was expressed in the contract. This is held in the paragraph "when however" in the Institutes on Purchase and Sale; the Law "in a sale" in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing; Law 39, title 5, part 5; and book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 1, the final paragraph; and often elsewhere. Understand the same on the contrary, when the risk, which otherwise would regard the seller, had been cast upon the buyer in the contract: for then the thing perishes for the buyer as well, as is established from the cited laws.

The fourth case is when the sold thing, before it is delivered, is confiscated on account of a crime of the seller: for then it does not perish for the buyer, but the price must be restored to him if he had already paid it. This is held in the Law "if a field" in the Digest on Hiring, and in the Portuguese Ordinances, title 1, paragraph 4. Where it is added that the same holds if the sold thing, before it is delivered, is taken by the King for some necessity.

The fifth case is if the seller affirmed something regarding the goodness of the wine, by which the buyer persuaded himself it would last longer in good condition...

<summary>This page discusses the legal principles determining whether the buyer or seller bears the "risk" (loss) if a specific item is destroyed before delivery. Generally, for individually identified items, the risk passes to the buyer upon agreement, but exceptions exist for seller negligence, legal delays, specific contract clauses, or government confiscation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of risk (periculum) in sales contracts, specifically focusing on the sale of wine and goods sold by measure versus those sold as a specific whole ("ad corpus"). It moves from the specific responsibilities of the seller regarding the quality of goods to the formal definitions of different types of sale.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 367

in quality, and if it is changed or deteriorates before delivery <note>original: "traditionem"</note>, the loss falls to the seller. The same applies if the seller knew the wine would not last and did not warn the buyer, even if the risk had already otherwise passed to the buyer: for if it becomes worse before delivery, the loss is the seller's. This is held in Law "if wines" 2 <note>original: "l. si vina. 2."</note> in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, and Law 39, title 5, part 5 <note>original: "p. 5"; referring to the Siete Partidas, a major Spanish legal code</note>.

Next, observe that if wine or anything similar is sold—whether as a specific whole <note>original: "ad corpus"</note> or by measure— and while not yet delivered, it is kept in a vessel or a place that the seller needs for storing something else: if the deadline has passed during which the buyer was bound to remove it, and the seller warns him in the presence of witnesses to take it away, then if the buyer remains in default <note>original: "in mora"</note>, the seller may throw it out into the public street without penalty. If the seller prefers, he may instead sell it to a third party so that the first buyer does not suffer a total loss, but receives at least the price found for it in good faith. He may also rent other vessels or a location at the buyer's expense to store it there.

<margin>14</margin>
The seller may likewise leave it where it was and receive a fair rent for the space, provided he would have otherwise rented those vessels or that place to another, or would have used them for his own goods. And although he does better if he does not throw the sold item into the public street but chooses one of the other options mentioned, the law—as a penalty for a defaulting buyer—permits him, setting aside the others, to throw it into the public street. When the vessels contain wine, if no deadline was set for the wine to be removed, they must always be left empty before the vintage <note>original: "ante vindemiatas"; the harvest time</note>, if the seller is a merchant who is accustomed to storing other wine there, before he needs them for storing new wine. These points are found in Law 1, the section beginning "it is permitted," and Law 2, and the Law "if anyone [buys] wines," the final paragraph, in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, and Law 24, title 5, part 5.

Fourth, we must discuss sales made under a future condition. In cases where it was said the risk pertains to the buyer, if the thing bought perishes entirely, the loss is the seller's. However, if it becomes better or worse and the condition is eventually fulfilled, the improvement or deterioration belongs to the buyer. 

<margin>15</margin>
An exception is made when the sale is by measure, and thus under the condition that it be measured; if the thing becomes worse before it is measured, weighed, or counted, then the deterioration is the seller's loss.

The first two parts of this conclusion are found in the Law "necessarily" <note>original: "l. necessario"</note> in the Digest on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, Law 26, title 5, part 5, and the 4th book of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 31, paragraphs one and two. In this latter source, it is rightly added that if the thing was made worse because the seller was in default of delivery, the risk belongs to the seller. To the first two points, it is added that if the condition fails, the sale is rendered entirely null; but if the condition is fulfilled after the death of the buyer and seller, the contract is valid and passes to the heirs of both parties.

The exception applied to the conclusion is clear from what we said above: when something is sold by measure under an implied condition that the thing be delivered, 

<column-break/>

measured, weighed, or counted. In that case, the risk—even of deterioration—before the condition is fulfilled rests with the seller, as is clear from the laws cited there. The gloss on the Law "that which often," the paragraph "in those," at the word "you shall have counted" <note>original: "adnumeraueris"</note> in the Digest on Contracting a Purchase, gives this reason: because that implied condition is "potestative" <note>a condition within the power of one party to fulfill</note>, depending on the seller's will, and he could easily have fulfilled it; therefore it is no wonder if the risk of deterioration of the sold thing is cast upon him before it is fulfilled.

Finally, in this disputation, one must observe with the gloss on the first Law of the Code on the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Thing, that there are three ways in the law and among the Doctors <note>learned legal scholars</note> that a purchase and sale is said to be "perfected." 

<margin>16</margin>
First, in such a way that the contracting parties can no longer withdraw from the contract. The ways this is perfected were explained in Disputations 337 and 338. Second, in such a way that the risk of the thing bought belongs to the buyer. This mode of perfection has been discussed throughout this entire disputation, and various laws speak of it in this way. Third, in such a way that the ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the thing bought is transferred to the buyer, and the ownership of the price to the seller, and finally, that the contract is fulfilled on both sides by delivery <note>original: "traditione"</note>.

We spoke of this matter in part in the latter portion of Disputation 338. As I remember saying more than once above, when any penalty is established for those selling something, it is understood to refer to a sale perfected in this third way—at least in the manner explained at the end of Disputation 338—unless the law expresses otherwise. The reason for this is that penalties must be interpreted restrictively.

***

### ->On sale, and universally on alienation,<- 
### ->by the whole and by measure.<-

### DISPUTATION CCCLXVII.

#### ->SUMMARY<-

1 *Sale or alienation is done either by the whole body or by measure.*
2 *When a sale or alienation is said to be made "by the whole" <note>original: "ad corpus"</note> and when "by measure."*
3 *Quantity in a contract can be expressed in three ways.*
4 *A sale by the whole is when one begins with the object itself and adds a measure or quantity; a sale by measure is when one begins with the measure and adds the thing.*
5 *If a sale is made by the whole, the entire thing is considered sold, even regarding any increase found in it (and the following number).*
6 *When the price should be increased or decreased by reason of the growth or shrinkage of a thing sold by the whole.*
7 *A sale is said to be "by measure" when it is made at a fixed price for every acre <note>original: "iugere"</note>.*
8 *When a sale is made by measure, that which grows by alluvion <note>land added by the flow of water</note> before it is measured belongs to the seller.*
9 *If a seller speaks falsely regarding the quality or quantity of a thing, he is held liable by an "action of purchase."*
10 *If a sale is made by quantity, when the price should be added to or subtracted from.*

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the transfer of property and risk. While the previous page focused on the risk associated with perishable goods like wine, this page transitions into the formal legal classification of sales: whether a thing is sold as a specific, whole object ("ad corpus") or by a specific quantity or measurement ("ad mensuram").</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts

<columns>
->**Luis de Molina: On Contracts**<-

When a sale or any other type of transfer <note>original: "alienationis"</note> of a thing occurs, and mention is made of both the thing being sold and its quantity, legal experts <note>original: "doctores"</note> distinguish two specific ways the sale can be conducted: first, **as a whole body** <note>original: "ad corpus"</note>; and second, **by measure** <note>original: "ad mensuram"</note>. They establish a significant distinction between these types of transfers.

<margin>1</margin>
A transfer is said to be made **as a whole body** when mention is made of the thing and its quantity, but the quantity is used only as a description, a sign, or an accidental feature <note>original: "accidente"; in legal philosophy, a non-essential characteristic</note>, in the sense explained in Disputation 211 (where it was discussed what jurists mean by "description"). An example is if someone says: "I bequeath to you," or "I sell to you, my specific estate, which consists of ten acres <note>original: "iugerum"</note>." In this case, the quantity is placed there as an accidental detail, a note to identify the thing being sold, rather than as a restriction on the contract. It is not as if the desire for that specific quantity restricts the legacy; thus, if the estate is found to be larger, the extra portion belongs to the buyer (or legatee) rather than the heirs. Conversely, if it is smaller, the heirs are not required to provide more to reach that total. On the other hand, they say a transfer is made **by measure** when the quantity is expressed not as a descriptive note, but as a restriction on the transfer, so that the sale is only understood to cover that specific amount. For example: "I sell to you ten acres *from* my field." If the field is then found to be larger, neither the legacy nor the sale is considered to include the extra land, but only the expressed quantity.

<margin>2</margin>
Because legal experts vary wonderfully on this matter—as can be seen in the works of Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva, a famous Spanish jurist</note> in *Practical Questions*, chapter 3, and Arias Pinelus <note>Arias Pinelo, another influential legal scholar</note> on the law regarding the rescinding of sales—I will state my view, particularly regarding "onerous" contracts (contracts involving an exchange of value) such as buying and selling. We must first note that the question of whether a sale is made "as a whole" or "by measure" can be examined regarding three effects. **The first effect** is whether the whole thing—of which a certain quantity was mentioned—is considered sold or not. That is, if the sale was "as a whole" and the object is found to be larger, the whole is considered sold, and the seller cannot keep the excess. But if it was "by measure," the whole is not sold, but only the expressed quantity; the seller remains free to keep or sell the excess to someone else, even if the buyer offers to pay for it at the same proportional price. **The second effect** is to determine whether the whole thing is considered sold for the price established at the beginning. If the sale is "as a whole" and the thing is later found to be larger or smaller, the buyer takes the whole for that same price (as some argue); the price does not increase for more land, nor decrease for less. However, if the sale was "by measure" and it is found to be larger, the buyer must either pay more or leave the excess to the seller; if smaller, the buyer can subtract from the price

<column-break/>

according to the decrease in quantity. **The third effect** is to determine whether the **risk** <note>original: "periculum"</note> of the sold thing belongs to the buyer or not. If a specific item (movable or immovable) is sold "as a whole," the risk passes to the buyer immediately. But if it is sold "by measure," the risk does not belong to the buyer until it has been measured out for him.

<margin>3</margin>
Next, it must be noted that the expression of quantity in a contract of sale (or any other) can be applied in three ways, which legal experts do not sufficiently attend to. **First**, strictly as a **description** of the thing being transferred—that is, as a note or accident irrelevant to the contract itself. While this can happen, unless it is clear from obvious clues that it was intended this way, and that the person paying for the thing did not rely on that quantity to determine the price, it should not be interpreted in this sense, but rather in the third sense mentioned below. In legacies and donations, however, which depend solely on the generosity of the giver, the giver usually does not rely on these descriptions of quantity or quality as if they meant the gift is void if the thing exceeds that size. Because the recipients are not giving anything in exchange, they do not rely on these expressions to balance the value. However, those who enter into "onerous" contracts (where there is a cost) usually *do* rely on such descriptions. Therefore, civil law rightly established that in wills and donations, unless the giver's intent is clearly otherwise, such "false descriptions" are treated as if they weren't written, as shown in Disputations 211 and 286. Thus, legal experts wrongly argue that the same applies to sales contracts, as Arias Pinelus correctly noted in the cited passage, number 15. **Second**, the expression of quantity can be used as a **restriction** on the transfer—namely, that the thing is only considered sold up to that quantity. For example: "I sell you ten acres of such a field of mine." **Third**, as a **warranty** <note>original: "modus"</note> of the thing being transferred, regarding which the seller formally (or effectively) assures the buyer, binding himself to that quantity. For if someone says, "I sell you this field and I assure you it is so many acres," or binds himself to that amount, he is formally making a guarantee. If he says, "I sell you this field of ten acres," he is effectively assuring the buyer it is ten acres and binding himself to that, if that assertion somehow motivated the contract; for the buyer, relying on that assertion, bought the field when he otherwise might not have, or might not have paid so high a price.

<margin>4</margin>
This third way seems to align with the legal term "mode of the field" in the Digest <note>original: "l. si seruus, §. si modus. ff. de actionib. empt." referring to the Body of Civil Law</note>, which says: "If the measure of the field is found to be less than the number of acres, the author (that is, the seller) is liable." Certainly, the fact that legal experts have not distinguished this third way of expressing quantity from the other two, and have not noticed the different considerations between sales "as a whole" and "by measure" regarding the first and second effects explained above, is the reason they have not fully reached a decision on this matter.

</columns>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property sales, specifically distinguishing between sales made "as a whole" (ad corpus) and sales made "by measure" (ad mensuram). This distinction determines who benefits from unexpected surpluses or who bears the loss of deficits in the quantity of the goods sold.</meta>

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 367</header>

<columns>

<margin>4</margin>
With these preliminary notes established, legal experts <note>original: "iurisperiti"</note> commonly hand down two rules. The first is: When in a sale one begins with the "body" <note>the specific object or property itself</note> and afterwards the measure or quantity is added, the sale is considered "to the body" <note>original: "ad corpus"; meaning as a single whole unit</note>. For example, if it is said: "I sell you such-and-such an estate, which is fifty acres <note>original: "iugerum"; a Roman unit of land area approximately equal to 0.6 acres</note>." This is understood to be the case whether the boundaries of the estate are explained—such as saying it is enclosed by certain borders—or if they are not explained, provided it is clear which estate is being discussed, and whether the boundaries are expressed immediately after the estate or after its quantity. Some restrict this rule, arguing it should only apply when the thing is sold for a single price for the total quantity; it would be different if a price is expressed for each individual measure. They claim that if it is said, "I sell you such an estate, which is fifty acres, at such a price for every acre," the sale is "by measure" <note>original: "ad mensuram"</note> and not "as a whole body."

<margin>The second-to-last law, paragraph "if jars," in the Digest on the actions of the buyer <note>original: "l. pen. §. si dolia ff. de actionib. empt."</note></margin>
The second rule is: When one begins from a certain measure and quantity of a thing, and afterwards the thing itself is added, the sale is "by measure." For example, if it is said: "I sell you thirty acres of such a field of mine," or "from such a field of mine." In that case, if the property is found to be of a greater quantity, the whole is not considered sold, but only the expressed measure. Regarding items sold as accessories, if one begins with their quantity, the sale is considered "by measure." For example, if it is said: "I sell you such an estate of mine with eighty jars <note>original: "dolijs"; large earthenware vessels used for storage</note>," or "with eighty jars existing there," the sale of the jars is by measure. Thus, if more are found there, only eighty (which must be sound) are to be delivered to the buyer, while the remainder belong to the seller. This is expressly stated in the second-to-last law, the paragraph beginning "if jars" <note>original: "l. pen. §. si dolia"</note>, in the Digest on the actions of the buyer.

However, if one begins with the thing sold as an accessory, the sale is considered "as a whole body." For example, if it is said: "I sell you such an estate, with the jars existing there, which are eighty." In that case, if more are found, all are considered sold. And since the transposition of words should not be a concern when it does not change the sense, it follows that whenever words, however arranged, sound like the sense of the first rule, the sale is to be considered "as a whole body." When they sound like the sense of the second rule, it is to be judged as made "by measure." Therefore, if it is said, "From such an estate of mine I sell you ten acres," the sale is by measure. But if the words are arranged so that the meaning is doubtful, it must be judged by conjectures as to what meaning the contracting parties intended.

Regarding these rules, I say this: if we are speaking of a sale "as a whole body" or "by measure" in comparison to the first effect explained above—namely, that the whole thing is considered sold, even regarding any surplus <note>original: "incrementum"</note> found in it, if the sale is "as a whole body"; but it is not considered sold regarding the surplus if the sale was "by measure," so that the seller can reserve the surplus for himself—then these rules are very true. However, the first rule does not need that restriction which some people apply to it.

<margin>5</margin>
Because, in truth, in that event the whole estate is considered sold, even if it is found to be of a greater quantity than fifty acres; nevertheless, in that case, according to everyone's opinion, the buyer is held to increase the price for the surplus found, according to the rate set for each acre. 

<column-break/>

And all of this, which we say regarding the proposed restriction, is clearly held in the law "he who a field" <note>original: "l. qui fundum"</note>, paragraph "he who a field" <note>original: "§. qui agrum"</note>, in the Digest on the contract of sale.

The entirety of the first rule is confirmed by the law "he who a field" <note>original: "l. qui fundum"</note> in the Digest on evictions <note>original: "de euictionib."; legal recovery of property by a judicial process</note>. There it states that if someone sells a field, saying it is one hundred acres, and it is later found to be larger, if after the delivery some part of the field is "evicted" <note>legally taken away</note>, even if what remains is still one hundred acres, the seller is nonetheless held liable for the eviction of that part, according to the quality of that part. The reason for this decision is that, since the sale was "as a whole body," the entire field is considered to have been sold, and therefore the seller is liable for the eviction of any part of it. And this is clearly the sense of that text. From these points, I conclude that if someone sells a jar of wine saying, "I sell you this jar, which holds one hundred amphorae <note>original: "amphoratum centum"; an amphora was a standard Roman liquid measure</note>, at such a price for every amphora," if more amphorae are later found in it, it is not within the seller's power to refuse to deliver the surplus to the buyer at the same price.

However, if he sells it thus: "From this jar I sell you one hundred amphorae at such a price for each of them," he is not held to deliver any surplus. All these things are to be understood when there is doubt about the intent of the contracting parties. But if it is established by conjectures either that the buyer did not intend to buy more than one hundred measures, or that the seller intended to sell only one hundred measures, then the buyer will not be held to receive more, nor the seller to give more. This pertains to the first effect.

<margin>6</margin>
As for what pertains to the second effect—namely, that when a sale is "as a whole body," the entire thing is considered sold for the same price established from the beginning, so that neither by reason of a surplus found in the thing should anything be added to the price, nor by reason of a deficit <note>original: "decremento"</note> should anything be taken away from the price—everyone agrees in the event of the restoration of the first rule. That is, when a specific price is expressed for each measure, the price must be increased according to the surplus found, and subtracted according to the deficit found. For example, if it is said, "I sell you such an estate of fifty acres at such a price for each acre," and it is later found to have more acres, the buyer is held to increase the price in the same proportion; but if it is found to have fewer, the seller is held to reduce the price in the same proportion, according to the law "he who a field," paragraph "he who a field," in the Digest on the contract of sale. Many, however, call that a sale "by measure" and not "as a whole body," and it should undoubtedly be called so, as was said in the preceding discussion, according to the law "what often," paragraph "in those," <note>original: "l. quod sæpe, §. in ijs"</note> and other laws. This is for the effect that the risk of the thing so sold does not look to the buyer until the thing has been measured, weighed, or numbered.

<margin>Question</margin>
But when a sale is "as a whole body" and the thing is sold for a single price for the total quantity, legal experts vary in a wonderful way—not only the ancients but also the moderns—as to whether the price should be increased or decreased for a surplus or deficit later found in the thing. Antonio Gómez <note>original: "Aut. Gom."; a 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 16, and many others assert that the price should be neither increased nor decreased. Their reasoning is that the contracting parties seem to have referred themselves to...

He cites Roman law from the Digest to clarify when prices must be adjusted based on the unit of measurement used in the agreement.</summary>

<page-num>293</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 368</header>

<columns>

...with reason a legal action will be granted, since he affirmed a falsehood regarding the quantity. The same is true, says the legal consultant, if a seller affirms that there are sixty acres <note>original: "iugera"</note> of vineyard and forty of meadow, which he sells together, but the opposite is true—even if the total area of both is found to be one hundred acres. In such a case, a lawsuit <note>original: "actio"</note> is granted against the seller. Furthermore, this agrees with the laws <note>The author cites various sections of the Digest, the Roman law code: "l. si qs cū fundū. l. & si vno, & l. si fundo. ff. eo. ti."</note>. Indeed, these cited laws are so clear that I greatly marvel that so many legal experts have held the contrary opinion.

<margin>10</margin>
**The third conclusion:** When a seller has expressed the quantity of a thing, and the thing is later found to be of a greater quantity—if from that greater quantity an inequality arises from the nature of the thing between the object and the price, such that the thing is truly worth more—the buyer is bound in conscience to restore the contract to equality, or to rescind the sale. Indeed, I believe that both in conscience and in the external court <note>meaning a human law court as opposed to the "court of conscience" or God's judgment</note>, if the found excess is notable, the buyer is bound to restore the contract to equality. This is done by adding to the established price an amount for the excess quantity, or by leaving the surplus quantity to the seller, or by rescinding the contract—unless the quantity was stated merely as a description or as an accidental detail irrelevant to the contract. The first part of this is self-evident and was proven in Disputation 350. The latter part is affirmed by Pinellus (citing Decius and Paulus Castrensis) in the place mentioned, number 9. This is consistent with natural equity, which demands that just as the buyer is assisted when a thing is found to be of lesser quantity than stated, so too should the seller be assisted when it is found to be of a notably greater quantity. And although such explicit laws are not found in favor of the seller—because it rarely happens that a seller is deceived in quantity, whereas it happens frequently to a buyer—support is found in the law <note>original: "l. si venditor, ff. de acti. empt."</note> which states: If someone sold a slave with the *peculium* <note>the personal savings or property a slave was allowed to hold</note> that the slave possessed, and affirmed that the slave had ten in the *peculium* and that nothing would be taken from it, then if it is later found that the slave had more in the *peculium*, the whole amount belongs to the buyer. From this, I gather by the opposite sense that if the seller had not affirmed that nothing would be taken, the surplus would belong to the seller. Observe what is said in this conclusion: if a seller expresses the quantity in this way—"I guarantee you that the estate I sell you is at minimum of such a quantity"—then if a larger quantity is found, the buyer would not be bound to increase the price, unless the excess was so great that an inequality in value arose between the thing and the price. For by those words, the seller is seen to have alienated the thing for that price alone, along with any increase it might have; and this seems to be the intent of the cited law. These are the things that occurred to be said regarding a sale "as a whole" <note>original: "ad corpus"</note> and "by measure" <note>original: "ad mensuram"</note> in comparison to the second effect. From these points, it is clear that the rule handed down by many is false—namely, that in a sale "as a whole" nothing is to be added for a discovered surplus, but in a sale "by measure," an addition must be made. For if a sale "by measure" is taken according to the second rule reported above, then the surplus is not considered sold to you. If, however, it is taken according to the limitation of the first rule (as is often done by legal experts and in law, and as we used in the preceding disputation), that rule is false:

<column-break/>

for it has been shown that in other sales "as a whole," an addition must be made to the price for a discovered surplus. Finally, as for the third effect—whether the risk of the sold thing belongs to the seller or not—it was sufficiently explained in the preceding disputation what ought to be said.

### To whom the fruits of a sold thing belong.

## DISPUTATION CCCLXVIII.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *When the fruits <note>profits, produce, or rents</note> of a sold thing belong to the buyer, and when to the seller.*
2 *The use of a sold house before the sale is finalized belongs to the seller; after it is finalized, it belongs to the buyer.*
3 *The labor of a sold slave, and to whom the payment for that labor is owed.*
4 *Expenses incurred on a sold thing by the seller before the sale is finalized, for the sake of gathering fruits, are the responsibility of the seller, just as the fruits themselves belong to him.*
5 *The rent <note>original: "pensio"</note> of a sold thing that was previously leased: when it belongs to the seller and when to the buyer. And what if the buyer was the Treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note>? Number 6.*
7 *When a buyer is bound to respect the rights of a tenant farmer or a resident tenant.*
8 *When a purchase and sale is considered finalized for the purpose of the fruits belonging to the buyer, if nothing else was agreed between the parties.*
9 *When a buyer is bound to pay interest <note>original: "usuras"</note> to the seller because of a delay in paying the price, and what kind.*
10 *When a seller is bound, beyond all fruits, to all "intrinsic interest" <note>actual loss or potential profit</note> regarding the sold thing.*
11 *How interest on an unpaid price is to be estimated.*
12 *When a buyer is bound to no interest toward the seller despite a delay in paying the price.*
13 *When ownership of a purchased thing is presumed to remain with the seller.*
14 *When interest on the price is not owed to the seller according to the value of the fruits.*
15 *When a sale is not called usurious or illicit while the price is in deposit under some condition.*
16 *A buyer offering the price to a seller who is in delay <note>original: "in mora"</note> in delivering the thing can sue for all fruits the seller perceived from that day, or could have perceived.*
17 *Cases in which a seller can sue a buyer for interest regarding lost profit <note>original: "lucri cessantis"</note> or emerging damage <note>original: "damni emergentis"</note>.*
18 *Fruits hanging from a purchased thing at the time of the contract, whether ripe or not, always belong to the buyer regarding the value at which they were estimated at the time of the contract.*

When it has been said and established between the contracting parties to whom the fruits of a sold thing ought to belong, the agreement made between them on this matter must be upheld. This is stated by Covarruvias (1. *var. res.* c. 15. n. 1), Antonio Gomez (2. *to. var. res.* c. 2. n. 11), and the Doctors of Law generally; the matter is clear enough in itself and is collected openly from the law...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 293 regarding the transition of rights from the seller to the buyer. It specifically focuses on "fruits" (economic yields like crops, labor, or rent) produced by a property during the period between the agreement of sale and the final "perfection" of the contract.</meta>

[Page 294]

->Ludovicus Molina, *On Contracts*<-

<note>Legal citations: Julian, Law "The one who [sold] the farm," paragraph "The one who [sold] the field," section "Of the farm," in the Digest on the contract of sale; and from the law of Julian, paragraph "If regarding the fruits," in the Digest on actions of purchase.</note>

When, however, nothing was explicitly stated in the contract regarding the fruits, then—once the sale is perfected <note>In Roman and Scholastic law, a sale is "perfected" (perfecta) when the object and price are fixed, even if the item hasn't been delivered yet</note> (in the sense to be explained below)—all fruits from the thing sold that have not yet been gathered belong to the buyer. Those fruits, however, which had been gathered up to the point of the sale’s perfection, would belong to the seller. For example, if a vineyard is bought shortly before the vintage, all the fruits found on it when the sale was perfected—even if they are already ripe and ready to be harvested—all belong to the buyer, and none of them to the seller. Consequently, a vineyard is worth more immediately before the vintage by reason of the hanging fruits than it is worth immediately after the vintage.

<margin>2</margin> In the case of a **house**, and in other similar things, since the fruits are nothing other than the use of that thing, the use of the sold house up until the perfection of the sale, and the price paid for that use, belong to the seller. The use after the perfection of the sale, and the price for that use, belong to the buyer. In the same way,

<margin>3</margin> the **labor of a servant**, and the price for those labors, up until the perfection of the servant's sale, belong to the seller; however, the labor and the price for them after the perfection of the sale belong to the buyer.

All these points are established from the law of Julian, the paragraphs "If regarding fruits," "If anything for the servant," and "From the sale," in the Digest on actions of purchase; from the second law, "The fruits," and the law "After perfection" in the Code under the same title. These are affirmed by Antonio Gómez and Covarruvias in the cited places. This is further confirmed because hanging fruits are legally considered parts of the land, as held in the law "The fruits" in the Digest on the recovery of property. However, as Covarruvias and others he refers to rightly affirm, the land is considered "whole" without them, as if no part of it were missing. Therefore, the fruits are considered sold with the land, and consequently belong to the buyer after the sale is perfected, just as the land itself does—notwithstanding the fact that the buyer has not yet acquired legal ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the land or the fruits before the formal delivery.

<margin>4</margin> Observe, however, that if the seller, after the contract was celebrated by mutual consent but before the necessary perfection for the fruits to belong to the buyer, had reasonably incurred some expenses in cultivating the land and bringing the fruits to their current state, those expenses and the industry <note>labor or skill</note> he applied must be paid back to him. The same applies to any other expenses reasonably incurred regarding the thing sold, when no other agreement was made. This is based on the law "After perfection" in the Code on actions of purchase and the law of Julian, the paragraph "Furthermore," in the Digest under the same title. Regarding the fruits that were hanging on the land at the time the contract was celebrated by mutual consent: to whom they belong if they are gathered before the perfection of the sale will be discussed at the end of this disputation.

<margin>5</margin> As for **rents** <note>original: "pensiones"</note>—for instance, if a sold field had previously been leased for a certain annual rent—Ulpian says in the law of Julian, paragraph "If regarding fruits," in the Digest on actions of purchase, that they belong to the person who leased it, and thus to the seller. The commentary of Accursius there, and Bartolus (whom Covarruvias refers to and follows, stating it to be the common opinion of the doctors), teach that this must be understood as follows: the seller must give the buyer a portion of that rent, or the whole amount, according to the time for which the fruits 

<column-break/>

belong to the buyer; or, the seller should certainly cede the legal action to the buyer so that the buyer may demand and receive that rent in the seller's place. Ulpian thus means that the personal action to demand and receive the rent from the tenant farmer <note>original: "colonus"</note> or resident belongs to the lessor who sold the thing, not to the buyer. For that reason, either the lessor himself must demand and receive the rent to give all or part of it to the buyer, or he must cede the action to the buyer so that the buyer may demand it in the lessor's name.

Covarruvias, in the cited place, along with Bartolus and many others, provides an excellent rule for discerning to whom the rent belongs—whether to the buyer or rather to the seller who had leased the thing. When the rent is derived from the yields of the leased thing, as is usual in leases, one must notice whether at the time the sale was made the fruits had been entirely gathered, whether none of them had been gathered, or whether they were partially gathered and partially not.

Indeed, if at the time of the perfected sale all the fruits were gathered (for example, if a vineyard was sold and the sale was perfected after the vintage), then the entire rent belongs to the seller. This is true whether the rent had already been paid or whether the day agreed upon for the tenant to pay had not yet arrived. The reason is that the rent is owed by reason of the fruits; and the fruits then, as has been shown, belong to the seller. This definition agrees entirely with the law "The deceased" in the Digest on usufruct.

If, however, at the time the sale was perfected no fruits had been gathered, then the entire rent belongs to the buyer. This is true whether the day prescribed for the tenant to pay had not yet arrived, or if it had arrived and the tenant had already paid the rent to the seller—in which case the seller is bound to restore it to the buyer. The reason is the same: namely, that the rent is owed by reason of the fruits, and in that event, all the fruits belong to the buyer, as we have seen.

When, however, at the time of the perfected sale a portion of the fruits was gathered and a portion remained to be gathered, the rent is to be pro-rated. This is not based on the portion of the year that preceded or followed the sale, but rather based on the ratio of fruits gathered before the sale's perfection to the remaining fruits. The seller receives the former and the buyer the latter, for the same reason.

Consequently, when the thing sold is a house or something similar, the "fruits" of which consist in daily use, the rent is to be divided pro-rata according to the time of the year that preceded the perfected sale versus the time that follows it. In this case, the division is naturally proportional to the fruits gathered before perfection compared to the fruits that will be or can be gathered after the sale is perfected.

<margin>6</margin> Nevertheless, an exception to this rule is made by Bartolus (in the final law, final paragraph of the Digest on the rights of the treasury), Covarruvias (in the cited place, numbers 4 and 5), and many others whom he cites, regarding the **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note>. When something belonging to the Treasury that was already leased to someone is sold, and at the time the sale is perfected part of the fruits were gathered and part remained to be gathered: then, they say, if the time for paying the rent had not yet arrived, the entire rent belongs to the buyer, as that paragraph expressly holds. They affirm this is granted to the buyer in compensation...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal entitlement to "fruits" (crops, labor, or rent) during a property sale. He establishes that once a sale is legally "perfected," future yields belong to the buyer, while past yields belong to the seller, with specific pro-rating rules for rental income and house usage.</summary>
