### Second Treatise, Disputation 368.

...compensation for the subsequent burden that it holds.
<margin>7</margin>
Indeed, other buyers are not held to honor the contracts of tenant farmers or renters for a duration of less than ten years established by the seller, but they may deprive them of the leased property; two outcomes excepted.

One is when the property was sold under the condition that the buyer be held to honor that contract, or if the buyer consents after the sale is celebrated that the tenant should persevere in the contract. The other is when that property was bound to the tenant by a general or special <term>mortgage<note>Original: "hypotheca." A legal claim on property used as security for a contract.</note></term> for the observance of the contract. So it is held in the *Ordinances of Portugal*, title 29, according to the Law "The Buyer" in the Code on leases, and other laws; and the common opinion affirms this, which Antonio Gómez relates in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 9, and follows. This matter must be discussed further under the contract of leasing and hiring. If, however, the tenant wishes to pay the buyer the full <term>interest<note>Original: "interesse." In this context, it refers to legal compensation for both "lost profit" and "actual damages" incurred.</note></term> of lost profit and emerging damage that comes to the buyer from the tenant staying in the contract, the buyer is compelled to consent, as is held in the cited place of the *Portuguese Ordinances*. When, however, the buyer does not wish to honor the lease contract (as he is not bound to outside of the listed outcomes), the tenant has a right of action for "interest" against the seller and lessor, as is held in the cited laws and will be said in its proper place. Although these things are so for other buyers, when someone buys from the **Treasury** <note>Original: "fisco." The public or royal treasury.</note>, he is absolutely held to honor the lease contract made regarding the thing sold by the Treasury; and this is a privilege of the Treasury, so that tenants do not later sue the Treasury for damages. Therefore, they are deemed to buy from the Treasury under that cited condition.

Those who buy from the Treasury, then, have this burden; in compensation for it, it is granted to them that, because part of the fruits at the time of the perfected sale were already collected and part remained to be collected—and the time for paying the rent had not yet arrived—the entire rent belongs to the buyer. In this way, the cited doctors reconcile the aforementioned paragraph with the established rule, regardless of what a few have said to the contrary. Because the cited paragraph is an exception, it ought not to be extended beyond the case contained within it.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
It must now be examined when a purchase and sale is considered "perfected" <note>A sale is "perfected" when it is legally finished and the risk/benefits transfer to the buyer.</note> to the effect that, if nothing else is agreed between the parties, the fruits of the thing sold belong to the buyer. Covarrubias, in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 15, number 2, affirms that a sale is considered perfected by the mere consent of the parties before the thing is delivered and before the buyer pays the price—even before the seller extends credit for the price—according to the Law of Julian, paragraph "if regarding the servant" in the Digest on the action of purchase. But Covarrubias seems to speak not of all fruits, but only of those "hanging" <note>Crops still attached to the plant or tree.</note> from the thing sold at the time of the contract, such as if a vineyard is bought immediately before the vintage. However, Angelus (under the word "purchase," near the end of number 11) and Sylvester (in the same place, question 3) say that a sale is then considered perfected so that the fruits belong to the buyer only when the price is already paid, or credit has been extended by the seller for the price.

Having established the distinction between fruits that were hanging from the purchased thing at the time of the contract (which, since 

<column-break/>

they already existed and were attached to the thing bought, are treated as parts of it, as has been said) and fruits that were not yet actually in the thing bought but could be perceived from it in the progress of time, the following conclusions must be established by which this question will be decided.

**First conclusion.** Speaking of fruits which at the time of the contract were not yet hanging from the thing bought, and when nothing else was established between the parties, they do not belong to the buyer before the buyer offers the price or the seller extends credit for it. Consequently, they do not belong to the buyer before the seller delivers the thing sold by extending credit, or before he is in <term>default<note>Original: "mora." A legal delay or failure to perform a duty on time.</note></term> of delivering it to a buyer who is offering the price. This is how the Law of Julian (the paragraph "if regarding the servant") must be understood. It follows that if, after the contract is celebrated, the seller receives any such fruits from the thing sold before the price is offered to him, they belong to him and not to the buyer—for example, if he receives some payment for the labors of a servant he sold before the price was handed over, or for the hiring of a beast of burden that he sold. In this conclusion, Antonio Gómez, Covarrubias, and others fully agree, especially following the Law "He shall care for" in the Code on the action of purchase. For equity does not allow that the seller should deliver the thing to the buyer, or that the thing should produce fruit for the buyer, before the buyer pays the price to the seller so that the seller may use it and it may produce fruit for him through his own industry.

**Second conclusion.** If the seller delivers the thing sold to the buyer, and the buyer is in default of handing over the price, or pays only part of the price and is in default of paying the rest, he is held to the seller not only for the price (or the unpaid part) but also for the **interest** <note>Original: "usuras." In a modern sense, "interest." In the 16th century, charging interest was morally complex, but allowed here as compensation for the buyer's delay.</note> on it. So it is held in the Law "He shall care for" and the final law in the Digest on the risk and benefit of a thing sold.

<margin>9</margin>
By this final law, it is added that he is held only to interest, and not to the "lost profit" <note>Original: "lucrum cessans." Profit the seller could have made if he had the money on time.</note> of the seller because the price was not paid at the proper time. For example, if the seller was a merchant and, because the price was not paid on time, he lost more profit than the interest on the price would be, the buyer is not held to that lost profit, but only to the interest on the price. Since, however, interest is prohibited by natural and canon law, some doubt the equity of this civil law provision. Omitting other opinions, it must be said with Covarrubias, Angelus, and others that this interest is granted as **compensation** for the fruits which belong to the seller in the meantime while the buyer is in default of paying the price. It follows that the buyer is held to pay as much interest on the unpaid price as equals the value of the fruits he received from that same thing during the whole time of the delay—or those he could have received but failed to due to his own negligence—and the seller cannot receive greater interest. If he paid part of the price and was in default on the rest, he is held to pay interest equal to the proportional part of the fruits he received or could have received.

It also concludes that a buyer only gains rights to future income from a purchase once they have paid or been granted credit, and must pay interest if they delay payment while enjoying the property's fruits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Luis de Molina’s legal and moral analysis of the "fruits" (economic yields) of a sold property. It specifically addresses what happens when there is a delay in payment or delivery, and how the law balances the rights of the buyer and the seller through compensatory interest.</meta>

For instance, if the buyer pays half the price, he is bound to pay the value of half the yields; but if he pays a quarter of the price, he is bound to pay the value of three parts of the yields, and so on for the remaining portions he has not paid. Therefore, because <term>usuries</term><note>In this 16th-century context, "usury" refers to any interest or growth on a principal, not necessarily illegal or exploitative "loan sharking."</note> of this kind are not for profit, but are "compensatory," as they are called, for the yields which equity does not allow to belong to the buyer while he is in <term>delay</term><note>Original: "mora." A legal term for a failure to perform a duty (like payment) on time.</note> of paying the price; it follows that they are not among the number of those usuries which natural and <term>canon law</term><note>The internal legal system of the Catholic Church, which strictly regulated lending and interest.</note> condemn. Thus, the provision of <term>civil law</term><note>Roman-based secular law.</note> on this matter contains no iniquity. The *Portuguese Ordinances*, Book 4, Title 14, § 3, not only agree with the second proposed conclusion, but they also very clearly explain the provision of common law in the manner we have just described.

For when usury is discussed in that title, the events are explained in which usuries—though improperly so-called—are licit. In § 3, among other things, they hold: "If the buyer, having received the thing purchased, does not pay its price as he is bound to do, the seller can demand from him not only the price, but at the same time the value of all the yields which he perceived from the thing purchased, or could have perceived during the entire time he was in delay of paying the price." With these words, the *Portuguese Ordinances* very clearly agree with the common law in the manner we have explained.

**The Third Conclusion.** If the buyer delivers the price, and the seller is in delay of delivering the sold item, not only do all the yields perceived from the time of the delay belong to the buyer, but also all those which <margin>10</margin> could have been perceived during that entire time and were not perceived due to the seller's negligence. Finally, the seller is bound for all <term>intrinsic interest</term><note>Original: "interesse intrinsecum." This refers to the actual value lost regarding the item itself, such as a drop in its market price or physical decay.</note> of that thing. For example, if at the time the thing was to be delivered it was worth more, and afterwards it was either returned in worse condition or decreased in price; and for that reason the buyer was deprived of that intrinsic interest in the thing due to the seller's delay, the seller is bound to him for it. However, he is not bound for <term>extrinsic interest</term><note>Original: "interesse extrinsecum." This refers to secondary losses or missed opportunities outside the item itself.</note> such as <term>lost profit</term><note>Original: "lucrum cessans." Profit the buyer would have made elsewhere if they had the item on time.</note>, or accidental damage emerging from the situation for the buyer. For instance, if the buyer was going to trade with that thing, and because the purchased thing was not delivered to him at the appointed time, some profit ceased for him which he would have had from transporting that thing or its yields to another place, the seller is not bound to him for such lost profit. Similarly, if because the thing was not delivered to him, some <term>slave</term><note>Original: "mancipium." Molina is writing in a period where the trade of enslaved persons was a standard part of legal and economic treatises.</note> of the buyer died of hunger, the seller is not bound to him for such an accidental emerging loss.

All these things are expressly contained in the Law "If Barren," in the paragraph "When through the seller" in the Digest *On Actions for Purchase*. They also prove the first part of the conclusions in the Law "Yields" and the Law "After Perfection" in the Code *On Actions for Purchase*. In the entire conclusion, the *Portuguese Ordinances* in the cited § 3 agree, while in the proposed event, they grant the buyer no action other than for all the yields which the seller perceived from the purchased thing, or could have perceived during the whole time of the delay, and did not perceive through his own negligence.

From these conclusions, and especially from the second, Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 4, infers several corollaries. The first is: The decision of civil law proposed in the second conclusion is not founded on "lost profit," as is clear enough from what has been said. For even if the seller was not going to make a profit with the price, he can receive usury on the unpaid price according to the quantity of the

<column-break/>

yields which belong to him during the entire time the buyer is in delay of paying the price. Nevertheless, the *Gloss* on the chapter "Conquestus" regarding usury, Panormitanus in the same place, and others, using the word more broadly, affirm that those usuries are licitly received by reason of "lost profit" on account of the yields which, in the meantime while the price was not paid, ought to have belonged to the seller.

<margin>11</margin> **The Second Corollary.** Usuries for the unpaid price are to be estimated according to the value of the yields which the seller *would have* perceived from that thing, not according to the value of the yields which the buyer *actually* perceived. Therefore, he says, if the buyer perceived greater yields than the seller would have perceived, the usuries must be paid only according to the value of the yields which the seller himself would have perceived. Although Covarruvias cites certain others for this opinion of his, the contrary view certainly seems more probable to me.
<margin>Refutation.</margin> Indeed, the yields which the buyer perceived are the yields of the thing itself. However, by provision of the law, the thing produces yields for the seller while the buyer is in delay of paying the price. Therefore, after deducting expenses and the reward for labor and industry, the remainder belongs to the seller. This is confirmed from the cited *Portuguese Ordinances* § 3, which grant an action to the seller for the value of all yields which the buyer perceived from that thing during that whole time, and those which he could have perceived and did not perceive through his own negligence.

**The Third Corollary.** The buyer is bound to pay usuries on the price according to the value of the yields, even if, due to the length of time, they exceed the value of the agreed price. The reason is that, in truth, during that entire time, that thing produces yields for the seller.

<margin>12</margin> **The Fourth Corollary.** It must be said, against Baldus, Paulus Castrensis, and certain others, that the buyer is bound to pay no usuries when the buyer neither perceived yields from the sold thing, nor would the seller have perceived them if he had kept it with him. The reason is clear, since usuries are only owed by reason of the yields and according to their value. Therefore, no usuries are owed when neither the buyer perceived yields, nor the seller would have perceived them.

Since, as was seen in the later part of Disputation 338, for the <term>ownership</term><note>Original: "dominium." Full legal title and rights to a property.</note> of a purchased thing to pass to the buyer, it is not enough that the contract was celebrated by mutual consent and that delivery of the purchased thing followed, <margin>† <gloss>Question 10</gloss></margin> but it is further required that the buyer pay the price, or offer it, or that the seller consider it as paid. For this reason, many affirm that the provision of the Law "He Shall Care" and the other laws we cited for the second conclusion have their force from the fact that, in the event of the second conclusion, ownership of the purchased thing does not pass to the buyer through delivery, but remains with the seller. For that reason, the thing produces yields for the seller as its own master. Therefore, they say, when ownership of the sold thing passes to the buyer (the seller granting it and waiting for the price until a certain day), the provision of the Law "He Shall Care" would cease; indeed, it would be a usurious contract by which the seller would bargain for usuries on the price according to the value of the yields for the time given for payment, or for any time if the buyer were in delay thereafter in paying the price. So say Panormitanus and many others, which Covarruvias relates in the cited chapter 4, fifth corollary.

Molina argues that a buyer who delays payment must compensate the seller for the property's yields, viewing this as fair compensation rather than exploitative usury.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 368.

Why, they ask, is this contract approved in the law *Sicut Emptio* and the following law in the <term>Digest</term><note>Original: "ff. locati." This refers to the Roman Digest, specifically the section on leasing and hiring (Locati-Conducti).</note>? The contract states: "**I sell you this house for a thousand gold coins**, and in the meantime, as long as you have not paid the price, I lease it to you for such-and-such a rate." Through this contract and the delivery of the house, <term>ownership</term><note>Original: "dominium." In Roman law, this is full legal title, not just physical possession.</note> is not transferred, because the price has neither been paid nor treated as paid; rather, only "holding" of the house is granted. Therefore, because the house remained the seller's and the price was not paid to him, it continues to "bear fruit" for him; thus, he was able to simultaneously lease it to the buyer until the price was paid.

<margin>13</margin> However, <term>Covarrubias</term><note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva (1512–1577), a famous Spanish jurist and theologian.</note> in his 5th corollary, cited above, says that the foundation of the law *Curabit* and of other rights is not that ownership of the purchased thing belongs to the seller. Rather, it is what we touched upon above: namely, that equity does not allow a thing to yield fruit for the buyer before he either delivers or offers the price to the seller, so that the price might also yield fruit for the seller through his own industry, or until the seller accepts the price as paid. Thus, in the event of the third proposed conclusion, ownership of the purchased thing remains with the seller in the meantime while he does not deliver it, and yet it yields fruit for the buyer. In the same way, it would yield fruit for the buyer even if it remained with the seller through no fault of his own—for instance, if the buyer paid the price but delayed in seeking or receiving the thing. This opinion of Covarrubias is pleasing.

<margin>14</margin> In the same corollary and the following one, Covarrubias indeed grants that when a seller transfers ownership of a thing to a buyer without any other agreement, treating the price as paid and granting a deadline for payment, he is not owed <term>usuries</term><note>Original: "vsuras." Here meaning interest or compensation for the delay.</note> on the price according to the value of the yields, even if the buyer is in <term>default</term><note>Original: "mora." A legal delay in fulfilling an obligation.</note> of paying the price after the given deadline. The reason is that the seller seems to have voluntarily renounced the privilege of the law *Curabit*. Therefore, he can only demand the "lost profit" resulting from the fact that the loan, in essence, was not paid to him at the due time; just as with formal loans, one can demand the profit that ceases because the loan was not paid by the prescribed deadline, as was said when usury was discussed. However, although Covarrubias grants this, he nevertheless asserts—along with many others whom he cites—that if the seller, when he thus transfers ownership and grants a deadline for payment, includes in the pact that the buyer must pay interest on the price according to the value of the yields for the entire time the price remains unpaid, the contract is valid and licit. This is argued first because, by the fact that the seller transfers ownership and grants a delay for paying the price, he imposes no burden on the buyer. This is because the risk of the purchased thing belongs to the buyer immediately once the sale is celebrated, even before ownership is transferred to him, as was said in *Disputation* 366. Therefore, by transferring ownership and granting a delay for the price, the seller improves the buyer's position. Thus, just as the seller justly receives interest on an unpaid price when the thing is delivered but ownership is not yet transferred, he can likewise choose to transfer ownership to the buyer and grant him time to pay, provided that he himself still enjoys interest in the same way, according to the value of the yields. Second, because by transferring ownership and granting time for payment, the seller deprives himself of the interest on the price which he could have justly received according to the value of the yields.

<column-break/>

...yields, as is clear from the second conclusion. Since this is estimable at a price, he may refuse to transfer ownership in that manner and grant time for payment unless it is with a pact that the "interest" of the value of the yields be paid to him in a similar way. I certainly incline toward this opinion of Covarrubias as the more probable one, although I see that <term>Silvester</term><note>Sylvester Prieras, a Dominican theologian.</note> (under the word "usury" 2, question 11), <term>Panormitanus</term><note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer.</note>, and many others—who do not seem to have sufficiently grasped the foundation of the law *Curabit* and other rights cited for the second conclusion—do not entirely agree with what has been said so far.

Following Covarrubias in the cited corollary 7, we advise that it is lawful at the time of the contract to estimate the value of the yields and establish that, whether their value is later found to be greater or lesser, a certain fixed price be paid for their value, which is believed to be what the fruits will be worth, more or less. This is clear enough from what has been said often above, especially when the discussion concerned "lost profit" by reason of a loan and a sale.

<margin>15</margin> From what has been said, I infer that a contract is neither usurious nor illicit if someone sells a vineyard and, for the benefit of the buyer, transfers ownership of it to him immediately, but on the condition that the price remains in deposit or with the buyer until some other property of equal quality is found to be bought with that price. This is with a pact that until that property is bought, the buyer is bound to pay the seller an annual <term>pension</term><note>Original: "pensionem." An annual payment or rent.</note> according to the value of the vineyard's yields. I have seen this contract celebrated, and its justice was doubted. I am led to assert that this contract is not usurious because this contract is licit: "I sell you this vineyard for two hundred gold coins, not to be delivered until another property is found to be bought with the price, from which equal yields in value may be perceived, so that I can be suitably sustained; for I do not wish to use the price for anything other than buying such a property, and in the meantime, while it is not found, I wish to enjoy the yields of my vineyard." Furthermore, after such a contract is celebrated, this other one is valid, by which, for the buyer's benefit, I grant him the yields and transfer full ownership of the vineyard to him for an annual pension according to the value of the yields in the meantime while that other property is not bought with the price. Since the right I reserve to the yields of my vineyard is worth that entire annual pension, if these two contracts are made together, as in the proposed case, neither usury is seen nor is anything unjust committed. You may find the corollary laws in Covarrubias if you wish.

<margin>16</margin> The fourth conclusion in order is this: If the buyer offers the price to the seller, and the seller is in default of delivering the sold thing according to the form of the contract—so that he neither wishes to deliver the thing nor receive the price—then the buyer can sue for all the yields which the seller has perceived from the purchased thing from that day forward, or could have perceived but did not perceive through his own negligence. This is proven because from that day, the seller unjustly deprived the buyer of the perception of all those yields; therefore, he is bound in conscience and in the external court to restore them all to him. Furthermore, the sale, as far as the buyer is concerned, was already consummated then, and the failure was solely due to the wickedness and fault of the seller. Since the yields belong to the buyer once the sale is perfected, it follows...

It then transitions into Disputation 369, which addresses the problem of a seller selling the same item to multiple buyers.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...the rule is that from that day, those yields are owed to the buyer. This conclusion is also clearly gathered from the law *If Sterile*, in the section *When through the seller*, in the <term>Digest</term><note>Original: "l. si sterilis. §. cum per venditorem. ff. de act. empt." This refers to the Roman Digest, the primary collection of Roman legal rulings.</note> on the action of purchase. The laws *Yields* and *After Completion* in the same title of the <term>Code</term><note>Original: "C. eo. tit." referring to the Codex Justinianus.</note> are also in agreement.

<term>Covarrubias</term>, in his 14th corollary in the place cited, says that perhaps the buyer, in the case of this conclusion, is bound to pay the seller not only the price of the thing bought, but also the profit, if any had been perceived from that price—even if the seller himself would have perceived no profit from that same price. However, that opinion is entirely improbable. For profit of that kind is not a yield of the thing itself, but a yield of <term>industry</term><note>Original: "industriæ." This refers to the human effort, skill, or business activity of the person using the money, rather than a natural growth of the object sold.</note>, as is clear from what was said in the matter of usury; therefore, it belongs to the buyer. This is confirmed because if a <term>depositary</term><note>Someone entrusted to hold money or property for another.</note> trades against the owner's will and makes a profit with the money he has on deposit, or a thief with the money he took by theft, or a usurer with the money he acquired through usury, the entire profit belongs to them. They are only bound to restore to the owners the principal money and any profit that the owners lost out on, or any damage that emerged, as was shown extensively in Disputation 327. Therefore, with much greater reason, the profit made from the price belongs to the buyer when the seller was not going to make any profit from that price. Indeed, even if the seller were going to make a profit, the entire profit still belongs to the buyer: because the seller, by his own fault, would have deprived himself of the use of that price, and the buyer was not an impediment to him such that he could not have traded if he wished.

Covarrubias, in the same 14th corollary, establishes this as the fifth conclusion: <margin>17</margin> When the seller has offered the sold item to the buyer, and the buyer was in <term>default</term><note>Original: "mora." A legal term for a failure to perform a duty at the proper time.</note> because he neither wanted to accept it nor pay the price according to the form of the contract, then the seller can offer him, if he wishes, the item and the yields perceived (or their value) and sue for <term>interest</term><note>Original: "interesse." This includes "lucrum cessans" (profit that ceased or was lost) and "damnum emergens" (actual damage incurred).</note> for the profit lost or the damage emerging because the price was not paid at the due time, when such interest exceeds the value of the yields. While this conclusion would be entirely true in my judgment if we were standing on <term>natural law</term> alone, it is certainly entirely false once the disposition of <term>human law</term> is considered—specifically the final law in the Digest on the risk and benefit of a sold thing, and the law *If Sterile* mentioned above. These laws, with which the Portuguese Ordinances (section 3, cited above) agree, were the ones we cited for the second and third conclusions. For if the laws do not grant the seller an action for "lost profit" or "emerging damage" external to the purchased thing when the seller has delivered the item but did not receive the price through the buyer's fault (but only grant the value of the yields, as the cited laws and conclusions 2 and 3 show), then they are certainly much less to be thought to grant that action when the seller has not yet delivered the item. <term>Angelus</term><note>Angelus de Ubaldis (1328–1400), a renowned Italian jurist.</note>, citing those two laws under the entry "usury," thinks that in the <term>court of conscience</term><note>The "internal forum" or moral/spiritual judgment, as opposed to a legal courtroom.</note> the buyer is held to the interest of lost profit and emerging damage—and so is any other promisor of a thing when profit ceased because the promises were not kept, and for that reason the person to whom it was promised did not provide for himself from elsewhere. I think, however, that this is false in a contract of buying and selling because of that disposition of human law regarding this contract. Indeed, civil laws are not easily to be condemned as unjust in the court of conscience. Therefore, since the power resides in the Sovereign to arrange matters

<column-break/>

concerning the very frequent and highly necessary contract of buying and selling in order to remove disputes and difficulties, and since all citizens enjoy that arrangement equally, and contracts are deemed to be celebrated according to the civil and canon laws passed concerning them, it follows certainly that those arrangements have no less force in the court of conscience than in the exterior court.

<margin>18</margin> Final conclusion: When nothing else was agreed between the contracting parties, the yields hanging from the purchased thing at the time of the contract—whether they were already ripe or not—always belong to the buyer as far as the value for which they would be appraised at the time of the contract. So says Covarrubias, Molina, and others. The reason is that "hanging fruits," which exist at the time of the contract, are considered as parts of the thing bought (as was said at the beginning of this disputation), and therefore they are bought for the money given along with the thing of which they were then already actually the yields. From this, I conclude that if a vineyard is bought after the fruit has been produced but before the vintage, and the yields are harvested by the seller (neither the seller offering the vineyard and demanding the price, nor the buyer asking for it and offering the price), then later in the month of January, when the buyer seeks it or the seller offers it, the price set must be reduced by the amount those hanging fruits were worth at the time the contract was celebrated. This is because those fruits are considered bought for a part of the price, and the buyer did not receive them, but the seller did. However, if the delivery were to happen in the following year, when equal yields were again hanging from the vineyard, nothing should be deducted from the price; nor, likewise, would the buyer be bound to pay the expenses for cultivating the vineyard up to that time.

### DISPUTATION 369.

->*S U M M A R Y*<-

1 *If there are multiple buyers of the same thing not yet delivered to anyone, the one who is first in time is to be preferred.*
2 *The rule of law, "he who is first in time is stronger in right," and how it should be understood.*
3 *The buyer to whom the sold thing is first delivered is to be preferred over the others, even if the others are prior in time. See note 7 for a clarification.*
4 *Ownership is not regularly transferred by a naked contract of sale unless delivery follows.*
5 *Buyers of the same thing to whom it was not delivered have a personal action against the seller for "interest" (damages).*
6 *A person selling the same thing to two people falls under the penalty for fraud.*
8 *A later buyer who paid the price and had the thing delivered to him is preferred over other buyers who did not pay the price, even if the thing was delivered to them.*
9 *The name "delivery" also applies to that which is done through a "fictional" or symbolic act.*

He also introduces the rules of priority when a seller fraudulently sells the same item to multiple buyers, emphasizing the legal weight of delivery over a mere contract.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of contracts, specifically transitioning into Disputation 369, which addresses the legal conflicts that arise when a seller sells the same item to multiple buyers and the criteria for determining who has the rightful claim to ownership.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 369

<margin>10</margin> When the delivery of the same thing is made to multiple buyers, in cases of doubt, it is presumed to have been made to the first buyer.
<margin>11</margin> Whoever first acquires **ownership** of a thing through **delivery**, or a **right in the thing** through a **mortgage**, is preferred in any contract over all others who have obtained neither ownership nor a right in the thing.
<margin>12</margin> Ownership of property is acquired immediately for churches or pious places at the time of the contract, without any other delivery.
<margin>13</margin> Whether a Prince transfers ownership immediately, without other delivery, in contracts celebrated by him.
<margin>14</margin> One holding a **mortgage** on a thing is preferred over all others to whom the thing was delivered.
<margin>15</margin> In what case a prior buyer can legally reclaim a thing bought from a later buyer.
<margin>16</margin> A later buyer is preferred over a previous one, even if the first sale was confirmed by an oath.

<margin>1</margin> Consequently, we must examine the proposal at hand. It is certainly established that when the item has been delivered to none of the buyers, and none has a privilege to acquire ownership without delivery (according to what we shall set forth below), nor has acquired a **right in the thing**—because the item was subject to a mortgage as security for the sales contract—the one to whom the thing was first sold is to be preferred over the others.

<margin>2</margin> For it is then that the legal rule applies: *he who is first in time is stronger in right* <note>Original: "qui prior est tempore, potior est iure." A fundamental principle of Roman and Canon law regarding competing claims.</note>, as found in the <term>Rules of Law</term><note>The "Regulae Iuris" are a collection of legal maxims at the end of the Liber Sextus of the Decretals.</note> in Book 6. This is expressly arranged in Law 7, Title 7, Part 7, following the Law *In Operis* in the <term>Digest</term><note>Original: "ff. locati." The Digest (Pandects) is a major part of the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Iuris Civilis).</note> regarding hiring, which arranges the same for a contract of leasing. <term>Covarrubias</term> and <term>Antonio Gómez</term> affirm that this same rule applies in leasing contracts, citing the decisions of the Rota. This, however, is to be understood when a specific, individual thing is sold to many people, to each in its entirety: because the one who first acquired the right to it individually should be preferred in its delivery and the completion of the contract. However, when indeterminate things are sold to different people as a class, one should follow what will be said in Disputation 36 regarding the order of restitution.

<margin>3</margin> Although the thing may have been sold to many in such a way that none of the others had acquired ownership or a **right in the thing**, then the one to whom it was delivered, and who acquired ownership through that delivery, will be preferred over the others—even if the sales contract had been celebrated earlier with the others. This is held in the Law *Quoties* in the <term>Code</term><note>Original: "C. de rei vend." The Codex Justinianus, another part of the Body of Civil Law.</note> on the sale of property, and several other laws in the Code and Digest. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias and Antonio Gómez report and follow. The reason is what we handed down in Disputation 2: namely, that by a "naked" or bare contract of sale, or any other, ownership is not regularly transferred unless **delivery** follows. This is clear from the Law *Traditionibus* in the Code and from the section *Per Traditionem* in the <term>Institutes</term><note>The "Institutes" were a textbook for first-year law students in the Roman Empire, later becoming law.</note> on the division of things. Likewise, a **right in the thing** is not acquired unless the item itself is simultaneously subjected to a mortgage to secure the contract. Therefore, since a buyer—by the sole contract of purchase—acquires neither ownership nor a right in the thing, but only a **right to**

<column-break/>

the thing, and likewise since no **real action** <note>An "actio in rem," a legal claim directed at the object itself regardless of who holds it.</note> regarding the thing itself arises from that contract (no matter whose hands it comes into), but only a **personal action** against the person of the seller, it follows that if the same thing is later sold and delivered to another, this other person is to be preferred in the sales contract over the other buyers. He should obtain the thing because, through the sale followed by delivery, he acquired a **right in the thing** and full ownership, with the prior sales being no obstacle. There remains, however, for the other buyers a personal action against the seller for their **interest** <note>Original: "ad interesse." This refers to legal damages—compensating the party for what they lost because the contract wasn't fulfilled.</note>; that is, that he should not only restore the price, if he had received any, but also as much as it was in each buyer's interest for the thing to be delivered to them and for them to be established as its owner at the proper time. This is held in the Code and the <term>Ordinances of Portugal</term><note>Original: "Lusit. ord." referring to the Manueline or Philippine Ordinances, the law of the land in Portugal at the time.</note>.

<margin>6</margin> Whoever sells one and the same thing to two people falls under the penalty for **falsification** <note>Original: "pœna falsi."</note>, which is deportation/exile, as held in the Digest. The same is arranged in the <term>Siete Partidas</term><note>Original: "p. 7" referring to the 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note>, which, however, seems to require that the seller has received a price from both buyers. The specific penalties incurred in Portugal are found in Book 5 of the Ordinances.

<margin>7</margin> However, several things must be observed here regarding the aforesaid. The first is: since in a contract of purchase and sale, for the buyer to acquire ownership of the thing bought, it is not enough for the contract to have preceded and the delivery to have followed, but it is further necessary for the buyer to pay the price, or offer it, or for the seller to accept it as paid (as we showed in Disputation 33). It follows that even if the sold item has been delivered to one of the buyers, if he has neither paid nor offered the price, nor has the seller accepted it as paid, he is not to be preferred over the prior buyers of the same thing. This is because he has not acquired ownership or a right in it. Instead, the prior buyers are to be preferred, even if he has already alienated the thing by sale or any other title and delivered it: for ownership always remains with the first seller. This is clearly hinted at in the Code and the Institutes.

<margin>8</margin> It is added that if the thing is delivered to a later buyer and he pays the price, he is to be preferred over earlier buyers if they did not pay the price—even if the thing had been delivered to them. The other cited laws agree, and the common opinion of the doctors affirms this: because the later buyer acquired ownership of that thing, whereas the earlier ones did not.

<margin>9</margin> Second: by the name of **delivery** in the proposed matter, even that which is done through a **fictitious act** <note>A legal fiction or symbolic delivery, such as handing over the keys to a house rather than the house itself.</note> is understood. We discussed in Disputation 13 which fictitious acts constitute delivery and possession. Therefore, if the sold thing is delivered to a later buyer by a fictitious pact and he pays the price, he is preferred over earlier buyers to whom delivery was not made, or who did not pay the price, even if a true delivery was made to them. The reason is that delivery through a fictitious act suffices to acquire ownership and possession. Thus says Antonio Gómez, following Bartolus and others.

<margin>10</margin> Third: In a case of doubt as to which of the buyers the delivery was made...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the priority of rights when a seller has entered into contracts with multiple parties for the same item. It focuses on the legal weight of delivery (traditio) and the special privileges afforded to the Church and the State.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

is made first, it is presumed to have been done for the benefit of the first buyer. Thus says Covarruvias with others, whom he cites in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 19, number 6.

<margin>11</margin>
**Fourth.** What has been said holds true not only in a contract of sale, but also in any other contract, whether it be **onerous** <note>A contract where both parties give and receive something of value, like an exchange.</note> such as a barter, or **lucrative** <note>A contract where one party benefits without providing payment, like a gift.</note> such as a donation. For the person who first acquires **ownership** through **delivery** <note>original: "traditionem" – the physical or legal transfer of a thing.</note>, or a **right in the thing** through a **mortgage**, is always preferred over others who have obtained neither ownership nor a right in the thing, whether those others first acquired a "right to the thing" through a similar or different contract. This is gathered from the law *Quoties*, the final paragraph in the Code *on the sale of a thing*, and from the law *Si ancillam* in the Digest *on actions for purchase*, and from other legal authorities. Antonio Gómez affirms this along with the common opinion of the doctors, which he relates in the cited number 20. However, for a thing to be reclaimed from prior creditors as if it were alienated in fraud of them, it matters greatly whether the subsequent person acquired ownership of it by an **onerous** or **lucrative** title, as we shall soon discuss.

<margin>12</margin>
**Fifth.** When something is donated or sold to **Churches**, monasteries, cities, for the redemption of captives, to hospitals, or other **pious places**, they acquire ownership of it immediately. A **real action** <note>A legal right to claim the physical object itself, rather than just a claim for damages against a person.</note> is granted to them as a special privilege according to the final law in the Code *on the most sacred Churches*. Consequently, if something is donated or sold to them, they are preferred over any other buyer to whom delivery was made after that donation or sale, whether the contract with that other person was celebrated before or after. The reason is clear: because the Church, city, or other entity enjoying this privilege would have acquired ownership and a **right in the thing** first. Thus say Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 19, number 2; Antonio Gómez as cited above; and the doctors generally. He observes, however, that through a mere **promise** or a **vow** to donate to the Church in the future, the Church does not acquire ownership nor a right in the thing, but only a "right to the thing." This is because such an act is not a donation, but a promise to donate. For that reason, if the same thing promised by vow is later alienated and delivered to another, the Church would not be preferred over them. He also observes that **individual clergy** do not enjoy this privilege, only the Churches themselves. Therefore, if something is donated or sold to individual clerics, they will not be preferred over others in that manner. Furthermore, when the Church itself donates or sells something, the buyer does not enjoy this privilege, but is treated just as if they had bought from a layman. Thus say Covarruvias as cited above, number 4, and Antonio Gómez as cited above, extension 6, and others whom they cite, regardless of what Hostiensis and certain others have said to the contrary without a legitimate reason.

<margin>13</margin>
Regarding things **alienated by a Prince** by onerous or lucrative title—specifically whether ownership is acquired before delivery, and thus whether the one to whom they are alienated should be preferred over others to whom delivery has not been made—read what was said in Disputation 3.

**Sixth.** Since by the very fact that a thing is subjected to a **mortgage** for someone, that person acquires a **right in that thing**, it follows that whoever was first in the mortgage for the fulfillment of the contract is to be preferred over others to <margin>14</margin> whom the thing was delivered later. Thus, if a thing is sold to one person and simultaneously subjected to a mortgage as security for the contract, even if it is later sold and delivered to another who pays the price, that first buyer to whom the thing was mortgaged is to be preferred. Thus say Covarruvias as cited above, number 7, and Antonio Gómez

<column-break/>

in the cited number 20, along with the doctors generally, arguing from the text in the law *Si creditor*, final paragraph of the Digest *on the sale of pledges*.

<margin>15</margin>
**Seventh.** When a subsequent buyer was **aware** of a prior sale, then, even if delivery was made to them and they paid the price, the prior buyer can **evict** <note>Legally reclaim or recover.</note> that thing from them as having been alienated in fraud of their rights. It is otherwise, however, if the subsequent buyer bought it in **good faith**, being ignorant of the prior sale. The exact same thing must be said if a subsequent creditor acquired the thing by any other **onerous title**. But if they acquired the thing by a **lucrative title**, such as through a donation, or because the thing was given to a daughter as a dowry and her husband has now died without surviving children from that marriage, or if something was donated to a daughter for her wedding and neither the wife nor children from that marriage survive—then the person to whom the thing was first sold will be able to evict it, as if alienated in fraud of them, even if the person to whom it was delivered received it in good faith, not knowing it had been sold before. Nevertheless, one who received a thing in fraud of creditors in the aforementioned ways is not bound in **conscience** or in the **external court** to hand over the thing, unless the prior creditors seek it within a **year** from the time they knew that the alienation was made in fraud of them. For if they never demand it, or if they seek it after a year has passed from such knowledge, the thing belongs to the one who received it in fraud of them, both in conscience and in the external court. All these points are established from what was said extensively in Disputation 328. Read also Covarruvias as cited above, number 5; Antonio Gómez at number 20, limitation 2; and the doctors they cite.

<margin>16</margin>
**Eighth.** What has been said so far is to be understood even if the prior sale was confirmed by an **oath**, while the subsequent sale (which includes delivery and payment of the price) was not. For since an oath does not cause the prior buyer to acquire ownership or a right in the thing, nor does it act as an impediment to the subsequent buyer acquiring ownership through sale, delivery, and payment of the price, it follows indeed that although the seller **sins gravely** by selling the same thing a second time and rendering himself unable to fulfill the oath, nonetheless the things said so far have no less force than if the prior sale had not been confirmed by oath. Thus say Covarruvias in his *Epitome*, part 1, chapter 5, number 9, and Antonio Gómez in the cited number 20, limitation 7, along with others they cite.

<margin>1</margin> **W**e must next discuss the **retraction** of things bought and sold. Legal experts call it <term>retraction</term> <note>Latin: *retractus*. This refers to the "right of first refusal" or "legal redemption," where a relative can step into a buyer's shoes to keep property in the family.</note> when someone, by a privilege, law, or other previously granted reason, takes back a thing sold to another for the same price at which they had bought it. This is because the one "retracting" has the right to be preferred for the purchase of that thing at the same price, regardless of the fact that it has already been sold and delivered to another who has already paid the price. Retraction can also occur in a similar way in contracts of leasing and hiring, and in other similar cases, when someone has the right to be preferred over others in the leasing of someone's property, or in receiving it as an <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of long-term lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent.</note> for the same payment, or in other similar matters.

<margin>2</margin> By the law of Castile... <note>referencing various Spanish legal codes including the Laws of Toro and the New Collection</note> ...it is granted to blood relatives up to the fourth degree <note>Counting generations back to a common ancestor and then down to the relative.</note> that within nine days from the moment a sale is celebrated and perfected, they may retract for the same price an **estate**—that is, a property—sold by one of their blood relatives, provided it belongs to the seller's patrimony; that is, it was delivered or left to them by their father or mother, or had come to them from one of their grandfathers or great-grandfathers. The words of Law 7 in the *New Collection* are these:

> "Every man who wishes to sell an estate of patrimony or ancestry <note>original Spanish: "abolengo" – property inherited from a grandfather.</note>, and anyone of that ancestry wishes to buy it for the same amount [as offered by another], etc."

And in explaining this same point, Law 15 following it adds:

> "Nor can they take back for the same price goods that were sold in such a way, except when such goods were sold by persons who had inherited them from their ancestry or from their patrimony, and those who had so inherited them were the ones selling them."

Behold in which goods alone the retraction by <term>right of blood</term> <note>original: "iure sanguinis"</note> has a place in this Kingdom. For it must be an "estate," that is, a property, acquired from the side of the father or the mother of the seller, or from one of the previous ancestors, not by an **onerous title** <note>A contract where something is given in exchange for something else, like a purchase or trade.</note> such as purchase or exchange, but by succession.

These matters, however, must be explained more fully. And first, observe that not just any blood relative of the seller up to the fourth degree has the right of retraction, but only those who descend from the ancestor from whom such a property was first derived. For example, if someone buys a property and leaves it to his son, who then sells it to a stranger, then the brother and other collateral relatives of the first possessor do not have the right of retraction; only the descendants of the first possessor, blood relatives of the seller up to the fourth degree, whether they be children, or grandchildren, or great-grandchildren, or great-great-grandchildren of the first possessor. This is the opinion of Antonio Gómez on the laws of Toro... and it is clearly evident from the words of those two laws cited a little earlier: for the one who ought to have the right of retraction must be "of that ancestry" of the first possessor—that is, descending from him.

<margin>3</margin> Nevertheless, for the right of retraction, it is not necessary that the property belonged to both the father and the grandfather of the seller; it is enough that it descended to the seller from the father or from the grandfather, whether by virtue of a division of goods among children or grandchildren, or as a "special gift" <note>original: "melioratio"</note>, or by a legacy, or by some other title as a son. So says Antonio Gómez in the cited place... and others whom he cites. But Antonio Gómez seems to require that the thing remained with the grandfather or...

->Ludovico Molina on Contracts<-

or from the father. I believe, however, that if he had given that property to a son or grandson while he was still living—perhaps for the purpose of taking holy orders, as a wedding gift, as a dowry for a daughter or granddaughter, or some other similar gift—and if that descendant sold it while the original owner was still alive, then the blood relatives descending from that same first owner would have the <term>right of retraction<note>The legal right of a family member to step into a sale and purchase ancestral property sold to a stranger for the same price.</note></term>. This is because such property is to be counted as part of the <term>patrimony<note>Inherited family estate, often subject to special protections to keep it within the lineage.</note></term> derived from that ancestor. And since, as a rule, at the time of such an ancestor's death, this property must either be brought into the general account of the estate or be accepted as a <term>legitime<note>The portion of an estate that a person is legally required to leave to their heirs.</note></term> or an <term>improvement<note>original: "melioratio"; a legal mechanism allowing a parent to give a larger share of the inheritance to one specific child.</note></term>, it should be regarded as a legacy or a pre-legacy in the division of the deceased’s goods. Ultimately, this is because we must stand by the intent of those laws rather than their mere words. 

If, however, the first owner were to sell or donate it before his death to someone who was not among the descendants, and that person later sold it, the right of retraction would not apply. This is clearly evident from the words of the two laws cited, joined with the principle of Law 15, and is affirmed by the cited doctors; nonetheless, there was once no small controversy on this matter in the <term>Chancery of Valladolid<note>original: "Cancellaria Pinciana"; one of the highest appellate courts in the Spanish Empire.</note></term>. If, however, a patrimonial item were sold once to an outsider (without the nearest blood relative retracting it) or exchanged or donated, and it later returned to the owner in whose hands it was patrimonial before such an alienation, it does not become patrimonial again upon its return. By the very fact that it ceased to be patrimonial when held by the outsider, that lost quality is not restored. This is the view of Antonio Gómez on Law 70 of Toro, number 34, following various laws which he cites.

<margin>4</margin>
Antonio Gómez in the place cited, number 4, and Gutiérrez in *Practicarum Quaestionum*, book 2, question 155, as well as the more common opinion which Gutiérrez reports, argue with several points that <term>natural descendants<note>Children born of a stable relationship between unmarried parents, who held more legal rights than "spurii."</note></term> have the right of retraction. Their opinion is pleasing, especially since in this kingdom they succeed to the nobility of the father, as was seen in Disputation 170. On the other hand, <term>illegitimate children<note>original: "spurij"; children born of "shameful" or prohibited unions (e.g., incestuous or adulterous), who had fewer legal rights than "natural" children.</note></term> do not have the right of retraction, as these same authors and most others affirm. If, however, they have been legitimized by a decree of the prince, they are born into the right of retraction, as was said with Covarruvias and others cited at the end of Disputation 173; Gutiérrez affirms the same in the cited question. It would be otherwise if a person were granted a general dispensation that did not specifically address this right, as is clear from what was said in the most recently cited disputation.

<margin>5</margin>
<insert>Those who are disinherited</insert> also have the right of retraction, as do those who have renounced their succession to their parents' goods with a just cause. This is because they are not deemed to have renounced the privilege of retraction, which belongs to them by <term>right of blood<note>original: "iure sanguinis"; a right inherent in one's biological lineage regardless of inheritance status.</note></term> out of a certain equity. So says Antonio Gómez in the same place, numbers 5 and 6.

<margin>6</margin>
Members of the <insert>clergy</insert> also enjoy the privilege of retraction both actively and passively. That is, they can retract property just as if they were laypeople, and property of their ancestors which they themselves have sold can be retracted by their relatives. The most powerful reason is that civil laws, which do not conflict with clerical immunity, are common to both the clergy and the laity, as was stated in Disputation 31, the final conclusion, and Disputation 364. Antonio Gómez (as above, number 7) and Gutiérrez (in the cited place, question 156, where he treats the matter extensively and brings forward many other foundations) agree; our reason, however, is the most powerful and broadly applicable, as do many others whom they cite.

Although Law 13, Title 10, Book 3 of the *Fuero Real*, which is Law 7

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
of Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, granted the right of retraction only to the relative closest in degree, and if that person was unwilling or unable to retract, it denied the right to the seller's other blood relatives; nonetheless, Law 73 of Toro, which is Law 12 of the *New Collection*, later granted the right to blood relatives up to the fourth degree. This was done so that if those closer in degree were unwilling or unable to retract, those further away could do so, provided it was within the same period of nine days from the completion of the sales contract. When, however, two or more people of equal degree approach to retract, the property must be divided among them, and the elder is not preferred over the younger. This is held in the cited Law 7 of the *New Collection*. However, when someone sells a paternal estate, if the seller has a son and also a brother (who is the son of the first owner), and both approach to retract, the son of the seller is preferred over the seller's brother (the uncle of said son). This is held in Law 8 at the end of Title 11 of the *New Collection*.

<margin>Doubt 7</margin>
It is <insert>doubtful</insert> if the relative who is closest in degree should die after a sale has been made, but before the nine days granted for retraction have elapsed, leaving an outside heir who otherwise would not have the right of retraction, whether the right of retraction belongs to such an heir in the name and place of the deceased. The answer must be in the negative. This is because that privilege is purely personal, belonging by right of blood, and it expires with the person of the deceased and does not pass to their heirs. So says Antonio Gómez on Law 70 of Toro, number 8.

<margin>Decision</margin>
He adds, however, that if the deceased had already initiated the legal claim before death, the right and the action pass to the heir. This is based on the argument of the text in the law *Posthumus*, the final section, and the following law in the Digest *On Inofficious Wills*. There it is held that if someone dies before preparing a complaint against an undutiful will, they do not transmit it to the heir; but if they die after the complaint has been prepared through the <term>joinder of issue<note>original: "litis contestationem"; the formal start of a trial where the issues are defined.</note></term>, they do transmit it. This is also supported by the argument of the single law in the Code *On the Crimes of the Deceased*, where it says that if a wrongdoer dies after the issue has been joined against him, the action for the full amount is available against his heirs. Faber and Bartolus, cited by Antonio Gómez, agree. For the same reason, a closer blood relative cannot cede the right of retraction to a third party, as Antonio Gómez joins with many others in saying there. This is clearly confirmed by Law 7, Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which requires that if a closer relative attempts a retraction, he must be compelled to swear whether he wants the property for himself and is using no other fraud. If he cannot attempt a retraction for the purpose of selling or handing the property over to another, much less can he cede his right to another.

<margin>Doubt 8</margin>
It is <insert>doubtful</insert> furthermore, if a closer relative enters a monastery capable of owning property and makes his profession there, whether the monastery can retract in the place of the religious person. The answer must be in the negative, for the same reason:

<margin>Decision</margin>
because the personal right of the monk does not pass to the monastery. Moreover, that monk would no longer be wanting the estate for himself, but for the monastery, which the cited Law 7 denies to a blood relative. Thus says Antonio Gómez, as above, number 9. Observe, however, that if he were still a novice, the right of retraction would belong to him so that he might acquire the property of his ancestors for himself while he is still capable of doing so, even if he intends to leave it later to the monastery or anyone else. By this same reasoning, the right of retraction belongs to our members <note>Molina refers here to his own order, the Jesuits.</note> after their novitiate and after taking their three vows...

<summary>This page discusses the legal eligibility for the 'right of retraction,' clarifying that while natural children, disinherited heirs, and clerics may exercise it, the right is a personal 'blood right' that cannot be easily transferred to outside heirs or monasteries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Disputation 37 regarding the "right of retraction"—the legal privilege of a family to reclaim ancestral property sold to outsiders—specifically looking at how this applies to members of religious orders, heirs, and judicial officials.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 37

customary, for as long as they have not yet made their profession or become <term>coadjutors<note>In the Jesuit order, a coadjutor is a member who has taken final vows but is not a "professed" father of the four vows.</note></term>. During this time, they retain the right of succession and are capable of owning property, according to the points explained at length in Disputation 37. However, after they have made their profession or become coadjutors, since neither they themselves nor the monastery (nor anyone else in their place) are capable of owning such property, it is established that the right of retraction cannot apply to them.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
There is likewise a doubt: if a monastery sells a piece of land belonging to someone who entered the order—land which had belonged to his ancestors—does the right of retraction apply to the closest blood relative of that religious person? The answer must be in the negative, following Antonio Gómez (as cited above, number 10). This is because that property no longer belongs to the religious person, but to the monastery to which it passed. When property has passed to a third party and that party sells it, the right of retraction does not apply, as is expressly stated in the <term>New Collection<note>original: "novae collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compendium of Spanish law.</note></term> (Book 1, Title 11, Law 5). However, if the goods of a novice were sold, or those of a member of our Society who had not yet made his profession or become a coadjutor, then the right of retraction would apply—unless that novice or religious brother had previously donated it to someone or exchanged it for something else, and that person then sold it. For in cases of exchange or donation, the right of retraction does not apply, as is clear from the cited laws 7 and 15.

<margin>Question 10</margin>
### 10 There is a further doubt: if the closest blood relative in degree is the heir to the seller of ancestral property, and the seller dies within the nine-day window for retraction, can such an heir retract that property? The side that says no can be argued as follows: First, because an heir cannot act against the deed of the deceased, even if the deceased bequeathed or alienated the heir's own property, as was partially stated in Disputation 196; therefore, he cannot retract a property sold by the deceased. Second, because such an heir is held liable to the buyer for <term>eviction<note>The legal duty of a seller (or their heir) to compensate a buyer if they lose the property due to a prior legal claim.</note></term> regarding that land in place of the deceased. Since actions that were valid against the deceased also pass to the heir, any heir who is liable for the eviction of a thing is barred by a legal exception from acting to obtain it, as is established in the law regarding "claimants" in the <term>Digest<note>original: "ff. de exceptionib."; a reference to the Roman Law *Pandects* or *Digest*.</note></term> and other legal sources. Nevertheless, the contrary must be affirmed along with Antonio Gómez (number 10), Gutierrez (Practical Questions, question 349), Pinelo (On the Goods of Mothers, part 3, number 79), and others whom they cite. The reason is that by retracting a thing sold by the deceased, one does not go against the deed and alienation of the deceased by disapproving of it; rather, it is confirmed by demanding the privilege of the law so that the heir himself is substituted in place of the first buyer to complete the contract. Thus, the first argument to the contrary fails. The second also fails: for eviction has no place in a retraction, since the thing is not "evicted" as if the seller had no right to sell it; rather, the second buyer is to be subrogated by legal privilege. Therefore, the premise of the second argument must be denied. Similarly for its proof: for even if the seller were alive, that action would not belong to the first buyer against him in a way that could pass to the heir. Gutierrez rightly limits this opinion to cases where the seller had promised the property was "safe from retraction"; in that case, since the seller would be liable for damages if the property were retracted, the heir is bound to the same burden and therefore could not retract it.

### 11 There is a further doubt whether a judge, who cannot buy 

<column-break/>

or enter into other contracts within the place of his jurisdiction, or a tutor and curator, who cannot buy the property of a minor committed to them, and others like them, might nevertheless be able to exercise the right of retraction. The answer must be in the affirmative, with Antonio Gómez (above, number 12). This is because these people are not the primary buyers; they are merely substituted in the place of the primary buyers after a price has been established by those against whom there is no sinister suspicion. Thus, others would have contracted, and these individuals merely step in to pay the price, with no new contract being initiated.

<margin>12</margin>
<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
### 12 Next, there is a doubt: if someone sells such a thing to a more distant relative, can a closer relative retract it? Although there have been some who answered in the negative, the more common and true opinion is that one can retract it in this Kingdom of Castile. This is the view of Antonio Gómez (number 13), Gutierrez (Practical Questions, volume 2, question 150), and others whom they cite. Indeed, the law (Law 7, Title 11, and Law 5 of the New Collection) says: <gloss>Every man who wishes to sell an inheritance from his father’s or grandfather’s side <note>original Spanish: "Todo hombre que heredada de patrimonio o abolengo quifiere vender"</note></gloss> (making no distinction whether to a relative or a stranger), and it immediately grants the right of retraction to the closer relative alone, denying it to the more distant one, even if the closer one does not wish to retract. Although later, in Law 12, they extend the retraction to more distant relatives in the event that the closer ones cannot or will not retract. Therefore, the intent of those laws was not only that the land should not leave the family of the first possessor, but also that it should come to the closest relative alone, if he were able and willing to buy it.

<margin>13</margin>
<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
### 13 There is also a doubt: if someone has sold to one of the relatives of a certain degree, whether a relative of the same degree can also retract, according to the cited Law 7, which states: <gloss>if two or more want it, and they are in the same degree of kinship, they shall share it between them. <note>original Spanish: "X si dos, o mas, la quifieren, si son en igual grado de prenterso, portanlo entre si."</note></gloss> Those who answer in the affirmative do so based on Antonio Gómez (number 13) and certain others whom Gutierrez (question 151) cites and follows; Antonio Gómez gave this advice in a question of fact. One should not depart from this opinion, even though it may seem harsh to us.

<margin>14</margin>
### 14 Whether the closest relative should be asked by a judge whether he wishes to retract, or whether he cannot be compelled to answer and choose one side or the other before the term of nine days has elapsed. Antonio Gómez (number 14) rightly answers in the negative, because the law grants him that entire time for deliberating and retracting, which the judge cannot shorten. He adds, however, that if he once answers that he does not wish to retract, he cannot retract afterward, because he is considered to have waived his right. This is proved by the final law (paragraph "but lest this") in the Code regarding <term>emphyteusis<note>A type of perpetual lease of land.</note></term>, and is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion which Antonio Gómez cites there. In number 21, Antonio Gómez correctly adds that if the closer relatives do not wish to declare whether they intend to retract before the deadline, the more distant relatives can then retract in that event and under the condition that the closer ones do not retract, based on the argument of the final law in the Code "because to be admitted." Also, in number 26, he adds that even if a more distant relative retracts in the presence of a closer relative while the closer one remains silent, the closer one can nonetheless still retract, because by that silence he is not deemed to have waived his right.
