<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "right of retraction" (the right of a family member to buy back ancestral land sold to a third party). It specifically addresses complex scenarios: bundled sales of different types of property, mixed payments of cash and goods, and property seized for debt.</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...one without the others: however, when they are sold at distinct prices, so that it is understood at what price each one is sold, a relative can reclaim one without the other or others. Both points are held in Law 71 of Toro, which is Law 10, Title 11, [and] Law 5 of the <term>New Collection<note>original: "nouæ collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, the 16th-century Spanish legal code.</note></term>.

<margin>Doubt 16</margin>
The doubt is: if a <term>patrimonial property<note>Ancestral family land or goods that have been passed down through generations, subject to the family's right of first refusal.</note></term> is sold together with another non-patrimonial property for a single price, can the patrimonial property be reclaimed?

<margin>Decision</margin>
It must be answered in the affirmative, following Antonio Gómez (as cited above, number 15), Gutierrez (Book 2, *Practical Questions*, question 162), Tiraquellus, and many others whom Gutierrez cites. This applies not only when both items were sold together in that manner fraudulently to prevent the patrimonial item from being reclaimed—a point on which everyone agrees—but even when it was done without fraud. Gutierrez, along with Tiraquellus, proves this from the chapter *Constitutus* regarding the restoration of the whole, where retraction is admitted for only one part of something that was sold as a whole for a single price; Antonio Gómez also cites many other laws for this. Furthermore, when many patrimonial items are sold together for a single price, the closest blood relative is entitled to reclaim them all. It is not surprising, then, that the cited law of Castile did not permit the retraction of one item without the others in that event. However, when one patrimonial item is sold together with others in which the right of retraction does not apply for a single price, it would be unreasonable to force the relative to buy everything; therefore, since it is not in the relative's power to reclaim the non-patrimonial items, he must be left free to reclaim only the patrimonial one. This is consistent with various Civil and Canon Laws. In such a case, it must be estimated by the judge’s discretion how much of that price should correspond to the patrimonial item, and it must be reclaimed at that price. If the estimation cannot be finished within the nine days granted for retraction, Gutierrez says it is enough to offer what the reclaimer calculates should be paid, while simultaneously offering suitable <term>guarantors<note>original: "fideiussores"; individuals who legally guarantee that the payment will be made.</note></term> to ensure that if the appraised value is higher, it will be paid immediately.

<margin>Doubt 17</margin>
Connected to the previous doubt is another: if someone sells a patrimonial property for a certain price and another item together—for example, a patrimonial house for eighty gold coins and a horse—when should the transaction be judged a "sale" (allowing the right of retraction) where the value of the extra item must be appraised, and when is it a "barter" (where retraction does not apply)? As we stated in Disputation 336, in a case where the rights of a third party are involved, if the cash price exceeds the value of the other item (even by a small amount), it must be considered a sale. If, however, the value of the item exceeds the cash price, it must be considered a barter. When no excess is found on either side, one should stand by the words of the contracting parties, as was said in the cited disputation; Antonio Gómez (number 15) does not contradict this.

<margin>Doubt 18</margin>
The doubt is: if a patrimonial item is given <term>in satisfaction of a debt<note>original: "insolutum" or "datio in solutum"; a legal act where a debtor provides an asset instead of money to settle a debt.</note></term>, does the right of retraction apply? Gutierrez (question 357) disputes this copiously, citing doctors on both sides. Briefly, I believe it must be said that if the debt is monetary and the item is given in satisfaction—whether by the owner himself (which lawyers call a "voluntary giving") or by the authority of a judge after an execution against the debtor's goods and a sale at public auction (which they call a "necessary giving")—retraction 

<column-break/>

does apply: because it is a true sale for the money owed. Thus hold Gregorio López, Antonio Gómez, Gutierrez, and many others. The reason is that it is a true sale of the item for the money that was supposed to be paid. This is consistent with the law *Si praedium* in the Code, which states that such contracts (where something is given in satisfaction) hold the place of a sale. Even if the debt is not monetary, if such a patrimonial estate is sold by judge's authority in a public auction to satisfy the debt according to the item's value, the right of retraction applies—even if the buyer is the creditor himself who bid on it when no one else would give a higher price. This is expressly held in Law 70 of Toro, which is Law 9, Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which states: <note>The following is translated from the original Spanish</note> "The law of the forum, which speaks about the closest relative reclaiming a sold patrimonial thing for the same price, shall also have a place when it is sold in a public auction, even if it is by order of a Judge." The reason is clear: two contracts are occurring there. One is the formal sale of the item for a price (where there is no reason retraction should not apply); the other is the payment of the past debt from that price, which is a distinct and very different contract. However, when a patrimonial item is given in satisfaction for something that was not a monetary price—such as for a horse owed, for another field owed, or for certain measures of wheat owed—without a prior sale of that patrimonial estate, then retraction would not apply. This is because it would be a true <term>barter<note>original: "permutatio"</note></term>, in which (according to Law 7, Title 11) retraction has no place. I would say the same when a patrimonial item is given for something that is not a price, such as an "innominate contract" distinct from barter: for example, if a patrimonial estate were given for services rendered for which no price had been fixed. The reason is that retraction only applies in a sale. Nor is it true, as Gutierrez claims, that only barter is excepted from retraction; rather, in all the laws of Castile, retraction is granted *only* in the case of a sale. Since the right of retraction is against common law, it should not be extended further in Castile than the laws specifically grant. The mention of barter in the cited Law 7 is clearly not an "exception" (since nothing had been said before that would include barter), but rather an example and clarification that when a contract is not a sale, the right of retraction does not apply.

<margin>19</margin>
When a patrimonial estate is sold on credit, the right of retraction applies within nine days of the contract being finalized. However, the person reclaiming is not bound to pay the price within those nine days; it is enough if he pays it at the same deadline originally granted to the buyer. He is, however, bound to provide suitable guarantors before the judge within those nine days to ensure he will pay the price at that deadline. This is held in Law 72 of Toro, which is Law 11, Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*. On this matter, see Antonio Gómez (number 22).

<summary>This page explores the limits of the right of retraction in Spanish law, determining that it applies to ancestral property sold alongside other goods or seized for monetary debt, but does not apply to barters or exchanges for services.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "right of retraction," specifically focusing on the strict nine-day time limit within which a relative must exercise their right to buy back ancestral property sold to a third party.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 370.

Thus, nine days are granted for reclaiming property in this Kingdom, such that even if the person is a minor, a ward, or absent, and does not reclaim it within those days, they are not subsequently granted the <term>benefit of legal restoration<note>original: "beneficiū restitutionis in integrum"; a legal remedy where a person is restored to their original legal position, effectively undoing a deadline they missed.</note></term>, nor any cutting back or deduction of that time. However, a tutor or curator can reclaim it in the name of the minor within those nine days. This is expressly stated in Law 8, Title 11, Book 5 of the <term>New Collection<note>original: "nouæ collec."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish law.</note></term>. Although there have been those who thought a minor should be granted the benefit of legal restoration on other grounds, Gutierrez (in the passage cited above, question 159) refutes this extensively and correctly; it is also clearly against the cited Law 8. If the provision of this law were absent, legal restoration would indeed take place, as is clear from the chapter *Constitutus* regarding the restoration of the whole.

<margin>20th Question</margin>
There is a doubt as to whether the nine days granted for reclaiming property begin from the time the contract of sale is celebrated and perfected, or truly from the time of the <term>delivery<note>original: "traditionis"; the physical or legal transfer of the property from seller to buyer.</note></term> of the thing sold. Antonio Gómez (on Law 70 of Toro, numbers 16 and 17) judges that it begins not from the time the contract is celebrated, but from the time of delivery—and not through a fictional act, but through a true and natural act of delivery. He makes an exception unless the sale occurs at a public auction; for then he admits it begins from the time of the <term>final bid<note>original: "remate"; the moment an auction is finalized.</note></term> or the perfection of the sale, and one need not wait for the time of delivery, as is expressly held in Law 70 of Toro, which is Law 9, Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection. There, when discussing a sale in a public auction by judicial authority, after the words we just related from the same law, it is added: <term>the nine days provided by the law of the code are counted, in this case, from the day of the final bid.<note>original: "los nueve dias, que dispone la ley del fuero, se cuente en este caso desde el dia del remate."</note></term> In this same opinion, insofar as it is affirmed that the days must be counted from the time of delivery, others agree, whom the same Antonio Gómez and more extensively Gutierrez (Book 2, question 152) have cited.

They argue firstly because the right of retraction is granted by these laws so that property does not leave the lineage or family of the seller; but before delivery, the property is not said to be <term>alienated<note>original: "alienata"; legally transferred to another's ownership.</note></term>, and therefore does not leave the family, as is clear from the law *Alienatum* in the Digest regarding the significance of words, whose words are:
> That which still remains in the ownership of the seller is not properly called "alienated," though it is correctly called "sold."

This is confirmed because ownership of the thing sold passes to the buyer not from the time of sale, but from delivery, as is clear from the law *Traditionibus* in the Code regarding pacts and other laws, as has been said often in the preceding sections. Secondly, because if those days did not begin from the time of delivery, notice of the sale might not easily reach the relative who ought to reclaim it; rather, a sale might be made secretly by word alone, and this might be done by fraud so that notice would not reach the relative until after the nine days had elapsed. Since the knowledge of the relative is not strictly necessary for those nine days to count against him, relatives could easily be deluded and prevented from reclaiming, which it is not to be presumed the authors of the laws of retraction intended.

The contrary opinion is more common and accepted in practice, as Antonio Gómez does not deny. It is embraced by Covarruvias, Lassarte, Gutierrez, and many others, and is approved by us as well. This is because the Spanish laws that grant retraction within nine days often affirm that they are to be computed 

<column-break/>

from the consummated sale, and never from delivery; moreover, a sale is perfected by mutual consent before delivery, as was shown extensively in Disputation 337. One may read in Gutierrez (cited above) various Spanish laws whose words he weighs, which clearly echo this opinion.

<margin>21</margin>
The doubt is: when a contract of sale is suspended until a written deed is completed (according to what was said in the cited disputation), are those nine days to be considered as beginning from the time of mutual consent before the writing is finished? Gutierrez affirms this. To me, however, the contrary seems true; since the contract is not perfected until the deed is finished—indeed, it is suspended until the writing is completed, and it is within the rights of either party to withdraw from it—I do not see why those days should be considered to begin before the deed is finished. Antonio Gómez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 27) affirms they begin from the completion of the deed, although he refers back to what he said on Law 7 of Toro regarding retraction; in this, he seems somewhat inconsistent with himself, unless you say he also excepts that event: because when a public deed is finished, it could sufficiently come to the notice of the relatives, just as when a sale is perfected in a public auction.

If the first argument for the opinion of Antonio Gómez had any force, its author would have to concede that those days also begin from delivery through a fictional act, because a fictional act suffices for alienation, and indeed for acquiring possession along with ownership. Likewise, since alienation is not yet a fact before delivery when a sale is perfected in a public auction, it is clearly evident that the intent of the lawmakers of Castile was not that those days should not begin before the alienation of the patrimonial estate was consummated. Therefore, it must be said that although the intent of those legislators was to grant retraction so that, if relatives wished, the property would be retained in the family, they nevertheless did not grant it except within nine days from the consummation of the sale.

Regarding the second argument, it must be said that those nine days begin from a sale openly consummated or manifested, so that by the very manner of its consummation, it may come to the notice of others. Therefore, if a sale is made only between the contracting parties while others are ignorant of it, the days will not begin to run; and much less will they begin to run when the sale was consummated by the fraud of the parties so that it could not reach the ears of the relatives, as Gutierrez correctly says following Tiraquellus and others. And from this is solved the argument that can be constructed from the words of Law 9 related above (and I am surprised it was not constructed by authors of the contrary opinion). For when the law says, <term>"And the nine days provided by the law of the code are counted, in this case, from the day of the final bid,"<note>original: "Y los nueve dias, que dispone la ley del fuero se cuenten en este caso desde el dia del remate."</note></term> it is implied, by an argument from the opposite sense, that in other cases they are not to be computed from the consummated sale, but from delivery. Nevertheless, it must be said that because in that event the contract could not be celebrated in such a way that notice could not reach the relatives, for that reason it was added...

Molina concludes that the period starts when the sale is publicly finalized, provided there is no fraudulent secrecy to hide the deal from relatives.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina On Contracts

...added words intended to suggest that in other types of sales, unless they were openly consummated or publicly manifested after consummation, the days do not begin to count except from the time of that manifestation.

22 A doubt then arises as to whether the nine days granted for the <term>retraction<note>original: "retractum"; the legal right of a relative to step into the shoes of a buyer and reclaim family land by paying the sale price.</note></term> should be calculated from moment to moment—so that if the sale was perfected on Monday at three o'clock in the afternoon, the nine days would end on the following Wednesday at the same hour—or whether the days should be calculated from midnight to midnight. This latter method can be understood in two ways: either by counting the starting point <term>inclusively<note>original: "inclusiue"; including the day the event happened as "Day 1."</note></term>, so that in the proposed example the days would end at the stroke of midnight dividing Tuesday from Wednesday (according to the Roman custom of counting days, as found in the law *More Romanorum*); or by counting <term>exclusively<note>original: "exclusiue"; starting the count on the day after the event.</note></term> from the starting point, so that Monday is excluded and the days end at the stroke of midnight dividing Wednesday from Thursday.

The Gloss on the chapter *Statutum* regarding prebends (Book 6), which many authors embrace and whom Tiraqueau refers to and follows, judges that when prepositions such as "From," "Away from," or "Out of" are used to denote the starting point from which a calculation must be made—for example, "within nine days *from* the day of the sale"—the day of the starting point must be excluded. Thus, the nine following days are counted so that, in the proposed example, the time expires at the midnight dividing Wednesday from Thursday. These authors are led to this conclusion because these prepositions, by the property of speech, signify the exclusion of the starting point; it is the same as saying "within nine days *after* the day of the sale."

Following this doctrine, Gutierrez judges that the nine days granted for retraction in this Kingdom <note>The Kingdom of Spain.</note> should be calculated from the day of purchase exclusively, and he affirms this to be the more common opinion. He is led by no other foundation than the aforementioned doctrine and because Law 70 of Toro (which is Law 9, Title 11, Book 5 of the *New Collection*), dealing with sales in a public auction, says:

> And the nine days, which the law of the code provides, shall be counted in this case from the day of the conclusion of the auction. <note>original Spanish: "Y los nueue dias, que dispone la ley del fuero, se cuente en este caso desde el dia del remate."</note>

"Behold," he says, the law says "from the day" of the perfected sale, and therefore that day must be excluded from the calculation of the nine days. He believes that the preceding laws are explained by this law, even though the opposite might seem to be gathered from them. He could also have cited the older Law 15 of the same title (from Henry II), which states:

> Let them demand them from the day the sale was made up to nine days. <note>original Spanish: "Que los demanden desde el dia que la uenta fuere hecha hasta nueue dias."</note>

<margin>Decision.</margin> However, Antonio Gómez (on Law 70 of Toro, number 25), assuming it as certain that the day of the perfected purchase or the delivery made must be counted, only asks whether we are speaking of natural days (so that the nine days end at the midnight dividing Tuesday from Wednesday) or of days calculated from point to point (ending Wednesday at three in the afternoon). He embraces this second view, along with many others cited by Gutierrez. And this opinion is pleasing. First, because all time regularly—

<column-break/>

or where nothing else is gathered from the law—and every legal term and delay is calculated from moment to moment. Thus, under the name of any prescribed or granted day, twenty-four full hours are understood, starting inclusively from the moment of the starting point. For instance, if one says "from the day of purchase" or "from the day of election or sentence," it follows the ancient method of calculation. This is proven in the laws regarding minors, adultery, and appeals; the doctors affirm it there, and it matches the property of speech and the customary manner of counting. The starting point is not excluded when it is something divisible, such as a day of the month, a year, or another thing in which the part containing the event is considered in the calculation—such as a birth, an appeal, an election, or a purchase. Thus, we call a fever "tertian" or "quartan" when it returns from the third to the third day, or fourth to the fourth. 

In the matter we are discussing, there is another very effective argument which the authors of the contrary opinion do not easily resolve. For they concede that if the law says "within nine days from the consummated sale," the days must be calculated from the exact point of the consummated purchase. This is because the starting point to be excluded is not the *day* of the purchase, but the *purchase itself*, from whose point of consummation the nine-day period begins to run. Now, Law 7, Title 1, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which was the first law passed regarding retraction, says:

> If after it has been sold, up to nine days, he should come and give the price for which it was sold, let him have it. <note>original Spanish: "Si despues que fuere vendida hasta nueue dias viniere y diere el precio porque es vendida, ayala."</note>

Behold, it said "up to nine days *after* the consummated sale," and not "after the *day* of the sale" or "from the *day* of the sale." And Law 8 following, which was given by Henry II in the year 1473 (and is called the Law of Nieva because it was passed in that town), states:

> Therefore we declare, ordain, and command that the nine days contained in the said law of the code, for the nearest relative to redeem the sold inheritance, shall run against minors under twenty-five years of age, etc. And further: And let this prescription of the said nine days take place against them, and let the said law be kept to the letter. <note>original Spanish: "Porende declaramos... que los nueue dias contenidas en la dicha ley del fuero... corran contra los menores... y que a la letra se guarde la dicha ley."</note>

Gutierrez responds that these laws were later declared by Law 70 of Toro. But certainly, that law has no appearance of being a declaration or restriction of the preceding ones; nor was the law any different in that regard after that law than it was before. Furthermore, although the law itself restricts that disposition to that single event, saying:

> And the nine days, which the law of the code provides, shall be counted in this case from the day of the conclusion of the auction, <note>original Spanish: "Y los nueue dias... se cuenten en este caso desde el dia del remarte."</note>

certainly, in Spanish phrasing (and even in Latin), "from the day of the conclusion" is the same as "from the conclusion" itself; that is how anyone hearing the law understands it. Add to this that, according to the opinion of the doctors we are opposing, more than nine days would be granted in this Kingdom for retraction—the contrary of which the laws themselves proclaim and which is the common usage of speakers.

Observe, however, that if, due to the authority of the cited Gloss and the multitude of doctors who follow it, you see that it has been received by established custom elsewhere that the starting day is excluded, one must stand by that custom, which...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 37

...is the interpreter of the laws, and has the force of law. In the matter we are discussing, however, since the <term>doctors<note>In this context, "doctors" refers to "Doctors of Law"—the highly influential legal scholars whose commentaries shaped early modern European law.</note></term> of our time hold opposing views, and Gutierrez himself admits that there is no fixed definition of this matter and nothing in it is certain, it must be judged that there is no established custom requiring that specific day to be excluded.

<margin>23.</margin>
23. Furthermore, there is a doubt regarding the days granted for <term>retraction<note>original: "retrahendum"; the legal right of a kinsman to "retract" or buy back ancestral property sold to a stranger by a relative.</note></term>: when do they begin in a sale made under a <term>condition<note>A "conditional sale" is one where the transfer of ownership depends on a future event, such as "I will sell you this land if the ship arrives from India."</note></term> pending in the future? Do they begin from the moment the contract is celebrated, or rather from the moment the condition is fulfilled?

An argument can be made that they begin before the condition is fulfilled, immediately from the celebration of the contract. First, because when a judicial sentence is passed under a condition, the days for filing an appeal begin immediately from the delivery of the sentence and not from the moment the condition is fulfilled (as is established in Law 1, section *biduum*, of the <term>Digest<note>original: "ff."; the Digest of Justinian, a massive collection of Roman legal writings.</note></term> regarding when appeals should be made). Therefore, the same should apply to the days granted for retraction if a sale is made under a condition.

Second, because in conditional contracts, one looks at the time they were celebrated, not the time the condition was fulfilled (as held in Law 6, *filiusfamilias*, at the beginning, in the Digest on verbal obligations, and other laws). Indeed, a conditional contract is considered perfected immediately, as is clear in the Law *in cessante*, section *si ita res*, in the Digest on the risk and benefit of a sold thing; there, the <term>Gloss<note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval commentary on Roman law.</note></term> says that neither of the contracting parties may withdraw from the contract against the will of the other. Therefore, the days for retraction should be calculated from the time of celebration.

Third, because if the condition is fulfilled later, it "acts backward" <note>original: "retrotrahitur"; a legal fiction where a later event is treated as if it happened at an earlier date.</note> to the time the contract was celebrated, as we show in various laws on page 337. Therefore, every effect of that contract is retroactive; consequently, the relative would no longer be able to retract, because by the logic of this legal fiction, the nine-day window granted for retraction would have already passed. For these reasons, Guido Papa and certain others have embraced this side of the argument.

However, the contrary view—namely, that those days do not begin except from the moment the condition is fulfilled—is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Covarruvias, Antonio Gomez, and Gutierrez. We should embrace this view. The reason is that, as stated in Disputation 337, although a right in "hope" and an obligation arise from a conditional sale (so that neither party can withdraw while the condition is pending), the contract is not yet "perfected" <note>In legal terms, a "perfected" contract is one that is fully binding and complete in all its essential elements.</note> before the condition is met. Since the days for retraction do not begin except from a perfected sale, it follows that they must be calculated from the moment the condition is met, and not before.

To the first argument to the contrary: even if we grant the premise, the conclusion must be denied. This is because by the very fact that a sentence is passed under a condition, the judge begins to "burden" the party against whom it is delivered; for that reason, the period for appealing begins then (as the Gloss says on Law 3, section 1, on the word *experitur*). But nothing similar is found in the conditional sale of an ancestral estate.

The first part of the premise of the second argument is 

<column-break/>

true; but only once the condition is fulfilled, which is then retroactive by a legal fiction to the time the contract was celebrated. For instance, if a son under his father's authority contracted under a condition, and the condition is met after he has become independent, the acquisition still goes to the father. This is because, once the condition is met, the law looks at the time the contract was celebrated, not the time it was fulfilled. However, the second part of the premise must be denied when a condition is pending in the future and the sale is properly and expressly conditional. Law *neccessariò*, section *si ita res*, speaks of a necessary condition, not a pending future one. What the Gloss says there remains true, even for future pending conditions.

To the third argument: granting the first premise, the first conclusion must also be granted if we are speaking of every effect that is a "proper effect" of the contract. However, the right to retract after a perfected sale is not an effect of the sale itself, but a benefit and privilege of the law. This privilege is only considered granted when the sale is truly perfected in reality, not through a legal fiction of retroactivity. Therefore, the further silent conclusion must be denied.

Tiraqueau, in his work on both types of retraction, thinks the recorded doctrine should be limited: if the seller delivered the thing to the buyer <term>before<note>original: "ante impletam conditionem"</note></term> the condition was fulfilled, and the relative became aware of this delivery, then the time for retraction is considered to begin from the moment of delivery. This is based on the idea that through that delivery, <term>ownership<note>original: "dominium"</note></term> is transferred. This limitation can be supported by the canon law chapter *per tuas* on conditions, where conditional betrothals are pronounced to have become a marriage if sexual intercourse follows. By that physical "delivery" of bodies, the spouses are deemed to have withdrawn from the condition that was still pending.

However, the opposite must be said, following Covarruvias and Gutierrez. For <term>delivery<note>original: "traditio"</note></term> in the case we are discussing is presumed to have been made under the same condition as the sale itself, unless it was expressly stated that they wished to withdraw from the condition and perfect the contract purely. Therefore, since the contract is not perfected by that delivery while the condition is still pending, it follows that the days granted for retraction do not begin before the condition is met. Nor does the example of betrothals before the Council of Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) changed marriage laws to require a priest and witnesses, ending the legal tradition where sex could automatically turn a promise to marry into a legal marriage.</note> prove anything. In that case, since intercourse could not happen without the sin of fornication unless they withdrew from the condition and celebrated the marriage, it is presumed by a "presumption of law" that they intended to withdraw from the condition. But in our case, delivery can occur without any fault under the same condition as the sale. Thus, there is no reason to presume—

Molina concludes that the clock only starts once the condition is actually met, rather than when the contract is first signed, because the sale is not legally "perfected" until then.</summary>

### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...he is presumed to have intended to withdraw from the condition.

<margin>Doubt 24</margin>
You ask whether, if a <term>kinsman<note>original: "consanguineus"; a blood relative who possesses the legal right to "retract" or buy back family property sold to an outsider.</note></term>, once a contract has been celebrated under a condition, and while that condition is still pending, wishes to retract the sale by offering the price, whether he can do so under that same condition. <margin>Decision</margin> It must be answered in the affirmative; Tiraquellus says this is the accepted custom in France, as does Matienzo in Spain, as Gutierrez records in the place cited above. But if he did this in court, having provided the necessary security for the matter, it will not be necessary to ratify the retraction within nine days of the condition being fulfilled; otherwise, it will be necessary.

<margin>25</margin>
There is a doubt whether, if someone sells and delivers a thing with a <term>pact of redemption<note>original: "pacto, ut redimere illam possit"; a clause in a sale contract allowing the original seller to buy the property back at a later date for the same price.</note></term> (meaning he can buy it back for the same price within a certain time), and a closer kinsman wants to retract that property within nine days of the contract being celebrated according to the laws of retraction—and at the same time the seller comes forward to redeem it—which of them should be preferred? Faber (in the Institutes, on Buying and Selling) asserted that the kinsman is to be preferred. He argues that by the very fact that the sale was perfected, the closer kinsman acquired a right to retraction. <margin>Decision</margin> Antonio Gomez rightly affirms the contrary, as do Tiraquellus and Gutierrez. Firstly, this is because the seller reserved the right of redemption for himself before anyone else. Secondly, it is because the laws do not grant the right of retraction to the closer kinsman except without prejudice to the pact made between the seller and the first buyer. Indeed, the one who retracts "steps into the shoes" of the first buyer and is bound by all the obligations that the buyer was bound to by the force of the contract, as was said above. This is because retraction is not a separate sale from the first one, as if the first were rescinded; this is the correct view of Antonio Gomez.

<margin>26</margin>
Connected to the preceding doubt is this other one: if the closer kinsman has already retracted the property, and the seller later wants to redeem it, is the closer kinsman bound to give it to him upon receiving the price for which it was sold? The side that says "no" can be argued thus: as we shall see later when discussing sales with a pact of resale, if someone sells a thing with that pact, and the buyer sells it again and delivers it to another person without any burden attached to it, the second buyer is not bound to deliver it to the one who wants to redeem it (unless certain specific conditions occur). Therefore, the same should be said in this case. However, the opposite must be said with Antonio Gomez and Gutierrez. The reason is that the person retracting steps into the shoes of the first buyer and retracts the thing by the privilege of the law in the same state in which it was sold, along with all the burdens the buyer was bound by. Therefore, he is bound to stand by the pact of resale in the same way the first buyer was bound.

Gutierrez (with Tiraquellus and Burgos de Paz) notes: when a thing is sold for "counted money" (cash), it is not enough for the person who wants to retract to deposit the price before a judge and then summon the buyer to deliver the thing. Rather, it is necessary to offer the price itself to the buyer within nine days; and if the buyer refuses to receive it, the person must go to the judge, narrate the facts, and deposit the price

<column-break/>

by the judge’s mandate, and summon the buyer within those same nine days to restore the property. Read the arguments he uses for this assertion and the form of practice he provides.

Covarruvias, Gutierrez, and others whom they cite, affirm: according to the <term>style of this Kingdom<note>original: "stylo huius Regni"; referring to the established legal customs and court procedures of Castile.</note></term>, when property is sold at a public auction by order of a judge to satisfy a debt, the debtor to whom the goods belonged is granted a right of retraction from the "day of the final bid" (<note>original: "del remate"; the moment the auction is finalized and the hammer falls</note>). For movable goods, this must be done within three days; for immovable property (land/buildings), within nine days. Furthermore, if the execution and sale are appealed—especially if the goods came into the power of the creditor because a bidder intervened, or if they were sold too cheaply—the supreme judges usually grant the defendant the ability to retract them within a certain time fixed at their discretion. However, this is done without the right to the fruits (profits) of the land, because that retraction is granted as a grace, and the expenses of the execution must be paid. Likewise, if it is proved that the goods were sold for less than half their "just price," the defendant can use the remedy of Law 2 of the Code regarding the rescinding of a sale within four years.

<margin>Doubt 27</margin>
<margin>From this arises the doubt: what does Law 9, Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection dispose?</margin>
When a thing is sold in a public auction, the nine days granted to the closer kinsman for retraction are computed from the "day of the final bid." Should this be understood as waiting for those three or nine days which, by the "style," are granted to the debtor for retraction, or not? Castillo and Matienzo (cited by Gutierrez) embrace the affirmative side. However, I fear the contrary is true, as Gutierrez affirms. This is both because of the express words of that law and because nothing prevents the debtor, within the time granted to him, from retracting the thing from someone else who bought it at auction, or even from a kinsman who had already retracted it. <margin>Decision</margin> For since the right passes to the kinsman with the same burden it had under the first buyer (as was said just before), the defendant will surely have the same right to retract it from the kinsman as he would have had from the first buyer.

* The retraction we have spoken of in this disputation (and which will be discussed in the next), which is peculiar to this Kingdom of Castile and certain other regions, is not rejected but rather approved by <term>Canon Law<note>The law of the Catholic Church, which often supplemented civil law in early modern Europe.</note></term>. In the Old Law, as is clear from Leviticus 25, the retraction of sold possessions by right of kinship was granted: specifically, that the relatives of the seller could take them back from buyers for the same price according to the number of years remaining until the Jubilee year, at which point possessions returned to their original owners. However, although by <term>Common Law<note>original: "iure communi"; referring to the revived Roman Law (the Corpus Iuris Civilis) used across much of Europe.</note></term> retraction was once granted to kinsmen and partners, today it is not granted, as is clear from the Code. The same is true under Portuguese Law (Book 4, Ordinance Title 25). Therefore, under Common Law and Portuguese Law, it is permitted for any of the partners or kinsmen to choose whichever buyer they wish, and the others do not have a right of retraction. This is added in the Portuguese Ordinances in accordance with the cited laws.

# Treatise the Second, Dispute 371

...nonetheless, if a testator leaves an inheritance or a legacy to someone, or if someone gives or sells property to another on the condition that they cannot alienate it except to a brother, a closer kinsman, or someone else, then any sale is legally void unless it is done according to that prescribed condition. Furthermore, when a thing belongs to many <term>partners<note>original: "socios"; here meaning co-owners or joint-holders of property.</note></term> and is of such a nature that it cannot be divided into parts without loss—such as a slave, a horse, a mill, a house, or a family estate—if one of the partners sells his share to an outsider, the sale is indeed valid and the <term>right of retraction<note>original: "retractus"; the legal right of a specific person (like a co-owner or relative) to step into the shoes of a buyer and purchase the property for the same price.</note></term> does not automatically apply. Nevertheless, the other partners can contend, either with the partner before he sells or with the buyer after the sale is finalized, through a legal action for dividing common property. They may ask that the thing be granted to them—whether they are a partner or an outsider—if they promise more than the <term>just price<note>original: "iusti pretij"; the fair market value as determined by legal and ethical standards of the time.</note></term> for the whole thing or offer a better condition than the other partners. This is established in Law 1 of the Code on dividing common property, and the Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, Title 77, Paragraph 19) agree. There, they decree that if none of these options are taken, the property should be leased and the partners should divide the income among themselves. The same applies to heirs who have a similar item to be divided among them. What has been said here regarding partners actually belongs to the following dispute; however, it was inserted here because the legal doctrines are so closely connected. We will also add some points pertaining to this dispute in the following one, since they are common to both types of retraction.

### Regarding retraction by reason of co-ownership in a thing with the seller. And certain matters common to this and the preceding retraction.

### DISPUTE CCCLXXI.

#### ->SUMMARY<-

1. A partner has the right of retraction in a portion sold by another partner as an <term>undivided whole<note>original: "pro indiviso"; a legal state where multiple people own a property together without specific physical boundaries marking who owns which part.</note></term>; it is otherwise if the parts were already divided.
2. Retraction and the <term>right of preference<note>original: "ius praelationis"; the right to be offered a purchase first, before it is sold to someone else.</note></term> differ.
3. If retraction by right of blood concurs with retraction by right of community (ownership of the soil or the structures), who is to be preferred.
4. And what occurs in the case of a <term>permanent tenant<note>original: "emphyteuta"; someone holding a very long-term lease, almost like ownership.</note></term> or a feudal holder. Number 4.
5. If a holder of surface rights sells the <term>beneficial ownership<note>original: "utile dominium"; the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property, as opposed to "direct ownership" of the title itself.</note></term>, the title owner is preferred in the right of retraction over partners and kinsmen.
6. A holder of surface rights competing with the partner or kinsmen of the title owner who is selling is preferred over them.
7. If a co-owner or co-participant competes with the kinsman of the selling partner in retraction, he is preferred. However, this is clarified and understood as stated there.
8. Who is understood to be included under the name of "partner" or "one holding a thing as an undivided whole."
9. A kinsman of the title owner who sold the thing to a <term>usufructuary<note>original: "usufructuario"; someone who has the right to use and harvest the fruits of a property but does not own it.</note></term> is preferred over the same in the right of retraction.
10. If a husband, during a marriage, retracts a thing sold by his kinsman by right of proximity, whether the wife or her heirs, upon the dissolution of the marriage, ought to receive half of that thing, or only half of the price.
11. If a husband, during a marriage, sells land from the 

<column-break/>

<term>accumulated assets<note>original: "superlucratis"; profits or property acquired during the course of a marriage beyond the initial dowry.</note></term> whose ownership belongs to the wife, whether the wife can retract it as one having a share in that land.
12. If a buyer purchases a field with hanging fruits (unharvested crops) and, from the day of the declared purchase until the retraction, he gathered some fruits, whether he is bound to restore the field along with the gathered fruits or their valuation.
13. The legal action by which retraction is made is personal, or written against the thing, and follows <term>strict law<note>original: "stricti iuris"; a legal interpretation that follows the letter of the law exactly, without equitable flexibility.</note></term>.
14. Full restoration of a thing is understood to include the fruits gathered from the thing to be restored.
15. The <term>Alcabala<note>original: "Alcanala"; a historical Spanish sales tax.</note></term> is owed by the very fact that the buyer purchased the thing which is later retracted.
16. Whether <term>excise taxes<note>original: "Gabelle"; generally refers to taxes on goods, often salt, but here used for intermediate transaction taxes.</note></term> are owed from intermediate sales celebrated by the first buyer up until the retraction.

<margin>1</margin>
In this Kingdom of Castile, in Law 55, Title 5, Part 5, it is ordained that if some people hold a thing common to them as an undivided whole—as the legal experts call it—that is, so that the whole belongs to everyone and one part does not belong to one more than to another, then each one of them, before the thing is divided, can indeed sell his part, both to other partners and to any outsider (provided that a judgment for dividing common property, according to what was said at the end of the previous dispute, has not been initiated before it is sold to the outsider). If, however, it is sold to an outsider, the partners can take it for themselves for the same price, which is to have the right of retraction. That this law is understood to apply when a thing is common as an undivided whole in the manner explained—and otherwise when the thing is so divided among partners that each one knows which part belongs to him—is evident not only from the words of that law, but is affirmed by Gregorio Lopez in his gloss on that passage and Antonio Gomez in Law 70 of the Laws of Toro, number 27. Antonio Gomez further confirms this from the law <italic>magis puto</italic>, the final paragraph, in the Digest regarding the same matter; its words are: "We ought to accept common estates if they are common as an undivided whole." He also cites many other laws. Therefore, the author says in the same place that perhaps that Law 55 was to be understood as applying only when the partner and the outsider were competing at the time of the contract, as if the partner were then to be preferred. It would be otherwise if the thing had already been sold to the outsider, as if that law did not grant retraction, but rather a right of preference. And indeed, that law seems to sound like that alone. Nevertheless, later Laws 74 and 75 of Toro, as we will soon report, do grant a true right of retraction.

<margin>2</margin>
Since the cited Law 55 speaks of property in a general sense, with no restriction made to immovable property, Gregorio Lopez in the same place and Gutierrez (Book 2 of Practical Questions, question 165) and others whom they cite, judge that the disposition of that law has a place in movable things—such as in a slave or a beast held in common—and likewise in a usufruct held by many in common, if one of them sells his part regarding the convenience (according to what was said in Dispute 7), and in a legal action or in any other incorporeal thing common to many, if someone sells the part that belongs to him. This is unless Gregorio Lopez and Gutierrez admit that they have never seen a retraction attempted regarding a movable thing common to many. This opinion certainly pleases me. However, because the Laws of Toro, which we will immediately relate and which grant a true retraction, speak only of immovable things, they do not extend the entire disposition of the cited Law 55 to retraction...

<summary>This page discusses the legal right of co-owners (partners) to "retract" or buy back a share of common property sold to an outsider. It clarifies that this right primarily applies to undivided property and examines its application to both movable and immovable goods under Spanish and Roman law.</summary>

# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...in the manner of that which is granted by right of blood. Certainly, in movable goods, rights of servitude, legal actions, and similar cases, we would judge that only the <term>right of preference<note>original: "ius praelationis"; a right of first refusal where a person has the priority to buy something before it is sold to a stranger.</note></term> should be admitted; namely, that at the time of the sale, a partner should be preferred over a stranger for the same price, according to the sense of Law 55. However, a true <term>retraction<note>original: "retractum"; the legal right of a specific person to step into the shoes of a buyer and "undo" a completed sale by paying the same price.</note></term> after the sale of the same items has been perfected would not be allowed.

**3** Law 74 of Toro, which is Law 13, Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection, deals with the overlap of the right of retraction by right of blood (which was discussed in the preceding Laws of Toro) and the right of retraction by right of community. To clarify who should be preferred when different people compete for the retraction of the same property, it established that among those competing—the owner, the surface-right holder, the one holding an undivided integral part, and the closer kinsman of the seller—the owner is preferred before all others. After the owner, the <term>surface-right holder<note>original: "superficiarius"; one who owns the buildings or improvements on land that belongs to someone else.</note></term> is preferred. After the surface-right holder, the one holding an undivided integral part is preferred, and the kinsman of the seller holds the last place—that is, provided none of the others have competed at the same time. Indeed, Law 75 of Toro, which is Law 14, Title 11 as cited, adds further: what was said in the preceding laws in the same title (from Law 7 onwards) regarding the right of retraction by proximity—concerning the offering of the price within nine days of the perfected sale and other matters—which we explained in the preceding dispute, must similarly apply and be observed in the retraction of an estate by right of community.

From the teaching of these two laws, many points are gathered and understood, by which a path is opened to resolve many very difficult and controversial questions. The first is, **4** that <margin>†</margin> what is said regarding the surface-right holder is, by much stronger reasoning, to be understood similarly regarding the <term>emphyteuta<note>original: "emphyteuta"; a tenant on a long-term or perpetual lease who holds "beneficial ownership" almost equivalent to full ownership.</note></term> and the <term>feudal holder<note>original: "feudatario"; one who holds land under a feudal lord.</note></term>. These do not only possess the <term>beneficial ownership<note>original: "utile dominium"; the right to use, enjoy, and profit from property, as opposed to "direct ownership" or legal title.</note></term> of the surface like a surface-right holder, but also of the soil itself, as was explained in Dispute 10. Likewise, any right lesser than that of a surface-right holder is not sufficient for retraction under the laws of Castile. For that reason, the law mentions the surface-right holder and not the emphyteuta or feudal holder, nor any lesser right, so that it might be understood that any greater right is included (by the argument from the lesser to the greater) and any lesser right is excluded. This is because whoever has a lesser right than a perpetual surface-right holder or emphyteuta is not said to have a part of the ownership—at least not in such a way that the property would not return to the owner by force of the contract. I say this regarding the <term>usufructuary<note>original: "usufructuarium"; one who has the right to use and profit from property for a set time, often for life, but does not own it.</note></term> who, as was said in Question 3, has beneficial ownership of the thing they enjoy, but because this must end with their death and be consolidated with the direct ownership, it falls far short of simple beneficial ownership, such as that of an emphyteuta, feudal holder, or surface-right holder. From this it follows that no right to which a servitude on another's estate corresponds—even if it be a usufruct—is sufficient for retraction if that estate is sold. Nor, likewise, if such a right or benefit from that right is sold, can the owner of the estate retract it. Regarding the usufruct, where this seemed more likely, Antonio Gómez (on Law 70 of Toro, no. 32 and the two following), Covarruvias (3 *Variarum Resolutionum*, ch. 11, no. 4), Gutiérrez (2 *De Practicis Quaestionibus*, q. 157 and q. 166), and others they cite, affirm this. And hence it is that whoever has the usufruct of a certain estate is not said simply to have a part of the ownership of that estate, but the entire ownership is said simply to per-

<column-break/>

tain to the owner alone, as is clear from the law *Rectè dicimus* [We rightly say] in the Digest, *On the Signification of Words*. Its words are: *“We rightly say that a field is entirely ours even if someone else has the usufruct of it; because usufruct is not a part of ownership, but of servitude”* (understand this as a <gloss>subjective part</gloss>), *“just like a path or a right of way. Nor is it falsely said to be mine, when no part of it can be said to belong to another.”* Thus the text. Antonio Gómez confirms the same in the cited number 32 with various other laws. Therefore, when Law 4 of the Digest, *On Usufruct*, and other laws say that usufruct is in many cases a part of ownership, they are to be understood as referring to when the usufruct is perpetual—as in the case of a perpetual surface-right holder, emphyteuta, and feudal holder. In those laws, the discussion concerns an integral part of the full ownership of the thing, along with the direct ownership, as was explained in Dispute 3. A usufruct that is not perpetual, however, is not called a part of ownership simply, but only in a certain respect. From what has been said, it follows that perpetual surface-right holders, feudal holders, and emphyteutas are called simple owners of estates regarding the beneficial ownership in which they have that right. And therefore, when they sell their rights, they are truly and properly said to sell those estates regarding the beneficial ownership within them. Just as an owner would be said to sell them simply if he sold only the direct ownership. However, a usufructuary, or anyone else who might have another servitude, even if they sold their right or benefit, would not be said to sell the estate; this is clear from common usage. Therefore, since the right of retraction in this Kingdom only takes place in the sale of estates, it follows that for one who only has a usufruct or a lesser right, even if they sell it, there is no place for retraction. It follows further that Covarruvias's opinion (3 *Var. Res.*, ch. 11, no. 3) is to be entirely approved in this Kingdom, along with Ferronus and others whom Gutiérrez (2 *De Pract. Qq.*, q. 145) cites, and with which Antonio Gómez (Law 70 of Toro, no. 31 and following) and Alvaro Valasco (*On the Right of Emphyteusis*, q. 17, no. 13) agree. It is no hindrance that the more common opinion is to the contrary, which Gutiérrez unmeritedly embraces for this Kingdom in the cited q. 145—namely, that there is a place for retraction in a perpetual <term>emphyteusis<note>original: "emphyteusi"; the contract granting emphyteutic rights.</note></term> if it is sold, even if it is ecclesiastical property. For since Law 74 of Toro (which is Law 13, Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection) grants retraction to a surface-right holder if the owner sells the estate, and prefers the surface-right holder to the close kinsman of the owner; and likewise grants retraction to the owner, and in his absence to a co-participant in the beneficial ownership of the surface, and in his absence to the closer kinsman of the surface-right holder if the surface-right holder sells his beneficial ownership, as is clearly evident from that law; both of these, by much stronger reasoning according to the prescription of the same law, must be judged to take place in the case of an emphyteuta and a perpetual feudal holder. Indeed, the right of the emphyteuta and feudal holder in an estate is much greater than that of a surface-right holder.

**5** The second point is, if <margin>†</margin> a surface-right holder sells the beneficial ownership he has in another's soil, the direct owner of the same soil can retract it within nine days, and especially in preference to those holding a part in the same surface and the closer kinsman of such a surface-right holder, as is clear from the cited Law 13. However, Antonio Gómez (in the cited no. 31) excellently observes that this is to be understood when the surface-right holder was not paying an annual pension, but received the surface from the owner without the burden of a pen-

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights under Castilian law, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of the "right of retraction." # Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...is made by title of purchase, donation, exchange, or another similar way. For if he paid an annual pension <note>original: "pensionem"; here meaning a fixed ground-rent</note>, he is equated to an <term>emphyteuta<note>original: "emphyteuta"; a tenant who holds a long-term or perpetual lease of land, possessing almost all the rights of an owner provided they pay a small annual rent and maintain the land.</note></term>, as Antonio Gómez affirms in the same place, following Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, and as was stated by us in Disputation 10. Therefore, just as an emphyteuta cannot sell his <term>useful ownership<note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property, as opposed to the "direct ownership" held by the legal landlord.</note></term> without consulting the direct owner; and the direct owner then has a much longer time to deliberate whether he wishes to buy that useful ownership for the same price offered to the emphyteuta (as we shall say in its proper place); so exactly the same must be said of the <term>surface-right holder<note>original: "superficiarius"; one who has the right to own or use buildings or structures on land owned by another.</note></term> in that event. However, once the sale of the surface rights, emphyteusis, or fief is entirely completed, if the direct owner does not wish to buy it for the same price, then first the co-participants (if there are any) may retract it, and secondly, the kinsmen of the seller.

<margin>6</margin>
The third point is that if the direct owner sells his <term>direct ownership<note>original: "directum dominium"; the ultimate legal title to land, distinct from the right to use its resources.</note></term>, the surface-right holder can retract it. He is preferred not only over the closer kinsman of the person selling the direct ownership, but also over someone holding a portion of the direct ownership of the estate of which he himself is the surface-right holder, if they both compete for the retraction. Law 13, previously cited, clearly establishes this, and Antonio Gómez affirms it in number 31. The exact same thing must be said regarding the emphyteuta and the feudal tenant if the direct owner sells his direct ownership, as is clearly gathered from the same law by an argument from the lesser to the greater.

<margin>7</margin>
Fourthly, if one of those holding a part in an undivided thing sells it, the co-participant has the right of retraction and is preferred over the blood relative of the seller. This is to be understood even if a part of the surface rights or emphyteusis is sold; for he who holds another part shall retract it. However, the direct owner is still preferred, as has been said. Furthermore, for someone to be called a co-participant and be able to retract, it is enough if he holds any part whatsoever, even the smallest, as Antonio Gómez, Gregorius Lopez, and others note following Baldus, according to the unique law in the Code regarding the manumission of common slaves.

<margin>8</margin>
Observe two things at this point. One is that the direct owner and the emphyteuta (or the feudal tenant or surface-right holder) can be called owners of the same thing, or co-owners, in an undivided sense. This is because each of them is the owner of the whole thing in terms of the totality of the thing they own, but they are owners by partiality of the <term>dominium<note>ownership</note></term>. This is because each of them is the owner of that whole thing in a different way: one by direct ownership, and the other by useful ownership. These two parts integrate into one full ownership in such a way that each part is measured against the whole thing. In another way, some are called owners of the same thing in an undivided sense because each one is the owner of the whole thing by the same kind of ownership, but simultaneously with another. In this case, the thing must be divided between both in terms of its integral parts or its valuation, which is how co-heirs and partners are owners of the goods of an inheritance or those they possess in a partnership before they are divided between them. Therefore, because those who own a thing in an undivided sense are owners of the whole thing—even if not totally by the totality of ownership—the legal consultants not undeservedly doubted whether they should be called owners of the whole or of a part. See the law "rectè," the last paragraph, in the Digest on the significance of words. The legal consultant Paulus reports this controversy between Quintus Mucius and Servius, saying: *And it is more true, what Quintus Mucius says, that the name of "part" signifies a thing held in common; for that which becomes ours in an undivided sense is not a part, but the whole.* Servius elegantly suggests that the name of "part" signifies both. Therefore, because undivided ownership of a thing is seen in both categories explained, the laws of Castile established retraction in both categories. However, because the direct ownership is the more principal part than the useful ownership, they granted the right of preference to the owner of the property in comparison to him who would have only the useful ownership; but after the owner of the property, they granted preference to him who had a part in the useful ownership, in comparison to a relative of the seller.

<column-break/>

<margin>9</margin>
The second thing to be observed is this: If the owner of the property sells the thing to someone who holds the <term>usufruct<note>original: "usumfructum"; the legal right to use and derive profit from property belonging to another.</note></term> in it, so that the usufruct is consolidated with the ownership in the buyer, the right of retraction is indeed granted to the closer blood relative of the seller, but only regarding that which was sold, as is most well known in itself. Therefore, the usufruct will remain with the buyer as it was before. Thus says Antonio Gómez on Law 70 of Toro.

<margin>10 Doubt</margin>
It is a matter of doubt: if a husband, while the marriage is standing, retracts a thing sold by his relative by right of kinship, ought the wife or his heirs, once the marriage is dissolved, obtain a half-share of it, or only a half-share of the price, if it pertains to the <term>community of gains<note>original: "bona superlucrata"; assets acquired during a marriage that are shared between spouses, similar to community property.</note></term> to be divided between both spouses? Antonio Gómez rightly says that the husband or his heirs can retain the whole thing for themselves. Since retraction in that event is granted so that it might remain with the husband as being of the family of the seller or his ancestors, I do not doubt through <term>epicheia<note>original: "epicheiam"; a legal principle of interpreting the spirit of the law rather than the strict letter to ensure equity.</note></term> that the laws of retraction should be understood this way. However, although Antonio Gómez says only half the price should be granted to the wife, perhaps it would be more appropriately said that she should be granted half the valuation of that thing at the time the marriage is dissolved, as that would pertain to the half of the profits then found. If, however, by the right of retraction on account of the wife, something was similarly extracted while the marriage stood—for instance, because the wife was closer to the seller, or held a part in the thing sold regarding her <term>dowry<note>original: "bona dotalia"</note></term> or <term>paraphernalia<note>original: "paraphernalia"; property belonging to a married woman that was not part of her dowry and remained under her own control.</note></term>—then similarly the whole thing would belong to the wife or her heirs, and the husband or his heirs should receive half of its valuation. Read the things added on this matter in Disputation 433.

<margin>11 Doubt</margin>
A doubt annexed to the preceding one is: If a husband, while the marriage is standing, sells a field from the community of gains, the ownership of which thereby belongs to the wife, can the wife retract it as if she held a part in that field? It must be said with Gregorius Lopez, Gutierrez, and others whom they cite, that although the wife has ownership and possession together with her husband in that field as a true partner in the gains (whatever others may have said to the contrary), nevertheless, because the entire administration and free alienation of those goods—since they are common to both spouses—belongs to the husband alone in this Kingdom while the marriage stands, the wife does not have the right of retraction. This is true even if the field is sold while the marriage stands and is not delivered until the marriage is dissolved; for it would then pertain to the settlement of debts contracted by another while the marriage stood, which would have to be paid before all else.

It also addresses how these rights function within a marriage, concluding that while a spouse may keep ancestral property retracted during marriage, they must compensate the other spouse for half its value under community property rules.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...and only what remained, after all debts contracted during the marriage were paid, would belong to the surplus property <note>original: "superlucrata"; assets gained during a marriage that exceed the original dowry or individual contributions</note>. Add to this that the field was sold by legal disposition in the name of, and for the loss or benefit of, both spouses; therefore, the wife, as a participant in the sale, does not have the right of retraction. However, if after the dissolution of the marriage it were sold by the husband or his heirs without the consent of the wife or her heirs, I believe the wife or her heirs do have the right of retraction: because by then his power to freely alienate the property would no longer belong to the husband.

<margin>12</margin> Next, there is a doubt: if a buyer purchases an estate with <term>pending fruits<note>Crops or profits, such as grain in the field or hanging fruit, that have not yet been harvested.</note></term>, and from the moment the purchase is perfected until the retraction occurs, he gathers any fruits or rents, is he bound to restore the estate along with the gathered fruits or their estimated value? Some authors, whom Antonio Gómez (Law 70 of Toro, number 29) and more extensively Gutierrez (Book 2 of Practical Questions, question 158) cite, assert that the fruits gathered in that middle period do not need to be restored, but belong to the first buyer.

Indeed, this is argued for several reasons. First, because that buyer held title, ownership, and good faith during that middle period, and paid the price—which the seller enjoyed the benefit of during all that time. Therefore, he justly gathered those fruits, made them his own, and consumed them; thus he is not bound to restore them.

Second, because although fruits are considered part of the estate while they are pending, and a person retracting the estate can take it with the fruits he finds still pending, once they have been gathered and separated from the estate, they are no longer called, nor are they, parts of the estate. Instead, they are movable things in which the right of retraction no longer has a place; therefore, they belong to the first buyer.

<margin>Question 13</margin> Third, because the action through which a retraction is made is personal, or based on a specific written provision, and is of "strict law" <note>A legal interpretation that follows the exact letter of the law rather than broad equity</note>, in which fruits are only included from the time the legal contest begins <note>original: "litis contestatio"</note> or at least from the time of a legal delay, following the arguments in the legal texts *l. hac, ff. de triticaria*, and *l. pen. ff. quae in fraud. cred.*

<margin>Question</margin> The contrary view—namely, that those fruits or their valuation must be restored—is asserted by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez and Gutierrez cite and follow in the places mentioned above. First, and most importantly, because retraction replaces the retractor in the full and same right to the sold property that the first buyer held at the time the sale was perfected, and it substitutes the retractor in his place, as was said in the preceding disputation. For that reason, just as the first buyer ought to suffer no loss (since all expenses he made must be paid to him, as well as the tax <note>original: "gabella"</note> if he paid it, as held in Law 70 of Toro), so too he should not carry away a profit from the purchase and subsequent removal. Therefore, he is bound to restore the fruits he gathered from the purchased property. Second, because fruits pending at the time of purchase were parts of the thing bought, and were bought together with it as parts of it. Furthermore, the property was worth more because of those pending fruits than it was before they grew or after they were harvested, as has been shown in the preceding sections. Therefore, they must be restored to the retractor together with the property; otherwise, he would not be retracting the whole of what was bought, but only a portion, which is against the law of retraction. Third, because in

<column-break/>

retraction there must be a full restoration of the thing bought. <margin>14</margin> Furthermore, full restoration, by legal disposition, is understood to include the fruits gathered from the thing to be restored, based on the texts in *l. restituere, ff. de verb. sig.* and *l. videamus. 2. §. in Faviana. ff. de vfut.* and other laws.

To the first argument for the contrary, even if the premise and the first conclusion are granted, the second must be denied. Since the buyer knew, or ought to have known, by the prescription of the laws that the property could be retracted—whereby his own purchase is effectively nullified and another person is substituted to take over the same agreement in his place—he surely ought not to have gathered the fruits before the time granted for retraction had elapsed. Or, he ought to have gathered them with the understanding and intent that if another retracted the estate, he would restore those gathered fruits or their value to that person.

To the second argument, it must be said that although fruits are no longer parts of the estate once they have been gathered, and therefore the right of retraction would not apply to them if they had been bought *after* they were separated from the estate; nevertheless, because they were bought while they were pending and were parts of the estate, the right of retraction applies to them. Nothing prevents this, even if they are already separated from the estate at the time of the retraction, because retraction substitutes the retractor in the place of the buyer, as if the buyer had bought the thing in the name and place of the retractor.

From this it is clear that the opinion of Covarruvias is not true (Chapter 15, number 8), where he asserts, without any other proof, that pending fruits from the time of purchase until the time of retraction should be divided between the retractor and the first buyer, proportional to the time in which the first buyer was the owner. Gutierrez rightly disapproves of this alongside Matienzo. For, besides the fact that it has been clearly shown that all those fruits belong to the retractor, it is not easy to understand how a "proportional time" of ownership would be calculated or accepted in comparison with the retractor’s time.

To the third argument, it must be said that it does not hold for fruits that were pending at the time of purchase; these are owed in their entirety to the retractor along with the purchased property. However, regarding fruits that were *not* pending [at the time of purchase] but were received by the buyer—who did not wish to restore the property and admit the retraction immediately after the price was offered to him, but only restored the thing after a lawsuit intervened—many authors, cited and followed by Covarruvias and Gutierrez, say that in terms of "fruits," only those received after the contest of the lawsuit are owed. However, in terms of "interest" (compensation for loss) from which the retractor was deprived, they are owed from the time the retractor offered the price. This is because from that time, the buyer was in "delay" <note>original: "mora"; a legal term for a failure to perform a duty on time</note> regarding the restoration of the thing, and unjustly deprived the retractor of the property and its fruits. Gutierrez adds, however, that if the buyer is excused by ignorance (because he did not believe the retractor was a blood relative, or had a share in the thing, or that the property belonged to his ancestors), then he is only held liable for fruits gathered after the publication of witnesses. He notes this with Antonio Gómez and adds that the retractor is held liable to the buyer for the interest the buyer would have gained from the price, from the day he bought and paid for the thing until the day the property was demanded from him via retraction after the price was offered.

<margin>15</margin> By the very fact that a buyer purchases a thing which is later retracted, the tax called the <term>alcabala<note>A historical Spanish sales tax, often around 10%.</note></term> is owed. Because when the sale is perfected, the treasury's right to it is established by that very fact...

<summary>This page debates whether a person exercising the right of retraction is entitled to the crops (fruits) harvested by the initial buyer before the buy-back occurred. Molina concludes that because the retractor steps into the exact legal position of the buyer at the time of the original sale, they are entitled to all fruits that were "pending" or growing at that time.</summary>
