<header>Treatise Two, Disputation 37 2.</header>

<margin>Question 16</margin>
...procured it for himself: but when it is later retracted, because it is not a new purchase—but rather the person retracting succeeds the first buyer in the same original contract, being substituted for him—no new <term>gabella<note>A type of excise or sales tax common in the early modern period.</note></term> is owed. Instead, the person retracting is bound to pay the past tax (if the buyer had paid it by some particular agreement) along with the other expenses incurred by the buyer, keeping him entirely free from loss. This is held in Law 70 of Toro, which is Title 11, Book 5 of the New Collection; Antonio Gómez affirms this in the place cited above at number 30, as does Lassarte on the *Taxes of Sales*, chapter 13, number 22, and others whom Lassarte cites. 

In number 24 of the same work, Lassarte brings into controversy a specific scenario: if, within the time granted for retraction, the first buyer sells the same thing to another, and this second person to another, and afterward a retraction is initiated, is a distinct tax owed for these intermediate sales? He thinks it is owed. Because, he says, those were perfected and distinct sales; and from every perfected sale, its own proper and <margin>Decision</margin> distinct tax is owed. 

I, however, judge the opposite to be more probable. Indeed, those intermediate sales contain a tacit condition: "provided that a retraction does not occur." Consequently, as long as some retractor is not substituted for the first buyer in the first sale, the intermediate sales are rendered null and invalid once a retraction is made in relation to the first sale. This is because a sale does not, and cannot, happen by reason of the subsequent buyers, since the subsequent sellers did not hold that property from a relative of the one retracting—something Lassarte himself admits. From a sale made under a condition, where the condition does not stand and the sale is rendered null by the disposition of the law itself, certainly no tax is owed, as Lassarte himself affirms elsewhere, and as was stated in Disputation 337.

Furthermore, it is argued that for intermediate sales to be valid, they would depend on a retraction not occurring in relation to the first sale; thus, they are considered to have been made under the aforementioned tacit condition by the disposition of the law introducing the retraction. 
First, because although the retractor before the retraction only has a right to the thing sold in the first sale, the second buyers have acquired ownership through the contract of sale, subsequent delivery, and payment of the price. Surely they would be preferred over the retractor in a claim for that thing unless, by the disposition of the law, intermediate sales were made under a tacit condition, and thus unless the ownership itself were revocable under that same condition. Just as a second buyer, to whom delivery was made and the price paid after an absolute sale, is preferred to the first buyer (as stated in Disputation 369); since, therefore, the retractor is preferred to them and can demand the thing from them by a personal action (as Lassarte himself confesses and all affirm), it follows that the sales were made under that condition and are rendered entirely null by the very fact that retractions are initiated, and the transferred ownership is immediately revoked.

Second, because the first buyer, who sold the thing a second time, and the subsequent sellers are not held liable for <term>eviction<note>The legal recovery of property from a purchaser by a person with a better title; a warranty against being legally "evicted" from the property.</note></term> toward the subsequent buyers when a retraction occurs. Just as a thief, who has sold someone else's property in an absolute and valid sale, is held liable for eviction to the buyer even if he did not transfer ownership (because it belonged to another); however, this 

<column-break/>

does not arise from anything else except that the subsequent sales, by the disposition of the law, rested upon the first sale and held a tacit condition: "provided a retraction was not made in relation to the first." For that reason, once the retraction follows, they are rendered entirely invalid. Therefore, no tax is owed from them; rather, if it was paid to a public official, it must be restored to them once the retraction follows.

Lassarte rightly says in the same place from number 28 that if the first buyer, after the nine days for retraction have passed, sells the thing to the person who had the right of retraction within those nine days, a new tax is owed. This is because it is no longer a retraction, but a new and distinct sale. 

If, however, he sells it within the nine days with some variation made in the price or in some other circumstance of the contract, a distinct tax is also owed: because it is considered a distinct contract of purchase and sale. But if the sale is made within nine days with no variation in price or other circumstances, a distinct tax is not owed: because it is considered a retraction. It does not matter that they do not use the word "retraction" but rather "purchase and sale," as he rightly affirms against <note>original: "Carolum Molinæum"</note> Charles Dumoulin; this is because in contracts one must attend rather to what is being done than to the words the contracting parties use.

## Whether the right of retraction has a place in the sale of a census.

### DISPUTATION 372.

#### SUMMARY.

> 1 *The census contract is of multiple types.*
> 2 *What a "reserved census" is.*
> 3 *The right of retraction is granted even for mixed census contracts and emphyteusis.*
> 4 *What a "common census" is.*
> 5 *The right of retraction is not granted to the relatives of one selling a common census.*
> 6 *If a census on some estate is sold, can it be stipulated in a pact that if the estate is sold, the owner of the census is preferred over other buyers for the same price if he wishes?*
> 7 *Whether there is a place for retraction for the nearest relative of one alienating an estate subject to a census, and when.*

<margin>1 2</margin> The <term>census contract<note>An annuity or rent-charge where a person pays a lump sum for the right to receive annual payments, or sells property while reserving an annual income.</note></term> is of multiple types, as will be said in its proper place below. One is <insert>reserved</insert>, of which there is talk in the chapter *Constitutus* concerning religious houses. Namely, when something is granted to someone regarding everything the grantor had in it, reserving an annual, monthly, or other similar payment, which the receiver is bound to pay either from the fruits or in some equivalent, such as money or another thing. Because through a contract of this kind the grantor gives the entire right he had in that thing, it follows that through it, not only the "useful ownership" but also the "direct ownership" is transferred whenever both were with the grantor. Thus, it is very distinct from an <term>emphyteutic contract<note>A long-term or perpetual lease of land for a yearly rent.</note></term> and from the census contract commonly discussed, which will be spoken of immediately.

<summary>This page analyzes whether sales taxes (gabella) are due when the right of retraction is exercised across multiple intermediate sales and begins a new discussion on applying retraction to various types of annuities or "census" contracts.</summary>
<keywords>retraction, sales tax, gabella, subrogation, Lassarte, Charles Dumoulin, reserved census, emphyteusis, property law, contracts</keywords>

--- Page 378 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "right of retraction" (the legal right of a relative or interested party to step into a sale and purchase the property for themselves). The previous page concluded that intermediate sales are effectively undone if a retraction is successfully claimed on the original sale.</meta>

<page-num>314</page-num>
<header>Ludovico Molina on Contracts</header>

When, however, a <term>census<note>A "census" in this legal context refers to a ground-rent or an annuity—a right to receive a regular payment from the income of a property.</note></term> is reserved in a grant of this kind, and no sale is seen to occur, it is clearly established that the right of retraction has no place when the grant is first made. If, however, the person who received the property under such a ground-rent later sells it, then the right of retraction will belong to the closest relative of the seller. It does not, however, belong to the one who granted the ground-rent, nor to the successor of the one to whom the life-payment or monthly pension from that estate is owed.

This is because that right to receive a pension from the estate is neither the estate itself, nor a part of the estate, nor the <term>beneficial or direct ownership<note>Molina distinguishes between "direct" ownership (the legal title) and "beneficial" ownership (the right to use and profit from the land).</note></term> of it. Rather, it is a certain right in the thing similar to an easement over an estate; as was said in the preceding dispute, such rights are by no means sufficient to trigger a retraction. If, then, someone were to grant an estate for a ground-rent in exchange for a certain sum of money and an annual or monthly pension at the same time; then, if the estimated value of the annual or monthly pension exceeded the value of the cash, there would be no room for retraction in the granting of such a ground-rent, according to what was said in Disputation 370. This is because such a grant of ground-rent would not be a sale, but would simply be a reserved ground-rent contract with some elements of a sale mixed in. If, however, the value of the money exceeded the estimated value of the annual pension, the right of retraction would belong to the seller's relative, because it would be simply a sale mixed with a reserved ground-rent contract, as is clear from the points made in that same dispute.

I should mention that a controversy of this sort came into my hands in days past. Once, a certain monastery held the direct ownership of certain estates, of which another person was the <term>emphyteuta<note>An "emphyteuta" is a tenant under a long-term lease (emphyteusis) who treats the land almost as their own, provided they pay a small rent and maintain the property.</note></term>, paying a certain annual pension to the monastery. In the course of time, that entire pension had been redeemed for a certain quantity of money which the person holding those estates in leasehold paid to the monastery. However, the monastery consented to the pension being redeemed for that money on the condition that the direct ownership of the same estates should nevertheless remain with it, with a very modest—nearly non-existent—payment of wheat to be paid thereafter as an acknowledgment of the monastery’s remaining direct ownership. The person into whose power those estates later came through a contract of purchase—without asking the monastery if it wished to buy them for the same price, and without paying the <term>laudemium<note>A transfer fee (usually 2% of the price) paid to the superior landlord when a leasehold was sold.</note></term> to the monastery for that sale—later sold them again to someone else, similarly without asking the monastery and without paying the transfer fee. The monastery opposed this, not on the grounds that the seller had incurred <note>original: "in commissum incidisset"</note> a forfeiture by selling without asking the monastery, nor as if a transfer fee were owed to it from that sale; but by the right of retraction, wishing to take those estates for the same price within the nine days granted by the law of this Kingdom, because it held the direct ownership in them. Some contended that the monastery's ancient right had passed into a reserved ground-rent by virtue of the last contract celebrated by the tenant for that sum of money, and therefore the direct ownership had also passed to that ancient tenant—according to the notes commonly made by the doctors on the chapter *Constitutus*—and therefore there was no place for retraction. As for that clause in the written contract by which the mona-

<column-break/>

-stery reserved the direct ownership for itself, they thought it had been added by the notary out of his own head, as is usually added in common ground-rent contracts, which attribute direct ownership of the rent-bearing estate to the buyer of the ground-rent, even though in reality no such thing happens. Therefore, they said no attention should be paid to that clause.

<margin>3</margin> Others, however, thought the right of retraction applied on the grounds that the contract had transitioned into a ground-rent contract. They argued that, universally, those who have a ground-rent in any estate—whether it be perpetual or redeemable—have the right of retraction when the estate is sold, because they hold the direct ownership of such an estate, as evidenced by the legal instruments usually drawn up for that purpose.

<margin>Decision</margin> I believe it must be said, however, that the monastery did have the right of retraction. This is not because owners of common ground-rents have it (as we shall say shortly), but because that ground-rent was a mixture of the <term>emphyteusis</term> from which it first originated and a reserved ground-rent. For this reason, the direct ownership never passed to the old tenant; indeed, the contrary was expressly included as a pact in the redemption of the pension. Instead, it always remained with the monastery. As a sign of this, that modest payment of wheat was reserved—not merely as a memory of a favor granted in the redemption of the old pension.

<margin>4</margin> There is another type of ground-rent contract in very frequent use, especially in this Kingdom of Castile, by which, for a certain sum of money, one buys the right of levying or receiving a certain annual or monthly pension in money, wheat, or another thing, from the estate or estates of someone. If the ground-rent is "real" (attached to the property), the estates remain with the person who owned them before, both in terms of beneficial and direct ownership, with only a "real" burden on the estates themselves so that the pension may be paid.

Regarding this type of ground-rent, it must be said that neither when it is sold does the right of retraction belong to the relatives of the seller, nor when the person who bought it sells it again to a third party does the right of retraction belong to the owner of the estate—even if that ground-rent were perpetual and irredeemable—nor to the relative of the seller. This is the view of Covarruvias in *Variarum Resolutionum*, book 3, chapter 11, number 5; Gutierrez in *Practicis Quaestionibus*, book 2, questions 146 and 166; and others whom they cite. The reason is that although this ground-rent is computed among immovable things, it is nevertheless neither an estate, nor a part of an estate, nor a part of the ownership of an estate. It is a certain right in the thing regarding that estate, similar to the rights corresponding to easements in estates. As was said at length in the preceding dispute, rights of this kind are not sufficient for retraction under the laws of this kingdom. Nor does it matter that when such ground-rents are sold in some estate, a clause is usually placed in the instruments by which the sellers of the ground-rent grant and transfer the direct ownership of that estate to the buyer of the ground-rent. For, as Covarruvias rightly says in the cited number 5, notaries add this from their own heads, beyond what the nature of the contract holds and what exists between the contracting parties; therefore, no attention should be paid to that clause.

<margin>6</margin> However, whether a pact can be included when such ground-rents are sold in an estate, stating that if the estate is sold, the owner of the ground-rent shall be preferred over other buyers for the same price if he so wishes: Gutierrez, in the cited work, book 2, question 167, deservedly defends the affirmative side.

<summary>This page discusses the right of retraction in the context of ground-rents (census) and leaseholds (emphyteusis), concluding that the right only applies when actual ownership is transferred, not merely the right to a pension. Molina uses a specific case involving a monastery to illustrate how symbolic payments can prove the retention of direct ownership.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "right of retraction," specifically focusing on how Papal decrees and Spanish royal law interact regarding property tied to a <term>census<note>A "census" was a common financial arrangement in the early modern period where a person provided a sum of capital in exchange for a steady, annual income (an annuity or ground-rent) derived from a specific piece of property.</note></term>.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 370. 315

Indeed, today, according to the bull of **Pius V** regarding the establishment of <term>censuses<note>This refers to the Papal Bull *Cum onus* (1569), which sought to regulate the terms of annuities to prevent usury.</note></term>, all other clauses were rendered completely void—specifically those by which the lord of the estate was prohibited from alienating it to whomever he wished. In compensation for this, it was decreed not only that if the lord of the census wished to buy the estate for the same price, he should be preferred over other buyers, but also that the lord of the estate was bound to notify the lord of the census of the price he found for it and the other conditions of sale before he sold the estate. He must then wait an entire month to see whether the lord of the census would rather take it for that same price and under those same conditions.

Whether this practice has been accepted in the **Spanish realms** is not clear to me. **Lassarte**, in his work *On the Tenth Part of a Sale*, chapter 10, at the end of number 20, reports that regarding the **Kingdom of Castile**, a petition was made by **King Philip II** concerning the bull of Pius V at the assembly <note>original: "comitijs"; referring to the Cortes or parliamentary assembly</note> held in **Madrid** in the year 1585, petition 2. **Gutierrez** reports the same in his second volume of *Practical Questions* at the end of question 177 in these words: 

*In the assembly of Madrid in the year 1587, our most invincible King Philip II, having been consulted on this matter by the representatives of these kingdoms, replied by royal law that this decree <note>original: "motum proprium"</note> had not been accepted among us by custom, and that a petition had been sent to the most holy Pontiff in the King's name regarding it.*

Therefore, as **Ignatius Salzedo** says most recently in his additions to the *Practices* of Bernardus Diaz, chapter 88, that "extravagant" decree <note>An "extravagant" was a papal decree not yet included in the official codified bodies of Canon Law.</note> should not be brought forward in court proceedings while the petition is pending. This is according to Gutierrez, who certainly calculates from the end of the assembly and the issuing of the response; Lassarte, however, calculates from the beginning of the assembly when the representatives were called. 

And truly, I believe that secular princes can, with a clear conscience, refuse to admit that their subjects, in a purely secular contract such as a census contract, should be subject to such a heavy burden: namely, that before they sell their estates subject to a census, they are bound to warn the lord of the census of the price they find, and wait through an entire month for the lord of the census’s deliberation, since by its very nature this contract contains no such thing.

Even if this had been drawn into a pact, or if the bull of Pius V had been accepted somewhere by custom, it is doubtful whether—if the lord of the estate nevertheless sells it and delivers it to a third party without requesting the lord of the census—the sale is valid and irrevocable. In the same way, when something was sold to one person but not delivered, if it is sold and delivered afterward to another, the second sale is valid, but the seller is held liable to the first buyer for damages, as was said in Disputation 369. Or is the situation different? Can the lord of the census "retract" <note>The right of "retraction" allows a preferred party to forcibly purchase the property from the new buyer at the same price.</note> and snatch that estate out of the power of the buyer for the same price? 

Certainly, if we consider the clause of Pius V's bull alone, I would not dare to say that there is room for retraction in that event. For the bull only establishes and commands that this be done; it does not, however, subject the estate to a <term>mortgage<note>original: "hypothecæ"</note></term> to secure that sanction and the obligation to which it subjects the seller of the census. Unless you argue that by the force of the law *Non Dubium* in the Code *On Laws* <note>A famous principle in Roman Law (C. 1.14.5) stating that acts done in violation of a legal prohibition are void by default.</note>, such an alienation is considered void, insofar as in the last part of the clause where Pius V establishes this, he imposes no penalty but only prohibits the sale from being made without that solemnity. For the law *Non Dubium* establishes that when something is prohibited by law, the act is considered void by that same law if it is done, even if nothing else is added in the law. This is how the doctors of law understand it when the law stops there,

<column-break/>

as it does in this bull of Pius V, and does not proceed further to add a penalty or something similar, as has been said elsewhere and will be said in the progress of this work. **Avendaño** and **Marienus**, cited by Gutierrez in question 167, held that when a pact on this matter had intervened between the lord of the estate and the buyer of the census, and the seller of the census nevertheless sold and delivered the thing, the second sale is valid. 

Gutierrez, however, asserted the opposite there. Because, he says, just as the estate is subject to a mortgage for the payment of the census and the observation of the census contract, so too is it subject to a mortgage for the observation of that pact added to the census contract. When a thing is subject to a mortgage for the observation of a pact, surely the fact that the same thing is sold and delivered to a third party does not block that prior obligation, as was said in the same Disputation 369.

In my view, however, one must inspect the legal instrument of the census contract itself. Indeed, if it appears from the instrument that the thing was subjected to a mortgage even for the observation of that pact not to alienate the thing unless the lord of the census was first requested and preferred over other buyers for the same price, then Gutierrez's opinion should be embraced. If, however, this does not appear from the instrument, his opinion should be rejected. This is because from the fact that a census is bought on a certain estate, it follows indeed that there is a **real right** in that estate so that the census may be paid from it and the census contract may be upheld; but it does not follow—if that other pact is added, which is entirely accidental to the census contract and foreign to it—that a "right in the thing" or a mortgage is created in that estate for the observation of that pact, unless it is clearly expressed in the instrument or the celebration of the contract. Remember, moreover, that the things said at the end of Disputation 369 also apply to the matter we are discussing.

<margin>7th Question</margin> Regarding the following contract, there is a major controversy: whether there is room for a "retraction by blood" <note>A "retraction by blood" (*retractus consanguinitatis*) is the right of a close relative to step into a sale and buy back ancestral land sold to a stranger.</note> for the nearest relative when an estate is alienated, and when exactly that right of retraction begins. 

Suppose **Peter**, having an estate, sold it to **Paul** for one hundred gold pieces, with this pact added: that until he paid them, he would return ten gold pieces annually as a census established on the same estate, redeemable for those same hundred gold pieces. Peter reserved for himself the <term>direct ownership<note>The legal title or "superior" ownership.</note></term> in the meantime until those hundred gold pieces were paid, and granted only the <term>beneficial ownership<note>The right to use the land and take its fruits.</note></term> to Paul for that same period. After one or two years had passed, Paul paid those hundred gold pieces and thus redeemed the census and acquired the full ownership of the estate. 

The question is: when do the nine days <note>In many jurisdictions, a relative had only nine days from the sale to exercise their right of retraction.</note> for the retraction of that estate begin for Peter’s nearest relative? Do they start from the day the price was paid and the census redeemed? Or from the beginning of that celebrated contract? Or, perhaps, never—because at the time of the redemption of the census and the acquisition of the direct ownership, Paul should be preferred over Peter’s nearest relative, as he already held the beneficial ownership and was a "co-sharer" with Peter in the ownership of the same thing, according to **Law 74 of Toro** <note>The Laws of Toro (1505) were a famous set of Spanish laws; Law 74 dealt with the rights of co-owners.</note>? The same doubt exists if Peter grants the estate to Paul for an annual census of ten gold pieces, redeemable for one hundred gold pieces.

<margin>Decision</margin> **Covarruvias** disputes this matter extensively on both sides in his *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 11. And indeed, regarding the first of the proposed points, his opinion...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal "right of retraction," specifically focusing on the timeline for when relatives can intervene in a property sale. It then begins a new Disputation regarding the dissolution of contracts by mutual consent.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>Luis de Molina on Contracts</header>

the opinion which he provides from number 5, and which **Gutierrez** follows in *Practical Questions*, book 2, question 145, number 6, along with others whom he cites.

Specifically, that sale of the <term>direct lordship<note>original: "dominium directum"; the legal title to property, often distinguished from the "useful lordship" or the right to use and profit from the land.</note></term> was, from the beginning of the contract, an absolute sale for one hundred gold coins, based on credit given for the price until **Paul** wished to pay it; in the meantime, while it was not paid, an <term>annuity<note>original: "census"; a financial arrangement where property generates a steady income for the holder.</note></term> of gold coins was established. Therefore, because that sale was absolute from the beginning of the contract, the nine-day period for the blood relatives of **Peter** to exercise their <term>right of retraction<note>original: "retractus"; a legal right allowing family members to step into a sale and purchase ancestral property themselves to keep it within the family.</note></term> begins to run from that same start of the contract. It does not begin at the point of the redemption of the annuity or the payment of the hundred gold coins. Furthermore, the relative may retract the entire estate, including the annuity and the <term>useful lordship<note>original: "utile dominium"; the right to use, inhabit, and take the profits from a piece of land.</note></term>, as **Covarrubias** correctly affirms in the same place, number 7. Nor does it matter that Paul did not obtain the direct lordship immediately from the start of the contract, but only from the point when the annuity was redeemed and those hundred gold coins were paid. I say it does not matter because, as was stated in Disputations 338, 367, and 368, even in other absolute sales, the ownership of the thing sold does not pass to the buyer (even if it has been delivered) before the price is paid or the seller accepts it as paid. This does not make the sale "conditional" (that is, dependent on whether the price is paid), nor does it prevent the sale from being "perfected" for the purpose of starting the clock on the days for retraction, as is clear from the two preceding disputations. Covarrubias confirms this same opinion with many other reasons in the place cited above; you should read him there.

Regarding the second point—namely, when Peter handed over the estate in exchange for an annual annuity of ten gold coins, redeemable for one hundred gold coins—Covarrubias, Gutierrez, and others they cite affirm that if, in one and the same contract, he hands over the estate for an annuity and grants that the annuity may be redeemed for one hundred gold coins (or if that redemption right is granted shortly after in a separate contract), then the right of retraction for Peter’s blood relatives begins as soon as the contract is celebrated and the power of redemption at that price is recognized. This is because such an arrangement is a "virtual sale" of that estate for one hundred gold coins, and it is presumed to have been done to defraud Peter’s relatives, so that the right of retraction might be taken away from them. However, Gutierrez says that if, at the beginning, the estate is only granted for an annuity, and then later, after an interval, the power to redeem the annuity is granted in a distinct contract—such that there is no presumption of fraud—then the right of retraction does not apply to Peter’s relatives from the start of the first contract. Instead, the right of retraction applies to them because of the second contract that created and manifested the power to redeem the annuity, provided it could have come to the knowledge of Peter's relatives.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I believe it must be said, however, that if it is a <term>reserved annuity<note>original: "census reservativus"; an annuity created when a seller transfers property but "reserves" a right to annual payments from it.</note></term>, whether the power to redeem is granted after an interval or at the same time, the right of retraction never applies to the relatives unless it is understood from the circumstances that it was done as a fraud, with the intention of selling the estate for the redemption price and disguising it in that manner so the relatives would not have the right of retraction. The reason is that since the first contract was not a sale, it does not trigger a retraction, as was said above; and since

<column-break/>

the second contract was neither a sale of the useful lordship nor the direct lordship, but only of the right to collect ten gold coins annually—which was the only right remaining to Peter in that estate—the right of retraction would not have a place by virtue of the second contract either. These matters will be made clearer from what is to be said in Disputation 382.

# Whether a purchase and sale may be dissolved by the mutual consent of the parties.

## DISPUTATION 373.

### SUMMARY

1 *How a purchase and sale is dissolved by the mutual consent of the buyer and seller.*
2 *And what of leasing and other similar contracts. Number 2.*
3 *Whether the tax, which is called the <term>alcabala<note>original: "alcauala"; a common sales tax in Spain and its colonies.</note></term>, is owed upon the dissolution of a contract by mutual consent, or rather from the prior contract.*
4 *When a sale made with the intention of gifting an appraised item is called a donation, so that the tax is not owed.*
5 *Whether a double alcabala is owed when a mutual consent to dissolve is made in the external forum.*
6 *Whether a double alcabala is owed when a contract is rescinded by mutual contrary consent.*

We must consequently discuss the ways in which a contract of purchase and sale, once celebrated, may be dissolved. And † first, whether it can be dissolved by the mutual consent of the buyer and seller. Briefly, it must be said that if the <term>matter is untouched<note>original: "res sit integra"; a legal phrase meaning neither party has yet performed their part of the deal (no delivery, no payment).</note></term>—that is, if delivery of the thing or the price has not been made on either side, even if a <term>deposit<note>original: "arrha"; earnest money or a down payment intended to bind the parties to a contract.</note></term> has been given by one side—the contract is dissolved, both in conscience and in the external court, by the mutual consent of the buyer and seller by which they will that the thing is no longer sold.

2 The same † must be said of leasing and other contracts that are perfected solely by mutual consent expressed outwardly. This is held in laws 1 and 2 of the Code, "When it is permitted to withdraw from a purchase," and in the law *iurisgentium*, paragraph *adeo*, and the law *ab emptione* in the Digest, "On Pacts," and in the final paragraph of the Institutes, "By what modes an obligation is removed." This is affirmed by the common opinion of the Doctors, whom **Antonio Gomez** refers to and follows among others in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2. The reason is that what is sufficient for a contract should also be sufficient for its "un-making" or dissolution, if the opposite action is taken. Therefore, when a contract is perfected solely by consent expressed outwardly regarding its binding force (even in the external court), equity surely demanded that if the matter were still untouched and no further progress had been made toward delivery and execution of the contract, the withdrawal of those same contracting parties through mutual consent expressed outwardly would also suffice for its dissolution, even in the external court.

What was said regarding the deposit is expressly held in law 2 of the Code, "When it is permitted to withdraw from a purchase." The reason for it is that a deposit is not an "execution" of the contract of purchase and sale, neither in whole nor in part, but rather something given as security that the contract will be upheld.

It then transitions to discussing how contracts can be legally canceled by mutual consent if no performance has yet occurred.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 3 of the Second Treatise, focusing on the legal and moral complexities of dissolving a contract of sale by mutual consent. It specifically addresses whether the Spanish sales tax (alcabala) is still owed when a deal is canceled.</meta>

<page-num>817</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 3</header>

The same principle applies if a **guarantor** <note>original: "fideiussor"</note> has been provided, even if a formal verbal agreement <note>original: "stipulatio"</note> intervened, and even if a sale and purchase, originally celebrated by mutual consent alone, were later strengthened by such an agreement. This is because these actions do not constitute the execution of the contract, but rather the formalizing of its stability, as is expressly stated in **Law 3 of the Digest on rescinding sales**. However, if **earnest money** <note>original: "arrha"; a deposit paid to seal a deal</note> was given not merely for security but as part of the price, then mutual consent would not suffice for the dissolution of the contract in the external court <note>the civil legal system, as opposed to the "court of conscience"</note>, as we shall soon discuss and as is held in **Law 2**, along with the gloss there, in the **Code on when it is permitted to withdraw from a purchase**.

---

<margin>Third Doubt</margin>
The doubt is whether, and when, a contract is dissolved in the manner explained, a tax—which is called an **alcabala** <note>a historical Spanish sales tax</note>—is owed, or not; and whether a double tax is owed: one from the prior contract which is dissolved, and another from the subsequent agreement by which it is dissolved (which might seem like a second sale made by the one who was previously the buyer).

<margin>Decision</margin>
When a contract is dissolved in the aforementioned way, all authorities agree that a double tax (the *alcabala*) is not owed. This is because, before a contract is perfected by the **delivery** of the goods and the **payment** of the price, the disagreement and revocation of what had been done is not considered a new sale, but rather the extinction and dissolution of the previous one. This is the view of **Charles Dumoulin**, **Lassarte on the Sale of Tithes**, chapter 14, number 9, and **Antonio Gómez** in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 1, number 31; this is consistent with various laws and the very nature of the matter.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
There is, however, a doubt as to whether the tax from the first contract is owed, or if the tax collector has already received it, whether he is bound to return it.

<margin>Decision</margin>
To this, it must be said—following **Paulus Castrensis** and the common opinion cited and followed by **Antonio Gómez**—that if the contract is dissolved **immediately** <note>original: "incontinenti"</note>, specifically before the contracting parties turn to other business, the tax is not owed. This is because the contract is regarded as if it had never been celebrated or perfected. See the penultimate and last gloss on the law **"Agreed Pacts"** in the **Digest on entering a purchase**. However, if it is dissolved **after an interval** <note>original: "ex intervallo"</note>, the tax from the original contract of sale and purchase is indeed owed. The reason is that the right has already been fully and perfectly acquired by the **treasury** <note>original: "fisco"</note> from the completed sale; it cannot be taken away by a later pact or reversal. Such a reversal can prejudice the contracting parties themselves, but not a third party (the state) who had already acquired a right from the contract being dissolved.

This is the common opinion followed by **Gómez** and **Lassarte**, based on the law **"If after death"** in the **Digest on possession of goods**, and the final law of the **Digest on pacts**. If the contract is not dissolved entirely, but the price is increased or decreased by mutual consent, or more goods are added for the same price, it is considered a withdrawal from the first purchase and the creation of a new one, insofar as the latter differs from the former. This is permitted because the matter is still "whole" <note>original: "res integra"; meaning no delivery or payment has yet occurred</note>. Nevertheless, the contract is in some way the same, merely varied in its essentials (goods, price, and consent), as is clear from **Law 2 of the Digest on rescinding sales** and more fully in the law **"Law of Nations," section "So much so"** in the **Digest on pacts**.

<column-break/>

Where it is added: if two people had previously entered a sale and purchase and, while the matter was still "whole," one of them died leaving two heirs, and one heir (while the matter remained whole) agreed with the surviving party to make a variation in the goods or price while the other co-heir refused, that variation is valid for the portion belonging to the consenting heir. In this situation, observe that when the price is lowered or the goods increased for the same price, although a new tax is not owed (since it is the same contract slightly varied), the tax collector is not bound to return or remit any of the tax from the first contract. He had acquired a full right to the whole tax from the start, which cannot be prejudiced by a variation made after an interval. However, if the price were increased, then an additional tax would be owed proportional to that increase. The reason is that, by that very act, the item has been sold anew for a higher price. Although the cited doctors do not speak of this specifically, none would oppose our teaching here, which is clearly deduced from the cited laws and is consistent with their other sayings.

4. **In passing**, I should add here that if a sale is made with the intention of **donating** an appraised item—and this is done so the recipient knows how much value is being given to them, but without any price actually being taken—it is not a sale, but a donation. Therefore, no sales tax is owed; this is held in the law **"When in a sale"** in the **Digest on entering a purchase**. If, however, a sale is made with the intention of selling, but without the intention of actually collecting the price (choosing instead to remit or gift it to the buyer), perhaps because the seller wishes to leave the **right of retraction** to relatives <note>a legal right for family members to buy back ancestral land</note>, then it is a true sale. This is according to the law **"If I [lease] a dwelling to you"** in the **Digest on letting and hiring**, and is confirmed by **Lassarte**, who affirms (with **Dumoulin**) that in this second case, the tax **is** owed.

5. When a sale and purchase is not merely celebrated by mutual consent expressed outwardly, but has proceeded further to some **delivery** <note>original: "traditionem"</note> or fulfillment by one party—such as the seller delivering the goods or the buyer paying the price—the matter is no longer "whole." In such a case, although the contract may be dissolved in the **court of conscience** through a mutual contrary consent (thereby removing the moral obligation to stand by the deal), and the person who received the goods or money is bound in conscience to return them, nonetheless, in the **external court** <note>the civil law</note>, the contract is not dissolved. This is because a **naked pact** <note>original: "pactum nudo"; an agreement not meeting all formal legal requirements</note> does not give rise to a civil obligation, as discussed in Disputation 25...

<summary>This page discusses the legal and tax implications of canceling or modifying a sales contract. It concludes that while immediate dissolution may exempt parties from sales tax (alcabala), a delayed cancellation does not forfeit the state's right to the tax already incurred.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 317 regarding the legal requirements for dissolving a contract and the tax implications thereof. It specifically moves from general dissolution by mutual consent to the specific legal mechanism of the "right of redemption" or "pact of resale."</meta>

<page-num>318</page-num>
<header>Luis de Molina on Contracts</header>

as was stated especially in Disputations 255 and 257. From this, it follows that for someone who has already delivered the goods and fulfilled their part of the contract, a subsequent **informal agreement** <note>original: "pacto nudo"; a "naked pact" is an agreement made without the specific legal formalities required to create a binding obligation in older civil law</note> does not grant a legal action to reclaim what they delivered. Instead, a legal action is granted only based on the preceding contract to compel the other party to fulfill their part of the purchase or sale, as is clear from the cited locations and held in **Laws 1 and 2 of the Code on when it is permitted to withdraw from a purchase**. 

However, if the party who has not yet fulfilled their side of the contract wishes for both parties to follow a subsequent informal agreement—meaning the sale and purchase would be dissolved—but the other party does not wish this and instead sues to enforce the first contract, then a **defense** <note>original: "exceptio"; a legal plea used to block an opponent's claim</note> is allowed in the **civil court** <note>original: "foro exteriori"; literally the "outer forum," referring to public legal systems rather than the "court of conscience"</note>. This defense argues that they are not bound to the contract because of the subsequent informal agreement to the contrary. Although such a pact does not create a civil obligation or a right to sue, it nonetheless creates a **natural obligation** <note>an obligation recognized by fairness and conscience even if not strictly enforceable by a lawsuit</note> and provides a defense in the civil court, as was explained in Disputation 257. 

But if that mutual consent to withdraw from the contract were formalized by a **solemn stipulation** <note>original: "stipulatione"; a formal verbal contract in Roman law that made a promise legally binding</note>, then a civil obligation would arise from it, and a legal action would be granted in the civil court to uphold it. According to **Canon Law** <note>the law of the Church</note>, and also within this **Kingdom of Castile**, a civil action is granted from that same informal agreement even if it is not formalized by a solemn stipulation, as we showed in Disputation 257 and as Antonio Gómez affirms in the place cited above at number 21. Therefore, what has been said only applies in **common civil law** <note>the shared Roman-based legal tradition of Europe</note> where nothing else has been decreed, as it has not been decreed in **Portugal**.

Nevertheless, according to that same common law, when the parties have proceeded to the delivery and fulfillment of the contract on one side, the contract is dissolved even in the civil court if there is not only mutual consent but also the **restoration** of what had been delivered. This is held in **Law 1 of the Code on when it is permitted to withdraw from a purchase**, and the **Law "from a purchase" in the Digest on pacts**, and is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The doubt is whether, when a contract is rescinded in this latter way, a single or rather a double **sales tax** <note>original: "alcauala"; the *alcabala* was a significant tax in Spain and its territories on the sale of goods</note> is owed. To this, Lassarte responds (cited above, number 8) that only a single tax is owed if everything is restored exactly as it was received, without introducing any changes to the goods or the price. In this case, it is entirely similar to the preceding act in reverse: for then no new purchase or sale is made, but only a rescission and extinction of the previous one, as the cited laws teach. However, if anything is changed—for example, if the price to be returned is increased or decreased, or if something similar happens regarding the goods to be returned—it is considered a distinct sale. Consequently, another distinct tax would be owed to the **tax collector** <note>original: "gabellario"</note> and the lord who are in power at that time. This is how Pinellus and Luis Peguera, whom he cites, understand **Law 2 of the Code on rescinding sales**.

<margin>Decision</margin>
One must add, along with the same author and Charles Dumoulin, that if the sale has been completed and consummated by delivery on both sides—that is, if both the goods and the price have been handed over—then the dissolution of a contract that is entirely perfected and consummated cannot take place. Even if the exact same goods and the exact same price are returned by mutual consent, the prior purchase and sale is not considered extinguished and dis-

<column-break/>

solved, but rather a new one is celebrated. This is gathered from **Law 2 of the Digest on rescinding sales**. The laws cited thus far do not speak to this specific event, as is manifest to anyone weighing them carefully. Therefore, a distinct tax must be paid to the tax collector and the lord who hold office at the time of the second contract.

A purchase and sale with a pact of resale occurs when a thing is bought or sold with a condition added in favor of the seller: that when they restore to the buyer the price given for it, the contract is dissolved, and consequently the buyer is bound to restore the item to the seller for that same price. For this reason, insofar as the one who bought the item returns it for the same price at which they bought it, the execution of the added pact is called a **resale**; whereas insofar as the one who sold it receives it again for the same price, it is called a **redemption** of that thing. From this it happens that when a **census** <note>original: "census"; here, a type of annuity or the right to receive an annual payment from a property's income</note>—that is, the right of receiving a certain annual payment from someone—is bought for a sum of money with a pact of resale, it means that whenever the seller returns that same money...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal nature of contract dissolution, focusing specifically on the "pact of resale" and how profits or produce from a property are divided when a seller exercises their right to buy the property back.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 374

quantity, he remains free from the burden of paying that 
pension, the <term>annuity</term> <note>original: "census"; a financial arrangement where a person receives a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment charged against property</note> is called "redeemable," to distinguish it from the type of <insert>annuity</insert> or contract celebrated without such a clause, which is therefore called "perpetual" and "irredeemable," as we shall see in its proper place. If, however, we were to speak <term>strictly</term>, the execution of that attached agreement should be called a "dissolution" of the previous contract rather than a "redemption" or a "resale." This is because there is no repeated or second purchase and sale, as we shall see, but rather a dissolving of the first one.

<margin>3</margin> The **agreement to resell** <note>original: "pactum de retrovendendo"; a clause allowing a seller to buy back their property within a certain time</note> is added in various ways for the benefit of the seller. First, it can be without any specific time limit, allowing the seller or their heirs to redeem the property whenever they wish. Second, it can be made with a <term>fixed time</term> limit, which happens in two ways: either the seller must redeem it within a certain time (for example, within three or four years) or not at all; or, the seller is barred from redeeming it for a certain period (such as the first two or three years) but can do so thereafter, either for a fixed time or forever, as agreed between the parties.

A limitation can also be added stating that whenever the seller wishes to redeem the property, they must give notice six months before the harvest—or a similar condition—to avoid disputes and ensure the contract does not unfairly harm the buyer. Since the buyer holds <term>possession</term> of the purchased item in the meantime, if it were redeemed just before the harvest, they might receive little or no profit for their efforts.

<margin>4</margin> The **fruits** <note>original: "fructus"; the produce, rent, or profits generated by a property</note> of a thing bought with a resale agreement belong to the buyer for as long as it is not redeemed, because during that entire time, the buyer is the legal owner. However, as soon as it is redeemed—or as soon as the price is offered and the buyer is in "delay" <note>original: "mora"; a legal state where a party is late in fulfilling an obligation, incurring penalties</note> regarding its return—the fruits belong to the seller, who was the original owner. This is held in Law 2 of the Code on agreements between buyers and sellers, and in Book 1 of the **Portuguese Ordinances**, title 14, section 2, and title 27 at the beginning, by which these points are confirmed throughout this dispute.

<margin>5</margin> However, legal scholars † doubt how this should be understood. Does it mean that all fruits hanging on the trees or in the fields at the time of redemption belong to the seller who redeemed it, while only those already harvested belong to the buyer? Or should they instead be divided **proportionally** according to the time that the property belonged to the buyer and the time remaining that now belongs to the seller? Although many authors cited by **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva (1512–1577), a famous Spanish jurist</note> in his *Varied Resolutions*, chapter 15, number 6, assert the first view, Covarrubias himself—along with many others—strongly prefers the second: that the fruits should be divided proportionally according to time, as this is more consistent with **equity**. Primarily, because since the property produced the fruits while the buyer was the owner, fairness requires that the buyer have a share in them, just as the property bears fruit for the seller once ownership returns to them.

Furthermore, since the seller has enjoyed the use of the purchase money and its benefits during the entire time the buyer held the property, it is only fair that the buyer enjoys the fruits that the property produced under their ownership, 

<column-break/>

sharing in them according to the time and state in which those fruits existed under their ownership; especially since the **risk** of the property remained with the buyer during that whole time. Therefore, for the best legal reasons, Covarrubias and others argue that if the fruits were already ripe and ready to be gathered at the time of redemption, they belong entirely to the buyer. This is because they gained no further growth or value after the property was redeemed and returned to the seller's ownership. This opinion of Covarrubias, which he takes from Alexander and Cumanus, and which Alvaro Valasco also cites in Consultation 37 without disapproval, is the one I certainly approve of. It should be understood not just as a strict division of the calendar year, but as a proportional division based on when the property began to produce fruits under the buyer, the estimation of their value until the buyer's ownership ended, and the remaining time needed for the fruits to reach maturity or for new growth to appear, to be divided by the judgment of a prudent person.

In the same way and in the same proportion, any **rent** <note>original: "pensio"</note> should be divided between them if the property was leased to a third party. It follows that if the property is redeemed before it even begins to produce fruit, the entire future harvest belongs to the seller who redeemed it. However, the seller would then have to compensate the buyer for any expenses or labor the buyer put into cultivating or preparing the land that year. Furthermore, when fruits are divided as explained above, both the buyer and the seller must first be reimbursed from the harvest for their expenses and the value of their labor up to the point of harvest, with the remainder divided as described.

<margin>6</margin> When the "fruits" of a thing bought with a resale pact consist of its daily use—such as the use of a house, a horse, or a servant—then the use belongs to the buyer until the moment of redemption, and to the seller after redemption. Therefore, if the item was rented to a third party, the rent must be divided between the buyer and the seller proportional to the time it was owned by each. However, when the thing being redeemed is an **annuity**, it will be stated in its proper place how much of the annuity payment must be paid.

<margin>7</margin> Regarding Law 2 of the Code on agreements between buyers and sellers, we must say † that it does not strictly affirm that all "pending" fruits belong to the seller from the moment of redemption or from the moment of the buyer's delay. Rather, it affirms that the seller may henceforth sue for the fruits gathered from the time of the delay. This is understood to mean not every single fruit hanging at the time of the delay, but rather that portion of the fruits that would belong to the seller (as explained above) if the buyer had not been in delay in handing over the property.

<margin>8</margin> At this point, one must observe the **gloss** <note>an explanatory note in the margin or between lines of a legal text</note> commonly approved by scholars on Law 2 of the Code: even if the resale agreement does not explicitly state that the seller's heirs can redeem the property or that it can be redeemed from the buyer's heirs, this is nonetheless understood from the very nature of the agreement...

It argues for a proportional division based on equity, time of ownership, and labor invested, rather than a winner-take-all approach at the moment of redemption.</summary>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts
### Page 320

...it is understood that this right, by its nature, passes to the heirs on both sides. Therefore, unless the contracting parties expressly agree that the **agreement** shall not pass to the heirs, it certainly extends to them from both parties. If, then, an agreement is added stating that the sold item can be redeemed within a certain time and not thereafter, even if the seller dies within that period, his heirs can redeem it within that same time. However, once that time has passed, there will be no place for redemption, even if the heir is a minor who did not redeem it through a guardian or curator; for in that case, the benefit of <term>restoration to the original state</term> <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy where a person is returned to their previous legal position, often used to help minors who failed to meet a deadline</note> will not be granted to him. The reason is that this time was established by the contract and the agreement of the parties, and for that reason, it runs against successors even if they are minors. The same applies to a <term>forfeiture clause</term> <note>original: "pactum legis commissoriae"; a provision where a contract is cancelled if the price is not paid by a set date</note> regarding the time given for payment. This is gathered from the law *Aemilius* in the Digest regarding minors, and is the common opinion of the doctors including Bartolus, which Antonio Gómez affirms in volume 2 of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 27. If, however, the heir—whether a minor or an adult—was ignorant of the agreement and for that reason did not redeem the property, restoration to the original state is granted to him so that he may still redeem it. So says Antonio Gómez in the same place with many others whom he cites, arguing from the text in the first law of the Digest on the grounds for restoring minors.

<margin>Question 9</margin> When it is stated in a contract of sale with a **pact of resale** that the seller may redeem the sold property whenever he wishes, with no fixed time limit, many authors—whom Antonio Gómez and Gregorio López (on the *Siete Partidas*, law 42, title 5, part 5, gloss 1) cite—argued that unless the property was redeemed within thirty years (others said forty), it would thereafter become irredeemable. They were led by the fact that from such an agreement a **personal action** <note>a legal claim against a specific person, rather than a claim on the property itself</note> results against the buyer to redeem the thing. A personal action, both under <term>Common Law</term> <note>original: "ius commune"; the shared legal system of Roman and Canon law in Europe</note> and under Justinian's law, is prescribed after thirty years—and under the law of Castile after twenty years, as was seen in Disputation 71. However, the opinion of Antonio Gómez and Gregorio López in the cited places is preferred (though López is somewhat hesitant because of the Law of Castile): namely, that the property can then be redeemed **forever**, both by the seller and by his heirs. The reason is that by the agreement of the parties, an action and obligation can be extended infinitely. In the matter proposed, since it is expressly stated in the agreement that the seller can redeem the property "whenever he wishes," it is deemed to have been agreed between the contractors that at whatever time in perpetuity the seller wishes, he can redeem the property.

<margin>Decision</margin> And this opinion, besides other laws cited by Antonio Gómez, is clearly proven from the law *quod si nolit* in the Digest on the Edict of the Aediles. There it is held that if an agreement is made between a buyer and seller that whenever the item displeases the buyer, it should be returned, it can be returned forever. Furthermore, in the <term>papal bull</term> on the creation of censuses, Pope Pius V decreed that the right which a seller of a census has to redeem it under a pact of resale can never be lost to time. Add to this that in a pact of resale, the seller reserves the faculty for himself so that whenever he or his heirs wish, they may redeem the sold property. For an action against the buyer, it is first necessary that the seller or his heirs choose to redeem and

<column-break/>

offer the price to the buyer, and only if he refuses does the action begin which ought to be limited by the time established by law. The action itself, and that other prerequisite which makes the action possible, are two very different things.

<margin>10</margin> The **doubt** is: if someone buys property with a pact of resale, and in the meantime while the seller has the right to redeem it, the buyer sells it and delivers it to a third party, does the first seller have the right and action to pull it out of the power of that third party? Johannes Medina (final question on usury) answers in the affirmative. For he thinks that through the pact of resale, a **right in the thing** <note>original: "ius in re"; a property right that follows the object itself, rather than just the person</note> remains with the first seller, and for that reason, a **real action** <note>an action to recover property from whoever possesses it</note> is available to him to extract it from the power of anyone into whose hands it has come. Covarrubias embraces the same sentence (chapter 8, number 3) along with Paolo di Castro and many others. He is led by the law *si cum venderet* in the Digest on pledge actions, which holds that if a creditor sold a pledge of his debtor to a third party with an agreement that whenever the debtor returned the price, he would restore his pledge, then the creditor is held to yield that action against that buyer, and the debtor may sue that buyer either by "reclaiming the thing" (*rei vindicatio*), which is a real action and supposes a right in the thing, or by an action based on the facts or the written words, which is personal. From this, Covarrubias and others conclude that a right in the thing and a real action result from a pact of resale, and for that reason, it can be extracted from the power of a third-party buyer to whom it was delivered.

<margin>11</margin> However, the **contrary opinion** is more common and should be embraced; Antonio Gómez and Gregorio López refer to and follow it. Namely, that from a pact of resale, the seller does not gain a right in the thing or a real action, but only a **personal action** against the first buyer to dissolve the first sale and return the purchased thing—provided it still remains in the ownership of the buyer or his universal successors. Otherwise, if it has been transferred to the ownership of another, the action is for **damages** <note>original: "id quod interest"; the difference in value or loss suffered</note>. Law 42, title 5, part 5 clearly contains this opinion, for it says:

> The buyer is obliged to return the thing in every way if it is in his power; and if it is not in his power, he must pay the seller for all damages and losses that came to him because he did not return that thing which he had thus sold.

Behold, when the thing is no longer in the power of the buyer, only a personal action for damages is granted to the first seller against the buyer, and no real action against the current possessor. The reason for this opinion is manifest: because a pact of resale is something less than an actual sale; it is only an obligation to sell the thing back, or to dissolve the prior sale, if the first seller wishes to redeem it. Therefore, since from an actual sale where delivery has not followed, only a personal action is available (as proved in Disputation 369), it follows that from a pact of resale, only a personal action is available. This is clearly confirmed by Law 2 of the Code on agreements between buyer and seller, which grants the seller only a personal action from a pact of resale. Unless, therefore, something intervenes for the reasons we discussed in Disputation 369, the prior creditor is preferred to the later one, nothing hindering the fact that to the later one there was...

Second Treatise, Disputation 374.

...if the delivery is made to the second buyer and not the first, the original seller will certainly not be granted a legal action to extract the property from the person to whom it was sold and delivered by the first buyer, even if an **agreement of redemption** <note>original: "pactum de retrouendendo"; a clause allowing the seller to buy back the item</note> was included in the first sale for his benefit. Note, however, that if in the first sale a condition was expressly added along with the redemption agreement stating that the buyer, while the seller still had the power to redeem the property, could not alienate it to anyone other than the first seller, then the first seller could extract that property from the power of the person to whom it was sold and delivered. This is because, according to what was reported at the end of Disputation 370 regarding both common law and <term>Portuguese law</term> <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, such a sale is null and void by the law itself.

Regarding the points that led Covarruvias and others to a different conclusion, it must be said that the text they cite should be understood as follows: a seller has a claim to recover the property <note>original: "rei vendicatio"; a legal action where an owner seeks to recover their property from someone else</note> if a creditor sold a pledge without observing all the requirements for selling it. In that case, through such a sale—especially one made with that specific agreement—the debtor did not lose ownership of the pledge, and for that reason, he can act through a claim to recover the property. Such a sale would be, in effect, like a second pledging. If, however, the creditor sold it while observing all the requirements, the debtor would only have a personal action based on the facts <note>original: "actione in factum personali"</note>. I should also mention that the <gloss>gloss</gloss> and Bartolus assert that the addition in that text regarding the "action based on the facts" is a correction of the words "claim to recover the property." Furthermore, as Bartolus notes in the same place from that same text, this is a privilege granted to a debtor in relation to his pledge; therefore, it is not permitted to extend this privilege to a seller with a redemption agreement.

<margin>Legal Question</margin>
### 12
The question is: if something is sold with an **agreement of redemption**, is the <term>sales tax</term> <note>original: "alcauala"; a common tax in Spain and its colonies on the sale of goods</note> owed, especially if the first sale is later dissolved by the fulfillment of the added agreement? The doctors of law commonly agree that the tax is owed from that first sale. The reason is that the sale was pure and perfect, and the added redemption agreement did not hinder it. Therefore, the right once acquired by the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fisco"</note> from that sale is not lost by the subsequent resolution of the contract by virtue of the added redemption agreement. This is the view of Antonio Gómez, volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 34, and Law 70 of Toro, number 30; Pinellus on the Code regarding the rescinding of sales, part 2, chapter 3, number 36; Laffarte on the tithe of sales, chapter 14, number 36; and many others whom they cite.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The same is established in Portugal <note>original: "en os artigos das sisas"; referring to the Portuguese tax regulations</note> on page 2, paragraph 1, where such a contract is considered purely made, regardless of the fact that the wording may sometimes appear to be conditional. It is commanded that the <term>tax</term> <note>original: "gabella"</note> be paid to the tax collector of the year in which the contract was celebrated, regardless of whether the condition under which the contract appeared to be made is fulfilled in another year.

### 13
A greater doubt is whether another tax is owed from the "un-selling" <note>original: "distractu"</note> and resale. However, it must be said, along with the aforementioned authors, that it is not owed. The legitimate reason is that this is not a second sale, but a resolution of the first, and it is done in execution of the agreement to dissolve the sale that was added to the first sale before it was perfected. Just as a sale can be dissolved by an added agreement before it is fulfilled by both sides and by the returning of what 

<column-break/>

was given by the other side (as was seen in the preceding disputation), so also it can be dissolved by a similar agreement added at the time, even if the execution of it happens after the sale is complete. No new tax is owed from the resolution of a sale, as was said in the preceding disputation.

If, however, after a sale has been perfected on both sides by the delivery of the goods and the price, with no redemption agreement added, the contracting parties should later agree that the thing be redeemed for the same price, then that would be considered an entirely new sale, and a new and distinct tax would be owed to the tax collector who was in office at the time of such a second agreement. This is because the resolution of a contract of buying and selling has no place after it has been perfected by fulfillment on both sides, as was said in the preceding disputation. Indeed, if at the time of the first agreement a redemption clause were added stating that the thing could be redeemed for a higher or lower price, or that part of the goods could be redeemed for the total price, it is considered a second sale, and a distinct tax would be owed from it, as Laffarte rightly says in the place cited above, number 41, and as is easily seen from what was said in the preceding disputation. For once the process has moved to delivery by one party, a variation in the contract is not permitted in such a way that it is considered one and the same slightly varied contract—which is what happens when the matter is still untouched and something regarding the goods or the price is increased or decreased, as was said in the preceding disputation. Much less can it be considered the same contract when, after the first has been entirely fulfilled by both sides, a variation should intervene by the consent of the parties in a second agreement and its fulfillment. Laffarte also well observes, along with <note>Charles Dumoulin</note> <gloss>Carolus Molinzo</gloss>, that if a sale were made from the beginning, not with a redemption agreement, but with an agreement that if the buyer wanted to sell the thing, he would be bound to offer it to the first seller before other buyers, then—even if it were later resold to the first seller for the same price at which it was first sold—a distinct tax would be owed to the tax collector of the time of such resale. This is because that would not be a resolution of the first contract, but a new sale by virtue of that old added agreement.

### 14
There is a doubt whether, if a sale was made with a redemption agreement for up to six years, for example, and before those years are completed, an extension of time is made by the consent of the parties so that the thing can be redeemed for another six years, and the redemption occurs within the second six years after the first six have passed, a distinct tax is owed. Laffarte rightly responds, along with Charles Dumoulin and <note>André Tiraqueau</note> <gloss>Tiraquello</gloss>, that it is owed. Since that redemption is not made by virtue of the first agreement, but by virtue of a second agreement after the sale was entirely completed regarding the first agreement, it is not considered a resolution of the first sale, but a new and distinct sale as far as the right of the treasury is concerned; and therefore, a distinct tax is owed.

X

It determines that while a standard redemption agreement does not trigger a second sales tax, any new agreement or extension made after the original contract is finalized constitutes a new sale subject to additional taxation.</summary>
