# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

## Whether a purchase with a buy-back clause is lawful.

### DISPUTATION 375.

### S U M M A R Y.

1. Whether a purchase with a buy-back clause <note>original: "pactum de retrouendendo"</note> is lawful.
2. The buy-back clause is not prohibited by any law.
3. The buy-back clause is not injurious to either of the contracting parties, nor is it prejudicial to the buyer.
4. Regarding the law of Castile and Portugal, see number 4.
5. Why a purchase with a buy-back clause is lawful.
6. Whether the buy-back clause makes the property worth less, such that the buyer is required to lower the price, and by how much; see number 8.
7. A purchase made with a buy-back clause involving a reduction in price is rejected and judged as usurious.
9. The price reduction that occurs due to a buy-back clause: how the "just price" <note>the fair market value determined by common estimation</note> should be understood.
10. How restitution in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal spiritual forum of the soul, as opposed to a public legal court</note> should be made in cases where property was bought at a reduced price with a buy-back clause.

<margin>Question 1</margin> While reserving for its proper place the discussion on the purchase of an annuity <term>census</term> <note>a "census" was a common financial contract where one party paid a lump sum in exchange for an annual return from the fruits of a property</note> with a buy-back clause, the question is asked whether the type of purchase discussed in the preceding disputation is lawful. The side that argues it is not lawful can be supported by the following: as held in **Leviticus 25**, all possessions that the children of Israel bought from one another were bought with a buy-back clause. The buyers were required to count the fruits they gathered as part of the price until the time of redemption. For instance, if someone bought a possession for forty gold coins, and the fruits gathered until the time of redemption were valued at ten gold coins, the seller would only be bound to return thirty gold coins to receive his possession back. Therefore, since that law was just—having been given by God—it follows that the opposite is unjust. Consequently, a purchase with a buy-back clause that does *not* count the gathered fruits toward the price would be unjust.

<margin>Decision</margin> Nevertheless, the common and true opinion is that it is lawful. This is the view embraced by Conradus in *On Contracts*, question 83; Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 8, number 4; and others whom we shall cite extensively when we examine the same issue regarding the annuity with a buy-back clause. It can be proven as follows:

<margin>2</margin> First, because a purchase is lawful without a buy-back clause, as is self-evident. However, a buy-back clause is not prohibited by any law, nor is it injurious to either party or prejudicial. Therefore, it is lawfully added, and consequently, the purchase with the buy-back clause is lawful. The first part of this—that the buy-back clause is prohibited by no law—will be clear from the citations of both divine and human law below. The second part—that it is not injurious or prejudicial to the contracting parties—is proven thus:

It is not injurious to the seller, since the clause is added for his benefit. It is the buyer who is burdened by it, as he cannot freely dispose of the property by virtue of this

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> agreement while the seller retains the right to redeem it; he is also bound to sell it back to the seller whenever the seller wishes to redeem it according to the agreement. That it is neither injurious nor prejudicial to the buyer is also proven. Not only because he consented to the agreement knowingly, willingly, and under no necessity, but also because this burden is estimable in money. Thus, if the price of the property in a sale with a buy-back clause is lowered by as much as a prudent person would estimate the burden to be worth, the buyer suffers no injury or prejudice by purchasing the thing for that price with that burden attached.

Second, if a purchase with a buy-back clause were inherently unlawful, it would be primarily because it seems usurious <note>usury was the sinful practice of charging interest on a loan</note>, as the buyer receives the full principal back when the property is redeemed—just as if he had given a loan—and yet he gains the fruits of the property in the interim. However, no usury is found in such a contract. First, usury requires a loan <term>mutuum</term> <note>a "mutuum" is a specific type of loan where the exact same amount or quality of a fungible item, like money or grain, must be returned</note>, at least in substance, as has been seen in the section on usury. For a loan, the lender must have the power to demand the return of the principal at some time. This is not seen in the case proposed: for we assume there is no power in the buyer to demand the price back, but only in the seller to buy the thing back for that price if he wishes. Furthermore, the buyer with a buy-back clause acquires ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the thing so purchased; if it perishes in the interim while it is not redeemed, it perishes for him, and the seller is not bound to return the price to him. In this, there is no loan, even in substance, but a pure purchase. Therefore, no usury can occur regarding his perception of the fruits of that thing, which at that time is his own. It follows, then, that this type of contract is lawful.

<margin>4</margin> Added to this, besides common law, are the laws of Castile and Portugal, which approve purchase with a buy-back clause. Furthermore, Pope Martin V in the first *Extravagant* <note>a term for papal decretals not originally included in major canon law collections</note>, Pope Calixtus III in the second *Extravagant* on buying and selling, and Pope Pius V in the bull on the creation of annuities, all approve the annuity <term>census</term> with a buy-back clause. At first glance, there seemed to be greater difficulty in that than in the purchase of other things with a buy-back clause, as we shall see in its proper place. This is also supported by our own laws on buying and selling: when a purchase with a buy-back clause is condemned because the price given was too low, it implies by contrary logic that it is approved when the price is commensurate with the thing being bought under that agreement. Finally, this is confirmed by **Leviticus 25**, where the Lord commanded that possessions be sold with a buy-back clause—especially houses that were not within walls nor belonged to the Levites.

<margin>5</margin> The fact that a purchase with a buy-back clause is lawful regardless of how the agreement is varied—according to the modes proposed in the preceding disputation—is proven as follows: Since it is entirely within the buyer's right to buy the thing at a just price without any agreement, the addition of the agreement (in whatever mode) works in favor of the seller. Even though it is more favorable if the power to redeem is granted in perpetuity than if it is granted only for a time, the buyer is still prohibited...

<sig>x</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...prohibited from [preventing the redemption]</meta>

<summary>This page argues for the legality and morality of buy-back agreements in sales. Molina concludes that such contracts are not usurious because the buyer assumes the risk of ownership and the seller is not forced to repay the money like a loan.</summary>
<keywords>buy-back clause, right of redemption, usury, Levitical law, just price, ownership risk, Spanish law, Portuguese law, papal bulls, annuities</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into the "pactum de retrouendendo" (buy-back agreement). The previous section established that these agreements are generally lawful; this page specifically addresses how such a clause affects the "just price" of a property and refutes the idea that a property's value remains unchanged when it is subject to redemption.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 375.

...the buyer may be allowed to redeem the property at a higher price: therefore, in whatever way the agreement is varied, the buyer remits something that was not strictly necessary to remit for the justice of the sale. If the pact turns in favor of the seller, it follows that by adding such a pact, no injustice is done to the seller. Rather, it is a "grace" <note>a favor or act of kindness</note>—strictly speaking, if the buyer does not decrease the fair price because of the pact; or loosely speaking, if he does lower the price so that an equality is maintained between the price and the property burdened by that pact. From this, it follows that no injury is done to the buyer by including such a clause.

**6** † There was a certain Henry of Oyta <note>original: "Henricus Oita," a 14th-century Viennese theologian</note>—cited by Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart</note> and reported by Medina <note>Juan de Medina</note> in his final question on usury—who asserted that a property with a buy-back clause is worth no less than a property without one. For this reason, he argued that a buyer with a buy-back clause cannot lawfully lower the price from what it would be without the clause. His reasoning was that the property retains the same nature and, therefore, the same value; thus, it is a sin to reduce anything from the otherwise just price because of that agreement. His other, less significant arguments and their solutions can be read in the works of the cited doctors.

The common opinion of the learned doctors rightly affirms the contrary. It is clear that the "burden" <note>original: "onus"</note> of not being able to sell the property to others in the meantime—since the seller has the right to redeem it—and the obligation of the buyer to sell it back whenever the seller wishes within the timeframe, is a burden that can be valued in money. This is no different than other burdens of service <term>servitūta</term> <note>legal obligations attached to land, like easements</note>, such as being required to grind grain at the lender’s mill and similar things discussed in the section on usury, which are estimable in price. Therefore, an additional burden attached to the property being bought surely makes it of lesser value. A buyer, in order to undergo that burden, may demand a competent compensation: namely, that the price be decreased relative to the valuation of the property as seen in itself. Furthermore, when a property is bought with such a pact, the buyer does not acquire full ownership <term>plenum dñium</term> <note>total legal control over a property</note>, which usually follows all the rights of full ownership. This is because the seller reserves a certain right for himself. Just as when a property has a legal easement, or when the seller retains either the direct or useful ownership <note>distinctions in feudal law between who owns the title and who uses the land</note>, it is worth less than when it is sold with full ownership; so too when it is sold with a buy-back clause, it is worth less because of the right the seller reserves than it would be if sold free of that pact.

Regarding the point that led that author [Oyta] to his conclusion, it must be said that the value of a thing is not estimated according to its "nature" <note>its essential existence</note>, but according to its use and the convenience derived from it. As was explained and shown when we dealt with the price of goods, for this reason, although the property retains the same nature with that pact, it does not have the same convenience for the uses that usually flow from ownership; therefore, it is not of such great value as it would be if sold without that pact.

As for the argument proposed at the beginning of this disputation for the negative side, it should be known that God—for the sake of His people, so that possessions would not leave the families among whom they were divided, and so that some would not hold many possessions

<column-break/>

while others remained with none—commanded in that place <note>referring to the Bible</note> that possessions could not be sold for longer than until the Year of Jubilee. At the Jubilee, they would return to their ancient owners freely and without any price. Therefore, a possession sold in that manner was worth only as much as the use and convenience of it could be valued until the Year of Jubilee. For that reason, if the Year of Jubilee was far off, those possessions were valued more; if it was near, they were valued at a lower price. Likewise, God perceived that by that law, possessions were bought such that if the seller wished to redeem the possession before the Year of Jubilee, he could do so for the price at which he sold it; however, the buyer was then bound to compensate, as part of the price, the value of the fruits [harvests] he had received.

From this law, only houses within the walls of a city or town were excepted, provided they did not belong to the Levites. When these two conditions met—that they were within walls and not owned by Levites—they were considered sold forever, with a right of redemption lasting only one year. However, houses that either belonged to Levites or were not within walls fell under the same law as other possessions that were not houses. All of this is found in Leviticus 25.

Regarding the proposed argument: even if the major and minor premises are granted in the sense that the [divine] law contained no injustice, the conclusion—that the opposite situation must contain injustice—must be denied. For it can very well happen that between two contradictory options, neither contains injustice. Just because God did no injustice in creating the world, it does not follow that He would have done an injustice if He had not created the world.

Observe at this point the law "To Our [People]" <note>original: "ad nostram," a reference to Canon Law regarding sales</note> regarding buying and selling, and in the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 14, § 2, and title 27, § 1.

**7** † When something is bought with a buy-back clause and the price is diminished, the contract is rejected and judged as usurious. To understand these laws, one must observe: If the contracting parties truly intend to buy and sell with a buy-back clause, usury does not occur in the "court of conscience" <note>internal moral standing before God</note>, even if the price is greatly reduced. This is because in that contract, neither in fact nor in spirit, is there a "loan" <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, without which usury cannot exist. However, the purchase will be unjust due to the inequality of the price. Hence, one who buys in that way at a greatly diminished price sins against justice and is bound to make restitution, but he does not incur the penalties for usurers in the court of conscience. The doctors commonly agree on this; on this matter, read among others Navarrus <note>Martín de Azpilcueta</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 248. However, in the "external forum" <note>public legal courts</note>, if a property is bought with a buy-back clause and the price is greatly diminished, it is presumed that the buyer's intent was not to buy, but to give a loan, taking the property as a pledge <note>collateral</note> and profiting from its fruits in the meantime while the loan is not repaid, without counting those fruits toward the principal. Therefore, in the external forum, that contract is judged usurious.

Many authors gather this opinion, among whom Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias</note> refers in the third volume of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 8, number 3, and the fourth; and Álvaro Valasco, *Consultation 70*, from the chapter "To Our [People]" on buying and selling, and those cited Portuguese Ordinances.

<summary>This page argues that a buy-back clause legally and morally reduces a property's value because it limits the buyer's ownership rights. It also explains how significantly low prices in such contracts are treated as usurious loans in legal courts, even if the parties' intentions were technically for a sale.</summary>
<keywords>buy-back clause, just price, ownership rights, usury, Leviticus 25, Year of Jubilee, Henry of Oyta, Portuguese Law, internal vs external forum</keywords>

--- Page 388 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal presumptions of usury in contracts featuring a buy-back clause (pactum de retrouendendo), specifically within the context of Portuguese and Canon law. It focuses on how the "just price" is calculated when such a clause is present and the obligations of restitution if a contract is found to be usurious.</meta>

...[the Portuguese jurists] decreed that this law must be observed. They added that if the price were diminished by a fourth part of the **just price** <note>The "just price" (pretium iustum) was a medieval economic concept asserting that there is a morally objective value for goods and services based on common estimation, rather than just supply and demand.</note>, the contract must be judged as **usurious**, and the buyer would incur the penalties of usurers.

From this, it follows that under **Portuguese law**, there is a legal presumption—specifically a "presumption of law and by law" <note>original: "praesumptio iuris et de iure," a legal term for a presumption that cannot be rebutted by evidence</note>—that the contract is usurious. Consequently, a person buying in this manner must be declared to have incurred the penalties of usury, with no proof to the contrary being admitted. Furthermore, since a usurious contract is void by the law itself, and ownership of the property (which is treated as a mere pledge) does not pass to the recipient, it follows that the seller is granted a **claim for the property** <term>rei vendicatio: a legal action by which an owner demands the return of their physical property from whoever possesses it</term>. This is a "real action" <note>an action against the thing itself, not just the person</note> and is not restricted by the time limits that usually apply to personal legal actions, as Alvaro Valasco rightly affirms in the cited location, number 5.

However, although perhaps the majority of doctors derive this doctrine from the chapter *Ad nostram* <note>A reference to a specific chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding usury</note> and believe it must be strictly observed in Portugal, Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note>, Covarrubias, and many others observe (not without reason) that this cannot be sufficiently concluded from that chapter alone. Indeed, in the case described in that text where someone is judged usurious by presumption, it was not merely those two circumstances <note>a low price and a buy-back clause</note> that occurred, but two others as well. First, the buyer was accustomed to lending at usury; fearing the penalties of usurers, he chose not to give a loan but instead "bought" the property in this manner. Thus, many authorities—whom Covarrubias, Alvaro Valasco, and Gama cite—believe this third circumstance should be added. The second additional circumstance was the inclusion of a pact in the contract stating that the buyer could not redeem the property before seven years, nor after nine years. Thus, the buyer intended to profit from at least seven years of fruits <note>the income or produce from the land</note>, while knowing that because of the low price, the property would certainly be redeemed after the seven years. Hence, Covarrubias rightly judges that, based on canon law alone, it should be left to the **discretion of a prudent judge** to define whether a contract should be held as usurious by legal presumption when not all four circumstances are present, but only some of them.

<margin>8</margin>
It was stated above that a **property sold with a buy-back pact** is worth less than if it were sold without such a pact. This is confirmed by various legal authorities, including Navarrus, Covarrubias, Alvaro Valasco, and Gama, who report the common opinion of the doctors affirming the same. Some of these doctors argued that a property with a buy-back pact is worth nearly **one-third less** than one without it; for example, if a property is worth 100 gold coins normally, it might be worth about 70 with the pact. Others said that the price should never be reduced by more than a third from the otherwise just price. However, the cited doctors rightly assert, along with others, that this matter must be defined by the judgment of a prudent person in each region, taking into account the local customs and the common estimation of people there—which matters greatly in determining the just price, as was discussed previously when we spoke on that topic. They adds with very good reason that a property is worth less if the buy-back pact is perpetual (or without a set time limit) than if it has a time limit; likewise, it is worth more if the buy-back period is short rather than long.

<column-break/>

<margin>9</margin>
A doubt arises: when our aforementioned rule on buying and selling considers a contract usurious because the price was greatly diminished and those other circumstances concur (and in the **Portuguese Ordinances** it is deemed usurious when the price falls short of the just price by a fourth part), should this be understood as the just price of the property *if it were sold without the buy-back pact*, or rather the just price of the property *with the buy-back pact*? As we have said, the just price of the property in the latter case is far lower than in the former. Alvaro Valasco and Pinellus think it should be understood as the just price of the property considered without any buy-back pact. I do not doubt, however, that this is false. The "just price" must be understood as the just price of the property considered **under that same buy-back pact**, as Gama and the rest of the doctors commonly affirm. This is more widely accepted in practice, as even Pinellus and Valasco admit, and equity itself demands it. Among other reasons, if the doctors we are disputing with concede that a buy-back pact can sometimes reduce the just value by a third, they would be forced to admit that the Portuguese ordinance (which calls a sale usurious if the price is reduced by a fourth) would label a sale usurious even if it were actually just when considering the burden of the buy-back clause. Nothing could be more absurd.

<margin>10</margin>
The next doubt is: when a property has been bought at a diminished price with a buy-back pact, and there is an **obligation to make restitution** in the "court of conscience" <note>the moral realm of the soul and the confessional, as opposed to a civil court</note>, how should that restitution be made? Specifically, should the price be increased to the "breadth of the just price" at the time the contract was made, while also paying the seller for the **lost profit** <term>lucrum cessans: a legal term for profits that were lost because money or property was withheld</term> caused by the missing portion of the price? Or should the buyer instead restore a portion of the yearly fruits gathered from the property, in the same proportion that the price deficit bears to the full just price? Following Juan Medina, we must say that restitution should be made in the **first way**; the buyer is bound to this whether it amounts to more than the portion of the fruits or not. The reason is that through that unjust purchase, the buyer acquired ownership of the whole thing; if the property had perished, it would have perished for the buyer, not the seller. For that reason, he made all those fruits his own, and he is only bound to bring the contract back to equality by paying for the damages—including lost profit—resulting from the fact that the price was not just from the beginning.

<summary>Molina discusses the legal and moral criteria for usury in buy-back contracts under Portuguese law, arguing that the "just price" must account for the decreased value caused by the buy-back clause itself. He concludes that restitution for an unfair price should involve paying the difference plus lost interest, rather than surrendering a portion of the property's produce.</summary>

Second Treatise, Disputation 376.

# Whether a purchase with a pact of resale at a higher price is licit. And whether the property, while it is not yet redeemed, can be licitly leased back to the seller.

## DISPUTATION 376.

### S U M M A R Y

1. *How buyers with a pact of resale may licitly lease the property to the seller while it remains unredeemed.*
2. *How a purchase with a pact of resale at a higher price than was set in the first sale is licit.*
3. *With two declarations. number 3.*

<margin>1</margin> Two proposed doubts remain to be explained. To begin with the latter, which involves less difficulty: it must be said that if the contracting parties truly intend to perform those two contracts simultaneously—namely, the purchase of a house at a certain price with a pact of resale, and a lease by which the buyer leaves that house to the seller as a tenant—and if the price of each contract is proportionate to the value of the thing for which it is given, these are licit; nothing prevents them from being celebrated at the same time. This is the judgment of Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist known as "Doctor Navarrus."</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 248; Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), an influential theologian.</note> under the word "usury," 2, question 15, second pronouncement; Conrad <note>Conradus Summenhart (1450–1502), an expert on contracts.</note> on contracts, question 83, at 12; and Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Dominican theologian.</note> on the *Second-Second*, question 77, article 1. The reason is that one is a just purchase and the other is a just lease; since they are done together, no injustice or other iniquity arises from that fact alone.

However, if the first contract were not a true purchase but a loan of money cloaked in the guise of a purchase—such that if the property perished during the time of the lease, the loss would fall on the seller—then both contracts would be a true usurious loan, simulated under the name of a false purchase and lease. Such contracts are presumed as such in the external court if they are made by someone who habitually lends at usury, as Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a great canon lawyer.</note> says in the chapter *Illos vos*, on pledges, number 5. Furthermore, if both contracts were indeed a true purchase and lease, but the purchase price was too low or the lease price too high, then the contract would be unjust (though not usurious), and the buyer and lessor would be bound to make restitution for the excess or deficiency in price. If the buyer were accustomed to lending at usury, or if other circumstances created a strong presumption that simulated usury was involved in these contracts, he could be condemned in the external court as a usurer, according to what was said shortly before and in the preceding disputation. He would also sin by the sin of scandal if, when he celebrated those contracts, he noticed (or ought to have noticed) that others might take scandal from them.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the second doubt—namely, whether a purchase with a pact that the resale be made at a higher price than the first sale is licit—Conrad, in his work on contracts, question 84, conclusion 4, seems to assert along with certain others that such a contract is illicit. This is because the condition of both contracting parties would not be equal; and because, if the price given for the property in the first purchase was a just price, the higher price brought into the pact for the redemption

<sig>X 3</sig>

<column-break/>

of that same property will be unjust. Medina <note>Bartolomé de Medina (1527–1581), a Dominican theologian at Salamanca.</note> in the last question on usury, whom Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> follows in his *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 9, number 5, is of the contrary opinion. Namely, that it is not always illicit to stipulate in a pact that if the sold property is redeemed, the redemption should occur at a higher price. For, they say, in a purchase with a pact of resale, two contracts of buying and selling are seen: one by which the property is first bought, and another by which it is later redeemed. Certainly, if each is celebrated at a just price, according to the value of the property at the time each contract is executed, both will be licit.

Therefore, since it can sometimes happen that the property is expected to be worth more at the time the second contract is executed than it is worth at the time of the first, there will be no injustice if the purchase is then celebrated with a pact that the price in the resale shall increase by as much as the property is estimated to be worth then (more or less), or that the resale price shall rise or fall according to what its value is found to be at that time. An example is if someone buys a horse's foal with a pact of resale within two years; in that time, speaking morally, it will be of far greater price. There will be no injustice if it is stipulated in the pact that the seller is bound to increase the price by as much as the foal is estimated to be worth then, or as much as it is found to be worth at the time of redemption. Indeed, if the pact of resale were made so that the seller only paid the price he originally received for it, the contract would surely be unjust to the detriment of the first buyer. For the buyer, having bought the property at a just price, would be forced to resell it below the lowest just price <note>The "lowest just price" refers to the bottom of the acceptable market range for a good's value.</note>. Nor does it matter that in the entire intermediate time he had made use of the foal's fruits—for instance, if he had leased it or used it himself. For not only had he incurred expenses for it, and had it perished in that middle time, it would have perished for him <note>Meaning the buyer bears the financial risk of the item being destroyed or dying while he owns it.</note>, but also because it had grown in quality and value while under his ownership, that value certainly belongs to him. Another example: if a merchant at the time of the new harvest buys several measures of wheat which he intends to keep until a time when he hopes they will be worth more, and the seller asks that the purchase be made with a pact of resale at that future time; then the buyer can justly demand that the redemption be at the price it is expected to be worth then, according to the chapter *Naviganti* <note>A famous decree by Pope Gregory IX regarding the maritime loan and risk.</note> on usury, or at the price it is actually found to be worth at that time.

This opinion certainly pleases me, especially if it is understood that if the price of the property was somewhat diminished in the first purchase because of the burden of the resale pact which the buyer took upon himself, then in the redemption, one should not seek as much of an increase in price as the property is expected to be worth above the price given for it, but rather how much it is expected to be worth above the price at which that same property would have been bought in the first sale without a pact of resale. For the seller should not be forced to pay that portion of the price in the redemption which he himself deducted for the buyer because of the burden of the resale pact. Medina argues that the contract should not be condemned even if the pact includes the total increase the property has gained over the price given for it. Although, however...

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "autem" (however), indicating the argument continues on the next page regarding Medina's stricter interpretation of price increases.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legality of leasing property back to a seller under a buy-back agreement and whether the buy-back price can be higher than the original sale price. It concludes that both are licit if the prices are "just" and reflect changes in market value or the growth/improvement of the property (like a foal) over time.</summary>
<keywords>just price, pact of resale, buy-back clause, usury, leasing, risk of loss, contract law, Navarrus, Medina, scholastic economics</keywords>

--- Page 390 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 376 regarding the "pact of resale" (buy-back clause). The previous page addressed the legality of leasing property back to the original seller. Here, Molina concludes his thoughts on price differences in buy-back agreements before moving to Disputation 377, which focuses on contracts where the option to rescind lies solely with the buyer.</meta>

...however, while that opinion regarding scholastic rigor <note>original: "de rigore ſcolaſtico"; Molina refers to the strict theological interpretations of usury common in the schools</note> does not seem worthy of condemnation, it does not seem to be something to be asserted without caution. For that reason, I said what I did, especially if the opinion of Medina and Covarrubias <note>Bartolomé de Medina and Diego de Covarrubias, prominent 16th-century Spanish theologians and jurists.</note> is understood in the manner I just explained.

<margin>2</margin>
I would advise two points † regarding this same opinion. The first is: When a buyer, by virtue of his profession, buys something to resell it at a higher price—such as a bookseller who buys the books of scholars to resell them and make a profit—a contract of resale for that higher price would be licit, provided it is the same higher price at which the same bookseller would justly sell those same books to anyone else. This is because that same item, under these two different modes of selling, is worth more in the second sale than in the first, according to what was said above regarding the price of things. The fact that both contracts are made with the same person at different times contains no injustice, provided that those two contracts are genuine and not fictions used to disguise usury—namely, giving a loan under that veil in order to receive something beyond the principal.

For this reason, those in Lisbon and elsewhere where there are soldiers can be excused from usury and injustice; these are people whose trade is to buy and resell swords, clothing, and similar items (the Portuguese call them *ropaveiros*, and they are also called *aljababes* <note>original: "ropaueiros, Luſitani aljababes vocant"; terms for second-hand dealers or "old-clothes men" who often acted as pawnbrokers for soldiers.</note>). Often, soldiers go to them and, pressed by necessity or to have money for gambling, sell them their swords, clothes, and the like, asking that they keep those same items for them until they receive their wages, and then sell them back to them at a certain higher price established at the time of the first sale. If this higher price does not exceed what the dealer could justly receive from others, such a contract is not to be strictly condemned. Nevertheless, such men should be advised to deal more gently with miserable soldiers, to be content with a very moderate profit, and to ensure their intention is sincere—not to give a loan under that veil—and that no scandal is generated among others by this practice.

The second point is this: It might perhaps seem to someone that since the prices of things do not consist in an indivisible point <note>A technical legal concept meaning the "just price" is not a single fixed number, but a range (latitude) between a "rigorous" high price and a "pious" low price.</note> but have a certain range within the limits of justice, and a buyer can justly buy at the lowest price and refuse to sell except at the middle or rigorous price, then one could licitly buy something at the lowest price with a pact to resell it at the middle or rigorous price—even if the item is worth no more at the time of the redemption than at the time of the first purchase. However, this is by no means to be tolerated in the external court <note>The public legal system/law courts.</note> but must be condemned as usury unless, as was just said, the buyer is a professional reseller who buys to sell to others and, at the seller's request, reserves the item for him, giving him preference over others at the same price; this is a kind of benefit. Nor is it to be tolerated in the court of conscience <note>The internal moral judgment of the soul, often managed through confession.</note> except in the aforementioned case or something similar. For although it would be just if the agreements were made separately, it is not just when they are made at the same time (even if the execution of the second pact of resale happens later), unless it is likely that the item will be worth more at the time of the second pact's execution than at the first. Indeed, there is no just title why, at one and the same time and with one and the same person, someone can—before the thing has even become his—arrange for the item to be sold to him at a certain price and then be redeemed at a higher price by the same seller, unless some of the explained circumstances are present by which

<column-break/>

he might receive that increase in profit, or some other similar circumstance that might perhaps occur to someone.

It remains for us to respond to those two arguments that led Conrad <note>Conradus Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts and usury.</note> and others to universally condemn a purchase with a pact of resale at a higher price. To the first, it must be said that the inequality between those two contracting parties is not within one and the same pact, but in different ones, and it arises from a change in the value of the item at the time of the second execution, or from the fact that the item is worth more under the mode of the second sale than under the first, as explained. Such inequality is not unjust, as an inequality between the price and the item within one and the same pact would be.

Add to this that the better condition on the part of the first buyer is partly compensated by the fact that if the item perishes in the time between the first pact and the execution of the second, it perishes for the first buyer, and the second is not bound to restore the price to him.

To the second, the consequence must be denied: for a higher and lower price can be measured for one and the same thing, not only if the item undergoes a variety in value due to different times, but also if, under different modes of selling, it is worth more under one mode than another, as has been said.

# Whether a purchase with a pact of resale in the buyer's favor is licit. And universally, when a contract is dissolved, to whom the fruits gathered from the sold item in the meantime belong.

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological examination of "pacts of resale." While the previous discussion focused on the seller's right to buy back property, Disputation 377 shifts the focus to the buyer's right to force the seller to take the property back, a practice that raised significant concerns about usury in the 16th century.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 377.

Thus far, we have spoken regarding a sale with a pact of resale <term>pactum de retrovendendo; a clause allowing a seller to buy back their property at a later date</term> in favor of the seller—specifically, so that he himself might redeem the item whenever he wished within a set time limit. Now, we must truly examine whether a sale with a pact of resale in favor of the buyer is also permitted; that is, whether a contract is licit where the seller is bound to redeem the item whenever the buyer wishes.

<margin>1</margin>
Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian and jurist at the University of Salamanca.</note> in his work *On Justice and Law*, book 6, question 5, article 3, conclusion 1, asserted that this kind of contract is illicit and usurious unless the buyer counts all the "fruits" <gloss>fructus; produce, rent, or income generated by the property</gloss> gathered from that thing as part of the repayment of the price. He argues that if the buyer wished to take any of the fruits beyond the price itself, it would be usury—either open or disguised. This is because, through such a contract, the buyer always keeps his principal capital secure and can demand it back whenever he wants. This, Soto argues, is the defining characteristic of a loan <term>mutuum</term>, even if the contract is called a "sale." Certain others hold this same opinion.

In this place, we must examine before all else: when the dissolution or voiding of a contract is left to the will of the buyer, do the fruits gathered in the meantime belong to the buyer by the nature of the contract, or rather to the seller? And more universally: when a contract is dissolved, to whom do the interim fruits belong—the buyer or the seller?

<margin>2</margin>
Regarding the first point, all agree on what the question assumes: namely, that the dissolution of a contract can be granted to the will of the buyer no less than to the seller. This is clear in itself, as there is nothing that prevents the one more than the other. Furthermore, this is clearly gathered from the laws <note>original: "l. si res ita. ff. de contrah. empt. & ex l. quod si nolit. §. si quid ita. ff. de ædil. edict." These refer to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law.</note> which state: if something is sold with a pact that it may be returned if the item displeases the buyer, such a pact is valid. If, however, the time is not limited in which the buyer must say the item displeases him, and it is not explicitly said he can dissolve it "whenever," then a time limit of sixty days is legally assumed. But if it were said he could dissolve the contract whenever it displeased him, then he could dissolve it in perpetuity. This same conclusion is reached by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canonist.</note>, Medina, Covarrubias, and others.

<margin>3</margin>
However, regarding the specific question this assumes, not everyone agrees. Panormitanus and certain others think that when the dissolution of the contract is left to the buyer's will, the fruits gathered by him in the meantime do not belong to him, but by the nature of the contract must be restored to the seller. Therefore, in the matter we are disputing, they consequently affirm that the buyer is bound to count the fruits gathered from the purchased item as part of the price. Others, including Medina and Covarrubias, assert that the fact that the dissolution is left to the buyer's will does not prevent the interim fruits from belonging to the buyer. Thus, they believe the interim fruits belong to the buyer as produce of his own property

<column-break/>

for that duration of time.

<margin>4 Question</margin>
As for the second point—namely, to whom do the interim fruits universally belong when a contract is dissolved after the item has been delivered and the price paid—legal experts vary greatly. One may read their opinions in the works of Covarrubias and others.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Setting aside other opinions, I believe a distinction must be made—not only in conscience but also in the external court—based on what the laws suggest and the light of nature (from which the laws proceeded) teaches. This is partly in agreement with Covarrubias and partly with Medina. A contract is dissolved either because of a "past cause" or because of an "added pact" that it may be dissolved in the future. If it is dissolved because of a past cause—for example, because the item is found to have been defective at the time the contract was made—then the fruits gathered in the meantime belong to the seller. In such an event (as shown in Disputation 353), a "redhibitory action" <term>actio redhibitoria; a legal claim to cancel a sale due to hidden defects</term> is granted to dissolve the contract, as the buyer would not have bought it had he known the defect. In this case, the contract is considered to have been invalid from the start.

If, however, the contract is dissolved due to an added pact for the future, then we must stand with Medina's distinction. Such a pact can be added to a contract of buying and selling in two ways. One: so that if a certain event occurs, the item is held as "unsold" or the contract is considered as never having been celebrated. The other: not so that the item is held as unsold, but so that the item may be redeemed <note>i.e., bought back as a new transaction</note>.

In the first case, because the contract (by the very agreement of the parties) is considered as never having happened, the interim fruits belong to the seller. It does not matter that the item belonged to the buyer during that time if it had been delivered to him. This is the reasoning behind an "addiction in diem" <term>pactum adiectionis in diem; a clause allowing a seller to cancel if a better offer is received within a certain timeframe</term>, which we will discuss in the next disputation. For example, if I sell you a thing for 100 gold pieces on the condition that if I find a better buyer within two months, the item is "un-bought" by you. If the contract is dissolved because a better offer arrived, the interim fruits belong to the seller, even if you had already paid and taken delivery. Similarly, in a "forfeiture clause" <term>lex commissoria; a clause that cancels a sale if the buyer fails to pay by a deadline</term> (discussed in Disputation 324), if I sell you something on the condition that if you do not pay within two months the item is "not sold" to you, and you fail to pay, the interim fruits belong to the seller.

<summary>This page examines whether a buyer can legally force a seller to buy back an item and who is entitled to the profits (fruits) earned from the property during the interim. Molina distinguishes between contracts voided by hidden defects and those dissolved by specific pre-agreed conditions.</summary>

<keywords>pact of resale, usury, interim fruits, redhibitory action, addiction in diem, lex commissoria, Domingo de Soto, Bartolomé de Medina, contract law, property rights</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate over whether a buyer is entitled to the "fruits"—the income or produce—of a property when a sale is later dissolved or the property is redeemed. It specifically addresses the potential for these arrangements to hide usury.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

There is, moreover, another specific reason why, when a contract is dissolved in this latter way, the fruits of the intervening time should not belong to the buyer. This is because, as the legal expert adds in the cited law, *Nothing ought to remain with the buyer from the thing in which he has broken faith.* <note>original: "Nihil penes emptorem residere oportet ex re, in quam is fidē fefelleretur." This refers to a buyer who fails to fulfill his end of a bargain, such as failing to pay on time.</note> It is observed that if a buyer had given "earnest money" <term>arrha; a deposit or down payment to secure a contract</term>, or had paid part of the price, and it was agreed in the pact that the sale would be voided if he did not pay the remainder within a certain time, he would then lose the deposit and the portion of the price he had paid. This is established in the laws *si fundus* and *de lege* in the Digest <note>The Digest, or *Pandects*, is a major component of the Corpus Juris Civilis, the body of Roman law.</note> and in the Laws of the Partidas. <note>original: "l. 38. tit. 5. part. 5." This refers to the *Siete Partidas*, a 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note> However, in compensation for the deposit or the part of the price he loses, the laws—following the more lenient interpretation of Neratius <note>Neratius Priscus, a Roman jurist of the 1st and 2nd centuries AD.</note>—intended for the buyer to keep the fruits he gathered in the meantime.

And this is what the law *si fundus* provides, as does the law of Castilla cited after it, and not what Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist often called the "Spanish Bartolus."</note> reports from those laws in the cited passage, as is clearly evident to anyone reading those laws. But if, in that case, the seller does not want the deposit or the part of the price, but prefers the intervening fruits, he may choose them for himself.

In the second scenario, however—namely, when the pact does not state that the thing is held as "unsold" and the contract as "uncelebrated," but rather that the thing is to be redeemed or can be redeemed—then if the contract is dissolved according to that pact, the fruits gathered in the meantime belong to the buyer. This is because the thing was entirely his during that time; and this holds true whether the dissolution of the contract depends on the will of the seller or the will of the buyer, as occurs in the matter we are discussing and which gave rise to all these points.

I should point out in this place that all the contracts we have spoken about since Disputation 374 are called in law, and truly are, "pure"—that is, not conditional. For although a conditional pact is added to some of them, the condition does not exist so that the sale may happen, but rather so that, after it has happened, it may be dissolved and cease to exist. This can happen either so that it is considered never to have been made, or so that it does not proceed further, as has been explained. However, if the contracts were celebrated in this form: "I sell this thing to you, or let it be sold to you, *if* you pay the price within such a time," or "unless another offers a higher price within such a time," or if some other condition is added that suspends the sale so that it only occurs (or doesn't) based on some future event: then the contract will be "conditional." If the condition fails, the sale is not dissolved because it never existed; rather, the contract never takes effect because the condition on which it depended for perfection was missing. If, however, the condition is fulfilled, the contract is said to be perfected and to take effect. This is held in various laws of the Digest. It is of no small importance whether a contract is conditional for various effects, which have been partly explained in the preceding parts of this work and will be partly discussed in the following sections, especially in the next disputation.

<margin>Question 6</margin>
From what has been said, it will be easy to understand what should be thought regarding the case in the chapter *Illo vos* concerning pledges. <note>Refers to a specific canon in church law regarding pawns or pledges.</note> Specifically, whether in that case, by the nature of the contract of purchase and sale, the buyer is bound to count the fruits gathered before the dissolution of the contract as part of the 

<column-break/>

price, as if they belonged to the seller; or not, as if they belonged to the buyer. This was the case: Peter had bought a certain possession from Paul for a fixed price on the condition that if the purchase displeased Peter within two years, Paul would be bound to return a certain *higher* price within a year; however, the intervening fruits would be counted as part of the price. The Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> defines that although the contract, in its external form, appears to be a pure purchase with a pact for dissolution, it is nonetheless presumed to be a usurious contract based on two things expressed in the pact: namely, that the gathered fruits should be counted as part of the price, and that the seller is bound to return a higher price than he received for the same possession. It should be judged as such, especially since the buyer was accustomed to practicing usury. For it is to be presumed that he intended to lend money under that cloak, and to accept that possession as a pledge <term>pignus; collateral</term> with a pact that something beyond the principal should be returned to him.

<margin>7 Decision.</margin>
The Doctors <note>Learned legal and theological scholars.</note> truly doubt this, for according to the form of that purchase contract (in which the resolution was left to the buyer's will), they disagree on whether the intervening fruits belong to the buyer or the seller. Various men say various things. However, according to what we have recently defined, I believe it must be said: If the condition added was that if the purchase displeased Peter, the contract would be held as if never made, then the fruits would have belonged to the seller. But in that case, the other contract—that the seller should return a higher price—would have been openly usurious; for once that is granted, no other title remained for that increase in price except a loan <term>mutuum</term>.

If, however, the added condition was that if the purchase displeased him, the contract would cease and be dissolved, then the intervening fruits belonged to the buyer. And this is the force intended by the form of that contract. Furthermore, it is condemned as usurious by legal presumption due to those two or three other points mentioned, taken together. This is because the presumption of usury in that contract is created not only by the fact that the buyer was accustomed to practice usury and exact more than the given price, but also by the fact that he waived the fruits so they could be counted toward the price. If they truly belonged to him because he really intended to celebrate a purchase, he would not so easily waive them to be counted toward the principal. Therefore, from all those things taken together, that contract is sufficiently presumed to be usurious.

<margin>8</margin>
Now, let us return to where we digressed. Conrad de Summenhart, Medina, Major in his epilogue, and Covarruvias are of an opinion contrary to Soto. <note>original: "Conr. de contract. q. 84. Med. q. citata, Maior, in 4. d. 15. q. 43... Cou. 3. vari. ref. c. 9. nu. 3." References to major Scholastic and legal writers.</note> They hold that by the nature of the matter and by "scholastic rigor," a contract of purchase with a pact that the seller must redeem what he sold whenever the buyer wishes is licit, without counting the intervening fruits toward the price (meaning the buyer keeps them), provided that the following conditions are met. First, that the redemption price is just. Second, that there is no evil intention to hide usury by celebrating a loan under the feigned name of a purchase.

<summary>Molina distinguishes between types of contract dissolution and argues that while a buyer's right to force a resale is generally licit, specific conditions—like counting income toward the price or paying back more than the original cost—reveal a hidden, usurious loan.</summary>
<keywords>usury, contract law, fruits, income, redemption, earnest money, legal presumption, Roman law, Luis de Molina, Soto, Covarruvias</keywords>

--- Page 393 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal and theological investigation into the morality of specific types of sales contracts, particularly those involving buy-back clauses that might be used to hide usurious loans.</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 378

Thirdly, let it be free from chance and the infamy associated with those who enter into such a contract. They add that these contracts should be discouraged entirely before they are made, because of the danger—which is more imminent in these than in others—of cloaking usury in this way, and because they have the "appearance of evil" and are inherently suspect. This is true even if they are not condemned as usurious by a legal presumption of law <note>original: "praesumptione iuris, et de iure"</note>, unless other circumstances are present that increase the suspicion, as is clearly gathered from that cited chapter *Vos*. <note>A reference to a specific chapter in Canon Law.</note> Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist.</note> makes an exception for the "censual" contract <term>censualis; a type of annuity or ground-rent agreement</term>, which he considers illicit when combined with such a pact.

Indeed, these authors prove their opinion. First, because if this contract were illicit when the mentioned conditions are met, it would be so either because it is usurious or because it is unjust for some other reason. It is not usurious because it does not involve a loan <term>mutuum; a loan of goods or money for consumption that must be repaid in kind</term>, but is a true sale and purchase. This is clear because it involves a commodity and a price. Furthermore, if the property perishes before it is redeemed, it perishes for the buyer, and the seller does not owe the buyer the price paid for it. This is far removed from the nature of a loan, because in a loan, regardless of whether the thing perishes, the principal is always owed to the lender. Therefore, there is no usury in that contract, as usury cannot exist without a loan.

By this same logic, it is proven that this contract is not a pledge <term>pignus; a security or collateral for a debt</term> where the income gathered is not counted toward the principal. For if a pledge perishes, it does not perish for the person who gave money under that pledge; however, a thing bought in this manner perishes for the buyer if it perishes before redemption. That the same contract is not unjust for any other reason is also proven: we assume the price is equal to the value of the thing sold, both in the first purchase and in the redemption, taking into account the burdens placed on one side or the other. We will speak on this shortly.

Secondly, they prove the same opinion because this contract is licit: "I buy such a house from you, provided that you are bound to buy another house from me, similar to it and located elsewhere, whenever I wish, with a just price intervening in both sales and considering the burdens on either side." Therefore, by the same reasoning, this contract will be licit: "I will buy this house from you, provided you are bound to redeem the same house whenever I wish at a just price, considering the burdens placed on both sides." For it does not make a contract illicit just because I bind you to buy back the same thing rather than something else similar to it.

Thirdly, because the exchange of one estate for another is licit with a pact that when one party wishes, the other is bound to rescind the contract without counting the intervening income toward the principal, provided that—according to the burden imposed on the other—due compensation is made for the greater value of one estate over the other. Therefore, by the same reasoning, a similar purchase of an estate with a pact that the purchase be rescinded when the buyer wishes will be licit, provided due compensation is made in the price according to the burden imposed on the other party.

Conradus <note>Likely Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on economic ethics.</note> and Medina <note>Juan de Medina (1490–1547), a Spanish theologian.</note> observe in the cited places that if a thing is bought with a pact of resale <term>pactum de retrovendendo; a clause allowing or requiring the seller to buy the property back</term> placed solely in favor of the buyer, the just price of the first purchase ought to be higher, not only than if the pact were only in favor of the seller, but even than if the thing were sold absolutely without 

<column-break/>

any pact of resale. Therefore, if the price of a thing with a resale pact in favor of the seller were seventy, and the price of the same thing without any pact were one hundred, the price with a resale pact in favor of the buyer ought to be more than one hundred. This increase should be as much as that burden is worth in a price—the burden that someone is bound to buy something back at a certain price when the other party wishes—which shall be estimated by the judgment of a prudent man. All these things are easily established. Since the purchase of that thing with a pact in favor of the buyer alone is a purchase of that same thing "irredeemably" on the part of the seller, the price with that pact will be equal to the price of the thing without any pact. Then, the added pact that the seller is bound to redeem it whenever the buyer wishes is a burden on the seller; therefore, it increases the price of the same thing without diminishing anything else.

The aforementioned authors also observe that a redemption pact is iniquitous if the seller is forced to redeem it for the same price at which he justly sold it. The reason is that when he sold it, he not only sold the thing without any power to redeem it on his part, but he also sold the burden he took upon himself to redeem it whenever the buyer wished. He received an increase in price for that burden if the first purchase was just. But when he redeems it, he buys it "naked," free from any such burden. Therefore, it is unjust that he should pay as much for it as he received for it when it was burdened with the obligation to redeem it whenever the buyer wished.

<margin>9</margin>
Therefore, because contracts with a resale pact in favor of the buyer alone are not usually celebrated with this explained equality of price—in both the first purchase and the second sale—they are regularly celebrated unjustly. By the best right, a sinister suspicion is held regarding them, and they are by no means to be permitted in any well-ordered republic.

However, when something is sold with a resale pact in favor of both the buyer and the seller simultaneously (which Conradus and Medina report is customary in some regions), so that whenever either of them wishes it first, the other is bound to dissolve the contract; then, because the seller is more burdened by the pact in favor of the buyer than the buyer is burdened by the pact in favor of the seller, the just price ought to be higher than that at which the thing would be justly bought with a resale pact in favor of the seller alone, and lower than that at which it would be bought if it were bought entirely irredeemably. This should be taxed by the judgment of a prudent man, determining how much it is fair for the just price to increase for the greater burden of the seller compared to the buyer.

## On the dissolution of a sale by the pact of the *lex commissoria* and the *addictio in diem*.

### DISPUTATION 378.

->**SUMMARY.**<-

1 *What is a pact of "lex commissoria."* <note>A clause in a contract where the sale is cancelled if the price is not paid by a specific date.</note>
2 *What is a pact of "addictio in diem."* <note>A clause where a sale is cancelled if the seller receives a better offer within a certain timeframe.</note>
3 *In which cases the pacts of "lex commissoria" and "addictio in diem" apply.*

<vocab>pact of resale, usury, contract, just price, purchase, sale, Covarruvias, Medina, lex commissoria, addictio in diem</vocab>

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of buy-back contracts, explaining that for such a sale to be "just" and not a hidden loan, the price must be adjusted to account for the legal burdens placed on the buyer or seller. It establishes that the risk of loss lies with the buyer in a true sale, distinguishing it from usurious lending.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of sales contracts, specifically focusing on clauses that allow a sale to be canceled if certain conditions are met, such as non-payment or a better offer from another buyer.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

### [Summary of Points]
4 *A sale with a better-offer clause or a forfeiture clause: in how many ways it can be dissolved or not.*
5 *Whether a seller reacquires ownership of the thing sold without delivery, if they sold it under a buy-back clause such as: "I sell this to you for this price, on the condition that if I return the price within a year, the thing shall be un-bought."*
6 *Ownership of a thing cannot be transferred without delivery <term>traditio; the formal transfer of possession</term>, neither through a contract nor through its dissolution. Note the limits, however, regarding the forfeiture clause and the better-offer clause in number 7.*
8 *Whether the sales tax <term>alcabala; a common tax on transactions in Spain and its territories</term> is owed when a sales contract is rescinded due to a forfeiture clause or a better-offer clause.*
9 *Whether a forfeiture clause placed in a contract with direct words dissolves the contract as if it had never been celebrated when the condition is not met, so that the tax is not owed.*

1 **T**he forfeiture clause <margin>†</margin> <note>original: "pactum legis commissoriæ"</note>, as was said in Disputation 324 and the preceding disputation, occurs when something is sold to someone with a clause or law attached stating that if they do not pay the price within a certain time, the thing shall be considered un-sold.
2 2 <margin>†</margin> However, the better-offer clause <margin>†</margin> <note>original: "adiectionis in diem"</note>, as we said in the preceding disputation, is when something is sold with a pact or law attached stating that if someone else offers a higher price or better terms for the purchase within a certain time, the thing shall be un-sold, as is held in Law 1 of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*.
3 <margin>†</margin> These pacts agree † first in that, since they are added solely for the favor of the seller, if the pact is not fulfilled, it is in the seller's power either to dissolve the contract or not to dissolve it, but rather to compel the buyer to pay the price, as the seller prefers. However, if the seller says once that they wish to dissolve the contract, they cannot thereafter compel the buyer to pay the price. Likewise, if they once demand the price, or a part of it, they cannot thereafter dissolve the contract. On the other hand, once the pact or law attached to the contract is not fulfilled, the buyer can immediately compel the seller to say which of these options they choose. Furthermore, if the thing perishes before the seller dissolves the contract, the loss falls on the buyer and not the seller. These points regarding the forfeiture clause are found in Laws 2, 3, and 4, paragraph *eleganter*, and Laws 6 and 7 of the Digest, *On the Forfeiture Clause*, Law 38, Title 5, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 37, the final paragraph. Regarding the better-offer clause, these are found in Laws 2 and 3, and the law *Eum qui* at the beginning, and Law *Sabinus* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*.
4 <margin>†</margin> Observe this: if, when a better-offer clause † is applied, a "fake buyer" is set up who offers a higher price or better terms, that is not sufficient to dissolve the contract. This is held in Law *Eum qui*, paragraph *cum igitur* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*. Even if a true buyer does not increase the price, if they offer a purchase that is better for the seller for any reason whatsoever due to intervening circumstances, the seller can withdraw from the contract if it was celebrated under the pact of a "better purchase." This is held in the same place, the final paragraph, joined with the following law. When a female slave is sold under a better-offer clause and she gives birth after the sale—

<column-break/>

—and a better offer is made because of the birth or any fruits of the thing sold in this way, the contract cannot be dissolved. This is because that better offer being made would not be regarding the thing itself that was sold, but regarding a different thing, even if it originated from the thing sold. This is held in Law *Si res* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*. If, however, two things were sold, such as two slaves, and one perished, and a better offer was made regarding the other, because both were sold together, the contract could be dissolved, as is held in Law *Si ex duobus* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*.

In a forfeiture clause, for the buyer to be said not to have fulfilled the pact, it is enough if they have not offered the price to the seller within the prescribed time; for it is not necessary for the seller to demand it. If, however, the buyer brings the price within the prescribed time but finds no one to give it to, they would not be said to have violated the pact. This is found in Law *Si fundus*, the final paragraph, and the final law of the Digest, *On the Forfeiture Clause*. Sometimes a pact is also added to a forfeiture clause stating that if the buyer does not pay the price within a certain time, not only is the thing un-bought, but the seller can also sell it to another, and if they sell it for a lower price, the first buyer is bound to make up what was lacking from the price agreed with them; such a pact is valid. This is found in the cited Law *Si fundus*, paragraph *in commissoria*.

In a better-offer clause, if it was expressed that just as the seller can dissolve the contract if another offers better conditions, so too the buyer is not bound to stand by it, then, if another offers a better purchase within the prescribed time, the seller cannot choose the prior sale by forcing the first buyer to stand by it. This is found in Law *Sabinus* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*.

When something is sold with a better-offer clause and the seller dies before the prescribed time, and lacks an heir who might enter into the inheritance within that time, then even if someone offers a better purchase within that time, the sale remains with the first buyer. This is because the pact is understood to refer to a purchase that pleases the seller within that time, and within such a time it cannot please either the seller or their heir, who at that time do not exist. This is held in Law *Si praedio* of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*.

Furthermore, the forfeiture clause and the better-offer clause agree in that if the contract is dissolved by such a pact, the fruits <term>fructus; products or income generated by the property, like crops or rent</term> gathered in the meantime belong to the seller, as was shown in the preceding disputation. Moreover, the buyer is bound, if the thing has been made worse through their fault, to pay the seller the estimated value of the damage to such a thing. This is found in Law *Si fundus* at the beginning of the Digest, *On the Forfeiture Clause*, and Law 38, Title 5, Part 5.

In the better-offer clause, however, when the thing remains with the first buyer—not because the seller chooses the first sale, but because, when another offers a better purchase, the first buyer increases their offer above the price offered by this other person and there is no one else to offer more—the fruits of the intermediate time belong to the seller, unless something else was expressed in the contract. This is found in Law *Item quod*, the final paragraph, joined with the two following laws of the Digest, *On the Better-Offer Clause*. The reason is that by the very fact that another offered more, it was signified to the first buyer (as the cited laws prescribe it must be signified) that the first sale was rescinded and withdrawn from.
