# Second Treatise, Disputation 378.

Third, the forfeiture clause <note>original: "pactum legis commissoriæ"; a clause stating a sale is void if payment isn't made</note> and the better-offer clause <note>original: "adiectionis in diem"; a clause allowing a seller to accept a better offer within a set timeframe</note> agree in this: once the condition is met and the sale is rescinded, ownership <term>dominium; legal title or right of a property owner</term> of that thing passes back to the original seller by that very fact, without any further delivery <term>traditio; the physical or formal handover of an item</term>. Consequently, the seller has the right to sue for the property <term>rei vindicatio; a legal action by which an owner claims their property from whoever possesses it</term>, regardless of whose hands the item has fallen into. 

This is clearly gathered regarding the better-offer clause from the law *Si quis hac* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de rei vend."; Digest of Justinian, Book 6, Title 1, On the recovery of property</note>. There it is held: If someone buys a thing under a better-offer clause, even though the buyer can bring a lawsuit for the property before the condition occurs (since the sale is considered valid until then), they cannot do so after it occurs; for by that very fact, ownership belongs to the seller. 

The same is gathered from the law *Si ex duobus* (alternatively beginning *Idem Iulianus*), in the section *sed & Marcellus* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de in diem adiect."; Digest Book 18, Title 2</note>. There it is held: If someone who holds a thing purchased under a better-offer clause has handed it over to a third party as a pledge, and the contract is subsequently rescinded because a better offer was made to the seller, the item is immediately freed from the burden of the pledge. From this, the legal expert concludes that until the better offer was made, the first buyer was the owner of the thing and could therefore pledge it, and all the conditions of a true owner applied to him in that middle period. However, he held ownership revocably and dependently on the fact that no better offer would be presented to the seller; thus, all other rights were held by him in a similar way.

The same regarding the forfeiture clause is gathered from the law *Commissoriae* in the Code <note>original: "C. de pact. inter empt. & vend."; Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 54, On pacts between buyer and seller</note>, specifically the words "not to choose the recovery of the thing," and from the final law in the Digest "On the forfeiture clause" <note>original: "ff. de leg. cõmis."; Digest Book 18, Title 3</note>, by the words: "it ought to be reclaimed by the female seller," etc. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, whom Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a Spanish jurist</note> and Antonius Gomez <note>Antonio Gómez, a prominent Spanish legal scholar</note> cite and follow.

<margin>Question 5</margin>
However, when a thing is sold under this form: "I sell this thing to you for such a price on the condition that if I return the price to you within a year, the thing shall be un-bought" (a case found in the law *Si a te* in the Code), does the seller, upon returning the price within the year, acquire ownership of it without delivery, just as ownership is acquired when a sale is rescinded by a better-offer or forfeiture clause? 

Some, whom Covarruvias and Gregorio Lopez <note>Commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> cite (referring to the phrase *que sea deshecha* <note>Spanish: "that it be undone"</note>), answer in the affirmative. However, the contrary opinion is more pleasing, which Antonius Gomez embraces along with Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note> and others, and which Covarruvias 

<margin>Decision</margin>
confesses above is the common view. The reason is that Rule 6 <margin>†</margin> is general: various laws establish that ownership is transferred neither through a contract nor through the dissolution of a contract without delivery, as was shown in Disputations 366 and 373. From this rule, only those things found to be excepted in the law should be excluded. No law is found in which it is expressly stated that ownership is transferred without delivery in that event, whereas the laws do express that it is transferred when a sale is dissolved by a better-offer or forfeiture clause. 

Furthermore, the text of the law *Voluntate* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. quib. mod. pig. vel hypoth."; On how a pledge or mortgage is released</note>, which Covarruvias cites to confirm his opinion, certainly does not prove it. For in that text, it is held that if a creditor legally sells a pledge, or someone else sells another’s property by the owner’s authority, and the

<column-break/>

sale is dissolved by the consent of the parties, the ownership of the pledge returns to the debtor who owned it before the sale, not to the creditor. Similarly, the ownership of another’s property sold by the owner's authority returns not to the seller, but to the person who owned it; because, as the text says, once the sale is dissolved, the matter returns to the state in which it was before. 

It is clear, however, that the text is not speaking of just any dissolution where the thing sold is handed over again. Rather, in that text, the discussion concerns dissolution by the mutual consent of the parties. Everyone agrees that in that type of dissolution, the buyer does not lose ownership until they deliver the thing back. Note, however, that in the proposed case, the fruits gathered in the middle period before the resolution of the contract belong to the seller, according to what was said in the preceding disputation. The reason is that in that contract, there was no pact for "resale" <note>original: "pactū de retrouendendo"</note>, but rather a pact for the "resolution" of the contract, so that it is considered as if it had never been celebrated from the beginning.

7 The Doctors agree that by a forfeiture clause, ownership is transferred to the seller without delivery: first, when it is done with "direct words," and second, when it is done with "oblique words." 

Legal experts call "direct words" those which signify the dissolution of the contract as if it had not been celebrated from the start—such as "the thing is un-bought," "the contract shall be held as not done," and similar phrases. They call "oblique words" those which either signify an interruption of the contract (so that from the deadline prescribed for paying the price, the contract is dissolved) or are indifferent words that can equally be adapted to the view that the contract is considered never to have happened. Such words are: "If you have not paid within such a time, the thing shall return to me," "the contract shall be dissolved," "it shall be dissolved from then on," and similar expressions. 

That ownership does not pass to the seller without delivery when the forfeiture clause is not made with direct words is clearly held in Law 3 of the Code "On pacts between buyer and seller." This is affirmed by the gloss on the word *mortis causa* in the Digest "On donations," by Bartolus, and the doctors commonly, whom Covarruvias and Antonius Gomez cite and follow. 

Furthermore, regarding the better-offer clause: when a sale is dissolved because of it, should we say ownership does not pass to the seller without delivery? The common opinion of the doctors, as Covarruvias reports, is that it does not pass. Nevertheless, he himself rightly leans toward the opposite view, led by the law *Si quis hac* in the Digest. There, a better-offer clause is proposed in oblique words, and despite what Bartolus explains there in trying to break down the text, it is said that ownership is transferred to the seller without delivery. 

I should advise that when the aforementioned pacts are made with oblique words, the fruits gathered in the meantime belong to the buyer and not the seller, according to what was handed down in the preceding disputation; since the contract is not dissolved in such a way that it is considered not to have happened from the beginning.

Furthermore, the doctors observe that if the forfeiture or better-offer clauses are not added immediately <note>original: "incontinenti"</note> when the sales contract is celebrated, but later after an interval, then even if they are made with direct words, ownership does not pass to the seller without delivery. So says the penultimate gloss on the law *Ab emptione* in the Digest "On pacts," and the doctors commonly with it.

<meta>This page continues the legal and fiscal analysis of sales contracts, specifically focusing on whether sales taxes (alcuala) must be paid when a contract is rescinded due to specific clauses like the forfeiture clause or the better-offer clause.</meta>

...commonly held, whom Covarruvias and Antonio Gómez refer to and follow in the cited places.
8. The question is whether, once a **sales contract is rescinded** <note>original: "resoluto contractu venditionis"</note> by a forfeiture clause <note>original: "pactum legis commissoriæ"</note> or a better-offer clause <note>original: "adiectionis in diem"</note>, the sales tax <term>alcuala; a historical Spanish tax on the sale of property</term> is nonetheless owed. Legal experts agree that based on the rescission, it is not owed, according to what was said in the preceding disputations. Likewise, they commonly agree that when the clause was made with "oblique" or indirect wording, even if it is rescinded, the tax <term>gabella; a general term for a tax or duty</term> is owed. This is because the contract is not rescinded as if it had never been made, but is only dissolved so that it proceeds no further. Therefore, since the tax authority's right was already established once the contract was fully formed, that right does not cease just because the contract later ends, even by the force of a preceding agreement. For the same reason, it must be said that when the clause was added after an interval of time—and not at the moment the contract was made—the tax is owed. Since the treasury's right was perfectly established at the initial celebration of the contract, independent of anything then existing in the contract that could dissolve it, any later agreement to rescind could not prejudice the treasury’s already fully acquired right.

<margin>Question.</margin>
The whole difficulty, however, is when the clause was included with direct wording during the very celebration of the contract. In such a case, if the condition or the law of the agreement is not subsequently met, it dissolves the contract just as if it had never been celebrated. This is the same in the case of the law *If from you* in the Code <note>original: "l. si a te C. de pact. inter empt. & vendit."; Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 54, Law 4</note> and in any other similar case where a rescission clause is applied at the contract's inception, making it as if it were never celebrated from the beginning.
The common opinion—which Antonio Gómez reports in his second volume of *Various Resolutions*, and which Lassarte also reports and follows in *On the Tithe of Sale* <note>original: "Lassatte de decim. vend. c. 14. n. 19."</note>—is that in that event, the tax is not owed from that contract. If it had already been paid, it must be reclaimed from the tax collector.
However, Antonio Gómez argues in the same place that it is owed. His reasoning is first: because the contract was "pure" <note>unconditional and immediate</note> and not conditional, as is clear from what was said in this and the preceding disputation. Therefore, since the treasury's right was established from the beginning, a later dissolution cannot harm the treasury, even if it happens by the force of a previous agreement.
Second, he relies on the legal scholar Bartolus’s commentary on the law <note>original: "l. vlti. §. fin. autē. C. cõia de leg."</note>, where he says: If someone burdened with a condition to restore a thing should sell it while the condition is pending, the sale is valid and the tax is owed, even if later, when the condition is met, the contract and sale are rescinded.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Nevertheless, one must not withdraw from the common opinion. For although the sale was pure, and therefore a right was acquired both by the treasury and the other contracting party, it was acquired according to the method or law applied at the very celebration of the contract. This law stated that if the price were not paid within a certain time, or if someone else offered a better deal within that time, the sale would be held as if it were never contracted. Thus, the right was only acquired by both parties depending on that condition not occurring, and on the seller not wishing to dissolve the contract if it did occur. Since the seller reserved this for himself at the very moment of sale and did not wish to sell otherwise, it follows that if the price is not paid, or if

<column-break/>

a better offer occurs and the seller wishes to rescind the contract for that reason, the effect is pulled back <note>retroactive</note> by the force of the included agreement. Thus, the sale is considered as if it were never made, and consequently, as if the treasury or the buyer had never acquired any right. Therefore, in this regard, that sale is treated as if the contract had been celebrated under a condition. Read Lassarte in the place cited above, who explains this more extensively.
Regarding the first argument of Antonio Gómez: once the major premise is granted in the sense explained, we must address the minor premise. A right was indeed acquired by the treasury from that contract, but only dependently on the fact that the seller, upon the condition being met, would not choose to dissolve the contract, as has been explained. Therefore, the conclusion does not follow.
Regarding the second argument: the teaching of Bartolus is very true, because a sale made of another person's property is valid, and the seller is held liable to the buyer for "eviction" <term>evictio; the recovery of a property by a third party who has better title, requiring the seller to compensate the buyer</term> and thus for damages, as shown in Disputation 327. Therefore, the tax is owed on it. That sale was rescinded not regarding the sales contract itself (as if it had become void), but regarding the transfer of ownership, which is understood to have been made under the same condition that the burdened heir who sold it held ownership at that time. For once the condition under which the thing had been bequeathed was fulfilled, just as the seller would have lost ownership and it would have passed to the legatee <note>the person receiving the legacy</note>, so also the buyer loses it, and it passes by that very fact to the legatee.
Observe this: when a sale is dissolved due to a better-offer clause and the thing is handed over to the person offering the better deal, this delivery is a distinct sale from the first one, as Lassarte proves in the place cited above against Menchaca. From that second sale, the tax is owed to the lord and the tax collector who are in office at that time—not to the old ones who were in office at the time of the first sale with the better-offer clause.

**A**lthough this disputation might seem superfluous after the various things said about conditional sales scattered throughout Disputation 337 and elsewhere above, it was decided to add it here so that we might bring those points together in a summary and add anything that was omitted.
1. A conditional sale occurs when a condition is added to it, not so that the contract may be dissolved...

<summary>This page discusses the tax implications of rescinding sales contracts and introduces the general principles of conditional sales, arguing that rescinded contracts should not be taxed as if they were completed.</summary>

Second Treatise, Disputation 380

...which can exist after it has already been made, but rather so that it is suspended, so that it only takes effect depending on that condition. This condition must therefore concern the future and be "contingent" <note>dependent on an uncertain event</note> in either direction. Otherwise, the contract is not truly conditional in the sense we are discussing here. If someone says, "I sell you this thing for such a price if you pay me within a certain time," or "if no one offers a better deal within a certain time," such contracts are indeed conditional. They are not merely contracts with a "better-offer" clause <note>original: "pactu adiectionis in diem"</note> or a "forfeiture" clause <note>original: "legis commissoriæ"</note>, as was discussed in the two preceding disputations and is held in Law 2 of the Digest <note>original: "ff."; referring to the Pandects or Digest of Justinian's Roman Law</note> regarding the better-offer clause, as well as other laws. In that form, the condition is not added so that a contract is dissolved after it has already existed and had force, but so that it is perfected and takes effect only depending on that condition. Thus, when the condition is fulfilled, the contract is said to be "purified" and perfected; but if the condition fails, it is rendered null, as if it never had any force. Therefore:

<margin>2</margin> In a conditional contract, while the condition is still pending and determined in neither direction, no obligation arises, nor is any legal action granted. No one is properly called a "debtor" except in a qualified sense <note>original: "secũdũ qd." (secundum quid)</note>—that is, conditionally or dependently, if the condition is eventually met. Consequently, only a "hope" <term>spes; a legal expectation of a future right</term> for all these things arises from it, as held in the Institutes <note>original: "Insti."; Justinian's legal textbook</note> regarding verbal obligations. From this qualified obligation and debt—and from this hope arising from a conditional contract while the condition still hangs—various effects emanate, which Antonio Gómez records in his *Various Resolutions* (Volume 2, Chapter 2, Number 30). Among others: the contract passes to the heirs of both parties, so that if one party dies while the condition is pending, the heirs are bound to stand by the contract. This is also held in the cited section of the Institutes. Likewise, neither party can withdraw from the contract against the will of the other.

<margin>3</margin> In a contract of buying and selling, any condition and any pact may be added, provided they do not conflict with good morals or the law. This is held in the *Siete Partidas* <note>original: "l. 1. tit. 5. par. 5."; the 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note> and the *Ordenamiento de Montalvo* <note>original: "lib. 4. Lust. ord. tit. 27."</note>.

<margin>4</margin> Which pacts are considered contrary to good morals is found in the Digest, under the title "On Pacts," and was explained copiously in Disputation 271.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding when a contract is conditional and to what extent the risk of the sold item belongs to the seller, this was discussed at the end of Disputation 366.

<margin>6</margin> If a thing is sold under a <insert>suspensive</insert> condition, any fruits <note>original: "fructus"; products or profits like crops or rent</note> gathered in the meantime belong to the seller, as noted in the Digest and by Covarruvias. I understand this to mean that even if the item has been delivered and the price received, if the condition later fails, the fruits gathered in the interim belong to the seller. This is because there is no "just title" <note>legal right to ownership</note> by which they could belong to the buyer. First, there is no title of sale, because the sale never took effect; the condition was not "resolutive" <note>canceling an existing deal</note> but "suspensive" <note>delaying the start of a deal</note>, and the contract's perfection depended on that outcome. Furthermore, there is no title of "compensation" for the price given, which the seller enjoyed all that time. For if that price, upon the failure of the condition, had to be 

<sig>Tt</sig>

<column-break/>

restored in full to the buyer, and if a pact had intervened stating that the interim fruits belonged to the buyer in exchange for the price given, the contract would be usurious. This is because something would be demanded beyond the principal for the retention of the price during all that time. However, when the buyer would suffer a "loss of profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note> or an "emerging damage" <note>original: "damnum emergens"</note> because he paid the price immediately, he could—by reason of that loss or damage—include a pact that the interim fruits belong to him, provided their value does not exceed the estimate of that lost profit or damage. I further understand that the fruits belong to the seller if neither the buyer has delivered the price nor the seller the item. For then, even if the condition is fulfilled and the contract perfected, the fruits gathered in the meantime belong to the seller. When nothing else is specified in the pact, fruits gathered before the payment of the price belong to the seller, as stated in Disputation 368. Moreover, when parties celebrate a sale under a condition and express nothing else, they seem to refer themselves to the time when the contract will be executed upon the fulfillment of the condition—namely, that execution happens according to the state the thing is in at that time. But if the item was delivered immediately and the price was paid, and the condition was fulfilled, then the fruits gathered in the meantime would belong to the buyer. This is because the rule is that once a condition is "purified" <note>fulfilled</note>, the contract relates back <note>original: "retrotrahi"</note> to the time it was celebrated, just as if it had then been celebrated purely and without any condition, as seen in Disputation 337.
Whether a tax <term>gabella; a sales tax</term> is owed or not owed from a conditional contract was discussed copiously in the cited Disputation 337.

### Louis Molina, On Contracts

11. If a member of the clergy sells an item to a layperson, they are required to defend them before the secular judge where the lawsuit was initiated.

**1** Finally, regarding the contract of purchase and sale, we must examine when a sold item is "evicted" <note>In legal terms, "eviction" refers to the loss of possession of a property because a third party successfully proves a better title or ownership in court.</note> and snatched from the power of the buyer because another proves it is theirs or pertains to them and not to the seller, and whether the seller is liable to the buyer for this eviction. It must be answered that, as a rule, the seller is held liable, and the buyer has a legal action against them not only for the price—based on what the item is valued at the time it is evicted—but also for the "interest" <note>original: "interesse"; refers to the financial loss or damage suffered by the buyer due to the loss of the item.</note>, so that the seller pays how much it mattered to the buyer that the item was not evicted, as well as for subsequent damages. This is held in the Code <note>original: "C."; referring to the Code of Justinian.</note>, law *libera*, under the title on sentences and interlocutions; law *si cum quaestio*, under the title on eviction; and the Digest <note>original: "ff."; referring to the Pandects or Digest of Justinian.</note>, law *evicta re*, under the same title; and the final chapter on purchase and sale; and law 32 and following, title 5, part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note>; and book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 30, § 12. There it is added that the buyer can sue either for the item and its "interest"—that is, how much it is valued at the time it was evicted and how much it mattered to them not to lose it—or for the price they originally paid for it, whichever the buyer prefers, as proved by law 1, final paragraph, of the Code on the exchange of things.

**2** Not only is the one who sold the item liable for eviction if it is lost, but also the one who exchanged it, as in law *si permutationes* of the Code on eviction, and law 1 of the Code on the exchange of things. This also applies to anyone who transferred an item to another through any other "onerous" contract <note>A contract where both parties give and receive something of value, as opposed to a gift.</note>, such as when someone gives an item in payment <note>original: "in solutum"; giving an object to settle a debt instead of money.</note>, as held in law *libera* and law *praedium* of the Code on evictions; or when heirs divide an inheritance among themselves, or partners divide common property. For if any of the things that one person received is evicted, the other partners or heirs are liable to them for that eviction, according to law *si familiae* and law *si fratres*, and other laws we cited at the end of Disputation 245, where we explained when co-heirs are not liable for eviction. Antonio Gómez discusses this extensively in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, numbers 33 and 34. Likewise, if something is promised as a dowry to a son-in-law, the one promising it is liable for eviction, as held in law 1 of the Code on the law of dowries. However, when something is given through a "lucrative" contract <note>A contract where one party benefits without giving anything in return, like a donation.</note>, such as a gift, the extent to which the donor is or is not liable for eviction was discussed in Disputation 252.

**3** In a contract of settlement <note>original: "transactionis"; a legal agreement to resolve a dispute or lawsuit.</note>, namely when something is given to someone so that they withdraw from a lawsuit and yield to another whatever right they had regarding the item in dispute: if after that settlement the thing is evicted by a third party, the person who settled with the one from whose power it was evicted is not liable for eviction, nor must they return what they received to drop the lawsuit. The reason is that they did not receive it for the item itself which is being evicted, but rather to withdraw from the lawsuit and in exchange for the "obscure right" <note>A legal right that is uncertain, disputed, or difficult to prove.</note> they believed they had to that thing, whether they actually had it or not.

<column-break/>

Rather, if what was given to that person is evicted by someone else, the person who gave it to them is liable for eviction. Both points are expressly held in law *si pro fundo* of the Code on settlements, and were asserted by Bartolus and others whom Antonio Gómez cites and follows in the work mentioned above. However, if the litigants settled the lawsuit in such a way that one received one part of the disputed property and the other received another part, then if either part were evicted, the other party would not be liable for eviction. The reason is that, for the sake of the obscure right that each believed they had in the whole, each conceded to the other the right they believed they had in the part, which they left to the other with full title, in the same manner they believed they held that right.

**4** If only a part of the sold item is evicted, the seller is liable for the eviction of that part. If it is a specific part, they are liable according to the valuation of that specific part, as well as for the "interest," per law 1 of the Digest on eviction and law 33, title 5, part 5. If a "usufruct" <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the fruits or profits of something belonging to another.</note> of a thing is evicted, the seller will be liable for its estimated value, according to law *vaccae* and law *si ab emptore* of the Digest. For a usufruct is valued as if it were a part of the estate, as held in law 4 of the Digest on usufruct and other laws cited by Antonio Gómez.

**5** If, however, another "servitude" <note>original: "servitus"; a legal burden or easement on a property, such as a neighbor's right of way.</note>—whether rural or urban—is evicted, such as if after a property is bought someone proves they have a right of way, a right to build higher, or another right: then if the person who sold the estate affirmed it had no servitudes (at least by saying it was "best" <note>original: "optimum"; a technical term in Roman law meaning the property is free from all encumbrances or servitudes.</note>, which means lacking defects), or if they knew it had a servitude and did not inform the buyer, the buyer can sue for eviction, including for interest and subsequent damages, at least through the "action on the purchase" <note>original: "actione empti"; the standard legal action for a buyer to enforce the seller's obligations.</note>. This is held in law 1, law *Iulianus*, and law *quaero* of the Digest on actions of purchase, and the penultimate law of the Digest on eviction. It is added in that law *quaero* that even if the seller had included a pact stating they did not wish to be held liable for any servitude the estate might have, if they knew it had one and did not disclose it, they are held liable by the action of purchase just as if they had not included that pact. All these things were stated in Disputation 353, especially conclusion 6, where it was also shown that the buyer can sue for a price reduction <note>original: "actione quanto minoris"; a claim to get back part of the price because the item was worth less than advertised.</note> or even a rescission <note>original: "redhibitoria"; an action to cancel the sale entirely and return the item due to a significant defect.</note> if they would not have bought the item had the defect been known. The reason is that a servitude or a defect in quantity are flaws for which those actions are available. When nothing was said by the buyer or seller about servitudes because the seller did not know the estate had one, then the buyer cannot sue for eviction even if a servitude is later proven, as held in the penultimate law of the Digest on eviction. The "gloss" <note>Interlinear or marginal commentary by legal scholars on the text of the law.</note> there understands this to apply to "interest" and subsequent damages. It can also be understood regarding the "double value" which is sometimes promised in an onerous contract if the item is evicted. Nevertheless, the buyer can still sue for a price reduction so that they are repaid the amount by which the item is worth less because of this servitude—though they cannot sue for rescission—as is clearly laid down in law *quoties* of the Digest on the Aedilian Edict, law *sed si quid* on eviction, and many other laws which we cited along with the common opinion in Disputation 353, third conclusion, when discussing hidden defects in general. Nor is it true that law 63, title 5, part 5, grants an action for rescission in a matter concerning...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of "eviction"—when a buyer loses a purchased item to a third party with a better legal claim. It specifically moves from general principles to the liability of the seller in cases of hidden defects and the specific requirements for legal notice under both Common Law and the Ordinances of Portugal.</meta>

Treatise Second, Disputation 3, Section 355

about which we are disputing, as Antonio Gomez <note>Antonio Gomez was a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentaries on civil law.</note> asserts in the cited number 45; for that law, which is taken from the penultimate law in the Code, under the title "On Aedilician Actions," refers to a certain other particular event regarding a hidden defect <term>vitij occulti (hidden defect): a physical or legal flaw in an item not apparent at the time of sale</term>, as was stated in the cited third conclusion.

Finally, observe this regarding evicted servitudes <note>In law, a servitude is a right to use someone else's land, such as a right of way.</note>: if someone sells a property with a servitude that is owed to it from another property, and afterward that servitude is evicted by the owner of the other property, the seller of the property with that servitude is held liable to the buyer for its eviction. This is held in the penultimate law of the Digest, under the title "On Evictions," and the law *tenetur*, paragraph *si tibi*, in the Digest, under the title "On the Action of Purchase," and Antonio Gomez affirms this in the cited place.

<margin>6</margin>
When † a seller, knowingly and intentionally, sells someone else's property to a buyer who is ignorant of this, the buyer—even before the item is evicted from him, and indeed even if no lawsuit is brought against him—can take action against the seller for the value of the item and the interest <note>original: "interesse"; the financial difference between the buyer's current state and their state had the contract been fulfilled.</note>, namely, how much it mattered to the buyer that the item had become his own. This is expressly held in the law *seruus*, paragraph *sciens*, in the Digest, under the title "On Actions of Purchase," and the common opinion of the doctors affirms this, which Antonio Gomez relates and follows in his second volume, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 39. Indeed, in the forum of conscience <note>The "forum of conscience" refers to the moral and spiritual standing of a person before God, often distinguished from the "exterior forum" of human courts.</note>, even if the buyer is ignorant that the item belongs to another, the seller is bound to pay him the price and the lost interest because it is being taken from him, and the seller must hand it over to the true owner. Furthermore, even if the seller, being ignorant that the item belonged to another, sold it, as soon as he learns it is another's, he is bound to return the price to the buyer and restore the item to the proper owner, without waiting for a lawsuit. However, I do not believe that in the forum of conscience he is then bound to the buyer for the interest or for subsequent damages: because he is not bound to them either by reason of the thing received or by reason of an unjust taking, since he did not sin by selling the item in that manner. These points agree with what we said in Disputation 153, conclusion 3.

Yet I judge this alone to be true: when the item is not evicted by a third party, such as the true owner, but the buyer himself, before the item is sought by law, attempts to return it to the person it belongs to; otherwise, by the force of the past contract, the seller would be held liable for eviction. For by the disposition of the law, onerous contracts are considered celebrated under this condition: that if the item is evicted, the interest must be paid, even if no fault occurred on the part of the seller. But if another's property had been sold in good faith with probable ignorance that it belonged to another, and it no longer existed, the seller would satisfy his part if he restored to the owner as much as he was found to have been made wealthier by it, or by the price received for it: because he is bound to nothing else, neither by reason of the thing received nor by reason of an unjust taking. Similarly, if the buyer had been made wealthier in any way from that item—after deducting the price he gave for it, and deducting expenses and the value of the labor applied—he would be bound to restore that to the owner of the item, and no more, for the same reason.

<margin>7</margin>
When † it is not established that the seller sold the item knowing it belonged to another, he is not held liable for eviction in the exterior forum (nor even in the forum of conscience when it is not clearly established to the seller himself that it belonged to another) until a final sentence is passed by which the item is evicted from the buyer, as is clear from law 3 and the law *si cum quaestio* in the Code, under the title "On Eviction," and the law *si plus* in the Digest, under the same title. Indeed, it is necessary that the buyer has already handed over the item in order to take action regarding the eviction, as is clear in the law *habere* in the Digest, under the same title. Furthermore, not even before that time

<column-break/>

is the seller bound to provide guarantors <term>fideiussores: individuals who guarantee that a debt or legal obligation will be met if the primary party fails.</term>, even if they are requested, stating that if the item is evicted, he will satisfy the buyer, as is clear in the law *illud* in the Digest, under the same title. Nevertheless, in the beginning, if after the contract is celebrated and the item is handed over, but the price (or some part of it) is not yet paid, a question or doubt arises that the sold item does not belong to the seller, the buyer is not bound to pay what remains of the price unless the seller first provides sufficient guarantors that, if the item is evicted, he will satisfy him for the eviction. This is held in the law *si post perfectam* in the Code, under the title "On Eviction," and the penultimate law, last paragraph, in the Digest, "On the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Item," and in the Laws of Portugal <note>original: "Lusit. ord."; referring to the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the legal code of Portugal.</note>, book 4, title 37, in the beginning. As is added in the same place concerning Portuguese law, when it is established that the seller has sufficient immovable goods <note>Real estate or land.</note> free from other debts from which he can sufficiently satisfy the buyer, he is not bound to provide guarantors to the buyer. Observe this: for greater caution, lest a lawsuit or doubt be moved simply to delay the payment of the price, both the buyer and the one moving the lawsuit or doubt can be compelled to swear that they are raising the lawsuit or doubt sincerely and without any fraud, based on the arguments of the laws which Antonio Gomez cites in the place mentioned above in number 39, where you may read the common opinion of the doctors, which he relates and follows concerning all these matters.

<margin>8</margin>
Next, † for the seller to be held liable for eviction, it is necessary that once a lawsuit is initiated, the buyer notifies him that it has been moved and requires of him whether he wishes to defend it, as is established in the law *emptor* and the law *empti actio* in the Code, under the title "On Eviction," and law 1 in the Code, "On the Risk and Benefit of a Sold Item," and the last chapter "On Purchase and Sale," and laws 32 and 36, title 5, part 5, and book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 30, paragraph 2, and in other laws. Although the more common opinion asserts that it is necessary for the buyer to send the complaint of the proposed lawsuit to the seller, it is accepted by custom that this is not necessary, at least when the notification is made to the buyer with the intervening authority of a judge. Furthermore, the common opinion, along with Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> and Panormitanus <note>Nicholas de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> on the last chapter "On Purchase and Sale," number 9, affirms that even if the seller knows from elsewhere that a lawsuit has been moved, it does not prevent the requirement that the buyer must notify him; and this is defined today in book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 30, paragraph 2.

The reason is because, although when notification is required for knowledge alone the obligation to notify ceases when the knowledge of the one who should be notified is established, nevertheless, when notification is ordained so that the one to whom it is made may perform something to which he is bound—as happens in the matter proposed—then the fact that he already knows it does not excuse one from the obligation of making the notification to him. I also judge, with the common opinion of the doctors, that a naked notification is not enough, but it is simultaneously necessary that the seller be requested whether he wishes to join in defending the case, whatever Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> may say to the contrary in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 17, number 3. Moreover, the notification must be made before the publication of witnesses <note>The stage in a Roman-canonical trial where the testimony of witnesses was made public to the parties.</note> occurs; otherwise, the seller will not be held liable for eviction, as is sanctioned by the last gloss on the law *si rem quae* in the Digest, under "On Evictions," and by the common opinion of the doctors on laws 32 and 36, title 5, part 5, and book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 30, paragraph 2, in Castile and in Portugal. Covarruvias, book 3 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 17, number 8; Antonio Gomez at the cited number 39; Gregorio Lopez on the cited law 32, with Bartolus and others, affirm that even if the notification was not made before the first sentence, if it is nonetheless made at the time of an appeal, it suffices—provided, however, that the rights of defense and proof remain intact.

### 336 Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...at that time, the seller should be present. Furthermore, notice <term>denunciatio (notice): a formal legal warning given by a buyer to a seller that a lawsuit has been filed regarding the purchased item</term> must be made to the seller himself in person, if he can be found; otherwise, it is sufficient if it is made at his home, provided he was sought there first, and in the presence of neighbors. But if it can be proven that the seller took care to ensure that notice could not be served to him, that would suffice, and no other notice would be necessary, as is clear from the law *si dictum*, in the section *simili modo* of the Digest, under the title "On Evictions." If, however, the seller is deceased, notice must then be made to all heirs; nor is it enough if it is made to only one, since each of them is only held liable for their proportional share, according to the law *si tem*, in the final section of the Digest, under the title "On Evictions," as is established from what has been said in the matter of testaments. The obligation for notice to be given to the seller—so that he may be held liable for eviction—can be waived or permitted by the seller in the contract of sale itself. If it is waived, even if the buyer neglects to give notice, the seller is held liable for the eviction, as is clear from the law *Herennius*, in the Digest, under the title "On Evictions." For this reason, notaries are accustomed to placing clauses in the instruments of purchase containing such a waiver. Because the buyer is bound to notify the seller of the lawsuit so that the seller may defend the case if he wishes, the Ordinances of Portugal <note>original: "ordi. Lusit."; refers to the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the legal codes of the Kingdom of Portugal</note>, Book 3, Title 30, at the beginning, establish that when a lawsuit is brought against a buyer or another possessor of a thing, if he names the "author" <term>author (autor): the person from whom the current owner acquired their title or right to the property</term> from whom he received the item and who is responsible for defending the case, he must be granted as much time as is sufficient based on the distance of the location for that person to be brought in, should they wish to join the defense of the case; in the meantime, the lawsuit shall not proceed further. However, the possessor must swear an oath—before the time limit is granted to him—that he is proceeding sincerely and not with the intention of procrastinating the lawsuit by inventing a false "author." But if that "author," appearing in court, names another "author," time must similarly be granted to bring that person in, and so on consequently for others, until the first "author" is reached. Regarding all these matters, read the laws and the doctors cited by Antonio Gomez in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 2, number 39, and Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, chapter 7, number 5.

<margin>9</margin> It must be observed that if it is so obvious that the thing did not belong to the seller, but rather to the person seeking it, so that the seller could not hide it through any evasion, then it is not necessary for notice to be given to the seller for him to be held liable for eviction; indeed, it is not even necessary then for the buyer to defend the case. This is clearly gathered from the law *emptorem* at the beginning of the Digest, under the title "On Actions of Purchase," and is affirmed by the Gloss on the second law *si cum quaest* in the Code, under the title "On Evictions," and many others whom Antonio Gomez refers to and follows at the cited number 39. Indeed, Covarruvias, in the place cited above at number 6, asserts along with the common opinion which he references, that even if the buyer does not give notice that a lawsuit has been moved, or if after giving notice he hands over the thing to the adversary before a judgment is rendered, if he nevertheless clearly proves that the thing belonged to that other person, the seller is held liable to him for the eviction. As to what the seller is held to in the "court of conscience" <note>This refers to the moral and religious obligation (Internal Forum), as opposed to the purely legal one (External Forum).</note> when he himself knows the thing belonged to someone else, this was discussed above.

When the buyer is a minor, it is enough if the seller knows that a lawsuit has been brought against the minor regarding the purchased item for him to be held liable for eviction, even if no formal notice was given to the seller. The reason is that, according to the law *in minorum* in the Code, under the title "In which cases restoration of the original state is necessary," a minor is not placed in default <term>mora (default): a legal delay in performing an obligation that triggers liability</term> without a formal demand or request. Moreover, since the Church enjoys the privilege of a minor <note>In medieval and early modern law, the Church was often granted the same legal protections as orphans or minors to prevent the loss of ecclesiastical property.</note>, the same must be said when 

<column-break/>

the Church buys something and a lawsuit is brought against the purchased item, as Covarruvias rightly proves in the place cited above at number 4, along with the common opinion of the doctors, against certain individuals who asserted the contrary. Covarruvias adds in the same place at number 5 that the same applies when the seller has affirmed by oath that he would assist the buyer in any lawsuit that might be brought against him. And I believe the same is true if he promised this without an oath; for while an oath binds more strictly, it does not obligate one to anything other than what the promise itself, confirmed by oath, obligates. The reason for both assertions is that when a defense is not promised, the seller is not specifically bound to it, but is bound either to defend it or, if he does not wish to, to pay the value of the item later along with the expenses of the lawsuit—provided, however, that once the lawsuit is started, the buyer requests his presence; because perhaps he will know how to defend the item better than the buyer, and will be able to apply greater diligence, since it is more in his interest than the buyer's that the item be retained. However, when the seller has promised a defense, he is specifically bound to it by the force of such a promise, whether it was confirmed by an oath or not; and for that reason, since he is then aware that a lawsuit has been moved, he is considered by that very fact to be in default if he does not come to the buyer's defense as he is bound. But if only the contract of sale was confirmed by oath, the seller is not bound to the defense otherwise than if the oath had not been added to the contract, because an oath regarding the sale does not extend itself to the defense if a lawsuit is moved against the item sold.

When a seller would be held liable for eviction if the item were lost, he may—as soon as the lawsuit has been moved, whether he has been given notice and requested for it or not, and whether he promised a defense to the buyer or not—approach on his own authority and oppose the lawsuit for his own interest and defend it, even against the will of the person moving the lawsuit. However, he must do this as if he were the buyer's representative in his own case, and take up the lawsuit in the state in which it currently stands. According to Portuguese law, it is added that he is then bound to provide pledges or competent guarantors so that, if a judgment is rendered against him, it will be executed without impediment and satisfaction will be given to the one who moved the lawsuit. Furthermore, it is added that if at the beginning, when the seller wishes to take up the lawsuit, the person moving it refuses this, showing it to be likely that it is in his interest to contend with the buyer instead (because the buyer might be more truthful or faithful), then the buyer is bound to pursue the lawsuit. All these things are held in the law *si parentes* in the Code, under the title "On Evictions," chapter 2, "While the suit is pending," law 33, title 5, part 5, and in the Ordinances of Portugal, Book 3, title 30, paragraphs 5, 6, 7, and 8; and it is established from various laws which Antonio Gomez cites in the place above at number 39.

<margin>11</margin> When a seller takes the lawsuit upon himself in the manner explained, he is bound to contend before the same judge where the case was started, even if he himself is the defendant and would otherwise be exempt from that judge's jurisdiction. Thus, if a cleric sold an item to a layman, he is bound to contend before the secular judge <note>The "secular judge" refers to civil/royal courts as opposed to ecclesiastical (church) courts.</note> before whom the claim against the buyer was begun. Conversely, if a layman sold an item to a cleric, he is bound to contend before the ecclesiastical judge before whom the claim against the cleric was begun. This is held in the law *venditor* of the Digest, under the title "On Judgments," law 57, title 6, part 1, and the Ordinances of Portugal, Book 3, title 30, paragraph 1; and Panormitanus <note>Nicholas de Tudeschis, a famous canon lawyer.</note> affirms this at the final chapter of "On Purchase and Sale," as does the common opinion, which Antonio Gomez refers to and [follows]...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "eviction"—the loss of a purchased property to a third party with a superior legal claim. ### Second Treatise, Dispute 380, Page 337

...carries and follows. From the cited section 1 of **Portuguese Law**, an exception is made when the item was given by the King and it pertains to him to defend it; for then the entire matter is referred to the judge of *the King's affairs* <note>original: "dos feitos del Roy"</note>.

In the following five <note>The author lists six in the body text</note> events, the person who sold the thing or alienated it under another title is not held liable for eviction.

<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>
**The first is**, if while the lawsuit is pending, notice <term>denunciatio: a formal legal warning</term> is not given to him, as has been said. An exception is made unless the buyer, or whoever received it under another title, was expressly exempted from that notice in the contract. Covarruvias, in *Variarum Resolutionum*, book 3, chapter 17, number 7, along with the gloss on the law *cum pena* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de arb." refers to the Pandects/Digest title "De arbitris"</note>, and with the common opinion which he cites, says: when a general clause was placed in the contract stating that in whatever way the thing is evicted, the seller is held liable for eviction, it must be understood provided that no fault on the part of the buyer intervenes. For that reason, he says, if the thing is called away either by a judge's sentence or by chosen arbiters, with the seller knowing this but not being called to the defense of the case, the seller is held liable for eviction. It is otherwise if this happens without his knowledge, because the buyer was bound to warn the seller. He says the same applies if the thing is adjudged to another not by arbiters, but by "arbitrators" or "amicable compounders" <note>informal mediators rather than legal judges</note> with the buyer's consent—at least so that, although in these two events he is held for eviction, he is only held for the price of the thing, and not for a penalty, if any had been placed in the contract for the event that the thing was evicted.

**The second**, when it was expressed in the contract that he would not be held for eviction; for then, if the thing is evicted, he is not held for eviction in this sense: that he is held neither for the "interest" <term>interesse: legal damages representing the buyer's loss beyond the mere price</term> nor for subsequent losses to the buyer. He is, however, held to return the price received, unless it had been specifically expressed that he was not held even for the price. These things, however, are to be understood when the seller sold it in good faith, not knowing the thing belonged to another; for then, by selling it in that manner, he is in the same position as one who sold the "cast of a net" <note>original: "iactum retis" — an aleatory contract where one buys the result of a fishing attempt, whether fish are caught or not</note>. If, however, the seller, knowing the thing belonged to another, sold it in that manner, then in either case he is held by the "action of purchase" <note>actio empti</note>, both for the price and for subsequent damages, and this because of the fraud <note>dolus</note> intervening in the contract. All the aforesaid are found clearly in the law *emptorem*, the final section, in the Digest on the action of purchase. And I understand the same when the seller expressed in particular that he did not wish to be held even for the price in some specific case, or if the thing were evicted by a specific person. For if he knew the thing did not belong to him on that account, or belonged to another specific person, he is certainly held for the price and for damages, unless he revealed his knowledge; because he is judged to have given cause for the contract through fraud. The opinion of Antonio Gomez at number 39, and of certain others whom he cites, is somewhat ridiculous when they assert that the seller in that case is not even held for the price received. For as Covarruvias sufficiently proves in the cited chapter 17, number 2, there is no just title by which that seller can make that price his own. Indeed, I add, when a seller knows that the thing is at risk from some specific cause or in relation to some person, if he then sold that thing without disclosing that danger, and agreed with the buyer that he would not be held for the price upon eviction, he is certainly held—not only for the price, but also for all subsequent damages—if the thing is evicted for the very reason he feared. In fact, the contract in conscience and in the external

<column-break/>

court would be void, because fraud would have given cause to it, according to what was said in disputes 352 and 353.

**The third**, when the buyer, after the sentence was passed and while the seller was absent from the judgment, did not appeal from it. So holds the law *Herenius*, the section *quia*, in the Digest "On Evictions," and law 36, title 5, part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas</note>. It must be understood, however, unless it is manifest that the sentence is just and the thing belongs to the one who evicted it. For if, when the matter is so clear, it is lawful to desist from the lawsuit, it will be entirely proper, with much greater reason, not to appeal from the sentence. However, when there can be some doubt in the matter, because perhaps the seller still has some proof or defense, the buyer is generally bound to appeal and pursue the lawsuit until the final sentence from which it is not permitted to appeal. So says Covarruvias in the cited place, number 9, and this is also decreed in the **Portuguese Ordinances**, the cited title 50, section 2. There it is added that the buyer is not held to "aggravate" the final sentence, which the Castilians call "to supplicate" <note>a higher form of legal appeal</note>. Therefore, we do not approve of those points in which Antonio Gomez, at the cited number 39, along with some others, disagreed with this doctrine.

**The fourth**, when the sentence is clearly unjust, whether it was passed through the judge's ignorance, or through wickedness, or out of hatred for the possessor, or because he wished to unjustly favor the plaintiff. So holds the law *si per imprudentiam* in the Digest "On Evictions," chapter "the last" on buying and selling, law 36, title 5, part 5, and other laws. The reason is that then the thing is judged to be taken out of the power of the buyer just as if it had been unjustly taken away by theft or force, or had perished by a chance accident; in which cases of eviction it is established that the loss falls upon the buyer. Therefore, in that event, the possessor only has an action against the judge. Regarding this matter, read Covarruvias in the final number of the cited place. Observe, however, that by **Portuguese Law**, even in this fourth event, the seller is held for the eviction, and he has the action against the judge, as is clearly arranged in the cited title 20, section 2.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Nor is this decreed without merit, for since it is taken from the buyer on the grounds that the thing was not the seller's when he sold it, it seems to pertain to the seller rather than the buyer to contend regarding that matter before the judge.

**The fifth**, when the buyer consented to have his dispute defined by a judge-arbiter, or by another to whom the jurisdiction of that case did not belong: law *si dictum*, the section *si compromisero*, in the Digest "On Evictions," and law 36, title 5, part 5.

**The sixth**, when the buyer at the time of purchase knew the thing belonged to another; for then, by Common Law, an action is not given to him even for the price, unless an express agreement was made that the seller would be held for eviction: then, he can sue only for the price. All these are gathered from the law *si fundum* in the Code <note>original: "C. de euic." refers to the Codex Justinianus</note> "On Evictions."

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>

At this point, observe that since such laws are penal, when the seller was not aware the thing belonged to another, he can retain the price for himself by the authority of the law; if, however, it is sought by the buyer, he can contend with him until it is awarded to him. But if the seller hands it over to the buyer, not knowing that he could lawfully retain it, the buyer can reserve it for himself until the judge's sentence awards it to the other; because he is not bound to execute a penalty against himself before the sentence is passed. When, however, the seller was aware the thing belonged to another, he cannot...

Nor is the seller to be condemned if he chooses this latter option, because it is not his official duty to ensure that the penalty of the law is executed. **Seventh**, when the buyer could have acquired the thing by prescription <term>usucapio: gaining legal ownership through long-term possession</term>: for then the seller is not held liable to him for eviction, because the thing was taken from him through the buyer's own fault or laziness. **Ninth**, when the buyer has purchased an inheritance: for then, if any particular item of the inheritance is evicted, the heir is not held liable for eviction, because that specific item was not part of the goods of the inheritance <note>Meaning the sale was for the legal "entity" of the estate, not a guaranteed list of items</note>. It would be otherwise if the entire inheritance were evicted by proving that the seller was not the legitimate heir, but that the inheritance belonged to another. See law 1 of the Code <note>original: "C. de euict."</note> and law 37, title 5, part 5. This law adds that the same applies if someone had purchased the rents of a certain territory or estate: for if something were evicted that was proven not to belong to the rents of that territory or estate, the seller would not be held liable for eviction. Gregorius Lopez observes there, and with him Lassarte in *De Decimis Venditionis*, chapter 18, number 86, that it is different if a part of the territory or estate is evicted, and as a consequence, a part of the rents is evicted; for then, just as the seller of an estate would be held liable for eviction if the estate itself were sold (as was said above), so also he who had leased or sold the rents of it—for example, the **gabelles** <term>excise taxes or tolls</term> from that territory—would be held liable to the buyer or lessee for the eviction of the part of the rents so lost. On these points, see Antonio Gómez, volume 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 2, number 43.

**Whether** the seller, when a thing is evicted, is held liable for **double the value** of that thing. The answer is that he is only held liable for double when it has been specifically included in the agreement, as is expressly held in the third book of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, title 30, section 2; and the law *emptori* in the Digest and other laws agree. However, when one sues for double the value, one cannot simultaneously sue for interest and subsequent damages; rather, the buyer must choose which of the two he would prefer to sue for. See law *emptore*, section *Cassius*, on actions for purchase.

<margin>

</margin>
**Whether**, moreover, the seller is liable to the buyer for the **expenses incurred in the lawsuit**. The answer is that when the thing is evicted and the seller is bound to provide a defense, no one doubts he is liable for the expenses of the suit; for expenses are part of the "interest" <note>legal damages intended to make the person whole</note> to which the seller is bound. But when the thing is not evicted, and the sentence is instead carried in favor of the buyer, although certain commentaries have asserted 

<column-break/>

that the seller is then not held liable for the expenses, nevertheless Bartolus, and after him Panormitanus in the last chapter on "Buying and Selling," number 11, and Sylvester under the word "purchase," question 25, and the common opinion of the doctors (which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in volume 2, chapter 2, number 47), all affirm that he **is** held liable, provided that the buyer notified him that the lawsuit had been initiated, and provided the adversary was not condemned to pay the legal expenses. The reason is that although the seller, once warned, is not forced to take the lawsuit upon himself, he is nonetheless held under a choice: either to defend the buyer (for which reason he is warned), or, if he refuses, he is held to pay all his expenses.

### DISPUTE CCCLXXXI.

#### S V M M A R Y.

1 *From where the word "census" is derived.*
2 *What a reserved census is.*
3 *In what ways a census contract differs from an emphyteusis.*
4 *A census is paid from one's own property, while a pension is paid from another's.*
5 *A pact or condition placed in a census contract, stating that if the debtor does not pay within a certain time, he falls into forfeiture—when this is valid.*
6 *Whether a census contract should be judged as such rather than as an emphyteutic one in cases of doubt.*
7 *Census contracts concerning temporal things are rare.*
8 *By what standard a reserved census contract should be judged.*

**S**ince the census contract is for the most part like a certain underlying part of buying and selling, as will be clear from what is to be said, after the treatment of buying and selling in general, we must now discuss the census contract.

1. To begin with the name: **census** is named from *censendo*, that is, "estimating." Indeed, the appraisal of each person's goods, which was done so that a tribute could be imposed according to their quantity and value, was called a "census," as is found in the laws *forma*, *vitia*, and *per discursum* in the Digest and laws 2 and 3 of the Code, book 11, and other laws which Covarruvias and Alvarez Valasco cite. From there, the name was adapted to signify, first, the resources and goods of each person, because they were accustomed to be "censused" and appraised so it could be understood how much each person could assist the Republic in war, or for the imposition of tribute; and then also to signify the tribute itself which was paid from them. And in this last sense, "census" is used in the Code, law 2, "without census or remains," etc. From there, the name was extended to signify even those tributes imposed per person (poll taxes), especially in recognition of subjection and the jurisdiction of lordship; in which sense it is used in Matthew 22, when Christ was asked: "Is it lawful to give **census** <note>Usually translated as "tribute" or "taxes" in English Bibles</note> to Caesar, or not?" It is also used more broadly in Canon Law for that which is paid annually to someone, even to someone inferior to a prince, by reason of subjection, foundation, or another just cause, as Alvarez Valasco says in the place cited above, and from the whole title in the Decretals on censuses and from other...

### Second Treatise, Dispute 381.

He confirms this with other laws. Where, along with Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as "the Abbot of Palermo"</note> and others, he adds: since an annuity of this kind can be paid for various reasons, even if someone proves it is owed to them and has always been paid, unless they prove the specific reason why it was owed, they do not prove a case; for instance, that it is owed as a sign of subjection, or for some other specific cause. He adds that Oralora also takes "annuity" in its most general sense for any burden imposed on someone. In none of these meanings are we speaking of annuities in this place; however, the annuities we will discuss have their origin in the second-to-last definition.

<margin>2</margin> As we were saying in Dispute 372, and as is gathered from the chapter *Constitutus* regarding religious houses <note>original: "cap. constitutus, de relig. domibus"; a reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX</note>, and as is affirmed by the second-to-last gloss there, and with it Panormitanus at number 18; Covarruvias, *Variae Resolutiones*, book 3, chapter 7, number 1; Antonio Gómez on law 68 of Toro, number 2; Conradus, *On Contracts*, question 72; Johannes Medina, *On Usury*, question 1 regarding annuities; Soto, *On Justice*, book 6, question 5, article 1; Alvarus Valascus, question 32, cited at number 7; Lassatte, *On the Tenth of Sales*, chapter 10, number 3 and number 45; and many others whom they cite: **an annuity contract** <term>contractus censualis: a contract involving the payment of a regular fee or annuity from the income of a property</term> under Canon Law exists when something is granted to someone in regards to everything that the grantor was able to grant, while reserving for himself an annual, monthly, or other similar pension which the receiver is bound to pay, either from the fruits <note>The produce or income of the land</note> or in something equivalent, such as money or another thing. And this kind of contract is frequent in spiritual matters, as when a benefice <note>An ecclesiastical office that provides income</note> is granted with an annual pension reserved, which is what the cited chapter *Constitutus* discusses. It can also be celebrated in temporal matters, as in the granting of land under an annual or monthly pension. In this kind of contract, a modest pension is usually reserved in memory of the ancient ownership and the benefit conferred, as well as for other purposes; however, it is customary for the reserved amount to be smaller when a spiritual thing is granted than when a temporal thing is conferred, unless another piece of land is granted at the same time in compensation for services rendered or something similar. Therefore, because through that contract everything is granted that the grantor is able to grant—with only that pension reserved—it follows that through it, not only the **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile: the right to use and profit from property</term>, as in a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis: a contract where land is leased for a long period in exchange for improvement and a small rent</term>, but also the **direct ownership** <term>dominium directum: the ultimate legal title or "naked" ownership</term> is transferred. But because the pension to be paid is called an "annuity" <note>original: "census"</note> in Canon Law, according to the second-to-last meaning of annuity explained shortly before, the result is that the right to receive it every year or every month—which is reserved in the thing granted—is called an "annuity," and the contract by which the thing is granted and the pension reserved is called "annuitant" <note>original: "censualis"</note>. However, such an annuity, or rather the contract, is called **reserved** <note>original: "reservativus"</note>, to distinguish it from another which is called **consigned** <note>original: "consignativus"</note>, which will be discussed in the following disputes. It is called "reserved" because from the thing itself which is conferred, the grantor reserves the annuity for himself or another without receiving anything in compensation for what he grants from that thing; for that reason, this contract has a place in spiritual matters without the vice of simony <note>The illegal buying or selling of church offices or spiritual things</note>, as Panormitanus notes in the cited chapter *Constitutus*, number 12, and it is manifest from the text itself.

<margin>3</margin> This annuity contract differs from a long-term lease <note>original: "emphyteusis"</note>, as the gloss, Panormitanus, and other cited doctors note: First, because through an emphyteutic contract only the "useful ownership" is transferred, and the "direct ownership" remains with the grantor, as was said in part in Dispute 10, and

<column-break/>

will be discussed more copiously below in its proper place; but through this annuity contract, even the "direct ownership" is transferred. Alvarus Valascus, *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 32, numbers 1 and 7, also establishes a distinction: that the leaseholder <note>original: "emphyteuta"</note> possesses only "naturally," while the owner possesses "civilly"; but he who possesses a thing from the annuity contract of which we speak possesses the thing both civilly and naturally. We, however, said in Dispute 12, regarding ownership, that the direct owner possesses civilly through himself, and naturally through the leaseholder, and thus the leaseholder possesses the property only naturally in the name of the direct owner; otherwise, the leaseholder can have both civil and natural possession of the useful ownership.

According to the distinction handed down (as Alvarus Valascus teaches with Everardus in the cited number, and Julius Clarus in book 4 of *Sententiae*, section *emphyteusis*, question 1), it is customary to say that we <margin>4</margin> pay an **annuity** <note>original: "censum"</note> on our own property, but a **pension** <note>original: "pensionem"</note> on someone else's, because the thing from which the leaseholder pays the pension belongs to another in terms of its ownership. Along with Panormitanus in the cited chapter *Constitutus*, these same authors warn that although what is paid from an annuity property is customarily called an annuity, and what is paid from an emphyteutic property is called a pension or a "canon," the terms are sometimes confused; indeed, sometimes an annuity contract is called a lease <note>original: "emphyteusim"</note>, and an emphyteutic contract is called an annuity, even though these two contracts are quite different in themselves. Hence, Alvarus Valascus there at number 28, following Panormitanus in the cited chapter *Constitutus*, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors which he relates, adds: although in the investing and celebration of the contract it may be said that something is granted in a lease <note>original: "in emphyteusim"</note> with the transfer of all rights that the grantor has in that thing, and the word "lease" is often repeated in the instrument of the contract, and no mention is made of an "annuity," the contract must be judged as an annuity contract and not an emphyteutic one. This is because in contracts one should attend more to what is done than to the names which the contracting parties use. And on the contrary, if in the celebration of the contract it is said that it is granted as a "perpetual annuity" with the reservation of the direct ownership, the contract must be judged as emphyteutic and not an annuity contract by the same reasoning.

**Secondly**, they differ in that in a lease <note>original: "emphyteusi"</note>, if the pension is not paid by the leaseholder for two or three years, he falls into **forfeiture** <note>original: "commissum"</note>—that is, he loses the useful ownership to the owner, as will be said below in its place. But in an annuity contract, even if he who is bound to pay the annuity does not pay it for many years, he does not for that reason fall into forfeiture, but is only bound to pay the unpaid pensions. This is gathered clearly from the chapter *Constitutus* regarding religious houses, and the glosses there affirm it, as well as Panormitanus and the common opinion of the doctors, which the doctors cited so far relate and follow. The reason, according to Panormitanus and others, is that in a lease contract the thing remains as far as direct ownership is concerned with the one granting the lease, and by the rule of law he is deemed to grant it regarding useful ownership as if under a condition, provided that the leaseholder does not fail to pay the pension within that time. In an annuity contract, however, the thing is fully and perfectly made the property of the one to whom it is granted as an annuity, and for that reason the law willed that if the annuitant <note>original: "censuarius"</note> failed to pay the pensions, he would not fall into forfeiture, but would only be compelled to pay them.

<summary>This page defines the "reserved annuity contract" (contractus censualis reservativus) and distinguishes it from long-term leases (emphyteusis). The key legal difference is that an annuity contract transfers full legal and useful ownership to the recipient, meaning failure to pay results in debt rather than forfeiture of the property.</summary>
