# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

<margin>Doubt 5</margin> The question is whether, in an annuity contract, a law or condition can be added stating that if the debtor does not pay the annuity within a certain time, they shall incur **forfeiture** <note>original: "incidat in commissum"; a legal penalty where the possessor loses their rights to the property due to a breach of contract</note>. Is such a condition or agreement valid?

<margin>Decision</margin> It must be said that if it is a "reserved annuity" <term>census reservativus: an arrangement where a person transfers property but "reserves" a right to an annual payment from it</term>, which we are discussing now, it is no less valid than in an emphyteusis. In this case, we should follow Law 68 of Toro <note>A famous set of Spanish laws promulgated in 1505</note>, which is today Law 3, Title 15, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which establishes this. Nor does the *motu proprio* <note>a decree issued by the Pope on his own initiative</note> of Pius V regarding the creation of annuities contradict this, because that decree only speaks of "consigned annuities" <term>census consignativus: an annuity where a person "buys" a right to income from property owned by another</term>. This is also affirmed by Covarruvias, Gutierrez (in several works), Alvarus Valascus, and others they cite. The reason is that since in this contract the property is granted in terms of ownership and title while the annuity is reserved, the person granting the property can justly refuse to grant both types of ownership except under the agreement and condition that if the annuity is not paid within a certain time, the property—in both forms of ownership—reverts to him. This is no different than someone who hands over property in an emphyteusis and can justly refuse to grant the "useful ownership" <note>the right to use and profit from the land</note> except under a similar condition. Furthermore, Gutierrez rightly argues against Covarruvias that this applies even if the property was handed over under a redeemable reserved annuity, because the same logic holds. Alvarus Valascus reports that according to the common opinion of Rolandus, the same should be said if the debtor of the annuity promised under oath to pay within a certain time and failed to keep the promise. However, Valascus adds that this is not certain. I personally think it is false: an oath merely makes the person a perjurer if they do not keep their promise; it does not, however, cause them to incur forfeiture if, without the oath, they would not have incurred it by failing to keep the promise. Whether these same rules apply to a consigned annuity will be discussed later in its proper place when explaining the Bull of Pius V.

Thirdly, these contracts differ because the **emphyteuta** <note>the holder of a long-term lease</note> cannot sell the leased property without seeking the lord's permission; otherwise, he faces forfeiture. Furthermore, he is required to pay a **laudemium** <term>laudemium: a fee, usually a percentage of the sale price, paid to the landlord when a long-term lease is transferred</term> to the owner from the sale price, as will be shown in its proper place. However, a debtor of an annuity of this kind can sell the property subject to the annuity without seeking permission from the lord to whom the annuity is owed, nor is he required to pay a *laudemium* from the sale price. This is the common opinion, which Alvarus Valascus and others report and follow.

<margin>Doubt 6</margin> The question is, if there is doubt about a certain contract—whether it is an emphyteusis or an annuity contract—because its clauses do not clearly imply one over the other, or because it is known that a payment has always been made but the reason or title is unknown, which should it be judged to be?

<margin>Decision</margin> It must be said that this should be judged based on other concurrent circumstances. For example, if emphyteusis is customary in that region and reserved annuities are not, or based on other such factors, one should judge which contract is more likely to be presumed. Such was the opinion of Alvarus Valascus. However, when circumstances do not tip the scales in one direction rather than the other, Julius Clarus

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> states that the common opinion is that it should be judged as an emphyteusis in favor of the grantor, rather than an annuity. But Covarruvias and Alvarus Valascus affirm that the common opinion is that it should be judged as an annuity in favor of the possessor. This is the view they embrace, as does Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a highly influential canonist and economist</note>, and we approve of it as well. Because in cases of doubt, the condition of the possessor is better, and no more of a burden should be imposed on him than is clearly established as likely. Indeed, the three cited doctors agree that the same should be said whether the person who handed over the property is the Church or a private individual; this is against those who thought that in such an event, the judgment should be in favor of the Church.

<margin>7</margin> The annuity contract explained thus far is not very frequent today regarding temporal matters, but rather quite rare. It is not the primary subject we intend to treat in this place, nor is it technically a part of "buying and selling." For when a piece of land is granted to someone with full rights, reserving only an annual or monthly payment, it is clear that this is not a *purchase* of a payment, but rather a **donation** of the property regarding the remainder (if the value of the payment is not as great as the total value of the land), combined with the right that the donor reserves for himself in that land. Or, it is an "innominate contract" of "I give so that you give" <note>original: "do ut des"; a standard legal category for reciprocal agreements that don't fit specific names like 'sale'</note>, or as will be explained in the following dispute, it is a contract by which one thing is conferred and another part of one and the same thing is reserved. If someone hands over land to another for a sum of money and simultaneously for an annual payment to be rendered from that land, it will not be a purchase of an annuity either, but a "mixed contract" consisting of the sale of the land for that money and an innominate contract of "I give this land (regarding the portion that is worth more than the money) so that you give me such an annual payment from it."

<margin>8</margin> Likewise, if someone bought or acquired a piece of land through exchange and later granted it to the same person with full rights in return for an annual payment—as Joseph did with the Egyptians in Genesis 47—it would not be a purchase of an annual payment. In that case, Joseph acquired all the lands of the Egyptians for Pharaoh in exchange for wheat, and later granted those same lands to the Egyptians for an annual payment. This was not a purchase of an annual payment, but rather two contracts: one of purchase or exchange of the land, and another of granting that same land while reserving an annual payment from it, which is thus a reserved annuity.

### Treatise Two, Disputation 382

<margin>4 A bare pact regarding a buy-back in favor of the seller, when clothed by the coherence of the contract, produces an "action for prescribed words" <note>original: "actio praescriptis verbis"; a flexible Roman law legal action used for contracts that did not fit into standard categories</note> against the buyer, so that he stands by that pact.</margin>

When no other contract is mixed into a contract for a reserved annuity—for example, if a property is handed over in terms of its "useful" and "direct" ownership <note>A distinction in medieval law: "direct" ownership belongs to the lord, "useful" ownership to the person who actually uses the land</note> in exchange for an annual annuity of ten gold coins—it is doubted whether an **alcabala** <term>alcauala: a significant sales tax in the Spanish and Portuguese empires, often around 10%</term> must be paid on it. Indeed, it could be argued not only that it is owed, but that a double tax is owed. This is because, by the laws of Castile and Lusitania <note>Portugal</note>, a double tax is owed on an exchange or a contract of "I give so that you may give" <note>original: "do ut des"; a standard legal formula for a reciprocal exchange of goods</note>, as is clear from Law 2, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Collection* and from the fiscal articles in Lusitania. A contract for a reserved annuity is truly an exchange of a property for the annuity itself—that is, for the right to receive an annual payment from that property. However, it must be said, following Lassarte <note>a noted Spanish legal scholar</note> in *On the Sale of Tithes* (Chapter 20, No. 52), that no tax is owed from that contract. The reason is that it is not an exchange or a "give-for-give" contract, for which two distinct things are necessary, handed over by the parties to one another in exchange. This is not seen in the contract we are discussing. For when Peter hands over his property to John for a reserved annuity of ten gold coins annually, only the property Peter hands over is considered; nothing is given back from John’s side. Instead, Peter reserves for himself from that property the right of receiving ten gold coins from its fruits. This right is like a part of the whole right and full ownership of that same property. We understand that he takes away something from that property—namely, from its formal or virtual lordship—leaving only the burden to John of cultivating and managing the property and paying ten gold coins annually from it. Nor does John, after accepting the property in its full and complete ownership, grant that right to Peter; rather, it is Peter himself who, while granting the property regarding everything else, reserves that right for himself, so that he never actually handed it over to John. In this, no exchange or "give-for-give" contract is seen. Rather, as Law *Ultima* of the Code *On the Exchange of Things* (which deals with this very contract) expressly states, the one granting the property prescribes a law upon his own property while he grants it, making it the recipient's property in all other respects. Therefore, as stated there, it is a certain "bare pact" <note>an agreement that doesn't technically meet all the formal requirements of a contract but is still binding here</note> celebrated by the mutual consent of both parties: the granting of the thing in other respects and the reservation of that right, with a burden on the part of the one receiving it and an obligation to fulfill it. This is "clothed" by the delivery of the property, from which an "action for prescribed words" is available against the recipient and his successors in the same property to fulfill that obligation, as the same law expressly holds...

<margin>1</margin>
When a sale is mixed into a contract for a reserved annuity—for instance, because a property was handed over for a certain amount of money along with the reservation of an annual payment—then, regarding the money accepted as the price, an alcabala would be owed by the seller in this Kingdom of Castile. In Lusitania, however, half would be owed by the seller and the other half by the buyer. But when an exchange is mixed in—for example, if a property were handed over for another thing (which is not money) and for

<column-break/>

an annual payment—then, from the value of the thing given for the property along with the annual payment, one alcabala would be owed. And from the value of the property, insofar as it corresponds precisely not to the payment, but to that thing given in exchange for the property, another alcabala would be owed. Lassarte agrees with this in the citation above at number 73.

<margin>2 Question</margin>
The chief difficulty, however, is when a property is given, for example, for an annual annuity of ten gold coins, with the faculty of redeeming it for a certain price. In that case, is an alcabala owed? And when? And to which tax collector should it be paid? In this place, two types of contracts must be examined for this purpose, which were mentioned at the end of Disputation 372.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The first case is when a property is sold for one hundred gold coins, with the pact that, while they remain unpaid, an annual annuity of ten gold coins established on that property shall be paid, redeemable for those same hundred gold coins. Regarding this contract, it must undoubtedly be said that a double tax is owed. One tax comes from that first contract of selling the property for those hundred gold coins, which is a true sale perfected immediately by the mutual consent of the parties. Therefore, that tax is owed immediately—in this Kingdom by the seller of the property alone, but in Lusitania, half by the buyer and half by the seller. It is owed to the tax collector and the lord who were in office at the time the contract was celebrated. The other tax is owed from the sale of the annuity for those hundred gold coins. It is owed not at the time of redemption, nor because of the redemption (since that is the dissolution of the prior contract based on the "buy-back" pact attached to it); rather, it is owed from the sale of the annuity itself for those hundred gold coins made at the beginning. Thus, it is owed to the tax collector who was then in office. In this Kingdom, it is owed by the seller of the annuity alone (who had just been the buyer of the property), but in Lusitania, half is owed by one and half by the other. The reason for this is that the establishment of that annual annuity of ten gold coins—until the hundred gold coins for which the property was sold were paid—was a true purchase and sale of that annuity, distinct from the sale of the property. For the sale of that annuity, its own peculiar tax is owed, according to what will be said in the following disputations. Lassarte agrees with these points in *On the Sale of Tithes*, Chapter 10, from number 47.

Note several things, however. First: In this case, the annuity is not "reserved" (which was the subject of the preceding disputation), but "consigned" <term>census consignativus: an annuity where a buyer pays a lump sum to a property owner in exchange for a guaranteed annual income from that property</term>, which will be discussed in subsequent disputations. This is because he sold the property for one hundred gold coins, reserving nothing for himself. Since those gold coins were not to be paid immediately, the seller of the property, while they remained unpaid and until the annuity was redeemed, "bought" that annuity on the same property. Thus, it is an annuity granted by the buyer of the property and "consigned" on the same property bought for one hundred gold coins, until he should pay them back.

Second: The price of this annuity in the proposed example—at the rate of ten to one <note>a 10% rate of return</note>—is **unjust** <note>illegal or usurious</note> in this Kingdom. It does not reach the legal price for a redeemable consigned annuity taxed in Law 6, Title 15 of the *New Collection*, which sets the minimum rate at fourteen to one <note>roughly a 7.1% rate of return; "fourteen to one" means you pay 14 units of capital to "buy" 1 unit of annual income</note>.

Third...

### Ludovico Molina on Contracts

Third: This same annuity is today legally void and presumed usurious wherever the Bull of Pius V has been accepted. That decree established that "consigned" annuities <note>original: "census consignativos"; these were annuities backed by specific property</note> which are redeemable but purchased with anything other than cash paid in the presence of a notary are legally null. By a legal presumption <note>original: "praesumptione iuris, & de iure"; a heavy legal term meaning a presumption so strong it is treated as a fact</note>, they are to be considered usurious.

The second type of contract is when a property is given in exchange for a reserved annual annuity of, for example, ten gold coins, which can be redeemed for one hundred and fifty gold coins. In this situation, first observe that this reserved annuity is not among those addressed by Pius V in his Bull. There has never been a doubt about its lawfulness, as it bears no resemblance to usury. Furthermore, it is not among those for which the price of purchase or redemption is capped by Law 6 of Castile, which sets a minimum ratio of fourteen to one. Such an annuity (unless a higher price is established from the start because of the right to redeem granted in the original contract) is certainly worth much more than a fourteen-to-one ratio. By its nature, it is perpetual and irredeemable; therefore, if the redemption is negotiated sometime after the first contract was made, the price should be much higher than the fourteen-to-one ratio. Consequently, in this Kingdom, for the redemption price of this annuity to be just, it must exceed the fourteen-to-one ratio, unless it was originally set at that rate specifically because the power to redeem was granted at the same time.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding this † redeemable annuity, there is a significant difficulty: whether a **tax** <term>gabella: refers here to the "alcabala," the standard sales tax</term> is owed, and if so, when and to which tax collector it should be paid. Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a major 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in *Various Resolutions* (Book 3, Chapter 11), although he does not explicitly debate the tax owed on the contract proposed here, does discuss the right of "retraction" <note>the right of a relative or co-owner to step in and buy back sold property</note>. He considers that two sales and purchases can be seen in such a contract. First, the sale of the property for the price at which the annuity may be redeemed (one hundred and fifty gold coins in our example). Second, the sale of the annuity itself for those same one hundred and fifty coins. From this, Lassarte <note>another legal authority</note> rightly infers that a double tax is owed: one from the seller of the property for the sale of the land, and another from the buyer of the property for the "sale" of the annuity. However, no additional tax is owed upon the actual redemption of the annuity, as that is merely the reversal of the second sale.

Lassarte also cites the opinion of Avendanius, who asserts that only a single tax is owed because of the "power to redeem" the annuity, which is the only part he recognizes as a sale. He argues this tax is owed by the seller of the property immediately when the contract is signed, and it belongs to the tax collector active at that time. No tax would then be owed at the later moment of redemption.

Lassarte notes that the

<column-break/>

daily practice followed in many places in this Kingdom is that a single tax is owed, to be paid by the seller of the property. This is paid not at the time the contract is signed, nor to the collector then in office, but rather at the time of the annuity's redemption, and to the collector and the lord who are in power at *that* future time. This custom should be embraced—as Lassarte does—not only as a legitimate interpreter of the laws but as the very truth of the matter.

To understand this, one must observe what was shown above: that no tax is owed from the contract and the handing over of property for a reserved annual annuity of ten gold coins. That contract is neither a purchase and sale, nor an exchange, nor a contract of "I give so that you may give." The entire difficulty lies in the "power to redeem" that annuity for one hundred and fifty gold coins added to the contract—the agreement that whenever the person who received the property pays those coins, the annuity is extinguished. Is a tax owed because of that agreement, or rather because of the redemption itself, as if the redemption were the "purchase" of the annuity? Avendanius and others thought the agreement itself was the sale. Since a contract of sale is perfected by mutual consent (triggering the tax) rather than by the delivery of money, Avendanius argued the tax was owed immediately. However, putting aside Lassarte's long dispute which does not seem to hit the mark, the matter should be stated briefly: That "power" or "pact" is not a contract of sale (neither pure nor conditional). Instead, it is a **bare pact** <term>pactum nudum: an agreement that, in Roman law, did not originally grant a right to sue unless it was "clothed" or attached to a formal contract</term> added to the annuity contract for the benefit of the person receiving the property. Because it is "clothed" by the coherence of the annuity contract, it gives rise to an "action for prescribed words" <note>original: "actionem praescriptis verbis"; a legal remedy for non-standard contracts</note> to force the person who gave the property to allow the redemption whenever the money is offered.

<margin>2</margin> Just as † when a pact of resale <note>original: "pactum de retrovendendo"; an agreement allowing a seller to buy back their goods</note> is added to a sale in favor of the seller, it is granted the "action for prescribed words" to force the buyer to stand by the pact. This is clear from the laws on agreements between buyer and seller. It is obvious from our previous discussion that the property was sold with the burden of that pact. Therefore, no sale of the annuity preceded the redemption; rather, the redemption follows the pact as a resolution of the

<meta>catchword: prioris (of the prior...)</meta>

of the prior sales contract, as is seen in a buy-back agreement: the consequence is that the redemption, in the case proposed, is a true purchase <note>original: "vera emptio"</note> of that annuity for those fifty gold coins, so that it is extinguished for the person to whom it was previously owed and is consolidated with the property. This is what the person who handed over the property for the annuity bound himself to do through that agreement. Therefore, because this redemption is a true purchase and sale, and not merely a reversal of some previous sale, it follows that the sales tax <term>gabellario (from gabella)</term><note>The "gabella" or "alcabala" was a significant sales tax in Spain and its territories, often around 10%.</note> who is in office at the time must be paid. This is the accepted practice, even though no tax is owed when a sale is simply reversed through a buy-back agreement.

From what has been said, it is clear that if a reserved annuity is established without a buy-back agreement and is later redeemed by the agreement of the parties, the tax is owed to the tax collector who is then in office; this is because it constitutes a true purchase and sale of that annuity. However, if after the property has been accepted for a reserved and redeemable annuity, the contracting parties agree that the matter should return to its original state, no tax is owed: because that is neither an exchange, nor a purchase, nor a sale. If, however, the person possessing the property sells or exchanges it, the tax is owed—a single tax for a sale, and a double tax for an exchange. Say the same if the annuity itself is sold or exchanged.

### What a consigned annuity is, and its fourfold nature.

## DISPUTATION 383.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 What a consigned annuity is, and the following numbers throughout.
2 When an annuity contract is called a purchase.
3 "Pension," "return," and "annuity" are understood in two ways.
4 What corresponds to a "real" annuity and what to a "personal" one.
5 The personal annuity is twofold.
6 What a "real" annuity is, and how it differs from a personal one with a mortgage.
7 If a real annuity is placed on certain specific properties, whether the annuity is considered dead if those properties are destroyed.
8 An annuity established on specific properties acts like a "servitude" <note>A legal burden or right over someone else's land, similar to a modern easement.</note>.
9 An annuity can be demanded in full from anyone possessing any part of the things subject to the annuity.
10 Annuities, pensions, and returns are counted among immovable property.
11 If an annuity is paid in money, it can be sold; otherwise, it would be an exchange or another "innominate" <note>A contract that doesn't have a specific legal name but is still binding.</note> contract. What is observed in Castile and Portugal.
12 What is an "annuitist" <note>original: "censuista"; the buyer/creditor</note> and what is an "annuitary" <note>original: "censuarius"; the seller/debtor</note>.
13 Both real and personal annuities are fourfold.
14 What a life annuity is.

In another sense, an annuity is what is called "consigned" <note>original: "consignativus"</note> because it is assigned, established, and produced from the assets of the person who grants it, while the ownership of those same assets—both the "useful" and "direct" ownership—remains with the grantor himself. If it is granted for a price (as is regularly done), it is a true purchase and sale, as we shall see. Viewed in this way, the annuity contract is like a sub-category of purchase and sale; and it is primarily about this that we speak here. I said "if it is granted for a price" because it can be granted by various other titles, such as exchange, or a donation as a reward for work or services, and various other ways; and then the grant will take on a different nature according to the type of title. We will speak primarily of the purchase and sale of an annuity, not only because this title is the most frequent, but also because, once this contract is explained, it will be easy to understand what should be said about annuities acquired by other titles.

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin> An annuity contract taken in this way is a purchase by which someone, for a certain amount of money, buys the right <note>original: "ius"</note> to receive an annual, monthly, or other similar return from a person or from property, whether in money or in any other thing, while the seller of the return remains the owner of his own goods just as he was before. This is what Gutierrez and others commonly affirm. In Disputation 372, along with Covarruvias and others, we said that we should not worry that notaries in this Kingdom, out of ignorance and corrupt usage, say in contracts that the seller of an annuity grants "direct ownership" of the property on which the annuity is placed to the buyer. Indeed, this annuity contract takes its name from the "return" <note>original: "reditus"</note> that is bought with it and which must be paid at set times; for that return is called an "annuity" in the sense explained in Disputation 381.

<margin>3</margin> At this point, it should be noted that if the purchased return is to be paid in money, nothing at all prevents the annuity contract from being a true purchase and sale. You will easily understand this if you consider that "return," "pension," "annuity," and similar terms are used in two ways. One way is **materially**, for the things that are paid every year or at other set times. In this way, returns, pensions, and annuities are the money, wheat, and other things paid at those times. They are called "returns" <note>original: "reditus"</note> from "returning" <note>original: "redeundo"</note> because they return to be paid from time to time. In the other way, they are used **formally**, not for the things being paid, but for the **right** to be paid from time to time. And in this sense we are accustomed to say, "Peter has an annuity on such-and-such property of John's"—meaning the right that a certain amount of money or produce be paid to him from it, as if that property were obligated to it. We also say, "Peter has such a pension from John's church-office," which is the right that a certain amount be paid to him from it every year. In this sense, annuity, pension, and return denote **incorporeal things** <note>In law, an incorporeal thing is an asset that has no physical existence, like a debt, a right, or an intellectual property.</note>. For that right, which those words formally signify, is nothing other than a certain "rational relation" <note>original: "respectus rationis"</note> in the person to whom the pension, return, or annuity is owed. Therefore, this relation is numbered among incorporeal things because it is not a thing that can be touched or handled with the hands, as physical things are touched and handled. Read what was said in Disputation 2 and following. Furthermore, to such a right, as a correlative, there corresponds an "obligation" and a "debt"; for a right is toward something that is owed in some way by that right. On the part of the one who owes it, there corresponds his obligation to such a debt. If it is owed from some thing in such a way that the thing itself is bound to it, there also corresponds a "real obligation" on the part of that thing.

Molina clarifies that this is a "true sale" of an incorporeal right (an intangible asset) rather than a physical object.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts I

4. the thing. Whence † it follows that in a real annuity <term>census realis (an income stream tied to land)</term>—that is, the right to an annual or monthly payment from someone who sold that annuity—there are three partial correlatives. The first is the thing itself which is owed, insofar as it is owed; such as money or wheat to be paid annually. The second is the **obligation of the thing**, from which it is owed, which is bound for that debt; and this is called a **real obligation**, because it is an obligation of the thing itself to whomever it may pass. The right in comparison to this is called a **real right**, because it is a right in the thing <note>original: "ius in re"</note>; that is, having a corresponding obligation of the thing to that which is owed from it. The third partial correlative is the **obligation of the person** who owes the annuity from such a thing. And this obligation is personal; for a personal obligation is always joined with a real obligation of the one to whom the thing belongs which carries the real obligation. For they are bound, at the very least, to surrender the thing for payment, or at least in the event of another's failure to pay the debt. However, when an annuity is **merely personal**—that is, a right that another pay an annual or monthly pension with no other thing bound to it—then only a double partial correlative corresponds to that right: namely, the thing which is owed (such as money, wheat, or something similar to be paid at set times) and the personal obligation of the one who owes it.

5. I said "when the annuity is merely personal," because † an annuity that is simply and absolutely personal is twofold. One is **merely personal**, because no real obligation corresponds to it, since no other thing is bound to it other than the person. The other is **not merely personal**, when, beyond the person, something else is bound for that annuity—not indeed as the thing *in* which and *from* which it is owed, but as a **mortgage** <term>hypotheca (property used as collateral)</term> for the annuity and the security of its payment. Such an annuity is simply personal, yet a real obligation corresponds to it, such that in the event the debtor of the annuity does not pay, and there are no other assets from which it can be paid, the mortgaged thing remains liable so that it may be paid from it, into whosever hands or ownership it may come.

6. From these points † it is established that a **real annuity** is only that which is so placed in some thing that it is owed in that thing and from that thing. There is no small difference between a real annuity and a personal annuity with a mortgage for its security. For when an annuity is **real**, if the thing in which it was placed perishes, the annuity perishes; because it was owed only in and from that thing, as if the buyer of the annuity, by so purchasing it, bought a part of the right to the fruits in that thing from the greater right which the owner held in it. But truly, when an annuity is **personal with a mortgage**, if the mortgage perishes, the annuity does not perish; because the annuity was not placed in the mortgage, but in the **person** from whom the annuity was bought. For that reason, only the security provided for the payment of the annuity perishes—the security from which the annuity was to be paid into whosever hands that thing might come, in the event the debtor did not have other assets from which to pay.
Connected with this distinction is another: namely, that when an annuity is **real**, the debtor of the annuity is the person to whom the thing in which the annuity is placed passes, because it is owed in and from that thing. But when an annuity is

<column-break/>

**personal with a mortgage**, if the mortgage passes to another, the one to whom it passes is **not** the debtor of the annuity. Instead, the debtor is the person in whom the annuity was placed and their heirs. The mortgage only remains liable for the payment of that annuity in the event that the person who owes the annuity has become unable to pay, such that they do not have assets from which it can be paid. In the meantime, as long as the person has assets from which it can be paid, execution must first be made against their assets rather than against the mortgage, according to the legal principle "this if the debtor" <note>original: "auth. hoc si debitor. C. de pignor." This refers to the Code of Justinian, specifically the section on pledges and mortgages, establishing the order of debt collection.</note>.
From this it is clear that although a real obligation corresponds to both a real annuity and a personal annuity with a mortgage, they correspond in different ways. To a **real annuity**, it corresponds from the very nature of the annuity and the annuity contract; it corresponds such that the payment must be made from the thing in which the annuity is placed, to whomever that thing may come. But to a **personal annuity with a mortgage**, a real obligation does not correspond by virtue of the annuity or the annuity contract, but by virtue of **another contract added** for the greater security of the annuity, by which certain goods are mortgaged for the security of the annuity contract. Furthermore, the real obligation does not correspond as if the payment were owed in and from the mortgaged thing, but because the mortgaged thing remains bound in default of the one who owes the annuity and his other assets. And for this reason, we said above: a personal obligation of the owner of the thing is always joined with a real obligation; I added this because they are bound at the minimum to surrender the thing for payment, at least in default of another who should pay the debt.

7. Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva (1512–1577), a famous Spanish jurist whose opinions Molina frequently critiques or refines.</note> in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 7, differs in some points from the doctrine we have handed down so far. First, at the end of number 5 and in number 6, he asserts that † when a **real annuity** is placed in one or more specific estates, unless it is expressly stated in the contract that it is so placed that the annuity perishes if the estates perish, the annuity does **not** perish. Instead, the seller of the annuity and their heirs are held to the payment. He relies on a certain foundation in which he also differs from our doctrine: he affirms that when a real annuity is placed in specific estates, those estates only have the character of a **mortgage**—though an irregular and more restrictive one, which therefore does not follow all the laws of other pledges and mortgages.
From this, he first concludes that if the things in which a real annuity is placed pass to a **third-party possessor** who is not the heir of the seller, the person to whom the annuity is owed has an action against that possessor to pay the annuity from the estate and to recognize themselves as the debtor of the annuity from that estate, without first demanding anything from the seller of the annuity or their heirs. And in this, he says, this mortgage is more restrictive and does not follow the laws of other mortgages. For if other common mortgaged things pass to a third-party possessor, no action lies against the third possessor to pay the debt from them unless execution is first made against the assets of the principal debtor and his sureties; only when no assets of theirs are found from which the debt can be paid, then execution...

<summary>Molina distinguishes between "real" annuities (tied to specific property) and "personal" annuities (tied to a person), explaining that a real annuity ends if the property is destroyed, while a personal annuity persists. He also begins a critique of the jurist Covarrubias, who argued that sellers remain liable for real annuities even if the property is lost.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 383.

[Regredia]tion <note>original: "Regrediatio"; referring to the right of the creditor to "step back" or return to a previous debtor for payment</note> can occur if it was done with mortgages <term>hypothecis (property pledged as security)</term>, and not before, as stated in the authentic text "Hoc si debitor" <note>A reference to the Code of Justinian, specifically regarding the rights of creditors against debtors</note> in the section on pledges. Secondly, in the same place (number 7), Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist</note> argues that if an annuity <term>census (an annual payment derived from property)</term> valued at a certain amount of gold is placed upon three estates—which then pass to three distinct owners—the individual owners cannot be sued for the entire annuity. Nor can they be forced to recognize the debt of the whole annuity; rather, they can only be sued for a portion of it, according to the proportional value of each estate. In this matter, he says, the mortgage on the things upon which the annuity is placed does not follow the laws of other common mortgages. For when properties are subject to a mortgage for some debt, and neither the debtor nor his guarantors have the means to pay, the entire debt can be demanded from any single item subject to the mortgage, without demanding anything from the owners of the other items. This is according to the law "Moschis" in the Digest on the rights of the treasury, as taught by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, though some disagree.

Thirdly, in the cited number 6, he argues that when an annuity has been placed on certain specific estates and those have passed to other owners, the person to whom the annuity is owed can bypass the current owners and sue for payment against the original seller and his heirs. He believes that since the annuity is "real" <note>meaning "attached to a thing" (res)</note>, it does not only create a real obligation—by reason of which an action is given against the person possessing the property—but it also simultaneously creates a personal obligation on the part of the seller to pay it. This personal obligation remains with the seller even after the estates are sold and passes to his heirs. In this respect, he says that the mortgage on things where a real annuity is placed agrees with other common mortgages. For even if common mortgages pass to a third-party owner, the principal and original debtor does not cease to remain obligated for the debt.

<margin>Decisions.</margin>

Alvarus Valascus <note>Álvaro Valasco, a Portuguese jurist</note> rightly affirms the opposite of all these points in his work "On Emphyteutic Law," question 32, number 13, as does Lassarte "On the Tenth of Sales," chapter 10. First of all, the foundation upon which Covarruvias leans—namely, that the things upon which a real annuity is placed have the character of a mortgage—is false and fabricated. For the form of the contract does not imply this, nor does it have any foundation in law that would make it an "extraordinary mortgage," as Covarruvias and others imagine.

8. Fifthly, an annuity established in this way is more like a servitude <term>servitutis (a legal burden on land, like an easement)</term> fixed to the estate in which the annuity is placed, as Alvarus Valascus correctly states above. Just as a servitude perishes when the estate to which it is attached perishes, and just as the servitude accompanies the estate when it passes to a third-party owner, no action for the servitude lies against the original person who granted it or his heirs (unless perhaps the estate is legally recovered by a previous owner), but the action lies only against the current owner. Thus it is entirely the same in the case of a real annuity. On this point, besides the doctors cited, Conradus "On Contracts" (question 83), Medina (final question on usury), Gabriel, Navarrus, and others commonly agree.

As for why a real annuity cannot strictly be called a servitude,

<column-break/>

it was discussed in Disputation 11; yet it cannot be denied that it is like a personal servitude. Furthermore, just as the annuity contract we are discussing was not recognized in the civil law of the *Digest* or the *Code*, it is no wonder that no mention of this "quasi-servitude" was made in civil law. It can be confirmed that when the thing in which the annuity is placed perishes, the annuity perishes and is no longer owed. For the sale of a purely real annuity is nothing other than the sale of a part of the right to the estate in which it is placed, as has been explained; and when the thing perishes, the part of the right in it also perishes.

From this, it is clear that what Covarruvias says is false: namely, that for an annuity to perish when the property perishes, it must be expressly stated in the contract. Since a real annuity has this quality by its very nature, it is certainly not necessary to express it in the contract. This is clearly established by the *Extravagantes* <note>Canon law collections</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III under the title "On Buying and Selling." There, when discussing this kind of annuity, it is said that if the possessions in which the annuity was established perish, no action is available to the buyers of the annuity to recover their money; because, obviously, the purchased annuity perished for them along with the estates in which it was placed. Pope Pius V established the same even more clearly in his bull on the creation of annuities, where he decreed that if the thing upon which the annuity is placed perishes or is rendered unproductive, in whole or in part, the annuity also perishes proportionally.

9. It is established† next that, although it is true that when the things upon which a real annuity is placed pass to other owners, the annuity-holder has an action against them to pay and acknowledge the annuity, it is nonetheless false that he cannot demand the entire annuity from anyone possessing even a part of those things. Indeed, the contrary is true and is accepted in Spain, as affirmed by Alvarus Valascus and Lassarte, followed by Navarrus and even Covarruvias himself, who admits it is the accepted practice.

The reason is that such seems to have been the intention of those celebrating the annuity contract: that each of those items should be obligated for the total annuity, in the manner of mortgages. A buyer of an annuity would not otherwise want to enter the contract, exposing himself to the risk that if those items passed to various owners, he would be forced to demand parts of the annuity from each one with great labor and loss. Since contracts are judged to be celebrated according to the custom of the place, even if nothing is expressed in the contract, it must be judged that such was the intention of the parties in Spain.

It is also clear that it is false to say that when the things pass to other owners, an action remains for the buyer of the annuity against the seller and his heirs, as is clear from what has been said. An exception is made unless the thing is legally evicted <note>lost to a superior legal claim</note>. For then, just as the original seller and his heirs would be held liable for eviction to the owners (each heir for their proportional share), so too they would be held liable to the holder of the annuity for the annuity along with those evicted things, as the cited doctors and Navarrus affirm.

<summary>This page argues that a real annuity is a legal burden attached to the land (like a servitude) rather than a personal debt of the seller. Consequently, if the land is destroyed, the annuity ends, and if the land is sold, the new owners are liable for the full payment, not the original seller.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

10 Let us return now to what we were explaining, and observe this final point: an annuity, pension, or rent—which is the right to a payment from a property at set times—is classified as **immovable property**, even if the items being paid are themselves **movable** <note>In legal terms, "immovable property" usually refers to land or buildings, while "movable" refers to things like cash or grain. Molina is explaining that the *legal right* to a payment is treated like land itself.</note>. This is established in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of Roman Catholic canon law</note> in the chapter "Exivi de paradiso," in the section regarding the meaning of words. The text states: *“Since annual rents are considered by law to be among immovable goods.”* In this context, "annual rents" does not mean the actual things being paid—as everyone knows no movable goods are immovable—but rather the **legal right** to receive those payments. Furthermore, "annual rent" is a general term covering both annuities and pensions, for every annuity and pension is a form of rent.

11 From what has been said, it is now easily understood that the "contingent contract" we are discussing is a true form of **buying and selling**. The fact that the annuity is paid in money does not change this. In such a contract, we first see a price—that is, the money given for the annuity. Next, we see the merchandise, which must be distinguished from the price. What is immediately and directly purchased is not the money or any other movable item to be paid at set times; rather, it is the **right** to receive those payments. This comes with an obligation on the part of the person selling the annuity, or an obligation tied to the property upon which the annuity is sold. The price is given so that the seller grants this right and takes this obligation upon themselves and their property; this right is what is being bought.

However, if the payment for the annuity is not money, but a horse, a piece of land, services to be rendered, or something similar, then the contract will not be a "buying and selling" agreement. Instead, it would be an **exchange** of a thing for an annuity, or another type of "unnamed contract" <note>original: "contractus innominatus"; a legal category for agreements that don't fit standard labels like 'sale' or 'lease'</note>, such as "I give so that you may do" or "I do so that you may give." An annuity can also be established as a gift, as we mentioned at the start of this discussion—for example, if someone grants an annuity based on their ownership of certain property or rights owed to them in a city. If the annuity is granted in return for services already performed, it is more like a contract of "I give because you have done" rather than a pure gift. If a prince grants more than the services were worth, it is a mixed contract, part gift and part unnamed contract.

<margin>The Law of Castile</margin>
In this Kingdom <note>Castile/Spain</note>, when the King grants an annual rent from the rights and revenues owed to him—such as from salt mines, a city, or a town—whether as a gift, as compensation for services, or for a price, these rents are called by the specific name <term>juros</term> <note>Spanish state-backed annuities or bonds</note>. This applies whether they are perpetual (cannot be bought back), redeemable, or granted for one or more lifetimes. Other similar rents are simply called annuities <term>census</term>, as is clear from the New Collection of Laws and common speech. In this and the following discussions, we include all these under the name "annuity." In Portugal, those who buy such rents from the King or nobility are also said to buy <term>juros</term>, even if they include a "buy-back" clause.

<margin>The Law of Portugal</margin>
When the King gives something as a gift—either from his own revenues, or by granting a town, or a title like Marquis, Count, or Duke—if he gives it forever to someone and their successors, it is called a gift <term>de juro</term>. However, if he gives it for the life of one or more people, or for a 

<column-break/>

limited time, it is not called a grant <term>de juro</term>, but a grant of **grace** <note>original: "de merce"</note>. When he grants certain rents for a lifetime, or gives them for services or a price, it is called conferring a <term>tença</term> <note>A Portuguese term for a pension or stipend</note>.

12 Regarding the first part of the title of this discussion, note this final point about the way scholars speak: some call the person to whom the annuity is owed the **annuitant** <note>original: "censuista"</note>, and the person who owes it the **debtor** <note>original: "censuarium"</note>.

13 As for the second part of the title, annuities are divided first by the type of property they are placed upon: **real** (tied to land) or **personal**. Personal annuities can be subdivided into **purely personal**—which have no mortgage <term>hypotheca (property pledge)</term> to back them up—and **not purely personal**, which are tied to a person but also supported by a mortgage for greater security. A "purely personal" annuity is rarely or never bought because of its low security. 

Annuities are also divided by what is being paid: **fruit-bearing**, paid in products like wheat, oil, or wine; and **pecuniary**, paid in money. In this Kingdom of Castile, the law prohibits "redeemable" annuities from being paid in anything other than money. It was also decreed that redeemable annuities created before that law, which were paid in other goods, should be converted to money at a rate of **one for fourteen** <note>Meaning the annual payment should be 1/14th of the total value given</note>.

In Portugal, however, non-money redeemable annuities paid in wheat are quite common. They are usually bought at a very low price compared to the high cost of wheat in that Kingdom today, often at a rate of less than **nine for one** <note>This indicates a very high interest rate of over 11%, which Molina suggests is exploitative</note>. It would certainly be right to either prohibit these or regulate them so that farmers, who take this money out of necessity, are not unjustly oppressed.

Furthermore, regarding the items paid, annuities are divided into those paid in a **fixed quantity** (such as a certain number of bushels of wheat or a set amount of money) and those paid as a **fixed share** of the total (such as a fourth or fifth of the crop). An example of this is the system established by Joseph, where the Egyptians paid a fifth part of their harvest to Pharaoh. However, this division applies to "reserved" annuities (discussed in the previous two sections) and not to the "assigned" annuities we are discussing now.
<margin>Thomas, 2</margin>

Additionally, regarding time, annuities are divided into those paid annually, monthly, or at other set times.

Finally, regarding duration, they are divided into **perpetual** and **temporary**. Perpetual annuities are split into **irredeemable** (simply perpetual) and **redeemable**, which are made with a "buy-back" agreement <note>original: "pacto de retrouendendo"</note>.

<summary>Molina defines annuities as a form of immovable property and explains the legal mechanics of buying the "right" to future payments. He also details specific Spanish and Portuguese financial instruments like juros and tenças, while warning against the exploitation of farmers through high-interest grain-based annuities.</summary>

A temporal annuity is divided into that which lasts for a fixed number of years—such as ten, twenty, or thirty years—and that which lasts for an uncertain number of years, such as one purchased for the entire life of the buyer, the seller, or a certain third party.

A temporal annuity can also be made with a "buy-back clause" <note>original: *pactum de retrovendendo*</note> or without it. # Whether the sales tax is owed on a contract for a consigned annuity.

## DISPUTATION 384.

->S U M M A R Y<-

1 **Whether the <term>alcabala tax</term> <note>original: *gabella alcauale*; a major sales tax in the Spanish kingdoms</note> is owed from a contract for a consigned annuity, and when.**
2 **In which case a double tax is owed, and in the following number.**
3 **The tax is not owed from a buy-back made by virtue of a buy-back clause included in the first sale.**
4 **Whether the tax is owed on the total value of the item sold with the burden of the annuity, or rather with that burden deducted.**
5 **Whether the tax collector is bound to restore the tax paid by someone for the sale of a property as if it were free of debt, when it actually carried the burden of an annuity.**
6 **The tax is owed on the sale of a life annuity.**

<margin>1</margin>
**S**ince it was shown in the preceding disputation that when money is given for a consigned annuity <note>An annuity secured against a specific piece of property</note>, a true purchase and sale of an annuity takes place, it follows logically that the <term>alcabala tax</term> <note>original: *gabella alcaualæ*</note> is owed as soon as the contract is perfected and celebrated, even before the price is handed over. 
This is true unless you argue that, following the Bull of Pope Pius V <note>Likely referring to *Cum Onus* (1569), which regulated the terms of annuities to prevent usury</note>, where that Bull has been accepted in that region, an annuity contract with a buy-back clause is not considered "celebrated" until the money has been counted out in the presence of a notary. The tax is owed to the tax collector who is in office at that time. Furthermore, in this Kingdom [Castile], it is owed by the seller of the annuity alone; Lassarte affirms all these points, along with others he cites, in *On the Tithe of Sale*, chapter 10, from number 4. In Portugal, however, half is owed by the buyer and half by the seller. Additionally, it belongs to the seller to pay the cost of the legal document (*instrumentum*) drawn up for the matter because, as Tiraquellus says, it pertains to the one who binds himself to pay for the document being made. Lassarte affirms this along with Picarro at the end of number 7. However, perhaps since the contract is celebrated for the benefit of both, the buyer should pay half. And perhaps that is the accepted custom.

<margin>2</margin>
If someone who already possesses a previously purchased annuity sells it to someone else, the tax is owed again from that sale. In this Kingdom, the whole amount is payable by this second seller; but in Portugal, part is by the buyer and part by the seller. It must be paid,

<column-break/>

however, to the tax collector of the place where the properties subject to the annuity are located; for this reason, the tax of the first sale of the annuity is also paid, as we shall soon say. So says Lassarte in the place cited above, number 8, with others whom he cites.

<margin>2</margin>
But if an annuity, once established, is exchanged by the possessor for another thing—such as for wheat, a slave, a house, or another similar thing that is not money—a double tax will be owed, according to what has been said regarding <term>exchanges</term> <note>original: *permutationib.*; legally, an exchange was often treated as two separate sales, triggering two sets of taxes</note>. Thus Lassarte, as above, number 9. The same will apply to the first constitution of an annuity if it is done by exchange, and today an annuity with a buy-back clause, following the Bull of Pius V, can be established by exchange and not only by money counted out immediately before a notary. Furthermore, one tax shall be owed to the tax collector of the place where the things subjected to the annuity are located; the other shall be owed to the tax collector of the place where the things exchanged for the annuity are located.

<margin>3</margin>
If, however, the purchased annuity was from the beginning made with a <term>buy-back clause</term> <note>original: *pacto de retrouendendo*</note> for the same price at which it was bought, as is commonly done, and later it is redeemed at that price, a new tax is not owed on the redemption. This is because, as was said above when discussing sales with a buy-back clause, this is not a new contract but a resolution of the prior one based on a clause attached to the first.
If, however, it was bought at the beginning without a buy-back clause, but is later redeemed by agreement of the parties for the same price at which it was bought, a new tax is owed. This is because it is not a resolution of the prior contract based on a clause attached to it, but a new contract of purchase and sale, as is clear from what was said in the place cited.
But if at the beginning it was bought with money, and a clause was added that it should be redeemed with some piece of land of the same value as that price, or for a different price (whether greater or smaller), then a new tax is owed—and a double one if the redemption is made with land or another thing that is not money, because it is then an exchange. I understand the same to apply if a clause had intervened at the beginning that the annuity be redeemed for the price at which it was bought, and later, by agreement of the parties, it is redeemed with a thing that is not money; for then it is not a resolution of the prior contract, but a new contract of exchange.
Lassarte agrees in *On the Tithe of Sale*, chapter 10, number 10 and the two following, and others whom he cites. Lassarte, in the same place, number 13, adds that the matter is different if the seller redeems the annuity by the cession (handing over) of one of the properties in which the annuity had been placed, based on an agreement made between himself and the buyer over time, thus freeing the other properties in which the annuity had been placed. He thinks that in that case no tax is owed. He seems to mean the same even if he redeems the annuity by the cession of some thing that was subject to a mortgage as security for the annuity. Whether both doctrines are true is not entirely clear to me; read him, though I lean rather toward the contrary.
When a "real" annuity <note>An annuity tied to physical property (realty)</note> is bought upon properties located in different places, where there are different tax collectors, then the tax on the annuity is owed to those various collectors in proportion to the value of the property in each of those places relative to the value of the other properties. For example, if an annuity is bought for 1,400 gold coins and is placed upon goods existing in various places...

# Luis Molina on Contracts

...of those things, which are all valued at four thousand gold pieces, and a property existing in one location is valued at one thousand gold pieces, then a fourth part of the <term>sales tax</term> <note>original: *gabella*; referring to the Spanish *alcabala*</note> from that annuity must be paid to the tax collector of that location, and so on for the remaining parts according to the proportion of the value of the properties. Thus it happens that the seller of that annuity can be summoned regarding the tax before various judges in a hundred different places where those properties are located. So Lassar. <note>Lassarte, a noted Spanish jurist</note> on the tithe of sales, chapter 4, number 31, and chapter 10, number 34, affirms this with others whom he cites, stating that this practice is accepted in Castile.

<margin>Doubt 4</margin>
The doubt is: if someone sells an annuity of one hundred on one of his properties for one hundred and forty gold pieces, and later sells that same property to a third party for three hundred gold pieces on the condition that the buyer pays him one hundred and sixty gold pieces and, in place of the other one hundred and forty, acknowledges and pays the annuity placed upon that property—is the tax owed on the entire three hundred gold pieces, or only on the one hundred and sixty?

<margin>Decision</margin>
To this, it must be said with Lassarte (chapter 10, cited above, number 16) and others whom he cites, that it is owed only from the hundred and sixty; because in truth, the property is only sold for those hundred and sixty gold pieces along with that burden of the annuity which it contains within itself. The burden of the annuity is transferred, along with the property in which it resides, to the buyer of the property. From the transfer of a property with such a burden, valued by the remaining part of the price, the tax is not owed.

But if the annuity were <term>personal</term> <note>An annuity tied to a person's credit rather than a specific piece of land</note>, and the property was merely placed as a specific mortgage for the security of that annuity, then, if that property were sold for three hundred gold pieces, the tax would be owed on that total price, as Lassarte rightly adds in the same place. He also, along with Faber, correctly adds that if someone sells a property for a thousand gold pieces—five hundred to be paid to himself and the other five hundred to be paid to his creditors—the tax is owed on both.

<margin>Doubt 5</margin>
The next doubt is: if a seller sells a thing upon which an annuity was placed as if it were "free" <note>meaning free of any liens or encumbrances</note>, and later the buyer discovers it has the burden of an annuity and brings an <term>action for price reduction</term> <note>original: *actione quanto minoris*; a legal claim to lower the price because of a hidden defect or burden</note> against the seller, and the seller is compelled by a judge's sentence to restore part of the price because the thing with that burden was not worth as much: must he pay the tax on the part of the price he restored? Or if he had already paid it, is the tax collector bound to restore it to him?

<margin>Decision</margin>
Lassarte (as above, number 37) affirms it is owed. However, I judge the contrary to be true, following what we said regarding a certain other similar event in Disputation 349 against the same author. For the tax is not owed except from the <term>just price</term> of the thing, as was said there. This opinion of ours should be most especially embraced when the seller sold the thing in good faith as if it were free, being ignorant that it was subject to an annuity.

<margin>Doubt 6</margin>
Whether the tax is owed from the sale of a <term>life annuity</term> <note>original: *vitalitij*</note> can be called into doubt because of the most illustrious prelate Master Francisco Sarmiento, who in Book 7 of his *Selected Interpretations*, chapter 1, number 40, judges that this contract is not a sale, but a certain "aleatory" contract <note>A contract based on chance or luck, like a bet</note>, such as insurance, lots, or gambling, from which it is established that the tax is not owed, because neither a sale nor an exchange

<column-break/>

takes place. Nevertheless, it must undoubtedly be said with Lassarte (as above, number 38) and with others whom he cites, that it is a sale, as is clear enough from what was said in the preceding disputation, and therefore the tax is owed on it.

Lastly, observe with Lassarte (as above, number 76) that the practice has obtained in this Kingdom that the tax is not owed on the sale or exchange of those annuities which in this Kingdom are called <term>juros</term> <note>original: *iūros*; Spanish state-funded annuities or royal bonds</note>, according to what was said at the end of the preceding disputation. And although no sufficient reason seems able to be given why, by the rigor of the law, the tax should not be owed when the possessor sells it or exchanges it for another thing, perhaps it was introduced in favor of royal grants, and so that men might be more inclined to serve the King and to purchase such annuities or rights when he sells them.

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into the nature of annuity contracts (census), specifically debating whether the inclusion of a redemption clause—allowing the seller to buy back the annuity—transforms a legitimate sale into a disguised usurious loan. This forms part of Luis Molina’s broader Disputation 385 on the justice of financial instruments.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 385.
---

...[an agreement] of resale <note>original: *retrovendendo*; a clause allowing the seller to buy back the asset, effectively acting as a redemption of a debt</note> is usurious, and therefore illicit. The premise is proven as follows: if Peter lends John one hundred gold pieces on the condition that, until he repays them, Peter receives a certain annual amount from the fruits of one of John’s estates, and that estate is held as security for the principal, the contract is usurious. In such a case, the lender is required to count those annual payments toward the principal, as all authorities agree and as established in Disputation 320. Now, an <term>annuity contract</term> <note>original: *contractus censualis*; a financial arrangement where one party pays a lump sum in exchange for a guaranteed annual income (pension) from a specific property</note> is similar to this. In it, Peter gives one hundred gold pieces to John as the price for an equal annual <term>pension</term> <note>original: *pensio*; the recurring payment of an annuity</note> which John is obligated to pay from a certain estate. This burden follows the estate to whoever owns it. If a clause for resale is added—meaning that if those hundred gold pieces are returned, the obligation is abolished—and yet the pensions received are not counted toward the principal, then the premise is true. Indeed, no distinction can be made between one contract and the other, especially since the parties are the same, the money given is the same, and the pension is paid until the principal is returned; likewise, the estate is tied to the debt in both cases. There seems to be no difference in reality, only in words: in the first contract, the money is called a "loan," while in the second, it is called the "price of an annuity with a right of resale." Therefore, this is not a true purchase and sale, but a loan for a certain annual payment masked as a purchase, and thus it appears to be true usury.

<margin>2</margin>
Secondly, in some places, an irredeemable annuity is bought at a rate of thirty, twenty-five, or twenty to one <note>This refers to the "purchase price" being 20 or 30 times the value of the annual payment</note>. Yet in those same places, a redeemable annuity—that is, one with a right of resale—is bought at a rate of fourteen, twelve, or even ten to one. In this case, the seller appears to be defrauded of more than half the just price. But whenever something is bought with a right of resale and the price is significantly diminished, the contract is rejected and judged usurious, as is clear from the Canon Law <note>original: *c. ad nostram, de emp. & vend.* (Chapter "Ad Nostram" on Purchase and Sale)</note> and the *Ordinances of Justice* <note>original: *de Iustit. ord.*</note> Book 14, § 2. Therefore, a redeemable annuity contract celebrated in that manner is illicit.

<margin>3</margin>
Thirdly, in an annuity contract, especially if the pension is to be paid in money, there appears to be no contract other than a loan. Money is given so that it may be repaid in parts over time with an increase beyond the principal. This is the very definition of usury. The "sale" argument fails because for a contract to be a sale, there must be "merchandise." If this were a sale, the thing sold would have to be either the land, the money paid annually, or the right to that money. It is not the land, for the land remains with the seller. Nor is it the money, for money as such cannot be sold; money is the price and measure of value for saleable goods and cannot itself be treated as merchandise. For a sale to occur, there must be both a price and merchandise.

<column-break/>

Finally, it cannot be the "right" to have the money paid; since that right is a mere <term>entity of reason</term> <note>original: *ens rationis*; a conceptual thing that exists only in the mind, rather than a physical object</note> and has no value in itself, the contract would be unjust if so much money were accepted for it.

<margin>4</margin>
Fourthly, for a contract to be just, equality is required between what is given and what is received. This equality is not found in the annuity contract. The money given for the annuity is finite and limited—for example, one hundred and forty gold pieces for an annual payment of ten. However, what must be paid back in a redeemable annuity exceeds that amount within sixteen years, and the entire principal is still owed! Or, the payments must continue forever. In an irredeemable annuity, the amount paid back within forty years is far greater than the price received, and yet the pensions remain to be paid forever. Thus, there is no equality. Even if one argues that they are not buying the "pensions" themselves but the "right to receive them," the argument fails. A right to receive something in the future is worth no less than the thing itself. Therefore, if there is a mismatch in value between the price and the total pensions, there is a mismatch between the price and the right to those pensions.

Fifthly, if these contracts were just and maintained equality, there should be a mathematical proportion between the price of a temporary annuity and a perpetual one. However, there is no proportion between a perpetual duration and a temporal one, nor between infinite pensions and finite ones. Since a finite, temporary annuity is bought for a finite just price, it follows that an infinite, perpetual annuity could never be justly bought for any finite price. Otherwise, you would have a proportion between the prices where no proportion exists between the things being bought.

<margin>5</margin>
Lastly, many evils follow from these annuity contracts...
