<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of the moral and legal status of annuities (census). Having previously discussed the potential for usury in redemption clauses, he now addresses the broader question of whether establishing an annuity contract is inherently illicit, examining the arguments of critics before presenting the "common opinion" of the Church doctors that these contracts are legitimate forms of sale and purchase.</meta>

# Luis Molina, On Contracts
---

[the following consequences] follow: therefore, this contract is illicit. The premise is proven, first, because those who buy these <term>annuities</term> <note>original: *census*; a financial arrangement where a person pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment from property</note> wish to live off the sweat of others when they ought to live off their own. From this, it further follows that they do not cultivate the land, nor do they practice other trades useful to the Commonwealth. Furthermore, the path to practicing charity through interest-free loans is blocked; for as soon as someone asks for a loan, the person who has money instead offers to buy an annuity. Moreover, those who sell annuities are greatly impoverished, as they burden their assets with the annual payments they must make.

Henry of Ghent (in *Quodlibet* 8, question 24; he should also be read in *Quodlibet* 1, question 39), Salycetus (on the *Authentica ad haec* in the Code regarding usury), and Gregory of Rimini as cited by Salycetus, all judge the purchase of annual payments that are newly created to be illicit and usurious, even if they are tied to a specific estate from which they are to be paid. This is the case, they argue, provided it is expected that such payments, even when received over intervals of time, will eventually exceed the money given for them. For, they say, in the purchase of these annuities, money is effectively given as a loan so that it may be restored with an increase in installments. The tying of these payments to an estate serves no other purpose than to make the estate act as a pledge or a mortgage. Consequently, by the reasoning of these authors, it is a far more usurious contract if cash payments are purchased without being tied to any estate, which is called a <term>personal annuity</term> <note>original: *census personalis*; an annuity tied to a person's credit or labor rather than a piece of real estate</note>.

If, however, they say, such payments had already been lawfully established—for example, through a gift from the owner of an estate who granted someone an annual payment from that land, or if the payments were lawfully established as taxes due to a King, or for some other reason—then they say a third party can lawfully buy such payments. This is because in that case, a true right is found to exist prior to the sale, acting as a commodity that is bought for a price; therefore, usury does not occur. Innocent and Joannes Andreae (on the chapter *In civitatem* regarding usury) seem to lean toward this same opinion, though they do not explicitly reject the contrary view.

9 **The contrary opinion**—namely, that a true purchase and sale occurs in a lawful annuity contract, and thus it is legitimate when it is a <term>real annuity</term> <note>original: *census realis*; an annuity secured by physical property</note> (provided the price is proportionate to the annuity according to local custom, because annuities are commonly bought that way in that place)—is the common doctrine and is to be embraced. This is affirmed by Conrad (on contracts, from question 73, especially 79 and 82), Juan Medina (on usury, in the questions on annuities, question 2 and the last question, which is on redeemable annuities), Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 5, articles 1 and 3), Covarruvias (Book 3, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7), Gabriel (on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, question 12), Major (ibid., questions 43 and 44), Panormitanus (on the chapter *In civitatem* regarding usury and other interpreters of canon law in the same place; also Panormitanus in his own questions, question 5), Navarro (chapter 14, question 3, from number 69), Alvaro Valasco (*On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 32, numbers 8 and 9), Antonio Gomez (on law 68 of Toro, number 2), Gregorio Lopez (law 28, title 8, part 5, on the word *a censo*), Sylvester (under the word *usury* 2, question 12), and others whom they cite.

7 First, however, it was shown in Disputation 383 that a true purchase and sale occurs in this contract. This is because a true commodity is found in it: namely, the **right** which the seller of the annuity grants in exchange for the price, and the **obligation** which he undertakes upon his property for the annual payment. These are the immediate

<column-break/>

object that is bought; and a price is found, namely the money given for that annuity. Even if the immediate object of the purchase were not that right and obligation toward the payments (viewed as material things), but the payments themselves, it could not be denied—provided the annuity is "fruit-bearing" <note>original: *fructuarius*; producing income like a crop</note>—that a true purchase and sale is seen in that annuity contract. This is because those fruits of the payments would truly have the character of a commodity. Nor would it be an obstacle that they do not yet exist; for whatever is expected to exist—such as the grapes of a vineyard, fish expected from a cast of a net, future offspring of livestock, and other things of this sort—can be sold, as was shown in Disputation 340.

8 Second, it is proven that the purchase of a **real annuity** is lawful when the price is proportionate according to local custom. First, because it is lawful to establish a real annuity under another title <note>i.e., another legal justification</note>, as those with whom we are disputing admit—namely, by a gift, as when someone grants annual payments from his field to a girl so she may marry, or to someone else; or by a just law, such as when a certain amount is paid from every field as a tax or for expenses for an aqueduct to irrigate those fields. Therefore, it will also be lawful to establish it under the title of purchase. Since this annuity is estimable in money, it is no less inherently in that field (whether established by the owner or by the title of purchase) than if it were established by any other means. Nor is it worth more after it has already been established by another title than it is worth when newly established by the title of purchase. Therefore, just as the doctors we are disputing with concede that it can be lawfully bought once it has been established by another title, they are bound to concede that it can be lawfully bought at that same price so as to be newly established—especially since, as has been said, it is not necessary for a purchase that the commodity exist prior to the sale.

Second, as is clear in itself and as common usage testifies, the **purchase of an easement** <note>original: *servitus*; a legal right to use another's land for a specific purpose</note> is lawful when it is newly established on an estate—such as a right of way through another’s field, the right to eavesdrop drainage, the right not to have a neighbor build higher, and similar things. As explained in Disputation 11, these are "real rights" in the things to which they are granted, with a "real obligation" on the estates on which they are granted. Likewise, as found in the Digest (*On the risk and benefit of the thing sold*, the last paragraph), the **purchase of a usufruct** <note>original: *ususfructus*; the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> of some field is lawful when it is newly granted. This newly granted usufruct is nothing other than the right of perceiving the fruits of that field while the ownership remains with another. After it is granted, it is called a "formal usufruct," to distinguish it from that which was previously joined with direct ownership in the hands of the proprietor, which is called a "causal usufruct," as seen in Disputation 7. Therefore, the purchase of a real annuity that is newly established is lawful in a similar way, since it is nothing other than the right to receive a certain part of the fruits from the field in which it is established.

10 The logic is clear, because an annuity of this kind is nothing other than a certain part of the right in that field derived from the greater right which the proprietor held in it—just as a usufruct and other easements are nothing other than certain parts of the right which the proprietor held, which he renounces and transfers to the person to whom he grants the usufruct or other easement.

<summary>This page discusses the morality of annuity contracts (census), contrasting the view of early critics who saw them as usurious with the "common opinion" that they are legitimate sales of rights. Molina argues that buying the right to annual income from land is legally and morally equivalent to buying a usufruct or an easement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological defense of annuity contracts (census). Having previously addressed the objections that these contracts might be usurious or socially harmful, Molina now begins to lay out the positive arguments for their legitimacy under both Canon and Civil law, specifically addressing the transfer of rights and the validity of paying these annuities in money rather than physical crops.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 385.
ii 3
<meta>catchword: pecu-</meta>

[...the right] passes.) And although in all these cases the numerically identical right that was in the seller is not transferred—because an "accident" <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that cannot exist without a "subject" or substance to hold it; here, the legal right is the accident and the person is the subject.</note> cannot migrate from one subject to another—nonetheless, a right to the same object is granted to the buyer, along with an obligation on the property corresponding to that right. Simultaneously, the right to that same thing that was previously in the seller perishes, as does the obligation on the property that corresponded to that right.

Thirdly (and this argument proves that the purchase of a <term>perpetual real annuity</term> <note>original: *census realis perpetuus*; a permanent annual payment tied to a piece of real estate</note> for a fixed price is lawful): as is self-evident and as common practice everywhere testifies, it is lawful to purchase a farm for a fixed price in terms of full ownership and entire right. Nothing prevents the fruits to be gathered from that farm from belonging to the buyer in perpetuity. The reason is that the value of those fruits, as they exist in the potential of the farm, does not make the farm of infinite value. However, the purchase of a perpetual real annuity on a farm is nothing other than the purchase of a portion of the right to the fruits which the owner held, as explained and proven in the preceding argument. Therefore, it is justly done for a lower price than the same farm would be bought for with full rights, and thus it is justly done for a fixed price.

<margin>11</margin>
Fourthly, this is proven from the definition of **Martin V** in the first *Extravagant* decree and **Calixtus III** in the second *Extravagant* decree <note>“Extravagantes” were papal decrees that “circulated outside” the primary collections of Canon Law</note> among the chapters on buying and selling. There, the contracts for the purchase and sale of real annuities are defined as just and lawful, provided certain circumstances expressed there are applied. However, although mention is only made there of a contract for a real annuity with a <term>redemption clause</term> <note>original: *pactum de retrouendendo*; a clause allowing the seller to buy back the annuity</note>—about which alone those Supreme Pontiffs were questioned, and which many at that time doubted was lawful—nevertheless, by an argument from the greater to the lesser, it is gathered that a contract for the purchase of an irredeemable real annuity is lawful, provided the price paid for it is commensurate with the annuity. Indeed, there has always been more doubt about whether a redeemable annuity contract was lawful than an irredeemable one, because the purchase of a redeemable annuity has a greater appearance of a usurious contract than an irredeemable one. This same point is confirmed by the bull of **Pius V** regarding the form of creating annuities, where the redeemable real annuity is also approved.

Fifthly, the same is proven by the definitions of Civil Law. For in the final Law (under the title "On the Exchange of Things" in the Code), a contract is approved by which someone grants their goods to another with the agreement that the receiver is bound to pay a certain amount every month or year to the one granting those goods. In that law, however, a <term>reserved annuity</term> <note>original: *census reseruatiuus*; where a seller keeps a right to annual payments when selling property</note> seems to be approved rather than a <term>consigned annuity</term> <note>original: *consignatiuus*; where a person creates a new annual charge on property they already own in exchange for cash</note>, which is what we are discussing now.

Furthermore, in the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian’s New Constitutions (Novellae) used in medieval law schools</note> (in the section "If any things are obligated," paragraph "But if," at the verse "it shall be permitted"), tutors and guardians are commanded to buy annual revenues for minors using the minors' money. In this command, the annuity contract is seen to be approved; and no annuity contract appears more lawful than the one we are discussing. **Covarrubias** (in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 7, number 2) and others cite another New Constitution of the Emperors, which is not found in the common codes, and which even more clearly approves the annuity contract. Otherwise, in the ancient law—not only of the *Digest* but also of the *Code*—no mention is made of the reserved annuity.

<column-break/>

The things said so far prove, at minimum, that a real annuity contract is lawful when it is "fruit-bearing"—that is, payable in the same crops that the field in which it is placed produces. 

<margin>12† Doubt</margin>
† But there is a doubt whether it is similarly lawful when it is **monetary**; specifically, in the sense that while it may not immediately produce money, it nonetheless produces other fruits that are valued in money and from which money can be made, and therefore it is enjoined that the annuity be paid in money. Likewise, there is a doubt whether a real annuity is lawful when it is indeed to be paid in fruits, but fruits which the field does not produce. For example, if an annuity of so many measures of wine is established upon an olive grove, or an annuity of so many measures of wheat upon a vineyard.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Whatever a few people may have said, it must undoubtedly be said that such a contract is lawful by the nature of the thing itself. This is affirmed by the doctors commonly: **Conrad** (on contracts, questions 75 and 79), **Giovanni di Medina** (on usury, question 1, and more extensively on annuities, question 2), **Covarrubias** (in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 7, number 2), **Soto** (book 6, *On Justice*, question 5, article 1, conclusion 3), **Major** (on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, question 42), **Gabriel Biel** (in the same place, question 12, first conclusion and following), **Alvaro Valasco** (on the law of emphyteusis, question 32, number 9), **Panormitanus** (on the chapter *In ciuitate* regarding usury, and the cited question 5, last number), **Sylvester Prieras** (on usury 2, question 12, pronouncement 4), and others. 

It can be proven:
First, because after a crop-based annuity is lawfully bought and placed on a certain farm, a contract of exchange is lawful whereby the debtor of that annuity wishes instead to bind himself to pay its value in money, or in some other fruits which the farm does not produce, and which are expected to have more or less the same value every year. Therefore, the contract was lawful from the beginning, whereby an annuity on the same farm was bought in money, or in fruits which the farm did not produce. The consequence is clear: because no absurdity follows from the joining of those two contracts, or rather from the fact that such an exchange only intervenes virtually from the beginning in the contract by which a monetary annuity is bought, or one payable in fruits the field does not produce. The premise is similarly manifest, because an exchange of equivalent for equivalent is lawful in itself when the things are not of a kind that are forbidden from being exchanged.

Secondly, the value of a monetary annuity and a crop-based annuity is equal when the payments are equal in value and are subject to the risk of payment in the same way. Therefore, just as the purchase of a crop-based annuity on a farm for a certain price is just, so will the purchase of an equal monetary payment in value on the same farm for the same price be just. The consequence is very well known. And the premise likewise, because the value of an annuity is assessed according to the value of the payment, assuming equality of risk and other things being equal.

Thirdly, the same is most clearly proven so that no room for doubt remains, because the annuities approved in the decrees of **Martin V** and **Calixtus III** were monetary, as will be clearly evident to anyone reading those decrees. 

Furthermore, many of them were established upon houses, as is clear from both decrees; but on a house, no annuity can be established other than [a monetary one].

<summary>Molina argues for the legal and moral legitimacy of annuity contracts (census), citing both papal decrees and the "common opinion" of major theologians. He demonstrates that paying these annuities in money is just as valid as paying them in crops, as it represents a fair exchange of equivalent value.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the legality of the *census* (annuity) contract. He is specifically arguing why it is lawful to pay these annuities in money rather than physical produce, and whether the payment remains due even if the land fails to produce a harvest in a given year.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

[...whether the payment is] monetary, or in other crops which the estate does not produce.

**Fourthly**, because a monetary **pension** <note>original: *pensio*; the regular annual payment made by the person who received the principal investment</note> is certain and invariable in its value. Thus, it is more suitable for determining the value and price of the annuity accurately without the risk of injustice or deception. Pensions paid in crops, however, are quite inconsistent in value; a measure of wheat might be worth four units one year and twenty the next, and so on for other crops, depending on their abundance or scarcity at any given time. Therefore, it is better to set the value and price of the annuity according to money. This was the reason why, in the **Kingdom of Castile**, it was rightly prohibited by law <note>New Recopilación, Book 5, Title 15, Law 4</note> to have any "crop-producing" annuities with a buy-back clause; only monetary ones were permitted, as we saw in Disputation 383. Therefore, a monetary annuity is lawful.

**Finally**, this is confirmed because even those we are disputing with admit that if a monetary annuity was lawfully established on a property through a gift or some other means, it can later be lawfully bought and sold for money. Therefore, by the same reasoning, it could have been lawfully established for money from the very beginning on that same property.

<margin>13</margin> The next **doubt** is whether an annuity contract is lawful if a <term>real annuity</term> <note>original: *census realis*; an annuity specifically tied to the income/fruits of a piece of land</note> is purchased that must be paid every year, regardless of whether the land it is placed upon actually produces crops that year or not. The answer is that such a contract is lawful by the nature of the thing, at least when the property is productive enough that the pension due in a barren year can be compensated for by the harvests of another year. In this way, the total collection of pensions over many years does not exceed the total of all the crops gathered over those same years. I understand this answer to apply when the price paid for the pension placed on a property is just and proportional to the right to receive that pension.

And primarily, those who believe a <term>personal annuity</term> <note>original: *census personalis*; an annuity tied to the person's credit rather than specific property</note> is lawful—and consequently that a "mixed" annuity of personal and real is lawful, such that if the property vanishes, the person is still held to the debt—will easily admit our response without the restriction I added. In that event, the annuity would be, at the very least, a mixture of the lawful real and personal types. Nevertheless, this is proven even for those who deny that a personal annuity is lawful.

**First**, because this contract is lawful: "I buy from you a certain annual pension from your field for a certain price, with the condition that if in some year it does not bear fruit, or does not bear enough for the full pension, you are bound to make up what was missing in the preceding years from the crops produced in following years." Therefore, a contract is lawful where an annual pension is bought for as long as the property remains intact, whether it produces fruit every single year or not.

The premise is proven because in that contract, nothing is bought except a purely real annuity—that is, a right to a portion of the crops of that estate—even if more of the right is exercised in one year than in another. Therefore, if the price is just (that is, proportional to the entire

<column-break/>

right being bought), the contract is just. The conclusion is proven by the fact that once the contract is made, it is a lawful exchange if the seller of the annuity chooses to pay the full pension every year from other funds, rather than being held to an increased pension from the crops of the same field in later years. Therefore, the contract mentioned in the conclusion is lawful from the start, as it essentially assumes that lawful exchange, just as I argued above regarding monetary annuities.

**Secondly**, this contract is lawful: "I buy from you a certain annual pension from this field, which usually bears much larger crops, on the condition that you are bound to sow the whole field every year and use manure on it, so that it yields sufficient and overflowing crops for the pension every year, regardless of whether it is a barren year." Therefore, this contract is lawful: "I buy from you a certain annual pension from this field, whether it yields it every year or not."

The premise is clear. The conclusion is proven because after the contract is made, the debtor of the annuity could choose to stop sowing that field for a while so the soil becomes more fertile, provided he still pays the pension from elsewhere. For the buyer of the annuity is not bound to grant him that rest for free; he can lawfully demand the price for the pension he was supposed to receive from that property that year.

**Thirdly**, by the nature of the thing, a contract is lawful where someone leases their field for a fixed annual pension, adding a pact that even if by accident or some other reason the field does not produce crops one year, the tenant is still bound to pay the full pension—provided the pension is moderate enough to compensate for the risk the tenant takes on. Therefore, by the same reasoning, a real annuity contract is lawful by nature where the seller of the annuity is bound to the annual payment every year, whether the property produces fruit or not, provided the price given for that annuity is appropriate, considering the risk taken by the seller. Note here: by the nature of the thing, an annuity is worth less if the payment is less secure. Accordingly, a price that is fair for a very secure pension (considering the quality and size of the property) would be a proportional price for an equal pension on a less secure property if the seller takes the risk of the payment upon himself.

**Fourthly**, it is lawful to join a contract of **insurance** <note>original: *assecuratio*; Molina is remarkably modern here, treating the risk management as a separate, billable contract</note> against accidents and any other events with a real annuity contract. Therefore, if the price is just, considering the risk the seller takes on, it will be lawful to buy a real annuity with the burden that the pension must be paid whether the property yields enough fruit each year or not. The conclusion is manifest, because in this contract, at most, there is only a just insurance contract joined with a just contract for the purchase of a real annuity. And since the payment of the pension for many...

He justifies this through principles of risk management, price stability, and the ability to bundle insurance-like protections into property contracts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal nature of the "census" or annuity contract. Molina is refuting arguments that these contracts are merely disguised usurious loans. # Second Treatise, Disputation 385

[...the more an annuity] is subject to dangers, the less it should be worth; and the more secure it is, the more it should be worth. Certainly, the same just price paid for a modest **pension** <note>original: *pensio*; the recurring annual payment</note> on a highly suspect property (where there would be no moral danger if paid in full every year) would also be a just price for an equal pension on a property where there was some physical danger of failing to yield enough fruit to pay it—provided there is a pact that the seller of the annuity is bound to pay the full pension from other sources, as was stated at the end of the previous argument.

**Fourthly**, this is confirmed by common practice, by which <term>real annuities</term> <note>original: *census reales*; annuities tied to the income of specific physical property</note> are customarily purchased by law with the understanding that while the property on which the annuity is placed remains safe, the pension must be paid whether the land yields those fruits or not. Whether anything regarding all these matters has been changed today by **Pope Pius V** <note>Referring to the Papal Bull *Cum onus* (1569), which restricted the conditions under which annuities could be considered non-usurious</note> concerning annuities created after the publication of his bull, will be made clear below when we explain that bull.

<margin>24</margin>
Regarding the **first argument** for the negative side proposed at the beginning of this disputation, the premise must be denied. As for the proof, following **Conrad Summenhart** <note>A significant 15th-century German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts</note> in his work *On Contracts* (question 83, in response to the first and two following arguments), a distinction must be made regarding that contract which is said to be similar to an annuity contract. First, either Peter gives those one hundred gold coins to John, giving up the power to demand them back while leaving John the power to return them whenever he wishes (so that as soon as he returns them, the right to receive the annual pension from the fruits of John's estate is extinguished); or Peter reserves for himself the power to demand back those hundred gold coins whenever he wishes, or at some certain term, so that in the meantime he receives that annual pension, which is not to be counted toward the principal.

Next, a distinction must be made regarding the same contract: if the estate on which Peter has that right perishes, and the right perishes along with the estate, is John nevertheless bound to pay Peter those hundred gold coins he received, or not? After establishing these two distinctions, if in that contract Peter does not reserve the power to demand back those hundred gold coins, but only John has the power to return them to extinguish the right to the pension; and furthermore, if the estate perishes, the right to the pension is extinguished so that John is not bound to restore the hundred coins (since they were received as the price for a right that has been extinguished and which perishes for the buyer), then it must be conceded that the contract is entirely similar to an annuity contract. Indeed, it should be said to be a true annuity contract with a <term>buy-back clause</term> <note>original: *pacto de retrovendendo*; a clause allowing the seller to repurchase the right to the annuity</note>. Therefore, it must be denied that a <term>loan</term> <note>original: *mutuum*; a loan specifically of fungible goods like money where the exact same amount must be returned, often associated with usury in this period</note> is involved, even if the contracting parties call it a loan.

For in contracts, one must attend to what is actually being done rather than the words the parties use, as stated in the law <note>original: *l. 3. C. plus valere quod agitur*; a legal principle from the Code of Justinian meaning "what is done carries more weight than what is said"</note>. That a loan is not involved in such a contract, so understood, is easily apparent. For a loan, by its very nature, includes the right to demand back what is given, either at a certain time or whenever the lender wishes. Furthermore, the principal does not perish for the lender, no matter

<column-break/>

what else might perish; the opposite is seen in that [annuity] contract when understood in this way. However, if in that contract Peter reserves the power to demand back those hundred gold coins, and if the estate perishes, John does not remain free from both the annuity and the restoration of the hundred coins he received, then it must be conceded that the contract is **usurious**, and Peter is bound to count the pensions received toward the principal. Nevertheless, it must be denied that such a contract is entirely similar to a [true] annuity contract.

In an annuity contract, even if made with a buy-back clause, the power to demand back the price does not usually remain with the one who bought the annuity; rather, the power to redeem it usually remains with the one selling the annuity. Furthermore, if the property on which the annuity is placed perishes, the annuity perishes for the buyer, and the seller is not thereafter bound to restore the price, nor likewise to pay the pensions of the annuity.

The **second argument**, to be solved more clearly, requires an explanation of how much the just price of an **irredeemable** real annuity should be valued, given that in this **Kingdom of Castile**, the law has fixed the price of an annuity with a buy-back clause at a ratio of fourteen to one <note>This means the principal cost is 14 times the annual payment (approx. 7.1%)</note>.

<margin>25</margin>
Regarding this matter, nothing certain can be established, and the scholars vary greatly. Some say the just price of an irredeemable annuity should be double that of a redeemable one, or something more, so that it is at a ratio of **thirty to one**. Others assert it should be greater only by about a "sesquialterate" proportion <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1</note>; specifically, if the price of a redeemable annuity is at a ratio of fourteen to one, the price of an irredeemable one should be at a ratio of **twenty to one**. This follows what was said above regarding the purchase of other things with a buy-back clause. Finally, others assert that the price of an irredeemable annuity ought to be higher when placed on more solid and fertile estates or rights.

And although nothing that is accepted by local custom should be easily disapproved, it certainly seems equitable to me that when a perpetual and irredeemable annuity is bought, its price should exceed the price of a redeemable one only by half again (the 1.5 ratio), provided there is equal stability and security in both. However, when someone sells their estate in such a way that they transfer the <term>direct ownership</term> <note>original: *directum dominium*; the ultimate legal title held by a lord or owner</note> to the buyer, and the seller remains the buyer’s **tenant** <note>original: *emphyteuta*; a person holding a long-term, heritable lease (emphyteusis) who pays a rent and improves the land</note>, then the seller must not only pay the annual pension but also a **transfer fee** <note>original: *laudemium*; a fee paid to the landlord whenever the leasehold is sold or transferred to a new person</note> if he alienates the property. In this case, subjecting himself simultaneously to the other laws of tenancy, a much higher price should be judged just—such as a ratio of **thirty to one** for the annual pension. Therefore, if the owner sells the entire right he has over the estate and the tenant to another, he could justly receive thirty times the value of the annual pension.

# 334 Ludovico Molina
## On Contracts
<meta>Catchword: CEN-</meta>

I hear that in this Kingdom of Castile, when an **annuity** <note>original: *census*; a financial arrangement where one party pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment</note> is entirely irredeemable, and is placed upon a very solid asset, it is purchased at a rate of thirty to one <note>i.e., a 3.33% annual return</note>, even if the direct ownership of the property in which it is placed, or from which it is owed, does not pass to the buyer. This practice is not to be condemned; because of the rarity and security of such annuities, and the abundance of buyers, they are valued as such for several reasons.

<margin>16</margin> This being established, regarding the **second argument**, it must be denied that a person selling an annuity in that manner with a **buy-back clause** <note>original: *pacto de retrovendendo*; a condition allowing the seller to "buy back" the obligation and end the payments</note> is defrauded, not only of half the just price, but even of any part of the just price. Indeed, an annuity with a buy-back clause is worth that much less than an irredeemable annuity because of the burden of that clause added in favor of the seller, as was explained above when we discussed sales with a buy-back clause regarding other things sold under a similar agreement.

<margin>17</margin> Regarding the **third argument**, the minor premise must be denied. As for its first proof, it must be denied that the immediate object of a pecuniary annuity contract is the money itself to be paid annually. Rather, it is the **right** <note>original: *ius*</note> to demand and receive that money every year, along with the obligation of some estate or other thing which is counted among immovable goods, so that it may be paid from there. Therefore, the right depends on the permanence of the estate, as part of the total right over that estate, as has been said.

Wherefore, just as there is nothing absurd in perceiving, over the course of time and in parts, more fruits in value from a justly purchased estate than the price given for the estate; so it is not absurd if, from that right to an annuity in that estate, so many payments are received over time that they exceed the price given for it in value.

Regarding the second point, it must be said: the right is seen as money to be paid annually. However, that right—nothing preventing it from being finite in itself—is worth that price, not indeed by reason of its own "being" <note>original: *entitativè*; its existence as a legal concept</note>, but by reason of the money to be received annually, to which there is a right. For the value of things is not judged by their abstract existence, but by the **utilities and conveniences** they bring, as was explained in Disputation 348.

<margin>18</margin> Regarding the **fourth argument**, the major premise being granted, the minor must be denied. As for the proof, it must be said that neither the payments themselves, as they exist in the potential of the estate in which the annuity is placed and dependent on the estate's permanence, nor the right to receive them as it depends on that same estate, are of greater value than the price for which they are bought. Nothing prevents it from happening that, through the passage of time, payments are received in a greater quantity than the price given, while perhaps the estate remains intact, or the full right to receive future payments remains intact.

Just as the fruits to be received successively from an estate, as they are in the potential of the estate and dependent on its consistency, are not worth more than the just price usually given for that estate; nothing prevents it from happening that through the passage of time they can be received in a greater quantity and value than the price given for the estate, and that the estate remains thereafter equally capable of producing fruits without any limit. Therefore, just as

<column-break/>

the fact that the fruits of an estate can be received forever does not imply their value is infinite, insofar as they are in the potential of the estate; nor does it imply the value of the estate is infinite insofar as it is capable of producing them: so, the fact that the payments of an annuity can be received forever does not imply an infinite value for them, as they exist by virtue and power in the annuity, nor does it imply an infinite value for the annuity in itself, as it depends on the estate in which it is placed.

From this it follows that in a <term>real annuity</term> <note>original: *censu reali*; an annuity secured by physical property</note> the proposed argument has no force. How much force it has in a **personal annuity** <note>original: *personali*; secured by a person's credit rather than land</note> will be discussed in the following disputation. Indeed, **Juan Medina** <note>A Spanish theologian (1490–1546) who wrote on ethics and economics</note> and others advise that it is not a legitimate rule for judging whether the price given for an annuity is just to say that an estate could be bought for the same price which, after expenses, would return as much annually as the annuity payment. For estates do not return fruits exactly according to their purchase value. Indeed, a house that is justly bought for a thousand gold pieces sometimes does not return a rent of thirty gold pieces; and yet elsewhere a vineyard, which is justly bought for a thousand gold pieces, is justly leased for fifty. Thus, just as one must stand by the common custom of each region to judge the just price of other things, so to judge whether the price of an annuity is just in any region, one must look to the common custom by which annuities are usually bought and sold there. Provided, however, that no human law intervenes to tax the price; for then, unless its injustice were clearly evident, one would have to abide by it.

Regarding the **fifth argument**, the major premise must be denied. For men do not care for their successors—especially if they are very distant—as much as they care for themselves. Furthermore, **present payments** are valued more than those which will occur after a very long time: both because the latter are subject to more dangers, and because one cannot enjoy or trade with them in the near future; and finally for other reasons. Certainly, the right to payments forever will be worth only a little more than the right to payments for a hundred years. Thus, in taxing the just price for a right to payments forever without a buy-back clause, common estimation takes place; just as in taxing the just price of estates that can yield fruit in perpetuity, the same common estimation takes place.

<margin>19</margin> Regarding the **sixth argument**, it must be said that all those things which are considered evil and absurd in the argument follow no less, and indeed more, from the fact that estates can be bought at a just price from those who need money. For those who abound in many estates can live in idleness through the sweat and labor of others by leasing to them, just as those live in idleness who have bought many annuities.

Also, those who sell estates are more easily reduced to poverty than those who sell annuities in them, especially if they are redeemable. Therefore, just as it does not follow from this that the purchase of estates at a just price is illicit, so it does not follow that the purchase of annuities is illicit.

Other things that could be said about redeemable annuities in this disputation will be more conveniently discussed below when explaining the **Bull of Pius V** <note>The 1569 decree *Cum onus*, which set strict rules for annuities to prevent usury</note>.

<summary>Molina defends the pricing of annuities in Castile, arguing that their value is determined by market custom and the security of the underlying property, rather than a simple mathematical formula. He also introduces the economic concept of the time value of money, noting that distant future payments are worth less than present ones.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s investigation into the justice of financial contracts. # Whether an annuity for a fixed number of years, whether real or personal, is licit.

## DISPUTATION 386.

### SUMMARY

1. *Whether an annuity for a fixed number of years at a lower price is licit, and when, with the following numbers throughout.*
3. *A perpetual real annuity <note>original: "census realis"; an annuity secured by physical property</note> at a price lower than the total sum of payments is licit.*
4. *If a personal annuity <note>original: "census personalis"; an annuity secured only by a person's credit or labor</note> perishes with the person and the goods of the payer, how it also perishes for the buyer.*
5. *From what factors the price of a thing is to be judged.*

---

<margin>Question</margin>
**S**ince the arguments we will use regarding annuities for a fixed number of years are to be used to prove that a perpetual personal annuity is illicit, we must first examine whether an annuity for a fixed number of years—such as ten, twenty, or thirty years—is licit at a price lower than the total sum of all the payments to be made from it. For example: may an annual payment of twenty gold coins for ten years be licitly purchased for a lower price than two hundred gold coins (say, for one hundred eighty or one hundred ninety), even when there is no "lost profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; the profit a lender loses by not having their money</note> or "emergent loss" <note>original: "damnum emergens"; an actual loss incurred by the lender</note> on the part of the buyer, and no just fear or probability that the payments will be poorly made?

Conradus, in his work *On Contracts* (Question 80), asserts that according to "scholastic rigor" it can be bought licitly; however, he adds that the contract has the appearance of evil and should be discouraged before it is made. Covarrubias arrives at the same opinion in *Various Resolutions* (Book 3, Chapter 7, No. 4), though he adds that such a contract should be entirely prohibited and expelled from the Commonwealth. Navarrus holds the same view in his commentary (Chapter 1, 14, Question 3, No. 71). Conradus argues for this as follows:

First, because if this contract were unjust, it would follow that a temporary annuity would be worth more than a perpetual annuity of equal payment—not only a redeemable one, but even an irredeemable one—and would have to be bought at a higher price to be just; yet this is clearly false. The consequence is proven because, let us suppose the just price of an irredeemable perpetual annuity is at a ratio of thirty to one <note>i.e., you pay 30 coins to receive 1 coin per year forever</note>. Then, if an annuity for a fixed number of years could not be justly bought for less than the total sum of payments received from it, then an annuity for thirty-four years could not be justly bought at a ratio of thirty to one, but the value of the four additional payments received beyond that would have to be added to the price.

Second, because for human convenience and use, one hundred gold coins ready and present are worth more than one hundred coins to be paid in installments over ten or thirty years. Therefore, one hundred gold coins to be paid through annual installments are justly bought for a lower price paid immediately than the total sum of the hundred coins.

Third, because in other annuities, their value is not estimated according to the total quantity of the 

<column-break/>

payments to be received; otherwise, he who buys an annuity could not receive more payments than would equal the price given—which, however, is clearly false. Therefore, it follows that even in an annuity for a fixed number of years, the value of the annuity ought not to be estimated as equal to the total quantity of the payments to be received.

The contrary opinion is held by Gabriel [Biel] (in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 12, Conclusion 3). He argues that an annuity for a fixed number of years cannot be justly bought for a price lower than the total sum of the payments, except by reason of the risk to which the annuity is subject, or by reason of some other similar factor that justifies that decrease in price. Johannes Medina (On Usury, Question 3, on annuities) and [Dominicus] Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, Question 5, Article 2) are of the same opinion; although these two authors hesitate slightly because of Conradus’s arguments, especially the first one.

I should warn that these authors, as well as Conradus and Covarrubias, speak indiscriminately of annuities for a fixed number of years, whether personal or real, thinking the reasoning is the same for both. Panormitanus also disapproves of both in his *Questions* (Question 5, penultimate column). Navarrus, however, and others who deny that a perpetual personal annuity is licit, ought much more strongly to deny that the same annuity for a fixed number of years is licit at a price lower than the total sum of payments. Nevertheless, as was said, Navarrus concedes that it is licit.

Our first conclusion is this: A **personal annuity** <term>census personalis: an annuity based on the payer's credit rather than physical collateral like land</term> for a fixed number of years is **illicit** and unjust at a price lower than the total sum of the payments, unless "lost profit" or "emergent loss" is present, or the annuity is subject to a risk of non-payment, or the price is justly diminished due to some other similar cause.

Furthermore, the price cannot then be justly diminished by more than the specific cause for the reduction deserves. Likewise, it cannot be diminished by reason of lost profit, emergent loss, or even risk, unless this is explicitly brought into the agreement—that is, by stating that the price is being reduced from what would otherwise be just for that reason—or unless it is understood that the seller of the annuity is content with that arrangement.

This conclusion, regarding all the limitations by which it is restricted, is clear from what was said in Disputation 361, and often elsewhere regarding the matter of usury and of buying and selling. Regarding the core of the current controversy, although it is also clear enough from what was said in that same disputation—where we effectively showed that the right and personal obligation to pay something in the future is worth no less than the thing itself at the time it is paid—it can also be proven.

First, because if the purchase of the right to receive twenty gold coins every year for ten years were justly made for one hundred eighty or one hundred ninety gold coins, then this contract would also be licit: "Take now one hundred eighty or one hundred ninety gold coins, and at the end of ten years you shall restore to me two hundred all at once"; it follows...

<summary>Molina argues that temporary personal annuities sold at a discount are generally usurious because they function like a loan where the lender receives back more than the principal. He disputes earlier authors who suggested the "time value of money" justified these discounts in personal credit contracts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 386 regarding the morality of temporary annuities. Molina is currently refuting the idea that personal annuities (secured by a person's credit) can be sold at a discount, arguing that this often masks usury, while distinguishing them from real annuities (secured by property).</meta>

# Whether an annuity for a fixed number of years, whether real or personal, is licit.

## DISPUTATION 386.

...but the following contains manifest usury; therefore, the preceding does as well.

The sequence of logic is clear. First, because regarding the nature of a loan <term>mutuum: a loan of fungible goods, like money, where the same amount must be returned</term> and the usury derived from it, it makes no difference whether the borrower is required to repay the loan with an increase all at once or successively in parts. Furthermore, the fact that annual payments are allowed to be paid together at the end of a ten-year period is a favor granted to the borrower, not a burden, since they are essentially granted as a loan until the end of the ten years. Therefore, if usury is seen in the consequence, it will also be seen in the antecedent. The same argument can be made if an annuity <term>census: a financial contract where a person pays a lump sum for the right to receive future payments</term> is purchased for twenty, thirty, or forty years at a price lower than the total sum of all the payments. From this same argument, it is clear that even if a right to annual payments is purchased when such an annuity is bought, usury still intervenes. This is because, in essence, a price is given for a loan so that it may be returned in parts with an increase by reason of the "expectation" <note>the time the lender must wait to be repaid</note> of the payment. This is no different than when something is sold at a certain higher price than the item is worth for cash paid immediately; usury intervenes because it is as if the price, which should have been paid immediately, were left as a loan to the buyer to be restored in the future with an increase.

Second, if anyone sells for credit—to be paid in installments over ten years—something that is worth at most one hundred and eighty in cash for two hundred, he commits usury, as is self-evident, unless the contract is justified by "lost profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; the profit a lender misses out on by lending his money elsewhere</note> or some other similar legal title. Therefore, by the same reasoning, if he gives money so that he may receive it back in parts with the same increase, he commits usury.

Third, if I give you two hundred gold coins and, in the meantime, while you do not repay them, I take from you a pledge <term>pignus: collateral or security for a debt</term> yielding twenty gold coins of income each year—which are not to be counted toward the principal—the contract is usurious. Once two hundred gold coins have been received from it over ten years, I ought to be content with those for the whole debt; nor can I further receive anything, whether of the fruits or the capital, without the vice of usury, as held in the legal codes <note>original: "c. 1. & 2. de usur. c. cum contra, & c. significasti, de pigno."; references to Canon Law regarding usury and pledges</note> and as explained in Disputation 320. But it is the same to make an agreement that you pay me twenty gold coins annually for ten years for two hundred gold coins as it is to make an agreement that I receive them from the fruits of a pledge. Therefore, a personal annuity <note>original: "census personalis"; an annuity based on the credit of a person rather than physical property</note> for a price lower than the total sum of the payments is illicit and usurious.

<margin>3</margin>
**Second Conclusion:** Just as a perpetual real annuity <note>original: "census realis"; an annuity secured by immovable property like land</note> is licit for a price lower than the total sum of the payments expected to be received—even if the property in which the annuity is placed is extremely secure, such as a massive forest for grazing or something similar that securely yields a large amount every year—so too, by the nature of the thing, a real annuity for a fixed number of years is licit for a price lower than the total sum of the payments expected to be received.

However, if the annuity were for only a few years, such as five, eight, or ten, it should be prohibited due to the danger of cloaking usury in that way, or of buying those annuities at a much lower price than they are worth—especially when the annuity is a monetary one, in which the value of the payments is fixed and certain. The first part is proven by the distinction between a real annuity

<column-break/>

for a fixed number of years and a personal annuity.

For in a personal annuity, one immediately buys the right and a personal debt to the payments, considered materially, to be paid in the future. This value is equal to the total quantity of the payments, as shown here and in Disputation 361. In a real annuity, however, one buys a part of the right to a thing, or the fullest ownership of a property, depending on the thing itself. For this reason, the payments are not bought except as they exist in the potential of the thing and depend on the thing itself, so that the risk of them, as such, belongs to the buyer of the annuity. On that account, they are worth less while they are in "potential" <note>as a future possibility</note> than they are worth in themselves at the time they are actually received. For just as the entire ownership of a property is worth less than the sum of all the harvests already collected which (after deducting expenses) are hoped for from that thing in perpetuity; and just as a portion of the right to receive a certain annual payment from that property in perpetuity is worth less than the payments themselves once they are in hand; so too a smaller part of that right (namely, to receive payments only for a fixed number of years) is worth less than the payments themselves which are hoped for from that property and in dependence upon it.

<margin>4</margin>
**You will say:** Just as the payments of a real annuity depend on the risk of the property in which the annuity is placed, so too the payments of a personal annuity depend on the risk of the person who pays it and their goods. For if the person perishes, and their goods perish at the same time, the annuity also perishes for the buyer.

To this, it is first responded that a real annuity is not worth less than a personal one solely because it depends on the risk of the property, but because—insofar as the payments exist in the potential of that property and are to be received depending upon it—they are worth less according to "common estimation" <note>the market value determined by the community</note> than they are in themselves. Second, it is responded that there is less risk for payments when they depend only on the risk of a single property than when they depend on a person and on every sort of income from their goods, which remain obligated to the payment of their debts even after the person's death.

Add to this that in a real annuity, if the property fails to bear fruit for one or more years by a "chance occurrence" <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an act of God or unavoidable accident</note>, the annuity is not owed for that year by the nature of the contract (unless another specific pact is added), as is clear from what has been said regarding the real annuity and as will be explained below in discussing the Bull of Pius V <note>A papal decree from 1569 that regulated these types of financial contracts</note>. A personal annuity, however, is not subject to this risk. Third, it is responded that the fact that a personal debt depends on the survival of the person does nothing to make the debt worth less than the total sum of what is owed, except for the tiny amount of risk that the debt might fail. Otherwise, one could licitly demand interest in a simple loan, since a loan also depends on the survival of the debtor; from which it would follow that usury is licit, which is heretical.

Next, the same part of the conclusion is proven by the first argument by which the opinion of Conrad <note>referring to the theologian Conrad Summenhart</note> is confirmed: that in a real annuity for a fixed number of years, by comparison to a perpetual real annuity, it is entirely...

<summary>Molina argues that personal annuities sold at a discount are usually forms of usury because they are essentially loans. However, real annuities secured by property are licitly sold for less than their total future payouts because the buyer assumes the risk of the land's productivity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from Disputation 386 to Disputation 387. ...completely convinces: and Medina, Soto, and Covarruvias <note>These refer to Juan Medina, Domingo de Soto, and Diego de Covarruvias, major Spanish Scholastic thinkers who influenced early modern economic theory</note> have sufficiently recognized and confess its force in the cited places. The latter part of the conclusion is clear enough in itself and is common among the doctors of law and theology.

To the first argument of the contrary opinion, it must be said that it sufficiently proves the established rule regarding a real annuity <term>census realis: a financial contract where the annual payment is secured by a specific piece of immovable property, like a farm</term> for a certain number of years, as has been said: but not regarding a personal annuity <term>census personalis: an annuity secured only by the debtor’s personal credit and general assets</term>. Indeed, as will be discussed in the following disputation, a perpetual personal annuity is not licit for a fixed price unless it is justified by one of the grounds upon which we said a personal annuity for a certain number of years can be justified—specifically, when the price is lower than the range of payments expected to be received. However, the argument assumes the contrary to be true.

To the second, it must be said that although one hundred gold coins in the present are worth more to someone using them for business than the same amount in the future, they are not worth more in themselves, nor are they "fruit-bearing" in their own nature <note>Latin: *fructiferos*; a central concept in medieval economics was that money, unlike a tree or a cow, does not naturally produce "fruit" or offspring</note>. Moreover, a person giving one hundred gold coins in the present cannot sell to the receiver the industry <note>the labor, skill, or effort</note> that the receiver is going to apply to that money. Therefore, he cannot sell the fruit or profit that can be gained with that money, as was stated in Disputation 304 and frequently elsewhere.

<margin>5</margin> Add that the price of an item is to be judged by the value of the item in itself, not by the specific convenience or utility that the item will bring to the individual buyer, as was seen in the section on buying and selling. However, a seller may licitly receive a price for the convenience or profit the item *would have* brought to himself, which he loses after handing it over to another—provided he gives it up for the sake of the receiver and includes the value of that lost convenience in the contract.

And for that reason, if the person giving one hundred coins today deprives himself of some profit because of it, he can include that "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the legal and moral concept allowing a lender to be compensated for the potential earnings they sacrificed by lending their capital</term> in the contract and receive something for it. At this point, observe: if Conrad’s <note>Likely Conrad Summenhart</note> argument had any force, it would also prove that usury <term>usura: charging interest on a simple loan, which was traditionally forbidden by the Church</term> is licit. For the hundred coins given as a loan today would be worth more than the same hundred to be paid in the future, and for that reason, something beyond the principal could be licitly received for the loan.

To the third, it must be said that the premise is true regarding a perpetual real annuity, but not a personal one, as has been said and will be shown in the following disputation. Therefore, the logical consequence of that argument is perfectly valid; the conclusion refers to a real annuity for a fixed number of years, but it does not follow if the discussion concerns a similar personal annuity.

The discussion concerns a perpetual annuity, whether it is purely personal or has an attached mortgage for the security of the annuity and its payment, and whether it is "redeemable" <note>the debtor can pay back the principal to end the obligation</note> or "irredeemable."

<margin>1</margin> In addition to those who affirm this, even when the annuity is monetary and purely personal, this view is embraced by Conrad [on contracts, questions 74, 75, and 79], Juan Medina [on usury, question 1; on annuities], Soto [on justice, question 5, article 1, conclusion 4], Covarruvias [Various Resolutions, book 3, chapter 7, number 5], John Major [on the 4th book of Sentences, distinction 15, question 44, at the end], Gabriel Biel [same place, question 12, conclusion 1], and several others. Indeed, among the doctors cited by Navarro for the contrary opinion, many do not deny that a personal annuity is licit in the sense in which the authors just cited affirm it to be so.

<margin>2</margin> To be sure, the cited authors do not affirm its licitness in the sense that a "right in the thing" <note>original: "ius in re"</note> can be established over a person—as if the buyer of the annuity acquires a real property right over the person selling it. This would be like how a buyer of a real annuity acquires a right in the land where that annuity is placed. It does not mean that if the person who sold the annuity runs out of money to pay the annual fee, the buyer could reduce that person to slavery or force them to serve as a laborer for a time to cover the value of the payment. Rather, they believe it can be licitly established in the sense that a person, for the money they receive as a price, can obligate themselves to an annual payment. This is the same way that someone who buys something on credit remains obligated to pay the price, or the way people normally obligate themselves to perform actions in other contracts. The legal order then grants a right to the one to whom they are obligated; by reason of this right, the creditor has a "personal action," not a "real action" <note>A "personal action" allows you to sue the person; a "real action" allows you to seize a specific physical object or piece of land</note>.

<margin>3</margin> Because, however, such actions and obligations pass—both from the giver and the receiver—to heirs by the very fact that they accept an inheritance, it follows that a personal annuity can endure in perpetuity for that reason. However, if the person who owes the annuity were to die and leave no sufficient assets, and for that reason no one wished to be their heir with such a heavy burden, then the annuity would expire by that very fact; only the goods the deceased left behind, if any, would remain obligated to...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legality of the "personal annuity" (census personalis). On the previous page, Molina concluded the arguments regarding fixed-term annuities and here transitions into the complex legal debate over whether a person can sell an annual "rent" based on their own labor or general assets rather than on a specific piece of productive land.</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

Furthermore, among those whom Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a leading canon lawyer</note> cites in favor of his opinion, Panormitanus <note>Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canonist known as "The Abbot"</note> in his *Inquiries*, question 5, column before last, in the section "or we ask" and the following section, clearly affirms that a perpetual personal annuity <term>census personalis: a contract where one pays an annual fee based on personal credit/assets rather than specific land</term> is licit in the sense just explained. Perhaps others among those cited by Navarrus and Covarruvias for that same opinion do not deny it, if they are read carefully.

<margin>1</margin> These doctors prove their opinion first because a human being is capable of a personal obligation in the sense explained. In the same way that a person can personally obligate themselves to pay a price for a thing they buy on credit, and other similar things (which is well known in itself), or just as one can obligate oneself to an annuity through a title of gift—promising an annual pension for a woman's dowry or for the support of a hospital—so too can the person to whom it is promised sell that right (acquired by gift) for a just price. Therefore, the person who obligated themselves could, from the start, bring that obligation upon themselves for a just price, which is to "sell" a personal annuity.

<margin>2</margin> Secondly, a personal † annuity can be licitly established by law. Indeed, by ecclesiastical law, tithes <note>decimae: a 10% tax for the church</note>—both "personal" tithes, as the laws call them—are paid from things acquired through craftsmanship, trade, military service, and other similar things, as is clear in chapters 10 and 16, question 1, and the chapter *Apostolicae*.

<margin>3</margin> Chapters *Non est* and *Pastoralis* on tithes show that this † custom persists in some churches. Indeed, in some churches, servants pay tithes from the wages they receive annually for their service; this is observed today in certain towns of this Diocese of Cuenca <note>The diocese where Molina lived and taught</note>. In the Old Law, personal tithes also seemed to be paid, as hinted in Deuteronomy 12. Likewise, in Nehemiah chapter 10 <note>original: 2 Esdrae</note>, the faithful established an annual return of a third of a shekel per head for the ministry of the temple, which was a personal annuity. Secular princes can also, for a just cause, introduce a personal tribute to be paid annually, which will be a personal annuity. The doctors say that Caesar Augustus introduced such an annuity in Luke 2. Therefore, by equal reasoning, anyone can sell a similar personal annuity to be paid annually from what they have acquired by their own work and industry, or from other goods that have come to them in any way. Covarruvias and Soto, in the places cited, confirm this further. Be-

<margin>4</margin> cause, they say, when a real † annuity <term>census realis: an annuity tied to a specific piece of real estate</term> is established on a designated estate, a purely personal obligation simultaneously results for the person and their successors in the person of the seller to pay it, even if the property in which the annuity was placed completely perishes. Therefore, the buyer of the annuity could have bought only that personal obligation from the beginning, without the real obligation of the estate. Since that obligation—the right to demand an annual return from the person—is a personal annuity, it follows that a personal annuity can be licitly bought and established.

These authors prove the first premise from the *Extravagantes* <note>Papal decrees circulating outside the standard codes</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III, where it is said that those selling real annuities on certain estates with a contract for back-purchase <note>pacto de retrovendendo: the right to buy back the annuity to cancel the debt</note> can never be forced to redeem the annuity, even if the estates on which the annuities were placed perish.

<column-break/>

From this, they conclude that even after the estates on which the annuities were placed are destroyed, the obligation remains in the persons who sold the annuities to pay them. Otherwise, there would have been no need to say that they cannot be forced to redeem annuities that would have already been completely extinguished. Likewise, if the obligation to pay the annuity did not remain after the destruction of the estates, those *Extravagantes* would have explained it, just as they explained that the seller cannot be forced to redeem it.

Hence Soto and Covarruvias, along with Charles Dumoulin <note>original: Carolo Molinaeo; a famous French jurist</note>, hold that when an annuity is placed on an estate, that estate serves only as a mortgage <term>hypotheca: collateral to secure a debt</term> for the security of the annuity. Thus, the annuity does not depend on the estate, but a personal obligation results in the seller to pay it, even if the estate is destroyed—provided this is not explicitly contradicted in the contract. However, Covarruvias and others hold that this mortgage is "irregular" and extraordinary.

But because all these matters were extensively reported and challenged by us in Disputation 383, there is no need to add more here. I should only point out that Soto, in the cited question, article 2, asserts that the personal obligation resulting from a real annuity for the seller to pay it (even if the estate is destroyed) does not pass to the seller's heirs; for that reason, the annuity expires if the estate perishes after the seller's death.

However, I do not see the reason why, if that personal obligation resulted in the person of the seller, it should not pass to the heirs, just as other obligations resulting from other contracts pass. On this point, Soto is somewhat inconsistent, while Covarruvias and others of the same opinion affirm the contrary.

Nevertheless, the more common opinion among the doctors is that a personal annuity is illicit, even if it is not merely personal but has a mortgage attached for its security. This view is embraced by many whom Navarrus lists and follows in his commentary on chapter 14, question 3, number 81. See also the latest edition of Alvaro Valasco on the Law of Emphyteusis <note>Emphyteusis: a long-term lease of land</note>, question 32; Gregorio Lopez on Law 28, Title 8, Part 5; Lassarte on the Sale of Tithes, chapter 10; and Gutierrez in *Practical Inquiries*, question 177.

They prove this first because Martin V and Calixtus III only approve annuities that are placed on estates or other fruit-bearing things <note>fructiferis: things like farms or mills that naturally produce "fruit" or income</note>, such that if those things perish, the annuity perishes, and the seller of the annuity does not remain obligated thereafter. Therefore, a personal annuity is illicit.

<margin>†</margin> Secondly, because civil law provides that a free person cannot be given as a pledge <note>pignus: a physical pawn or security</note>. One cannot establish a real right over a person such that they could be sold for a debt, reduced to slavery, or forced to serve for that reason. Rather, if someone accepts a free person as a pledge, they lose the debt and fall under other monetary and physical penalties, as is clear in the law *Ob aes alienum* and the following *Authentica*. See also the Code *On Actions and Obligations* and the Digest *What things can be pledged*. Therefore, with much greater reason, an annuity cannot be established on a free person.
