<meta>This page continues the legal and theological analysis of annuities (censibus). On the previous page, Molina discussed the arguments for why a person might be able to sell an annual payment based on their personal credit. Here, he moves to the counter-arguments regarding risk and the inherent nature of purchase contracts, ultimately weighing in on the morality and legality of these financial instruments.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 387.

Third, it is part of the nature of a purchase that, once the contract is finalized, the risk of the thing purchased belongs to the buyer, as was seen in Disputation 366. However, if an annuity <term>census: a financial contract where an investor provides capital in exchange for annual payments</term> is established upon a person rather than on specific determined goods, the risk of the annuity will never belong to the buyer. This is because the person of the seller, and their heirs, will always remain obligated to pay the annuity. Therefore, the purchase of a personal annuity is unjust, as it is repugnant to the very nature of what a purchase is.

<margin>6</margin>
I will explain in a few words what I think about this matter. First, I believe there should be no doubt that a human being is capable of a purely personal annuity. Thus, a purely personal annuity can, by the nature of the thing, be established upon a person so that only a personal legal action applies to that annuity. If it can be established by the nature of the thing in this way, it can also be established backed by a mortgage <note>original: "hypothecæ"</note> on some or all of the assets of that same person, or another. The arguments proposed for the previous opinion sufficiently prove this.

However, the real difficulty lies in whether such an annuity can be lawfully purchased at a price lower than the total range of payments <note>original: "latitudo pensionum"</note> expected to be received from it—especially when there is no "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: profit that an investor misses out on by choosing one investment over another</term> or "accrued loss" <term>damnum emergens: actual financial loss or expenses incurred</term> affecting the buyer, no fear that the payments won't be made without great expense and difficulty, nor any other similar reason why the otherwise just price could be lawfully reduced. This is in contrast to a "real" annuity (one based on land), which, even without those factors, is lawfully purchased for a price lower than the total payments expected from it, as shown in the two preceding disputations. Indeed, the reasons cited for the later opinion cause me no difficulty; as we shall see, they are resolved with very little effort.

What *does* cause me difficulty is that in the purchase of a personal annuity, nothing else is being bought except a personal debt to be paid gradually in the future, and a personal right to demand and receive it. As was shown in Disputation 361 and the preceding disputation, a personal debt for the future (or the right to receive it) is worth no less than the thing itself which is owed, provided no risk is feared. For example, the right to receive fifty units of currency over one, two, three, or more years is worth fifty. Therefore, just as a personal annuity to receive a certain annual payment for only a few years cannot be bought for a price lower than the total of all those payments, so too a perpetual personal annuity—whether it can be bought back or not—can never be justly bought for a finite price. This is because the personal debt being bought would always be worth more than the price given for it. These conditions do not apply in the same way to a "real" annuity (based on land), as was explained and proven in the two preceding disputations.

Since this is the primary foundation for why a personal annuity should be condemned as illicit and usurious <term>vsurarius: relating to usury, the practice of charging unethical or illegal interest on a loan</term>—whether it is perpetual or for a set number of years—if it is sold for a price lower than the sum of the payments. For indeed, as in Disputation 361...

<column-break/>

...it appeared, if one affirms that a future debt can be lawfully bought for a lower price paid immediately than the total amount of the debt (even if the buyer suffers no lost profit or accrued loss, and even if no risk or trouble is feared in the payment), I truly do not see by what reasoning one can defend the idea that a purely personal annuity, even for a fixed number of years, is illicit and unjust for being sold at a price lower than the sum of the payments. I do not see how such a person remains consistent with themselves.

<margin>7</margin>
Let us therefore establish this conclusion. A perpetual personal annuity sold for a price lower than the total payments expected to be received forever cannot be justified by any other grounds than those mentioned in the preceding disputation regarding a similar personal annuity for a fixed number of years. Namely: the risks to which the payments to be received forever are subject; the "lost profit" or "accrued loss" of the buyer; and other similar factors, with the added point that the person who buys the annuity will not enjoy it forever, but rather their successors will. Therefore, this kind of perpetual personal annuity, in and of itself and in terms of its price—even with the mortgages usually used for security—seems to me to be unjust and usurious by its very nature. For that reason, it was never defined as just by the Supreme Pontiffs; on the contrary, it is rightly prohibited today by Pius V in his bull regarding the creation of annuities <note>Pope Pius V's 1569 bull *Cum Onus* strictly regulated the conditions under which annuities were considered legal rather than usurious loans.</note>. Nevertheless, such circumstances could intervene that, by the nature of the thing, it could be rendered licit.

For if someone wanted to buy properties that would yield them equal and secure annual returns forever, or wanted to buy a perpetual "real" annuity based on the large and secure property of another, and yet that other person asked them to instead buy a perpetual "personal" annuity from them as a favor; I believe that then, by the nature of the case, it could be done lawfully on the grounds of "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans</term>. This is because the properties or the real annuity would have been worth just as much to the buyer, and would have yielded returns just as securely as they hope for from the personal annuity. Anyone can lawfully sell their own convenience to another when they give it up for that person's sake, by buying a thing from them for a lower price than it would otherwise be worth, as is clear from what has been said regarding purchase and sale.

Likewise, the just price for a perpetual personal annuity could be set so that—taking into account the "lost profit" because an equal amount will not reach the buyer's hands through payments for a very long time (during which time they would likely have bought estates or engaged in trade if they hadn't bought the annuity)—the value of the payments expected after a very long time can be significantly discounted. This is both because the original buyer will not enjoy them (but rather their remote successors) and because over a very long time they are subject to many risks. Thus, the purchase of a perpetual personal annuity could be just at a finite price, considering the condition of the annuity and all other concurrent circumstances.

However, I say then that it is also licit to have a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note> of an equal amount of money to be paid in installments in the future with all that excess...

<summary>Molina argues that personal annuities (based on a person's credit rather than land) are generally usurious and unjust if the purchase price is less than the total expected payments, though he notes specific exceptions for "lost profit" or extreme long-term risks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s examination of the legality of personal annuities. He has just introduced the idea that a purely personal annuity—one not tied to physical property—might be seen as a form of loan, which raises the specter of usury. He is now moving into specific arguments and papal rulings that restricted these contracts.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 387 (Continued)

...that annuity, which is potentially infinite <note>original: "syncategorematicè infinitus," a logic term meaning the annuity continues indefinitely as long as the line of heirs exists</note>, would be considered just only if it were accepted in exchange for "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the profit a lender misses out on by not having their money available to invest elsewhere</term> because the money was given as a loan in that manner, and for the risks to which the money is subject by being paid back in parts forever. However, because personal annuities are not usually justified in this way, their purchase was most rightly prohibited and rendered void by **Pope Pius V**, and such a contract was declared usurious. To put it briefly, the purchase of a personal annuity must be judged no differently than if the price were given as a loan, to be repaid in parts in the same way the annuity is paid.

The main point asserted in this conclusion can be proven by almost the same reasons used in the preceding dispute regarding a personal annuity for a fixed number of years. First, because what is actually being bought in that annuity is a right and a personal debt to a certain quantity of money or fruits to be paid successively in the future. Now, a personal debt to be paid in the future is only worth as much as the thing itself at the time it is to be paid, unless its value is diminished by risks, lost profit, or some other similar reason, as was proved in Disputation 361. Second, because if a perpetual personal annuity were licit at a rate of thirty-to-one, then this contract would also be licit: "Accept a loan of thirty on the condition that at the end of thirty years you restore them to me in full, and in addition, you are bound to pay me one every year forever." Yet in this, usury is clearly seen, unless the contract is excused by the head of lost profit or something else. The logic follows because, regarding the nature of a loan, it makes no difference whether the thirty given now are required to be paid in parts over thirty years, or if they are required to be paid all at once at the end of thirty years. Indeed, a favor is granted in that the payments, which were to be paid each year, are allowed to be paid at the end of the thirty-year period.

Third, because if the annuity we are discussing were licit, it would also be licit to sell a credit—which is worth only thirty in cash—for thirty to be paid thirty years from now, and additionally for one to be paid thereafter forever, as was deduced more extensively in the preceding dispute regarding personal annuities for a fixed number of years. Likewise, since it is a sin to receive more fruits from a pledge <note>original: "pignore"</note> within thirty or forty years for thirty given than would equal the value of thirty, it is therefore a sin to bargain for more payments to be made than equal the value of thirty, as was also more broadly deduced there. Fourth, because if a perpetual personal annuity were licit, it would follow either that a personal annuity for a fixed number of years would be licit for a lower price than the total sum of the payments received from it, or that a personal annuity for a fixed number of years would be worth as much as, or even more than, a perpetual personal annuity of equal payment. This is clearly demonstrated by the first argument for the opinion of **Conrad Summenhart** proposed in the preceding dispute. This argument rightly caused **Medina** and **Soto** to tremble <note>Molina often uses "trembling" or "hesitating" to describe theologians struggling with difficult moral questions</note> regarding whether the purchase of a personal annuity for a fixed number of years was licit for a price lower than the total of the payments, and it forced **Conrad** and **Covarruvias** to assert that it was licit in 

<column-break/>

rigor and by the nature of the thing, based on the opinion of those same authors that a perpetual personal annuity was licit. Since, therefore, it has been shown that such a purchase of a personal annuity for a fixed number of years is illicit, it follows that one must concede that the purchase of a perpetual personal annuity for a set price, in the manner it is usually done, is illicit. Furthermore, the **Decrees of Martin V and Callixtus III** <note>original: "extrauagantes," referring to papal decrees found outside the main bodies of canon law</note> favor our opinion. For although they do not explicitly define a perpetual personal annuity as illicit, they emphasize that for an annuity to be justified, it must be placed upon some possession or estate <note>original: "prædio"</note>, such that if the estate perishes, the annuity perishes for the buyer. If a perpetual personal annuity were equally just, certainly those Decrees would not mention so accurately that the annuities in that controversy must be placed on a specific estate, nor would those most wise Popes have insisted so much on that condition. Moreover, the **Decree of Pius V** openly establishes our opinion, pronouncing all personal annuities to be usury and declaring that none are to be held as valid henceforth. It seems he included those words at the beginning of that decree for their sake:

> *While performing the duties of the Apostolic service, we have learned that countless annuity contracts have been celebrated, and are celebrated daily, which not only are not contained within the limits established by our predecessors for those same contracts, but even—what is worse—prefer contrary agreements in every way, on account of the burning sting of greed and manifest contempt for divine and human laws, etc.*

<margin>8</margin>
Observe this: even today, in places where the **Bull of Pius V** is accepted, once a "real annuity" <term>census realis: an annuity tied to the income of a specific piece of land</term> is established on a specific estate or estates, a mortgage <note>original: "hypotheca"</note> on other goods can be applied for two effects. One is that if the estate on which the annuity is placed is recovered by a legal claim <note>original: "euincatur"</note>—either while the annuity is in the power of the seller or after it has passed to another possessor—the seller must pay the "interest" <note>original: "intereſſe"</note>, that is, the value of the annuity, along with interest for lost profit and subsequent damages. Thus says **Navarrus**. The other effect is that in the meantime, while the annuity has not been extinguished, if the estate in which it is placed is destroyed, the payment <note>original: "pensio"</note> must still be paid.

However, since the estate itself in which the annuity is placed is a sufficient mortgage for the sole purpose of paying the pension, any other mortgage is surely superfluous for this second effect.

<margin>9</margin>
Then observe this: if in the purchase of a real annuity on some estate it is simultaneously stipulated in the agreement that if the estate is destroyed, the seller of the annuity is still held to the payment of the pension, then the contract will be "mixed." It is part real annuity and part personal annuity, or rather, a contract of a real annuity combined with a contract of insurance <note>original: "aſſecurationis"</note>. Insofar as that contract is a real annuity, the burden of the annuity passes to a third-party possessor along with the thing in which the annuity is placed; the owner of the annuity can compel only that person to pay the pensions as long as the estate remains intact.

Insofar as that other personal obligation of "insuring" the annuity is mixed into the contract in the event the estate is destroyed, the owner could, if the estate is destroyed, compel the seller of the annuity and their heirs to pay the pension, but not...

<summary>Molina argues that personal annuities are fundamentally usurious loans because they lack the risk associated with property-backed annuities. He cites Papal decrees to show that for an annuity to be moral, it must be tied to a specific piece of land (a real annuity), though he allows for mixed contracts that include insurance-like personal guarantees.</summary>

### Page 361

...not in any other event: and the mortgages <term>hypothecæ: assets pledged as security for a debt</term> would be subject to this burden if any, beyond the property itself, had been given by the seller of the annuity as insurance for the contract. One must always consult the clauses attached to the contract to understand how much of a burden the seller of the annuity has taken upon himself, beyond the <term>real annuity</term> <note>original: "censum realem," an annuity tied specifically to a piece of real estate or productive land</note>; he should not be considered obligated for more than what those clauses state.

<margin>10</margin> To understand whether a contract with such a burden is just by its very nature, one must consider whether the price given for the annuity is proportional to the real annuity itself, strictly considered, along with that burden of insurance. 

Today, however, wherever the **Bull of Pius V** <note>The papal decree *Cum Onus* (1569), which restricted annuity contracts to prevent hidden usury</note> has been accepted, all such clauses are null. In fact, the contract is presumed by the law itself <note>original: "praesumptione iuris, & de iure"</note> to be usurious if it was celebrated in that manner after the publication of that bull. If a contract were made with the burden that—in any event, even if the property where the annuity is placed remains intact—the seller of the annuity is held to the payment of the pensions, then the contract would be "mixed," consisting of both a real and a personal annuity. Consequently, insofar as it had a personal annuity mixed in, the buyer could force the seller, his heirs, and even a third-party possessor to pay the pensions indifferently, as **Covarruvias**, **Charles Dumoulin**, and **Soto** used to say. However, this no longer holds place today where the Bull of Pius V is received. 

But where it has not been received, one must see whether the price given for that real annuity is equal when comparing both the real annuity and that personal burden imposed on the seller simultaneously. If it is found to be equal in the judgment of a prudent man, the contract should not be condemned by its nature. This is because it is primarily a real annuity, with the support of that other burden for the greater security of the buyer. Since this "support" does not mean the seller is always bound to pay from his own pocket beyond the income of the property, and since it will rarely happen that he must pay extra, it should be valued at a modest price; thus, the contract with that burden can be just by its nature. The authors cited above believe that all real annuity contracts are presumed to be bought and sold with this burden, even if it is not expressed in the contract, provided the contrary is not explicitly stated. This, however, is false and asserted freely without any solid foundation. Indeed, a contract for a real annuity by its very nature holds the opposite, as explained and proved in this and the preceding disputations, and as the common opinion of the learned doctors affirms.

From what has been said so far, it will be easily understood that **Soto** (in the place cited above) unfairly accuses **Juan Medina** of inconsistency for asserting in Question 1 on annuities that an annuity cannot be established except in a productive thing whose fruits exceed the annual pension, and later asserting that a personal annuity is licit. For, as Soto says, if a purely personal annuity is licit, then an annuity could also be licitly established on a thing whose fruits do not reach the value of the annual pension, with the obligation remaining on the seller for the remainder of the pension. However, it must be said that Medina only denies that a purely real annuity can be established on an unproductive thing, or one where the fruits are less than the pension to be paid. He admits, nonetheless, that a "mixed" annuity (real and personal) can be established on such a thing, as he 

<column-break/>

promises to explain later in that same question, and indeed did explain at the end of the final question on annuities.

It remains for us to respond to the arguments for both opinions proposed above, insofar as they might seem to conflict with our own. 

To the first and second arguments for the opinion of **Conrad** and others, it must be said that they prove a human being is capable of a personal annuity obligation, but they do not prove that a perpetual personal annuity can be justly bought for a finite price, unless the contract is rendered licit by one of the specific categories explained—contrary to what it possesses by its own nature. 

To the third argument of **Covarruvias** and **Soto**, the premise must be denied, as is clear enough from what was said in this and the two preceding disputations, joined with Disputation 383. Regarding the proof, it must be said that those words are found in the narration before the definition; they were added as a way to lighten the burden on the part of the sellers and to justify the contract. In that sense, it was said that the seller of a real annuity cannot be forced to redeem it, even if the thing it is placed upon is destroyed, because when the thing is destroyed, the annuity perishes and the prior obligation expires. Therefore, from those words follows the opposite of what Covarruvias and Soto infer.

<margin>11</margin> From the "Extravagants" <note>original: "extrauagantibus," referring to papal decretals not included in the main codified collections of canon law</note> themselves, it is clear enough that when the thing in which a real annuity is placed perishes, the obligation to pay the annuity does not remain. **Pius V** later defined this even more clearly. Since the annuities discussed in those decretals were celebrated in Germany (as is evident from the decretals themselves), surely if they were such as Soto, Covarruvias, and Dumoulin claim, this would not have escaped **Conrad the German** <note>Conrad Summenhart</note>. Yet he affirms, as a matter doubted by no one, that they expire along with the thing in which they are placed.

To the first argument of **Navarrus** and others, it must be said that it has no force. For although personal annuities are not approved in those decretals, they are not strictly condemned by them either.

<margin>12</margin> To the second argument, it must be said that it only proves that, by the disposition of human law, an annuity cannot be established on a free person in such a way that the buyer acquires a "right in the thing" <term>ius in re: a property right that follows the object regardless of who owns it</term> over the free person, as if he could sell them or reduce them to slavery for payment of the annuity. It does not prove that there cannot be a personal annuity in the sense that the person selling it remains bound by a personal obligation only, whether or not they simultaneously subject their other goods to a mortgage as security for that annuity. Add to this that in some events, a man can reduce himself to slavery (as explained in the section on slaves), and in those same events, the commentaries and doctors affirm that a "real obligation" can be established on a person to pay something.

<margin>13</margin> To the third argument, it can first be said that the risk <note>original: "periculum"</note> of a purchased thing never pertains to the buyer except when the purchased thing perishes. A personal annuity, however, never perishes regarding the personal obligation of the seller, unless the seller perishes along with all his goods (which, in the place of the deceased, are subject to all the personal obligations of the deceased). For that reason, not before...

...first that a personal annuity <term>census personalis: an annuity secured by the person's assets rather than a specific piece of productive land</term> perishes for the buyer before all the aforementioned things perish. Second, it can be said that although this is part of the nature of a purchase—as a concomitant consequence and agreeable to its nature—it is nonetheless not of its essence, nor an inseparable property of it. Matters that are of such a kind can be waived by a specific agreement <note>original: "pacto"</note> without the contract being rendered invalid for that reason, especially if a just compensation in the price is made for that reason, and such a contract has not been made void by positive law.

### Whether the purchase of a life annuity, or an annuity for an uncertain number of years, is lawful.

### DISPUTATION 388.

### SUMMARY.

1 *How the purchase of a life annuity, or an annuity for an uncertain number of years, is lawful.*
2 *A life annuity can be bequeathed or donated, and thus also purchased.*
3 *A precarious contract <term>precariarium: a contract where one party grants the use of property to another for a duration, often for life</term> is lawful under both canon and civil law.*
4 *By what reasoning a life annuity is rendered lawful.*
5 *How the just price of a life annuity is to be assessed.*
6 *When a life annuity is a real annuity, placed upon some estate or royal revenues, its price must be assessed by the judgment of a prudent person.*

Henry of Ghent <note>A 13th-century theologian known for his strict views on economics</note> (Quodlibet 1, q. 39) asserted that the purchase of an annual pension for the life of the buyer or the seller, or for any other uncertain number of years, is unjust and usurious if it happens that more pensions are received in quantity than the quantity of the price given for them. For example, if for one hundred gold pieces it happens that one hundred and ten are received over eleven years, by receiving ten gold pieces each year. Nor does it matter, he says, if at the time of the contract it was doubtful whether the buyer of the annuity would receive that many pensions. The arguments by which this opinion is confirmed—which will be easily understood to contain no difficulty from what follows—can be read in Conrad [Summenhart] on contracts (q. 81), in [Juan] Medina (the penultimate question on annuities), and in others.

<margin>Question 1</margin> The contrary opinion is the common view of the doctors. Namely, that such a purchase is lawful, provided the price is commensurate with the expectation <note>original: "spem," meaning the statistical hope or probability</note> of whether the annuity will last more or less time, and considering other intervening circumstances. Nor is it an obstacle that it can happen that more pensions are received than the quantity of the price given to receive them; for it can also happen that far fewer are received than the price, and therefore there is a risk for both parties. Likewise, it is no obstacle that the one who buys does so with the hope of profiting and receiving more pensions: since other contracts of purchase and sale are not vitiated by the hope of profit, and merchants ordinarily engage in them with the hope of profit. Thus Conrad on contracts and Juan Medina in the places cited, [Domingo de] Soto (Book 6 on Justice, q. 5, at the end of art. 2), [Diego de] Covarruvias (3rd Variar. Resol. c. 7, no. 4), Gabriel [Biel] (on the 4th, dist. 15, q. 12, conclusion 3), [John] Major (ibid. q. 44), Navarro [Martín de Azpilcueta] (commentary on c. 1, 14, q. 3, no. 71), Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note> (in his Questions, q. 5, penultimate column), and many others.

<margin>2</margin> This can be proven. First, because it is pos-

<column-break/>

-sible for a life annuity to be bequeathed or granted as a gift, as everyone admits. Once it has been granted in this way, it can be lawfully purchased, because it is of some value and not of infinite value. Therefore, it could also be lawfully established from the beginning for a commensurate price; especially since in that contract, both the buyer and the seller expose themselves to the risk of losing, just as they do to the probability of profiting, because of the uncertainty of the duration of that annuity. Once the annuity is finished, nothing of the capital is to be restored, but the buyer loses it entirely. Second,

<margin>3</margin> a "precarious" contract <note>original: "contractus precariarum"</note> is lawful, by which the Church grants some possession or possessions to someone for their use and profit for their lifetime, in exchange for some possession of that same person which they return to the Church upon their death, as is well known. For this contract is approved by canon and civil law (10. q. 2. c. 2. § if the administrator, and c. *precariae*, and in the *Authenticum* regarding non-alienation § if anyone however, and other laws which we cited above in Disputation 298). A contract of this sort is nothing other than the granting of a life annuity in exchange for some estate. Observe, however, that in such "precarious" grants which Churches commonly provide, a donation often intervenes on the part of the one who receives them. In a way, they "buy" it out of devotion to the Church and as an alms for their soul, wishing to leave far more to the Church after their death than the support they receive from the Church via this route for the duration of their life. Therefore, in such precarious grants—which are made without any involuntary mixture by the one who receives them—it is not necessary for what is returned to be perfectly commensurate with the life annuity, for it is not a pure contract of life annuity, but has a donation and alms mixed in for the things to be received after life. Third, the *Clementina* <note>A collection of canon law</note> (1. regarding the non-alienation of Church property) states that a prelate, if the necessity or utility of the monastery requires it, can grant someone a possession or an annual income of the monastery for their life in exchange for money, provided the solemnities discussed there are observed (which will be discussed in the matter of *emphyteusis* <term>emphyteusis: a long-term or perpetual lease of land</term>). This, however, is to grant a life annuity for a price; therefore, the contract of a life annuity is lawful.

It must be observed that if a life annuity is not granted upon some estate or another thing considered immovable (so that it is a "real" annuity), but is established upon a person with a mortgage of goods or without it (and is therefore "personal"), the contract is lawful from the

<margin>4</margin> nature of the thing, provided however that the price in this sense is equal to the pensions which are hoped to be received. That is, the risk of loss and hope of profit should be more or less equal for both contracting parties. Indeed, by reason of the risk to both parties, this contract is lawful. However, when there is a much greater probability that the pensions to be received will exceed the quantity of the price given, then, if the annuity were personal and were not justified on the grounds of "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the profit lost by not investing the money elsewhere</term> or something similar, the contract would be unjust and usurious, according to those things said in the two preceding disputations regarding personal annuities. For this reason, a contract for a life annuity will rarely be lawful if it is a personal annuity.

<margin>5</margin> The entire difficulty of this disputation is how the just price of a life annuity should be assessed, namely...

<summary>Molina discusses the legality of life annuities (vitalitium), refuting Henry of Ghent's view that they are inherently usurious. He argues that the inherent risk to both parties regarding the length of a human life justifies the potential for profit, provided the price is set fairly based on probability.</summary>
<keywords>life annuity, vitalitium, usury, Henry of Ghent, precarious contract, canon law, personal annuity, risk, just price, ecclesiastical property</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 388 regarding the calculation of the "just price" for a life annuity. It transitions from a mathematical formula of lifespans to a more nuanced view based on regional custom and the nature of the security (real vs. personal property), eventually moving into Disputation 389 regarding the conditions for perpetual annuities with repurchase clauses.</meta>

namely, by attending to the ultimate limit to which his life, for which the annuity is granted, can reach both morally and naturally; and by taking half of the years which remain from the day the life annuity begins until that limit, so that the just price is that which equals the quantity of the payments <term>pensiones: the periodic payments of the annuity</term> for all those years. For example, if a life annuity is ten ducats annually, and the person on whose life it is granted is sixty years old (and is expected to be able to live until eighty years), the just price of that life annuity would be one hundred gold coins, which equals ten years of payments—and thus half of the span which is from sixty to eighty. And if the person on whose life it is granted is forty years old, and is expected to be able to live until eighty, the just price would be two hundred gold coins, and so on.

And for the affirmative side <note>supporting this mathematical rule</note> we can argue thus: Just as a sixty-year-old can reach his eightieth year, so he can die in the first year; and just as he can reach his seventy-fifth year, so he can die in his sixty-fifth year, and so on. Therefore, the condition of the buyer and the seller is equal at that middle price, and consequently, that is the just price of that life annuity; and likewise for the others, if the price is equal to the payments of half of all those years.

But for the negative side, I can argue: because if the just price were to be taxed in that way, it would follow that sometimes the just price of a temporary annuity (which <margin>*</margin> is to end with someone's life so that the capital is not restored) ought to be the same as, or even more than, the price of a completely perpetual annuity—which is clearly absurd. This consequence is proven because if someone buys such a life annuity and is twenty years old, and is expected to live until eighty, the price will be three hundred ducats, and thus at the rate of thirty for one <note>original: "rationē triginta pro vno" — a common way of expressing interest rates as a ratio of capital to annual payment; 30:1 is roughly 3.3%</note>; at which price (and even a lower one) a perpetual, irredeemable annuity is justly bought. But if a father buys the same life annuity for a ten-year-old son, the just price will be three hundred and fifty ducats, at the rate of thirty-five for one; even though a completely perpetual annuity is bought for a much lower price.

Because of this second argument, in the penultimate question cited, Covarruvias (3 *Variar. Resol.* cap. 9, num. 7) and many others reject that rule. It certainly must be rejected if the annuity is a real annuity <term>census realis: an annuity secured by specific real estate</term>. It is otherwise, however, if it is a personal annuity <term>census personalis: an annuity secured by the person's general assets</term> and with a mortgage, unless it is justified on the grounds of "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the profit a lender loses by not having their money available to invest elsewhere</term> to the one who buys the annuity, or by some other reason, according to those things said in the two preceding disputations. Therefore, as a rule, I do not think a life annuity of a personal nature is licit, but rather usurious, unless it is made according to that rule; and for that reason, I think it is not to be permitted. I believe it is included in the Bull of Pius V <note>Pope Pius V's 1569 decree *Cum onus* which strictly regulated the terms of annuities to prevent usury</note>, as we shall see in the first clause of that bull in the following disputation; although I do not think Pius V spoke in that bull about a life annuity that is a real annuity, which there was no reason to prohibit, as we shall say in its proper place.

<margin>6</margin> However, when the life annuity is a real annuity placed upon some estate, or upon royal revenues, or some other similar thing, then its just price is not to be taxed according to that mathematical rule, but is to be established by the judgment of a prudent person, considering the age, complexion,

<column-break/>

and the dangers to the life of the person for whom the life annuity is bought. One must descend from the price at which a perpetual real annuity of equal payment is justly bought in that same region by as much as is fair to descend—not only considering those circumstances, but also considering that the life annuity is to end in such a way that the capital is entirely lost and remains with the one who bought it. Therefore, one must descend not only from the price of an irredeemable real annuity, but also from the price of a redeemable one. However, I do not approve of a life annuity being bought or sold for the same price regardless of whether the one whose life it is based on is a youth or an old man, or whether he is sickly or healthy and robust; for it is worth less if his death can be reasonably feared sooner. In judging the just price of a real life annuity, one must rely on the custom of the region regarding the price at which it is commonly bought and sold, just as we are accustomed to rely on custom in judging the just price of other things; provided, however, that it is not established that it is commonly bought at a greatly diminished or greatly excessive price. Gutierrez (*De Pract.* qq. lib. 2, at the end of q. 17) says that by the pragmatics <note>royal decrees</note> of this Kingdom of Castile, it is taxed so that a life annuity is valued and sold at the rate of seven for one. I should advise that in the purchase of a life annuity, a pact for resale <note>original: "pactum de retrouendendo" — an agreement allowing the seller to buy back the annuity</note> has no place, at least at the same price for which it was sold. Since as more time passes in the life for which it was bought, and more payments have been made, the annuity is worth less; therefore, unless there was an agreement that the price to redeem the annuity would be reduced by some proportion to be determined by the judgment of a prudent person as time progressed, such a contract would be unjust.

Moreover, from the fact that it could happen that the debtor of the annuity desires the death of the one upon whose life it was granted, the contract is certainly not to be condemned—not only as being unjust, which is most obvious, but also not as being illicit. For such a vice would belong to the contracting parties, not to the contract itself. Just as the law which ordains that children should succeed their parents is not condemned simply because children might desire the death of their parents in order to succeed to their goods; so the contract of a life annuity ought not to be condemned on that account.

Having previously discussed how to value a life annuity based on age and probability, Molina now transitions into the strict legal requirements for perpetual redeemable annuities, specifically focusing on the reforms instituted by Pope Pius V to prevent these contracts from being used as a cover for usury (charging illegal interest on loans).</meta>

# Luis Molina on Contracts

<margin>1</margin> It was shown in Disputation 385 that a perpetual redeemable annuity—that is, one with a "buy-back" clause—is licit if it is "real" (secured by property) and the price is proportionate. In Disputation 387, it was stated that a "personal" annuity (secured only by a person) is, by its nature, illicit and usurious in the way it is typically conducted; we also discussed the grounds upon which it might be rendered licit by natural law, setting aside human law. Now, we must examine the conditions provided by various authorities to ensure a redeemable annuity contract is licit. At the same time, we must explain the Bull of Pius V <note>The Papal Bull *Cum Onus* (1569), which strictly regulated annuities to prevent usury.</note> so it may be understood which conditions are necessary today for such a contract to be licit and valid in places where that Bull has been accepted. Through the explanation of this Bull, the entire matter of annuities will be made clearer.

Miranda <note>Luis de Miranda, a 16th-century Franciscan theologian.</note>, in his summary of councils, immediately after the Council of Florence, provides a summary of the "Extravagants" <note>Decrees of popes that were not included in the main collections of Canon Law.</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III. He added his own conditions, without which, he says, the purchase of an annuity with a buy-back clause is in no way to be tolerated. He affirms that the omission of certain conditions makes the contract usurious by its very nature. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a leading canonist known as "Navarrus."</note> holds the same opinion in his commentary. Both of them spoke before the Bull of Pius V and gathered those conditions from the decrees of Martin V and Calixtus III. (Though Navarrus later expanded his commentaries and added an explanation of the Bull of Pius V). The conditions are as follows:

**First:** That the annuity be placed on a specific thing or specific things, which alone remain obligated for the payment of the annuity, and not on the person (except by reason of the thing) nor on the other assets of the person.

<margin>2</margin> **Second:** That the annuity be bought at a just or proportionate price.

**Third:** That the price be paid in full at the time the contract is celebrated.

**Fourth:** That the seller of the annuity be granted the faculty in the contract to redeem the annuity in whole or in part, whenever they wish, for the same price.

**Fifth:** That the seller is not obligated to ever redeem the annuity, but always remains free from the obligation to buy it back.

**Sixth:** That if the property upon which the annuity is placed perishes, the annuity perishes entirely for the buyer; thus, the seller is neither bound to pay the annuity from then on, nor to return the price <note>This is the "risk of loss" principle: if it were a loan, the borrower would still owe the money even if their house burned down. In a licit annuity, the buyer takes the risk.</note>.

**Seventh:** That the property on which the annuity is placed yields, at minimum, as much as the annuity payment to be made. This is because to place an annuity on a thing is to buy the right to receive a certain amount of <term>pensionis: periodic annuity payments</term> from the fruits of that thing, or from something equivalent to its value.

It matters little whether Miranda reduced these conditions to six, or Navarrus divided them into eight.

These conditions, except for the last one, are indeed contained in the decrees of Martin V and Calixtus III. However, it is not as if those Supreme Pontiffs were condemning the annuity contracts they were consulted about; rather, the contracts they approved were those celebrated with these conditions. Thus, it cannot be concluded from those decrees that annuity 

<column-break/>

contracts lacking these conditions are illicit, as Navarrus confesses in the aforementioned passage (number 78), and as we have said in the preceding disputations. Therefore, it remains to be examined whether the omission of these conditions makes a contract illicit by its very nature, or not.

Because Pius V later, in his Bull on the creation of annuities, rendered void any contracts for redeemable annuities celebrated after that Bull without these and other conditions, he did so to remove injustices and usurious disguises and to provide for the salvation of souls. He established significant penalties for those who do not observe them. At the same time, he left contracts celebrated before that Bull to their own natures, not condemning them. Therefore, by explaining the conditions of his Bull, we will examine which of them make a contract illicit by its very nature. This will clarify which contracts are just and which are unjust among those celebrated before the Bull, as well as those celebrated after the Bull in places where it has not been received.

### FIRST CLAUSE
### Of the Bull of Pius V

The first clause or condition of the Bull of Pius V reads as follows: *By this our constitution, we decree that an annuity or annual return can in no way be created or established except upon immovable property, or things held as immovable, which are by their nature fruit-bearing, and are specifically designated by certain boundaries.*

<margin>3</margin> Through this clause alone, supported by what follows in the same Bull, the "personal" annuity is excluded, and only the "real" annuity <note>A "real" annuity is tied to "real estate" or physical property; a "personal" annuity is a contract tied only to an individual's credit or labor.</note> is approved. Although the primary intent of this Bull is to speak of the annuity with a buy-back clause (as we shall see and as is clear from the Bull itself), and although this was the only subject in the decrees of Martin V and Calixtus III—since it looks more like usury than others do—nevertheless, it must be considered that every personal annuity whatsoever is excluded by this clause. This is because when an annuity is redeemed, the entire capital or price for which it was bought is restored, and the buyer has gained the profit of the payments received in the meantime while the seller enjoyed the price. All such personal annuities are, by their nature, illicit and usurious, as shown in previous disputations. They are rarely justified by surrounding circumstances and are liable to burden consciences and induce various evils; the clause itself, as it sounds, encompasses them all.

For this reason, I also believe the "life annuity" (*vitalitium*) is included when the annuity is personal—unless the price were set so that it equaled half of all the payments expected to be received, so that there was an equal hope of gain for both buyer and seller, as discussed in the previous disputation. If celebrated in that way, there would be no danger of usury or injustice. However, it is not usually celebrated that way, and therefore it must be considered prohibited in the manner it is typically conducted.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase in that clause, *or things held as immovable*, Pius V expressly approved the "real" annuity which is placed on annual or monthly rights and revenues, such as the right to <term>gabellas: taxes or duties, often on salt or trade</term>...

He emphasizes that annuities must be "real" (secured by productive property) rather than "personal" to avoid falling into the sin of usury.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 389. Page 365

...[of the city], and in other perpetual revenues in any city, town, forest, fishery, meat market, or other similar thing, and in any others: for these are considered **immovable things** <note>In legal terms, "immovable" refers to real estate or assets tied to a specific location, as opposed to "moveable" personal property like clothes or tools.</note>, and are accounted as such, as is clear from the *Clementina* <note>A collection of Canon Law named after Pope Clement V.</note>, in the decree *Exivi de Paradiso* regarding the meaning of words, and from other laws; the common opinion of the learned doctors affirms this.

Whether one annuity (*census*) can be placed upon another, larger real annuity. One must answer with Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> in the place cited above, number 87, that it can be established not only on a larger one, but even on one of equal value. I would warn, however, that the annuity on which another is placed must be **unredeemable**; otherwise, if the first annuity were redeemed, the annuity placed upon it would perish, or it would turn into a **personal annuity** <note>An unsecured annuity tied to the person rather than property, which was often considered usurious.</note> if the seller of the second annuity is still bound to pay it—which Pius V prohibits in this and following clauses. Once one annuity has been placed upon another real, unredeemable annuity, the first cannot be sold without the burden of the second annuity (which is likewise real) being placed upon it. Therefore, it cannot be redeemed or removed from the estate where it was placed, because it must always retain the burden of the second annuity for as long as the property in which the first annuity was placed remains safe.

Because the annuity discussed in this Bull is perpetual, even if it is redeemable, it follows that all **moveable things** are excluded from the list of things on which it can be placed, because they are not perpetual. And although some moveables have a very long duration and great value—almost like perpetual things, such as gems—they are excluded because they do not produce "fruit" (income). Therefore, their ownership does not include the right to perceive an annual revenue from them, of which a **real annuity** <term>Real annuity: A contract where the payment is secured by a specific, productive piece of real estate.</term> placed upon them ought to be a part. Thus, even these moveable things, no matter how precious or durable, are excluded from the category of things in which a perpetual annuity may be placed.

As for the addition in the same clause: *by its nature fruit-bearing*: this excludes annuities placed on immovable property that is by nature unproductive—that is, property which, even if cultivated, either brings no fruit or so little that it would not be sufficient to pay the annuity or pension, once the labor and expenses of harvesting have been deducted. Such annuities would effectively be created with a mortgage on other goods and a personal obligation; they would therefore be **mixed** (partly real and partly personal), which the Supreme Pontiff rightly excludes. This is surely the legitimate sense of these words, as Navarrus rightly says in his commentary. No one would buy a purely real annuity on a thing that, even when cultivated, did not return as much as the pension; for by surrendering that thing, the debtor would remain free from the payment of the annuity—and the Supreme Pontiff presupposes this. Therefore, to prevent **personal annuities** from being mixed in (which he intends to exclude entirely as usurious and unjust), he added those words, which have the meaning we have handed down.

There are some who think that by these words Pius V intended to exclude an annuity of a certain pension if the property was not a producer of that specific crop—for example, an annuity of so many measures of wine secured by an olive grove, or so many bushels of wheat secured by a vineyard. However, since those words do

<column-break/>

not mean that the thing must be fruit-bearing of the **exact same** fruit that is to be paid, but only that it must be generally "fruit-bearing by its nature"; and since a real annuity paid in fruits of a different species from those which the property immediately produces is licit by the nature of the thing, and was approved in the "Extravagants" <note>Papal decrees circulating outside the main legal collections.</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III (as we showed in Disputation 385), it must undoubtedly be said that such cases are not excluded by the decree. Furthermore, a constitution that departs from common law and the nature of things should not be extended, but rather narrowed as much as its sense allows; it has been explained that the intention of Pius V in those words was far different. 

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> Observe this: although the *Portuguese Ordinances* (Book 4, Title 65, last section) prohibit houses or their ground from being given in *emphyteusis* <term>Emphyteusis: A long-term lease of land where the tenant is required to improve the property in exchange for a low rent.</term> under a pension of wheat, wine, oil, or other fruit, and only permit a money pension (or perhaps some birds as well), and declare void any contract of *emphyteusis* celebrated otherwise regarding houses; it is not therefore considered to prohibit the placement of an annuity of bread, wine, or other similar things upon houses or their ground. This is because that regulation departs from common law and should not be extended to other cases: those ordinances there speak only of the *emphyteutic* contract, not the *censual* (annuity) contract. Remember that in Disputation 385 it was said 

<margin>Castilian Law.</margin> that in this Kingdom of Castile, a *censual* contract with a buy-back clause is not admitted unless it is **pecuniary**—that is, one whose pension cannot be paid in anything other than money.

The last part of the clause—*and which is specifically designated by certain boundaries*—was added to exclude annuities placed over **all goods**, both present and future, of the one who sells the annuity. In such cases, the goods only seem to take on the character of a mortgage, and the annuity seems to be personal, with the risk of the annuity being thrown back onto the seller. So that there would be no room for such annuities, and so that the risk would belong to the buyer if the specific part of the goods in which the annuity was placed were to perish (as is added below in another clause), Pius V willed that an annuity could not be placed otherwise than in a **certain and determined thing**, upon whose risk the buyer's risk of the annuity would also depend. 

In this place, observe that an annuity cannot be established on a designated thing while adding "and upon the rest of the seller's goods, including future ones": for this would similarly be to throw the risk of the annuity onto the seller, as Navarrus says. However, an annuity established before that Bull would not be rendered invalid, as Navarrus adds. The reason is that since it was truly "real" as placed upon that particular thing, the addition of the other goods was nothing other than the mixing in of an insurance contract for the real annuity, which is licit apart from the Bull of Pius V, provided the price is equal and proportionate. When you hear "a certain and determined thing," understand it to mean one or many, as Navarrus well says. Indeed, the intention of the Supreme Pontiff was not to prohibit one annuity from being placed upon several specific and determined immovable things.

<margin>5</margin> **Whether, after this Bull of Pius V, a mortgage has a place in a real annuity.** <note>A "real annuity" (census realis) is a financial arrangement where a buyer pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment drawn from the income of a specific piece of real estate.</note> Gutierrez, in his *Practicarum Quaestionum* book 2, question 177, answers in the affirmative. He understands this to mean that if the property on which the annuity is placed is seized or lost <note>original: "evicta re"</note>, the owner of the annuity may act against the seller for the interest and securely obtain it. However, regarding the collection of the annual payments, as long as the property subject to the annuity remains intact, although it is not illegal to require another mortgage, it is nonetheless superfluous and of no advantage, since the property itself in which the annuity is placed is sufficient.

## Five following clauses in the same bull are explained.

### DISPUTATION CCCXC.

### THE SECOND CLAUSE of the Bull of Pius V.

> The second clause, or condition, reads as follows: *Again, [the contract is valid] only if the full just price is truly counted out in cash, in the presence of witnesses and a notary, and at the time of the execution of the legal instrument, and not before.*

### SUMMARY

1. *What the second clause or condition of the Bull of Pius V effects, with its declarations.*
2. *How an annuity contract is judged void based on the second clause of the Bull of Pius V.*
3. *How annuities before the Bull of Pius V, or where it was not received, are to be judged valid. numbers 5, 7, 9, & 11.*
4. *The third clause of the Bull of Pius V, its effects, and declarations.*
*Likewise the fourth, fifth, and sixth clauses, with their effects and declarations. numbers 6, 8, 10.*
*And regarding the sixth clause according to the law of Castile. number 12.*

---

<margin>1</margin> This clause was added to remove the injustices that often occur in annuity contracts. Sometimes, when those buying annuities see that the sellers are pressed by a need for money, they force them to take part of the price in cash and part in goods <note>original: "mercibus"</note> which they do not need and which are sold to them at an immoderate price. At other times, they give a certain part of the price immediately, but later pay the remainder in installments over time. These two practices are indeed most unjust. In the first case, there is an obligation of restitution <note>Molina argues that the buyer must pay back the seller because the seller was essentially cheated through price manipulation.</note> for all the damages that follow for the sellers, because they force them to sell a larger annuity than they would have otherwise sold for cash, and because they force them to buy those goods at a high, immoderate price only to resell them for very little. 

<column-break/>

In the second case, there is an obligation of restitution for that portion of the annual payment which they receive for the part of the money not yet delivered. For no equity allows an annual payment to be received from an annuity except from the time the price for that part of the annuity has been paid. Nor does the seller of the annuity consent that it be owed and paid except involuntarily and in a "mixed" way, in the same manner that interest <note>original: "usurae"</note> is paid. A person who sells an annuity in this way would not find the money they need otherwise, except by selling the annuity with the price partly on credit, as Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a leading scholar on law and morality.</note> rightly says among others in his commentary on chapter 1, question 3, number 78.

This same clause also seems to have been added for the public good <note>original: "in rempublicam bonum"</note>, so that debtors would not be forced by their creditors to take on an annuity for old debts and pay annual returns while the debt remains unpaid, and to avoid similar damages that tend to burden the assets of others with annuities and reduce them to poverty. 

Because this clause was added as a <term>solemnitas</term> <note>A legal formality required for a contract to be valid.</note> and a required form, if it is not observed, the contract becomes void by the law itself (*ipso iure*), even if it might otherwise be considered just by its nature. This is clear from what the Supreme Pontiff adds after all these clauses and conditions in the same bull. Certainly, where this bull has been received into use, even regarding this clause, the contract will be null both in the external court of law and in the forum of conscience if the prescribed formality was omitted, as Lassarte affirms regarding this clause in particular in his work on the sale of tithes, chapter 10, number 49.

<margin>*</margin> From this clause, it is established that where this bull has been received into use, it is unlawful and void to enter into an annuity contract where one buys a real annual annuity from their debtor with a "buy-back" agreement <note>original: "pacto de retrovendendo" — a clause allowing the seller to buy back the annuity later.</note> using money that the debtor already owes and is late in paying, even if the price is otherwise just. However, excluding positive law, I do not think this annuity should be condemned by the nature of the thing itself. 

Next, it is established as unlawful and void to have a contract where someone hands over a property justly valued at, for example, 1,400 gold coins <note>original: "aureis"</note> for a real annuity with a buy-back agreement of 100 gold coins annually (at a rate of 14 to 1), or where someone justly sells an estate for 1,400 gold coins and, having received a price of 600 coins, buys an annuity from the buyer of that same estate (or from another estate) for the remaining part at 50 coins per year at the same rate, because the buyer of the estate does not have the full price to pay immediately. Here, too, there is no reason to condemn the contract by the nature of the thing itself, excluding positive law. 

Likewise, it is established that no contract exists unless, in the presence of a notary <note>original: "tabellionis"</note> and witnesses, the full price is truly counted out in cash and delivered to the seller of the annuity at the moment of the celebration or drafting of the legal instrument, and not before, as the words of the clause we are explaining contain. It will be safe for the money to be counted and delivered before the notary and witnesses; although if it was truly counted beforehand and is entirely present before the notary...

However, when only a part of the price is shown and handed over before the notary and witnesses—with the seller of the annuity confessing that he is receiving the full price, while the buyer retains the other part because the seller owed it to him—this would not suffice, as **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian known as "Navarrus."</note> says in the cited commentary, number 88. But if he should hand over the full price, yet with an agreement made with the seller that he should immediately pay back from that sum the part he owed him, I certainly would not dare to condemn that. For the buyer of the annuity truly pays the full value of the annuity in counted-out money <term>pecunia numerata</term> <note>original: "pecunia numerata" refers to cash physically counted out in public to prove the transaction isn't a legal fiction or a hidden usurious loan.</note> before the notary and witnesses; and that he pays with the intention and agreement that what is truly owed to the same buyer be paid back from it—which the seller is indeed bound to do—certainly contains nothing evil or fraudulent.

I would point out that although the formality of this clause was established out of holy zeal and suggested to the Most Holy Pope **Pius V**, it might perhaps be expedient for it to be abolished. For there are very few who observe it, even where that Bull is received and observed in many other respects. This is partly because the contracting parties are ignorant that this formality is necessary for the contract to be valid, and partly because it is extremely troublesome for them—nor can it be done without expense—for a sum of six gold pieces, or a thousand gold pieces, to be counted out before a notary and witnesses, or even for the whole sum to be handed over to them during the very drafting of the legal instrument. Nor should all those things be decreed which, viewed in themselves, are judged expedient for some good end, when, considering human frailty, they can be fulfilled only with difficulty and by a few. Such things can become an occasion for **ensnaring consciences** and for doubting whether contracts, otherwise just in themselves, are void and null, carrying the burden of restitution or of counting the accepted payments toward the principal price. Especially since experience has shown that on the occasion of the formalities of that Bull, many lawsuits have arisen, both in secular and ecclesiastical courts, concerning many annuities entered into in good faith after that Bull and just in themselves; from which it follows that many, due to ignorance of so many formalities, suffer no small detriment to their property.

Finally, I would point out that **Navarrus**, in the cited commentary number 88 and more clearly at number 121, asserts that the buyer of an annuity at a just price is safe in conscience even if he did not pay it before a notary or witnesses, nor in counted-out money, but in goods that were worth that amount, or in compensation for an old debt. This indeed seems harsh to me, because the Bull itself does not seem to say that, for it renders the contract void and null; nor does it seem to be based on a presumption, as Navarrus seems to want in cited number 88. Unless you say that all these things were established as a penalty, and thus do not take place before a sentence has been passed. Or that the omission is a light one, and therefore—even if it pertains to the required form—it does not vitiate the act, according to those things said with **Alvarez**, **Valasco**, **Barbosa**, and others in Disputation 218. However, in truth, this does not seem to be the case, nor would it vitiate the contract in the external court; the contrary of which Navarrus affirms.

<margin>3</margin> As † pertains to annuity contracts celebrated before that Bull, or after it in places where it has not been received, or where it has not been received regarding that formality,

<column-break/>

it is established that they are valid, provided they suffer from no other defect than the omission of those formalities. However, when the price was not just—because it did not reach the limits of the lowest just price—I judge in the matter proposed that the buyer is bound to moderate the annuity, so that a smaller payment is paid thereafter (that is, one which is judged equal to the quantity of the price given for the annuity), and at the same time the buyer is bound to restore the excess of the payments he received up to that time. Nor is the reasoning in this part the same for an annuity bought with a **right of redemption** <term>pactum de retrovendendo</term> <note>A clause allowing the seller to buy back the property or annuity at a later date for the original price.</note> as it is for estates similarly bought, such that restitution of the excess price would not be made in the same way, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 375. For if the estate and the annuity placed upon it should perish, the seller is in no way relieved regarding that larger portion of the payment which he has paid up until then. Furthermore, all the fruits of the estate (beyond the just portion that the buyer justly purchased) belonged solely to the seller, who is the owner of the estate, for the entire past time; but the matter is far different in a purchase made with a right of redemption.

### THE THIRD CLAUSE.

> The third clause reads as follows: *We prohibit payments, which are commonly called "anticipated" (prepaid), to be made or to be included in a contract.*

<margin>4</margin> To understand this clause, it must be observed: although the rule is different regarding other things bought with a right of redemption concerning their fruits from the time of purchase until the time of redemption (as explained in Disputation 374), nevertheless in an annuity contract, unless something else is specifically included in the agreement, this general rule must be observed: If an annual payment is established, for example, as so many measures of wheat, so many measures of wine or oil, or such a quantity of money, or of any other thing, the payment is owed only in proportion to the time of the year that has elapsed. For instance, if an annuity consists of twelve measures of wheat to be paid at the end of August, and the annuity was bought and its price paid four months before the end of August; when that first end of August arrives, only four measures are owed. But if it was bought two months before the end of August, two measures will be owed; and so the measures will be owed in the same proportion of elapsed time. If the contract was celebrated with a right of redemption, and it is redeemed one month after the end of August, only one measure will be owed [for that period]; if two months after the end of August, two measures will be owed, and so on consequently for the rate of elapsed time. This is affirmed by **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> in *Variae Resolutiones*, book 1, chapter 15, numbers 10 and 11, and many others whom he cites. The reason is that since an annual payment was bought, it must be paid according to the rate of the time of the year in which the annuity lasts—especially since the seller of the annuity was in possession of the price for no longer a time. These are the legal points by which Covarruvias confirms the same in that place.

This being established, although many have doubted what Pius V intended by this clause and various people have asserted various things, I do not doubt that it was added to prevent any more of a payment being received or included in the contract than that which is owed by the nature of the contract, if it were celebrated absolutely without any other agreement, and...

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

For whatever payment is further included in the agreement to be paid would certainly be an anticipated payment <term>solutio anticipata</term> <note>original: "solutio anticipata"; this refers to paying the interest or rent before it has technically been earned by the passage of time.</note> of the annuity, or part of the annuity. According to this, therefore, it would be an anticipated payment not only if it is included in the agreement that one full installment of the annuity be paid at the very beginning of the purchase, with full annual installments paid thereafter, but even if the annuity is bought four months before the fixed payment date and it is included in the agreement that a full installment be paid at that first due date. Finally, it will be an anticipated payment if any amount is established as being owed before it is due proportionally for the time elapsed. This is because it is properly called an "anticipated payment" if you look at the nature of the contract itself and at what is customarily observed within it.

Contracts celebrated before this Bull <note>The Bull *Cum Onus* issued by Pope Pius V in 1569, which set strict moral and legal rules for annuities to prevent hidden usury.</note>, or in places where it has not been received, are not to be judged as unjust—and much less as void—due to the lack of this condition, provided that the price given for the annuity, including that burden, does not exceed the bounds of a just price. For since no inequality is seen between the price and the goods, there is certainly no reason why such a contract should be judged unjust by its very nature. If, however, it did exceed the bounds of justice regarding only the added burden, then that burden should be remitted, or if already accepted, it should be restored.

### THE FOURTH CLAUSE.

**T**he Fourth Clause holds: *We will that agreements—directly or indirectly—obliging a person to be liable for fortuitous cases <term>casus fortuitos</term> <note>original: "casus fortuitos"; these are "acts of God" or accidental events like fire, flood, or war that occur through no fault of the parties.</note>, who otherwise by the nature of the contract would not be held liable, shall in no way be valid.*

<margin>6</margin> Some † have argued that this clause should be understood as referring to the property in which the annuity is placed, as if the Supreme Pontiff intended to annul agreements providing that if the property itself perishes, the seller is nevertheless bound to pay the annuity. They argue it should not be understood as referring to a fortuitous case regarding the *fruits* (the produce or income) of that property, as if he intended to annul agreements stating that if the crops perish in some year by accident, the seller is still bound to pay the annuity installment. They are led to this because, they say, just as a long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>original: "emphyteuta"; a tenant under a specific Roman law lease who has near-ownership of the land.</note> is bound to pay the rent as long as the leased property remains safe, regardless of whether the crops perish by accident, so too the seller of an annuity is bound to pay the installment as long as the property in which it is placed remains safe, even if its crops perish by accident.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
However, the contrary must undoubtedly be affirmed. Firstly, because the Supreme Pontiff later adds a specific clause annulling agreements by which the debtor of an annuity is obligated for fortuitous cases regarding the *property* itself; he certainly would not have added this other specific clause if it meant the same thing. Secondly, because it is false to say that it is in the nature of a "real" annuity—which is the only type Pius V approves in this Bull—that if the crops perish by accident in any given year, the debtor is still bound to pay. For since the purchase of a purely real annuity is nothing other than the purchase of the right to receive a portion of the fruits that the property subject to the annuity yields each year—either in the fruits themselves or in some equivalent—it follows that

<column-break/>

if the property perishes by accident, the debtor of the annuity is thereafter not bound to the payment. Likewise, if the crops perish by accident in any year, he is not bound by the nature of the contract to pay the installment for that year. It will be enough if he leaves to the buyer of the annuity whatever fruits he may have gathered that year, after deducting expenses and labor, since these are not "fruits" but the expenses of the landowner. Therefore, if an annuity is placed on a certain house and that house cannot be inhabited during a certain year due to a plague or war, no payment is owed for that year from such an annuity. 

Observe two things in this place. One is: regarding the fruits of the property on which the annuity is placed, the buyer of the annuity is, by the nature of the contract, to be preferred over the owner of that property. Thus, the first thing to be taken from the fruits is the annuity payment, and only what remains belongs to the owner of the property. Second: by the very fact that Pius V only invalidated the agreement regarding the failure of crops when they fail due to an *accident*, he tacitly approved such agreements when they fail for other reasons—namely, from the negligence of the debtor, or because it was better for him to cease cultivation for a year so that it might yield more fruit later, or some other similar reason. Indeed, such agreements are understood to exist by the nature of the annuity contract, even if they are not explicitly stated in it.

<margin>7</margin> Regarding annuities created before this Bull with agreements rendered void by this clause, or those created after the Bull where it is not received, this must be said: if the price given does not exceed the limits of justice when comparing the annuity with that burden, there is no reason why it should be condemned by the nature of the thing (as shown in Disputation 385), and thus they should be judged licit. If, however, the price given exceeds the limits of justice because of that defect, then the buyer of the annuity will be bound to restore whatever is lacking in the price to reach the level of justice.

### THE FIFTH CLAUSE.

**T**he Fifth Clause reads as follows: *Just as we do not wish for any agreement to be valid that takes away or restricts the power to alienate <note>To "alienate" means to sell, transfer, or give away ownership to another person.</note> the property subject to the annuity. For we will that the property itself may always be alienated freely and without payment of a transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>original: "laudemium"; a fee paid to a superior landlord when a leasehold was transferred. Molina is saying the annuity-holder cannot demand such a fee.</note>, or a "fiftieth," or any other quantity or thing, whether between living persons or in a last will. However, where it is to be sold, we will that the owner of the annuity be preferred over all others, and the conditions under which it is to be sold must be announced to him, and he must be waited for during one month.*

<margin>8</margin> This clause † was added because, since neither the "useful" nor "direct" ownership of the property in which the annuity is placed belongs to the buyer (as is clearly established from the preceding disputations), but only the right to receive a payment from its fruits, it is certainly within the debtor's power to alienate the property by any title, to anyone, and whenever he wishes. Just as it is within anyone else's power to alienate their own estate to whomever they please, with nothing preventing them even if someone else holds a servitude <note>A "servitude" is a legal right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, like a right-of-way or, in this case, a right to the income from the land.</note> upon it; because the full...
