# Second Treatise, Disputation 390.

remains whole. Thirdly, his right remains for him. However, it is with far greater reason that the debtor of an annuity <term>census</term> <note>original: "census"; a fixed annual payment charged against property, often used as a way to circumvent usury laws by treating the loan as a purchase of future income.</note> is free to alienate <note>To "alienate" in this context means to sell or transfer ownership to someone else.</note> the property itself without being bound to pay a transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>original: "laudemium"; a fee, usually a percentage of the sale price, paid to a superior landlord when a leasehold interest is transferred to a new party.</note> to the lord of the annuity. This is unlike a long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>original: "emphyteuta"; a person holding a long-term lease who has "useful" ownership of the land but must recognize a "direct" owner.</note>, who is bound to pay such a fee to the owner in recognition of his direct lordship if he sells his leasehold right in the owner’s property to another, as will be discussed in its proper place below.

Because of this, those buying annuities—seeing the sellers hard-pressed by the need for money—often imposed burdens on them beyond the nature of the annuity contract. Sometimes they did so unjustly, considering the price paid, by requiring that the seller not alienate the property on which the annuity was placed without the buyer's permission. They also required that if they did alienate it with permission, they were bound to pay a transfer fee; that is, a specific portion of the price—perhaps a fiftieth, a thirtieth, or some similar amount—in the same way a long-term tenant is bound to pay. Therefore, to keep the annuity contract within its proper limits and to avoid dangers to conscience, this clause of Pope Pius V <note>Referencing the Bull *Cum Onus* (1569).</note> renders void every agreement that takes away or restricts the power to alienate the property subject to the annuity by any title, or that imposes an obligation to pay a transfer fee from the price received for it. 

Nevertheless, when the property was already subject to a transfer fee if sold—independent of the annuity contract—Pius V does not prohibit it in this place, as Navarrus <note>original: "Naua."; Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canon lawyer and theologian.</note> noted in the cited commentary, number 93, and from the preceding section of the summary. However, Pius V, as compensation for the annulment of these agreements and so that annuities might be extinguished more quickly, imposed a burden on the seller of the annuity: if he wished to sell the property subject to the annuity, he would be bound to notify the lord of the annuity. This was so that if the lord wished to buy it for the same price and under the same conditions, he should be preferred over other buyers. Furthermore, the seller was ordered to wait for one month from the day of notification of the price and conditions to see if the lord wanted it. 

If the debtor of the annuity sells the property to another without notifying the lord, I believe he falls into a forfeiture <note>original: "commissum"; a legal penalty where a right or property is lost due to a breach of contract.</note>, as if he were losing the property to the lord of the annuity, just as a long-term tenant falls into forfeiture if he sells the leased property without notifying the owner. The reason for the distinction is that neither in this Bull nor elsewhere is that penalty applied to the seller of an annuity, whereas in law it is applied to the long-term tenant; penalties are not to be extended beyond the case in which they are imposed by law. 

Whether a sale is valid if a debtor sells and delivers the property to someone after this Bull without first consulting the lord of the annuity was discussed in Disputation 378. It was said there that the burden of notifying and preferring the lord of the annuity over other buyers, and waiting for him for a month, is a very heavy one. Some argue that secular princes are not bound to admit this in their kingdoms because the nature of the annuity contract, which is purely secular, does not demand it, nor does it prevent the danger to souls. Navarrus says in his commentary that it could have been justly omitted, and that to introduce it is to turn an annuity contract into a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term>.

<column-break/>

There are those who affirm that nothing in this fifth clause prevents a lawful agreement being made that the property cannot be sold to anyone more powerful <note>original: "potentiori"; referring to high-ranking nobles or the Church.</note>. It is said that a long-term tenant cannot sell his right to someone more powerful, either by privilege—such as monasteries and clerics—or for other reasons, such as powerful secular lords from whom it would be more difficult to recover the payment, as will be said in its place. 

However, I believe the contrary should be said. For the right of an annuity, neither from the nature of the thing nor from the disposition of human law, possesses the rule that the property subject to it cannot be sold or pass by any other title to a more powerful person without the consent of the lord of the annuity. This is just as any other right in a property—such as an easement <note>original: "servitutis"; a legal right to use another's land for a specific purpose.</note> or any other—does not prevent the property in which it is placed from passing to a more powerful person without the consent of the one holding that right. If the owner, by the disposition of human law regarding a property in which another has a leasehold right, possesses such a privilege, it is surely because the ownership <term>proprietas</term> is the principal thing in that matter. If the leasehold right were to pass to a more powerful person, not only the annual payment but also the ownership itself, which is far more valuable, would be endangered. Furthermore, if the annuity right does not have this restriction from the nature of the thing or from legal disposition, it certainly cannot be denied that such an agreement restricts the faculty of alienating that property, and is therefore prohibited by this fifth clause.

9. Regarding annuities created before this Bull, or where it has not been received, containing agreements voided by this clause: Johannes Medina <note>Johannes Medina (1490–1546), a Spanish theologian.</note> rightly affirms in his last question on usury that they are not to be condemned, provided the price was commensurate with the annuity along with those burdens. He correctly observes that an annuity is worth more when it is made more secure—either by the possessions in which it is placed or by the burdens imposed. Likewise, the hope of receiving a transfer fee makes it worth a higher price, depending on how much and how often the fee is expected, based on the value of the property and its likelihood of being sold frequently. In all these and similar circumstances, one must judge whether the contract is just or unjust regarding the price, and thus determine whether the buyer is bound to restore what was lacking in the just price or to waive the burdens. Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a major figure in the School of Salamanca.</note>, in book 6 *On Justice*, question 5, article 2, does not seem to disagree with Johannes Medina on the matter, but says these burdens seem inequitable—understand this to mean unless they are compensated by a just price, as they frequently are not.

-> THE SIXTH CLAUSE. <-

THE Sixth Clause states: Agreements containing provisions that a debtor who is late <term>morosus</term> <note>original: "morosus"; legal delay in performing an obligation.</note> in paying the annuity is bound to pay for "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; the profit a creditor could have made if they had been paid on time.</note>, or for damages, or specific expenses, or specific salaries; or to pay salaries or expenses to be determined by the creditor's fair assessment; or to lose the property subject to the annuity or any part of it; or to lose any other right from the same contract or any other right acquired elsewhere; or to fall under any penalty; are entirely void and null. Moreover, we altogether prohibit that an annuity be increased or created upon the same or another property in favor of the same person or their proxy for payments of time either past or future.

<meta>This page continues Molina's commentary on the Bull of Pope Pius V regarding annuity contracts. It specifically addresses the "Fifth Clause," which invalidates certain penalty clauses and compound interest arrangements that were historically used to exploit debtors.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina / On Contracts

Just as a long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>original: "emphyteuta"; a tenant who holds "useful" ownership of land but must pay a fixed rent to the "direct" owner</note>—if they do not pay their rent for two or three years—falls into a forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>original: "commissum"; a legal penalty where a person loses their right or property due to a failure to fulfill an obligation</note> and loses the leased property to the owner (as will be discussed in its proper place), so too did buyers of annuities <term>census</term> begin to impose various burdens on the sellers. Beyond what the nature of an annuity contract requires, they would demand that the debtor fall into forfeiture for non-payment, among other things, often doing so unjustly. Therefore, this clause of Pope Pius V renders void any agreements where, due to unpaid rent, the seller of the annuity was bound to pay interest for lost profit <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; a legal concept referring to the profit a creditor loses because they did not receive their money on time</note>, or to pay for currency exchange <term>cambium</term>, or to cover specific expenses and salaries for the recovery of the rent, or salaries and expenses that the creditor swore they spent on such recovery. It also voids agreements for the loss of the property on which the annuity is placed (or part of it), the loss of any other acquired right, or, finally, any other penalty whatsoever.

Regarding these matters, observe that the Supreme Pontiff does not forbid the collection of reasonable and moderate expenses that the lord of the annuity incurred due to the debtor’s delay in paying. To put it briefly, he does not forbid demanding anything that could be lawfully demanded based on the nature of the situation itself, without any specific agreement; he only forbids demanding anything else by virtue of an added clause in the annuity contract.

Regarding interest for lost profit <note>original: "lucrum cessans"</note>, observe that he does not forbid "intrinsic" interest for lost profit resulting from unpaid rent. For example, if the rent was to be paid in wheat at a time when a measure was worth two gold coins, and the lord of the annuity intended to sell it immediately (or if that wheat was meant to offset the purchase of another item at that same price), and later the rent is paid at a time when the wheat is only worth half a gold coin, the Pope does not forbid demanding that lost profit. This is because that loss is owed by the very nature of the thing, even without any extra agreement added to the annuity contract. He only forbids taking "extrinsic" lost profit—for instance, if the lord of the annuity was a merchant and, because the rent was not paid on time, they lost profit from their trade. Such a profit is said to be "extrinsic" to the matter at hand, as explained in Disputation 368, conclusions 3 and 5. Therefore, since an annuity contract is a form of buying and selling, and the payment of rent is like a partial delivery of the purchased goods, when the seller is delayed in delivering the "goods" (the payment), they are only held to the interest intrinsic to the goods, not extrinsic interest. This is established by civil law <note>original: "l. si stetit l.§.cum per venditorem, ff. de actionib. emp."; references to the Digest of Justinian regarding the actions of buyers and sellers</note> and other laws we cited in the aforementioned disputation. It follows that, by the nature of the annuity contract, extrinsic lost profit is not owed; thus, for it to be owed, a specific additional agreement would be necessary—which is exactly what Pius V renders void here.

In the second part of the same clause, the Supreme Pontiff forbids an annuity from being created upon the same property (or any other property) based on past unpaid rent or even future rent yet to be paid. This is to prevent debtors from being reduced to poverty through the accumulation of annuities upon annuities, losing their property in the same way they usually are by compound interest 

<column-break/>

on interest or by re-exchanges <term>secambia</term> <note>original: "secambis"; a banking practice involving repeated currency exchanges that often hid usurious interest</note>. However, this part of the clause is already contained in the second clause proposed above: such a purchase of an annuity would not be made in ready money paid in the presence of witnesses and a notary.

<margin>11</margin>
11. Regarding annuity contracts celebrated before this Bull, or after it in places where it has not been received, it must be said: there is no reason to condemn the inclusion of clauses containing agreed-upon penalties if the rent is not paid at the appointed time, provided the penalty is moderate and proportionate to the fault, and is not demanded if no fault occurred. This is also provided that the other conditions we discussed in Disputation 317 (along with Disputation 97) are observed, so that a conventional penalty may be collected lawfully and justly. There is no reason why such agreements cannot be applied to a lingering debtor of an annuity rent just as they would be to any other debtor in any other contract. This is the consensus of Conradus <note>original: "Conrad. de contract. q. 85"</note>, Juan Medina <note>original: "Ioã. Med. de vsur. q. vlt."</note>, Domingo de Soto <note>original: "Sotus 6. de iust. q. 5."</note>, Martín de Azpilcueta <note>original: "Nauarr. in commen. c. 1."</note>, and doctors commonly. However, Pius V rightly prohibited such agreements in this specific contract because of the excessive penalties many were imposing and the injustices being committed. Indeed, to impose the penalty of losing the property subject to the annuity if the rent is not paid for two or three years is an excessive and unjust penalty, since the property is of much greater value than the annuity itself.

<margin>12 † Canon Law is approved, and in the external court, the ownership of the annuity is awarded; therefore Medina in the cited place, and others, rightly judge this law to be unjust and not at all to be observed in the court of conscience.</margin>
12 † Nothing prevents this penalty from being approved in this Kingdom by Law 68 of the Laws of Toro <note>original: "l. 68. Tau."; the Laws of Toro (1505) were a famous set of Spanish laws</note>, where it is commanded in the external court <note>The "external court" refers to public, secular, or ecclesiastical legal proceedings, as opposed to the "court of conscience" or internal forum.</note> that the ownership of the annuity be awarded. Nevertheless, Medina and others rightly judge that law to be unjust and not to be followed in the court of conscience. And Covarruvias, Alvarez Valasco, Gutierrez, and others they cite assert that this law is not accepted in practice regarding that penalty, except when the annuity is a "reserved" one <term>census reservativus</term>. For just as in a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> that penalty has a place because the owner hands over the "useful" ownership to the tenant—and can lawfully refuse to grant it except on the condition that if rent is not paid for two or three years, it reverts to the owner—so too in a reserved annuity, the person who grants the property to another grants both the useful and direct ownership together. They can lawfully refuse to grant both except on the condition that if possession (rent) is not paid within two or three years, both types of ownership revert to them. However, in a "consigned" annuity <term>census consignativus</term>—which is what we are discussing here and what Law 68 of Toro addresses—the reasoning is not the same, as Azpilcueta <note>original: "Nau." (Navarrus)</note> also says. For the person who grants an annuity to another does not receive either useful or direct ownership from the buyer of the annuity; rather, for a price, they merely grant the "bought annuity," which is the right to receive a certain annual rent from that property. It is not fair for such a heavy penalty to be established—namely, that if they do not pay the rent within two or three years, they lose the useful and direct ownership of their own property, which is worth far more than the annuity.

### The five following clauses are explained. Also, whether "real" annuities without a buyback agreement are included within them.

## DISPUTATION 391.
## THE SEVENTH CLAUSE.

The seventh clause reads as follows: "We also likewise annul agreements containing provisions that the payment of taxes and burdens shall belong to the person to whom they would not otherwise belong by law or by the nature of the contract."

<margin>1</margin>Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> in his commentary provides an example: such as if the buyer of an annuity includes a pact that the seller is required to provide lodging <term>hospitio</term> for the buyer's family members. Observe, however, that regarding the property in which the annuity is placed, those taxes <term>tributa</term> imposed based on the value of each person's goods, or the quantity of income from the estates from which taxes are collected, belong partly to the owner of the estate and partly to the owner of the annuity <term>dominus census</term>, according to the proportion of the right they hold over the fruits of that estate. In this clause, therefore, Pius V renders void those agreements by which these and similar burdens, which partially belong to the owner of the annuity, are cast upon the debtor of the annuity. However, he did not by this clause forbid taking guarantors, nor [did he forbid] that the property in which the annuity is placed belong to the seller of the annuity, or that the payment be made at the [due] time, as some have thought. For those things are not invalid or illicit after this Bull, as was said above. Nevertheless, it is illicit and void to take guarantors [to ensure] that if the property subject to the annuity perishes, the annuity would still be paid:

<column-break/>

just as it is illicit and void to demand this from the seller of the annuity.

<margin>2</margin>As for annuities created before this Bull, or where it has not been accepted, which were created with agreements now rendered null by this clause: it must be said that if the price does not exceed the limits of justice when compared to an annuity with these burdens, there is no reason they should be condemned. If, however, the price does not reach the limits of justice, there is an obligation to either increase the price to a just level or to remit the burdens.

## THE EIGHTH CLAUSE.

> **E**ighthly, regarding annuities to be created in the future, if the property is destroyed in whole or in part, or rendered fruitless in whole or in part, we will that the annuity perish proportionally.

<margin>3</margin>By this clause, Pius V established that in annuities created after this Bull, if the entire property in which the annuity is placed perishes, or is rendered entirely fruitless, the entire annuity perishes. If, however, the same property perishes in part, or is rendered entirely fruitless in part—for instance, because a half, a third, a fourth, or some other part has perished or been rendered entirely fruitless—the annuity perishes in that same proportional part (that is, in a half, a third, a fourth, or another similar part). At this point, observe that a property is not said to be "rendered fruitless" <term>infructuosa</term> simply because it fails to bear fruit for two, three, or more years; rather, it is because it has become incapable of yielding fruit in the future. For example, if a field is not merely hit by a bad season, but is simply and without hope of remedy swallowed by the sea, or because a river changed its course and made its bed through that place; or because a house in which the annuity was placed collapsed entirely or was burned down. Observe further, it is a very different thing for the property in which the annuity is placed to fail to produce its usual fruits due to sterility or some other accidental case, but produces far fewer, than for the same property to perish in part or be rendered fruitless. In the first scenario, the full payment is owed from whatever fruits are produced, if they suffice for it, even if nothing remains for the owner of the estate, as was said in the previous disputation regarding the fourth clause. In the latter scenario, however, the payment is only owed in proportion to what remains of the property in which the annuity is placed, as is contained in this clause. This remains true even if the part of the property that survives produces far more fruit than is necessary to pay the full installment. The reason for this difference is that an annuity is a right *in the thing* <term>ius in re</term> subject to the annuity, and it is a "real" obligation of that entire thing to produce the payment—first from the fruits it bears, whether the whole is cultivated and bears fruit, or only a part. Since that obligation is extended over the whole, such that the whole is in the whole property and a part is in the part, it follows that when a part of that property perishes or is rendered entirely fruitless, a part of that obligation perishes as well, and thus the right to the installment perishes along with it. Meanwhile, as long as the thing remains whole, the full installment is owed, whether the thing bears fruit according to its whole self or according to a part, and whether the debtor is rendered [more or less] capable of producing fruit, or whether it remains in the same state. Therefore, because the annuity is spread across the property in which it is placed, when a part of the property perishes, a part of the annuity perishes.

...remains in its entirety and is owed. From this, it is clear that according to the nature of a divided matter, when an annuity <term>census</term> <note>original: "census"; a financial arrangement where one person pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual income from a specific property</note> is split among multiple heirs or buyers, each individual only owes the portion of the annuity corresponding to the share of the property they possess. However, the fact that the lord of the annuity can take action against any one of them for the full amount arises because no one would want to buy an annuity unless it carried such a weight <note>The "weight" or "burden" refers to a legal obligation making the debt easier for the creditor to collect from any single part-owner</note>. This practice has prevailed—with no law hitherto opposing it—so that the contract is celebrated with this burden and privilege for the buyer, as was stated in Disputation 383.

4 Regarding annuities created before this Bull <note>The Bull *Cum onus* issued by Pope Pius V in 1569 to regulate annuities and prevent usury</note>, or where it has not been received, we must say: if they are simply placed upon a specific thing with no additional agreement, and the thing or part of it perishes, the debtor is nonetheless held to the full annual payment. This applies to the provisions of this clause whether the annuity is redeemable or irredeemable. The reason is that the arrangement of this clause relies on the nature of a "real" annuity <note>An annuity tied to physical property or "real" estate, rather than a person</note>, as has been explained, when no other agreement is added. Regarding annuities created in the future, Pius V intended by this clause to invalidate agreements that would state anything to the contrary. If, however, the annuities are placed on a thing with an added agreement that even if the thing perishes, the debtor is still bound to the full payment; certainly, since such an agreement is nothing other than a contract of insurance <term>assecuratio</term> mixed with an annuity contract—and the insurance contract is by its nature valid and lawful—it is just, provided the price given for the annuity with that burden is equal and proportionate to both risks. This was shown in Disputation 389. It is unjust, however, if it does not reach the limits of a fair price, requiring either an increase in price or a removal of the burden. That such a contract can be valid and just by its nature is clearly hinted at by Pius V when he expressly restricted this clause to annuities created after this Bull.

->CLAUSE NINE.<-

It states:
> We also will that [annuities] can be extinguished for the same price, notwithstanding the prescription of even the longest and immemorable time—even of one hundred or more years—notwithstanding any agreements directly or indirectly taking away such power, in whatever words or clauses they are conceived.

5 By this † clause, joined with the following one, Pius V established that an annuity can always be redeemed for the same price. No prescription <note>A legal principle where rights are lost or gained over a period of time, such as losing the right to buy back a debt because too many years have passed</note> of any duration in which the annuity was not redeemed can prevent this. Nor can it be blocked by any agreement or words added to the annuity contract. The first part is intended to nullify any agreement that the annuity be redeemed for a higher price than it was originally bought for. The second part excludes the opinion of those who claimed that the right to redeem (which arises from a buy-back agreement) is lost after thirty years. We showed the opposite to be true in Disputation 374, as does Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a famous Spanish jurist</note> in *Various Resolutions* chapter 9, specifically regarding

<column-break/>

the annuity, where he discusses this point at length. The third part is added to render void any agreements that remove or restrict the power to redeem the annuity. Thus, annuities created after this Bull, where it is accepted, can be redeemed at any time without any restriction.

6 Regarding † contracts created before this Bull, or after it in places where it is not received, which were made with an agreement that they cannot be redeemed beyond a certain time (such as four or seven years), or that they cannot be redeemed *within* a certain time but can be afterward: Some authors—whom Covarruvias mentions and follows in *Various Resolutions* book 3, chapter 8, numbers 7 and 8—specifically disapprove of any agreement in an annuity other than one where the seller is left with full and perfect power to redeem the annuity whenever they wish, without any restriction. Covarruvias adds that in the High Court of Granada, sentences have often been pronounced stating that any such restriction should be treated as if it were not there, and the seller retains the free power to redeem the annuity at any time, just as if the restriction had never been added.

These authors are led by two reasons. First, because the buying of annuities is "odious" <note>In legal terms, "odious" refers to something viewed with suspicion or disfavor because it borders on an illegal or immoral act, like usury</note> and has a greater similarity to a usurious loan than the buying of any other thing.

Second, because Martin V in the first *Extravagant* and Calixtus III in the second *Extravagant* <note>The "Extravagantes" were papal decrees that circulated outside the main organized collections of canon law</note> regarding buying and selling, only mention and approve of annuities with a free agreement to redeem them whenever one pleases, without restriction.

However, I believe we should say, along with the author of **On Doubts** <note>original: "Dubiis"; likely referring to the work of a contemporary scholastic theologian</note> regarding contracts questions 83 and 84, Medina *On Usury*, and Soto *On Justice* book 6, question 5, article 3, that such agreements are not illicit by their very nature if added to an annuity; provided that the more the freedom of redemption is restricted, the more the buyer of the annuity increases the price. This is because the more risk there is that the annuity might become irredeemable, the more it is worth, since an irredeemable annuity is of much greater value than a redeemable one. This requires no other proof than that there is no inequality seen between the price and the thing bought with such a burden. Nevertheless, because of the dangers of cloaking usury <term>usura</term> in this way and committing injustice, such agreements can and should be rendered void by positive law.

Regarding the first argument of the opposing opinion, we must say: although the subject matter is "odious" and dangerous, if the due circumstances are kept when adding these restrictions to a buy-back agreement, there is no reason why they should be condemned by their nature alone.

Regarding the second, although those papal decrees only mention annuities with the convenient freedom to redeem them whenever one wishes, other annuities are not thereby condemned; they are neither approved nor condemned there. Nor does Pius V in this Bull condemn such annuities that were celebrated before its issuance.

7 Observe † this: since in this Kingdom <note>Referring to the Kingdom of Castile/Spain</note> redeemable annuities cannot justly be bought for less...

<summary>Molina discusses the Ninth Clause of the Bull of Pope Pius V, which grants debtors the perpetual right to redeem annuities at their original price, regardless of time elapsed. He argues that while restrictions on redemption might be naturally fair if the price is adjusted, they are legally prohibited to prevent the exploitation and hidden usury common in such financial contracts.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 391.

...at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one, as if it were a purchase of those same annuities <term>censuum</term> <note>original: "censuum"; financial arrangements where a lump sum is paid for the right to receive an annual income from a property</note> with the restoration of the power to redeem for the same price. Consequently, the tribunals of this Kingdom rightly pronounce as null any pacts restricting the power to redeem them, if the annuities were purchased only at the ratio of fourteen to one, as they are regularly accustomed to doing.

<margin>8</margin>
Regarding contracts celebrated before this Bull, or where it has not been received, which include a pact that the annuity must be redeemed at a higher price than it was purchased: we must say this. Although the price of a redeemable annuity does not consist in a single fixed point when it is not taxed by law—and therefore, the prices of annuities in different regions, or at different times in the same region, should not be easily condemned when no public legal tax is set, whether they are at the ratio of fourteen, sixteen, twelve, or ten for one, or other intermediate prices—provided that it is the common price then in that region. This can even be confirmed by *Martin V*, who, in the "Extravagantes" <note>A collection of canon laws not included in the primary decree of Gratian</note>, mentions larger prices and does not condemn them as unjust; indeed, he seems to approve as just a price at the ratio of ten to one <note>A 10:1 ratio means paying 10 coins to get 1 coin annually (a 10% rate), which is more expensive for the debtor than a 14:1 ratio (roughly 7%)</note> if it is customary in some region. However, it should not be denied, following *Medina*, that according to scholastic rigor, a pact to redeem an annuity at a higher price is sometimes permitted by the nature of the case—specifically when it is likely that it will be worth more at the time of redemption, just as we showed was permitted in Disputation 376 for other things. Nevertheless, because it is very rarely expected that an annuity will be worth more in the same region at the time of redemption than at the time of purchase, and since the matter itself has the appearance of evil and usury <term>usuræ</term>—regularly serving as a reservation for usury—it is undoubtedly to be condemned simply. Rightly, therefore, *Pius V* rendered judgment on such a pact; namely, that by the Bull of *Pius V*, it should be condemned as usurious by both ecclesiastical and secular judges. Thus, such a pact is not so much to be condemned based on the decree of *Martin V*, as *Covarrubias* suggests in *Variarum Resolutionum*, book 3, chapter 9, but rather from the very nature of the matter and the disposition of this clause by *Pius V*.

<margin>9</margin>
The doubt at this point is whether *Pius V*, through this clause, intended to remove all "real" irredeemable annuities <note>Annuities tied to property that the debtor has no right to end by paying back the principal</note> from Christian Republics and to decree that in the future only redeemable ones should be created.

The side that affirms this can be persuaded because he spoke of annuities indistinctly and universally throughout this whole Bull; therefore, the disposition of this clause and the entire Bull extends even to irredeemable ones. This is especially so because this clause and the preceding one were issued in a single flow of speech, so much so that it seems to be one clause rather than two if you attend to the connection of the words in the Bull of *Pius V*. We, however, in order to provide a clearer teaching, have divided it into two, removing from the first clause these words: "not only"; and at the beginning of the second, in place of the word "but," repeating the word "*we will*." Hence, the words of *Pius V* are as follows: "*Finally, regarding all annuities to be created in the future, [we will] not only that they perish in whole or in part if the thing is destroyed, etc., but also that they can be extinguished for the same price, etc.*" Here you see that he willed for all annuities created in the future universally 

<column-break/>

to perish with the thing in which they were placed and to be redeemable for the same price for which they were bought; and consequently, that an irredeemable annuity cannot be created in the future.

<margin>10 Decision.</margin>
The side that denies this is undoubtedly to be asserted, which *Navarrus* also embraces through equity <term>epicheia</term> <note>original: "epicheia"; a legal principle of interpreting the spirit of the law rather than the strict letter to avoid injustice</note> in commentary, chapter 1, question 14, number 98: namely, that irredeemable annuities from Christian Republics are not removed. By this, I mean a "real" life annuity <term>vitalitio</term> <note>An annuity that lasts for the duration of a person's life</note>, and even a real annuity for a fixed number of years, which are not redeemable but completely expire at the end of the established number of years—whether that number is certain or uncertain and dependent on fortune. For there was no reason why life annuities and completely perpetual ones should be banished from Republics.

And *Navarrus* seems to admit that a life annuity is permitted after the Bull of *Pius V*, though he speaks of it as a contract celebrated in the manner of a mutual donation of the price and the payments.

I am led to this first because "real" irredeemable annuities have always been judged just in the Church by learned men, without any scruple or doubt, and they do not have that appearance of usury that redeemable ones have. The reason is that since the price—which was given for the right to collect annual payments from the estate in which the annuity was established—is not returned in these cases, there is no appearance of a loan with profit for the time the buyer lacked the money; thus, there is no usury, as there is in redeemable annuities. Therefore, because the contract of a "real" irredeemable annuity has always been judged just and lawful in the Church without danger or shadow of sin—no different from a contract of buying other things or leasing—it surely should not be thought that *Pius V* intended to include them in this clause and deprive secular Christian Republics of a useful and just contract without any legitimate cause. Nor does his jurisdiction extend to that: for his jurisdiction in temporal matters, compared to that of secular princes, extends only as far as the salvation of souls and the spiritual end requires, as was shown in Disputation 29.

Secondly, as is clear from the beginning of the Bull itself, *Pius V* intended therein only to speak of the annuities of which *Martin V* and *Calixtus III* had spoken, and to apply greater force to remove and prevent the abuses that had arisen and were increasing around them. However, as is clear from their own decrees, *Martin V* and *Calixtus III* spoke only of redeemable annuities, which have the appearance of usury and in which usury can easily be disguised; but not of irredeemable ones. Added to this reason is that *Pius V* was only speaking about annuities that some had complained about to him, and whose pious petitions he says he is satisfying in that Bull. But no one had ever complained before him about real irredeemable annuities, but only about annuities with a pact of "buy-back" without the conditions under which *Martin V* and *Calixtus III* approved them. It also follows that burdensome and extraordinary sanctions—such as those which would prohibit evidently just contracts that are without danger or appearance of sin—are not to be extended, but rather narrowed, consider-

# Ludovici Molina On Contracts, Volume I

rather in them, and by following the intent rather than the words of the legislator: for I am entirely persuaded that if Pius V were consulted on whether he intended to include irredeemable real annuities <term>census reales irredimibiles</term> <note>These were investments where the investor paid a lump sum for a permanent annual income from a property, with no option for the property owner to "buy back" the obligation.</note> in this clause and to abolish them from the commonwealths, he would answer in the negative.

Thirdly, because buying an irredeemable real annuity is nothing other than buying a certain perpetual right and an obligation on the part of the property subjected to the annuity. This is nothing other than buying, as it were, a certain part of the ownership of that thing, not unlike when an easement <term>servitus</term> <note>A legal right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way.</note> is purchased on another’s estate; as all these things were explained in Disputation 383 and those following. Who, then, could persuade themselves that the legislator—much less the Most Holy Pius V—intended to prohibit an estate from being sold, or an easement and right that is like a part of the thing from being purchased, without a buy-back agreement <term>pactum de retrovendendo</term>? And to do so because of the "image and danger of usury," when in such a purchase there is absolutely no image of usury or other injustice? In contrast, in a sale made with a buy-back agreement, usury could easily be cloaked.

Fourthly, because a King can grant someone a perpetual annual income on some estate, or from the revenues of some city, either because of their service and merits or by a completely liberal gift, as frequently happens. Who would say that Pius V, by his own initiative <term>motu proprio</term>, intended to prohibit this person (even with the King’s permission) from selling that annual income irredeemably if they wished to move elsewhere or if selling it were advantageous for another just and legitimate cause? Yet Pius V inhibits those annuities which he prohibits from being newly created from being similarly bought and sold after they have been created.

Nevertheless, these points notwithstanding, I likewise think that the rules Pius V established in this bull regarding redeemable annuities—of which it chiefly speaks—if they were established precisely so that they might be purely "real" <note>Meaning tied to a specific physical asset like land, rather than a personal debt.</note> and at a lawful price without any mixture of injustice, should also be extended to irredeemable annuities through equity <term>epicheia</term> <note>A legal principle allowing for a flexible interpretation of the law to follow its spirit when a literal application would be unfair.</note>. For if he were consulted on this matter, there is no doubt he would answer in the affirmative. The language in his bull is universal and without restriction, and in interpreting laws, one must chiefly attend to the mind of the legislator. Such rules include: that the annuity must be placed on a specific thing; that advance payments are not demanded; that the debtor of the annuity is not liable for accidental losses to the crops; that they can alienate the property subject to the annuity whenever they wish and without paying a transfer fee <term>laudemium</term>; that they are not liable for a penalty, nor can the annuity be increased due to unpaid or future pensions; and that if the property subject to the annuity perishes or becomes unfruitful in whole or in part, the annuity perishes in the same proportion.

### THE TENTH CLAUSE.

> *The tenth clause states: When the income is to be extinguished by the delivery of the price, we will that it be denounced two months prior to the one to whom the price is to be given; and after the denunciation, within a year, the price may be reclaimed even from an unwilling party. And where the price is neither paid willingly within the two months, nor exacted from an unwilling party within the year, we will nonetheless that the income can be extinguished at any time, provided the price is always denounced,*

<column-break/>

as mentioned above, and notwithstanding the things mentioned above. And we command this to be observed even if the denunciation had been made many times over and the effect had never followed.

11 By this † clause, Pius V ordained that when an annuity is to be redeemed, the debtor of the annuity must announce <term>denunciare</term> this to the lord of the annuity two months before the redemption. Once that announcement is made, the lord of the annuity can, if he wishes, compel the debtor to redeem the annuity within a year from the day of the announcement. However, if the debtor does not redeem the annuity within the two months, nor is compelled to redeem it during the remainder of the year, he ordained that the matter returns to its original state. Thus, it remains entirely up to the debtor to redeem it at the same price whenever he wishes, provided a similar announcement is made; and similarly, the lord of the annuity retains the power to compel him to redeem the annuity within a year of the announcement, as often as it is made in the future.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
12 A doubt † can arise concerning this: whether by this disposition Pius V intended for the debtor of the annuity to be bound to continue in the annuity for two months from the day the announcement is made, such that he could not redeem it before those months have elapsed if the lord of the annuity so wished. I think the answer <margin>Negation.</margin> should be in the negative. Indeed, he only <margin>Decision.</margin> intended to grant two months of the year from the day of the announcement in which it is lawful for the debtor of the annuity to redeem it in whatever part of them he wishes; this is clearly suggested by those words he adds: *and where the price is neither paid willingly within the two months,* leaving the rest of the year to the lord of the annuity so that he can compel the debtor to redeem it, since the debtor said he wished to redeem it. However, I believe that secular princes are not bound to admit into their Commonwealths this burden imposed on the debtors of annuities. Instead, they can simply leave them free to redeem or not redeem the annuity whenever they wish, as was customary in the Spains before this bull. And so Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> affirms in his commentary, that neither this nor the rule that the one to whom the annuity is owed must be preferred over other buyers of the property binds those who are outside the temporal jurisdiction of the Supreme Pontiff. Therefore, outside the lands of the temporal dominion of the Church, it is not necessary for such announcements to be made.

### THE ELEVENTH CLAUSE.

> *The eleventh clause states: Pacts containing that the price of the annuity can be reclaimed from an unwilling party outside the aforesaid case, either because of a penalty or for another cause, we altogether prohibit.*

Since the purchase of other things with a buy-back agreement <term>pactum de retrovendendo</term> in favor of the buyer (that is, where the seller is bound to redeem the thing whenever the buyer wishes) is illicit if the pact is that the thing be redeemed for the same price at which it was bought—as was seen in Disputation 377—and since it is very rarely or never done in practice so as to be licit, as is clear from what was said there; surely the same must be said with far greater reason regarding an annuity. It is no hindrance that if the thing underlying the annuity perishes while the buyer of the annuity is not demanding its redemption, the annuity perishes for the buyer by the nature of the thing.

He also examines the procedural rules for redeeming annuities, noting that secular rulers outside the Papal States may not be strictly bound by the Pope's specific notification requirements.</summary>

Molina is specifically examining the twelfth clause, which deals with the penalties for non-compliance and the legal classification of "usury" by papal decree versus natural law.</meta>

...it might perish, since nothing else was brought into the agreement. For this reason, to remove the cloaks of usury and injustices, Pius V rightly decreed in this clause that an annuity could not only not be created simply with a pact that the seller could be forced to redeem it whenever the buyer wished, but also with a pact that, as a penalty if the seller did not pay the annual payments, or for any other cause, he could be forced to redeem it. Medina [writing] on usury, final question on annuities, and Olanus, cited by Gutierrez (Book 2 of *Practical Questions*, question 175), do not consider an agreement inherently illicit by which the burden of redeeming the annuity is joined to the seller in the event that he does not pay the installments. I also do not dare to condemn this, although it was most holily and prudently prohibited by Pius V. I should advise this regarding Covarruvias (3 *Varied Resolutions* chapter 9) and Gutierrez (cited above): it is not gathered from the *Extravagantes* <note>original: "extrauagantibus"; refers to canon law decrees circulating outside the standard official collections.</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III that an annuity with a buy-back agreement in favor of the buyer is illicit. For although the annuities approved in those decrees were not created with such an agreement, it does not follow that annuities celebrated otherwise are there condemned, as has often been said in the preceding sections.

### The remainder of the Bull is explained, except for the final clause.

### DISPUTATION 392.

### THE TWELFTH CLAUSE.

The twelfth clause holds: "Contracts to be celebrated hereafter under another form, we judge to be usurious; furthermore, notwithstanding those things, we will that whatever happens to be given, remitted, or dismissed—either expressly or tacitly—against these our mandates, may be adjudged by the treasury."

### SUMMARY.

1 The twelfth clause or condition of the Bull of Pius V, with its declarations and effects.
2 Whether an annuity contract celebrated against any of those things disposed in the Bull of Pius V should be judged entirely void, or truly only in that part found against said Bull.
3 The thirteenth and fourteenth clauses, with their dispositions, declarations, and effects (number 4).
5 How annuities created before the Bull of Pius V are to be judged valid regarding the 13th and 14th clauses, even in the Kingdom of Castile.

By this clause, Pius V established penalties for those celebrating annuity contracts under a form other than that which has been handed down so far in this Bull. And in the first place, he pronounces that those contracts are to be judged usurious, and consequently subjects those celebrating them to the penalties of usurers. Then he condemns the contracting parties to the loss, by the very fact <term>ipso facto</term> <note>By the act itself, without need for a separate judicial sentence.</note>, to the treasury of all things which were given, remitted, or dismissed tacitly or expressly against the form handed down; and he grants the treasury the right to claim those things from whoever’s hand or power they have come into. Moreover, when he judges these contracts usurious, you should understand this as a "presumption of law and by law" <term>praesumptio iuris et de iure</term> <note>A legal assumption that cannot be rebutted by evidence.</note>, or rather as "positive usury"...

<column-break/>

...to the effect that the penalties of usurers are incurred just as if they were usurious in themselves from the nature of the thing. For just as a double simony <note>The buying or selling of sacred things or ecclesiastical offices.</note> is distinguished—one from the nature of the thing, staying within the sole limits of natural and divine law, and another "positive," for the effect of incurring the penalties imposed on simoniacs—so also a double usury is to be distinguished after this Bull: one from the nature of the thing, staying within the limits of natural and divine law; the other "positive," introduced by Pius V for the effect of incurring the penalties of usurers. For as is clear from the Bull itself and from what has been said so far, he does not think that all contracts to be celebrated in the future, which he judges here to be usurious, are such by the sole nature of the thing; otherwise, those that had been similarly celebrated before this Bull would also be such by the same definition—the contrary of which the Supreme Pontiff himself clearly intends in the same Bull. Which things from the dispositions in this Bull are of natural law, and which are not, has been explained by us. Secular princes in their kingdoms are held to admit from this Bull only those things whose opposites are against natural law, or are very dangerous to the salvation of souls. However, that an annuity cannot be created except in counted money in the presence of a notary and witnesses, and that it cannot be created from the exchange of a thing—such as a slave, a horse, an estate, or another thing—for an annuity, I do not think they are held to receive. Navarrus disputes this matter copiously in his commentary (Chapter 1, 14, question 3, from number 15).

<margin>Question.</margin>
2 It is a doubt whether, if an annuity contract is celebrated against anything disposed in this Bull, the annuity contract itself should be judged usurious, and therefore void by law; or truly only that part which is found in that contract against the disposition of this Bull. Gutierrez (Book 2 of *Practical Questions*, question 176) judges that only that which is found contrary to the disposition and form of this Bull in the annuity contract should be judged usurious and void, but not the contract itself. [He excepts] numbers 4 and 6, unless some pact added against the disposition of this Bull at the petition of the buyer (or lord of the annuity) were put into execution; for then, he says, the whole contract would fall. Likewise, if the price of the annuity were not paid in counted money before a notary and witnesses; for then he similarly judges the annuity contract itself to be void. I think, however, where <margin>Decision.</margin> this Bull has been received, that whatever is applied against its disposition vitiates the annuity contract and makes it usurious by legal presumption and void. Navarrus seems to feel this in the cited commentary, number 98, although he rightly adds that in this Bull there is only talk of "onerous" contracts <note>Contracts where both parties exchange something of value, such as a sale.</note> of purchase and the exchange of an annuity for a price or some other thing, and it only approves a contract of purchase with the conditions handed down in this Bull. It is not truly speaking in that [Bull] about an annuity established by will, donation, as a dowry, or as a wedding gift; and therefore it is not necessary to observe the conditions prescribed in this Bull for those. Moreover, it can be confirmed that by this Bull, not only the pact added to the annuity contract against its disposition is judged usurious and void, but also the annuity contract itself.

### THE THIRTEENTH CLAUSE,

The thirteenth holds: *Moreover, we wish this health-giving sanction to be observed perpetually and in all things, not only in the creating of a new annuity, but also in the transferring of one already created at any time, provided it was created after the publication of this constitution.*

<margin>3</margin> In this † clause, Pius V established that as long as the annuity was originally created after the publication of this Bull, in transferring it through onerous titles <note>A "title" involves a transfer of property; "onerous" means both parties give something of value (like a sale), as opposed to a gift.</note> (about which we spoke with Navarro in the preceding clause), those things which have been said so far must be observed, just as they must be observed in establishing a new one.

### THE FOURTEENTH CLAUSE,

The fourteenth holds: *They declare that the price once established for an annuity can never be decreased or increased on account of the times, the quality of the contracting parties, or any other accident, nor even with respect to the final contracting parties.*

<margin>4</margin> In this † clause, Pius V established that the price once set for any annuity not only cannot be decreased or increased due to the variety of times or other accidents (from which the prices of things usually vary), but also that the lord of the annuity cannot sell an annuity bought at its price to a third party for a higher price, even if times or other circumstances change; nor can a third party buy it from him for a lower price. And with this clause, Pius V finishes the form for creating annuities in the future.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding † annuities created before this Bull, or those that will be created where it has not been received: it must be said that if a tax <note>A legally fixed rate.</note> on the prices of annuities has not been established in that place, since the prices of annuities do not consist in an indivisible point, it is not illicit for an annuity bought at a lower price to be sold at a higher price

<column-break/>

to a certain third party. Nor likewise is it illegal to buy or redeem it at a lower price by agreement of the parties, when the prices do not exceed the latitude of what is just. These circumstances—from which the natural price of things varies (of which we spoke in Disputation 348, such as when voluntary goods lose value and other factors explained there)—have a place regarding annuities where the prices are not taxed by law, just as they do regarding other things. This clause was established to remove the injustices and oppressions that buyers of annuities usually commit by buying annuities cheaply from those they see pressed by the necessity of money, and reselling the same at a higher price. However, whether Pius V intended to prevent an annuity from being bought and sold at a lower price even when it becomes of less value in itself—for instance, because the property on which the annuity is placed begins to be at risk, or because the installment is paid with difficulty, labor, and expense due to the power of the debtor or some other similar cause—I believe the answer should be in the negative. Because here, an exception should be sought through equity <note>term: <term>epicheia</term> (the interpretation of a law's spirit over its literal wording in specific cases)</note>; if the legislator had been asked whether he intended to include such a case in that law, there is no doubt he would have answered in the negative. And so the doctors commonly affirm that where the price of an annuity is taxed by law (as in this Kingdom of Castile, where the redeemable price of annuities is established), it cannot be less than at the rate of fourteen to one <note>The "14 to 1" ratio means a buyer pays 14 gold/silver pieces to receive 1 piece annually (approx. 7.14% interest).</note>. Nevertheless, it is licit for the reason we just spoke of to buy an annuity for a lower price than the rate of fourteen to one, with nothing hindering the law that taxed the price.

## Whether annuities (especially in this Kingdom of Castile) can be redeemed or bought from previous buyers for a lower price than they were bought. And whether the condition that they cannot be redeemed in parts is lawful. The final clause of the Bull is also added.

### DISPUTATION 394.

#### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *Whether a redeemable annuity in the Kingdom of Castile can be bought for a lower price than the rate of fourteen to one.*
<margin>2</margin> *A perpetual and irredeemable annuity is worth more than a redeemable one.*
<margin>3</margin> *Whether a redeemable annuity, once established, can licitly be bought for a lower price than the rate of fourteen to one.*
<margin>4</margin> *Irredeemable annuities are not included in the Bull of Pius V.*
<margin>5</margin> *Whether the clause or condition that an annuity can be redeemed in parts must necessarily be added to the Bull of Pius V so that a redeemable annuity is not usurious or unjust.*
<margin>6</margin> *For an annuity to be redeemable in parts is as much a burden as when it is redeemed in its entirety.*
<margin>7</margin> *That an annuity can be redeemed in parts does not come from the nature of a buy-back agreement, but must be specifically brought into the agreement.*
<margin>8</margin> *The practice of allowing redeemable annuities to be redeemed even in large parts is not observed in the Spains.*

He also introduces the specific legal standards for the Kingdom of Castile, including the 14-to-1 purchase ratio.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 393.

<margin>1</margin> Indeed, on the occasion of the preceding clause, several matters must be examined in this place. The first, which will open the way to the rest, is: **Whether in this Kingdom it is lawful to purchase a redeemable annuity <term>census redimibilis: a financial contract where a buyer pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment, which the seller can later "buy back" or redeem</term> at a price lower than the ratio of fourteen to one.** 

This matter is disputed by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a celebrated Spanish jurist.</note> in his *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 10, numbers 2 and 3, at a time when there were only three decrees in this Kingdom, which are recorded and established in Book 5, Title 15, Law 4 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* of 1567, a major compilation of Spanish laws.</note>. Some—not very firmly—propose, along with Juan Medina, that this is permitted, as that law does not impede it. They argue that the law only speaks of annuities whose installments <note>original: "pensiones"</note> were not in money, but in wheat, oil, or other things, and specifically that the law required those installments to be reduced to a monetary value at the ratio of fourteen to one in comparison to the price for which the annuity was originally bought. 

Both Juan Medina and Covarruvias judge that the disposition of that law should not be extended to annuities bought from the beginning with a monetary installment, which were customary at that time in many places—specifically in the jurisdiction of Granada—at a ratio of twelve or even ten to one. He mentions that sentences were handed down in the court of Granada in which these annuities were approved, with nothing in that law standing in the way. 

<margin>Decision</margin> However, King Philip <note>Philip II of Spain.</note> later, in the year 1563, passed Law 6, Title 15, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which encompasses all places in Castile. By this law, he decreed that no redeemable annuities could henceforth be sold, imposed, or established at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one. Furthermore, if they were sold or established otherwise, they are null regarding the excess of the higher payment. A penalty was added for notaries <note>original: "tabellionibus"</note> who might draft the instrument of such an annuity or provide a certification of it: the loss of their office. 

Moreover, he established that annuities created before that law at a lower price should be reduced to the ratio of fourteen to one, and by that very act, he reduced them to that price. He added that nothing should stand in the way, even if they had been imposed a long time ago and celebrated in a place or province where it was customary to sell at a lower price. Since this was so decreed by King Philip, and since to this day there is not, nor could there be, a custom to the contrary that would prejudice that law, it must certainly be said that such a practice is illicit today, carrying the burden of restoring the excess of the installments that were received. This very point was added in the Saragossa edition of Covarruvias at the cited number 3 after the third edition; and therefore, some writers today incorrectly call this into doubt, as if the matter could still be considered doubtful today.

If in this Kingdom a property is delivered, valued at, for example, 140 gold coins, and because the buyer does not have the price immediately, an annual redeemable annuity is established on that property (or together with other goods) for more than ten gold coins—so that the payment is greater than the ratio of fourteen to one—the contract is null regarding the excess because of the cited Law 6. For that is the same as buying an annuity at less than the ratio of fourteen to one. This is the view of Gutierrez in his *Practical Questions*, book 2, question 172. 

If, however, a property is delivered in *emphyteusis* <note>A type of long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land.</note> or as a reserved annuity <note>original: "census reservativus": an annuity where the seller of a property keeps the right to an annual payment as part of the sale.</note>, with a certain annual payment established and with a pact that it can be redeemed for less than the ratio of fourteen to one, this pact will not be against the said Law 6, as Gutierrez rightly affirms along with others in the same place.

For just as in a contract of emphyteusis or

<column-break/>

reserved annuity, if the payment is established in produce—such as wheat, wine, or oil—it is not against Law 4 of the same title, nor is it necessary to reduce that payment to a monetary one at the ratio of fourteen to one. This is because in that law, as in the *motu proprio* <note>A document issued by the Pope on his own initiative.</note> of Pius V, mention is only made of a redeemable annuity of consignment <note>original: "census redimibilis consignationis": a standard financial annuity where money is paid for a return.</note>. Thus, the fact that that other payment can be redeemed for less than the ratio of fourteen to one is not against the cited Law 6, in which similarly there is no mention of the contract of emphyteusis or reserved annuity, but only of the monetary and redeemable consignment annuity. 

The only exception would be if the contract was entered into in fraud of that law, with the intention of selling the property for 140 gold coins and delivering them to the buyer of the property as an annuity for a higher payment than the ratio of fourteen to one; and to cloak this, a contract of emphyteusis or reserved annuity was celebrated for that annual payment with a pact of the power to redeem it for 140 gold coins. In that event, the payment would be null regarding the excess of that payment beyond the ratio of fourteen to one, with the burden of restoring the excess of such payment that was received.

<margin>2</margin> At this point, observe that if a contract of emphyteusis or reserved annuity were justly celebrated for a certain annual payment without the power to redeem it, then that payment is worth far more than the ratio of fourteen to one. This is because it is perpetual; and a perpetual and irredeemable annuity is worth more than the ratio of fourteen to one. Add to this that in an emphyteutic contract, by the very fact that it is granted that the payment may be redeemed for a certain price, not only is the right to that payment sold for that price, but also the "direct ownership" <note>original: "directum dominium": the underlying legal title held by the lord, as opposed to the "useful ownership" held by the tenant.</note>, which remained with the seller along with the right to the payment, and which is extinguished when the payment is redeemed. Therefore, that payment is worth more than if it were an irredeemable consignment annuity. 

From this, you will easily understand that in the redemption of such a payment for a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one, there is no imminent danger of injustice against the one buying or redeeming that payment for that price. This is unlike when a redeemable annuity is bought at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one, where there is a danger of injustice against the seller of the annuity. For that reason, it is prohibited in this Kingdom to buy one for a price lower than the ratio of fourteen to one.

<margin>3 Doubt</margin> There is a doubt whether in this Kingdom, notwithstanding the cited Law 6, an annuity—after it has <note>The cross (†) indicates a point of debate or a specific reference in the text.</note> once been established—can be lawfully bought for a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one. Some, whom Gutierrez refers to in *Practical Questions*, book 2, question 173, affirm and respond that it can. For they judge that the law is only to be understood as applying to the *first* purchase of a redeemable annuity.

In order to submit our own opinion, it must be observed: although a redeemable annuity in this Kingdom, after that law, cannot lawfully be bought for a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one, it can nevertheless be lawfully sold for a *higher* price. It often happens in practice that it is sold for a higher price, namely at a ratio of fifteen or sixteen to one. The reason is that the law was passed solely in favor of the seller, so that the annuity could not be bought from him at a lower price...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral examination of annuities (census) within the Kingdom of Castile, focusing on the price limits (the "ratio") and the conditions under which these financial instruments can be sold or redeemed. ...than at the ratio of fourteen to one <note>The "ratio" refers to the purchase price relative to the annual payment. At 14:1, an annual payment of 1 gold piece would cost 14 gold pieces to purchase—an effective interest rate of roughly 7.1%.</note>, he himself might be able to sell it at a higher price if he finds a buyer. Indeed, it sometimes happens that a higher price is found because there are many buyers of annuities and few sellers, or because the annuity being sold is very secure and in a location more convenient for the buyer, so it is bought at a higher price with less risk, because it may be quickly and easily redeemed.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
This being established, it must be said: Although, if a redeemable annuity was bought at a price higher than the ratio of fourteen to one, it may lawfully be bought afterward at the ratio of fourteen to one—since this does not deviate from the price established by Law 6—it is nevertheless a crime <note>original: "nefas"</note> in this Kingdom to buy a redeemable annuity a second or third time at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one. Rather, the contract is null regarding the excess of the installment <note>original: "pensionis"</note>, with the burden of restoring it if it is accepted. This is held by many whom Gutierrez cites and follows in the place mentioned.

This can be proved. First, because in that Law 6 (as we related above), you have it that an annuity cannot be sold at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one. Moreover, the sale of an annuity that occurs a second or third time is truly a sale of an annuity; therefore, it can be done neither a second nor a third time at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one. Second, because that law commands that annuities previously sold at a lower price be reduced to the ratio of fourteen to one; therefore, it does not permit any annuity to be sold henceforth at a lower price than the ratio of fourteen to one, even if it had been established previously.

Thirdly, because by the very fact that the price of grain or any other thing is fixed <note>original: "taxatum"</note>, it is a crime to sell that thing a second or third time at a higher price; therefore, the same will apply to a redeemable annuity. Nor is it to be doubted that if the legislator, while founding that law, were asked whether he left it free to buy an annuity at a lower price once it had been established at that price, he would have answered in the negative—especially since an annuity has no less value when it is sold a second or third time than when it is sold the first time. This same point is confirmed by the clause of Pius V <note>Pope Pius V, referring to the Bull *Cum onus* (1569), which sought to regulate these contracts to prevent usury.</note> regarding which we are examining these matters, which decreed that the price once established for an annuity can neither be increased nor diminished, even by the most recent contracting parties. Wherefore, if this Bull had been received in this Kingdom, it would be a crime <margin>†</margin> because of this clause to buy a redeemable annuity at the ratio of fourteen to one that had already been sold at a ratio of fifteen or sixteen to one. However, it has not been received here.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding redeemable annuities bought in this Kingdom at the ratio of thirty to one, or at any other price, it must be said that they can lawfully be bought afterward at a lower price, provided that, considering the concurrent circumstances and the manner of selling, the limits of justice are not exceeded. The reason is that no price is fixed by law for this specific annuity in this Kingdom, nor does the *motu proprio* <note>A type of papal document issued on the Pope's own initiative.</note> of Pius V speak of this annuity, as shown in Disputation 390. Read on this matter Navarrus in his commentary, chapter 1, question 3, number 112.

<margin>Question 5</margin>
Since Pius V in this entire Bull makes no mention of the condition that an annuity might be

<column-break/>

partially redeemed <note>original: "pro parte redimi"; the right of the debtor to pay back the principal in installments rather than all at once.</note>, it is doubted whether that condition is necessary so that a redeemable annuity is not usurious or at least unjust. All agree that if the price of the annuity is increased enough to compensate for the burden of not being able to redeem the annuity in parts (but only as a whole), the contract is neither usurious nor unjust. Thus says Soto, *On Justice*, book 6, question 5, article 3; Navarrus in his commentary; and others whom Gutierrez refers to and follows. Gutierrez, however, judges that in this Kingdom a contract for a redeemable annuity at the ratio of fourteen to one is unjust if it includes a pact that the annuity cannot be redeemed in parts, but that an annuity with such a pact ought to be bought at the ratio of fifteen or sixteen to one.

Furthermore, if that pact is added and the price is not increased, should the contract be called usurious, or merely unjust because it is unequal, yet without the vice of usury? Navarrus, in the place cited above, thinks it should be called usurious. Soto, however, whom Gutierrez and others follow, thinks it lacks the vice of usury and is only unjust because it is unequal.

I, along with Lord Francisco Sarmiento and others, judge that it should be said: A redeemable annuity is no more "by the nature of the thing" redeemable in parts than other things which are enumerated with a <margin>Decision.</margin> pact of repurchase <term>pactum de retrouendendo: a legal clause allowing a seller to buy back the property or right they sold</term>. Regarding those other things, everyone agrees that unless it is specifically stated in the pact that they can be redeemed in parts, they cannot be redeemed except all at once.

<margin>6</margin>
I confess † indeed that an annuity is more suited by its nature to be redeemed in parts than other things are, but what I deny is that it is inherent by the nature of the thing in an annuity contract (if celebrated with a pact of repurchase) that it is within the power of the seller to redeem it in parts, excluding the custom of the place. Rather, I judge that, excluding a contrary custom, it is not in the power of the seller to redeem it in parts unless it is specified in the pact.

<margin>7</margin>
Wherefore, just as it would be a burden † on the buyer of other things with a pact of repurchase if it were specified in the pact that they could be redeemed in parts—and they would be worth less with that pact than if sold absolutely—for that reason, the price should be reduced from the otherwise just price. So too, the fact that an annuity can be redeemed in parts is a burden to the one buying it, although a smaller one than the ability to redeem other things in parts. Consequently, an annuity with that burden is worth somewhat less than if it were sold absolutely with only a pact of repurchase. Our opinion can be confirmed: first, because no legitimate reason can be given why one sale with a pact of repurchase should have, by the nature of the thing and excluding other pacts or local custom, one of these qualities while another does not. Second, because when an annuity is sold with a pact of repurchase, what is sold is not the installments themselves materially—that is, the money to be paid every year—but the right <note>original: "ius"</note> to receive them from the property in which the annuity is placed. Such a right is a certain whole, having fewer "parts" in comparison to the breadth of the installment to be paid than do estates and other things which with a pact...
