Second Treatise | Disputation 393.

...bought with a <term>right of repurchase</term> <note>original: "pacto de retrovendendo"; a clause allowing the seller to buy back the asset or cancel the annuity by returning the principal</note>; therefore, it is no more inherent to the nature of an annuity bought with a right of repurchase—setting aside other agreements and customs—that the seller has the power to redeem it in parts, than it is in any other things sold in a similar way.

Thirdly, because just as it is a burden to the buyer for an annuity to be sold with a right of repurchase (and for that reason an annuity with such a right is worth less than one without it), so too is it a burden to the same buyer if it can additionally be redeemed in parts. It is worth even less with that burden than with the simple right of repurchase. 
<margin>Distinction 3</margin> Indeed, a person will buy the right to an annual pension much less willingly if there is a clause allowing it to be redeemed in parts—even large ones like a half, a third, a fourth, or a fifth—than without that burden. 
<margin>30</margin> This is because money returning to him in installments is less useful for buying estates or other sources of income, and it is more easily spent than if it were received all at once. Furthermore, small returns, which must be collected from various sources, are less useful and very troublesome. However, with a clause stating that the annuity can be redeemed in any parts whatsoever, even the smallest—such as redeeming individual gold coins of the pension one by one—there is a far greater burden, which greatly reduces the price. 
<margin>Soto</margin> A seller of an annuity will hardly find anyone willing to buy it with such a burden. The doctors with whom we are disputing affirm that it is not within the power of the seller to redeem an annuity with a right of repurchase in such tiny parts, but only in large ones, such as thirds or fourths. Consequently, they must confess that it is not inherent in the nature of an annuity contract sold with a right of repurchase that it can be redeemed in tiny parts; rather, an express additional agreement is necessary for that power.

If a contract for an annuity sold with a right of repurchase does not, by its nature, allow for redemption in tiny parts (excluding specific agreements and custom), then surely it does not allow for redemption in larger parts by its nature either. Instead, custom (according to which the contract is understood to be celebrated) or an express agreement is necessary for that. Add to this—as was assumed regarding how the right of repurchase in an annuity contract is a burden to the buyer—that the ability to redeem in parts is another added burden to the same buyer. 
<margin>to 2.</margin> Burdens that are not inherent to the nature of buying and selling are not considered owed unless they are brought into the agreement or accepted by custom; and unless they are considered tacitly included in the agreement. Just as the fact that an annuity *can* be redeemed is not inherent in the nature of the contract, but requires an agreement to exist, so too the fact that it can be redeemed in parts (whether large or small) is not inherent to the contract; it must be included in the agreement, either tacitly or expressly.

<margin>8</margin> In Spain, however, there is no custom that annuities redeemable in parts, even large ones, are actually redeemed that way; they are redeemed all at once. If sometimes, rarely, an annuity has been redeemed in parts without an express agreement allowing it, this was surely done with the free consent of the owner of the annuity, or certainly with the consent of those doctors

<column-break/>

of the contrary opinion, claiming he is bound to consent. That opinion, however, seems to have had its origin in the <term>Extravagantes</term> <note>A term for Papal decrees that circulated "outside" the official primary collections of Canon Law</note> of Martin V and Calixtus III, insofar as it is proposed in them that the annuities with a right of repurchase discussed and approved there were celebrated with the condition, among others, that they could be redeemed in parts.

However, from the fact that those were celebrated in that way, it is not correctly inferred that all *must* be celebrated so, or that they are otherwise unjust, or that it is a necessary condition for contracts with a right of repurchase to be lawfully celebrated, as Miranda and Navarrus <note>referring to Martín de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canonist</note> conclude. For as was said before, because the contracts proposed in those decrees—celebrated with those conditions and agreements—are approved, it does not follow that others celebrated differently are condemned in those same decrees. And in the matter proposed, it does not follow that all those conditions are inherent to the nature of the contract with a right of repurchase, or that there is a universal custom for them to be celebrated in the same way. Indeed, the fact that Pius V did not mention that condition is a manifest sign that it is not necessary for the contract to be just.

From what has been said, I infer that what Gutierrez affirms is false: namely, that it is unjust in this Kingdom to have an annuity with a right of repurchase at the ratio of fourteen to one if it is explicitly stated that the annuity cannot be redeemed in parts. For since the contract has this by its nature, stating it does not increase the price of the annuity; nor, if it did increase it, would it be such a burden that it ought to increase the price by one above fourteen, let alone two. Rather, if an agreement were made that it *could* be redeemed in parts, that ought to *decrease* the price from the ratio of fourteen to one fixed by law. This is because, as has been shown, that is a burden on the buyer, which by its nature reduces the price of an otherwise just annuity, just as the right of repurchase itself reduces it.

### THE LAST CLAUSE.

Finally, the clause states:
> And although we do not extend this law
> -> to contracts already celebrated, <-
> we nevertheless exhort in the Lord all those into whose hands annuities have come under another form, to subject their individual annuity contracts to the rules governing the property of religious orders, and to look to the salvation of their souls. Notwithstanding etc. Given at Rome in the year 1568, on the 14th day before the Kalends of February <note>January 19, 1568</note>.

This clause is clear enough and needs no explanation.

# Louis de Molina: On Contracts #

<margin>Question 1</margin>
1 **T**he first doubt is: whether—notwithstanding the Bull of Pius V <note>A 1566 papal decree, *Cum onus*, which strictly regulated annuities to prevent them from being used as a cover for usury</note>—when someone is legally sentenced to pay a sum of money but cannot pay it immediately, they can be sentenced under a "disjunction" <note>An "either/or" ruling</note> to either pay that sum or to pay an annual annuity in the meantime until it is paid. Navarrus (in commentary chapter 1, title 4, question 3, n. 99) says this is customary in this Kingdom of Castile. Navarrus (ibid. n. 101) affirms it is a matter of faith, provided that it is issued as compensation for the profit the creditor loses because the money is not paid immediately, and as a just penalty for the debtor's "contumacy" <note>Legal jargon for a stubborn refusal to obey a court order</note>. The reasoning is that the Bull of Pius V is only understood to apply to annuities created by contract and the agreement of parties, not to those created by other just titles—among which is the just sentence of a judge. An exception is made if the debt consisted of goods determined by weight, number, or measure.

<margin>Decision</margin>
However, I consider it irrelevant where the sum of money comes from, as long as it is truly owed; otherwise, there would be fraud and deceit. Although a penalty agreed upon at the time of a contract is more suspect when something is owed in goods of weight, number, or measure than when it is owed from other things, this penalty we are discussing is not a "conventional" (agreed) penalty, but a judicial one. It arises from money truly owed and not paid in its proper time. After the money is already owed, if a judge enjoins the debtor under a disjunction to either pay or yield an annual annuity—due to the penalty for contumacy for not paying and the interest lost by the creditor due to the delay—it is irrelevant how the debt originated. Yet the judge must take care that no simulation <note>A legal sham or pretense</note> occurs between the parties to create a personal annuity (which would be illicit) or one without the necessary conditions for lawfulness. Furthermore, it should be added that the Bull of Pius V has not been formally accepted in this kingdom.

<margin>Question 2</margin>
2 **T**he second question is whether a person who has sold an <term>†</term> annuity can give part of the price to a third party on the condition that the third party pays the portion of the pension that corresponds to that part of the price. Navarrus (in the place cited, number 113) answers in the negative. I believe, however, that the answer should be affirmative. This is especially true even in Navarrus’s own opinion, as he believes an annuity can be redeemed in parts. Since the seller of the annuity could have used that part of the price he hands over to another to redeem part of the annuity, he certainly grants a benefit to the other person by giving him that part of the price with the same burden with which he himself received it, while leaving the annuity secured upon his own assets.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Add to this that because of the loss emerging for himself from not redeeming part of the annuity with that money,

<column-break/>

this is licit: especially since the seller of the annuity derives no profit from it. From the beginning, when he sold the annuity, he could have sold half so that he himself would pay it, and the other half so that it would be paid by someone else who needed that money, placing the entire annuity on some property of his own. This is to confer a benefit on that other person without any profit of his own; in this, neither usury nor any other injustice is seen. However, when the person who sold the annuity has idle money and it is not permitted for him to redeem part of the annuity, then it would indeed be usury to hand that money over to another person in need with the burden of paying part of the annuity. Perhaps Navarrus is speaking only of this specific event.

<margin>Doubt 3</margin>
3 Third: if the property in which the <term>†</term> annuity was placed was, for example, a house, and that house collapses or is burned down, and another similar house is erected again on the same plot, is the annuity still owed? Following Navarrus in the cited place (number 118), the answer is that it is not owed. Since the specific thing in which the annuity is placed has perished, the annuity perishes entirely. Even though the ground of the house remains, it is simply true to say the "house" has perished. However, when the thing in which the annuity was placed perishes through the fault of the debtor, he is bound to place it on another thing of equal value, or he is bound to pay the value of the annuity.
<margin>Decision</margin>

<margin>Doubt 4</margin>
4 Fourth: if an <term>†</term> annuity is bought on a property that is not "free"—that is, one in which an annuity could not be placed because it was tied to an entail <note>original: "maioratus"; a legal arrangement where property is kept within a family line and cannot be sold or burdened</note>, or it belonged to someone else, or for some other similar reason—are the pensions licitly received? For this, one must distinguish, as Navarrus does above (number 118): either the buyer of the annuity knew the property was such that an annuity could not be placed on it, or he was ignorant of it. In the latter case, he licitly receives the pensions as long as that ignorance persists, nor is he bound to count them toward the principal price; this is true whether or not the seller of the annuity knew the property was incapable of supporting that annuity. The reason is that the buyer received them in good faith, and they were owed to him by virtue of the contract of purchase. But if the seller was aware that the property was incapable of supporting the annuity, fraud has entered the contract (according to the discussions in 352 and 353), and he will be bound to reveal the defect; his fraud should not protect him such that he is exempt from paying pensions during that time.
<margin>Decision</margin>

<margin>Law of Castile</margin>
5 Fifth: In this Kingdom, even if a property is not entailed and is the seller's own property, if it was nevertheless burdened by other prior annuities or taxes and the seller did not disclose this to the buyer, the seller is punished by the loss of double the price he received for the annuity. He is also forced to secure the annuity again on safe property so that the annuity may be paid from it. This is held in Law 2, Title 15, Book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collect."; the *Nueva Recopilación*, a major compilation of Spanish laws published in 1567</note>. Furthermore, in the following Law 3, to avoid the lawsuits that often arise from the concealment of burdens on properties where annuities are placed, it is established that in every place that is a seat of jurisdiction, a person should be appointed to keep a book. In this book, a catalog should be made of all contracts by which a burden of mortgage, annuity, or tax is imposed on property. Those entering such contracts are bound to ensure they are written in this book within six days of the contract's celebration, under the penalty that if made otherwise, they shall not be considered evidence, nor...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 394 #

...nor should they be judged according to those registers, nor should a third-party possessor of those things be held to any prior burden.

It is further commanded that this register <note>original: "libellum"</note> should not be shown openly. Instead, the person whose duty it is to record these contracts in a catalog must provide a certification as to whether the property to be sold (or on which a burden is to be placed) has any existing burden; this is done at the request of the person selling the property or placing a burden upon it. Gutierrez (cited in *Practical Questions*, book 2, question 9, decision 169) says that the provision of this third law was never actually put into execution. Therefore, as long as no official is appointed to hold that office, that law does not bind the conscience.

However, suppose the seller of an annuity <note>original: "census"; a financial arrangement where a capital sum is paid in exchange for an annual income secured by property</note> was unaware at the time of the sale that the property on which the annuity was placed was "incapable" of supporting it. In that case, the buyer of the annuity nonetheless justly receives the annual payments <note>original: "pensiones"</note>, and these are not to be counted as part of the principal price for as long as the buyer himself remained unaware of the defect. This is because the seller of the annuity is liable for "eviction" <note>original: "de evictione"; a legal guarantee that the seller has the right to sell and the property is free of hidden claims</note> as soon as it is discovered the property was not capable of supporting the burden. Thus, the seller is liable for damages to the buyer, according to what was said in Disputation 380. But when an annuity is redeemable <note>can be paid off by the debtor to end the obligation</note>, since it is in the seller's power to redeem it whenever they wish, the full damages are sufficiently paid if, beyond all the payments due from the annuity up to that point, the entire principal price is restored, or the annuity is relocated to property that is equally good and secure.

On the other hand, when the annuity is irredeemable <note>a perpetual obligation</note>, in addition to the payments due up to that point, the seller of the annuity should be compelled to relocate it to another property that is good and secure, if they have one and the buyer chooses it. If that cannot be done, the seller should be compelled to pay the full and just price of such an annuity, as that would constitute the full damages. In the first scenario, however—where the buyer of the annuity *knew* that the property was of such a nature that an annuity could not be placed upon it—it must be said that they cannot accept those annual payments; if they do accept them, they are bound to count them as part of the principal price paid.

The reason is that in such an instance, the guarantee against eviction does not apply, as we showed in Disputation 380. This is because such an annuity does not truly exist as a "thing"; and since it does not exist, there can be no income from it. Therefore, income cannot be justly perceived by one who was aware the annuity did not exist. If such payments are taken, they are subject to restitution. Indeed, if it is established in a secular court that they were perceived in this way, the one who accepted them shall be punished with the penalties for usurers, as Navarrus affirms (cited above, n. 119); for in that case, there is no title by which they are received other than by way of a loan <note>Under Catholic canon law of this period, charging interest on a simple loan (mutuum) was considered the sin of usury, whereas an annuity was a legitimate sale of future income</note>.

<margin>Question 6</margin>
Conversely, if a property on which an annuity was legally placed is sold to someone without disclosing that the property carries such a "real burden" <note>a legal claim attached to the land itself</note>, it is doubted whether the buyer, upon discovering the burden, can rescind the sale. The side that argues "yes" can be supported by the fact that a property with such a burden is considered defective <note>original: "vitiosa"</note>, no differently than if it had a hidden easement <note>original: "servitutem"; a right for someone else to use the land, like a path</note>. A person who sells property knowing it has an easement without disclosing it is considered to be knowingly selling a defective thing without revealing the defect; thus, the buyer can rescind the contract once the easement is discovered. If the seller unknowingly sells property with an easement, the buyer is granted an action for a "price reduction" <note>original: "actio quanto minoris"; a legal claim to refund part of the price because the item was worth less than advertised</note>

<column-break/>

against the seller, as was shown in Disputation 353. Therefore, the same should apply in the case proposed here.

It must be stated, following Gutierrez (*Practical Questions*, book 2, question 9, decision 169): First, the seller of that property does not fall under the penalty of the second law, title 15, book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a 1567 compilation of Spanish laws</note>. This is because that law only establishes a penalty for the seller of an *annuity* on a property already burdened by another annuity or tax without disclosing that burden. Penalties should not be extended to different cases, even if it might seem more reasonable to establish them in that other case.

Next, it must be said that if the annuity is redeemable, the buyer cannot sue to dissolve the contract, nor can they use the action for a price reduction. Instead, they can only sue to have the annuity redeemed and the payments due from it paid. Once that is done (which is within the seller's power), the property will remain free from that annuity and thus free from the defect. When a defect is such that it is within the power of the seller to remove it, the rules mentioned in the cited disputation do not apply; rather, the seller must be compelled to remove the defect or flaw. Meanwhile, as long as the annuity is not removed, the buyer may withhold the price if they have not yet paid it.

All of this is confirmed because when a property is sold that was specifically subject to a mortgage <note>original: "hypothecae"</note>, and that real burden is later discovered, one cannot sue for the rescission of the sale. Instead, one sues to have the property cleared of that burden by the seller, if it is within their power. This is clearly gathered from the law *Ex praediis* in the Code under the title *On Eviction*, and is noted there by the Gloss, Bartolus, and others whom Gutierrez refers to above. However, if the annuity were irredeemable, the arguments for the affirmative side would hold weight.

<margin>7th Doubt</margin>
The fifth doubt <note>Molina's numbering of specific doubts within the disputation</note> is whether, in places where the Bull of Pius V is accepted—even though it is forbidden to *buy* an annuity except with ready cash—it is nevertheless lawful to *redeem* and extinguish it using other goods that the owner of the annuity is satisfied with in place of money. One must respond with Navarrus (*Commentary*, chapter 1, decision 14, question 3, n. 123) that this is licit. This is because that Bull only speaks of the *purchase* of an annuity, and since it deviates from common law, it should not be extended to redemption. Certainly, that was not the intention of Pius V.

Furthermore, in the extinction of an annuity, there was no danger of using that method to cloak usury or commit injustice, as there is in its purchase. Moreover, that Bull aimed to decrease and extinguish annuities. Navarrus adds in the same place that an annuity can also be extinguished by "compensation" <note>offsetting</note> for an equal, liquidated debt that the owner of the annuity owes to the debtor of the annuity. This can happen not only by mutual consent but even if the owner of the annuity refuses, provided the debtor petitions a judge or protests before witnesses that they wish to redeem the annuity with that equal debt and will no longer be held to pay the annual installments. However, simply because an amount equal to the price of the annuity is owed in that manner, the annuity is not considered redeemed unless the debtor of the annuity petitions for it or protests, as Navarrus rightly adds in the same place, n. 125.

<margin>8th Doubt</margin>
Sixth, whether, if the Bull of Pius V is accepted anywhere—even regarding the clause stating that in the sale of property subject to an annuity, the owner of the annuity is preferred over others—is that owner to be preferred even over those who have a "right of retraction" <note>original: "ius retractus"; the legal right of certain people, like family or co-owners, to step in and buy property for the same price offered by a stranger</note> by reason of co-ownership of the same property, or by reason of kinship? Such a right of retraction exists in this...

The reason is that the grace and privilege granted to the lord of an annuity <term>census: a financial arrangement where an investor provides capital in exchange for a yearly return secured by property</term> in this Papal Bull neither removes nor hinders prior graces and privileges granted earlier. ### Concerning annuities celebrated many months after the Bull of Pius V was issued in Rome, but without the conditions contained in it, in dioceses where it was not published and was commonly ignored: what should be judged.

## DISPUTATION 395.

### SUMMARY.

1. Laws and canons bind everyone, even those who are ignorant of them, in every province after two months from the day of their publication.
2. Indeed, a law would have force after two months from publication even to the point of rendering contracts invalid. However, this must be fully declared and understood as in number 4.
3. Annuity contracts celebrated many months after the publication of the Bull of Pius V by those ignorant of it: when they are valid.
5. A contract celebrated before two months have passed since the publication of a law that invalidates such contracts, by someone who has notice of it: when it is null, even in the "forum of conscience" <note>The internal moral judgement of an individual before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note>. And what is the case regarding Portuguese law, number 6.

After many months, and indeed after several years from the day the Bull of Pius V <note>The Bull *Cum onus* (1569), which set strict rules to ensure annuities were not used as a cover for usury.</note> was published in Rome, many annuity contracts were celebrated in a certain diocese of Portugal. These included a "pact of redemption" <note>An agreement allowing the borrower to buy back the annuity and clear the debt.</note> but lacked the specific conditions prescribed in that Bull for such contracts to be licit and valid. At that time, in that diocese, the Bull had not only not been published, but was also commonly unknown, and there was no one who raised any moral scruple regarding those contracts.

Nevertheless, such contracts were of a kind that—setting aside the Bull of Pius V and looking only at the nature of the thing—they were valid. This was true even if, in some cases in the forum of conscience, it might have been necessary to reduce the burden on the seller of the annuity or increase the price at which the annuities had been bought. Lawsuits regarding these contracts began to be moved in the Ecclesiastical court, with the debtors of the annuities contending that the contracts were null because they were celebrated contrary to the Bull of Pius V. They argued that the payments already received should be returned and counted as part of the principal price given for those annuities.

<column-break/>

Various learned men were consulted on this matter. Many affirmed that contracts celebrated after two months from the publication in Rome were null, and that the common ignorance of that Bull in that diocese was no obstacle. They argued that even if they were celebrated in good faith, the payments accepted from those annuities must be returned or counted toward the principal price.

Indeed, this can be argued as follows: regarding common law, just as the laws of Emperors and Kings have force so that ignorance of them is not presumed—and so that the ignorance of the contracting parties is no obstacle to rendering contracts null—it is required that in the Court and Metropolis of the Kingdom, two months pass from the day of publication. In the remaining provinces subject to that same Kingdom and Metropolis, however, it is required that two months pass from the publication made in each one of them (as held in the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's legal "Novels."</note>, regarding "how constitutions are made," collation 5, constitution 1). Nevertheless, the common opinion of the doctors is that for the laws of the Supreme Pontiff to have that force in the whole Church and to render contracts invalid, it is enough if two months pass from the publication made in Rome, as many affirm. A peculiar publication in every single Metropolis or diocese is not necessary. They argue this:

First, from the distinction between the Church and a Kingdom that has many provinces or sub-kingdoms. For the Church is a unique spiritual Republic; whereas many kingdoms subject to the same King are many republics depending on one principal one to which they are subjected. Therefore, while different publications are required in distinct provinces because the Republics are different, and in each of them one publication suffices for everyone in that province (even if they belong to different towns or cities), so in the Church, for papal laws to have force after two months, one solemn publication performed in the Roman Court will suffice.

Second, because perhaps no constitution of the Supreme Pontiff among those inserted into the body of the law was published in every single province or diocese. Therefore, if it were necessary for a law to be published in each province for it to bind them, no law would bind the entire Church—which is in no way to be affirmed.

Third, because Pius IV, in the Bull concerning the declaration of the time for observing the decrees of the Council of Trent, referring to the fact that it is established in common law that new constitutions do not obtain force except after a certain time, says: "Just as we have judged it to meet reason, law, and equity, we have seen fit to declare that the decrees pertaining to reformation and positive law began to bind everyone from the Kalends of May, and after that day no one’s excuse that they were ignorant of them is to be admitted." Yet they were published in Rome and began to be observed in Rome at the end of January. He adds that if anything was judged to the contrary, it should be null and void. See, he designates only three months after the publication...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of contract validity, specifically debating when a Papal law becomes binding on the public. It transitions from a general discussion of local privileges to the specific legal timeline of the Bull of Pius V regarding annuities.</meta>

Tract. Secund. Disp. 395. 383.

...publication made in Rome, requiring no other publication in particular dioceses; however, it seems to designate that increase [of time] beyond two months because of the delay in printing and sending the Council's decrees to the provinces, a delay which he mentions in the same bull.

<margin>2 †</margin> From these points, the following argument is drawn: The laws of the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> have force even to render contracts invalid after two months from the publication made in Rome. It does not matter if they were not published in particular dioceses, or that the contracting parties suffer from invincible ignorance <note>Ignorance that cannot be overcome by ordinary care; in legal terms, it often excuses a person from guilt but not necessarily from the civil effects of a law.</note> of those laws. Therefore, although invincible ignorance of the Bull of Pius V <note>Pope Pius V issued the bull *Cum onere* in 1569 to regulate "census" (annuities) and curb usury.</note> might excuse those who celebrated annuity contracts after two months from the Roman publication from guilt and penalties, the contracts are nonetheless void by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>. Consequently, the buyers of the annuities are bound to restore the payments <note>original: "pensiones"</note> they received through those contracts, as they were received under a title that was legally null.

At this point, observe what is said: namely, that two months from the day of publication are necessary for the laws of the Supreme Pontiff (or other princes) to have the force to invalidate contracts and render other things void, regardless of the ignorance of the parties or any other factor. This is generally limited by the doctors [of law] to mean: unless something else is specifically arranged in those same laws. If, for instance, more time is granted from the day of publication, or less, or if it is stated that they begin to take effect from the moment they are published, one must abide by their specific provisions. Thus say Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canonist.</note> and Felinus <note>Felinus Sandeus (1444–1503), another influential canonist.</note> on the second book of "De constitutionibus," and the doctors commonly.

<margin>3</margin> I think, however, that the contrary should be affirmed, even where the Bull of Pius V is fully accepted. Namely, that those contracts celebrated in a diocese by those in ignorance are valid, and the buyers of the annuities are not bound to restore the payments or count them toward the principal price. I am led to this:

First and most importantly, because—whatever may be said of the Supreme Pontiff’s rulings regarding matters whose administration and disposal belong to him without injury to anyone (such as the granting of church benefices)—in other rulings where something is rendered void for the common good, such an annulment would result in injury to those performing the act unless the law were first properly promulgated <note>Officially proclaimed or made known.</note> to them and sufficient time granted in which it could reach everyone's knowledge. Certainly, the Supreme Pontiff would not be doing well if, to the injury of his subjects, he wished to render something void by law before it was promulgated to them in their own provinces and dioceses, allowing them a competent amount of time in which knowledge of it could normally arrive. Since, therefore, the annulment of the contracts we are now debating results in injury to those celebrating them (unless it could first sufficiently reach their knowledge, as I will soon show), and since it should not be presumed that the Supreme Pontiff intends his laws to contain anything unreasonable or to bind his subjects to their own injury, it must surely be said that the mind of Pius V was that the bull he issued should not render contracts void—

<column-break/>

—otherwise lawful by the nature of the thing, and void in relation to those celebrating them in ignorance, until it was effectively promulgated in each individual diocese or could have reached the knowledge of all by some other way.

Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and theologian.</note> agrees with us in his book *On Justice*, question 1, article 4, asserting that similar laws of the Supreme Pontiff ought not to bind in any province before they are promulgated there; because otherwise, they would be full of dangers, and for that reason, he says it must be judged that this is the mind of the Supreme Pontiff.

He rightly affirms the same consistently regarding laws that take away the privilege of granting absolution; for it is not to be believed that the Supreme Pontiff intends to render void sacramental absolutions performed according to those privileges before such laws are sufficiently promulgated in each diocese. This would be unreasonable and a great burden to the faithful. Furthermore, the Council of Trent <note>The major Catholic reform council held between 1545 and 1563.</note> in Session 24, chapter 1 "on reform," while rendering clandestine marriage void, saw that this could result in grave injury to those who might celebrate it while ignorant that it had been made null. Therefore, the Council did not want that law to have force in any parish except thirty days after the publication of the decree in that same parish. Moreover, it is clear enough that the annulment of the contracts we are speaking of would result in injury to those celebrating them unless it could first sufficiently come to their knowledge.

For they would celebrate a contract that is lawful by the nature of the thing, and they would hand over a price [the principal] while ceasing to gain some other profit or incurring a loss [of opportunity] greater than the payments they received; and nonetheless, they would be forced to restore those payments (otherwise lawfully accepted) and receive only the bare price which the sellers of the annuities had enjoyed the whole time. It is clear that this results in their injury.

For the sellers of the annuities would not be held liable to them for that lost profit or emerging loss, as if they could compensate for it from the payments; since they would not be held to it on account of the thing received (since the buyer’s lost profit or loss is not something that passed to the sellers), nor would they be held to it on account of an unjust acceptance, given that they did not sin, but acted in good faith in celebrating those contracts with them.

<margin>4</margin> Secondly, I am led [to this conclusion] because that opinion—that Papal laws bind the whole Church immediately after two months from their publication in Rome, and that their publication in individual provinces or dioceses is not necessary to ensure that no one is presumed to be invincibly ignorant of them and that what they annul is invalid—is certainly not as certain as is usually assumed. Rather, in my judgment, the contrary opinion is more probable.

For as Panormitanus, Felinus (on chapter 3 "De constitutionibus"), and others argue: since Civil Law <note>The Roman Law tradition.</note> establishes two months from the publication made in each province before what the Prince's law annuls is judged invalid there (as is clear from the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's 'Novels' or new laws.</note> regarding the "new constitutions," which speaks expressly of a law annulling a will due to a lack of formalities), and since Canon Law has established nothing to the contrary, one must surely abide by the Civil Law in this matter...

Molina argues that laws should not be binding to the point of causing injury to people acting in good faith until they have been properly proclaimed in their specific diocese.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

### Page 384

[Column 1]

...it will be unique to that provision of the civil law: for when canon law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership.</note> establishes nothing, one must recur to the provision of civil law <note>The secular legal system, primarily based on Roman Law (Justinian's Code).</note> in the ecclesiastical court; and one must stand by it, as is clear from chapter 1 *concerning the announcement of a new work* <note>original: "de noui oper. nunc." refers to a title in the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note> and from other laws. Nor is that distinction of any value—that the entire Church is a single Republic, while diverse provinces subject to the same principal Kingdom are diverse Republics.

Indeed, the reason why in the cited *Authentic* <note>The *Authentica* or *Novels* of the Emperor Justinian, which were later additions to Roman Law.</note> two months from publication were judged sufficient so that, regularly, no one could claim ignorance of the law—and thus, so that the law, without injury to anyone, might annul wills after that time due to a defect of formality, or contracts for that or another cause—is that the law was to be published throughout individual provinces. That time was judged competent so that, after publication in each of them, notice of the law could regularly reach everyone. But if the entire Roman Empire, then widely diffused throughout the world, were a single temporal Republic in the same way the whole Church is, certainly a time of only two months from the day of publication made in the imperial court would not be prescribed for the whole world to be deemed not to have ignorance of that law, or for wills or contracts to be deemed void due to a defect of formality or other causes that moved the legislators. For it would be unreasonable, because in such a short time notice of the law could not reach the whole empire and its individual towns and persons. Hence, heirs appointed in a less formal will would rightly recur to the imperial court and propose that the testator, through just ignorance of the law, had so appointed them heirs, and that it was unworthy for the testator's will to be shattered without his own fault. Many did recur and obtain the inheritance before that *Authentic* was established, with nothing in the law preventing it by voiding the will; and for that reason, that *Authentic* was established, as is clear from its own text. Therefore, since the Church is as widely diffused throughout the world as the Roman Empire was then, and is divided into Metropolises and dioceses just as the empire was divided into provinces, and since Pontifical laws derived from the Roman court are accustomed to be promulgated to Patriarchates, Metropolises, and dioceses (or in a certain order through Patriarchs, Archbishops, and Bishops by order of the Supreme Pontiff, as is clear from the bulls themselves containing them), it is clearly evident. It follows surely that when canon law—consistent with civil law—speaks of two months regarding Pontifical laws, those months are to be understood as starting from the publication made in each diocese. Otherwise, such a brief time would be unreasonable—both so that ignorance in the universal Church would not be presumed (which is clear enough in itself) and so that acts otherwise lawful in themselves would not be void in the whole Church. For they would be rendered null for no one <note>meaning no valid reason</note>, which could not happen without injury to many. Since these things are not to be presumed regarding the will of the Supreme Pontiff and the order and disposition of the Church, it must undoubtedly be said that those two months are to be understood from the day of promulgation in each diocese. And so I understand that phrase in this bull of Pius V: *Provided it was created after the publication of this bull.*

<column-break/>

[Column 2]

Cited in favor of this opinion are the gloss on chapter 2 *concerning constitutions* <note>original: "gl. c. 2. de const." refers to the standard legal commentary on Church law.</note> and others; chapter 1 *concerning the standing of statutes* <note>original: "de post. stat."</note>; and another, *let him know*, *concerning the sentence of excommunication* <note>original: "c. nouerit, de sent. excō."</note>. While these affirm that Pontifical laws bind after two months from publication according to the *Authentic* as "newly made constitutions" and add nothing more, they clearly intend them to bind after two months in the same manner sanctioned in the aforementioned *Authentic*. In that text, it is provided that they bind in each province after two months from the publication made therein. In the same opinion are Panormitanus, Felinus, Cardinal Zabarella, Henricus, and Decio <note>A list of heavyweight 15th and 16th-century legal scholars and canonists.</note> in the lecture on the cited chapter 2 *concerning constitutions*; likewise Panormitanus on chapter 1 *concerning the postulation of prelates*; Angelus under the word "law," number 13; and certain others.

Joannes Andreae, however, in the final gloss of the *Sixth Book of Decretals* <note>original: "lib. 6. decretaliū," a major collection of Canon law published in 1298.</note> regarding the date of that book, seems to suggest that Pontifical laws compiled in that *Sixth Book* bind everyone in the Church after two months from the publication of that same book, even if they are not published in the provinces. After him, many have asserted generally that the constitutions of the Supreme Pontiff bind the universal Church after two months from the publication made in Rome. This opinion has flourished so much that it seems it should be called the "more common" one. Indeed, Sylvester, who embraces the same (under "law," question 6, pronouncement 3), and many others affirm it is observed in practice. And Panormitanus, on *let him know*, *concerning the sentence of excommunication*, being little consistent with himself, seems to incline toward the same, although he adds that it is most true regarding constitutions inserted into the "Body of Law" <note>The *Corpus Iuris Canonici*.</note> of which Joannes Andreae speaks. He seems moved by that argument proposed above which moved Joannes Andreae and most other authors of his opinion: namely, that otherwise many of the constitutions inserted into the body of canon law would not bind the universal Church, because they have not been promulgated in individual provinces.

But this argument ought not to have moved them to depart from that other opinion proved by the authority of the law and the firmest reasons. Rather, it should only limit it, so it is understood that unless the constitution was inserted into the body of law which the province uses, and is learned there in the university and practiced among literate men—for that suffices for promulgation in each province—no other promulgation is necessary, whether the law is canon or civil. And in this way, Felinus limits that opinion in the place cited, and this is what Panormitanus seems to want in the cited *let him know*.

We are warned, however, that if some body of law were newly issued in Rome in which there were some new constitutions, and sufficient notice of them did not reach some province within two months, nor were they published in it, then they would not bind those who are ignorant in that province before notice of them was commonly held there, and this because of the things already said.

Hence, as far as it pertains to the bull we are now disputing, I say: If it has not been published in some province, and it is not practiced among learned men, and the notaries and contracting parties have not been commonly warned of it, it does not void contracts celebrated by those ignorant of it against its form, until notice of it is commonly held among that people.

One doubt for the completion of those things that have been said...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 39.

### Page 385

¶ ...we ought to examine this. Namely, if some people, before two months have passed from the publication of an **invalidating law** <note>original: "legis irritantis"; a law that renders certain acts or contracts null and void from the outset.</note> regarding a contract, have sufficient notice of it and yet enter into the contract, whether that contract is invalid and null in the **court of conscience** <note>The internal moral realm of an individual's relationship with God.</note> and in the **external court** <note>The public legal system or ecclesiastical court.</note>, as if the law binds those who know during those two months, but not those who are ignorant. Some have asserted that such laws, within those two months, bind neither those who know nor those who are ignorant, and for that reason, the contract is valid. However, the more common opinion of the doctors is that when a law does not specify within <margin>Decision.</margin> what time it begins to be valid and binding, it binds those who know immediately, and in regard to them, it renders null any contracts it invalidates. 

The two months, however, which are granted by **common law** <note>The general body of legal principles applicable across Christendom.</note>, are granted for this purpose alone: that within that time, ignorance is presumed when the contrary is not sufficiently proven, and so that contracts are not null in regard to those who are ignorant. For this reason, they affirm that it binds those who know within those two months, not only in the court of conscience but also in the external court; nevertheless, in the external court, it is required to be proven against them that they had knowledge. Among others of this opinion are the **gloss** <note>Standard legal commentary on a text.</note> on chapter 2 *concerning the non-alienation of Church property* <note>original: "de reb. Eccles. non alien."</note> in Book 6; Panormitanus and Felinus on chapter 2 *concerning constitutions*; the same Panormitanus on chapter 1 *concerning the postulation of prelates*; Sylvester under the word "law," question 6, pronouncement 4; Angelus in the same place, number 21; and many others whom they cite. Barzosa also moves toward the same opinion in the cited **Authentic** <note>A collection of Roman laws by Justinian.</note> at number 6. He confirms this from chapter 1 *concerning the granting of prebends* <note>original: "de concess. præben."</note> in Book 6, at the words "nor would it stand in the way," where the text clearly hints at this, and that text is almost an exposition of the cited *Authentic*; the cited gloss also relies on that same text. Furthermore, the **bull of Pius IV** regarding the declaration of the time in which the decrees of the **Council of Trent** <note>A major 16th-century ecumenical council that shaped Catholic doctrine and reform.</note> began to bind agrees with this, when it says that from the publication of the Council made in Rome, the decrees began to be observed there, with no mention made of a prior lapse of two months.

The doctors observe, however, that although contracts invalidated by a law are null after the passage of two months from its publication even if performed by someone having **invincible ignorance** <note>A state of ignorance that cannot be overcome by reasonable diligence, excusing the person from moral guilt.</note> of that law (the reason for which is rejected because to annul contracts for the **common good** <note>The welfare or benefit of the community as a whole.</note>, it is enough if a time is granted in which it is presumed that ignorance of the law will no longer exist, nor is it necessary to account for the few in whom invincible ignorance might exist by accident); nevertheless, for someone to be held to a penalty established by law after those two months, it is required that they are not invincibly ignorant of it at that time. The reason is that a penalty presupposes **fault** <note>original: "culpa"; legal or moral culpability.</note>; where there is invincible ignorance of the law, there can be no fault in its transgression. From this it follows that although, after two months from the promulgation of a law, no one is presumed to be invincibly ignorant of it—and thus, unless invincible ignorance is established, every transgressor of that law must be punished with its penalty—nevertheless, proof of invincible ignorance is to be admitted in the external court, and once it is sufficiently proven, the transgressor of the law should not be punished. What kind of proof is required, and whether the oath of the transgressor is sometimes sufficient, may be read in Panormitanus and Felinus in the places cited.

From what has just been said, it will be easily understood that if any rules established in the bull of **Pius V** regarding the invalidity of **census contracts** <note>original: "contractuū censualium"; a type of investment contract involving annual payments, often debated in the context of usury laws.</note> were enacted as a penalty, they have no force against those who are invincibly ignorant of that law—which describes those for whose sake all these things have been said.

6 <margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> It is to be † observed regarding **Portuguese law** <note>original: "Ius Lusitanu."</note> that Royal laws have force in the place where the King resides eight days after their publication in the Royal Chancery or in the House of Supplication. In the rest of the Kingdom, however, they have force after three months from that same publication in the Chancery or the House of Supplication, regardless of whether they are published in the remaining parts of the Kingdom, which they call **comarcas** <note>Administrative districts or judicial regions in Portugal and Spain.</note>, even if it is commanded in those same laws that they be published through the *comarcas*. Indeed, such a command is not added as if that publication were necessary for the law to have force in the whole Kingdom, but so that the law might better come to the notice of all. All these things are found in Book 1 of the **Portuguese Ordinances** <note>original: "Lusit. ord."; referring to the *Ordenações Manuelinas*, the compiled laws of the Kingdom of Portugal.</note>, title 2, paragraph 9. However, that paragraph is to be understood as applying when nothing else is expressed in the law regarding the time in which it ought to bind. Furthermore, I believe that under Portuguese law, royal laws do not bind those who know until eight days pass in the Court, and three months in the rest of the Kingdom. The reason is that in the cited paragraph, it is clearly established that laws do not have vigor until that time elapses.

Regarding the argument by which we were persuaded of the contrary opinion and the first proof of it, it must be said: it has been shown clearly enough that such a distinction accomplishes nothing, nor is that the reason why publication is required in every single province under imperial laws.

But if that distinction does effect anything, it will only be in this regard: that by the very fact that it is fully evident to some people of a certain diocese that some law has been passed by the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope.</note>, and it does not seem to be of such a kind that one must petition the Supreme Pontiff against it, it binds them before it is promulgated in their own diocese; this is because the universal Church is like a single Republic governed by the same laws. But indeed, when many provinces are subject to the same Kingdom, any of which is governed by its own peculiar laws—as are today the Kingdoms of **Portugal** and **Aragon**, and likewise **Belgium** and the **Kingdom of Naples** in comparison to the **Kingdom of Castile**—it will not be enough to know that the King of Castile has promulgated a law in Castile which he wishes to be common to the other Kingdoms that obey him, for it to bind those who know in them before he promulgates it in those very Kingdoms of theirs.

Regarding the second point, it has already been said that it is enough for some constitution to be inserted into the **body of law** <note>The official collection of statutes or canons.</note> by which a province is commonly governed, and which is preached in it, for it to be considered promulgated there.

Regarding the third point, it must be said—considering the notice that was already held throughout all the provinces concerning the Council of Trent, which had already been completed, and because it had reached all provinces in printed form in parts before its confirmation—and considering also the notice of its confirmation and publication made in Rome, which reached all provinces of Europe subject to the Roman Church within a short time, as a matter so distinguished and so greatly...

...longed for everywhere; furthermore, considering the publication of the rest of those decrees, which was carried out everywhere (for if I remember correctly, in the province of Portugal, which is so distant from the Roman Court, it was promulgated a full two months before the Calends <note>The "Calends" refers to the first day of the month; here, May 1st.</note> of May), Pius IV rightly declared that all began to be bound from the Calends of May. However, through *epikeia* <note>original: "epicheiam"; a principle of legal interpretation that allows for exceptions to the letter of the law in favor of its spirit or equity when unforeseen circumstances arise.</note>, the interpreter of laws, it must be judged that he did not mean this to apply to those who dwell in the Indies and in the most remote parts of the New World, to whom notice of the confirmation of the Council could not have reached in such a short time. For if these people had occurred to the Supreme Pontiff, or if they had been presented to him when he issued that declaration, he certainly would have excepted them. He would have judged that they suffered from invincible ignorance of the confirmation and publication of the Council, even many months after those Calends of May. Indeed, this confirms that our opinion was the intention of Pius IV in that bull, and not what the opposing argument intends.

Since the declaration contained in that bull was made after the Calends of May had already passed—whereas the Council had originally been promulgated in Rome in an absolute sense, with no time prefixed for when the decrees would begin to bind—it follows that if papal laws bound the entire Church immediately after two months had elapsed from their publication in Rome, Pius IV would surely not have declared (consistently with common law) that they began to bind after three months; rather, he would have said they began to bind immediately after two months, so that whatever had been done against those decrees afterward would be void and empty.

Therefore, our opinion is confirmed by that declaration rather than being challenged by it.

## Barter and Exchange: In How Many Ways They Are Used. And on Barter Strictly Defined.

### DISPUTATION 396.
### SUMMARY.

1 *Exchange and barter are the same in their implied meaning.*
2 *Exchange and barter are used in three ways in their meaning.*
3 *What barter is, properly speaking.*
4 *What exchange is, properly speaking.*
5 *Barter, properly speaking, is similar to buying and selling.*
6 *Things can be bartered while they do not yet exist, for a time when they will exist.*
7 *Exchange can be made concerning a thing not yet existing for a time when it will exist.*
8 *Whether ownership in barter and exchange is transferred by delivery on one side, if it has not been transferred on the other side, or if the thing was offered or held as delivered.*
*And regarding Portuguese Law. number 9.*

Since barter and exchange—as held in Law 2 of the Digest regarding the exchange of things—are very closely related and similar to buying and selling, they must be discussed next.

<margin>1</margin> Exchange <note>original: "Cambium"</note>, by the force of its † meaning, signifies the same as barter <note>original: "permutatio"</note>. For "to exchange" and "to barter," taken broadly, are exactly the same thing; on which matter read,

<column-break/>

among others, Covarrubias in his treatise on coinage, chapter 7, number 5. However, both terms are used in three ways.

<margin>2</margin> First, † they are taken in the broadest sense for any kind of trade <note>original: "commutatione"</note>. Taken in this way, they encompass in their scope all non-gratuitous or reciprocal contracts, such as buying, hiring, loans <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, and others, both named and unnamed <note>term: "innominatos" (unnamed); in Roman law, these are contracts that do not fall under specific established categories like "sale" or "lease" but are still legally binding if one party has performed their duty.</note>. Indeed, they are called non-gratuitous contracts for this reason: that in every one of them, something is done, given, or promised in compensation for another thing. This was the first meaning and usage of these words; the others, which are less broad, derive their force from the adaptation of usage. This is why the contracts signified in those usages are not called "named." For as was said with a certain gloss, Bartolus, and others in Disputation 253, for a contract to be called "named," it is not enough for it to retain a common generic name from the adaptation of usage; it is necessary that it claim a proper and peculiar name for itself. However, since we are now discussing contracts in particular, we are not speaking here of barter and exchange in such an ample meaning.

Secondly, they are used less broadly for that "unnamed" contract which is called "I give so that you may give" <note>original: "do vt des"</note>; that is, one by which one thing (as distinguished from "doing" or an action) is traded for another. This applies whether one thing, uncertain as an individual item but certain in its species or type, is traded for another, or whether one specific individual thing is traded for another specific individual thing (as was said in Disputation 253 with Padilla, Pinello, and others whom they cite, and with whom Lassarte agrees). This is the contract which, by adaptation of usage, is peculiarly called barter and exchange. It is distinguished from other contracts, both named and unnamed, and it encompasses two sub-categories. One, where a thing that is not "price" <note>i.e., not money</note> is traded for a thing that is also not price—such as a horse for an ox, wheat for oil, or a horse for a horse, etc. The other, where a thing that is "price" is traded for a thing that is also "price"—such as gold money for several silver pieces, or money in one place for other money to be paid in another.

For the contract of a thing that is not price for a price is a "named" contract: namely, buying and selling. insofar as it was said in the explanation of barter and exchange in this second usage that it is an "unnamed" contract, all named contracts like buying, hiring, and the rest are excluded from its definition. Insofar as it was added that it is a contract by which a thing (as distinguished from "doing") is traded for another thing, three other unnamed contracts are excluded: namely, "I give that you may do," "I do that you may give," and "I do that you may do," in which, at least on the part of one side, an action <note>original: "facere"</note> is traded. In this place, however, we intend to deal with barter in this second usage and the parts subject to it. Nor will it be necessary to add peculiar disputations about the other unnamed contracts, in which there is no peculiar difficulty; they will be sufficiently understood both from what we discuss regarding barter and other contracts, and also from what was said about them from Disputation 253.

<margin>3</margin> Thirdly...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral definitions of barter and exchange. The previous discussion established the general nature of these contracts; here, the author narrows the definitions and addresses when ownership transfers and how specific regional laws (Spanish and Portuguese) apply to these transactions.</meta>

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 397.</header>

<margin>3</margin> Thirdly, based on the adaptation of common usage, the terms "barter" <note>original: "permutatio"</note> and "exchange" <note>original: "cambium"</note> are used even more precisely. Specifically, barter is used for that sub-category where a <margin>4</margin> thing that is not currency is exchanged for another thing that is also not currency—for example, a horse for an ox. On the other hand, exchange is used for that sub-category where a thing that is currency is exchanged for another thing that is also currency, such as one type of money for another. In this third sense, "exchange" is a distinct category from "barter," and it is in this specific sense, following common human usage, that we shall speak of them from here on.

<margin>5</margin> Barter, when taken in this third sense, is very similar to buying and selling. For that reason, the rules stated regarding buying and selling are to be applied to barter insofar as they are compatible, provided the law does not expressly state the contrary. This is clearly gathered from Law 2 of the Digest <note>original: "ff." refers to the Pandects or Digest of Justinian</note> on the barter of things, and from Law 2 of the Code <note>original: "C." refers to the Codex Justinianus</note> under the same title, as was mentioned in Disputation 253. Hence, legal remedies like the "rescission of sale" <note>original: "reutiō" likely referring to "redhibitio"</note>, the "action for latent defects" <note>original: "actio redhibitoria," which allows a buyer to return a defective item</note>, and the "action for a lower price" <note>original: "quanto minoris," an action to reduce the price if a defect is found</note> have a place here. In situations where these would apply to buying and selling (as explained in their respective sections), they also apply to barter. <margin>6</margin> Furthermore, things can be bartered even if they do not yet exist, to be delivered at a time when they will exist. As Martin de Azpilcueta <note>referred to as "Navar."</note> rightly affirms in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 87, against the opinions of Soto and Sylvester: since things can be bought and sold for a future time (as we showed in Disputation 340), and nothing to the contrary is found in the laws regarding barter.

<margin>7</margin> These same rules also apply in a "presumed exchange." Indeed, by the very fact that the sale of a certain thing is prohibited, it is also considered prohibited to barter it; and so it goes for other rules adapted from buying and selling.

<margin>Question</margin> <margin>Disagreement</margin> <margin>8</margin> A doubt arises: in a sale, ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the sold item is not transferred by delivery unless the price is paid, offered, or considered as paid (as stated in Disputation 338). Does it follow that in barter and exchange, delivery by one party does not transfer ownership until delivery is likewise made by the other party, or the item is taken or considered as delivered? The Gloss on Law 2 of the Code on the barter of things, and another on the Digest under the same title, as well as another on the Code regarding pacts, affirm that this requirement is unique to the contract of buying and selling by a special privilege of that contract. They argue that in barter and other contracts that transfer ownership, ownership is transferred by delivery before the contract is completed by the other side. They strongly agree with the sections "By Delivery" and "Sold Items" in the Institutes on the division of things, where it is said ownership is transferred by delivery, and only sale is excepted (where payment of the price is further required for the transfer of title). However, Bartolus <note>a famous 14th-century Italian law professor</note>, commenting on Law 2 of the Code on the barter of things (along with a certain addition to the gloss of that law cited just before), and the same Bartolus on the Digest regarding theft, is of the contrary opinion, agreeing with certain other glosses. Namely, he believes that in barter and other contracts, ownership is not transferred by delivery alone, but it is further required that the contract be fulfilled by the other party; he cites Law 3 of the Digest on the action of pledges in confirmation of this.

<margin>Decision</margin> To me, however, the first opinion is far more proven, which is gathered quite clearly from those two cited sections of the Institutes.

<column-break/>

For nothing should be excepted from that rule—that ownership is acquired by delivery based on a preceding title—unless the exception has been expressly stated in the law. Furthermore, that ownership is transferred in barter by delivery before the contract is fulfilled by the other side is stated so expressly in the law *With Prayers* <note>original: "l. cum precib."</note> in the Code on barter, that it is a wonder Bartolus did not attend to that law. Nor does the law that Bartolus cites for his opinion prove anything, even on the surface. For in that law, it only states that if a debtor should go to his creditor and demand the pledge he gave as security for the debt, saying he wants to pay the debt, and having received the pledge he throws it through a window to another person waiting there for that purpose, and then does not pay the debt—the creditor then retains the right of the pledge over that thing, which was snatched from his power by deceit in that manner, until the debt is paid to him.

From this, I do not see by what logical consequence Bartolus can infer his opinion. Regarding barter accepted in this third way, one must observe <margin>9</margin> a rule of Portuguese law (Book 2 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, last title). To avoid the evils that used to arise from it, it is prohibited to barter wheat, wine, oil, or anything else belonging to the food supply <note>original: "annonam"</note> for another thing to be paid in the future—even if the person with whom the barter is made does not have the item of his own but is going to buy it or acquire it by another title from someone else to pay it. And upon the person who has bartered in this way, the penalty is imposed of losing the item he gave by the very fact of the deed; it is forfeited to the one to whom he gave it, such that he is never bound to make any compensation for it. Nor is a waiver of the privilege of this law valid, even if the receiver makes one. Regarding the barter of ecclesiastical benefices, however, this will be discussed when we speak of benefices.

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

sold for a fixed price, and later the parties agree that another appraised item should be accepted in place of the price.
12. On which things the *Alcauala* <note>A significant sales tax in the Spanish kingdoms.</note> is not owed.
13. Which of the contracting parties ought to pay the *Alcauala*.
14. The *Alcauala* is not owed on a remunerative gift <note>A gift given in return for a past service.</note> in Castile and Portugal.
15. When a barter is to be considered a gift.
16. The *Alcauala* is not owed on a currency exchange strictly defined.

<margin>1</margin> **A**ccording to the law of this Kingdom of Castile, not only is the *alcauala* tax owed on a barter, but it is actually owed twice. One tax is for the first item which is bartered for another, and the second tax is for the other item which is bartered in return. <margin>2</margin> For in every barter, a double sale is considered to have occurred, following the law *sciendum*, paragraph *sed si quis permutaverit* of the Digest regarding the edicts of the city officials <note>original: "l. sciendũ. §. sed si quis permutauerit, ff. de ædil. edictis." The Digest was the primary source of Roman Law.</note>. One sale is for the first item bartered, and the other is for the second item bartered for the first. Consequently, in this Kingdom, both parties to the barter are bound to pay the full *alcauala* according to the value of the item each receives in exchange for the item he gave. This is because what one receives as compensation for the item he barters takes on the nature of a "price." In this Kingdom, a seller is bound to pay the full *alcauala* based on the price of the item he sells. All of these points are clearly gathered from Law 2, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Compilation* <note>original: "nouæ collect." referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century collection of Spanish laws</note>, and they were discussed in the section on buying and selling. In Portugal, a double tax is similarly owed for the same reason—a tax they call the *sisa* there—as is clear from the articles on the *sisa*. However, in that case, one party to the barter pays half of both taxes, and the other pays the other half. This is because in that Kingdom, the buyer pays half and the seller pays half, as was noted in the section on buying and selling. Regarding this matter as it pertains to the law of this kingdom, read Lassarte <note>Geronimo de Lassarte, a contemporary legal authority</note> in his work on the tithes of sales, in the commentaries on the aforementioned Law 2, before Chapter 1 and in Chapter 17 from number 1.

A doubt arises at this point. Since a barter is not considered perfected and brought into existence until the delivery <note>original: "traditio"</note> has been made by both sides, and since it is not enough for delivery to have been made by only one side (as is clearly evident from what was said in Disputation 253, and as Lassarte admits in the cited Chapter 17, number 3, following Fortunio Garcia, and as is expressly held in Law 1 of the Digest on the barter of things), <margin>3</margin> the question is whether the tax <note>original: "gabella"</note>, or the taxes owed from the barter, only begin to be owed when delivery has been made by both sides. If delivery never happens, is the tax never owed? Furthermore, if after delivery has been made by only one side, the person who delivered the item changes his mind—as he is permitted to do under common law (as seen in Disputation 258)—or if the contract is dissolved by the mutual consent of both parties, is the tax never owed?

Staying strictly within the common law, which has force in Portugal because nothing to the contrary has been enacted there on this matter, Lassarte (cited Chapter 17, number 25) admits, along with Bertachino Firmius in his work on taxes (Part 3, Section 8, number 48), that this tax is not owed until the barter is perfected by the mutual delivery of both parts. Menchaca (Book 1, *Controversies*, Chapter 11, number 21) and Parladorius (cited by Lassarte in the same place, number 35) believe the same to be true in this Kingdom. Their reasoning is that, although in this Kingdom a legal action is granted based on a bare agreement <note>original: "pacto nudo"</note> to barter, and it is not lawful to back out—not only when delivery has been made by one side, but even when neither side has reached the point of delivery (as seen in Disputations 257

<column-break/>

and 258)—nevertheless, an agreement or pact to execute and perfect a barter is one thing, and the barter itself is another. The barter is not considered perfected or brought into existence before delivery is made on both sides. In this Kingdom, however, the aforementioned Law 2 does not impose the *alcauala* tax (or the two *alcaualas*) upon the *agreement* to barter, but upon the *barter* itself.

Lassarte, starting from the cited number 25, holds the opposite opinion. He argues that this tax is owed in this Kingdom from the moment the pact of barter is perfected and concluded, even if delivery never follows, and even if the contracting parties withdraw from the contract by mutual consent before delivery. He says this because, since a civil obligation and a right of action arise from a bare pact in this Kingdom, and since backing out is not permitted against the will of the other party (whether delivery was made by one side or by neither), a barter is surely perfected by mutual consent in this Kingdom no less than a sale is perfected by mutual consent. Consequently, just as the state treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> acquires a perfected right to the tax from the mutual consent of a sale—a right which cannot be prejudiced by a withdrawal from the contract before delivery—so too the tax is owed to the lord or tax collector who held office at the time of that mutual consent, not to the one who might be in office at the time of delivery (as was shown in the material on sales). Therefore, the same must be said regarding barter. Otherwise, the contracting parties might defraud the tax owed on barter by making a contract and then, by mutual consent, delaying the execution and progress toward delivery until they actually needed the items. Then, if circumstances arose that might disrupt the barter, they would withdraw from the contract by mutual consent.

<margin>Decision.</margin> For my part, the opposing opinion of the other doctors is far more persuasive to me, because of their fundamental principle: "barter" does not signify the *agreement* to barter, but the barter itself, completed by the work and mutual delivery. Just as "a loan" <note>original: "mutuum"</note> does not signify an agreement to lend, but the actual execution of the lending. Hence, just as a loan is among those "named contracts" which are perfected by deed and action, rather than by mutual consent or words alone (as seen in Disputation 254), so too <margin>4</margin> barter is among the number of contracts perfected by deed and action. This is what the word "barter" <note>original: "permutatio"</note> signifies; it does not mean mutual consent or a stipulation to barter, as Law 1 of the Digest on the barter of things expressly holds. Therefore, since the tax we are discussing is imposed upon *barter*, it follows that before the barter is completed by mutual delivery, the tax is not owed, nor is the right to it perfectly acquired by the treasury. It does not matter that those making an agreement to perform a barter can delay the execution and withdraw from the pact; they are simply using their own right, and they do no injury to the state treasury. At this point, observe that just as in common law, although an action is not granted from a bare pact to make a loan, an action *is* granted if a formal stipulation is added or if that pact is linked with another contract (as stated in Disputation 253); yet even then, there is not yet a contract of loan, but rather a stipulation...

<meta>catchword: ...of [stipulationis]</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the taxation of barter in Castile and Portugal, debating whether the Alcauala tax is triggered by the initial agreement to exchange goods or only upon the physical delivery of those goods. Luis de Molina argues against contemporary legal scholars, asserting that because barter is a contract perfected by action (delivery), no tax is owed if the parties cancel the deal before the items change hands.</summary>
