### Second Treatise, Disputation 337

...made concerning a loan, or otherwise a "naked pact" <note>A *pactum nudum* (naked pact) is an agreement that, under Roman law, did not automatically grant a right to sue unless it followed a specific legal form or was accompanied by the delivery of goods.</note> <unclear>clothed</unclear> by its connection to another contract. For this reason, if a tax were imposed on a loan contract, the tax would not yet be owed under common law, because it would still be a mere naked pact. Thus, according to common law, or in Portugal where common law prevails in this matter, if a tax is imposed on an exchange, and a formal promise is added to the agreement to exchange, or if that agreement is linked with another contract, a legal action may indeed be granted based on such an agreement. However, because it is not yet a completed barter, but rather an agreement to barter "clothed" by the formula of a formal promise or the connection of another contract, the tax—which is imposed only on the contract of barter, or of purchase and sale—is not yet owed. Consequently, under the law of this Kingdom, it is irrelevant whether a legal action is granted based on a naked agreement of barter (as with any other naked agreement) or whether the right to withdraw from the deal is removed; one cannot conclude from those grounds that the tax imposed on the contract of barter is already owed.

7 Regarding the contract of purchase and sale, however, the reasoning is far different. The tax is owed for it, and the right to that tax is acquired by the treasury by the very fact that the contract is perfected through mutual consent. Since purchase and sale are perfected by consent alone (as explained in Disputation 254 and elsewhere), the terms "purchase" and "sale" signify a contract perfected in that manner; therefore, the tax imposed on the contract of sale is owed from that moment.

From what has been said, it is easy to understand that if in this Kingdom, or in Portugal, during the time of one lord and tax collector, an agreement was made to barter one thing for another, and during the time of a second collector the barter is completed by the delivery of the goods, the tax is owed to the later lord and collector in whose time the barter was perfected and finished. It is not owed to the prior lord and collector in whose time the agreement was merely a naked pact, even if that agreement was then "clothed" by a formal promise or by connection with another contract.

The reason is that the tax is not owed based on the agreement to barter—even if a civil obligation to complete the barter arises from it—but rather from the completed barter itself, or when it is brought into actual existence, as has been stated. It was completed not in the time of the first lord and tax collector, but in the time of the later one.

<margin>Question</margin>
5 Laffarte <note>The jurist Enrique de Villalobos, often cited as Laffarte.</note> in the place cited above at number 43, because he believes the tax from a barter is owed by the very fact that a civil obligation arises from the agreement to barter, brings into dispute whether—when a naked agreement to barter preceded in the time of one tax collector (from which no civil obligation arises in common law unless a formal promise is used, or it links with another contract, or delivery occurs)—and in the time of a second collector it is "clothed" by delivery—whether, I say, a civil obligation having then arisen, the tax is owed to the first collector or the later one. He cites the opinion of Antonio Gómez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his "Varias Resolutiones."</note> in volume 2, chapter 8, number 2, who is followed by Parladorius in his book *Daily Matters*, chapter 3, section 3, number 35. They assert it is owed to the first collector. They are led to this because they believe the obligation does not arise from the fulfillment of the agreement or from the delivery, but from the agreement itself once delivery follows,

6 since delivery is only a † condition without which

<column-break/>

an obligation does not arise from the agreement, as is gathered from the law *Ex placito* in the Code regarding the exchange of things, in these words: *From an agreement of barter, where no delivery has followed, it is established that no one has a right of action.* <note>original: "Ex placito permutationis, nulla re sequuta, constat nemini actionem competere;"</note> From this, it follows by an argument from the opposite sense that from the agreement and contract itself, once the thing has followed (i.e., been delivered), an action arises and is available. Therefore, they say, since the agreement from which the action arises was celebrated during the time of the first tax collector, it follows that the tax is owed to him, even if the condition without which the action does not arise from that agreement (the delivery) arrived during the time of the later collector. The glosses on the same law *Ex placito* and another in the Institutes regarding actions seem to agree. However, the opinion of Laffarte in the same place is far more pleasing—namely, that it should rather be affirmed that the tax is owed to the later collector and not the first. First, because the civil obligation arises from both parts as integrating and perfecting that contract; thus, just as the completeness and perfection of the contract depend on both, so too does the emergence of the civil obligation.

7 This † is gathered clearly from the first law of the Digest regarding the exchange of things, in these words: *Barter, however, provides the beginning of an obligation from the thing delivered;* <note>original: "Permutatio autem ex re tradita initium obligationis præbet;"</note> understand this as being from the completion that perfects the contract. If the words cited from the law *Ex placito* prove anything by an argument from the opposite sense, it is only that the obligation arises partially from the agreement, which we do not deny—but it does not prove that it does not also arise simultaneously from the delivery itself as a part and completion of the same contract. Furthermore, even if we say it arises from the agreement alone (with delivery being a condition without which it does not arise), it cannot be denied that the contract is not perfected and finished before that delivery, and thus the obligation does not arise before that delivery. Consequently, it cannot be denied that the contract is finished and the civil obligation arises during the time of the later tax collector, and therefore the tax is owed to the later collector. This is just like when a contract of sale is suspended so that a written document may be completed; the tax is not owed until the writing is finished, because the contract is not yet perfected. Thus, the tax is owed to the collector who is in office at the time the writing is completed, as Antonio Gómez himself confesses and as was said regarding the matter of purchase and sale.

Just as when the parties intend for a purchase and sale to be perfected by a written document, the contract celebrated by mutual consent is suspended so that it is not considered perfected before the writing is fully finished; so it is in a barter, as is clearly arranged in the law *Contractus* in the Code regarding the faith of instruments, and as Laffarte and the Doctors generally affirm. And in Ca-

<margin>Law of Castile</margin>
8 stile, if either before the celebration † of the contract, or during the celebration itself, mention was made of a written document to be prepared, the contract is considered suspended until the writing is perfected, according to those things said in Disputation 337 regarding the contract of sale—unless it is clearly understood from the concurrent circumstances that the intention of the parties was that the writing should only serve for proof and greater security.

<summary>This page discusses the legal timing of tax obligations for barter and sale contracts, concluding that while sales are taxed upon consent, barter is only taxed upon delivery, meaning the tax belongs to the collector active at the time of completion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina's discussion on the legal nature of exchange (barter) and the specific conditions under which the "alcabala" (a sales and transfer tax) becomes due to the treasury. It follows the previous page's distinction between contracts perfected by consent alone versus those requiring the delivery of goods.</meta>

### Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

Lassarte <note>Ignacio Lasso de la Vega, a Spanish jurist often cited by Molina regarding tax law.</note> advises in the section cited above that, since an exchange is perfected by the delivery of the goods, it is not a sufficient guess to assume that delivery has proceeded on both sides just because a written document was mentioned. If mention was made of preparing a deed during the celebration of the contract or beforehand, that mention should be considered as made only for the sake of proof, and not for the completion of the contract itself. This is similar to what was said in the cited discussion regarding the opinion of the same author and Gregorius Lopez: that in a contract of buying and selling, it is a sufficient guess that the parties proceeded to the delivery of the merchandise and the price, because buying and selling are perfected by consent alone. He adds, however, that if the delivery has proceeded on both sides and the tax has been paid to the tax collector who was then in office, this is a sufficient guess to understand that by mentioning the preparation of a deed, they did not intend to suspend the contract, but only intended for the deed to be made for proof and greater security. He reports that he judged in this way in a case of no small importance, and the sentence was confirmed by the higher judges.

When, however, a contract of exchange has been suspended so that a deed might be perfected, then before that deed is entirely completed, it remains legal for either of the contracting parties to change their mind and withdraw from the contract. This is true not only under common law but also under the law of Castile <note>Castilian law often provided specific statutory modifications to the general Roman "Common Law" (Ius Commune) used throughout Europe.</note>, as long as the deed is not fully completed, even if delivery has proceeded from one or both sides. This is because, before a contract is consumed <note>meaning "finalized" or "legally binding"</note>, it remains open to both parties to withdraw from it. Furthermore, the tax from that contract would be owed to the tax collector who was in office at the time the deed was completed, because that is when the contract is perfected—not to the collector who was in office at the time of the agreement and mutual delivery, if those collectors were different individuals. This is the view of Lassarte as cited above, and it is clear enough from what has been said.

Regarding those contracts where "I give you such a thing so that after a certain time you give it to Peter," or "I give you a hundred so that you grant fifty of them to John," or "I give you such a field of mine so that you pay a certain pension annually to me or another," Lassarte rightly says in chapter 17, number 7, that the tax is not owed. For a tax to be owed from the contract of "I give that you may give" <note>Latin: *do ut des*, a standard category of reciprocal exchange in Roman law</note>, it is necessary that the things given on both sides be different things, and not one thing included within another, or a fruit or a right reserved within it. Although Lassarte thinks all these contracts are included under the unnamed contract of "I give that you may give," I would rather say they are "donations with a condition" <note>Latin: *donationes sub modo*, a gift that carries a specific obligation for the recipient</note>. From a donation and its conditions, the <term>alcabala<gloss>A substantial sales and transfer tax in the Spanish Empire, typically around 5–10%.</gloss></term> is not owed, because it is strictly neither a sale nor an exchange, but a far different type of contract. Read what was said in Disputation 382 regarding the reserved census <note>A type of ground-rent or annuity</note>, as to whether the alcabala is owed from it.

<margin>Question</margin>
All agree that when a thing of one species is given for something of another species—such as a horse for an ox, wheat for oil, etc.—or an individual of one species for another of the same species that is different in value—such as one horse for another—it is an exchange, and therefore a double tax is owed. 9 They doubt, however, whether an exchange occurs when an individual of one species is given for another of the same species that is similar in value, such as one measure of wheat for another equal measure of wheat, or one measure of wine or oil for another similar one, and whether

<column-break/>

the tax is owed or not. Parladorius <note>Juan Yañez Parladorio, a 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> in the place cited above, number 33, along with Bartolus and others, says that it is a <term>mutuum<gloss>A "loan for consumption" involving fungible goods (like grain or coins) where the borrower is expected to return the same quantity and quality, rather than the specific physical items borrowed.</gloss></term>, and therefore the tax is not owed from that contract. However, Lassarte (number 9) speaks better and more in harmony with Law 2, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a major compilation of Spanish laws promulgated in 1567.</note>, which concerns <note>original: "de las trueques que se hizieren de vnas cosas a otras semejantes o desemejantes"</note> "exchanges that are made of some things for others, whether similar or dissimilar." He says we must look at whether, from the circumstances, the contracting parties intend a loan (mutuum), as they often do from the manner of contracting itself and the concurrent circumstances; in that case, the tax is not owed. This occurs when someone asks for a loan of wheat, bread, wine, oil, or even money, to be paid back later in an individual thing of the same species and value, more or less. Or we must look at whether they intend another contract that is not an exchange, such as a deposit—whether it is to be returned as the exact same item or not—or the consignment of a dowry, so that the same amount is returned when the marriage is dissolved. In these cases, the tax is not owed, even if, after the thing is consumed by the depositary, he pays it back in another similar thing in another place by consent of the parties (for instance, if he pays back wheat he had in deposit and consumed by his own authority in another place).

But if, from the circumstances and the manner of celebrating the contract, they intend an exchange, then the tax is owed, even if the contracting parties want to cloak and pretend the contract is a loan under the name of "mutuum." There is, however, no certain rule for judging it to be an exchange simply because what is done is convenient for both parties. For if someone who has wheat in another place asks an inhabitant here for a loan of several measures of wheat for daily use, intending to pay them back when his own arrives from that other place, then—even if the borrower would prefer to have them in that other place—it should not be considered an exchange, but a true loan. Likewise, if someone asks for a loan of wheat now, intending to pay back the same amount from his own future harvest, even if this is convenient for the lender, it should not be considered an exchange, but a loan. 

If, however, someone gives wheat here so that the same amount is paid to him in another place where he will sell it for more, it should be considered an exchange, even if it is cloaked under the name of a loan, unless there are circumstances suggesting that the one receiving the wheat here is truly asking for and receiving a loan. Likewise, if two people live in different places, and each has wheat in the place of the other, and they swap, it will be an exchange of one wheat for another, even if cloaked under the name of a loan. Therefore, these matters must be committed to the judgment of a prudent person, so it may be judged whether, considering all concurrent circumstances, it should be judged that a loan is occurring, or rather an exchange.

10 When two things are exchanged, the valuation of both—so that it may be understood how much tax is owed—pertains to the judge, or to another whom the judge has appointed for that valuation, as held in Law 2, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Collection*. Therefore, one must not rely on the valuation of the parties, even if they expressed the value of each thing being exchanged in the contract. If, however, from the beginning a thing is sold for a certain price, and later the parties agree that instead of the price, another thing estimated by the agreement of both 11 parties is accepted, then it is not an exchange, but a double sale, and the tax will have to be paid according to the price established by the contracting parties in both contracts. So says Pinellus in his commentary on the Code, "On Rescinding a Sale," part 2, chapter 1, number 16, and Lassarte in chapter 17, number 17.

<summary>This page discusses the legal criteria for distinguishing between a taxable exchange (barter) and a non-taxable loan (mutuum) or donation, emphasizing that the intent of the parties and the physical delivery of goods determine tax liability. Molina notes that swapping similar goods like wheat can be a taxable exchange if used for profit across different locations, rather than just for mutual convenience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the alcabala tax in the context of exchanges. It specifically addresses "inestimable" things (like spiritual rights), privileged goods (like books), and the distinction between a true exchange and a gift given in gratitude.</meta>

Second Treatise. Disputation 398.

When a thing is inestimable, and therefore not saleable—such as the **right of burial**, and other things discussed in Disputation 340 and elsewhere—if an exchange of that thing is made for another estimable thing, the alcabala <note>A Spanish sales and transfer tax, typically a percentage of the value.</note> 
<margin>12</margin>
† is not owed by either party. This is because a tax is not owed on a sacred thing, as it is inestimable; nor does the law (Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Compilation*) <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a major collection of Spanish laws compiled in 1567.</note> apply here, which requires an appraisal of things being exchanged. Just as the sale of such a thing is null because it is simoniacal <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred or spiritual things.</note>, so too an exchange of it for a secular thing is null. Furthermore, no alcabala is owed on a null sale or exchange. For these same reasons, no alcabala is owed on the exchange of a secular thing for an inestimable thing, especially since the alcabala would have to be paid according to the appraisal of the inestimable thing, which in that exchange would take the place of the price. Although spiritual things may be exchanged for one another (as held in the chapter *Ad Quaestiones* <note>original: "c. ad quæstiones"</note> and the gloss there on the exchange of things), even if laypeople exchange them—such as one burial right for another, or one chapel for another—the tax is not owed, because such things are inestimable. All of this is cited by Lassarte <note>Ignacio Lasso de la Vega, a Spanish jurist and expert on tax law.</note> in chapter 17, number 18.

In this Kingdom, many things are exempt from the alcabala, as contained in Law 34, Title 18, Book 9 of the *New Compilation*, such as **books**, a **horse** adorned with saddle and bridle, and other items. However, when one of these is exchanged for something else—for example, books for cinnamon—the person exchanging the books is exempt from paying the tax, since such things are considered privileged in that they take the place of the merchandise. Thus, no alcabala is owed on the price received for them or the thing received in place of a price.

However, the person who exchanges cinnamon for books owes the alcabala based on the appraisal of the books. This is because books are not considered privileged when they take the place of the price, as if they could make the thing sold for them exempt from the tax; this is clear enough in itself. This is easily proven: by that same law, money is made exempt from the alcabala specifically when it takes the role of the merchandise (which is why no alcabala is owed on a strict money-exchange); and yet, when money serves as the price, it does not make the thing sold for that money exempt from the alcabala. Instead, the seller pays the tax according to the amount of the price. These points are made by Lassarte in the place cited above, number 19.

When a thing is sold for a certain price and simultaneously for another thing, even if this other thing is of much less value than the price, it was stated in Disputation 336 that in this Kingdom (according to Law 2, Title 17, Book 9 of the *New Compilation*), 
<margin>13</margin>
† both items must be appraised by a judge or someone designated by a judge. The person selling the thing of greater value shall pay the alcabala on the full value of the price and the thing given with it, according to the appraisal that was made. The person giving the price and the thing, however, shall pay the alcabala only according to the appraisal of what he receives for his specific item. For example: if Peter sells John a farm for 1,000 gold pieces and a mule, and if the mule is appraised at 100 gold pieces, Peter will pay the alcabala on 1,100 gold pieces.

But if the farm is appraised at 1,100 gold pieces, John will only pay the alcabala on the 100 gold pieces

<column-break/>

which he is considered to have received for the mule. If the farm is appraised at more or less than 1,100 gold pieces, John will pay the alcabala on the eleventh part of the sum at which the farm was appraised; for the other ten parts correspond to the price of 1,000 gold pieces (on which he owes no alcabala), and only the remaining eleventh part corresponds to the mule, for which alone he owes the tax. Thus says Lassarte, as above, from number 20.

<margin>14</margin>
It is quite clear that the alcabala is not owed on a **remunerative donation** † in Castile and Portugal. This is because it is not an exchange, even if it is a return for something that was not a physical act. Indeed, a remunerative donation <note>A gift given to someone as a reward or in gratitude for a past favor or service.</note> is not a compensation based on justice, as occurs in an exchange, but arises solely from liberality and gratitude.

Nor does it matter that in the law (specifically the section *sed & si §. consuluit* <note>A reference to the Digest of Roman Civil Law regarding the petition of inheritance.</note>) it is said to be a kind of exchange. It is not actually an exchange; rather, a similarity to exchange is seen in it, insofar as a benefit previously received is compensated, as Lassarte correctly noted in chapter 17, number 53.

<margin>15</margin>
If † certain things are given as mutual gifts, such that one person gives on the condition that the other gives back, it must be considered an **exchange**, and the alcabala will be owed. If, however, it is not conditional, but absolute, and out of mutual love and liberality they give to each other immediately, it should be considered a donation—provided the circumstances suggest the intent on both sides was to give a gift. If the circumstances do not suggest this, it will be judged as an exchange disguised under the name of a donation, and a double tax will be owed.

<margin>16</margin>
Since in a **strict money-exchange** † money is traded on both sides, and money is privileged so that no alcabala is owed on it (as said above), it is established that no alcabala is owed on a strict exchange.

## What a strict exchange is. Whether the practice of money-changing is licit. Of how many types exchange consists.

### DISPUTATION CCCXCVIII.

->SUMMARY<-

> 1 *What exchange properly is.*
> 2 *Of what things exchange properly consists.*
> 3 *Who is called a money-changer.*
> 4 *How the art of money-changing is licit.*
> 5 *How many types of exchange there are.*
> 6 *Time and place are especially to be considered in exchange.*
> 7 *What real and "dry" exchange are.*
> 8 *Why "dry" exchange is so called, and from where.*

1 A strict exchange <note>original: "Cambium presse"</note>, as † is clear from the discussions in Disputation 396, is nothing other than the **exchange of money for money**. # Luis de Molina, On Contracts

in the sign <note>The "sign" refers to the official stamp or face value of a coin, as opposed to its intrinsic metal value.</note>, are different, as Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican scholastic theologian and jurist.</note> rightly noted in Book 6, *On Justice*, question 8, article 1.
It should be observed that since the concrete things or the extremes between which a barter occurs (explained in Disputation 339) share the same name—as stated in the first law of the Digest *On the Exchange of Things* <note>original: "l. 1. ff. de rerū permut."</note>—for each of those between whom a barter takes place is called a "barterer" or "exchanger." Nevertheless, the concrete things or extremes between which a currency exchange <note>original: "cambium"</note> is perceived do not have the same name, nor are they entirely of the same nature and character. For the one from whom the exchange is requested can lease his labor and industry, which he applies at the request of the other; for this reason, he can justly receive something beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note>, as will become clear in what follows. And thus, for the sake of distinguishing them, the extremes of this contract receive different names. The one from whom the exchange is requested, and who applies his work and industry at the other's request, is called the **money-changer** <note>original: "campsor"</note>, especially if he held a public office of exchanging. He is also called a **banker** <note>original: "nummularius, trapezita, collybista, & argentarius"</note>, although some of these names have broader meanings, regarding which one should read Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> *On the Collection of Ancient Coins*, chapter 7, from the beginning to the end of number 4. In Spanish, he is called a **banker** <note>original: "banquero"</note>. However, the one who requests the exchange is called a **client** <note>original: "campsarius"</note> by Conradus <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian.</note> in *On Contracts*, question 99, by Medina <note>Juan de Medina (1490–1547), a Spanish theologian.</note> in question 1 *On Exchange*, and by others; just as one who receives a loan is called a borrower, one who receives a gift is a donee, and one who receives a legacy is a legatee.

<margin>4</margin> † Whether, moreover, the art of money-changing—insofar as profit is intended beyond the principal—is licit in its practice. It must be said that although it is inherently dangerous, even more so than the art of trading which intends profit through buying and bartering, and although it is unbecoming for certain persons, such as Clergy, and is prohibited to them; nevertheless, if it is practiced in the manner to be explained in the following sections, it is to be condemned neither as unjust nor as illicit. Rather, it can be practiced meritoriously, as was shown regarding the art of trading concerning buying and exchange in Disputation 339. Indeed, that it is useful to the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note>, just like that other art, will be manifest from what follows.
Leaving aside that exchange in which no profit is intended—as when, in the same place, money of higher value is exchanged for other smaller coins which, taken together, have equal value according to the law and the common estimation of men—in which contract there is no doubt. The exchange in which profit is intended, and in which a difference is seen regarding the range of value between the money that is exchanged and that for which it is exchanged, is divided into

<margin>5</margin> three species or modes, which are for now to be abstracted from whether they are licit or illicit. Since exchange does not happen except for some difference in the monies: and this is considered either regarding the monies themselves in their essence—because they are of different material, or different sign, or different sign and material simultaneously—or regarding the place—because one is given in one place, such as **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olissypone"</note>, to be returned in another, such as **Seville** <note>original: "Hispali"</note> or **Rome**—or regarding the time, because one is given at one time to be returned at another; it follows that three species of exchange are distinguished. One, in which monies are exchanged because of their difference in themselves. Because this

<column-break/>

usually involves exchanging money of higher value for small change, it is customarily called **small exchange** <note>original: "cambiū minutū"</note>. It can also be called **manual exchange** <note>original: "cābiū manuale"</note>, as it is named by some, because it is done from hand to hand in the same place. Another is that in which monies are exchanged because of a difference in place. And because this is frequently done by providing letters so that the money may be paid in a distant place, it is customarily called **exchange by letters** <note>original: "cabium per literas"</note>. And the other is that in which money is exchanged because of a difference in time, which can be named **exchange due to time difference**.
This is improperly called an "exchange"; for if it is correctly examined, one only finds a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note> in it. Accordingly, if anything beyond the principal is received in such exchanges, <term>usury</term> <note>Taking interest on a loan, which was heavily regulated or forbidden in Catholic moral theology unless specific justifications existed.</note> is committed, unless the contract is rendered just on the grounds of **lost profit** <note>original: "lucri cessantis"</note>, **emerging loss** <note>original: "damni emergentis"</note>, or some other just reason. And for this reason, in the proposed division, I said it was abstracted from licit and illicit exchange, so that this species might be included under "exchange" so that it might be discussed, and thereby be disapproved

<margin>6</margin> and recognized. † Universally, however, in exchanges it must always be observed whether something beyond the principal is received by reason of time; for whatever is received by reason of time—unless it be excused on the grounds of lost profit or something else—is received unjustly, and usury intervenes in that receipt, because it is received by reason of a loan, either formally or virtually. It should be observed that the aforementioned three species or modes of exchange are sometimes mixed. For it can happen that in the monies themselves a difference of places is found, and thus in the exchange by which they are bartered, there will be simultaneously an exchange due to difference of places and a difference of the monies in themselves. Likewise, a difference in time is usually joined with a difference of places, specifically the time in which the money is to be paid in the distant place.

<margin>7</margin> Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 8, article 2) distinguishes a fourth species or mode of exchange, due to the difference in value which the same money has in different places. For one and the same money—for example, a ducat—although as many silver coins would be given for it in **Flanders** as in Spain or in the New World, nevertheless it is worth more in Flanders than in Spain, and in Spain than in the New World. This is because there is a smaller supply of coins and many more goods can be bought with it in Flanders than in Spain, and in Spain than in the New World. However, I think it is not necessary to distinguish this fourth species, since this difference arises from the circumstances of distant places; rather, while explaining the grounds upon which it is licit to receive something beyond what the money-changer gives in an exchange due to distance of place, that ground will be sufficiently explained. Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and economist.</note>, however, in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 286, and from his commentary on the chapter *Last* regarding usury, number 10, distinguishes seven species of exchange, some of which only contain certain grounds upon which it is licit for the money-changer to receive something beyond the principal. But it will not be necessary to multiply so many species of exchange; it will be enough, among the proposed species to be explained, to examine the grounds upon which it is or is not licit to receive something beyond the principal. Likewise, it will suffice to explain "small exchange" and "exchange due to difference of place," and simultaneously examine the other grounds upon which it is or is not licit to receive an increase...

...then to receive something.
<margin>7</margin> Furthermore, the learned doctors divide exchange into "real" and "dry." They call "real" that which is a true exchange, legitimate by its very nature, so that something beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note> can be licitly received. However, they call "dry" that which is not truly an exchange, but is instead a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, and for that reason it is not legitimate for anything beyond the principal to be received. Specifically, this occurs when an increment is taken in the exchange solely because of a delay in time or a waited-for payment, which constitutes usury. It is called "dry," as if lacking moisture, sterile for producing fruit or bringing in profit. These terms are used in this sense in the Bull of Pope Pius V regarding exchanges <note>Referring to the 1571 papal decree *In eam pro vicario*, which sought to regulate banking and suppress usurious "dry" exchanges that hid interest-bearing loans under the guise of currency trade.</note>. Some understand "dry exchange" to mean an exchange where the money-changer gives first, so that he may later receive it back with an increment, even if the future receipt is in a distant location.
<margin>8</margin> They believe this interpretation has its origin in the same root: because such an exchange was considered usurious by its nature and sterile for licitly receiving anything beyond the principal, as many doctors affirm and as the Portuguese Ordinances define in Book 4, Title 14, penultimate section. This matter must be examined in what follows, and we shall show that it was improperly defined. Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist known as "Doctor Navarrus."</note>, in the cited passage, says it is called "dry" by these doctors because the money-changer gives before he receives. However, what I said previously pleases me more.
Medina <note>Juan de Medina (1490–1547), a Spanish theologian.</note> in Question 2 on exchanges, along with Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502).</note> in *On Contracts*, Question 99, Supposition 5, also divides exchange into "impure" and "pure." They call "pure" that in which no other contract is mixed. "Impure" is that in which another contract is mixed, such as a loan or a lease of the labor and industry of the money-changer or something similar. But Soto <note>Domingo de Soto.</note>, in the second article cited, says it is more significant to call just exchange "pure" and unjust exchange "impure." These things are said so that the various ways doctors speak on this matter may be understood.

## Whether it is licit for a money-changer to receive an increment beyond the legally fixed prices of coins for "minute exchange"
### DISPUTATION 399.
->SUMMARY<-

1 *To what end "minute exchange" is useful.*
2 *What exchange requires so that it can be called just.*
3 *What private money-changers may receive for their office and service.*
*And what is observed in Castile and Portugal. number 4.*
*Understand, however, and declare as in number 6.*
5 *Whether private money-changers may receive anything for their services, just as public money-changers do.*
7 *Whether a money-changer sins and is bound to restitution if he justly retains something for his office that is otherwise prohibited to him by law.*
8 *Whereby a private money-changer may licitly receive a profit.*

<margin>1</margin> That "minute exchange" <note>This refers to "small change"—exchanging a large-denomination coin for many smaller ones, or vice versa, within the same local economy.</note> is useful to the State <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note> is clear from the fact that men often need small coins to buy daily items of cheaper price, to give smaller alms, and for other such things for which high-value money is not

<column-break/>

suitable. On the other hand, those who are about to store a large sum of money, or transport it to another place, need the exchange of lower-value coins for others of much higher value. Also, for those about to travel to a place where the money of the place they are leaving has no value, it is necessary to exchange money for other coins that have value in the destination. For these reasons, therefore, and for others, it is useful to the State that there be some money-changers who have coins of various kinds ready and prepared for exchange, as each person may need them in place of others.
<margin>2</margin> This being established, it must be set down as a foundation in this matter, according to the common opinion of the doctors: just as in buying and selling, and other exchanges, it is necessary that equality and commensuration occur between what is given and what is received in return so that the contract is just and no obligation of restitution arises; so also it must occur in an exchange where money is traded for money. Indeed, this is common to all contracts of "commutative justice," <note>The branch of justice governing private transactions and the equal exchange of goods or services.</note> of which exchange is one. Since money has a value fixed by public authority and law—which, viewed from the perspective of price, consists in an indivisible point for both sides of the exchange—what we are primarily inquiring into in this matter is: what are the grounds upon which a money-changer can justly receive something beyond the equal amount he himself gives, considering the value of both currencies as fixed by law?
<margin>3</margin> First, it must be said according to the common opinion of the doctors: it is licit for money-changers to receive a just price for the duty and service <note>original: "munere, ac obsequio"</note> they perform in the exchange for the benefit of those who request it from them. This price may come from the State or from those who seek the exchange, provided they do not already receive a salary from the State; however, the price they receive must not be disproportionate or exceeding the service they perform. If it were to exceed a rigorous price for the service, the excess would be unjust and subject to restitution. The services of the money-changer include: collecting and keeping ready coins of various kinds for whoever wishes to exchange; staying in the public house by himself or through servants destined for that task, waiting for those who wish to exchange; and counting the money, both what he gives and what he receives. All these things are certainly worthy of a just wage <note>original: "stipendio"</note>.
<margin>4</margin> In this Kingdom of Castile, the duty of a public money-changer is free and immune from any burden for all; however, they must be chosen in the Royal Court by the King himself, and in other places by the judges and governors (called *regidores*) of the city or town where they are to exercise their office, as held in Law 1, Title 18, Book 5 of the *New Collection*. By Law 4 of the same title, they are permitted to receive four maravedis for the exchange of one *Castellano*, three maravedis for a ducat or *dobla*, and two maravedis for one florin; the same for the ducat is repeated in Law 62, Title 21 of the same title. Navarro, in his commentary on the chapter *fina, de usuris*, reports that in Salamanca, during the time he was teaching in that distinguished academy, the public money-changer...

### Ludovicus Molina On Contracts

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
...it was said that it was customary to receive one maravedí <note>A small Spanish copper coin.</note> for the exchange of one ducat <note>A gold coin used across Europe.</note>. In Portugal, however, in the fourth part of the *Extravagantes* laws, Title 1, Law 4, § 9, it is forbidden—both for giving and for receiving gold coins that have value in that Kingdom, whether they were minted in that Kingdom or another—to receive any increment beyond their just value. The penalty is the loss of the value of the coins, with half going to the accuser and the other half to the **redemption of captives** <note>A common charitable fund in the 16th century used to ransom Christians captured by Mediterranean pirates.</note>; furthermore, one faces the penalty of two years of exile to the regions of Africa. An exception is made if someone is appointed by the King as a **public money-changer** in a certain place, with a specific increment prescribed to him by the King; in that case, he may lawfully receive it. However, if a specific increment is not prescribed, he can receive nothing under the same penalties, even if the King granted him permission to exercise the office of a public money-changer. Since the increment that a money-changer justly receives in this way is not taken for the money he gives, but for the **service** he provides, it follows that in this type of exchange, two just contracts are found joined together. One is the exchange of money for money of equal value. The other is the **hiring of the money-changer's labor** for that just increment. For just as was said in Disputation 304 (along with Medina, Navarrus, Maior, and others), although a lender can receive nothing beyond the principal for a loan <note>original: "mutuo"</note>, he can nevertheless, by the very nature of the matter, receive a moderate stipend for the counting of the money and for other services which he performs for the benefit of the borrower. In the same way, a money-changer can receive a moderate stipend for the aforementioned services.

<margin>Question.</margin>
The doubt is whether even **private money-changers**, who do not have an official duty to serve the Commonwealth in that office, may lawfully receive any increment for the labor they expend for the sake of the person requesting the exchange, such as in the counting of money or anything else they perform. Cajetan, in his small work *On Exchanges* (Tract 7, Chapters 1 and 6), answers in the negative.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Cajetan says this because counting money is not worthy of payment but is usually done for free. Furthermore, sometimes the person requesting the exchange counts more money than the money-changer himself. Likewise, the act of counting on the part of the money-changer is balanced by the act of counting on the part of the requester. However, the **common opinion of the doctors** affirms the contrary: namely, that it is lawful by the nature of the matter even for private money-changers to receive a modest increment for the act of counting or any other similar service they provide, just as was said of a private lender in the place cited above. However, it is less lawful for them to receive as much as public money-changers who are appointed to this by the Commonwealth; for the latter are subject to far more expenses and burdens, as mentioned before.

This is affirmed by Medina (Question 2 on exchanges, though the penultimate section of Question 1 might seem to suggest the contrary at first glance), Soto (Book 6 on Justice, Question 9, single article), Navarrus (in the *Manual*, Chapter 17, number 288, and in the *Commentary on Usury*, number 19), and Contra (on contracts, Question 99, conclusion 5), Gabriel (in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 11, article 3, doubt 12), Maior (in the same place, Question 37), Covarruvias (in his work on old collections, Chapter 7, number 4), and Silvester arrives at the same opinion (under the word "usury," 4, Question 7, pronouncement 3), and

<column-break/>

others agree. The reason is that this service is indeed estimable at a price, even if a very small one. Therefore, one must deny the first point that moved Cajetan. Regarding the second, it must be said that although the money-changer counts both the money he gives and that which he receives, he performs both at the request of the person who demands the exchange; for that reason, both acts of counting are worthy of a price. Just as a lender is worthy of a price for counting both when he gives the loan and when he receives payment, because he undergoes both for the sake of the borrower and would be free from both if he did not wish to grant the benefit of the loan. From this, the third point is denied: no "compensation of labor for labor" is seen there, just as such compensation is not seen in a loan. Indeed, in both contracts, whatever labor is undertaken arises to accommodate the person requesting the loan or the exchange.

6 These things that have been said should be understood as they pertain to the nature of the matter. For the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Respublica"</note> can prohibit anyone from receiving anything for an exchange beyond the value of the money, and this is for the good of the Commonwealth itself.

This is done, first, so that the prices of currencies do not increase, and second, so that foreigners, by offering a higher price for gold or silver coins, do not export them to the detriment of the Commonwealth. Soto, in the passage cited above (Conclusion 3), says that a law was passed long ago in this Kingdom <note>Referring to Spain.</note> that no one could receive an increment for **small exchange** <note>original: "cambio minuto," referring to changing large denominations into small change.</note> except for public money-changers deputized for this by the Commonwealth. He affirms that this law, by its nature, binds under the threat of mortal sin, and transgressors are bound to restore the increment. On the contrary, Navarrus (at the cited number 19) says that although it is prohibited in this Kingdom for anyone to take up the office of a public money-changer by their own authority, it is not forbidden for private individuals to exchange money and to receive a just stipend for the exchange. He cites the royal decrees <note>original: "pragmaticas"</note> which establish only this, and he rebukes Soto for not citing a specific law for his opinion. Covarruvias, in the cited work, embraces Soto's opinion and cites the *Ordinances* (Title 8, Law 5, which today is Title 18, Law 5 of the *New Collection*). In that law, it is only prohibited for anyone to take up the office of a public money-changer unless they are chosen in the Court by the King, or in other towns by the judge and governors, as was related above; but this does not prohibit others from exercising exchange privately. From the laws by which gold coins are taxed today (which we will relate in the following sections) and by which it is prohibited to receive more by any means, it should perhaps be considered forbidden for private individuals to receive an increment for small exchange, as Gutierrez (Book 2, Practice 99, Question 178) concludes. What has been decreed in Portugal was related above. I believe, however, that in neither Kingdom is it the custom for private individuals to receive anything for small exchange based on the principle we are discussing.

7 They affirm that if a law is given which forbids receiving anything for small exchange, if something is received, it is subject to **restitution**. This is not without its difficulties if the discussion is about a price that would otherwise be "just" for the act of exchanging according to their own opinion. For although a Prince, for the common good of the Commonwealth, can in that event make the recipient incapable of holding that increment...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the legality of charging for currency exchange. Molina is arguing that while civil laws (like those in Portugal or Castile) might forbid money-changers from taking a fee, this is often a "penal law"—meaning it carries a fine but does not necessarily mean the changer has committed a mortal sin of injustice if they take a fair payment for their labor, as long as the payment is intrinsically "just" based on the work performed.</meta>

Second Treatise.
Disputation 400.
395

...that something be prohibited by law so that, if it is done, it is considered void and null; nevertheless, when a just compensation is established in it by the nature of the thing between what is received and that for which it is received, and laws of this kind are usually penal <note>A "penal law" in scholastic thought is one that binds the citizen to pay a penalty if caught, but does not necessarily bind the conscience as a sin of injustice.</note>, in which this does not apply, there is no doubt—as is clear from many other things we have said about that law in Disputation 88, especially regarding the confirmation of the first argument proposed there—that such laws do not usually make those who receive a just stipend incapable of receiving it. I believe that in such a transgression of the laws, only the sin of disobedience to the prince occurs, which by its nature is by no means lethal <note>A "lethal" or mortal sin would jeopardize the soul's salvation; Molina argues this is a lesser, venial matter.</note>. Furthermore, before a sentence is passed by a judge, there is no obligation to restore a stipend that was just based on the nature of the thing. However, if what was received exceeded the limits of a just stipend based on the nature of the thing, then it would be a lethal sin by its nature to take an increment beyond those limits, with the burden of restoring it.

<margin>8</margin> For another reason, however, even a private money-changer can lawfully receive a profit: namely, by giving in the place where he practices exchange less for certain money—not less than it is worth in that place, but less than it is worth in another place. He does this by transferring that money to that other location, or by exchanging it with those traveling to that other location for the value it has there, if they are willing to grant him that benefit without any disadvantage to themselves. Until now, those who are at the borders of Kingdoms are accustomed to profiting by exchanging asported <note>Carried out or brought across a border.</note> money from another Kingdom—which has no value in the place where the exchange occurs—for a lower price than it is worth where it came from. This is lawful because the money has no legal value where the exchange takes place. They then carry it to a place where it has a value fixed by law, or exchange it for that value with those traveling to that place. Doctors of law such as Medina (Question 3 on Exchange, final section), Cajetan (in his work *On Exchanges*, Chapter 6), and others agree. Observe, however, that the price can sometimes be so low, considering the material of the coinage (for instance, if it were Portuguese silver), that the contract would be unjust, carrying the burden of restitution down to the lowest just price. For if the price for an equal piece of silver were below the lowest just price at which silver bullion is usually bought in a similar mode of sale, the contract would certainly be unjust, with the burden of restoring it to the lowest just price.

To shed light on the things that must be said, it will be worthwhile for us to examine the matters proposed, of which we have greater knowledge than of the coins of other Kingdoms. From those things we shall say about such coins, however, it will be easily understood what should be judged in other Kingdoms, once knowledge of the laws and the quality of the coins of those Kingdoms is obtained.

To proceed more clearly, it must be observed that a <term>selibra</term> <note>A half-pound.</note> of gold or silver—called a <term>marco</term> <note>A Mark.</note> by the Spanish, and in certain other regions a <term>marca</term>—is a weight of eight ounces. An ounce is divided into eight "eighths" <note>original: "octauas".</note>, which the Hebrews call <term>adhareon</term> <note>Likely referring to the biblical *adarkon* or darkemon.</note>, the Greeks call <term>drachmas</term>, and the Latins call <term>drachmas</term>. The Spanish, with the name corrupted from the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, call them <term>drama</term> and <term>adarame</term>, and others call them <term>adarme</term>. I suspect, however, that the word <term>adarame</term> flowed into Spanish from the Saracens <note>The Moors/Muslims of the Iberian Peninsula.</note> who occupied the Spains, whose language is very closely connected with Hebrew, just as many other Spanish words did. In this Kingdom <note>Referring to Portugal, where Molina was writing.</note>, however, they call half of an eighth—that is, the sixteenth part of an ounce—a <term>drama</term> or <term>adarame</term>. From this it is already easily established that a half-pound contains sixty-four eighths of an ounce. For the eight ounces that make up a half-pound, multiplied by the eight eighths that make up each ounce, produce sixty-four eighths.

<margin>3</margin> An eighth of gold contains seventy-two grains.

<margin>4</margin> Next, it should be observed that to better judge and express the purity or impurity of gold, goldsmiths divide a half-pound, or any other weight of gold, into twenty-four parts, which they call <term>caracta</term> <note>Karats.</note>. In Spanish, we call these <term>quilates</term>. Furthermore, they subdivide each karat into quarters of a karat, into eighths, and into other similar proportional parts, larger and smaller. When gold is at its purest, having nothing mixed in from another metal, it is said to be of twenty-four karats—in Spanish, <term>veinte y quatro quilates</term>—because clearly the half-pound, or whatever other weight of such gold, has all twenty-four parts consisting of gold and nothing of another metal. And such gold is what is called <term>obryzum</term> <note>Pure or refined gold.</note>, which in Greek signifies "sincere" and "delicate." Others claim it is named after Ophir <note>The biblical land of gold.</note>. However, that etymology is quite harsh. When, however, a half-pound of gold, along with twenty-three parts of gold, has...

# Ludovicus Molina

...contains one mixed part of another metal, whether it be silver, copper, or any other, it is called **gold of twenty-three carats.** When, however, it has twenty-two parts of gold mixed with two parts of another metal, it is called **gold of twenty-two carats**, and so on.

In a similar way, to better judge and express the purity or impurity of silver, they divide a pound or any other weight of silver into twelve parts, which they call *denarii* <note>original: "denarios". In the context of silver fineness, these are "pence" or "pennyweights," representing 1/12th of the total mass.</note>. When a pound of silver has no other metal mixed in, but is pure silver, it is called **twelve-penny silver.** But when one part of another metal is mixed with eleven parts of silver, it is called **eleven-penny silver**, and is said to have one penny of *alloy* <note>original: "ligæ", the Spanish term for the base metal added to a precious metal</note>. And so it is called silver of fewer pennies according to how many more parts of other metal it has mixed in.

<margin>6</margin> They divide a penny <note>original: "denarium"</note> further into twenty-four parts, each of which they call a **grain** <note>original: "grana"</note> of silver. Thus it happens that a grain of silver has far more weight than a grain of gold.

It should furthermore be observed that in this Kingdom of Castile, by Ferdinand and his wife Isabella—as reported by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and expert on numismatics.</note> in *On the Comparison of Ancient Coins*, chapter 3, at the beginning, number 2, and section 1, number 4, and as held in law 1, title 21, book 5 of the *New Collection*—

<margin>7</margin> **ducats** <note>original: "ducatos"</note> were ordered to be minted from gold of twenty-three and three-quarters carats, so that only a quarter part of a carat was missing for that gold to be the purest. Perhaps that small portion of another metal was mixed in for somewhat greater firmness, because the purest gold is not very hard, but easily bent. Sixty-five ducats and a third part of another were minted from a half-pound <note>original: "selibra", a Spanish weight unit of 6 ounces</note> of gold. Thus, each ducat had one-eighth of an ounce of gold, after subtracting from each of the sixty-four ducats as many grains for the expenses of minting the money as would suffice to produce one other ducat and a third of another. Consequently, each ducat had less than an eighth of an ounce of gold by nearly a grain and a half. These same Sovereigns also ordered another coin to be minted from the same gold, double the size of this one, which was called a *dobla* <note>original: "dobla", a "double" coin</note> in that Kingdom, and another five-fold (five gold pieces), another ten-fold, another twenty, and another fifty gold pieces. Since a ducat in this Kingdom is worth eleven silver **reals** <note>original: "regales"</note> and one **maravedi** <note>original: "marauedinum"</note>, and a silver real is worth thirty-four maravedis, a ducat is worth three hundred seventy-five maravedis. All these things are held in law 4, title 21, book 5 of the *New Collection*. Thus, a half-pound of that gold in bulk was valued then at the price of twenty-four thousand maravedis. For sixty-four ducats, at the rate of three hundred seventy-five maravedis, make twenty-four thousand maravedis. The ducat and a third of another, which were additionally made from the half-pound of gold, were for the expenses of minting those coins from that bulk. Thus, the bulk of a half-pound of that gold was valued at twenty-four thousand

# Second Treatise, Disputation 400.

...of twenty-three thousand, three hundred thirty-one maravedis. <note>The maravedi was the smallest unit of account in early modern Spain.</note> A half-ounce <note>original: "semivn." or "semi-uncia"</note> contains twelve grains of gold and is worth two silver reals; one and three-quarter carats <note>original: "semivn verò, & tres quartæ", likely referring to quarter-carats</note> contain twenty-one grains and are worth three and a half silver reals—that is, one hundred nineteen maravedis. When added to the escudo <note>A gold coin worth a specific number of maravedis.</note>, which at that time was worth three hundred fifty maravedis, they make four hundred sixty-nine maravedis. If you subtract these from twenty-three thousand eight hundred maravedis, you will find that a half-pound <note>original: "selibram", a weight of 8 ounces</note> of that mass of gold was worth twenty-three thousand, three hundred thirty-one maravedis at that time.

Since, however, a half-pound of gold of twenty-three carats contained ninety-five quarters of a carat of gold and one quarter of alloy <note>original: "ligæ", referring to the base metal mixed with gold</note> of other metals; while a half-pound of gold of twenty-two carats only contains eighty-eight quarters of a carat of gold and eight quarters of alloy of other metals; and twenty-three thousand, three hundred thirty-one maravedis, divided into eighty-eight quarters of a carat, makes each quarter worth two hundred sixty-five maravedis and an eleventh part of one maravedi; it follows that a half-pound of gold mass of twenty-three and three-quarter carats—which has seven more quarters of gold—is worth, after the escudos of that value are minted, twenty-five thousand, one hundred eighty-six maravedis and seven-elevenths of a maravedi. 

Furthermore, since a half-pound of gold of twenty-two carats has two carats of alloy—and two parts of this alloy are silver and the third part is copper—it follows that a half-pound of gold of twenty-two carats has one and a third carats of silver and two-thirds of a carat of copper. Therefore, since a half-pound of silver in this Kingdom has a value of sixty-five silver reals, as is found in
<margin>Law 1, title 21, book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a 1567 compilation of Spanish laws.</note></margin>
a carat of silver is worth ninety-two maravedis and a twelfth part of a maravedi; and thus one and a third carats are worth nearly one hundred twenty-one maravedis. If you subtract these from twenty-five thousand, one hundred eighty-six maravedis, you will find that after the escudos of that value are struck, a half-pound of gold of twenty-three and three-quarter carats is worth twenty thousand, sixty-six maravedis. And thus an eighth of an ounce <note>original: "octauam vncię", equivalent to a drachm</note> of that gold mass is worth three hundred ninety-one maravedis and thirty-nine sixty-fourths of a maravedi. This was the value of each ducat <note>The ducat was a standard gold coin across Europe.</note> at that time, if you add five hundred maravedis for the expenses of minting them.

Our King Philip II, in the year 1566, as is found in Law 13, title 21, book 5 of the *New Collection*, declared that while changing nothing in the weight and carats of these escudos, he raised the value of each to four hundred maravedis, so that a half-pound of these escudos was worth twenty-seven thousand, two hundred maravedis, as it is worth today. But if you subtract one escudo (now worth four hundred maravedis) as a tax for the King, and one hundred forty-one maravedis for expenses (which today are paid in Seville <note>original: "Hispali"</note>) instead of the one hundred nineteen maravedis that were once paid—because since the escudo was raised to a value of four hundred maravedis, the one and three-quarter carats are worth more today—and thus from that total sum you subtract

<column-break/>

five hundred forty-one maravedis, you will find that a half-pound of this kind of gold mass is worth today twenty-six thousand, six hundred fifty-nine maravedis. If you divide these into the eighty-eight quarters of a carat of purest gold which that half-pound contains (for the other eight are alloy), you will find that each quarter-carat of purest gold is worth today nearly three hundred and three maravedis. Furthermore, the seven quarters of purest gold, which a half-pound of gold mass of twenty-three and three-quarter carats has in excess, are worth today nearly one thousand, two hundred twenty-two maravedis. 

Therefore, a half-pound of the gold mass used for ducats (meanwhile not deducting what must be subtracted for the alloy) is worth today approximately twenty-seven thousand, nine hundred maravedis. Today, however, almost nothing is to be subtracted for the alloy, because it is entirely copper and has no silver in it, as was reported to me from Seville. An eighth of an ounce of this mass is worth about four hundred thirty-five maravedis—that is, twelve silver reals and twenty-seven maravedis. And that same ducat is worth just as much today, if you add the five hundred forty-one maravedis of minting expenses, which compensate for what is missing in gold to make a full eighth of an ounce. 

However, the cited Law 13 set a fixed price <note>original: "taxam", a legally mandated value</note> for them at four hundred twenty-nine maravedis, and that should rather be followed. For perhaps something is hidden from me which causes that decrease, or perhaps, because I am ignorant of arithmetic <note>A humble admission that he may have made a calculation error.</note>, I used someone else's help to make these calculations and something was not calculated correctly. Nevertheless, what has been said will bring no small amount of light to what needs to be discussed.

<margin>12.</margin> I would advise three things. First, that Castilian goldsmiths and mint officials do not practice the calculation of carats on a half-pound of gold, but on that gold coin called the *Castellano*. This coin, if it is of twenty-two carats, is worth today sixteen silver reals, or five hundred forty-four maravedis, as held in the cited Law 13. They say that a carat of purest gold in a *Castellano* is worth today twenty-four maravedis, plus some fractions of another maravedi. Because fifty of these coins weigh exactly a half-pound, they find that coin suitable to use as a measure for other weights in their practice of carats.

Second, although in this Kingdom the price of silver mass is fixed so that a half-pound cannot exceed the value of sixty-five silver reals (as we will say shortly and as was cited above), no price has been imposed on the mass of gold itself, but only on the coins made from it. However, if the mass today is twenty-two carats, it will never exceed the value we said it has based on the coins that can be made from it, once the costs of minting and the tax paid to the King are subtracted.

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...of twenty carats. In the same law, they almost subject those selling manufactured goods to a penalty if the item contains less gold than required for any of those three qualities of gold.

<margin>13</margin> In this same Kingdom <note>Referring to Castile.</note>, under Ferdinand and Isabella, silver reals were ordered to be minted of a fineness of eleven deniers and four grains <note>A "denier" (dinero) was a measure of silver purity divided into 12 parts; eleven deniers and four grains indicates high purity silver.</note>. These were minted at sixty-seven reals per half-pound <note>original: "selibra", a weight of 8 ounces</note>, which consequently contained twenty grains of alloy <note>original: "ligæ"</note> of another metal, namely copper. This is according to the New Collection of laws, book 5, title 21, law 2. The value of these was thirty-four maravedis, as per law 4 of the same title. However, the half-pound of this silver mass was taxed so that it could not be sold for a higher price than sixty-five silver reals, as per law 5. Since they mint sixty-seven reals from it, as noted in laws 8 and 2, it follows that the reals themselves only contain thirty-two maravedis worth of silver <note>Molina is showing that the face value of the coin is higher than the raw metal value to cover costs and taxes.</note>. Since only one real is paid for the expenses of the half-pound of these reals, and furthermore one maravedi—as a public official of the mint confirms to me—it follows that the remaining thirty-three maravedis go as profit to the person who provides the silver to be made into reals; this is clearly indicated in law 5. Regarding silver reals, nothing has changed concerning all these matters until the present day, as is established in the text of law 13. One exception exists: by a Royal decree sent to the mints of Spain, a tax of fifty maravedis was imposed to be paid to the King for every half-pound of silver minted; this tax is called **seigniorage** <note>original: "señorage", the crown's profit on minting currency.</note>. Therefore, today, for someone minting a half-pound of silver, sixty-four and a half silver reals are returned as the price.

<margin>14</margin> Around the time that Ferdinand and Isabella ordered the ducats mentioned earlier to be minted, in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> other similar coins were minted from the purest gold of twenty-four carats, which they call **cruzados** in that Kingdom. The simple *cruzado*, or ducat, contained an eighth of an ounce of gold, minus three-quarters of a grain for expenses; it had seventy-one grains plus a quarter of another grain. The ten-ducat cruzado, which is called a **Português** in that Kingdom, contained one and one-eighth ounces, and sixty-four and a half grains; it only lacked seven and a half grains to equal ten-eighths of an ounce, as cited in law 4, section 3. Since the ducat in that Kingdom has a value of four hundred **reais**, it follows that a half-pound of that gold mass was then valued at twenty-five thousand, six hundred reais. Indeed, sixty-four eighth-ounces of that gold, at the rate of four hundred reais per eighth, yield that number of twenty-five thousand, six hundred reais. But a half-pound of gold reduced into those coins was worth twenty-five thousand, eight hundred reais, with some increase because of the forty-eight grains extracted from the sixty-four ducats for expenses, which made up more than half of another ducat. A grain of gold at that time was worth five and a half reais, and a certain seventh part. For seventy-two grains at the rate of five reais per grain make three hundred sixty reais. If truly

<column-break/>

you divide each of the forty reais that remain to complete the four hundred into two halves, you get eighty halves. Then, if you subtract seventy-two halves for the seventy-two grains, you will find that each grain was worth five and a half reais, and additionally a seventy-second part of four reais, which contains twenty-four sevenths.

<margin>15</margin> In the time of Charles V, John III <note>King of Portugal, reigned 1521–1557.</note>, moved by the same reasons as Charles V, had ducats minted in Portugal which he calls **cruzados of the small cross** (*cruzados de cruz piquena*). Today they are called **middle cruzados** (*cruzados do meio*), because they were minted between those first ones of purest gold and others of even lower gold. Their gold was twenty-two carats and five-eighths of a carat; they only had an alloy of one carat and three-eighths of another metal mixed in. Each of them weighed seventy-one grains and a quarter part, just like the ducats of pure gold. Because these ducats retained the price of four hundred reais, a half-pound of this less pure gold began to be worth the price that the half-pound of the other pure gold was worth before. Later, the same John III ordered other ducats to be minted, which he calls **cruzados of the cross of Mount Calvary** (*cruzados de cruz de monte caluario*), made of gold of twenty-two carats and one-eighth, weighing seventy-one grains, with a half and three-eighths of a grain; thus it only lacked one-eighth of a grain to be an eighth of an ounce. Because these ducats also retained the price of four hundred reais, from then on a half-pound of this less pure gold began to be worth the price at which a half-pound of pure gold was formerly valued.

Most recently, the same John III ordered coins to be minted which were very common in Portugal when I was teaching there <note>Molina taught at the University of Coimbra in Portugal.</note>, made of gold of twenty-two carats and one-eighth. Some of these were of such weight that thirty of them weighed a half-pound, and the value of each individually was one thousand reais; hence from their value they were called **thousand-reais coins** (*monedas de mil reais*). Others had half the weight of these, and sixty of them weighed a half-pound of gold, each worth five hundred reais, and similarly they were called **five-hundred-reais coins** (*monedas de quinhētos reais*). Thus it happens that whereas formerly a half-pound of pure gold of twenty-four carats had a value of twenty-five thousand, six hundred reais, from the time of these coins, a half-pound of a much less pure gold mass—namely twenty-two carats and one-eighth—began to be worth thirty thousand reais. And the value of other purer coins increases according to this rate, not only so that an equal weight yields an equal price to the thousand-reais coins at the rate of thirty thousand reais per half-pound of weight, but also so that a greater quantity of pure gold yields a higher price in the same proportion by which the quantity of purest gold in older coins exceeds the quantity in the thousand-reais coins (after subtracting something for the value of the mixed alloy, as was deduced regarding the coins of Castile). This is what the extra-legal statutes of Portugal, law 4, decree, as will be discussed later.
