### Second Treatise, Dispute 400.

Although in the cited law 4 a specific price was imposed on those newest gold coins, and in paragraph 11 of the same law it was forbidden to take any profit for their exchange—under penalty of losing the value of the coins and two years of exile to locations in **Africa**—and though that was their common price, foreign merchants nevertheless began to offer one thousand one hundred <term>reais</term><note>The *real* (plural *reais*) was the basic unit of account in Portugal.</note> for coins worth one thousand, and five hundred and fifty for coins worth five hundred. Suddenly, at the time I was teaching these matters, with the Senate and other public ministers knowing but not contradicting it, a great abundance of these coins was given at that higher price by many, even by those who were in charge of the government and the King's assets. Perhaps what I will subjoin below was a significant aid in making this happen.

The silver of Portuguese coins is of eleven <term>deniers</term><note>A measure of silver purity where 12 deniers represents pure silver; 11 deniers is roughly 91.6% pure.</note> fineness; however, they contain one full denier of another metal mixed in as alloy, as is established in the first law, title 8, part 5 of the Extraordinary Laws. This is the reason why in **Flanders**, **Germany**, and among other nations, they are not valued except according to the quantity of the silver mass they contain, with further consideration given to that impurity. King **Sebastian** <note>Sebastian I of Portugal, reigned 1557–1578.</note>, in the cited law, ordered twenty-four <term>tostões</term><note>A *tostão* (testoon) was a silver coin.</note> to be minted from a half-pound <note>original: *selibra*, a weight of 8 ounces</note> of this silver, each with a value of one hundred reais. By this calculation, a half-pound of them was worth two thousand four hundred reais, or (which is the same thing) six <term>cruzados</term><note>The *cruzado* was a major Portuguese coin, originally gold, later silver.</note>. However, since those who provided the silver for minting them paid only sixty reais for the expenses, as the same law holds, it follows that a half-pound of that silver mass was then worth two thousand three hundred and forty reais.

His grandfather, **John III**, had ordered twenty-six *tostões* to be minted from a half-pound of the same silver; thus, in the time of John III, a half-pound of these *tostões* was worth two thousand six hundred reais <note>original: *mille sexcentus*, but context and the reference to 6.5 cruzados indicate 2600 is intended</note>, or six and a half *cruzados*, as is held in the same law. Before the time of John III, the *tostões* were of even greater weight. All these *reais* mentioned were always of the value of one hundred reais, with nothing hindering the fact that some of them had more silver and others less. Indeed, King Sebastian, in the cited title, law 2, commanded that the *tostões* ordered to be minted by John III should retain the same value, and no one could reject them when they were handed over in payment for goods or debt.

During this whole time, the silver <term>real</term><note>Here referring to the physical silver coin, as opposed to the *real* unit of account.</note> was of the value of thirty-six and two-sevenths reais in **Portugal**, so that eleven of them were worth four hundred reais, or one *cruzado*. King Sebastian, in the cited title, law 3, in the year 1588 <note>Molina likely means 1558, as Sebastian died in 1578; 1588 would be during the Philippine Union.</note>, established that this should be their price and that no one, under certain penalties, should receive more for them. But since at that time it was worth sixty reais in **East India**, forty <term>maravedis</term> in **Africa**, and it was sought after among all nations—and everywhere men traded with them, rather than with Portuguese silver money—and since in that region called **Mina** in **Ethiopia** <note>Referring to Elmina (São Jorge da Mina) in modern Ghana, a major source of gold for Portugal.</note>, from where a huge abundance of gold is transported to Portugal, much gold is given in exchange for these coins, many during all this time (with nothing in the reported law hindering them) bought them in Portugal at a higher price. Even the King himself, or his ministers, did so, in order to send a huge quantity of them every year to the East Indies and other places. Everything was full of scruples <note>Moral/legal doubts</note> as to whether they could be licitly bought at a higher price in Portugal.

<column-break/>

While things were thus, suddenly, while I was teaching this matter and King Sebastian was preparing to cross over into Africa <note>The ill-fated 1578 expedition to Morocco.</note>, the price of the silver *real* in all of Portugal happened to rise to forty reais, so that ten of them began to be worth four hundred reais, or one *cruzado*. This happened by no law, but because the King was thus paying wages and the price of goods, and public ministers were compelling private men to receive silver *reals* in their accounts. And from then on, *tostões* began to be minted with the weight of two and a half silver *reals*, and from one half-pound, twenty-eight *tostões* are minted, each of the same value of one hundred reais. Who pays the expenses, and how much is taken for expenses, I do not know, as I am currently distant from that kingdom.

Therefore, this increase in the value of silver in that kingdom was of no small help in causing those coins <note>The gold coins mentioned earlier.</note> previously worth one thousand and five hundred reais to be bought at such a high price, and caused that kingdom to be suddenly stripped of the greatest abundance of them that was then in it, as they shortly disappeared, carried away to other kingdoms. I hear that merchants have brought a huge quantity into this kingdom of **Castile** and sold individual coins of one thousand reais for thirty-three silver *reals*, which, when brought back to Portugal, were worth one thousand three hundred and twenty reais. 

At that time, I caused King Sebastian to be warned that it was expedient for the price of gold to be increased, and I taught this from the pulpit, yet I achieved nothing. But up to the present day, *tostões* both old and new—the latter being of such small weight—are exchanged at the same price of one hundred reais. Gradually the old ones disappear, either carried to foreign nations or taken by goldsmiths who reduce them into a mass of silver and sell it at a far higher price, which is what silver is worth now in Portugal. Similarly, even those gold coins, although they are rare today, are exchanged by many at the price of one thousand reais, or certainly were being exchanged until my departure from that Kingdom.

At this point, I should advise that although the copper coin, which is called a *real* in Portugal, retains the same value whether gold or silver coins are raised or lowered in value—to the effect that the sum of gold or other coins that was owed, or in tribute, or in penalty imposed by law is paid by it, as shown in dispute 312—nevertheless, for exchange <term>from place to place</term><note>original: *de loco ad locum*, referring to international bills of exchange.</note>, it does not have the same value. This is as the practice of merchants has always maintained and maintains today, and will be discussed in its proper place below. For ten *reals*, which today in Portugal are worth four hundred reais, will not be paid in Castile as eleven *reals*, even though in Castile eleven *reals* are worth only three hundred seventy-four maravedis; instead, only ten *reals* will be paid, the exchange being made to equality, saying nothing meanwhile of the increase due to the exchange itself. In such exchanges, account is taken rather of the quantity of silver, by comparison made with an equal quantity of silver, or of the quantity of gold, by comparison similarly made with an equal quantity of gold of the same goodness, than of the quantities of copper and its value in different places.

Therefore, the maravedis of Castile—since the silver *real* in Portugal was worth thirty-six reais and two-sevenths—were of greater value among merchants than the copper Portuguese *real*, in that proportion by which thirty-six and two-sevenths reais exceed thirty.

### ## Ludwig Molina on Contracts

#### ### Dispute 400 (Continued)

...thirty-four <term>maravedís</term><note>A small Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account.</note>, and accordingly, the silver <term>real</term><note>The *real* (royal) was a standard silver coin used in both Spain and Portugal, though their internal values differed.</note> was exchanged at an equal rate from **Portugal** to **Castile** and vice versa. Similarly, a <term>ducat</term><note>A gold coin used throughout Europe as a standard of value.</note> was exchanged for a ducat, even though it was worth four hundred <term>reais</term> in **Portugal** and three hundred and seventy-five maravedís in **Castile**. Therefore, since the silver real in **Portugal** was raised to forty reais, it is now of lesser value than a maravedí in the same proportion that forty reais exceeds the number thirty-four. Because the silver real was raised to forty reais and the Portuguese silver <term>tostão</term><note>A Portuguese silver coin originally worth 100 reais.</note> was reduced in weight, the value of the Portuguese copper real decreased accordingly. Consequently, when compared to that same copper coinage, the value of those Portuguese currencies has increased among merchants. In the same way, the value must increase in the exchange of other things for them; a law that does not increase their price in comparison to the same copper coinage is irrational. For who but a fool would today give a gold coin in **Portugal**—which was previously worth 27.5 silver reals—for only 25, simply because the silver real was raised in **Portugal** to a price of 40 reais? This is especially true since the same currency is worth far more when brought to the Kingdom of **Castile** or any other nation, and since forty reais today buys no more goods in **Portugal** than thirty-six did previously. Instead, the prices of all things have continually increased in **Portugal** relative to that copper coinage. Therefore, on this occasion, since the silver real was raised to forty reais, the value of gold coins rightly began to increase continually in relation to that same copper coinage. From this, you will understand that today in **Portugal**, half a pound <note>Original: *selibra*. In this context, a half-pound (8 ounces) of gold.</note> of 22 and 1/8 carat gold is worth far more than 30,000 reais, in the same proportion that 40 reais exceeds 36 and 2/7. We have said so much about the price of silver coins in **Portugal** to elucidate and demonstrate these points, which will shed no small light on what is to be said in this entire matter concerning <term>exchanges</term><note>The "exchange" (Latin: *cambium*) refers to the professional business of trading currencies between different locations.</note>.

<margin>A Question</margin>
Since in **Castile** and **Portugal** the price of gold bullion is not fixed by law, nor likewise silver—except for that in **Castile** which is eleven <term>deniers</term><note>A measure of purity where 12 deniers is pure silver.</note> and 4 grains, such that a half-pound of it cannot be sold for more than sixty-five reals—and since it is not forbidden to buy it at a lower price, and it is daily bought and sold at that price or lower as each person is able, the answer to the following question will be easy: is the purchase of silver unjust, carrying an obligation of restitution? Many, when they need money, are forced to sell silver artifacts they own. But when they offer them to goldsmiths or merchants for purchase, they find no higher price for them than if the silver were not fashioned into items, even though the <term>workmanship</term><note>Original: *opificium*. The labor and artistry involved in creating the object.</note> may sometimes be worth a great deal. Sometimes they do not even find a price for that silver higher than sixty-four reals per half-pound, so that, besides losing the value of the workmanship, they are forced to drop one real below the bullion value for every half-pound.

<margin>Decision 16</margin>
It is asked, therefore, whether such a purchase is unjust and requires restitution. I believe it must be answered that,

<column-break/>

since in this matter no transgression of human laws occurs (as has been said), and since the goldsmiths or other merchants who buy these items invest a great deal of money to resell them later at a higher price after refining and preparing them, the business should not be condemned as unjust. This is provided that, considering the manner of purchase (which falls to goldsmiths by their office just as it falls to booksellers to buy books offered to them at a lower price to resell them at a higher price), the price they pay is not judged by a prudent person's arbitration to fall below the <term>minimum just price</term><note>The "just price" (*iustum pretium*) in Catholic economic theory was not a single point but a range (lowest, middle, and highest) determined by common estimation.</note>, taking into account all concurrent circumstances—including the fact that the goods were offered voluntarily. For the workmanship can be of such value, and there could be such hope of reselling the item shortly at a far higher price, that the purchase could rightly be judged unjust by a prudent person, requiring restitution for the amount it fell short of the minimum just price. This remains true even if the half-pound were bought for sixty-five reals. The fact that the prices of such things do not consist in an indivisible point, but have a wide range between the highest and lowest, does not prevent this. However, do not condemn what you find to be the accepted custom in this area, for that custom does much to ensure the price in such a transaction is not considered unjust.

<margin>A Question</margin>
Sometimes those who sell such silver are accustomed to bargain with the buyers that they shall not resell it to another within a certain time, but that the sellers themselves may redeem it within that time at a certain price higher than what they received for it. 

<margin>17</margin>
Some doubt whether this is licit or whether a <term>palliated usury</term><note>A "palliated" or "hidden" usury was a contract designed to look like a legitimate sale or partnership but which functioned as a guaranteed interest-bearing loan, which was forbidden by Church law.</note> is involved. 

<margin>Decision 17</margin>
I believe it must be answered that if a true sale takes place—such that if the silver is lost during that middle period, it is lost to the buyer—and the first contract was just according to what has been said, and in the second contract no higher price is set than what the first buyer could justly receive from any other buyer for the same silver, then neither usury nor injustice occurs in that contract. Rather, it is a favor the first buyer does for the first seller by making himself unable to sell that merchandise to anyone else during that time. This has also been shown in Dispute 376 using other examples.

Finally, you will easily understand this from this whole dispute: in the past, when there were <term>ducats</term> in this Kingdom of **Castile** worth 375 maravedís and the same ducats (or <term>crusados</term><note>The *cruzado* was the Portuguese equivalent of the ducat.</note>) in **Portugal** were worth 400 reais, money exchanges were made from place to place. Many other things were established with mention of the ducat, not only in these Kingdoms but from them to other provinces and vice versa. Today, likewise, exchanges and contracts are made under the name of the "ducat," even though, after variations in the value of gold over time, there is no longer any coin in these Kingdoms of that exact value. Instead, that value which was once understood by the name "ducat," and is still understood today, is paid by making an equalization with that value in other coins, as daily usage testifies.

## Whether it is lawful to receive more for money whose value, while it is coined, has been established by public authority.

### DISPUTE 401.
### SUMMARY.

1. *The value of money is fixed by public authority; however, if there is a loss of potential profit <note>original: "ratione lucri cessante"</note>, it may undergo some increase in price.*
2. *In Portugal, it is prohibited under heavy penalty to destroy silver coins, even those of another kingdom.*
3. *The same applies in Castile, number 3.*
4. *When it is lawful for the price of money to be increased, even if its value is fixed by public authority.*
5. *The Portuguese and Castilian laws that imposed a price on gold coins do not bind the conscience today.*

The things said in the preceding dispute will shed light on this one. It should be observed, however, that a custom has been accepted in some provinces, especially in **Italy** and **Flanders**, where although certain coins have a common price among them, it is not so fixed that it cannot—like other merchandise not taxed by law—increase or decrease in price according to their abundance or scarcity, or according to the number of people seeking them. And so I hear that although the common value of a gold <term>scudo</term><note>A gold coin used in various Italian states.</note> in **Rome** is eleven and a half <term>Giulii</term><note>A silver coin named after Pope Julius II.</note>, nevertheless their value suddenly increases by a few copper coins (sometimes even twice in a month) and then decreases again. This increase or decrease of more or fewer copper coins happens according to the demand and rarity of those scudi, and according to other occurring circumstances. Where such a custom flourishes, no one can doubt that it is lawful to receive that increase.

<margin>1</margin>
The entire difficulty, therefore, is where the prices of coins are fixed by public authority and law so that they are stable, as they are usually taxed in the **Spains** <note>Referring to the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula under the Spanish Habsburgs.</note> and regularly in other provinces, especially when the coins are native to those provinces. Indeed, it must be said that even then, by reason of "lost profit" <note>A legal and ethical concept where a person is compensated for the profit they could have made if they hadn't performed a specific transaction.</note>, it is lawful to receive something beyond the price fixed by law, equivalent to what that profit is estimated to be. For example, if someone possessing certain money could transport it to a place where it is worth more, or use it to buy merchandise in a place where the currency of the Kingdom in which he resides is not accepted (or only accepted at a loss), then he can receive, for the exchange of such money for another, as much as the profit is estimated to be which would actually be lost to him from that exchange. Johannes Medina <note>Juan de Medina (1490–1546), a prominent Spanish theologian who wrote on the ethics of business and exchange.</note> affirms this with others in his third question on exchange. And in a similar event, we said at the end of Dispute 364 that regarding the "lost profit" on wheat fixed by law—which someone wanted to transport to a place where it was worth more—something could be received beyond the legally fixed price, provided no scandal arises. On this same basis, if a goldsmith has money ready for gilding, or for making an artifact out of it in which he will profit by reason of the very pure material, and in order to grant it to someone who is pleading for it, he deprives himself of that profit, he will be able to receive,

<column-break/>

beyond the common price of those coins, an estimation of that profit of which he deprives himself for that reason.

<margin>2</margin>
In **Portugal**, in Book 5 of the Ordinances, Title 6, last paragraph, it is prohibited to destroy silver coins, or to order them to be destroyed so that an artifact may be made from them, or for any other reason, even if they belong to another Kingdom. The established penalty is ten years of exile to the regions of **Africa** and the loss of half of one’s goods, to be divided equally between the accuser and the King’s treasury. And under the same penalties, it is forbidden to pick out coins of greater weight and sell them by weight. Moreover, if someone does any of these things and is among the number of the King's ministers whose duty it is to receive the King's money, he incurs the death penalty and the loss of all his goods. I do not know, however, whether that law is executed with such rigor that a goldsmith or another private person who destroys some silver coins to make an artifact should be condemned for a mortal sin. This is especially true after the royal silver <term>real</term> reached the price of forty <term>reais</term>, and the quantity of the <term>tostão</term> was diminished, as was related in the preceding dispute. But if that law remained in its full strength, with the circumstances persisting as they were when it was passed, and if it were fully enforced, I would not hesitate to say it binds under pain of mortal sin, considering the bitterness of the penalty and the damage that happens to the Republic when coins of equal value but greater weight are destroyed, as usually happens when any coins are destroyed. However, that law is not understood to apply to silver coins that do not have a set value in **Portugal**, as clearly established in Law 3, Title 18, Part 4 of the *Extravagantes* laws.

<margin>3 † <insert>Castilian Law.</insert></margin>
In this † Kingdom <note>Referring to Castile, where Molina was likely writing.</note> also, by Law 67, Title 21, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, joined with Law 6, Title 17, Book 8, it is prohibited under penalty of death and loss of all goods to destroy gold, silver, or copper coins, or to export them from this Kingdom. However, this law, which was passed by the Catholic Monarchs <note>Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon.</note>, I do not understand to apply to those ancient coins which today are very rare and in whose place others have succeeded, if any are destroyed for the purpose of gilding. For it is a small matter, and the change of times and circumstances renders it lawful.

Although the exchange of coins in the same place ought to be done at an equality of value, nevertheless, if there were a probable fear that a certain coin would shortly be reduced in value by public authority, it could lawfully be bought at a lower price than that fixed by law. Because that fear and probability that it is to be reduced in value makes it of lesser value: not unlike money that has been placed in a storm or depends on the danger of the sea, which is justly bought at a lower price than the one fixed by law. So says Medina in the place cited, last paragraph. Meanwhile, however, until that money is diminished by public authority, it is lawfully given at the taxed price, because in truth it still retains its ancient value to the effect that it can be lawfully given and spent for those uses in which it would be spent if there were no such fear.

<margin>4 ‡ <insert>Question.</insert></margin>
Medina, in the cited question, contends that while the law of public taxation of money holds its force, it is a sin to receive a greater price for money than the one fixed by law, even if the material has many advantages—for example, because the gold is of higher purity <note>original: "plurium caracterum"</note>, as ancient coins usually are, and is more useful for gilding and decoration...

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

<column-break/>

...to health, and to other similar things. Medina’s reasoning is that when money is "taxed" <note>In this context, 'taxed' (taxatur) means having its value legally fixed by the state.</note>, an account is made of the purity of its material and its various uses; once all these factors are weighed, the value of the material is established by the "stamp" <note>original: "signo"</note>, which constitutes its existence as money. Because of this, he says, just as it is a sin to accept a higher price for grain that has a legally fixed price—because the "just price" established by law exists as a single, indivisible point—so too it is a sin to accept a price for such coins beyond what the law mandates. If such a premium is taken, it is subject to restitution. However, he adds that if a custom begins to prevail where something extra is accepted for certain gold coins, and the Prince or his Senate knows this and does not punish or contradict it, then it must be judged that it is not his will for the law to be binding in that regard; thus, that increase can be safely accepted. I would even add that, from that point on, such an increase enters the limits of the **natural just price** <note>The 'natural just price' was a concept in Scholastic economics referring to the market value determined by common estimation, as opposed to a 'legal price' fixed by decree.</note>, and can subsequently be extended within those limits—which, unlike a legally fixed price, is not a single fixed point. By this reasoning, Medina defends as free from guilt and the burden of restitution the custom of accepting a price increase for certain ancient gold coins. According to this opinion, however, one would have to say that those who first began to accept such an increase—before that silent and presumed consent of the Prince—not only sinned but were also bound to restore the difference to those from whom they took it, since the law still retained its force.

<margin>TO su... lis n</margin> However, **Soto** (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 9), **Navarrus** (in *Manual*, ch. 17, n. 288), **Covarruvias**, and **Sylvester**—with whom **Gaius** agrees in his work *On Exchanges*—assert that a coin can be viewed in two ways. One, insofar as it is money, in its "essence as money." The other, regarding its material: namely, as it consists of a certain amount of gold, of greater or lesser purity, weight, etc. They say that by reason of the material, if the concurrent circumstances warrant it, it is lawful to accept an increase beyond the legally fixed price. This is because the coin is "taxed" only in its essence as a coin, serving as a price for buying things; even if, when it is taxed, its material value is taken into account to establish its value as money. Many of them add that no one can be forced to give a higher price for it, or to accept it at a lower valuation than its legally fixed price. For this reason, it is lawful to purchase it at the legal price and later exchange that same coin for a price above the legal rate.

Regarding this matter, I will state my opinion in a few words. First, I believe it must be observed and established: whenever coins are minted and their price is set, the material—viewed with all the benefits that can be derived from it—is **never** worth more than the price imposed on the coins; indeed, it is worth less. This is because the expenses incurred in minting the coins are drawn from the material, and any tax owed to the Prince is paid from it. A Prince would be very foolish to impose a lower price on the coins he orders to be minted than the value of the material from which they are made. Therefore, based on the abundance of the material at that time, all its uses, and all other occurring circumstances, the price is imposed on the coins; at that time, no one would find a higher price for them by reason of the material or any other circumstance. In this, Medina speaks the truth.

<column-break/>

Next, it must be said that when an "inferior" money <note>A coin with less gold content or lower purity.</note> is minted in terms of carats or weight, and a price is imposed on it equal to or greater than the preceding money, the law that had imposed the price on the previous money is considered to have ceased. People may then increase the price of that preceding money within the limits of its "natural just price," considering all concurrent circumstances, unless the Prince commands otherwise for a rational cause. A law establishing the contrary would be irrational and unjust unless there is a valid reason for it, since it is irrational and injurious to subjects to set equal prices for things of unequal value without a rational cause. With this doctrine of ours—which is clear and manifest in itself—the laws of **Castile** and **Portugal** regarding gold coins agree. For **Philip I** <note>Philip I "the Handsome" (r. 1506). Molina is citing the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century legal code.</note>, in the third law of the declarations, after he had taxed <term>scuta</term> <note>The 'escudo', a gold coin.</note> so that they would henceforth be worth 400 <term>maravedis</term> <note>A Spanish unit of account.</note> and commanded that no one for any reason could accept a higher price for them, he declared that the value of those <term>ducats</term> of purer gold (which **Ferdinand and Isabella** had ordered minted) was of greater value than they were when they were first ordered to be struck. This was due to their greater weight and the greater quantity of gold they contained. He commanded that they be worth 429 maravedis, as explained in the preceding dispute. Surely, no one could rightly condemn someone who, before that increase in the price of the scuta, accepted a price for the ducats proportional to the scuta, taking into account not only their weight but also the greater quantity of very pure gold they contain. Similarly, in **Portuguese law**, it is explained that the value of a grain of gold in a <term>cruzado</term> <note>A Portuguese gold coin.</note> of 24 carats is higher than the value of a grain of gold in coins of 22 carats and one-eighth. It is stated that the grade of gold in these latter coins is worth six and a half <term>reais</term> <note>The 'real', the Portuguese unit of currency.</note>, while a grain of the former is worth seven reais and a third of a "septil," and thus the value of the grain in intermediate coins is declared in a certain order. Third, it must be said that when gold coins are minted and their price is first set, there is usually a great abundance of that gold; according to that abundance and other circumstances, the price is set. Surely, if over time the circumstances vary—the purer gold coins are taken out of the Kingdom, or consumed in gilding and other services, leading to a great rarity and penury of them—and they are much desired for gilding, or for ornament and pomp, or other similar things, and for that reason the value of their material increases greatly, one must not believe that the legislators intend for the old "tax law" to persist. Even if they did, it would not be just or equitable. Therefore, at that time, without...

<summary>Molina argues that while money has a legally fixed price, this law ceases to bind when the state issues inferior currency or when the intrinsic material value of older coins increases due to scarcity or alternative uses like jewelry. He supports this by citing Spanish and Portuguese monetary laws that adjusted the value of older, purer gold coins relative to newer ones.</summary>
<keywords>monetary value, just price, legal price, gold coins, ducats, maravedis, reais, carats, Castilian law, Portuguese law, Philip I, Ferdinand and Isabella, Bartolomé de Medina, Domingo de Soto</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of currency valuation from the previous page. It concludes Dispute 401 regarding the "natural" versus "legal" price of coins and begins Dispute 402, which examines the ethics of agents or "ministers" who profit from fluctuating exchange rates while transporting funds.</meta>

...can be sold without sin and without the burden of making restitution at their natural just price. This applies not only when they are used as a price in exchange for other things, but as objects of trade themselves. The reasoning remains the same for money regardless of how it is viewed, as João Medina <note>original: "Io. Med." referring to the Spanish theologian Juan Medina (1490–1546)</note> rightly affirms. Thus, upright public officials—who do not use the law to harshly or unjustly vex their subjects—rightly do not oppose or punish this. Instead, they interpret such laws through *equity* <term>epicheia: a legal concept where the spirit of the law is followed over its literal wording when circumstances change</term>, recognizing that these laws no longer apply because the circumstances that existed when they were first passed have changed. 

<margin>Decision</margin> Therefore, although the laws of Ferdinand and Isabella <note>The "Catholic Monarchs" of Spain (r. 1474–1516)</note>, included in Title 2, Book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compendium of Spanish law</note>, contain many other provisions that still hold power today, the specific regulations regarding the fixed value of ducats no longer apply. This was declared by King Philip <note>Likely Philip II of Spain</note> in the cited Law 13. Even before that declaration, as has been said, those laws lacked force; likewise, the words commanding that those fixed rates be observed no longer carry authority today. 

Furthermore, although Philip commanded that no one should receive more for *scudos* than the price he fixed (because there was a great abundance of them at the time the law was passed), when he addressed the "old ducats," he merely defined their current value by comparing them to the *scudo*. He did not add those restrictive words forbidding anyone from accepting a higher price. This is because, due to their rarity, necessity, and utility for certain purposes, it is perfectly lawful to accept their full natural value, considering all the current circumstances. 

To summarize: at any time, it is lawful to receive for any coin whatever amount could be lawfully received for an equal amount of gold of the same weight and purity. The value of the metal is not lessened simply because it has been struck into a coin; rather, it is in a better condition and of greater value when coined. For this reason, one might even receive a bit more for the coin than for an equal weight of raw gold.

From what has been said in this preceding dispute, it is clear that the Portuguese laws which impose prices on gold coins do not bind the conscience today. Instead, for coins made of less pure gold, for which a price of one thousand or five hundred *reais* <note>The *real* (plural *reais*) was the standard unit of currency in Portugal and Spain</note> was established, a higher price may be accepted within the limits of their natural value. The law that fixed the price of silver *reals* lost its force the moment the silver *real* was raised to the value of forty *reais*. At that same moment, the moral scruples and difficulties vanished regarding whether one could accept a price beyond the official rate for the purpose of transporting them elsewhere; for today, there is no one who would offer more than forty *reais* for them.

Since the laws of both Castile and Portugal now declare how much old gold coins have risen in price and what they are worth today, it is established that if a debtor wishes to pay a creditor in those coins, the creditor must be compelled to accept them at the price declared by the laws. Nor can they be justly accepted for a lower price, because that is the minimum just value they hold today; no one would give them for less unless they were ignorant of their value. Regarding a 

<column-break/>

higher price—which is found today for certain coins and is justly accepted beyond what is declared by law (as was said regarding the Portuguese one thousand or five hundred *reais* coins)—no creditor can be forced to accept them at that higher price. This is because that premium or "increase" <note>original: "incrementum"</note> belongs to their natural price, not their legal price. The natural price is not a single fixed point; usually, there are those who give them at the old legally fixed price, which (as long as nothing else is decreed) should not be considered to fall outside the limits of the lowest just price. Therefore, the debtor himself should find someone willing to give a higher price for them, and then pay his debt in other forms of money.

---

## Whether a minister delivering payment in gold coins, and justly exchanging them for a higher price on the journey, can retain the increase for himself.

# DISPUTE CCCCII.

### SUMMARY

1 *When a minister or depositary may keep for himself the increase in value of the money he was delivering to a creditor.*
2 *The difference between profit <note>original: "lucrum"</note> and the "fruit" <note>original: "fructus"</note> of a thing.*
3 *What constitutes the "fruit" of a thing.*
4 *In what case a depositary is not bound to return the increase gained from a deposit.*

The scenario proposed in this dispute was a frequent occurrence in Portugal at the time I was explaining these matters. Since there were many coins of one thousand and five hundred *reais*, and debts were paid in them or they were handed over to agents so that goods could be bought for their owners, a doubt arose. According to what has been said, these coins could be justly traded with a premium <note>An "increase" above face value</note> once they ceased to circulate at the fixed rate. 

The question is: if a minister <note>An agent, official, or servant</note> is given these coins to deliver to a creditor or to buy something, and he first exchanges them for a premium (knowing the creditor would accept them at that premium, or seeking someone else who would), can he justly keep that profit for himself? Could he then pay the debt in full using other money, or buy the goods as if he had used the gold coins, while pocketing the difference? Or is he bound to restore it, and to whom should restitution be made? 

The same doubt applies to the King’s ministers who receive his revenues and other debts, and to other similar agents. Since they receive many payments in these types of coins (which they are not bound to accept at a higher value), and later, according to the orders of the King or their employer, they pay out stipends or debts, can they keep the profit for themselves if they exchange that money for a premium in the meantime? Or are they bound to restore it?

### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

Regarding the proposed conclusions. **First:** In all the scenarios presented, if an agent or a custodian, after exchanging gold coins at a profit, uses that profit to buy back similar gold coins at a lower price and then carries out the transaction as originally instructed by his employer, he may lawfully keep the profit as the "fruit of his own industry" <note>Molina uses "industry" (*industria*) to mean the personal skill, effort, and cleverness of the individual in business.</note>. This holds true even if he used someone else’s money as the instrument to acquire that profit. This is proven because he caused no loss, neither to the person whose business he was conducting nor to the person to whom the money was to be delivered. Indeed, since he delivered the money at the proper time—and as we assume, it was of the exact same type and value as what he had originally received for the task—he has sufficiently satisfied his duty by returning that money. Therefore, he can keep the increase and the profit for himself. This conclusion will be further strengthened by what is said in the third section.

**Second conclusion.** If the owner’s will—at least his "habitual" or implied will—was that the debt be paid in that specific currency because he desired the benefit of the recipient more than that of the messenger, and the recipient would have sold those coins at the same or a higher profit, then the messenger is bound to restore the entire profit to the recipient (unless he delivered coins of the exact same quality). This is proven because, against the will of both the sender and the recipient, and therefore unjustly, he deprives the recipient of money of that specific quality, and consequently of the just profit the recipient would have perceived from it. Therefore, he commits an injury and is bound to make restitution.

**Third conclusion.** If either the recipient was not going to make any profit from money of that quality (because he would have spent it at the lowest, common price), or if the sender was habitually content that the messenger should enjoy the profit rather than the recipient, or if the sender simply did not care about the matter, I believe the messenger can lawfully keep that profit for himself. It does not matter if the sender might have preferred the profit for himself rather than his servant. In proving this conclusion, we must recall what we showed in Dispute 327: namely, that whatever a usurer, a thief, or a custodian acquires by trading with someone else’s "consumable" property <term>consumptibili: goods like money or grain that are "consumed" or used up when they are traded</term>—whether acquired through usury, theft, or held in deposit—belongs to them. They are not bound to restore the profit, but only the original property itself or its equivalent value. Additionally, they must pay for any "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: a legal term for the profit a person would have made if their money hadn't been withheld</term> that the owners suffered because of a delay in restitution, whether that amount be large, small, or nothing at all. From this, we can construct an argument to prove the first part of the conclusion: In this event, the profit belongs no more to the recipient or the sender than it would if the messenger had stolen the money from them or extorted it via usury. But in those cases, neither a thief nor a usurer would be bound to restore the profit made from the trade, but only to keep both parties "harmless" (indemnity), as we clearly showed in the cited dispute. Therefore, the messenger is not bound to restore the profit either, but only to keep the parties harmless—which he indeed does by delivering to the recipient 

<column-break/>

the value that the money would have had in the recipient’s own hands. Furthermore, we can argue this way: if the messenger had gained nothing with that money, but had lost it gambling or spent it buying something at its lowest value, the recipient would not have gained any higher value from it. Therefore, no confessor would command that restitution be made except at the value the money would have otherwise had. Thus, in the case proposed, the messenger is not bound to any other restitution. 

**Objection:** You might object that the profit—whether obtained by a thief, a usurer, or a messenger—is derived from someone else's property and from its inherent value, since it is that property which is traded. Therefore, the profit does not belong to them but to the owner, or to the intended recipient, acting as the "fruit" of that property and not of the skill of the person exchanging it. This would be true even if the owner or recipient were not going to perceive that fruit, just as the offspring of a horse or the crops of a field belong to the owner of the horse or field, even if the owner was not the one to harvest them. To this argument, while the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied.

<margin>2</margin> For although that profit is perceived *from* that thing and its value, it is nonetheless not the "fruit of the thing," but the fruit of the "industry" of the person trading and exchanging it at his own risk and for his own benefit. The owner of the property does not lose the thing through that exchange as long as he is sufficiently satisfied, and the person trading it is responsible for the "eviction" <term>evictio: a legal guarantee that the seller has the right to transfer ownership</term> to the one with whom he exchanges or sells it, should the original owner reclaim it. The fruit <note>† original: "fructus"</note> of a horse or a field, however, is not the thing itself or its value, but the *use* of it, or something emanating from it, or the price received for such fruits (which is a further fruit perceived from the fruit itself, such as the work of a horse or apples from a field). But what is acquired by trading a thing solely at the risk of the one trading it is the fruit of "industry." Therefore, the profit we are discussing belongs to the messenger who exchanges the money at his own risk and benefit.

<margin>3</margin> The **second part of the conclusion**—namely, that if the sender was habitually content that the messenger should enjoy the profit rather than the recipient, or did not care, the messenger may lawfully keep the profit even if the recipient would have made the same or more—is proven thus: whether the money is sent as a gift, as payment for a debt, or in exchange for something else, the money does not belong to the recipient until he accepts it. Before acceptance, it still belongs to the sender, who can revoke the gift or the mandate, as has been said in Dispute 263 and elsewhere. Therefore, whatever the agent or messenger does with that money based on the presumed will of the owner (at least assuming the owner would not be displeased) before the recipient accepts it, he does no injury to the recipient. Consequently, by depriving the recipient of the profit he would have made, he neither commits an injury nor is he bound to restore the profit that ceased to exist for that reason. If, however, the person carrying the money was the *servant* of the recipient, or someone else who received it specifically in the name of the recipient, then the recipient would have acquired ownership of it at that moment, as discussed elsewhere. In that case, the messenger would indeed be doing an injury by depriving

He distinguishes between the natural growth of property (like crops) and the profit generated by a businessman's risk and skill.</summary>

...when he acquired that profit, and therefore he is bound to restore to the owner the entire profit that would have been perceived from that money, even if the messenger <note>original: *inter nuncius*</note> had reported less or no profit from the sale and exchange of it. The third part of the conclusion—namely, that it is true that nothing prevents the sender from being so disposed that he would rather the profit go to himself than to the messenger—is proven as follows: if the messenger had stolen that money from the sender, such a profit would not belong to the owner of the money, despite the fact that the owner would have preferred the profit for himself rather than the thief. Instead, the messenger would only be bound to keep the owner "harmless" <note>meaning to compensate for any actual loss or missed gain caused by the theft</note>. Therefore, in the case proposed, the profit does not belong to the owner of the money but to the servant, regardless of the owner's personal desire for the profit.

<margin>4</margin> Observe this: when a depositary <note>a person or institution with whom money is lodged</note> is of such a kind that the ownership of the deposit belongs to him and not to the depositor—because he accepts the deposits at his own risk and is not bound to return the exact same coins he received, but rather an equivalent sum (as is usually the case with public depositaries of money and receivers called *Almoxarifes* <term>Almoxarife: a Portuguese or Spanish tax collector or treasurer</term> or Royal Treasurers, and others like them)—then what has been said applies even more strongly. For even if they receive gold currency, they satisfy their obligation by returning what was deposited in any form of money, paying the King or others to whom they are ministers according to their instructions. Therefore, if they gain anything by exchanging such gold coins, the profit belongs to them. This is one of the advantages and, as it were, the stipends <note>regular payments or perks of office</note> that they receive from their duty.

->The utility of the exchange of money from place to place, and concerning such exchange when the banker receives payment in advance.<-

### DISPVTATION CCCCIII.

**SUMMARY**

1 *Why the exchange of money from place to place is useful and necessary.*
2 *How it is lawful for bankers <note>original: *campsoribus*</note> to receive some profit or increase for the commutation of money from place to place (also in number 4).*
3 *Exchange from place to place occurs in two ways.*
5 *The transportation of money from place to place is a disadvantage to the one seeking exchange, and its value can be estimated in price.*
6 *The just price to be given to the banker for exchange between places is left to the judgment of a prudent person; indeed, it is accustomed to be increased or decreased according to various circumstances.*
7 *A double contract occurs in the exchange from place to place.*
8 *How a banker in the exchange from place to place can commit injustice and usury.*

<margin>1</margin> Having explained "minute exchange" <note>the local changing of small currency or different coins within the same city</note> up to this point, we must consequently speak of exchange from place to place, or "exchange by letters" <note>referring to letters of credit or bills of exchange</note>. This exchange is useful and necessary to men for many reasons. For they frequently lack money in one place which they possess in another, whether for transporting goods from the place where they need it, or for residing there, or for

<column-break/>

making any other expenses there. Nor can they always transport the money from the other place, either because it is prohibited under heavy penalties to take currency out of that kingdom, or because it could not be transferred without great danger from the sea, robbers, or other similar threats, or not without great expense, labor, and trouble. Or perhaps the money is needed more quickly in the other place than it could be moved, or, even if none of these obstacles exist, that specific money is not valid in the place where they need it, or is not worth as much as it is in the place where they have it. For these and other reasons, it is often useful to men—both for private good and for the common good of republics—to exchange money in one place for money in another. What we intend to examine, however, is whether it is lawful for bankers to receive some profit or increase for such a commutation of money from place to place.

<margin>2</margin> Because money can have different values in distinct places for various reasons, it must be considered in the following discussion whether, by reason of that diversity of value, the price may rise or fall for the contract to be lawful and just. Above all, it must be examined here whether—assuming the value of the money is equal in both places—it is lawful for the banker to receive an increase as a "just stipend for transportation" on account of the formal or virtual transportation of the money from place to place for the sake of the person requesting the exchange.

<margin>3</margin> Such an exchange can be done in two ways. First, the banker receives the money first in one place so that he may later give it, either himself or through his correspondent, in another place. In this way, no appearance of a loan <note>original: *mutui*</note> or usury <note>the illegal practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates</note> is seen on the part of the banker. For example, if someone going to Rome gives 100 to a banker here so that when he arrives in Rome, he may receive 90 from the banker or his correspondent <note>The person pays a fee of 10 for the convenience and safety of not carrying the cash</note>. Second, the banker provides the money first, so that he may receive it back with an increase, either himself or through his correspondent, in another place. In this latter case, a loan is mixed in. Legal scholars do not speak of both types of exchange in the same way; we will speak first in this disputation of the former type of exchange, and in the following disputation of the latter.

<margin>5</margin> The scholars agree that the first method of exchange with some increase is lawful, provided that the increase does not exceed the value of that formal or virtual transportation of money from place to place according to the judgment of a prudent person, taking into account the distance, the dangers, and other concurrent circumstances. This is the view of Conradus, Johannes Medina, Soto, Cajetan, Navarro, Gabriel, Major, and others. The Portuguese Ordinances also agree, and King Sebastian did not prohibit this exchange in the law he passed in the year 1570; rather, he approved it, as is clear to anyone reading it. Furthermore, Pope Pius V agrees in the Bull <note>a formal papal decree</note> he issued concerning exchanges. The reason for this assertion is as follows:

<margin>6</margin> Because that transportation for the benefit of the one seeking the exchange has an estimable price. For a muleteer <note>original: *agaso*</note> or a sailor lawfully receives a competent stipend for the transportation of money from place to place, and this stipend is greater as the places are further apart, as the journeys are subject to more dangers, and as the sum of money is larger; and so it is with other circumstances that can increase the value of transportation.

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

...Therefore, the banker <note>original: *campfor*</note> lawfully and properly accepts a suitable stipend for this type of transportation. It does not matter that, for the most part, the banker does not formally <note>meaning physically moving the specific coins</note> transfer the money himself, but instead has servants or correspondents in distant places who pay the money to the clients. For, as the doctors of law and theology commonly and correctly observe, he provides the same convenience and the same effect to those who seek exchange in those places as if he were formally transferring the money to them. The fact that he can do this more easily than others, with very few or almost no expenses, and without risk or labor, is a result of his own industry and his successful status in that field. This does not prevent him from being able to receive a suitable stipend for the effect he provides to others for their own convenience. It must be observed, however, that the ease he has in many places—being able to transport money to them, and from there to others, not for one person but for many, and being able to simultaneously attend to other negotiations and profits—decreases the value of that transportation. Thus, the banker cannot then justly receive as much from each individual as he would if he were formally transporting only the coins of that one person or

<margin>6</margin> of a few. However, the just price <note>original: *pretium iustum*</note> for this kind of exchange, if it is not fixed by law (as it is usually not fixed), does not consist of an indivisible point, but has a certain range to be defined by the judgment of a prudent person, in the same way we described in Discussion 348 regarding the range of the natural just price of other things. Custom contributes not a little to judging whether a price in this matter is just, provided that the custom was not introduced through the tyranny of monopolies or an insatiable thirst for profit, which increase the prices of things more than the nature of the matter requires. Indeed, a multitude of those seeking exchange and a scarcity of bankers increases this kind of price; just as, conversely, a multitude of bankers and a scarcity of those seeking exchange decreases it. This is no different than in other things where a multitude of buyers and a scarcity of sellers increases the price, whereas a scarcity of buyers and a multitude of sellers decreases it—a point noted regarding the price of exchanges by Medina, Navarrus, and Major <note>Bartholomew de Medina, Martin de Azpilcueta (Navarrus), and John Major, prominent 16th-century scholastic thinkers</note> in the places cited. Although Medina does not seem to have fully grasped that reasoning regarding "virtual transportation."

In the type of exchange being discussed in this and the following dispute, 
<margin>7</margin> a twofold † contract is mixed together. One is a contract of permutation <note>an exchange or barter</note> of money for money. And this must be done according to equality of value. The other is a contract of hiring out labor and industry for the purpose of transferring money, at least virtually, from place to place; it is by reason of this second part that a premium <note>original: *incrementum*</note> is accepted. Ownership is transferred as much in the exchange of the money as it is in the payment of the premium for the labor applied (or to be applied), as is clear in itself.

<margin>8</margin> In the exchange we are discussing in this dispute, injustice can occur on the part of the banker—carrying the burden of restitution—if a greater premium is taken than is worthy of the industry and service provided. However, usury <note>original: *vsura*; the sin of charging interest on a loan</note> cannot occur here, because the banker himself is not giving a loan, either formally or virtually. But because the person who enters the contract of exchange with him gives a virtual loan to the banker (insofar as he first pays him in one place so that the banker may return it later in another), that client could commit usury, with the burden of restitution. For example, if the client sees that the banker needs money here, and gives it to him with the condition that he restore the same amount in a distant place, then the client is seeking a burden over and above the principal—namely, the burden of transporting the money to a distant place—which

<column-break/>

burden is estimable in money. Consequently, the client commits usury, with the burden of restoring as much as that burden is valued. So say Navarrus, in the places cited, and others. Furthermore, the client is held to a far greater restitution if it was agreed that an equal quantity of money be given in a place where it is worth more (based on the reasons to be explained in the following sections), because he would virtually receive a far greater premium for that anticipated delivery of money. When, however, money is of equal value in both places and the distance between locations is not great, since the price of transportation would then be modest, it can often be presumed that the banker wishes to waive it out of liberality and in compensation for the benefit he received through that modest premium. But when the premium is large, slight conjectures would not suffice for one to safely persuade himself that the waiver is being made out of liberality and gratitude. But if two people mutually needed to transport money—one, for example, from Lisbon <note>original: *Olyssipone*</note> to Toledo, and the other from Toledo to Lisbon—then even if one were a banker by profession and the other were not, it would be lawful for one to give money in one place so that the other would return the same amount in the other. For, as will be said in the two following disputes, it is lawful for each of them to "sell" to the other the virtual transportation of money which the other needs; and it will be lawful with much greater reason to make a mutual compensation of transportation.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 404.

...able to receive that increase by reason of the service he provides. Nor is there any other title under which he might receive that increase, except for the expectation of payment, in which—either formally or virtually—the nature of a loan <note>original: *mutuum*; a traditional loan where charging interest was forbidden</note> is perceived; and therefore, the acceptance of such an increase is usurious. This opinion is embraced and defined by the **Portuguese Ordinances** (Book 4, Title 14, § 6), as they condemn this contract as usurious and subject such a banker <note>original: *campsor*</note> to the penalties reserved for usurers.

<margin>Decision 1</margin>
<margin>†</margin>
However, the contrary opinion seems more common among the doctors of law: namely, that a contract of this kind is not usurious, provided the increase is not accepted because of the "waiting" for payment, but rather for the service or the virtual transportation of the money. This is the view of **Conradus** (on contracts, question 99), in the places cited in the preceding dispute; **Cajetan** (in the treatise on exchanges, chapter 9); **Soto** (Book 6 on Justice, question 10, article 1); **Navarrus** <note>The famous economist Martin de Azpilcueta</note> (in his commentary on usury, number 25, and in his Manual, chapter 17); **Johannes Medina** (questions 4 and 5 on exchange); and many others. This is supported by the law enacted by **Sebastian, King of Portugal**, on November 5, 1577, in which he established four fairs <note>original: *nundinas*; major seasonal markets for trade and debt settlement</note> in Portugal, though they were never fully implemented. By that law, he permitted the acceptance of exchange to be paid in **Seville** <note>original: *Hispalis*</note> and later in **Portugal** with an increase, not only during the fairs but also outside of them in other parts of the Kingdom. This same sentiment is not only not disapproved, but actually approved by **Pope Pius V** in his bull on exchanges.

It can be proven because money in a distant location is not worth as much in compensation for what is given in *this* location as it would be if it were not distant from the debtor. Distance itself implies an annexed cost of transportation, labor, and expense, which must be borne by the one who has to make the compensation. Truly, this transportation of money has an estimable value. Therefore, when a banker gives money in one place, if the person who receives it is relieved of the burden of transporting the money they have in another place to compensate for what they received—and this occurs because the banker accepts the repayment in that distant location—the banker may accept a just price for that transportation. This is the same amount that another banker might charge to take that money in the current location and provide it in the distant one where the exchange is finalized.

It does not matter if this first banker already has a correspondent in the location where his money is, and thus can relieve the recipient of the burden without any new labor or expense of his own. This is an "accidental" circumstance <note>In scholastic logic, a secondary detail that doesn't change the essence of the act</note> and pertains to his own fortunate condition; the effect he provides through that route still holds that value. This is the reasoning intended by **Cajetan** in the place cited, and which **Navarrus** treats at length in his commentary (numbers 62 and 63). Likewise, it does not matter that the banker gives the money before he receives compensation for it and for the relief from the burden of transport. Even though both are owed to him in the settlement, the fact that he waits for compensation—both for the money and for the price of the transportation—is a favor he provides. As long as he accepts nothing *because* of the waiting (unless perhaps he loses some profit because of it), but only for those other two factors, it is lawful.

This same reasoning is confirmed: a banker who first receives money here to give it elsewhere—for example, in **Rome**, to facilitate the processing of papal bulls—does not perform more labor or expend more industry than a banker in Rome who, for the same purpose, first gives

<column-break/>

money there to receive it later here. In fact, the latter performs a greater favor, insofar as he gives the money before he receives compensation and waits for the payment. Therefore, whatever increase the first banker may lawfully accept for the initial exchange, this second banker may also accept here for the subsequent exchange, since he accepts nothing solely for the sake of the "waiting" for payment.

<margin>2</margin>
Regarding the reasoning of the contrary opinion, it must be said that the banker *does* transfer the money, at least equivalently, insofar as he frees the one receiving the exchange from the burden of transferring it himself, as explained. This is a just title for receiving the increase. As for the **Portuguese Ordinance**, it must be said that while it decrees the contract to be illicit and usurious by its nature—and for that reason prohibits it and subjects the banker to penalties—it has been shown that the contract is *not* such by its nature as the authors of that ordinance imagined. Therefore, that law does not hold force, even in the external court. Furthermore, King Sebastian, by the law he passed later, approved such contracts.

From what has been said, it is understood that it is lawful <margin>†</margin> for a buyer of a thing that is absent and far distant to buy it at a lower price than it is worth in the place where it sits. This is because the buyer is purchasing from someone who, due to the distance, cannot sell it where it is, nor can they transport it without great expense. It does not matter if the person buying it can enjoy it there without expense or can easily sell it for a just price. The reason is that, at that moment, the item is truly worth less to the *seller*, and the fact that it is bought helps the seller avoid a great burden and expense. Cajetan and Navarrus teach all this in more detail in the cited places.

<margin>3</margin>
From this I gather that what the **Genoese** used to do in this **Kingdom of Castile** was not illicit by its nature. Many people living in distant places had annual incomes <note>original: *reditus*; likely referring to 'censos' or government bonds</note> in Seville from their own money, which the King had taken as a census <note>A type of long-term loan or annuity</note>. Because the fleet from the **New World** would arrive in Seville, the Genoese would provide these people with smaller annual returns in the places where they lived, in exchange for the ones they held in Seville. I do not condemn this exchange, provided the difference was moderate, taking into account the burdens from which the owners of those annuities were relieved, and perhaps also the difficulty of recovering those funds from the King's ministers.

I also gather from these points that something I was often consulted about in **Lisbon** <note>original: *Olyssipone*</note> is not illicit. Many noblewomen of Lisbon have annual incomes in Castile, which are paid to them by the King's ministers at certain times of the year. They pay a certain portion of these to a merchant so that he might demand and receive them from the King's ministers, transfer them to Lisbon, and deliver them to the women. Indeed, some even allow a gift to be given to the King's minister—leaving him a portion of the debt—so that when the merchant arrives to receive it in her name, the payment is not delayed.

In this matter, the King ought to provide oversight by investigating such ministers, so they do not take such gifts unjustly or make the payments of debts "for sale" <note>i.e., requiring bribes to do their jobs</note>. He should punish them and compel them to restore such gifts. Confessors should also examine these ministers and compel them to restore gifts that were offered "voluntarily-mixed" <note>meaning the giver 'voluntarily' offered it only because they felt forced by circumstances</note> to redeem themselves from the harassment of the creditors. On this matter, <margin>4</margin> some God-fearing merchants have often consulted me...

...stating that they travel to those same places and require money there for their business dealings, which they pay in Lisbon out of the funds they hold in Lisbon. I responded: the fact that this is useful to them and that they achieve it with almost no additional labor of their own does not prevent them from lawfully receiving what is worth the management of those women’s <note>Likely referring to widows or female investors mentioned on the previous page</note> business in such a distant place. This also accounts for the value of the virtual transportation of that money, which will become clearer from what is said in the following dispute. Regarding the fee <note>original: *stipendium*</note> they usually receive: they pay the full number of gold coins to these women, each of which is worth four hundred reals in Portugal, while in Castile they are worth only three hundred and seventy-four maravedis. However, for each coin, they receive eleven silver reals in Castile and return only ten in Portugal. Thus, on every gold coin or ducat, they gain one silver real. This is surely not an immoderate fee for recovering those funds in Castile and transporting them to Portugal. Nonetheless, these matters are left to the judgment of a prudent person, and merchants should always be advised to behave with moderation in such fees and profits—especially since they involve little labor or trouble and no risk in this matter.

Regarding the exchange <term>cambium: the business of exchanging different currencies or transferring funds between cities</term> that we are discussing in this dispute, it must be observed universally: if nothing is received by reason of the "expectation of payment" <note>the time spent waiting for the money to be repaid</note>, then whatever is received beyond the strict just price is legitimate. However, if anything is received specifically because the payment is delayed, that is entirely usurious and subject to restitution. Therefore, one cannot lawfully receive more because the payment is to be made later in another place than what could be lawfully received if the payment were made at the same moment, or what could be received if the money had been paid in the other place first. This was established by Pope Pius V in his bull on exchanges. This must be understood, however, unless there is a reason of true "loss of profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the profit a person loses out on because their money is tied up elsewhere</term> arising from the expected payment—at least in the "court of conscience" <note>an ecclesiastical term for the internal moral judgment of the individual before God</note>, as Navarrus says in his Manual (chapter 17, number 301). For although Pius V in his bull prohibits the banker <note>original: *campsor*</note> from bargaining for a certain and determined interest from the start or otherwise (even in cases of non-payment), Navarrus, explaining these very words, says this is based on a legal presumption: that the fee is taken not for lost profit, but as a way to cloak usury under that name because of the delay. However, when it is truly taken by reason of lost profit, it is taken justly and lawfully in the court of conscience and is not subject to restitution. This is because a law based on a presumption does not hold power in the court of conscience when the contrary of that presumption is evident in that same court.

To remove occasions for usury due to delayed payment, Pius V also prohibited in the same bull that exchanges be given for a term longer than the next "fairs" <term>nundinae: major seasonal markets where international debts were settled</term> in the place where fairs are held. If fairs are not held in the place to which the exchange is directed, they should not be given except for the next standard term, according to the custom of granting exchanges to that place. Note, however, if the next fairs are so close in time to when the exchange is made that the letters of exchange could not reach them in time for

<column-break/>

payment to be made, then in this bull, "the next fairs" should not be understood as those immediately following, but the ones after them, since the text refers to the next fairs in which payment *can* be made. Navarrus, in the cited number 301, explaining these same words, says it is not forbidden to grant payment for the second, third, or fourth fairs when—despite the longer delay—the price of the exchange is not increased more than if it had been granted for the very next fair. In such a case, it would be an act of benefit and charity to grant that longer time without any increase, which the Supreme Pontiff did not intend to prohibit.

A certain God-fearing merchant <note>original: *timoratus quidam mercator*</note> who did not grant exchanges except for the next fairs (according to the command of Pius V’s bull) consulted me in Lisbon in this manner: "You know," he said, "that the instrument by which we merchants trade and profit is money, and the more money we have, the more we can trade and earn. From this," he said, "it follows that the further away the next fairs are in a certain place, the more merchants—and with greater intensity—seek exchanges for the fairs of that place. Conversely, the closer they are, the fewer merchants want them, and they seek them with a smaller 'increment' <note>the fee or interest added to the exchange</note>. Therefore, if the fairs of Medina <note>Medina del Campo in Spain, a major financial center</note>, for example, are four months away at the start, then regularly the market price <note>original: *forum*</note> for exchange to those fairs is higher than after one month has passed, and higher after one month than after two. Thus, the less time there is until those fairs, the lower the increment regularly given and received in the common market. This has no other origin than the fact that the more the payment is deferred, the more increment is given for the exchange because of the greater profit merchants make from that delay." <margin>6</margin> "Will it be a sin for me," he asked, "when the fairs are far off, to receive the full increment that the common market currently charges? Or must I abstain from that large increment as if it were usury taken for the long delay? If I must abstain, surely, since merchants trade for profit, no one will be willing to grant an exchange then. And if we God-fearing men abstain from granting such exchanges, then only the unscrupulous will profit in that way. Furthermore, since the increment increases when fewer people offer exchange and more demand it, this will result not only in the detriment of the God-fearing, but also in damage to the Commonwealth and those seeking exchange." I responded that he need not abstain from that exchange according to the common price then current in the market for that location. For the abundance of those seeking exchange increases the price—if not strictly by reason of transportation, then certainly due to other factors to be discussed later. The fact that it is the common price in the public market for exchanges strongly suggests it should be considered just. Additionally, the common need of merchants (both those giving and those receiving) for money to trade, and the profit reported from such trade, is a circumstance that increases the price of exchange—even in comparison to those who seek exchange not for trading and profiting, but for other purposes.
