<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of currency exchange. While the previous page discussed the legitimacy of fees for the "virtual transportation" of money between Lisbon and Castile, this page addresses "fictitious" or "dry" exchange—a deceptive practice used to hide usury—and the legal penalties established by the Church and the Portuguese Crown.</meta>

<margin>7</margin>
There is a burden of restoring the entire amount accepted beyond the principal <note>original: *sortem*</note> when someone grants money to another to be paid in a different location with an increase, yet understands that the recipient has neither money there nor anyone else to pay it on their behalf. Instead, the lender presumes the money will be paid back with that increase in the very same place where the exchange <term>cambium: the business of exchanging different currencies or transferring funds between cities</term> was originally contracted. These are the types of exchanges that nobles in Spain usually accept—for example, to be paid in Flanders or France with the increase typically charged at merchant houses <note>original: *cambijs ad casas*</note>—even though they have neither funds there nor anyone to pay on their behalf in those places. Since in this type of exchange there is no formal or virtual transmission of money from place to place, nor any real connection to someone who has funds there, it is not a true exchange of one location’s currency for another’s. Rather, it is an exchange of money in this location for other money with an added cost in the same location, based solely on the delay of payment. Therefore, in such an exchange, nothing is seen other than a loan <note>original: *mutuum*</note> with an increase for waiting for payment, which is usurious <note>Charging interest on a loan was traditionally considered the sin of usury</note> or a fictitious exchange. It is much more unjust when money is granted to people in this way, to be paid with an increase in a place where they have no means to pay, such that if it is not paid there by the fixed time, the letters of exchange <note>documents used to transfer funds</note> are "re-exchanged" from that place back to this one with a new increase.

<margin>8</margin>
In such a contract, a double injustice is seen, carrying the burden of restoring both increases. Nor are the takers <note>the bankers/lenders</note> excused if they send letters to the places where the first exchange was supposedly taken and claim that the fault lay with those who entered the exchange for not paying there, or that they themselves were ready to receive the money in that place. This is the opinion held by, among others, Cardinal Cajetan in his *Opuscula on Exchange*, chapter 1; Soto in *On Justice*, book 6, question 10; Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer</note> in his commentary on usury; and Sylvester. Today, this is also defined by Pope Pius V in his bull on exchanges <note>referring to the 1571 papal bull *In eam pro vobis* which cracked down on deceptive banking</note>. Regarding those celebrating this kind of exchange in Portugal, King Sebastian I <note>reigned 1557–1578</note> established a law in 1570 as a penalty: that the person giving the exchange in this manner would lose the entire amount given to the recipient immediately, even before any formal sentence was passed. Furthermore, the recipient could not waive this law; even if they paid it back, both they and their heirs could sue to recover it. Indeed, for the person who accepted such an exchange, the King established heavy penalties if they returned any of what they received to the banker <term>campsor: a professional money-changer or banker</term>. The law that the King later passed in 1577 regarding such exchanges did not change this. Navarro, in the cited commentary, along with Sylvester, says that for an exchange not to be usurious or fictitious, it is sufficient that even if the person accepting the exchange for a certain place has neither money nor an agent <note>original: *respondentem*</note> there at the time of the contract, it is likely they will have it by the fixed time of payment—whether they intend to have it there through another loan, or by taking it there with interest to another place, or by some other means. However, I believe this should be understood to mean that they will obtain that money from someone else, and not from the very person (or their agent) to whom they are supposed to pay it.

<column-break/>

<margin>Doubt</margin>
The question is: What if a banker gave an exchange to a certain place in good faith <note>original: *bona fide*</note>, believing the person would pay in that place, but it was later discovered that the recipient had neither money nor an agent there and would instead pay in the same place where they received the exchange? Could the banker then justly accept that increase in the place where they originally gave the money? <margin>Decision</margin> Regardless of what others may say, I judge that in this case, the banker can accept not only the damages resulting from having given his money to that person (because perhaps he would have given it to someone else for a legitimate exchange or used it for another honest business venture), but even if those damages are minor, he can accept as much as it concerns his interest <note>original: *quantum sua interest*</note> that the money be given to him with the increase in the place established in the contract. He can also compel the one who accepted the exchange to place that money, with its increase, in that location at their own expense, if it is possible to do so.

I am led to this because the contract was lawful in itself and was celebrated and fulfilled in good faith on the part of the banker. Since it is an innominate contract <term>contractus innominatus: a legal category for agreements that don't have a specific name (like 'sale') but are still binding</term>, it follows that he can compel the one who contracted with him to also fulfill it on their part, if possible, or to pay in the place where they currently are. This is because it was in the banker's interest for the contract to be fulfilled in that other location, according to the legal dispositions discussed previously.

These principles hold not only in the court of conscience <note>the internal moral judgment of the person</note> but also in the external legal court. However, in the external court, if it is presumed by circumstances that the banker knew—or ought to have known—that the person he was contracting with had neither money nor an agent in that other place, the contract will be condemned as usurious, and the banker may be subjected to the penalties for usurers. This is further confirmed because fraud and deceit should not protect anyone. Furthermore, the legal sale of another's property is a valid contract, so that if the buyer is deprived of the item <term>evictio: the legal recovery of property by a third party with a better title</term>, the seller is held liable for as much as it was in the buyer's interest to become the owner. This agrees with what we said about someone who buys oxen in good faith, believing the seller owned them, and then leases them back to him.

## Decision on certain doubts regarding the two preceding disputes. And likewise concerning those who bring back pack animals for a fee, which they were going to hire. And whether exchange with an increase from one place to another within the same Kingdom is lawful.

### DISPUTE CCCCV.

-> SUMMARY <-

1. Lawful exchanges with an increase for public bankers are also lawful for private individuals.
2. The increase in value that occurs when an exchange is made from one place to another also occurs in the same way when an exchange happens between the same locations due to a need.

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

<margin>3 The hiring of a horse, which is done from one place to another, can conversely be done by the same hirer from the destination back to the starting point for the purpose of the return journey.</margin>

<margin>4 An exchange in which the transportation of money from one place to another follows "by accident" <note>original: *per accidens*; a Scholastic term meaning a secondary or incidental result rather than the primary intent</note> for the benefit of the needy party, is lawful even with an "increase" <note>A fee or profit added to the principal</note>.</margin>

<margin>5 When an exchange with an increase is lawful between one place and another within the same kingdom. And concerning the laws of Castile and Portugal.</margin>

<margin>6 Whether an exchange with an increase between one place and another in the same kingdom—otherwise lawful before prohibitive laws—is subject to restitution without waiting for a legal sentence.</margin>

<margin>Doubt</margin>
<margin>Decision 1</margin>
The doubt is whether the two types of lawful exchange with an "increase," which were explained in the two preceding discussions, are permitted not only to public bankers <note>original: *camporibus publicis*; officials authorized to change money</note> who do this by office, but also to other private individuals. The answer must be in the affirmative. This is because the service provided for the benefit of the person seeking the exchange is worth that increase, regardless of who provides the service; furthermore, there is no law that prohibits such exchange to private individuals.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
A second doubt arises: suppose someone has money in Lisbon <note>original: *Olyffipone*</note>, for example, which they need to transfer to Flanders because they need it there to buy merchandise, pay a debt, or for some other purpose. They were planning to give it to a banker so that they could receive a smaller amount of it themselves in Flanders. Then, another person approaches them who needs money in Lisbon but has money in Flanders, and asks for an exchange of the money in Lisbon, to be repaid with an increase in Flanders. Is it lawful for the person who has the money in Lisbon to accept that increase? This is especially questionable since it is just as much in their own interest for the other person to transport that money to Flanders as it is for the other person to receive money in Lisbon.

<margin>Decision</margin>
This doubt must be answered in the affirmative. The reason is that the service and labor provided to the other party is truly worth that increase. It is merely "by accident" <note>incidental</note> that this also results in a benefit to the provider by another route. In contracts, what must be considered to judge if they are just is whether what is done by one party is equivalent to that for which it is done. Regarding the matter proposed, this is affirmed by Domingo de Soto <note>A 16th-century Spanish Dominican theologian</note> (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 10, article 1) and Juan Medina <note>A Spanish theologian known for his works on ethics and economics</note> (Question 5, *On Exchanges*).

<margin>3</margin>
Something similar is seen when someone has hired a horse to a certain place and was going to incur expenses in returning it to the owner. If they find a traveler who wants to be carried to that [original] place, they can rightly hire the horse to them for a just price. It is no obstacle that the owner additionally profits by saving the expenses they would have incurred in returning the horse. Since there is an equality between the use of the horse granted and the price received for it, the contract they make is just, even if they incidentally gain another benefit from it.

In a similar way, I say: Suppose someone intended to hire a horse to go to a certain place. If they find someone who wants to hire them to deliver a horse to that same place, they can lawfully hire themselves out to that person, accepting a just wage for the labor and industry of returning the horse. It is no obstacle that they themselves travel to the place they intended to go at someone else's expense, saving the costs they would have spent on hiring another horse. The reason is the same: the service provided for the benefit of another is worthy of the wage that person would have given to anyone else. It is incidental that the person receiving the wage gains another greater benefit from the same service.

Hence I say, if the person looking for someone to deliver a horse knows about the other's need for a horse to that place, and the one needing the horse knows about the owner's need to have the horse delivered, they can mutually waive either the whole price or part of it. Whatever they agree upon will be just. No one is bound to enter a contract that purely benefits the other, but can choose to enter a contract that benefits themselves without linking it to another contract. If, however, someone chooses to waive something due to their own necessity, that is their choice. The same should be said of merchants who both know of the mutual necessity of transporting money. These things are said regarding Scholastic rigor and justice. However, moral decency and brotherly charity demand that one grant a relaxation of such rigor. Nevertheless, one should not condemn a person for a mortal sin if they are unwilling to waive the fee.

<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
Juan Medina, in the cited question, asserts that <term>usury: the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender</term> is committed if a person needing a thousand ducats in Flanders gives them to a merchant who then seeks someone else wanting them for an exchange in Spain, to be paid with an increase in Flanders. Thus, the first person, through their own profit, replaces their money in Flanders. However, I do not see why this should be considered usury. In truth, that person is using their right by giving that money for an exchange in which anyone else—even someone who did not need money in Flanders—could lawfully profit. Because the transportation of their own money to Flanders follows incidentally, as they hoped and intended, the contract is not rendered unlawful, as has been explained and as Juan Medina himself agrees. Nor is it rendered unlawful because they, personally or through another, invite someone to an otherwise just exchange.

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
As for the latter part of the discussion—namely, whether an exchange with an increase is lawful from one place to another within the same kingdom, such as from Seville <note>original: *Hispalim*</note> to Medina del Campo <note>original: *Metinam*; a major center for trade fairs in Spain</note>—Domingo de Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 10, article 1) denies it. However, Martín de Azpilcueta <note>Known as "Navarrus," an influential canon lawyer and early economist</note> in the cited commentary (number 28) and in his *Manual* (chapter 17, number 190) affirms it is lawful by the nature of the thing, provided the increase is moderate according to the distance. This opinion is entirely pleasing to me. It can be proved because just as the industry of transferring money from a place in one kingdom to a place in another is estimable by a price, so the industry of transferring from one place to another in the same kingdom is estimable by a price—albeit a smaller one if the distance is shorter and the risks in transportation are less. This is especially true since there is no prohibition on the removal of money to a place within the same kingdom, as there usually is from one kingdom to another; whence...

<summary>Molina argues that currency exchange fees are legitimate even for private individuals and even when the exchange provides an incidental benefit to the person providing the funds. He uses an analogy of hiring out a horse on a return journey to illustrate that saving one's own costs does not invalidate charging a fair price for a service.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 410 regarding the justice of exchange fees (cambium). ...solely transfer the money, taking it in the place where they receive it, and paying it back where the students reside. Nor do I believe that Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a major Spanish Scholastic philosopher</note> intended to deny this, but only that it is not worth as much as merchants charge nobles for the money they give them in the Royal Court, to be received later in the places where the nobles have their revenues and homes; for in that way, merchants are accustomed to mask usury under the name of exchange.

<margin>The Law of Castile.</margin>
Although this may be the case by the nature of the matter, in this Kingdom, by Law 8, Title 18, Book 5 of the New Collection <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* (1567), a compilation of Spanish laws</note>, it is prohibited—for both natives and foreigners—to give money for exchange with any increase or interest from one place in this Kingdom to another in the same Kingdom, or to fairs held in the same Kingdom. This is under the penalty of losing all the money given to the person receiving it for exchange, and the one who gave it is subject to all the penalties for usurers.

<margin>The Law of Portugal.</margin>
In Portugal, however, although King Sebastian prohibited the same in the law *Qualis* in the year 1570, it was afterwards permitted by a law passed in 1577, when money was received at any of the four fairs established in Portugal, and as fortunes allowed, was paid at others of those fairs; or when money was received outside the locations of the fairs to be paid at the nearest of those fairs. Furthermore, the same King Sebastian, by a certain provision of his (of which I have a transcript), revoked that law passed in 1570 before the law of 1577 was passed, regarding all exchanges which, according to the Bull of Pius V or according to Portuguese ordinances, or by the nature of the matter, can be lawfully practiced. Thus, today in Portugal it is not illegal to have an exchange with an increase from one place in the Kingdom to another, provided the increase is moderate.

Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), also known as Doctor Navarrus, a prominent canon lawyer</note>, in the cited passages, says that such laws prohibiting exchange between places in the same Kingdom ought to be limited. They should only apply when the money-changer gives the money first, which he later receives with an increase in another place; for in this kind of exchange, usury can be masked, as the increase is taken by reason of a loan's delay or payment. However, they should not apply when the money-changer first receives the money, which he later gives in some smaller quantity in another place. In such a contract, there is no danger of masking or committing usury, and prohibiting it could be an impediment to the lawful transfer of money—to the detriment of both the Commonwealth and private individuals—from one place to another in the same Kingdom where students and others need it. I believe, moreover, that the cited law of Castile does not encompass this second type of contract, since that is not "giving money for exchange with interest" according to the intent of that law.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
<margin>Decision.</margin>
The doubt is: what if, contrary to the prescription of such laws, something is accepted for an exchange from place to place in the same Kingdom which, setting aside such laws, would otherwise be lawfully and justly accepted? Would it be subject to restitution without waiting for a court sentence? I believe the answer is no. Because in truth, the service provided is worth what was accepted for it. Even if the contract were void because of such laws (which the cited law of Castile does not say, but only

<column-break/>

prohibits it being done under heavy penalties), the person who accepts it is nonetheless not bound to return it before a sentence is passed condemning him to do so, unless he first receives just compensation for the service he did not provide for free. Just as if a contract for the exchange of certain things for others were annulled, the person who carried out that exchange would not be bound to return what he received unless what he gave for it was returned or compensated. Even if the law demands this, it would be penal in that regard, and therefore would not hold in the "court of conscience" <note>original: *in foro conscientiae*; a theological concept referring to a person's moral responsibility before God, distinct from civil legal liability</note> before a sentence is passed.

# On the double value of the same money in different places.

## DISPUTATION 406.

### S U M M A R Y

1 Money can have more value in one place than in another in two ways.
2 The necessity and abundance of money cause its value to increase and decrease.
3 How money of one place to be exchanged for money in another acts like a commodity.

In the three preceding disputations, we examined one reason by which exchange from one place to another can be lawfully granted with an increase. To examine the two other reasons, we must first explain what has been proposed.

Money can have more value in one place than in another in two ways. First, by public law or accepted custom, it has a different value in comparison to other currencies in different places. Thus, in Portugal, a ducat <note>A gold coin</note> is worth four hundred reais, and in Castile three hundred seventy-five maravedis; and a silver real <note>A silver coin</note> is worth thirty-four maravedis in Castile, but in Portugal today it is worth forty. In the Kingdom of Valencia, it is worth fewer of the lowest copper coins, which they call *dines* there, and in Catalonia more; and it has different values in various other places. Thus, while eleven silver reals are worth three hundred seventy-four maravedis in Castile, in Portugal today they are worth four hundred forty reais—to omit other places for now. Likewise, the gold *escudo*, which was once worth ten silver reals and ten maravedis (or three hundred fifty maravedis) in Castile, was worth eleven and a half *Giulios* in Rome; the *Giulio* <note>A silver coin of the Papal States</note> corresponds to a silver real. It had various other prices in France and other places, and today in Castile it has been raised to the value of four hundred maravedis.

In the second way, a certain money can have a greater value in one place than in another because there is a smaller supply of it in one than in the other. For, other things being equal, the greater the supply of money in any place, the less it is worth there for buying goods and for obtaining other things that are not money.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the fluctuations of monetary value across different geographic regions, building on the previous analysis of exchange laws in Castile and Portugal. Molina here explains the economic principles of supply and demand as they apply to currency itself.</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

<margin>2</margin>
Just as an abundance of goods causes their price to decrease when the supply of money and the number of merchants remains the same, so too does an abundance of money cause the price of goods to increase when the supply of goods and merchants remains the same. This abundance is the reason why money itself becomes "cheaper" <note>original: "vilescat" — loses its purchasing power</note> in terms of buying and acquiring things. Hence we see that money is worth far less today in Spain for purchasing goods than it was eighty years ago, precisely because of its abundance. Indeed, what could then be bought for two is bought today for five, six, or perhaps even more. In the same proportion, the wages of laborers have increased, as have dowries, the value of estates, the income from ecclesiastical benefices, and all other things.

From this we also see that money is worth much less in the New World—especially in Peru, where there is a greater abundance of it—than in Spain. Conversely, in places where the supply of money is smaller than in Spain, it is worth more. Its value is not the same everywhere in other locations either, but varies according to the quantity of the supply, while also considering other circumstances. This value does not consist of a single fixed point <note>original: "in indiuisibili" — a technical term meaning a price that cannot fluctuate</note>, but has its own range of flexibility, much like <term>untaxed goods</term> <note>original: "merces lege non taxatæ" — goods whose prices were not capped by government decree, but left to market forces</note>, to be determined by the judgment of prudent merchants. Furthermore, the value of money is not equal everywhere even within Spain, but varies; as a rule, money is usually worth less in Seville, where the fleets from the New World arrive and where the supply is therefore greater, than it is worth in other parts of the same Spanish kingdoms.

Next, a greater necessity for money in one place than in another—whether for buying goods there and transporting them elsewhere, or for some other business, or for the expenses of war, or for the King's Court in that place, or for any other reason—makes money worth more in one place than in another. Indeed, these very factors are usually the reason why money is worth more in the same place at one time than at another.

<margin>3</margin>
In fact, the money of one place, when exchanged for money in another for the purpose of trade, the profits of merchants, and the other reasons mentioned, behaves like a <term>commodity</term> that is not at all regulated by law. Its value increases at one time and decreases at another, depending on whether the need for it is greater or lesser in one place than in another. Just as the abundance or scarcity of any good, a greater or lesser need for it, or a greater or lesser number of merchants seeking it causes its value to rise or fall in a certain place; so too the smaller or larger supply of money in one place compared to another, the greater or lesser need for it there, the greater or lesser number of people demanding it for exchange to different places, and the greater or lesser supply of those who can or will provide it for exchange, is the reason why money is worth more at one time in one place than in another. This even happens at different times within the same trade fairs, such that it is worth more or less at the beginning, middle, or end of the fair, depending on how many people need it or want it for exchange to different locations, and how many are able or willing to provide it.

Therefore, when the value of money is regulated in Republics <note>referring to states or commonwealths</note> by comparing higher denominations to lower ones, that

<column-break/>

regulation applies only to the exchange of money for money in that same place, and for buying goods and paying the prices of things in that same location. However, Republics never intended to regulate money regarding the value we are discussing—that is, in exchange for money in other locations. This is because this value is inconstant and is not hindered by that other value fixed by law; and because this value is just, even when that other value is fixed by law; and finally, because to do otherwise would be to the greatest detriment of the Republics themselves, which would thereby lack necessary goods and many other conveniences. Hence, practice has rightly always maintained that, without the legally fixed price interfering, money should have this other fluctuating value for exchange with other money in a different place. Pope Pius V, in his bull, approved of this type of exchange with an "increase" <note>original: "incremento" — referring to the exchange fee or rate difference</note>.

I said that the money of one place, to be exchanged for money in another, etc., behaves like a commodity not regulated by law, etc., because in comparison to the place where it is currently located, it always retains the value fixed by law or received by custom. For although in Medina <note>Medina del Campo, the site of major international trade fairs in Spain</note> or any other place where exchange is accepted, the value of money varies—because exchange is given at a higher rate to one place than to another, and to the same place not only at different times but even at the same time one person gives it more dearly and another more cheaply, since that value does not consist of a fixed point—nevertheless, in Medina itself, in comparison to the goods bought there at different times and the debts paid there, money always retains the price fixed by law. Goods are bought and debts are paid at that legal rate, whether that other exchange value increases or decreases.

Indeed, in every place where an exchange is to be paid, the sum of money to be paid according to the contract made is always paid at that value fixed by law which the money has in that place.

### 2 If a measure of wheat is worth more in one place than in another, an exchange of that same measure becomes unjust.

<margin>2</margin>
**T**his is a very useful question and necessary to know, concerning which the practice of merchants and exchange-banks holds one view, while the assertions of many learned doctors hold another. Some of these doctors attempt to introduce very weak arguments to avoid condemning the practices of certain places; yet, if their primary assertion were true, that practice would have to be condemned as usurious <note>original: "vsuraria" — the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated or forbidden by Church law at the time</note>, especially if the money-changer gives the money first and only later receives it in another place.

It should be observed, however, that in this dispute we are not dealing with the profit <term>incrementum</term> <note>the "agio" or fee a banker charges for the service of moving funds</note> that a money-changer may legally receive by reason of the exchange, nor with the matter of <margin>†</margin> where—from which he might legally receive it—but rather we are inquiring into the † exchange itself (setting aside those other matters and that profit). We are asking whether the exchange is made according to equality when money that is worth less in one place (in comparison to small copper coins) is exchanged for similar money to be paid back in a place where it is worth more (in comparison to copper coins). Or is it rather unequal, such that the excess must be compensated for the contract to be just? Thus, should the person exchanging money where it is worth less have to "descend" (take a lower rate) in the exchange for similar coins to be returned elsewhere? And conversely, should the one exchanging it where it is worth more be allowed or required to "ascend" (take a higher rate) to account for that increase?

<margin>†</margin> Here are the examples. Let us take the <term>ducat</term> <note>a gold coin used as a standard unit of account across Europe</note>. When it first circulated, it was worth 375 maravedis in Castile, 400 <term>reais</term> in Portugal, and its estimation in Flanders—in the "gros" <note>original: "glossis," likely referring to the Flemish "gros" or "groot"</note> as they call them in that province—corresponded to 400 reais or maravedis according to the common consensus and calculation of merchants in exchanges and other business. And since today there is no gold or silver coin that is precisely worth that amount (as was said in Disputation 400), this value of the ducat persists to this day in these three regions, in whatever coins it is to be paid. Since in exchanges or any other business or agreement today, if mention is made of a "ducat" and nothing else is specified, that value is understood: in Castile it is to be paid at 375 maravedis, but in Portugal and Flanders at 400 reais or maravedis. We ask, therefore, whether in the past (when that gold coin had that value) and today (when no such gold coin exists, but we speak of ducats of that defined value in exchanges), the exchange of a ducat in Castile for a ducat in Portugal or Flanders is made according to equality—and likewise for a ducat in Portugal or Flanders for one in Castile.

Another example concerns the silver <term>real</term>, which in Castile is worth 34 maravedis and in Portugal 40. Similarly, in the Kingdom of Valencia, it is worth fewer <term>dines</term> <note>original: "dines" — a local Valencian currency unit; Molina notes each is worth one and a half maravedis</note> than it is worth in Catalonia. We ask whether the exchange of 100 reals in Castile for the same number in Portu-

<meta>The catchword "nia" links to the start of the next column's word, "Lusitania."</meta>

<column-break/>

-gal is made according to equality, and conversely, 100 in Portugal for the same in Castile; and similarly 100 reals of Valencia for the same in Barcelona, and vice versa. And since a much larger increase results from the ducat—which eleven silver reals and one maravedi make up today in Castile (at 375 maravedis), and ten silver reals and a quarter make up today in Portugal (at 400 reais)—we ask whether the exchange of 100 ducats in Castile for 100 ducats in Portugal is equal, and vice versa. For if the greater value of a certain coin in one place compared to another (in terms of small copper coins) creates an inequality in the exchange from place to place, then we certainly have another reason why profit can be legally taken in an exchange from a place where it is worth more to a place where it is worth less. It would also be necessary to "descend" in the exchange rate from a place where it is worth less to a place where it is worth more, so that the contract remains equal and just on both sides.

Navarrus <note>referring to the influential theologian Martín de Azpilcueta</note> in his commentary on usury (Chapter 11, numbers 60 and 61) and in his Manual (Chapter 17, number 295) judges that this is not an equal exchange, and that it is an unjust and usurious loan if someone gives 100 ducats in Castile to have the same number returned in Portugal, or if he gives 100 silver reals in Castile for the same in Portugal.

Because, he says, the ducat and the silver real are worth more in Portugal than in Castile. He is speaking of the time when the silver real in Portugal was worth a little more than 36 reais, and when the ducat was worth eleven reals (making up 400 reais). Navarrus would say the same for the other examples we proposed. Certain others who wrote after him affirm the same thing. Although Sotus <note>referring to Domingo de Soto</note> (Book 6, *On Justice*, question 12, article 1) thinks the same when the same coin is worth more in one place than in another—using the example of a ducat being worth more silver reals in Italy than in Spain, even though the reals themselves were of the same value as Spanish reals, or if a ducat was worth more *grossi* in one place than another—I do not know if he would say the same in the examples we have proposed.

Navarrus is led to this because the copper coin which is called a *real* in Portugal is of the same value as the Castilian *maravedi*. For just as in Portugal that copper coin is worth six *ceptis* <note>small Portuguese copper coins</note>, and half of it is worth three, so in Castile at that time there were <term>cornados</term> or <term>meajas</term> <note>obsolete small Spanish coins</note>: six were worth one maravedi, and three were worth a half-maravedi (which is called a <term>blanca</term> in Castile). And today in the Kingdom of Galicia, six cornados are worth one maravedi. Since, therefore, the value of the maravedi and the Portuguese copper real is the same and equal, it is unjust to receive in Portugal a silver real worth 36 reais for a silver real of 34 maravedis received in Castile, or to receive in Portugal a ducat of 400 reais for a ducat of 370 <note>Molina likely means 375 here, based on previous context</note> maravedis received in Castile.

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

### The Valuation of Currency and Regional Exchange

Castile, as is normally the case, makes for an unjust exchange if one measure of wheat in Castile is traded for an equal measure in Portugal, even if the wheat of Castile is of better quality than that of Portugal. It would be usury to lend one measure of wheat in Castile in exchange for an equal measure in Portugal because a greater value of wheat would be received in Portugal than what was given in Castile. Therefore, by the same reasoning, it is unjust and usury to accept a loan of one hundred silver reals or one hundred ducats in Castile, with the burden of restitution, for the same amount to be paid back in Portugal. This is because a greater value is returned in Portugal than was received in Castile.

<margin>Decision 3</margin>
In opposition to this view is—and always has been—the practice of merchants, who understand the valuation of things better than the scholastic doctors. It is to the judgment of merchants that we should most strongly defer regarding the value of things, especially when they follow these practices among themselves in the business they conduct, with none of them complaining or protesting. In the matter at hand, regarding the exchange of money from place to place, they prioritize the ratio of gold and silver. These metals, when taken from any location, retain their value everywhere. This stands in contrast to the status of money as "coinage," which is regularly different in various regions and kingdoms; what is valid in one place is not valid in others. Regarding copper money, it is valued at almost nothing, and the costs of transporting such money from place to place would be greater than the value of the copper itself.

For this reason, merchants involved in exchanges and other business from place to place do not make small copper coins the measure for silver and gold. On the contrary, they make gold and silver the measure of the value for the copper coins of each place. Therefore, in many places, they conduct exchanges to different locations under the name of "silver trade" (our people call these measures *marks* and the Latins call them *felibras* <note>original: "marcos... felibras" — these refer to units of weight for precious metals rather than specific coin denominations</note>). When they conduct exchanges under the name of ducats or shields (*escudos*), as is customary among the Spanish and from the Spanish to other places, they want the silver real to have the same value everywhere, since the silver real is accepted in every place and is the currency in which exchanges are largely settled. 

Because the copper coins in various places have different values fixed by law or received by custom, merchants do not want the small copper coins (which are the local measures of the silver real and consequently the ducat or shield) to have the same value when buying goods, paying debts, or exchanging small coins for larger ones. Instead, they want the value to differ in the same proportion by which the number of copper coins given for a silver real in one region exceeds the number of coins paid for it in another.

And so it has always been established among them that the *maravedi* <note>A small copper coin of Castile</note> of Castile is of greater value than the copper *real* of Portugal. It is of far greater value today compared to that same Portuguese coin, now that the silver real in Portugal has been raised to the value of forty *reais*, whereas previously the silver real was worth only thirty-six *reais* in Portugal. Merchants hold the same view 

<column-break/>

regarding the *maravedis* of Castile when compared to the *grossi* <note>original: "grossis" — groats, a type of silver coin used in Flanders and across Europe</note> of Flanders. The same should be said of the copper *denarii* of the Kingdom of Valencia compared with the copper *denarii* of Catalonia.

This opinion actually agrees with the law that Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (r. 1516–1556)</note> passed regarding exchanges, which Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer and economist</note> cites in his *Commentary on the Chapter 'Finalis' regarding Usury*, number 30. There it is said that 375 *maravedis* of Castile are worth 400 *reais* in Portugal. This discussion took place before the silver real was worth 40 *reais* in Portugal. Although Navarro says in number 60 of the same work that this law should not be followed, the opposite is certainly true. This is because reason demands it, and that law relies on the common estimation and practice of merchants, which carries great weight in defining the just prices of things.

It is no small argument that the price of small copper coins decreases and is diminished in itself when a greater number of them are required by public law to be given for a silver real and other silver and gold money. Experience proved this: as soon as the silver real in Portugal was raised to 40 *reais*, the prices of goods immediately increased in comparison to those copper coins. If Navarro’s opinion were true, one would have to say that usury is committed today if someone in Castile gave a loan of 1,100 silver reals to be repaid as only 1,000 in Portugal. Or (which is the same thing) if someone gave a loan of 100 ducats (each worth 11 silver reals) for only 110 reals to be received in Portugal, with the lender in Castile being obligated to return 26 *maravedis* for each of those ducats.

The reason is that the 11 reals of each ducat given as a loan are worth 374 *maravedis* in Castile; yet in the 10 reals received in Portugal, 400 *reais* would be paid. If each of those was of equal value to the *maravedis* of Castile, the lender would indeed receive in Portugal an excess value of 26 *maravedis* for every ducat beyond the value given in Castile.

But who would be so foolish as to give 11 silver reals and 26 *maravedis* in Castile only to receive 10 silver reals in Portugal? Or who in Portugal would accept only 10 reals in exchange for 11 reals and 26 *maravedis* to be paid back in Castile? Or who could persuade himself that such a contract is equal and just? Surely no one.

However, I should advise that the increase in the value of silver or gold coins compared to copper in the very province where that increase is decreed is of some weight and importance. It means that henceforth, larger debts are paid in that province with those same gold and silver coins than were paid before; more goods can be bought with them than before; and it causes more gold and silver money of the same sort from foreign regions to flow into that province because of that profit. Therefore, that increase will somewhat decrease the price of the exchange and the bank-fee.

<summary>Molina argues that currency exchange should be based on the intrinsic value of silver and gold rather than nominal copper denominations, defending merchant practices as a more accurate reflection of "just price" than strict theological theories. He uses the changing exchange rates between Castile and Portugal to demonstrate how legal devaluations of copper coins affect international trade and debt.</summary>

of those currencies from a place where they are worth less in that manner, to a place where they are worth more in the same manner. No better rule can be given in this regard than to observe the common price of the exchange among strong merchants <note>original: "forti cambiorum mercatorum," likely referring to established, high-volume merchant bankers</note> between one place and another, and to abide by that price as just, being the one accepted in the common estimation of merchants.

I should also point out that since the Portuguese silver real was raised to the value of 40 reais, and ten reals there make up a ducat of four hundred reais, it follows that if exchanges from Portugal to Castile, and vice versa, are made in the name of ducats (as is regularly the custom), the exchange has decreased from its ancient value by nearly an eleventh part from Portugal to Castile. This is because the ducat in Portugal has decreased by an eleventh part. Conversely, from Castile to Portugal, it has increased by nearly an eleventh part, by which amount the Castilian ducat exceeds the Portuguese ducat. Indeed, there are today some Portuguese who, from Lisbon <note>Latin: "Olyssipone"</note> to Medina del Campo <note>Latin: "Metina," a major Spanish trade fair city</note>, grant exchange at an equality of ducats while waiting for payment for a full year. In this, usury is clearly open. A certain god-fearing merchant of Medina warned our brothers about this while I was also in Lisbon, so that they might oppose this usury and evil of conscience. For if they grant one hundred ducats in this way in Lisbon for exchange—specifically for one thousand silver reals which they hand over in Lisbon—they want one thousand one hundred to be paid in Medina after a year. They deceive confessors and other learned men by saying they granted the exchange at an equality of ducat for ducat, when in fact they do not disclose that the ducat in Castile exceeds the Portuguese ducat by an eleventh part of its value, nor do the confessors notice it.

Against the argument of Navarrus <note>referring to Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous canon lawyer</note>, it must be denied that the Portuguese copper real is of the same value as the Castilian maravedí for exchanges from place to place. For although both were once worth six other copper coins (called *ceutis* in Portugal and *cornados* or *meajas* in Castile), since the silver real was made of greater value in Portugal in comparison to those copper coins, the copper coins called *reais* in Portugal have become of lesser value in the same proportion compared to the maravedís and those coins once called *cornados* or *meajas* in Castile, as has been explained.

To the confirmation, even if the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied. For it has been shown that the ducat was never of greater value in Portugal than in Castile, and today it is of far lesser value.

## On those who gather to conduct exchanges from place to place.

### DISPUTATION 408.

#### SUMMARY.

1. Three types of merchants who participate in exchanges, numbers 3 and 4.
2. The origin of exchanges among merchants, and their inclination.
4. The nature of the office of bankers.

<column-break/>

5. In what way bankers differ from depositaries.
6. Two types of bankers.
7. When bankers of the first type sin mortally in their office and are bound to restitution.
8. Whether bankers of the first type, who receive nothing for the deposit, can justly receive a salary from the depositors, and how.
9. And what concerning bankers of the second type, number 9.

Before we set down the final chapter on how the price of exchange from place to place may rise or fall, and conclude this whole matter of exchanges, some things regarding the practice of exchanges must be explained. First of all, who are the ones participating in this business.

Three types of men, depending on one another and participating in exchanges in various ways, are distinguished. Some are merchants who, either by themselves or through agents appointed for this purpose (whom they call factors), or through correspondents, conduct trade in various places, such as Lisbon, Seville <note>Latin: "Hispali"</note>, Medina del Campo, in Flanders, Genoa, Florence, Venice, Cape Verde, the Island of Saint Thomas, in various places of the New World, in the East Indies, and in other similar places. They carry from certain places those things which are worth more in others, and send to those places what has greater value there.

To provide some examples to make the matter clearer: from Portugal, oil, salt, wine, pepper, and other things brought from the East Indies, the region of Brazil, and other lands of Portuguese commerce are sent to Flanders. From Flanders, however, all sorts of merchandise are brought into Portugal that are necessary in Portugal, the East Indies, the region of Brazil, and other places of Portuguese trade. Similar trade exists from the Kingdom of Portugal to various provinces and cities of Spain, France, Italy, etc. For from there they transport paper, books, silk, scarlet cloths, *rajas* <note>a type of coarse cloth</note> as they call them, and other merchandise necessary for the Kingdom of Portugal and other provinces of Portuguese trade. And from Portugal, they transmit to those places what is useful there from Portugal and Portuguese commerce. To Seville, goods are brought from many provinces of Europe and cities which are suited for it and for various places in the New World and the islands of the Ocean subject to the crown of Castile. And again, from Seville, those things in which Seville abounds are transmitted to various provinces; namely, besides a huge supply of money and bullion of gold and silver which flows there from trade in the New World, innumerable other goods, both specific to the region of Andalusia <note>Latin: "Betica"</note> and especially those brought there from various overseas places.

Other similar examples can be applied to other provinces and cities. Hence it happens that the principal merchants of each province trade in various places, and that sometimes money is owed to them in those places for the goods they sent there, and sometimes they themselves owe money for the goods they brought from there; and sometimes they lack money in those places, and sometimes they have an abundance. From this it follows, again, that in all these places they have need of ministers, or correspondents, and credit <note>original: "credito"</note> as they call it.

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...that is to say, so that they are present there to recognize their letters <note>original: "literas," referring to bills of exchange or letters of credit</note>, and to pay out what they have been prescribed to give, and to receive from others what was prescribed to be given to them by similar letters, and to dispatch their other business in those places.

<margin>1</margin>
Truly, since it happens from such manifold and varied business in different places that merchants often lack money in various places for their trade and profits—money which they have in abundance in other places—from this arose the practice of those who lacked money in one place seeking it as an <term>exchange|cambium: a financial contract where money is provided in one location/currency to be repaid in another</term> from those who had an abundance of money there, in return for other money which they had in a different place, or which they could more easily pay in another place. In this way, merchants might mutually assist one another through exchanges for their own profits and business dealings in various locations. And this was the origin of **exchanges** among merchants, who alone practiced them among themselves in the beginning.

<margin>2</margin>
Furthermore, because an exchange is usually delivered with a profit in the place where it is to be paid—both because the thing itself is worthy in its own right for the <term>exchange dealer|campsor: a professional who specialized in the business of currency exchange and bills of credit</term> to receive a profit, as was shown above, and also because regularly those to whom money is so given for exchange profit much more by trading and buying merchandise to transport to those places where they are worth more than the increase and profit they grant to the exchange dealers—the result has been that many who had money, attracted by the profit they saw in exchange and the security of it without manual labor, began to assist merchants in the principal **trade centers** and places of business. This they did either by themselves, or through their servants or correspondents, so that they might supply money for exchange to those merchants in various places. Such profit began to arise from this kind of business, and from the skill in practicing it and transporting a huge supply of money to places where, due to various circumstances, it is believed it will be worth more. This is sometimes done by first taking money for exchange in various places at a lower interest rate, so as to later deliver it from those places to others at a much higher rate. As a result, many have abandoned general trade to intend primarily to this business. And **this is the second class of men**, who are exchange dealers either exclusively or primarily by office; they stand, as it were, as assistants to the merchants and depend upon them in their business.

<margin>3</margin>
Moreover, it is no less necessary for men of this kind to have correspondents in the places where trade is practiced—both in the places from which and to which exchanges are accepted—and to have credit there, just as the merchants themselves do. Indeed, it is necessary for them to have men in those places who, having received the letters of exchange which they transmit to them, may receive the money which they gave for exchange in those locations. These agents also, in their name, give the money they have there back into exchange, either to the places where the principal exchange dealers themselves reside, or to other places where it can be given with a greater increase, or where it is believed it will be worth more in the future, according as the principal exchange dealers have prescribed to them, or as those men, having considered the concurrent circumstances, judge to be expedient. Likewise, since the principal exchange dealers themselves often need to take money for exchange in the place where they are to other locations, so that they may deliver it with a greater increase to certain other places, or so that they may transport it via exchange to places where they will need it, or where

<column-break/>

they believe it will be worth more, and for other useful causes; and since it is likewise often useful and necessary for them to take money for exchange in other places—either because they lack money in those places to pay the exchanges they took for those locations, or to transmit it from exchange to exchange to the places where they will need it or where it is believed it will be worth more, and for other reasons—they certainly have no less need of correspondents and credit in various places than the merchants themselves. For this business of exchanges is often carried out with more profit through credit, correspondents, and the skill of prescribing to them how to receive and give for exchange in different places, than through an abundance of money which the exchange dealers hold as their own and free from debt; although an abundance of one's own money held in various places contributes much to this kind of profit. For even if some exchange dealer does not have much money, if he nevertheless has credit and correspondents in various places, and is skillful in commanding that in his name—at a time when money is worth less—it be taken for exchange to places where it is given with a smaller increase and where he can better pay, and that it be given back for exchange with a greater increase at a time when it will be worth more, and to places where it is worth more or is hoped to be worth more; certainly, by thus taking from some for exchange and giving to others for exchange, he will profit much with the money accepted for exchange in that manner.
Likewise, if the exchange dealer has skill in guessing the place and time in which money will be worth much because of a huge shortage at that time and the necessity of merchants or others—as, for example, if perhaps a **Prince** in that place is preparing for **war** and is collecting the entire money of that region from every side, whence it is likely believed that merchants in the **fairs** of that region will have a great lack of it (as used to happen not infrequently in **Flanders** when **Charles V** <note>Charles V (1500–1558) was the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain; his massive military expenditures in the Low Countries often caused extreme liquidity crises and spikes in exchange rates</note> was staying there); and if at the same time he has the skill to bring together from exchange to exchange a great supply of money to have ready in that place at that time; he will surely profit much from that money, which he will grant for exchange with a huge increase to the places from which he transported it, and he will receive it back after four or more months in those same places greatly increased.

<margin>4</margin>
**The third class of men** intending to the business of exchanges are those whom they call **bankers** <note>original: "banqueros"</note>. Their role in places where trade and exchanges are primarily practiced is this: to receive the money of those merchants and exchange dealers who wish to consign it to their **bank** <note>original: "banco"</note>, and to be the depositors of their money. Likewise, to pay out to others those sums which those who deposited them have prescribed. Furthermore, to keep accounts in writing, both of what is received and what is given, according to their prescription. Finally, to settle their accounts with others and to have them always ready.
Men of this kind, however, before they undertake this duty, provide sureties and legitimate security to the **Commonwealths** in which they must exercise that duty, ensuring that they will exercise it sincerely...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 408.

...they will pay out in full those things which have been consigned to their deposit.

**4** Mercado says that these men are of a somewhat different character in Seville and in places where trade fairs are held, such as Medina and other similar locations. In Seville, the advantage that comes to them from such a deposit is so great that they receive no additional fee; rather, they consider it a significant benefit that merchants and <term>money-changers|campsores: specialists in currency exchange and credit</term> wish to deposit their money in their bank and use their services in that regard. Navarro says the same in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 293, regarding Rome and certain places in France and Spain. Indeed, such men sometimes earn two or three thousand ducats within three or four months from the money deposited with them by putting it out for <term>exchange|cambium: the business of dealing in bills of credit and different currencies</term> while various merchants or money-changers do not need it. They also trade with it, sending merchandise to the <term>New World|nouum Orbem: the Americas</term> and other places, from which they report a significant profit. However, it sometimes happens, when fortune fails them, that they are reduced to extreme poverty, to the peril and detriment of the guarantors they provided.

When they fall into such poverty that they cannot pay the deposits and other debts, they are said to **break the bank** <note>original Spanish: "quebrar el banco," the origin of the term "bankruptcy"</note>. As long as they do not experience very adverse fortune, since they hold the money of many men in their deposit—such as merchants and money-changers from Lisbon, Genoa, Florence, Venice, Medina, Toledo, and many others—and since they hold many thousands of ducats for some individuals, it never happens that all the depositors need their money at the same time. Thus, many thousands of ducats always remain in the deposit, which the bankers can trade with for their own benefit and without detriment to others.

**5** Truly, both these and other bankers are the **true owners of the money** which they have deposited with them. In this, they differ greatly from other types of depositaries, as will be discussed later when we speak of deposits. Therefore, if the money is lost, it is lost to them and not to those who deposited it. For they receive it not to guard and return the *exact same coins* <note>original: "eandem numero," referring to the specific physical objects</note>, but so that they may be ready to return an equal quantity of money whenever the depositors demand it. From this, it follows that they receive it as if it were a <term>gratuitous loan|precario mutuo: a loan where ownership of the goods passes to the borrower, to be returned on demand</term>, and thus at their own risk, to return it all at once or in parts whenever and however it is demanded.

**6** There are other bankers, especially in places where trade fairs are celebrated, who receive the money of those who wish to consign it to their bank. They pay out the letters which the depositors of money transmit to them, and they deliver and receive money according to their instructions. They keep accounts of "given and received" <note>original: "dati & accepti," standard accounting entries for debits and credits</note> for themselves and, finally, they settle the accounts of those who frequent their bank. For this reason, at the end of the fairs, they receive a fee for their labor from each person—more or less, depending on how much business each one settled through their bank. For example, they might receive eight ducats from one, ten from another, and more or less from others, according to how much business they handled for them. Mercado reports that these salaries are ordinarily worth fifteen hundred or two thousand ducats to them in a single fair.

<column-break/>

**7** Regarding bankers, especially of the **first type**, it must be observed that they sin mortally if they spend the deposited money in such quantities in their own negotiations that they are rendered unable to pay at the proper time what the depositors demand or order to be paid from the money held in deposit. Furthermore, they are bound to restore the damages and the <term>lost profit|lucri cessantis: the profit a person would have made if they had been paid on time</term> that followed because they did not return the money according to the depositor's instructions. Since by law they accepted that money in deposit on the condition that they would pay it when prescribed, by not paying it then, they surely sin against justice and against the agreement they entered into with the depositors; they are therefore bound to the restitution of damages and also of the lost profit arising therefrom. Likewise, they sin mortally if they engage in such negotiations that they expose themselves to the danger of falling into a state where they cannot pay the deposits. For instance, if they send so many goods to overseas locations that, if the ship were to wreck or be captured by enemies, they could not pay the deposits even by selling their paternal inheritance. Nor do they sin mortally only when the matter turns out poorly, but also when it succeeds prosperously, because of the danger to which they exposed themselves of harming the depositors and the guarantors who gave security for the deposit.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
**8** Regarding those who deposit with such bankers—who take no stipend for the deposit nor for the other services we mentioned they perform for the depositor's benefit—the **doubt** is whether the depositors are bound to pay them a competent stipend, despite the advantage the bankers gain by trading with the deposited money, lest they otherwise commit <term>usury|vsura: charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated by Church law</term>. Navarro, in his *Commentary* on the final chapter regarding usury, number 40, and in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 195, answers in the affirmative. This is supported by the following argument: Since such a deposit is in truth a loan (*mutuum*), as has been said, and the ownership of the money so deposited passes to the banker—and thus if it is lost, it is lost to the banker—therefore, regardless of any profit, even a great one, that the banker acquires through his own industry by trading with that money, the depositors cannot demand or receive anything of value from the banker for the deposit and loan. Otherwise, they commit usury with the burden of restoring what was presented to them. Unless, therefore, the depositors pay a competent stipend for those services, they sin mortally, with the burden of restitution.

<margin>Decision</margin>
While this argument proves that this is not so much a deposit for the benefit of the depositor alone as it is a true loan for the benefit of the banker—although it results incidentally that the money of those who consign it to the bank is preserved in that way, just as the money of other lenders is preserved with the borrower while the loan lasts—the argument does not have as much force as it appears at first glance. For, as we said in Disputation 405, when two people have a need at the same time—one needing to return a horse to a certain place, and the other needing to hire a horse to that same place—each of them can refuse to enter the contract unless the one who benefits the other receives a competent price for it, even if that contract has a joint...

->Luis de Molina, On Contracts.<-

his own other great advantage: so in the matter proposed, it must be said that a banker might, in the first place, not wish to accept the money of others into his bank unless he is paid for the service of guarding that money and, moreover, unless he is paid for the other administrative services he is to perform for their benefit. This is not hindered by the fact that the deposit provides him with his own advantage—namely, that he can trade and profit with that money. Therefore, a banker can lawfully make an agreement for a suitable <term>stipend|stipendio: a fee or salary for services rendered</term> for all those things and receive it, despite his other, much greater profit and gain.

Next, however, it must be said that, on the other hand, merchants and <term>money-changers|campsores</term>—noticing the banker's profit from trading with that money and his need for that money to make such a profit—may wish to enter into no other contract with him than a <term>loan|mutui: specifically a "mutuum," a loan of fungible goods where ownership transfers to the borrower</term> in that manner. Such a contract yields to the banker's advantage, and it is therefore a favor they do for him. They choose to employ his services and offer him the loan rather than others who desire the same, regardless of the fact that they receive the guarding of their money through that loan, so that it may be returned either all at once or in parts when they prescribe it. Therefore, if they intend to enter only into that contract of a loan, as they are able to do and as it is to be assumed they intend, they certainly owe the banker nothing at the start for the guarding of the money, which is accidentally joined with that contract and follows from it by happenstance—just as nothing is owed to other borrowers for a similar guarding of money. Furthermore, they owe him nothing for the labor and service of counting the money, both when he receives it and when he pays it out, whether to the depositors themselves or to others at their direction. Likewise, nothing is owed to any other borrower for similar tasks, which he must perform for free by the very fact that the contract yields to his own advantage. Moreover, they owe him nothing for the keeping of accounts of receipts and payments, even if it is necessary to draw up certain <term>instruments|instrumenta: formal legal documents or contracts</term> for that purpose. Similarly, a person who gives a loan to others owes the borrower nothing for the documents created, whether at the time of the loan for the security of the debt, or at the time of payment for the security of the borrower himself. Since the loan was celebrated for the sake of the borrower, he is bound to pay for everything himself, and nothing is owed by the one who provides the benefit of the loan.

But if the banker provides other greater services for the benefit of the depositors than those which are inherently joined with that kind of loan (which yields so much to his own benefit), a suitable stipend is owed to him for those things alone—unless he provides them for free in compensation for the benefit received, namely that he, rather than others, was chosen for that deposit, as it is right for him to provide them for free; and unless he provides them as gifts to entice merchants and money-changers to consign their money in his bank rather than in others. Therefore, I would instill a <note>scruple: a moral or ethical hesitation</note> in merchants and money-changers in this regard. Especially since, if any banker were ungrateful, or sought fees beyond such great advantage and so great a benefit conferred upon him, he would be worthy of having his office taken away. And since merchants and money-changers should rightly judge that these things are done for free, and if he does not wish to provide them for free, there are many 

<column-break/>

others who would willingly provide them for free. Surely, if the merchants later discover that someone, by whom they thought the services were provided for free, did not actually provide them for free, they are held to no restitution toward him.

For they did not intend to buy those services, but to receive them as favors in compensation for the greater benefit they provided, and they could easily find others who would provide them as favors. Therefore, if a banker intends to charge a price for them, he is bound to notify the merchants before he provides them, so that the merchants may be held to a stipend through an <note>action for business transacted: original Latin "actione negotiorum gestorum," a legal claim for services rendered without a prior contract</note>, as will be discussed more extensively below when we speak of business transacted.

<margin>9</margin> As † pertains to the second kind of bankers, the <note>doctors: the learned legal and theological authorities</note> agree that they may lawfully receive a suitable stipend from each of the merchants who have business with their bank. For receiving, counting, and guarding money; counting it again when it is to be returned; writing and settling their accounts with others (sometimes with personal risk lest an error creep into the counting or in examining and finalizing the accounts); accepting <term>bills of exchange|literas cambij: credit instruments used to transfer funds between different locations and currencies</term> for those who do not currently have money in their bank, making themselves debtors in their place; and other similar things are worth a price. This price is all the greater because a man of no small reputation is required to perform these things, one of significant intelligence, dexterity, and resources, and because these services serve greater profits and gains.

However, this stipend is not fixed by law, but is discretionary. For that reason, each of those for whose advantage the banker performed such services is accustomed, at the end of the <term>trade fairs|nundinarum: the periodic gatherings where international debts were cleared</term>, to pay him according to the judgment of a good man, based on the business he settled, as was said above.

It should be observed that although in some places the three kinds of men we have spoken of in this disputation are distinguished, nevertheless in some other places, it is the merchants themselves who exercise the office of money-changers and who are called bankers. 

Indeed, even in those places where there are some who have provided a guarantee to the State to be the depositaries for others and to exercise the specific office of bankers, often the merchants themselves, in addition to those men, are the ones who give money they have on hand for exchange.

Also, public bankers themselves practice trade with their own money, and by their own authority and for their own advantage or loss, they grant their own money for exchange.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 409.
#### Page 419

<margin>4. The practice of exchange at all fairs, and where it originates.</margin>
<margin>5. When someone is considered to have bought on credit at a fair.</margin>

To understand certain other matters pertaining to the practice of exchange, and to simultaneously examine whether bankers may lawfully receive a certain other <term>stipend|stipendium: a fee for service</term>—which many report they receive in various places, though Mercado in his book *On Exchanges*, chapter 13, asserts is not the custom in either Seville or Rome—it must first be observed that money is consigned to bankers <margin>1</margin> in two ways. One way is in <term>counted money|numerata pecunia: physical cash or coin</term>, which they receive in person. The <margin>2</margin> second way is through a <term>letter of exchange|litera cambij: a financial instrument used to transfer funds between different currencies or locations without moving physical gold</term>, or any other letter they receive. By virtue of this letter, the bank is owed a debt in the name of the person consigning it, payable by the one who is to settle what is contained therein.

<margin>3</margin> Just as money is consigned to them in two ways, they also pay it out in two ways. One is in counted money. The other is without counted money, either by transferring the debt to another person who owes the bank an equal or greater sum, or by delivering a letter of exchange to another location where the person owed prefers to have it. Alternatively, the banker might establish himself as the debtor for that sum on behalf of the person to whom it is owed, who wishes to have it consigned in that bank; or on behalf of others whom the creditor designates as the recipients of that sum, who also wish it consigned in that bank or want to use it to pay another debt they owe to the same bank.

<margin>4</margin> For this reason, at the fairs of <note>original: "Metinensibus," referring to Medina del Campo, the premier financial center of 16th-century Spain</note> Medina del Campo, or any other fairs where many people gather with letters of exchange to buy necessary goods, although much is paid in counted money, the majority of business is conducted through <term>written notes|chirographis: hand-written promissory notes or ledger entries</term>. Some pay with notes for money owed to them in the bank, others accept the payment and consign it into the same bank, and still others settle through the offsetting of debts or the granting of letters of exchange to various locations.

<margin>5</margin> It must then be observed that letters of exchange are written in various forms. In some it is said: "as soon as this has been delivered to you," or "when you have read it," or "when it reaches you," or something similar, "you shall pay this much." In such a case, the money must be paid immediately, without delay. Such payments are usually called <term>at sight|altera vista: a term meaning the bill is due as soon as the recipient sees it</term>, because by the very fact that the letters are inspected and read, the money contained in them must be paid.

In other letters it is said: "on such a day," or "within so many days or months after you receive these letters," or something similar, "you shall pay this much." In those cases, the money must be paid at the time prescribed in the letters. In still others, it says: "at such a fair," namely at Medina del Campo, Antwerp, or others, "you shall pay this much." In those cases, one must follow the custom regarding the time of payment. For if the custom is that such letters are paid at the beginning of the fair, they must be paid at the beginning;

<column-break/>

but if the custom is that they are paid in the middle or at the end, they must be paid at that time.

However, I believe it is regularly the custom for them to be paid at the end of the fair, and that a certain time is prescribed when the fairs are finished, or nearly finished, for such payments. Before that time, as many transactions as possible are conducted through written notes, because there is not a large enough supply of physical money to allow such a vast multitude of goods—which are brought there and sold—to be bought with immediate cash, or for so many business deals to be settled back and forth with physical coins. This period, in which accounts are settled and counted money is paid to those who are still owed something after all calculations, or when letters of exchange to other places are granted to them, is called by merchants "the settlement of the tables" at the fairs and the "opening of the exchanges."

In light of this, I understand what <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a famous Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic philosopher</note> Soto reports in his 6th book *On Justice*, question <margin>12, article 2, regarding the practice of fairs and exchanges based on the accounts of merchants.</margin> He says that four principal fairs are established in the Kingdom of Castile, divided throughout the four seasons of the year. He says four others in Flanders correspond to these, as do others in various places. At these fairs, exchanges are taken for various other fairs in different locations, and for various other places where fairs are not held; and similarly, in other places and fairs, exchanges are taken for these.

<margin>1</margin> The first of these four fairs is held at Medina del Campo in the month of May. There, the banking tables are set up and the exchanges are opened on the fifteenth day of July, and the payments last until the tenth day of August. To this fair correspond others in Flanders in the month of September; there the tables are set up, or the exchanges opened, on the tenth day of November, and payments continue through that entire month. <margin>2</margin> The second fair is held in the other Medina, which is called <note>Medina de Rioseco</note> Rioseco. In that fair, the exchanges open on the fifteenth day of September and continue until the tenth day of October. To this correspond others held in Flanders around the birth of the Lord <note>Christmas</note>, and the exchanges in those open on the tenth day of February, with payments lasting until the end of the month. <margin>3</margin> The third are held at Medina del Campo in the month of October, and the exchanges in those open in the month of December, with payments lasting until the end of the month. To these in Flanders correspond the fairs of the Resurrection <note>Easter</note>, in which the exchanges open on the tenth day of May and last through the whole month. <margin>4</margin> The fourth are held in the town of Villalón, for which the exchanges open in the middle of Lent and continue until the Resurrection. To this correspond the fairs of June in Flanders, whose exchanges open in the month of August and continue until the end of the month. Sometimes, however, the four fairs held in Spain—especially those at Medina del Campo—are extended by royal order so that they last longer, either until the arrival of the fleet from the New World <note>original: "classis ex nouo Octobre" - referring to the Spanish Treasure Fleet</note> or for other reasons. Soto says that for this practice of exchange from a fair held in Castile to a fair in Flanders, only three months are usually granted for payment until the next fair held in Flanders, which is considered sufficient time for...
