### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts
#### Page 420

the transmission of letters from the Kingdom of Castile to Flanders. The same amount of time is granted in reverse, from the Flemish <term>fairs|nundinae: periodic markets that served as the primary centers for international trade and clearing financial debts</term> to the fairs of Castile. For example, if at the <note>Medina del Campo was the site of the most important trade fairs in Spain.</note> Medina fairs in May a money-changer counts out money at the end of June or the beginning of August for the Flemish fairs, the money is to be paid in Flanders at the next September fairs, when in the month of November the <term>exchanges|cambia: the financial tables or booths where foreign currency was traded</term> are opened in them; and so it goes for the remaining fairs in the manner they correspond to each other.

This is the view of <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a dominant Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> Soto. However, I do not understand these things to mean that at the beginning of the fairs or during the rest of the year, physical cash is not taken for exchange if necessary, or as if letters sent to be paid on a certain day (or immediately upon arrival) should not be paid in cash at the prescribed time. Rather, it means that letters which prescribe payment at the fairs are understood to be due when the "tables" of those fairs are set up and the exchanges are opened.

<margin>§ 5</margin> 5. It should be observed that a person is not considered to be buying on credit at a fair if they pay by consigning the price to a <term>banker|bancarius</term>, even if they do not pay in physical cash immediately. This is because the banker, at least by the end of the fair, is going to pay in physical cash whatever remains to be paid after all accounts are balanced. The same applies if one buys goods by consigning the price to any other person who will eventually pay in the same manner as a banker. Therefore, someone is only considered to buy on credit at a fair if they buy with the price to be paid at another time.

<margin>6</margin> 6. Finally, it should be observed that <term>letters of exchange|literae cambii</term> are regularly sent not to the banker, but to a correspondent, who pays or receives the money contained in them. The correspondent then consigns those letters to the bank so that the banker may pay the money at the time prescribed in the letters, if the letters state that payment should be made to the bearer; or so that the banker may receive the money in the name of the one sending the letter, if the letters state that the money should be paid in that place to the sender or their correspondent.

<margin>7</margin> 7. With these things thus explained, <note>Tomás de Mercado, a Spanish economist and theologian known for his work on trade ethics.</note> Mercado (in chapter 13, cited), Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, Question 11, sole article), and <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), also known as Doctor Navarrus, a famous canon lawyer.</note> Navarrus (Chapter "On Usury," number 37 and following, and in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 293) report that in many places the custom prevails that when a banker pays letters of exchange in physical cash, he receives a fee at the rate of five or six per thousand <note>0.5% to 0.6%</note> for what he pays out. However, this is not the case if he does not pay in physical cash, but rather when the person to whom the money is owed consigns it to others from whom they bought goods or to whom they owe something—with the banker accepting this transfer in the bank, or by some other method explained above where no physical money is counted out. Therefore, when someone recovers their debt from a banker in this way, they receive the full amount contained in the letter of exchange. This is because the banker accepts the entire consignment of that sum to be paid at the proper time in physical cash, unless, due to some compensation [offsetting], it does not need to be paid in cash then. Finally, however, if the banker pays either the whole sum or part of it in physical cash to those to whom it was consigned, he takes a fee at the rate of five or six per thousand for what he so pays. For this reason, those who sell goods to people who will consign the price in a bank sell them at a higher price: both because at the time of payment

<column-break/>

<margin>*</margin> the banker is going to take from the price at a rate of five or six per thousand, and also because they must wait for payment until the end of the fairs. Hence, merchants at fairs, when they sell goods, are accustomed to ask the method of future payment so that they may sell at a higher or lower price accordingly.

To better understand when the matter we are discussing takes place, and to simultaneously reveal other abuses, it should be observed: When someone has deposited physical cash with a banker, so that the depositor may withdraw it, the banker does not take five or six per thousand, but the depositor withdraws it purely for free. By the same logic, if the depositor sends letters of exchange or others so that something may be given to someone else from his own money, the banker takes nothing to pay it in physical cash. This is because he has no just title to it, nor do I believe it is a settled custom in that event. On the contrary, it is said that in some places, because of the great profit the banker makes from the use of the deposited money, he is accustomed to give the depositor some interest—for instance, at an annual rate of four or five per thousand. In certain other places, it is a received custom that if a depositor deposits, for example, ten thousand ducats in physical cash, he has credit with the banker for another five thousand beyond those ten thousand. That is to say, if the depositor consigns to others in that bank up to fifteen thousand ducats, the banker accepts the letters and binds himself to pay all those things in his place, receiving no <term>stipend|stipendium</term> from that depositor for that greater credit and obligation which he takes upon himself. Although Soto (Book 6, *On Justice*, Question 18, at the end of the last article) seems to approve of this, it is worth asking whether it is usurious by the nature of the thing if the banker does this by an agreement and not out of a liberal and grateful mind. This is clear because it is a profit from a loan, since this kind of deposit is effectively a loan, as has been shown. Navarrus (in his commentary on "On Usury," number 4, and in his *Manual*, number 293) and Mercado (as cited above) agree with our opinion. However, if the banker provided this out of a liberal and grateful mind, in recompense for a benefit received and with the intention of attracting the depositor to continue the deposit, it would be neither usury nor a sin, provided no scandal occurs.

Mercado (Chapter 13, cited) says that the matter we are discussing only takes place when the person who transmits the letters of exchange has no deposit with the banker where they are to be consigned. In that case, for the banker to bind himself to the payment of that money at the end of the fairs, it is an accepted custom in some places that he receives a fee at the rate of five or six per thousand for what he pays in physical cash. This is in addition to the stipend he otherwise usually receives for handling the business of those who frequent their exchange. Mercado affirms that this is a just title. For just as a <term>guarantor|fideiussor: a person who takes responsibility for another's debt</term> can receive a fitting price for the obligation he takes upon himself by standing surety for another (as seen in Disputation 319), so the banker, to take upon himself the burden of paying money at the end of the fairs in place of the one who sends the letters, justly receives that price. Furthermore, he indicates that letters are sent to the correspondent under this form: "You shall give..."

### Second Treatise, Dispute 409. 421

"You shall give a thousand for such fairs, by consigning these letters in the banks at six per thousand," which were thus paid. He implies the meaning to be that one thousand and six are consigned in the <term>bank|banco: a money-changer's table or stall where accounts were settled by ledger entry</term>, all of which the person who brought the letters can assign to those from whom he buys goods, or to whom he pays another debt, so that they are paid in the bank at the end of the fairs. However, when the banker at the end of the fairs pays any part of that sum in <term>counted money|pecunia numerata: physical coins as opposed to ledger transfers</term>, either to the one who brought the letter or to others to whom he assigned the debt in that bank, the banker shall receive his fee at the rate of six per thousand for what he has thus paid. The result is that the one who sent the letter eventually pays those six extra; he granted them above the thousand to the recipient so that the recipient would be satisfied with that less useful method of payment in the bank, and so that the same amount would reach the banker if he were to pay it in physical cash.

He adds that the one who sends the letter looks out for his own interest by granting those six above the thousand: because, since he does not have the money in that bank, that sum would have to be taken up there as an <term>exchange|cambium: a financial transaction involving the transfer of funds, often across different locations or currencies</term> in his name. Exchanges, while the fairs last, are very expensive, since many people are then taking up money at exchange to conduct their business; but once the fairs are finished, exchanges are not usually so expensive. Therefore, so that money may be taken at exchange with less interest after the fairs are over to satisfy the banker and pay the debt, the sender of the letter chooses instead to grant the banker a fee at the rate of six per thousand, so that the banker may take upon himself the burden of paying that thousand at the end of the fairs in his place.

<note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560) was a Dominican theologian whose "De Iustitia et Iure" was a standard text on law and economics.</note> Soto almost reaches this same opinion in Book 6, *On Justice*, Question 1, single article, although he does not explain it quite so clearly. He suggests there is a law in the Kingdom of Castile by which those six are granted to the banker when he counts out the money. However, <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), known as "Navarrus," was the leading canon lawyer of the age and an expert on the morality of money.</note> Navarrus rightly criticizes this in the cited commentary; for if anything had previously been decreed regarding this matter by <note>The "Catholic Monarchs" who unified Spain.</note> Ferdinand and Isabella, it was revoked by them in Law 5, Title 18, Book 5 of the *New Collection*.

Navarrus, in the cited commentary, number 37, and in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 293, absolutely condemns the custom of taking five or six per thousand from the person to whom money is counted out according to the instructions of the person who consigned it in the bank. He argues that the banker is bound to restore those five or six to the person to whom he counts the money. He makes an exception only when the person to be paid sold his goods for a higher price because of the burden he was about to undergo, or when he voluntarily and out of pure grace wished to give those five or six to the banker—which, however, is not to be presumed. It is said that the labor the banker spends, and whatever else he does that can be valued at a price, he does entirely in service to the one who instructed him to pay the money and whose place he takes. Therefore, he can only seek payment from that person, not from the one to whom he counts the money.

Navarrus assumes, moreover, that the practice is such that one thousand is not consigned in the bank along with an additional six that the banker will eventually receive when he counts the money, but only the thousand owed to the person to whom the money is consigned. Indeed, he relates that it happened to him when he was about to receive money from a banker based on letters of exchange brought from elsewhere, that the banker refused to pay him unless he took from that money a fee at the rate of six per thousand, and that he 

<meta>catchword: gained</meta>

<column-break/>

gained nothing by warning the banker that he could not justly take those fees.

<margin>8</margin> In the following conclusions, I shall finally state what I think about this matter. The first is: In the event that a banker takes upon himself the obligation of paying money at the end of the fairs in place of someone else, which that person does not have on deposit with the banker, it does not seem condemnable for the banker to receive five or six per thousand for what he has thus paid, especially where this is established by custom. This is proven because he has a just title for it—namely, taking that obligation upon himself—as <note>Tomás de Mercado (c. 1525–1575) was a Spanish economist and theologian famous for his work on trade and the "School of Salamanca."</note> Soto and Mercado rightly affirm.

The second conclusion: The interest should be paid, either formally or in effect, by the person in whose name that money is first consigned in the bank, not by the one to whom the money is to be paid. This is proven by Navarrus's reasoning: because the burden the banker undergoes, he undergoes in the place of the one in whose name the money is first consigned in his bank and for whose sake he binds himself to pay it; therefore, that person ought to pay the fee, not the ones to whom the money is to be paid.

If, however, someone who owes a thousand to another consigns one thousand and six in the bank on account of the fee the banker is eventually to receive (as Mercado affirms is done), then in truth he is the one who formally pays such a fee. But if he consigns only a thousand, and the reason he consigns them is worth no more than those thousand thus consigned, from which the banker is to subtract six for his fee, and the person in whose favor they are consigned understands this (or ought to understand it), then in truth the person who first consigns the thousand effectively pays the banker six from them, since he consigns the thousand on the condition that the banker will eventually take six from them at the time of payment.

The third conclusion: When only a thousand are consigned in the bank to be paid in that manner, and all of that is owed in physical cash to the person to whom it is consigned, and the person to whom it is owed had no reason to think otherwise, the banker can nonetheless take his fee from those thousand when he counts the money. This is because he is considered to have willed to bind himself to that payment on the condition that he receive the customary fee from the money to be counted. However, the person to whom the full amount was owed has a legal right against the person who consigned it to have the fee restored to him which the banker took from it, for that person is surely bound to pay it.

The fourth conclusion: When no prior obligation was undertaken by the banker to count and pay money in another's name, he can subtract nothing from the money he counts and pays, but must be content with the fee he ought otherwise to receive from the one whose business he manages, and which he deserves for the services he performs for that person's sake. This is proven because the counting and payment of that money—if he gives it so that it may be restored again in the same place—has the nature of a <term>loan|mutuum</term>; and for a loan, one cannot lawfully receive anything beyond the principal.

<margin>9</margin> At this point, another abuse which bankers are accustomed to practice must be mentioned. For when some money has been consigned in their bank, to be paid at the end of the fairs,

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...occurred, if the person to whom the money was first consigned—to be paid either to him or to others from whom he bought goods—should want that money before the end of the fairs, the bankers are sometimes accustomed to give it to them. However, this is done on the condition that they pay <term>interest|interesse: here used in the sense of a fee for the loss or cost incurred by the banker</term>, at the rate for which money is given at exchange for other locations at that time, or some other interest.

However, whatever is received in this way is <term>usurious|usura: the practice of making an unethical or immoral monetary loan that unfairly enriches the lender</term>, since there is an obligation to restore it; for that advance payment is essentially a <term>loan|mutuum: a loan of fungible goods like money where the same amount must be returned</term>, and thus anything received for that reason is usury. An exception might be if it is received because of an equal profit that the banker actually loses because the payment was made early; however, this will rarely happen. They sin with far greater reason and are bound to make restitution when the time for counting out the money has already arrived, and yet they receive something from the creditor in order not to delay the payment and to settle with him immediately.

For what is received in that way is entirely <term>involuntary mixed|involuntarium mixtum: a legal concept where an action is chosen only because the alternative is worse, making it partially forced</term>, and is received unjustly, unless it is established that it comes from the liberal spirit of the giver.

->**Regarding exchange based on the diverse value that money has in different places—not by comparison of small coins, but from concurrent circumstances: a conclusion on the whole matter of exchange.**<-

### DISPUTE 410.

->**SUMMARY.**<-

> 1 Whether exchange should be varied and regulated according to the greater or lesser value of money which it has from place to place.
> 2 An equal exchange for an equal value is lawful by the nature of the thing.
> 3 When the exchange of money in a greater or lesser quantity is lawful.
> 4 To determine whether exchange from place to place is just, one must look to three main points.
> 5 A money-changer can lawfully receive something for the universal transportation of money.
> 6 The just price of exchanges is inconsistent and variable.
> 7 How the common price of money is to be judged just in different places.
> 8 How the diverse value of the <term>Ducat|ducatus: a gold coin used as a standard of trade across Europe</term> is to be understood and regulated.
> 9 Instruction for confessors regarding the matter of exchanges.
> 10 When brokers, servants of money-changers, and others cooperating in illicit exchanges sin and are bound to restitution.

We distinguished a double genus of the value of money in Dispute 406. The latter was that by which money—not this or that specific coin of a place, but money in its totality—is worth more in this place than the total money of another place is worth in this other place. This is determined by a comparison of an equal quantity of money of one place with an equal quantity of another, even if the money in both places is of the same material in quality, quantity, and weight, and bears the same mark, and has an equal value imposed upon it by law compared to other coins of the same place. We said this value does not arise from the

<column-break/>

money itself, but from circumstances, and is very inconsistent and variable as circumstances change. It does not consist in a single point but has a range of what is just, no different than how the value of goods does not consist in a single point as long as it is not fixed by law. What we therefore inquire in this dispute <margin>1</margin> is whether, because of this diverse value, it is sometimes lawful to increase the cost in the exchange of money from place to place, and whether it is sometimes necessary to decrease it, according to the greater or lesser value that money has in those places.

To this question, one must answer in the affirmative, along with <note>original: "Soto 6. de iustit. q. 12. art. 2." refers to Domingo de Soto, a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> Soto and <note>original: "Nauar. in com. c. vult. de usur." refers to Martín de Azpilcueta, known as Dr. Navarrus.</note> Navarrus and others. It can be proven because an exchange of equal for equal in terms of value is lawful by the nature of the thing. Therefore, if at a certain time 360 <term>maravedís|marauedini: a Spanish unit of account</term> in Flanders are worth as much as 400 in <note>original: "Metinae" refers to Medina del Campo, the site of the most important trade fairs in Spain.</note> Medina, on account of the scarcity of coins in Flanders and the abundance in Medina, and because of other concurrent circumstances, then (all other things being equal) an exchange of 360 maravedís given in Flanders for 400 to be paid in Medina will be lawful. Conversely, an exchange of 400 given in Medina for 360 to be paid in Flanders will be lawful.

Just as it is lawful to exchange 100 measures of wine or oil in Spain for, say, 80 to be delivered in Flanders—and conversely, 80 given in Flanders for 100 to be delivered in Spain—because 80 measures of wine or oil in Flanders are worth as much as 100 in Spain (which is why they transport wine and oil to Flanders). Thus, for this reason, it is often lawful to exchange a larger quantity of money given where it is worth less (according to the principle we are discussing) for a smaller quantity to be paid where it is worth more. And conversely, it is lawful to exchange a smaller quantity of money in a place where it is worth more for a larger quantity to be paid where it is worth less. Regarding this greater or lesser value of money, Soto (cited above) and <note>Tomas de Mercado, author of "Summa de Tratos y Contratos."</note> Mercado in his treatise on exchanges, chapter 5 and following, say that money-changers of our time look especially to this, and that their exchanges are justified by it.

Against this primary foundation of the exchanges that are made today from place to place, someone might object. **Objection:** If it is lawful to exchange a smaller quantity of money for a larger one to be paid where there is greater abundance and less need, simply because circumstances make money worth less in one place than another, then it would follow that it is also lawful to exchange a smaller quantity of money at a time when there is a scarcity and greater need in a certain place, for a larger quantity to be paid in the *same* place at a time when there will be a greater abundance and less need. But no one would grant that this consequence is lawful (as it would be blatant usury); therefore, neither should the premise be granted.

Soto, in article 2 cited above, denies that this follows. Nor does he provide any other reason except that when money is to be paid in the same place but at a different time, it is perceived...

Molina argues that money's value fluctuates between locations based on supply and demand, making it ethical to exchange different quantities of currency if their regional values are equivalent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dispute 410, focusing on the distinction between a loan (mutuum) and currency exchange (cambium). It addresses whether fluctuating market values of goods or money can justify receiving a larger quantity than what was originally given, and begins a three-part summary of the criteria for a just exchange.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 410

...loan; however, by reason of a <term>loan|mutuum: a contract where fungible goods are given and the same amount is returned</term>, nothing extra can be accepted. But when the money is to be returned in another location, it is seen as an exchange of two things equal in value, even if they are unequal in quantity, which is lawful. However, this explanation is not sufficient. For even in a loan, if that which must be returned is equal in value at the time it is returned to that which was given at the time it was lent, the contract is lawful. It is no hindrance that a greater quantity is returned than was received. For example, a person may lawfully lend two measures of wheat when each is worth two ducats, to be repaid with four measures at the time of the new harvest, if it is probably believed that each measure at that time will be worth, more or less, one ducat. In this case, equality is seen regarding the value between what is given and what is received, even though there is an inequality in the quantity or number of measures. On the contrary, it would be <term>usury|usura</term> if I were to lend four measures of wheat at a time when each is worth one ducat, to be repaid with the same number when each is expected to be worth two ducats, as was stated in its place according to the <note>original: "cap. Naviganti, de usuris" — a reference to a specific decretal in Canon Law regarding maritime loans and risk.</note> chapter *Naviganti* on usury, and as <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian and jurist.</note> Soto himself affirms. Therefore, if in the same place a smaller quantity of money is worth as much now because of its scarcity and the need for it, as a larger quantity will be worth later in the same place because of its expected abundance, there is no reason to deny that this principle follows.

<margin>3</margin> However, the legitimate reason why this should be denied is given at the end of Dispute 406. Namely, because money—whether there is a great scarcity and need for it, or a very great supply and abundance—never holds the status of <term>merchandise|merx</term> in comparison to the place where it is located. Instead, it always retains the price or value fixed by law or received by custom (I am speaking of regions where the prices of currencies are fixed and do not depend on the will and agreement of private individuals). For that reason, in comparison to that same place, it does not have a greater value at one time than at another, but only when it is exchanged for money in another place, as was explained there. Observe, however, that by reason of <term>lost profit|lucrum cessans: a legal concept where a person is compensated for the profit they missed out on by lending their money</term>, if someone gives money at a time when there is a smaller supply and greater need for it, to be restored in the same place at a time when there will be a greater abundance and less need, an increase can lawfully be accepted, as much as that lost profit is valued. For instance, if at a time of great scarcity and need for money, the price of goods decreases for that reason, and the one who has the money was going to buy goods then to make a profit or support his family, but by granting it to another to be restored in the same place, he is deprived of that profit or suffers an <term>accrued loss|damnum emergens: actual loss incurred by the lender</term> because he must later buy necessities for his family at a higher price; then, when he grants the money, he can include in the agreement an increase beyond the principal, as much as such lost profit or accrued loss is valued. Similarly, if he were going to give that money for an exchange to another location with a notable profit, and by granting it to be returned in the same place he is deprived of that profit, he can certainly lawfully include in the agreement as much of an increase as the profit he is deprived of is valued.

<column-break/>

So that we may bring this entire matter of exchange from place to place to a summary and conclude it in the remainder of this dispute, we must look at three main factors together to judge whether an exchange is just or not, how much of an increase it is lawful to receive in each exchange, and when it is necessary to receive nothing more than the sum given for the exchange to be just. We are not speaking here of "dry exchange" <note>A "dry" exchange (cambium siccum) was a fictional exchange used to hide a usurious loan where no actual movement of money between cities took place.</note>, about which enough was said in Dispute 404, but only about the remaining exchanges from place to place. Furthermore, we will mention those three factors not in the same order in which they were explained.

The first factor is the different value that the same money has in different places in comparison to small coins. And if exchanges are made under the name of major currencies—such as ducats, scudi, or silver <note>A Spanish silver coin.</note> reals—as is usually done, and the value of such currency is different in the place from which and to which it is exchanged, it was shown in Dispute 407 (against some doctors) that although some consideration must be had for that greater or lesser value, the price in the exchange should rise only very little for it to remain just.

On the other hand, if the exchange were carried out under the name of the smallest coins (which, however, is not customary)—for example, under the name of <note>A small Spanish copper coin.</note> maravedis, so that they were traded for <note>The Portuguese equivalent of the real.</note> reais in Portugal, or vice versa—then, because maravedis are worth more in Castile than reais in Portugal (as shown in the same dispute), one would have to take account of that greater or lesser value. For if, setting aside the other factors that allow the price of an exchange to rise or require it to decrease, the exchange were not made to equality, it would therefore be unjust and carry the burden of restitution if, for 374 reais given in Portugal, the same number of maravedis were received in Castile; for in Portugal one would be giving only a little more than nine silver reals, while in Castile one would be receiving eleven whole reals.

The second factor is the transportation of money, either formally (physically) or virtually, from the place where the <term>banker|campsor</term> gives it to the place where he receives it. Based on this factor, the banker may lawfully increase the price of the exchange by as much as the transportation is estimated to be worth in the judgment of a prudent person, considering the distance between places, the difficulty, and other concurrent circumstances, as explained in Dispute 408 and the two following.

The third factor is the different value of money in distinct places, explained in this and Dispute 406, arising from the abundance or scarcity and need for it, and from other circumstances. And although from this factor, as well as from virtual transportation, it is often lawful for the banker to increase the price in an exchange, sometimes it will be necessary to decrease it from this factor so that the contract is equal and just, due to the lower value of the money where he gives it compared to the place where he is to receive it. If the money is worth exactly as much less in the place where it is given as the transportation is worth, then for the contract to be equal and just, the exchange must be made at an equality of quantity between the money given and that to be received, with the value of transportation being compensated by the lower value of the money where it is given.

<meta>This page continues Molina's investigation into the justice of exchange contracts (cambium). Specifically, it deals with the 'third reason' for exchange: the difference in the value of money across different geographic locations and the costs associated with moving it.</meta>

### Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

If, however, the cost of transportation exceeds the amount by which the money is worth less where it is given than where it is to be received, then that excess may be added to the exchange rate according to the quantity of money to be received. Conversely, if the lower value of the money where it is given exceeds the cost of transportation, then it will be necessary to increase the quantity of money given in comparison to what is received for the contract to be just. However, because neither the cost of transporting money nor the excess value that money possesses in distinct places (the "third head" or reason for exchange) consists of a single indivisible point, but rather has a certain <term>latitude of the just|latitudo iusti: a range of prices or values within which a transaction is considered morally fair</term>, it is enough for the contract to be just if the parties do not step outside these fair limits. From this, it follows that the range of justice in exchanges—when all the reasons for increasing or decreasing the rate are calculated—is not a single fixed point. Rather, the range is larger when more factors concur; by looking at all of them together, one must judge the fair range for an exchange from one place to another.

<margin>Objection</margin>
<note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> Soto, in book 6 of *On Justice*, question 12, article 2, says that when the "third reason" applies—namely, when an increase is taken because the money is worth more where the <term>banker|campsor: a person who exchanges money, often at trade fairs</term> provides it than where he receives it—it is a sin to take an additional increase for "virtual transportation" <note>Moving money through bills of exchange or accounting rather than physical transport.</note>, unless perhaps it is a very small amount.

We can indeed support this objection: when you transport money for me from a place where it is worth less to a place where it is worth more, it ought to be worth more to *me* (at whose expense it is transported) and not to *you* (who are moving it at my expense). Therefore, if the banker accepts a price for the formal or virtual transportation of money to a place where it is worth more, it would be wrong for him to also accept a price for the higher value the money has in that location. Or certainly, if he accepts a price for that higher value, it would be wrong for him to also accept a price for the transportation, since in that very act, nothing is deemed to be transferred to the person receiving the exchange.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Despite this argument, I believe it is more probable that one can <insert>licitly</insert> accept something for virtual transportation, or rather for the "relief" (*leuamine*) by which the person requesting the exchange is spared the burden of transporting that money. This is proven because, by returning to him an equivalent value in the place where he needs the money, I am indeed relieving him of the burden of transporting and placing that value there. This service is estimable and can be sold in comparison to that burden. Therefore, I can licitly receive a just stipend for performing that service in his favor. It is no hindrance that I might perform it easily and without personal expense due to the <term>correspondent|correspondentem: a business partner or branch office in another city</term> I have there, as was explained in Dispute 403.

This is confirmed: let us grant, according to the judgment of prudent merchants, that 370 in Flanders is worth as much as 400 in <note>Medina del Campo, a major center for Spanish trade fairs.</note> Medina, and furthermore, that the virtual transportation (or rather the relief from transporting that money from Flanders to Medina) is worth 10. In that case, an exchange of 400 given by the banker in Medina for 370 to be returned in Flanders is licit. Thus, 360 are returned to achieve equality in value for the money

<column-break/>

given in Medina, and the remaining 10 are returned for the relief from transportation from Flanders to Medina. By the same reasoning, if the banker gives 360 in Flanders, he can receive something more than 400 in Medina, so that the 400 serves as compensation to reach equality for the money given in Flanders, and the excess is for the relief from the burden of transporting money from Medina to Flanders. The logic is clear, since in neither exchange is there a formal physical transfer of money, but only a relief from the burden of transferring it. In both exchanges—excluding what is taken for the relief from the burden—there is an equality in value between what is given and what is received, accounting for the different values the money has in those places due to circumstances.

Soto would not deny the first part of this, because in that exchange nothing is taken for the higher value where the banker gives it; indeed, it is worth *less* in Medina where he handed it over than in Flanders. For that reason, less money is received in Flanders than was given in Medina. Soto himself affirms that when no increase is taken based on the higher value of money in different places, it is licit to take an increase for the virtual transportation of the money.

At this point, observe that the banker—excluding what he receives for virtual transportation—never takes an increase in value or quantity in the place where the money is worth more. Rather, in the place where it is worth less, he takes an increase, not in value, but in the *quantity* of money, to compensate for the higher value his money has in the other location.

Regarding the argument we constructed for the opposing view, it must be said: First, it assumes something false—namely, that the banker takes an increase in the place where money is worth more. Second, the premise is true when there is an actual physical transfer of money; but it is otherwise when, by giving an equivalent in one place for an equivalent in another, the recipient is relieved of the burden of transporting it. In that case, what is given by each party is worth what it is worth *where* it is given, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, he who, at another's request, relieves them of transportation through that exchange, can accept a just stipend for that relief.

From what has just been said, it is easily seen that we should not condemn the fact that a banker, for 360 given in Flanders, receives more in Medina than that same banker gives in Medina for 360 to be returned to him in Flanders.

For Soto says that even when the value of money did not vary in either place, it was customary in his time for a banker in Medina to give 410 in exchange for 360 to be received in Flanders; but on the other hand, when he provided exchange from Flanders to Medina, for the 360 he gave in Flanders, he received 430 in Medina.

Soto condemns this because, he says, if the first exchange was equal, the second is unequal. However, it can be perfectly well answered that both exchanges can be just for this reason: because 360 in Flanders, due to various circum-

<meta>The catchword "circun-" indicates the start of the word "circumstances" on the next page.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 410

And then, if an exchange is sought from Medina to Flanders, the <term>banker|campsor: a professional money changer or dealer in bills of exchange</term> justly subtracts ten from the four hundred and twenty because of the burden he lifts from the one seeking the exchange. If, however, the exchange is sought from Flanders to Medina, he justly adds ten above the four hundred and twenty, to be paid back to him in Medina, because of the burden he takes on for the person seeking the exchange.

<margin>6</margin> Since, as has been said, the <term>just value|iustus valor: the moral and economic worth of a currency based on local conditions</term> of money in distinct places at one and the same time does not consist of a single fixed point, but rather has a <term>latitude|latitudo: a range of prices within which a transaction remains morally acceptable</term>—no differently than goods that are not strictly regulated by law—and furthermore, since the just price for the virtual transportation of money from place to place also does not consist of a fixed point; it follows that the just price of exchanges has a range of flexibility, not only between different places, but even in one and the same place at the same time. Likewise, since the circumstances of affairs—from which the value of both money and its transportation increases and decreases—change easily even in the same location relative to others, it follows that the just price of exchanges is inconsistent and varied, not only between different places but also at different times in the same place. This is especially true because, just as the just prices of other things vary as money increases or decreases in value, so too do the just profits intended from exchange vary; people are unwilling to apply their money to exchange without a greater profit, preferring instead to turn those funds toward other profitable business dealings. Hence, I should warn that in the examples of exchange from place to place that we have proposed, and those read in the works of other <term>doctors|doctores: learned scholars and theologians of the era</term>, one should not look for a absolute truth as if the practice of exchange in those places must always correspond to them. For with the progress of time and the changing of circumstances, these things change, and in practice, they are often found to be quite different.

<margin>7</margin> Furthermore, since the natural just price of any thing in any place depends greatly on the <term>common estimation|communis aestimatio: the collective market value determined by the community rather than an individual</term> of that thing in that place—as was said in Disputation 348 and elsewhere—it follows that the common price determined at different times in the exchange market from one place to another should not be condemned. Rather, it should be held as just and as the measure by which we judge those who, through excess or deficiency, deviate significantly from it and thus overstep the limits of a just price. This doctrine, however, must be understood provided that such a common price was not introduced through the fraud of a <term>monopoly|monopolium: the exclusive control of a market, which was considered a sin</term> or something similar. For if those who hold money at the <term>trade fairs|nundinae: major international commercial gatherings where debts were settled and money exchanged</term> should agree among themselves that no one shall give money for exchange except at a certain high rate, and that rate is beyond the "rigorous" just price that would have existed without that monopoly, then those who caused that excess beyond the otherwise just price have not only committed a mortal sin but are also bound to make restitution of that increase to those from whom it was taken. In a similar way, if before the fairs, or immediately at their start, someone should take up all the money in that place through exchange to various other places at a lower rate, so that during the fair or as it progresses, they may give it out for exchange at their own pleasure with a much higher increase to those needing it—because they are the only ones who have it—then certainly, if they grant it beyond the rigorous just price

<column-break/>

at which it would otherwise have been granted at the fairs, and which equity demands it be granted (considering the quantity of money they hold), they likewise commit a mortal sin with the burden of making restitution. But if neither these people nor those mentioned previously exceed the rigorous just price that would have otherwise existed, they would not be compelled to make restitution, according to what was said and proven more extensively regarding all these matters in Disputation 345. Even then, however, a sin against the charity owed to one's neighbors and country may occur, which is worthy of being most sharply prohibited and punished, as was said there. When, however, some people—presuming that money will be worth a great deal at certain fairs—take up all the money in a place for exchange to various locations before the fairs arrive, so that they might later grant it for exchange at a higher just price that equity would then demand according to the concurrent circumstances, there is no reason they should be condemned for mortal sin. For in all these things they would be using their own right, and they would be doing injury to no one, since this pertains to the art and dexterity of business. Furthermore, this same doctrine must be understood provided that the common price does not include some "head" or reason by which something is unjustly taken. For example, if money were commonly given for exchange at a higher price than it otherwise would be purely because of a longer extension of time, it would then be a sin, with the burden of restitution, to accept that increase when nothing else is involved beyond what is commonly accepted. For as <note>original: "Nauar. in cō. cap. vlt. de vsur. n. 57"</note> <term>Navarrus|Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586): a famous Spanish canonist and early economist</term> well notes, an abundance of buyers when a thing is sold unfairly does not increase the price of the thing; nor is the just price of that thing to be determined by their common use.

<margin>8</margin> Finally, two things are to be observed. First, in exchanges, sometimes the name "ducat" is understood to have the same value in the place where the exchange is granted and where it is later to be paid; and then the increases or decreases are expressed by the addition or subtraction of ducats to be paid in the place to which the exchange is granted. For example, if one hundred and ten or one hundred and fifteen <term>ducats|ducati: a gold or silver coin used across Europe</term> are received in one place, for which letters are granted to another place so that one hundred ducats may be paid; in that case, an increase of ten or fifteen ducats is taken. I understand this to be the case even when ducats have a different value in different provinces, whether fixed by law or received by custom. For example, in <term>Portugal|Lusitania</term> a ducat is worth four hundred <term>reais|reais: Portuguese currency units</term> today, but it is only worth ten silver <term>reales|regales: Spanish silver coins</term>. On the other hand, in <term>Castile|Castella</term> it is only worth three hundred and seventy-five <term>maravedis|marauedini: Spanish accounting units</term>, but it is worth eleven silver reales and one maravedi. Therefore, when today exchanges are made from Castile to Portugal under the name of ducats, they are understood as just explained. Furthermore, because the ducat of Castile exceeds the ducat of Portugal by one silver real, if an exchange is given from Castile to Portugal with an increase of three or four percent, one hundred ducats are received in Castile, for example, and letters are granted in Portugal for one hundred and thirteen or one hundred and fourteen ducats. Since one hundred ducats of Castile and one hundred and ten in Portugal are equal, because...

The person who grants that exchange from Castile to Portugal receives an increase of three or four Portuguese <term>ducats|ducatos: a gold coin used throughout Europe</term>. But if the exchange were granted with the same increase from Portugal to Castile, one hundred ducats would be received in Portugal, and letters of exchange for ninety-three and a half, or ninety-four and a half, or a little more, would be granted in Castile.

And because in Flanders there was frequent variation in the value of currencies, in the year 1527, merchants established a certain fixed estimation and value for currencies that would last perpetually among them, regardless of changes in the value of money within the state. And so, in letters of exchange given for Flanders, it is customary to say: "you shall pay so many ducats, for example, a third part in gold and the remainder in silver, according to the valuation of currencies made in the year 1527." Sometimes, however, in exchanges, merchants do not use the name of the "ducat" according to the valuation used in the place where the exchange is granted or paid, but rather according to a valuation they themselves devise and establish in the exchange contract they enter into. That is, they increase or decrease the value of the ducat in the place where the exchange is to be paid as much as they agree, considering the concurrent circumstances, relative to the value of the ducat in the place where the exchange is given. In this way, it is customary in Flanders to receive one hundred ducats valued, for instance, at three hundred and sixty <term>maravedis|maravedinorum: a small Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account</term>, in exchange for the same number of ducats valued at four hundred maravedis to be paid in Medina. Letters of exchange are then given in Medina in this form: "you shall pay one hundred ducats, each at the value of four hundred maravedis." However, neither in the past nor today are there ducats of that specific value in Medina; rather, they are <term>imaginary ducats|ducati fictitii: accounting units used by merchants to standardize contracts across different currencies</term> devised by merchants for their exchanges and business dealings. In a similar way, ducats or <term>scudi|scuta: gold or silver coins, often called 'crowns' in English</term> of various values are devised for other locations, as the merchants agree among themselves. Although <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, known as Navarrus</note> Navarrus, in his commentary on the chapter *vlt. de usuris*, number 53, rails against these imaginary and fictitious ducats, he later, in his *Manual*, chapter 17, at the end of number 302, does not judge them as something to be condemned, but rather to be accepted.

<margin>8</margin> The second point is this: what has been said in this matter of exchanges should be understood with a spirit of indulgence. <margin>9</margin> Indeed, we extend this teaching for the instruction of <term>confessors|confessariorum: priests who heard the confessions of merchants and needed to know if a business deal was a sin</term> and others who are asked about these matters, as far as the limits of justice allow. This is so that they do not command restitution when the <term>money changers|campsores</term> are not bound to it, and so they do not condemn what should not be condemned. However, this does not mean that exchanges should not very often be discouraged, because of the abuses men frequently commit in them, and because of the dangers of losing eternal happiness to which those who are not God-fearing expose themselves when they devote themselves to this business.

<margin>10</margin> Furthermore, as pertains to the brokers, the servants of the money changers, and others cooperating in illicit exchanges—whether they sin and are bound to make restitution—the exact same thing must be said as was stated in Disputation 331 regarding those who cooperate in <term>usury|usuram: the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated by the Church</term>.

### What a Partnership Is.
## DISPUTATION 411.
### S U M M A R Y.

<margin>1</margin> *What a partnership is.*
<margin>2</margin> *Whether a partnership or a hiring is presumed in case of doubt, when someone hands over animals to someone else to be guarded, promising them a certain portion of the offspring. And what of the agent, or factor, and other ministers of a merchant. number 3.*
<margin>4</margin> *A partnership can be contracted in two ways.*
<margin>5</margin> *Why a partnership can be contracted so that one provides the capital or part of it and the other provides the labor, whereas it is otherwise in a loan.*
<margin>6</margin> *The capital placed in a partnership by one of the partners is made common to all partners.*
<margin>7</margin> *To which of the partners the ownership of those things acquired from the capital after the partnership is contracted is understood to be acquired.*

Having explained exchanges, we must now discuss the contract of partnership. A <term>partnership|societas</term>, according to <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> Cicero and <note>Azo of Bologna, a medieval legal scholar</note> Azo in his summary of the Code *pro socio*, whom others follow, can be defined as follows: It is a contract, or agreement, of two or more people to contribute toward a common profit or use. Those who enter into this agreement among themselves are called partners. A partnership is perfected solely by the mutual consent of the contracting parties expressed outwardly; for that reason, it requires neither a formal hand-over of goods nor a written document to be considered complete, unless the parties wish to suspend the contract until a writing is finished. It can be celebrated not only between those who are present but also between those who are absent, via letter or a messenger, in the same way that all these things were explained regarding buying and selling in Disputation 337. These points are established from the single paragraph in the *Institutes* regarding obligations from consent and from law 4 of the Digest *pro socio*, and the common opinion of the learned doctors agrees. Thus, the contract of partnership consists solely in the agreement to contribute toward a common profit or use. The actual contribution, the business dealings, the administration of the contributed items, and the subsequent division of profit belong to the execution and fulfillment of the obligation of the partnership contract. A contribution is understood to be proposed whether the thing contributed is money, or animals, or something similar, or whether it consists of the labor or the <term>skill|industria: professional expertise or diligent effort</term> of one or more of the partners. For, as will be clear from what is to be said, sometimes a partnership is contracted with one partner contributing money and the other contributing labor and skill to trade with it; or one contributing animals and the other contributing the guarding and administration, or even the fodder.

It was said in the definition: "for a common profit." For if one person hands over animals to another for guarding, or money for trading, such that the entire profit belongs to the person handing it over, and the other receives a certain fixed payment for his labor and skill, it will not be a partnership, but rather a <term>hiring|locatio</term> on the part of the one providing the labor and skill, and a <term>leasing|conductio</term> on the part of the one paying the wage for the labor and skill. This is the case if the payment is in money; but if it is something...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 411.

...anything else, such as so many young animals handed over for safekeeping, or something similar, it will be an **innominate contract** <note>In Roman law, "innominate" contracts are those that do not fit into standard categories like "sale" or "partnership" but are still legally binding based on an exchange of performance.</note>: *I give, so that you may do.* <note>Latin: *do: vt facias*.</note> In a similar way, if someone receives the sheep or goats of another, so that he may receive the milk and some cheeses from them for several months, and pays the owner a certain salary for such fruits, it will not be a partnership, but a **hiring** of those sheep or goats for the purpose of receiving those fruits. This is the case if the payment is made in money. If, however, it is to be paid in another thing, such as in cheeses or something similar, it will be an innominate contract: *I give, so that you may grant me the goats or sheep for the purpose of receiving those fruits.* If, however, along with the money or cheeses to be paid, the person who receives the sheep or goats binds himself to their care, or pasture, or something else, then another innominate contract will be mixed in with the aforementioned contracts: *I shall do, so that you may grant them to me for the purpose of receiving those fruits.* Nevertheless, all these innominate contracts are similar to the contract of **hiring and leasing**; and they should be judged and evaluated according to that, as was said in Disputation 253.

<margin>Doubt 2</margin>
The question is: if someone hands over animals to another and, to make them more diligent in their care and management, grants them a portion of the fruits as a salary—say, an eighth or a tenth part of the lambs, wool, and cheeses—or some other similar portion that is uncertain in its future extent, but whose expectation, by the judgment of a prudent person, is equal to a certain and determined just salary that he would otherwise have given him: is such a contract one of **partnership**, or rather an **innominate contract** that should be reduced to a contract of hiring, and judged according to the laws of hiring?

<margin>Decision 3</margin>
The same doubt exists regarding a **merchant** who puts someone in charge of his business, establishing as a salary some portion of the profit that remains after the capital and expenses have been deducted when the partnership ends. This contract is frequent among merchants and their ministers, or **factors** <note>A "factor" was a business agent or manager who traded on behalf of a merchant, often in a different city.</note>, as they call them. First, I say that when it is not expressed—at least implicitly—that the portion is for a salary, but the contract is celebrated simply by stating that so many parts of the future profit belong to the person providing the capital and such a portion to the one in charge of the business or the animals, then the contract is one of **partnership**. This is because it is truly a contract of contributing toward a common profit to be divided afterward. Hence, it should be judged according to the laws and privileges of the contract of partnership, and not according to the laws of the contract of hiring and leasing. 

If, however, it is expressed that the portion is for a **salary**, insofar as that expectation is equal to a certain and determined salary of which he would be worthy if he were leasing his labor and industry for that business, the contract is not one of partnership, but of the **hiring of labor and industry**. For then the application of labor and industry is solely for the profit of the one providing the capital, who established a salary for it; but by accident, it results in a common profit, insofar as by the agreement of both parties, the salary (which otherwise would have been something certain in value) is exchanged for a portion of the future profit—uncertain in its extent and value, and dependent on a greater or lesser

<column-break/>

quantity of future profit. 

In this matter, observe that it matters a great deal whether such a contract, by the intention of those celebrating it, is one of **partnership** or rather of **hiring and leasing of labor and industry**. For if it is a partnership, besides the fact that it must be judged according to the laws and privileges of a partnership contract, then it must certainly be weighed whether equality and justice are maintained in that contract. This is done by comparing the capital to the labor and industry, both between themselves and in comparison to the profit, to judge how much profit equity requires to come to each partner, considering what each of them contributes to that partnership. According to this consideration, more profit is often due to the one who contributes labor and industry than if he were to lease himself for that same labor and industry to the one providing capital—who could easily find a servant to lease themselves for the same labor and industry for a much smaller salary. 

If, however, that contract is one of **hiring**, then for equality and justice to be preserved in it, it is sufficient if the expected profit established for the one providing labor and industry is equal to the value of the labor and industry provided, without any relation made between such labor and industry to the capital, or both to the profit that is hoped for. This must be noted so that merchants are not undeservedly condemned when they engage in similar contracts, in which—due to the magnitude of the profit they receive from the capital—they grant less to those they put in charge of their businesses than equity would require them to grant if they entered into a partnership contract with them. For they are not bound to enter into a partnership contract with them, but they can hire their labor and industry. As long as they grant them a just salary, taking into account both the value of such labor and industry and the risks to which they expose themselves, there is no reason they should be condemned for injustice.

Regarding the definition of partnership, observe that it was said to be an agreement to contribute toward a **common profit**. This is because for the nature of a partnership, common ownership in future profit is sufficient; common ownership in the capital is not necessary—although there can be a partnership with an agreement for common ownership in both. 

<margin>4</margin>
Indeed, it can be contracted in two ways. One, with an agreement for common ownership in the **profit alone**, so that the capital remains the property of those who provided it, and when the partnership is ended, it must first be withdrawn by those same people, and only the profit is to be divided among all the partners. Some call this kind of partnership a sharing only in the *interusurio* <note>Original: *interusurio*. In this legal context, it refers to the "interest" or "use-value" produced by the capital, i.e., the profit, rather than the capital itself.</note>, that is, in the **usufruct** or the profit from the capital. 

The other way is contracted with an agreement for common ownership in **both**. For example, if three people each contribute one thousand gold coins, and a fourth contributes labor and industry which is valued as a salary of one thousand coins, and the agreement is made that, when the partnership ends, the total aggregate of capital and profit shall be divided into four equal parts to be distributed among the partners: that partnership will be one of common ownership both in the profit and in the capital.

<margin>5</margin>
In a partnership contract, therefore, the one who contributes capital or a part of it, even if he does not contribute industry, justly earns a profit. Yet, if he were to give that as a **loan** <note>Latin: *mutuum*. A simple loan where ownership of the money transfers to the borrower, and the lender cannot legally or morally demand more than the principal back without committing usury.</note> to the one who was going to contribute industry, he could justly receive no profit from it, for that would be **usury**. This is because...

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

As Saint Thomas rightly says in the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 78, Article 2, Reply 5, and as others agree, a person who puts only their capital into a contract of partnership does not renounce ownership of it, as happens in a **loan** <note>original: *mutuo*; in a traditional loan, ownership of the money passes to the borrower, whereas in a partnership, it remains with the investor</note>. For that reason, that capital works toward a profit as the person’s own property and at their own risk. Therefore, they may justly receive a portion of the profit as the fruit of their own money, which has been exposed to the risks of that business.

<margin>6</margin>
It must be † observed that in a contract of partnership, by the very fact that some contribute to the capital, it becomes common to the partners. All of them acquire ownership of it, even if the contribution is not physically delivered to each individual. Indeed, even without such delivery, each acquires possession of it because, by a **legal fiction** <note>A legal assumption used to achieve a just result, even if the physical reality differs.</note>, they are said to possess it through the one or many who physically hold it, as if any one of them were appointed to possess and acquire ownership in the place and name of all. These things hold true whether the capital is to be divided among the partners in equal or unequal parts upon the dissolution of the partnership. This is held in Laws 1, 2, and 3 of the **Digest, "On the Partner"** <note>original: *ff. pro socio*; "ff" is a standard abbreviation for the Digest of Roman Law</note>, along with the cited gloss on Law 1; Bartolus and others note the same there, as does Law 6, Title 10, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]. Although those laws only speak of a partnership of all universal goods, the same must be understood for any other particular partnership, such as one for profit in a specific business. When capital is handed over to be common among the partners, the reasoning is the same. Those laws expressed this regarding the universal partnership because in that type of partnership, the doctrine is universally true; however, when a partnership is for profit in a specific business, that doctrine is not always true. This is because there is not always communal ownership of the capital in such a partnership; sometimes ownership is only in the profit from the capital, such as when one person provides the livestock (which remain theirs alone) and the other provides the pasture and labor for a common profit regarding the offspring or products.

The cited Law 3 adds that when something was owed to one of the partners before the partnership was contracted—even if such a debt is part of the capital—the other partners cannot bring a legal action against the debtor to demand payment unless the partner to whom it was owed first assigns that action to them. Therefore, either he alone can pursue the action, or he must first assign it so the partners can pursue it.

<margin>7</margin>
Regarding † those things acquired from the capital after the partnership is contracted by buying and trading with that same capital, Law *Si quis societatem* [If anyone... partnership] in the Digest, "On the Partner," suggests that only the one who acquires them by trading in this way gains ownership; however, they are bound to communicate and divide them with the other partners. Covarruvias (Book 3, *Variae Resolutiones*, Chapter 9, Number 1) and others he cites understand this to apply when a partner has traded with the capital in his own name. It is different, however, when he acts in the name of the partnership, intending to act on behalf of the partnership: in that case, all partners acquire ownership and possession without a specific delivery being made to each individual, as equity clearly demands. For this reason, in this **Kingdom of Castile**, Law 47, Title 28, Part 3 has rightly decreed that even if one of the partners acquires something by trading with the capital in their own name, the others acquire ownership of it by that very fact. Covarruvias (in the place cited), Antonio Gomez (Volume 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, Chapter 5, Number 3), and other Spanish doctors agree.

<column-break/>

In the definition of partnership, it was said to be an agreement to contribute toward common profit or **use**. This is because in a partnership of all goods, there is also a contribution toward common use and expenses from the goods held in common. There are also many other particular partnerships for common use and expenses, such as among students living in the same house for ordinary expenses from a common purse, and among soldiers, who are called **comrades** <note>original: *camarada*</note> by the Spaniards, and among similar groups.

### Multiple Types of Partnership.

# DISPUTATION 412.

->SUMMARY<-

1. How many types of partnership there are, and the ways they can be contracted (also numbers 5, 7, and 8).
2. A partnership contracted simply is understood to be of all present and future goods (also number 6).
3. Indeed, unless otherwise expressed, it is understood that all goods are divided into equal parts (number 3).
4. A partnership of all goods can even be contracted between those who do not have equal assets, so that when the partnership is dissolved, they are divided into equal parts.
6. A partnership contracted absolutely is to be understood broadly.

<margin>1</margin>
**A** partnership † is sometimes contracted between people for all their goods. And then, even if it is not so ex-
<margin>2</margin>
pressed, it is understood to be of † all universal goods, both present and future, which will be acquired while the partnership lasts, by whatever title they are acquired—whether from business, inheritance by law, legacy, or gift. Indeed, even if those goods pertain to someone’s **military savings** <note>original: *peculium castrense*; property a son in a Roman family could own independently of his father, usually earned through military or civil service</note> or quasi-military savings, they all become common. They are to be divided among the partners when the partnership is dissolved according to the portions established, either tacitly or expressly, at the start of the partnership.

<margin>3</margin>
And when nothing has been established, it is understood † that they are to be divided into equal parts. But for a partnership to be understood as contracted in this way, is it necessary for it to be expressly agreed among the partners that it be for "all goods," even if "future goods" are not mentioned? Yes, because that is understood by the very fact that it is expressed as being for "universal" or "all" goods. If it is stated that it is for all goods acquired by whatever title, that is sufficiently expressed.

<margin>4</margin>
Such † a partnership can indeed be contracted even among those who do not have equal assets, so that when the partnership is dissolved, they are divided into equal parts. This is partly because the industry of the one who has fewer goods can be compensated by what the other has in assets. And also because in the future, it might happen that the one who has fewer goods might acquire more by chance or by their own industry.

Furthermore, the greater assets of one person can be compensated by other things, such as nobility, beauty, or other qualities, by which some people entering into marriage may decide to contract a partnership of all universal goods together. This is something that frequently happens in **Portugal** <note>original: *Lusitania*</note>, as will be seen below.

<meta>The catchword "infra" (below) indicates the discussion of Portuguese marriage customs continues on the next page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of partnership (societas), transitioning from the definition of general partnerships to specific rules regarding illegal gains, the duration of contracts, and the liability of partners for damages.</meta>

...as will be discussed below. Then finally, because a partner who has more capital can grant that favor to another partner by title of gift and generosity. All these points are found in Law 3, section "specifically"; Law 5; Law "if brothers," section "the same says Pomponius"; and Law "on the partnership of all" in the Digest, *On the Partner* <note>original: ff. pro socio; "ff" is the standard abbreviation for the Digest of Roman Law</note>; and in the Institutes, *On Partnership* at the beginning. Antonio Gomez agrees in Volume 2 of his *Various Resolutions*, chapters 1, 2, and 3, as does the common opinion of the Doctors.

<margin>5</margin> Sometimes, however, a partnership is contracted for a specific thing or for certain particular matters, such as for one or more specific <margin>6</margin> business ventures. If, however, people contract a partnership absolutely, without expressing that it is "of all goods," nor expressing certain determined things for which they are partners, it is understood that they are partners universally. This does not mean a partnership of all goods simply, but of everything they might acquire by **onerous title** <note>original: titulo oneroso; this refers to property acquired through effort, cost, or work, such as a salary or a purchase, rather than through a gift</note>, whether by hiring out their labor or any other thing, or by buying, selling, exchanging, or any other onerous title. If anything was owed to one of the partners before the partnership began, that debt belongs to him alone. If anything is given or bequeathed to him, or if he acquires it by title of inheritance—even if the partnership provided the opportunity for it (for example, if someone became well-disposed toward him through partnership business and thus named him heir or left him a legacy or gift)—the whole of it belongs to him. All these rules are found in Law "on entering" and those following, and Law "the partner who in it," section "partner" in the Digest, *On the Partner*, where Bartolus agrees in his commentary on the text; and in his treatise *On Two Brothers*, note 11, he notes the point mentioned last. However, to some partnerships contracted in this second way, certain pacts may be added to expand or restrict them—for instance, if it is added that if anything is bequeathed or given to any of the partners while the partnership lasts, it shall become common property. In that event, it will be common to the partners. And generally, any pact is valid that is not repugnant to good morals or the disposition of the law. But if a pact is added stating that if any **rightful inheritance** <note>original: iusta hæreditas</note> comes to any of the partners, it shall become common, then by "rightful inheritance" are understood those things that come from a relative who died without a will [intestate], but not those granted by a specific will, as is held in Law 3, section "on that" in the Digest, *On the Partner*.

<margin>7</margin> A partnership may also be formed for a shameful or illegal purpose. Such a partnership is void by the law itself, per Law "nor should it be permitted" in the Digest, *On the Partner*, and Law 2, Title 10, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]. Another kind is for a matter that is not shameful, which includes any partnership, whether of all goods or specific ones, in which it is not expressed that it includes illegal activities. Therefore, once any such partnership is entered into—even if it is of all goods universally—if one of the partners acquires something by theft or another crime, it does not belong to the partnership, nor does it become common to the other partners. If, however, the one who acquired it contributes it to the partnership of his own accord, he is not allowed to reclaim it. But if he is condemned by a court to restore it, the partners are bound to contribute what they received from that matter so that it may be handed over to the person to whom it must be restored by sentence. If, when they received it, they were aware it had been poorly acquired, they are bound to contribute to full restitution, even including the penalty imposed. This is found in Law "what however" and the three following in the Digest, *On the Partner*.

<margin>8</margin> A partnership † can be contracted to last for the whole life of the contracting parties, or until a certain time, or to begin from a certain time. It can also be contracted under a 

<column-break/>

condition—both so that it begins to have force depending on some condition, and so that it ends when some condition arrives. However, it cannot be contracted so that it continues with one of the contracting parties after his death, because the contract of partnership does not pass to heirs, except in some events which we will present in <margin>414</margin> Disputation 414. Indeed, this is so true that even if it were expressly stated in a pact that the partnership contract should pass to the heirs, the pact would be void; the heirs would need to enter into the same partnership anew for it to be continued further. Indeed, by the death of one partner, the partnership is dissolved even regarding the remaining survivors, unless it was specified in a pact that by the death of one or more, the partnership is not dissolved regarding the survivors, as will be said in Disputation 414. All these rules are found in Law 1; Law "plainly if they"; Law "by action," section "by death"; and Law "no partnership" in the Digest, *On the Partner*; the penultimate law of the Code, *On the Partner*; section "it is dissolved" in the Institutes, *On Partnership*; Law 1, Title 10, Part 5; and the Portuguese Ordinances agree in Book 4, Title 60, at the beginning, joined with section 1.

### To what degree of fault a partner is liable, and universally how far they are liable to other partners even without fault; and what it means for someone to be liable only for "as much as they can conveniently do."

### DISPUTATION 413.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> A partner is liable to another partner in **both forums** <note>original: vtroque foro; the "external" court of civil law and the "internal" court of conscience or confession</note> for the total damage that arises even from **slight negligence** <note>original: leui culpa</note>. 
<margin>2</margin> This rule fails [is not applied] in cases of the slightest negligence or accidental chance. number 2.
<margin>3</margin> What is understood to be included under the name of "slight negligence."

Indeed, this also applies to the partnerships of students living in the same house.
<margin>5</margin> It fails, however, in certain cases, as in numbers 5 and 9.
