# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

16 *The privilege enjoyed by a person, preventing them from being sued for more than they are able to perform: does it pass to their heirs?*
17 *The holder of such a privilege, preventing them from being sued for more than they are able to perform: what precautions can they take so that another acting in their name may also enjoy this privilege?*
18 *A partner is bound to contribute their share until all have an equal portion.*

---

<margin>1</margin> **IN** partnerships, every partner is bound—both in conscience and in the secular courts—to the other partners for any loss that arises through their own **fraud** <note>original: "dolo"; intentional wrongdoing or deceit</note>, **gross negligence** <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>, or **light negligence** <note>original: "leui culpa"</note>. Nor is a partner excused even if their industry and hard work have otherwise brought great profit to the group. The reason is that, by the law of partnership, they are participants in all the profit that occurs; however, if a partner causes them loss through fraud or negligence, they commit an injury against them. Certainly, even if no "theological" guilt <note>moral sin</note> were joined with the legal fault, they would still be bound by the force of the contract to make good on the damage so caused. But if, <margin>2 †</margin> † through the **very lightest negligence** <note>original: "leuissima culpa"</note> of one of the partners, or by a **fortuitous accident** <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an event that could not be foreseen or prevented</note>, some loss should befall the partnership, then it is a common loss to be divided among the individual partners. The reasoning for this entire doctrine is that the contract of partnership is celebrated for the benefit of all partners. It is a regular rule of law that when a contract is made for the benefit of all contracting parties, no one is held liable to the others except for fraud, gross negligence, or light negligence, as was stated in *Disputation 295*. All of this is established in the *Institutes* (on partnership) and the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. pro socio"; Molina uses the standard "ff" abbreviation for the Digest of Roman Law</note>.

<margin>3</margin> At † this point, observe that the laws express that under the name of "light negligence," it is understood if a partner has not applied that diligence which he would commonly apply, or which it would be fitting for him to apply, to his own personal affairs, considering his own quality and character. For the two laws cited first and last clearly hand down this rule, adding that he who takes on a partner who is not very diligent or industrious has only himself to complain about. If it were specifically agreed in a pact that a partner should be liable even for the lightest negligence or for an accident, that pact would be valid, provided it were equitable. However, for it to be equitable, it would be necessary that no inequality result; rather, this greater burden which one partner takes upon himself should be compensated from elsewhere, such as by a larger portion of the profits being assigned to him, or from some other source. Similarly, if it were agreed that a partner should not even be liable for gross negligence, the pact would be valid, provided that inequality did not result. But a pact stating that a partner is not liable even for fraud would be against good morals, and for that reason, it would be void. All these things are clear from what was said in *Disputation 295*, and therefore I do not reinforce them here. This concludes what pertains to the first of the proposed points.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding † the second point, the contract of partnership has this privilege: if one partner is sued by another or by the rest regarding matters pertaining to the partnership, and because of poverty he is unable to pay the full amount, he is not bound to them beyond what he is able to perform. This is found in the *Digest, On the Partner* <note>original: "l. verum... ff. pro socio"</note>.

<column-break/>

There are those who discuss this in the *Digest, On Res Judicata* <note>matters already judged</note>, the *Institutes, On Actions*, and the *Siete Partidas* <note>original: "par. 5"; the foundational 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>. This holds true not only in a partnership of all goods, but also in a partnership concerning a single thing, as is expressly stated in the law cited above. Therefore, when the law says "a partner of all goods" should be understood, it means "especially," as the **Gloss** <note>the standard medieval commentary on the law</note> explains in both places and the common opinion of the doctors affirms—which, among others, Gutierrez relates and follows in his work *On Confirmed Law*. This also takes place in partnerships of students <note>original: "scholasticorum"</note> living in the same house: if something is owed by one of them to the other partners by reason of the partnership, he is not bound to them beyond what he is able to do, as Gutierrez and Gregorio Lopez affirm, citing others.

<margin>5</margin> However, † a partner does not enjoy this privilege if, when sued regarding such a debt, he denied that he was a partner. For once he is convicted of being a partner and owing the debt, he is compelled to pay it in full, regardless of whether he can comfortably pay it. This is held in the *Digest, On the Partner* and *On Res Judicata*, and is affirmed by Gutierrez and Gregorio Lopez.

<margin>6</margin> This † privilege—namely, that a partner or anyone else who enjoys it is not bound beyond what he can perform—is to be understood as "beyond what he can *comfortably* perform." Hence, the **Gloss** on the aforementioned law says that by the judge's discretion, enough goods should be left to the partner so sued so that he does not fall into want, but can be comfortably sustained, according to the law on condemnation in the *Digest, On the Rules of Law*, whose words are:
> In the condemnation of persons who are condemned to pay what they are able, not everything they have is to be extorted from them; rather, consideration must be given to them so that they do not lack the necessities of life.
And this opinion of the Gloss is sanctioned today in the *Siete Partidas*.

<margin>7</margin> However, † in judging how much should be left to the person, one must take into account their status and social condition. More must be left to one person for suitable sustenance than to another, in proportion to their condition, status, and other concurrent circumstances. Yet, as Gutierrez well says (following Paolo di Castro), he should not be left as much for sustenance as he used to spend while in his prosperous fortune and dignity, but rather what is fitting for him to spend, living far more sparingly according to his present circumstances, after he has reached such poverty and state at the loss of others. Thus, these things are to be committed to the discretion of a prudent judge, according to the cited authors.

Gregorio Lopez, Gutierrez, Antonio Gomez, Bartolus, and many others note that to judge whether enough remains for someone so they do not fall into want, one must look at what income is received or can comfortably be received from their **patrimony** <note>inherited estate or assets</note>, rather than looking at the total value of the assets or how much money could be made by selling them, following the argument of the text in the law *On the Surrender of Goods*.

<summary>This page discusses the liability of partners for damages caused by negligence or fraud and introduces the "privilege of competence," which prevents a partner from being sued into absolute destitution, ensuring they retain enough for basic sustenance based on their social status.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 413

...since, according to other laws cited by Gutierrez, when <note>original: "Gutier." referring to the jurist Juan Gutiérrez</note> someone is owed support <note>original: "alimenta"; the basic necessities of life including food, clothing, and housing</note>, or such support is left to them, they are not considered to have more than a "fitting maintenance" <note>original: "competentia alimenta, congruâve sustentationem"</note> if they only possess assets which, even with diligent effort appropriate to their social status, produce no more than is necessary for their survival. Indeed, such fitting support must be left to them for their entire life, and not just for a limited time, as noted in a certain marginal gloss on the section "Likewise if regarding a dowry" <note>original: "§. itē si de dote"</note> in the *Institutes* regarding actions, and other sources cited correctly by Gutierrez in the passage mentioned above at number 3. However, with Giovanni da Imola and others, Gregorio López <note>A famous Spanish jurist and commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> and Gutierrez (at number 13) excellently observe that if such a partner possesses high-value immovable property <note>real estate or land</note> that yields very little profit, that property should be sold. Part of the proceeds should then be used to purchase other assets of lower value, or an annuity, or be placed into an honest business that provides fitting support for the partner; the remainder of the price must then be used to pay the debt owed to the other partners.

<margin>8</margin> This must be observed: If a partner, or † anyone else who holds the privilege of not being compelled to pay more than they are able, holds a public office or some other means by which they are fittingly supported—considering the quality of their person and their own hard work—then their remaining assets must be sold to pay the debt. But if they only receive a portion of their fitting support from that office or elsewhere, then they should be allowed to keep enough of their assets to complete that support, and the rest must be sold. The reason is that only "fitting support" is to be left to them, and in this manner, it is preserved for them. This is affirmed by the gloss on the law "If a husband" <note>original: "l. si maritus"</note> regarding the dissolution of marriage, and it is established today in Law 15, Title 10, of the Fifth *Partida* <note>The Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish law code</note>, as affirmed by Gregorio López in the final gloss there and by Gutierrez at number 5.

<margin>9</margin> When † a partner has acted with "evil fraud" <note>original: "dolo malo"; intentional deceit</note> and is the cause of their own inability to pay the debt, they do not enjoy this privilege of only paying what they are able; however, it is different if the inability arises from mere fault or negligence without fraud. This is held in the law "Truly" <note>original: "l. verum"</note> at the beginning and in the section "But the time" <note>original: "§. tempus aurē"</note> in the Digest regarding partners. It is also affirmed in the gloss on the section "Likewise if regarding a dowry." Furthermore, when the other partner—excluding what is owed to them from the partnership—would not have fitting support themselves, then the partner who owes the debt does not enjoy this privilege regarding that portion which the other needs for their own basic survival. This is the view of Bartolus, Paulus de Castro, and others, as well as Gregorio López on the cited Law 15 at the word "lives" <note>original: "uiuir"</note>, and Gutierrez at number 4. Likewise, when a partner has promised the other partners that they will pay in full, adding that they will use no legal or factual defense, and has confirmed this with an oath, they shall not enjoy this privilege. So say Alexander and others, as does Gregorio López at the words "To the company" <note>original: "A la compañia"</note> and Gutierrez at number 38. Gutierrez also notes, following Alexander, that the same applies if there was a "naked promise" <note>original: "nuda promissio"; a simple verbal agreement</note> even without an oath.

<margin>10</margin> When † a partner, because of this privilege, does not pay the full debt, they must provide a "caution"—that is, a simple promise—that they will pay in full if they should come into "fatter fortune" <note>original: "pinguior fortunā"; more prosperous circumstances</note>. They are compelled as time goes on to pay that debt as soon as they have the means to conveniently 

<column-break/>

pay. This is held in the law "Truly," in the section "That which a partner" <note>original: "§. id quod socius"</note> regarding partners, and in Law 15, Title 10, of the Fifth *Partida*, which should be understood as referring to a simple promise according to Gregorio López in the penultimate gloss and Gutierrez at number 9.

<margin>11</margin> It must be observed that in order to judge † how much a partner who is sued is "able to perform" so that they do not fall into want, other debts <note>original: "æs alienum"; literally "another's copper/money"</note>—that is, what they owe to third parties—are not to be deducted, unless those debts arose from the partnership itself. Instead, one must only ensure that after the partnership debt is paid to the other partners, the sued partner is not left in want, even if they remain burdened by other debts. This is expressly stated in the law "Truly," in the section "That which a partner." The same rule applies to others who enjoy this privilege, <margin>12</margin> except for † a donor <note>original: "solo donatore"</note> alone. When a donor is sued for a gift they have promised but not yet fulfilled, all of their other debts must be deducted first. Enough assets must remain for the donor after those debts are paid so that they do not fall into poverty. Both points are expressly stated in the law "Between them" <note>original: "l. inter eos"</note> regarding matters judged. There, after stating that this applies to all debtors who enjoy this privilege (namely, that other debts are not deducted), the following words are added in the section "He also": *"He also, who is sued on account of a donation, is condemned for only as much as he is able to perform, and indeed he alone is granted the deduction of other debts."* The reason why this was specifically established for a donor is this: because they became a debtor solely out of their own generosity <note>original: "liberalitate"</note>, it was therefore considered reasonable that, when sued, they should not be forced into greater poverty because of that act. When, in the manner explained, assets are left to them so they do not suffer want, the rest is used to satisfy the creditors. And when debts are owed to several people for the same reason—as in the case proposed, by title of donation—and without any right of priority, then the one who first receives what is owed to them is in a better position, as is added in the same section. The same was also said at the beginning of that law: when debts arise from another title without priority, whether other debts were to be deducted or not, when assets are to be left to the debtor so they do not suffer want, the condition of the one who first receives what is owed is made better by that very fact. Gutierrez, at number 20, shows extensively that all other debts must be deducted even if the donation was made with a general or specific mortgage. Read him.

<margin>13</margin> I rightly said above that a donor enjoys this privilege when sued for a donation that has been made but not yet fulfilled; for if the † donation has been completed by "delivery" <note>original: "traditione"</note>, a recovery of the gift is not granted on that basis, and therefore this privilege has no place. The same must be said, with even greater reason, for other debts in which a person is not sued for more than they are able to perform. This is the view of Padilla and Gutierrez at number 33. An exception to this doctrine is made when, in this Kingdom of Castile, a son or another descendant has been "bettered" <note>original: "melioratus"; given a larger share of an inheritance</note> in the "third and fifth" <note>The *tercio y quinto* were portions of an estate that a parent could legally use to favor one heir over others under Spanish law</note>. In that case, even if that betterment was made as a gift between living persons and delivery had been performed, at the time of the donor's death, the descendant so bettered would be bound to contribute to all the debts of the deceased, as held in Law 21 of Toro (which is Law 5, Title 6, Book 5 of the *New Collection*), joined with Law 17 of Toro. For the "third and fifth" portions must be calculated according to the assets which, at the time of death, were...

<summary>This page discusses the legal "privilege of competence," which ensures that debtors—particularly business partners and donors—are not forced into destitution by lawsuits. It explains that while partners generally cannot deduct outside debts from their liability, donors are given special protection because their debt arose from an act of unforced generosity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "privilege of competence," specifically how assets are valued at the time of death and how this protection applies to donors and business partners. It transitions into a new disputation regarding the dissolution of partnerships.</meta>

...were found: however, at the time of death, only those goods are considered to belong to the deceased which were found then, after all debts have first been deducted; it is therefore logical that this was rightly decreed in that Kingdom. So says Gutierrez <note>Juan Gutiérrez, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> in the same place.

14 When you hear that a donor † enjoys the explained privilege <note>The "privilege of competence," allowing a debtor to keep enough to live on</note>, make an exception unless the donation is a remunerative one <term>remunerative donation: a gift given as a reward for a service or to settle a moral debt</term> of the first of the three types explained in Disputation 292. In that type of donation, even if the delivery of the gift has not been made, the donor does not enjoy the privilege—when sued—of only providing as much as he conveniently can. This is because a true debt preceded the donation, or rather, preceded the promise of it. However, the situation is different in the remaining two types of donation explained there. Read also what was said at the end of Disputation 282, and you will understand to what extent this privilege applies or does not apply in donations made for a cause <note>donations with a specific purpose or condition</note>, which includes remunerative ones. And the teachings of Gutierrez (cited above at number 34) should be understood according to these principles.

15 When † someone enjoys the privilege of being compelled to pay only what they conveniently can when sued, they can raise this defense <note>original: "exceptione"</note> during the entire time the trial is pending. They may even do so after a judgment has been passed into a "settled matter" <term>res judicata: a legal case that has been definitively decided and cannot be appealed</term>, provided the judgment has not yet been fully executed and the debt has not been paid in full. The reason is that a defense which does not destroy the judgment, but serves to moderate or reduce its burden—as this one does—can be raised even after a judgment has become final. This is because it assists in the execution, according to the law *Nefenius* in the final paragraph of the Digest on judgments <note>original: "l. Nefenius. §. vlt. ff. de re iud."</note> and the law *& ex diuerso* in the final paragraph of the Digest on the dissolution of marriage, as Gutierrez affirms with the common opinion of the doctors in the passage cited above at number 37.

16 You may ask whether † the privilege enjoyed by a partner, or anyone else, not to be held liable for more than they can conveniently afford, passes to their heirs. The answer is no. For a deceased person is not considered to have left more goods to their heirs than were found after all the debts of the deceased were subtracted across the board. This is held in the law *verum* at the beginning of the Digest on partnerships <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>, the law *& si fideiussor*, and the law *Nefenius* at the beginning of the Digest on judgments. Although this same privilege is personal to the partner or whoever else enjoys it, and does not apply to a guarantor <term>fideiussor: a person who guarantees another's debt</term>, as held in the three laws just cited,

17 if † the guarantor uses this precaution—that as a necessary defender of the principal debtor, they undertake the trial in the place and name of that debtor (which they can very well do)—the privilege will redound to them. This is expressly stated in the law *verum* at the beginning of the Digest on partnerships. Gutierrez (at number 15 above) brings forward another precaution along with Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note> and many others: namely, that when a guarantor is sued, they should notify the principal debtor. The debtor should then oppose the suit and take the trial upon themselves, because it is in their interest that the guarantor not be condemned, since the guarantor would immediately have recourse against the debtor to be reimbursed for what was paid in their place. Since the principal debtor does not enjoy that privilege against their own guarantor as they do against other creditors, they can therefore argue that they are not liable beyond what they can afford, and that their guarantor cannot be compelled beyond that sum either. Otherwise, the burden would immediately fall back on the debtor, and the privilege granted to them by law would be rendered useless.

18 Finally, observe: If there are † three or more partners, and one of them, who possesses the assets of the partnership,

<column-break/>

pays one partner the full share owed to them, but later, when the other partners demand their portions, he does not have the means to conveniently pay them, that partner who received what was owed to him is compelled to contribute to the others from that portion. This ensures everyone is satisfied equally according to a certain proportion. This is held in the law *verum* in the paragraph *tempus autem* of the Digest on partnerships, and Law 13, Title 10, Part 5 <note>of the *Siete Partidas*</note>. There, following the opinion of Azo <note>Azo of Bologna, a medieval legal glossator</note>, it is further defined that if the remaining partners were aware that payment had been made to one of them and did not ask for their own payment for a long time (to be defined by the judgment of a prudent judge), then that partner is not held to give them any part of it.

# How a Partnership is Dissolved.
## DISPUTATION 414.
### SUMMARY.

1 *In how many ways a partnership is dissolved; also at numbers 12, 13, 14, 20, and following.*
2 *To what extent a partner's heir is required to continue things started by the deceased.*
3 *Whether a contract is a partnership or an emphyteusis* <term>emphyteusis: a long-term lease of land where the tenant pays a small rent and must improve the property</term> *in cases of doubt, such as when someone gives land to another to be cultivated with an agreement to return half, a third, a fourth, or another portion of the fruits.*
4 *An agreement that a partnership shall pass to heirs is void. However, see the declaration in the following number.*
6 *A partnership is considered continued between partners by tacit consent.*
*Indeed, even by an heir through the same tacit consent. Number 7.*
*And even if the heir were a minor <note>original: "pupillus"</note>, provided they tacitly consent through their guardian. Number 8.*
*And also between spouses, or if one dies, it may be considered continued by the heir through tacit consent. Number 9.*
10 *In which cases a partnership passes to the heirs.*
11 *A partnership contracted with an oath to pass to heirs—when it obligates the heirs to stand by it.*
15 *An agreement that a partnership can never be dissolved is void.*
16 *If communities have common boundaries between them, they are not forced to remain in common ownership.*
17 *If several co-owners of a single thing held in common <note>original: "pro indiuiso"</note> are found, one of them can seek division if they wish, even if the others are unwilling.*
18 *If one of the partners wishes to renounce the partnership, what conditions they must observe.*
19 *In which cases it is permitted to renounce a partnership before the pre-arranged time.*

1 A partnership is dissolved and ended in many ways. First, † by the natural death of any of the partners. And then it is dissolved not only regarding the person of the deceased—because partnership does not pass to his heirs—but also regarding the remaining surviving partners, unless they had agreed among themselves that it would not be dissolved for the survivors upon the death of one or more of them, as was said at the end of Disputation 412. So it is held in the paragraph *soluitur* of the *Institutes* on partnership, and several laws in the Digest and Partidas.
2 Those things, † however, which were begun before the death of the partner, the heir is bound to continue and complete in the place of the deceased with the other partners, in the same manner the deceased was bound. And in a similar way, he is bound...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 414.

...regarding **fraud**, **gross negligence**, or **slight negligence**, if any loss occurred to the other partners through his negligence in projects that had already begun, the deceased would be held liable to them. Likewise, the heir is bound to divide with the partners those assets of the partnership which the deceased held, and to provide an account of them in the same way the deceased was bound. The heir stands in the place of the deceased regarding **fraud**, **gross negligence**, and **slight negligence** committed by the deceased before his death. Similarly, the other partners are bound to all the same obligations toward the heir. 

<note>In Roman law, which this text follows, "fraud" (dolus) is intentional harm, "gross negligence" (lata culpa) is extreme carelessness, and "slight negligence" (levis culpa) is a failure to show the standard care of a prudent person.</note>

Legal actions, whether they involve collecting debts or paying them, which arise from a contract pass to the heirs. However, the heir is not bound to continue the partnership regarding business matters and assets that had not been started at the time of the partner's death. All these points are found in the Digest <note>original: "ff.", the standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Justinian's Roman law</note> in the laws titled "For a Partner" and "On Business Conducted." 

It is also established in this final area of law that if one partner dies and another partner begins a new project while being unaware of that death, then the partnership is not considered dissolved regarding that specific act. Instead, it must be continued by the heir until that specific project is finished. It would be otherwise, however, if the project was started after the death of the partner was known. This is similar to a **mandate** <note>a contract where one person acts on behalf of another</note>: although a mandate expires upon the death of the person giving it, if the agent performs an act while ignorant of that death, the act remains valid, as is stated in the law and will be explained later in its proper place.

<margin>3</margin> Consistent with this doctrine, Book 4 of the **Portuguese Ordinances** <note>original: "Lusitanarum ordinationum," the national legal code of Portugal</note>, title 60, establishes the following: If someone hands over a vineyard or another field to someone else for cultivation, with a pact that they return a half, a third, a fourth, or some other portion of the fruits, then—if the contract is for ten years or more—it is considered an <term>emphyteutic</term> <note>a long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights as long as they improve the land and pay rent</note> contract. According to what will be said later when we discuss emphyteusis, this contract passes to the heirs of both contracting parties. 

If, however, it is for a shorter time, it is considered a contract of partnership, and it is extinguished by the death of either partner and does not pass to the heirs. An exception is made if the person who received the land for cultivation had already performed some labor for that year when the other partner died—for instance, if he had pruned the vineyard, plowed or sowed the field, or done something similar. In that case, the contract passes to the heirs for that year only, because the matter was no longer "untouched" <note>original: "res non esset integra," a legal term meaning the status quo had already been changed by action</note>, but the cultivation for that year had already begun. In rural estates, even by tacit consent, when a contract is continued, it is understood to be continued for a full year. 

If, however, the field was taken not for a portion of the crops but for a determined pension or fixed rent, then if the contract was made for ten years or more, it was emphyteutic; if for a shorter time, it was a contract of **leasing and hiring** <note>original: "locationis et conductionis"</note>. In either of these cases, the contract passes to the heirs.

So it is written there. Indeed, in the final section of that same law, it is commanded: When someone receives the field of another for a portion of the crops to be paid annually, he must not remove the wheat or any other grain of that field from the threshing floor unless he has first summoned the lord of the field or his representative. If they are absent from that town or the surrounding districts, he must not remove it

<column-break/>

except in the presence of two trustworthy witnesses. Otherwise, it shall later be estimated by the judgment of prudent men how much he likely harvested from that field, and he shall pay double what he would otherwise have been required to pay.

<margin>4</margin> As was said at the end of Disputation 412, not only does a <term>partnership</term> <note>original: "societas"</note> not pass to heirs, but even a pact or agreement that it should pass to them is void. This is held in the laws of the Digest under the title "For a Partner." The reason why such a pact is rendered void by civil law is because, as cited in the *Institutes* <note>a foundational legal textbook for students of Roman law</note>, in a partnership, the specific **industry of the person** is chosen. It is unknown what sort of person the heir will turn out to be. Furthermore, as Gregorio López <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> says, if the person of the heir were designated to whom the partnership should pass, the person making such a contract would be stripping themselves of the freedom to change their heir.

<margin>5</margin> However, although a partnership does not pass to heirs and a pact for it to do so is void, if the heir of the deceased partner reaches an agreement with the remaining partners to continue the partnership, it is considered to have been entered into anew and is therefore valid. Indeed, **tacit consent** is sufficient for this, which is assumed to exist if the partnership is continued with the same capital and the same type of business, with neither the heir of the deceased nor the other partners objecting.

<margin>6</margin> Since a contract of this kind is perfected by consent alone expressed outwardly, certainly tacit consent suffices—both in this case and in leasing, or in any other similar contract—for it to be held as if entered into anew and continued. Consent is deemed tacit if, when the contract has ended, the execution of it continues with both parties knowing this and not objecting. This is confirmed by the law and is treated at length by Alvaro Valasco <note>a prominent Portuguese jurist</note>. 

Based on this principle, when certain people had entered into a partnership for a specific time, and that time had ended, the one to whom the business had been committed by the other partner continued the business with the same capital. When the partner later sought a share of the profit from that time, the other contended that the profit was not owed because the partnership had ended long before. Alvaro Valasco, in the cited consultation, judged that it was indeed owed, and he records that the sentence was carried out in favor of his client.

And when the adversary objected that the partnership contract had been celebrated in writing only for that specific time, according to the **Portuguese Ordinances**, and that when a writing is required for a contract, it is not considered renewed unless a new writing intervenes in the renewal, Valasco responded excellently. Following Paulo de Castro, Bartolus, and others, he argued that this applies only when the writing is essential to the substance of the contract (as in <term>emphyteusis</term>, especially ecclesiastical ones). In the Kingdom of Portugal, however, if such writings are used for partnership contracts and others according to the Ordinances, it is not because the writings are part of the substance of such contracts, but because they are necessary for **proof** in that Kingdom when such contracts exceed a certain sum.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 414 regarding how partnerships dissolve or continue upon the death of a partner. It specifically explores the legal mechanisms of "tacit consent" and the validity of oaths in binding heirs to a partnership contract.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

As we have often stated in the previous sections: I am of the opinion that even if the contracting parties had initially suspended the contract—stipulating that it would not be valid unless a written document were first drawn up—it could still be continued through tacit or express consent without a new written document. For, just as it could have begun from the start without writing through the mutual consent of the parties, so too could it be extended and renewed without writing.

7. That this **tacit consent** <note>original: "tacitum consensum"; in law, this refers to agreement implied by actions rather than words</note> is sufficient to consider a partnership renewed with the heir of a deceased partner is affirmed by Gutierrez in his work *On the Confirmation of Oaths*, chapter 48, number 2 (following Baldus, Alexander, and many others), by Gregorio López on Law 10, Title 10, Part 5, at the words "by death" <note>original: "por muerte"</note>, and by Alvaro Valasco in Consultation 63, cited from number 9. 
8. This holds true even when the heir is a **minor** <note>original: "pupillus"; a child under the age of legal responsibility</note>, provided they tacitly consent through their guardian by employing the same managers. This also has the effect that the minor is bound to stand by the contract and bear any loss, if perhaps something occurs by chance from the partnership or its denial; many authorities confirm this. Indeed, I believe that for the minor to enjoy the benefit, it is not strictly necessary for them to have a guardian or curator, according to what was said in Disputation 224. However, in a certain event debated by Alvaro Valasco (where he asserts that certain minor heirs of a deceased partner were owed nothing of the profit acquired after their father's death), he defends this on the grounds that the original partnership had been entered into under the condition that the deceased was bound to renew his **guarantors** <note>original: "fideiussores"; people who legally promise to pay a debt if the principal debtor fails</note> every year. Since neither the minors nor the guardian provided this, even when requested, that partnership was not considered renewed. For a partnership to be renewed by tacit or express consent, the forms and pacts established at the beginning must be observed. He adds, however, that if the other partners had shared any profits acquired after the father's death with the minors *as partners*, then they would be seen to have waived that condition regarding the annual renewal of guarantors. Consequently, the partnership would be considered renewed according to the doctrine of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists</note>, which he then cites.
9. This same **tacit consent** is sufficient so that, upon the death of one spouse, if the goods remain undivided, the partnership is considered renewed between the survivor and the heirs regarding common profits until a division of assets is made. This is the opinion of Palacios Rubios, Alvaro Valasco (as cited above), and Gutierrez.

Although, as stated, a partnership regularly does not pass to heirs—even if a pact was added stating that it should— 
10. an exception is made when the **partnership** concerns **taxes** <note>original: "vectigalia"; public revenues or customs duties farmed out to private collectors</note> or other public leased items. In such a case, if no pact was added to pass it to the heirs, the same rules apply as in other partnerships. However, if a pact *was* added that it should pass to the heirs, it certainly passes to them for the sake of the **public benefit** <note>original: "favorem publicum"</note>. Any profit or loss occurring after a partner's death is shared between the heir and the other partners. This must be understood, however, provided that the heir is **suitable** for the partnership. For if the deceased had been admitted and placed in charge of the partnership because of his specific **industry** <note>skill or specialized labor</note>, and he leaves an heir who is inept for that task, then the partnership does not pass to him, regardless of the pact. This is because such a pact carries the tacit condition: "provided the heir is a suitable partner for the task." All this is found in the laws *Adeo* and *Verum*, in the section "Regarding the Heir" in the Digest <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>, and it agrees with Law 

<column-break/>

1, Title 10, Part 5, as well as the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvaro Valasco and Gutierrez follow.

<margin>Question.</margin>
11. Whether, if a partnership in other matters is contracted with a pact that it pass to heirs, and all partners take an **oath** to observe it, does the contract pass to the heirs in the sense that the surviving partners cannot go against it, but are bound to continue the partnership with the heir? Gutierrez and Gregorio López respond in the affirmative. However, López and Gutierrez believe this should be limited: it only applies if a certain and determined heir is designated. Otherwise, they believe such an oath is **against good morals** <note>original: "contra bonos mores"; legal principle that certain acts are void if they violate social or ethical standards</note>, because it takes away the power to appoint a different heir, and therefore it does not bind. Alvaro Valasco, however, thinks it *never* passes. His reasoning is that a party's oath does not validate an act forbidden and prohibited by law to the prejudice of a third party. Also, because the nature of the act does not seem to change even with an oath. However, I believe Fabrus's opinion is true, even without the restrictions of Lopez and Gutierrez. For that pact—standing on the nature of the thing alone and excluding human law which might make it void—is neither evil nor a nullity in itself, as is manifest. If it were inherently evil, it would not be admitted as valid even in a partnership for taxes. Therefore, if it is corroborated by an oath to observe it, an obligation to keep it arises both **in conscience** and in the external court, based on such an oath, as discussed in Disputations 149 and 150.

As for the first point by which Alvaro Valasco convinces himself of the contrary: it must be denied that the pact, or its execution, is "prohibited." The pact is merely rendered **null**, but not forbidden. Even if the pact were forbidden, that would not prevent an obligation from arising to carry it out if it were confirmed by an oath, as is clear from Disputation 151. Furthermore, that the execution is not forbidden by civil law is clear from the fact that the partners and heirs are free to continue the partnership; by doing so, it is considered renewed by them, as Valasco himself affirms.

To the second point: although the nature of the act is not changed by an oath (as if an oath could make a bad act good or a good act bad), the oath nevertheless has the power to make an act or pact—which is not inherently bad but merely void by human law—valid and obligatory, as shown in the three previous disputations.

Regarding the limitation proposed by Gregorio and Gutierrez, I have shown quite clearly in Disputation 151 (against the opinion of many) that it is groundless. There, I explained in what sense it is said in law that "stripping oneself of the power to make a will" is against good morals. Additionally, anyone entering a partnership who has descendants or ancestors (whom he is bound to leave as heirs by law) does not take away his power to make a will simply because he designates which of them should enter the partnership...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the limits of partnership contracts (societas), specifically looking at when these contracts bind heirs and the various ways a partnership is legally dissolved, such as through civil death, bankruptcy, or the completion of a specific task.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 414.

...through whom the acts of the partnership might pass.

<margin>11</margin> Gregorio López, in the cited gloss, adds another limitation to this rule, along with Bartolus, Baldus, and others, with whom Alvaro Valasco and Gutierrez agree. Namely, if a testator commands his heirs to persevere in a partnership, they are bound to obey the testator's command—provided it is not in perpetuity, but for a certain time, as Gutierrez observes and as will be clear from what follows. However, I would understand this teaching of these doctors to be true regarding the heirs themselves: they would be bound to continue the partnership among themselves if the other partners wish it. But I do not believe an obligation arises for the *other* partners to continue the partnership with the heirs, even if a pact regarding that matter had been made between the partners and the deceased. I also understand this to apply when the testator leaves the heirs something beyond their legal shares <note>original: "legitimas portiones"; the portion of an estate that laws require be left to immediate family</note>; for if he left only the legal share, he could not impose such a burden upon it. Likewise, when such a command is imposed for the benefit and favor of the heirs, they could renounce it by mutual consent. It is otherwise if they are **minors**, as Alvaro Valasco affirms along with Oldradus, Bartolus, and Decio. Here, he rightly adds that this is not properly a limitation of the doctrine handed down above—namely, that a partnership contract does not pass to the heirs even if a pact was made to the contrary.

<margin>12</margin> **Second**, a partnership is dissolved by the **civil death** <note>original: "morte ciuili"; a legal status where a person loses their civil rights (e.g., through life imprisonment or religious profession), being treated as dead in the eyes of the law</note> of any of the partners, in those events discussed in Disputation 9, where it was said that a life-interest <note>original: "vsumfructum"</note> is ended by civil death. One is also dissolved by the very fact that all the goods of one of the partners are confiscated. This is held in the Institutes, title *on partnership* <note>original: "inst. de societate"</note>, and in the Digest <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>.

<margin>13</margin> **Third**, if any of the partners surrenders his assets <note>original: "cedat bonis suis"; essentially declaring bankruptcy</note> because of debts. This is also found in the Institutes and the Digest.

<margin>14</margin> **Fourth**, if the partnership was established precisely for a certain thing and that thing is finished. For example, if it was established for the single purpose of transporting wheat from one place to sell it in another: once that wheat is sold, the partnership is ended. If one of the partners then trades with that money, the profit and loss are not shared but belong to him alone. By the same reasoning, if the entire capital perishes by a chance accident or for another reason, the partnership is ended. (To whom the loss falls will be discussed in what follows). Similarly, if the thing around which the partnership centered perishes or changes its condition so that it is no longer fit for the partnership, the partnership ends. For instance, if a church is built by public authority on land that someone had received to cultivate (intending to divide the fruits with the owner). Also, if a partnership was contracted for a certain time, once that time expires, the partnership is finished—unless it is considered renewed and continued by **tacit consent**, as was said above.

<margin>15</margin> Just as it may have been agreed that a partnership should not be dissolved within a certain time (and thus cannot be dissolved before that time against the will of the partners), so too is a

<column-break/>

pact invalid which states that a partnership can *never* be dissolved. For a pact is not valid if it seeks to pass the partnership to heirs, and consequently, it cannot be made so that it is not dissolved by the death of any partner, as seen above. Therefore, when no time has been set within which a partnership cannot be dissolved—either expressly or tacitly (as a partnership between spouses cannot be dissolved while the marriage lasts, because the partnership is deemed contracted for that entire time)—it is within the rights of the partners, or those who hold something in common, to seek a division and dissolve the partnership.

<margin>16</margin> From this, Avendaño and Gutierrez also gather that if certain peoples or towns have common boundaries, they are not compelled to persevere in that communion. Nor does **prescription** <note>legal ownership gained through long-term use</note> have a place there, even if it has been possessed in common from a time beyond memory; rather, any of those peoples can seek a division if it can be done conveniently, provided it does not depend on royal authority or a prior legal sentence of perpetual communion.

<margin>17</margin> Furthermore, it is inferred that when private individuals have common places for grazing, which are called **dehesas** <note>original: "dehesas"; a Spanish term for a multifunctional agrosylvopastoral system (woodland pasture)</note> in this Kingdom—which is frequent when many heirs succeed to one estate—they usually hold it in common and undivided, leasing it for grazing and dividing the price of the lease according to the portion each holds. In this event, I say, nothing prevents any of them from seeking a division, even if they and their predecessors have possessed it in common from time immemorial. This holds as long as it can be done conveniently without notable prejudice to the others; that is, each divided part must bring a benefit roughly proportional to what the whole brought. For if a notable disadvantage would follow for the others who resist the division—because the divided parts would be of little use, or no one would want to lease them because of their small size, or because some parts have water and others do not—then surely the division should not be granted, especially when the thing was destined for undivided use since ancient times. Indeed, Gutierrez reports that such a division of a common inheritance has been made more than once when one owner sought it and obtained a royal requisition. He also says he has often seen divisions of common houses, supported by enough legal sentences and executions, provided the division can be made conveniently. Whether a husband can seek division when a dotal estate <note>property brought into a marriage</note> is common to his wife and others, or whether a minor or the Church can seek division, you may read in Gutierrez.

Having explained these things, when a partnership was entered into without a fixed...

<meta>This page continues the legal and ethical analysis of the dissolution of partnerships (societas). The previous page established that partnerships generally end upon the death of a partner, but this page explores the rules for voluntary resignation and the specific conditions required for a lawful exit from a business agreement.</meta>

436
->**Luis de Molina on Contracts**<-

...if no specific time was set for how long it should last, it is lawful for any of the partners to dissolve the partnership whenever they wish. 
<margin>18</margin> Then, the partnership is truly dissolved when one of the partners renounces it—that is, signals to the other partners that they wish to withdraw. However, several conditions must be observed. First, they must inform all the partners of their departure. For if they renounce the partnership in the absence of any partner, then whatever the renouncing partner acquires through business using the shared capital while the absent partner is unaware of the resignation must be shared between them. On the other hand, if any loss occurs, the renouncing partner alone is bound to bear it. Conversely, whatever the absent partner acquires in the meantime while ignorant of the change belongs to them alone, but any loss remains shared between both. The reason for this, according to Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note>, is that it is within the rights of the absent partner, once they learn of the resignation, to either ratify it so they are not a participant in the loss, or—if there is no loss or the profit exceeds the loss—not to ratify it, so that they may participate in the profit with the one who renounced the partnership up until that time. However, from the moment they have knowledge of the resignation, they are no longer allowed this choice. 

Second, one must not renounce the partnership at an inopportune time <note>original: "intempestivè"</note>, such that the resignation is damaging to the partnership. Therefore, the partner is bound to complete business already begun and grant a suitable time for its conclusion. For example, if they have purchased slaves <note>original: "mancipia"; Molina writes within the legal framework of the 16th century where slavery was a standard legal category in Roman and Civil law</note>, or wheat, or anything else, and it is not a favorable time to sell them for a profit, the partner is bound to wait for a suitable time. In short, they are bound to bring no harm to the partnership by that dissolution. 

Third, one must not renounce the partnership with fraudulent intent <note>original: "cum dolo"</note> to participate alone in some profit which otherwise, by the force of the preceding contract, would have belonged to the whole partnership. For example, if a "partnership of all goods" <note>original: "societas omnium bonorum"; a contract where partners share all current and future assets</note> had been contracted, and someone, seeing that a large inheritance was about to be left to them, renounced the partnership so that they alone might possess that inheritance and deprive the others of a share in it. In that case, the resignation would be valid in its effect such that if a loss resulted from accepting that inheritance, it would pertain only to them; however, it would not be valid in the sense that they would still be bound to share the benefit with the others if any profit came from the inheritance. The same applies if they renounced the partnership for the purpose of depriving partners of a share of profit from some particular business deal that was imminent. However, this does not apply to business deals entered into *after* the renunciation which they would not have renounced the partnership to avoid; in such cases, they are not judged to have acted with fraud or deceit. But if, from the very beginning when the partnership was formed, a pact was made allowing for resignation even at an inopportune time, then such an untimely resignation would be valid. All these points are clear from the laws *Si coierit*, *Sed & socius* (§ 1 and 2), and *Actione* (§ Diximus) in the Digest <note>Roman legal code</note> under the section "On Partnerships" <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>, and from Law 11, Title 10, Part 5 <note>of the *Siete Partidas*, the Castilian statutory code</note>.

<margin>19</margin> When a partnership has been entered into for a predefined certain time during which it ought to persevere, it is then unlawful for the partners to renounce the partnership unless other factors intervene. But if one of them does renounce it, from that point forward, any loss begins to pertain to them alone, whereas profit is made common in the same manner explained just above regarding partnerships initiated without a fixed time, when a renunciation was made in the absence of one of the partners.

<column-break/>

Several events are excepted in which it is lawful to renounce that partnership before the fixed time has expired. First, if the pacts and conditions under which the partnership was formed are not kept for the one who renounces. Second, if the partners are abusive or harmful to them, such that they are not to be endured in the judgment of a prudent person. Third, if the very purpose for which the partnership was formed ceases to exist. Fourth, if one of the partners renounces the partnership because they will be absent for a long time and against their will for the sake of the State <note>original: "Reipublicæ causa"</note>. However, this is only if they cannot conveniently manage the partnership through another person or commit the partnership to the other partners without loss to themselves; in that case, it would be unlawful for them to renounce. All these things are clear from the law *Coire*, along with the three following laws, and from the law *Actione*, § *Diximus*, at the verse *Item qui societatem*, in the Digest "On Partnerships," and from Law 14, Title 10, Part 5.

<margin>20</margin> It must be observed universally that in whatever way a partnership is entered into, it is dissolved by the mutual tacit consent of the partners—for instance, if they individually begin to act separately for their own private benefit. This is expressly held in the law *Itaque cum* in the Digest "On Partnerships." For just as a partnership is entered into and can be continued by mutual tacit consent, as was said above, so also can it be dissolved by mutual tacit consent.

<margin>21</margin> If someone who was of sound mind entered into a partnership and then falls into madness <note>original: "amentiam"</note>, their guardian <note>term: curator; a court-appointed protector for a person deemed legally incapable</note> can dissolve the partnership in the same way that the person themselves could have dissolved it if they had remained of sound mind. The other partners may also then renounce the partnership, according to the final law in the Code "On Partnerships" <note>original: "C. pro socio"</note>. 

A person can also renounce a partnership either through their general proxy <note>term: procuratorem; a legal representative or agent</note> or through a proxy specifically appointed for that purpose. However, if the partner had prohibited the proxy from doing so, then a renunciation made through that proxy would not be valid. If one partner delivers a renunciation to the proxy of another, it remains within the rights of the partner whose proxy he is to either ratify that renunciation (if they judge it expedient for themselves) or not to ratify it and instead participate in the acquired profit. Therefore, to be excluded from profit, it is necessary that the renunciation be made to the partner themselves. This is held in the law *Actione*, § *Renunciare*, and the following paragraph in the Digest "On Partnerships."

## Various ways in which a partnership for trade and profit is contracted, and how to judge whether it is just.

# DISPUTATION 415.

### SUMMARY.

1. *In what ways a partnership for trade and profit may be contracted.*
2. *By what rules it can be known whether a partnership for trade and profit is just or unjust.*
3. *What the valuation of many things that occur in a partnership consists of.*
4. *A partnership contracted simply for profit is understood to be regarding equal shares and equal division.*
5. *How equal profit in a partnership is computed and understood.*
6. *A partnership with a pact that someone should judge the portion belonging to each partner is void by the law itself once that person dies.*

<margin>
7 When an agreement to submit to a third party, whether acting as a formal judge or an informal mediator, is considered valid.
8 When a partnership involving unequal shares of profit and loss is considered valid.
9 When a partnership entered into where specific losses apply to only one of the partners is considered valid.

<margin>1</margin> Thus far, we have explained partnerships in general. Now, we must first examine the partnership formed for business and profit, which is our current objective. Such a partnership is contracted in many ways. First, where each partner contributes capital, whether equally or unequally with the others, so that expenses are paid from it, while the industry <note>In this context, "industry" refers to professional skill, business expertise, or management effort.</note> and labor are treated as if they were hired for a wage. Then, when the partnership is dissolved, only the capital that each partner brought in is considered when calculating the resulting profit and loss. This type of partnership is one where justice is easily recognized. For if the partners divide the resulting profits and losses among themselves according to the proportion of the capital they contributed, the contract is just; otherwise, it is unjust and unequal. Second, a partnership can be formed where the partners provide capital equally or unequally, but one or more of them contributes all the "industry," or more industry and labor than the others, or provides a ship to carry the goods, or other tools necessary for the business and profit—such as nets for fishing, pack animals for transporting goods, and so on. Third, it can be contracted where one or more contribute the capital, and another or others contribute their labor and industry, or both labor and tools.

<margin>2</margin> In whatever manner and with whatever agreements a partnership is celebrated, the contract must be measured against the following rule to judge whether it is just or unjust, and consequently, whether an obligation to make restitution arises from it or not. Once everything that each individual partner has contributed has been calculated—regarding capital, industry, labor, tools, or anything else—if a proportional equality is found in the contract (that is, if the proportion of what each person contributes to what the others contribute matches the proportion of the profit they are to receive compared to the others, as well as the portion of capital they will withdraw at the end, and the risk and loss to which they expose themselves), then the contract is just. Or certainly, if some inequality is seen in one of these areas, it must be compensated for elsewhere, so that when all things are considered, a "proportional equality" (<term>proportionalis æqualitas</term>) <note>Proportional equality means that fairness is not found in everyone getting the exact same amount (arithmetic), but in everyone getting an amount that fits the size and value of their contribution (geometric).</note> is found among the partners according to the judgment of a prudent man. Otherwise, the contract is unjust and unequal, carrying an obligation to make restitution and to bring the deal back to equality. At this point, it should be observed—

<column-break/>

—taking into account the greater or lesser danger to their own person to which they are exposed (for example, if they are to transport goods by sea or through dangerous places), and taking into account the greater or lesser labor and hardship they will undergo, along with other concurrent circumstances. Certainly, this value does not consist of a single fixed point <note>original: "in indivisibili," a legal term meaning a value that cannot be divided or varied; Molina argues here that prices and values actually have a flexible range.</note>, but has a wide range within the limits of a "just value." Likewise, the valuation of the industry <note>expertise</note> that someone is to provide, even if they stay at home, because they possess great dexterity in organizing and executing business for profit, does not consist of a single fixed point, nor is it valued lightly. This is because profit depends heavily on such dexterity and skill in negotiating, just as much labor and industry are valued in the first category explained above. Hence, in the law "If it was not" <note>original: "l. si nō fuerit," referring to a specific law in the Roman Digest (Digest 17.2.6)</note>, at the beginning of the section "On Partnerships" <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>, we read: "Frequently, the industry of a partner is so great that it contributes more to the partnership than money." The same applies if he sails alone, travels alone, or undergoes dangers alone. These are the words of the law. Furthermore, the valuation of the use of a ship or any other tool necessary for business and profit is certainly not set at a single fixed point, but has much latitude within the limits of what is just. Since the valuation of these things—and many others that occur in a partnership contract—does not consist of a single fixed point, it follows that the proportional equality required for a partnership to be just also has its own range, greater or lesser, depending on what was contributed. Therefore, when everything involved is calculated and the full range of the just value of each part is weighed, if no departure from proportional equality is found, the contract is just. But when the judgment of a prudent man detects a departure, the contract is unjust, with the burden of restitution to the extent necessary to reach the limits of justice. However, this is understood to apply when the partner who is burdened by the inequality does not "pardon" or allow it out of "liberality" <note>generosity or charity</note>, but suffers it involuntarily (either because they are unaware of it or because they feel it is better to suffer it than not to enter the contract at all, as often happens). For if they chose to suffer that inequality out of liberality—perhaps because the partner is a relative or friend, or to reward past services, or as an act of charity—then clearly, since no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting with full freedom, neither injustice nor any other iniquity would be seen in that contract.

<margin>4</margin> If the partners entered into a partnership for profit but did not express how the profit should be divided among them, it is understood that it must be divided into equal parts. This is held in the *Institutes* <note>A foundational Roman law textbook</note> in the section "On Partnerships" at the beginning, and in the law "If it was not" in the *Digest*. The gloss <note>A standard medieval commentary on the law</note> in both places understands this to apply when the capital was contributed equally by the partners. 

<margin>5</margin> This is finally to be understood as referring to equal shares of profit, not always according to <term>arithmetic proportion</term> <note>Strictly equal amounts (e.g., $5 each).</note> but according to <term>geometric proportion</term> <note>Proportional amounts (e.g., 10% of what you put in).</note>: specifically, that the proportion of the share of capital contributed by one person matches the shares contributed by others.

<summary>This page analyzes how to ensure justice in business partnerships by balancing financial capital against "industry" (skill) and physical risk. It argues that fairness is found in "proportional equality," where rewards match the value and danger of the contribution, rather than a simple 50/50 split.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 416. ###

<margin>
2. A partnership simply entered into without an explicit statement on the shares of profit and capital is understood to be regulated according to the custom of the place where it was contracted.
3. If a partnership is entered into where one provides capital and the other labor, if the capital is destroyed, it is dissolved at the risk of the one who provided it, without any restitution from the other for labor not performed.
4. If one of the partners provides money and the other labor, how the profit of the money is to be estimated.
5. When a partnership is contracted where one provides capital and the other labor, when does the ownership of the capital become common?
6. It is also to be called a contract of partnership when one provides capital and the other a ship along with the labor of a servant.
</margin>

**Question.** This matter is highly controversial among the Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the "Doctors of the Church" or learned scholars of theology and law</note>. Examples are as follows: If someone hands over money to a craftsman to practice the skills of his trade and make a profit; or to a merchant who is to transport and export goods by land or sea; or to someone similar who alone is to trade with that money. The question is whether, once the partnership is dissolved, only the profit should be divided between them (with the entire capital belonging to the one who provided it), or whether the capital itself should also be divided between them. The same doubt arises when someone contributes the use of some property to a partnership—such as a ship or something similar—and another, or others, provide capital: should only the profit found after the capital has been deducted be divided with him, or indeed the capital itself?

Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534) was a prominent Italian theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note>, in his commentary on the *Secunda Secundae*, question 78, article 2, reply to the fifth objection, asserted that both the profit and the capital are to be divided in a certain proportion with the person who provided the labor, industry, or the use of a ship or other item. For example, if one person provided two thousand ducats <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe in the Renaissance</note> for trade, and another provided labor and industry (or even the use of a ship) which were valued at one thousand ducats, and upon the dissolution of the partnership four thousand five hundred ducats are found: the one who provided only the labor and industry (or the use of a ship) ought to receive a third part of that entire sum found—that is, one thousand five hundred ducats. The other should receive the remaining two parts—that is, three thousand ducats. It is as if, from that entire sum found, three thousand ducats are first extracted as the "established capital" (made up of the two thousand ducats one partner provided and the one thousand ducats the other's labor, industry, and ship-use were worth). These are divided so that one receives the two parts of the whole capital he provided, and the other receives the remaining third which he provided in labor, industry, and ship-use (which no longer exist as physical assets). Afterwards, the remaining one thousand five hundred ducats, which exist as profit, are divided between them in the same way, according to the proportion of the share of capital each provided. If, however, those partners should report a loss from that partnership—for instance, if at the end only one thousand five hundred ducats are found of the capital—then the one who provided the labor, industry, and use of the ship would receive a third of that capital (namely, five hundred ducats), and the other would receive the remaining two parts (namely, the remaining one thousand ducats).

Later, however, the same Cajetan, in his *Summa* under the word "partnership" (*societas*), 

<column-break/>

changed his opinion. Namely, he argued that only the profit remaining after the capital has been deducted should be divided between them, and the entire capital belongs solely to the person who provided it. Likewise, if the capital perished, either in whole or in part, that entire loss would belong to the same person, and no part of it would fall to the one who provided labor, industry, and the use of a ship; instead, this person would only bear the loss of the labor, industry, and use of the ship he had contributed. This same opinion is embraced by Soto <note>Dominic de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican and leading figure in the School of Salamanca</note> in *On Justice*, Book 6, question 6, article 1, and by Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canon lawyer and economist</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 251 and following. Silvester (under the word "partnership," question 6), Angelus (in the same place, number 10), and many others agree with it. Nevertheless, many of these authors add that it is sometimes lawful to include in the agreement that the capital belongs to everyone, or even that if it perishes in part, some portion of the remainder should go to the one who provided the labor and industry.

The following conclusions will reveal how I feel about this matter. **The First Conclusion.** When <insert>†</insert> the labor, industry, use of a ship, or other property that one partner provides are equal in value to the capital provided by the other, the contract is lawful if both the profit and the capital are divided equally between both partners, according to the opinion Cajetan followed in his commentary on the *Secunda Secundae*. Indeed, in that case, an agreement that only the profit be divided equally while the entire capital belongs to the one who provided it is inequitable, carrying the obligation of restoring half of the capital. If, therefore, such partners had agreed that at the end of the partnership they would make a division between themselves in equal parts, without expressing whether it was of profit alone or of the whole sum, in case of doubt they should be judged to have intended the whole sum. The same must be said when the labor, industry, and ship-use were equal in value to half of the capital, and the agreement was that the one who provided these should receive a third of the whole sum; or when they were equal to any other fractional part, and the agreement was that he should receive a corresponding proportional part of the whole sum. Conradus agrees with this conclusion in *On Contracts*, question 93, corollary 3; as does Major <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, question 47; Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist</note> in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 2, number 2; and others cited by Covarruvias. This can be proven regarding the first two parts, because if in that event the whole sum is to be divided equally, equality is preserved among the partners; for they contribute equal values to the partnership, and they report equal amounts when the partnership ends. But if an agreement is made that only the profit is divided and the entire capital belongs to the one who provided it, an inequality is seen. This is because, while the partners are equal in other respects, one of them provides an equal value of labor, industry, and ship-use (which he spends entirely), and the other provides the same value in money (which he keeps safe and whole). In this, surely, inequality and injustice are seen, with the burden of restoring as much as is necessary to bring the contract back to equality—that is, half of the capital provided in money. Thus, the first two parts of the proposed conclusion are true. The third part is proven by the fact that, in doubt,

# Luis de Molina on Contracts #

It must not be presumed that the contracting parties intended to enter into an unjust contract. This is especially true since, if a notable and manifest inequality exists, a judge can and should compel the contract to be reduced to a state of equality. Indeed, the cited doctors <note>Legal and theological scholars</note> observe most correctly that in the event described—if the capital is lost after the labor, industry, and use of the ship have been applied—the partner who provided those things is not bound to return anything to the partner who provided the capital. This is because the capital had become common property, and the value of the labor, industry, and use of the ship provided was equal to the risk. However, if the capital were to perish before these things were applied, then the labor-partner would be bound to pay half of the capital to the other. This is because they had not yet contributed their portion of the value they were bound to provide, and half of the valuation of that partnership belongs to the one who contributed the capital in money or goods. But if the capital should perish after the other partner has provided a portion of the labor, industry, and use of the ship, with a portion of the value still remaining to be contributed, then they would only be bound to return half of the value of what remained to be provided.

**The second conclusion.** If the labor, industry, and use of the property provided by one of the partners are not equal to the capital in terms of market value, but are equal to the capital in terms of profit by the judgment of a prudent person <note>Latin: *arbitrio prudentis*; a standard legal term for reasonable assessment</note>—that is, so that the partner providing labor participates equally in the profit because of it, just as the other does because of the capital—then the contract is licit. In such a case, when the partnership ends, they share the profit equally (or in whatever proportion was agreed), and the capital, if it remains safe, belongs solely to the one who provided it. I believe that partnership contracts are frequently celebrated in this manner; indeed, such contracts are understood this way when nothing else is specified in the agreement. Namely, that the labor, industry, and use of a ship or other item are valued only in comparison to the profit—specifically, how much is fair for the provider to share in the profit, considering the capital others provided. One must also consider that these efforts are entirely "lost" (spent) by the one who provides them, while the other partners must receive back the full portions of the capital they provided if it remains safe after the partnership is dissolved, and only the profit remaining above that is to be divided among all partners.

<margin>
2.
</margin>
Therefore, because † contracts are deemed to be celebrated according to the custom of the place in which they are made when nothing else is expressed (as is clear from the laws *quod si nolit* <note>Digest 21.1.31.22</note> and *prius* <note>Digest 39.3.1.2</note>), it follows that as a rule, if persons absolutely celebrate a partnership contract where some provide capital and others provide labor and industry, and they agree on what share each will receive at the end without specifying whether it is a share of the whole sum or only of the profit after deducting capital, it must be understood as referring to the profit alone and not the capital. However, if a custom prevailed in some place that, as a rule, partnership contracts in any business (or a specific one) were celebrated so that both profit and capital were to be divided among all partners, then a contract celebrated in that manner would be understood to include both capital and profit, either in any business

<column-break/>

or in a specific one, according to the prevailing custom. But if in some place the partnership contract is celebrated interchangeably in both ways, then the contract should be understood in whichever way contains more equity: for in doubt, it is to be presumed that the contracting parties wished and intended to observe equity.

That the contract discussed in this conclusion is licit is quite clear in itself. This is because equality is preserved in it, and I do not see the Doctors disagreeing about it; rather, they agree if they are read carefully. In this matter, observe that in order to share in the profit alone, labor, industry, and the use of property must be valued much higher than if they were being valued for the purpose of sharing in the capital itself as part of the total principal alongside money or goods. For instance, labor, industry, and the use of a vessel which are worth only one hundred in themselves, if applied toward sharing only the profit, might be equivalent to seven hundred or a thousand. Thus, if one person provides those and another provides seven hundred or a thousand, the profit should be divided between them in equal parts. This accounts for the fact that the labor and industry are entirely "lost" to the one who provides them <note>The worker cannot get their time back</note>, and the other must first deduct the seven hundred or thousand they provided before the remaining profit is divided. It also accounts for the fact that the partner providing labor bears the total loss of both capital and profit if it occurs through even their slight negligence—which is surely no light burden to take upon oneself.

<margin>
3.
</margin>
When † a contract is celebrated according to this second conclusion, what the Doctors are accustomed to say (both those we cited before the first conclusion and those for it) remains true: namely, if the capital perishes, the whole loss falls upon the one who provided it. Likewise, if the one who was to provide labor has not yet provided it, or has not yet provided it in full, and the capital is entirely lost, they are not bound to restore anything by reason of the labor or use of property not yet provided. The contract is deemed to be celebrated under the condition that the risk of the total capital belongs to one partner, because the whole capital belongs to that same partner if it remains safe. The other partner is only expected to provide labor or the use of a thing as long as the capital remains safe; if it is entirely lost, they are no longer bound to provide it, for it is enough to be bound to that alone, since they lose everything they provided from their own side.

I would further advise two things regarding a partnership contract celebrated in the aforementioned way. The first is that, as Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous canon lawyer</note> well observes in his *Manual*, chapter 12, number 251, Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Dominican theologian</note> affirms something false in his *On Justice*, book 6, question 6, article 1. Soto
