For it would follow from this that if someone provided ten thousand ducats for a very safe business from which a huge profit was expected, but which required little industry and labor, they could receive almost no profit, but almost the en-

...then it would pertain to the one who had provided moderate labor, which the owner of the money could have hired for a small price for that business; however, the intellect rejects this as manifestly false. Furthermore, since such a large amount of money cooperates primarily toward that profit, and works as a lasting instrument for the person who applied it toward that end and at his own risk, it is indeed absurd to claim that the one who provided the money can only share in the profit to the extent that the risk he exposed it to is valued, and not also to the extent that the result depends on and is produced by that money.

This opinion of ours is clearly confirmed in the chapter *Per vestras*, concerning donations between husband and wife. <note>Refers to a specific decree in Canon Law regarding the management of dowries.</note> There, the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> ordered that the dowry of a certain woman—which was at risk in her husband's possession because the husband was verging on extreme poverty—be handed over to a merchant in a partnership contract for some secure business. This was so that the husband might live and support the wife from the profit of that money. If one could not justly receive more profit from that money than what corresponded to the risk of losing it, then either the wife’s dowry would be at great risk, or the husband would be able to receive very little from it to support his wife. However, the Supreme Pontiff assumes the opposite of both to be true in that teaching.

<margin>5</margin> The second point is this: When a partnership contract is celebrated in this manner, the ownership of the capital does not become common to the partners; rather, as long as the capital remains the same in identity as what was contributed, the ownership belongs solely to the one who contributed it. However, by the very fact that it is traded for profit, and that goods are bought with it or other money is acquired, the ownership of those goods or that money becomes common to the partners. Thus, the entire sum, in its totality, belongs to each individual partner; yet partially, by partiality of ownership. <note>This is a legal distinction: while they own the whole pot together, their individual legal claim is to a specific share.</note> The reason for this is that in that sum, the capital is mixed with the profit, so that one part no more belongs to the profit than the other, nor one part more to the capital than the other.

<margin>6</margin> Along with the contract I affirm in this conclusion, we can include a contract that is quite frequent in maritime places. Some are accustomed to contribute capital, and another provides the ship, with an agreement entered into that a certain part of the profit be divided between the owner of the ship and the crew of the ship, with a certain portion of that part given to each of the crew. Some merchants are accustomed to pay the price of one of the ship's crew members, so that the portion of the profit that would fall to that crew member belongs to them; this is what the Portuguese call *emere vnmarinaagem* <note>original: "emere vnmarinaagem" — to buy a seaman's share.</note>. In this case, if the ship perishes or no profit is gained, the merchants lose that price; but if profit is gained, the portion of one crew member belongs to them, and nothing of the price they gave. This is a partnership contract by which the labor of one ship's crew member is contributed in exchange for that profit which is hoped for; and it is a licit contract. It would indeed be illicit if the price contributed were required to remain safe in any event. <note>This would be considered usury if the merchant's investment was guaranteed regardless of the voyage's success.</note>

# Whether a contract can be licit where the entire risk of the capital belongs to the one providing labor.

## DISPUTATION 417.

### SUMMARY.

1. Whether a partnership contract is licit if the entire risk of the capital belongs to the one who provides labor, and how, and in what events; also number 7 and following. And what applies in other contracts, number 2.
3. A licit partnership contract where the one providing labor also takes part of the risk of the capital upon himself.
4. A merchant receiving dowry money for trading is also compelled to take the risk of it upon himself.
5. A partnership contract joined with an insurance contract: when it is illicit. Explain and understand as in number 10.
6. The proper nature of partnership, and what the conditions are, and what is called a "Leonine partnership." <note>A "Leonine partnership" (societas leonina) is an illegal partnership where one party takes all the profits and the other takes all the losses, named after Aesop's fable of the lion's share.</note>

12. A partnership contract: when it is licit if one provides the capital with only a third part of the risk and profit, and the other provides labor with the risk of the remaining parts of the capital and profit.

Frequently in Lisbon <note>original: "Olyssipone"</note> and in other places, widows and many others are accustomed to hand over money to craftsmen and other merchants for some profitable business with a pact: that it be entirely up to them to withdraw from the partnership whenever they please, or after a certain fixed time; and with a pact that the capital, or part of the capital which they contribute, always remain whole and safe for them, and the merchant takes the entire risk upon himself; and furthermore with a pact that from the profit, a certain amount be returned to them annually—for instance, at the rate of four, five, or six percent—whether the merchant gains much, little, or nothing; or that a proportional share of the profit be returned to them, so that if no profit is gained, nothing but their capital is returned to them, but if it is gained, a third or fourth part of the profit is returned to them. And because merchants, the greater the amount of money they trade with, the more they profit, they gladly enter into these contracts.

And so that they may free themselves from the care and labor of accounting, and from scruples, and also to free the partners contributing capital from the suspicion of whether more profit was gained and they were deceived by the merchants, both parties more willingly agree that a certain fixed amount of profit be paid annually—at a rate of four, five, or six percent—rather than a proportional share of the profit being paid. We inquire, therefore, about this kind of contract and other similar ones, whether they can be licitly celebrated, or whether they are always...

# Luis Molina, On Contracts

### Page 442

...whether they are illicit and usurious: because such an arrangement seems more like a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"</note> with a pact to return something extra, rather than a true **partnership** <note>original: "societas"</note>.

<margin>1</margin>
John Major (in book 4, distinction 15, questions 48 and 49), Martín de Azpilcueta (in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 253, and in his *Consilia*), Diego de Covarrubias, and others whom they cite, assert that this contract is licit. However, this is only provided that the person handing over the **capital** <note>original: "capitale"</note> does not intend to give that money as a loan, but truly intends to enter into a partnership contract in that manner. Furthermore, the increase in profit specified in the agreement must be commensurate with the money, given that the other party takes the risk upon themselves. Specifically, the amount subtracted from the profit that the capitalist could otherwise legally receive must be equal to what he would have to pay a third party to insure that same capital.

This opinion is proved first: Because a person who hands over a thousand gold pieces for a business venture where the capital is at little or no risk, and from which he expects a share of eighty gold pieces, can legally enter into an insurance contract for his capital with a third party for twenty gold pieces (or a proportional share of the expected profit). He can also legally enter another contract with a different third party to sell the remaining expected profit for thirty or forty gold pieces. Therefore, from the beginning, when he entered the partnership, he could legally enter all three of those contracts simultaneously with the partner who provided the labor and industry. Namely: first, a partnership for a share of the profit (roughly eighty pieces); second, insurance of the capital for twenty pieces; and third, the sale of the hope of the remaining profit for thirty or forty pieces. The logic holds because when many individual contracts are just and legal, no injustice arises from combining them; the combination is nothing more than a union of just contracts. <note>This "Triple Contract" allowed investors to secure their principal and a small profit while staying within the Church's anti-usury laws.</note>

<margin>2</margin>
Second, in cases of **loans for use** <note>original: "commodato"</note>, **leases** <note>original: "locato"</note>, and **deposits**, although part of the risk for the item belongs to the lender or owner (as seen in the section on loans for use and as will be discussed later), a pact is nonetheless legal where the entire risk—even for accidents—belongs to the borrower, tenant, or deposit-keeper. Therefore, by the same reasoning in a partnership contract, although the nature of the contract suggests that when one provides capital and another labor, the risk to the capital belongs (entirely or partly) to the one who provides it, a pact is nonetheless legal where the one providing labor takes the entire risk upon himself. This is done through compensation: in exchange for the risk he assumes, he receives a larger share of the expected profit than he otherwise would. Such a pact is not "against the nature" of a partnership in a way that destroys its essence; rather, it is "beside its nature," as an accidental pact added and joined to it.

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin>
This reasoning is confirmed because it is legal for the one providing labor to take a portion of the risk to the capital upon himself, provided he is granted a larger share of the expected profit (as discussed in preceding disputes and agreed upon in legal texts like the *Institutes* and the *Digest*). Therefore, by the same logic, a pact will be legal where he takes the *entire* risk of the capital, provided there is due compensation in the form of a greater share of the expected profit. This might sometimes be more desirable and useful for the person providing the labor than the alternative, especially if the risk is nearly non-existent and the potential profit is of much greater value.

<margin>4</margin>
Third, the aforementioned authors prove the same from the chapter *Vestras* (regarding donations between husband and wife), where a husband is compelled to hand over dowry money to a merchant for "secure negotiation." This is so the dowry remains safe for the wife while the husband supports himself and her from the profit. This cannot happen unless the merchant takes the risk of the capital upon himself.

<margin>5</margin>
However, Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note>, Domingo de Soto (in *De Iustitia et Iure*, book 6, question 6), and others believe that while a partnership contract is legal when it is joined with an insurance contract from a *third party*, it is illegal when that same contract is made with the *partner* who provides the labor—regardless of whether a portion of the expected profit is sold for a smaller, fixed profit or not.

<margin>6</margin>
Panormitanus is led to this because it is of the nature of a partnership that both partners are exposed to the risk of losing either their labor or their capital. Otherwise, the partnership would be "Leonine." <note>A "Leonine partnership" refers to a fable where the lion took all the spoils; in law, it describes an illegal partnership where one party takes all the profit and the other all the loss.</note> Therefore, while the laborer can shift the risk of the capital onto the person providing it (because the laborer still risks losing his work), the person providing the capital cannot shift the risk of both the labor and the capital onto the laborer without destroying the nature of a just partnership.

Soto, however, argues that by the very fact that the capitalist shifts the entire risk onto the partner, he loses **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of it and transfers it to the partner. This is because the owner of a thing is the one for whom the thing perishes. From this, it follows that as soon as the risk is shifted to the partner through an insurance contract, the partnership ceases to exist and becomes a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>. This applies whether the insurance pact is made at the start of the partnership or later. Since nothing can be taken from a loan without the sin of **usury** <note>original: "vsuræ"</note> and the burden of restitution, it follows that a partnership for profit with a capital insurance pact made with the partner is illicit and usurious.

Cardinal Cajetan, in his 17th work, response 11, says that if an insurance pact is added to a partnership contract after some time has passed—and likewise a pact for a certain profit for the remaining share of hope—nothing unjust or illicit is created...

<summary>This page discusses the legality of the "Triple Contract," specifically debating whether a partner providing capital can legally shift all financial risk to the working partner in exchange for a lower profit share. Molina presents arguments from both sides, weighing the nature of partnership against the freedom to contract insurance.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 417.
#### Page 443

...it may be done lawfully, provided that what is surrendered from the expected profit in exchange for the insurance of the **capital** <note>original: "capitale," the principal sum invested</note> is a price commensurate with the risk to the capital, and provided that the certain profit established for the remainder of the expectation is also commensurate with it. If, however (he says), those three contracts are celebrated together with the partner, or if the second and third are presupposed—that is, if from the beginning the one who is to provide the capital to the **partnership** <note>original: "societas"</note> first agrees with the craftsman or merchant that, for the capital he is to hand over, the merchant shall pay a certain amount of profit annually and furthermore take upon himself the entire risk of that capital—then the contract is unjust and **usurious** <note>original: "usurarius," referring to the sin of charging interest on a loan</note>, carrying the burden of restitution for whatever was accepted in this way.

**Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canonist</note>, as reported by **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445)</note> and others, asserted that a pact for a certain profit is licit, throwing the entire risk of the capital onto the partner, and that this is permissible due to the risk of "fortuitous cases" <note>accidents or "acts of God"</note>.

**Conrad** <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian</note>, however, in his work *On Contracts* (question 97), agrees with the authors of the first opinion mentioned: that the contract can be celebrated licitly within the limits of justice. Yet he says that, simply speaking, it is illicit because it has the appearance of a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum," a loan for consumption where ownership transfers and interest is forbidden</note> with a pact for usurious increase; for this reason, it is prone to generate scandal, defame the contracting party, and open a path for introducing and cloaking usury.

<margin>Decision 7</margin> In order for me to state my opinion on this matter, it must be observed that money can be given with the aforementioned pacts in many ways. One way is to someone who is believed not to be going to trade with it. Another is to someone who is believed to be going to trade, but without caring whether he will trade or not; rather, the one who gives it abdicates his **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> and transfers it to the receiver with a pact that after a certain time (or whenever the giver wishes), he shall return it with some increase established between them.

Another way is by giving it precisely for trading, so that the receiver cannot spend it on anything else; but in this sense, by throwing the risk onto the receiver, so that after a certain time (or at the giver's discretion) he is bound to restore it in full. And, as it were, as a price for being permitted to trade with the hope of profit and convenience, he is bound to pay some moderate increase—for example, four or five percent annually, or a portion of whatever profit he acquires.

Finally, one can give it for trade so that it may cooperate and produce profit, with the giver's ownership persevering. However, he does not wish to give it except for a share of the expected profit that is owed to him, either by a third party or by the person who receives it. He does this either because he fears losing it, or because he fears the receiver might not be faithful in the accounting to be done later—denying him both the profit and the capital (or part of it) by claiming the capital was lost in trade through no fault of his own, leading to lawsuits and troubles. For a similar reason, he might only be willing to give it if the receiver simultaneously enters a third contract of "sale" regarding the remaining part of the expected profit, in exchange for a certain and determined profit to be paid to him annually. Merchants who receive such money for trading often prefer all these conditions, as they are usually more useful to them than if the money were handed over under a simple partnership contract alone.

<column-break/>

This being established, our first conclusion is:

8 If money is handed over for trading in the fourth way explained, with those pacts, and if the certain and determined profit is commensurate with the quantity of the expected profit, then the contract is "mixed." This is true not only if the pacts are added after an interval, but even when they are added from the beginning, either formally or virtually. They are considered added "virtually" if the one providing the labor says: "Give me so much money for such trade, and I will take the risk of the capital upon myself, and furthermore I will give you annually so much certain profit, and leave the rest of the profit to me." Or if the one providing the capital offers a similar pact; for in that agreement, those three contracts are virtually contained.

Two arguments prove this conclusion, along with the confirmation of the second argument, which were proposed in favor of the opinion of the majority, **Navarrus** <note>Martín de Azpilcueta</note> and **Covarrubias**. Nor is it true what **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Dominican theologian</note> says: namely, that by the very fact that a pact for insuring capital is added to a partnership contract with the partner, the ownership of the capital passes to the one providing the labor, the contract ceases to be a partnership, and it turns into a loan. We shall address this when responding to Soto's fundamental argument. On the contrary, as long as the capital is not alienated, its ownership belongs solely to the one who provided it. Consequently, a **vindicatory action** <note>original: "rei vendicatio," a legal claim to recover property from someone else</note> is available to him if someone steals it while it is in the power of the partner providing the labor. Likewise, if the partner dies, and for that or any other reason the partnership is dissolved or proceeds no further, the one who handed it over has a right to reclaim the property. Nor could any seizure be made upon that capital for other debts of the working partner that do not pertain to the partnership; for it is not yet his, but belongs to the one who provided it. Therefore, no creditor of such a debtor could be preferred over the one who provided the capital, even if those creditors had a general mortgage on the debtor's goods. All these things are entirely foreign to a **loan** <note>mutuum</note>, the ownership of which passes by that very fact to the borrower and ceases to be with the lender.

Indeed, if that merchant alienated that capital and bought merchandise from it, or acquired other money, all of that belongs to the partnership. Consequently, each of the partners acquires ownership of it—totally as to the whole of the thing, but partially as to the portion of ownership, as was said in the preceding disputations. For that reason, each of the partners, insofar as it concerns him (either regarding the capital or the share of profit), ought to be preferred over all other creditors of the other partner. The fact that one partner enters an insurance contract with the other does not hinder this any more than if a third party had entered the same insurance contract for a share of the profit with the same partner. In that event, it is clear that the ownership of the capital and profit belongs to the partner with whom the insurance contract was made, just as if such a contract had not been celebrated with him.

Therefore, because that money, handed over for trade in that manner, cooperates toward profit—and the insurance contract entered with the other partner does not impede this—and because the ownership of it remains with the one who provided it, even if it is [passed] to the other...

<summary>Molina argues that the "Triple Contract"—combining partnership, insurance, and the sale of uncertain profit—is a licit "mixed contract" because the investor retains legal ownership of the capital until it is traded, distinguishing it from a usurious loan.</summary>

I should advise that, even if we were to grant for the sake of argument that the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the capital passes to the partner by the very fact that an insurance contract is added with the other partner, and ceases to remain with the one providing it—certainly when the one providing the capital was about to enter into that same true contract of **partnership** <note>original: "societas"</note>, even if the insurance contract were not added—especially if he believes the partner will conduct the business honestly, he could lawfully receive his capital back safe and sound. This is due to the **lost profit** <note>original: "lucrum cessans," the concept that an investor deserves compensation for forgoing other profitable opportunities</note> ceasing for him by withdrawing from the partnership in that way, and granting the person providing the labor all the profit expected therefrom. Furthermore, he could receive a certain moderate profit as a just price for that lost profit. Many people do not pay attention to this, yet it would be a legitimate title to justify the contract at that time.

<margin>9</margin> **Second conclusion.** When † money is handed over for trading with these agreements in any of the three ways explained in the first place, the contract would be unjust, carrying the burden of restoring the increase, unless it were excused on the grounds of **lost profit**. This is because, in that way, the one who gives would, for the sake of the receiver, deprive himself of an equal profit that would otherwise have lawfully come to him from that money. This conclusion is proven because, in those events, a partnership is not truly seen, but rather a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>; immediately the ownership of that money passes to the receiver, and the one who gives it loses it. Even if it is applied to trading, it does not cooperate toward profit as belonging to the giver, but as belonging to the receiver and the one trading.

However, I should advise two things. One is that when money is truly given to a merchant with these agreements, and the one who gives it judges that he wants it for trading and making a profit—since everyone intends to hand it over in the best way they lawfully can—and since he could lawfully give it in the fourth way explained; simple people who do not know how to distinguish these things should never be condemned if they hand over their money with such agreements to someone whom they do not doubt wants it for trading and profit. For, at least by virtue of their intent, they intend to hand it over in the fourth way explained. The other thing is that if the merchant later does not trade with it, he is nonetheless bound to pay the entire capital and the increase of profit; for it is his own fault that he does not trade, and he may not pursue the partnership contract at his own risk and loss.

<margin>10</margin> **Third conclusion.** When † some thing can produce fruit or a benefit through its use without being sold, or provide it in some other way, then a contract is licit by which that thing is granted for the fruit or benefit to be perceived from it, with an agreement for its insurance, and in addition the payment of some certain **interest** <note>original: "interesse," here meaning a return or fee</note>—provided that the benefit hoped for from it is worth both that insurance and also that certain interest. For example, it is licit to lease one hundred sheep to someone to perceive the fruits from them, with an agreement for their insurance and the payment of such and such interest in money, or in their fruits, or in some other

<column-break/>

thing, provided the fruits hoped for from them are worth both the undertaking of that risk and the interest to be paid in addition.

Similarly, the use of a horse can be granted for a certain time for a certain amount of money, and with the burden that the hirer takes the risk of the horse upon himself, provided the granted use is equal in value to both things. The reason is that such things are not like money and other things that are consumed by use, and which do not bear fruit unless they are distributed and alienated by transferring ownership to another; and thus they only bear fruit as they are subject to human industry and trading. Therefore, since the things discussed in this conclusion yield fruit estimable in money while their ownership remains with the person who previously held it, they can be granted for perceiving those fruits for a certain interest. If as much is remitted from that interest as is fair to remit for the undertaking of their risk, the contract will be licit by which the one who receives them to perceive their fruits takes their risk upon himself; and in addition, he pays a certain interest, or an uncertain one—that is, a certain portion of the fruits.

It remains for us to run through the arguments for other opinions. The first two for the opinion of **Major**, **Navarrus**, and **Covarrubias** <note>Leading theologians and jurists of the 16th century</note> only confirm our own, as was said. Regarding the third, it must be observed that **Giovanni d’Andrea** <note>A famous 14th-century canonist</note> thought that this concession was made specifically in favor of a dowry, as if handing over money in that way were intrinsically illicit, but allowed in that event by privilege. However, **Panormitanus** and the doctors commonly and rightly rebuke this.

For if that contract were usurious by its very nature, it would be licit to practice it for no cause, however pious, because usury is prohibited by natural law, which positive law cannot override—as we said in a similar case regarding the conservation of the goods of minors in the matter of usury. Also, that text does not support the opinion of Major, Navarrus, and Covarrubias, because the Supreme Pontiff only ordained that the money be given for subsequent trading, but not without almost no risk to that capital. For just as it was to be left in the power of the husband—unless experience had shown that it was greatly endangered in his power, even though it could perish by chance or by trading beyond hope—so the Supreme Pontiff ordained that it be handed over for equally secure trading for profit; yet not without all risk whatsoever, even of chance or omission, in trading that is secure by its nature.

Regarding the point that led Panormitanus, it must be denied that it is of the essence of a just partnership that both partners be exposed to risk. For when the shifting of the entire risk onto one partner is sufficiently compensated, no injustice is seen in the partnership because the entire risk belongs to only one of the partners. Nor is this what the laws call a **lion’s partnership** <note>original: "leonina societas," an unfair partnership where one person takes all the profit or none of the risk, named after Aesop's fable</note>, but rather when it is shifted without compensation or any benefit.

Regarding the point that leads **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Dominican theologian</note>, the first premise must be denied, along with the proof added to it. For when a stranger insures merchandise for another which he is transporting by sea, he certainly does not acquire ownership of it; rather, it remains his whose it was before the insurance, and nothing prevents this even if they

<summary>Molina explains that financial contracts are not usurious if risk is properly managed and compensated. He distinguishes between "consumable" goods like money (which usually transfer ownership) and "fructifying" goods like livestock, which can be leased with insurance and interest.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 418

...they perish not for their owner, but for the insurer. Likewise, as **Navarrus** <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note> rightly says in the cited commentary, number 36: from the fact that the entire risk of a thing lent, deposited, or hired is thrown upon the borrower, depositary, or renter, the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of that thing does not pass to them; yet, if it perishes, it perishes for them and not for its owner. Consequently, one must deny that a **partnership** <note>original: "societas"</note>, through a contract of insurance celebrated with a partner, ceases to be a partnership and turns into a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum," a type of loan where ownership of the goods transfers to the borrower, which was the basis for usury accusations.</note>.

<margin>31</margin>
Fifth, we say rather that—nothing in the insurance contract hindering it—he who, according to our first conclusion, hands over money into a partnership, remains the owner of it and a co-owner of the aggregate of profit and capital when they begin to be mixed, as was said in the second conclusion. Consequently, we add that he can not only compel the partner to use the capital for nothing other than the trade for which the partnership was entered, but also, if they should consume it in some other way, he will be granted a **legal claim for the property** <note>original: "rei vendicatio," a legal action to recover a physical object from whoever possesses it.</note>, into whomever's hands it may come, as a thing whose ownership still belongs to him. Read a longer refutation of the opinion of **Soto** <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Dominican theologian who was more restrictive regarding these contracts.</note> in the work of Navarrus at the cited number 36.

Finally, that which **Conrad** <note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian.</note> affirms—namely, that such a contract, though just in itself, is illicit because it is apt to generate scandal and bring ill repute to the contracting party—is certainly false. For if those agreements are added after an interval during the progress of the trade and partnership, there will be no appearance of a loan or usury at all. Likewise, if from the beginning the trades are made in the manner we explained as licitly possible, there is no reason why there should be a suspicion of usury or why scandal should be generated. Nor have I experienced any such thing in **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olyssipone"</note>, where this contract is very frequent, even though some are hesitant due to the opinions of the doctors we cited to the contrary. Nor does Conrad mean that it is illicit against justice with the burden of restitution, but only against charity.

<margin>32</margin>
From what has been said, it will be easy to understand what should be said regarding the following doubt: What if, in a partnership, one person gave 300 gold coins to another who was only to contribute work and industry, on the condition that only a third of the risk of the capital belonged to the one who provided it, while the other two-thirds belonged to the one providing the work? And similarly, that only a third of the profit should go to the one providing the capital, and the other two-thirds to the one providing the work? It was doubted whether this contract was licit. **Sylvester** <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), an Italian theologian.</note>, under the word *societas*, question 5, and others condemn it as usurious.

For, they say, it is the same as if the one providing the capital gave two parts of the capital as a loan to the other, with an agreement that in exchange for that loan, he would provide work regarding the remaining third part, the entire risk and profit of which would belong to the one who provided it. Therefore, since the provision of labor regarding that third part is something estimable in money, and it is received in compensation for the loan of the other two parts of the capital, it follows that usury is committed, with the burden of restoring however much that labor is valued at.

I think, along with **Major** <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Dist. 15, Q. 47)...

<column-break/>

...in the fourth doubt, that it must be said: If it is a true partnership of the whole capital and labor toward profit (according to the fourth way of handing over money for trade explained before the first conclusion), the contract can be licit and just. For since the whole money, and not just a third part of it, works toward the whole profit as an **instrument** <note>In Scholastic thought, capital was often viewed as a "tool" or "instrument" of the owner, justifying their claim to profit.</note>, and as the money of the one providing it together with the works and industry of the other partner (as was explained and shown in conclusion 1), and since the ownership of it remains with the giver, surely the contract is just if the profit—which is justly hoped to have come to the one providing the capital in the event he took the whole risk upon himself—was such that his being content with only a third of the profit and leaving the other two parts to the one providing labor sufficiently compensates him for taking on the risk of two parts of the capital. Generally, this will be a sufficient compensation.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
For just as one can justly and licitly cast the whole risk of the capital upon a partner by compensating for it with a sufficiently larger share of the profit than would otherwise justly come to him (as shown in conclusion 1), so with much greater reason can one justly and licitly cast upon him the risk of two parts of the capital by compensating with a larger share of the profit. And indeed, I wonder that Sylvester, in the cited place, question 1, admits the first case and then in question 5 denies the second. However, when there was no true intention of entering a partnership regarding the whole capital, but only of giving two parts as a loan in exchange for labor on the third, then the contract would be usurious, with the burden of restitution, as Sylvester affirms.

Likewise, when leaving two parts of the profit to the partner would not compensate for taking on the risk regarding two parts of the capital (which will rarely happen), the contract would be unjust with the burden of restoring as much as would be enough to reduce it to equality. Indeed, by a similar rate, it must be judged in many other similar events whether a contract is usurious and just, or unjust. When one partner provides only capital, and the other provides a part of the capital plus labor and industry, then, for the contract to be just, a share of profit is owed to the latter proportional to the part of the capital he provides, and additionally another share measured by the labor and industry he applies to the whole capital.

<summary>Molina defends the legality of risk-shifting in partnerships, arguing that as long as ownership of capital remains with the investor, trading a share of potential profit for insurance against loss is not usury. He emphasizes that the intent to form a partnership, rather than a disguised loan, is the deciding factor in its moral and legal validity.</summary>

Specifically, it transitions from the ownership of capital to the practical rules for deducting business expenses and handling personal losses or injuries sustained by a partner while conducting company business.</meta>

# 446 Luis de Molina on Contracts

...in another way he might lose his own goods, or be captured by enemies. See number 5.
However, clarify and understand this as in number 6.
<margin>7</margin> When a partner is not bound to contribute to a partner to repair a loss brought upon him.
<margin>8</margin> Whether a partner is bound to make expenditures for the preservation of merchandise, as if lending those funds to the other partners.
<margin>9</margin> All expenses are to be extracted at the time of the dissolution of the partnership, as well as that which is owed by the partnership, unless it is owed under a condition still pending in the future.

<margin>1</margin> **T**he question arises † whether the expenses made by the partner who provides labor and industry <note>In a "triple contract" or standard partnership, one partner often provides the money (capital) while the other provides the work (industry).</note> should be extracted from the partnership’s assets, so that, once deducted, the capital is withdrawn from the remainder, and whatever is left over is the profit to be divided among the partners. It must be said † that some expenses concern the merchandise itself: for example, if it is necessary to hire pack animals or a ship to transport them; or if it is necessary to rent a house to guard or sell them; or if it is necessary to hire jars or other vessels to contain, carry, or guard them; or to make other expenses to preserve or improve them. These and similar expenses, which are not the personal expenses of the merchant but are incurred in and with the goods themselves, are to be paid from the partnership’s assets, unless a different just agreement was expressly made, or unless in some particular event the local custom holds the contrary (which will rarely happen). Indeed, a contract, when nothing else was expressed, is considered to have been celebrated according to the custom of the place in which it is made. On these points, everyone agrees, and the matter is clear enough in itself, and is openly confirmed by the law *si fratres* in the section *si quis ex socijs* in the Digest's title "On Partnership" <note>original: "l. si fratres §. si quis ex socijs. ff. pro socio." This refers to the Roman Law Digest, 17.2.52.10.</note>.

Other expenses belong to the person providing the labor and industry, which he incurs for food and drink, for his pack animal, and for a servant or servants for the business, as well as according to the quality of his person in paying for lodging and similar things. Regarding these, it must be said: If something was specified in an agreement, or if the intent of the contracting parties is clear from conjectures in this regard, one must stand by such an agreement or intent. However, if nothing was specified in the agreement, nor is the intent of the parties clear, then one must stand by the common custom of the place, if there is any custom received by common use in that area; because a contract, when nothing else is expressed, is considered celebrated according to the common local custom. But when this matter cannot be defined by any of these headings, it must be said:

If the one providing the labor leaves his place of residence for the business of the partnership, then the expenses he incurs must be extracted from the common assets of the partnership, provided they are competent and reasonable. For if he spends anything irrationally and superfluously, such as on banquets or other things not at all necessary, he shall pay for those out of his own pocket <note>original: "de suo marsupio," literally "from his own purse."</note>. Major, in his commentary on the *Sentences* <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian.</note>, along with Balduinus and others whom Silvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523).</note> and Angelus <note>Angelus de Clavasio (1411–1495).</note> cite and follow, asserted that expenses should only be extracted from the common assets regarding the amount he spent while away from his own residence *over and above* what he would have spent in his own home; and that he is bound to pay the remainder himself. On the contrary, however, with Salicetus...

<column-break/>

...Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta.</note> affirms in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 283: namely, that those expenses should be extracted in their entirety from the common assets of the partnership, when it is not specified in the agreement that only the "increment" <note>The extra cost of travel versus staying at home.</note> should be extracted.

And this opinion is pleasing, especially when he sets out to trade in remote places, such as India, or even just for several leagues, so that he stays for several days outside his own residence for that business. All these points are confirmed by the law *cum duob.* in the section *quidam Sagariam* and the law *si fratres* in the section *si quis ex socijs* according to Julian in the Digest <note>Roman law citations: Digest 17.2.52.4 and 17.2.52.10.</note>, and from the laws of the *Partidas* <note>original: "l. 16. tit. 10. par. 5." This refers to the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish legal code.</note>. In these laws, it is established that when any of the partners sets out for the business of the partnership, the expenses he incurs must be extracted from the common assets of the partnership, with no mention made that this applies only to the increment beyond what he would have spent in his own home. Furthermore, since the laws only speak of when he sets out for business, they clearly imply—by the argument from the contrary sense—that when he conducts business in his own home, he is not to be supported by the common assets; and the cited doctors imply the same. However, that he supports himself at his own expense then [at home] helps to ensure that the labor and industry he provides are valued at a higher price.

<margin>2</margin> These same cited laws establish that if any of the partners, having set out for the business of the partnership, falls ill and reasonably spends anything on doctors, pharmacists, and other similar things, all of that must be extracted 
<margin>3</margin> from the common assets of the partnership. This † however I understand to apply to those things he spent while outside his own residence; otherwise, however, after he has arrived at his own home, even if the ill health persists.
<margin>4</margin> Likewise † the same laws establish that if he is plundered by robbers, or suffers shipwreck, and loses any of his own personal goods which he brought for the sake of the business—such as the horse on which he was traveling, his sword, cloak, or the slave he brought as a servant—all those things must be extracted from the common assets of the partnership. And in a similar way, if he is captured by enemies and reduced to slavery, whatever is necessary to spend for his ransom must be entirely extracted from the common assets.

<margin>5</margin> Understand † all these things, however, unless the loss happens by his own fault, at least through slight negligence; for whatever damages occur through his own fault belong entirely to him, as was said in Disputation 413. The same laws also establish that if, while he is resisting the common slaves of the partnership who wish to flee, he is wounded by them, the costs he incurs for medical treatment and the damages arising from it must be repaired from the common assets of the partnership. The reason is that since these things happen while he is intending the common good of the partnership, just as the profits that were to come from it were to be common to the partners, so it is consonant with reason that the losses should also be common. The same applies in similar events; regarding which, understand that if the event we just spoke of, or another similar one, happens to him while he is in his own home, the partners would be bound in the same way to repair those losses from the common assets. This is because the reasoning is the same, whether the cause of the partnership brings these events upon him outside his residence or within his own home.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 419.

7 **O**bserve † however, if some loss comes to such a partner on the occasion of the partnership’s business which he was conducting, but not because he was intending it for the partnership, then the partners are not bound to contribute to repairing such damage. For example, if while he was traveling for the partnership’s business, he got into a brawl with someone on the road—even if he would not have had that occasion for a fight unless he had undertaken that journey for the sake of the partnership—and even if he were wounded by the other person through no fault of his own, the partners are not bound to contribute to that loss. In the same way, if an enemy by chance finds him on that road and wounds him because of an old hatred—even if the enemy would not have found him if he had not undertaken that journey for the partnership—the partners are bound to him for nothing. For he is not said to expose himself to such dangers for the sake of the partnership in the same way he is said to expose himself to the dangers of robbers or capture by enemies of the state. There is a great difference between a partner having a benefit or disadvantage "on the occasion" of the partnership, and it arriving "because of" or "out of" the partnership itself. In the first of these events, just as the benefit is not common to the partnership, neither is the disadvantage, as affirmed by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357) was one of the most influential legal commentators of the Middle Ages, specializing in Roman Law.</note> on the law *socium*, section *socius*, in the Digest under the title *pro socio* <note>The "Digest" (ff.) is a massive collection of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian. *Pro socio* is the specific title dealing with the law of partnerships.</note>, and the doctors of law commonly. In the second case, however, just as the benefit is common to the partnership, so too must the disadvantage be common, as the doctors have also commonly asserted.

<margin>Question.</margin> When one of the partners makes expenditures from his own purse <note>The original Latin *marsupium* literally means a pouch or purse, referring here to personal private funds rather than the partnership's capital.</note> which he was permitted to make from the common goods, he will be able to recover them from the common goods of the partnership, just as if they were given as a loan to the partnership. But is it true that when it is necessary to make certain expenditures for the preservation of the merchandise—which if he did not make, the goods would perish or be rendered worse—he is bound to make them as if lending them to the other partners? It must be said, first of all, that he is bound by the precept of charity.

Furthermore, he has at least an "action for business conducted" <note>Latin: *actio negotiorum gestorum*. A legal claim under Roman law allowing someone who manages another's affairs without an express mandate to recover their costs.</note> to recover what he has thus applied, with nothing hindering him even if all the profit, and even the capital, should perish. The reason is that in that matter he advantageously managed the business of the partners, and for that reason, whatever follows afterward, they are bound to pay the expenses made for their benefit. As for the obligation arising from justice—as if the merchandise should perish because he did not make those expenditures—is he bound to restore those goods to the partners?

Some might answer in the negative. Because, they say, by the force of the contract, those expenses were to be made from the common goods; and for that reason, even if the merchandise perishes because the partner did not pay from his own purse, he is bound to no restitution to the other partners. This is similar to public officials who are bound by justice to guard the city; if some evils occur which they could have avoided if they had taken another man along with them besides those assigned by the King or the State, they do not sin against justice, because they are only bound by justice to avoid evils that they were able to avoid with the men assigned or constituted for them.

<margin>Decision.</margin> Although this opinion does not lack the appearance of probability, perhaps the contrary is more probable. The reason is that such a partner, by the force of the contract,

<column-break/>

is held responsible for all damages which arise even from his "slight fault" <note>Latin: *culpa leuis*. A legal standard of negligence where a person fails to exercise the degree of care that a prudent person would use for their own property.</note>; therefore, if by seeking a loan from some third party he could avoid the loss of the goods, and did not seek it, he would certainly be compelled—both in conscience and in the external court <note>The "external forum" refers to the public legal system, while the "internal forum" or "conscience" refers to moral accountability before God.</note>—to pay for the subsequent damages. This is because he was bound to apply such diligence so that the goods would not perish. In the same way, if by spending something from his own purse (which he was going to recover in due time without any personal disadvantage) he could have preserved the goods committed to him, and did not spend it, they would surely be said to have perished by his fault, and therefore he will be bound to restore the subsequent damage to the partners. For the other partners are deemed to have entered into that contract under that condition, and any other similar one, since they intended him to be held responsible even for slight fault, and therefore to be held to the diligence which he would apply to his own affairs.

Regarding the comparison to public officials, it must be said that if they similarly understand it to be necessary to avoid some great evil in a particular case by employing another man here and now, whom they could provide for themselves to be paid back at a suitable time, they are bound by justice to employ him. If they neglect to employ him, they are bound to the restitution of the subsequent damages and shall be punished for that reason by the higher powers.

9 Here it must be observed that at the time of the dissolution of the partnership, before all else, all expenses are to be extracted, and that which is owed by the partnership must be paid immediately. But if something is owed under a condition pending in the future, or something else is owed in the future, then that is not to be extracted from the common goods before the division; rather, all goods are to be divided. However, he who contributed his labor, and who obligated himself in the name of the partnership, ought to receive from the partners a due guarantee that they will contribute to the payment at the proper time. This is held in the law *omne æs*, in the Digest *pro socio*, and the law *cum socijs*, in the Digest *communi diuidundo* <note>Commonly dividing (assets).</note>, and in law 16, title 10, part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note>.

->Whether one who enters a partnership by contributing labor with others who contribute capital can enter other similar partnerships with others.<-

## DISPUTATION 419.
### SUMMARY.

1 *Whether a partnership can be entered into with others by one who only contributes labor.*
2 *When a later partnership can be entered into by a partner who only provides labor.*
3 *A partner who only contributes labor, contracting a later partnership against a pact placed in the first one: to what is he bound?*
4 *And what if a pact was not placed, but the later partnership prejudices the first?*

Regarding this question, a distinction must be made. Since either † in the first partnership it was drawn into a pact that he should not enter another partnership, nor any other [undertaking]...

He concludes that a partner must exercise high diligence—similar to how one cares for their own property—and is liable for damages caused by even slight negligence.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...undertook these business affairs so that he might be more efficient for that reason, and better serve that partnership—which is something many people are accustomed to include in a contract—or if no such thing was included in the contract. And again, one must ask whether devoting time to later partnerships and the business affairs he has undertaken prejudices the first partnership, because he was not able to devote himself as well to its business, or whether it does not prejudice it because he is able to manage all those business affairs quite sufficiently.

<margin>2</margin> Having established this distinction, the first conclusion is: If the second partnership neither prejudices the first, nor was it stipulated in the contract that another partnership or other business should not be entered into, it is lawful to enter into a later partnership or several later partnerships. This is proven because no injury is done to the first partners in this case, since they are not defrauded, nor is there a transgression of the contract entered into with them. This matter is very similar to when someone hires himself out as a servant to another; for if, without prejudicing his service to his master, he accomplishes something at the request of another, he may lawfully receive a just wage for it. Nor does he cease to be worthy of the full stipend he receives from his master for the service and obedience in which he does not defraud him.

You might object: In the first partnership, it was estimated how much profit he is worthy to receive for his work, assuming he intends no other business; therefore, by the very fact that he receives profit in another partnership, he is made worthy of less profit in the first partnership than was appraised for him. To this argument, the premise must be denied. For in each individual partnership, it is only estimated how much profit he is worthy of precisely as he contributes to *that* partnership. For if he is taken on to trade with one thousand ducats, less profit is established for him, and he is worthy of less profit, than if he is taken on to trade with twelve thousand ducats in the same kind of business.

For although in this later business a smaller aliquot <note>aliquot: a portion of a whole that leaves no remainder; in this context, a specific percentage or fixed share.</note> part of the profit might be established for him than in the first one, nevertheless, the smaller aliquot part of the profit from trading with 12,000 ducats can be a much larger part—and in reality will be—than the larger aliquot part of the profit from trading with only one thousand ducats.

And although someone might sometimes demand more profit in a first partnership than he would seek in a certain proportion if he were entering it and other partnerships simultaneously—insofar as the convenience of many partnerships might invite him to reduce the profit in each one (just as someone who sells many goods at once reduces the price at which he would sell them in parts over time)—this nevertheless does not prevent him, after he has justly entered the first partnership, from being able to lawfully receive profits later from other partnerships he enters, and from which he did not bind himself not to enter, either formally or by implication, when entering the first partnership.

All these things are confirmed because it is an accepted custom, after someone has entered a partnership by contributing his labor to transport the partnership's goods to India, or to the New World, or to other places, to also take the goods of others (our people call these *encomiendas* <note>original: "encomiendas". In this context, these are commissions or consignments of goods entrusted to a merchant to sell on someone else's behalf for a fee.</note>)—one worth five hundred ducats, another six hundred, and others of greater or lesser value—which he may sell in those places and bring back their price

<column-break/>

in other goods; and for that industry, a certain profit is paid to him, or a specific share of the profit.

I should advise this: when someone enters into many partnerships in such a way that his personal expenses should be taken from the common goods of each one (if each were entered alone) while he is staying away from his own home, then equity requires that he not take those full expenses from each one, but only one set of expenses from all of them, taking a proportional part of them from each.

<margin>3</margin> Second conclusion: When it was stipulated in the contract of the first partnership that the one contributing his labor should not enter another partnership nor undertake other business, if in fact the other partnership does not prejudice the first, then the one who enters another against that contract would indeed sin by transgression of the agreement. The other partners could, for that reason, contend with him in court, and he is bound to pay them the penalty that would be adjudged to them for such a crime and infidelity. However, he would be bound to restore <note>original: "restituere". Restitution is a key concept in Scholastic economics, involving the returning of ill-gotten gains to their rightful owner to satisfy justice.</note> nothing to them from the profit acquired in the other partnership.

He would, nonetheless, be bound to restore to those first partners any extra profit that was granted to him in the first partnership for that burden—that is, the restriction that he could not involve himself in other partnerships and business—beyond what would otherwise have been granted to him. The first part of this conclusion is clear enough: since the transgression of a just contract is a fault, and therefore he is bound after a sentence is passed to pay the penalty adjudged to the partners because of that fault. The second part is proven because he justly acquired the profit from the subsequent partnership and in reality did not inflict any prejudice on the other partners; therefore, he is not bound to restore such profit. The third part is proven from this: because the increase in profit was granted to him by the prior partners for that burden which he took upon himself; when, therefore, he rejected the burden for which it was granted, it follows that he is bound to restore that increase in profit, as it was given for a cause, and the cause did not follow through.

<margin>4</margin> Third conclusion: Even if in the first partnership it was not stipulated in the contract that he should not involve himself in another partnership or undertake other business, if the later partnership or other business affairs impede the business of the first partnership, he is bound to restore to the partners the whole loss that followed for them, both in the capital and also in the profit which they could have acquired, but which was not acquired through his fault because he involved himself in other business.

This is proven because that partner, by the very nature of the contract of partnership, is bound to the other partners for all losses—both regarding the capital and regarding the profit that was to be acquired—that followed from his fault, even a slight one, as was seen above.

From this it is clear that if a partner consumes common goods of the partnership superfluously in banquets or other similar things, or steals anything from there, he is not only bound to restore that to the partnership, but also the increase in profit that was not acquired because of it.

Likewise, if he managed the partnership negligently, he is bound to restore the profit that would have been obtained if he had applied reasonable <note>original: "moralem... diligentiam". Molina refers to "moral diligence," the standard level of care an honest and prudent person would take.</note> diligence.

<summary>This page discusses whether a business partner can take on side ventures. Molina argues that it is generally allowed unless it harms the main partnership or breaks an exclusivity clause, though expenses must be shared across all ventures and any loss caused by negligence must be compensated.</summary>

Second Treatise. Disputation 420. 449

## On the contract of partnership concerning animals.

### DISPUTATION 420.

#### SUMMARY

1 The various ways animals can be handed over for profit and loss.
2 In which cases a partnership contracted through the delivery of animals is considered lawful.
3 If a partnership is formed where one party provides labor and industry and the other provides the animals, how the valuation must be made for it to be called lawful.
4 The same principles apply to fishing and other similar ventures.

<margin>1</margin> Animals can be handed over to someone through a contract for the hiring of their services, or for both services and grazing, such that the owner of the animals hires the labor, industry, or grazing from the person receiving the animals. In this case, the one receiving the animals is effectively leasing his services to the owner. Conversely, animals can be handed over through a contract for the hiring of the animals themselves by the person who receives them, so that he may take the fruits <note>In legal terms, "fruits" refers to products like milk, wool, or offspring.</note> from them, while the owner acts as the lessor. This may or may not involve an insurance contract for the animals on the part of the one receiving them. Regarding these types of contracts, sufficient points were made in Disputations 411 and 417, especially in conclusion 3.

In another way, animals can be handed over to a monastery, a Church, or anyone else in exchange for a certain annual payment <note>Original: "pensione"</note> to be paid to the person handing them over for as long as he lives, regardless of whether the animals perish or not. This is done on the condition that, by the very act of being handed over, the ownership of the animals passes forever to the monastery, Church, or whoever receives them. Since this contract is nothing other than the establishment of a **life annuity** <note>A "vitalitium" or life annuity was a common way for individuals to secure retirement income by giving capital to an institution in exchange for a guaranteed lifetime payout.</note> in exchange for those animals, its justice and lawfulness can be easily understood from what was said in Disputation 388, by estimating the value of the animals against the payment to be made.

<margin>2</margin> In a third way, animals can be handed over for a **true partnership**, seeking profit from their offspring and products, as well as from their purchase and sale. Indeed, when many partners buy animals in common, pay all expenses, and divide the fruits and profit among themselves—so that each contributes to expenses and divides profit according to the proportion of the capital he provided—and they all take upon themselves the risks to the capital, there is no one who can rightly call such a partnership into question. Rather, this should be held as the standard for all others. If, in other partnerships, a variation is found regarding one or more of these points, but it is sufficiently compensated for from elsewhere, the partnership will be just; otherwise, it will be unjust, carrying the burden of restitution to the extent necessary to bring the contract back to equality, as was said generally regarding partnerships for profit in Disputation 415.

<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, when one partner provides labor and industry in grazing the animals, taking their fruits, working with them, buying new ones, and selling others, or providing for their

<column-break/>

pasture and other similar things, these can be valued in two ways, as was generally stated regarding labor and industry in partnerships for profit in Disputation 416. In the first way, the labor is valued only for the purpose of participating in the fruits and profit. In the second way, it is valued to achieve equality with the value of the animals and the other expenses incurred in the partnership. If they are valued in the first way, then only a proportional share of the fruits and profit belongs to the person providing the labor; the entire capital, along with the remaining share of the fruits and profit, belongs to the owner or owners of the animals. The risk of the animals also remains with the owners, unless they perish through at least the slight fault of the one providing labor, according to what was said in Disputation 413; for in that case, the animals perish for him <note>Meaning the laborer bears the financial loss if his negligence caused the death of the animals.</note> and not for the owners.

But if they are valued in the second way, then the capital becomes common property. In fact, the valuation of the labor and industry constitutes the total capital along with the animals and other things contributed to that partnership, as explained in Disputation 416. Both the capital and the fruits and profit found at the end of the partnership must be divided among the partners according to the proportion of that first total capital (which includes the value of the labor) that each partner contributed, as was shown there. Sometimes, the entire risk of the capital, or a part of it, can even be shifted onto the one providing the labor, regardless of which of the two valuation methods is used, provided this burden is sufficiently compensated—either by granting him a larger share of the profit than he would otherwise be due, or by some other means, as stated in Disputation 417, especially conclusion 3.

And when the risk of the capital is shifted to the one providing labor in this way, the animals may be handed over to him with a set valuation so that it is clear how much he must pay for each one if they perish. This valuation does not cause the ownership of the animals to pass to the laborer, nor is that delivery seen as a **loan** <note>Molina is distinguishing this from a "mutuum," a type of loan where ownership transfers and the borrower must return the equivalent value. If it were a loan with a guaranteed profit, it might be accused of usury.</note>, as some have wrongly argued. Instead, it can be seen as a true partnership, a contract for the leasing of animals regarding their fruits, or an "innominate" <note>An "unnamed" contract that doesn't fit a standard category but is still legally binding.</note> contract that can be reduced to a contract of leasing and hiring, according to what was said in Disputation 417, combined with the explanations in Disputation 415.

<margin>4</margin> I have deemed it superfluous to pour out more words on this matter, as many others do, including Conrad Summenhart in *On Contracts* (question 88), John Major (in book 4, distinction 15, question 46), and Sylvester and Angelus under the word "partnership" <note>Original: Conrad. de contractibus, Maior, Sylvest. & Ang. verb. societas.</note>. From these points, joined with what was said in the preceding disputations and applying them to the partnership of animals, fishing, and other similar ventures, one can easily understand whether, after calculating everything, an inequality is perceived that requires restitution, or whether equality is found, making the contract just. I do not approve of many things taught by the cited doctors on this subject; it will be easily understood from what has been said where they deviate from our opinion and from the truth.

Ff

Luis de Molina on Contracts. 450

## On the partnership of all goods. And simultaneously on that partnership which is customary among brothers who hold a paternal inheritance without dividing it.

### DISPUTATION 421.

->SUMMARY<-

1. A partnership of all goods can be contracted in two ways.
2. When a partnership of all goods is understood to be tacitly contracted.
3. When losses and gains occurring after the partnership of all goods is contracted are made common. And what about losses that occur after a marriage is contracted (no. 4).
5. When a partner in a partnership of all goods can provide dowries for daughters from the common assets.
6. When a partnership of all goods among brothers is considered contracted, and when it is not.
7. Whether, and when, a partnership contracted with a minor is valid.

<margin>1</margin>
**H**aving explained the partnership for profit <note>This refers to a business partnership where only profits from trade are shared.</note>, let us approach the partnership of all goods. Today, this is rare, except between spouses, especially according to Portuguese law, where marriage is celebrated with a contract for half of the assets, as it is called in that Kingdom <note>Original: "Lusitano iure... contractu medietatis bonorum." This refers to the Portuguese legal tradition of "metade de bens," a community property regime.</note>. Because we intend to deal with partnerships of particular goods between spouses in the following disputations, in this disputation, regarding what pertains to the partnership of all goods in general, we will add a few points to those said in Disputation 412.

<margin>2</margin>
The first point is this: both this partnership and any other less universal partnership can be contracted in two ways, as is easily clear from the things said in Disputation 414. One way is express, namely through a pact and an express agreement. The other way is tacit, namely through acts by which the partners in reality carry out the partnership among themselves, with no preceding pact. Indeed, such a partnership is to be judged as universal as is gathered from the acts themselves. For if some people were accustomed to hold all things universally in common, so that whatever came to each of them—whether from their own industry <note>In this context, "industry" refers to professional labor or skilled work.</note> or from elsewhere, and whether by an onerous or lucrative title <note>An "onerous title" involves a purchase or trade; a "lucrative title" refers to gifts or inheritances.</note>—he brought it all in and shared it with the others, and expenses were made and losses paid indiscriminately from all the assets, then a partnership of all goods is deemed tacitly contracted among them. But if they only shared among themselves what each acquired from his own industry, or from an office, or what he gained by trading, and these were common to them for expenses and other things, then a partnership is deemed tacitly contracted among them, not of all goods universally, but of everything they acquire by trading and through an onerous title. If, however, they only shared in certain business dealings, even if various dealings were carried out by different partners for their common benefit, then only a partnership of that specific business or those businesses is deemed tacitly contracted among them. Therefore, when no express pact has intervened between them, a partnership is deemed tacitly contracted between them precisely as great as is gathered from the acts themselves, and no

<column-break/>

greater. Thus say Bartolus and Baldus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis were the most influential legal commentators of the Middle Ages.</note> on the Law *Si patruus* in the Code *Communia utriusque iudicii*; and the same Bartolus on the Law *Titium*, paragraph *Altero*, in the Digest *De administratione tutorum*; and Baldus in the additions to the treatise of Bartolus on the two brothers; and Silvester under the word *peculium*, number 2; and Angelus under the same word, number 27; and the doctors of law commonly. Although Baldus spoke more accurately on some of these points than Bartolus, all these things are easily established from the cited disputations.

<margin>3</margin>
Secondly: once a partnership of all goods has been contracted, whether expressly or tacitly, all losses, debts, and gains universally that happen after the partnership was contracted—from wherever they come, provided they do not come from the crime or fault of one of the partners—are made common. This goes so far that, if a stranger is condemned to pay something to one of the partners on account of an injury inflicted on that person, even that is made common to the partners. If, however, one of the partners is condemned to pay something for a true fault which he committed, then that loss will not be common to the partners, but his own, according to those things explained in Disputation 413. If, indeed, he were condemned unjustly, then the loss would be common to the partners: because every loss that happens without the partner's fault is made common, just as a benefit is. In a similar way, if one of the partners was bound to appear in court and through his own negligence did not appear, and it followed from this that he was condemned, that loss is not common, but his own: because it happened through his own fault. All these things are held expressly in the Law *Si fratres* (otherwise beginning *Papinianus*), the final paragraph, in the Digest *Pro socio*.

<margin>4</margin>
These things are very much to be noted: because the same must be said about losses which happen after a marriage is contracted through the fault of either spouse, such as from a crime for which one is condemned, or for the repairing of which something is spent, or from any other fault of their own. And by the same reasoning, the same must be said of those things which a husband spends wickedly with prostitutes, or if it be a wife, with adulterers, or what one spends against the will of the other spouse on donations and other things that are inconsistent with the proper and permitted administration or consumption of common goods. For that spouse is bound to take all those things upon their own share, as was said in Disputation 275. Although in the administration of common goods, which falls to the husband, he should not be so strictly bound as to be held liable for a slight fault <note>Molina distinguishes between "slight fault" (culpa levis) and "gross negligence" (culpa lata).</note>, according to those things said in the cited disputation, but only for gross negligence and fraud. In that same place we showed that, in this Kingdom of Castile, the husband, regarding gains, is not held liable to the wife for any fault, except when he has alienated something in fraud of the wife. These are the laws which were spoken of there at length. Likewise, if before contracting the partnership of all goods, one of the partners had debts which he did not manifest to the others, nor did he formally or by implication include them in the pact so they would be paid from common goods, then those debts are not made common, but remain his own personal and peculiar debts; for the other partners, by the very fact that they contracted a partnership of all goods with him, are not to be deemed to have consented that those debts should be made common to all.

<margin>5</margin>
Moreover, when some have contracted a partnership of all goods universally, whether one who has daughters can provide them with dowries <note>Original: "dotare." A dowry was the property or money brought by a bride to her husband.</note> from the common assets, when nothing was expressly included in the pact regarding that matter, is a matter greatly controverted among the doctors.
