Second Treatise, Disputation 422.

Indeed, the law titled "the partner for the daughter" in the Digest under "on the action of partnership" <note>original: "lex socius pro filia.ff.pro socio," a reference to Roman civil law regarding whether a partner can use shared funds for a daughter's dowry</note>, which speaks to this matter, only affirms that this could be done when it was expressly included as a pact at the time the contract was celebrated. Therefore, by an argument from the contrary sense, one concludes from that law that it is *not* possible if it was not included in the pact, rather than that it is possible. 

Whatever the case may be, when people of different families have contracted a partnership of all their universal goods—which is very unusual—we shall discuss in the following sections what should be judged when one of the spouses wishes to provide a dowry for their own daughter, or a daughter common to both: specifically, whether they can do this from the common goods even against the will of the other spouse. This concludes what pertains to the partnership of all universal goods.

<margin>6</margin> Sometimes brothers, after the death of their parents, are accustomed to hold the parents' goods undivided in the manner of a partnership <note>This was a common historical practice to keep a family estate intact rather than splitting it into smaller, less productive plots.</note>, either because it is advantageous for the assets themselves and the utility of the brothers, or for some other reason. And so they are accustomed to hold them undivided such that the losses, benefits, or profits are shared. 

Indeed, when nothing else has been expressly included in a pact, or cannot be sufficiently gathered tacitly from the mutual sharing of all universal goods, that partnership is not to be considered one of all goods universally. Instead, it only applies to the inherited goods and the profits and losses arising from them, or from some particular business and administration of those goods, or perhaps also regarding the labors of the brothers and sisters which concern the administration and support of the family. Finally, the partnership should be considered to extend to all these things only so far as was included in the pact, or was sufficiently established by the mutual sharing of labors and profits. 

As for the remaining goods, if anything comes to one of them from elsewhere—either by gift, or by title of inheritance, or legacy, or from any other personal industry of theirs which is not owed to the partnership—that whole amount becomes their own. This is held in the law titled "if brothers" at the beginning of the section "on the action of partnership" <note>original: "l. si fratres in prin.ff.pro socio"</note>.

Therefore, each of these partners shall take ordinary and appropriate expenses from the common goods of the partnership. But if they have unequal portions in the inherited goods, when they agree that those goods should remain undivided and that they should administer them and live from them, then, when the partnership ends, the goods shall be divided according to the portions which each held in the inheritance, unless something else was included in the pact. Nor may any of them receive more than the others for greater industry or labor in administering the goods, unless it was similarly included in the pact. 

However, if one of the brothers was appointed as a <term>tutor</term> <note>a legal guardian for a minor under the age of puberty</note> or a <term>curator</term> <note>a guardian for a young person who has reached puberty but is not yet of full legal age</note> for the others to administer all those goods which it was expedient to keep undivided, then strictly speaking there would not be a partnership between them regarding those goods. In that case, the brother who administered them for the common good of all could receive a fee, which was said at the end of Disputation 224 to be receivable by tutors and curators from the goods of the minors they administer. But for the goods of minors to remain undivided and be administered in that way, it is necessary in Portugal that at least the authority of the "judge of orphans" <note>original: "iudicis orphanorum," a specific Portuguese official tasked with protecting the interests of fatherless children</note> intervene.

<margin>7</margin> It must be observed that since a partnership contracted with a ward <note>original: "pupillo," a child under legal guardianship</note>—whether tacitly or expressly—is not binding unless the consent of a tutor is added (as held in the law "on leases" in the section "on the action of partnership" <note>original: "l. in conductionibus.ff.pro socio"</note> and the law "he who for a certain" 

<column-break/>

in the section "on hiring" <note>original: "l. qui ad certum, ff. locati"</note>), when it is contracted without the authority of a tutor, its validity depends on whether the ward wishes to ratify it after reaching the proper age. This is because a ward can obligate others to himself for his own convenience and utility, but he himself does not remain obligated to others, as was said in Disputation 224 and others preceding. 

Furthermore, when a partnership is contracted with any minor with the intervening authority of a tutor or curator, although it is valid, the minor may nevertheless seek <term>restitution in integrum</term> <note>A legal remedy where a contract is cancelled and the parties are restored to their original positions as if the deal had never happened.</note> and liberation from the partnership and its losses when he finds himself notably harmed. It is otherwise if the contract was originally entered into usefully by him, but later, as things turned out poorly, it began to decline to his detriment; for then, "restitution to the original state" is not granted to him, as was said in the cited places and will be said below in its proper place. Since these things are so, it follows that if among brothers who contract a partnership of this kind some are wards or minors, the partnership is not valid unless it was contracted with the authority of a tutor or curator, except depending on his later ratification. And even if it was contracted with the authority of a tutor or curator, if the minor later discovers himself to be harmed in the manner just explained, he may seek restitution to the original state. Read what Bartolus, Baldus, Sylvester, and Angelus <note>References to famous medieval and Renaissance legal and theological commentators: Bartolus de Saxoferrato, Baldus de Ubaldis, Sylvester Prierias, and Angelus de Clavasio.</note> hand down on this matter in the places cited above.

-> ### Luis de Molina On Contracts ### <-

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the matter of marriage: leaving aside that contract by which spouses grant each other power over their own bodies for the act of procreation—which serves as the foundation of that sacrament—it truly belongs to this second treatise on justice concerning external goods to discuss the other contracts regarding external wealth that are usually joined with the marriage contract. (Although discussing the former matter otherwise pertains to the following treatise on justice regarding the goods of the body). Since we spoke in Disputations 239 and 290 about donations between spouses, bridal gifts, and donations made before or because of nuptials, the remaining contracts in this social union will be appropriately introduced here. For indeed, the <term>contract of the half of goods</term><note>Latin: "contractus medietatis bonorum." This is a form of community property where everything is shared 50/50.</note> is most properly a partnership, not only in profit and loss, but also in the capital itself. Furthermore, the contract of <term>earnest money</term><note>Latin: "arrhae." This refers to assets or money pledged by the husband to the wife as security.</note> and of <term>dowry</term>, especially as they are celebrated in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, is also most properly a contract of partnership—not indeed with a communion in the capital, but only in the profit, if any is found when the partnership is dissolved. This is true even though that contract may have certain other elements mixed in, as we shall say.

<margin>2</margin> Concerning the contract of the half of goods between spouses, I find no mention in the <term>common law</term><note>Latin: "ius commune." The shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law.</note>, but it is specific to the Kingdom of Portugal. Although it is lawful in that Kingdom for spouses to celebrate marriages with a contract of earnest money and dowry, those who are not nobles usually do not celebrate them that way, but rather by the contract of the half of goods. Indeed, in that Kingdom, all marriages in which nothing else has been expressed are deemed to be celebrated by the contract of the half of goods, as held in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 7, at the beginning.

<margin>3</margin> When a marriage in Portugal is celebrated by the contract of the half of goods, the spouses' assets do not become common until the marriage has been <term>consummated by sexual union</term><note>Latin: "per copulam consummatum."</note>. From this it follows that if the marriage is found to be void due to impotence for union, or if it is dissolved before union by the death of one spouse or by the profession of religious vows, each spouse (or their heirs) shall keep for themselves the specific goods they brought, and the fruits of those goods, as their own property. Each spouse is also bound to pay whatever expenses were incurred regarding those goods. However, once the marriage is consummated by union, all goods, rights, and legal actions belonging to them at that time—as well as those they might acquire by any title while the marriage persists—become common to both. Thus, each of them is the owner of all the goods of both, by a "partnership of ownership" and a "totality of the things." In a similar way, they have a right to all those things for which they have a right without ownership; and likewise, the possession of any of their goods belongs to each of them by a partnership of possession and totally over the things possessed.

<margin>4</margin> When the partnership between them is dissolved by the death of one, or for any other reason such as divorce, all their goods and rights must be divided into two parts: one half goes to one spouse (or their heirs) and the other half to the other. If the husband dies before the wife, the wife <column-break/> remains in possession of all the goods as the head of the family, and the husband’s heirs must receive from her the portion that belonged to the husband. Likewise, if the wife departs from this life before the husband, the husband remains in possession of all the goods as the head of the family, and the wife’s heirs must receive from him the portion that pertained to the wife. However, when the partnership is dissolved by divorce, the wife must receive from the husband—as from the head of the family and the universal administrator of all goods up to that time—the portion that falls to her. All these things are established in Book 4 of the Portuguese *Ordinances*, Title 7, § 1, and Book 2, Title 47, § 2 and 3.

<margin>5</margin> An exception is made to this doctrine if among those goods there are any that are <term>entailed</term><note>Latin: "vinculata." Property legally tied to a specific lineage or purpose that cannot be sold or split.</note>, such as a <term>majorat</term><note>Latin: "maioratus." An estate that must pass intact to the eldest son.</note>, a chapel, a fief, or a crown grant belonging to one of the spouses; or any <term>emphyteutic</term><note>Latin: "emphyteutica." A type of long-term lease where the tenant improves the land.</note> goods which do not belong to both spouses (as we shall say below in its place), such as those called "of nomination." Indeed, although the fruits perceived from such goods while the marriage lasts are common to both spouses, once the marriage is dissolved, the assets themselves remain the specific property of the spouse to whom they belonged (or their heirs). The surviving spouse does not remain in possession of them after the death of the one to whom they belonged.
   Understand this, however, unless they were bought with common funds or improvements were made upon them. In that case, because the surviving spouse is owed half the price for which they were bought, or half the value of the improvements made, that spouse remains in possession of them until paid what is owed. The same applies if such goods belonging to one were subject to a mortgage in favor of the survivor, with the authority of the one whose consent was necessary. In that case, the survivor remains in possession until satisfied in those matters for which the mortgages were secured. These points are found in Book 4 of the Portuguese *Ordinances*, Title 7, § 2.

<margin>6</margin> Likewise, if either spouse who contracted in this manner owed anything to anyone when the marriage was celebrated, such debts are not common to both spouses. Instead, only the one who was the debtor is bound to pay them, specifically from the goods they brought into the marriage and from the half of the profits acquired during the marriage that pertained to them. Execution of debt can only be made against these goods while the marriage lasts, not against the goods belonging to the other spouse. Finally, when the marriage is dissolved, the spouse who owed the debt is bound to take into their own share the fact that the debt was so paid. This is held in the cited Title 7, in the next to last section. I would add that whoever stood as a debtor and did not disclose it before the marriage was contracted is liable to the other spouse for damages and losses—including lost profit—that followed from that cause.
   When a woman has denied someone was her husband, and by that route escaped the penalty for an adulteress, or has obtained a judgment for some other reason that he was not her man; then she cannot later be admitted to prove that he was her husband for the purpose of participating in his goods, as if by that marriage...

I would say the same if someone had obtained a legal judgment stating that a woman was not his wife: he would not later be permitted to prove she *was* his wife simply so he could share in her property.

<margin>
Question 7
</margin>
When a marriage was "putative"—meaning it was contracted in good faith by the party seeking to share in the other’s goods—and was consummated in that same good faith, but a legal impediment is later discovered and the marriage is found to be null, a doubt arises: should the property of such spouses be considered shared so that it is divided into two equal parts, or not? Or should each person simply take back what they brought into the union? Indeed, if after the impediment is uncovered some <term>surplus profits</term><note>Latin: "superlucrata." This refers to wealth acquired by the couple during the time they lived together as husband and wife.</note> are found, it must be said—whether the marriage was celebrated under a "contract of the half" or under a contract of earnest money and dowry—that those surplus profits are communal and must be divided equally between both spouses. The reason is that the partnership was contracted in good faith and continued until that time, with each spouse contributing the capital that helped produce those profits, and each spouse providing administration, labor, industry, and the duties expected of them. Therefore, the profit ought to be common, no differently than if the marriage had been valid and true. This is the common opinion cited and followed by Gama (Decision 89 and 204), Antonio Gómez (on the Laws of Toro, 50, number 77), and Covarrubias (Part 2, Chapter 7, section 1, number 7). However, regarding the <term>capital</term><note>The original assets or property each person owned before the marriage.</note>, when the marriage was celebrated as a "contract of the half," the matter is doubtful, and the doctors of law in Portugal have spoken of it quite a bit; this is because no mention is made of such a marriage in the <term>common law</term><note>The general Roman-canonical legal system used across Europe.</note>, nor is it usually in use in other places. Gama disputes this in the cited Decision 89.

<margin>Decision</margin>
And although in a certain other case he reports that it was ruled the property should be shared, in that specific decision he leans toward the view that it is more probable that the capital should *not* be shared; and this is the view I prefer. For the sharing of capital presupposes a valid marriage, and the partnership regarding that communication is considered contracted as if under the condition of marriage. Therefore, by the very fact that the marriage is found to be null, the partnership must also be considered null. I believe, however, that if any loss occurred to the capital, it should be divided proportionally between the spouses according to the amount of capital each one contributed, since the partnership—contracted and continued in good faith—requires this.

<margin>8</margin>
When persons in Portugal celebrate a marriage with a "contract of the half," the administration of all goods belongs to the husband as the head of the family. The wife has no administration except what is granted and permitted to her by her husband. Read what was said in Disputations 274, 275, and 343. However, when a wife, at the time the marriage was celebrated, reserved certain goods for herself through a specific pact—the administration and disposal of which would belong to her alone—then she would have administration of those goods independent of her husband. Yet this rarely happens. In some matters, however, the husband depends on the wife. Indeed, <term>immovable property</term><note>Real estate, such as land or buildings.</note> and things categorized as such, like

<column-break/>

rights to annual rents for ten years or more, cannot be sold by the husband without the express consent of the wife, or without a power of attorney from her for that purpose. If he sells them otherwise, the sale is invalid. It does not matter if <term>guarantors</term><note>Latin: "fideiussores." People who promise to pay if the primary party fails.</note> were provided (who are bound to nothing by such an obligation), nor does it matter if the husband bound himself under a specific penalty to produce his wife’s express consent: all such acts are void and null.

<margin>9</margin>
To prove the wife’s express consent, nothing is admitted except a <term>public deed</term><note>Latin: "scriptura publica." A formal legal document recorded by a notary.</note>. Nevertheless, a husband may sell or resign any public office without his wife’s consent. Regarding the consent of the husband—or if the husband refuses, with the consent of the King or a local judge—a wife may revoke the sale of immovable property sold by the husband without her express consent. The heirs of a deceased wife can do the same. The husband who sold the property can also do this, as can his heirs, but only with the consent of the wife (or her heirs if she is deceased), and certainly not without that consent.

<margin>10</margin>
When property sold without the wife’s consent is recovered in the ways explained, a distinction must be made. If the price paid was used for the benefit of both the husband and wife, or if the wife shared in it in some way, then the price must be refunded to the buyer from the common property and the husband’s property. But if the wife did not share in it at all, a further distinction is made: either the buyer knew the seller was married (or had a just reason to know), or he did not. In the first case, the buyer loses the price paid, and in addition to returning the property, he is bound to return all profits earned from it, minus expenses. In the second case, the husband is bound to pay back the price; if he cannot pay, he is thrown into prison until he does. These rules apply not only if the sale without consent happened after the marriage was consummated through sexual union, but also if it happened before consummation. All of this is found in the <term>Portuguese Ordinances</term><note>Latin: "Ord. Lusit." The "Ordenações Manuelinas" or "Filipinas," the primary law codes of the Kingdom of Portugal.</note>, Book 4, Title 6. In that place, it was also established that a wife should appear before a judge to give her consent and be questioned under oath in her husband's absence as to whether she consented freely. That requirement, however, was later revoked in the "Extravagant Laws" (Part 2, Title 22, Law 6), which decreed that she should give consent before a notary without a judge, and it was forbidden to question her under oath. To what extent a husband depends on his wife’s consent regarding gifts of money or other movable goods, or regarding alms—and likewise regarding gifts a husband gives to a mistress or anyone else with whom he commits fornication—see what was said in Disputation 275.

<margin>11</margin>
If a husband acts as a guarantor for someone without his wife’s consent, he can only obligate the half of the property that belongs to him, not the wife’s half. An exception is made when he is a guarantor for the price of someone leasing royal taxes: in that case, all movable property of both spouses remains obligated, but of the immovable property, only the half belonging to the husband. If, however, the husband himself leases royal taxes or those of another and obligates all his goods for it, then all common property of himself and his wife—whether movable or im-

...or if they are immovable goods, they remain obligated. This is held in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 13.

<margin>12</margin>
From this, it is clear that Gama (Decision 108) rightly asserts against certain others that, under Portuguese law, it is lawful to <term>mortgage</term><note>original: "hypothecare." To use property as security for a debt without transferring possession.</note> an immovable thing without the wife's consent, even though the husband cannot <term>alienate</term><note>To sell or transfer ownership of the property to another.</note> it without her consent. However, Gama well observes in the same place that if an immovable thing were given as a pledge or subjected to a mortgage for so great an amount that there was no hope of redeeming it, it is then considered an alienation; consequently, such a pledge or mortgage is invalid without the wife’s consent. Read his work.

Spouses are also interdependent—the husband on the wife, and the wife on the husband—insofar as neither of them can contend in a legal judgment regarding immovable goods (or those counted as immovable) without the consent or <term>proxy</term><note>Latin: "procuratione." A legal authorization for someone to act on another's behalf.</note> of the other. Anything attempted otherwise is completely void and empty. In the same way, the spouse of the person with whom one is litigating must be summoned simultaneously; otherwise, the proceedings will be similarly void and empty, unless perhaps the defendant held a proxy or the consent of their spouse to proceed in that lawsuit. If, however, the summoned spouse does not appear in court in person or through their proxy within the prescribed time, then, after one public proclamation has been made, whatever actions are taken after that proclamation are valid. Heavy penalties are established for judges unless, at the start of a lawsuit, they inquire of both the plaintiff and the defendant whether they are married, and unless they ensure that these rules are carried out. If, in the progress of a lawsuit, one of the litigants takes a wife, the same rules must be carried out regarding the new wife. But if the progress of a lawsuit occurs through the judge's justifiable ignorance, then—because it was lawfully begun—the actions continued in that ignorance are not void. When one spouse wishes to initiate a lawsuit regarding their own similar goods, and the other does not wish to grant consent or proxy for it, then the local judge where they live is bound to provide that consent if he foresees the matter is reasonable and the one wishing to sue is fit for it; the judge's consent is sufficient without the consent of the spouse who refused to provide it. These matters are held in Book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 32.

<margin>13</margin>
In this <term>partnership contract</term><note>Latin: "societatis contractu." Here referring to the legal union of assets in marriage.</note>, if anything is consumed or lost due to the crime of one spouse, or due to their notable fault or negligence (greater than "slight"), or due to improper and disordered administration, that spouse is bound to accept the total loss out of the portion of goods that falls to them. This was stated in the preceding disputation and is clear from the law *si fratres*, the final section (Digest, *pro socio*). The Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, title 6, final section) agree, as they command the husband to take from his own share any donations he made without the wife’s consent. How this is to be understood was explained in Disputation 275. Furthermore, in title 8, they grant wives the right to recover what husbands have given to concubines or others with whom they have sexual relations—a matter also discussed in the cited disputation. This is confirmed because, in all those cases, one spouse does an injury to the other and causes them loss unjustly, since their own fault is the cause of the communal goods being so consumed

<column-break/>

or lost; therefore, they are bound to restore the loss thus inflicted. At a minimum, this is half of what was consumed or lost.

I said "at a minimum" because fraud is also seen in the fact that further profit could have been acquired with those goods. In this place, observe that for a spouse who consumed assets in this way to be freed from the burden of restitution, it is enough if they obtain a free release from the other spouse; this is because that alienation would have been valid if it had been carried out with their consent. It is also sufficient if the spouse understands without doubt that, although the other spouse grieves that the asset was consumed, they nevertheless wish for no restitution. In these matters, <term>offsetting</term><note>Latin: "compensatio." A legal balancing where debts or losses on both sides cancel each other out.</note> also has a place. For if one spouse understands that the other has poorly spent just as much or more goods, they are bound to no restitution. Observe also that the spouse who is bound to take poorly spent things into their own share is not forced to take them from the "Third" of goods (which in Portugal they can freely dispose of), but they may declare that it be deducted from the entire portion of goods that would otherwise belong to them, and they may still dispose of the entire remaining Third of goods at their pleasure. The reason is that this pertains to a debt, which must be deducted from the entire mass of one's goods before all else; in Portugal, one can freely dispose of the remaining Third, while the other two parts are the <term>forced share</term><note>Latin: "legitimae." The portion of an estate that by law must go to the children or parents.</note> of descendants or, in their absence, of ancestors. Other things that could be said about this contract will be understood from what follows.

### ->Concerning the partnership of those celebrating marriage in Castile and Portugal under the contract of earnest money and dowry. And which dowry is called "profectitious" and which "adventitious." And concerning certain privileges of the dowry, even on the part of the one to whom it is promised.<-

### ->DISPUTATION 423.<-

#### ->SUMMARY.<-

1 *What a dowry is.*
2 *A dowry cannot exist without a marriage.*
3 *The promise and delivery of a dowry implies a tacit condition that the marriage follows.*
4 *From what point the time for the payment of the dowry begins to run.*
5 *For what purpose a dowry is given to a husband under common law.*
6 *A partnership contract between husband and wife is not granted under common law; it is otherwise under Portuguese and Castilian law.*
7 *By whom a dowry can be given or promised under common law.*
8 *And what the law is in Castile and Portugal (number 8).*
9 *The cause of a dowry carries a tacit agreement regarding both its restitution and its payment. Likewise, it carries a tacit mortgage (number 10). And what the law is in Portugal (number 11).*

When spouses celebrate marriage under a contract of <term>earnest money</term><note>Latin: "arrharum." Gifts or money given at the time of betrothal to seal the agreement.</note> and dowry, there is indeed, by the law of this Kingdom and by the custom of Portugal, a partnership between them regarding the sharing only of profit—if any is found when the marriage is dissolved or a divorce occurs—but not regarding the capital.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of marital property, specifically transitioning from the management of assets to the definition and division of the dowry and communal profits in the kingdoms of Castile and Portugal compared to Roman Common Law.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 4, 23.
Ff 4
<meta>catchword: esset</meta>

To better understand this entire matter—to establish which communal profits are to be divided between the spouses, how all goods should be distributed once the partnership ends, and to make clear the difference between marriage as celebrated under **Common Law**<note>original: "iure comuni." This refers to the Roman-based legal system used across much of Europe at the time.</note> and as it is practiced in these two Kingdoms—we must begin by explaining the **capital**<note>The core assets or principal wealth brought into the marriage.</note> of each spouse. First, we must speak of the principal part of the wife’s capital: the **dowry**.

<margin>1</margin> The dowry is defined by Azo, in accordance with various laws, in this manner: it is that which is given or promised to the husband by reason of marriage to sustain its burdens—that is, to provide for and support the wife, their common children, and the household.

<margin>2</margin> From this it follows that without † marriage, a dowry can neither exist nor be understood, as held in Law 3, "By promising," in the Digest *On the Law of Dowries*, and the Law "While many," in the section "Just as," in the Code *On Donations Before Marriage*. This is the consensus of the teachers, followed by Antonio Gómez in his commentary on Law 50 of the Laws of Toro, number 25; Gregorio López on Law 1, Title 11, Part 4, final gloss; and Emmanuel Acosta on the Law "Since such," in the section "If by judgment," limitation 6.

<margin>3</margin> n. 30. It further follows that a promise of a dowry, or even its physical delivery, carries an implied condition: "provided that the wedding follows." A promised dowry cannot be demanded before the marriage is celebrated. This is expressly stated in the Law "Of stipulations," in the Digest *On the Law of Dowry*, and Laws "Frequently," in the section "If before," "In things," section 1, and "For not," under the same title. These are also express in the Law "Likewise, because," section 1, in the Digest *On Pacts*, and Law 11,

<margin>4</margin> Title 11, Part 4. From this it is further concluded that if a specific time was set for the dowry to be paid—for instance, "within a year"—that time begins to run from the moment the wedding is celebrated, not from the moment the contract was first signed. This is found in the Law "With such a deed," at the beginning, in the Digest *On the Law of Dowry*, and Law 12, Title 11, Part 4. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows. However, it is different if it was expressly stated that the time should run from the moment of the agreement, or if a specific, designated day was fixed for payment, such as **St. John’s Day**, † **St. Michael’s Day**, or the **Nativity of the Lord**<note>Christmas.</note>. In those cases, if the wedding was celebrated within that time, the dowry would be due at the time established when the agreement was made. Likewise, if it were agreed that the dowry should be paid *before* the celebration of the wedding, it must be paid at that time. If, however, the wedding does not actually take place, whatever was given as a dowry may be reclaimed. This is held by Baldus and others, and cited by Antonio Gómez and Gregorio López.

<margin>5</margin> A partner in this legal system must observe that under † Common Law, a dowry is given to the husband regarding its use and its "fruits"<note>The income, interest, or produce generated by the asset.</note> to sustain the burdens of marriage. Thus, when the marriage is dissolved, the entire dowry under Common Law would revert to the wife or her heirs, but all the fruits and profits from it up until the dissolution belonged entirely to the husband. This is found in Laws 1 and 2, and the Law "Fruits of the dowry," in the Digest *On the Law of Dowry*, and other various statutes. Furthermore, the wife was bound during the entire time the marriage lasted to perform that part of the household administration that pertained to her, and to apply those efforts in managing it which were fitting for her social condition.

<column-break/>

<margin>6</margin> From this † it is clear that under Common Law, there was no "partnership of goods" contract between husband and wife, as affirmed by Covarruvias and others. This is because they did not share in the profits. Instead, there was an **innominate contract**<note>A contract that does not fall under a specific standard category (like sale or lease) but is binding nonetheless.</note> between them: "I give you a dowry for your use and the enjoyment of its fruits for the duration of the marriage so they may be yours, and in addition, I will manage the household in matters pertaining to me and provide the labor fitting for me, so that you may perform or sustain the remaining burdens of the marriage."

<margin>The Law of Castile and Lusitania</margin> Under the law of Castile and the custom of **Lusitania**<note>Portugal.</note>, it was later added that not only the administration of the dowry but also of the wife's other goods pertains to the husband. There is a communion between them regarding *only* the profits of all the goods of both, from wherever they might come. Thus, under Castilian law and Portuguese custom, this contract is a true **partnership**<note>original: "societas."</note> regarding the communion of profits alone, which is not the case under Common Law. What the law or custom might be in other kingdoms must be learned from their own statutes and practice. Note, however, that in Castile and Portugal, this is not a pure partnership contract, but a mixed one on the wife's part: "I provide all these things, and I will provide all my effort and industry in assisting you as is fitting, so that you may sustain all the burdens of the marriage in full and always keep my entire capital safe." Insofar as it further adds: "if, however, any profits are found resulting from all your goods and mine, and from your industry and mine, half shall belong to me and the other half to you," a true partnership is seen in that contract.

<margin>7</margin> A dowry can be given, established, or promised † to the husband by the wife’s father or another ancestor in the male line, such as a paternal grandfather or great-grandfather. If it is given or promised from their own goods, or by someone else in their name, so that those goods are considered to proceed from these ancestors into the woman's dowry, it is called a **profectitious dowry**<note>original: "dos profectitia." A dowry provided by a father or paternal ancestor.</note>. It can also be given, established, or promised to the husband by the wife herself from her own property—even if the father gives it to the husband from the daughter’s goods which she inherited from her mother or obtained elsewhere. Alternatively, it can be given by the wife's mother or any other relative not in the paternal male line, or by a stranger; in these cases, it is called an **adventitious dowry**<note>original: "dos aduentitia." A dowry coming from any source other than the father/paternal line.</note>. This is found in the Law "Profectitious," in the Digest *On the Law of Dowries*, and Law 2, Title 11, Part 4. Among other things, there was this difference between an adventitious and profectitious dowry: when the dowry was profectitious, if the husband died and the wife was not **emancipated**<note>Freed from the legal control of her father.</note>, the dowry reverted to the parent who gave it if they were still living, rather than to the wife. However, that parent was bound to restore the whole dowry to the woman in the event that she married again, unless the parent's wealth had significantly diminished; in that case, the parent was only bound to hand over what they conveniently could. When the dowry was adventitious, it returned to the wife and not to the person who had given it, even if the person who gave it was...

# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

<margin>Castilian Law</margin>...were the mother, unless perhaps the dowry was given under the condition that, upon the husband's death, it would return to the one who gave it. All these matters are contained in the single law, in the section "it happens," and the section "this," with the authentic text added there, in the Code *On the action regarding the wife's property*. Today, however, in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, this distinction does not apply. This is because a woman, by the very fact that she marries, is emancipated and remains in her own right <note>original: "sui iuris"</note>, as was stated in Disputation 227 and elsewhere frequently in this treatise. Thus, even when a dowry is a **paternal dowry** <term>profectitia; a dowry provided by the father or a paternal ancestor</term>, it returns to the wife and not to the parents. Note here that when a dowry was provided by the mother, although it is not called "paternal" for the purpose just explained, it is still called "paternal" in relation to the mother for the purpose of **collation** <term>the bringing of gifts into a common pool before the division of an inheritance</term> in the partition of the mother's goods, as seen in Disputation 233 and those following. However, the fruits of a paternal dowry received by both the son-in-law and the daughter are not to be brought into the collation, as was shown in that same place.

<margin>9</margin> Whether † a dowry is paternal or **external** <term>adventitia; a dowry provided by the woman herself, her mother, or a third party</term>, the cause of the dowry is considered by legal privilege to have a **silent agreement** <term>tacitam stipulationem</term>. This is not only so that the wife, parents, or her heirs may reclaim it once the marriage is dissolved, but also so that the husband can demand the dowry promised to him with his wife—even if not yet paid—from whoever promised it to him, whether it be the wife herself, parents, other relatives, or anyone else. Consequently, in a case involving a dowry, a "naked" or informal pact is "clothed" by the help of the law, which grants it this silent agreement. Therefore, from such a pact, not only a natural obligation but also a civil legal obligation arises, as was said at the end of Disputation 255. This is held in the single law, sections 1 and "that more fully," in the sentence "and no one," in the Code *On the action regarding the wife's property*, and the law "to the exaction" in the Code *On the promise of a dowry*. This is affirmed by the common opinion, which Antonio Gómez records and follows in his commentary on Law 30 of the Laws of Toro, number 29.

<margin>10</margin> Furthermore, † the cause of the dowry holds a **silent mortgage** <term>tacitam hypothecam; a legal lien on property created by law rather than a contract</term>. This exists not only over the husband's goods so the dowry can be reclaimed when the marriage ends (which will be discussed fully in its proper place below), but the husband also has a silent mortgage over the goods of the person promising the dowry. This serves both to ensure it is paid to him and to cover his interests if any part of the dowry is lost through legal claim <note>original: "evincatur," referring to evictio, where a third party proves they own the property</note> after it has been paid to him. This is held in the cited single law, the section "that more fully," and Law 23, Title 12, Part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas</note>.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin> <margin>11</margin> These rules apply whether a written document was involved or not, as in the cited single law, the sentence "and no one." In the Kingdom of Portugal, however, although these rules have the same force, proof regarding a promised dowry is not admitted except through a **public instrument** <note>a notarized or official deed</note> or the confession of the promisor (or their heirs after death), as we showed in Disputation 260. Gregorio López, Antonio Gómez, and the common body of doctors observe that the mortgage the husband holds over the goods of the one promising him a dowry is not **privileged**. This means the husband is not preferred over earlier creditors in that regard. This is different from the privileged mortgage the wife holds over her husband's goods to recover her dowry, as will be discussed below. The reason is that nowhere in the law is such a privilege found to be granted to the husband, whereas it is found granted to the wife.

All these things said regarding the husband's mortgage on the goods of the one promising a dowry, and regarding the silent agreement, apply similarly to a dowry promised when a marriage is celebrated under a contract for a **half-share of goods** <note>a community property arrangement</note>.

->SUMMARY<-

14. A large gift given by a father to a son: to what extent it can be revoked by the subsequent birth of more children.

<margin>1</margin> A father can be compelled by the authority of a judge to give his daughter in marriage when he is negligent in the matter. † This would be the case if the daughter exceeded the twenty-fifth year of her age and wished to marry, but the father did not seek a husband for her. At the same time, he can be compelled to provide her a dowry, even if the daughter has other goods of her own from her mother or elsewhere. This is held in the law "those children" in the Digest *On the rite of marriage*, the final law of the Code *On the promise of a dowry*, and Law 8, Title 11, Part 4. The common opinion of the doctors agrees, as recorded and followed by Gregorio López and Antonio Gómez.

<margin>2</margin> The † measure, however, up to which a father can be compelled to provide a dowry for a daughter is the **legal share** <term>legitima; the portion of an estate that a child is entitled to by law</term> owed to such a daughter from the father's goods. For if the father can conveniently give her the whole share, he can be compelled to present it to her, as Gregorio López says following Saliceto and Alexander.

<margin>3</margin> A † mother, however, is not bound to provide a dowry for a daughter, as held in the law "nor a mother" in the Code *On the law of dowries*, and Law 9, Title 11, Part 4. Indeed, it is the father's own duty both to provide a dowry for daughters and to grant sons a gift for marriage or toward the wedding, as held in the final law of the Code *On the dowry*...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 424.

*Column 1:*

...promised. An exception is made when some urgent cause is present such that the mother should provide a dowry for her daughter, such as if the daughter were destitute and had no other source for a dowry. For just as a mother is bound to provide nourishment to her daughter on account of poverty when the father is unable to provide it—as we showed in Disputations 168 and 228 regarding the fifth effect of paternal power—so too is she bound to provide her with a dowry. And this is clearly suggested in the law <note>original: "l. neque mater"</note> cited in those words: "unless for a great and probable cause." A further exception is made if the mother were a heretic or otherwise an unbeliever, and the daughter were a believer; for then the mother could be compelled to provide a dowry for the daughter up to the full **legal portion** <term>legitima; the share of an estate that a person's natural heirs cannot be deprived of without legal cause</term> owed to such a daughter from the mother’s goods, even if the daughter had a competent dowry from the father or elsewhere. This is held in the law <note>original: "l. cognouimus"</note>, in the Code *on heretics*, and in law 9, title 11, part 4; and the law "neither mother" in the Code *on the law of dowries* is in agreement.

<margin>4</margin> When † a father held other property belonging to the son or daughter—such as property from the side of the deceased mother, or from elsewhere—if the father sends a certain sum to such a daughter or son as a dowry or a **gift on account of marriage** <term>donatio propter nuptias; a gift given by the groom or his family to the bride, often mirroring the dowry</term>, and does not specify from which goods he will pay it, he is judged to promise it entirely from his own personal goods. Therefore, he is bound to deliver the whole amount in addition to that which such a daughter or son holds from elsewhere. If, however, he expressed that he would give it from his own goods and from the goods of the daughter or son, but did not express how much of that sum he would give from his own and how much from the child's, then he is only judged to have promised from the child's goods to the extent that he himself, due to poverty, could not pay from his own. In this case, he is judged to have promised from his own goods as far as he could conveniently pay, and only the remainder from the child’s goods. The reason is that, since it is the father’s own duty to provide dowries for daughters and gifts for sons for marriage, in cases of doubt the law presumes he intended to provide from his own property in accordance with his duty, rather than from the children's property, even if he is the administrator of the children's goods. The law established this in favor of marriage, and so that parents would explain themselves sufficiently when promising something to sons or daughters as a dowry or gift. This prevents them from appearing at first glance to be giving out of their own personal generosity—as if boasting of their liberality, as the law soon to be cited says—and thereby deceiving the sons-in-law or daughters-in-law, only to say later that they only intended to give from the children's own goods, except for what was necessary to complete the promised sum. However, when the father explicitly states how much he would give from the children’s goods and how much from his own, then he is only bound to pay from his own what he had specified, and the rest from the children's goods. All these matters are expressly contained in the final law of the Code *on the promise of a dowry*.

<margin>5</margin> Several things should be observed regarding this. The first is: When † a father truly intended to promise part of the sum from the children's goods, then in the **forum of conscience** <note>original: "in foro conscientiæ"; referring to moral and religious duty before God rather than civil liability</note> he is not bound to pay the whole sum from his own goods, but only up to the legal portion owed to the daughter, or whatever more he intended to promise from his own. Unless, perhaps, by the manner in which he promised, he had by his own fault deceived the son-in-law

<column-break/>

*Column 2:*

or daughter-in-law to whom he had promised it, who believed he intended to promise the whole amount from his own property. The reason that moves me to assert this is that the cited law is founded on a presumption and was established so that parents would speak clearly and not deceive those who contract marriages with their sons or daughters; however, in the forum of conscience, one stands by the truth and not by a legal presumption.

The second point is that the contrary holds true when a father holds some property of a son or daughter and consumes something for that child's nourishment or for some other useful purpose for the child. In case of doubt, he is judged to have spent it from the child's goods, not from his own, as seen in Disputations 234 and 239. The final law of the Digest *on claiming an inheritance* and the law "Nefenius" in the Digest *on the management of affairs* agree. The reason is that the final law of the Code *on the promise of a dowry* was introduced in favor of marriage, in which it is the father's specific duty to provide a dowry for a daughter and a gift for a son for the wedding from his own property.

The third point is that today, in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, by the name "gift on account of marriage," one must understand that which is given to the male for the wedding. As was said in Disputation 290, it is called a "gift on account of marriage" in these Kingdoms, and it can be called a "gift for the wedding." It is far different from the "gift on account of marriage" or "before marriage" discussed in **Common Law** <note>original: "iure communi"; the Roman-canonical legal tradition</note>, which it succeeded, as was stated in the cited disputation.

The fourth point is that certain authors—whom Antonio Gomez refers to and follows regarding Law 30 of the Laws of Toro, number 21—wished to argue that when a father who held goods of his daughter (understand the same for a gift promised to a son) said "I promise such an amount as a dowry for my daughter, counting in it everything of hers that I hold," he is bound to pay the entire promised sum from his own goods, counting nothing of the daughter's own property. They are led by the final law of the Code *on the promise of a dowry*. I, however, consider this opinion improbable. For that law only speaks in cases of doubt, when the father has not sufficiently explained what he wished to give of his own and what of the daughter's goods; but in the proposed event, the father sufficiently explains what he wants to be counted toward the dowry from the daughter's goods, and to what he wishes to bind himself from his own property.

<margin>6</margin> When someone promises a dowry or a gift on account of marriage and is not the father of the person for whom they promise—but rather the mother, another relative, or a stranger who had the administration of some of that person's property—then in case of doubt they are not judged to promise from their own goods, but from the goods they manage. This is gathered from the law "afterward" in the Digest *on the administration of tutors*; the final law of the Digest *on claiming an inheritance* and other laws agree. Thus, the provision of the final law of the Code *on the promise of a dowry* only applies to a father, who is bound by duty to provide dowries for daughters and gifts for a son's marriage. But if a stranger having the administration of someone’s goods, such as a **curator** <term>a legal guardian appointed to manage the affairs of a person over the age of puberty but under twenty-five</term>, promises a dowry or gift for that person's marriage beyond their own goods, then in case of doubt they are not judged to promise the increase from their own property, nor are they bound to pay it.

<margin>7</margin> An exception is made if, † knowing that the one whose goods he administered did not have that much in property, [he promised] the whole sum...

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

For then, because he is presumed to have intended to give it, or if he did not intend to give it, he acted deceitfully to the prejudice of a third party, he is bound to pay that increase from his own personal goods. Nefenius"</note> in the Digest *on the management of affairs* and the law "nourishment" in the Code *under the same title*. Read Antonio Gomez, cited above, number 24.

<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>
**8** In this Kingdom, however, when † only the husband promises something as a dowry for a daughter, or as a wedding gift for a son while the marriage still exists, he is considered to promise it from the goods held in common with his wife, and it must be paid from them, even if the wife did not consent. If there are no communal goods, or they are insufficient, then the deficiency must be paid from the husband’s own goods. This was enacted in Law 53 of the Laws of Toro <note>original: "l. 53. Tauri"</note>, which is Law 8, Title 9, Book 5 of the New Collection. The reason for the first part of this assertion is that in the common profits shared by a husband and wife, the husband has free administration and full power to **alienate** <term>alienate; to transfer ownership of property to another</term> them, provided he does not do so to defraud the wife of her share, as held in Law 5, Title 9, Book 5 of the New Collection. He especially has full power to alienate for a just and reasonable cause; such a cause is a daughter’s dowry or a wedding gift for a son. For this reason, he does not need his wife's consent, just as he does not need it for any other reasonable cause. Added to this is the fact that the debt for providing a daughter's dowry or a son's wedding gift arises during the marriage; therefore, since debts contracted during marriage are to be paid from communal property unless only separate property is found, it follows that when there are communal goods for both spouses, the daughters' dowries and sons' wedding gifts should be paid from them. Covarruvias (Various Resolutions, book 3, chapter 19, number 3), Antonio Gomez (cited number 24), and others they cite, agree.

<margin>Question.</margin>
**9** The learned doctors doubt whether, if the marriage is already dissolved by the death of the wife, a husband provides a dowry for a daughter or a wedding gift for a son without expressing from which property he does so, he is thought † to do so from the goods that were common to him and his wife during the marriage, or from his own personal property alone. Antonio Gomez (cited number 24) and several others assert that he is considered to have promised from his own goods alone. They are moved by the fact that the cited law only speaks of when the father does this while the marriage exists. Furthermore, once the marriage is dissolved, the profits that were previously communal remain as the property of the wife's heirs as far as her half-share is concerned, and the husband no longer has free administration over them. Covarruvias, however (in Various Resolutions, book 3, chapter 19, number 3), along with Gregorio Lopez (on Law 6, Title 10, Part 5), affirms that it is rather considered to have been promised from the communal goods. He says that by the more frequent vote of judges, this opinion is accepted over the contrary. They are moved by the fact that the debt of providing dowries for daughters and gifts for sons on account of marriage was contracted

<column-break/>

after the marriage was celebrated and while it continued; for which reason, just as it must be paid from communal property, so too must it be considered promised and given by the father from those same goods. Neither opinion is improbable. And if this latter one is more widely accepted, as Covarruvias says, he would embrace it. Yet the former opinion has great probability because such a debt is not like other debts, but is a specific paternal burden by the disposition of common law. However, out of a certain equity, Law 35 of the Laws of Toro <note>original: "l. 35. Tauri"</note> enacted that since by the law of this Kingdom profits acquired while a marriage exists are made common to the wife and husband, and the husband has free administration of them with full power to alienate them, he can also alienate them for such a reasonable cause as a dowry for a daughter or a wedding gift for a son common to both spouses. Therefore, since that Law 53 of the Laws of Toro only speaks of the time while the marriage exists—at which time the husband has full power to alienate those goods—that provision clearly does not seem to extend to establishing a dowry or wedding gift after the marriage has already been dissolved. Additionally, if many children were left from that dissolved marriage, each now has their own specific portion in the property and the half-share of the profits, which the father cannot prejudice by promising it as a dowry or wedding gift to another child. In any event, whenever a daughter’s dowry or a son’s wedding gift is not established from the communal property of both parents, that son or daughter is bound to bring back to the **collation** <term>collation; the legal requirement for an heir to account for gifts received during the benefactor's lifetime to ensure a fair distribution among all heirs</term> half of it upon the death of one parent, and the other half upon the death of the other parent, as Antonio Gomez affirms at the cited number, and as we have said in Disputation 238.

**10** When both † the father and the mother have promised something together as a dowry for a daughter or a wedding gift for a son, then each of them is bound to pay half, both according to common law and the law of Castile. This is based on the argument of the text in the law "debtors," the section "when in the tablets" <note>original: "l. reos, §. cum in tabulis"</note> in the Digest *on two debtors*, joined with the laws "to provide a dowry" and "generally" in the Code *on the Velleianum Decree*, or "the wife" in the Digest *on donations between husband and wife*, and the law "Lucius Titius" in the Digest *on the ways pledges or mortgages are dissolved*, and the law "any" in the Digest *on the dissolution of marriage*. In the first of the laws cited, it is held that when two people promise something and specify nothing else, each is bound to pay half. In the others, it is held that a wife's transfer of property for the sake of a dowry is valid in cases where it would otherwise not be valid.

**11** Although everyone agrees that when that wife, at the time she made the promise, had other goods besides **dotal property** <term>dotalia; property constituting a woman's dowry</term> from which she might promise it, there are others who nonetheless deny that the promise is valid regarding what should be paid from dotal property, unless the promise was confirmed by an oath. Today, however, by the law of Castile, Law 53 of the Laws of Toro <note>original: "l. 53. Tauri"</note>, which is Law 8, Title 9, Book 5 of the New Collection, it is enacted that it is valid even regarding dotal property. And this same opinion seems more probable when standing on common law, as the cited laws suggest. Therefore, since nothing has been enacted on this matter in the law of Portugal, the disposition of common law must be followed in Portugal when that wife [contracts] for pledges and the dowry of the marriage...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal source of funds for dowries and wedding gifts, explaining that under Castilian law, such promises made during marriage are primarily paid from communal property managed by the husband. He also addresses the distribution of liability when both parents make a joint promise and how these rules apply after a marriage is dissolved or under Portuguese jurisdiction.</summary>

# Second Treatise. Disputation 424.
### Page 457

When, however, she married under a **contract of half of the goods** <note>original: "contractu medietatis bonorum"; a legal arrangement where all assets are shared equally between spouses</note>, there is certainly no difficulty in that Kingdom. For then, she can alienate <note>sell or transfer ownership</note> all goods together with her husband, both immovable <note>real estate</note> and movable, and obligate them, not only for the dowry of daughters and for the **gift on account of marriage** <term>donatio propter nuptias; a gift given to the groom or his family, often balancing the dowry</term> for sons, but also for any other purposes. This is because all goods are common to both spouses, and they can be alienated by them for whatever they wish, as was said in Disputation 422. From the cited disposition of common law, Antonio Gomez concludes (at Law 50 of Toro, number 25) that if a father and some outsider, such as a stepmother, promise a dowry to a daughter and do not express how much each of them is to pay, each of them is held to pay half; he reports that it was so judged in a certain particular event.

<margin>22</margin>
Concerning <insert>†</insert> **Portuguese law**, when a father alone promises a dowry to a daughter, or a wedding gift to a son, and pays them: if the promise and payment were made from movable goods, and were not **undutiful** <term>inofficiosa; a gift that unfairly reduces the mandatory inheritance of other heirs</term> to the other children, nor to the wife regarding her dotal goods, **paraphernalia** <term>assets belonging to the wife outside of her dowry</term>, the wedding bounty, and the **earnest money** <note>original: "arrhas"; a security or gift given at the time of the marriage contract</note>—when the marriage was celebrated under a contract of earnest money and dowry—or regarding the wife’s half-share of goods when it was celebrated under a contract of half of the goods: such a promise and payment made without the wife's consent would be valid. 

This is proven because under Portuguese law, whether the husband celebrated the marriage under a contract of earnest money and dowry or one of half of the goods, he has the free administration of movable goods and the power to alienate them for a reasonable cause without the wife's consent. This is clear from Book 4 of the Ordinances <note>The *Ordenações*, the primary legal code of Portugal</note>, Title 6, final paragraph, joined with the beginning of that title and the following paragraphs, and it was partly stated in Disputation 422. Since a dowry is conferred on a daughter and a wedding gift on a son for a reasonable cause—indeed, as was said, it is the father's duty to provide them—it follows that when such a promise and payment are made by the husband alone from movable goods, it is valid. This is no different than how other contracts involving similar goods celebrated by the husband alone would be valid. 

I said "not undutiful to the other children," because if it happened to touch the **legitims** <term>legitima; the portion of an estate that must by law be left to one's children</term> owed to them from the parents' goods, it would be invalid regarding that portion which touched them, as was said in Disputation 238. I also added "nor to the wife regarding dotal goods, etc.," because, as said above, a wife is not bound to provide a dowry, and much less a wedding gift, from her own proper goods while she lives, unless the husband lacks sufficient goods to provide the dowry. Nor can a husband, against the wife's will, give anything to a common daughter from the wife's goods, as the law "neither the mother" <note>original: "l. neque mater"</note> in the Code *on the law of dowries* expressly holds. 

From this it follows that if she had married under a contract of earnest money and dowry, and the dowry or wedding gift made by the husband alone touched the dotal goods, paraphernalia, and other things belonging to the wife, she could complain and seek recovery during her life for what was given without her consent to the prejudice of her goods. 

Concerning communal profits acquired during the marriage contract, the husband could dispose of these by dowering daughters and giving wedding gifts to sons without the wife's consent, for the reasons we said this is possible under the law of this Kingdom; provided, however, he gave from movable things. For he is entirely prohibited in Portugal from alienating immovable goods without his wife's consent, even if he

<column-break/>

contracted the marriage under a contract of earnest money and dowry, as is clear in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 6, at the beginning and in the following paragraphs. In the same way, if that dowry or wedding gift made from movable goods by a husband who had married a wife under a contract of half of the goods were to prejudice the wife's half, the wife could for the same reason complain and reclaim during her life that which prejudiced her. This is because she herself is not bound to provide a dowry for a daughter while she lives, but the husband is. 

However, a dowry made by a husband for a daughter from immovable goods without the wife's consent, or a wedding gift made from the same goods to a son, is invalid in Portugal in the sense that the wife, or the husband with the wife's consent, can reclaim the immovable good thus given, according to what was said in Disputation 422. For what was said there in this regard similarly takes place when the marriage was celebrated under a contract of earnest money and dowry, and the husband alienates immovable goods without the wife's consent, as is established in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 6. 

But if, for the purpose of dowering a daughter according to the amount the father can confer on her, or for giving a wedding gift to a son, it were necessary to hand over an immovable good to them or to sell it for that purpose, and the wife were unreasonably unwilling to consent to that alienation, she could be compelled by the authority of a judge to provide consent. Indeed, the judge could even supply her consent by granting the husband the power for that alienation, following the argument in the final paragraph of Title 32, Book 3 of the Ordinances.

<margin>23</margin>
If a husband has sons or daughters from another, prior wife, he may dower those daughters and give wedding gifts to those sons from movable goods without the consent of the later wife, provided that what he gives does not touch the legitims owed to his other children from his goods, and provided it does not prejudice the goods of the later wife. The reason is that he has full administration of those goods and the free power to alienate them for a reasonable cause, which this is; for he owes a dowry and wedding gift no less to the children of the first marriage than to those of the second. Therefore, if it were necessary to alienate an immovable good for that purpose and the later wife would not consent, she could be compelled by the authority of the judge to provide consent, or he could alienate it against the wife's will by the judge's authority, as was said a little earlier. 

In the same way, if a wife wished to dower a daughter of a prior marriage who did not have a suitable dowry from elsewhere, or similarly wished to give a wedding gift to a son, and the husband would not consent—even though she is not the administrator of the goods, but the husband is—she could compel the husband by the authority of the judge to consent, based on the argument of the same final paragraph cited. The reason is that the wife is then bound to dower the daughter according to the law "neither the mother" <note>original: "l. neque mater"</note> in the Code *on the law of dowries*, and the husband is then acting unreasonably in being unwilling for the wife to dower her daughters or hand over wedding gifts to sons of a prior marriage.

<margin>24</margin>
This last point regarding what has been said so far must be observed: if a father <insert>†</insert> promises or even hands over a large dowry to a daughter, and afterwards other children are born to the same father for whom that dowry is rendered undutiful <note>leaving them less than their legal share</note>, then standing on common law alone—and likewise in Portugal, where nothing to the contrary has been enacted—it is to be revoked or rendered invalid only insofar as it touches the legitims of the children. It is not revoked regarding that portion in which the father could favor such a daughter, such as regarding the **third of the goods** <term>tertium bonorum; the one-third of an estate that a parent was legally allowed to distribute freely to one heir over others</term> of the father in Portugal, as we showed in Disputation 283...

# Second Treatise. Disputation 415.
### Page 461

...sustaining the **burdens of marriage** <term>oneribus matrimonij; the expenses of a shared life, such as housing, food, and clothing</term> with those assets. For that reason, if those who promised the dowry as a price—or as a sort of price—for sustaining the burdens of marriage fail to deliver, the husband is not bound to stand by the contract or sustain those burdens. This is the opinion of **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> (in *c. per vestras. de donat. inter vir. & vxor. nu. 4*), **Sylvester** (*word: dowry, q. 10*), **Covarruvias** (in *Epitome 4, book of decrees, ch. 7, num. 1*), **Antonio Gomez** (on *Law 50 of Toro, num. 31*), and the common opinion of the doctors, which they cite in agreement with various laws. I stated above that he is not required to bring her into his home to support her or sustain the marriage's burdens; for, as **Covarruvias** (in *num. 1* cited above) rightly notes, because the dowry was not paid, the husband cannot deny the wife her "marital debt" <note>original: "debitum"; the sexual rights within marriage</note> or marital companionship, but he can deny her maintenance, which includes providing competent servants. Nor do the other doctors seem to have intended the contrary, regardless of what Covarruvias says there. However, if a man were to marry a woman where no dowry was promised, and her parents were capable of providing one, they should be compelled to do so according to what was said in the preceding disputation. In that event, whether they endowed her or not, the husband would be bound to support her, and she would be bound to provide him with her services, as the cited doctors affirm based on various laws (Covarruvias in the cited *Epitome part 2, ch. 3, § 8, num. 5*, along with many other legal experts).

<margin>7</margin>
When, however, a daughter marries in the presence of the Church without the consent of her parents, she cannot be **disinherited** <note>original: "exhæredari"</note> by her parents. For that reason, parents could then be compelled to endow her just as if she had married with their consent; any civil laws stating the contrary have no force, because this matrimonial cause pertains to **Canon Law** <note>the law of the Catholic Church</note>, which wills marriage to be free and immune from this or any other penalty. However, we have shown the opposite at length in **Disputation 176**, concerning the eleventh cause of disinheritance, and there is no need to repeat those points here. Consequently, in such an event, parents are by no means held to endow their daughters.

<margin>8</margin>
As for the last of the proposed points: You know that if the person who promised the dowry is the **father-in-law** <note>original: "socer"</note> (the wife's father or another male ancestor), he is not held to pay the dowry before the marriage is dissolved except **according to his means** <note>original: "in quantum facere possit"</note>. This means (as explained in Disputation 413) he is only required to give and pay what he can without lacking what he needs to support himself, keeping in mind his social status; he cannot be harassed for the remaining part of the dowry. If, however, he should come into a greater fortune, that part can then be sought from him. But once the marriage is dissolved, if by custom, local statutes, or the force of a contract, the **son-in-law** <note>original: "gener"</note> gains the dowry or a part of it, the father-in-law is held to pay the son-in-law **in full** <note>original: "in solidum"; the total amount without deduction for his own needs</note>, beyond what he could do in the sense explained above, just as one is regularly held for other debts. This is held in the laws of the *Digest*. Nevertheless, in another law of the *Digest*, it is added that this

<column-break/>

should be understood to apply when the father-in-law deceitfully promises a dowry to his son-in-law which he saw he could not conveniently pay. It is otherwise when he promised the dowry in good faith, believing he would pay it in full, and was later found to be unable to pay it conveniently and entirely; in that case, even after the marriage is dissolved, he is only held to pay as much as he conveniently can. Regarding what is owed to the daughter herself and the grandchildren after the death of the son-in-law and daughter, he is only held to what he can conveniently do. The same must be said of a mother who promised a dowry to her daughter. The reason is not only because, in comparison to the daughter, the dowry is not owed by **burdensome cause** but by **lucrative title** <note>original: "titulo lucratiuo"; meaning she receives it as a gift/gain rather than as a balanced exchange for costs</note>. Anyone who promises something by lucrative title is only held to what they can conveniently do, as we showed extensively in Disputation 413. It is also because parents are only held to their children according to what they can conveniently do, as stated in the *Institutes*. **Heirs** † indeed

<margin>9</margin>
of the father or father-in-law who promised a dowry to a daughter or son-in-law are held to pay the dowry **in full** <note>original: "in solidum"</note> from the goods of the deceased, provided the goods are sufficient and the dowry does not infringe upon the **legal portions** <term>legitimas portiones; the mandatory inheritance share reserved for certain family members</term> if any are due from those same goods. The same applies to the heirs of one who had promised a dowry as a gift, and even to **guarantors** <note>original: "fideiussores"</note>; although in Disputation 413 we discussed what caution guarantors might use so that, while the principal debtor lives, they are not compelled to pay more than the principal debtor himself is able. For this privilege does not pass to heirs or guarantors; rather, upon the death of the one who promised, his goods remain obligated to this debt just as to other debts of the deceased, as was said in Disputation 413.

<margin>10</margin>
Furthermore, a person who promised a dowry but was neither the wife's father nor any male ancestor is held to her husband **in full** <note>original: "in solidum"</note>, even while the marriage lasts, even if he promised it out of pure generosity. The reason is that, in comparison to the husband, he is held by **burdensome title** <note>original: "titulo oneroso"; because the husband takes on the actual costs and duties of marriage in exchange</note>. But in comparison to the wife, since he is only held by lucrative title, he is only held to what he can conveniently do. Thus, if the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death or by divorce and the dowry must be paid to the wife, then the one who promised the dowry out of generosity is held to her only to the extent he can conveniently pay. Nevertheless, for the husband's children, even if the mother has died, the right of the father is believed to remain, and thus the debt remains as one of burdensome cause. These points, besides the cited laws, are clear from the *Digest*. To what extent a husband is held when the dowry must be restored to the wife will be discussed below in its proper place. What could be added here was said in Disputation 413, where we explained the things common to all who enjoy the privilege of being sued only for what they can conveniently do. The things said in this disputation concerning the dowry and the gift on account of marriage also take place when the marriage is celebrated under a **contract of half the goods** <note>original: "contractu medietatis bonorum"; a communal property arrangement</note>.

<summary>This page explains when a father-in-law or third party is legally required to pay a promised dowry in full versus only what they can afford without falling into poverty. It distinguishes between the "burdensome" obligation to the husband (who manages the marriage's costs) and the "lucrative" gift to the wife or daughter.</summary>
