<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of dowry obligations, specifically focusing on the liability for lost property (risk) and the distinction between valued and unvalued dowry assets. Note: while the previous page was marked Disputation 415, the header here indicates Disputation 426; however, the subject matter follows the same legal discourse on the rights and duties of husbands and wives regarding property.</meta>

### Second Treatise. Disputation 426. 
### Page 464

...celebrated between husband and wife for the benefit of both. The general rule is that when a contract is celebrated for the benefit of both parties, one is held liable to the other only for **slight negligence** <note>original: "leui culpa"; a standard level of fault in Roman law where one fails to show the care of a "good householder"</note>, but not for the **slightest negligence** <note>original: "leuissima"; a very high standard of care</note>, as I stated on pages 295 and 413. **Antonio Gomez** <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>, in his commentary on *Law 50 of Toro, number 43*, says that when it is not clear that a thing perished without the husband's fault, it is his responsibility to prove it perished without his fault; otherwise, he is compelled to pay the value of the item that perished. I refer you to that law.

<margin>5</margin> When a **herd** <term>grex; a collective group of animals such as sheep or cattle</term> is given to the husband as an **unvalued dowry** <note>original: "inæstimatus"; a dowry where the items are not assigned a specific monetary value at the start, meaning the specific items must be returned rather than their cash value</note>, if some heads of that herd perish, they are replaced by the offspring of the same herd—if there are any then, or if they are born in the future—so that the herd remains whole for the wife. The remaining offspring of the same herd are counted among the **fruits** <note>original: "fructibus"; the legal term for income or produce generated by an asset</note>, which by common law belong to the husband for sustaining the **burdens of marriage**, as reported from the *Digest, on the law of dowries, law "plerunque"* and found in the *Siete Partidas, Part 4, Title 11, Law 21*. Read what was said on this matter in Disputation 7.

<margin>6</margin> When unvalued things that consist of **weight, number, or measure** <note>fungible goods like grain, wine, or coined money</note> are given to the husband as dowry, then **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> is seen to be transferred entirely to the husband, in the same way we say it is transferred when valued things are given to him by an appraisal that constitutes a **sale**. In this case, the risk of those items pertains to the husband, not to the wife. However, when the marriage is dissolved, the husband or his heir is bound to restore to the wife or her heirs an equal amount of the same **kind** <note>original: "speciei"; referring to the logical category of the item</note> and quality, regardless of whether the things are worth more or less than they were at the time they were given to the husband as dowry. Thus, if by consent of the parties they are to be restored by price, they must be paid at the price they are found to be worth at the time of restoration, the dissolution of the marriage, and the conclusion of this "loan"; not at the price they were worth at the time the marriage was celebrated when they were handed over as dowry, as **Antonio Gomez** rightly noted at the end of *Law 50 of Toro, number 43*. The reason for all this is that such things are handed over so that the husband can alienate and consume them. Therefore, he takes them at his own risk, just as if he were receiving a **loan of fungible goods** <term>mutuo; a loan where the borrower consumes the goods and returns an equivalent amount later</term>. For this reason, I said above that the ownership of them appears to be transferred entirely to the husband. All these points, together with the reason just given, are expressly found in the *Digest, on the law of dowries, law "res in dotem"* and the *Siete Partidas, Part 4, Title 11, Law 21*. Read **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, a famous Spanish canonist</note>, *Practical Questions, chapter 28, number 6*, where he discusses many things pertaining to this entire dispute.

When all things, or some of them, are given to the husband as a **valued dowry**, a distinction must be made. Either the appraisal was made solely to know their value—so that the husband understands whether a competent dowry is being handed over to him with his wife, or to establish how much the husband must return for them if, at the time the marriage is dissolved, they are found to have perished by his fault or to have been made worse—or the appraisal was made so that from that moment the dowry items are handed over to the husband as if **sold** at that price, so that a specific monetary value is handed over to him as dowry.

<margin>7</margin> In the **first scenario** of this distinction, the risk, loss, and benefit of the things thus handed over as dowry belong to the wife, in the same way that was said regarding

<column-break/>

things that do not consist of weight, number, and measure when handed over without an appraisal. Thus, if they perish without the husband's fault, or are rendered worse, or in the progress of time increase or decrease in quantity or in value, the loss and benefit look to the wife. Therefore, just as the husband is not bound to return the value fixed at the beginning if they decrease in value (unless it was originally agreed that he would pay if they perished by his fault), but satisfies the obligation by returning the items themselves; so too, if they increase in value, he does not satisfy the obligation by returning the value fixed at the beginning, but must return the items themselves, or in their absence, the value they would then have. Indeed, if the things still exist, the wife or her heirs can compel him to return the items themselves, not permitting only their value to be returned. All these points are established by the *Codex, same title, law "cum inter virum"* and from the *Siete Partidas, Part 4, Title 11, Law 19*, and other laws to be cited agree.

<margin>8</margin> In the **second scenario** of the same distinction—namely, when the appraisal constitutes a **purchase** (as is usually the custom for dowries handed over as valued in these Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal)—ownership of the things handed over as dowry passes entirely to the husband. All risk, profit, or loss regarding them pertains to him. When the marriage is dissolved, neither he nor his heirs are compelled to return those things even if they still exist, but only the **price** at which they were valued, just as if he had bought them. Likewise, the wife is not compelled to accept the items back, but can refuse them and demand the price at which they were valued. All these points are clear from the *Codex, on the law of dowries, laws "quoties" and "cum dotem"*; from the *Digest, same title, laws "plerunque" and "cum post," paragraph "in dotem"*; from the *Digest, on the dissolution of marriage, law "æstimatæ"*; and from the *Siete Partidas, Part 4, Title 11, Laws 16 and 18*.

<margin>9</margin> From this **it follows** that if a man bequeaths to his wife any item from those which had been handed over to him as a valued dowry, both the item itself is owed to the wife as a **legacy** <term>legatum; a gift left in a will</term>, and the value at which it was originally appraised is owed as dowry, as the commonly accepted gloss on the *Digest, on legacies 2, law "Lucius Locuta"* affirms.

There are, however, several things to be observed regarding this. **First**: When any item is handed over as a valued dowry, and it is not clear whether the appraisal was intended to effect a **sale** or not, it must be **presumed** that it was made to effect a sale. So affirms the accepted gloss on the *Codex, on the law of dowries, law "si inter virum"*. The *Digest, on leasing, law "cum fundus"* agrees. **Gregorio Lopez** <note>The primary 16th-century commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> concludes the same in his second gloss on the cited *Law 18 of the Siete Partidas*, based on that law itself and other legal authorities; and **Covarruvias**, *Practical Questions, chapter 28, number 1*, and many others affirm this.

<margin>11</margin> **Second**: If an item is handed over as a valued dowry and perishes **before the marriage** has followed, the risk pertains to the wife and not to the husband, notwithstanding the appraisal and the delivery. This is expressly stated in the *Digest, on the law of dowries, law "plerunque," paragraph "si ante"*, and the *Siete Partidas, Part 4, Title 11, Law 18*. **Ulpian** <note>A famous Roman jurist</note>, in the cited law "plerunque," provides this elegant reasoning:

Since the delivery of a dowry, and whatever else occurs in a dowry contract, is understood to be under the **condition** that the marriage follows—for which all these things are ordered, and without which the logic of a dowry cannot remain intact (as was said in Disputation 413)—for that reason, that sale which occurs when dowry items are appraised...

<summary>This page analyzes the legal risks and ownership of dowry assets, distinguishing between unvalued items (where the wife bears the risk) and valued items (where the husband often becomes the owner as if by sale and bears the risk). It also clarifies that dowry contracts are conditional upon the actual occurrence of the marriage.</summary>

# Louis de Molina, On Contracts

...are handed over; it is conditional, provided that the marriage follows. As shown above at the end of Disputation 366, when a sale is conditional, if the sold item perishes before the condition is fulfilled, the loss falls on the seller, and it does not matter that the item was delivered or the price paid. From this, I conclude that if dowry items were delivered with a valuation, and they still exist but the marriage did not take place, the items themselves must be returned, not their monetary value, because the sale was never completed.

<margin>12</margin> Third: When delivered items are valued, and it is clear that the **valuation** <note>original: "æstimationem"</note> was outside the limits of a **fair price** <term>iusti pretii; the standard market value of an item at the time</term>—whether it was valued to the detriment of the wife or the husband—redress is given to either party. The valuation is reduced or raised to the limits of a fair price, even if the deception was not more or less than half of the fair price. This is a special rule regarding dowry agreements, as held in the laws *Iure succursum*, the final section, and *Si res*, the section *Si mulier* in the Digest regarding dowry law, and the law *Si circumscripta* in the Code regarding dissolved marriages; it is most clearly established in Law 16, Title 11, Part 4 <note>Molina is citing the *Siete Partidas*, the famous medieval Spanish legal code</note>.

<margin>13</margin> Fourth: When a marriage is dissolved and no other assets of the husband are found from which the dowry can be sufficiently paid to the wife, then—even if the dowry assets delivered to the husband had been valued at a price that would normally effect a sale—the **ownership** <term>dominium; the full legal right to a property</term> of those assets returns to the wife if they are found among the husband's goods. It is as if they had been delivered to the husband without a valuation. She can claim them as her own property and is preferred over any prior creditors. This is established for the support and favor of the wife when there are no other assets to pay her dowry. This is the interpretation of the law *In rebus* in the Code on dowry law, specifically the words: *whether they are valued or unvalued*. **Arrius Pinellus** and **Antonio Gomez** <note>Influential 16th-century legal commentators</note> affirm this with various glosses and many doctors of law whom they cite.

<margin>14</margin> Fifth: When something delivered as a dowry to a husband is valued at a price that effects a sale, and the item is **evicted** <term>evinceretur; legally recovered from the husband by a third party with a better title</term>, if a prior agreement required the husband to be paid double in place of that item, then that increase which he receives for the lost dowry item must go toward increasing the dowry itself. Upon dissolution of the marriage, he is bound to restore the dowry along with that increase. The reason is that the sale which occurs when a dowry item is delivered with a valuation is not an absolute sale, but one with the added condition that it is for the dowry; for that reason, the increase must be treated as part of the dowry in the same way. This is held in the law *Quoties* in the Digest on dowry law.

<margin>15</margin> Sixth: In those events where it is said that a dowry item delivered with a valuation effects a purchase and sale, no **tax** <note>original: "gabellam"</note> is owed from that contract, which is called the **alcabala** <note>original: "alcauala"; a significant 16th-century Spanish sales tax, usually 10%</note>. Indeed, by favor of the dowry, it is exempt from that tribute by Law 35, Title 8, Book 9 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish laws</note>. **Lassarte**, in his work on sales taxes, understands this to apply even if a certain quantity of money was promised at the beginning but later paid in valued items, as is commonly done. In truth, those things are delivered into the dowry as valued items and are therefore considered exempt from that tax by the cited law. If, however, after some time had passed since an unvalued item was delivered as a dowry to the husband, it were valued by agreement between the spouses and converted into money,

<column-break/>

which was thereafter considered to be given as a dowry, Lassarte thinks the *alcabala* is owed on that sale. He considers that sale valid, even if it were converted into money from a dowry estate, provided it resulted in a benefit for the wife, following the law *Si constante* and the preceding law in the Digest. **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a major Spanish jurist and bishop</note> disagreed with this, thinking that such an **alienation** <term>alienatio; the transfer of property rights to another</term> made by a wife to her husband is invalid after the dowry has already been established and the marriage contracted—and especially after the property has become an immovable dowry estate. I prefer this opinion of Covarrubias. For after an estate has become part of a dowry, a wife can no more alienate it to her husband than to any stranger. If the husband could first take it for himself by converting it into a monetary valuation with mutual consent, which only the husband would thereafter owe, a dowry estate could always be alienated to any stranger by the consent of both spouses. Regarding the laws Lassarte relies on, it must be said that they speak of a time when a dowry estate could be alienated with the wife's consent; however, that was later revoked by the later law of the *Code*, as we observed in Disputation 428.

<margin>16</margin> Seventh: When a dowry item is given with a valuation, but with the agreement that either the item itself or its value may be paid back at the choice of the wife or her heirs, then any loss that happens pertains to the husband, insofar as if a loss follows, the wife will be able to choose the monetary valuation.

<margin>17</margin> And in this event, the ownership of such a thing seems to remain with the wife, just as if it had been delivered unvalued. The husband cannot alienate that thing, just as he could not alienate it if it were unvalued. However, if the choice belonged to the husband (which happens not only when it is expressed in the agreement, but also when it is simply stated that either the thing or the valuation should be paid, without specifying to whom the choice belongs), then the risk of **deterioration** <note>original: "deteriorationis"</note> would fall on the wife. If, however, the item perished entirely, the husband would be bound to pay the valuation. All these points are held in the law *Plerumque* and the following law in the Digest, and Law 18, Title 11, Part 4. Furthermore, when the choice belongs to the husband, the ownership of that thing passes entirely to him; the husband can alienate that thing no differently than if it had been delivered with a valuation that effected a sale. Note also that an agreement is valid where the husband takes upon himself the risk of an unvalued dowry item, or a valued one that does not effect a sale. Likewise, an agreement is valid that the risk belongs to the wife, even if the husband's negligence occurs, provided it does not occur through the husband's **fraud** <term>dolo; intentional deceit or bad faith</term>.

<margin>18</margin> What has been said about ownership, benefit, or risk of dowry items does not apply when certain people in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> by a contract...

...celebrated the marriage under the dictates of the goods, but only when they celebrated it by a contract of **earnest money and dowry** <note>original: "contractu arrharum, & dotis"; this refers to a traditional dowry arrangement where specific assets are set aside</note>. In a **contract for half of the assets** <note>original: "contractu medietatis bonorum"; a form of community property where spouses share half of all belongings</note>, all things become common to both spouses regarding ownership, risk, and benefit. However, because in that contract the goods do not become common until the marriage is **consummated by intercourse** <note>original: "per copulam sit consummatum"</note>, as stated in Disputation 422 and elsewhere, it follows that the risk for dowry items that occurs before the marriage is consummated belongs to the wife, provided it was not caused by the husband's fault. This is true whether the goods were valued to meet a specific promised dowry amount or not. Consequently, if the marriage is dissolved before its consummation, all losses occurring to the dowry assets without the husband's fault are the responsibility of the wife.

### Regarding the husband's negligence in obtaining the dowry promised to him, and when the person who promised it becomes unable to pay; to what extent the risk belongs to the husband. Likewise, when something given to the husband as a dowry is legally recovered by a third party, to what extent the husband can take legal action.

# DISPUTATION 427.

## SUMMARY

1. To what extent the risk of a promised dowry, not collected through the husband's negligence, falls upon the husband.
2. To what extent a husband can take legal action for the **eviction** <term>evictio; the loss of property to a third party who has a superior legal claim</term> of a dowry item taken from him.
3. Whether the provision of Law 1 in the Code *On Dowry Law* has been corrected today.

<margin>1</margin> **As** for the first of these points, a distinction must be made. If the person promising the dowry was the wife’s father, another ancestor in the male line, or the wife herself, then the risk belongs to the wife. Upon the dissolution of the marriage, the husband is not required to pay that amount to the wife or her heirs.

However, if it was someone else, we must further distinguish. Either they promised it as a gift (*gratuitous title*) for the wife’s benefit, or they were a debtor to her (*onerous title*). If they were a debtor, then whatever is lost in this way is lost to the husband; he is therefore bound to restore it to the wife or her heirs when the marriage ends. But if the person promised it as a gift, then the loss is the wife's, not the husband's. Nevertheless, if the husband was negligent in collecting the dowry from the heirs after the death of the person who promised it (whether a stranger or the father-in-law), then whatever is lost for that reason is the husband's loss. These rules are found in the laws *Si extraneus* in the Digest *On Dowry Law*, combined with *Ob res*, the final section, and *Nesenius* at the beginning. These rules also apply when a marriage is celebrated in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> under a contract for half of the assets; the effect is that the husband, upon dissolution, must restore to the wife or her heirs the half she would have held in those goods in cases where, if the marriage

<column-break/>

had been celebrated by a contract of earnest money and dowry, the risk would have belonged to the husband.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the second point—namely, when a thing given to the husband as a dowry is **evicted** <note>legally reclaimed</note> by a third party—the laws make a distinction. If the item was given with a **valuation** <note>original: "aestimata"</note> that functions as a sale (according to what was said in the previous disputation), then whether the dowry began upon delivery or upon the promise, the husband may sue for eviction. However, if it was given without such a valuation, then if the dowry began with a promise—meaning the whole dowry or that specific item was promised first and delivered later—the husband can also sue for eviction. But if the dowry began only upon delivery, the laws distinguish further: If the item was given in **bad faith** (that is, with the knowledge or suspicion that it belonged to someone else), then the husband can sue for eviction. If it was given in **good faith**, he cannot sue unless it was specifically agreed in a contract that he would be protected against eviction. In that case, the item is lost to the wife, to whom it belonged, and not to the husband. All this is expressly stated in Law 1 of the Code *On Dowry Law* and Law 22, Title 11, Part 4 <note>The *Siete Partidas*</note>, which agree with what we said in Disputation 252.

<margin>3</margin> At this point, note that some claim Law 1 of the Code *On Dowry Law* has been corrected. They argue that even when a dowry of valued items begins with delivery and involves good faith, the husband should still be able to sue for eviction. They say this was updated by the "Single Law" in the Code *On the Wife's Action*, which generally grants husbands a legal action for evicted dowry items. However, it is not sufficiently clear from that law that the earlier law was corrected, as noted by the **glosses** <note>marginal legal commentaries</note> on both laws. Law 22 of the *Siete Partidas* also agrees, maintaining the original rule. Nevertheless, observe that this law arguably *should* be corrected in that regard. Since a husband does not receive a dowry as a mere gift, but for the purpose of supporting the wife and the burdens of marriage, it stands to reason that if the dowry is lost to a third party, he should be granted an action for eviction against the wife or the one who was bound to provide the dowry. At the very least, it should be granted that he is not required to support the wife or hand over a "profit portion" of the estate in proportion to the lost dowry—at least when the wife has other assets from which the dowry could be completed. On this matter, read **Gregorio López** <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> on Law 22. However, in Castile and Portugal, these rules do not apply regarding the basic support of the wife; the dowry need not be "completed" from other assets simply to ensure her maintenance.

However, when a marriage is celebrated in Portugal under the **contract of half of the assets** <note>community property</note>, if any of the things they brought at the beginning is later **legally recovered by a third party** <note>original: "euincatur"; referring to eviction where a true owner proves their title</note>, the person who brought it is required to count it toward their own portion, as if they had held that much debt before the marriage contract, which would later be paid out of the common goods, according to what was said in Disputation 423. Indeed, if they had contracted in **bad faith** <note>original: "mala fide"</note> by not disclosing that the property belonged to someone else, I believe they would be held liable to the other spouse for **compensation for interest** <note>original: "intereße"; a legal term for damages covering both loss and lost profit</note> as well as for the injury inflicted on them in that regard.

### To what extent dotal goods can be alienated or not, especially the dotal estate, and what defines it. If it is legally recovered during the marriage, whether the wife has recourse afterward.

### DISPUTATION 428.

### SUMMARY.

1 *What is called a dotal estate.*
2 *A dotal estate cannot be alienated during marriage, even with the consent of both spouses; and any alienation performed is void.*
3 *Indeed, today it is not enough for the wife to consent again two years after the alienation, even if the husband retains sufficient goods from which he could later pay the wife the price of such an estate. No. 3.*
4 *A husband can reclaim a dotal estate that he himself alienated.*
5 *When a husband is held liable for legal recovery (eviction) and for interest regarding a dotal estate sold by him. And what the Portuguese law says. No. 6.*
7 *What is required for the alienation of a dotal estate performed during marriage to be valid.*
8 *Whether the alienation of a dotal estate performed by the wife with her husband's consent is confirmed if the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death.*
9 *A guarantor given in the alienation of a dotal estate is held liable for legal recovery.*
10 *In which cases the alienation of a dotal estate is valid. Also no. 12.*
11 *If a dotal estate is awarded to another by a court sentence, whether the woman can seek its return after the marriage is dissolved by proving her husband did not defend that estate correctly.*
13 *A husband can manumit (free) a dotal slave against the wife's will if he has the means to pay her the value.*
14 *When the alienation of a movable dotal item, which can be preserved by keeping it, is valid.*
15 *A husband can alienate valued dotal goods consisting of weight, number, and measure against the wife's will. With a declaration, as noted there.*

<margin>1</margin> From the goods given to a husband as a dowry with his wife, any **immovable property** <note>such as land or buildings</note> given to him that has not been valued at a price that would constitute a sale (according to what was said in Disputation 425) is called a **dotal estate** <note>original: "fundus dotalis"</note> in law. This is held in the *Unique Law* of the Code, section *And when the law*, under the word *on the estate* regarding the action for a wife's property.

<column-break/>

Law 1 of the Code regarding dotal estates, and the law *But if the estate* in the Digest regarding dotal estates. And in these latter two legal sources, it is said that when an estimated estate is given such that the choice remains with the wife—whether the valuation or the estate itself should be restored—as far as the woman can choose the latter, it is considered a dotal estate and cannot be sold, as we shall discuss.

<margin>2</margin> Although a dotal estate could formerly be sold by the husband with the wife's consent, today, however, it cannot be sold or subjected to a **mortgage** <note>original: "hypothecæ"; which is a type of alienation in a broad sense, as will be discussed regarding Emphyteusis (long-term leases)</note> while the marriage lasts—neither by the husband with the wife's consent, nor by the wife with the husband's consent, nor by both together. If such a thing is attempted, the contract is **void by law** <note>original: "ipſo iure nullus"</note>, and both the wife and her heirs can reclaim that property once the marriage is dissolved. This is held in the *Unique Law* of the Code and the Institutes.

<margin>3</margin> Nor is it sufficient today for the alienation to be valid if the wife consents to it again two years later, even if the husband has enough property left to pay the price of such a farm to the wife later. Some have wrongly thought this was enacted later in the **Authentica** <note>original: "authentica"; a supplement to the Roman Law Code</note> *Sive a me*. I say this is not sufficient because, as is clear enough from the supplement itself and affirmed by the glosses and the common opinion of the doctors (which Covarruvias follows), that supplement only speaks of immovable property given to a wife by her husband **on account of marriage** <note>original: "propter nuptias"</note>. This type of gift is not in use today in Castile or Portugal, as was stated in Disputation 290; and he does not mean the same for a dotal estate.

<margin>4</margin> It is doubted, however, whether the husband himself can reclaim a dotal estate he sold while the marriage is ongoing. The answer must be in the affirmative; it is no obstacle that he was the one who sold it. This is affirmed by the glosses and the common opinion of the doctors. The reason is that a person can go against their own act when they do so in the name of another person in whose favor the law was granted—as in the case proposed, the husband reclaims the estate he sold in the wife's favor.

<margin>5</margin> When a dotal estate sold in this way is recovered from the possession of the buyer (or anyone else to whom it has passed), a distinction must be made. Either the buyer knew it was dotal when they bought it, or they were ignorant of it. In this latter case, the husband and his heirs are held liable to the buyer for the **legal recovery** <note>eviction</note>, not only for the price but also for **interest** <note>damages</note>, just as a seller of other things bought in good faith is held liable. The woman and her heirs, however, are held liable for nothing to the buyer. In the former case (where the buyer knew), the buyer can only sue for the price paid.

It also outlines the legal rights of the husband and wife to reclaim such property and the liability toward buyers who purchase dotal land in good faith versus bad faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 428 regarding the legal restrictions on selling or transferring (alienating) land that has been given as a dowry. It specifically addresses the roles of consent, the husband's quasi-ownership, and regional variations in Portuguese and Spanish law.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 428.
Gg 2

...the **Authentica** <note>original: "Authenticæ"; a collection of later laws added to the Code of Justinian</note> regarding the property already mentioned in the **Code on Sacred Churches**. Nor does it matter that—as was stated in Disputation 380—when someone buys what they know to be another's, they cannot sue for the price, but lose it: for that is understood when the property was entirely another's. This does not apply to a **dotal estate** <note>landed property given as part of a dowry</note> in relation to the husband, who is in a sense its master while the marriage lasts, as was said in Disputation 425. This is even less applicable when the wife has consented to its transfer. See the laws cited for all these points by **Antonio Gómez** <note>a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> on **Law 50 of Toro**, number 61, and the doctors of law whom he references and follows. 

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
According to **Portuguese law**, however, when someone buys an estate from a man they know to be married without the wife’s consent, they would lose the price paid, unless the wife shared in that price, as held in Book 4, Ordinance Title 6, and as stated in Disputation 422. This ordinance, moreover, applies not only when a couple has celebrated their marriage under a contract for half of the assets, but also when they have celebrated it under a contract of **arras** <note>a bride-price or earnest money given by the husband</note> and dowry.

7. For the transfer of a dotal estate made with the wife's consent during the marriage to be valid, it is not enough if a **ratification** <note>formal confirmation of a previous act</note> by that same wife is added after the marriage is dissolved, unless that ratification followed her having recovered possession of that estate. Indeed, neither the transfer nor the sale of that estate made by the same wife to a third party before she recovers possession would be valid. The reason is that until the dowry is restored to the woman and acquired by her, it still retains the nature and **privileges of a dowry** <note>legal protections that prevent dotal land from being sold to protect the woman's future</note>, and it cannot be transferred. This is gathered from the text of **Law 2 of the Digest on dotal estates**, whose words are: "A dotal estate cannot be transferred as often as the woman has a legal action, or is entirely likely to have one." The same is gathered from the text of the **Constitution**, which says: "A dotal estate is understood to remain such even when the marriage is dissolved." All these things are confirmed by **Antonio Gómez** in the place cited above, number 59, and he asserts this is the common opinion of the doctors. By the very fact that a woman recovers dotal assets once the marriage is dissolved, she can transfer them by her own authority, because they then cease to have the nature and privileges of a dowry. Therefore, if she restores the assets to the person to whom they were transferred after she has recovered them—thereby approving the transfer made during the marriage—that transfer is made valid. Likewise, if the marriage is dissolved by the wife's death and her heirs approve the transfer of the dotal estate made during the marriage, that transfer is made valid, even if the estate had not yet been restored to them; for the prohibition against transferring that estate ceases with the heirs. Thus says **Antonio Gómez**, number 59, at the end.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
8. There is a **doubt** <note>a formal legal question or point of contention</note>: what if the woman herself transfers a dotal estate with her husband’s permission, and afterward the marriage is dissolved by the husband’s death? Will that transfer remain confirmed? The reason for doubting is that, as held in the law "When a man" in the **Digest on Usucaption**, if a dotal estate is transferred during marriage by the husband or with his permission, although the transfer is invalid and can be reclaimed, nevertheless if the marriage is dissolved by the wife's death and the husband succeeds to her goods, it remains confirmed by that fact. This is true whether the person to whom the estate was transferred knew it was dotal or was ignorant of it. Therefore, since the ownership of the dowry passes to the wife with full legal right when the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death,

<column-break/>

it should be judged by the same reasoning to remain confirmed when it was performed by the wife with the husband's consent. The contrary has been affirmed so far due to the arrangement of the law. Thus, regarding the argument, while the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied. The reason for the difference is twofold. First, because the husband, once the marriage is dissolved and the wife’s dowry passes to him, can transfer it before he is put into possession of it—which is denied to the wife. Second, because in that event, the husband was held liable to the buyer for **eviction** <note>original: "euictione"; when a buyer is legally forced to give up property to a third party with better title</note> from that estate, at least regarding the price, and sometimes even regarding interest, as has been said. For these reasons, it was rightly decreed that in the event described by the law cited, that transfer would remain confirmed. However, when it was the woman who transferred the estate with the husband's permission, neither of these two reasons applies: because she is not held liable for the price when she reclaims her own estate, unless she happened to become wealthier from that price in some way beyond her dowry and her other goods, which rarely happens. This is especially true when a couple celebrates a marriage under a contract of **arras** and dowry, particularly under **common law** <note>original: "iure communi"; referring here to the Roman-based legal tradition</note>, according to which profits found beyond the goods the husband and wife brought were not common to both spouses; rather, the wife received only her dowry and **paraphernal goods** <note>original: "bona paraphernalia"; property belonging to the wife outside of her dowry</note>, and the rest belonged to the husband.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
9. But if you ask whether a **guarantor** <note>original: "fideiussor"</note> is held liable for eviction if they intervened when a woman was transferring a dotal estate by the husband's authority, or for a husband transferring with the wife's consent, if the wife later reclaims the dotal estate. **Panormitanus**, **Antonio Gómez**, **Bartolus**, and others respond: Since a guarantor

<margin>Decision</margin>
is not bound more than the person for whom they pledged their faith, and since the wife is not held to the price for eviction, it follows that the guarantor is held to nothing when they pledged their faith for the wife. But when they pledged their faith for the husband, they are held for those things for which it was said the husband is held; however, they are only held when the husband is unable to pay. There are many laws with which the cited Doctors, especially **Antonio Gómez**, confirm these points.

When a **pledge** <note>original: "sponsio"</note> is given as a dowry before the marriage is contracted, it is called a **quasi-dotal estate**: because nothing can have the status of a dowry before marriage. Just as the transfer of a dotal estate is void, so the transfer of a quasi-dotal estate performed by the betrothed man is void. So it is held in the **Julian Law**, in the **Digest on dotal estates**.

10. In certain events, however, the transfer of a dotal estate is valid. The first: when it is done for a **necessary cause**, that is, independently of the will of the husband and wife. For example, if a part of a mill or another estate was given to the husband as dowry, which cannot be conveniently divided into parts, and a partner sues for division and asks that it be sold to whoever offers the highest price: for then, if it is transferred for that reason by a judge compelling it, the transfer is valid. In that event, however, the husband cannot sue for division—even with the wife's consent—by asking that it be divided; but when challenged by a partner, he may consent to the division and the transfer. These things are held in the final law of the **Code on dotal estates**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 428 concerning the "alienation" (the sale or transfer) of dotal property—assets provided as a dowry. It specifically addresses legal disputes where a court awards dotal land to a third party and the rights of the wife to recover that property after the marriage ends.</meta>

-># Luis de Molina on Contracts<-

regarding dotal land. Other examples of the necessary transfer of dotal land are provided in **Law 1 of the Digest under the same title**, where this outcome is generally discussed.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
11 Connected with this outcome is the discussion of the following difficulty. A lawsuit was brought regarding a **dotal estate** <note>landed property given as part of a dowry</note> while the husband was in possession of it, and that land was awarded by the court to another person. The doubt is whether, once the marriage is dissolved and after that matter has already become a **judged case** <note>original: "rem iudicatam"; a final legal judgment that cannot be appealed</note>, the woman will be heard if she wishes to reclaim that land from the hand of the possessor by proving that it was not rightfully withheld and that it belongs to her.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The answer must be given through a distinction. For either the land was awarded to that other person through the **fraud or fault** <note>original: "dolo, aut culpa"</note> of the husband—at least because the husband was negligent in providing witnesses or producing the documents proving the land belonged to the wife, or some other similar way—or it was awarded without any fraud or fault of the husband. In this latter case, the woman will not be heard, but the objection of a **judged case** <note>original: "exceptio rei iudicatæ"</note> will be held against her. Since the husband was not at fault, and for that time he was in his own way the master of that land, or certainly the legitimate administrator of those goods in place of his wife, for that reason the sentence passed against him harms the wife. It creates the exception of a judged case no differently than if it had been passed against the wife’s own **procurator** <note>a legal representative or agent</note>, following the argument in **Law "If a mother," the section "In this law" in the Digest on the exception of a judged case**.

In the former case, however, neither she nor her heirs will be heard against the person to whom the estate was awarded, provided the husband has the means to pay the **damages** <note>original: "interesse"; the financial interest or value lost</note>, or left behind enough property from which it can be sufficiently paid. However, she will be heard against the husband or the husband's heirs. Yet, if the husband does not have, nor did he leave, property from which the wife can be paid the damages resulting from the husband's fault, she will be heard against the person to whom the land was awarded. This follows the argument in **Law "Titius [owed] a hundred," the section "To Titius the son-in-law," the last verse, in the Digest on conditions and demonstrations**, and other laws which **Antonio Gómez** <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> cites in his commentary on **Law 50 of Toro**, number 32, where he teaches all these things along with many others.

<margin>12</margin>
12 The second case in which the transfer of a dotal estate is valid was handed down in Disputation 149. Namely, when the wife, induced by neither fraud nor fear, confirmed that transfer by her command. An exception is made in **Portuguese law**, unless permission is first obtained from the King to confirm that transfer lawfully. But because the things that could be said on this matter were stated at length in that disputation and the two following ones—since many of the points explained there regarding a lawfully confirmed will apply similarly to the matter proposed here—it will not be necessary to say more in this place. This, however, should be observed: in the event that the transfer of a dotal estate would be valid, unless the woman consumed the price solely for her own benefit, but instead (as is commonly done in **Spain**) the husband disposed of it as the administrator of the goods and the family, then upon the dissolution of the marriage, that **valuation** <note>the monetary value of the property</note> is owed to her by the husband or his heirs. This is the view of Antonio Gómez on Law 50 of Toro, number 57; **Gutiérrez** on the law of confirmations, part 1, chapter 1, number 14; and others whom they cite.

Other goods delivered as dowry that were **not valued** <note>original: "non æstimata"; property intended to be returned in its original form rather than as a cash equivalent</note>—provided they are not among those things that consist of weight, number, or measure—can be sold with the wife's consent (at least presumed consent), if

<column-break/>

however, they are sold without her consent, that transfer is invalid. The first part is based on the **Law "Thus while [the marriage] stands"** joined with the following law and the **Law "From the stone-quarries" in the Digest on dotal law**; and **Law "If a woman"** and **Law "When a husband" in the Digest on dotal pacts**. This is affirmed by the **Gloss** on the **Institutes** regarding those who are permitted to alienate, at the beginning of the word "dotal," although it adds: "provided the husband is solvent." And although some of these laws speak of **immovable property** <note>land or buildings</note>, that was according to the old law, which was afterwards revoked regarding immovable property by the law of the **Code** <note>the Code of Justinian</note>. By these same laws, it is established that an estate or another thing can be bought with dotal money with the wife's consent, so that the dotal property remains **unvalued** <note>to be returned in its current form</note> in place of the money, and belongs specifically to the wife's ownership. See **Law "The thing which" in the Digest on dotal law**, and **Law 49, title 5, part 5** <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the Spanish law code</note>. If, however, it was not bought with the wife’s consent so as to be an unvalued dotal thing, it would remain entirely the husband's, as held in **Law "From the money" in the Code on dotal law**. In the alternative, however, when there is nothing else from which the dowry can be paid in full, it would remain the wife's, so that she could claim it as her own; for that reason, she is preferred over any other prior creditor in that matter, as noted in the cited **Gloss on Law "From the money"**, according to **Law "The wife of the husband" in the Digest on donations between husband and wife**. So says Antonio Gómez on Law 50 of Toro, number 36, and **Gregorio López** on Law 49, title 5, part 5, in the second-to-last gloss. The second part of the distinction is gathered from the opposite sense of these same laws and is clear from what has been said so far: because the ownership of those things remains with the wife, and for that reason, if they perish, the loss does not belong to the husband except regarding the use and the **fruits** <note>the profits or produce</note> to be received from them. Therefore, if he sells them without the wife's consent, the transfer is invalid, as it concerns another's property without the true owner's consent.

<margin>13</margin>
13 However, in favor of **liberty** <note>referring to the legal favor shown to manumission</note>, the husband is permitted to **manumit** <note>to legally free</note> a dotal slave, provided the husband has the means to pay the wife her value. This is held in **Law 1 and the last law of the Code on slaves given in pledge and manumitted**. Note, however, the **Gloss on Law "Liberty to all" in the Digest on the rules of law**, with which another **Unique Law, section "And when the law," at the word "to alienate" in the Code on the wife’s action for property** agrees. These are followed by **Bacil.** on the first law of the Digest on dissolving marriage, and Gutiérrez on the law of confirmations, part 1, chapter 1, number 5, who

<margin>14</margin>
14 asserts that if the things are **immovable**, which can be preserved by being kept, the transfer is invalid even with the wife's consent, unless the formality of the **Authentica "If any woman"** <note>original: "Authenticæ si qua mulier"; a law in the Code of Justinian protecting women from being pressured into acting as sureties for their husbands</note> in the **Code on the Velleian Decree** is observed. Namely, that the wife consents again two years after the transfer, that she holds the transfer as rare, and that the husband retains sufficient goods from which the wife can be satisfied. This, however, is not clearly gathered from the cited **Authentica**, which is why other glosses do not teach it very firmly.

<margin>15 <unclear>ūdoci</unclear></margin>
15 Dotal things given into the dowry as **valued** <note>original: "æstimatas"; property given with a fixed price so the husband effectively buys it and owes that sum back</note>—with that valuation which effects a sale—whether they are **movable** <note>personal property</note> or immovable, and likewise things given as valued if they consist of weight, number, or measure, the husband can sell without the wife's consent. The reason is that ownership passes to the husband by full right, as was said in Disputation 42. For these, however, and for other dotal goods, all the husband's property remains **mortgaged** <note>original: "hypothecata"</note> to the wife, as will be said below. Moreover, even things thus transferred by the husband, if they still exist, the woman can claim them, and she will be preferred in them over prior creditors. This was established for the wife's protection in the **Law "In things" in the Code on dotal law**, and is affirmed by Gregorio López on Law 17, title 11, part 4, and many others whom Gutiérrez cites in his work on the law of confirmations, part 1, chapter 1.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
1. Gutierrez <note>referring to Juan Gutiérrez, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> reports and follows this in number 9. If a price is offered to the wife at which the items were valued, the **action to reclaim the property** <note>original: "rei vendicatio"; a legal action where a plaintiff demands the return of a specific physical item</note> ceases. This is because reclaiming the physical property is only granted if the husband's own goods are insufficient to pay the valuation; it is strictly a backup measure if the monetary value is not paid, as Gutierrez adds with many others in number 10. See what was said in Disputation 426. However, regarding **Portuguese Law**, a husband cannot **alienate** <note>sell or transfer ownership of</note> any immovable property <note>land or buildings</note> without the express consent of his wife, even if it was given to him as part of a valued dowry where the property technically becomes the husband's. If he alienates it without the wife’s consent, that transfer is invalid, as held in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 6. The matters discussed regarding this in Disputation 422 apply when the marriage was celebrated with a contract of **earnest money** <note>original: "arrharum"; a down payment or pledge for the marriage</note> and dowry.

### Whether a wife can ever reclaim her dowry from her husband while the marriage is still standing.

### DISPUTATION CCCCXXIX.

1. Under what circumstances a wife can reclaim her dowry from her husband while the marriage is still standing.
2. Whether a wealthy husband who manages property poorly can be forced to return the dowry to his wife.
3. Precise proof is not necessary to show that a husband is verging toward poverty.
4. If a husband provides guarantors for the dowry, can the wife reject them and still demand the dowry itself?
5. If a husband verges toward poverty by some accidental event, can the woman withdraw the dowry?
6. Can a wife withdraw her dowry from the power of a man she knew was poor and a bad manager when she married him?
7. Can a third party who provided the dowry withdraw it, just as a wife does?
8. Should the dowry be returned to the husband if he becomes wealthy again and manages his goods properly?

Regarding this question, it must be said: That a wife regularly cannot reclaim her dowry before the marriage is dissolved, at least through divorce, as is clear from **Law 2 of the Digest on the dissolution of marriage**. However, if the husband verges toward poverty such that the wife's dowry is endangered in his hands, she can reclaim it. This is not so the wife may alienate it, but so that she, or someone else, may manage it for the family; that the family may be supported by its fruits <note>income or produce</note>, or that it may be placed with a merchant for some safe and honest business so the family is sustained by the profit. In this way, the fruits are handed over to the husband to bear the burdens of the marriage, while the substance of the dowry remains whole and safe for the wife. This is held in **Law "If with a dowry"** and **Law "If standing [the marriage]"** in the Digest, and the **Authentic "On the equality of the dowry"** in the Code, as well as the Decretals and **Law 29, Title 11, Partida 4**.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The doubt is: if a husband indeed manages the goods poorly—for example, he consumes them through gambling or manages them badly for some other reason—but the dowry itself is not yet in danger because he has so many assets that, in the judgment of a prudent

<column-break/>

man, no danger yet threatens the dowry,
<margin>Decision</margin>
2. whether the husband can then be forced to restore the dowry to the wife in the manner explained. To this, regardless of what some may say, the answer must be in the negative. Because the intent of the laws in the cited provisions was only to provide for the safety and the danger to the wife’s dowry. In this case, no danger threatens the wife's dowry, and the wife is no better provided for than if the dowry remained with the husband. However, one does not have to wait until the husband squanders all the goods until only the wife's dowry remains; rather, the wife can and should be assisted when the dowry *begins* to be endangered. This is when it is justly and likely feared that the dowry will be lost in the husband's power. To prove that a husband has come to such poverty that the dowry begins to be at risk, exact proof is not necessary. It is sufficient that it is likely, based on the debts he has already contracted, his habits, and his general reputation, considering his status and his goods, as **Bartolus**, **Antonio Gómez**, and others note. The reason is that this concerns the "favor of the dowry" <note>a legal principle that the law should be biased toward protecting dowries</note> and involves only a slight prejudice to the husband—indeed, it is in some part for his benefit, since all the fruits of the dowry are to be handed over to him.

There is then a doubt: What if the husband provides sufficient **guarantors** <note>original: "fideiussores"; third parties who pledge to pay if the husband cannot</note> for the dowry? Is it then the wife's choice to reject them and demand that the dowry be taken out of the husband's power? The common opinion of the interpreters of **Civil Law** <note>Roman Law</note> is that the choice belongs to the wife, and she can reject guarantors at her will. However, the cited **Canon Law** and **Law 29 of the Partidas** clearly imply the opposite: that the wife's danger is sufficiently met by guarantors. Indeed, I approve the opinion of **Panormitanus**: namely, that when a husband offers guarantors, or if those fail, offers to place the assets in **sequestration** <note>escrow</note> in the hands of a third party, it should be committed to the judgment of a wise judge. The judge should see whether the wife's danger is better, or at least sufficiently, addressed that way. If he finds it sufficient, he should admit it; otherwise, he should do everything he judges necessary to ensure the wife's danger is sufficiently addressed. The reason for this is that laws must be judged by their purpose and intent. Therefore, since the cited laws intend nothing other than that the wife's danger be sufficiently addressed, it is certainly not their intent that another remedy be applied against the husband's will unless it is judged absolutely necessary. In this way, the Canon Law and the Partidas, which are later laws, seem to have interpreted the **Imperial [Roman] laws**. And one should stand by the exposition of these laws rather than the exposition of Bartolus and other interpreters of the Roman Law.

<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>A Doubt</margin>
5 There is a further doubt: What if, through no fault or bad management of the husband, but by some accident, he verges toward poverty? Will it then be lawful to withdraw the dowry?
<margin>Decision</margin>
I believe it should be said: if the dowry is then in no more danger with the husband than with someone else, and he will manage it sufficiently in the future, neither exposing it to greater dangers through business than others would, nor consuming more than its income for the support of the family, it cannot be withdrawn from his power, nor is he bound to provide guarantors for...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of when a wife may reclaim her dowry from her husband's administration during the marriage, specifically addressing cases of poverty and mismanagement, before moving on to "paraphernalia"—assets the wife owns outside of her formal dowry.</meta>

its safety. And this is the intent of the cited Castilian law, which denies that the dowry can be extracted from the husband's power in this event. Indeed, it is also the intent of the cited "Authenticum" <note>A collection of Justinian's legal decrees (Novels)</note> (which, as the doctors of law affirm, grants a greater power for extracting the dowry than other older civil laws) while it only allows the extraction when the husband begins to use the assets poorly.

<margin>Question 6</margin>
There is also a doubt whether, if a wife contracted marriage with a man whom she knew to be poor and likely not to be a fit administrator of the assets, she can then extract the dowry from his power.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Bartolus and Panormitanus <note>Influential medieval legal commentators</note> in the cited places, and the doctors generally respond, that she can nonetheless extract the dowry. This is because a woman could not, before the marriage contract, act in a way that would make the condition of the dowry worse. However, the limitation of Antonio Gómez in the cited place along with Salicetus is pleasing: namely, that this does not apply when the husband does not slide toward greater poverty than he was in when the dowry was handed over to him, nor begins to administer it poorly. For as long as these two conditions remain as they were, there is no reason why the dowry should be extracted from him.

<margin>Question 7</margin>
There is likewise a doubt if an outsider gave the dowry for the wife with a pact that, if the marriage is dissolved by the death of the wife without children, the dowry should return to him or to his heirs, whether † in the events in which it is said the wife can extract the dowry, he himself can also extract it.

<margin>Decision</margin>
To this, the common opinion responds in the negative. Because that privilege is only found granted in the law to the wife. Moreover, that outsider only stipulated in the pact that the dowry should return to him upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the wife without children. However, Bartolus in the cited place, Antonio Gómez in number 34, and the common opinion of the doctors affirm that he is nonetheless entitled to the remedy of the law in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de iud." referring to the Roman law section 'On Judgments'</note>. Specifically, that guarantors <note>original: "fideiussores"</note> be given to him for security regarding the full restitution of the dowry in that event.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
Finally, there is a doubt if a husband, after the dowry was taken from him, becomes wealthy and now administers his own assets rightly, whether † the right to the dowry ought to be restored to him.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Bartolus and the common opinion deny this, which Antonio Gómez follows in part in number 35. To me, however, the contrary seems far more probable. Indeed, by the very nature of the matter, the dowry is owed to the husband regarding its administration, use, and fruits, for sustaining the burdens of marriage, which he in fact sustains. And since the impediment because of which he was deprived of the administration has ceased, it ought therefore to be restored to him: for when the cause ceases, the effect should also cease. Especially since the reason for the marriage continues, for which the contrary effect was granted to him and is owed. Nor is it merely that the husband being deprived of the administration of the dowry is a loss of security for the wife's dowry, as Bartolus’s foundation assumes, but at the same time it involves an injustice, that he should now be deprived of the administration owed to him without a legitimate cause. I add that such deprivation now does little or nothing for the greater security of the dowry.

When spouses in the Kingdom of Portugal have celebrated a marriage under the custom of "half-property" <note>original: "medietatis bonorum"; a system where assets are shared equally</note>, I do not see the wife being helped when the husband slides toward poverty because of improper administration of assets, unless he were so much of a spendthrift <note>original: "prodigus"</note> that a curator <note>a court-appointed guardian for assets</note> ought to be appointed for him, and the administration of his assets should be taken from him and handed over to the wife, or to someone else, according to those things which are in Book 1 of the Ordinances, Title 67,

<column-break/>

disposed: and as was said in part in Disputations 200 and following. But if in any other event the wife were to be helped, it would be necessary to obtain this from the King. This covers the wife’s dowry while the marriage is standing. Whether, however, she loses it after adultery, will be discussed in Treatise 3. Regarding the dowry after the marriage is dissolved, there will be a discussion below.

# On the wife’s paraphernalia goods, and other things pertaining to her capital.

## DISPUTATION CCCCXXX.

->SUMMARY<-

1. *What paraphernalia goods are, and where they get their name.*
2. *Whether, and when, the ownership of paraphernalia goods belongs to the husband.*
*And what of the law of Castile and Portugal.*
3. *Which assets can also be counted among paraphernalia goods.*
4. *Things given to both spouses at the time of the nuptials by outsiders become common property.*
*The same also applies during the marriage.*
*The same also in things given by blood relatives to both of them.*
5. *Things given to the spouses by the blood relatives of the husband or groom become the husband's, unless the contrary is proved regarding the intent.*
*The same in things given by the blood relatives of the wife, so that they become the wife's own, unless the contrary is proved.*
6. *Things given to the groom by the groom's blood relatives at the time of the betrothal: whose they become, even by the law of Portugal and Castile.*
*And what conversely if it is given to the wife by the husband's blood relatives. number 7.*
8. *Things given to the groom or bride by the father or mother become their own.*

1 **B**eyond the dowry, all "paraphernalia" goods belong to the wife's capital <note>original: "capitale vxoris"</note>. These include all her other assets, so called in Greek from *para*, which is "beside," and *phernia*, which is as if to say "goods beside the dowry," or "outside the dowry." Therefore, whatever other goods, besides the dowry, belonged to the wife at the time the marriage was celebrated, or will come to her in the progress of time, are called her paraphernalia goods, and they belong to her capital along with the dowry. So it is held in Law 17, Title 11, Part 4, and all the doctors of law agree.

2 When, however, assets of this kind were handed over to the husband having been valued at a price that would effect a sale, or were assets that consisted of weight, number, or measure, and were handed over to the husband so that he might consume them—as they are customarily handed over today—the ownership would belong to the husband; otherwise, it would belong to the wife, as was similarly said above regarding dotal goods, and the reasoning is the same in both cases. But always, when they are handed over to the husband for administration, as they are customarily handed over in Castile and Portugal, the wife has a **tacit mortgage** <note>a legal claim or lien that exists automatically by law without a written contract</note> for such goods upon all the husband's assets. So it is held in the last law of the Code, "On agreed pacts," and Law 17 cited above.

3 Along with the paraphernalia goods and the wife's capital, we can calculate whatever the wife acquires through

through the nuptial generosity bestowed upon her by the husband, according to what was said in Disputation 290. And those things which are given to her by the husband after the marriage has been celebrated, in those instances where it is valid or confirmed, are treated as a gift between husband and wife according to what was explained in Disputation 289. To these two cited disputations, add the following conclusions:

<margin>4</margin> **First.** Whatever is given to both spouses at the same time by friends and strangers <note>original: "extraneis"; meaning those outside the immediate family unit</note> at the † time of the wedding or betrothal—that is, by those who are not blood relatives of the spouses—becomes the common property of both. It is to be divided between them just like assets gained during the marriage <term>bona superlucrata: assets acquired through labor or investment during the marriage, rather than through inheritance</term>. Say the same of things given to both in a similar way while the marriage is ongoing. This is affirmed by Antonio Gómez in his commentary on the Law of Toro, and matches the Civil Law regarding joint debtors and the *Partidas* <note>The "Siete Partidas," a famous 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>. I would say the same if the gifts were given by those who were blood relatives to both spouses simultaneously.

<margin>5</margin> **Second.** Whatever is given to such spouses together by the blood relatives † of the husband or groom becomes the property of the husband. This is because the gift is presumed to be made to him unless the contrary is clear regarding the intent of the donors. This is the opinion of Antonio Gómez, Julius Clarus, Gutierrez, and others whom they cite. In a similar way, I believe that if a gift is made to both together by the blood relatives of the wife, it becomes the property of the wife alone. This is because the gift is similarly seen as being made to the wife; Julius Clarus seems to agree, and Gutierrez affirms it.

<margin>6</margin> **Third.** If something is given by the † blood relatives of the groom at the time of the betrothal (which in Portugal is before the marriage is contracted by "vows of present consent" <note>original: "per verba de praesenti"; these are vows that make a marriage legally binding immediately, as opposed to "vows of the future" which are just a promise to marry later</note>, and in Castile even after such a contract, but before it is consummated by physical union, according to the explanations in Disputation 290), Antonio Gómez says it is considered a gift from those relatives to the groom, and from the groom to the bride. Therefore, it belongs to the bride in the same way as other wedding gifts made to her by the groom. And in those events discussed there—where there was no kiss or the marriage was not completed—just as other wedding gifts return to the groom, he affirms these do as well. However, Gutierrez more correctly affirms with others that, universally, these are not considered to be made by the groom to the bride. For that reason, they always remain with the husband unless the donors expressed that they were giving only to the bride, or the groom similarly expressed that he wished to grant them to her as a wedding gift.

<margin>7</margin> **Fourth.** Those things † which the husband's blood relatives give to the wife—in Portugal after the marriage is completed by vows of present consent, and in Castile after consummation—are considered given to the husband by his own relatives. Antonio Gómez adds, however, that they are then considered given by the husband to the wife. For that reason, they should be judged just like other gifts given by a husband to a wife (known as "gifts between husband and wife"), and such a gift is confirmed or can be revoked just like others between spouses, according to Disputation 289. But Gutierrez affirms the contrary: namely, that the husband is not presumed to give them to the wife unless he expresses this sufficiently, and therefore those assets belong to the husband alone.

However, when it is sufficiently established through circumstantial evidence

<column-break/>

that the intent of the donors was to give to the wife—for instance, if the gift was made to her by the husband’s relatives because of services she provided to one of them during an illness, or for some other specific reason—the gift would belong primarily to the wife. But if those services were performed using communal resources <note>original: "de communibus bonis"</note>, or if the benefit was considered to be bestowed by both spouses, then whatever was given would be common to both. It would not matter if, for the sake of politeness or honor, the gift was sent specifically to the wife.

<margin>8</margin> **Fifth.** Those things † which the father or mother of the groom give to the bride, whether before the consummation of the marriage or after, are considered given to the groom, as stated in the third and fourth conclusions. For that reason, the groom is bound to bring those items into "collation" <term>collation: the legal requirement for an heir to account for gifts received during the parents' lifetime so that the total inheritance is shared fairly among all siblings</term> with his other brothers, just like other assets given to him on account of the marriage. This is affirmed by Antonio Gómez and was stated above in Disputation 238.

## Concerning the wife’s arras.
# DISPUTATION 431.
### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *What the arras for contracting a marriage are, and whether they differ from others.*
<margin>2</margin> *Who might lose the arras.*
<margin>3</margin> *Why arras are granted in marriage, and why they are prohibited as a penalty.*
<margin>4</margin> *What the marriage arras are in Castile and Portugal.*
<margin>5</margin> *For what reason marriage arras are promised.*
<margin>6</margin> *Marriage arras and pre-nuptial gifts differ.*
<margin>7</margin> *Whether marriage arras can be established or increased after the marriage is contracted, and when.*
<margin>8</margin> *Whether a woman entering a second marriage can dispose of the arras to the prejudice of the children of the first marriage, and in which cases.*
<margin>9</margin> *Whether the husband's assets should be appraised regarding the arras promised by the husband, and how; and what of the wife's entailed estate given as a dowry.*
<margin>10</margin> *If a promised dowry is not paid to the husband, is he bound to pay the arras to the wife or her heirs when the marriage is dissolved?*
<margin>11</margin> *In Portugal, should marriage arras be paid from the husband’s entire estate, or only from the third part that belongs to him, if he has descendants or ancestors?*
<margin>11</margin> <note>Note: numbering error in original; appears twice</note> *If one promises arras beyond a tenth part of his assets according to Castilian law, or beyond a third according to Portuguese law, and confirms it with an oath, is he bound by the power of the oath to fulfill the promise?*

**The Arras** <note>original: "Arrhae"; a traditional gift of coins or assets pledged by the groom to the bride as security</note> which are today promised by husbands to wives according to the custom of the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, are something quite different from the *arrhae* that were formerly in use and of which the ancient laws speak. For indeed, the † *arrhae* discussed in those laws were what was handed over as a pledge <note>original: "pignus"</note> when an agreement was made for a future marriage, serving as strength and security that the marriage would indeed be celebrated. This is evident from the Code of Justinian and is affirmed in the *Partidas* and by the legal commentators.

# Ludouicus Molina on Contracts

The chapter "Gemma" concerning betrothals <note>original: "capit. gemma de ſponſalibus"</note>, and the Teachers who are cited and followed—such as Covarruvias in his *Summary*, chapter 3, section 7, number 6; Antonio Gómez on Law 50 of Toro, number 12; and Aluarus Valafchus in *Consultation* 2, number 1—discuss these matters. These **earnest monies** <term>arrhae: a deposit or "pledge" given to confirm a contract, which is forfeited if the giver backs out</term> were not unlike those used in contracts of buying and selling, or other similar agreements, to ensure that the work would be completed (as discussed in Disputation 338). Therefore, once the marriage was celebrated, these pledges were returned to the person who gave them. If the groom or bride passed away before the marriage could be celebrated, they were similarly returned to the giver, unless that person was at fault or responsible for the delay of the marriage.

<margin>2</margin> For the one whose fault prevents the marriage from being celebrated always loses the pledge, as seen in the cited laws. If the failure lies with the one who received the pledges, they must return them plus an equal amount <note>i.e., double the original value</note>, unless they are a minor, in which case they simply return what was given. If the receiver was a father or another ancestor of one of the betrothed, and he was the reason the marriage did not take place without a just cause (either a new reason arising or one he just discovered), he was formerly required to return them **fourfold**. Today, however, he must return **double**, unless it was expressly agreed that he would return three or four times the amount; in that case, the contract must be upheld. These points are established by the final law in the Code regarding betrothals, as affirmed by the doctors cited by Aluarus Valafchus and Antonio Gómez. 

However, if a groom or bride enters a religious order <note>original: "ad religionē tranſeant"; becoming a monk or nun</note> and the marriage is not celebrated for that reason, they do not lose the pledge they gave, nor are they required to return double what they received. This is held in the law *Deo nobis* and the chapter *ex publico* concerning the conversion of spouses. Although a penalty <note>original: "pœna"</note> is prohibited from being attached to a betrothal to force someone into marriage—and such a penalty is legally void—all legal experts agree that the use of a pledge is valid. It is neither invalid nor forbidden for the person responsible for the failure of the marriage to lose their pledge or return it double.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the reason † why one (the pledge) is permitted rather than the other (the penalty), the experts do not agree. Some, followed by Covarruvias and Antonio Gómez, argue that a penalty is usually promised by word alone and might be agreed to too easily or without mature reflection. A pledge, however, involves the physical delivery of goods or money, which usually involves more careful consideration. Aluarus Valafchus rejects this reasoning; he argues that the same concern—not restricting the freedom to marry—applies to both. He suggests another reason: a pledge is given as a sign and security for a completed act, whereas a penalty is not for security but to coerce the parties into the wedding. I believe, however, that both are used to ensure the parties stand by their agreement to marry. Neither one removes the freedom to marry any less than the other; in fact, if one restricts freedom more, it is the pledge rather than the penalty (if both are of equal value). A person is more likely to be driven to celebrate a wedding they otherwise wouldn't by the fear of

<column-break/>

losing a pledge already handed over—which the receiver already possesses—than by the fear of a stipulated penalty that might never be collected and which would require a difficult lawsuit to extract. 

Therefore, I believe that while both would have force under natural law alone, positive law <term>ius positivum: man-made laws enacted by a government or church</term> removed the power of the penalty but not the pledge because a penalty is easier to promise in much larger amounts, leading to greater lawsuits later. This is the reason intended by the doctors whom Aluarus Valafchus criticizes. Pledges in this specific sense <note>as earnest money to ensure a wedding happens</note> are not in use in Spain.

<margin>4</margin> However, the **arras** <term>arrhae: in Hispanic law, this refers to a gift from the husband to the wife rather than earnest money</term> which are today promised by husbands to wives by the custom of Castile and Portugal, are a type of promise the groom makes to his bride. The woman acquires this right immediately upon the marriage being contracted and consummated through intercourse (as per Law 5, Title 2, Book 3 of the Forum). It is to be paid and delivered along with her dowry when the marriage is dissolved <note>usually by death</note>. This is the view of Covarruvias, Antonio Gómez, and many others cited by Aluarus Valafchus. Laws regarding *arras* in this sense are found in the Laws of Toro (Law 50) and the New Collection of Portugal. Because these pledges are not usually handed to the wife while the marriage lasts, but are a debt owed from the husband’s assets upon dissolution, they are not strictly part of the wife’s "capital" <note>initial dowry</note>. Instead, they are a debt the husband or his heirs must pay the wife (or her heirs) above her original capital. Consequently, the wife can dispose of this debt even if she dies before her husband; if she does not, her heirs inherit it according to the Law of Toro and Portuguese custom.

<margin>5</margin> There is some doubt † as to why these pledges are promised. Aluarus Valafchus says common people believe it is a **reward for virginity**, citing Covarruvias as if he held this opinion because he calls it a "reward for modesty," quoting Juvenal’s *Satire 6*: "Nor is that given for the first night." Valafchus points out that if this were true, it would follow that widows entering second marriages could not be promised *arras*. He and Rodrigo Xuarez rightly mock this opinion and cite the common consensus of Spanish doctors to the contrary—including Antonio Gómez and Gregorio Lopez. Thus, Antonio Gómez defines *arras* as a gift made by the groom to the bride in remuneration for her dowry, her virginity, **or** her nobility. Aluarus Valafchus adds that while the laws do not restrict the gift to any specific cause, modern custom views it as a way for the wife to be wealthier so she may maintain her "widowed honor," as she is presumed to remain in that state. For my part, while I agree the gift should not be restricted to any one cause—the free will of the giver is enough—it is for this reason that in the definition...
