### Second Tractate, Disputation 431

Regarding the definition of marriage pledges <term>arrhae: a settlement or "earnest money" pledged by the husband to the wife</term>, I mentioned no specific cause for them. I believe it is not without merit that Covarruvias is attributed the view that pledges cannot be promised to a widow. However, this is not necessarily gathered from his words. The "reward for modesty" <note>original: "premium pudicitiæ"</note> is a broader category than the "reward for virginity." It applies equally to a widow who gives herself to be known by a husband <note>i.e., enters into a second marriage</note>; and it does not seem that Covarruvias intended otherwise.

<margin>6.</margin>
From what has been said, it is easily apparent that the marriage pledges we are discussing are not the same thing as the "gift on account of marriage" <term>donatio propter nuptias: a Roman law concept where the husband gives property to the wife, often mirroring the dowry</term> mentioned in the laws, which we discussed at the end of Disputation 290. We asserted there that it is not in use today in the Spanish kingdoms, even though Rodrigo Suárez and Joannes Lupus claimed they were the same, led by Law 1, Title 1, Part 4 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish law code</note>. In Spain, the marriage pledges have succeeded in the place of the "gift on account of marriage," as we said there, following the common opinion of the doctors. However, they differ in several ways. The "gift on account of marriage" became the property of the wife throughout the marriage, even though the husband held the profits and administration (it served to help the husband better sustain the burdens of marriage for the wife's benefit). Once the marriage dissolved, it returned entirely to the husband or his heirs. In contrast, the marriage pledge remains with the husband during the marriage; but upon dissolution, it must be paid to the wife or her heirs so that it remains theirs. You may read many other differences and similarities between pledges and gifts on account of marriage in the works of Aluarus Valascus, *Consultation* 2, among others.

<margin>Quest. 7</margin>
The question is whether marriage pledges can be established or increased after the marriage has been contracted. The Spanish doctors—whom Gregorio López refers to in Law 1, Title 11, Part 4 under the word "in Spain," and Aluarus Valascus in *Consultation* 4, number 1—along with Antonio Gómez and Covarruvias, believe they can be established then. They are led by the idea that a gift on account of marriage could be made or increased after the marriage was contracted. Law 1, cited above, explicitly affirms this, saying that pledges are the same as the gift on account of marriage and can be established or increased after the wedding. However, Gregorio López rightly considers this opinion quite doubtful. A pledge is a true gift, through which the wife acquires a perpetual right to the promised property so that it becomes hers and her heirs' upon the dissolution of the marriage. Yet, gifts between a husband and wife are invalid if made after the wedding, unless they are confirmed by the death of the donor and a prior delivery of the property <term>traditio: the formal legal transfer of possession</term>. Aluarus Valascus thinks it is valid in the Kingdom of Castile because of the cited law. However, in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, he considers it invalid and says he has always advised this and seen the courts judge it so. Indeed, I

<margin>Decision</margin>
think it is invalid, even in this Kingdom, for the reason just given, which is most pressing. Furthermore, the cited Law of Castile speaks on the assumption that pledges are the same as the gift on account of marriage, and perhaps refers to a time when there was no difference; it does not refer to the pledges mentioned in later laws and the Laws of Toro <note>A famous set of laws passed in 1505 to clarify the *Siete Partidas*</note>,

<column-break/>

which are in use today, as Covarruvias himself says.

Rodrigo Suárez, whom Gregorio López cites and follows, and with whom Aluarus Valascus expressly agrees, says that the establishment of pledges after the marriage contract is valid without scruple in the event that the husband dies before the wife. He argues that even if we say these are like any other gifts between husband and wife made after the marriage, they are confirmed by the husband's death and thus rendered valid. However, these learned men fail to notice that no delivery <gloss>traditio</gloss> of the pledge is made to the wife before the husband's death. For a gift between husband and wife to be confirmed by the donor's death, it is necessary that the delivery of the gifted item precedes it.

Similarly, the aforementioned authors think the establishment of pledges after marriage is valid when a commoner husband has married a noblewoman. In such a case, out of gratitude or to compensate for her nobility, or because he received a large dowry with her, he might establish or increase the pledges after the wedding. When such reasons exist, many believe it is presumed he established them for that cause, even if not explicitly stated. In Disputation 289, we said that the common opinion of doctors is that any other gift from husband to wife for such a reason is immediately valid and does not need death to confirm it. Although, we noted that Iulius Clarius <note>Giulio Claro, a prominent 16th-century Italian jurist</note> affirms the contrary unless the gift is made at the time the marriage is contracted. If the common opinion is true, the establishment of pledges in that event would also be valid after the marriage. Aluarus Valascus, in approving this, suggests that in these cases, the establishment might be held valid even in the Kingdom of Portugal. But he adds: "I fear that even in these cases, the Portuguese Senate might not admit this." There is nothing in the Portuguese Ordinances that excludes these two scenarios if, by common law, a gift between spouses for those reasons were immediately valid. The same author adds that these reasons are sufficient to obtain a faculty <note>special permission</note> from the King to secure pledges after the marriage has been celebrated.

<margin>8. Quest.</margin>
The question is whether a woman who enters a second marriage while children from the first marriage are still living can dispose of the pledges she received from her first husband as she would her other property. Or is she bound to preserve them entirely for the children of the first marriage? Rodrigo Suárez, followed by Molina and Gutierrez, asserts that such a woman is bound to keep them whole for the children of the first marriage, and they must be divided equally among them. She cannot use them to favor one child over another or to establish an entail <term>maioratum: a legal arrangement (majorat) where property is passed to a single heir, usually the eldest, to keep the estate intact</term>.

The reason, according to all these authors, is that

# 474 Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

A wife who has received anything from her first husband, whether through a gift made during his lifetime or through his last will and testament, is bound—if she enters into a second marriage—to reserve that entire amount specifically for the children of the first marriage. This is established in the law beginning *Feminae* <note>original: "l. fœminæ in prin. C. de secun. nup."; referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 5, Title 9, Law 3, which governs the property of women who remarry</note> and Law 26, Title 13, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Castilian law code</note>. Furthermore, whatever was given to her in consideration of her husband is likewise to be reserved for the children of the first marriage. The ownership <term>dominium: full legal ownership</term> of all these mentioned items does not remain with the wife; she holds only the usufruct <term>usufructus: the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term> for as long as she lives. This is expressly stated in the *Authentica* <note>a later legal update to the Roman Code</note> regarding gifts, found after the law *Feminae*, and in the *Authentica* regarding marriages in the section "If indeed it is expedient." Indeed, by the law *Hac Edictali* <note>referring to the Edictal Law, Code 5.9.6</note> and the cited Law 26, all the property of such a wife—both what she possessed from the moment she received it from or because of her husband, and what she acquires later—is subject to a mortgage <term>hypotheca: a legal lien or security interest</term> to ensure the full restitution of those assets to the children of the first marriage.

Although the cited law *Feminae* permitted a woman entering a second marriage to divide what she had obtained from her first husband among the children of that marriage at her own pleasure, or even to give the whole amount to just one of them, that power was later taken away by the *Authentica Lucrum*. It instead mandated that she must divide it equally among them. For that *Authentica* states:
> This profit shall be distributed equally among the children by law; it is not permitted to be left to the parent’s discretion.
The same is provided in the *Authentica* regarding marriages, in the section "They come," the words of which are:
> For we do not permit parents to exercise an improperly introduced choice <note>original: "electionem"; referring to the choice previously allowed by the law *Feminae*</note>.
The gloss <note>interlinear or marginal commentary by legal scholars</note> on the word "possession" in the law *Feminae* asserts that these same rules must be understood to apply to a man who enters a second marriage. He is likewise bound to reserve for the children of the first marriage whatever he obtained from his wife through the methods explained, and to divide it equally among them. This is expressly sanctioned today in Law 15 of Toro <note>the Laws of Toro (1505) were central to Spanish succession law</note>, which is Law 4, Title 1, Book 5 of the New Compilation, and in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 75, section 3. There, the regulations concerning a woman remarrying—regarding the assets coming from her husband that must be reserved and distributed among the children—are said to be understood similarly for a man remarrying, regarding the assets coming from his first wife. Indeed, this is most clearly established in common law by the law *Si quis prioris* <note>Code 5.9.5</note>, where the husband's property is subject to a mortgage for the children of the first marriage, in the same way it was reported shortly before from the law *Hac Edictali* regarding the wife’s property. The same is held in Law 26, Title 13, Part 5.

These rules were not introduced out of hatred for second marriages, but out of favor for the children of the first marriage, as Alvarus Valascus rightly observes with others. Consequently, they have not been abolished by Canon Law <note>the law of the Church</note>. On all these matters, read among others Alvarus Valascus in the cited consultation, Antonio Gomez on Law 1 of Toro, and Molina in the place cited above from number 59. Add this entire doctrine to what we said in Disputations 162 and 163.

<margin>::</margin> Based on this most true and accepted doctrine, Rodrigo Suarez, Molina, and Gutierrez (in the places cited above) maintain that a woman who enters a second marriage, while children of the first marriage are still living, is bound to reserve 

<column-break/>

for them the marriage pledges <term>arrhae: earnest money or property pledged by the husband to the wife at the time of marriage</term> which she received from their father. These must be divided equally among them, whether by will or by intestacy <note>dying without a will</note>. Nor can that woman use those assets to establish a majorat <term>maioratum: an entailed estate that passes to a single heir, usually the eldest son, to keep the family fortune intact</term> or favor any one of those children over the others.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Alvarus Valascus, in the cited consultation number 6, affirms the contrary along with Joannes Lupus. Namely, that such a woman is *not* bound to reserve those marriage pledges for the children of the first marriage, but may dispose of them just as she does her other property. Consequently, she can use the "third" of those assets in Portugal, or the "third and fifth" <note>the "tercio y quinto" were portions of an estate that a parent could freely give to one heir to "improve" their share under Spanish law</note> in Castile, to establish a majorat or to favor any of her children. She could even leave it to a complete stranger (except for the "third" in Castile), just as she can do with the third or the fifth of the rest of her assets. Alvarus Valascus notes that he has always advised this. The reasoning is: because the law *Feminae*, which introduces this reservation, and which the cited *Authenticae* presuppose, only speaks of assets acquired from a first husband by "lucrative title" <note>i.e., as a pure gift or profit</note>. This is what the cited laws clearly sound like, and the authors of the contrary opinion do not deny it. Marriage pledges (*arrhae*), however, are acquired from the first husband not by lucrative title, but by "onerous title" <note>i.e., a contract involving exchange or obligation</note>. This is because they are considered given in compensation for the dowry, for her virginity, etc. Furthermore, he says that things acquired from a husband by a "remuneratory gift" <note>a gift given to reward a specific service or merit</note> are not considered to be included in the law *Feminae*, as he teaches from certain doctors. Certainly, this opinion seems probable enough to me: especially because today in Spain, marriage pledges are not usually established as a free gift, but are drawn into the agreement as an onerous contract. Neither the wife nor those acting on her behalf are willing to agree unless a certain amount of pledges is promised to her.

I believe the same should be said regarding the "daily bed" <note>original: "lecto quotidiano"</note> usually given to widows in Castile, which they call the *cama viudal* <note>the "widow's bed," a legal right for a widow to keep the household furniture and bed</note>. For it is not given as a gift, but as a debt prescribed by law. However, a woman loses this if she enters a second marriage. But if you object regarding the pledges citing Law 52 of Toro (which is Law 4, Title 2, Book 5 of the New Compilation), it stipulates that if betrothal gifts <term>sponsalitia largitas: gifts given during the engagement period</term> preceded and pledges were also promised, then upon the dissolution of the marriage, the wife or her heirs can choose within twenty days only one of the two, whichever they prefer. After those days, the choice passes to the husband or his heirs. Now, the law *Feminae* and the cited *Authenticae* apply to betrothal gifts because they are true gifts proceeding from the man to the woman; therefore, they should also apply to the marriage pledges.

If you object in this way, I reply: granted the major and minor premises—when betrothal gifts are not taken in place of marriage pledges—the conclusion must be denied. This is because marriage pledges are not a simple gift in the way that betrothal gifts are. When, in this Kingdom, marriage pledges are left aside and the betrothal gift is chosen instead, then the cited laws would not apply to the betrothal gift regarding the precise value that corresponds to the pledges. For in that case, regarding that value, it would have the legal force of marriage pledges in the matter proposed, and not that of a betrothal gift. For that law intended, in that part, to provide a remedy for the "blind love" by which husbands are accustomed to despoil themselves of their goods by giving them...

It highlights a debate on whether "arrhae" (marriage pledges) should be treated as restricted gifts or as earned assets that the spouse can freely control.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the legal restrictions on marriage gifts, specifically focusing on the "arrhae" (marriage pledges) and how they are calculated in the kingdoms of Castile and Portugal when an entailed estate is involved.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 43.

...regarding wives in the matter of marriage pledges and bridal gifts, just as the laws by which marriage pledges are limited in Castile and Portugal—laws which we shall discuss shortly—aimed to remedy that same loss. Finally, I should mention that Alvaro Valasco, in the cited consultation number 9, affirms he learned from elder senators and most experienced advocates that the decision of the law *Feminæ* <note>Latin: *l. fœminæ*; a reference to the Roman Code regarding the reservation of profits for children of a first marriage</note> regarding the reservation of profits for children of a prior marriage is not observed by the custom of the Kingdom of Portugal.

<margin>9</margin>
Regarding the marriage pledges <term>arrhas; a gift of property or money pledged by a husband to his wife as security for her future</term> which a woman received from her husband, and from whom children remained to her: Rodericus Xuarez (following Gomez Arias) similarly considers that a wife who does not proceed to a second marriage, but remains in perpetual widowhood, is bound to reserve three-quarters of those pledges for her husband's children. He argues she cannot use those portions to establish an entail <term>maioratum; a form of inheritance where property is kept together and passed to a single heir, usually the eldest son</term> or favor one child over the others, but they must be divided equally among them according to the cited "Authentica" <note>A reference to the *Authentica Lucrum*, a decree regulating inheritance</note>. However, regarding the remaining fourth part, she may do as she wishes, including establishing an entail or favoring whichever child she chooses. These authors are guided by Law 1, Title 2, Book 3 of the *Fuero* <note>Local Spanish laws</note>, which establishes that such a woman in this event may only dispose of a fourth part of the pledges for the sake of her soul, but is bound to reserve three parts for the husband's children; these same authors believe these parts must be divided equally among them.

Molina (Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, Chapter 10, number 64), Alvaro Valasco, Gutierrez, and others affirm the opposite: namely, that she can dispose of the marriage pledges just as she does her other goods, including establishing an entail or favoring any of the children she wishes. The reason is that the laws of the Code and the

<margin>10</margin>
Authentica only speak of a wife who passes to a second marriage, not of one who remains in perpetual widowhood. Furthermore, that law of the *Fuero* has not been received into use regarding that part; in the Kingdom of Castile, the laws of the *Fuero* do not have force unless they are received by use, and this must be proven for a judgment to be made according to them. See what was said in Dispute 289.

It should be observed that, by the law of this Kingdom of Castile, the marriage pledges <note>original: *arrhas*</note> must not exceed the tenth part <note>A "tithe" of the groom's wealth</note> of the groom's assets, after first deducting all debt and calculating everything owed to the groom and what he possesses in good faith. If they exceed this, they are invalid regarding the excess, as held in Law 1, Title 2, Book 5 of the *New Collection*. It is added there that a man cannot renounce this law, and even if he does renounce it, the law must nevertheless be upheld. A notary <note>original: *tabellio*</note> who records in any instrument that a renunciation of this law was made loses his office; if he uses it thereafter, he is punished as a forger. We also said a little earlier that if the groom makes any bridal gifts, the wife or her heirs in this Kingdom must choose to receive either the marriage pledges or the bridal gifts alone.

In the Kingdom of Portugal, however, these cannot exceed a third part of the value of the wife’s dowry; if they exceed it, they are invalid regarding the excess. Likewise, if the husband had children or other descendants from a prior wife, and they (or any of them) are surviving at the time the marriage pledges are to be paid upon the dissolution of the later marriage, such pledges cannot exceed a third part of those assets of the husband

<column-break/>

which he possessed when he promised those pledges; this is so they do not prejudice the children or descendants from such a prior marriage regarding the excess. This is held in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 9, Paragraph 11.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
Concerning these matters, it is asked: If in this Kingdom a husband who promised marriage pledges held an entail <note>original: *maioratum*</note>, should the goods of the entail be appraised, and in what way, to determine if the promised pledges exceed the tenth part of the husband’s assets? Similarly, it is asked if a wife in Portugal brings an entail as her dowry, should the goods of the entail be appraised, and how, to determine if the pledges exceed the third part of the value of the wife’s dowry?

<margin>Decision 1</margin>
Indeed, all agree that they must be appraised according to how much the income of those goods is estimated to be worth for the life of the one possessing the entail. Alvaro Valasco and many others whom he and the cited doctors mention, assert that they should be appraised according to the rule of the law *Hereditatum* <note>A Roman law from the Digest regarding the valuation of a life interest or usufruct</note> provided for appraising a bequeathed usufruct <term>usufructus; the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property belonging to another</term> so that the Falcidian portion <term>lex Falcidia; a Roman law requiring that at least one-quarter of an estate go to the legal heir</term> may be deducted from it. Gutierrez (following the gloss of Accursius and Bartolus on that law) considers that the calculation fixed in that law is to be understood such that, if the person holding the life interest is later found to have lived fewer years, the amount over-deducted from the Falcidian estimation should be returned; but if they are found to have lived longer, the increase should be deducted.

And so, in the matter proposed, Gutierrez wants this: if in this Kingdom a wife dies before her husband, the value of all the income of the entail perceived in all those years from the start of the marriage must be calculated, deducting the expenses for collecting them. The marriage pledges would then be valid up to a tenth part of that total value, as far as the husband’s entailed goods are concerned. However, Covarruvias and others rightly reject this; they believe the appraisal of the law *Hereditatum* should be understood to hold regardless of what the eventual outcome proves. Molina (Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, Chapter 10, from number 39), although he thinks it probable in this case that the appraisal of the law *Hereditatum* should be followed, says with Covarruvias and many others that it should only be understood for the purpose of deducting the Falcidian portion from legacies, not for this and other similar effects.

And so, with Covarruvias and most others, he judges that the value of the entailed goods for the entire life of the possessor should be appraised by the judgment of a prudent person, considering the age, health, and other circumstances of the possessor. This would be done in the same way a life annuity of some annual income would be appraised for the life of that person—an opinion from which Gutierrez does not dissent above. Molina says the income of such an entail should be appraised at a ratio of eight to one; thus, if an entail yields two thousand ducats annually after expenses, it would be valued at sixteen thousand ducats for the total life of the possessor. From this, he could validly promise marriage pledges of one thousand six hundred ducats, which is a tenth part of sixteen thousand.

Gutierrez, however, says those incomes should be appraised at a ratio of seven to one, according to the pragmatic decree of Castile, because a life annuity is appraised and sold in that manner.

<summary>This page analyzes the legal limits on "arrhae" (marriage pledges) in Castile and Portugal, specifically how to calculate these limits when the groom's wealth is tied up in an entailed estate (maioratum). It concludes that the value should be based on a professional appraisal of the possessor's life interest, often using a 7:1 or 8:1 ratio of annual income.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

(Column 1)

We have stated in Dispute 188 that it is irrational and unjust to set an equal price for all life annuities <term>vitalitiis; a financial arrangement providing annual income for life</term> of equal annual returns. Instead, the value and price must be assessed according to the age and health of the person for whose life the annuity is granted, as well as other concurrent circumstances. We hold the same view in assessing the value of an entailed estate <term>maioratus; a property that stays within a family, usually inherited by the eldest son</term> based on the life of the person currently possessing it. This is done to understand how much can be permitted as marriage pledges <term>arrharum; a gift of property or money pledged by a husband to his wife as security for her future</term> in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, regardless of how things turn out later. Indeed, in both Kingdoms, the items promised as pledges must be established according to the value of either the husband's property or the wife's dowry, whatever may later happen to their assets, as is clear from the laws of those same kingdoms cited above.

<margin>Doubt 10</margin>
The doubt † is whether, if the dowry <term>dos; the property or money brought by a bride to her husband at marriage</term> promised to the husband is not paid to him, he is bound to pay the marriage pledges to the wife or her heirs upon the dissolution of the marriage. To this, Alvaro Valasco (Consultation 3) and Gama (Decision 370, no. 2) respond, along with others they cite, that the husband is only bound to pay them in the same proportion in which the dowry was paid. Thus, if nothing of the dowry was paid, he is bound to pay nothing of the pledges; if a third or fourth part of the dowry was paid, only a third or fourth part of the pledges must be paid, and so on for other proportional parts of the pledges and dowry. The aforementioned authors report that it has been judged this way in Portugal. This is proven first because the Portuguese law cited above only permits marriage pledges up to a third of the dowry which the wife "brought"; however, a wife is not considered to have "brought" that part of the dowry which was promised but not actually paid.

Furthermore, because marriage pledges are given as a compensation for the dowry, equity does not allow that a person who fails to keep their promise and agreement regarding the dowry should have the promise and agreement regarding the pledges upheld, since the latter is supported by the promise of the former. This is confirmed by a significant legal text <note>original: "authentica sed quæ. C. de pact. conuen." referring to a section of the Code of Justinian</note> which holds that a wife who provided nothing of the recorded dowry ought to receive nothing from the husband's gift upon his death; and she who gave less than she promised should receive a profit only in proportion to the amount provided. This discussion concerns the agreement to gain a pre-marriage gift upon the husband's death. Although marriage pledges differ from pre-marriage gifts, they do not differ much when there is an agreement to gain them through the husband’s death; thus, the argument from a similarity of reasoning holds in this case.

Therefore, Alvaro Valasco does not correctly weaken the argument from that text which Gama and others rightfully use. The same is confirmed by the law <note>original: "l. pollicitationes. C. de don. ante nuptias"</note> which states that a woman who deceived her husband regarding the dowry cannot seek from the husband a gift made in contemplation of the marriage. Valasco admits this text is convincing if the woman deceitfully promised a larger dowry than she intended to pay. However, Gama rightly affirms above that the full pledges are owed when the husband waived the part of the dowry that was to be paid, since what is waived is considered as paid. Valasco also affirms the full pledges are owed when the dowry was not paid simply because the time prescribed for its payment had not yet arrived when the marriage was dissolved; he notes that in such an event, he prevailed in a certain case where the full pledges had to be paid.

<margin>Doubt 11</margin>
The doubt is whether in Portugal marriage pledges should be paid...

<column-break/>

(Column 2)

...from the husband's entire estate, or only from the "third" <term>tertio; the portion of an estate (usually one-third) that a person could freely bequeath, as opposed to the "legal portion" reserved for heirs</term> which belongs to him, if he has descendants or ancestors. Gama (Decision 308, no. 14, and Decision 370, final number) asserts they must be paid only from the third. However, I believe a distinction must be made. If the marriage pledges were promised in a first marriage, they must be paid from the whole estate, whether they exceed a third of the husband's goods or not, as is clearly established from the Fourth Book of the Ordinances (Title 9, last paragraph), provided they do not exceed a third of the wife's dowry; for then they would be invalid regarding the excess, as has been said. And such pledges, in comparison to the husband's goods, are to be calculated alongside the husband's debts to others; once these are deducted, the remaining goods are considered his property, from which he has the "third" he can freely dispose of. The other two parts belong to the "legal portions" <note>original: "legitimas"; the shares of an estate that cannot be legally denied to direct heirs</note> due in his goods to his descendants or ancestors.

If, however, the marriage pledges were promised in a later marriage while descendants of that man from a previous marriage were still living, then in that event the Portuguese Ordinances (in the last paragraph cited) intended that the man could only promise them from the third of his goods which he had at the time of such a promise. He cannot promise them from the two remaining parts, which already at that time belong to the descendants of the first marriage. Therefore, the pledge should not exceed that third, and must be paid only from it, rather than from the entire mass of goods the man then possessed. This is surely the only thing the Portuguese Ordinances intend and clearly state.

<margin>Question 12</margin>
Finally, the doubt is: if someone in Castile promises marriage pledges beyond a tenth part of their goods, or in Portugal beyond a third part of the wife's dowry, and confirms the promise with an oath, is he bound by the power of the oath to fulfill the promise? Regarding Portugal, it is easily seen from the things said in Dispute 149 that not only does an oath fail to create an obligation to fulfill the excess, but the entire promise is null by law unless a legal provision for Royal permission is included. Alvaro Valasco (Consultation 26, second to last number) says he thinks the King would not grant permission for an excess to be promised, because every noble would then ask for the same thing; if it were not granted, they would think an injustice was being done to them by denying them what was granted to another. Regarding the law of Castile, however, Palacios Rubias, Segura, and certain others followed by Antonio Gomez affirm that from such an oath arises an obligation to pay the excess. The reason is that although the matter is otherwise legally null, it is not an evil thing. In the Kingdom of Castile, as seen in Dispute 149, although a contract or promise to which an oath is attached may be null, an exception is made when the contract or promise is rendered valid by the oath, as happens in the case proposed. Also expressly excepted are promises of pledges and dowry, to which it is permitted in this Kingdom to attach an oath, as shown in the cited dispute. However, the more common opinion of the learned doctors, which among others Covarruvias and Gutierrez cite and follow...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, moving toward a discussion of the common legal opinion on oaths and pledges.</meta>

# Second Treatise. Dispute 432.

...confirmed by oath (Part 1, chapter 14, number 2 and *On Practical Questions*, book 2, question 19), even if it is confirmed by an oath, it is invalid regarding the excess amount.

Covarrubias is led to this first because Law 1, Title 2, Book 3 of the *Fuero* <note>original: "l. 1. fori. ti. 2. lib. 3." referring to the *Fuero Real*, a 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> renders a promise of marriage pledges <term>arrharum; property pledged by a husband to a wife</term> void if it exceeds a tenth part of the husband's goods, even if confirmed by an oath. However, that does not apply in that specific law, but only that no excess is rendered if it is given; likewise, nothing is rendered if a "pleito" <note>original: "pleito," here meaning a formal agreement or contract</note> is made concerning its delivery. He is led to this secondly because this was enacted not so much for the benefit of the one making the promise, but for the benefit of the next of kin, to whom the law grants the right to reclaim the excess from the place of the giver after it has been paid.

I believe, however, that this was enacted primarily for the benefit of the giver, although, so that the sanction might have greater force, the right of recovery is granted to the closest blood relatives. Some are also led to a third point: that the law prohibits an increase from being given; for it states:
<margin>he cannot give more pledges to his wife than a tenth <note>original Spanish: "no pueda dar mas arras d su mugier del diezmo"</note></margin>
An oath, however, has no power to make something happen that is prohibited by even positive human law, as was explained in Dispute 149. Certainly, I do not doubt that this is not a prohibition in the sense that one sins by promising or paying an increase, but the meaning is "he cannot give" in such a way that it is done validly; hence it immediately follows: "And if he should give her more, or make an agreement regarding it, it shall not be valid." <note>original: "Et si mas le diere, o pleito sobre ello hiziere, no uala"</note> It is in this sense that it is said "he cannot give more," just as we are accustomed to say a wife cannot alienate dotal land, and a minor cannot alienate immovable property without a judge's decree—because, clearly, it would be done invalidly. Yet, if they confirm the alienation with an oath, it becomes valid, as everyone concedes and as was shown in the cited Dispute 149. Therefore, I strongly incline toward the former opinion, so long as in this Kingdom a promise of that excess is not more clearly rendered null, even if confirmed by an oath.

I should, however, advise that the law which allows an oath to be attached to a promise of marriage pledges is to be understood as applying when the pledges are promised within the limits prescribed by law. Furthermore, a notary <term>tabellio; a public official authorized to draw up legal documents</term> who certifies a renunciation of the law of the *Fuero*, even if the renunciation is confirmed by an oath, will fall under the penalties imposed by Law 50 of Toro. <note>The Laws of Toro (1505) were a landmark set of Spanish laws regulating succession and marriage.</note>

### Regarding what belongs to the husband from the wife's goods according to Common Law.

### DISPUTE 432.

->**SUMMARY**<-

1 *Which goods are those that belong to the husband from the wife's property.*
2 *What things are necessary for the fruits of the dowry to belong to the husband (also numbers 5 and 6).*
3 *When the fruits of the dowry and of the wife's other goods go toward their own increase.*
4 *Whether the fruits of the dowry belong to the husband if he supported the bride before the wedding.*
7 *What is included under the term "fruits of the dowry."*
8 *If the wife's right of use <term>usufructus; the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</term> is given to the husband as a dowry, what else is considered given.*
9 *When the offspring of a female slave <term>ancillae partus</term> belongs to the husband and when to the wife.*
10 *A husband cannot donate the fruits of the dowry to his wife to the extent that she would be made wealthier by them.*
11 *From which day of the year and time the calculation is made so that the husband may profit from the fruits of the dowry.*

---

**H**aving explained the wife's capital, we must consequently speak of the husband's capital, so that we may further explain which goods in these Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal are called "surplus-earned" <term>superlucrata; assets acquired during the marriage above the initial capital</term>—that is, earned beyond the capital of both, and common to both spouses. It is by comparison to these that a partnership of goods exists between them in these Kingdoms, as was said in Dispute 423. First, however, it must be taught which things belong to the husband from the wife's goods according to Common Law <term>ius commune; the general body of Roman and Canon law used in Europe</term>, so that it may be understood both that there was no partnership of goods between spouses under Common Law, and also the difference in this matter between Common Law and the law of Castile and the custom of the Kingdom of Portugal, as was partially handed down in the cited dispute.

<margin>1</margin>
Regarding Common Law, it was said in the same place that only the fruits <term>fructus; the income, produce, or profit</term> of the dowry <term>dos</term> belonged to the husband from the wife's goods. The fruits of her other goods, however, belonged to the wife herself. Likewise, everything she acquired by her own industry and the labor of her hands belonged to her, after she had provided those services which pertained to her role in the administration of the family. Law 25, Title 11, Part 4, with the gloss on the law "fruits of the dowry" (*ff. de iure dot.*) and Azor, agree across various laws in defining that for the dotal fruit to belong to the husband in that way, three things are necessary.

<margin>2</margin>
The first is that the marriage must already be contracted through "words of the present" <term>per verba de praesenti; a formal legal declaration of marriage that is immediately binding</term>. Otherwise, fruits of the dowry perceived before that point go toward the increase of the dowry and do not belong to the husband. This is held in the law "if before marriage" (*ff. solut. mat.*) and the law "fruits of the dowry" (*ff. de iure dot.*). There it is added that if it was included in a pact that fruits perceived at some time before the marriage should belong to the husband, then they do belong to him.

<margin>3</margin>
The rule that the fruit of the dowry and other goods of the wife goes toward their increase—and thus belongs to the wife's capital—if perceived before the marriage, also holds place in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, provided nothing else was settled in a pact. Just as, in that case, fruits perceived at that time from the husband's capital go toward the increase of the same husband's capital.

<margin>4</margin>
There is a doubt: what if the husband supported the bride before the wedding? Will the fruits then belong to the husband just as if they were perceived after the marriage was celebrated? The final gloss on "before the wedding" cited above raises this question and says the more common opinion, which it follows, is that by the strictness of the law they do not belong to the husband but go toward the increase of the dowry. However, out of a certain equity, they belong to him, since he is then sustaining the burdens of marriage just as if the marriage had been celebrated. And this second view is to be embraced where it has been enacted by municipal law out of equity, as it is reported to have been established in Bologna. This same thing is enacted in Law 28, Title 11, Part 4, and therefore has force in this kingdom, as Gregorio Lopez noted on the same law. Thus it happens that today, if he supports the bride from the dowry and her goods, the groom is considered from that point in this Kingdom to have entered a partnership between groom and bride, and the fruits of the goods...

<summary>This page discusses the legal limitations on marriage pledges (arrhae) and introduces the rules of "Common Law" regarding property rights between spouses, specifically focusing on when a husband is entitled to the income (fructus) generated by his wife's dowry.</summary>
<keywords>marriage pledges, arrhae, dowry, dos, fructus, common law, ius commune, Castile, Portugal, marriage partnership, legal equity, property rights</keywords>

--- Page 539 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights within a marriage, specifically focusing on the conditions under which a husband is entitled to the "fruits" (income or produce) generated by his wife's dowry. It transitions from general requirements to specific cases involving various types of property and compares Roman "Common Law" with the local statutes of Spain (Castile) and Portugal.</meta>

<margin>5</margin> The second necessary [requirement] for the fruits of the dowry to belong to the husband is that the dowry must have been delivered to him. Indeed, the fruits of any dotal property that had not been delivered to him would belong not to him, but to the wife, or to the person who had promised the dowry on the wife's behalf, even if the marriage had been celebrated and the husband was bearing its financial burdens. This is held in the cited Law 25, as well as the law regarding division in the Digest <note>original: "ff. sol. matr." referring to the Digest of Justinian, book on the dissolution of marriage</note>. However, if a pact had been made that the fruits of that period should belong to the husband, then they would belong to him, just as was said regarding the first requirement; for the reasoning is the same in both cases. Furthermore, when such a pact has not been made, the husband could sue for damages if the dotal property were not delivered to him for his enjoyment at the appropriate time, as stated in Dispute 423.

<margin>6</margin> The third [requirement] is that the husband must bear the burdens of marriage, supporting the wife and the family common to both. This usually begins from the day he brings the wife into their common home. However, the fruits that the husband might collect after the dowry is delivered and the marriage celebrated, but during a time when he is not yet bearing the burdens of marriage, would go toward the increase of the dowry itself. This is gathered from the cited Law 25, the law on the fruits of the dowry in the Digest, and the law on burdens in the Code. If, however, a pact had been made that the fruits should belong to the husband for some time before he began to bear the marriage burdens, such a pact should be honored, as was said regarding the other two requirements for the husband to gain the fruits of the dowry; since the reasoning is the same.

<margin>7</margin> Under the name "fruits of the dowry" are also understood the fruits of the wife’s <term>maioratus</term> <note>an entailed estate that descends through a specific line of heirs and cannot be sold</note> if that estate was given as a dowry. This is true even if some of those fruits consist of fines or profits arising from some dignity or jurisdiction of such an estate, even if those penalties are sometimes immovable goods from confiscation due to someone’s crime. This is affirmed by Antonio Gómez (Law 50 of *Toro*, number 33) along with Bartolus and others, based on certain laws he cites, and it is clear enough in itself.

<margin>8</margin> If a wife's <term>usufruct</term> <note>the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> is given to the husband as a dowry, the right of enjoyment itself is considered given as the dowry, unless otherwise expressed; therefore, the fruits collected therefrom during the marriage belong to him. If, however, the marriage is dissolved by the death of the husband, the usufruct reverts to the wife. But if it is dissolved by the death of the wife, it is entirely extinguished and consolidated with the ownership, according to the law on the fruits of the dowry in the Digest. If unappraised slave women and slave men are given in the dowry, then the offspring of the slave women, and anything donated or left to the male or female slaves by a will, would belong to the wife; because these are not counted among "fruits." However, what they might have earned by their own industry and labor, such as by hiring themselves out for gold, would belong to the husband, because these are fruits gained from them. This is held in Law 25 joined with Law 20, Title 11, Part 4, and the unique law in the Code regarding dotal property, which agree with what we said in Disputes 7 and 423.

<margin>9</margin> When, however, the husband takes the entire risk of the slave woman upon himself, then her offspring would belong to him, as held in the cited Laws 20 and 25, and the penultimate law in the Digest on the dissolution of marriage.

<column-break/>

<margin>Antonio Gregorio López, on the cited Law 20 at the words "otherwise the husband" <note>original: "otro si el marido"</note>, observes that by the law of Castile (and I think the same is true by the custom of Portugal), the offspring of slave women do not belong to the wife's capital, but to the "surplus gains" <term>bona superlucrata; property acquired during the marriage through the couple's industry</term>. The same must be said of the offspring of slave women brought by the husband. The reason is that, as held in the last law of the title on gains (Book 5 of the *Ordenamiento*, which is Law 5, Title 19, Book 5 of the *New Collection*), not only do the fruits of the capital belong to both spouses in common, but all their rents as well; for that law states:</margin>

> But the fruits and rents from them, and from all other offices whatsoever, even if they are by right "nearly military" <note>referring to property or income a son might keep separate from his father's estate, here applied to marital property</note>, and the other goods that were gained or improved during the marriage, and the fruits and rents of such military goods, and offices, and gifts—let them both have them in common. <note>original Spanish: "Peroque los fructus y rentas dellos..."</note> Under the name of rents, the offspring of slave women are also understood, as held in the law of Paulus in the Digest on usufruct.

Read what was said concerning this matter in Dispute 188. Gregorio López confirms this, because by the general custom and the laws of this Kingdom, all things acquired from anywhere are shared between the husband and wife, because there is a universal partnership between them in matters of acquisition, according to the Digest on partnerships. And since in this Kingdom the risk of the slave woman, even if she belongs to the wife, pertains in a way to the husband (just as if she were the husband's, the risk pertains in a way to the wife, since she must be compensated from the surplus gains, as will be said in the following dispute), therefore the profits and rents from her must belong to both spouses.

<margin>10</margin> Since the fruits of the dowry belong to the husband by common law, it follows that if the husband, while the marriage was standing, had donated them to the wife, he could reclaim them while he lives; the donation would not be valid insofar as the wife was made wealthier by them. However, if the wife had supported herself and the family from those same fruits, she would not be held to restore what she had consumed with the express or tacit consent of her husband, since she is not considered to have been made wealthier by them. This is held in the law on burdens in the Code regarding the law of dowries, and other laws cited by Antonio Gómez.

Regarding the same common time, when an unappraised dowry was delivered, the fruits of that year in which the marriage was dissolved belonged to the husband or his heirs in proportion to that part of the year in which he sustained the burdens of marriage up until the dissolution, and to the remaining time of that year in which he did not sustain them.

<margin>11</margin> The years, for the purpose of making the fruits his own, were computed from the day on which, after the marriage was celebrated and the dowry delivered, the husband began to bear the burdens of marriage, according to what was said above. Thus, if in the final year, computed from that day, only three months had elapsed until the day the marriage was dissolved, the husband would receive only a fourth part of the fruits or the pension of that year. If four months had elapsed, he would receive a third part, and so on for other proportional parts of that year. The same must be said regarding the part of the first year in which the husband sustained the marriage burdens up to the time when the fruits are gathered or the pension received, according to the proportion of that part of the year to the rest.

<summary>This page outlines the three conditions required for a husband to claim the income from a dowry: the delivery of the assets, the celebration of the marriage, and the actual fulfillment of the husband's duty to support the household. It also highlights the differences between Roman law and Iberian custom, particularly regarding how the offspring of slaves and other "surplus gains" are shared between spouses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the division of marital assets and income (the "fruits"). ...since the time of that same year had not yet passed, the income was divided between the husband and the wife. However, he contributed to the expenses of harvesting that income in proportion to the time he was married, or the expenses were taken out of the income itself, so that the income to be divided between both was only what remained after the expenses were deducted.

And the income was to be divided in that same proportion between them, whether the field bore fruit twice or three times in a year, or once every two years, or more. For the income was divided between the husband and wife in proportion to the part of that entire time in which the husband had sustained the burdens of marriage, relative to the total time period. This is held in the law *divortio* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. soluto matrim." referring to the Roman law on the dissolution of marriage</note>, in the single law, paragraph beginning *cumque ex stipulatu*, at the verse *sed & nouissimi*, according to the commentary there in the Code <note>original: "C. de rei vxor. act."</note>, and Law 26, title 11, part 4.

Today, however, in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, such income is made communal between the spouses if any of it remains after the entire capital of both has been deducted. Indeed, Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note>, at the end of the cited Law 26, correctly observes that if the wife had renounced the common gains—according to what will be discussed later—then the rules of the common law <note>The *Ius Commune*, or Roman law used as a general legal framework.</note> just explained would apply in these Kingdoms. Other matters that could be added regarding these points will be more conveniently discussed in the following sections.

# Concerning the husband's capital. And which goods in Castile and Portugal are called "super-gains," and are common to both spouses.

## ->centered DISPUTE 433.<-

### ->centered *SUMMARY*<-

1 *The husband’s capital: what goods it contains and what belongs to it.*
2 *Wedding gifts also belong to the husband’s capital.*
3 *The right to use a property [usufruct] whose ownership belongs to another: when it belongs to the husband, is it common to both husband and wife, or is it the husband’s separate property?*
4 *Improvements made by the husband to entailed property [maioratus]: is the successor to the entail required to pay the wife or the children of the man who made them?*
5 *If a husband sold his field with a "buy-back" agreement and redeems it during the marriage: does the increase in the field's value belong to the husband alone?*
6 *Property reclaimed by the husband through "blood right" [lineal kinship] during the marriage: does half belong to the wife, or half of the price?*
7 *If one spouse brought something as part of their capital which they began to possess in good faith, but the period for legal ownership [prescription] was completed during the marriage: does it count as communal gain?*
8 *A field purchased during the marriage by one spouse with their own money: to whom does it belong?*
9 *A gift given as a reward: is it the separate property of the person it was given to, as in a simple gift?*
10 *Items sold or consumed from the capital of either spouse: how should they be compensated from the gains?*
11 *The decrease in value of an unappraised item brought by one spouse as part of their capital: should it be repaired from the communal gains?*

<column-break/>

12 *Expenses made by either spouse: when and from what funds should they be deducted?*
13 *Income gathered from the property of both spouses up to the time the marriage is dissolved: in which cases are they made communal, and in which cases not?*
14 *Does a "putative" wife <note>A woman who entered a marriage in good faith that was later found to be legally invalid.</note> acquire half of the gains, just as when a marriage is valid?*

<margin>1</margin>
**T**o the husband's capital belong whatever things were his, or those to which he had a right, up to the moment in which the partnership regarding revenues and gains begins between the husband and wife.

All things also belong to it which come to him over time through a will, or from someone dying without a will, or through a gift. This is held in Laws 1 and 2, title 3, book 3 of the *Fuero*, which are Laws 2 and 3, title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*. Likewise, according to the law of this Kingdom (and I believe the same is true in Portugal), whatever he has acquired in war through his soldier's pay, or by any other means, belongs to the husband's capital, so that they are "military goods" <note>original: "bona castrensia"</note>, according to what was said in Dispute 230: provided that he did not serve at the common expense of himself and his wife. In that case, things acquired in war in that manner belong to the gains common to himself and his wife. This is held in Law 2, title 3, book 3 of the *Fuero*, which is Law 3, title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*.

<margin>2</margin>
To the same husband also belongs anything given to him by the wife as a wedding gift, according to what was said in Dispute 290 and 430 regarding the wife. Likewise, anything given to him by the same wife after the marriage was celebrated—that type of gift called "between husband and wife"—in those instances where such a gift is legally confirmed, according to what was said in Dispute 289 and 430. All other things which are acquired by either the husband or the wife from the point at which the partnership between them begins—which is normally (according to the preceding dispute) after the marriage has been celebrated and the dowry handed over to the husband, when they begin to live together and the husband sustains the burdens of marriage—are called "super-gains" <note>original: "superlucrata," meaning profits or acquisitions made during the marriage</note>, and they are common to both spouses. This is according to Law 1, title 3, book 3 of the *Fuero*, which is Law 2, title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*, in those words, "living together" (that is, inhabiting the same home), "let them both have it halfway."

And this is true not only for all income from the capital of both, even if one brought more capital than the other, as is held in the final law of title 3, book 3 of the *Fuero* (which is Law 4, title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*). This remains true even if the income and revenues are from "military goods," quasi-military goods, or an office belonging to one of them, as held in Law 5, title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*. It also applies to any goods acquired by the industry and labor of either spouse, or newly purchased, and finally to all goods in general that do not belong to the original capital, as is clear from the cited Laws 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of title 9, book 5 of the *New Collection*.

<margin>3</margin>
<margin>Question</margin>
A doubt arises: if the husband, for example, brought a certain property of which the "right of use" [usufruct] belonged to another—either because it had been bequeathed to them, or because they were a long-term tenant [emphyteuta], or for some other reason—and during the marriage that right of use returns to the ownership and is merged with it (either because the user died, or because the time for the lease ended, or for any other cause), is such a right of use then communal...

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

...whether it belongs to the husband and wife, as a thing acquired while the marriage was standing, or whether it is truly the separate property of the husband. In this way, the husband would receive not only the ownership but also the **usufruct** <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another.</note>, and thus the **direct ownership** <term>dominium directum: legal title</term> together with the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile: the right to use the property</term>, upon the dissolution of the marriage, as his own separate capital.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The same doubt exists if the ownership belonged to the wife, and the usufruct was merged with it while the marriage was standing: whether both should belong to her when the marriage is dissolved. Faber, Rodrigo Suárez, and certain others cited by later doctors have asserted that this usufruct—at least in terms of its monetary value—should be divided between the husband and wife upon the dissolution of the marriage as a gain and a thing acquired during the marriage. However, the opposite opinion should be embraced, following Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> in his *Epitome*, part 2, chapter 7; Antonio Gómez in his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 15; Law 50 of Toro; Gregorio López on Law 18; Gutierrez; and others they cite.

The reason is that the usufruct merges with the ownership based on a "prior cause" <note>A legal concept where a new right is seen as stemming from an old one rather than being a brand new acquisition.</note> by right of that very ownership. It is seen as something previously missing from the ownership that now completes it into a full and integrated title. Therefore, just as soil added to a wife's dowry land by **alluvion** <note>Land added to a riverbank by the flow of water.</note> belongs to her (as shown in Dispute 426), and just as any other addition by alluvion belongs to the separate capital of either spouse, so too does a usufruct that is added and merged into the capital of either spouse belong to that spouse alone.

This is confirmed by Law 4 of the Digest <note>original: "l. 4. ff. de iure dot."</note> on the law of dowries, the words of which are: *“If the usufruct is added to the naked property given in a dowry, it is seen as an increase of the dowry, not a different dowry; just as if something had been added by alluvion.”*

This is found in that law and others by which the cited doctors confirm this point. However, observe here that when a dowry is handed over to a husband with a valuation that functions as a sale, then any usufruct added to the wife's dowry would be considered a communal gain, if the property with that usufruct exceeds the valuation at which it was given to the husband. This is because, in that case, the usufruct would not be added to a property that remained the separate property of one of the spouses.

In the reason I gave just before, I deliberately said: "because it is merged based on a prior cause, by right of the ownership itself." For if the usufruct returned to the ownership through a purchase or any other "onerous title" <note>A title acquired for a price or through labor, rather than by gift or inheritance.</note>, then the amount by which the property is worth more than it was before (when there was only a hope of merger) would be considered communal gain. This is no different than how improvements made to the same property at communal expense belong to the communal gains. Regarding the "fruits" harvested from that estate after the usufruct has merged with the ownership—by whatever means it merged—there is no doubt that they belong to the communal gains, as Covarrubias rightly affirms.

<margin>Law of Portugal. 4</margin>
In this Kingdom, however, Law 46 of Toro (which is Law 6, Title 7, Book 5 of the New Collection), states that if a possessor of a **maioratus** <insert>†</insert> <note>An entailed estate that must pass to the next heir, usually the eldest son, and cannot be sold.</note> makes improvements or constructs buildings on the lands of that estate, the successor of the estate is not bound to pay the value of those improvements to the wife or children 

<column-break/>

of the one who made them, even if he made them using the communal gains shared with his wife. Molina <note>The author refers here to his own work, *De Hispanorum Primogeniis*.</note> understands this not only regarding the buildings and improvements expressed in that law, but also regarding any others. However, I do not consider this to be true, because that law is harsh and departs from common law; therefore, it should not be extended further than its specific wording and arrangement, as I shall discuss more fully in the section on entailed estates.

Palacios Rubios <note>A Spanish jurist who helped draft the Laws of Toro in 1505.</note> thinks that this law is not only against ancient prior laws, but also considers it unjust and believes it should be changed. Antonio Gómez and Molina, in the place cited, defend the law as just and equitable. They argue that equity does not allow a successor to an entailed estate—who must leave it to the person designated by the original founder—to be forced to pay for improvements made by his predecessor. Especially since, by that same logic, every successor who paid for them would seek to recover the cost from the next successor, and such recovery would proceed to infinity, which is quite absurd.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Indeed, although I agree that it was rightly established by law that the successor in an entailed estate is not bound to pay for improvements made by a predecessor, I do not see why the "poor wife" and the legitimate children should not be helped. It could be established that a husband could not spend communal funds in that way beyond a **fifth** of his goods, or even a **third** if the successor was to be one of his own descendants. This amount should be taken from his portion of the goods so that the wife remains unharmed and the children’s legal portions remain intact. Otherwise, a man could easily rob his wife of all gains, however large, by using them to increase an entailed estate that is destined for his own blood relatives. We will discuss this more in the section on entailed estates.

Following the doctrine on usufruct (which merges with ownership during a marriage and belongs to the owner), Gregorio López and Gutierrez infer that if a husband <insert>†</insert> sells his property with a **pact of resale** <note>original: "pacto de retrovendendo," a clause allowing the seller to buy the property back later for a set price.</note> and redeems it while married, the increase in the property’s value (insofar as it is worth more than the price paid) belongs to the husband's separate capital. This is because that increase comes from a "prior cause"—namely, the original sale with the freedom to redeem it.

This is confirmed because a property sold with a pact of resale is worth less than one sold absolutely without the burden of a redemption clause. As was seen in the discussion on sales with resale pacts: no equity allows a husband to lose his separate property or share the increase of his estate with his wife just because he sold it with a right of repurchase, perhaps for the benefit of the wife to help support the family.

<margin>Question</margin>
However, if a husband, by "right of blood" <term>ius sanguinis: the right of family members to buy back ancestral land</term> during the marriage, buys back an estate that belonged to his relatives...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 433

<margin>Decision</margin>
6 ...of his ancestors, does only half the price he paid for it belong to the wife, or does half the estate itself belong to her? Avendanio was of the opinion that half the estate also belongs to her. However, Antonio Gómez <note>Law 70 of Toro, number 28</note> and others, whom Gutierrez <note>Question 16, cited at number 3</note> references and follows, affirm the opposite. This is because the **right of redemption** <term>retractus: a legal right to buy back ancestral property sold to a stranger</term> belongs to the husband by reason of his own person and by a privilege of the law specifically granted to him so that he may possess the property of his ancestors. Therefore, the wife does not share in that estate. The same would be true if the wife redeemed property as belonging to her ancestors; for the husband would not participate in that property, but only in the price. Read other laws upon which Antonio Gómez relies and what was said in Disputation 371 on this matter. Note, however: if while the marriage was standing, a portion of some estate had been purchased as a shared expense, and a right of redemption arose by reason of that portion, then, just as that portion would belong to the communal gains, so too would the remainder of the estate obtained through the right of redemption.

<margin>Question</margin>
7 There is a doubt: if one of the spouses brought something as part of their capital which they had begun to possess in good faith, but the **period of prescription** <term>praescriptio: acquiring legal ownership through long-term possession</term> was completed while the marriage was standing, does it belong to the communal gains? Palacios Rubios <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> affirms that it becomes the private property of the spouse who brought it, as it was acquired from a "prior cause" without a new act; although he adds that this matter requires further thought. Covarrubias, however, <note>in his *Epitome*, article 2, chapter 7</note> judges that it becomes the common property of both spouses, since it was obtained through continued possession while the marriage was standing. I, however, am more inclined toward the opinion of Palacios Rubios. Not only because it is acquired from a prior cause, but also because it is "prescribed" as the capital and separate property of that spouse, and thus becomes their own by virtue of the prescription.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Law 11, Title 4, Book 3 of the **Fuero** <note>The *Fuero Real*, a traditional Spanish legal code</note> stipulates that if the estate of one spouse is exchanged for another, then although the "fruits" <note>profits or produce</note> of the estate so exchanged are shared by both spouses, the estate itself stands in place of the one for which it was exchanged, and therefore belongs to the spouse who owned the original estate. Likewise, it stipulates that if the estate of one spouse is sold, and another estate is bought with that money, the estate thus purchased stands in place of the former and belongs to the same spouse, even though the fruits gathered from it are made common to both.

<margin>Question</margin>
8 From this a doubt arises: if an estate is bought while the marriage is standing using money that one spouse brought in at the time of the marriage, does that estate become the property of the one who owned the money? Montalvo, Rodrigo Juárez, and others whom Gutierrez <note>Book 2, question 117</note> cites, affirm this, moved by the provision of the aforementioned Law 11. I, along with the same Gutierrez, find the opposite to be proven. For Law 1, Title 3, Book 3 of the *Fuero* <note>which is Law 2, Title 9, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación*</note> stipulates that whatever is bought while the marriage is standing becomes common to both spouses; nothing is to be exempt from this rule unless it is found to be specifically excepted, and the law does not except this particular outcome.

<margin>Decision</margin>
As stated above, Law 3, joined with Laws 2 and 5 of Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación*, stipulates that things given to either spouse while the marriage is standing are the private property of the one to whom they are given, even if the fruits gathered from them while the marriage stands

<column-break/>

9 are common to both. However, there is a highly controversial question among Spanish doctors whether this should also be understood regarding **remunerative donations** <term>donatio remuneratoria: a gift given as a reward for services rendered</term>. Many deny this, affirming instead that these are common to both spouses, no differently than other things acquired for a price while the marriage stands. Among their number are Rodrigo Juárez, Montalvo, Covarrubias, and Gregorio López, though López adds that if the merits and services exceed the value of the gift, the gift is the separate property of the spouse to whom it was made regarding that excess. Gutierrez follows this same opinion.

<margin>Question</margin>
The opposite—namely, that a remunerative donation becomes the private property of the one to whom it was made—is affirmed by Arias Pinel, Matienzo, and Palacios Rubios. Rubios records that it was so judged in the High Court of Valladolid in the case of a certain Doctor Montalvo, to whom the King had given certain annual rents for life on account of his merits and services. Upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the wife, it was judged that while the rents actually collected during the marriage were common to him and his wife, the **right itself** <note>original: "ius vero ipsum"</note> to those annual rents remained solely the husband's, as a gift to him from the King.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Burgos de Paz the Younger follows the same opinion. I believe that a reconciliation can be made between these doctors' opinions. We must say: if the remunerative donation is of the "first kind" <note>Molina refers to three types of rewards explained in Disputation 292</note>—namely, where services or benefits are compensated so equally that if the gift were not given, it would be an act of ingratitude or even grounds for a lawsuit—then such a gift becomes common to both spouses. This is because it is not a "gift" in the simple sense, but is rather considered to have been acquired by the work and industry of the recipient. Whatever either spouse acquires by their own work and industry while the marriage stands becomes common to both. Also, I believe things given as a recompense for favors and services could become common property. An exception: unless the services were performed in war and were rewarded at a time when the husband was not serving at the common expense of himself and his wife.

Following the first part of this reasoning, I judge that things given or sent to doctors, lawyers, notaries, and others like them, in view of services to be performed (to encourage them to act more promptly or better) or in view of services already performed—even if they were otherwise paid a salary—become the common property of both spouses. This is because all these things are considered "fruits" and "wages" of their services and the practice of their office; thus, they are considered acquired by the work and industry of the recipient. However, the second part of the reasoning is clear from what was said above. Hence I say: if someone served the King at the common expense of himself and his wife, whether in the fleet or in the royal court, and because of such service he is given a gift by the King—such as if he is made the governor of some fortress in the In-
