### Luis de Molina on Contracts

...a grant <note>original: "media," likely referring to the *media anata* or a similar royal grant of office or revenue</note> or something similar, and sells it with the King's consent—as is sometimes done in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>—it seems to me that the price becomes common property for both spouses. It is otherwise, however, if the grant was given due to military service which the spouse performed either on the King's salary or at his own expense (rather than from communal funds); for in that case, the value of that reward, being donated to him for that specific reason, would be his own private property.

Lastly, it must be said that when a prince occasionally gives an extraordinary gift to a minister who serves him, beyond the usual salary—whether the minister himself requested it or the prince offered it, as often happens—then that gift becomes the minister’s own private property. However, if any fruits <term>fructus: income or produce generated by an asset</term> are gathered from that gift while the marriage is standing, they are communal to both spouses. This is what is provided for in the Laws of the New Compilation <note>Book 5, Title 5, Laws 2, 3, etc.</note>. Such were the annual revenues of Doctor Montalvo <note>Alfonso Díaz de Montalvo, a famous 15th-century Spanish jurist</note> granted by the King, which were therefore rightly awarded to him in the High Court of Valladolid <note>original: "Pinciano Praetorio"</note>. When such things are donated, whether they should be judged as private or communal is to be decided by the judgment of a prudent person based on the surrounding circumstances.

Regarding the offspring of female slaves belonging to either spouse, it was stated in the preceding discussions that although they do not belong to the "fruits" of the capital, they nevertheless belong to the communal gains as a form of return and profit perceived from the capital while the marriage was standing.

Regarding the capital of either spouse that has been consumed or sold, the whole amount must be compensated from the gains. For before all else, the full capital must be set aside, and the remainder—after all debts have been paid and the total capital withdrawn—is considered to be the communal gains, to be divided equally between both spouses. This is according to what was said at the end of Disputation 415 and is clear enough in itself; it is also affirmed by Gregorio López <note>on Law 55, Title 5, Partida 5</note> and Antonio Gómez <note>Law 50 of Toro, number 69</note>. From this, it follows that if one spouse brought a slave, a beast of burden, or anything else, and it has died, been consumed, sold, or otherwise alienated, it must be restored from the communal gains.

<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
11 You might ask: if one spouse brought something unappraised <term>inaestimatum: an item not given a fixed cash value at the start of the marriage</term> as part of their capital, and upon the dissolution of the marriage it still exists but has been made worse by use, should that † decrease in value be compensated from the communal gains? I believe that regarding immovable property (real estate), the custom is that it is received back in whatever condition it is found; any increase or decrease belongs to the person who owned it, according to the common law explained previously. An exception is made if the property belonged to the wife and was made worse by the fault or negligence of the husband, who was responsible for the administration; in that case, he would be held to restore the loss to the extent that it happened through his fault, according to what was said in Disputation 413. When the item brought is movable, I have no doubt that in Castile and Portugal, the decrease caused by wear and tear or aging should be compensated from the communal gains, if there are any from which to compensate; otherwise, it must be accepted in the condition it is found. The reason is that in these kingdoms, the partnership entered into between spouses is considered to be for gain alone; and in a partnership, "gain" is only understood

<column-break/>

to be that which remains after the full capital has been deducted and all debts paid. And since equity does not allow movable goods brought by the husband—which were consumed or worn out for the benefit of both spouses and the partnership—to go uncompensated from the common gains, the same applies to unappraised movables brought by the wife. Ordinarily, however, the movable goods a wife brings are handed over to the husband with an appraisal; and it would be wise for the items she brings to be valued from the start of the partnership so that it can be better understood later how much should be restored from the common gains.

12 Expenses † incurred for the preservation of immovable property (real estate) belonging to one of the spouses are not counted against the gains, but rather among the consumption expenses of family administration. However, if something was spent in a legal dispute to defend that property, the spouse whose benefit those expenses served would be responsible for paying it; therefore, it should be extracted from the portion that falls to that spouse upon the dissolution of the marriage. Likewise, if any of that spouse's debts contracted before the marriage were paid while the marriage was standing—or a debt of their parents or another person whom that spouse inherited—the whole amount must be deducted from the portion belonging to that spouse. When something has been improved in a spouse's immovable or movable property through the expenses and industry of the couple, then that improvement—and the increase in value—belongs to the communal gains to be divided between both. Formerly, under common law <note>Roman civil law</note>, if necessary expenses (those without which the thing would perish or worsen) were made on unappraised dotal property <note>dowry</note>, the wife was held to pay them, and the husband could retain the dowry until they were paid. The wife was also liable for "useful" expenses made with her consent (those that made the property better), and similarly, the property could be retained until paid; if they were made without her consent, she was only liable through a legal action for "business managed" <note>actio negotiorum gestorum</note>. As for "voluntary" or luxury expenses—for instance, if the husband had painted the wife’s house of his own accord or done something similar—the wife was not liable. However, the husband could remove what he had added if he could do so without damage to the property, unless the wife wished to pay him the value of what he could have removed. This is found in the Code <note>Code of Justinian, "On the actions of a wife's property"</note> and the Digest <note>Digest, "On expenses made on dotal property"</note>, and the Institutes <note>"On actions"</note>, where the gloss excellently explains what are called necessary, useful, and voluntary expenses. Today, however, in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, whatever improvement is found in such things is calculated among the gains to be divided between both spouses, provided that gains remain after deducting the capital, as was said a little earlier. If, however, no gains remain, but the wife's property is found to be improved in a way that was necessary to the husband's capital, the wife pays the value of that improvement to the husband or his heirs.

13 Fruits † gathered from the property of both spouses up until the time the marriage is dissolved are common to both. Regarding those which are not yet...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of marital property, specifically addressing the division of agricultural produce, livestock, and the burden of proof regarding separate versus communal assets upon the dissolution of a marriage. It then transitions to a new Disputation regarding the wife's legal standing and ownership rights during the marriage.</meta>

...of those perceived <term>percepti: crops or profits that have been physically gathered or collected</term>, a distinction must be made. For if they already appear in the fields, they belong to both spouses in common, and they are to be gathered at their common expense. If, however, they do not yet appear, they belong to that spouse who owned the estate, but that spouse is bound to pay the expenses incurred for those fruits up to that time.

An exception is made for fields where seeds are sown: for if the seeds were committed to the earth at the time the marriage was dissolved—even if they have not yet appeared above the ground—they belong to both spouses in common and are to be gathered at common expense.

But if the seeds were not yet committed to the earth at the time the marriage was dissolved, the field remains his who owns the estate; however, he is bound to pay the expenses, if any were made, in tilling the land.

All these matters are arranged in Law 10, Title 4, Book 3 of the *Fuero Real* <note>original: "fori," referring to the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>, and Antonio Gómez affirms this in his commentary on Law 5 of the *Leyes de Toro*, number 71. Gregorio López agrees in Law 26, Title 11, Part 4, final gloss. Nevertheless, he adds that this does not apply in Córdoba, where the cited Law 4 is not received. The offspring of animals, even if not yet born, are made common to both spouses if they were conceived during the time the marriage was standing, and they are to be gathered at common expense. This is affirmed by the *Glossa Ordinaria* on the cited Law 16, and by Palacios Rubios, who affirms it is practiced this way, as does Antonio Gómez in the place cited above. However, whether these rules similarly hold place in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, although I have consulted learned men experienced in practice, I have been able to find nothing certain.

When a marriage is dissolved, it is the responsibility of each spouse, or their heirs, to prove what goods they brought into the marriage, or which came to them while the marriage was standing; otherwise, they are considered surplus profits <term>superlucrata: assets acquired during the marriage through the industry or investments of the couple</term>, to be divided equally between both spouses. This is held in Law 1, Title 9, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish laws</note>, and is affirmed by Palacios Rubios and Rodrigo Juárez, whom Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in the place cited above, number 70.

Thus, it is sound advice—as the cited doctors affirm—that from the beginning an inventory should be made of those things which each spouse brings, and it should be updated later if anything comes to any of them by hereditary right or for any other reason, after an estimation of the value of each thing has been made—especially if it is a consumable item or one that becomes worse through use.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
Whether, when a marriage was null on account of a hidden impediment, but was nonetheless contracted in good faith on the part of the wife, does the wife acquire half of the profits, just as when the marriage is valid?

<margin>Decision</margin>
The answer must be "yes," in accordance with the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias refers to and follows in his *Epitome*, part 2, chapter 7, section 1, number 7; also Gama, decision 204, number 1 and following; and Antonio Gómez, Law 50 of the *Leyes de Toro*, number 77. The reason is that this partnership was contracted in good faith for the purpose of profit, and therefore, what was thus acquired by the labor and capital of both partners must be divided equally between them according to the laws of the partnership entered into.

This is especially true since children born from such a marriage are legitimate—as was shown when discussing the succession of illegitimate children—and thus regarding the half of the goods acquired by contract, as was stated in Disputation 422.

<column-break/>

# On the ownership and possession of surplus profits: whether they belong to the wife even while the marriage is standing. And how fully the disposal of her half belongs to her when the marriage is dissolved; and when she might lose it.

## DISPUTATION CCCCXXXIV.

-> S U M M A R Y <-

<margin>Question</margin>
1 *The wife immediately acquires ownership and possession of the same surplus profits that the husband himself acquires. However, clarify and understand this as in number 2.*
2 *A husband and wife, even if they pass to second marriages, can freely dispose of the half of the profits acquired in the prior marriage.*
3 *A dowry promised to a daughter or a gift for a son’s marriage while the marriage is standing must be fulfilled from the surplus profits common to the husband and wife.*
4 *A wife can, on account of a crime, lose her own goods, her dowry, or her surplus profits while the marriage is standing. Indeed, a woman remaining a widow and living luxuriously <note>meaning immorally or promiscuously</note> loses the profits gained during the marriage by the industry of her deceased husband, as well as her own acquisitions, and they revert to the husband’s heirs. Number 6.*
5 *And what if she fornicates only once or twice? Does she lose those surplus profits? Number 7.*

---

<margin>Question</margin>
Regarding the first of those things proposed, Castillo (on Law 60 of the *Leyes de Toro*) and certain others, whom the doctors to be cited refer to, had asserted that surplus profits acquired while the marriage is standing belong to the husband alone regarding ownership and possession, and not truly to the wife. This is despite the wife having a right so that, upon dissolution of the marriage, the ownership and possession of half the profits found at that time might be delivered to her. They argue this is an action based on the partnership contracted between them in Castile and Portugal for all profits acquired. They are led by this: that by common law <note>original: "iure communi," likely referring to Roman Law</note>, although when there is a partnership of all goods between some persons, the ownership and even possession of the entire capital and all parts belongs to the individual partners without any delivery of the partiality of ownership and possession—indeed it belongs to all—which are later acquired in the name of the whole partnership, as was shown in Disputation 411. We showed there that the same is to be understood similarly in other particular partnerships when there is a communion in the capital. In these, whatever each of the partners later acquires with the goods of the partnership, by obligating themselves in their own name, belongs to him alone regarding ownership and possession, even if the other partners have a legal action to have their share of the things acquired in that manner delivered to them regarding ownership and property, according to the law *Si quis societatem* in the Digest *Pro socio*; and it was stated there. Hence, Ancharano in a certain counsel felt the same, there being a certain statute that what was acquired should become common to the wife with the husband. Therefore, the cited doctors say, since the laws of these particulars are to be interpreted so as not to depart from common law as far as possible, it must be affirmed that what a husband in this Kingdom acquires by his own industry, obligating himself alone, as if from the goods of both spouses...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding property ownership between spouses, specifically focusing on whether the wife holds actual ownership of gains made during the marriage or merely a right to a future share upon the marriage's dissolution.</meta>

-># Luis de Molina: On Contracts<-

the administrator <note>referring to the husband in his role as the legal manager of the household</note>, he would have acquired it for himself alone as far as ownership and possession are concerned, and not for the wife; nonetheless, he would owe the wife and her heirs half of those gains found once the marriage is dissolved, the ownership and possession of which they would obtain when it is delivered to them, and not before.

<margin>1</margin>
The contrary opinion is today common among the Spanish doctors, namely that in this Kingdom <note>The Kingdom of Castile</note>, by the very fact that the husband acquires ownership and possession of <term>surplus gains: *bona superlucrata*, property acquired through industry or profit during the marriage</term>, the wife also acquires ownership and possession of those same goods without any other delivery being made to her. Therefore, she is the mistress of them together with the husband, just as the husband is master of them together with the wife, even regarding what the wife acquires by her own industry and labor. This is affirmed by Covarruvias (3 *Variar. Resol.* c. 19 n. 2), Antonio Gómez (Law 53 of Toro, n. 76; and Law 60, n. 1), Gregorio López (Law 55, Title 5, Partida 5), Gutiérrez (*De Pract.* qq. lib. 3, q. 118), and others whom they cite. Besides Law 47, Title 28, Partida 3, according to which this must be said by custom in this Kingdom, the same is clearly gathered from Laws 1 and 2 and from the others following in Title 9, Book 5 of the *New Compilation*, which Covarruvias, Gregorio, and Gutiérrez examine at length in the cited places. Regarding Portuguese law, the same is clearly established in Law 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 7, § 1, where it is decreed that if a marriage is dissolved by the death of the husband, the wife remains in possession of the surplus gains, and the husband’s heirs must receive their partition from her. In this regard, the matter is held as if they had celebrated the marriage under a <gloss>contract of half-property</gloss>. It is well known in Portugal that when any are joined in marriage by a contract of half-property, the wife is the mistress of all goods that are not <gloss>entailed</gloss> <note>not tied up in a trust or *mayorazgo*</note>, and she is in possession of them together with her husband.

<margin>2</margin>
Because the wife, as we shall see, can renounce the surplus gains, and by that repudiation behave toward them as if she had never been their mistress, the three cited doctors rightly affirm that her ownership in them before she occupies them is <gloss>revocable</gloss>. This is just like the ownership an heir has in the property of a deceased father immediately upon the father's death, before the heir actually enters upon the inheritance or repudiates it; and just like the ownership a legatee acquires in a specific thing bequeathed to him as soon as the heir enters the inheritance. These are revocable by the repudiation of the inheritance or the legacy, as was said in Disputations 180 and 181.

Because the wife is also a co-owner with the husband of those things acquired while the marriage stands, the free administration and alienation of them—even if they are <term>immovables: real estate or land</term>—belongs to the husband in this Kingdom independently of the wife's consent while the marriage lasts, provided the alienation is not made to defraud the wife. From this it follows that she does not obtain all the effects of ownership regarding those goods until the marriage is dissolved, and then only depending on the fact that they have not been alienated by the husband up to that time. Charles Du Moulin, Covarruvias, Gutiérrez, and others call this the wife having ownership <gloss>in habit but not in act</gloss> <note>original: *in habitu & non in actu*; meaning she has the legal status of owner but cannot exercise the power of an owner until a specific event occurs</note>—namely, a full and unimpeded ownership regarding its effects. From this it also follows that although the wife is a co-owner of those goods, a <gloss>right of retrieval</gloss> <note>original: *retractus*; the right to buy back property sold to a third party</note> does not apply to her if they were alienated by the husband while the marriage stood, as Gregorio

<column-break/>

López rightly affirms in the cited place, and as was said by us and others in Disputation 371. I said a little earlier that the husband in this Kingdom can alienate those goods independently of the wife, even if they are immovables; however, in Portugal he cannot alienate immovable property without the wife’s consent, nor does he have such ample power to alienate other goods as he has in Castile, as we shall see. These things concern the first of the proposed points.

<margin>3</margin>
As for the second point, in Law 14 of Toro, which is Law 6, Title 9, Book 5 of the *New Compilation*, it is sanctioned that both the husband and the wife, once the marriage is dissolved—even if they move on to a second, third, or more marriages—can freely dispose of half of the gains acquired in the prior marriage, just as they can with any other of their goods. Nor are they bound to reserve for the children of the prior marriage either the ownership or the <term>usufruct: the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</term> of that half.

Also, by Law 16 of Toro, which is Law 7 of the cited title, it is further established that if a husband leaves a legacy to his wife, it is not to be counted toward the half of the surplus gains that falls to her, but she ought to obtain that legacy in addition to her half and all her other goods. This was also said by us in Disputation 200.

<margin>4</margin>
A dowry promised to a daughter, or a donation for a marriage made to a son while the marriage stands—even if made by the husband alone—must be fulfilled from the surplus gains common to the husband and wife, as ordered in Law 53 of Toro, which is Law 8 of the cited Title 9, and as said by us in Disputation 424.

To proceed to the third point: in Law 7 of Toro, which is Law 10 of the cited Title 9, it is pronounced that even if a husband or wife loses their property due to the crime of heresy or any other, the other spouse does not thereby lose their own property, nor their half of the surplus gains acquired while the marriage stood; rather, it must be left to them. It is further pronounced that in such an event, the surplus gains are to be divided between the spouses, of which one half pertains to the <term>Treasury: *fiscus*</term> and the other half is to be left to the innocent spouse. This is all to be understood as applying to gains made up to the point of the sentence by which the other spouse is condemned for that crime, even if the crime is such that the penalty is incurred by the law itself <note>original: *ipso iure*</note> or by the very fact <note>original: *ipso facto*</note>.

<margin>5</margin>
Law 78 of Toro, which is Law 11 of the cited title, adds that a wife, while the marriage continues, can lose her property—either entirely or in part, according to the quality of the crime—due to an offense, including her dowry property, surplus gains, or any others. For although they were given to the husband as a dowry for sustaining the burdens of marriage, or were acquired by the husband's industry, insofar as they belong to the wife, she can and ought to be punished through them, just as the husband is in the goods that belong to him. It is no obstacle that this may result in accidental detriment to the other spouse and their common children; for everyone should see whom they marry, and understand that the goods of both spouses are exposed to that danger. It is expedient for the common good that crimes do not go unpunished, which is to be preferred over private benefit or loss, especially when such damage follows only by accident. Furthermore, the fact that the half belonging to the wife is occupied by the Treasury for her crime immediately upon the passing of the sentence—without waiting for the dissolution of the marriage—clearly confirms that she was the mistress of it before the marriage was dissolved.

6 Law 5, Title 9, of the cited work <note>referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a collection of Spanish laws</note> establishes that if a wife, remaining a widow, lives unchastely <note>original: *luxuriose*; in this legal context, it refers to sexual promiscuity or profligacy</note>, she shall lose the <term>surplus gains: *bona superlucrata*, profits acquired through the industry of the deceased husband or her own during the marriage</term>, and they shall revert to the husband's heirs.

<margin>Question 7</margin> However, it is a matter of doubt whether if that widow commits fornication only once or twice, † that is enough for her to lose those surplus gains. Covarrubias, in his *Epitome* (part 2, chapter 7, § 6, number 12), before the final edition, was of the opinion that a single act of fornication was sufficient. Antonio Gómez thinks the same (Law 50 of Toro, final number). And although Law 14 (number 17) affirms the same regarding a widow who "lives unchastely," he nevertheless understands the term "one who lives unchastely" to include her who commits fornication once, as is easily established from what he adds in that same place. However, Emmanuel Acosta (chapter *si pater*, part 1, at the word *legavit*, numbers 33, 38, & <margin>Decision</margin> 39) rightly asserted that although that law is to be understood as referring to a widow who lives unchastely even after the first year of mourning, nevertheless, for her to be judged as living unchastely—and thus to incur that penalty—it is not enough for her to have committed fornication once, twice, or thrice. Instead, it is necessary that she be accustomed to that vice. For she alone is said to live unchastely, based on the argument of the law *& mulieri* (Digest, *de curat. furio.* <note>referring to the Title on curators for the insane and spendthrifts</note>) and the consensus of other legal authorities. Many doctors whom he cites are of this view, among whose number is Arias Pinel (on the final Law, Code, *de bon. mater.*, number 22). Covarrubias later proved in his final Saragossa edition that the cited Law 5 must be understood in this way. Gutiérrez (*De Pract.* qq. book 2, question 122) and others whom he cites embrace the same opinion. I would advise this: that law is penal, as it deprives the widow of goods for that crime—goods of which she had acquired ownership by a just title and which she was possessing. Consequently, that widow is not held to restore those goods to the heirs of the deceased husband except after a sentence has been passed.

->D I S P V T A T I O N CCCCXXXV.<-

->S V M M A R Y<-

1 *The renunciation of future gains made by a wife or husband before the marriage is celebrated is valid, whether it is made in whole or in part.*
2 *The renunciation of future gains made during the marriage in favor of the other spouse is included under the category of a donation between husband and wife, just as it is for gains already acquired.*
3 *Gains to be acquired by spouses; by what gains and contracts they are obtained.*
4 *A new sense and understanding of Law 60 of Toro, Title 9, Book 5 of the New Collection.*
5 *The reduction of a disposition to common law, and when it should be done.*
6 *Whether a renunciation of common gains made by one spouse is valid if the one renouncing has creditors.*

<column-break/>

We must speak in detail about the renunciation made before the marriage is celebrated, during the marriage, and after the marriage is already dissolved.
<margin>1</margin> The doctors agree that a renunciation † of future gains made before the marriage is celebrated is valid, whether it is an absolute renunciation or a partial one. For it is common for a very wealthy man, or a rich and very industrious merchant, to be unwilling to contract marriage with a poor wife unless she either renounces the gains entirely—being content with her dowry and her own goods when the marriage is dissolved, or with a certain fixed amount added to them—or unless she renounces a specific portion of the gains, being content with only a third, fourth, fifth, or some similar part of the gains. In a similar way, a very wealthy wife who has many incomes might be unwilling to contract marriage with a poor man unless, in her favor, he renounces a portion of the gains, being content with a third or fourth part, or another similar portion of them. Since at the time of celebrating such a contract they are not yet husband and wife, that renunciation will not be a "donation between husband and wife" <note>under Roman and Civil law, gifts between spouses were often restricted or revocable to prevent one from impoverishing the other</note>, which would be revoked by the death of the recipient before the donor (that is, the death of the one in whose favor the renunciation was made) or which the one who renounced could revoke at will while still living.

Rather, that shall be considered an <term>onerous contract: a contract involving an exchange of value or mutual obligations</term>, and entirely valid and irrevocable as soon as it is celebrated. For it is the right of anyone arranging to celebrate a marriage with another to refuse to contract with them except under such conditions and laws regarding the partnership of goods and gains that they wish to enter into together. No injustice at all is seen in such a contract, especially since that inequality can be compensated for—namely, on account of nobility, beauty, or some other better condition of the one who is unwilling to celebrate the marriage except under those laws and conditions. Read among others Gutiérrez (*De Pract.* qq. book 2, question 126, at the end of number 1). In number 2, however, following Palacios Rubios (on the chapter *per vestras*, § 6, 3, number 2), he adds that if a renunciation of this kind regarding future gains (or a part of them) is made by only one party before the marriage is celebrated in the presence of a silent daughter, it is invalid; he argues it is necessary for the daughter also to consent for it to be valid. Regarding this matter, I doubt much, since the contract is "onerous" as has been said; it would seem that the silent consent of the daughter suffices, for she ought to have protested if she did not wish to stand by the conditions without which the other was unwilling to contract with her, and who expressly contracted with her only under those conditions.

<margin>Question</margin> Regarding a renunciation made while the marriage is standing, the more common opinion of the doctors is that it is valid and firm, not only if it concerns gains yet to be acquired, but even if it concerns those already acquired—whether some of them or all—especially if it is made by the wife. This is affirmed by Rodrigo Suárez (Law 1, Title 3, *De las ganancias*, Book 3 of the *Fuero*), with Palacios Rubios, Juan López (on the Title *De donat. inter vir. & uxor.*), and with many others whom Covarrubias cites (*Epitome*, part 2, chapter 7, § 1, number 11), Antonio Gómez (Law 50 of Toro, number 66, case 5; Law 60, numbers 1 and 2; volume *Var. Res.*, chapter 4, number 24), and Gutiérrez (*De Pract.* qq. book 2, question 126).

They are led to this primarily because, as we showed at the end of Disputation 128, a donation between husband and wife immediately...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights between spouses, specifically whether a wife can validly renounce her share of the "gains" (profits made during marriage) in favor of her husband while the marriage is still active.</meta>

### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...is valid, if the donor does not become poorer because of it; for as we have proved there by many laws and examples, in similar donations a person is not considered to become poorer by the fact that they do not acquire something to which they had a right that was dependent on their own acceptance. Consequently, this applies when one renounces that right in favor of the other spouse. Therefore, since spouses—especially the wife—while the marriage lasts, only have a right and ownership of half the gains dependent upon their own acceptance (and thus by a <term>legal fiction: *iuris fictio*, a transition where the law treats a situation as true for the sake of justice even if it isn't a physical fact</term>), it is no different than a <term>legatee: someone left a specific item in a will</term>. Just as a legatee is considered by legal fiction to have acquired ownership of a specific thing left to them from the moment of the testator's death once the heir accepts the inheritance—yet this is revocable because it depends on their own acceptance, as seen in Disputation 18—it follows that a renunciation of half the gains (not only those to be acquired in the future but also those already acquired) made by the wife in favor of the husband while the marriage is ongoing is valid, firm, and irrevocable.

<margin>1</margin>
Secondly, because Law 60 of Toro <note>original: *l. 60 Taur.*, a famous set of Spanish laws from 1505</note>, which is Law 9, Title 9, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, states: *When the woman renounces the gains, she shall not be obligated to pay any part of the debts that the husband might have made during the marriage.* <note>original Spanish: "Quando la muger renunciare las ganacias..."</note> Behold, the law leaves it entirely to the wife to renounce the <term>surplus gains: *bona superlucrata*, the profits or assets accumulated during the marriage</term>. And since the law does not restrict this to the time after the marriage is dissolved, neither should we restrict it; it speaks clearly even regarding gains already acquired. Therefore, that renunciation is valid and irrevocable, even if it is made while the marriage is ongoing.

Thirdly, because through such a valid renunciation made by the wife during the marriage, this matter is returned to the terms of <term>Common Law: *ius commune*, the Roman-based legal tradition used across Europe</term>, according to which no gains belonged to the wife. In interpreting the particular laws of Kingdoms, one should lean toward the interpretation that returns the matter to the terms of Common Law rather than the contrary.

<margin>2</margin>
The contrary opinion is embraced by Gregorius Lopez (on Law 5, Title 11, Part 4, final gloss), Menchaca (Book 1, *Controversies*, chapter 13, number 6), and Burgos de Paz (Question 9, civil, number 10). They argue that such a renunciation—not only of acquired gains but also those to be acquired—made in favor of the other spouse, should be numbered among those <term>donations between husband and wife: *donationes inter virum et uxorem*</term> which are not valid unless they are confirmed by the delivery of the gift, followed by the death of the donor before the death of the recipient, without the gift being revoked. And we embraced this opinion in Disputation 289, led chiefly by this reason: that given the law of Castile and the custom of Lusitania <note>Portugal</note>, by the very fact that marriage is celebrated in these Kingdoms with a contract of <term>earnest money: *arrhae*, a traditional marriage payment</term> and dowry, half of the gains is owed to the wife by the power of the contract alone. This is independent of her acceptance; indeed, ownership is acquired as shown in the preceding disputation. For this reason, either spouse transmits this right to their heirs if they depart from this life before the other. Therefore, since a donation (even a release of a debt) made between spouses is invalid unless confirmed by the death of the donor in the manner explained—as is clear in the law *si sponsus*, paragraph *circa venditionem* (Digest, *on donations between husband and wife*) and as Navarro affirms in his *Manual* (chapter 17, number 149)—it follows that such a renunciation is invalid unless confirmed by the death of the donor, and unless it is <term>registered: *insinuetur*, the formal public recording of a large gift</term> if it exceeds the sum that

<column-break/>

one is permitted to give without registration. This is confirmed because, by the disposition of the law of Castile and the custom of Lusitania, the marriage contract we are discussing is truly a partnership regarding the gains found when the marriage is dissolved, with both husband and wife cooperating, as well as the capital of both, toward common gains—even though it includes the burden on the husband's part to preserve the wife's capital intact, and the administration and disposal of the goods is committed to the husband alone for the entire time the marriage lasts. Therefore, the wife acquires the right to the surplus goods and their ownership by the very fact that they are acquired, and they are owed to her by the power of the contract for the time when the contract is dissolved, no less than if she had entered the same contract with some third party. But if the wife had a contract with a third party and, while the marriage was ongoing, she renounced the gains from that contract in favor of her husband or gave them to him (whether already acquired or to be acquired), transferring the right to him so that he might acquire and receive them in her place, that gift would be among those that are not confirmed otherwise than by preceding delivery and the subsequent death of the donating wife before the husband, with the wife having the free power to revoke that gift as long as she lives. Therefore, the same must be said of the renunciation we are now discussing. Secondly, our opinion is proven because if the husband renounces in favor of the wife, not only gains already sought but also those to be sought, it will be a donation of the sort that is only confirmed by the death of the donor; therefore, the same must be said of a renunciation made by the wife in favor of the husband. Covarrubias, in the place cited above, thinks that even a renunciation of gains made by a husband in favor of his wife is immediately valid and firm, and does not need to be confirmed by the donor's death. However, that is clearly false regarding gains already sought, of which the husband has acquired full and complete ownership as to his half, without any legal fiction or dependency on a new acceptance, as is clear enough in itself and denied by no one. Therefore, giving those to his wife would be the same as giving any other of his goods, under the condition that they are not found to be consumed or sold at the time the marriage is dissolved. It is also false regarding gains to be acquired: since they will be acquired by the work and industry of the husband, the wife would not have a right to them by virtue of that gift otherwise than if they were acquired by the husband and ownership of them was gained. See other laws by which Gregorius Lopez confirms the same opinion in the place cited.

But let us turn to the arguments for the other opinion, from the solution of which our own judgment will become more transparent. Regarding the first argument: while both parts of the <term>major premise: the first part of a logical argument</term> are granted, the <term>minor premise: the second part of the argument</term> must be denied—namely, that spouses (especially the wife) only have a right and ownership to half the gains dependent on their own acceptance by a legal fiction. For it has been shown that they have a right to the gains simply, and acquire ownership of them by the power of the partnership contract entered into between them, and that half the gains found at the time the marriage is dissolved is entirely owed to the wife, and this without any legal fiction and not at all dependent on acceptance.

<summary>This page discusses whether a wife's renunciation of marital gains in favor of her husband is immediately valid or treated as a revocable gift. Molina argues that under Spanish and Portuguese law, marriage is a partnership where the wife's right to gains is an immediate contractual right, making her renunciation subject to the standard restrictions on gifts between spouses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from the previous page regarding whether a wife’s ownership of communal gains is a mere legal fiction or a true right, and the implications this has for her ability to renounce those gains to avoid her husband's debts.</meta>

->### Second Tractate, Disputation 435.<-

Hence, the ownership that spouses acquire in their "gains" <note>original: *lucris*, referring to profits or property acquired during the marriage through the industry of either spouse</note> is not like the ownership that is imagined for <term>legatees: people designated to receive specific gifts in a will</term> regarding the thing left to them. In the case of a legatee, ownership is viewed through a <term>legal fiction: *iuris fictio*, a transition where the law treats a situation as true for the sake of justice even if it isn't a physical fact</term> as having been acquired from the time of the testator's death, provided that the heir later accepts the inheritance. If that same legatee does not accept the legacy after the inheritance is opened, they are considered never to have acquired ownership at all; therefore, that ownership, seen as existing before acceptance, was a fiction dating back to the death of the testator by a legal maneuver, as was discussed in Disputation 181.

However, the wife’s ownership regarding her half-share of the gains is far different. Suppose the marriage is already dissolved and the wife has been put in possession of her half of the gains and has used them. If her husband's debts are then revealed and demanded from her, she is granted the power to renounce the half-share of the gains in her own favor and hand them over so that she may be freed from the obligation of the debts. By doing so, she abdicates the *true ownership* of that half-share which she held up to that point. Therefore, before the renunciation, her ownership was not a fiction but a reality. Nevertheless, for the purpose of not being held liable for the debts, she is treated after the renunciation as if she had never been the owner. This is because, by the privilege granted to her, she does not wish to keep those goods, and consequently does not wish to continue their ownership with the burden of being liable for her husband's debts. The following solution will make this even clearer.

Observe, in passing, that the matter is far different for a wife (who, by renouncing the gain, is not liable for her husband’s debts) than it is for an <term>heir: a person who succeeds to the entirety of a deceased person's estate</term> (who, by renouncing the inheritance, is not liable for the debts of the deceased). For a wife can renounce the gains even if she has already taken possession of them and used them as her own. An heir, however, cannot repudiate the inheritance if they have once "intermingled" with it <note>original: *se immiscuit*, a legal term for taking actions that imply acceptance of the estate's responsibilities</note> and accepted it either tacitly or expressly—unless they accepted it with the <term>benefit of inventory: a legal protection where the heir is only liable for debts up to the value of the inherited assets</term>, as was discussed in its proper place.

Regarding the second point, it must be conceded that the law speaks also of a renunciation made while the marriage is still ongoing, and of a renunciation made in relation to creditors, so that she may free herself from the burden of paying the husband’s debts contracted during the partnership of the marriage. This is according to the privilege granted—or rather explained—by the law for her own benefit and utility. And this is clearly the intended sense and mind of that law: it was not as if the law intended to grant the wife a greater power to donate those goods to her husband during the marriage by renunciation (to her own detriment) than she would have had if the law had not been passed. Likewise, the husband, by virtue of the same law, does not have a greater power to donate those same gains to the wife while the marriage lasts than if that law had not been enacted.

Several things must be observed at this point. First: as was said in the response to the first argument, the fact that the wife (either during the marriage or after its dissolution by the husband's death) continues the ownership, possession, and administration of the half-share of the gains that belongs to her—or that the wife’s heirs (after the marriage is dissolved by her death) receive and administer that half-share—does not cause them any prejudice in the meantime. As long as they are not sought out by creditors, or by the husband or his heirs, they are no more liable for the debts contracted by the husband during the marriage than if they had neither administered nor occupied those goods. Rather, it is necessary that they be asked by the aforementioned parties whether they wish to renounce the gains or rather

<column-break/>

to accept them with the burden of paying half of all the debts. After they have been thus notified and requested, a certain time should be established for them by a judge—for instance, ten days—within which they may deliberate. Once this time has passed, if they do not expressly renounce or accept the gains, they are considered to have renounced them if it is to their disadvantage to keep them, based on the argument of the law <note>original: *l. ult. §. sin aut*, referring to the Code of Justinian on the right of deliberation</note> and the commentaries there. This is affirmed by Gutteriez <note>Gutiérrez, a Spanish jurist</note> among others. But if they accept the gains, they are held liable for half the debts. If, however, they once renounce them—even if it is the wife herself who renounced—she is not afterwards admitted to go against that renunciation, even if she has suffered an "enormous loss" or even if she is a minor, as Gutteriez affirms citing Burgos de Paz and others.

The second observation is this: The "gains" we are discussing here truly have the nature of profits when compared to the original capital and the partnership entered into between the spouses, because they are acquired beyond the starting capital. In this sense, following common usage, they are called "gains" in the laws of Castile <note>original: *iuribus Castellae*</note> cited by Gutteriez and by the doctors he cites, in the same way that acquisitions beyond the capital in other partnerships are called the profits of those partnerships. This, however, does not change the fact that they were acquired through the <term>onerous title: a legal basis involving an exchange of value or effort</term> of the partnership contract, the capital, and the industry of both spouses, just as other things acquired in other partnerships are. Therefore, it does not prevent them from being excluded from the category of goods that a spouse must reserve for the children of the first marriage if they enter into a second marriage, as is provided in Law 14 of Toro <note>original: *l. 14 Taur.*</note>. By the name of "goods gained from the first marriage" (which a spouse must reserve for children if they remarry), the law understands what one spouse obtained from the other by <term>lucrative title: a gift or inheritance received without providing anything in exchange</term>, or what the law similarly granted to them from the goods of the other. This is correctly affirmed by Covarrubias and many others whom Gutteriez refers to and follows. Gutteriez also mentions that Arias Pinel denies that these "surplus acquisitions" should be called gains, and consequently argues that if the wife does not accept them, they are not transmitted to her heirs. However, Pinel is speaking of "gain" in the latter sense (as a gift), and he does not clearly affirm that they are not transferred. Whatever he may have felt, it must be affirmed without a doubt that they *are* transferred to the heirs, according to Antonio Gómez and many others. For since the goods and the "actions" (legal rights) of the deceased, both active and passive, pass to the heirs, surely these types of gains—of which the wife had acquired ownership and right through the partnership contract between herself and her husband—pass to her heirs. And they pass with that same privilege of repudiating them that she herself possessed, as the cited doctors affirm. Regarding the transmission of inheritances and legacies, this was discussed in Disputation 180 and 181.

It also clarifies that these rights and the privilege to renounce them are transmissible to the wife's heirs upon her death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of marital property, specifically focusing on Law 60 and Law 61 of the Laws of Toro (1505), which governed the rights of wives in Castile and Portugal regarding "gains" (marital profit) and liability for their husbands' debts.</meta>

### Luis de Molina / On Contracts

<margin>4</margin>
The third point concerns Law 60 of Toro <note>original: "l. 60. Taur."</note>, which is Law 9, Title 9, Book 5 of the *New Compilation* <note>A 1567 collection of Spanish laws</note>. In my judgment, this law did not grant a new privilege to the wife but merely explained what was permitted to her by the nature of the matter regarding gains, assuming other laws—both common and those of the Kingdom—remained in effect. We alluded to this in our response to the second point. Indeed, since according to common law and the law of Castile, a wife’s capital <note>The property or dowry she brought into the marriage</note> must always remain intact for her, protected by <term>hypothecs: legal claims or mortgages on property</term> and privileges that give her priority over her husband's other creditors (as will be discussed later), and since the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal established a "partnership of gains" <note>original: *societas ad lucra*; similar to modern community property</note> between husband and wife beyond that capital, it follows that at the dissolution of the marriage, the wife is only liable to the husband's creditors to the extent of the gains acquired during the marriage. This is conditional on her choosing to participate in those gains according to the contract entered into between her and her husband.

Therefore, if she wishes to abstain from the gains by renouncing them, she shall not be held liable for anything at all to her husband's creditors, provided she did not specifically obligate herself to them. This is precisely what the law we are discussing established and declared. In light of this, I agree with what Gama <note>Antonio da Gama, a prominent Portuguese jurist</note> reports in Decision 366: the high court judges have often ruled that a wife is not held to her husband’s debts from her dowry or her own capital, even if those debts were contracted to feed the wife and the family, provided she renounces the common gains. This holds true even if the husband has no other assets to pay those debts. The reason is that the entire burden of support belonged to the husband in exchange for the <term>fruits: the income or interest generated by a dowry</term> of the wife’s capital. Although Gama protests, asserting that in such an event the debts should be paid from the wife's dowry because they were spent on her and the family's food, I certainly do not agree; he proves this with no solid foundation. Nor do the arguments regarding expenses in other types of partnerships—which suggest expenses should be paid from capital when there are no gains—conclude anything for *this* specific marital partnership through an argument of equal reasoning.

The reason is that this marital partnership exists solely for the common gains, while the wife's capital is always preserved intact, as has been said, with a legal claim and privileges of priority over the husband's other creditors. Nor should one be moved by the authority of Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century legal commentator</note> regarding whether children would be held for a father's debt contracted for their food. Some recent doctors use this to argue that a wife should be held liable if the money was spent on feeding her or the common family. In my judgment, this is significantly refuted by Law 61 of Toro (Law 9, Title 3, Book 5 of the *New Compilation*), which reads as follows:

> *From this point forward, the wife may not obligate herself as a guarantor for her husband, even if it is said and alleged that the debt was converted to the benefit of the wife. And likewise, we command that when a husband and wife obligate themselves jointly <note>original: "a mancamun"</note> in one contract or several, the wife shall not be obligated to anything, unless it is proven that the debt was converted to her specific benefit; and then we command that she be obligated for her share of said benefit. However, if that which was converted to her benefit was in those things that the husband was already obligated to give her, such as clothing, food, and other things*

<column-break/>

> *necessary, we command that for this she shall not be obligated to anything. All of which is said shall be understood unless the said guarantee or joint obligation was for maravedis <note>Spanish currency</note> of our taxes, tributes, or rights.*

Behold: even when the wife obligated herself together with her husband for debts contracted, this law establishes that the wife is not held liable from her own capital for those debts. Although they were contracted for things converted to the wife's benefit, they were only converted regarding things the husband was already bound to provide for her. How much more, then, should the same be judged when the husband alone, without the wife, obligated himself to those debts?

<margin>5</margin>
Regarding the third argument, it must be said that a reduction to the <note>original: "terminos iuris cois"</note> terms of common law <note>The general Roman law used across Europe</note> should only be made when there is no specific local law that demands the opposite. In the matter proposed, there is no contract for a "partnership of gains" between spouses under common law; however, such a contract exists under the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal. As long as this particular law of these Kingdoms persists, equity does not require us to reduce things back to common law terms against those specific statutes.

<margin>6</margin>
From what has been said, we can easily resolve the question: is the † renunciation of common gains made by one spouse valid if the person renouncing has their own creditors? Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a Spanish jurist</note> and others cited by Gutierrez argue that it is valid. They are led by the principle that one is not considered to act in fraud of creditors—and thus creditors are not granted an action to revoke the act—if a debtor simply refuses to accept an inheritance or a legacy offered to them. For although they did not increase their estate (from which they could pay debts), they did not actually diminish it. Gutierrez, however, along with others he cites, asserts that once gains are already acquired and incorporated into the partnership, neither spouse can renounce them in fraud of creditors. This is because all debts contracted during the marriage must be paid from the common gains, even if one spouse yields them to the other. Furthermore, they cannot renounce them to the fraud of their parents or children (to whom a <term>legitime: a mandatory minimum portion of an estate</term> is owed), nor to the fraud of the royal treasury if the spouse's goods are to be confiscated or used to pay a fine. They say, however, that regarding gains *not yet acquired* or incorporated into the partnership, either spouse can validly renounce them in favor of the other, regardless of the detriment to creditors or heirs. I do not see, however, how the first part of this doctrine is consistent with the opinion of the same Gutierrez cited above, where he states that a wife's renunciation of already acquired gains in favor of her husband is immediately valid and firm.

<margin>Question. Decision.</margin>
In accordance with what we have stated above, we must say regarding the proposed question that neither a renunciation of goods already acquired nor of those to be acquired is firm when compared to the rights of creditors or those who have a legal claim to the assets of the person renouncing. The reason is that gains, even those yet to be acquired, are truly "owed" as a half-share to each spouse by reason of the partnership contract entered into between them. As stated above, a renunciation of things owed by reason of a contract is not firm if it brings prejudice to creditors.
->Hence<-

Refer to the law "He who" <note>original: "L. qui aut"; Digest 42.8.6</note> in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the *Pandects* or Digest of Roman Law</note> regarding things done in fraud of creditors. It should be stated that this text does not discuss the renunciation of debts arising from a contract. Indeed, such a renunciation is considered to diminish one's estate and the assets of the person renouncing. Note this: if someone has creditors to whom they owe something, which they could pay by accepting a legacy or an inheritance offered to them, they would commit a mortal sin by renouncing such a legacy or inheritance if that renunciation made them unable to pay their debts. This is an act against justice toward the creditors, even if, in the secular courts <note>original: "foro exteriori"</note>, the creditors are not granted a legal action to obtain those assets that were renounced in this manner.

It remains to speak of the renunciation of communal property—or the portion of it that falls to her and which is in her possession—made by a widow after the marriage has been dissolved. In this matter, there is little or no difficulty. Since she is now entirely her own master <note>original: "sui omnino iuris"; a person with full legal capacity</note>, if the renunciation is made in her own favor—namely, to free herself from the burden of paying debts contracted by her husband while the marriage was standing—it is undoubtedly valid and binding immediately, as stated above. If, however, it is made in favor of another, since it is a gift of assets over which she is now the complete and perfect owner, that gift should be judged in the same way as any other gift made by a widow from her own private property.

# Whether a wife, or her heirs, if they desire half of the gains, are bound to persevere in contracts celebrated by the husband but not yet finished. And whether, if the husband acted as a guarantor and paid something, he is entitled to take that whole amount from the half of the gains that falls to him.

## DISPUTATION 436.

### SUMMARY.

> 1 *A wife is bound to persevere in a contract of partnership with her husband’s heirs if she wishes to have half of the gains.*
> 2 *A husband acting as a guarantor and paying a debt is bound to take that payment out of his own share of the half-profits.*
> *This is clarified, however, as noted there.*
> *And regarding Portuguese law.*

<margin>Question 1</margin> Regarding the first of these points, Gutierrez <note>Juan Gutiérrez, a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in *Practicarum Quaestionum*, book 2, question 130, reports a case: a certain husband had leased taxes or a farm for several years, and died before the years were up. The wife, having accepted half of the profits, did not want to continue the contract for the following years that still remained according to the form of the contract, because it was not profitable for her. Some advocates argued that this was perfectly permissible for the wife, because a partnership is ended by the death of one spouse (according to what was said in Disputation 414). Therefore, the other spouse, or their heirs, once the marriage is dissolved, are not bound to accept the aforementioned lease but can reject it as something divided and 

<column-break/>

separated from the years already passed; especially since a certain price was established for each individual year, and for that reason, they seemed to be multiple distinct obligations, according to the law "We ought" <note>original: "l. scitè debemus"; Digest 45.1.29</note> in the Digest regarding verbal obligations.

<margin>Decision 1</margin> However, Gutierrez rightly says in the same place that he argued the opposite in that event. Along with Matienzo and others whom he cites, he asserts that in similar events, the contrary must be affirmed. This is because the obligation to persevere in that lease for the following years descends from a contract celebrated while the partnership between the two spouses was standing, and in which the business of the partnership was conducted. Although a partnership ends with the death of one spouse, and neither the surviving partners nor the heir of the deceased are bound to enter into *new* business pertaining to the partnership, they are nonetheless bound to continue and complete—both they and their heirs—all business started while the partnership was still active, as was shown from many laws in Disputation 414; the common opinion of the doctors <note>Legal scholars</note> agrees with this. Therefore, in the matter proposed, the wife or her heirs must either renounce the profits or persevere in the lease. Nor can they be barred from it, if it is profitable to them, until the time of the contract is finished.

<margin>Question 1</margin> Regarding the second point proposed, the negative side can be argued. First, because that debt was contracted while the marriage was standing; but a wife, if she wants half of the profits, is held equally with her husband for debts contracted during the marriage. Therefore, the husband is not bound to take the whole amount he paid as a <term>guarantor: one who takes responsibility for another's debt (fideiussor)</term> out of his own half of the profits.

Second, because (as will be said in the following disputation) the husband, while the marriage stands, is the legitimate administrator of all profits, with full power to alienate <note>To sell or transfer</note> them, provided he does not do so to defraud the wife. But by acting as a guarantor for another, he does nothing to defraud the wife; rather, he performs a work of charity and piety. Indeed, right reason demands it for the benefit of the partnership; for just as he himself often needs others to be his guarantors for the benefit of the partnership, so it is necessary that he himself act as a guarantor for others, otherwise he will find no one willing to be a guarantor for him. Therefore, what he pays for that reason ought to be common to both spouses from the earned assets.

<margin>Decision 2</margin> **T**he affirmative side, however, is to be embraced with Gutierrez, Montalvo, Matienzo, Menchaca, and Ayora, whom he cites, and with whom Gama agrees in Decision 162. The most powerful reason is because it is so decreed in Law 7, Title 3, Book 5 of the *New Compilation*, which reads: <term>We command that for any guarantee the husband might make in any manner, or for any reason, his wife shall not be obligated, nor shall her assets be:</term> the assets of the wife also include her half of the profits. Indeed, that law was undoubtedly established with regard to the earned assets, for there could be no doubt regarding her other [private] property. The same is provided in Law 5, Title 18, Book 3 of the *Fuero Real*. Because no benefit could come to the wife from a guarantee, it was established by the cited laws that no loss resulting from that same guarantee should fall upon the wife. This is especially because husbands could easily lose the profits belonging to their wives through such guarantees. However, Gutierrez rightly excepts, along with Ayora, the case where the husband and someone...

It concludes that a widow must either fulfill the entirety of her late husband's active contracts or forfeit her share of the marital profits, while also shielding her share of profits from her husband's liabilities as a third-party guarantor.</summary>

This follows the reasoning of the law "with two" in the section "Dama" in the Digest regarding partnerships <note>original: "l. cum duobus §. Dama. ff. pro socio"; Digest 17.2.52.18</note>.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Under Portuguese law, however, when a husband acts as a surety without his wife’s consent, not only is the wife’s capital not obligated, but neither is her half of the gains that belong to her, unless he acted as a surety for the King’s revenues. In that case, all gains would remain obligated if they consisted of moveable goods, along with half of the immovable property <note>such as land or buildings</note>. Furthermore, when a husband alone leases something—whether from the King or anyone else—without the wife also obligating herself, none of the wife's capital remains obligated, though all the gains would be. This is held in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 13, *On the husband as surety*, and was discussed in Dispute 422 regarding marriages celebrated under the contract of "half of the property."

To the first argument to the contrary: while the major premise is granted, we must address the minor premise. That rule is true for debts involving "onerous title" <note>contracts involving a mutual exchange of value, like a sale or lease</note>, or those arising from the burdens of marriage and the partnership. It is not true, however, for debts arising from mere "liberality" <note>generosity or a gift</note>, which the husband chose to exercise toward another by acting as their surety, providing no benefit or advantage to the wife—especially since express laws, passed as a privilege for wives, exempt such debts contracted while the marriage is standing.

To the second argument, it must similarly be said that the major premise is true regarding administration and alienation <note>selling or transferring property</note> under onerous title, or according to the burdens of marriage and the partnership. It is otherwise, however, when exercising the "liberality" of suretyship with a third party, as has been said, especially since there are express laws which, in favor of wives, exempt such debt as a loss. This aligns with the teaching regarding excessive gifts made by a husband from the acquired gains, as discussed in Dispute 275.

Regarding the points added to the minor premise: although right reason sometimes demands it, and it might seem to benefit the partnership in that way, nevertheless, because it more frequently results in the detriment of wives without any benefit to the partnership, the law has rightly rejected this entire category of loss as being to the detriment of husbands. However, when it is effectively an "onerous contract" and equal between two people—considering the circumstances where they mutually agree: "You be my surety in this matter, and I will be yours in that other"—I believe that if any loss happens to the husband by chance from that suretyship, it ought to be common to the wife regarding the acquired gains. The cited laws would not prevent this, as they are not to be understood through "equity" <note>original: "epicheiam"; a legal principle allowing for exceptions to the letter of the law to follow its spirit</note> in this specific event. This entire doctrine—that if a husband pays something because he acted as a surety, he must take that from the half of the gains that belongs to him—is confirmed by the fact that he must also take from his own half any excessive gifts he has made from the acquired gains, as stated in Dispute 275.

<column-break/>

->The administration of property, especially acquired gains; to what extent it belongs to the husband and to what extent to the wife. And whether a husband can, from the acquired gains, provide a dowry for a daughter of a prior marriage, or establish a "maioratum" <note>term: <term>maioratum</term>; an entailed estate that passes to a single heir, usually the eldest son, to keep the family wealth intact</note> without the wife.<-

### DISPUTATION 437.

#### SUMMARY.

1 *To whom the administration of all property belongs under the law of Castile and Portugal.*
2 *Under Common Law and the law of Castile, which property the husband can alienate without the wife’s consent, and which under Portuguese law.*

1 It has been stated in Dispute 274 (combined with the additions in Dispute 343) that the administration of all property under the law of Castile, and by custom and law in Portugal, belongs to the husband alone. Any actions the wife takes to administer or dispose of property without at least the husband's tacit consent are invalid, unless they pertain to her appropriate maintenance which the husband is unjustly denying her, or unless the wife specifically reserved something for herself at the time she contracted the marriage, the administration of which would belong to her alone—which rarely happens. Likewise, in Dispute 275, it was added to what extent gifts or wasteful spending by the husband from the acquired gains are valid or invalid under both Castilian and Portuguese law. To these, add what we subjoined at the end of Dispute 422, which has relevance when something is wrongly given or spent by the husband from the acquired gains (especially in Portugal).

2 Under Common Law and the law of Castile, a husband can alienate all property, even immovable property, without the wife's consent, unless it was delivered to him as "unestimated" <note>original: "inaestimata"; property where the specific item, rather than its cash value, must be returned at the end of the marriage</note>, in which case the ownership belongs to the wife alone, as stated in Disputes 426 and 428. In Dispute 428, it was explained when property owned solely by the wife cannot be validly sold even with her consent, and when it can. Under Portuguese law, however, the husband cannot alienate any immovable property—even if it is his own private property or part of the acquired gains—without the express consent of the wife. Indeed, all that was said in Dispute 422 regarding the sale of immovable property in Portugal without express consent holds true not only when the marriage contract was for "half of the property," but also when it concerned "earnest money and dowry" <note>original: "arrharum & dotis"</note>, as is clear from the laws cited there. Furthermore, when such immovable property is a "dotal estate" <note>land specifically set aside as part of a dowry</note>, the husband could not sell it even with the wife's consent if the marriage contract was for earnest money and dowry, which is the only type of marriage where something can be considered a dotal estate. For what was said in Dispute 428 regarding dotal estates under Common Law also applies in Portugal, since nothing to the contrary...

the contrary is defined in that Kingdom.
In Castile, Law 5, Title 9, Book 5 of the *New Compilation* <note>original: "nouæ collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish laws</note> grants the same power to the husband during the marriage to alienate assets earned as gains. <note>original Spanish: "Otro si á los bienes, que fueren ganados y mejorados y multiplicados, durante el matrimonio entre el marido y la muger, que los pueda enagenar el marido durante el matrimonio, si quisiere, and que el contrato de enagenacion vala, saluo si fuere probado, que se hizo cautelosamẽte por defraudar o damnificar a la muger."</note> *Furthermore, regarding assets gained, improved, or multiplied during the marriage between husband and wife, the husband may alienate them during the marriage if he wishes, and the contract of alienation shall be valid, unless it is proven that it was done deceitfully to defraud or harm the wife.* However, although the law grants such ample power to the husband while the marriage lasts, it was shown in Dispute 275 that this does not extend to making excessive donations from these assets. For this same reason, if a husband wishes to provide a dowry for a daughter, or give a wedding gift to a son from a prior marriage—since that burden belongs to him alone and not to the second wife, who is considered a stranger in relation to such a daughter or son—he may indeed do so from the assets gained in the later marriage, provided it does not infringe upon the legal portions <note>original: "legitimas"; the portion of an estate that must by law go to the children</note> of the other children, nor the second wife’s half of the gains. Nevertheless, he is required to take that amount from his own half of the gains, or, if it exceeds that, to reimburse the wife from his own private assets. This is the rule not only in other Kingdoms, as stated generally in Dispute 424, but also in the Kingdom of Castile. This is the view held by Palacios Rubios, Burgos de Paz, Ayora, and others, as well as Gutierrez in *Practical Questions*, Book 2, Question 128, number 5.

For the same reason—and because the law should not be interpreted as granting the husband the power to prevent the wife’s free disposal of her half of the gains which belong to her—he cannot, in place of the wife and against her will, grant a special advantage <term>præcipuum: a portion of an estate given to one heir above their standard share</term> to one or more of their common children. Certainly, while it is lawful for a husband during the marriage to establish an entailment <term>maioratum: an estate that is inherited by a single heir, usually the eldest son, to keep the family fortune intact</term> from the half of the gains belonging to him, or to "better" <note>original: "meliorare"; a legal term for increasing one child's inheritance share</note> whichever son he wishes from that half (provided he does not prejudice the legal portions of the other children), it is nevertheless unlawful for him, without the consent and permission of his wife, to do the same during the marriage with the half of those same gains belonging to the wife. Instead, he is bound to leave the disposal of that half free to the wife; this is the accepted practice in Castile and Portugal. This is the opinion of Molina, Book 2, *On Primogeniture*, Chapter 10, number 67; Gutierrez, *Practical Questions*, Book 2, Question 121, number 6; and others whom they cite.

## When a marriage is dissolved, the wife or her heirs extract the dowry by a privileged action, and what kind of mortgage they have over the husband’s assets for that dowry.

### DISPUTE CCCCXXXVIII.

->SUMMARY<-

1. What action a woman has for recovering her dowry, and which creditors she is preferred over.
2. Whether the same applies to a "quasi-dowry" <note>gifts given in anticipation of a marriage that did not take place</note>, number 2.
3. The privilege by which a woman, in demanding her dowry, is preferred over

<column-break/>

all prior creditors, does not pass to her heirs.
4. To recover her dowry, a wife has a tacit mortgage <term>tacita hypotheca: a legal lien that exists automatically by law without a written contract</term> on all the husband's assets, even if the husband is a minor. The same is to be said for a putative <note>supposed or apparent</note> dowry, number 5.
5. This is also extended so that she has this right against a guarantor, number 6.
6. It is limited in the case of a bride betrothed by "words of the future" <note>an engagement to marry later, rather than a present marriage contract</note>, number 7.
8. In her tacit mortgage for recovering her dowry, the wife is preferred over other prior creditors who likewise have tacit mortgages, according to common opinion. He explains and interprets this, however, in the following number.
10. Whether the wife’s tacit mortgage for recovering her dowry is preferred even over someone holding an express mortgage.
11. To whom the privilege of preference in the same matter belongs most among several people holding it.
12. Whether the privilege of preference is only personal, or whether it contains a tacit mortgage within itself.
13. Whether wives having express mortgages by contract are preferred over prior creditors who also have express mortgages.
14. At what time the wife’s tacit mortgage begins.
15. A wife can renounce the tacit mortgage she held on her husband's assets for the payment of her dowry. And what regarding an express mortgage.

---

<margin>1</margin>
Having thus far explained the partnership between spouses regarding the division of assets when the partnership ends, we must now speak of how the wife or her heirs extract, before all else, the dowry that the wife brought. For the recovery of the dowry from the husband or his heirs, they possess, first of all, a "privileged action from stipulation" <note>original: "actio priuilegiata ex stipulatu"</note>, as if a contract had been made between the wife and husband at the time the dowry was delivered regarding its return once the partnership ended. This is similar to what was said in Dispute 423 regarding the action a husband has to demand a dowry promised to him with his wife but not yet paid. This is found in the Law *Vnica*, section 1, and the sections *maneat* and *illo*, joined with the section *sed & si* in the Code, *On the wife's property* <note>original: "C. de rei vxor."</note>, and the section *fuerat* in the Institutes, *On actions*. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez relates and follows in Law 50 of the *Laws of Toro*, numbers 37 and 445. Furthermore, in demanding her dowry, a wife is preferred over all other prior creditors who have only a personal action. Thus, the dowry must be paid to the wife from the husband's assets in the first place, even if no assets remain from which the prior creditors can be paid. This was indeed decreed as a privilege for women and for the public good; it is by this law that men are understood to celebrate their contracts: that if any dowry is owed to women, it must be satisfied to them first, even if they are later in time regarding their legal claim.

<margin>2</margin>
This privilege is extended to a "quasi-dowry"—that is, to what was given as a dowry to a bride-to-be, even if the marriage did not follow. All these things are found in Law 2, the final section, and the two following laws in the Digest, *On the privileges of creditors*. These have force with much greater reason <margin>3</margin> when the marriage was contracted in good faith on the wife's part, but was later found to be null.

<margin>3</margin>
However, the privilege that a woman be preferred over prior creditors in demanding her dowry does not pass to her heirs, because it is a personal privilege. This is held in the Law *Vnica* in the Code, *On the privilege of the dowry*, the words of which are: *You ought to know, the privilege of the dowry...*

<summary>This page discusses the legal rights of a husband to manage marital gains in Castile and Portugal, while establishing the wife's "privileged" right to recover her dowry first when a marriage ends. It introduces the concept of a tacit mortgage, or legal lien, that protects the wife's assets against other creditors.</summary>
