<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal protections for a wife’s dowry. The previous page concluded by noting that while a husband has broad power over marital assets, he cannot use them to disadvantage his wife's legal claims. Here, Molina explores the "tacit mortgage"—a legal lien—that secures the return of the dowry.</meta>

# Luis Molina, On Contracts
#### [Page 492]

...[the privilege] which women use in a dotal action <note>An "action de dote" is a legal claim brought to recover a dowry after a marriage ends.</note> does not pass to an heir. An exception is made if the heirs are children or other descendants of the wife: for then they enjoy the mother's privilege, according to Law *assiduis*, section *in praesenti*, Code: *Who are preferred in a pledge* <note>original: "l. assiduis §. in præsenti. C. qui potiores in pignor." refers to the Code of Justinian</note> and the second gloss on the single law of the Code: *On the privilege of the dowry*. The common opinion agrees on these points, which Antonio Gómez relates and follows in the place cited above.

<margin>4</margin>
Furthermore, for the purpose of recovering her dowry, a wife holds a tacit mortgage <note term="tacit mortgage">A "tacit mortgage" (hypotheca tacita) is a legal lien that arises automatically by operation of law, rather than by a written contract, over all the property of the debtor to secure a specific claim.</note> over all the goods of her husband. This is held in the single law, section *and that more fully*, Code: *On the action for the wife's property* <note>original: "l. vnica §. & ut plenius. C. de rei vxo. act."</note>; in the section *it had been*, Institutes: *On actions*; in the chapter *from the letters*, *On pledges*; in Law 17, Title 11, Part 4; and Law 23, Title 13, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]. This is affirmed by the common opinion, which is related and followed by Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 7, number 1; Antonio Gómez as cited above; Gregorio López in his notes on the cited laws; and Gutiérrez in *On the Confirmation of Oaths*, part 1, chapter 46, number 1.

<margin>5</margin>
This holds true even if the husband is younger than twenty-five years <note>Under Roman and Early Modern law, twenty-five was the age of full legal majority.</note>, according to the doctors of law whom Antonio Gómez relates and follows in number 37: because, since he is capable of contracting at that age, he is also considered capable regarding the accessories to the marriage contract. Likewise, this takes place when the dowry is "putative" <note term="putative dowry">A dowry given for a marriage that the woman believed in good faith was valid, but which was actually legally void.</note>, because the woman celebrated the void marriage in good faith. This is proven excellently by the gloss on Law *assiduis* at the word *the previous one*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*, and it is the common opinion which Antonio Gómez relates and follows.

<margin>6</margin>
This tacit mortgage is also available to the wife against a guarantor <note>original: "fideiussorem"; a person who promises to pay if the husband cannot.</note> in those instances explained in Dispute 425 where such a guarantee can be given; for the guarantor's obligation is an accessory one and follows the husband’s principal obligation. Thus says Antonio Gómez with others; and Gregorio López, with Bartolus and others, affirms in Law 23, Title 13, Part 5; and Gutiérrez, number 3 and 4, says that a husband's father can be compelled to bind himself to ensure the husband restores the dowry. In that case, by the very fact that the father consents to the marriage and the reception of the dowry, his own goods remain mortgaged to the wife for the payment of the dowry. They add, however, that this only takes place for a son who is under his father's legal power <note>original: "in potestate patris"; the Roman concept of *patria potestas*.</note>. Consequently, since in Portugal—and also in Castile if the marriage has been veiled <note>"Veiled" refers to the nuptial blessing in the church ceremony.</note>—a son leaves his father's power through marriage, this doctrine will apply in these Kingdoms unless, perhaps in Castile, the dowry is delivered after the marriage is celebrated but before the son is veiled, with the party's consent.

<margin>7</margin>
This privilege of a tacit mortgage does not apply to a betrothed woman by "words of the future" <note term="verba de futuro">A promise to marry in the future, as opposed to "verba de praesenti," which created a marriage immediately.</note>, as affirmed by the second gloss on Law *eos*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*, and the common opinion of the doctors. Nor does it apply to one who provided the wife's dowry with a pact that the dowry should return to him in a certain event—for example, if the marriage were dissolved without children. The reason is that this privilege is found to be granted to the wife alone. This is the common view of the doctors, whom Antonio Gómez relates and follows.

<margin>8</margin>
The wife not only possesses a tacit mortgage for her dowry in the manner explained, but she also has a privilege within it so that she is preferred over all other earlier creditors, even those who have tacit mortgages that are not similarly privileged. This is expressly stated in Law *assiduis*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*, and the section *it had been*, Institutes: *On actions*, and Law 33, Title 13, Part 5; and it is affirmed by Antonio Gómez, Covarruvias, and the doctors commonly. 

<column-break/>

Observe, however, that the privilege of the tacit mortgage granted to the wife passes to all her heirs, even "stranger" heirs <note>Heirs who are not direct descendants, such as those appointed by a will.</note>; for it is handed down and granted to the dowry and the legal action itself, not to the person of the wife, as is gathered from the single law, section *and that more fully*, Code: *On the action for the wife's property*, joined with Law *assiduis*, section *and therefore*, and the gloss there on the words *we gave a mortgage*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*. Furthermore, it is clearly gathered by an argument from the opposite sense from the section *it had been*, Institutes: *On actions*; and the addition to the gloss at the word *to her* affirms this, as do Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez relates and follows in Law 50 of the *Laws of Toro*, number 45. 

However, the privilege of *priority* <note>The right to be paid before other creditors who might have older claims.</note> over those holding earlier non-privileged tacit mortgages does not pass to the heirs, but is personal to the wife; this is because it was granted to the wife, not to the dowry or the action. This is held in Law *assiduis*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*, and the section *it had been*, Institutes: *On actions*, in these words: *We gave her a mortgage; however, we then judged she should be preferred to other creditors in mortgages only when the woman herself seeks her dowry, for whose benefit alone we introduced these protections.* <note>original Latin: "Ei dedimus hypothecam, præferri autē alijs creditoribus in hypothecis, tunc cēsuimus, cum ipsa mulier de dote sua experiatur, cuius solius prouidentia hæc induximus."</note> The same is gathered from the single law, Code: *On the privilege of the dowry*, and affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors. 

When you hear, however, that this privilege of priority does not pass to the wife's heirs, except if they are children or other descendants of hers, as held in Law *assiduis*, section *in the present*, and clearly in the *Authenticum* <note>The *Authenticum* is a collection of Justinian's Novels (new laws).</note> *Regarding the pending action for dowry*, at the beginning. This is affirmed by the cited gloss and the doctors commonly. Indeed, when children of a first marriage remain, they are preferred over a second wife and her children regarding the tacit mortgage for the payment of the first wife's dowry, as is expressly held in Law *assiduis* and the *Authenticum* *If anything from the assets*, Code: *Who is preferred in a pledge*, and Law 33, Title 13, Part 5. 

The reason, as held in the cited *Authenticum*, is that a mortgage that is prior in time is preferred to a mortgage from a later time, and then that rule applies: *He who is first in time is stronger in right.* <note>original: "qui prior est tēpore, potior est in iure." A fundamental legal maxim.</note> Nevertheless, regarding goods found to have belonged to the second wife, the second wife and her heirs are preferred over the children of the prior marriage, as held in the cited *Authentica* and Law 33, and they agree with Law *In assets*, Code: *On the law of dowries*, Dispute 426, around point 4, which we observed in that place.

---

I said above that the wife has a privilege in her mortgage so that she is preferred over other earlier creditors holding tacit mortgages that are not similarly privileged. However, if any of those creditors hold a tacit mortgage that is similarly privileged to be preferred over others—just as 

<margin>9</margin>
the Treasury <note>original: "fiscus, camerave Regia"; the royal treasury or chamber.</note> possesses—then whoever was first in the right of the mortgage is preferred to the other. For example, if the husband entered a contract with the Treasury before he contracted marriage with the wife, the Treasury’s tacit mortgage is preferred to the wife’s mortgage. But if he contracted with the wife first, the wife’s mortgage is preferred to the Treasury's. This is held in Law 2, Code: *On the privilege of the Treasury*; and Law *of your dowry*, Code: *On the law of dowries*; and noted by Gregorio López on the cited Law 33, gloss A.

<summary>This page discusses the legal protections for a wife's dowry, specifically the "tacit mortgage" (lien) she holds over her husband's assets and her right to be paid before other creditors. It distinguishes between the mortgage itself, which can pass to any heir, and the privilege of priority, which is generally restricted to the wife and her direct descendants.</summary>

#### Second Treatise, Dispute 43. 493

...according to the text there, and the preceding Law 29. Regarding the tacit mortgage of the treasury <note>The "fiscus" or state treasury often had automatic legal claims over the property of those who managed public funds.</note>, see Laws 23 and 25. If it should be uncertain which of these mortgages was established first, the mortgage of the dowry is preferred over the mortgage of the treasury. This is affirmed by Gregorius Lopez, citing the gloss of Baldus, according to the rule: *In ambiguous cases, [judgment is] in favor of dowries* <note>original: "in ambiguis pro dotibus." Digest, *On the rules of law*.</note>. Antonio Gómez affirms the same, citing Bartolus and many others for the same opinion, in Law 50 of the Laws of Toro, number 40.

<margin>10</margin>
The Doctors of Law <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established legal commentators and university professors whose interpretations shaped the Common Law of Europe.</note> doubt whether the † tacit mortgage—which a wife holds over her husband's goods by benefit of law—should be preferred to an earlier express mortgage <note term="express mortgage">A mortgage created by an explicit written contract or agreement between the debtor and creditor.</note> held by other creditors. For example, if the husband had previously granted a specific possession or all his goods to another person through an express pact. Although some authors, whom Antonio Gómez refers to in Law 50 of Toro, number 39, affirm that the wife's tacit mortgage should be preferred; the contrary must be asserted. This follows the gloss on the section *it had been*, Institutes: *On actions*; the gloss on Law *assiduis*, Code: *Who are preferred in a pledge*; and the gloss on the chapter *from the letters*, *On pledges*. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez and Covarruvias (in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 7, number 1, conclusion 3) follow. This is now defined in Law 33, Title 13, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]. It can also be proved because the wife and the treasury enjoy an equal privilege of priority regarding their tacit mortgages, as is clear from what was said just above; but the treasury is not preferred to earlier creditors who hold an express mortgage, as is clear from the Digest and the Code. Therefore, the wife is not preferred either. Likewise, because he who is first in a real right <note>A "real right" is a right that is attached to the property itself (like a lien), rather than just a personal claim against a person.</note> is preferred to others, unless the contrary is expressed by law: but nowhere is it found expressed that the wife's tacit mortgage is preferred to an earlier express one. Therefore, she is not preferred to it. In this place, it should be observed that the wife’s tacit mortgage *is* preferred to the *later* express mortgages of others. So says Covarruvias with others whom he cites. They believe the same should be said regarding private citizens who hold an earlier tacit mortgage without a specific privilege of priority. The reason is that an earlier right in a thing is always preferred to a later one, unless a privilege of priority over the earlier one has been expressly granted by law to the person holding the later right.

On the occasion of what I have just said, observe: When someone has first subjected all his goods to a mortgage for someone, and later accepts a loan from another person to buy a field, and while 

<margin>11</margin>
† receiving that loan, he subjects that same field to a mortgage; this later creditor is preferred regarding the field bought with his own money (even though it was subjected to the mortgage later) over the earlier creditor who held a mortgage right over all the debtor's goods, including that field. This is held in the Code: *Who are preferred in a pledge*. Likewise, in Law *if to the womb*, section 1, Digest: *On the privileges of an heir*, the privilege of priority is granted to one who gave a loan for the purpose of repairing or restoring a building, even if they gave it to the craftsman at the command of the building's owner. The same is held in the Digest: *If a certain thing is sought*. What it means "to repair" is explained in the Digest. Although from these laws only a privilege of priority is gathered, nevertheless from Law 1 of the Digest: *In which cases a pledge or mortgage is tacitly contracted*, it is clearly established, together with Law *if to the womb*, cited

<meta>catchword: above</meta>

<column-break/>

above, that the Emperor Marcus [Aurelius] granted a tacit mortgage on the building itself to secure that money. Furthermore, in the Digest: *On the privileges of an heir*, it is held that he who has provided money for the construction of a ship—for example, for provisions and other things necessary for sailing, or for arming it, or even for buying it—has a privilege of priority. And although a similar privilege of priority is gathered from this, nonetheless from the Digest: *Who are preferred in a pledge*, a tacit mortgage is also gathered along with the privilege of priority. Indeed, the discussion in those laws concerns a privilege in a pledge or mortgage, as is clear from the title under which they are placed; and because Law *of this* states: *for the money of this man saved the cause of the whole pledge* <note>This is a foundational legal principle: if a loan saves an asset from being destroyed or lost, that lender gets paid first because, without them, the other creditors would have nothing to claim.</note>, where the discussion is about priority in a pledge. It is established by these two laws that if a later creditor gave something for the preservation of a thing previously pledged, he is to be preferred to the earlier creditor in recovering what he thus spent. For instance, if he gave something to arm or repair a ship already pledged to another, or for the provisions of the sailors (without which the ship could not arrive safely), or if he gave money so that goods already pledged to another would be made safe, or if he paid for the ships to carry them away, or if he paid the price for warehouses or other things in which those goods were preserved, or the price for the transport of the pack animals by which they were brought. However, Molina warns in Book 1 of *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10, number 23—along with Negusantius and Ripa, with whom Gregorius Lopez agrees in his final gloss on Law 26, Title 13, Part 5—that for the mortgage and right of priority to apply in these events, it is necessary that the money was necessary for that purpose, that no more was spent than was necessary, and that the thing itself still exists; otherwise, there will be no mortgage from which that money can be paid by real right.

<margin>Quest. 2</margin>
There is, in truth, no small controversy among the doctors whether, standing in the Common Law <note>Molina refers here to the *Ius Commune*, the synthesized Roman and Canon law used across Europe.</note>, especially in the events of Law *sometimes* and Law *of this*, there is only † granted to the later creditor a personal privilege of priority over earlier creditors (even if they have a mortgage), or whether a tacit mortgage is granted along with the privilege of priority. The gloss on the cited Law *sometimes* affirms that a tacit mortgage is not granted, and with it Bartolus and the common opinion, which Covarruvias, Molina, and Gregorius Lopez relate. The contrary view—namely, that a mortgage is indeed granted—is held by others; and that is what is sanctioned today in this Kingdom of Castile in the cited Law 26. This is clearly gathered from the *Authenticum* regarding the equality of the dowry, section *consequent to these*, whose words are: *“It is consequent to these things to decree that which we know has been doubted in cases of this kind; namely, [we know] that certain younger mortgages arising from privileges given by the laws are placed before older creditors. Such is the case when someone has arranged with his own money to acquire, or build, or repair a ship, or perhaps to build a house, or even to buy a field, or any of these things. For in all these cases, the later creditors, with whose money the thing was bought or renewed, stand prior to those who were much older.”*

<summary>This page analyzes the priority of the wife's tacit mortgage over her husband's property, concluding that while she beats later creditors, she generally does not displace earlier contract-based mortgages. It also discusses the legal exception for lenders whose money "saves" or creates an asset (like a ship or building), granting them top priority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "tacit mortgages" (automatic legal claims) and their ranking. It focuses on the specific privileges granted to a wife’s dowry to ensure her financial security, comparing her claims against other types of creditors under both Roman and Spanish law.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

...are older. In that passage, you see clearly that the condition of that decree <note>original: "authentici." This refers to the *Authentica*, a collection of Justinian’s later Roman laws (Novels).</note> has established that all these later creditors hold stronger mortgages. This discussion pertains to the various legal cases we have reported, many of which involve tacit mortgages <note term="tacit mortgage">A claim on property that is created automatically by law (such as for a dowry or taxes) rather than by a written contract.</note>, while others are express. Therefore, since the Law of Castile <note>The legal code of the Kingdom of Castile, including the *Siete Partidas* and the *Laws of Toro*.</note> agrees, and the laws we have cited and weighed point clearly to this, we must undoubtedly follow this latter opinion.

It should be added—which is the reason the above was mentioned—that in the cited decree, although a privilege of priority was granted to the later creditors mentioned against earlier creditors who hold prior mortgages (sometimes tacit, sometimes express), a **unique privilege** is nevertheless granted to **wives**. This is done so that they may be enticed to enter into marriage and not live dishonestly outside of marriage; namely, that in a case regarding a dowry, the aforementioned later creditors, or any others, are not preferred over them. 

An exception is made if someone lent money to the husband to purchase a military post <note>original: "militia." In this context, it often refers to a purchased administrative or military office that generated income.</note> with a mortgage specifically on that post; in that case, this later creditor is preferred over the wife regarding the mortgage on that post. I specified "the aforementioned later creditors" because, as clearly stated in Law 29, Title 13, Part 3 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Spanish legal code.</note> and noted there by Gregorius Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist who wrote the standard commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note> in the final gloss, it would be different if such creditors were *earlier* in time. However, standing solely on Common Law <note>The *Ius Commune*, the shared legal tradition of Roman and Canon law in Europe.</note>, there would be contrary opinions on that matter, as Gregorius Lopez reports in the cited place. 

From this unique privilege granted to wives in that decree, a certain legal axiom becomes clear: "If I defeat the one who defeats you, I will all the more defeat you." <note>original: "si vinco vincentem te, à fortiori vincam te." A logic rule often used in legal priorities.</note> This rule is not always true in matters that depend on human legal arrangements, as noted in the gloss on the law *assiduis* and by others. For indeed, those who hold earlier express mortgages are preferred over wives who hold later tacit ones, as has been said; and yet, while the later creditors we have discussed defeat those earlier creditors with express mortgages, they do not defeat wives in dowry cases—rather, they are defeated by the wives. This very point—that a wife is preferred over such privileged later creditors—is also extended to the treasury <note>original: "fiscus." The state's financial office.</note> by the cited Law 29. As Gregorius Lopez notes there, this was not so clearly expressed in Common Law, even though the only argument for that opinion was that the privileges of the wife and the treasury are equal to one another, as stated above.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The next doubt is whether—just as wives holding later tacit mortgages for the recovery of a dowry are preferred over earlier creditors who hold earlier mortgages that are also 
<margin>13</margin>
tacit and not privileged—those same wives should be preferred over earlier creditors holding **express** mortgages, if the wives hold an express mortgage on the husband's goods by a **specific contract**. 
<margin>Decision</margin>
The more common opinion, which should be embraced, says no. This is followed by Antonius Gomez <note>A prominent Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the *Laws of Toro*.</note> and Covarruvias. The reason is that the first privilege is found granted to wives in the law; 

<column-break/>

but the latter is not.

<margin>14</margin>
A wife's † tacit mortgage for her dowry begins from the time the dowry is handed over to the husband, not from the time the marriage is contracted. This agrees with the glosses and various laws affirmed by Antonius Gomez and Gutierrez. Law 17, Title 11, Part 4 <note>From the *Siete Partidas*.</note> agrees with these words: *As soon as the husband receives the dowry, all his goods are bound to the wife, both those he has then and those he has afterward.* <note>original Spanish: "Ca luego que el marido recibe la dote, son obligados a la muger todos sus bienes..."</note> However, Bartolus <note>One of the most influential medieval legal commentators.</note> and others, whom Gomez and Gutierrez cite, thought that the mortgage begins on the day the marriage is contracted. 

From our opinion, I conclude that if, before the wife's mortgage begins, any goods are alienated by the husband which were pledged to other creditors, or which were entirely free of debt, the wife has no right to have her dowry paid from those goods; only the prior creditors have rights in the goods previously pledged. However, when the mortgage for the dowry is **express**—because the husband pledged his goods for the payment of the dowry through a specific contract—then by everyone's opinion, that mortgage begins from the moment the marriage contract is celebrated, even if the dowry is handed over to the husband later. This is gathered from the laws and the common opinion of the Doctors, followed by Gomez and Gutierrez.

<margin>15</margin>
A wife † can renounce the tacit mortgage she holds over her husband's goods for the payment of her dowry, as found in the laws of the Code. However, it is not enough if she renounces it in general terms regarding one person contracting with her husband, or in a single contract made with her husband, for the renunciation to be valid in relation to all who contract with the husband, or in relation to other contracts that the same person might make with the husband. 

Bartolus and the glosses understand this to mean that the renunciation is only valid if, at the time the woman renounced it, the husband had sufficient goods to pay the dowry; otherwise, they judge the renunciation invalid. Some also affirm that although a woman can renounce a tacit mortgage, she cannot renounce an express one. Antonius Gomez follows both of these points. However, I do not see where these points are sufficiently proven. Gutierrez, cited above, along with others, judges that a wife cannot renounce a tacit mortgage at all; they seem to mean she cannot do so in favor of the husband himself. They affirm, however, that the renunciation is valid if it is confirmed by an **oath**. I agree with them on this second point. Regarding the first point, I do not see how they sufficiently prove it, or how they satisfy the laws which seem to affirm the contrary. The explanation given by Gutierrez on this matter is frivolous.

<summary>This page discusses the legal priority of a wife's dowry claims over other creditors, explaining that while she has a "unique privilege" to recover her dowry, the timing of when this right begins depends on whether the claim is automatic (tacit) or written (express).</summary>
<keywords>dowry, tacit mortgage, express mortgage, legal priority, Siete Partidas, Laws of Toro, marital property rights, renunciation of rights, Antonius Gomez, Gregorius Lopez</keywords>

Tract. Second. Disp. 439.

# The defense of a dowry not paid, and how long it is available to the husband and his heirs against the wife and her heirs.

### DISPUTE 439

#### ->SUMMARY<-

1 *Within what period of time is the defense of a dowry not paid <note>original: "Exceptio non numeratæ dotis." This is a legal defense where a person admits they signed a contract for a debt or dowry but claims they never actually received the money.</note> granted to a husband or his heirs after the marriage is dissolved.*
2 *Indeed, it can even be initiated by way of a formal complaint or protest. See number 2.*
3 *Limitations on this defense: cases where it is not admitted. See numbers 3, 4, 5, 6.*
7 *Whether the defense of a dowry not paid is granted when the confession of the received dowry was confirmed by an oath.*
8 *When a husband has confessed to receiving a dowry, but it is not clear that he actually received it, should he be thought to have made that confession in the hope of a future payment, or rather with the intention of making a gift to his wife?*
10 *Whether a presumed gift between husband and wife, made by the husband granting a dowry he did not truly have, is confirmed by an oath.*
*And what if the husband says, "I swear I have received this much dowry"—is it by that very fact considered a gift confirmed by oath and irrevocable? See number 11.*
11 *When a confession of a received dowry has the force of a gift after the marriage is contracted, it does not matter whether the time limits for the defense of a dowry not paid have passed or not.*
13 *A wife does not have a mortgage or priority over the husband's assets in competition with other creditors regarding a dowry that the husband only confessed to receiving but did not actually get.*

---

<margin>1</margin> Just as with a loan <note>original: "mutuo." A standard loan where ownership of the thing lent passes to the borrower.</note> (as was stated in Dispute 302), the law provides that if someone has confessed—whether by a private note, a public document, or before witnesses—that they owe a certain amount of money given to them as a loan, they may, within two years of making that confession, raise a defense or opposition stating that the money was never actually paid out. In such a case, the burden of proof falls on the creditor to show that the money was indeed handed over. If they cannot prove it, the person who made the confession is released from the debt, because the law presumes that the confession was made in the hope of a future payment.

Similarly, if a husband confesses in a private or public document, or before witnesses, that he has received a dowry or a certain amount of a dowry, the civil law grants him and his heirs the right—once the marriage is dissolved—to raise the defense that the dowry was never counted out or delivered. It then becomes the responsibility of the wife or her heirs to prove that it was indeed paid or delivered to him. If they fail to prove this, the husband or his heirs are released from the obligation to return the dowry, because it is presumed that his confession was made in the hope of a future delivery. This is established in the final law of the Code, *Concerning a cautioned dowry not paid* <note>original: "l. vlt, C. de dote cauta non numerata." This refers to the *Codex Justinianus*, a foundational body of Roman law.</note>, and is affirmed by Antonio Gomez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentaries on the Laws of Toro.</note> and the common opinion of the doctors of law, whom we shall cite as we proceed.

<margin>2</margin> In former times, however, a husband, his heirs, or anyone else who had confessed to receiving a dowry could raise the defense that

<column-break/>

the dowry had not been paid or delivered, not only during the entire time the marriage lasted, but also within one year after the marriage was dissolved by the death of one spouse, or within one year after a divorce. This was the rule in the aforementioned final law of the Code. 

Today, however, the rule is different. If the marriage is dissolved or separated by divorce within two years of the confession of the dowry's receipt, an additional year from the time of dissolution or separation is granted to raise the defense. However, if the marriage is dissolved after two years but before ten years have passed since the confession, then only three months are granted to raise the defense after the marriage ends. 

If the marriage has lasted for a full ten years from the moment the confession was made without being dissolved or separated, then once those ten years have passed, no defense of an unpaid or undelivered dowry is allowed, whether the marriage is still intact or has been dissolved. In this case, the husband or his heirs must prove that the dowry was *not* delivered; otherwise, they will be compelled to pay it. An exception is made if the husband or his heirs were minors under the age of twenty-five during that entire time; in that case, they are granted "restoration to their original legal state" <note term="restitutio in integrum">A legal remedy where a person is restored to their previous position, often used to protect minors from the consequences of unfair contracts.</note>. All of this is expressly stated in the *Authentics* <note>The *Authentica* are a collection of Justinian's later laws (Novels) integrated into the Code.</note> and discussed at length by Antonio Gomez and Alvaro Valasco.

On this point, observe: during the entire time granted for raising this defense, it is not only possible to use it as a shield if the dowry is being sued for, but also to proactively file a complaint or a protest <note term="querela/protestatio">A formal legal declaration intended to preserve a right or prevent a legal presumption from taking effect.</note> stating that the dowry was not delivered. This must be done in a way that notifies the wife or her heirs so they have the chance to prove the contrary. This complaint must be put in writing and presented as described in the cited laws.

<margin>3</margin> However, when a notary <note term="tabellio">A public official in the Roman and civil law traditions authorized to draw up and attest to legal documents.</note> testifies in the document of confession that the dowry was actually delivered in his presence, then the defense of an unpaid dowry is not admitted. In this case, the wife or her heirs are not required to prove the delivery; rather, the husband or his heirs are compelled to return it based solely on the notary's word. This follows the same logic we cited regarding loans in Dispute 302, and is affirmed for dowries by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> and the common opinion.

<margin>4</margin> Likewise, when someone has formally renounced the defense of a dowry not paid or delivered, neither they nor their heirs can later raise that defense to shift the burden of proof onto the wife or her heirs. According to the Law of Castile, it is sufficient for this renunciation to be made at the time of the contract in the very same document where the receipt of the dowry was confessed. According to the more common opinion of the general law, as held by Bartolus...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "defense of an unpaid dowry" (exceptio non numeratae dotis). It specifically addresses the conditions under which a husband loses the right to claim he never actually received the money he formally acknowledged in writing. It builds on the previous discussion of time limits and formal documents.</meta>

->Luis de Molina on Contracts<-

it ought to be done after an interval <note>Latin: "ex interuallo"; meaning a significant period of time has passed between two legal acts.</note> in another instrument so that it is valid. And this is especially necessary for it to be valid in Portugal. Thus, Antonio Gomez (at the cited number 51) and Alvarus Valascus (in the cited consultation 5, numbers 12 and 13) affirm this, along with the gloss on the final law of the Code *Concerning a dowry secured but not paid* <note>Latin: "l. vlt. C. de dote cauta non nume."</note> and Bartolus and others. For the reasoning is the same regarding the renunciation of the defense of an unpaid dowry as it is for the renunciation of unpaid money, which was discussed more copiously in Dispute 302. Read what was said there.

Jason and certain others, whom Antonio Gomez (cited number 52), Alvarus Valascus (cited consultation 5, number 14), and more copiously Covarruvias (Book 1, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7, number 6, at the passage "there is also another") refer to, affirm that if a husband has indeed confessed to having received a dowry, but not from the wife, nor from the father-in-law (the wife's father), but from some stranger <note>Latin: "extraneo"; a third party not directly part of the marriage contract.</note>, the defense of an unpaid dowry does not apply to him. Nevertheless, the three doctors cited rightly assert that even in that event, the defense of an unpaid dowry is available to the husband and his heirs. This is because the laws that grant that defense do not exclude that event, nor is there any reason why it should be excluded. Indeed, the authentic text <note>A term for a decree or law, often from the "Authenticum," a collection of Justinian's Novels.</note> *Concerning the time for non-payment of money regarding a dowry* <note>Latin: "de temp. non solu. pecu. super dot."</note> in the section "but if neither," clearly teaches that the defense is equally available whether the wife, the father of the wife, or any stranger promised the dowry. Covarruvias, in the same place with Bartolus and others, judges that if, after the husband's confession of the received dowry, some stranger promises the dowry and the husband accepts, the defense of an unpaid dowry no longer applies to him or his heirs, because the acceptance of such a promise is held to be equivalent to payment. However, I do not believe this to be true unless the husband is content at that time to take that promise in place of the payment of the dowry which ought to have been made by the wife or father-in-law.

<margin>5</margin> Item: when a promise of a certain dowry preceded in a dowry instrument, and later, after an interval, the husband confessed that he had received the aforementioned promised dowry, from such acts—namely, the prior promise of the dowry in the instrument and the subsequent confession of the received dowry after an interval—there arises such a powerful presumption of the dowry having been paid or delivered that thereafter the defense of an unpaid or undelivered dowry is denied to the husband and his heirs. Thus the text proves, according to its more common exposition, in the law *In contracts*, the section "but because," at the words "to those also," in the Code *Concerning money not paid* <note>Latin: "l. in contractibus. §. sed quoniam ver. illis etiam C. de non numerata pecunia."</note>, which Covarruvias (Book 1, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7, number 6), Alvarus Valascus (cited consultation 5, number 9), and Antonio Gomez (cited number 52) refer to and follow. Its words are these:

> We decree that no defense of unpaid money at all may be opposed to those security documents <note>Latin: "securitatibus"; documents proving a discharge of debt or payment.</note> which, after the drafting of the dowry instruments (by which the dowry was established and promised), are set forth regarding a dowry paid in part or in full. Nor does the law "As in the beginning" <note>Latin: "l. vt, in prin."</note> in the Code *Concerning a dowry secured but not paid* contradict this with these words: "In dowries which are customarily recorded as given in dowry instruments, when as yet no giving but only a promise has followed, it shall be permitted to oppose the defense of unpaid money."

For in this text, there is no mention of a confession of a received dowry made after an interval from the promise of the same dowry, but rather of a confession which, on account of only

<column-break/>

the promise of a dowry, was made at the same time when the dowry was promised, as is clear from the words themselves. I said above, "according to its more common exposition," because the gloss of Accursius there, Bartolus, and certain others (whose opinion Emmanuel a Costa refers to and follows in the law *If by caution*, Exception 14) explain that text as referring to a "doubled confession" <note>Latin: "geminata confessione."</note> made by the husband regarding the received dowry, with one made after an interval from the other, as if the defense of an unpaid dowry were then denied. However, that prior, more common exposition is more true to the words of that section quoted a little earlier, as is clear to one weighing them.

<margin>6</margin> Item: when the confession of the received dowry was doubled after an interval, in the manner explained just above, the defense of an unpaid dowry is denied to the husband and his heirs, as Alvarus Valascus (cited consultation 5, number 10), Emmanuel a Costa, and Antonio Gomez affirm in the place cited above, along with the gloss of Accursius, Bartolus, and many others. And besides other things by which they confirm it, this reasoning of Emmanuel a Costa seems to prove it: because the first confession of the received dowry rests upon the promise of the same dowry made to the husband and presupposes it; therefore, if with a preceding promise and a subsequent confession of the received dowry after an interval, the defense of an unpaid dowry is denied to the husband and his heirs according to the more common opinion and interpretation of the text discussed in the preceding section, it will also be granted in the event we are now discussing. Therefore, whether you explain that text in one way or the other, it is always gathered from it that when a doubled confession of a received dowry exists after an interval, the defense of an unpaid dowry is denied to the husband and his heirs.

<margin>7</margin> When, however, the confession of a received dowry is confirmed by an oath, a distinction must be made. For either it was confirmed by an oath that the dowry *had been* received—as if the husband affirmed by oath that he had already received the dowry—or he did not affirm this by oath, but having confessed that he had received the dowry, he bound himself by oath to return it. In the first case, the oath is not promissory of something in the future, but assertive of a past thing—namely, that he received the dowry. And in that case, I believe (with Alvarus Valascus, Emmanuel a Costa, and others whom they cite) that the husband is not granted the defense of an unpaid dowry to the effect that it should fall to the wife or her heirs to prove she delivered it. This is because it ought not to be presumed that the husband was a perjurer; for he would have been a perjurer and would have sinned mortally if, even in the hope of a future payment, he had affirmed by oath that he received a dowry which he did not receive. However, he can and should be admitted to prove that he did not receive it, so that if he proves it sufficiently, he is not compelled to return it—even if, by proving this, he simultaneously manifests his own disgrace and perjury, for which cause he should be punished, as Emmanuel a Costa rightly teaches with others in the cited exception. In the second case, however, the oath is promissory, and nothing prevents it, if that confession was made in the hope of future payment, and relying on the same, the husband promised to return the dowry...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the "defense of an unpaid dowry." It focuses on whether a husband's formal acknowledgment of receiving a dowry should be interpreted as a genuine receipt, a hope for future payment, or a gift to his wife, particularly under Portuguese law.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute VIII

...can seek a remedy, both in the court of conscience and in the external court, etc., by claiming that the dowry was never actually paid. In a similar case, this is expressly held in the final law of the Code *Concerning money not paid* <note>Latin: "l. ult. C. de non numer. pecun." Referring to the Code of Justinian, a foundational Roman law text.</note>, which affirms the common opinion of the doctors, as stated in Dispute 302. The reason for this is that an oath regarding promises follows the nature of the promise itself; a promise regarding a future event, or one made in the hope of the dowry being paid, contains an implied condition: "if the dowry is actually paid or delivered." Covarruvias, in *Various Resolutions* (chapter 7, number 6, at the passage "thus also from confession"), affirms that when a husband’s confession of receipt is accompanied by other evidence that he truly received it, the defense of an unpaid dowry ceases to apply. For instance, if he is presumed to have received a companion or if there are witnesses who affirm the husband received it, as is read in the works of many doctors.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
Having established these points, we proceed further into matters where the Doctors vary greatly and are divided. Alvarus Valascus (at the cited Consultation 8, number 3) refers to the principal opinions more distinctly than others. When it is established that a husband confessed to receiving a dowry, but it is not clear from the facts that he actually received it, should he be judged to have made that confession in the hope of future payment or delivery, or rather with the intent of making a gift <note>Latin: "animo donandi"; the legal intention to give something without receiving anything in return.</note>? Joannes Andreas, in his additions to the *Speculum* under the title *On dowries between husband and wife*, says that if the confession of a received dowry was made before the marriage was contracted, it is presumed to have been made in the hope of future payment. If, however, it was made after the marriage was already contracted and ongoing, it is judged to have been made with the intent of gifting it to the wife. The second opinion is that of Baldus, whom many follow, asserting without any distinction that whether the confession was made before or after the marriage, if it is not proven that the dowry was delivered, it is always presumed to be a gift made to the wife. Consequently, if the husband dies, the gift is confirmed by his death, in accordance with what was said in Dispute 289 regarding gifts between husband and wife and the laws in the Code *Concerning a dowry secured but not paid*. But if the marriage is dissolved by the wife's death or by divorce, the confession is judged null. The third opinion is that of Alexander and others (also asserted by Bartolus), that whether the confession is made before or after the marriage, if there is no proof of delivery, it is always presumed to have been made in hope of future delivery.

To better understand what should be held, one must observe that a confession of a received dowry—when it was not received, or was received in a smaller amount—is sometimes made by husbands in a public instrument neither in the hope of future payment nor with the intent of gifting it, but rather as a simulation <note>A "simulated" contract is one made for appearance's sake, with no intention of it being legally binding between the parties.</note> by the mutual consent of both spouses. This might be done so the husband may preserve his and his family's honor (as it would be a disgrace to be known that he took a wife without a dowry or with a very small one), or so the husband may appease his parents and relatives who would be upset if they knew he married a woman with little or no dowry. In this event, the confession of a received dowry, being a fiction and made without any true consent to be bound in the future...

<column-break/>

...induces no obligation, nor is the defense of an unpaid dowry strictly necessary, as Alvarus Valascus rightly affirms with others (cited Consultation 5). However, if in an external court the husband’s confession of receiving the dowry is established but the simulation is not, and the dowry is demanded by the wife or her heirs, the husband could and should protect himself with the defense of an unpaid dowry, provided the legal time limit for raising it has not passed. It is customary to prove in court that the confession was simulated, sometimes by a private "secret" document <note>Latin: "chirographo"; a handwritten note or bond.</note> which the husband usually takes from the wife and her parents for his own security, in which they admit she did not actually have as much dowry as was confessed. And although in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances* <note>Latin: "Lusitanorum ord."; refers to the *Ordenações Filipinas*, the legal code of Portugal.</note>, title 15, all simulated agreements are prohibited under heavy penalties, Alvarus Valascus understands this not to apply to those simulations which prejudice neither the royal treasury nor any other private party, as is the case here; he affirms that judges have always ruled this way. Indeed, such a judgment should be made through *epikeia* <note>A legal concept meaning "equity" or a "reasonable deviation" from the strict letter of the law to achieve justice.</note>, since the act was not done with the intent of defrauding the treasury of the portion of the penalty the husband might incur for a crime—which is not usually the case in Portugal, especially where marriages are largely celebrated under the contract of "half-and-half" ownership of goods <note>Latin: "contractu medietatis bonorum"; a communal property arrangement between spouses.</note>.

<margin>Question</margin>
More frequently, husbands make a confession of a received dowry which they have not received (or not in such a quantity) sometimes in hope of future payment which never followed, and sometimes with the intent of gifting to the wife what was not actually received. There is no small controversy among the doctors when it is not clearly evident from the circumstances which of these occurred. If the payment or delivery of the dowry is not proven, should it be presumed in the external court that the husband’s confession was made in hope of payment, or with the intent of gifting it to the wife?

<margin>Decision</margin>
Indeed, when the confession was made before the marriage was celebrated, and the marriage subsequently followed, it is the common opinion of almost everyone that unless it clearly appears otherwise that the husband intended to give a gift, it must be presumed and judged that it was made in the hope of future payment. This is especially true since a husband could easily be led to confess receipt of a dowry in the hope of future payment simply to speed up the marriage and gain his bride. The doctors referred to by Alvarus Valascus (Consultation 5, number 5) follow this view. This is confirmed because it is not to be presumed that a husband wished to marry without a dowry or with a very small one. Furthermore, before a marriage is contracted, there is usually not such great passion between the spouses that they would intend to forgive such a large sum. Likewise, the intent to donate is regularly not presumed in law (as seen in the law *Concerning the Undue*, at the passage "for it is not," in the Digest *On Proofs* and other laws). And as we shall add below, if the intent then had been to donate, the act would have been entirely invalid; an interpretation should not be chosen that would render the act a nullity. Finally, if a confession of receipt made before marriage were not interpreted this way, the laws cited regarding an unpaid dowry would never have a place.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of dowry confessions, specifically addressing whether an acknowledgment of receiving a dowry made by a husband before or after the wedding ceremony should be legally treated as a genuine receipt, a strategic gift to the wife, or a mere "hope" of receiving the money later.</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

### Page 498

When it is established that a confession of a received dowry was made before the marriage was celebrated, and it was done with the intent of gifting that amount to the wife and binding oneself to return it upon the dissolution of the marriage, Alvarus Valascus (in the passage cited above) along with others he cites, asserts that such a confession is void as a gift. Consequently, neither the husband nor his heirs are bound to return it. This is proven from the first law of the Code *Concerning gifts before marriage* <note>Latin: "l. 1. C. de donat. ante nupt."</note>, which states: *“It makes a great difference whether the things a husband gives were actually delivered to the wife and later received back as a dowry, or whether he increased the dowry with the intent of gifting so that he appears to have received what he did not actually receive. In the first case, the gift is not hindered... in the latter case, however, nothing was achieved by the gift; and what was not given as a dowry cannot be reclaimed.”* Thus far the law.

Otherwise, you might object: In Dispute 289, following Navarrus, we taught that a gift made between a man and woman before marriage, but intended to remain during the marriage, is treated just like gifts made between spouses while already married. We confirmed this with various laws. Furthermore, a gift of a dowry or an "increase of dowry" made by a husband to a wife during the marriage is valid to the effect that if the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death, it remains confirmed and is owed to the wife. Therefore, in a similar way, that gift of a dowry made before the marriage should be valid so that if the marriage ends by the husband's death and was not revoked by him while alive, the wife can reclaim it from the husband's heirs. To this argument, while the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied unless that gift had been repeated and confirmed by the husband while the marriage was ongoing. The reason is that for a gift between spouses to be valid in that way, it is necessary that delivery of the gifted thing occurs. Since a dowry does not legally function as a dowry until the marriage follows—at which time, although it is owed to the wife by the husband, it must remain with the husband to support the burdens of marriage—it follows that an increase or establishment of a dowry made by the husband’s gift during the marriage is regarded as if it were "virtually delivered" by the husband to the wife and then placed back with the husband by the wife to be returned when the marriage ends. For this reason, that gift is valid. However, when the increase or establishment of the dowry is made by the husband’s gift before the marriage contract, since that virtual delivery from husband to wife does not then occur, the gift is entirely invalid. This is what the law defines.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
When the acknowledgment of a received dowry was made *after* the marriage was celebrated, and it is not clear from the circumstances or otherwise whether it was made in the hope of the dowry being counted out <note>i.e., actually paid in cash later</note> or with the intent of gifting it to the wife, the more common opinion of the doctors (which Covarruvias reports and Alvarus Valascus follows) is that it should be presumed to have been made with the intent of gifting it to the wife. They are led to this because this controversy can only arise when a husband contracted marriage with no dowry previously promised or received. Indeed, if a promise or confession of receipt had preceded the marriage, and it was clear it had occurred, and then a *new* confession was made during the marriage, the husband would be truly judged to have received the dowry and compelled to pay it. He would not be allowed

<column-break/>

to use the <term>defense of the unpaid dowry</term> <note>Latin: "exceptio dotis non numeratæ." A legal defense where a party admits to signing a contract for money but claims they never actually received the physical cash.</note>, because a profession made after an interval, or a doubled confession of receipt, excludes that defense. Therefore, since this controversy only applies when a husband married without a prior promise, it is not likely that the husband later issued a confession of receipt solely in the hope that it would be paid in the future. Rather, there is a strong presumption in that case that the husband, led by his wife’s charms, intended to gift it to her. They argue further that gifts between spouses are generally prohibited unless delivery intervenes and it is confirmed by the death of the donor. Regularly, when a confession of receiving something comes from "suspicious persons" <note>In legal terms, "suspicious persons" often refers to those in a close relationship (like spouses) where collusion or fraud to protect assets from creditors might occur.</note>, it is presumed fraudulent. Thus, a confession of a received dowry is presumed to be made simply with the intent of gifting. Altriatus and others cited by Covarruvias believe this opinion is true only when the husband not only confessed to receiving the dowry after the marriage but also renounced the defense of the unpaid dowry; otherwise, if he did not renounce the defense, the presumption of a gift is less certain.

Covarruvias, however, along with Ancharanus and others, thinks instead that a confession of receipt made after the marriage contract should, in cases of doubt, be judged as made not with the intent of gifting, but in the hope of future payment. He holds this even if the husband renounces the defense of the unpaid dowry.
The first reason is that when another reason can be given, a gift should never be presumed. In this matter, a reason for the confession can be clearly given: the hope of future payment.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Second, if it were presumed to be a gift from the husband to the wife, it would surely be confirmed by his death, and thus his heirs could not argue after his death that the dowry was never paid. Yet, the law <note>The Code and subsequent authentications</note> grants the heirs of the husband the defense of the unpaid dowry.

I, certainly, do not dare to depart from the common opinion of the doctors, especially because of the first reason we proposed, which you will not find presented with such force by others.
Hence, regarding Covarruvias's first point, it must be said that his premise is true when a "suitable" alternative reason can be given based on the circumstances and the law. But in this case, a confession made after the wedding cannot suitably be explained as a mere "hope of future payment."
To the second point, while granting the premise, it must be said that those laws and others Covarruvias cites are to be understood as applying when the confession was made *before* the marriage was celebrated—as is usually done when there is hope of future delivery—or when it is openly clear that it was made after the marriage specifically because of that hope.

<summary>This page discusses the legal presumptions surrounding a husband's confession of receiving a dowry. Molina argues that if such a confession is made after the wedding without prior promises, it should be legally treated as a gift to the wife (animo donandi) rather than a mere expectation of future payment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the "confession of a dowry"—a formal legal acknowledgment by a husband that he has received a dowry, even if the money has not yet changed hands. It focuses on the legal implications of such acknowledgments when made after the wedding ceremony.</meta>

# Second Treatise: Dispute 439

There are indeed several things to be observed regarding these matters. The first is: if a confession of a dowry made after the marriage has been celebrated is, in case of doubt, to be considered a gift from the husband to the wife, it does not require any other formal delivery <note>Latin: "traditio"</note> to be valid. This is because a gift of a dowry made by a husband to his wife is then considered as a delivery, as was explained above. This is established in Law 1 of the Code *Concerning a secured dowry not yet paid* <note>Latin: "l. 1. C. de dote cauta non numerata"</note> and is confirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvarus Valascus (Consultation 5, cited at number 16) and Covarruvias (number 5) cite and follow. It would be otherwise, however, regarding a confession of a received dowry made with the express intent of giving *before* the marriage was celebrated, as was stated and explained above according to Law 1 of the Code *Concerning gifts before marriage*.

Second: if that same confession made after the marriage is celebrated is, in case of doubt, to be considered a gift, then upon the death of the husband before the wife, it is confirmed by law, and consequently must be paid to the wife by the husband's heirs. Meanwhile, however, as long as the marriage lasts, it is considered able to be revoked by the husband; and it is considered revoked if a divorce occurs between them.

Likewise, if a husband has confessed to having received a specific piece of his own property as a dowry from his wife, and then he alienates <note>To "alienate" here means to sell, gift, or transfer ownership to someone else.</note> that property, the gift is considered revoked in regard to that item. Furthermore, the gift expires and is rendered invalid if the wife departs from this life before the husband. All these points are established from what was said regarding gifts between husband and wife in Dispute 289, and they are affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvarus Valascus and Covarruvias (as cited above) refer to and follow. In this context, observe whether the husband, after the marriage was celebrated, confessed to receiving something from the wife as a dowry in a situation where (as explained in the cited Dispute 289) a gift between spouses is immediately confirmed and rendered irrevocable. In such a case, the gift made through that confession is rendered irrevocable even before the death of the husband. For example, if a commoner who has become wealthy has married a noble woman, or an old man has married a young, beautiful virgin, and after the celebration of the marriage—in compensation for her nobility, virginity, youth, or beauty—he confesses to having received such-and-such a dowry from her which he did not actually receive: by that very act, that establishment or increase of the dowry remains confirmed and irrevocable according to the points discussed in the cited dispute. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvarus Valascus (Consultation 5, cited at numbers 17 and 18) refers to and follows.

<margin>
10
Decision
</margin>
However, as we showed in the cited dispute, although a gift between husband and wife may be confirmed by law and become irrevocable, there is no small controversy among the doctors as to whether a presumed gift of this kind—arising from a confession of a received dowry made by a husband after the celebration of marriage—is also confirmed by an oath <note>Latin: "iuramentum"</note> and rendered irrevocable. The common opinion of the doctors, which Covarruvias (cited at numbers 4 and 5) and Alvarus Valascus (cited at number 18) refer to and follow, asserts that if there is an oath regarding the dowry (confessing it as received but to be paid in the future) or an oath not to go against that confession, then it is confirmed and rendered irrevocable. And this must undoubtedly be affirmed, regardless of what Covarruvias adds at the cited number 5. For just as it is judged a gift in the <term>external forum</term> <note>The "external forum" refers to the public, secular, or ecclesiastical legal courts, as opposed to the internal "forum of conscience."</note> according to the more common opinion of the doctors (which we embrace), so in the same forum it must be judged to be entirely confirmed by such an oath. I said "in the external forum" because in the <term>forum of conscience</term>, if the confession was not made with the intent of giving, but rather in the hope of future payment, then the oath to pay it in the future does not bind. This is because that promise confirmed by an oath contains a tacit condition: "if

<margin>Question</margin>

<column-break/>

the dowry is actually counted out and delivered," as was said above.

<margin>11</margin>
However, there is a greater controversy: if that promise is confirmed by an oath in this manner—"I swear that I have received so much of a dowry"—whether by that very fact it is considered confirmed by oath and irrevocable as a gift. Indeed, many deny this. They argue that such an oath is "assertory" (asserting a past fact) and not "promissory" (promising not to contest the gift in the future); and an oath that is not promissory does not confirm a gift. Also, because an oath creates no binding force when it is applied to a simulated <note>A "simulated" contract is a legal fiction or a "fake" agreement made for appearances, lacking true intent.</note> contract, since true consent is missing. Therefore, when such an oath is taken regarding a confession that simulates a received dowry—when in truth it was not received—the consequence is that it induces no obligation. However, Alvarus Valascus (cited above at number 19) believes it *is* confirmed by that oath. <margin>Decision</margin> And I judge that this latter opinion should be followed. For those words have and produce this meaning (in which they must be judged to have been uttered, so that we do not say the oath was taken in vain, which should not be presumed of anyone if it can be reasonably avoided): "I swear that I give so much dowry to my wife, which I therefore confess I have received from her by virtue of this act." This follows what was said above regarding Law 2 of the Code *Concerning a secured dowry not yet paid*, from the gloss there, and from the common opinion of the doctors. Furthermore, an assertory oath, by which one affirms that he is giving something, contains by its nature a promissory commitment to always stand by the gift; and for that reason, it firms up a gift that would otherwise be revocable. In the forum of conscience, however, if it was not the intention of the one confirming it in that way to actually receive the dowry, but rather to falsely affirm he received what he did not, then even if he had the intent to give that same dowry under that "cloak," nevertheless that gift is not confirmed by that oath. Instead, in the same forum, it would be within his right to revoke it while he lived; and the same would apply in the external forum if that intention were established there. To the first argument to the contrary, it must be said that it has been explained how that oath by its nature includes a promise. To the second, it must be said that it has been similarly explained how the oath applies both to the promise that the confession presupposes, and also to the virtual receipt of the dowry which is truly signified by that confession. Observe also that when there is a true intention of swearing—even if it is applied to a thing that someone feigns or lies about doing, or rather is done while swearing in anger—nevertheless, if the thing about which the oath is taken is not evil, the oath obliges him to fulfill it. For instance, if I swear that I will give you a hundred, with the intention of deceiving you and not giving it, I am nonetheless bound to give it to you by virtue of the oath employed. Similarly, if I swear that I will enter a religious order, with the intention of swearing but not of entering, I am similarly bound under the guilt of mortal sin to enter the order.

<margin>12</margin>
Further regarding this matter, Covarruvias (cited at number 4) observes with others whom he cites: when a confession made after the marriage contract has the force of a gift, it does not matter whether the time for the "exception of an unpaid dowry" <note>A legal defense where a husband could argue he never actually received the money he confessed to receiving.</note> has elapsed or not. By the very fact that the gift is confirmed by the husband's death, or has been confirmed otherwise beforehand, it can be demanded by the wife or by her heirs after the husband's death, whether the time for the exception of an unpaid dowry has passed or not.

Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

Furthermore, in the same place, he observes along with many others and records it as the common opinion that, in the same event <margin>13</margin>, a wife does not possess a right of <term>mortgage</term> <note>Latin: "hypotheca"</note> or priority over other creditors—even personal ones—regarding a dowry that was simply confessed by the husband in this way. Nor should this case be handled differently than other gifts between a husband and wife. This is surely correct: since there may be a suspicion that this was done to defraud creditors, the wife certainly ought not to enjoy the privileges of a dowry to the detriment of creditors when dealing with such a "confessed" dowry. This follows the reasoning of the <term>Authentica</term> <note>A term for a specific decree in Roman law</note> titled *Sed iam necesse* in the Code *Concerning gifts before marriage* <note>Latin: "C. de don. ante nup."</note>, where it is decreed that if a husband is burdened by debt and the wife increases the dowry in movable goods, that increase lacks dotal privileges; this is because there is a suspicion that it was done to defraud creditors.

### The defense of the unpaid dowry: to what extent it is available to the husband's creditors against the wife and her heirs.

## DISPUTATION 440

->SUMMARY<-

1 *Whether the husband's creditors can always raise the <term>defense of the unpaid dowry</term> <note>Latin: "exceptio non numeratæ dotis"; a legal claim that the money was acknowledged but never actually handed over</note> against the wife or her heirs regarding a documented dowry, and the following numbers.*
2 *If a confession of a dowry is proven to have been made in fraud, it will never harm the husband's creditors.*
3 *A husband’s confession alone that a dowry was received does not prejudice his own creditors, unless the time limits for raising the defense of non-payment have passed, or the defense was waived.*
4 *A confession of a received dowry made before the marriage or during the celebration itself—once the time for the defense has passed—not only prejudices the husband's creditors, but the wife is actually preferred over them regarding that dowry. (Note the clarification provided there).*
5 *A waiver of the defense of the unpaid dowry made by a husband does not harm his creditors.*
6 *When a confession of a received dowry made by a husband during the marriage harms the creditors, and when it does not.*
7 *If a promise of a dowry preceded the marriage, and a confession of the received dowry followed during the marriage, whether the wife is preferred over the husband’s creditors regarding such a dowry.*

<margin>1</margin> The gloss of Accursius on the law *Assiduis* (under the word "datæ" in the Code *Who may have a pledge*) taught without distinction that a confessed dowry does not harm the husband's creditors. Instead, the creditors are always preferred over the wife in the case of a merely confessed dowry; they can raise the defense of the unpaid dowry so that, if the wife or her heirs do not prove it was truly paid, the creditors are preferred over the wife regarding that dowry. Imola and others followed this same opinion, whom Alvarus Valascus records in Consultation 6, number 2. However, Bartolus, on the cited law *Assiduis*—whose opinion is recorded in the addition to the cited gloss of Accursius—and others judge that if the time limits granted to the husband and his heirs to claim that the dowry was not paid have not yet passed, and the husband has not waived the defense, then

<column-break/>

the husband’s creditors can raise the defense against the wife or her heirs that the dowry was not actually paid. They are preferred over the wife and her heirs if these cannot prove the payment occurred. If, however, the time limits for raising the defense have passed, or the husband has waived the defense, then the wife is preferred over the husband’s creditors, even if they have prior <term>tacit mortgages</term> <note>A legal claim on property that exists by law without needing a formal contract</note>, according to what was said in Disputation 438. Alexander, however, on the first law of the Digest *On the dissolution of marriage* <note>Latin: "ff. solut. mat."</note>, while agreeing with Bartolus on other points, argues that a waiver of the defense made by the husband brings no prejudice to the creditors; he believes that within the entire time given to the husband and his heirs to raise the defense, the creditors themselves can claim the dowry was never paid. This dispute, however, must be resolved by the following conclusions.

<margin>2</margin> **First conclusion.** If the fraudulent nature of a confession of a received dowry is established by proofs or strong conjectures, that confession will never harm the husband’s creditors. This is clear and is affirmed by Alvarus Valascus (Consultation 6, cited at number 3) and Covarruvias (1 *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7, number 7, second part). Alvarus Valascus, along with Alciatus, says this matter should be left to the judge's discretion, as the proofs or conjectures must be sufficient for that purpose. The same is confirmed by the *Authentica* "Sed iam necesse" in the Code *On gifts before marriage* and other laws cited by Alvarus Valascus.

<margin>3</margin> **Second conclusion.** In the meantime, while the time limits for the defense of the unpaid dowry have not expired—if the husband has not waived that defense—the husband’s confession of a received dowry alone does not prejudice his creditors. This holds even if the creditors only have a personal right; they can raise the defense against the wife and her heirs that the dowry was not paid. Everyone agrees on this, as is evident from the doctors cited and followed by Alvarus Valascus (Conclusion 2), Antonio Gomez (Law 50 of *Toro*, number 52), and Covarruvias (1 *Various Resolutions*, chapter 7, number 7). Furthermore, it is clearly gathered from the law *Si cui* in the Code *Concerning non-numbered money* <note>Latin: "C. de non nu. pec."</note>. It says that since the defense (either of unpaid money or unpaid dowry) is available to the principal debtor—even if he does not raise it—his creditors can nevertheless raise it. This is certainly true as a minimum and is accepted by everyone during the period in which the principal debtor himself can raise the defense.

<margin>4</margin> **Third conclusion.** If the confession of a received dowry was made before the marriage was celebrated, or during the celebration itself, and the time granted to the husband and his heirs to raise the defense has passed, then the husband’s creditors cannot raise the defense against the wife and her heirs that the dowry was not paid. Instead, the wife is preferred over them regarding that dowry, even if they have prior tacit mortgages on the husband's assets. This is the opinion of Bartolus and is the common view, as recorded and followed by Antonio Gomez (Law 50 of *Toro*, number 52) and Covarruvias (number 7, cited at the word "de creditoribus"). Antonio Gomez and Covarruvias excellently explain the law *Si cui* in the Code *Concerning non-numbered money*. They argue it only means that while normally no one can use a privilege granted to another against that person's will, creditors in this specific case can raise the defense even if their debtor is unwilling or silent—but only within the time allowed to the debtor. No greater or different privilege is granted to them than to their debtor. However, Antonio Gomez and Alvarus Valascus observe...

<summary>This page discusses the "exception of the unpaid dowry," exploring when creditors can challenge a husband's formal acknowledgment of receiving a dowry to prevent fraud. It concludes that creditors are generally bound by the same legal time limits as the husband unless active fraud can be proven.</summary>
