<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "defense of the unpaid dowry" (exceptio non numeratæ dotis). It builds on the previous discussion regarding whether a husband's confession of receiving a dowry is binding against his creditors, especially when there is a suspicion of fraud or "gift-giving" between spouses to shield assets.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 440.
Ii 3
catchword: Which

consultation 6, cited at the end, number 5, and others whom they cite. If the creditors had neglected to raise this defense against the wife and her heirs during that whole time because they were <note>Latin: "ignorarent"</note> unaware that the husband possessed it, then they could be helped by the general clause regarding the benefit of <term>restitution to the original state</term> <note>Latin: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy to restore parties to their original position before a contract or judgment</note>. However, although *Alvaro Valasco*, at the cited number 5, seems to establish this third conclusion of ours as the common one and affirms it has been judged so in practice (number 12), nevertheless, in that same number 12 and the two following, he thinks the opinion of *Accursius* <note>A famous 13th-century Italian jurist</note> should rather be embraced. This opinion holds that even after the time limits given to the principal debtor to object have passed, his creditors still have the right to object that the money or dowry was <note>Latin: "non numeratam"; literally "not counted out," meaning the funds were never actually transferred</note> never actually paid. Therefore, the wife should not be preferred over the husband’s creditors regarding such a dowry. He argues that the husband’s sole confession—since he is usually very affectionately disposed toward his wife—ought not to bring prejudice or harm to the husband's creditors. Nevertheless, I believe we must stick to the common opinion: because a confession of debt in other instances counts as delivery; however, in the case of a debt involving a loan or a dowry, a unique privilege is granted to debtors to object, and this same privilege is extended to the debtor's creditors by the law *si cur.* in the Code *Concerning the defense of unpaid money*. Yet, this is granted in no other way, nor for a longer time, than it is granted to the debtors themselves.

Regarding the outcome of this third conclusion, *Covarruvias* <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> (where cited above at the section *from the premises*) rightly affirms that whether the debt to the creditors arises from a loan, a dowry, or any other title, and whether the defense of unpaid money applies against them or not, the wife is always preferred over them. For if, in the outcome of this conclusion—when what is owed by the husband is certain—the wife is preferred over creditors even if they have <term>tacit prior mortgages</term> <note>Legal claims on property that exist automatically by law without a written contract</note>, she will be preferred with much greater reason when the debt is not so firm, but the defense of unpaid money remains available against the husband's creditors. Nor does *Alvaro Valasco* (at numbers 8 and 9 above) seem to contradict this. For, as is clear from the conclusion he adds at number 10, he is not speaking about the outcome of our third conclusion.

<margin>5</margin>
**The Fourth Conclusion.** A renunciation of the defense of the unpaid dowry made by the husband, although it may harm him and his heirs, does not harm the husband's creditors. Therefore, with nothing hindering them, they can object within the time granted for objecting that the dowry was not actually paid. This stands against *Bartolus* and many others whom *Antonio Gomez* follows (at cited number 52); however, *Covarruvias* (at the section *but if the confession*) and *Alvaro Valasco* (at number 6) affirm it along with *Alexander* and others. The reason is that although the husband can renounce the privilege of objecting within the times granted to him to his own detriment and that of his heirs, he cannot renounce a privilege granted to creditors for their own advantage and benefit within those same times.

<margin>6</margin>
**The Fifth Conclusion.** When the confession of a received dowry was made by the husband while the marriage was already in progress, even if the time limits granted to the husband and his heirs to object to the unpaid dowry have passed, the wife and her heirs are not preferred over the husband's creditors. Instead, the creditors can object that the dowry was not actually paid. This is affirmed by *Covarruvias* (Chapter 7, number 7), *Antonio Gomez* (Law 50 of Toro, number 42), and *Alvaro Valasco* (Consultation 5, cited at the end, number

<column-break/>

11). This is consistent with *Bartolus*, as *Covarruvias* shows in the section *that furthermore*. It is confirmed because a confession made at that time is presumed to be a gift from the husband to the wife, as was said in the preceding disputation. In the case of gifts from a husband to a wife, the wife is not preferred over other creditors, as was also stated there.

When a confession of a received dowry is made while the marriage is ongoing, then, if the husband's creditors prove their own debt based solely on the husband's confession under a title of purchase, deposit, or another that is not a loan or a dowry, they are to be preferred to the wife regarding such a dowry confessed by the husband. This is because, under such titles, the sole confession of the debtor sufficiently proves the debt when there is no evidence of fraud in such a confession. If, however, they prove it from a confession of a loan alone, then if the two-year period granted for objecting to unpaid money has passed, and there is no evidence of fraud in the confession, the same must be said. Otherwise, such creditors will be excluded both by the wife and the heirs of the deceased husband by the defense of unpaid money; and thus, the wife will prevail if the time limits for the defense of the unpaid dowry have passed. According to these points, one should approve what *Alvaro Valasco* (numbers 8 and 9) and *Covarruvias* (number 7, section *from the premises*) hand down on this matter along with others.

<margin>7</margin>
**A Doubt.** What if a promise of a dowry had preceded the marriage, and the confession of the received dowry followed while the marriage was already in progress? Would the wife then be preferred over the husband's creditors regarding that dowry? *Covarruvias* and *Alvaro Valasco* report that not only do many assert this, but even *Matthaeus de Afflictis* <note>A Neapolitan jurist</note> affirms it was decided by the unanimous consent of the Neapolitan Senate and later confirmed by a Royal sentence. All these authors argue this because, in that event, the law strongly presumes that the dowry was delivered. For that reason, it denies the husband and his heirs the defense of the unpaid dowry, as was seen in the preceding disputation. Thus, in that event, the wife is no less to be preferred over the husband's creditors regarding the dowry than if it were established that the money had been paid. However, *Alvaro Valasco* affirms the contrary there: because that presumption and the denial of the defense of the unpaid dowry in that event only exist in comparison to the husband and his heirs, whom he could prejudice in that way, but not in comparison to the creditors. *Covarruvias* also seems to approach this same opinion along with *Baldus Novellus*, especially when the husband was already burdened by debt at the time of the confession.

Finally, one must observe what *Covarruvias* and others whom he refers to say. What has been said in this and the preceding disputation regarding a dowry confessed by a husband primarily applies to **movable goods**. For if the husband had confessed that he received certain **immovable goods** <note>Real estate, such as land or buildings</note> as a dowry, surely, if the delivery were not established, and neither the wife nor her heirs specified and sufficiently proved what those goods were and that they had been delivered to the husband as a dowry, that confession would be regarded as false and null. It is clear enough that if any immovable goods had been delivered to him, it ought to be easily established what they were, and that they had once belonged to the wife or to another who had delivered them as a dowry in the wife's place.

It establishes that while a husband's acknowledgment might bind him, it cannot easily be used to defraud creditors, especially if the acknowledgment happened during the marriage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how assets are divided between a husband and wife (or their heirs) when a marriage ends. It builds on the previous analysis of the dowry, now moving to other types of property like personal belongings and betrothal gifts.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

### Which other goods the wife and her heirs may set aside, and which privileges they enjoy. Likewise, what the husband or his heirs may take, and how the partition of property is finalized.

## DISPUTATION 441.

->SUMMARY<-

1. *The wife possesses a tacit mortgage on the husband's goods even for her paraphernal goods, provided he administered them.*
2. *However, she does not have the privilege of preference against other earlier creditors, as that is granted only to the dowry (number 2).*
3. *Beyond paraphernal goods, the wife also sets aside betrothal gifts from the husband’s goods. Likewise, donations confirmed upon the dissolution of the marriage, and the earnest money promised to her (numbers 4, 5).*
6. *The earnest money must be paid to the wife from the husband’s goods alone, after the division of profits between husband and wife has been performed.*
7. *How the partition of goods is to be made between the husband and wife, or their heirs.*

**A** In Disputation 438, we began to speak of the partition of goods between spouses or their heirs when a marriage is dissolved. Regarding the dowry, which the wife or her heirs set aside <note>Latin: "extrahunt"; literally 'to draw out' or extract from the shared marital estate before division</note> before all else, much was said in the three preceding disputations. Now let us continue and complete the same partition of goods. Beyond the dowry, the wife or her heirs next set aside all the wife's <term>paraphernal goods</term> <note>Latin: "bona paraphernalia"; from the Greek 'para' (beside) and 'pherne' (dowry). These were personal items like clothing and jewelry that remained the wife's property outside the formal dowry</note>.

1 <margin>1</margin> Regarding these goods, † all the husband's assets are also under a <term>tacit mortgage</term> <note>Latin: "tacita hypotheca"; a legal lien that exists by law even without a written contract</note>, provided that the husband had the administration of those paraphernal goods, either tacitly or expressly. This is regularly the case in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, as has often been said above. This is held in the Code <note>The Code of Justinian</note> under the titles *On Agreed Pacts* and *On the Right of Dowry*, and in the *Siete Partidas* <note>A 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note> (Partida 4, Title 11, Law 17). This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which is followed by Gregorio López, Antonio Gómez, Covarrubias, and Gutiérrez.

2 <margin>2</margin> However, † the woman does not have the <term>privilege of preference</term> <note>Latin: "praelatio"; the right to be paid first among several creditors</note> over other earlier creditors regarding these goods. The privilege of preference is found to be granted to the dowry alone. This is affirmed by the gloss on the Digest and the common opinion of the doctors cited above.

3 <margin>3</margin> Beyond † paraphernal goods, the wife sets aside <term>betrothal gifts</term> <note>Latin: "sponsalitia largitas"; gifts given by the groom to the bride before the wedding</note>, which were discussed in Disputation 290, unless she has already received and consumed them for her own use. However, in the Kingdom of Castile, as stated in Disputations 290 and 431, if <term>earnest money</term> <note>Latin: "arrhae"; a gift or deposit given at the time of the marriage contract to confirm the union</note> was also promised to her, she may only set aside either the earnest money or the betrothal gifts, whichever she or her heirs prefer. Antonio Gómez asserts that the wife has a tacit mortgage on the husband's goods for betrothal gifts if the husband sold them during the marriage.

<column-break/>

But she does not have the right of preference compared to the husband’s creditors. However, I do not see the law—nor does he cite it—from which such a tacit mortgage would be inferred.

4 <margin>4</margin> Likewise, † if any gift was given by the husband to the wife while the marriage stood, and the donation was confirmed at least upon the dissolution of the marriage (according to what was said in Disputation 289), the wife also sets that aside, if it can still be found. She does not, however, have a tacit mortgage on the husband's goods regarding these donated items.

5 <margin>5</margin> Beyond † all these, <term>earnest money</term> <note>Latin: "arrhae"</note> is owed to the wife if any was duly promised to her. Regarding these, Antonio Gómez (at number 41) affirms that the wife has a tacit mortgage on the husband's goods, though without the privilege of preference over other creditors. But I consider this to be false, because there is no legal text from which it can be inferred. Furthermore, in <term>Common Law</term> <note>Latin: "ius commune"; the shared legal system of Roman and Canon law in Europe</note>, these were not used in the sense we are now discussing. Therefore, a tacit mortgage is not granted for earnest money in that sense under common law. Unless, therefore, the husband obligates his goods for the payment of the earnest money by a specific contract, the wife does not have a mortgage for them on the man’s goods.

<margin>Decision.</margin> Whether the earnest money should be paid to the wife from the shared profits <note>Latin: "lucra communia"</note> of the husband and wife (if any are found after the marriage is dissolved), or rather from the husband's goods alone, after the division of both the capital and the profits has been made.

6 <margin>6</margin> It must † be said that they are to be paid from the husband’s goods alone. First, because it is a debt of the husband alone in relation to the wife; therefore, it comes from his half, while the other half of the estate belongs to the wife. Second, because even when there are no profits, the earnest money is paid in full from the husband's capital; therefore, to maintain equality for wives, they should be paid from the husband's portion alone even when there are profits, and not from the goods common to both. Third, because only those debts contracted for the sake of profit *after* the marriage began and the partnership was formed are paid from the shared profits. Earnest money, however, is promised by the husband *before* the partnership begins, and is owed by him because of that contract once the marriage follows. Therefore, it must be paid from the husband's goods alone. For this reason, we do not compute the earnest money with the capital that the wife or her heirs set aside before the profits; rather, we reserve it as a debt to be paid from the husband's goods alone after all profits have been divided. This covers the capital that the wife or her heirs set aside before all else from the goods found at the time the marriage is dissolved.

7 <margin>7</margin> Afterward, the husband † or his heirs set aside the husband's entire capital, which was explained in Disputation 433. They set it aside if enough goods remain to do so; otherwise, the entire loss falls on the husband and his heirs alone. If, however, after the capital of both spouses has been set aside and all debts paid, any goods remain, these are called "surplus profits" <note>Latin: "superlucrata"</note> common to both spouses. These are to be divided into two halves: one belongs to the husband or his heirs, and the other to the wife or her heirs. Additionally, the earnest money must be paid to the wife or her heirs from the husband's goods, if any was duly promised. And thus, the partition of goods between husband and wife is completed. What either the husband or wife receives...

Treatise Second, Disputation 442. <note>Note: While the header says 442, the internal heading below identifies this section as Disputation 444, reflecting the complexity of early modern legal indexing.</note>

...ought to be specifically considered, or calculated into their respective parts, has been explained in various places throughout the progress of this work on justice; those matters which still require explanation will be set down in their proper places in the following sections. A similar division of goods must be made between spouses when the property of one of them is confiscated due to the crime of heresy <note>Heresy was a capital crime often resulting in the total seizure of assets by the state or church</note> or another offense. Indeed, the capital of the spouse whose goods are confiscated, along with half of the profits found to belong to them up until the passing of the sentence, pertains to the treasury; furthermore, the <term>arrhae</term> <note>original: "arrhæ"; betrothal gifts or earnest money</note>, if it is the wife whose goods are seized and to whom the gifts were owed, also belong to the treasury. To the other spouse, however, all their own goods remain intact.

When the wife has brought an office, or if certain gifts and offices are found among the surplus profits—such as the <term>regimiento</term> <note>A municipal administrative office</note> in this Kingdom of Castile, which are considered valuable but cannot be physically divided—and because a woman may not be capable of holding the office herself, whether the valuation pertains to the dowry or the wife's capital, or whether half the valuation belongs to her as a "surplus profit" <note>Latin: "bonum superlucratum"</note>, and when it does not, was discussed in Disputation 241. Covarruvias, in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 19, number 5, states: If a husband, during the marriage, builds a church from their common goods and reserves for himself the <term>right of patronage</term> <note>The right to nominate a priest to a vacant benefice</note> for presenting candidates to it, that right is common to the wife and husband; the wife, in turn, transmits the right of presentation to her heirs along with the husband’s heirs. Although that right is indivisible in itself and exists as a whole by the nature of the law, it belongs to the heirs of the husband and the heirs of the wife by virtue of their partial shares; it is nevertheless divisible regarding the exercise of presentation, and in that way they can divide the exercise of it among themselves.

## DISPUTATION 444

### SUMMARY

<margin>1</margin> Within what time the dowry and other goods of the woman must be paid by the husband’s heirs to the woman herself or her heirs.
And concerning the law of Castile and Portugal (number 2).
<margin>3</margin> From what time the fruits of the dowry begin to be owed to the woman.
<margin>4</margin> The wife must be maintained from the husband’s goods, if she does not have support from elsewhere, until the dowry is paid to her.
And much more so if she remained pregnant, whether the dowry has been handed over to her or not (number 5).
And what is observed in Portugal.
<margin>6</margin> A husband is bound to the payment of the dowry only insofar as he is able to perform it.
However, see the declaration there.
The same must be said for certain other persons who enjoy this privilege (number 7).

<margin>1</margin> **A**S was stated in Disputation 235, according to common law, not only when a marriage is dissolved by the death of the wife

<column-break/>

does the husband remain in possession of the goods as the head of the family, and from him the wife’s heirs must receive what belongs to her; but also, when a marriage is ended by the death of the husband, the husband’s heirs remain in possession of the goods as the head of the family, and from them the widowed wife receives what belongs to her. And the same is observed in Portugal, when some celebrate a marriage with a contract of <term>arrhae</term> and dowry, except regarding the goods which, upon the dissolution of the marriage, are found to be common to both spouses. For when the marriage is dissolved by the death of the husband, the wife remains in possession of these goods, and from her the husband’s heirs must receive the portion that pertained to the husband. This is found in the *Ordinances*, Book 4, Title 7, § 4. Often in that same Kingdom, it is customary to include a pact in the dotal instruments <note>Legal marriage contracts</note> that the wife, if the marriage is dissolved by the husband’s death, shall remain as the head of the family in possession of all goods, and from her the husband’s heirs shall receive what belongs to the husband; and according to the ordinances of that Kingdom, such a pact must be upheld. According to these things, therefore, we say in the first place, in those events in which the wife and her heirs must receive the dowry and other goods of the wife from the hand of the husband or his heirs, within what time they must be paid to her.

<margin>2</margin> Although it was once ordained by common law that the wife or her heirs were bound to restore the dowry on the "annual, biennial, or triennial day"—that is, within three years, restoring one-third part on the last day of each year—nevertheless, it has now been established today that when the dowry consists of unvalued immovable goods <note>Real estate whose value was not fixed in the contract</note>, it must be restored immediately without delay regarding those goods. When, however, it consists of movables, or self-moving things <note>Livestock</note>, or in unvalued physical things, or finally when a certain sum of value is to be returned, then regarding all these things the dowry is to be restored within a year from the day the marriage was dissolved. This is expressly held in the "unique law" in the Code *on actions concerning a wife's property* <note>Latin: "l. vnica. §. exactio. C. de rei vxor. act."</note>, the words of which are: *The extraction of the dowry shall be celebrated not on the annual, biennial, or triennial day, but in every way within a year for movable things, or self-moving things, or physical objects; other things, namely those which are contained in the soil, being restored immediately.* The same is held in the *Siete Partidas* <note>Latin: "l. pen. tit. 11. par. 4."; the foundational law code of Castile</note>, and is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez relates and follows. Where he adds that today in the Kingdom of Castile, it is customary to include a pact in dotal instruments that the dowry be paid within thirty days of the dissolution of the marriage; and such a pact, or any other that was applied in that regard, must be upheld. I believe the same custom is observed in Portugal. Observe this: once the time within which the dowry was to be restored has passed, the woman and her heirs can sue for interest, as is gathered from the same law in the Code and affirmed by Molina, Gomez, and the doctors commonly.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the fruits of the dowry, a distinction must be made. For if the dotal things are immovables and were handed over to the husband unvalued, then their fruits from the day the marriage was dissolved belong to the wife or her heirs. Similarly, if they are movables handed over unvalued and are productive <note>Latin: "fructiferæ"; e.g., pregnant animals or interest-bearing loans</note>, their fruits also from the day the marriage was dissolved belong to the wife, or to her...

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...the wife's property, such as the offspring of livestock, the hire-fees of a leased ship, of pack-animals, and of leased slaves; the same applies to the payments of rights. However, the use of all these revenues, and even of the dowry itself—when it consists of a sum of money which the husband is bound to pay the wife—belongs to the husband or to his heirs for the entire duration granted to them by law or by agreement for the restoration of the dowry. This is held in the Law *Unica*, section *Sin autem*, at the word *Fructibus*, in the Code on the Action for the Wife’s Property <note>Latin: "l. unica. §. sin auté, ver. fructibus. C. de rei vxor. act."; referring to Justinian’s Code 5.13.1. These were standard Roman Law references used in the 16th century.</note>, the words of which are: *The fruits of immovable property are to be provided to the wife’s side from the time the marriage is dissolved; in like manner, the pensions or freight-charges of ships, or of pack-animals, or the labor of servants, or the profit of civil grain-provisions, and others similar to these, are to be restored to the wife’s side.* The common opinion of the doctors is the same, which Antonio Gómez relates and follows in Law 50 of the Laws of Toro, number 47.

<margin>4</margin>
In the meantime, while the dowry is not yet handed over to the wife within the time established by law or agreement, maintenance <term>alimenta</term> <note>Support including food, clothing, and housing</note> must be provided to her if she does not have it from elsewhere and she requests it. But if any income from the dowry and her own goods belongs to her at that time according to what was just said, she is to be supported from those; if anything is lacking, it must be supplied from the husband's goods. This privilege, however, belongs only to the wife, not to her heirs, as if they ought to be supported in the aforesaid manner during that time. Also during that time, the wife is bound to perform competent and customary duties within the husband's house, such as are fitting for her to perform. If, however, the wife remains

<margin>5</margin>
pregnant, she must be supported entirely from the husband's goods, whether the dowry has been handed over to her or not, and whether she has means of support from elsewhere or not. Furthermore, in the meantime while the dowry is not restored to her, the wife can retain the house in which she lived with her husband, and all the goods found within it. Antonio Gómez affirms all these points at number 48, cited according to various glosses, laws, and doctors which he cites. And Covarruvias affirms almost all of them in his *Epitome on the Fourth Book of the Decretals*, part 2, chapter 8, section 9, numbers 9 and 10. In this place, remember that it was said by us in Disputation 235

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
that in Portugal, with great equity—considering the partnership of goods between spouses at least regarding profits, and that the dowry is given for the support of the wife—it has been received by custom that, upon the dissolution of marriage, the mourning clothes of the surviving spouse, the funeral expenses, and the maintenance of the surviving wife and family until the partition of goods between the spouses occurs, are understood to be paid from the common goods of both spouses, if any surplus profits exist. Otherwise, the wife or her heirs extract in full all those things which, according to what was said in the preceding disputations, belong to the wife; the remainder pertains to the husband or his heirs.

<margin>6</margin>
Regarding the final point proposed in the title of this disputation, it must be said: that a husband is only bound to pay the wife's dowry insofar as he is "comfortably able" <note>Latin: "quantum commodè facere poterit." This is the legal *beneficium competentiae*, a privilege where a debtor is not reduced to destitution to pay a debt.</note>, in the sense explained in Disputation 413 and at the end of Disputation 425. This is true unless he had diminished his substance through fraud; for then he would be compelled to pay it even beyond what he could comfortably do. Furthermore, if the husband cannot comfortably pay the whole dowry, he is bound to provide a guarantee that, if he comes into a more plentiful fortune, he will pay it in full. All these things are expressly held in Law *Unica*, section *Cum autem*, in the Code on the Action for the Wife's Property, and similarly in the Institutes, on Actions, and the Digest, on the dissolution of marriage.

<column-break/>

If, however, the marriage is dissolved by the death of the husband, his heirs are bound for the full amount <term>in solidum</term>; for this privilege belongs to the husband and not to the heirs (Digest, on the dissolution of marriage). An exception is made unless the heirs are the children of the same wife, for these also are only bound for as much as they can comfortably perform (Digest, on the dissolution of marriage, and Law 11, title 11, part 4 <note>The *Siete Partidas*, the foundational law code of Castile</note>). Also, the father-in-law of the wife (the husband's father) can only be sued by the wife regarding the dowry for as much as he can comfortably perform. Yet, if the wife did not have means from elsewhere to feed herself, then any debtors would be bound to grant her as much of her dowry as was necessary for her to support herself, even if it went beyond what they could comfortably do. In this event, no debtor enjoys that privilege against the creditor, as was said with Bartolus, Paulus de Castro, Gregorio López, and Gutierrez in Disputation 413. Likewise, if certain "unvalued" goods <term>bona inæstimata</term> <note>Goods given as dowry that were not assigned a fixed cash value; they remained the property of the wife, whereas "valued" goods became the property of the husband who then owed their cash value.</note> had been given to the husband as dowry, then, because the ownership of them returns to the wife by full right without any delivery upon the dissolution of marriage, the wife is preferred over any creditors in those goods. She will be able to act for the full amount against any heirs of the husband to claim them for herself. And I think the same should be said of the wife's heirs in comparison to the surviving husband, since those goods are not the husband's, so that he may enjoy that privilege in them. Likewise, when the marriage is dissolved by the husband's death, and there are found in the husband's possession any dotal goods which were rightfully delivered as "valued," since these return to the wife regarding ownership so that the dowry may be paid to the wife (as said in the Code and Disputation 426), neither the wife's children (as the husband's heirs) nor the father-in-law enjoy that privilege regarding them. On all these matters, read Antonio Gómez on Law 50 of Toro, number 49.

### Where the dowry and the wife's goods are to be claimed. And according to the laws of which place the marriage contract is considered celebrated. And how far the cause of the dowry pertains to the Ecclesiastical judge.

## DISPUTATION 443.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *The dowry is claimed in the place of the husband's domicile at the time the contract was celebrated, according to the common opinion.*
2 *The laws and customs of the place where the husband had his domicile at the time of the celebration of the dowry contract must be observed, not those of the place where the contract was celebrated.*
3 *Advice for a woman who enters into marriage with a foreigner.*
4 *An ecclesiastical judge can incidentally take notice of a dowry case.*

It is peculiar in the marriage contract that the dowry is not claimed in the place where the contract was celebrated, but in the place of the husband's domicile at the time the contract was celebrated.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the dowry and marital property, specifically focusing on which local laws apply when a husband and wife move between regions. It then transitions into a new Disputation regarding the nature and origin of the emphyteusis contract (a form of long-term land lease).</meta>

<page-num>505</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise. Disputation 444.</header>

<margin>1</margin> The reason is that a wife is held to follow her husband, and she therefore acquires the legal domicile of the husband. For this very reason, it is defined in the law *Exigere dotem* <note>Latin: "l. exigere dotem. ff. de iudicijs"; Digest 5.1.65, a foundational Roman law text regarding where a dowry should be claimed.</note>, and this is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarruvias relates and follows in his *Epitome*, part 2, chapter 7, at the beginning of number 6, as does Antonio Gómez in his commentary on the Laws of Toro, Law 50, number 50.

<margin>2</margin> For the same reason, when nothing else was explicitly stated in the contract, one must abide by the customs and laws of the place in which the husband had his domicile at the time the contract was celebrated. This applies rather than the laws of the place where the contract was signed or where the wife had her domicile, both regarding shared profits <term>lucra</term> or the administration of the wife’s <term>paraphernalia</term> <note>Personal property of a married woman such as clothing and jewelry that was not part of her dowry</note>, as well as any other matters. This is the view of Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarruvias and Antonio Gómez follow in the locations cited above.

An exception is made when the marriage is celebrated with the intention that the husband will live in the place where the wife has her domicile: for then, regarding all these matters, one must abide by the laws of the place of the wife’s domicile. So says Covarruvias, number 8, along with many others whom he cites, and indeed right reason demands it. That is to say, if a man and woman contract in any other place with the intention of living there, then the laws and customs of that place must be followed.

If they celebrate the marriage in one place with the intention of staying there, as usually happens, and later they move to another place with the intention of staying there permanently, and if there are different laws and customs in each place, then one must abide by the laws and customs of the place where the marriage was celebrated, not the laws of the place to which they moved. This is the only thing defined by the law <note>original: "l. 24. tit. 11. par. 4." referring to the Siete Partidas, a major Spanish law code.</note> if its words are correctly weighed. Covarruvias affirms this along with Rodrigo Juárez, and finally Gregorio López agrees regarding that same law. This is not to say that the law intends to contradict those things we have defined up to now from common law and the consensus of the doctors, whatever Antonio Gómez might argue to the contrary. Nor do we approve of what Gregorio López contends regarding the cited law.

Namely, if a contract was celebrated in one place with the intention of staying there, where certain laws and customs regarding profits exist, and later they move to another place with the intention of staying there, where there are different laws: some argue that regarding things acquired in the first place, the first laws apply, but regarding things acquired in the second place, the second laws apply. This, I say, we do not approve. Since a marriage contract is celebrated for a whole lifetime, it is therefore deemed celebrated for a whole lifetime according to the laws and customs of the place where it was celebrated, and according to the other express agreements added at that time.

<margin>3</margin> When a woman contracts with a foreigner with the intention of moving with him, she should inquire into the laws and customs of the place where she is moving, or specify what she wants in the agreement; otherwise, she must blame herself if she contracted to her own detriment according to the laws of the place where she moves. This is especially true when the husband celebrated the contract with her in good faith, not intending to circumvent her in her ignorance. However, when 

<column-break/>

the wife did not know that the man she was contracting with was from another region, and she celebrated the marriage with the intention of staying in the place where she was contracting, then the laws and customs of the place where the contract was celebrated must be followed. Covarruvias agrees on these points in the place cited above.

<margin>4</margin> Since a case involving a dowry is in itself purely secular and between lay persons, it certainly belongs to the secular judges alone to take primary notice of it. However, incidentally and as an accessory, an ecclesiastical judge can also take notice of it, and command and compel that it be paid. For example, if he is taking primary notice of a marriage—whether it is valid or not, or whether there are legitimate causes for a divorce—he can simultaneously command that the dowry be paid to the husband or that the husband restore it to the wife.

The same is noted in the gloss on the chapter *De prudentia*, consistent with the text there regarding donations between husband and wife. According to this doctrine, many canonical laws should be understood which sound as if it belongs to the ecclesiastical judge to take notice of the dowry. Read, among others, Antonio Gómez on the Laws of Toro, Law 50, number 53.

## Where the name "Emphyteusis" comes from.

-> DISPUTATION 444. <-

-> S V M M A R Y <-

1 *Where the name 'Emphyteusis' comes from, with the opinions of others reported.*

After the contract of partnership, we must speak of contracts by which something is granted for use or for its fruits, while the ownership is retained—at least the "direct ownership"—of the thing being granted. Of this sort are <term>Emphyteusis</term> <note>A long-term or perpetual lease of land where the tenant pays a small rent and improves the property</note>, the fief <term>feudum</term>, the *libellarius* contract, the *superficiarius* contract, and the contract of letting and hiring <term>locatio et conductio</term>. We shall begin with emphyteusis, and at the same time we will mix in discussion of the *libellarius* and *superficiarius* contracts if anything needs to be added to what was said in Disputation 10 regarding those two.

Discarding the inept origin of the word *emphyteusis* which the *Speculator* provides and Alvarez Valasco reports, Accursius affirms in the *Authenticum* that emphyteusis is named from <term>emponemata</term> <note>Greek: ἐμπόνημα (emponema), meaning an improvement or something worked upon</note>, as if it were a "contract of improvement." For *emponemata* in Greek means the same as *melioratio* (improvement) in Latin. Accursius taught this same thing in the Institutes, and Sylvester and many others follow him. Accursius gives the reason in the second gloss cited: because in the beginning, only sterile lands were usually handed over in emphyteusis so that they might be improved and brought back to cultivation—though he adds that today even fertile lands, and those not believed to need improvement, are granted in emphyteusis.

For it is not necessary that the thing from which a name is derived should apply universally to everything to which the name is adapted. Others, more correctly along with Alciatus and many others whom Valasco follows, and whose opinion Calepinus approves, think...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the legal nature and origins of the emphyteusis contract—a specific type of long-term land lease. The author is moving from etymological origins to a formal definition and distinguishing it from other types of contracts like standard leases or fiefs.</meta>

<page-num>506</page-num>
<header>Luis de Molina on Contracts</header>

...they argue that **emphyteusis** is named from the Greek word *emphyteusis*, which in Latin means "I bring in" or "I contribute," <note>original: "emphyteusi verbo graeco, quod latinè significat infero, ac cófero"</note> as if emphyteusis were the same as "planting," and to give something in emphyteusis were the same as giving it for planting or cultivation. This is because, as was said, in the beginning only uncultivated and deserted lands were typically handed over by this contract regarding their use, fruits, and beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile</term>, in exchange for a modest payment <term>pensio</term>, so that they might be brought back to cultivation and made better and more useful. Although both derivations lead to the same practical result and effect, the latter seems more true and genuine.

Alvarus Valascus, in the place cited above (number 5 and question 1, number 5), rightly rejects the opinion of Alciatus and Paris de Puteo. Based on the origin of the word *emphyteusis*, they asserted that it is of the nature of an emphyteutic contract that the thing handed over and received must be sterile and unproductive. On the contrary, the common opinion of the learned—together with the cited gloss of Accursius—affirms that this practice has prevailed. This is clearly gathered from the perpetual imperial constitution <note>original: "authentica perpetua C. de sacrosan. eccl"</note>, from the decree on not alienating church property <note>original: "authentico de non alienandis §. quia vero Leonis"</note>, and from the canon law <note>original: "c. ea enim. §. perpetua. 10. q. 1."</note>. For it is not necessary that the original reason for a name must apply to every single thing to which the name is later adapted.

# What is Emphyteusis.

## DISPUTATION 445.

-> S U M M A R Y <-

1 *What emphyteusis is, and in what ways it differs from leasing and hiring, and in number 2.*
3 *For how long a time emphyteusis can be granted.*
4 *The two-fold nature of leasing.*
5 *A lease made for a "long time"—how that time is to be understood.*
6 *In a lease for a long time, beneficial ownership, the right to the thing, and possession are acquired.*
7 *Whether emphyteusis and a long-term lease are distinct contracts or not.*
8 *In how many ways emphyteusis and long-term leasing are accepted in law, and in the following number.*
10 *The emphyteutic right and the right to improvements, which the tenant makes on the property, are different things.*

<margin>1</margin> Setting aside other definitions, we can define emphyteusis thus: It is a contract by which an immovable thing is granted regarding its beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile</term> in exchange for a fixed payment <term>pensio</term> to be paid at stated times to the owner of the property for that reason. The "genus" (general category) is given as a contract. It is added, "by which an **immovable thing**," because an emphyteutic contract cannot exist except for an immovable thing, as the laws presuppose. This is gathered from the Code, on the right of emphyteusis, by these words: *To repel from emphyteutic estates* <note>original: "A predijs emphyteuticaris repellere"; Code of Justinian 4.66.2</note>, and from the Institutes, on leasing, by these words: *as for example, concerning estates which are handed over to be enjoyed forever by certain people* <note>original: "ut ecce de prædijs, quæ perpetuo quibusdam fruenda traduntur"</note>, etc., and from other laws. This is also held in the *Partidas* <note>The Siete Partidas, the statutory code of Castile</note> (Law 3, Title 14, Part 5 and Law 28, Title 18, Part 5). This is the common opinion of the doctors, which, among others, Alvarus Valascus relates and follows in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*. He proves at length that an emphyteusis cannot be established not only in movable things, but

<column-break/>

neither in those things which are accounted as immovables, such as annual rents, even perpetual ones. Although a fief <term>feudum</term> might be established in them. Read him.

<margin>2</margin> And in this, among other things, emphyteusis differs from **leasing and hiring** <term>locatio et conductio</term>, which can also concern movable things. Regarding trees, however, while they are attached to the ground, they are considered as part of the immovable soil in which they have roots. Gregorio López and Alvarus Valascus, with others they cite, believe that an emphyteusis can be established in them. It is then added, **regarding beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile</term>. In this, the emphyteutic contract also differs from leasing and hiring, which does not usually transfer ownership—even beneficial ownership—of the leased thing to the hirer, according to the laws. But by an emphyteutic contract, the beneficial ownership of the thing is handed over and passes to the tenant <term>emphyteuta</term>. Read what was said in Disputation 3 regarding the beneficial ownership of a usufructuary and a tenant.

Furthermore, it is added, **under a fixed payment** <term>sub reali pensione</term>, to distinguish it from a fief, in which personal service and fidelity are paid (if it is a pure fief, having nothing of emphyteusis mixed in). Likewise, it is said "under a fixed payment" without restricting it to being paid in money or something else; for it is irrelevant to the nature of emphyteusis in what form the payment is made, as is gathered from the Institutes and the common opinion followed by Valascus. Nor is it said that the payment must be a small or large amount. That too is irrelevant to the nature of emphyteusis, despite what many have said, being deceived by the words of Baldus. They asserted that it is of the nature of emphyteusis that the payment be modest, otherwise the contract would turn into a lease. They were led by the fact that in the beginning, when only sterile and uncultivated fields were given in emphyteusis, a modest payment was paid. But this was entirely accidental to the contract, no less than it was accidental that only uncultivated fields were then given, as Valascus rightly affirms. Finally, by the rest of the definition, the emphyteutic contract is distinguished from buying and selling, and from other contracts, and even from the transfer of an emphyteusis from one tenant to another (whether by sale, exchange, legacy, or any other title). For that transfer is not the emphyteutic contract itself, but rather a transfer of the emphyteutic condition, an exchange, or another contract or last will, depending on the title by which it is transferred.

In the proposed definition of emphyteusis, I have placed nothing to express whether the things are granted by that contract forever or for a certain term of time. For although by the original institution of this contract things seem to be granted in perpetual emphyteusis, as is gathered from the Institutes: *concerning estates which are handed over to be enjoyed forever by certain people*...

It distinguishes this from standard leases, which do not transfer ownership rights, and from fiefs, which require personal service rather than just material payment.</summary>

It specifically addresses whether these contracts must be perpetual or can be limited to specific lifetimes or generations, and how "long-term" leases transfer specific property rights.</meta>

<page-num>507</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 445.</header>

From the law *Quicunque* [Whosoever], law 1 of the Code on patrimonial lands, book 11, and from the authentic decree *De non alienandis* [On not alienating property] in the section beginning *alienationis autem nomen* [the name of alienation], the common opinion of the learned confirms this. Alvarus Valascus (question 1, number 12, cited) refers to and follows this view, regardless of what a few have wrongly asserted to the contrary. From this, it seems to have arisen that among the Spanish, the term <margin>3</margin> **a foro** <note>This refers to the *contrato de foro*, a traditional Galician and Spanish land lease similar to emphyteusis.</note> is understood to mean only a perpetual grant. Nevertheless, things can and usually are granted in **emphyteusis** <term>a long-term land lease</term> for only the life of the person to whom they are granted, or for two or three generations. By the word "generation," we understand the life of each individual tenant <term>emphyteuta</term>. Thus, an emphyteusis granted for two generations is considered granted for two lives, and one for three generations is considered granted for three lives—namely, the life of the person who receives it and two others—according to what was agreed upon between the grantor and the recipient. 

Indeed, in this type of contract, the specific agreements <note>original: "pacta"</note> serve as the law, as stated in laws 1 and 2 of the Code on the law of emphyteusis, and in the Institutes on leasing, where the accepted gloss affirms the same. The learned doctors, whom Alvarus Valascus refers to and follows at number 12, teach this as well. Nor do emphyteutic leases that are granted for one, two, or three lives cease to be true and proper emphyteuses, as all the doctors commonly acknowledge and affirm, according to Valascus. The condition that a thing be granted to be enjoyed in perpetuity is accidental to the emphyteutic contract; therefore, if that condition varies, the nature and essence of the contract itself do not change. For that reason, I included nothing in the definition to express that the thing is given in perpetuity or for a fixed term of time; instead, I left the definition broad enough to encompass both temporary and perpetual emphyteusis within its scope.

Because the original institution of these leases was usually for perpetuity, such contracts—by which ownership is transferred—are considered perpetual unless the contrary is expressed, as noted in the final law of the Code on legacies. This is supported by the text which Alvarus Valascus (at number 12) rightly uses to conclude, along with Angulo and others, that when an emphyteusis is found to be established and it was not expressed whether it was granted for a certain time or certain lives, it is presumed to be granted in perpetuity. Covarruvias asserts the same along with many others in book 3 of his *Variarum resolutionum* [Various Resolutions], chapter 10, number 4. 

Alvarus Valascus and others make an exception for an ecclesiastical emphyteusis. Since it is prohibited to grant church property for more than three lives (as established in the decree *De non alienandis* in the section *emphyteusim*), unless the form of the contract explicitly states it was granted in perpetuity, in case of doubt it is presumed to be granted only for three lives. Covarruvias agrees in volume 2, chapter 17. The same should be said of a secular emphyteusis where the custom is to grant it only for three lives, as Valascus says seems to be the case in Portugal; in that kingdom, the custom is that lay emphyteuses are regularly granted only for three lives. On this matter, see Gama, decision 276. Furthermore, concerning emphyteuses, one must stand by the custom of each region when nothing else is expressed in the contract, as taught by the doctors referred to by Valascus, Molina (book 1, chapter 3), and Covarruvias.

<margin>4</margin> To arrive at the main question concerning the proposed definition, it must be observed that there are two types of leasing <term>locatio</term>. One is that which is said to be for a 

<column-break/>

short time, namely under ten years, as almost everyone agrees. The other is that which is said to be for a long time. And this is primarily that which is for ten years or more, as affirmed by the common opinion of the learned and accepted practice, following the final gloss on the Clementines (on not alienating church property) and the gloss on law 3 of the Digest. This is cited and followed by Navarrus, Covarruvias (volume 2, chapter 15), and more extensively in chapter 16, Alvarus Valascus (question 29), Molina (book 1, chapter 21), Aries Pinellus, Antonius Gomez, and Franciscus Caldas. 

Although the gloss on law 1 of the Digest (concerning surfaces) says it should be left to the judge's discretion to decide what should be called <margin>5</margin> a "long time," the judge † ought to understand "long time" as ten years or more, according to the titles and laws of the Code on long-term prescription of ten or twenty years. With much greater reason, a lease is called "for a long time" when it is made for the life of the lessor or the lessee, as taught by Navarrus, Covarruvias, Valascus, Molina, Aries Pinellus, and many others. This is gathered from law 1 of the Digest on partnerships, where a partnership entered into for the whole life of the partners is called "perpetual." It is also gathered from the Clementines and other laws cited by Covarruvias. Navarrus provides an elegant reason for this: a human life is considered much longer than ten years according to the Code on the Most Holy Churches and the Digest on the Falcidian law. 

However, when the person for whose life something is leased is already so aged that, according to the legal calculations, he is not expected to live ten years, the lease would not be considered "for a long time," as Covarruvias says. When a lease is made for as long as the lessee or the lessor wishes, Decius, Socinus the Younger, Jason, Molina, and Aries Pinellus consider it should be reputed as a lease for a long time. Nevertheless, Valascus (at number 4) rightly thinks this should be restricted to when it is for as long as the *lessor* wishes.

<margin>6</margin> A lease for a long time transfers beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile</term> and a right in the thing to the lessee, and consequently, it is compared to the possession of that ownership and right, as discussed in Disputation 12. That beneficial ownership and a right in the thing are transferred is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned following Bartolus, whom Valascus, Covarruvias, Molina, Julius Clarus, Antonius Gomez, and Caldas follow. This is proven by the text of law 3 joined with law 1 of the Digest (on emphyteusis) and more clearly by law 1 of the Digest (on surfaces) with these words: *“And certainly, for good reason, he who has leased a surface right not for a short time has a legal action in rem [against the property].”* Molina says no suitable answer can be given against this text. Likewise, for that reason, a long-term lease is considered an alienation <term>the transfer of property rights</term> according to the Clementines. Hence, the contrary opinion of Aries Pinellus—who contends through various interpretations that neither beneficial ownership nor a right in the thing is acquired by a long-term lease—is not to be approved, as it goes against the common opinion of the learned.

<summary>This page discusses the duration of emphyteutic contracts, arguing that while often perpetual, they can be limited to specific lifetimes or generations without losing their legal essence. It also defines "long-term" leases as those exceeding ten years or lasting a lifetime, noting that such leases transfer beneficial ownership and legal rights in the property to the tenant.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

<margin>† Question 7</margin>
From this arises a doubt: whether **emphyteusis** <term>a long-term land lease granting near-ownership</term> and a **lease for a long period** <term>locatio ad longum tempus</term> are distinct contracts, or if a long-term lease is truly an emphyteusis and is therefore included in the definition of emphyteusis we have provided. Alvarus Valascus, in his work *On the Law of Emphyteusis* (question 26, number 19), discusses this doubt; after citing various authors on both sides, he judges them to be different contracts—not only in name but in substance and effect. He argues that an argument applied to emphyteusis is not necessarily valid for a long-term lease, and he asserts this to be the common opinion of the learned doctors. Furthermore, in the progress of that question, he contends that many provisions established as penalties or otherwise regarding emphyteusis do not apply to a long-term lease. In this, he follows the footsteps and teachings of Aries Pinellus in the three sections cited above, attempting in part to weaken the common opinion which asserts that a long-term lease conveys **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from property while another holds legal title</term> and a "right in the thing." However, he eventually adds that one should not depart from the common opinion, which he admits is corroborated by **canon law** <note>Laws established by the Church, which often governed land and contracts in this period.</note>—something even Aries Pinellus does not deny in the passage discussed above.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I believe it should be said: By the very fact that the law allows a long-term lease to transfer beneficial ownership and a right in the thing to the tenant, it is equivalent in effect and in the nature of the contract to an emphyteusis. Consequently, all things decreed concerning emphyteusis in both civil and canon law apply to it. This is affirmed by Molina in *On Primogeniture* (book 1, chapter 21, number 21), along with Faber, Aretinus, Felinus, Jason, and many others; as well as Caldas in *On the Renewal of Emphyteusis* (question 16, from number 8, especially number 11), and most others. The **Portuguese Ordinances** <note>The *Ordenações*, the primary legal code of the Kingdom of Portugal.</note> (book 4, title 64, at the beginning) clearly agree, where they state: <insert>The tenant (that is, the emphyteuta) who holds any estate, house, vineyard, or other leased possession forever, or for certain persons, or for a fixed time exceeding ten years, shall not be able to sell the leased thing, etc.</insert> <note>original Portuguese: "O foreiro... que traz alguna herdade... non pordera uender a couſa aforada."</note> Here, under the name of emphyteusis, the law understands a long-term lease and equates it in all respects to a perpetual emphyteusis, such that the tenant **forfeits the grant** <note>original: "cadat in commissum"</note> if he alienates the property without requesting the **direct lord** <term>the superior owner who holds the legal title</term>. And in Title 65, at the beginning, it says: <insert>If the tenant who received any possession from the lordship for a certain rent or pension, or quantity of fruits, or price, forever, or for certain persons, or for a fixed time of ten years and upward, does not pay the rent or pension for three years, etc.</insert> <note>original Portuguese: "Se oforeio que recebeo... non pagar o foro ou penſam per tres annos."</note> Here, the law includes a long-term lease under emphyteusis and decrees that a long-term tenant, if he fails to pay the rent for three years, forfeits the grant just like any other emphyteuta. Another similar ordinance is in book 4, title 6, paragraph 9: <insert>This shall likewise take place regarding goods leased or set aside, if the lease is for ten years and upward.</insert> <note>original Portuguese: "beens emprazados ou arredados... de dez annos e di acima."</note> This is also found in book 3, title 32, at the beginning. Indeed, I do not see why a lease for the entire life of the tenant or the landlord should be called an emphyteusis—being equated entirely in nature and effect to a perpetual emphyteusis, as Alvarus Valascus and others with whom we dispute wish—and yet a lease for ten years or more should not be treated similarly, if by this lease beneficial ownership and a right in the thing is also transferred to the tenant (as Alvarus Valascus concedes is transferred). For by that very fact, the contract acquires a nature distinct from a lease for a

<column-break/>

short time, no less than a lease for a whole life acquires a nature different from a short-term lease. And indeed, Gregory Lopez (on law 28, title 8, part 5, at the words "for his whole life") and Silvester (under the word "emphyteusis," number 1) agree with you, as they include a lease for ten years or more under the category of emphyteusis.

So that you may understand the laws and the doctors, observe—as found in the **Institutes** <note>A foundational law textbook forming part of the *Corpus Juris Civilis* of Emperor Justinian.</note> in the section on leasing—that it was once doubted whether emphyteusis was a lease or a distinct contract. Because of the great connection and affinity it had with leasing, it was discussed alongside leasing and under the broad name of "leasing." Whence in law 1 of the Digest (*If a tax-paying field or emphyteusis is claimed*), emphyteusis is discussed under the name of leasing with these words: <insert>They are called "tax-paying" fields [vectigales] which are leased in perpetuity; that is, under the law that as long as the tax is paid for them, it is not permitted to take them away either from those who leased them or from those who succeed to their place.</insert> <note>original Latin: "Vectigales uocantur, qui in perpetuum locantur..."</note> Behold: the emphyteutic contract is discussed under the names of "hiring" and "leasing." Because in those times, before the **Zenonian Law** <note>A law by the Byzantine Emperor Zeno (r. 474–491 AD) that finally settled that emphyteusis was its own third type of contract, neither purely a sale nor purely a lease.</note> in the Code on the law of emphyteusis established the proper nature of this contract and explained it as distinct from a lease, the discussion of emphyteusis used the term "lease" in a broad sense. In the law *Non solet* in the Digest on leasing, these words are found: <insert>A lease does not usually change ownership;</insert> by which it is hinted that although for the most part it does not change ownership, sometimes it *does* change beneficial ownership—namely, when it is in perpetuity or for a long time. Therefore, I say that the terms "emphyteusis" and "lease" are **equivocal** <note>Used with multiple meanings.</note> in law and among the learned. For sometimes "lease" is used broadly to include emphyteusis and perpetual grants; at other times it is used strictly, and this in two ways, especially among the doctors. In one way, it is used very strictly and most properly for only a lease for a short time, by which beneficial ownership is not transferred, and which is a contract distinct in kind from emphyteusis broadly taken. In another way, it is used somewhat more broadly, so as to exclude perpetual emphyteusis or those for a life or lives, but to include a lease for ten years or more—which is how the Portuguese Ordinances use it in the two places cited later.

<margin>†</margin>
"Emphyteusis" is also used in two ways: one strictly, for only perpetual emphyteusis or those for a life or lives; and another way broadly, insofar as it also includes a lease for ten years or more. In this latter way, it constitutes a true species of contract distinct from a lease in its most proper and strict sense. And it was in this way that it was defined by us in this place, and it is in this sense we shall speak of it hereafter. Therefore, the definition of emphyteusis proposed by us also applies to a long-term lease, which is similarly contained within the thing defined.

Finally, in this dispute, one should observe (with Alvarus Valascus, question 1, number 19, and others) that the emphyteutic right, which we have explained thus far, is distinct from the **right to improvements** <note>The legal right of a tenant to be compensated for "meliorations" or betterments they have made to the land, such as planting vineyards or building walls.</note> which the emphyteuta makes on the property, and which belongs to the same emphyteuta. This is both evident in itself and is gathered from the final law in the Code on the law of emphyteusis, which deals with these two rights...

Indeed, the **right of emphyteusis** <term>the legal right to a long-term lease</term> arises from the emphyteutic contract as defined and explained thus far; however, the **right to improvements** <term>Latin: ius meliorationum; the value added by the tenant's work</term> arises from the labor, expense, and industry of the tenant regarding the leased property. Yet, because the right to improvements presupposes the emphyteutic right and depends upon it—and because the owner of the property acquires ownership of those improvements precisely because they are made upon and attached to the leased thing (as shown at the end of Disputation 10 and Disputation 57)—it follows that the tenant cannot sell the emphyteutic right without first notifying the **direct lord** <term>the legal title holder or landlord</term>, as we shall see. Likewise, the tenant cannot sell the right to improvements without notifying the same lord, unless a different agreement was made in the contract, as held in the final law of the Code, *On the Right of Emphyteusis* <note>original: "l. ult. C. de iure emphy." refers to the Code of Justinian, the foundation of civil law</note>.

# Emphyteusis: One Common, Another Ecclesiastical. Whether Civil Law Applies to the Latter.

## DISPUTATION 446.

-> SUMMARY <-

1 *Fourfold division of emphyteusis.*
2 *Ecclesiastical emphyteusis is regulated according to canon law and not civil law, except where civil law has been tacitly or expressly approved by the Church.*
3 *Whether a civil law admitting illegitimate children to succession in the absence of legitimate ones also extends to an ecclesiastical emphyteusis.*

<margin>1</margin> **Having provided** the definition of emphyteusis, we must next speak of its division into **common** and **ecclesiastical**. As we shall see in the following sections, these do not agree in all respects; rather, many things are peculiar to ecclesiastical emphyteusis. An **ecclesiastical emphyteusis** is defined as one involving the property of the Church, or specifically, a property where the direct ownership belongs to the Church. Any other such lease is called a **common emphyteusis**.

<margin>2</margin> **Regarding** † ecclesiastical emphyteusis, one must abide by the provisions of **canon law** <term>the internal legal system of the Catholic Church</term>, rather than **civil law** <term>secular state law</term>, except insofar as the civil law has been tacitly or expressly approved by the Church. The Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, Title 65, Paragraph 2) acknowledge this, and it is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Julius Clarus (Book 4, *Sentences*, section on Emphyteusis, question 48), Alvarus Valascus (*On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 20, number 6, paragraph 4), and others whom we shall cite in the progress of this disputation, follow.

The reason for this is that civil provisions regarding both ecclesiastical persons and the Church and its goods do not have force except where they have been tacitly or expressly approved by the Supreme Pontiff, because they are exempt from civil power, as is clear from the chapter *Ecclesiæ Sanctæ Mariæ*, *On Constitutions*, and other laws.

However, the cited doctors and many others rightly affirm that since the property of the Church is handed over to a layman in emphyteusis, the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the land</term> of that property does 

<column-break/>

not belong to the Church, but to the lay person. Therefore, it is subject to civil law and lay power, and civil laws have force regarding it. From this, it follows that **taxes** <note>original: "tributa"</note> imposed on the goods of laymen by civil decree are owed by lay tenants according to the value of the beneficial ownership they hold in the leased property. It is no hindrance that the emphyteusis is "ecclesiastical," or that the layman's beneficial ownership is joined with the Church's direct ownership (which is exempt from such taxes). Furthermore, it does not matter if the Church is indirectly deprived of some profit—insofar as the property might have been leased for a higher rent if the layman's ownership were tax-exempt. That is entirely accidental; it should not and cannot impede the lay power, nor the profit and right of the secular prince over all goods by the very fact that they become the property of the laymen who are his subjects, as Alvarus Valascus rightly affirms (question 17, from number 21) along with many others he cites.

From this it follows that lay laws regarding **retraction** <term>the right of a relative to buy back property sold to a stranger</term>, which we discussed in Disputation 370, have a place in ecclesiastical emphyteusis if the tenant sells his beneficial ownership to a stranger. For a relative closer in degree can "retract" <term>redeem</term> it within the time granted for retraction, as Alvarus Valascus and many others he cites there (number 13) assert. For the direct lord always retains his full right (of which we will speak below) to be preferred over other buyers, and to wait for the full time allowed to him for deliberating whether he wishes to take that beneficial ownership for the same price, as granted by law and discussed in Disputation 371.

The whole difficulty is whether, when some are excluded from succession in an ecclesiastical emphyteusis by the disposition of canon law—such as **illegitimate children** <note>Canon law traditionally restricted the inheritance of Church-leased lands to legitimate offspring to ensure stability and moral standing.</note>, as we shall see—this holds even if a civil law has been established in a Kingdom admitting certain illegitimate children to the succession. For example, the Portuguese law (Book 4, Ordinance Title 62, Paragraph 4) admits illegitimate natural descendants (not only of commoners but even of nobles) in the absence of legitimate descendants.

<margin>3</margin> **The question is, I say,** whether † by virtue of such a law, these illegitimate children succeed in an ecclesiastical emphyteusis, even when it was not granted by the Church with a specific clause or agreement admitting them, or if that law only applies to a common emphyteusis.

Likewise, when an emphyteusis is granted to someone and "the person whom they shall name," this involves a condition: *if they have named someone*. Therefore, if the first tenant dies without naming anyone for the lease, the emphyteusis is extinguished, and the beneficial ownership reverts to the property owner, as all concede and as the Portuguese Ordinances (Title cited, Paragraph 3, at the beginning) acknowledge. This being established, when the Portuguese law (in the cited Paragraph 3 and the following Paragraph 4) states that if such a tenant dies intestate and leaves descendants or ancestors, the nearest descendant is "deemed" to be named, and in the absence of descendants, the nearest ancestor is "deemed" named to succeed in the lease—the question is whether that law applies to an ecclesiastical emphyteusis or only to

<meta>This page continues the legal debate over whether secular laws—specifically those of the Kingdom of Portugal—can govern long-term leases (emphyteusis) involving Church property. The author, Luis de Molina, explores the tension between civil statutes and Canon Law.</meta>

510 Ludovici Molinæ De Contractib.

<column-break/>

in a common **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis; a type of lease where the tenant has permanent use of the land provided they pay a rent and maintain the property</term>: for that would result in the detriment of the Church, because the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the property</term> would not be merged with the **legal title** <term>proprietas; the underlying ownership</term> as quickly, nor would it return to the Church. Civil law that results in the detriment of Church property, and any agreement by which the Church grants those goods, has no force until it is tacitly or expressly approved by the Church. There is almost the same difficulty regarding the Portuguese ordinance in the same title, at the beginning and the two following paragraphs, insofar as it decrees that if such a tenant should appoint an heir or heirs without making a specific nomination in the lease, that heir or heirs are considered nominated in the order and manner explained therein.

For many grave authors believe that the appointment of an heir should not be considered a nomination for a long-term lease under common law, and therefore that law has no place in an ecclesiastical lease. Among their number are Antonio Gomez in the second volume of his *Various Resolutions*, chapter 11, at the end, number 7; and Emmanuel à Costa in his work *On Entails*, part 2, decision 16. Likewise, since the pension for a lease can consist of any things whatsoever, the Portuguese law (Book 4 of the Ordinances, title 65, final paragraph) decrees that in a lease of houses, or of some plot of land for building houses, the pension cannot be established except in **money or birds** <note>original: "pecunia, aut auibus"; it was common to pay rents in poultry, such as capons</note>; otherwise the contract is void and of no effect.

It is asked, however, whether such a law has a place in an ecclesiastical lease, or only in a common lease. For neither a secular prince nor civil laws can restrict the power of the Church regarding contracts to be celebrated concerning Church matters, when those contracts are otherwise valid and lawful in themselves.

Therefore, regarding these and other similar secular laws that would restrict or loosen ecclesiastical contracts concerning leases—so that they would be open to the Church’s disadvantage more than they otherwise ought to extend, or so that they would be invalid when they otherwise would have been valid—against the power the Church has to dispose of its own things, there is a doubt whether they can extend to ecclesiastical leases without the tacit or express approval of the Supreme Pontiff, whether the intention of the secular legislators was to include them or not. And certainly, of no Christian legislator should it be thought that they intended to include them under the hypothesis that such a thing would be wicked or invalid.

Gama, in his *Decisions* 2 and 149, around number 6 regarding the first of the proposed matters, considers that **natural children** <term>filios naturales; children born out of wedlock but recognized by their father</term> succeed in an ecclesiastical lease in Portugal, and this according to the Portuguese law of which we have spoken.

For, he says, that disposition concerns the succession in the beneficial ownership once it has already been transferred from the Church to a lay tenant, and thus when it is already subject to the disposition of civil law. He reports in that second decision that it has often been so judged in Portugal, although he also reports that it has sometimes been judged to the contrary. But as for the second of the proposed matters, Emmanuel à Costa and Antonio Gomez, in the places cited, believe that those dispositions do not extend to ecclesiastical leases.

Caldas, in his work *On Emphyteutic Nomination*, question 

<column-break/>

7, copiously and diligently disputes the question, citing authors on both sides and bringing many reasons for and against. On the point of law, he leans toward the opinion of Emmanuel à Costa and Antonio Gomez, especially when the one who ought to have nominated dies **intestate** <term>without leaving a will</term>. Finally, at number 56, he resolves that this hardly has a place in practice in Portugal, even in the ecclesiastical court: because, he says, the ecclesiastical courts are accustomed, in so doubtful a matter, to yield to the disposition and equity of the Royal law; and thus he says he has seen it judged and obtained many times.

By which it happens, he says, that this can today be called a mixed custom and disposition in Portugal, and is entirely to be observed by both laity and ecclesiastics. Finally, as for the third point, Alvaro Valasco in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 20, number 6, paragraph "likewise I ask," considers that the Portuguese law does not extend to leases of the Church, but only to lay ones: because the laws of particular kingdoms have no force against the power of the Churches regarding the celebration of their contracts about Church matters. This is especially true when one and the same contract is celebrated in one way by the laity and in another way by the Churches, as happens in the matter of leases. Valasco adds that the Portuguese law could be extended to ecclesiastical leases if only it were received in the ecclesiastical tribunals by long use and time: because from that promiscuous and long use, it becomes a mixed custom of the laity and ecclesiastics, which must be observed in the **canonical court** <term>the Church's legal system</term>, according to Panormitanus... and Felinus... and Decio. In this matter there can be no doubt: for, if it were received in Portugal by a prescribed custom in both courts, it certainly derogates from Canon Law. However, whether a prescribed custom exists in Portugal on this matter, he does not affirm.

But to say what I feel: I certainly judge, on the point of law in all these and similar events, that secular laws do not extend to ecclesiastical leases, because they bring prejudice to ecclesiastical lease contracts, and thus to ecclesiastical things. In that event, secular laws have no force unless they are tacitly or expressly approved by the Supreme Pontiff, or have already been extended to ecclesiastical leases by prescribed custom.

And from those things which Gama and Alvaro Valasco teach, and likewise Emmanuel à Costa, it is not established that those Portuguese laws have been extended in Portugal to ecclesiastical leases by prescribed custom: but it is the secular judges who, in their constant effort to extend lay jurisdiction into Church matters as much as they can, easily persuade themselves of that **pseudographic** <note>original: "pfeudographa"; here meaning a false or forged reasoning</note> reasoning—namely, that civil laws regarding the beneficial ownership of ecclesiastical tenants are valid—and they often deliver sentences that those Portuguese laws also have a place in ecclesiastical leases.

Nonetheless, although it is very true that civil laws regarding the beneficial ownership of tenants of Church property—when it does not follow that the lease contracts in the Church are restricted or loosened...
