<meta>This page transitions from specific discussions of Portuguese ordinances regarding Church property to a broader legal analysis of the nature of the emphyteutic contract—a form of long-term lease. It addresses the contract's origins in Roman law, its classification as a "strict law" contract, and the essential requirement of a written document for its validity.</meta>

Second Treatise. Disputation 4.

# On the origin of the long-term lease contract, whether it is of strict law, a named contract, and whether it is finalized by writing.

## DISPUTATION 447.

### ->SUMMARY<-

1 *The long-term lease <term>emphyteusis; a type of lease where the tenant has permanent use of the land provided they pay an annual rent</term> was introduced by civil law.*
2 *The long-term lease contract is one of strict law <term>stricti iuris; a legal category where the court interprets the contract exactly as written, without the flexibility of "good faith" equity</term>.*
3 *The long-term lease is a "named" contract <term>contractus nominatus; a contract with a specific legal name and established rules in Roman Law</term>.*
4 *Whether the long-term lease contract is finalized by writing. And what applies in an Ecclesiastical lease. number 5.*

**1** Since the long-term lease contract was unknown to many nations in the world, both formerly and up to the present day, and was not at all in use, it is quite clear that this contract did not originate from the Law of Nations <note>original: *gentium iure*; the universal laws perceived as common to all humanity</note>, but rather from † civil law <note>original: *ciuili*; specifically the Roman statutory law</note>. This is despite what certain others have said, whom Alvaro Valasco <note>a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> mentions and refutes in his work *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 1. It is established that in the times of the Emperor Zeno <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 474–491 AD</note>, it began to be reduced to a better and more exact form, as is clear from the first law of the Code *On the Law of Emphyteusis* (1.1. C. de iure emphy.), and other following laws in the same title, as well as from the section *Adeo* in the Institutes regarding leasing. All these points are asserted by the Gloss <note>The "Standard Gloss," the standard medieval commentary on Roman law</note> on the law *From this law* (l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iustit. & iure), which is the common opinion of the doctors of law, and which Alvaro Valasco mentions and follows above in number 7.

**2** Furthermore, that the long-term lease is a † contract of strict law is clear from those things said in Disputation 259; Alvaro Valasco disputes this extensively in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 5. Therefore, the legal action that results from it is also of strict law, as is evident from what was said in that same disputation.

**3** Indeed, that the long-term lease is a "named contract" was explained in Disputation 253. It is clear from the first law of the Code *On the Law of Emphyteusis* and the section *Adeo* in the Institutes on leasing, where it is taught that it was introduced and perfected by civil law with a peculiar form and name. On this matter, see Alvaro Valasco extensively, as cited above, question 6.

<margin>Question</margin>
**4** However, the question is whether it is finalized by writing. The common opinion of the doctors—which is followed by Giulio Claro (Book 4, section *Emphyteusis*, question 4), Caldas (On the Renewal of Emphyteusis, question 2, number 2 and question 18, number 36), Antonio Gomez (Volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 16), and Gregorio Lopez (on law 18, title 8, part 5, on the word "by writing" <note>original: *por escrita*; Spanish</note>)—and from which Alvaro Valasco concludes one should not recede, is that writing is necessary for a long-term lease contract.

This is affirmed by the Gloss on the section *Adeo* in the Institutes regarding leasing, on the words "nor for leasing" <note>original: *neque ad locationem*</note> at the end; the Gloss on the law "it is contracted" <note>original: *contrahitur*</note> regarding pledges; and the Gloss on the law "a pact, because in good faith" <note>original: *pactum, quod bona fide*</note> in the Code regarding pacts. And although Accursius <note>the 13th-century author of the Great Gloss</note> asserts the same in his Gloss on the fourth law of the Code *On the Law of Emphyteusis* on the word "writing" <note>original: *scriptura*</note>, he nevertheless adds two interpretations concerning that text by which it might be defended that a long-term lease contract is valid without writing. Where an addition is made to that same Gloss, he affirms it is valid according to that Gloss, and adds that Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, perhaps the most influential medieval jurist</note> affirmed that this was received by custom.

That writing is necessary for a long-term lease contract is confirmed by the first law of the Code *On the Law of Emphyteusis* in those words: *with agreements held through the intervention of writing* <note>original: *pactionibus scriptura interueniente habitis*</note>. The cited Gloss explains these words in one way: that they should be understood as referring to the specific agreements inserted into the long-term lease contract, but not as if the writing itself were necessary for the long-term lease contract itself. However, there is no fitting reason why the law should require this for agreements inserted into the contract rather than for the contract itself. The same is confirmed by the second law of the Code in the same title, with those words: *If indeed any agreements were written down in the emphyteutic instruments* <note>original: *Siquidem aliquae pactiones in emphyteuticis instrumentis fuerint conscripta*</note>. These words have the same force as the preceding ones.

It is also confirmed by the third law of the Code in the same title: *if indeed the emphyteutic instrument has any agreements regarding this, let them be observed* <note>original: *si quidem emphyteuticum instrumentum super hoc aliquas pactiones habeat, eas obseruari*</note>. These words also have the same force as the others cited. This is expressly asserted in the laws of the *Siete Partidas* (Law 28, Title 8, Part 5, and Law 3, Title 14, Part 5 <note>The primary legal code of medieval Castile</note>). Regarding ecclesiastical long-term leases, this is held far more expressly than in the common laws just mentioned, in the *Authenticum* <note>a collection of Justinian's Novels</note> on "not alienating," specifically in the section *We permit therefore* <note>original: *sinimus igitur*</note>, joined with the preceding section *Anastasius*, and the section *What however was said* <note>original: *quod autem dictum est*</note>, in which places the discourse is only about ecclesiastical emphyteusis. The Portuguese Ordinance (Book 4, Title 36, at the beginning) confirms this very thing openly, where among the contracts that are perfected by writing—and for whose substance it is required that writing intervenes—it commemorates the ecclesiastical long-term lease, saying: *and in the emphyteutic contract of an ecclesiastical thing* <note>original: *e no contrato emphyteotico da cosa ecclesiastica*</note>.

<margin>Decision</margin>
What I think about this matter, I will say in a few words. First, where a prescribed custom has been established that a long-term lease contract can be made without writing and be held as firm, that custom must be stood by. There can be no doubt in that matter, because a prescribed custom derogates <note>overrides</note> the law, both Canon and Civil. However, many affirm against Bartolus that there is no such custom; indeed, it is clear that in most places at least, there is none, and Caldas affirms that there is no such custom in Portugal.

Neither does there seem to be such a custom in Castile, even in a common long-term lease, as is gathered from the laws of that Kingdom just cited; for one should not believe that a contrary custom was introduced in that Kingdom against such express laws.

And Gregorio Lopez, cited above, affirms that writing is necessary, not only for proof but also for the very substance <note>validity</note> of the contract. Where also it has been received by use and custom that writing is necessary for a long-term lease contract, and that a contract celebrated without writing has no strength, that custom must also be stood by: especially since the common opinion of the doctors and the cited testimonies of the law support it.

As for what must be said on the point of law, and also

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 511 regarding the legal formalities of the emphyteutic contract (a permanent land lease). It specifically focuses on whether a written document is a strict requirement for the contract's validity (substance) or merely for providing evidence in court (probation).</meta>

# Luis de Molina
# On Contracts

...where it is established that no custom has been prescribed for either side. 
<margin>5</margin> First, I judge that it is of the essential substance <term>de substantia; a legal term meaning a requirement without which a contract is null and void</term> of an Ecclesiastical long-term lease contract <term>emphyteusis; a type of lease where the tenant has permanent use of the land provided they pay an annual rent</term> that a written document be drafted and completed, because of the testimonies from the authorities cited. Indeed, the cited Portuguese law <note>original: *lex Lusitana*</note> affirms this, and many authorities on these same authentic texts consider it a crime to think otherwise in Portugal, as Alvaro Valasco <note>a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> states above in number 11, and as Caldas also asserted in question 18.

However, regarding common (secular) long-term leases, I do not think we should stray from the more common opinion of the doctors of law, both because the laws agree with enough probability, and especially in the Kingdom of Castile <note>modern-day central Spain</note> where it is established by law. Because, however, the matter is not so certain regarding a common long-term lease when standing on common law alone <note>original: *iure communi*; the underlying Roman-canonical legal system of Europe</note>, for that reason, in Disputation 254, when using examples of contracts that are completed by writing, I made no mention of the common long-term lease, nor of the lease in general, but only of the Ecclesiastical long-term lease. Alvaro Valasco, in question 7, cited at number 3, agrees; where above, Caldas in question 18 judges, along with others whom he cites, that writing is not so necessary for a common long-term lease as if it were of the substance of the contract (such that without it the contract would be void), but rather that it is only necessary for the proof <note>original: *probationem*</note> of it—as if proof of that contract by witnesses or any other means is not admitted, but only through a public document or the confession of the party with whom one is litigating over the contract. And indeed, in Portugal this must be affirmed, if we are speaking of common law and that writing is not necessary for its proof. Truly, in that Kingdom, neither in this contract nor regularly in others is any proof admitted other than by public writing or confession of the party, as is established in Book 3 of the *Ordinances*, title 45, and as was explained by us in Disputation 260. And so I judge it should be affirmed in Portugal. For the founders of the *Ordinances* of that Kingdom seem to have thought that writing was necessary for the Ecclesiastical long-term lease alone when standing on common law, as is clear from Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, title 36, at the beginning; nor did they establish it as necessary for a common lease in any other way than for the rest of the contracts in that Kingdom, according to the specific disposition of that Kingdom in Book 3, title 45. Therefore, standing on common law alone, it is not certain to me whether, according to the more common opinion reported above, it is necessary only for proof, or rather for the substance of the contract. I judge that whatever Alvaro Valasco and others he cites may have thought, the more common opinion was that it is necessary even for the substance of the contract; this is what Gregorio López <note>a famous Spanish jurist, 1496–1560</note> affirms in the place cited above.

### When a writing is of the substance of a contract, or necessary for its proof, if it is lost after being legitimately made, whether proof by witnesses is admitted.

## DISPUTATION 448.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *When a writing is of the substance of a contract, if it is lost by chance or without the fault or fraud of the person*

<column-break/>

*who has an interest, witnesses can be used to provide evidence of it.*
2 *Two trustworthy witnesses suffice for proof, even if more would have been necessary for the validity of the original writing.*
3 *How many witnesses must be proven in order to provide evidence of a writing and its loss.*
4 *What kind of witnesses they must be to prove the truth or falsity of a lost writing.*
5 *What witnesses testifying about the loss of a writing ought to state.*
6 *Witnesses are not to be examined regarding the loss of a writing that was not necessary for the contract.*
7 *A non-necessary formality, if it intervenes less aptly, does not invalidate the contract.*
8 *If a writing was lost through malice or fraud, two witnesses of any kind suffice to prove what was contained in it.*

<margin>1</margin> **O**n the occasion of those things said in the latter part of the preceding disputation, this question is raised. It must be said that even if a writing is of the substance of a contract, and even if it is established by some law that regarding a certain contract or disposition no other proof has force except through public writing <note>original: *scripturam publicam*; a document drafted by a notary or public official</note> or the confession of the opposing party; nevertheless, if the writing perishes by chance or without the fault or fraud of the interested party, and if it is proven by witnesses to have perished and what it contained, then that which is suspected [as missing] pertains to providing evidence in place of legitimate proof, just as the instrument itself would if it were exhibited in court. So say Bartolus, Panormitanus, Felinus, and the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvaro Valasco refers to and follows in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 7, numbers 1 and 8; and Antonio Gómez, question 41 of the *Laws of Toro*, at the end of number 2, and question 3, according to the Law of Witnesses <note>original: *l. testium*; referring to the Code of Justinian</note>, final paragraph, Title on Witnesses. Also the law *Sicut iniquum* <note>Justinian's Code, "As it is unjust"</note>, together with the gloss there, and the law *Emancipationem* in the Code on the Faith of Instruments, and Camp. Observation 1 on Privileges, and the second-to-last paragraph of title 64, book 3 of the Portuguese *Ordinances*.

<margin>2</margin> Furthermore, two trustworthy witnesses suffice for such proof, even if more would have been necessary for the validity of the writing, as the glosses on the cited law *Sicut iniquum* affirm, along with Bartolus, Paulus de Castro, and others whom Alvaro Valasco refers to and follows in the place cited.

<margin>3</margin> Three † things, however, must be proven. First, the fact itself: for example, that such and such a contract was celebrated between such persons. Second, that a public writing was drafted regarding that matter, of such and such a tenor <note>original: *tenoris*; the specific wording or content of the document</note>. Third, that the writing was lost. If only two things are proven—namely, the tenor of the writing and that it was lost—then any witnesses who are otherwise trustworthy do not suffice to prove it; rather, they require witnesses who are highly suitable and skilled <note>original: *periti*</note> in that matter, who can correctly know the falsity or defect of the writing and its contents from before or from use. Such are those skilled in law, like advocates and others similar, or notaries, or scriveners, and their ministers, and other similar persons.

Furthermore, it is not necessary to prove that the witnesses have sufficient skill for this, but it is enough if the judge recognizes it from the interrogations and responses, or from elsewhere. Besides, the witnesses must be "co-witnesses" <note>original: *contestes*; witnesses who testify to the same specific facts</note>. These things Alvaro Valasco agrees with in the same place, along with many others whom he cites, in the chapter "with others" cited, and the Portuguese...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal requirements for contracts, specifically focusing on how to prove the contents of a legal document (instrument) that has been lost or destroyed, and the role of witnesses and oaths in such cases.</meta>

### Treatise Two, Disputation 448. Page 513

The cited Portuguese ordinance uses these words: <note>original: "Per homens discretos e entendidos, que declaradamente digan o teor do dito instrumento, e como foi notado e perdido."</note> "By discrete and knowledgeable men, who clearly state the content of said instrument, and how it was noted and lost." But if the witnesses are not of the quality described, then the proof is not "full" <term>plena probatio; evidence that is sufficient on its own to convince a judge</term>, even if there are two witnesses who are otherwise suitable; rather, it will only be "semi-full" <term>semiplena; incomplete evidence that requires additional support</term>, as the cited Portuguese ordinance affirms, and as the doctors of law, whom Alvaro Valasco and Antonio Gomez refer to and follow above, also state.

And then, says Alvaro Valasco in his last gloss on the chapter previously cited, and in agreement with the final law in the Code regarding the "trustworthiness of instruments," and along with many others whom he cites: that incomplete proof can be supplemented by the oath of the party who lost such a document. In this oath, they must swear that it was truly lost without any fraud, and that the document contained exactly what is claimed, free from any defect. Hence, Alvaro Valasco warns in the same place that the party striving to prove the content of a lost document through witnesses should always ask, after the witnesses have been produced, that the oath be administered to them as a "supplementary proof" <note>original: *iuramentum in supplementum probationis*</note> to better protect themselves. This is because such a supplementary oath is not granted unless the party requests it before the case is concluded.

<margin>5</margin> Witnesses of this kind must be able to testify as to where the lost writing was drafted, on what day, in what year, and in what month, since these details are necessary for its credibility and validity. This is taught by Covarruvias in *Practical Questions*, chapter 20, by Alvaro Valasco as cited above, and many others whom they reference. Antonio Gomez partially agrees in his second cited point, adding that they must also testify regarding the "sign" <note>a unique mark or seal</note> of the notary <term>tabellio; a public official authorized to draw up legal documents</term>. The Portuguese Law, Book 1, Ordinance, title 59, paragraph 3, agrees; it commands that all these details be applied to public documents, and additionally the name of the notary. Indeed, Alvaro Valasco says in the same place that they must testify to the "complete similarity" of that document with other writings of the same notary, so that the opposing party retains the ability to challenge that writing, according to the "Best Law" in the Code regarding contracts.

Finally, he adds that they must testify to all things that are "substantial" to the writing—that is, the parts without which it would not be valid—in which matter the others he refers to rightly agree. Thus it happens that for the validity of a lost writing, more witnesses than two might be necessary; for example, if the lost writing was a will, as many witnesses must testify to it as were necessary for its original validity.

It also follows that they are bound to testify that the lost document was "authentic," without defect or erasure, such that its credibility did not waver in any part. This agrees with the first chapter on privileges (at the end) and the final law in the Code on the "Edict of the Divine Hadrian." Alvaro Valasco affirms this in the same place, as do others whom he references. However, regarding those things that are customarily included in public documents but are not "substantial" to such an instrument—such as invoking the name of the Lord at the beginning—it is not necessary for witnesses to testify, according to Alvaro Valasco, Covarruvias, and many others.

Regarding the "subscription" <note>signing at the bottom</note> of witnesses, according to common law <term>ius commune; the Roman-canonical legal system used across Europe</term>, it is not necessary for them to testify to this: because 

<column-break/>

their signature is not regularly required in public documents. Instead, the "inscription" of witnesses—that is, naming them within the document—is sufficient, as the common opinion of the doctors affirms, which Covarruvias and Alvaro Valasco refer to and follow above. In Portugal, however, it is necessary to testify regarding the witnesses' signatures, because in that Kingdom, signatures are necessary for the validity of public documents, as held in Book 1 of the Ordinances, title 59, at the beginning, and as Alvaro Valasco affirms.

The reason so many things are required to be proven when a document is said to be lost is this: when the document is of the "substance of the contract" <note>essential to the contract's existence</note> or absolutely necessary for proving the contract, an easy path would otherwise be opened to many frauds. For anyone might claim a document was lost so that they could prove whatever they wanted by bribing witnesses, or to prevent a forgery or defect in the document from being discovered. One must provide a defense against the trickery <note>original: *calumnijs*</note> of litigants.

<margin>6</margin> And although the proof of so many things is very difficult and almost impossible—especially since, when the witnesses read the document before it was lost, they were not thinking about its loss and thus did not sharply observe all the formalities or commit them to memory—this difficulty is nevertheless aided by the "supplementary oath" of full proof, which was discussed above.

<margin>9</margin> However, when a writing was made solely for "easier and safer proof" <note>meaning the contract could exist without it</note>, then it is not necessary to prove that the writing was lost or that it lacked forgery or defect, even if the agreement was committed to a public writing; rather, it is enough to prove the truth of the transaction itself.

<margin>7</margin> Since the truth of a matter can be proven by witnesses alone without a writing being drafted for that purpose, it should not be a hindrance that a writing *was* drafted, or that the writing was somewhat flawed. This follows the rule: "An unnecessary formality, if it intervenes in a flawed manner, does not void the contract." This is affirmed by Alvaro Valasco, along with Afflictis and Purpuratus, and is the mind of everyone regarding the previously cited chapter.

<margin>8</margin> Finally, this must be observed: if the document was lost through the "malice or fraud" of the opposing party—who perhaps stole it, tore it up, or was otherwise the cause of its destruction or disappearance—then, once that fraud is proven, two witnesses are sufficient to prove whatever was contained in it. This is proven by the law "If regarding possession" in the Code on Proofs, and the Gloss on the law "Just as it is inequitable" in the Code on the Trustworthiness of Instruments. It is also found in the third book of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 46, second to last paragraph, as Alvaro Valasco asserts.

<margin>10</margin> In that event, it would not even be necessary to prove what was contained in it [via witnesses], but one would rely on the oath of the party who had an interest in the document appearing, who would affirm what was in it. This is gathered clearly enough from the cited law "If regarding possession," and agrees with the law "If ever" in the Code on "Where by force," and is affirmed by many whom Alvaro Valasco refers to and follows in his final paragraph.

Luis de Molina, *On Contracts*

# Whether a perpetual tenant is bound to produce the deed of lease for the direct lord, and concerning the prescription of the lease.

## DISPUTATION 449.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> 1 *A perpetual tenant <term>emphyteuta; a tenant under a long-term or perpetual lease who pays a fixed rent</term> is bound to produce the deed of lease for the direct lord, as well as the lands and their boundaries; otherwise, all his lands are presumed to be held under that lease.*
*The same should be said of a vassal <term>feudatarius; one who holds land in exchange for service</term>, in number 2.*
*However, see the declaration and understanding in number 3.*
<margin>4</margin> 4 *An owner seeking the production of the lease deed from the tenant is bound to swear an oath against calumny <term>de calumnia; an oath that the legal action is not brought in bad faith or for harassment</term>.*
<margin>5</margin> 5 *If the tenant hides the deed or loses it through fraud, the owner’s oath is accepted if he claims the lease has ended or the title was void.*
<margin>6</margin> 6 *A tenant protected by the prescription <term>praescriptio; the acquisition of a right through the lapse of time</term> of paying rent is not bound to produce another lease deed.*
<margin>7</margin> 7 *When a lease is considered renewed through tacit consent without writing, and how the tenant must respond to preserve his rights.*
<margin>8</margin> 8 *How a sharecropper or farmer <term>colonus</term> may protect himself by prescription against an owner or a perpetual tenant.*
<margin>9</margin> 9 *A lessor for a fixed term who allows a farmer to continue after the time has expired is understood to grant this under the same type of contract and conditions.*
<margin>10</margin> 10 *Once the lease term has passed, how long the contract is considered renewed by the tacit consent of the parties.*
<margin>11</margin> 11 *A farmer who continues to cultivate Church lands under a uniform rent for a period sufficient for prescription cannot be expelled by others who have been invested as tenants by the same Church at different times. Indeed, he is to be judged a perpetual tenant, as in number 12.*
<margin>14</margin> *Limit and clarify this, as in number 14.*
<margin>13</margin> 13 *How much a farmer must prove to be declared a perpetual tenant.*
<margin>15</margin> 15 *What period of time is required to prescribe "useful domain" <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from property, as opposed to the underlying ownership</term>.*

---

<margin>1</margin> Although a defendant in a lawsuit—except in certain cases—is not bound to produce his own documents for the plaintiff, as will be discussed elsewhere, nor is a possessor bound to produce the title of his possession; nevertheless, the more common opinion of the legal experts, which Alvaro Valasco relates and follows in his *On the Law of Emphyteusis* (Question 8, from number two), affirms that a perpetual tenant can be compelled to show the direct lord <note>The "direct lord" or *dominus directus* holds the underlying title, while the tenant holds the right of use.</note> upon request not only the documents and titles of such a lease, but also the lands and their boundaries in which he is a tenant and for which he pays rent. Otherwise, if he does not show the documents and titles, the judge may pronounce that the lease is finished and consolidated with the direct ownership, or certainly that such a lease never existed. However, the judge must first warn the tenant of this and later, if he does not comply, carry it out into 

<column-break/>

execution, as Alvaro Valasco affirms in the cited question, number 19, along with others. If, however, he does not show the lands and their boundaries, all his lands are presumed to be under that lease, and thus the burden of proof will fall on such a tenant to show which of them are not part of the lease.

<margin>2</margin> 2 That a vassal is bound to both—namely, to show the documents or the investiture of the fief, and to show the feudal lands and their boundaries in comparison to the direct lord—is affirmed by the final gloss on chapter one, paragraph *illud quoque*, regarding the prohibition of feudal alienation. This argument from a fief to a lease holds weight in this part. This can also be confirmed not only because the lease document was drawn up for the common benefit of the tenant and the owner (and documents common to both plaintiff and defendant must be disclosed by the defendant according to the law *praetor ait* in the Digest, "On Disclosure"), but also and especially because since the leased land is acknowledged to belong to the owner in terms of property—and thus simply belongs to him—the owner has a well-founded intention. Therefore, unless the tenant shows that the "useful domain" belongs to him, the owner may claim it for himself entirely and simply. Read Alvaro Valasco in the place cited above, numbers 5 and 6. If the owner were the Treasury <term>fiscus</term>, this would have weight for another reason: because by special privilege, documents that relate to the Treasury's case must be produced by the adversary (Digest, "On Disclosure," and "On the Law of the Treasury"). Alvaro Valasco affirms in the same place (number 7), along with Panormitanus and many others, that the Church and holy places also enjoy this privilege.

<margin>3</margin> 3 This entire doctrine, however, is to be understood when the lease is not denied by the tenant, or it is established from elsewhere that he is indeed the tenant; for then, as stated, the direct lord has a well-founded claim. If, however, someone denies that he is the tenant of the one demanding the documents, and the matter is not certain, then he shall not be compelled to produce his documents for him, according to the rule of the laws *qui accusare* and the final law in the Code, "On Disclosure," and the law *cogit* in the Code, "On the Petition for Inheritance." These laws teach that, as a rule, a defendant should not be compelled to exhibit his own documents. This is affirmed by many whom Alvaro Valasco cites and follows above (number 9). If, however, the owner convicts the denying tenant of a lie, the tenant by that very fact loses the lease, and it is consolidated with the property. This argument is deduced from feudal law: for if a vassal denies to the direct lord that he is his vassal, and the direct lord convicts him of the lie, he loses the fief by that very fact and it is consolidated to the property (as held in the final paragraph of the Law of Conrad). Both are affirmed by many whom Alvaro Valasco cites and follows (number 10). The same is asserted by Valasco (number 11) along with others: if a tenant says the lease is perpetual but it is proven to be temporary, he loses the lease. He also reports that it was so judged in the Portuguese Senate while he was the advocate.

<margin>4</margin> 4 It should also be observed that when an owner asks a tenant to exhibit the lease document, he can be compelled to first swear

<margin>† If, however, it is proven that the document was lost or hidden on purpose, then the oath of the owner will be upheld if he affirms that the lease <term>emphyteusis; a perpetual or long-term lease of land</term> has ended, or that the title was null, and the leasehold will be merged with the ownership, according to the law *si de possessione* <note>original: "if concerning possession"</note> in the Code *de probationibus* <note>original: "on proofs"</note> and those things said in the preceding dispute. So says Alvarez Valasco in that place, number 15.</margin>
regarding calumny <term>de calumnia; a formal oath that a party is acting in good faith and not to harass the opponent</term>, which is to say, I do not seek the production of that document with a malicious mind, but for the sake of protecting and preserving my own right. Thus it is with the *Speculator* <note>A nickname for the famous jurist William Durand</note> and others, as cited by Alvarez Valasco, number 13.

But if the tenant <term>emphyteuta</term>, when asked by the owner to produce the deed, responds that it has been lost without any deceit or fraud—which is certainly to be presumed if he confirms it by an oath and the contrary is not established—then he is not bound to produce a document that he does not have.

When a tenant, from whom the lease deed is demanded, asserts that he is protected by the title of law alone—because, for instance, for a very long time of 30 years (if the lease was common), or 40 years (if it belonged to the Church), or 60 years (if it belonged to a monastery of Saint Benedict or another order enjoying the Benedictine privilege), or 100 years (if it belonged to the Roman Church, according to what was said in disputations 70 and 72 above)—he was in peaceful possession of the leased property without any controversy from the direct lord <term>dominus directus; the primary owner of the land</term>, paying him throughout that very long time a single and uniform rent as its tenant, and therefore has prescribed <term>praescriptio; gaining a legal right through long-term use</term> that right,
<margin>6</margin> then † he is not bound to produce another deed. This is because prescription grants as much as an express agreement would grant with all the required qualities, and even with a writing drawn up regarding that matter. Nor in this event does Portuguese law <note>original: "lex Lusitana"</note> require proof by a public writing. So says Alvarez Valasco, number 18, and the extensive Caldas regarding the renewal of leases, with the common opinion of the doctors which he cites.
<margin>7</margin> He says † the same is true if, after the end of the last life for which the lease was granted, the successor continued in the same way in the lease, paying a uniform rent for the entire time required for prescription. For by that very act, the lease is considered renewed by tacit consent without writing, due to the time sufficient for prescribing that lease.

However, he warns that in pleading or responding, one ought to allege that he paid the uniform rent for the whole property as a tenant, which the direct lord received. Otherwise, he would not have possessed the whole property in good faith, and therefore would not have prescribed it. These points are confirmed by the law <note>original: "c. 1. §. si quis per triginta"</note> regarding feudal disputes between a lord and the kinsmen of a deceased vassal, where it says: If anyone has possessed something as a fief <term>feudum</term> for 30 years and has performed service to the lord, even if he was not formally invested in that matter, he can nonetheless protect himself by the 30-year prescription. Behold, without investiture, and thus without writing or an express contract, it says he can protect himself; and this refers to a common fief, which is prescribed in 30 years.

Alvarez Valasco, in the cited number 18, and the extensive work in question 7, number 33, to which Caldas agrees in the place above at number 12, as well as many others (especially those Caldas cites), assert that it is enough to have paid a uniform rent for ten years, with the lord accepting it and not contradicting it,

<column-break/>

so that the tenant can protect himself in the lease without showing a deed. For the law then presumes that a title has intervened, according to the law *cum de in rem verso* in the Digest *de usuris* <note>original: "on interest"</note>, which in a similar event involving uniform payment and reception of interest for ten continuous years presumes that a pact for interest has intervened. This is especially true since in that payment and reception, the action of both parties intervenes, and not just knowledge and patience. Proof from a legal presumption is equivalent to proof by writing. I do not know, however, whether this holds true especially in an Ecclesiastical lease. For in that case, a mere agreement is not sufficient, but a public writing is simultaneously required as being of the substance of that contract. Although from that continuous and uniform payment of rent we may say the law presumes an agreement intervened, it does not, however, presume that a writing intervened, nor is there any reason why it should reasonably presume so. Add to this that immovable things, and those counted with immovables (such as a lease), cannot be prescribed against the Church with a title in a space of less than 40 years, as seen in disputation 72.

Caldas warns in the cited question 15, number 15, that when Ecclesiastical estates pertain to the housing and specific maintenance of Abbots and the seats of Churches (which the Portuguese call *Passaes* <note>The parsonage or manse lands</note> or *assento da Igreja* <note>The seat of the church</note>), since such estates are not accustomed to be alienated in any other way nor handed over in lease, and therefore according to the *Extravagante* decree *inter communes* <note>A type of Papal canon law</note> regarding the non-alienation of Church property, which is accepted in Portugal, they cannot be alienated or leased without the license of the Supreme Pontiff; otherwise, the alienation is null. In such a case, a presumed title of either ten or 40 years from the continuous presentation of uniform rent is not sufficient for the one possessing them to protect himself against the direct lord. Because just as an old title together with a public writing is not sufficient for it without the consent of the Supreme Pontiff, so much less will a presumed one suffice, which that pontifical law completely opposes. Read that author.

<margin>Doubt 8 Decision</margin>
The doubt here is whether, just as we have said a perpetual tenant can protect himself by the title of prescription against the owner from the continuous uniform payment of rent without a deed, so † a farmer <term>colonus; a tenant farmer or sharecropper</term> can similarly protect himself by the title of prescription against the owner or a perpetual tenant from whom he received the field for cultivation, by proof of continuous uniform payment of rent for forty years, or even thirty if the prescription is against a private person and not the Church. However, whatever Baldus and certain others may have said, it must be said without doubt that even if one has received a field for hire under a certain annual rent, and has thus continued for forty or more years, cultivating the field through himself or his successors and paying an annual uniform rent, he has prescribed nothing at all. Therefore, he cannot protect himself but can be expelled by the one from whom he received the field to cultivate, or by any other manner of lease. The reason is that, as we said in disputation 12, § 2, the perpetual tenant possesses the leasehold right or "useful ownership" both civilly and naturally, and for that reason can prescribe it; but neither a farmer nor a lodger <term>inquilinus</term> possesses the thing they have under hire...

516 Ludovicus Molina on Contracts.

they have [possession], either civilly or naturally; rather, it is the landlord who possesses the land civilly through himself and naturally through the farmer <term>colonus; a tenant farmer</term> or the tenant <term>inquilinus; an inhabitant of a property who does not own it</term>. Furthermore, without possession, no one can prescribe <term>præscribere; to gain a legal right or title through the passage of time</term>, as stated in the rule *sine possessione* <note>original: "without possession"</note> in the Rules of Law (Book 6) and as discussed in the section on prescription.

This is most strongly confirmed by the law *malè agitur* <note>original: "it is poorly handled"</note> in the Code, regarding thirty-year prescription, which reads: *“It is a bad deal for the owners of estates if such a great privilege is granted to those possessing land by prayerful request <term>precario; a grant of land held only at the will of the owner</term> that it is not permitted to disturb them after a period of forty years has passed for whatever reason.”* And further down: *“It is not appropriate to call those people 'possessors' who hold land in such a way that they must pay the customary rent for that very reason. Therefore, let no one who enters as a tenant <term>conductor</term> into possession usurp the right of ownership for himself by holding another’s property for a long time, lest owners be forced either to lose what they have leased, or lessors be forced to exclude those who might be useful to them, or to make a public protest every year regarding their own ownership.”* These are the words there. At this point, one should also note the words of Ulpian in the law *in reb.*, the final paragraph, in the Digest on *precarium*: *“Likewise, he who requested a grant at will for a certain time, once that time has ended—even if he did not request it for that specific time—is still seen to possess the land at will.”* For the owner is understood, when he allows the person who requested the grant to possess it, to be granting it at will once again.

<margin>9</margin>
From these words and this doctrine, it is gathered that by the same reasoning, if someone who has leased a property for a fixed time allows the farmer to retain the same property after that time has ended, he is understood to grant this under the same type of contract and under the same conditions. This is clearly confirmed by the law *legem* in the Code on leasing, where it is held that when something was leased for a fixed time and the tenant continues to hold the same property after the time has expired, the prior contract is considered renewed by tacit consent <note>original: "tacito consensu"</note> under the same laws and conditions. The law *item quæritur*, paragraph *qui impleto*, in the same title of the Digest, adds the same.

A transaction made at the time of the lease, by that tacit consent of both parties, is only considered to have renewed the contract for the following year, and once that has passed, for the next, and so on; thus, the landlord can expel the tenant at the end of any subsequent year. This same principle should be understood regarding the heir of the tenant if they similarly retain the property, as Caldas asserts in the cited Question 15, number 45, following Balbus and many others, according to the law *neq;* in the Code on usufruct. Thus it happens that a tenant or his heirs can never defend themselves by prescription of the leased property based on the fact that they have consistently paid the rent to the owner of the estate at any given time. Caldas (cited above from number 41), Alvarez Valasco in *The Law of Emphyteusis* (Question 20, number 12), and apparently Gama (Decision 297, last number), and many others whom they cite, all agree on this.

Although elsewhere Gama asserts with others that a perpetual tenancy <term>colonia perpetua</term> can be prescribed in a space of 40 years, Caldas (in the cited Question 15) asserts that this is not in use in Spain. Nor indeed do I see what else a "perpetual tenancy" could be other than an emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a permanent lease where the tenant improves the land</term>, if one weighs what was said in Disputation 445.

From this, it is easier to understand what should be said in the event that Gama (cited Decision 297) reports as a settled matter, and which Caldas (cited Question 15 from number 23) reports and examines along with other cases.

<column-break/>

Referring to the first event of which Gama speaks: as if a farmer <term>colonus</term> (who was truly a long-term leaseholder <term>emphyteuta</term>) had received through his ancestors certain sterile lands from the Church under a certain larger annual rent, which they paid uniformly in perpetuity. And as if afterward the same Church had granted those same lands—now brought under cultivation—to a certain third party as a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> for three lives <note>A common legal term where a lease lasted for the lifespan of three successive generations</note> under a smaller rent. From this person, that lease finally came to someone else, while those original farmers continued in the cultivation of the same lands and in the payment of that uniform rent. However, the farmer paid that smaller rent, which the new leaseholder was going to pay to the Church, to the Church itself, and paid the surplus to that new leaseholder.

But when the new leaseholder later wanted to expel that farmer from those lands on the grounds that he held them only as his tenant, Gama and Caldas report that the judgment was given in favor of the farmer. The farmer defended himself by title of prescription, saying that he and his ancestors had received those lands in long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> from the Church, had brought them under cultivation, and had paid a uniform rent for the time necessary for prescription. If the matter was proposed and proven in that way, it certainly contains no difficulty; however, Gama does not propose the matter quite like that, but Caldas seems to have devised this explanation to defend that decision and to respect the honor of the senators [judges].

Secondly, he refers to the same and certain other events: as if lands had first been granted by the Church in long-term lease for three lives to someone for a certain rent, from whom (or from one of his successors) they had been granted to another for a certain larger rent. This second person and his successors paid that rent uniformly in this manner for a period of forty or more years.

They paid the rent directly to the Church that the person from whom they first received it was obliged to pay to the same Church; the surplus, however, they paid to that same man and his successors. But later, in the progress of time, the successor in the long-term lease wanted to expel from those lands the one who was cultivating them and paying that larger rent in the manner explained. He claimed that the cultivator was his tenant, and had therefore never possessed the lands in his own name, and that it was therefore lawful for him to expel the cultivator in whatever year he wished, according to what we said above.

But the one who was cultivating the lands proved (as Gama reports) that he and his ancestors had possessed them for forty or sixty full years, had paid the uniform rent in the manner explained, had brought those lands under cultivation, and were perpetual leaseholders <term>emphyteutas</term> of the Church.

<margin>22</margin>
The senators, as Gama in that place and Caldas report, delivered the sentence in favor of the farmer: that he was a leaseholder not only until the three lives were finished, but even in perpetuity. They were led to this not only by the title of prescription, but also because, according to the final law in the Code on alluvion and marshes, it is not equitable to exclude that defendant from those lands which were brought under cultivation by his own labor and expense, and those of his ancestors. This also agrees with the ecclesiastical acts regarding not alienating the property of the Church.

It concludes that while temporary tenants cannot claim ownership through long-term stay, those who improve sterile land and pay consistent rent over decades gain protected legal rights that can even override the claims of intermediate landlords.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion on property rights, specifically focusing on whether a tenant farmer can claim the status of a perpetual lessee (emphyteuta) against the Church or a primary leaseholder based on long-term cultivation and rent payment.</meta>

->Second Treatise, Dispute 450.<-

<margin>23</margin> Quite rightly, Caldas <note>Francisco de Caldas Pereira y Castro, a famous 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> stated in the passage cited above that for that tenant farmer <term>colonus; a person who works land they do not own</term> to be declared a perpetual lessee <term>emphyteuta; a tenant with a long-term, inheritable lease that grants quasi-ownership</term>, he would have had to prove two things. First, that he did not receive those lands from another lessee, but directly from the Church, before the Church had handed them over to that other person in a lease. However, Caldas asserts the opposite is true. It is evident from the legal instruments that the plaintiff produced against him that the lands were first handed over for "three lives" <note>A common lease term lasting for the duration of three successive generations</note> to the person from whom the plaintiff eventually acquired his leasing right. Therefore, since the farmer and his predecessors held their right from a lessee, they could not claim a legal right through time <term>præscribere; to gain a right via prescription</term> for any longer than the period until those three lives ended. The second thing he had to prove was that he had received those lands while they were sterile. By that very fact, they could have been given by the Church in a perpetual lease according to the chapter *ad aures* <note>original: "c. ad aures"; a reference to Canon Law regarding the management of Church property</note>, and it was to be presumed that they had been handed over in that state. But Caldas asserts the truth was the opposite: namely, that before that event, he had received those lands from a lessee after they had already been brought under cultivation. And let me give this one warning: it is surely false to claim that lands brought under cultivation by someone (or their ancestors) cannot be taken away from them, or that they must be left to that person and their successors in a perpetual lease under the same rent, if this claim is taken universally. For the law *vlt. C. de alluvio. & palud.* <note>The last law in the Code of Justinian regarding alluvial lands and marshes</note> only establishes this for "taxable estates" from which the Prince or the Republic receives a rent or tribute—estates which the Castilians call <term>realencos</term> and the Portuguese call <term>regengos</term> <note>Both terms refer to royal or crown lands</note>.

For since it is in the interest of the Republic that estates be brought under cultivation, this was rightly established by that law for the public benefit. It does not follow from this that the law has the same force regarding Church estates or those of other private individuals. Furthermore, the chapter *ad aures* only permits that the Church *may* leave lands brought under cultivation to those very people (or their successors) who turned them from uncultivated to cultivated under the same rent—provided, as the text adds, that there are no others who are willing to take them under a higher rent. For in that case, the others shall be preferred, unless the original cultivators increase the rent as much as the others are willing to increase it. Note also in that text, before the case is even presented, that it is remarked that those lands, because they were handed over while sterile, were promised to the cultivators under a perpetual lease, even if a written contract had not been drawn up for the matter.

<margin>24</margin> Since the matter, as proposed in the second place by Caldas, was settled by an arbitrator, it must be defined as Caldas suggests, and as Gama <note>Antonio da Gama, another prominent Portuguese jurist</note> records in Decision 329. If it is clear that the property which a lessee had received directly from the Church had been handed over from the beginning by that same lessee to someone else, and leased to them for a certain rent, then, no matter how long that contract continues—even for forty or sixty years—it is always considered a lease for the following year and the year after that. Therefore, no right is acquired by the passage of time <term>nullū ius præfcribitur</term>, according to what was said above; instead, the farmer can be expelled by the lessee at the end of any given year. If, however, it is not clear that it was a simple lease from the beginning, and the person who received it from the primary lessee for a certain rent has paid a uniform rent for thirty years—whether he paid part to the Church and part to the lessee, or the whole to the Church or the lessee who then paid his own rent to the Church—then the contract is 

<column-break/>

to be considered "libellary." This is a sub-lease from a lessee, a contract which the Portuguese call <term>prazo de prazo</term> <note>literally "lease of a lease" or a sub-emphyteusis</note>, about which we spoke in Dispute 10. For although a lessee cannot grant a sub-lease of what he received himself without the owner's consent, he can validly grant it with the owner's consent, as will be discussed below. Since he has paid a uniform rent for such a long time, with the direct lord <note>The ultimate owner, usually the Church</note> knowing and allowing it, either to the lessee or the owner, the direct lord is deemed to have consented to that contract. Therefore, by such tacit or express consent, the libellary contract is valid. This was so decided in Decision 329, cited above, and Decision 244, and Caldas affirms it should be defined this way in the place cited. In that case, the final lessee remains with the "useful ownership" <term>dñio vtili; the right to use and profit from the land</term>, while the intermediary remains only with the right that the final lessee pays the rent to him, or a part of it, and the rest to the primary lessee, as they agreed among themselves. But if the final lessee commits a forfeit <term>in commiffum cadat; fails to fulfill the contract terms</term>, he loses the useful ownership not to the first lessee, but to the direct lord, as Gama rightly says in the final number there.

<margin>25</margin> I said a little while ago "if he has paid rent for thirty years," because, since the final lessee was acquiring useful ownership and the leasing right, a span of 30 years is sufficient even without a title deed, as was said in Dispute 70. This is because he is not claiming this right against the Church, but against another lessee, whether of the Church or a common person.

Indeed, if a written document is not essential to the substance of this contract (which is celebrated not with the Church but with a private individual), then even though at least the tacit consent of the direct lord is required, it will be enough to have paid a uniform rent for ten consecutive years. This allows the one who paid it to protect himself against the previous lessee without any legal instrument at all, according to what was said above based on the law *cum de in rem verfo* in the Digest on interest.

## Whether for an emphyteutic contract it is necessary, beyond the rent, for something to be paid for entry. And to whom it is prohibited to receive it.

## DISPUTE CCCCL.

### SUMMARY.

1. What an emphyteutic contract requires beyond the payment of rent.
2. And regarding Portuguese law, number 2.
3. When a lease for entry should be judged as a purchase and sale instead.

**M**any among the ancients thought that for an emphyteutic contract it was necessary that, beyond the rent, something should be paid for "entry" or "entrance," as they call it. And in this they felt that the emphyteutic contract—which in law is called a middle ground between purchase and sale, and between leasing and hiring (Institutes on leasing, paragraph *adeo* and the first law of the Code on emphyteutic law)—approached the nature of purchase and sale.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of emphyteusis—a type of long-term lease that functions like ownership—specifically investigating whether a one-time entry fee is a legal requirement for such contracts and how this affects Church and Crown lands.</meta>

### Louis Molina: On Contracts

Among their number are included the glosses on the law *c. potiss.* concerning leases, Bartolus on the first law of the Code regarding the law of emphyteusis, and many others whom Alvarus Valascus <note>original: "Alu. Valas."; a prominent Portuguese jurist</note> cites in his work *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 10, number 1. This same opinion seems to be held in Law 3, title 14, part 1, and Law 69, title 8, part 5. Gregorius Lopez, in his commentary on the cited Law 69 under the phrase *for certain maravedis* <note>original: "por ciertos marauedis"; a Spanish currency of the time</note>, argues that it should be interpreted this way: since an emphyteutic contract can be celebrated with a payment for entry, if nothing is paid for entry, that law prescribes the form by which the contract ought to be celebrated in the former manner. However, regarding Law 3 and the two other contrary laws cited, it must be said that they only mean that when such a contract is celebrated in that first way—where a price is paid for entry—it approaches the nature of a purchase and sale.

The more common and true opinion of the doctors, however, is that it is not necessary for an emphyteutic contract <term>emphyteuticus contractus; a long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights in exchange for rent and land improvement</term> to have something paid for entry beyond the annual rent <term>pensionem; the fixed yearly rent paid by the tenant</term>, since it can be perfectly well celebrated in either way. This is the view of Bartolus on the law *si mihi & tibi* in the Digest concerning verbal obligations, and others whom Julius Clarus cites and follows in his *Sentences*, book 4, section on emphyteusis, question 3, as do Alvarus Valascus and Gregorius Lopez in the places cited above. In Law 28, title 8, part 5, under the word *given* and the following gloss on the word *added*, the same is gathered from that law. This opinion is embraced by Silvester under the word *emphyteusis*, number 3, and Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 7, number 1.

<margin>Portuguese Law, 2</margin>
Indeed, this is confirmed by Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, title 66. There, a payment for entry is so far from being considered necessary to the nature of an emphyteutic contract that if those who hold lands from the Crown, or administrators of chapels, or entails <term>maioratūm; an estate that must be passed down whole to a single heir</term>, or commendataries <note>officials holding a "commenda," or a beneficial grant of land or revenue</note> who have the faculty of granting the goods of chapels, entails, commendams, or the Crown in emphyteusis, should accept anything for entry—whether they grant those goods in perpetual emphyteusis or for a set number of lives, or when they renew an emphyteusis—the contract is by that very fact null and void. Furthermore, the emphyteutic property is immediately reunited with the ownership <note>the "useful" right of the tenant merges back into the "direct" ownership of the landlord</note>, without the tenant having any power to contest this with the owner in court or to summon him for that cause. Moreover, whoever gave that entry fee is punished by the loss of the amount to the person who received it, for which no judicial sentence need be awaited. In addition, if it is proven that they gave it, they are forced to pay the same amount again: half to the accuser and half for the redemption of captives <note>a common charitable cause in the 16th century, often for ransoming Christians captured by Mediterranean pirates</note>. The reason for this prudent law is found in the sanctions of the Portuguese Order, chapter 25, where it prescribes the same for the commendataries of that order. Namely, because all these people possess those goods that must pass to another upon their death according to the original founder's decree or return eventually to the Crown; therefore, lest they grant those lands for a meager annual rent to the detriment of their successors or the Crown, having accepted a large upfront price for entry for their own sole enjoyment, this was most rightly decreed. This agrees with the law *Titius rogatus* in the Digest, where it is held that when an heir was burdened with restoring what remained of an inheritance at his death, he does not have to restore what he consumed in good faith, thereby diminishing the inheritance; but it is otherwise for what was consumed for the purpose of subverting the trust <term>fideicommissum; a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of another</term>, as Bartolus and others note, whom Alvarus Valascus cites and follows.

This cited ordinance is not contradicted by another ordinance of the same

<column-break/>

kingdom in Book 2, title 17, paragraph 23. There it is defined that if the King's grantees—to whom certain things are granted during their life at the King's pleasure—should grant the property so donated in emphyteusis without the King's permission, the King is not bound to observe that contract from the moment the donation expires, though it holds until the donation ceases. This second point is gathered from the law *necessario*, final paragraph, in the Digest on the risk and convenience of a sold thing, and from the law *si quis domum*, and as Antonius Gomez affirms in Law 40 of Toro, number 84, and others cited by Alvarus Valascus. This ordinance, I say, does not contradict the other, as Alvarus Valascus rightly observes in the same place. For the first speaks of when something was accepted for entry, in which event the emphyteutic contract celebrated regarding Crown lands donated by the king is null by law; but this latter one speaks of when nothing was accepted for entry.

From what has been said, Alvarus Valascus rightly concludes that emphyteuses granted by Church prelates with the acceptance of money or gifts for entry, beyond the annual rent, can be overturned and declared invalid insofar as it was to the prejudice of their successors—for instance, if the annual rent is meager and the amount accepted for entry was significant.

And this was clearly established by the Council of Trent <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council that defined the Catholic Reformation</note>, session 25, chapter 11, on reform, where it states: "Great ruin is often brought upon churches when their property is leased to others in prejudice of successors in exchange for immediate cash. Therefore, let all such leases, if they are made with anticipated payments, be understood as in no way valid to the prejudice of successors, notwithstanding any indulgence or privilege. Nor should leases of this kind be confirmed in the Roman Curia or outside of it." This seems to be extended to the emphyteuses we are discussing.

When the price or other thing given for entry, together with the annual rent, does not exceed the limits of equal compensation for the emphyteusis being granted in the judgment of a prudent person, there would be no reason to condemn such a contract as unequal or unjust; it is otherwise when it exceeds it, and then there would be an obligation to restore the excess. However, it will rarely happen that more is given for an emphyteusis than it is worth; the danger is far greater when something is given for entry so that, out of a desire to receive it immediately, the emphyteusis is granted for a smaller return than it is worth. In that case, if it does not reach the limits of what is just, it should be increased in the court of conscience. Although, because things were usually granted in emphyteusis for a meager rent from the beginning so that they might be improved by the recipients, and because there are many burdens that remain for the tenant—such as paying the *laudemium* <term>laudemium; a fee paid to the landlord when the tenant's right is sold to someone else</term> if he sells his right, and other risks of forfeiture we shall see—there is usually no scruple on that matter, especially when the emphyteuses are ancient.

I should mention this along with Alvarus Valascus: if for the entry into an emphyteusis a much higher price is given than the value of the annual rents, the contract should be considered not an emphyteusis, but a purchase and sale of the "useful domain" <note>the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to legal title</note>, according to what we said in Dispute 336. If, however, it does not exceed it by much, it should be considered an emphyteutic contract, as was said there. Unless, however, it is conducted...

I also believe, following what was said there and elsewhere, that whenever a price is paid for entry, it should be considered a purchase and sale to the extent that an *alcauala* <note>original: "alcauala"; a Spanish sales tax, typically 10%</note> is owed based on the amount of that price. The same applies if another thing is given for entry, such as a horse, an ox, wheat, or something similar, so that it is considered an exchange, and a double *alcauala* is owed according to its value. Read what was said there and in Disputations 382 and 397. However, from an emphyteutic contract <term>emphyteuticus contractus; a long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights in exchange for improving the land and paying rent</term> as such, the *alcauala* is not owed: because it is neither a sale nor an exchange, but an entirely distinct contract. So says Lassattus in *On the Tenth of Sales*, chapter 1, number 42.

# How much the emphyteutic pension should be, in what matter, and when it should be paid.
## DISPUTATION CCCCLI.
### S U M M A R Y.

<margin>1</margin> 1 Pension, return, canon, and census are appropriate to the emphyteutic contract and are accepted as the same thing.
<margin>2</margin> 2 How much the pension is required to be in an emphyteutic contract so that it differs from a standard lease.
<margin>3</margin> 3 In what way an emphyteutic contract differs from a standard lease.
<margin>4</margin> 4 The pension in an emphyteutic contract can be established in any type of thing.
<margin>5</margin> 5 And what is observed in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> in number 5.
<margin>6</margin> 6 Likewise, it can be established as a certain quantity or a share of the fruits. Number 6.
<margin>7</margin> 7 At what times the pension must be paid.
<margin>8</margin> 8 Whether emphyteutic property is tacitly mortgaged for the payment of the pension.

<margin>1</margin> **T**hat which must be paid at stated times from an emphyteutic contract in recognition of the superior ownership <term>dominij directi; the ultimate ownership held by the landlord, as opposed to the tenant's right of use</term> is called both a † pension and a return <note>original: "pensio" and "reditus"</note>, as is clear from those words in the section "Adeo" of the Institutes on Leasing: *as long as the pension or return is provided for these.* However, both names have a much broader meaning, as Alvarus Valascus <note>original: "Aluar. Valas."; a 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> says in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 1, number 1, citing Paris de Puteo; and as is clear from common usage and what we have handed down in the section on *censuses* and elsewhere.

It is also called a *canon* in the chapter *Potuit* concerning leases, in those words: *By ceasing in the payment of the canon for a two-year period.* This name also extends to other things. For, as Covarruvias and Alvarus Valascus (cited above) hand down following Budé, all returns to the Crown of the Kingdom are called *canons*. It can also be called a *census*, according to what was said in Disputation 381, and it is used this way in Law 28, title 8, part 5. This name is also common to many other returns, as was explained in the same place.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the † substance of the emphyteutic contract, it does not matter whether the pension is large or small. Although many, deceived by Bartolus on the first law of the Code regarding the law of emphyteusis, have asserted that it is required for an emphy-

<column-break/>

-teutic contract that the pension be modest; otherwise, if it is large, it turns into a standard lease <term>locationem; a typical rental agreement</term>. On the contrary, Alvarus Valascus, in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 1, number 8, rightly asserted with Laurentius Silvianus that there is no text from which this can be gathered. And the contrary is quite clearly evident from what was said in Disputation 445.

<margin>3</margin> Indeed, the † emphyteutic contract differs from leasing and hiring <term>locatione, & conductione; the standard Roman law terms for a rental contract</term> (taking "leasing" somewhat broadly, as including that in which something is given for use and fruit in exchange for something that is not money) only in regards to time. For if an immovable thing is given to be used and enjoyed for ten years or more, it will be an emphyteutic contract; but if it is given for less than ten years, it will be a lease and hire, as was explained there. Therefore, I do not approve of what Alvarus Valascus adds in the cited question 1, numbers 9 and 10.

<margin>4</margin> Likewise, the † pension can be established and paid either in money or in some other thing, such as in grain, wine, oil, or another thing, as the common opinion of the doctors notes with the gloss on the word "pension" or "return" in the section "Adeo." Alvarus Valascus cites this in question 1, number 7, and follows it in question 20, number 3; and the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 60, last section, agree. And in this, emphyteusis differs from leasing and hiring in the strict sense, in which that which is to be paid for the enjoyment of the thing must be money, as we shall see in its proper place.

<margin>5</margin> However, as was said in Disputation 446, regarding Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, book 4 of the Ordinances, title 66, last section, it is decreed that in the † emphyteusis of houses, or of ground for building houses, the pension cannot be established except in money and birds; otherwise the contract is null and of no effect. Alvarus Valascus gives the reason for this decree in the cited question 20, number 6. He says there, however, that if the birds are not of the number of those which are accustomed to be delivered dead (namely those caught by hunting, such as partridges and quails), they must be delivered alive and not dead, arguing from the law *qui de cem*, last section, in the Digest on payments. Whether that Portuguese law extends to the Ecclesiastical emphyteuses of that Kingdom was discussed in the cited disputation.

<margin>6</margin> Likewise, the † emphyteutic pension can be established either as a certain quantity or as a proportional share of the fruits that have been harvested from that estate, as is gathered from the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 60, section 2, and affirmed by Alvarus Valascus in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 30, number 3. This can be confirmed because the agreements applied in this contract are valid, provided they are not against the substance of the contract, as is clear from laws 1 and 2 of the Code on the law of emphyteusis, and Law 28, title 8, part 5. Moreover, for a pension to be established for payment in that manner is certainly not against the substance of an emphyteutic contract.

<margin>7</margin> The law establishes no specific † time for the pension to be paid, but it is to be paid at the times established by the contracting parties, either every year or every two years (as happens with the pension of oil in some places where olive groves only bear fruit every two years), or at any other time as the contracting parties agree. For although it is of the substance of the con-
