nature of an emphyteutic contract <term>emphyteuticus contractus; a long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights in exchange for improving the land and paying rent</term> that a pension be paid, yet it is not essential to its nature that it be paid at this or that specific time. In this matter, one must stand by the agreements made by those entering the contract, according to what was said shortly before. But if the contracting parties have expressed nothing in this regard, one must follow the custom of the place; for when nothing else is specified, contracts are assumed to follow local custom. However, when the matter cannot be settled by local custom, one must judge what the parties intended based on the surrounding circumstances. This is the view of Alvaro Valasco in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 1, number 14; Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 16, number 6; and others whom he cites.

When the contracting parties have established a specific part or day of the year for the pension to be paid, it must be paid then. But when nothing has been established, custom shall be followed; if there is no consistent and universal custom, the pension should be paid at the end of the year, counting from the day the contract was celebrated. This last point is affirmed by Giulio Claro in *Sentences*, book 4, § emphyteusis, question 12, as being the standard practice.

<margin>8</margin>
Furthermore, is the emphyteutic property † tacitly mortgaged for the payment of the pensions? Baldus and others, cited by Alvaro Valasco in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 4, number 6, believe that it is mortgaged. On the contrary, Valasco rightly judges in the same place that it is not. This is because there is no legal text from which such a thing can be gathered, and for other reasons that you may read in his work.

## For an emphyteutic contract to be valid, is it necessary to establish a certain and determined pension? And what pension should be considered just? And does Law 2 of the Code on Rescinding a Sale apply to this contract?

->DISPUTATION CCCCLII.<-

->S U M M A R Y.<-

1 *A determined pension must be established in an emphyteusis for the contract to be valid.*
2 *A renewal [innovation] is not a new title, but a continuation of the preceding one.*
3 *What pension should be considered just.*
4 *Whether Law 2 of the Code on Rescinding a Sale applies to an emphyteutic contract.*
5 *Whether injury in an emphyteutic contract is more or less than half the just price, and how it is to be judged.*

**R**egarding the first of these points, the same things must be said as were said regarding the contract of purchase and sale—specifically, whether a determined price must be established for it to be valid—which we discussed in Disputation 337.

<margin>1</margin>
For † that reason, I will not dwell on this matter. Alvaro Valasco disputes it at length in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 11, from number 5. However, when an emphyteusis is renewed <note>original: "innouaretur"; a legal 'innovation' or 'novatio' where an old contract is replaced by a new one</note>, it is not necessary to make mention of a specific price for which it is renewed, since it is deemed renewed at the previous 

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin>
price. Nor is a renewal † considered a new title <note>a legal basis for ownership</note>, but a continuation of the preceding one. So says Alvaro Valasco in the place cited above, number 15, along with Bartolus and the common opinion which he reports. This is confirmed by the laws *Item quaeritur* § *qui impleto* and the penultimate law § *uxor* in the Digests.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the second point, many have taught that a "just" † pension for an emphyteusis is one which, when collected over twenty years, equals the value of the property granted in emphyteusis. This is according to the *Authenticum* <note>a collection of Justinian's legal novels</note> regarding the non-alienation of church property, § *si vero alicuius Ecclesiastici*, and is affirmed by the final gloss on the text *Perpetua* in the Code *On the Most Holy Churches*. The authors of this opinion are cited by Pinellus on Law 2 of the Code *On Rescinding a Sale*, part 3, chapter 4, number 29; Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 3, chapter 9, number 5; and Alvaro Valasco, question 11, number 2.

However, it must be said, along with the same Pinellus in the cited law (part 1, at the end of chapter 3), Covarruvias, and Valasco, that this is not a certain and constant rule. Rather, it must be established by the judgment of prudent men, taking into account the circumstances and the local custom regarding the granting of similar properties in emphyteusis. Indeed, the custom by which similar things are usually traded in a region contributes greatly to the just price of things, as was explained in Disputation 348.

Regarding the cited *Authenticum*, it must be said that it was wisely established for that specific time—not universally, as is clear from the text itself—but concerning certain suburban estates of the Church which were of great value but returned small pensions, such as towers, as the gloss there explains. Furthermore, in the *Authenticum* regarding alienation and emphyteusis, § *sanctissimas*, the Church of Jerusalem is permitted to alienate certain houses belonging to it at a price no less than what fifty-five annual pensions of those same houses would amount to. Covarruvias cites various other laws in which the prices of things are sanctioned differently when compared with pensions. Therefore, just as the just price of a census <note>an annual payment or tax</note> does not consist in an indivisible point, nor is it the same at different times in the same place, or at the same time in different regions (as was said in the section on censuses), so it is with emphyteusis.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding the third point—namely, whether † Law 2 of the Code *On Rescinding a Sale* <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescind. vendit."; a famous Roman law allowing a seller to rescind a sale if they received less than half the "just price" (laesio enormis)</note> applies to an emphyteutic contract—many, following the *Speculator* in the title on purchase and sale (cited by Valasco and Pinellus), judge that it has no place in it. This is partly because that law only applies to "good faith" contracts, whereas emphyteusis is a contract of "strict law," as was stated in Disputation 447. It is also because the pension in an emphyteutic contract is not paid as a price or wage, but as a recognition of the direct lordship <term>dominium directum; the ultimate ownership of the land retained by the grantor, as opposed to the tenant's right of use</term>; therefore, by the nature of the contract, it is usually modest compared to the rent paid in a standard lease.

This very point seems to be echoed in Law 68 of the Castilian *Laws of Toro*, which states: *If anyone should place upon his estate any census with the condition that if he does not pay at certain terms, the estate is forfeited, let the contract be kept and judged by it, even if the penalty be great and more than half the value.* <note>original Spanish: "Si alguno pusiere sobre su heredad algun censo..."</note> And so it is understood...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 520 regarding whether the legal protections against "enormous loss" (where a price is less than half or more than double the fair value) apply to long-term land leases known as emphyteusis.</meta>

<header>Second Treatise. Disputation 453.</header>

<margin>Antonio Gomez understands it this way at the end, number 4.</margin>
Antonio Gomez understands this law in the same place at the end, number 4. See Title 12, Book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collectiōnis", referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compilation of Spanish laws</note>, which, dealing with the provision of Law 2 of the Code on the rescinding of sales, adds: *“And this same thing must be observed in such sales and in exchanges and in other similar contracts, as in those of good faith.”* <note>original: "Y esto mismo deue ser guardado en tales ventas y en los cambios y en los otros contratos semejantes, vtique bonæ fidei."</note>

The opposite opinion is more common, along with the same Speculator <note>Guillaume Durand, a famous medieval legal scholar</note> (though he contradicts himself elsewhere) in the title on <term>emphyteusis</term> <gloss>a long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights in exchange for improving the land and paying rent</gloss>, section "if indeed any," number 14. Panormitanus follows this in the chapter "with cause," on buying and selling, stating it is the common view; it is also cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco and Pinellus in the places mentioned above. This is undoubtedly the law in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, as it is decreed in Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 90, § 1, in those words: *Leasing agreements* <note>original: "Eaforamentos", the Portuguese term for emphyteutic leases</note>.

The reason is not only because an emphyteutic contract is similar to a standard lease <note>original: "locationi"</note>, in which that law applies, but also because that law, in terms of its effect, even has a place in contracts of "strict law" <note>contracts interpreted literally according to the letter of the agreement rather than general equity</note>. However, because there was a controversy among the doctors on this point in Disputation 349, we only stated that the law applies to contracts of "good faith," asserting nothing about contracts of "strict law," but leaving that to be examined in other places.

Nor is it certain that in the Kingdom of Castile <note>original: "Regno Castellæ"</note> this does not apply to emphyteusis. Regarding Law 68 of Toro <note>original: "L. Tauri"</note>, it should be said that it only speaks of the penalty of forfeiture <note>original: "pœna commissi"</note> even if it exceeds half the just price; it does not, however, speak of the annual rents <note>original: "pensionibus"</note>, or the right to them, proceeding from a comparison of the price's value. Furthermore, in Disputation 92, when explaining the sixth clause of the Bull of Pope Pius V with the doctors we cited there, we said that that law is not just regarding that penalty in a "constituted census" <note>a type of financial annuity secured by property</note>, of which there is talk there, nor is it received in practice in that Kingdom. Add to this that the law speaks of the "constituted census," which is a contract of good faith and a certain part of buying and selling; in such a census, no one can deny that Law 2 of the Code on rescinding sales applies, once a comparison is made between the value of the right to the rents and the price given for that right.

Regarding Law 1, Title 12, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, it must be said that those words—*“And in other similar contracts”*—are to be understood as those in which one thing is given for another, whether they are of "good faith" or "strict law."

But as for what was said before those laws—namely, that in an emphyteutic contract the rent is not given as a price or payment, but only in recognition of <term>direct ownership</term> <gloss>the ultimate legal title held by the landlord</gloss>—that must be flatly denied, as Alvaro Valasco also denies it in the place cited. For although it is given in recognition of direct ownership, it is simultaneously, and equally primarily, given as compensation for the <term>useful ownership</term> <gloss>the right to use and profit from the land</gloss> which is granted to the tenant by the emphyteutic contract.

Therefore, observe that Alvaro Valasco tries too hard in other questions of his work to distinguish the emphyteutic contract from hiring and leasing <note>original: "locatione, & conductione"</note> on the grounds that in a lease, the rent is paid as a price and compensation for the use and fruits of the hired thing, whereas in emphyteusis it is not, but is for the recognition of direct ownership.

<margin>5</margin>
Furthermore, † to judge whether the loss <note>original: "læsio"</note> in an emphyteutic contract is more or less than half of the just price, one must estimate the value of the "useful ownership" granted to the tenant, keeping in mind that the tenant

<column-break/>

is left subject to many burdens by that same contract. These we will explain, such as the risk of forfeiture <note>original: "commissum"</note> for various reasons, the payment of a <term>transfer fee</term> <gloss>laudemium; a fee paid to the landlord when the lease is sold to a new tenant</gloss>, and so on. One must also estimate the value of the right to the rents which is returned to the "direct owner," making a comparison of one value with the other. In estimating these things, account must be taken of the amount of rent that is customarily granted for similar things handed over in emphyteusis in the same region, as was said above.

Neither do I judge that the opinion of Pinellus, in the cited number, should be approved—namely, that Law 2 of the Code on rescinding sales applies if the tenant says he is harmed, but not if the direct owner complains he is harmed. For the direct owner is also to be heard, as Alvaro Valasco and others more rightly maintain. However, as we said in Disputation 450, controversies will rarely arise where the contract was unjust, let alone where one of the contracting parties is harmed by more or less than half of the just value. Alvaro Valasco, however, affirms that he has seen this second controversy once.

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

13. If someone accepts an <term>emphyteusis</term> <gloss>a long-term lease where the tenant acts as a near-owner, paying a small rent and improving the land</gloss> for themselves, their children, and their descendants, and if an intermediary leaseholder incurs a <term>commissum</term> <gloss>a forfeiture of rights due to a breach of contract</gloss>, does this harm the others to whom the leasehold rights ought to pass?
14. If a leaseholder does not pay for two or three years, do they fall into forfeiture if a different penalty was imposed in the contract for non-payment of rent?
15. An agreement that the leaseholder shall not forfeit the lease for unpaid rent is valid.
16. The same must be said of an agreement that if they do not pay within a period shorter than two or three years, they shall forfeit the lease.
17. If it is contended that a leaseholder has forfeited the lease, does it fall to the owner to prove the rent was not paid, or to the leaseholder to prove they paid it?
18. If a leaseholder incurs forfeiture and the owner has not executed the penalty, can the owner's heirs do so?
19. If an owner does not execute the penalty of forfeiture against a leaseholder, can they do so against the leaseholder's heirs?
20. If a leaseholder offers the owner rent for several subsequent years, the owner is not bound to receive them.
21. Can a leaseholder who incurs forfeiture for unpaid rent be expelled by the owner on the owner's own authority?
22. If a leaseholder wishes to give up the property to the owner, is the owner bound to accept it, or can the owner compel them to persist in the lease?

<margin>1</margin>
If the lease is "common"—that is, not involving Church property—and nothing else has been specifically agreed upon in the contract, and the leaseholder has not paid the rent for three continuous years, they lose not only their leasehold right but also any <term>improvements</term> <note>original: "melioramenta"</note> made to the property. The entire property, along with the improvements, reverts to the owner if the owner desires it, even if the owner has not demanded the rent from the leaseholder during that whole time. In this case, the passage of time "stands in" for a formal demand by the owner; consequently, the leaseholder is bound to pay the rent even if not asked.

<margin>2</margin>
When a leaseholder incurs this penalty, it is called "falling into <term>commissum</term>" <gloss>forfeiture</gloss> or "falling into lapse." This also refers to the loss of the property to the owner due to unpaid rent. All of this is established in *Law 2 of the Code on the Right of Emphyteusis*; *Law 28, Title 8, Part 5*; and *Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 65*, at the beginning and in section 1. These rules hold true even if the Church is the leaseholder of a layman's land; however, in that case, the Church is entitled to "restoration to its original state" <note>original: "restitutio in integrum," a legal remedy to cancel the effects of a law that would otherwise cause an unfair loss</note>, just as a minor is. This is correctly affirmed by Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist who commented on the *Siete Partidas*</note> in his commentary on the aforementioned Law 28, at the words "for two years." 

If, however, the lease involves Church property and the leaseholder does not pay the rent for two continuous years, they similarly incur forfeiture, and all the aforementioned consequences apply. This is established in the chapter *Potuit* regarding leases. 

Furthermore, this privilege for Churches had previously been granted in civil law in the *Authenticum* regarding non-alienation <note>original: "authentico de nõ alienandis"</note>, section *Scire*, and in the *Authenticum* regarding alienation and emphyteusis, section *If indeed anyone or by lease* <note>original: "si verò quis aut locato"</note>, and it is found in the *Authenticum* titled *Who*:

<column-break/>

and in the *Code on the Holy Churches*; *Law 28, Title 8, Part 5*; and *Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 65, section 2*. The common opinion of the learned doctors agrees with what has been said so far. If a private person's lease is transferred to the Church, and the leaseholder had not paid the private person for a year and a half, and subsequently does not pay the Church for a year, I believe they incur forfeiture—provided the previous owner transferred to the Church the right they had partially acquired to execute the penalty of forfeiture. This follows what was said regarding prescription at the end of Disputation 72. However, Gregorio Lopez, in the passage cited above, requires a full lapse of two years after the lease begins to belong to the Church. I consider this to be true if the previous owner does not transfer their right to the Church.

<margin>3</margin>
At this point, observe that since laws of this kind are "penal," they do not create an obligation unless the owner wishes to enforce the penalty. This is sufficiently hinted at in *Law 2 of the Code on the Right of Emphyteusis* and is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Giulio Claro <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist</note> cites and follows in his *Sentences, Book 4, section on Emphyteusis, question 9*. Therefore, as long as the owner does not move to execute the penalty, the leaseholder is safe in their conscience while continuing in the lease. Nevertheless, a formal court sentence is not strictly necessary to end the right, as the cited doctors and others mentioned by Silvester <note>Sylvester Prieras, a 15th-century theologian</note> under the word "emphyteusis," question 2, affirm and follow.

Diego de Covarrubias <note>A prominent Spanish canon lawyer and bishop</note>, in his *Varied Resolutions, Book 3, chapter 16, number 6*, along with Baldus, Alexander, Jason, and Catiline Corta, asserts that if the fruits of the leased property are not gathered every year, but every two years, a common leaseholder does not incur forfeiture unless they fail to pay the rent for six continuous years. They argue this from the law *If so* in the *Digest* concerning how services are lost. I believe this is true only when the land does not yield fruit except every two years, and the rent was likewise paid every two years. If, however, the rent was paid annually in money or in some other form, then one falls into forfeiture in the customary time of three years. In cases where a common leaseholder would not forfeit the lease before six continuous years for that reason, a Church leaseholder would not forfeit it before four continuous years, as the same reasoning applies.

<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
There is a doubt whether, when a leaseholder has confirmed by oath that they will pay the rents every year, they incur forfeiture by the very fact that they fail to pay once at the proper time. In such a case, should one not wait for the lapse of three years in a common lease, or two years in a Church lease? And further, would there be no room for "purging the delay" <note>original: "purgatio moræ," a legal concept where a debtor can avoid penalties by paying before a formal legal action is finalized</note>, which will be discussed shortly? Baldus, in the chapter *Complaint* regarding oaths, and after him the more common opinion of the doctors (which Gutierrez cites and follows in his *On Oaths, Part 1, Chapter 31*), embrace the affirmative view. They are moved chiefly by the law *If anyone of age* in the *Code on Transactions*, which states that someone who has sworn to keep an agreement and fails to do so is deprived of the entire benefit of the contract.

<margin>Decision</margin>
However, I believe the opposite should be maintained, along with Covarrubias in his *Although an Agreement* on pacts, part 1, section 4, number 5, and others whom he cites. Giulio Claro also leans toward this in his *Sentences, section on Emphyteusis, question 8, number 2*. For that law is penal and clearly speaks only of an agreement for a legal settlement <note>original: "pacto transactionis"</note> confirmed by an oath, as is clear from the text itself and the glosses there; it should not be extended to other contracts. And therefore, while one who

<meta>The catchword "qui" at the bottom indicates the next page begins with that word, continuing the thought that someone who breaks an oath is a perjurer, but perhaps not automatically a forfeit-holder of the lease.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the forfeiture of long-term leases (emphyteusis). It specifically addresses whether a tenant who has failed to pay rent for the required period (two or three years) can still save their lease by paying the arrears late—a process known as "purging the delay."</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation I.

...one who has sworn to pay rent at the appropriate times, but does not pay when they are able, does not immediately incur <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; the loss of the leasehold rights due to breach of contract</gloss> unless the rent remains unpaid for the entire period established by law for that purpose.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The question is whether, once the two or three-year period has passed—in which the <term>leaseholder</term><gloss>Latin: emphyteuta</gloss> normally incurs forfeiture—there is still room for <term>purging the delay</term><gloss>Latin: purgatio morae; a legal remedy allowing a debtor to fulfill an obligation late to avoid a penalty</gloss>. Specifically, can the leaseholder be freed from the penalty of forfeiture and retain the lease by offering the owner the rent for that entire elapsed time?

<margin>Decision on the Law of Castile</margin>
The common opinion among legal scholars is that in a standard lease, there is no room for purging the delay once the time has passed; this seems to agree with the Code of Justinian <note>original: "l. 2. C. de iure emphy."</note> and is expressly defined in the Portuguese Ordinances. However, the Law of Castile <note>original: "Lex 28. tit. 8. part. 5." referring to the Siete Partidas</note> establishes that in both standard and <term>Ecclesiastical leases</term><gloss>leases involving land owned by the Church</gloss>, there is a window for purging the delay within only ten days after the two or three-year period has expired. This is the rule to be asserted in the Kingdom of Castile regarding standard leases, as affirmed by Gregorius Lopez, Covarruvias, and Gutierrez.

<margin>B. 14.</margin>
Regarding Ecclesiastical leases, it is granted that after the two-year period has passed, the leaseholder can purge the past delay by a "swift offering" of the rent payments, thereby escaping the penalty of forfeiture, as is expressly held in the canon law chapter *Potuit*. This was granted out of the Church's kindness toward such leases as a compensation for the privilege granted to the Church itself—namely, that a leaseholder falls into forfeiture in the shorter time of two years (whereas in civil law it is usually three).

<margin>Question</margin>
However, a doubt exists among scholars as to how much time is allowed to purge the delay so that it is considered "swift" after the two years have passed, according to the disposal of the chapter *Potuit*. The <term>Gloss</term><gloss>the standard marginal commentary on legal texts</gloss> on that passage cites many opinions. Omitting others, one opinion is that it must be within ten days, as this is considered a "modest time." This view, which is certainly not improbable, was embraced by the cited Law of Castile; it extends this timeframe to standard leases so that in that Kingdom, a common leaseholder can purge a three-year delay within that period. Another opinion is that the delay can be purged until the <term>joinder of issue</term><gloss>Latin: litem contestatam; the formal start of a trial when the defendant answers the plaintiff's claim</gloss> in the legal execution of the forfeiture penalty.

This is the rule established in the Portuguese Ordinances. However, Gama thinks that in this "hateful matter" <note>Molina refers to forfeiture as "odious" or "hateful" because the law generally dislikes penalties that strip people of their property rights</note>, a mere general denial before a judge is not enough; rather, a true and formal joinder of issue is required—answering the plaintiff’s specific complaint—to bar the leaseholder from purging the delay. The cited Gloss on the chapter *Potuit* rightly disagrees with this opinion. It argues that the rule where a leaseholder loses the lease after two years was introduced in favor of the Church; in return for this shorter timeframe, the Church granted the "swift" purging of delay, which does not normally apply to other leaseholders. Furthermore, the word "swift" does not support a long delay. The intent of the Church was not to allow a leaseholder to purge a delay after three, four, or more years simply because they had not yet been summoned to court. If that were the case,

<column-break/>

the Ecclesiastical lease would be in a worse condition in this regard than a standard one. Another opinion is held by the Gloss, Panormitanus, Cardinalis, Navarrus, and Covarruvias.

Julius Clarus and the common opinion suggest that it should be left to the judge's discretion to decide what period constitutes a "swift satisfaction" for purging the delay. I have learned that in Portugal, a certain <term>Papal Legate</term><gloss>an official representative of the Pope</gloss> judged in a particular case that someone who had not purged the delay within two months had not acted "swiftly," and therefore had forfeited the lease. There is a question as to whether that Portuguese law has force in Ecclesiastical leases.

Whatever Gama may say to the contrary, I believe it does not have force, as the Portuguese law itself immediately adds that in Church property and Ecclesiastical leases, one must follow Canon law rather than Civil law. The opinion established in the Portuguese Ordinance is truly improbable, greatly detracts from the Church's privilege concerning its leases, and is not at all consistent with the disposal of Canon law.

Some authors report that a <term>direct lord</term><gloss>the actual owner of the land to whom the tenant pays rent</gloss> to whom rent has not been paid (for two years by a Church tenant or three by a common tenant) should immediately declare—even in the tenant's absence—that they wish for the lease to be forfeited. This, they say, is the best precaution to prevent any late purging of the delay. However, Gregorius Lopez and Gutierrez believe this does not apply in the Kingdom of Castile unless that declaration is made after the ten-day grace period has passed.

This is because such a declaration cannot prejudice the rights granted by Law 28, which allows those ten days to purge the delay. They add, however, that if the owner grants the lease to someone else or alienates the property before those ten days are up—so that the matter is no longer "whole"—then the tenant cannot purge the delay. Nevertheless, I believe, along with Covarruvias, that it must be stated absolutely: within the term granted either by the Law of Castile (for common leases) or by Canon Law (for Ecclesiastical leases), the tenant can generally purge the delay. The owner's actions cannot override the rights granted to the tenant by the Church's sanctions or Castilian law, especially while the tenant is still in possession of the property; they cannot be stripped of it before that term expires if they wish to pay.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
The question is whether, after a tenant has incurred forfeiture and can no longer purge the delay, the owner is considered to have forgiven the penalty if they accept the past-due rent from the tenant. If so, could the owner still take the lease away?

<margin>Decision</margin>
Panormitanus and, following him, Silvester answer this excellently: if the owner accepts rent payments from the leaseholder, even for the time *after* the forfeiture was incurred, they are considered to have remitted...

<summary>This page analyzes the "grace period" allowed for tenants to pay overdue rent to avoid losing their long-term leases, comparing Spanish (Castilian), Portuguese, and Church (Canon) laws. It concludes that while laws vary on the exact timeframe, owners who accept back rent after a deadline may unintentionally waive their right to evict the tenant.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

...remitted the penalty of <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; the loss of the leasehold rights due to breach of contract</gloss>, and intended to continue the contract. By that act, he tacitly continued the leasehold contract for the following period. This is based on the legal argument found in the chapter "Solicitudinem" regarding appeals <note>original: "c. sollicitudinē de appell. in fine"</note>. Legal scholars such as Giulio Claro <note>original: "Iul. Clarūs verb. emphyteu. q. 10. nu. 1."</note> and Gigas affirm against Bartolus that this is true, even if the owner, while receiving the rent for that time, protested that he did not wish to prejudice his own rights regarding the penalty of forfeiture.

However, if he only receives the rents from the past period—those which were not paid and thus caused the forfeiture—then all scholars agree that if a protest was made stating he did not wish to prejudice his ability to execute the penalty of forfeiture, he may still execute it. If, however, he received them without making any such protest, the <term>gloss</term><gloss>a standard marginal commentary on legal texts</gloss> on the Code regarding the law of <term>emphyteusis</term><gloss>a long-term or permanent lease of land</gloss>, Giulio Claro, Gigas, and others they cite, have asserted that he prejudices his rights and tacitly waives the penalty of forfeiture. Yet, Panormitanus and Sylvester rightly affirm in the same place that he can still execute the penalty of forfeiture: because in a case of doubt, no one is deemed to surrender his own right. This was also the opinion of Bartolus and Afflictis, as reported by Gama, and it has been enacted in the **Portuguese Ordinances**, Book 4, Title 65, Paragraph 1.

From this, you will easily understand that we should reject the opinion of Giulio Claro, Gigas, and others they cite, who assert—against Bartolus and most others—that an owner who expels a private leaseholder for not paying rent for three years cannot additionally demand the rents for those three years. They hold this even though they concede that an owner expelling a leaseholder of the **Church** can recover the rents for those two years <note>Under Roman and Canon law, Church land was often protected by a shorter two-year window for forfeiture compared to the three years allowed for secular land.</note>.

Since the rents for those three years are not owed as a penalty, but by contract as compensation for the <term>useful ownership</term><gloss>the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to "direct ownership"</gloss> and for the fruits gathered from the leased property in those years, they are certainly owed in justice beyond the penalty of forfeiture, and therefore they can be recovered.

<margin>Doubt 8</margin> The next doubt is whether, in order for the leaseholder to avoid forfeiture, it is sufficient for him to offer the rent to the owner within that two or three-year period. The final gloss on the Code regarding the law of emphyteusis raises this doubt. In the second place, it records the opinion of those who said there was a special rule in this contract: that it was not enough to offer payment, but that a <term>consignation</term><gloss>a formal deposit of the money with a court or third party</gloss> or deposit of such rent was also necessary.

<margin>Decision</margin> And this is quite consistent with the words of that law. However, the common opinion is the one the cited gloss records in the first place, which Giulio Claro affirms with many others: namely, that it is sufficient to offer it, provided the leaseholder offers it in a suitable place and time, and offers it truly, and not in words alone. This is unless, perhaps, when the leaseholder offers it in words, the owner responds that he does not want it.

And I do not think one should depart from this opinion, as it is both common and equitable. As for the words of the Code which seem to also require a deposit, it must be said that this should be understood as necessary not for the leaseholder to 

<column-break/>

escape the penalty of forfeiture, but so that he may be entirely free from the obligation of payment. It is sufficient, moreover, for the leaseholder to pay the rent through a third person, or to report it to the owner, to avoid the penalty of forfeiture—especially if that third person was deputized for that purpose by the leaseholder, as Giulio Claro affirms with the common opinion of the doctors.

It should be observed that when the owner owed something to the leaseholder that could be balanced by withholding the rents, the leaseholder is not considered to have incurred forfeiture simply because he did not pay the rent for two or three years.

This is because, as noted by Panormitanus, Navarro, Innocent, and others whom Sylvester and Gama follow, **compensation** <note>original: "compensatio"; a legal offsetting of mutual debts</note> takes place, at least in a "hateful" matter <note>In legal terms, a "hateful" or "odious" matter is one involving a harsh penalty or loss of rights; the law often seeks ways to avoid such outcomes.</note> and for the purpose of avoiding a penalty, as is seen in the present case. This applies not only when the leaseholder signifies to the owner within that time that he wishes to retain the rents as compensation for the debt, but even when he says nothing at all to him, according to the law and its primary gloss regarding compensation.

<margin>Doubt 9</margin> The doubt is: What if the leaseholder was ignorant that the rent was owed? For example, because he was an heir and succeeded to property that he did not know was held under a lease, and because of that ignorance he did not pay the rent for a full two or three years—will he incur forfeiture for that reason? The final gloss on the Code regarding the law of emphyteusis raises this doubt at the end.

<margin>Decision</margin> It responds that by the rigor of the law he does incur it, but a <term>restitution to the original state</term><gloss>Latin: restitutio in integrum; a legal remedy where a person is restored to their previous position as if a loss had not occurred</gloss> is granted to him. Even if he is older than twenty-five years, this is granted under the general clause "if any just cause appears to me," etc. This gloss is followed by the common opinion of the doctors, including Giulio Claro, Gutierrez, Arias Pinel, Gama, Caldas, and Sylvester. The latter judges the same when a leaseholder does not pay the rent because he was legitimately hindered. Gigas affirms this same thing with many others whom he cites.

The doctors observe, however, that a leaseholder who is an heir has the weight of the law on his side; therefore, it is up to the owner to prove that the heir had knowledge, in order for him to be judged to have incurred forfeiture. In the absence of proof, the owner can compel such an heir to swear an oath as to whether he was ignorant. As soon as knowledge arrives, according to Gutierrez, and it is contended that he has incurred forfeiture, he must seek "restitution to the original state" and offer the rents. If, while the lawsuit is pending, the owner does not wish to receive the rents that are now owed due to the passage of time, the leaseholder must deposit them.

Furthermore, when it is not clear that the property is held under a lease, I believe it will be sufficient to protest that one will pay all the rents in the event that the property is pronounced to be a leasehold.

Pinel correctly says that if the heir had the legal instruments in his possession which showed the property was a leasehold, then it must not be presumed that there was ignorance on his part.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of long-term leasehold contracts (emphyteusis). It specifically addresses whether the leaseholder loses their rights for failing to pay very small or partial rents.</meta>

### Treatise Second, Disputation 453

<margin>Doubt 10</margin>
There is also a doubt: if the <term>emphyteutic property</term><gloss>property held under a long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</gloss> is of great value, but the <term>rent</term><gloss>Latin: pensio</gloss> to be paid is very small, does the <term>leaseholder</term><gloss>Latin: emphyteuta</gloss> incur <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; the loss of the lease for breach of contract</gloss> if that rent is not paid for two or three years? This matter is debated in the <term>gloss</term><gloss>standard legal commentary</gloss> on the <term>Authentica</term><gloss>a collection of Justinian's laws</gloss> regarding the word "repell." in the Code regarding Sacred Churches <note>Original: "gl. in authentica qui rem verb. repell. C. de sacrosan. Eccles."</note>. It argues both sides, and perhaps leans toward the negative side, which it proposes last.

<margin>Decision</margin>
And it is argued that it does not seem equitable that for such a small fault, so grave a penalty should be imposed. However, the common opinion is to the contrary, which Giulio Claro <note>A famous 16th-century Italian jurist</note> reports and follows in Question 8, number 3. This is because, first, the rent is primarily given in recognition of the <term>direct ownership</term><gloss>the ultimate legal title held by the owner, as opposed to the right of use held by the tenant</gloss>; the harm to that recognition is equal whether a small rent or a large rent, intended for that purpose, goes unpaid.

Furthermore, such a penalty is not a deprivation of other assets that belong to the leaseholder, but of the <term>beneficial ownership</term><gloss>the right to use and profit from the land</gloss>, which originally belonged to the owner. The owner granted it to the leaseholder only for as long as he did not stop paying the rent, as is clear from the Digest and the Institutes <note>Legal citations: "l. 1. §. vectigales. ff. si ager vect. vel emphyte. & §. adeo. Insti. de locat."</note>. Therefore, since it was granted under that condition and law, it is no wonder if—the condition failing through the leaseholder's fault, whatever it may be—that beneficial ownership returns to the owner. The law prescribed a period of two or three years, with or without the opportunity to remedy the delay; if the rent were not paid for that whole time, the leaseholder would be considered to have incurred the lapse, and not before. From this, you will understand why, although the will and action of the owner are required for the leaseholder to incur this penalty (because it is established as dependent on the owner's will), a judge's sentence is not required—as was said above according to the common opinion of the doctors. Rather, he incurs it by the very fact from the moment the legal term expires. Because the property was only granted in leasehold for that time from the beginning, he falls into that penalty by the law itself from that point.

<margin>Question 11</margin>
A greater doubt is when the rent-payer pays the rent every year, but not the whole amount. Through the omission of a part of the rent, even a small one, for two or three continuous years, does he incur forfeiture of the entire property, or only for the portion of the rent not paid? Many, including the <term>Speculator</term><gloss>Guillaume Durand, a famous 13th-century jurist</gloss> and others, seem to assert that through the omission of any part of the rent, however small, the leaseholder incurs forfeiture of the entire emphyteutic property.

Gama, in Decision 41, number 2, and others whom he cites, seem to be of this number. They use an example in that decision of a <term>bundle of straw</term><gloss>Latin: rete paleæ</gloss> that a beast of burden could carry. The leaseholder was bound to pay this in addition to another large rent, and he had not paid it for many years, even though he had faithfully paid the rest of the rent. However, it was rightly judged there that the leaseholder had not, in that event, incurred forfeiture. Since it did not appear that the owner had ever demanded it, and the leaseholder had never been stubborn in not paying it, it was presumed from the owner's silent consent that he had allowed that very small thing to go unpaid.

<column-break/>

Regarding this matter, I believe a distinction should be made, following Giulio Claro, Book 4, Opinions, section on Emphyteusis, Question 8, number 4.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Either one single rent was rendered for the whole property (as is regularly done), or it was rendered pro-rata according to the parts of the property—for instance, twenty silver pieces for twenty <term>acres</term><gloss>Latin: iugeribus</gloss>, at the rate of one silver piece for each acre. In this latter case, it must be said that the leaseholder only incurs forfeiture of that part of the property proportional to the unpaid rent, since he paid the rent for the other parts. In the former case, however, if he did not pay a notable part of the rent (such as a half, a third, or a quarter), and this was due to error, poverty, or some other inability, then he does not incur forfeiture but is <term>restored to his original state</term><gloss>Latin: restituitur in integrum; a legal remedy to undo a loss</gloss>, as was said above. But if error or inability is not proven, then he incurs forfeiture of the entire property, as the common opinion of the doctors affirms. If, however, he failed to pay a small part (such as a sixth, an eighth, or another smaller portion), Giulio Claro thinks, following the opinion of the Speculator, that he should only lose a proportional part of the property; but in his own opinion, he should be excused from the penalty entirely. Perhaps by the rigor of the law, he incurs forfeiture of the entire property unless, as said above, it can be presumed from circumstances that it went unpaid by the owner's will.

<margin>Doubt 12</margin>
The next doubt is: if the leaseholder leaves many heirs, and while the others pay their portions, one alone does not pay, do all of them incur forfeiture of the entire property, or only that person for the portion of the property that belongs to him?

<margin>Decision</margin>
The more common opinion of the doctors, following the gloss on the law "communi diuidundo" regarding the word "confundueretur" <note>Digest 10.3</note>, which Giulio Claro reports and follows, is that all of them incur forfeiture. This is because a leasehold (*emphyteusis*) is by its nature indivisible, as will be said in its proper place below, and the leaseholder was bound for the whole amount; therefore, the leasehold right passed to his heirs with that same burden.

<margin>Doubt 13</margin>
When someone receives something in leasehold for himself, his children, and his descendants: if the first or an intermediate leaseholder incurs forfeiture, does this harm the others to whom that leasehold right was supposed to pass?

<margin>Decision</margin>
One must respond in the affirmative, following Bartolus and Sylvester <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato and Sylvester Prierias, major legal and theological authorities</note>, and the common opinion of the doctors, which Giulio Claro reports and follows. The reason is that, as said above, the property is handed over in leasehold by the owner himself under the condition that the rent be paid, and only for the time during which it was paid. However, if the leaseholder deliberately incurred forfeiture to defraud his successors, then Giulio Claro rightly says the successor ought to be restored to his full rights.

<margin>Doubt 14</margin>
When another penalty was imposed in the leasehold contract for one not paying the rent, does he still incur forfeiture if he does not pay the rent for two or three continuous years?

<margin>Decision</margin>
One must respond in the affirmative, following the gloss on the Code regarding the word "repellere" <note>C. de emph.</note>. However, he cannot...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the rights and obligations of the property owner and the leaseholder (emphyteuta) in a long-term land contract. # Section 26. Luis de Molina / On Contracts

The owner can demand either penalty, or rather, whichever one he prefers, unless it had been specifically stated in the agreement that he could demand both. This is the opinion of the <term>Gloss</term><gloss>standard legal commentary</gloss> and of Giulio Claro in the place cited above, number 12.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
Whether, however, an agreement is valid stating that the <term>leaseholder</term><gloss>Latin: emphyteuta; a tenant with a long-term, inheritable interest in the land</gloss> does not incur <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; the loss of the leasehold rights due to a breach of contract</gloss> even if the <term>rent</term><gloss>Latin: canon; the annual payment acknowledging the owner's title</gloss> is not paid. I respond, along with the cited Gloss, that it is valid.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Because the property owner can renounce a right that was introduced for his own benefit. Furthermore, this forfeiture is not part of the <term>substance</term><gloss>the essential, unchangeable nature</gloss> of the contract, but is an <term>accident</term><gloss>a non-essential feature that can be modified</gloss> that can be removed from it, being attributed to it only by the disposition of the law. Agreements entered into regarding this contract are valid; the law only dictates that forfeiture occurs after a period of three years when nothing else has been specifically agreed upon, as is clearly indicated in the Code regarding the law of emphyteusis, Law 2 <note>Original: "l. 2. C. de iur. emph."</note>.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
Whether, however, an agreement is valid stating that the leasehold is forfeited if the rent is not paid within a shorter period, such as one or two years. I believe the answer should be in the affirmative.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Because agreements entered into concerning emphyteusis are valid. The law establishes the three-year time limit only when nothing else has been brought into the agreement, as is evident from the aforementioned Law 2. Álvaro Valasco agrees with this in his work *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 4, number 4, section 4.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
There is a doubt: when a leaseholder is accused of having incurred forfeiture, is it the owner’s responsibility to prove that the rent was not paid for two or three consecutive years, or rather

<margin>Decision</margin>
is it the leaseholder's responsibility to prove that he did pay it? One must respond with the Gloss on Law 2, regarding the word "repel" <note>Original: "verb. repellere"</note> in the Code on the law of emphyteusis: the owner has his claim founded upon the emphyteutic contract (or the <term>investiture</term><gloss>the formal act of granting the lease</gloss>), and it belongs to the leaseholder to prove he paid the rent. Otherwise, it shall be pronounced that he has incurred forfeiture. This is the common opinion, which Giulio Claro reports and follows in his section on emphyteusis, question 10, number 4, as does Gigas in his work *On Pensions*, question 76, last number.

<margin>Question</margin>
There is likewise a doubt: if the leaseholder incurs forfeiture, and the <term>direct owner</term><gloss>the ultimate legal owner of the land</gloss> did not execute the penalty of forfeiture nor initiate a lawsuit, can the heirs of the owner initiate the lawsuit and execute the penalty? Gama, in Decision 17, section 5, answers in the affirmative, along with many others whom he cites. However, Gigas asserts the contrary in his work *On Pensions*, question 74, number 3, along with others he mentions. This is because the penalty of forfeiture for unpaid rent does not take place unless the owner wishes to execute it, as was said above from Law 2 of the Code on the law of emphyteusis.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Nevertheless, the heir of the owner stands in the place of the deceased and succeeds to the rights of the deceased. I would say that if there are indications that the deceased did not wish to execute the penalty of forfeiture, the heirs cannot execute it unless the leaseholder incurs forfeiture again from the time they became the heirs. If, however, there are no such indications, they can execute it; for they are both the owners and they succeed to the rights of the deceased to execute that penalty.

<margin>Question</margin>
There is also a doubt: if the leaseholder incurs forfeiture for unpaid rent, and the owner did not attempt to execute the penalty against him while the leaseholder was alive, can he attempt to do so against the leaseholder's heirs? Gama, in the cited decision, says that the <term>Portuguese Senate</term><gloss>the high court of Portugal</gloss> is accustomed to approve the opinion of <term>Baldus</term><gloss>a famous 14th-century jurist</gloss> and others whom he cites as being truer and more common—namely, that

<column-break/>

he cannot attempt it against the heirs. This is because "crimes" <note>Original: "delicta"</note> usually expire with the wrongdoer regarding the execution of the penalty when a lawsuit was not initiated against him while he was alive (Code, *That action is not taken for the crimes of the deceased* <note>Original: "C. ne ex delict. defunct."</note>). He also cites Gigas in support of this opinion, question 74. The same is affirmed and discussed more extensively (referring to other doctors on both sides) in Decision 17, number 2. Yet, the same Gigas, at the end of that question, leans toward the opposite side.

<margin>Decision</margin>
And I consider this latter opinion to be truer. Because this is not strictly a "penalty," but rather the termination of a contract by the disposition of the law due to a condition not being kept—though it still depends on the will of the owner by the disposition of that same law. Furthermore, the execution of this "improper penalty" is not taken from the other assets of the deceased, but only from the <term>beneficial ownership</term><gloss>the right to use and profit from the land</gloss> which belonged to the property owner; since the contract term has ended and the condition under which it was granted to the leaseholder was not kept, it returns to the ownership and is consolidated with it.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
There is a further doubt: if the leaseholder offers the owner the rents for several subsequent years at once, is the owner bound to receive them? The answer must be in the negative. Because the owner is not bound to yield his right to have the leaseholder, by paying the rent successively each year, also recognize the direct ownership each year. This is the view of Silvester in the section on emphyteusis, question 8, with others he cites.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Although he mentions that Bartolus <note>Another influential medieval jurist</note> affirms that one can be compelled to accept three years of rent at once (following Law *Placuit*, Code, *On the contribution of the father's estate*, book 11). However, that law only speaks of the rent to be paid to the Emperor and received by a public collector.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
It is asked: can a leaseholder who has incurred forfeiture for unpaid rent be expelled by the owner by his own authority, without waiting for a judge's sentence? The common opinion

<margin>Decision</margin>
of the doctors, following the Gloss on Law 2 of the Code on the law of emphyteusis, affirms that he can expel him by his own authority. This is reported and followed by Giulio Claro, Book 4 of the Sentences, section on emphyteusis, question 11; Gutierrez; Álvaro Valasco; and Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous Spanish jurist who commented on the Siete Partidas</note> on Law 28, Title 8, Part 5, regarding the words "without the judge's command" <note>Original: "sin mandado del juez"</note>, and that very law dictates the same there.
Nevertheless, they all say it is better if it is done by the order of a judge to avoid <term>scandals</term><gloss>public disorder or moral outcry</gloss>, and in many places, this is how it is regularly done. Gregorio Lopez, with many others he cites, thinks this should be limited: unless the leaseholder resists—at least by asserting that he has paid the rent, or that he has not failed to pay for as long a time as is necessary to incur forfeiture, or something similar whereby the case becomes a matter of controversy.
For when a matter is controversial, neither party ought to declare the law for themselves against the other party, but rather the judge should. Gama affirms this same thing in Decision 4, number 2. But Giulio Claro thinks this limitation only applies when the leaseholder resists by deed (force), and not when he resists only with words.
Gregorio Lopez, Gutierrez, and others agree that if the owner goes to a judge to expel the leaseholder, he must not have protested that he would not yield by that path...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of emphyteusis, specifically addressing whether a leaseholder can be forced to maintain a contract they wish to abandon, and the impact of property destruction or crop failure on the obligation to pay rent.</meta>

...to yield what he holds; the <term>leaseholder</term><gloss>Latin: emphyteuta; a tenant with a long-term, inheritable interest in the land</gloss> cannot thereafter expel him by his own authority, but only by the authority of a judge.

<margin>22</margin> It is <term>doubted</term><gloss>a standard "dubium" or legal question for debate</gloss> whether, if the leaseholder wishes to return the property to the owner—either of his own free will, or because he has committed a <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; a breach of contract</gloss>, or for some other cause—the owner is bound to accept it, or if the owner can instead compel him to persevere in the lease.

It must be said that the owner can compel him to persevere in the lease. This is the opinion of the <term>Speculator</term><gloss>Guillaume Durand, a 13th-century jurist</gloss>, Panormitanus, and others cited by Silvester, Alvaro Valasco, and Aries Pinel. The laws of Portugal also agree. The reason is clear: although contracts are voluntary at their inception, once they are finalized, the parties are necessarily bound to stand by them. Just as the owner is bound to honor the contract with the leaseholder, so too is the leaseholder bound to honor the contract with the owner.

### Whether misfortune regarding the leased property, its fruits, or crop failure, excuses the leaseholder from paying rent.

->DISPUTATION 454.<-
->SUMMARY.<-

<margin>1</margin> The leaseholder is freed from the lease if the property is entirely destroyed.
Indeed, the contract itself is ended. no. 2.
This fails, however, if the leaseholder took upon himself the risk of <term>fortuitous events</term><gloss>unforeseeable accidents or "acts of God"</gloss>. no. 3.
It also fails if the property or house was destroyed through the fault of the leaseholder. no. 4.
It also fails if it is only partially destroyed. no. 6. See also no. 8.
<margin>5</margin> If a vineyard or olive grove is granted in lease and is destroyed by accident, the lease ends; it is otherwise if the bare land was leased and the tenant later planted the vineyard or grove.
<margin>7</margin> When the leased property is said to have perished "in part," what is understood by the term "part."
<margin>8</margin> If the property perishes in part, in which cases the rent must also be reduced.
<margin>9</margin> The rent is not remitted due to misfortune or sterility affecting the crops. This is limited unless the sterility is so great that it removes the fruit entirely. no. 11.
Note the explanation for this limitation at no. 12.
<margin>13</margin> Whether the leaseholder is freed from rent and the penalty of forfeiture due to war, plague in the region, or other similar causes.

---

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the leased property, the first conclusion is this: if the <term>substance</term><gloss>the physical existence</gloss> of the property is entirely destroyed—such as if a house is demolished or burned down, or if a field is permanently submerged by the sea or destroyed by <term>alluvion</term><gloss>soil deposited or washed away by water</gloss> so that it can no longer be cultivated, or if it is occupied by enemies with no hope of recovery—the leaseholder is not bound to pay rent from that point forward. The loss of the property falls entirely on the owner. This is expressly stated in the Code <note>original: "l. 1. C. de iure emph. §. adeo"</note> and is the common opinion of the doctors, including Bartolus and Alvaro Valasco.

<margin>2</margin> Indeed, in such an event, the contract is terminated. If by chance the property that was lost is later recovered, neither party—the owner nor the former leaseholder—is bound to the old contract, as Silvester and Valasco affirm.

<margin>3</margin> Note, however, that if the leaseholder specifically took upon himself the risk of fortuitous events, such that he agreed to pay rent even if the property was utterly destroyed, such a pact is valid. In that case, he remains bound to pay even after total destruction.

<margin>4</margin> When a house is burned or otherwise destroyed through the fault of the leaseholder, Alvaro Valasco agrees with Baldus that the owner has an option: he can either sue the leaseholder for damages and end the contract, or he can compel him to rebuild the house (or any other building) and continue the lease. In this situation, the contract "limps" <note>a legal metaphor meaning the contract is valid for one party but voidable by the other</note>, and it is left entirely to the owner’s will whether to continue or to expel the tenant.

<margin>5</margin> However, when the house is destroyed through no fault of the leaseholder, Valasco rightly disagrees with Baldus. Baldus asserted that the leaseholder could choose to rebuild the house on the remaining plot—since the plot is the principal part of a house—and continue the lease, or choose to abandon it. If the leasehold is considered to remain because of that principal part (the land), then the leaseholder would be bound to pay rent for that part alone, and the contract would not be finished. Some authors, like Jason and Afflitto, argued the leaseholder must persevere and pay. Yet, with the best legal reasoning, Valasco and Bartolomé Philippo affirm the contrary.

<margin>6</margin> For although the plot is the "principal part" of a burned house, the "house" itself does not remain when the structure is destroyed. A house consists essentially in its form, which does not exist in the plot alone, nor even in the materials if they are leveled to the ground. Destru-
<meta>Catchword: destru- (continuation of "destroyed")</meta>

It concludes that while tenants are generally bound to their contracts, total destruction through no fault of their own typically terminates the lease and the rent obligation.</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

when the form of a thing is destroyed, since its essence consists in that form, its substance is considered to have perished even if the material remains. This is established in the <term>Digest</term><gloss>Latin: ff.; the largest part of the Corpus Iuris Civilis, or Roman law</gloss> under the sections on production of evidence <note>original: "l. sul. §. si quis... ad exhib."</note> and the ways in which a <term>usufruct</term><gloss>the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</gloss> is lost.

This same opinion is clearly indicated in the <term>Siete Partidas</term><gloss>The 13th-century Spanish statutory code</gloss> <note>original: "l. 28. tit. 8. par. 5."</note>, as Gregorio López correctly observes regarding the phrase "by fire." He confirms this using the same foundations as Alvaro Valasco. For the same reason, Gregorio López believes the same must be said when the <term>emphyteutic property</term><gloss>property held under a long-term, hereditary lease</gloss> was a vineyard or an olive grove. Indeed, if the plants are destroyed by some <term>fortuitous event</term><gloss>an act of God or an unforeseeable accident</gloss>, even if the ground remains, the vineyard or olive grove no longer exists, and thus the contract of <term>emphyteusis</term><gloss>a long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</gloss> is ended. However, understand this to apply unless the land was handed over in emphyteusis before the planting of the vineyard or olive grove. In that case, even if a vineyard or olive grove is planted later and the entire property becomes an emphyteutic one, the contract—which was originally celebrated regarding the soil alone—does not cease if the plants are destroyed.

<margin>6</margin> **Second Conclusion:** When the emphyteutic property does not perish entirely by a fortuitous event, but only in part, the <term>leaseholder</term><gloss>Latin: emphyteuta</gloss> is bound to pay the full <term>rent</term><gloss>Latin: pensio</gloss>. This is held in the Code <note>original: "l. 1. C. de iure emphyteu."</note> and the Institutes regarding leasing. It is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco, Julius Clarus, and others. Hence the verses:
> *If the thing perishes entirely, the leaseholder shall be freed;*
> *but if it perishes in part, he shall be freed by no art.*

<margin>7</margin> However, the doctors doubt when an emphyteutic property (pertaining to the present discussion) should be said to have perished "in part." The <term>gloss</term><gloss>standard marginal commentary on legal texts</gloss> on the law regarding the names of daughters <note>original: "l. nomen filiarum"</note> says it is when up to half perishes, and no more. Other commentaries on the Code and Institutes discuss the matter and finally conclude that it perishes "in part" whenever *any* portion of the emphyteutic property remains, even if it is less than half.

Indeed, the Code clearly indicates this when it says:
> *If a disaster emerges so great that it causes the utter destruction of the thing itself which was given in emphyteusis, this should not be blamed on the leaseholder (to whom nothing remains), but on the owner of the thing. But if a partial loss or some other light damage occurs, from which the substance of the thing itself is not entirely harmed, the leaseholder should not doubt that this is attributed to his own portion.*
And in the Institutes:
> *If the destruction of the whole thing has occurred, the risk falls back on the owner; but if it is a partial destruction, such loss comes to the leaseholder.*

Nothing could be said more clearly. The *Siete Partidas* agrees, stating that when at least an eighth part of the emphyteutic property remains, the risk belongs to the leaseholder, and he is therefore bound to pay the full rent. If a portion smaller than one-eighth remains, such a tiny part would be considered as nothing. Therefore, on this point of law, I agree with the opinion followed by Panormitanus and many others, who affirm it is the common view.

<column-break/>

This is also supported by Julius Clarus and Gregorio López. We can confirm it thus: if the leaseholder had taken the entire risk of fortuitous events upon himself, he would be bound to pay the full rent even if the property perished entirely, as was said above. Therefore, since by the disposition of those laws (according to which the contract is deemed made when nothing else was expressed) the risk of the emphyteutic property belongs to the leaseholder when it perishes only in part and not entirely, it follows that the leaseholder is then bound to pay the full rent.

Regarding the text in the law concerning the "names of daughters" mentioned earlier, it should be said that it explains itself: it says "half" is to be understood unless something else is expressed. However, the two laws cited above sufficiently express that if any part of the emphyteutic property remains, even if it is less than half, the risk falls to the leaseholder. Alvaro Valasco, although he agrees with this opinion along with many others, adds that when the part that remains is not sufficient to pay the rent, a portion of the rent should be remitted, as <term>Bartolus</term><gloss>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</gloss> and others noted. He says he has seen it practiced in Ecclesiastical tribunals that when emphyteutic property is rendered notably unfruitful by the sands of the sea or rivers (which happens not infrequently in Portugal), a reduction of the rent is made at the judgment of honorable men. Certainly, it is equitable that the owner—especially if it is the Church—should consent to such a reduction of rent. However, I do not see that they are strictly bound to it by the nature of the contract or the disposition of the law, or that judges can enforce it against the owner’s will.

Julius Clarus, Gregorio López, and Valasco, along with Bartolus, believe the taught doctrine should be limited to when the leaseholder pays only a modest rent in <term>recognition of direct ownership</term><gloss>a token payment to acknowledge the landlord as the true owner</gloss>.

<margin>8</margin> However, when he was paying a large rent corresponding to the value of the fruits, they believe the rent should be reduced in proportion to the part that perished or the deterioration of the property, since the contract then has the force of a <term>hire</term><gloss>Latin: locatio; a standard rental agreement</gloss>. They argue the cited laws only speak of emphyteusis in which a modest rent is paid.

Strictly speaking on the point of law, I believe this distinction is also false, except when the rent was set according to the proportions of the parts of the property—for instance, if twenty silver pieces or twenty measures were set for twenty acres of field, at the rate of one piece or measure for each acre. For it is unbelievable that rent in emphyteusis is set solely to acknowledge direct ownership with no consideration of the fruits to be gathered from it, unless a purchase of the <term>useful ownership</term><gloss>the tenant's right to use and profit from the land</gloss> had occurred at the same time.

Furthermore, it was shown in Disputation 445 that by the very fact that a contract is for ten years or more, it is a true emphyteusis. Those laws speak of emphyteusis in general without making any exception, and Bartolus’s opinion seems to have originated from that...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 454

...regarding another opinion of the same Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note>, in which he judges that for the nature of an <term>emphyteusis</term><gloss>a long-term, inheritable land lease requiring improvement of the property</gloss> it is necessary that the <term>rent</term><gloss>Latin: pensio; the yearly payment made by the tenant to the owner</gloss> be modest and not at all equivalent to the value of the crops; otherwise, it is considered a regular lease. Add to this that never is such a high rent established in an emphyteusis—even taking the crops into account—as is established in a standard lease. Perhaps Bartolus's opinion, because it is equitable in itself regardless of the strict letter of the law, will have been accepted by usage in some places. We, however, are explaining what the truth of the matter is according to the established disposition of the law. This concerns the emphyteutic property itself.

<margin>9</margin> But regarding the crops, the common opinion is that on account of misfortune or sterility occurring among them, the rent is not to be remitted but must be paid in full. So says the <term>Gloss</term><gloss>The standard medieval commentary on Roman or Canon law</gloss> on the chapter *Potuit* regarding leases <note>original: "c. potuit de locat."</note>, and with it Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> in the same place at numbers 16, 17, and 18; also in the chapter *Propter sterilitatem* <note>original: "on account of sterility"</note> at number 3 under the same title. This is the common opinion which, among others, Julius Clarus <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist.</note> records and follows in Book 4 of his *Opinions*, section on emphyteusis, question 8, number 7; and Alvaro Valasco in question 27, cited from number 7. This is clearly proven from Law 2 of the <term>Code</term><gloss>The Code of Justinian</gloss> regarding the right of emphyteusis, and from the section *Adeo* in the <term>Institutes</term><gloss>An introductory textbook of Roman law</gloss> regarding leases. In these laws, all misfortunes that occur—which do not entirely destroy the emphyteutic property itself—pertain to the leaseholder; and thus, because of them, he is not exempted from paying the full rent.

<margin>10</margin> Many, following Bartolus, whom Alvaro Valasco records in the same place at number 11, and whom Julius Clarus follows at the cited number 7—as well as Navarro in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 190, and Gregorio López in the passage cited—judge that this <term>†</term> should be limited, provided that the rent is a modest one imposed precisely as a recognition of the <term>direct ownership</term><gloss>Latin: dominium directum; the ultimate ownership held by the landlord</gloss>, rather than being based on the value of the crops. For in the latter case, they judge it to have the nature of a lease, and that the rent ought to be reduced in proportion to the misfortune or sterility. Indeed, Alvaro Valasco reports that he has often seen the Portuguese Senate judge according to that opinion, and thus it does not seem one should depart from it in Portugal. I, however, along with the more common opinion (which makes no such exception), think that on the point of law the same must be said as I said a little while ago regarding a similar limitation: when a misfortune happens regarding a part of the emphyteutic property, it is for the reasons I gave in that place. And Alvaro Valasco thinks the same at the cited number, saying that interpreters of the civil law everywhere—and wrongly—confuse leases with emphyteusis on this point.

<margin>11</margin> Some also judge that another limitation should be added following Bartolus, whom Alvaro Valasco records at number 12 of the cited question: namely, <term>†</term> provided that the sterility is not so great that it entirely takes away the crops, or does not leave enough of them to suffice for paying the rent; and he suggests that the Portuguese Senate judges according to this limitation. He thinks, however, that this has no place in the Kingdom of Castile, unless the remaining part of the crops does not reach an eighth part, according to Law 28, title 8, part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the Castilian law code.</note>. Furthermore, that law does not speak of a portion of the crops, but of a portion of the emphyteutic property itself; nor do I see by what reasoning that could have a place regarding crops, unless one considers the quantity of crops which the emphyteutic property usually yields, neither in an abundant year nor a sterile one, but in a middling and ordinary one. Gama also, in Decisions 150 and 232, reports judgments according to this same limitation; yet he notes that in the Kingdom of Portugal, judgment was rendered according to those things decreed in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, title 61, regarding leases, when sterility comes upon the thing leased. Namely, that

<column-break/>

if no crops were harvested, no rent should be paid. <margin>12</margin> <term>†</term> But if something was harvested, either all of it should be left to the lord of the field, or the full rent should be paid to him. An exception is made when the seeds were committed to the earth: for then the one who cultivated the field takes out the seed, and leaves the remainder to the lord of the field. First, however, he takes from the whole heap the tithe owed to the Church, as Gama reports was judged in the cited place; then the seed is taken from the remainder, and the residue belongs to the lord of the field. I, certainly, on the point of law, think the same should be said of this limitation as of the preceding one, for the same reasons; and Alvaro Valasco agrees in the same place, as does Julius Clarus above. Moreover, the Portuguese law does not speak of emphyteusis, but of the contract of leasing, which will be discussed in its own place. Added to this is a significant reason for the distinction between a lease and an emphyteusis: a <term>tenant farmer</term><gloss>Latin: colonus; a simple renter who does not hold the "useful ownership"</gloss> is not the owner of the crops of the field while they have not yet been harvested; rather, the lord of the field is their owner, as has been said elsewhere, and the tenant farmer only has the right to harvest them and make them his own once they have been gathered and separated from the soil. Therefore, it is no wonder if they perish before they are collected; they perish for the lord of the field (that is, the lessor) and not for the tenant. The leaseholder in an emphyteusis, however, since he holds the <term>useful ownership</term><gloss>Latin: utile dominium; the right to the use and profits of the land</gloss> of the emphyteutic property, is undoubtedly the owner of the crops even before they are collected and separated from the emphyteutic property. Hence, they perish for him and not for the proprietor, unless something else was deducted by agreement; and therefore he is bound then to pay the full rent.

<margin>Question</margin> The doctors doubt when, on account of war in that region—whether it be just or unjust (for it matters nothing to the present case)—or on account of a just fear of war, the farmers were unable to work, or the emphyteutic houses could neither be inhabited nor leased, or on account of plague or another similar just and reasonable cause no crops, or very few, could be harvested from the emphyteutic property, whether <margin>13</margin> <term>†</term> the leaseholder is freed from the payment of the rent, and thus from the penalty of forfeiture. Many, whom Alvaro Valasco records in the cited question 27 from number 13, and with whom Julius Clarus largely agrees in the cited question 8, number 6—and whose opinion the same Alvaro Valasco thinks should be followed in practice—assert that the leaseholder is then excused from paying the rent, especially if the rent is not very small (which would be paid only in recognition of the direct ownership), and much more so from the penalty of <term>forfeiture</term><gloss>Latin: commissum; the loss of the lease for failure to pay</gloss> for not having paid the rent. Alvaro Valasco, with others, makes an exception unless the leaseholder took all fortuitous cases upon himself. For since such an agreement is valid regarding the substance of the emphyteutic property, as has been said, it will be much more valid regarding the crops. He further excepts unless it were the custom of the region that, notwithstanding the impediments of wars, the rent should be paid. Likewise, he excepts unless the leaseholder himself was the cause of the war, or unless he could have prevented it or resisted it and did not do so; and if he did not warn the proprietor, who, having been warned, might have harvested the crops from the emphyteutic property.

<margin>Decision</margin> I, certainly, as far as the rent is concerned, think the question is entirely the same whether the crops are not gathered due to the impediments of wars, or due to any other misfortune or sterility, provided the leaseholder is not despoiled of the emphyteutic property itself so that it is possessed by enemies without hope of recovering it; because—
