# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...judgment <note>original: "sententiam," continuing from the previous page's catchword</note>, and therefore regarding the point of law, I believe the same should be said about this question as was said regarding the two preceding limitations; it is for those same reasons. Alvaro Valasco <note>Alvaro Valasco (1526–1593), a prominent Portuguese jurist who wrote extensively on emphyteusis.</note> agrees with us, as cited above at number 20, although he adds that the contrary common opinion should not be abandoned.

As for the penalty of **forfeiture** <term>commissum; the loss of a legal right or property as a penalty for a breach of contract</term>, certainly in a region where a custom has been accepted that the rent must be paid in a time of war, or in another event discussed in the two preceding limitations, the <term>emphyteuta</term> <gloss>a tenant holding a long-term, inheritable lease on the condition of improving the land</gloss> would fall into forfeiture if they did not pay for two or three years. 

However, where such a custom has not been accepted, and the tenant has not taken upon themselves all accidental risks, then a tenant who does not pay the rent—contending that it is not owed either due to the impediments of war, or other misfortunes or sterility—certainly, even if they were condemned according to our opinion to pay all unpaid rents, they neither should nor could justly be condemned to have fallen into forfeiture. This is because they did not fail to pay through their own fault, and it was lawful for them to test their right by defending themselves, especially since they were supported by the opinion of so many highly authoritative legal experts.

Where, however, there is no fault in the failure to pay the rent, the penalty of forfeiture for that unpaid rent does not apply.

# A tenant falling into forfeiture: which improvements made to the emphyteutic property do they lose to the owner, and from what point do the fruits of the property belong to the owner?

## DISPUTATION 457.

### SUMMARY.

1 *When a tenant falls into forfeiture, which improvements do they lose to the owner?*
*And what is the case for a feudal vassal? number 2.*
3 *Whether a tenant falling into forfeiture loses improvements made afterward.*
4 *From what point the fruits of the emphyteutic property that has fallen into forfeiture begin to be owed to the owner.*
5 *Produced goods are not called "fruits" unless the expenses incurred in the property for the purpose of gathering the fruits have been deducted.*
6 *Whether fruits perceived from improvements belong to a possessor in bad faith, and when.*

<margin>Question.</margin>
Since it was stated at the beginning of Disputation 453 that a tenant falling into forfeiture for non-payment of rent not only loses the emphyteutic property to the owner, but also the **improvements** <note>original: "melioramenta"</note> made upon it, we must examine whether they lose all of them universally, or only some.

The common opinion, which Julius Clarus <note>Giulio Claro (1525–1575), an influential Italian jurist and magistrate.</note> follows in Book 4 of his *Opinions*, at the section on emphyteusis, question 45, number 1, and which Alvaro Valasco reports more extensively than others in his *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 25, number 2, asserts absolutely: a tenant falling into forfeiture—not only on that ground but on any other which we shall explain as we proceed—loses all improvements to the owner. 

Alvaro Valasco, in the beginning of the following number 3, along with

<column-break/>

a certain other author whom he cites, says it can be called into doubt whether a tenant falling into forfeiture for non-payment of rent loses the improvements to the owner, except for those specifically included in the contract that the tenant was required to make—those made in place of the price they were going to give at the start, and because of which they paid a very small rent. The same Alvaro Valasco spoke of these in number 1, and we shall discuss them below in their proper place when we examine to whom the improvements belong when an emphyteusis is ended without the fault of the tenant. 

The reason why this might not undeservedly be called into doubt is as follows. First, because improvements according to their nature belong to the tenant, and therefore the tenant transmits them to their heirs, even external ones, with nothing preventing it, even if the emphyteusis is ecclesiastical, as will be said in its place. For they are something far different from the emphyteutic right itself: the emphyteutic right arises from the contract and the <term>investiture</term> <gloss>the formal legal act of granting the lease</gloss>, and is granted by the owner to the tenant; the improvements, however, proceed from the tenant himself, because he produced them by his own industry and at his own expense. Therefore, even if the tenant, falling into forfeiture as a penalty, loses the emphyteutic right to the owner which he received from him, there is no reason why he should similarly lose his own improvements to the same person. 

Furthermore, a penalty must not be extended beyond what has been expressed in the law; for "hateful" things <note>A legal maxim: "Odia restringi, et favores convenit ampliari" (Hate/penalties should be restricted, and favors/benefits expanded).</note> are to be restricted, and favors are to be expanded. The law (Code, *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, law 2), on which the authors of the common opinion rely, although it establishes that a tenant not paying rent falls into forfeiture of the emphyteutic property, it does not, however, establish that they fall into forfeiture of the improvements. For it states: *It shall be permitted to the owner, if they wish, to repel them from the emphyteutic lands, with no allegation on the grounds of improvement, or those things called "emponemata" <note>Greek term: emponemata, referring to labor or improvements added to land.</note>, or penalty to be opposed against the owner.* 

Behold: it only says that the tenant is not excused from being expelled from the emphyteutic lands and the emphyteutic right even if they claim to have made improvements, or if they claim a penalty was placed in the contract against the owner if they expelled the tenant—since that is to be understood as expulsion without a legitimate cause. Therefore, although it is established from this that the claim of improvements made on the emphyteutic property does not excuse the tenant from the penalty of forfeiture of the emphyteutic right, it is not established from this that they also fall into the penalty of forfeiting the improvements. 

Indeed, one might embrace this opinion, were the contrary not the common opinion of the doctors and the one received in practice—not only in emphyteusis but also in **fiefs** <term>feudum; a feudal land holding</term>, as Alvaro Valasco affirms there along with others. 

<margin>3 Decision.</margin>
And unless it were supported by the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's Novels (new laws).</note> regarding alienation and emphyteusis, in the section "if however someone," which denies the tenant a legal action for improvements. And unless the final law of the Code, *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, while speaking of the penalty of forfeiture for alienating <note>selling or transferring to another</note> the improvements and the lease without consulting the owner, did not speak clearly about the loss of the improvements. Therefore, Alvaro Valasco, even though such laws are minimally cited, does not think one should depart from the common opinion, which Aries Pinellus <note>Arias Piñel (1512–1563), a Spanish jurist.</note> also follows in law 2 of the Code, *On Rescinding a Sale*, part 2, chapter 3, number 7. Although I do not approve of Pinellus's opinion in that regard...

While Molina acknowledges arguments for the tenant's right to their own labor, he notes that prevailing legal tradition and practice favor the landlord's total repossession.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 455.

...judgment <note>original: "sententiam"</note>, insofar as in number 8 following, he makes an exception to the common opinion when something is granted in **emphyteusis** <gloss>a long-term lease of land in exchange for a fixed rent and a promise to improve it</gloss> for ten years or more, and sometimes perpetually, or at least beyond a new life-term.

Next, Gregorio López <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> in the cited law 28, title 8, part 5, penultimate gloss; Pinellus in the place cited above, number 9; and Alvaro Valasco in the cited question, number 3, along with Charles Dumoulin <note>original: "Carol. Molina," a French jurist (1500–1566) known for his work on customary law.</note>, understand the common opinion to refer to **common and ordinary improvements**, to which the tenant is bound either tacitly or expressly by the contract. However, it is otherwise regarding **extraordinary improvements** of great value—for instance, if the tenant builds a house on the leased land, or a mill, or something similar that is extraordinary and of great expense. The tenant would not lose these even if they fall into **forfeiture** <term>commissum; the loss of the lease as a penalty for breach</term>. Indeed, Valasco reports that he saw this so judged in the Portuguese Senate. Nevertheless, a significant difficulty arises from what was reported in the final law of the Code *concerning emphyteutic law*. However, we shall discuss how such improvements are to be paid for in the cited place.

<margin>3</margin>
The question is: what if the tenant, after falling into forfeiture, made certain improvements? Would they lose those just like the others they made before the forfeiture occurred? One side argues in the affirmative, on the grounds that the tenant is then a **bad faith possessor** <term>malae fidei possessor; someone who holds property knowing they have no legal right to it</term> of the leased property, knowing that the **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the land, distinct from the landlord's legal title</term> has already devolved back to the property owner. A bad faith possessor does not recover the cost of improvements they make on the property they so possess, because they are deemed to have made them with the intent of donating them; and if they wished to claim them, they could be charged with the fault of having made them on soil they understood to be another’s. This is evident from the Institutes and the Digest. 

However, it must be said, in agreement with Alvaro Valasco, number 4, that since the tenant does not lose the useful ownership—even after falling into forfeiture—except as it depends on the will of the property owner, and thus depends on the penalty being put into execution by the owner demanding the useful ownership back from the tenant, the tenant is not considered a bad faith possessor of the leased property except from that point forward. Therefore, if the matter is brought to court, they are only in bad faith from the **joinder of issue** <term>lis contestata; the formal start of a trial when the legal issues are defined</term>. For this reason, the tenant can recover the improvements made to the leased property from the moment they fell into forfeiture until that point. If they made any after the joinder of issue, they will lose them. An exception is made if the expenses incurred on the leased property were **necessary**—that is, those without which the property would perish or be rendered worse—whether they consist of building or repairing. These the bad faith possessor may recover by the office of the judge, retaining the property until they are paid, as Bartolus and others, including Valasco, affirm.

<margin>2</margin>
Regarding **useful expenses**, if they were made for repairing, a bad faith possessor is permitted to remove them, provided it does not damage the prior state of the same property. However, if the owner wishes to pay the tenant as much as the removed material would be worth to them, the tenant is not permitted to remove it. This is to be understood in the same way as the cited law 44, which establishes the same. Yet, if the expenses cannot be removed without detriment to the property, the tenant loses them entirely.

<column-break/>

As for **luxurious expenses** <gloss>voluptarias; spending on ornaments or non-essential comforts</gloss>, the tenant does not recover them, even if the owner does not object, but loses them entirely. Law 44, title 28, part 3 so disposes. What constitutes "luxurious" expenses is excellently explained in the cited law 44, and we have discussed it in Disputation 453. This concludes the first of the points proposed in the title of this disputation.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding the second point, I believe that the **fruits** <gloss>fructus; the produce or income of the land</gloss> of the leased property—just like the property itself regarding the useful ownership—do not belong to the owner except from the point at which they attempt to execute the penalty, or from the joinder of issue. Until that point, the emphyteutic contract is considered to have continued, because the penalty of forfeiture is not incurred except as it depends on the will of the owner attempting to execute it, as has been said often. 

Therefore, up until 그 point, the unpaid rents are owed to the owner, together with the leased property itself, which is then reclaimed as a penalty for forfeiture. However, the fruits perceived <note>original: "percepti"; crops already harvested</note> up to that point would belong entirely to the tenant as the owner of the useful ownership. Hence, I do not favor the opinion of Alvaro Valasco (number 4) that there should be an offset of the expenses the tenant made on the property against the fruits they gathered from the point they fell into forfeiture, unless he means the fruits gathered *after* the joinder of issue. Nor do the laws that dispose this concerning other possessors have a place in the case proposed here. All those laws speak of a possessor of another's property for the time during which it was another's; this does not apply to the tenant's useful ownership except from the point of the joinder of issue. 

Therefore, the fruits from the point of the joinder of issue belong to the property owner, but the owner is bound to pay the tenant all the costs incurred by them up to the point of the joinder of issue regarding the gathering of the fruits for that year, and any other costs the tenant incurred regarding those same fruits. This is because the costs incurred in gathering the fruits of another's property are always paid to the possessor, whether they are in good or bad faith. Indeed, "fruits" are not considered to exist except for those that remain after expenses have been deducted. This is affirmed by Valasco and others whom he cites.

<margin>5</margin>
Hence, the same author in number 5 concludes that a tenant who is condemned to have lost their lease and improvements through their own fault can still recover the expenses they incurred in seeking and preserving the fruits of the year in which they are condemned to leave the land. I should warn, regarding other bad faith possessors, that they are required to deduct the value of the fruits they received from that property from the necessary expenses they incurred on it, as is very well known. We shall speak of the **good faith possessor** in Disputation 463. Whether this should be understood only regarding fruits gathered from the property itself, or also from the improvements made by a bad faith possessor, is a matter we will examine in Disputation 463 concerning the good faith possessor, where we will embrace the negative side.

<sig>Ll 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Quod</meta>

<margin>6</margin> Regarding the **possessor in bad faith** <note>original: "possessorem malae fidei"; someone who occupies property knowing they have no legal right to it</note>, the more common opinion—which Alvaro Valasco reports in his work on emphyteutic law (question 25, number 26) and which Covarruvias follows—is that although a possessor in bad faith must deduct from their expenses the **fruits** <gloss>the profits, crops, or income produced by the land</gloss> they actually gathered from another's property, as well as those they *could* have gathered (a point on which everyone agrees), they are indeed required to deduct fruits gathered from their own improvements, but not those they *could* have gathered. This last point is gathered from the law *caeterum* in the Digest regarding the recovery of property. However, Alvaro Valasco notes that in the courts of Portugal, it is judged and accepted that they are not required to deduct the fruits they gathered from their own improvements, but may keep those for themselves. This same opinion was held by Matteo d'Afflitto and Capicius, whom Valasco cites. One might say that in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiae"; the internal moral judgment or ecclesiastical jurisdiction, as opposed to a civil court</note> before a legal sentence is passed, the fruits gathered from improvements belong to the possessor in bad faith; however, after a sentence is passed, one must stand by the judgment delivered in whichever court it was heard.

Although the law grants a possessor in bad faith the right to necessary and useful improvements—at least so far as being able to remove them—I judge it more in accordance with the law that the fruits gathered from those improvements should also belong to them, and they should not be condemned to lose them as a penalty.

# Whether the emphyteutic tenant is bound to expenses regarding the leased property, and to its burdens and taxes.

### DISPUTATION 456.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> *Which expenses made on the leased property the tenant can seek from the owner.*
<margin>2</margin> *What the Portuguese law says on this, number 2.*
<margin>3</margin> *The tenant is bound to pay burdens and taxes, both real and personal, imposed by reason of the leased property.*
<margin>4</margin> *Including a declaration on the matter.*
<margin>5</margin> *The same is to be said regarding a feudal tenant, number 4.*
<margin>6</margin> *Whether a tenant of the Church is bound to collections by reason of their beneficial ownership.*
<margin>7</margin> *What happens in fiefs and usufructs when the direct owner is the Church and the tenant or usufructuary is a layperson, or vice versa, number 6.*

<margin>1</margin> **A**mong the expenses made on a property held in **emphyteusis** <gloss>a type of perpetual or long-term lease</gloss>, some pertain to the conservation of the property or the gathering of fruits. The tenant is bound to make these at their own expense during their tenure, even if they are great. They cannot seek compensation for them when the lease ends, nor can they reduce their rent because of them. Thus, the tenant is bound to repair the leased houses or any other building on the land. However, they are not bound to rebuild if a building collapses or is burned down through no fault of their own. They are also bound to repair dikes and clean the ditches or water-channels of the fields, as well as repair and clean the well. Furthermore, if by law, statute, local custom, or command, everyone is required to pave the road with stones according to the location and quality of the house they possess, or contribute to cleaning a nearby street

<column-break/>

or a place designated for dumping street refuse, or anything similar, the tenant is responsible for all such outlays. They cannot reduce the rent because of these, nor demand anything from the **direct owner** <note>original: "proprietario"; the person who holds legal title to the land, as opposed to the tenant</note> for such expenses when the lease ends. This is the view of Bartolus, Baldus, and others cited by Alvaro Valasco. It agrees with the laws *hactenus* and *pendentes* in the Digest concerning usufruct. For if a **usufructuary** <gloss>someone with a right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another for their lifetime</gloss> is bound to some of these things, as is clear from the cited laws and as was discussed in Disputation 7, how much more should the emphyteutic tenant be bound, who transfers **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile; the right to use, possess, and profit from property while another holds the ultimate title</term> to their successors, and who receives the property in terms of beneficial ownership so that they may conserve it at their own expense and enjoy it with all the burdens attached to it.

<margin>2</margin> Although this doctrine as proposed—and that which we shall add in the second part of this disputation—is generally agreed upon (as noted in Gama's Decision 301), Gama rightly reports in that same decision that the Supreme Senate of Portugal judged otherwise in a specific case. When the King had ordered that the owners of certain lands contribute to the construction of dikes to resist the force of a river (lest the fields be lost, covered in sand, and rendered infertile) and to create channels to drain marshes and make them fit for bearing fruit, it was decided that not only the tenants but also the direct owners should contribute. This was to be done proportionally, according to the judgment of a prudent man, based on the greater or lesser time the tenant or their successors were expected to remain in the lease. This was because it was an unusual event that the contracting parties could not have foreseen, even if the tenant had expressly obligated themselves to the burdens and taxes of that field. Furthermore, it pertained not only to the utility of the tenant (who held the land for a few lifetimes), but to the perpetual benefit and utility of the owner. Gama indicates that the King's decree, which ordered the contribution, expressed this very thing: that the owners should also contribute. Indeed, with nothing in the general law preventing it, it was rightly decided and judged so in that event. For the sanctions of general law and the common opinion of doctors are not to be understood as applying to such extraordinary circumstances.

<margin>3</margin> When, however, the expenses the tenant makes pertain to a greater perpetual utility for the property—such as if they enlarged a building, or rebuilt one that had collapsed or burned without their fault, or if they usefully dug a well, built new dikes, or opened ditches and channels that make the fields more useful not just for their own use, but after the lease ends—if they are forced by public authority to do these things, they can compel the owner to contribute. This is as was said regarding the dikes and channels ordered by the King of Portugal. But if they do them of their own accord, the owner is not bound to contribute while the lease lasts; however, when the lease ends (especially if it ends without the fault of the tenant), the tenant must be paid either the value the property has gained beyond its original state, or the amount spent, at the discretion of the owner, as will be discussed in its proper place.

### Second Treatise, Disputations 4, 5, 6.

An exception is made unless the **emphyteuta** <note>a tenant holding a long-term, heritable lease known as an emphyteusis</note> was bound by the force of the contract to do otherwise—not in that general sense by which a tenant receives property in order to improve it, but specifically as compensation for a lower **pension** <gloss>the annual rent or fee paid to the owner</gloss> imposed upon him for that reason. In such cases, it is customary to express in the emphyteutic instrument <note>the written legal contract</note> that the tenant is bound to perform this or that task at his own expense, with no price to be demanded for it once the lease has ended. Thus Alvaro Valasco writes in the place cited above, along with others whom he references, although he may not explain these matters as accurately as we do.

2. From what has been said, one will easily understand which "expressed items" are discussed in **Portuguese Law** <note>original: "lege Lusitana"; referring to the Ordinances of the Kingdom of Portugal</note> (Book 4, Title 77, Paragraph 3) at the end. There, when discussing improvements made by a predecessor which a successor in the lease would be required to bring to a partition with other co-heirs, it is added: *“And this shall not be understood to apply to some small expenses and improvements, nor to certain others which the tenant is required by common law to perform out of necessity, without any other agreement between the parties or condition placed in the emphyteutic contract.”* Truly, these types of expenses to which a tenant is bound by **common law** <note>original: "iure communi"; the Roman-Canonical legal tradition shared across Europe</note> are none other than those mentioned in the first part of this disputation, as Alvaro Valasco rightly observed in the place cited above, number 5. This concludes the first of the topics proposed in the title of this disputation.

3. Regarding **burdens** <gloss>legal obligations or services attached to the land</gloss> and **taxes** <gloss>tributes or payments to the state</gloss>, it must be said that the tenant is required to pay not only **real burdens** <note>original: "onera realia"; taxes or duties attached to the physical property itself, regardless of who owns it</note> and taxes owed from the emphyteutic property, but also **personal burdens** and city taxes imposed by occasion of the property. Furthermore, he is required to pay future taxes that may be imposed while the lease continues, unless—as stated in the prior part of this disputation—something is imposed extraordinarily for a purpose concerning the perpetual utility of the property. In that case, the **owner** <note>original: "proprietarius"; the ultimate legal owner or landlord, as opposed to the tenant</note> is required to contribute, as was said there. If something were imposed on subjects according to the quantity and value of each person's goods, then the tenant would only be bound to pay as much as the value of his **useful domain** <note>original: "utile dominium"; the tenant's right to use and profit from the land, which is distinct from the owner's "direct domain"</note> is estimated, after deducting the rent or the burden of the rent; for the remaining portion, the owner to whom it belongs would be held responsible.

The first part of this entire assertion is proven by the law (Law 2, *On Emphyteutic Law*) in these words: *“unless he has provided the receipts of public functions,”* that is, the written document acknowledging that he has paid the burdens and taxes due by reason of that estate. It is as if the tenant himself is bound to those payments beyond the rent owed to the owner, as the **Gloss** <note>the standard medieval commentary on Roman law</note> explains, along with Alciatus, Baldus, Jason, and others whom Alvaro Valasco (Question 17, number 1) refers to and follows. The same is proven by Laws 2 and 3 of the Code (*That a farm cannot be purchased without the census or arrears*), the law *Imperatores* in the Digest (*On publicans*), the law *Inter emptorem* (*On pacts*), and the final law of the Code (*On the estates and all property of ship-owners*, Book 11). All these laws speak of real burdens and taxes on estates and establish that the burden of paying them passes to the possessors of the estates, even regarding past taxes not yet paid from those estates. It is as if the **fiscus** <note>original: "fisco"; the state treasury</note> has the right to demand past payments from the new possessors of the estates or from the old ones.

Laws 1 of the Code (*If for public payments*) and Law 1 (*In which cases a tacit mortgage...*) also speak of these same real taxes.

<column-break/>

And Law 25, Title 13, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>, which affirms that taxable estates are **tacitly mortgaged** <gloss>automatically pledged as security by law without a written contract</gloss> for the payment of taxes. Indeed, Law 25 establishes that all the goods of a person owing tax are tacitly mortgaged for those taxes. On this point, I read the opinion of **Jacobus de Ravanis** <note>Jacques de Révigny, a 13th-century French jurist</note>, which I do not believe to be true under common law, because there is no text from which it can be gathered. **Gregorio Lopez** <note>a major 16th-century commentator on Spanish law</note>, in his commentary on that same law, understands it—though not very firmly—to apply to all taxes, even personal ones, because that law speaks universally without restricting itself to real taxes. However, I think this is not true under common law, as there is no law from which it can be gathered. That law of Castile <note>Spain</note> should be understood according to the common law. Furthermore, those laws cited a little earlier establish that a **pact** <gloss>a private agreement</gloss> between a new possessor and an old one—stating that the burden of paying these taxes belongs to the old possessor and not the new one—is invalid. Therefore, with that pact offering no obstacle, the tax can be demanded from the new possessor. This must be understood, however, in terms of its effect: that it may not prejudice the treasury or any other person to whom the real burden of the estate belongs, so as to prevent them from demanding it from the new possessor. It does *not* mean that the old possessor is not bound by that pact to pay it back to the later possessor in the event that the later possessor pays it, as held in the law *Epistola*, section *pactum* (*On pacts*) and affirmed by the glosses on the laws *Inter emptorem*, *Imperatores*, and the others cited. By this same reasoning, if a new possessor pays old burdens or taxes which the predecessor was bound to pay, he has an action against that predecessor to be repaid the same amount, as the cited glosses affirm and Law *Idem Julianus* proves.

Regarding the rule that a new possessor is held to pay past taxes, there is an exception: unless the treasury has sold the estate. In that case, he is not held to past burdens and taxes, but only to future ones, as held in the final law of the Code (*On the celebration of sales*, Book 11) and affirmed by the gloss on Law 3 cited. Add to this: if someone sells an estate subject to real burdens and taxes to another, and the buyer is found to be less suitable for paying them, the seller is held to pay them in his place—even those belonging to a future time. This is held in the **Authentica** <note>a later addition or clarification to the Code of Justinian</note> *Sed et periculum* and the final law of the Code (*On estates and ship-owners*). On all these matters, read Alvaro Valasco (number 17) and Arias Pinel (*On the law of paternal property*, Part 2, number 72).

Regarding the second part—namely, that the tenant is also bound to pay personal burdens and taxes imposed by reason of the emphyteutic property, including those that will be imposed in the future while the lease lasts—this, along with the first part of the assertion, is proven primarily by Law 2 of the Code (*On emphyteutic law*) in these words: *“public functions, which comprise all public burdens and taxes,”* whether they be real or personal, by reason of the emphyteutic property. Furthermore, both parts of the conclusion are proven because a **usufructuary** <note>someone who has the right to use and enjoy the fruits/profits of another's property without owning it</note> is bound to all burdens and taxes, whether they are real taxes on the property or personal taxes by reason and occasion of that property, as was said in Disputation 7. This is proven by the laws *Hactenus*, section *modica*, and *Si pendentes*, section *Si quid cloacarii*, and the law *Usufructu relicto* (*On usufruct*), which says the same regarding taxes and burdens to be imposed while the usufruct persists.

# Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

**Column 1:**

This is also proven by the law *Neither stipend* in the *Digest* regarding expenses on dotal property <note>original: "l. neq; stipendiũ. ff. de impẽf. re. dot."; "dotal property" refers to a dowry</note>, where a husband, as the **usufructuary** <note>one who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> of his wife's dotal goods under common law, is held to pay all the tributes on the dotal estates. According to the law, he cannot later reclaim from his wife what he has paid. The text provides the reasoning: because, it says, all these expenses are a **burden upon the fruits** <note>original: "onus fructuum"; meaning the costs are tied to the profits/crops produced</note>, and they therefore follow the person who perceives the fruits of the estate or on whose occasion they are paid. Therefore, since the **emphyteuta** is the usufructuary of the leased property and holds the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile: the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to the underlying title</term> of it—which is generally not ended by his death—it follows that he is held to all burdens and tributes, whether **real** <gloss>tied to the land itself</gloss> or **personal** <gloss>tied to the individual</gloss>, by reason of the leased property. He is considered to have accepted the property to be enjoyed along with that burden, unless something else was specified in the contract, or if the local custom of the region dictates otherwise; for in those cases, the contract or custom must be upheld.

The common opinion of the doctors <note>learned legal scholars</note> agrees with both parts of this assertion, as cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco (in the place mentioned above, number 1), Arias Pinellus (on the Code, *concerning maternal goods*, part 2, number 72), and Julio Claro (Book 4, *Sentences*, section on emphyteusis, question 46). I do not approve of Julio Claro's opinion, nor does Alvaro Valasco (question cited, number 4), insofar as they suggest both parts of the assertion should be restricted provided that only a modest **pension** <gloss>annual rent</gloss> is paid. Indeed, Alvaro Valasco and Pinellus (in the places cited) do not think the rule should be restricted even if the lease is not for a lifetime, but for ten years or more.

The restriction we applied to both parts of our assertion was explained in the earlier part of this disputation; Antonio Gomez (Decision 301, cited) agrees with this and with both parts of the assertion.

The final part of the assertion is clear enough in itself; Alvaro Valasco affirms it along with many others whom he cites. It must be kept before one’s mind to discern when a **pensioner** <gloss>the recipient of a fixed payment</gloss> is held to the burdens imposed on **benefices** <note>church offices or properties</note>, and when he is not, and for many other matters.

<margin>4</margin>
The entire † proposed assertion similarly applies to a **feudatory** <note>a holder of land under a feudal lord</note>, since the reasoning is the same, as Alvaro Valasco rightly affirms.

When a thing affected by a burden or a **real tribute** <gloss>a tax on property</gloss> passes to the Church or an ecclesiastical person (through the life of an emphyteuta or otherwise), then that Church or ecclesiastical person is held to pay that burden or tribute. The exemption of Churches and ecclesiastical persons from burdens on their own goods does not stand in the way. The reason is that the property passes to any possessor whatsoever with its own real burden with which it was affected. The *Authentica* "Likewise the estate" <note>original: "authentice item prædiũ"; referring to a late-Roman legal update in the Code of Justinian</note> and other laws in the Code regarding sacred churches and the extraction of tributes agree on this. The same applies to property subject to a burden or real tribute that comes to the Church or an ecclesiastical person by way of a **fief** <note>original: "via feudi"</note>. The common opinion of the doctors agrees on this, as cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco and Gregorio Lopez.

Therefore, because in Portugal the tribute from certain fields, which they call the **jugada** <note>original: "iugada"; a tax based on the "yoke" (iugum) of oxen used for plowing</note>, is a real tax, it was rightly necessary for the King to grant a privilege to Churches and certain others so they would not have to pay it. To what extent it should not be paid by reason of that privilege—whether the Churches hold the beneficial and **direct ownership** <term>dominium directum: the ultimate legal title</term> or only the beneficial—and when it must be paid, is found in the *Ordinances of the Kingdom of Portugal*, Book 2, Title 16, Paragraph 8 and following. Read Alvaro Valasco on this.

When the tribute is personal—not by reason of the leased property

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

but based on the goods and income of each individual—the owner of the title must pay the tax imposed on the pension, and the emphyteuta must pay on the remaining income. In that case, the expenses incurred in collecting the income should be deducted from the emphyteuta's returns, because only the remainder is considered "fruits" and "income" for this purpose, as was stated in the preceding disputation. So says Alvaro Valasco (Question 17, number 10) along with the common opinion of the doctors.

<margin>5</margin>
When the emphyteuta holds land from the Church, although a real tribute cannot be imposed on the property (because the property is truly ecclesiastical, and once the lease ends and the beneficial ownership is consolidated with the direct ownership, that burden would persist upon a purely ecclesiastical thing), the doctors nevertheless doubt whether † a secular emphyteuta of the Church is held to **collections** <gloss>general taxes or levies</gloss> which are personal burdens. Specifically, whether he is held to pay collections based on the quantity of fruits or income (after deducting the pension) by reason of his beneficial ownership. And indeed, whatever Bartolus and a few others have said to the contrary, it must be said with Alvaro Valasco (Question 27, number 11) and the common opinion he cites, that the tenant is held to these collections. The reason is that they are paid by him solely by reason of his beneficial ownership; that beneficial ownership, while the lease lasts, is his own and not the Church's. Therefore, it is a **lay thing** <gloss>secular property</gloss>, subject to the secular jurisdiction of princes and the tributes rightly imposed by them.

For the same reason, if the lease is sold by him to a third party, the **right of first refusal** <note>original: "ius retractus"; the right of the owner to buy back the lease before it is sold to a stranger</note> applies, as was discussed in the section on contracts of buying and selling; Alvaro Valasco and others rightly affirm this. On the other hand, if a Church or ecclesiastical person holds a lease from a layman, although they are held to real burdens previously imposed on the property, they cannot be forced to pay collections and tributes from which clerics are exempt, as Valasco rightly asserts. This is because the beneficial ownership of such an emphyteuta belongs to the Church as an ecclesiastical person.

<margin>6</margin>
All these points similarly apply to fiefs and generally to usufructuaries when the direct lord is the Church and the feudatory or usufructuary is a layman, or vice versa, as Alvaro Valasco rightly advises. An emphyteuta of the **Supreme Prince** <gloss>the King</gloss> is excused from new tributes on the same property according to laws in the Code regarding the estates of the Emperor and leases; Alvaro Valasco affirms this with Rebuffi, although both say it is poorly observed in practice. In the same place, with the same author, he adds that those who pay a **fourth part** <note>original: "quartam partem"</note> of their land's produce to the King (in those same fruits or an equivalent) ought to be kept immune from other tributes from those same fields. This is based on many legal arguments he cites, and also alluded to in **Portuguese Law** (Book 2, Title 16, Paragraph 3), which renders those estates immune from paying the *jugada*. The reason is that estates already burdened with tributes ought to be exempt from paying new tributes unless a great necessity urges it.

However, this too is not usually observed in practice. Yet, none of the aforementioned are exempt from those **extraordinary burdens** imposed for the sake of piety and common utility, such as the repair of roads, fountains, walls, and bridges, according to the Code; as Alvaro Valasco adds in the same place.

It also examines complex cases where the Church is either the owner or the tenant, distinguishing between land-based taxes and personal levies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the rights and duties of the emphyteuta (a long-term tenant). While the previous page discussed the responsibility for taxes and public burdens, this page shifts to the penalties for mismanaging the property—specifically, whether a tenant loses their lease if they allow the property to deteriorate.</meta>

### Whether a long-term tenant incurs forfeiture if they make the leased property worse.

### D I S P V T A T I O N  CCCCLVII.

->S V M M A R Y<-

1 Whether and when a <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>a tenant holding a long-term or perpetual lease</note> incurs <term>commissum</term> <note>forfeiture of the lease</note> if they make the leased property worse.
2 A tenant who cuts down an old olive grove and plants a vineyard: does this cause forfeiture? Distinguished in number 7.
3 A tenant who destroys a <term>coppice-wood</term> <note>original: "syluam caeduam"; a forest managed for timber</note> without the owner’s permission to plant a vineyard incurs forfeiture.
4 Destroying houses and cutting down trees are considered equal offenses.
5 An owner is not permitted to change the form of property held in <term>usufruct</term> <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> even if they make it better.
6 A tenant has more rights than the owner or a usufructuary to change the leased property to make it better.

---

<margin>Question</margin>
**I**t is established that a tenant of Church land who makes the leased property worse incurs forfeiture. Consequently, they can be deprived of the lease and cannot reclaim the costs of other improvements made to the property. This is because, as previously stated, they lose these rights when they forfeit the lease due to unpaid rent. This is expressly stated in the *Authentica* regarding alienations and long-term leases <note>original: "auth. de alien. & emph."</note> in the section "But if anyone or the lessor," and in the *Authentica* "He who a thing," in the Code regarding the most sacred churches. However, regarding non-Ecclesiastical leases, because it is not found as expressly in the law, the scholars Imola, Jason, and a few others—whose opinion Aluarus Valascus cites and does not consider improbable in his 50th Counsel, number 5—believe the tenant does not incur forfeiture. Nevertheless, he notes that in Portugal, one must not depart from the contrary opinion, as it is the view of Bartolus and the common consensus. He confirms this by noting that the law is not sufficiently clear regarding <term>fiefs</term> <note>land held under the feudal system</note> either. Indeed, in the section "Public Robbers" regarding the keeping of peace, it is only held that a vassal who misuses feudal property by making it worse can be punished; the laws do not say they must be deprived of the property. Since a milder penalty should be chosen, it ought only to be understood that the tenant should be condemned to pay for the full interest of the lord, rather than being deprived of the property. For this view—that the vassal does not incur forfeiture for this reason—he cites Baldus, Paulus de Castro, Decio, and Ludovicus Romanus. I wonder, however, that Valascus cites the section "Public Robbers" in support, as that section explicitly deals with the penalty of deprivation, even if it specifies that this happens if they mistreated the thing and did not stop after being warned by the lord.

<margin>Decision</margin>
However, the common opinion of Bartolus on the law regarding divorce <note>original: "l. diuortio."</note> in the section "If a field," in the *Digest* on the dissolution of marriage, and of others followed by Giulio Claro, Aris Pinel, Molina, Gama, and Silvestro, which states that forfeiture *does* occur,

<column-break/>

and from which Aluarus Valascus himself (in the cited counsel) judges we should not depart, is the one we must embrace. This is based on the reasoning established for Church leases. Since the contract was entered into for the improvement of the property, equity does not allow the owner to be bound to the contract when the tenant does the opposite. However, the doctrine taught so far regarding both Church and private leases must be understood to apply only if the deterioration is in the very substance of the property, and not merely in the fruits <note>the crops or annual profits</note>, which belong only to the tenant and not the owner. Yet, as Silvestro rightly observes above, if a vineyard is not pruned for several years and thus becomes barren for the future and of less value, it is considered to have deteriorated in its substance, no differently than if the vines had been cut down and uprooted by the tenant. Furthermore, this is understood to refer to deterioration that is not minor, but notable, based on the judgment of a prudent person (arguing from the law "I know" in the *Digest* on restitution). It must also result from the fraud or "gross fault" of the tenant, as Gama affirms with many others. Although Silvestro asserts that "slight fault" <note>original: "culpa levis"</note> is sufficient, rather than "very slight fault," because the contract was made for the benefit of both owner and tenant; in such contracts, one is liable for slight fault, as has often been said above.

<margin>1</margin>
From what has been said, one can understand what should be judged regarding the question Valascus raises and which Gama disputes in many places. A tenant cut down and uprooted an old olive grove which they held in a perpetual lease (or for several lifetimes) and began to plant a vineyard in that same soil. The owner contended that the tenant had incurred forfeiture because the olives were cut and uprooted without the owner's permission. The tenant, conversely, defended himself by arguing that he had improved the owner's position, because the vineyard he was planting would be of far greater value than the grove of very old olive trees.

<margin>2</margin>
Against the tenant, the teaching of Bartolus and many others was cited, as followed by Giulio Claro and Aries Pinel. Molina also absolutely affirms that a tenant who cuts down fruit-bearing trees incurs forfeiture; and such were those olives. Likewise, Baldus and Jason affirm that a tenant who <margin>3</margin> destroys a coppice-wood <note>a forest grown for harvest</note> without the owner's permission to plant a vineyard there incurs forfeiture; for once the wood is destroyed, neither it nor the vineyard remains [as the original contracted thing]. The same is seen in the proposed case. Also, <margin>4</margin> destroying houses and cutting down trees are considered equal acts (as gathered from the law "Elegantly" in the *Digest* on fraud); a tenant who destroyed houses on the leased land would certainly incur forfeiture.

Nonetheless, it must be said, along with Aluarus Valascus, Gama, and others, that when the property is not notably deteriorated by such a change, the tenant does not incur forfeiture...

<sig>Ll 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: and so</meta>

<summary>This page debates whether a long-term tenant (emphyteuta) loses their lease if they change or degrade the property. It concludes that while substantial damage through neglect or fraud leads to forfeiture, improvements—like replacing an old olive grove with a more valuable vineyard—might be permissible depending on the degree of change to the property's "substance."</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina On Contracts

...and thus it was judged in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, as Alvaro Valasco and Gama report there. This is especially so because it is said to be the custom in Portugal that this occurs, as Alvaro Valasco (ibid. no. 6) and Gama (Decision 147, no. 5) affirm: in this matter, one must truly abide by the custom of the place.

The doctrine of Bartolus and the common opinion cited in the first place is true in itself: however, it must be understood to apply when other plants are not growing back, and when other more useful plants are not substituted in their place, such that the leased property <note>the <term>emphyteutic</term> thing</note> is rendered notably worse. The doctrine of Baldus and Jason is similarly to be understood to apply when the <term>coppice-wood</term> <note>original: "sylua cædua"; a forest managed for timber</note> was more useful and better—at least due to its longevity—than a vineyard. Regarding the point brought up in the third place, it must be said that if the leased property consists not only of houses but of the farm on which they are situated, the tenant does not then incur <term>commissum</term> <note>forfeiture of the lease</note> if they destroy those houses in order to build better and more convenient ones, either in the same spot or in another part of the same farm, or if they do so for the greater utility and convenience of the leased property.

<margin>5</margin>
But if someone objects to us using the final law of the Digest on use and habitation <note>original: "l. vlt. ff. de vsu & hab."</note>, where the legal owner is not permitted to change the form of property held in <term>usufruct</term> <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> even if they make it better by that means; or the law regarding a usufructuary's new building <note>original: "l. vsufructuarius nouū. §. ædificium, ff. de vsufructu"</note>, and other laws in which a usufructuary is not permitted to complete an unfinished building on the property without the owner's permission, even if it is made better.

<margin>6</margin>
It must be said, following Arias Pinellus and Alvaro Valasco, that there is a far greater reason to favor the long-term tenant. The tenant has more legal right <note>original: "plus iuris"</note> in the leased property and for a longer time; they receive the property from the origin of the <term>emphyteutic</term> contract specifically to make it better. Hence, without the direct owner's permission, the tenant can construct a building on the property and make it better by any other means.

<margin>7</margin>
However, to say what I think: I believe a distinction must be made. Either the property received in the long-term lease from the beginning was a vineyard, an olive grove, or a coppice-wood, or it was the soil itself in which those were planted. And again, either a single large farm—containing houses, a vineyard, an olive grove, and other things—was given in the lease by one contract, or only a house, or only a vineyard or olive grove was given.

If, from the beginning, the soil itself in which things were planted was given, or a large farm was given in which houses, olive groves, vineyards, or woods were parts of the whole leased property, then the entire doctrine handed down so far is true. This is because the long-term lease contract is not considered finished by the destruction or change of form of just one part, as was stated in Disputation 454.

Likewise, the leased property is not considered destroyed by the destruction of the vineyard plants or olive trees when the soil itself was given in the lease from the beginning, as was said in the same place. In other cases, however, based on what was said there, I think that—standing on the sole disposition of the law—by the very fact that the olive grove, vineyard, woods, or house given in the lease was destroyed, the <term>emphyteutic</term> contract is finished.

<column-break/>

It is then at the option of the owner, when the tenant has destroyed the property, to either take possession of the soil and compel the tenant to pay for damages <note>original: "interesse"</note>, or to compel the tenant to repair what they destroyed and continue the contract, as was stated in the same place.

I said, "standing on the sole disposition of the law," because if there is a custom anywhere that allows the tenant to change an olive grove into a vineyard, or vice versa, or do something similar without requesting the owner's permission, that custom must be followed.

## Whether a long-term tenant can be expelled from the leased property because the owner needs it for their own use, or because the tenant is abusing it for bad purposes. And whether, if the tenant sells produce from the leased property, the owner should be preferred in their purchase.

# DISPVTATIO CCCCLVIII.

### SUMMARY

<margin>1</margin>
1 *Whether a long-term tenant can be expelled from the leased property because it is necessary for the owner.*
*And what happens when they abuse it for bad purposes.*
*And whether, if they sell the produce from the leased property, the owner should be preferred in their purchase.*

<margin>1</margin>
Alvaro Valasco disputes these three points in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 22 and the two following. He rightly concludes with the negative side regarding all of them.

First, because the long-term tenant holds the <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to the use and profits of the land</note> of the leased property, they cannot be expelled for those two reasons proposed in the first two questions.

But if they must be restrained due to a depraved use of the leased property, that should be done by another means through a judge's order, just as if someone who held both the beneficial and <term>direct ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium directum"; the legal title</note> simultaneously had to be restrained if they were abusing the same property in a similar way.

Nor does the tenant have any less right—by reason of their beneficial ownership—to sell the produce of the leased property to whomever they wish, without any right of first refusal <note>original: "iure prælationis"</note> for the owner, than if the same tenant also held the direct ownership of the same property. Furthermore, none of those three things are found sanctioned in the law: and without express law, none of those things should be asserted. What should be said regarding a tenant farmer or a tenant of a house concerning those three points will be examined below in its proper place.

# Whether a long-term tenant incurs forfeiture by selling the leased property without asking the owner if they wish to buy it at the same price, and regarding the payment of the recognition fee to the owner if the property is sold to another.

## DISPUTATION CCCCLIX.

### S V M M A R Y.

1 A long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>a tenant under a perpetual or long-term lease</note> who sells the leased property without asking the lord incurs forfeiture <term>commissum</term>. However, understand and clarify this as noted there.
2 A long-term tenant may offer improvements and the leasehold right for sale without asking the lord. Understand and clarify this as in number 7.
3 A long-term tenant wishing to sell their right, if they do not have a license from the owner, is bound to wait for them for two months.
4 And what about Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> even in the case of a Church lease, number 4.
5 Once the long-term tenant has obtained a license to sell from the owner, they may sell their right to whomever they wish, provided it is not to those who are typically forbidden from buying leasehold rights.
6 Which persons are prohibited from buying leasehold rights.
8 The mere sale of the leasehold right without asking the lord, if no delivery of the property occurs, is not a sufficient cause for incurring the penalty of forfeiture.
9 Whether delivery through a "fictional act" <note>a legal formality rather than physical handover</note> is sufficient cause for the tenant to incur forfeiture.
10 A long-term tenant who sells and delivers the leasehold right without asking the lord, but under the condition "if it pleases the lord," does not incur forfeiture. The same applies to a sale made with a forfeiture clause <note>original: "lex commissoria"</note>, or a "day-addition" clause <note>original: "in diem addictio"; a clause allowing a better offer within a certain timeframe</note>, or other similar conditions, number 12. The same applies in a void alienation, even if the owner's permission was present, number 13.
It is limited, however, unless they say "saving the right of the owner," number 11.
14 A long-term tenant who recovers their alienated leasehold right is not freed from the forfeiture. Limit this, however, as noted there.
15 Whether a long-term tenant who alienates part of the leasehold right incurs forfeiture for the whole.
16 A long-term tenant wishing to alienate their right must ask all the owners of the same property; otherwise, they incur forfeiture.
17 When a wife is the owner, it is sufficient for the tenant to notify the husband so that they may sell their right.
18 When the leasehold right passes from one person to another, the final tenant must ask the owner about the price, as the owner is preferred over other buyers for the same price.
19 When the long-term tenant has notified the owner of the price and has rightfully sold and delivered the property, if the contract is later rescinded by the remedy of Law 2 of the Code on rescinding sales <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescind. uend."; a law allowing rescission if the price was less than half the fair value</note>, a new license from the owner is not required.
20 An owner who accepts the rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note> from a new tenant...

<column-break/>

...is deemed to have consented to the contract and to have freed the first tenant from the penalty of forfeiture. Understand this, however, as noted there.
21 A long-term tenant who unknowingly sells the leased property without asking the lord does not incur forfeiture; this ignorance transfers the burden of proving knowledge onto the owner.
This is extended even to a necessary sale <note>such as an estate sale or forced auction</note>, number 22.
23 When a leasehold right is sold, the <term>Alcabala</term> <note>original: "Alcauala"; a sales tax</note> is owed.
24 From what things the recognition fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>a fee paid to the landlord on the transfer of a lease</note> must be paid to the owner, and when not.
25 Whether the recognition fee is owed from a lease for ten years or more, if the person who has the leased property sells that right to another.
26 If the lease was granted with the power for the tenant to sell it to whomever they wish, the new tenant will still be bound to pay the recognition fee.

Although a long-term tenant may offer improvements and the leasehold right they hold in the property for sale without having to ask the owner, they cannot actually sell them unless they have consulted the owner and disclosed the price that others are offering. This is so that if the owner wishes to acquire them at that same price, they may be preferred over others.
However, once the owner says they do not wish to buy them, or grants the tenant the power to sell to whomever they wish, or—having been informed of the price—responds that they do not wish to buy or not at such a high price, the tenant may then sell to another. But if the owner remains silent or says they wish to deliberate on the matter, the tenant is bound by common civil law, the law of Castile, and Canon law to wait for two months from the moment the owner was notified of the price. By Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, however, the tenant is only bound to wait thirty days. Within that time, if the owner does not say they wish to buy at that price and thus pay the price themselves, the tenant may thereafter sell to another, provided the buyer is not among those typically forbidden from buying leasehold rights.
If, however, the long-term tenant sells and delivers the property without observing these requirements, they incur forfeiture <term>commissum</term> and immediately lose the entire leasehold right and all improvements to the owner. When, however, they sell to a stranger (that is, to someone other than the owner) while observing these rules, a fiftieth part of the price must be paid to the owner according to common civil law, the law of Castile, and Canon law. By Portuguese law, a fortieth part is due. Understand this to be the case unless, when the lease contract was first made, a pact was included for more, less, or nothing to be paid.
This payment is what legal experts typically call the <term>laudemium</term> <note>recognition fee</note>. In the Portuguese ordinances <note>original: "Lusitanis ordinationibus"</note>, the part that is paid (when nothing else was specified in the pact) is called the <term>quarentena</term> <note>the "fortieth"</note>; elsewhere it is the "fiftieth." Many in Portugal call it the "payment to the lord" <note>original: "pagaro domino"</note>, because it is paid on account of the lord's direct ownership. In the Alentejo region <note>original: "trasstagana"</note> of that kingdom, it is customary to call it <term>pagar otteradego</term>. What has been said in this whole section is to be understood unless something else regarding these matters is...

# Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...unless something else was specified in the agreement when the long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>a type of perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land</note> was first established: for in that case, the original convention must be upheld regarding all these matters.

<margin>2</margin>
All these points must be further corroborated and explained. The first point asserted—namely, that the long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term> may put the improvements and the leasehold right up for sale without first requiring the owner's permission—is clearly gathered from the Code of Justinian <note>original: "l. 3. §. sed ne. C. de iure emph."</note> in these words: *A notification should be sent to the lord, and he should be told beforehand how much price can truly be received from another;* and from the decretals regarding leases <note>original: "c. potuit de locat."</note> in the words: *And having notified him of how much is offered to him by others;* as well as from the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. vlt. tit. 8. par. 5." - a 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note> and the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "lib. 4. Lusit. ord. tit. 64."</note>. This is affirmed by Panormitanus, Gregorio López, and others. For if the tenant must notify the owner of the price others are offering him, he certainly has the power to put the improvements and the leasehold right up for sale so that he can make the owner certain of the price he has found for them.

<margin>3</margin>
The second point will be more conveniently discussed along with the fifth. The third point, however, is that if the owner does not first grant the power to sell the improvements and leasehold right to another, or does not say he is unwilling to buy them at that price, the tenant is bound to wait for a period of two months. Once that has passed, if the owner has not said within that time that he wishes to buy at that price and has not paid the price, the tenant may sell them to another. This is expressly held in the Code of Justinian, the decretals, and the Siete Partidas. However, Monterroso <note>a Spanish legal authority</note> says in his *Practica* that by custom today in the Kingdom of Castile, a clause is added to leasehold contracts stating that only thirty days are expected. If such a clause is included, it must be observed, even if it is a Church lease.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding the fact that under Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> one is only bound to wait thirty days, this is found in the Portuguese Ordinances. Although that ordinance would not normally take place in that Kingdom regarding a Church lease (where, according to Canon Law, two full months should be expected), while I was staying in Portugal, I learned that it has become established by custom in that Kingdom that even in Church leases, only thirty days are expected. It seems that the common lease provided the occasion for this custom; people followed the timeframe of the Ordinances and did not notice that in Church leases, one should not stand by the local ordinances but by the disposition of Canon Law. Thus, that custom in that Kingdom has overridden Canon Law in this regard.

<margin>5</margin>
Furthermore, it is clear enough that the tenant can sell the leasehold right to another as soon as the owner gives him permission. By that very act, the owner waives his right so that the time granted to him by law is not waited for; "to one who is willing and consenting, no injury is done" <note>a legal maxim meaning a person cannot claim to be wronged by an action they agreed to</note>. Likewise, it is clear that if the owner responds that he does not wish to buy at that price, the tenant can sell it; for that time is granted to the tenant <gloss>the owner</gloss> to deliberate and prepare the price if he chooses to buy. By responding that he does not wish to buy at that price, he has finished deliberating and waives his right. All of this is indicated

<column-break/>

quite clearly in the decretals, the Siete Partidas, and the Portuguese Ordinances, and it is commonly accepted.

<margin>6</margin>
The fourth point—namely, that the buyer must not be among those to whom it is usually forbidden to buy a leasehold right—is found in the Code of Justinian and more explicitly in the Siete Partidas. The commentary on the Code says regarding the word "forbidden" <note>original: "vetari"</note> that, first of all, if it was stipulated at the beginning when the lease contract was made that the leasehold right should not pass to certain persons, it is unlawful to sell the right or the improvements to them. Next, it must be said that if the buyer is someone from whom the owner will have more difficulty obtaining the rent <term>pensionem</term> than from the current tenant—either because of their power, their privileges, or their extreme poverty, or for some other reason—then it is unlawful for the tenant to sell the leasehold right and improvements to them.

This is the only point expressed by the Portuguese Ordinance in the place cited. Finally, if the buyer is someone from whom the owner justly fears some harm—either for the reason just explained, or because they might usurp the ownership, or because they will rarely try to sell or exchange the leasehold right (which means the "useful ownership" would rarely be reunited with the "direct ownership," or the recognition fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>a fee paid to the landlord when the lease is transferred</note> would rarely be paid to the owner)—it is unlawful to sell to such a buyer. All the cited laws intend this, and it is affirmed by the doctors cited by Giulio Claro and Gregorio López.

Hence, the legal experts hold that a tenant cannot sell the leasehold right to a Church or a monastery, nor exchange it with them, because the owner would be burdened; the "useful ownership" <note>the right to use and profit from the land</note> would return to him with greater difficulty, the recognition fee would be paid to him less often, and because of the privileges of the Church. Therefore, although a leasehold right can be left to the Church in a will or come to a monastery through the possession of a monk (as was said in Disputation 140), the Church or monastery is bound to sell it within a year, as affirmed by the doctors cited by Silvester Prierias. They testify that this is accepted by custom. Among "privileged persons" are counted soldiers, courtiers, and clergy. Understand this doctrine to apply when the tenant is not as privileged as the person to whom the leasehold right would pass.

<margin>7</margin>
Regarding the second and fifth points: namely, that he cannot sell the improvements and leasehold right without first asking the owner and manifesting the price offered by others, so that if the owner wants to take them at that same price, he is preferred over others; and that if the tenant sells them without observing the third and fourth requirements and delivers the property, he incurs forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>loss of the lease rights as a penalty</note> not only of the leasehold right but also of the improvements. This is expressly held in the Code of Justinian, the decretals, and the Siete Partidas, along with the commentary of Gregorio López and the Portuguese Ordinances.

<margin>8</margin>
These things are certainly to be understood even if the owner has said he does not want to buy them, if the tenant then sells to a buyer...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 459.

...to the buyer, to whom it is usually forbidden to purchase the leasehold right <term>ius emphyteuticum</term> <note>the specific legal right of a tenant in a long-term, transferable lease</note>, as is sufficiently gathered from the laws cited. The same applies if the tenant lies about the price, telling the owner that he is receiving less than what is actually being found, as Gregorio López affirms in his commentary on the last law cited, specifically on the phrase "and how much it is" <note>original: "e quanto es"</note>, following Saliceto and others. In this place, observe that a sale of a leasehold <term>emphyteusis</term> made without the power of the owner—even if a physical transfer has followed—is null and void by the law itself, as is clear in itself and gathered openly from the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusita. ordina. §. 1."</note>. Therefore, if a leasehold property is first sold and delivered to one person without the owner's consent, but later sold to another with the owner's consent, the second buyer is preferred over the first, as Gama rightly teaches along with others.

<margin>8</margin>
It has been said, "if he has sold and delivered" the leasehold property: because a mere sale, if delivery <term>traditio</term> <note>the formal legal transfer of possession</note> does not follow, is not sufficient for ownership <term>dominium</term> to be transferred, nor for the thing to be said to be alienated entirely and simply, as was said in Disputations 2, 3, and 338. Moreover, the common opinion of the doctors affirms that a sale consummated in this way is necessary to incur the penalty of forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>the loss of the lease as a penalty for breach of contract</note>. This is the view followed by Julius Clarus, Alvaro Valasco, Antonio Gomez (where he confirms it with many arguments), Covarruvias, Gutierrez, and Sylvester.

<margin>Question 9</margin>
But is delivery through a "fictitious act" sufficient—such as through a "clause of possession" <note>original: "clausulam constituti" - a legal fiction where a seller agrees to hold the item on behalf of the buyer, effectively transferring legal possession without moving the object</note>—for the tenant to fall into forfeiture? Antonio Gomez denies this, led by certain testimonies from the books of feudal law, which require a physical delivery so that a vassal who alienates a fief without consulting the lord falls into forfeiture. Julius Clarus says this opinion is more equitable and can be upheld in court, especially if judging based solely on the truth of the facts; he notes that Guido testifies this is how they judge in the region of Dauphiné.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The contrary opinion, however, is more common, as Julius Clarus himself reports, asserting it is the true one according to the rigor of the law; it is also followed by Gutierrez and Gama, and we should embrace it. This is because delivery through a fictitious act truly transfers possession and ownership, and is therefore sufficient for a consummated and perfected alienation <note>the legal transfer of property to another</note>. Those testimonies from the feudal books should be understood to include delivery by either a real or a fictitious act.

<margin>Point of Doubt 10</margin>
Furthermore, if a tenant sells or delivers the leasehold right without requesting the owner's permission, but under the condition "if the owner consents," or using other words that amount to the same thing, does he fall into forfeiture?

<margin>Decision</margin>
It must be said that he does not fall into forfeiture, because a sale under a condition is not a perfected or consummated alienation until that condition is fulfilled. Moreover, a condition of this sort, which we are discussing, requires the owner's consent and thus requires that the owner be asked whether he consents to the sale so that it may be perfected. This is held by Sylvester, Gregorio López, and Gama. Nor do I think

<column-break/>

it is necessary that after the tenant says he is alienating "saving the consent of the lord" or "on the condition that he consents," he must also add "and not otherwise, nor in any other way," as Julius Clarus (following Baldus) wishes in a certain place.

The reason is that these latter words are contained by implication within the former ones, and there is no law from which it can be gathered that they must be added for the tenant to be freed from the penalty of forfeiture. However, I agree with Baldus, Julius Clarus, and Gregorio López on this: if the tenant delivers something that is difficult to recover—such as a fortified castle delivered to a powerful person—and generally if there were signs that once delivered, it would be difficult for the owner to recover it, then the tenant falls into forfeiture by so delivering the leasehold property. In such a case, the protestation or condition added would be hindered by nothing, for it would be judged to have been added in fraud, and the tenant would be at fault for so delivering the owner's property.

<margin>11</margin>
If, however, the tenant sells and delivers the leasehold property adding the phrase "saving the right of the owner," the cited doctors commonly say (and Molina follows them in his work *On Primogeniture*) that the tenant falls into forfeiture. This is because protestations that are contrary to the actual deed are of no weight.

Based on the same principle—that for a tenant to fall into forfeiture, it is necessary for the sale to be entirely consummated so that the sold thing is considered simply alienated—the following must be said:

<margin>12</margin>
If a tenant sells and delivers the leasehold right, but under a "forfeiture clause" <note>original: "lex commissoria" - a clause where the sale is void if the price isn't paid by a certain date</note> or a "better offer clause" <note>original: "addictio in diem" - a clause allowing the seller to cancel the sale if a better offer comes within a set timeframe</note>, such that if the condition occurs, the contract is dissolved as if it had never been made from the beginning, then the tenant does not fall into forfeiture if the contract is so dissolved. He is not considered to have fallen into forfeiture before that contract is entirely perfected. This is the view of Gama, Baldus, Jason de Mayno, and others.

<margin>13</margin>
From this same foundation, whenever an alienation of the leasehold right made by the tenant is legally null—even if the owner’s permission was present—he would not fall into forfeiture through that alienation. This is because a void alienation cannot be called "consummated," nor is it simply an alienation. This is the view of Gregorio López, following Speculator, Bartolus, and others, based on various laws he cites.

<margin>14</margin>
When a tenant has sold and entirely alienated the leasehold right, and has thus fallen into forfeiture, even if he later recovers that same leasehold right, he is not freed from the forfeiture. This is because a right once perfectly acquired by the owner for that reason cannot be snatched away from him without his own act. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus, Gutierrez, Alvaro Valasco, Sylvester, and Gama.

However, some judge that this should be limited based on a certain equity, as reported by Gama and Caldas, when a person who has sold the leasehold without consulting the owner...
