-># Ludovicus Molina on Contracts<-

sold it back to the owner, he immediately recovered it. However, Gama believes that the tenant has restored his status if he recovered the property before a lawsuit was contested against him by the owner; he says that he once judged a case alongside other senators according to this limitation. However, just as this limitation does not please Jason <note>Jason de Mayno, a famous 15th-century legal commentator</note>, it is likewise not approved by me.

<margin>15</margin> When a leaseholder <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>a tenant under a long-term, heritable lease</note> has alienated only a part of the leasehold right without requesting the lord's permission, Giulio Claro (in question 13, cited above) says the more common opinion is that he does not incur forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>the loss of the lease as a penalty for breach of contract</note> of the whole right, but only of the part alienated; he notes that the Senate of Naples has judged according to this opinion. On the contrary, Sylvester (in his 2nd pronouncement, cited above) affirms along with Jason that the tenant incurs forfeiture of the entire right, saying that this is how the law is held. Regarding this same question, Gregorio López (in the place cited) refers the reader to the same Jason. I believe this latter opinion to be the true one in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, where the leasehold property is indivisible, as will be discussed in the following disputation; it is otherwise in other places where it is divisible, as we shall also see in the following disputation.

<margin>16</margin> When there are two owners of the same leasehold property held in common, both must be asked whether they wish to exercise their right of first refusal for the price offered by others; it is not sufficient to ask only one and have permission from him; otherwise, the leaseholder incurs forfeiture. However, whether he then incurs forfeiture of the entire leasehold right or only a part, Gregorio López (on the last law, title 8, part 5, at the word "to the lord" <note>original: "al señor"</note>) refers to Johannes Andreae, Speculator, and Jason. Sylvester, however, in the cited 2nd pronouncement, correctly affirms that he only incurs forfeiture for that portion: because he should only be punished insofar as the ownership of the leasehold property belongs to the person against whom he offended, and according to the proportion of the leasehold that corresponds to that person. However, if one of those owners does not want the leasehold right for that price, but the other does, this owner should be preferred over other buyers for the entire leasehold right at the same price. Gregorio López (cited above) correctly responds along with Albericus and Jason that he is to be preferred, based on the argument of the law *in bello* <note>a reference to Digest 49.15.12.2</note>. This is an undisputed point in this Kingdom of Castile, according to the law of retraction <note>retractus: the right to buy back property</note>, of which we spoke in Disputation 371.

<margin>17</margin> When a wife is the owner, it is sufficient for the leaseholder to notify the husband and sell the leasehold right with his consent. This is the view of Jason and Gregorio López in the same place, based on the argument of the law *aut qui aliter* <note>Digest 43.24.11</note>. This is undisputed in Castile and Portugal, where the husband is the administrator of all assets.

<margin>18</margin> When the leasehold right passes from one leaseholder to another, the final leaseholder must ask not the intermediate leaseholder, but the actual owner regarding the price; and the owner alone is to be preferred for that price over other buyers, unless something else was agreed upon in the contract when the owner first granted the property in lease. This is the view of the last gloss on the Code *de iure emphyteutico* <note>on the law of emphyteusis</note> at the words "to sell to others" <note>original: "alijs uendere"</note>, and according to the text there, as cited by Gregorio López, Gama, Caldas, and many others. Therefore, Caldas rightly

<column-break/>

rejects the contrary opinion of Alvaro Valasco regarding the law of emphyteusis, who claims (against the common opinion of the doctors) that when a leaseholder, with the consent of the owner, appoints a sub-leaseholder who pays a higher rent, while reserving the increase for the first leaseholder, the second leaseholder is bound to notify the first leaseholder and pay the transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>a fee, usually 2% of the price, paid to the owner upon the sale of a lease</note> to him, and not to the owner.

For the owner, by granting that power to sub-lease, did not abdicate any right that belongs to him as owner; therefore, the permission to alienate must be sought from him, and the transfer fee must be paid to him, not to the first leaseholder.

<margin>19</margin> When the leaseholder has notified the owner of the price and has properly sold and delivered the property, if the contract is later lawfully rescinded <note>undone or cancelled</note> according to the second law of the Code *de rescindenda venditione*, the owner's permission is not necessary for that reversal. This is because it is not a new alienation (sale), but a resolution of the prior one for a just cause. Likewise, when the leasehold right has been properly sold and delivered with a "buy-back" agreement <note>pacto de retro uendendo</note>, if it is later redeemed and recovered, the owner's permission is not necessary; for similarly, it is not a new contract, but the resolution of the former one based on a clause included within it. However, when the same leasehold right is bought again as a completely new transaction, the owner's authority is necessary, as it would be a new sale. All these points are made by Gregorio López (cited above) and are clear in themselves. Read what was said in Disputation 273 and at the end of Disputations 374, 378, and 379.

<margin>20</margin> <margin>Molina</margin> If, after the leaseholder has incurred forfeiture for alienating the property without following the procedures explained in this disputation, the owner accepts rent <term>pensionem</term> from the new leaseholder, he is considered to have consented to the contract. Consequently, the first leaseholder is freed from the penalty of forfeiture, and the owner cannot expel the new leaseholder from the property. This is the view of Gregorio López, Gama, and Caldas; they agree with what was said in Disputation 453, and the Portuguese ordinances cited there do not contradict this.

Just as if someone incurs forfeiture for not paying rent, and the owner then accepts not only the overdue rent but also rent for the time following the forfeiture, the owner is considered to have waived the forfeiture. Thus, in this case, if he receives rent for the time after the forfeiture was incurred for this other reason (unauthorized sale), he is considered to have waived it. The Portuguese ordinances speak of the specific rents whose non-payment causes forfeiture, not about other rents paid after the fact; I do not know if Gama sufficiently considered this in his cited decisions.

However, I understand these points to apply when the owner accepts the rent while *not* being ignorant of the forfeiture. Regularly, he will not be ignorant of it, since he sees a new leaseholder paying the rent, unless the forfeiture was incurred because the previous leaseholder reported a much lower price to him than

### Second Treatise, Disputation 49. ###

...be offered for the leasehold right: when it is that for which something else is sold, or for another similar cause which the owner might be ignorant of: to receive the rent from him while ignorant of the forfeiture <note>original: "caducitatis"</note> is not sufficient for the owner to be deemed to have waived the forfeiture. For this reason, if the tenant, after he has alienated the property, seeks the faculty from the owner to alienate it, although the owner is deemed to waive the forfeiture if, knowing it was alienated, he grants the same faculty, as Gregorio López rightly affirms in the cited place.

<margin>21</margin> Just as was said in Disputation 45, section 3, if you are ignorant that a property is leasehold for two or three years and do not pay the rent, you do not fall into forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>the loss of the lease as a penalty for breach of contract</note> for that reason: so too if, ignorant of the trust, you alienate it without the owner's request, you do not incur forfeiture: because where there is no fault, there is no place for punishment. It belongs to the owner to prove that knowledge was present, because the matter is not manifest, as was said there by Gregorio López, where he discusses the word "the sale" <note>original: "la uenda"</note>, and Gama in Decision 91, number 1, and others whom they cite. I believe, however, the sale is null.

<margin>22</margin> These things said have a place not only when the sale of the leasehold right is voluntary—that is, made by the tenant himself—but also when it is necessary, such as when it is done to satisfy his debts, or for another cause by the authority of a judge, as held in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusitan. ordin."</note>, title 64, at the beginning; and along with others, Alvaro Valasco (on the Law of Emphyteusis, question 38, number 9) and Gregorio López (on the last law, title 8, part 5, on the word "the sale" <note>original: "la uenda"</note>) assert this. Otherwise, if no fault of the tenant intervenes and what has been said is not observed, the sale will indeed be null, as held in the cited place, and is clear enough in itself: because a transfer made by the authority of a judge can in no way prejudice the right of the owner. The tenant, however, does not fall into forfeiture: since he committed no fault, he should not sustain the punishment.

These all likewise have a place when the leasehold property is given in payment to a creditor, whether by the tenant himself or by a judge. For the owner is indeed [affected], and he has the right of first refusal <term>ius praelationis</term> <note>the legal right of a landlord to buy back the leasehold by matching the price offered by another</note> for the same price, assisting in that place of the debtor to the creditor himself; and the transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>a fee paid to the landlord upon the transfer of a lease, usually a percentage of the price</note> must be paid to him if he does not want the property for the same price. Thus Gregorio López [affirms] above.

<margin>23</margin> When the leasehold right is sold, whether to the owner himself or to anyone else, the sales tax <term>alcavala</term> <note>a common tax on sales in Spain and its territories</note> is owed: because that is a true sale, and it is not against the leasehold right, from which the tax is not owed, as Lassarte (on the tithe of sales, chapter 1, number 42) rightly asserts against Menchaca. These things regarding the second and fifth assertions are at the beginning of this disputation.

<margin>24</margin> But then indeed—namely, that when the leasehold right and improvements <term>meliorationes</term> <note>investments or physical upgrades made to the land by the tenant</note> are sold to someone who is not the owner—a transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> is owed to the owner. This is the fiftieth part of the price by Common Law and the law of Castile, and the fortieth part by Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, if at the beginning, when the leasehold contract was celebrated, nothing else was deducted in the pact. This is held in the last law, section "and lest" <note>original: "§. & ne."</note>, of the Code on the Law of Emphyteusis; the last law, title 8, part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]; and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 64, at the beginning. Although in Portugal, when

<column-break/>

the leasehold is Ecclesiastical, the payment of the transfer fee should be according to Common Law, and not the Portuguese Ordinances; because in Ecclesiastical leaseholds the Portuguese Ordinances do not have a place, but rather Canon Law. And by Canon Law, when nothing is found disposed regarding something, one must stand by the disposition of the common Civil Law; nevertheless, a custom has been prescribed in that Kingdom that only the fortieth part be paid, and therefore that custom must be stood by.

Moreover, the transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> is not only to be paid on the price of the leasehold right, but also on the price of the improvements, as is quite clearly held in the last law of the Code on the Law of Emphyteusis and other cited laws. The reason is that the owner also acquired the direct ownership <term>dominium directum</term> <note>the ultimate legal title to the land, as opposed to the 'useful' right of the tenant</note> of the improvements, because they adhere to the leasehold estate itself.

The new tenant must pay the transfer fee: as the gloss on the word "to receive" <note>original: "accipere"</note> in the last law of the Code on the Law of Emphyteusis, and Gregorio López on the last law, title 8, part 5, on the words "he should not take" <note>original: "noli deue tomar"</note>, Giulio Claro on the word "emphyteusis" question 24, number 4, and others whom they cite, affirm. The reason is that it is paid for the new investiture and the placing into possession, which must be done by the owner, as the last law of the Code on the Law of Emphyteusis quite openly teaches; and Giulio Claro (cited above, numbers 2 and 3), Alvaro Valasco (on the Law of Emphyteusis, question 9, number 4), and others whom they cite, affirm this.

And for this reason, when the leasehold is sold to the owner, the transfer fee is not paid to him, but he must hand over the entire price that others offer for it: as the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, title 64, teach, and Sulla and others whom he refers to affirm. I believe, however, it is received by usage in Spain that the seller of the leasehold pays the transfer fee from the price he agreed upon with the new tenant.

If the owner departs from life, with the ownership of the leasehold property bequeathed to one person and the right of use <term>usufructus</term> <note>the right to enjoy the fruits and profits of a property owned by another</note> from it bequeathed to another, the transfer fee must be paid to the usufructuary, and not to the owner. For although it is paid by reason of ownership, the fruit nonetheless belongs to the ownership: so says Sulla on the word "emphyteusis," question 22, and Giulio Claro in the same place, last number, with Giovanni Andrea Socius and the common opinion of the doctors which they cite. For this reason, if a son under paternal power <term>filiusfamilias</term> <note>a son still legally subject to his father's authority and property rights</note> is the owner, the transfer fee belongs to the father, as Sulla (question 22, cited) rightly affirms with others.

<margin>25</margin> Finally, whether the transfer fee is owed from a lease of ten years or more, if someone who has the property thus rented sells that right to another. Alvaro Valasco (on the Law of Emphyteusis, question 29, number 16) cites Covarruvias (2 *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 16, number 2) and Antonio Gómez (volume 2, *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 3, number 11) in the negative. However, they are not speaking of the transfer fee in particular, but Covarruvias, with Charles Dumoulin <note>original: "Carolo Molin."</note>, speaks of the penalty of forfeiture <term>commissum</term> due to leasing to another again for a long time without the owner's request; and Antonio Gómez speaks of the penalty established for leaseholds in general, and whether they apply to long-term lessors. However, I would say the same about the transfer fee.

And although, as to strict dispute, Alvaro Valasco's opinion is pleasing, it must be affirmed with the common opinion of the doctors that the transfer fee is owed and forfeiture is incurred: which
-> Caldas <-

# Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts #

Caldas, in *On the Renewal of Emphyteusis*, question 16, number 8, and Alvarus Valascus in the place cited, report and follow this, and the Portuguese Ordinances define it in Book 4, Title 64, at the beginning. For emphyteusis is truly that form of leasing <note>original: "locatio"</note>, as has often been said and shown above. I added to this sixth assertion that this amount must be paid as a transfer fee <term>laudemium</term> <note>A fee paid by a new tenant to the landlord when a long-term lease was transferred or sold, usually a percentage of the price</note> if, from the beginning when the leasehold contract was solemnized, nothing else was brought into the agreement.

For whatever was brought into the agreement at that time must be observed, whether it was that less should be paid, or nothing at all, or that it should be paid to the first tenant, or even that more should be paid. I have heard, however, that in Portugal—especially in that region between the Douro and Minho rivers—it is sometimes brought into the agreement that half of the price received for the leasehold right and improvements should be paid to the owner. This seems truly harsh, if not to say unjust, unless it is compensated for from elsewhere. Gaspar Monterroso, in his *Practice*, treatise 7, folio 235, handing down the form for drafting a leasehold instrument, says:

> and that in recognition of the lordship <note>original Spanish: "señorío"</note> you are obliged to pay us the twentieth, or tenth part of the price, that they give you for the said house. <note>original: "y que en reconoscimiento del señorío seais obligada a nos pagar la ueintena, o decima parte del precio, que por la dicha tal casa uos dieren."</note>

From these words, it is gathered that in the Kingdom of Castile, it is customary to enjoin in the leasehold instruments that a part be paid, sometimes a twentieth, sometimes a tenth part of the price.

The final assertion—namely, that all the aforesaid things are to be understood unless something else was agreed upon in the contract when it was first made—stands because those agreements must be upheld. This is held in the final law of the Code, *On the Right of Emphyteusis* <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de iur. emph."</note>. For it is specifically sanctioned regarding such a leasehold contract that the agreements placed within it should be upheld, even if they are contrary to those things established by law, provided nothing else is brought into the agreement, as is clear from that same law and the two preceding it, from the section "Indeed" <note>original: "§. adeo"</note> in the *Institutes* on leasing, and from the penultimate law of Title 8, Part 5. Therefore, in this contract more than any other, by the very disposition of the law, one may vary from those things otherwise handed down and sanctioned in law; a point noted in part by Gama in Decision 323, final number, and more clearly by Caldas in *On the Naming of Emphyteusis*, question 23, number 46, along with Rolandus à Valle and Baldus.

<margin>26</margin> From this it is gathered that if the lease is granted with the faculty that the tenant may sell it to whomever they wish, then they can sell it without requesting the owner's permission, as Julius Clarus says in the cited question 13, number 9. Nevertheless, the new tenant will be bound to pay the transfer fee, and before being put into possession, the owner must be notified of the sale so that he may put the new tenant into possession and receive the transfer fee, as Julius Clarus affirms in the section on emphyteusis, question 23, number 3, with others.

By this same reasoning, if a lease is granted to someone "and such persons," or "to whomever the tenant wishes," the nomination can be made without requesting the owner's permission. Likewise, if it is granted to someone "and to whomever he wishes to give it," he can confer it without the owner's faculty, as Julius Clarus affirms in the same place, number 7, with others; though Alvarus Valascus in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 18, calculation 28, asserts that the practice does not observe this, and the owner is required

<column-break/>

to put the nominated person into possession, or another to whom the lease is freely transferred.

Finally, regarding the things said in this disputation, it must be observed: just as one who falls into forfeiture <term>commissum</term> <note>the loss of the lease as a penalty</note> for unpaid rent is safe in conscience until the owner intends to execute the penalty—even though before the sentence is passed, the tenant is bound to submit to it simply because the owner executes the penalty, as was said in Disputation 453—so it must be said in this proposal. Because for this reason also, one falls into forfeiture by the very fact, yet it depends on whether the owner wishes to execute the penalty, as Julius Clarus says in the section on emphyteusis, question 13, number 2, with the gloss on the final law of the Code, *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, and the common opinion of the doctors.

Hence, the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 64, paragraph 1, rightly establish that the owner can compel the tenant in this event to recover the property so unduly alienated, and to persevere with him in the leasehold contract.

The things which were said in Disputation 453—whether the penalty of forfeiture can be intended by the heirs of the owner, and against the heirs of the tenant—also have their place in their own way regarding this other penalty of forfeiture.

Likewise, those things we examined in Disputation 455—namely, which improvements the tenant loses when falling into forfeiture to the owner, and from what point the fruits of the leasehold property belong to the owner—similarly have a place in the matter proposed.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the legal complexities of emphyteusis (long-term heritable leases). Following the discussion of transfer fees (laudemium), he now explores how these leases are handled when an original tenant dies and leaves multiple heirs, specifically comparing general Roman law (Common Law) with the specific statutes of the Kingdom of Portugal.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 459 ###

<margin>1</margin> For the sake of clarity, we must begin with these last two points. Under **Common Law** <note>The *ius commune*, the shared legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</note>, a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of contract where a tenant improves land in exchange for a low, fixed rent and the right to pass the lease to heirs</note> is a divisible thing. Therefore, co-heirs, or those participating in it in any other way, can divide it among themselves according to common law. Such is the common opinion, which is followed by Julius Clarus (Book 4, Opinions, § emphyteusis, q. 14), Alvarus Valascus (Consultation 53, no. 1, and *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, q. 38, no. 12), and Caldas (*On the Naming of Emphyteusis*, q. 24, no. 14). This is established from the laws *item praedia* (Digest, On the division of an inheritance) and *item videndum* (§ last, where it says "whether they be rights or bodies") (Digest, On the petition of inheritance). However, the Law in Portugal (Book 4 of the Ordinances, Title 77, penultimate paragraph) commands that the land be divided among heirs only by valuation, so that the lease remains whole and undivided in itself, falling to one person alone.

<margin>2</margin> Indeed, it adds: "Since property of this kind, according to the nature of the lease, should not be divided but ought to be possessed by one person only, we command that within six months of the death of the previous possessor, the lease be registered <note>original: "incapitarentur," or in Portuguese "se encabeçen"</note> in the name of one of the heirs upon whom all, or the majority, agree. That person shall pay the remaining co-heirs the valuation of their portions and pay the landowner the pension according to the form of the contract."

But if the majority of co-heirs do not agree on one person, they are commanded to sell those leased goods within those six months—having first notified the landowner to see if he wishes to buy them for the price they have found. The buyer then pays the pension to the owner, while the co-heirs divide the price among themselves according to their inherited shares. If, however, within those six months, they have neither registered the lease in one heir's name nor sold it, the law establishes that the lease is automatically forfeited <note>original: "devoluatur"</note> to the owner, falling into a state of seizure <term>commissum</term> <note>A legal penalty where the tenant loses the lease for failing to meet conditions</note>. Nevertheless, Gama (Decision 242, no. 3) argues that if the registration is done before a lawsuit is filed against them for that reason, they are freed from the penalty of forfeiture. You may read him on this.

Alvarus Valascus (question 38, cited above, no. 17) and with him Caldas (cited above) explain those words of the Ordinances—"since property of this kind according to the nature of the lease should not be divided"—as referring not to the nature the lease has in itself, but to the nature it has from the disposition of Portuguese law; for in itself and by common law, it could be divided.

However, I think the meaning is "according to the nature of the lease," that is, in a way *more suited* to the nature of the lease. It is as if the authors of those Ordinances wanted to say: "Since it is more suited to the nature of the lease that it be established as indivisible, we so decree." Indeed, it is more suited to the nature of the lease so that the pension <note>The annual rent paid to the landlord</note> is not divided and required from many people. This is what the same Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, Title 62, § 1) teach: for such division is troublesome, has many inconveniences, and is therefore to be avoided, as held in the Digest (On Transactions; On the division of an inheritance; and On the legacy of food and provisions).

<margin>3</margin> Observe, however, that although this is sanctioned in Portugal, I nevertheless learned while staying in that Kingdom that in the region between the Douro and Minho rivers, leases are indeed registered so that only one person must pay the whole pension and it is demanded from him alone; yet, because of the poverty of those people, it is an accepted custom for the heirs to divide the leased land among themselves, and for each to contribute their share of the pension to the one in whose name the lease is registered, so that he may pay the whole to the owner. Gama (Decision 242, no. 1 and 2) seems to assert that this is permitted in Portugal, even if the tenants are not poor, led by the reason that this does not prejudice the landowner regarding the payment of the pension.

<column-break/>

Alvarus Valascus (in the cited consultation, no. 3) says that even in the properties called *regengos* <note>Royal lands in Portugal</note>—from which a pension is paid to the King, even though the direct and useful ownership belongs to the possessors—he has seen it judged in Portugal that they should be divided among heirs by valuation and fall to one person alone, so that the pension would not have to be demanded from many to the detriment of the King or those to whom the King granted that right.

<margin>4</margin> <margin>Doubt / Decision</margin> In the same place, number 4, Alvarus Valascus asks whether the registration <term>incapitatio</term> in Portugal must be done before a judge. He answers in the negative, since the law does not require it. An exception is made if a minor is involved: because then, in that Kingdom, the presence of the specific Judge of Orphans is required, through whom the affairs of minors are handled (Ordinances, Book 1, Title 67, § 66). He says, however, that a judge’s decree is not required for that registration.

For although a division has the force of a sale (as he proves with many points), since the matter at hand is a necessary act because it is commanded by law, it does not need a judge’s decree. He uses the argument from the Digest (On the property of those under guardianship), where it says a creditor can exercise his right. Thus, even in the division of immovable property, a judge’s decree is not necessary when a minor is called to division by an adult; for then the act is necessary (Digest, On the property of those under guardianship, and Code, On the estates of minors).

Indeed, if one adult calls many minors to division, those so called can divide not only with him but also among themselves without a judge's decree. If, however, it is the minor who calls for the division, then it is invalid unless a judge's decree intervenes. Read Alvarus Valascus there.

In the same place, number 6, the same Alvarus Valascus asks whether, if heirs are appointed to unequal shares, the registration of the lease must still be done according to the majority vote of the heirs. He rightly responds (whatever others may have said) in the affirmative: for where the law does not distinguish or restrict, we ought not to distinguish or restrict.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>Doubt / Decision</margin> Indeed, this matter is clearly gathered from the Portuguese law itself, which establishes that when the majority of heirs do not agree, the lease is sold and the price divided according to how the heirs were appointed; in this law, heirs appointed to unequal shares are also included.

<margin>6</margin> Whether, however, the form passed down by the Portuguese Ordinance (cited § last) being omitted, it is lawful for a judge to adjudge the lease to the one who [holds] the larger part... <note>Text ends mid-sentence</note>

Unlike general Roman law, Portuguese law requires the lease to remain undivided and be registered under a single heir's name to ensure the landlord receives a single, consistent rent payment.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 461 ###

Mm Maius

...put him into possession and receive the **transfer fee** <term>laudemium</term> <note>A fee, often 2% of the value, paid to the landlord when a lease is transferred to a new tenant</note>. For everyone agrees that based on a contract of **exchange** <note>original: "permutationis"</note> of an emphyteutic property, the new tenant owes a transfer fee. Gregorio Lopez, in the place cited above, references a commentary on the law regarding the "transposing" of emphyteutic rights. He suggests that the tenant is required to notify the owner before the exchange, effectively treating an exchange as equal to a sale in all respects regarding the property in question. However, truly nothing of the sort can be gathered from that commentary; rather, the opposite is true. For the text where the commentary explains exchange only spoke of the new tenant's offering to the owner—so that the owner might approve him, invest him, put him into possession, and receive the transfer fee based on the valuation of the improvements and the lease itself into which he was being inducted, as will be clearly evident to anyone looking at that text.

Julius Clarus, in the place cited above along with Baldus and others, correctly affirms that if a contract is truly and in effect a **sale** of the emphyteutic property but is disguised <note>original: "palliatus"</note> under the name of an **exchange** or a **donation** so that the owner is deprived of his **right of first refusal** <term>iure praelationis</term>, such fraud does not prevent the owner from being able to exercise his legal right of preference. I do not know, however, why Julius Clarus hesitates in this event—namely, whether a tenant who thus alienates the emphyteutic right without consulting the owner falls into **forfeiture** <term>commissum</term> <note>The loss of the lease as a penalty for breaching the contract</note> of the property. It is quite clear that he does. Gregorio Lopez, following Panormitanus and Innocent, says that when an emphyteutic property is exchanged for another thing that the owner can equally provide—such as wheat, oil, wine, rams, etc.—the tenant is bound to notify the owner of the quantity offered in exchange before he completes the trade. He must observe everything that was said in Disputation 459 regarding the sale of a lease; otherwise, he falls into forfeiture.

And this opinion seems true, especially since the **Portuguese Ordinances** (Book 4, Title 64, at the beginning and § 1) establish that an exchange and a sale of a lease are to be treated exactly the same. These laws should be interpreted to mean that when the item for which the lease is exchanged is of a type that the owner can provide in kind—equally good and convenient for the tenant—we should not say that the ordinance departs irrationally from the common opinion of the doctors or the disposition of the common law. One thing must be noted: generally, when an emphyteutic property is exchanged for another real thing, a **double sales tax** <term>alcauala</term> <note>The Alcabala, a common tax on transactions in the Spanish and Portuguese empires</note> is owed, based on the valuation of the emphyteutic property (including improvements) and the valuation of the thing for which it is exchanged, as is clear from what was said regarding purchase, sale, and exchange.

<margin>Question 3</margin>
Furthermore, can a tenant lease the property for a **long term** <note>original: "ad łlongum tempus"</note> of ten years or more without consulting the owner? Many deny this, as cited and followed by Molina (Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, ch. 21), Julius Clarus (Book 4, Opinions, § emphyteusis, q. 19)—limiting this to where there is no contrary custom—Gregorio Lopez, Gama, and Caldas. Finally, Alvarus Valascus does not dare to depart from their opinion and defends it (*On the Right of Emphyteusis*, q. 29, no. 23). These doctors assert that if a tenant does the opposite, he falls into

<column-break/>

**forfeiture**. Nevertheless, the opposite is affirmed by Covarrubias, Pinellus, Molina (Book 3, ch. 20), and others. Their reasoning is that in "odious" matters <note>In legal terms, "odious" refers to penalties or burdens; the principle is that laws imposing penalties should be interpreted strictly and narrowly</note>—such as the incurring of a penalty of forfeiture—the term "**alienation**" <note>The transfer of property rights</note> ought to be taken strictly and properly. However, we approve of the former opinion. Firstly, because a long-term lease is an alienation of the emphyteutic property for a price; therefore, it cannot be done unless the lord is first consulted to see if he wishes to take the property for the same price for that same time. Secondly, and most importantly, because—as shown in Disputation 445 and following—a long-term lease is truly a form of emphyteusis itself and transfers **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile</term> <note>The right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to the 'direct ownership' held by the landlord</note>. A tenant cannot grant a sub-lease <note>original: "subemphyteuticare"</note> without the owner's consent; otherwise, he falls into forfeiture, as the common opinion teaches. This is followed by Julius Clarus, Alvarus Valascus (who affirms this is the practice), Molina, Silvester, and Caldas.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The reason is that to hand over a thing in emphyteusis is to alienate it, as held in the Code (*On things alienated*), and as shown below. A tenant cannot alienate the emphyteutic property without consulting the owner. As for the claim that in "odious" matters alienation must be taken strictly and properly, that is plainly false. If that were so, the penalty of forfeiture would only be incurred for the alienation of **direct ownership** <note>original: "dominij directi"</note>, which is the only form of "strict" alienation; but that is false. It is one thing to say that in odious matters alienation should be taken properly (by which logic a sale without delivery would not trigger forfeiture, because that is "improper" alienation); it is quite another to say it must be taken "strictly" to include only the transfer of direct title. Molina does not seem to have considered this distinction.

Although a tenant can neither grant the property as a leasehold to another nor lease it for a long term without the owner's consent, he can
<margin>4</margin>
nevertheless grant an **easement** <term>servitutem</term> <note>A right to use the land for a specific purpose, like a right of way</note> without necessarily consulting the owner. This is because such an easement expires with the death of the one who grants it, and therefore it brings no prejudice to the owner or the successor to the lease after the tenant's life. Thus, it expires if the one who grants it ceases to be the tenant before his death. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus, Molina, and Pinellus. The commentary on the Digest (regarding surfaces) affirms this, saying that granting such an easement is permissible by reason of the **useful ownership** which they hold in the emphyteutic property or the surface.
<margin>5</margin>
Indeed, this is clearly proven by the Book of Feuds, where this was clearly established regarding a **fief** <note>original: "feudo"</note>. In this matter, the argument holds from a fief to an emphyteusis. That a feudal vassal can grant an easement in feudal property in this manner is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Julius Clarus, Molina, and Pinellus.

<summary>This page discusses the legal penalties and fees associated with transferring or sub-leasing emphyteutic property, clarifying that exchanges (barter) and long-term sub-leases are treated as "alienations" that require the landlord's notification and consent to avoid forfeiture. It also notes that while a tenant cannot sub-lease without permission, they may grant temporary easements that expire upon their death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis by Luis de Molina regarding the rights of long-term tenants (emphyteutae) and feudal tenants to grant rights to others, specifically focusing on usufruct and donations.</meta>

->### Luis de Molina on Contracts ###<-

<margin>6</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>
A greater doubt arises: just as a **long-term tenant** <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>A tenant under a long-term, heritable lease known as emphyteusis</note> and a **feudal tenant** <term>feudatarius</term> <note>One who holds land in exchange for service or allegiance under a feudal lord</note> can grant other **servitudes** <note>Rights to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way</note> in the manner already explained, can they also grant a true **usufruct** <term>usufructus</term> <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the fruits and profits of another's property without destroying it</note>? This usufruct would similarly expire with their own life and would not prejudice the legal owner or the successor in the long-term lease or the fief. Molina, in Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 19, number 23, along with Bartolus and others whom he cites—although he mentions a commentary on Law 3 of the Digest regarding servitudes which does not actually discuss usufruct—and in chapter 20, number 6, he judges that a long-term tenant can grant a usufruct in that manner. However, in chapter 20, number 7, he denies this for a feudal tenant. 

But I believe it should be said, along with many others whom Aries Pinellus refers to in numbers 70 and 71, that they cannot grant a true usufruct. Otherwise, there would be a manifest contradiction among the doctors <note>Legal scholars and experts</note>, as many whom Aries Pinellus cites and follows rightly affirm. For indeed, a **usufructuary** <note>The person holding the right of usufruct</note> holds the **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile</term> <note>The right to the use and profits of a property, as opposed to "direct ownership" held by the landlord</note> of the thing they enjoy, as was seen in Disputation 3. 

While a long-term tenant and a feudal tenant may grant other servitudes on the leased or feudal property for the time they themselves are the tenants (during which no ownership of the property passes to those who receive the rights), they cannot grant a servitude through which the useful ownership itself is transferred, which is what a true usufruct is. This is because to do so would be to **alienate** <note>To transfer ownership to another</note> their own useful ownership, at least for the duration of their life, which is forbidden to a long-term tenant without the legal owner's consent. And this is precisely what Julius Clarus teaches under the word "fief," question 37, number 2. Nor do I see by what reasoning any distinction should be made in this part between a long-term tenant and a feudal tenant, as Molina and others do. 

Nevertheless, a long-term tenant or feudal tenant can, without seeking the owner's permission, grant to someone for the duration of their own tenancy the **benefit of usufruct** <note>The financial advantage or use of the property, rather than the legal status of usufructuary</note> by granting them the right to use and gather the fruits in the tenant’s place. This is not strictly a "usufruct." This is not for the reason Aries Pinellus suggests (that it depends on the life of the grantor), which Molina rightly challenges; for granting a usufruct for a set time does not destroy the nature of a usufruct. Rather, it is because it is of the nature of a usufruct to be the right of using and enjoying in one's **own name**. This does not apply to one who only has the right to the utility to be perceived in the **name of another**, as explained with the common opinion of the doctors at the end of Disputation 7. Furthermore, the useful ownership does not pass to the person to whom this kind of right to utility and benefit is granted, but remains with the long-term tenant, feudal tenant, or naked usufructuary, as is clear from what was said in that place. 

And it seems that many of the doctors who are cited for the contrary opinion are speaking of this "improper" usufruct, including Gregorio Lopez and Alexander in their commentary on the laws of the *Siete Partidas* <note>A 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>, where he says that Alexander gives this reason: because the long-term tenant does not transfer the useful ownership, nor his improvements, and therefore we are not in a case of prohibited alienation. Gregorio Lopez agrees with this same law. Molina also speaks of this type of usufruct in Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 20, number 11, quite 

<column-break/>

consistently with our doctrine here.

Hence I say, if a lease is made for a long term—not of the property itself, but of the benefit derived from it—by transferring the right to use and perceive the fruits in the name of the long-term tenant, and thus under the condition that it lasts only as long as the tenant lives, the contract is valid. The tenant does not lose the lease <note>original: "incidere in commissum," referring to the forfeiture of the lease for breach of contract</note> because of it. The reason is that granting a servitude or a benefit from the property while the tenant lives or the lease persists is equally valid whether it is done for free or for money or other profit, as is established from Disputation 7. A long-term tenant is not found to be prohibited from leasing their benefit, or the property in regards to their benefit, for many years any more than for a few years. Also, because this is not "sub-emphyteusis" <note>Granting a new long-term sub-lease</note> nor the granting of a lease, and thus not the granting of useful ownership. For sub-emphyteusis is a contract which by its nature does not end with the life of the tenant, nor even with the life of the owner; but the contract we are speaking of ends with the tenant’s life, because it is nothing other than the right of perceiving fruits in the place and name of that tenant. Indeed, if the tenant were to lose the lease, whether by forfeiture or another cause, the contract we are speaking of would end for that same reason.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>

Whether a long-term tenant can **donate** the property and its improvements to whomever they wish without the owner's consent. The common opinion of the scholars—which Julius Clarus, Sylvester, and Gregorio Lopez follow—is that the tenant can donate it without seeking the owner's permission. Since there is no sale price or other compensation involved here, there is no reason why the owner should be preferred <note>The owner usually has a "right of first refusal" to buy back the lease if it is being sold</note> if the tenant wishes to give it away. The tenant is not bound to grant the property to the owner for free rather than to someone else. Therefore, there is no need for the owner to be pre-consulted, as must be done when the property is sold and sometimes when it is exchanged. 

However, the donation must be made saving the rights of the owner, so that only the useful ownership is donated. Likewise, the recipient of the gift <note>original: "donatarius"</note> must not be put into possession of the property by the donating tenant, but must be introduced through the owner. The owner must be notified and requested to put the new tenant into possession. Upon this notification, the owner will see whether the new tenant is a suitable person, or whether he has any legitimate objection and does not wish to approve him for the lease or admit him to the formal investiture and possession. And I understand the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 64, at the beginning, to be speaking of this notification when they say:
>And in the case that [the tenant] wishes to donate it, or give it as a dowry, they shall nonetheless make it known to the landlord, to see if he has any legitimate objection.< <note>original: "Eno caso que a quiser doar, ou dotar, o fara toda via saber ao senhorio, para ver si tem algum legitimo embargo."</note>

Molina concludes that while they cannot transfer "useful ownership" without consent, they can lease out the benefits of the land and donate the lease, provided the landlord is notified to vet the new tenant.</summary>

Second Treatise, Disputation 461. | Page 547

If the **long-term tenant** <term>emphyteuta</term> <note>A tenant who holds a heritable, long-term lease known as emphyteusis</note> should omit any of these requirements, they fall into **forfeiture** <term>commissum</term> <note>original: "incidet in commissum"; the legal loss of the lease as a penalty for breaching the contract</note>, as Giulio Claro and Silvestro affirm in the citations above. This is consistent enough with the final law of the Code <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de iure emph."; referring to the Codex of Justinian regarding the rights of emphyteusis</note> and the Portuguese Ordinances mentioned above, in conjunction with section 1. (Though Alvaro Valasco, in his work *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 18, at the end of number 28, says that practice does not observe this, and it is not customary for the owner to be required to formally put the person—into whom the property is freely transferred—into possession.) However, I believe it is false what Giulio Claro and Silvestro affirm above: namely, that after such a notification, one must wait two months for the owner to see if they wish to grant **investiture** <term>investitura</term> <note>The formal legal act of admitting a new tenant to the property</note> to the new tenant.

Indeed, the final law of the Code regarding the right of emphyteusis only grants that period of time when the property is being sold—and sometimes, for the same reason, when it is exchanged—so that the owner may deliberate whether they wish to buy the property for the same price and prepare the funds. But this does not apply when the owner is only burdened with granting investiture and admitting the new tenant to possession, as is the case when the property is alienated under other titles. This is quite clear to anyone looking at that law. Therefore, if the owner responds during a sale that they do not wish to buy the property at that price, it can be sold to another immediately. After the sale, it will not be necessary to wait two months for investiture, but only a reasonable amount of time for the owner to determine if the new tenant is a fit person or if there is a legitimate objection to be made.

<margin>8</margin> Furthermore, when the property is given as a gift, a **transfer fee** <term>laudemium</term> <note>A payment made to the landlord by a tenant upon the transfer of the lease to a new person</note> is owed to the owner for the investiture based on its valuation. This is clearly established from the final law of the Code on the right of emphyteusis and is affirmed by the consensus of the legal experts whom we have cited and followed. In the Kingdom of Portugal, however, this fee is not owed in that event, but only when the property is sold or exchanged. I believe the same is observed in practice in this Kingdom of Castile, and by the consensus of the form of the emphyteutic contract which Gaspar Monterroso provides in his *Practice*, treatise 7, folio 135.

<margin>9</margin> Regarding a **dowry** <term>dos</term>, according to the **Common Law** <term>ius commune</term> <note>The general legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</note>, Bartolus, Jason, and others followed by Silvestro and Gama, judge that if the lease is given as a dowry to a daughter (even if it is appraised) or as a marriage gift to a son, it is not necessary to notify the owner, nor must a transfer fee be paid. It is otherwise if it is given as a dowry to a stranger; in that case, the owner must be notified and the fee paid. However, Portuguese law (Book 4, Ordinance title 64) orders that the owner be notified whenever the property is given as a dowry; otherwise, forfeiture is incurred.

<margin>10</margin> Nevertheless, regarding property given as a dowry, the law generally commands there that a transfer fee should not be paid. Gama, in the cited decision, says that if the tenant is a Church, it is not necessary in Portugal to notify the owner when the property is given as a dowry for a daughter <note>Likely referring to the family of a tenant on Church-owned land or specific clerical legal structures</note>. This is because cases regarding Ecclesiastical emphyteusis in that Kingdom must be judged according to Common Law, not according to the Portuguese Ordinances, as the Ordinances themselves prescribe. This was judged to be the case in that Kingdom,

<column-break/>

the Portuguese Ordinance notwithstanding, which establishes that the owner must be notified or forfeiture is incurred. When, however, the lease is not Ecclesiastical, Gama attempts to explain the Portuguese Ordinance according to the received opinion of Common Law: that it should be understood as applying when the property is given as a dowry to a stranger. Yet, in Decision 283, he leans more toward the view that the Portuguese Ordinance should be understood to require notification of the owner even for a dowry given by parents to a daughter, or else forfeiture is incurred.

<margin>11</margin> Regarding **succession** in the property by title of heir, or legacy, or by virtue of a **nomination** <note>The right to name a successor to the lease</note> granted to the tenant in the original contract, I judge that it is neither necessary to notify the owner, nor is a transfer fee owed for that succession. Alvaro Valasco and others agree. The reason is that an emphyteutic contract, by its very nature, passes to heirs, even if it is only for ten years or more. Therefore, to put this into execution, no new permission or notification of the owner is required. The same applies to a **legacy** <term>legatum</term> <note>A specific gift of property left in a will</note>, because in this regard, a legacy is like the appointment of an heir. For this reason, Gregorio Lopez correctly says that if a lease is granted so that it can pass to any heirs, the term "heir" also includes a legatee.

This is not hindered by the fact that if the heir, legatee, or nominee is an unsuitable person, the owner can object. This is not to the effect that a forfeiture is declared, but only to compel them to alienate the lease to someone else within a certain time. This is the custom when a lease falls by succession to a monastery or to a person less suitable than the previous tenant. Hence, in the final law of the Code and the Portuguese Ordinances, no mention is made of succession by right of inheritance or legacy, but only of transfers by "contract" (taking that term broadly to include gifts and dowries), as distinguished from a "last will."

Thus, the rules established regarding transfer fees or notifying the owner only apply to the transfer of improvements and the leasehold rights by contract, not to the succession of the tenant upon death while the contract still persists. By this reasoning, the confusing and varied theories offered by some regarding succession through a last will or **intestacy** <note>Dying without a will</note> are resolved, while many others have remained silent on these questions, perhaps because

12. Finally, as for the **mortgage** <term>hypotheca</term>, although the tenant is prohibited from transferring improvements and the emphyteutic right to another through a contract (broadly speaking) without the owner's consent in the ways explained so far, they are nonetheless not prohibited from subjecting those same things to mortgage and pledge, provided it is without prejudice to the owner. This is established by law <note>original: "l. iutor. §. vlt. & l. sanè. ff. de pign. act." refers to the Digest of Justinian regarding the action of pledges.</note> and the common opinion of the doctors of law confirms this, as cited and followed by Giulio Claro <note>A prominent 16th-century Italian jurist.</note> and Valasco. From this, Giulio Claro rightly infers that if a tenant subjects their goods to a mortgage, they are also deemed to have mortgaged the emphyteutic right and the improvements.

### To whom the growth of emphyteutic property and the acquired easements belong.

## DISPUTATION 462.

-> SUMMARY <-

1 *To whom the growth in emphyteutic and even feudal property belongs.*
2 *Easements acquired by the tenant or vassal belong to the owner.*
3 *Otherwise if they were acquired for a price (onerous title). no. 3.*

1. In Disputation 57, it was said that growth—whether obvious or gradual—acquired by **alluvion** <term>alluvio</term> <note>The gradual deposit of soil by a river which increases the size of a piece of land.</note> in emphyteutic property belongs to the owner regarding the **direct ownership** <term>dominium directum</term>, and to the tenant regarding the **beneficial use** <term>dominium utile</term>, but only for as long as the lease continues, according to the more probable opinion. However, once the lease is finished, it belongs by full right to the owner along with the property itself to which it was added. Thus, nothing is to be paid to the tenant for such growth, as affirmed by Alvaro Valasco, Charles Dumoulin, and others. Giulio Claro, however, refers to what he teaches regarding **fiefs** <term>feudum</term>, where he considers our opinion more consistent with equity, though he leaves it for further thought. Regarding fiefs, we have said (citing Valasco and Gregorio López) that growth in feudal property belongs to the owner. In Castile, Law 30, Title 28, Part 3, decrees that only obvious growth belongs fully to the owner, while gradual growth, as long as the fief continues, belongs to the vassal regarding beneficial ownership. Read what has been said, and also

<column-break/>

Disputation 454, which states that because of such increases or decreases in emphyteutic property, the **rent** <term>pensio</term> is neither to be increased nor decreased; the same applies to the service owed for feudal property.

2. Regarding **easements** <term>servitutes</term> <note>Rights to use another's land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way or water access.</note>, Giulio Claro says that the common opinion is that easements which a tenant or vassal has acquired for the benefit of the emphyteutic or feudal property at a price are added to the property and follow it. Therefore, when the lease or fief ends, they belong to the owner and not to the tenant, the vassal, or their heirs. Alvaro Valasco asserts the same. However, purchased easements, or those acquired through other costly means, are compared to **improvements** <term>melioramenta</term>. Consequently, the price that was paid for them, or their appraised value, must be paid back—whichever the owner prefers—if the lease or fief ends without the fault of the tenant or vassal, according to what will be said in the following disputation. Read what is said there regarding easements acquired through gift (lucrative title). If, however, the lease or fief ends through the fault of the tenant or vassal, the same must be said as was said regarding other improvements in Disputation 455. This is according to Valasco and Dumoulin.

Regarding improvements, when a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of lease where the tenant has a permanent or very long-term right to use the land, provided they pay an annual fee and improve the property.</note> ends through the fault of the tenant, it was discussed in Disputation 45. However, when it ends without their fault, the following conclusions are to be established.

1 The first conclusion: That improvements made by the tenant out of the necessity of the agreement—arising from a special pact, such as being bound to build a house, plant a vineyard, insert a certain number of plants, or do some other specific thing on the leased property—belong by full right to the owner when the lease ends. The owner is not bound to pay anything for them. This is because they were made by the necessity of the contract as a "part of the price" along with the annual **rent** <term>pensio</term>. For this reason, a far lower rent is imposed from the beginning than would otherwise have been charged. Therefore, since such improvements are owed by the tenant by virtue of the contract (to the point that if they had not made them, the owner could compel them to do so or pay the value of the interest, beyond the restitution of the property), it follows that the owner is not bound to pay anything for them. So hold Alvarez Valasco, Arias Pinellus, Caldas, Gama, and many others whom they cite. The same would apply if the tenant were not bound to make specific improvements, but a pact was added stating that, upon the end of the lease, whatever improvements are found on the property belong to the **direct lord** <term>dominus directus</term> <note>The legal owner of the land, as opposed to the tenant who holds the "useful" ownership.</note> without any compensation. This is the view of Jason, Batista, Valasco, and Gama; Pinellus does not disagree. The law <note>original: "l. 24. tit. 8. par. 5." referring to the Siete Partidas, a major Spanish legal code.</note> affirms the same regarding improvements similarly made by a **sharecropper** <term>colonus</term>.

2 This can also be confirmed because pacts included in an emphyteutic contract must be observed if their injustice is not evident,

<column-break/>

as held in the Code of Justinian and the Institutes. In such a pact, injustice will generally not be evident. This is especially true because, when the property is given under such a pact, it is understood that improvements are to be made for the sake of the profit the tenant will derive from them—such as planting a vineyard in a suitable place, or an olive grove, or bringing forest land under cultivation. To ensure these improvements belong to the owner without repayment at the end of the lease, the rent that would otherwise have been imposed for the future is usually reduced. 

However, if a pact is added stating that the tenant is bound to "keep the property improved," or that the property should "revert freely to the owner with the improvements found therein," the improvements would nonetheless have to be paid to the tenant in the manner we will describe below. This is because those former words signify nothing other than the purpose for which the emphyteutic contract was originally invented, which does not prevent the improvements from being paid for, despite what Gregorio Lopez and Baldus have said to the contrary. The latter words (that the property "reverts freely") mean either that the improvements are not to be removed from the property (as Valasco argues) or that no "renewal" of the lease is sought because of the improvements, but rather the property and improvements revert to the owner—which, as Gama says, also does not prevent the improvements from being paid for. 

Furthermore, such general clauses are usually added by **notaries** <term>tabelliones</term> without a specific agreement between the owner and tenant that the improvements should belong to the owner without compensation. In cases of doubt, no one is presumed to intend to give a gift, nor should an interpretation be made that someone intended to donate. Valasco, Pinellus, and Gama report this. Gama notes that regarding those latter words, he had seen a judgment in favor of the tenant. Although he adds that he later saw a judgment by both senates in favor of the owner, this was not so much out of equity as out of the broadness of the words, which can be interpreted to mean the property reverts "free" of the obligation to pay any compensation for them.

3 Second conclusion. In other circumstances, improvements made to the leased property belong to the tenant and their heirs (even outside heirs) when the lease ends. This is not in terms of legal ownership (for they follow the title of the property), but in terms of their **appraised value** <term>aestimatio</term>. This holds whether the lease is secular or Ecclesiastical. This is the common opinion of the doctors of law, following the Digest and the feudal laws, which define the same for a **fief** <term>feudum</term>. This is followed by Valasco, Pinellus, Gama, Giulio Claro, and Caldas. It is confirmed because:

4 A **usufructuary** <term>vsufructuarius</term> <note>Someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property belonging to another.</note> recovers the improvements they made to the property they enjoy, as the gloss on the Digest affirms; and a sharecropper recovers improvements made to the rented property.

It distinguishes between improvements required by contract (which usually belong to the landlord) and those made voluntarily (for which the tenant is typically entitled to compensation for the value added).</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

The aforementioned conclusion remains true even if the improvements were made from the fruits of the property held under a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A permanent or long-term lease where the tenant is obligated to improve the land in exchange for a low annual rent.</note> or a **feudal grant**; for the fruits are the property of the tenant or the vassal. This is the opinion of Alvaro Valasco in the cited passage, along with Paris de Puteo, and it is a most well-known principle in itself. Likewise, it holds true even if the improvements were made by the labor and industry of the tenant or vassal; for they shall receive not only the expenses they incurred along with others in improving the property, but also the price of their own labor and industry in the event they incurred such costs. This should be understood according to what we will add below. This is the view held by Papinian and others, as cited by Arias Pinel. It also holds true if the property was improved by a friend for the sake of the tenant, or by a **good-faith possessor** <note>Someone who occupies land believing they have a legal right to it, even if their title is technically flawed.</note> to whom the tenant is bound to pay. This follows the laws regarding mandates and the legal principles noted by Alvaro Valasco at the end of his tenth point.

<margin>5</margin>
Furthermore, note that in the matter proposed, the "improvements" include **servitudes** <term>servitutes</term> <note>Legal rights to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way or water access.</note> acquired for the leased property through payment, as was discussed in the preceding dispute. This even applies to those acquired for free if they were donated or bequeathed to the tenant; for the value of these rights belongs to the tenant, just as things donated to them would. However, regarding rights acquired through **prescription** <note>Gaining a legal right or title through long-term, uninterrupted use.</note>, the same cannot be said; since these are prescribed to the leased property itself as something owed to it, and not to the tenant—except by reason of the property, which belongs simply to the owner—they belong by full right to the ownership. Moreover, necessary expenses made by the tenant on the property, if they are not of the type that the tenant is legally bound to perform at their own expense, must be paid to the tenant or their heirs along with the value of the improvements. This is the view of Jason and Alvaro, as cited above.

Even if the **direct owner** <term>dominus directus</term> <note>The ultimate legal owner of the land, who receives the annual rent from the long-term tenant.</note> forbids the tenant from making improvements and protests that he will not pay for any made in the future, the owner is nonetheless bound to pay for them to the tenant or their heirs when the lease ends. Indeed, the tenant or their heirs can use those improvements to petition for a renewal of the lease; the fact that the owner protested against them before they were made does not stand in the way. The reason is that a lease contract, from its very beginning, implies that the tenant can make improvements to the property, both for their own benefit and for the benefit of the owner.

Although it is decreed in the law regarding **unauthorized management** <term>negotiorum gestio</term> <note>When someone manages the affairs of another without being asked, often out of necessity or kindness.</note> that a manager should not recover expenses made after the owner’s contradiction and prohibition, that rule is understood to apply when the action depends on the owner’s will, as with a personal manager. It is different where it does not depend on his will, as in the present case after a lease contract has been signed. However, as noted by Alvaro Valasco following Boerio, if there is a delay in a lawsuit against the tenant—as if the lease no longer belongs to them—and the owner protests (either in court or outside of it) that the tenant should not make improvements, or because it is expected the lease will end soon (such as when the tenant is old, sickly, and the last person entitled to the lease), and the tenant makes them anyway, then no compensation is owed for improve-

<column-break/>

ments made after that protest. This is because a notification made according to the law prevents the recovery of expenses incurred after it, even in cases where expenses were previously allowed.

<margin>6</margin>
This, however, is to be understood as applying when the notification was made due to a pending lawsuit, provided the owner emerges victorious; for if the tenant were to win, there would be no reason why such improvements should not be paid to them or their heirs. Furthermore, he adds that if the tenant makes **excessive improvements** which they knew the direct owner would not be able to pay for at the time the lease ends, the owner is not then bound to pay for them. Instead, the tenant is permitted to remove what they can without damaging the property's prior state; but they must lose the rest. It is quite unjust for anyone to reap fruit from their own **deceit** <term>dolus</term>. Arias Pinel and Gama agree on this, even if they speak on different matters. Alvaro Valasco adds that he heard it was once judged in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> that in such an event, the owner should pay from the annual returns each year until the improvements are fully satisfied, according to the Portuguese Ordinances. However, he rightly adds that the Portuguese Ordinances speak of a very different matter in those sections. He does not see why an owner should be forced to pay for improvements made deceitfully by a tenant with the intention of forcibly retaining the property. When, however, the owner is unable to pay for improvements made by the tenant without any deceit, then the leased property can be left to the tenant so that they may satisfy themselves from the annual returns.

<margin>7</margin>
It must also be observed that if the expenses incurred for the improvement are **modest**, then the owner is not bound to them, even if they concern the permanent utility of the property. The reason is that this type of lease was invented so that the tenant would make the property better, and this also yields a benefit to the tenant; for this reason, if they make the property better at a modest cost, the owner is not bound to pay it, and he enjoys the improvements when the lease ends. This is established in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 77, Section 32, at the end, with the words: *This shall not be understood to include some small expenses and minor improvements* <note>original: "Esto nam se entenderão em algumas despesas e bemfeitorias pequenas"</note>. This is according to the common opinion of the doctors, also accepted in feudal law, which is followed by Alvaro Valasco, Arias Pinel, Gama, and Caldas. It is confirmed by the fact that under common law, a husband is not paid for modest expenses made on **dowry property**, but only for large ones.

<meta>catchword: no. ff.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property improvements (melioramenta) within the context of long-term leases (emphyteusis) and feudal grants. It specifically addresses how to categorize the magnitude of expenses and the rights of the owner (proprietarius) versus the tenant (emphyteuta) regarding the valuation and removal of those improvements.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 43, 6.

...according to the laws on expenses in dowry property <note>original: "no. ff. de impen. in reb. dotalib." referring to the Digest of Justinian.</note> and provides the legal reasoning, which would otherwise seem to pertain to the management of affairs <term>negotiorum gestorum</term> <note>A legal concept where one person manages the affairs of another without their express authority, often entitled to reimbursement for expenses.</note> rather than a judgment on dowry; this same reasoning applies similarly to long-term leases <term>emphyteusi</term> and feudal grants <term>feudo</term>.

<margin>Quest. 8</margin>
A doubt arises regarding which expenses, both in the proposed case and in dowry matters, should be called minor and which major. Alexander Tartagnus, whom Carolus Ruinus and a few others follow, calls those expenses "minor" which concern only the gathering of fruits during the time they are to be received by the tenant or husband, even if the cost is large in itself; conversely, they call those "major" which concern the permanent utility of the property, even if they are small in themselves.

<margin>Decis.</margin>
The doctors <note>Legal scholars or authorities.</note> commonly and rightly reject this opinion; these are cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco and Caldas in the passage above, Arias Pinel in Book 1 of the Code *on maternal goods*, part 2, number 70, and Molina in Book 1 *on primogeniture*, chapter 27, number 6. Instead, it is judged that it should be left to the discretion of a prudent judge, following the Gloss and Bartolus in the cited passages, to determine which expenses, when they concern the permanent utility of the property, should be considered minor so that the owner and wife are not held to pay them, taking into account the quantity and benefit of the property and other concurring circumstances. From this, Alvaro Valasco (number 15), following Paulus de Castro and others, infers that if, in the judgment of a prudent person, a non-major expense is made in bringing fallow lands into cultivation, considering the benefit that comes from it even to the tenant, the size of the estate being cultivated, and other circumstances, or in grafting and planting trees, the owner is not held to pay them. If, however, in the prudent person's judgment, the expense is considered major, the owner must be compelled to pay it.

<margin>Quest. 9</margin>
Many, whom Alvaro Valasco refers to in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 25, number 16, affirm that it is at the option of the direct lord <term>domini directi</term> <note>The superior owner who holds the legal title, as opposed to the tenant who has the right of use.</note> either to pay the valuation of the improvements or to allow them to be removed; since this seems to be established in chapter one, section *if a vassal* <note>original: "§. si vasallus"</note>, under the title *how a fief is ended*. They judge the same if, while the lease or fief continues, the tenant or vassal wished to remove the improvements; for the owner can prohibit it by paying their valuation. Baldus holds both views, even if at the beginning, when the lease contract was celebrated, it was agreed in a pact that the tenant could remove the improvements; because the owner could still prohibit it by paying their valuation.

However, the question is whether the valuation of the improvements should be paid according to the value they have in themselves before they are demolished and removed, or according to the value of only the demolished and removed material. Many, whom Alvaro Valasco refers to in the same place, judge that they should be paid only according to the value the material will have once demolished and removed, to the point that Baereus affirms this to be the more common opinion. However, Alvaro Valasco, with Charles Dumoulin <note>Original: "Catolo Molinzo", likely a typographical error for Carolus Molinaeus.</note>, rightly says that one should not stand by the decision in the section *if a vassal* cited above, compiled by certain followers of Barbatus <note>Referring to the legal commentator Andreas Barbatius.</note>; especially, he says, since it is a local law which should not be drawn into a general legal consequence.

Nor would the argument regarding what was decreed in feudal law on this matter have a place in a long-term lease, in which things are handed over for the purpose of improvement, which is not the case in a fief. Especially since the contrary seems to be...

<column-break/>

...taught and decreed in the last law of the Code *on the law of emphyteusis*, and in the chapter *it was possible* <note>original: "c. potuit"</note> on leases, law 28, title 8, part 5, and the Royal Ordinances <note>original: "Lustit. ordin." referring to the Spanish Royal Ordinances.</note>, book 4, title 64 (which I am surprised Alvaro Valasco and others did not bring forward). For before the lease is finished, the tenant is permitted to sell not only the right of the lease, but also the improvements he has in the leased property, as they persist in it, and according to the value they have thus, with the right of first refusal <term>iure praelationis</term> in buying them granted to the owner. Furthermore, imagine the improvements are very cheap mounds and ditches made in the leased property, on which much was spent and which make the leased property of great value; surely, if the owner were only held to pay how much they were worth destroyed, he would be held to pay nothing at all. Also, if the improvement consisted of a vineyard planted at great expense and utility, and nothing were to be paid except how much the uprooted vines were worth when removed from the estate, the tenant would receive very little.

<margin>Decis.</margin>
Therefore, it must be said first that always, in the event that the tenant or vassal wishes to remove the improvements, it is at the owner's option either to permit it or to prevent it by paying their value. Then it must be said that the tenant or his heirs, who succeed him in the right to the improvements, can always compel the owner to pay the value of the improvements as they exist in the leased property itself, or what was spent on them, whichever the owner prefers, as we will soon say. Thus Julius Clarus affirms it is received practice and should be done, not only in long-term leases but also in fiefs, in the 4th book of his *Sentences*, section *emphyteusis*, questions 10 and 25, in the addition joined to them, and section *feudum*, question 88, number two; and Alvaro Valasco follows the same in the place cited above with Charles Dumoulin, nor do I see why there should be any doubt about the matter.

<margin>10</margin>
But this must be observed: when the improvements are something separate and distinct from the leased or feudal property, even if they are joined to it and useful to it, then they neither accrue to the leased or feudal property, nor do they become leased or feudal property, and therefore the direct ownership of them does not belong to the owner of the leased or feudal property. Therefore, it is not at the option of the owner of the leased or feudal property to pay their valuation and take them for himself; rather, while the lease or fief still continues, the tenant or vassal can sell them to whomever he wishes. Examples include if the tenant buys a field adjacent to the leased field that is very useful to it, and from both they make one; for the field so joined is not leased property, nor is it to be counted among the improvements of which we speak, as Alvaro Valasco (number 17) rightly affirms with others. Likewise, if one holding a town in fief later buys jurisdiction <term>iurisdictionem</term> <note>The legal right to administer justice and exercise authority in a territory.</note> in it which he did not have, or acquires it by some other title, surely that jurisdiction, which is separable from the rest of the town's lordship, does not become feudal, nor is it calculated with the improvements of which we speak, as Julius Clarus rightly teaches with others in the cited question 88, last number.

<summary>This page discusses how to distinguish between major and minor improvements on leased land and the owner's obligation to reimburse the tenant. It argues that improvements should be valued based on their current state on the land rather than as scrap material, and clarifies that independent acquisitions like adjacent land or new jurisdictions do not automatically become part of the lease or fief.</summary>
