# Louis de Molina, On Contracts

However, to explain how improvements made to a property held under a long-term lease <term>emphyteutica</term> <note>A type of contract where a person enjoys the use of land for a long duration, often generations, in exchange for rent and improvements.</note> or a feudal grant should be valued and paid for, one must observe that the reasoning is quite different for a "good faith" possessor of another's property—who had no right to enjoy it—than for one who held "useful ownership" <term>dominium utile</term> <note>The right to the use and profits of a property, as opposed to the "direct ownership" held by the landlord.</note> or a right to enjoy it, even if the property was subject to being returned. In the first case, if a good-faith possessor of someone else's property made necessary improvements because the property would have perished or deteriorated without them, and the owner then claims the property back, the possessor may recover those necessary expenses. They do this by holding onto the property until paid, raising an "exception of fraud" <term>doli exceptionem</term> <note>A legal defense claiming that the owner is acting unfairly by taking the property back without paying for the work that saved it.</note> against the claiming owner unless the expenses are first settled. This is proven by the law *Domum* in the Code on the sale of property, where even a "bad faith" possessor is granted the right to seek repayment for such expenses through the judge's office, as was stated in Disputation 455. Therefore, it is with much greater reason that this should be granted to a good-faith possessor. The same is proven by the law *Si in area* at the end of the Digest on the recovery of undue payments, and by Law 44, Title 28, Part 3 <note>References to the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish law code.</note>. This is the common opinion of the legal scholars, which Gregory Lopez <note>A famous Spanish jurist (1496–1560) known for his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> and Antonio Gomez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> follow. In cases where such a good-faith possessor also recovers "useful expenses" <note>Costs that improve the value or profit of the property but were not strictly necessary to save it from ruin.</note>, they recover them by retaining the property and blocking the owner’s claim with the exception of fraud, refusing to give up the item until the expenses are paid.

<margin>12</margin>
However, Antonio Gomez (in the passage cited) says that for a good-faith possessor to recover expenses—whether necessary or useful—no remedy is available other than retaining the property and raising the exception of fraud, according to the cited laws. From this, he concludes that if the property in which the expenses were made has perished, or if the good-faith possessor has already handed it over to the owner, no remedy remains to recover the expenses. The reason for this is that because the person making such expenses believed they were working on their own property, they did not intend to obligate another person by their actions; therefore, the law granted that remedy only out of a kind of fairness <note>original: "ex aequitate quadam"</note>. He makes an exception for an heir or anyone else against whom a general judgment for many things is brought at once: for although that specific piece of inheritance might have perished or been handed over, the possessor can retain the remaining parts and raise the exception of fraud unless the expenses made on that other item are paid. This is because they made those expenses on it as a part of an inheritance they believed belonged to them. And this is what the law *Plane* in the Digest on claiming inheritance seems to teach regarding someone who possessed an inheritance in good faith, believing themselves to be the heir when they were not. Otherwise, the

<margin>13</margin>
rule is universally true: if someone possesses property in good faith and makes expenses on it as if it were their own, not intending to manage another's business, and that property perishes before they claim and recover the expenses, just as the property is lost to the owner, so too are the expenses lost to the one who made them. This teaching of Antonio

<column-break/>

Gomez is common, as Alvaro Valasco <note>A Portuguese jurist specializing in emphyteusis.</note> admits, citing many others for the same opinion. However, Paulus Castrensis <note>An influential 15th-century Italian jurist.</note>, seeing that a great inequality or rather an "iniquity" arises from this—whereby the owner of the property becomes enriched <term>locupletior fiat</term> by the existing improvements made in good faith by another at such great loss to that person—stated that he had advised in the legal councils <note>original: "vltra montes" (beyond the mountains, likely referring to legal practice in France/Italy)</note> that those expenses can be recovered out of equity <note>original: "ex aequitate"</note> by a legal action. Antonio Gomez, however, thinks this opinion should be rejected because, he says, that legal remedy is only granted when no other remedy exists. But surely, after a good-faith possessor has restored the property with its improvements out of ignorance or inadvertence, not realizing (due to the technicality of civil law rather than fairness) that the property should have been retained until the improvements were paid for, no other remedy is available to him except that based on the law of fairness. By the very act of handing it over, the benefit of the one who handed it over passes to another, in which case repayment is granted out of equity. Therefore, I do not see why the opinion of Paulus Castrensis should not be admitted on that basis. Indeed, Alvaro Valasco adds there that the Portuguese tribunals embrace the opinion of Paulus Castrensis because, in judging, they follow the "truth of the matter" rather than the technicality of civil law; he says Charles Dumoulin <note>A famous 16th-century French jurist known as Carolus Molinaeus.</note> and Balduinus follow the same opinion. He also adds that if the expense was necessary, it is not "uncivil" to say that even after the property is handed over, an action for recovery is available. I, however, believe it is available based on fairness <term>epicieia</term> <note>From the Greek 'epieikeia', meaning the correction of a law where it is defective due to its universality; legal equity.</note>, even for useful expenses. Since even a "bad faith" possessor can use the office of the judge to recover or remove expenses even after the property is returned, it must be judged all the more that the same remedy is available to a good-faith possessor after a return made out of ignorance. This is supported by the law *Plane* if read carefully. Gregory Lopez agrees with Antonio Gomez but makes an exception when the good-faith possessor made the expenses that the owner was bound to make and could have been compelled to do: in this case, the good-faith possessor may recover them in full. The same applies when the expenses were made because a judge compelled them. Gregory Lopez also adds that if the expenses are made with the intention of obligating the owner and managing their business <term>negotiorum gestorum</term>, even if the one making them is a bad-faith possessor, they can recover them after returning the property.

<margin>4</margin>
When a good-faith possessor has gathered some fruits <note>Profits, such as crops or rents.</note> from another's property in which they made necessary or useful expenses that they can reclaim, then the value of the fruits gathered must be deducted from the expenses. This is expressly held in the law *Sumptus* in the Digest on the sale of property.

<summary>Molina discusses the legal rights of individuals who improve property they do not own, arguing that while strict civil law requires retaining the property to get paid, "equity" (epieikeia) demands they be reimbursed even after the property is returned.</summary>

It specifically addresses the calculation of "fruits" (profits or produce) and the distinction between different types of legal holdings.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 463

...sold, and Law 41 and 44, Title 28, Part 3 <note>References to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Spanish legal code.</note>.

<margin>15</margin> Regarding the extent to which fruits <term>fructus</term> <note>In legal terms, "fruits" refers to the natural produce (like crops) or civil income (like rent) generated by a property.</note> should be valued, one should look to the law *Ab domino*, the final paragraph, joined with the following law in the Digest on claiming an inheritance <note>original: "l. à dñō. §. vlt. iuncta. l. sequenti ff. de peti. hær."</note>. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Antonio Gomez (in the cited number 2), Arias Pinel (on Law 2 of the Code regarding the rescinding of a sale), Gama (Decision 310), and the doctors to be cited shortly. However, there is a doubt as to whether this should be understood only regarding the fruits taken from the thing itself, excluding improvements, or also regarding the fruits perceived from the improvements themselves. Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a prominent Spanish jurist.</note> reports that it is the accepted practice in the courts of Castile that this includes fruits perceived from improvements. Conversely, Alvarus Valascus, along with many others he cites, rightly asserts in his work on the law of long-term leases <term>emphyteusis</term> that this is the accepted rule in the Portuguese courts. Indeed, equity does not allow a good-faith possessor to be forced to deduct the fruits they obtained from their own improvements from the expenses they incurred on someone else's property. Consequently, the same Covarruvias later inclined toward this opinion in the Zaragoza edition, referencing Valascus and noting that he knew of cases where the courts of Castile judged in the same way, citing Massa who asserted that the auditors of the Rota <note>The Roman Rota, the highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church.</note> judged a certain case in the same manner.

Therefore, when a good-faith possessor has incurred expenses that were not strictly necessary but merely useful, they may recover them in the manner described, deducting any fruits perceived as stated. They may recover either the total expenses incurred or only the amount by which the property was improved at the time the work was done. This choice is at the discretion of the owner of the property, who is only bound to pay whichever of these two amounts they prefer. This is held in the law *Adeo*, paragraph *Certe*, in the Digest on acquiring ownership, and more fully in the law *In fundo* in the Digest on claiming property. Alvarus Valascus affirms this, along with Bartolus and many others, who nearly all warn lawyers to be careful in their legal arguments <term>articulo</term> to state both that the property was improved and that it was made more valuable by the amount spent; both are required together, otherwise the owner is only required to pay the lesser amount.

<margin>16</margin> An exception to this rule occurs when the owner of the property is poor and neither intends to sell the property with its improvements immediately, nor has the means to pay for the improvements or expenses. In such a case, the good-faith possessor is only permitted to remove what they added to the property, provided they do not leave the property in a worse state than it was originally before the improvements; otherwise, they lose the right to remove them.

However, if in this situation the owner wishes to pay the possessor the value that those improvements would have *after* being removed, the possessor must be content with that price and cannot remove them. This is expressly stated in the law *In fundo* and in Law 41, Title 28, Part 3.

<margin>17</margin> But what if the person was a good-faith possessor at the beginning, but by the time they improved the property at their own expense, they were already acting in "bad faith" <term>mala fide</term> <note>Acting with the knowledge that the property belongs to someone else.</note>? In that case, the owner is not bound to pay them for either the expenses or the value of the improvements. The possessor is only permitted to take away what they added, if it can be done without damage to the property’s

<column-break/>

original state. If the owner offers to pay the estimated value of what the improvements would be worth after being removed, the possessor must be content with that valuation and cannot remove them, as was just said. This is gathered from the law *Domum* in the Code on the sale of property and other laws, and is decreed in Law 41, Title 28, Part 3. It is also the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez cites and follows. As for "voluntary" expenses <note>Luxurious or decorative improvements rather than functional ones.</note> or improvements, a good-faith possessor is only permitted to remove them without damage to the original state of the property, unless the owner wishes to pay their estimated value.

This is found in the law *Pro voluptuariis* in the Digest on expenses and decreed in Law 44, Title 28, Part 3, and affirmed by the common opinion. Regarding the "bad faith" possessor, this was discussed in Disputation 455.

In the second scenario proposed above—namely, when the person who incurred the expenses and improvements held "useful ownership" <term>dominium utile</term> <note>The right to use and profit from the land, typical of feudal or long-term lease arrangements.</note> of the property or a right to enjoy it, but the property was subject to return—this applies to long-term leaseholders <term>emphyteutæ</term>, feudal vassals, usufructuaries, and those holding property through a trust <term>fideicommissarius</term>. It also applies to cases where a contract is rescinded because the price was less or more than half the "just price" <term>iusti pretij</term> <note>A legal concept where a sale can be cancelled if the price was extremely unfair (laesio enormis).</note>. In these cases, the rules are not exactly the same. First, if the property was improved by the labor and industry of such a possessor, the value is not paid based on what it cost when the work was done, but based on its value at the time of restitution (the return of the property). If that value is less than what was spent, or if more was spent than the current value, the owner who receives the restitution chooses which to pay.

Alvarus Valascus affirms this with the common opinion, though he adds that by custom in Portugal, it is accepted that improvements are valued at the time of restitution, and that amount is paid regardless of whether it is more or less than the original expense. Antonio Gomez affirms the same with the common opinion of doctors, and confirms it from the laws on legacies. These laws prove that a person holding property in trust <term>fideicommissario</term> must be reimbursed for expenses incurred on the property subject to return.

Gama also affirms this, and more clearly in Decision 310. Nor is this contradicted by the Portuguese Law (Book 4, Title 77, Paragraph 32) regarding a son receiving a lease from his father while the father was alive. If the father made improvements, the son is held to bring those improvements to the partition with his brothers, either at their value at the time he received the lease or the amount the father spent, as the son prefers. This law, while agreeing with the general doctrine, does not contradict the rule regarding the time of valuation, as the reasoning for a partition among heirs is quite different from the restitution of property...

It highlights differences between Castilian and Portuguese legal practices regarding the valuation of "fruits" and improvements at the time of the property's return.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property restitution, specifically focusing on how a long-term leaseholder (emphyteuta) or a good-faith possessor should be compensated for improvements made to a property before they return it to the owner.</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina / On Contracts

...the ownership of a property held by long-term lease <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of contract where a person enjoys the use of land for a long period in exchange for a fee and improving the land.</note>, once the lease has ended. Indeed, a son is held to bring to the partition of assets the benefit which he received from his father out of his goods: however, he received improvements according to the state they were in at the time they were handed over to him, and accordingly he is ordered to bring their value at that time, or what the father had spent in making them. 

The reason why all those mentioned above should only receive the value of the improvements at the time when the property, which is subject to restitution, must be handed over, and not at the time they were made, is this: because those improvements were made on a thing that belonged to them—at least regarding the fruits and the use—and for their own benefit, not just for the benefit of the person to whom the property was to be restored. Therefore, equity did not demand that the person receiving the restitution should pay for what had perished or deteriorated through the passage of time (as usually happens) up to the point of restitution. Instead, they should pay only the value the improvements had at the time of restitution, or what was spent on them from the beginning, at the discretion of the person to whom restitution is made.

This is especially true since, as we shall add, the fruits <term>fructus</term> <note>The profits or produce, such as crops or rent, generated by the property.</note> which the person restoring the property perceived from the thing itself and from the improvements in the preceding time are not to be deducted; rather, they belong entirely to the former possessor. Furthermore, in estimating the expenses made on improvements, when the person to whom restitution is to be made chooses to pay those expenses rather than the value of the improvements at the time of restitution, the value of the labor and industry of the former possessor must also be estimated—whether he performed the work himself or through his sons, servants, or friends. This was stated above, following Pinel (on Law 2 of the Code regarding the rescinding of a sale, part 2, chapter 3, number 4), along with Panormitanus, Baldus, Aretinus, and others whom he cites.

Next, just as a good-faith possessor who had no right to the fruits of the thing possessed can retain the property until the expenses made on it are paid to him, and can raise a plea of fraud <term>exceptio doli mali</term> <note>A legal defense claiming the other party is acting in bad faith or unfairly.</note> against the one demanding it unless the expenses are paid: so too the leaseholder and the others of whom we are now speaking can retain the property to be restored until the improvements made on it are paid for. This is based on the same laws we cited for the first case, joined with the law *Qua ratione* at the beginning of the Digest on acquiring ownership of things <note>original: "ff. de acquiren. rer. dominio"</note>, as affirmed by Antonio Gomez (at the end of number 2) and Alvarus Valascus (on the law of long-term leases, question 25, number 22).

By this same reasoning, in Portuguese Law (Book 4, Title 7, § 1), a wife—though she does not otherwise remain in possession of certain things as the head of the household—nevertheless retains them if improvements were made in them, until the portion of the improvements that belongs to her is paid. Regarding this law, Alvarus Valascus rightly says (in the place cited above) that the word "possession" concerning such goods signifies "bare holding" or "retention." In the same place, following Gozadinus, he excellently adds that even if a person has been condemned by a final judgment to give up the leased property or another thing subject to restitution, they can nonetheless hinder the execution of the judgment by raising a plea regarding improvements, until their value is paid, according to the law *Nefenius*, the final paragraph of the Digest on judgments <note>original: "ff. de rei iud."</note>, and the Portuguese Code (Book 3, Title 71, § 18 at the end).

However, when it is not clear how great or of what

<column-break/>

<margin>18</margin> value the improvements are, the Portuguese Senate has rightfully been accustomed to decree that, after an oath is taken by the person to whom they are owed as to their value, that amount should be deposited by the party bound to pay. Thus, it is ordered that the execution of the judgment not be hindered, so that once the liquidation is later completed to determine the exact amount, they may be paid from the deposited money. In this way, both parties are looked after without detriment to either.

For equity does not allow the execution of a judgment regarding the handing over of a thing to be hindered for a long time by litigation over liquidating the value of improvements. So says Gama (Decision 4, number 3) and more fully Alvarus Valascus (cited above, number 23). He adds that when a sentence expressly states that the thing should not be handed over unless the improvements are paid first, a deposit is not sufficient, and one must not proceed to the execution of the sentence before the actual payment for the improvements. Following Paulus Castrensis, he also adds that if some things have been improved and others have not, one should proceed to execute the sentence regarding the things that were not improved, and this should not be hindered because of the improvements on the others. 

The doctors agree that when expenses or improvements are made on a thing by someone who knew it had to be restored to another, the recovery of those expenses and improvements is available not only through the retention of the thing and the plea of fraud, but also through an action based on contract, or even the "management of affairs" <term>negotiorum gestorum</term> <note>A legal concept where someone acts on behalf of another without their explicit permission, creating an obligation for reimbursement.</note>. This is because the person who made them intended by that very act to bind the other; therefore, even after the property has been handed over, the improvements can be demanded from the owner by the leaseholder and the others we are discussing. This is the opinion of Alvarus Valascus, Antonio Gomez, and Gama, and the common opinion of the doctors, based on the law *Divortio*, the paragraph *Impendia* <note>original: "ff. soluto matrimonio"</note> and other laws.

The leaseholder and the others of whom we now speak are not bound to deduct from the expenses and improvements the fruits <term>fructus</term> which they perceived from the thing to be restored. The reason is that those fruits belonged to them, and they made them their own by the very fact that they were gathered. This is similar to what was said in Disputation 349 regarding a buyer of a thing for more than half the just price, and even for less than half the price (at least regarding the fruits corresponding to that diminished price). Therefore, if a buyer for less than half the just price must deduct anything from such improvements, it is only the fruits corresponding to that part of the price which was missing to reach the limit of the lowest just price. Our principal assertion is affirmed by Bartolus (with the gloss on the law *Emptor* in the Digest on the sale of things), and by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Alvarus Valascus, Arias Pinel, Antonio Gomez (on Law 46 of Toro), Covarruvias (1 *Variar. Resol.* chapter 8), Gregorius Lopez (on Law 41, Title 28, Part 3), and Gama (Decision 310).

Alvarus Valascus (cited above, number 27), rightly following Tiraquellus, says that if the leaseholder and the others we are discussing, when the time for restitution arrives, retain the property in the meantime while the improvements are not paid to them, and...

...that they may perceive some fruits from the improvements, making those fruits their own; nor are they required to deduct the value of those fruits from the value of the improvements themselves. This is because they perceive such fruits from the improvements which—during the time that the value of those improvements has not yet been paid to them—rightfully belong to them. This is clearly gathered from the final law, the final paragraph, of the Digest <note>original: "l. vlt. §. vlt. ff. de fundo dotali"</note> regarding dotal land.

They may also take for themselves the use of the remaining fruits from the time the property is to be restored, and not deduct them from the value of the improvements. Alvaro Valasco seems to affirm this in the same place: because, he says, this proceeds in a judicial pledge, and he cites in confirmation the law beginning "Titia cum propter" in the Digest concerning payments. However, the opposite seems to be affirmed by that text and is proved by the final law, final paragraph, of the Digest regarding dotal land cited just above.

->How many types of alienation there are.<-

### DISPUTATION 464.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *In how many ways alienation may be understood.*
2 *What alienation includes when understood broadly.*
3 *How a pledge and a mortgage differ.*

**I**n order to explain who (especially within the Church) and to what extent one can grant a property in <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of contract where a person enjoys the use of land for a long period—often generations—in exchange for a fee and a commitment to improve the land.</note>, we must first explain what is included under the term "alienation," how many types of alienation there are, and a few things must be remembered regarding the explanation of the alienation of Church property and the formal requirements needed for it.

<margin>1</margin> Alienation is used in two ways. One, strictly and properly, for the act by which <term>dominium</term> <note>Legal ownership or "domain."</note> is transferred—specifically <term>dominium directum</term> <note>Direct or ultimate ownership, as opposed to the right to use the property.</note>. Such acts are usually sales, donations, exchanges, etc. It is understood this way in the Code <note>original: "leg. vnic. C. de fund. dotal."</note> regarding dotal land, the words of which are: *Alienation is the act by which ownership is transferred.* It is understood in the same way in the Fifth Partida <note>A famous 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note> and it agrees with the Digest concerning the meaning of words, where it is held that a sale—unless delivery follows by which ownership is transferred—is not properly and simply an "alienation." It is understood in another way more broadly.

<margin>2</margin> In this broad sense, anyone who is prohibited from "alienating" is not only forbidden from transferring the direct ownership, but also from granting the <term>dominium utile</term> <note>Beneficial ownership; the right to use and profit from the land while someone else holds the underlying title.</note> by granting it as a fief or in emphyteusis, or even by leasing it for ten years or more. They are also forbidden from handing the thing over as a <term>pignus</term> <note>A "pledge" or pawn; a physical object given to a creditor as security for a debt.</note> or a <term>hypotheca</term> <note>A mortgage; a legal claim on property as security for a debt without the creditor taking physical possession.</note>. This is because the thing thus obligated remains subject to the risk of being alienated (sold off) to satisfy the creditor if there is no other source from which the debt may be paid.

There is, however, a difference between a pledge and a mortgage, as Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> rightly affirms with others, and as we stated and showed through legal authorities at the end of Disputation 2. A mortgage <margin>3</margin> is a certain thing which is obligated to a creditor but is not handed over, remaining instead with the person who owes the debt. A pledge, however, is when the thing obligated to the creditor is handed over to them or to someone else in their place. Therefore, they only differ in whether the thing being used as security is handed over or not. Nevertheless, these terms are sometimes confused in the law, and one is taken to include

<column-break/>

the meaning of the other, as was said in Disputation 2. Whoever is prohibited from alienating in this latter (broad) sense is not only forbidden from the acts mentioned above, but also from establishing a "servitude" <note>A legal right for someone else to use the property in a specific way, such as a right of way.</note> upon the thing, even a personal servitude such as a <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it.</note>, as is expressly held in the law next to be cited. All these things—implying at the same time the first definition of the word—are decreed in the final law of the Code regarding things not to be alienated. There it is added: for whoever is prohibited from alienating, whether by law, by a testator, or by a contract, all the things mentioned are considered prohibited unless some of them were specifically permitted by the person making the prohibition. This agrees with the Seventh Partida.

->Which Ecclesiastical goods cannot be alienated without a legitimate cause and the formalities of which we shall speak below, and which may be validly alienated.<-

### DISPUTATION 465.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Which Church goods may be alienated without cause and formalities, and which may not.*
2 *The rights and names of debtors, under which category of "goods" they are included.*
3 *What is included under the name of "noble goods" which cannot be preserved by keeping them.*
4 *And what concerning those things which can be preserved by keeping them.*

**I**t should be observed that regarding the prohibition of alienating Church property, various laws were established over time, both civil and canonical.

Indeed, the Emperor Leo established the law beginning "jubemus" in the Code regarding the most sacred churches. Later, Justinian established a decree <note>original: "authenticum"</note> concerning things not to be alienated, and later another decree concerning alienation and emphyteusis. From these two places were taken the decrees inserted into the Code after the law "jubemus." One must always stand by the later laws if they disagree with the earlier ones by adding, granting, or changing anything. However, because this is an ecclesiastical matter and canon law <note>The internal legal system of the Catholic Church.</note> has provided sufficiently for it, it will not be necessary to rely on the dispositions of civil law, as Panormitanus and others have rightly noted—especially regarding the causes and formalities necessary for alienating. Consequently, it is enough to observe those formalities that are established by the sacred canons.

There is no one who doubts that the term "alienation" is taken broadly in this matter of Church property, which is a "favorable" area of law <note>In legal interpretation, a "favorable" matter is one interpreted broadly to protect the interests involved—in this case, protecting the Church's assets.</note>. This is clearly evident from the chapter "nulli" concerning not alienating Church property, and from the decree concerning not alienating, and from other laws.

To speak universally about this matter in this disputation, as we shall examine it more broadly in the following sections, and...

# Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

<margin>1</margin> **Ecclesiastical goods**, including both immovable property and precious movables that can be preserved by keeping them, cannot be alienated <note>The legal transfer of ownership, such as selling or giving away.</note> unless a just cause is present and certain forms and <term>solemnities</term> <note>Official legal formalities and procedures required by Canon Law.</note> are observed, which will be discussed in the following sections. However, movables that are not precious, or those that—even if precious—cannot be preserved by keeping them, do not require such a cause, nor the same form and solemnity, to be validly alienated. All of this, as well as the penalties established for those doing the opposite and whether an alienation performed otherwise is void, will become clear in what follows.

<margin>2</margin> Although rights to movable or immovable things, under the name of "debts," are indeed included under the category of "goods," they do not regularly fall under the name of "movable" or "immovable" goods; rather, they constitute a certain third genus of goods, distinct from both, as was explained in Disputations 68 and 301. However, when there is something that compels them to be included under the names of movables and immovables—either from the subject matter or the intention of the person disposing of them—they are understood to be included. In such cases, we added (along with Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in Canon Law.</note> in the chapter *Nulli*, regarding the non-alienation of Church property <note>original: "c. nulli, de reb. Eccl. non alienan."</note>, numbers 9 and 10; Bartolus; and others) that they should be considered included under the name of movable and immovable goods.

And so, regarding the matter at hand, Panormitanus says in the same place—and the common opinion of the doctors agrees—that they are included under the name of movables and immovables. This is because the laws, both Canon and Civil, speak universally of all Ecclesiastical goods, and they only prohibit the alienation of immovables and precious movables that can be preserved, unless there is due cause and the observation of certain solemnities as a matter of form. Thus, rights to immovable things—such as all debts involving immovable things, legal actions regarding those things, and all <term>servitudes</term> <note>Rights to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, like a right of way.</note>—are included here under the name of immovable goods.

It also follows that rights and revenues for a period of ten years or more, even if they are to be paid in movable things, are nonetheless included under the name of immovable things. Indeed, rights of this kind, because they are firm and stable, are counted with immovable things, as is clearly evident from the Clementine decree *Exivi de paradiso* <note>A famous 1312 decree by Pope Clement V regarding Franciscan poverty and Church property.</note> in the paragraph "tunic," regarding the meaning of words, and from other laws cited in the gloss on chapter 2, "On not alienating Church property," Book 6, at the word "rights," and as was said in Disputation 68. This is the reason why, in the alienation of Ecclesiastical <term>benefices</term> <note>A church office that provides an income to the holder.</note> and other rights for receiving annual revenues for ten years or more, the same causes and solemnities are required as are necessary in the alienation of immovable goods, as is established in chapter 1, "On not alienating Church property," and often elsewhere. It likewise follows that other rights to immovable things are counted with immovable things.

Finally, you should know that both immovable things (and those counted as immovables) and precious movable things that can be preserved, as well as the rights to such things, cannot be alienated by prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> without due cause and the form and solemnities prescribed for that purpose. Remaining movables, however, and the rights to them (unless they involve repeated installments for ten years or more), may be alienated without those causes and solemnities.

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> Under the name of movable goods "that cannot be preserved by keeping them"—according to the law *Lex quae* in the Code regarding the administration of wards, and other laws we cited in Disputation 224 in the paragraph on movables—Panormitanus says (along with a certain gloss on the cited chapter *Nulli*, numbers 8 and 11) that this includes not only fruits such as wheat, wine, oil, wool, lambs, and other revenues or produce, but also clothing, which grows older and more worn day by day, and similar items.

Among these are counted beasts of burden and <term>slaves</term> <note>original: "mancipia". In this legal context, it refers to unfree laborers. Molina distinguishes those "affixed" to the land (serfs) from movable ones.</note>, though not those who, in the ancient manner, were rural and as if fixed to the estates. Indeed, such unfree laborers are prohibited from being alienated by the cited chapter *Nulli* and in the *Authenticum* regarding not alienating property, in the paragraph "We therefore" <note>original: "§. nos igitur"</note>, and are counted with immovable things. Also counted with goods that cannot be preserved by keeping them is money intended for daily use, as Panormitanus rightly says in the cited place, number 11.

<margin>4</margin> However, under the name of "precious movable goods that can be preserved by keeping them," we understand gold and silver vessels, precious garments that are far from perishing and can be conveniently stored, gems, and similar things. You should also understand this to include a flock of sheep or goats, from whose fruits a monastery or Church is accustomed to receive profits and revenue. For although it would be lawful to sell rams, lambs, he-goats, and kids, it would nonetheless not be lawful to alienate the **entire flock** without the concurring causes and the observation of the form that must be observed in the alienation of precious things that can be preserved.

### DISPUTATION 466.

->SUMMARY.<-

<margin>1</margin> *Whether ecclesiastical goods can be mortgaged or granted in emphyteusis without the required cause and solemnities; also in number 3.*
<margin>2</margin> *Ecclesiastical goods can be subject to a mortgage in general, but not in particular.*

### Second Treatise, Disputation 4, Section 66

<margin>1</margin> To come to the alienation <note>The legal transfer of ownership or rights to another party.</note> of specific Ecclesiastical goods, we must address the first of the points proposed. It must be stated that no such goods can be specifically subjected to a **mortgage** <note>original: "hypothecæ"</note> unless there is a just cause and the forms and <term>solemnities</term> <note>Formal legal procedures required by Canon Law, such as obtaining consent from a superior or a council.</note> required for alienating Ecclesiastical goods are observed. With even greater reason, a good cannot be handed over as a **pledge** <note>original: "pignus"; a physical item given as security for a debt.</note> except in the same manner. This is held in the chapter *Nulli*, regarding the non-alienation of Church property <note>original: "c. nulli, de rebus Eccles. non alienand."</note>, and was decreed by Pope Paul II in the decree *Ambitiosæ* <note>A famous papal constitution from 1468 that strictly limited the sale or pledging of church assets.</note> under the penalty of automatic excommunication for both the one pledging the item and the one receiving it, as well as other penalties which will be discussed later.

I have said that it is not possible to specifically subject a good to a mortgage: because in the cited chapter *Nulli*, in agreement with the authentic text on non-alienation <note>original: "authenticū de non alienandis. §. nos igitur"</note>, only the mortgaging of something **in particular** is prohibited. From this, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a major canon lawyer.</note> rightly concludes—and others agree—
<margin>2</margin> that it is lawful for † prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> to obligate the goods of their Church **in general** under a title of mortgage without these formalities. This is because, in a general mortgage, individual items remain less burdened and less subject to being sold off. This is clearly hinted at in the cited chapter *Nulli*. And although Paul II in *Ambitiosæ* speaks of mortgages indistinctly and without restriction, he nevertheless excepts cases expressed by law, and thus does not contradict the common opinion of the doctors of law.

Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist.</note> agrees with all of this. However, he suggests that while a contract specifically mortgaging Church property without just cause is void, the penalties are not incurred until the item is actually handed over, since the "alienation" is not considered finished before then. I have great doubts about this teaching. The laws establish penalties for those who merely *subject* the items to a mortgage. Furthermore, if his view were true, even handing over a pledge would not be enough to trigger the penalties; one would have to wait until the pledge was sold to pay the debt.

Furthermore, if that opinion were accepted, one would have to say that legal penalties are only incurred for "alienation" in the strictest sense (where ownership is transferred). But the laws suggest the opposite. The penalties here are established for those who pledge or mortgage specific Church items because of the **danger** they are placed in—the risk that they must be sold and lost forever. Therefore, the act of mortgaging is completed the moment the item is obligated, even if it hasn't been sold yet.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding † **emphyteusis** <note>A type of long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent.</note>, it is clear enough that under the name of "alienation" in the context of Ecclesiastical goods, perpetual emphyteusis is included. Consequently, no Ecclesiastical goods can be granted in perpetual emphyteusis without a legitimate cause and the required formalities.

<column-break/>

This is gathered from the final law on the non-alienation of things <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de reb. alien. non alienā."</note>. It is also expressly stated in the chapter *Nulli* and the decree *Ambitiosæ*. The same penalty is established by Paul II for those handing over Church property in emphyteusis as for those alienating it in other ways.

<margin>4</margin> However, when a certain thing was accustomed from ancient times to be granted in emphyteusis (whether perpetual or not), Paul II allows it to be granted again in that same manner without new formalities. Yet, he restricts this by saying it must be for the **evident utility** of the Church or the pious place that holds the direct ownership. Other matters regarding this will be more conveniently discussed in the following three sections.

Regarding other types of alienation—such as gift, sale, exchange, and the like—it is well known from the cited places that these are prohibited without due cause and the proper formalities. Those who alienate Church goods without these requirements incur the established penalties.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>Question.</margin> Therefore, it only remains for us to examine whether the **leasing** <note>original: "locatio"</note> of these same goods for ten years or more—or even for the life of one or more persons—is lawful without the formalities required for alienation. Or is it unlawful, triggering the penalties for improper alienation? As shown previously in Disputation 445, such a lease transfers <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>original: "dominiū vtile"; the right to use and profit from the property, while the Church retains the "direct" title.</note> and is truly a form of emphyteusis. Therefore, there is no doubt: because these Ecclesiastical goods are prohibited from being alienated without just cause, they are also prohibited from being leased for a long term without the same cause and formalities. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Molina, Covarrubias, and Alvarez Valasco. It agrees with the chapter *Nulli*, where some versions read that the term "alienation" includes <gloss>leasing for a long time</gloss>, donation, sale, and perpetual emphyteusis.

This is even more clearly supported by the *Clementine* decrees <note>A collection of Canon Law issued by Pope Clement V.</note>, where it is forbidden to grant Ecclesiastical rights, revenues, or possessions for the life of a person or for a set time, even if money is received, unless the grant is for utility or necessity. The person granting it is automatically suspended from office. However, the same decree allows leasing for a "modest time." It should be noted that this specific decree only speaks of religious superiors (like priors); therefore, the penalty of suspension does not extend to others.

<summary>Molina explains that specific Church assets cannot be mortgaged, pledged, or leased long-term (emphyteusis) without strict legal "solemnities" and a just cause, as these actions are legally equivalent to selling the property. He distinguishes these from general mortgages on all Church property, which are often permitted more easily because they pose less immediate risk to specific sacred items.</summary>

<keywords>alienation, mortgage, pledge, emphyteusis, long-term lease, beneficial ownership, Canon Law, Pope Paul II, ecclesiastical property, legal formalities</keywords>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts #

<column-break/>

Furthermore, the final law of the Code regarding the non-alienation of others' property <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de reb. alien. non alienand."</note> agrees; it states that when the **alienation** of a thing is prohibited, the granting of its **usufruct** <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another.</note> is also understood to be prohibited. The only reason for this is that the granting of usufruct transfers <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to use and profit from property, as opposed to "direct ownership" (dominium directum) held by the title-holder.</note>. Therefore, since beneficial ownership is also transferred by a long-term lease, it follows that by the prohibition of alienating such Ecclesiastical property—unless for a just cause and observing a specific form—a long-term lease of the same is likewise understood to be prohibited. Add to this that it is truly a grant in **emphyteusis** <note>A type of contract where land is leased for a very long period or forever, provided the tenant improves it and pays a small rent.</note>, as we have shown extensively in Disputation 445; for this reason, it is considered prohibited under the name of 'prohibition of alienation' of those same things.

From this it is clear that it is a sin to lease Church property for the entire life of the lessor, unless it is under the condition that it ends within a ten-year period. Read what was said in the cited Disputation 445. Therefore, when Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in Canon Law.</note>—along with the second gloss on the final chapter of "Lest Prelates [delegate] their roles" <note>original: "c. vlt. ne Prælati vices suas"</note>—notes that a rector of a Church can lease the fruits for the entire time of his life, he understands this negatively: that is, not for a time *beyond* his life, as he explains himself in the following sections of the same chapter. For if the lease is made in his own name, as is regularly done, the successor is not bound to stand by the lease beyond the time of the previous lessor’s life, even if it was made for only a few years. However, he does not mean that a rector can lease in his own name, in a single lease or all at once, the fruits of the Church for the entire time of his life if his life lasts ten years: for he immediately adds that this is a sin and is done invalidly. This is because it would transfer beneficial ownership, which cannot be done without just cause and the required <term>solemnities</term> <note>The formal legal procedures and witnesses required by Church law to make a contract valid.</note>. Law 9, Title 17, Part 1, which hands down the same doctrine as Gregorio Lopez explains there, must be understood in the same way. Both Panormitanus and that law spoke before the <insert>Papal decree</insert> *Ambitiosæ*, which, as we shall see, reduced the time for leasing Church property to a three-year period.

One must observe that the **Synod of Trent** (Session 25, Chapter 11 on Reform) decreed that those leases of Church property made within the last thirty years for a long term are void, even if they were confirmed by Apostolic authority, if a provincial Synod (or those appointed by it) judges them to have been contracted to the damage of the Church and against Canonical sanctions.

Alvarez Valasco <note>A Spanish jurist.</note> and Arias Pinelo, along with many others they cite, believe that beneficial ownership is *not* transferred by a long-term lease, even if it is made for a hundred years, provided that a pact is added at the same time stating that beneficial ownership is not transferred, but remains with the lessor. They are led to this because such a pact is not against the substance of a lease, which does not inherently require that beneficial ownership be transferred. Therefore, if the pact is added, it is valid, and ownership is not transferred by a lease of any length. However, they add—along with Covarrubias, Baldus, and others—that if a thing were prohibited from being alienated (as Church property, <term>entailed estates</term> <note>original: "maioratum"; property that must stay within a family line and cannot be sold.</note>, and the property of minors are), then if it were leased for a long time, even if an express pact were added stating that beneficial ownership

<column-break/>

would not pass to the tenant, such a long-term lease must be considered an **alienation**. This is because, they say, the convenience of the fruits, when transferred for a long time, is held to be a true alienation in prohibited matters, specifically to avoid fraud.

More correctly, however, Molina, in his book 1 *On Primogeniture* <note>original: "de primog."</note>, distinguishes three possible outcomes in this matter. Either, he says, the property of an entailed estate or a church is leased simply for a long time; or it is leased for a long time not simply, but with a pact added that its beneficial ownership does not pass to the tenant; or finally, not the property itself, but only the **convenience** <note>The right to use or benefit from the property.</note> of the thing is leased for a long time or a hundred years. In the first case, he says, that lease is undoubtedly to be considered an alienation of the thing, since through it, as has been said, beneficial ownership is transferred. And in this, the cited doctors also agree. In the second case, however, he says the same thing must be said even if the thing were not prohibited from being alienated. In this, he disagrees with Alvarez Valasco, Pinelo, Covarrubias, and the other doctors they follow. They all think that when a thing is not prohibited from being alienated, it is not considered alienated by a long-term lease if a pact is added that the beneficial ownership does not pass to the tenant. 

Molina is best guided here: since a long-term lease—given the disposition of civil law—transfers beneficial ownership to the tenant and is therefore an alienation, it is only a "lease and hire" in name and by equivocation. In reality, it is simply **emphyteusis**, a contract distinct in kind from a lease, as shown in Disputation 445. Therefore, since pacts that are against the nature and substance of a contract (as established by civil law) have no strength or weight, it follows that the transfer of beneficial ownership cannot be prevented by such a pact in a long-term lease. It is just like if a thing were handed over in perpetual emphyteusis with a pact that beneficial ownership should not transfer; the authors we are arguing with would not allow that in perpetual emphyteusis. Clearly, their opinion arises from that other view of theirs: that a long-term lease is not emphyteusis, but a contract distinct from it and of the same kind as a short-term lease—an opinion we challenged in Disputation 445.

In the third case, however—when specifically a long-term lease or a hundred-year lease is made not of the thing itself, but only of its <note>dagger-like mark in text</note> **convenience**, or the thing regarding its convenience and the gathering of fruits in the name of the lessor—then as long as the right remains with the lessor, Molina rightly affirms that beneficial ownership is not transferred. No **real right** <note>A right over a physical thing (ius in re), rather than just a personal right against a person.</note> is acquired in the thing so leased, but only a personal obligation regarding the lease to receive fruits from it. And therefore, such a lease is not an alienation, nor is it considered prohibited, even if alienation is prohibited.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "tio," part of "alienatio."</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legal status of long-term leases for Church property, arguing that they typically count as "alienation" because they transfer beneficial ownership, making them subject to strict prohibitions. Molina critiques other jurists, asserting that long-term leases are essentially emphyteusis contracts and cannot be legally disguised as simple rentals through special clauses.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 466 ###

...of the thing which is so leased: therefore, for whatever time it is made, it expires when the right that the lessor had in that thing ceases, and the property passes freely to the person to whom it would have passed if it had not been leased. Just as that benefit—or the thing in respect to that benefit—can be leased for a long time, so too can that entire benefit be sold for a single price for the entire life of the person on whose life it depends, or for the entire time it depends on them. This is affirmed by many authors whom Molina <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600), a highly influential Spanish Jesuit priest and jurist.</note> cites in the same place. He testifies that he has often seen the entire benefit of a **majorat** <note>An entailed estate that passes to the eldest son and cannot be divided or sold.</note>—which, due to a crime committed by the holder, belonged to the royal treasury for the duration of that person's life—being sold, and likewise in other circumstances.

All these points are sufficiently established from what we said in Disputation 461, in the section "A greater doubt," joined with the following section. However, Molina says in number 25 (cited above) and the preceding number 24—along with Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a 14th-century legal scholar whose works were foundational to European law.</note> and others whom he cites in the gloss on the law regarding codicils <note>original: "gloss. l. codicillis. §. instituto. ff. de legat. 2."</note>—that if the matter is weighed correctly, the law speaks only of the **leasing** for one hundred years of the benefit of a thing that is prohibited from being alienated, but not of the leasing of the thing itself. This is despite the fact that many cite it as if it spoke of the leasing of the thing itself and commonly reject it in that sense. 

He also states that in a long-term lease, just as in a sale, no fraud is found in alienating only the **benefit** of a prohibited thing, since this is permitted by many laws, and because no fraud can be found in someone exercising their own right. Perhaps because in the leasing of an **Ecclesiastical benefice** <note>A church office that provides an income, such as a parish or a cathedral post.</note>, only the benefit is leased to the tenant—so that they receive the tithes belonging to the beneficiary in the name of the beneficiary, not their own—as was said in Disputation 7. Law 9, Title 17, Part 1 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note> asserted that a beneficiary can lease the benefice for their entire life without any explicit statement that only the benefit was being leased. This interpretation is followed by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish bishop and jurist.</note> in his *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 16, at the end of number 6, although we previously provided another sense of the same law along with Gregorio López.

Furthermore, the chapter *Vestra* regarding leases <note>A specific chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX, the main body of medieval Canon Law.</note>, when it declared that monasteries could lease **tithes** <note>A tenth part of agricultural produce or income, paid as a tax to support the Church.</note> to laypeople for certain periods, seems to have added a condition: that such a lease should not be seen to extend to a **fief** <note>Property held on condition of feudal service.</note> or to an **alienation**. Since the right to those tithes was perpetually annexed to the monastery and would not pass to anyone else in the monastery's place, laypeople could, over time, claim that the <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to use and profit from property while another holds the title.</note> of all those tithes belonged to them. As I will shortly add with Molina, that would in effect be an **alienation of Ecclesiastical property**.

Molina, in the place cited above at number 27, excellently observes that a prelate or beneficiary either leases what belongs to him for his own sustenance—such as his own benefice or a field annexed to it—or he leases things and revenues as an **administrator**, which belong not to him but to the Church, a hospital, or another pious place. He says that in the first case, a long-term lease (or one for the entire life of the lessor) of the benefit of that thing is lawful and valid without any formal ceremony, according to what has been said.

In the second case, however, he rightly says it is unlawful and void without a just cause and without the formal ceremonies required for **alienating Church property**. The reason, he says, is that in the first case, upon the death of the lessor

<column-break/>

or if they do not continue in that benefice, the lease immediately expires, as has been said and as Covarruvias rightly resolves in *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 15, number 6. In the second case, however, the lease does not expire upon the death of the lessor or the termination of their administration, as the same Covarruvias rightly shows. Instead, it continues for the entire time for which it was made. Therefore, if a lease of the benefit of that property for any long period through such administration were valid without a just cause—and without observing the formal ceremonies required for alienating Church property—it would result in prejudice to the Church's holdings and to the Churches themselves. A way would be opened for frauds, by which Ecclesiastical property would in effect be alienated without just cause and without the required ceremony, which must not be allowed for any reason.

<margin>6</margin>
From what has been said in this entire disputation, it will be understood what should be said regarding the question: whether a **Prelate** <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> who swears not to alienate the property of the Church without consulting the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> is a **perjurer** if he leases such property for a long time without consulting him. Covarruvias, in *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 16, number 2, although he concedes that a prohibition on alienating a thing is considered a prohibition on leasing it for a long time, adds with Calderinus (though he says the matter is doubtful) that a Prelate who swore not to alienate Church property without the Pope's consent is **not a perjurer** if he leases it for a long time without consulting him. Alfonso Valdes does not reject this same opinion in his work on emphyteusis. Covarruvias is led to this because an oath is a matter of "strict law"—meaning it should not be extended but rather restricted. A long-term lease is not an **alienation** except in a broad and less proper sense of the word; for that reason, it should not be understood as included under the name of "alienation" to the effect that one who leases for a long time should be judged a perjurer or incur the penalty for perjury.

<margin>Decision</margin>
However, the contrary opinion is proven to me by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer.</note> in his commentary on the chapter *Intellecto* regarding oaths, number 10. I am convinced of this because an oath must be understood according to the subject matter, and it extends as far as the promise upon which it is based. Therefore, since in the matter of alienating Church property, "alienation" is understood to include long-term leases—and since the oath is required from prelates according to the subject matter and the sacred canons—it follows that the promise (and consequently the oath based on it) extends to long-term leases.

This is confirmed because if the reasoning used by Covarruvias were true, then even the **pledging** of Church property and the granting of it in **perpetual emphyteusis** <note>A type of long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant is required to improve the land.</note> would not be included under the Prelates' oath. Indeed, pledging and perpetual emphyteusis are not "alienations" unless the word is used broadly and less properly. Yet Covarruvias himself would say the opposite, and the opposite is clear from the very form of the oath, which I saw in a certain public instrument while I was staying in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania".</note>. These are the points regarding long-term leases.

### Louis Molina, On Contracts ###

<margin>7</margin> It should be observed <note>ornamental mark</note> that in "favorable matters" <note>A legal term referring to interpretations that expand a person's rights or benefits.</note>, such as the one at hand, when the sale of something is prohibited, it is also understood to be prohibited from being alienated by all the methods previously explained.
<margin>This is according to the gloss on the word "vendi" (to be sold) in the law "Quemadmodum" in the Code of Justinian, Book 10, and as affirmed by Panormitanus, Valasco on the law of emphyteusis, and Caldas.</margin>
Regarding the final point proposed in the title of this disputation: although it pertains more closely to the contract of "hiring and leasing" <note>original: "locationis, & conductionis"</note> strictly speaking (which will be discussed in its proper place later) than to the contract of a long-term lease <note>original: "emphyteusis"</note> in the broad sense which we are now discussing; nevertheless, because the matter is closely tied to the alienation of Church property—and was joined to it by Pope Paul II in the decree <note>original: "extrauagante"</note> titled *Ambitiosae*—with common penalties applied both to the leasing of Church property for more than three years and to the alienation of those same goods, it must be discussed here.

<margin>8</margin> It is clear that until the time of Paul II, it was lawful to lease Church property without special formalities for a short period, that is, for less than ten years, as is evident in the laws regarding the non-alienation of Church property. For example, when someone had leased the annual income of a certain Church for seven years and the lessor later did not wish to stand by the contract, the Pope ordered that if the contract was established, the lessor should be compelled to observe it for the full seven years. However, Paul II, in the decree *Ambitiosae*, restricted these leases of Church property to three years. Consequently, a lease made for more than three years without a just cause and the proper legal formalities is not only void by the law itself, but both the person leasing out the property and the person taking the lease are automatically excommunicated. If the lessor is an Abbot or a Bishop, they are barred from entering the Church. If they do not repent within six months, they are automatically suspended from the administration of the Church or monastery they head, in both spiritual and temporal matters.

Lower prelates, holders of "commendams" <note>A practice where a person held a church office "in trust" to receive its income.</note>, and any others holding benefices or administrative roles are automatically deprived of the benefices, commendams, or administrations whose property they have leased out. He likewise established all these penalties against those who alienate Church goods and those who receive them.

Cardinal Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note>, Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note>, and others observe that this law is not accepted everywhere. In some places, it is accepted only in part, and it only has the force of law where it has been received and to the extent of its reception; this is because laws are not considered binding unless confirmed by the usage of those who use them, and a contrary custom can abolish them. They say one must learn from the episcopal court in each place how far that decree has been accepted. Navarrus adds that it seems to be accepted in few places regarding the external penalties, but only regarding the internal nullity of the contract. He says it is accepted nowhere regarding the penalty of losing a benefice. He mentions that once in Salamanca, in a case involving a lease for more than three years, he gave the opinion that the contract was void, yet the lessor had not incurred excommunication

<column-break/>

nor was he "irregular" <note>A legal state of being barred from performing religious duties.</note> for having celebrated Mass after that contract. He also says that the decree does not seem to be accepted in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> regarding the three-year limit because, he says, contracts for four years are frequently made there. However, while I was lecturing on these matters in Évora, after making a diligent inquiry with ecclesiastical judges and advocates of long experience, I discovered that this decree is accepted not only in that Archbishopric but in the whole Kingdom of Portugal, and judgments are made according to it. I believe, however, that this applies only to the nullity of the contract for the time exceeding three years, and not to the penalty of excommunication or other external penalties. Nevertheless, it is accepted with this limitation in that Archbishopric and in other places (where there are lands called "four or five leaf" lands because they need four or five years to be fully cultivated and <term>harvested</term> <note>original: "eminentur." In this context, it refers to the process of bringing the land to full production or clearing it.</note>): that such estates or inheritances may be leased for as many years as they need to be fully sown.

Later, Gama <note>António da Gama (1520–1595), a prominent Portuguese jurist.</note> published a legal decision in which he firmly asserts against Navarrus that in all the tribunals of Portugal, that decree is accepted regarding the three-year limit, and contracts are declared void regarding the excess time. He says the fact that contracts for four or more years are tolerated when they are not brought to court does not prevent the decree from being accepted in that Kingdom in the way explained. Diego de Covarruvias <note>A famous Spanish jurist (1512–1577).</note>, besides the limitation from Portugal we reported, adds another: the three-year rule applies if the estate being leased produces fruit every year. If, for instance, olive groves produce fruit every two years, it would be lawful to lease them for six years; if they produce every three years, it would be lawful to lease them for nine years.

This limitation is quite reasonable and should be understood through *epikeia* <note>The principle of interpreting a law according to the spirit and intention of the legislator rather than its strict literal word.</note> from the same decree. This agrees with what was said in Disputation 453 regarding a long-term tenant not losing their rights unless the required time has passed two or three times over when the property did not bear fruit except every two or three years. Regarding the Kingdom of Castile, and whether this decree is accepted there, Covarruvias says: "Among the Spanish, it is doubtful whether this constitution has been set aside; for I have often seen it cited and discussed in several controversies, sometimes admitted and sometimes neglected; therefore, we leave this to the examination of the judge."

So he says. I hear that in our city and Diocese of Cuenca <note>original: "Conchensi"</note> it is accepted to the same extent as Navarrus's opinion in Salamanca, and as Gama testifies it is accepted in Portugal, as we said just before. And I believe it is accepted in the same way in the rest of this Kingdom of Castile.

# Second Treatise. Disputation 467. #

to you this Church property for nine years, in such a way that there are as many individual leases as there are **three-year periods** <note>original: "triennia"</note>, or in such a way that, once one three-year period is finished, it is considered leased for another three-year period from that moment, and once that is finished, for another. Whatever Baldus may have felt, it must undoubtedly be said—following Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias (cited above, number 4) and Alvaro Valasco in *On the Law of Emphyteusis* <note>A long-term land lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a fixed rent.</note> (question 29, number 15) report and follow—that such a contract is invalid regarding the remaining time beyond the first three-year period. The reason is that this is considered to be **in fraud of the law** <note>original: "in fraudem legis"; an act that follows the letter of the law but subverts its intent.</note>, which prohibits a lease beyond three years and renders it void. Pacts made in fraud of the laws are null; rather, they are considered prohibited by those very laws they seek to evade, because one must attend not so much to the words of the laws as to the intention of the legislators within them, as will be discussed in the first treatise. This common opinion is clearly confirmed by the legal text *De non alienandis rebus ecclesiasticis* <note>Regarding the non-alienation of Church property.</note> in the section "quod autem," near the end. There, since it had been prohibited to grant an ecclesiastical **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis: a type of perpetual or long-term lease of land belonging to the Church or the state</term> except for the life of the recipient and two subsequent generations or lives, it is pronounced that any pact added by some is void—namely, the pact that, once those two other generations were finished, the ministers of the Church would be bound to grant that lease again to the next successor and prefer him over others. And the text provides this reason: "In this, there is nothing else being done through this cycle and perpetual machinations than the granting of leases, or rather, the deprivation of Church property." But even if such a thing was done, there is no necessity for the most reverend administrators to hand it over to others once the two inheritances have ceased. Thus far the text. Alvaro Valasco (at the cited number 11), along with Cardinal and Alexander, adds that if a lease is made only for three years, and at the end of the first year a lease is made again for another three years to begin after the first ends, the contract is invalid because the prior lease is considered extended beyond three years. However, Alvaro Valasco rightly adds there that a distinction must be made if it is made to the same person and for the same **rent** <note>original: "pensione"</note>. For if it were made to a different person, or to the same person for a different rent, the prior contract would not be considered extended, but a new one instituted. However, this opinion is suspicious to me when it involves the same person, even if the rent varies, because fraud could easily intervene. No one would say it is lawful from the start to enter into those two contracts with the same person for those different rents; indeed, that would truly be leasing to the same person beyond three years. The laws do not look so much at whether it is for the same or a different person, but rather that it is not leased to the same person beyond three years. Covarrubias (cited above, number 6), along with Decius, adds that not only is a lease beyond three years prohibited, but it must also be considered prohibited to grant someone the faculty of leasing more than once for a three-year term. For example, if someone is given a mandate or faculty to lease a certain Church property for nine years, and they lease it once for three years, once that lease is made, the mandate and faculty cease. Therefore, when the first three years are finished, they cannot lease that property again, even to a different tenant, without a new mandate and faculty. He adds, however, that this opinion of his and Decius's might seem doubtful to some.
To me, indeed, it seems not only doubtful, but excessively 

<column-break/>

scrupulous, and even entirely false, as it rests on no solid foundation or law, and would establish something irrational. For why should an ecclesiastic, who reasonably departs for Rome or the Indies, not be able to grant the faculty of leasing Church property in his place, according to the prescription of the law, for the entire time he is away?

## Whether an alienation or lease for a longer time than is permitted by law is valid for the shorter time permitted by law that is included within that longer period. ##

### DISPUTATION 467. ###

#### S V M M A R Y ####

1. Whether a lease or alienation of Church property beyond the time permitted by law is invalid only regarding the excess, or truly in its entirety.
2. Time permitted by law can be separated from prohibited time, just as the useful can be separated from the useless.
3. When a lease or any other alienation of Church property is invalid even for the shorter time included within the invalid longer term.
4. How the decree of Clement I regarding the non-alienation of Church property is to be understood.

---

<margin>Question</margin>
This dispute is, as it were, an appendix to the preceding one. Here are examples: If Church property was handed over in **emphyteusis** for only three lives—whereas the legal text *de non alienandis* prescribes it not be given for more—and the lease is finished but not yet incorporated into the estate; according to what will be said in the following pages, it is then lawful for a prelate to hand it over for the same number of lives without new formalities, but not for more; otherwise, it will be void and useless. He asks, therefore, if a prelate hands over that lease for four or five lives, is that delivery valid for the three lives included in those four or five, being invalid only regarding the excess? Or is it entirely invalid, even for the first three lives? Likewise, it is forbidden to lease Church property beyond a **three-year period**, and if anything else is done, it is void and useless, as shown in the preceding dispute. It is asked, therefore, if Church property is leased for four or six years, whether that lease is valid for only the first three years and invalid regarding the excess; or whether it is entirely invalid, even for the first three years. Bartolus and others whom Covarrubias cites (in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 16, number 5) and Molina (in *On Primogeniture*, book 1, chapter 21, number 28)—and toward whose opinion Covarrubias clearly leans—judge those and other similar dispositions to be entirely invalid.
This can be argued, first, because in the papal decree <note>original: "extrauagāti"</note> *Ambitiosae*, it says a lease made beyond three years is of no strength or moment whatsoever. And in the legal text regarding non-alienation in the section "emphyteusim," while forbidding a lease to be given beyond three lives, it is added: "we permit it to be given in no other way, nor do we allow what is done to have any strength." And in the section "if indeed," if anyone presumes to receive a perpetual lease, which is not allowed, or at least one not according to the observation of this our law (that is, beyond three lives), then he indeed loses...

<meta>Catchword: indeed</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legal limits on leasing Church property, specifically the three-year limit for standard leases and the three-generation limit for emphyteusis, debating whether contracts that exceed these limits are entirely void or valid for the permitted duration.</summary>
