<meta>This page continues the legal debate from the previous page regarding the validity of contracts that exceed the time limits allowed by law, specifically focusing on whether a contract for an illegal duration (such as a ten-year lease of Church land) can be "saved" by being considered valid for the legally permitted period (three years).</meta>

### Ludovici Molina ###
### On Contracts ###

indeed regarding **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis: a long-term land lease where the tenant pays a small rent and improves the land</term>, and what has been given should remain with the venerable house <note>The "venerable house" refers to the Church or the religious institution owning the land.</note>. In these words, Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist</note> weighs that word, "forfeit" <note>original: "cadat"</note>, which signifies that they lose even that right which could have been lawfully granted to them; otherwise, it would not be a fitting way of speaking. Indeed, when a contract, or that part of an agreement, is null, it is not properly stated that the contracting parties "forfeit" it. Finally, in the *Clementines* (Book 1, *On the alienation of Church property*), it is said: "Nor let any right be acquired by the recipient." Moreover, that negation—"nor any"—is verified in even the smallest part, as noted by the glosses on the *Clementines* and by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> and others whom Covarrubias cites.

Secondly, because in those matters which depend on the will of two parties, and where it concerns the undertaking of an obligation, if the act is not valid as it was performed, it shall not be valid as it *could* have been performed. This is noted by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note>, who is widely accepted. To this is added the response of the Rota <note>The Roman Rota, the highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church</note> (Decision 66), stating that the election of a counselor for a three-year term is not valid even for one year when the statute states that the election is for one year and no more, and if done otherwise, it is null.

The **common opinion** <note>original: "communis opinio"; the consensus among legal experts</note>, along with Baldus, affirms that those and similar other dispositions or agreements are valid for the lesser time in which they could have been lawfully and validly made (which is included within the greater time), and are invalid only regarding the excess. Covarrubias reports and admits this is the common opinion in the place cited above; Molina (at number 28) and Julio Claro follow the same, as does Gamez, asserting that it has been very frequently judged according to this view in the **Portuguese Senate**. However, he adds that he once saw a judgment rendered according to the contrary view. This is primarily confirmed by the section "quod autem" at the end of the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's Novels (new laws)</note> regarding non-alienation. There, an emphyteusis was given for the life of the recipient and two heirs besides, but with a pact that upon the death of the last of those two heirs, it should again be handed over to his heir, who would be preferred over others for that lease. It is added: "If such a thing has been done (that is, if the emphyteusis was granted with that pact), there is no necessity for the most reverend administrators to hand it over to the others once the two heirs have ceased." Here you see the contract pronounced valid for the first three lives, but not for the remaining lives included in the same contract's pact. Covarrubias responds, however—not without a hope of probability—that the emphyteusis there was granted only for three lives according to the law's prescription, but an additional pact was added in **fraud of the law** <note>original: "in fraudem legis"; bypassing the intent of the law while following its letter</note>, so that when those lives ended, it would be granted again for as many lives to the heir of the last person. For that reason, the first contract was pronounced valid and the additional pact in fraud of the law was invalid. Furthermore, since that pact was celebrated at the same time as the first contract, and thus in effect the contract was for six lives at once, it constituted a transgression of the law prohibiting ecclesiastical emphyteusis beyond three lives. Truly, the common opinion is greatly strengthened by that text, and a path is opened to explain the texts cited from the same source.

It is then further confirmed because in such contracts the time permitted by law can be perfectly separated 

<column-break/>

from the prohibited time. Moreover, when the **useful can be separated from the useless**, the useful is not spoiled by the useless <note>original: "utile per inutile non vitiatur"; a fundamental legal maxim</note>, as seen in the laws regarding verbal obligations. Thirdly, it is confirmed because a donation made without registration <note>original: "insinuatio"; the formal recording of a gift in public records</note> above the sum which it is lawful to donate without registration, although it is invalid by legal disposition, is understood to be so only regarding the excess. It is not invalid regarding the sum which was lawful to donate without registration, which is included in that total quantity. All admit this, and it has been discussed in the material on donations. The reasoning is the same in the matter we are disputing, because the quantity of "useful" time (not prohibited by law) can be separated from the prohibited excess, just as in a donation the amount allowed can be separated from the excess that could not be validly given without registration.

<margin>Decision.</margin> This common and true opinion is to be understood in instances where the useful time can be separated from the useless. But if it cannot be separated, then it will not be valid even for the time in which the contract could have been validly made on its own. And in this, as Molina says at the cited number, all seem to agree: because the primary and fundamental reason of the authors of the common opinion is that the useful time can be separated from the useless. However, as Molina rightly says at the end of the cited number—and as we also once taught—the useful time cannot be separated from the useless when a person, who could have validly leased for three years (or some other modest time below ten years), instead invalidly leased for ten years, or invalidly handed over property in emphyteusis forever, or for a life or several lives. In that case, the contract is not valid even for the three years included in the ten years or the longer time; rather, it is entirely useless for the whole time. The reason is that, as shown above, a lease for ten years transfers **beneficial ownership** <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to use and profit from property owned by another</note> and is a true emphyteutic contract, distinct in kind from a lease for a modest time. No part of it—not even the first three years—is of a different nature than the whole. Therefore, since in an emphyteutic contract (even if only for ten years) there is no part that has the character of a "lease" strictly speaking (that is, for a modest time), it follows that in that contract the "useful" part cannot be separated. From this it follows that although the holder of an entailed estate (*majoratus*), an emphyteuta, or a feudal lord can validly lease for three years, they cannot validly lease for ten years or more. If they attempt to do so, I say, the contract is invalid even for the three years or other modest time included within that greater period. It also follows that since Church goods cannot be leased beyond three years without just cause and the observance of legal formalities, nor can they be granted anew in emphyteusis or otherwise alienated, if they are granted anew in emphyteusis without due cause or leased for ten years or more, the contract is invalid [altogether].

<summary>This page analyzes whether a contract that exceeds legal time limits (like a 10-year lease when only 3 years are allowed) remains valid for the legal portion. Molina argues that while the "useful" can often be separated from the "useless," an emphyteusis is a legally distinct type of contract that cannot simply be reduced to a shorter lease.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of whether a contract that exceeds legal limits—such as a lease of Church property for more than three years—is entirely void or remains valid for the legally permitted duration. It specifically addresses the arguments of jurists like Covarrubias and Molina regarding the severability of contract terms.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 467 #

the contract would be entirely [invalid], even regarding the first three years. However, if a lease were made for nine years, the contract would be valid for the first three years—which are of the same nature and type of leasing as the full nine years—and invalid only regarding the remaining six years. I should advise that if a contract concerning Church property were made in this manner: "I lease this estate to you for three years, and once those are finished, I lease it to you from this moment again for another twelve years until fifteen are reached"; in my judgment, the contract is valid for the first three years and invalid for the rest. This is because the first contract was truly a lease regarding the first three-year period; the remaining agreements for the other twelve years, which were added at the same time in fraud of the law, were null, yet they did not spoil the three-year term of the first contract, which is separable from them. In the same way, if the holder of a **maioratus** <term>maioratus: an entailed estate that must be passed down whole to a single heir</term> leases an entailed estate for nine years, with a pact added at the same time that, once those are finished, it is leased from this moment for the same number of years, I believe the first contract is valid, even though the added pact is null. And this is confirmed, regardless of the legal opinion held, by the words from the *Authentica* regarding non-alienation <note>original: "authē. de non alien. §. quod autem," referring to a section of Roman/Civil Law</note> cited above.

<margin>3</margin>
Furthermore, when † it is established by conjectures that the contracting parties would not have entered into the contract for the shorter time included within the longer one, the contract is invalid even for the shorter time included within the invalid longer period. This is the view of Bartolus and others, as cited by Molina (number 28) and Covarrubias (number 5). They provide an example of when a property is leased for the entire life of the tenant; for it is not to be believed that they would have similarly entered into a contract for only three years, or another modest amount of time, for the same annual rent. However, Molina correctly observes later at the end of that same section that this is primarily true based on the chapter cited shortly before. Specifically, this is because a life lease is a type of **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis: a long-term land lease where the tenant pays rent and improves the land, distinct from a standard short-term lease</term>, a distinct species of contract from a lease for a modest period. Therefore, a lease for a modest time cannot be separated as a part of it, since it belongs to a different legal logic and category. Molina adds, following Alexander and Tiraqueau, that even if it is not clear from other conjectures that the parties would have refused the shorter term, if it nonetheless matters greatly to one of them to have the contract for the full time and not just for a part—because, for instance, harm would follow for them from a contract for only a partial term—that is sufficient for it to be judged that they would not have contracted otherwise, and therefore the contract is invalid for that part. This is gathered from the law *Fundus*, joined with the gloss there, and the common doctrine of the writers on the Digest <note>original: "ff. de contrah. emp." referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 18, Title 1</note>. Covarrubias, in the cited section, along with Baldus and others he references, judges that if a lease of Church property is made invalidly for a certain time—say, for six or nine years—for a single price for that whole time, then, even according to the common opinion, it is invalid even for the first three years included in that longer time. This is because, from the fact that it was made for a single price for the whole time, it must be thought that the contracting parties did not wish to enter into a contract for just the part included in that whole time. However, I agree with the esteemed Julius Clarus <note>Giulio Clareti (1525–1575), an Italian jurist</note> and with Molina (number 28): unless there are conjectures from elsewhere that the same parties did not wish to contract for the part included in the whole time, that argument is not sufficient when the entire time of the lease is uniform and the price can be conveniently divided equally by individual years. Nor does it follow that because the lease was made for a single price for all years, it must be considered a single inseparable lease for that whole time, such that the "useful" part cannot be divided from the "useless" <note>In legal terms, "useful" refers to the legally valid portion, and "useless" to the void portion.</note>. Indeed, in a single donation that exceeds the amount allowed without formal registration, the useful is separated from the useless, as Molina rightly adds in the same place.

Regarding the first argument of the contrary opinion, it must be said that all those laws are to be understood regarding the *excess*; as to that excess, not even the smallest part is valid. However, those laws do not speak of the "useful" part, which is permitted by the laws, even if it is joined with an invalid excess prohibited by those laws and rendered null.

<margin>4</margin>
Observe † moreover, that the *Clementine* decree <note>Referring to the "Clementines," a collection of Canon Law issued by Pope Clement V.</note> mentioned above does not speak of a lease for a modest time as if it prohibits any part of it or renders it null, but rather of alienations. In those cases, as was said with Molina, it does not apply that a modest lease is included within them and remains valid. Furthermore, the word "forfeit" <note>original: *cadat*</note>, which Covarrubias weighs there, actually fights on our side: for it means that one "forfeits" the emphyteusis after the legally valid time included in such a grant has elapsed, as if by the force of this prohibition one truly falls away from an emphyteusis that was legitimately possessed up to that point.

If, however, according to Covarrubias's opinion, the entire time of the grant is excluded from the start, one could not properly be said to "forfeit" an emphyteusis which one never even obtained.

Nor is it a satisfying explanation when Covarrubias says that one "forfeits" the right that *could* have been lawfully granted. For if that right was never obtained, and was not granted to him, he certainly could not properly be said to forfeit it by force of that grant. Indeed, no one is said to forfeit a status or rank which he never held, at least as a matter of obligation.

To the second point, it must be said that the doctrine is true in those instances where it is stated that the intent was so focused on what is uselessly done that they are not judged to have wanted the useful part included in it, even if they could have done so usefully. Furthermore, it must be said that the doctrine is simply true because, regarding the law as to what is done in vain, it is not valid even if it could have been done [another way]. For example, if an entire act and its individual parts are invalid as they are performed—because some law annuls the whole and all its parts if done in a certain way—they are not valid even if they could have been performed otherwise. However, the acts we are speaking of now are valid as to *some* part of how they are performed, and not valid as to another part; hence, regarding that for which they are valid, it is false to say they are not valid as they are performed.

<summary>This page discusses whether an illegal long-term lease of Church property can be partially upheld for the legally allowed three-year period. The author argues that if the contract's terms (like price and duration) are uniform and divisible, the "useful" (legal) part remains valid even if the "useless" (excessive) part is void.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of contract duration (Disputation 467) to the specific legal requirements for the "alienation" (selling, leasing, or giving away) of Church property. It begins the detailed examination of Disputation 468.</meta>

# Who may alienate the property of the Church. What cause and what formality are required for alienating immovable and precious movable goods. And which goods are said to belong to the "mensa." <note>The "mensa," literally meaning "table," refers to the fund or estate reserved for the maintenance of a bishop or a religious community.</note>

## DISPUTATION 468.

### SUMMARY.

1. Who can alienate the property of the Church.
2. What is required for the alienation of immovable Church property, or precious movable goods, to be valid.
3. And what if such goods or things belong to a cathedral church.
4. What "authority" is.
5. What "discussion" <note>original: "tractatus"</note> is.
6. Express consent is the same as praise and approval.
7. When a signature for a matter or contract is necessary by a prelate of the Church.
8. Prelates take an oath before the Supreme Pontiff not to alienate Church property.
9. A Bishop alone, without other formalities, can alienate a thing of small value belonging to the Church.
10. A Bishop and an Abbot alone can grant "mensa" goods to someone, but only for the lifetime of the one granting them.
11. A prelate may refuse a legacy left to the Church without formality or the consent of the chapter, provided he does not incur a penalty.
12. With what formalities the property of a monastery may be alienated.
13. What is required for the property of a secular church subordinate to a cathedral to be alienated.
14. For the alienation of Church things to be valid, beyond other requirements, a just cause and the proper formality prescribed by law are required.
15. If an alienation is null by law, the alienated thing—along with all profits gained from it—is restored to the Church.
16. If Church goods are pledged, mortgaged, or alienated in another way, a legitimate cause and proper formality are necessary; otherwise, the alienation will be null by law.
17. Things of the Church usually granted as a fief <term>feudum: a landed estate held on condition of noble service</term> or a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis: a type of contract where land is leased for a very long time, often generations, provided it is improved</term>, before they are incorporated into the "mensa," can be granted anew without the required formalities.
18. With a declaration, however, as noted there and at number 19.
19. And what is required if such a thing belongs to a monastery, college, or chapter, for it to be granted anew.
20. When a thing of the Church should be said to be "usually granted" as a long-term lease or fief.
21. And when it should be considered "incorporated" into the mensa, so that it is called a "mensa" good.

<margin>1</margin> Regarding this matter, the first conclusion is: By common law <note>original: "iure cōi," referring to the universal law of the Church used across Europe</note>, the prelate alone can alienate movable goods that are not precious, or those which cannot be preserved by keeping them <note>such as perishable foodstuffs</note>. Say the same for anyone else who has the administration of Church goods. This is affirmed by the gloss in the *Summa* (that is, at the beginning of the whole question) 12. q. 2. Likewise the gloss on the chapter *Tua*, regarding those things done by a prelate without the consent of the chapter <note>original: "de his quæ fi. à pręl. sine consensu c."</note>, on the word "discussion," and Panormitanus <note>a famous 15th-century legal scholar</note> at the same place, number 7. Likewise the gloss on the chapter *Nulli*, on the word "immovables," regarding not alienating Church property, and Panormitanus there, number 8. Also the gloss on the chapter *Is cui*, regarding elections in Book 6, on the word "immovables." The text there agrees and can be clearly gathered from the first entry on not alienating Church property. For if, as said there, the prelate alone can lease out immovable property and sell the fruits of benefices for a short time (that is, for less than ten years), he will be able—with much greater reason—to sell individual harvested fruits, and even movable goods that cannot be preserved by keeping them, even if they are valuable. This is held clearly in the decree *Ambitiosae*, regarding not alienating Church property, where Pope Paul II prohibits alienating or leasing for more than three years all Church goods, both immovable and precious movables that can be preserved, but allows the alienation of movables that cannot be preserved. The same is confirmed by the chapter *Nulli* and from the *Authenticum* regarding non-alienation <note>legal citations to the Corpus Iuris Canonici and the Code of Justinian</note>; in these places, while the alienation of Church property is prohibited, mention is only made of immovables, with which the glosses include precious movables that can be preserved.

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin> The second conclusion: In order for the alienation of immovable goods and those precious movable goods that can be preserved to be lawful and valid, a legitimate cause is required first and foremost. When such a cause is present, it is said to be a case permitted by law for alienating. Furthermore, the legitimate causes for alienating are reduced to four, which that distinguished gloss records in the *Summa* 12. q. 2., which doctors <note>legal scholars</note> commonly follow—including Panormitanus in the cited chapter *Nulli*, number 5, and others whom Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a Spanish jurist</note> mentions and follows in his *Variarum Resolutionum*, chapter 17, number 2.

**The first cause is necessity.** Such as when debts press upon the Church, or another similar necessity, and it cannot be conveniently helped from other goods or by another way than by alienating immovable goods or precious movables.

**The second is utility.** For one immovable good or precious movable can be exchanged for another more useful to the Church; or one may be sold so that another more useful to the Church may be bought or built.

**The third is piety.** Such as for redeeming <note>captives</note> and for helping not only the extreme, but also the grave necessities of neighbors—not only those who belong to the same church, but also those who are of others. Indeed, for this purpose, not only immovable and non-consecrated precious movables may be sold, but even those that are consecrated, such as chalices, as is established in the law *Sancimus* (Code, *On the Most Sacred Churches*) and in the *Authenticum* on alienations. In 12. q. 2, Augustine is praised by Possidius <note>Saint Augustine's biographer</note> for having the vessels of the church broken and sold to redeem captives and to relieve the poverty and misery of the needy. He records that Ambrose did the same—whose words are in the cited chapter *Aurum*—and the necessity of neighbors could be so great that a prelate would be held under the guilt of mortal sin to help them from such goods when he could not otherwise. However, it is not lawful to alienate Church goods for just any necessity of neighbors, but only for an exceedingly grave one—especially those goods without which proper divine worship could not be maintained. Nor is it lawful for these goods to be sold or alienated for the purpose of rescuing wrongdoers from a just punishment, even if that punishment is grave and very painful.

<summary>This page discusses the legal conditions under which Church property may be sold or leased, defining what counts as "precious" goods and outlining the four justifications for such actions: necessity, utility, and piety.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of Disputation 468, moving from the justifications for selling Church property to the specific legal formalities required for such actions to be valid.</meta>

Tract. Secund. Disp. 468

When a cause exists for alienating such goods of the church, one must begin with those things that are not dedicated to divine worship, unless the dedicated items are superfluous. When it becomes necessary to proceed to the alienation of items dedicated to divine worship, one should start with those that are not consecrated. Consecrated items, however, are not to be alienated or given as a pledge—especially to laypeople <note>Non-clergy or people not ordained into the church's service.</note>—except for the most urgent reasons. All these matters are learnedly and extensively treated by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop known for his work on canon law.</note> in *Variarum Resolutionum*, book 2, chapter 16, numbers 8 and 9. Read him.

The fourth cause is **inconvenience**. This occurs when a certain thing brings more trouble to the church than profit; for example, if it is located far away and yields little fruit, or brings other disadvantages, as established in the canon *Terulas* (12, question 2). This cause, along with the previous one, can be reduced to the two primary categories of **necessity** and **utility**; for this reason, sometimes the law only mentions those first two. This entire second conclusion is common; everyone agrees that for an alienation to be lawful, a legitimate cause is required. As to whether a legitimate cause is necessary for the alienation to be *valid*, the common opinion of the doctors affirms that it is necessary, even if a few dissent—a matter to be discussed below, after first explaining the formality <note>original: "solemnitas"</note> required for alienating church property.

<margin>3</margin>
**Third conclusion.** In order that **alienation**—strictly understood as selling, exchanging, or otherwise transferring direct ownership—be not only lawful but also valid, if it concerns a cathedral church, the following formality is necessary. Namely, that in addition to the consent and authority of the Bishop, a **discussion** <note>original: "tractatus"</note> must precede it, and after the discussion, the **consent of the chapter** <note>The college of clergy (canons) who advise the bishop.</note> and their **signature** must be added. This conclusion is clear from various canons and laws, and is affirmed and handed down extensively by Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canonist called "Panormitanus" because he was Archbishop of Palermo.</note> and the doctors generally in various places. Something must be said regarding each specific element contained in the aforementioned formality.

<margin>4</margin>
First, it was said that the **consent and authority of the Bishop** is necessary. Regarding this, observe that the authority of the bishop is nothing other than his consent. For as the gloss <note>An interpretive commentary on a legal text.</note> rightly notes, the consent of one who presides by public office is called "authority." Hence, the consent of the Pope is called the authority of the Pope, and the consent of an Archbishop, bishop, or Prelate is called the authority of the Archbishop, bishop, or Prelate. Although in the past the authority of two bishops was necessary, today the authority of the bishop with the consent of the chapter suffices; the authority of the Archbishop is not necessary except in his own Archiepiscopal church.

<margin>5</margin>
Second, it was said that a **discussion** is necessary. Indeed, a discussion is something distinct from consent and prior to it. For a discussion, as Panormitanus says, is the proposal and deliberation on whether it is appropriate to alienate the thing, so that the causes and reasons for and against may be weighed. After this deliberation and discussion, consent or dissent usually follows. From this, Panormitanus concludes

<column-break/>

that when something is prohibited from being discussed by some statute under a penalty, it is enough if the matter is proposed and debated in the manner explained for those proposing and discussing it to incur that penalty; it is not necessary for consent to follow, much less for the matter to be executed. Some have said that three discussions ought to precede the alienation of any such ecclesiastical goods, otherwise the alienation would be invalid. However, from the cited authorities, it clearly stands that one is sufficient, provided it is diligent according to the quality of the matter being handled; for they only require "discussion" in the singular, not "discussions" in the plural.

<margin>6</margin>
Third, it was said that **consent** is necessary. This must be understood as **express consent**, as is clear from the law. This is what is called "praise" <note>original: "collaudatio"</note> there—that is, approval and express consent. Nevertheless, the consent of the majority of the chapter is sufficient; the consent of those absent is not necessary, but the consent of those present suffices. However, if a bishop alienates something while the chapter protests, or without the chapter's consent, is it enough if the chapter later ratifies it by providing consent after a prior discussion?

The answer must be in the affirmative. However, it must be understood that the alienation then becomes valid through the chapter's consent not from the time the prelate alienated it without that consent, but from the time the chapter consented. For that which preceded the consent was null by the law itself. But if a prelate lacks a chapter due to war or another cause, Panormitanus says he ought to convoke other clerics and, having discussed the matter with them, he can alienate with their consent what is judged to be expedient.

<margin>7</margin>
Fourth, it was said that a **signature** is necessary. This is only necessary in cases expressly stated by law, such as when something is donated, sold, or exchanged. Indeed, Panormitanus adds that the signature of the chapter is not observed in many places. And Armilla <note>Likely referring to the "Summa Armilla," a manual for confessors by Bartholomaeus de Fumo.</note> says it is not necessary for the signature to be made by the hand of the canons or religious, but it is enough if it is made by the hand of a notary, because custom holds this. Therefore, in this matter, one must stand by the custom of each place.

<margin>3</margin>
Panormitanus and others observe that today, prelates promoted by the **Supreme Pontiff**, or consecrated by his mandate, swear an oath that they will not alienate the immovable goods of the church, nor pledge them, nor grant them as a new fief <note>A grant of land in exchange for service or fee.</note> or emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis: a type of long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant must improve the land</term>, even with the consent of their chapter, without consulting the Roman Pontiff. Abbots take the same oath, as became known to me in our times in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> through a certain public instrument.

<sig>Nn 3</sig>

It highlights the mandatory "discussion" phase and the specific oaths taken by high-ranking clergy to prevent unauthorized loss of Church assets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of church property alienation, specifically focusing on the binding nature of the oath taken by bishops and abbots, and the exceptions for small items or specific types of church income.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

He affirms that Abbots, during their blessing, take the same oath that Bishops take during their consecration. Regarding an oath of this kind, however, observe that when an alienation would otherwise be valid—because, for instance, a legitimate cause and the formalities established by law were present—this oath would not prevent it from being valid, even if it had been done without consulting the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>. This is because the observance of this oath is not counted among the formalities that are necessary for an alienation to exist.

Therefore, the transgression of this oath would indeed constitute perjury for the person breaking it, but it would not render the alienation invalid. Panormitanus <note>original: "Pan." Referring to Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canonist known as the "Abbot of Palermo."</note> in the place cited at number 15, and in the final chapter of "On the Building of Churches" from number 3, says that this oath can be sworn in two ways. One way is to simply swear not to alienate property without consulting the Roman Pontiff or without his license. In that case, he says that if it is offered in the first way, it is only understood as swearing regarding cases prohibited by law; it is otherwise in cases permitted by law, and therefore one can alienate for some legitimate cause and the four reasons explained above, provided the due formality is observed, with the oath being no hindrance.

For that oath is not applied to restrict the power of alienating by one’s own authority, but for greater stability, so that one does not alienate in cases which, even without that oath, are prohibited. And regarding an oath sworn in this manner, the final chapter of "On the Building of Churches" is understood, where the Supreme Pontiff responds that, notwithstanding the oath not to alienate church property, Bishops can establish new basilicas as they judge appropriate, by applying to them a portion of the revenues of other churches already built. But if, he says, the oath is offered in the second way—as is customary for prelates to offer today—where they bind themselves to seek counsel or the faculty to alienate from the Roman Pontiff, this is not to be understood only when the alienation is unjust, but even when it is just. In that case, one cannot alienate even in cases permitted by law without consulting the Roman Pontiff. And he reports this to be the common opinion of the Doctors along with Johannes Andreae <note>A celebrated 14th-century canonist.</note>. Although a few have contended that even the oath sworn today only binds in cases otherwise illicit—because an oath is a matter of strict law—the opinion of Panormitanus, Johannes Andreae, and the common consensus is to be embraced by us. It is, however, limited with Panormitanus in the cited final chapter, and with others, to be understood as applying except in a case of notable necessity, which would not allow time to first approach the Supreme Pontiff. For an oath is not a bond of iniquity, nor ought it to obstruct a greater good; especially in the matter we are discussing. Through **equity** <note>original: "Epicheiam." From the Greek *epieikeia*, the principle of interpreting the law according to its spirit and fairness when the literal application would be harmful.</note> it must be judged that the Supreme Pontiffs do not intend to bind someone in such an event, because if they did intend it, they would be acting wrongly.

<margin>9</margin> Although the aforementioned formalities are regularly necessary both for the alienation to be lawful and for it to be valid, it must nevertheless be observed that when a **matter is minor** <note>original: "res est modica."</note> and of little utility to the Church, and it is expedient to alienate it, the Bishop alone can perform it without any other formality. This is established in the chapter *Terrulas* (34, question 2) and affirmed by the gloss in the same summary and Panormitanus with certain others in the chapter mentioned above regarding the building of church property, number 9. He adds that nothing prevents the oath, which Bishops today swear regarding not alienating property without consulting the Roman

<column-break/>

Pontiff, from allowing Bishops to alienate such small things, because they are not understood to be included in that oath.

And although the chapter *Terrulas* speaks only of Bishops, Panormitanus considers that lower Prelates can also alienate such minor things without a formal discussion or the consent of the chapter, according to certain laws which he cites there; the gloss on the chapter *Abbatius* (12, question 2) agrees. In this case, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian and cardinal.</note> is also to be understood in his summary under the word "excommunication," chapter 75, when he says that in the alienation of the smallest immovable things, one does not incur the excommunication of Paul II in the decree *Ambitiosae* <note>A famous decree by Pope Paul II (1467) restricting the sale of church lands under pain of excommunication.</note>. For in that decree, cases permitted by law are excepted, and the one we are speaking of is among their number.

<margin>10</margin> When **certain common goods** do not belong to the Bishop together with the chapter, or the Abbot together with the convent, but belong to the **episcopal or abbatial table** <note>original: "mensa." Property set aside specifically for the support and maintenance of the prelate.</note>, Panormitanus says (chapter *Continebatur*, "On those things done by prelates," number 7), along with Federico of Siena and Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a leading canonist.</note> whom Panormitanus cites, that the Bishop or Abbot alone can grant those to someone, but only for the lifetime of the grantor, without any other formality. The reason is that this is not "alienating," nor is it leasing for longer than three years (which is prohibited in the decree *Ambitiosae*), nor does it result in prejudice to the chapter or the church, but only to the prelate granting it. It seems to be nothing other than granting the benefit of that thing for the life of the one granting it.

Perhaps the contrary is true, and that grant seems to be disapproved in chapter 3, "On Arbitrators." The reason is that it is beyond three years, and because it is destructive to the church. For it often happens that such a thing is recovered only with difficulty and not without a lawsuit after it has been in the hand of a layman, as I have sometimes learned from experience in a serious matter. When something has been given to a layman in perpetual **fief** <note>original: "feudum." A land grant held on condition of service.</note>, and he does not wish to return it to its own church, then if he wishes to donate it to some other church or monastery, the authority of the bishop would suffice for that donation to be valid, without the consent and discussion with the chapter, and without the consent of the clergy of the church whose direct ownership of that thing was held. This is expressly stated in the chapter *Cum Apostolica*, "On those things done by prelates," and is affirmed there by Panormitanus at number 7, and the gloss on the *Clementines* <note>A collection of canon law promulgated by Pope Clement V.</note> (2, "On not alienating church property," on the word "table"). Since, however, the chapter *Cum Apostolica* says that this is not so much a prelate alienating what the church possesses as it is reclaiming for ecclesiastical use what is held by a layman, it does not seem to oppose the oath about not alienating without consulting the Roman Pontiff which is taken today; therefore, it seems it can be done without consulting the Roman Pontiff.

<margin>11</margin> There is a doubt: if a prelate, without formality and the consent of the chapter, **repudiates a legacy** <note>Refuses an inheritance.</note> of immovable property made to the church, whether that repudiation is valid, and whether that prelate is a perjurer if he did it without consulting the Roman Pontiff. Panormitanus (chapter *Tua*, "On those things done by prelates," number 9, and chapter 1, "On total restoration," also number 9) disputes this question. Although he says the matter is doubtful, he nevertheless inclines toward the view that the repudiation is valid and that the prelate is not a perjurer.

It explores the distinction between legal validity and the moral sin of perjury in the context of church administration.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 468.

<margin>Decision.</margin> The reason for this is that it is not considered "alienating" a piece of Church property if a prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> refuses to accept a legacy <note>A gift left in a person's will.</note> before it has been formally received. This is because the Church is not yet the mistress or owner of the bequeathed item, as is clearly established in the discussions of Disputations 2, 3, and 18. Instead, this is viewed as a failure to acquire something for the Church that could have been acquired. Legal formalities, however, are only strictly required for the act of alienating (giving away) what is already owned. Nevertheless, Panormitanus <note>original: "Panor." Referring to the famous canon lawyer Nicola de' Tudeschi.</note> adds that if the refusal was prejudicial to the Church, a legal action can be brought against the prelate and his heirs to restore any interest or damages that followed. However, the opposite opinion seems far more probable to me, in line with what was said with Panormitanus in Disputation 465. Namely, in this matter of transferring ecclesiastical goods, rights to immovable property <note>Real estate, like land or buildings.</note> are calculated alongside the immovable goods of the Church. Therefore, if the legacy consists of immovable property, or a price that can be preserved by keeping it (which is the only type of legacy where difficulty arises), the right to it must be calculated alongside the immovable goods or precious movable goods. Since the Church acquires the right to that thing before the prelate’s acceptance, it follows that although that refusal is not an alienation regarding the physical item bequeathed, it is nonetheless an alienation regarding the *right* to that item, which the Church had acquired upon the testator’s death. By that refusal, the prelate abdicates that right from the Church. Consequently, such a refusal is invalid if it involves a Bishop or Abbot and the right pertained to immovable property, which is of greater value.

**2** **The Fourth Conclusion.** In the alienation of such goods belonging to a monastery, if the monastery is not privileged and exempt from the Bishop's authority, then in addition to the discussion and consent of the chapter <note>The governing body of monks or canons.</note> and the monastery’s superior, the consent of the Bishop is also necessary. Otherwise, the transfer will be null and void. However, if the monastery is privileged and exempt—as almost all monasteries are today—the consent of the chapter and the prelate is sufficient, provided it is handled according to the constitutions and privileges of each specific religious order. In our Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits), of which Molina was a member.</note>, according to its privileges, the consent of a chapter is not necessary; rather, it is sufficient to have a discussion with advisors in the manner customary to our Society. The first part of this conclusion is affirmed by the glosses and doctors <note>Legal commentators and theologians.</note> generally, as seen in the chapter *Abbatibus* and the chapter *In Venditionibus*. The second part is affirmed by Turrecremata <note>A prominent 15th-century Dominican theologian.</note> and needs no further proof, as it is contained in the privileges of each exempt religious order or monastery. The third part is established by the privileges of our Society in the Bulls of Pius V (1566) and Gregory XIII (1575), which prescribe a method for making contracts and transferring property without a chapter, suited to the constitutions and governance of the Society. Nor is the faculty of the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> necessary for such transfers, except in cases not granted by law, as is clear from the Bull of Pius V.

**3** **The Fifth Conclusion.** If the property to be transferred belongs to an inferior secular church <note>A smaller, local church not part of a monastery.</note> and is being moved to a cathedral, then if the Bishop is the primary author of that transfer, a discussion and the assent of his own Cathedral Chapter is required. However, if the Bishop is not the author, but the rector of that specific church is, then if that

<column-break/>

inferior church has its own college <note>A group of clergy assigned to a specific church.</note>, a discussion by the Rector with his college and the consent of the college together with the Rector is necessary, as well as the authority or consent of the Bishop. But if the church lacks a college, the rector alone can transfer the property with the authority or consent of the Bishop alone. This conclusion belongs to Panormitanus. The first part is gathered from the law regarding "the property of the Church not to be alienated." However, the rector of the inferior church must be heard if there is one; if there is no rector and the position is vacant, a defender must be appointed to act on behalf of the Church. For a Bishop, even with the consent of his chapter, cannot transfer the goods of an inferior church without necessity and without the consent of the rector and the college (if it has one). It is different where a necessity exists. In such a case, the rector or an appointed defender must still be heard, even if their consent is not strictly necessary. This same part can be confirmed by the chapter *Cum Apostolica*. The latter part of the conclusion is affirmed by the gloss and is clear from the chapters *Abbatibus* and *Placuit*. The reason why a discussion and consent of the Bishop’s own chapter is required in the first scenario, but not in the second, is according to Panormitanus: in the first, the transfer is made by the Bishop himself; to prevent him from squandering the goods of an inferior church, it was necessary to prescribe these full formalities. In the latter case, because the transfer is made by the rector, it was necessary first to prescribe that he follow the formalities prelates use—discussing the matter with his college—and then, it was fitting that the authority or consent of his own Bishop be added as a necessary requirement.

**4** **The Sixth Conclusion.** For the transfer of such ecclesiastical items to be valid, it is necessary that two things occur simultaneously: there must be a "just cause" from among the four explained in the second conclusion, and the "due formality" prescribed by law and explained by us in the preceding conclusions. This conclusion stands against the glosses and a few others cited by Panormitanus and Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish canonist.</note>, who asserted that if the due form or formality is observed, the transfer is valid even if a legitimate cause is absent. They add, however, that if the Church is significantly harmed by the transfer, it can seek "restoration to the original state" <note>term: *restitutio in integrum* — a legal remedy to cancel a contract and return things to how they were.</note>, meaning the transfer is rescinded. However, our conclusion is the common one: namely, that the transfer is null by the law itself <note>note: original: "ipso iure nullam"</note>, whether it lacks a legitimate cause or the legitimate formality required for the transfer.

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

They affirm this <note>The legal experts and glossators mentioned in the citations.</note> in the *penultimate gloss on chapter 1, "On the restoration to the original state"* <note>original: "de in integr. restit." referring to the legal remedy of returning parties to their original position before a contract.</note>; *Panormitanus in the same place at number 17; chapter "Tua," on those things done by prelates, number 8; chapter "Nulli," on not alienating Church property, number 7; and elsewhere. Covarruvias at number 2, already cited, and many others whom he references.* This is clearly gathered from *chapter 1, "On not alienating Church property," book 6,* in which place a certain transfer is pronounced void, both because the required formality was not observed, and especially because a legitimate cause was not present.

It is also gathered from *Clementine 1, "On not alienating Church property."* There, a lease for life, or for another long term, is pronounced void by the law itself if either a legitimate cause is absent or the required formality is missing. It is gathered even more clearly from the *extravagant "Ambitiosae" under the same title,* <note>The "Extravagantes" were decretals not included in the primary collections of Canon Law; "Ambitiosae" is a specific decree by Pope Paul II.</note> where every transfer made, except in cases permitted by law, is pronounced void by the law itself. The same is gathered from *chapter "Sine exceptione," 12, question 2; from chapter "Cum apostolica," and from chapter "Tua," regarding things done by prelates.* Therefore, a transfer is only valid—allowing for "restoration to the original state"—when both the required formality was observed and a legitimate cause for the transfer existed; otherwise, the Church is "enormously harmed" <note>A legal term for a loss exceeding half the value of the object.</note> by the transfer because the price was far too low, or the established rent was extremely small compared to the quality of the item transferred. This occurred in the event mentioned in *chapter "Ad nostram," on not alienating Church property.* It is regarding this and other similar events that *chapter 1, "On the restoration to the original state"* must be understood.

Observe, however, that for a transfer to be valid, it is sufficient that the cause was considered legitimate by the contracting parties when the transfer was made, even if it is later found to be insufficient. So says the *gloss on chapter "Ad nostram," on not alienating Church property, and others whom Covarruvias references and follows at number 2.* But if the Church then finds itself "enormously harmed," restoration to the original state is granted to it; it is otherwise if the Church does not feel enormously harmed in the price or rent. Likewise, when it is clear that the required formality was observed, it is presumed that a legitimate cause was also present when the contrary is not evident; although the Church is then admitted to prove that a legitimate cause did not intervene. So it is with the *gloss on the law "Hoc ius porrectum," Code, on the most sacred Churches; Baldus, Jason, and others, cited by Covarruvias in the same place.* It must also be observed that the *Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Lisbon, title 18, constitution 2,* hold that even if no mention of the required formalities is made in the document by which something was handed over in <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>A type of perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent.</note>, the contract is confirmed if a space of thirty years has passed. Regarding common law, *Gama, decision 49,* also contends that the required formalities are presumed to have occurred even if it is not evident from the writing, and he cites many doctors affirming this. Moreover, regarding when a transfer is made to satisfy the Church’s debts and to pay back a loan—specifically how far the burden of proof lies with the lender and other creditors to show those debts were turned to the benefit of the Church—this was explained extensively by us in Disputation 300.

<margin>15</margin>
When a transfer was void by the law itself, then the transferred property must be restored to the Church along with all the fruits <note>Profits, crops, or interest derived from the property.</note> gathered from it, as is clear in *chapter "Si quis," on not alienating Church property.* The buyer is also punished by the loss of the price paid, which goes to the benefit of the Church, as held in the *law "Iubemus," and in the passage "Qui res," Code, on the most sacred Churches.* However, when the buyer bought the thing in good faith, then the person who illicitly

<column-break/>

transferred it is bound to pay the price back to the buyer; and in that person's default, the Church is bound to pay back only the amount by which it was made wealthier from that price, as *Panormitanus rightly noted on the cited chapter "Si quis."*

<margin>16</margin>
**Seventh conclusion.** For the purpose of pledging or subjecting to a specific <term>hypothec</term> <note>A mortgage or security interest where the debtor keeps possession of the property.</note> an immovable item belonging to the Church (and I say the same for a precious movable item that can be preserved by keeping it), and likewise for leasing it for a long time, or for granting it anew as a <term>fief</term> <note>Land held on condition of feudal service.</note>, or in perpetual emphyteusis, or for certain lives <note>A lease lasting for the duration of specified people's lifetimes.</note>, both a legitimate cause and the required formality are necessary. If either of these is missing, the transfer will be void by the law itself. The same must be said for a lease longer than three years and shorter than ten years, where the decree of Paul II <note>original: "extrauagans Pauli II."</note> has been received in that region. The first part of this conclusion is common opinion and can be proven.

First, because, as shown in Disputation 466, all those types of transfer are prohibited in law; therefore, being done without a legitimate cause and required formality, they are illicit and void. Since they are not more strictly prohibited than the transfers we spoke of in the preceding conclusions (which are transfers in a more proper and narrow sense), it follows that they are licit and valid under the same causes and formalities as those.

Second, because for a lease of ten years or more, both a legitimate cause and required formality are simultaneously required; otherwise, such a lease is void by the law itself, as is clear from *Clementine 1, "On not alienating Church property."* Therefore, since this type of transfer is the least significant when compared with the others, it follows that for the others to be valid, they similarly require a legitimate cause and formality, and if done otherwise, they are entirely void. In this place, observe: if all these types of transfer are included under that "alienation" which Bishops and Abbots today swear they will not perform without consulting the Roman Pontiff (as we showed they are included above), then, for them to be done licitly and without the sin of perjury by Bishops and Abbots, it is additionally required that they be carried out only after the Roman Pontiff has been consulted. However, this is not necessary for them to be valid, as was said above regarding another type of transfer.

One must also apply to these types of transfers the limitations that were made there regarding transfer in the strict sense. The latter part of the conclusion is proven because a lease longer than three years and shorter than ten years is prohibited; therefore, at least without a legitimate cause and formality, it will be illicit and void, as is established from the *extravagant "Ambitiosae."* Since it is not considered more strictly prohibited than transfers of far greater weight and importance, it follows that when a cause and legitimate formality concur in the manner explained, such a lease is valid and licit. However, because a regular urgent cause will not be present, it will also regularly be illicit and void. And, since it is not technically a full "alienation," it will not be necessary for Bishops and Abbots to consult the Roman Pontiff about it beforehand.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from the previous section regarding the "alienation" or transfer of Church property. Second Treatise, Disputation 468.

...or a **long-term lease** <note>original: "emphyteusim"</note> was traditionally granted, it can—before it is fully incorporated back into the **church table** <note>original: "mensa"; the specific assets or income set aside for the support of a prelate or the cathedral chapter</note>—be granted again as a **fief** <note>original: "feudum"</note> or a long-term lease. This can be done without formal ceremony, provided that a sufficient cause persists or is present; or, as Paul II says in the decree *Ambitiosae*, provided it is handled for the evident benefit of the Church—that is, judged to be advantageous to the Church without any ambiguity. 

This is the opinion of **Panormitanus** <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis, a leading 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in the chapter cited above, "On the non-alienation of church property," from number 9. This is affirmed as the common opinion of the doctors of law, which is referenced and followed by **Julius Clarus** in his sections on "long-term leases" (question 6, number 1) and "fiefs" (question 13, numbers 1 and 2); **Gregorio Lopez**; **Gama** (decisions 24 and 161); **Alvaro Valasco** on the law of long-term leases (question 11, number 15); and **Covarruvias** (2. *Variae Resolutiones*, chapter 17, number 4). Julius Clarus, in the cited question 13, adds that this opinion is true even if the fief or lease became vacant during the time of a predecessor, provided they are granted by the successor before those assets are incorporated into the "table" in the sense explained. This opinion is gathered from chapter 2 "On Fiefs" and from the decree *Ambitiosae*.

It is also clearly confirmed by chapter 1, joined with the **gloss** <note>an interpretive commentary written in the margins of legal texts</note> there, "By whom investiture is made." There it is held that a minor under 25 years old, who cannot transfer property without the required formalities, can nevertheless grant investiture for an **ancient fief** <note>original: "feudo antiquo"</note> that has returned to him. This is because he is not "alienating" (transferring away) the property, but rather reforming what had already been transferred. This clearly accords with the logic upon which the common opinion rests: namely, that this is not considered a new alienation, but a continuation of a previously made transfer, as long as it is not re-incorporated into the church table. For that reason, it does not require the same formal ceremony by which it was first transferred. Instead, the authority of the prelate (or whoever would be responsible for the transfer if no legal formality had been established) is sufficient. Similarly, when a tenant or vassal commits a default, the authority of that same person is sufficient—without other formalities—to allow the lease or fief to continue. From this doctrine, **Gama** (decision 14) notes that he determined, following the teaching of a certain very learned teacher of his, that a **ward** <note>original: "pupillum"; a child under legal guardianship</note> can nominate someone for a long-term lease.

Just as a minor can grant investiture for a long-term lease or fief according to chapter 1, "By whom investiture is made," because it is not considered a transfer of ownership, so too can he nominate someone; for this is also not a "new" grant of a lease. From this same doctrine, it follows that to grant a fief or lease again for property usually held this way, it is not necessary for Bishops or Abbots to run to the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note> before it is re-incorporated into the table. The oath they took—not to alienate property without consulting the Roman Pontiff—does not stand in the way. This is because it is not judged to be a *new* alienation, but a continuation of one made previously, as Panormitanus rightly affirms in the place cited.

**Covarruvias**, in the place cited, said that property could be granted again in lease with the same formality with which it was usually granted. However, Panormitanus and the other cited doctors assert that it is not necessary to apply the old formalities anew when it was originally granted with the due ceremony (or is presumed to have been). This is certainly proven by the cited laws and is persuaded by the reasoning given above with the common opinion. Perhaps Covarruvias did not mean otherwise. **Caldas**, on the renewal of long-term leases (question 14), although he confesses that our conclusion 

<column-break/>

is the common opinion of the doctors (whom he references both at the beginning and the end of that question), says at number 3 that the common practice in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> is different. This practice is strengthened by the synodal constitutions of that Kingdom: when a finished lease is to be renewed, a new negotiation occurs. Through arbitrators and with the consent of both parties, the leased property is inspected anew and explored regarding its quality and value. Thus, the annual rent to be paid is estimated and defined by their judgment; this rent is never lower than what was previously established. In this way, a new consent from the direct lord is added for the renewal, which is finally concluded and celebrated through a formal writing and a public instrument. In question 20, he relates the entire process by which these things are done in that Kingdom, with the authority of the **ordinary** <note>The local Bishop or official with standard jurisdiction</note> interposed so that arbitrators may be appointed and the matter carried out.

<margin>18</margin>
He says that when the property belongs to a monastery, college, or **chapter** <note>the governing body of a cathedral or collegiate church</note>, the matter is first brought for consultation. Once the college or chapter is assembled, they deliberate whether it is expedient for the property to be granted as a new lease or renewed. After diligent negotiation and finding that it would result in the evident benefit of the church, one or two people are appointed to carry out the matter on behalf of the chapter. Caldas contends that this practice or formality used in Portugal is also necessary by **common law** <note>original: "iure communi"</note>. However, one should not depart from the common opinion, which is also approved by Portuguese authors. Therefore, I believe it should be said that this custom in Portugal took its origin from the decree *Ambitiosae*, insofar as it prescribes that property usually granted in lease can indeed be granted again, but only if it results in the evident benefit of the church. To examine whether it truly results in evident benefit, that preliminary negotiation seems to have been introduced. Nevertheless, it is not strictly necessary; it is enough that the one granting the lease again understands it to be useful to the church. Therefore, since that practice does not require renewals made without those formalities to be rescinded, they are certainly not necessary in Portugal today for a contract to be valid.

<margin>19</margin>
Our conclusion proposed above must be understood, however, provided that the manner in which the property was usually granted in fief or lease is not exceeded. For if it was only accustomed to be granted for **three lives** <note>a lease term lasting through the lives of three successive named people</note>, and it is granted for more, or in perpetuity, or so that it passes to persons of a different kind than those for whom it was usually granted (for example, if it was only granted to descendants of the recipient, but is now granted so it can pass to strangers), and if this new grant is made without a just cause and without applying new legal formalities, then according to the common opinion it is invalid regarding the excess, as Julius Clarus says in the cited questions 6 and 13. As to whether it remains valid for the rest, we showed in the preceding disputation (along with Julius Clarus and others) that it is indeed valid, because "the useful is not vitiated by the useless" <note>A legal maxim meaning a valid part of a contract isn't ruined by an invalid part</note>. This agrees with what Gama (decision 161) relates was judged in the Portuguese Senate.

Two points regarding the proposed conclusion must be examined...

<summary>This page discusses whether Church-owned lands previously under lease or fief can be re-granted without the complex papal permissions usually required for "alienating" Church property. Molina argues that such renewals are continuations of old contracts rather than new transfers, though he notes stricter regional customs in Portugal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of church property from page 569. The first word "nanda" completes "consideranda" from the previous sentence, discussing the conditions under which church lands are treated as being part of a specific endowment or "table."</meta>

...must be considered. The first is when a thing should be said to be customarily granted in a **long-term lease** <note>original: "emphyteusim"; a type of contract where a tenant improves land in exchange for a low rent and long-term rights</note> or a **fief** <note>original: "feudum"</note>. The second, truly, is when it should be considered incorporated into the **table** <note>original: "mensæ"; the specific fund or assets designated for the support of a bishop or monastery</note>. 

Regarding the first point, setting aside other opinions which **Julius Clarus** (section on *fiefs*, question 13, number 4) and **Gregorio López** (where cited above) report and weigh, we must speak to the present matter. If a property has been granted even once as a long-term lease or a fief—with the proper cause and legal formality—and it has not yet been incorporated into the "table" (according to what will be said), then it must be affirmed that it is "customarily granted." The effect of this is that it can be granted again without new formal ceremonies, provided a just cause persists. The reason is that in such a case, the property is not being **alienated** <note>transferred out of Church ownership</note> anew; rather, given that a legitimate transfer was made previously, that transfer is merely being continued. This is the reason why it can be done without new formal ceremonies. If, however, it is not clear that it was previously granted with the proper cause and formality, such a state is presumed when the property has remained granted in a long-term lease for thirty or forty years. When the original contract is not available, the property is still considered customarily granted in lease or fief, meaning that as long as a just cause remains, it can be granted again without new formal ceremonies.

Regarding the second point, as gathered from the commentary on the **Clementine Constitutions** <note>original: "gl. Clem. vnic. de exces. præl."; a collection of canon law</note> and from **Innocent** and **Panormitanus** <note>leading medieval legal commentators</note> in the chapter cited above, and from others: the goods of any Church or monastery are said to belong to the "table" of that Church or monastery for this reason—that they serve the table. That is, they serve the maintenance of the poor and of those who belong to that Church or monastery, and they serve their interests. If any churches are annexed for this very purpose to another Church, monastery, or the office of an Abbot or Bishop, they are said to belong to the "table" of that Church or monastery, or to the Episcopal or Abbatial table, as the cited commentary teaches and Panormitanus recommends. Panormitanus and Innocent add that when the **useful ownership** <note>original: "dominium vtile"; the right to use the land and take its profits</note> of a property belongs to another person, that property is not said to be "of the table," because its utility does not look toward the table.

Perhaps, however, it would be more accurately said that it is "not of the table" only with the addition of "as far as the useful ownership" is concerned; it is, however, "of the table" regarding the **direct ownership** <note>original: "dominium directum"; the underlying legal title held by the Church</note> and the pension paid from the useful ownership to the owner. With these foundations laid, the cited authors teach that when something granted in a fief or long-term lease becomes vacant regarding its useful ownership—and it reverts to the owner because there are no heirs, or the leaseholder committed a crime, or for any other reason—it is not considered to be "of the table" as long as it is not formally applied to the table by the **prelate** <note>a high-ranking church official like a bishop or abbot</note>.

Truly, it is first considered "of the table" when the prelate or the community of monks, deciding not to grant it again as a fief or lease, applies it to the table. If, regarding such goods that have become vacant, it is not clear whether the prelate applied them to the table, Panormitanus approves a saying of the **Archdeacon** <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous canonist</note> (32, question 8, chapter 1), who affirms that if the prelate retained those goods for a whole year without granting them again in fief or 

<column-break/>

lease, he is considered to have applied them to the table. However, a successor could still grant them again in fief or lease without a formal ceremony.

Panormitanus restricts this teaching to cases where a legitimate cause is present; otherwise, as soon as they are vacant, they are considered to have been applied to the table. This is no different from goods donated to a church or monastery; as soon as they are given, they become part of the "table," and the prelate cannot transfer them without formal ceremony. Thus, if in the beginning sterile lands were granted in long-term lease with the proper ceremonies for the just cause of bringing them under cultivation and making them fruitful; or if they were granted again to the successors of the person who cultivated them (because such a promise was usefully made to the original cultivator); then, if they become vacant after they have been cultivated and made fruitful, and there is no legitimate cause why they should be leased again, they immediately become "of the table." If they are granted in lease again without cause, that transfer is invalid, as is clearly established in the decree **Ambitiosae** <note>a famous papal decree by Paul II in 1468 restricting the transfer of Church property</note>. Indeed, Panormitanus seems to feel that a Bishop or Abbot who does this without consulting the Roman Pontiff is guilty of **perjury**.

Regarding goods called "of the table," this must be added: sometimes in monasteries, the goods are divided between the Abbot and the community. In that case, the goods belonging to the Abbot are called the "Abbatial table," while those belonging to the community for the relief, support, and utility of the monks are called the "Conventual table."

Similarly, in cathedral churches, goods are usually divided between the Bishop and the **chapter** <note>the college of clergy serving a cathedral</note>. Those belonging to the Bishop are called the "Episcopal table," while those deputed for the support of the canons and other clergy of that Church are called the "Capitular table."

Distinguished from all these goods are those belonging to the **fabric** <note>original: "fabricam"; the fund for the maintenance of the church building itself</note>. If anything is also deputed and annexed to another office, such as a deanery or archdeaconry, it is said to belong to the "table" of that specific office.

# Whether Church property can be granted in perpetual lease. And whether, if granted to the recipient and his heirs or successors, it is understood only as descendants or also as outsiders.

## DISPUTATION 469.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *In what way church property can be granted in a perpetual lease.*
<margin>2</margin> *If an ecclesiastical lease is granted in perpetuity for oneself and one's heirs, whether this includes ancestors and any external heirs whatsoever.*
