Second Treatise. Disputation 469. 371

granted without an expression of time, until such time as it is considered granted.
4 *A **long-term lease** <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note> acquired by right of long-term possession <note>original: "praescriptionis"</note> is considered to last for three lives.*
5 *A long-term lease granted up to the third generation does not pass to outsiders, but only to descendants.*
6 *A long-term lease granted for a fixed number of years passes to any successors within that time.*
7 *Before a property is incorporated into the **church fund** <note>original: "mensa"; the specific assets designated for a bishop or monastery</note>, it can be granted anew without the required formal ceremonies in the same way it was before, provided the same legitimate cause continues.*
8 *A long-term lease granted without the formal ceremonies required by law is valid according to the established custom of the place.*

The **R**eason for doubt, as far as the first of the proposed points is concerned, is this: In the legal text *Authenticum de non alienandis* <note>A collection of laws by Emperor Justinian concerning the prohibition of selling Church property</note> in the section on long-term leases, and in other places cited in Disputation 467, it is only permitted to grant ecclesiastical property in a long-term lease for the life of the recipient and two descending heirs—that is, some of the sons or daughters, and some of the grandsons or granddaughters. This is what they call granting to the "third generation only," which is to say, for the lives of descendants only. In the same place, it is granted that it can also be given for the life of the recipient and a spouse, along with one descendant. However, all other long-term leases of church property are prohibited, and are declared void and null by the very fact of their creation.

The reason for doubt regarding the second point is this: Although many authorities—including **Bartolus**, the **Speculator**, and others whom **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century expert in Church law</note> refutes (from number 25 to 30), and whom **Felynus** also cites at number 27—believe that the original law was later corrected by the *Authenticum de alienatione and emphyteusi* <note>Justinian's legal update regarding the transfer and leasing of property</note> in the section on "licensing," where it is granted that church property can be handed over in a perpetual lease; nevertheless, **Johannes Andreae** and others judge that while it was indeed corrected regarding the time and number of generations (meaning they can be granted in perpetuity for children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and other descendants), it was not corrected regarding the *quality* of the heirs. Thus, they argue that beyond descendants, ancestors or other "outsiders" <note>original: "extraneos"; heirs who are not direct blood descendants</note> cannot succeed to the lease.

And so, opinions vary. Some assert it can only be granted for three generations, according to the section on long-term leases, and that they should be understood as granted in this way even when they are granted "absolutely" or "in perpetuity." Others, however, assert it can indeed be granted in perpetuity according to the cited section on "licensing," but not for outsiders—only for descendants—since on this point, the law has not been found to be corrected. Finally, others affirm it can be granted in perpetuity for any heirs or successors whatsoever, even outsiders. This matter is to be settled by the following conclusions.

<margin>1</margin> **First conclusion.** For a just cause, and with the legal formal ceremonies intervening (of which we spoke in the preceding disputation), church property can be granted in a perpetual long-term lease, even for outside heirs. And it is to be understood as granted in that way if it is said: "I grant this property to you in a perpetual long-term lease, even for outside heirs," or if it is said: "for any heirs whatsoever," or "for any 

<column-break/>

successors whatsoever," or "for whomever you please to leave it." This conclusion is held by **Panormitanus** (as cited above, numbers 28 and 29), **Felynus** (number 27), and is the common opinion, as reported and followed by **Covarrubias** (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 16, number 5, conclusions 3 and 4) and **Julius Clarus** (Book 4, *Sententiae*, section on long-term leases, question 6, number 4, and question 25, numbers 5, 9, and 10).

Indeed, this is proven not only because the law in the *Authenticum* on alienation and long-term leases corrected and extended the earlier prohibition so that church property could be granted in perpetual lease; since it added no limitation, it follows that they can be granted even for outside heirs and successors. This is how it should be understood as long as it is sufficiently expressed, as it is in the words proposed in our conclusion. 

But it is proven most of all because—as Panormitanus notes above, and as Julius Clarus pursues more broadly in the cited question 28—when a specific provision is given in **Canon Law** <note>Church law</note> regarding its own proper subject matter, such as this matter of the transfer of church property, the two heirs and the formality prescribed by **Civil Law** <note>original: "iure civili"; secular Roman law</note> regarding it are considered. Therefore, since Canon Law, while otherwise prohibiting all types of transfer of Church property, has granted all of them without any exception when a due cause and the formalities explained in the preceding disputation occur together, and since it has not excepted anything or established anything in that regard concerning long-term leases, it follows that just as it is lawful to transfer church property entirely when a legitimate cause and formality occur, it is much more valid and lawful to hand them over in perpetual lease, even for outsiders. This is provided that a legitimate cause and due formality occur, and that it is understood to have been handed over in that way when it is sufficiently expressed, as it is in the words discussed in our conclusion. 

Nevertheless, as Panormitanus observes above, it must be noted that a just cause may often exist for granting a lease for a certain number of lives, but not for granting it in perpetuity. This is because the former might be advantageous to the church, while the latter might not, and this for many reasons.

And this seems to be the reason why in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> and elsewhere, they are most often customarily granted for three lives and not in perpetuity, and why it was so enacted in the law regarding non-alienation. Yet, in my judgment, a sufficient cause will rarely occur to grant it only so that it passes to descendants and not to outsiders, even though it could be ended somewhat more easily with a clause stating it only goes to descendants, rather than a clause stating it can also go to outsiders.

<margin>2</margin> **Indeed, there is no small debate among the learned doctors: if a church property is handed over for just cause and with due formality in a perpetual lease to someone and his heirs, should it be considered granted only to his descending heirs, or truly also to ancestors and any other outside heirs?** I say this if the church property is granted in that manner: because everyone agrees that if it is *not* a church lease, and it is granted in that way, the name of "heirs" is understood to include anyone, even outsiders; because he...

the name of "heirs" <note>original: "hæredis nomen"</note>, how far it extends, including even outsiders <note>original: "extraneos"; those who are not blood descendants</note>, and if there is nothing in that long-term lease <note>term: <term>emphyteusis</term>—a type of perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</note> that suggests a restriction should be made to descendants alone. This is the view held by Alvaro Valasco in *On the Right of Long-term Leases*, question 39, number 9, following the law *prædia* in the Digest *familiæ erciscundæ*, as well as Caldas in *On the Naming of Long-term Leases*, question 23, number 11 and following, and Julius Clarus, question 28, cited at number 6, which is the common opinion he reports. 

However, the reason for disputing this in the case of a **Church lease** <note>original: "emphyteusi Ecclesiastica"</note> is as follows: In the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Roman laws by Justinian</note> regarding the prohibition of alienation, in the section on long-term leases, it is decreed that a Church lease is only granted to two descendants—or, what is the same thing, only to the third generation. Therefore, under the name of "heirs," only descendants would seem to be understood in such a lease, unless something else is explicitly stated. 

This view, based on that foundation alone, is the more common opinion of the doctors and is received in many regions, as Julius Clarus reports extensively at number 6. He does not dare to depart from it, although he says the opposite view seems truer in point of law. This same opinion (that the broader view is truer in law) is embraced by Alvaro Valasco and Caldas, especially at numbers 25 and 26. The Portuguese Senators followed this in a sentence which Gama reports as having been handed down in Decision 50, numbers 3 and 4. Truly, what Gama argues there to the contrary regarding the disposition of **Portuguese law** <note>original: "legis Lusitanæ"</note> which he cites has no weight; for, as we showed in Disputation 446, that Portuguese law has no force regarding Church leases, but only regarding secular ones. They followed the same in Decision 72, number 1, and Decision 326, numbers 4 and 5. 

The contrary opinion—namely, that in such a grant, outsiders should also be understood under the name of "heirs"—was held by Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> and is followed by Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 16, number 5, conclusion 4. However, Covarruvias adds that the opposite view is safer. Many others follow this, whom Julius Clarus cites, noting that it is the accepted practice in many other places. These authors are led by the fact that the name "heirs" most properly includes even outsiders. Furthermore, the *Authenticum* regarding non-alienation was later corrected and extended by the *Authenticum* regarding alienation and long-term leases, in the section "licentiam," without any limitation to descendants. Moreover, that civil decree does not bind in Ecclesiastical matters, especially since the sacred canons later allowed the alienation of Church property for every kind of case, provided there was a just cause and the proper ceremonies. 

I judge this opinion to be true with this limitation: that where a custom has been received that in a Church lease, under the name of "heirs," only descendants are understood when nothing else has been sufficiently expressed, that custom should be upheld. This is because a contract is considered to have been celebrated according to the custom of the place. This is observed by Panormitanus and Julius Clarus, and it is the common opinion of the doctors which they report. In this matter of long-term leases, one must stand by the custom in similar cases.

<margin>3</margin> **Second conclusion.** If a Church lease is granted anew, with a legitimate cause

<column-break/>

existing and the proper ceremonies observed, but it is granted in this form—"I grant you this thing in long-term lease"—without expressing the time it should last or to whom it should pass, it is considered granted to the recipient and two of his descendants only. If, however, it is a **secular lease** <note>original: "emphyteusis non Ecclesiastica"</note>, it requires neither a specific cause nor formal ceremonies to be granted, and it is considered granted for the life of the recipient and his two successors, whether they be descendants or outsiders. This is affirmed by Julius Clarus and Covarruvias, and it is the common opinion they report. 

The reason is both because the cited law so disposes it, and when nothing else is expressed, it must be judged as such—especially where the custom is to grant it regularly in that way, as is the **custom in Portugal**. It is also because a sufficient cause is more frequently present to grant it in this way, rather than in perpetuity. When it is not to be considered granted in perpetuity, and the "lives" are not specified, it should be estimated as granted in the manner most frequent in Church leases. I do not see why Julius Clarus, though he warns that practice should not depart from this doctrine, added that there is a "clear text" <note>original: "textum rotundum"</note> in the cited law stating that in this event it ends with the life of the person to whom it was granted; for no such thing is gathered from that section, but rather the contrary. Since a secular lease requires neither cause nor ceremony to be validly granted, and descendants and outsiders may succeed indifferently in it, the latter part of the conclusion is certainly true—especially where even secular leases are accustomed to be granted for three lives, as in Portugal.

<margin>4</margin> Hence it must be said that if a long-term lease is acquired by **title of prescription** <note>original: "titulo præscriptionis"; gaining legal rights through long-term uninterrupted use</note>, it is not considered prescribed for a longer time than for three lives—either of descendants only, if it is a Church lease, or also of outsiders, if it is secular. The reason is that a title acquired by prescription is not considered to cover a longer time than the minimum, and especially that which is most frequently accustomed to be handed down. Thus it is with Baldus and Covarruvias.

<margin>5</margin> **Third conclusion.** If a long-term lease is granted "up to the third generation": since a "generation" is only made by comparison of descendants, such a lease does not pass to outsiders, even if it is not a Church lease, but only to descendants. This is very well known, and Julius Clarus affirms it.

<margin>6</margin> **Fourth conclusion.** When a long-term lease is granted for a fixed number of years, if it is not a Church lease, it passes within 그 time to any successors, even if nothing else was expressed. Julius Clarus considers the same to be truer even if it is a Church lease, although he says it is doubtful whether it passes only to descendants within that time; in this, he does not seem very consistent with himself. However, according to the opinion we followed at the end of the first conclusion, it must be said that it also passes to outsiders.

7 **Fifth conclusion.** If a piece of Church property is not being granted as a long-term lease <note>term: <term>emphyteusis</term>—a type of perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a lower rent</note> for the first time, but rather, once a previous lease has ended and before the property is re-incorporated into the Church's main holdings, it is granted again, then it may be granted without the new legal formalities usually required for the disposal <note>original: "alienandū"; the legal transfer of property rights</note> of assets. This is allowed provided that the "just cause" (the valid reason) for leasing it out in that specific way still exists, even if it passes to outsiders <note>original: "extraneos"; those who are not direct family heirs</note>, if that was the original arrangement. However, if the terms of this new lease exceed the original terms, the grant is invalid regarding that excess. Likewise, if the "just cause" for leasing it in perpetuity or to outsiders no longer exists, the grant will only be valid for the portion or duration for which a valid reason remains. This entire conclusion is clear from what was said in the final conclusion of the previous dispute. I am actually surprised by Julius Clarus, who—while agreeing with us on other points in his cited question 28, number 6—makes an exception here. He claims that even if all conditions in this conclusion are met, the property cannot pass to outsiders unless the full legal formalities for a complete transfer of property are performed again (an opinion Diego de Covarruvias also seems to share at number 5). In truth, this is not a brand-new transfer of property, but rather a continuation of the old transfer based on a sufficient cause. We assume in our conclusion that this cause persists and that the property was originally granted under those terms.

8 **Final conclusion.** In places where there is an established custom that Church property can be leased out without the legal formalities required by common law—as Julius Clarus affirms is the case in many places (citing the legal scholars Speculator and Azo)—then such a lease is valid. This holds true as long as the custom is locally accepted, even if it includes the understanding that "heirs" can include outsiders. I see no reason why this should be an exception if the custom supports it, since custom can easily take precedence over specific laws, no less than it can over Canon laws that establish certain ceremonies. However, in cases of doubt as to whether such a custom exists, I do not dislike the opinion of Julius Clarus and Covarruvias: that under the name of "heirs," only direct descendants should be understood unless the contract explicitly states otherwise. These things are said here so it may be understood how far Church property can be leased and by whom. The remaining details will be added a little further down when we discuss the succession of long-term leases in general.

# Whether the possessor of a majorat can lease out the property of the majorat, and concerning other types of alienation.

## DISPUTATION 470.

### SUMMARY.

1 *The possessor of a majorat <note>term: <term>maioratus</term>—an "entail" or "majorat," a legal arrangement where an estate is passed down to a single heir, usually the eldest son, and cannot be sold or divided</note> cannot grant majorat property in a long-term lease.*
*And what about an easement <note>term: <term>servitutem</term>—the right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, like a path or water access</note>: can he establish one on the aforementioned property? Number 2.*
3 *How many types of transfer are considered forbidden under the*

<column-break/>

*prohibition of transferring any property.*
4 *The possessor of a majorat can grant the benefit of a usufruct <note>term: <term>vfusfructus</term>—the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property without owning it</note> or another easement to someone for the duration of their life, provided it is a personal obligation only, not a permanent legal claim on the land.*
5 *Whether a majorat possessor can grant a usufruct on the estate that lasts only as long as he himself is the lord of the majorat, and when.*
*And what if he is a son still under his father's authority: can the father hold the usufruct? Number 6 and decided at number 10.*
7 *A true usufruct is a type of alienation (transfer of rights).*
8 *The interpretation of the law "I ask" (l. peto), section "the estate" (prædium) in the Digest.*
9 *When the Treasury <note>original: "Fifcus"</note> can acquire a usufruct in the goods of a majorat that is forbidden from being sold.*
11 *The possessor of a majorat cannot grant majorat goods in a long-term lease for the first time without the permission of the founder's terms or the King.*
*This fails if there is a custom to the contrary, as in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>. Number 11.*
*The same must be said regarding long-term rentals. Number 12.*
*Indeed, they cannot even be subjected to a general mortgage, just as is the case with Church property. Number 14.*

Regarding the possessor of a majorat, although this section only strictly requires us to examine whether he can lease out majorat property (and thus rent it for a long period, which is a type of long-term lease, as is clear from what has been said), these issues are easily explained by the principles discussed regarding Church property and long-term leases. Therefore, we should briefly discuss all types of property transfer <note>original: "alienationis"</note> regarding majorat property.

<margin>1</margin>
By the very fact that property is tied to the bond of a majorat—both by the legal disposition that allows such bonds and by the act of the person who founded the majorat—it is understood that the property is forbidden from being sold or transferred. This is to ensure the estate is preserved whole and undivided, passing to all those called to the succession by the founder. This is part of the very nature of a majorat, as explained elsewhere by Molina and others. Consequently, all types of transfer are not only forbidden to the possessor, but if attempted, they are void by law and cannot harm the future heirs.

<margin>2</margin>
However, as we said regarding the long-term tenant and the feudal holder in dispute 461, they have a "useful ownership" <note>term: <term>dominium vtile</term>—the right to use and benefit from property, distinguished from "direct ownership" or legal title</note>. Because of this, they can grant an easement on the land without the owner's consent, provided it only lasts as long as their own lease or feudal right lasts, and does not harm the owner or the next heir. Similarly, because a majorat possessor has not only the useful ownership but also the "direct ownership" <note>original: "directum dominium"</note> of the property while he lives (and has not lost his right to the majorat), he can grant an easement to someone without asking the next heir. This easement would only last as long as he himself remains the possessor and lord of the majorat property, and would bring no harm to the successor.

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...bring a judgment. Thus Molina, in book 1 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 2, number 1 and following; Aires Pinellus on the Code regarding maternal goods, part 3, at the end of number 71; and Padilla on the Code regarding servitudes, number 33. These authors prove the points we made regarding this matter in Dispute 461, as well as other points cited by Molina in the place mentioned above. Antonio Gomez, in his commentary on Law 40 of Toro, number 85, holds the opposite opinion. His reasoning is that someone who is prohibited from **transferring** <note>original: "alienare"; to legally sell or give away</note> a property is also prohibited from imposing a **servitude** <note>term: <term>servitude</term>—a legal right to use another person’s land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way</note> upon it, as is established in the final law of the Code *On things that cannot be alienated*. Therefore, just as he cannot impose a servitude for the time after his life, he also cannot do so for the time while he is alive and holds ownership of that property.

Molina, in the same work (numbers 4 and 14), states that when the assets of an **entailed estate** <note>term: <term>majorat</term> (Latin: *maioratus*)—an inheritance of landed property that is legally bound to pass to the eldest son or a specific line of heirs, preventing it from being sold or divided</note> are only prohibited from being transferred by the general disposition of the law and the nature of the entail itself, then—just as a long-term tenant <note>term: <term>emphyteuta</term></note> or a feudal vassal can grant a servitude that lasts only as long as they hold their respective rights—the possessor of an entailed estate can likewise grant a similar servitude. In this specific scenario, Molina considers the opinion of Aires Pinellus and Padilla to be preferable to that of Antonio Gomez.

However, Molina adds that when the person who originally established the entail included a specific clause prohibiting the transfer of the estate's assets, then the granting of a servitude is invalid, even for the period during which the person granting it possesses the estate. The logic is that a double prohibition—one from the law and one from the founder of the entail—is stronger and must extend to more cases than the simple legal prohibition alone. In this specific case, he judges Antonio Gomez’s opinion to be superior to those of Aires, Pinellus, and Padilla.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Indeed, I do not think this reasoning of Molina is firm enough, unless the specific clause prohibiting transfer has a broader reach than the general legal prohibition and the nature of the entail. For example, it would have to explicitly state that no servitude can be granted, even during the lifetime of the possessor's ownership. For although two bonds might bind more tightly than one, they do not encompass more objects or extend further than a single bond unless the second bond specifically adds a broader scope. If an oath is added to confirm a valid promise, although the oath binds more strongly than the promise alone, it does not extend to more things than were contained in the original promise. Furthermore, the final law of the Code *On things that cannot be alienated*...

<margin>3</margin>
...which explains how many and what types of transfers are considered prohibited when a thing is forbidden from being alienated, speaks regardless of whether the prohibition comes from the law or a private individual, and whether it is made by contract or a final will. The commentary there rightly teaches and proves that whether the prohibition is by law or by will, the transfer is invalid *ipso facto* <note>meaning "by the fact itself" or "automatically"</note> if it is attempted or carried out against that prohibition. Therefore, all types of transfer listed in that law are considered prohibited, and none are valid regarding the assets of an entailed estate by the mere disposition of law and the nature of the institution itself. Therefore, even if a clause from the founder of the entail is added to prohibit the transfer of those assets, unless that clause expresses more or creates a larger...

<column-break/>

...extension of the rule that is clear from the words of the clause itself, no more things are considered prohibited by that clause than were already prohibited by the general law and the nature of the entail. Thus, despite the aforementioned law of the Code which states that a prohibition on transferring a thing includes a prohibition on imposing a servitude, it is sufficiently clear from other sources that this should be understood as referring to a **permanent** servitude.

It is different for a servitude that does not transfer the **beneficial ownership** <note>term: <term>utile dominium</term>—the right to use and profit from property, as distinguished from the legal title held by the direct owner</note> and only lasts while the granter remains in possession. Such a servitude does not bring any prejudice or harm to the successor in the estate or to the direct lord, even if the person granted the servitude acquires a right for that specific duration. It follows, then, that even if there is a strict clause from the founder prohibiting transfer, unless it explicitly states that one cannot grant a servitude (even one that does not transfer beneficial ownership and only lasts during the granter's possession), that clause should not be interpreted as prohibiting it. This is because such an act is not truly a "transfer" of the family assets, nor does it harm the assets or the future heirs—which is the only thing the law and the founders of entails are presumed to want to prevent.

At this point, observe that neither Antonio Gomez nor Molina denies that, even with an express prohibition from the founder, a possessor of an entailed estate can grant someone the convenience of **usufruct** <note>term: <term>usufruct</term>—the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property for a time, usually for life, without damaging it</note> or any other servitude for the duration of their own life. This is allowed as long as it is not granted as a "right in the thing" (a real right) but only as a personal obligation of the granter to allow the use. In fact, Molina admits this in numbers 12 and 13, along with many others he cites. The controversy we have examined and defined here concerns a servitude granted with a "right in the thing" for the duration of the granter's life; this is properly called a servitude, but only for that time and without prejudice to the successors.

Regarding usufruct, Molina (in the cited chapter 20, number 5 and following) asserts, along with many others, that if there is only the legal prohibition inherent in the nature of the entail, the possessor can indeed grant a true usufruct in the estate's assets that lasts as long as they are the lord of the estate. However, if an additional prohibition was made by the founder, then such a grant is invalid. He argues that the double prohibition is stronger and extends to more things, as he said of other servitudes. In that case, he says that even during the life of the current possessor, the **successor** to the entail (and not the possessor himself) can revoke that transfer, following the rules of the laws *cum pater* and *quoties* in the Digest and Code.

He holds the same view regarding other servitudes. In the same way, he says, if there is only the legal prohibition and the possessor of the estate commits a crime for which...

### Second Treatise. Dispute 470.

that his goods should be confiscated, then the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"; the state or royal coffers</note> acquires the true **usufruct** <note>term: <term>usufruct</term> (Latin: *ususfructus*)—the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another, provided the property itself remains undamaged</note> of the assets of that **entailed estate** <note>term: <term>majorat</term> (Latin: *maioratus*)—an inheritance of landed property bound to a specific line of heirs</note> for the entire duration of the possessor who committed the crime. If, however, he says, the founder of the majorat prohibited the **alienation** <note>original: "alienationem"; the legal transfer of ownership to another</note> of those assets, then the treasury does not acquire the usufruct of those goods. This is because it would follow that an alienation to the treasury was taking place, since usufruct is considered a type of alienation, as held in the final law of the Code *On things that cannot be alienated*. Instead, the treasury acquires the right to perceive the **benefit** <note>original: "commoditatem"</note> of those assets, in the place and name of the offender, for as long as the offender lives; he cites many others in support of this opinion.

Following this same opinion and doctrine, the same author [Molina], in chapter 19 of the preceding sections, teaches several points concerning the usufruct which a father holds over the assets of a majorat belonging to a **son under paternal authority** <note>term: <term>filius familias</term>—a son who, regardless of age, remains under the legal control and "power" of his father</note>. These points are simple and should be examined alongside those previously reported from the same author. <margin>6</margin> First, from number 18: because the possessor of a majorat is the "owner" of the majorat’s assets and not merely a "bare usufructuary," he correctly infers that when the possessor of a majorat is a son under paternal authority, the father is entitled to the usufruct of those bound assets, just as he is to the rest of the assets of the same son while he remains under the father's power. In number 20, he correctly adds that although the father's usufruct over a son's goods does not normally expire upon the son's death but continues for the father's entire life, in the case of **entailed assets** <note>original: "bonis vinculatis"; literally "chained" or legally bound assets</note> or assets subject to restitution for any other reason, the usufruct expires and immediately passes to the successor along with the ownership. The reason is that this depends on the will of the majorat's founder, who decreed that the entire thing should pass immediately to the successor. Furthermore, the father did not hold the usufruct except as it depended on those goods remaining the son's; they ought not to pass to another in their entirety according to the founder's will.

And all these things we, along with Antonio Gomez (Law 48 of Toro, number 4), taught above in Dispute 232. He also correctly observes, following Rodrigo Suarez and Molina (at the same number 24), that if the majorat had been established by the King himself from assets donated by him for that purpose, then—because the son is considered to have received the gift from the King and not from the previous possessor—the father would certainly not have the usufruct in those assets. This is because a father does not have usufruct in the assets of a son under his authority that were donated to him by the King, as we showed in Dispute 8. However, if the King had donated certain assets to someone so that they might establish a majorat, which eventually came to a son under paternal authority, then, as Rodrigo Suarez correctly states, those assets would not be considered a gift from the King to that son. Consequently, the father would have the usufruct of those assets for as long as the son remained under his power. These points are correct and do not strictly pertain to the present undertaking.

He adds in the same place (number 29) that if the founder of the majorat included a clause in the foundation prohibiting the majorat's assets from being alienated, then, <margin>7</margin> since true usufruct is a form of alienation—as is clear from the final law of the Code *On things that cannot be alienated*—the father will not have the usufruct in the assets of his son’s majorat, though he will have the entire "benefit" of the same assets. He is led to this (as is clearly 

<column-break/>

evident, since he refers the reader to those points we reported from him in the first place regarding usufruct) because the legal prohibition, arising from the nature and institution of a majorat, against alienating the assets does not prevent the granting of other **servitudes** <note>term: <term>servitude</term>—a right of way or easement</note> upon the majorat's assets. Such servitudes only last while the one granting them remains the owner and do not prejudice the successors. Likewise, it does not prevent the granting of a usufruct that similarly lasts [only for the term of ownership] and does not prejudice the successors. However, an *express* prohibition by the founder, in his opinion, will prevent the granting of other servitudes and also prevents the granting or acquisition of "true usufruct," as was reported from him above.

In the same place, from number 30, Molina adds that if the founder of the majorat specifically prohibited parents from having usufruct in the majorat’s assets when it comes to their children, then they are not usufructuaries of those assets; this is sufficiently clear from what we said in Dispute 8. However, as to whether they then have the "benefit" of those assets, he mentions Angelus and certain others answering affirmatively, while Rodrigo Suarez and Gregorio Lopez doubt that teaching. He himself judges that they should not even have the benefit then, because the intent of the majorat's founder in that event is not to be cheated by legal subtleties. Indeed, he advises founders of majorats that if they wish to exclude parents—who will sometimes be outsiders to the founder's family—from the benefit of usufruct and to cut off doubts and lawsuits, they should express this by saying that they shall perceive neither usufruct nor benefit from those goods. Instead, they should receive only a certain amount for the administration of the assets, or only a certain amount from the fruits or rents, and from the remainder, they should buy rents or other immovable property, whereby the majorat increases.

All these things must be examined one by one. And beginning from the first: namely, whether the possessor of a majorat <margin>Decision 2</margin> can grant a true usufruct in the majorat’s assets (regarding mere "benefit," there is no one who doubts it, as was said in Dispute 465 and 466) that lasts only as long as he himself is the owner of those assets, when no specific prohibition against alienation was made by the founder. It must be argued *against* what Molina asserted.

Specifically, it must be said that it cannot be granted, or if it is granted, the grant is invalid. This is due to the points made in a similar question regarding the **long-term tenant** <note>term: <term>emphyteuta</term></note> and the **feudal vassal** <note>term: <term>feudatarius</term></note> in Dispute 461. For the reasoning is not the same for other servitudes (by which **useful ownership** <note>term: <term>dominium utile</term>—the right to use and profit from property, as opposed to holding the legal title</note> is not transferred) as it is for usufruct, by which useful ownership is transferred to the usufructuary, even if it is granted only for the time of the majorat's possessor, as was said there.

Hence, in the final law of the Code *On things that cannot be alienated*, usufruct is distinguished from other servitudes as a distinct species or mode of alienation. Nor should that which is found as an exception in the law regarding other servitudes be applied—namely, that they can be granted by a long-term tenant or feudal vassal (since they hold useful ownership in the leased or feudal property) without the consent of the title-owner, for only the time that the grantors...

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding whether the possessor of an entailed estate (majorat) can grant a usufruct to another party, and how this relates to the general prohibition against transferring such property out of the family line.</meta>

# Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

...either as feudal lords or holders of a **majorat** <note>original: "maioratûs"; a landed estate that must descend to a specific heir and cannot be sold</note>, and the same is rightly said of a possessor of a majorat who holds even the **direct ownership** <note>term: <term>direct ownership</term> (Latin: *dominium directum*)—the legal title to property, as opposed to the right to use it</note> of the assets. This must also be extended to a true **usufruct** <note>term: <term>usufruct</term> (Latin: *usufructus*)—the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note>, which is a distinct and far greater method of **alienation** <note>original: "alienationis"; the legal transfer of property to another</note> than other **servitudes** <note>term: <term>servitude</term> (Latin: *servitutes*)—a right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, like a right of way</note>, seeing as it transfers the **beneficial ownership** <note>term: <term>beneficial ownership</term> (Latin: *dominium utile*)—the right to the use and profits of land, even if someone else holds the legal title</note>. This is especially true since that exception regarding other servitudes deviates from common law and should not have been granted concerning things prohibited from being alienated, unless it were found to be granted by law; and exceptions that deviate from the law should not be extended further than they are found to be granted. Furthermore, the foundation upon which Molina relies—namely, that the prohibition of alienation by the founder of a majorat extends further, together with the prohibition of law, nature, and the institution of the majorat itself, than this latter prohibition would extend on its own—is entirely false, as has been copiously proved above regarding other servitudes. Therefore, since he concedes that if a prohibition is made by the founder of the majorat (without specifically mentioning usufruct) it cannot even be granted for the life of the possessor, it must also be said that no grant of usufruct for the life of the possessor of the majorat is valid, even if no prohibition of alienation was expressed by the founder, but only the prohibition of the law, of nature, and of the institution of the majorat itself.

But if you should object to us the law *peto*, paragraph *prędium* <note>original: "l. peto. §. prędium: ff. de leg. 2"; a reference to the Digest of Roman Law, Book 31, Title 1, Law 77, Paragraph 12</note>, with which paragraph Molina confirms his opinion, and where it is held that if an estate is left to someone bound so that it does not leave the family (and thus prohibited from being alienated to outsiders), and due to the necessary debts of such an heir it is sold by a **necessary alienation**—that is, by the authority of a judge and for a price to satisfy the debts—then the buyer can retain that estate for as long as the possessor was going to hold it. However, upon the possessor's death, if no heir succeeds who is from the family, the estate shall revert to the family, and such an outside heir must restore it to the family, provided the buyer is satisfied.

<margin>8</margin>
If you object this to us, observe first that there is no talk there of any alienation other than a sale. Thus, if anything were gathered against us, it would follow that majorat goods could be sold for the duration of the possessor's life, which no one would say. Next, observe that the text only speaks of a *necessary* alienation; therefore, by reasoning from the opposite sense, it clearly hints that the contrary should be said of a *voluntary* alienation—namely, that the buyer cannot retain it even for the time the prior possessor was to have it. Thus, that text actually fights for us, who are disputing only voluntary alienation.

What is established in that text is this: because the possessor did not alienate it himself, but a judge did so to pay his debt, the buyer may retain it only as long as that individual was to possess it and while it was not yet due to pass to another in the family. For in the meantime, this outside buyer possesses it by public authority in the place of that other family member, which in effect is nothing other than granting him the benefit of that estate for all that time which he perceives in the name of the person who was to retain it.

Regarding what Molina adds—namely, that if a clause from the founder of the majorat preceded it which prohibited the alienation of those goods, because the grant of a true usufruct in those goods is then invalid,

<column-break/>

even for the life of the possessor of the majorat (and we say the same by force of the prohibition of law alone, and from the nature and institution of the majorat, even if such a clause is not added)—that in such a case, not the possessor himself, but the successor in the majorat can revoke that alienation during the life of the possessor; this, I say, is certainly not approved by us, unless it is understood in the event that by that alienation the possessor of the majorat would incur the penalty of immediately losing the majorat or the alienated property to the successor. Yet Molina does not mean it this way.

Since the possessor of the majorat does not incur that penalty, he is undoubtedly the one who, while he lives, can revoke that alienation as being void by the law itself. If, however, he granted it by an **onerous contract** <note>term: <term>onerous contract</term>—a contract where both parties give and receive something of value (like a sale or lease)</note>, he will be bound to the person to whom he granted it, either for **eviction** <note>term: <term>eviction</term> (Latin: *evictio*)—the recovery of property from a purchaser by a third party with a better legal title; the seller must usually compensate the buyer</note> or to refund what he received for it, according to the concurrent circumstances. The two laws which Molina cites in confirmation of his opinion clearly speak of when the person who alienates a thing loses the thing so alienated by that very act to others in the family, who can immediately claim it. For since no right to that thing then remains with the old possessor, but only with others of the family, those laws rightly stand, so that not the old possessor, but the others of the family may claim it.

For the case proposed in those laws is when a thing is left to many people with the burden that the thing shall not leave the family, but whoever alienates a part of it shall lose it to the rest of the family. If one then alienates a part without the consent of the others, the rest can claim it, even if some of them later alienated their own parts; but the one who alienated it cannot claim it, as established by those laws. And always, those who did not alienate nor consent to the alienation will be able to claim the parts alienated by others, and not those who alienated them. But when all have alienated or consented to the alienation, then none of them can claim what was so alienated, as those laws establish.

<margin>9</margin>
Furthermore, what Molina adds—namely, that if a possessor of a majorat falls into a **crime** <note>original: "crimen"; likely referring to treason or another high crime resulting in asset forfeiture</note> for which his goods are confiscated, and no clause preceded it by which the founder prohibited those goods from being alienated, the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"; the state or royal coffers</note> acquires a true usufruct in the goods of that majorat for as long as that possessor lives; but if such a clause did precede it, the treasury does not acquire a true usufruct, but only the right to the benefit to be perceived from those goods in the place and name of the offender—this, I say, as to the first point Molina asserts, is not approved by us. For in either event, it does not acquire a true usufruct, because the prohibition of alienation of those goods, which is made by the disposition of law and from the nature and institution of the majorat, is sufficient to prevent its acquisition, as has been said and proved by us. Because even then the possessor of the majorat holds the beneficial and direct ownership of those goods, which cannot pass to the treasury by force of the institution of the majorat; and by reason of that ownership and right, there belongs to him even then the right to the entire benefit from those goods for the whole time of his life; when, by force of the institution of the same majorat, by reason of the crime, both do not pass...

The author emphasizes that the law protects the family's right to the estate even in cases of debt or criminal confiscation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights within an entailed estate (maioratus), specifically focusing on whether a father retains the right to the income (usufruct) of an estate held by his son, and the rules governing long-term leases (emphyteusis).</meta>

->Second Treatise, Disputation 470.<-

...ownership remains with the successor in the **majorat** <note>original: "maioratu"; a legal arrangement where an estate is inherited by a single heir to keep it within the family</note>. In either event, the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscum"; the state or royal coffers</note> only looks to the right of receiving the benefit from those goods for the duration of the delinquent's life, in the name and place of the offender, as was stated in Disputation 9.

This concludes the first of those points we cited from Molina.

<margin>10</margin>
As for the second point, it must be said: whether the goods of the majorat are prohibited from being **alienated** <note>term: <term>alienation</term> (Latin: *alienari*)—the act of transferring property or rights to another person</note> solely by the disposition of the law and the nature and institution of the majorat, or by a clause added by the founder of the majorat—provided that it does not specifically forbid the father from having the **usufruct** <note>term: <term>usufruct</term> (Latin: *vsumfructum*)—the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> of those goods should they pass to a **dependent son** <note>term: <term>dependent son</term> (Latin: *filium-familias*)—a son who remains under the legal authority of his father</note>—the father is truly the usufructuary of those goods.

The foundation I rely upon for this claim is as follows: in a general prohibition, whether issued by law or by a person, something is not considered included if it did not enter the mind of the one making the disposition, nor was he moved to prohibit it, and which he would have excepted had he been asked. Just as in a general grant, something does not pass which the grantor would not have granted specifically (following the general **rule of law** <note>original: "reg. iuris"; referring to the "Regulae Iuris" or Rules of Law in the Sixth Book of Decretals</note> in the 6th book). Therefore, since the father's true usufruct in the majorat goods of a dependent son does not prevent the majorat goods from passing whole to the successor at the proper time, nor causes them to be divided or diminished—which is why the law and the founders of majorats are moved to prohibit their alienation—and since the usufruct of all **adventitious goods** <note>term: <term>adventitious goods</term> (Latin: *bonorum aduentitiorum*)—property acquired by a child from a source other than their father</note> of a dependent son is granted to the father by law (among which are majorat goods), and the **administration** <note>original: "administratio"</note> of those goods belongs to the father for that entire time: it is not consistent with reason that the law, through a general prohibition of the alienation of majorat goods, intended to block the father's usufruct while the son is alive and under his power. This is something Molina himself concedes. For, through **equity** <note>term: <term>equity</term> (Latin: *epicheiam*)—the interpretation of a law according to its spirit and fairness rather than its strict literal letter</note>, those things which right reason teaches the legislators and disposers did not intend to include must always be excepted from general laws and dispositions.

Moreover, if the father's usufruct in those goods is not included in the general prohibition of alienation by law—arising from the nature and institution of the majorat—as Molina asserts, it certainly will not be included in the prohibition of the founder of the majorat when he made no mention of the father's usufruct. Furthermore, as has been shown, the prohibition of the founder, alongside the legal prohibition, does not extend to more things than the latter unless there is a specific expression of those things not covered by the legal prohibition. Above all, it is ridiculous to believe that a founder, by his general prohibition, intended to forbid the father's legal usufruct of the son's majorat goods, but did *not* intend to forbid the general **benefit** <note>original: "commoditatem"; the practical use or profit</note> of those goods. There is no reason why, while leaving the benefit (which is equivalent to usufruct) to the father, he would forbid the legal usufruct itself. Yet Molina, in his opinion, asserts that the founder, by prohibiting alienation, blocks the father's usufruct while nonetheless leaving him the entire benefit of those goods.

Regarding the controversy that Molina subjoins—

<column-break/>

if the founder of the majorat expressly prohibits the father from having the usufruct in that majorat, does that father, though he lacks the usufruct, still possess the benefit of those goods while the son (the possessor of the majorat) remains under his power? Correcting the views of **Angelus** <note>likely Angelus de Ubaldis, a famous medieval jurist</note> and others, he rightly asserts that the father would then not even have the benefit. This is not only because the founder's will in that event makes it (as we said shortly before) ridiculous to think he intended to deprive the father of only the formal usufruct while leaving the benefit, which is equivalent in that case; but also because it must undoubtedly be stated according to the principles and disposition of the law itself. For civil law only granted the father the true right of usufruct in the adventitious goods of a dependent son (except for some cases explained by us in Disputation 8, of which this is one). Nowhere do we read that the law granted—either in those events or any other—the benefit of those goods while excluding the usufruct. Therefore, by the very fact that the father is prohibited by the founder from the usufruct of those goods, no right or title is left to him for the benefit. This reason is so evident that I consider it superfluous to add more to exclude the father from the benefit, even though Molina teaches it should be added for greater caution—though one might prudently add what the father ought to receive for the administration of those goods and what should be done with their revenues. However, **maintenance** <note>original: "alimenta"</note> for such a dependent son from the revenues of his majorat, appropriate to those revenues, ought deservedly to be left.

Regarding **emphyteusis** <note>term: <term>emphyteusis</term>—a long-term or perpetual lease of land where the tenant improves the property in exchange for a fixed rent</note>, since granting property in emphyteusis is a true species of alienation (as is clear from the final law of the Code *concerning things that may or may not be alienated*, and from what has been said previously), and since it transfers **beneficial ownership** <note>original: "dnium vtile"</note>, it is clear that

<margin>11</margin>
the possessor of a majorat cannot grant majorat properties anew in emphyteusis unless the power to do so was granted by the founder or obtained from the King; otherwise, the grant is void. So says Molina (Book 1 *on Primogeniture*, ch. 21, no. 31), **Aries Pinedus** (on the Code *concerning maternal goods*, part 3, no. 65), **Caldas** (*on renewal of emphyteusis*, question 16, from no. 1), and the common opinion of the Doctors which they cite. Furthermore, since emphyteusis transfers beneficial ownership, and since the possessor is not allowed to transfer the beneficial ownership of majorat property to another, the grant of majorat property in emphyteusis will be so invalid that it will be void for any period of time, including the duration for which it was given. The exception is if the founder permitted majorat property to be given in emphyteusis for a certain time (such as for specific lives), or if the King granted the power, or if it is accepted by prescribed custom in a place. In those cases, majorat property can be validly and lawfully granted in emphyteusis for that time; and even if it is granted for a longer period invalidly, the grant will be valid for the shorter period included within the longer one. So Molina (as above, no. 34), to whom **Gama** subscribes (Decision 192, no. 3). I also believe that if the person who founded the majorat included properties in it which others already held in emphyteusis, and did not decree that once the emphyteusis ended (provided there was no obligation to renew it) the properties should no longer be leased, the possessor of the majorat can grant them in emphyteusis again in precisely the same way they were customarily granted...

<summary>This page discusses whether a father can claim the income (usufruct) from an entailed estate inherited by his son and concludes that general bans on selling the property do not usually strip a father of these rights unless the founder specifically says so. It also explains that long-term leases (emphyteusis) are considered a form of selling the property and are generally forbidden without special permission.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights within an entailed estate (majorat), focusing on whether these lands can be leased long-term or used as collateral for debts, specifically referencing Portuguese law and the opinions of legal scholars like Molina and Gama.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

The reason is that the bond of the **majorat** <note>original: "maioratus"; an inheritance system where an estate is kept whole and passed to a single heir, usually the eldest son</note> is not considered to extend further than to the property in the state in which it then exists, nor does it prohibit any **alienation** <note>the transfer of ownership or rights to another</note> except that which would degrade the property from that state.

<margin>12</margin>
Although Gama <note>Antonio da Gama, a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> in Decision 192 concedes that if the founder of a majorat or a **chapel** <note>a religious endowment often attached to family estates</note> prohibits the goods bound in the majorat or chapel from being alienated—specifically mentioning that they should not be granted in **emphyteusis** <note>term: <term>emphyteusis</term> (Latin: *emphyteusim*)—a long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a fixed rent</note>—then such a grant is invalid not only in other places but even in Portugal. However, in Decisions 16 and 222 (numbers 3 and 4), he reports that when it was not specifically expressed that a grant in emphyteusis was forbidden, but was only inhibited by the general disposition of the law or by the nature and institution of the majorat (or even by a general prohibition of alienation by the founder), there has been controversy in Portugal. The question was whether a grant of majorat property in emphyteusis would then be invalid or not, and there were various opinions on both sides. Nevertheless, it has been much more frequently ruled that such grants are valid, but only for **three lives** <note>original: "tres vitas"; a lease lasting for the duration of three successive generations of the tenant's family</note>, even if they had been granted for a longer time or in perpetuity.

This opinion is embraced primarily on the basis that it is an accepted custom in that Kingdom [Portugal] for the possessors of a majorat to grant property in emphyteusis, provided it is only for three lives and when not expressly forbidden by the founder. If that custom flourishes and is established in that Kingdom, there is no reason to doubt the matter. However, the fact that the matter remains controversial to this day, with rulings being pronounced on both sides, is a significant argument that the custom does not seem to be firmly established. Hence, Caldas <note>Fernão Diaz de Caldas, another contemporary jurist</note> in Question 16 (cited at the end, number 1), although not entirely faithful to what Gama teaches in Decision 192, absolutely embraces the contrary opinion from number 3 onward. He adds that Gama asserts there is a custom to the contrary in Portugal. In number 13, he explains the Portuguese ordinance which some thought permitted such goods to be granted in emphyteusis.

Molina, in the final number of the section cited above, judges that a possessor of a majorat who has invalidly granted a bound property in emphyteusis cannot revoke that alienation during his own lifetime; Gama subscribes to this in Decision 192, even when the founder expressly prohibited the majorat property from being granted in emphyteusis. However, Molina says the successor can revoke it even while the previous possessor (who granted the emphyteusis) is still alive, provided the founder of the majorat expressly prohibited the alienation of the majorat property. It is otherwise when it was not expressly prohibited, but the prohibition arises only from the law or the nature and institution of the majorat.

Although Molina does not explain the source of this doctrine, he is surely leaning on the same foundation from which he delivered similar teachings regarding the granting of **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> in majorat property. For our part, we must say what we said regarding that other matter: namely, if the possessor of the majorat who granted the emphyteusis does not incur the penalty of immediately losing those goods to the successor, then he himself (and not the successor) can revoke that alienation as being void

<column-break/>

by the law itself. If, however, because of that alienation he incurs the penalty of immediately losing those goods to the successor, then the successor can immediately claim those goods, but the one who alienated them cannot—and this is for the reasons stated regarding the granting of usufruct.

<margin>13</margin>
What has been said regarding emphyteusis is to be understood similarly regarding the leasing of majorat goods for a long period, because such a lease is truly an emphyteusis: it transfers the **useful ownership** <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right of a tenant to use and profit from land, as opposed to the "direct ownership" held by the lord or estate owner</note> to the tenant. Nevertheless, the possessor of a majorat may grant the entire benefit of the majorat goods for free as long as he lives, or even sell that benefit for a price for that entire time, or lease the majorat property (as far as receiving its fruits is concerned) not in his own name, but in the name and place of the possessor of the majorat for all that time. Since these things are clear from what was said in Disputation 466, joined with Disputations 445 and 461, there is no reason to say more on this.

<margin>14</margin>
The property of a majorat cannot be subjected to a **universal mortgage** <note>original: "hypothecae uniuersali"; a pledge of all of one's current and future assets as security for a debt</note>. In Disputation 466, it was said that the immovable property of the **Church** could be subjected to such a mortgage, even if it could not be subjected to a **particular mortgage** <note>a pledge of a specific, named piece of property</note> without a just cause and the legal formalities required for alienating Church property. The reason for the difference between Church property and majorat property is that subjecting Church property to a universal mortgage does not result in prejudice to a third party, but only to the Church itself, whose business is being conducted for its own benefit while the contract is celebrated. It is for the security of these contracts that Church property is subjected to a universal mortgage; because no one would want to contract with the Church unless its goods could be subjected to such a mortgage, it is permitted that they be validly subjected without the usual cause or formalities.

But truly, since subjecting majorat goods to a universal mortgage could lead to the consumption and dissipation of the majorat and the prejudice of successors, this is not found to be permitted, nor was it expedient to permit it. Especially since the contracts entered into by the possessor of a majorat would not result in the benefit of the majorat itself, but of the possessor, who could subject his other private goods to mortgage or find people to act as his **guarantors** <note>original: "fideiussores"; people who take responsibility for another's debt</note> and bind their own goods. Therefore, when a thing is prohibited from being alienated—as majorat goods are—it is considered forbidden to subject it to a mortgage, even a universal one, because of the "right in the thing" <note>original: "ius in re"</note> which the creditor thereby acquires, and because of the danger that follows: that the property might later be alienated and sold to pay the debt. This is clear from the law *lastly, Code, on the alienation of things not to be alienated* <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de reb. alie. non alien."; a reference to the Code of Justinian</note>. It follows, therefore, that since it is not found to be permitted for majorat goods (as it is for Church goods), they can in no way be validly subjected even to a universal mortgage, unless the prince grants a faculty for a reasonable cause, or the founder of the majorat permits it, which is almost never done.

Regarding other types of alienation by which **direct ownership** <note>original: "directum dominium"; the ultimate legal title to property</note> is transferred, it is clear that they are illicit and invalid concerning majorat goods, unless the prince's permission or the founder's consent in some event is obtained.

Treatise Second, Dispute 471.

# To what extent a long-term tenant may grant a sub-lease, and whether they retain beneficial ownership.

### DISPUTE 471.

->SUMMARY<-

1 **When a long-term tenant may again grant the property in a sub-lease or a "leveling" contract.**
2 **Whether a tenant sub-leasing the property transfers the beneficial ownership to the final tenant, or whether it remains with them, or exists in both simultaneously; decided in numbers 5, 6, and 11.**
3 **A King, if he holds a kingdom as a fief, is called the owner in one respect and a vassal in another.**
4 **The vassal of a vassal is bound to obey the supreme lord rather than his own immediate lord.**
**The same applies to a secondary long-term tenant.**
7 **Natural possession of the leased property, along with the "quasi-possession" of beneficial ownership, passes to the second tenant, such that the owner is said to possess it naturally through him.**
8 **What the right to rent and the penalty for forfeiture entails if the rent is not paid.**
9 **An owner buying the tenant's right from a second sub-tenant is bound to pay the increase in rent to the first tenant.**
10 **If the right of the first tenant is dissolved, the right of the second is dissolved by that very fact.**
11 **A vassal may sub-lease feudal property with the consent of the lord.**
13 **A second tenant who forfeits their right due to unpaid rent loses that right to the property owner, not to the first tenant.**
14 **A vassal can create a sub-fief in two ways.**

<margin>1</margin> In Dispute 461, following the common opinion of the scholars, we showed that a long-term tenant <note>term: <term>emphyteuta</term>—a person holding land under a long-term lease (emphyteusis) where they pay a fixed rent and improve the land</note> cannot grant the property in a sub-lease or a "leveling" contract <note>original: "liuellare"; referring to a *libellus* or written lease contract</note> without the consent of the property owner. This is because such an act is considered an <term>alienation</term> <note>the transfer of rights or ownership to another person</note> of the leased property, which is not permitted without the owner's permission.
<margin>1</margin> However, with the owner's consent, the tenant can indeed grant a sub-lease. This consent might be granted at the very beginning when the first contract was made (if it was included as a specific clause), or it might be provided later. In Portugal, this sub-leasing is known as <term>emprazar a face do seu prazo</term> <note>original Portuguese: "to lease out based on the face of one's term"</note> or <term>a sombra do seu prazo</term> <note>original Portuguese: "under the shadow of one's term"</note>. Although some authors cited by Alvaro Valasco <note>a 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> claimed that in certain places custom does not require the owner's consent for this, the custom in the Spanish kingdoms follows the general law in requiring it. This is the view held by Valasco, Caldas, and Antonio da Gama. Gama rightly notes at the end of his Decision 269 that the owner's consent may be presumed if they have knowledge of the arrangement and remain

<column-break/>

silent over a long period of time. He teaches extensively in other decisions that this "knowledge and patience" over a long duration creates a presumption that consent was previously given, a view shared by Silvester and others.

<margin>2</margin> The principal difficulty, however, is whether the <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>term: <term>dominium utile</term>—the right to use the property and claim its profits, as opposed to the "direct ownership" (dominium directum) or legal title held by the landlord</note> passes to the final sub-tenant, or if it remains with the first tenant, or perhaps exists in both at once in different ways. Certainly, one and the same beneficial ownership, unchanged and in its entirety, cannot exist in two people at the same time. To explain my view on this matter—which involves a great variety of opinions as detailed by Caldas—certain points must be observed.
First, a tenant or a <term>vassal</term> <note>a person holding land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service</note> may be granted precisely the beneficial ownership. Usually, this is shared with other tenants or vassals with the power to sub-lease, and this is assumed to be the case unless otherwise specified. Secondly, that same ownership can be granted along with certain "prerogatives" and effects that usually belong to <term>direct ownership</term>. For example: that the tenant may grant a sub-lease or a sub-fief with their own consent alone, without requiring the original owner's permission; or that the first tenant has the right of first refusal to buy the lease back at the same price (rather than the owner); and that the <term>laudemium</term> <note>a fee paid to the landlord when a long-term lease is transferred to someone else</note> or service should be paid to the first tenant as well as the owner. Furthermore, if a sub-tenant forfeits their right, that benefit should go to the first tenant rather than the owner. All of these are aspects of direct ownership, not beneficial ownership. Just as an owner can share only the beneficial ownership with a tenant—which was originally part of his direct ownership before he separated them—so too can he share these other "fruits" of direct ownership that usually stay with the owner. There is nothing in the nature of the thing to prevent this. As we showed at the end of Dispute 459, such agreements added to a contract are valid, even if the nature of the contract would suggest otherwise without them. This is affirmed by Gama and is also true in the case of fiefs.

<margin>3</margin> Hence, when a Kingdom is granted to a King as a <term>fief</term>, such as the example often used of the Kingdom of Sicily, the King holds all power and administration as if he were the direct owner. The supreme title (the <term>proprietas</term>) is reserved for the High Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, and the King owes a certain service in recognition of that ownership. In such a case, beyond the full beneficial ownership of that Kingdom, the Prince also possesses almost all the "rights and effects" of ownership; therefore, he can grant sub-fiefs and sub-leases of

<meta>catchword: towns (pida);</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...towns, castles, and estates of that Kingdom, with no other consent required from the owner; and he holds all rights over the long-term tenants <term>emphyteutas; those holding land under a long-term lease</term> and vassals exactly as if he himself were the owner. Thus, he can be called the owner, or rather, he is like an owner in comparison to them. This view is more pleasing than that which Baldus, Decius, and Alexander (whom Caldas cites and follows in question 13, number 30) are led to affirm: that he is the owner in comparison to the individual parts of that Kingdom, though not in comparison to the whole Kingdom. For as much ownership as he has over the individual parts of that Kingdom, to that extent only—in my judgment—does he have ownership over the entire collective entity of the Kingdom.

<margin>4</margin>
On the contrary, however, when <note>† marks a key point in the legal argument</note> someone subject to a supreme prince grants something as a fief or a long-term lease, they are never exempt from performing service and aid to the supreme prince when the common good of the state demands it. This is true not only if they are merely the beneficial owner <term>utilis dominus; the person who has the right to use and profit from the land, though not the legal title</term> of those goods (with whatever power to alienate or sub-lease them under the burden of service), but even if they are the legal owner of those goods and grant them as a fief. If necessary, they must deny service to their immediate lord—which would otherwise be owed—and even take up arms against him. Likewise, such a vassal cannot take up arms to help his own immediate lord against another private lord without the authority of the supreme prince, in whom alone resides the authority and right to wage war, as we showed in Dispute 100. Caldas affirms all these points, along with many others whom he cites, in the passage mentioned above at number 37. These points can be confirmed because in every oath and promise of fidelity, the loyalty owed to the supreme King is always excepted, or understood to be excepted, as held in chapter 1, the final paragraph, *On the alienation of a fief* by Frederick, where it is written:

> We also decree that in every oath of fidelity, the Emperor shall be specifically excepted.

The things we stated in Dispute 74 confirm these same points.

<margin>5</margin>
Once these matters are established, we must say: When <note>†</note> it is not evident that the first long-term tenant was granted more than precisely the beneficial ownership <note>dominium utile</note> usually granted to other tenants, then—whether from the beginning or later through the passage of time—if the owner grants them the power to sub-lease (or they are deemed to have it), and by virtue of that power they sub-lease the land, they transfer their beneficial ownership to the second tenant. Nothing remains with the first tenant except the right to demand the new rent imposed on the second tenant. This is done either by receiving the entire rent and then paying the owner the portion due from the first contract while keeping the remainder (which is the more frequent practice and should be done unless otherwise agreed), or by receiving only the "increase" and leaving the new tenant bound to pay the remainder to the owner, as the first tenant, the second, and the owner shall agree among themselves.

Furthermore, the first tenant retains the right to execute the penalty of forfeiture <term>commissum; the legal seizure of the lease if the tenant fails to pay rent</term> against the second tenant if he should fall into forfeiture for unpaid rent, thereby recovering the beneficial ownership that he had transferred to him. However, the other rights which belonged to the owner by reason of ownership in comparison to the first tenant likewise apply in comparison to the second.

<column-break/>

Vnde... <note>original: "Hence..."</note> Hence, if the second tenant wishes to sell his long-term lease right and the improvements made to the land, he must go to the property owner to announce it, not to the first tenant. The property owner must be given preference at the same price, and the transfer fee <term>laudemium; a fee (usually 2% of the price) paid to a landlord when a long-term lease is sold</term> must be paid to him if he does not buy the right himself but someone else does.

Nevertheless, the first tenant possesses a right against the new tenant regarding the rights he reserved for himself: namely, receiving the rent from him in the manner explained above, and executing the penalty of forfeiture if the new tenant fails to pay. Indeed, if the property owner buys the lease right from the second tenant and the beneficial ownership is consolidated with the legal title, the owner will be bound to pay the first tenant the "increase" in rent that was owed to him from that leased property.

It must also be observed that by the very fact that the lease ends for the first tenant, it ends for the others; for he is not deemed to have transferred any more right to them than he himself had. Nor is the owner, by granting the power to sub-lease, deemed to have granted any right to his own prejudice unless he expressly stated it or it was included in the agreement.

Furthermore, once the beneficial ownership is transferred to the second tenant, just as previously the owner possessed the property civilly <note>legally, via title</note>—and possessed the interests and other effects of it through himself, and naturally <note>physically</note> through the first tenant (who had natural possession of the thing by reason of beneficial ownership and its use and administration, as stated in Dispute 12)—so now he possesses it naturally through the second tenant, to whom those rights were transferred by the first. The second tenant, for his part, possesses (or "quasi-possesses") the beneficial ownership both civilly and naturally, as was said of the first tenant in the cited dispute.

However, the right which remains with the first tenant to the rent and to the penalty of forfeiture (if forfeiture is incurred for unpaid rent) is not indeed the beneficial ownership of the leased property, but a certain incorporeal right <term>incorporeal right; a legal right that has no physical presence, such as the right to collect a debt or rent</term> reserved to himself in the leased thing itself. He remains in possession (or "quasi-possession") of that right by the very fact that he reserved it for himself when handing over the beneficial ownership to the new tenant. He continues this possession through acts of that right, such as demanding and receiving rent from the new tenant, or executing the penalty of forfeiture against him, as was explained and shown regarding similar points of law in Dispute 14.

All these things must be further explained and corroborated, though not in the order in which they were proposed. Starting from what we said—namely, that in that event, nothing remains with the first tenant except the right to demand the new rent imposed on the second tenant, and the right to execute the penalty of forfeiture—surely there is no one who would deny these rights to the first tenant, since they are the minimum that must be granted to him. Both rights are attributed to him by the commonly accepted gloss on the section *Adeo*, at the word *Propriam*, in the Institutes *On Leasing* <note>original: "Instit. de locat."</note>. This implies that when the first tenant, by the owner’s power, transfers his beneficial ownership to a second party for that rent, that contract is not properly...
