### Second Treatise, Dispute 471
**Oo 3**

...it is not strictly a long-term lease <term>emphyteutic; a type of contract for land use</term>, but rather a "give so that you may give" <note>original: "do vt des"; a category of contract where both parties exchange something</note> arrangement. Consequently, an "action for unspecified terms" <note>original: "actionem praescriptis verbis"; a legal remedy for contracts that don't fit into standard categories</note> is available to recover the rent by virtue of that contract, and subsequently to enforce the penalty of forfeiture <note>original: "poenam commissi"</note> for non-payment. For by the very fact that the first tenant reserves the rent for himself with the owner’s consent, all other rights reserved to him are considered secondary, established by the long-term lease contract to ensure that rent is recovered—such as the execution of the penalty for forfeiture. This is the opinion of Caldas <note>Francisco de Caldas, a prominent 16th-century jurist</note> in the work cited above at number 44, and others whom he cites.

<margin>6</margin> Indeed, the common opinion of the doctors of law—along with the cited gloss mentioned by Alvarez Valasco <note>a Portuguese legal scholar</note> in his work on emphyteutic law, question 13, number 1—affirms that the beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the land</term> passes to the second long-term tenant and does not remain with the first. Only those other rights remain which are, as it were, the "remnants" of the preceding beneficial ownership that was once in him. This is followed by Caldas (number 11), Julius Clarus (at the section on fiefs, question 32, last number, where he teaches this regarding feudal law), and Gama (Decision 244, number 7). Besides the fact that this matter is quite clear within the terms we are discussing, it can be proven as follows.

Since beneficial ownership of the same thing cannot belong to many people individually in its entirety, it follows that when the first long-term tenant transfers the beneficial ownership and the administration of the leased property to a second person, and reserves nothing for himself except those mentioned rights—which clearly do not constitute beneficial or direct ownership—we must say that the beneficial ownership passes to the second tenant. It does not remain in the first, except for those specifically mentioned rights. Because possession is linked with ownership, let us move to that subject, and later return to other matters.

<margin>Quest. 7</margin> Does the "natural" (physical) possession of the leased property also pass to the second long-term tenant along with the "quasi-possession" of the beneficial ownership? And can the legal owners be said to naturally possess the property through the second tenant, just as they were previously said to naturally possess it through the first? This is affirmed by the gloss on the Digest <note>original: "ff. de acq. poss."; referencing the Roman Law Pandects</note> and the Code, as well as by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors cited by Valasco and Caldas. Therefore, it is quite clear from the preceding doctrine: if the beneficial ownership does not remain with the first tenant but passes to the second along with full administration of the property, then the natural possession of that same property does not remain with the first tenant either, but passes to the second.

<margin>8</margin> Finally, as for the added point regarding the right † to the rent and the penalty of forfeiture if the rent is not paid—which the first long-term tenant reserves for himself—this is not beneficial ownership. Rather, it is a certain "incorporeal right" reserved in the leased property. He remains in "quasi-possession" of that reservation while the beneficial ownership is handed over. This is clear from the discussion cited there. Indeed, when someone is in possession of a thing and transfers that possession to another, reserving something for himself by mutual consent, he remains in possession of what he so reserved. By the very act of transferring possession only regarding the rest, no other 

<column-break/>

act is necessary for this. Hence it is established that the legal glosses rightly assert that when the first tenant, with the owner's consent, hands over the property to another in a long-term lease, the original owner remains in "civil" (legal) possession of the property, while the second tenant remains in "natural" (physical) possession. The middleman (the first tenant), however, retains no possession of the property itself, not even through the second tenant. Truly, he does not possess that property; he only remains in possession (or quasi-possession, both legal and natural) of the right to receive rent from it and to execute the penalty of forfeiture if it is not paid. On this point, I do not approve of the opinion of Francisco Caldas (question 13, number 35), who rejects those glosses regarding the first tenant's possession—glosses which Bartolus and others rightly approve.

Furthermore, the other rights that belonged to the owner by reason of his ownership in relation to the first tenant now belong to him in relation to the second. Therefore, if the second tenant wishes to sell his emphyteutic right and his improvements <note>original: "meliorationes"; physical upgrades made to the land</note>, he must notify the original owner and not the first tenant. The owner must be given preference at the same price <note>the right of first refusal</note>, and the transfer fee <term>laudemium; a fee paid to the lord/owner for the privilege of transferring a lease</term> must be paid to the owner if someone else buys it. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, consistent with the glosses on the Code. This is cited and followed by Alvarez Valasco, Caldas, Julius Clarus (in feudal matters), Gama, and Silvester (under the word "emphyteusis," question 34), and it follows clearly from what has been said.

For if neither the beneficial ownership nor the civil or natural possession of the leased property remains with the first tenant, there is certainly no reason why the rights belonging to the owner by reason of his ownership should not apply to the second tenant. This is especially true since the second tenant holds his emphyteutic right not merely from the first tenant, but from the owner, who provided consent and authority for it. Indeed, as Caldas rightly says, even if it were granted that the first tenant retained some "superior" beneficial ownership compared to the second tenant, one should not have to turn to him for a further sale of the lease, nor should he be given preference at the same price or paid the transfer fee. All these rights are granted in law to the "owner" by reason of his ownership, and are never found to be granted to a beneficial owner <term>utilis dominus</term>. The name "owner" used in law refers only to the owner simply speaking (the person with the legal title), not to one holding beneficial ownership. Additionally, if the first tenant had to be consulted for further alienation instead of the legal owner, the owner's situation could easily be made worse: the property could pass to a powerful or privileged person without his consent, potentially causing him great loss.

<summary>This page argues that when a primary tenant sub-leases land, the beneficial ownership and physical possession pass to the new tenant, leaving the primary tenant with only an incorporeal right to collect rent. It reinforces that the original owner maintains their rights (such as the right of first refusal and transfer fees) directly over the new tenant.</summary>

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

Add also that in the granting of the right to sub-lease <term>subemphyteusis; a secondary long-term lease granted by a tenant to another person</term>, nothing more seems to be granted than the ability to hand over the property to another under a higher rent for the benefit of the first tenant. This power does not imply that the owner <term>proprietarius; the person who holds the ultimate legal title to the land</term> intends to yield their ownership rights in favor of others by reason of the property rights they hold, unless this is explicitly stated.

9. We add this: if the owner buys the beneficial right from the second tenant, so that the beneficial ownership and the legal property are consolidated, the owner is bound to pay the first tenant the increase in rent that was owed to them from that lease. This is self-evident. For just as the second tenant could not transfer their beneficial right to anyone else without the burden of paying that higher rent to the first tenant (which was owed to them as long as the lease continued), the owner also has the right of first refusal <term>ius praelationis; the right to match an offer and buy back the lease</term> only under that same burden. The owner must pay the rent increase to the first tenant for as long as the lease would have persisted in the hands of the tenant or their successors if it had not been sub-leased.

10. Finally, it is quite clear that when the lease of the first tenant or their successors ends, the lease also ends for those to whom it was sub-leased. This follows from what we have noted elsewhere: when the right of the grantor (upon whom the recipient’s right depends) is dissolved, the right of the recipient is also dissolved.

<margin>Question</margin> 11. Another view: Valasco <note>Alvarez Valasco, a 16th-century Portuguese legal scholar</note> in his work *On Emphyteutic Law*, question 13, number 12, judges that the opinion we have relayed so far should only be understood to apply when the first tenant transfers their entire leasehold right to a second person, reserving nothing for themselves—neither rent nor the penalty for forfeiture if the second tenant fails to pay. In that case, the second tenant is simply substituted in place of the first regarding the owner, to whom they pay rent and who can enforce penalties. 

However, he adds that when the first tenant, with the owner’s consent, truly sub-leases the land and the rent is to be paid to that first tenant, then the first tenant possesses a true "superior" beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the land</term> over the "inferior" beneficial ownership that they transferred to the second tenant. It is not absurd for two beneficial ownerships of the same property to exist simultaneously in different people, provided one is superior and larger, and the other is inferior and smaller; though it would be absurd for two identical beneficial ownerships to exist entirely and equally in two people. He further adds that the first tenant, having made the sub-lease, remains in "civil possession" <note>possession in the eyes of the law, even if not physically occupying the land</note> of the property they transferred.

- Likewise, the second tenant must go back to the first tenant if they wish to sell their leasehold right, notifying them of the price offered so that the first tenant may be preferred over other buyers at that same price. Furthermore, the transfer fee <term>laudemium; a fee paid to the landlord, usually 2% of the price, when a lease is sold</term> must be paid to the first tenant. The first tenant is also the one who should enforce the penalty of forfeiture <note>original: "poenam commissi"</note> for whatever reason the second tenant might fall into default. These rights do not belong to the

<column-break/>

owner simply because they granted the power to sub-lease.

In these matters, he largely follows the footsteps of Charles Dumoulin <note>Carolus Molinaeus, a famous French jurist known for his work on customary and feudal law</note> and certain others cited by him and Caldas. Indeed, Dumoulin judges that both a first tenant who sub-leases with consent, and a first vassal <note>vassallus; a person granted land by a lord in exchange for service</note> who grants a sub-fief, retain the full beneficial ownership of the property. They transfer only the "right of convenience" and the use itself to the sub-tenant or sub-vassal under the burden of a higher rent or service. Therefore, the owner has no direct right over the sub-tenant or sub-vassal. 

Others cited by Caldas held that although the first tenant or vassal is the beneficial owner, if the owner consents to the sub-lease, the first tenant becomes the "direct lord" <term>dominus directus; the legal superior in a property hierarchy</term> in comparison to the beneficial ownership of the sub-tenant. Similarly, if a vassal creates a sub-fief, they act as the direct lord to the sub-vassal. Valasco confirms his opinion (number 11) by stating it is a contradiction to say a tenant can sub-lease but then retains no rights. If no rights remained in them, they would no longer be a tenant under the owner, and thus could not establish another tenant under themselves, as they would no longer be the party immediately connected to the owner.

12. Second, because a feudal holder <term>feudatarius; one who holds a fief</term> has beneficial ownership and can sub-lease with the owner's consent. Not only can they do this, but what is more, they can (without fraud) grant a sub-fief <term>subinfeudatio; the process of a vassal granting land to a lower-tier vassal</term> even without the lord's knowledge or consent, provided it is to a person of suitable quality and dignity who can serve just as well as the grantor, and under the same conditions. In such a case, the first person remains the owner's vassal, and the second is the sub-vassal. This is established by several chapters of feudal law. Just as the first vassal then retains the beneficial ownership and the sub-vassal is immediately subject to them in all things, the same holds true for the first tenant in comparison to their sub-tenant.

- Third, because if the law permits a tenant to sub-lease, it should be understood according to the nature of an emphyteutic contract. The nature of such a contract is that some right and superiority must remain with the one granting it. Therefore, in a first tenant sub-leasing with the owner's permission, there remains a beneficial ownership superior to that which is transferred to the sub-tenant. The sub-tenant is subject to the first tenant, not the owner, in all matters.

<summary>This page explores the legal hierarchy of sub-leasing, arguing that a primary tenant who sub-leases land retains a 'superior' beneficial ownership and acts as a middleman-lord over the sub-tenant. This arrangement entitles the primary tenant, rather than the original owner, to transfer fees and the power to evict for non-payment.</summary>

<keywords>emphyteusis, sub-leasing, beneficial ownership, dominium utile, laudemium, forfeiture, right of first refusal, Carolus Molinaeus, feudal law, subinfeudation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding the rights of a primary tenant (emphyteuta) when they sub-lease property to a second tenant. It specifically addresses the arguments of Alvarez Valasco and explores whether the primary tenant retains any form of "beneficial ownership" or "superiority" over the sub-tenant.</meta>

<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 47.</header>

<margin>Decision.</margin> However, we must not depart from the common opinion of the legal scholars, which we have sufficiently explained and supported. This opinion was certainly interpreted poorly by Alvarez Valasco, who truly twists it to support his own view. Thus, regarding his first argument, we must first state that the authors of that opinion do not claim that no right remains with the one who grants a sub-lease <term>subemphyteuticantem; the primary tenant who sub-leases to another</term>. Rather, they only claim that the beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from the land</term> does not remain with them, but passes to the sub-tenant <term>subemphyteuta; the secondary tenant</term>. What remains with the primary tenant are those rights we have explained: the right to receive the annual rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note> and the right to enforce the penalty of forfeiture <term>commissum; the legal loss of a lease for failing to meet its terms, such as non-payment</term> if the rent is not paid. They call these rights "certain traces and remnants of beneficial ownership," as Valasco himself reports from Baldus and others. By reason of these rights, they asserted that the primary tenant holds a position of superiority and eminence over the sub-tenant regarding those effects. And although they should not be said to have either direct or beneficial ownership over the leased property by reason of those rights, they can be said to stand in the place of a direct lord <note>original: "instat domini directi"</note> in comparison to the sub-tenant, because of the superiority and eminence they hold over him due to those rights.

<margin>1</margin> Furthermore, if at the time the first tenant was granted the power to sub-lease, they were also granted other aspects of property ownership (which we explained at the beginning of this disputation), then—even though they should not be called the beneficial or direct owner of the leased thing—they will stand even more in the place of a direct lord in relation to the sub-tenant, depending on how many of those rights were shared with them. The same must be said of a vassal: the more rights of property ownership granted to him, the more freely he can grant feudal property into a lease or a fief <term>feudum; land held under a feudal agreement</term>, and the greater his right over the tenants and feudal subjects. This was mentioned above regarding the King of Sicily, who is a vassal of the Apostolic See <note>The Pope in Rome</note>. The same could be said of the King of Aragon when he was a vassal to the King of Castile, before the fief was remitted to him because of the military aid he brought to this, our city of Cuenca <note>original: "Conchēsem ciuitatē"</note>. At that time, the city was very well fortified by its location and industry, and it was finally captured from the power of the Moors <note>original: "manūrum potestate"</note> on September 21, in the year 1177.

Next, it must be said in response to the argument: although it would be a contradiction to say a tenant could sub-lease with the owner's consent while retaining no rights at all, there is no contradiction in saying they can sub-lease and yet not retain the beneficial ownership. For, to speak accurately and properly in teaching this art, it is not necessary that the primary tenant transfer as much right, or as perfect and complete a beneficial ownership, to the sub-tenant as they themselves held. Indeed, it is clear they transfer a weaker right, because they retain certain remnants of it for themselves. Furthermore, they transfer it subject to the condition that the primary tenant does not forfeit the lease by failing to pay the rent to the owner. For if the lease expires for the primary tenant, it must also expire for the sub-tenant, as was explained above. Likewise, to speak accurately and properly, it is not necessary that as much right

<column-break/>

remains in the primary tenant after the sub-lease is made as was there before, or that the beneficial ownership that was in him should remain in him. It is enough that, by reason of the beneficial ownership he received and transferred to the new tenant with the owner's consent, he is held responsible for paying the rent to the owner. Thus, if he does not pay it, he incurs forfeiture—even if the sub-tenant has paid well—and he must see to it that the sub-tenant does not cause a forfeiture against the owner by damaging the property or selling it without following the rules required by the owner. Otherwise, this will harm him in relation to the owner, though he may be able to sue the sub-tenant for damages.

<margin>2</margin> Therefore, because of that hierarchy—where the first tenant is subordinate to the owner and the second is subordinate to the first (as well as to the owner)—that arrangement is aptly called a "sub-lease" <note>original: "subemphyteuticatio"</note>. I should warn in passing that I do not agree with what Gama says in Decision 244, no. 7, and Decision 329, no. 5: namely, that if a sub-tenant incurs forfeiture for not paying the rent, they lose the beneficial ownership to the original owner and not to the first tenant.

<margin>3</margin> For although that may be true if the forfeiture happens for any other reason, it is not true if it happens for unpaid rent. This is because the rent must be paid by the sub-tenant to the primary tenant, not to the owner. Therefore, it belongs to the primary tenant to execute the penalty of forfeiture in their own favor for the rent not paid to them, as has been said.

<margin>4</margin> Before solving the second argument, one must observe: under the laws of fiefs granted to a vassal, there are two ways he can transfer the fief to another. First, in such a way that the new vassal serves the owner in place of the first, so that the burdens of the first pass to the second. For such a transfer of a fief to be valid, the person to whom it is transferred must be of such a status that he can serve the owner just as well as the one who transfers it. For example, if the first vassal was a soldier and the fief was granted with the burden of serving in war, he cannot transfer it except to another soldier who can serve the owner equally well in war. This type of transfer is discussed in various legal chapters.

<margin>7</margin> Secondly, it can be granted so that the new vassal is bound to serve not the owner, but the first vassal. He takes on the imposed burdens in relation to the first vassal, not the owner, while the burdens of the first vassal in relation to the owner remain as they were before. And since in this kind of sub-fief <term>subinfeudatio; creating a new subordinate fief under an existing one</term> the issue is not about the prejudice or benefit of the owner, but of the vassal, it does not seem so necessary that the one to whom the right is granted be of such a status that he can serve the owner as well as the first vassal could. This kind of sub-fief is discussed in other laws.

This being established, as far as the second argument is concerned, Caldas (in *On the Renewal of Emphyteusis*, question 13, no. 42) responds by conceding that the beneficial ownership remains in the first vassal, and only the utility...

He uses the historical example of the Kings of Castile and Aragon at the siege of Cuenca to illustrate complex feudal hierarchies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal debate over whether a primary tenant (the one who first leases land from a lord) retains "beneficial ownership" once they sub-lease that land to someone else. Molina is specifically refuting the famous French jurist Charles Dumoulin (Carolus Molinaeus) and clarifying how these rights function in both feudal and emphyteutic law.</meta>

<header>Luis de Molina, *On Contracts*</header>

...transfer the right to receive profits from the feudal property in his own name to the sub-vassal <note>original: "subfeudatarium"</note>, as Charles Dumoulin used to assert. Furthermore, within the specialized rules of fiefs <note>the "exorbitantia" or unique legal exceptions of feudal law</note>, which allow sub-leasing without the owner's consent, the beneficial ownership <term>dominium utile; the right to use and profit from land</term> is left with the one who sub-leases; however, these rules should not be extended to emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term or perpetual lease requiring the tenant to improve the land</term>.

The opinion of Charles Dumoulin—that the beneficial ownership remains with the first tenant and only the "convenience" or "utility" of the land is transferred to the sub-tenant—is false and contrary to the common consensus of legal scholars. This is clearly confirmed by the laws of King Conrad <note>original: "c.1.§.similiter, de leg. Conrad."; referring to the Libri Feudorum, a collection of feudal laws</note>, where it is stated that a second tenant can sub-lease again, and so on infinitely, without prejudice to the original owner and according to the laws of the first fief. However, someone who only possesses the "commodity" or benefit of a thing cannot sub-lease it; if they only enjoy the benefit while the first tenant remains the master of both aspects of the property, that right should not pass to another. This is because they would only be perceiving the benefits in the name of the first tenant, acting as a mere administrator.

Therefore, in response to the second argument, we must deny that a tenant who sub-leases retains the beneficial ownership. He does not retain it, except for certain "remnants" of it, as Giulio Claro asserts in the common opinion <note>original: "Iul. Clar. 4. lib. sent. §. feudum. q. 32. nu. vlt."</note>. By reason of these remnants, he holds a position of superiority and eminence over the sub-vassal, and stands in the position of a direct lord <note>original: "instar domini directi"</note> in comparison to him. This is especially true when more effects and rights of ownership were granted to him by the original owner than he granted to the sub-tenant, as was discussed regarding sub-leasing with the owner’s consent. But why is it that a vassal is permitted to sub-lease without the owner's consent (provided proper conditions are met), while an emphyteutic tenant is not? Giulio Claro says in the cited question that he has so far found no good reason for this among the doctors of law.

Although these interpretations depend on the law and the will of the legislators—who could establish one rule for fiefs and another for emphyteusis—there is perhaps a reason. Fiefs were usually granted in exchange for military or personal service, rather than with a focus on improving the property or providing other profits to the owner, which is why emphyteusis is granted. Therefore, as long as the service is adequately performed, whether by the immediate vassal or another equally suitable person, the power to sub-lease should be left more free than the power to sub-lease an emphyteutic property. This is especially true since a vassal, by having other sub-vassals, can make himself more capable of providing personal services to the owner.

Regarding the third argument, it must be granted that if the law permitted an emphyteutic tenant to sub-lease, this should be understood according to the nature of the emphyteutic contract. However, as far as the nature of sub-leasing allows, once beneficial ownership is transferred to the sub-tenant, it cannot remain with the one who granted the sub-lease. Nevertheless, the "superiority" we explained remains with him in comparison to the sub-tenant. For this reason, we must deny the conclusion that the primary tenant retains a "superior" beneficial ownership over the one transferred to the sub-tenant, or that in all matters one must 

<column-break/>

turn to the sub-leaser and not to the original owner.

## Emphyteusis: Some New, Others Old. Also Some Hereditary, Others by Contract and Provision (or Family), and Others Mixed. The Same Applies to Fiefs.

### DISPUTATION 472.

### SUMMARY.

1. *Emphyteusis is twofold: new and old.*
2. *Emphyteusis and fiefs can be called "hereditary" in two ways.*
3. *What constitutes a strictly hereditary emphyteusis or fief.*
4. *Under the name of "heirs and successors," even in Church-related emphyteusis, outsiders are included.*
5. *Whether a fief granted simply is considered granted also for outside heirs.*
6. *What constitutes a fief or emphyteusis "by contract and provision."*
7. *When they are by contract and provision, it is not necessary for the successor to be the legal heir.*
8. *Whether fiefs and emphyteusis "by contract and provision" are found in law.*
9. *What constitutes a mixed hereditary fief or emphyteusis.*
10. *When they are hereditary, is it enough to be the heir of the first possessor, or must one be the heir of the last?*

In order to next explain succession in emphyteusis—and whether a father can prejudice his sons' rights within it, and when and to what extent it should be subject to division—we must begin by explaining the terms proposed.

<margin>1</margin> An emphyteusis or a fief is called **new** when it is first granted by the direct lord, and a new investiture <term>investitura; the formal legal act of granting possession of land</term> is made. For the person to whom it is first granted, it is called new. It is called **old** <note>original: "antiqua"</note> when it had already been granted previously and passes to another, or is renewed under the same agreements (for example, by the last possessor or his successor) so that it continues in the same way it was granted before. Because fiefs were usually granted to someone and his male descendants, we must say that when a fief is held by the first person it was granted to, it is called "new." But when it is derived from there to another of his lineage or family—whether the person it passes to is a descendant of the last possessor or a kinsman <note>original: "agnatus"; a relative through the male line</note> descending from the first possessor—it is called both an "old fief" and a **paternal fief** <note>original: "feudum paternum"</note>, as if derived from that first "father" of the entire kinship. Today, doctors of law call any fief that is not "new" by both names: "old" and "paternal." However, as stated in Chapter 1, Section 1, at the end, regarding the succession of fiefs, only that fief is properly called "paternal" which descends from a common father within the fourth degree, and not...

<page-num>585</page-num>

...who is derived from some lower, primary parent. This is the common opinion of the learned doctors, which is reported and followed by Giulio Claro <note>original: "Iulius Clar. lib. 4. sent. §. emphyteusis. q. 16. nu. 1."</note>, Alvaro Valasco <note>original: "Aluar. Valaf. de iur. emphyt. q. 42. nu. 2."</note>, and Caldas <note>original: "Caldas de renouat. emphyt. q. 1. nu. 3."</note> and those following.

However, Caldas, following Salyceto, observes in the same place <margin>2</margin> that a person is called a "new tenant" <term>emphyteuta; a long-term tenant under a contract to improve the land</term> if they are not included under the first investiture <term>investiture; the formal legal ceremony or act of transferring possession of land from a lord to a tenant</term> or grant of the lease. For example, if someone acquires the lease from another tenant through purchase, donation, or another title, they are considered a "new" tenant. Consequently, this person is required to receive possession from the owner and renew the lease contract. However, when someone is already included in the original investiture or grant of the lease, then not only is the lease itself not considered "new," but the successor is not considered a "new tenant" by virtue of that first grant. For this reason, they are not required to seek either investiture or possession from the owner.

Hence, when a lease is granted for three generations, or to three specific persons, or to those whom the current possessors name for the lease, then those who succeed by virtue of such a primary grant are not required to return to the owner for investiture or possession. Caldas testifies that this is the accepted practice in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>. The same applies when the lease was taken for oneself, one's children, and one's descendants: because they succeed by virtue of that first grant, they are not personally bound to seek investiture or possession, as Jason and Paris de Puteo asserted (cited by Caldas).

<margin>2</margin> The matter stands differently, however, in the case of a fief <term>feudum; land held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for military or other service</term>. In a fief, the successor is always bound to seek investiture from the owner within a year and a month, unless a just cause prevents them; otherwise, they are deprived of the fief. The same applies if the owner dies: the tenant is similarly bound within that same timeframe to seek a new investiture from the owner's successor. This is held in the laws of King Radbot <note>original: "c. 1. in prin. quo tempore miles & c. Ratib." referring to the Libri Feudorum</note>, where this specific requirement was established for fiefs. This is not only because the feudal vassal is regularly bound to personal service and burdens for the owner, but primarily because they are bound to swear an oath of fidelity to him—two requirements that have no place in a standard long-term lease <note>original: "emphyteusi"</note>. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

### Regarding the second point,

From the knowledge of whether a lease or fief is "hereditary," or whether it exists by "pact and provision" (also called "familial"), the resolution of many grave questions depends, as will be clear from the following sections. <margin>2</margin> As it pertains to the present instruction, a lease or fief can be called "hereditary" for two reasons. First, because they are considered granted for any heirs whatsoever, including outsiders <note>original: "extraneis"; those not of the bloodline</note>. Second, because by the power of the grant, no one can succeed in them unless they are simultaneously the legal heir of the tenant or vassal; it is not enough to be a son or to have some other quality unless one is also the heir.

Those leases or fiefs which are called hereditary for the first reason are termed "simply hereditary" by the doctors. Those which are so called only for the second reason are not undeservedly called "mixed hereditary" by many. Among those who use this classification are Giulio

<column-break/>

Claro <note>original: "lib. 4. sent. §. emphyteusi. q. 16. nu. 1."</note>, Caldas <note>original: "q. 22. à nu. 11."</note>, and Arias Pinelo <note>original: "l. 1. C. de bon. mater. par. 3."</note>.
<margin>3</margin> Hence, we can define "simply hereditary" leases or fiefs according to the common opinion of the doctors as those which are considered granted for any heirs, even outsiders. This is the view of Giulio Claro and the doctors cited, although many of them do not speak as distinctly on this matter as we do.

<margin>4</margin> If the lease is not an ecclesiastical one <note>i.e., not involving Church-owned land</note>, it is "simply hereditary" according to the common opinion if it was granted under any of the following formulas: *I grant this thing to you for a lease and to your heirs.* This is because, as stated in Dispute 4.69, the name of "heirs" includes everyone, even outsiders. Nor is there anything in a private or non-Church lease (which can pass to anyone by its nature) that would suggest a restriction. The same is true if it is said: *I grant this thing to you for a lease and to your successors*; for under the name of "successors," even outside heirs are included—that is, those who are not descendants. The same applies if it is said: *I grant this thing to you and to whomever you wish*; for by that name, outside heirs are likewise included.

The same is also true if it is said: *I grant this thing to you, and to your children and heirs, and successors*; or *to you and your descendants, and heirs, and successors*; or if only "heirs" or "successors" is added. As Caldas rightly says, this will become clear from the discussions in the following dispute.

But if the lease is an Ecclesiastical one, as we resolved in Dispute 4.69, the common opinion of the doctors is that in such a case, the name of "heirs" or "successors" is understood to mean only descendants. Therefore, the common opinion holds that by virtue of these formulas—insofar as they mention heirs and successors—only descending heirs and successors are understood. Thus, unless a greater expression is made to show it is granted even for outside heirs, it is not considered "simply" hereditary in the first sense, but only in the second or "mixed" sense. However, in that same place, along with Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and others, we weighed the idea that even in an Ecclesiastical lease, the name of "heirs" or "successors" should include outsiders. Nevertheless, we added that where custom has been accepted to understand only descendants in such a lease—as seems to be the case in Portugal—one must stand by that common opinion.

<margin>5</margin> The same applies to a fief, because it is only considered granted for the descendants of the recipient, and not for ancestors or other outsiders, unless this is specifically expressed. This is clear from the feudal laws regarding the nature of succession <note>original: "c. 1. de natura succes. feudi"</note> and is affirmed by the common opinion followed by Caldas, Alvaro Valasco, and others. If a fief is granted under similar formulas, by the name of heirs...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s detailed classification of feudal and emphyteutic successions. The previous page established when a successor is considered a "new" tenant and when they are covered by the original grant. Here, Molina distinguishes between purely hereditary grants and those governed by specific "provisions" or family compacts.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...or successors; in the case of the one receiving the fief <term>fief; a landed estate held on condition of feudal service</term>, only his descendants are understood.

Therefore, a fief granted under such similar forms is not simply hereditary, but only mixedly so. For a fief, or an ecclesiastical emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term lease where the tenant must improve the land in exchange for a low rent</term>, to be considered simply hereditary, it is necessary to include words in the grant from which it can be understood that it is also granted for outside heirs. This occurs primarily if it is stated: "I grant you this thing in emphyteusis, or as a fief, for any of your heirs, even outside ones." For in such a grant, there can be no doubt that the grant extends even to outside heirs. The same applies if it says, "for any of your heirs," or "for any of your successors," or "for whomever you wish." Indeed, that word, "whomever," denotes that the grant is made to all successors or heirs whatsoever, even outside ones. This is the common opinion of the learned doctors, which is reported and followed by Gigas <note>original: "Gigas de pens. q. 19. nu. 3."</note>, Covarruvias <note>original: "Couar. 2. var. res. c. 17. nu. 5."</note>, Julius Clarus <note>original: "Iul. Clar. §. emphyteusis, q. 28."</note>, and Caldas. However, in the following discussion, the conversation will return to whether—when in a fief or an ecclesiastical emphyteusis only "successors" are mentioned—it should be judged as being by agreement and foresight, or truly mixedly hereditary.

<margin>6</margin> Before we speak of mixed emphyteusis and fiefs, there are those established "by agreement and foresight" <note>original: "ex pacto et prouidentia"</note>—also called "family" grants. These are the ones in whose grant or investiture <term>investiture; the formal ceremony of transferring land possession</term> no mention of "heirs" was made; consequently, by the strength of the grant, they do not require the successor to be a legal heir. This is the common view of the doctors, including Julius Clarus, Luis de Molina in his work on primogeniture, Alvaro Valasco, Arias Pinel, and Caldas, with whom Covarruvias agrees.

Examples include cases where a fief or emphyteusis is granted to the recipient and their children, or the recipient and their descendants, or the recipient, their sons, and descendants, with no mention of "heirs." Or if the emphyteusis is granted to the recipient, his wife, and one son, or to descendants for three generations, or to the recipient and two others named in a certain order by the first and second possessor, or under any other similar form in which no mention of "heirs" is made.

<margin>7</margin> At this point, observe—as the doctors commonly assert—that when an emphyteusis or fief is by agreement and foresight (or "family" based), it is not necessary for the one who succeeds to be the legal heir. For one could renounce the inheritance <note>In Roman law, inheriting often meant taking on the deceased's debts; "renouncing the inheritance" allowed a person to avoid those debts while still trying to claim specific rights like these land grants.</note> and still succeed in the fief or emphyteusis. An exception is made unless the person succeeding in the fief is a direct descendant of the last possessor; in that case, they cannot succeed in that fief if they have renounced the inheritance, but are bound to accept the inheritance if they wish to succeed in that fief.

However, it is different if the person succeeding in that fief is not a descendant of the last possessor, but is an agnate <term>agnate; a relative related through the male line of descent</term> to him, and is only a descendant in relation to the *first* possessor. In that case, they can succeed in that fief even if they have renounced the inheritance of the last possessor. Both points are

<column-break/>

expressed clearly enough in the legal chapter *whether an agnate or a son* <note>original: "c. 1. an agnat. vel filius"</note>, and the more common opinion of the doctors explains it this way. For this reason, in the definition or explanation of emphyteusis and fiefs "by agreement and foresight," we included those words: "which by the strength of the grant do not require the successor to be the heir." Although a descendant of the last possessor cannot succeed in such a fief if the inheritance is renounced, this does not happen by the strength of the *grant*, but by the strength of a peculiar statute established out of reverence for parents. Nor can an argument be drawn from this that the same applies to an emphyteusis established by agreement and foresight.

Furthermore, that the discourse in that chapter concerns fiefs "by agreement and foresight," rather than hereditary fiefs (even mixed ones), is excellently proven by Covarruvias, Arias Pinel, Alvaro Valasco, and many others. This is because, if the discourse there were about a hereditary fief, even a mixed one, it would be false to say that an agnate could succeed in it while renouncing the inheritance. This is because in every hereditary fief or emphyteusis, it is necessary for the successor to be the heir, as will become clear in the following sections.

Nor is the response of Julius Clarus sufficient, who says that the text is verified in the case of the first possessor of a hereditary fief: for if a descendant succeeds him, they cannot renounce the inheritance and succeed in such a fief; but if an agnate succeeds, they can renounce the inheritance and succeed. In my judgment, there is an inevitable argument against Julius Clarus: for if a fief is simply hereditary, then not even an agnate can succeed the first possessor unless they are his heir. If, however, it is only mixedly hereditary—as in being accepted only for the descendant heirs of the first possessor—then the agnates of the first possessor cannot succeed in that fief at all, since they are not his descendants, and the fief was granted only for the descendants of the recipient.

<margin>8</margin> Regarding the names by which such emphyteusis and fiefs are called—"by agreement and foresight" and "family" grants—Arias Pinel condemns the name "by agreement and foresight." Firstly, because there is no specific legal text from which it is gathered or proven. Secondly, and most importantly, because a fief or emphyteusis is called "by agreement and foresight" because one succeeds in them according to the tenor of the agreement of investiture; yet, even in hereditary fiefs and emphyteusis, one succeeds according to the tenor of the agreement. Nevertheless, he says he will use those terms since they have been introduced by the doctors of law.

Alvaro Valasco, citing Pinel, says that better names could have been found and adapted by the doctors for this purpose. Certainly, it is not unusual for teachers of a discipline, having adapted a specific name to one part of a subject—as in the present matter of fiefs and emphyteusis, where the name "hereditary" was adapted—to call the remaining part by a common name. Thus Aristotle, having applied the name "habit" to one part of the subject of "disposition," called the rest "disposition." There are many other such examples.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of feudal and emphyteutic law, specifically focusing on the distinction between familial, hereditary, and "mixed" successions, and the legal requirement of being an heir to the previous possessor.</meta>

<header>Second Treatise, Dispute 473.</header>

Regarding the name "familial," it should be observed that although it is fit for distinguishing a "familial" fief or emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term lease of land for improvement</term> from hereditary ones—in the same way that we distinguished familial tombs from hereditary ones in Dispute 188 (following the law regarding family matters and the following law in the Digest concerning religious matters and funeral expenses)—there are nonetheless some emphyteuses created by pact and provision <term>pact and provision; a specific legal agreement that overrides general customary law</term> in which someone who is not from the family of the first possessor can succeed. This occurs when an emphyteusis is taken up "for those who shall be named," whether they are of that family or not. Similarly, some fiefs <term>fief; land held from a lord in return for service</term> can be granted by pact and provision which, by the force of that agreement, can pass to someone outside the family of the first possessor; for names sometimes have a broader application than the specific reason for which they were first adapted. Furthermore, observe that just as when one must succeed in a fief or emphyteusis because they are the possessor’s heir, it is called "succession by hereditary right"; so too when one succeeds by right of kinship, it is said to be "succession by right of blood." This distinction is applied to many other things, such as succession in a majorat <term>majorat; an estate associated with a title of nobility that descends to the eldest son</term> and other similar cases.

Hereditary emphyteusis and fiefs are "mixed" when they are granted for heirs, but not for all heirs. Insofar as they are not granted for all heirs, they are called "mixed" by pact and provision. A fief granted to the recipient "and his heirs" is of this kind; and, according to the common opinion of the doctors, an ecclesiastical emphyteusis granted in the same way is similar, though a private emphyteusis is not, according to what was said above and in Dispute 469. For a fief and an ecclesiastical emphyteusis granted in that manner do not extend to outside heirs, but only to heirs who are descendants. Therefore, those who, by virtue of such a grant, ought to succeed in a fief or ecclesiastical emphyteusis must be both descendants and heirs; if they lack either of these qualities, they cannot succeed in such a fief or emphyteusis.

A private emphyteusis granted to someone "and the heirs of his descendants," or with any other limitation so that it does not extend to all his heirs universally, is also of this kind. This is stated by Julius Clarus <note>original: "Iulius Clarus, §. emphyteusis q. 16. nu. 1. & §. feudum, q. 9. nu. 4."</note>, Aries Pinellus <note>original: "Aries Pinel. vbi sup. nu. 85."</note> (where he says the opinions of many doctors are reconciled by this distinction between a mixed hereditary fief and a simply hereditary one), and Caldas <note>original: "Caldas, q. 23. citata, nu. 20."</note>. Covarruvias agrees <note>original: "Couar. 2. var. resol. c. 18. num. 3."</note>. And Molina also speaks of this fief <note>original: "Molina, c. 8. cit. à num. 3."</note>.

<margin>Question 10.</margin>
Since the doctors agree that when an emphyteusis or fief is hereditary, it is necessary for the successor to be the heir, and it is not enough to be a son or have another quality unless he stands as the heir; they nevertheless doubt whether it is sufficient to be the heir of the *first* possessor through some intermediary who eventually became the heir of the first possessor—meaning it would not be necessary to be the heir of the *last* possessor, but one could succeed in the fief or emphyteusis even after repudiating the last possessor's inheritance—or whether it is truly necessary to be the heir of the last possessor. The more common opinion of the doctors, which Julius Clarus and Aries Pinellus report and follow:

<column-break/>

the Code of Justinian on maternal goods <note>original: "l. 5. C. de bon. mater. par. 3. n. 91."</note>, Caldas on nominated emphyteusis <note>original: "Caldas de nominate emphyteu. q. 22. nu. 39."</note>, and Alvarus Valascus on the law of emphyteusis <note>original: "Aluuar. Valaf. de iur. emphy. q. 44. nu. 19."</note>. According to this view, Julius Clarus says that in a certain case, the Neapolitan Senate judged that it is sufficient to be the heir of the first possessor in that way, and it is not necessary to be the heir of the last possessor.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
They say this because descendants receive from the first possessor, not from the immediate one. However, the contrary opinion seems true to me, along with Curtius Junior and others: namely, that it is necessary to be the heir of the last possessor, and one cannot repudiate that inheritance and still accept the fief or emphyteusis. It is false that an emphyteutic tenant or vassal who succeeds by hereditary right after the first possessor receives it from the first possessor. For they do not receive it from the first possessor as if from the origin, but from the owner <term>owner; the 'dominus' or lord who holds the ultimate title to the land</term>, who granted the fief or emphyteusis under those laws and conditions so that it might be derived and pass down in a certain order. They actually receive it immediately from the last possessor and from his disposition, which was made with the owner's consent according to the laws of investiture <term>investiture; the formal legal act of putting a person in possession of a fief</term>.

Add that in an emphyteusis or fief, especially those that are simply and entirely hereditary, it is not enough for a successor to have eventually become the heir of the first possessor through some intermediary; rather, the application and grant of such an emphyteusis or fief by the last possessor is necessary.

# Various Forms in which things are transferred into emphyteusis or fief. And an evaluation of which of them create a hereditary emphyteusis or fief, and which are by pact and provision.

## DISPUTE 474.

### SUMMARY.

> 1. The form of a fief and emphyteusis by pact and provision.
> 2. Whether a fief granted under this form—"I grant you this thing in fief"—ought to be called hereditary.
> 3. Whether ecclesiastical and secular emphyteusis differ if both are granted to someone for himself and his children or descendants.
> 4. Emphyteusis and fiefs granted to oneself, one's children, and heirs are to be considered hereditary, or at least mixed.
> 5. What name should be given to a fief or ecclesiastical emphyteusis if they are granted under this form: "to you and your male heirs," or "born of your body."
> 6. And what if it is said: "I grant you this thing in fief or emphyteusis to you and your legitimate heirs."
> 7. And what if it is said: "I grant you this thing in fief according to Frankish law" <note>original: "iure Francorum"; a specific legal custom where the eldest son typically inherits the whole fief</note>.
> 8. Likewise, what if it is said: "to you and yours."
> 9. Likewise, if it is said: "to you and your successors."

It also begins a new dispute categorizing the specific phrasing used in land grants and their legal implications.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion from Dispute 472 regarding the legal nature of succession. Having previously defined "familial" and "hereditary" tenures, he now moves into specific phrasing used in contracts to distinguish between grants made by "hereditary right" and those made by "pact and provision."</meta>

# Louis Molina, On Contracts

### Dispute 473

Doctors commonly affirm, and it is easily seen from what was said in the preceding dispute, that when no mention of heirs is made in the granting of an emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term lease of land for improvement</term> or a fief <term>fief; land held from a lord in return for service</term>, the emphyteusis or fief is not hereditary, but exists by "pact and provision" <term>pact and provision; a specific legal agreement that follows the grantor's intent rather than general inheritance law</term>. Thus, the following formulas are considered to be by pact and provision: "I grant you this property in emphyteusis (or as a fief) for thirty years," "for your life," "for three generations (or lives)." "To you, your wife, and one of your surviving sons at the time of the last of your deaths." "To you, your wife, and a son to be born to you." "To you and two other persons, such that you name the second, and the second names the third."

<margin>1</margin>
These forms are frequent in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> in the granting of an emphyteusis: "To you and all your generation." "To you and your children." "To you and your kin." Or "To you and for the whole generation." "To you and your descendants," whether it is added "born of your body" or "legitimate," or not, and whether it is added "through the masculine or male line," or not, and whether the power of naming a successor is granted, or not. On this, read among others Alvaro Valasco in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 4, and question 43, number 3. This also agrees with what Julius Clarus teaches in book 4, *Sentences*, section on emphyteusis, question 37.

<margin>
Question 2
Decision.
</margin>
Alvaro Valasco, in the following question 44, number 2, says that if a fief is given to someone under this form—"I grant you this property as a fief"—without expressing anything else (which they call being given "simply" and "informally" as a fief), it is considered given for the recipient and his heirs; and thus, it seems to suggest that such a fief is hereditary. Among others, he cites for this opinion Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 18, number 4, and Julius Clarus, section on fiefs, question 9, number 6, and question 76.

<margin>2</margin>
However, it must be said without a doubt that this is by pact and provision; since no mention is made there of heirs, neither expressly nor tacitly from the nature of such a fief. Covarruvias openly asserts this in the place cited, at the end of numbers 3 and 4. For he says that in such a fief, by everyone’s opinion, the rule applies <note>original: "c. 1. an agnatus"</note> that a son or a descending grandson can succeed in it even after repudiating the inheritance <term>repudiating the inheritance; formally refusing to be the legal heir, usually to avoid the deceased's debts</term>. Indeed, an agnate <term>agnate; a relative through the male line</term> and successor of the first possessor can succeed in it having repudiated the inheritance; which would not be true unless that fief was by pact and provision.

Nor does Julius Clarus seem to have intended anything else in the cited places, if read attentively, but only that it should not be considered granted for the recipient alone, but also for his descendants, according to the proper nature of a fief; and that in that event, by everyone’s opinion, that distinction holds which was established for the descendant and the agnate in the chapter first cited, as Covarruvias affirmed. And perhaps he incautiously added those words, "given for himself and his heirs."

<margin>3</margin>
The same Alvaro Valasco, in the cited question 44, number 6; question 49, number 2, and at the end of number 6; and question 50, number 5—along with Bartolus and others whom he cites—establishes this distinction between a secular (or private) emphyteusis and an Ecclesiastical emphyteusis. If an Ecclesiastical emphyteusis is granted to someone and his children or descendants, it is considered to be by pact and provision, and thus the children will be able to succeed in it even if they are not heirs or if they repudiate the inheritance; because such an emphy-

<column-break/>

-teusis does not pass to outside heirs unless it was granted for heirs in such a way that it is understood to extend even to outsiders. But truly, if a secular emphyteusis is granted to someone and his children or descendants, it is considered hereditary, and the children cannot succeed in it if they are not the legal heirs; because such an emphyteusis, by its nature, passes to outside heirs.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Jason and Imola reject this distinction, as reported by Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 18, number 2, the fifth conclusion; and Covarruvias seems to lean toward their opinion there, judging that even a secular emphyteusis granted under that form is by pact and provision, and a son can succeed in it even if he is not the heir, or if he repudiates the father’s inheritance. Julius Clarus also embraces this opinion in the section on emphyteusis, question 37, number 1, with many others whom he mentions.

The same is proven to me. First, because it is entirely consistent with the foundations laid down from the common opinion of the doctors in the preceding dispute. Second, because the contrary opinion rests on no solid foundation for establishing that distinction between those two types of emphyteusis. Finally, because Ecclesiastical emphyteusis is commonly granted for "heirs," just like secular ones, and thus in such a way that it is hereditary—or at least "mixed"—and it can even be granted so that it is simply hereditary. Therefore, that primary reason of Alvaro Valasco and Bartolus is by no means solid in the matter we are disputing: namely, that a father, by stipulating or contracting for a son, is in case of doubt considered to contract for him *as an heir*. This logic applies in the same way to Ecclesiastical emphyteusis; since, therefore, it does not hold for Ecclesiastical emphyteusis in their opinion, it should not be thought to have any force in secular ones either.

And Caldas asserts this must be affirmed absolutely in question 22, from number 19, regarding Portuguese law <note>original: "de iure Lusitano"</note>, according to those things which we will relate in the following disputes; and he adds the same is true under common law, although from number 14 he seemed to lean toward the opinion of Bartolus, Alvaro Valasco, and others. Of the same opinion as Caldas is Gama in *Decisions*, 8, numbers 6 and 7.

<margin>4</margin>
An emphyteusis or fief granted to someone "for himself, his children, and his heirs" is to be considered hereditary, at least "mixed." I said "at least mixed" because if it is a secular emphyteusis, and in it by the name of "heirs" even outsiders are understood (as was said in the preceding dispute), it will certainly be an emphyteusis that is simply hereditary. If, however, it is a fief—since in that the name of "heirs" is understood to mean only descendants unless something else is expressed (as was explained in the preceding dispute)—it will only be a "mixed" hereditary fief. And the same, according to the common opinion of the doctors, is true in an Ecclesiastical emphyteusis, for the same reason, as was seen there and in Dispute 469.

Therefore, not only can others included under the same form not succeed in that emphyteusis or fief unless they are heirs, but even the children cannot succeed unless they are the legal heirs. This is the common opinion of the doctors following Bartolus, which Covarruvias relates and follows in *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 18, number 3; and Julius Clarus, in the section on fiefs, question 9, number 8, and the section on emphyteusis.

<summary>This page discusses the specific phrasing required to distinguish between hereditary grants and those made by "pact and provision," arguing that if a grant does not explicitly mention "heirs," it is generally considered a specific contractual provision rather than a standard inheritance. Molina highlights debates over whether secular and ecclesiastical leases should be treated differently under the law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of the specific legal language used in property contracts. He is distinguishing between "hereditary" grants (which follow general inheritance laws) and those by "pact and provision" (which follow the specific, restricted intent of the person granting the land). This section focuses on how the inclusion of the word "heirs" changes the legal obligations of the successors.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 473

...emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term land lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for low rent</term>, question 37, numbers 2 and 3; and Alvaro Valasco, question 44, cited number 9. For that word, "and to heirs," has the same weight as saying "and to all other heirs," and consequently it affects the sons such that they cannot succeed to the property unless they are also the legal heirs. If, however, it were stated, "for the sons as heirs," or "for the descendants as heirs," without the conjunction "and" being included, then, as Alvaro Valasco well adds following Bartolus, it would indeed be an emphyteusis or a "mixed" fief <term>fief; land held from a lord in return for service</term>, even if the emphyteusis were secular <note>original: "secularis," meaning non-church related</note>. This is because the word "heirs" would qualify the specific "descendants" to whom it is joined, and in that form, the right would not extend to outside parties. Pinelo agrees in his commentary on Law 1 of the Code *concerning maternal goods*, part 3, number 90, inference 5. With much greater reason, if an ecclesiastical <note>church-owned</note> fief or emphyteusis were granted under this form—"to you and your heirs"—it would be a hereditary fief or emphyteusis. This means that descendants could not succeed in such a holding unless they were the legal heirs; as, against certain people asserting the contrary, Alvaro Valasco rightly maintains in the place cited above, number 11; Julius Clarus, question 9, cited number 7; and Covarruvias, cited number 3, in the section "the same entirely."

<margin>Question 5</margin> When a fief or ecclesiastical emphyteusis is granted under this form—"to you and your male heirs," or "those born of your body"—some legal scholars have judged the fief or emphyteusis to be by "pact and provision" <term>pact and provision; a specific agreement that follows the grantor's private rules rather than general inheritance law</term>, just as if the word "heirs" had not been included at all. Aretino calls this the truer and more accepted opinion. Pinelo and Alvaro Valasco (although Valasco later holds the opposite) say: "I would support this opinion in the formula 'for himself and the heirs born of his body.'" For then, he says, the word "heirs" designates only the sons, because "heirs" in a biological sense are not born, but are "made" by the law or by a person's will. He also adds that in the form "for himself and male heirs," the text in chapter 1, section *but different*, "on the alienation of fiefs," is quite pressing with these words: *If he dies without a legitimate male heir*, which word is to be understood in a fief as meaning "without a male son."

<margin>Decision</margin> Nevertheless, the contrary opinion is undoubtedly to be maintained along with Covarruvias (near the end of number 3), Julius Clarus (at the last number of question 9), Alvaro Valasco, and others whom he cites. For the addition of those words, "male" or "born of his body," ensures that the fief or emphyteusis is not *simply* hereditary <note>meaning open to any heir at all</note>, but it does not mean they are not "mixed hereditary," as if the word "heirs" included there lost its legal force. Nor is there any solid foundation for the contrary. Rather, the intention of the grantors must be considered, as well as the force of that word "heirs," rather than the metaphysical argument Valasco puts forward—namely, that heirs are not born but are created by the disposition of law or man. For those who are heirs by law or will are divided into categories: those heirs born of the body of the grantor, and those heirs not born from them. Even if they are "born" before they become "heirs," the terms still apply. Furthermore, the words from the section "on the alienation of fiefs" are cited incorrectly; for it is established that a "legitimate heir" is truly an heir, while in a fief it is understood that by that name, only a son

<column-break/>

or a male descendant is meant—specifically one who is an heir. For those words only signify that in fiefs, when nothing else was specified, neither women nor ancestors nor other outside heirs succeed, but only male descendants.

<margin>6</margin> And what was said about the previous form should also be said about this one: "I grant to you and your legitimate heirs this thing as a fief or emphyteusis." For such a holding is hereditary and not by pact and provision, as Alvaro Valasco rightly says against certain authors. The word "legitimate" only excludes illegitimate children; it does not strip the word "heirs" of its legal power. The same applies to this form: "I grant you this thing in emphyteusis or as a fief, to your children and heirs, so that they succeed according to sex and the priority of age," or "so that they succeed by the law of the Franks" <term>law of the Franks; a legal custom favoring primogeniture, where the eldest son inherits the entire estate</term>. This means the firstborn is always preferred over the others. Such a holding is hereditary to the effect that one cannot succeed to it unless he has first been established as the heir, as Valasco rightly says against Pinelo and others. The word "heirs" is not to be thought of as having been added in vain.

<margin>7</margin> However, if a fief is granted under this form—"I grant you this thing as a fief by the law of the Franks," meaning the firstborn is always preferred—the fief is held by pact and provision, because no mention of "heirs" was made. This is taught by Alvaro Valasco and Molina <note>The author referring to his own work on primogeniture</note> in book 1, chapter 7. But the matter is otherwise when "heirs" are mentioned; then it is hereditary.

<margin>8</margin> When an emphyteusis or fief has been granted under the form "to you and yours," Alvaro Valasco rightly affirms with Emilio Ferretti that it is by pact and provision. This is because by the name "yours," we understand those who are of the family and connected by blood; thus it is the same as if it were said, "to you and your descendants." Pinelo rightly rebukes the one who asserted it was then a "mixed hereditary" holding, claiming that "to you and yours" is the same as "to you and your heirs." Therefore, even if the emphyteusis were secular, it would not be hereditary under that specific form, but would be governed by pact and provision.

<margin>9</margin> When an emphyteusis or fief is granted under the form "to you and your successors," I would say that if it were a secular emphyteusis, it would be simply hereditary, as we said in the preceding dispute. This is because the term "successors" includes even outside parties who succeed by hereditary right. If, however, it were an ecclesiastical grant or a fief—which do not extend beyond descendants unless explicitly stated—the term "successors" is appropriately understood in that context to mean "descendants," and therefore they will be held by pact and provision.

If, however, as Alvaro Valasco and the more common opinion of the doctors hold, there is doubt as to whether a fief or emphyteusis is hereditary...

<summary>This page analyzes how specific legal formulas in contracts determine whether land is inherited through general law (hereditary) or specific restricted agreements (pact and provision). Molina argues that the inclusion of the word "heirs" is the decisive factor in making a grant hereditary, even when specific preferences like primogeniture or male-only succession are added.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina On Contracts

...ry <note>original: "ria," continuing the word "hereditaria" from the previous page</note>, if it is to be proposed that those rights are hereditary, they should certainly be considered mixed-hereditary: because the word "successors" can best be adapted to "descending heirs," even insofar as they are truly heirs and the term includes them. This agrees with what Caldas teaches in *On the nomination of emphyteusis* <term>emphyteusis; a long-term lease of land where the tenant must improve the property in exchange for low rent</term>, question 23, numbers 13 and 14, joined with the two preceding points, and what he reports regarding Portuguese law, which will be discussed below.

I have spoken according to the opinion of Alvaro Valasco and the more common view of the doctors: since Pinelo, in his commentary on Law 1 of the Code *concerning maternal goods*, part 3, number 91, argues so strongly against the common opinion of the doctors that he thinks in fiefs <term>fief; land held from a lord in return for service</term> one should rather lean toward them being by "pact and provision." Even in many arrangements where he had previously taught they were hereditary following the common opinion, he adds that they should rather be judged as being by pact and provision, with the word "heirs" placed in them being no obstacle. However, as Alvaro Valasco rightly adds in the place cited above, one must not withdraw from the common opinions received in practice, especially since Pinelo relies on no solid foundation for leaning toward the contrary.

From what has been said in this and the preceding dispute, it will be easy to judge—when any other forms are presented by which an emphyteusis or a fief are granted—when they are to be judged as being by pact and provision, and when they are simply or mixed-hereditary.

### Whether women succeed in emphyteusis and fiefs.

### DISPUTE 474.

-> SUMMARY <-

<margin>1</margin> Women are regularly not admitted to the succession of a fief, according to common opinion.  
*And the same applies to illegitimate children.*  
*Exceptions occur, however, as in numbers 2, 3, 4, and 5.*  
<margin>6</margin> *Whether the Prince can grant a dispensation so that a woman may succeed in a fief to the prejudice of the male agnates <note>agnates: relatives related through the male line</note>.*  
<margin>7</margin> *Whether a male descended from a woman excludes women who would succeed in a fief in the absence of males.*  
<margin>8</margin> *Whether a woman once excluded by a male is always considered excluded.*  
<margin>9</margin> *Whether, and when, an emphyteusis passes to women.*  
<margin>10</margin> *Whether women succeed in an emphyteusis taken for oneself and one's children.*  
*And what the rule is in Portuguese law. Ibid.*  
<margin>11</margin> *When women are not excluded from an emphyteusis, grandchildren from a woman of either sex succeed in it.*  
<margin>12</margin> *Whether a grandson from a daughter can succeed in an emphyteusis taken for oneself, children, and grandchildren and males, or for oneself and male descendants.*

Before we come to the other effects that arise from whether an emphyteusis or a fief is by "pact and provision" or "hereditary"—which is our goal—we must examine in this dispute and the following one whether illegitimate children succeed in an emphyteusis or a fief.

And to begin with the fief: the common conclusion, received and approved by the movements of fiefs, is that wo-

<column-break/>

men are regularly not admitted to succession in a fief. This is held in chapter 1, paragraph "however this" <note>original Latin: "hoc autem"</note>, *concerning those who can give a fief*; chapter 1, paragraph "but the daughters," *concerning the succession of a fief*; and chapter 1, paragraph "to the daughters," *concerning the succession of brothers or degrees of succession*; and the common opinion of the doctors affirms this, which Alvaro Valasco (on emphyteutic law, question 41), Julius Clarus (Book 4 of *Sentences*, section "fief," question 73), Covarrubias (1 *Varied Resolutions*, chapter 18, number 1), and Caldas (on the nomination of emphyteusis, question 23, number 8) report and follow.

<margin>1</margin> The reason, which the doctors commonly give along with the Gloss <note>Gloss: a standard medieval legal commentary</note> on the cited paragraph "however this," is that fiefs are usually granted with the burden of personal service, especially fighting and assisting in war, for which women are unfit. This reason is not entirely approved by the same Gloss and Julius Clarus in the place cited above: because, as is clear from the cited laws, even males descending through a female line are excluded from fiefs; in which cases that reason has no force.

Hence that Gloss and Julius Clarus subjoin that the "will of the legislators," or of those introducing the use of fiefs in this part, stands as the reason. Nevertheless, that common reason of the doctors is not to be despised or rejected, as they use it sometimes to define certain things received by use in the matter of fiefs. For from that reason, it was likely established and introduced in fiefs, with the extension that, once women were excluded, their male offspring would not be admitted to the fief either.

<margin>2</margin> When † however women are called to the fief in the investiture <term>investiture; the formal legal act of granting possession of a fief</term> or grant of the fief, then they succeed in it, but only in the absence of males, as Julius Clarus (question 73, number 3) affirms both points expressly from the three cited laws and others. It matters, however, whether in the investiture the fief is granted "for males and females," or "so that women may succeed in it along with the males." In the former event, women do not succeed except in the absence of males, according to the three cited laws; but in the latter, they succeed equally alongside them, as Julius Clarus subjoins in number 4 with Baldus and the common opinion of the doctors.

<margin>3</margin> When † a fief is "maternal" or "feminine"—because, for instance, it was granted to a woman from the beginning—women succeed in it, as held in chapter 1, *concerning the nature of the succession of a fief*; yet it must be understood that women succeed in the absence of males: because even in that event, males are preferred to women, as per chapter 1, *concerning the fief of a woman*. So says Julius Clarus in the same place, number 5, and the common opinion which he reports.

Julius Clarus (section "fief," question 16) along with many others whom he reports, testifies that it is received by custom that property is sometimes granted into a fief by the owner for a price; and there is no reason why it cannot be done so, even if such a type of fief deviates from the most proper form of a fief.

<margin>4</margin> Concerning † this kind of fief, therefore, there is a doubt whether women succeed in it. And indeed, when only males and not women were called in the investiture, it must be said that women do not succeed in it, even in the absence of males; because the tenor of the investiture must always be stood by.

When, however <note>original catchword: "men," from "tamen"</note>, no other service had been imposed, or personal service had not been imposed, then women would succeed in the absence of...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal restrictions on women inheriting fiefs and emphyteutic leases, explaining that while they are generally excluded due to the historical requirement for military service, exceptions exist if explicitly stated in the original grant or if the fief was originally established for a woman.</summary>
