<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of inheritance laws, specifically transitioning from the general nature of land grants to the specific rules governing when women may or may not succeed to a fief or an emphyteusis.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 474, Page 591

...of males, according to what we will soon add. But when these conditions are absent, since no other outcome remains except when personal service has been imposed, I believe—along with Isernia and Bruno, whom Julius Clarus mentions in question 73, citation number 6—that women do not succeed, rather than following Odofredo (whom Julius Clarus also follows there), who says they do succeed. This is especially true since Julius Clarus agrees with us on those other outcomes.

<margin>5</margin> When † for a fief <term>fief; land held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service, often military</term> no service has been imposed, then women are not excluded from it in the absence of males, unless the investiture <term>investiture; the formal legal act of granting possession of a fief</term> calls only for males. This is according to Baldus and the common opinion of the doctors, as Julius Clarus notes in question 72, citation number 7. The same applies if a service were imposed for the fief that a woman could perform just as well as a man, provided the investiture does not similarly call only for males, and where no contrary local custom has been accepted. This is affirmed by the common opinion cited by Julius Clarus, from which he says one must not depart in practice. Caldas asserted the same with others whom he cites in question 23, number 8. However, in places where there has been a custom that women succeed in fiefs, that custom must be upheld, as is very well known and affirmed by the common opinion mentioned by Julius Clarus at number 9.

<margin>Doubt</margin> Whether the prince <note>original: "princeps"; referring to the sovereign or head of state</note> can grant a dispensation so that a woman may succeed in a fief to the prejudice of the agnates <term>agnates; relatives related through the male line</term>.

<margin>Decision 6</margin> Julius Clarus responded there in the negative, following the common opinion of the doctors: because the prince cannot take away a right already acquired by another. He adds that even if he could, he ought not to do so. What should be said on this matter has been explained extensively by us in Dispute 170, especially before the seventh conclusion.

<margin>Doubt 7</margin> There is a doubt in those cases where it is said that women succeed in a fief in the absence of males: if, after a woman succeeds due to the lack of males and obtains the fief, a male is later born—either from her or from her sister—does that male exclude her from the fief? Andreas Isernia answers affirmatively.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, the common opinion to be embraced is the opposite, as reported and followed by Julius Clarus (on Fiefs, question 38, number 1) and Molina (Book 1 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 10, number 13). This is gathered from the chapter "Concerning him who to himself or his heirs" <note>original: "c. 1. de eo qui sibi, vel heredibus"</note> at the beginning: where, when a woman obtained a fief due to the lack of males, a son born to her while she was still alive did not obtain it. The reason is that this type of "useful ownership" <term>useful ownership; the legal right to use and profit from property, while the "direct ownership" remains with the lord</term> was obtained perpetually and irrevocably; it ought not to remain pending on the outcome of another’s birth.

<margin>Question 8</margin> There is a doubt on the other hand: if a woman, in those cases where she succeeds due to the lack of males, is once excluded from the fief because a male was present to succeed in it, does she remain excluded forever? Does this mean she cannot succeed even if the males later fail? The common opinion of the doctors affirms this, following the text in chapter 1, paragraph "Furthermore" <note>original: "quin et"</note>, under the title "Bishops or Abbots," as Isernia understands it (cited by Julius Clarus, question 80, number 2). The doctors, along with the Gloss <note>standard medieval legal commentary</note> there, limit this unless the male who excludes the woman dies immediately after the death of the last possessor: for then he is considered as if he had never existed, and therefore does not exclude her. I prefer the contrary opinion of Julius Clarus: namely, that she is only excluded forever as long as there is a male or another woman closer to him,

<column-break/>

who was the future last possessor. That text should be understood in this way: it is not the case that she must be excluded when the closer female relative of the last possessor is missing, as if in that event the fief ought to revert to the owner <note>original: "proprietarium"; the lord who holds the underlying title</note>. So much for fiefs.

<margin>9</margin> As far as emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term land lease where the tenant pays a small rent and must improve the property</term> is concerned, Baldus, Alexander, and a few others (cited by Covarruvias at number 1) judged that † emphyteusis does not pass to women. They were moved by the fact that a fief does not pass to them unless the opposite is expressed in the investiture. Likewise, Johannes Andreas (on the chapter "He was able" <note>original: "c. potuit"</note>, regarding Leases) and certain others (cited by Caldas, question 19, number 10, and the cited question at number 9), among whom is Gama (Decision 233, number 8), asserted that women do not succeed in ecclesiastical emphyteusis.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, the contrary opinion must be maintained, even in ecclesiastical emphyteusis, according to the more common view of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Covarruvias (Miscellaneous Resolutions, book 2, chapter 18, number 1), Julius Clarus (on Emphyteusis, question 32), Alvaro Valasco (on the Law of Emphyteusis, question 41, number 2), and Caldas (the cited question 23 from number 8, and question 24 from number 27). Namely, when no word excluding women is placed in the grant of emphyteusis, both women and males succeed in it. This is clearly proven by the "Authentic" <term>Authentic; a collection of Emperor Justinian's legal decrees</term> regarding non-alienation, paragraph "Emphyteusis," where even ecclesiastical emphyteusis is said to be granted indifferently for sons and grandsons, males and females, and for a husband and wife, if mention was made of the wife. Nor is the reasoning the same as for a fief: because a fief, as stated, is usually granted for personal service in war, which is not suitable for women.

<margin>Question 10</margin> Whether, when an emphyteusis is accepted for oneself and one's "sons," † women also succeed in it? The Archdeacon and the more common opinion of the doctors asserted that women do not succeed then, but only males. They were moved by the idea that in contracts, the masculine does not include the feminine, and the contracting parties should blame themselves if they wanted to include women; since they could have expressed it, they used ambiguous words.

<margin>Decision</margin> Rightly, however, along with Salycetus and many others whom they cite, the contrary was asserted by Covarruvias (at number 1), Julius Clarus (at question 32, number 3), Aries Pinelo (on Law 3 of the Code regarding maternal goods, number 33), and Alvaro Valasco (at question 41, number 3). And this opinion is approved by Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>: for in book 4 of the Ordinances, title 93, in the second to last paragraph, under the name of "one son" whom he wished to name, a daughter is also understood. This is confirmed because under the name of "sons" <note>original: "filiorum"</note>, daughters are also included, as proven by the law "Whoever" <note>original: "quisquis"</note> in the Digest *on the meaning of words*, and as the Gloss on the section "If anyone to daughters" <note>original: "si quis filiabus"</note> affirms regarding the word "sons" in the Institutes *on those who can appoint guardians in a will*. It is also proven by various other laws which we cited in Dispute 220. This especially takes place in "indifferent" matters <note>meaning matters where the specific gender of the person does not affect the function of the grant</note>, such as emphyteusis, so that both women and males succeed in it. This should apply no less in contracts, if the matter is indifferent, than in last wills; in a will, it is no less within the power of the testator to express daughters specifically if he wants his disposition to extend to them. When a father takes an emphyteusis for himself and his sons, or male and female descendants, then women succeed with males in such an emphyteutic grant, and it is to be divided equally among them—at least as far as the valuation—in Portugal, according to what was said in Dispute 460. So say Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, whom Covarruvias and Alvaro Valasco follow.

Molina argues that in "indifferent" contracts like emphyteusis, the term "sons" should legally include daughters, particularly under Portuguese law.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts

Valasco, in the place cited above, number 4, states that if there is a custom or a statute in a particular place that males are preferred to females, then the common opinion of the doctors is rightly followed (which they cite against Salicetus and which Covarrubias, Alvarez, and Valasco follow, as does Julius Clarus in question 32, the last number cited). This opinion asserts that females do not succeed in an <term>emphyteusis; a type of long-term or perpetual lease of land where the tenant enjoys the use of the property in exchange for a yearly rent and upkeep</term> unless there is a lack of males. This is because the contracting parties are presumed to celebrate their contracts according to the local statutes and customs. A similar rule exists in Portuguese law, Book 4, Title 62,

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> sections 2, 3, and 4. There it is decreed that if someone holds an emphyteusis for themselves and for a person they might nominate, and if that person—or their ancestors or many descendants—establishes heirs without nominating anyone specifically for the emphyteusis, then the rules for intestate succession (dying without a will) must be followed. In such an event, it is arranged that descendants are always preferred to ancestors in the emphyteusis. This applies even if such descendants are "natural" children <note>children born to unmarried parents who were legally capable of marrying</note> of a commoner, or even if they are "spurious" <note>children born from an illicit or prohibited union, such as adultery</note>. However, spurious children must be legitimized by the Prince <note>the sovereign ruler</note> to succeed a parent who dies intestate. Nevertheless, these rules regarding illegitimate children should not be extended to an ecclesiastical (Church) emphyteusis, as will be discussed in the following dispute. Among descendants or ancestors of equal degree, males are always preferred to females and are considered the "nominated" heirs; among male descendants of the same degree, the eldest is preferred over the rest. In the absence of a male of the same degree, the eldest female is preferred. Likewise, a legitimate descendant is always preferred to an illegitimate one, unless it is a natural son of a commoner, who succeeds equally with legitimate children in this Kingdom. Alvarez and Valasco, in the place cited at the end of number 3, and others, observe that this regulation is noteworthy.

When women are not excluded from an emphyteusis, grandchildren of either sex born from a daughter certainly succeed to it. This is the view of Alvarez and Valasco (question 41, cited at number 5) and Julius Clarus (section on emphyteusis, question 36, number 1), and it is the common opinion and an undisputed matter.

<margin>Question.</margin> A greater doubt, however, is whether a male grandson—the son of a daughter—can succeed in an emphyteusis that was taken for "himself, his sons, and his male grandsons," or for "himself and his male descendants." Julius Clarus (question 36) and others cited by Aries Pinellus (Book 3, Code on maternal goods, number 19) deny this. They follow the rule that when a female is excluded from a <term>maioratu; an inheritance restricted to the eldest son to keep an estate intact, similar to primogeniture</term> or other similar arrangement, the males descending from her are also considered excluded. This is the common opinion of many whom Molina refers to and follows (Book 3 on Primogeniture, chapter 5, number 41). Alvarez and Valasco (at number 5) affirm the opposite. He argues that a grandson descending from a daughter is truly a male and is the grandson of the person who took the emphyteusis. Indeed, Alvarez, Valasco, and Aries Pinellus, as well as Molina (at number 48, though Molina is speaking of primogeniture rather than emphyteusis), all agree on this: if the intent of excluding females from succession is to keep the property within the family or the <term>agnatio; relationship through the male line or the father's side</term>, then by excluding the female, the males descending from her are also considered excluded. This is because the family name of the head of the house is not preserved in them. However, if the intent was not to exclude the female's line specifically, but rather to ensures the property passes to males for administration, then the males 

<column-break/>

descending from her are not considered excluded. Alvarez and Valasco judge that this second interpretation should be applied when only "male descendants" are called to an emphyteusis.

<margin>Decision.</margin> I, however, judge that the matter must be decided by conjectures regarding what the mind of the person (or persons) excluding the females was. Based on these conjectures and the concurrent circumstances, one must judge whether males from a female line ought to be admitted or not. Perhaps the most frequent intent will be that the emphyteutic property should not leave the family; this is what Aries Pinellus seems to have felt, and the opinion of the other doctors seems to lean this way. Furthermore, what Alvarez and Valasco cite from Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 63, section *Essendo*, in confirmation of his opinion, actually contributes nothing to the matter; in that section, the discussion concerns a case where the female is *not* excluded from the emphyteusis. The same Alvarez and Valasco confess that if the emphyteusis was taken for "descendants through the male sex," then males descending from a daughter are indeed excluded.

### Whether an illegitimate person succeeds in an emphyteusis or a fief.

1 Illegitimate children, even if they are natural sons and later legitimized, do not succeed in a fief, according to the common opinion.
2 And what the rule is in an emphyteusis. (Number 2).

# Second Treatise, Dispute 475.

<margin>26</margin> *The power to legitimize granted by the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, a Legate, or a Count Palatine is not understood to include the right to succeed in an entail <note>original: "maioratu"; a system where an estate is kept whole and passed to a single heir</note>, a fief, or an ecclesiastical perpetual lease <note>original: "emphyteusi ecclesiastica"</note>, unless this is expressly granted.*
<margin>27</margin> *Declare and understand this, however, as in number 17.*
<margin>28</margin> *Whether an illegitimate person who obtains an ecclesiastical perpetual lease before being legitimized may lawfully retain it after their legitimization.*

<margin>1</margin> **A**s far as the fief <note>original: "feudum"</note> is concerned: illegitimate children, even if they are "natural" children <note>children born to parents who were legally able to marry each other at the time of conception</note> and are later legitimized, do not succeed in the fief. This is established in chapter 1, paragraph "naturales," concerning the fiefs of the deceased. This is also the common opinion of the doctors of law, which is cited and followed by Gigas in *On Fiefs*, question 19, number 5, and by Julius Clarus in Book 4, *Sententiae*, under the section on fiefs, question 82, numbers 1 and 2. What should be said regarding someone legitimized specifically to succeed even in a fief will become clear from what is to be said regarding legitimization for succeeding in an ecclesiastical <term>emphyteusis; a type of long-term or perpetual land lease where the tenant (emphyteuta) has the right to use the land in exchange for an annual rent</term>.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the <term>emphyteusis</term>, we must say the following: If it is a secular or private lease and is not strictly limited to the children or offspring of the recipient, then illegitimate children can succeed in it (or not) just as they can (or cannot) succeed in the other property of the person in question. This follows the general rules of succession for illegitimate children explained in Disputes 166 and 167. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which Julius Clarus (question 30) and Caldas (question 19, from number 5) cite and follow, even if Caldas does not state it in exactly these terms. This can be effectively proved: since a secular lease granted without restriction to a specific class of persons can pass even to strangers, the judgment regarding succession must be the same as for any other free property held by the possessor of such a lease. Therefore, illegitimate children face no greater or different prohibition against succeeding in that lease than they do in any other property held by the possessor. It follows that if they can succeed in the other property—according to what was said in the two cited disputes—they can also succeed in such a lease. If they cannot succeed in other property, they cannot succeed in the lease either.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding legitimized children: if they could not have succeeded in the other property of the person in question unless they were legitimized, then the same applies to the lease. In the cases discussed in Dispute 362 and the two following it—where it was said that legitimized or dispensed persons can succeed in someone’s property—they can also succeed in this kind of lease, because the reasoning is exactly the same. 
And this is what the common opinion of the doctors intends, which Julius Clarus (as cited above, question 31) and Caldas (question 21, from number 25) cite and follow; there can be no difficulty in this matter.

<margin>Question 4</margin> There is, however, no small controversy among the doctors if a secular lease is granted to a recipient "and his children." Should the <column-break/> name of "children" be understood as only those who are legitimate, or also illegitimate ones, especially "natural" children? Baldus, Decius, and others cited by Caldas (number 9, above) asserted that only the legitimate are to be understood, and therefore natural children cannot succeed in the lease. They argue that by the name "children" used simply, only the legitimate are meant, based on the law *Filium eum* (Digest: On those who are their own masters or under the power of another), which states:
> For we have defined a son as one who is born of a man and his wife.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, the common opinion—which Julius Clarus (cited question 30) refers to and follows, along with Alexander, Felinus, and others cited by Caldas (number 11)—affirms the contrary: namely, that natural children are also to be understood, and therefore can succeed in that lease. In last wills and testaments, when "children" are named, natural children are also considered to be called, at least in the absence of legitimate ones. This is gathered from the law *Ex facto*, paragraph *Si quis rogatus* (Digest: On the Trebellianic Decree), where a thing is left to someone with the clause that "if he dies without children," it should pass to a third party. If he dies leaving a natural son, that son excludes the substitute heir. Furthermore, the argument from last wills to contracts is valid in this specific area. Caldas (number 12) leans toward the former opinion, arguing that last wills allow for a broader interpretation than contracts. In wills, the name "children" also includes grandchildren and other descendants, which is not the case in contracts. Therefore, although natural children might be understood by the name "children" in wills, they should not be in contracts like a lease—especially today, when cohabitation with a concubine kept at home is condemned by Gospel law and Canon law, which more recent civil laws have embraced.

Finally, from number 16, he adds that one must judge from the concurrent circumstances in the proposed case whether the contracting parties intended to include natural children. This is similar to what we were saying (citing Molina, Emmanuel Acosta, and others) at the end of Dispute 147: one must judge from the circumstances whether a testator intended to include natural children under the name "children" for the purpose of excluding a substitute heir, as the paragraph *Ille* clearly teaches.

In the case at hand, the contracting parties are not acting to preserve the lease among successors to increase the nobility of the family (as those who establish entails or trusts usually do to ennoble their family line, which the succession of a natural child might hinder). Rather, the "direct lord" <note>the original owner who granted the lease</note> might only intend that the lease end and be reunited with the property sooner if there are no legitimate children. Since this is not of great importance and does not happen frequently, I lean toward the latter opinion: unless there are probable conjectures to the contrary, the contracting parties are not usually presumed to have intended to exclude natural children.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of inheritance rights regarding perpetual leases (emphyteusis). It specifically addresses whether "natural" children (born to unmarried parents who could have legally wed) and "spurious" children (born of prohibited unions) can succeed to these estates under various regional laws, particularly those of Portugal.</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts

**A**nd this can be further argued, because concerning this kind of <term>emphyteusis; a perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant has near-ownership rights in exchange for rent</term>, the judgment regarding succession is the same as for other "free" assets <note>assets not tied up in an entail or specific legal restriction</note> belonging to the possessor, as has been stated. Now, natural children, in the absence of legitimate ones (especially descendants), are accustomed to succeed their parents in those free assets, as was said in Dispute 166. 

This opinion of ours holds true especially in **Lusitania** <note>Portugal</note>, where not only do the natural children of commoners succeed their parents in all assets equally with legitimate ones, but even the natural children of a nobleman dying intestate <note>without a will</note>—in the absence of all legitimate descendants—are considered named for the father’s perpetual lease. They are preferred in that succession over any legitimate ancestors <note>such as the deceased's parents</note>, as is held in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 62, the penultimate paragraph. Moreover, contracts are considered to be made in accordance with the laws and customs of the kingdoms in which they are enacted. 

Nor should the law "filius eum" (*Digest, On those who are their own or another's right*) sway the matter. For there, for the purpose of distinguishing various human conditions and statuses, it was said that he is considered a "son" simply who is legitimate. However, in the strictness and property of the word—which must be stood by simply when the circumstances of the matter do not demand otherwise—the name of "sons" includes natural children no less than legitimate ones.

**Caldas**, along with others whom he cites, and according to his own earlier opinion, considers that if the person to whom the lease is granted only had natural children at the time of the grant, and this was not hidden from the grantor, the lease granted to him and his "sons" is extended to the natural ones. This circumstance is a sufficient indication that by the name of "sons," the contracting parties intended to include even natural ones. He thinks the same must be said, following Aluarotus, regarding a **fief** <note>feudal land held on condition of service</note>, even if natural sons are not normally admitted to a fief (as said above), provided nothing else was said tacitly or expressly in the investiture. 

Likewise, because a lease was granted to an illegitimate person himself and his "sons," he considers—with **Baldus** and others—that natural children succeed in it. This is a sufficient circumstance to show the grantor did not intend to exclude sons because of the quality <note>illegitimacy</note> which he already accepted in the parent. 

Furthermore, although the law "generaliter" (*Code, On institutions and substitutions*) provides that when someone appoints a natural son as heir and substitutes another for him, the substitute is excluded if the appointee has legitimate offspring, but not if he has natural offspring—a provision to which the *Gloss* <note>standard legal commentary</note> applies many solutions—the natural son nonetheless excludes the substitute. This is especially true when the clause "if he should die without children" was express rather than merely presumed. Certainly, the circumstance of illegitimacy in the person to whom the lease was granted carries little or no weight in the proposed matter. We are not speaking of a lease which, by legal disposition or presumption, does not pass to illegitimates—such as an **Ecclesiastical lease**. A secular lease, by its nature, can pass to illegitimates. The only controversy is whether the person granting it to a recipient and his "children" intended only legitimate ones so that the lease might end sooner. To this, whether the recipient is legitimate or not is entirely irrelevant. Caldas, with many others, considers the same to be true if the person handing over the property in a lease to a recipient and his children

<column-break/>

is himself illegitimate. For he is not presumed to have intended to exclude in the children of the recipient the very quality which he himself possesses. Indeed, regarding this, there is a somewhat greater conjecture that such was the mind of the one handing over the property in that manner.

Caldas, in the place cited above at number 22, asserts with others that if a secular lease is granted to a recipient and his children, even **illegitimate** ones, then an illegitimate child can succeed. He seems to mean even a <term>spurious; a child born of a union the law considered "shameful," such as adultery or incest</term> child, if the grant was also made to him. He gives this reason: because then the illegitimate child does not so much take the lease from the parent as from the <term>proprietarius; the ultimate legal owner or landlord</term> granting the property. In comparison to the owner, such an illegitimate person is not incapable of receiving it. 

He confirms this from the doctrine which we handed down from the law "si is" (*Digest, On vulgar and pupillary substitution*), Dispute 167, before the fourth conclusion, with **Bartolus**, **Covarrubias**, and others. Namely, that a father can substitute a spurious son for a legitimate son in a "pupillary" manner <note>appointing an heir for a minor child</note>—not indeed in the assets that flowed from that parent to the legitimate son, but in the other assets of that same legitimate son. This is because, by virtue of such a substitution, the spurious son (though receiving through the agency of the father) does not receive from the father, nor assets that flowed from the father, but receives from his brother assets which the brother had from elsewhere. Therefore, in a similar way, since in the proposed matter the son does not receive from the father but from the owner—even if the father applied the lease to such a son through the power granted to him by the owner—it follows that a spurious son of the tenant can succeed in that lease.

An exception is made in the following twenty-fourth number, with others he cites: unless the father had purchased that lease with a **price**. For then, since the lease takes the place of the price (or is subrogated for it), just as such an illegitimate child could not succeed the father in the money/price, so neither can he in the lease bought with that price. 

**H**owever, I judge it to be **false** that a spurious son can succeed in that lease, even if it was not purchased. I am led to this because by the very fact that a property is handed over in a lease, the <term>useful ownership; the right to use and profit from the land</term> or the "emphyteutic right" becomes the proper asset of the first tenant. Thus, by a certain order of successors, such ownership and right are estimable by a price. And although the owner in the first contract could prescribe the laws and conditions by which it would be destined—and regarding the receiving of the thing, it is said to be from the owner prescribing those laws—it nonetheless cannot be denied that subsequent tenants receive that useful ownership and right from the prior ones in a certain order. In comparison to this, the spurious son of the prior tenant is no less incapable than he is in comparison to the other assets of the same tenant. Therefore, unless he has been dispensed or legitimized by the **Prince** <note>the sovereign or monarch</note> to succeed in that lease, he can no more succeed in it than in the rest of the assets of the same tenant, even if the owner granted the faculty to succeed in it.

This is clearly confirmed: because by the very fact that a secular property is granted without any restriction...

Molina explores Portuguese law and various legal opinions, ultimately arguing that without sovereign legitimization, spurious children cannot inherit these rights as they are considered personal property of the previous tenant.</summary>

### Treatise Two, Dispute 475

...granted, by the power of the owner's concession, it can pass to anyone, even outsiders, and even to <term>spurious children; those born from prohibited unions, such as adultery or incest</term>, provided they are otherwise legally capable. Thus, a <term>tenant; specifically an emphyteuta, the holder of a perpetual lease</term> can leave it to a spurious child who is an outsider to his family. Yet, no one would say a father can leave it to his own spurious son unless that son has been legitimized or granted a dispensation by the prince. Hence, in the **Portuguese Ordinances**, Title 62, the second-to-last paragraph, although it is established that if a tenant—who had the power to name anyone, even an outsider, to the lease—dies intestate without a legitimate descendant, he is considered to have named his <term>natural child; a child born to unmarried parents who were legally free to marry</term> if he has one (even if the father is not a commoner). However, regarding a spurious child, it is added in the same place that they are not considered named unless they are legitimized by the prince so they may succeed their parents in an intestate death.

Regarding the point used to confirm the opposite opinion, it must be said that the reasoning is not the same in the matter we are debating and in the case of a father <term>substituting; a legal arrangement where a second heir is named if the first cannot take the inheritance</term> a spurious son for a legitimate son in a "pupillary" fashion. For in that substitution, not only does the spurious son receive nothing at all from the father, but he cannot even receive from his brother the assets that came to the legitimate son from the father by virtue of that substitution. These points concern secular leases.

<margin>6</margin> But regarding † **Ecclesiastical** leases, it must be said: not only is it true if the lease was granted to the recipient and his children for three generations, or in perpetuity, but even if it was granted with the power to transmit it to any heirs or successors (even outsiders), illegitimate and natural sons cannot succeed in it. This is the common opinion of the learned doctors, which is cited and followed by **Gigas** (On Pensions, question 19, number 6), **Julius Clarus** (on Emphyteusis, question 30), **Gama** (Decision 2, number 1 and Decision 377, number 2), and **Caldas** (On the Nomination of Emphyteusis, question 7, number 38). The reason is that the Church rightly holds all illegitimate children in <note>original: "exosos," meaning loathed or viewed with legal disfavor</note> disregard, as they were conceived in a sinful act. It should not be presumed that the Church intends—through the general words of a concession of its property—to include those whom it would refuse if asked specifically, as it seeks to oppose the sins in which they are conceived.

<margin>Question</margin> From this, a doubt arises: whether the Portuguese law (Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 62, second-to-last paragraph) should also apply to Ecclesiastical leases. This law states that when a tenant who had the power to name anyone dies intestate, he is considered to have named his natural son (even if the father is not a commoner) when he lacked other <margin>7</margin> legitimate descendants. † Consequently, since this law assumes a tenant *can* name such a son, does it apply to Church property, or is it only understood to apply to secular leases? Likewise, does another Portuguese law (Book 4, Title 71), which allows the natural son of a commoner to succeed equally to his parents' property alongside legitimate children, also apply to obtaining an ecclesiastical lease?

**Gama** (Decision 2, number 4), speaking of that first law, says that it does extend even to ecclesiastical leases. He notes that it has been judged this way several times in the 

<column-break/>

**Portuguese Senate** <note>the high court of Portugal</note>, although he admits that it has often been judged to the contrary. He follows the same opinion in Decision 377, number 7.

It is argued that in such cases, the issue is only the succession of the <term>useful domain; the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to the "direct domain" or ultimate ownership</term> of the leased property. This "useful" right no longer belongs to the Church but to the lay tenant. Therefore, while it belongs to laypeople, the civil law governing succession is valid, even if it decrees that the property should go to illegitimate children (who, under common Church law, could not receive an ecclesiastical lease). However, the opposite must be affirmed, following what was said in Dispute 446 and according to **Caldas** (question 7, number 39). That law should only be understood to have force in secular leases, not ecclesiastical ones. Regarding succession to property held from the Church, civil laws can have no force to the prejudice of the Church and its own sanctions. Caldas reports that the Portuguese Senate has often judged this way, and he has seen such rulings himself. He affirms this same view in question 19, numbers 28 and 31. Regarding the second law mentioned, I believe the same should be said: that law does not apply for the purpose of obtaining an ecclesiastical lease. Caldas asserted the same (question 21, at the end of number 48). I believe, however, that if a natural son is rejected from the lease, he ought to be compensated from the parents' other assets, so that he does not receive a smaller <term>legitimate portion; the minimum share of an estate guaranteed by law to certain heirs</term> of his parents' goods than he would have if the lease were secular or if other brothers had obtained it. Furthermore, it should be seen whether there is a <note>original: "consuetudo praescripta," a custom established over time</note> prescribed custom in Portugal regarding this law, such that natural children do succeed in them. I am unaware of this, as I am currently far from that Kingdom and cannot inquire.

<margin>8 †</margin> There is a doubt whether a **grandson**, born from the legitimate marriage of an illegitimate son, is incapable of succeeding to his grandfather's ecclesiastical lease because he descends from an incapable son. **Caldas** (question 19, starting at number 35) disputes this matter at length and finally agrees with the following points. Briefly, following what we said in Dispute 167 (conclusion 9, with **Barros**, **Covarrubias**, **Pinelo**, **Gama**, and **Antonio Gomez**), we must say: such a grandson is not incapable of succeeding his grandfather in that lease. Therefore, the grandfather can leave it to him, provided he does so for the sake of the grandson himself (which is always presumed) and not for the sake of the illegitimate son, and provided he does not do so to the prejudice of other legitimate descendants to whom the lease is owed.

The reason is that this grandson, being the legitimate son of his father, is not incapable of an ecclesiastical lease, just as he is not barred from <term>ecclesiastical benefices; church offices that provide an income</term>. Just as a grandfather can appoint him as an heir and leave him other assets, he can also leave him his ecclesiastical lease. An exception is made if the grandson were the legitimate son of a <term>spurious; here specifically meaning "incestuous"</term> son born of an incestuous union. For then, just as it was said that he cannot succeed to any of that grandfather's assets, he could not succeed to his grandfather's lease, whether secular or ecclesiastical. In the event, however, in which it was said that such a grandson can succeed in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the inheritance rights of illegitimate children within the context of emphyteusis (long-term leases). # Luis de Molina, On Contracts

In an **Ecclesiastical emphyteusis** <note>original: "emphyteusi Ecclesiastica"; a long-term or perpetual lease of Church land</note>, even if a **son under paternal power** <note>original: "filiusfamilias"; a son who remains under the legal authority of his father</note> is established in his father's power, the father does not have the **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of the property</note> of such a lease, nor of other goods that come to that grandson. This is consistent with the views of Bartolus and Antonio Gómez; the reason is that a father of a **spurious child** <note>a child born of a prohibited union</note> should not receive any profit from his son's assets. Instead, such usufruct belongs to the grandson himself, along with the lease. Regarding a **son-in-law** married to an illegitimate daughter, I believe the same must be said as we stated in the cited conclusion regarding the question of whether he can be appointed as an heir by the same father-in-law.

When an Ecclesiastical lease is granted directly by the Church to an illegitimate person, such a grant is valid, even if the person is spurious—provided that the grantor is not unaware that the recipient is illegitimate. For if the grantor were ignorant of this, and would not have granted it had they known of the illegitimacy, the grant would be void. It would be considered an involuntary and "surreptitious" <note>obtained by withholding the truth</note> acquisition, as the quality of the person was not disclosed—a quality that would have entirely deterred the grantor from making the grant. The first point is proved because the Church never renders an illegitimate person inherently incapable of an ecclesiastical lease; it is merely presumed that the Church does not *intend* to grant it to them, because it is generally more beneficial for the public good and the salvation of souls. However, if a legitimate cause exists—such as the person or their parent having served the Church well, or if it is more expedient for the Church because they will manage the property better or offer a higher rent—there is no prohibition against the Church handing over its property in a lease to an illegitimate person. Even if the grantor does not act rightly in doing so without a legitimate cause (for the reason stated above), the transfer is valid if all other necessary conditions for alienating the property are met.

The second point—namely, that if the grantor was unaware of this status and otherwise would not have granted it, the grant is invalid because it was involuntary—is clear in itself. **Caldas** (Question 19, number 70) followed **Afflicto** on this, noting that it has been so judged in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>. This is further confirmed by the law (Chapter 1, Paragraph *Personam*), which states that many are excluded from a **fief** <note>original: "feudo"</note> unless a grant is expressly made for them. Regarding the original grant, it says: *We do not distinguish the person of the one receiving the investiture, for even a slave can be invested, unless ignorance is claimed regarding the quality of the person.* If a quality is unknown which would normally prevent someone from being admitted to a fief, the grant is null. This is quite clearly hinted at there and affirmed by the gloss. The same reasoning applies to an Ecclesiastical lease regarding an illegitimate person.

However, the fact that either the grantor of the Church property or the recipient is illegitimate is not a sufficient sign for us to believe that the grant is made for future illegitimate successors, especially those not yet born. To do so would be to **favor future sins**, which

<column-break/>

must not be presumed of the Church as a grantor. Even if the Church property is leased by a spurious prelate <note>a high-ranking Church official</note> using the words "to you, and to any of your successors," or "to you, and to whomever you wish," it is not understood to include illegitimate successors if none are currently born to the recipient. This is even more true if the prelate making the grant is not illegitimate. Furthermore, a prelate alone cannot lease property in this way before it is incorporated into the "table" <note>original: "mensæ"; the portion of Church revenue set aside for the prelate's support</note>, as this is not the traditional way of preserving property. In this matter, the argument from fiefs or the establishment of a **mayorazgo** <note>original: "maioratus"; an entailed estate that passes to a single heir</note> does not apply to an Ecclesiastical lease. In those cases, based on the status of the grantor or the first recipient, it might be presumed that the grant was made for those of similar status, even those yet to be born. There, such a provision could be made without indecency and lawfully. But in the matter we are discussing, such a grant would be not only indecent but also illicit, as it would encourage future sins; therefore, it cannot be presumed from the circumstances alone. Additionally, prelates do not grant what is their own in an Ecclesiastical lease, but what belongs to the Church, over which they do not have as free a power of disposal as if it were their own. This is supported by Caldas (Question 39, number 68 and Question 20, number 3).

<margin>9</margin>
When, however, property is granted in an Ecclesiastical lease to someone who *already* has illegitimate children, then—whether the recipient is legitimate or illegitimate—it could be presumed from those circumstances that the grant "to himself and his children or descendants" includes those illegitimate children already born. This is because doing so is not "favoring" or providing an occasion for those sins in the future. If there were no hope of him having other descendants in the future, then that circumstance would strongly suggest the grant extends to his illegitimate children.

Even if there were hope of him having legitimate children, or if at the time of the grant he had both legitimate and illegitimate children, the clause "to himself and any of his children," or "to whomever he wishes to leave it," or "to whomever he shall name," certainly extends to the illegitimate ones.

I believe it is only in this specific event that such general clauses in a Church lease extend to illegitimate children. I do not believe they do so in other cases where it would be done indecently or wrongly, regardless of what **Gama** (Decision 2, number 3 and Decision 377, number 6) says or claims to have seen judged. For when an extension to illegitimate children would be wrong or indecent, it must rather be presumed that those clauses are to be understood as applying only to those to whom the extension can be made without indecency or fault.

When someone has only illegitimate children born to them, and this fact is not unknown to the grantor of the lease...

...would be included, then; if he were to say, "I grant this property in **emphyteusis** <term>a long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land</term> to you, and to your others, both those already born and those to be born," it is clear that illegitimate children are included. This is because there are no others for whom that part of the grant—"those already born"—could be verified <note>If the grant mentions children already born to someone who only has illegitimate ones at the time, the law assumes the grantor intended to include them</note>. According to this, the teachings of Caldas <note>Francisco de Caldas Pereira y Castro (1543–1597), a prominent Portuguese jurist</note> in his cited question 19, from number 61, and question 20, from number 4, are to be approved or rejected.

<margin>10</margin> A person legitimated by a prince’s **rescript** <term>a formal legal decree or reply from a ruler</term> cannot succeed in an Ecclesiastical emphyteusis. This is the common opinion of the doctors of law, along with Baldus, which is cited and followed by Gigas in *On Pensions*, question 19, number 6; Giulio Claro on *Emphyteusis*, question 13; Gregorio López on law 4, title 15, part 4, at the words *all the honors*; Gama, decision 307, number 3; and more extensively by Caldas on the naming of emphyteusis, question 21, from number 29. This holds true not only if the Ecclesiastical lease was expressly granted for "legitimate children" or "those born of legitimate marriage," but even if it was granted for "children" or "descendants" generally, or even if granted without qualification.

The reason for this is that, although those legitimated by decree are equated with legitimate children (as seen in Disputation 173), they are nonetheless not truly legitimate, but were truly conceived from the sin of their parents. For this reason, they are barred from Ecclesiastical leases. Therefore, even if an Ecclesiastical lease was granted with a clause stating that it could also pass to "outside successors" <note>heirs who are not direct family members</note>, an illegitimate person legitimated by a prince's decree does not succeed in it, even though I may have suggested the contrary in the cited Disputation 173 along with Gama. 

Indeed, the reason why someone legitimated by a prince's decree cannot succeed in an Ecclesiastical lease is not simply because it would result in a loss for the Church (to which the **useful ownership** <term>the right to use and profit from the land</term> would return sooner if such a person did not succeed). A secular prince's legitimation could not block such a benefit to the Church. While that specific reason might seem to fail when the lease is allowed to go to outsiders anyway, the true legal reason is the one we just provided <note>the moral/legal status of the birth</note>, which a secular prince cannot override with his decree.

<margin>11</margin> It is further confirmed that one legitimated by decree cannot succeed in an Ecclesiastical lease because such a person cannot even succeed in a **fief** <term>land held in exchange for service, usually military</term> by a prince’s decree unless they are specifically legitimated for that purpose, as was stated at the beginning of this disputation. The reason is far stronger regarding Ecclesiastical leases due to the aforementioned logic, which a prince cannot prejudice through his decree. Therefore, an illegitimate person cannot be granted a dispensation to succeed in an Ecclesiastical lease except by the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, or by someone having express faculty from the Supreme Pontiff for that purpose. Nor is someone considered legitimated for this purpose by a general legitimation from the Pope, unless specific mention is made of legitimation for an Ecclesiastical lease, or a clause is added to the dispensation making it clear that such was the Pope's intention, as noted by Gigas, Caldas (citing Decio), and others.

Where Caldas adds: when the Supreme Pontiff merely grants a dispensation to an illegitimate person so they can succeed in an Ecclesiastical lease, and does not add anything to indicate he grants this even to the prejudice of the Church, then for that person to succeed in a lease already granted by the Church, the consent of the Church's **rector** <term>the administrator or head of the specific church institution</term> is necessary. This is because 

<column-break/>

similar dispensations have no force when they prejudice a third party—unless the loss to the third party is mentioned in the narrative or something is added to the grant making it clear it is granted regardless of such loss—unless that third party freely consents.

<margin>12</margin> When a lease is granted for "lawfully born children," or (which is the same) for "children born from a legitimate marriage," if that grant were secular, someone legitimated by a prince's decree would not succeed in it. For although such a person is equated to legitimate children, they were still not "born from a legitimate marriage." Such a lease was granted only for those born from marriage. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which Caldas relates and follows.

However, the question is whether a prince can legitimate someone to succeed in a lease granted in that way. Certainly, if the lease were secular, he could not do so; for he cannot, in that regard, prejudice the rights of the **direct lord** <term>the ultimate owner of the land to whom the tenant owes duties</term> so as to extend the lease to more people than were granted in his favor from the beginning.

If, however, the lease were Ecclesiastical, since the Supreme Pontiff can, for a reasonable cause, dispose of all the goods of particular Churches, he could certainly grant a dispensation and legitimate someone for a reasonable cause so that they could succeed even in an Ecclesiastical lease granted in that way. This is no less than what the particular Church itself could do: for a reasonable cause, it could grant that the lease be extended to one or more illegitimate persons. However, for the Supreme Pontiff to be deemed to have legitimated someone even for that effect, words would have to be included that sufficiently express it.

<margin>13</margin> But can one legitimated by **subsequent marriage** <term>when parents of a child born out of wedlock later marry each other</term> succeed by that very fact in a lease or fief granted in that manner? Rubeus and others, cited by Caldas above, deny it. They argue that although one legitimated by subsequent marriage is "legitimate," they were still not "lawfully born," nor "born from a legitimate marriage." Rather, they were conceived through the mortal sin of both parents. This was the reason why someone legitimated by a prince's decree could not succeed in an Ecclesiastical lease granted under the common form, even though such a person *can* succeed in a secular lease granted in that way.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, it must be said without a doubt that both the child who was conceived before marriage but born after it was celebrated, and also the child who was legitimated by subsequent marriage after being born, succeeds in both secular and Ecclesiastical leases granted under that form. The reason is that, as stated in Disputation 162 with the common opinion of the doctors, those legitimated by subsequent marriage—by the disposition of both **civil and canon law**—have all their legal disabilities completely wiped away. These disabilities were introduced and established by both laws against those born out of wedlock. They are so thoroughly cleared that they require no further dispensation at all, even to be elected as Bishops, and they are regarded as if they had been conceived as legitimate from the start. Thus, legitimate...

It distinguishes between legitimation by a King's decree (which is generally insufficient for Church land) and legitimation by the parents' subsequent marriage (which fully restores inheritance rights in both secular and Church law).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of inheritance rights, specifically focusing on the status of "legitimated" children—those born outside of marriage whose status was later corrected by law or by the marriage of their parents—and their right to inherit entailed estates and church-leased lands.</meta>

# Luis de Molina | On Contracts

The status of these children relates back <note>original: "retrotrahitur"</note> to the moment of their conception. For this reason, in **maioratus** <term>an entailed estate that passes to a single heir to keep the family property intact</term> and in any other form of succession, they are preferred over children born after them, even those born within the marriage that performed the legitimation. They are also preferred over children from any other subsequent marriage and are counted alongside those born of a legitimate marriage. Because of this, for such children to be considered excluded from a specific entailed estate, **fief** <term>land held on condition of feudal service</term>, **emphyteusis** <term>a long-term lease of land</term>, or any other property, it is not enough to simply state that the property is for "legitimate children only" or "only those born of a legitimate marriage." By legal disposition, legitimated children are already counted as such. Instead, it is necessary to expressly exclude those "legitimated by a subsequent marriage," as we demonstrated in the cited discussion. Therefore, the common legal opinion, which we have cited there, asserts that children legitimated by a subsequent marriage succeed in both secular and Ecclesiastical emphyteusis, as well as in fiefs granted only for those "born of a legitimate marriage." However, it is different if those legitimated by subsequent marriage are expressly excluded, as was said in the same place. This is expressly affirmed regarding fiefs by the common opinion of the doctors, which Julius Clarus <note>Giulio Claro (1525–1575), an influential Italian jurist</note> reports and follows in his section on fiefs, question 82, final number. Regarding emphyteusis, it is the common opinion reported and followed by Caldas <note>Francisco de Caldas Pereira y Castro</note> in the section above from number 35.

<margin>14</margin>
Furthermore, does a child born from a marriage that was publicly celebrated in the Church and believed to be valid <note>original: "in Ecclesiae facie reputato valido"</note>—where there was **good faith** <term>honest intent or belief</term> at least on the part of one of the contracting parents—succeed in an emphyteusis, fief, or entailed estate granted for "legitimate children" or "those born of legitimate marriage"? Curtius the Younger, cited by Caldas above at number 42 and by Molina in book 3 *On Primogeniture*, chapter 1, number 15, says no. His reasoning is that although such a child is legitimate (as is clear from discussion 165), they were not conceived from a *truly* legitimate marriage, but from one *thought* to be legitimate when it actually was not.

However, in a case of great importance, Molina says he saw that this opinion of Curtius was quite controversial. Nevertheless, it must undoubtedly be said that such a child succeeds in that emphyteusis, fief, or entailed estate—not only if these come from the parent who acted in good faith, but even if they come from the other parent. Indeed, in comparison to both parents, the child is truly legitimate for all effects, including succession, as we stated with Emmanuel Acosta in the cited discussion 165. The reason for this common assertion, followed by Molina, Caldas, and others they cite (and whom we cited in the aforementioned discussion), is as follows:

The Church considers that marriage legitimate—not necessarily in itself, but for the effect of legitimizing the offspring—so that the child is deemed legitimately born from a legitimate marriage. This is clear from the laws cited in discussion 165. Therefore, that offspring should not just be called "legitimated" but "legitimate" and "legitimately born," as they were born from a marriage that was legitimate for that purpose by the Church's decree. Faithful subjects are presumed to accommodate their own language to this decree when they call someone to an emphyteusis, fief, or entailed estate. Truly, the contrary opinion would bring confusion, if not outright injustice, into the Church. To prevent this, the Church pronounced that such a marriage must be considered legitimate for the effect of the total legitimation of the children born from it.

When legitimation or a **dispensation** <term>an exemption from a legal requirement</term> to succeed in an emphyteusis (whether secular or Ecclesiastical-
<column-break/>
-al) or in a fief would result in prejudice to others—who would otherwise have succeeded or whose rights are otherwise harmed—to what extent can a prince legitimate or grant a dispensation, and to what extent can he not? Likewise, regarding what follows or what must intervene so that such legitimation or dispensation is not considered "surreptitious" <note>obtained by concealing the truth</note>, or what clauses must be added for it to be valid, this can be understood from what was said in discussions 173 and 174.

<margin>15</margin>
When someone should be considered "legitimated" and when merely "dispensed" was explained in discussion 173. If someone were considered legitimated for the purpose of obtaining **Ecclesiastical benefices** <term>a church office that provides an income</term>, they should also be considered legitimated for Ecclesiastical emphyteusis and Ecclesiastical fiefs, unless something was added to expressly state they are not admitted to them. The reason is that, as stated there, legitimation is to be interpreted broadly and favorably. Therefore, an argument from the greater to the lesser <note>original: "a maiori ad minus"</note> holds, provided it is not expressly denied. Temporal goods of the Church (in terms of the "useful ownership" granted in an emphyteusis or fief) are "lesser" than the spiritual Ecclesiastical benefices themselves. However, if someone was *only* granted a dispensation for Ecclesiastical benefices, then—because a dispensation must be interpreted strictly and not extended to things not expressly granted, even if they are lesser—they would not be considered dispensed for an emphyteusis or fief. So says Gigas, question 86, number 4; Caldas, number 63; and many others whom he cites.

<margin>16</margin>
The power of legitimizing granted by the **Supreme Pontiff** <term>the Pope</term> to a Legate or a Count Palatine is not understood to include the right to succeed in an entailed estate, fief, or Ecclesiastical emphyteusis unless it is expressly granted for that purpose. This was said above in this discussion and in discussion 173. Besides Covarruvias (cited there), this is affirmed by Julius Clarus and Caldas. This is because even the Supreme Pontiff himself, when legitimizing in a general sense for spiritual matters, is not deemed to be legitimizing for those earthly successions, as we have said in both places.

<margin>17</margin>
I believe, however, that if the Supreme Pontiff granted someone the power to legitimate in spiritual matters, adding "also for benefices with and without the **cure of souls**" <term>the responsibility for the spiritual welfare of parishioners</term>, the power to grant a dispensation for Ecclesiastical fiefs and emphyteusis would also be considered granted. This is because such a power is a "grace" <note>a favor or privilege</note> that is to be interpreted broadly, and thus the argument from the greater to the lesser applies. However, such a dispensation is not to be understood to the prejudice of a third party who already has a right to that emphyteusis or fief, or to the prejudice of the owner who had previously granted it (and whose lease would end sooner to his benefit if the legitimated person did not succeed). But when a fief or emphyteusis is granted *after* such legitimation has been obtained, the legitimated person can succeed in them, because at the time of the grant, he was capable and had the right to succeed if it were granted. See Caldas, number 69, and others. Likewise, when an emphyteusis or fief was granted before legitimation but was set up so it could pass even to "outsiders" <note>non-family members</note>, then the dispensed person could succeed in the place of an outsider, since this would not result in prejudice to any specific person.

It argues that such children should generally be treated as fully legitimate in inheritance matters, especially regarding Church-held lands, unless expressly excluded.</summary>

Not indeed to the prejudice of the owner <note>original: "proprietarij"</note>: because whether by a will or by dying without a will <note>original: "ab intestato"</note>, the successors would have similarly been outsiders. Nor likewise is it to the prejudice of any other person in particular: since the property could equally be left by the last possessor to any other person, and even if such a prejudice existed, it would not be of such weight that it ought to be taken into account.

28 Furthermore, if an illegitimate person obtained an ecclesiastical **emphyteusis** <term>a long-term land lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent</term> before obtaining a dispensation to hold it, whether they may lawfully retain that lease after subsequently obtaining a dispensation is discussed at length by Caldas in the place cited above at number 84. He finally resolves the matter: if they only obtain a dispensation, they cannot hold such a lease unless the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>, knowing that they had previously held that lease, nonetheless grants the dispensation; for then, even in the retention of the lease previously obtained, he is deemed to grant the dispensation. This is argued for the first point: because the act by which they previously obtained the lease was null; and a dispensation must be interpreted strictly, and thus only applies to obtaining it validly anew, when the one granting the dispensation had no prior knowledge. When such knowledge exists in the grantor at the time of the dispensation, it is presumed that he also wishes to dispense for the lease previously held invalidly. If, however, the person was not merely dispensed but was fully "legitimated" for spiritual matters and for obtaining ecclesiastical leases, then, because legitimation is to be interpreted broadly, the impediment is considered to have been removed so that the past act, which had been null due to such impediment, becomes valid. This opinion does not lack probability. Read that author.

### When each spouse shares in a perpetual emphyteusis, even if only one of them brought it.

#### DISPUTATION 476.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Whether and when a perpetual emphyteusis under Portuguese law is made common to both spouses if one of them brought it to the marriage, and at number 3.*
*And what the rule is in an ecclesiastical emphyteusis, number 2.*
4 *The provision of the final paragraph of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 77; in what sense it is to be understood.*
5 *An ecclesiastical emphyteusis accepted for "descending heirs" under Portuguese law does not belong to the widow left as heir by the last possessor, but to the grandson of the possessor.*
6 *Leases in Portugal are sometimes common to the wife and husband, and sometimes the private property of the deceased.*
*But feudal goods, properties of the Crown of the Kingdom, or **maioratus** <term>entailed estates</term> are not held in common.*

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
In Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 77, the final paragraph (to which a reference is made in the same Book 4, title 62, final paragraph, joined with the second-to-last paragraph), it is first established, or rather explained, when—after a marriage has been celebrated with a contract for "half the goods" <note>a community property arrangement</note>, and after the goods have been made common be-

<column-break/>

tween them—both spouses, or one of them, took something as a perpetual emphyteusis (the same applies if they bought a perpetual emphyteusis). Regardless of the words used in the contract—that is, whether those words create a simple hereditary lease, a mixed hereditary lease, or one by agreement and provision <note>original: "ex pacto, & prouidētia"</note>, according to the points explained in Disputations 472 and 473—that lease is made common to both spouses. Consequently, upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of one of them, it must be divided by appraisal between the surviving spouse and the heirs of the deceased, in the same manner as the preceding paragraph explained for a simple hereditary lease which must be divided by appraisal among the heirs. We have discussed this method of division at length at the beginning of Disputation 460.

2 These same rules apply even if it is an Ecclesiastical emphyteusis which does not pass to outside heirs: since in that paragraph, the discussion concerns a perpetual lease, even if it is not strictly hereditary, and indeed even if it exists only by agreement and provision. However, when a marriage was celebrated with a contract of **arras** <term>earnest money or a bride-price</term> and dowry, whether in Portugal or in Castile, that lease would certainly be counted among the goods acquired during the marriage. Therefore, if the capital of both spouses were extracted and the lease remained whole, or some of its value remained, it would similarly be divided between the surviving spouse and the heirs of the deceased.

3 In that same paragraph, it is added that when one of the spouses obtained a perpetual lease before a marriage celebrated with a community property contract, a distinction must be made: because, if in the lease contract no mention was made of "heirs," but the property was granted only as a lease for children or descendants in perpetuity, then, upon the dissolution of the marriage, that lease belongs only to the spouse who owned it before the marriage, or to their heirs. Nothing of it belongs to the other spouse or their heirs, because that lease was not made common to both spouses. If, however, it was granted for "heirs and successors," or for "heirs or successors," then upon the dissolution of the marriage, it is to be divided by appraisal between the surviving spouse and the heirs of the deceased. However, it must be "headed" <note>original: "incapitetur," meaning assigned to the primary title-holder</note> so that it remains with the spouse who owned it before the marriage was celebrated, or with one of their heirs, and only half of the appraisal of such a lease is paid to the other spouse or their heirs. Here you see that if the lease is not hereditary, it is not shared with the other spouse, but remains the whole and primary property of the spouse who owned it before marriage. But if it is hereditary, it is shared only to the effect that half the appraisal value belongs to the other spouse or their heirs upon dissolution. Exactly the same must be said if the lease comes to one of the spouses after the marriage contract by right of inheritance, legacy, or other gift from someone who already held the lease: for the reasoning is exactly the same, even if that Ordinance does not mention this specific outcome.

### Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

Alvaro Valasco, in his work *On the Law of Leases* <note>original: "de iur. emphy."</note> (Question 43, number 9), expresses surprise at a certain regulation. This rule states that when a lease <term>emphyteusis: a long-term land lease where the tenant pays a small rent and improves the land</term> is inheritable, it allows one spouse to receive half of its appraised value. This is surprising because, normally, a spouse is only the heir in an "intestate" situation <note>when someone dies without a valid will</note> if there are no blood relatives of the deceased up to the tenth degree, as we saw in Dispute 146, Conclusion 10. Valasco offers a somewhat flawed interpretation of that regulation, which differs from common practice in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitana"</note>. Later, however, he provides the true meaning of that regulation, which Caldas explains and pursues at length in his work *On the Naming of Leases* (Question 23, from number 11).

<margin>4</margin>
The provision of that regulation applies when a lease is "simply inheritable" <note>original: "hæreditaria simpliciter"</note>, such as a secular one (which is the only type mentioned in that section). This occurs when the lease was taken for "heirs and successors," or "heirs or successors," following the explanations in Disputes 172 and 173. In these cases, the lease becomes common to both spouses who entered marriage under a contract for the "sharing of half of the goods" <term>contractu medietatis bonorum: a marriage contract where all assets are pooled and shared equally</term>. This is because such a lease is just as alienable <note>able to be sold or transferred</note> and divisible among any heirs—not being restricted to direct descendants—as the other assets of the spouses, which are called "allodial" <term>allodialia: property held absolutely by the owner, free from any superior lord or feudal duties</term>. This is the teaching of Julius Clarus (Book 4, Sentences, section on emphyteusis, Question 16, number 1), as well as Alvaro Valasco, Caldas, and legal scholars generally. Therefore, just as other entirely free assets of such spouses become common property once the marriage is consummated through physical union, so too does a simply inheritable lease.

The same should be said regarding an entirely inheritable fief <term>feudum: a feudal land holding granted by a lord</term> for the same reason: it is equally alienable and divisible among any heirs, even outsiders, and is not restricted solely to the descendants of the first possessor, just like other free assets. This is the common view of scholars, including Julius Clarus (Section on Fiefs, Question 40, number 2). However, because such a fief is not in use in Portugal, no mention of it was made there.

When, however, a lease is not "simply inheritable" but only "mixed inheritable" <note>original: "hæreditaria mixtè"</note>, it would not pass to outside heirs and would be restricted to the family of the person who first received it. In that case, the other spouse would not share in it. Instead, upon the dissolution of the marriage, it would remain the "separate property" <note>original: "præcipua"</note> of the spouse (or their heirs) who held it before the marriage, or to whom it came by right of inheritance or other free gift after the marriage. The reason for it becoming common property—which applies to leases or fiefs that are "simply inheritable"—does not apply here. Caldas agrees with this, as does the reasoning provided by Alvaro Valasco.

Consequently, an ecclesiastical <note>Church-owned</note> lease granted to "heirs and successors"—when it is not explicitly stated to include outsiders—does not pass to outsiders according to the common opinion accepted in Portugal (as stated in Disputes 172 and 173). Thus, it does not become common to both spouses but remains the separate property of the one who held it before the marriage or who received it by free title during the marriage.

<column-break/>

The situation is different, however, if it was granted also for outside heirs, so that it is "simply inheritable." The same applies to a fief, following the explanations regarding fiefs in the cited disputes. Also, a secular lease—not only if it exists entirely by "pact and foresight" <note>original: "ex pacto, & prouidentia," meaning a specific negotiated contract</note> but also if it is mixed inheritable—does not become common to both spouses. It remains the separate property of the one who held it before the marriage or who received it by free title during the marriage. For if it had been bought by both or one of the spouses, or if the property had been newly accepted as a lease by them, it would generally become common to both, whether the lease was by pact and foresight or mixed inheritable, according to what was said at the beginning of this dispute.

Perhaps the Portuguese Ordinance (in the final cited section) spoke only of secular leases because there were differing opinions regarding when an ecclesiastical lease should be considered "simply inheritable." Furthermore, it is primarily the role of a secular legislator to deal with secular leases; for this reason, the Portuguese Ordinances rarely mention ecclesiastical leases in the titles where leases are discussed.

<margin>5</margin>
From what has been said, you will understand that it was rightly judged in Portugal that a certain ecclesiastical lease, accepted for descendants and ancestors, did not belong to the widow left as heir by the last possessor, but to a certain grandson of that possessor, as Gama reports in Decision 50 (noting that it was decided despite the widow's protest).

From what has been said, you will also understand why the Portuguese Ordinance (Book 4, Title 7, Section 1) established that when spouses marry under a contract of "sharing half of the goods," the surviving spouse, upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the other, remains in possession of the goods, and the heirs of the deceased must receive from that spouse the portion belonging to the deceased. Section 2 added that this is to be understood regarding the common goods of both spouses, but not regarding feudal goods of the Crown of the Kingdom, or an "entailed estate" <term>majoratus: a legal arrangement where an estate is kept intact and passed to a single heir, usually the eldest son</term>, which are specific to the deceased spouse; nor regarding leased property, when it is not common to both spouses (except perhaps regarding some improvements made to them during the marriage), but is the separate property of the deceased.

<margin>3</margin>
For indeed, leases are sometimes common to the wife and the husband, as is partially clear from what has been said, but sometimes they are the specific property of the deceased. Feudal goods, those of the Crown, or entailed estates are not usually common in that Kingdom. When a marriage was celebrated with a contract of "earnest money" <term>artharum: a pre-nuptial gift or pledge, often related to the dowry</term> and dowry, generally a lease that belonged to one spouse before the marriage, or came to them by hereditary right or other free gift after the marriage, belongs specifically to that person as part of their capital.
