### When a long-term lease should be divided according to hereditary portions, and when in equal portions, among heirs. Also, when one who is assigned a specific object participates in the lease; and when an heir is held liable for the deceased’s creditors regarding the lease.

### DISPUTE 477.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *How a hereditary long-term lease is to be divided among heirs.*
*And what is the rule in Portuguese law? number 2.*
3 *How one who is assigned a specific object can have a share in the lease.*
4 *Whether a son lawfully disinherited from a share still succeeds to the father's lease and fief.*
5 *When an heir is bound to pay the deceased's creditors from the lease.*

Regarding the first point, the doctors of law make a distinction. If the long-term lease <term>emphyteusis: a type of contract where land is leased for a very long period or forever, provided the tenant improves it and pays a small rent</term> is "simply hereditary," it can be sold or divided among any heirs—even those outside the family—just like other unrestricted assets, as was said in the preceding dispute. In this case, it must certainly be divided among the heirs according to their hereditary portions, just as other inherited goods are divided between them.

Therefore, if one person is appointed heir to two parts of the inheritance and another to one part, just as the first receives two parts and the second one part of the remaining assets, so too with the lease: one receives two parts and the other one. This is based on the logic of Law 1 in the Code <note>original: "C. de impub. & alijs subst."</note> and other statutes. This is further supported by the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusitanar. ordin."</note>, book 4, title 77, the next to last section. When discussing the division of a hereditary lease, it says: *“The said heirs shall divide the price among themselves”* (referring to the value of the leased property) *“according to how they are heirs,”* <note>original: "Eos ditos heredeiros partiraam entre si o preço segundo forem heredeiros"</note> that is, according to their hereditary portions. In that Kingdom, the division is made only by valuation <note>appraisal of the monetary value rather than dividing the land itself</note>, as is stated in that section and in Dispute 460. However, if the lease is not simply hereditary, but is created by a specific agreement and provision, or is "mixed hereditary," then it must be divided among the heirs in equal parts, even if the heirs were appointed to unequal shares of the estate. This is affirmed by Bartolus, following the text of the law. This is also held by Covarruvias, Alvaro Valasco, Caldas, and Gregorio Lopez, whom they cite. Valasco says the same rule applies to fiefs <term>feudum: a landed estate held on condition of feudal service</term>.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
Hence, Alvaro Valasco (cited above, number 8) says that a Portuguese law (book 4, title 62, section 1) could be contested. This law establishes that if a lease was taken for specific persons to be named, with no mention of "heirs," and the possessor names many "stranger" heirs <note>heirs who are not direct descendants or ancestors</note> in their will without naming them specifically for the lease, they are all

<column-break/>

considered to be "tacitly named" for that lease by the very act of being appointed heirs. The law adds that the valuation of that lease must then be divided among those heirs according to the hereditary portions in which they were appointed.

Based on what was said earlier, however, it would seem that the valuation should be divided equally among them, even if they were appointed to unequal portions, because that specific lease is not strictly "hereditary" by its original nature. But Valasco adds that one must stand by the law as it is written. Caldas, in his work on the naming of leases, says this law was rightly decreed. He argues that since all these heirs are considered named by the act of institution itself, it is only right—based on the "affection" <note>dilectio: the legal term for the testator's intent and preference shown in the will</note> shown toward them regarding the rest of the assets—that they should be considered loved in the same proportions regarding this tacit naming for the lease. This is especially true since these matters derive their power from human law, and equity shines more clearly here than it would if heirs appointed to unequal portions were suddenly considered "tacitly named" to equal portions of that lease. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the second point, the doctors of law again make a distinction. If the lease or fief is hereditary (either simply or mixed), then since a person must be an "heir" to succeed in it, someone who is only "assigned a specific object" <term>institutus in re certa: a person given a specific item in a will rather than a percentage of the total estate</term> is not technically an heir. Rather, such a person has the status of a "legatee" <note>someone who receives a specific gift from an estate but does not represent the person of the deceased</note> when a "universal heir" <note>someone who inherits the whole estate or a percentage of it</note> is also appointed. As explained extensively in Dispute 155, the person assigned a specific object has no part in that lease or fief but is entirely excluded from them.

However, if no one else was appointed as a universal heir along with the person assigned the specific object—or if the universal heir died before the testator, or before accepting the inheritance, or if they refused it—then the entire inheritance "accrues" to the person assigned the specific object. In that case, they become the universal heir by default and succeed to the lease or fief, provided they are within the class of persons to whom the grant extends.

When the lease or fief exists by a specific agreement and provision <note>rather than standard inheritance law</note>, then the person assigned a specific object—if they are among the number of those to whom the grant extends—succeeds to it in equal parts, according to what was said in the first part of this dispute. This second point is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, citing Bartolus and Baldis, and followed by Covarruvias, Valasco, Julius Clarus, and Caldas. Indeed, Arias Pinellus asserts that if a lease is granted to "any heirs and successors whatsoever,"

## Ludovico Molina: On Contracts

even if it is granted in the name of "any successors whatsoever," whether a person appointed to a specific item is included to succeed in such a hereditary long-term lease <term>emphyteusis: a permanent or long-term lease of land in exchange for a rent and a commitment to improve the property</term> along with the universal heirs. I do not doubt that the contrary is true. In such concessions made in the name of "any heirs and successors," the term "heirs" is understood to mean those designated by civil law, by the praetor’s law, by a will, or through intestacy—whether they are descendants or outsiders—but not "particular successors" <note>A "particular successor" is someone given a specific item, like a legatee, rather than a share of the whole estate.</note>. Furthermore, since such a lease is simply hereditary and is counted among the rest of the inherited assets, the very fact that someone was appointed for a specific item and was not expressly called to the lease (or a portion of it) means they should be considered excluded by the testator, just as they are from the rest of the hereditary assets.

**4** Whether a son who was lawfully disinherited by his father may still succeed to his father’s long-term lease or fief. Setting aside other opinions, Alvaro Valasco <note>Alvaro Valasco was a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist specializing in property and inheritance law.</note> makes a distinction in his work *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 45. If the fief or long-term lease is "hereditary," the son does not succeed to it, because he does not truly exist as the father’s heir. However, if they exist "by pact and provision" <note>original: "ex pacto & prouidentia" — this refers to a lease or fief where the succession rules were specifically written into the original contract, rather than following standard inheritance law.</note>, he does succeed. This is because one can succeed in these cases even if one is not the general heir, and disinheritance does not extend to what is not part of the general heritage; after all, "deprivation presupposes a right to hold." Nor does it matter that in a fief "by pact and provision," a son or descendant does not succeed unless they are the heir (as stated in Dispute 472). That rule is understood to apply when someone refuses to be the heir by rejecting the inheritance; the case is different when they were ready to be the heir, but the father prevented it by disinheriting them. 

Alvaro Valasco, in the cited question 45—noting that many believe a disinherited descendant cannot succeed even in a fief "by pact and provision"—debates whether, even holding that opinion, one should say the descendant cannot succeed to a *grandfather’s* fief when a grandson is justly disinherited by his own father. He rightly judges that the grandson *does* succeed to the grandfather's fief. This is most clear if the disinheriting father dies before the grandfather, as the grandson succeeds the grandfather immediately. But even if the father dies after the grandfather, the grandson succeeds to the grandfather's fief immediately after his father. This is proven by the Law of the Head of the Family <note>original: "l. filiusfamilias. §. cùm pater"</note> where disinherited grandsons are admitted to property which a grandfather had left first to his son and then to the family. This is confirmed by the Book of Feuds <note>original: "c. 1. in prin. de succeſ. feud."</note>, with the words: *No ordinance of the deceased remaining or being valid regarding the fief.* From this it is gathered that the disinheritance by the last possessor does not prevent the person who ought to succeed according to the original grant <note>original: "investituram" — the document granting the fief</note> from succeeding to the grandfather’s fief. It does not matter if someone objects using the law regarding patrons, where a grandson disinherited for bad behavior is excluded from the rights of patronage over a grandfather’s freedmen <note>In Roman law, "patronage" involved rights over formerly enslaved people who had been freed.</note>. One cannot draw a valid argument from the rights of patronage to fiefs and long-term leases, because in a grandfather's fief or lease "by pact and provision," a son can dispose of nothing to the prejudice of the next successors according 

<column-break/>

to the terms of the original grant. Read Alvaro Valasco, question 45, as cited. This concludes the second of the proposed points.

**5** As for the third point, the doctors of law make a similar distinction. If <insert>†</insert> the long-term lease or fief is not hereditary but "by pact and provision," then even if the person who obtained it according to the form of the grant enters into the inheritance of the previous possessor—even with the "benefit of inventory" <note>A legal protection where an heir is only liable for the deceased's debts up to the value of the assets they inherited.</note>—they are not liable for the deceased’s debts from that lease or fief, but only from the rest of the deceased's assets belonging to that estate, and only according to their value. The reason is manifest: that lease or fief is not part of the general inheritance. The new tenant or vassal does not hold it from the immediate previous possessor so much as from the "direct lord" who granted it so that it would come to him according to the form of the grant. An heir making an inventory is only liable for the deceased's debts from the inheritance itself, according to its value, as was said in Dispute 216. 

However, when the lease or fief is hereditary, then the person who obtains it must be the heir and must enter into the predecessor’s inheritance to obtain the lease or fief. Therefore, they are liable for the deceased’s debts from those assets, even if they made an inventory. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Covarruvias, Valasco, Caldas, Gama, and Giulio Claro. Claro, however, thought that if a fief was not simply hereditary but "mixed," an heir who made an inventory would not be bound to pay the deceased's debts if they were also an heir to the first possessor through someone other than the very last possessor. Nevertheless, the contrary must be said: as we shall see in the following dispute, an inventory does not release one from things in which one succeeds as an heir, but only from those things which are the heir's own property or to which they have a right from elsewhere. 

Gama, in the place cited above, correctly observes that if a lease "by pact and provision" had been *purchased* by the last possessor, or if the last possessor had made improvements to it, the successor is liable for the deceased's debts up to the amount of that price or the value of those improvements. To that extent, the lease is considered the deceased's own property, no less subject to debts than their other assets. He also rightly teaches (in number 8) that for the debts of the person currently holding a lease or fief "by pact and provision," a seizure can be made against the lease or fief while they are alive—but only for the duration of their life. It cannot extend to the time after their death, as that would result in harm to the next successor who holds rights by the original grant. He correctly adds, along with others he cites, that such a seizure should be made against the *profits* or convenience of the lease or fief during the possessor's life, rather than against the lease or fief itself.

# Whether a father can prejudice his children in a long-term lease or a fief, especially by selling them or pre-bequeathing them to one of them.

## DISPUTATION 478.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> *In a long-term lease or a fief that is simply hereditary, a father can prejudice his children.*
*This fails in the case of a lucrative title if he does so "inofficiosely" <note>original: "inofficiose" — This refers to a legal action that ignores the moral duty to provide the "legitimate share" for one's heirs.</note>.*
*It also fails in a long-term lease or fief held by "pact and provision" <note>original: "ex pacto & prouidentia" — A specific legal arrangement where the order of succession is fixed in the initial contract/deed rather than left to the holder's will.</note>. See number 2.*
*Clarify and understand this limitation as explained fully in number 5.*
<margin>3</margin> *Leases and fiefs held by pact and provision are owed to those for whom they were accepted.*
<margin>4</margin> *A long-term lease accepted for one of the sons, or for common children born to both parents, cannot be renewed to their prejudice.*
<margin>5</margin> *When a leaseholder or vassal by pact and provision can prejudice those called by the investiture <note>The formal deed or ceremony granting the land.</note>.*
<margin>6</margin> *In a mixed hereditary long-term lease or fief, a father can dispose of it to the prejudice of his children with the consent of the owner, where it is necessarily required.*
*The same applies in a lease or fief by pact and provision. See number 9.*
*This is limited, however, as seen in number 7.*
*It is also limited if the alienation was made by him through a free title, insofar as he acted inofficiosely. See number 8.*
<margin>10</margin> *Whether a son entering into a paternal inheritance with the "benefit of inventory" <note>A legal protection allowing an heir to limit their liability for the deceased's debts to the value of the assets inherited.</note> can revoke the sale of a lease or fief when they are mixed hereditary assets.*
<margin>11</margin> *A father, even in a lease and fief by pact and provision, can prejudice his children by "falling into commission" <note>original: "incidendo in commissum" — Forfeiting the property due to a breach of contract or failure to pay the required rent/dues.</note>.*

---

<margin>1</margin> This dispute is to be settled by the following conclusions. The first is: if a long-term lease <term>emphyteusis: a permanent or long-term lease of land in exchange for a rent and a commitment to improve the property</term> or a fief are simply hereditary, the father can to that extent prejudice his children in them. He can pre-bequeath them to one of them, or even bequeath them to a stranger, or sell them to anyone, or exchange them with another, provided the owner’s consent is first obtained. In short, he can dispose of them as far as the prejudice of the children is concerned just as he can with his other free assets. Therefore, just as he cannot "inofficiosely" give away, bequeath, or leave his other assets by hereditary right to others—so that the "legitimate portions" <note>The "legitima" is the mandatory minimum share of an estate that must by law go to children or parents.</note> due to descendants or ancestors are preserved—and if he does so, such dispositions are invalid to the extent they touch those portions; so too he cannot inofficiosely give away, bequeath, or leave such long-term leases or fiefs by hereditary right to the prejudice of legitimate descendants or ancestors. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Julius Clarus, book 4 of *Sentences*, section on emphyteusis, question 16; and section on fiefs, question 40, number 2, and question 41, last number; Caldas, *On the Naming of Emphyteusis*, question 24; Aries Pinellus, on law

<column-break/>

1 of the Code *On Maternal Assets*, part 3, number 93; Covarruvias, *Varied Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 18, number 2, conclusion 4; and Alvaro Valasco, *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 49, from number 3. Although these last three speak somewhat mixedly about hereditary leases and fiefs, it is clear that they agree with the proposed conclusion. Indeed, the reason for the proposed conclusion is quite clear: because such a lease or fief, as far as the prejudice of successors is concerned, behaves exactly like entirely free assets.

<margin>2</margin> The second conclusion: If the long-term lease or fief is held "by pact and provision," the more probable and common opinion of the doctors is that the possessor—even with the consent of the direct lord—cannot sell it to the prejudice of those who are called to it by the investiture, nor can he bequeath or give it away to their prejudice. This is held by Bartolus and many others; Covarruvias; Alvaro Valasco; Caldas; and Gama in *Decisions*, decision 5, number 7, where he cites many sentences passed according to this opinion; and decision 233. Indeed, they understand it thus: even if the lease or fief was accepted for himself and his children, if the power of naming whomever he wished was not given to the one accepting it, he cannot leave that lease or fief to one of the sons to the prejudice of the others.

They also understand it to mean that he cannot even renounce such a lease or fief to the owner to the prejudice of those called by the investiture, as Alvaro Valasco affirms along with others. Likewise, they understand it to mean that the possessor cannot enter into a legal settlement regarding it to the prejudice of those called to it, as Gama reports was judged in Portugal. Alvaro Valasco asserts with Bartolus that a secular long-term lease accepted for sons or descendants is "hereditary," because in that lease the father is considered to stipulate for the sons as heirs, and thus the father can prejudice the sons in that lease. We, however, in Disputation 473, rejected that opinion, and Gama affirms it is false in the matter proposed, especially under Portuguese law <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, by which it is established that the contrary is true. Regarding what Alvaro Valasco taught, some have hesitated, as if it could be said—not without some color of truth, as he says—that in a lease, whether ecclesiastical or secular, taken up for "freedmen," the father can prejudice them by selling it with the consent of the direct lord. Gama, however, says that Valasco does not firmly hold that opinion there, nor does he think Valasco was of that opinion, and rightly adds that even if he did affirm it, it should not be embraced in judging.

<margin>3</margin> The conclusion thus explained is proven because, by the father's stipulation and pact, such a lease or fief is owed to those for whom it was accepted. From this, a "beneficial action" <note>A legal right to sue for the use or possession of the property.</note> belongs to them for the time when, according to the investiture, they ought to succeed. The direct lord must blame himself for granting the lease or fief in such a form of concession that, even with his own consent, it could not be sold to the prejudice of those for whom it was granted; who indeed

-># Ludovicus Molina on Contracts<-

Indeed, the successors are not so much considered to hold these rights from the last possessor as they are from the **direct lord** <note>original: "domino directo" — the ultimate owner of the land who grants the lease or fief</note> who granted them under that specific form; for this reason, the possessor can vary nothing regarding those rights, as is gathered from Chapter 1, at the beginning, on the succession of a fief. Thus, it follows that those for whom the rights were granted cannot be deprived of that right without their own fault.

The Portuguese law agrees in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 63, Section 5, as Gama rightly observes in Decision 8 and others cited there. It establishes that if someone took a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual lease where the tenant improves the land and pays a small rent</term> for himself, his wife, and one son to be born to them, the last parent can name which of the sons he wishes to succeed to the lease, but he cannot name a stranger. For this is established for no other reason than that naming a stranger would be against the right acquired by the sons by virtue of the **investiture** <note>the formal legal act or document granting the property</note>. Truly, it would be no less against that right to sell that lease to a stranger or to alienate it outside the children in any other way.

<margin>4</margin>
Hence it is clear that when a lease was taken for one of the sons born of both parents, or for common children born of both parents, it cannot be renewed or granted for any of their other children to the prejudice of these first children, such that the grant would extend only to the children of the other parent born from a second marriage, while this could prejudice the common children of both parents from that prior marriage. On this matter, you may find a long dispute in Caldas, *On the Nomination of Leases*, Question 1, <unclear>number 1.</unclear>

<margin>Question</margin>
Julius Clarus (Question 16, section on long-term leases, number 2, joined with number 3; and the section on fiefs, Question 40, before number 3 and at number 3; and Question 41, number 2) and Arias Pinelo (on the law regarding maternal goods, part 3, number 98) and others—reported by both those authors and by Alvaro Valasco at number 6—although they confess that the contrary is the more common opinion, they nevertheless make a distinction.

<margin>5</margin>
If the lease or fief, held by pact and provision, are **new**, it is because they began with the one who currently possesses them; or they are **ancient**, meaning they were derived by the current possessor from a previous leaseholder or vassal.

In this latter event (ancient holdings), they agree with the more common opinion of the doctors. But in the first case, namely when the lease or fief is **new**, they judge that even if they are held by pact and provision, the possessor or vassal can prejudice those called by the investiture by alienating the property with the consent of the owner. They are led to this because the first recipient seems to take it for himself first, and not for the successors unless his own death follows without a prior disposition made with the direct lord's consent. They add, however, that if the owner had granted it even to the sons, or if the sons were present at the time of the contract and stipulated or accepted it together with the parent, then they would have a perfectly acquired right immediately upon the grant of the lease or fief to the parent; therefore, the parent could not then alienate that lease or fief to their prejudice, even with the owner’s consent. Arias Pinelo, at the end of number 98, observes that it is one thing to speak of the alienation of a new fief or lease by an **onerous title** <note>a contract involving a sale or exchange for value</note>, and another by a **last will** <note>a testament or gift upon death</note>. Since alienation by onerous title cannot be done without the intervening consent of the owner,

<column-break/>

the possessor can alienate it with the owner's consent; this is because the will of the direct lord joined with the will of the possessor is more powerful than the will of the possessor alone. However, since alienation by a last will is usually done by the sole will of the testator, the possessor cannot alienate such a lease or fief by such a **gratuitous title** <note>a gift or legacy without an exchange of value</note> to the prejudice of those called by the investiture. This is what Julius Clarus concedes and asserts in the section on fiefs, Question 40, last number, and Question 41, number 2.

However, it must be said, following the Doctors reported above and the common opinion, that even if the lease or fief are **new**, the possessor cannot—whether by onerous or gratuitous title—alienate them to the prejudice of the successors, even if the direct lord consents. This is because a right is immediately acquired by the successors from the investiture through the mutual contract and consent of the first possessor and the direct lord, which they cannot later contravene or prejudice.

And indeed, I do not see why a possessor could dispose of a **new** lease or fief with the owner's consent to the prejudice of successors, yet cannot do so in **ancient** ones. For after the death of the first possessor, no new pact is made; rather, solely by virtue of the first investiture and the pact celebrated between the first possessor and the direct lord, those later called obtain and retain their right. The second or third possessor and the direct lord cannot prejudice this right. Therefore, since the first possessor and the direct lord did not celebrate the contract with any power reserved to themselves or subsequent possessors to prejudice those called by the investiture, but rather celebrated the contract absolutely, the first possessor can no more prejudice the right belonging to those called by the investiture under that pact (even with the lord's consent) than subsequent possessors could prejudice them with the same consent.

Arias Pinelo (number 98), Alvaro Valasco (on the law of leases, Question 49, number 7), and many others whom they report (especially Alvaro Valasco) assert with Balduus that if a lease or fief acquired by pact and provision were bought with the parent's money, or in exchange for another thing belonging to the parent, that parent can alienate them with the direct lord's consent to the prejudice of those called by the investiture. This is because, insofar as they were acquired with the father's property, they are considered a gift from the father, which he can revoke in the circumstances explained in Disputation 219, number 1. Perhaps, however, it could not be revoked even in this event; but the father could charge the son so that he takes the price given as part of his **legitimate portion** <note>the portion of an estate that must by law go to the heirs</note> or brings it to the partition of the inheritance.

Alvaro Valasco, in the same place, number 8, with Aretinus and Ruinus, adds: when a lease or fief by pact and provision is extended to a son out of regard for the father, whatever is conferred on the son out of regard for the father is "profectitium" <note>property derived from the father's estate or effort</note>; the father can then alienate that lease or fief to the prejudice of the son as if it were the father's own good, even regarding that extension made in the investiture. However, I judge that to be false; because that extension...

Molina argues against the common view, stating that once the contract is made, the rights of the heirs are fixed and cannot be undone even with the landlord's permission.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding the rights of children to succeed in a long-term lease or fief. It specifically examines whether a father’s actions or the acceptance of an inheritance binds the children to a father's decision to sell or give away that property.</meta>

->### Second Treatise, Disputation 478.<-

...that right, and the claim to such a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a type of land tenure where the tenant has permanent use of the land in exchange for improvements and a small rent</term>, or **fief** <term>feudum — land held on condition of feudal service</term>, after the death of the father, is not the father’s own property. Nor was it granted to the son simply so that it would become the father’s property—which would be necessary for it to be considered "property derived from the father" <note>original: "boni profectitij" — property a child receives from a parent or through their means</note>. Instead, it is a benefit granted to the son’s own son, out of favor to the father, and a benefit bestowed upon the son through the simultaneous consent and will of both the father and the **direct lord** <note>the ultimate owner of the land</note> to confer it upon him in that way. Clearly, this opinion of Alvaro Valasco would differ in no way from the opinion of Julius Clarus and Pinellus, which Valasco himself challenges in number 6.

The same Alvaro Valasco, in the same place at number 12, along with Angelo and others, adds that a father can prejudice his son’s interest in a lease or fief through a specific **agreement and provision** <note>original: "ex pacto, & prouidétia" — terms specifically written into the grant or contract</note>, provided that he leaves the son an equal or greater amount in compensation. Furthermore, the son must expressly accept the legacy as being left to him in compensation and under the condition that he consents to that sale or transfer. Otherwise, if it is not left to him under that condition, or if the son does not wish to accept such a legacy, the sale will be invalid. I also believe that if this acts to the prejudice of a descendant of such a son (who is called by the **investiture** <note>the formal legal document granting the property</note> to that fief or lease), they can later act to annul such a sale insofar as it harms their interests.

<margin>6</margin>
Regarding a lease or fief that is considered "mixed hereditary" <note>property that follows both the rules of the specific grant and the general laws of inheritance</note>, this third conclusion is usually established: whether they are "new" or "old," the possessor can dispose of them to the prejudice of the sons, provided the consent of the owner intervenes when it is necessary for the sale to be valid. This is the common opinion, which is cited and followed by Covarruvias (Book 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 18, number 2, conclusion 4) and Valasco (*On the Law of Long-term Leases*, question 49, from number 3), as well as Caldas. The reason for this conclusion is that in such a lease or fief, the sons cannot succeed unless they accept the inheritance and act as heirs. Because the property is "mixed hereditary," an heir cannot go against the actions of the deceased, according to the law *cum a matre* and other statutes. This follows the rule: "From whatever person someone receives a benefit, they must stand by that person's deeds." Valasco and Caldas extend this conclusion even to leases or fiefs held by "agreement and provision," provided the sons accept the inheritance. The reason is the same: by the very fact that they accept the inheritance, they cannot challenge the father’s deed, even in a lease or fief governed by specific agreement.

<margin>7</margin>
Covarruvias, and with him Valasco, Decius, and others followed by Pinellus and Caldas, limit this conclusion unless the person is among those specifically named in the investiture. For example, if in an ecclesiastical lease only the descendants are named, and it is sold to a stranger, then because the sale is null, the descendants can reclaim the lease or fief even if they accepted the inheritance. However, this opinion is not without doubt—and no small doubt at that. The fact that the sale is null does not prevent the heirs from being bound

<column-break/>

to stand by it; just as the sale of a son's property made by a father is null, it does not prevent the son from being bound to uphold it if he remains the father's heir. This is proportional to the share of the inheritance the son receives from the father. If that son is the sole heir, he is bound to the entire sale; if he is an heir alongside others (to a half, a third, or a fourth part), he is similarly bound to uphold the sale of a half, third, or fourth part of the property. This follows the opinion of Covarruvias, Valasco, and the common view, even regarding the mandatory **legitime** <term>the legal minimum share of an estate that must go to the children</term> due to such a son. However, according to my own view and that of Bartolus, he is only bound regarding the **surplus** <note>the value of the inheritance that exceeds the son's mandatory legal share</note> beyond the legitime, as I explained extensively in Disputation 216. Therefore, if the sale of the lease or fief was made with the owner's consent, the heirs cannot challenge it. If it was made without the owner's consent, it is up to the owner to challenge it, not the heirs, even if it harms them.

<margin>8</margin>
Regarding the conclusion itself, if the transfer was made for free—such as a gift, a final will, a dowry, or a marriage gift—and it was "inofficious" <note>legally "uncourteous" because it ignores the children's mandatory share</note> toward the children by infringing on their legal shares, it would be invalid to that extent. This holds even if the children accept the inheritance, as was said regarding the first conclusion and affirmed by Caldas and others. We provided the reason for this in the first conclusion.

<margin>9</margin>
Regarding the extension of the conclusion to leases and fiefs by "agreement and provision," observe that generally, when a lease or fief must come to a son by the terms of the investiture such that he is not required to count it toward his mandatory legal share, then even if he accepts the inheritance, he is only prevented from challenging the sale of that property (even if it was sold for a price) in the same proportion in which he is his father's heir. For instance, if the entire lease or fief should have come to him by the grant, but he is heir to only half the father's estate, he can only be barred from challenging half of the alienated property. If he is heir to only a third or fourth, he can only be barred from challenging a third or fourth part; he can challenge the rest. Furthermore, if he has made an **inventory** <note>a formal list of the estate's assets to limit the heir's liability</note>, the mandatory legal share due to him must be deducted from his portion of the inheritance. He is only barred from challenging the sale to the extent of the surplus value beyond that legal share. If the portion of the alienated lease is worth more than the surplus he received, he can challenge the part of the value that exceeds it, as I clearly showed in Disputation 216. This is because a testator cannot place any burden upon the mandatory legal share.

Read what has been said extensively in that place.

<margin>Question.</margin> Julius Clarus (at the section on emphyteusis, question 16, last number; and the section on fiefs, question 40, number 2; and question 42, last number) and others, whom both he and Alvaro Valasco (cited above at number 4) record, are of the opinion that a son who **accepts a paternal inheritance with the benefit of inventory** <note>A legal protection allowing an heir to be liable for the deceased's debts only up to the value of the inherited assets</note> can revoke the transfer of a long-term lease or fief when these are held through a "mixed hereditary" title and the transfer was made to his detriment. They are led to this because the benefit of inventory preserves all rights and legal actions for the heir just as if he had not accepted the inheritance, as was shown in Disputation 216.

<margin>Decision.</margin> However, the contrary must be affirmed along with the common opinion of the doctors, which is recorded and followed by Covarruvias (at the cited verse 8), Alvaro Valasco (at the cited number 4), Arias Pinellus (on the Code concerning maternal goods, part 3, number 93), and Caldas (at the cited question 24, number 20). The reason is that an inventory does not free an heir from those matters in which he succeeds the deceased by hereditary right, but rather from those things which are his own or to which he has a right from another source.

¶ **The fourth conclusion.** By falling into **forfeiture** <note>original: "commissum" — the loss of a right or property due to a breach of contract or law</note> in the ways explained in the progress of this contract of emphyteusis, a father prejudices his sons, even if the lease exists by specific **agreement and provision** <note>original: "ex pacto, & prouidentia" — terms specifically written into the contract rather than standard law</note>. This is the view of Bartolus and many others cited by Alvaro Valasco (on the law of emphyteusis, question 49, number 2). The reason is that a wrong is committed against the contract; and because the lease is granted under that law and condition: that if a forfeiture occurs, the lease reverts to the owner. If, however, someone falls into forfeiture through deceit or fraud to harm those named in the **investiture** <note>The formal act of granting the lease or fief</note>, especially if the owner was a participant in that deceit, then the injured parties would be helped, as Alvaro Valasco adds in the same place, because the laws decree that frauds must be countered.

->Whether a long-term lease or a fief is included in the restoration of a universal trust. And whether a long-term lease or a fief ought to be counted toward the forced share.<-

### DISPUTATION 479.

#### SUMMARY.

1 *When a long-term lease or fief is included in the restoration of a universal trust <term>fideicommissum — a request in a will for an heir to hand over the estate to another</term>.*
2 *Hereditary leases or fiefs, even mixed ones, are counted toward the **forced share** <note>original: "legitima" — the portion of an estate that must by law go to the children</note>, according to the common opinion.*
3 *Whether a secular long-term lease taken out for the benefit of children is hereditary or not.*
4 *Leases or fiefs held by agreement and provision are not counted toward the forced share, according to the common opinion. Indeed, neither the **Falcidian** nor the **Trebellian portions** <note>Roman law rules allowing an heir to keep at least one-fourth of an estate before paying out legacies or trusts</note> are deducted from them, according to common opinion.*
*It is declared, however, that such a fief is counted toward the forced share, as in numbers 5, 6, 7, and 8.*
9 *Improvements which by agreement belong to the owner before the lease ends are counted toward the forced share.*

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the first point, the doctors commonly agree that if a **long-term lease** or **fief** is simply hereditary and is among the number of assets of the deceased (who burdened the heir to restore the inheritance to someone else), that lease or fief is included in the restoration of such a **universal trust**. Because they do not differ from other assets regarding transmission and the power of sale, they are included in the inheritance ordered to be restored. Similarly, they agree with Bartolus that if the lease or fief exists by **special provision** <note>original: "ex prouidentia" — a grant specifically naming successors rather than following general inheritance law</note>, they are not included in a universal trust; for these do not come to the burdened heir insofar as he is an heir, and therefore they are not part of the inheritance to be restored. If, however, they are "mixed hereditary," although they come to the descendant as an heir, the heir is not considered burdened to restore them with the rest of the estate assets unless, by the terms of the grant, the trust-beneficiary is called to that lease or fief, nor can the heir be burdened for that purpose. These are the points intended by the doctors whom Julius Clarus (Book 4 of Sentences, section on fiefs, question 85), Alvaro Valasco (on the law of emphyteusis, question 48), and Caldas (on the naming of emphyteusis, question 24, number 26) record and follow.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding the second point, the first conclusion is: A long-term lease or fief, if it is hereditary (even mixed), is counted toward the **forced share** <note>The "legitime" or legal minimum inheritance for children</note>, just like other **paternal property** <note>original: "profectitia" — property coming from the father’s estate</note>. Thus, they must be numbered in the heap of the father's assets so it may be understood how large each child's forced share is. Whoever obtains that lease (or part of it) is bound to bring it to the "collation" <note>The process of bringing gifts received during the parent's life back into the estate pool for fair division</note>, or count it toward their share, or toward the assets in which they were properly improved by the father.

This is the common opinion of the doctors, recorded and followed by Alvaro Valasco (question 46), Julius Clarus (section on fiefs, question 46), and Caldas (question 18, number 27). The reason is that such leases or fiefs are then passed down by hereditary title and are considered parts of the inheritance.

<margin>3</margin> The **Portuguese Ordinances** <note>The *Ordenações*, the legal code of the Kingdom of Portugal</note> (Book 4, Title 77, penultimate section) agree. Alvaro Valasco, as we recorded in Disputation 473, thinks along with Bartolus and others that a secular lease taken out for children is hereditary, on the grounds that the father is considered to have made the agreement for the children as heirs; thus, he also thinks it must be counted toward the forced share. However, we taught the opposite there: namely, that it is not hereditary. Therefore, in the matter proposed, it must be asserted that it is not counted toward the forced share, but the children have it as a **special gift** <note>original: "præcipuam" — a portion of the estate given to one heir above their standard share</note>. The Portuguese Ordinance (in the cited title, section 32) agrees; there, when a lease is taken for the children with no mention made of heirs, it is asserted that it ought not be counted toward the forced share, in the same way we will soon add regarding leases by agreement and provision. Caldas affirms the same (cited above, number 28). Just as a hereditary lease is counted toward the forced share because it comes by title of heir, so also the Falcidian and Trebellian portions <note>Legal deductions</note> ought to be subtracted from it, as from a hereditary asset or part of an inheritance, as [it is] affir-

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of how specific types of property—specifically long-term leases and fiefs—affect the calculation of a child's mandatory inheritance (the forced share). ...[this] confirms the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Alvaro Valasco (cited at question 46) records and follows.

<margin>4</margin>
**The second conclusion.** If a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a permanent land lease requiring the tenant to improve the property</term> or a **fief** <term>feudum — land held on condition of feudal service</term> are established by contract and foresight, they are not counted toward the **forced share** <note>original: "legitimam" — the portion of an estate that must by law go to the children</note> of the person who receives them through nomination or other means. Instead, they are held as a special right above and beyond the forced share, except for certain outcomes which we will list below. Furthermore, no deduction is made from them for the **Falcidian** <note>A Roman law allowing an heir to keep one-fourth of an estate before paying out legacies</note> or **Trebellianic portions** <note>A similar deduction allowed for an heir who must restore an inheritance to a third party under a trust</note>. This last point is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, along with the gloss on the law *si patroni*, under the word *apud hæredem* in the Digest (Ad Trebellianum), which is cited and followed by Alvaro Valasco (at question 46) and Caldas (concerning the naming of emphyteusis, question 18, from number 11), following the rule in the law *pater filiam* at the beginning (Digest, Ad legem Falcidiam). Indeed, the Trebellianic and Falcidian portions are only deducted from those things which come to someone by the title of "heir," but not from those things which would come to them even if they were not the heir.

The first point—that these are not counted toward the forced share—is affirmed by the more common opinion of the doctors, including Angelus on the law *si patroni* mentioned above, in the addition to the gloss on the word *apud hæredem*. This is recorded and followed by Caldas (at number 11) and others. This opinion is also defined by **Portuguese law** <note>original: "lex Lusitana"</note> (Book 4, Ordinance title 77, § 2), where it decrees regarding such a long-term lease or *prazo*:

> And if it was not given to him during the life of the father or mother, but he was only named as the person for the said lease to take effect after their death, in such case he shall not be obliged to bring the said lease or its value to the partition and **collation** <note>original Portuguese: "colaçam" — the process of returning gifts received during the parent's lifetime to the general estate pool for fair division</note>, nor shall it be counted in his forced share, nor discounted from it, unless the said lease was purchased, etc.

The reason is that a son does not receive such a long-term lease or fief from the father so much as from the **direct lord** <note>The actual owner of the land</note>, who arranged for it to be passed down and descend in this way, even if the choice or nomination of who should succeed to that lease or fief was entrusted to the father. This is supported by the text in the law *unum ex familia* (Digest, De legatis 2): "For what can he be seen to have left of his own, who was entirely obliged to return what he left?" In other words: nothing. Therefore, such a lease or fief is not considered **property derived from the father** <term>profectitium — assets originating from the parent's own estate</term> such that it should be counted against the successor's forced share, but rather **external property** <term>aduentitium — assets coming from a third party</term> from the direct lord, which he should therefore hold as a special right, just like other external goods.

<margin>5</margin>
**And indeed, if such a fief or long-term lease** was "ancient"—that is, acquired and agreed upon not by the person being succeeded, but by a grandfather or another ancestor—many more authors agree that it should not be counted toward the forced share or brought into the partition of the estate. Caldas (cited above, number 22) records these authors, to the extent that in such an event, it must be said that this is not only the more common opinion, but the universal opinion of the doctors.

The reason is that, since it is not then considered to come from the father (as if acquired by him to be passed down), but from ancestors, it is not considered property originating from the father's own patrimony, but external property, just like other goods that descend from grandfathers or great-grandfathers to grandsons or great-grandsons. Only property derived directly from the father's estate must be shared; external property does not.

However, when such a fief or long-term lease is "new"—that is, acquired by the person who is being immediately succeeded—many authors (whom Caldas

<column-break/>

cites at number 15) want it to be shared. Their opinion is embraced by Alvaro Valasco (at question 48, though he admits the Portuguese Ordinance states the contrary) and Julius Clarus (Book 4, Sententiae, § feudum, question 46). They argue such a fief or lease must be shared and counted toward the forced share. Alvaro Valasco and most others are led to this because, in that event, the assets are considered to have originated from the father, and thus must be shared and computed in the forced share. Julius Clarus says this because, since the father who first acquired the fief or lease could have sold it (even to a stranger, in his view), it should be numbered among his own assets, and therefore shared and counted in the forced share.

Nevertheless, according to what was said in the previous disputation (Conclusion 2) and in the final part of Disputation 477, it must undoubtedly be said, along with Angelus and the more common opinion of the doctors, that even if such a fief or lease is "new," it should not be shared or counted toward the forced share. This is because they are not considered to derive from the first leaseholder, but from the owner, who granted them so that they might descend in this way. They do not have the character of property derived from the first leaseholder, nor can they be sold or otherwise alienated by him, even with the owner's consent, as we have sufficiently shown in the previous disputation by citing these and other authors and the more common opinion.

Therefore, the argument of certain others fails: they argue that military service and other similar rights which can be sold or transmitted to others are shared and counted in the forced share (as was said according to the law *commodo* in the Code regarding inofficious testaments, and the law *illud* regarding collations, Disputation 241). They argue that because such fiefs and leases can be sold and transferred to heirs, they must be shared and counted.

But one must deny that such fiefs and leases can be sold, even with the owner's consent, as was seen in the previous disputation. One must also deny that they are transferable to others in any way other than according to the agreement, arrangement, and rule of the owner in the first grant of that lease or fief. This is not enough to make something shared or counted toward the forced share; just as the fact that an **entail** <term>maioratus — a property succession limited to a specific line of heirs</term> or a **trust** <term>fideicommissum</term> is transferable according to the arrangement of the first founder does not make it shared or counted toward the forced share of the new successor. When a military office or something similar is sellable or transferable as the father's own property, then it is shareable; and that is the only meaning of the two laws cited in the proposed argument and what we asserted in the cited disputation. Hence I say: if a long-term lease is granted for several lifetimes, such that the first leaseholder may nominate whomever he wishes without restriction to sons or descendants, and the second and third may likewise nominate whomever they wish, then—because such a lease is not by specific contract and foresight but is hereditary—it can pass to anyone just like the leaseholder's other free goods. In that case, just as such a lease can be sold (with preference given to the direct lord if he wants it for that price)...

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...and it can be freely transferred to anyone, if one of the sons is named to it, he is bound to bring it to the partition and accept it as part of his **forced share** <term>legitima — the portion of an estate that laws require be left to the children</term>.

<margin>6</margin> However, when a father purchases a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a permanent land lease requiring the tenant to improve the property</term> or a **fief** <term>feudum — land held on condition of feudal service</term> through a contract or foresight, or receives it in exchange for another thing of estimable price, then the son who succeeds to it—whether by the father’s nomination or another title—is bound to bring it to the partition. He must count toward his forced share either the price the parent paid for it or the value of such a lease or fief at the time the son received it, whichever the son prefers. This is well-stated in the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Book 4, Title 77, § 32, and the same should be said regarding common law. Caldas (at the cited question 18, especially number 26), Alvaro Valasco (on the law of emphyteusis, question 38, number 27), and others they cite, agree with this.

The reason is that such a lease or fief, in terms of its price, is considered **derived property** <note>original: "bonum profectitium" — property that comes to a child from the father's estate or efforts</note> passing to the son. Therefore, the son is bound to bring it to the partition with his brothers and count it toward his forced share. If at the time he received the lease or fief it was worth less than the price paid for it, he is bound to bring its value to the partition; for that reason, he is given the choice to bring either the original price or the current value.

By this same reasoning, whatever the son brought to the partition and counted toward his forced share because of such a fief or lease, a grandson to whom it passes after that son is also bound to bring to the partition with the other brothers. He must bring either what it was worth at the time it reached him, because in terms of that valuation, it is similarly considered **derived property** from the son to the grandson. So says Caldas (on the naming of emphyteusis, question 18, number 23).

Nothing in the *Portuguese Ordinances* (at the cited title, § 34) contradicts this definition when it establishes that when such a lease was bought during a marriage where a contract for "half of the goods" <note>community property</note> was in effect, or improvements were made while that marriage lasted, the son named by the father to that lease is bound to pay the wife (whether she is his mother or not) half the price or value of those improvements. I say nothing contradicts it because when the ordinance establishes this, it adds a restriction: "unless that wife expressly consented to that nomination."

Indeed, by that consent and ratification, or "express grant" <note>original: "otorga expreſſa"</note> as the ordinance says, she is considered to have forgiven the nominee, so that the half-share is not paid to her by him. However, this does not prevent the son—if she is his mother—from being bound to bring that value to the partition with his brothers during the division of his mother's goods, taking it as part of the forced share that falls to him from those goods. From what has been said, you will understand that the doctrine of Antonio Gomez (on Law 29 of the *Laws of Toro*, number 21) is false.

If he understands it to apply to fiefs and leases created by contract and foresight, the foundation on which he relies is false. For he says that if a father or mother obtained a fief from the Prince with money for themselves and their descendants, and handed it over to one of their sons, it is brought to partition because it is transferable, even if it is not alienable <note>meaning it can be passed to heirs but not sold to strangers</note>. And he says the same applies if they received a fief or

<column-break/>

lease for a certain price and money, and gave or granted it to a son, because it can similarly be transmitted, even if it cannot be sold. All these points are false insofar as they disagree with what has been said so far and what is about to be said.

<margin>7</margin> Likewise, when a father—who, without any price or compensation (except the annual payment owed to the owner), held a lease by contract and foresight—transmitted it to one of his sons while he was still alive, without reserving the **income** <term>fructus — the "fruits" or profits generated by the land</term> for himself for his lifetime, whether by giving it as a dowry for a daughter, or giving it to a son for his marriage, or transferring it to him in some other way, then the following applies: Since that benefit which the father would have enjoyed during his life belonged to his own estate, it is considered **derived property** from him to the son. Therefore, that son (in a matter held in common) is bound to bring the valuation of that benefit to the partition with his brothers and count it toward his forced share. It is different, however, regarding the value the lease has for the time *after* the father's life; for he is not considered to have received that value from the father, but from the arrangement of the owner, as has been said.

The *Portuguese Ordinances* (§ 32, cited above) establish that in this event, the son is bound to bring to the partition and count toward his forced share either the lease itself or its valuation at the time it was given, as he prefers—unless the lease ends with the father’s life because the father was the "last person" named in the contract. In that case, he is bound to bring the valuation of it at the time it was given to him. Here you see that in that Kingdom, it is commanded to bring to partition not only the estimated **usufruct** <term>ususfructus — the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term> of which the father deprived himself during his life, but either the lease itself or its full value; and this is followed in practice in Portugal.

Caldas says that since the opinions of the learned doctors were contradictory as to whether a lease by contract and foresight had to be brought to partition and counted toward the forced share, the Portuguese legislator chose this path for that event. Because these matters depend greatly on the arrangement of human law and do not conflict with natural law, that law must be upheld until it is changed. Furthermore, it is pleasing that Caldas affirms (against the professors of Coimbra) that it is not enough for a son to be bound to bring such a lease or its valuation to partition if the father, while living, names him to it irrevocably; rather, it is necessary that he actually hand it over to him, even regarding the use and income, without reserving them for himself while he lives.

This is because the *Portuguese Ordinances* clearly suggest this, and the nature of the matter requires it, according to everything said in this second conclusion. Read Caldas throughout that cited question 18. This same author in the same place (at number 7 and from number 52) considers that even if a father renounces a lease of Crown lands (which he held for several lifetimes) into the hands of the King so that the King may grant it anew to his son to be enjoyed during the father's life, such a son is bound to bring the value of the income to the partition—the income of which the father deprived himself by that renunciation during his life—even if the King's authority intervened.

It concludes that if a father provides such property to a son using his own funds or by giving up his own lifetime income from the land, the son must account for that value as part of his legal inheritance share during the partition of the estate.</summary>

Second Treatise, Disputation 480, Page 609

Since a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a permanent land lease requiring the tenant to improve the property</term> of this kind regarding the properties of the Crown of the Kingdom is subject to the same laws as the long-term leases of private individuals, as held in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 62, the second to last paragraph. And since that lease is not among the number of gifts from the King which—by the very fact that it is transferred to a son at the father's request—the son is not bound to bring to the **partition** <term>partitionem — the legal division of an estate among heirs</term> (as was said in its proper place), but is rather an **onerous contract** <term>contractus onerosus — a contract where both parties give and receive something of value</term> first celebrated by the King with the father or another ancestor, and later celebrated with the son at the father’s consent and request. In doing so, the father deprives himself, to the detriment of his other children, of the benefit of the **usufruct** <term>usufructus — the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property owned by another</term> of that thing for his entire life. Likewise, since in the renunciation of a long-term lease into the hands of the King or another **direct lord** <term>domini directi — the ultimate owner of the land, as opposed to the tenant</term>, frauds could easily occur; by the father depriving himself of the usufruct for the whole time of his life, that benefit could be transferred to one of the sons by a new grant from the owner to the detriment of the others. By this same artifice, a son could be excused from bringing to the partition the price that the father had given for that lease, with the father renouncing the lease into the hands of the owner and the owner granting that same lease anew: this fraud, indeed, must be blocked.

<margin>8</margin> Likewise, when some improvements have been made to the leased property by agreement and foresight; since those improvements or their valuation—if nothing else was deducted in the agreement from the start of the lease contract—belong to the **patrimony** <term>patrimonium — the inherited estate</term> of the leaseholder (as was explained extensively in Disputation 463), they must be brought to the partition with the other brothers and counted toward the **forced share** <term>legitima — the portion of an estate that laws require be left to the children</term> of the one to whom such a lease has come. However, by Portuguese law (Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 77, § 32), a choice is given to the person to whom the lease has come: either to bring to the partition their valuation at the time they received the lease, or what was spent in completing them, whichever they prefer. We provided the reason for this provision in Disputation 463. Caldas agrees in *On the Name of Emphyteusis*, Question 18, number 29, and others whom he cites.

<margin>Question 9</margin> But a greater doubt arises when it was specified in the agreement that those improvements which the leaseholder was bound to make would belong to the owner, with no price or compensation paid for them (according to what was said in the cited disputation). In that case, is the person to whom that lease came before it ended bound to bring to the partition and count toward their forced share the value of those improvements, or what was spent in making them? Regarding this matter, as Caldas reports in the same place from number 31, there was a dispute in Portugal; and indeed, the *Portuguese Ordinances* in the cited § 32 seem to suggest the affirmative side by an argument from the contrary sense.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, I think it should be said that since the burden of making those expenses and improvements, and leaving them for free to the owner when the lease ends, is regarded as a sort of price given for the lease along with the annual rent—and because of those expenses, a much lower annual rent is imposed than would otherwise be required—surely, staying within common law alone, when other improvements were not to be made while the lease continued, that son is bound by the judgment of a prudent person to bring to the partition and count toward his forced share a proportional part of what was spent in completing them. This should take into account the time elapsed from the beginning of such a lease, and the time that still remains

<column-break/>

to be completed, and having considered the benefit perceived from that leased thing and what is to be perceived in the future, and having looked at other concurrent circumstances.

And I would say the same regarding the price that was given for the lease. The *Portuguese Ordinances*, however, command that the entire price for which the lease was bought be brought to the partition, or the total value of the lease at the time it came to that son. Regarding such improvements, however, it seems harsh to decree that the new leaseholder should bring the whole amount spent in making them, or however much they are valued at, since they belong not to him but to the owner. Therefore, out of **equity** <note>original: "epicheia" — a legal concept where the spirit of the law is applied to correct the letter of the law in specific cases</note>, the interpreter of the laws should only say that a proportional part of what was spent must be brought, in the manner explained; for the Portuguese law did not express what should be done in this particular event.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion of the legal technicalities surrounding the "nomination" of successors to a long-term land lease (emphyteusis), specifically addressing whether a successor can be named through non-verbal signs or conditional statements in a will, followed by a detailed breakdown of Portuguese inheritance laws when no specific successor is named.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...when a person possesses the judgment of reason and sufficiently expresses their consent and will by a nod of the head: so too in the matter proposed, it must be said that a nomination to a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a permanent land lease where the tenant holds the property so long as they improve it and pay a small fee</term> made similarly by a mere nod is valid. For indeed, dispositions that are sufficiently expressed outwardly are valid when the law has not stipulated otherwise regarding specific cases—as is decreed concerning the institution of an heir, which is invalid if done by a mere nod, as was stated in the cited disputation. However, no such statute is found regarding the nomination to a long-term lease. Thus says Caldas <note>original: "Ita Caldas"</note>, after a long disputation on the nomination of a long-term lease, question 1, especially at number 29; and Gama speaks harmoniously with this in decision 287.

<margin>Question</margin> Caldas, in *On the Nomination of a Long-term Lease*, question 2, number 1, reports a case where a certain father held a long-term lease with the power of nominating a successor in it. He had handed it over to a certain son or daughter who was being joined in marriage with these words: "the father said that for the maintenance of his son (or daughter) and for the support of the future family, he gave and granted to them such a long-term lease as he held, etc." Afterward, however—either while he was still living or at the time of his death—he nominated another son to that lease. It was as if the prior grant had not been a "nomination" <note>the formal naming of a successor to the leasehold</note> but had only been a transfer of the **usufruct** <term>usufructus — the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property without owning it</term> of that lease for the entire time that son or daughter should live, reserving to himself the right of nominating anyone else he wished to the lease, who would then be the tenant and enjoy the property after the death of said son or daughter.

<margin>2</margin> It was doubted, however, whether † that prior grant was a true nomination—given the context of the transfer and that **onerous contract** <term>contractus onerosus — a contract where both parties give something of value, in this case, a marriage agreement</term> of marriage, which rendered it irrevocable—or whether it was not a nomination but merely a grant and transfer of the usufruct of that lease, as the father later intended it to be.

It must be said, as Caldas also concludes in that same place, that the grant should be considered a nomination unless the father said in other, more express words that he was only transferring the usufruct for the duration of the life of that son or daughter. Those words, "for maintenance and the support of the future family," only signify the "impelling cause" <note>the motivation for the gift</note> why the father immediately abdicated that lease from himself and transferred it with its fruits as a dowry or a wedding gift. Since the contract was onerous, if the father intended something else, he was bound to express it clearly so as not to deceive the other contracting party and their parents. Besides the many points with which Caldas confirms this, read what was said by us in Disputation 208, especially at the paragraph beginning "at which place, in passing."

<margin>Question</margin> The same author in the same place, number 4, reports a case where someone held a similar long-term lease and, having a son absent in India, had nominated a successor in his will as follows: "If my son is dead, or does not return to Portugal, I nominate Sempronius <margin>3</margin> to such lease of mine." It was † doubted, however, whether that son should be considered nominated if he were alive and did return to Portugal. Many thought he was not nominated, because mention was only made of him in the "condition" <note>the "if" clause</note> under which another person was nominated, but not in the actual "disposition" <note>the legal naming</note> and nomination itself. Caldas disputes this matter at length, bringing many arguments for both sides. It must be said, however, that without a doubt he should be considered

<column-break/>

nominated: for that was clearly the mind of the testator from the concurrent circumstances, and he expressed it sufficiently by an **argument from the contrary sense** <note>a logical inference: if "if he does not return, X gets it" is stated, it implies "if he does return, he gets it"</note> of those words. <margin>Decision</margin> That doctrine—that a person mentioned in a condition but not in the disposition is not considered "called" to the inheritance—is to be understood only when it is not clear from concurrent circumstances that the mind of the person disposing was otherwise. In events of this kind, one should stand by the truth and the clear intention of the disposers rather than by subtleties and doctrines, which are true only when concurrent circumstances do not persuade us of the opposite; especially when the favor of children is at stake.

<margin>Decision</margin> When a thing is granted in a long-term lease for several "lives" <note>successive generations</note>, so that the first tenant can nominate whomever he wishes to the lease, and the second person so nominated can similarly nominate whomever he wishes, etc., then if the tenant who still holds the right of nomination expressly names someone, that person succeeds to the lease, as is very well known.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin> When, however, he has expressly nominated no one, it is decreed by **Portuguese law** <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> that if he appoints someone as heir to the whole of his goods, that person is considered nominated. This is held in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, Title 62, at the beginning. If, however, he appoints many heirs who are not among the number of his descendants or ancestors, then they are all considered nominated. Yet, either one of them ought to receive that entire lease as part of the inheritance falling to him, refunding the excess to the others if the value exceeds his hereditary share; or, if the co-heirs do not so agree among themselves, they are bound to sell or exchange the lease with other goods within six months to divide among themselves. This requires first asking the **direct owner** <term>dominus directus — the ultimate owner of the land, such as the Crown or a lord</term> if he wants it for that price, or in exchange for equal goods, and paying him the **transfer fee** <term>laudemium — a fee paid to the landlord when a lease is transferred</term> in this event if he does not want it for equal value. But if they perform none of the aforesaid within six months, the lease reverts to the owner, if he wants it. This is held in the same place, paragraph 1. If the tenant dies with no heir appointed and leaving neither descendants nor ancestors, the lease reverts to the owner. This is held in the same place, paragraph 3.

If, however, in his will he appoints descendants or ancestors as heirs (even if he leaves a third of his goods to some stranger), or if he dies intestate leaving descendants or ancestors, then the eldest legitimate son is considered nominated. In the absence of legitimate sons, the eldest legitimate daughter is considered nominated, and she excludes a male grandson who is the son of an older son. In the absence of sons and daughters, the eldest legitimate male grandson is considered nominated; and in the absence of such grandsons, the eldest legitimate granddaughter is considered nominated; and so on for great-grandchildren or great-great-grandchildren. In the absence of legitimate descendants, a **natural son** <note>a child born out of wedlock but legally recognized</note> is considered nominated, even if he be of a man who is not a commoner; and he is preferred in that lease over legitimate ancestors (the same is to be said of a natural grandson or great-grandson in the absence of a natural son or daughter). A "spurious" <note>an illegitimate child not legally recognized</note> child, however, is not considered nominated in that lease unless he has been legitimized by the Prince so that he may succeed to such a tenant as an intestate heir.

It also details the hierarchy of succession in Portuguese law, prioritizing legitimate descendants by age and gender, followed by recognized natural children.</summary>
