### Second Treatise, Disputation 480.

If all the aforementioned descendants are lacking, the closest male ancestor in degree is considered nominated, and the elder is preferred over the younger, as was said regarding descendants; Acosta affirms this regarding pacts and grandsons, part 2, number 46, as does Caldas in *On the Nomination of a Long-term Lease*, question 11, numbers 1 and 2. In the absence of the closest males, the closest female ancestor is preferred. Moreover, the closest ancestor in degree succeeds a natural son <note>An illegitimate child</note> or grandson. These points are found there in sections 2, 3, and 4.

5 However, what has been said so far similarly applies to **long-term leases** <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual lease where the tenant holds the land so long as they pay a rent and improve the property</term> of the assets of the Royal Crown, granted for a certain number of lives, which are likewise to be nominated in a certain order. This is found there in the penultimate section and in book 2, title 17, section 6. Note, however, if the King has granted such assets of the Royal Crown to someone in a long-term lease so that they are henceforth the owner and receive the pension <note>The annual rent or fee paid for the lease</note>, these assets cannot be divided, nor can they pass to anyone other than the eldest legitimate male son who survives the death of the parent. In the absence of sons, it passes to the legitimate grandson (the son of the eldest son), or to the male great-grandson directly descending through the male line. If these are lacking, such assets immediately revert to the Royal Crown. This is the case even if the grant is phrased in different words, unless it was granted otherwise with an express derogation <note>A formal repeal or exemption</note> of that law (which is called the **Mental Law** <note>original: "mentalis" — The *Lei Mental* was a famous 1434 Portuguese law by King Duarte I which established that crown lands could only be inherited by the eldest legitimate male descendant to prevent the fragmentation of royal property</note> in that Kingdom). This is arranged and explained at length throughout that title, especially in section 5.

Furthermore, as Caldas contends at length in *On the Nomination of a Long-term Lease*, question 12,
6 these rules apply even if someone dies **intestate** <term>dying without a valid will</term> because they are a **ward** <term>pupillus — a minor under the care of a guardian</term> and cannot make a will. In such a case, the closest ancestor is considered nominated in the manner explained. The same applies when someone dies intestate because there is no one to accept the inheritance, or for some other similar cause. He adds in the cited question 12 from number 45 onwards that in all events where Portuguese law dictates that a nominated heir (whether instituted by will or by intestacy) is held to succeed, this must be understood as the "heir with effect"—that is, the one who actually accepts the inheritance. For if they repudiate <note>Refuse to accept</note> it, they are not considered the one nominated to the lease; rather, the one who actually receives the inheritance through intestacy is considered nominated, as he teaches at length in question 13, with those prior in degree always being preferred without representation; read that passage.

7 Exception: When by a peculiar privilege of the law, someone is considered nominated by a descendant dying intestate who cannot be an heir—such as the natural son of a **non-commoner** <note>original: "homini non plebei"</note>, as found in the cited section 4. In order for such a person to be considered nominated here in the long-term lease and preferred over the legitimate ancestors of the leaseholder, it is not necessary for him to be the heir to such a leaseholder.

Hence, it was not necessary for Caldas, because of this outcome (which is very clear in section 4), to resort to certain distorted interpretations of that paragraph to exclude such a son from the number of tacitly nominated successors in the event that he was not truly the son of a commoner and, consequently, could not be the heir of the father who held the lease. Nor do Gama (decision 229) and certain others correctly conclude from this peculiar event that in Portugal, others who are tacitly nominated to a lease by the disposition of the law are considered nominated and can succeed in it even if they have repudiated the inheritance of the leaseholder by whom they are tacitly nominated.

<column-break/>

8 Whether such tacit and virtual nominations have a place while standing in **common law** <term>ius commune — the general legal system based on Roman and Canon law, distinct from local statutes</term>, or whether, by the very fact that no one is found expressly nominated, such a lease devolves back to the owner, and whether such tacit nominations in ecclesiastical leases have a place in Portugal, was discussed in Disputation 446. Likewise, whether what is said in this Portuguese ordinance regarding the succession of natural sons and their tacit nomination in a lease applies to ecclesiastical leases in Portugal was examined in the cited disputation, as well as in Disputation 475, where the succession of illegitimate children in both ecclesiastical and secular leases was discussed at length.

Although a minor below the age of puberty cannot make a will, and therefore cannot tacitly nominate outsiders as heirs to the lease by appointing them in a will, nevertheless, if a father, by making a **pupillary substitution** <note>A legal arrangement where a father names an heir for his child in case the child dies before reaching the age of legal capacity</note> for that ward (according to what was said in Disputations 182 and 184), appoints an outsider or outsiders as heirs for the child, they will be considered by that very fact as nominated to the long-term lease of such a ward if the ward dies while still a minor. This is because that will and that institution of heirs are considered to be the son's and not the father's. Thus says Caldas in *On the Nomination of a Long-term Lease*, question 4, numbers 2, 3, and 4. The same must be said if someone appoints heirs through an **exemplary substitution** <note>A substitution made for an insane person or someone otherwise incapable of making a will</note> for an insane person or others for whom exemplary substitution is allowed, according to what was explained in Disputations 182 and 185. They will be considered by that very fact as nominated to the lease of the person for whom the exemplary substitution is duly made, as the reasoning is the same. Caldas, in the same place from number 5, disputes whether, once a tacit nomination to the ward's lease has been made by the father in that manner—or even an express one in that pupillary institution—the ward, from the age of seven until the years of puberty, can make another nomination for the same lease. In this way, the one nominated by the ward would be preferred over the one previously nominated by the parent, as if the nomination made by the parent through that pupillary substitution expires through the nomination made by the ward outside of a will.

He contends with many arguments that the ward can do this, and that the nomination made in the pupillary substitution expires because of it. The reasoning is that the nomination or choice of a successor to a lease consists of an act that is not denied to a ward, and through it, he does not grant his own property but another's—that is, the property of the owner, according to the owner's own disposition. However, he thinks it necessary for the authority of a guardian and the decree of a judge to intervene for that nomination to be valid, according to what was said in Disputation 224, since it concerns the alienation of the **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile — the right to use and profit from property without owning the legal title</term> of the lease, which is an immovable good. Yet, in my judgment, an event will rarely occur in which a judge can and should interpose his authority to make that nomination, especially if it is irrevocable, according to what was said in the cited disputation regarding the interposing of a judge's decree for alienating the immovable property of a minor. And when the nomination is revocable, I greatly doubt whether a judge's decree is necessary for it, especially since the minor does not thereby renounce the useful ownership or the fruits of the lease for the duration of his life...

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...of that [successor], but only chooses a successor to the **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual lease where the tenant holds the land so long as they pay a rent and improve the property</term> for the period following their own life. And since a revocable nomination is considered equal to a last will and testament—which, in the case of a minor, does not require a judge’s decree (as is established regarding a minor who has reached puberty)—this opinion holds.

I like this author’s <note>Referring to the jurist Caldas mentioned later</note> opinion, but not the foundation upon which it rests: namely, that nomination consists solely in a matter of fact, and that the person nominating does not dispose of their own property, but rather the property of the owner <note>original: *proprietarij* — the "direct owner" or landlord</note> and according to the owner’s instructions. From this false foundation, he deduces many other things in the following questions which we do not approve of. For it is one thing when someone disposes of their property solely at their own pleasure so that it might be derived in a certain way and pass to certain people, and commits the choice of those people to someone else—either because they trust that person's prudence and integrity, or to grant them a favor by entrusting them with that choice. In this way, the founders of **entailed estates** <term>maioratus — an estate that must pass to the eldest son</term>, **trusts** <term>fideicommissum — a legal arrangement where property is held by one party for the benefit of another</term>, and legacies for pious causes, or those who endow churches, are accustomed to commit to someone the choice of a family member to succeed in the estate or trust, or the choice of the poor or the pious cause to which those legacies should be applied, or the choice of the person to be presented to that church, granting the right of patronage <note>original: *ius patronatus*</note> to such an elector. But it is a far different matter when someone, through an **onerous contract** <term>contractus onerosus — a contract where both parties give and receive something of economic value</term>, grants something to someone in a long-term lease, with the power for themselves and their successors to nominate a further successor.

In that first scenario, since the arrangement was made solely by the first founder and at their sole discretion (or by church prelates granting it as a favor or reward for endowing a church), the choice and nomination to one of those positions, according to the founder's instructions, consists solely in the "fact" of choosing. No personal profit depending on the elector or nominator results for them; they are merely carrying out a duty enjoined upon them or a favor granted to them.

In the second scenario, however, the first leaseholder <note>original: *emphyteuta*</note>—through that onerous contract celebrated with the owner for themselves and their successors—has essentially purchased the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile — the right to use and enjoy the profits of property, as distinct from the legal title</term> or the leasehold right, along with the power (be it broad or limited) to nominate a successor. Therefore, both belong to them: namely, the leasehold right itself (the beneficial ownership of the property) and the power to nominate a successor. Both were, in a sense, purchased by them and granted for their own benefit.

Therefore, although when they nominate a successor they are following the owner's instructions (in that they cannot exceed the power of nomination granted for their benefit in that contract), they are nevertheless using their own proper right acquired by that contract. Thus, they contribute something of their own when they choose and nominate one person rather than another, and confer upon them their own beneficial ownership and leasehold right. Hence, that choice and nomination does not consist solely in a "fact," as Caldas and others contend.

In this place, note that the reasoning for a long-term lease of nomination based on a "pact and providence" is far different—because in that case, the nomination is tied to a specific group of people by the arrangement and the contract itself

<column-break/>

between the owner and the first leaseholder (for example, to one of the sons or descendants)—than the reasoning for a **hereditary nomination** long-term lease, which we are discussing now. This latter type includes the power to nominate anyone, even a stranger, to the succession. Regarding the former type of lease, the leaseholder cannot dispose of it to the prejudice of those who are called to it, even if the choice among them is committed to them. But regarding the latter, they can dispose of it freely, even by selling it and thereby nominating the buyer, or any other successor to the buyer, who is found to possess it at the time of the nominator's death. Thus, if the seller was the "first life," the person found to be the possessor at that time is the "second life," with the power to nominate a "third life," as is clear from the two preceding disputations and will be discussed in those following.

Therefore, when a long-term lease of nomination is based on "pact and providence," although the leaseholder—in choosing and nominating—is similar to those whose right of nomination consists in "fact" (insofar as they choose one uncertain person from a certain group, and cannot cause them prejudice by choosing another or alienating the thing), they nevertheless differ from them. This is partly because that right and power to nominate whomever they wish from that group and to confer the leasehold right they possess is their own, acquired by the force of the first contract. It is also because they can transfer the leasehold right to that person while they are still alive, renouncing their own beneficial ownership of the property without any reservation of the fruits <note>The income or produce of the land</note> if they so wish, which certainly does not consist in a mere "fact."

However, when the long-term lease is one of hereditary nomination, the leaseholder differs far more from those whose right of choice and nomination consists in "fact." Indeed, they choose and nominate by their own right, which was essentially bought and acquired for them by an onerous contract. And they choose and nominate not just one person from a certain group, but whoever they wish. Furthermore, they confer upon that person their own beneficial ownership of the property, acquired similarly by contract, which they could have sold and kept the price.

Likewise, they can nominate that person so irrevocably that, while the nominator is still alive, the nominee immediately enjoys that ownership and leasehold, with no income reserved for the nominator; these things surely do not consist in a naked "fact." Therefore, the foundation upon which Caldas relies crumbles when he says that a **minor** <note>original: *pupillum*</note> can nominate for their lease in such a way that the nomination overrides a nomination previously made by their parent in a **pupillary substitution** <note>A legal provision where a parent names a successor for their child in case the child dies before reaching the age of legal capacity</note>. The legitimate foundation of this assertion, however, is that if the minor is near puberty—that is, if a male has reached ten and a half years or a female nine and a half—just as they can enter into any contracts and dispose of their goods with the authority of a guardian and a judge's decree (in matters requiring such a decree), they can likewise nominate for their lease, even irrevocably, and by transferring [the right]...

<summary>Molina argues that the right to nominate a successor in a long-term lease (emphyteusis) is a property right acquired by contract, not just a procedural act. This allows minors near the age of puberty to legally nominate successors, potentially overriding their parents' previous arrangements.</summary>

It specifically addresses whether a minor can override a nomination made by their deceased father and transitions into a new discussion regarding the rights of those condemned of crimes (slaves of punishment) to manage such leases.</meta>

...by immediately transferring the **beneficial ownership** <term>dominium utile — the right to use and profit from property owned by another</term> of the leased property to another, as was shown in Disputation 224. Therefore, after the death of a father who had appointed a substitute for his minor child and named someone to the lease, the minor himself—with the authority of a guardian and a judge’s decree—may name another person. By doing so, he revokes the nomination made by his deceased father. However, he cannot do this if he is an infant or very close to infancy, because before that stage of life, he cannot dispose of his property even with a guardian’s authority and a judge’s decree, as was stated in the same place. Furthermore, the right of nominating is a personal right granted only to the **leaseholder** <term>emphyteuta — the person holding the long-term lease</term>, and therefore a guardian cannot exercise it in the name or place of such a minor.

The question arises whether, once a nomination for the lease has been made by a minor, they can seek **legal restoration** <term>restitutio in integrum — a legal remedy where a person is restored to their previous condition as if a contract or act had never occurred</term> for the purpose of revoking it. On this cited question, Caldas correctly notes that if the nomination is revocable, the minor neither needs that remedy nor should it be granted.

This is because the minor can revoke the nomination by their own authority without that remedy. If, however, the nomination is irrevocable (according to what will be said below), they can seek the remedy if they are found to have suffered a loss.

I understand this to apply not only if they transfer the lease and its fruits for the duration of their own life, but also if the nomination is only made for the period after their life. For such an act could result in their own harm, insofar as that nomination would deprive them of the right to sell the lease or to nominate someone else whom it might be more beneficial for them to name.

### Whether a slave of punishment can nominate
### for a long-term lease. And when the lease
### of one whose goods are confiscated
### belongs to the treasury.

### DISPUTATION 481.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A **slave of punishment** <term>servus poenae — a person who has lost their civil rights due to a criminal sentence</term> in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal can nominate for a long-term lease, even if condemned to natural death; see also number 7.*
2 *When the lease of one whose goods are confiscated belongs to the **treasury** <term>fiscus — the public or royal treasury</term>.*
3 *An ecclesiastical lease not granted by nomination, so that it might pass to an outsider, does not belong to the treasury; instead, it reverts freely to the Church if the Church wishes it. It is otherwise regarding improvements made to the property.*
4 *The same applies to a lease based on a contract or provision that excludes outsiders, even if it is a secular lease, so that the treasury does not succeed to it; see number 4.*
5 *However, understand and clarify this as noted in number 5.*
6 *The children of one who has committed **high treason** <note>original: "crimen lęsæ maiestatis"</note> or fallen into heresy are incapable of holding the lease, even by contract or provision.*
8 *The lease of nomination belonging to one whose goods are confiscated does not belong to the treasury when the offender is made a slave of punishment due to a crime.*

<column-break/>

The definition of who is called a "slave of punishment" was explained in Disputation 9. Many things were said in that place upon which the solution to this question depends. And according to what was said there, it must undoubtedly be said that a slave of punishment, even if condemned to natural death, can nominate for a long-term lease in this Kingdom of Castile. This is because, as shown there, those so condemned in this Kingdom retain the power of making a will, and of administering and disposing of their property. Therefore, they can both sell the lease (unless it is confiscated because of that specific crime) and nominate someone to it.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin>
The same must be said in the Kingdom of Portugal regarding other slaves of punishment who are not condemned to natural death. For, as stated in the cited disputation, the authors of those **ordinances** <note>Referring to the *Ordenações Filipinas* or earlier Portuguese legal codes</note> undoubtedly assume—following the opinion of many doctors which we cited and challenged there—that today, under **common law** <note>original: "iure communi" — the shared legal tradition of Roman and Canon law in Europe</note>, the status of "slave of punishment" has been removed from them for the purpose of allowing them to make a will and dispose of their goods. Therefore, in Book 5 of the Ordinances, Title 9, the discussion concerns only those condemned to death as slaves of punishment. This is for the effect that their wills (even if made before the crime) are void by established law, and their goods either go to the treasury or pass to their heirs as if they had died intestate immediately upon committing the crime. Nevertheless, those who are not condemned to death for the crimes of heresy, high treason, or sodomy are permitted to bequeath one-third of their goods to pious causes, and the remaining two parts—if not confiscated due to the crime—pass to their heirs as if they had died intestate. Therefore, beyond doubt, for slaves of punishment who are not condemned to natural death, the free administration and disposal of their property is left to them, both among the living and by will, according to the intent of the ordinances and the practice of that Kingdom; consequently, they can nominate for a lease.

Regarding those condemned to death in that Kingdom, I believe they remain slaves of punishment, not only if condemned for heresy, treason, or sodomy, but for any crime whatsoever, as they are under common law. The only exception is that those not condemned for those three specific crimes may make a will and dispose of a third of their goods for the pious causes expressed in that ordinance. Consequently, they retain their goods and the **usufruct** <term>ususfructus — the right to use and enjoy the fruits/profits of another's property</term> of them until their natural death, as stated in the cited disputation. Indeed, the Portuguese ordinance itself clearly teaches that they remain slaves of punishment regarding the other effects established by common law.

However, since we showed in Disputation 9 that the status of slave of punishment under common law—regarding those condemned to natural death, civil death, or those who have otherwise suffered a "maximum" or "middle" **loss of status** <term>capitis diminutio — a change or reduction in a person's legal standing</term>—has not been removed for other effects (except that a marriage contracted by them is valid), we must examine whether under common law all the aforesaid slaves of punishment, and under Portuguese law those condemned to natural death, can nominate for a long-term lease.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal analysis of long-term leases (emphyteusis). While the previous page focused on the rights of minors to nominate successors, this page examines what happens to these leases when a person's property is confiscated by the state (the treasury) due to a crime.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina On Contracts

In light of this difficulty, we must simultaneously explain to what extent a person's **long-term leases** <term>emphyteuses — long-term land leases where the tenant improves the property</term> belong to the **state treasury** <term>fiscus — the public or royal treasury</term> when their goods are confiscated, whether those leases are by specific nomination or not. We shall begin with this second point, which will also clarify the first. The following conclusions are to be established:

<margin>2</margin>
**First conclusion.** If the long-term lease of the person whose goods are being confiscated is not an Ecclesiastical one, nor is it based on a specific nomination—and is thus hereditary in such a way that it could pass to a stranger—then it belongs to the treasury. However, the treasury can be compelled to sell and transfer it to a person who does not hold special legal privileges. The first part of this is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by, among others, Julius Clarus (Book 4, Opinions, § emphyteusis, question 29) and Simancas (*On Catholic Institutes*, title 9, numbers 97 and 99). This is because the treasury does not succeed in a lease unless it could have passed to a stranger, based on the legal argument concerning the rights of freedmen in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff. de iure patronatus" — a reference to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note>. This opinion is expressly established by **Portuguese Law** <note>original: "lex Lusit. li. 7. ord. tit. 3. §. 17." — referring to the Ordinances of the Kingdom of Portugal</note>. The second part is clear enough: since the treasury holds many privileges and never "dies" or disappears, the landowner’s situation would be far worse in many respects if the lease remained with the treasury indefinitely. Therefore, the landowner can force the treasury to transfer it to another private individual, as was stated in Disputation 459.

<margin>3</margin>
**Second conclusion.** If an Ecclesiastical long-term lease, not involving a specific nomination, was granted such that it could pass to a stranger, it does not belong to the treasury; instead, it reverts freely to the Church, should the Church want it. However, the **improvements** <term>melioramenta — enhancements made to the property that increase its value</term>—the valuation of which would have belonged to the leaseholder or their heirs upon the end of the lease—belong to the treasury in terms of their monetary value. The first part is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion, followed by Julius Clarus and Simancas in the places cited above.

The reason is not so much that the Church’s position would be worsened if the lease passed to the treasury (since that harm could be avoided by forcing the treasury to transfer it to a private party, as discussed in the previous conclusion regarding secular leases); rather, it is because this privilege was granted to the Church in the **Authenticum** <note>original: "authentico de alien. & emphy. §. r. vers. si verò contigerit" — a collection of legal decrees</note> and has been widely accepted. This is evident from the decree *si qua vero* concerning penalties (Book 6) and from the cited Portuguese Ordinances.

The second part of the conclusion is clear enough against the view of Simancas. Although the legal ownership of the improvements belongs to the landowner, the *value* of those improvements is the personal property of the leaseholder. This value ought to pass to any of his heirs unless otherwise stipulated in the contract at the time it was signed, as stated in Disputations 463 and 479. Therefore, since the treasury succeeds to all the goods of the person whose property is confiscated, it also succeeds to these values. Consequently, the Church is bound to pay that value to the treasury if it wishes to reclaim the leased property. The argument does not hold that because a leaseholder loses the lease due to a crime, they also lose the improvements to the landowner (as mentioned in Disputation 455). That rule only applies to a "crime of commission" <note>a specific breach of the lease contract itself</note>, not to a crime for which 

<column-break/>

the person's goods are generally confiscated. In this latter event, the leaseholder does not lose the improvements to the landowner, but rather to the treasury.

<margin>4</margin>
**Third conclusion.** When a long-term lease is not by nomination but exists by contract and provision (even mixed), such that according to the form of the **investiture** <term>investitura — the formal legal document granting the lease</term> it cannot pass to a stranger, the treasury does not succeed to it, whether it is Ecclesiastical or secular. Instead, those who are called to it according to the terms of the investiture succeed to it, provided they are legally capable. Otherwise, those called further down the line in the investiture succeed. If no such people exist, the lease reverts to the landowner and is consolidated with the property ownership.

-> However, if there are any improvements in it which, according to what was said in the previous conclusion, would belong to the estate of the person whose goods are confiscated, the treasury succeeds to the valuation of those improvements. <-

The first and primary point asserted in this conclusion—namely, that the treasury does not succeed in such a lease, but rather those called by the investiture succeed as if the person had died intestate—was asserted by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors. This is cited by Julius Clarus, and by myself in *On Primogeniture* (Book 4, chapter 11, number 4). Simancas agrees, stating that the treasury is considered a "stranger" and therefore does not succeed to a lease unless a stranger could have succeeded to it. The Portuguese Law (title 3, § 14 and 17) defines the same.

<margin>5</margin>
The cited paragraph 14 also adds that if the person whose goods are confiscated flees so that the death penalty cannot be carried out, then the treasury succeeds to the **profits** <gloss>commoditate</gloss> of that lease for as long as the person lives. Upon their death, the lease passes to the person named in the investiture. This confirms what we drew from the Digest regarding the Trebellian decree in Disputation 190 and what we said in Disputation 9 regarding the confiscation of goods.

This same rule applies when someone is condemned for the **crime of heresy** <note>theology and law were deeply intertwined; heresy was a capital crime involving property confiscation</note> and their goods are confiscated, but they are mercifully reconciled to the Church. In the meantime, while they live, the profit from the lease in question belongs to the treasury; but upon their death, it passes to the person named in the investiture who is capable of holding it. If no capable person exists, it returns to the landowner because the lease expires and ends at that point.

I specified "whether the lease is Ecclesiastical or secular" because the privilege stating that an Ecclesiastical lease returns to the Church and is consolidated with the property ownership only applies when it would otherwise go to the treasury, as is clear from the cited *Authenticum*. No sense of equity allows for a situation where, if an Ecclesiastical lease could not pass to the treasury because of a crime by the current holder, those called by the same investiture should be robbed of it because of that same crime. It would not be equitable for such a privilege to be granted to the Church. Therefore, in the legal chapter *saeltis* <note>original: "c. sælteis" — likely a reference to a specific canon law chapter</note>, if long-term leases are included under the name of "rentals," only those should be understood as included which would have passed to the treasury due to such a crime. The Portuguese Law (title 3, § 16) should be understood in the same way.

<header>Second Treatise, Part 1, Disputation 482, Page 615</header>

<margin>6 Title 3, § 12</margin>
It was added in the conclusion "provided they are capable of it," etc., because, as held in the law *Quisquis* <note>original: "l. quisquis. C. ad l. Iul. Mai." — referring to the Code of Justinian regarding the Julian Law on High Treason</note>, and the Laws of the Kingdoms <note>original: "l. 2. tit. 2. par. 9. & lib. 3. Lusit. ordin. tit. 3. §. 12." — referencing Siete Partidas of Castile and the Ordinances of Portugal</note>, the children of one who has committed the **crime of high treason** <term>laesa maiestatis — treason against the king or state</term> remain in perpetual poverty and are incapable of succeeding others, whether by a will or by intestacy. Furthermore, in the Portuguese Ordinances in the cited section, it is added that this must also be understood to include receiving and succeeding by gift or contract among the living. Hence, in Portugal, they are incapable of obtaining **long-term leases** <term>emphyteuses</term>, even if they are by agreement and provision. It is otherwise, however, according to common law and the law of this Kingdom of Castile, when these do not arise from a last will; as they regularly do not. Therefore, in Portugal, if they are called by the investiture <note>the formal handing over of the lease rights</note>, they are excluded from them, and those called to succeed the last possessor lose their right. But if no further successors exist, the lease expires and reverts to the owner of the property, as held in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 3, Title 3, § 12.

The last part of the conclusion is manifest of itself and from what was said in the latter part of the preceding conclusion. For the **treasury** <term>fiscus — the royal or state treasury</term> always succeeds to the entire estate of the person whose goods are confiscated.

<margin>7</margin>
As for leases by **nomination** <term>nominationis — a lease where the current tenant has the right to name the next successor</term>, Caldas <note>a noted legal commentator</note> contends at length that a **slave of the penalty** <term>servus poenae — a person who has lost all civil rights due to being condemned to death</term>, according to common law and even Portuguese law, could still nominate someone to those leases. He bases this on the idea that nomination to a lease consists in a matter of fact, and those things consisting in fact are not denied to a "slave of the penalty." To us, however, the opposite seems true, along with Emmanuel Acosta and others whom Caldas cites there. We are led chiefly by the reason that nomination to a lease does not consist in a mere matter of fact, but is a legal disposal by the tenant of his own right, as was shown in the preceding disputation where we overturned Caldas’s foundation. Therefore, since any disposal of goods made by a "slave of the penalty" is null by the law itself, it must be said that such a person cannot validly nominate for a lease.

The Portuguese Ordinance, Title 3, § 18, openly agrees with us. Where it speaks of one who committed the crime of high treason, it says:
> <note>original Portuguese: "se foro dado en certas pessoas..."</note> if a lease was granted to certain persons who were to be nominated, it should immediately be returned to the lordship from which it proceeded, because he who committed the said wickedness cannot nominate any person after it was committed. And if he had made any nomination before, it is held as null and void, as if it had never been.

However, I understand this regarding a nomination by a last will or a gift in anticipation of death made before the crime, which is rendered null by the very fact that the person becomes a "slave of the penalty." It is otherwise for an irrevocable nomination, or even a revocable one, which is a disposal among the living. For disposals among the living, even revocable ones, made by someone before a crime was committed, are not rendered null by a subsequent crime, even if that crime is high treason against man or God, as we shall show in Disputation 659. This being established,
<margin>8</margin>
the conclusion is: **long-term leases by nomination** belonging to one whose goods are confiscated do not belong to the treasury, whether they are by agreement or hereditary, such that a stranger could be nominated to them, when

<column-break/>

the delinquent becomes a "slave of the penalty" due to a crime. Rather, upon the death of the delinquent, they revert to the owner of the property, as if granted under the condition "if he shall have nominated," and the condition not being met because he was rendered incapable of nominating. In the meantime, while the delinquent lives, the benefit of the lease belongs to the treasury in the place of the delinquent. In the Kingdom of Castile, however, I believe that a tenant whose goods are confiscated can nominate, according to what was said previously and in Disputation 489. I judge the same in Portugal if, in some event, someone's goods were confiscated but they were not condemned to natural death; and this is for the same reason. Furthermore, if any **improvements** <term>melioramenta — enhancements made to the value of the land</term> had been made in such leases that belonged to the delinquent’s estate in terms of their valuation, those would also belong to the treasury. This entire conclusion is sufficiently clear of itself and from the previously mentioned conclusions, and needs no further proof.

### Whether a member of a religious order can nominate for a long-term lease, and when the lease of a religious person belongs to the monastery.

# DISPUTATION 482.

-> SUMMARY <-

1 *When the long-term lease of a member of a religious order belongs to the monastery, and when it belongs to his heirs by intestacy.*
2 *Whether a member of a religious order, having made their profession, can nominate for a long-term lease, and when.*

It is clear enough from what was said in Disputations 139 and 140 that a **religious person** <note>a monk, friar, or member of a religious order</note>, before they profess their vows—or in **our Society** <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits)</note>, before being admitted to the grade of spiritual or temporal coadjutor—can nominate for their lease. The whole difficulty is whether they can nominate if they have already made their **profession** <term>professus — taking the final, solemn vows of the order</term> or become a coadjutor in our Society. But first, we must explain when a religious person's lease belongs to the monastery.

When a religious person has disposed of their lease before professing their vows, then there is no reason it should belong to the order, as is clear from Disputation 140. However, when they have not disposed of it and have professed their vows, the order then has a right to the goods of its member, and a distinction must be made. For if the lease is not hereditary—meaning those succeeding to it are called by name—the monastery is not among that number.

The benefit of the lease belongs to the monastery while such a religious person lives. But upon their death, the lease passes entirely to the one or more persons called by the investiture. Likewise, if there are any improvements in that lease whose value belonged to the estate of that religious person before they professed, those also belong to the monastery because it succeeds to all the goods of such a person. If however...

...nevertheless, if 그hat religious person has descendants or ancestors, their legal share <note>original: "portio legitima" — the portion of an estate that by law cannot be willed away from certain heirs</note> would be owed to them, just as in the case of other goods belonging to such a religious person, as was discussed in Disputation 140; this applies also to the valuation of **improvements** <term>melioramenta — enhancements made to a property that increase its value, such as buildings or irrigation</term>.

The first of these points is affirmed by the common opinion, which **Julius Clarus** cites in his *Sentences, Book 4, § Emphyteusis, Question 33*. This is clear enough in itself and from what was said in the preceding disputation. The remaining points are also quite manifest from the previous discussion and from Disputation 140, requiring no further proof. However, if that religious person belongs to an order that does not have a legal right to the goods of its members, or if they are admitted to the rank of **coadjutor** <note>a specific grade of membership in the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) who took vows but retained certain technical relationships to their previous property</note> in our Society, then that **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual or long-term lease of land</term> immediately belongs—at least regarding its use and benefit—to those who are called to it by the original grant. The valuation of the improvements, however, would belong to the heirs-at-law <note>original: "hæredes ab intestato"</note>, whether they are the same people succeeding to the lease or others, as is established from the cited Disputation 140.

When, however, there are no persons who would be called to that lease by the grant, then the lease expires and reverts to the owner of the property. The owner is then bound to pay the value of the improvements either to the monastery (if it has the right to the religious person's goods) or to the heirs-at-law of that religious person, as is clear in itself and from the preceding discussion.

If, truly, the lease is hereditary so that an outsider could succeed to it, and it is not a "lease by nomination" <note>a lease where the tenant has the right to name their successor</note>, and the profession is made in a monastery that acquires rights to the person's goods, then that lease belongs to the monastery just like the rest of that person's assets. However, the monastery is required to **alienate** <note>to sell or transfer to someone else</note> it. This is because, due to the monastery's privileges and other inconveniences that might follow for the owner, the owner's condition would be made worse, as was stated in the previous disputation and Disputation 140. This is the view of **Julius Clarus** as cited above and is the common opinion; the matter is quite clear in itself.

And what we said in Disputation 140 should be understood as referring only to this type of lease. But if the religious profession is made in a monastery that does not acquire rights to the person's goods, or if the religious person is admitted to the rank of coadjutor in our Society, then by that very fact, such a lease—along with the improvements—passes to the heirs-at-law of that religious person. This is because the person is considered naturally dead for that purpose, as is clear from Disputation 140.

<margin>Question 2</margin>
Whether a religious person, after making their profession—or after taking the vows of a coadjutor in our Society—can **nominate** someone to the lease. **Caldas**, in his *On the Nomination of Emphyteusis, Question 6*, says yes. He is led by his own reasoning that nominating a successor to a lease consists in an act of fact, and therefore is something even a professed religious person can do.

<margin>Decision</margin>
However, the contrary must be said: because this is truly a legal disposal of property and rights, as was stated in the two preceding disputations. No right to temporal goods remains to a religious person once they have made their profession, nor to the coadjutors in our Society; no power to dispose of such things as

<column-break/>

their own remains to them once their profession is made.

For this reason, in Disputation 140, following **Panormitanus, Navarrus, Covarruvias**, and the common opinion of the doctors, we said that a religious person, once professed, cannot revoke a will they made before their profession—even if they wish to revoke it in favor of the monastery or another pious cause. Because through profession they are **dead to the world**, they can no longer dispose of the goods they previously held. Therefore, just as they cannot make a will after profession, they cannot revoke a will made before profession. And in Disputation 141, following **Navarrus**, we said that although in the *Authentica* <note>a collection of Byzantine legal decrees</note> "If any woman" <note>original: "si qua mulier, C. de Episc. & cleric."</note> it is permitted for a professed religious person (if they did not make a will before profession) to divide their goods among their children—provided the children's legal share is not diminished and a portion is left to the monastery—outside of that specific event and the manner granted there, they cannot dispose of anything from their goods among their children. This is because they lack ownership and administration over them, and they no longer have a legal "will" to choose or refuse.

Therefore, if a religious person who held a "lease by nomination" makes their profession (or coadjutor vows in our Society) without having made a nomination, the lease expires. It reverts to the property owner, as the condition under which it was granted—namely, that they should nominate someone—has failed.

Unless, in **Portugal**, you say that one making a profession without having previously made a will is considered to have died intestate. Therefore, if they have descendants or ancestors, they are tacitly considered to have nominated one of them in the order recorded in Disputation 80 from the **Portuguese Ordinances**. Even if a lease by nomination expires because no one was nominated, it nevertheless does not expire before the physical death of that religious person. Thus, the benefit of the lease belongs to the monastery where the profession was made for as long as the religious person lives, provided the monastery has rights to that person's goods. Otherwise, if it does not have those rights, the benefit passes to the heirs-at-law, whether the lease was hereditary or by agreement and provision.

The same must be said regarding the value of the improvements to that lease, if such value belonged to the person's estate before profession, as both points are clear enough. Finally, I should warn that even if the lease by nomination were hereditary, it would not have been lawful for that religious person to nominate the monastery to it before their profession. This is because the monastery's succession would make the owner's situation much worse, as has been said many times.

# Some other matters regarding nomination to an emphyteusis.

## DISPUTATION 483.

### SUMMARY.

1 *A tenant <term>emphyteuta — the holder of a long-term lease</term> who has the power to nominate a successor before their death may, at their own pleasure, vary and change that nomination up until the moment of death. With further clarification, as noted therein.*
2 *A tenant who has the power of nomination without any mention of death being made in the contract cannot revoke a nomination once it is made. However, this fails and is limited in certain cases, as noted therein.*
3 *If an emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual or long-term lease of land</term> passes to various persons through sale by the first tenant (who holds the power of nomination) while that first tenant is still alive, the "second person" to be nominated is considered to be whoever is found holding the lease at the time of the first tenant's death, and so on.*
4 *If an emphyteusis is granted for several specific lives, which persons the last survivor may nominate, and who are considered expressly nominated.*

The following conclusions regarding nomination to an **emphyteusis** <note>a lease where the tenant enjoys the land as if they owned it, provided they pay a small annual rent and improve the property</note> under Portuguese law (where such cases are frequent) are to be established.

<margin>1</margin>
The first conclusion is this: If the contract for the nomination of the lease contains a clause stating that the persons granted the power of nomination may name whom they wish before their death, or at the time of death, then they may nominate once, twice, or many times, naming different persons as they please. The later nomination always revokes the earlier ones. The reason is that arrangements ordered for the time of death can be changed and revoked before death. However, if the person holding this power of nomination has transferred the leasehold right to someone else—whether as a dowry, a gift for a marriage, or any other cause—then they cannot nominate anyone else afterward, even if they reserved the **usufruct** <term>usufruct — the right to use and enjoy the fruits/profits of a property without owning it</term> of that leased property for themselves. This is because the right to dispose of such a lease belongs thereafter to the person to whom it was transferred. Furthermore, when a public document exists recording a nomination to an emphyteusis made to someone, then the Kingdom’s law does not allow proof by witnesses of another, prior nomination—unless it was made in a **nuncupative will** <note>original: "testamento nuncupativo" — an oral will declared by the testator in their final illness before witnesses</note> spoken at the time of death and with six witnesses, whether male or female; in that case it is valid in this Kingdom, as explained in Disputation 126. If, however, there is no public document regarding another nomination, a nomination proved by three witnesses is considered valid.

These rules are found in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances* <note>original: "Lusitan. ordin." — referring to the *Ordenações Filipinas*, the legal code of Portugal</note>, Title 63, at the beginning and in sections 2 and the penultimate. However, what is said regarding proof should, in my judgment, be understood as applying to the **external court** <note>the public, legal court system</note> of the Kingdom. In the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiae" — the moral or spiritual judgment before God</note>, a nomination will be valid even if a public document preceded it and the later nomination was made before few-

<column-break/>

er than three witnesses. Indeed, it would even be considered valid in the external court if the person otherwise rightfully nominated confesses that the tenant had made that nomination.

<margin>2</margin>
The second conclusion: If the power of nomination is granted in the lease contract without any mention of death, then by the very fact that a person has been nominated—even if they are unaware of the nomination—no one else can be named. If another is named, any subsequent nomination is invalid and does not revoke the first. An exception is made when someone nominates in a will; for just as a will can be revoked before the death of the testator, so too can a nomination contained within it.

Likewise, when someone has nominated in a will that is void by law or for some other reason, the nomination contained in it is void. Except, however, if the will is void only regarding the institution of an heir (for example, because someone was passed over or disinherited without just cause); in that case, nominations to an emphyteusis made in it remain valid under Portuguese law, as we have shown at length in Disputation 175 against **Alvaro Valasco** <note>a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note>. Furthermore, when someone has first nominated someone outside of a will according to the terms of this conclusion, but without transferring the lease to them, if the nominee dies before the nominator, the right and power to nominate again remains with the nominator. This is because the first nomination neither achieved, nor could achieve, the effect of transferring the leasehold right to the person so named. For the same reason, the same must be said if someone was nominated under a condition that fails before the death of the nominator.

Therefore, if someone has nominated one person under a condition pending in the future, they can simultaneously nominate someone else in the event that the condition fails. What was said in the preceding conclusion regarding proof of nomination by public document, witnesses, or an oral nuncupative will applies similarly to the nomination discussed in this conclusion. Both conclusions apply whether the emphyteusis and the power of nomination were granted by contract (even a lucrative one), by testament, or by a last will. These are found in Title 63, sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and the last two.

<margin>3</margin>
The third conclusion: When dealing with an emphyteusis of the kind discussed in the two preceding conclusions and from Disputation 480, if the "first person" (for example) who has the power to nominate another person sells, gives, or transfers the leasehold right to someone else by any other title, the right to dispose of that lease no longer remains with that first person. Instead, it belongs to the new tenant, who can sell, give, or transfer that right to another. If the tenant dies—whether having nominated someone or with no one nominated—all rules must be observed which we stated were to be followed from Title 61 of the *Portuguese Ordinances* and Disputation 480. Nevertheless, as long as that *first person* is alive, none of those to whom the leasehold right descended during that whole time is considered the "second person" to be nominated. Rather, whoever is found in possession of the lease at the time of the death of that first tenant is considered the "second person." And what was said regarding that first person should be understood...

the same is to be understood for the second person, and for the others who, according to the form of the contract or the grant of the **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis — a long-term land lease where the tenant acts as a near-owner</term>, have the power to nominate. For none of those to whom the lease descends is considered the "second person" until that other second person, who was found in the lease at the time of the first, has died. However, the final person, who has no power to nominate further, may sell or transfer their **emphyteutic** right to another under a different title during their lifetime; and that person may transfer it to another, and so on, likewise for the duration of that final person's life. But if anything else was established between the person transferring the right and the person receiving it by the authority of the **owner** <note>original: "proprietarius" — the underlying landlord or lord of the land</note>, that must be observed. All these points are found in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 64, final sections.

Regarding the three preceding conclusions and what was said in Disputation 480, I should give this warning: While I was staying in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, it was reported to me that in some places in that kingdom, such as the region between the **Douro** and **Minho** <note>original: "Durius et Minius" — rivers in northern Portugal</note> rivers, a custom has been accepted. When an emphyteusis is taken for several "lives" <note>a "life" refers to the lifespan of a specific person named in the contract</note>, the leased property is divided among the heirs of the person who currently possesses it. The "nomination," however, serves only two purposes: first, so that when the life of the last person named in the contract ends, the lease expires and the property returns to the owner; and second, so that the persons so named act as the "heads" of the lease. These heads are held responsible for paying the full rent to the owner, while the others among whom the property is divided contribute their proportional shares of the rent. We reported that this same practice is observed regarding emphyteusis in general in Disputation 460, and that **Gama** <note>Antonio da Gama, a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> asserts this is lawful in itself because no loss results to the owner from it.

<margin>4</margin> The fourth conclusion: When an emphyteusis is established for a certain number of lives, both as to the number and the specific persons (for example, if it is granted to someone, their wife, and a son born or to be born to them), then the last surviving parent can nominate whichever son or daughter they wish. If at the time of death they lack children but have grandchildren, they can nominate whichever grandson or granddaughter they wish, even if the contract only mentioned "children." This is stated in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 63, section 5. I believe the same applies to great-grandchildren in the absence of grandchildren. If, however, the person dies **intestate** <note>without a will</note>, or with a will but with no one expressly nominated for that lease, the eldest son is considered nominated; and in his absence, the order reported from Title 62 in Disputation 480 is to be followed.

It is established, however, that ancestors or collateral relatives <note>such as siblings or cousins</note> are not included in such a contract, as they cannot be understood under the name of "children." When a contract is celebrated under the form of this conclusion in that region between the Douro and Minho, it was also reported to me that custom dictates that upon the death of one spouse, the leased property is divided between the survivor and the children of the deceased; and when the last parent dies, their portion is divided among their descending heirs. These nominations serve only to clarify when the lease ends, and so that the person named in the contract (or by the last parent) acts as

<column-break/>

the "head" of the lease, in the manner explained just above.

## Whether, when the lease has ended, the owner is bound to renew the contract for the successor of the last tenant.

### DISPUTATION 483.

### SUMMARY

1 *An emphyteusis ended through **forfeiture** <term>commissum — the loss of a right due to a breach of contract or law</term> returns absolutely to the owner.*
2 *This is expanded and limited as in number 2.*
3 *In which cases and for which persons the owner is bound to renew the lease once it has ended.*
4 *What applies to Church-owned <note>Ecclesiastical</note> leases. See numbers 4 and 8.*
6 *Understand this as in number 6.*
*However, see the contrary view in number 9, which goes against the common opinion.*
7 *Agreements placed within the lease contract must be observed.*
8 *Whether the owner is bound to renew the lease for the successor of the last tenant if they request it within the due time, even if the owner has already granted it to someone else, and thus the matter is no longer **untouched** <note>original: "re non integra" — a legal state where a new obligation has already been entered into</note>.*
10 *Interpretation of Law 1, section "It is permitted," in the Digest regarding daily and summer water.*
11 *Interpretation of the law "It is fitting" in the Code regarding leasing.*
12 *The opinion of **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note> and the common opinion on the matter of renewing a lease for the successor of the last tenant, and whether it is observed in Portugal.*
13 *Whether the owner is bound to renew the lease for the successor of the last tenant on account of **improvements** <note>original: "meliorationes"</note> made to the property.*

It remains for us to speak about the renewal of the emphyteutic contract, and let us examine the notable question proposed. It must be observed that if the lease ends because the tenant has fallen into **forfeiture** <note>original: "in commissum"</note> by any of the ways explained in the preceding sections, the property then returns to the owner in such a way that he is not bound to renew the contract either for the tenant who defaulted or for his successors, as everyone admits. This is stated by **Caldas** <note>Peregrinus de Cassis, often cited as Caldas, a commentator on leases</note> in *On the Renewal of Emphyteusis*, question 8, number 1, and others whom he cites.

This holds true even if, when the lease was originally handed over, an agreement was added about renewing the lease when the contract ended; this is the common opinion reported by the same Caldas in *On the Renewal of Emphyteusis*, question 9, number 5. Likewise, if the lease was granted to someone, his wife, and one of their sons, and they have no children or descendants; or if it was granted to someone and his descendants down to the third generation; certainly, if the matter reaches a state where there are absolutely no descendants of the first tenant, the lease is considered extinct and reverts to the owner, so that he is not bound to renew the contract. For he is not bound to renew and continue it except according to the original form of the contract. And this is all that is asser-

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of emphyteusis (long-term leases), specifically addressing whether a landlord is legally obligated to renew a lease once the specified "lives" or terms have expired, and how this intersects with both Civil and Canon Law.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 4, Question 4. Page 619

Caldas seems to assert the same in that place, along with others whom he cites. Therefore, in an **emphyteutic** <term>emphyteusis — a type of perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</term> contract granted for a certain time or for certain "lives," one must consider whether it is simply hereditary. In that case, the heir or heirs of the last tenant may seek a renewal, according to the opinion of those who assert that the owner is bound to grant a renewal.

If, however, the lease is granted through a mix of a specific agreement and "providence" <note>original: "pactum et providentia" — a legal arrangement considering both the contract terms and the landlord's foresight for the tenant's family</note>, then only those who were heirs of the last tenant and were called according to the form of the first contract may seek a renewal, and no others—provided the lease did not end with the preceding person. But if it is simply from agreement and providence, then those who likewise possess the required qualities according to the form of the first contract (at least in respect to the first tenant) may seek it, and no others. Hence, if only the descendants of the first tenant are called to a certain lease, and the last tenant appoints his own wife as his heir, she cannot seek a renewal because she is a "stranger" in comparison to the first tenant. In these matters, Gama seems to agree with others whom he references in Decision 326, as does Staphyleus in his work on letters of grace.

According to this teaching of ours, the contrary opinions must be reconciled, and the question must be settled—a question which Julius Clarus and Caldas raise but do not define as they ought. From these points, you will easily understand in which event, and toward which persons, the proposed question applies: whether the owner, once the lease has ended, is bound to renew the **emphyteutic** contract. For based on Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors followed by Caldas, Julius Clarus, Gama, Staphyleus, Alvarez Valasco, and Emmanuel Acosta, they affirm that once the lease has ended in the manner explained, the successors of whom we have spoken can seek a renewal of the contract from the owner. <margin>3</margin> They argue that they will obtain one easily; indeed, if it is not granted by the owner, an "injury" <note>original: "iniuria" — a legal injustice or violation of rights</note> is done to them. For that reason, under **Canon Law** <term>Canon Law — the internal legal system of the Catholic Church</term>, they can appeal and have recourse to a superior to compel the owner to renew the lease.

<margin>1</margin> They are led to assert this for several reasons. First and most importantly, from the section *permittitur* <note>a reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding water rights</note>, where it is held that the Prince, and no other, can grant water to be drawn from a stream or other public place to irrigate a field. Sometimes the grant is made to the estates themselves, and sometimes to the persons who own the estates. <margin>2</margin> If the grant of that water is made to the estate, it does not expire when the person to whom it was granted dies, because it is a "real" grant <note>a right attached to the "res" or thing/land itself</note> made to the estate, which persists with the estate regardless of whose ownership it falls under. If, however, it is made to a person, then it expires with that person, because it was a personal grant; therefore, it does not pass to that person's heirs, nor to other owners of the same estate, if by chance the person to whom the grant was made sells the estate

<column-break/>

or transfers it into the ownership of another by some other title.

It is added that in such an event, the new owner of the estate will easily obtain the grant of water to irrigate that field. For, if he shows that the water is "due" to his fields, even if it previously flowed in the name of the one from whom ownership passed to him (as something granted personally), he undoubtedly obtains the right to draw the water. Nor is this (namely, the grant of such water) merely a "benefit," but rather an injury if someone should fail to obtain that water from the Prince. In the **Gloss** <term>Gloss — a standard medieval commentary on legal texts</term> on the word *impetrabile* (obtainable), it explains that the word means it "can be easily obtained" and "ought to be easily granted." It adds that this is similar to the **investiture** <term>investiture — the formal ceremony of granting a fief or office</term> of feuds: for when a vassal dies, the male heir can easily obtain investiture, because it must be given to him, and he must take the oath.

From this text, joined with the Gloss, Bartolus and his followers conclude that the same applies to feuds and to emphyteusis: namely, that when the final "life" for which they were granted ends, an injury is done to the successors of the last tenant or feudal holder if they seek renewal and it is not granted. Therefore, they can then have recourse to a superior to compel the owner to grant the renewal.

Next, Bartolus cites in confirmation of this opinion various laws regarding the leasing of estates and certain feudal laws.

Likewise, Bartolus and others, in confirmation of the same opinion, cite the final gloss on the chapter *bonae memoriae* regarding postulations, and the final gloss on the 100th Distinction. These two glosses affirm that although the **pallium** <note>original: "pallium" — a circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and bond with the Pope</note> which the Supreme Pontiff is accustomed to grant to Archbishops is a personal privilege, an injury is nevertheless done to the successors in the archbishoprics unless it is granted to them by the Supreme Pontiff in the same way it was customarily granted to their predecessors. Those glosses prove this from the aforementioned section *permittitur*. Thus far, however, I do not see that the opinion of Bartolus and the common view rests on any other foundation.

<margin>4</margin> There is, however, a debate as to whether this common opinion of Bartolus also applies to **Ecclesiastical emphyteusis** <note>leases involving land owned by the Church</note>, or only to secular leases. And although the more common opinion of the doctors (which Julius Clarus and Caldas follow) is that it applies even to Church land, many others whom Caldas names specifically deny it. They confirm this from the *Authenticum* <term>Authenticum — a collection of Justinian's legal decrees</term> regarding non-alienation. There, a pact is disapproved by which the Church might promise that, after the third generation ends, it will renew the lease for the descendants of the last tenant and that they should be preferred over others. It decrees that such a pact poses no obstacle to the Church taking back the land once the third generation is over. If the Church were bound to renew the lease in that manner, such a pact would certainly not be disapproved; indeed, if successors could compel the Church to such a renewal, tenants would not bother to include such a pact in the first place. Nor would the law speak so freely in the cited *Authenticum*.

# Louis Molina: On Contracts

### Page 620

It was declared that the Church, once the final generation had ended, could take back the **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis — a type of long-term or perpetual lease where the tenant pays a modest rent and improves the land</term> for itself. Antonio Augustinus records these words from the "New Constitution" (Novella 7, chapter 4). Indeed, the constitution commands that any agreement—or rather, any "crafty machination"—should be rejected if it was made with the administrators, a pious Bishop, or other officials I have listed, by the person contracting the lease. This refers to schemes where, even after three persons (the "three lives") have passed away, the successors might still be allowed to take immovable property from the Church under the title of emphyteusis and be preferred over others. The constitution condemned such a machination as being done in bad faith. This is drawn from that constitution.

<margin>†</margin>
Panormitanus, in the cited chapter *bona memoriæ*, number 28, judges that the opinion of Bartolus should be restricted. It should only be understood to apply when the Church (or another owner) wishes to grant a new lease to an outsider after the old one has ended; in that case, the successors of the last tenant should be preferred. However, it is different when the Church wishes to take the property for its own use, for then it cannot be forced to renew the lease. This opinion is embraced by Emmanuel Acosta at the last cited number, by Gama in Decision 41, and Julius Clarus inclines toward it as well. Many others whom Caldas refers to also embrace it. As Panormitanus says: if the Church could never deny a finished lease to the successors of the last tenant, it would have been useless to decree in the *Authenticum* <note>original: "authentico de non alien." — referring to Justinian's legal updates on not selling church property</note> that Church property cannot be granted in emphyteusis except for "three lives" <note>A common legal term for three generations of tenants</note>.

Some scholars hold generally that when a clause is included in the contract—as is customary in Portugal—stating that after the three lives, the leased property shall return to the Church or the direct lord "free and clear and without any impediment," then the owner is not held to renew the lease for the successors of the last tenant.

<margin>†</margin>
For indeed, one must † stand by the agreements and conditions placed in contracts, especially in a lease contract, as is often said in the preceding sections (based on the Institutes and the Code). And so Gama reports in Decision 41 and 326 that it has sometimes been so judged in the Portuguese Senate, and should be judged so. Although Caldas stubbornly judges that the Church should be forced to renew the lease for the successors—both in this and the preceding case—he does report that sometimes the contrary has been judged in that same Senate.

<margin>6</margin>
Those who affirm that the owner is held to renew the lease for the successor of the last tenant (if they ask for it) add a condition: if that successor † does not ask for the renewal within a year from the moment the lease ended, they lose the right to seek it by that very fact. Consequently, the owner is not thereafter held to grant it to them. This is based on the text of feudal law regarding heirs of a deceased vassal. There, someone who had a right to a **fief** <term>feudum — a feudal land grant</term> but did not seek it within a year (while being aware of it) is rejected if they seek it later. Likewise, this follows the rule that a year of silence has the force of a repudiation, according to Baldus and others. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which Julius Clarus and Caldas follow, and which they assert is the accepted practice in Portugal. However, they debate extensively whether a minor can be granted "restitution" <note>legal restoration of a lost right</note> to seek a renewal after that year has passed, or if others can seek it if they were prevented by a just cause or impediment.

<column-break/>

This involves the power of the owner to redeem a fief sold by a vassal at the same price. If the owner, knowing this, does not do so within a year, he loses the power to redeem it later. Indeed, that year-long silence is considered a rejection of the right. This is the common opinion of the learned, which Julius Clarus and Caldas follow, asserting it is the accepted practice in Portugal. Whether a minor should be granted a full restoration of rights to seek renewal after the year has passed—or if others who had a just cause or impediment should be granted the same—is discussed at length by Caldas and Gama.

Furthermore, if the matter is "no longer whole"—that is, if the owner, immediately after the lease ended or within the year, granted it to an outsider before the successor <margin>7 Question</margin> of the last tenant could ask for a renewal—does the successor still have the right to claim it? Julius Clarus denies this, along with others cited by Caldas. On the other hand, Caldas and others affirm that even when the matter is no longer whole, one can still seek the renewal within the year, and it should be granted.

Given the common opinion of Bartolus, I believe a distinction must be made. If the successor of the last tenant is in possession of the property because they occupied it based on their right to seek renewal, then they should be preferred even if the owner has made a new deal with someone else; for their right overrides the right of the other. However, if the owner had already granted the lease to an outsider and had placed them in possession, then the newcomer—having acquired a "right in the thing" and **useful ownership** <term>dominium utile — the tenant's right to use and profit from the land, distinct from the landlord's legal title</term> through title and possession—must be preferred over the successor. The successor only had a right *to* the thing, and that only based on a certain equity. This is similar to what <margin>†</margin> has often been said before: if a thing is sold to one person but not delivered, and later it is sold and delivered to another, the second buyer is preferred over the first. This is because the second buyer acquired ownership through delivery, while the first buyer only acquired a personal action against the seller to fulfill the sale.

Regarding the legal form for requesting a renewal and the customary style for granting it in Portugal—and when the rent (pension) may be increased during renewal—one can find this in Caldas's work.

Having thus explained the opinion of Bartolus and the common view, let us add what we ourselves think about the proposed question.

<margin>8</margin>
And † first of all, I believe the same must be said regarding an ecclesiastical lease as is said of a secular or private one. As the more common opinion of the doctors affirms, the reasoning is the same: it is no less fitting and necessary for the Church to observe equity than it is for private individuals. To preserve this equity...
