<meta>This page continues the legal and moral argument regarding the expiration of emphyteusis (long-term land leases). Molina is specifically refuting the common legal opinion that a landlord is morally or legally obligated to renew a lease for the heir of the previous tenant once the original contract has expired.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 43, Chapter 1

[The owner] can be compelled by ecclesiastical superiors if equity <note>moral fairness rather than strict legalism</note> in the matter at hand has such force that a secular owner would be bound to renew the **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis — a long-term land grant where the tenant improves the land and pays a small rent</term> for the successors of the last tenant, and could be compelled to do so by his own superiors.

9 However, I believe that the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note>, and the common opinion regarding both types of emphyteusis, is undoubtedly false and conflicts with justice. It is wrong to compel an owner—whether that owner is the Church or a private individual—to renew an emphyteusis for the successor of the last tenant once the contract has reached its end.

I am led to this because an emphyteutic contract is certainly an **onerous** one <term>onerous contract — a legal agreement where both parties have obligations and receive benefits, such as land use in exchange for rent</term>. It is a grant of a piece of land in terms of its "useful ownership," either in perpetuity, or for certain lives, or for another period beyond ten years, as the parties have agreed. This is done for a specific rent to be paid at set times, with various burdens arising either from the law or the agreement of the parties. Therefore, since contracts receive their "law" from the agreement of the parties—as stated in the rule "contractus" in the *Rules of Law* in the *Sext* <note>original: "regula, contractus, de reg. iuris in 6"; refers to a standard collection of Canon Law rules</note>—this is most well-known. Especially here, the pacts and agreements of the parties must be observed exactly as they were agreed upon, as seen in the Code of Justinian and the Institutes. Truly, unless it is sufficiently shown from the law or elsewhere that the emphyteutic contract was celebrated for certain lives or a finite time with the condition that the owner is bound to renew it when that time ends, such a claim should no more be admitted than it would be in a standard lease, a loan, or any other onerous contract. In those cases, no one would assert that one of the parties is bound to renew the contract. Whoever claims that an owner is bound to renew a contract has the burden of proof; otherwise, they should not be heard, as is clear enough. Therefore, since the arguments upon which Bartolus and the common opinion rely are of no weight at all—as I shall clearly show—it follows that their opinion is entirely false. Indeed, an injury is done to the owner against **commutative justice** <term>commutative justice — the fairness required in private exchanges and contracts</term> when such a person is forced to renew a contract.

This reasoning is confirmed: no greater burden can be imposed on anyone regarding their own property than that to which they obligated themselves by contract, unless a sufficient reason is shown either from the prescription of laws or elsewhere. Therefore, since it does not appear from the form of the contract that the owner obligated himself to renew it—indeed, the opposite is clear—and since the reasons of Bartolus and the common opinion do not sufficiently prove an obligation from elsewhere (as I will show by overturning each one individually), it follows that the opinion is false and inflicts an injury upon the owner by forcing him to do what he is not truly bound to do.

Regarding the paragraph "permittitur" [it is permitted] <note>a reference to a specific section of Roman civil law</note>: first of all, that text speaks of a grant of water given as a favor to irrigate a private estate. However, this grant is made from a public stream or other public water source by the Prince <note>the sovereign or head of state</note>, whose role it is to grant and apply common resources to private individuals for a fitting, reasonable, and just cause for the common good.

<column-break/>

In the case proposed, the grant was made to a certain private individual to irrigate his field because equity demanded it for the common good. Because of the location of the field, it was appropriate for it to be irrigated by that water (just as other similar fields were), making it fertile for the common good. Thus, that water was "owed" in a certain way to that estate for that purpose—not indeed out of strict justice, but out of decency and moral equity.

Hence Ulpian <note>a famous Roman jurist</note> says that if the new owner of that estate shows that the water is "owed" in that manner, even if it had flowed there until then only in the name of the previous owner (because it had been granted to the person rather than the land), he will easily obtain it. This is because granting it is not so much a "benefit" as it would be an "injury" or a denial of what is due if the Prince refused it to someone asking for it rightfully. Since the Prince had previously granted it to the predecessor out of the same equity, he is bound to maintain equity and equality among his subjects in the republic when distributing common resources.

However, from this, I do not see by what logic Bartolus and the common opinion correctly infer their conclusion. They argue that just as a Prince—who by his office granted a favor and privilege regarding water to a previous owner—is bound by equity to grant it to a successor who asks for it (because otherwise he would be acting with inequality), so too a private owner who entered into an emphyteutic contract for a set time of his own free will is bound to renew it with the successor of the last tenant.

Truly, I do not see where this "injury" lies. Why should this follow any more than saying a lessor, a lender, or a depositor is bound to renew their contracts with the heirs of the other party once the time has expired? No one in their right mind would say that this follows, or that any injury is done to these people if the contracts are not renewed when they ask.

10 Furthermore, it should be observed that in the cited paragraph "permittitur," the text is not speaking of an "injury" in the proper sense—as if a strict injustice occurs in the denial of that water and the Prince could be legally compelled to grant it to the successor. Rather, it speaks of "injury" in an improper sense, as something opposed to "honesty" and "moral decency," which a Prince ought to observe toward his subjects in the execution of his office. In such an "injury," no strict injustice is seen; nor can the one who does it be compelled to stop and do the opposite, as we said in Disputation 262 following Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note>. This is clearly what the final gloss on the text feels: while discussing this "injury," it adds that a judge using such a denial cannot be compelled to stop or do the opposite.

We can further confirm that in that section, there is no talk of a "personal injury" in the proper sense that would create an injustice. For it is said there that the privilege and right which the predecessor had from that grant...

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts #

[The argument] held that it was personal and expired with that person: therefore, he transmitted no right to a successor, such that by acting against that right, an "injury" in the proper sense or an "injustice" is committed against him by denying him that water. Furthermore, as it is stated in that same place, the successor will easily obtain the right to draw water if he requests it; therefore, he lacks the right to draw it before it is granted to him.

And the commentary <note>original: "glossa," referring to the standard medieval legal annotations on Roman law</note> on the word *water* (*aquae*) clearly affirms this: therefore, by denying the drawing of water, one does not violate the right of justice for such a new possessor of that estate to draw from that stream, but only a right based on **equity** <term>equity — moral fairness and natural justice rather than the strict letter of the law</term>, namely that the power to draw it should be granted to him by the sovereign. Likewise, since that text says a new possessor must prove that the water is "owed" to his estate in the manner we have explained so that he may undoubtedly obtain the right to draw it: therefore, even once that is proven, he still lacks the right until the privilege is granted to him.

And truly, unless that text is interpreted as referring to "injury" in an improper sense—which is opposed only to moral equity—Ulpian <note>one of the most famous Roman jurists of the 2nd-3rd century AD</note> himself would be in conflict with his own words in that text. Therefore, even if we were to grant Bartolus and other authors of the "common opinion" that it follows correctly from that text that an owner is bound to renew an **emphyteutic contract** <term>emphyteusis — a long-term land grant where the tenant improves the land and pays a small rent</term> for the successors of the last tenant in the same way the sovereign is bound to grant a new successor the water for irrigating that estate which he had granted to the predecessor (the contrary of which we have shown more clearly than light), they still wrongly conclude from that text that an owner can be compelled to do so. For even the sovereign cannot be compelled to grant water, since he is not bound to grant it out of justice, but only out of moral equity. Furthermore, the commentary on the word *obtainable* (*impetrabile*), in those words we have cited from it, neither disagrees with our opinion nor agrees with Bartolus and the common opinion.

For that discussion does not concern a petition for **investiture** <term>investiture — the formal legal ceremony or act of recognizing a tenant's right to land</term> after a contract for a **fief** <term>feudum — a land grant held on condition of loyalty and service</term> has ended—as if the owner should easily grant it because it is requested by the successor of the last vassal whose contract has expired, and would commit an injury if he denied it. Rather, it concerns the petition for investiture by a male heir already included in the contract, upon the death of the vassal who held the fief.

As shown in Disputation 472, in a fief, any new successor—even if included in the contract—is bound to request investiture from the owner within a year and a month from the death of the vassal he succeeds in that fief, and to swear an oath of loyalty to him; otherwise, he loses the fief. Therefore, the commentary there is speaking of that kind of petition for investiture, and it says it is among those things that are "easily obtained" because it must be granted by the owner to a vassal to whom the fief is owed by virtue of the contract, and the vassal in turn must swear loyalty to the owner.

<margin>31</margin> Regarding the law *congruit*, it must be said that it only grants a privilege to those who possess leased public lands, so that they are preferred over any other lessees who might offer new price increases for those same estates, provided they pay those same increases themselves. But this does not speak of emphyteutic tenants, nor of lessees of other private properties. For by the law *necui* <note>C. de locato, law 18, title 8, part 5; and book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 57</note>, at the 

<column-break/>

beginning, those who have leased houses or other private property are denied the privilege of retaining them against the will of their owners, even if they offer as much payment as others to whom the owners wish to lease them.

Truly, the law *praedia* has nothing in it from which even an apparent argument for Bartolus's opinion could be drawn. Say the same of the law *nullus* regarding decurions; for there are many in that title which begin that way, and none of them serve Bartolus’s purpose. Furthermore, the feudal laws he cites do not speak of a fief after the contract has ended and the fief has returned to the owner, as will be clear to anyone looking at them.

Indeed, those two commentaries that Bartolus and others cite say nothing about emphyteusis. Nor does it follow from the teaching they then provide regarding the **pallium** <term>pallium — a circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and communion with the Pope</term> for an archbishop that an injury is done to the successors of the last emphyteutic tenant if renewal is denied to them. That teaching regarding the pallium is correctly supported by the section *permittitur* for this reason: since the pallium is customarily delivered to individual archbishops by the Supreme Pontiff as the dispenser and distributor of privileges and ecclesiastical honors, surely by that very custom and the arrangement of the Supreme Pontiff, it is owed out of decency and moral honesty to individual archbishops by reason of their archiepiscopal dignity. This is no less than how water from a public stream is "owed" by the sovereign to the owners of those lands which can be conveniently and properly irrigated from that public stream without harm to the common good. Therefore, if that pallium is denied to any archbishop without some special cause, when it had been granted to all his predecessors in that dignity by reason of the same dignity, an "injury" is done to him against honesty, decency, and moral duty—very similar to the injury done to one to whom water from a public stream is denied, which had deservedly been granted to all his predecessors as possessors of the same field.

From what has been said, you will understand that when nothing intervenes by which something is somehow "owed" out of decency and moral honesty, not only in **onerous contracts** <term>onerous contract — an agreement where both parties provide something of value, like rent for land</term> does an obligation to renew the same contract with a successor not arise from the celebration of a contract with one person (as the light of reason itself clearly teaches); but neither does it follow in matters of "grace" <note>favors or privileges granted freely</note> that because a privilege is granted out of pure grace to someone established in some dignity for them to use and enjoy, there is an obligation to grant it to successors in that same dignity if they request it.

For example: the Supreme Pontiff granted the pallium to the Bishop of Coimbra, Lord João Soares <note>original: "Ioanni Soarez," Bishop of Coimbra (1545-1572)</note>, upon his return from the Council of Trent and from a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. He was succeeded by the fourth successor, the most illustrious doctor Lord Alfonso de Castro <note>original: "Alfonsus ab albo Castro," Alfonso y de Castro (1495–1558), a famous theologian and legal theorist</note>, now the most deserving Bishop of that same city and Count of the town of Arganil, who was once a most sharp debater with us while we were engaged in studies together. From this, it does not follow that it is "owed" to the successors in that Bishopric; for that was a purely personal grace, without any...

...due by reason of the Episcopal dignity.

<margin>A Doubt</margin> You may ask whether, after such great light has been shed and it has been clearly shown that the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential jurist of the Middle Ages; his opinions often held the weight of law.</note>—which is the common opinion—is entirely false and contrary to justice, 12 should it nonetheless be followed in judgments in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>? This is considering the Ordinance of that Kingdom (Book 2, Title 5, Paragraph 1), which prescribes that when there is no specific law of the Kingdom, nor custom, nor Roman law, nor a generally accepted gloss of Accursius <note>a famous 13th-century legal commentator</note>, one must stand by the opinion of Bartolus in judging, provided it does not contradict the common opinion of those who wrote after him.

<margin>Decision</margin> I respond that the intent of that Ordinance was not to turn the opinions of Bartolus into laws that bind the subjects in such an event. Rather, it was only to instruct judges that when the falsity of those opinions was not clear to them in a particular case, they should judge according to them. This is evident from the reasoning of the precept itself, which the Ordinance adds: "because," it says, "the opinions of Bartolus are regularly more in harmony with reason than those of others."

However, when it is established by effective reasoning that the opinion of Bartolus is false, surely it was not the intent of that Ordinance to command that one must stand by such an opinion in judging. This is clear from the very reasoning of the precept, which fails in that instance. Furthermore, if it did command such a thing, it would not be a just precept, but an openly iniquitous one, which would therefore not render the consciences of the judges safe and which, for no reason, should be followed. In that event, the words of Peter in Acts 4 would apply: <note>original: "obediendum potius est Deo, quã hominibus"</note> "We must obey God rather than men." And according to this interpretation of ours, I have found that while I was in Portugal, that Ordinance was observed in practice.

<margin>Question 13</margin> Whether, however, on another ground, the owner is sometimes bound to renew an **emphyteusis** <term>emphyteusis — a long-term lease of land where the tenant improves the property in exchange for a low rent</term>, namely because the last tenant, or his predecessors, made improvements on that leased property. Many authors answer in the affirmative. They are guided by the last law in the Code on alluvion, and other laws in the Code regarding deserted fields and the private property of the Emperor.

<margin>Decision</margin> I, for my part, although I judge it pious and equitable that those who by their industry and expense have brought leased lands to cultivation or made them far better should be affected by such a reward—especially when it is a Church lease—nevertheless, I think that owners are not bound to do so, nor can they be lawfully compelled.

I am moved by this: because all those civil laws that are cited, besides the fact that they speak only of public lands or the Emperor's treasury, do not speak of lands given in lease for certain lives or for a finite time. Rather, they speak of lands given in perpetuity. It is commanded because they were made fertile and fruitful by the expense and industry of the possessors or their ancestors, so that the land should remain with them and pass to their successors forever, rather than being given to others.

The chapter "To the Ears" <note>original: "ad aures," a specific decree in Canon Law</note> only permits the lease to be renewed at that time, even in perpetuity, but with a limitation: provided that they cannot then be given to others for the far greater benefit of the Church.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, because the value of the improvements belongs to the last tenant and must be paid to him when the contract ends (as was seen in Disputation 463), unless it was specifically agreed in the lease contract that the improvements would belong to the owner and the rent was lowered for that reason. Therefore, no injury is done to the tenant or his successors, and no inequality is seen in the fact that—notwithstanding the improvements made to the property—the contract is not renewed for the successors of the last tenant once the term is finished and all conditions agreed upon between the owner and the first tenant have been fulfilled. This is especially true since there is no law that decrees otherwise.

## DISPUTATION 485.

### SUMMARY

<margin>1. In which places fiefs are more frequent.</margin>

Having finished the disputations on the long-term lease, I should have spoken in this place about the **fief** <term>fief / feud — land held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for military service</term>. However, although the use of fiefs is frequent in Germany, France, and Italy, there is no use, or almost no use, for them in Spain. Therefore, content with what I have mixed in regarding fiefs during the discussion of leases, and what was said in Disputation 10 and elsewhere, and what will be added in the progress of this material on justice (especially when the discussion turns to entailed estates), and following the custom of Spanish doctors in this regard, I shall make the transition to the contract of leasing and hiring, according to the order of teaching prescribed at the beginning of Disputation 444.

I might mention this in passing: among the Japanese, nothing seems to be more frequent than fiefs. For since princes contend among themselves in perpetual wars on that huge island, by an ancient custom among them, whatever each one obtains in war, he immediately divides among his leaders and others whom he loves, with the burden of serving him in war and performing other duties. He changes lords from one place to another, taking from them what they possessed and granting them other things.

Moreover, the greater lords <note>original: "dinastę"</note> stationed under some supreme prince have their governed territories divided among others inferior to them, with the same burdens of serving them in war and performing other physical duties. These in turn divide them among others, until it reaches the lowest **tonos** <note>original: "tonos," a phonetic rendering of the Japanese word "tono" (殿), meaning a lord or landholder</note>, as they call them, each of whom similarly rules in his own town under a nearly similar law, so that vassals accompany him to war and perform other such services.

## What are Letting and Hiring?

### DISPUTATION 486.

->SUMMARY<-

1. What letting is, and what hiring is.
2. In how many ways "letting" is understood, and in what ways it differs from emphyteusis <note>A long-term land lease</note> and other contracts, both named and unnamed.
3. Whether it is strictly called a lease if a price is not given, but something else instead.
4. What the price may consist of in both a strict and a broad lease.
5. The various names by which a renter, a tenant farmer, and a tenant are called in Spain and Portugal.

<margin>1</margin>
We can define letting <note>original: "locatio"</note> in this way: It is a contract by which an immovable thing (for less than ten years) or a movable thing (for any length of time) is granted for use, or even for its fruits, in exchange for a price.
We can define hiring <note>original: "conductio"</note> thus: It is a contract by which an immovable thing (for less than ten years) or a movable thing (for any length of time) is taken for use, or even for its fruits, in exchange for a price. Just as one and the same contract is called "selling" from the perspective of the one granting the goods for a price, and "buying" from the perspective of the one receiving them; so too, one and the same contract is called "letting" from the perspective of the one granting the thing for use or fruits for a price, and "hiring" from the perspective of the one receiving it in that manner for a price. It was stated in the definition: "by which an immovable thing is granted for less than ten years." This is because, as was shown in Disputation 4, if an immovable thing is granted in this way for ten years or more, the <term>useful ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium utile"; the right to the use and profits of a property, distinct from the ultimate legal title</note> is transferred to the receiver by legal disposition. Consequently, it becomes a true emphyteutic contract, which is a distinct species from a lease strictly and properly understood, which is the only subject we are discussing here.

<margin>2</margin>
I just said "from a lease strictly and properly understood" because, as explained in the cited disputation, there are various uses in law (especially among the doctors) for both the word "letting" and the word "emphyteusis." In law, letting sometimes includes even a perpetual emphyteusis. Among the Doctors, it is sometimes used only for a lease strictly and properly understood, which we are defining now; if this involves an immovable thing for less than ten years, it is called a "lease for a short time." At other times, it is used broadly to include the leasing of an immovable thing for ten years or more, which is called a "lease for a long time."
Read what was said in the cited disputation. By that part of the definition—"by which an immovable thing is granted for less than ten years"—every emphyteutic contract is excluded from the definition of a lease.

<column-break/>

An emphyteutic contract is always a grant of an immovable thing for ten years or more, as explained in the cited disputation. Furthermore, "immovable thing" in this definition is taken broadly to include even rights to income: for <term>benefices</term> <note>Church offices that provided an income</note>, <term>commenda</term> <note>a form of land grant or trust</note>, tributes, and other rights of that kind are also leased. Under the name of "movable thing," even the person doing the letting is included. For someone "lets" not only his own property or things entrusted to him to be leased, but also himself—to serve another, to teach, to provide legal advocacy, to judge, to sew, and to perform various other ministries and duties. Things are sometimes leased for use alone, such as a horse for a journey, a craftsman for building, or a house for habitation; at other times, they are leased for the sake of gathering fruits and profits, such as goats for milk and cheese, sheep for wool, vineyards for their harvest, and rights for the sake of collecting their income. Therefore, by the part of the definition "for use, or even for its fruits," we exclude from the nature of a lease: buying and selling, loans <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, deposits, pledges, mortgages, and other contracts in which things are not granted for use or fruits.

Finally, by the last part of the definition—namely, "for a price"—we exclude all contracts in which a price does not intervene. This refers especially to the <term>unnamed contract</term> <note>Latin: "contractus innominatus"; a contract that does not have a specific name in Roman law but is enforced based on performance</note> of "I give, or I do, so that you may grant something for use or fruits." For example, if I give you a certain measure of wine or oil so that you give me your vineyard for use and fruits, or if I prune your vineyard so that you let me use your field. These contracts are excluded from the definition of letting and hiring strictly understood because, in compensation for the grant of the thing, a price is not returned, but rather something else that is not a price.

And although these contracts are reduced to the contract of letting and hiring—and are to be judged according to its rules (excepting only those points where unnamed contracts differ from named ones, as stated in Disputation 253 and 411)—indeed, they can even be called "hiring" and "letting" when the terms are used broadly, and they are sometimes called such in law. Nonetheless, they are not leases and hirings in the strict sense, because it is of the essence of a strict lease that a price be involved, just as a price is essential to the nature of buying and selling.

That a price is essential to a lease—and for that reason, those other contracts are not strictly leases but unnamed contracts, meaning they do not trigger a "legal action for a lease" <note>original: "actio ex locato"</note> but rather an "action on the facts" <note>original: "actio in factum"</note> or an "action for prescribed words"—is clearly established in the *Institutes*, in the chapter "On Letting," at the beginning. It states there: "Letting and hiring is very close to buying and selling, and consists of the same rules of law. For just as buying and selling is contracted once the price is agreed upon, so too letting and hiring is understood to be contracted if a fee <note>original: "merces"</note> (fixed and in counted money, as the gloss explains and other cited laws teach) has been established: and the 'action for a lease' is available to the letter, while the 'action for hiring' is available to the hirer." Thus it is stated there. And in the paragraph...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 624 (noted as Disputation 486 there, though this header reads 586, likely a printer's error or a jump in the text's numbering system) regarding the legal definitions of letting and hiring. It specifically addresses whether a contract can be strictly called a "lease" if the payment is something other than money.</meta>

<header>Second Treatise. Disputation 586.</header>

Furthermore, these words are added: *Just as it was commonly asked whether a sale and purchase is contracted by an exchange of things, so it used to be asked regarding letting and hiring <note>original: "locatio et conductio"</note>, if perhaps someone gave you a thing to be enjoyed or used, and in turn received another thing from you to be used or enjoyed. And it was decided that this is not letting and hiring, but is a unique type of contract.* And below: *Neither an action for letting, nor for hiring, nor for a loan <note>original: "commodatum"</note> is applicable, because the loan was not free of charge; rather, one must proceed by an action based on the "prescribed words" <note>An action for "unnamed contracts" that do not fit standard categories like sale or lease</note>.* What could be said more clearly? And in Law 1, paragraph "if anyone a slave" <note>original: "si quis servum"</note>, in the Digest under "deposits" <note>original: "ff. depositi"</note>, we find it written thus: *If someone puts a slave in a mill to be guarded, and if indeed a fee intervened for the guarding, I think there is an action against the miller for hiring. If, however, I was receiving a fee for this slave whom he was receiving into the mill, I could act based on letting. But if the work of that slave was being compensated by the guarding, a kind of letting and hiring intervened; but because money is not given, an action is given based on the prescribed words.* End quote. From these words, you see first of all that the same opinion is clearly proven.

Next, by the name of "rent" <note>original: "merces"</note>, both in this text and in the Institutes under "on letting," at the beginning, only money is understood. Likewise, such an "unnamed contract" is called a "sort of" genus of letting and hiring, yet it is not strictly and properly letting and hiring, because a price does not intervene in it. And in the Law "Naturalis," paragraph "But when I give" <note>original: "at cum do"</note>, in the Digest under "on prescribed words," we have: *But when I give so that you may do, if the deed is such that it is usually leased—for example, that you paint tablets—if money is given, it will be a lease, just as in the previous case (namely, when I give money to receive a thing) it is a sale. If it is a thing <note>rather than money</note>, it will not be a lease, but there will arise either a civil action for what is in my interest, or a claim to recover what was given.* End quote. By these words, it is clearly stated that for a deed that can be leased, if money is not given, but a thing which is not money—such as wheat, wine, or something similar—it is not a lease, nor is an action for letting granted, but an action "on the facts" <note>original: "in factum"</note> or based on "prescribed words" for the interest, or for recovering what one gave. The same is gathered from the Law "Insulam," in the Digest under "on prescribed words," and the same is held clearly in Law 1, title 8, part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas</note>; and the legal glosses affirm this, as do Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors elsewhere, as everyone admits.

<margin>†</margin> Although Arias Pinellus <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in his commentary on the Code "on rescinding a sale," part 2, last chapter, from number 29, admits that this is the common opinion of the glosses, of Bartolus, and of the doctors, and although he thinks with that same common opinion of doctors that the "price" is part of the intrinsic nature of buying and selling, he nevertheless agrees with Corrasius <note>Jean de Coras, a French jurist</note> against the common opinion insofar as it affirms that a "price" <note>specifically in money</note> is also part of the intrinsic nature of a lease properly so-called. For he says that <margin>3</margin> it is a most proper lease, even if in compensation for the thing leased a price is not given, but something else; and he says it is a "named" contract <note>A contract with a specific legal name and standard protections</note> and one of "good faith," and that the action for letting applies to it. Aluarus Valascus follows the same opinion in *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 20, number 5, citing certain others in its favor, and in question 30 at the beginning.

They are led mostly by the Law "And this distinction," final paragraph <note>original: "l. & hæc distinctio. §. vlt."</note> in the Digest under "on letting," where it is held that it is a true lease if two people, who each have their own individual fields, agree that one shall have the other's field as a hiring, such that the fruits are compensated in the name of rent.

Likewise, it is said in the Law "If of oil" <note>original: "l. si olei"</note>, in the Code under "on letting," of which these are the words: *If the fruits of a year are leased for a certain weight of oil, based on a contract held in good faith, one ought not to withdraw from it for this reason alone, that another has offered a greater weight.* Here, the contract for the fruits of a field for one year in exchange for a certain quantity of oil is called a "lease." It is also called a contract of "good faith," which does not apply to an "unnamed contract" such as "I give that you may do," as is clear from the paragraph "Action," in the Institutes under "on actions," and as was said in Disputation 259. Likewise, it is defined as a wrong to withdraw from it before fulfillment by the other side; which would be false according to common law if it were an unnamed contract of "I give that you may do," as was seen in Disputation 255. He also brings forward other laws, which are of less importance.

However, one must not depart from the common opinion confirmed by such clear laws; which certainly Arias Pinellus does not sufficiently answer, as will be clear to one reading him, and as Lassarte extensively proves in *On Deciding Sales*, chapter 1, from number 24.

Therefore, regarding the Law "And this distinction," final paragraph, one must say with the gloss in that place, and with Lassarte as cited above at number 30: those parties agreed in such a way that those fields were leased for a certain rent in money, and therefore it was a true and proper lease, but nevertheless the fruits which each one received from the other's field were compensated against the rent he was to receive from his own field, whether those fruits were many or few: for in this way it happens that the fruits are compensated in the name of rent (which, as the gloss explains there, had been previously agreed upon).

But regarding the Law "If of oil," setting aside other responses, one must say with Lassarte in the same place, number 31, that similarly a convention for a certain rent in money preceded it, so that it was a true lease and a contract of good faith, and one could not withdraw from it, and that money was exchanged for that certain weight of oil. This solution is confirmed in the following number 32 by an excellent text on the matter proposed, Law "If a debtor," paragraph "it is likely" <note>original: "l. si debitor. §. verisimile"</note>, in the Digest under "on contracting a sale," where similarly hanging olive fruits are said to be sold for ten pounds of oil: which were certainly established by a formal promise in place of a price previously established; for even in the opinion of Corrasius and Pinellus, a sale is not without a price.

<margin>4</margin> This must be observed: that the price † in a proper lease, or the rent in another thing in an improper lease, or an "unnamed contract" of giving or doing so that you might grant something for use or even for fruits, can be something "certain" as to the range of quantity—for instance, ten or twenty gold coins, or ten or twenty measures of wheat or oil. Or it can be something "certain" as to a proportional part of the profit reported from some business or from the fruits of some field which is handed over to someone to be cultivated; and "uncertain" as to the range of such a proportional part, provided it is established as a reward for labor and industry, and not as something responding to the labor and industry with regard to the remaining capital, as if a partnership <note>original: "societas"</note> of capital and industry were entered into for the comparison of profit hoped for from such a partnership. For then it is not a contract of letting and hiring, but is a contract of partnership, as explained in both parts of Disputation 411.

And this second interpretation is presumed to have been the intent rather than the first, when to the one applying labor and industry, a proportional part of the fruits was established...

### How similar letting and hiring is to buying and selling.

### DISPUTATION CCCCLXXXVII.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin>
1. In what ways letting and hiring agree with buying and selling.

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
Letting and hiring is very closely related to buying and selling, as is held in the Institutes under "letting" <note>original: "Instu. de loca."</note> at the beginning, and in Law 2 at the beginning of the Digest under "letting" <note>original: "ff. locati"</note>. First, they agree because both are part of the law of nations <note>original: "ius gentium"; laws considered common to all humanity</note>, as held in Law 1 of the Digest under "letting" and the law "from this law" in the Digest under "justice and law." Second, they are perfected by consent, as was said in Disputation 254, and explained regarding buying and selling in Disputations 336 and 337; regarding letting and hiring, this is held in Law 1 of the Digest under "letting" and the Institutes under "obligations which arise from consent," in the single paragraph.

Therefore, what was said extensively in Disputations 336 and 337 regarding when buying and selling is considered perfected should similarly be understood regarding letting. Third, because each is a "named contract" <note>A contract with a specific legal name and established rules</note>, as explained in Disputation 253. Fourth, because each is a "good faith" contract <note>original: "bonae fidei"</note>, as we showed in Disputation 259. Fifth, because in both it is necessary that a certain price be established; otherwise, the contract is neither considered perfected nor is it valid, as was said regarding buying and selling in Disputation 337, and regarding letting and hiring in the Institutes and Law 2 of the Digest. Therefore, what was said extensively on this matter regarding buying and selling in Disputation 337 should be understood similarly for letting and hiring.

Sixth, they agree in what was said in Disputation 338 regarding "earnest money" <note>original: "arrha"; a down payment or deposit to seal a deal</note> in buying and selling; for it is to be understood similarly in letting and hiring, as we added there, and as practice observes in Castile and Portugal. However, when a contract should be judged as buying and selling, or letting and hiring—in those cases where the matter could be doubtful—was explained at the end of Disputation 336.

Seventh, they agree because just as Law 2 of the Code regarding the rescinding of a sale <note>original: "C. de rescind. vendit."</note> has a place in buying and selling when the buyer or seller is injured below or above half of the just price <note>This refers to "lesion beyond half," a legal principle where a contract can be voided if the price is less than 50% or more than 150% of the fair market value</note>, so it has a place in letting and hiring when a similar injury beyond or below half of the just price occurs, as was shown in both cases in Disputation 349. Nor does it matter if the contract is already completed, or if the option to lease does not remain for the one who leased beyond half the just price, so that he might receive the fruits or use of his thing and return the full price, or return the increase of the price beyond what is just; nor likewise does the option remain for the hirer who hired below half the just price, so that he might either return the fruits or use of another's thing and receive the price, or increase the price up to the limits of what is just. It does not, I say, matter. Both because even in buying and selling, in many events in which there is no place for the dissolution of the contract (because the goods perished or are with another), that law still holds place, as was said in the cited disputation. And also because what is said about buying and selling according to that law must be accommodated to letting and hiring, considering the nature of the thing itself, in which the use or even the fruits of the thing being hired do not usually remain. Thus Arius Pinellus (Law 2, Code on Rescinding Sale, Part 1, Chapter 2, Number 20) and Gama (Decision 19), who report that it has often been judged according to this opinion in Portugal. However, some advocates have contended that it has also sometimes been judged to the contrary, on account of that reasoning which we just excluded; among their number is Alua. Vala.

# Who Can Lease and Hire.
## DISPUTATION CCCCLXXXVIII.
### SUMMARY.

<margin>a</margin> 1 *All those who can likewise sell and buy can lease and hire.*
<margin>2</margin> 2 *Which persons are prohibited from hiring, also according to Castilian and Portuguese law.*

<margin>1</margin> Those who can buy and sell can likewise lease and hire, as is most well-known in itself and from Law 2, Title 8, Partida 5 <note>A reference to the "Siete Partidas," the 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>. No more is required for leasing and hiring than for buying and selling. Regarding those who generally can or cannot celebrate contracts, this was explained in Disputation 261. Furthermore, regarding what kind of hiring by an Ecclesiastic is <margin>a</margin> prohibited as a form of business, it was discussed in Disputation 342. For nobles and ministers of the Court, hiring is prohibited: this is to be understood as that which pertains to business <note>original: "negotiationem"</note>. Law "Curialis," Code on Letting, and Law 2, Title 8, Partida 5 agree with the final law of the Code on the Rescission of Sale; these things were said regarding nobles in Disputation 342 according to Portuguese law. The same is decreed regarding soldiers in the final law of the Code on Letting. Which Law 2, cited above, Gregorio Lopez and others whom he cites understand as referring to soldiers who are not at leisure, but in actual military service. These things are not to be accepted otherwise than when they have been received by custom. Furthermore, he who, being ignorant that someone is a soldier, leases to him, is excused from the penalty established for soldiers in the cited laws; and Gregorio Lopez says the same in the cited Law 2 regarding a lessor who is ignorant that the person is a noble. So it is here in the law "if you are ignorant," in the Digest on Letting.

What was said regarding tutors and curators in Disputation 224 regarding the prohibition against tutors and curators buying the goods of those minors committed to their care, should be similarly understood regarding the hiring of those same goods: because the reasoning is the same.

In the Kingdom of Castile, the following prohibitions exist regarding hiring and leasing. *Law 3, Title 5, Book 7 of the New Collection <note>original: "nouæ collec." or Nueva Recopilación, a 1584 compilation of Spanish laws</note> holds thus: We command that no judge <note>original: "alcalde"</note>, nor justice, nor councilor <note>original: "regidor"</note>, nor juror, nor judicial officer <note>original: "merino"</note>, nor constable <note>original: "alguazzil"</note>, nor steward <note>original: "maiordomo"</note>, nor scribe of the council, nor of the number <note>a notary with a fixed public office</note>, nor other officials who have to oversee the council’s property, shall be lessees or collectors, in large or small amounts (what "large or small" means is explained in Law 1, Title 11, Book 9 of the New Collection), nor shall they be guarantors, nor endorsers, nor insurers of the rents of municipal properties <note>original: "proprios"</note> and councils, nor of the royal rents of the cities, towns, and places where they hold said offices, nor of their butcheries; nor through themselves, nor through intermediaries, shall they have a part in them: under penalty of losing their offices and also a fourth part of their assets, etc. And we command that the said officials, when they are received into the said offices, shall swear that they will observe the abovementioned, and that they shall not be received into possession of the said offices until they make the said oath, etc.* One also reads *the following Law 4. ## What can be leased, and whether even a leased thing can be re-leased. And whether the contract of leasing and hiring passes to the heirs of the lessor and the lessee.

# DISPUTATION 489

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> One can lease all things that can be sold, and even oneself, a servant, and a leased thing. *Understanding, however, for the same use for which it was leased. Number 2.*
<margin>3</margin> A second lessee <note>the sub-tenant</note> is not held by a personal action to the owner, but only to the one who sub-leased the thing to him.
<margin>4</margin> A leased thing is considered intended for that use for which it was designed or customarily leased.
<margin>5</margin> Real servitudes <note>term: "servitutes reales" — legal rights over land, such as a right of way</note> cannot be leased: it is otherwise for personal ones.
<margin>6</margin> The contract of leasing and hiring passes to the heirs of both the lessor and the lessee. *This fails, however, as noted from number 7 to the end.*

Not only can those things be leased which can be sold, but also many other things, as is easily clear from the definition of leasing provided in Disputation 486. <margin>1</margin> And a person can lease himself, and his servant, to perform that which the servant was bound to do for him: and universally, one can lease a thing already leased to him. In the law *Nemo* <note>original Latin: "No one is prohibited from leasing a thing he has hired to others for their enjoyment, unless otherwise agreed."</note> in the Code on leasing, and in the Digest on the same title: *If I have leased to someone the doing of something which I myself had hired, it is established that I have a legal action based on the lease.* <margin>2</margin> This is to be understood, however, provided that he leases it for the same use, and to a suitable lessee, as the commentaries on the cited laws note. This is argued from the text in the law *Equissimum* and in the law *Sed et si quid* regarding the use of slaves in the Digest on usufruct, and in the law *Non aliter* on use and habitation. Antonio Gómez affirms this along with Baldus... with whom Alvarez Valasco and others agree... <margin>3</margin> He correctly adds that the second lessee is not bound to the owner of the house for the payment of rent by a personal action <note>term: "actione personali" — a lawsuit against a specific person based on a contract</note>, but is bound by personal action to the first lessee who leased it to him; nevertheless, he is bound to the owner of the house regarding the goods which he has permanently brought into that house and which are found there, by a hypothecary action <note>term: "actione hypothecaria" — an action to seize property used as collateral, like a landlord's lien</note>, insofar as the owner holds a tacit mortgage: both on goods permanently brought onto his rural estate with his knowledge, and on goods brought into his...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion of the legal rights and obligations in leasing contracts (locatio et conductio). Having previously discussed who is prohibited from leasing, he now moves into the specifics of sub-leasing, the rights of landlords over a tenant’s property, and how leases are handled when a party dies.</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts ###

Similarly, if goods are brought into an urban property <note>In Roman and Canon law, "urban property" (praedium urbanum) refers to buildings or houses, regardless of whether they are in a city or the countryside.</note>, whether with the landlord's knowledge or without it—as held in the law *certi iuris* in the Code regarding leases, and others we shall cite below in Disputation 497—it is so that the rent may be paid from them. Therefore, the owner of the house can compel payment of the rent from those goods if the first tenant fails to pay, even if the second tenant <note>The sub-tenant</note> has already paid his rent to the first tenant. By reason of this real obligation, or "tacit mortgage," which the goods of the second tenant carry, the second tenant is permitted to pay the rent directly to the house owner if the first tenant has not yet paid. The first tenant is bound to accept this as valid, as is clear from the cited law and the commentary upon it.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
In accordance with this, the Portuguese Ordinances <note>Book 4, Title 57, last paragraph</note> first forbid a house owner from personally seizing a pledge <note>A "pledge" or distraint (pignus) involves seizing property to guarantee payment of a debt.</note> from a tenant for unpaid rent or executing a seizure of goods. Instead, they grant that he may remove such a pledge or perform such execution through a public official called an *alcayde* <note>original: "alcayde" — a local administrative or judicial officer in Portugal and Spain</note>, without needing further judicial authority. They immediately add that if the house owner does not find the person to whom he leased the house, but finds another in it, he may demand the rent from whoever he finds there, or from the person whose goods he finds. If that person refuses to pay, the owner may, in the manner described, seize a pledge from him or execute against his goods.

However, if it is later discovered that the rent had already been paid, or that he seized a pledge from either the first or second tenant for something not owed to him, he is compelled to pay triple the amount he claimed was due. Furthermore, the tenant may keep the house and live in it without paying any rent until that triple amount is compensated, based on the rent established in the original contract. Álvaro Valasco <note>original: "Alu. Vela." — a prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> maintains that this execution is granted in Portugal specifically for unpaid rent and should not be extended to other matters, as it deviates from common law.

**4** When a thing is designated for a certain use, or is customarily leased for that use, if nothing else is expressly stated or brought into the agreement, it is deemed to be leased for that use alone. This is the opinion of Bartolus and Gregorio López <note>regarding Law 3, Title 8, Part 5</note>. In the same way, if a thing is customarily leased at a certain price, that price is deemed established when no other price is brought into the agreement, as gathered from the law *exceptio* at the end of the Code regarding leases. This is confirmed by the glosses and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows.

**5** Easements <note>original: "Seruitutes" — legal rights to use another's land for a specific purpose, such as a right-of-way.</note> cannot be leased. Where the gloss rightly says this must be understood as "real easements" <note>rights attached to the land itself</note>, which neither the owner of the burdened land nor the owner or tenant of the benefiting land can lease. However, the matter is different for personal easements. For although someone who only has the "use" of something cannot lease it (as shown in Disputation 5), someone who has the right of "habitation" in a house can lease it, as proved at the end of that same disputation. Also, one who holds a "usufruct" <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the fruits or profits of another's property without destroying it.</note> can lease it, as stated in the Digest and the Institutes.

<column-break/>

If, however, the usufructuary <note>The person holding the usufruct rights</note> dies, then just as the usufruct expires and is consolidated back with the ownership of the property, so too the contract of lease and hire ends. For when the right of the giver is dissolved, the right of the receiver is dissolved and ceases <note>original: "resoluto quippe iure dantis, resoluitur, ac cessat ius accipientis"</note>. But if the tenant had paid any rent to the usufructuary beyond the proportional time elapsed up to the usufructuary’s death, the heirs of the usufructuary are bound to restore it to the tenant. If he had paid less or nothing, he is bound to pay only the portion due to the heirs. The property owner is not liable for anything. 

With much greater reason, a holder of a long-term lease <note>original: "emphyteuta"</note> or a feudal tenant can lease out the emphyteutic or feudal property. However, once the long-term lease or feud ends and is consolidated with the ownership, the lease contract similarly expires, and the owner is not liable for anything. In short, the same things must be said here as were said regarding the death of a usufructuary, for the reasoning is the same. Whether ecclesiastical property can be leased for more than three years was discussed in Disputation 466. These are the points regarding the first and second items proposed.

**6** Regarding the third point: the contract of lease and hire passes to the heirs of both the landlord and the tenant, as long as the time for which the thing was leased has not expired. This is held in the Institutes and the Code. The common opinion of the doctors agrees, which Antonio Gómez, Álvaro Valasco, and Covarrubias refer to and follow. An exception is made unless the contract was made "at the good pleasure" of the landlord or the tenant, or "while this shall be his will." 

**7** For since "good pleasure" and "will" cease at death, the contract expires with the death of the person to whose pleasure or will it was entrusted. It is different if a thing is leased as a *precarium* <note>A "precarious" loan or lease is one granted by request and held only as long as the grantor allows.</note> in another way; for any other precarious grant passes to the heirs of the person who granted it until it is revoked, but it does not pass to the heirs of the person to whom it was granted. We have spoken copiously on this in Disputation 298. 

A further exception is when someone has leased their services for something that cannot be fulfilled by another. In that case, upon that person's death, the contract does not pass to their heirs. When the contract can be fulfilled by another, even if it is a manual craft, the contract passes to the heirs of the one who leased his services and industry for it, as is expressly held in the law *veteris*, which explains and corrects the laws that Gregorio López seemed to interpret to the contrary.

<summary>This page discusses the legal complexities of sub-leasing, particularly the landlord's right to seize a sub-tenant's goods for unpaid rent, and the conditions under which lease contracts expire or pass to heirs, such as in the case of usufructs or personal service contracts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of leasing contracts (locatio et conductio). Tract. Second. Disp. 490. 631

# Whether a lease contract transfers to a buyer, or another particular successor who holds a title from the lessor, such that the new successor is bound to stand by the lease made by the lessor.

## DISPUTATION 490.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *A buyer is not bound to honor a lease made by the seller, but may evict the tenant.*
2 *The same applies if the property is alienated by any other title, even a legal one, and passes to a particular successor. no. 2.*
3 *The same applies even if the leased property is alienated only regarding its beneficial ownership. no. 5.*
*The same applies conversely: the tenant is not bound to stay for the buyer. no. 3.*
4 *This rule fails unless the lessor assigns the right and the legal action they have against the tenant to the particular successor in order to continue the contract. no. 4.*
6 *The principal rule fails if the property was leased for ten years or more, since the tenant is then effectively an emphyteuta <note>An "emphyteuta" is a tenant under a long-term or perpetual lease who possesses a "real right" in the land, similar to ownership, rather than just a personal contract.</note>. no. 6.*
*The rule also fails regarding short-term leases in many cases or events, from no. 7 to the end.*
8 *Whether a particular successor in a property subject to a mortgage is bound to honor the lease.*

<margin>1</margin> **I**t must be said that a buyer is not bound to honor a lease <note>original: "stare † locationi"</note> made by the seller, but may evict the tenant. However, the tenant possesses a personal action for damages <note>original: "actionem personalem ad interesse"</note> against the lessor, or their heirs if they are deceased, so that they may pay what it was worth to the tenant for the contract to be continued for the full time for which the property had been leased. This is held in the law *Emptorem* <note>original: "l. emptorem" — a famous Roman law principle: "A buyer is not bound by a lease."</note> in the Code under the title "On Leases"; the law *Si merces*, paragraph *Si qui fundum* in the Digest "On Leases"; Law 9, number 8, Partida 5; and Law 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lust. ord." — referring to the Lusitanian/Portuguese Ordinances</note>, title 29.

<margin>2</margin> The principle is the same if the property is alienated by any other title, even by a legacy, and passes to any particular successor <note>A "particular successor" is someone who acquires a specific item (like a buyer or legatee), as opposed to a "universal successor" like an heir who inherits everything.</note>. For the successor is not bound to honor the lease of the predecessor, and the tenant may similarly sue for damages against the lessor or their heirs. This is held in the law *Qui fundum* in the Digest "On Leases," and the law *Nihil*, the final paragraph in the Digest.

<margin>3</margin> By the same reasoning, the tenant is not bound to stay for the buyer, the recipient of a gift, a legatee, or any other particular successor to the lease contract, as is clearly gathered from the two laws just cited.

<margin>4</margin> An exception occurs unless the lessor assigns to the particular successor the right and the legal action they held against the tenant to continue the contract; for then the tenant can be compelled to continue it, as Bartolus and Joannes de Platea <note>Two influential medieval legal commentators.</note> affirm along with Gregorio

<margin>5</margin> Lopez <note>The primary commentator on the Siete Partidas.</note> on the cited Law 19, gloss 2. What has been said so far holds true even if the leased property is alienated only regarding its beneficial ownership <note>term: "dominium utile" — the right to use and enjoy the profits of property, as distinct from the "direct ownership" held by the legal title-holder.</note>, such as if a usufruct is granted to someone in *emphyteusis*. For the emphyteuta and the usufructuary <note>One who has the right to use and harvest the "fruits" (profits) of another's property.</note> are not bound to honor the lease contract made by their predecessor, but can evict the tenant. This is expressly held in the law *Arbores* in the Digest "On Usufruct." The reason is that a right in the thing <note>original: "ius in re"</note> is acquired not only through full ownership, but also through beneficial ownership alone; whereas the tenant, by virtue of the contract, only held a personal action, which does not pass against the successor in the leased property, but only

<column-break/>

remains against the lessor and their heirs. On what has been said so far, read Antonio Gómez, volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 9; Gregorio López on the cited Law 19; Alvarez Valasco *On the Law of Emphyteusis*, question 20, number 19 and Consultation 76, number 4; and Covarrubias

<margin>6</margin> *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 15, number 1. However, when the property is leased for ten years or more, since the tenant is then effectively an emphyteuta and acquires a right in the thing—even beneficial ownership, as shown in Disputations 445 and 469—the particular successor in that property is bound to honor this contract. This is the common teaching on the law *Ac ius* and the gloss on the law *Emptorem*, and Bartolus, whom Covarrubias (book 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 15, number 2), Antonio Gómez, and Alvarez Valasco (cited above) follow. They also affirm that the Portuguese Ordinances, book 4, title 29 in the beginning, and title 60, and elsewhere, and the Castilian Law 19 cited at the end, only asserted that a particular successor is bound to honor the contract when the property was leased by the predecessor for the entire life of the recipient or in perpetuity, making no mention of a lease for ten years or more. However, in the following events, the particular successor is bound to honor a lease contract made for a short time by

<margin>7</margin> their predecessor. The first is when it was enjoined upon them by the predecessor, by adding that burden and manner, or by including it as a pact when the property was granted to them. This is held in the law *Emptorem* in the Code "On Leases"; the law *Si merces*, paragraph *Qui fundum* in the Digest "On Leases"; and Law 4, number 8, Partida 5; and in the Portuguese Ordinances, title 29, cited at the beginning. Read also the law *Si mercedem*, the final paragraph in the Digest "On the Action of Purchase," where it says: if the seller of a house includes a pact for the buyer that they must not evict those living in the house, then they cannot evict those living there for a certain rent; however, they can evict those living there for free, unless it was expressly included in the pact that they should not evict those living there for free. Covarrubias (*Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 15, number 1), along with others he cites, considers the reason to be that the buyer, when nothing else was expressed, is presumed only to have intended to grant habitation to those who, if evicted, could sue for damages against the seller. According to this, these authors, along with the gloss there, hold that when someone was living there for free such that if they were evicted they could sue the seller for breach of warranty <note>original: "de evictione ad interesse"</note>, then they cannot be evicted by the buyer. Perhaps that text is founded on the presumption that the buyer, when nothing else was expressed, thought they were living there for a rent which would thereafter belong to him. Be that as it may, since that law is founded on a presumption, surely if it was established to the buyer that they were living there for free, he cannot evict them in the court of conscience <note>The "court of conscience" (forum conscientiae) refers to moral and religious obligation, as opposed to the "exterior court" of civil law.</note>, nor in the exterior court if a presumption to the contrary is established in that court. The second case is when the successor in the leased property, after the alienation was made to them, agrees with the tenant to persevere in the same contract, or grants that to them in some way. This is held in the cited Law *Emptorem*, Law 19, and Title 29. The third is if the tenant, when they leased the property, included a pact that the property itself should be bound under the title of a mortgage <note>original: "hypothecae"</note> for the security of the contract, and furthermore, that the lessor, while the contract lasted, could not alienate it. For then they could not be evicted by the one to whom the lessor tried to alienate it. The reason is because that alienation would then be invalid, as held in the law *Si creditor*, the final paragraph in the Digest "On the Sale of Pledges," and the final law of title 5, Partida 5. I said "included a pact that the property itself should be bound under the title of a mortgage for the security of the contract," because for this purpose, a pact added furthermore—that the lessor, during the contract, cannot alienate the leased property—hinders the transfer of ownership and renders any alienation null, if the lessor...

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts

...the successor intends to carry it out, a universal mortgage <note>A "universal mortgage" (hypotheca universalis) covers all of a person's assets, whereas a "particular mortgage" (hypotheca particularis) is tied to one specific piece of property.</note> on all goods is not enough; rather, a particular mortgage on the leased property itself is necessary. This is the common opinion of the learned doctors, affirmed by Caldas on the renewal of emphyteusis, question 13, number 16; Alvarus Valascus, consultation 76, number 7; Antonio Gomez, number 9 (already cited); and Covarruvias, *Various Resolutions*, book 2, chapter 15, number 3. This is because the cited laws, being exceptions to the norm, are only to be understood as applying to a particular mortgage. Thus, the contrary opinion of Gregory Lopez (on Law 19, Title 8, Part 5, at the words "two cases" near the end) must be rejected, where he asserts with certain others that a general mortgage of goods is sufficient in this event.

**Fourthly**, when the lessor, for the security of the lease contract, had subjected the leased property to a mortgage—whether he subjected it specifically or universally by subjecting all his goods to a mortgage as security for that contract. In that case, although the sale <note>original: "alienatio"</note> of such a leased property (which was subject to a mortgage for the security of the lease) is valid, the tenant <term>conductor<gloss>The tenant or lessee who pays for the use of the property.</gloss></term> can nonetheless resist if a particular successor <note>A "particular successor" is someone who acquires a specific property through sale, gift, or legacy, rather than an heir who inherits an entire estate.</note> attempts to evict them. The tenant may do so by retaining the property and objecting that it was obligated to them by title of mortgage as security that the contract would be upheld. This is the opinion of Bartolus and the common sentiment of the doctors, which is followed by Covarruvias (cited above), Antonio Gomez (volume 2, chapter 3, number 9), Caldas (as above, number 18), Alvarus Valascus (consultation 76, numbers 6 and 11), and Gregory Lopez (on Law 19, at the words "two cases"). This is due to the "right in the thing" <note>original: "ius in re"</note> previously acquired by virtue of the mortgage. This was also defined in the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusit. ordin."</note>, book 4, title 29, at the beginning. Thus, Alvarus Valascus (above, number 9) rightly criticizes the Portuguese Decision 243 (approved by Gama), which defined that a buyer of a leased property could evict the tenant even when the property was subject to a mortgage for the lease. Gama and those who agreed with him thought that for a mortgage to prevent eviction, it had to be a mortgage securing a promise *not to sell* the property, rather than a mortgage securing the *performance* of the lease contract. However, this is false and contrary to the common opinion of the doctors and the cited Portuguese Ordinance. Nevertheless, Decision 30 was correctly decided: when a property was leased to one person and mortgaged to them as security for the contract, but not yet delivered, and then later leased and delivered to another, the first tenant is to be preferred. This is not only because the mortgage (and thus the "right in the thing") came first for the first tenant, but also because the second tenant has no right in the thing itself, but only a personal action. Even if delivery was made to the second person, the first tenant must be preferred because they first acquired the right to that specific property to be delivered for their enjoyment through the lease.

<margin>Question 8</margin>
The doctors doubt whether, when a property was subject only to a mortgage for the security of a lease contract, it is enough for a particular successor in that property to pay the tenant the full "interest" <note>In legal terms, "interest" (interesse) refers to the monetary value of the benefit the tenant would have received if the contract had been honored—essentially, damages.</note> or estimated value of the lease being upheld, so that the successor can evict the tenant against their will; or whether they are bound to stand by the lease contract. The common opinion of the doctors, which follows Bartolus and is followed by Covarruvias, Alvarus Valascus (consultation cited, number 5),

<column-break/>

Caldas on the renewal of emphyteusis (question 12, number 23), and Gregory Lopez (at the words "two cases"), judges that it is enough to offer the tenant their "interest." This is based on the law of Paulus (in the Digest, "By what means a pledge or mortgage is dissolved"), which states that if a property was obligated to someone by title of mortgage for a debt that is not paid, the person possessing the property is not bound to hand it over to the requesting creditor, but it is enough if they pay the debt. And because the mortgage, in the case proposed, was only for the security of a personal action (which only seeks the "interest" or damages from the lessor who sold the property).

**I**, however, believe the contrary to be true, along with the few cited by Caldas (as above, number 22) and others. Namely, that it is not enough to offer and pay the interest, but that the successor is bound to honor the lease contract if the tenant so wishes. This is very clearly defined in the Portuguese Ordinances (title 29, cited at the beginning), to the point that Alvarus Valascus admits it is judged this way in Portugal and must be so stated in that Kingdom. I am moved by this: because that property was truly subject to a mortgage for the security of the lease itself, so that it might be upheld. If the lessor had not sold the property, he could not satisfy the tenant by simply offering the interest; thus, that "real right" <term>ius reale<gloss>A right tied to the physical property itself, which generally follows the property even if it changes hands.</gloss></term> remains with the tenant, regardless of the sale.

As for that cited law and other similar laws, it must be said that they apply because nothing else was owed to the person holding the mortgage than the money being paid; therefore, the property is freed from the burden of the mortgage by that payment. In our proposed case, however, the thing owed (and for which the property is obligated) is different from the "interest" being offered: namely, the continuation of the lease contract, which *can* be fulfilled. Laws do not state that when the very thing for which a property is mortgaged can be fulfilled by the owner, they may instead satisfy it by paying an equivalent value or interest. Regarding the final point, it should be said that the mortgage in this case is indeed for the security of a personal action against the lessor; but since the lessor himself could not satisfy the tenant with damages if he still owned the property, but would be bound to honor the contract, this right always perseveres in the tenant by reason of the mortgage. Thus, it follows that the successor cannot satisfy the obligation by merely offering the interest.

**Fifthly**, when the State Treasury <term>fiscus<gloss>The public treasury or the financial interests of the crown/government.</gloss></term> has sold or otherwise alienated a leased property, and the tenant could sue the Treasury for damages: in that case, the person to whom the property was alienated by the Treasury cannot evict the tenant, unless (as I understand it) they satisfy the tenant's interest, if the Treasury was only bound to that interest. This is according to the teaching of Bartolus (on the law regarding the rights of the Treasury) and is consistent with the text there. Gregory Lopez (as above, Law 19, "two cases") and Covarruvias agree. In that place, it is said that this is not an unusual extension. Therefore, this privilege of the Treasury does not apply to the Church, as Gregory Lopez contends at length against certain others.
