# Whether the Treasury succeeding to confiscated goods is bound to stand by a lease made by the condemned person, and whether a successor in an entail is bound by a lease made by his predecessor, and a beneficiary of a trust by a lease made by the burdened heir.

## DISPUTATION CCCCXCI.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *The Treasury is not bound to stand by a lease made regarding specific determined goods; it is otherwise if all goods, or a portion of them, are confiscated.*
*Exceptions apply, as in number 2.*
3 *A successor in an entail <note>original: "maioratu"</note>, or a beneficiary of a trust <note>original: "fideicommissarius"</note>, is not bound to stand by a lease made regarding the goods of the entail or the trust.*
*Clarified in number 5.*
4 *The rule that "when the right of the giver is terminated, the right of the receiver is terminated," and when it takes place.*
6 *Whether a tenant expelled by a successor of the leased goods can sue for damages <note>original: "ad interesse"</note> against the heirs of the lessor.*

<margin>1</margin> Regarding the first point, it must be said: If some specific good or determined goods are confiscated, the Treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> is not bound to stand by a lease made regarding those goods, according to what was said in the preceding disputation regarding a particular successor in a leased thing. The reason is that the Treasury is a particular successor in those goods, no differently than a buyer or a legatee. However, the condemned person is not then held to the tenant for damages, but only for the remission of the rent (or the restitution of it, if he had already received it) for the remainder of the time during which the tenant was not permitted to enjoy the property for that reason. Both points are found in the law *si fundus*, in the Digest *locati* <note>Digest 19.2.33</note>. The first point is affirmed by Antonio Gomez and others whom he cites in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 10. The second point is supported by Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 187.

Perhaps, however, that text (regarding this second point) does not speak of confiscation due to the crime of the lessor, but for the public good—such as if it were given to soldiers, as is clearly said in the law *item si verberatu*, paragraph *item si forte*, in the Digest *de rei vindicatio*. Indeed, the cited law *si fundus* openly teaches that if it was within the lessor's power to prevent the tenant from being deprived of the leased thing—at least because he could have acted so that another did not impede him—then he is held even for damages. Since the leased thing is confiscated through the fault of the lessor, and for that reason the tenant is prohibited by the Treasury from enjoying it, the lessor, by abstaining from that fault, could and should have acted so that the tenant was not prohibited. Therefore, according to that same law, the lessor is then held to the tenant for damages. But if all the delinquent's goods are confiscated, or a proportional part of them (such as a half, a third, a fourth, or another similar part), then—because the Treasury is a universal successor to the delinquent, like an heir—it is bound to stand by the contract celebrated by the delinquent, according to what was said in Disputation 489. This is gathered openly from Law 2 of the Code *de vi publica*, and is affirmed by Antonio Gomez (cited above) and others.

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin> One should except, with the same Antonio Gomez in the same place, cases where the goods are confiscated by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> due to a crime, such as when the goods of heretics are confiscated. For then, if the goods were leased after the crime was committed, the Treasury would not be bound to stand by the contract, according to what was said in Disputation 95. The reason is that before the lease, the Treasury had acquired a right in those goods, and for that reason, the lease that followed afterward was void by the law itself.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the successor in an entail <note>original: "maioratu," a legal arrangement where property is kept within a family line</note> and the beneficiary of a trust <note>original: "fideicommissarius"</note>, it must be said that neither is bound to stand by a lease made regarding the goods of the entail or trust by the preceding possessor or the burdened heir. The reason is that neither of those predecessors had the power of disposing of those goods (even through a lease) for a time after their own life, or after the arrival of the time for the restitution of the trust. For that reason, neither could lease those goods for a longer time, or prejudice the successor during the time of his succession, preventing him from having free and total administration of them—just as was said regarding a usufructuary <note>someone with a right to use property but not own it</note> in Disputation 489. This is the common opinion of the doctors, which Molina refers to and follows in Book 1 *de primog.* chapter 21, from number 1; also Antonio Gomez on Law 40 of *Toro*, number 84; and *Various Resolutions* chapter 3, number 8; Gregory Lopez on Law 2, Title 8, Part 5; and Aluarus Valascus. This is also gathered from the law *peto*, paragraph *praedium*, regarding the beneficiary of a trust, and the same reasoning applies to the successor in an entail. It is also found expressly in the law *si quis domum*, paragraph *hic subiungi*, regarding a usufructuary.

<margin>4</margin> In this matter, the rule of the law *lex vestigali* and other similar laws applies: "when the right of the giver is terminated, the right of the receiver is terminated" <note>original: "resoluto iure dantis, resoluitur ius accipientis"</note>. Just as in these events the successor in the entail or the trust is not bound to stand by the lease made by the predecessor, so too is the tenant <term>conductor<gloss>The person paying to rent or use the property.</gloss></term> not bound to continue the lease contract with them. For an onerous contract, such as this one, ought not to be "limping" <note>original: "claudicare," meaning one-sided or legally unstable</note>, but must bind both parties mutually or not bind them at all. Thus says Molina (above, number 4) with Panormitanus and others. Hence, with Dr. Antonio de Padilla, he gives the counsel that if a tenant of these goods wishes to bind the successor in an entail or trust to stand by the lease, he should have them be obligated along with the current possessor of those goods.

<margin>5</margin> When a successor was not bound to stand by the lease contract made by his predecessor, if he receives the rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note> of that lease, he is deemed to have consented that the contract entered into with his predecessor be continued—but only for the year for which he receives the rent (or part of it), when a certain rent was established for each individual year. Thus says Molina...

6. Whether <gloss>†</gloss> in these circumstances, tenants can sue for damages <note>original: "agere ad interesse"</note> regarding eviction against the heirs of the lessors on the grounds that the successors do not wish to abide by the contract. Molina disputes this at length from number 8 onwards in the place cited above. Briefly, it should be said: if the tenants knew, or had just cause to know, that those items were part of an entail <note>original: "maioratus"</note>, or were burdened with a duty of restitution, or that the lessor only held the use and fruit <note>term: "usufruct" (the right to enjoy the use and advantages of another's property without destroying it)</note> of them, or was the last perpetual tenant <note>original: "emphyteuta"</note> of them, then they cannot sue the heirs of the lessors for damages. This is because no deception occurred in that contract; rather, the lease is considered to have been celebrated only for that specific period, and it is judged to have ended just as if the leased thing had perished by a chance accident. Therefore, the heirs are only bound to return any rent paid to the lessor in excess of the proportional time he lived; and the tenants are only bound to pay the heirs if they paid less rent than was proportional to that same time. However, if the lessors deceived such tenants—either by leasing those goods as if they had more right in them than they did, or because they expressed to the tenants that they could lease them beyond their own lifespan when the tenants had no just reason to know otherwise (which is to deceive them in effect by not disclosing what they were bound to disclose)—then they can certainly sue the heirs of the lessors for damages.
All of this is expressly held in the Law "If anyone [leases] a house," in the section "Here is added," joined with the following verses in the Digest on leases <note>original: "ff locati"</note>, with this single exception: that the law does not explicitly state the final scenario in which the lessors deceive the tenants in effect by not revealing what they were then bound to reveal; nonetheless, this is implicitly contained in the teaching of that law.
And this is clearly what Molina intends in the place cited above, along with the others he quotes.

# Whether a minor is bound to stand by leases made by his tutor or curator; and a wife, upon the dissolution of marriage, by leases made by her husband; and a husband by leases of dotal goods made before the marriage; and a beneficiary or prelate by leases of Church property made by his predecessors.

## DISPUTATION 492.

### SUMMARY.

1. *A minor is bound to stand by a lease made by a tutor or curator, and conversely the tenant is bound; however, restitution to the original state is granted to the minor himself if he is notably harmed.*
2. *A wife is bound to stand by a lease made by her husband regarding her separate property <note>term: "paraphernalia" (property belonging to a married woman that is not part of her dowry)</note>, and even more so by the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal.*

<column-break/>

Regarding the lease of dotal [dowry] goods... number 2.
And what regarding the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal... number 4.
And what conversely of the husband, whether he is bound to stand by a lease made by himself regarding dotal things... number 5.
6. Whether a prelate or a beneficiary is bound to stand by leases of Church property made by their predecessors.

As far as the minor is concerned, the legal experts agree that once the tutorship or curatorship has ended, both the minor and his heirs are bound to stand by the leases made by the tutor or curator. Conversely, the tenant and his heirs are bound to stand by the contract with the aforementioned minor (even if he has now reached adulthood) and his heirs.
The reason is that when someone is a legitimate administrator of certain things in another's name—such as a tutor, curator, or proxy—then the person in whose name they administer is no less bound to stand by the contracts made by them than if he had celebrated them himself. Thus says Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 15, number 5, following the common opinion of the doctors, which they support by the argument of the law "If of tutorship" in the Digest on the administration of tutors. However, if the minor is found to be notably harmed, he would be granted "restitution to the original state" <note>term: "restitutio in integrum" (a legal remedy where a party is restored to their previous position before a contract or act, often used to protect minors from unfair deals)</note>.
<margin>2</margin> From the teaching passed down regarding the minor, Antonio Gómez concludes in the place cited above that since <gloss>†</gloss> a husband administers the separate property <note>original: "paraphernalia"</note> of the wife not in his own name, but in the name of the wife as her proxy, the wife is bound to stand by the leases made by the husband concerning those separate goods. Although this is concluded from that principle when following Common Law (because under Common Law the administration of separate property does not belong to the husband but to the wife, and thus if the husband administers them, it is by the wife's consent and in her name), nevertheless, according to the law of Castile and the custom of Portugal, when a marriage was celebrated with a contract of dower and dowry, the administration of separate property belongs to the husband as the head of the family and as the primary partner in the community of property between him and his wife regarding the acquisition of profits (as was explained at length when discussing the contract of partnership between spouses). Thus, from a far different principle, which we will explain next, the wife in these Kingdoms is bound to stand by the leases of those goods made by her husband.
<margin>3</margin> Regarding wives in relation to leases made by a husband during the marriage concerning dotal [dowry] goods, the common opinion of the doctors (as reported by Covarrubias in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 15, number 5, and Antonio Gómez, volume 2, chapter 3, number 8, conclusion 1) is as follows: First, the husband or his heirs are bound to the tenant for damages if the tenant is expelled by the wife or her heirs upon the dissolution of the marriage; nor can the tenant raise any objection against the wife or her heirs in order to persevere in the contract.
Second, the wife and her heirs are bound to keep the husband harmless in that regard, and thus are bound to one of two things: namely, either to not expel the tenant...

Second Treatise, Disputation 492.

All of this is clearly proven by the law *si filiofamilias*, paragraph *si vir in quinquennium* in the Digest regarding the dissolution of marriage, where the jurist Paulus says: <note>original: "Si vir in quinquennium locauerit fundum, & post primum forte annū diuortium interuenerit, Sabinus ait, non alias mulieri fundū reddi oportere, quam si cauerit, si quid post vnius anni locationem maritus damnatus sit, id a se prestitū iri."</note> *“If a husband leases land for five years, and perhaps after the first year a divorce occurs, Sabinus says the land should not be returned to the woman unless she gives security that if the husband is condemned for anything related to the lease after that one year, she will provide for it.”* Panormitanus the elder, and a few others, affirm that the wife is no less bound to stand by a lease made by her husband than a minor is bound to a contract made by a tutor or curator; this is because the husband administers those goods as a curator of the wife and of those goods.

To this, others rightly respond that while the marriage lasts, the husband administers those goods in his own name, as the <term>usufructuary</term> <note>One who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another.</note> of them for that whole time, and for that reason, the contract does not pass to the wife once the marriage is dissolved. But certainly, if the husband administers those goods as their owner and usufructuary at that time, I do not see why he should be held liable for damages if the tenants knew those goods were part of a <term>dowry</term> <note>Property brought by a bride to her husband on their marriage.</note>, or ought to have known it—or if, when they were ignorant of it, he explained it at the time of the contract as he was bound to do. This is the same as was said in the preceding disputation regarding the possessor of an <term>entail</term> <note>An inheritance of land restricted to a specific line of heirs (majorat).</note>, a usufructuary, or an heir burdened with a trust when they lease something. However, if he did not explain it as he was bound to do when they were entirely ignorant, I do not see why the wife should be bound to keep him harmless, while a successor to an entail, a property owner, or a <term>fiduciary</term> <note>A person to whom property is entrusted for the benefit of another (fideicommissarius).</note> would not be bound to keep their predecessor in the entail, the usufructuary, or the burdened heir harmless.

Regarding these matters, I do not see what else could be more conveniently said under <term>common law</term> than that this "middle way" in the paragraph *si vir in quinquennium* was chosen because the marriage contract—specifically the providing of a dowry for the usufruct during the whole time of the marriage to support the wife and sustain the burdens of marriage—is celebrated for the benefit of both spouses.

4 <gloss>†</gloss> Under **Portuguese law**, however, when a marriage was celebrated with a contract for half of the goods <note>A community property arrangement.</note>, and under the **law of Castile** and the custom of Portugal when it was celebrated with a contract for <term>earnest money</term> <note>A sum of money (arrhae) given to seal a marriage contract.</note> and dowry, it must be said that the wife is bound to stand by leases made by the husband, whether of dotal goods or <term>paraphernal goods</term> <note>Property belonging to a married woman that is not part of her dowry.</note>. The reason is that such leases are celebrated in a common name and for the benefit of both in terms of profit, by the husband as the head of the family and society, and the universal administrator of those goods by the law of those Kingdoms. Although that partnership of goods is dissolved when the marriage ends, the partners are nevertheless bound to fulfill those things undertaken while the partnership lasted after it has ended, as was said in Disputation 414. If, however, among the wife's goods there is found some property tied to the marriage bond that is dissolved by the wife's death, then the successor to that tied property is not bound to stand by a lease made of that thing, even if the wife consented to the lease or if she leased it with her husband’s permission, as was stated in the preceding disputation.

<column-break/>

5 <gloss>†</gloss> As for the husband, specifically whether he is bound to honor leases made of dotal property before the marriage contract: Covarruvias (at number 5 cited with others) affirms he is not bound to honor them. This is because he is a <term>particular successor</term> in those goods, just like a buyer, a donee, or a legatee; it was shown in Disputation 490 that all such persons are not bound to honor leases of this kind. This is despite the fact that the <term>Gloss</term> <note>A standard legal commentary on the text of the law.</note> on the law *diuortio* at the beginning, on the word *sequantur* (Digest: *solutio matrimonii*), says the opposite, which it not only claims should be embraced but even says is received in practice, because the husband knew at the time of the wedding that they were leased; at that time, it says, he is deemed to have consented to the past leases. However, in my judgment, the Gloss that Covarruvias cites affirms no such thing.

6 <gloss>†</gloss> Finally, regarding a **prelate** or a **benefice holder**, as to whether they are bound to honor leases of Church property made by their predecessor, it must be said: If a prelate or benefice holder leases property assigned to his own dignity or benefice for his own income and sustenance, then the successor is not bound to honor the lease made by such a predecessor in that prelacy or benefice. Furthermore, the tenant is not bound to the same contract to continue it with the successor, just as was said regarding the successor in an entail and the fiduciary in the preceding disputation. For the contract is ended by the very fact that the dignity or other Ecclesiastical benefice passes by any means to a successor. This is just like leases made by a prior possessor of an entail or an heir burdened with a trust, which end by the very fact that the entail or trust passes to another. Indeed, that lease is made by the prelate in his own name, and concerning things about which he cannot contract except for the time of his life, as was said regarding similar leases in the preceding disputation.

Understand the same if a <term>commendatory</term> <note>A person (often a layman or secular priest) holding a church living in "commendam" (trust).</note> leases a commendary or something pertaining to it; for the successor is not bound to honor that lease, nor is the tenant bound to continue the contract with the successor in such a commendary. This is the commonly received Gloss, Chapter *vlt.* (on prelates not delegating their duties), Covarruvias (2nd volume of various resolutions, chapter 15, number 6), Molina (Book 1 on primogeniture, chapter 21, number 2), and the common opinion of the doctors. If, however, the prelate or benefice holder leases property not pertaining to their own private income, but belonging to their Church or monastery as the legitimate administrators of those goods, and they lease them for a time permitted by law, having observed the solemnities required for it (according to what was said in Disputation 464 and especially 466), then the successor is bound to the contract, and the tenant is similarly bound to continue the contract with the successor. If, however, the Church is found to be notably harmed, it may seek the benefit of <term>restitution to original state</term> <note>A legal remedy (restitutio in integrum) to cancel a contract that was legally valid but caused unfair loss.</note>.

All these things are proven by the fact that such an administrator acted in that lease just like a curator in the lease of a minor's goods, or any other legitimate proxy in the lease of those goods for which he was appointed proxy. Therefore, just as those in whose name these men leased are bound to honor the lease made by them...

# If the leased thing perishes, or if by any other impediment the tenant is unable to use or enjoy it, to what extent the lessor and the tenant are bound, or not bound, to one another.

## DISPUTATION 493.

->SUMMARY.<-

<margin>§</margin> 1 *If the leased thing perishes, or if by any other impediment the tenant is unable to use or enjoy it, to what extent the lessor and the tenant are bound to each other.*
2 *The lessor's knowledge of the danger to the property is not sufficient to excuse the tenant from the duty of notification.*
3 *What suffices for a tenant to be released from the payment of rent due to the danger of the property.*
4 *Whether a tenant is bound to continue the lease once a war or other danger to the property has ceased.*
<margin>§</margin> 5 *An impediment to the leased thing arising on the part of the tenant does not release him from the payment of rent.*
6 *If the leased thing perishes or is seized through the fault of the lessor, the lessor himself is bound to the tenant for all damages, and even for the interest of lost profits.*
7 *Whether a lessor, who is bound to the tenant for the interest of lost profits, is also bound for extrinsic interest.*
8 *If the leased thing is recovered by legal claim <note>original: "euicta"</note>, to what the lessor is bound to the tenant.*
9 *One who leases his services to someone and does not work faithfully, to what he is bound to the employer.*

<margin>§</margin> When a leased thing perishes by a chance occurrence <note>original: "casu fortuito"</note>, or is seized from the tenant's control without the fault of the lessor—such that there was no fault on the part of either, nor could the lessor have prevented it—then the tenant is only bound to pay the rent <note>original: "pensionē"</note> proportional to the time in which he used the leased thing. The lessor, however, is not liable to the tenant for anything, except for the restitution of the rent if he had received more than was owed for that portion of time. By the same reasoning, if another impediment arises to the use and enjoyment of the leased thing on the part of the property itself due to supervening circumstances, or circumstances that were unknown—as when a leased house threatens to collapse, or because, due to a sudden plague or enemies, habitation in it is not safe, and for these reasons it is deserted out of a just fear, or due to the fear of evil spirits and apparitions <note>original: "spirituum malignorum, ac phantasmatum"</note> that appear there, or for other similar

<column-break/>

causes it is rightfully deserted—the tenant is only bound to pay the rent proportional to the time before he rightfully deserted it out of just fear. In the same way, if someone hires a servant, and because that servant falls ill, he cannot make use of his services, he is not bound to pay the wages to him for the portion of time in which he could not use him.

All these things are gathered and established, first from the law *item quaeritur*, paragraph *exercitu* in the Digest *On Leases*. <note>original: "ff. locati"</note> Where it is held that if, when an army arrives, a tenant moves out and deserts the farm he had leased, and the soldiers, while staying there, took away the windows and other things, the tenant is not held liable under the lease (understand: except regarding the rent for the proportional time), provided however that he notified the lessor and restored the property, if he was able to notify him (as is added there), and could have resisted and avoided the damages without danger to himself. For if he could have notified him, and could have resisted and avoided the damages without danger to himself, and did not do so, then he will be liable under the lease, both for the full rent and also for the subsequent damages, as is clear from that text.

I believe, however, that if the tenant's failure to notify the lessor of his departure due to enemies or other danger caused no damage to the lessor—neither regarding the rent nor other matters—then the tenant is bound to him for nothing in the forum of conscience; nor in the external forum, if that were clearly established even there. Alvaro Valasco agrees in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 27, at the end of number 13, with others whom he cites. <margin>†</margin> Where he adds that when the notification would have been beneficial, the lessor’s knowledge is not sufficient to excuse the tenant from the duty of notification.

In the same number, he rightly affirms that the aforementioned holds true whether the war is just or unjust, provided the tenant did not provide the cause for it, as he adds in number 17 with others whom he cites. If, however, someone were to lease something while a war or other danger was already present, then he would not be excused from paying rent if he deserted the leased thing because of such a war or danger, unless the danger increased and grew far beyond what was expected. Thus Alva. Valasco rightly adds and affirms in the same place, number 18, along with others he cites, as does the Gloss on the law *habitatores*, the final paragraph, on the word *vere* in the Digest *On Leases*. The aforementioned points are then gathered and established from the law *habitatores*, final paragraph, whose words are: *“If there were a just cause why the tenant feared danger, even if the danger had not truly existed, nevertheless the rent would not be owed. But if the cause of fear was not just, he must nonetheless pay the rent.”* Where you see that it is enough for the tenant to desert the leased thing because of a just fear to be released from the payment of rent, even if that which was justly feared did not happen.

The law *Pedius*, in the beginning, in the Digest *On Fires* <note>original: "ff. de incendijs"</note> agrees, and many affirm this, whom Alva. Valasco cites and follows in the cited number 13. Likewise, all the aforementioned are more copiously gathered and established from the law *si fundus* and the two following, joined with the law *si uno*, paragraph *item cum quidam* in the Digest *On Leases*, and from law 21, title 8, part 5. <note>original: "par. 5" refers to the Siete Partidas</note> In what has been said so far, Navarro agrees in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 187; Covarruvias in *Practical Questions*, question 30, number 3, where he speaks of the plague, war, and any other just cause; and in *Various Resolutions*, book 4, chapter 6, where he affirms the same regarding just fear due to evil spirits and apparitions, and reports that it was so judged in the high court of Granada.

<summary>This page discusses legal principles regarding property leases when use is interrupted by external disasters like war, plague, or "evil spirits." It establishes that tenants are generally only liable for rent during the time they actually used the property if they had a "just fear" for their safety.</summary>
<keywords>lease law, rent liability, force majeure, just fear, war, plague, hauntings, Luis de Molina, Roman law, legal successors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of lease contracts (location-conductio) during times of crisis, such as war or plague. It specifically addresses whether a tenant who flees a plague is still obligated to pay rent or return to the property once the danger has passed.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 439. <note>The header says 439, but the context continues Disputation 493 from the previous page; this is likely a printer's error in the original volume.</note>
761

indicated, and in Book 3 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 8, where the common opinion of the doctors regarding a sick servant affirms what has been said and proves it, rejecting the contrary opinion of a few. See also Alvarus Valascus on the *Law of Emphyteusis* <note>A type of long-term land lease</note> as cited above, at numbers 21 and 22, and Question 22, numbers 6 and 7; Sylvester under the word "leasing" <note>original: "locatio"</note>, Question 12; Antonius Gomez, volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, numbers 1, 2, and 3; and others whom they cite. Panormitanus, however, in his commentary on the chapter *Propter sterilitatem* under the title *On Leases* <note>original: "de locato"</note>, number 8, says that although a house can be abandoned because of the plague and the tenant <note>original: "conductor"</note> is not bound to pay the rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note>, this can hardly be upheld in practice. Covarruvias, at the cited number 3, adds that this assertion by Panormitanus agrees with what Matthæus de Afflictis reports: namely, that the Neapolitan Senate in the time of Alfonso II decreed that tenants were not immune from paying rent on account of the plague. Nevertheless, the cited doctors constantly assert that they *are* immune. Covarruvias in the same place, and Alvarus Valascus at the cited number 6, say that the Neapolitan decree pertains to the specific statutes of that Kingdom, and that the contrary view, according to the dispositions of civil law, should be embraced in other Kingdoms.

<margin>Question 4</margin>
Whether, however, when the war, plague, or other danger—on account of which someone had deserted the leased property—ceases, the tenant is bound to continue the lease contract, if there was still time remaining according to the contract entered into from the beginning. Covarruvias, at the cited number 3, along with others he cites, asserts against certain people that the tenant *is* bound to continue the contract; Alvarus Valascus embraces the same opinion in the cited Question 22, number 6.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I think, however, a distinction must be made. Since the matter is no longer "whole" <note>original: "res non fit integra," a legal term meaning the situation has changed significantly</note> because the landlord <note>original: "locator"</note> found someone else to lease it during the time the previous tenant was absent, the previous tenant certainly cannot compel the landlord to continue the contract with him. For this reason, the burden of notifying the landlord of his departure was placed on that tenant, so that the landlord could look out for his own interests and not suffer the loss of rent. Likewise, the landlord cannot compel the tenant in this case.

If, however, the matter is still "whole," and there is nothing to suggest that the tenant should not be compelled to continue the contract, then the tenant and landlord can mutually compel each other to continue the contract, as Covarruvias and Alvarus Valascus affirm. But if there is something which, considering the concurrent circumstances, suggests the tenant should not be compelled to continue the contract—as when the plague or war persisted for a long time, and the tenant moved far away and it is no longer expedient for him to return to the same place, or other similar reasons—then I do not think he should be compelled to continue the contract. For if it had been included in the agreement from the start that he would be bound to continue the contract in that event, he certainly would not have accepted it; in contracts, as in other matters, that which would not have been accepted if specifically proposed is not considered to be included in a general agreement.

When the leased property, before the completion of the term for which it was leased, is rendered notably worse for the purpose for which it was leased, and it cannot be restored or repaired, then it can be abandoned by the tenant. Alternatively, the tenant can compel the landlord to reduce the rent proportionately to the decrease in usefulness. This is held in the law *Habitatores* at the beginning, and the law *Si merces*, in the section *Si vicino*, in the Digest under the title *On Leases* <note>original: "ff. locati"</note>.

<column-break/>

I said above, not without reason: "if an impediment to the use and enjoyment of the leased thing should arise," <margin>5</margin> holding this to apply when the impediment is on the part of the property itself. For if the impediment is on the part of the one who leased it (for example, if the leased property is a house and he cannot inhabit it due to a circumstance arising from his own side), or if he leased the services of someone and cannot use them because he no longer needs them, or because it was necessary for his own convenience or to avoid his own particular loss to move elsewhere—even if these things happened by chance—he is bound to pay the rent in full to the landlord. This is unless he makes a peaceful arrangement with the landlord's consent, so that the landlord remits something in exchange for the power to lease the same thing to someone else, as can be seen from what was said in Disputation 489. This is held in the law *Sed addes*, in the section *Cum quidam*, and the law *Qui operas*, in the Digest under the title *On Leases*, and it is affirmed by Sylvester at the cited Question 12, and Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, numbers 197 and 198.

In this place, observe that if the landlord leases that same thing to someone else for the same time, he is bound to deduct that from the rent which the first tenant promised him for that same time. For that use of the thing and its enjoyment for that time which he leases—or the purpose for which he leases it—does not belong to the landlord, but to the first tenant. Just as one who sells someone else's property is bound to restore the price to the owner of the thing when the owner tacitly ratifies the sale, so too the one who receives a price for that lease is bound to deduct it from the price that the first tenant owed him for that same use and enjoyment.

And this is what is commanded in the cited section. Therefore, although the landlord is not bound to lease the thing to another and could receive the full rent from the first tenant, if he *does* lease it without first making a settlement or composition with the first tenant, he is certainly bound to deduct from the first rent the price he receives for the second lease. This applies unless the first tenant leaves that use as if abandoned, giving up his right to the enjoyment of that thing for the whole time it was owed to him, even though he himself could have leased it to another.

<margin>6</margin>
If the leased thing perishes, or if it is found to be by the fault of the landlord, or by someone the landlord could have prevented, or if it was leased while the landlord knew it belonged to someone else and it is legally recovered by the owner <note>original: "euincatur," referring to evictio, where a third party proves ownership</note>, then the landlord is liable to the tenant not only for all damages that followed from that cause, but also for the interest of lost profit <note>original: "lucri cessantis," literally "gain ceasing," referring to the income the tenant expected to make</note>. Understand the same regarding one who leased his services and through his own fault did not provide them: he is liable to the employer for the whole interest, including lost profit. This is held in the law *Si in lege*, in the section *Colonus*, and the law *Si fundus*, in the Digest under the title *On Leases*, and in Law 21, Title 8, Part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the Castilian law code</note>.

<margin>7 Question</margin>
Whether, however, one is liable only for intrinsic lost profit—that is, how much more the fruits and use of the leased thing would have been worth than they are worth at the time of restitution—or also for extrinsic profit, that is, how much the tenant was going to gain by trading with them. Gregorius Lopez, commenting on the cited Law 21, says one is liable only for the intrinsic profit, according to the law *Si sterilis*, in the section *Cum per venditorem*, in the Digest under the title *On Actions for Purchase* <note>original: "ff. de actionib. empt."</note>. He adds: unless the one who leased it was a merchant; for then he affirms that one is also liable for the intrinsic profit <note>The text likely intended "extrinsic" here based on the preceding logic</note>.

We have reported a similar opinion of the same author along with Bartolus in Disputation 299, in which he affirmed...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of lease and service contracts (locatio-conductio). It moves from the specific issue of rent abatement during plagues to the broader question of liability for damages and lost profits when one party fails to fulfill their end of the agreement.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts #

...maintained that a borrower is indeed held to the interest <note>original: "interesse"; here meaning compensation for loss or the "difference" in value</note> of the loan if they do not restore it within the fixed term. However, he argued they are held only to "intrinsic" interest (loss within the thing itself) and not "extrinsic" interest (consequential losses), unless the lender was a merchant.

Just as we rejected and challenged that opinion in that section, this other one must also be rejected here. It must be affirmed that the lessor <note>The person leasing out the property or service.</note> is held liable to the lessee <note>The person paying for the use of the property or service.</note> even for extrinsic interest. This is because the lessor is truly the cause of both types of damage for the lessee. Thus, setting aside the law *si sterilis* <note>A specific Roman law regarding barren land</note> and standing on the nature of the matter alone, or on natural law alone, whenever someone is at fault for not standing by a contract (especially a burdensome or "onerous" one), they are liable for the full interest, including extrinsic interest and lost profits. The law *si sterilis* (specifically the section "when through the seller") only speaks of contracts of buying and selling; since it deviates from the standard and recedes from the nature of the thing itself, it should not be extended to other contracts, as has often been said.

8. If, however, someone has leased something to another in good faith, and that thing is "evicted" <note>term: eviction <gloss>the legal recovery of property by a third party who has a better title, resulting in the lessee losing access</gloss></note>, the lessor is then bound to petition the one who evicted it to leave it to the lessee for the same rent for the entire duration of the lease contract. Or, the lessor is bound to provide another thing equally as good for the lessee’s enjoyment for that entire time. If they can achieve neither, the lessor is bound to reduce the rent for the lessee in proportion to the time that they were not permitted to enjoy the leased property. This is held in the law *si quis domum* under the title *on leasing* <note>original: "ff. locati"</note> and Law 21, Title 8, Part 5.

Since each party to a contract is bound to fulfill the agreement for the other in whatever way they conveniently can, the lessor is justly obligated to those two prior options—providing the original or an equivalent—and through them sufficiently fulfills the contract on their part. In such a case, the lessee is also bound to stand by the contract and pay the rent.

In the absence of those two options, the lessor is bound to waive the rent in proportion to the time the lessee could not use the property. I would say the same if the leased property is confiscated without the lessor's fault, according to what was said regarding the law *si fundus* in Disputation 491. For the lessor is bound to obtain the use of the property from the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note> for the same rent if possible; otherwise, they are bound to provide another equally good thing to the lessee. When they can perform neither, the rent must be remitted proportionally.

9. One who has hired out their labor <note>original: "operas"; services or work</note> for a day or another period, but has not worked faithfully within the limits of the labor and care owed (to the point that, by the judgment of a prudent man, they do not reach the minimum just labor owed for that stipend), is bound to restore to the hirer a portion of the wage proportional to the labor and work they were bound to provide but did not. Indeed, they are also bound to restore any other detriment, including lost profit, that followed for the hirer—for instance, if they were hired for fishing or something similar. This is the view of Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 196, and the matter is quite clear in itself.

-> Regarding what level of fault a lessee is held liable to a lessor, and a lessor to a lessee. <-

### DISPUTATION 494 ###

---

<columns>2</columns>

-> SUMMARY <-

1. *A lessee is held liable to a lessor for fraud, gross negligence, and ordinary negligence, but not for the slightest negligence.*

<column-break/>

**A** lessee, who has received a leased thing for use or for its fruits, is held liable to the lessor for fraud <note>term: dolus <gloss>intentional deceit or harm</gloss></note>, gross negligence <note>term: lata culpa <gloss>extreme carelessness or recklessness</gloss></note>, and ordinary negligence <note>term: levis culpa <gloss>the failure to take the care that a reasonable person would take</gloss></note>. They are not, however, held liable for the "slightest fault" <note>term: levissima culpa <gloss>a very minor slip or oversight that only the most extremely diligent person would avoid</gloss></note> or for a fortuitous event, according to what was said in Disputation 295 joined with Disputation 293. The reason is that this contract is for the benefit of both parties. When a contract is of such a kind, and nothing else is expressly found, the contracting parties are only held for fraud, gross negligence, and ordinary negligence; but not for the slightest fault or accidental events. In a similar way, when someone hires out their labor regarding someone else's property—such as a tailor for making clothes, a miller or baker for grinding wheat, a shepherd for guarding a flock, and various other craftsmen and servants to perform something else regarding another's property—then, if that thing perishes or is made worse by their negligence, they are held for fraud, gross [negligence...]

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of lease and service contracts (locatio-conductio). While the previous page focused on compensation for damages when a contract is broken, this page examines the degrees of negligence for which a person is liable and how specific agreements can shift the risk of accidental loss.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 484 ###

**Column 1**

...or for a slight fault <note>original: "leui culpa"; standard negligence where one fails to act as a reasonable person would</note>, but not indeed for the slightest fault <note>original: "leuissima"; an extremely high standard of care where even the smallest oversight results in liability</note>; or for a fortuitous accident <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an unforeseen event like a storm or sudden fire, often called an "Act of God"</note>.

<margin>3</margin>If, however, it was specifically included in a pact <note>A formal agreement or clause within a contract</note> that such lessees or lessors should be held liable for a minor fault, or even for a fortuitous accident; or even that they should not be held liable for any fault, the contract must be upheld. This is provided that no inequality <note>A lack of balance between the risk taken and the price paid</note> arises therefrom, considering the danger to which they expose themselves and the payment they receive; and provided that it is not agreed that they are exempt from liability for fraud <note>original: "dolo"; intentional deceit or harmful intent</note>. Such an agreement would be against good morals and would therefore be invalid. All these matters, and others that could be said here, were explained at length in dispute 295 and the two following, regarding this and other contracts. In all these things the doctors of law commonly agree, and they are established by the law *item quaeritur* in the section *si gemma*, the law *si quis fundum* at the beginning and in the section *Celsus*, and from the law *sed et damno* in the Digest <note>The *Digest* is a massive collection of Roman legal opinions</note> under the title "On Hiring," and from the final section of the Institutes "On how an obligation is contracted," and from law 7 and others up to 17 in title 8 of the fifth *Partida* <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the primary legal code of medieval Castile (Spain)</note>.

<margin>4</margin>For greater clarity on these matters, several points expressed in the law must be added. In the law *videamus*, at the beginning, joined with the law *qui insulam* in the final section of the Digest "On Hiring," it is held that a lessee <note>The person who hires or rents the property</note> is liable to the lessor; not only for their own fault, but also for the fault of their household, and even of outsiders whom they have brought into the house or into a similar leased estate.

Likewise, in the section *si merces* of the law *qui columnam* in the Digest "On Hiring," it is held that if someone is hired to transport a column, or to transport vessels of wine, or oil, or other similar things, such as glass vessels, they are held to a level of diligence to ensure they are not endangered or broken, such as the most diligent person <note>original: "diligentissimus"</note> would apply. Both from these words and from those preceding and following, that text seems to exclude fortuitous accidents and thus includes even the slightest fault.

<margin>5</margin>And law 8, title 8 of the fifth *Partida* seems to establish this very thing openly. The gloss by Accursius <note>A famous 13th-century legal scholar whose commentary (gloss) on Roman law was authoritative</note> on the cited section explains "the most diligent" as meaning "diligent," so that only slight fault is included, according to the standard rule and confirmed by many laws in dispute 295. And indeed, this interpretation and opinion is approved by me: it should be understood that the diligence applied should be what a diligent person would apply, as the nature of the thing being transported requires. Certainly, an elaborate marble column requires greater care from the transporter to prevent it from breaking than common things do; and similarly, glass vessels or a jar full of wine or oil require greater care and diligence than common things.

I am led to embrace this interpretation and opinion not only by the authority of Accursius, and because—as the same Accursius rightly says there—in law, the diligence opposed to slight fault is often expressed by those words; but also because in the Institutes "On Hiring," in the second to last section, when speaking of hired clothing, silver, or a pack animal <note>original: "iumento"</note>, the diligence to which the lessee is held is expressed in a similar way. Accursius explains it there in the same manner: for no one would say that the hirer of a pack animal is held to the slightest fault in caring for and guarding it, unless they wish to contradict other clear laws and create an irrational exception for a pack animal, or clothing,

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

or silver, from the general rule of this contract.

<margin>6</margin>I am further moved because, in such laws that sound like something departing from reasonable and general rules, a somewhat "strained" interpretation <note>original: "violenta... interpretatio"; a legal term for a non-literal interpretation used to harmonize conflicting laws</note> is permitted so that laws may harmonize with other laws. Or perhaps the section *qui columnam* and the cited law 8 intended to signify only this: that the slightest fault can scarcely, or not at all, be distinguished from slight fault in those things which, by the very nature of the object, demand greater than common diligence. It is as if a fault that would be "slight" in preserving other things does not even reach the limits of "slight" in these matters. Thus, in these cases, there is no exception to the general rule of the contract of lease and hire.

Even if there was no pact between the lessor and the lessee for one of them to be liable for a fortuitous accident, if the one who was held to guard the thing <term>custodia <gloss>the legal duty to watch over and protect a piece of property</gloss></term> transgressed some other agreement, and that was the occasion for the thing to perish by accident, then they are liable for such an accident. However, it is otherwise if that was not the occasion for the thing to perish by accident—because the thing would have perished in the same way even if that occasion had been removed. Examples are found in the law *videamus*, in the section *si hoc*, and the final section of the Digest "On Hiring."

<margin>7</margin>For if it was agreed between the lessor and lessee that there should be no fire at all in the leased property, then certainly if a fire were there, and the leased property were burned by a fortuitous accident without any fault of anyone, the lessee would be liable for that accident, because that fire, forbidden by the lessor, was the occasion of the blaze. It would be otherwise if they had only agreed that there should be only an "innocent fire"—that is, one from which no danger was imminent; then the lessee is not liable for that accident, because there was no transgression of the pact, since the fire was innocent. Both points are in the cited section *si hoc*, joined with the preceding law *si quis fundum* in the section *quod si in*.

Another example: if it was agreed between the lessor and the lessee that hay should not be put in a certain estate, and the lessee transgressed this, and a fire happened to reach the hay by accident and the estate was burned, the lessee is liable for that accident, because that transgression was the occasion of that fortuitous event. So it is held in the final section cited. In a similar way, if someone hired something for a certain time, and that time having passed, they were in delay <term>mora <gloss>a legal default or failure to perform an obligation on time</gloss></term> in restoring the thing, and that was the occasion for the thing to perish by accident—because if it had been restored, it would have escaped that danger and not perished—they are held liable for that accident. Understand this if they detained it against the lessor's will; it is otherwise if they presumed the lessor was not unwilling, and the person was not unwilling themselves.

If, however, the thing was going to perish by a similar accident anyway, then, because the transgression of the pact was not the occasion for it perishing by accident, the lessee is not liable for that accident, as was proved at length in dispute 295. For that reason, I do not linger here in proving this or citing the authors of our opinion. And according to these points, what is held in the cited law 8 of Castile <note>The laws of the Kingdom of Castile</note> must be accepted. From this, you will understand what should be said in the following event: Someone hired a horse for a journey on the condition that they would only cover seven leagues daily on it; but they covered eight, and the horse died. It is asked whether they are held to restore the price of it to the lessor.

<summary>This page discusses the legal liability of tenants and hirers (lessees) for damages, distinguishing between standard negligence and accidental loss. It establishes that while lessees are generally only liable for "slight fault," they become responsible for accidental losses if they have violated specific terms of the contract or delayed the return of the property.</summary>

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts ###

It must be said that one is held liable if they were the cause or the occasion for someone's death. However, it is otherwise if they were neither the cause nor the occasion for the death, because the person was going to die in a similar manner anyway—as usually happens if they died of a disease. For traveling one league beyond the standard seven is not usually a sufficient reason for someone to die who would not have died otherwise.

<margin>8</margin>
Furthermore, it should be observed that when a pact <note>A specific clause or agreement within a contract</note> is made regarding liability for a fortuitous accident <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an unforeseen event such as a natural disaster or sudden accident</note>, whether this is understood to cover every accident, or only one or several specific types. This must be judged from the concurrent circumstances: to which accidents did the person intend to bind themselves by virtue of the contract when it is not sufficiently expressed? One should not be judged to have intended to bind themselves to more than the current circumstances suggest. For example, if a goldsmith <note>original: "aurifex"</note> undertakes to engrave a gem or set it in gold, and out of the owner’s fear that he might break it during the engraving or setting, he binds himself to the risk of accident; in this case, he is understood to be liable only for the accident of breaking it while engraving or setting, and not for other types of accidents. This is the meaning of the law *item quaeritur* in the section *si gemma* <note>References to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman law</note> and Law 10, Title 8, Part 5 <note>A reference to the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish legal code</note>. Whether one is held liable for unusual and unexpected accidents when they are not specifically mentioned, or only for common and foreseeable ones, will be discussed in the following dispute.

<margin>9</margin>
Read this, but add: section 1 of the title on leasing and Law 14, Title 8, Part 5. A person who leases out defective vessels <note>original: "vasa vitiosa"</note> for wine, oil, or similar liquids to be stored in, is held liable for damages <note>original: "interesse"; the legal value of the loss suffered</note> to a lessee who was unaware of the defect, even if the lessor himself did not know of it. The same applies to a person selling similar defective vessels, according to the law *tenet* in the section *sed si vas*.

<margin>a.</margin>
Nevertheless, in the two laws cited first, the opposite is established regarding one who leases a field for grazing in which there were poisonous herbs. If he knew those herbs were there and did not warn the lessee, he is liable for the resulting damages. If, however, he did not know they were there, he is not liable for the damages; but no price is owed to him for the lease of that field, and if he had already received payment, he is bound to restore it. The reason for this latter ruling seems to be that the field is worth nothing as a grazing lease since it does not serve that purpose but rather causes harm. Regarding the leased or sold vessels, the reason the lessor or seller is held liable even if they didn't know of the defect is that they ought to have paid attention to the quality of the vessels they were delivering. The law presumes that such ignorance is "culpable" <note>negligent or blameworthy</note> in someone selling or leasing vessels for that purpose. However, it does not presume this in someone who leases a field that happens to be harmful for grazing, which no one had previously experienced. Therefore, because that law is based on a presumption, it does not have force in the "forum of conscience" <note>The internal moral judgment of the soul, as opposed to a legal court</note> when, in the judgment of a prudent person, there was no fault on the part of the seller or lessor. But it will have force in the external court unless the contrary of that presumption is established. This is the view of Navarro <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, a famous 16th-century canon lawyer</note> and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras, an influential theologian</note>.

When, however, someone sells or leases such vessels as being "not defective," explicitly stating they are selling or leasing them as such, then even if they were invincibly ignorant of the defect, they would be held liable to the lessee or buyer for the damages and subsequent losses,

<column-break/>

as is expressly stated in the law *tenet* in the section *sed si vas* and affirmed by the cited doctors. This is because by that very statement, he is deemed to have taken upon himself any damages that might follow.

<margin>11</margin>
These laws (*quaeritur* section *si fullo*, and *si quis fundum* section *Celsus*) state that if someone receives an item to perform some task related to their profession—such as a tailor <note>original: "sartor"</note> receiving clothes to sew, a fuller <note>original: "fullo"; someone who cleans and thickens cloth</note> receiving cloths to wash, or a dyer to color—and they either swap the item (giving one person's goods to another) or the item suffers some damage while in their power (such as being gnawed by mice), they are held liable to restore an equally good item or its value to the owner, even if it happened through their ignorance. The Gloss of Accursius <note>The standard 13th-century commentary on Roman law</note> gives the reason for this ruling: fault is always presumed—at least a "slight fault" <note>original: "culpa leuis"</note>—due to inattention or lack of skill.

If those laws are based on that presumption, then those who received the items are not bound to restitution in the forum of conscience if no fault (at least a slight one) occurred on their part. Indeed, they are not even bound in the external court if the opposite of what those laws presume is sufficiently proven. For such things, if they perish without fault of the receiver, they perish for the owner, unless there was a pact to the contrary. Therefore, unless the receiver is deemed to accept the items with that burden by the decree of these laws (so that he is liable even for invincible ignorance or inattention), he is not bound to restitution.

<margin>12</margin>
If someone had chartered a ship to carry merchandise, and the shipowner, being unskilled in the art of navigation, sailed without a pilot <note>original: "magistro"</note> or refused to follow the pilot's advice during the voyage, and for that reason the ship perished, he is held liable for damages to the charterer. Also, if he transferred the goods to another, inferior ship without the consent of the owner of the goods, and this other ship perished, he is likewise held liable to the owner of the goods.

All these points are found in the law *item quaeritur* and Law 13, Title 8, Part 5. But if he transferred them to another ship that was equally good or better, yet did so against the express protest and will of the owner of the goods, and this other ship perished, he is still held liable for damages; because by transferring them against the owner's will, he provided the "occasion" for them to perish. If, however, he did this without the owner's knowledge, but the owner did not protest, he is not liable.

If he transferred the goods to another ship heading to the same place without the owner's knowledge or protest, and both ships were wrecked without any fault of the sailors, then the shipowner is not liable for damages to the owner of the goods. This is because the goods would have perished similarly even if they had remained in the first ship; thus, that transfer was not the occasion of their destruction. This is held in the law *vlt.* in the section *si ea conditione* in the passage by Paulus.

<margin>13</margin>
When someone who has leased a rural estate makes it worse for future crops through untimely or poor cultivation...

He emphasizes that while the law may presume fault for the sake of public order, moral restitution is only required if actual negligence or a specific agreement exists.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of liability within the contract of hiring and leasing (locatio et conductio). ### Second Treatise, Disputation 494. ###

...the heirs themselves, such that if one were to care for a vineyard—where it might bear more fruit and be better situated—in such a way that they rendered it worse for the following season, they are held liable to the lessor for the damage caused. Likewise, if a tenant were to cut down and destroy trees more than is reasonable, or if they were to take for themselves wood blown down by the force of a storm against the owner's will; and finally, if any damage should come to the estate through their own fault or negligent guarding—for instance, if they allowed a servitude <note>A legal right to use another's land, such as a right of way; if not defended, this right could be lost through "prescription" or lapse of time.</note> owed to that estate to be lost by prescription—they would be held liable for the damage that subsequently followed for the owner of the estate. See here in the Digest, Book 19, Title 2, Law 15, section 1 <note>original: "ff. locat." refers to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman civil law.</note>.

<margin>14</margin>
And by the same reasoning, if a neighbor was doing something about which the owner of the house could very well have issued a notice of new work <note>A formal legal protest to stop a neighbor's construction that might infringe on one's rights.</note>, and the tenant did not warn the ignorant owner so that he might look out for himself in that or another way; or if a neighbor’s house was threatening to collapse, which could bring harm to the leased house, and the tenant did not seek security against threatened damage <note>original: "cautionem... de damno infecto"</note> nor informed the owner of the house to look out for himself, the tenant is held liable to the owner for the loss of interest. This is gathered from the final part of the law cited above, and is affirmed by Antonio Gómez in chapter 3, number 20, along with others whom he cites.

<margin>15</margin>
Furthermore, if because of enmities that someone had with the tenant, some damage was inflicted on the estate by that enemy, the tenant would be held liable for that damage: provided, however, that if he himself was the cause of the enmities, he is held strictly liable for that damage. If, however, he was not the cause of the enmities, he is only held liable if he did not apply competent care and guarding to prevent such damage from being inflicted. If, on the other hand, the damage is inflicted because of enmities with the owner of the field, or because of public enmities, then the tenant is not held to such a high degree of guarding—except that which he is normally bound to provide for the field—nor is he bound to provide the greater guarding necessary for that situation, since the enmities are not with him. When, however, the enmities are with a business partner, he is held to contribute to that greater guarding. All these points are found in the Digest, under the laws concerning hiring, and in the *Siete Partidas*, Law 7, Title 8, Part 5, along with the commentary of Gregorio López <note>Gregorio López de Tovar (1496–1560) was a Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Castilian law code.</note>.

<margin>16</margin>
He who professes the exercise of any art is by that very fact deemed to promise sufficient skill for it, and that he will apply competent diligence; wherefore, if because of his lack of skill <note>original: "imperitiam"</note>—because, namely, he did not have as much skill for it as men of his art are commonly accustomed to have—or because of his negligence, he brings some detriment to the thing committed to him according to his art, he is held liable to the person who hired his labor and industry for the loss of interest. This is found in the Digest, Law 9, section 5, and in the *Partidas*, Law 10, Title 8, Part 5.

When a tenant undertakes to do something in its entirety for a certain price—which the Castilians call *a destajo* and the Portuguese call *de empreitada* <note>These terms refer to "piece-work" or "fixed-price contracts" rather than work paid by the day.</note>—if it is then discovered to be defective, either because it was done too hastily, or because such material (or so much of it) was not applied as ought to have been applied, or for some other reason, then, with the assistance of experts skilled in that matter, it must be judged whether it is defective or not. If it is found to be defective, he who leased his labor for it is held liable for the loss of interest. However, whether someone has leased their labor in that or another way, yet contracting with the hirer that he would perform it so that it would please and be approved by the hirer; such a pact is regarded as if the approval were committed to the judgment of a good man <note>original: "boni viri arbitrio"; a legal standard of a reasonable, fair-minded person or expert.</note>.

<column-break/>

Therefore, if the hirer later says that it displeases him, and he who leased his labor contends that such a judgment is unreasonable, good men skilled in that matter must be chosen to judge the case, and their judgment must be stood by. Likewise, if the hirer delays giving judgment, he ought to be compelled to give it; and if he refuses, others must similarly be chosen to judge the work. When, however, the hirer, having established a certain wage for each day, hires someone to do something on the condition that whenever that person's labor displeases him, he may dismiss him; then, once the work is finished, he is not heard if he says it displeases him or is not well-made. This is because by persevering in the hiring and paying the wages, he is deemed to have approved the work. If the thing, while it was being made or after it was finished, but before it was approved by the hirer, perished by a fortuitous accident, then it is sufficient for the hirer to prove that there was a defect in it for the risk to remain with the worker. All these points are found in various laws of the Digest and the *Partidas*.

<margin>17</margin>
When someone had hired themselves out to finish some entire work for a certain wage, and by a fortuitous accident they cannot complete it—for example, because they have died—then they or their heirs must be paid only a proportionate share of the wage for what they have done. This is found in the *Partidas*, Law 9, Title 8, Part 5. And as Gregorio López says there, the gloss <note>A marginal or interlinear commentary on a legal text.</note> on the Digest agrees, noting that the heirs may finish the work themselves if they wish, provided it is through another equally suitable person. Gregorio López notes there that he had never read it defined in such a way.

<margin>18</margin>
However, he thinks this should be limited unless the person of the deceased was specifically chosen for the task <note>In legal terms, an "intuitu personae" contract, where the specific individual's talent is why they were hired, such as a famous artist.</note>. Certainly, when nothing else was specified in the pact, nor is it presumed from the circumstances that the intention of the contracting parties was otherwise, I believe that the heirs of the deceased can compel the person who had hired the deceased for that work to allow it to be finished by another equally suitable person whom the heirs provide. Similarly, the hirer can compel the heirs to finish it through another equally suitable person, provided they find someone who will finish it at a fair price, since the contract of hiring and leasing passes to the heirs, as was said in Disputation 489. But when such a person is not found who will finish it for a fair price, or the industry of the deceased was specifically chosen for it, then one must stand by the first part of the definition in Law 9 and the cited gloss.

When anyone accepts the guarding of something for a wage—as a shepherd does for a flock—many, led by the law in the Digest, believe they are held liable for interest even for the slightest fault <note>original: "culpa levissima"</note> if some detriment comes to the thing committed to their guard because of their negligence. Gregorio López records and follows this in his commentary on Law 15. Nevertheless, I believe they are only held liable for slight fault <note>original: "culpa levis"</note>, according to what was said above regarding those hired to carry a column or wine vessels, or to sew, dye, or wash clothes. For a very heavy yoke, both unreasonable and unbearable, would be imposed on shepherds if, since they are hired for so many things concerning the flocks—such as defending them from wolves and foxes, curing them of mange and other diseases, keeping them away from others' crops, gardens, and vineyards, and grazing them by night in winter, and other such things—they were held liable for the slightest fault if anything should happen.

<summary>This page examines the liability of tenants, heirs, and professional craftsmen under Roman and Spanish law. It specifically addresses the duty to warn landlords of property threats and argues that shepherds should only be liable for ordinary negligence rather than the "slightest fault" due to the difficulty of their work.</summary>

...any danger or loss that might occur regarding them. Nor does the law <note>original: "l. qui mercedem"</note> speak of shepherds in particular, but only teaches that if danger arises for a thing belonging to another because of a failure in guarding it, the person who received a payment for guarding it is held liable for that loss. This is to be understood if the loss occurs through their fault—at least slight negligence <note>term: "culpa levis" — a legal standard meaning the failure to exercise the degree of care that a reasonably prudent person would use in managing their own affairs.</note>—according to the general rule of this contract.

<margin>20</margin> It is not enough for someone who had received a thing for guarding to say it was lost or returned in worse condition without his fault; rather, he must prove both: namely, he must show it was lost or damaged, and that this happened without his own fault. This is the view of Gregorio López <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist who annotated the *Siete Partidas*.</note> regarding the law cited above, and it is found in the law itself. However, if a shepherd brings the hides of dead livestock and does not claim more have died than is customary, or if more have died, he proves that a similar proportion died from other flocks in the same region, or gives a specific, likely reason why more died from his flock than others, and no other proof can be brought against him, then he can be compelled to swear an oath that it was so, and he will be cleared. But if he does not offer sufficient evidence as to why so many died without his fault, his oath will not be accepted, and he will be compelled to pay for the loss according to the judgment of a prudent person. These points are gathered from the Digest <note>original: "ff. locati" and "ff. de eden." refers to the Digest of Justinian, the core of Roman Law.</note> and confirmed by Gregorio López. Therefore, because the death of a hired beast of burden usually occurs from natural causes or disease without the hirer’s fault, if the hirer proves it died and the lessor does not prove fault intervened, the hirer’s oath that it died without his fault will be accepted, because the presumption is in his favor—that it died by a natural course of disease. Following this, one should accept what Antonio Gómez <note>Another prominent Spanish legal scholar.</note> teaches, in which he agrees with the doctrine we have handed down in this section.

# Whether, on account of supervening sterility, the tenant should be released from rent, and whether due to an unusual increase, they are held to a higher rent.

## DISPUTATION 495.

### SUMMARY.

1. When a tenant is freed from paying rent on account of sterility arising from any cause.
2. When the sterility of crops is said to be so great that the rent ought to be reduced proportionally.
And what the law is in Castile and Portugal, numbers 4 and 5.
3. When the remedy of the law regarding the rescinding of a sale <note>original: "l. 2 C. de rescind. vend." — a law allowing a contract to be voided if the price was less than half the fair value.</note> also applies to the tenant of a farm.
6. Cases in which rent is not remitted to a tenant despite sterility; also numbers 7, 8, 9, 11, and 14.
10. Compensation of sterility with abundance: how much it must be for it to take place, and the abundance of preceding or following years.
12. Whether a tenant renouncing fortuitous events is also deemed to renounce unusual ones.
And what if such a renunciation is confirmed by an oath?

<column-break/>

<margin>no. 13</margin>
15. Whether the rent should be increased because of an unusual increase in crops; discussed at length.

On account of supervening sterility <note>term: "sterilitas" — in this context, it refers specifically to crop failure or a lack of harvest, rather than biological infertility.</note> in the leased property occurring without the tenant's fault—whether it occurs due to armies plundering or destroying crops, or due to flooding from the sea or rivers, or due to excessive abundance of rain, or due to great drought, or because of locusts, other worms, and other animals, or because of fire, or any other cause—the tenant is released from paying the rent. This is held in the Digest and the Code <note>original: "l. si merces. §. vis maior. l. ex conducto. §. si vis ff. locat. l. licet. j. C. eod. tit."</note>, as well as in the laws of Castile and Portugal. All agree that if the sterility is so great that absolutely no crops are harvested, the tenant is freed from paying the rent such that they are not bound to pay anything at all, according to the law which states: *But if a landslide occurs and takes away all the crop, the loss is not the farmer's, lest he be compelled to pay the rent for the field on top of the loss of the seeds he sowed.* This is established even more clearly in the laws cited above. And in this event, the law holds that the remission of rent ought to be made in proportion to the time in which the crops were not gathered. If, however, the sterility is notable and great, but not so great that absolutely nothing is perceived, the rent must be reduced proportionally, as is agreed by other laws, especially: *Superior force <note>term: "vis maior" — an overwhelming force or "Act of God," like a natural disaster or war, that cannot be controlled.</note> ought not to be a loss to the tenant if the crops are damaged more than is tolerable; otherwise, the farmer ought to bear a moderate loss with an even mind.* Here you see that even when not all the crops perish, but the damage to the crops is not just anything, but great and intolerable—so that it is truly notable and great sterility—the farmer must be helped. This is not done so that the entire rent is remitted as if all the crops had perished, but so that it is remitted proportionally, taking the sterility into account. You see, moreover, that for a moderate damage to crops, nothing of the rent is to be remitted; this is also held in the Digest, which says: *When a certain person complained about the scantiness of crops, the response was that no account should be taken of it. Likewise, in another response: You desire a new thing, that a remission be given to you on account of the age of the vines.*

<margin>2</margin> The doctors <note>Legal scholars and experts in civil and canon law.</note> doubt when the sterility of crops is to be called so great that the rent ought to be reduced proportionally. Panormitanus, Alvarez Valasco, and others cite a gloss which suggests that sterility is only considered sufficient to reduce the rent when no crops—even in the amount of the seed sown—are gathered. They rightly reject that gloss (if that is indeed what it meant). I believe, however, it did not mean that, but only referred there to the rule that in such a case, no rent at all is to be paid; for the gloss immediately follows by saying that if the sterility is such that no fruits...
