<meta>This page continues a legal analysis regarding the contract of hiring and leasing (locatio et conductio). Specifically, it examines the conditions under which a tenant farmer is entitled to a reduction or "remission" of rent due to crop failure (sterility), weighing different historical legal opinions on what constitutes a significant enough loss to warrant relief.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 495.

If the fruits of the land are collected, some argue the tenant <note>original: "colonus"</note> is freed from the entire rent; however, if the harvest is not so small, they argue he is only held to pay a proportional amount. We can compare this opinion with another by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists</note> regarding the law on rent and superior force <note>original: "vis maior"</note> in the Digest, which states that crop failure <note>original: "sterilitas"</note> is understood to occur when, after deducting expenses, absolutely no fruit remains. He argues that the term "fruit" should only refer to what remains after expenses are subtracted; if nothing remains, the tenant should pay no rent. This view is cited but rightly challenged by Panormitanus, Covarruvias, and Aluarus Valascus. Their reason is that under this rule, rent would almost always be remitted whenever there was a poor harvest, which contradicts the established law on leasing.

Another opinion, originating from Johannes Andreae and followed by Panormitanus, asserts that crop failure occurs when a tenant <note>original: "conductor"</note> collects a third less than the amount usually gathered from that field. In such a case, the rent should be reduced in proportion to that loss—so if a third less is collected, a third of the rent is remitted, and so on. This view is also rightly rejected by Covarruvias, Valascus, and Gregorio López. They argue that a loss of only one-third, or indeed anything up to half of the usual harvest, is considered "moderate damage" <note>original: "modicum damnum"</note>, which the tenant must endure without a reduction in rent, according to the laws cited above. Having set these opinions aside, three following views are more celebrated.

The **first** is that crop failure should be recognized when, according to the common opinion of the local people, it is affirmed that there is a failure in that place. This is supported by the glosses on the Code and the Digest. Many authors cited by Valascus and Covarruvias hold this, though Covarruvias—citing Baldus and Barbatias—states that it should rest on the judge’s discretion to decide when the failure is great enough to warrant a rent reduction. He adds, however, that evidence must be presented so the judge can determine the quantity of fruits gathered. Furthermore, he notes that while proving crop failure through "common public opinion" is not entirely certain or sufficient—as it can be vague—lawyers still use such questioning in witness examinations. Proving that there is a general consensus of failure is useful and contributes greatly to defining the case, thereby justifying the judge's decision. Valascus adds that if there is general proof that there was a failure in the region where the field is located, it serves as proof for that specific field unless the opponent proves otherwise.

<column-break/>

However, when there is proof that common opinion holds there was a crop failure in that specific field, it is considered effective evidence for the matter.

The **second** opinion is that crop failure is sufficient to remit rent proportionally when the tenant does not receive half of the fruits that are commonly gathered from that field. This opinion, alongside the previous one, is embraced by the Gloss and followed by many authors who are cited without disapproval by Covarruvias, Valascus, and Gregorio López.

The **third** opinion is that crop failure should be considered sufficient for a proportional rent reduction when so few fruits are collected that, if the cost of seeds and expenses are subtracted and the full rent is then paid from the remainder, the tenant would suffer a loss of more than half of the "just price" <note>term: "iustum pretium" — a legal concept of a fair or objective market value</note>, or more than half of the rent in fruits that he paid for the lease. For example, if ten measures of wheat are the rent to be paid, and the fruits gathered are so few that, after seeds and expenses are deducted, less than three measures remain, then the rest (up to ten) should be remitted from the rent due. If, however, five or more measures remain, nothing is remitted, because the failure is not considered great enough to deserve a remission of rent. This is the most recent view of Bartolus and, after him, the common opinion of the learned doctors. It is accepted as the most reasonable view by Covarruvias, Aries Pinellus, Antonio Gómez, and others. As Valascus notes, this applies when the loss happens because the harvest is physically small compared to the usual yield, rather than just because the market price of the crops has dropped.

<margin>3</margin> It should be observed, following Valascus and Covarruvias, that this last and more common opinion by Bartolus does not rely on the law regarding the rescission of sales <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescind. vend."</note>—which was passed after the civil laws on crop failure—but rather relies on the fact that the interpretation of those earlier laws is consistent with equity. Therefore, the law on rescinding sales (which also applies to leases) is a distinct protection from this one. Both protections are available to a tenant, but in different ways. The protection under the sales law regards the *start* of the contract: if the tenant was deceived by more than half the just price at the beginning (e.g., he paid ninety for future crops valued at less than sixty), he can seek a remedy regardless of whether a crop failure later occurs. The protection of rent remission, however, regards a "fortuitous event" <note>term: "casum fortuitum" — an unforeseen accident or act of God, like a storm or drought</note> affecting the crops *after* the contract was made.

<summary>This page discusses the legal criteria for "sterilitas" (crop failure) and when a tenant is entitled to rent reduction, concluding that relief is generally granted only when losses exceed half the expected yield or result in significant financial deficit after expenses.</summary>

### 644 Luis de Molina on Contracts

...reasoning: therefore, even if the contract was just from the beginning and fair to both parties, and no protection under the second law applies, if the crop failure <note>original: "sterilitas"</note> is so great that, after subtracting the cost of seed and expenses, the remaining produce does not reach half the value of the rent due, this other protection applies. This is because equity does not allow a tenant <note>original: "conductor"</note> to suffer such a great loss through no fault of his own.

Depending on which of the reported opinions one deems truer and more worthy of acceptance, one ought to understand and judge accordingly when a remission of rent for crop failure should or should not be granted to a tenant. This applies whether one is following common Imperial law, the chapter on crop failure <note>original: "caput propter sterilitatem"</note>, Law 22, Title 8, Part 5, or even—as Alvarez Valascus argues at the end of his 24th point—the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "ord. Lusit."</note>, Book 4, Title 61. If the crop failure is not so great as to reach the limits of failure discussed in the opinion one has chosen as truer, then a remission of rent should not be granted; but if it does reach those limits, it should be granted. This is the view of Covarruvias in the cited second point, Alvarez Valascus in the passage above, and the doctors of law commonly.

<margin>4</margin>
To resolve difficulties that arise when some crops are actually gathered—meaning the entire rent should not be forgiven, but only a part—the Law of Castile <note>Law 22, cited above</note> establishes the following: *But if it should happen that the crops were not entirely lost, and the laborer gathers some portion of them, then it shall be his choice either to pay the full rent to the lord of the estate, if he dares to pay it, or if not, to set aside for himself the expenses and the outlays he made in working the estate, and whatever remains, let him give it to the lord of the thing he had leased.* <note>Molina is quoting the Spanish text: "Pero si acaescie se, que los fructos no se perdiesen todos..."</note> In this passage, Gregorio López believes the law has chosen the second of the three opinions mentioned later. Namely, that this remission and the option granted to the tenant only apply when the fruits gathered do not reach half of the produce usually harvested from that land. For by the term "some portion," he understands "less than half," as he proves from many legal sources. Alvarez Valascus approves of this same view, saying that Tiraquellus adorned that doctrine with almost infinite authorities, even though he incorrectly cites Covarruvias as asserting the same thing as Gregorio López. Valascus adds that this doctrine can be adapted to the Portuguese Ordinance. According to that law and this interpretation of it, only when a tenant has gathered less than half of the usual harvest is he given the choice: either pay the full rent, or deduct the costs spent in gathering the crops (among which the seed and the labor put into the land must be understood) and give the remaining produce to the landlord. Covarruvias says that when a tenant wishes to choose this second option, to ensure the matter is handled more safely and justly, he ought to call upon and require the landlord to be present, either in person or through another, to assist in the gathering of the harvest or other fruits. This is so that the landlord may better know how much fruit was received and may accept it after the expenses have been deducted. He further adds that even if the tenant omits this precaution, he can still exercise the choice granted by the royal law through legal action, provided it can be proven legitimately and without suspicion of fraud how many crops he gathered from the 

<column-break/>

estate and what expenses he incurred in gathering them.

Covarruvias adds that in the High Court of Granada <note>original: "Granatensi praetorio"</note>, he saw that in questions of crop failure—when the failure is not entirely clear, or is clear but not so great that it should fall under the formal legal statutes, and when a certain knowledge of the produce received and expenses cannot be had due to disputes and varying witness testimonies—he saw, I say, that when there is some pressing proof of crop failure, the court would set aside the form of the Royal Law. Instead, through a definitive sentence, they would grant a remission of the rent based on the judges' discretion, perhaps for a third or a fourth part. He says that he himself has subscribed to such sentences because of their great equity. Alvarez Valascus approves of this practice as well. 

I, however, would rather think that sentences should be rendered in favor of the landlords, ordering that the rents be paid to them in full, unless it is clearer than the light of day that the crop failure was great enough to trigger the sanctions of common law. Nor do I think the form of the Royal Law should be set aside; rather, the expenses should simply be estimated by the judgment of a prudent man, according to the concurrent circumstances, when it cannot be fully and certainly established how great they were. 

I am led to this because the provision in a lease contract regarding the remission of rent in the event of crop failure has force only out of a certain equity, given the legal disposition in this matter. Indeed, if that legal provision were set aside, the fruits of the leased property would surely stand at the risk of the tenant alone, without any remission of rent for that cause—just as a purchased item stands at the risk of the buyer, even before it is delivered, without any obligation on the seller to return any of the price. Thus, a tenant can waive that legal provision and take upon himself the entire risk of such accidental events, as we shall discuss; this is sanctioned by law and happens daily. Therefore, it is wrong to extend the legal provisions for remitting rent further than what is found established in common law and in each Kingdom. 

And perhaps it would be more useful for the commonwealth to repeal all such laws and decree that tenants take the outcomes of the harvests at their own risk and for their own profit. This would be better than opening the door to as many lawsuits as are filed daily because of such laws, with so many expenses for both contracting parties and such liberty for judges to deliver sentences in favor of whomever they wish. In such a variety of opinions and subtleties, judges may choose what pleases them most to favor the person to whom they are more inclined due to entreaties, gifts, or other reasons. Hence, rightly in the same Kingdom of Castile (Law 2, Title 9, Book 9 of the *New Compilation* <note>original: "nouae collect." referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* of 1567</note>), to entirely cut off the lawsuits and evasions of tenants regarding the King's property, it was decreed that the tenants of royal revenues and goods must take upon themselves the entire risk of any events whatsoever.

I am also moved by the fact that if such legal provisions were not extended by judges at their own discretion based on a supposed equity, but were instead observed exactly as they sound, so many lawsuits would not be stirred up around such contracts to the great loss of the parties involved.

<summary>This page discusses the legal thresholds for rent reduction due to crop failure, contrasting the flexible "equity-based" approach of some courts with a stricter, more pro-landlord interpretation intended to reduce litigation.</summary>

# Treatise Second, Disputation 495

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
Law 1 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 61, regarding the outcome of a rent reduction <note>original: "remissionis partis pensionis"</note>, states as follows: <gloss>But if it should happen that the crops are not entirely lost, and the laborer harvests some portion of them, it is then his choice to surrender all the crops of the said estate; however, if the failure occurs on grain-producing land, he may set aside the seed for himself, and whatever remains over, he shall give to the landlord of the estate he holds under lease.</gloss> Here you see that the option is granted only to the tenant <note>original: "conductor"</note>: he may either pay the full rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note> or leave all the crops of that year to the landlord <note>original: "locator"</note>, deducting only the seed for the grain, but no other expenses. When this happens through no fault of the tenant, since he deducts no expenses except the seed, it is not the practice to check whether the crops amount to less than half of what is usually gathered—which would otherwise allow the landlord to compel the tenant to harvest and take them and pay the full rent. This is not implied by the cited Portuguese law, nor is it the accepted practice; in Portugal, all crops are offered to the landlord for him to take for himself, a process they call *returning the estate's produce* <note>original: "emcambar a herdade"</note>; though Alvarez Valascus in question 27, number 32, claims the opposite.

In that Kingdom, however, it is rightly established by custom that the tenant must formally notify <note>original: "interpellet, ac denunciet"</note> the landlord that he wishes to use the protection of the law and surrender the crops. This allows the landlord to gather them himself (or through another) or be present at the harvest, so that no fraud occurs and he is certain of the quantity of the crops. This notification must be made before the crops are separated from the earth; otherwise, it will be of no use, as it was made at an improper time. It is not sufficient if the notification happens while the crops are already on the threshing floor <note>original: "area"</note>, because fraud could occur during the harvest itself. Alvarez Valascus reports that he saw a poor farmer condemned by the Portuguese Senate because he did not notify the landlord before the crops were gathered; it did him no good to prove the crop failure or that he had given notice while the crops were on the threshing floor. In this event, it is not enough for the landlord to simply know about the crop failure unless a formal notification is made. Since notification is not required solely for the sake of sharing knowledge, the landlord’s prior knowledge is not enough; the formal act of notification itself is required, as Alvarez Valascus rightly affirms at number 32. If the lord is not present, it is sufficient to notify a general proxy or one appointed for that purpose, as is clear from the law and the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 6. If neither the landlord nor a proxy can be found, the notification should be made to a judge. Valascus considers this to be established by common law, even if it is not specifically decreed in Portuguese or Castilian law.

I, however, although I see that it is consistent with reason and the text that this should be done, do not think that the specific text is strictly binding. That text speaks of a situation where a tenant was abandoning a leased house because of an approaching army. In that case, if the landlord had been warned of the tenant's departure, he could have looked out for himself, both to prevent the house from being damaged by the army and to find another tenant or other profit from the house. Therefore, standing on the strictness of the law alone, and excluding

<column-break/>

custom to the contrary, I agree more with the opinion of Ripa and Covarruvias: namely, even if that notification is omitted, the protection of these laws should be granted to the tenant, provided he proves without suspicion of fraud how many crops he gathered from the field. Valascus admits that this opinion has equity on its side. In the same place at number 33, Valascus says the tenant is bound to harvest the crops; he proves this because the tenant is only released from paying rent by the actual presentation of the crops, and also by the words of the Portuguese Ordinance: <gloss>give what remains over to the landlord.</gloss> This implies the landlord ought to receive them from the tenant’s hand. When the landlord is not present at the harvest, either personally or through a representative, the tenant ought to bring two witnesses beyond all reproach, as the Portuguese law establishes for sharecroppers in Book 4, Title 60; or he should gather them in the presence of a person appointed for that purpose by a judge.

In the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, when an urban property <note>original: "urbana praedium"</note> is leased and its fruits or returns are greatly diminished by a chance event—for example, if a mill or an inn was leased and a bridge providing access to that place was destroyed by the force of a river, so that very few people came to grind grain or seek lodging—I believe that regarding the reduction of rent, one should follow the arrangements of common law and embrace one of the reported opinions, because nothing specifically decreed is found in these Kingdoms for such events.

In the following cases, no remission of rent is granted to the tenant. The first case usually cited is when the calamity that took the crops is very common in those places. For some regions are very subject to rains and the flooding of the rivers that nourish them. Examples in Portugal include the fields along the banks of the Mondego <note>original: "Mondae"</note> near Coimbra <note>original: "Conimbricam"</note>, and those along the banks of the Tagus <note>original: "Tagi"</note> at Santarém <note>original: "Scalabim"</note>. In Lombardy, storms that destroy crops are said to be frequent. Therefore, when such causes of destruction are frequent in certain places, they say the rent should not be reduced for that reason. They derive this from the law: <gloss>if damage happens from an unaccustomed heat or rot of the olives, the loss shall be the landlord's; but if nothing happened outside of the usual custom, the loss is the farmer's.</gloss> Law 22 agrees with these words: <gloss>by some occasion that happened, which was not very accustomed to occur,</gloss> and there Gregory Lopez notes and affirms this with others.

The Portuguese Ordinance, Book 4, Title 62, agrees with these words: <gloss>by some case that was not very accustomed to come;</gloss> and the great glosses at the end of the law affirm this, as do others followed by Aries Pinellus and Alvarez Valascus. I, however, although I do not think we should depart from this opinion if it is understood correctly, am not greatly moved by those specific words.

For that phrase regarding "unaccustomed heat of the sun" was said because accustomed heat of the sun, that is—

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding when a tenant is entitled to a rent reduction due to environmental disasters. ### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...is not very abundant and is unusual, it does not usually bring so much damage to the olive trees that the risk should fall to the landlord <note>original: "locatorem"</note>, as if the rent <note>original: "pensione"</note> ought to be reduced for that reason. And those other words signify the same thing: if nothing happens "contrary to custom" (that is, against the usual order of natural causes), the loss belongs to the farmer <note>original: "coloni"</note>, because the loss is not typically so great that the rent ought to be remitted on its account.

I said that I do not believe we should depart from the well-understood opinion: for if it is understood that when a specific property being leased is particularly subject to misfortunes and crop failure <note>original: "sterilitati"</note>, and for that reason is leased for a much lower rent than it would be otherwise, then that opinion is true. In such a case, the risk of that failure is considered to have been transferred to the tenant <note>original: "conductorem"</note>, and he accepts it at his own peril. However, if it is understood that when a whole region where something is leased is very subject to some misfortune, but not this specific estate in particular, the rent should not be remitted, then that is surely false. It is against common practice and against the examples provided by the laws which state the conditions under which rent must be remitted due to crop failure.

For instance, the region of this Diocese of Cuenca <note>original: "Cochensis Episcopatus"; Cuenca is a city in central Spain</note> is very subject to hail in the summer which devastates the fruit. Yet, no specific estate there is uniquely prone to it; hail falls now in one town, now in another, and it does not usually devastate every estate within the boundaries of the town where it falls. Therefore, the fact that a region is generally subject to hail in this way does not prevent a rent reduction if hail happens to devastate the fruit of a particular estate. Thus, in every place, one must consider whether a custom exists where, because certain estates are highly subject to misfortunes and crop failure, they are leased for a much lower price than they otherwise would be. In that case alone, the tenant is viewed as having taken all those risks upon himself, and only then is it considered that the rent should not be reduced despite frequent failure. But if such a custom does not exist, the remission of rent due to crop failure will certainly take place.

From this it is clear that Arias Pinellus <note>a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> wrongly denies—in the cited point 30—the need to distinguish between unusual and unexpected "accidental cases" and those that are common and expected to happen. He wrongly suggests that for all these, the rent must be remitted according to what has been said, but if they are common, no remission should occur according to the paragraph *but if also* <note>original: "sed & si"</note> and other laws. For indeed, in many common events which we expect might happen, and which happen not so rarely, it is the rule that the rent should be remitted on their account, as has been stated.

**7.** The second case <note>original: "† euentus"</note> in which rent is not remitted to the tenant despite crop failure is: When that failure occurs through the fault of the tenant <note>original: "culpa conductori"</note>. This might happen because he farmed the land poorly or at the wrong time, or gathered the fruit prematurely, or because he did not clear the crops of weeds when it could have been done usefully, or because he guarded the fruit negligently given the circumstances, or for any other reason. See Law "From the Lease" <note>original: "l. ex conducto"</note>, section "if force," in those words: *if the crops are ruined by worms or weeds* (that is, through the farmer's negligence); also Law "if wages" <note>original: "l. si merces"</note>, section "tenant" in the *Digest* under the title "on hiring"; and the chapter "on account of sterility" in the same title; and Law 22 at the end of Title 8, Part 5; and Book 4 of the Institutes,

<column-break/>

Title 6, the final law; and the doctors of law commonly affirm this. However, when the fault was not directed toward that outcome, nor was it such that it could be certain that the failure happened because of it, then that fault does not prevent a rent reduction when a failure occurs.
Thus, Alvarez Valascus <note>a Portuguese jurist</note> in the cited question 27, number 40, rightly rejects the opinion of Hostiensis, Barbosius, and certain others—which Gregorio López follows in the cited Law 22 at the word "possible fault"—who assert that if a tenant had not paid the church tithes <note>original: "decimos Ecclesiae"</note> and a crop failure followed, the rent should not be remitted to him, as if the failure had its origin in that fault. For such a fault (or any other committed against God) is not of itself ordered toward causing a crop failure, nor can it be certain that the failure was sent by God because of it. Valascus had asserted the same in the preceding number 30: if a crop failure were brought about by a tenant’s enemy because of enmities that arose from the farmer's own fault, the fault is not inherently directed toward a crop failure following from it. He affirms the same if the failure should follow from the fact that the farmer was thrown into prison for a crime, sent into exile, or taken into captivity because of his own fault.

I believe the opposite is true, however, as is clearly gathered from Law "if wages," section "of fault" <note>original: "l. si merces. §. culpæ"</note> in the *Digest*, and from the points discussed in the preceding dispute. For that fault is sufficient for that effect to follow; and although the tenant did not intend it for that effect, he ought to have avoided the fault so that the effect would not follow. Therefore, since he did not avoid it, and it is clear that the effect followed from it, it ought not to result in a loss for the landlord, but for the tenant. The citation from Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a Spanish canonist</note> which Valascus uses to confirm his opinion does not actually apply to the matter proposed, nor would Covarruvias assert it regarding this case.

However, if the tenant were not already in such enmity, and had not been negligent in guarding the estate so that the failure was not induced by an enemy, then the rent should be remitted. If the tenant had not farmed the leased estate at all, and then an accidental event occurred which would have totally destroyed the fruits even without his fault, the tenant would still not be released from paying the full rent. This is expressly held in Law "tenant," final section, in the *Digest* under "hiring," and it is the common opinion of the doctors which Valascus records and follows.

When crop failure follows from fire <note>original: "incendio"</note>, as the final cited section notes, one must distinguish. Either the fire was caused by outsiders, in which case it can very well happen without the fault of the tenant, and thus the rent should be remitted. But if it was not caused by outsiders, it is presumed to have happened through the fault of the inhabitants; for, as held in Law 3, section 3, regarding the office of the night watch <note>original: "de præf. vigil."</note>, a fire usually happens through the fault of the inhabitants. In this sense, Law "if sold" in the *Digest* on the risk and benefit of a sold thing must be understood when it says that if a sold block of houses <note>original: "insula"</note> was burned, the fire could not have happened without fault.

Understand this to mean "usually," as held in the cited section 3, or as a legal presumption, because fault usually occurs—even if not by the master inhabiting the house, then by the master's household or servants, as the same Law "if sold" adds. Because however it happens—whether the fire occurs by the fault of the master or the fault of his servants—the rent is not to be remitted to him for the crop failure that follows from it,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and ethical obligations between landlords and tenants when natural disasters or "acts of God" occur. Specifically, it moves from regional risks (like those in Cuenca mentioned previously) to the specific legal burdens of proof regarding fire and the "balancing" of good and bad harvest years.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputations 4 & 5

...following from the law, as gathered from the chapter *qui infula*, the final paragraph, joined with the law *videamus* at the beginning of the section on leasing <note>original: "ff. locat," referring to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman law</note>, a doubt arises: when a fire occurs (provided it was not started by outside enemies) and results in crop failure, is the tenant <note>original: "conductorem"</note> required to prove that the fire happened without his fault or the fault of his household in order to receive a rent reduction? Or is it the landlord's <note>original: "locatorem"</note> responsibility to prove that the fire was their fault so that the rent is *not* reduced? Alvaro Valasco <note>A prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> resolves this excellently in Question 27, number 41: it belongs to the landlord to prove that the fire happened through at least "slight fault" <term>culpa leuis: a legal standard of negligence where one fails to take the care a bonus paterfamilias, or good householder, would take</term> on the part of the tenant or his household. This is because, as the final gloss on the Institutes states, a fire is only presumed to have started through the very slight fault of the inhabitant; however, a tenant is only held liable to the landlord for "slight" or "major" fault, which is not presumed but must be proven.

**8** The third situation occurs if the crops are spoiled or perish after they have already been fully received into the house or granary. For example, if the wine turns sour, or is spilled, or the wheat rots after it has been received, or if these things are taken by force or theft: in these cases, the rent is not reduced. This is gathered from the law *ex conducto*, paragraph *si quis*, in the Digest under 'Leasing,' with these words: *if, however, any defects arise from the thing itself, these are at the loss of the farmer—such as if the wine sours.* This is affirmed by Bartolus and many others whom Antonio Gomez and Alvaro Valasco cite and follow. However, it is a different matter if the wheat perishes on the threshing floor <note>original: "in area"</note>—before it is cleaned and brought into the house—due to a flood, fire, robbery, or otherwise without the fault of the master or his people, as Antonio Gomez rightly states in the same place.

The reason for this decision is not simply that the crops, once separated from the land, belong to the tenant. While they were still attached to the soil, the ownership of them belonged to the landlord along with the land itself. Rather, the reason is that the law did not intend for the loss of a crop failure to fall upon the tenant before the crops were fully and safely collected. This is Valasco's view, rejecting the opinion of those who think it is enough for the grain to simply be cleaned on the threshing floor to transfer the risk to the tenant.

**9** The fourth situation is when the abundance <note>original: "vbertate"</note> of a preceding or following year within the same lease contract compensates for the failure of a barren year. If the abundance of any previous years of the same contract—whether immediately preceding or earlier—fully compensates for the barren year, no rent should be reduced. If it only compensates in part, then only a proportional part of the rent is to be reduced. If there is no compensation at all from other years, the whole rent for that period is to be reduced. If, however, a rent reduction was already granted, but a following year of the same contract proves abundant enough to compensate, the landlord can reclaim what was reduced—even if the reduction was originally given under the name of a "gift" or "forgiveness."

An exception exists if the crop failure happens in the very last year of the entire contract, and the landlord was aware of the abundance of the previous

<column-break/>

years. In that case, if he reduces the rent under the name of a gift, it cannot be reclaimed later. It is different, however, if the landlord was unaware of the abundance of previous years and reduced the rent as a gift; in that case, he can reclaim it. All these points are found in the law *si vno* in the Digest. Furthermore, everything—except for the point about the gift—is found in the Code of Justinian and the chapter "Regarding Crop Failure" <note>original: "c. propter sterilitatem"</note>, as well as in the laws of Castile <note>The *Siete Partidas*, law 23, title 8, part 5</note> and the Portuguese Ordinances <note>Book 4, title 61</note>. The common opinion of the learned doctors agrees with this.

It is specified that this applies if the failure is compensated by the abundance of years *within the same lease contract*. If there is a different lease contract for the same estate—even if it is between the same people and for the same price—the years do not compensate each other. It is different if one and the same contract is extended further by the silent or express agreement of the parties; in that case, compensation does occur. This is the view of Gregorio Lopez, Alvaro Valasco, and others they cite. When the failure of the current year is not compensated by previous years of the same contract, the rent reduction must be granted immediately. One should not wait to see if following years will compensate for it before granting the relief at the end of the contract. This is because the law allows for compensation from future years not to *delay* the initial rent reduction, but rather to justify *reclaiming* that reduction later if a bountiful harvest follows. This is clear from looking at the law itself. Therefore, Valasco rightly says that some in Portugal have judged incorrectly by deciding the opposite.

**10** The entire difficulty <note>marked with a cross † in text to denote a crux or difficult point</note> in this matter is how great the abundance of the preceding or following years must be for this compensation to take place. The Portuguese Ordinances refer back to the common law without stating or declaring anything specific on this point. Setting aside other opinions, there are two main views. The first is that the preceding and following years should be calculated alongside the year of failure. If, when all are added up, enough was collected to pay the full rent for all those years, and *furthermore* to cover all the expenses the tenant incurred—including what is owed to him and his family for their own labor and industry—then there is a full compensation, and no rent should be reduced. If some rent was already reduced, it should be reclaimed if the subsequent years meet this calculation. If, however, not enough was collected to meet these marks, a proportional reduction of the rent should be made.

One must understand that what is missing from the total amount needed for full expenses and full rent is what must be taken off the rent. For example, if a fourth of the total amount needed is missing, a fourth of the rent is reduced; if a third is missing, a third of the rent is reduced, and so on. In this way, both parties feel the loss proportionally. This is clearly what Law 33 of Castile defines, which is quite consistent with the canon law "Regarding Crop Failure" and is not contradicted by the Roman Digest. And that is the very thing...

# Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts
### Page 648

...on account of which Gregory Lopez <note>original: "Greg. Lop." — A 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his definitive commentary on the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval law code of Spain.</note> commends those views there under the word *abondaria*, and Antonio Gomez <note>original: "Ant. Gom." — A highly influential Spanish legal scholar often cited alongside Molina.</note> in his *Various Resolutions* affirms that this legal arrangement must not be abandoned in this Kingdom of Castile. This rule is indeed quite fair: for the laws usually only intend to help the tenant <term>conductor: the person who leases or hires the property</term> so that, on account of crop failure, after everything has been calculated, they should not be left suffering a loss. They rightly established that the loss should be divided between the tenant and the landlord <term>locator: the owner or lessor of the property</term> in a certain proportion, in the manner already explained. And this opinion entirely pleases me, even when standing on the ground of common law <term>ius commune: the traditional legal system of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</term>.

However, observe that beyond the complexities of when "sterility" <note>original: "sterilitas" — crop failure or lack of productivity</note> should be declared so that a rent remission occurs, and when it should be judged so great that the whole rent or part of it must be remitted—of which we spoke above—and when the fault belongs to the tenant or not, and other points by which the landlord is excused from granting a remission; observe, I say, that all these things are the greatest breeding grounds for lawsuits <note>original: "litium seminaria" — literally "nurseries of litigation"</note> by which the contracting parties consume their own goods, and from which hatreds arise. This is especially true given the great ambiguity of the laws and the variety of opinions. Consider what a massive "nursery of lawsuits" arises in calculating the fruits of all the years of a lease contract, in establishing the value of them all, and in determining the estimation of expenses, industry, and the labor of the tenant and his people. All this is done just to understand whether sterility occurred, how much, and whether it is compensated by the abundance of preceding or following years, so it can be understood how much rent should be remitted. Certainly, as I touched upon above, it would be far better for the public good if these laws were reformed by establishing that tenants take the property at their own risk and for their own benefit—as they usually do in practice—taking upon themselves all fortuitous cases <term>casus fortuitus: "acts of God" or accidental events like floods or war</term>, both usual and unusual. This would be better than leaving open such opportunities for endless lawsuits, to the great detriment of both landlords and tenants.

The second opinion is that "abundance" <note>original: "vbertas" — a bountiful harvest</note> is judged to exist when the leased estate bears more fruit than usual. According to the proportion of the excess of fruit in a year of abundance over the usual amount, compensation is made for that portion of the rent which would have been remitted in a year of sterility. For example, if the leased estate usually produced thirty measures <note>original: "modios" — a Roman/Spanish unit of volume for grain</note> of wheat, then in whatever proportion it produced more than thirty in a given year, the amount that had been remitted from the full rent of a sterile year would be repaid. For instance, if in a year of abundance it produces forty, a third part of one full rent is repaid; if it produces fifty, two parts of a full rent are repaid; but if it produces sixty, one full rent is repaid.

<margin>11</margin> The fifth eventuality is when the tenant has renounced <note>original: "renunciauit"</note> the right to claim for fortuitous events or sterility. In that case, even if sterility occurs, he is held to pay the full rent. This is held in the law *si quis fundum* at the beginning <note>original: "ff. locat." — referring to the section on Leasing in the Digest of Justinian</note> and the law *licet* in the same title of the Code, as well as in the *Siete Partidas* <note>original: "l. 23. tit. 8. part. 5."</note>. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez and others follow.

<column-break/>

This rule holds even if someone renounces "fortuitous cases" in a general sense without specifying any in particular, according to the cited doctors and the laws. This is true even if the tenant only says he is leasing the property "at his own risk." However, Gutierrez and others disagree unless the contract says "at *all* risk" [omni periculo]. The text in the law *sed & si quis* does not stand in the way, where it is held that a general renunciation of exceptions is not enough to prevent an excuse if an unexpressed act of God occurs.

I say that this is not an obstacle because, as the cited doctors affirm, that rule is only to be understood regarding renunciations like a promise made to present someone in court. Matters are handled far differently regarding renunciations of fortuitous events made in the types of contracts we are discussing here. Indeed, some argue that even in judicial renunciations, while a general waiver of all exceptions is not enough, a renunciation of certain specific fortuitous events with an added general clause—"and other similar events"—is sufficient to count those events as waived.

Indeed, it is affirmed that it is enough to renounce through a general clause for fortuitous events, even if nothing is expressed in particular, although it is not sufficient to renounce through a most general clause for "any exceptions whatsoever." When someone renounces certain specific fortuitous cases and adds a general clause "and other fortuitous cases," that clause should be understood to cover events of equal or lesser severity, but not "greater and more unusual" [maiores, ac magis insolitis] events. This is based on the argument from the *Clementines* <note>A collection of Canon Law</note> which decrees that such clauses added after specific examples only include things equal to or smaller than those expressed, not greater things. This is the view of Gigas on Pensions and others.

<margin>12</margin> There is a doubt: if a tenant renounces "fortuitous cases," should he be thought to renounce only the "usual" ones [solitis] that could be imagined as possibly happening, or also "unusual" ones [insolitis] for which there was no fear at all in that region—perhaps because they had been unheard of for forty years or from the memory of man? Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Antonio Gomez and others, judge that he only renounces the "usual" ones. This is because the intention of the contracting parties, under those general words, does not seem to extend beyond the usual acts of God which one could then think might happen. This is also supported by the two laws of the Church cited shortly before. Although Bartolus and others confirm this from the law *fistulas*...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral obligations regarding rent remission. Specifically, it addresses whether a tenant who has waived their rights to claim "fortuitous events" (accidents) is still protected against completely unforeseen or extraordinary disasters, and introduces the concept of sharecropping.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 49
#### Page 649

The words are: *“When you had sold the grain that was still in the blade, you said that if anything should happen by force or by storm, you would be responsible. Snow ruined that grain. If the snows were immoderate and contrary to the usual pattern of the season, an action for purchase <note>original: "ex empto" — a legal claim based on a contract of sale</note> can be brought against you.”*

So it is written there. However, as many observe, that text can be turned against the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most famous medieval jurists</note> and the common view, rather than confirming it. For it pronounced that he who obligated himself for "fortuitous cases" <term>casus fortuitus: an accidental event that could not be foreseen or prevented, like a natural disaster</term> is held liable for those that happen against the usual pattern of the season. The more recent Alvaro Valasco <note>a 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> responds that an event might be contrary to the usual pattern of the season and yet not be "unexpected" in that region, but rather believed to be possible, even if very rare, and therefore included under the "usual" risks. Aires Pinhel <note>original: "Aties Pinel." — a Portuguese law professor</note> disputes this matter in the place cited above at number 29; he believes, along with Baldus and others he cites, that someone who renounces their rights regarding fortuitous cases is considered to renounce not only common ones but also unusual ones. However, since the other opinion is more common, and the arguments Pinhel relies on are not of great weight and are easily dismissed by what has been said, I do not think one should depart from the common opinion.

Whether, however, one who renounces "foreseen and unforeseen" fortuitous events is thereby considered to have renounced "usual and unusual" ones. Aires Pinhel and Alvaro Valasco affirm this, reporting that the Royal Senate judged it so: because the term "unforeseen" sufficiently expresses "unusual" events. Gutierrez, cited above at number 7, although he agrees, thinks along with Ripa and Corneus that a person who renounces "foreseen and unforeseen" events—but not specifically "usual and unusual"—is considered to renounce events that even wise men could not foresee might happen, but is *not* considered to renounce events that even the most prudent could not possibly imagine. I believe, however, that such excessive subtleties, which only provide fuel for lawsuits, should not be listened to.

It has already been stated above that in this Kingdom of Castile, all collectors of royal revenues and properties renounce all fortuitous events, both usual and unusual, and both foreseeable and unforeseeable, with absolutely none excepted, no matter how unusual or unforeseeable, as is held in Law 2, Title 9, Book 9 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collect." — referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, the 1567 compilation of Spanish laws</note>.

<margin>13</margin>
But if, in all the events we have discussed, the renunciation of fortuitous cases is † confirmed by an oath, that renunciation would certainly not extend to more cases than if it had not been confirmed by an oath. The reason is that the strengthening of an oath does not extend further than what is included in the promise or pact being confirmed, according to the final law of the Code *on non-enumerated money* and other similar laws. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Alvaro Valasco and Gutierrez follow. If, however, the intention of the one renouncing had been to renounce more fortuitous cases than explained according to the reported opinions, then certainly in the "court of conscience" <note>the moral/spiritual realm rather than the civil court</note> he would be held to those other events—not only under the guilt of perjury if the renunciation was fixed by oath, but also simply by the strictness of justice if the renunciation was not confirmed by an oath.

<margin>14</margin>
The sixth scenario in which a tenant is not granted a remission

<column-break/>

of the rent is: if he is a sharecropper <term>partiarius: a farmer who pays rent with a fixed portion of the harvest, such as a third or a fifth</term>. For then it is not a lease, but a contract of partnership <note>original: "contractus societatis"</note>. Therefore, even if sterility occurs, the debtor still owes that specific portion of the crops that he actually gathered. This is held in the law *if the rent* <note>original: "l. si merces"</note>, paragraph *force majeure* <note>original: "§. vis maior"</note>, at the end of the Digest's title on leasing.

<margin>15</margin>
It remains for us to say something about the second point proposed in the title of this dispute. Namely, whether † on account of an unusual increase in crops, the tenant is bound to pay a higher rent? Certainly, if the tenant renounced all fortuitous events, even unusual ones, he will not be bound to a rent increase because of an unusual harvest. For those who claim the rent should be increased due to a crop increase argue that just as the landlord suffers a loss of rent due to notable sterility—rent otherwise owed to him by contract—so too he ought to feel the benefit of a rent increase due to an unusual abundance. For he who feels the loss should also feel the benefit, and vice versa, as the rule states. The question, therefore, only arises when the tenant has *not* renounced fortuitous events.

And indeed, all agree that when an extraordinary increase in crops results from the tenant's own industry <note>original: "industria" — hard work or skill</note>—because he sowed more, cultivated the land more diligently, or made improvements to the leased property—the rent is not to be increased. This is established in Law 23, Title 8, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and the Great Gloss affirms it at the end of the law *if the rent*, paragraph *force majeure*. However, when the increase comes from elsewhere and reaches double what the leased property usually yielded, Law 32 cited above establishes that the rent must be doubled, based on that equity: that he who suffers the loss of rent reduction due to unusual sterility should also feel the benefit of a rent increase due to unusual fertility. The cited glosses, Bartolus, and others (including Antonio Gomez) affirm this. However, many understand this to be true only when the crops increase in such abundance due to a fortuitous event—for example, if someone has leased a mill, and by a fortuitous event other mills are destroyed, which causes this mill to yield far more than usual. In that case, the rent should be increased in proportion to the increase beyond the highest yields that mill used to produce. But it is otherwise when the crops increase much beyond the usual due to the fertility of the year, even if the goodness of the leased land contributes much to it. Among those who hold this view are Gregory Lopez, Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), an influential canon lawyer</note>, and Sylvestre.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I am of the opinion that the rent should not be increased because of an increase in crops, excluding the specific fortuitous event explained above or something similar. This is clearly gathered from the paragraph *force majeure* cited, whose words are: *“A tenant ought to bear a small loss with a level mind, from whom an immoderate gain is not taken away.”* Here you see that on account of a great gain, and where the property [yields] fruits, it does not increase the rent. This is to be understood through "equity" <term>epicheiam: the interpretation of a law not by its literal words but by its underlying spirit or fairness</term> when the gains do not arrive due to a fortuitous case like the mill example, but because of the fertility of the year and the land. And thus understood...

He also argues that landlords shouldn't raise rent just because of a "good year," unless the extra profit comes from a specific external accident.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Luis de Molina’s legal and moral analysis of lease contracts. The previous page discussed whether a tenant who waived their rights to claim "fortuitous events" was still protected against extraordinary disasters. This page concludes that discussion and begins a new section on who is responsible for the costs of maintaining and repairing a leased property.</meta>

Having understood this opinion, so as to exclude the abundance of a fortuitous case <term>vbertas casus fortuiti: an unexpected "bumper crop" or stroke of good luck that makes the land more productive than usual</term>, I believe we should accept what Aires Pinhel <note>Aires Pinhel (1512–1563) was a prominent Portuguese jurist</note> says in his commentary on the Code, book 2, "On Rescinding a Sale," part 1, chapter 3, number 34, and what Alvaro Valasco says in the place cited above, at the final number: namely, that this opinion has been accepted in practice.

This is supported by the following reasoning: when an abundance of profit arises because of the high price of the crops, the doctors <note>Legal scholars or "Doctors of Law"</note> of the contrary opinion agree that the rent should not be increased. However, when the abundance arises due to the great fertility of the year, surely the abundant crops gathered then are worth only a little more than the usual amount, because the very abundance of the crops causes their market value to decrease. Therefore, it is not equitable that the tenant’s rent should be increased for crops that are worth no more to him than the usual harvest. But in that other event of abundance due to a fortuitous case, right reason certainly demands that just as rent is to be decreased because of a contrary accidental event, so it should be increased because of this one. And indeed, if that specific case had been proposed to the legislator, he would surely have made an exception for it; for when he uttered those words cited above, he had his mind’s eye fixed on the fertility of the year and on that which usually happens.

## To which expenses of the leased property the lessee is bound, and to which the lessor. And when the lessor is bound to pay the lessee for expenses he made on the property.

### DISPUTE 496.

-> *SUMMARY* <-

<margin>1</margin>
1 *The lessee <term>conductor: the tenant or person hiring the service</term> is bound to the expenses of the leased thing according to the custom of the place, unless it was otherwise agreed; and the same must be said for the lessor <term>locator: the landlord or owner</term>.*
2 *And what if there is no custom, as to which of them is bound; see number 2, where this is treated fully.*
3 *The lessee can compensate <note>original: "compensare" — meaning to deduct from the debt</note> useful expenses from the rent owed for the leased thing, according to the common opinion.*
4 *Whether the lessor is bound to pay for expenses made by the lessee when there is a general pact that the property should be improved by the lessee, but it was not said that it should be at his own expense.*
5 *Whether the lessee of a usufructuary <note>A "usufructuary" is someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</note> can recover from the owner the expenses made on the leased property which has returned to the owner upon the death of the usufructuary.*
6 *The lessee can retain the thing leased to him until the expenses made on the leased thing are paid to him.*

<margin>1</margin>
Alvaro Valasco, in his work on emphyteutic law <note>Emphyteusis is a long-term lease of land where the tenant is obliged to improve the property</note>, question 26, number 6, correctly notes—along with Bartolus on the law of expenses in the Digest <note>original: "l. impensæ. ff. de impens." — refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> and with others—that in this matter, the custom of each region must be observed above all else. Thus, if the custom in a certain region is that certain expenses on certain leased things are to be borne by the lessees, that custom should be followed. For contracts, when nothing else is specified in them, are deemed to be made according to the custom of the place in that matter, as per the law "Always in stipulations" in the Digest's rules of law. The same is specifically held regarding the contract of letting and hiring in the laws "Excepted" and "Around" in the Code <note>original: "C. de locat." — The Code of Justinian</note> 

<column-break/>

and the law "Owners of estates" in the Digest under "On farmers and tax-collectors."

<margin>2</margin>
2 Setting custom aside, Bartolus in the cited law, and certain others whom Alvaro Valasco cites at number 6—among whose number is Antonio Gómez in his *Various Resolutions*, volume 2, chapter 3, number 20—judge that if the expense is for the perpetual utility of the estate, or for a longer time than the duration of the lease, the lessee is not bound to it, as it is a "great" expense. However, if it is not to last except for the time of the lease, and therefore is only for the use of the lessee, then the lessee is bound to make it as a "small" expense; nor can he recover it when the lease is finished; from which it follows that he cannot deduct it from the rent paid. 

Nevertheless, Alvaro Valasco in the same place, at number 7, rightly affirms—along with many others whom he cites—that the lessee is bound to make no expenses on the leased thing, but rather he can compel the lessor to make those that are necessary and customary for the convenience and use of the leased thing. And if the lessee performs them in the lessor's stead, he can recover them or deduct what was so spent from the rent to be paid for the lease. For only those expenses which pertain to gathering the fruits of the lease—such as plowing, digging, pruning, reaping, etc.—belong to the lessee. But that other necessary expenses pertain to the lessor is clear from the law "But you will add," section "The tenant," in the Digest under "Lease." 

There it is held: If a tenant had brought a vaulted and very large chest into a rented house, and the landlord—whether knowingly or unknowingly—narrowed the entrance of the house so that the chest cannot be taken out, the landlord is bound to the necessary costs for widening the entrance so the chest may be removed. See, the lessor is bound to those expenses which are necessary for extracting a chest previously brought into that house by the lessee. This is also clear from the law "From the lease" at the beginning of the same title, where it is held that an action from the lease is given to the lessee against the lessor if the farmhouse <note>original: "villa"</note> is not repaired, or the stable, or where his flocks ought to stay. And the Gloss <note>The standard medieval commentary on Roman law</note> there, on the word "repaired," affirms that the lessor is bound to such expenses, and in this, a lessee differs from a usufructuary, to whom the owner is not bound for such expenses, as is held in the law "But with the fruit-user," final section, in the Digest "On Usufruct"; and the Gloss affirms both points in the same place.

And by the same reasoning, the lessor is bound to repair the roof of the leased house when it needs repair to avoid leaks, or for some other reason. Likewise, he is bound to repair the rest when they threaten to fall or have already collapsed. By the same reasoning, the lessee is not bound to taxes by reason of the thing leased, nor to public duties <note>original: "functiones publicas"</note>, such as repairing the public road with stones next to the leased house, or cleaning and repairing a well. So it is held in the law "The aediles," section "Whoever live," in the preceding words of the Digest "On the public way," where we read it written thus:
> "Let each person build the public ways in front of their own house, and let them clean the aqueducts that are under the open sky, and build them so that a vehicle is not prohibited from passing. Whoever lives there for a price <note>i.e., tenants</note>, if the owner does not build, they themselves building may calculate the expense into the rent."
Thus it is said there. Where you see that even these necessary expenses, by reason of the thing leased, pertain to the lessor, and if they are done by the lessee, they are to be deducted from the rent or recovered.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on lease contracts (location-conduction). The previous page concluded that while rent shouldn't typically increase due to high crop prices, an extraordinary "lucky break" or fortuitous abundance might justify an increase, just as a disaster justifies a decrease. This page transitions into the responsibilities for maintenance and the reimbursement of expenses incurred by a tenant.</meta>

From what has been said, it is established that the tenant (<term>conductor</term>: the person who leases the property) is not bound to build embankments or ditches on the leased property, as Alvaro Valasco <note>Alvaro Valasco (c. 1526–1606) was a prominent Portuguese jurist.</note> states at the end of question 26; nor is he bound to repair them, unless this was specifically included as a requirement in the contract. From what has been said, it is also quite clear that in this Kingdom of Castile, the custom of the realm is much to the point: that the tenant only pays for food and lodging. If he necessarily spends anything else on the property—such as for the forging of iron tools or similar necessities—he can reclaim it or deduct it from the rent owed for that lease.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding "useful expenses" <note>original: "vtilibus expensis"</note>—those which make the leased property better and more profitable—although neither the landlord (<term>locator</term>) nor the tenant is strictly bound to make them, if the tenant does make them, he can offset them against the rent to be paid. Alternatively, he can reclaim them once the contract has ended, even if the tenant is evicted from the property due to some fault of his own. In this respect, a tenant differs from a "permanent leaseholder" (<term>emphyteuta</term>: a holder of an emphyteusis), according to what was said in Dispute 451. This is the rule in the law *The owner of the granaries* <note>original: "l. dñs horreorum," referring to Digest 19.2.55.1</note> in the section "if" under the title *on hiring*, which states: "In a leased field, if the tenant, by his own labor, has increased the value through something necessary or useful, or has built or established something, even if it was not agreed upon, he can sue the owner of the field under the lease contract to recover what he spent." The same is held in the law *The tenant farmer* <note>original: "l. colonus," referring to Digest 19.2.61</note> at the beginning of the same title, in these words: "A tenant farmer, although it was not included in the terms of the lease that he should plant vines, nevertheless established vines on the farm, and because of their fruit, the land could be leased for ten gold pieces more per year. The question was asked: if the owner sues this tenant, who has been evicted from the farm, for the debt of rent, can the tenant account for the useful expenses incurred in planting the vines by raising a plea of 'malice and fraud' (<term>doli mali exceptione</term>: a defense that the landlord is acting in bad faith)? Scaevola answered that he should either obtain his expenses or not be required to pay anything more."

Understand, however, that the tenant can compel the landlord to pay the surplus of the expenses if the improvements are worth more than what is owed in rent, as is clear from the law *The owner of the granaries*. Conversely, the landlord can compel the tenant to pay the difference if more is owed in rent than what was usefully spent. From the law cited most recently, Tiraquellus <note>André Tiraqueau (1488–1558), a French jurist.</note> notes that this rule holds even when the form of the thing is changed by the useful expenses—as in the case proposed, where a field was changed into a vineyard. However, Alvaro Valasco, in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 25, number 32, says the "form" is not said to be changed when the change is for the benefit of the other contracting party. Yet, these two legal points do not prove that the form is not considered changed, but rather that it is lawful to change it for the benefit of the other party. That a tenant can reclaim or offset useful expenses against the rent due for the leased thing in the manner explained is also expressly stated here in Law 24, Title 8, Part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish legal code.</note>. This is agreed upon in Law 1 of the Code *on mandates*, and affirmed by the common consensus of the doctors, which Alvaro Valasco (at number 32) and Antonio Gomez (volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 20) and Gregory Lopez (on Law 24) follow. However, Gregory Lopez, following Paulo de Castro, limits this to cases where the improvements were made with the consent—at least tacit—of the landlord; or, if made without his consent, that they are not excessively burdensome to him. Valasco (at number 38) agrees. He also adds that the tenant can remove the improvements he made to the leased property if he wishes, provided he can do so without damage to the property. This is also

<column-break/>

to be understood regarding such heavy expenses, as well as necessary ones, and even those that are not useful but entirely voluntary or for pleasure <note>original: "voluptuarijs"</note>, as is held in the law *But you will add* <note>Digest 19.2.19.4</note> in the section "if a tenant," and affirmed by Alvaro Valasco (at number 37). Read all these matters which were discussed extensively in Dispute 463.

When it has been specifically included in the contract that the tenant should make such-and-such improvements at his own expense, then certainly—whether they be necessary or useful—the landlord is not bound to pay for them, nor should they be deducted from the rent established hereafter, as is self-evident; for an agreement makes the law between the contracting parties. This is the sense of the two laws cited in the first place, and Law 24, cited above, clearly establishes this.

<margin>4</margin> However, when property is handed over with a general agreement that "the property shall be improved by the tenant," and it is not specified that it be at his own expense, some (whom Valasco cites at number 34) assert that the landlord is not bound to pay for them. Gregory Lopez (on Law 24, final gloss) embraces this same opinion. Nevertheless, Valasco (at the cited number) affirms the contrary, and not without great probability. He argues that such an agreement does not prevent a permanent leaseholder (<term>emphyteuta</term>) from being paid for useful expenses or improvements made to the leased property, as was said in Dispute 456; it is enough that the agreement functions to bind the tenant to improve the property, but not necessarily at his own cost, as if such expenses were never to be repaid to him. I believe, however, that in similar situations in leasing, one must infer from the concurrent circumstances what the intent of the contracting parties was, and one must stand by that. In case of doubt, I would not dare to depart from the opinion of Alvaro Valasco.

<margin>5</margin> It is common, however, when a "usufructuary" <note>A person who has the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another.</note> has leased a property in which they held a usufruct for a certain time—say, for five years—and then dies, the lease contract is consequently dissolved, and the leased property returns free to the owner, according to what was said in Dispute 452. If the tenant has made any useful expenses on the leased property, is the owner bound to pay him as much as is expedient, or as much as the property is worth more because of those expenses? Valasco (at number 35) reports that some affirm nothing should be paid, led by the law *If someone [leases] a house* <note>Digest 19.2.35</note> in the section "the same is asked," the words of which regarding such a tenant are: "the same is asked, if he spent money on the farm, as if he were to enjoy it for five years, whether he receives it back." And it says he shall not receive it, because he ought to have foreseen that this [the death of the usufructuary] could happen. Thus far Ulpian, from the words of the jurist Marcellinus. And Valasco thinks Ulpian's mind failed him in that decision. He adds, however, that the Senators in Portugal <note>The high court or *Relação* of Portugal.</note> rightly decide the contrary: for it is not equitable for the owner to be enriched by the expenses of such a tenant; and because, if the usufructuary had made those useful expenses, the owner would be bound to pay their valuation to his heirs; just as a "fideicommissary" <note>A person who receives property to be held in trust for another.</note> pays for useful expenses made on property committed to his trust. Hence he says, since that decision of Ulpian rests on no solid reason, it is rightly not followed in judicial practice in Portugal, where the imperial [Roman] laws are admitted for the purpose of judging by them when there is no law or custom of the Kingdom to the contrary—since they are considered to be based on the best reason, as is held in Book 2 of the *Ordinances*, Title 5. I, however, think that Ulpian decides no such thing there...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal rights of tenants regarding expenses and introduces the timing of rent payments. It specifically examines the opinions of the Roman jurist Ulpian regarding when a landlord's heir is liable for a tenant's improvements and moves into Dispute 497, which covers "tacit mortgages"—legal liens the landlord holds over the tenant’s goods and crops to ensure the rent is paid.</meta>

[Ul]pian, or had even entered his mind. But, since the expenses incurred on a leased property by a tenant over a five-year period are usually much greater—given the hope of enjoying them for the full five years—than the value of the utility that remains in the property after the lease, Ulpian asks whether the heir of the usufructuary <note>An "usufructuary" is someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property owned by someone else.</note> is bound to pay the tenant for that increase, or even for the total expenses if they brought no utility to the property.

And he responds that the heir is not bound, because the tenant ought to have foreseen that this could happen: namely, that the usufructuary might die before the five-year period ended, thus terminating the lease contract. Ulpian says nothing, however, in comparison to the owner, regarding whether the owner is bound to pay the landlord the value of the utility that accrued to the estate from those expenses. That this was Ulpian’s intention is clear, both from the preceding passages, which discussed the heir of a usufructuary landlord, and from the following passages, in which the same Ulpian held that if the landlord leased the thing not as a usufructuary but as the owner, and thereby deceived the tenant, then his heir is bound to pay the expenses of the lease.

<margin>6</margin> A tenant can recover **useful or necessary expenses** by retaining the leased property until they are paid. For to whomever an "action" <note>An "action" is a legal right to sue or bring a case to court.</note> is granted, the right to retain the thing in which the expenses were made is much more strongly granted, according to the law *If on a plot* <note>original: "l. si in area," Digest 12.6.40</note> in the Digest on *the recovery of what was not owed*. And so the Portuguese law, Book 4, Ordinance Title 50, § 1, grants a borrower the right to retain a borrowed thing for expenses made upon it until they are paid. If the rent has not been paid, the tenant can recover expenses by "compensation" <note>In legal terms, "compensation" refers to offsetting a debt—effectively deducting the repair costs from the rent owed.</note> made against the rent itself. If, however, the rent has already been paid, he can recover them through an action based on the lease, as is established in the laws *The owner of the gardens*, section 1, *But you will add*, the section *If a tenant*, and the law *A farmer* <note>original: "l. dñs hortorum... l. sed addes... l. colonus," referring to Digest 19.2.55, 19.2.13.8, and 19.2.61</note> in the Digest on *Leasing*; likewise in the law *The aediles*, the section *In whatever way* <note>original: "l. ædiles §. qualicunque," Digest 43.8.2.38</note> on *Public roads*; and this is affirmed by Alvaro Valasco in Question 25, cited at the very end.

## When the rent of a leased thing is to be paid: And whether the things brought onto it, as well as the crops, are tacitly mortgaged for the payment of rent and for any deterioration of the leased property.

### DISPUTE 497.

### SUMMARY.

1. *At what time the rent of a leased thing is to be paid.*
2. *Rent to be paid in crops must be paid after the crops are gathered, unless otherwise agreed.*
3. *What is required for the ownership of a sold thing to pass to the buyer.*
4. *The crops of a leased property are tacitly mortgaged to the landlord for the payment of rent.*
*The same applies to things brought into or onto the leased estate. Number 5.*
5. *What is required for goods brought into or onto a leased estate to be tacitly subject to a mortgage. And what of things brought in permanently that were later transported from elsewhere. Number 7.*
6. *However, these limits do not apply to the goods of others brought in, number 8, with the declaration as stated there.*

Regarding the first point, just as we said in Dispute 451 concerning a "ground rent" <note>original: "pēfione emphyteutica," referring to a long-term or perpetual lease.</note>, so

<column-break/>

now must we speak concerning the rent for a leased thing. Namely, if a time was expressed in the contract in which the rent was to be paid, the contract must be upheld. If, however, nothing was expressed, the custom of the place must be upheld, as held in Law 4, Title 8, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinance in Title 48, § "But if..." If there is no certain custom from which it is clear that payment is usually made earlier, it is to be paid at the end of the year. So it is held in Law 4 of the Code on the same subject; and all these things are clearly gathered from the law *Always in stipulations* <note>original: "l. semper in ftipulationibus," Digest 50.17.34</note> in the Digest on *Rules of Law*, because the fact that rent is paid at the end of the year is the minimum that can be chosen, and is the more "benign" option in comparison to the debtor. That rule teaches that this path should be followed when nothing else has been agreed upon and the custom of the region holds nothing else; and the law *Always in obscure matters* <note>original: "l. semper in obscuris," Digest 50.17.9</note> prescribes the same thing to be done. All these same points are affirmed by the final gloss on the law *A house* <note>original: "l. ædem," Code 4.65.1</note> on *Leasing*, and the common doctors whom Gregory Lopez cites and follows in the aforementioned Law 4; Navarro in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 198; Panormitanus <note>Panormitanus was the nickname of Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> on the chapter *On account of sterility* regarding leases, number 18; and Antonio Gómez in Volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 13.

When, however, a thing is leased for many years for a certain annual rent, and it is not expressed when the rent should be paid, nor does the custom of the region have anything certain, then the rent for that year is to be paid at the end of each year; for those are considered distinct leases for each of those years, according to the laws *We ought to know* and *In many [stipulations]* <note>original: "l. scire debemus & l. plurib.," Digest 45.1.4 and 45.1.29</note> and as Gregory Lopez affirms in the place cited above. When the rent is to be paid in crops, and nothing else has been agreed, it is to be paid after the crops have been collected, and not before; so says Gregory Lopez there, according to the law *To Firmius*, the final section <note>original: "l. Firmio. §. vlt.," Digest 36.2.12</note>. Likewise, when from the cause for which the rent is given, from the person, or from other circumstances, it is understood that the contracting parties intended for the rent or part of it to be paid before the lease contract ended, then it must be paid at the time the matter requires, and it is presumed that the contracting parties intended this. So says Panormitanus in the place cited above, number 9, and Navarro, number 198. If there is a doubt whether a tenant (the same applies to a permanent leaseholder) has paid the rents of past years, and he produces receipts by which he proves he paid for three continuous years, he is considered to have paid for all the years preceding those three, unless the contrary is proved against him. Thus proves the law *Whosoever* <note>original: "l. quicunque," Code 10.22.3</note> in the Code on *Public Receipts*, and the common opinion of the doctors affirms it, which Antonio Gómez cites and follows. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

<margin>Question</margin> Regarding the second point, to begin with the crops of the leased property, it must be observed: as was said in Dispute 338, for the ownership of a sold thing to pass to the buyer, it is not enough for the sold thing to be delivered to him, but it is further necessary that the price be paid, or that the buyer offer it and it be the fault of the seller that it is not received, or that sureties or pledges for its payment be presented by the buyer and accepted by the seller, or certainly that the seller considers the price as paid by trusting the buyer. Thus the gloss on the law *If a common slave*, at the section *I leased*, on the word *to do* <note>original: "l. si feruus communis §. locaui, verb. facere," Digest 47.2.52.2</note>, and Bartolus, and the common opinion which Alvaro Valasco cites and asserts in *On the interest of emphyteusis*, question 20, number 15...

It also introduces the concept of "tacit mortgages," where crops and personal property brought onto a leasehold serve as legal security for the landlord.</summary>
