<meta>This page continues the discussion within Dispute 497 regarding the legal relationship between a landlord and tenant, focusing specifically on the "tacit mortgage"—a legal lien the law automatically grants a landlord over a tenant's goods to ensure rent is paid.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 497.

[The previous author] had held that the natural fruits <note>original: "fructus naturales"; in legal terms, these are the organic products of the land, such as crops or livestock.</note> of a leased property—such as apples, wheat, wine, etc.—do not belong to the tenant in terms of ownership until he pays the rent to the landlord, or offers it, or it is considered paid through the methods explained in the section on sales. This would apply even if such fruits have already been harvested from the leased field, or even carried into the tenant's house, or sold and delivered by him to others, as was discussed in the cited dispute regarding purchased items. Instead, in the meantime, while the price is not paid, ownership belongs to the owner of the estate, just as it did before the fruits were separated from the land. For this opinion, I do not see any other pressing legal argument than that the reasoning for sales and leases appears to be the same. To me, however, a different view is far more 

<margin>4</margin> persuasive: the opinion of Alvaro Valasco <note>original: "Alua. Valaf."; a 16th-century Portuguese jurist known for his work on legal rights and emphyteusis (long-term leases).</note> in the same place. He argues that by the very fact that such fruits have been separated from the land, ownership belongs to the tenant, even if he has not paid the rent. The landlord possesses only a **tacit mortgage** <note>A "tacit mortgage" (hypotheca) is a legal lien that exists by operation of law, even if not explicitly written into a contract.</note> on them to ensure the rent is paid. First, because there is no text that establishes this for leasing; that which is specifically decreed for sales—as an exception to the common rule of law that ownership is acquired through title and delivery—should not be extended further than what is found defined in the law. Therefore, there is truly no argument to be made here from the similarity between sales and leases. Second, because the natural fruits of a leased thing, even if not subjected to an express mortgage by agreement of the parties, are nonetheless tacitly subjected to a mortgage by provision of law for the payment of rent. This is found in the law *in fructibus* in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the Digest is a massive collection of Roman legal juristic writings compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding when a pledge or mortgage is created, the words of which are: *in rural estates, the fruits that grow there are tacitly understood to be a pledge to the owner of the leased land, even if it was not specifically agreed upon.* This is also found in the law *si in lege* in the section on "tenant," where it is expressed that this remains true even if the tenant had sublet the field to someone else. For the fruits gathered by the second tenant are similarly subject to a tacit mortgage to the owner of the field for the rent owed to him. However, no one can have a pledge on his own property, as stated in the law *neque pignus* in the Digest's rules of law. Therefore, the owner of the land does not have ownership of the fruits after they are separated from the land, but only a tacit mortgage, or even an express one if it was agreed between the contracting parties. It is added that in a sale, the sold item is said to be retained *as if* it were a pledge for the unpaid part of the price, as held in the law *Iulianus*, yet it is not truly a pledge. But in a lease, the fruits of the leased thing are not called "as if" a pledge by the cited laws, but a *true pledge* for the 

<margin>5</margin> rent. In the section *locavi* <note>meaning "I have leased"</note> of the Digest regarding theft, the owner of the land is granted an **action for theft** <note>An "action" is the right to sue; an action for theft allowed the victim to seek penalties against the thief.</note> if the fruits are carried away from the estate secretly and against his will before the rent is paid. However, theft cannot be committed against one’s own property by the person taking it, since theft is defined as the "handling of another's property." It must be said that under the term "another's property" in the definition of theft, items belonging to someone else are included—not just by ownership, but also those held as a pledge. This is clear not only from that section *locavi*, where those fruits had been expressly subjected to a pledge for the payment of rent by the agreement of the parties, but also expressly from law 3 in the Digest regarding pledge actions. It is surprising that Bartolus <note>A highly influential 14th-century Italian law professor.</note> cited this in 

<column-break/>

confirmation of his own aforementioned opinion.

<margin>5</margin> Likewise, goods brought into a leased property <note>original: "invecta et illata"; items carried in, like furniture, or driven in, like livestock.</note> are tacitly subjected to a mortgage to the owner of the leased estate for the payment of rent, and also for repairing damages caused to the leased thing by the tenant's fault. However, this distinction is applied: if the leased estate is **urban**, such as a house, then whatever was brought into it—whether the owner who leased it knew they were brought in or not—is subject to the mortgage. But if it is a **rural** estate, then only those things brought into that estate with the owner's knowledge are subject to the mortgage, not those brought in without his knowledge. This is held in the law *certi* in the Code <note>The Code of Justinian, a collection of imperial laws.</note> joined with the final law of the Code regarding the causes of a pledge, and the law *item quia* regarding pacts, and the section *et serviana* in the Institutes <note>A textbook for law students in the 6th century.</note> on actions. These sources also express that such goods are subject to a mortgage for damages caused to the leased thing. All these same points are expressly held in Law 5, Title 8, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], and the common opinion of the doctors <note>Legal scholars.</note> agrees. Furthermore, it has been explained in Dispute 439 that items brought into a property by a primary tenant are mortgaged to the first landlord for the rent owed to him.

<margin>6</margin> Observe, however, that for goods brought into a leased estate to be tacitly subjected to a mortgage in the manner explained, it is necessary that they be brought in with the **intent to remain there permanently**—that is, not temporarily, but for as long as the lease lasts. This applies whether the intent is later changed and they are removed or even sold, or not. This is held in the law *in praediis* in the Digest regarding pledges, and is affirmed by the Gloss on the law *certi* on the word "brought in," as well as by Alvaro Valasco and Gregory Lopez <note>Gregorio López de Tovar, the primary commentator on Spanish law in this era.</note> in the cited Law 5. From this, he says that Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, a famous medieval jurist.</note> infers that merchandise brought into a leased house by a tenant for the purpose of being sold is not tacitly mortgaged, because it is not brought in to stay there permanently. For that reason, the buyers of such goods are not bound to pay the rent or the costs of the house's deterioration if the tenant fails to do so.

<margin>7 Decision on Doubts</margin> Is it only those goods found on the leased property at the time the rent is demanded (or when compensation for damage is sought) that are tacitly mortgaged? Or does it also include those that were once brought in permanently but are no longer there? The common opinion of the scholars affirms that even these are tacitly mortgaged. The current possessors of these goods can be sued so that, in the event of the tenant's default, they may pay the rent and the damages caused to the leased property from those goods, as reported by Gregory Lopez. However, that law of Castile seems to establish only that those goods found at the time the rent or damage is demanded are mortgaged, as Gregory Lopez notes. Nevertheless, one should not depart from the common opinion, which is more in harmony with the common law. Nor should anyone object using the law *est differentia* from the Digest, which states that if certain slaves are specifically obligated for the payment of rent or damage, they cannot be **manumitted** <note>Set free from slavery.</note> (as if manumission would free them from the burden of the mortgage). However, if they are only tacitly obligated, they can be manumitted, provided they are not held on the leased property at the time the rent is demanded or before the damage to the property has been settled.

<summary>This page discusses the "tacit mortgage," a legal lien landlords hold over a tenant's crops and personal property to secure rent. It explores legal debates over ownership of harvested crops and distinguishes between urban and rural properties regarding which goods are automatically subject to this lien.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of leases (locationes) within Luis de Molina’s "On Contracts." It concludes the discussion on the landlord's right to a "tacit mortgage" over goods on the property and begins a new Disputation regarding the penalties for tenants who refuse to return property once a lease has expired.</meta>

Luis de Molina / On Contracts

...relinquishment. Let no one, I say, object to this: because it was specifically decreed in favor of liberty.

**Alien goods** <note>original: "Bona aliena"; goods belonging to someone other than the tenant.</note>, even if they are brought onto a re-leased property, are not considered tacitly mortgaged for the rent or for the deterioration of the leased thing. Indeed, an alien thing, which in no way belongs to the person who would obligate it, cannot be expressly subjected to a pledge or mortgage. This is gathered from the law [citations of Roman and Canon law]. These laws are limited unless the owner of the goods knew and permitted the tenant to bring them onto the leased property. In that case, they are deemed to have contracted a tacit mortgage. Gregorio Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note>, in the cited law, rightly says that doctors of law commonly affirm the contrary to that interpretation, unless fraud is deemed to have intervened on the part of the owner against the landlord. This occurs when the owner silently watches his property be brought into a leased estate so that the landlord, relying on that pledge, would not seek the rent or damages in a timely manner. For simply by seeing his property brought in and remaining silent, he is not deemed to intend to subject it to a mortgage; yet such intention would be necessary to subject it to a pledge.

The cited Law 5 prescribes that when a landlord wants to take goods brought onto a leased estate as a pledge for unpaid rent or for damage caused to the property, and the tenant is not present, he must do so in the presence of neighbors. He must create a written inventory of what was found there in their presence, so that no fraud is committed against the tenant. This law agrees in part with the law regarding leases which states that if a house or granary is leased and the tenant does not appear, nor pays the rent for two full years, then at the landlord's request, it can be opened in the presence of public officials and an inventory made, so that the landlord may finally be paid. Regarding how execution <note>Legal enforcement or seizure.</note> against a tenant and the goods on the property for unpaid rent should be carried out under **Portuguese law** <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, this was discussed in Disputation 489.

### When the lease period is finished, under what penalty is the tenant bound to restore the leased property to the landlord requesting it. And whether the tenant has a right of preference or retention for the same price. And when, by continuation, the contract is deemed tacitly extended, and for how long.

# DISPUTATION 498.

## S U M M A R Y.

<margin>1</margin> When a lease is finished, what penalty a tenant is punished with if he does not restore the property. n. 1.
<margin>2</margin> And whether the same applies to a borrower <note>original: "commodatario"; someone using an item for free.</note>, a depositary <note>original: "depositario"; someone holding an item for safekeeping.</note>, and others. n. 2.

<margin>1</margin> When the lease time has ended, if the landlord (who leased the property as its owner) or his heirs request it, and the tenant or his heirs do not restore it but instead contend the matter in court, they are punished with a penalty of the appraised value of the thing in addition to the thing itself, once a final judgment is rendered. However, it is different if, having begun to contend, they restore it before such a sentence is passed. <margin>2</margin> The same penalty applies to a borrower or his heirs if they do not restore the thing at the end of the term, but fight it in court until a final judgment. The same should be said of a depositary, as held in Law 12, Title 10, Part 7; and indeed of anyone else who does not possess the thing as owner but holds it in the name of another, such as a **tutor** or **curator** <note>Legal guardians for minors or the incapacitated.</note>. This is affirmed by Gregorio Lopez. Thus it is held regarding the tenant and others in the Code [of Justinian] and the Portuguese Ordinances. The landlord, borrower, or their heirs can demand this penalty either after the final sentence is given, or while the lawsuit is being contested, but under the condition that a final judgment is eventually rendered. <margin>3</margin> Furthermore, for this penalty to apply, the landlord must demand the leased property through an "action on the lease." ### Second Treatise, Disputation 49.

<margin>4</margin>...resists until a final definitive sentence is passed, as noted by the commentaries on the cited laws and Gregório López <note>original: "Greg. Lopez"; a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the Siete Partidas</note> in Law 18, cited gloss 3, and as indicated in the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "ordinationes Lusitanæ"; the Manueline or Philippine Ordinances that governed Portuguese law</note> mentioned above in section 3, in agreement with the law *si quis conductionis* <note>original: "if anyone [seeks] a lease"</note> in the Code on Leases. 

From the very fact that a landlord seeks the return of the property that was leased, he is presumed to be the owner based on the prior lease, unless the contrary is established elsewhere, as Bartolus <note>A foundational medieval Italian jurist</note> notes along with Gregório López. However, he does not sufficiently prove the property is his simply by proving he leased it, as held in the law *ad probationem* <note>original: "for the purpose of proof"</note> in the Code on Leases. 

Furthermore, the heirs of a tenant or a borrower <note>original: "commodatarij"; someone who holds property through a 'commodatum' or a loan for use without payment</note> will incur the explained penalty if they do not restore the leased or borrowed property to the landlord or lender when it is demanded, but instead wait for a definitive sentence—provided, however, they know the property was leased or borrowed. It is different if they are ignorant of this, as Gregório López rightly says, following Bartolus. 

When a landlord or lender seeks property as if it were leased or borrowed, and the tenant or borrower contends that the property is their own and wishes to retain it for that reason, they are not heard. Instead, they are compelled to restore it immediately to the landlord or lender, while their right is reserved so that after restitution they may bring an action and prove the property belongs to them. This is held in the law *si quis conductionis* and in the Portuguese Ordinances, section 3. 

When a third party contends that the leased or borrowed property is theirs and asks the judge not to restore it to the landlord, then the Portuguese Ordinance (section last) rightly decrees: if the item is movable and the one who leased or lent it is suspect, or lacks sufficient goods to pay safely if it is proven to belong to the other, the item should be placed in **sequestration** <note>original: "sequestrum"; held by a neutral third party until the dispute is resolved</note> with a trustworthy person, and that third party should be heard summarily to prove the item is theirs.

<margin>5</margin>What has been said so far does not prevent a tenant from being able to retain the leased property until they are paid for the **useful expenses** <note>original: "vtiles expensæ"; improvements made by the tenant that increased the value of the property</note> made upon it, as was stated at the end of Disputation 496. Nor do they prevent a tenant who acquires ownership of the property through some clear title after the lease began—whereby the landlord loses ownership—from safely and without penalty retaining it. In such a case, the tenant cannot be compelled to restore it to the landlord, because by **equity** <note>original: "epicheiam"; the principle of interpreting law according to its spirit rather than its literal letter</note> this is judged not to be covered by the cited laws. 

Thus, in Portugal, as reported and defended by Álvaro Valasco <note>original: "Aluar. Valaf."; a famous Portuguese legal authority</note> in Consultation 42: when, after the leasing of a property, an execution of the landlord’s goods was made at the request of a creditor, and the leased property was sold at a public auction and bought by the tenant, and the landlord later sought the property through a lease action, demanding the tenant restore it to him so he could then dispute it with him, it was judged (despite the aforementioned laws) that it should not be restored. Read those points in the cited consultation by Álvaro Valasco *On Confirmations*. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

<margin>6</margin>Regarding the second point: One who has leased a house or other property does not have a privilege such that, when the time for which he leased it ends, he is preferred over other tenants for the same or even a higher price. Instead, the landlord can freely remove him

<column-break/>

and lease that property to another. This is held in the law *ne cui* in the Code on Leases, Law 18, Title 8, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 57 at the beginning. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez <note>original: "Ant. Gomez"; a 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> reports and follows in Volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 3. 

An exception is made for **public lands** <note>original: "prædijs communibus"; lands belonging to a municipality</note> or those of the treasury; in these cases, the tenant is preferred over any other tenant, provided that if another offers a higher rent, he himself is willing to pay that increase. This is held in the final penal law of the Code on Leasing Civil Lands, Book 11, and is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez (cited at number 5) reports and follows. 

The first chapter *On Leases* and Law 5 of the final title, Part 2, prohibit **scholastics** <note>original: "scholastici"; specifically university students and teachers</note>, masters, or doctors from leasing houses in which other scholastics or masters live, until those living there wish to leave them. And it should be added for each place whether this is observed in practice or if there is some other privilege of preference granted to certain tenants.

<margin>8</margin>In Portugal, in the cited Title 57, sections 1 and 2, it is decreed that when a house is leased for a certain time, the landlord is bound, thirty days before that time ends, to warn the tenant to vacate the house at the end of the lease. Or, if the landlord wishes the tenant to continue in the contract if he chooses, he is bound thirty days before the contract ends to ask whether he wishes to persevere further in the contract and retain the leased house. If the tenant gives no response within three days, the landlord can compel him to persevere in the contract for the entire following year. But if the landlord does neither of these two things thirty days before the lease ends, then it is at the tenant's option either to persevere in the contract for the following year—even against the landlord's will (unless the landlord wants the house for his own residence)—or to leave the house and not continue the contract. So much for the second point.

<margin>9</margin>Regarding the third point: If a tenant, with the landlord’s knowledge and sufferance, continues in the leased property after the time for which it was leased has expired, the contract is considered prolonged by the **tacit consent** <note>original: "tacito consensu"</note> of both parties, but with this distinction: 

If the leased property is **urban** <note>original: "urbanum"</note>, such as a house, the contract is only considered prolonged until one of the contracting parties wishes to withdraw from it. But if the leased property is **rural** <note>original: "rusticum"</note>, the contract is considered prolonged only for the following year, even if the first contract was made for a five-year period or for many years. If, at the end of that following year, the tenant again continues in the same property with the landlord's knowledge and sufferance, the contract is similarly considered prolonged for the next year, and so on, until at the end of some year of such tacit extension, a departure from the contract occurs, with the tenant leaving the property or the landlord evicting the tenant. 

This is expressly held in the law *item quæritur*, section *qui impleto*, joined with the following law in the Digest on Leases, and Law 20, Title 8, Part 5. This is affirmed by Gregório López there, and Álvaro Valasco *On the Law of Emphyteusis* <note>original: "de iur. emphy."; a type of long-term ground lease or perpetual lease</note>, question 20, number 20, and Antonio Gómez, Volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 3, number 15, as well as the common opinion of the doctors they cite. <meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 49 regarding the legal mechanisms of leasing. Specifically, it addresses the conditions under which a lease is considered "tacitly" renewed—meaning renewed by the silence or inaction of both parties—and whether this applies to specialized long-term contracts like emphyteusis.</meta>

### Luis de Molina: On Contracts

A contract of leasing and hiring is completed by mutual consent; thus, a renewal is certainly not considered to have occurred by tacit consent on the part of the landlord unless he, being aware and acting with foresight, allows the tenant to remain on the estate. Therefore, if the landlord should fall into a state of insanity at the time the first contract ended, or if he were already dead, a renewal of the contract is not considered to have been made by the tacit consent of such a landlord, as held in the law *qui ad certum* <note>original: "the person who [leases] for a fixed [time]"; a reference to the Digest of Roman Law regarding leases</note> in the Digest on Leases. However, it can certainly be made by the tacit consent of the heirs, if the heirs, knowing the situation, allow the tenant to remain on the leased rural estate.

<margin>10</margin> However, as to how much time a tenant's persistence on a rural estate after the contract has ended is sufficient for the landlord—knowing he remains there—to be considered to have tacitly renewed the contract for the following year: this is not defined in common law <note>The *Ius Commune*, the standard legal system based on Roman and Canon law used across Europe at the time</note>. Instead, it is left to the discretion of the judge to be decided, as affirmed by Alvaro Valasco <note>original: "Alu. Val."</note> at number 20 as cited, Antonio Gómez <note>original: "Ant. Gom."</note> as above at number 16, and Gregório López <note>A famous Spanish jurist</note> on the cited Law 20 at the word *tres dies* [three days], along with Bartolus and others. However, by the cited Law 20, it is specifically distinguished in the Kingdom of Castile that three days are sufficient. Gregório López, in the cited gloss, reports that Odofredus and Baldus asserted the contrary, saying that two or three days are not enough, but that a "competent time" is necessary. Antonio Gómez, however, at number 16, says the best advice is for a contracting party who does not want the contract extended beyond the time of the first contract to make a formal protest before the contract ends, stating that they do not want it renewed, and to have that protest formally delivered to the other party. This is because in matters that depend on the mind's intent, a protest to the contrary is sufficient to prevent a tacit consent from being assumed, according to various laws he cites; the matter is quite clear in itself.

<margin>Doubt 11</margin> Whether, in a lease for ten years, and generally in an emphyteutic contract <note term="emphyteusis">A long-term land lease where the tenant (emphyteuta) has many of the rights of an owner, provided they improve the land and pay a yearly rent</note>, if the contract ends and the owner, knowing the situation, allows the tenant to remain without taking the emphyteutic estate away from him, he is considered to have renewed the contract by tacit consent. <margin>Decision</margin> It must be said that, without a doubt, he is not considered to have renewed the emphyteutic contract specifically as an emphyteutic contract. First, because renewal by tacit consent, according to the cited laws, is only for one year and does not grant "useful ownership" <note term="useful ownership">The right to use and profit from property, as opposed to 'direct ownership' held by the ultimate landlord</note>; whereas an emphyteutic contract is not just for one year, and through it, useful ownership is transferred. Second, because a written document is essential to the substance of an emphyteutic contract—either entirely or for the most part—as was seen in Disputation 447. Therefore, bare consent, not only tacit but even expressed, is not sufficient for renewing an emphyteutic contract into the status of an emphyteutic contract. And in this, Gregório López agrees on the cited Law 20 at the word *entendiese* [it should be understood], along with other doctors.

<margin>Doubt</margin> However, whether it should be considered renewed in the status of a different contract—that is, as a one-year lease—if the emphyteutic estate is a rural one. Gregório López, as cited above, inclines toward it being renewed. <margin>Decision 12</margin> Nevertheless, the contrary must be affirmed along with Antonio Gómez at the cited number 16, and with Alvaro Valasco also at number 20, and the common opinion of the doctors. This is because a renewal is an extension of the preceding contract, and thus into a new part of a contract of the same nature and species as the preceding one, not into a contract of another nature and species. Nor should the knowledge and patience of someone regarding an estate, to the use of which

<column-break/>

he previously had a right, be considered a tacit consent by legal presumption, except for a use of the same nature as the preceding one.

<margin>Doubt 13</margin> There is a greater doubt when the first contract for a lease of a rural estate for a short time was suspended so that a written document could be finalized. If the landlord, knowing the situation, allowed the tenant to stay in that estate after the contract's time ended, is he considered to have tacitly renewed the contract for the following year? Antonio Gómez, at the cited number 16, denies it, and this is the common opinion of the doctors, as even Gregório López admits above, based on certain very ambiguous and obscure words in the law *item quaeritur* <note>original: "likewise it is asked"</note> at the final section in the Digest on Leases, which are commonly explained this way. And since, when the first contract was suspended so that a written document could be finalized, the parties were not satisfied with mere mutual consent expressed outwardly, it does not seem to be renewed by tacit consent alone. <margin>Decision</margin> Gregório López, in the cited place, inclines to the opposite side, led by the reasoning that just as—according to the teaching of Bartolus—even if the first contract had been celebrated and fortified by a formal stipulation, it would be considered renewed by tacit consent alone; so, although the first contract was suspended for the completion of a document, it could be renewed by tacit consent. This is because, just as a written document is not essential to the nature of a lease, neither is it essential to the nature of its renewal. And this opinion seems sufficiently probable to me. Since no one can doubt that the first contract can be renewed without a written document by the express mutual consent of the parties, because a written document is not required for such a renewal, why then can it not also be renewed by the tacit consent of the same parties?

<margin>14</margin> The renewal of a lease contract by the tacit consent of the parties also takes place in the estates of a community or a republic <note>Referring to municipal or public lands</note>, as held in the law *item quaeritur* in the section *qui impleto* at the clause *eadem causa* <note>original: "for the same reason"</note> in the Digest on Leases. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Gregório López and Antonio Gómez (in the cited chapter 3, number 15) report and follow. In such cases, there must be the knowledge and patience of those who administer those lands and whose duty it is to lease them. The same applies to the estates of the Church, hospitals, and wards <note>Minors or orphans under legal guardianship</note>: for the knowledge and patience of those who administer and lease them is sufficient for the contract to be considered prolonged, as the cited doctors assert.

<margin>15</margin> However, in the case of moveable things <note>Items like tools or furniture</note> or self-moving things <note>Livestock or animals</note>, the rule from the law *item quaeritur* at the section *qui impleto* does not apply, as the final gloss on the last words there affirms, along with the doctors generally. In fact, the gloss says there that if the tenant does not restore the thing when the contract's time is finished, he is considered to be committing theft. This is how the gloss itself, Bartolus, and others (whom Gregório López follows in the cited Law 20, gloss 1) understand it—unless the tenant believes the landlord will approve of it. This is always to be presumed if the thing is of a type that is customarily leased and there are no circumstances that would suggest the contrary. In fact, I believe that if someone has leased a beast of burden for a journey to a certain place and returned, and then, with the landlord’s knowledge and patience, makes another journey either to the same place or another, it is considered a tacit renewal of the contract for that other journey, to the extent that the landlord cannot withdraw from the contract before the appropriate time for returning from that other place.

<margin>16</margin> In the events in which it has been said that a tacit renewal of a lease contract is considered to have been made, it must be understood that it is considered made for the same annual [rent]...

## Under what circumstances the landlord can expel the tenant before the contract time has finished:

### DISPUTATION CCCCXCIX.
->SUMMARY<-

1 *In what cases a landlord can expel a tenant before the finished time of the contract, even if there is a penalty clause, and numbers 5, 11, and 12.*
2 *An oath does not extend beyond that which is contained in the contract.*
3 *The understanding of the section "between the landlord" in the law "Likewise I ask" in the Digest on Leases, others being rejected.*
4 *The understanding of the law "When the owners" in the Digest on Leases.*
5 *If the landlord needs the leased house, he can expel the tenant from it.*
*This is expanded, even if he needs only a part, and his necessity increased afterward, number 10.*
*This is limited, as in number 8.*

<margin>Question</margin>
**IN** the following events, the landlord can expel the tenant from the rented property before the finished
1 time of the contract. First, if he † does not pay the rent <note>original: "pensionem"</note> at the due time, according to those things said in Disputation 497, the law *aedem* <note>original: "the house"</note> in the Code on Leases, Law 5 at the beginning of Title 8, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>The laws of the Kingdom of Portugal</note>, Title 58, Section 1. The law *in quaero*, section *inter locatorem* <note>original: "between the landlord"</note> in the Digest on Leases creates no small difficulty in this matter. For when it had been agreed by a stipulation between the landlord and the tenant that if the landlord expelled the tenant from the leased property before the finished time of the contract, he would pay ten to the tenant as a penalty; and similarly, if the tenant departed from the rented property before the same finished time of the contract, he would pay ten to the landlord as a penalty; it was asked: Whether, when the tenant has not paid the rent for two full years, he can be expelled by the landlord without fear of the penalty. And Paulus the jurisconsult <note>A famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> responds in the affirmative. Because, although nothing was expressly stated in the penalty stipulation regarding the payment of rent, nevertheless it is likely (as if he were to say, it must be judged through *epikeia* <term>epicheia: a legal principle of interpreting the law by its spirit or equity when the literal letter seems too harsh</term> of the laws, and as an interpreter of other continuous dispositions) it had been so agreed regarding not expelling the farmer within the predefined times—that is, under this tacit condition—if he complied with the rents, and cultivated as is proper (that is, by not bringing harm to the estate). And therefore, if a tenant who has not paid rent demands the penalty, he can be repelled by a plea of "malicious fraud" <note>original: "doli mali exceptione"; a Roman legal defense against someone acting in bad faith</note>. This is found there. From which text it is gathered by the way, that even if a pact exists about not expelling the tenant, and even if a penalty has been attached if he is expelled, he can nonetheless be expelled when the rent...

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts #

<column-break/>

...otherwise he does not pay, or he brings damage to the leased property; for all things are understood under that **tacit condition**, <note>A "tacit condition" is an implied agreement that exists even if it is not written down explicitly.</note> provided that he pays the rent, and thus fulfills his part of the contract, and does not cause damage to the estate, when nothing else was expressly stated in the agreement. From this, the doctors <note>original: "doctores"; referring to learned legal scholars.</note> further conclude that if he does not pay the rent—since the lease contract is held under the tacit condition that he pays—then even an **oath** † <insert>3</insert> does not extend to more than what is confirmed by the contract itself, joined with the final law of the Code regarding non-enumerated money and other rights. Thus argue Alvarus Valascus on the law of emphyteusis, <note>Emphyteusis is a type of long-term or perpetual lease of land, often used in agricultural contexts.</note> question 21, number 4; Gregorio Lopez on Law 6, Title 8, Part 5, at the words "the house falls"; and others whom they cite. However, that text creates a difficulty in the matter proposed, insofar as it seems to require the **lapse of two years** during which the tenant has not paid rent at all, before he can be expelled from the leased property. Hence, there are various interpretations by the scholars regarding this. The Gloss on the same passage, at the word "two-year period" (biennium), in its second explanation, and others—including Panormitanus on the chapter *Regarding Sterility*, under the section on leases, number 10; and Antonio Gomez in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 6—with whom Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, known as Navarrus, a prominent canon lawyer.</note> partially agrees in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 193, understand this to apply to a **long-term lease**. That is, a lease for ten years or more, in which the tenant is not expelled unless he fails to pay for a full two years; and by "canonical leniency," <note>original: "benignitate canonica"; a principle in church law allowing for mercy or flexibility.</note> he may quickly "purge his delay" <note>To "purge a delay" (purgare moram) means to pay the overdue amount immediately to stop the eviction process.</note> once the two years have passed. This interpretation is favored by the chapter *Regarding Sterility*, paragraph "Truly," at the end, where among the causes for which a tenant can be expelled before the contract ends, the last is said to be if he does not pay rent for two years and does not provide for a quick satisfaction of the debt. However, Alvarus Valascus rightly rejects this interpretation in the citation above, numbers 5 and 7, as do others. This is because a long-term lease is truly an *emphyteusis*; and an emphyteutic tenant, by civil law, is not expelled unless he fails to pay for a full **three years**, as was proven in the section on emphyteusis. Likewise, because the chapter *Regarding Sterility*, paragraph "Truly," clearly speaks of a simple lease—such as one under ten years—and it had handed down three other legitimate causes according to civil law for which a landlord can expel a tenant before the time is up, which will be discussed shortly; it is not likely that in the fourth cause it would shift the meaning of "lease" to mean a long-term one. Others, such as Bartolus and those they cite, offer a different explanation in the first interpretation of the Gloss, which they do not disprove; rather, they seem to agree with them most closely. Alvarus Valascus and Gregorio Lopez, and Covarruvias (who seems to embrace their opinion based on common law), explain the text to mean it only applies when there was a **specific agreement not to expel the tenant**, and the lease was made for more than two years. In that case, because of the agreement, <insert>3</insert> it is necessary that the tenant fail to pay for a full two years before he can be expelled. But if no such agreement was made, or if it was made but the lease was not for more than two years, he can be expelled immediately if the rent is not paid at the appointed time. Others understand that

<column-break/>

text to speak universally of a lease for a certain annual rent, whether or not an agreement was included about not expelling the tenant; however, in that paragraph, it speaks of a lease made for **more than two years**. And some, such as Navarrus and others, require that it be made for five years or more. Law 6 at the end, Title 8, Part 5, requires it be for four or five years or more—as if all these authors mean that if a lease is made for such a long time, it is necessary for the tenant to miss his annual rent for a full two-year period before he can be expelled. But if it is for a shorter time, he can be expelled immediately upon failing to pay at the set time, according to the laws cited at the beginning of this constitution. And according to these opinions, or some of them, one must interpret the chapter *Regarding Sterility*, which both requires the lapse of two years for expulsion and, moreover, by canonical leniency, allows for a quick purging of the delay once those two years have passed. Finally, some understand these opinions to mean that when a lease is for more than two years in the ways explained, once the two years pass, the tenant can be expelled without being granted any purging of the delay, except by canonical leniency. Before the two years, however, the tenant could be expelled immediately and deprived of the use of the property if he doesn't pay, but he is allowed to "purge the delay" as long as the matter is "whole"—that is, as long as the property has not yet been leased to another or the landlord hasn't taken it for his own use. This is what Alvarus Valascus says, following Baldus and others. Read also Gregorio Lopez on the cited Law 5, Gloss 1. However, Jason and Decius, cited by Valascus, argue that from the paragraph "Between Landlord," it cannot be concluded that it is ever necessary to wait for a two-year lapse of non-payment to expel a tenant. For in that section, the legal expert Paulus was responding to a specific event that had occurred and about which he was questioned, as is clear from the text itself, and he never taught that one **must** wait for a two-year lapse.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
If you ask what I think of the matter? I answer that, standing on **Civil Law** alone, excluding the chapter *Regarding Sterility* and the cited Law 6 of Castile, the opinion of Jason and Decius seems true to me. For the law *Aedem*, which was passed later, mentions nothing at all about a two-year lapse, even though it lists all the reasons a tenant can be expelled before the end of the contract; surely it would not have omitted this if a two-year period were necessary for expulsion. Indeed, the section "Between Landlord" made no mention of the two-year lapse as a necessary requirement, regardless of what Alvarus Valascus claims, as is clearly evident from the text itself. However, because a tenant cannot be effectively expelled the very moment a payment is missed if he offers the debt, but rather **stubbornness** (contumacy) in not paying is required, it was relevant in that decision to mention that the tenant had been in delay for so long—namely two years—that...

<margin>4</margin> But if you should object to us using the law *Cum domini* in the Digest regarding leases, <note>original: "l. cum domini. ff. locati"; referring to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law.</note> where it is commanded that a two-year period be expected from the point when the rent was due: setting aside other explanations of that text, it must be said, following Alvarus Valascus (cited above, number 6), that there is no mention therein of every lease in general. Rather, it concerns the leasing of **warehouses** or **houses**, and the specific circumstances mentioned there—namely, that the tenant is absent and has left the property locked. In such a case, since merchandise and the tenant's goods are usually left there, it is commanded that such warehouses and houses should not be opened until two years have passed from the time the rent was due, while the absence of the tenants continues; and that this should be done in the manner described at the end of Disputation 497.

Alvarus Valascus, along with others he cites in the aforementioned question 21, numbers 9 and 10, observes two things. First, that the landlord has his legal claim established against the tenant based on the lease contract if the tenant does not prove he has paid the rent. Therefore, it belongs to the **tenant** to prove that he paid the rent, not to the landlord to prove that it was not paid. Read what was said at the end of the first part of Disputation 397. Second, a landlord who expels a tenant for unpaid rent can, in addition, sue to recover the unpaid amounts.

<margin>5</margin> The **second circumstance** in which a landlord can expel a tenant before the end of the contract term is if he leased a house and, due to a supervening cause <note>A "supervening cause" is a new, unforeseen event that changes the situation.</note> which could not likely have been foreseen at the time of the contract, the house becomes **necessary for his own use and habitation**. This is supported by the law *Aedem* in the Code regarding leases; the chapter *Propter sterilitatem*, section *Verum* under the same title; Law 6, Title 8, Part 5; and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 58, penultimate section. This is the common opinion of the scholars, which is cited and followed by Alvarus Valascus in *On the Right of Emphyteusis*, question 22, number 3; Antonio Gomez at the cited number 6; Gregorio Lopez on the cited Law 6; Covarruvias in *Practical Questions*, chapter 30, number 3, second to last; and Navarro in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 193. <margin>6</margin> An example is given in the glosses on the word "necessary" in the cited law *Aedem*, and in the gloss on the words "was not imminent" in the cited section *Verum*, as well as in the cited Law 6: for instance, if the house in which the landlord was living **unexpectedly collapses**, or cannot be safely inhabited, and the landlord has no other house where he can comfortably live. Another example is given: if **enemies** begin to occupy that neighborhood, or some other danger arises so that his habitation in that house is not safe, and he has no other suitable house besides the one he leased. Alvarus Valascus says the same above: if, due to some sudden and urgent cause, it is necessary for him to move from the place where he was living to the one where

<column-break/>

he had the leased house, and he has no other suitable house for his own habitation. They provide another example—Portuguese Law and the Ordinances, along with the two cited glosses—if the landlord **takes a wife**, which he did not expect at the time of the contract, and the leased house is necessary for him to live with her because he has no other suitable one for that purpose. Covarruvias and other scholars commonly approve this same example. The cited Law 6 and the Portuguese Ordinances say the same if he should unexpectedly join one of his **sons or daughters in marriage**, and similarly would need the leased house for their habitation. And the Portuguese law extends this same principle to the necessity of a son or daughter living in it, regardless of where that necessity came from, or a brother or sister, and with much greater reason a father or mother. Regarding the father and mother, Antonio Gomez affirms this with Baldus at the end of the cited number 6.

I do not know, however, whether outside of Portugal, and standing solely on **Common Law**, <note>Common Law here refers to the *ius commune*, the shared Roman and Canon law of Europe, rather than English Common Law.</note> a necessity for anyone more than a son is admitted; for a father first provides a house to a son, which is seen to pertain to the duty of a father. For the Common Law only grants this privilege to a landlord due to a necessity coming upon **himself**. The necessity of persons related to the landlord—when they were already established in their own futures and it belonged to them to provide for themselves, not the landlord—is not a necessity for the "habitation of the landlord," which is what is discussed in that privilege. Nor is that privilege to be extended further than it is found to be granted, especially since it is "odious" <note>In legal terms, an "odious" rule is one that is restrictive or burdensome to a party—in this case, the tenant.</note> in comparison to the tenant, who by force of the lease contract has a right to live in that house and not be expelled from it. I do not believe that, setting aside that privilege and the provision of human law, one could be expelled even for the necessity of the landlord himself. However, given that provision, since contracts are considered initiated according to the provisions of the law and the customs of the place, **no injury is done to the tenant** if, in cases expressed by the law, he is expelled from the house.

Antonio Gomez rightfully provides another example at the cited number 6: if the landlord attains a **dignity** <note>A "dignity" refers to a high office, title, or ecclesiastical position.</note> because of which he requires a larger household, and for that reason the leased house is necessary for his habitation. Law 6 also provides another example: namely, if the landlord's son is **created a knight**; because perhaps (as Gregorio Lopez says there), according to the ancient custom of Spain, a son created a knight used to live separately from his father, and for that reason needed a house. From this, Gregorio Lopez concludes that the same should be said if a son becomes a **priest** or a **lawyer**.

And Alvarus Valascus, at the cited number 3, says that in Portugal it was sometimes judged the same regarding one created a **governor** or a **judge**. However, after listing all these events with Gregorio Lopez, he adds that he does not so willingly dare to extend the Portuguese law to those cases. And much less would I judge that the provisions of Common Law ought to be extended to them, for the reasons we stated a little earlier regarding Common Law alone. # Ludovicus Molina on Contracts #

...cannot be inhabited by him due to some just and urgent cause, which Alvarus Valascus (in the place cited above) rightly does not approve if the landlord previously looked elsewhere than from that house. <note>original: "æde"; referring to the specific dwelling or building being leased.</note>

<margin>7</margin>
Although the leased property was subject to a mortgage <note>original: "hypothecę"; here used as a legal pledge or security for a contract.</note> for the security of the lease contract, the tenant can nevertheless be expelled from the leased property, both in this second case <note>the landlord's personal need</note> as well as in the first <note>non-payment</note> and the two following cases. This is held against several authors cited by Covarruvias (Varied Resolutions, Book 2, Chapter 15, number 4) and Alvarus Valascus (Question 22, cited number 4). The reason is that a mortgage, just like an oath, only confirms a contract within the limits of the agreement; and thus the right or mortgage by which a contract is confirmed does not extend to more than what was tacitly or expressly agreed upon in the contract. For that reason, neither an oath nor a mortgage extends to the cases expressed by law in which it is understood that the contract does not hold—as if no agreement had been made regarding them. These four cases, which we are discussing in this disputation, are of that number. Nor are the authors of the contrary opinion supported by what was defined in Disputation 490—namely, that although a buyer or any other particular successor <note>term: "particular successor" — someone who acquires a specific piece of property, such as a buyer or a recipient of a gift, as opposed to an heir who inherits an entire estate.</note> in the leased property is not bound to stand by the lease contract except in certain outcomes explained there, they are nonetheless bound to stand by it if the property was subject to a mortgage, either by a universal or particular title, for the security of the contract. This is one of the outcomes in which we said a particular successor is bound to uphold the lease contract. This, I say, does not support them. Because, as was explained in that same place, even when some particular successor succeeds in the leased property, and nothing else is applied by which that particular successor is bound to uphold the lease, the lease contract has force—but not against that particular successor, who is preferred over the tenant because he acquired a right from that particular succession. The tenant only has a right to the use of that thing; but against the landlord, against whom the tenant has a personal action for damages <note>original: "intereſſe"; the legal interest or compensation for loss.</note>, as was said there. However, since the leased property was subject to a title of mortgage for the security of the lease contract, because by that very act the tenant acquired a prior right in the leased property so that the lease contract would be upheld for him while the contract had force, a later right in the same property acquired by a particular successor cannot prejudice that right. From this, it follows that he is bound to uphold the lease contract. However, whether a universal successor <note>term: "universal successor" — an heir who steps into all the legal rights and obligations of the deceased.</note> to the landlord, such as his heir, can expel the tenant in these four cases even if the property was subject to a mortgage for the security of the contract, Covarruvias rightly affirms. This is because the heir represents the person of the deceased and succeeds to his entire right; nor in these cases is it deemed <meta>Catchword: successor</meta>

<column-break/>

that a particular successor can expel the tenant in these four cases in the same way that the heir of the landlord can expel him, even if the house was subject to the title of mortgage for the tenant for the observation of the contract. The reason is that the heir succeeds to the entire right of the landlord. Therefore, for his own necessity alone, which similarly would not have been the landlord's, he will not be able to expel the tenant, as has been said concerning the universal successor. Otherwise, when the landlord himself could have expelled him, the heir also could expel him—especially if the landlord had transferred the entire right, including the privilege of expelling in the case of his own necessity, to the particular successor. And according to these points, one must accept what Covarruvias teaches at the cited number 4, Gregorius Lopez at the cited Law 6 in the word *oſamerar*, and Alvarus Valascus in the place above at the final number.

Certainly, I would say that it must be judged from the concurrent circumstances whether the landlord intended to renounce his privilege, namely that in the event of his own necessity he can expel the tenant for habitation. For if it is likely understood that he intended to yield and renounce his right, then surely, since he could validly do so because it is a renunciation of a private privilege and benefit, it must be judged that he cannot expel the tenant. But if it is likely not so understood, at least because the matter is doubtful, he can expel him, as Covarruvias and Gregorius Lopez rightly think. For not only when the tenant is at fault can he be expelled in a case excepted or permitted by law, with that pact added to the lease contract being no impediment, but also when no fault of his intervenes—as is clear in the third case to be explained immediately: namely, when the leased house begins to threaten ruin and needs swift repair. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the four legal circumstances under which a landlord may break a lease agreement. It concludes the second case (the landlord's urgent need), details the third (necessary repairs) and fourth (tenant's misconduct), and then debates whether these rules apply to all types of property and how they affect rent payments.</meta>

### Second Treatise. Disputation 499. ###

<margin>10</margin>
...added to the lease contract, it is understood that the landlord intended to renounce this outcome granted by express law. Furthermore, the landlord will be able to expel the tenant even if, at the time of the lease, he lacked some part of the house he was leasing, but later his necessity increased quite unexpectedly; this is according to Barbatias, as cited by Alvarus Valascus in question 22, number 9. Likewise, the landlord has the right to expel the tenant due to the landlord's unexpected necessity, even if the tenant is a student <note>original: "scholasticus"; students in university towns often held significant legal protections and privileges.</note> or another privileged person, who nevertheless could not expel the landlord from his own house. Thus says Alvarus Valascus in the same place, number 5, against certain authors whom he cites; for the general determination of the laws granting this privilege to landlords also includes privileged persons among tenants.

However, Baldus and Antonius Gomez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 3, at the end, number 6) note very well that since the power to expel a tenant in the case of the landlord's supervening necessity is a privilege granted by human law—which, without the specific provision of the law, would have no force—it should not be extended further than what is found to be granted by law. Therefore, since it is only found to be granted regarding houses, it ought not be extended to other estates <note>term: "praedia" — a general term for landed property, including farms and rural estates.</note>.

<margin>11</margin>
The third event in which the landlord can expel the tenant is when the house, after it has been leased, begins to require necessary repairs <note>original: "refectione necessaria"</note> that cannot be carried out while the tenant is living in it. This is found in the law *Eadem*, Code: *On Leasing*, the chapter *Propter sterilitatem*, section *Verum*, in the same title; and Law 6, Title 8, Part 5; and Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 9, sections 5 and 3; and the common opinion of the doctors affirms this. However, once the repair is finished, the landlord is bound to restore the house to the tenant so that he may finish the time of the entire contract; so it is held in the cited section 3, and with the Gloss and Bartolus on the law *Si duo*, section *Cum inquilinus*, Digest: *As You Possess*, as affirmed by Gregorius Lupus on the cited Law 6.

<margin>12</margin>
The fourth event in which a landlord can expel a tenant is when the tenant abuses the leased property by causing damage to it—for instance, if he causes notable damage by introducing his own structural changes into the leased house, or by some other means. Likewise, if he abuses it against good morals by bringing in prostitutes or pimps, or by practicing something else shameful or indecent in it, from which harm or scandal to the neighborhood follows (Law *Eadem*, Code: *On Leasing*; chapter *Propter sterilitatem*, section *Verum*, same title; and the cited Law 6 and the *Portuguese Ordinances* as above, section 2). Regarding prostitutes and pimps, Alvarus Valascus (*On Emphyteutic Law*, question 23) rightly understands this to apply when the leased house is among honorable men and women; for if the house were next to a brothel, or among other houses in which similar things are practiced, then because no corruption of morals or scandal to the neighborhood would follow, the tenant could not be expelled by the landlord for that reason. He adds that from this last cause, even a student who abuses a leased house can be expelled from it.

<margin>Decision on the Doubt</margin>
There are, however, several points to be examined regarding these four explained events. The first is whether they take place only regarding houses. To this I respond that the power to expel a tenant based on the **second event** <note>the landlord's personal need</note> only has a place regarding houses, as explained therein, because it is a privilege and is not found granted regarding other things; for that reason, it cannot be extended beyond that for which it is found granted, as was said in that place.

<column-break/>

The remaining events, however, in their own way have a place even regarding movable things; for they are not privileges, but through **equity** <note>term: "Epicheia" — a Greek legal concept meaning the interpretation of a law where the literal words fall short, focusing instead on the spirit of the law and the "presumed will" of the parties.</note> as an interpreter of the laws of contracts and other dispositions, those events are excepted by consent from the silent and presumed will of the contracting parties. This certainly has a place equally in rural and urban estates, and in leased movable and immovable things, as is gathered clearly enough from the law *Quaero*, section *Inter locatorem*, Digest: *On Leasing*, in which the rule regarding a farmer not paying rent or abusing a rural estate is established. The same lawyer, Paulus, would have responded regarding an urban estate—indeed even regarding a movable thing—if he had been questioned about them in a similar way. Hence, if rent is not paid, one can equally take away a rural estate as an urban one, and for the same reason a leased movable thing; for a landlord is not bound to stand by the contract for the tenant when the tenant does not stand by the contract for him. Likewise, if a leased thing requires repair or "medicine" <note>original: "medicina"; here meaning restoration or specialized maintenance.</note> due to an unforeseen event, it can be taken from the tenant if he cannot use it at the same time, even if that thing is movable. Likewise, if a tenant abuses a leased thing to its damage, or to the scandal and destruction of the morals of others, it can certainly be taken from him even if it is a movable thing or a rural estate, of which the cited section *Inter locatorem* speaks.

The second point is whether, in all those four events, when the tenant is expelled, the rent <note>original: "pensio"</note> should be remitted to him in proportion to the time in which he does not use the leased thing. To this it must be said that all agree that in the **second and third events**—in which the tenant is expelled from the leased thing for the landlord's benefit without any fault of his own—the rent should be remitted 

<margin>14</margin>
to him in proportion to the time; or certainly in the third event, the landlord ought to offer him another house equally good and equally convenient for the tenant to live in for the meantime, as the cited Law 62 of Castile says. And indeed, that in the second event the rent should be remitted to him in proportion to the time is clear enough, and is affirmed by the chapter *Propter sterilitatem*, section *Verum*, *On Leasing*, and the cited Law 6. In the third event, it is expressly held that the rent must be remitted in the same way in the law *Qui insulam* at the beginning, Digest: *On Leasing*, section *Verum*, and the cited Law 6 and section 3 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*.

In the other **two events** <note>non-payment and misconduct</note>, however, the matter is a controversy among the doctors. Indeed, section *Verum* and Law 6 seem to suggest, by an argument from the opposite sense, that the rent should not be reduced proportionally. For having mentioned the second and third events, they subjoin: "and in these two events, the rent is to be reduced in proportion to the time the tenant lacked the use and enjoyment of the leased thing." They say no such thing about the other two, which these two laws subjoin immediately. Cinus and Azzo add to this (whose opinion Navarrus follows in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 194), speaking of the fourth event: they affirm the rent should not be reduced, because the tenant was ejected from the leased thing due to his own fault. The Gloss, however, on the law *Eadem*, Code: *On Leasing*, and another Gloss on the cited section *Verum* (which Salicetus and Speculator follow), judge that the rent should be reduced in proportion to the time, but that the landlord can sue the tenant for the damage caused. Johannes Andreae and Panormitanus on the cited chapter *Propter sterilitatem*, Hostiensis, and others, try to bring the two opinions into harmony...

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts #

<margin>Decision</margin>
...of the leased property, the latter opinion should prevail. However, when there was an abuse of the leased property without damage caused to it—such as when activities against good morals and causing a neighborhood scandal were carried out in it—the former opinion should hold. To me, the opinion of Gregorio Lopez <note>original: "Grego. Lope."</note> in the cited Law 6, at the word *dos casos* <note>original: "two cases"</note>, is proven; following Barbatias and certain others he refers to, he distinguishes between the first and fourth outcomes. For if the landlord, having expelled the tenant, finds another who would lease it for the remaining time at a rent proportional to the time <note>term: "pro rata temporis" — a Latin phrase meaning in proportion to the time elapsed or remaining</note> equal to what the prior tenant paid, or if the prior tenant offers someone who would lease it without abusing the property, then the first tenant should be released from the rent for that portion of the time. In this case, action can only be taken against him for any damage he caused to the leased property. If, however, no one is found to lease it at that price, then the first tenant is bound to pay that portion of the future rent which the landlord fails to receive, so that the landlord suffers no loss due to the fault of the first tenant. And this is clearly what the two cited glosses intended: indeed, that ought to be calculated among the damages inflicted. Nothing more than this is gathered from Law 6 and the cited paragraph *verum*, by an argument from the contrary sense. Because a reduction in rent for the proportional future time is not always to be made in these two outcomes (compared to the other two in which a remission must always be made), they taught this only regarding those cases.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
The third question is whether, in these four outcomes, the landlord can expel the tenant from the leased property by his own authority.

<margin>Decision</margin>
The common † opinion, which Aluarus Valascus <note>original: "Alu. Val."</note> in *On the Right of Emphyteusis* <note>term: "emphytensis" — a permanent lease of land for a fixed rent</note>, question 21, number 2, and Gregorio Lopez in the cited Law 6, gloss 1, refer to and follow, is that according to common law, he can expel him by his own authority; this is consistent with the law *si duo*, paragraph *cum inquilinus*, joined with the gloss there (Digest, *uti possidetis*). Although some say it is safer to go to a judge and request a public official from him to carry out the execution; and Aluarus

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
Valascus says in the same place that the judge is bound to grant this immediately. Portuguese law (Book 4, Ordinance title 58, final paragraph), rightly aiming to prevent the evils that could follow from such actions, decreed that a landlord may not expel a tenant by himself, but must request the official of that place—whom they call an *alcaide* <note>term: "alcaide" — a local administrative or judicial official in the Iberian Peninsula</note>—so that, by explaining to the tenant the cause for which he is being expelled, he may command him to leave, and if he is unwilling, expel him by force. And that official is commanded to carry it out in this manner. If, however, it is later found that the landlord ejected the tenant out of malice, without just cause, and improperly, the tenant is immediately restored to that house, and he inhabits it for free for a period triple the time he was still supposed to inhabit it according to the contract. Aluarus Valascus, at the end of the cited number 2, says that if the tenant prefers, he can instead sue for interests <note>term: "interesse" — legal compensation for loss or damages</note>, according to the law *qui insulam*, at the beginning (Digest, *locati*).

### Whether it is lawful to lease something which is understood to be used by the tenant for a mortal sin. ###

-> DISPUTATION 500 <-
-> SUMMARY <-

1 *To lease something is a sin if the intention of the lessor is directed toward the sin; this is entirely illicit.*

<column-break/>

2 *To lease something to someone who will use it for a mortal injury to another is a mortal sin, and for that reason, it is illicit.*
3 *To lease a house to prostitutes, not with the intention that they practice fornication there, but only for their habitation, is not a sin.*
4 *When it is lawful and when it is not to lease something because of which an abuse for sin can be suspected.*

This disputation must be briefly satisfied by the following conclusions. The first is:
1 It is illicit, in that sense, to lease † something for sin if the intention of the lessor is directed toward the sin itself, such that he leases it specifically so that it may be used for sin. As, for example, to lease a house so that it may be used for usury or for fornication. This is most well-known, since that would be to participate in the sin of the tenant. And since a thing ordered toward an end takes its nature from the end to which it is ordered.
2 The second conclusion. It is a mortal † sin to lease something when it is understood that its use will be for a mortal injury to another. As if a sword or a horse were leased to someone who is understood to be going to use it for an unjust war, or to unjustly wound, or to kill a neighbor—even if the intention of the lessor is not directed toward that injury and sin. This conclusion was shown above in this part (2. 2, question 43, article 7), while we were discussing scandal.
3 The third conclusion. Granted † that prostitutes are permitted by the state to avoid greater evils, it is not a sin to lease a house to them, provided the lessor does not intend their fornication there, but leases the house only for their habitation, even though he knows they will abuse that habitation for sins. This is proven because the leasing of a house for them to live in is not evil by its nature. Likewise, the permitting of sins which he foresees will happen through the malice of those living in it is not evil for him, because he is not bound to prevent their abuse and sins. This is especially true since their permission is ordered toward avoiding greater evils for the common good—if it is true that through brothels <note>original: "lupanaribus"</note>, as they are permitted today, greater evils are avoided rather than increased in the republic. Therefore, that lease is lawful, although it should be discouraged, and every upright man should rather see his house burned than leased to women of this kind. Read Martin de Azpilcueta <note>original: "Navarr." — referring to the famous Spanish canonist known as Dr. Navarrus</note> in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 195, who, though hesitant, finally agrees with this conclusion.
4 And, to † speak summarily: in those events in which it is lawful or illicit to sell something when an abuse for sin is believed or feared to follow from that thing, it is likewise lawful or illicit to lease something. Because this was discussed copiously in the cited question 43 and deduced from its own principles (namely, when in such an event it is lawful or illicit to sell), it is sufficient to have touched upon these few points regarding leasing in this place.

# Whether the leasing of clothing allowances <note>original: "vestuariorum"</note> for an advance payment lower than the expected return is usurious, as sometimes occurs in the Diocese of Cuenca.

## DISPUTATION 501.

### SUMMARY.

1 **All the revenues of the episcopal and chapter table <note>term: "mensa" — a common fund or endowment intended for the support of a specific ecclesiastical office or group</note> in the Diocese of Cuenca, and what they consist of.**
2 **Whether the leasing of clothing allowances for a lower price paid in advance than the expected return is usury, when there is a burden of restitution, as sometimes occurs in the Diocese of Cuenca.**

In the following disputations, some specific cases regarding leasing and hiring must be decided. However, so that the proposed question, about which I have often been asked, may be unraveled, we must begin with the practice and the explanation of the terms.

<margin>1</margin> In this Diocese of Cuenca <note>original: "Conchensi episcopatu"</note>, almost all the revenues of the episcopal and chapter table consist of that portion of the tithes <note>term: "decimae" — a tenth part of agricultural produce given to support the church</note> of bread (grain), wine, and meat—that is, lambs, kids, and certain herds—which belongs to the cathedral church. For the entire tithe of wool, cheese, and other things belongs to the ministers of the individual parishes. Moreover, the tithes of bread, wine, and meat, as far as the present matter is concerned, are partly owed from the fruits of the goods of those who have been initiated at least into the first tonsure <note>note: The "first tonsure" was the ceremony of clipping the hair that marked the entry of a person into the clerical state</note>, which they call "tithes of the goods of the tonsured" <note>original: "de bienes de coronados"</note>; and partly from the fruits of the goods of those men who have not been initiated into the first tonsure, which they therefore call "of the goods of laypeople" <note>original: "de bienes de legos"</note>. Such tithes collected in each parish, if they are from the fruits of those initiated into the first tonsure, are divided into only two equal parts: one belongs to the ministers of the parish, and the other to the Cathedral Church. If, however, they are from men not initiated into the first tonsure, they are divided into nine equal parts: three belong to the Cathedral Church, just as many to the ministers of the parish, and from the three remaining parts, two belong to the King—which are therefore called the Royal Thirds <note>original: "tertiæ Regis"</note>—and the remaining part is assigned to the building fund <note>original: "fabricæ"</note> of the parish.

These explained tithes, which belong to the Cathedral Church, are divided between the bishop and the chapter (or the episcopal and chapter funds) according to an ancient agreement, such that the tithes of certain places are assigned to the episcopal fund and the tithes of certain other places to the chapter fund, except for some places in which such tithes belong indiscriminately to both the episcopal and chapter measures; therefore, these two funds divide them equally between themselves. And the administration of those which belong to the episcopal fund pertains to the bishop alone; but the administration of those which belong to the chapter fund pertains to the chapter alone.

The tithes of the various towns that belong to the chapter fund are called "refectory rents" <note>original: "refitores"</note>, and it is customary to say "the refitory" of such

<column-break/>

or such a town. Perhaps the name takes its origin from the time when the chapter members lived in community, because those goods belonged to the refreshment <note>original: "refectionem"</note> and sustenance of the members. Now, the chapter fund is divided among the canons, the portionaries (whom they call *rationeros* in Spanish), and the semi-portionaries. Regarding these revenues, there is a difference between the canons and the portionaries: certain primary "refectory rents" are reserved for the community of canons to be divided among them alone. The portion which falls to each of the canons annually from such "refectory rents" is called the clothing allowance <note>original: "vestuarium"</note>, as if it were a special amount reserved for their clothing, greater decoration, and a larger household. Thus, these tithes of the chapter are divided into two parts. Some, from certain designated places, belong to the canons alone, and the portions that fall to each canon annually from these are called *vestuaria*. But the remaining tithes and goods of the chapter are divided equally between the portionaries and the canons; and that which falls to each person annually from there is called a portion <note>original: "portio", in Spanish: "racion"</note>. Some of these portions are divided equally between two ministers, who are therefore called semi-portionaries. Thus, the income of any canonry consists of the clothing allowance and the portion. Moreover, the portion consists of two types of revenue. For some revenues are in bread (grain): there is the grain of certain specific places assigned to be divided equally among all portionaries and canons; and as that supply is greater in some years and smaller in others, or some canon or portionary is absent (who did not produce his fruits that year), or no one is absent, in one year a greater quantity of this grain falls to each canon or portionary, and in another a smaller amount.

Other revenues of the portion are in money, which, after expenses are deducted, is sometimes in greater supply and sometimes in smaller.

Furthermore, from this money a certain amount is assigned to be distributed to each person present for each individual hour [of service]; the remainder of this money—which always exists, both because of the absence of some and because the total supply is greater than what is assigned to each person for the individual hours (which they therefore call the "surplus" <note>original: "superauit"</note>)—is distributed at the end of the year. For this purpose, the year is calculated from the first day of January to the last day of December, and it is distributed among those who were present for the hours throughout the whole year, in proportion to the time <note>original: "pro rata temporis"</note> that each is found to have been present. Those days which they call "rest days" are counted as days of attendance; that is, those days which, according to the statutes of this Church, each person is allowed to be absent without loss of those daily distributions, as they are called.

Only this portion of money is distributed among the canons and portionaries according to the stated attendance of each of them. And that is what is called the "hand-money" <note>original: "manualia"</note> and "daily distributions." However, the clothing allowances <note>original: "vestuaria"</note> and that other portion of grain common to both canons and portionaries are not acquired according to the rate of days of attendance, but in the following way—
