# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...in which I will speak only of clothing allowances <note>original: "vestuariis"</note>; the same should be understood regarding the portion of bread shared by the portionaries <note>term: "portionariis" — clergy members who receive a specific portion of church income</note> and the canons.

Canons earn their clothing allowances every year in the following manner. Whoever, for example, on the upcoming feast of Saint Michael in this year 1594 <note>September 29</note> is present for first vespers and the procession which takes place on the morning of that feast in the cathedral church, earns in this sense the entire clothing allowance of the fruits that will be collected from then until the next feast of Saint Michael in the year 1595. This is conditional: if afterward, during the course of the year from that feast of Saint Michael until the next in 1595, he is present for one hundred and twenty days, or if he dies while one hundred and twenty days in which he could have been present still remain—at least by counting the days in which he was present at the Church—then they earn the allowance in full. 

If, however, he is neither present for one hundred and twenty days, nor dies while those days remain (in the manner explained) in which he could have been present, he loses the entire clothing allowance to the community of canons, to be distributed among the others who earned their clothing allowances that year. 

Regarding those canons who were not present for the first vespers and the procession of the feast of Saint Michael, a distinction must be made. For if they had already completed their "first year residency," as they call it, and were actually present for one hundred and twenty days throughout the whole year, they earn the clothing allowance just like the others. But if they either die before they have actually been present for those one hundred and twenty days, or for some other reason are not actually present for those full one hundred and twenty days, they lose the entire clothing allowance to the community of those who earned them that year. 

However, if those who were not present for the first vespers and the procession of Saint Michael had not yet completed their first year residency, then they lose the clothing allowance entirely, even if they are actually present for one hundred and twenty days afterward. Thus, those who acquire possession of a canonry after the feast of Saint Michael do not obtain the clothing allowance for that year, even if they are present for one hundred and twenty days. The reason for this rule seems to be that if the predecessor was present for the first vespers and the procession of Saint Michael and then died, he earned the clothing allowance for that year's canonry, and there is no allowance remaining for the successor to earn through actual presence.

To come to the point, it must be observed that the Collectors <note>original: "Restores"</note> of the fruits of the year 1595 (from which the revenues for that year's clothing allowances are formed) manage these while the canons earn them in the manner explained at the first vespers and procession of the feast of Saint Michael in this year 1594. I say that those collectors are appointed around the feast of the Trinity in 1594, so that the lessees pay the money partly by Shrove Tuesday <note>original: "carnisprivium"; the start of the Lenten fast</note> of 1596, and partly by the feast of the Trinity in that same year, 1596. But since the canons need money, and it will be so long before they receive it from their clothing allowances, they are accustomed to lease the money

<column-break/>

for the anticipated clothing allowances immediately after they earn them at the first vespers and procession of the feast of Saint Michael in the manner explained. They provide guarantors <note>original: "fideiussoribus"</note> that, if they live, they will reside for the necessary one hundred and twenty days so as not to lose the allowances they have thus earned, or that they will otherwise pay the lessees the amount the lessees stood to lose by the allowance being forfeited. Indeed, sometimes before they even earn them, they are accustomed to lease the money for anticipated clothing allowances for one, two, or three years, likewise providing guarantors that they will earn them or pay the lessees what it was worth to them to receive such revenues. 

Now, since experience over twenty or twenty-five years has shown that the clothing allowances (counting in them a certain portion of bread belonging to the allowance which they receive in grain) have never yielded less than one thousand gold coins <note>original: "aureos"; likely referring to the ducat or similar high-value currency</note>—so much so that the allowance for the very sterile past year of 1593, which began to be paid at Shrove Tuesday of this year 1594 in which I am writing, reached one thousand gold coins—and they regularly yield one thousand two hundred and fifty, or one thousand three hundred, and sometimes rise to one thousand five hundred or one thousand six hundred gold coins, and occasionally, though very rarely, have been found to yield one thousand seven hundred or one thousand eight hundred gold coins; and since prudent men experienced in this matter judge the "middle price" (in which the lessee exposes himself to an equal risk and advantage of profit or loss) to be one thousand two hundred and fifty or one thousand three hundred gold coins, because it is equally possible for the revenues to decrease or increase between one thousand and one thousand six hundred or one thousand eight hundred; such a contract for anticipated money is usually celebrated in one of two ways. First, by paying only eight hundred or nine hundred gold coins for them. Second, by paying eight hundred or nine hundred gold coins, but with a pact that if the revenues increase above one thousand or one thousand one hundred gold coins, the increase belongs to the canon who leased the allowance.

The question regarding such a lease of clothing allowances is whether it is usurious, carrying the burden of restitution. And it must undoubtedly be said that it is usurious, with the burden of restitution, at least up to the completion of the one thousand two hundred and fifty gold coins, unless something should be deducted for "lost profit" <note>term: "lucrum cessans" — a legal concept where interest is permitted to compensate the lender for profits they could have made elsewhere</note> or "emerging loss" <note>term: "damnum emergens" — compensation for a direct loss incurred by the lender because the money was not available</note> to the lessee due to the advance payment of money, about which I will speak shortly. 

The reason is that, according to the chapter *Naviganti* <note>note: A famous decree in Canon Law regarding the morality of investment and risk in maritime and commercial loans</note> concerning usury and right reason, that "middle price" is the lowest just price for each clothing allowance while it is still a future hope—if the faithful practice of this matter as reported by us thus far is true. For the one leasing at that price exposes himself equally to profit and loss. It is usury, however, with the burden of restitution (which is missing up to the lowest just price), to lease something by advance payment for a price below the lowest just price, unless it is excused on the grounds of lost profit or emerging loss. This is because that advance payment of the price is a virtual loan for the duration until the fruits of the allowance are to be paid, and for that loan, the discount from the lowest just price is accepted as interest. And in the matter proposed, it should be observed that the lessee of the clothing allowance undergoes no labor in receiving the revenues, nor does he expose himself to any risk. For nearly all the revenues are...

Second Treatise. Disputation 502.

They are received in cash; and when the collectors <note>original: "refitores" — the agents who lease the right to collect church revenues</note> from whom that money is paid are hired, they are hired under the condition that the lessee renounces all claims to any fortuitous events, even those entirely unusual and unexpected. Furthermore, the best guarantors are required, so that there is morally no risk that the price will not be paid in full. If, however, as very rarely (or rather never) happens, something were not paid, it concerns the entire mass of clothing revenues, so that there would be almost no loss to individual clothing allowances. Likewise, if before the collectors are hired on the Feast of the Trinity, some damage happens to a collector due to hail or something similar, because of which he is hired for a lower price than would otherwise be paid (which happens very rarely, especially since the whole bishopric can suffer little or no damage at that time because the land is very late-ripening), that loss falls upon the entire pool of clothing revenues, which is nearly nothing in comparison to individual allowances. All these things—along with the sterility or abundance of the year and other circumstances—pertain to the full range of the decrease and increase of clothing revenues, from one thousand gold coins <note>original: "aureis"</note> up to one thousand six hundred or one thousand eight hundred. For this reason, we say that the lowest "just price" <note>term: "iustum pretium" — a theological concept referring to a fair market value that avoids the sin of usury</note> of any clothing allowance, as it exists in expectation, is only one thousand two hundred fifty gold coins.

The lessees of these collections are bound to bring the money from these revenues to the house of the canon to whom they are assigned to pay, or to the house of the person the canon has substituted in his place. If they are late, they are compelled to pay by excommunications <note>Molina describes the use of church law to enforce financial contracts</note> against both themselves and their guarantors, who are bound as principals. They are also forced to pay the expense of one gold coin daily to the person sent to execute the collection or demand the debt, along with all other expenses incurred for that reason. As I said above, if it should happen that a lessee does not pay in full, that loss affects all canons equally. Therefore, the purchaser of a clothing allowance cannot subtract anything from that lowest just price for each allowance while it is still in expectation on account of labor, administration, expenses, or risks. Nor indeed, considering that the clothing revenue is paid in cash in this way, is it strictly a lease, but rather a loan of money for money to be received in the future. In this way, one exposes oneself equally to the event of losing or gaining, just as in wagers, which are called <term>apuestas</term> <note>Spanish for "bets"</note> in Spanish. If, beyond an equal amount of money in the manner aforesaid, an increase in money is negotiated, it is pure usury <note>term: "vsura" — the charging of unethical or illegal interest on a loan</note> regarding that increase received for the loan. Therefore, I do not see any other grounds from which an increase can be accepted—at least in expectation—other than for "lost profit" or "emergent loss" <note>terms: "lucri cessantis" and "damni emergentis" — legal justifications for charging interest when a lender loses money or potential profit by making a loan</note> for the person providing the money in advance.

Regarding the "lost profit" or "emergent loss" pertaining to the purchaser of such clothing allowances due to the anticipation of money, it must be said: it is entirely necessary that a profit truly ceases or a loss truly emerges, in the sense explained in Disputations 315 and 316. In that case, no more increase can be accepted than the value of this lost profit or emergent loss; if more is accepted, as far as that increase is concerned,

<column-break/>

usury would be committed with the obligation to restore it. Certainly, such purchasers of clothing allowances do not enter into this contract for the benefit of the canons, merely claiming for themselves the value of the lost profit and emergent loss, but rather so that they themselves may profit far more. This can be argued because they would not lend that money to a canon to be received only from the clothing revenue with an increase equal to the loss they incurred from the missed profit or emergent loss from that loan. It should be observed, however, that sometimes such leases of clothing allowances are made for eight hundred or nine hundred gold coins, which the lessees give to the canons for their expenses, granting them a pro-rata amount each month from those eight hundred or nine hundred coins. In this event, less profit can be lost or less damage emerge than if they paid the whole sum at once; indeed, no loss occurs if they are wealthy, because they do not cease other lawful business dealings for that reason.

I would advise two things. First: although in these times the just price of clothing allowances paid in advance is estimated at one thousand two hundred fifty or one thousand three hundred gold coins, as times change and the revenues of the clothing allowances increase or decrease, such a just price for advance money also varies, and no certain rule can be established regarding this.

The second is: I hear that even "portions" <note>referring to the income of "portionaries," a lower rank of clergy</note> are sometimes leased with advance money—sometimes regarding only the revenues of bread, and sometimes also regarding cash revenues—with the portionary binding himself to be present in such a way that he earns as much as the one who earns the most by being present. Thus, if he does not earn that much, he refunds the lessee whatever less he earned. Regarding such a contract, the same thing must be said, in a certain proportion, as was said regarding the leasing of clothing allowances.

# If a price is paid for a place on a ship to the Indies, for example, and due to contrary winds or another cause, the ship does not arrive there but returns to port, should at least part of the price be restored?

### DISPUTATION 502.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> Whether a merchant can reclaim the price given to a shipmaster for carrying his goods if the ship, having set out partway, returns to port due to the winds.
<margin>2</margin> Freightage <note>original: "Vectura"</note> is not owed for a slave <note>original: "mancipio"</note> who dies before being transported to the destined place.

This is a matter about which, as reported by Alvarez Valasquez (Consultation 75), there was a controversy in Lisbon <note>original: "Olyssipone"</note> and a sentence was passed. It is customary on ships going to the Indies <note>the Spanish and Portuguese overseas empires</note> for space to be granted to certain officers of the ship. A certain shipmaster gave a merchant the space granted to him for a certain price, for the purpose of carrying goods to the Indies. The ship set out, and halfway through the journey, due to contrary winds, it returned to port.

...has returned. The merchant contended that the price ought to be returned to him, at least in proportion to the journey that he did not complete. The shipmaster, however, defended himself by arguing that the ship had indeed departed from the port, and he had not bound himself to the absolute completion of the journey.

On behalf of the merchant, the following was proposed: First, that the contract was, in effect, one of **letting and hiring** <note>original: "locationis, & conductionis"</note> of that space in the ship, just as if a contract were made regarding a space in a house, a bedroom, or a cellar; it was not a contract of sale, because neither the house nor a part of it was sold, nor was ownership of any thing transferred by that contract. Therefore, since it was not a sale, there is an express text that seems to decide the matter in favor of the merchant in the law *si uno*, paragraph *item cum quidam*, in the Digest under "Hiring," the words of which are:

> When a certain person, having lost his ship, sought the return of the freight-charge <note>original: "vecturam"</note> which he had received for the cargo, the response was: Not without merit, the Imperial Procurator may seek the return of this freight-charge from him; since he did not perform the service of carrying. This must be observed similarly in all persons.

Thus far the text. From this, it is established that what was given for the service of carrying is to be reclaimed when the one who received it did not perform that service due to a fortuitous event. In the case proposed, the ship did not perform the service of carrying to India due to a fortuitous event.

Second, that it is the custom in Portugal in such an event that half of the freight—that is, the price given for carrying the goods—is returned to the hirer; and contracts are judged to be celebrated according to the custom of the place in which they are made.

Third, because if the freight is established for transporting slaves to a certain place, and some of those slaves die on the journey before they are transported to that place, the freight is not owed for the dead slave, for the reason that they were not transported to the destined place, as **Stracca** <note>Benvenuto Stracca (1509–1578), an Italian jurist and foundational figure in commercial and maritime law.</note> affirms in his *Treatise on Ships*, part 3, number 19, according to the text of the law *Seio amico* at the beginning, and the law *illis libertis* at the end. Therefore, the same should be said in the case proposed.

Although **Alvaro Valasco** <note>A prominent 16th-century Portuguese jurist.</note> objects and thinks that the sentence should have been given in favor of the merchant, it was nevertheless rightly given in favor of the shipmaster. First, because it was truly a **sale of the right** granted to the shipmaster to occupy or assign space in that place, wherever he wished on that voyage to India. He transferred that entire right to the merchant for that price, taking upon himself no risk if the ship returned from the middle of the journey or did not reach India for another reason, but rather transferring such a right to the merchant for that price as was competent to himself and had been granted. Common usage of speech in Portugal agrees with this when such a contract is celebrated; for the contracting parties say, *I sell you my lodging in such a ship for such a price* <note>original Portuguese: "vendo vos o meu gasalhado em tal nao tanto pretio"</note>. When the words can fit the matter at hand, such a contract must be judged to be celebrated as the words signify. But by that very fact, because a contract of buying and selling has been celebrated—especially if delivery followed on both sides, as in the case proposed, where the shipmaster received the price and the merchant began to use that right—the risk of the thing bought belongs to the buyer, as was seen in Disputation 366. Therefore, the shipmaster was held to return nothing of the price to the merchant. Nor is it true what **Alvaro Valasco** 

<column-break/>

affirms in the same place, number 10: namely, that in the case proposed, even if we say it is a contract of buying and selling, what is sold is not yet in existence but is hoped for in the future—namely, the navigation to India—and it is sold by measure. In this event, **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval continental jurists.</note> says the risk of the sold thing regarding what did not happen falls upon the seller and not the buyer. This, I say, is not true: because a **present right** to inhabit and carry goods in that place is sold, and the whole right is transferred to the buyer, whether the full use of it follows afterward or not.

Second, because, even if we were to grant that it is a hiring of that space in the ship (or of the ship regarding that space), since a hirer of a thing can lease it to another for the time he himself has it hired (as was said in Disputation 489), and for the same reason, one who received as a gift or in recompense for a service what could have been leased to him for a price can also lease it himself; still, in the proposed case, it should be said that the shipmaster is bound to restore nothing of the price to this merchant. In the first place, because for as long as he carried his merchandise there, he prevented the shipmaster from occupying that place for the duration of the voyage toward India; and it is no less worthy of payment to permit the goods to return to port than to grant that the goods be carried to the place from which the ship returned. For those goods were not to be thrown into the sea to prevent them from returning. Furthermore, although the laws state that if a hirer cannot use the hired thing due to some fortuitous event—not on the part of the hirer, but on the part of the thing hired—he is not held to pay the rent in proportion to the time he was prevented from using it (as seen in Disputation 493); nevertheless, in legal matters one must use <term>epicheia</term> <note>A term derived from Greek meaning "equity" or a "reasonable correction of the law" where it is deficient due to its universality.</note>. One must attend to the circumstances of things, and by right reason it must be weighed and judged whether a general legal provision also has a place in certain events to which it would be irrational to extend that legal dispute, or whether they should rather be excepted from it. 

Truly, in the proposed case, since the India ships are built at such great expense, last such a short time, and are exposed to so many dangers, and so many expenses are incurred for the officers and servants necessary for navigation—and moreover, if the ships return to port due to adverse winds or another reason, a loss is made of all these things, and the voyage cannot be made that year—the hiring of spaces in those ships cannot reasonably be understood according to the common rules of hiring other things. Namely, that if the ship does not reach India, they should pay only a portion of the <term>naulum</term> <note>A Latin term for "freight-money" or the fare paid for sea transport.</note> or the price of hiring for the time they used the ships. As if, should the ship suffer shipwreck or be captured by pirates, the voyagers themselves or their heirs could reclaim part of the price given for the use and habitation of the ship! Surely that is not in use, nor would it be done reasonably; nor, if such a condition were brought into the agreement by the hirers when the hiring is made, would they be heard, or would the lessors consent to them. Therefore, there is no reason why such hirers or their heirs should be heard in court regarding this matter.

# Second Treatise. Disputation 503. 667

To the first argument to the contrary, it must first be denied that the contract in question is not one of sale. For a contract of sale to exist, it is not necessary that the ship itself, or a part of the ship, be sold, or that ownership of a physical thing be transferred to the buyer. Instead, it is sufficient that the **right** <note>original: "ius"</note> which the shipmaster held—to use that space in the ship for whatever he wished during that voyage—be sold. He transfers a similar right to the merchant for a price, according to what was stated in Disputation 336. Furthermore, even if we were to admit that it is a **lease** <note>original: "conductionem," the hiring of a service or space</note>, we must deny that the paragraph "likewise when a certain person" <note>a reference to the Digest of Roman Law, §. item cum quidam</note> decides this matter in favor of the merchant. For the ship discussed in that paragraph did not even sail, but was lost in the very port; this ship, however, not only sailed, and the merchant used the space, but it sailed for such a length of time and reached such a point that it would have been sufficient to arrive in India.

To the second argument, it must be denied that such a custom exists in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>. Indeed, for the opposite side, it was stated and proved by two witnesses that the custom in Portugal is for such a contract to be considered a sale and not a lease, and that the price (or part of it) should not be returned, as **Alvaro Valasco** <note>original: "Aluar. Valaf.," a famous 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note> reports in that same place. Although Valasco himself protests that this second custom is not sufficiently proven, the other claim is proven even less—and it would be irrational. If it were proven, a judgment would certainly never have been rendered in favor of the shipmaster.

To the third argument, it must be said that unless it had been expressly stated in the agreement that the price was paid only for those **slaves** <note>original: "mancipijs"</note> who reached the place to which they were being transported, the price is owed even for those who died. The contract should be understood in this way because it was not due to the sailor that he did not transport them, but due to the slaves themselves, who died. Nor would it be reasonable to pay him a price only in proportion to the journey of each slave on the ship, especially since the sailor could not have taken on other goods in the middle of the sea to carry in place of the deceased slaves. The two laws cited only prove the case where the price for transporting slaves was promised under the **condition** that they arrive at the location, as is clear enough to anyone looking at those laws; but that has no place in the matter proposed here.

# Whether it is lawful to lease animals with a pact that the lessee is always bound to keep the number whole from their offspring or elsewhere.

## DISPUTATION 503.

### SUMMARY.

1. Whether the leasing of animals with a pact that their number be kept whole from their offspring is lawful, and in how many ways it may be done. Number 1.

<margin>1</margin>
I have found that this contract is celebrated in two ways, and something must be said about each. In the first way, someone is given, for example, one hundred sheep or goats—whether some rams

<column-break/>

or he-goats are mixed in or not—with a pact that he is always bound to keep the number whole, either from offspring of a certain age or from elsewhere, by replacing those that have died, or those he has sold or otherwise disposed of. Additionally, he must provide all care and necessary expenses; and finally, he must pay a certain amount of money annually in addition, while the fruits and profit belong to him. This same contract is sometimes celebrated with a pact where he only replaces the number of dead cattle from the offspring or elsewhere, and does not dispose of any others, applying all care and expense to them; the fruits are then divided equally, or in some other proportion, between himself and the owner of the animals. It is usually asked whether such a contract, celebrated in either way, is lawful, or rather unjust and **usurious** <note>original: "usurarius," involving the sin of charging illicit interest</note>.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
To this question, it must be briefly said that in this case, a contract of **capital insurance** <note>original: "assecurationis capitalis," ensuring the original stock is not lost</note> (or the insurance of that number of cattle) is mixed with a contract of **leasing** <note>original: "conductionis"</note> regarding the fruits of those cattle—or a **partnership** <note>original: "societatis"</note>, if it is celebrated in the second way, according to what was said in Disputation 411. This contract, first of all, is free from any stain of usury. Secondly, it is just and lawful if, considering the risk to which the lessee exposes himself and the expenses and industry he applies, the fruits of those cattle (as they are expected) are worth such a great fee to be paid annually. Or, if such risk, expense, and industry are sufficiently compensated by a portion of the fruits so expected, which the owner reserves for himself. And since these points contain no difficulty, I will not dwell on them further. Read Disputation 462, which could be added here regarding the letting and hiring of livestock.

<margin>2</margin>
I saw this contract celebrated in another way, and I was consulted about it in **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olyssiponæ"</note> when a lessor and lessee were contending over it in court. A certain nobleman had a large rural estate on which a herd of livestock—oxen and cows—belonging to that nobleman was raised. Furthermore, seeds were sown on that estate, and oxen from the same herd were used for cultivating the land and for wagons. The nobleman had leased that estate and those two herds for a certain sum of money to be paid annually, with the law that the lessee was bound to keep the number of animals in both herds whole, replacing from offspring or elsewhere those that died, or those the lessee wanted to sell or otherwise dispose of for his own benefit. However, in a certain year that was very barren due to excessive drought, many animals from both herds—especially the oxen and cows—perished, causing the lessee to suffer great loss. The nobleman demanded both the rent and that the lessee restore the herds. The lessee, among other things, defended himself in court by contending that the contract had been usurious because the lessor had shifted the risk of both leased herds onto the lessee along with the estate. A very skillful advocate for the lessee referred the lessor and lessee to me to ask whether the contract was usurious. I responded:

<margin>Decision.</margin>
That contract is a mixed one, consisting of a contract of insurance for both herds regarding the number of animals...

...and from the contract of leasing <note>original: "conductionis"</note>, both of the estate and of both herds: first, for using the oxen for cultivation and other necessary and useful services; and second, for perceiving the offspring from both herds and the profits. This includes selling for his own benefit those animals that had reached full maturity, or which, with the passage of time, would become useless for labor, and replacing their number from the new offspring. I argued that a contract of this kind is entirely free from any moral defect <note>original: "omni prorsus carere labe," likely referring to usury or injustice</note> and is highly beneficial to the state and to both contracting parties. I added that it was also just—provided that, considering the risk of replacing the herds from elsewhere and considering the fruits and profits which the owner hoped to receive annually from the estate and both herds at the time the contract was made—the wages or rent to be paid was not judged by a prudent person's estimation to exceed the limits of a **just price**.

Since contracts of this kind, which have been discussed in this dispute, are not illicit by their very nature, nor are they found to be prohibited in law—so long as the rent imposed is not unjust in the manner explained—it must undoubtedly be said that they are not included among the prohibited contracts in **Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 42** <note>The "Ordenações" were the primary legal code of the Kingdom of Portugal</note>. This is because that law only speaks of contracts involving animals that are illicit in themselves and prohibited by law regardless of that ordinance, as is clear from the ordinance itself; these contracts, however, are not of that type. Furthermore, if that ordinance is read carefully, these are not among the number of those listed there. Therefore, if they are entered into, they are not void by that ordinance, nor do those who enter into them incur the penalties of that ordinance.

->What should be said regarding two contracts pertaining to leasing and hiring.<-

### DISPUTATION 504.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> 1. How certain contracts are recognized as pertaining to leasing and hiring <note>original: "locatum, & conductum"</note>, and number 2.

Since skill and light for defining many other cases are gained from the decision of specific events in particular, some must be unraveled by us. A contract of this sort is said to have been entered into in **Valencia**. A certain **nobleman** agreed with a **baker** <note>original: "pistor"</note> that the baker would be bound to provide him for an entire year with baked bread of a certain good quality necessary for his household. The conditions were as follows: the nobleman would sell measures <note>original: "modios"</note> of wheat to the baker, from which the baker would make the bread, at the price for which other wheat—far inferior in quality—is valued at the time of the new harvest in a town nine leagues distant from Valencia, where that inferior wheat is abundant. Because of this, the price fell short of the **just price**. This was first because the wheat was sold and delivered in Valencia, where it was worth more; second, because it was to be sold and delivered in baked bread throughout the entire year at the price the wheat was worth at harvest time, even though the price of wheat would rise during the course of the year. Finally,

<column-break/>

because the wheat sold and delivered to the nobleman in the form of bread was of much better quality and higher price than that of the other town. Furthermore, the baker was compelled to return so much weight in bread for every measure of wheat that only the **bran** <note>original: "furfures," the outer husks of the grain</note> remained for him, despite his own industry, labor, and the expenses incurred in baking the bread.

However, the nobleman bound himself to the following conditions, which were of such great profit to the baker that he would gain more from them than he would lose in the other contracts. First, the nobleman granted the baker a capital sum <note>original: "statum"</note> of two hundred gold crowns <note>original: "scuta"</note> with which the baker could trade, on the condition that a twelfth part of them each month would be counted toward the price of the measures of wheat he provided in bread to the nobleman; and the nobleman would pay each month the increase in the price of the measures for that month. Next, the nobleman bound himself to obtain a license for the baker so that he could daily receive three sacks of wheat for his business from the public warehouse where wheat is sold; even though, by public law, bakers are only permitted to take one sack daily. Likewise, he bound himself to obtain for him a license to buy and export five hundred or six hundred measures of wheat from other towns in the Kingdom for his business, even though this was also prohibited by public law.

There are those who think this nobleman is held to no restitution to the baker, because he sufficiently compensated him for the loss of the first two contracts with the profit of the three subsequent ones. But they add that he is held to restore to the **common good** the damage he caused it by obtaining and using those two licenses for the baker.

Indeed, that damage to the common good seems to be nothing or very slight, and you would not know how much it should be valued, or to whom or how restitution should be made. Rather, it seems to be an injustice done to the community that such licenses are granted and obtained for one person without any just cause, and that he alone uses them for his own benefit and that of the one who obtained them, while they are denied to others. For laws and prohibitions ought to be common to all subjects when there is no legitimate reason why one individual in particular should be exempted from them—a reason which would not similarly apply to the rest. And certainly, no burden of restoring to the common good would be enjoined upon the baker if he, without any license, had bought and exported the same number of measures from other towns at his own risk, or if he bought those three sacks of wheat and removed them from the public warehouse where wheat is sold, either by himself or through intermediaries. Indeed, he would be judged to have brought no true damage to the common good, but only to have violated the laws passed to the contrary. Add to this that no one, in the event we are discussing, would order the baker to restore to the common good the damage he brought it by using those licenses; however, he would have to be ordered to restore it in the nobleman’s stead, as the nobleman was the true cause of that damage (if any had been brought to the common good for that reason) through the use of those licenses.

I believe it should be said that the nobleman is held to restore to the baker as much as is sufficient so that those two contracts...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 504

...the contract for the purchase of that wheat, and the hiring of the baker—on the condition that he should provide so much bread from every bushel <note>original: "modio," a Roman unit of dry volume</note> that only the bran <note>original: "furfures," the outer husks of the grain left after milling</note> remained for him—should be reduced to the limits of justice, unless something ought to be deducted for the nobleman’s effort <note>original: "industria"</note> in obtaining those legal privileges. I am led to this because those two contracts are truly unjust in themselves, carrying the burden of restitution to the extent necessary to bring both to a state of equality. Or (and it comes to the same thing), the purchase of that baked bread for that specific price must be reduced to equality, a point upon which everyone agrees. 

Furthermore, that advance payment of two hundred gold scudi <note>original: "scutorum aureorum," a common gold coin of the period</note> does not excuse the nobleman from the burden of restitution, even if the baker earned more profit from them than the amount needed to bring those two contracts to the limits of justice. This is because that advance is effectively a **virtual loan** <note>original: "virtuale mutuum," a concept where a payment functions as a loan in practice even if not called one</note> of those scudi. For such a loan, the nobleman can receive no profit or excuse from the burden of restitution without the **stain of usury**. Indeed, those scudi do not generate profit except through the labor of the baker, and because they have already become the property of the baker, the risk associated with them belongs to the baker. Therefore, just as the risk is his, so is the benefit—as the fruit of his own industry using that money as an instrument. Since the money is now his own and does not remain with the lender, the profit belongs solely to the baker; the lender cannot sell him a profit that does not belong to the lender, but to the baker himself. On this point, too, all agree.

Next, the two legal privileges which the nobleman obtained for the baker do not excuse him from the burden of restitution. This is because the profit the baker acquires—by purchasing bushels of wheat at a just price in other places, extracting it, and making bread from it, and similarly by buying those three sacks of wheat daily at a just price in the public house and making bread from them—is the fruit of his own industry. He carries out these just contracts with his own money, applying his own work, industry, and other necessary expenses. Those legal privileges merely serve to allow him to do this without being penalized. Therefore, that profit belongs to the baker as the fruit of his industry and money, and not to the nobleman. Thus, the nobleman is not freed by the baker’s profit from the burden of restoring enough so that those two other contracts, which he unjustly made with the baker, are reduced to the limits of just contracts. 

This is confirmed because those two privileges certainly contribute no more to the baker's profit than if someone (if the baker lacked money for trading) were to assist him by lending him two thousand gold pieces. As everyone admits, the lender could take nothing from that profit, nor compensate anything with it, because that profit belongs solely to the baker as the fruit of his industry and money. Therefore, the nobleman cannot compensate for anything from that profit on account of those two privileges he obtained, because the profit truly becomes the baker’s and not his own. 

It is further confirmed because the public authorities who granted those privileges to the baker could not receive anything from the baker’s profit as a price or compensation for those privileges, nor could they settle any of their own debts with it. On the contrary, if they did so, they would be bound to restitution, since they have no just title to receive it. 

<column-break/>

Therefore, neither can the person who obtained those privileges from the public authority through his petitions receive anything from the profit in recompense for them, or compensate his own debt with it. For just as a lender can receive nothing from the profit that comes to the borrower by trading with that money in recompense for the loan, so too a person who, through his petitions and authority, brings it about that someone lends to another, can receive nothing from that same profit in recompense. Indeed, it would be a strange thing if the lender could receive almost nothing as the price of the loan, yet the mediator—by whose petitions and authority the loan was given—could receive something, except perhaps a wage worthy of his labor and industry in interceding. 

The same must be said in the case proposed: just as the public authorities could receive nothing for granting that privilege, so the nobleman of whom we speak can receive nothing, except perhaps as much as he would be worth for the service, labor, and industry of interceding. And certainly, since he acts wrongly by interceding and obtaining these privileges to the detriment of the commonwealth and to the injury of others in the community, even if he could receive something from that profit without the burden of restitution according to the strict rigor of justice, a **prudent confessor** <note>original: "prudens confessarius," a priest providing moral guidance in the sacrament of Penance</note> ought to command him, at least as a penance, to restore it—at least to the poor—so that such abuses do not creep into the commonwealth, as was said regarding other things that public ministers receive in Disputation 88.

<margin>2</margin> The following † contract is also said to be practiced in some places. A person who owns a farm <note>original: "praedium"</note> in which fifteen *fanegas* <note>original: "faneccae," a Spanish dry measure of about 55 liters</note>, as they call them, are sown every year, leases it to a peasant for thirty *fanegas* to be paid annually: fifteen of wheat, and the same amount of barley or rye <note>original: "secalis," which he notes is called *centeno* in Spanish</note>. Furthermore, he gives him two oxen to cultivate the farm, or twenty-two ducats with which to buy those oxen, which are never to be returned. However, he imposes on him the burden of paying twenty *fanegas* annually—ten of wheat and as many of barley or rye—and this only for the eight years for which the contract is made. It is asked whether this contract is licit? 

<margin>Decision.</margin> Since it includes two parts—one, the leasing of the farm for those thirty *fanegas* to be paid annually; the other, the exchange of those oxen for those twenty *fanegas* to be paid annually for eight years, or the purchase of the same *fanegas* for those twenty-two gold pieces—each part must be discussed separately. Regarding the first part, it must be said: depending on the quality of the farm—whether the land is fertile or sterile—and considering other concurrent circumstances and the custom of the region, it must be judged by the **judgment of a prudent person** whether that rent exceeds the limits of justice or not. Accordingly, the contract is either just, or unjust with the burden of restitution up to the limits of justice; no other safer or more certain rule can be established.

As for the second part, it must be said that it is entirely unjust, with the burden of remitting those *fanegas* which exceed the number of those that can be bought for those twenty-two gold pieces at the lowest just price. Or, if they have already been received, there is a burden of restoring the profit received. But if that profit was drawn into the agreement because of the advance...

### On servants who hire themselves
### out for service.

## DISPUTATION 505.

### SUMMARY.

1. Whether a servant who hires himself out for a specific time is bound, once that time has ended, to make up for time in which he was unable to serve due to illness.
2. And what the law of Castile and Portugal says in points 2 and 3, until the end.

In Disputation 493, it was stated that if a servant falls ill, or is unable to provide his services due to some similar hindrance, the master is not bound to pay the wages for that time. To this, add that if the master incurs any expenses in caring for the servant, he can demand those from him; for those expenses belong to the servant who hired himself out, not to the master.

You may ask: If such a servant hired himself for a year, or for another period of time, is he bound—once the contract period has ended—to persevere in service until he makes up for that time in which he was hindered from serving? It must be said that neither can the master compel him to stay, nor can the servant compel the master to let him make up for that time by extending the period of service. This is because the burden of serving was precisely for the time prescribed in the contract; therefore, once that time has passed, the burden does not remain for the following period. This is just like a person who does not fast, or does not recite the Divine Office <note>The daily cycle of prayers required of clergy and religious orders</note> at the time prescribed by the Church; he is not bound to make it up afterward, because it was a burden specific to that day or time. The same must be said of other leases: if, on the part of the thing leased (according to what was said in the cited Disputation 493), the hirer cannot use it—for instance, if because of war or plague he cannot inhabit it for several months—the contract should not be extended, once the initially established time has ended, for as much time as the hindrance lasted. This has always been the observed custom.

<margin>The Law of Castile.</margin>
By Law 1, Title 20, Book 6 of the *New Collection*, under penalty of twenty thousand maravedis <note>A common Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account</note> and exile from that place, it is commanded that no one at all, of whatever condition, may have more than two of these servants whom they call lackeys <note>original: "lacaios," typically liveried footmen or personal attendants</note>. By Law 2 of the same title, it is commanded of any male or female servant, of whatever condition and in whatever ministry they serve, that if they withdraw themselves from the master’s service, they cannot serve another in that same place, nor in its suburbs, without the express permission and goodwill of the former master. The penalty is to be cast into chains for twenty days and exiled for one

<column-break/>

year from that place; and whoever receives him into his service shall pay six thousand maravedis. However, if the male or female servant did not withdraw from the master's service, but the master himself expelled them, they may serve another in the same place. Yet, the second master ought to first ask the former master whether he expelled them, and the answer of the former master must be stood by. Nonetheless, it is permitted for a servant who has withdrawn from a former master to commit themselves in the same place to the service of someone from whom they may learn a trade, or to hire out their labor for wages in agricultural work. Furthermore, they may serve anyone else in a different location. These things are understood provided they are not done to defraud the prior prohibition. They are considered to be done in fraud if the servant, within four months in the place where he deserted the former master, commits himself to the service of another. If, however, the one who withdrew from someone’s service had received from him some advance payment or clothing, and withdraws from that service before the contract time is completed and the payment earned, he falls under the aforementioned penalties—even if he leaves the place where he served the former master, or serves someone else to learn a trade at the same time. This law, although passed to prevent the evils that usually arise from one person taking a servant who served another, and to that extent seems to do less injury to servants (since it is established before they commit to anyone's service, and they can foresee that they accept service under that law and condition), nevertheless seems rigid to me, and contrary to the liberty of servants, if it is understood to apply even when the servant departs from the master after the time originally prescribed by both parties in the contract has ended.

<margin>The Law of Portugal.</margin>
In Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 18, it is decreed that when one has served with no set wage, if he has received a tunic and a cloak <note>original: "tunicam, & pallium"</note> from the master, he cannot depart from him without his consent before a full year of service is completed. If, however, he received only one of those two, or any other clothing, he cannot depart except after completing a half-year of service. The same applies if he serves by tending horses and has received the same or something equivalent. Whoever does not observe these rules is cast into chains until he pays double, plus all expenses incurred in the matter. But if someone who was serving the King, Queen, Prince, or the Infantes <note>Royal princes or princesses of Spain or Portugal</note> departs from their service, he is brought to the Royal Court in chains. Whoever receives these people into his own service, if—having been warned by the former master or another by his command—he does not expel them, he pays just as much as the servant was bound to return to the former master: half to the King, and half to the accuser. Moreover, a servant of someone from the King’s court, with no set wage, cannot thereafter be the servant of another from the court who dwells in it, without the permission of the former master. If, however, one receives him and, after being warned, does not dismiss him, he pays ten gold coins <note>original: "aureos"</note>: half to the former master and half to the King, and is compelled to dismiss the servant. Furthermore, it is commanded that no one, of whatever condition, shall take as a servant, or under his protection and care, the servant of another who has been...

But if they do not lay hands on him, yet draw a sword or take up arms against him: if the said servant be a <term>nobleman</term> <note>original: "hijo de algo," literally "son of something," the lowest tier of nobility</note>, in addition to the other penalties, he shall be imprisoned in jail for thirty days and banished for two years. If he is not a nobleman, in addition to the said penalties, he shall be <term>subjected to public shame</term> <note>original: "traido a la verguenza," a punishment involving public exposure or parading</note>. If the injury is not by deed or by taking up arms, but by words only, our judges and justices shall proceed according to the quality of the case and the persons involved.

Law 4 of the same title states as follows: We command that any servant to a person, serving in whatever service or office, who shall involve himself in and have carnal access with any woman, servant, or slave of the house of his lord and master—if he is not a nobleman—shall be given one hundred lashes publicly and banished for two years; and the said servant girl or woman shall receive the same penalty. But if he is a nobleman, he shall be subjected to public shame and banished from the kingdom for one year, and for four years from the place where this occurred. However, if the aforementioned occurs with a relative of the lord or master, or with a maiden being raised in his house, or a wet-nurse raising his child, justice shall be done with greater rigor as the quality of the case requires. And the same penalty shall be incurred by those male or female servants who are proven to have been intermediaries or go-betweens for others from outside the house to commit the said crime.

And Law 2, Title 1, Book 5 states: Any man who lives with a master, and while living with him, becomes betrothed to or marries the daughter or a female relative whom that master keeps in his house, without his command,

<column-break/>

the one who commits such an error shall be cast out of the kingdom forever; and if he returns to it without our license, the justices shall put him to death. The woman shall be disinherited, and her closest relatives shall have her goods. The father, mother, lord, or lady with whom she lived may accuse her. If they do not accuse her, any of the closest relatives up to the third degree may do so. But if the father, mother, or lord with whom she lived pardons her, no one else may accuse her.

And in Book 8, Title 20, Law 6, it is held: We command that anyone who commits fornication with the recognized <term>concubine</term> <note>original: "barragana," a woman in a legally recognized but non-marital union</note> of the master, or with a maiden he has in his house, or with the lady’s maid, or with the relative of the one with whom he lives (the relative residing in the master's house), or with the wet-nurse who nurses the child as long as she is giving milk, shall be put to death for it. And the woman who commits this error shall be placed in the power of the one with whom she lived, that he may give her the penalty he wishes, whether death or another kind. And he who commits such wickedness with a house servant who is not among those mentioned above, each of them shall be given one hundred lashes publicly through the town. And if he who commits this error with a servant is a nobleman, and she is a noblewoman, he shall serve one year in chains; and if either of them is not noble, they shall be given one hundred lashes. I observe that if in any of the laws previously related a different penalty is established for committing one of these crimes, those other laws must stand as they were enacted later.

Book 5 of the <term>Portuguese Ordinances</term> <note>original: "Lusit. ordi.," likely the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*</note>, Title 18, states: Every man who lives with another, whether for wages or for "well-doing" <note>original: "a bē fazer," serving for favor or future advancement rather than a set salary</note>, and marries the daughter, mother, sister, or female cousin of the one with whom he lives—whether they are within the doors or outside the house—without the command or license of the master; or sleeps with any of the above-mentioned, whether inside or outside the house; or marries or sleeps in the master's house with a servant who is "within the doors" and does not serve outside the house: he shall die a natural death for it. No defense shall be received by his claiming he was married to said servant or married outside the house, if it is proven he slept with her in or out of the house, whether she was there for wages or for "well-doing." And if he marries or sleeps with a second cousin of the master or mistress, or marries or sleeps with a servant who is not "within the doors" but serves outside the house, he shall be <term>exiled forever</term> <note>original: "degradado pera sempre"</note> to the <term>island of São Tomé</term> <note>an island off the coast of Africa used as a penal colony</note>. However, for those condemned to death for such a crime, the execution shall not be carried out until they inform us, so we may see the case with its qualities and circumstances, and thus we shall command what is our mercy. And if he sleeps with any white slave of the master who is kept "within the doors," he shall be exiled forever to the island of São Tomé.

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal and moral analysis of the relationship between masters and servants, transitioning from the duration of service to the determination of "just wages" under Portuguese and Castilian law, as well as moral theology.</meta>

# On the just wage of servants.
## DISPUTATION 506.

->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> What constitutes a just salary or wage for servants according to Portuguese law.
<margin>2</margin> Two types of servants (continued in paragraph 5).
<margin>3</margin> What the laws of Portugal and Castile establish regarding male and female servants.
<margin>4</margin> When a servant is held responsible for a theft committed by another.

---

<margin>1</margin>
Regarding the wages of servants: although it was formerly decreed in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 19, that when someone served "to do well" <note>original: "a ben fecer," a legal term for serving without a predefined contract</note>—that is, with no set wage established—if the service was of the kind for which a wage is ordinarily paid, the servant could demand a wage. In such cases, they were to be awarded as much as was customarily paid to others in that location for similar services. However, if the service was not of the kind for which a wage is ordinarily paid, but rather the kind usually performed by those who leave it to their masters to reward them as they wish—a manner in which many are ordinarily accustomed to serve the nobility—then the male or female servant could demand nothing for such services. Nevertheless, later, in the sixth part of the <term>Extravagant Laws</term> <note>original: "legum extrauag.," referring to laws promulgated outside the main systematic collections</note>, Title 1, Law 3, that former law was rightly revoked in this second regard. It was decreed that even in that event, male or female servants could demand a just price for their services, and they should be awarded whatever is judged to be worthy compensation, considering the duration of the service and the quality of the servants and their labors. This rule is observed in practice in Portugal, especially when a prelate or another nobleman departs this life without having compensated the services of such servants.

<margin>2</margin>
To state my view on the just wage of servants, two types of servants must be distinguished. Some serve for a specific, fixed wage established for them. Regarding these, it must be said: unless it is clearer than the midday sun that the established wage—considering all concurrent circumstances—falls outside the limits of the <term>lowest just price</term> <note>Molina refers to the "just price" theory, where a price/wage has a range (highest, middle, lowest) rather than a single fixed point</note> and is therefore openly unjust, it is not to be judged unjust, not only in the civil courts but even in the "forum of conscience" <note>the moral judgment of the soul, often in the context of confession</note>. Consequently, such a servant can neither demand anything more as a debt, nor, if it is not granted, can they secretly take anything from the master’s goods as compensation for their services. If they do take it, knowing the master is presumably unwilling (or if it is doubtful whether he is unwilling), they commit theft and are bound to restore it. This remains true even if the servant can barely sustain themselves on that wage and lives miserably, unable to support children or their own household; for a master is only bound to give the just wage for the services, considering the concurrent circumstances, and not as much as might be sufficient for the servant to maintain themselves—and much less for the support of their children or family. These points hold true whether one serves any other person for an established stipend, or serves the King. These things are well known in themselves: for when the injustice of a
<meta>catchword: contract</meta>

<column-break/>

contract is not evident, one must abide by it; and whatever was established by both parties is to be considered just. However, when the injustice of the wage is evident—because it clearly does not reach the limits of the lowest just rate—then, unless it were below half of the lowest just price, the servant would certainly not be assisted in the civil courts. But they could make <term>occult compensation</term> <note>a controversial theological concept where a person secretly takes what they are morally owed but cannot obtain through legal means</note> in the forum of conscience alone, only for that which is missing to reach the breadth of the lowest just wage, and no more—and only by observing those conditions for licit compensation which will be explained in their proper place in this second treatise on justice.

To make these matters and those that follow—which are daily occurrences in confessions—clearer, the following should be observed: there are many offices or ministries to perform which many people would be found who would gladly hire themselves out for a certain annual or monthly wage, even though that wage is not sufficient to sustain themselves, and much less their entire family. Many gladly hire themselves out for those tasks for that wage because, although it is not sufficient for a fitting livelihood, it nevertheless contributes to and suffices when combined with other goods that the person has, or with the industry they can apply to other things at the same time. And when many people are found who will gladly hire themselves out for that task for that wage, the wage is not to be considered unjust for performing that duty or office, even if it is given to someone for whom it is insufficient for their sustenance—perhaps because they lack other goods or industry, or because they have many children, or because they wish to live more splendidly and with a larger household than they otherwise would.

By this reasoning, you can easily dismiss the excuses and pretexts of many in the confessional who, while holding royal or other public offices, or serving the nobility by accompanying them or their wives, or assisting in their homes, or performing other duties in their houses, take something beyond their stipend—either from those who have business with them by virtue of their office, or secretly from the royal goods, or from the goods of those they serve. They claim they do this because their stipend is meager and they cannot sustain themselves, their children, or their household with it, as if that were a just cause for such usurpation and something that would excuse them from the burden of restitution. For if there are others who would gladly undertake that duty for that stipend, it is clear the stipend is just, and therefore these people are bound to restore what they have thus usurped.

Therefore, regarding those who serve for a fixed stipend, I believe this rule should be established: if, considering the ministry in which one serves, and considering the multitude or rarity of those who are found at that time to serve in such a way, at least the lowest stipend that is customarily established in that region at that time for those serving in such a ministry is set, the stipend is to be judged just. Consequently, if that servant should secretly usurp anything, where it is not certain that the master is willing, he is bound to restore it. But if he is paid less than the lowest customary stipend—either because the servant was ignorant of it when they agreed to it, or because they were unwillingly forced to serve for it by royal ministers or anyone else...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal and moral standards for servant wages, arguing that a wage is "just" if others are willing to work for it, regardless of whether it meets the servant's personal needs, and strictly limits the practice of "occult compensation."</summary>

# Second Treatise. Disputation 507. 673

...and with another, or finally; because someone was compelled by necessity—since he found no one better—and yet there is some other circumstance why his service is worth less than others; in that case, the person hiring is bound to restore the increment to the person hired, up to the limits of what is just. Indeed, I believe that when a person was forced to serve, especially if he suffers a loss through that compulsion, at the very least this restitution should reach the midpoint of a just salary. This is because he himself may not wish to hire himself out for the lowest just price; the master is not entitled to that when the servant was unwillingly compelled to serve for that price. From this part of the rule, an exception must be made when the hirer does not actually need the labor or ministry of that servant, but took him into his service at the request of the servant himself or someone else. In that case, the master is not bound to give the salary he would in an ordinary situation, unless out of mercy he grants a just remuneration until the servant finds a place where he can stay for a just wage. Regarding this limitation, even if the master did not find the servant's work so useful that he would pay any wage worthy of what he receives from it, he is then bound to provide nothing beyond the perceived utility, up to a just wage for the service. According to these points, the teachings on this matter by Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 168, and Soto in book 5 of *On Justice*, question 3, article 3, reply to the 1st, can be understood and brought into harmony.

->Two Admonitions.<-

The first is: when, according to the contract entered into from the beginning, the servant is owed maintenance <note>original: "sustentatio," referring to food, housing, and basic needs</note> in addition to a continuous wage (as is usually the case), that maintenance must be of the kind customarily provided to similar servants. Therefore, if it does not reach the moderate or even the lowest level usually provided in that rank, the servant is not to be blamed if—provided he can demand it without shame or other danger—and it is not given, he secretly takes something to compensate for it. This is because he is taking what is owed to him but not paid; and if he were to seek it in court, he would either not be heard, or he would spend more in obtaining it, and receive more trouble from the master for that reason than the item is worth.

<margin><unclear>Soto, On Justice, q. 3. art. 3.</unclear></margin>
The second is: when a servant is taken on by a craftsman to serve and learn a trade from him, or is taken on by someone to serve and devote himself to studies (as servants are customarily taken on by scholars in universities), and for that reason only food and shoes are usually provided to them—and sometimes something is even paid to the craftsman to help support such a servant—then, if the master prevents him from learning the skills or the scholar prevents him from studying by ordering him to do other things, the master sins gravely. He is bound to restore the serious loss of the trade’s skill or the loss of knowledge. Likewise, if a craftsman is negligent in teaching him the art, but expects him to leave time to finish the works of the trade, he sins and must restore the loss of skill in the craft. So says Navarrus in the place cited above, number 109.

<margin><unclear>Soto, On Justice, q. 3.</unclear></margin>
It should also be observed that if someone serves another for a wage established at a lower rate than would otherwise be just, but does so because he wishes to grant the master the difference—either because of benefits received or to gain favor with him in the hope of obtaining a greater

<column-break/>

good from him or through his intercession—then, because this is not a simple hiring but one mixed with a gift of the deduction from a just wage, the person hiring such a servant or such labor is bound to no restitution, even if the one hired is frustrated in the hope that led him to give the discount. This is because that hope was only the motivating and final cause for giving, not a condition under which it was given (as if the gift would be void if the hope were not realized), as was said in the matter of donations and in Disputation 210 and the two preceding ones.

3 The other † kind of servants consists of those who serve someone with no certain wage established. Indeed, if such services are those which are regularly performed for a certain established wage—such as a servant taken on for plowing, for guarding a flock, for carrying wood from the field on pack animals, and for other similar things—even if no certain wage is established but the servant has left it to the master's judgment, the master is bound, both in conscience and in the external court, to pay him the just wage customary for those ministries in that region and place, as is decreed in Book 4 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 19.

If, however, the services are not of the kind that, considering the status of those serving and those served, are regularly done for a certain established wage, then if the services are worthy of a greater retribution than the honest maintenance of the servant (also providing him with suitable clothing), then compensation is certainly owed to him according to his quality, the proportion of time, and the quality of the services. This is what Law 3 of the *Extravagant Laws* of Portugal, Title 1, Part 6, establishes; whereas previously in the cited Title 19, the opposite had been established regarding the external court. I said, "if the services are worthy of a greater retribution than the honest maintenance of the servant, also providing him with suitable clothing," because many people—not without reason—assert that by the rigor of justice, this is the suitable provision for the service of those boys born of honest rank whom the Spanish call <term>pages</term> <note>Spanish: "pajes," young men serving in noble households to learn courtly manners</note>. They serve nobles such as counts, marquises, dukes, prelates, and others like them, at the request of their parents. For although they are handed over in the hope of a even greater reward, relying on the nobility, liberality, and power of the masters, the nobles nevertheless bestow a significant benefit upon both the boys and their parents (which many others would desire), as they relieve the parents of the expenses they would have had to incur for them. They support and clothe such boys honorably, instruct them in courtly and urban manners, and make them more capable of greater service and duties. Therefore, where the custom is that by the rigor of justice nothing more is given for such services, the nobles are bound to nothing else in conscience or in the external court.

However, when a retribution beyond maintenance is owed for services, nobles are accustomed to provide it in many ways: namely, by establishing for those they have nurtured in some lower ministry some salary until they ascend to a higher grade of service, which may be...

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...be the entire wage due, or a portion of it. Later, indeed, they fulfill it in various ways—namely, when the servants depart from the service itself—by prescribing a stipend to be given to them every year for as long as such servants and the masters themselves live; or when the male servants marry, or the maidservants wed, by bestowing something upon them, either in money, or in clothing, or by obtaining some office for them from the King; or, if the granting of any office belongs to such masters, by conferring it upon them, or some other benefit. In these same ways, they are accustomed to pay for complete services. It is also customary, especially in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, to pay for services by obtaining from the King that he receive their servants into his own service, or that he grant them some office in **India**, or on the Indian ships, or in any other matter. Since Kings grant these things in consideration of those petitioning, and partly in that way pay the petitioners for the merits they have with the King, once these things are obtained from the King, the masters are rightly accustomed to satisfy their servants when these rewards exceed the service rendered by the servants. However, when masters have not fully satisfied the servants for the services rendered by these or other means, then in the **forum of conscience** <term>the internal realm of moral and religious duty, as opposed to legal courts</term> they are bound to pay them in full, and in the **external forum** <term>the public legal court system</term> the servants can demand this from the masters or from their heirs.

It is common for such servants, while they are serving their masters, to secretly misappropriate many of their goods and consume them poorly; this is a very frequent case in **confessions** <note>referring to the Sacrament of Penance where such thefts were admitted to priests</note>. However, when they do not exceed the just and certain wage that is already owed to them for their services, they are first of all to be sharply and seriously restrained from doing anything similar in the future. Next, care must be taken so that, as far as possible, they restore the damages inflicted on the masters, and that they hope for and demand their full stipend from them when it is likely to be paid by the masters in due time. Otherwise, it must be allowed that they compensate themselves from the wage already earned and owed to them by the rigors of justice; yet under this condition: that they take care that their masters do not pay it to them or their successors a second time. Rather, the masters should understand at an appropriate time that they do not owe it, because an equivalent amount was taken from their goods due to human fragility in the course of the time they served them. Indeed, it is very expedient that what was said in the second-to-last place be done as much as possible, rather than this last option, because of the danger that the masters might pay the wage twice to deceased or absent servants, or that the servants, at the time of receiving the wage, might accept it and demand it in full—either out of greed or because shame overcomes them, preventing them from revealing that less is owed to them because the remainder was secretly taken during the course of time.

It should be observed that in some places, maidservants and servants who serve with no established wage are sometimes so miserably supported and treated by their masters that they are provided neither with the necessities of food—which are commonly accustomed and ought to be given to similar servants in other houses—nor are they given what is necessary for clothing, undergarments, shoes, hats, and the like. Instead, the masters expect that such servants, who have no other source of income to buy these things, should seek and buy them for themselves. However, since competent support (even if meager) and competent clothing (even if modest) is owed to them according to the contract

<column-break/>

and common custom, in addition to other compensation for their services, those who secretly take something from the masters' goods for these necessities alone are certainly not to be blamed; provided that they first ask the masters for what is necessary for food and clothing, if they can do so without detriment to themselves and great embarrassment, and the masters do not provide them.

<margin>4 †</margin>
In **Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 21**, it is decreed that when a master expels a servant from the house before the finished time—if the servant was taken for a certain defined period for a certain wage—the master must be compelled to pay him the full wage. This, however, is to be understood as applying when he was expelled without just cause, and the servant was fulfilling his part of the contract as he ought. And then I believe (according to what is immediately added there concerning servants departing before the finished time) that a servant unjustly expelled is not bound to return to complete the time. For this is established as a penalty for the unjust expulsion, and not as if he is only compelled to fulfill the contract on his part, as he is bound to do when it does not depend on the servant but he wishes to fulfill it on his part. Similarly, it is established in the same place that if a servant departs before the time is completed without the master's fault, he is to be compelled to both restore the wage (or part of it, if he had already received it) and to serve the full time, with no payment of the wage being made to him. This part, however—namely, that he loses the payment already earned and to be earned—since it is established as a penalty, is not owed by the servant before a sentence is passed. Hence, if he departed after receiving some earned payment, he is not to be ordered to restore it before it is sought by the master. However, when he had earned part of the payment but had not received it, and departed by his own fault before the time was completed, then neither in the external forum nor in the forum of conscience is the master bound to pay him the earned wage; rather, he can retain it for himself as a penalty, even if a judge's sentence does not award it to him. For to whom an action is given to recover something if he had already paid it, an exception is granted so that he is not bound to pay it if it is demanded from him. Consequently, as long as it is not demanded, he lawfully retains it, being prepared to object and ask that it be awarded to him as a just penalty established by law if it is demanded. This whole case is quite frequent in confessions in **Portugal** because of that law.

<margin>Portugal and Castile</margin>
The eighth law, title 4, book 4 of the **Forum** <term>referring to the *Fuero Real* or local statutory law</term> also establishes in this Kingdom that if a master expels a servant before the finished time without the servant's fault, he is bound to pay him the entire wage. If, however, the servant departs before the finished time without the master's fault, he loses the entire wage and, moreover, must pay an equivalent amount.

Furthermore, within what time a servant is bound to demand his wage after he has departed from the master's service—otherwise an action to demand it is not granted to him by the law of **Castile** and **Portugal**, and how this is to be understood—was stated in Disputation 67.

If the servant has caused damage to the master, the master may demand it from the servant, or compensate for it in the wage, as held in Book 4 of the **Portuguese Ordinances**, title 22, and the cited law 8 of the Forum; this is very well known in itself. Otherwise, by Portuguese law, it happens...
