<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral obligations regarding servant wages and damages, specifically referencing Portuguese law, before transitioning to a new section on the nature and morality of insurance contracts.</meta>

In the cited Title 22 <note>This likely refers to the *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the historical legal codes of Portugal</note>, it is decreed that when a servant has not left before the end of the contract term, the master is required at the time of the servant's departure to declare any damages before a judge or before honest men. Otherwise, when the servant later demands his wages, the master will not be able to claim damages from him. This is because it is presumed the master only brings up the damage to avoid paying the full wages truly owed. However, when the master has formally protested the damage, he is granted only four days to prove it from the moment the servant demands his wages—unless the master wishes to pay the full wage immediately; in that case, a longer time will be granted as the judge deems fair. Note, however, that these rules were established as a prudent caution so that masters do not harass their servants or defraud them of their just wages. Nevertheless, when a servant has truly caused damage to a master through his own fault—even a minor fault—he is bound in the **internal forum of conscience** <term>the realm of moral and religious duty</term> to restore it fully to the master, regardless of these provisions of **Portuguese law** <note>original: "iuris Lusitani"</note>.

<margin>A Question</margin>
Whether a servant is bound to restore something to his master if it is stolen from the house or if damage is done to the master with the servant’s knowledge, provided he was able to prevent it and did not.

<margin>The Decision</margin>
It must be said that if the **care** <note>legal responsibility or custody</note> of that thing was entrusted to him—at least at the time it was stolen or damaged, perhaps because he was given the key to open a place and do something there—then he is liable. This also applies if his specific office in the house involves the care and custody of all things or specific items committed to him as part of his duty. He is held to make restitution to the master if any of these are stolen or damaged through even the "slightest fault" of the servant, let alone when he knows of it and is able to prevent it.

Indeed, if he could not prevent it due to **superior force** <note>original: "maiore vim," referring to an unstoppable event like an armed robbery</note>, he is bound to warn the person taking or damaging the item to restore it. If that person refuses and the servant is able to do so, he is bound—not only out of **charity** <note>moral love for neighbor</note> as others are, but also out of **justice**—to ensure the master is compensated. This includes identifying the offender if that is the only way the damage can be repaired and no other effective way exists. This applies, however, only if he can reveal the culprit safely and without great danger to himself.

On the other hand, when the servant does not have the care of the specific thing being stolen or damaged in any of these ways, then even if he sees it being taken or damaged by other servants or anyone else and does not prevent it, he is bound by **charity** to stop it and later ensure it is restored. In this case, he is in the same position as a stranger rather than a servant, because he is not considered the "cause" of the damage since he was not bound by his office or a specific trust to prevent it.

# On the contract of insurance, and on a certain other contract similar to it, common in Seville.

## DISPUTATION 507.
### SUMMARY

1 *What the contract of insurance is, and to what species of contract it belongs (also in number 2).*
3 *What is required for a contract of insurance to be just.*
4 *How to prove the knowledge of the one seeking insurance that the thing had already perished.*
5 *If one insures for a certain quantity which is later found to be less, is one bound to the whole sum or only the actual quantity?*
6 *If one insures a ship loaded with goods for a certain sum if it does not reach a destination, is one bound, and how, if there are no goods or another accident occurs?*
7 *A contract in which someone secures the life of another for a certain time for a price is valid.*
8 *The contract usually made in **Seville** <note>original: "Hispali"</note> for the sake of goods and business: what name it is called by, and when it is lawful.*

We must now speak of those contracts in which fortune is mixed with skill and industry. We shall begin with the contract of **insurance** <note>original: "assecurationis"</note>, which we may define as follows:
<margin>1</margin>
It is a contract by which the risk of a thing is undertaken for a price or other interest. Because by undertaking the risk, the thing is made "secure" in its own way for the person for whose benefit the risk is taken, this is called a contract of **insurance**. According to **Alvaro Valasco** <note>A 16th-century Portuguese jurist</note>, there is a public insurance board in **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olyssiponę"</note> where a notary is appointed by royal authority for these contracts. The same appears to be the case in other major commercial centers, such as **Seville** and **Genoa**.

As to what category this contract belongs: setting aside the opinions of those who claim
<margin>2</margin>
it should be reduced to a contract of hiring and leasing, or a contract of suretyship <note>acting as a guarantor</note>—in which I see no probability—there are two main opinions. The first asserts it is an **innominate contract** <term>a contract that does not fall under a specific traditional Roman law category</term> on the part of the insurers: "I will do" or "I will take the risk on myself so that you may give"; and "I give so that you may do" on the part of the person offering the price. This is affirmed by **Sylvester Prieras**, **Baldus de Ubaldis**, and others. Others in our time judge it to be a contract of **buying and selling**, or reducible to it, by which the undertaking of risk (or the obligation to pay the value of the thing if it perishes) is sold for a certain price. Just as the "cast of a net"—that is, the right to the fish that will be caught by the cast—is bought and sold <note>This is a famous Roman law concept: *emptio spei*, or buying a hope/chance</note>, so the burden or obligation of paying for the thing if it perishes can be sold and bought. I incline toward this opinion, along with Alvaro Valasco. Therefore, when a price is promised for the insurance of a thing, as is regularly done...

### Luis de Molina on Contracts

<margin>Disputations 254 and 259 were discussed.</margin>
It is common practice—and rightly so, since such a contract is a form of **buying and selling**—that it is finalized solely by mutual consent. It shall be a **contract of good faith** <term>a legal agreement based on trust and fairness rather than strict technicalities</term>, according to what was said in Disputations 254 and 259. Note this: although the risk of a thing can be undertaken for free (in which case the contract is not "onerous" but "gratuitous," falling under the category of a gift or act of generosity), it is normally not celebrated in that way. Therefore, we have defined the **insurance contract** as specifically "onerous," and our discussion in this disputation concerns that type alone.

<margin>
Conrad [Summenhart] in *On Contracts*, question 71, says that when someone who is going to apply their effort toward preserving a thing takes the risk upon themselves for a moderate fee, the contract is just—for example, if a sailor takes on the risk for the goods he carries on his ship. He gives this reason: because insurance then leads to the "spiritual health" of the sailor, who will take more diligent care of those goods than he is strictly bound to do. It also benefits not only the owner of the goods but the **public good**, because the goods will be better preserved and brought into the state. However, when someone who takes on the risk is not going to apply any effort toward the thing, Conrad says the contract is illicit. He argues this because it does not lead to the public good, and because those who insure in this way want to profit while being idle, contrary to **Genesis 3**: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." <note>original: "In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo."</note> Nevertheless, this opinion is rightly rejected by everyone. This contract often serves the public good because many would stop transporting goods under the danger of huge losses unless there were people willing to take on that risk for a certain price. It also often benefits those paying the price, because in this way they are freed from a much greater potential loss. Furthermore, the wealthy are not bound to perform manual labor to eat their bread, nor is that strictly commanded in Genesis 3; rather, that was a pronouncement of punishment for Adam’s sin—that it would henceforth be necessary for him and his descendants to work so that the earth would provide what was necessary for their survival. Additionally, such a contract can be entered into while simultaneously intending to engage in other negotiations and services useful to the state. Therefore, there is no reason for Conrad to condemn this or other contracts that depend on fortune (which we will discuss later) based on this point.
</margin>
There is no one who doubts that this contract is just, provided the price is equal to the proportion of the risk one takes on; indeed, the undertaking of risk for a thing is something that can be valued and sold. Nor does the **just price** <term>the fair market value as determined by moral theology</term> for such a thing consist of a single fixed point; it has a range—lowest, middle, and "rigorous" (highest) just price. And this price increases or decreases not only according to the greater or lesser value of the thing being insured, but also according to the greater or lesser risk to which the insurer exposes himself—for instance, if the ship carrying the goods is to make a longer and more difficult voyage, or if there are many pirates, and so on.

3. For an insurance contract to be just, it is necessary that the outcome of the thing being insured be uncertain, at least in comparison to the knowledge that each of the contracting parties has about the matter. For both parties must be exposed to profit and loss for the contract to be just. The insurer 

<column-break/>

stands to lose by paying the indemnity for a smaller fee, or to gain that fee entirely if no loss occurs. The one seeking insurance, on the other hand, stands to lose the price he paid, but to obtain a much greater indemnity from the insurer in exchange for it. In this exchange of one risk and advantage for another, the contract is just, provided that **equality** (a certain proportion) is seen on both sides, considering the concurrent circumstances. Therefore, if the person seeking insurance knew, at the time they made the contract, that the thing they were insuring had already perished, the contract is void. They cannot receive the value of the lost item, but can only recover the price they paid for the insurance, while being required to pay all expenses incurred in making the contract. Furthermore, they must pay the insurer for any other loss that arose or profit that ceased because of the contract—perhaps because the insurer passed up another profitable contract for this reason.

<margin>Disputations 352 and 353 were discussed.</margin>
By this same reasoning, if rumors had reached the person seeking insurance that the thing had perished, or if they had suspicions about the outcome which they hid from the insurer—certainly, if the insurer would not have entered the contract or would have charged a much higher price had they known—then fraud has "given cause" to the contract. In such a case, the seeker of insurance either cannot receive any value for the thing (if the fraud was the primary reason for the contract), or they are bound to restore the difference in price to the insurer, according to what was said in Disputations 352 and 353. However, given the risk the seeker was exposing himself to—the risk that the thing might *not* have perished and he would have lost his premium to the insurer without any benefit—he might perhaps be able to keep something beyond the premium he paid, in consideration of that risk, even when fraud gave cause to the contract. In the same way, if the insurer knew the thing was already safe when he made the contract (for instance, knowing the ship had already reached port), the contract is void. He is bound to restore the price he received for the insurance, plus any expenses incurred. If he did not *know* for sure but had suspicions that it was safe which the buyer did not have, or knew the ship was so close to port that there was little to no danger, and he did not disclose this, he is bound to restore either the portion of the price the buyer would not have paid, or the whole price if the buyer would not have contracted at all—unless something should be deducted for the small risk he still faced of the ship sinking between its current location and the port.

<margin>Alvaro Valasco, *Consultation* 64, cited from number 9.</margin>
How, then, is the knowledge of the one seeking insurance (that the thing perished) or the insurer (that the thing was safe) to be proven? Alvaro Valasco, in *Consultation* 64, rightly says it is not sufficiently proven by the mere lapse of time in which a messenger *could* have arrived.

<summary>Molina defends the moral validity of insurance as a contract based on the sale of risk, refuting earlier claims that it constitutes "idle gain." He establishes that justice in insurance depends on mutual uncertainty and the honest disclosure of information regarding the safety of the goods.</summary>

### Second Treatise. Disputation 507.

...was determined, by calculating twenty-four leagues, or parasangs <term>an ancient unit of distance, roughly 3 to 4 miles</term>, for each day, according to the practice accepted among merchants. This is considered the minimum distance a ship usually covers when there are no contrary winds. Those who travel by relay horses (which our people call *by the post*) are expected to cover at least thirty leagues daily. Because a messenger might fail to arrive within that time for various reasons, and the person who insured or sought insurance might be ignorant of this, it is rightly said that the matter should be left to the judgment of a prudent person based on the surrounding circumstances. In cases of doubt, it should be presumed in the public court <term>the 'outer forum,' or secular legal system</term> that knowledge of the loss was not present.

I have said that for an insurance contract to be just, the event being insured must be uncertain—at least in comparison to the knowledge that each of the contracting parties had about the matter. This is enough so that, by the very act of making the contract, both parties expose themselves to profit and loss. This suffices for the contract to be equal and just, even if the thing has already perished or is already safe, provided they are deemed to consent that the insurance contract is valid regardless of the current state of the thing. This is similar to a contract of betting—which some call a "wager," others a "deposit," and in Spanish is called an *apuesta*—regarding a past event. It is enough if the outcome is uncertain to both parties for the contract to be equal and just. Both parties are deemed to consent because each equally exposes himself to profit and loss based on the knowledge he possesses. This is the view of Gama in Decision 181 and Aluarus Valascus in Consultation 64, number 6. From this, as Aluarus Valascus notes in numbers 1 and 7, it is common to express in a contract that insurance is understood to apply from the time the ship leaves port, even if it perishes through the ship's own fault, and even if it takes a different route to stop at another port, which the Portuguese call *making a port call* <note>original: "fazer scala"</note>. Even if such clauses are not added, one must judge from custom and the concurrent circumstances whether the parties intended this. For example, if a contract for insurance on goods carried in an Indian ship is made in Portugal two or three months after the ships usually depart from India, it is clear that the goods are insured from the moment the ship leaves India.

When someone living in Portugal, for instance, instructs their business agent in India to send them goods valued at four thousand gold coins on a specific ship, and believing they are coming, enters into an insurance contract in Portugal for all of them, a doubt arises: if it is later discovered that the goods were not sent, or not in such a large quantity, is he held to the full price of the insurance? Similarly, if that ship perishes, is the insurer bound to pay him the full value of four thousand gold coins for those goods? This is the situation discussed by Gama in Decision 181, number 2, and Aluarus Valascus in Consultation 64, number 5. They rightly respond, following Pedro Santerna, that it was decided in the Portuguese Senate that if no goods were loaded, the contract was null. Consequently, neither is one party held to the premium, nor the other to the value of the goods. However, if fewer goods were loaded, one is held only to the insurance premium for the quantity of goods actually put on the ship, and the other is held only to the value of those specific goods if they perished—not to the full four thousand gold coins. The reason is that the "matter" of the contract is missing, without which it cannot stand. The contract is deemed to be made on the hypothesis that the goods would be loaded; therefore, if they were not loaded, consent was lacking. If only a part was loaded, consent was likewise lacking regarding the remainder that was not loaded.

<column-break/>

<margin>Question.</margin>
The scenario discussed by [Domingo de] Soto in Book 6, *On Justice*, question 7, article 1, is quite different. Namely, if someone with an empty ship claims it is loaded with goods and valued at forty thousand gold coins, and for a premium of two thousand gold coins, he bargains with someone that the insurer will pay forty thousand if the ship does not arrive safely at the destination port. This assumes the contract would be just if it actually carried goods valued at that total price. Soto responds that if the person taking on the risk knew the ship carried no goods and yet entered the contract, the contract is valid. This is because no injury is done to him; it is like a type of betting (what the Spaniards call *a wager* <note>original: "de apuesta"</note>): "if the ship does not arrive safely, I will give you forty thousand, provided you give me two thousand." This opinion is true. However, observe that if the ship perishes through the owner's fault so that he might collect the forty thousand gold coins, then the one who took the risk is not held to anything. For the fraud <term>Latin: 'dolus,' meaning intentional deception or wrongdoing</term> and injustice of the ship owner should not protect him, and it would excuse the insurer from the burden of paying that valuation. Soto adds that if the person who took the risk on the ship and goods believed the story was true—that the ship and its goods were worth that entire valuation—the contract is invalid. This is because fraud was the cause of the contract; the insurer would not have entered it if he feared the ship owner might deliberately lose the ship for the hope of such a great profit. I would say that this is how it should be judged in the public court, and it is safe in the court of conscience <term>the 'inner forum,' or the individual's moral standing before God</term> for the one who took the risk, since he would not have entered the contract if he knew the ship lacked goods, and since he could presume that through the negligence or wickedness of the owner, the ship failed to arrive safely at port. I add, however, that if the ship owner applied as much diligence toward the ship as he would have if it were loaded with goods of that value, he should not be forced in the court of conscience to return those forty thousand gold coins, nor should he be prohibited in that same court from demanding them. I am led to this because the one taking the risk did not consider the value of the ship and goods so much as he considered taking on the risk of paying forty thousand for two thousand in that event, and in that, he was not deceived.

Furthermore, if he truly knew the ship owner would apply as much diligence to the preservation of the ship as he would if it had that full value in goods, he would not have backed out of the contract. Therefore, all those things said in the first place are based on a presumption, and thus they have no place in the court of conscience for an insurer who is fully aware of the truth. I have only this to advise: when...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral obligations of insurance contracts, specifically focusing on the valuation of goods and the limits of liability when losses occur at sea.</meta>

-># Ludovicus Molina on Contracts<-

If a certain value is insured in the event that everything is lost, the insurer is held to pay the total amount. However, if only a part of the shipment is lost, the insurer is only bound to pay for the value of that specific part, and not for the part that remains safe. If a falsehood were involved—for instance, if the ship were lost but the goods remained safe, either in whole or in part—and the ship was carrying goods of less value than claimed, then the value of the goods that remained safe must be deducted from the forty thousand gold pieces <note>original: "aureorum," referring to gold coins such as ducats</note> that the insurer is obligated to pay.

Hence, I say that since in the trade with the Indies <note>the Spanish Americas</note> and many other routes where merchants transport their goods, the care and management of the ship does not belong to the merchants themselves but to the owner and the ship's crew, the merchants pay for the transport of their goods. Consequently, the sailors manage the ship in the same way whether the goods are insured or not. Since insurance is regularly made only for fear of shipwreck or pirates—events in which all goods are usually lost along with the ship, rather than just a part of them—it seems very likely to me that if a merchant, looking after his goods, should lie by saying he is carrying more goods or goods of greater value, and pays the insurance premium according to that higher value without hope of recovering part of it if the goods arrive safely (as I hear is the custom), he may in good conscience, and even in the secular courts, receive the full value he insured in the event that all the goods are lost. This is because he paid the price for that entire value, and it does not matter to the insurer whether the goods were worth that much or less, as the insurer entered the contract in the same way regardless of the value. However, the reasoning is quite different when insurance is made in the hope that goods of a certain value would be placed on the ship, and it is later discovered that nothing was loaded, or only a part was loaded, a situation discussed above with Gammarius and Alvarez Valascus. In that case, since the basis upon which the contract was celebrated (the hope and presumption of the goods being present) does not exist, the contract is void for both parties, as it was made under the unspoken condition that the goods be placed on the ship. If the condition and the subject matter of the contract do not exist, the contract fails. But in the case proposed here, the goods were indeed loaded; there is only an error in their valuation, which the contracting parties do not care about. Indeed, the custom is for the estimation of the insured items to be made at the discretion of the person seeking insurance, whether they are worth much more or not, so that he pays the insurance premium based on that valuation, and the insurer pays out based on that same valuation if the item is lost. In this event, however, if only half of the goods were lost, only half of that higher valuation would be paid, and so on for other proportional parts that might perish.

Those who transport a large quantity of goods usually do not insure the whole amount, but only a part, so they do not have to pay a high premium and so that if all the goods are lost, they are not left with nothing, but at least retain the value of the insured portion. For example, if they transport goods worth six thousand gold pieces, they might insure only the value of two thousand. In this case, if it is specified which particular part is being insured, then if that part or a portion of it is lost,

<column-break/>

only what was lost from that specific part must be paid; nothing is owed if other uninsured parts are lost and the specified insured part remains safe. If, however, nothing is specifically designated, but simply two thousand gold pieces' worth of those goods are insured, then if all the goods are lost in a shipwreck or taken by pirates, the full two thousand gold pieces are paid. But if half of all those goods (which were valued at six thousand) are lost, only one thousand gold pieces are paid, and the same proportion applies to whatever other amount of goods might be lost.

If someone who has no assets insures a ship for a certain price, intending in his heart to flee to another region where nothing is known of him if the ship is lost, the contract is void. This is because deceit <note>original: "dolus," referring to intentional fraud</note> was the cause of the contract, and thus he is bound to return the price he received.

This contract is also licit: "Give me this much, and I will guarantee you that in this fair <note>a large seasonal market</note> where you are, or to which you are traveling, you will make such and such a profit, so that if you earn less, I will pay you the difference." This is a form of insurance and an assumption of risk for a price. So says Soto in the place cited above.

Whether it is usury to lend money and receive a price for taking the risk of the thing lent was discussed in Disputation 318.

<margin>
Question.
Decision 7.
</margin>
Furthermore, is a contract licit by which someone guarantees the life of another for a certain price, such that if that person dies before a certain time, the insurer pays a certain amount of money? Despite what some have said to the contrary, it must be answered in the affirmative, along with Soto and others. Indeed, it will rarely happen that the person to whom the money is to be paid (if the person whose life is at risk dies within that time) would wish for that death just to gain the money. Often, this contract is celebrated out of a great desire for the life of the person whose risk is being insured, and because it is of great interest that they do not die. Therefore, it cannot be doubted that it can be justly celebrated within the limits of justice.

Additionally, just as a gift given in anticipation of death <note>original: "donatio causa mortis"</note> or the appointment of an heir are not condemned—even though the recipient or heir might wish for the death of the giver or testator to receive the benefit—this does not mean the contract provides the *occasion* for that evil desire; rather, the individuals take that occasion from their own wickedness. The same holds true in this matter.

<margin>3</margin>
It remains for us to examine the following contract, which is customary in Seville <note>original: "Hispalis"</note>, about which I have been consulted and which Mercado examines in Book 4 of *On Contracts*, chapter 13. Those in Seville who need money to travel to the New World <note>original: "nouum orbem"</note>, which they will repay in the New World itself, find that currency exchange <note>original: "cambium," often referring to bills of exchange</note> does not exist from Seville to the New World. This is perhaps due to Law 8, Title 18, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, which we mentioned in Disputation 405, and which prohibits under heavy penalties the giving of exchange from any place in the Kingdoms of the Crown of Castile to another place in the same Kingdoms. The New World belongs to the Crown of Castile and is governed by the same laws. However, there will be no one willing to grant an exchange from Seville to the New World without some increase in the money, because money is worth far less in the New World than in Seville, due to its greater abundance there. Because therefore...

--- Page 739 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal and moral examination of maritime contracts, specifically addressing the high-interest loans provided to those traveling from Seville to the Americas and whether these constitute usury or a fair assessment of risk.</meta>

-># Second Treatise, Disputation 507<-

Therefore, those who prepare to cross to the New World <note>original: "nouum orbem," referring to the Spanish Americas</note> find that neither those who provide standard loans nor those who provide currency exchange are willing to give money for the journey, even though they often seek it with a great "thirst" <note>a metaphorical expression for desperate need</note>. Consequently, those in Seville who have an abundance of money—seeking to profit more than they would in any other type of business—offer them the following contract:

They grant them the money they request, to be repaid in the New World, but with an increase of sixty or fifty percent. This rate varies according to whether money is plentiful or scarce in Seville, making the market for this business more or less broad or restricted. However, they grant this capital under a specific condition: a particular ship is chosen or designated from those departing for the New World. If that ship should perish, the person who provided the capital loses it entirely, and the receiver is not bound to pay anything back. For this reason, they usually call this grant a "grant at risk of such a ship" <note>original Spanish: "concessionẽ a daño sobre tal naue"</note>. If, however, the ship arrives safely, the receiver must pay the capital in the New World along with the increase of sixty or fifty percent, as agreed between them.

Regarding this contract, there is a justified doubt as to whether it is unjust and carries the burden of restitution <note>the legal and moral obligation to return ill-gotten gains</note>. Indeed, those who hand over that money would earn less profit if they instead sent merchandise bought with that money to the New World—and they would face the same risk to their capital, because if the ship carrying the goods perished, they would likewise lose their investment. Furthermore, they would earn that profit through far greater industry and labor, and also with the risk that an abundance of similar goods in the New World might cause the value to drop, resulting in little or no profit. Additionally, capital sent from Seville to the New World is usually insured in Seville at a rate of eight or nine percent. All of these factors make such a contract highly suspect of injustice.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I will say briefly what I think. This contract is entirely to be discouraged and condemned as unjust, carrying the obligation of restitution. When all the concurrent circumstances are considered, it is entirely unequal. However, so that it may be understood how it might be reduced to equality by the judgment of a prudent person—and thus to what extent a similar prudent person should judge that restitution is required for contracts already entered into in that manner—I observe the following:

This contract is not one of insurance <term>assecuratio; a contract where one party takes on the risk of another's loss for a fee</term> regarding the capital being given, as is clear enough from the facts. Rather, regarding the risk to the capital, it is a contract of wagering <term>sponsio; a bet or mutual promise based on an uncertain outcome</term>. Specifically: "if such a ship perishes, I lose my capital to you; if it does not perish, you will pay the agreed amount, and my capital will be returned to me in full."

Since it is far more probable that the ship will not perish than that it will—because ships much more frequently arrive safely in the New World than sink—equity does not allow the person betting the ship will perish to stake as much as the person betting it will not. This must be noted for the following disputation we will conduct regarding wagers: when one outcome is far more probable than the other, the parties must not wager equal amounts if the contract is to be just. In the case proposed, for the contract to be just, the person asserting the ship will arrive safely may lawfully contract for a bit more to be returned to him if it arrives, compared to if he had simply insured the same amount of capital

<column-break/>

and would have lost it in the event the ship perished. This is because if the ship sinks, he loses his capital in such a way that he retains nothing as a price; however, someone who insures a certain amount, whether the ship sinks or not, always retains the insurance premium <note>original: "pretium assecurationis"</note>.

Next, I observe that—notwithstanding Law 8 of the "New Collection" <note>referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compendium of Spanish laws</note> previously cited—it is lawful to exchange currency from Seville to the New World with a significant increase. This is not only because of the "virtual transportation" of money from the New World back to Seville, but much more so because of the far greater value that money holds in Seville than in the New World. This difference exists because of the greater abundance of money in the New World than in Seville, according to the principles explained at length in Disputation 406. 

The exact amount of a just increase in such an exchange—based on both of these factors and others—must be determined by the judgment of a prudent person, after considering all relevant circumstances. This value is not the same for all parts of the New World, nor is it the same for the same place at different times when different circumstances arise. It is not fixed at an indivisible point. I, being far away and ignorant of various changing circumstances, and possessing no expertise or skill in the art of trading, cannot define it precisely. Although Mercado <note>Tomás de Mercado, a Spanish Dominican economist of the School of Salamanca</note> attempts to define it by comparing different locations in the New World, I judge it more prudent to leave this definition to experienced and God-fearing merchants.

I am persuaded that, Law 8 notwithstanding, exchange with an increase from Seville to the New World is lawful. Through "equity" <term>epicheiam; a legal principle where the spirit of the law is followed when the literal words would be unfair</term>, it must be judged that this law only speaks of exchanges from one place in the Kingdoms of Castile in Spain to another place within those same Spanish kingdoms; it is different regarding the New World. One should not believe that the legislator intended to prohibit useful and necessary exchange from Spain to the New World, nor does that law say so. Nor should it be believed that the law intended only to permit exchange to the New World that was unjust for the receiver—who would receive something worth much more in exchange for something worth less—thereby permitting injustice and consequently wanting to abolish exchange to the New World altogether. Indeed, no one would be so insane or such a squanderer of his own goods as to grant an exchange where he gave more value for something worth far less. 

Therefore, merchants are wrong to avoid moderate increases in New World exchanges out of fear of that law, and for that reason, they turn to illicit and unjust contracts. What is most notable in the proposed matter—as we showed in Disputation 405—is that even if that law prohibited exchange with an increase from one place in the Kingdoms of the Spanish Crown of Castile to another and rendered the contract void, nevertheless, a person who received a moderate and (aside from that law) just increase would not be bound to restore that increase in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal forum of moral duty and sin</note>. They would certainly not be bound to restore it before a legal sentence was passed. This holds even more true in the case of exchange with an increase from Seville to the New World, rather than...

<meta>The catchword "in" at the bottom of the page indicates the next sentence continues "in the case of..." or "in these matters..."</meta>

<summary>Molina argues that the high-interest maritime loans (50-60%) commonly used for New World voyages are often unjust because they function as unequal wagers. He suggests that while currency exchange with a moderate profit is morally acceptable due to the different values of money in Spain versus the Americas, current laws are being misinterpreted by merchants, driving them toward these more predatory contracts.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on maritime exchange contracts and begins a new inquiry into the morality of wagering and betting contracts.</meta>

in exchange from one place in Spain to another within the same Spanish territories.

Following these points, I therefore say that the contract in question is reduced to equality <note>meaning it becomes a fair and balanced exchange</note> if the capital is handed over in that manner, but is to be repaid in the New World <note>original: "nouo orbe," the Spanish Americas</note> with an increase that is moderate and does not exceed just limits. This is judged both by comparing the risk of losing the capital if that ship does not arrive safely at the New World, and also in the exchange of the value of the money received in Seville. For an equal quantity returned in the New World does not equal the value of what was received, but a far greater amount is required, as has been said. Something can even be received additionally for "virtual transportation" <note>the service of moving funds across the ocean without physical transport of the same coins</note>. How much this total increase ought to be, so that it does not exceed the limits of justice, will be for the judgment of prudent merchants to decide; it seems it should be much less than the rate of sixty or fifty per hundred <note>60% or 50%</note>. And according to this rule, restitution <note>the moral obligation to return unfair profits</note> must be commanded regarding such contracts that have been unjustly celebrated until now. Other grounds upon which some think this increase can be raised are generally not solid if the matter is carefully weighed, nor do they have a place once the two or three grounds explained here are accepted. These are the things which, subject to the judgment of others, occur to me to be said concerning this contract.

### On the Contract of Wagering.
#### DISPUTATION DVIII.
->SUMMARY<-

<margin>1</margin> What a wager is; and it is a just and lawful contract unless stained by some circumstance.
<margin>2</margin> In how many ways a wager can be made.

<margin>1</margin> A wager <note>original: "Sponsio"</note> (or betting; in Spanish *apuesta*) is a contract in which, regarding a doubtful matter, one person pledges for one side and another for the other, whether money or anything else, so that the one who hits upon the outcome or the truth may gain it. It is a lawful contract unless stained by some circumstance, as Covarrubias, Gomez, Medina, and others affirm. For indeed, one of those so wagering exposes himself to the risk of losing for the benefit of the other if what he says does not happen or if he does not hit upon the truth; this is exchangeable for a similar risk to which the other similarly exposes himself. This is provided that what is pledged, considering the amount of risk on both sides, is equal in a certain proportion—that is, in whatever proportion one person exposes himself to a smaller risk than the other, what he pledges should be greater than what the other pledges, as was said in the preceding disputation. And indeed, when a wager is made concerning some future contingency, which therefore could turn out either way—such as that on such a day, or within such a time, several Indian ships <note>original: "naues Indicæ," the Spanish treasure fleets</note> will arrive, or that a pregnant woman will give birth to a male, etc.—no one doubts that the wager can be just, because each person exposes himself to both disadvantage and

<column-break/>

gain. Skill <note>original: "industria"</note> also usually plays a part in such arrangements, as when a wager is made on which of two people will arrive at a certain place first, or who will draw better characters <note>calligraphy or writing</note>. However, when a wager is made concerning a present or past matter, which is therefore already outside its own causes, it is necessary for the wager to be just that the matter be doubtful in some way to both parties wagering. They must not be so certain of it that they cannot be deceived, as Juan Medina rightly affirms and others agree; and this is what the phrase "in a doubtful matter" signifies in the definition of a wager. For someone who is entirely certain that the thing for which he wagers is as he says, since he exposes himself to no risk of losing, can gain nothing from the other—even if the other, deceiving himself, also thinks himself certain of the contrary and says that, despite the certainty the first claims to have, he wishes to stake and lose. Medina and Covarrubias say this even when the certain party does not warn the other of his certainty. The reason for our assertion is that the contract would be unequal; the one who "wills" to be deceived does not truly grant the money with full freedom, but rather wills to lose involuntarily due to a mixture of ignorance and error. Therefore, just as someone who is certain a stone is not a gem, and thus not worth as much as another thinks (who is deceived into believing it is a gem and offers a higher price), cannot keep that increase—because it is given involuntarily due to ignorance and deception—so it is in this case. If, however, someone who does not want to wager because he is certain of the matter begins to doubt whether he might be deceived because the other person insists on wagering, and because he remembers that sometimes he thought he was certain but was later found deceived; if he then wagers because he nonetheless persuades himself the thing is as he thinks, then because in his own estimation he exposes himself to some risk of losing, he lawfully wins and accepts what the other loses due to his excessive credulity.

This should be observed: if someone thinks that what he wagers on is absolutely certain, and he wagers; if he later finds that it was not absolutely certain but that he had exposed himself to a risk of losing, and yet the matter turns out as he predicted; although he sinned by wagering with that erroneous conscience (thinking he risked nothing), he can nevertheless lawfully keep what he gained in that way. For just as someone who gains from a contract he thought was usurious or otherwise unjust, if he later finds it was actually just, is not bound to make restitution; it is enough that it was justly gained in itself, or "materially" <note>term: materialiter; meaning the objective facts of the case, regardless of the person's intent or mistaken belief</note>, so that he is not bound to return it. Even though he sinned against justice by entering the contract and gaining with that erroneous conscience, the matter stands similarly in this case.

<summary>Molina concludes that maritime interest rates must be moderate and based on risk and currency value. He then defines wagering (betting) as a valid contract based on mutual risk and uncertainty, provided neither party has hidden certainty.</summary>

# On the contract of drawing lots.

## DISPUTATION DIX.

->SUMMARY<-

1 *In how many ways lots are conducted.*
2 *What lots are.*
3 *When lots are licit <note>lawful or morally permissible</note>, and when they are not.*
   *And what concerning the law of Castile. number 4.*

<margin>1</margin> Lots, as St. Thomas Aquinas establishes in *Summa Theologiae* 2.q.95 art. last, are of certain types: † **divinatory** <note>original: "divinatoriæ," used to predict the future</note> or **consultive** <note>original: "consultoriæ," used to seek divine guidance on a course of action</note>. To dispute concerning these types does not belong to this section, but rather to the study of the virtue of religion or the vices opposed to it <note>such as superstition</note>. Others, however, are **divisory** <note>original: "diuisoriæ"</note>, such as when certain goods must be divided among many people, and they cannot agree on which portions each should receive; they then cast lots to see which part should fall to each individual. Although the name seems to be derived from this use, so that they are called "divisory lots," the practice is actually broader. Sometimes several people agree that a thing to which they all have a right should be tested by lots to see who should receive it in its entirety—either because it cannot be easily divided, or because they prefer this method even if it could be divided. And sometimes a "contribution" <note>a pool of money</note> is made to buy a certain thing or things, so that they may test by lot which of the contributors should receive them. Occasionally, such contributions and drawings are conducted by public authority, with public officials appointed to tax the value of the items for which the lots are cast, to receive the contributions and names of the participants, and to execute the whole matter faithfully. These officials are assigned a competent salary, sometimes established by law, so that from the contributions something may be applied to some **pious work** <note>charitable causes such as hospitals or orphanges</note>. Indeed, sometimes, so that the matter is settled more quickly, a prize is established for the one who offers larger contributions sooner, so that, according to the number of contributions, more **slips** <note>original: "schedulæ," small pieces of paper or tickets</note> containing his name are placed into the **urn** <note>the vessel from which lots were drawn</note>. Furthermore, in many places, many public offices involving significant prestige are conferred by casting lots among certain members of the republic to whom they are assigned, so that the person to whom the lot falls may hold that office for that year or another period. Sometimes also, when people cannot otherwise come to an agreement regarding a certain matter, they are compelled by public authority to cast lots over it. In this place, however, our discourse concerns the contract by which those having a right to a thing, or in a thing, agree that lots be cast to determine who should obtain it, or which part of it. We say, indeed, that if fraud and injustice do not intervene in that contract and its execution, it is just. Since it is an exchange where individuals, in favor of the others, expose to the risk of the lot an equal right to a thing (or a right they have in a thing, or which part of those things they ought to receive), the exchange is surely equal, and therefore just.

<margin>2</margin> Because, if we speak of those lots sometimes instituted by public authority where individuals contribute to buy another thing or things beforehand, 

<column-break/>

around which the lots are cast, no doubt will remain regarding the rest; thus, we must speak briefly of them.

When many people contribute to buy those things for which lots are to be cast among them, it is clear that a contract of purchase intervenes, by which those things are bought from the contributed money. If it happens that those things are sold for a higher price than they are worth, injustice occurs, carrying the burden of **restitution** <note>the moral requirement to pay back ill-gotten gains</note> for the excess on the part of the seller to those who contributed (or for their benefit) if possible; otherwise, it must be restored to the poor for the sake of their souls. But if any official appointed for this purpose has unjustly valued those things, or was a co-cause of that unjust contract for any other reason, he is also bound to restore the increase, but only in the default of the seller or the one who received that unjust increase.

If something is done in the casting of lots whereby some of those among whom the lots are cast are less exposed to the risk of losing or the benefit of winning, injustice is committed in that contract or its execution. This carries the burden of restoring, according to the judgment of a prudent man, the profit of which someone was deprived for that reason. Hence, if someone arranges the matter so that the lot falls to one in particular and not the others, he is bound to restore to the rest the total amount they contributed. If, however, he arranges it so that the lot falls to one of three, when twenty have contributed, he is bound to restore to the other seventeen (to whom the lot could not fall) what they contributed.

Officials chosen and appointed to the business of lots may receive a just **stipend** <note>salary or fee</note> for their labor and industry, for they are not bound to provide these services for free. Indeed, if it is to be paid from the just price of the goods being sold (so that lots may be cast for them), such that the person selling the goods pays the stipend, they can receive as much as the price established for those goods allows. If, however, it is to be paid from the contributions—such that the contributors must pay not only the just price of the things, but also these stipends—then officials should only be chosen if they are absolutely necessary. Their stipend must be moderate, and the business must be completed in the shortest time possible so that such stipends do not accumulate. And I believe it ought to be announced from the start when the laws of the drawing are promulgated: how much each person must contribute for each **slip** <note>ticket</note> to be placed in the urn with their name inscribed, so that each person may take heed and consider whether they wish to contribute to those stipends, lest they pay it involuntarily or through deception.

In the same way, when something beyond the value of the items is to be extracted from the contributions for a **pious work**, it should be announced from the start in the manner explained, so that the contributors may take heed and consider whether they wish to contribute to that as well, lest they similarly pay it involuntarily and while deceived.

When a prize is established for the one who contributes more to the lots sooner: if that prize is not bought from the contributions, but from the generosity of the one selling the goods so that lots may be cast for them...

It emphasizes that such contracts are just only if they are transparent, free from fraud, and the odds are equal for all participants.</summary>

<margin>4</margin> Finally, it must be observed that in the laws of the <note>original: "l. 12. tit. 7. lib. 8. nouæ collect." refers to the Nueva Recopilación, a 16th-century compilation of Spanish laws</note> New Compilation, casting lots is prohibited without Royal permission. The reason given is that whatever is put up for a lottery is usually sold for a much higher price than it is worth. It is stated there that the King will ensure that permission for casting lots is not granted. For the same reason, the same law prohibits **raffling** <note>original: "rifar"</note>—that is, contributing money to buy something which is then played for among the contributors, so that the winner of the game takes the whole thing. A penalty is imposed there on those who propose such a game: they lose the item itself. Furthermore, those who contributed money to buy it must lose the amount they contributed and pay an additional fine of the same amount. One-third of this total penalty goes to the treasury, another third to the informer, and the final third to the judge who delivered the sentence.

# Concerning which type of game is discussed in this place. And whether it can be practiced justly and lawfully.

-> DISPUTATION DX. <-

-> SUMMARY. <-

<margin>1</margin> In how many ways "game" is used, and what it means in the broad sense.
<margin>2</margin> A game joined to a contract: what it is, and whether it is lawful.

<margin>1</margin> **Play** <note>original: "Ludus"</note> is used in two ways. First, in a broad sense, for words and deeds intended for the delight of the soul. Indeed, when it is practiced through words, it is specifically called a **joke** <note>original: "iocus"</note>. Whether play happens through words or deeds, if it is practiced in accordance with right reason and with the proper circumstances observed, it is an act of virtue. Aristotle, in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 4, Chapter 8, calls this **wittiness** <note>original: "eutrapelia"</note>—that is, urbanity or social grace. St. Thomas Aquinas, in the *Summa Theologiae* <note>2. 2. q. 168. art. 2</note>, says we can call it **cheerfulness**. It is situated as a "middle way" between excess and deficiency in playing. For although one more frequently sins through excess in play—since, as Cicero says in *On Duties*, Book 1, life should be seasoned with play as sparingly as food is with salt, and we are naturally prone to seeking delight in play—it can nevertheless happen that one sins through deficiency, though this rarely occurs. One who sins through deficiency is called **harsh and boorish** <note>original: "durus & agrestis"</note> by Aristotle. Disputing about play in this sense belongs not to this treatise on justice, but to the treatment of temperance; for that reason, St. Thomas discusses it later in the place cited.

<margin>2</margin> In the second way, **play** is used more strictly, as it involves an added agreement where the players put at stake some interest in the outcome of the game, which, according to the rules and the varying results of the game, one loses and the other acquires. This kind of agreement is sometimes joined to games of cards, dice, and

<column-break/>

tables, to jousting, ball games, and chess (which our people call <term>axedrez</term> <note>Spanish for chess</note>), and sometimes to other games. A dispute concerning play in this sense certainly belongs to this treatise: for it is a kind of **unnamed contract** <note>original: "contractu innominato," a legal term for a contract that doesn't fall into standard categories like 'sale' but is still binding</note>. In this contract, one player, according to the rules and the uncertain outcome of the game, exposes an interest to risk for the benefit of the other, so that the other may similarly expose another interest for his benefit. This involves the industry of the players cooperating toward the same outcome of the game according to the greater or lesser skill and dexterity of each. This is true whether they simultaneously intend the delight of the game for its own sake (from which this matter takes the name "game") or not. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

As for the second point, this conclusion must be established:
**Conclusion.** Relying on natural law alone, and excluding the prohibition of human law, play taken in this second sense can be practiced justly and lawfully, even if it involves cards or dice. This is proven because the agreement involved can be equal on both sides, and therefore just. Both parties have the power to alienate the interest they have staked in this contract; the game can be practiced without force, deceit, or fraud; and it can be directed toward a fitting delight taken according to the rule of reason—considering the quality and condition of the players, and observing the proper time, place, and other circumstances. As for the fact that profit is hoped for, besides containing no injustice (because the contract is equal on both sides), it can serve to foster delight. Indeed, the spirits of the players flag when no prize is proposed to them; they are not as delighted as when they play with some prize proposed, as experience testifies. Therefore, the game of which we speak—even cards and dice—relying on natural law alone and excluding human prohibition, can be practiced so justly and lawfully that the acts of two mentioned virtues may intervene: namely, **justice** and **wittiness** <note>eutrapelia</note>. Thus, it can even be practiced meritoriously. Add to this that it can be directed toward avoiding idleness and other sins into which men easily fall when they are not occupied with other matters.

# A game is rendered vicious by circumstances. And whether it becomes vicious because profit is intended, or because money is subjected to fortune.

-> DISPUTATION DXI. <-

-> SUMMARY. <-

<margin>1</margin> From which circumstances a game is rendered bad and vicious.
<margin>2</margin> Whether a game is rendered vicious if it is directed toward profit.
<margin>3</margin> What "loss" actually is.
<margin>4</margin> Whether a game is lawful in which money is subjected to fortune <note>chance</note>.

Although...

<summary>Molina defines "play" as both a social virtue (eutrapelia) and a legal contract. He argues that gambling is not inherently against natural law if the risks are equal, the participants are willing, and it serves as reasonable recreation.</summary>

--- Page 743 ---
<meta>This page continues Molina’s investigation into the morality of games of chance. Page 682 concluded a discussion on state-regulated lotteries; page 683 shifts to the moral theology of private gaming, specifically whether playing for profit is inherently sinful.</meta>

<page-num>683</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 511.</header>

<margin>1</margin> Although gaming is not evil in itself—standing solely on the grounds of natural law, as shown in the preceding disputation—this is also gathered from Saint Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "D. Th. 2.2.q.168.art.2." refers to the Summa Theologiae</note> and those following him. It is affirmed by Juan Medina <note>Spanish theologian, 1490–1546</note>, Domingo de Soto <note>Influential Dominican jurist, 1494–1560</note>, Major, and many others. However, due to various circumstances, gaming can be rendered evil and vicious. For instance, if more time is spent on it than is proper; or if it happens at a time or place where it should not; or by a person for whom it is inappropriate given their status—such as a cleric, a member of a religious order, or a high-ranking prelate playing a game unbecoming of them. This is especially true when the profit in a game is not directed toward the enjoyment to be found in playing—where a modest prize is set to make the game serious and more delightful for the players—but rather when the game is directed toward the profit hoped for. In such cases, players usually become disordered in various ways: sometimes through perjury, brawling, or even blasphemy if things go badly; sometimes through fraud, deception, and other injuries against fellow players. At times, they turn nights into days and days into nights, neglecting sacred duties on feast days. Sometimes they squander their own inheritance and the goods of their wives and children, spending vast amounts of time on it to the great detriment of their families and other affairs. From all these things, various losses tend to arise to their own ruin and the harm of the commonwealth. Evils and losses most commonly arise from games of dice and cards. Indeed, with dice (which our people call <note>original: "dados"</note> **dice**), a great deal of money is usually lost in a short time; the same happens with certain card games. Yet, these are the vices of the players, not of the game itself, which by its very nature can be done well—just as we said regarding the art of trade in Disputation 339. Nevertheless, some games are of such a nature that similar outrages are frequently attached to them, as was said in that same place regarding trade. This concludes the first of the proposed points.

<margin>Question 2</margin> Regarding the second point, Gabriel Biel <note>Late scholastic philosopher, d. 1495</note>, Panormitanus <note>Famous canon lawyer, d. 1445</note>, and certain others believe that a game is rendered so vicious if it is ordered toward profit—that is, if the player primarily intends to gain money—that they affirm it is a mortal sin, provided the intended profit is notable.

They are led to this because the player intends a notable loss to his neighbor, and the neighbor's property is coveted to his detriment, which is against the Tenth Commandment of the Decalogue <note>The commandment: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s goods"</note>. Nor does it matter, they say, that the fellow player voluntarily subjected himself to the rules of the game and voluntarily pays what the other wins; for in that payment, there is a "mixed involuntary" element <note>A technical term for an action done with regret or under pressure, like throwing cargo overboard during a storm to save a ship</note>, no different than in the payment of usury.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, this opinion is rightly rejected by Medina and Soto in the places cited, and by many others. For in the Tenth Commandment of the Decalogue, what is prohibited is the coveting of a neighbor’s property by an *unjust* means or path (the external act of which was already prohibited by the Seventh Commandment). Coveting via a *just* means and path is not prohibited. In the type of gaming we are discussing, we see an equal and just contract. One person intends that, for his own benefit, the other should expose his money to the rules and outcome of the game, so that

<column-break/>

he himself might likewise expose an equal amount for the other’s benefit. He wants the other to expose it not for free, but in compensation for an equal risk taken in his own favor. Since, when conditions are equal, no one is bound by the law of charity to prefer another's benefit over his own—but may perfectly well prefer his own benefit to another's, as is clear from what we have said in this "Second of the Second" <note>Referring to the second part of the second part of the Summa Theologiae</note> when discussing the order of charity—it follows that by intending profit in this way, one not only does not sin against justice, but neither against charity toward one’s neighbor. Just as one does not sin by entering into other just contracts with him, intending one's own benefit—such as leasing a field to him for a certain annual rent and including a pact that he is bound to pay it even if a sterile year occurs, as explained in Disputation 495. Clearly, if the opinion of Gabriel and Panormitanus were true, it would similarly be a mortal sin to intend profit from games prohibited by no law, such as ball games or chess. Indeed, it would even be a mortal sin to intend or accept a less-than-notable profit from a game, since it is not permitted to covet a neighbor's property even in a small way in the manner prohibited by the Tenth Commandment.

Furthermore, regarding what Gabriel says about the "mixed involuntary": if that proved anything, it would also prove that the winner of a game is bound to restore his winnings, just as a usurer is bound to restore interest already accepted. Yet Gabriel himself asserts that things acquired in this way through gaming are not subject to restitution. Therefore, just as we said when discussing usury and as has been said often elsewhere, we must say the same in this case: namely, that a "mixed involuntary" state prevents the transfer of ownership and makes acceptance illicit only when something is given for free; but not when it is given in a non-gratuitous contract as compensation for something else that the other either gives or subjects to a similar risk, as happens in the case proposed. For the fact that a man who sells his house does so with a "mixed involuntary" will—insofar as he would not sell it if he had other money—does not make the contract vicious on the part of the buyer. And so that you may better know how to respond formally to Gabriel's argument, take note:

<margin>3</margin> **Loss** <note>original: "Damnum"</note> properly speaking, as the Doctors note, is not just any decrease in one’s inheritance or goods; rather, it is that decrease which occurs against the owner's will and unjustly. From this, it follows that, speaking properly, one must deny that a person who intends profit through a just path in gaming intends "loss" to his neighbor. He only intends his own profit and benefit, and the other's loss occurs only incidentally <note>original: "per accidens"</note> through a just path and with the other's intervening consent. This is much like how a recipient of a gift, when he asks for the gift, indirectly intends a loss in the giver’s goods via a just path.

From what has been said, it is established that not even a venial sin arises precisely from the fact that someone orders a game more toward just profit than toward taking pleasure from the play; in this, Medina agrees with us. I said "precisely from that fact" because if the appetite for profit is immoderate, as it often is in many people, it can be a sin of greed (by its nature venial). This greed can be the cause for the player to be drawn into many other evils by that unbridled appetite, as was proved in the first part of this disputation.

<summary>This page discusses the morality of gambling, arguing that playing for profit is not inherently a mortal sin because it constitutes a just contract involving mutual risk and consent. It refutes earlier theologians who compared gambling profit to usury or a violation of the Tenth Commandment.</summary>
<keywords>gaming, gambling, profit, contracts, mortal sin, Tenth Commandment, mixed involuntary, dice, cards, Luis de Molina, morality of risk</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 511 regarding the morality of gambling, specifically addressing why seeking profit through games is often seen as a vice and transitioning into the legal prohibitions found in Civil and Canon law.</meta>

<page-num>684</page-num>
<header>Louis Molina, On Contracts</header>

However, this does not arise from the fact that profit is sought through the game, but rather that it is sought excessively and inordinately. For this reason, Aristotle, in the 4th book of his *Ethics*, chapter 1, toward the end, calls gamblers—that is, those who give themselves entirely over to play out of a greed for gain—**"illiberal"** <note>original: "illiberales," meaning stingy or lacking the virtues of a free person</note>. He asserts that they are occupied with sordid gain and do everything for the sake of profit and lucre, taking from friends to whom they ought rather to give. This concludes the second of the points proposed.

**4** Regarding the third point, some have argued that the gambling we are discussing is illicit by its very nature, because that money is subjected to luck and it fosters idleness. However, this opinion is rightly rejected by the law. Firstly, because it is not inherently illicit to commit something to the outcome of fortune. Secondly, as was stated in Disputation 507, men are not always bound to work; they may lawfully pause from other occupations and devote themselves not only to other contracts but also to gaming for the sake of delight, and even for profit, to avoid idleness and other sins.

->To what extent gaming is prohibited by human, civil,<-
->and canon law.<-

->DISPUTATION 512.<-

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Which games are included under the name of "alea" <note>games of chance</note>.*
2 *By what law, and to what extent, gaming is prohibited.*
3 *Regarding the law of Castile (number 3) and Portugal (number 5).*
4 *Whether what is lost in a game can be recovered by the player, even after the time granted for recovery has passed.*
6 *Penalties established by Portuguese law against players and those who receive them into their houses.*
7 *Under what penalty gaming is prohibited by canon law.*

Since no law is found in positive divine law <note>scripture or direct revelation</note> concerning the prohibition of gaming, we must explain to what extent gaming is found to be prohibited by human law—both civil and canon—based on what was said at the beginning of the preceding disputation. We shall begin our arrangement with common civil law.

<margin>1</margin> Under the name of **alea** <note>Latin term for dice or games of hazard</note>, every game is included that is governed more by fortune and chance than by skill, such as <term>tesserae</term> <note>six-sided dice</note>, <term>tali</term> <note>four-sided knucklebones</note>, and small dice; likewise **cards**, which had not been invented in the time of the Romans and the imperial laws. <margin>2</margin> Although gaming was prohibited by the law of the *Digest* <note>a collection of Roman legal writings</note> if played for money or things valued in money—unless it was played at a banquet where one is eating, or played for money from which something to eat is bought—and it was prohibited to make wagers <note>original: "sponsiones," which Molina notes are called "atruefas" in Spanish</note> in these types of prohibited games, and the recovery of what someone had won and received was granted, as is established in laws 2, 3, and 4 of the title *On Gamblers* <note>original: "de aleæ lusu"</note>. Nevertheless, the same gaming is much more expressly and extensively prohibited in the <term>Authentica</term> <note>a collection of Justinian's decrees</note> under the title *Concerning Religious Places and Funeral Expenses*. There, an action to demand what someone has won in such a game is denied if it has not yet been paid; and if he has already received it, recovery against him is granted. Not only can the person who

<column-break/>

lost it in the game recover it, but also his heirs, parents, and any others whose role it is to act on his behalf. If these do not seek recovery, the <term>fiscus</term> <note>the state treasury</note> is granted the right of recovery. This recovery is granted to all these parties within fifty years from the day it was paid, as all these things are expressly contained in the cited *Authentica*.

In Law 1 of the title *On Gamblers* and Law 6, Title 14, Part 7 <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the Castilian statutory code</note>, out of hatred and as a punishment for those who receive gamblers into their homes for the purpose of playing (provided they have a custom of receiving them, and not just once or twice or on a rare occasion, as the gloss on the cited Law 1 says), it is decreed that if they are beaten, wounded, or otherwise injured—provided they are not killed (as Law 6 says) nor mutilated (as Gregory Lopez says in the same place, since mutilation is equated to death)—whether in their own home or elsewhere, and whether while playing or afterward, provided it happens on account of the game, it shall be done with impunity. No action against the one inflicting the injury shall be granted to the host of the gamblers, at least because the gamblers are convicted, and he did not provide them with necessities. Likewise, if during the time of the game something is stolen from the house of the person receiving them for play, this also happens with such impunity that no action is granted to the host, even to recover or claim what was thus stolen from him. If, however, something is stolen either outside his house where the playing occurs, or in his house but at a time when there was no gaming in it, then an action is granted to such a host against the thief, as is held in the cited laws. But if one of the fellow players strikes another fellow player, or if something is stolen from one of the fellow players by another, then the player who suffered the injury is granted an action against the wrongdoer, even if one of the players compelled the other to play, either at the beginning or during the progress of the game. Furthermore, he who thus compels another to play shall be punished with a monetary fine or cast into chains. This is held in laws 1 and 2 of the title *On Gamblers*.

<margin>3 Law of Castile.</margin> In this Kingdom of Castile, various laws have been passed regarding gaming. King Alfonso in the year 1386 passed a law <unclear>†</unclear> which today is the first of Title 7, Book 8 of the *New Collection* <note>the Nueva Recopilación of Spanish laws</note>. In this law, he prohibited the game of dice and <term>tabellas</term> <note>likely a form of backgammon or board game</note> (perhaps cards were not yet in use in Spain) during military expeditions, under penalty of six hundred <term>maravedis</term> <note>Spanish currency</note> for the official, who is called an <term>alguazil</term> <note>bailiff or constable</note>, and by casting the player into chains. He also decreed that if the official did not put the player in chains, the official should pay double the penalty to the King’s treasury. Likewise, he decreed that whoever won anything in such a game should immediately return it to the person from whom it was won. If he did not have the means to return it, he should be cast into chains for thirty days. Today, however, in military expeditions and in garrisons, nothing is found more frequently than the game of dice and cards.

Afterward, John I in the year 1387 and Ferdinand in the year 1476, in Law 2 of the same title, prohibited the game of dice and cards under the penalty that he who was caught playing for the first time should pay six hundred maravedis, or if he was unable to pay, be cast into chains for ten days. He who was caught a second time should pay one thousand two hundred maravedis, or if unable to pay, be cast for twenty days into chains...
