And he who was caught a third time would pay one thousand eight hundred maravedís <note>a copper coin used in Spain</note>, or, if he was unable to pay, he would be cast into chains for thirty days. Thereafter, if he were caught again, he would pay three thousand maravedís each time, or, if unable to pay, be detained for thirty days in chains. Later, the same Ferdinand, in Law 5 of the same title, granted immunity from such penalties to those who played for fruit, wine, or money to buy something to be eaten or drunk immediately, provided they did not play with dice. And Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain</note>, while in Law 10 of the same title he had granted immunity from that penalty to those who only played for two reales <note>silver coins</note> to buy something to be eaten, in the following Law 11 he granted immunity universally to those who only play for up to two silver reales, even if the money is lost, and even if it is not used to buy something to eat.

Law 2, cited above, records that someone who has lost and paid anything in a prohibited game can reclaim it within eight days from the moment he paid it; and if he won, he is bound to return it if it is reclaimed. If, however, the one who lost does not reclaim it within eight days, then any other person can demand it and keep it for himself. But if no one reclaims it, then any judge is bound by virtue of his office to demand it and adjudge it to the King’s treasury. If, however, knowing of it, he does not do so, the judge himself is bound to pay six hundred maravedís—half to the accuser and half to the King’s treasury. Later, Charles V in Law 10 of the same title commanded that players could not be condemned to the penalty of the game, nor could they be investigated, unless it was within two months of the crime being committed. Since the recovery of what someone has won in a game is granted as a penalty, it will certainly not take place except within those two months, as Gutierrez rightly affirms in *On the Confirmation of Rights*, part 1, chapter 53, number 2. The same Charles V, in the following Law 11, decreed that those caught playing should only lose the money they were caught playing with, which would be enough to pay the penalty, and that the money for paying that penalty should then be deposited with someone until the judge's sentence followed. Likewise, those who were not caught in the act of playing could not be accused or condemned before an investigation into that crime was made, by which it is discovered that they played a prohibited game.

<margin>Question 4</margin>
However, it is doubted whether, after those eight days granted to the one who lost something in a game to reclaim it have passed, he can nevertheless reclaim it during the remaining time until the full two months have elapsed. Aviles, cited by Gutierrez in number 3, says no.

<margin>Decision 1</margin>
It must be said, however, with Avendaño and the same Gutierrez, that he can reclaim it, provided that after those eight days no one else from the public, or the judge himself by virtue of his office, has demanded it. The reason is that the law grants the fellow-player those eight days in which he alone can reclaim what he lost in the game, and not others; but the remaining time of the two months is common to him and others, and it is a matter of preemption <note>first come, first served</note>. Therefore, if after those eight days have passed, someone else begins to demand it, the one who lost it shall be excluded.

In Law 7 of the same title, it is strictly forbidden for everyone universally, even foreigners, to play with dice in any kind of game, or to manufacture dice, or to order them to be manufactured, or to sell them, or to order them to be sold

<column-break/>

by oneself or through an intermediary, directly or indirectly; or to bring them into these kingdoms, under penalty of exile for two years from these Kingdoms. Those caught playing with them shall lose the stakes they were caught playing with, provided the condemnatory sentence is delivered within eight days of the moment they were caught. Furthermore, those who play with dice shall pay twenty thousand maravedís to the King’s treasury. Likewise, the house in which it is found that dice were played, and the tavern (*tienda* in Spanish) in which they were sold or found for sale, are confiscated to the King’s treasury. Ministers of justice who do not carry this into execution are deprived of their office and rendered unfit to hold others. Later, our King Philip II, in Law 15, title 26, book 8 of the *New Collection*, established a penalty for those making or selling dice, by themselves or through an intermediary, directly or indirectly, or those playing with them or having them in their possession: if he is a nobleman or enjoys the status that the Castilians call *hidalguía* <note>the rank of a minor noble or gentleman</note>, he shall be exiled for five years from these Kingdoms and, furthermore, pay two hundred gold crowns—a third to the King’s treasury, another third to the judge, and another third to the informer. If, however, he is of lower rank, he shall be publicly flogged and serve five years in the galleys <note>original: "triremibus," referring to penal labor as an oarsman</note>, and furthermore lose up to thirty thousand maravedís of his goods, to be divided in the aforesaid manner between the treasury, the judge, and the informer. Furthermore, the house in which dice were played, and where they were sold or found for sale, shall be confiscated, and its value similarly divided between the treasury, the judge, and the informer. Likewise, it is commanded that whoever falls into any of the aforesaid crimes shall not be released from chains until the sentence is passed and becomes a final judgment, nor shall he be permitted to leave before that time under bail or for any other reason; and that whichever of the listed penalties can be carried out immediately should be executed without delay.

Charles V, in Law 8, title 7, book 8 of the *New Collection*, forbade playing on credit in the following words <note>original: Spanish</note>:

> We command that henceforth no person, of whatever state or quality they may be, can play, nor shall play, on credit or on trust, even if it be the game of pelota <note>a traditional Spanish ball game</note> or others permitted and tolerated in these kingdoms. And if they play the said games on credit or trust, we command our justices not to condemn or take execution against such persons nor their goods, nor their guarantors, for what they may owe from the said games on credit or trust. And by the present document we declare null and void any obligations, deeds, or promises that such persons may make regarding this, etc.

> And in the following Law 9, it is held thus: We command that no persons, of whatever quality and condition they may be, can play in one day at the game of pelota, nor at other games, even if they are permitted, for more than thirty ducats <note>a high-value gold coin</note> in money, even if they say they play for others; nor in the said games shall there be side-bets (*treviesas*); and they cannot play, nor shall they play, for jewels or pledges (*preseas o predas*) nor any other thing in small or large quantity, nor on credit or trust, nor on one's word: under penalty that for the first time, both the one who loses it and the one who wins it or makes a side-bet, shall fall into and incur the penalty of whatever he plays beyond the said quantity. By Law 3 of the same title, tables set out for gambling are prohibited, and a penalty of five thousand maravedís <note>a copper coin</note> is imposed on him who has them set out in his house. And in Law 4 following, it is forbidden for a town to lease out space so that someone may have tables set out for gambling. And in Law 5, the penalties established for gamblers are extended to those who lease from towns or lords of towns so that they may have tables set out for gambling, and against those setting out tables for gambling, and against those granting a house so that gambling may be practiced in it. Read there the penalties that were established for the lords of towns, unless they saw to it within a certain time that such tables were not set out for gambling. And in Law 6, it is prohibited for those to whom the gambling penalties belong to be able to grant permission, or make a composition <note>a legal settlement to avoid prosecution</note> with anyone, so that gambling might occur with impunity.

**5** In the Kingdom of Portugal <note>original: *Lusitaniæ Regno*</note>, all games of cards and dice are universally prohibited, except when dice are played in the "game of tables" <note>a family of board games like backgammon</note>, as they call it: for this is permitted in that Kingdom. This is established in Book 5, Title 48 of the Ordinances <note>The *Ordenações Manuelinas*, the legal code of Portugal at the time</note>, in the beginning and §3.

To whomever in that Kingdom it shall be proved to have played cards in any kind of game, or to whomever cards shall be found in his house, or whomever shall be found carrying them with him—if **6** he be a commoner <note>original: *plebeius*, whom they call a *peon*</note>, he incurs the penalty of paying two thousand réis <note>Portuguese currency</note> while in chains. If indeed he be of a higher order, he is not cast into chains, yet he pays ten gold coins as a penalty. Likewise, both incur the penalty of paying whatever it is proved they had won in the game. And half of all these penalties belongs to the accuser, and the other half to the King’s treasury. Those who are likewise caught gambling incur the penalty of losing all that money which they had set out for gambling; but not what they had in their purses or elsewhere; half goes to the one catching them in the game, and the other half to him who is called in the Kingdom the *alcaide mor* <note>the chief magistrate or governor</note> of that town in which they were caught gambling. Thus it is held there, §2 and the last. Slaves, however, do not incur these penalties, but rather the penalty of 

<column-break/>

twenty lashes at the place of the gallows (at the "foot of the pillory" <note>original: *ao pe do peiorinho*</note>, as the ordinances say) unless their masters prefer to pay a monetary penalty. Thus it is held in the cited last paragraph.

Whoever makes playing cards, or brings them from another Kingdom, or sells them in Portugal, if he be a commoner, incurs the penalty of paying twenty gold coins while in chains, half to the accuser and half to the King’s treasury, and furthermore lashes "with rope and proclamation" <note>original: *com barazo e pregā*, a form of public shaming where the criminal was led through the streets</note>. If indeed he be of greater status, he incurs the penalty of paying forty gold coins to be divided in the same way, and furthermore one year of exile to the city of Ceuta <note>a Portuguese stronghold in North Africa</note>. And those who play with dice, except for the game of tables, incur the same penalties in a similar way. Thus it is held in the cited title, §1, 3, and the last.

Whoever falsifies dice or cards, or, knowing they are falsified, plays with them, as well as he in whose possession they are found—if he be a commoner, he incurs the penalty of lashes "with rope and proclamation," and ten years of exile to the island of Saint Thomas <note>São Tomé, then a penal colony</note>. Whatever he has won with those dice or cards, he pays ninefold for each one won, to be divided equally between the accuser and the King’s treasury. If, however, he has won twenty gold coins or more in that way, he is exiled forever to the island of Saint Thomas; and beyond all these things, whoever plays in this way incurs the penalties established for those playing dice or cards, as related above. Whoever is not a commoner incurs all the same penalties, with only the penalty of lashes excepted. Thus it is held in the cited title, §4 and the last.

Whoever receives any people for gambling in his house, and receives some payment from them for that reason, or provides food or drink for a price, incurs a penalty of fifty ducats, to be divided equally between the accuser and the treasury, and ten years of exile to the island of Saint Thomas, and furthermore, if he be a commoner, he is publicly whipped. Ibid. §5.

Against those who play with cards or dice, a legal action is granted only within four months from the day the crime was committed. But against those who make, bring, or sell cards, or falsify cards or dice, or, knowingly, play with falsified ones, and likewise against those who admit people for gambling in the manner explained, an action is granted within one year of the crime being committed. Thus it is held in the cited title, the penultimate paragraph.

Rightly also King Emmanuel <note>Manuel I of Portugal, r. 1495–1521</note> decreed that whoever played ball <note>original: *a la bola*</note> on feast days before the solemn mass should be cast into chains and pay fifty réis from there, as is held in part 4 of the laws, Book 1. This pertains to the prohibitions of civil law.

<margin>Canon Law</margin>
**7** Regarding what pertains to Canon Law <note>the law of the Church</note>, in the penultimate chapter concerning the life and conduct of clerics, clerics are forbidden from playing with dice or small dice <note>original: *aleis, ac taxillis*</note>, or from being present at those games; and in the decree *interdicimus* <note>a section of the Justinian Code incorporated into Canon Law</note> under the title "On bishops and clerics," the same is forbidden to them regarding the "game of tables" under the penalty that they be barred from ministry for three years and be confined to a monastery; provided, however, that if they repent within that time, it is permitted for the bishop to reduce the time for them and restore them to their ministry before the three-year period. <meta>This page continues the discussion of legal prohibitions on gambling, specifically addressing how canon law and local diocesan statutes (such as those in Portugal and Spain) treat clerics who gamble, and whether winnings from illegal games must be returned.</meta>

[...according to] canon law, prelates are not bound to order the execution of that law. Indeed, they should not make such a great matter of that game which in Portugal <note>original: *Lusitania*</note> is permitted to laypeople as moderate and honest, even though in the constitutions of the Archbishopric of Evora (title 10, chapter 7) it is prohibited to clerics—perhaps because of 그 법령 <note>the *Authentica*</note> and because it is not so becoming for clerics. In the same way, one should not be so concerned about certain games which, in the cited Law 57 of Castile, are forbidden to clerics under heavier penalties than those established for clerical gamblers in canon law, which I set down immediately below. For the game of ball <note>Latin: *pila*</note> and of the tile <note>Spanish: *el tejo* or *teiuelo*, a game involving throwing stones or tiles at a mark</note> are mentioned there; although these are not so becoming for clerics if practiced publicly (because clerics sometimes must strip down to perform them), yet if they are practiced where they cannot be seen by any but their own household, they have very little or no indecency. 

From those civil laws joined with canon law, one may gather what great composure is required of clerics, and how great it was in those times when even being seen at such games was so severely prohibited. Likewise, in the chapter *Inter dilectos*, concerning the excesses of prelates, a certain cleric was rejected from obtaining a certain ecclesiastical dignity in France because he was a public gambler, being considered an unworthy person. It did not benefit him to claim that it was the custom in France for clerics to play dice; for the Supreme Pontiff says there that this was a corruption not to be tolerated, but punished. And in chapter 1, distinction 35, we read: *A Bishop, priest, or deacon addicted to dice <note>original: "aleæ deseruiens", literally serving the dice</note> must either stop or certainly be condemned.* This means he should be deprived of his benefice or suspended from office. 

Wherefore the Gloss on the penultimate chapter of *The Life and Honesty of Clerics*, and Panormitanus in the same place (number 12), Gregório Lopez where cited above, and others, excellently observe that for a cleric to be barred from obtaining a benefice, it is enough if he is a public gambler, even if he has not been warned to restrain himself from the game, according to the cited chapter *Inter dilectos*. However, for him to be deprived of a benefice already obtained, or to be suspended, it is necessary that he first be warned. If, after being warned, he ceases the habit of playing, he is not to be deprived of his benefice or suspended. But if he does not cease, then he must be deprived or suspended, according to distinction 35. To be called a "public gambler" and thus incur these penalties, it is not enough for a cleric to play once, twice, or thrice; rather, it is required that he do so often. Hence the Gloss on distinction 35, on the word *addicted* <note>original: *deseruiens*</note>, says it means "greatly serving."

<margin>§ In the Archbishopric of Evora, chapter 7.</margin>
In the cited chapter 7 of the Archbishopric of Evora, if clerics—playing publicly or secretly with cards, dice, or tables—are caught, a penalty is imposed: for the first offense they pay five hundred reais; for the second, double; and for the third, they pay the same and are first cast into chains. Furthermore, they must restore whatever they gained in the game. Half of all these fines is awarded to the fabric <note>the building fund or maintenance office</note> of the church where the cleric was caught playing, and the other half to the *meirinho* <note>a bailiff or official</note> of the clerics. Moreover, it is commanded that they be punished according to the quality of the offense. Under the same penalty, clerics are commanded not to play publicly at *bola* or *eboca*; however, they are permitted to use games not prohibited by law in their own homes or in other decent places.

# Whether things acquired in a prohibited game are subject to restitution.

## DISPUTATION DXIII.

->SUMMARY<-

1. *How things acquired in a game prohibited by human law are subject to restitution.*
2. *Gambling is a contract according to natural law.*
3. *Interpretation of the law "Non dubium" in the Code of Laws.*

It must be explained at this point whether such a game prohibited by human laws constitutes a mortal sin, especially for ecclesiastics; however, we shall speak of that more conveniently after first explaining all those matters regarding gambling that pertain to this subject.

There is no one who doubts that things rightly acquired in a game not prohibited by human law are not subject to restitution. <margin>Question.</margin> Regarding things acquired in a game prohibited by human law, Saint Bonaventure (in Book 4, distinction 15) says that a gambler does not acquire ownership of those things he wins in a game, but is held to restore them to the person from whom he won them, or to the poor if the other person induced him to play. He would say the same of things acquired in any other prohibited game, as he expressly affirms this regarding things acquired in tournaments prohibited by law. 

Many interpreters of canon law embrace this same opinion, though they do not agree whether restitution should be made to the poor or to the person who lost it in the game. Saint Thomas is of the same opinion (in Book 4, distinction 15 and in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, question 32), as is Paludanus (distinction 15). Paludanus adds that when the loser was able to alienate that money, and the winner gained it without force or deceit and without enticing him to play, then the winner is not held to restore it to the loser before a sentence is passed, but is held to restore it to the poor. If, however, he restores it to the poor before he is condemned, he can object to a judge ordering him to restore it to the winner, stating he has already given it to the poor. Richard [of Middleton] also propounds this view, stating that the opinion of Bonaventure and others is the more common and secure one, and he leans toward it, as do several others.

<margin>Decision.</margin> However, the contrary opinion is today common among the doctors: namely, that things acquired through a game—solely because the game is prohibited by human law and because the law allows for the recovery of what was thus won—are not subject to restitution before a sentence is passed ordering them to be restored. They argue that the winner acquires ownership by the very fact that the items were handed over. So says Alexander of Hales and Adrian [of Utrecht] in his question on gambling...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of gambling, specifically addressing the obligation of restitution—whether a winner of a prohibited game is morally or legally required to return their winnings to the loser before a court order is issued.</meta>

<page-num>688</page-num>
<header>Ludovicus Molina on Contracts</header>

...because in the previous sections, Medina [cited on restitution, question 23], John Major [on book 4, distinction 15, question 13], Gabriel Biel [on the same distinction and question], Domingo de Soto [book 4 of *On Justice and Right*, question 5, article 2], Alfonso à Castro [book 2 of *On Penal Laws*, chapter 2, corollary 3], Diego de Covarrubias [on the rule *peccatum*, part 2, § 4, from number 1], Martín de Azpilcueta (Navarrus) [in his *Manual*, chapter 19, number 19], and many others. It is proved because, as shown in Disputations 510 and 511, gambling is a <term>just contract</term> <note>A contract that meets the basic requirements of natural law, such as mutual consent and equal risk, even if civil law later prohibits it for social reasons.</note> according to natural law. Consequently, it is a contract that transfers <term>ownership</term> <note>original: *dominium*</note> to the one who wins the thing lost, provided that the physical delivery follows; otherwise, it provides only a right to the thing, and an obligation arises in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>original: *in foro conscientiae*; this refers to the internal moral realm or the confessional, where one's standing before God is judged, as opposed to a civil courtroom.</note> to deliver it, just as these things are firmly binding in any other just contract. 

However, human laws—which were reported in the preceding disputation—only prohibit certain games without making the contract itself void (unless you exclude the law of Charles V regarding items gambled and delivered, which will be discussed below). Instead, these laws merely grant, as a penalty for transgressing the law, a <term>repetition</term> <note>original: *repetitio*; the legal right to demand the return of money or property that was lost or paid out.</note> of what was acquired through that game. Furthermore, this right is not granted forever, but only within a certain time, beyond which the law does not permit such recovery, as was stated in the previous disputation. Therefore, since the winner—like any other transgressor of a penal law—is not bound to the penalty before a sentence is passed, it follows that by the very fact that the thing won is delivered, he acquires ownership of it, and is not bound to restore it before a legal sentence is handed down.

<margin>2</margin>
I would add that even if the mind and intention of the legislators had been to make the gambling contract void and to prevent the transfer of ownership (which is false, as is clear to anyone examining the laws), such laws would today be abolished in this regard through contrary custom. Indeed, it is the custom for those who win at gambling not to restore the winnings, but to retain them as their own. Saint Thomas Aquinas [Second Part of the Second Part, question 32, article 2, reply to objection 7] asserts that laws can be abolished in this respect by contrary custom, and no one objects to this. However, as Panormitanus [on the penultimate chapter, *concerning the life and honor of clerics*] observes, the fact that losers are not accustomed to sue for what they lose does not strip the force from those same laws insofar as they grant the right of recovery. The reason is that a law which permits something is not abolished by the non-use of that permission, but by a use to the contrary. Therefore, for that law to lose its force regarding the recovery of gambling losses through contrary use, it would be necessary for a recovery to be demanded within the time required for prescription against the law, and for that demand to be denied.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the law *Non dubium* [Code, on laws], and that rule of the legal experts stating that when an acquisition is bad, the recipient is bound to restore what was so received—either to the giver (if the giver committed no disgrace in giving), or to the poor, or to the treasury—from which authors of the contrary opinion seem moved to embrace it; we have already shown above in Disputation 88 (especially at the end, while resolving arguments) that nothing prevents a winner in a prohibited game from holding what he has won until a sentence is passed ordering him to restore it.

<column-break/>

# On the recovery of what someone has won in a prohibited game, and how far the winner is bound to return it.

### DISPUTATION 513.

### SUMMARY.

1 *In Portuguese law, the loser of a prohibited game is not granted recovery; instead, the loss is applied half to the accuser and half to the treasury. The same applies in the law of Castile.*
2 *Whether a winner in a prohibited game is immediately bound in the court of conscience.*
3 *If a loser in a prohibited game cannot obtain recovery through a judge, whether he may lawfully take an equal amount secretly, or retain the winner's goods, as compensation for what he lost.*
4 *Whether a loser may strike a bargain with the winner for the return of part of the losses to avoid suing for the whole amount in court.*

---

<margin>1</margin>
Above all, it must be observed that under Portuguese law, the loser of a prohibited game is not granted the recovery of what he lost. Instead, the one who won is forced to return it: half to the accuser and half to the Royal Treasury, as reported in Disputation 512. Indeed, under Portuguese law, when there is a specific law of that Kingdom arranging something, the arrangement of the same matter under <term>common law</term> <note>original: *ius commune*; the general Roman-canonical legal system of Europe, as opposed to local royal statutes.</note> ceases, as found in Book 2 of the *Ordinances*, title 5. In the matter proposed, there is not only a specific law, but one that arranges things contrary to the arrangement of common law. While I was staying in that Kingdom, many legal experts in Portugal did not pay enough attention to this, thinking that the recovery granted to the loser under common law applied in Portugal. However, since under Portuguese law the profit is not to be paid to the loser, but to the treasury and the accuser, and the winner cannot be condemned to pay more profit than was proven, as stated in Disputation 512, it is quite clear that in that Kingdom the gambling contract is not void, but the winner acquires ownership of what he wins. Likewise, the penalties established by common law for gamblers and those who host them do not apply in Portugal, where there are specific penalties established for the same crimes. The same must be said for this Kingdom of Castile, where specific penalties are also established for these crimes.
<margin>Law of Castile.</margin>

<margin>2</margin>
<margin>Doubt</margin>
The doubt is whether someone who has won something in a prohibited game is bound in the court of conscience to return it to the one who lost it as soon as it is demanded outside of court; or whether, with a safe conscience, he may deny it until he is condemned by a judge's sentence. It should be said, following Alfonso à Castro [Decision 2, *On Penal Laws*, chapter 2, corollary 3], Medina [on restitution, question 22, the section beginning "neither does it stand in the way"], Covarrubias [on the rule *peccatum*, part 2, § 4, number 8], and others—to whose opinion Soto [book 4 of *On Justice*, question 5, article 2] also moves (though with doubt)—that he may deny it until he is condemned by a judge's sentence.

<summary>Molina argues that gambling winnings, even from prohibited games, represent a valid transfer of ownership under natural law. In the kingdoms of Portugal and Castile, winners are not morally obligated to return funds to the loser until a formal legal sentence is issued, as local statutes prioritize the state treasury over the loser's recovery.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral obligations of gamblers, specifically focusing on when a winner is legally required to return winnings and whether a loser can use "secret compensation" to recover their losses before a court sentence is passed.</meta>

<page-num>689</page-num>
<header>Treatise Two, Disputation 515.</header>

...is granted. The reason is that such restitution is established only as a penalty, by granting an action to recover the profit in court to the person who lost it. Since a penalty can be withheld and denied until a sentence is passed—because it is not owed except as a result of a condemning sentence being issued—it follows that this profit can be denied, not only outside of court, but even in court, while the sentence has not yet been issued. Nor is the reasoning the same for one who swore to pay, or did swear and paid, to whom a <term>petition for recovery</term> <note>original: *repetitio*; a legal action to reclaim something paid that was not legally owed.</note> is granted according to the chapter *Debitofes* on oaths. For because a usurer acquired neither ownership nor any right to those usuries, but fully owes them by right to the giver, he is certainly bound to restore them—not only to one seeking them outside of court, but even if the person remains silent and does not seek them. 

However, in the case proposed, the one who won acquired <term>ownership</term> <note>original: *dominium*</note> of the profit; he does not owe it to the one who lost it, but only as a penalty and out of a legal hatred for the game is a right granted to the loser to obtain it by initiating a legal action. Once the judge's sentence follows, he is bound, but before that, the winner is not bound to pay it. Indeed, I add that since it is established as a penalty, the defendant—when interrogated—is not bound to confess his crime unless it is <term>half-proven</term> <note>original: *semi plene*; a legal standard in Roman-canonical law where the evidence of one credible witness or strong circumstantial evidence is present, but not yet enough for a full conviction.</note> in court. Certainly, before it is half-proven (that is, by one witness beyond all exception) that he won the money, he is not bound to confess it, even if interrogated by a judge through false questioning; since the judge does not interrogate legally, the winner can rightly retain the profit or that money. 

If, however, he were to justly impede the passing of the sentence through deceits, or by certainly denying the winnings when they had been half-proven in court and he was questioned by the judge, then—as an unjust cause preventing a just sentence by which it would be awarded to the other—he would be bound to restore it, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 45. He is also bound to pay the legal expenses which the other party incurred beyond what they would have otherwise spent, due to his deceits or other injustices. In Portugal (*Lusitania*), it is quite clear that the winner is not bound to restore the profit before a sentence is issued demanding it; for it is to be restored as a mere penalty, not to the one who lost it in the game, but to the accuser and the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: *fisco*</note>. Nor is the winner bound to return more profit than was proven that he won, as has been said.

<margin>Doubt 3</margin>
3 From what has been said, the answer to the following doubt is easy: Whether, if someone who lost something in a prohibited game cannot obtain it through a judge via a recovery action, they might lawfully and secretly take or retain an equal amount from the winner's goods in <term>compensation</term> <note>original: *recompensationem*; the practice of "secret compensation" where a creditor takes what is owed to them by stealth if the legal system fails them.</note> for what they lost. Medina, Soto, and Castro, in the places cited, attribute to Adrian [on Restitution, question on gambling] the claim that such compensation is lawful. But if he is read carefully, he asserts the contrary. For he says that when something is applied to someone as a penalty—not automatically (*ipso facto*), but through the intervention of a judge's sentence, as in the case proposed—compensation cannot be made, because it is not owed before the sentence is passed. But when, he says, something is applied as a penalty automatically, compensation is lawful. In this, he seems to affirm the opinion of Castro, which we challenged in Disputation 95: namely, that when something is established as an automatic penalty, it is owed

<column-break/>

immediately upon the fault being committed, as if the sentence had been passed, and secret compensation could be made when it cannot be obtained otherwise. Therefore, regarding the proposed doubt, it must be said that such compensation is entirely illicit and carries an obligation of restitution. Except when the winner has unjustly impeded the passing of a just sentence by which it would have been awarded to the person seeking compensation. In the same way, compensation would be unjust (and require restitution) if someone who lost in a prohibited game wanted to compensate by playing again with the winner and, through fraud or trickery, winning back the same amount. The reason for both assertions is that the amount is not "owed" to the loser except by initiating a recovery action and depending upon the judge's sentence.

<margin>Decision</margin>
4 There is also a doubt: When a recovery of money acquired in a prohibited game is granted, is it lawful for the loser to threaten a lawsuit for recovery and make a deal with the winner so that the winner restores part of it, to avoid having to return the whole amount in court? The answer is yes. For just as it is lawful to seek recovery, so it is lawful to threaten a just recovery action and accept the whole or a part in order not to initiate the action, or to desist from an action already started. However, if someone—whether out of shame, fear of infamy, or any other cause—was never actually going to seek recovery, but faked the intention to sue so that the other, being deterred, would restore part of the profit, I believe he could not retain it in good conscience. For the one who restores it was justly retaining it as his own, and the one who faked the intention to sue extracted it unjustly through deceit and simulation; there was no cause for which one gave it or for which the other could justly receive it.

<margin>Decision</margin>
# Whether one who lost something on credit in a prohibited game is bound in conscience to pay it. And whether, in Castile, the one who won it can accept and retain it.

->### DISPUTATION 515.<-
->#### SUMMARY.<-

1 *When one who loses something on credit in a prohibited game is bound in conscience to pay it. And number 2 with the following.*
3 *One who loses on credit in Portugal is bound in conscience to pay.*

6 *If a gambler swore he would pay what he lost, he is bound; but see there whether he can recover what he paid.*
7 *Whether one who swears to pay what he loses in a game can lawfully recover it after payment is made, and when.*
8 *When one who receives gambling winnings sins and is bound to restore.*

As far as the first part of this disputation is concerned, Medina [on Restitution, question 22] and Castro [book 2 of *On Penal Laws*, chapter 2, corollary 3]—against the opinion of Adrian—affirm that one who loses something on credit in a prohibited game is bound in con...

<summary>This page discusses the legalities of recovering gambling losses, concluding that since recovery is a civil penalty, a winner is not morally bound to return winnings until a judge orders it. It also argues that "secret compensation" (stealing back losses) is generally illicit because the loser has no natural right to the money until a legal sentence is passed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on gambling debts from page 689, specifically whether a person is morally or legally bound to pay a debt incurred through gambling when human law might offer a way to avoid or recover that payment.</meta>

690
-> Ludovicus Molina on Contracts <-

in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>original: *in conscientia*; referring to one's moral standing before God, regardless of civil law</note> to pay that debt, and cannot withhold or deny payment to the winner; even if, after paying, he might safely in conscience seek to recover it by the benefit of the law granting him <term>recovery</term> <note>original: *repetitionem*; the legal right to reclaim a payment.</note>.

The first arguments are these: since the contract between the parties is valid, as is clear from what has been said so far, it follows that the one who won has acquired a true right to the thing won, and it is truly owed to him. Otherwise, even if it were paid, the winner would not acquire <term>ownership</term> <note>original: *dominium*</note> of it and would be bound to restore it without waiting for any court sentence—which is false, and denied even by authors of the opposing view. Therefore, since nothing prevents a loser from being granted recovery after payment, he is bound by <term>natural law</term> <note>The concept that certain rights or values are inherent by virtue of human nature and perceivable by reason, independent of man-made laws.</note> to pay what he lost, because the contract creates a prior right not invalidated by human law, at least until a judge's sentence awards it back to him.

Secondly, the payment of a thing lost in such a game is neither evil on the part of the payer nor the receiver, and a mutual promise preceded it through a just contract. Since it is a matter of natural law that a just promise must be fulfilled, it follows that—provided nothing prevents the recovery being granted to the payer afterward—he is bound to fulfill the promise. This is similar to the way one who has sworn to pay usury is bound to pay it, and yet, after payment, can seek to recover it.

Thirdly, there must be equality between the players in a game, since it is a contract pertaining to <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Justice regarding the exchange of goods and ensuring that what is given is equal to what is received.</note>. But if two people play, one with cash in hand and the other only on credit, if the latter wins, he truly acquires ownership of the present money he receives. Therefore, the other person acquires—if not ownership, for lack of physical delivery—at least a true right to the promised money, making it truly owed to him, so that the loser is bound to pay it. Otherwise, equality would not be maintained in that contract.

The following conclusions are to be established:

<margin>2</margin>
The first is this: **Excluding all human law, and standing on natural law alone, anyone who loses something on credit in a game is bound to pay it in the court of conscience.** Indeed, even if that game were prohibited by human law, and a penalty were simply imposed on the players without adding anything further, one would similarly be bound to pay it in the court of conscience. The first part is clear because, as we showed in Disputation 510, gambling (standing on natural law alone) is a just contract, and through it, a right and ownership of the thing won are acquired if delivery follows. Therefore, if you set aside human law—which might grant recovery of the thing won or its retention before it is paid—the loser is bound in conscience to pay. This is proven by the arguments already proposed. The second part is clear because the simple prohibition of a contract and the imposition of a penalty on those who practice it does not strip it of its power to bind in the court of conscience, just as if it were not prohibited under that penalty.

<margin>3</margin>
The second conclusion: **One who loses something on credit while gambling in Portugal is bound to pay it in the court of conscience.** This is proven because, as was said in the preceding disputation, in Portugal, recovery is not granted to the loser, nor does the <term>exception</term> <note>original: *exceptio*; a legal defense used to block a claim.</note> (which will be discussed below) have a place in that Kingdom.

<column-break/>

Rather, among other penalties, this one is imposed on the winner in that Kingdom: he shall lose what is proven to have been won to the <term>exchequer</term> <note>original: *fisco*; the public treasury.</note> and the accuser. Therefore, no penalty is determined for him except as it depends on sufficient proof and a formal condemning sentence. In fact, if a loser in that Kingdom attempts to recover something lost in a prohibited game, he could be condemned based on his own confession to pay the penalty established for gamblers.

<margin>4</margin>
The third conclusion: **In this Kingdom of Castile, following the laws of Charles V** <note>original: *Catoli V*; referring to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who was King Charles I of Spain.</note> (8 and 9, title 7, book 8 of the New Collection, cited in Disputation 512), **one who has lost something on credit in a game—even if otherwise permitted and promised—is not bound to pay it, not only in the external court, but also in the court of conscience.** On this point, Castro, Soto, Covarrubias, Navarro, and Gutierrez agree in their cited works. The reason is that by those two laws, not only was gambling on credit prohibited (even in games otherwise allowed) and legal action to seek winnings denied, but the promises and obligations that might arise from it or were made concerning it were rendered void and null.

<margin>5</margin>
The fourth conclusion: **Standing on common law alone, a person is bound neither in the external court nor in the court of conscience to pay what was lost in a prohibited game if it has not yet been paid.** Instead, before a sentence is passed—and even before the matter is brought to judgment—the loser can raise an <term>exception</term> or objection against the winner, stating he is not bound to it, as the law exempts him from that obligation. This is found in the legal commentaries on gambling. It is proven first because in the <term>Authentica</term> <note>A term for a summary or extract of a law in the Code of Justinian.</note> *Ut Alearum* (Codex: *On religious matters and funeral expenses*), it is stated:

> *Let no condemnation follow (as if the loser were compelled to pay the game).*

But let what has been paid be recovered by competent actions; therefore, the mind of the legislator in that law is to render the loser immune from the obligation to pay before he pays, and to grant him recovery after he has paid. The legislator was able to effect both of these, and it was expedient to do so out of hatred for prohibited gambling. Secondly, because in that law, out of hatred for the prohibited game, it is openly granted to the loser that he need not pay. Although that law is penal, because that penalty requires no execution on the part of the one punished by it, a judge’s sentence is certainly not necessary for that penalty to have force and place; rather, the denial—by which the one who otherwise owes it denies it to the one to whom it would be paid—is sufficient.

<margin>Question</margin>
Thirdly, because to whomever an <term>action</term> <note>original: *actio*; the right to sue.</note> is granted to recover what he gave, an <term>exception</term> is also granted so that he does not have to pay it to the claimant. This is held in the Digest and the Code regarding rules of law and pacts. Since the loser is granted an action to recover what he paid, it is granted with far greater reason that he has an exception, without any fault, before he pays.

<margin>6</margin>
The doubt is whether one who has sworn that he would pay what he lost in a game is bound to pay it, notwithstanding civil laws and even the laws of Charles V. The answer must be given according to the opinion of all...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 690 regarding the moral and legal obligations surrounding gambling debts, specifically focusing on whether an oath makes a debt binding and if such payments can be reclaimed under the law.</meta>

691
### Second Treatise, Disputation 515.

...are affirmed by this opinion. The reason is that it does not concern an evil or illicit matter; for he who loses something in a game may lawfully pay it, and a lawful oath made regarding a matter that is not prohibited must be fulfilled. However, if—excluding the oath—it would be a sin (at least a <term>venial</term> <note>A minor sin that does not result in complete separation from God's grace, unlike a mortal sin.</note> one) to pay it, perhaps because it would cause detriment to his wife’s property or for some other reason, then, because an oath is not a "bond of iniquity" <note>A legal and theological principle that an oath cannot bind someone to do something sinful or unjust.</note>, he would not be bound to pay it.

<margin>Question 7</margin>
Furthermore, can one who has so sworn, once the payment is made, lawfully seek to <term>recover</term> <note>original: *repetere*; the legal action to get back money paid under an invalid or voidable contract.</note> it? Navarrus in his *Manual* (chapter 19, number 17) and Gutierrez (Part 1, chapter 53, numbers 7 and 8), along with others, affirm that he not only can lawfully recover it, but can even lawfully seek and obtain a <term>release from the oath</term> <note>An official dispensation by a church authority that cancels the spiritual obligation of an oath.</note> before he pays. Once obtained, he need not pay. This is no different from one who swore to pay <term>usury</term> <note>Interest on a loan, which was largely prohibited or strictly regulated by Church law at this time.</note>; he can reclaim those payments after they are made, and before paying, he can obtain a release from the oath and then refuse to pay, as is established in the chapter *Debitores* regarding oaths. However, there is a great difference between one who swore to pay usury and one who swore to pay what he lost on credit. For he who accepts usury from one who swore to pay it sins by accepting it and is bound to restore it to the one from whom he received it. He does not acquire ownership of that money, nor did he acquire a right to it by virtue of the oath before it was paid. Rather, the one who swore is only bound by the oath to pay so as not to take God’s name in vain—unless he is first released from the oath by the usurer himself or by a superior, as was explained at length in Disputation 149 and the two following. But he who receives what he won on credit does not act wrongly in receiving it, and he acquires ownership of it, even if the loser had not bound himself by an oath to pay, as has been said. Therefore, when the bond of an oath is added, since it falls upon a lawful promise—even if that promise is void by <term>human law</term> <note>Civil or statutory law made by monarchs or states, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note> without the oath—it nonetheless grants the winner a true right to be paid. This is similar to one who buys <term>dotal land</term> <note>Land belonging to a wife's dowry, which usually could not be sold without specific legal protections.</note> or something from a <term>minor</term> <note>A person under the legal age of majority, whose contracts were often voidable to protect them from exploitation.</note> with an added oath; the contract, otherwise void by human law, is confirmed, and the buyer acquires true right and ownership. If the delivery of the item follows, there is no place for recovery, nor can a release of the oath be granted to the prejudice of the third party to whom it was sworn, provided no force or injury was involved, as was explained in the cited Disputation 149.

<margin>Decision</margin>
For this reason, I would say that if the intention of the swearer was only to bind himself not to deny the delivery of the goods to the winner (as the law allows), then the opinion of those doctors is true: the oath does not prevent him from reclaiming what he paid. By delivering it, he fulfilled the oath, and the winner acquired no special right other than that the delivery should not be denied. But if the swearer’s intent was to bind himself to make that thing the winner's own—as if the oath were strengthening the promise and the mutual contract—then he cannot reclaim it. Indeed, I do not believe a

<column-break/>

public power could then release him from that oath so that he might reclaim it or refuse to pay, just as we said in the cited disputations regarding the sale of dotal land or a minor’s property confirmed by oath. Therefore, I do not see by what other reasoning it could be entirely prevented that a winner on credit would acquire an irrevocable right and ownership when such an oath is added, unless the public law voids the oath itself before the recipient acquires a true right. That supreme powers (even secular ones) can do this was proved in Disputation 149. Although Gutierrez says (in numbers 9 and 10) that even if one swore not only to pay what he lost on credit but also not to reclaim it, he could still reclaim it by first obtaining a release from both oaths. This is argued because one could similarly reclaim payments if he had sworn to pay and not reclaim usury. He also believes that following the laws of **Charles V**, anyone who receives such a payment is bound to restore it in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>The internal moral realm where one is accountable to God, distinct from civil courts.</note>, even if it is not reclaimed. I believe the contrary opinion is true, based on what was just said. Just as in the case of dotal land or a minor’s property sold in that manner, recovery cannot be sought nor a release of the oath granted. As for the first point regarding usury, I have shown there is a wide difference between a usurer and a gambler. As for the second point, we shall immediately show it to be false.

Regarding the second point proposed in the title of this disputation, Soto (in *On Justice and Right*, book 4, question 5, article 2) says that after those laws of **Charles V** <note>Referring to the 16th-century Spanish laws (such as those in the *Nueva Recopilación*) which heavily restricted gambling and the enforcement of gambling debts.</note>, not only can a person who loses on credit refuse to pay in the court of conscience, but he who accepts it sins by doing so. He is bound in conscience to restore it to the giver without waiting for a legal sentence, even if it is not requested. Gutierrez holds the same opinion. They argue that those laws make the contract and the obligation to pay void and null; but from a null contract, neither ownership nor right can be acquired. Therefore, since the receiver acquires neither ownership nor right to the thing, but ownership remains with the giver, it follows that the receiver is immediately bound in the court of conscience to restore it. To me and certain others, the opposite seems true: namely, that the receiver acquires ownership and is not bound to restore it unless a legal action for recovery is initiated and a sentence is passed.

Firstly, because it was not the intent of those laws to prevent the transfer of ownership to the receiver, nor to "entangle consciences" by mandating restoration in the court of conscience without any recovery action. Rather, the intent was only to remove the *obligation* to pay from the loser, in the same way it was removed under <term>common law</term> <note>In this context, *ius commune*, the shared legal system of Roman and Canon law used in Europe.</note>. Because there were differing opinions on this in common law, the laws of Charles V established it more explicitly by voiding those promises and obligations, but only to the effect that the promisor should not be bound to pay and should be acquitted in court...

<summary>This page discusses whether a gambling debt confirmed by an oath is morally binding and whether such payments can be recovered. Molina argues that while certain laws by Charles V attempt to void gambling debts, an oath may still create a moral obligation, and ownership transfers once payment is made unless a court explicitly orders its return.</summary>

in the <term>external forum</term> <note>The public system of civil or ecclesiastical law and courts.</note>, it is not as if the ownership would not be transferred if he paid of his own accord and the winner accepted it. Nor would the winner be bound to restore it in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>original: *animæ foro*; the internal moral judgment of an individual before God, often addressed in confession.</note>, which secular legislators do not wish to oversee. Secondly, even if we were to grant that <term>Charles V</term> <note>Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (1516–1556), who issued strict edicts against gambling to prevent social disorder.</note> intended this (which we do not believe to be true), a <term>prescription</term> <note>A legal principle where a law loses its force because it is no longer observed or enforced by the community.</note> has today taken effect against those laws in that regard. It has never been heard of that anyone who won in this way restored what was paid to him, or that confessors enjoined such a thing—even though nobles often play on credit and pay what they lose. Laws do not bind any more than they have been confirmed by the practice of those using them, and custom is their best interpreter.

It remains for us to respond to the arguments proposed at the beginning. To the first: granted that the contract was valid and the winner acquired a <term>right to the thing</term> <note>original: *ius ad rem*; a legal claim to a specific object or sum.</note> he won—making it his own if it is paid to him—it must be said that it is truly owed to him. However, this is dependent on the loser not wishing to use the <term>privilege of the law</term> <note>A specific legal protection or "out" provided by the state to a certain class of people or in certain situations.</note>, which allows him not to pay if he chooses to invoke or apply that legal privilege. Because the law does not void the contract itself (except for the law of Charles V, which we are not discussing here, and that only to the effect that the loser can choose not to pay if he wishes, as just explained), the winner truly holds a right to that thing from the contract. Thus, if it is paid to him without the loser using the legal privilege, it becomes his own. Yet, because <term>positive law</term> <note>Man-made laws enacted by a government, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note> grants the loser the faculty of not paying if he wishes to object and use that privilege, the result is that if the loser objects and wishes to use the privilege of the law, the winner loses the right he otherwise held from the contract. Therefore, these two things stand together: that the winner may demand what he won from the loser and make it his own if it is paid to him according to the contract, and that the loser can deny it to him by using the privilege and benefit of the law. However, by the very fact that the loser denies it, the winner is bound not to proceed further, since the loser does not need a judge’s sentence to exercise his right. Nevertheless, if he had already paid and then sought to <term>recover</term> <note>original: *repeteret*; a legal action to reclaim money already handed over.</note> it, because the winner is not bound to return it unless a sentence follows condemning him to that penalty, the winner is not bound to return it as soon as it is demanded, but can wait for the judge's condemnatory sentence.

Therefore, regarding the argument in its formal structure: having granted the premise in the sense explained, the conclusion must be denied. The loser can use the privilege of the law, but he is not *required* to, except in a way that depends on his choice not to use the privilege which the law grants him as a penalty against the winner.

To the second point: having granted the <term>major premise</term> <note>The first part of a logical argument.</note>, it must be said regarding the <term>minor premise</term> <note>The second part of a logical argument.</note> that it is a matter of <term>natural law</term> <note>Universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> that a just promise be fulfilled, provided that the law has not granted a privilege for the common good (and as a penalty for the one to be paid) allowing the promiser to refuse fulfillment if he wishes, as is granted in the matter at hand. Regarding the example of one who swore an oath to pay <term>usury</term> <note>Interest on a loan, which was traditionally viewed as a sin and often legally prohibited.</note>, it must be said that he is bound to pay by virtue of the oath out of reverence for God—lest he should have called God as a witness to a faithless promise—and he is not excused from that obligation on any

<column-break/>

grounds, even though the usurer himself is bound to release him from that obligation before the usury is paid, and after payment, is bound to return it to him. But in the matter at hand, the privilege of the law grants the loser the power not to pay what he promised, if he wishes to use that privilege.

To the third point: regarding the major premise, it must be said that in a game there ought to be equality between the players for it to be just, unless one of them voluntarily wishes to waive some part of that total equality, either expressly or tacitly. This is because, even assuming the penalties or privileges granted by law in some types of games, he nonetheless chooses to play with that inequality. No injury is done to one who is willing and consenting. Thus, having then granted the minor premise, the conclusion is to be denied—if the conclusion is understood to mean that the loser, because of the legal privilege, cannot safely deny payment in both the <term>external forum</term> and the <term>court of conscience</term>. He who plays for ready cash with someone should blame himself if, while that legal privilege stands, he chooses to play; for no injury is done to him since he is willing and consenting. Observe two things, however. One is that he who plays with ready cash enjoys nearly the same privileges. For after he has lost, if he has not yet paid, he can similarly deny payment. And after he has paid, the law grants him the right of recovery. The other is that if anyone plays on credit with the intention of not paying if he loses, he cannot keep his winnings; he is bound to restore anything won in that game because of the inequality in the contract at the time the game was played. In the same way, he who plays for ready cash, if he has the intention at that time of reclaiming what he might lose, is bound for the same reason to restore what he may have won.

## Whether one who entices another to gamble is bound to restore what he won from him.

### DISPUTATION 516.

### SUMMARY.

> 1. Whether a player who draws another into gambling is bound to restore what he won from him, and when. Also numbers 2 and 3.

<margin>Question</margin> 
**Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian.</note> (2. 2. question 32, article 7, reply to the 2nd objection) answers in the affirmative, speaking of one who, out of a desire for gain, has drawn another into gambling. **Hadrianus** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a Dutch theologian known for his strict moral views.</note>, however, in his treatise *On Restitution*, the question on gambling beginning with the words "Because in the above," disagrees with him. He says that just as someone who, out of greed, entices another to celebrate some other just contract on a Sunday—although he sins against the virtue of religion or the sin of avarice through an inordinate desire for gain—does not thereby sin against justice and, for that reason, is bound to no restitution of the gain; so too, he who out of greed entices someone to a game that is otherwise just, is not bound to restore the gain, even if he sins by the sin of avarice because of an inordinate appetite for profit.

<summary>This page explores the tension between civil laws that allow gamblers to default on debts and the moral obligation of an oath, concluding that while a loser may legally refuse to pay, the winner’s right to keep a voluntary payment is generally upheld by custom. It also begins a debate on whether "luring" someone into a game constitutes an injustice requiring restitution.</summary>

693
Second Treatise, Disputation 17.

<term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> on the same passage of <term>Saint Thomas</term>, <term>Soto</term> <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a Spanish Dominican priest and scholastic theologian.</note> in book 4 of *On Justice*, question 5, article 2; <term>Castro</term> *On Penal Laws*, chapter 2, column 3; <term>Covarruvias</term> in the rule *Peccatum*, part 2, section 4, number 7, and others, distinguish that there are two ways one can draw another to a game. First, in such a way that the enticement creates an involuntary act mixed with an <term>injury</term> <note>In a legal sense, *iniuria* refers to a violation of a person's rights or dignity.</note> to the person drawn in—for instance, if someone is drawn in by insults, threats, some force, or by such words that they approach the game against their will due to shame or fear. In this case, they say the winner is bound to restore what was won in that manner, because the contract was void due to the involuntary nature mixed with the injury to the person כך enticed; they argue that Saint Thomas was speaking of this kind of enticement to play. In the second way, they say someone can be drawn to play by requests that do not inflict injury nor create a mixed involuntary state. In that case, they say the winner is not bound to restore any winnings to the person drawn in this way, as <term>Hadrian</term> <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a scholar and theologian.</note> affirms.

<margin>2</margin>
I would advise two things. First, it seems to me that a person who entices another to a game in the "mixed involuntary" way explained above is not bound to restore the *whole* of what was won, but only a greater or lesser part, according to the judgment of a prudent person, considering the degree of the injury and other concurrent circumstances. Indeed, if the injury only occurred but otherwise the person could have equally won or lost—and thus the contract was fair—I believe they are bound to no restoration. For, as we shall show in the material on restoration, by reason of an injury specifically distinct from a loss caused, no restoration is owed; rather, for an injury distinct from a loss, only a penalty is required, which is not owed before a legal judgment is passed. I am led to assert that the winner is not bound to restore the whole profit because none of the doctors with whom we are disputing affirms that a person enticed to a game in this mixed involuntary way is bound to restore to the enticer anything he might have won from him in that game. Therefore, the contract was not null; otherwise, if it were null, just as the enticer is bound to restore the whole profit if he wins, so the enticed person would be bound to restore the whole profit. Certainly, from a null contract, neither ownership nor any right is acquired. If, therefore, the contract was fair in itself and equal—because, considering the concurrent circumstances, either party could equally win or lose—then surely, just as that consent was sufficient for the contract to be valid on the part of the enticed person, it was also sufficient for it to be valid in comparison to the enticer. For "mixed involuntary" consent is simply voluntary, and only involuntary in a certain respect, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Arist. 3. Ethic. c. 1." referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> and all the doctors affirm. And although this might not be enough to transfer ownership or a right when no <term>onerous title</term> <note>A legal basis for a contract involving an exchange of value (like a sale), as opposed to a "gratuitous title" like a gift.</note> intervenes—but only a gratuitous title, as in the granting of usury or a promise to a highwayman so that he does not unjustly kill—it is nevertheless sufficient when an onerous title is involved. Furthermore, although one who is led to enter into a contract through injury (mixed involuntary) has just cause to seek and obtain the rescission of that contract by returning what he received and reclaiming what he gave, nevertheless equity does not allow him to ask for what he gave to be restored to him while giving nothing back. In the matter proposed, however, the equal hope of winning and the equal danger of losing have been exchanged on both sides, and therefore there is no place for the res-

<column-break/>

-cission of the contract unless the person who was led to play in a mixed involuntary way returns what he received and demands what he gave in compensation. If anyone should say that it is fitting for one who draws another to play in a mixed involuntary way to have the whole profit taken from him as a just penalty and given back to the enticed person without any compensation, I respond: although that might be just—especially if the injury was grave and much of the involuntary was involved, or even out of hatred for the game itself, even if the injury were not grave—this nevertheless does not take place except after a legal sentence by which the enticer is condemned to it.

<margin>3</margin>
The second point concerns whatever Saint Thomas may have said in the cited response to the second point. Yet, <term>Saint Bonaventure</term> <note>Bonaventure (1221–1274), a major Franciscan theologian.</note> in book 4, distinction 15, part 2, article 2, question 1; Saint Thomas in the same distinction, question 2, article 4, final short question; and others whom we cited in Disputation 513, when they assert that the enticer is bound to restore the profit to the enticed person, they mean it to apply regardless of how he entices them by inviting them to play. They are led to this because they believe that, given the civil law, the profit must always be restored. However, they say, when someone was enticed in some way, the law grants them the right to reclaim the money in the <term>external forum</term> <note>The public system of civil laws and courts.</note> because of the greater wickedness present in the enticer; for that reason, restoration should be made to the loser in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>The internal moral judgment of the individual's soul.</note> and not to the poor, and therefore alms cannot be made from such profit. But when the enticer won because he was himself drawn into the game, they say the right to reclaim is not granted to the enticer in the external forum; therefore, that profit is not to be restored to him (as he is unworthy due to the wickedness in him), but must be given to the poor. Hence <term>Medina</term> <note>Bartolomé de Medina (1527–1581), a Spanish scholastic.</note> on Restoration, question 42, not without merit, attributes to Saint Thomas and others the opinion that an enticer, regardless of how he draws someone to a game, is bound to restore the profit to the enticed person, and likewise that alms should be given to the poor from it.

# Fraud and deception in a game: when they are unjust and consequently oblige one to restoration.

## DISPUTATION 517.

->SUMMARY<-

1. *Fraud and deception in a game: when they are unjust and oblige one to restoration.*
2. *When a player is not bound to restore and does not commit a sin by playing.*
3. *When those present at a game are not bound to warn the players.*
4. *When deception and fraud are said to occur unjustly in a game. Number 5.*

<margin>1</margin>
**In** a game, deception is not considered unjust, nor is there unjust or evil guile or fraud, when one of the players deceives the other according to the rules of the game common to both; consequently, no obligation to restore arises from what one wins from the other through that deception, guile, or fraud. The reason is that the contract is equal and just,

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

settling with the person committing the act, they might agree that, whether it is worth more or less, it should be sold at a fixed price. In that case, whether it is later found to be worth much more or much less, neither party is bound to restore anything to the other, because of the risk and hope to which both exposed themselves. <term>Medina</term> <note>Juan de Medina (1489–1545), a Spanish theologian known for his work on restitution.</note> agrees with all of this in his work *On Restitution*, question 22.

Next, unjust deception, or unjust trickery or fraud, occurs if someone profits by stealing a card, or by marking cards with signs so that he knows what should be hidden from him according to the rules of the game; or by playing with cards he recognizes from the back by habit while the other is ignorant of this; or by some art or industry arranging the cards so that a better hand falls to himself. Or if he plays with someone advising him about the adversary's hand, or if an adversary's partner does not help the adversary as much as he can and is bound to do. According to the rules of the game, a partner is bound to help his own teammate as much as he can by playing with whatever skill he possesses, and by advising him on all things where it is helpful and lawful to be advised according to the rules of the game. Otherwise, he is bound to <term>restitution</term> <note>The act of making points right by returning stolen goods or compensating for loss.</note> for the <term>emerging loss</term> <note>original: "damni emergentis"; direct financial loss incurred.</note> and the <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucri cessantis"; potential income that was prevented.</note>—both he himself and the opponent who, knowing this, continued to play.

Likewise, deception and unjust fraud occur, carrying the burden of restitution, if an opponent has won and did not notice it, or through forgetfulness did not ask for what he won, and the winner keeps it for himself. This is the case unless perhaps there is a law or custom in some place that says this negligence harms the one who does not notice or ask for his winnings; for one must always abide by the laws and customs of the game. Furthermore, in all these and similar cases, the burden of restitution lies not only on how much was gained by such deceptions and frauds by the one who committed them, but also on how much was found to have prevented the other from winning.

If, however, it is doubtful who would have won if such unjust frauds and deceptions had not intervened, then one is not bound to restore what was thus doubtful—unless perhaps it was more probable that the adversary would have won. In that case, based on the degree of that greater probability, something should be restored according to the judgment of a prudent man, insofar as an unjust impediment was placed to prevent the just effect of profit following from that higher probability.

From this it is clear that it is not enough to exempt someone from the burden of restitution for frauds and deceptions committed unjustly while playing if he says that he carried away no profit at the end of the game, or even if he says he suffered a loss. For if it is certain that through those frauds and deceptions he was an obstacle to his adversary winning more, he is bound to restore to him the profit that he unjustly prevented—unless (outside of Portugal) he had a true intention, after the game ceased, of seeking back what he lost or would have lost had those frauds not intervened; however, this rarely happens.

<column-break/>

### Gaming with a thief, a custodian, a usurer, or another possessing and playing with someone else’s property, and to what extent it creates an obligation of restitution on both sides.

## DISPUTATION 518.

->SUMMARY<-

1. When someone playing with a thief, a custodian, or a usurer—or another possessing someone else's property—is bound to restore what he won from them, and vice versa.
2. Whether a thief, a usurer, and others like them who win at gambling are bound to restore their winnings, and when.

<margin>1</margin>
Whether a <term>usurer</term> <note>A person who lends money at interest, which was often considered a sin or a crime in this period.</note> acquires ownership of the interest or of the things he further acquires with that interest—and likewise whether a robber and a <term>depositary</term> <note>original: "depositarius"; someone entrusted with another's property for safekeeping.</note> acquire ownership of things they acquire using others' property—was explained in Disputations 326 and 327. Therefore, if anyone plays with a thief, a custodian, or a usurer and wins from them a thing which did not belong to them, nor did they have the power from the owner to alienate it in that way, he is bound to restore it to the rightful owner as soon as he knows it belongs to another. The reason is that the one who lost it in the game is in default regarding its restoration to the true owner. The reasoning is this: even if someone won it in good faith, thinking the fellow player could alienate it in that way, he is nevertheless bound to restitution by reason of the thing received. However, the person who lost it in the game is then bound to restore its value to the winner. Because, as we showed in Disputation 327, that gambling contract was valid in the <term>forum of conscience</term> <note>The internal "court" of one's own moral standing before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note>, and the usurer or custodian is bound in the forum of conscience for the <term>eviction of the property</term> <note>original: "evictione rei"; a legal term for the loss of property to a third party with a better claim.</note> which they lost in the game.

<margin>2</margin>
Because that gambling contract was valid, certainly the thief, usurer, or custodian, if they won anything in that game, acquire ownership of it. They are not bound to restore it, even if they won it using money or other property belonging to someone else, as is clearly established from what was said in the same disputation. Note, however: if those who played with another's property and won did not have the means to pay back its value in the event that it was recovered and snatched from the power of the fellow player, or in the event that the fellow player, knowing it was another's, restored it of his own accord (as he would be bound to do), then those who played with the stolen property must be compelled to restore a portion of the value they acquired in that game. This is because of the risk to which they exposed the fellow player—the risk of not obtaining his winnings if he had been the one to win. They should be compelled to restore a larger or smaller part of the profit depending on how great or small the risk was to which they exposed their fellow player. This is especially true since, in the <term>external forum</term> <note>The public, legal court system.</note>, the fellow player would not be granted a legal action for the recovery of property gained in a prohibited game. Therefore, if they exposed the fellow player to an obvious risk, they should be compelled to restore the entire profit they acquired in that game, keeping nothing for themselves.

Observe, however, that since the thing was taken by theft and both players knew it, perhaps the thief would be bound to restore whatever he won with it, because the gambling contract is then void by the law itself, just as a contract of buying and selling the same stolen item would be.
