# On gaming with a son under paternal authority, or with a minor; when an obligation to restore arises.

## DISPUTATION 519.

### SUMMARY.

1 *When someone playing with a son under paternal authority or a minor is bound to restore what was won from them.*
2 *In the case where the gambler is bound to restore, should he restore to the parents, and after their death to the same son from whom he won? And conversely, if a son or another person incapable of transferring property wins in a game, is he bound to restore it? number 3.*
4 *If a son under paternal authority wins more from the father's profectitious property than he himself could transfer through gaming from those goods, is he bound to restore the increase?*

Regarding the <term>son under paternal authority</term> <note>original: "filiusfamilias"; a son who remains under the legal control and "potestas" of his father, regardless of his age, until the father dies or legally emancipates him.</note>, a distinction must be made. For <gloss>†</gloss> if he is an adolescent—that is, if he is a male over the age of fourteen—and someone wins from him property which such a son has the power to <term>alienate</term> <note>The legal right to transfer ownership of property to another person.</note>, then the winner is not bound to restore what was won. This applies if the son wagers <term>military property</term> <note>original: "bona castrensia"; property or wages earned by a son through military service, over which he had full control even if under his father's authority.</note> or <term>quasi-military property</term> <note>original: "quasi-castrensia"; property earned through civil service, the church, or liberal professions.</note>; for he has the free administration and disposal of these, provided he is an adolescent, as was explained in Disputations 230 and 231 (where we explained what constitutes military and quasi-military property) and Disputation 261. Therefore, whatever someone wins from those goods is not subject to <term>restitution</term>.

If the son also wagers his <term>adventitious property</term> <note>original: "bona adventitia"; property coming to the son from any source other than the father, such as an inheritance from his mother or a gift from a stranger.</note>, the administration and <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another (in this case, the father's right to the son's property profits).</note> of which belong to him—either because the law left it to him in the many cases explained in Disputation 8, or because the father does not claim it from him but leaves it to him, according to what was explained in Disputations 8 and 232—then the person who wins it is not bound to restore it. This is because, by that very fact, the son has the administration and disposal of those goods. The same must be said of <term>profectitious property</term> <note>original: "bonis profectitiis"; property that comes directly from the father’s estate.</note> which the father grants him for his own enjoyment and play. From this, you may gather that since young sons have some property, either given and granted by parents for their enjoyment, or acquired by their own labor, industry, or service, or given to them by someone else which the father does not claim, if they wager these things, those who win them are bound to no restitution to the sons or their parents. And hence, those who play with youths living in their father's house are excused from restitution when it is certain or likely that they are not wagering what they have stolen from their parents or others, but what is their own property, with the parents not demanding it back from them. By this same reasoning, such sons are excused from the burden of restoring what they have won from others using those goods, provided the others were able to alienate the property they lost; for such profit

<column-break/>

falls into the increase of the <term>adventitious peculium</term> <note>A "peculium" is a personal fund of money or property allowed by a master or father to a slave or son. "Adventitious" refers to funds from outside the father.</note> of those sons.

With even greater reason are those excused from the burden of restoring who play with sons living outside the paternal home—either in the service of someone else, or acquiring goods for themselves through a trade or other ministry—and win something from them. For such sons are the administrators of the adventitious property which they so acquire and possess, and which the father does not claim. In this matter, observe that even if the father does not claim the administration and usufruct of the son's adventitious property because of ignorance—not ignorance that the son possesses them, but ignorance that the right belongs to him—if he were to wish to claim them and use that right, the usufruct certainly belongs to the son for the time being. The administration and disposal made by the son at that time is valid. The reason is that the grant of law which gives the head of the family the usufruct and administration of the son's adventitious property is understood to apply only if the father wishes it and claims it, as is clear from what was said in Disputations 8 and 232. Furthermore, he must bear the responsibility for his own ignorance of the law. Observe also that as long as the father permits the son the administration of adventitious goods, even if he would not wish him to gamble with them, the transfer made by the son through gaming is valid; for, in order for him to be able to transfer them through gaming, it is enough that he has the administration and disposal of them.

In Disputation 234, in the section "hence I gather," we said that if a son living in his father's house and receiving food and necessities from the father's goods earns more for the father through some trade than the father spends on him, and for that reason, without the father's knowledge, reserves something for himself or takes from the father's goods because he does not wish to grant it to the father, and he wagers that: neither the winner is bound to any restitution, nor is the son himself bound to the father, or to his brothers after the father's death. This is because he wagers what is his own and not his father's—except perhaps regarding the usufruct and administration while the father lives, which is not of such great importance, as I immediately add: especially if such a son still leaves more to the father from his own labor than what the father spends on him.

When a son wagers his adventitious property, the administration of which the father does not permit him, but he wagers it secretly against the father's will, then such a son, though he sins, would not be bound to restore what he so wagered to his brothers later. This is because he wagered what is his own, and he did not deprive the father or the brothers (as a consequence of the father's rights) except of the usufruct of those goods, which would then belong to the father. Such usufruct is usually of little value to the father when such adventitious goods are <term>movables</term> <note>Personal property that can be moved (like money or jewelry), as opposed to "immovables" like land.</note>, as those things which sons wager usually are. It is rarely to be believed that any father is so harsh and inhuman with his son that he would want to compel him to restore the small profit of such a usufruct, and much less would he want to compel him to restore it to his brothers after his death. Moreover, the father can freely forgive such usufruct to the son, as was said in Disputations 8 and 232.

<margin>A Doubt</margin> A greater doubt is whether those who have won such goods from these sons are bound to restore them to the parents—since they were won against the parents' presumed will—and whether after...

<summary>This page examines the legal and moral obligations of restitution when gambling with "sons under paternal authority." It concludes that if a son has legal control over his earnings or inheritance, his losses are generally valid and do not require the winner to pay back the family.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into gambling involving dependents. It focuses on 'sons under paternal authority' and minors, specifically examining whether winnings are valid when the person betting does not technically own the property they are wagering under Roman and Civil law.</meta>

Second Treatise. Disputation 519.

...after the death of those parents, is the winner bound to restore those goods to the children from whom they were won? And similarly, if children who play with their <term>adventitious goods</term> <note>original: "bonis adventitiis"; property a son acquires from outside the father's estate, such as an inheritance from his mother or a gift from a third party.</note> win something, are they bound to restore it to those from whom they won it? 

The reason for both doubts is that, as stated in Disputation 161, the <term>alienation</term> <note>The legal transfer of ownership of property.</note> of such adventitious goods—where the administration and <term>usufruct</term> <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another person.</note> belong to the father—is null if performed by a <term>son under paternal authority</term> <note>original: "filiusfamilias"; a son who remains under the legal control of his father until emancipated or the father's death.</note> before the age of puberty. If, however, it is done with the father's consent, it is valid; if done after the age of puberty without the father's consent, it is invalid. Therefore, since no ownership or right can be acquired from a null contract, it follows that what others have won from sons under paternal authority without the father's consent does not belong to them. Instead, they are bound to restore it to the father while he lives, and after his death, to the son from whom they won it. Likewise, what the son has won from them would not belong to him, but he would be bound to restore it to those from whom he won it.

<margin>Decision.</margin> It must be said, however, that winners are bound to no restitution to such sons. The reason is that, as we showed in Disputation 261, although that transfer of property is legally null and the father could reclaim what the son intended to lose through gambling (or any other contract to his own detriment), the contract remains valid between the parties. By it, the son is bound not only in the <term>court of conscience</term> <note>The internal moral forum of the soul and religious confession.</note> but also in the external court, unless it were a prohibited game for which the law grants no legal action. Therefore, because of the right the winner acquired through the game and the natural obligation the son owes him, the winner is not bound to restore anything to the son. 

In a similar way, if the son won something using those goods, he is not bound to restore it, because the contract was similarly valid and both parties are bound by it. As for the father, if he were to reclaim the property (as is his right) and obtain what was gambled away without his consent, the son is then bound to <term>indemnify</term> <note>original: "de evictione"; a legal obligation to compensate a buyer if the property is reclaimed by a third party with a better title.</note> the winner in the court of conscience. This holds unless the son uses the legal privilege granted to him to avoid paying it back, or unless he is a minor under twenty-five years old and qualifies for <term>restitution in integrum</term> <note>A legal remedy where a person is restored to their original state before a contract was made, usually to protect young people from the consequences of bad decisions.</note>. 

However, unless the father specifically reclaims it, it is rarely or never required of the winner to restore anything to the father. This is because the father’s loss is usually minor—essentially just the temporary use of the property during his lifetime. Furthermore, the son would be morally bound to pay back the winner if the winner were to restore the money to the father. Finally, a father will rarely be found who, despite his grief over his son's gambling, wishes to pursue such a small personal gain at the cost of burdening his son and causing public disgrace to both father and son.

<margin>Decision.</margin> What has been said regarding a son under paternal authority gambling with adventitious goods he does not manage should likewise be said of a minor who is not a

<column-break/>

son under paternal authority and who gambles away goods without the authority of a <term>tutor</term> or <term>curator</term> <note>Legal guardians: a 'tutor' managed the affairs of a child under 14; a 'curator' assisted a young adult between 14 and 25.</note>. For the contract is valid, and for that reason, no obligation of restitution arises on either side, unless the minor or the guardian wishes to rescind the contract through the legal benefit of "restitution in integrum," as discussed extensively at the end of Disputation 224.

What <term>profectitious goods</term> <note>original: "bona profectitia"; property that comes directly from the father’s own estate or assets.</note> are was explained in Disputations 233 and 234. These include funds the father sends to the son for his support while he is away at school, at court, or elsewhere, as well as property he manages while conducting his father's business. In Disputation 242, it was explained to what extent a son is bound to restore what he has wasted from these goods in gambling to his father, or to include those losses in the division of inheritance with his brothers after the father's death. It also covered to what extent a person who wins such goods is bound to restore them to the father or his heirs. Therefore, what was said in that place relieves us of the burden of repeating it here.

<margin>Doubt 3</margin> The doubt is whether, in <term>winnings</term> <note>original: "quaestibus"</note> where someone cannot win from a son under paternal authority because the contract is null due to his inability to transfer property, such a son (or another person similarly restricted) can nonetheless keep what he wins from others, or whether he is bound to restore it. <margin>Decision.</margin> The answer is that he cannot keep the winnings, but is bound to restore them. This is the view of Castro, Covarrubias, and Soto. The reason is that just as the contract is null so that others cannot win from someone who cannot legally lose his property, it must also be null so that the person who cannot lose cannot win from others. Otherwise, the contract would be unequal: one person would face no risk of losing anything, while the other would face the risk of losing whatever the first person might win.

<margin>Question 4</margin> The doubt is: if a son under paternal authority wins more from his father's profectitious goods than he himself was legally allowed to wager, is he bound <insert>†</insert> to restore the excess? For example, if he could only wager one gold coin but wins twenty, must he restore the nineteen? Soto suggests he must restore the increase. However, Navarro argues against him, asserting that he is <margin>Decision.</margin> bound to restore nothing. It must be said, however, that if in every individual toss of a continuous game he does not win more from any player than he himself could have lost in that toss—even if he wins a large total from many people or over many tosses—he is bound to no restitution, provided the losers were legally capable of wagering that money. Soto would deny this. The reason for our view is that he always has a right to win in each toss as much as he can lose; because the contract is equal, it does not matter if, by losing it all in one toss, nothing remains for him...

<summary>This page discusses the legalities of gambling with family property, concluding that while a father may have a right to reclaim property lost by a son, the gambling contract itself often creates a moral obligation between the players. It also establishes the principle of "equality of risk," arguing that if a person cannot legally lose money, they cannot legally keep their winnings.</summary>

that he can play, while it nonetheless remains with the co-player; for this only proves that if, having lost it, he plays further, he will be bound to restore what he had won: just as he who plays with him is bound to restore what was further won from him. At this point, observe that the more such a son under paternal authority <note>original: "filiusfamilias"; a son who is not legally independent from his father's control.</note> has legitimately won from his <term>profectitious goods</term> <note>original: "bonis profectitiis"; property derived from the father's estate, as opposed to "adventitious" property from other sources.</note> in one continuous game, the more he is able to alienate in that same game, and even in others. Since he becomes more capable of losing at play from those things he has won without prejudice to his father's property—not only in the continuation of the same game (as all agree, since nothing is considered simply won before the entire game is finished), but even in a game he might start anew later, whether with the same co-player or someone else. This is because everything he legitimately acquires through play increases his means, so that he can spend those winnings on his own stakes. This is true unless it were a huge sum which, being acquired by the father's money, he could not gamble away but would be bound to keep for the father; though even then, he could always play for more from that sum than from only the goods he received from his father. When, however, this son wins more from each of the co-players in a single throw than he himself could alienate in that throw, then he would be bound to restore the excess to the co-players. According to the <note>original: "Sotisoniam"; referring to the school of thought of the theologian Domingo de Soto.</note> opinion regarding the excess, the contract would be unequal and invalid.

<margin>Soto</margin> This must be observed concerning one who has won profectitious goods from a son under paternal authority which the son could not legally alienate: if that son had previously won just as much from him, or were to win it in the future, <term>compensation</term> <note>original: "compensatio"; a legal principle where two debts cancel each other out.</note> takes place. The one winning from him is not bound to restore anything except the excess, if perhaps he won more from the son out of those things the son could not alienate than the son won from him. Understand this, however, unless the son had already vainly consumed what he won, or someone else had legitimately won it from the son, and the son no longer had anything he could legitimately lose at play; for then compensation would not take place, because the first contract with that son was valid, and the second was invalid.

Likewise, even if the son had not legitimately won before, but were bound to restore to the winner what was won from him—if, when he later loses at play, he possessed none of those goods, nor their value (because he was in no way wealthier then on account of those goods which he had vainly consumed, but only possessed his father’s profectitious goods which he could not alienate at play), compensation would clearly not take place. The only exception is if it were presumed to be the father’s will, because the son remained obligated to restore what he had previously won.

The reason why compensation does not take place in this event, except by the presumed will of the father, is this: Because the goods which the son thus finally lost are the father’s and not the son’s; for which reason they are not obligated to the one from whom the son had previously unjustly won. Instead, they must be restored to the father; for which reason, against the father’s will, compensation cannot be made in them.

On account of these and similar things, confessors must take care to seriously advise penitents not to play with sons under paternal authority, unless they certainly understand that they are playing with those goods which they may lawfully expose to chance.

<column-break/>

### Gambling with a religious person, with a slave, or with married persons, and when it induces an obligation to restore.

# DISPUTATION 520.

## SUMMARY.

1 *Gambling with a religious person: whether one is bound to restore what is won from them, and when.*
2 *And what concerning a servant or slave. number 2.*
3 *And whether the same should be said of a wife, and also a husband. numbers 3 & 4.*
4 *A husband cannot play to the prejudice of his wife and family.*
5 *Whether one playing with a husband is bound to restore a portion of the winnings to the wife.*

---

CONCERNING a religious man or a nun, since they can alienate nothing without the permission of a <term>prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy or the head of a religious house.</note> (at least a presumed one), if anyone should win anything from them at play against the expressed or presumed will of the prelate, he is bound to restore it to the prelate, to the monastery, or to the religious person themselves. This is the case unless it is feared the person would spend it again vainly and against the prelate’s will, or unless they have already been removed from the administration of those goods with which they played; in that case, restitution must be made to the monastery and not to that religious person. By the same reasoning, if that religious person had won anything in that game, they are bound to restore it to the one from whom it was won. The reason is that the contract would have been null by the law itself, as is clear in itself and from what was said in Disputation 14: from a contract that is null by the law itself, neither of the contracting parties can gain. <note>original: "Navar. in Manic."; referring to Martín de Azpilcueta, known as Dr. Navarrus, likely in his "Manual for Confessors."</note> says: Just as one who is supported by a father at school or elsewhere outside his own home can spend from what the father grants for his support—at a rate of four or five gold coins per hundred—for his own amusement; so a religious person, who is supported by the monastery in study or in another place where he conducts some business, can spend a similar amount on his own honest amusement, even by gambling. However, this is not to be understood or affirmed of prohibited gambling, or gambling unbecoming of a religious person; for that would not be "honest amusement" in comparison to such a religious person, and because a prelate would be senseless and acting wrongly if he expressly or tacitly granted such a faculty to his subordinate. Therefore, a person who wins money in a prohibited or unbecoming game from a religious person would not be safe in conscience or immune from the burden of restoration. When, however, a religious person lives outside the monastery, either by license of the Supreme Pontiff or having been expelled from the order, and has the use and administration of goods independently of his monastery and prelate (according to what was said in Disputation 141), then, although he would be doing wrong by playing a prohibited or unbecoming game, the one who wins something from those goods would not be liable for restitution.

As far as <term>slaves</term> <note>original: "mancipia"; refers to servants or enslaved persons with limited legal rights to property.</note> are concerned, if they have anything from the category of those goods which they are permitted to have...

as if it were their own: as we mentioned in Disputation 38 joined with Disputation 26, or if their masters permit them to have certain things over which they allow them to dispose freely. Because when masters know, or presume, that their <term>slaves</term> <note>original: "mancipia"; referring to individuals in a state of legal servitude.</note> have acquired these things by their own hard work or by the gift of another, and they do not seize them but leave them to the slaves, then whoever wins such goods from them in a game is not bound to restore them. By the same reasoning, slaves are not bound to restore what they might win from others in a game from such goods; rather, these winnings go toward increasing their <term>peculium</term> <note>original: "peculij"; a small amount of property or money that a master allowed a slave to manage as their own.</note>, which they may freely dispose of. If, however, slaves gamble with things they have taken by theft from their own masters or others, or which they acquire for their masters but the masters retain them against their will—or certainly in cases where it is not clear that it is the masters' will for the slaves to keep them—then those who win these things from them are bound to restore them to the masters or to the others from whom the slaves stole them. The reason is truly that they are winning property belonging to another. In a case of doubt, anyone who wins something from slaves is bound to inquire whether the slaves were able to alienate <note>To "alienate" in a legal sense means to transfer the ownership of property to another.</note> those goods. In the same way, if such slaves win anything from others through gambling with such goods, they are bound to restore it to them. Understand this to mean that if it is discovered from elsewhere that those were the slaves' own goods, they would not be required to indemnify those who had won from them by paying them an equal amount or restoring it to them from another source.

<margin>3</margin>
It remains for us to speak of spouses. And regarding what pertains to wives, it must be said first: they can † gamble as much as their husbands have expressly or tacitly permitted them; because it is clearly established that the husbands are not unwilling. Furthermore, from what was said in Disputation 274, it is clear that they can gamble even if their husbands are unwilling, and spend on their own honest amusements as much as women of average status and condition are accustomed to gamble and spend; provided there are no particular reasons why the husband should forbid it. The reason for this assertion, as we said in that place, is: that on account of the dowry and the <term>partnership of goods</term> <note>original: "societatem bonorum"; the legal community of property between husband and wife.</note> contracted between them, they are owed a fit and competent maintenance. This surely includes all expenses for all those things which wives of the same condition and status are accustomed to spend, including competent and honest amusement. Therefore, if others win anything from them within these limits, or if the wives themselves win while playing with those who can alienate property, it is not subject to restitution. If, however, they gamble anything beyond all these limits, the contract is null, as is clear from Disputation 343; and therefore, what they have lost must be restored to their husbands, just as they themselves are bound to restore anything they may have won by gambling outside those boundaries.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding what pertains to husbands. † First, they can gamble what others of their status, wealth, and condition commonly gamble, and which is by no means unbecoming to their status. Indeed, even if they exceed this, provided the excess is not particularly notable, as long as no notable detriment to their own goods or those of the family is found to result from the gambling, not only do the others acquire ownership of what was won (and are bound to no restitution), but the husbands themselves are not bound to restore anything to their wives, even if they lose a notable quantity. For, beyond their own amusement, they were able to test that contract—and a kind of business dealing, as it were—to the disadvantage and

<column-break/>

advantage of the partnership between the husband and the wife; for they themselves are the administrators of the goods of that partnership. When, however, it is already known by experience from the husband’s gambling that a notable detriment to the wife follows—because by gambling he consumes many goods to her detriment, and because on account of gambling he abandons the business and profits by which the goods ought to be preserved or even increased—then in <term>Portugal</term> <note>original: "Lusitania"; Molina frequently references Portuguese law as he taught at the University of Coimbra.</note> that husband would be bound to restore it to his wife. This applies not only when the marriage was celebrated with a contract of <term>half-share of goods</term> <note>original: "medietatis bonorum"; a community property arrangement where assets are split 50/50.</note>, but also when it was celebrated with a contract of <term>earnest money and dowry</term> <note>original: "arrharum & dotis"</note>. This is the case because either the capital of the wife (who contracted under a half-share of goods) would be diminished, or the goods already acquired would be notably diminished, regardless of how the marriage was contracted in Portugal, as will be easily understood from Disputation 422. For a man, as was said there, is bound to his wife (and similarly a wife to her husband) if he spends or loses anything through a crime, or a notable fault, or negligence on his part that is greater than "slight," or through undue and disordered administration. It is clear that in the event we are speaking of, a fault greater than a "slight" one, and a very undue and disordered administration of goods, is involved. Furthermore, in this event, the man is not bound to restore to the wife the entire detriment that would have actually come to the wife on account of his blameworthy gambling, but rather a certain part of it, according to the judgment of a prudent person, having considered all the concurrent circumstances. The reason that leads me to assert this is as follows: because if the man had won by that gambling, as could have happened, half of the profit would belong to the wife (nothing hindering the fact that the man sinned by gambling in that way), and it would have been used for the wife's benefit. Thus it happens that equity does not allow that, since half of the profit would have come to the wife from that contract, the entire loss of the wife should belong to the husband. Rather, only a part, as much as the risk is estimated, joined with that hope of profit to which he unjustly subjected her against her will—and given the husband's prior experience that gambling in that way would bring notable detriment to the goods of the wife and the partnership. Therefore, if the total detriment that comes to the common goods after that experience, through the fault and gambling of the husband, is estimated at two hundred gold coins—and consequently one hundred are considered the wife's loss and one hundred the husband's loss—sometimes it will be enough if the husband restores forty or thirty to the wife for that reason, or more or less, as the concurrent circumstances shall be. However, such restitutions are rarely or never made: either because husbands and others do not attend to these matters, or because wives, although they grieve over such a loss of goods, easily forgive their husbands for it and do not demand restitution; especially if they have children in common from that marriage. Nevertheless, we are explaining here what the nature of the matter itself holds.

<margin>Decisive Doubt.</margin>
You ask whether he who has won in this way from a husband is bound to restore a part of the winnings to the wife. It must be said that if the husband, when he lost it, still had goods remaining pertaining to his own share from which he could satisfy the wife, then he who won from him is bound to no restitution to the wife. The reason is that he who played with the husband in that way celebrated a just contract...

if the marriage was celebrated, and the husband was the administrator of the assets, which he then lost through gambling; if the husband, in carrying out and exercising that contract, caused injury to his wife, he himself is bound to compensate her from his own assets, even if this results in a loss for the children common to both spouses. This is confirmed because when a husband has excessively donated something from the common assets without his wife's consent, the recipient is not bound to restore it to the wife, but the husband is bound to count it toward the portion that belongs to him, as is held in the <note>original: "Lusitan. ordin. tit. 6. §. vlt."</note> Portuguese Ordinances, title 6, final paragraph, and as was stated in Disputation 275. Therefore, with much greater reason, one who has gained from the husband through a burdensome gambling contract is not bound to restore it to the wife; rather, it is the husband who must repair the damage unjustly caused to her in that way.

However, when the husband is unable to pay the <term>dowry</term> <note>original: "dotem"; the property a woman brings to her husband at marriage.</note> or the wife's <term>paraphernalia</term> <note>original: "bona paraphernalia"; property belonging to a married woman that the law allows her to keep in her own right, separate from her dowry.</note> which were involved in the contract, and he celebrated the marriage either in Portugal or in Castile, then the wife would certainly have the right to take action to reclaim the assets alienated through gambling, if they still existed in the possession of the winners or others. This is because all the husband’s assets are <term>tacitly mortgaged</term> <note>original: "tacitè hypothecata"; a legal assumption that property is pledged as security for a debt even without a formal contract.</note> for the dowry and the wife's personal goods, as we showed in Disputations 438 and 441. However, when in Portugal the only damage to the wife from the husband's gambling would be in the <term>surplus profits</term> <note>original: "bonis superlucratis"; assets acquired by the spouses during the marriage beyond their initial capital.</note> or in half of her assets (if they had celebrated the marriage under a contract of shared halves), I believe that the person who won those assets from the husband through gambling is not bound to any restitution to the wife. Likewise, the husband and wife would not be bound to restore anything to him if the husband had won anything from him in that game. The reason is that the husband, by the disposition of the law, is appointed the administrator of those assets; and although the husband may have committed an injury against his wife by gambling in that way more than was proper—and would be bound to restore the damage thus caused to her in the manner explained—nevertheless, the things he administered and alienated through a burdensome contract are valid. If, however, in Portugal, the husband gambled away <term>immovable property</term> <note>Real estate, such as land or buildings.</note> without the express consent of the wife, then the wife could reclaim that property, according to what was said in Disputation 422.

When the husband, with the wife's free consent, gambles inordinately more than is right, he is bound to no restitution to the wife: since the contract would have been celebrated by common consent. The wife's true presumed consent would be sufficient for this, provided that no alienation of immovable property occurred in that manner. Likewise, if before the wife's death the husband had obtained from her a free remission of those things he had lost in gambling (which carried the burden of restitution), that remission would be valid, according to what was explained in Disputation 522.

I said above that when experience shows that grave harm to the wife follows from the husband's gambling, he is bound in Portugal to restore it to the wife, etc. Because in this Kingdom of Castile, if it only brings her detriment regarding surplus profits, he is bound to no restitution to her, as is copiously explained and shown in Disputations 275 and 437 from Law 5, Title 9, Book 5 of the <note>original: "nouæ collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compilation of Spanish laws.</note> New Collection. Other damages, however, which he might bring to the assets through gambling or any other reason beyond the gains, he is bound to take upon his own

<column-break/>

share, and consequently his own capital would be diminished, but not the wife’s capital, which he is always bound to preserve intact.

### Whether gambling prohibited by human law is sometimes a mortal sin. And concerning those who keep tables set out for gambling.

#### DISPUTATION 516.

-> SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENTS <-

<margin>1</margin> 1. When a person gambling in a game prohibited by human law falls into mortal sin.
<margin>2</margin> 2. When card games in the kingdoms of Castile and Portugal are prohibited under the penalty of mortal sin.
And what about those who manufacture or sell cards for gambling, and dice, number 2.
And whether the same should be said of those who keep houses and tables set out for gambling, number 5.
<margin>6</margin> 6. Whether the game of dice is simply forbidden to clerics and those in religious orders under the penalty of mortal sin, without any modification or declaration.

<margin>1</margin>
In this place, we are only explaining how much fault there is in a game prohibited by human law precisely for the reason that it is prohibited by human law, and consequently in which disobedience and transgression of human law occur. From other headings and circumstances, anyone will easily understand from what has been said, and from the quality of the circumstances, when a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>original: "culpa lethalis"; a grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> occurs or not. For instance, if because of gambling, the Holy Mass is skipped on a feast day, or if perjuries, blasphemies, or deadly brawls are mixed into it, or if frauds or other injustices occur in it, from which an obligation arises to restore a value sufficient to constitute a mortal sin.

<margin>2</margin>
In the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, card games are not to be considered prohibited under the penalty of mortal sin, as is clear from the penalties established in the laws cited in Disputation 512 for those gambling in those Kingdoms. Indeed, even if today some gamble more than two silver <term>reales</term> <note>A Spanish silver coin.</note> (which is permitted for games in Castile), provided they do not exceed an amount that is fitting for them to gamble for the sake of recreation according to their social standing, they do not sin even venially, both in Castile and in Portugal. This is because those laws have not been received into use with such rigor; indeed, it is customary for kings and public officials—who know of it and gamble themselves—to gamble for far more. Nor does it matter that people are rarely fined for card games; for that seems to serve to restrain the practice of gambling from spreading too much. And, if it is permissible to say so, it serves so that public officials have a source from which to extract fines, which they usually take not from the powerful who gamble publicly, but from the "little people" caught just once. Nevertheless, God-fearing judges, as I have heard is the case in Portugal, when those caught are not among the number of those excessively devoted to gambling, but are those who occasionally gamble moderately for recreation, usually let them go unpunished. For equity does not allow them to pay a penalty for something they do without any sin, and which is therefore permitted to others everywhere, because such laws are not [enforced] with that rigor...

<header>Second Tractate, Disputation 522.</header>

undertaken. In these cases, however, I do not include students (especially those of the University of Évora) who play games: since the statutes prohibiting them from playing are in <note>original: "in viridi sunt obseruantia"; literally 'in green observance', meaning currently and strictly enforced</note> force, and whenever they are caught playing, they pay penalties; furthermore, it is less fitting for them to play than for other laypeople. Add to this that almost all of them are <term>sons of families</term> <note>original: "filios familias"; individuals under the legal authority of the head of their household</note> and aspire to holy orders, for whom it is therefore beneficial to be restrained from gambling.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding those who manufacture or sell playing cards, or those who bring them into Portugal from other kingdoms: considering the punishment of flogging and other penalties established for those crimes in Portugal, those crimes should be condemned as mortal sins in that kingdom if those laws were executed with such rigor. However, since men in that kingdom are permitted to play with cards, and cards are sold with impunity, and it has never been heard that the punishment of flogging was inflicted for these crimes, you would not today condemn those crimes as mortal sins. Indeed, perhaps they are not even venial sins, since gambling, those instruments, and the business of selling them are permitted. It is much less to be condemned as a fault to manufacture or sell playing cards in Castile, where we read of no prohibition or established penalty regarding that matter.

<margin>4</margin>
In this Kingdom of Castile, especially after Law 15, Title 16, Book 8 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouę collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación*, a 16th-century compilation of Spanish laws</note>, I would not dare to excuse from mortal sin those who manufacture or sell—either by themselves or through an intermediary—dice, or those who play with dice; since the punishment of flogging and of rowing for five years in the galleys, in addition to other penalties, are established for those crimes. Unless it is understood that those penalties are placed only <note>original: "ad terrorem"; as a deterrent to inspire fear</note> and are not carried out, even if some are caught having fallen into those crimes. I say the same regarding those playing dice in Portugal (except for backgammon) if the punishment of flogging established for that crime in the kingdom is carried out, and is not merely placed as a deterrent.

<margin>5</margin>
Regarding those who have tables set out for gambling, or who receive men to gamble in their houses: since in Portugal the punishment of flogging is established for them if they receive payment for that reason or sell them food or drink, they ought to be condemned for a mortal sin, considering the severity of the penalty. However, because that penalty is not seen to be inflicted today, I certainly would not condemn that crime as a mortal sin on that ground. In Castile, however, I do not see a penalty so severe imposed that I would dare to condemn that crime as a mortal sin based on the penalty alone. From the quality of the game and the players, however, one must judge whether they are to be condemned for mortal sin or not. For if they admit men to play dice in Castile, I would not dare to excuse them from mortal sin, especially if they provide the dice for them. This is both because that game does not seem to be excusable from mortal sin in Castile, and also because having and supplying dice for gambling seems to be a mortal sin in that kingdom. Finally, because the penalty of confiscation of the house in which dice are played is not light, but severe, and suggests a mortal sin. Furthermore, since those might be admitted to the game who cannot alienate what they lose, or who might practice the game with mortal sin in various other ways, the hosts would not be excused from mortal sin, and therefore ought not to be absolved unless they effectively

<column-break/>

abstained from setting out tables for gambling and from receiving men for the game.

<margin>6</margin>
As for clerics, members of religious orders, and prelates: the game of dice is forbidden to them under penalty of mortal sin, as is clear from the canon laws cited at the end of Disputation 512, which decree for clerics who are public gamblers the penalty of removal from a benefice they hope to obtain, deprivation of those already held, and suspension if, having been warned, they do not cease from that vice. Penalties of this kind are not imposed except for mortal sin. Likewise, the Council of Trent (Session 22, Chapter 1 on Reformation) renewed all those penalties and canons. And so Navarrus <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a highly influential canonist</note> feels, along with others whom he cites in the *Manual*, Chapter 19, Number 9. However, since those penalties are imposed only on public gamblers—who do not play once or rarely, but are devoted to the game—I do not judge those clerics to be condemned for mortal sin who, without scandalizing others and for the sake of recreation, play cards for modest amounts that do not misbecome their condition and status, considering their income and assets. Nor does Navarrus (in the cited number 9) seem to condemn these for mortal sin; he only condemns those who play for a notable quantity. Nevertheless, such playing of cards, and much more so of dice, is very unseemly for them and is altogether to be discouraged: especially since many speak more strictly on this matter, and I would speak so too if the customs of the clergy had not deflected so far from that ancient state of the primitive Church. For then, such gambling was more unseemly for them and generated greater scandal for the laity than it generates today; for today people do not expect from them such a strict life, dedicated to God, as was customary and expected in the past. Fourthly, card playing is far more unseemly for religious <note>members of monastic or mendicant orders</note> and more scandalous to others than for secular clerics; and it is more unseemly for them and scandalous to others the more they profess a strict life, the more regular discipline flourishes in that order, and the higher the opinion the people have of their observance and sanctity. Similarly, I would say it is far more unseemly and a greater sin for secular clerics to play cards or other similar games in regions where it is less customary and their customs are less corrupt, than where they are more corrupt and the practice is more customary.

<page-num>702</page-num>
<header>Ludovico Molina on Contracts</header>

<margin>1</margin>
A **deposit** <note>original: "depositum"</note> is that which is given to someone for safekeeping; or (which amounts to the same thing) it is a contract by which something is handed over to someone to be guarded, and consequently, so that he may restore it whole. According to the same author, Ulpian, in the same place, the word is derived from "placing" <note>original: "pono"</note> and "from" <note>original: "de"</note>, which is a preposition that increases the force of the word, as if placed in the hands of another. However, it is not enough for someone to be considered to have made a deposit with another if he merely puts something in that person's house, unless the other person undertakes the guardianship of it, or it is declared to him: "I hand this thing over to you for safekeeping," or "keep this," as is gathered from the law <note>original: "l. si ego §. ult. ff. de iur. dot."</note> and noted by others including Gregorio Lopez and Antonio Gomez. Understand this, unless the person has a duty by virtue of his office to guard it, such as **stable-keepers**, **sailors**, and the like; for then it will be sufficient that it is placed in his house while he sees it or knows of it. Furthermore, the person with whom something is deposited is called the **depositary** <note>original: "depositarius"</note>.

A deposit is regularly made of movable things; for immovable things are not usually deposited, except when there is a controversy regarding a certain matter; then it is deposited with a **sequester** <note>a neutral third party or stakeholder</note> until it is established or decreed to whom it belongs.

<margin>2</margin>
Thus, a deposition with a sequester is a true and proper deposit, as it is a specific type of deposit in general. Consequently, an **action of deposit** <note>original: "actio depositi"; a legal claim to recover the item</note> is granted against the sequester. Although some have wished for an "action on the prescribed words" <note>original: "actionem præscriptis verbis"</note> to apply, the law states that a sequester is one with whom several people, by common consent, deposit the same thing about which there is a controversy as to whom it belongs. He is so named, as Modestinus says, as if he "follows" <note>original: "sequatur"</note> the litigants, to give the deposit to the one who wins; or, as Gellius says, as if the litigants "follow the faith" <note>original: "fidem illius sequantur"</note> of the man. Nonetheless, the term has a wider scope: for sometimes it is done by the office of a judge when the parties do not agree; and sometimes it occurs for other reasons, such as when someone’s goods are to be confiscated for a crime <note>original: "delictum"</note>, or he loses them for another reason. Meanwhile, until the sentence is passed adjudging them to the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note> or another, they are usually **sequestrated**—that is, taken out of his power and placed with a sequester who possesses them in the meantime. The form for how a sequestration ought to be done today when a delinquent person cannot be captured, and the crime is such that his goods ought to be sequestrated, is prescribed in the **New Collection** <note>original: "nouæ collegtionis"; referring to the Nueva Recopilación of Spanish law</note>. Today, legal experts call a deposition with a sequester "the sequestration of a sequester" <note>original: "sequestrum, sequestri"</note>; and it is in that sense we have used the term in the title of this disputation.

Rightly, however, in the Code regarding the prohibition of the sequestration of money <note>original: "l. C. de prohib. sequestr. pecun."</note>

<column-break/>

it is decreed that because someone contends that something is owed from a contract or another reason, a sequestration of that thing ought not to be made. Instead, the person contending that it is owed to him or belongs to him must first prove it; and after providing legitimate and sufficient proof, he should then petition for it to be handed over to him. In that event, there is no need for any sequestration to occur. However, when neither of the contenders is in possession of the thing, and each contends it belongs to him, or one of them has entered into possession of it unduly, then sequestration has a place.

<margin>3</margin>
In the following events, however, sequestration is granted even when it otherwise ought not to be. **First**, if someone contends for a movable thing, and the one who holds it is suspected of fleeing with it <note>original: "suspectus est de fuga"</note>; then, unless he gives sufficient sureties, it is sequestrated. The same applies if there is a fear he will consume the thing and later be unable to pay; for unless he gives a competent surety, it is sequestrated. Regarding this entire first event, read the **Portuguese Ordinances** <note>original: "Lusitanæ ordinationes"</note>, which dispose of these matters at length in accordance with what we have said. **Second**, if a husband wastes the dowry of his wife. This seems to be understood when he wastes dotal lands out of hatred for his wife. **Third**, when someone possessing a thing has appealed a judgment concerning it; if he wastes the fruits of it before the final sentence, the thing is put into sequestration. **Fourth**, when an appeal is made against an execution; if the execution is suspended because of that appeal and the execution was to be made on a movable thing, it is sequestrated; if on an immovable thing, the fruits perceived thereafter are sequestrated until the final definition. **Fifth**, one who must offer certain goods for partition which he received from parents; unless he gives competent sureties, they are sequestrated until the partition is completed. **Sixth**, if one who was possessed as a slave proclaims his freedom <note>original: "proclamet ad libertatem"</note>, contending he is free; while the lawsuit is pending as to whether he is free or a slave, he must return to the master what was in his possession and which he confesses belongs to the master. Concerning those things which he denies belong to the master, and the master says belong to himself, the slave must provide competent surety; otherwise, they are sequestrated so that when the litigation over freedom is finished, it may be examined to which of them those things belong. Finally, sequestration of a thing which someone possesses does not regularly occur except in cases expressed by the law.

<margin>4</margin>
When it is agreed with a sequester in what place he should return the thing deposited with him, he is bound to return it in that place. When, however, it is agreed that he should return it in any one of several places under a disjunction, the option belongs to the sequester as to which of those places...

## How many types of deposits exist. And whether, in a deposit that has the nature of a loan, there is room for the "exception of non-counted money." And to whom the ownership and possession of the deposited item belongs. A certain notable outcome is decided.

### DISPUTATION 523.

### SUMMARY.

1 How many types of deposits exist.
2 When a deposit transitions into a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"; a loan of fungible goods like money or grain where the same kind is returned, not the specific item</note>.
3 When a deposit transitions into a loan, whether the "exception of non-counted money" <term>exceptio non numeratæ pecuniæ: a legal defense where a debtor claims they never actually received the funds they are being sued for</term> applies within a two-year period.
4 To whom the ownership of the deposit belongs when the deposit transitions into a loan.
With declarations as in number 6.
And what applies in the case of a sequester, number 5.

1 One kind of deposit is that made under the pressing necessity of fire, collapse, shipwreck, riot, or other similar events, where things are deposited with another so they do not perish in the sudden emergency that is at hand; another kind is that which occurs when no such necessity is pressing. This is held in law 1, section 1 of the Digest on deposits and law 1, title 3, part 5. Likewise, one kind of deposit is a sequestration, as explained in the preceding disputation; another is not a sequestration but a **simple deposit**. Furthermore, one kind of deposit is entirely and properly so-called; another is not, but instead transitions into a different contract or has one mixed with it. This occurs in two ways. First, because a price or some benefit is received for the deposit or the guarding of the item; in this case, it transitions into a contract of **hiring and leasing** <note>original: "locati et conducti"</note>, or mixes with it in some way, as held in the Institutes "on hiring," and the Digest on mandates, and law 2, title 3, part 5. For example, when clothes are given to a tailor to be mended or to a **fuller** <note>a person who cleans and thickens cloth</note> to be washed. Likewise, things handed over to a **stable-keeper** or a sailor for safekeeping: for although a specific price is not paid for that reason, a price is nonetheless paid for lodging and transportation, which have

<column-break/>

an annexed duty of guarding those things brought into the stable or the ship. Therefore, these people are held more strictly to the duty of guarding, and are liable for even minor negligence, compared to a mere depositary, as will be discussed in the following sections.

2 In the second way, this occurs when something is handed over for safekeeping such that the exact same item does not necessarily have to be returned, but rather something of the same type, and of the same quantity and quality. And a deposit of this kind transitions into the nature of a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, and the ownership of the deposited thing does not remain with the depositor (as it does in the other types of deposits mentioned), but passes to the depositary. Consequently, if it perishes before it is returned, the loss falls on the depositary and not the depositor. For example, if someone deposits money, wheat, or something else that consists of weight, number, or measure with someone so that an equal amount of equal quality is restored when requested, that is not so much a deposit as it is a loan, as is clear from the law "Lucius" and the law "regarding betrothals" in the Digest under the title "On Hiring." However, it is not a sufficient guess to assume the contract is a loan rather than a deposit—and thus that ownership passes to the receiver—simply because the money, wheat, or similar item is handed over by count, measure, or weight (which law 2, title 3, part 5 seems to suggest). For often something is handed over by count, measure, or weight so that the depositary understands how much he is receiving into his care and must return, even though it is handed over solely for safekeeping, with no power of use or consumption granted. In such a case, ownership remains with the depositor, and the loss of the item falls on him and not the depositary, unless it perishes through the depositary's fault. This is sufficiently indicated by the two laws cited. Therefore, it must be judged from the concurrent circumstances, the person to whom it is given, and the manner in which it is given. However, when something consisting of number, weight, or measure is handed over to someone for safekeeping while closed or sealed, then it is a **pure deposit**, as is clear in itself and gathered from the law "if money" and the law "a small bag" in the Digest on deposits, and from other laws. When someone deposits things in such a way that ownership remains with them, but with the power for the depositary to consume or sell what he wishes from them—provided that he later returns an equal amount—then the contract only begins to transition into a loan when the depositary consumes or sells something. Specifically, it transitions into a loan regarding those things he consumes or sells, but not regarding the remainder, the ownership of which remains with the depositor. Thus says Navarro in his Manual, chapter 17, at the end of number 180, and it is held in the section "although this condition" and the following law of the Digest "if a certain thing is sought."

3 <margin>Question.</margin> There is a doubt: when a deposit transitions into a loan, does the "exception of non-counted money" (about which much was said in Disputation 502) apply within a two-year period? Bartolus and Portius—cited by Emmanuel Acosta in his commentary on the law "if from a caution" in the Code on non-counted money, under exception 2, number 4—affirm that it does apply. However, the contrary opinion held by Baldus is more common, which the same Emmanuel Acosta embraces in that same place. <margin>Decision.</margin> The reason is that, although a deposit of this kind transitions into a loan because the ownership of the thing

<page-num>704</page-num>
<header>Luis de Molina: On Contracts</header>

the deposit belongs to the depositary, and they may freely use and consume that thing; whatever the reason for its loss, the loss is theirs and not the depositor's. Nonetheless, the transaction retains certain characteristics of a deposit. For this reason, it should be called a "mixed contract" of deposit and loan <note>original: "mutuo"</note>, rather than a mere loan or a mere deposit. Indeed, a pure loan is made for the benefit of the borrower alone; however, this kind of deposit is made for the utility and good of the depositor, to whom the depositary provides a service—even if, by chance, it also benefits the depositary, who can use and trade with the thing while the deposit lasts. Furthermore, in a loan, as stated at the end of Disputation 299, the lender cannot immediately demand back what was given if no time limit was set; under the Law of Castile <note>Molina often references Spanish regional law</note>, if no urgent reason arises, they must wait at least ten days, and under Common Law, whatever time a prudent judge deems fit. But in this kind of deposit, the person who deposited the money is not required to wait at any time; they can demand it back immediately, and payment cannot be delayed, just as other deposited things cannot be delayed, as we shall see. Likewise, "compensation" <note>the legal practice of offsetting a debt with a counter-claim</note> has a place in loans, but in this kind of deposit, as in all other deposits, compensation is not permitted.

<margin>4</margin>
Therefore, because this kind of deposit is not a pure loan but retains much of the nature of a deposit, the **exception of non-counted money** <note>original: "exceptio non numeratæ pecuniæ" - a legal defense where a person claims they signed a contract for money they never actually received</note> only applies to a pure loan. It is granted there because it is the borrower who seeks the loan, and in their eagerness to obtain it and relieve their necessity, they often confess to having received money they haven't actually gotten yet but hope to receive. However, in the deposit we are discussing, it is the depositor who offers the deposit for their own convenience; thus, the reason that exception was granted for pure loans does not apply here. Consequently, a depositary who receives something on the condition that they return an equal amount of the same quality cannot use the "exception of non-counted money" against the depositor. To this is added what appears to be an express text in the Code <note>original: "C. de nō num. pec."</note>, where the exception of non-counted money is openly denied in the case of a deposit of a specific sum of money. This concludes the second point proposed in the title.

<margin>4</margin>
As for the final point: in a deposit that has the force of a loan, the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> and possession of the deposited thing pass to the depositary, as is clear from what has been said. In other types of deposits, ownership remains with the depositor, if it was theirs before. The same must be said of possession, even "natural" possession; for the depositor possesses naturally through the depositary, and "civilly" by themselves <note>Natural possession is physical control; civil possession is the legal right/intent to hold something as one's own</note>, if they were the one who held it both ways before.

<margin>5</margin>
An exception occurs in **sequestration** <note>holding property during a legal dispute</note>: for then both civil and natural possession pass to the sequestered party, and the person from whose power the thing is taken and placed in sequestration ceases to possess it, if they possessed it before. Both points are held in the law "It is permitted" <note>original: "l. licet"</note> in the Digest on deposits.

<column-break/>

<margin>Law [unclear] Law [unclear]</margin>
This, however, is to be understood as occurring when the sequestration is done so that the sequester is the one who possesses it while it is decided to whom the thing should be awarded, as in the law "Interest" <note>original: "l. interesse"</note> in the Digest on acquiring possession. This is always how it is understood when nothing else is specified, as the gloss affirms there. In such a case, the **prescription** <note>the process of gaining ownership through long-term possession, like a statute of limitations</note> is interrupted because possession has ceased. But when a thing is placed in sequestration solely for the sake of custody—perhaps because the possessor was suspected of fleeing, or so they would not consume the thing and later have nothing to pay with—and it is not otherwise taken out of their power, then possession does not pass to the sequester. Instead, it remains with the current possessor, who possesses "civilly" through themselves and "naturally" through the sequester. In this case, the sequester is merely a "holder" <note>original: "tentoris"</note>. Thus, the fact that the thing is sequestered does not interrupt the prescription; it continues, provided that the possessor is the one who ultimately wins the case.

<margin>6</margin>
On the occasion of what has been said regarding the ownership of deposited goods, I will add a decision on an event about which I was consulted in **Lisbon** <note>original: "Olyssipone"</note>. On a certain ship, many crates of **sugar** <note>original: "saccari" — the Portuguese call them *caxones*</note> were being transported from overseas to Lisbon. When the ship arrived at an island in Portugal, a certain man who was transporting several crates of his own, and many others entrusted to him, feared pirates. He wanted to sell some of his own crates on that island and send the proceeds to Lisbon by letter, so that if the ship were captured by pirates, he would not lose everything. However, his own crates were stored deep in the hold, with many crates belonging to others stacked on top of them. They could not be extracted without great labor and trouble. Certain that the owners of the other crates would not take it badly—but would rather be grateful, since all the crates were of the same weight, quality, and value of sugar—he took an equal number of crates marked with other people's signs. His intention was that, if the ship arrived safely in Lisbon, he would return an equal number of his own crates to the owners of the others. In this, he did them no wrong and caused them no loss; their crates were in no more danger than his—in fact, less, because his were at the bottom of the hold. It happened that the ship was captured. Some people wanted to force this merchant to pay the price of the crates he had sold to their original owners. They argued that the ownership of the crates he sold had remained with the original owners, while his own crates were lost to him because they were still in the hands of the pirates. Nonetheless, I responded that he was not bound to make any restitution to them, but had acquired that money for himself. The reason is that the sale of those crates belonging to others, in place of his own, was done as a "permutation" <note>an exchange or swap</note> of those crates for an equal number of his own, based on the **presumed will of the owners**, who truly would not have been unwilling if they had been asked. Therefore, the sale was valid, and the ownership of the crates he sold passed to the buyers; he acquired the money for himself and not for the original owners.

<summary>Molina discusses "irregular" deposits that function like loans, explaining that ownership transfers to the recipient. He also provides a legal ruling on a merchant in Lisbon who swapped identical sugar crates to avoid total loss from piracy, concluding the swap was valid based on presumed consent.</summary>

<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 525.</header>

the price of those slaves. He would not have sold them himself so that the price would belong to others in the event that the ship perished; nor, if the ship had arrived safely in Lisbon <note>original: "Olyssiponem"</note>, would the owners of the sold captives have been content with only the price obtained for them on that island. Therefore, since he did not conduct the business of those captive owners through that exchange and sale, but rather his own—and since the owners were not at all unwilling regarding that exchange when it was made, but rather consented by a very true presumption—it follows as a certainty that the loss of those captives from that ship would fall upon them and not upon him, and that he, not they, would acquire that price. 

However, if pirates had plundered part of the ship's merchandise (as sometimes happens), or if part of the merchandise were thrown into the sea by the force of a storm, and those goods he had sold would have been among the lost while all his own goods in the depths of the ship remained safe, he would similarly be bound to restore an equal amount from his own goods to the owners of those he sold. But if only half of his own goods remained safe, then he would be bound to restore to them half of what he sold, proportionally. For by the very fact that he made that exchange without designating any specific items from his own stock in place of those he took, a corresponding amount from his own goods—held "in a confused state" or "as an undivided whole" <note>original: "pro indiviso"</note>, as the legal experts <note>original: "iurisperiti"</note> rightly call it—belonged to them. Consequently, the risk of all those goods belonged proportionally to those others and to himself.

## The use of a deposited thing, and the profit from it: to whom do they belong?

### DISPUTATION 524.

### SUMMARY

1 **The use and profit of a deposited thing belong to the depositary when the deposit transforms into a loan; otherwise they do not. Indeed, a depositary who uses the thing is held liable for an action of theft. However, this is clarified in number 2.**

<margin>1</margin> When a deposit transforms into a loan <note>original: "mutuum," a loan of fungible goods like money or grain where ownership transfers</note>, it is clear from what was said in the preceding disputation that the depositary may use the deposited thing; if he makes any profit by trading with it or by any other means, it belongs to him. In all other types of deposit, however, it is a grave wrong <note>original: "nefas"</note> for the depositary to use the deposited thing. In fact, if he uses it against the depositor's will, he is bound—not only in conscience but also in the external court—to restore the value of that use to the owner. Furthermore, the depositor is granted an "action of theft" <note>original: "actio furti"</note> against him, allowing the depositor to proceed against him as a thief, as established in the laws <note>Molina cites various Roman and Canon law sources here, including the Digest and the Institutes</note>. According to the fourth book of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusit. ord. tit. 52"</note>, he is ordered to be cast into chains so that he may pay for the use and any damage he caused by using the thing. If a complaint is duly filed against him, he may undergo the penalty for "deceptive litigation" <note>original: "de burla è lizador"</note>. <margin>2</margin> It is added that if someone uses a deposited thing (and the same applies to things borrowed or given as a pledge) because he believed the owner would approve, he is not held liable for an 

<column-break/>

action of theft, even if he was mistaken. This elegant reason is given: a theft is not considered committed without the "intent to steal" <note>original: "animo furandi"</note>, or the intention of handling a thing against the owner's will. This is supported by the legal authorities Angelo, Silvester, Panormitanus, Gabriel, and Covarrubias. Covarrubias rightly adds that since such use against an owner's will is not as harmful to the state, nor does it possess the same inherent dishonesty as other thefts, this crime should be punished more mildly than other thefts, and the infamy of theft should not be inflicted for such an offense.

<margin>3</margin> It must be observed that when the deposited item is money, wheat, or something else consisting of weight, number, or measure, if the depositary is morally certain that he will restore the deposit in full when the depositor asks for it—by substituting an equal amount of money or equally good wheat—he does not usually sin, at least not mortally, nor is there a reason to admit an action of theft against him. For in this, he does no injury to the depositor; rather, it somewhat turns to the depositor's advantage and causes no detriment. This is because if the thing were to perish by chance or by a slight fault of the depositary, the loss would fall on the depositor, but by this use, the value is preserved for him. Whatever profit the depositary gains by using the deposited thing in this way belongs to him and not to the depositor, as taught by Cajetan and Soto. This is clear from what we said in Disputation 327, Conclusion 2. The reason is that the profit is the fruit of his own industry, and he trades at his own risk when consuming and distributing the deposited goods.

## Who can be a depositary? And concerning a deposit made to the Church.

### DISPUTATION 525.

### SUMMARY

1 **Anyone who possesses the use of reason can be a depositary, including a woman. And what of Portuguese and Castilian law? See number 5.**
2 **A ward <note>original: "pupillus," a minor under guardianship</note> is held by an action of deposit to the extent that they have been made wealthier by the deposited thing; indeed, they are liable for fraud if they are capable of it.**
3 **A cleric or a member of a religious order can be a depositary.**
4 **How the Church is held liable for a deposit made with a cleric or religious person.**

<margin>1</margin> All those who possess the judgment of reason can be depositaries. <margin>2</margin> Even a woman can be, as is established in law. If a ward is appointed as a depositary, an action is always granted to ensure they return the deposited thing as it exists. For the item is reclaimed as belonging to the depositor when found in the ward's possession. This is expressly held regarding borrowed things, even when borrowed by a person lacking reason <note>original: "furioso"</note>. The same reasoning applies to a deposited thing, whether with a ward (even an infant) or someone lacking reason, or in any other way...

By the same reasoning, even if the item is no longer in their possession, if they have been enriched by it, a legal action certainly applies for them to return as much as they were enriched. This is held in Law 3 at the beginning, joined with the end of Law 1 of the Digest, *commodati* <note>original: "ff. commodati"; this refers to laws regarding loans for use</note>, and Law 1, section "an in pupillum," of the Digest, *de deposito* <note>original: "ff. de pos."</note>.
