<margin>3</margin>
Not only can a † cleric be a depositary, as gathered from chapter 1 *de deposito*, but also a member of a religious order, as both are affirmed in Law 3, title 3, part 5 <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish law code</note>. However, a religious person acts wrongly if they undertake the duty of a depositary without the silent, express, or undoubtedly presumed consent of their superior. Nor is the monastery held liable for the deposit—even if the superior allows a religious person to be a depositary—except to the extent that the deposited item was converted to the monastery's use, or the monastery was enriched by it. In the same † <margin>4</margin> manner, the Church would also be held liable for a deposit placed with a cleric, to the extent it was converted to the Church’s benefit, as held in the title *de deposito*, Law 7, title 3, part 5, and other laws, and is clear in itself. For always, the person with whom the deposit is found is bound to return it to the depositor to the extent it is found with them, or at least in any part by which they were made wealthier. But since a depositary is only held liable for deceit <note>original: "dolo"</note> and gross negligence <note>original: "lata culpa"</note> when the deposit no longer exists or is returned in worse condition (as we shall see below), and since a monastery or superior is not held liable for the wrongdoing of their subordinate (as was said in Disputation 140), certainly the monastery will not be held liable for a deposit placed with its subordinate when it perished through that person's fault or was returned in worse condition. Nevertheless, the religious person will be bound in the forum of conscience to restore the loss following from their own fault and wrongdoing, if there is any way they can eventually pay, in the manner explained in Disputation 140. It will be the responsibility of the superior, as the competent judge of such a religious person, to punish his subordinate for such a wrongdoing.

Regarding a deposit made to the Church, the same should be said as was said regarding a loan made to the Church, as was copiously explained in Disputation 300. Except that the depositor, if the deposit does not exist in whole or in part, is not bound to prove it was converted to the Church's benefit, as a lender is bound to do. And according to what was said there regarding loans, I judge that those things held in Law 7, title 3, part 5 regarding a deposit made to the Church should be accepted and explained, regardless of what Gregorio López <note>A famous Spanish jurist and commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> explains there.

<margin>Portuguese Law 5</margin>
In Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 34, the penultimate section, all those who have any role in the administration of justice or

<column-break/>

government are forbidden—even if they are notaries <note>original: "tabelliones"</note> or other similar ministers—from receiving, either by themselves or through others, anything that is lawfully deposited, under penalty of losing their offices and paying double: half to the accuser and half to the King’s treasury, as well as two years of exile to locations in Africa. And in the final section, it is added: If another person who received that deposit gives it by loan or any other reason to any of the aforementioned ministers, they are nonetheless bound to return it to the rightful owner within nine days from the moment they are ordered to return it; otherwise, they are cast into chains and not permitted to be released until they pay it in full.

<margin>Castilian Law</margin>
In the Kingdom of Castile, in Law 13, title 10, book 2 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish royal laws</note>, deposits are prohibited which are made because someone of the Senate is recused; and generally, deposits made by order of the Senate are forbidden from being placed with the scribes of the chamber who are the notaries in that business or case.

In Law 2, title 21 of the same Book 2, notaries are prohibited from being depositaries of money or any other thing taken by theft in a criminal case.

In Law 22, title 1, book 3 of the same collection, the governor and the ministers whom they call *alcaldes mayores* <note>senior judges/magistrates</note> are commanded to appoint a "trustworthy and solvent" <note>original: "llano y abonado"</note> depositary for the deposits they order to be made, who must not be the scribe of the court—whom they call the *escriuano del aiuntamiento* <note>town council scribe</note>. Also, that he should have a book in which such deposits are written, which shall remain with the governor; and that at the beginning of each month, there shall be written in it what was received as a deposit in the preceding month and what was returned. And in the preceding Law 20, it is commanded that these same ministers apply no penalty to themselves, or to their subordinate ministers or household members.

In Law 23, title 2 of the same Book 3, it is commanded that in the high court (which they call the *audiencia*) of every jurisdiction, there be a book in which deposits and fines are written by the hand of each notary before the deposits and fines are made; and that the notaries be bound to report them to the depositary within three days after they are made. Otherwise, they themselves must pay them, plus six hundred maravedis <note>original: "marauedinos"; a Spanish currency</note> to the King’s treasury. Likewise, it is commanded that according to that book, the depositary shall give an account of all those deposits to the judges at the end of each year.

In Law 13, title 9 of the same book, judges are commanded to appoint a depositary in every single place—a trustworthy and solvent person—with whom those things they order to be deposited shall be placed, and that he not be the notary of that case.

The same is commanded in Law 28, title 25, book 4, under the penalty that a judge who orders a deposit to be made with the notary of the case shall pay ten thousand maravedis, and the notary who accepts such a deposit shall pay the same amount; the penalty is to be applied to the common goods of the people in the place where it was done.

In the single law of title 12, book 4 of the same collection, it is established that when any goods are sequestered or prohibited from being returned to someone, it is nonetheless lawful for the owners of those things to ensure they are harvested or repaired; and if, during the sequestration or prohibition, any fruits are to be gathered from there, the public ministers of that place shall cause them to be faithfully gathered at the expense of the same...

### When a deposit must be returned. Whether a set-off for another debt has a place in that situation. And how the depositor is preferred over other creditors of the depositary.

# DISPUTATION 526.
## SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> A deposit must be returned as soon as it is requested, even if the item was deposited until a certain time. This is explained and limited in number 5.
<margin>2</margin> The deposited item must be returned where it was deposited, or in the place where it is found, unless it was moved to another place through the deceit or fault of the depositary <note>The person holding the item for safekeeping</note>.
<margin>3</margin> One who denies the duty to restore a deposit is condemned to restore it along with its fruits and interest.
<margin>4</margin> Indeed, if the deposit was made out of necessity—such as during a fire or similar event—the person is condemned to pay double. (See number 4).
<margin>6</margin> A stakeholder <note>original: "sequestratarius"; a third party holding property during a dispute</note> ought not return the deposit before the lawsuit is finished and it is clear to whom the thing should be returned.
<margin>7</margin> A depositary cannot set off <note>original: "compensare"; a legal 'set-off' where one debt cancels out another</note> a debt owed to them against the deposited item, nor can they raise an objection or claim a right of retention.
<margin>8</margin> However, a "contrary action of deposit" is granted to them for expenses rightfully incurred on the deposited item. (See number 8).
<margin>9</margin> When a depositor is preferred over other creditors of the depositary.

<margin>1</margin> A deposit must be returned as soon as it is requested, unless circumstances arise by which it cannot or should not be returned, as we will explain below. This holds true—that it must be returned as soon as it is requested—even if the item was deposited until a specific time. Since a deposit, by its very nature, is made for the sake and convenience of the depositor, it is entirely up to them to revoke their will and demand it back even before that time has expired. This applies when it is a true deposit <note>original: "verum depositum"</note> and not a contract of hiring or leasing for some work, such as for washing or sewing clothes, and also when the deposit is not converted into a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, as was said in Disputation 523. This is held in the chapter *bona fides* regarding deposits, in these words: "surely it was permitted for the depositor to revoke the deposit at his will." See Law 1, section "it is however," and the penultimate section of the Digest, *on deposits* <note>original: "ff. depos."</note>, and Law 5, title 3, part 5.

<margin>2</margin> Moreover, the deposited item is to be returned where it was deposited, or in the place where it is found, provided it was not moved to another place through the deceit or fault of the depositary. See Law "If in Asia," section "deposit," of the Digest, *on deposits*, and affirmed by Gregorio López <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in the cited Law 5, gloss 2.

<margin>3</margin> But if anyone denies the duty to restore a deposited item and is condemned by the court, they will not only be forced to restore the thing with its fruits—according to Law 1, section "this action," of the Digest, *on deposits*, and Law 5 at the end of title 3, part 5—but also the interest,

<column-break/>

or the damages that followed, based on a just oath regarding the value in the lawsuit, as held in Law 3 of the Digest, *on the oath in a lawsuit*, Law 1, section "in a deposit," of the Digest, *on deposits*, and Law 8, title 3, part 5. Furthermore, the person is rendered infamous <note>original: "infamis"; a legal status involving the loss of certain civil rights and reputation</note>, provided they are condemned in their own name—that is, as the depositary. It is otherwise if they are condemned as a proxy, guardian, or curator of the depositary, or under some other name. See Law "on theft," section "if anyone in another's [name]," of the Digest, *on those marked with infamy*, Law "he who [denies] a deposit" in the Code, *on deposits*, and Law 8, title 3, part 5. And book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusit. ord."</note>, title 52, penultimate section, orders that such a person be thrown into chains until they return the item.

<margin>4</margin> But if the deposit was made under the pressure of necessity, such as due to fire, shipwreck, or another similar urgent danger (according to what was said in Disputation 523), a depositary who denies such a deposit will be forced to pay double its value, in addition to the aforementioned penalties. This is held in Law 1, sections 1 and 2, of the Digest, *on deposits*, the section "but indeed every action" in the Institutes, *on actions*, and Law 8, title 3, part 5. Indeed, Law 12, title 10, part 7, following the law "not without reason," states that if any depositary delays restoring a deposit until a final sentence is passed, they fall under a penalty: they must restore the valuation of the item to the depositor in addition to the item itself, as discussed extensively in Disputation 498.

<margin>5</margin> In the following events, the deposit is not to be returned to the one who deposited it. First, when they demand it during a fit of insanity—either their own or affecting others—such as if someone falls into a rage and demands back a deposited sword. Because damage to the one demanding it, or to others, could arise from this, it must not be returned. This is held by Augustine in the chapter "lest anyone," at the end of question 2, and Law 6, title 3, part 5. However, if someone who was already insane deposited a sword, it should still not be returned to them, because it could similarly lead to the harm of the one demanding it or others; Law 6 cited above does not intend the contrary, but only used the first situation as an example of what usually happens.

Second, when the goods of the depositor have been confiscated or assigned to the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>: for then the deposit is to be returned not to the one who deposited it, but to the treasury. Law *bona fides* at the beginning, of the Digest, *on deposits*, and the cited Law 6.

Third, when a thief and the true owner of the item demand it at the same time: then, out of hatred for the theft, it is not to be handed to the thief, but one must wait to see if the owner can prove the item is theirs and was stolen. If they prove this, it must be returned to them and not to the thief who deposited it. By the same reasoning, if a stolen item is deposited with its own true owner, the owner is not bound to return it. See the cited Laws *bona fides* and Law 6.

<margin>6</margin> However, when something is placed in sequestration <note>Held by a neutral third party during a dispute</note>, the stakeholder <note>original: "sequester"</note> ought not return the deposit before the lawsuit is finished and it is clear to whom the item should be returned, according to Law 5, title 3, part 5. Yet, if a thing was placed with a stakeholder by the common consent of two parties, and those two agree that it should be handed to one of them, it can be handed over, as recorded in a judgment by Gregorio López in the penultimate gloss there.

<margin>7</margin> In the case of a deposit, a "set-off" <note>original: "compensatio"</note> has no place—where a depositary wants to subtract from the deposited item what the depositor owes them from elsewhere. Nor does a claim for an exception or retention of the deposit have a place until another debt is paid to them. Indeed, even if two people are reciprocally depositaries for one another, one cannot hold the other's deposit until his own deposit is restored; rather, it must be restored immediately to the one who first demands it.

This is held in the law *si quis vel pecunias*, joined with the authentic text added there <note>referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 34, "On Deposits"</note>. However, this Portuguese law <note>original: "Lex tamen hæc Lusitana"</note>, if it is read carefully, seems to allow the offsetting of one deposit with another.

8 Regarding expenses incurred <margin>†</margin> for the deposited item, the depositary <note>the person looking after the item</note> is granted a "contrary action of deposit" against the depositor. A legal gloss <note>an interpretive commentary</note> on the law affirms that it is lawful to retain the deposited item for expenses incurred in its care, just as it is lawful to retain a borrowed item for its expenses. However, the last law of Title 3, Partida 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> establishes the opposite, and that is what must be observed in this Kingdom of Castile. Gregorio López <note>a famous Spanish jurist</note> asserts there that the common opinion among doctors is the opposite of that gloss. Villalobos, however, says that by common law one can retain the item for expenses, but it is otherwise under Royal law.

9 Regarding <margin>†</margin> the final point proposed in the title of the disputation, a distinction must be made. If the deposit is such that ownership of the item does not pass to the depositary, and the item still exists, the depositor is preferred over all the depositary's creditors across the board, as is well known; for then the depositor claims it as his own property. If, however, the deposit is such that it transforms into a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note>, and therefore the depositary acquires ownership of it—and such a deposit was made with a banker <note>original: "argentarium"</note>, that is, a public depositary established by the state for that purpose—then, if the depositor received no interest for that deposit, he enjoys a privilege. He is preferred over other creditors who do not have a tacit or express mortgage on the depositary’s goods, and thus he is preferred over the personal creditors of such a depositary. And although the law cited seems to extend this privilege to depositors with *any* depositary, the common legal opinion only grants it to those using public depositaries established by the state for the public good, to foster and increase the trade of merchants. The law seems to grant this privilege not only over non-privileged personal creditors, but even over privileged ones, so that such depositors are paid in the first place before others. Exception is made if something is owed to someone for burial expenses <note>original: "ratione sepulturæ"</note>, because they lent or spent money for the debtor’s burial or for someone the debtor was responsible for burying, such as a son or a servant. 

<column-break/>

For a debt of this kind is preferred over all other debts of the deceased across the board, even if they have tacit or express mortgages on the deceased's goods. All depositors are admitted equally to be paid from the assets of a public depositary, even if some were earlier in time and others later. When the exact same money deposited still exists with the depositary, or something was bought with that money, the person who deposited it is preferred in that specific instance, even if they were receiving interest from the deposit.

->For which degree of fault is a depositary held liable: even when the deposit is attached to another duty.<-

### DISPUTATION 527.

#### SUMMARY.

> 1 *When a depositary is held liable only for deceit and gross negligence.*
> *Also when for light negligence and accidental events. Number 2.*
> *Also when for light negligence but not the slightest negligence. Number 3.*
> 4 *Stable-keepers, innkeepers, and sailors; millers, tailors, and fullers, and others similar are held liable for light negligence, and sometimes even for the slightest negligence, but not for accidental events; and Number 5.*
> *It fails, however, in a case where he is held liable for nothing but deceit. Number 6.*
> *And regarding Portuguese law. Number 7.*
> 8 *When a depositary is held liable even for the slightest negligence, but not for accidental events.*

1 A depositary, when the deposit is made for the benefit of the depositor alone (as usually happens), if the deposited item perishes or is returned in worse condition, is <margin>†</margin> held liable only for deceit <note>original: "dolo"</note> and gross negligence <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>, which is equated to deceit; but not for light negligence <note>original: "leui"</note> or the slightest negligence <note>original: "leuissima"</note>, and much less for an accidental event <note>original: "casu fortuito"</note>. If, however, an agreement was made that he should be liable for lighter negligence, or even for accidents, the agreement must be upheld. If the depositary was in default <note>original: "in mora"</note> in returning the item, or by using the item against the depositor's will, or for another unauthorized reason, and the item perishes or is worsened (so that it would not have otherwise perished in the same way for the depositor), he is held liable even for accidental events. We have discussed these matters at length in Disputation 295 regarding loans.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 528.

...for the benefit of both parties, he is held liable for **light fault** <note>original: "levis culpa"; refers to ordinary negligence or the failure to use the care that a reasonable person would provide</note>, but not for the **lightest fault** <note>original: "levissima culpa"; refers to the slightest degree of negligence</note>. This is because the contract then transforms into one of hiring and leasing for the purpose of guarding that thing. Consequently, one who hires himself out to guard a thing would only be liable for light fault, as was stated in Disputation 494. All of this is established by Law 1, § "if clothing," and § "if anyone a servant" in the Digest on deposits <note>original: "ff. deposit."</note>, as well as the law on good faith in the same title, and Law 3, Title 3, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*</note>.

<margin>4</margin>
The same must be said when something is given in deposit to someone whose office includes the duty of guarding things, and who derives a benefit from that office. Such people are <margin>†</margin> stable-keepers, innkeepers, and shipmasters, regarding the things brought into the ship or the inn. Likewise are those who have care of a mill regarding the wheat brought to be ground, and those who have care of public buildings where wheat or other things are sold and they derive some benefit from it—unless there is a local custom where the guarding of things sold in such houses belongs to the sellers rather than the managers. Furthermore, such people include factors <note>commercial agents</note> and fullers <note>those who clean or thicken cloth</note>, regarding the items given to them to be finished or washed, and others like them. All of these are held liable for at least light fault for the same reason: namely, because the deposit also serves their own benefit by reason of the contract of hiring and leasing joined with it. Thus it is in the law on shipmasters in the Digest <note>original: "l. nautae, ff. nautae caupones"</note>. Indeed, these men are deemed to have received things into deposit by the very fact that the items are left in the ship or in their houses in the sight of them or their servants or staff assigned for that purpose, as was said in Disputation 522 following Antonio Gómez and others, and as gathered from the first law, final paragraph, and the second law in the Digest on shipmasters and innkeepers. I have said that those mentioned are held to at least

<margin>5</margin>
light fault, because <margin>†</margin> some of them, for whom it is specifically decreed in law, are held even for the **lightest fault**, though not for a **fortuitous event** <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an unavoidable accident or "Act of God"</note>. Certainly (as listed in the cited first law, § 1 and following), the shipmaster—that is, he who transports people, merchandise, or other things for a fee in a ship or any other vessel, even a small boat—and stable-keepers and innkeepers: all of these, by the very fact that something is placed in their inn or ship in the sight of them or their servants assigned for that purpose, are held liable for the lightest fault if the item perishes or is returned in worse condition, but not for a fortuitous event. This is held in Law 3, § "and this edict," joined with those preceding and following in the Digest on shipmasters and innkeepers, and in Law 26, Title 8, Part 5. Indeed, even if things to be transported are placed on the shore by the ship, the shipmaster is liable for the lightest fault if they perish or are damaged from the moment he takes charge of them, as held in the same Law 3 cited at the beginning. However, Angelus and Sylvester <note>famous 15th-century legal commentators</note>, both under the word "shipmaster," judge that although he is held liable for the lightest fault in the **exterior forum** <note>the public legal court</note>, in the **forum of conscience** <note>the moral or religious realm</note> he is only held for light fault. Because, they say, this was decreed out of hatred for such men, since they were known to commit frauds and thefts against guests and those they transported. Thus, they say that law is based on a **presumption** that a greater fault than the "lightest" occurred; and a law founded on a presumption has no place

<column-break/>

in the forum of conscience. Nevertheless, the contrary must be affirmed: namely, that this law has force in the forum of conscience and is not merely based on a presumption of greater fault. For although it says in the beginning of Law 1 of that title that this was decreed because it is usually necessary for men to trust these people and commit their things to their custody—and that this regulation should not be considered harsh because it is within these men's choice not to exercise this office, and because if this were not established, opportunity would be given to conspire with thieves against those they receive—nevertheless, that is the motivating or impulsive reason why this was decreed for the public good. It does not truly imply a presumption of greater fault. Furthermore, the contract of hiring and leasing is equitable in that one may be held to a lesser fault than would otherwise be the case, and one must stand by that contract, whether it is celebrated by the sole agreement of the parties or by the prescription of the law, as is clear from what was said above.

<margin>6</margin>
However, in the following <margin>†</margin> event, these men will not be held liable except for **fraud** <note>original: "dolo"; intentional harm or deceit</note>. For example, if when they received people into the inn or the ship, they told them beforehand that they received them on the condition that the guests themselves would take care of their own things; or if, while telling them to take care of their things, they handed over the key to the house or place in which they might keep their belongings. Thus it is in the final law, § 1, joined with the gloss there in the Digest on shipmasters and innkeepers, and the cited Law 26. The cited gloss adds that for these men to be held only for fraud, it is not enough if they say the guests should look after their own things *after* they have already received them; rather, it is necessary to say this at the beginning when they receive them. What has been said so far similarly applies if shipmasters, innkeepers, or stable-keepers receive people for free, as in the penultimate law at the beginning of the Digest on shipmasters and innkeepers. However, those who are not shipmasters, innkeepers, or stable-keepers by profession—even if they receive people for money—are not held for the lightest fault. This often happens when the **King's Court** <note>the traveling royal administration</note> comes to a place, and those accompanying the court are distributed among private houses for lodging. The cited laws do not speak of these people, and since those laws are "odious" <note>a legal term meaning they impose a burden or penalty</note>, they are not to be extended beyond those explicitly named in the law. So say Angelus and Sylvester.

In Portugal, in Book 5 of the Ordinances, Title 39, it is decreed that <margin>7</margin> stable-keepers and whoever <margin>†</margin> are accustomed to receiving money for lodging must lock all entrances through which the house can be exited with a key at night. They must not open for anyone until all guests are asked if they are missing anything; and they should allow no one to leave until they go and notify the local judge, and he performs his duty. If they do otherwise, the stable-keepers themselves, or those who received money for lodging, are held liable to pay for whatever the guests claim is missing.

<margin>8</margin>
When <margin>†</margin> someone offers himself as a depositary, the laws affirm that he is held even for the **lightest fault**, but not for a fortuitous event. This is held in Law 1, § "often," in the Digest on deposits, and Law 3, Title 3, Part 5. This is supported by the chapter on good faith regarding deposits. Argus, however, and Sylvester in the same place, question 2, understand this to mean when the depositor was looking for a very diligent person, and the depositary

<meta>This page continues the discussion of liability in contracts of deposit from the previous page, specifically focusing on the degrees of negligence (fault) for which a depositary is held responsible depending on who benefits from the arrangement. It then transitions into a new disputation regarding the legal definitions of pledges and mortgages.</meta>

...by offering himself, he excludes the most diligent person from the task. However, it must be said, as Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> states in the cited chapter *bona fides* at number 3, that this is to be understood when the deposit was made for the sake and benefit of the depositary alone, and not the depositor. In such an event, Law *si quis nec*, at the beginning of the Digest *si cert. pet.* <note>original: "ff. si cert. pet."; Digest 12.1.9</note>, holds that the depositary is liable even for **lightest fault** <note>original: "culpa levissima"; the highest standard of care, where even a minor oversight results in liability</note>. 

For example, when someone desired to buy estates and asked for a loan from another, which he would receive as a loan from the moment he bought those estates with that money and not before; if the lender, being about to go on a journey, leaves that money in deposit with him so that if he buys the estates, he would receive it as a loan from the moment he pays the price—it is defined by law that such a depositary is liable for the slightest fault if the money should perish while it is in deposit, because the deposit was made solely for his own benefit. If, however, the deposit was made for the benefit of both the one offering himself as depositary and the depositor, he will only be liable for **light fault** <note>original: "culpa levis"; ordinary negligence</note>. But if it was made for the benefit of the depositor alone, and the depositary offered himself out of friendship and to perform a service for the depositor, he shall be liable only for **gross fault** <note>original: "lata culpa"; extreme negligence</note>, even if he excludes someone else from the task. Navarrus agrees with this in his *Manual*, chapter 17, at the end of number 181, and more extensively in chapter 4, number 10.

<margin>9</margin>
If anyone deposits a servant <note>original: "servum"; in the Roman legal context this refers to an enslaved person</note>, knowing him to be a thief, he is held liable to the depositary for the theft, unless he warned him of the servant's vice. If, however, he was ignorant of it, he is only held either to make satisfaction for the theft or to hand over the servant for punishment <note>original: "reddere servum pro noxa"; a legal principle called noxal surrender where the owner avoids further liability by surrendering the offending party or animal</note>, whichever he prefers. This is defined in Law 10, Title 3, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas* of Castile</note>, following Law *si quis servum* in the Digest on the action of pledge <note>original: "ff. de pig. act."</note>, which seems to decide the same thing. And so it must be affirmed in the Kingdom of Castile, as Gregorio López says there, and Villalobos in his *Antinomia*, law 11, D. number 9. Nevertheless, the contrary must be said regarding common law, following the gloss on the cited law *si quis servum*: namely, that one who deposited a servant, being ignorant that he was a thief, is held to make satisfaction for the theft; because that is clearly decided in Law *si servus*, paragraph *quod vero*, in the Digest on thefts <note>original: "ff. de furtis"</note>, when the deposit was made solely for the benefit of the depositor; for equity does not allow the depositary to suffer a loss in place of a benefit.

The remaining matters that could be said in this place—and especially whether deposited things should be preferred over the depositary’s own things when all cannot be saved; and why a deposit perishes if it is sent to the depositor through a third party—were discussed at the end of Disputation 295 and the two following ones, where those same things were simultaneously examined regarding loans for use (*commodatum*).

# Pledge and Mortgage: what they are, and how they are manifold. And what is comprised in a universal mortgage.

### DISPUTATION DXXVIII.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Pledge: from where the word is derived.*
2 *Mortgage: in how many ways it may be taken.*
3 *Pledge and mortgage in a broad sense; and in a strict sense. number 5.*
4 *The contract of pledge and mortgage in a broad sense; and in a strict sense. number 5.*
6 *Whether a statute making mention of a pledge includes a mortgage taken in the strict sense.*

<column-break/>

7 *How manifold a mortgage is, both taken broadly and strictly.*
8 *What is a tacit mortgage, and what is an express one. number 9.*
10 *What is a conventional pledge; what is a praetorian one; and what is a judicial one.*
*And how they differ from each other and from a mortgage. number 11.*
12 *How manifold a conventional mortgage is; and what is an express universal mortgage.*
*What is an express particular mortgage. number 13.*
*What is a tacit universal mortgage. number 14.*
*What is a tacit particular mortgage. number 15.*

<margin>1</margin>
Pledge <note>original: "Pignus"</note> is a Latin word, derived from **fist** <note>original: "† pugno"</note>, as the jurist Gaius says in Law *plebs*, § *pignus* in the Digest on the significance of words: because, he says, the things given in pledge are delivered by hand. From which he adds, it can even be seen that what some people think is true: that a pledge is properly established for a movable thing. This is his view. Although, according to this etymology of the name, a pledge is most properly for movable things which are taken by hand, it nevertheless has a wider application. Not only is a **pledge in the broad sense** everything that is obligated for the security of a debt so that satisfaction may be made from it unless the debt is fulfilled; but even a **pledge in the strict sense** (as it is distinguished from a mortgage in the strict sense) is everything that is obligated in the aforementioned way so that it is delivered—whether it be a movable or immovable thing; although movable things are more frequently delivered as pledges in that manner than immovable ones.

<margin>2</margin>
Mortgage <note>original: "Hypotheca"</note> is indeed a **Greek name**, derived from *hypo*, which is "under," and *thesis*, which is "placing"—as if a thing placed under and obligated to a creditor for a debt. And indeed, a mortgage taken in the broad sense is exactly the same in Greek as a pledge taken in the broad sense is in Latin; and thus, in law, "pledge" often comprises mortgage in the strict sense, and "mortgage" comprises pledge in the strict sense. Hence Law *res*, the last paragraph in the Digest on pledges, states: *Between a pledge and a mortgage, only the sound of the name differs.* However, it is very often taken in a strict sense, as distinguished from a pledge in the strict sense: namely, for a thing subjected and obligated for a debt in such a way that it has not been delivered to the creditor, nor to another in his place. In that way, not only immovable things, but also movables are subjected to mortgages without a delivery being made to the creditor. Hence, in the Institutes on actions, § *item serviana*, and Law *si rem alienam*, paragraph *proprie* in the Digest on the action of pledge, it is stated: *By the term "pledge," we say that thing is properly contained which is simultaneously delivered to the creditor; but that which is contained by a bare agreement without delivery, we say is properly contained by the term "mortgage."* And a little before in the cited place of the Institutes, it was said: *Between a pledge and a mortgage, as far as the mortgage action is concerned, there is no difference; for whatever thing was agreed upon between creditor and debtor to be obligated for a debt, is contained under both these terms.* So it says there.

<margin>3</margin>
Following these, we can define pledge or mortgage in the broad sense thus: It is a † thing subjected or obligated for a debt so that, unless the debt is fulfilled, satisfaction may be made from it. Whence the creditor acquires a **real right** <note>original: "ius reale"; a right that attaches to the property itself, not just a person</note> in the mortgage or pledge, as we showed extensively at the end of Disputation 2. And therefore, to whomever that thing passes, it passes with that real burden, so that satisfaction may be made from it unless satisfaction has been made from elsewhere. We can define the contract of pledge and mortgage in the broad sense thus: It is a † contract by which something [is given] to a creditor for the payment of a debt...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 528

...the person is obligated, so that satisfaction may be made from that source if it has not been satisfied otherwise. This contract is perfected by solely expressed outward consent, even through an intermediary or letters, whether the things subjected to the pledge or mortgage are present or not, as was said regarding the contract of buying and selling. This is well-established in the laws *contrahitur* and *creditur* <note>original: "ff. de pign. l. 1. in prin. ff. de pign. act."; Digest 13.7.1 and 20.1.1</note> and Law 6, Title 13, Partida 5 <note>The "Siete Partidas" was a famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>. Hence, in the cited Law 1, § 6, it is inserted that when some parties entered into a contract with gold shown as a pledge, and it was agreed it would be the pledge, but later brass <note>original: "auricalcum"; an alloy resembling gold, often used in fraud</note> was delivered, the gold shown is the pledge. If, however, brass was asserted to be gold and was agreed upon and delivered as a pledge, then that brass is indeed the pledge, but the creditor can take action against the debtor through a "contrary pledge action" <note>original: "contraria pignoratit-tia actione"</note> so that another pledge of equal value to gold may be established, in addition to the crime of **stellionate** <note>original: "crimen stellionatus"; a term for fraud or swindling, especially in contracts where the same thing is sold or pledged twice</note> into which the deceiver falls if he did so knowingly; we shall speak of this crime 
<margin>5</margin>
in Disputation 532. You will arrive at the definitions of a **pledge** <note>original: "pignoris"</note> in the strict sense, and a **contract of pledge** in the strict sense, if you add to the traditional definitions that delivery has been made to the creditor, or to another in his place, of the thing so obligated. It is concerning this kind of pledge that the *Institutes* speak regarding "obligations arising from a delict" <note>original: "Inst. de oblig. quæ ex delic. §. furti"; Institutes 4.1.14</note> when it says that a creditor can sue for theft of a stolen pledge even if he has a solvent debtor, because it is more advantageous for him to rely on the pledge than to sue the person. Similarly, you will arrive at the definitions of a **mortgage** <note>original: "hypothecæ"</note> in the strict sense, and a **contract of mortgage** in the strict sense, if you add to the same definitions that delivery of the thing so obligated has *not* been made.
<margin>
Doubt
6
Decision
</margin>
Whether, however, if mention of a "pledge" is made in some statute, it should be judged that a **mortgage** can be included under that name? Although Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> (though hesitantly) answers in the negative; Panormitanus and Gregorius Lopez <note>A famous commentator on the Siete Partidas</note> rightly say that when a statute is **odious** <note>In legal hermeneutics, an "odious" statute was one that restricted common rights or imposed penalties; these were to be interpreted as narrowly as possible</note>, it is not included, based on the argument of certain laws they cite and because "odious things are to be restricted"; it is otherwise, however, when it is not odious. These points pertain to the first of the matters proposed.
<margin>7</margin>
As for the second point: A mortgage, taken broadly, is first divided into a **pledge** (strict sense) and a **mortgage** (strict sense), as is clear from what has been said. Next, 
<margin>8</margin>
a strict mortgage is divided into **tacit** and **express**. A **tacit** mortgage is one established by the authority of the law, even if no agreement occurs regarding it, and for this reason, it can also be called a **legal mortgage**. Such is the mortgage of a wife upon the property of her husband for the payment of her dowry, and there are many 
<margin>9</margin>
others, of which we will speak in the progression of this work. An **express** mortgage is that which is made by the express agreement of the parties, for which reason it is called **conventional**. As when one of the contracting parties, or some third party, obligates all his goods, or some of them, to another as security that something will be done or paid. Indeed, in the Law *res*, the final section of the Digest *de pign.* <note>Digest 20.1.5</note>, it is held: "Anyone can give a mortgage, whether for his own obligation or for that of another."
<margin>10</margin>
A **pledge** in the strict sense (which is always express), taken more broadly than defined above, is divided into **conventional**, **praetorian**, and **judicial**. A **conventional** pledge is that which is made solely by the agreement of the parties. A **praetorian** pledge <note>Named for the Praetor, a Roman magistrate</note> is when, by the mandate or decree of a judge, before a sentence is passed and due to the contempt <note>original: "contumaciam"; failure to appear in court or obey an order</note> of one party, the other litigant is put into possession or

<column-break/>

<margin>11</margin>
holding of that thing; for through that "immission" <note>The legal act of being put into possession</note> he acquires a right in that thing, and that thing takes on the nature of a **praetorian pledge**. A **judicial pledge**, however, is when one of the litigants—in execution of a sentence previously delivered, or in execution of a **guarentigian obligation** <note>original: "obligationis guarentigiæ"; a contract drafted before a notary that carries the same weight as a court judgment and allows for immediate enforcement</note>, or another that brings with it ready execution—is put into possession or holding of the property of the other without waiting for a judge's sentence, so that he may be satisfied from it. That thing then takes on the nature of a judicial pledge, and not before. A praetorian and judicial pledge differ in this from a conventional pledge and mortgage, in which a right is acquired by consent alone, as is clear from the Law *non est mirum* <note>Digest 13.7.1</note> and Law 13, Title 13, Partida 5. It will become clearer below that Gregorius Lopez, with Bartolus, affirms that for something to take on the nature of a judicial or praetorian pledge, it is not enough if the person to whom it is to be delivered is put into possession by a judge (or by a minister by the judge's mandate) through a **fictitious act**. For example, if he is put into possession by "sight" in his presence, with the judge or minister saying, "I deliver to you the possession of that," and the other accepting it without **real apprehension** <note>original: "reali apprehensione"; physical seizing or touching of the property</note>. For, he says, although a fictitious act is sufficient for one who possesses to transfer possession to another, it is not sufficient for one who does *not* possess (such as a judge or his minister) to transfer it. Panormitanus relates the same opinion, citing the *Speculator* and Antonius de Butrio, saying he followed it for a long time. However, from number 10 onwards, with Joannes Andreae, he proves copiously that it is enough if possession is delivered by the judge or his minister by sight; and this opinion does not displease me. From that rule, however—that for something to take on the nature of a judicial or praetorian pledge, it is necessary for the person to be put into possession—except where there is an impediment: for example, if the land is **flooded** by water and cannot be possessed, or because he is prevented by force; in such cases, it becomes a judicial pledge by the act of apprehension. This is held in Law *quavis* <note>Digest 42.4.7</note>. Finally, observe that a praetorian pledge can also be called "judicial" in a broader sense because it is done by the authority of a judge. Thus, "judicial pledge" is sometimes used to include "praetorian." Read Negusantius *On Pledges* regarding all these matters.
<margin>12</margin>
A **conventional mortgage** is subdivided into **universal** and **particular**. It is **universal** when someone obligates all his goods to another. Under the term "all goods," it is then understood not only all present goods but also future ones which he will acquire in the course of time, even if this is not expressed. This is held expressly in the final Law of the Code *quæ res pignor. oblig. poſſ.* <note>Code 8.16.9</note> and Law 5, Title 13, Partida 5; Covarruvias and Gregorius Lopez affirm this as well.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Disputation 528 regarding the legal nature of mortgages and pledges, specifically focusing on what is excluded from a "universal mortgage" (one covering all of a debtor's assets) and the distinction between express and tacit obligations.</meta>

...and it is the common opinion of the learned doctors. The reason for this is that a **mortgage** <note>original: "hypotheca"; a legal claim against property as security for a debt without transferring possession</note> does not cause great prejudice to the debtor, because the debt itself does not increase because of it; rather, only the creditor's security that he will be paid increases. An exception is the case mentioned in the last law of the Code on the redemption of pledges <note>original: "leg. vlt. C. de rem. pign."; referring to Justinian’s Code</note>. If a debtor, with the creditor's consent, alienates <note>transfers or sells to another</note> any item from those included in a universal mortgage and thus tacitly waives the mortgage obligation by which that item was bound, and if by chance that item later returns to the ownership of the same debtor through another cause, it is not considered subject to the mortgage, as will be explained in Disputation 557.

They also except those things which, if a person obligating his goods were asked specifically, he would not have intended to obligate. This is held in the law *obligatione* in the Digest on pledges <note>original: "ff. de pign. l. 1. C. quæ res pig."</note>. Such items are, as those laws express (along with the law *vel quæ* and the two following): a maidservant who is his concubine, the children born of him by her, slaves necessary for his daily administration or for nurturing his children, daily winter and summer clothes for both himself and his wife, household furniture entirely necessary for daily use, weapons for his own person, and a horse—as the cited law expresses—and any other similar things. These exceptions are to be understood also in a **tacit universal mortgage**, which will be discussed shortly.

Note, however, that if these specific items (which are usually not considered part of a universal mortgage) were explicitly named in a universal mortgage, then those specifically expressed items *are* considered included, as Negusantius observes with others in his treatise on pledges. Under the name of "all goods," those things are included in a mortgage which belong to the debtor in such a way that they can be alienated by him, as Gregorius Lopez notes on the phrase "all other things" (*todas las otras cosas*).

Things meant for sale are also included, as was said with Bartolus and Covarruvias in Disputation 201, and affirmed by Gregorius Lopez above. In that place, I add with others: this does not impede trade; because, in place of the sold item, the price succeeds it in the universal mortgage. Therefore, by the very fact that a merchant's goods are alienated, they cease to be included under the mortgage. This is the view of Negusantius and Covarruvias.

<margin>13</margin> A **particular mortgage** occurs when not all goods are obligated, but only certain ones, whether one or many. When all goods of a certain *kind* are obligated, the items of that kind meant for sale are considered obligated, unless a restriction is made to those in a specific place.

<margin>14</margin> A **tacit mortgage** is also subdivided into universal and particular. A universal one is that by which all goods are obligated by provision of law. Such is the mortgage a wife has over all her husband's goods for the payment of her dowry and her own property. In such a universal mortgage, all present and future goods are similarly included, just as in an express universal mortgage. This is gathered from the law *hac edictali* in the Code and is the common opinion followed by Covarruvias and Gregorius Lopez on the phrase 

<column-break/>

"those who are understood to have been cited." However, those things we said were excepted in an express universal mortgage must also be excepted here.

<margin>15</margin> A **particular tacit mortgage** is one where not all, but some specific good or goods are obligated by legal provision. An example of this is the claim held by one who has lent money for the repair of a ship or a house; for that very house or ship remains mortgaged by legal provision for the payment of that money, as we shall see, and as was mentioned when we spoke of the mortgage for a dowry above.

However, a **pledge** <note>original: "pignus"; usually referring to a physical object handed over to the creditor</note> is always considered express and particular, because it requires delivery of the item; the same is true for a judicial pledge for the same reason. Therefore, we have made the divisions into tacit and express, and into universal and particular, only for the mortgage, not for the pledge.

## What things can be subjected to pledge and mortgage, what are considered subjected, and who can subject them.

<margin>1</margin> Not only things that already exist can be subjected to mortgage and pledge, but also those that will exist or are hoped for in the future, such as hanging fruits, the offspring of cattle, and the children of slave-women, even if they have not yet been conceived or born; just as they can also be sold, as was seen in Disputation 349. This is held in the Digest and in the *Siete Partidas*. # Second Treatise, Disputation 526.

subject to a similar reasoning as a pledge, just as a conditional **mortgage** <note>original: "hypotheca"; a legal claim against property as security for a debt</note> is, if it comes into existence: for that which does not exist cannot undergo the logic of an actual pledge or mortgage.

<margin>2</margin> However, for the **fruits** <note>original: "fructus"; legal term for the natural produce of land or interest on money</note> or the **offspring** <note>original: "partus"; usually referring to the young of animals or, historically, children of enslaved women</note> of any thing to be subjected to a pledge or mortgage while they are still "in hope" <note>original: "in spe"; expected but not yet realized</note>, it is necessary that at the time the contract of pledge or mortgage is celebrated, the thing from which they are expected to be gathered belongs to the person who subjects them to the pledge or mortgage. This is held in the law *potior*, in the section *de futura* in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff."; the *Pandects* or Digest of Roman Law</note> on who is prior in pledge. The reason is that another person's property cannot be bound to a pledge or mortgage without the owner's knowledge and without the owner ratifying it; such an obligation is null, unless the owner consents or later ratifies it, as found in the law *aliena res* at the beginning, and the law *si fundus*, section 1, in the Digest on pledges, and the law *quae praedium*, and the final law of the Code on if another's property is given as a pledge, and law 9, title 13, of the fifth **Partida** <note>original: "part. 5"; referring to the *Siete Partidas*, a famous Spanish legal code</note>.

<margin>3</margin> I should mention here in passing that when another's property is given in pledge without the owner's knowledge, and the owner later ratifies it, that **ratification** <note>original: "ratihabitio"; the act of giving retroactive legal force to a prior unauthorized act</note> is pulled backward, so that from the beginning the thing is considered to have been delivered in pledge or subjected to a mortgage. However, this is not to the prejudice of a third party to whom the same thing might have been subjected as a mortgage before that ratification; in this case, the prior creditor, who first had a right in the thing, shall be preferred to the other creditor. So says Negusantius on pledges, part 3, member 1, number 19, by the argument of the law *potior*, section 1, in the Digest on who is prior in pledge.

<margin>4</margin> Observe that when someone to whom a thing was subjected as a pledge or mortgage was ignorant that it belonged to another, they can act by a "contrary action" <note>original: "contraria actione"; a legal claim to recover damages or expenses</note> against the one who bound it, so that they may bind another equally good thing as a pledge or mortgage, as held in the law *quae praedium* cited above, and the law *rem alienam* in the Digest on pledges. Add to this that if that thing later comes to the person who subjected it to the pledge or mortgage, a "pledge action" <note>original: "pignoraticiam actionem"</note> is available to the creditor against that thing, because it remains subjected to the pledge or mortgage for the creditor by that very fact; and the same is held in law 7, title 13, of the fifth Partida at the end. Whence I do not doubt that a thing which is in some way "in the hope" of someone can be subjected by them to a pledge or mortgage, insofar as it is in hope, and under the condition that it comes into their **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note>. Indeed, the law *si fundus*, in the section *aliena* in the Digest on pledges, has it thus: *Another's property can be usefully bound under the condition that it becomes the debtor's*, and this very thing is affirmed more clearly in law 7, title 13, of the fifth Partida. Nor is the law *potior*, section *si de futura*, in the Digest on who is prior in pledge, intended to the contrary; but its main intent is what I shall subjoin in the following section.

<margin>5</margin> When someone subjects another's property to a mortgage without the owner's knowledge, and then the person who subjected it to the mortgage acquires the ownership of it from the owner, it does not remain subject to that mortgage. This is held in law 7, title 13, of the fifth Partida, and Bartolus agrees there, as cited by Gregorio Lopez in the last gloss; although the gloss on law 1 at the beginning, on the word *difficilius* in the Digest on pledges, asserts the contrary, and Angelus agrees with it. However, when another's property is given as a pledge to someone who knows it belongs to another, if the one who delivered it acquires ownership of it, the creditor will be able to retain it until the debt is paid to him, as held in the cited law 3, and as those things which must be said in Disputation 531 agree.

<margin>5</margin> <note>Note: The original text repeats the number 5 in the margin</note> This must be observed: When any thing or things are subjected to a pledge or mortgage, the fruits of those things, if they are produced by the debtor, and the offspring of a maidservant or other animals, if they were conceived

<column-break/>

while those mortgages belonged to the debtor, are also subjected to the mortgage together with the things of which they are the fruits. Even if those things are alienated and have already passed into the ownership of another, and are gathered by another, or if those offspring from the animals are fed and the ownership of them is acquired, [they are still subject]. And this is what is primarily intended by the law *potior*, section *si de futura* in the Digest on who is prior in pledge.

<margin>6</margin> Where it is also held that if a **usufruct** <note>original: "vsusfructus"; the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</note> was subjected to a pledge or mortgage by the usufructuary to a creditor, the fruits produced and gathered from such a usufruct while that usufruct belonged to him are considered subject to the pledge or mortgage. They are considered subject to the pledge or mortgage by reason of such usufruct, even if they are gathered by someone else. For although, as the gloss on the word *utifrui* says there, and as we have said in Disputation 7 and elsewhere, those fruits do not pertain to the ownership of the usufructuary but to the ownership of the proprietor while they are "pending" <note>original: "pendent"; crops still growing and attached to the land</note> (as they are then considered as one with the land of which they are fruits), they only finally become the usufructuary's when he gathers them while the usufruct continues, or another does so in his place. Nevertheless, the right which the usufructuary has by reason of the usufruct to make them his own if he gathers them while the usufruct continues is enough so that, by reason of the usufruct being subjected to a pledge or mortgage, they too are considered subject to the pledge or mortgage—dependent, however, on their being gathered while the usufruct continues. For if the usufruct ends while they are still hanging, they belong entirely to the proprietor, as was said in Disputation 7. And just as the pledge or mortgage of such a usufruct ends, so also the pledge or mortgage of those same fruits expires. However, that fruits which were born, produced, or conceived at the time when the pledge or mortgage belonged to the debtor are likewise subject to the pledge or mortgage while they exist—even if ownership has passed to another and that person has gathered them—is supported not only by the cited law but also by the gloss there. It is expressly held in the law *quis* in the Code on in which cases a pledge or mortgage is tacitly contracted; the law *in praediis* in the Digest of the same title; the law *greg.* at the beginning; and the law *et quem* at the beginning, joined with section 1; and the law *Paulus*, section *si mancipia* in the Digest on pledges; the law *si convenerit*, section 2 *si fundus*, joined with the gloss there in the Digest on pledges; and the law 1 joined with the gloss there in the Code on the offspring of a pledge; and law 16, title 13, of the fifth Partida. But by the very fact that such fruits no longer exist, they cease to be subject to the pledge or mortgage. Indeed, if the person to whose ownership they passed buys something with them, or acquires something by exchange with them, the thing so acquired is not subject to the pledge or mortgage, but only those fruits themselves, while they exist, are subject to the mortgage, as held in the law *quamvis* in the Code on in which cases a pledge or mortgage [is contracted]. Hence the laws say that when a mortgage is **particular** <note>original: "particularis"; a mortgage on a specific item rather than all assets</note>, and some fruits are gathered from the thing thus subjected to the mortgage by the one who subjected it in that way, then, for those fruits to be considered subject to the mortgage by that very fact, it belongs to the creditor to prove they were born or conceived from that thing after it was subjected to the mortgage. It is otherwise when the mortgage is **universal**; because then all things of that person universally, both present and future, and therefore all those fruits, at whatever time they were gathered by him, are subject to the mortgage. So it is held in the law *et quae*...

-># Ludovicus Molina on Contracts<-

<page-num>714</page-num>

...which is found in paragraph 1 of the **Digest** <note>original: "ff."; the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> on pledges. Generally, however, when a creditor brings a **Servian action** <note>A legal action allowing a creditor to take possession of a debtor's property held by a third party</note>, or an action regarding a pledge or mortgage against a third-party possessor to ensure a debt is paid from a thing held by that possessor—as if it were a mortgage—the burden of proof lies with the creditor. He must prove that the item was indeed subject to the mortgage and that, at the time the contract was made, it belonged to the debtor, or that the true owner consented to it being mortgaged or later ratified the agreement. This is held in the law *Before all things* in the Digest on proofs, and in Law 18, Title 13 of the **Fifth Partida** <note>A foundational Spanish legal code</note>. Furthermore, if after a thing was mortgaged, the person who mortgaged it loses a court case regarding that item, and a sentence is passed stating it belongs (or belonged) to someone else, the creditor still has the right to prove it actually belonged to the debtor at the time it was mortgaged, so that his debt may be paid from it. It is otherwise, however, if the debtor had already lost the case before he mortgaged the thing; in that case, the creditor would not be heard even if he wished to prove it belonged to the debtor, but would be blocked by the exception of **res iudicata** <note>original: "rei iudicatæ"; a matter already judged by a court which cannot be relitigated</note>. This is the rule in the law *If defeated* in the Digest on pledges. To return to the **fruits** <note>Produce, rent, or offspring generated by a property</note> of a mortgaged thing: if, after the thing was sold, the fruits were sown and gathered (or conceived and gathered) by the person who became the new owner, so that the person who mortgaged it never had ownership or rights to them, then those fruits are not subject to the mortgage, even if they currently exist. This is found in the law of *Paulus*, in the section *If slaves*, and Law 1, in the section *As soon as*, noting the gloss at the end on the words "never the debtor's," and Law 16, Title 13 of the Fifth Partida.

<margin>Doubt 7</margin>
Regarding the fruits gathered by an **heir** from such a thing, there is a doubt as to whether they are subject to the mortgage. From the law of *Paulus* at the beginning of the Digest on pledges, it seems to follow that they are subject, because they are truly gathered from the inherited property; it is said there that only those things an heir acquires from somewhere other than the deceased’s estate are not subject to the mortgage. And **Gregorio López** <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>, commenting on Law 5, Title 13 of the Fifth Partida on the words "those he expects to have," discusses cases where the deceased’s goods were bound by a general mortgage. He adds that the natural fruits of the inherited thing are subject to the mortgage; however, it is different for goods the heir acquires through his own **industry** <note>Personal effort, business, or labor</note> by trading with the deceased's goods. Following the jurist **Angelus**, he affirms these are not subject to the mortgage.

<margin>Decision</margin>
I would say that the fruits of the deceased's property that were sown or conceived at the time when those goods already belonged to the heir are subject to the mortgage, but only after subtracting the expenses and the price of the heir’s labor and industry in cultivating the property and gathering the fruits. For only the remainder is truly counted as "fruit" from that thing.

<margin>Doubt 8</margin>
I have a greater doubt, however, regarding the fruits that a **tenant** <note>original: "conductor"; someone leasing the property</note> of a mortgaged thing gathers, whether during the time of the person who mortgaged it or during the time of that person's heir.

<margin>Decision</margin>
It seems to me that they should not be subject to the mortgage once they have been gathered. This is because they are the fruits of the tenant's industry and the rent he pays under a valid lease contract. The fact that they are simultaneously the produce of a mortgaged thing does not prevent this; just as the fruits an authorized buyer gathers from the same property are not subject to the mortgage by operation of law, even though the mortgage obligation on the land itself persists. The same should be judged by **equity** <note>original: "epicheiam"; a legal principle of fairness that looks at the spirit of the law rather than just the letter</note> regarding these kinds of fruits. However, while the fruits are still "hanging" (unharvested) and not yet gathered, they are considered part of the mortgaged property

<column-break/>

itself. Therefore, they are considered subject to the mortgage, whether the thing was leased, or bought, or acquired under any other title of ownership. This is found in the law *If a field*, in the section *In a claim*, in the verse *Sometimes*, joined with the final gloss in the Digest on pledges, and is affirmed by Gregorio López in the previously cited Law 16. Nevertheless, expenses—which include the price of labor and industry—must always be subtracted from such fruits.

<margin>9</margin>
Not only physical objects but also **incorporeal things** <note>Intangible rights, such as debts or legal claims</note> like rights can be given as a pledge. This is found in Law 2, Title 13 of the Fifth Partida and is gathered from the laws to be cited. Therefore, a thing accepted as a pledge by one creditor can be handed over by him to another person as a pledge for a different debt, by reason of the right of pledge he holds in it. For the same reason, a thing mortgaged to one person for one debt can be subjected by him to a mortgage for another person for a different debt. [See] the law *The flock*, section *When as a pledge*, and Laws 1 and 2 of the Code on *If a pledge is given as a pledge*, and Law 35, Title 13 of the Fifth Partida. However, the moment the first debtor pays in full what he owed under that pledge, the second pledge is dissolved. For that reason, the debtor can reclaim his pledge through a **property claim** <note>original: "vendicare"; an action to assert ownership</note>; because once the primary right on which the secondary pledge rested is cleared, the second right is dissolved. [See] the Digest on pledges and the Code on the same. However, the second creditor can demand from the first creditor that he either pay his debt immediately or hand over another pledge of equal value. When, however, one person owed another a certain amount of money, and since the debtor did not then have the money to pay, he handed over a pledge so the creditor could seek the money from someone else and receive it, and that was carried out; then, if the first debtor pays the first creditor the money owed, and the pledge has already been recovered by the first creditor, he is compelled to produce it in a property claim. But if it is still in the hands of the second creditor <note>The text here says "second debtor," likely a slip for "second creditor" or the person holding the sub-pledge</note>, the right of pledge is not considered dissolved, because it was handed over to the second creditor by the authority of the first debtor. Thus, the first debtor cannot act against him with a pledge action or a property claim to have the pledge restored until satisfaction is made; he will, however, act against the first creditor with an **action on the prescribed words** <note>A flexible legal action used when no specific named action fits the contract</note> to force him to pay the debt to the second creditor, take back the pledge, and restore it to him. This is what is held in the law *To the petitioner* in the Digest on the action of pledge.

<margin>10</margin>
The **names** <note>original: "Nomina"; a Roman legal term for debts or accounts receivable</note> of debtors—that is, the debts owed to someone—can also be handed over as a pledge or subjected to a mortgage. This is held in the law *The flock*, section *But he can*, and the law *It is agreed* in the Digest on pledges... and Law 2, Title 13 of the Fifth Partida. In such a case, the second creditor uses a **useful action** <note>A legal remedy extended by a judge to cover a case not strictly within the letter of the law</note> to demand the debt from the first debtor, unless the first debtor has already paid the first creditor, being unaware that the debt had been pledged to the second creditor. For if he were warned by the second creditor and still paid the first creditor, the second creditor could nevertheless demand the same amount from the first debtor. Following **Bartolus** <note>A highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> against the gloss on the cited law *The name*, an addition to that same gloss says that if the first debtor...

-># Second Treatise, Dispute 529<-

...debtor <note>original: "tor", completing "debitor" from the previous page</note>, being aware that a debt has been given as a pledge to a second creditor, pays it instead to the first creditor. If, however, the debt consists of money, the second creditor who recovers it may offset the total amount of money owed to him and deliver the remainder to the first creditor. The same applies if both debts consist of things that can be exchanged for one another, such as if both debts are in wheat or some similar commodity. But if it is a specific thing where such an exchange <term>compensation: a legal mechanism where two debts cancel each other out</term> does not apply, then the thing so paid takes on the nature of a pledge, and the second creditor retains it as a pledge until what is owed to him is paid in full. All of this is cited in the Law *Nomen*, and the Law *Grege*, paragraph *But it can*, in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff."; the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> on pledges; Law *If it shall have been agreed*, at the beginning, in the Digest on actions regarding pledges; and Law 2, Title 13 of the **Fifth Partida** <note>The *Siete Partidas*, a major Spanish legal code</note>; and other cited laws agree.

11 **Usufruct** <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> can also be subject to a pledge and mortgage, according to Law *Prior*, paragraph *If regarding a future*, in the Digest on who is prior in a pledge; Law *If anyone*, paragraph *Usufruct*, in the Digest on pledges; and Law 1, paragraph 1 of the **Code** <note>The Code of Justinian</note> on if a pledge can be pledged. However, the right of the pledge expires by that very fact when the usufruct ends and is merged with the ownership of the property. This is because neither a pledge nor anything else can be established to the detriment of the owner against his will. Nevertheless, with the owner's consent, it could be given as a pledge even for the time when it would be merged with the ownership—just as any other property belonging to another can be given as a pledge with the consent of the owners, as has been said.

12 **Emphyteusis** <note>A long-term lease of land, often for agricultural purposes, in exchange for an annual rent and improvements</note> can also be subject to pledge and mortgage, provided it does not prejudice the owner. The same applies to **superficies** <note>the right to a building standing on another's land</note>, as was clearly shown at the end of Dispute 461. The situation is different regarding a **feud** <note>land held under the feudal system</note>; for a **vassal** <note>a person granted the use of land in return for homage and labor</note> is prohibited from pledging or mortgaging it without the lord's permission, lest through the pledging or obligating of the feud, the vassal becomes too weak to follow his lord and serve him in war. This is according to Chapter 1, at the beginning, on the prohibition of alienating feuds by Emperor Frederick, along with the **gloss** <note>standard legal commentary</note> there on the word "commerce"; and Negusantius affirms this with others in his work *On Pledges*, part 2, member 2, number 43. Read there for certain limitations.

13 Regarding **real servitudes** <note>often called "easements" today, such as a right of way over a neighbor's land</note>, a distinction must be made. Since a servitude owed to a piece of land—whether urban or rural—is considered subject to a pledge or mortgage by the very fact that the land itself is pledged, as it is annexed and owed to that land. The laws we will soon cite do not teach or intend otherwise. However, a servitude taken by itself, if it is an urban one, is prohibited from being pledged or mortgaged; but it is otherwise for a rural one. The first is held in Law *He who*, the last paragraph, in the Digest on pledges; and the second in Law *But also whether*, in the same title of the Digest. This is how the gloss on Law *Which a field*, paragraph *They shall have been*, in the Code on if another's property is pledged, and Law *Who sons*, at the word "subject," in the Digest on what things can be pledged, and Ripa (as reported by Gregorio López in Law 2, gloss 2, title 13, Partida 5) understand it—specifically regarding the convenience of the servitude on another's land which the creditor might have while the debt is unpaid. Law *But also whether*, cited above, seems to grant this. And Silvester, at the word "pledge," number 2, rightly says that one must beware of **usury** <note>charging illegal or excessive interest</note>, which that civil law seems to grant by its disposition.

14 Regarding **jurisdiction** <note>the legal power of a lord or official over a territory</note>, whether it can be subject to pledge and mortgage: Bartolus denied it when it is "mere jurisdiction" over men which has no annexed revenues. However, Gregorio López, in Law 2, gloss 

<column-break/>

2, title 13, Partida 5, with others, rightly affirms the contrary. Especially since today such jurisdiction is sold, and for no small price. Insofar as it can be sold, it can be subject to a pledge or mortgage, so that the debt may be paid from its price.

15 Regarding the **right of patronage** <note>original: "ius patronatum"; the right of a founder of a church to nominate a candidate for the clergy</note>, it should be said (following Panormitanus on Chapter *Since Bartholdus*, on sentences and res iudicata, numbers 38 and 39, along with Gregorio López in the cited gloss 2 and others) that if it has some temporal revenues annexed and assigned to such a right of patronage, it can be subject to a pledge or mortgage regarding the right to those revenues. Indeed, by the very fact that a right of patronage is annexed to certain temporal goods, such as a villa or another thing, if the villa or property to which the right is annexed is given as a pledge, the right of patronage is also considered pledged regarding the temporal right to the revenues annexed to it. However, the right of patronage itself—in terms of the right to present a candidate for an Ecclesiastical **benefice** <note>a church office that provides an income</note> in which it essentially consists—is neither considered subject to a pledge or mortgage, nor can it be subjected to one by any means. All of this is clearly gathered and established from the cited Chapter *Since Bartholdus*, even if that villa or other property to which the right was annexed were sold or passed into the ownership of another by some other title, the right of patronage would pass along with it. The reason why the right of patronage (as far as the right of presentation is concerned) is not considered pledged when the villa or property is pledged is this: the use of the right of presentation is not a saleable thing, nor can it be valued at a price. Therefore, it is not something that can be returned to the debtor by the creditor when the debt has been satisfied, nor something the creditor can count toward the principal debt—unlike the revenues annexed to the right of patronage. For the creditor can indeed return these to the debtor once the debt is paid, or count them toward the debt. A creditor is always bound to return the revenues of a pledge to the debtor once the debt is paid, or to count them toward the debt, because the ownership of the pledge remains with the debtor and does not pass to the creditor; only the possession of the pledge passes. This is established from Law 1 of the Code on the sale of pledges; Laws 1, 2, and the last of the Code on actions regarding pledges; Law 2 of the Code on the offspring of a pledge; Law *If ownership* in the Code on pledges; Chapter *Since on the contrary* on pledges; and Chapters 1 and 2 on usury; and Law 2, Title 13, Partida 5.

16 Those who can alienate <note>sell or transfer</note> property can also subject it to a pledge or mortgage; it is otherwise for those who cannot alienate them, according to Law 7, Title 13, Partida 5; Azo on the Code on pledges in summary; and the gloss on Law 1, at the beginning, at the word "more difficult," in the Digest on pledges. However, although **prelates** <note>high-ranking church officials like bishops</note> cannot, without just cause and due solemnity, alienate immovable property or precious movable goods that can be preserved, nor subject them to a specific mortgage or pledge, they can nevertheless, without solemnity and just cause, subject all the goods of the Church to a **universal mortgage**, as we showed at the beginning of Dispute 466, following the common opinion of the doctors.

17 Whoever has a right in a thing can give it as a pledge, and thus subject it to a mortgage, according to Law 3, paragraph *Since from a cause*, in the Digest on who is prior in a pledge; and Law 3, Title 13, Partida 5. If the person who subjected it to a pledge later acquires full ownership of it, it remains subject to the pledge or mortgage...

Molina emphasizes that while the financial income from these rights can be pledged, the essential personal or spiritual duties (like military service or clerical appointments) are often legally protected.</summary>
