<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal analysis of pledges and mortgages, moving from how debts are pledged to defining specific categories of things and people that are legally prohibited from being used as collateral.</meta>

### Which things cannot be subject to a pledge or mortgage.

->DISPUTE 530<-

->SUMMARY<-

1. Things that cannot be sold or transferred to others cannot be subject to a pledge or mortgage.
2. When sacred things may be pledged (see also no. 5).
3. The same must be said regarding the right of patronage.
4. What applies to public property and a free person (no. 5 and 6).
7. A free person may be given as a hostage or a pledge for the sake of peace between warring parties.
8. What if they are given for a matter not related to war?
9. Regarding the laws of Portugal and Castile.

<margin>1</margin>Regarding those sacred things mentioned at the end of Dispute 268—where it was stated that any agreement or promise made regarding them is entirely useless—and in Dispute 340—where we showed that any attempted sale is void—such as churches and tombs, these cannot be subject to a pledge or mortgage. If such a thing is attempted, it has no force or significance. This is because, <margin>1</margin> † generally speaking, things that cannot be sold cannot be subject to a pledge or mortgage, according to the Law *But also*, paragraph *Which purchase* in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff. de pign."; the Digest of Roman Law, title on pledges</note> and Law 1, final paragraph, in the Digest on what things can be pledged or mortgaged. This same rule regarding sacred things is found in Law 1, paragraph *That thing* in the Digest, and the Law *If a monument* in the **Code** <note>original: "C. eod. tit."; the Code of Justinian, under the same title</note>; these laws entirely deny that such things can be pledged.

<margin>2</margin>However, just as such things cannot be sold on their own, they can be sold together with the land of which they are parts or to which they are attached—indeed, they pass along with the land so sold even if it is not explicitly stated that they are sold with their attachments, as we showed in Dispute 340. In the same way, if that land is pledged or mortgaged, those sacred things are also considered subject to the pledge or mortgage by virtue of that agreement. If the land is sold so that a debt or obligation can be satisfied from the price, those things are likewise considered sold.

<margin>3</margin>The same must be said regarding a <term>right of patronage: the legal right of a benefactor to nominate a member of the clergy to a specific church or office</term> attached to such a place. Even though the place is handed over as a pledge, the exercise of the right of patronage—specifically the act of presenting a candidate—does not belong to the creditor, but remains with the debtor as long as the property remains a pledge and has not yet been sold to satisfy the debt. It should also be noted that if a sacred thing (or any other thing that cannot be sold) is sold to someone who is unaware of the quality that makes it unsellable, the seller is liable to that person for <term>eviction: the recovery of property by judicial process, or the compensation owed when a buyer loses property due to a defect in the seller's title</term>, as shown at the end of Dispute 268 and 340. Similarly, if that same thing is pledged to someone who is ignorant of the quality that prevents it from being pledged, that person has a legal action against the debtor to demand that another thing of equal value be pledged in its place, based on the argument of Law 1, final paragraph, on pledge actions, and other laws cited in the preceding disputes.

<column-break/>

<margin>4</margin>Other sacred items, such as chalices, vestments, and other things which, though not consecrated, serve and are dedicated to divine worship, cannot be sold except in cases of urgent necessity—such as to relieve famine, to ransom captives of that same Church who cannot be redeemed by their own people, or to pay the Church's debts which cannot be settled otherwise, as discussed in Dispute 340. Consequently, they cannot be pledged or mortgaged to laypeople except for a similar urgent cause, according to Chapter 1 on pledges and Law 3, Title 13, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the Castilian legal code</note>. In Portugal, however, such items and other gold or silver objects—which they call the "jewels of the Churches or monasteries"—cannot be accepted as a pledge even in cases permitted by law, unless the matter is first disclosed to the King and done by his authority. Otherwise, the recipient is compelled to return the item to the Church for free and, in addition, pay nine times the value of the item: part of this penalty goes to the accuser and part toward the ransom of captives, as held in Book 2, Title 13 of the **Ordinances** <note>The *Ordenações Manuelinas* or *Filipinas*, the laws of the Kingdom of Portugal</note>. Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> correctly says in his commentary on Chapter 1 regarding pledges, number 4, that when the property of a Church is mortgaged as security for a contract, it is not understood to include things that serve divine worship, which cannot be pledged except for urgent cause. This follows the argument of Law 1 in the Code on what things can be pledged, which states that when something specifically cannot be pledged, it is not considered included when property is pledged under a general mortgage.

<margin>5</margin>Public property, such as squares, public roads, and other things † designated for the common use of the people, cannot be sold without the consent of the supreme prince, and any sale made otherwise is void, as stated in Disputes 340 and 268. Thus, they cannot be pledged or mortgaged without the permission of the same supreme prince, following the same reasoning used for the first category of sacred things.

<margin>6</margin>A free person, just as they † cannot be sold (even for a limited time as a slave, as discussed in Dispute 340 and 268, except in the specific events explained in Dispute 33 under the third title where someone is lawfully reduced to servitude), cannot be pledged or mortgaged where Roman laws have force. The exceptions are cases where a father may sell his children, or when someone held captive pledges themselves for the price of their ransom until they pay it or satisfy it through service, according to Chapter 2 on pledges and the Law *Those children* in the Code, and Law 3, Title 13, Part 5. Anyone who knowingly receives a son of a family as a pledge is to be <term>relegated: a form of exile where a person is banished to a specific place</term> under the final law of the Digest on what things can be pledged; moreover, they lose the debt and are forced to refund an equal amount to the person, their parents, or their heirs. The same applies if they receive any other free person as a pledge.

<margin>9</margin>
It is established that for no civil debt—even if it is a tax owed to the King—can animals used for plowing be seized or sequestered, nor other things belonging to the cultivation and harvesting of any fruits of the earth. An exception is made when the debt is a tax owed to the King or to the lord of the town, or is something owed to the lord of the estate which that farmer cultivates. In those cases, if the farmer has no other goods, whether movable or immovable, upon which seizure can be made, the aforementioned things belonging to cultivation can be seized. It is otherwise if he has other goods upon which seizure can be made. Any official who carries out a seizure otherwise is forced to restore the pledge and all damages following from it, and moreover pays four times the value of the pledge—half to the one who complained of the matter, and the other half to the King’s treasury. However, when a seizure is made for a debt or a guarantee of a private person, the creditor by that very act loses the entire debt or guarantee, or whatever other right he had in that part. Nor is any renunciation made by the debtor regarding this matter valid, no matter what clauses he used to renounce it or bind himself to the debt. If it was confirmed by an oath, the creditor loses the debt by that very act. The same is established in the following Law 6, and there only two oxen used for plowing are exempted from the burden of tax. Any public official who does the contrary is punished by the officials they call the *Alcaldes* <note>judges</note> of the Brotherhood.

And that in one pair of oxen, mules, or other beasts for plowing, they cannot be seized in the said three cases, nor for any other." And in the second paragraph he established: "That the persons of the said farmers cannot be imprisoned for any debt that does not arise from a crime, in the months of July and those following until the end of December. And the creditor who requested it, by that same act, shall have lost and loses the said debt, and the farmer shall be free from it." -> **Whether a pledge or mortgage of another's property made by an agent, a business manager, a tutor, or a curator, or a son, is valid, or even one made of one's own property in favor of another.** <-

### DISPUTE 531.
#### SUMMARY.

1. *A litigious thing <note>property subject to a lawsuit</note> cannot be placed under pledge, just as it cannot be sold.*
2. *When an agent <note>procurator</note> and a business manager may place a thing under pledge, and when they may not. The same is to be said for a tutor and a curator, in number 3.*

It was stated in Dispute 529 that the property of another cannot be subjected to a pledge or mortgage except with the consent of the owner or with their later ratification of what was done at the beginning. And this holds true even if an emancipated son or a son still under parental authority subjects the father's property to a pledge or mortgage without his consent, according to the law *Nec si* in the Code on the pledging of another's property. For the same reason, just as a litigious thing <note>original: "res litigiosa"</note> cannot be alienated <note>transferred to another</note>, so also it cannot be subjected to a pledge or mortgage, according to Law 1, the final paragraph, in the Digest on what things can be pledged, and Bartolus there, and Negusantius on pledges, part 2, member 3, number 46. Because, however, there is a particular difficulty in the events proposed in the title of this dispute, that must be examined in detail.

Regarding an agent <note>original: "procuratore"</note> or a business manager <note>original: "negotiorum gestore"</note>, a distinction must be made. Because if he has not only the administration of assets, but even the free administration of all assets—which must necessarily be granted to him according to the law *Quam Tuberonis*, paragraph *Alia ex causa*, in the Digest on peculium—then, since he can alienate property by an onerous title (such as by selling, exchanging, hiring, or leasing), but not by a gratuitous title (such as by giving it away), he can also subject the things of the person for whom he is agent or manager to a pledge or mortgage. However...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the management of property and the rights of creditors, specifically focusing on when an agent or manager may validly pledge the property of another as security for a debt.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 531
### Page 719

...acting in the business of that person <note>original: "l. procurator cui generaliter, ff. de pig. act." — referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 13, Title 7, on the action of pledge.</note>. I said, however, "acting in his business": for one who acts for another's benefit cannot subject the property of the person for whom he is an agent <term>procurator</term> or manager of affairs <term>negotiorum gestor</term> to a pledge or mortgage for his own advantage, even if he has "free administration" (full power of attorney). To do so would be equivalent to giving the property away, which is not permitted <note>original: "l. 1. §. 1. ff. quæ res pigno."</note>. If, however, he has universal administration of the assets, but not "free" administration, then the pledge is valid only if the owner was accustomed to pledging property in that manner. In such a case, the agent, manager, or administrator may similarly subject the property to a pledge or mortgage; otherwise, it is not valid. However, when he has a specific mandate to pledge or mortgage something, there can be no doubt that he can effectively do so. And in those circumstances where he can validly pledge something, he is entitled to the pledge action <term>actio pignoratitia</term>.

In other circumstances, if a steward—whom we call a <margin>steward</margin> *mayordomo* in Spanish—subjects something belonging to the person whose business they manage to a pledge or mortgage in exchange for money or another item they receive, without the owner of the property consenting or later ratifying it, a distinction must again be made. Either this was done with the owner of the property knowing and remaining silent while it was pledged, and the creditor being ignorant that the property belonged to another; or it was done with the owner being ignorant of the pledge, or with the creditor knowing that it was the owner's property. In this latter case—namely, when the owner was ignorant of the pledging, or if he knew but did not consent, and the creditor knew it was the owner's property—we must distinguish further: was the money or item taken under that pledge converted to the benefit of the owner? If so, and if the pledge was delivered to the creditor, the creditor may retain it until the owner pays back what was used for his benefit. Against an owner seeking to reclaim his property, the creditor is granted an "exception" (a legal defense): that the value received was used for the owner's benefit, and therefore the owner must first pay that amount, or the pledge will not be restored. This is found in the Code <note>original: "l. 1. C. si aliena res pign." — Code of Justinian, Book 8, Title 15.</note> and the *Partidas* <note>original: "l. 8. titu. 13. par. 5." — Referencing the Siete Partidas, the medieval Spanish law code.</note>. If, however, the pledge was not delivered to the creditor, then the creditor can sue the owner with a personal action to pay what was used for his benefit, but the owner is not compelled to hand the property over to the creditor. This is because the law recognizes the owner owes what was used for his benefit, and for that reason allows the creditor to keep the item if he already has it, but does not grant a right to seize it.

<column-break/>

If the entire amount was not converted to the owner's benefit, the owner is not bound to pay the whole debt; instead, the person who received the money under that pledge is bound to pay. That person is liable for the whole if nothing was converted to the owner's benefit, or if the business was not managed usefully or reasonably in that part. If, however, it was managed reasonably, even if the matter did not turn out successfully, the owner is bound to pay the whole amount via the action for business managed <term>actio negotiorum gestorum</term>, as was said in Dispute 300. Although the owner is not bound to hand over the pledge to the creditor, if by chance that property later comes into the ownership of the person who pledged it (provided the creditor was ignorant that it belonged to another), it then becomes subject to the pledge or mortgage by that very fact. The creditor then has a legal action to have the property delivered to him. Otherwise, the person who pledged it is forced by the pledge action to provide another item of equal quality as security. These rules generally apply when someone else's property is pledged without the owner's consent and without the creditor knowing it belonged to another. However, when the creditor knew it belonged to someone else, he is only entitled to be repaid his debt; he cannot demand another item be pledged in its place.

Returning to the first scenario mentioned: when property was pledged while the owner knew and remained silent at the time, and the creditor was ignorant of the ownership. In this case, the property remains subject to the pledge just as if the owner had consented. This is supported by the Code and the fifth *Partida*. This also agrees with common law regarding a husband who pledges his wife's separate <note>original: "paraphernalē"</note> property; if the wife knows and is silent, and the creditor is ignorant, the pledge stands. In such a case, the wife is not helped by the Velleian Decree <note>The *Senatus Consultum Velleianum* was a Roman law that prohibited women from standing as sureties or taking on the debts of others; here, Molina notes it does not apply if she acted fraudulently through silence.</note> because of the fraud. If she had been ignorant of it, the pledge would be invalid. Furthermore, it is the creditor's responsibility to prove that the owner knew the property was being pledged. The ninth law of Title 13, Partida 5, which says that if the owner is present and silent while another pledges his property, he is deemed to consent, is the express provision of the common law, despite what Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous Italian jurist.</note> or Gregorius Lopez <note>Gregorio López de Tovar (1496–1560), a Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> might have said to the contrary.

A tutor or curator <note>A legal guardian for minors or those deemed unfit to manage their own affairs.</note> can also subject property to a pledge...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property management by agents. ...pledge movable property belonging to a minor by his own authority, provided that they subject those items to the pledge while conducting the minor's business and not their own, or that of another <note>original: "l. curator, & leg. si in rem. C. si aliena res pign. l. tutor, in prin, ff. de pignorat. act, & l. 8. tit. 13. part. 5." — citing the Code and Digest of Roman law alongside the Spanish Siete Partidas.</note>. However, this is not to be understood as applying to "precious" movables that can be kept safely (such as jewelry or heirlooms); for a tutor or curator cannot alienate these without a judge's decree, and consequently cannot subject them to a pledge or mortgage, because that is considered a form of alienation <term>alienatio</term> (transfer of ownership rights), as we showed extensively in Dispute 224 and as the glosses on the cited laws affirm. Nor do I approve of the opinion of Gregorio López <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist who wrote the standard commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> regarding the cited Law 8, who asserts that in the Kingdom of Castile, tutors or curators can pledge or mortgage even precious movable goods that could be preserved. Although he eventually leaves it as a matter for further thought, that law speaks in the same way as the other common laws cited, and therefore must be interpreted in the same manner as they are. Regarding **immovable property** (real estate), tutors or curators cannot subject it to a pledge or mortgage without a judge's decree, as is expressly stated in the cited Law 8, the laws "curator" and "tutor," and as is evident from the arguments in Dispute 224. 

Observe, however, that it is one thing for a tutor or curator to subject a minor's movable property to a pledge or mortgage while conducting the minor's business; it is quite another for the thing for which they were pledged to have actually been converted to the minor’s benefit. This second condition is only necessary when the reason for the pledge is a loan <term>mutuum</term>. Unless the creditor later proves that the loan was converted to the minor's benefit—just as the minor is not held to repay such a loan (as shown in Dispute 500)—the minor's goods do not contract any obligation of pledge or mortgage for that loan. The cited laws "curator" and "tutor" do not deal with this second issue, but only with the first: they establish that when a minor's movable property is pledged while conducting the minor's business, the property truly contracts that burden, even if it is not later converted to or results in the minor’s benefit. For in contracts other than loans, the creditor is not required to prove that the transaction was converted to the minor's benefit, as seen in Dispute 300. In the law "if into the matter" <note>original: "l. si in rem"</note>, it is held that when a tutor or curator pledges a minor's property while conducting his own business and not the minor's, the pledge is invalid unless the minor later consents and ratifies it after reaching the age of twenty-five <note>In Roman and early modern law, "minority" often extended to age 25.</note>. In that case, the obligation arises from such consent or ratification; this is to be understood even if the tutor or curator had obligated the minor's immovable property.

However, when a tutor or curator subjects some of his own property to a pledge or mortgage as security for a contract he was making in favor of the minor, the pledge is valid. The same is true if anyone else subjects their own property to a pledge or mortgage on behalf of another. <note>original: "l. & si is. §. vlt. C. de præd. min. & l. 8. tit. 13. part. 5."</note>

<column-break/>

# Pledge and mortgage: in which obligations they have a place, and whether they can be established under a condition or for a specific day. And whether a thing obligated to one person can be subjected to a pledge or mortgage to another.

## DISPUTE 532.

-> SUMMARY <-

1 *Pledge and mortgage can be provided and have a place in every contract and obligation. Likewise for a whole debt or a part, even for a "natural" obligation alone, and even for someone else's debt.*
2 *A pledge and mortgage are understood to be suspended until a condition is fulfilled.*
3 *When a thing already obligated to one person can be subjected to another.*
4 *When a later creditor can act against a debtor to compel them to subject another suitable thing to a mortgage and pledge. Likewise, when one can act regarding the crime of swindling.*
5 *When the crime of swindling is considered to have been committed.*

1 Items can be subjected to a pledge or mortgage in any contract and obligation, whether it is "pure" (unconditional), for a future day, or under a condition; and whether the contract is made in the present or was already celebrated previously; indeed, they can be subjected for the entire obligation. They can likewise be subjected for the whole debt or obligation, or for only a part of it; and not only for a civil obligation but also for a "natural" one <term>naturalis obligatio</term> (an obligation that is morally binding but not legally enforceable by action); and not only for one's own obligation and debt, but also for another's. However, when things are pledged for a conditional obligation, just as the condition suspends the obligation so that it does not fully arise except depending on the fulfillment of the condition—and at the time the condition is fulfilled (as said in Dispute 406)—so, even if the thing was pledged unconditionally for that obligation, it does not remain obligated for it except depending on that same condition existing. Therefore, the creditor cannot bring a mortgage action <term>actio hypothecaria</term> in the meantime while the condition has not been fulfilled. All these points are found in the law "property of mortgage" <note>original: "l. res hypothecæ. ff. de pign."</note>. This last point is also found in the law "flock" <note>original: "l. grege. §. si sub conditione. ff. eod. tit."</note>, where it is defined that if the creditor brings a mortgage action in that event before the condition is fulfilled, they will lose the case; nevertheless, if the condition is fulfilled later, they can bring the action, with nothing hindering them because they lost previously.

2 When, on the other hand, the debt or obligation is "pure" (unconditional), but something is pledged for that obligation under a condition or for a future day, then before that condition is fulfilled or the day arrives, one cannot take action regarding the pledge or mortgage. This is because before that day or the fulfillment of the condition, the thing is not obligated for that debt or for the fulfillment of that obligation. This is held in the law "flock" and the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. 17. tit. 13. part. 5."</note>.

## Second Treatise, Dispute 53, Part 2

If, however, there exists some just cause—which, as Gregorio López <note>original: "Greg. Lop. l. 17." — referring to his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> rightly says along with Bartolus, might arise after a thing has been subjected to a future date or condition as a pledge or mortgage, or which the creditor was previously unaware of—for which it is necessary for the pledge or mortgage to be delivered beforehand, or for the owner of the pledge to be forced to provide suitable security (for instance, because he is suspected of fleeing with the pledge or mortgage, or some similar reason), then he must be compelled to either provide suitable security or to deliver the pledge or mortgage before that day or before the condition is fulfilled. This is held in the paragraph "if under condition" <note>original: "§. si sub conditione"</note> as cited, and in the law "it was asked" <note>original: "l. quæsitum est." — references to the Digest of Roman Law (ff.).</note> regarding pledges, the law "in all things" regarding judgments, and the cited law 17.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the last of the points proposed, it must be said: the fact that things are bound to one person by a **universal mortgage** <note>A mortgage covering all of a person’s current and future property.</note> does not prevent them from being bound to another by a universal mortgage, or for some of those things to be subjected to a **particular mortgage** or pledge for another person. This is consistent with Angelo <note>Angelo de Ubaldis, a famous medieval jurist.</note> on the Code regarding the crime of fraud, and Gregorio López on law 10, title 13, part 5, gloss 1; otherwise, trade and commerce would be greatly hindered without just cause.

However, when a thing already subjected to one particular mortgage or pledge is then bound to another person, a distinction must be made. If it is of such value that it suffices to pay both debts, then this is done lawfully and without penalty, as held in the law "if anyone in a pledge," final paragraph <note>original: "l. si quis in pignore. §. vlt."</note> and the cited law 10. But if it is not sufficient, and it is done with the knowledge of both creditors, then since no injury is done to one who is willing and consenting, it is also done without penalty. Unless the first creditor consents in such a way that he wishes the other to be preferred over him in that pledge or mortgage, the first creditor is certainly preferred over the later one; thus, that property will not remain bound to the later creditor except regarding any surplus value, and only after the first creditor has been fully satisfied from other sources, as held in the law "and those not yet," final paragraph.

The same applies if it is bound without the first creditor's knowledge, but with the second creditor's knowledge or warning, as is clearly gathered from the law "tutor" <note>original: "l. tutor. §. 1."</note> and the law "if anyone in a pledge," because no prejudice is done to the first, and there is no injury to the second since they knew the situation. 

If, however, it is bound with the knowledge of the first creditor but without the knowledge of the second, then unless the first creditor objects and warns the second creditor, I believe the second creditor should be preferred in that pledge. This is based on the arguments made in the preceding dispute: when a thing is subjected to a pledge or mortgage with the owner's knowledge while another person is unaware that it belongs to someone else, unless the owner objects and warns the creditor, the thing remains subject to that pledge or mortgage. The same reasoning applies here: the pledge or mortgage remains fully bound to the later creditor, with the prior claim posing no obstacle, as the first creditor is deemed to have waived his right due to the fraud he consented to, with the effect that the thing remains entirely bound to the later creditor.

<margin>4</margin> When, however—as frequently happens—the debtor binds a thing to a second person that was already bound to a first, without either creditor knowing, and the thing is not sufficient for both debts, then † first and foremost, the later creditor can act against the debtor with a **mortgage action** <term>hypothecaria actione</term> <note>A legal claim to seize property used as collateral.</note> 

<column-break/>

to force him to subject another thing sufficient for paying the debt as a pledge or mortgage. This is held in the law "tutor," paragraph 1, and the law "if anyone in a pledge," final paragraph, and law 10, title 13, part 5.

Furthermore, he can bring a case for the **crime of stellionate** <term>stellionatus</term> <note>A term in Roman and Civil law for fraud, specifically selling or pledging the same thing to two different people.</note> against him, unless the debtor, before the action for stellionate is brought against him, actually offers payment of the debt to either both creditors or one of them. For by the very fact that he has fully paid one, the later creditor remains without any loss from the fact that the thing, previously bound to another, was bound to him while he was ignorant. The crime of stellionate has this privilege: if the fault is cleared in the aforementioned way before the action is brought, the action has no place, and consequently 

<margin>5</margin> neither does the penalty for that crime. † The crime of stellionate is considered to be committed when, through craftiness and imposture, something is done for which no ordinary penalty is found imposed in the law, but the crime is left to be punished at the judge's discretion, as held in laws 1, 2, and 3 of the Digest regarding the crime of stellionate. 

This crime was named after the **stellion** animal <note>A type of spotted lizard.</note> (called a *tarantola* in Spanish <note>In this historical context, Molina likely refers to a gecko or a wall lizard, which was often confused with the "stellio" due to its spots.</note>), which is of various colors and decorated as if with stars <note>original: "quasi stellis depicto"</note>. It is said that every year it sheds its skin, which is a most potent remedy for the "comitial disease" <note>Epilepsy.</note>; yet as soon as it sheds it, it devours the skin so as to snatch away this potent remedy from man. Its bite, though it rarely kills a man, nevertheless causes numbness and affects him in various ways. Because of its variety of color, its craftiness, and the quality of its bite, the name was given to this crime from this animal. 

Among the types of this crime (listed in the cited law 3 and other laws soon to be cited) are: if someone binds, sells, or alienates by another burdensome title a thing already bound to one person to another person who is ignorant of it. Likewise, if, when he has first bound a thing to one, he later pretends it was previously bound to another, so as to prefer that other person over this one. Likewise, if he knowingly says he is delivering gold as a pledge and delivers brass <note>original: "aurichalcum"</note>, or deceives the creditor in some other similar way. Likewise, if, after promising something as a pledge, he delivers or substitutes another thing in its place; for if, after the pledge is delivered, he secretly takes it and substitutes another, he is considered to have committed **theft**. 

Likewise, if he knowingly and prudently subjects someone else's property to a pledge or mortgage to a person who is unaware of it. For if he did this while ignorant that it belonged to someone else, he would not incur the crime of stellionate, as his ignorance would excuse him; nevertheless, he would still be compelled by a mortgage action to subject another thing as a pledge or mortgage, just as if he had knowingly bound it to a second creditor. Both points are held in the law "tutor" and "if anyone in a pledge." The first point is also found in law 3 of the Digest on the crime of stellionate. That the action for stellionate is available to a creditor against one who bound a thing already pledged to another to him while he was ignorant is held in the two laws just cited. That the crime is cleared if the debtor offers full payment of his debt to either or both creditors before the action for stellionate is brought is held in law 1, joined with the gloss there.

### Whether a thing subjected to a pledge or mortgage remains subject to it if it undergoes some change, increase, or decrease.

## DISPUTATION 533.

-> SUMMARY <-

1 *If a house pledged as security collapses or is burned down, the land remains bound.*
2 *The same must be said of a vineyard and an olive grove. Number 2.*
3 *The same applies to land destroyed by a flood where some part remains. Number 3.*
4 *If a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage is changed, it remains similarly bound.*
5 *An option is given to a third-party possessor who has improved the property: either to pay the value of the property as it was before the improvement, or to receive the value of the improvements and surrender the property itself.*
6 *If a forest is subject to a pledge, even its cut timber is subject to it, unless they were intended for some specific work.*

<margin>1</margin>
If a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage is partially destroyed, and some of it remains, that which remains continues to be subject to the pledge or mortgage. For instance, if a house which was subject to a † pledge or mortgage collapses or is burned down, the ground itself remains subject to the pledge or mortgage. <note>original: "l. domo ff. de pig. act." — Law regarding the action for pledges in the Roman Digest.</note> This is also held in Law 15, Title 13, Part 5. And the same

<margin>2</margin>
can be said if a vineyard or olive grove subject to a pledge or mortgage is destroyed, for the ground itself remains similarly subject. The same is true if an estate subject to a pledge or mortgage is destroyed by **accretion** <term>accretion: the gradual addition of land by the action of water, known as alluvio</term>; for whatever remains stays subject to the pledge or mortgage.

<margin>4</margin>
But if a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage is changed—such as ground being converted into a vineyard or olive grove, or a house into a garden—or if something is added to the thing, such as land added to an estate by a flood, or the right of use <note>original: "usufructus"</note> being added to the ownership, or a house being built on the ground, all these things are similarly subject to the pledge or mortgage. <note>Molina cites several laws from the Digest to support the idea that improvements and natural growth belong to the creditor's security.</note> However, if some increase or improvement has been made, not by the effort and expense of the debtor, but by the effort and expense of some third-party

<column-break/>

possessor, then, although the thing (with that increase) is subject to the pledge or mortgage, the third-party possessor is not bound to hand it over to satisfy the debt for which it was obligated unless he is first paid what he spent, or the amount by which the value of the thing increased due to his industry and expenses. This is held in the Digest <note>original: "l. cum postulaffem. §. damni, ff. de dam. infect." — Law regarding damage not yet committed.</note>. (I do not think, when the buyer is compared there with one who repaired a house handed over to him because of a threat of damage, that the discussion is about the price the buyer first gave for that house, but rather about what he likewise spent in repairing and improving the purchased house). The same is held in the cited Law 15. Therefore, if someone granted the surface of a plot of land—which was subject to a pledge and whose house had been burned and destroyed—to another so that he might build a house on it again, and that third party built the house; certainly, although the house built by this third party is similarly subject to the pledge or mortgage, he is not bound to hand it over to satisfy the debt unless he is first paid what he spent in building that house, insofar as the ground with that house is worth more than it would be if the house had not been rebuilt.

However, Gregorio López, in the cited Law 10, under the words "in good faith" <note>original: "en buona fe"</note>, excellently asserts along with Bartolus and others that when a thing has been improved by a third-party possessor, an **option** is given to him: either to pay the value of that thing as it stands without those improvements (since the thing is not liable for more than that in satisfying the debt), or to produce the thing after first receiving the amount it is worth more by reason of the improvements, as has been said. I do not approve of the contrary opinion of Covarrubias, who confesses it goes against Bartolus and the common view; namely, that a third-party possessor who improved the thing does not satisfy the law if he offers the creditor as much as the thing is then worth without improvements, but can be forced to hand it over with the improvements, receiving their price. Indeed, the laws he relies on do not prove his opinion. The reason why increases that happen while the thing belongs to the debtor are subject to the pledge (even if done at his own expense and industry) is because they merge with the principal thing and form one whole with it; and because the debtor is not more burdened by paying from there, if he does not pay from elsewhere, than by what he truly owes and for which debt he subjected that thing as security. When the creditor himself held the pledged thing and made some improvements to it or spent something usefully, then these are similarly subject to the pledge; however, when the debt is paid to him and he returns the pledge, he must be paid for what he usefully spent; otherwise, he can retain the pledge for those expenses. Yet he is bound to return the thing with the fruits perceived from it, and those which through his own fault he did not perceive.

Which fruits from a thing subject to a mortgage are considered subject to the mortgage when the thing is possessed by a third party, and which are not, was explained in Disputation 529. However, when some such fruits are to be considered subject to a mortgage according to...

what was said in that place should not be understood only regarding the fruits of the thing itself, viewed strictly apart from the improvements made to it by a third-party possessor, but also regarding the fruits corresponding to those improvements. Covarruvias <note>original: "Couar. vbi sup. nu 4"</note>, in the place cited above at number 4, along with others, holds that this includes the fruits corresponding to the improvements. We, however, showed the contrary in Dispute 455 and Dispute 463, noting that Covarruvias later revoked this opinion in the Zaragoza edition, as was stated in those places.

<margin>6</margin> Finally, it must be observed that when someone holds a forest, for example, that is subject to a pledge or mortgage, the wood cut from it remains similarly subject to the pledge or mortgage, as they are considered parts and fruits of the pledged item. However, if a ship, a house, or another manufactured object is made from that wood, they cease to have the status of a pledge or mortgage, unless this had been specifically provided for. The reason for this is that the material has now been changed into another thing. This is held in Law 6, Section 2 <note>original: "l. 6 conuenerit. 2. §. si quis ff. de pign. act." — referring to the Digest of Justinian regarding the "action of pledge."</note> and is affirmed by Gregorio López on the cited Law 13, at the word "similar," along with Bartolus and others. Negusantius <note>original: "Negat de pignorib."</note> in his work on pledges, part 6, member 3, says that if a thing perishes in its substance, and not merely in its quality, the status of the pledge or mortgage that was upon it is extinguished, following the law "as in the beginning" in the Digest on how a pledge is ended. From this it follows that if a mortgaged ship is destroyed, the wood does not remain subject to the mortgage; and if an animal dies, the hide and the meat are not subject to the mortgage. This opinion is pleasing, although it could be said regarding that text that it only speaks of cases where the thing perishes so entirely that nothing of it remains. But if a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage perishes through the fault of its owner, then a mortgage action is available against him to compel him to subject an equivalent amount to the pledge or mortgage. Thus says Negusantius at the cited number.

->**When the delivery or obligation of a pledge is made through some instrument, the property contained in it is considered obligated as a pledge. And how a general mortgage action can be brought against the debtor or the possessor of the mortgaged property.**<-

### DISPUTATION 534.

<margin>1</margin> One who delivers a writing or instrument as a pledge is considered to have obligated that which is contained within them.
<margin>2</margin> However, the thing itself is not necessarily considered delivered; see number 2.
<margin>3</margin> One who delivers a thing as a pledge remains in **civil possession** <term>civil possession: legal ownership and right to possess, even if physical control is held by another</term>.
<margin>4</margin> When a debtor should be warned to pay before an action is brought against him, whether by a personal or mortgage action.
<margin>5</margin> When and in what order a mortgage action should be brought against a third-party possessor.
<margin>6</margin> What must be proven before a mortgage action is brought against a third-party possessor.
<margin>7</margin> In what events a mortgage action can be brought against a third-party possessor, whether regarding the seizure of goods or the pursuit of guarantors; see number 8.
<margin>9</margin> In what case a creditor may swear an oath in court against

<column-break/>

the debtor or a third-party possessor who holds the property subject to the mortgage.
<margin>10</margin> The right of mortgage is far different from an **annuity** <term>census: a censo, or a right to annual income</term>, whether real or personal.

**I**f anyone obligates or delivers as a pledge a writing or an instrument of gift, sale, or another title by which some property belongs to him, he is considered to subject to the pledge that property which belongs to him by that title. This is held in Law 2 of the Code on what things can be obligated as a pledge <note>original: "l. 2. C. quæ res pignor. oblig. poss."</note> and Law 14, Title 13, Part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*.</note>. However, Gregorio López observes there in gloss 1, agreeing with Azo and consistently with the gloss on the cited Law 2, and much more consistently with the cited Law 14, <margin>1</margin> that from the sole delivery of such an instrument as a pledge, the property described in the instrument is indeed considered obligated as a pledge, but the property itself is not considered delivered as a pledge until the physical delivery of that same property occurs.

Nor does it stand in the way, he says, that—as was stated in Dispute 13 regarding the second method by which possession is considered delivered by a **fictitious act** <term>traditio ficta: a "fictional delivery" where the law treats a symbolic act, like handing over keys or papers, as the transfer of the actual object</term>—possession of the property contained in an instrument is considered delivered by the delivery of the instrument. For, he says, that is true when a title has preceded it, such as a sale, gift, or exchange of that property for another, and the delivery of the instrument for that same property follows. For then, it seems to have been delivered for no other purpose than that the delivery of possession of the property contained within it should be made through it. But the matter is different when only the instrument is delivered or obligated as a pledge, as happens in the case proposed, lest two fictions be understood to occur simultaneously in a single act—namely, the obligation of the property as a pledge by the delivery of its instrument, and the delivery of that same property through that same delivery of the instrument.

Hence I would say: if a contract preceded it by which some property was subjected to a pledge, and afterward the delivery of the instrument for that property followed, then the property is considered delivered as a pledge through the instrument, which property had previously been subjected to the pledge by contract without delivery. I would say the same if the thing itself and its instrument were simultaneously subjected to the pledge and the instrument was delivered; for then that delivery of the instrument seems to serve no other purpose than to deliver the thing as a pledge, which is simultaneously and expressly subjected to the pledge in itself. However, we are not dealing with that matter now, but with the delivery of instruments as a pledge.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding those things added in the cited Law 14, I should give a warning. In that law, in my judgment, as is clear from its entire sequence, the discussion is not about "pledge" in the broad sense (which includes "mortgage" strictly speaking), but about "pledge" in the strict sense, as it is distinguished from "mortgage" and from specific pledges (which I do not know if Gregorio López sufficiently attended to in that law). The discussion in that law, therefore, concerns one who obligated a thing as a pledge but has not yet delivered that obligated thing to the creditor. Thus, it is immediately added in that law that the creditor can compel him or his heirs to deliver it to him. This surely has no place in a mortgage or a specific pledge; for the debtor is not bound to deliver it to the creditor as security for the debt, since in this a mortgage is distinguished from a pledge: <margin>3</margin> a pledge is made to be delivered as security for the debt before the time for payment arrives.

<margin>3</margin> ...the mortgage is established, but a pledge is not. It is added in the same law that if the person who was bound to deliver a thing as a pledge sells, exchanges, or otherwise alienates it—or subjects it to a later pledge—before delivering it and putting the creditor in possession of it, certain rules apply. (Understand this regarding the effects for which a conventional pledge is delivered, for which the creditor possesses it, even civilly, as held in Law *Cum & fortis*, final paragraph <note>original: "l.cum & fortis. §.vlt. ff. de pignor. act." — referring to the Digest of Justinian regarding the "action of pledge"</note>, and Law *Si de eo* at the beginning <note>original: "l. si de eo, in princ. ff. de acquir. poss." — regarding the acquisition of possession</note>. For in other respects, the one who delivers the thing as a pledge remains in civil possession of that thing, and possesses it naturally through the creditor who holds it, as explained in the gloss on Law *Sciendum*, paragraph *Creditor* <note>original: "gl. l. sciẽdum. §. creditor ff. qui satisd. cog."</note>). In such a case, the creditor to whom it was first pledged but not delivered can seek satisfaction of the debt from the debtor. If the debtor chooses to pay, he leaves the person to whom it was delivered free of the claim. However, if the debtor does not satisfy the debt, the creditor can then seek from the possessor or holder of the item that it be delivered to him, as it was previously bound to him by a real burden <note>term: real burden <gloss>a legal obligation attached to the physical property itself, rather than just the person</gloss></note> and was due to be delivered for the security of his debt. It is also added that if the debtor alienated the thing or pledged it to another after the creditor had already demanded its delivery, the creditor has the full right to either first demand payment from the debtor or immediately seek from the possessor or holder that the item be delivered to him to be held as security for his debt.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding the mortgage <note>term: mortgage <gloss>original: "hypotheca" — a legal claim on property as security for a debt where the debtor typically keeps possession</gloss></note>, when the time arrives for payment or satisfaction of the debt for which the thing or things were mortgaged, either a specific day was set for that payment or not. In the latter case, it was left as if "precarious" <note>term: precarious <gloss>original: "praecarium" — a legal arrangement where something is held by the permission of another and can be revoked at any time</gloss></note>, to be paid whenever demanded, or no date was set for some other reason. In the first scenario, where a payment date was established, the debtor should be warned to pay out of courtesy and decency before an action is brought against him—whether a personal action or a mortgage action—but this is not strictly necessary by law, as held in Law *Debitores* <note>original: "l. debitores, C. de pig." — referring to the Code of Justinian</note>, because "the day demands on behalf of the creditor" <note>original: "dies pro creditore interpellat" — a legal maxim meaning that when a deadline is set, the passing of the date itself serves as a legal demand for payment</note>. In the second scenario, however, he must be warned first to pay, as the glosses on the cited Law *Debitores* and others affirm; otherwise, the debtor is not yet considered to be in "default" <note>term: default <gloss>original: "mora" — a legal delay or failure to perform an obligation on time</gloss></note> of payment. Meanwhile, as long as the debtor is not in default, a personal or mortgage action cannot be brought against him, and much less a mortgage action for the items subject to the debt, as Negusantius notes along with Bartolus and others in his work *On Pledges*.

Therefore, when the debtor is already in default of paying that for which the thing or things are mortgaged, a distinction must be made. Either the action is intended to be brought against the debtor himself, or his heirs, or against the "unclaimed estate" <note>term: unclaimed estate <gloss>original: "haereditatem iacentem" — an estate where no heir has yet formally accepted the inheritance</gloss></note> (because no heir has yet approached it), or a mortgage action is intended against a third-party possessor of the mortgaged thing to whom that thing has been alienated. I say "to whom it has been alienated," because if someone holds it only as a borrower or a de-

<column-break/>

-pository <note>term: depository <gloss>someone holding an item for safekeeping</gloss></note>, the thing still belongs to the debtor, his heirs, or his unclaimed estate. We are not speaking here of such a holder as if we were calling him a "third-party possessor." In the first scenario, then—when the action is intended against the debtor, his heirs, or the unclaimed estate—the creditor has the option either to bring a personal action, or a mortgage action, or both simultaneously. He may request in his lawsuit that they either pay the debt or deliver the mortgaged items to him so they may be sold and the debt paid from the proceeds. By the very fact that the delivery or seizure of those items is carried out by judicial authority so they may be sold and the debt satisfied, they begin to take on the character of a "judicial pledge." That both actions can be brought against the debtor or his heirs in the manner explained is expressly held in the *Authentic* collection regarding guarantors <note>original: "authentico de fideiussoribus" — referring to the "Novels" or new laws of Justinian</note> in the section *Sed neque*, which states: "Against the principals, however, whose things are in their possession—whether personal or mortgaged—we grant full permission to use either or both [actions] as they wish." This was granted long ago by us in the final Law of the Code *On Actions and Obligations* and other laws.

<margin>5</margin> However, in the second scenario—when the action is intended against a *third-party possessor* of the thing or things mortgaged for that debt—the rules have changed. Formerly, if the mortgage was "implied" <note>term: implied <gloss>original: "tacita" — a mortgage created by law rather than by specific contract</gloss></note>, it was forbidden to act unless an "exhaustion of assets" <note>term: exhaustion of assets <gloss>original: "excussione" — the legal requirement to first seize and sell the primary debtor's property before going after property they sold to others</gloss></note> was first performed on the debtor's goods. If the debt was not satisfied from that, then it was permitted to bring a mortgage action against the third-party possessor for the remainder, as held in Law *Moschis* <note>original: "l. Moschis, in prin. ff. de iure fisci"</note>. If, however, the mortgage was "express" (specifically contracted), one could immediately bring the mortgage action against the third-party possessor without any exhaustion of the debtor's assets, according to various older laws. Today, however, under the "Authentic" law, whether the mortgage is implied or express, it is forbidden to bring a mortgage action against a third-party possessor unless an exhaustion of assets is first performed on the goods of the debtor and the guarantors <note>original: "fideiussorum"</note> who were provided for the same debt. One must bring both personal and real actions (if the debtor has other property bound for the same debt) against the debtor, his heirs, or the unclaimed estate, as well as against the guarantors or their heirs. After seizing the goods they possess—whether they specifically mortgaged them for that debt or not—and once a judge's sentence has been passed (as Bartolus and others affirm, whom Negusantius follows), if it is found that they do not have enough goods to satisfy the debt in full, then finally the mortgage action can be brought against the third-party possessor of the mortgaged thing to satisfy what is lacking. This is expressly held in the cited *Authentic* on guarantors and other related statutes. Therefore, if a mortgage action is brought against a third-party possessor before such an exhaustion of the debtor’s or guarantors' assets is performed, then according to the laws most...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 534.

...as cited above, he is entitled to the defense <note>original: "exceptio"</note> that an exhaustion of assets <term>excussio<gloss>a legal requirement that a creditor must first attempt to collect a debt from the primary debtor's own property before seizing mortgaged property held by a third party</gloss></term> must first be performed on the goods of the debtor or the guarantors. Because this type of defense is merely dilatory <note>meaning it delays rather than cancels the action</note>, it must be raised by the third-party possessor before the case is formally contested <note>original: "ante litem contestatam"</note> while the mortgage action is being moved against him; otherwise, it has no place afterward, even in a second instance or during an appeal, as observed by Negusantius (cited above, number 36) along with Bartolus and others.

<margin>6</margin> Therefore, when a mortgage action <term>actio hypothecaria<gloss>a legal proceeding to foreclose on property used as collateral for a debt</gloss></term> is brought against a third-party possessor, all these things must be proven by the creditor for the action to have force against that third party. First, that the specific thing or things he possesses, and regarding which the mortgage action is intended, were bound by the debtor for that debt, and that they belonged to the debtor when he bound them (or that they subsequently came into his ownership, if it was a general mortgage), or that they were bound by the debtor with the owner's consent or subsequent ratification, as was said in Disputation 529. Next, he must prove that the debtor was in default <note>original: "in mora"</note> of paying the debt for which the mortgages were subject, as stated above. Likewise, he must prove that an exhaustion of assets was performed on the goods of the debtor, or even the guarantors, and that the debt cannot be satisfied from their goods, as was just stated. However, if any third-party possessor against whom the mortgage action is brought effectively offers the debtor what is owed in good faith, the mortgage action would cease; for once the debt is paid in full, there is no reason for further action, nor can the creditor refuse that payment. This is held in Law *Si fundus*, paragraph *Si in vendicatione* <note>original: "ff. de pig." — referring to the Digest on pledges</note>; Law *Mulier* <note>original: "ff. qui potior. in pig."</note>; Law *Paulus*, final paragraph <note>original: "ff. quib. mod. pign. vel hypot. sol."</note>; and Law 18, Title 13, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish legal code</note>. And then, if the possessor who paid the debt demands it, the creditor is bound to yield to him the rights he held against the debtor and the mortgage. This is held in the cited Laws *Mulier* and Law 18.

<margin>7</margin> However, in the following events, a mortgage action can be brought against a third-party possessor without first performing an exhaustion of the assets of the debtor and guarantors. First, if after a lawsuit was initiated against the debtor regarding that debt, the debtor alienated <note>transferred ownership of</note> the thing subject to the mortgage. For although it is within the debtor's right, even after a lawsuit is brought against him, to alienate things subject to a mortgage for that same debt—and even things given as a pledge to a creditor—so that he may pay the debt from the price, and the creditor cannot prevent this (though he can retain the pledge in his possession until the debt is paid to him from the price); nevertheless, if the debtor alienates them and does not pay the price, the creditor can immediately bring a mortgage action against the third-party possessor so they may be handed over and sold, so that the debt is satisfied from the price. This holds unless there is someone else who has a prior or more privileged mortgage on the same things and who contends he must be paid first; for then he will be preferred in the payment of his debt from the price of those things. This is held in the *Authenticum de litigiosis* <note>a collection of Justinian's laws regarding property in litigation</note>, paragraph *Ad hoc autem*, and in the *Authenticum hoc ita* <note>C. de pign.</note>. For by the very fact that a lawsuit or execution for the debt is initiated against the debtor, the things existing in his possession and mortgaged for that debt are considered, as it were, "litigious," and therefore prohibited from being alienated, unless it is done wisely so that the debt is effectively paid from the price. For that reason, if the debt is not effectively paid from the price, a mortgage

<column-break/>

action is granted against the possessor, even if no exhaustion of assets was performed on the goods of the debtors and guarantors. And this is what is intended in the cited *Authenticum de litigiosis* and in the *Authenticum hoc ita* regarding pledges, which is taken from the former where the matter is more fully defined; Bartolus and others, whom Negusantius (above, numbers 10 and 17) refers to and follows, affirm this.

<margin>8</margin> The second scenario is when the debtor is notoriously insolvent, nor has guarantors who are solvent; for then a mortgage action is granted against a third-party possessor without first performing an exhaustion on the principal debtor, because it cannot then be done upon him. This is held by Negusantius (above, number 34) with Bartolus and others. By this same reasoning, when the debtor's property is in another territory and an exhaustion of assets regarding them would not be easy, or if they were in a fortified place so they could not be obtained, an action could be brought immediately against the third-party possessor, as the same Negusantius asserts with many others (ibid., number 42). The same author discusses certain other scenarios (ibid., from number 16) as does Gregorio López (Law 14, Title 13, Part 5, on the word *primeramente*).

<margin>9</margin> If, once a mortgage action is initiated—whether against the debtor still possessing the thing subject to the mortgage, or against a third-party possessor of the same thing—the possessor fraudulently <note>original: "dolo"</note> sends it to another place or disposes of it so that he can say he can no longer obtain it, then the creditor is granted the right to swear to the value in the lawsuit <note>term: jurare in litem<gloss>a legal oath where the plaintiff estimates the value of the disputed object when the defendant has fraudulently made its recovery impossible</gloss></term> against that possessor, after an estimation of the damage is first made by the judge, so that the damage which the creditor swears followed from it is paid to him beyond the debt. But if, not through fraud but through the fault <note>original: "culpa"</note> of such a possessor, that thing perishes after the lawsuit is moved, then he is only compelled to pay either the debt (if the thing was worth as much as or more than the debt) or the estimated value of the thing. But if by chance, when the lawsuit was initiated, the thing was absent so that it could not be delivered immediately, then he is compelled to provide security <note>original: "cautionem"</note> that within a certain time—to be prescribed by the judge's discretion after considering the concurrent circumstances—he will bring and deliver the thing or pay the debt; and once that security is provided, he is meanwhile released from the judgment. These things are held in Law *Si fundus*, paragraphs *In vendicatione* and *Si pluris*, and Law *Si inter*, final paragraph <note>Digest on pledges</note>, and more clearly in Law 19, Title 13, Part 5. Although what was said regarding the oath in the lawsuit for paying damages (in the cited paragraph *Si pluris*) is said to be understood according to the rigor of the law, it is otherwise according to equity as far as it pertains to the debtor himself, and Law *Si inter* (final paragraph) seems to agree. However, the cited Law of Castile 19 establishes that the rigor of the law is to be followed.

<margin>10</margin> Observe, as was discussed more copiously in Disputation 382, that it is a far different thing for a certain "real ground-rent" <term>census realis<gloss>an annual payment tied specifically to a piece of land; if the land is destroyed, the debt typically ends</gloss></term> to be placed on a certain estate, such that the estate itself owes an annual pension, or it is owed from it in such a way that if the estate perishes, the right of collecting that pension or the real ground-rent itself perishes; and it is a far different thing for that estate to be subject to a mortgage. For when a thing is only subject to a mortgage—whether for the security and payment of a personal ground-rent, or for the security and payment of a real ground-rent placed on another thing, or for the security of the payment of any other debt—and the thing so mortgaged...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights and debts. Specifically, it distinguishes between a general mortgage and a "real annuity" (census realis) attached to a property, then transitions into Disputation 535 concerning the rules for physical pledges (pignus).</meta>

# Ludovico Molina on Contracts
## Page 726

<column-break/>

When property subject to a mortgage passes to a third-party possessor, in both cases <note>likely referring to the previous page's distinction between types of debt</note>, before the property can be seized for that annuity or debt, there must be an exhaustion of assets <term>excussio<gloss>the legal requirement for a creditor to first pursue the primary debtor's other assets before seizing property held by a third party</gloss></term> against the goods of the original debtor and his guarantors. However, when the property upon which a real annuity <term>census realis<gloss>a fixed annual payment tied specifically to a piece of land, similar to a ground rent</gloss></term> is placed passes to a third-party possessor, that burden or debt is owed by the property itself or by reason of the property. Therefore, the debt passes to the new possessor along with the property. It is the new possessor who owes the burden by reason of the property having become his own, rather than the original debtor. He can and must be immediately compelled to acknowledge himself as the debtor of that annuity because of that property, as was stated in the cited disputation. Therefore, to seek the annuity from him or to execute the debt against him, there is no need to first exhaust the assets of the original debtor or his guarantors. Indeed, subsequent payments <note>original: "pensiones"</note> of that annuity cannot thereafter be demanded from the original debtor; since the ownership of the property upon which the annuity was placed (and by reason of which the payments are due) no longer belongs to him, he no longer owes them. Instead, they must be demanded from the new possessor and owner of that property.

Thus, when a property is subject to an annuity in this way, it is not considered a simple mortgage; rather, it is a far tighter bond and a "real burden." Consequently, the rules regarding the exhaustion of assets against the primary debtor and guarantors—which are standard for mortgages—do not apply here. Gama, in Decision 315, did not sufficiently attend to this distinction. Exactly the same must be said for any other thing where a real burden is placed upon it to be paid from the thing itself or by reason of it—such as an Ecclesiastical benefice <note>a church office that provides an income</note> in which an annual pension is established to be paid to someone, or a field subject to a tribute to be paid annually or at other fixed times. This even applies to fields from which tithes <note>a one-tenth tax on produce</note> are paid to the Church, under the condition that they bear fruit. For that burden is a real obligation of such fields, and to whomever they pass, they pass with that burden. The same is true for other similar things having a real burden to be paid from themselves or by reason of themselves.

Furthermore, payments that were not yet paid by the first possessor can be demanded indifferently when the property has passed to a new owner: either from the later possessor (who owes them because he is the current owner of the thing) or from the prior possessor (who still owes them because they fell due during the time he held the property). However, if the later possessor pays them, he is granted a right of recourse to demand them from the prior possessor who truly owed them. All of this, along with many other points, is correctly taught by Alvaro Valasco in *On the Right of Emphyteusis* <note>a type of long-term land lease</note>, question 4, numbers 6 and 7; question 17, from number 17; and question 32, from number 13. Therefore, although many doctors <note>legal scholars</note> often call such things "mortgages," they are not truly the mortgages and pledges discussed in the Law or in this specific treatise on pledges and mortgages; they involve a much tighter legal bond. For this reason, in Disputation 536, we do not number them among mortgages, even though Negusantius, in *On Pledges*, part 2, member 6, does include them.

In this disputation, the discussion concerns a pledge <term>pignus<gloss>a physical object handed over to a creditor as security</gloss></term> taken in person, as distinguished from a mortgage <term>hypotheca<gloss>a lien where the debtor usually retains possession of the property</gloss></term>, when it has already been delivered to the creditor for the security of a debt. As it pertains to the first and second points proposed: since a pledge is delivered solely for the security of a debt, and the ownership of it belongs to the debtor, surely both the use and the fruits <note>the income, produce, or profits</note> of it, or their valuation and price, belong to the debtor and not to the creditor. Therefore, if the creditor uses the pledge for his own private benefit without the knowledge and against the will of the owner, he commits theft—not of the value of the pledged object itself, but of the value of its use. This is affirmed by the gloss on the law *quia iumenta* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de fur."</note>, and by Bartolus and Gregorio López on Law 3, and the final gloss. <meta>This page continues the legal discussion of the rights and duties of creditors regarding physical security, known as a pledge (pignus). The previous page established that when property is transferred, certain debts follow the property. This page focuses on how a creditor must account for the income or benefits (fruits) generated by a pledged item while it is in their possession.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 535
## Page 727

...the owner, a distinction must be made. If he consents involuntarily or in a mixed manner—in the same way that someone who pays interest <term>usura<gloss>the practice of charging interest on a loan, often considered a sin or a crime in this period if excessive or poorly structured</gloss></term> consents involuntarily—then the creditor commits usury. This is an open usury if the pledge was given for a loan, and a "cloaked" usury if it was done in expectation of a payment or the fulfillment of another contract. In this case, the creditor is bound to restore the value of that use to the debtor. This is the view of *Navarrus in the Manual, chapter 17, number 203, and Sylvester under the word "pledge," number 7.* If, however, the owner consents out of pure liberality, or at least if such consent is presumed, then it is done lawfully and without any crime. It is in this light that we must understand *Law 20*, which affirms this.

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the fruits <term>fructus<gloss>the produce, income, or profits generated by a piece of property, such as crops from a field or rent from a house</gloss></term> of a pledge, although the creditor may collect them because they are part of the pledge (as is clear from what was said in *disputation 529*), and for that reason he may sell them (as *Panormitanus* affirms in *chapter "cum contra" on pledges, number 1*, following the text there, and with him *Gregorio Lopez on Law 3, title 14, part 7, final gloss*), this is provided that they cannot be preserved until the time of the debt's payment and the return of the pledge. If they could be preserved, he could not sell them, as *Gregorio Lopez* affirms with others in *Law 2, title 13, part 5, second-to-last gloss*. Although, I say, he may collect and sell them, he is nevertheless bound to calculate those fruits, or their price, toward the debt or toward necessary or useful expenses made on the pledge; thus, they ultimately belong to the owner of the pledge. By the name "fruits," we mean what remains after expenses have been deducted. That the creditor may collect the fruits for the stated reason, but is bound to account for them toward the debt, is expressly held in *Law "qui domum," Code on actions concerning pledges; Laws 1 and the last, Code on actions concerning pledges; Law 1, Code on the sale of pledges; Law 2, Code on the agreement of a pledge; Laws 2 and 21, title 13, part 5; and chapter "cum contra" on pledges.*

<margin>4</margin> Therefore, if from the † fruits collected—whether by the first creditor and his heirs, or by another to whom that same pledge was given—the entire original debt is exhausted, the debtor or his heirs must immediately be put back into possession of that thing. For once the right of the first creditor is resolved, and the debt is fully paid from the fruits, the rights of subsequent creditors who held a claim on that same pledge are also resolved. This is what is found in the cited *chapter "cum contra"* and *Law 1, Code on the sale of pledges*, where it is stated that by the law itself, once the creditor has obtained his debt from the fruits, the thing given as a pledge is liberated from that burden.

<margin>5</margin> Furthermore, † it is defined as usury if a creditor does not count the fruits of the pledge toward the debt, or does not return them to the debtor, but instead keeps them for himself as a special profit. This is established in *chapters 1 and 2 on usury, and the chapter "significante" on pledges*, and was also discussed in *disputation 320*.

<margin>6</margin> These things † that have been said about the fruits of a pledge are to be understood similarly regarding a "praetorian" <term>pignus praetorium<gloss>a pledge or seizure of property ordered by a judge or court official (the Praetor) to satisfy a legal judgment, rather than one agreed upon privately</gloss></term> or judicial pledge, while it still retains the character of a pledge and has not yet been sold or transferred by public authority. This is held in *Law "is cui," paragraph "sed quaeri potest," Digest on the possession of legacies; Law "Titia," Digest on payments*; and *Negusantius* affirms this with *Bartolus* and others in *On Pledges, part 5, member 2, number 4*.

<margin>7</margin> However, † must the creditor also account toward the debt, or return to the debtor, the fruits which he *could* have collected from the pledge but did not?

<column-break/>

The side affirming this seems to be expressly supported by *Law 2, Code on actions concerning pledges*, the words of which are: *A creditor who has held a field attached as a pledge must necessarily calculate toward the discharge of the debt the fruits which he collected, or which he ought to have collected.* Likewise, it is held in *Law 2, Code on the agreement of a pledge*: *The labor of these slaves, which the creditor collected or could have collected, shall be counted toward the interest, and afterward toward the principal.* The same is affirmed by the *Gloss on chapter "cum contra" on pledges*, and with it *Panormitanus at number 9*; *Negusantius* in the cited *member 5, number 3*; and it is the common opinion of the doctors against *Hostiensis*. Hostiensis, led by the argument that a "good faith possessor" is not liable for fruits he could have collected, asserted that such a creditor is not liable for fruits he could have collected (subject to certain exceptions). *Gregorio Lopez* also favored this opinion in *Law 2, title 13, part 5, on the word "el qual mo,"* although he was not entirely firm on it and left the matter for further thought.

However, the common opinion is the one to be embraced: if through fraud, gross negligence, or even slight negligence <term>levis culpa<gloss>a legal standard of failure to exercise the degree of care that a reasonably prudent person would take in managing their own affairs</gloss></term>, the creditor did not collect fruits from the pledge which he could have collected, he must count them toward the debt or hand them over to the debtor.

For since the fruits of the pledge go to the creditor, and the contract of the pledge was entered into for the benefit of both the creditor and the debtor, it is rightly decreed that the creditor is bound to account toward the debt—or return to the creditor—even those fruits which he could have collected and, at least by his slight negligence, did not.

Furthermore, when a creditor is put into possession of a praetorian pledge, he is only liable for fraud or gross negligence if the pledge is returned in a worse condition—not for slight negligence (in which a praetorian pledge differs from a conventional one). As is held in *Law "praetor," paragraph "est praeterea,"* joined with the *Gloss there, Digest on the authority of judicial possessions*, *Negusantius* (as cited above, number 5) rightly says that the creditor is liable for fruits he could have collected but did not due to fraud or gross negligence, but not for those he missed through slight negligence.

When a creditor could have found someone to rent a house handed to him as a pledge, and he did not lease it to them, then—whether he lived in the house himself or not—he is liable to the debtor for the full rent. For if he lived in that house, he owes that rent as the price of his own habitation; if, however, he did not live there but left it empty of an inhabitant, he is bound to pay the same rent as a "fruit" which he could have collected from that house and, by his own fault, <margin>8</margin> did not. But if † he could not find a tenant and he lived in the house himself, then a distinction must be made. If he himself was intending to rent another house, then he is the debtor for as much rent as he would have paid for the other house—not necessarily the full value of the pledged house's habitation if that habitation is worth more. This is unless he gained a greater benefit from that habitation and would have willingly paid something more for it than for the inferior house he would have rented; in that case, he pays only that increased amount. But if he would not have rented any other house at all, then he owes nothing.

<summary>This page discusses the legal obligations of a creditor holding a pledge, specifically the requirement to account for any income (fruits) generated by the property toward the repayment of the debt. It establishes that failure to do so constitutes usury and clarifies that creditors are liable for income they could have collected but neglected to through their own fault.</summary>
