# Luis Molina on Contracts
## Page 728

...the debtor is not obligated to pay for the housing; for he provides a benefit to the master of the house by living in it <note>original: "pro habitatione debet... beneficium præstat domino"</note>, and he does not become wealthier because of it. If, however, he would have willingly given something for the residence of that splendid house, then he shall be bound to return only that amount to the debtor, or to subtract it from the debt. These matters should be understood according to what Gregorio Lopez teaches with Paulus de Castro regarding *Law 21, title 13, part 5*, on the words *if he should dwell in it* <note>original Spanish: "si morare en ella"</note>. This concludes the first and second points of those proposed.

<margin>9</margin>
Regarding the third point: if the purpose for which the pledge was given was not fulfilled—for instance, if the money intended as a loan was never actually given—then the item ceases to have the character of a pledge. Consequently, it must be returned immediately. The person who delivered it has a "direct action on the pledge" <term>directa pignoratitiia actio<gloss>a legal claim used by a debtor to demand the return of their property once the obligation is finished</gloss></term> against the creditor to have it returned. The same applies if something was given as a pledge under a condition and that condition was not met; it immediately ceases to be a pledge. Similarly, it must be returned according to the law *solutum* <note>refers to Digest 13.7.9.3</note>. If a slave girl is given as a pledge and the creditor forces her into prostitution or compels her to do something impious, the items cease to be pledges, and an action may be brought against the creditor for their return. Furthermore, if the debt is paid in full, or satisfied by any other means, or if the creditor accepts something in place of payment, the item given as security ceases to be a pledge and must be returned at once. However, if the creditor had purchased the item in the meantime, he may retain it.

<margin>10</margin>
When an item given as security ceases to be a pledge and its return is demanded, if the creditor does not return it and lacks a just cause for retaining it (either the one mentioned or others we will add), the debtor is permitted to take an "oath for the lawsuit" <term>iurare in litem<gloss>a formal oath where the plaintiff estimates the value of the damages or the item, often used when a defendant wrongfully refuses to produce property</gloss></term>. This forces the creditor to pay for the damages resulting from the retention, after the judge has made an assessment of those damages.

<margin>11</margin>
If the creditor † has incurred any expenses, even daily ones—such as feeding a beast of burden given as a pledge—whether those expenses were necessary or merely useful, the debtor is bound to pay them. The creditor may retain the pledge until they are paid, provided the "useful" expenses are not excessive or of the sort that the debtor, due to poverty or another just cause, would not have wanted made. In such a case, the pledge cannot be held because of them, though in the course of time the debtor might be bound to pay them out of the fruits (income) of the pledge. See the discussion at the end of *disputation 297* and *disputations 463 and 496*.

<margin>12</margin>
When † a pledge was obligated by a debtor to a creditor for a specific debt, if the same debtor later owes something else to the same creditor but did not specifically pledge that same item for the second debt,

<column-break/>

but the creditor only had a personal action for that second debt, then, once the first debt is paid or otherwise abolished, the creditor may nonetheless retain the same pledge until the second debt is paid to him. This is held in the single law <note>refers to the *Constitutio Gordiana*, Code 4.23.1</note>. However, he cannot *sell* the pledge for the second debt as he could for the first; because for the second debt, he is only granted the right of retention <term>retentio<gloss>the right to keep possession of property until a debt is paid, distinct from the right to sell it</gloss></term>. This is the view of the glosses and Gregorio Lopez. If, however, he were to sell the pledge for the first debt and a surplus remained from the price, he could use that surplus to offset the second debt. If the creditor had accepted a pledge for the second debt but it was insufficient, then upon payment of the first debt, he could also retain the first pledge until the second was satisfied. Just as a pledge can be retained for a debt contracted later, so too for a debt contracted before the pledge was received. Likewise, a pledge delivered by a debtor can be retained for another debt of that debtor's heir. However, if the debtor had sold that pledge or obligated it to a third party, and that third party offered the debt for which the pledge was originally given and asked for its return, the creditor could not then claim he wants to keep it until another debt of the same debtor is paid. This is because that right of retention is only granted to the creditor in relation to the debtor, not in relation to a second creditor of the same debtor.

<margin>13</margin>
All these points—namely, that a pledge for one debt can be retained for another debt of the same debtor—similarly apply to "praetorian" and judicial pledges <term>pignus praetorium<gloss>a security interest created by a court order or legal official rather than by a private contract</gloss></term>.

<margin>14</margin>
Regarding the last † of the proposed points: if the pledge perishes or is returned in worse condition, the creditor is only liable for fraud <term>dolus<gloss>intentional wrongdoing or deception</gloss></term>, gross negligence <term>lata culpa<gloss>extreme carelessness, almost reaching the level of intent</gloss></term>, and ordinary negligence <term>leuis culpa<gloss>the failure to act with the care of a reasonable person</gloss></term>. He is not liable for the "slightest negligence" <term>leuissima culpa<gloss>a very minor lack of care that only the most diligent person would avoid</gloss></term>, and much less for an accidental occurrence <term>casus fortuitus<gloss>an act of God or unforeseen accident, like a fire or earthquake</gloss></term>. This is because the contract is celebrated for the benefit of both the debtor and the creditor. In this, the 

<margin>15</margin>
conventional pledge † differs from the praetorian one; for he who holds a praetorian pledge is only liable for fraud and gross negligence, not for ordinary negligence, as was said above. However, if they should agree that if the thing perishes by the slightest fault or by accident, the loss falls on the creditor, or that if it perishes by ordinary or gross negligence, the loss falls on the debtor, such a contract would be valid. But a contract stating that the loss falls on the debtor even if the thing perishes through the fraud of the creditor would not be valid.

...of the debtor equally, he is not bound to pay it: because such an agreement would be against good morals <note>original: "contra bonos mores"</note>, as all these things were extensively proved in Disputation 295.

When someone uses a pledge against the owner's will—at least their presumed will—or when the creditor believes the owner would not truly agree to it, and this use becomes the occasion for the pledge to be destroyed by an accidental event <note>original: "casu fortuito"</note>, then the loss falls upon the creditor and not the debtor. However, it is otherwise when that use was not the cause of the pledge perishing, because it would have perished in a similar way even if the creditor had not used the pledge in that manner. The same is said when the creditor was in "mora" <term>mora<gloss>a legal delay or failure to perform an obligation on time</gloss></term> in returning the pledge, and that delay was the reason the pledge perished; for, if it had been restored at the proper time, it would not have perished in the same way, as shown in the cited Disputation 295. When a pledge is returned in a worse condition through the fault of the creditor in any of the ways explained so far, so that the creditor is held liable for that damage, if the appraisal of the damage is as much as the debt was, then it is compensated <note>set off</note> against the whole debt; therefore, the item ceases to have the legal status of a pledge. The same must be said if the appraisal of the damage is greater, in which case the creditor additionally pays the surplus. However, when the appraisal of the damage is less than the debt, then it is compensated against an equal part of the debt, according to the Code of Justinian, *Law: If a creditor 1 & 2* <note>original: "l. si creditor 1. & 2. <meta>This page continues Molina’s legal and theological analysis of the "tacit mortgage" (hypotheca tacita), which is a legal lien that arises automatically by law rather than through a specific written agreement. Having previously discussed physical pledges, he now moves to the various categories of people—spouses, the state, minors, and the Church—who hold these automatic legal claims over the property of others to ensure debts or obligations are met.</meta>

# Luis Molina on Contracts

<margin>1</margin>In the first place, a husband, regarding the dowry promised to him with his wife, holds a **tacit mortgage** <term>tacit mortgage<gloss>a legal claim or lien on property that exists by operation of law without needing a written contract</gloss></term> on the assets of the person who promised it, so that it may be paid, and also for interest if any part of the dowry, after it has been paid to him, is lost through **eviction** <term>eviction<gloss>the recovery of property by a third party who proves they have a better legal title to it than the current possessor</gloss></term>. However, this is not a "privileged" mortgage, meaning the husband is not preferred over other creditors who hold earlier tacit mortgages, as was discussed in all of Disputation 423. When a husband can take action regarding the eviction of a dowry so that he may be entitled to interest was discussed in Disputation 427.

<margin>2</margin>Next, a wife has a **tacit mortgage** on all her husband's assets for the recovery of her dowry, and on the assets of the husband’s guarantors for the same dowry in cases where it is appropriate for the husband to provide guarantors for the return of the dowry. Furthermore, this privilege of a tacit mortgage passes to all the wife’s heirs and even to outside parties. Likewise, the wife holds a privilege such that in this tacit mortgage she is preferred over other creditors who hold earlier tacit mortgages that are not similarly privileged. This, however,

<margin>3</margin>† **privilege of preference** over those holding earlier tacit mortgages that are not similarly privileged belongs only to the wife, her children, and her other descendants—not to her other heirs. Additionally, a first wife and her descendants are preferred in that mortgage over the mortgage held by a subsequent wife and her descendants for a dowry held in the assets of the same husband. However, if among the husband's assets any are found that belonged to the second wife, the second wife and her descendants are preferred over the first wife and her descendants regarding those specific assets. Although a wife is not preferred over someone holding a prior mortgage that is similarly privileged—such as that held by the **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note>—when mortgages are similarly privileged, the one who is first in time is stronger in right <note>original: "prior fuerit tempore, sit potior in iure"</note>. Nevertheless, in a case of doubt as to who was first, the wife, by "favor of the dowry" <note>original: "fauore dotis"; a legal principle giving preference to dowry claims to protect women's financial stability</note>, is preferred over the Treasury and any other party. Yet, the tacit mortgage of the wife (and of the Treasury), although preferred over the later **express mortgage** <term>express mortgage<gloss>a mortgage specifically created by a written contract or agreement</gloss></term> of other creditors (which is similarly understood for those holding prior non-privileged tacit mortgages), is not preferred over an earlier express mortgage of other creditors. If in a dowry contract an express mortgage is added for the dowry on the husband's assets, this express mortgage does not have the privilege of preferring the wife over earlier creditors holding earlier express mortgages on those same assets of the husband. All these points were proved in Disputation 438, and for that reason, I have only reviewed them here. **Negusantius** <note>Antonio Negusanti, a 16th-century Italian jurist</note> treats this same matter extensively in *On Pledges* <note>original: "de pign."</note>, part 2, member 4, from number 24 to 112. In the same disputation, it was explained when a mortgage for a dowry begins and whether a wife can renounce it.

<margin>4</margin>Similarly, for **paraphernal goods** <term>paraphernal goods<gloss>property owned by a married woman that is not part of her dowry and remains her own, though often managed by the husband</gloss></term>, when the husband administers them (as is the case in Castile and Portugal), the wife holds a † **tacit mortgage** on the husband's assets. However, this is without the privilege of preference over other creditors, as shown in Disputation 441. For other things owed to a wife upon the dissolution of marriage, I do not see that she has a tacit mortgage on the husband's assets; however, there could be an express one if it was included in an agreement, as was said in the same place.

<column-break/>

<margin>5</margin>The **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note> † or the King’s Chamber also holds a **tacit mortgage** on the assets of anyone who owes it something, whether as a tax or by contract. Thus, those who have leased the King’s revenues tacitly have their assets mortgaged for the payment of the price. However, if a minor buys from the Treasury, the item purchased is indeed tacitly subject to a mortgage to the Treasury, but not the minor's other assets, according to Law 2 of the Digest *on their assets* <note>original: "ff. de bon. eorum"</note>; and Negusantius affirms this with Jason <note>Jason de Mayno, a prominent medieval jurist</note> in the place cited above, number 113. Indeed, the tacit mortgage that the Treasury acquires in the things of someone owing it something is equally privileged with the mortgage a wife holds in the assets of her husband for the restitution of her dowry, as proved in Disputation 438. However, although when someone’s assets (or part of them) are confiscated by the law itself for some crime, the later sentence is retroactive to the time the crime was committed, the Treasury acquires a right in that thing or things (as was said at the end of Disputation 2). Nevertheless, when someone incurs a penalty to be applied to the Treasury that is not incurred by the law itself but requires a prior sentence, then surely—since that penalty is not simply owed until the sentence is passed—the assets of the delinquent person are not obligated to the Treasury for that penalty until after a condemnatory sentence has been passed by which that penalty is applied to the Treasury. Understand Negusantius’s teachings regarding penalties applied to the Treasury accordingly in number 115 above; see also **Gregorio López** on Law 25, Title 13, Part 5, at the word "obligated" <note>original: "obligados"</note>, and the doctors he cites.

<margin>6</margin>A **minor** † also holds a **tacit mortgage** on the assets of a **guardian** <term>guardian<gloss>Latin "tutor" or "curator"; a person legally responsible for the person or property of a minor</gloss></term> without the privilege of preference, from the moment the guardianship or care is undertaken, both for the minor's assets and for their lawful administration, as said in Disputation 223. But if a mother who is a guardian or curator of her son enters into a second marriage without resigning the guardianship, the assets of the second husband also remain simultaneously mortgaged to that same minor, as was also said in Disputation 220. Read a longer discussion in Negusantius, cited above, starting at number 6.

<margin>7</margin>**Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in the chapter *from the letters* <note>original: "cap. ex literis"</note> on pledges, number 11, along with the gloss in the same place, asserts that prelates and, universally, administrators of Church property, have their own assets tacitly obligated to the Churches for the assets they manage and for their lawful administration. They give this reason: because Churches enjoy the **privilege of minors** <term>privilege of minors<gloss>a legal doctrine treating the Church or the state as a "minor" to allow them special protections and the ability to undo harmful contracts</gloss></term>, as in chapter 1, *on the restoration of the whole*. Negusantius agrees, cited above, from number 20, along with others he cites.

<margin>8</margin>The assets of those administering the assets of cities, says Negusantius in number 119 above (along with Alexander), are also tacitly mortgaged to the cities for the assets they manage and their lawful administration. This is derived from the final law of the Code, *by which someone is convened in order* <note>original: "C. quo quis ord. conueniatur"</note>, book 11. However, I do not see that the text sufficiently proves that. It would be better proven because a city enjoys the privilege of minors, just as the Church does; this is the foundation on which the cited gloss, Panormitanus, and he and others are led to assert this regarding the assets of those administering Church goods.

<margin>9</margin>When a thing, previously † mortgaged to another, is bought with a minor's money, then that minor—because the price given for it was from his own money—has in that thing a **tacit...**

<meta>This page continues Molina’s systematic catalog of "tacit mortgages"—legal liens that arise automatically to protect vulnerable parties. Having previously discussed the rights of husbands and wives, Molina now moves to the rights of wards (minors), children whose property is managed by their parents, and landlords. He engages in a detailed legal debate over whether a son must first exhaust his father's personal assets before reclaiming property his father sold without permission.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 536

...a **tacit mortgage** <term>tacit mortgage<gloss>A legal claim or lien on property that arises automatically by law to secure a debt, without a written contract.</gloss></term> which, as is established, is not universal but particular. It is "privileged," meaning that in regards to that money, the **ward** <term>ward<gloss>A minor under the care of a legal guardian (pupillus).</gloss></term> is preferred over earlier creditors, even if those creditors hold an explicit, prior mortgage on that same property. This is held in the Law *Idemque* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. qui potior. in pign. hab." refers to the Digest, Book 20, Title 4.</note>, the penultimate law of the Code <note>original: "C. de seruo pig. dato manumis." refers to the Codex Justinianus.</note>, and Law 25, Title 13 of the Fifth **Partida** <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the primary legal code of Castile (Spain).</note>. See also Law 30 of the same, where **Gregorio Lopez** <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist and commentator on the Siete Partidas.</note> discusses whether this should be extended to a minor who has lost his father but has already reached puberty.

<margin>10</margin> Likewise, if a wife has received any assets by **gratuitous title** <term>gratuitous title<gloss>Acquiring property for free, such as through a gift or inheritance, rather than buying it.</gloss></term> from her husband, or because of her husband, and she moves to a second marriage while leaving behind children from that first husband, those assets belong to those children. To protect those assets, the children hold a mortgage on all the assets of that woman, starting from the moment those other assets from the first husband came to her. The same applies to assets that come to a husband by gratuitous title from his first wife when he moves to a second marriage and has children from the first, as is established in the Law *Hac edictali* <note>A famous Roman law concerning second marriages and the protection of children's inheritance.</note> and Law 26, Title 13, Partida 5, as discussed in Disputation 431.

<margin>11</margin> Likewise, a son has a tacit mortgage on all the assets of a father who is administering the son’s **adventitious property** <term>adventitious property<gloss>Assets a child acquires from sources other than their father, such as from a mother, grandparent, or through a legacy.</gloss></term>. This is so that he may recover those assets or their value. This mortgage begins from the moment the father undertakes the administration of such property, even before he manages it poorly or alienates it improperly.

<margin>12</margin> It is asked, however, whether a father is only held liable for **fraud** <term>fraud<gloss>In a legal sense (dolus), this refers to intentional wrongdoing or deceit in management.</gloss></term> in the poor administration of his son's assets. I believe the answer should be in the affirmative; however, fraud or **gross negligence** <term>gross negligence<gloss>Lata culpa, or a failure to exercise even the most basic care that any person would use.</gloss></term> is considered to have occurred whenever a father squanders the adventitious property of his son, as **Gama** <note>Antonio da Gama, a prominent Portuguese jurist.</note> in Decision 330 confirms along with others whom he cites. Law 24, Title 13, Partida 5 grants this same mortgage to the son, but it commands that an **exhaustion** <term>exhaustion<gloss>Also known as "excussion," this is the legal requirement to seize and sell the debtor's own property before going after property the debtor sold to third parties.</gloss></term> of the father's assets must be performed first. Only when the father's assets are insufficient to fully satisfy the son can the **mortgage action** then be brought against those who possess the assets that belonged to the father after he took over the administration of the son's property. **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias, a leading 16th-century Spanish legal scholar.</note> examines this law at length and judges it to be a correction of the **Common Law** <term>Common Law<gloss>Ius commune: the shared legal system of Roman and Canon law used across Europe.</gloss></term> disposition. As we discussed in Disputation 216, under Common Law, a son is granted the right to reclaim (*rei vindicatio*) his adventitious property which the father sold without a necessary cause (such as paying the son's debts) or alienated in any other way. For although the father, as the legal administrator, may sell a child’s immovable property without a judge's decree for a necessary and just cause, and the son cannot later reclaim it, if he sells it *without* such a cause, the son does not lose

<column-break/>

ownership of it under the Common Law. He can reclaim it immediately, without any exhaustion of the father's assets being performed first, and he can refuse any other compensation offered to him. Therefore, Covarrubias judges that this Common Law disposition is corrected by Law 23 <note>Likely referring back to the Partidas law mentioned previously.</note>, establishing that the son cannot reclaim the thing alienated by the father unless an exhaustion of the father’s assets is performed first and full satisfaction is not found there. However, the opinion of **Gregorio Lopez** on this same law is much more approved by me. Namely, that this law does not correct the Common Law, and it leaves the son's right intact to reclaim adventitious property that the father sold or alienated without a just or necessary cause, without any prior exhaustion of the father's assets and having refused all other compensation.

->But what is established by that law is this: When the father<-
has alienated adventitious money, or adventitious grain, wine, oil, and similar goods that had come to the son, or other movable things that could not be kept without spoiling (which were more useful for the son to have sold), or a piece of land sold out of necessity from which some price remained for the son—then, when the time comes for the restitution of the adventitious assets to the son (either because the father died or the son was emancipated while the father was still living), an exhaustion must first be made of the assets found to belong to the father at that time. This is done so that the value of those assets may be paid to the son. And when sufficient assets are not found among the father's property to satisfy the son, only then may he bring a mortgage action for the remainder against those who possess assets that were the father’s after he began the administration of the son’s adventitious property. This disposition in no way contradicts the sanctions of the Common Law; rather, it agrees with them entirely.

<margin>13</margin> The fruits of a rented property are also tacitly subjected to a mortgage to the landlord for the payment of rent. However, the fruits of an **emphyteutic property** <term>emphyteutic property<gloss>Land held under a long-term lease (emphyteusis) where the tenant has near-ownership rights as long as they pay a fixed rent and improve the land.</gloss></term> are not tacitly mortgaged for the payment of the ground-rent, as was stated at the end of Disputation 451. Likewise, items **brought onto** <note>original: "inuectæ" - things like furniture or livestock.</note> a rented property are tacitly subjected to a mortgage to the landlord, both for

<margin>14</margin> the payment of rent and for damages caused by the fault of the tenant. However, if the rented property is rural, this applies only if the items were brought in with the landlord’s knowledge. Both points were shown and explained in Disputation 497. I do not, however, agree with **Baldo**, **Alvarez**, or **Valasco** regarding the law of emphyteusis when they say that items brought onto emphyteutic property are mortgaged to the direct lord for the rent or for the deterioration of the property. I find no law that establishes the former, even though there are laws that establish the latter for standard leases. But if the **emphyteuta** <note>The holder of the long-term lease.</note> should sublet the emphyteutic property, then the items brought onto the property so sublet will be tacitly mortgaged to the emphyteuta for the rent and for any damage to the property.

<margin>15</margin> A mortgage is also available to a **legatee** <term>legatee<gloss>A person who receives a specific gift or "legacy" in a person's will.</gloss></term>...

It also details the rights of landlords to claim a tenant's goods or crops as security for unpaid rent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the hierarchy of legal claims (priorities) among various creditors. It addresses how the law treats debts inherited from a deceased person and the specific "privileged" status given to those who provide funds for purchasing, repairing, or preserving property.</meta>

### Louis Molina, On Contracts
<meta>catchword: tem</meta>

...an action against all the assets of the deceased, so that the **legacy** <term>legacy<gloss>A specific gift of property or money left to someone in a will, distinct from the general inheritance.</gloss></term> may be paid to them, as we showed in Disputation 3. However, since only those assets that remain after all debts are deducted are considered the "assets of the deceased," it is established that no **legatee** <gloss>recipient of a legacy</gloss> is to be preferred over the creditors of the deceased. This remains true even if the creditor only holds a personal action against the deceased, the **vacant estate** <term>vacant estate<gloss>An inheritance that has not yet been accepted by an heir (haereditas iacens).</gloss></term>, or the heirs of the deceased, as is clear from what was said in Disputation 216 and elsewhere.

<margin>16</margin> When someone has previously subjected all their assets to a **mortgage** <term>mortgage<gloss>In this context, "hypotheca," a legal claim on property used as collateral for a debt.</gloss></term> (and the same is said with even greater reason if the assets were tacitly mortgaged by law), and later accepts a loan from another person specifically to buy a field, and at the time they took that loan they subjected that same field to a mortgage for that lender: this later creditor is preferred regarding that specific field purchased with their money and subsequently mortgaged to them. They are preferred over the prior creditor or creditors who held mortgage rights over all the debtor's goods in general, including that field. Likewise, anyone who provided a loan to repair or restore a building—even if they gave the money to the craftsman who provided the labor and materials at the owner's order—is granted a mortgage on that building to recover that money. This claim takes precedence over other creditors who held prior mortgages on that same building. 

<margin>18</margin> Likewise, one who gave money to outfit a ship with provisions or other necessities for sailing, or to arm or purchase it, is granted a mortgage on that ship to receive that money. This also carries a **privilege of preference** <gloss>legal right to be paid first</gloss> over other creditors holding an earlier mortgage on the same ship. 

<margin>19</margin> Similarly, if a later creditor gave something for the **preservation** <gloss>conseruatio</gloss> of a thing already pledged to another, they are preferred in receiving payment from that thing for what they provided, over the others to whom the thing was previously pledged. For example, if someone gave money to arm or repair a ship already pledged to another, or provided for the sailors' provisions (without which the ship could not arrive safely), or gave something so that goods already pledged to another would be made safe, or paid the **freight charge** <gloss>naulum</gloss> for transporting them, or paid the rent for the warehouse or other place where those goods were stored, or paid the price for the pack animals that brought them: in all these cases, they are preferred in recovering these costs from those goods over prior creditors to whom the goods were mortgaged. All these points were shown above in Disputation 438. 

<margin>20</margin> In that same place, we added that although this privilege of mortgage is granted to these later creditors in such matters against those holding prior mortgages (sometimes tacit and sometimes expressed), the mortgage granted to a wife for her **dowry** <term>dowry<gloss>Property brought by a bride to her husband at marriage, which must be returned if the marriage ends.</gloss></term> in her husband's assets is nevertheless preferred over these otherwise privileged mortgages. This is done out of favor for the institution of marriage (Law 29, Title 13, Partida 5 extends this also to the mortgage of the **fiscus** <term>fiscus<gloss>The state treasury or government tax office.</gloss></term>, as stated there). 

<margin>21</margin> An exception occurs when someone gave a loan to the husband of such a wife to purchase a **military office** <term>military office<gloss>In the 16th century, many administrative and military posts (militia) were treated as property that could be bought, sold, or mortgaged.</gloss></term> under a mortgage of that same office. In that case, the creditor is preferred over the wife regarding the mortgage of that office, as was stated there. In that location, we also added that in matters which depend on the disposition of human law, that rule is not always true: *if I conquer the one conquering you, I necessarily conquer you* <note>original: "si vinco vincentem te, a fortiori vincam te"</note>. Indeed, one holding an express prior mortgage is preferred over a wife holding a later tacit mortgage for her dowry; and yet, while the privileged creditors we just discussed are preferred over those holding a prior express mortgage, wives are nonetheless preferred in the mortgage of their dowry over these privileged creditors.

<column-break/>

<margin>22</margin> Although it is the rule that he who first subjects something to a **pledge** <gloss>pignus</gloss> or mortgage is stronger in right <note>original: "potior in iure"</note>, and therefore should be preferred in the payment of debt from that pledge or mortgage over someone to whom the same thing was later subjected; this must be understood to apply only when the contract was fully celebrated. This means an obligation was born on the part of the one pledging the property that did not depend solely on their own free will—what legal experts call an obligation "not depending on a **potestative condition**" <term>potestative condition<gloss>A condition that is entirely within the power of one of the parties to fulfill (e.g., "I will pay you if I feel like it").</gloss></term> of the one pledging the thing. 

<margin>23</margin> From this it follows that if someone subjects a thing to a pledge or mortgage for a loan they are *going* to receive, but before that money is delivered to them, they subject the same thing to another person for a different loan that *is* delivered to them: even if the first loan is delivered later, the second creditor (who was the first to actually provide the money) is preferred in that pledge or mortgage over the first creditor (to whom the thing was first pledged but who provided the money later). The reason is that before the delivery of the money, there was no contract of loan (*mutuum*), and consequently no completed contract of pledge for that loan. Instead, it was entirely within the borrower's free will not to accept that loan, and thus not to complete either contract. Both are considered celebrated under a tacit, purely potestative condition on the part of the pledger: "if I choose to accept the money." This is expressly held in Law 1 at the end, and Law *Qui balneum*, in the section *amplius* at the verse *si modo*, and Law *Potior* at the beginning of the Digest <note>original: "ff. qui potior. in pig." refers to the Digest title "Who is preferred in a pledge."</note>, and in Law 27, Title 13, Partida 5. 

From this same foundation, it follows that if someone subjects something to a pledge or mortgage for a loan they were going to receive, and before receiving that money they sell the thing, even if the money is later delivered to them, the thing does not remain subject to the pledge or mortgage. This is because when the loan contract was perfected, the thing was no longer among the borrower’s assets. This is held in the next-to-last law of the Digest, "What things can be pledged" <note>original: "ff. quae res pig."</note>.

The matter is far different when the contract was fully celebrated, even if under a **casual** <gloss>beyond human control</gloss> or mixed condition, such that an obligation was born on the part of the pledger that did not depend solely on their free will. In that case, whether the contract was absolute (pure) or conditional, if the condition is eventually fulfilled, the first creditor is preferred over the second. This is because the fulfillment of a condition "relates back" to the time the contract was celebrated, as if it had been a pure contract from the start. This is held in Law *Qui balneum* and Law *Potior* at the beginning of the Digest, and Law 32, Title 13, Partida 5.

However, when someone has promised a dowry with a certain woman under a condition—or rather, a provision—that if the marriage is dissolved (for example, by the death of the woman without children), the dowry should be restored to them by the husband; and for security...

<summary>This page discusses the legal hierarchy of creditors, explaining that those who provide funds to purchase or preserve specific property (like ships or buildings) often have "privileged" claims over earlier general creditors. It also clarifies that a mortgage is only legally "perfected" when the loan money is actually delivered, rather than when the agreement is first signed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of the "hierarchy of creditors"—the legal order determining who gets paid first when a debtor has multiple obligations. It specifically addresses how a third party or a junior creditor can "step into the shoes" of a senior creditor by paying off the earlier debt.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 536.
<meta>catchword: was</meta>

...[if] a husband has subjected something to a **pledge** <gloss>pignus; a physical asset held as security</gloss> or a **mortgage** <gloss>hypotheca; a legal claim on property without physical possession</gloss> while promising a **dowry** <note>original: "dotem"</note>, as defined in the laws regarding who has the better claim to a pledge. If that husband later subjects the same property to a pledge or mortgage for someone else before the dowry is fully recovered, the first creditor must be preferred in that mortgage.

This is because the first contract was fully completed by the party promising the dowry, such that the husband and the woman were compelled to fulfill it. The second contract regarding the restoration of the dowry was connected to the first; the promisor did not wish to bind himself to pay that dowry except in connection with the second contract. This second contract was likewise fully completed from the beginning, and a simple obligation was born on the husband's part to fulfill it. Therefore, since something was subjected to a pledge or mortgage for the security of the person promising the dowry, it follows that even if it is later obligated to another, the first creditor is to be preferred over the later one.

**24.** Anyone who buys a property from a debtor that was subjected to a pledge or mortgage for **two creditors** <note>This refers to "junior" and "senior" lienholders</note>—if the first creditor is satisfied from the purchase price—the buyer **succeeds to the rights** <term>succession of rights<gloss>A legal mechanism, often called subrogation, where one person takes over the legal standing and priorities of another.</term> of the first creditor. This is not so the buyer can hold the property as a pledge (since it has truly become their own property), but so they may defend themselves against the second creditor up to the value of the property that went from their payment to the first creditor. For just as the first creditor was to be preferred over the second up to that value, so the buyer is defended in comparison to the second creditor. This is held in the laws regarding those who succeed to the place of a prior creditor.

However, if the first creditor had accepted that property from the debtor **in lieu of payment** <note>original: "in solutum"</note> or by sale, then if the second creditor pays the first creditor what was owed (so that they might hold the property as obligated for that debt), or effectively offers it to them, the second creditor can bring a mortgage action against that property. This is the case just as if the property had been sold or handed over in payment to some outsider who had no prior claim.

If a later creditor, to whom the same property is mortgaged, pays the debt of the prior creditor (who has a better claim to the pledge or mortgage), or offers it and deposits it in the event the senior creditor refuses to accept the payment, they succeed to the place of the prior creditor in the pledge. They gain that person’s **privilege** <gloss>priority rank</gloss>, though precisely only up to the value of what they paid. This is affirmed and excellently distinguished by the legal commentaries on the rights of prior creditors.

The same applies if a third, fourth, or even more distant mortgage creditor pays or offers the debt to the first; they succeed to the place of the first and are preferred even to those who were originally senior to them, but junior to the first. This is stated by **Gregorio López** <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note> and the laws he cites.

<column-break/>

**25.** The same would apply if there were many prior creditors holding **tacit mortgages** <term>tacit mortgage<gloss>A mortgage created automatically by law rather than by a written contract, such as the state's claim for taxes.</gloss></term>, and the last creditor was a woman seeking her dowry or the **State Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note>, both of whom have a legal right of preference over prior creditors. If any later creditor among those over whom the wife or the Treasury is preferred—for instance, the second or third—offers the debt to the Treasury or the wife, they succeed to that person's place and are preferred to the earlier creditors up to the value paid. However, if an earlier creditor offers this same amount to the one who paid it, they themselves succeed to that privilege. When a later creditor offers a prior creditor who possesses the pledge what is owed to them, if the senior creditor in turn offers the other what is owed, they can retain the pledge with their own right and the right of the other whom they paid.

If, however, an **outsider** <gloss>someone with no prior legal interest in the property</gloss> pays the debt to a creditor holding a prior or more privileged mortgage, two things are necessary for them to "step into the shoes" of that creditor. First, they must pay with a **covenant** <gloss>pactum; a formal agreement</gloss> that the property remains mortgaged to them. Second, they must pay with a covenant that they succeed to the place of that creditor. Note, however, that if they pay with a covenant that the creditor transfers all rights they held in that property to them, then these two conditions are included within that single agreement.

**26.** But if an outsider hands money over to a **debtor** so that the debtor may pay a creditor holding a prior or more privileged mortgage, then three things are required for the outsider to succeed to that place and preference. First, they must provide the money with a covenant that they succeed to the place of such a creditor. Second, that the money actually reaches that creditor. And third, that the pledge or mortgage is released and dissolved by that money.

In laws concerning the privileges of the Treasury, it is held even more clearly that the **State Treasury** (at least by right of preference) can take action to recover money paid by a debtor to a later creditor, even if the money was accepted in **good faith** <note>original: "bona fide"</note> and spent by that later creditor who was unaware that it was owed to the Treasury first—and even if that creditor was not made wealthier by that money. If, however, they had accepted it in **bad faith** <note>original: "mala fide"</note>, knowing it was owed to the Treasury, or spent it in bad faith after learning of the debt, they would fall under the penalty of paying **double** the amount to the Treasury.

**27.** A **doubt** <gloss>a formal legal question for debate</gloss> has arisen: whether the Treasury's ability to sue for money accepted and spent in good faith is a unique privilege belonging only to the State, or whether it similarly applies to any other prior creditors who hold a mortgage on the debtor's goods, allowing them to take action for what was paid...

<summary>This page details the legal mechanisms of subrogation, explaining how junior creditors or third parties can acquire the priority status of senior creditors by paying off existing debts. It highlights specific protections for dowries and the State Treasury, including the Treasury's power to reclaim funds even if spent in good faith.</summary>
<keywords>subrogation, mortgage priority, dowry rights, State Treasury (Fiscus), Gregorio López, good faith (bona fide), bad faith (mala fide), legal succession, debt satisfaction</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the rights of creditors, specifically focusing on whether a senior creditor can reclaim payments already made to a junior creditor, and the legal weight of public versus private documents in establishing debt priority.</meta>

-> # Ludovico Molina on Contracts <-

...[was] for the later creditors, even if it was received and consumed in **good faith** <gloss>bona fide; acting honestly without knowledge of the other's prior claim</gloss> by them. The **Gloss of Accursius** <note>Accursius (c. 1182–1263) was a celebrated Roman law jurist whose "Great Gloss" became the standard authority</note> on the law *pecunia* and the final paragraph cited, and another gloss on the first law, but whether here—as the common opinion of the doctors affirms, as **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop</note> reports in *On Pacts*, question 29—a few others, whom Covarruvias also reports there, deny it. I believe it should be stated: If the thing was received or consumed in **bad faith**, or if it was received in good faith and still exists, a right of action is granted to any creditor holding a prior or more privileged **mortgage** <gloss>hypotheca; a legal claim over property</gloss> to reclaim from the later creditor what was paid to them by their common debtor. On this point, no one doubts. However, if it was received and consumed in good faith, and the one who consumed it was made **enriched** <term>locupletior<gloss>Better off or wealthier as a result of the payment</gloss></term> in some way, it must be said that a similar reclamation is granted for the amount by which they were enriched.

The entire difficulty, however, is when it is received and consumed in good faith, whether that later creditor is bound to pay what they consumed if they were not made enriched by it. **Papinian** <note>A famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note>, reported in the law *deferte*, in the final paragraph cited, denied it. **Marcian** <note>Another influential Roman jurist</note>, however, whose law it is, says that they should be compelled to pay the **Treasury** <note>original: "fisco"</note>. On this, the Gloss on the word "but it is pleasing" refers to **Johannes** <note>Johannes Bassianus, a 12th-century jurist</note> saying that he grieves that Marcian contradicts Papinian. For my part, I do not judge that response of Marcian to be equitable, but rather unjust. Since that later creditor is not bound to restore what they were not enriched by—neither on account of the thing received (which no longer exists) nor on account of an unjust receipt (since they received and consumed it in good faith)—surely by the nature of the thing, and standing on **natural law** <gloss>ius naturale</gloss> alone, they are not bound to pay. Furthermore, **positive law** <gloss>ius positiuum; laws created by human authority</gloss> cannot grant the Treasury a privilege to reclaim from someone what it is in no way owed, nor even from a tacit pact or condition that if they consume it, they must restore it; for that would require the consumer to know that the item belonged to the Treasury. Therefore, I judge not only that this law should not be extended to other older creditors, but also that it should not be observed even for the Treasury, because it is unjust. Furthermore, it belongs to the **moral philosopher** and the **theologian** to discern and deduce from their principles whether a certain law is unjust or iniquitous or not.

**28.** When, however, a debt is considered only by a **private document** <gloss>scriptura priuata; a non-notarized contract</gloss>, and that a thing was subjected to a **pledge** or mortgage for it, or if it were proved only by two witnesses who did not testify to the debt itself but to the **confession of the debtor** regarding the debt and the mortgage—even though this would suffice to compel the debtor to pay and to seize the thing from them or whoever holds it—it would not suffice to give that creditor preference over one to whom the thing was later obligated by a **public document** <gloss>scriptura publica; a document witnessed and sealed by a public official/notary</gloss>; for in this case, the latter would be preferred over the prior creditor. If, however, the creditor held a private document written by the debtor's hand or signed by him, and additionally signed by the hand of **three other witnesses**, then the first creditor would be preferred in the mortgage over the later one, because a private document signed by the debtor and three witnesses is equivalent to a public document. So it is held 

<column-break/>

in the law *scripturas* regarding who is more powerful in a pledge, and in law 3, joined with **Gregorio López** <note>A Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*</note> there, title 13, part 5. However, it must be understood that in the scenario explained, the later creditor is preferred over the prior mortgage holder in the **external forum** <gloss>the public legal court</gloss> regarding the weight of proof; but it is otherwise in the **internal forum** <gloss>the forum of conscience/moral accountability</gloss> if the later creditor knows for certain that the thing was previously mortgaged to the first one; or even in the external forum if the later creditor confesses that it was previously mortgaged to the first. According to **Portuguese law** <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note>, no proof is admitted other than by a public document or by the confession of the later creditor who holds a public document, as was seen in Disputation 260. This concludes the first and second points of those proposed.

**29.** In order to explain at the same time in what **order** creditors must be satisfied, we must here introduce a third point: namely, among creditors who only have a **personal action** <gloss>a claim against the person, not a specific piece of property</gloss> against the debtor, those who have a privilege to be preferred over others in the payment of their debt.

When something is owed to someone by reason of the **funeral expenses** of the debtor, or of another whom the debtor was responsible for burying (such as a son or a servant)—because they lent, gave, or spent something for a moderate burial, considering the circumstances at the time—even if the debt is purely personal, the creditor to whom it is owed is preferred universally over other creditors, even those holding tacit or express mortgages on the goods of the deceased, as was said at the end of Disputation 527 and Disputation 235. The same is said of expenses made for the opening and copying of the **will** of the deceased, and in the making of the **inventory**, even against the inheritance or the goods of the deceased. This is both because these expenses are considered to have been made from the hereditary goods and because they result in the benefit of the creditors, so that those goods might be preserved for them. On this matter, it was discussed in Disputation 316, regarding the sixth benefit of those making an inventory.

<margin>By a law passed by **King Philip** <note>Philip II of Spain and I of Portugal</note> in this year 1594, and mentioned above in Disputation 530, section 3: **lords of estates** who have them leased out are preferred over all other creditors universally regarding the **fruits** <gloss>produce/income</gloss> harvested from them, as far as the payment of the rent is concerned. And I believe the same is true regarding what they lent to them for the cultivation of those estates.</margin>

Those who deposit with **public depositaries** appointed by the state, in that kind of deposit which has the force of a loan (where ownership of the deposited thing passes to the depositaries), provided they do not receive **usury** <gloss>interest</gloss> for it, have the privilege that they are preferred in the repayment of their deposit—not indeed over creditors holding tacit or express mortgages on the goods of such depositaries, but over other creditors holding only personal actions (who are also called **signature creditors** <term>chirographarii<gloss>Creditors whose claim rests only on a handwritten note without security</gloss></term> in law), even if those others have a privilege of preference. Such depositors are all admitted equally to be paid from the goods of such a public depositary, even if some were earlier and others later. However, when the exact same money that was deposited is found...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal priority of creditors, specifically addressing the hierarchical order of repayment when a debtor's assets are insufficient to cover all debts. It moves from general principles of "good faith" to specific categories of privileged creditors, such as depositors, brides, and minors.</meta>

-> ## Treatise Two, Disputation 53, Section 6 ## <-

[The money] is placed with a depositary, or if something is bought with it, then the person who deposited that money is preferred over all other depositaries, even if they were receiving interest <gloss>usury</gloss> on such a deposit. All these matters were stated and proven at the conclusion of Disputation 26.

A bride-to-be, if the dowry has been handed over to the groom but the marriage did not follow, does not indeed have a **tacit mortgage** <term>hypotheca<gloss>A legal claim or lien over a debtor's property that exists by operation of law without a written contract</gloss></term> on the groom's goods in the same way a wife has on a husband's goods. However, she holds a **personal privilege** <note>original: "personale priuilegiū"</note> to be preferred over other personal creditors. Furthermore, this privilege does not pass to her heirs unless they are descending children, as shown in all of Disputation 43, section 8.

A ward <term>pupillus<gloss>A minor under the care of a guardian or tutor</gloss></term> also has a personal privilege of preference over other creditors, so that they are paid from the assets of their tutor <note>A legal guardian responsible for the person and property of a minor</note> before other creditors. And because this privilege is personal, it does not pass to the ward's successors. The ward has the same privilege against a manager of their affairs <note>original: "negotiorum gestorem"</note>, even if that person is not in charge of all their affairs. Likewise, a minor who is a spendthrift, mentally incapacitated, or one who is both deaf and mute has a privilege to be preferred over the other creditors of their curators <note>Legal overseers for those unable to manage their own affairs due to age or disability</note>. This is held in the law *dabimus*, paragraph 1, and the three following laws in the Digest <note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* is a major part of the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Juris Civilis) compiled under Justinian I</note> regarding the privileges of creditors, and the final law of the Digest regarding the administration and distribution of accounts. Therefore, the ward and the minor in general have both a mortgage on the assets of their tutors or curators and a privilege of preference over other creditors. Because if that privilege of preference is not a "real" mortgage <note>A "real" right attaches to the property itself, whereas a "personal" right is against the individual</note>, then those holding prior mortgages on the same tutor's or curator's assets—as well as those holding a right of preference in a mortgage, such as a wife or the **Treasury** <term>fiscus<gloss>The public or royal treasury</gloss></term>—will be preferred over the ward or minor in payment from the assets of that same tutor or curator. The final gloss on the law *eos* agrees with this.

<margin>Code [of Justinian], "Who is more powerful in pledge."</margin>
When someone has given money so that it may be paid from that sum to an unsecured privileged creditor <term>chirographarius<gloss>A creditor whose claim is based on a handwritten document but lacks a formal mortgage/security</gloss></term>—that is, to one who had a privilege of preference but not a mortgage—then, if payment is actually made from that money, the person who gave the money succeeds to the place of the one to whom payment was made. They are then preferred over other unsecured creditors who are not so privileged. This is held in the law *si ventri*, in the last paragraph, joined with the gloss there in the Digest on the privileges of creditors. This concludes the third of the points proposed.

<margin>30</margin>
Regarding the final point—namely, the order in which creditors must be satisfied when a debtor does not have sufficient assets or where not enough remains to satisfy everyone fully—first of all, when some goods are found among the debtor's assets whose ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> belongs not to the debtor but to some creditor or creditors (perhaps because the debtor had stolen them, or they were lent, or deposited with him, or for any other reason), then it is quite clear that their owner must be preferred over all other creditors. This is held in the law of the "procurator," in the paragraph *plane*, at the verse *sed si dedi*, in the Digest on the "tributary action," and the law *cum fundus*, in the paragraph *seruum tuum*, and the imperial decree *si quid* in the Code, and Law 11, Title 14, Part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous Spanish statutory code</note>.

This is so true that even if the owners of those things, or those to whom they belong, are uncertain—that is, it is not known who they are specifically—nevertheless, satisfaction should not be made from those goods

<column-break/>

to the other creditors of the debtor, however prior or privileged they may be. Instead, the goods must be restored to the poor or spent on other pious works for the souls of those to whom the goods belong, provided that competent diligence is first performed to seek out those to whom they belong so they may be restored. The reason is manifest: because satisfaction cannot be made to a debtor’s creditors from the property of others that does not belong to the debtor.

By this same reasoning: when something is sold and delivered to someone, if they have not yet paid the price, nor offered it in such a way that the seller's refusal was the only thing stopping the payment, nor given guarantors or pledges for the payment, and the seller has not treated it as paid; then, whether that thing is found with the buyer, his heirs, or any other possessor under any title, the price must first be satisfied to the seller from that thing before satisfaction is made to any other creditor of the buyer or the third-party possessor. This holds even if that creditor has a prior and highly privileged mortgage on the assets of such a buyer or third-party possessor. For, as we showed in Disputation 33, section 8, the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of that thing still remains with the seller, and they have the right to reclaim it <term>vindicatio<gloss>A legal action by which an owner claims their property from someone else</gloss></term> as their own property. Consequently, the seller is to be preferred in that thing over any other creditors, even those with mortgages, and even over the funeral expenses of the buyer or the third-party possessor.

Indeed, if the thing sold belonged to the Treasury, a minor, or the Church, since ownership of it does not pass to the buyer or a third-party possessor until the price has actually been delivered to the Treasury, minor, or Church (as proven in the cited disputation), as long as the price has not been paid, the Treasury, minor, or Church is preferred in that thing over any other creditor. **Navarrus** <note>Martín de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a leading canonist and theologian</note> in the *Manual*, chapter 17, number 49, following **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian</note> under the word *restitutio* 6, question 5, although they agree with us in this doctrine, they nonetheless did not touch upon the root of this matter. For Navarrus believes that the ownership of the thing bought is transferred to the buyer by the very fact that it was delivered to him, which is against the most clear laws cited by us in Disputation 33, section 8, and against the common opinion of the doctors. In the same place, number 50, he adds that the same applies in any other **onerous contract** <gloss>A contract where both parties give and receive something of value</gloss>, such as in an exchange <note>original: "permutatione"</note> and others: namely, if a thing is delivered by one party and the contract is not completed by the other, the one who delivered it should be preferred in that thing over the other creditors of the same debtor. However, we clearly showed the contrary in Disputations 396 and 497: namely, that it is a privilege of sale alone that ownership is not considered transferred to the buyer by the delivery of the thing until he fulfills the contract on his part. Therefore, for that reason, the seller is to be preferred in the thing sold over any other creditors of the buyer or any other possessor of the same thing.

After all these creditors who hold ownership in a thing—and who must be preferred—preference over all other creditors, even those with mortgages, is given to those to whom something is owed by reason of a moderate burial of the debtor (or of another whom it was the debtor's duty to bury). Likewise, preference is given to those to whom something is owed by reason of the registration of the debtor's will, the inventory of his goods, or because something was spent...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "insum-" (spent/expended), which will likely lead into a discussion of administrative costs or estate management on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Molina details the hierarchy of debt repayment, emphasizing that true owners of property (including unpaid sellers and depositors) have priority over all other creditors because the debtor never legally owned the assets. He also outlines the personal legal privileges of brides, minors, and those covering burial costs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal hierarchy of creditors. It specifically addresses how landlords in Castile are prioritized for rent and how the principle of "first in time, stronger in law" applies to mortgages and pledges.</meta>

-> ## Luis de Molina: On Contracts ## <-

...were spent in preserving those goods; and in this Kingdom of Castile, the landlord who leased the estate is preferred in receiving the rent from the crops <gloss>fruits</gloss> of that estate, or for what he lent for the purpose of harvesting those crops, over all other creditors, as all these points were demonstrated above.

After all those mentioned who have a right of **pledge** <term>pignus<gloss>A type of security where the creditor takes physical possession of the debtor's property</gloss></term> or **mortgage** <term>hypotheca<gloss>A legal claim over property where the debtor retains possession, but the creditor has a right to seize it if the debt is unpaid</gloss></term> on the debtor's assets, they are preferred over all other creditors who only possess a **personal action** <note>original: "actio personalis"; a legal claim against a specific person rather than a specific piece of property</note>, regardless of whether those personal creditors have a "privilege of preference." This is because such a privilege is understood to apply only in comparison to **unsecured creditors** <term>chirographarii<gloss>Creditors who have a written acknowledgment of debt but no physical collateral or legal lien</gloss></term> who do not have a right of pledge or mortgage. This is expressly stated in the law *Eos*, under the title "Who is prior in pledge," which states: *It is well established that those who have received pledges (which includes mortgages) have an "action in the thing" <note>original: "in rem actionem"</note> and are preferred over all privileges that belong to personal actions.*

Among those holding a pledge or mortgage on the debtor's goods, those who first obtained the right of pledge or mortgage in those goods are generally preferred over others, whether the mortgages are **tacit** <gloss>implied by law</gloss> or **express** <gloss>written in a contract</gloss>, general or specific. This remains true even if nothing is left from those goods to pay the later creditors. For among such creditors, that famous rule holds: **"He who is first in time is stronger in right."** <note>original: "qui prior est tempore, potior est iure"</note> This is expressly found in the laws *Si fundum* and *Si generaliter*. I noted that among such creditors, those who first contracted the right are *regularly* preferred because exceptions are made for those who have a specific "privilege of preference" over earlier mortgage holders; who those individuals are has been explained above.

In the Code, under the law of pledges, the strictness of the law was set aside in favor of a certain **equity** <note>A legal principle used to reach a fair result when the strict letter of the law would be too harsh</note>. When a prior creditor has a mortgage on a specific thing or things, and simultaneously a general mortgage on the rest of the debtor's goods, and later the same debtor obligates certain goods to a second creditor, the first creditor cannot stop the second creditor from pursuing a mortgage action against the debtor regarding the general goods. Nor can the first creditor block payment to the second creditor from those general goods when the specific goods pledged to the first creditor are sufficient to satisfy his debt. In case of doubt, it is presumed they are sufficient, and it is up to the first creditor to prove otherwise. As the commentary on the law says, and as Covarrubias and the common opinion of the learned agree, this law was established in favor of the **second creditor**. Specifically, he should not be blocked from obtaining his debt by the first creditor when the first creditor's specific collateral is enough. It is irrelevant whether the debtor himself, the first creditor, the second, or some third party possesses those general goods;

<column-break/>

for this purpose, the second creditor can bring a mortgage action regarding them. On the same basis, it is affirmed that this law has equal force whether the second creditor has only a general mortgage, or a specific mortgage on things already generally obligated to the first creditor. Likewise, it applies whether the first creditor was first granted a specific mortgage with a general one added, or first a general mortgage with a specific one added. On the same basis, it is affirmed that the first creditor *can* take action regarding the general goods against the debtor, his heirs, or a third-party possessor if the debtor or his guarantors do not have enough assets, as stated in Disputation 534, without being forced to first go after the specific collateral. This is because the cited law was not passed for the benefit of the debtor or heirs, but solely for the second creditor. 

Furthermore, if the first creditor had only a general mortgage which perhaps covered more than the second creditor's mortgage, the first creditor can pursue the goods obligated to the second creditor. The second creditor cannot object by claiming that the other goods held by third parties are enough to pay the first debt. Indeed, a creditor is free to bring a mortgage action against any goods obligated to him, ignoring other obligated goods, as is clear from the law of Modestinus <note>original: "l. Moschs." appears to be a typo for Modestinus</note> and the law *Creditoris*. The cited law, which relies solely on equity against the rigors of the law, must not be extended further than its specific provisions allow.

When creditors hold a mortgage, because they have a "right in the thing" regarding the goods mortgaged to them, they can demand those goods from those who were paid first or from those who currently possess them. This applies even if the other creditors have personal or mortgage actions, provided they should have been ranked lower in priority.

An exception exists: unless it was an **heir** who created an **inventory** <term>inuentarium<gloss>A detailed list of a deceased person's assets and debts, which limits the heir's liability to the value of the estate</gloss></term> and paid the deceased's creditors. In that case, the prior mortgage creditors can demand the value from the lower-priority creditors who received payment. However, they cannot disturb or sue the heirs who paid them after completing the inventory, nor can they sue the buyers who purchased estate goods from such heirs that had been mortgaged to the deceased's creditors.

This is found in the final law of the Code regarding the "right of deliberation," as discussed in Disputation 216 regarding the third benefit of creating an inventory.

<summary>This page discusses the legal priority of creditors, establishing that those with specific property claims (pledges and mortgages) generally outrank those with only personal claims. It highlights the principle of "first in time, stronger in law" while explaining equitable exceptions that prevent senior creditors from blocking junior ones if their primary collateral is already sufficient.</summary>

-> ## Second Treatise, Disputation 538 ## <-

In this place it is added what should be decided when heirs, who have prepared an inventory, know that the resources of the inheritance are not sufficient for all the legatees <term>legatarii<gloss>Individuals named in a will to receive specific gifts or sums of money</gloss></term> and creditors. This applies if they have either prioritized the legatees over the other creditors, or prioritized unsecured creditors <term>chirographarii<gloss>Creditors who hold a written note of debt but no specific collateral</gloss></term> over those holding a mortgage, or prioritized mortgage creditors who ought to be ranked below other mortgage creditors who should have come first.

An exception is made, furthermore, when an execution is carried out by public authority against the goods of the debtor in the presence of a mortgage creditor—or with that creditor's knowledge—and he does not seek to be preferred or to be paid first. In such a case, he loses his right of preference by that very fact. Nor is the person who received payment of his own debt through that route bound to return anything to that mortgage creditor, whether the one who received payment in that manner was a mortgage creditor himself or merely a personal creditor. This is gathered, arguing from the lesser to the greater, from the Law 1 and the law *If mortgages* in the *Code of Justinian, On the release of pledges* <note>original: "l. 1. & l. si hypothecas, C. de remiss. pig."</note>.

<margin>Portuguese Law 32</margin> Concerning **Portuguese Law**, when a creditor has obtained a judgment against a debtor and the execution begins—so that the goods are seized as a **judicial pledge** <term>iudiciale pignus<gloss>Property seized by court order to satisfy a debt</gloss></term> and begin to be sold, or are already sold and the debt is paid—if another creditor then arrives, whether a mortgage or personal creditor who claims he should be preferred in payment, a distinction must be made. Either this late-arriving creditor was in the same place where the other creditor was litigating with the debtor before the judge, or he was absent and ignorant of it. If he was present and did not protest before the judge that he was the prior creditor and ought to be preferred, then he loses his right of preference at that time, even if he were a mortgage creditor, and the other person obtains or keeps the full payment of the debt. However, if he was absent, being rightfully ignorant that the other creditor was litigating with the debtor, or if he was present and did indeed protest that he was the prior creditor and ought to be preferred, then—even if the debt has already been paid to the creditor who should have been ranked lower—the late-comer is preferred over him. He obtains his full debt by extracting it from the power of the one who had received it, if necessary. If, however, the debtor has other goods from which the preferred creditor can be competently paid, he must be paid from those other goods of the debtor, rather than from what the first creditor received in payment of his debt. These matters are held in Book 3 of the *Portuguese Ordinances*, Title 34, at the beginning and in paragraph 1. Other matters related to these concerning Portuguese Law, and pertaining in their own way to the mortgage creditor, will be added a little further below.

After mortgage creditors, among the personal creditors, those who have a **privilege of preference** are to be preferred over the rest, even if nothing remains from which the others might be paid; for the privilege of preference consists in exactly that. So says Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 51 <note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), known as Navarrus, was a highly influential legal scholar and theologian.</note>, and the doctors of law commonly agree. Who specifically enjoys that privilege was explained above. The very last place is held by personal creditors who do not have a privilege of preference. These, however, are preferred over all legatees and heirs, as was said in Disputation 216 and elsewhere: this is because the "goods of the deceased" (the disposal of which belongs to the deceased) is only that which remains after the entire debt has been deducted and all creditors universally have been paid.

33. When there are **personal creditors**, and none of them enjoy a privilege of preference, none of them is preferred over the others, even if some of them are prior in time and 

<column-break/>

others are later. Rather, all have an equal right to the debtor's goods. For that reason, if the debtor’s goods are not sufficient, they must be divided among them **proportionally** <term>pro rata<gloss>A method of distribution where each person receives a share in proportion to the total amount they are owed</gloss></term>. Thus, whatever the proportion of one debt is to another in terms of quantity, such shall be the proportion of what each person receives compared to what others receive. The same must be said when many enjoy the same personal privilege of preference, as happens to those who deposit money with the same public depositary, and universally, when the personal privilege of one does not have preference in comparison to the personal privilege of another. From this it follows that in all these cases of creditors, that famous rule—*he who is prior in time is stronger in law* <note>original: "qui prior est tempore, potior est iure"</note>—does not have a place. This is expressly held in the law *Privileges* in the *Digest, On the privileges of creditors* <note>original: "l. priuilegia. ff. de priu. cred."</note>, and in the law *If a man*, last paragraph, in the *Digest, On deposits*, and the law *For a debt* in the *Code, On the authority of a judicial sale*. Navarrus affirms this in his *Manual*, chapter 17, number 51, as do the doctors commonly.

34. At this point it must be observed that if any of the personal creditors receives what is owed to him from the debtor before the other personal creditors receive their debts in court, then—even if he knows this will result in a loss for the other creditors because no goods remain from which their debts can be paid—he is certainly not bound, neither in the **external court** <gloss>civil law</gloss> nor in the **court of conscience** <term>forum conscientiae<gloss>The internal moral judgment of a person before God, often addressed in manual for confessors</gloss></term>, to give anything to those creditors, even if some of them have a privilege of preference and he does not. That he is not bound to this in the external court is expressly held in the law *He who*, paragraph *At Labeo's*, and the paragraph *It should be known*, and the law *A ward* in the *Digest, On things done to defraud creditors*, and other laws cited there by the glosses. For since that was truly owed to him already, and he received it through his own vigilance and diligence before all the other creditors (perhaps with the debtor's affection being moved toward him rather than toward others), the law did not wish to grant a **rescissory or revocatory action** <note>legal actions to undo a transfer of property</note> for what had been so received. This is handled differently than when an "onerous contract" <note>a contract where both parties give something of value</note> is newly made in fraud of creditors, as was said in Disputation 328. That he is not bound to this in the court of conscience either is proven. Firstly, because the law that established this for the external court is not to be judged unjust; therefore, it also has force in the court of conscience. Secondly, because the laws that prescribe the order of restitution or satisfaction for creditors are matters of human or positive law, and they imitate the laws recently cited, which decree this other outcome. What has been said—that when a personal creditor receives what is owed to him from the hand of the debtor while there are other personal creditors (even privileged ones) for whom sufficient goods do not remain to pay their debts—must be understood similarly when, upon the death of the creditor, he receives it from the hand of the heir. This is clear from the final law in the *Code, On the right of deliberation*, from the paragraph *And if the aforementioned*, where a "right of recovery" <note>original: "repetitio"</note> is granted only to mortgage creditors, but not to personal creditors. And the gloss there on the word "be repelled" affirms this our doctrine based on the same foundations.

35. It must then be observed that when one of the personal creditors seeks what is owed to him by way of a judge, if he obtains a judgment first, before the other personal creditors, and puts it into execution—either by the debtor's goods being sold and his debt being paid from their price, or by the debtor's goods being handed over by the judge's authority as a judicial pledge so that satisfaction may be made from them—he is preferred over the other personal creditors, even those with privi-
