is sanctioned by law, he should not be preferred over others. The question is whether a debtor sins if he prioritizes one creditor in payment who should have been ranked later, simply because another creditor holds a <term>privilegium praelationis<gloss>A legal right to be paid before others regardless of the date of the debt</gloss></term>. I respond that when the creditor being paid uses the court to demand payment while others remain silent, and the judge orders the payment—or will certainly do so soon, causing the debtor distress, loss of assets, and legal expenses—the debtor does not sin by paying that debt in full. This is because the law aids the "vigilant"—those who quickly demand what is owed—granting them a better position than those who are idle, as is established in the Law "He who [has increased his wealth]" <note>original: "l. qui au'" referring to Digest 42.8.6.7</note>, the Law "A ward" <note>original: "l. pupillus" referring to Digest 42.8.10.16</note> regarding "acts done to defraud creditors," the final law of the "Right of Deliberation" in the Code <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de iur. delib."</note>, and other legal sources. Even when one creditor asks for payment and others do not, I would not dare condemn the debtor, especially if there were a compelling reason, such as that creditor being particularly troublesome or the debtor fearing being hauled into court, or if that creditor were much poorer than the others. Nevertheless, I would advise the debtor to undergo a <term>cessio bonorum<gloss>A formal surrender of all assets to creditors to avoid imprisonment for debt</gloss></term> so they might be distributed according to the legal order, especially when there is no hope of the debtor coming into a greater fortune to pay everyone in full eventually. However, if the debtor, of his own accord, calls certain creditors to pay them while knowingly excluding others to their detriment, although the payment stands and the recipients are not bound to return it to the others, the debtor sins by committing this injustice against those left out.

The other matters that could be discussed here regarding the order of restitution will be more conveniently added in the final disputation of this second treatise on justice. However, what has been said here will greatly lighten our burden at that time.

### In what ways the obligation of pledge and mortgage is removed.

### DISPUTATION 537.

-> SUMMARY <-

<margin>1</margin> The number of ways a pledge or mortgage obligation is ended, with the following numbers.

<margin>2</margin> A creditor consenting to the sale <term>alienatio<gloss>The transfer of ownership of property to another person</gloss></term> of a thing mortgaged to him is deemed to have waived his right of pledge or mortgage.

Indeed, this applies even if he consents to the same property being pledged to a subsequent creditor.

But whether, in a case of doubt, he is deemed to have waived his entire right absolutely, or only in relation to that specific creditor, see number 3.

<margin>4</margin> If two creditors holding a mortgage on a thing buy it from the debtor, they are deemed to have mutually waived the mortgage to one another.

<margin>5</margin> A creditor who signs a debtor’s personal note <term>chirographum<gloss>A handwritten debt instrument not necessarily secured by collateral</gloss></term> or another document professing that the property is not subject to a mortgage is deemed to have waived his mortgage right.

With a clarification, as noted there.

Likewise, by the creditor delivering the legal instrument of debt back to the debtor, number 6.

Or by tearing or canceling the document.

Though there are exceptions, as noted there.

<margin>7</margin> A pledge is not deemed waived by mere knowledge, presence, or silence when the property subject to the pledge is sold.

This fails in many cases, as in number 8.

<margin>9</margin> A creditor consenting to the sale of property mortgaged to him, but with a formal protest that his right remains secure,

<column-break/>

is not deemed to have waived his right of mortgage.

The same applies if he consents to a sale on the condition that the debt be paid from the price, number 10.

<margin>11</margin> Whether a creditor consenting to one act of transfer is deemed to consent to any other.

<margin>12</margin> If a debtor sold property subject to a mortgage with the creditor's consent but has not yet delivered it, or if it was delivered but the price not yet paid, the mortgage right is nonetheless deemed waived.

<margin>13</margin> A creditor consenting to the sale of mortgaged property that never actually occurred is not deemed to have waived the pledge right.

The same applies in a fake sale.

Or if the sale was not legally valid.

The same applies when the creditor who consented was a minor, number 14.

The same for a general agent <term>procurator<gloss>A legal representative authorized to act on another's behalf</gloss></term> of the creditor consenting to the sale by the debtor or his agent, number 15.

However, it is different conversely if the creditor consented to the debtor’s general agent.

<margin>16</margin> A creditor consenting to the sale of mortgaged property which later returns to the same debtor for a different reason does not recover the mortgage; however, it is different if it returns for the same reason.

<margin>17</margin> A <term>novatio<gloss>The replacement of an old debt with a new one, which usually cancels the old obligation</gloss></term> of a debt extinguishes the prior obligation of pledge or mortgage unless express mention is made of it.

<margin>18</margin> An enslaved person <term>mancipium<gloss>A term for property, here specifically referring to an enslaved person who could be used as collateral</gloss></term> subject to a general mortgage can be freed by the debtor if he has other assets to pay the debt.

Indeed, in favor of liberty, a minor under twenty-five years of age can consent to the freeing of the person, even if he loses his pledge right, number 19.

<margin>20</margin> Whether one who subjects his property to a pledge or mortgage for another's debt can compel the debtor to release that property from the burden.

Consequently, we must speak of the dissolution of the obligation of pledge and mortgage, assuming what was said in the preceding section on this matter.

<margin>1</margin> First, it is dissolved by **payment** of the debt for which the property was pledged or mortgaged (Law 1 and the law "He is released" in the Digest <note>original: "l. 1. & l. liberatur, ff. quib. mod. pign."</note>). This remains true even if any other person pays the creditor in place of the debtor, and even if the debtor is unaware of the payment. The reason is that when the principal obligation is removed, the accessory obligation—which depends on it—is also removed. The same applies if payment is made to someone whom the creditor must acknowledge as having been paid, such as a legal agent or a servant appointed to receive his money, or to someone for whom the creditor is the heir. This also applies if the creditor had rented a house from a third party and sublet a part of it to me under a pledge, and I pay that third party the portion of the rent I owed the creditor. These points are held in the law "Paid," sections "Paid" and "Wherefore" <note>original: "l. solutum. §. solutam, & §. vnde fi. ff. de pig. act."</note>. It is also the same if the creditor accepts something else as full payment in place of what was owed, or if he cancels the debt through <term>acceptilatio<gloss>A formal verbal acknowledgment that a debt has been discharged, even without payment</gloss></term> or any other valid legal reason.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of security interests, specifically moving from the priority of creditors to the formal ways a pledge or mortgage can be extinguished or canceled under Roman and Canon law.</meta>

# Louis de Molina: On Contracts #

<margin>1</margin>
...through a formal release <note>original: "acceptitationẽ," a formal verbal release from an obligation in Roman law</note>. The same applies if satisfaction is provided in any other way, such as if the creditor accepts another debtor in place of the original (which we understand today as <term>novation<gloss>The replacement of an old contract with a new one, or an old debtor with a new one</gloss></term>), or if he agrees to receive another thing in the future in place of the original debt, or if he accepts other pledges or another mortgage in place of the former ones, or guarantors in place of the pledges or mortgages. Finally, whenever he is satisfied as he himself wished—whether regarding the debt itself or the previous mortgages or pledges—the obligation of the prior pledges or mortgages ceases, even if he was deceived by his own leniency, provided there was no fraud by the other party. This is held in the Law "Likewise he is liberated" <note>original: "l. itẽ liberatur" referring to Digest 13.7.9.pr.</note> at the beginning of the section "On the ways a pledge or mortgage [is dissolved]" <note>original: "ff. quib. mod. pign. vel hypot."</note> and more extensively in the Law "If a thing," section 1, "all," joined with the final gloss there <note>original: "l. si rem j. § ois iuncta gl. vlt."</note> in the Digest under "On the action of pledge." 

If, however, the debtor offers the creditor what is owed and the creditor refuses to accept it, a distinction must be made. For if he offers payment in court, it is considered sufficient for the obligation of the pledge or mortgage to be deemed canceled. This is seen in the Law "If a thing," the final section, joined with the gloss there and affirmed by another gloss according to the text in the Law "Another's property," the section "If to several," in the verse "If the creditor acts to return" <note>original: "l. aliena res. §. si pluribus, ver. si per creditorem verb. ređđẽ agitur"</note> in the Digest under "On the action of pledge." But if he offers payment outside of court, it is further necessary that he seals the counted money and deposits it in some public and safe place, as stated in the Law "A tutor for a ward," at the end <note>original: "l. tutor pro pupillo"</note> in the Digest on the administration of tutors, and the Law "Neither creditors," and the final law in the Code "On the action of pledge," and Law 38, title 13, of the fifth *Partida* <note>original: "l. 38. tit. 13. par. 5," referring to the Siete Partidas, a famous 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>.

Although an <term>alienation<gloss>The transfer of ownership of property to another person, such as through sale or gift</gloss></term> by which a debtor transfers property subject to a pledge or mortgage does not dissolve the right of pledge or mortgage held by the creditor, but rather the ownership passes to whoever receives it along with that burden—as held in the Law "If a thing" in the Code under "On the release of pledge," the Law "The debtor," and the Law "If a debtor" in the Code on the distribution of pledge—it is clear from what has been said, <margin>2</margin> especially in Disputation 334, that if the creditor consents to the thing being sold, exchanged, given as a dowry, or otherwise alienated, or if he ratifies it after the alienation has been made, he is deemed to remit (give up) his right of pledge or mortgage. This is found in the Law "If a debtor," section 1, and the Law "Just as," the section "If by will," and the section "On sale" <note>original: "ff. qb. mod. pig. vel hyp."</note> in the Digest. Also the Law "The creditor" in the Digest under "On the rules of law," and the Law "Lucius," which speaks of a creditor consenting to a dowry. Indeed, if a creditor to whom something was pledged or mortgaged consents to it being pledged to a subsequent creditor, he is deemed to have remitted his right of pledge or mortgage over that thing. This is in the Law "Paulus" (otherwise "Lucius," section "The same Paulus"). 

However, the gloss there and another law (Law 3. in the Code on the release of pledge) understand this only in comparison to that creditor to whom he consented it be pledged; thus, that creditor henceforth has a right of preference in comparison to the creditor who gave his consent, but not absolutely in comparison to other creditors. The Law "A second creditor," the final section <note>original: "Lex creditor scđa, §. vlt."</note>, says that the question—whether one who consented to property already pledged to himself being pledged to another intended to remit his whole right or only in comparison to the one to whom it was pledged—is a matter of fact rather than of law. Thus, if it is clear either from the manner of consent or from the surrounding circumstances what he intended, one must stand by his mind and will. <margin>3</margin> Fourthly, the whole difficulty is what should be decided in a case of doubt. Two cited glosses assert that it should not then be thought he intended to remit his whole right, but only in comparison to that later creditor. However, **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential legal commentators of the Middle Ages</note>, along with the final gloss on the Law "The creditor" cited above, says that if the person who remitted the right of pledge or mortgage in that manner was a man, he should be deemed to have remitted it entirely; but if it was a woman, it should be 

<column-break/>

<margin>4</margin>
judged that she remitted it only regarding that creditor to whom the thing was later pledged. This is because in the Law "We command" <note>original: "l. iubemus"</note> in the Code under the *Senatus Consultum Velleianum* <note>A Roman law that generally prohibited women from standing as surety for the debts of others</note>, it was decreed in favor of women that even if they grant permission for someone holding their pledged assets to pledge them to others, that permission is understood to apply only in comparison to that debtor with whom the contract was then intended to be made, and only in comparison to that contract, not to other contracts or with the same person. This last point concerning a woman's consent entirely pleases me, following Bartolus and **Negusantius** <note>Antonio Negusanti (1465–1528), an Italian jurist known for his work on pledges and mortgages</note> in "On Pledges," part 6, member 3, number 14, against Salycet. Regarding the first point about a man's consent, Negusantius’s distinction and the harmony of Salycet please me: namely, that if a man consented to a thing being pledged to someone in particular, he is deemed to have remitted his right only in comparison to them. But if he granted the faculty of pledging that thing to others absolutely, he is understood to have remitted his right entirely, according to the Law "Paulus" cited.

Similarly, if two creditors having a mortgage on some property buy it from the debtor, they are deemed to mutually remit to each other the mortgage that each of them had on that property. This is because, by mutual tacit consent, each of them buys that thing from the debtor. See the Law "Titius" at the beginning and Bartolus there. 

<margin>5</margin>
Likewise, if a creditor † signs his name to a debtor's handwritten note <note>original: "chirographo," a private bond or debt instrument</note> or another instrument in which he declares that the property is not subject to a mortgage, or not subject to a mortgage to himself, he is deemed by that very act to remit the right of mortgage. This is found in the Law "Titius," final section. The same is true if he signs an instrument of sale by which the property is sold to a third party; for he is deemed to remit the right of mortgage. There, the gloss says it is different if he is merely used as a witness to the instrument of sale, because from the fact that he is a witness to the sale, he is not deemed to consent to the sale for the purpose of being considered to remit the right of mortgage; just as from the fact that he knows a mortgage is being sold and remains silent, he is not deemed to consent to that effect in the sale, as is said there and will be explained more fully below. 

However, it is said to be different if he were used as a witness in an instrument which contains a statement that the property is mortgaged to no one. Then, by consenting to be used as a witness for that instrument, he would be deemed to tacitly consent to the remission of the right of mortgage; for otherwise, he would be providing testimony to a lie and would deceive the creditor. This specific event is not what is discussed in the cited section "Not as," but rather the former one—a point Negusantius did not sufficiently attend to above. Under the section "We are advised," when someone, being deceived, consents in any of these ways or another, or even expressly, then if this is sufficiently clear and proven, the right of pledge or mortgage is not deemed remitted. The same is true if it is clear he consented through force or fear, as held in Law 40, title 13, part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*]. Let the Law "A guarantor," 2, the section "A father" <note>original: "Lex fideiussor. 2. §. pater"</note> in the Digest be cited in confirmation of the aforesaid; however, that law does not speak of the remission of a mortgage, but of a tacit grant so that something may be bound as a pledge or mortgage. For it says there that if he to whom something belongs writes an instrument in which someone else subjects that thing to a mortgage or pledge to a third party, then he is deemed to have tacitly consented that it be so subjected.

<margin>6</margin>
Likewise, by the † delivery to the debtor by the creditor of the instrument <note>the physical debt contract</note> by which something was owed to him under pledge or mortgage, both the debt contained in that instrument and, consequently, the right of pledge or mortgage are deemed remitted. See the Law "From him" <note>original: "leg. ab eo"</note> in the Digest on pacts and the Law...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the cancellation of debts and securities (pledges and mortgages). It specifically examines how a creditor's actions, such as returning legal documents or remaining silent during the sale of a pledged item, affect their legal rights to that security.</meta>

Tract. Secund. Disp. 537.
Aaa 3
catchword: that po-

to the creditor <note>original: "creditricé," a female creditor; the text refers to Law 2 of the Code of Justinian, title 8.25(26)</note>, and Law 40, title 13, Partida 5 <note>The "Partidas" refers to the *Siete Partidas*, a famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>. The same is true if the creditor takes up or cancels the legal document <note>original: "instrum̄," the written contract of debt</note>, as seen in that same Law 40. An exception is added by the gloss on the cited Law: unless it is proven that the creditor handed the document over to the debtor for some other purpose. Similarly, if a creditor <term>bequeaths<gloss>leaves a gift in a will</gloss></term> to the debtor the document for that same debt, pledge, or mortgage, he is judged to be bequeathing both to him. If, however, the creditor hands over or bequeaths the **pledge** under which something was owed to him, he is indeed judged to remit the right to that pledge, but not the debt itself; rather, the debtor is still bound to pay it, unless it is expressed or clearly understood from other evidence that he intended to remit the debt as well. This is stated expressly in Law "Afterward" <note>original: "l. postq̄," Digest 2.14.2</note>, Law 1, the final section, in the title "On legacy of liberation," and the cited Law 40. The reason is that the return of a pledge only indicates the remission of the *right* to the pledge; but the remission of an accessory <note>the security/pledge</note> does not mean the principal <note>the debt itself</note> is remitted. See Negusantius where cited above, number 19, and the doctors he cites. And these things we say regarding the document and the pledge should be added to the discussions in Disputation 196.

<margin>7</margin>
Although the right of pledge or mortgage is deemed remitted not only through express consent—which is well known—but also through tacit consent, which is gathered and presumed from some other act (such as consenting to the <term>alienation<gloss>the transfer or sale to another</gloss></term> of the thing subject to the pledge or mortgage), nevertheless, it is **not** deemed remitted through mere knowledge, presence, and silence when the thing subject to the pledge is sold. This is expressly stated in Law "Just as," section "It does not seem" <note>original: "l. sicút, §. nō vī," Digest 20.6.8.15</note>, and Bartolus affirms it there, as does the common opinion of the doctors; it is also aptly hinted at by many other laws. They do, however, except several events in which a creditor, knowing and staying silent, is deemed to remit the right of pledge or mortgage. First: if a slave subject to a pledge or mortgage is <term>manumitted<gloss>formally set free from slavery</gloss></term>; indeed, out of favor for liberty, a creditor knowing of the manumission and remaining silent is deemed to remit the right of pledge or mortgage he had in that slave (Law 1, Code "On the remission of pledge," and Law 37, title 13, Partida 5). By the same logic, if, with the creditor knowing and allowing it, that slave takes holy orders, the creditor is deemed to remit the right of pledge he has in him; just as an owner, if he knows and allows it, is deemed to grant him liberty; or if he learns of it afterward and does not object within a year (Authenticum "If a slave," Code "On bishops and clerics"). A Bishop, however, who ordains someone knowing he is a slave while the owner is ignorant of it, is compelled to restore double his value to the owner. And those who petitioned the Bishop while ignorant of the status are compelled to pay the same (Chapter "If a slave," distinction 54).

<margin>8</margin>
Second: if the <term>fiscus<gloss>the state treasury</gloss></term> sells a thing subject to another's pledge or mortgage and the creditor, knowing this, stays silent, he loses his right of pledge in favor of the treasury (Law "If mortgages," Code "On the remission of pledges"). Third: when the creditor stays silent with the intent of deceiving the one to whom the thing is transferred—especially in a contract for value—when the buyer is unaware that the thing is obligated to a pledge or mortgage. This is argued from the laws cited in Disputation 531 and asserted by Negusantius, number 25. Fourth: when a pledge or mortgage is sold at the instance of a subsequent creditor and proclamations are made by judicial authority; for if the prior creditor knows this and does not come forward within that time, he is deemed to remit his right of pledge (Law "If at that time," Code "On the remission of pledges").

<margin>9</margin>
When a creditor has indeed consented to the sale or other transfer of a thing subject to his pledge or mortgage, but not simply, but with

<column-break/>

a protestation that his right would remain safe for him, he is not deemed to remit his right of mortgage (Law "If of a debt," section 1, Digest "On the ways a pledge or mortgage is dissolved").

<margin>10</margin>
Likewise, if a creditor consented that the debtor sell the thing subject to the mortgage or pledge under a **condition**—such as that the debt be paid from the price—then, if the condition fails and the debtor does not pay the debt from the price, he is not deemed to have remitted the right of pledge. For he only tacitly consented to the remission of the pledge under that condition, which was not fulfilled. In this event, he can sue indiscriminately both the debtor (to subject something of equal value to the pledge) and also the third-party possessor of the sold item, so that the debt may be paid from it in the absence of the debtor and the <term>guarantors<gloss>fideiussorum; those who promise to pay if the debtor fails</gloss></term> (Law "Just as," section "That," joined with the gloss and Bartolus there, Digest "On the ways a pledge or mortgage is dissolved"). If, however (as Bartolus correctly notes), he granted the power not under a condition but under a **mode** <note>a "mode" (modus) in Roman law is a duty or purpose attached to a gift or act, but unlike a condition, it does not suspend the act's validity</note>—namely, that the debtor *should* pay him from the proceeds—then he cannot sue the third-party possessor if the debtor does not pay the debt from the price. This is because he is truly deemed to have consented to the remission of the right of pledge or mortgage without any dependency on a future event. He can, however, sue the debtor who failed to fulfill the mode, so that he may provide another equal pledge. So says Negusantius, number 1.

<margin>11</margin>
When a creditor consents to one act of transfer, is he deemed to consent to any other? Marcellus correctly states (Law "Just as," section "But also if he permitted") that this question is more one of fact than of law, and therefore must be weighed from the surrounding circumstances as to what the creditor's intention was. If he consented so that he might be paid from the price, he is not deemed to permit a gift or any other transfer from which he gains no profit. If, however, he permitted a gift, he is deemed to have permitted a sale or exchange, unless perhaps he permitted the gift out of consideration for a specific friend; for then he is not to be judged as permitting a sale or exchange, and much less a gift to anyone else. And if he permitted a sale for twenty, he is not deemed to permit a sale for ten; but conversely, if he permitted a sale for ten, he is deemed to permit a sale for twenty—provided the permission was made so that the debt could be paid and there are no circumstances suggesting the contrary, as there usually are not. Similarly, if a creditor consented to a pledge being sold or transferred within a certain time, such as a year, and it was transferred after that time, he is not deemed to have consented to the remission of the mortgage. Also, if he permitted the *debtor* to sell or transfer the pledge, and the debtor did not transfer it, but perhaps it came into the possession of another, he is not deemed to remit the pledge if this other person sells it. Both points are held in the cited Law "Just as," penultimate section. Exception: unless that possessor is the heir of the debtor; for if the heir transfers it, the creditor loses his right of pledge. So it is held in the cited Law "Just as," section "If to the debtor."

<margin>12</margin>
If a creditor consented to the sale of a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage and the debtor sold it, but has not yet delivered it, or delivered it but the buyer has not paid the price nor is ready to pay, is the right of pledge deemed remitted? In the first case, the seller is bound to deliver the thing, or to...

<margin>33</margin>
If, however, the creditor consented to the sale <note>original: "venditioni"</note> or transfer <term>alienation<gloss>the legal transfer of property ownership to another</gloss></term>, and the transfer did not follow, the right of the pledge or mortgage is not considered waived; because by that consent, the pledge is tacitly considered waived only under the condition that the transfer actually follows, according to the cited Law *sicut*, paragraph *by the will*. For this same reason, if a transfer follows that is 
**fictitious**, the right of the pledge or mortgage is not considered waived: because a fictitious transfer is no transfer at all. This is the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> based on the text in the same Law *sicut*. By the same reasoning, if the transfer was not legally valid, the right of pledge or mortgage is not considered waived: because an invalid transfer is no transfer. This is held in Law *if a debtor*, the final paragraph, in the Digest title "In what ways a pledge or mortgage [is dissolved]." From this, Bartolus generally infers, and the others agree, that if the act for which consent is given is not valid, that consent does no harm: because it is treated as if it had never been granted.

<margin>34</margin>
By the same reasoning, consent granted by a **minor** regarding the transfer of a thing subject to a pledge or mortgage for their benefit does not waive the right of the pledge or mortgage, unless it was granted in the presence of a <term>tutor or curator<gloss>legal guardians for minors or those unable to manage their own affairs</gloss></term>, and with the simultaneous authority of a judge, or unless it was granted by the tutor with the judge's authority. See Law *if he consented*, at the beginning, in the same Digest title.

<margin>35</margin>
Likewise, when someone has been appointed as a **general agent** <note>original: "procurator generalis"</note> for a creditor, even if they consent in the name of the creditor to the transfer of a thing subject to the creditor's pledge or mortgage, if they do not have a specific mandate from the creditor for that purpose, the creditor would not lose the right of the pledge or mortgage. If, however, the creditor permitted the debtor's general agent to transfer the thing pledged or mortgaged to him, he would be considered to waive the right of the pledge or mortgage, even if such an agent did not have a specific mandate for it from the debtor. This is from Law *if he consented*, paragraph 1. If, however, someone was appointed by the creditor as an agent "in his own interest" <note>original: "in rem suam," a legal term for an agent who has the rights of the principal</note>, as they say, then if he consented to the transfer, he would be considered to waive the right of the pledge or mortgage, according to Law *sicut*, paragraph *the agent*.

When a creditor, who held a **universal mortgage** over all goods, or a particular one over a specific thing, consents to something being transferred that was contained under that universal mortgage, or that specific thing in which he had a 
<margin>36</margin>
particular mortgage, even if the debtor **afterward** recovers ownership of it for a different reason—either because he became the heir of the last possessor, or because someone donated it to him, bequeathed it, or gave it as a dowry—the creditor does not recover the mortgage on that item. This remains true even if the debtor had subjected all his present and future goods to the mortgage, as is discussed from the final law in the Code "On the remission of a pledge" <note>original: "C. de remiss. pignor."</note> in section 28; it is established from Law *sicut*, paragraph *superfluous*. However, it is otherwise if he recovers it for the **same reason** for which it was transferred, or for a connected reason; for example, because it was sold with a pact to buy it back and was redeemed, or because it was returned due to a defect, or the sale was cancelled due to a time-limit clause or a forfeiture clause,

<column-break/>

and finally for any other such reason; because through that cancellation, the debtor is restored to the ownership of that thing in such a way that the creditor is restored to his own right of mortgage which he had before. This is held in the said Law *by the will*, at the beginning and in the final paragraph, and the glosses on the final law of the Code "On the remission of a pledge," Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors, which Negusantius <note>Antonio Negusanti, a 16th-century legal scholar</note> refers to and follows at point 21.

When some debt is subject to a pledge or mortgage, if a valid **voluntary novation** <term>novation<gloss>the replacement of an old contract or debt with a new one</gloss></term> of that same debt occurs—whereby, the prior obligation being extinguished, another succeeds it into which the first is changed, either with the same debtor taking on the obligation or by a <term>delegate<gloss>a third party who takes over the debt</gloss></term>—then, 
<margin>37</margin>
unless the same pledge or mortgage is explicitly repeated in the later obligation, the obligation of the pledge or mortgage is extinguished. See Law *paid*, at the beginning, in the Digest "On the action of pledge," and Law *by novation* in the title "On novations." We specify "voluntary novation": because by the contesting of a lawsuit against the debtor, and much more so by a judgment rendered against him, a **necessary** novation is considered to have occurred; however, this does not extinguish the prior obligation of the debt, nor does it extinguish the obligation of the pledges or mortgages provided as security for the prior obligation. See Law *otherwise* in the Digest "On novations." What a novation is, and what is required there for it to be considered done, will be discussed below in its proper place. However, when a **delay** <note>original: "dilatio"</note> of the deadline for payment is granted to the debtor, because that is not a novation but a prolongation of the term under the same obligation, the right of pledge or mortgage is not extinguished; rather, the prolongation of the term is considered made under the same pledges, mortgages, waivers, and established penalties as was prescribed from the beginning. This is argued from Law *the law* in the Code "On hiring," and the gloss on Law *Aemilius* affirms this. Read Negusantius in the cited section 3, starting at number 3.

If, however, they are freed, although the manumission is valid so that the debtor cannot reduce them back into slavery, they nevertheless remain bound to the creditor for the debt, so that they can be sold to pay the debt, unless the debtor, or the enslaved person themselves, or another in their place, pays the debt in full. See Law *if to creditors*, joined with Law 1 and following in the Code "On an enslaved person given as a pledge and manumitted," and Law 37, title 13, Partida 5. Nevertheless, 
<margin>38 †</margin>

See Laws 2 and 3 in the same Code title and the cited Law 37. But if the debtor frees them not having other goods to pay the debt, the person remains liable for the debt alone, so that they can be sold as long as the debtor, the enslaved person, or someone else has not paid the debt in full, as was said regarding an enslaved person subject to a specific mortgage and freed without the creditor's knowledge. # On the sale of a pledge due to debt, and the agreements regarding the sale which usually precede it.

## DISPUTATION DXXXVIII.

### SUMMARY.

1 **An agreement stating that if the seller does not pay the debt within a certain time, the pledge remains sold at a fair price—to be assessed by the judgment of a fair-minded person—is valid.**
**Indeed, even if nothing is said about the price, it is understood to be at the judgment of a fair-minded person.**
2 **A creditor, through an agreement to sell, cannot sell the pledge before the debtor is in default of payment.**
3 **When a debtor is considered to be in default of payment.**
4 **When a creditor may proceed to the sale of a pledge without any formal notice being made, and what is the rule in the Law of Castile.**
5 **A creditor cannot be compelled to sell his debtor's pledge. However, he is bound to produce it once the debtor has provided the required security.**
6 **In what order a creditor ought to proceed to the sale of his debtor's pledge when no agreement is present.**
**And what is the rule in the Law of Castile.**
7 **What is the effect of an agreement that a creditor cannot sell his debtor's pledge.**
8 **Notice regarding the sale of a pledge can be waived by agreement between the creditor and seller, but a warning cannot.**
9 **What a judicial pledge is.**
10 **A judicial pledge can be sold after four months have elapsed from the day the final sentence was passed.**
11 **Whether the time given to condemned persons for payment can be shortened or extended at the judge's discretion.**
**And what is the rule in the Law of Castile.**
12 **Regarding the "ready execution" in the newest Law of Castile, how those things are done, and in what order execution must be made.**
**And what is the rule in the Law of Portugal. number 13.**
14 **If a buyer is not found for a judicial pledge, it is to be awarded to the victor for a fair price, by the judgment of a fair-minded person.**
15 **The time in which a praetorian <note>a pledge seized by court order</note> pledge can be sold is at the judge's discretion.**
16 **In what order and within how much**

<column-break/>

**time a conventional pledge can be sold when no agreement is present.**
17 **A primary creditor who has the right of priority, if he sells the property subject to his mortgage, cannot be sued by the debtor or a subsequent creditor by offering him or the buyer the price.**
**However, clarify and understand this as in numbers 19, 20, and 21.**
18 **Whether a creditor possessing a pledge by a court sentence can petition the judge to prescribe a certain time limit for the debtor to recover it, so he is not forced to count its fruits <note>profits or produce from the property</note> against the principal debt.**
22 **If a debtor bequeaths property to another that is mortgaged, or prohibits its transfer in a will, it does not prejudice the creditor.**
**Clarify and understand as stated there.**
23 **In what order a creditor is bound to sell many pledges obligated to him specifically and generally for the same debt.**
24 **A debtor cannot buy his own property from a creditor; if he buys it, it will not be a purchase, but a payment of the debt.**
**The same must be said of a creditor when he sells a pledge and later buys it back from the buyer: hence the debtor can offer him the price.**

29 **To what a creditor is bound in those cases in which he is not held liable for the eviction of a sold pledge.**
30 **In events where the creditor is held liable for eviction by reason of a sold pledge, he is also held liable for damages.**
31 **When a creditor has recourse against the debtor for an evicted pledge.**

<margin>1</margin> It remains for us to speak concerning the <term>distraction<gloss>the legal sale or disposal</gloss></term> of a pledge or mortgage for the debt for which they are obligated. Regarding the "forfeiture clause" <note>original: "pacto legis commissoriae"; a clause where the creditor keeps the property if the debt isn't paid</note> concerning a pledge and concerning a sale, it was said in Disputations 24 and 278 that while it may be valid regarding a sale, it is nevertheless utterly void regarding a pledge or mortgage. However, as was said in Disputation 324, an agreement is valid whereby, if the debtor does not pay the debt within a certain time limit for which something was given as a pledge, the pledge remains sold to the creditor—not indeed for just any price, but for a determined fair price to be estimated by the judgment of fair-minded men. According to the opinion of Bartolus, Panormitanus, and many others, it was said to be the same if the agreement is that if the debtor does not pay within that time, the pledge remains sold to the creditor: because it is understood to be for a fair price which fair-minded men shall then have judged. It is also customary to add an agreement that if the debtor does not pay the debt in his own time, the creditor may sell the pledge so that the debt may be satisfied from the price: such an agreement is valid for the effects immediately to be explained, as held in the Code <note>original: "l. vlt. §. sancimus. C. de iure dominii impetrando," referring to Code 8.33.3</note>, and Law 41, Title 13, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the Castilian statutory code</note>.

<margin>2</margin> Whether an agreement preceded it that the creditor could sell the pledge or not, the creditor cannot proceed to sell it before the debtor is in **default** of paying the debt, because the power granted to him by the agreement to sell is understood to begin from the day of default. But if a day was fixed for paying the debt, the debtor is not [considered in default before then]...

->Luis de Molina, On Contracts<-

is considered to be in **default** <note>original: "mora"; a legal delay that triggers penalties or rights</note> once that day has passed without the debt being satisfied. Consequently, before that day has passed, the creditor cannot proceed to sell the pledge, as held in the law *Since [debts] are to be paid* <note>original: "l. cum soluendæ. ff. de distract. pign."; Digest 20.5.4</note>. However, once that day has passed, the debtor is considered to be in default even if the debt is not specifically demanded, according to the law *The Great* <note>original: "l. magnā. C. de contrah. & commit. stipul."; Code 8.37.12</note>, because "the date stands in for the creditor" <note>This is a legal maxim meaning that if a deadline is set, the passing of the deadline itself serves as a formal demand for payment.</note>. If, however, no date was specifically fixed for the payment, the debtor is not considered to be in default simply by the passage of time—which reason requires for payment—until he has been formally summoned by the creditor, which is to say, warned to pay. This is found in the law *If by cause of legacy* <note>original: "l. si ex legati causa. ff. de verb. obl."; Digest 45.1.122</note> and was discussed in Disputation 532; it is also affirmed by Negusantius in *On Pledges*, part 6, and is the common opinion of the doctors of law.

<margin>The Law of Castile</margin>
4 When the power to sell the pledge was granted to the creditor, then, standing on Common Law alone, by the very fact that the debtor is in default of payment, the creditor may proceed to the sale of the pledge without any further <term>denunciation<gloss>a formal legal notice or warning</gloss></term>; that is, without a warning to the debtor that he intends to sell it. This is the gloss on the law *A creditor [may sell] mortgages* <note>original: "l. creditor hypothecas, verbo testato, C. de distra. pign."; Code 8.27.4</note>, and is affirmed by Negusantius and the common opinion of the doctors cited by Gregorio López and Villalobos. They agree with the laws *If it was agreed* <note>Digest 13.7.4</note> and *We sanction* <note>Code 8.33.3</note>. However, regarding the **Law of Castile**, in the laws cited above, even if an agreement preceded it allowing the creditor to sell the pledge, before he actually sells it, he is bound to warn the debtor that he wishes to sell it. If the debtor is absent, he is bound to make the warning at the debtor's house, unless perhaps this is impossible—such as when the debtor and his entire household are absent or there is an impediment. If the sale is made otherwise, it is void, and the debtor can reclaim the pledge by paying the buyer the price up to the amount of his debt. Whether the creditor sells the pledge under Common Law without prior warning, or under the Law of Castile with prior warning, he is bound to sell it in good faith, at the best price he can conveniently obtain, and through a <term>public auction<gloss>original: "subhastatione"; a sale "under the spear," referring to the Roman custom of marking an auction with a spear</term>. If any of the price remains leftover, he is bound to return it to the debtor. In both cases, the debtor has a "direct action of pledge" <note>original: "pignoratitia actio directa"</note> against the creditor to recover the surplus. If, however, the price does not suffice to pay the whole debt, the creditor has a personal action against the debtor to pay what is missing.

5 However, a creditor is never forced to sell a pledge, as held in the law *Although* <note>Digest 13.7.6</note>, since the debtor himself, if he wishes, can sell it and pay the debt from the price. But if the debtor asks for the pledge to be produced so that it may be sold, the creditor is bound to show it, provided that due <term>security<gloss>original: "cautione"; a guarantee or bond</gloss></term> is provided, either by another pledge or a guarantor. These rules apply to sales in good faith and the other procedures for selling a pledge that will be described.

<column-break/>

6 When no agreement preceded regarding whether the creditor could sell the pledge, and it was not prohibited by agreement, although under the law of the *Digests* the creditor could still proceed to the sale without further notice once the debtor was in default, nevertheless, as the glosses and other laws suggest, at least one **denunciation** (notice) is required. According to the Law of the *Partidas* <note>The *Siete Partidas*, the primary statutory code of Castile</note>, after that notice is given, the creditor is bound under Common Law to wait a **two-year period** <note>original: "biennium"</note> before he sells the pledge. This two-year period should be counted from the notice given if the debt is clear; otherwise, from the sentence handed down by a judge stating that the debt must be paid and the pledge can be sold.
<margin>The Law of Castile</margin>
However, under the **Law of Castile**, if the pledge is a movable item (personal property), he is only bound to wait **twelve days**; if it is an immovable item (like land or a house), he is only bound to wait **thirty days**. This difference between Common Law and the law of Castile is noted by Gregorio López and Villalobos, and there are various laws on this matter in different kingdoms, as the learned doctors advise.

7 When an agreement preceded stating that the creditor *cannot* sell the pledge, such an agreement is not valid to the extent of preventing a sale entirely—because that would be against public utility, for if a creditor could never sell a pledge, no one would want to lend to the needy. However, it is valid to the extent that the pledge cannot be sold unless a **threefold notification** <note>original: "trina denunciatio"</note> is made to the debtor to pay. It is as if the agreement contains a silent condition: "unless he is first warned three times to pay." This is the express holding of the law *If it was agreed*. These notifications should not be made all at once in a single context, but, as the doctors affirm, at least a **three-day interval** should occur between one and the next, or as others prefer, it should be left to the judge's discretion. After those three notifications, he must wait two years before the pledge is sold, according to Common Law. In this specific event, the Law of Castile does not differ from the Common Law, as the law of the *Partidas* expressly holds.

8 In the three scenarios explained above—whether no notice is necessary for the sale to be valid, or one is necessary, or three—whenever one proceeds to the sale of a pledge, it is furthermore appropriate to warn the debtor to **be present at the sale**. This is not because the sale would be void without that warning (in the way it would be if the other warnings and time periods discussed so far were not observed), but

<meta>This page continues Disputation 538, transitioning from the sale of "conventional" pledges (private agreements) to "judicial" pledges (property seized by court order). It compares the grace periods allowed for debtors under the Roman-based Common Law (Ius Commune) versus the specific statutory laws of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

### Second Tractate, Disputation 538.

...let suspicion of fraud be absent, nor should the debtor afterwards be able to bring a **pledge action** <note>original: "pignoratitiâ actione"; a lawsuit used to recover a pledge or its value</note> for damages against the creditor on account of fraud committed in the sale. This specific warning is primarily discussed in the law *The creditor of mortgages* <note>original: "l. creditor hypothecas. C. de remif. pig."; Code of Justinian 8.25.1</note>. This doctrine is handed down by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Negusantius relates and follows (as cited above, number 6), etc.

Thus far we have spoken of the sale of a conventional pledge. As for the **judicial pledge** <note>original: "iudiciale pignus"; property seized by authority of a court to satisfy a judgment</note>, which is taken for the execution of a final judgment in which the defendant is condemned to pay some amount; or which is taken for the execution of payment for a similar debt that the defendant has confessed in court to owing—according to the laws *By the Divine Pius* and *To Debtors* <note>original: "l. à Diuo Pio, & l. debitoribus. ff. de re iudicata"; Digest 42.1.15 and 42.1.31</note>, as well as the penultimate law of title 27, part 3, to which Law 4, title 13, part 5 refers—a far different order must be followed. 

For from the moment a condemnatory judgment is issued from which there is no appeal, or which is final so that no appeal is granted; and likewise from the moment of a confession of debt in court, which the defendant is then ordered to pay, by **Common Law** <note>The "Ius Commune," a blend of Roman and Canon law used across Europe</note> a space of four months must be granted before judicial pledges are taken from the defendant and his sureties and sold to pay that debt. This time is granted to those condemned to pay as a period for settlement <note>original: "l. à bē. l. 12. & c. C. de vfur. is rei iudicatæ"; Code 7.54.2</note>. The same is true in Canon Law. However, such a period may be shortened or extended by a judge for a reasonable cause, based on the amount of the debt and other concurrent circumstances. By the **Law of Castile**, however, only a space of ten days is granted from the confession of the debt or from the issuance of a judgment that has become *res iudicata* <note>A matter already judged and no longer subject to appeal</note>.

<margin>Law of Portugal</margin>
Whether anything has been changed in that Kingdom today, we shall add a little below. Note, however, that when the case involves the sale of a thing, or if someone is condemned to deliver a specific item, then the judgment is immediately commanded for execution without waiting for those four months of common civil or canon law, or the ten days of the Law of Castile. If, however, the item to be returned is absent, or if some legitimate impediment occurs why the defendant cannot return it immediately, a deadline is prescribed for him by the judge in which he must return it, or pay its value if it cannot be returned at all, with the defendant providing sureties. 

Once the four-month space granted to the debtor for payment by common civil and canon law has elapsed, if the debtor does not pay within that time, pledges are seized. Within two other months from the point of their seizure, the sale must be made by the authority of the ordinary judge who heard the case in the first instance. This was later established by the law of the Code to be four months, unless it seemed to the judge—having heard the case and weighed the circumstances—that for a just and reasonable cause the time should be

<column-break/>

shortened or extended. Another period, after the pledges are taken, consists of two other months—not indeed for the debtor to pay, but for the pledges to be sold during that time; the sale is not to be finalized until those months have elapsed, so that a fair price may be found. If, however, before the sale is finalized, the debtor pays the debt, the sale is not completed, but the pledges are returned to him upon his paying the expenses incurred. 

That the four months established by the law of the Code are a distinct time from the two months established for selling pledges after they are taken is asserted (against the *Gloss* and Cyanus, whom Gregory Lopez wrongly follows) by Bartolus, Alexander, and Jason, whom Negusantius refers to and follows. By the Law of the *Partidas* <note>The "Siete Partidas," the foundational statutory code of Castile</note> of Castile, pledges are taken after ten days, as was said, and only twenty days are established for selling them publicly (and ten if they are movable goods); when these are finished, the sale is finalized with the person who offered the most for them.

Today, however, by the Law of Castile <note>referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* or New Collection of laws</note>, judgments that pass into *res iudicata*, confessions of debt in court by the debtors themselves, as well as public contracts, and even private ones—provided they are recognized in court—have **ready execution** <note>original: "paratam exequutionẽ"; an expedited legal process where the creditor can seize assets immediately without a full trial on the merits</note>. No exception is admitted against this that would prevent it from being carried out until the debtor's goods have fully satisfied the creditor, except for a few cases mentioned in the law, which must be proven by the debtor within ten days. 

Although only those few exceptions prevent execution, if the debtor raises any other defense, the execution cannot be carried out unless the creditor provides sureties [guarantees] that, if a judgment is later issued against him, he will restore everything, including expenses. In that case, the sale of the debtor's goods is dissolved, and everything is restored to him along with any damages.

Furthermore, in Law 19 of the same title, the following form is prescribed for performing such executions:

> "We ordain and command that when any execution is requested, and it appears to the judge that the document for which it is requested ought to be executed, he shall issue his order of execution without summoning the executed party for it. He shall command by it that execution be made upon movable goods, and in their absence, upon real estate (for executions must be performed this way, beginning with movable goods, as in the law *By the Divine Pius* <note>Digest 42.1.15.8</note>) with guarantees to be given for indemnification... in default of the said guarantees..."

It highlights the significant difference between Roman Common Law, which granted a four-month grace period, and the Law of Castile, which reduced this to ten days for "ready execution."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Disputation 538 regarding the legal enforcement of debts. It transitions from the general rules of "conventional" pledges to the specific statutory procedures of the Spanish and Portuguese kingdoms, focusing on how property is seized and auctioned to satisfy a court judgment.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...guarantees that the debtor be arrested <note>original Spanish: "fianchas sea preso el deudor"</note>, provided he is not of such status that, according to the laws of these Kingdoms, he cannot be arrested for debt. In this manner, execution shall be carried out against movable goods, and in their absence, against real estate. If carried out against movable goods, public proclamations <note>original: "pregones"; public announcements of an auction</note> shall be made for nine days, one every three days. If it involves real estate, three proclamations shall be made over twenty-seven days, one every nine days. Once these proclamations are made, the debtor shall be summoned in person for the final auction <note>original: "remate"</note>, if he can be found; if not, at his house, informing his wife, children, or servants if he has them, and if not, the closest neighbors. Once the summons is made, if he opposes it within three days and alleges a legitimate legal exception according to the first and second laws of this title, a ten-day period shall run from the opposition, provided it is made within the third day. If no opposition is made within the said three days, the judge shall order the final auction and payment to the party, provided the party seeking execution gives the guarantees required by the Law of Toledo (namely the second of the same title) and other laws of these Kingdoms. The final auction and payment shall proceed regardless of any appeal.

<margin>Portuguese Law 13</margin> Regarding Portuguese Law, in Book 3 of the *Ordinances*, Title 71, it is established that judgments which have passed into a "judged matter" <note>original: "rem transeunt iudicatam"; a final judgment that can no longer be appealed</note> regarding the debts we are discussing must be sent for execution as soon as the creditor demands it from the judge. (The same applies to similar debts which the debtor confesses in court.) When execution is first attempted, the debtor must be warned to pay, or to immediately hand over sufficient pledges to satisfy the debt and the expenses. Once this warning is made, it is not necessary to warn him again later at the time of the sale of the pledges. Whatever the debtor might object, the execution must nonetheless be carried out, and the debt must be paid to the victor from the price of the pledges; provided he provides sufficient surety that, if a judgment is later issued against him regarding those exceptions, he will restore everything without any evasion, including expenses. Otherwise, the money from which the debt was to be paid is placed with a competent depository until a judgment is rendered regarding the exceptions. But if the defendant is acquitted, his pledges are restored to him, the sale notwithstanding, except for the fruits <note>original: "fructibus"; the profits or produce, such as rent or crops</note> harvested from them, which are left to the buyer; however, the one who caused the execution to be carried out must pay the defendant the value of such fruits. If the buyer made any improvements to the pledges, he is paid by the owner of the pledges, offsetting in that event the value of the fruits the buyer took from the pledges. Read there which exceptions can be raised by the defendant and which cannot. Likewise, in what manner execution should be carried out: first on movable goods, and if those are lacking or the debtor does not hand them over when requested, on immovable goods. Movable goods are to be sold by daily proclamation in public places of the town where the execution occurs for ten continuous business days, and immovable goods for thirty days, counting from the day the pledges were seized. On the last day, even if it is a holiday, once the proclamation is made in places where people usually gather for this purpose, the sale is to be finalized by order of the judge with 

<column-break/>

the person who offers the highest price for them. These and other matters are contained in that title.

Just as was said above regarding conventional pledges <note>private agreements between parties</note>, so must it be said here regarding judicial pledges <note>property seized by a court</note>: namely, if they are sold for a higher price than the debt for which execution is made (including expenses), the surplus must be returned to the debtor, according to the law *To Debtors* <note>original: "l. debitoribus"; Digest 42.1.31</note> at the end, and the last law of title 27, part 3. But if the full debt is not satisfied from the price of the pledges, execution shall be made again against the debtor’s goods until the full debt is paid; for the previous pledges alone would not constitute a full execution of the judgment and debt. Thus holds the last law cited, and the matter is clear enough in itself; the laws *Which Mortgages* and *Specially* <note>Code of Justinian 8.27 and 8.25</note> agree, even though those laws only speak of conventional pledges and mortgages. If, however, within the time prescribed for the sale of the pledge, no one is found who wishes to offer a price for it, or who wishes to offer as much as it is worth, the judge grants the person in whose favor the execution is made the right to bid for it himself, or through the person seeking execution in his name, or to increase the price just like anyone else, so that the sale may be made to him.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin> Thus holds the Code, Law 2, *If in a judged case a pledge was taken*. The Portuguese *Ordinances* at the cited title 71, §13, establish that this should only happen on the final day when the sale must be completed; and that the power to do so must then be requested from the judge, which he is bound to grant. But if, due to fear or the cleverness of the person against whom execution is made, no one is found who wishes to offer a price, or who wishes to offer what the pledge is worth under that mode of sale, then the last law of the Code, *If in a judged case a pledge was taken*, decrees that the pledge be granted to the person in whose favor the execution is made, in exchange for what is owed to him, and that he acquires ownership of it. At that point, the common laws seem to suggest that whether the pledge is worth more or less, he should be content with it and cannot demand more, as is clear from *The Divine Pius* <note>Digest 42.1.15.3</note>, the law *Order* <note>Code 7.53</note>, and the last law of the Code regarding the right to claim damages. In this last law, however, the talk is of a conventional pledge, and it is granted that in such an event the creditor may approach the Prince (understand this, following Negusantius and others, as referring to the judge as his minister) who may adjudge the pledge to him for the debt. Once obtained, he acquires ownership of it; provided, however, that if the debtor, within two years from the moment the pledge was granted to the creditor for the debt, offers him the full debt along with all damages resulting to the creditor from the debtor’s stubbornness <note>original: "contumacia"; legal term for willful disobedience or failure to appear</note>, including lost profits, he may recover his pledge.

<margin>Castilian Law</margin> Rightly, however, the last law of Castile, title 27, part 3, ordains that if, whether through fear or love of the debtor, or for any other cause, a just price is not found for the pledge, the judge should assign it to the victor as if sold to him for the price that the judge himself has judged to be just. Therefore, if such a just price exceeds the debt and expenses, the victor is bound to return the surplus to the condemned party; but if it does not reach the amount of the debt and expenses, the person who owned the pledge shall be compelled to pay, in addition, what is lacking to complete the debt and expenses. These are nearly all the resolutions or modes of carrying out this execution.

## Second Treatise, Disputation 5
## Page 389

...regarding the delivery of property, in the gloss on the section "if pledges" <note>original Latin: *si pignora*</note> as cited. I am entirely of the opinion that, if there is no one else who offers a fair price for the pledge under the terms of the sale, the winning creditor <note>original: *victor*; the party who won the court judgment</note> should first be admitted to bid. But if the bidding does not reach the minimum fair price under those sale conditions, the judge should award it to him at that minimum fair price. If the winning creditor does not want it for that price, and it is understood to be the fault of the owner of the pledge <note>the debtor</note> that a higher price is not found, the judge shall award it to the winning creditor as payment for the debt. However, the owner of the pledge shall have the right, within two years, to pay the debt in full along with all subsequent damages, and thus redeem his pledge. If, however, no fault is found on the part of the debtor, the judge should hand the pledge over to the winning creditor to be held for the debt until someone is found who will meet the fair price for that pledge. This concludes the discussion on judicial pledges <note>property seized by court order</note>.

<margin>15</margin> As for the **praetorian pledge** <note>original: *pignus praetorium*; a seizure initiated by a high official or magistrate, as distinct from a strictly judicial seizure</note>, the common opinion—along with Bartolus <note>a famous 14th-century Italian jurist</note>, whom Negusantius refers to above at number 8 and follows—is this: since it is not found to be established by the law itself within what time it ought to be sold, it should be committed to the judge's discretion to decide the timing of the sale, after considering all concurrent circumstances.

<margin>16</margin> To return to **conventional pledges** <note>original: *pignora conventionalia*; collateral agreed upon by private contract rather than court order</note> in the broad sense, Alberto and Gregorio Lopez (on Law 42, Title 13, Part 5, at the word *treynta*) advise that if no prior agreement was made regarding the sale of the conventional pledge, or if there was an agreement not to sell it, a shorter path to selling it and recovering the debt is found—especially according to the laws and statutes of certain kingdoms—if recourse is made to the judge’s executive authority. Thus, by turning the conventional pledge into a judicial one, the creditor should demand payment from the debtor before the judge. If he does not pay, and execution is sought against his goods for that debt, the conventional pledge is converted into a judicial one.

<margin>17</margin> It must be observed that when a thing is obligated to many people in a certain order as a pledge or mortgage <note>original: *hypothecam*</note>, if the person to whom it was first obligated—or who has the **right of preference** <note>original: *ius praelationis*</note> to sell it and recover his debt—sells it rightly (according to what has been said), then the right of pledge or mortgage is entirely extinguished in that thing. It remains completely free for the buyer, so that it cannot be reclaimed by the debtor (by offering the debt to the creditor or buyer), nor by a subsequent creditor to whom it was obligated later. Say the same when it is rightly sold by the person to whom alone it was obligated, or to whom it remains obligated first because the debtor, by paying the debt to the prior creditor or creditors, extinguished the right of mortgage by which it was previously bound. In that case, no right remains for the debtor against the buyer, nor for any other subsequent creditor. This is held in Law 3 at the beginning and Law 2 of the Code, "If an older creditor has sold the pledge" <note>original: *C. si antiquior creditor pign. vendiderit*</note>, and Law "He who from a creditor" <note>original: *l. qui à creditore*</note> in the Code, "On the selling of pledges" <note>original: *C. de distract. pign.*</note>, and Law "When the prior" <note>original: *l. cum prior*</note> in the Digest, same title, and in other laws.

<margin>18</margin> At this point, I should mention in passing that I do not see what difficulty is contained in the question raised by Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a 16th-century Spanish canonist</note> in *Various Resolutions*, Book 3, Chapter 18, final number. Specifically: whether a creditor, to whom a thing obligated to him is delivered by judicial sentence so that he may hold it by right of pledge or mortgage until his debt is satisfied,

<column-break/>

can ask the judge to prescribe a certain time limit for the former possessor (from whom it was taken) to pay the debt, otherwise it shall be solemnly sold. This is so the creditor is not forced to receive his debt bit by bit by counting the fruits <note>income, such as rent or harvests</note> of that thing toward the principal sum. For first of all, a mortgage cannot be seized from a **third-party possessor** <note>someone who bought the land from the debtor</note> to be delivered to the creditor as a pledge before the principal debtor is in default <note>original: *in mora*</note> of paying the debt, and before execution has been made against his goods, and even against his guarantors (if any were provided for paying that debt), as was said in Disputation 534. But when the debtor is in default of paying the debt, whether the pledge is judicial or conventional, it can and ought to be sold at the request of the creditor in the ways explained so far. Nor can there be any doubt that a creditor cannot be delayed from receiving his debt by forcing him to receive it bit by bit from the fruits of the pledge. Meanwhile, however, as long as the principal debtor is not in default of payment, a mortgage cannot be seized by the judge's authority to be delivered to the creditor as a pledge, even if it is possessed by the debtor himself, let alone if it is possessed by some third party who has become the owner of that thing.

<margin>19</margin> Having noted this in passing, to return to the sale of a thing obligated to many as a pledge or mortgage: the same is not to be said if the debtor delivers it **in lieu of payment** <note>original: *in solutum*; giving property instead of cash</note> or sells it to the first creditor to whom it was previously obligated, or to him who has the right of preference over the rest of the mortgage creditors. For if a subsequent creditor offers the first creditor what was owed to him under that pledge or mortgage, the first creditor is bound to return such a thing to the subsequent creditor—unless (as said in Disputation 536) the first creditor wishes to pay the subsequent creditor what was owed to him under that same pledge or mortgage. This is held in Law 1 of the Code, "If an older creditor has sold the pledge," and Law "When the prior" in the Digest, "On the selling of pledges," and Law 46 joined with the first gloss of Gregorio Lopez there, Title 13, Part 5. Gregorio Lopez says the same thing applies there if the same thing, mortgaged to many, is assigned by the judge as payment to the first creditor, because the act of the judge is considered the act of the debtor himself, according to the Law "If for a cause" <note>original: *l. si ob causam*</note> in the Code, "On Evictions." But if the first creditor—who thus bought from the debtor the thing mortgaged to himself and others, or received it as payment from the debtor or judge—sells it to some third party, or even that third party sells it to a fourth, the subsequent creditor can nonetheless reclaim it by offering what was owed to that first creditor under that mortgage. Thus says Gregorio Lopez in the place cited above, with others whom he cites. The reason is that the first creditor did not sell it then by the right of a "first creditor" to receive what was owed to him from the price, but rather sold it as a thing previously sold or delivered to him by the debtor as payment. Therefore, he could transfer no more right to the buyer through that sale than he himself acquired by right of purchase or delivery as payment from the debtor.

Observe, however, that when the first creditor truly acquires ownership of that thing by buying it from the debtor or receiving it as payment (even if with the burden explained regarding the subsequent creditor), it is no different than if some stranger had bought it from the same debtor or received it as payment...

### Luis Molina: On Contracts
### Page 748

The income or profits <note>original: *fructus*; this refers to crops, rents, or any revenue produced by the property</note> which the senior creditor himself gathered from that property, or which another person gathered after the senior creditor transferred ownership to them, belong to those parties up until the moment a junior creditor effectively offers to pay the senior creditor the debt owed. These profits do not remain subject to the junior creditor's mortgage. However, a different rule applies to "pending" fruits—those still attached to the land, or those conceived or born <note>referring to livestock</note> while the property was still in the debtor's possession, provided they still exist. This is explained more fully in Disputation 529. Thus <margin>20</margin> says Gregorio Lopez <note>a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in Law 46, citing the phrase "to abandon it" <note>original: *dexelo desamparar*</note>.

If the first creditor—or whoever holds the right of priority <term>right of priority: the legal standing to be paid first before other lenders</term> over the other mortgage creditors—sells the pledge or mortgage to a junior creditor, and the debtor then offers to pay that junior creditor both what was owed to the first creditor (who sold the property) and what was owed to the junior creditor himself, the debtor recovers his property. However, the debtor would not retain this right to recover the property if the first creditor had sold it to an outside stranger who was not a mortgage creditor regarding that specific property. In the same way, another junior creditor, by offering to this second creditor what he paid the first for the property plus what was owed to that second creditor, may obtain the property so that he may be paid what is owed to him from it. This is found in the Law *if the prior* <note>original: *l. si prior*</note>, in the section *it should be known* <note>original: *§. sciendum*</note> in the Digest, "Who is more powerful in a pledge," and Law 46, Title 13, Part 5 <note>of the *Siete Partidas*</note>. 

Nevertheless, all profits gathered by the person who bought the property from the first creditor—during the time the ownership remained with them—belong absolutely and primarily to that buyer, even if the debtor eventually redeems the property. This is affirmed in Law 46 and the final gloss of Gregorio Lopez on that passage. This is because the property is not mortgaged to the debtor in the same way it is mortgaged to the other junior creditors. On this point, note that Gregorio Lopez rightly says regarding the phrase "the other debt" <note>original: *la otra deuda*</note> that although a junior creditor might have paid the senior creditor a higher price for the property than what was actually owed to the senior creditor, if that surplus was not handed over to the debtor, the debtor is not required to pay that extra amount to the junior creditor to redeem his property. He only owes what was due to the senior and junior creditors; the junior creditor must instead recover that surplus from the senior creditor, to whom it was not legally owed. 

Likewise, if the same property is mortgaged to two people, but the senior creditor was also given guarantors <note>original: *fideiussores*; people who promise to pay if the debtor fails</note> for the same debt, then if the senior creditor demands payment from a guarantor (which he is entitled to do) and the property is later sold by a judge to that guarantor for the money paid on the debtor's behalf, the guarantor steps into the shoes of the senior creditor. Nevertheless, both the junior creditor and the debtor can offer the guarantor the full amount he paid to the senior creditor. By doing so, the sale is dissolved and either the junior creditor or the debtor will recover the mortgaged property, depending on which one of them paid the guarantor. This is held in Law 2 and the accompanying glosses in the Digest under "On the sale of a pledge" and Law 45, Title 13, Part 5.

<margin>21</margin> Although a creditor who—according to what has been said so far—lawfully sells a pledge or mortgage bound to him for a debt is not himself the owner of that pledge or mortgage, he nonetheless transfers ownership to the buyer.

<column-break/>

This is because, by legal provision in these events, he sells the property as the agent <note>original: *procurator*</note> of the debtor (who is the owner), even if the debtor is unwilling. See the Institutes, "To whom alienation is allowed or not" <note>original: *§. contra autem. Instit. quib. alien. licet, vel non*</note> and the Code of Justinian, "The debtor cannot impede the sale of a pledge" <note>original: *C. debitorem venditionem pignoris impedire non posse*</note>. There are many other instances where one who is not the owner transfers ownership of a thing to another. However, for the buyer to acquire ownership of the thing so purchased, as taught in Law *He who a farm* <note>original: *l. qui predium*</note> in the Digest, it is necessary that the buyer first be placed in possession of the pledge. This is affirmed by Balduinus and Negusantius at number 11. 

Law 43 seems to suggest it is also necessary for the buyer to hand over the price, as if it were not enough (as in other sales) for the creditor to take it on credit <note>original: *fidem habere*; to trust the buyer for the payment</note>. Gregorio Lopez interprets this to mean that when a creditor sells the property for a higher price than what was owed to him, he cannot grant credit for the surplus—which belongs to the debtor—without the debtor's consent. This is unless he could not have sold the property otherwise, and thus sold it reasonably given the circumstances. For a longer discussion on this, read Negusantius at number 37.

If a debtor, after the property has been pledged to a creditor, creates a legal bond on it (such as a trust or entailment), leaves it in a will, or prohibits its sale in his testament, or makes any other arrangement—indeed, whatever happens afterward that does not arise from some older, prior right—it cannot prejudice the creditor's prior real right <term>real right: a legal right over a physical object rather than just a person</term> to that same property. Consequently, it cannot prevent the creditor, his heir, or anyone holding the creditor's right, from selling it in the ways explained. This is self-evident and is held in the Code, Law 1, "The debtor cannot prohibit the sale of a pledge." 

Furthermore, unless the debtor effectively offers full payment of the entire debt to the creditor, he cannot prevent the sale of that property in the aforementioned events, regardless of any protest he makes to the creditor or the buyer. This is clear from Law 2 of the same title and Law 48, Title 13, Part 5. In the same way, another junior creditor cannot prevent the same sale unless he similarly offers full payment of the entire debt to the senior creditor. Read Negusantius on all these matters at number 15.

It was said: "unless the debtor effectively offers full payment of the entire debt." This is because as long as any part of the debt for which the property (or properties) was pledged or mortgaged remains unpaid—even if most parts of the debt were paid earlier—the creditor or his heirs are not required to return any part of the pledge to the debtor. This is because the right of a pledge or mortgage is indivisible <term>indivisible: the entire collateral secures every single penny of the debt; you don't get half the property back for paying half the debt</term>, covering all the items at once. Therefore, the creditor can proceed to the sale of them until the entire debt is fully satisfied. This is held in the Code, Law *As long as* <note>original: *l. quandiu*</note>, "On the sale of a pledge," and Law 43, Title 13, Part 5. From the same root...

It emphasizes that a creditor acts as a legal agent for the debtor during a sale and that a debtor cannot block a sale through testamentary changes or partial payments.</summary>
