### Second Treatise, Disputation 538.
### Page 749

It is said that the right of a pledge <note>original: *pignus*; movable property held as collateral</note> or a mortgage <note>original: *hypotheca*; immovable property held as collateral</note> is indivisible. From this, it follows that if the principal debtor dies before the entire debt is paid, leaving many heirs, it is not enough for one of them to pay only the portion of the debt for which he is responsible based on his share of the inheritance to free any part of the pledges or mortgages from the obligation. Rather, the creditor can sell the whole item, according to Law 6, *necessarias*, in the Codex *de distractione pignorum* <note>on the sale of pledges</note>, the law *si unus ex pluribus haeredibus*, and other statutes. Likewise, from the same principle, it follows that if the creditor dies and leaves many heirs, it is not sufficient for the debtor to pay one heir the portion of the debt owed to him to free any of the pledges or mortgages. Instead, the remaining heirs can proceed to sell the pledges and mortgages for the rest of the debt. This is found in the law *solutum*, paragraph *si creditori*, in the Digest *de pigneratitia actione* <note>on the action regarding pledges</note>, and Law 2 of the Codex, *si unus ex pluribus haeredibus*. Furthermore, even if the entire debt has been paid, if any expenses were incurred regarding the pledge or in demanding the debt, or if interest or anything else is owed because of it, the pledge can be retained and sold for these costs so that they too are paid, per Law *si necessarias*, the final paragraph, and the law *cum & fortis*, at the beginning, in the Digest *de pignoratitia actione*, and Law 1, *in his*, paragraph *imperator*, in the Digest *de solutionibus* <note>on payments</note>. All these points are affirmed by Negusantius <note>Antonio Negusanti, a 16th-century Italian jurist</note> in the section cited above, number 21, along with others he references.

<margin>23</margin>
When many items have been subjected to a creditor as a pledge or mortgage for a debt, although it is within the creditor's choice to proceed with the sale of whichever item he prefers to recover his debt in the scenarios explained (as found in the law *creditoris* in the Digest *de distractione pignorum*), nonetheless, if one item was specifically pledged and others only generally, he ought first to proceed to the sale of the item specifically pledged to him, provided it is sufficient to satisfy the debt. This is always presumed unless the creditor proves otherwise; after that, he may proceed to sell the other items if the first was not enough, per Law 2 of the Codex *de pignoribus* and the law *quae specialiter* in the Digest *de distractione pignorum*. Likewise, when many items are pledged or mortgaged, if selling one is enough to pay the debt, the creditor cannot proceed to sell them all. Furthermore, if a lower-quality item <note>original: *deterior*; literally "worse" or less valuable</note> is sufficient to cover the full debt, the creditor cannot proceed to sell a better-quality one. This is the opinion of the Gloss, Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note>, and others on the law *quandiu* in the Codex *de distractione pignorum*. This accords with the law *a Divo Pio*, paragraph *in venditione*, in the Digest *de re iudicata* <note>on judged matters</note>, and is supported by the law *magis*, paragraph *item praetor*, in the Digest *de rebus eorum*. For an execution of debt should always be carried out with the least possible harm to the debtor, provided it can be done conveniently. For that reason, if a creditor sells all the pledges when one would suffice, or sells a better item when he could conveniently recover his debt by selling a cheaper one, he will be judged to have acted in bad faith <term>bad faith: Latin *in dolo*; acting with intent to deceive or harm</term>. The debtor will then be able to sue for damages, as Bartolus, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note>, and the common opinion (which Negusantius cites and follows above at number 28) rightly assert. The same must be said regarding a judicial pledge, which is discussed in the cited paragraph *in venditione*. From this, it follows that if a creditor attempts to sell several items, or a better one, and the debtor claims that one is enough, or a lesser one is enough, and asks the creditor to allow him to sell that one, he ought to prevail, according to Bartolus and others whom Negusantius

<column-break/>

refers to and follows at number 22, based on the argument of the law *quamvis*, at the beginning, in the Digest *de pignoratitia actione*. I believe, however, that a specific time should then be prescribed for the debtor to sell the item, and that proper security <note>original: *cautio*</note> should be provided if the creditor possesses the item and it must be handed over to the debtor or someone else for the sale, as was said previously regarding the law *quamvis*.

Even if the creditor had granted the pledge back to the debtor "precariously" <note>original: *precario*; a legal term for a loan that can be revoked at any time at the owner's will</note>—that is, so that the debtor would restore it to the creditor whenever the creditor asked for it—the creditor could still proceed to its sale in the ways explained above, per Law 2 of the Codex *de distractione pignorum* joined with the law *cum & fortis*, paragraph 1, in the Digest *de pignoratitia actione*. But if the debtor were delayed in restoring it to the creditor or the buyer, the creditor could sue him for damages through a "contrary action of pledge" <term>contrary action: a legal claim filed by a defendant or a secondary party in a contract to recover expenses or losses</term>, and furthermore to recover the property through a "precarious interdict" <note>a legal order to return property held by favor</note>, per the law *si pignore*, paragraph *si post*, joined with the Gloss there in the Digest *de pignoratitia actione*, as Negusantius affirms with others in number 26.

<margin>24</margin>
Although a creditor can sell a pledge in the ways explained, and can buy it from the debtor (as stated above), the debtor himself cannot buy it, whether he does so knowingly or unknowingly. This is because a purchase by which someone buys their own property is legally null. Hence, if he buys it from the creditor for a lower price than the debt, the price the creditor receives is credited toward paying part of the debt, and the creditor can retain the pledge for the remaining part of the debt not yet paid; he can even recover it if it has already been delivered to the debtor, per the law *debitor*, at the beginning, in the Digest *de pignoribus*. Likewise, the creditor himself, while legally selling the pledge in the ways explained, cannot buy it either by himself or through an intermediary. If he does buy it, the debtor can at any time pay him his debt and recover the pledge along with any profits gathered from it. A creditor is presumed to have bought it through an intermediary when he has continued to hold possession and never delivered it to the buyer. This is found in the law *& quae sub imagine* in the Codex *de distractione pignorum* and Law 44, Title 13, of the fifth *Partida* <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the major statutory code of Castile</note>. However, Law 44 defines that if no other buyer is found, the property can be sold and assigned to the creditor by the authority of a judge at a just price. If the price exceeds the debt, the creditor shall return the surplus to the debtor; if it does not equal the whole debt, the creditor will be granted an action against the debtor for what is missing to pay the debt in full. This agrees with Laws 2 and 3 of the Codex *si in causa iudicati*, even though these two laws speak of judicial pledges and not conventional ones. Yet, when a buyer is lacking—at least one who will pay the minimum just price—equity demands that the same rule be applied to a conventional pledge as is legally arranged for a judicial one. Nor should the cited law *& quae sub imagine* be understood to apply in this event, in which it would be entirely irrational. Thus, what was said above regarding this event for judicial pledges—both under common law and the law of Castile and Portugal—is similarly to be understood for conventional pledges.

<margin>25</margin>
When a creditor has sold a pledge or mortgage rightfully according to what has been said so far, but has sold it for a lower price than it was worth through fraud <note>original: *dolo*</note>, if this is proven, and if the buyer was aware of the fraud and participated in it, then the debtor can take action against the cre...

It also explains that neither debtors nor creditors can simply "buy" the collateral for themselves under normal circumstances, though Spanish and Portuguese law provide exceptions via judicial oversight when no other buyer exists.</summary>

# Ludovico Molina: On Contracts
## Page 750

the creditor for damages <note>original: *interesse*; the legal interest or loss suffered</note>, and if the creditor is insolvent, against the buyer, so that they restore the purchased item with all its profits <note>original: *fructibus*; any income, crops, or rents generated by the property</note>, upon the buyer being paid the price they gave for it, provided it did not exceed the value of the debt for which the thing was pledged or mortgaged. However, if the price exceeded the debt, it is enough to pay the buyer the price up to the full extent of the debt; the debtor will recover the remainder from the creditor. In this event, when the buyer participated in the fraud, the buyer is not granted the option of increasing the price to the fair limit and keeping the item unless the owner of the item also wishes it. Rather, the owner of the item can take it back with its profits from the buyer, and nothing prevents this, even if the buyer offers the owner an increase in price up to the fair limit. These rules are found in Laws 1 and 3 of the Codex, *If the sale of a pledge is contested* <note>original: *C. si vend. pig. agat.*</note>, and Law 49, Title 13, Partida 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Spanish legal code</note>. Except for this last point: although it is found in the cited Law 49, it is not found in other common laws <note>original: *iuribus comunibus*; the standard Roman-based legal system of Europe</note>; nevertheless, this is affirmed by the final gloss on the penultimate law of the Codex, *If the sale of a pledge is contested*. This is also noted by Azo, reported by Gregorius Lopez in the final gloss of the cited Law 49, and by Baldus and others, whom Negusantius refers to and follows in the passage cited above, number 27. However, Negusantius adds, following Baldus, that if the buyer did not participate in the fraud, but only knowingly and prudently bought the item at a lower price, then the buyer is given the option of increasing the price to the fair limit. I understand this to apply in the external court <note>civil or public court as opposed to the court of conscience</note> when the item was bought for less than half the just price, according to Law 2 of the Codex, *On the rescission of a sale*. However, when the fraud occurs only on the part of the creditor, the buyer is held to nothing at all. This is held in the law *If it ceases* <note>original: *l. si cessante*</note> in the Codex, *On the sale of pledges*, and the cited Law 49, and is affirmed by the final gloss on the cited Law 1, and the doctors of law commonly agree. But when the trickery and fraud occur only on the part of the buyer, who fraudulently induced the creditor to sell at a lower price, then the buyer alone is held liable. Consequently, the debtor can reclaim the item from them with its profits, having paid the buyer only the amount of the debt for which the item was subject as a pledge or mortgage. If the buyer paid the creditor more for the item than that, they must recover that surplus from the creditor. Rightly, however, the final gloss at the end of the cited Law 1 is criticized by Saliceto, Gregorius Lopez, and Negusantius, in so far as it suggests that when fraud occurs only on the part of the buyer, the creditor is held liable, and the buyer is only held liable as a backup in the creditor's default. Indeed, fraud ought not to extend beyond the person who committed it, according to the law of Fulcinus, paragraph *If against* <note>original: *ff. ex q b. cau. in poss. eat.*</note>, and the law *If it ceases* in the Codex, *On the sale of pledges*.

<margin>26</margin> When † a creditor has sold an item outside of the circumstances permitted by law, and has not at all observed the order prescribed by law in that matter—as has already been said often above—the purchase and sale are null. The debtor can sue for damages against the creditor, or can reclaim the item thus sold, along with all its profits, having paid the buyer only the amount of the debt for which the item had been obligated as a pledge or mortgage; or, if they bought it at a lower price, having paid them the price for which they bought it, with the surplus up to the full amount of the debt being returned to the creditor. If, however, the buyer had already acquired the item through prescription <note>original: *praescripsisset*; acquiring legal ownership through the passage of time</note>, then no action would be available to the debtor against the buyer, but they could only sue the creditor for damages. All these points are found in Law 2 and 

<column-break/>

the penultimate law of the Codex, *If the sale of a pledge is contested*, and Law 48, Title 13, Partida 5. And these things hold true even if a judge's decree had intervened in the sale. For although it would then be presumed that all necessary steps had been taken so that the sale was done rightly, if the contrary were proven, all the aforementioned rules would similarly apply. So says Negusantius in the place cited above, number 28, with others whom he cites.

<margin>27</margin> When † something has been rightly subjected to a pledge or mortgage by the Church or a minor <note>a person under the age of 25 in Roman law</note>, with the necessary legal formalities preceding it, if the debt is not paid afterward, one can proceed to the sale of the pledge or mortgage in the ways explained, just as if the pledge or mortgage belonged to any private person, and this without other formalities. Thus, according to the law *If of the pupils* <note>original: *l. si pupillorum*</note>, paragraph 1, in the Digest, *On the property of those* <note>original: *de reb. eorum*</note>, as Bartolus and Florianus hold, whom Negusantius refers to and follows, and the laws immediately to be cited suppose this. However, if from the subsequent sale the minor or the Church is found to be notably harmed <note>original: *notabiliter laesi*; suffering a significant financial loss</note> because the pledge or mortgage was sold for less than the lowest fair price, they are granted—within four years from the time the minor reaches twenty-five years of age, or for the Church from the moment the sale was celebrated—a total restitution <note>term: <term>restitutio in integrum</term> — a legal remedy that restores the parties to their original condition as if a contract had never happened</note> against the buyer. Then, by returning to the buyer the price up to the amount of the debt for which the thing was subject as a pledge or mortgage, the minor or the Church recovers the pledge or mortgage. The same applies to someone absent for the sake of the republic, and to anyone else to whom total restitution is granted by a general clause, according to those things which are to be said below in their proper place. For if, while they are absent, a pledge or mortgage is sold and they are found to be notably harmed, then similarly within four years from their return, or from the cessation of another impediment, the sale is rescinded in a similar way upon their petition. This is held in the law *If the creditor*, paragraph *That should be known* <note>original: *ff. de distract. pign.*</note>, and Law 47, Title 13, Partida 5.

<margin>28</margin> It remains for us to explain whether, if a creditor sells a pledge or mortgage and it is "evicted" <note>term: <term>eviction</term> — in this legal context, when a buyer loses the property they just bought because a third party proves they have a superior legal title to it</note>, the creditor is held liable for the eviction or not. It must be said that they are not held liable, whether the selling creditor is the public treasury or some private person, as is held in Laws 1 and 2 of the Codex, *That a creditor does not have liability for the eviction of a pledge*, the law *danger* <note>original: *leg. periculum*</note> in the Digest, *On pledges*, and the final law of Title 13, Partida 5, and other laws—provided, however, that the following conditions are kept. First, that they sell it *as a creditor*, not as the owner of the thing. This is gathered from Law 1 at the beginning of the Codex, *A creditor ought not be liable for the eviction of a pledge*; the final gloss there affirms it, and it is found in the final law of Title 13, Partida 5, and the common opinion of the doctors of law asserts it. For if they were to sell that thing as their own, they would be held liable for the eviction. They are deemed to sell it as a creditor when they sufficiently express this to the buyer. They would be deemed to express it sufficiently if they said, "I, Peter, creditor of John, sell this pledge or mortgage to you," as Negusantius teaches with other doctors in the place cited above, number 40. It is otherwise if they only said, "I, Peter, sell this thing to you." Exception: unless it was clear that the buyer knew it was a pledge or mortgage and was being sold as a pledge or mortgage, as Gregorius Lopez rightly observes with Baldus on the final law cited, at the word *pledged* <note>original: *empeñada*</note>, according to the law *Who a tavern* in the Digest, *On entering a purchase*. <meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the sale of pledges (collateral) by a creditor. It focuses on the liability of the creditor and the debtor when the purchased item is later legally reclaimed by a third party—a process known as "eviction."</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 538

...the final gloss on Law 1, as cited, according to the text observed there, and the doctors of law commonly agree. If, however, the creditor could not prove that the item was obligated to him as a pledge or a mortgage, and he sold it, he would be held liable for **eviction** <note>original: *evictio*; this refers to a situation where a buyer is legally deprived of a property because a third party proves they have a superior title to it</note>. **Third**, if a prior creditor—superior to the others at least by a right of preference—should evict the buyer by that right of preference, the selling creditor would be held liable for the eviction, as the same gloss affirms according to the text there, and other legal experts agree. It is not necessary, however, for the creditor to have a better right to the item than the true owner who later evicts the buyer, as this is self-evident. **Fourth**, if the creditor sells the item knowing it does not belong to the debtor who pledged it, but rather to someone else: in that case, by selling it, he would be acting with **fraud** <note>original: *dolus*; intentional deceit or bad faith</note>, and would be held liable for the eviction. This is held in Law 2 of the Code, *That the creditor ought not to be liable for the eviction of a pledge*, and the final law of Title 13, Partida 5; this is affirmed by the cited final gloss and the common opinion of the doctors. **Fifth**, when the creditor could not yet sell the pledge or mortgage—neither by the terms of the contract nor by the prescription of the law—if he sells it and it is later evicted, he is deemed to have acted with fraud and is held liable for the eviction. So says the final gloss on Law 1, which agrees with the final law of Title 13, Partida 5, as the doctors commonly assert. However, if he were deceived by a **just error** <note>an understandable mistake made in good faith</note> and thought he was permitted to sell, he would not be held liable for the eviction; it is otherwise if the error was **gross and supine** <note>original: *errore crasso, & supino*; a legal term for a mistake so obvious or negligent that it cannot be excused</note>. This is the view of the cited gloss, Salicetus, and others, as well as Negusantius (number 40) and Gregorius Lopez in the first gloss. **Sixth**, the creditor is liable if, when he sold the item, he **promised** to be responsible for eviction; for if he promised, he is bound by it. This is held in Law 1 (at the beginning) and Law 2 of the Code, *That the creditor... not be liable*, and the final law of Title 13, Partida 5, as affirmed by the frequently cited final gloss and the common opinion of the doctors.

<margin>29</margin> Observe, however, that while a creditor (except in the specific events explained) is not held liable for eviction, he is nevertheless bound to **cede his mortgage action** <note>original: *cedere actionem suam hypothecariam*; to transfer his legal right to sue based on the mortgage to the buyer</note> against the debtor to the buyer, as held in the law *In creditore*, under the Digest title *On Evictions*. Furthermore, the debtor himself is then held liable to the buyer for eviction, up to the price given to the creditor for the evicted item, along with the **interest** <note>original: *usuras*; here referring to legal interest or compensation for the loss of use of the money</note> accrued after the item was evicted. This is held in the law *Rescriptum*, paragraph 1, together with the gloss on the word "held," in the Digest *On the Distraction [Sale] of Pledges*, and the final law of Title 23, Partida 5, with the gloss of Gregorius Lopez on the phrase "what they pledged." Even though these last two laws speak of a **judicial pledge** <note>property seized by a court order</note> that is sold and evicted, the reasoning is the same for either type of pledge sold when the creditor's debt is satisfied from the price and the item is later evicted. Since the full extent of the price redounded to the benefit of the debtor—either because it satisfied the debt or because any surplus belonged to him—equity demands that he be held liable for the eviction regarding the total price and the interest after the eviction, as sanctioned by the cited laws. Add to this, as was said above, that the creditor sold the pledge as the **agent** <note>original: *procuratorem*; a legal representative or proxy</note> of the debtor according to the prescription of law or contract; therefore, the debtor is rightly held liable for eviction, at least for the price given to the creditor.

I said *at least*: because, if the debtor fraudulently subjected that item to a pledge or mortgage knowing it belonged to another, I believe then, on account of the fraud, he is also held liable to the buyer for **damages** <note>original: *interesse*; the "interest" or "difference" between the buyer's current position and where they would be if the contract had been fulfilled</note> and not just for the repayment of the price. I must also add that if the debtor is **insolvent** <note>original: *soluendo non sit*; literally "is not for paying"</note>, in the

<column-break/>

debtor's default, the creditor is held to return the price received to the buyer, if it still exists or if the creditor has been made wealthier by it. The reason is that the payment and satisfaction of his debt ought to come from the debtor's goods, not from a third party's evicted property nor from the price of such property, which belongs to others. Therefore, as soon as it is discovered that the item subjected to the pledge or mortgage belongs to another, the creditor can retain neither the item nor the price received for it in satisfaction of his debt, unless the debtor restores the price to the buyer of the third party's property. Instead, he must demand his debt from the debtor alone, or lose it if he cannot recover it from him. Furthermore, it should be noted that the creditor himself cannot **evict** the pledge or mortgage he sold from that buyer, even for some other cause that comes to his notice, whereby he learns that the item belonged to him and not to the debtor who obligated it to him (Law *And if he*, Digest *On the Distraction of Pledges*). The same applies to the heir of that creditor, as the final gloss asserts there, along with Negusantius (number 41).

<margin>30</margin> In the events in which it was said that the creditor is held liable for eviction, he is certainly held liable to the buyer even for **damages** <note>original: *interesse*</note>: because he was either at fault for selling that item to the buyer in such a way, or he bound himself by an express or tacit agreement to be fully liable for eviction. Observe, however, that in the default of a creditor who is unable to pay the buyer what is owed for the eviction, the buyer is granted **recourse** against the debtor, so that the debtor pays the buyer the price they gave for it. This is because the creditor’s debt was satisfied by that price; equity does not allow the debtor to be enriched by the discharge of his debt at the buyer's loss. This is the view of Salicetus and others, Negusantius (number 40), and Gregorius Lopez on the final cited law, on the phrase "what they pledged," following the law *Rescriptum* and the law *Plainly* in the Digest.

<margin>31</margin> <margin>A Doubt</margin> <margin>Decision</margin> Finally, in those events where it was said the creditor is liable for eviction, if he pays anything to the buyer after the item is evicted, is he granted recourse against the debtor to recover it? It must be said that in the event where he **promised eviction**—whether he promised a simple refund or double the value—if he was a **private creditor** (for the **Treasury** <note>original: *fiscus*; the state or imperial treasury</note> or its agent, when selling something and promising double or triple if evicted, is only held to pay the simple value, as in the law *If the procurator*, Digest *On the Law of the Treasury*), a distinction must be made. For if there was no custom of promising eviction, or of promising double, and he could have conveniently sold the item without such promises, and the promise of double value was not made for the benefit of the debtor (namely, to sell the item at a higher price), then no recourse is open to him against the debtor. If, however, it was the custom to promise eviction—even when a pledge was sold as the creditor's property—or to promise double value, or if he could not otherwise conveniently sell the pledge, or if the sale was thus made profitably for the debtor's benefit because the pledge was sold at a higher price for that reason, then recourse is granted to the creditor against the debtor, even if the creditor promised and paid double. This is held in the law *If in a pledge*...

### What is a guarantor, and of how many types?

## DISPUTATION 539.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> What a guarantor is, how many types there are, and see number 12 and 13.
For what purpose the obligation of a guarantor was invented. See number 2.
From where the word is derived. See number 3.
It can be applied to any obligation whatsoever. See number 4.
Indeed, not only for a specific obligation, but also in general for any future contingency. See number 5.
Furthermore, even for an obligation arising from a crime <note>original: *ex delicto*</note>. See number 6.
And also for an obligation arising from the decree of a public authority correctly establishing something. See number 7.
<margin>8</margin> When a guarantor’s obligation is rendered void, and when it is not.
<margin>9</margin> A guarantor can be added even for a natural obligation <term>natural obligation: a debt that is morally binding but might not be legally enforceable in a civil court</term> alone.
<margin>10</margin> A contract for a guarantee is valid under Canon Law and the laws of Castile <note>Spain</note> even without a formal verbal agreement <term>stipulation: a specific, formal question-and-answer ritual required in ancient Roman law to make a contract binding</term>.
<margin>11</margin> How the obligation of a guarantor takes on the character of a mandator <note>one who gives an order</note> and a mandatory <note>one who carries it out</note>.
<margin>13</margin> For what purpose a guarantor is given for a "judged payment" <note>original: *iudicatum solui*; security that a court's judgment will be paid</note>, and what that obligation entails.
And what the law is in Castile and Portugal. See number 14.
<margin>15</margin> For what purpose a guarantor is given "to stand trial" <note>original: *de iudicio sisti*; security that a defendant will appear in court</note>, and concerning that obligation.
<margin>16</margin> A guarantor "against brawling" is included under judicial guarantees.
The same applies to a guarantor for one's own affairs. See number 17.

---

<margin>1</margin> Following the order prescribed at the beginning of Disputation 522, we must next speak about guarantors. A **guarantor** <term>fideiussor: someone who promises to pay a debt if the original debtor fails to do so</term> is one who takes another’s obligation upon themselves, or binds themselves to fulfill it in the event that the other person does not. Thus, the guarantor’s obligation is "accessory," meaning it assumes and relies upon another principal obligation to such an extent that without the main debt, the guarantee can neither exist nor be understood. However, it does not assume it in such a way that the guarantor’s promise cannot happen first. Indeed, a guarantor can bind themselves to a creditor before the principal debtor, at the same time as him, or after him, as held in the Institutes <note>Justinian's legal textbook</note> and the *Partidas* <note>the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>. Yet, if the guarantor’s promise comes first, it is dependent and under a "tacit condition"—meaning it only counts if the principal debtor’s obligation follows. For instance, someone might say, "I constitute myself as guarantor for the money you are willing to give Peter." Therefore, a guarantor's obligation always rests upon and depends on the principal debtor's obligation. The guarantor's obligation was invented for the sake of greater...

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin> ...firmness of the principal obligation and greater security for the creditor, ensuring that what the principal promisor bound themselves to will be fulfilled. This is held in the Institutes and the laws of the *Partidas*. Because the guarantor’s obligation rests upon and assumes another's principal obligation, it follows that—whereas in other contracts or promises made without a "cause" <note>original: *sine causa*; a legal reason or consideration for a contract</note>, a person may use a "plea of fraud" <note>original: *exceptio doli*; a defense that the contract was made in bad faith</note>—in a guarantee contract, that defense does not apply just because the guarantor personally had no specific reason to guarantee the debt. No other cause is necessary for the guarantee than the principal obligation itself, upon which the accessory promise rests. However, if the principal debtor himself had bound himself without cause, then whatever plea of fraud would be available to the principal debtor would also be available to his guarantor, even against the principal debtor’s will.

<margin>3</margin> The word **guarantor** <note>original: *fideiussor*</note> is derived from "faith" <note>original: *fides*</note> and "I authorize" <note>original: *iubeo*</note>. This is because formerly (as is clear from the Digest and other laws), the verbal formalities for a guarantee used to be done in this way: "Do you authorize this on your faith?" That is: do you take it up, or do you wish for that to which Titius binds himself to me to be so? And the guarantor would reply, "I authorize it." Thus, according to this etymology, a guarantor is the same as one who takes into their own "faith" <note>trust/credit</note> the fulfillment of another's obligation, binding themselves to it in that person's default.

<margin>4</margin> A guarantor can be provided for every kind of obligation, whether it is contracted through formal words or by consent alone, and whether it is "civil" <note>legally enforceable</note>, "natural" <note>morally binding</note>, or both—provided it is valid in its own way. The guarantor will be held liable even civilly, even if the principal debtor is held only naturally. This is found in the Institutes and the *Partidas*. A person can also be a guarantor not only for a specific and determined obligation, but also generally for any obligation someone might contract in the future with a certain creditor or creditors, and they remain bound for all of them. This is the common opinion of the legal experts.

<margin>6</margin> Furthermore, a guarantor can be given for an obligation arising from a **crime** <note>original: *delictum*</note>, and they will remain bound. Although a guarantee is invalid if it is for a "bad thing" or a future crime—for example, a pact that thieves will divide their loot equally, or that if someone is caught for a crime they intend to commit, the guarantor will pay their fine—it is nevertheless valid if, *after* someone has committed a crime, another acts as a guarantor that the person will pay the fine they are sentenced to, or will present them to the court so they may be released from chains. This is held in the law...

<meta>catchword: crime</meta>

<summary>This page defines the legal role of a guarantor (fideiussor), explaining that it is an accessory obligation dependent on a principal debt and can cover various types of legal and moral obligations, including those arising from crimes after they occur.</summary>
<keywords>guarantor, fideiussor, accessory obligation, natural obligation, civil law, canon law, Castile, Portugal, legal security, contracts, crimes, etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 539, specifically point 7 regarding the types of obligations a guarantor can secure. It follows from the previous page's discussion on obligations arising from crimes.</meta>

crime, as seen in Law 6, Decree 20, and the final law of the Digest concerning guarantors <note>original: "ff. de fideiuss." refers to the Digest, a massive collection of Roman legal rulings</note>. Indeed, a guarantee can even be provided for an obligation that arises from the decree of a public authority correctly establishing a rule—such as the lawful imposition of a tax <note>original: "tributum"</note>, or if the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> grants a portion of the tithes to a prince for a reasonable cause, as held in the law titled "Greek," section "for that," in the Digest regarding guarantors. From such a precept and decree arises not only a civil obligation but also a natural obligation <term>natural obligation: a moral or social duty that might not be enforceable in court on its own, but has legal effects once paid or guaranteed</term> to pay what is rightly ordered. This is a point that Gregorius Lopez <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> did not sufficiently attend to in the 3rd law cited.

<margin>8.</margin>**8** I stated above: "provided it is valid in its own way." For if the principal obligation is entirely invalid—either by the nature of the matter itself or by a decree of human law rendering it void—then, since the guarantor's obligation rests upon the principal one (as has been said), the guarantee will also be completely null. Therefore, if a sale is invalid and a guarantor was provided to ensure its fulfillment, just as the seller is not bound to fulfill or stand by it, neither is the guarantor bound to the buyer in any way. This is held in the law "when the law" <note>original: "l. cum lex"</note> in the Digest regarding guarantors. However, when the obligation is purely civil—such as when someone, having provided a guarantor, confesses to having received money in the hope of it being counted out to them, though they never actually received it—then just as that obligation is valid only in the external forum <note>legal court</note>, the guarantee is valid only in that same forum. Nevertheless, the defense of "money not counted" <term>exceptio non numeratae pecuniae: a legal defense used when a person signed a contract for a loan but never actually received the funds</term>, which is available to the principal debtor, is also available to the guarantor. I said "regularly" <note>meaning as a general rule</note>, because if a good debtor has yielded <note>declared bankruptcy or transferred assets</note>, the defense that becomes available to him—should the debt be demanded while he is unable to pay—does not apply to the guarantor. The guarantor is bound to pay in place of the principal debtor precisely because the principal debtor has become powerless to pay. The same applies to certain other defenses that belong to the principal debtor by reason of their personal status. This is found in the final section, joined with the commentary on the Institutes regarding replications. Furthermore, what was said regarding purely civil obligations is affirmed by the commentaries on section 1, under the word "civil" in the Institutes regarding guarantors, and the law "a guarantor to be bound," section "guarantor," under the word "civil" in the Digest on the same title.

<margin>9.</margin>**9** I also said above that a guarantee can be handed over for a natural obligation alone, and in that case, the guarantor is bound to the creditor not only by a natural obligation but also by a civil one. Regarding what constitutes a purely natural obligation, and what is both natural and civil together, this was discussed in Disputation 252. Much was also said regarding purely natural obligations—and to what extent a civil action is granted in many events under Canon Law or the laws of Castile <note>Spain</note>, where under common civil law only a natural obligation would arise and thus a civil action would be denied—in the following disputations up to 258. As it pertains to the present topic, an example is found in the case of a slave <note>original: "mancipio"</note>, who can be naturally obligated but not civilly; however, if a guarantor is added, the guarantor is held responsible even civilly, as held in the Institutes regarding guarantors, section 1, and at the end of the law "naturally" in the Digest regarding the recovery of undue payments, and Law 5, Title 13, Part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas, the Castilian law code</note>. We also, in Disputation 140 (from the section "whether indeed at the same time"), provided an example in the case of a member of a religious order who, without the permission of their superior, enters into a contract while providing a guarantor for the validity of the contract. And in Disputation

<column-break/>

224 (from the section "to the causes of minors," especially the section "although however"), we provided the example of a minor who enters into a contract without the authority of a guardian or curator, with a guarantor provided. But observe this: standing in common law <note>Roman Law</note>, not only if the principal debtor is obligated only naturally, but even if they are obligated both naturally and civilly, for a guarantor given for that same debt to remain bound (not just naturally but civilly), it is necessary that the guarantor's obligation be made with a formal verbal agreement <term>stipulation: a specific, formal oral contract in Roman law that made a promise legally binding</term> intervening. Otherwise, a civil obligation does not arise under the common Imperial Law, according to the law section "satisfactory acceptance" in the Digest regarding verbal obligations, the law "if naked" in the Code regarding guarantors, and Law 6, Title 12, Part 5.

However, when a guarantor is found written into the principal contract, all things are judged to have been done correctly, and therefore a formal stipulation is presumed to have occurred unless the contrary is proven. So it is in the law "to be known," joined with the commentary there, in the Digest on verbal obligations. Perhaps also, if the contract of guarantee were joined and celebrated at the same time as the contract of the principal debtor from which the civil obligation arises, the "naked pact" <note>an informal agreement normally not enforceable in court</note> of the guarantee would be considered "clothed" by its connection to the principal contract, even if no formal stipulation intervened. Consequently, a civil obligation would arise from it, no differently than from the principal contract to which it is attached, according to what was said in Disputation 253. Unless you say that those points are only to be understood regarding a naked pact that is attached to the principal contract of the *same person* who makes the naked pact; which is not seen in the matter proposed. This latter view seems more in line with the cited laws. However, under Canon Law and the laws of Castile (Law 3, Title 8, Book 5 of the *Ordenamiento*, which is Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación*), even if the contract of guarantee is not fortified by the solemnity of a formal stipulation, a civil obligation still arises from it, and a legal action is granted against the guarantor, as was stated in Disputations 254 and 257; Gregorius Lopez agrees in his commentary on the 6th cited law.

It must be observed that although the guarantor enters into a contract in relation to the creditor (the one to whom the principal debtor is bound), by which he binds himself to something should the debtor fail, nevertheless, in relation to the person for whom he binds himself, he takes on the role of a "mandatory" <note>an agent carrying out a task</note>. And the one for whom he binds himself takes on the role of the "mandator" <note>the principal giving the order</note>, as if asking him to act as a guarantor—provided that the one for whom he acts asks for it or knows of it and stays silent, for by that very silence he is judged to be ordering it (Law "if of remunerating," section "if he allowed," and law "if for you" in the Digest on mandates; section "if anything" in the Institutes on guarantors; Law 12, Title 13, Part 5; and other laws).

But if the principal debtor is unaware of it, the guarantor, in relation to him, takes on the role of a "manager of affairs" <term>negotiorum gestor: someone who steps in to manage another's business or debts without being asked, out of necessity or benefit</term>, whether the principal debtor later ratifies it or not; provided, however, that it was done usefully or reasonably (Law "from mandate," final section, in the Digest on mandates, and the cited Law 12). Therefore, if a guarantor suffers any loss on account of the guarantee without his own fault, the person for whom he acted as guarantor is bound to him, either by an action of mandate or an action for the management of affairs. However, if the person for whom he acted as guarantor refuses to reimburse him—perhaps because he forbade the guarantee in the first place, or because the guarantor acted with the intention of giving a gift to the principal debtor if he paid anything in his place, or for his own...

It also discusses the shift from strict Roman formal requirements to the more flexible standards of Canon and Spanish law regarding how such contracts are formed.</summary>

...guaranteed for his own benefit, because the principal obligation was contracted for him, then the debtor is held to him by no action. This is held in the law "if remunerating," section "if he suffered," and the law "if for you," cited in the final law of the Code on the management of affairs, and in the cited Law 12. Read on all these matters Antonio Gómez, volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 11 <note>Antonio Gómez was a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>.

<margin>12</margin> There are two types of guarantors. One is judicial (within a court case), and the other is extra-judicial (outside of court); it is regarding the latter that we primarily speak in this place. A judicial guarantor, however, as gathered from the law titled "Greek," section "and after the lawsuit" in the Digest regarding guarantors <note>original: "l. græcè. §. & post litem ff. de fideiuss."</note>, is also 
<margin>13</margin> of two types. The first is one who binds himself not only to present the defendant or debtor in court whenever necessary or requested, but also to ensure that whatever is judged will be paid. This type of guarantor is called in Spanish a <term>fiador de saneamento</term> <note>a "guarantor of satisfaction" or "indemnity guarantor"</note>. If such a defendant appears in court at the appointed times and is condemned by the conclusion of the trial, the guarantor is not released. Therefore, if the guarantor is required to pay what was judged so that the defendant pays, the guarantor cannot use the legal defense <note>original: "exceptio"</note> that he is freed from the burden of the guarantee because the trial ended in that manner, as is held in the section "and after the lawsuit" cited above.

<margin>14 Law of Castile.</margin> According to the law of Castile (Law 19, Title 21, Book 4 of the *New Collection*), as related in the preceding disputation, when a proceeding moves to the execution of the debtor's movable or even immovable assets (if movables are insufficient) based on a guaranteed instrument or other cases explained there, the debtor is thrown into chains until the debt is paid in full—unless the debtor provides such a guarantor <term>de saneamento</term> <note>of satisfaction</note> to ensure the debt and all expenses are paid in full from those assets and that those assets will not be legally reclaimed. This applies as long as the debt is not of a type for which one cannot be imprisoned, as related in the preceding disputation. Gutierrez, in *Practical Questions*, book 1, question 152, rightly proves that after that law, it is not enough to provide the other type of guarantor, which we will discuss next. Furthermore, in Book 3 of the Portuguese Ordinances, title 69—consistent with common law (as taught by Giulio Claro, book 5, *Sentences*, final section, question 46, number 19, and question 95, number 1, following Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors)—it is held that when someone has acted as a guarantor for the payment of a judgment, once the final definitive sentence is passed against the defendant, execution can be made against the guarantor's assets immediately without further summons or process. However, this is only after a "discussion" <note>original: "excussio," the legal process of first exhausting the principal debtor's assets before turning to the guarantor</note> of the principal debtor's assets has been performed, in the same manner that will be explained regarding the "discussion" of the assets of an extra-judicial guarantor in the following sections. Likewise, the guarantor retains the right of recourse against the principal debtor in the manner that will also be explained later regarding extra-judicial guarantors.

<margin>15 Law of Portugal.</margin> The other type of judicial guarantor is one who does not bind himself to pay the judgment, but only to ensure the defendant appears in court to trigger the litigation, as held in the cited section "and after the lawsuit." Thus, if the defendant does not appear, the guarantor binds himself to pay the judgment or incurs another penalty, as agreed upon in the contract of guarantee. This guarantor is called in Spanish a <term>fiador de la haz</term> <note>literally "guarantor of the face," meaning one who ensures the person's physical presence</note>. If, however, the defendant appears in court at his appointed times and is condemned, then, once the trial is finished, the guarantor remains entirely free

<column-break/>

from the obligation of the guarantee. Consequently, if the judgment is demanded from him because of the defendant's default, he has a legal defense <note>original: "exceptio"</note> that he is freed from the entire burden of the guarantee because the trial ended with a final sentence, as held in the cited section "and after the lawsuit." Within what time such a guarantor can "purge the delay" <note>original: "purgare moram," a legal term for fixing a default before a penalty is finalized</note> so that, if he presents the defendant in court, he avoids the penalty, will be more conveniently discussed in Disputation 547, which we will compose regarding such guarantors.

<margin>16</margin> Along with judicial guarantors, we can include the guarantors of those who, having brawled and being held in chains (or about to be), bind themselves under a certain penalty imposed by a judge not to brawl in the future, providing guarantors on both sides to ensure no further evil follows. If the one who brawled defaults and thus incurs the penalty, the execution of that penalty is commanded against his guarantors.

<margin>17</margin> Also belonging to judicial guarantors are those who are given and named "for one's own matter" <note>original: "in rem propriam"</note>. For instance, when a lawsuit is intended against someone and they appoint a representative <note>original: "procuratorem"</note> to defend them and provide guarantors that the judgment will be paid; such guarantors are said to be given for the own matter of the one presenting them. You have an example in the law "if the deceased" in the Digest regarding representatives. Other things that could be said here regarding judicial guarantors will be more conveniently discussed in the cited Disputation 547.

### Who may be guarantors and who may not; concerning the privilege of the Velleian Decree granted to women, and concerning guarantors for minors.

->DISPVTATIO DXL.<-

->SUMMARY<-

1. Anyone who can bind themselves can be a guarantor, unless expressly prohibited.
2. This rule fails in many persons and cases, as in the following numbers.
3. A woman acting as a guarantor for another is bound, but she is defended by the legal exception of the Velleian Decree, even in the "forum of conscience" <note>meaning she is not even morally bound to pay if the law protects her</note>.
4. Today, however, no obligation arises from such a guarantee. (Number 3).
5. Indeed, she can reclaim what she paid through a "claim for something not owed" <note>original: "condictione indebiti"</note>. (Number 4).
6. Understand this, however, as in number 6.
7. The Velleian exception is perpetual and can be raised at any time, even after a final definitive sentence, before payment is made. (Number 7).
8. It is clarified, however, as stated there.
9. Whether a woman can renounce the privilege of the Velleian Decree, and when.
10. And what of the law of Castile (numbers 9, 11) and of Portugal (number 12).
11. Anyone can renounce things that were introduced in their own favor.
12. A woman swearing that she will not resort to the Velleian privilege is bound by such an oath.

16 Which persons cannot be guarantors, and from number 17 through number 21.

Generally, those who can bind themselves by promising or by entering into other contracts can be guarantors <note>original: "fideiussores"</note>, unless they are found to be specifically excepted in the law (Digest, book 3, title "On guarantors" <note>original: "l. 3. ff. de fideiu."</note> and the *Siete Partidas*, part 5, title 12, law 1). This is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Antonio Gómez relates and follows (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 16). Regarding those who can bind themselves by promising or entering other contracts, this was discussed in Disputations 261 and 274.

2 However, if a woman stands as a guarantor for someone, the obligation is valid by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>; nevertheless, it is struck down and rendered null by the use of the legal defense <note>original: "exceptionis"</note> of the Velleian Decree <note>The *Senatusconsultum Velleianum* was a Roman law from 46 AD that prohibited women from undertaking liability for the debts of others</note>, if the woman acting as guarantor wishes to use that privilege and defense. She can do this not only in the external court but also in the court of conscience, as asserted by Panormitanus, Baldus, and the common opinion of the doctors cited by Antonio Gómez (number 16) and Gutierrez (*On the Confirmation of Oaths*, part 1, chapter 20, number 5). The reason for this is that the prince, for the common good and on account of the fragility of women <note>The "fragilitas sexus" was a common legal justification in historical law for protective or restrictive measures regarding women</note>, can grant them this privilege; therefore, they can use it in the court of conscience. Those who admit women as guarantors should look out for themselves and see whether it is expedient for them to accept those who enjoy such a privilege as guarantors. However, the fact remains that if a woman is a guarantor for someone, such an obligation is valid by the law itself but is struck down and rendered null by the help of the Velleian defense (Digest, book 3, joined with the gloss on the word "woman" <note>original: "mulierem"</note>; Code of Justinian, title "On the Velleian Decree," law 1 and following). This is how law 1 and the following in the Digest under the same title, law 2 at the end of title 12 of the *Siete Partidas*, and the Portuguese Ordinances (book 4, title 12, at the beginning) must be understood. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors cited by Antonio Gómez and in his commentary on Law 61 of Toro (number 1), as well as Gutierrez (chapter 20, number 1). Note this: women are no less helped by the Velleian privilege if they take another's debt upon themselves from the start in place of another, or if they transfer another’s debt to themselves by a substitution <note>original: "nouatione," a legal term for replacing an old obligation with a new one</note>, than if they stood as guarantors. This is held in law 1 and the law "The Decree of the Senate" in the Code under the Velleian title. It is otherwise if, without taking another's debt upon themselves, they pay it in place of another as if by gifting it, as is held in those same laws.

It must be observed, however, that—excepting the events in which a woman does not enjoy the Velleian privilege, as we shall explain—many older laws were corrected or narrowed by the "Ancient Law," final section, of the Code regarding the Velleian Decree. Those older laws left the guarantee obligation or the assumption of another's debt valid by the law itself until the women struck it down and made it null by pleading and using the Velleian privilege. Indeed, in that cited "Ancient Law," it was sanctioned that unless a woman acts as a guarantor or takes another's debt upon herself in a public instrument <note>a formal legal document drafted by a notary</note>, with three witnesses present and signing it, the guarantee or the assumption of that debt is null by the law itself. Consequently, since in that case 

<column-break/>

no obligation at all arises from that guarantee or from such an assumption of debt, it is not necessary for such a woman to use the privilege and Velleian defense to be freed from the obligation. Therefore today, if a 
3 woman in some private instrument, or outside of an instrument by word of mouth in front of a thousand witnesses, stands as a guarantor for someone or takes a debt upon herself in their place, no obligation arises from it. The same is true if the guarantee exists in a public instrument, or such a debt is assumed, but without the three witnesses being present. This is clearly taught by that text when compared with the preceding parts of the same law, which the following parts do not correct at all; for to affirm that would indeed be ridiculous. This is affirmed by the final gloss there, by Baldus, and by the common opinion of the doctors, which Gutierrez relates and follows (*On the Confirmation of Oaths*, part 1, chapter 20, number 6). However, the same Gutierrez, along with Paulus de Castro and Salicetus, warns that today, by common custom, it is not necessary for three witnesses to sign in a public instrument, but it is enough if the notary <note>original: "tabellio"</note> testifies in the instrument that they were present. Gutierrez testifies that this is the accepted custom in the Kingdom of Castile, and he says this custom is supported by the fact that under the law of that Kingdom, it is not necessary for witnesses present for public instruments of contracts to sign them, but it is enough for the Notary to testify that they were present.

Antonio Gómez (at number 16 and on Law 61 of Toro) 
4 rightly warns that even if a woman, in the event explained (namely when she enjoys the Velleian privilege), has paid the creditor without using the Velleian defense, she can reclaim what she so paid by a claim for recovery of an undue payment <note>term: <term>condictio indebiti</term> — a legal action to recover money paid by mistake when no debt was actually owed</note>.
5 The reason is that this Velleian defense is perpetual—that is, it is granted absolutely without a fixed time limit—as the gloss on law 6 "not the principal," section "undue," in the Digest explains. It is so favorable that it was granted for the benefit of the women themselves to whom it applies, and not out of hatred for the creditors—unlike the Macedonian defense <note>The *Senatusconsultum Macedonianum* prohibited lending money to sons who were still under their father's authority</note>, which was granted out of hatred for creditors who gave loans to sons-of-the-family. Whenever a defense is perpetual and favorable in that first way, recovery of payment is granted; it is otherwise when, although it is perpetual, it is not favorable in that way (just as the Macedonian defense is not favorable in that way). Both points are held expressly in the law "he who [pleads] an exception," at the beginning, in the Digest regarding the recovery of undue payment, and the law "on fraud," section "diverse," joined with the preceding parts, in the Digest regarding substitutions. The first point is also held in the law "although," section "sometimes," in the Digest regarding the Velleian Decree. The common opinion, related by Antonio Gómez in the 
6 cited places, affirms this to be the case. Understand this, however, provided that the one who paid did so by error, not knowing she could defend herself with the exception. If, indeed, she pays knowing that she could protect herself with the defense, recovery is not granted to her, as is held in law "if not the principal," section "undue," in the Digest. Antonio Gómez (at number 16) adds that a certain widow, who had stood as a guarantor in a "guarentigiate" instrument <note>a type of contract that allowed for immediate execution/seizure of assets upon default without a full trial</note> and had paid after an execution of judgment without using the Velleian defense, sought recovery of what she had paid with him acting as her lawyer, and she won. # Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

...law 1 and various other rights which the gloss cites there under the word "judged" <note>original: "iudicata"</note> in the Code, "On the recovery of what was not owed" <note>original: "C. de condict. indeb."</note>. Indeed, it says this should be understood when payment is made after a final judgment in which the case has been fully examined, but not when execution and payment are made by virtue of a guarantee instrument <note>term: "instrumenti guarentigij" — a notarized document where a debtor acknowledges a debt and submits to immediate execution without a trial</note> in which no prior examination of the case took place. 

7 Furthermore, it is argued that the defense of the Velleian Decree <note>The *Senatusconsultum Velleianum* was a Roman law that allowed women to avoid liability for the debts of others</note> can be raised after the final judgment during the execution phase, as long as the actual payment has not yet been made by the woman acting as guarantor. This is also held regarding the defense of the Macedonian Decree <note>A Roman law prohibiting lending money to sons still under their father's authority</note>, law *tamen*, in the Digest "On the Macedonian Decree," and is affirmed by the glosses there, as well as by Bartolus and the common opinion of the learned doctors. Regarding these matters, observe: If payment is made to the creditor by a woman guarantor out of ignorance—meaning she could have used the Velleian defense in an event where her obligation was not void by law but could have been struck down and rendered null by that defense—then the creditor can rightly retain the payment in the **court of conscience** <note>The "internal forum" or moral standing before God, as opposed to a secular court</note> until it is reclaimed by the woman. The reason is that the woman truly owed it and still owes it, naturally and civilly, as long as she does not use the Velleian defense or a claim for recovery after payment. However, when no obligation at all arose from the woman’s guarantee—because it was not made in one of the circumstances expressed by law, or because it was not made in a public instrument before three witnesses—then the creditor cannot retain the payment made by the woman’s error in the court of conscience, because in truth that woman did not owe it. Likewise, when a woman pays knowing she could use the Velleian defense but not caring to use it, or even if she is ignorant of it but pays after a final judgment, the creditor similarly retains the payment with a clear conscience: for the woman truly owed it to him, and in those circumstances, the law does not grant her the right to reclaim it.

8 The doctors doubt whether, according to common law, a woman can † **renounce** the privilege of the Velleian Decree. That is, if she acts as a guarantor with a renunciation of that privilege, would she be fully bound as if she were not a woman, such that the Velleian defense would no longer help her? This controversy only applies when, under common law, a woman remains bound by her contract and thus, unless she renounced the Velleian privilege, she could protect herself with it. For if no obligation arose from her contract because it was rendered void by human law, then just as the Velleian Decree would not apply (since it would be unnecessary), this controversy would also not apply. From this it follows that when a woman does not act as a guarantor in a public instrument with three witnesses present, this controversy ceases: because, as has been said, no obligation arises then, and consequently the Velleian Decree has no place. Gutierrez rightly understands this in *On the Confirmation of Oaths*, part 1, chapter 20, number 7, even in the Kingdom of Castile. It does not matter that in that Kingdom a private writing, later recognized by the one who bound themselves by it, is made public; because in the matter proposed, for a guarantee obligation to arise from a woman's contract, it is necessary as a matter of form—without which it does not arise—that the contract be made from the beginning by a public instrument

<column-break/>

before three witnesses, according to the Law *Antiquae*, final paragraph, of the Code "On the Velleian Decree." Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist who commented on the *Siete Partidas*</note> hesitated undeservedly in title 12, part 5, when he called into doubt whether this applies in the Kingdom of Castile, moved by the fact that the "Ancient Law" <note>original: "lex antiqua"</note> is not found to be formally approved in that Kingdom. However, for it not to apply in that Kingdom, it is not enough that a specific decree is not found approved; rather, it is necessary to find a decree that rejects or abolishes that law by decreeing something contrary or repugnant to it. When nothing contrary or repugnant is found established in that Kingdom, one must stand by the decrees of the common law. From the same foundation, it follows that although a woman acts as a guarantor for her husband, or takes his debt upon herself in a public instrument with three witnesses present and signed, the same controversy remains: for then the obligation is void by the law itself, even if it was made and confirmed repeatedly, and even if it was made for a public debt, such as what is owed to the treasury or the King. The woman is held to no more than can be proven to have been spent from such debt for her own benefit. This is held in the *Authenticum* "If any woman" <note>original: "auth. si qua mulier"</note> and in the *Authenticum* "That no judges," and is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Gregorio Lopez and Antonio Gómez (Law 61 of Toro, number 2) record and follow.

9 This very thing is more strictly decreed in part by Law 61 of Toro, which is Law 9, title 3, book 5 of the *New Compilation*, where it is said:

> From this time forward, a woman may not bind herself as a guarantor for her husband, even if it is said and alleged that the debt was converted to the benefit of the woman. And likewise we command that when a husband and wife bind themselves jointly in one contract or several, the woman shall not be bound to anything, unless it is proven that the said debt was converted to her benefit; for then we command that she be bound for the portion of the said benefit. But if what was converted to her benefit was in things that the husband was obliged to give her, such as clothing her, feeding her, and other necessary things, we command that she shall not be bound to anything because of this. All that I have said is to be understood unless the said guarantee and joint obligation was for maravedis <note>A historical Spanish currency</note> of our rents, or taxes, or rights thereof.

Where you see that even if that for which the wife stood as guarantor was spent for her benefit, the wife is not held to pay the creditor in place of her husband, as she would be held under common law. She would be held under the law of Castile if she were bound jointly with her husband for that debt and it were sufficiently proven to have been spent for her benefit, beyond those things which the husband was bound to spend on her by reason of the dowry. Indeed, that law intended that, notwithstanding the wife's guarantee for her husband, her entire dowry and **paraphernalia** <note>term: "bona paraphernalia" — property belonging to a married woman that was not part of her dowry</note> should remain hers, even if a contract celebrated with a third party by the husband was the reason the wife had all her goods intact or less diminished. And so Antonio Gómez understands that law in the same place, number 2.

# Second Treatise. Disputation 540.

although he does not explain it so clearly: However, when a wife has obligated herself **jointly** <note>original: "de mancomun," a Spanish legal term for shared liability</note> with her husband, that law intended that if anything from that contract was converted to the benefit of the woman—because the assets held by the husband and wife were increased such that the woman was going to receive more of her dowry and personal property than she otherwise would have—this is sufficiently proven so that the wife remains obligated to the creditor for that portion of the debt alone, but not for the remainder. Likewise, the same law restricts the common right established in favor of wives in the cited authorities: if a wife acts as a **guarantor** <note>term: "fideiussor" — someone who guarantees another person's debt</note> for her husband regarding revenues owed to the King, or obligates herself together with her husband regarding them, the guarantee and obligation are valid, and she does not enjoy the privilege of the Velleian Decree.

Having explained the case in which the controversy occurs, we ask whether a woman who renounces the privilege of the Velleian Decree still enjoys it or not. The Gloss, Azon, and many others assert that if a woman renounces the Velleian privilege, she no longer enjoys that protection; many of them affirm that this has been accepted by custom in many places.

<margin>10</margin>
Indeed, they persuade themselves of this opinion. First, because anyone can renounce those things which were introduced for their own benefit. We read this in the Code, "On Pacts," where it is written: *Since it is a rule of ancient law that all have the liberty to renounce those things introduced for their own benefit.* Since the Velleian Decree was introduced for the benefit of women, it remains entirely within their power to renounce it.

Second, in the Digest "On the Velleian Decree," it is held: *Since she can raise the exception of the Decree of the Senate, she truly ought to declare that she will not use that exception, and thus go before the judge.* Here you see that a woman can renounce the Velleian defense.

Third, in the Code regarding when a woman may take the office of tutor, where a mother and grandmother are admitted to the guardianship of children and grandchildren—indeed, they are preferred over other appointed guardians—provided they first renounce the privilege of the Velleian Decree, as was stated in Disputation 220.

<margin>11</margin>
But this opinion has been refined today in this Kingdom of Castile by Law 3, Title 12, Part 5; therefore, one must stand by that law. It must be understood, however, that a woman may renounce the Velleian privilege only if she knows she enjoys it in that event, and renounces it after gaining that knowledge. This is the view of Azon and the Gloss, and it is sanctioned in the cited Law 3 in these words: *The third is when the woman is knowledgeable and certain that she could not nor should not enter as a guarantor, if afterward she renounced it of her own will, having set aside the right that the law granted to women in this matter.* <note>original: "La tercera es, quãdo la muger foesse sabedora..." from the Siete Partidas</note> In this passage, Gregorio Lopez (on the word "knowledgeable") and Gutierrez noted that in the **public courts** <note>original: "foro exteriori"</note> it is not presumed that a woman knew of the privilege or was informed of it before the renunciation unless it is proven; for it is presumed that women are ignorant of the law. If, however, a **notary** <note>term: "Tabellio" — a public official who drafted and authenticated legal documents</note> certifies in the instrument of renunciation that the woman, having been informed of the privilege, renounced it, then one must stand by the faith of the notary. This is the view of Gutierrez and Covarrubias, who add that it is more cautious if the notary expressly says in the document: "She was informed by me,

<column-break/>

the undersigned notary, of the Velleian benefit in favor of women—namely, that a woman cannot obligate herself for another—and knowing this, she renounced it." He says this is the accepted practice of notaries.

Gutierrez rightly says in the same place (number 8) that a general renunciation of privileges is not sufficient for it to be deemed that she also renounced the Velleian privilege; rather, a renunciation of it in particular is necessary. This is required even when a mother or grandmother renounces the Velleian Decree to undertake the guardianship or care of children or grandchildren. This opinion is pleasing. Both because the laws speaking of mothers and grandmothers require an express renunciation of it in particular, and because knowledge of that privilege in particular must precede the renunciation—which is not inferred, nor presumed in court, from a general renunciation of privileges. In the same place (number 9), he reports a case where a certain woman had given a power of attorney in public form to a representative to obligate her for another, with the power of renouncing all privileges granted to her by law, which she then renounced; however, she did not expressly name the Velleian privilege. Afterward, the representative obligated the woman, using all required solemnities and renouncing the Velleian Decree and other privileges of the woman in particular. The woman later argued that she had not renounced the Velleian Decree in particular, nor had she given the power to renounce it in particular, nor had she been informed of that privilege before the renunciation was made, and therefore the obligation was null. He reports that the sentence was pronounced by the **Royal Senators** <note>referring to the high court judges of the Royal Council of Castile</note> in favor of the woman. It did not matter that it was proven she had been informed of it and renounced it in other contracts where she had obligated herself for others.

Certainly, in that event, if the woman were put under oath as to whether she was conscious of that privilege when she gave that power to her representative with the intent of renouncing even the Velleian privilege, and she answered affirmatively, I would judge that by **equity** <note>term: "epicheia" — the principle of interpreting the law according to the spirit of justice rather than the strict letter</note> she should be considered obligated. The subtleties and external words of the laws should not hinder this, because they are based on a presumption of the woman’s ignorance of the privilege—the opposite of which, in the case proposed, is clear. It is not to be thought that the authors of those laws intended to release that woman from her obligation in such an event, to the loss of the creditor, who could easily be deceived in that way by the woman and the principal debtor. In delivering sentences, one should stand by the intent rather than the words of the laws.

Although the opinion of Azon, the glosses, and others is that if a woman renounces the Velleian privilege in the manner explained, she does not enjoy it, and this is sanctioned by law in this Kingdom of Castile; nevertheless, Bartolus, Panormitanus, and the common opinion of the doctors—to which Gregorio Lopez leans and which Antonio Gomez and Covarrubias embrace—assert...
