# Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

...remain, standing in common law, even if a woman renounces the Velleian Decree <note>The *Senatus consultum Velleianum* was a Roman law that prohibited women from taking on the debts of others; it was intended to protect them from being pressured into risky financial guarantees.</note> in the aforementioned manner, she does not therefore lose that privilege, except if she renounces it in court, or if she is a mother or grandmother renouncing it in order to undertake the **guardianship** or care of her children or grandchildren.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin>
12. And this is today established by law in the Kingdom of Portugal (Book 4 of the Ordinances, title 12, penultimate section), even if the renunciation is made in court; Portuguese law only makes an exception when a mother or grandmother takes up the guardianship or care of children or grandchildren. The reasoning is that since women are easily led to act as **guarantors** <note>original: "fidejubendum"</note> or to obligate themselves for someone else, they could be just as easily led to renounce the Velleian privilege. Therefore, since that privilege was granted to them for that very reason, they ought to retain it even if they renounce it; otherwise, the legal protection would be of no use to them. This is the same reasoning provided by the Portuguese Ordinance in the cited section.

According to this opinion, regarding the first argument of the opposing view, it must be said that one can indeed renounce a privilege introduced for one's own benefit, provided that the cause for granting it is not the person's age or weakness. For as long as that same cause persists, such a renunciation of the privilege is not valid; because that renunciation would be, in a way, against good morals, and therefore void, as argued by the text in the law *in alia* (section *eleganter*).

Regarding the second argument, it must be said that the discussion there concerns a renunciation made in court, which is valid due to the authority and vigor of the judicial process. Under Portuguese law, however, it is not valid even in that event, as has been said.

Regarding the third argument, it must be said that the exception was granted there for the public office of guardianship or care of one's own offspring, to which it was fitting they be admitted, but only if they renounced their privileges, including the Velleian Decree, as it pertains to that duty.

13. This must also be observed: if a woman swears an oath that she will not use the Velleian privilege, then she cannot be helped by it. Likewise, if she obligates herself for someone else under an oath, promising that she will fulfill the obligation and not contest it, then—even if she had not obligated herself with the standard legal formalities (established in the law *antiquae*, final section)—she would be bound to fulfill the obligation by the force of the oath alone, and she could not contest it. The reason is that fulfilling such an obligation is not inherently evil, but merely void under human law; it is valid and binding in itself if the required formalities are used. However, human law allows it to be nullified by the benefit of the Velleian Decree, as has been explained. Therefore, if an oath is added to fulfill that promise, or not to use the Velleian privilege, since such an oath concerns a lawful matter, it certainly binds. This is no less than when the sale of property belonging to a minor, or dotal land <note>land designated for a dowry</note>, or the renunciation of a legal inheritance are confirmed by an oath; regarding such matters, we have spoken extensively in Disputation 149 and the two following. **Except in Portugal**, where, as stated in Disputation 149, an oath attached to any contract or promise without Royal permission is void, and the contract or promise itself is rendered void. However, regarding the fact that in the case we are discussing, the oath binds and the Velleian Decree has no place, this is affirmed

<column-break/>

by the common opinion of the doctors <note>the "doctors" refers to established legal and theological scholars</note>, which is cited and followed by Covarruvias, Gregorius Lopez, Antonio Gomez, Gutierrez, and others. Beyond the laws cited in Disputation 149 and what was said there, this is confirmed by the chapter *ex prescripto* and the gloss on the words "and the wife," where a woman who had acted as a guarantor while using an oath is commanded to fulfill the guarantee entirely.

Covarruvias, in the cited number 5, although he admits that a woman who is aware of her privilege and promises by oath to fulfill the guarantee does not enjoy the Velleian privilege; and although he also admits the common opinion is that she does not enjoy it even if she was unaware of the privilege when she bound herself by oath; he nevertheless thinks in this latter case—along with others he cites—that the oath does not prevent her from enjoying the privilege. He says this because the oath does not extend to things unknown, and therefore does not include a promise not to use a privilege granted to her by law in that matter. Thus, he argues that the oath does not prevent her from using the Velleian Decree. I, however, do not favor this opinion. For a woman who promises by oath to fulfill a guarantee understands that she will fulfill it in every way as far as she is concerned, and therefore without using any loophole. I understand this to be the case when, if she had known of the privilege, she would have similarly bound herself by oath to fulfill the guarantee, as regularly happens.

Gutierrez, in the cited number 2, along with Padilla and Menchaca (whom he cites), says that if a woman first swore *not* to act as a guarantor, and later acted as a guarantor and confirmed it with an oath—namely, that she would fulfill it and not contest it—she can still use the Velleian privilege. They are led to this because the second oath would not be binding, since the first oath aligned with the common law. However, the opposite must undoubtedly be affirmed, as is clear from what was said in Disputation 151. The reason is, first, that for a woman to act as a guarantor is not an evil thing, nor is it prohibited to her by human law; rather, it can sometimes be a good thing for a reasonable and just cause. Therefore, if the oath not to act as a guarantor was not made for the benefit of a third party, it merely has the status of a **vow** <note>original: "voti"</note> made to God and confirmed by oath. For that reason, unless it were better not to act as a guarantor given the circumstances, it would not bind; rather, the woman could licitly act as a guarantor despite that oath. Furthermore, even if she sinned by acting as a guarantor and confirming it with an oath, she would not sin—even given the prior oath—by *fulfilling* the guarantee. For to fulfill a guarantee and not contest it through the Velleian privilege is not an evil thing, nor is it the object of a wicked promise, but rather one confirmed by a second oath. Therefore, since it is not evil, she is bound under the penalty of mortal sin to fulfill that second promise confirmed by oath.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Senatus Consultum Velleianum, shifting from whether a woman can renounce her legal protections to the specific legal scenarios where those protections are automatically voided or do not apply, followed by a new section on other classes of people, such as soldiers and clerics, who are restricted from acting as guarantors.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 5, Section 40.

<margin>14</margin> In the following circumstances, a woman does not enjoy the protection of the Velleian Decree. <note>The Velleian Decree (Senatus Consultum Velleianum) was a Roman law that protected women by making any contract where they took on another person's debt invalid.</note> This is understood to be the case even if the formalities mentioned in the law *Antiquae* <note>original: "l. antique. C. ad Velle." referring to a specific law in the Code of Justinian</note> have not been met. 

**First**, if she obligates herself to pay something or acts as a **guarantor** <term>fideiussor: a person who legally promises to pay a debt if the original debtor fails to do so</term> for the sake of manumitting a slave. <note>original: "pro libertate mancipij"</note> This is established in favor of liberty itself, as seen in the Code and the Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, title 12, §1).

**Second**, if a woman promises something as a **dowry** <term>dos: property or money brought by a bride to her husband on their marriage</term> for another woman, or acts as a guarantor for a promised dowry. This is valid provided the marriage is celebrated according to Canon Law, as the Portuguese laws rightly add. This exception was created to favor marriage and the provision of dowries.

**Third**, if, after a woman has obligated herself for another or acted as their guarantor, a full two-year period passes from the initial obligation and she then gives a **pledge** <term>pignus: physical collateral or security for a debt</term> or renews the same obligation. In this case, she does not enjoy the Velleian privilege. However, if she gave the pledge or renewed the debt within the two-year window, she remains protected. The reasoning given by the law is that after two years, she is presumed to act with "mature counsel" and to be managing her own affairs. Gregory Lopez <note>A famous Spanish jurist known for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note> notes that if the original contract stipulated from the start that a pledge would be given after two years, this would be seen as an execution of the first contract rather than a fresh "innovation" <note>legal renewal of a contract</note>, and thus the protection would still apply. **However**, this third case does not apply in Portugal. The Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4, title 12, last section) decree that a woman enjoys the Velleian protection regardless of how many times the obligation is renewed.

<margin>15</margin> **Fourth**, when a woman receives a price, or something of equivalent value, in exchange for taking on another’s debt or acting as a guarantor. Whether the obligation is verbal or written, or whether she receives the payment at the start or later, she loses the Velleian protection. However, it must be proven—either by a public instrument with three witnesses or by other legal proof—that she actually received the payment. Otherwise, she retains her protection. The amount received must be significant enough that it is not considered a sham to trick the woman into being bound; this is left to the judge's discretion. We discussed the limits of a guarantor accepting payment for their services in Dispute 319.

**Fifth**, when a woman deceives a creditor. For example, if she dresses in men's clothing and pretends to be a man, or uses some other trick so the creditor does not realize she is a woman. Likewise, if she deceives him into thinking she does not have the Velleian protection when she actually does, she is not protected by it. 

<column-break/>

The same reasoning applies if a husband binds his wife’s property with her knowledge while the creditor remains ignorant; if the woman remains silent, she is considered a participant in the fraud against the creditor and remains bound.

**Sixth**, if a woman was already a debtor to someone and takes on an equal amount of debt for her own creditor, or consents to be substituted as the debtor to a third party. Or, if she acted as a guarantor and then received from the debtor the very thing she guaranteed so that she might pay it herself. Or, if she bought an inheritance and acted as a guarantor for the debts of the deceased that were to be paid from that inheritance. Or, if she was a guarantor for someone and later became their heir, she is bound to pay that debt in proportion to her share of the inheritance. In these and similar cases, she does not enjoy the Velleian protection because she is effectively paying what she already owed, or an equivalent amount, to the person whose debt she assumed. The same applies if she acts as a guarantor for someone in the same amount that they act as a guarantor for her. All of these are found in the Civil Law and the Portuguese Ordinances.

### Those who follow cannot be guarantors.

<margin>16</margin> **Soldiers**, first and foremost, who are not at rest but are on active expedition. Common law prohibits them from being guarantors for tenants of the prince's property. Although some laws refer specifically to leasing, legal experts generally agree that soldiers are prohibited from being guarantors in a universal sense. This is affirmed by Antonio Gomez, who states it is the common opinion of the doctors of law. This should be understood according to how it has been received by local custom.

<margin>17</margin> A **cleric**, although he should not frequently act as a guarantor for others (especially laypeople), and should be punished if he does so frequently. The law states that a cleric "serving" <note>meaning frequently occupied with</note> guarantees should be cast out. However, if he acts as a guarantor for a layperson out of piety or for a rational cause, far from sinning, he does so meritoriously. Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canonist.</note> and others affirm that such a guarantee is always valid, whether for another cleric or a layman. He can obligate his own personal property and even the income of his church office <note>original: "reditus sui beneficij"</note> to satisfy the debt. However, a cleric cannot be imprisoned for a guarantee.

### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts
#### Page 760

...but from the income of the benefice and his other goods, the creditor should be satisfied, leaving the cleric enough so that he does not suffer want, as is gathered from the decree on sureties <note>original: "c. 2. de fideiuss."</note> and noted there by Panormitanus, Antonio Gómez (citation 18), and doctors of law commonly.

<margin>18</margin> Regarding a **Bishop**, it is suggested in the canon *Te quidem* <note>original: "ca. te quidem 11. q. 1." citing a canon attributed to St. Ambrose</note> that he cannot be a **guarantor** <term>fideiussor: a person who guarantees the debt of another</term>. However, Gregorio López says in that same place that he believes in practice, if a Bishop does act as a guarantor, he is held liable.

<margin>19</margin> As for a **Member of a Religious Order**, if he acts as a guarantor without the permission of his superior and the majority of the chapter, the guarantee does not hold, and he is to be punished. In a religious order where a chapter is not traditionally assembled, the permission of the person who holds authority according to the statutes and privileges of that order is sufficient—as is the case in our Society <note>Molina refers here to the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), of which he was a member.</note>.

<margin>20</margin> **Farmers** who till the land themselves, or through their servants or family, cannot today be guarantors in this Kingdom of Castile for the lords of the towns under whose jurisdiction they live. Thus King Philip II, in a law passed in the year 1594 in favor of farmers, rightfully decreed in section 5, speaking of the aforementioned farmers in these words:

> That the said farmers cannot obligate themselves as principals, nor as guarantors, in favor of the lords of the places in whose jurisdiction they live, and that any legal documents executed to the contrary of what is contained in this chapter, or of any other protections for farmers expressed here, shall be null; regardless of any renunciations <note>A "renunciation" was a standard legal clause where a person waived their rights to specific legal protections.</note> they might make, nor shall the notaries allow such documents to be executed before them, under penalty of losing their offices and being barred from using them from that time forward.

<margin>21</margin> Regarding a **Minor under twenty-five years of age**: although an obligation is not void by the law itself <term>ipso iure: by the law itself, or automatically</term> if he acts as a guarantor for someone, it is nonetheless dissolved and annulled through the benefit of **full restoration** <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy where a person is restored to their original position as if a contract never happened</term>. This applies even if he is a guarantor for his father and the principal debtor is insolvent; for the very fact that such a minor would have to pay for the principal debtor, he would be considered "harmed" by that guarantee. This is held in the Code regarding the sons of families and the Praetor’s edict. Antonio Gómez affirms this is the common opinion of the doctors. Hence, the Portuguese Ordinances (Book 4) rightly advise that in cases where women do not enjoy the protection of the Velleian Decree <note>A Roman law protecting women from being held responsible for others' debts.</note>, they still enjoy the benefit of "full restoration" if they are minors. Antonio Gómez limits this, following the common opinion: unless the minor acted as a guarantor for his father who was in prison, in order to get him out. Since any prudent adult would do this—and would indeed be bound to do so—a son could even be disinherited if he were male and refused to help his father in such a state.

<margin>22</margin> When someone acts as a guarantor for a minor, and the minor sees himself harmed, or if there was **fraud** <term>dolus: intentional deception or trickery</term> involved, the situation is as follows. Even if the fraud was not intentional, but the harm is such that neither a **civil obligation** <note>A debt enforceable in court.</note> nor a **natural obligation** <note>A debt that is morally binding but might lack a legal mechanism for enforcement.</note> arises from the contract for the minor—for example, if the minor

<column-break/>

sold a property for less than half its just price <note>This refers to the legal concept of *laesio enormis*, where a contract can be rescinded if the price is extremely unfair.</note>, or if the other party did not intend to deceive him, but the minor remained obligated at least "naturally"—if the minor rescinds the contract due to this harm through the benefit of full restoration, then the guarantor is affected. In the first case, whether the fraud was formal or merely material, if no natural obligation arose for the minor and he is helped by the benefit of full restoration, the guarantor is not held liable to the creditor. This is because the obligation of a guarantor always rests upon some obligation—at least a natural one—of the principal debtor. Therefore, if the debt does not exist for the person for whom he guaranteed, he himself is not held for it. This is found in the Code regarding the sureties of minors and the *Partidas* <note>The *Siete Partidas*, the foundational law code of Castile.</note>. 

That this should be understood not only when there is formal fraud, but even when the harm is "material" (as explained), is gathered clearly from the laws on verbal obligations. Gregorio López affirms this, noting that it applies not only to the guarantor's obligation but also to a principal one, as if someone had taken over a minor’s debt after the contract to confirm it. Since this new obligation rests on the minor's first obligation, if that first one was entirely void, the second one must also be considered entirely void. 

From this it is easily established: if a minor sold real estate (or valuable movable goods that could have been preserved) without a judge's decree, the sale is void by law. Thus, no natural obligation arises for the minor (as we showed in Dispute 224). In that case, the minor is not bound to stand by such a contract—he can reclaim the item by returning the price—and the guarantor is not held liable for **eviction** <term>evictio: the recovery of property by a third party with a better legal title, leaving the buyer without the item</term>. Since no obligation (not even a natural one) arose for the minor, no obligation exists for the guarantor. Gregorio López affirms this against the "Gloss," which argued that a guarantor is always held liable. But in the case the Gloss cited, it was not the minor who sold the item, but a tutor or guardian who obligated himself and gave his own property as a pledge. 

However, when a minor has sold movable property for which a judge's decree was not necessary, and used a guarantor, then if he acts only to increase the price or rescind the contract because it was sold for less than half the just price, the guarantor is not liable. This is because the minor contracted neither a natural nor a civil obligation...

If, however, he should seek the rescission of the contract through the benefit of **restitution to the original state** <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum," a legal remedy allowing a person, typically a minor, to be restored to their previous legal position if a contract was unfair</note>, not being satisfied with an increase in the price up to what is just—or when he has not been deceived by more than half of the **just price** <term>just price: the fair market value as determined by moral and legal standards</term> he should seek the rescission of the contract because he finds himself harmed, or should seek an increase of the price up to the full just amount—then certainly the guarantor would be held liable in the secular court for **eviction** <note>original: "evictione," meaning the loss of property due to a third-party legal claim</note> if the contract were rescinded, or would be held liable for that increase in price which he would receive anew. This is held by **Gregorio López on law 4**, cited in the **penultimate gloss.** In the second outcome of the two proposed at the beginning—namely, when no material fraud intervened, but the minor who provided a guarantor sought and obtained restitution to the original state—then that restitution benefits only him, but not the guarantors. They remain liable for eviction or for the increase in price to the creditor. Nevertheless, they have recourse through an **action of mandate** <note>original: "actione mandati," a legal claim based on the agreement between the debtor and the guarantor</note> against the minor, unless the minor himself, as he is able, seeks restitution to the original state against the guarantors as well. This is expressly stated in **laws 1 & 2 of the Code on the guarantors of minors**, and by **Marcellus in the Digest, law 4, as cited.** And these same things are to be said concerning one who acts as a guarantor for a **spendthrift** <note>original: "prodigo"</note> or a **madman** <note>original: "furioso"</note>, as is held in the **cited law of Marcellus.**

# Whether a guarantor can be obligated for more than the principal debtor, or for a different thing?

-> ## DISPUTATION DXLI. <-

### SUMMARY

<margin>Law 1, title 12, part 5</margin>
1 **In what way it is to be understood that a guarantor is not obligated for more than the principal.**
<margin>Law 2</margin>
2 **In which cases a guarantor cannot be obligated for more than the principal.**
<margin>Law 3</margin>
3 **A guarantor can obligate himself for less than the principal debtor.**
<margin>Law 4</margin>
4 **When a guarantor is obligated for more than the principal, whether the obligation is rendered void in its entirety, or only for the excess amount.**
5 **And what if an oath is present. Number 5.**
<margin>Law 5</margin>
6 **A guarantor can be more strictly bound than the principal, though not for more.**
7 **In which cases and outcomes. Number 7.**
8 **How a guarantor can be obligated for a different thing from that which the principal debtor is obligated.**
9 **When the obligation of a guarantor is said to be different from the obligation of the principal.**

<margin>Laws 2, 3, & 4, title 12, part 5.</margin>
<margin>Laws 1 & 2 of the Code on the guarantors of minors.</margin>
A guarantor cannot be obligated for more than the principal debtor who is obligated in whatever way, as stated in the **Institutes on guarantors, and the Digest under the same title**, and **Law 7, distinction 22, part 5** <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>; the common opinion of the doctors of law agrees with this. The reason given is that the guarantee is secondary to the principal obligation and inherent to it; it cannot extend further than the obligation of the principal debtor, as recorded under **guarantors in the Digest and the Institutes.** In this place, observe that it is one thing for a guar-

<column-break/>

-antor to be obligated for "more"—that is, more strictly—than the principal debtor is obligated, yet only toward the same thing to which the principal debtor is bound; and it is not denied by the cited laws that this can be the case, as we shall explain. It is quite another thing, however, to be obligated for "more"—that is, for more extensively—than the principal debtor is obligated; and this the cited laws deny can be the case.

2 <margin>Paragraph "more than is just" and the following in the Institutes on actions.</margin> Furthermore, regarding the four points explained in the **Institutes on actions, in the paragraph "more than is just" and the following**, it is said in the cited laws that a guarantor cannot be obligated for more than the principal debtor. Primarily regarding **quantity**. For example, the principal debtor cannot be obligated to pay only five, while the guarantor is obligated to pay ten for him. Conversely, the guarantor can certainly act as a surety for only five, while the principal debtor remains obligated for ten. Secondly, regarding **place**. For example, the principal debtor cannot be obligated to pay something in a specific place, and the guarantor be obligated to pay it in a place more favorable to the creditor <note>The text suggests "gratiori fideiussori," likely meaning a place more demanding for the guarantor or more advantageous for the creditor</note>. Thirdly, regarding **time**. For example, the principal debtor cannot be obligated to pay within two years, and the guarantor be obligated to pay within a shorter time. For then the guarantor is said to be obligated for more in terms of time when he is bound to a shorter period, as is rightly stated in the cited laws. Conversely, the principal debtor can well be obligated to pay within a shorter time, and the guarantor within a longer time. To the category of a "greater obligation regarding time" is reduced the case where the principal debtor is obligated under a condition, but the guarantor is obligated purely <note>original: "purè," meaning unconditionally</note>; hence, that is not valid. However, the guarantor can be obligated only under a condition, or only for a specific day—that is, up to a certain time, or starting from a certain day—while the principal debtor is obligated purely or absolutely. For this latter obligation is greater, or extends further, than the former. That a guarantor can obligate himself only under a condition, or for a day, or from a certain day, is held in **Law 6, title 12, part 5**, in addition to the cited laws, and is very well known in itself. Fourthly, regarding the **cause**, as is said in the **section on place cited above.** Omitting the example found there (because that section does not discuss guarantors), appropriate examples are applied in the **Digest on guarantors.** For instance, if a debtor is obligated to give a man <note>meaning a slave</note> or ten—that is, some indeterminate slave or ten coins—which is understood to mean as the debtor himself chooses, and the guarantor is obligated to give one of those two as the creditor chooses, the obligation of the guarantor is harsher than that of the principal debtor, and therefore it is void. Conversely, if the principal debtor were obligated to give a man or ten as the creditor chose, and the guarantor were obligated to give a man or ten as the guarantor chose, the obligation would be valid; for the guarantor would be obligated for less than the principal debtor. For the same reason, if the principal debtor is obligated to give Stichus and Pamphilus <note>common placeholder names for slaves in Roman legal texts</note>, and the guarantor is obligated to give Stichus *or* Pamphilus, the obligation would be valid; because similarly, the guarantor would be obligated for less than the principal debtor. These are the examples **reported by Ulpian from the jurist Julian.**

3 <margin>Question.</margin> There is a doubt as to whether, when a guarantor is obligated for more than the principal debtor in the ways explained...

### Luis de Molina, On Contracts

**4** ...or whether the **guarantee** <term>guarantee (fideiussio): a legal promise to pay a debt if the original debtor fails to do so</term> remains void only regarding the excess, so that the person remains obligated precisely for that amount for which the principal debtor remains obligated; or whether it remains entirely void, so that he remains obligated to the creditor for nothing at all. The law "Graece," in the section "Illud" regarding guarantors, clearly seems to suggest the second option: namely, that the obligation is rendered completely void. For since the discourse is generally about all those who are obligated for others, it is said: *If they were obligated for a more burdensome cause, it was decided they are not obligated at all.* <note>original: "Si fuerint in duriorem causam obligati placuit omnino eos non obligari." This is a principle from Roman Law (Digest 46.1.8.7) suggesting that if a guarantor promises more than the debtor, the whole contract fails.</note> And this seems to be the meaning of the doctrine added in the following paragraphs; this is the opinion of the "Gloss" there, and of several others like Bartolus and the common opinion, as reported by Covarruvias, Gutierrez, and Gregorio López in his commentary on Law 7.

The contrary opinion—namely, that it is only rendered void regarding the excess—is also reported by the cited "Gloss" and the first "Gloss" on the Institutes regarding guarantors. The addition to the "Gloss" leans toward this view, and Antonio Gomez embraces it. Whatever the case may be in common law, this latter opinion has rightly been established as law in this **Kingdom of Castile** <margin>Decision: Law of Castile.</margin> by the cited Law 7, so that the guarantor is then held only to that for which the principal debtor is held; for the law does not wish that which is useful to be spoiled by that which is useless. <note>A reference to the legal maxim "utile per inutile non vitiatur."</note> Indeed, Gregorio López and Gutierrez warn that the guarantor's obligation regarding the excess is invalid under the law of Castile even if the creditor and guarantor expressly agree that the guarantor is held for the excess, and even if the guarantor renounces that law; this is because the law is not established as a private privilege for the guarantor, but as a mandatory legal form. The same must be said regarding the whole obligation under common law, according to the common opinion which asserts the obligation is invalid in its entirety.

<margin>A Doubtful Decision.</margin>**5** The question arises whether, if a guarantor who has obligated himself for more than the principal debtor confirms his obligation and guarantee with an **oath** <note>original: "iuramento." In the early modern period, a religious oath could make an otherwise legally "void" contract binding in the "court of conscience" or even in civil courts.</note>, he is held for the whole amount. To this, it must undoubtedly be said that he is held for the whole, even standing under civil common law. This is because a matter confirmed by such an oath is not illicit, but merely void in the absence of the oath—under the law of Castile only regarding the excess over the principal debtor's obligation, and under common law in its entirety. When a promise that is not illicit is confirmed by an oath, even if it were void without the oath, it assumes strength from the oath and creates an obligation. An action is granted even in civil law, provided it is not illicit on the part of the recipient. Nor can the oath be relaxed when it was made in favor of some person and the acceptance is not illicit on their part, as was shown in Disputations 149 and 256. This is affirmed in the present case by Covarruvias, Gregorio López, and the common opinion of the doctors.

The doctors agree, however, that since the principal debtor is not held for the excess, but only the guarantor is held for it by virtue of the oath, he is held for it as a **principal** and not as a guarantor. Therefore, regarding that excess, one must not

<column-break/>

wait for an **excussion** <term>excussion (excussio): the legal right of a guarantor to demand that the creditor first seize and sell the property of the principal debtor before coming after the guarantor</term> to be made against the goods of the principal debtor; we shall speak of this excussion in its proper place below.

Regarding the breadth of the quantity which the principal debtor also owes: Bartolus and others whom Covarruvias cites judge that a guarantor who (under common law) is held by the sole power of an oath is not held even then as a guarantor, but as a principal. Consequently, they argue it is not necessary to first perform an excussion of the principal's goods before the guarantor is compelled to pay by the strength of the oath provided. This is the opinion which Covarruvias rightly affirms for a long time, but from which he eventually departs—and I believe one should depart from it, despite what Gutierrez proclaims to the contrary.

The opposite of our and Covarruvias’s opinion can be asserted on two grounds. One is that by the very fact that a guarantee is confirmed by oath—even if the guarantor does not obligate himself for more than the principal—the guarantor does not enjoy the privilege granted by law to guarantors (namely, that excussion is first made against the principal's goods). Gutierrez seems to affirm this, but its falsehood will be discussed below. An oath that confirms an otherwise valid guarantee, although it binds the law, does not extend itself further than other promises confirmed by oath. The guarantee, if not confirmed by oath, would not bind one to payment unless an excussion was first made against the principal debtor's goods.

The second ground for that assertion is: since under common law the guarantor (without the oath) is not held even for the principal debt, and the obligation arises only from the oath, he seems to be held not as a guarantor of the debtor, but as a "debtor of the oath," and thus as a principal. Therefore, it seems he is held without waiting for the excussion of the principal.

Nevertheless, the contrary must undoubtedly be said with Covarruvias. For that guarantor intended only to obligate himself for that amount **as a guarantor** of the principal debtor, standing in his place in the event he does not pay. He employed the oath for greater firmness and so the creditor would be more secure. Although common law may render that guarantee void without the oath, once the oath is applied, the obligation of the guarantor arises—but not for anything other than what that guarantee would bind him to if it were not void. Clearly, given the legal disposition that excussion must first happen, the guarantor does not intend to obligate himself to anything else by adding an oath, nor does the creditor intend to bind him to anything else; he only wanted the oath added so that the obligation would remain more firm.

Remember, however, regarding **Portuguese Law**, if the oath was not provided with the King's permission, then the person is not held either by the oath or by the guarantee...

<summary>This page discusses whether a guarantor is liable if they promise to pay more than the original debtor. Molina concludes that under Castilian law, the guarantee is valid up to the principal's amount, and if an oath is taken, the guarantor may be liable for the excess, though they should still retain the right to have the debtor sued first.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 541

...but valid, to testify to the obligation, according to what was said in Disputation 149. In the same way, an obligation will not result in this Kingdom of Castile from a **guarantee** <term>guarantee (fideiussio): a legal promise to pay a debt if the original debtor fails to do so</term>, even if otherwise valid, if it is confirmed by an oath, according to what was said in the same place.

Gutierrez, in the cited chapter 22, number 5, along with Menchaca, asserts that if a guarantor had previously affirmed by oath that he would not guarantee more for anyone than that person was bound for, then, if he does guarantee more for him and confirms that guarantee with an oath, it is not valid regarding the excess. This is argued because the prior oath was in harmony with common law. However, this opinion is false, and is overturned in the same way that another similar opinion of theirs was overturned in the preceding disputation; for that reason, I will not dwell further on this matter.

<margin>6</margin>
It was said above that a guarantor cannot be obligated for **more** than the principal debtor, but can be obligated **more strictly** <term>stricter obligation (arctius obligari): when a guarantor's legal burden is heavier or more direct than the debtor's, even if the financial amount is the same</term> than him. Since, as was said in Disputation 539, for one who is only **naturally obligated** <term>natural obligation: a debt that is morally binding but cannot be legally enforced in court</term>, a guarantor can be added who will remain obligated both naturally and civilly <term>civil obligation: a debt that is legally enforceable in court</term>, and therefore more strictly, as Gregorio López affirms in the cited Law 7, gloss 1, and Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 2, along with the common opinion of the doctors which they report. Likewise, as is easily established from what has been said so far, he can be obligated with an oath, even though the principal debtor is obligated without an oath.

<margin>7</margin>
From this foundation—that a guarantor can be bound more strictly than the principal debtor—Antonio Gómez concludes in the same place, along with many others whom he cites, that a guarantor can be obligated by a **guarentigio instrument** <term>instrumento guarentigio: a public legal document that allows for immediate execution or seizure of assets without a full trial</term>, even when the principal debtor is not obligated by such an instrument, or is only naturally obligated. He then concludes, with Faber, that a guarantor can be obligated with a **mortgage** <term>hypotheca: a pledge of property as security for a debt</term> when the principal debtor is obligated without a mortgage. Thirdly, from the same foundation that a guarantor can be bound more strictly than the principal debtor, he rightly concludes, with many others whom he cites, that it can happen that sometimes a guarantor can be forced to pay for the debtor without any **discussion** of the debtor's goods <term>excussio (discussion): the legal right of a guarantor to demand that the creditor first try to seize the debtor's assets before coming after the guarantor</term>, even if the debtor has those goods present in the same place. For if the principal debtor is only naturally obligated, then, since he cannot be sued for the debt in the **external court** <note>The 'external court' (forum exterior) refers to public civil or ecclesiastical courts, as opposed to the 'internal court' of conscience or confession.</note>, no seizure can be made of his goods, even if he has many present goods, and yet the guarantor will then be forced to pay for him. From this same foundation we can conclude that a guarantor can bind himself to a penalty if he himself does not pay what he guaranteed, even when the principal debtor has bound himself to no penalty if he failed to pay, as the *Gloss* on the law *Sicut reus* affirms, consistently with the text there in the Digest on guarantors <note>original: "ff. de fideiuff." refers to the Digest, part of the Corpus Iuris Civilis, the foundation of Roman law</note>, and as Gregorio López and most others affirm, whom he reports on the cited Law 7, gloss 1. This agrees with the law *Si pupillus* at the end of the Digest on verbal obligations. The reason is because that is, in itself, being bound more strictly to the guarantee than the debtor is bound to the payment, and it is incidentally being bound to something else; for from the fact that the guarantor does not stand by his promises, it follows incidentally that he pays as a penalty for his own fault, and further, he promised it if he should fall into that fault. We can likewise conclude from the same foundation that he can bind himself to abide by the creditor's oath in a lawsuit regarding the **interest** <term>interest (interesse): the loss suffered or profit missed by the creditor due to a delay in payment</term> that the creditor might lose because the guarantor did not pay 

<column-break/>

at the appointed time, when the principal debtor has not bound himself to stand by a similar oath of the creditor, as Gregorio López asserts with Faber above. For that is, in itself, to bind oneself more strictly, and incidentally to bind oneself to something else, as if in a penalty, if he does not stand by his promises. This agrees with the fact that this is not, in itself, binding oneself for more, according to Law 1 of the Digest on taking an oath in a lawsuit. These points cover the first of the matters proposed.

<margin>8</margin>
As for what pertains to the second matter, namely whether a guarantor can be obligated for **a different thing** from that to which the principal debtor is obligated—and so that the first point may be more clearly illuminated at the same time, and so that certain difficult laws may be explained and brought into harmony—it must be observed with Lassarte in *On the Tithe of Sale*, chapter 8: In common civil law, not only is a guarantee invalid if the guarantor is bound for more than the principal debtor, but it is also invalid if the guarantor is bound for a different thing than that to which the principal debtor is bound, according to the law *Graece*, in the section *Si qui Stichum*, and the section *Idem Iulianus*, and the laws *Si ita* and *Si a reo*, section *Si a reo*, in the Digest on guarantors. However, although if the principal debtor is bound to a certain quantity of money, and the guarantor is bound for it to certain measures of wheat, wine, or oil, or to the payment of any other thing, the guarantor is considered bound for a different thing, and therefore the obligation is void (as is clear from the cited laws); and the same applies if the principal debtor is bound to a thing that is not money, such as wheat, wine, a slave, or another similar thing, and the guarantor is bound to a different thing that is not money; nonetheless, if the principal debtor is bound to a thing that is not money, such as wine or oil, and the guarantor is bound for him to a certain quantity of money, he is not considered bound for a different thing, as is expressly held in the cited law *Si ita* in the Digest on guarantors. The reason is that money, in regards to its value, is that by which all other things are estimated, and acts as their measure regarding value; and therefore, in the case proposed, the obligation of the guarantor to a certain quantity of money, when the principal debtor is bound to wheat, wine, oil, or another thing that is not money, is not considered an obligation for a different thing. The words of the law *Si ita* are as follows:

> *If I have accepted a guarantor thus: "Regarding the ten [coins] I have loaned, do you authorize a thousand measures of wheat to be on your faith [guarantee]?" the guarantor is not bound: because a guarantor cannot be bound for a different thing than what was loaned; for just as the estimation of things which are considered merchandise can be made in counted money, money cannot likewise be estimated by merchandise.* <note>original: "Si ita fideiuborem accepero... ita pecunia quoque merce aestimanda est." Digest 46.1.42.</note>

These are the words of the jurist Iambolenus, to whom that law belongs. There he expressly teaches that the obligation of a guarantor to pay wheat, when the obligation of the principal debtor was to pay money, is an obligation for a different thing, and therefore void; on the other hand, the obligation of a guarantor to pay money, when the principal debtor was obligated to pay wheat, is not considered an obligation for a different thing, and therefore is valid.

However, the *Gloss* of Accursius there, on the word "can" (*potest*), which Bartolus follows, asserts the opposite is true: when the debtor is bound to give a thing that is not money, such as wheat, and the guarantor binds himself to pay money for it; for they affirm that the obligation...

<summary>This page clarifies that while a guarantor cannot promise a higher amount than the debtor, they can accept 'stricter' terms (such as waiving the right to seize the debtor's assets first). It also establishes the Roman law principle that a guarantee is void if it involves a different commodity than the original debt, unless the guarantor promises money for a debt of goods, since money serves as the universal measure of value.</summary>

#### Of the Contracts of Luis de Molina

...that the obligation is for a different thing, and therefore is null. They rely on the gloss of the law *If anyone, Stichus* <note>original: "si quis Stichum"</note> in the Digest regarding **guarantees** <term>guarantee (fideiussio): a legal promise to pay a debt if the original debtor fails</term>, where Ulpian, reporting from Julian, states that if the principal debtor binds himself to deliver **Stichus** <term>Stichus: a generic name used for a slave in Roman legal examples, like "John Doe" today</term>, and the guarantor binds himself to deliver "Stichus, or ten [gold pieces]," the guarantor's obligation is null. This is because it is "harsher" <note>original: "durior"</note> than the principal debtor's obligation. For if Stichus dies [without fault], the principal debtor is released; meanwhile, the guarantor, being unable to return Stichus, would still be bound to pay the ten pieces. Since, I say, he reported this from Julian, he adds from Marcellus that the guarantee is null not only on that head, but also because the guarantor is bound to deliver a **different thing** <note>original: "rem diversam"</note>. Here you see that binding a guarantor to pay ten in place of Stichus is considered being bound for a different thing.

Ulpian adds: if the principal debtor is bound to pay ten, and the guarantor binds himself to pay "ten, or Stichus," the obligation is null; not because the guarantor's obligation is harsher—since it is lighter to be held to pay ten or Stichus at one's own choice than to be held to pay ten specifically—but because the guarantor is bound to a thing different from that which the principal debtor owes. Bartolus adds, along with the gloss on the law *If anyone for him* at the beginning, in the final words of that gloss, and with the gloss on the law *When a son of the family*, section 1, at the word *neither* <note>original: "neuter"</note> at the end of the Digest regarding verbal obligations: although if the debtor is bound to give a thing that is not money, and the guarantor is bound to give money, the guarantor is considered bound for a different thing (and thus the obligation is null, as stated); yet if the principal debtor is bound **to do** something, and the guarantor is bound to pay money equal to the estimated value of what the debtor ought to have done, or the **damages** <term>damages (interesse): the monetary value of a lost benefit or an unperformed act</term>, the obligation is valid, according to the law *it was stipulated* <note>original: "stipulatus est"</note> in the Digest regarding guarantees.

Paulus de Castro, Arias Pinellus in the commentary on the Code regarding the rescinding of a sale, part 1, chapter 3, number 19, and Lassarte in the cited chapter 8, rightly affirm—against the cited glosses, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors—that we should not depart from the doctrine clearly expressed in the law *If so* <note>original: "si ita"</note> in the Digest regarding guarantees. Namely, that when the principal debtor is bound to a thing that is not money, the guarantee for a certain amount of money is valid, provided the guarantor's obligation is not made "harsher" in some way than the principal debtor's. Indeed, no suitable reason can be given why, if the principal debtor is bound to an act, the guarantor’s obligation to a certain amount of money (the estimation or value of the interest in that act) is considered valid, yet it would not be valid if the debtor is bound to give a physical item that is not money, such as wheat, wine, a slave, or anything else. For money is no less the measure of the value of wine, oil, or any other non-monetary thing than it is the measure of an act. In fact, whenever someone is bound to give a specific individual thing, and another acts as guarantor that the principal debtor will fulfill this, he is understood to bind himself to the value or interest in that thing in the event that the principal debtor, through his own fault, cannot deliver it because he destroyed, consumed, or sold it, and cannot pay the damages.

<column-break/>

<margin>9</margin> While setting aside the opinion of Paulus de Castro, the opinion of Pinellus is certainly not to be despised, whatever Lassarte may say; although what Lassarte adds explains the matter further. For in the event discussed in the cited section *If anyone, Stichus*, and in the sense in which those words are used by Julian, Marcellus, and Ulpian, it cannot be denied (as Pinellus says) that it is a "different thing" for a guarantor to bind himself to "Stichus or ten," compared to the obligation to "Stichus" alone as the principal debtor had bound himself, even if the ten are to be delivered in place of Stichus. For the principal debtor had only bound himself to Stichus, a single item; and so, if the slave perished without his fault before the time of delivery, his obligation would expire, as those three jurists agree in that section. But the guarantor's obligation—as the words sound and as those three jurists understand them in that section—was such that even if Stichus perished before the time of delivery, the guarantor would be held to give either Stichus or ten, and thus fulfill one part of that **disjunction** (or "alternative," as the legal experts call it). Now, this second condition is "more" than the first; and it cannot be understood that something is "more" than another without it being understood as "different," especially if we speak of that increase regarding the valuation. And this is what Ulpian meant, following Marcellus, in that same section.

But if the guarantor's obligation had been made in this way: that in the event that at the time destined for delivery, the debtor (his obligation still persisting) did not deliver Stichus, the guarantor would be held to deliver the same Stichus, or ten in his place—surely this obligation would be far less than the debtor's, as is clearly evident from the sections *If anyone, Stichus* and *The same Julian*. Marcellus and Ulpian would never assert that this obligation is "different" from the debtor's obligation, because it is an obligation for money in place of Stichus without an increase—indeed, with a decrease in the obligation. And truly, in this sense, through **equity** <term>equity (epicheia): the interpretation of a law according to its spirit rather than its literal, harsh letter</term> based on the subject matter, those words should be understood, rather than the sense in which Julian, Marcellus, and Ulpian accept them. In the same way, they would be understood by judges today if they were found in any contract; for it is not to be believed that a guarantor intended to bind himself for more than the principal debtor.

However, when the principal debtor has bound himself for ten, and the guarantor for "ten or Stichus," Ulpian rightly says that although the guarantor's obligation is "less," it is nonetheless for a "different thing." This is because he substitutes Stichus in place of money if he so prefers, rather than money in place of Stichus. **Would that so many subtleties and trifles, invented by pagan men [the ancient Romans] and left to us, were rescinded from civil law! They are nothing but fuel for lawsuits, and they make the civil law obscure and exceedingly difficult to learn, to remember, and to reconcile.** It would be much better to provide this brief rule: that a guarantor cannot be bound for a greater value than the principal debt. If he were so bound, the guarantee should be null only regarding the excess. Nor do I see (as I should warn once regarding this whole dispute) by what just title a creditor could bind a guarantor for more...

<summary>Molina criticizes the rigid Roman law principle that a guarantee is void if it promises a "different thing" (like money instead of a slave) than the original debt. He argues that money is the natural measure of value for all things and suggests law should be simplified to focus on value rather than technical substitutions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Luis de Molina’s analysis of legal obligations, specifically focusing on the relationship between a guarantor and a principal debtor. The previous page explored how a guarantor cannot be bound for more than the debtor; here, Molina applies this to specific types of goods and moves into a new discussion on joint liability among multiple debtors.</meta>

...matter, or to receive more from him than the principal debt. For it should not be believed that more is promised or given by a donation than what is actually promised or given: such as **usury** <term>usury: the practice of charging excessive or illegal interest on a loan</term>, which, because it is given involuntarily or under mixed pressure, is granted and promised invalidly and received unjustly. Moreover, Law 7, Title 12, Part 5 <note>original: "l. 7. tit. 12. part. 5." — referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> seems to hand down this rule, and as I believe, for the purpose of rescinding all these vain and harmful elements of the common law. However, the Spanish doctors do not wish to understand it in this way, accumulating these other points from the common law. Nevertheless, Lassatte <note>Gabriel de Lasarte y Molina, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> rightly observes in chapter 8, number 12, that Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish laws updated in the 16th century</note> does not oppose the provisions of the common law regarding the annulment of a **guarantee** <term>guarantee (fideiussio): a legal promise to pay a debt if the original debtor fails</term> for more than, or for a different thing than, that to which the principal debtor was bound. For there, only the formal ceremony of a **stipulation** <term>stipulation: a formal Roman legal contract made by verbal question and answer</term> is excluded, and men are permitted to bind themselves by a simple bare agreement.

Lassatte also rightly observes in the cited chapter 8, starting at number 8: If the principal debtor owes a determined, specific thing <note>original: "rem determinatam in individuo"</note>, and if that thing perishes without his fault, he remains entirely freed from the debt; in this case, a guarantee is not valid if the guarantor binds himself to pay, for example, one hundred gold pieces (the estimated value of the item) in its place. This is because he is bound for "more," since the one hundred gold pieces (which are generic) do not "perish," whereas that specific determined thing can perish, and by its destruction, free the debtor from the obligation by which he was held. Since the guarantor is bound in that way for "more," he is not bound for the exact same thing, but for something different in value. This is because an obligation for one hundred gold pieces in general is worth more than an obligation for a specific determined item—for example, a slave named **Stichus** <term>Stichus: a common name used in Roman law examples for a specific slave or item</term>. Consequently, the hundred gold pieces are worth more as they fall under that obligation than Stichus is as he falls under the other. However, if the guarantor’s obligation for one hundred gold pieces was strictly limited to the duration that the principal debtor’s obligation for Stichus remained, then indeed one obligation would not be greater than the other, and the guarantee would be valid. Likewise, if the principal debtor is bound to something generic—that is, not a specific individual item, such as ten measures of wheat or a servant in general—and the guarantor is bound for one hundred gold pieces (the estimated value), then the guarantee is valid. This is because one is not bound for more than the other, and the guarantor is bound for money equivalent to the value of the thing. In this case, it is not considered a "different thing" from what the debtor owes, as held in the law *If so* in the Digest regarding guarantees <note>original: "l. si ita ff. de fideiuss."</note>. There, an example is used where the principal debt was an indeterminate thing, such as measures of wheat, rather than a specific individual thing like Stichus. A guarantee would also be valid if the debtor were bound for ten measures of wheat and the guarantor for the same, or for a certain amount of money by which they were valued; for the obligation would be lighter if the guarantor had the choice of either, rather than just the wheat, and because substituting money for wheat is permitted by the law.

# If many are bound together for something as principal debtors: when can they be sued individually for the whole, and when not?

## DISPUTATION 542.

->**SUMMARY**<-

1 *The ways in which a common obligation is said to be shared by many as an undivided whole.*
2 *Who are called "parties to a promise" and who are "parties to a credit."*
3 *When several debtors can be sued for the whole amount, and when for a portion. From number 10 to the end.*
4 *If several people are bound to a single indivisible thing, each of them is held for the whole amount.*
5 *Who are properly called "joint debtors." How they can be sued by the creditor (number 6). What the law of the "Authentics" says (number 7). And whether such a privilege and the law of the "Authentics" is observed in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal (numbers 8 and 9).*

---

Before we explain in the following disputation whether, if there are many guarantors for the same debt, each is held for the total or for a part, we must first explain this regarding debtors who are bound to something principally—that is, not as an accessory like a guarantor. For one of these is closely related to the other, and it will lead to a fuller knowledge of the matter; therefore, we have rightfully reserved for this place those things concerning the proposal.

1. An obligation can be common to many as an undivided whole, either on the part of those who are bound (because many are bound to one whole thing) or on the part of those to whom the obligation is made (because the obligation is made to many who acquire the right to it as an undivided whole). When the obligation is common to many as an undivided whole on the part of those to whom it is made—for example, if Peter promises one hundred to John and Francis—those to whom it is made (John and Francis) are called "joint creditors" <note>original: "plures rei stipulandi" — literally "several parties of the stipulation"</note> if they intend to make a stipulation. This is found in the Institutes *On two parties to an obligation* <note>original: "Inst. de duob. reis"</note>. This name is taken (as the gloss affirms) not from the word for "guilt" <note>original: "reatus"</note>, but from the word for "thing" <note>original: "res"</note>, as if they were holding someone bound to them for the same thing as an undivided whole. If that obligation is contracted by stipulation, or any other contract completed by consent, words, or the thing itself, they are called "parties to the credit" <note>original: "rei credendi"</note>, as if they were creditors holding someone bound to them for the same thing. Conversely, when the obligation is common to many as an undivided whole on the part of those who are bound—for example, if John and Francis promise one hundred to Peter—then those so bound are called "joint debtors" <note>original: "plures rei promittendi"</note> or "parties to the debt."

# Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...the last law of the Code under the same title; as if several were promising or owing the same thing **undivided** <term>undivided (pro indiviso): a joint obligation where the shares of each person are not yet separated or specified</term>. For there can result several "parties to a credit" or "parties to a debt," not only if the obligation is contracted by a **stipulation** <term>stipulation (stipulatio): a formal Roman legal contract made by a verbal question and answer</term>, but also if it is contracted by any other type of contract or in any other way. This is seen in the law "the same thing" in the Digest *On two parties to an obligation*, and is affirmed by Antonio Gómez <note>Antonio Gómez (1501–1572) was a highly influential Spanish jurist whose "Various Resolutions" became a standard legal reference</note> in volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 12, at the end of number 1, and the common opinion he reports. Furthermore, although the titles in the Institutes, Code, and Digest are inscribed "On two parties" <note>original: "duobus reis"</note>, there can nonetheless be three, four, or more parties, both on the side of the creditors and the debtors.

<margin>3</margin> See the law "out of two" in the Digest *On two parties to an obligation*, and the last paragraph of the Institutes under the same title. There is no disadvantage if there are two parties promising or owing, one of whom is obligated **purely** <term>purely: an unconditional obligation that is due immediately</term>, and the other under a condition or for a specific day. Neither the condition nor the date upon which one’s obligation depends prevents the debt from being demanded from the other when the time for payment arrives. Once the condition is fulfilled or the date arrives, both remain simply and equally obligated. If the condition fails, however, the one who was bound under it ceases to be obligated entirely, and only the other remains bound, as is well known.

When two or more are obligated to something undivided, such as to pay one hundred, unless it is formally or effectively expressed that each of them is held **for the whole** <term>for the whole (in solidum): a legal arrangement where each individual debtor is responsible for the entire debt, not just a portion</term>, each of them is held only for their own part, or **proportionally** <term>proportionally (pro virili): literally "by the man's portion," meaning divided equally among the number of people involved</term>. Thus, in the proposed example, if there are two parties who bound themselves, each is only held for fifty. This is found in the law *reos*, the paragraph beginning "with tables," in the Digest *On two parties*, and Law 2, Title 13, Book 5 of the *Siete Partidas* <note>The "Seven Parts," a 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note> (which is Law 1, Title 26, Book 5 of the *New Collection*), and many other laws cited by Antonio Gómez. He affirms this is the common opinion of the doctors, which he follows. In the same way, if one person is obligated to several creditors for something undivided, and does not formally or effectively express that he is bound to each of them for the whole, he is only bound to each for the proportional part that falls to him. This is found in the cited paragraph "with tables," and the common opinion of the doctors follows this. If the obligation is invalid for one party among the contractors in either case, only the remaining parts are owed. This is found in the law "if to me and Titius" in the Digest *On verbal obligations*.

<margin>4</margin> Observe, however, that if many bind themselves undivided to something that is **indivisible** <term>indivisible: a performance or object that cannot be split into parts without losing its essence, such as a legal right or a specific living animal</term>, such as a **servitude** <term>servitude: a legal right to use another's land for a specific purpose, like a right-of-way</term> (especially a real servitude), or the slave Stichus, or something similar that cannot be divided or paid in parts, then each is held to the creditor for the whole. Similarly, if such a thing is promised undivided to two people, it must be paid in full to each of them. In the first case, once payment is made by one of the debtors, the other is freed. But if the promise was invalid on the part of one of the creditors, the debtor is held to pay half the valuation. Similarly, in the second case, once payment is made to one of the creditors, nothing more is owed to the other. If the obligation was invalid regarding one creditor, the one to whom payment was made will be held to return half the valuation. This is found in law 2, paragraph "from...

<column-break/>

...these" and the law "stipulations are not divided" in the Digest *On verbal obligations*, and other laws cited above by Antonio Gómez.

<margin>5</margin> When some bind themselves undivided to something, and it was formally expressed that each is held for the whole, or effectively so because it was said "any one" or "each one" binds themselves to the whole, or something else was added from which this would be sufficiently understood, then most properly there are constituted several parties to a debt. These are the primary subject in the Institutes, Code, and the **Authentic** <term>Authentic (authentica): a summary or excerpt from Justinian's *Novels* (new laws) inserted into the Code by medieval jurists</term> regarding two parties; here, anyone is held for the whole and not for just a proportional part. In the same way, when someone binds himself to several people for something undivided, and to each of them for the whole, then there are most properly several parties to a credit. The debtor is held to each of them for the whole. This is expressly stated in the law *reos*, the paragraph "with tables" at the end, and other laws agree. About such parties, the Institutes say that each of the debtors owes the whole, and the whole is owed to each of the creditors, and in such obligations a single thing is involved. When one debtor pays or obtains a release, the other co-debtors are freed; and when payment is made to one co-creditor, the others are considered satisfied.

<margin>6</margin> When there are many debtors in this most proper sense, according to the **ancient law** of the Digest and Code, they could be sued by the creditor and compelled to pay either by demanding from each their proportional part, or from one whom the creditor preferred, demanding the whole debt. Antonio Gómez adds: or by demanding from all for the whole, protesting that he will be satisfied with one single complete payment. Although this is consistent with their obligation, the laws Gómez cites do not prove any such thing. From the fact that a creditor chose one to sue, if he has not yet obtained the debt from him (either because he was insolvent or for any other reason), he can sue another or the rest.

<margin>7</margin> Today, however, according to the law of the **Authentics** <note>Specifically referring to Justinian’s *Novels* 99, which changed the Roman rules on joint liability</note>, if all are solvent and none are absent, they cannot be sued for the whole, but only for their proportional parts. But if someone is absent outside the territory of the place so that they cannot be summoned (as the **gloss** <term>gloss: a marginal or interlinear note in a medieval legal text explaining a term or concept</term> on the Authentic *On guarantors* explains, and the Doctors commonly follow), the others are also held for that person’s part. If indeed someone is poor, then the others are compelled to pay what that person cannot. This is found in the Authentic "this way" in the Code *On two parties*, and in Law 10, Title 12, Part 5. Debtors can, however, renounce this benefit so that they can be sued for the whole even when the others are solvent and present: because...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal distinctions between joint obligations (pro indiviso) and solidary obligations (in solidum), explaining when multiple debtors are responsible for the whole debt versus just their individual share. He notes the historical shift from ancient Roman law, which allowed creditors to sue any single debtor for the full amount, to the "modern" Justinian law which favors proportional liability unless otherwise specified.</summary>

...that it was granted in their favor, as gathered from the law *if anyone in writing* <note>original: "l. si quis in cōscribendo"</note>, Code, *on pacts*, and from the law *what by favor* <note>original: "l. quod fauore"</note>, Code, *on laws*. Regarding the matter at hand, this is affirmed by the gloss on the **Authentic** <term>Authentic (Authenticum): a collection of New Constitutions (Novellae) by Emperor Justinian that updated the Roman Code</term> concerning *two parties to an obligation* <note>original: "de duobus reis"</note> at the words "to yield," the final gloss on the same title in the Code, and the final gloss on the final paragraph of the Institutes under the same title. This is also the opinion of Bartolus and the common view of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez reports and follows (cited above, number 2), as does Gutiérrez (on confirmed rights, part 1, chapter 23, at the end, number 9) and Gregorio López (on the cited law 10, penultimate gloss). Hence, if they **renounce** <term>renunciation: a formal statement in a contract where a party gives up a specific legal protection or right</term> that privilege, as is commonly done, they can be sued **for the total amount** <term>for the total amount (in solidum): a legal status where a single debtor can be held responsible for the entire debt of a group</term>, even if the other joint debtors are present and able to pay. Angelus, whom Gregorio López cites in the penultimate gloss, says that if the joint debtors are bound by a **guaranty deed** <term>guaranty deed (instrumentum guarentigium): a notarized document that allows for the immediate enforcement/execution of a debt without a lengthy trial</term>, they do not enjoy that privilege in a place where execution of such a deed occurs with all exceptions set aside. Rightly also, Gregorio López and others affirm that a guaranty deed does not block a legal defense <note>original: "exceptionem"</note> that arises from the very arrangement of the action being granted—such as the one we are discussing—which, according to Bartolus, includes the defense that the money was never actually paid. Furthermore, in the Kingdom of Castile, it is not entirely forbidden to raise a defense when proceeding to execution based on a guaranty deed; however, the defenses must be proven within ten days from the moment they are raised, otherwise they do not hinder the execution, as held in Law 1 and following, especially Law 19, title 21, book 4 of the *New Collection*, as was said in Disputation 538.

8 In another chapter, in the Kingdom of Castile, debtors who are bound **for the total amount**, whether by a guaranty deed or any other means, do not today enjoy that privilege granted to joint debtors by the law of the **Authentics** and Law 10 of the *Partidas*. This is because later, in Law 2, title 13, book 5 of the *Ordenamiento*, which is today Law 1, title 16, book 5 of the *New Collection*, that privilege was removed, and the matter was returned to the terms of the common law of the Digests and the Code. For that law states:

> We establish that if two persons bind themselves simply by contract, or in any other manner, to do or fulfill something, by that very fact they are understood to be bound each for one half, unless it is stated in the contract that each is bound **for the total amount** <note>original: "insolidū"</note>, or if it was otherwise agreed and settled between them. And this shall hold notwithstanding any laws of common law that speak against this <note>he says this because of the laws of the Authentics</note>, and this shall be observed both in past contracts and those to come.

Therefore, today in this Kingdom of Castile, such debtors do not enjoy that privilege, even if they do not renounce the law of the Authentics. Rightly, then, Gutiérrez (part 1, chapter 23, number 10) rejects the distorted interpretations of this very clear law, and especially the interpretation of Gregorio López (book 8, title 12, part 5, on the words "each of them"), who claims it should be understood only when they are bound as principals. Gregorio López is led to this because this law derogates <note>derogates: partially repeals or overrides a previous law</note> from the common law; he argues that if the law were speaking of principal debtors, there would be no need to derogate from common law, since it would already agree with it. Truly, this law most clearly speaks of principal debtors; and as has been said, it derogates from the common law of the Authentics (which would otherwise stand), but not from the law of the Digests

<column-break/>

and the Code. Similarly, the same Gutiérrez rightly says that although notaries in this Kingdom of Castile are accustomed to include a renunciation of the law of the Authentics in instruments where many are bound for the total amount, this is not necessary, and it has been so judged at times. However, Monterroso, in his *Practice* (treatise 7, folio 147, title *on exchange obligations*, paragraph *and if the obligations*), whom Gutiérrez criticizes as if he had forgotten the cited Law 1, asserts the renunciation of the **Authentic regarding two debtors** to be so necessary that without it they could not be sued for the total amount. Perhaps Monterroso, in the place cited, is merely prescribing the form that notaries commonly follow for "greater firmness," rather than asserting that if the renunciation is omitted, one cannot be sued for the total amount.

<margin>Portuguese Law</margin> 9 Regarding **Portuguese law**, I believe the same must be concluded. Namely, that every one of these debtors bound for the total amount can be sued for the entire debt, even if they have not renounced the law of the Authentics. For in Book 4 of the *Ordinances*, title 46, in the final paragraph, although the discussion in that title is about guarantors, it states:

> *And when one binds themselves as a guarantor and principal payer, or as a principal payer only* (note these immediately preceding words, which speak only of one bound as a principal, whom he regards as a guarantor, according to what we add at the end of this disputation), *even if they did not renounce this law or any other, they can always be sued first, before the principal debtor, even if the latter is present and has the means to pay.*

10 Several things should be observed regarding what has been said in this whole disputation. First, it is established from Law 10, title 12, part 5, and from Law 1 cited above, that when several are bound as principals to a certain "fact" <note>fact: a specific act or performance rather than just a payment of money</note>, they are bound for their share, and execution is made for the share of the thing in dispute. Gregorio López on the cited Law 10 at the words "or to do," agrees with the laws cited in the gloss on the law *reos* <note>original: "teos" [likely OCR error for reos]</note>, paragraph *with tablets*, at the words "they seemed," in the Digest *on two parties to an obligation*. But if the act is **indivisible**, execution against one of the debtors will be made for the total valuation, according to what Ulpian reports from Celsus and Tubero in the law *stipulations are not divided*, at the beginning, in the Digest *on verbal obligations*.

Second, that which was decreed regarding multiple debtors under the law of the Authentics—namely, that one cannot be sued for the whole if the others are present and solvent—does not apply to **multiple creditors**. That is, one creditor cannot sue the debtor for the whole amount without the others. This is affirmed by the gloss on the word "to believe" at the end of the Authentic *on two parties to an obligation*. This is because neither the heading of that title includes "creditors," nor is there any mention of them in the whole Authentic, but only of "debtors."

Third, Antonio Gómez (volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 12, at the end of number 3), along with Bartolus and the common opinion he reports, asserts that when there are two debtors and only one received the full benefit while the other received nothing—even if they renounced the benefit of the Authentics or are in the Kingdom of Castile where renunciation is unnecessary—if the one who received no benefit is sued, he can raise a defense so that he is sued...

<summary>Molina explains that in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal, joint debtors can be sued for the full amount of a debt (in solidum) even without a formal renunciation of Roman legal protections, as local laws have overridden the older "Authentic" privileges. He also distinguishes between the liability for divisible actions versus indivisible "facts" and the rights of multiple creditors versus multiple debtors.</summary>
