# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

...the other party may be sued, though at his own risk and expense, and he shall be heard. Indeed, he proves this by the argument of the law *Whence it is sought* <note>original: "l. vnde quæritur"</note>, Digest, *on loans* <note>original: "ff. commod."</note>, and the law *When among many*, the paragraph *garments* <note>original: "l. cum in plures. §. vestimēta"</note>, Digest, *on hiring* <note>original: "ff. locat."</note>. To me, however, this opinion is highly doubtful. For the obligation of **two joint debtors for the whole** <term>two joint debtors for the whole (duorum reorum in solidum): a legal arrangement where two or more people are each individually responsible for the entire debt, not just a portion of it</term> was invented precisely so that the whole amount could be demanded from each of them—whether that person received the whole, a part, or none of the benefit—and they would be bound to pay the whole without any exception. Furthermore, if we granted the opinion of Antonio Gómez, it would follow that when individuals had each received half of the benefit, any one of them sued for the whole debt could object, demanding that the other half be sought from the other party at his own risk and expense. This agrees neither with common practice nor with the established doctrine regarding joint debtors for the whole. For the same reasoning that applies to the whole benefit applies to a part; and in the laws he cites, the same logic will hold for a part as for the whole. As in the cited paragraph *garments*, if someone had handed over many clothes to a clothes-cleaner to be washed, and part of them were stolen such that the cleaner was held liable to the owner who delivered them, and it was known who had them in their possession and recovery was easy, the cleaner would be granted an objection so that the clothes might first be recovered from the thief or possessor at the cleaner's risk and expense, in order to return the specific items to the owner, no less than if all the clothes delivered for cleaning had been snatched from his power by theft.

Fourthly, a co-debtor who has paid something in place of the others is granted an action against his fellow debtors so that they may repay him, according to the law *The creditor*, Code, *on two joint debtors* <note>original: "l. creditor C. de duob. reis."</note>. However, regarding which specific action should be used to seek this, the doctors and the final gloss on that law dispute the matter at length. Those who believe that joint debtors for the whole are mutual **sureties** <term>surety (fideiussor): a person who takes responsibility for another's debt or performance</term> for one another in relation to the creditor—as seems to be clearly hinted at in the **Authentic** <term>Authentic: a decree updating Roman law</term> concerning *two joint debtors*, in the beginning—argue this because the Emperor there says he is providing an explanation and expansion of the decree on sureties, and also because he calls co-debtors "bound by mutual suretyship." Those who hold this view (among whom was Martinus, as the gloss and other cited sources report, and Bartolus, whom Aluarus Valascus follows in his 36th legal opinion, starting at number 3) consequently judge that the money should be sought through an **action of mandate** <term>action of mandate (actio mandati): a lawsuit used when one person performs a service for another based on an agreement or instruction</term>, following what was said in the cited Disputation 339. However, those who deny they are sureties (including Joannes, as both cited glosses report) judge that it should be sought through an **action for business managed** <term>action for business managed (actio negotiorum gestorum): a claim for reimbursement when someone looks after another's affairs without a formal contract</term>. I judge it cannot be denied that, at least in relation to the creditor, they stand toward one another like sureties; a mandate should be considered to have occurred, at least a tacit and implied one, and therefore it can be sought by either action. But if there were three co-debtors and, standing on common law, they **renounced** <term>renunciation: formally giving up a legal right</term> the decrees on joint debtors, the gloss on the law *The creditor* says at the end: if one paid thirty on behalf of all, and each was supposed to contribute ten, then he who paid can sue each of the other two for the full twenty that he paid for their share of the debt. This same rule will apply in this **Kingdom of Castile**, even if the renunciation of those decrees was not formally made.

### If there are many Sureties for the same debtor, when can individuals be sued for the whole, and when not.

### DISPUTATION DXLIII.
### SUMMARY.

1 When multiple sureties of one debtor can be sued for the whole, and when for a part; and the following number.
2 The **privilege of division** of action, and the exception or benefit of the **Epistle of the Divine Hadrian** <term>Epistle of Hadrian: a Roman legal rule allowing a guarantor to demand that a debt be split among all solvent guarantors</term> among multiple debtors and sureties; when it applies, even against the public treasury.
3 The objection based on the Epistle of the Divine Hadrian is considered an "anomalous" defense among temporary and permanent legal objections.
4 And when it may be raised.
5 It is not available to a surety after he has already paid (number 8).
6 Indeed, in this it differs from the **Velleian benefit** <term>Velleian benefit (Senatus Consultum Velleianum): a Roman law that prohibited women from standing as sureties for others</term>, under which a woman can reclaim what she paid.
7 A surety who raises the objection of the Epistle of Hadrian while another surety is solvent is freed, even if that other surety later becomes insolvent.
8 Indeed, it is even sufficient to raise the objection at the time of payment, provided that at that time the other surety is solvent.
However, it fails—meaning such an objection cannot be raised—in certain events, as in number 7.
And regarding the law of Castile and Portugal (number 8).

If many are simultaneously sureties for the same debtor, and it was agreed by them that they would be sureties for proportional shares of the debt, or if each of them guaranteed a specific determined amount or quota of the debt, then each can be sued only for that portion, and not for the whole. In that case, the privilege or objection does not apply to one who bound himself for a larger share, as if the others were forced to pay more in the debtor's place than that to which each bound himself. These things are well known in themselves, since no one can be forced to pay more in a debtor's place than the amount for which he bound himself for him. This is expressly established in the law *Among them*, at the beginning, Digest, *on sureties* <note>original: "l. inter eos in prin. ff. de fideiuss."</note>, where it is held that if many promised for the same debt under a distinction—that each would pay the whole debt or a proportional part—each is only held to the proportional part, even if the others are not solvent. The reason given is that they promised under that alternative; and because to fulfill an alternative it is enough to fulfill one part, those individuals are only considered bound to proportional parts, and then the privilege from the Epistle of the Divine Hadrian (which will be discussed shortly) has no place. This is held entirely and expressly in the 4th book of the **Revised Ordinances** <note>original: "Recop. ord."</note>, title 46, at the beginning. Likewise, when different sureties are given separately for different debts of the same debtor, then each is held only for the total to which he bound himself, and no division of the debt is made between them to pay it equally according to the Epistle of the Divine Hadrian, as is clear enough in itself; just as the creditor cannot be forced to divide the debt among the sureties...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s analysis of liability, transitioning from the obligations of joint debtors to those of co-sureties (guarantors). He explores whether multiple people who guarantee the same debt can be forced to pay the whole amount individually or if they have the right to split the debt.</meta>

...guarantors, who are given separately for distinct debts by distinct debtors, as is held in that Law *Titus*, and the Law *Between them*, the paragraph *Two things*, Digest, *on suretyship* <note>original: "ff. de fideiuſſ."</note>.

The proposed question, therefore, only contains difficulty and has a place where many sureties are given for the same debt for an undivided portion of the entire debt <term>undivided portion (pro indiviso): a shared responsibility that has not been legally split into specific parts</term>, without expressing that each is held **for the whole amount** <term>for the whole amount (in solidum): a legal term meaning an individual is responsible for the entire debt, not just their share</term>, or without adding anything from which it might be understood that each is not bound for the whole, but only for a proportional share, or some other certain and determined part. And indeed, in either event, standing in common law, each is considered bound for the whole, so that it is in the power of the creditor either to sue each for their proportional share, or one of them for the whole amount—whichever the creditor prefers—or all of them for the whole amount, while protesting that he will be satisfied with a single payment. This follows the way it was stated in the previous dispute, standing in the law of the Digests and the Code, that two joint debtors of a debt could be similarly sued, each being bound for the whole. However, although individual sureties of this kind are considered bound for the whole and can be sued for the whole, nevertheless, by the **Letter of the Divine Hadrian** (which is nowhere found written today, but mention of it is made only by citing legal authorities), a surety sued by a creditor for the whole amount can compel the creditor—if the other sureties are solvent—to seek their proportional shares from them. He does this by using against the creditor the defense from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian. This is expressly held in the Institutes, *on suretyship*, the paragraph *If many* <note>original: "iſt: de fideiuſſ. §. ſi plures"</note>, where there is a discussion about sureties for an undivided debt, without expressing whether each is bound for the whole or not. It is also held in Law 4 at the beginning, joined with the following paragraphs of the Digest, in the same title, where it is held that even if each is bound cumulatively for a part and for the whole debt, the defense from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian has a place. All these things are held more clearly than elsewhere in the Law *Not rightly*, in the Code, *on suretyship* <note>original: "l. non rectè. C. de fideiuſſ."</note>, where it is held that if many sureties are bound for an undivided debt, whether it was added that each is bound for the whole or not, each is held for the whole, yet enjoys the **benefit of division** of action from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian. This means each is sued for a proportional share, provided they are solvent, and this can be raised as a defense by the one who is sued for the whole amount. The same is held in the Law *Surety*, in the Code, in the same title, and in the last law of the Code, *on promised money*. And, after the pattern of the Letter of the Divine Hadrian, the provision of the *Authentica* regarding two debtors was established, about which a discussion was held in the preceding dispute.

<margin>2</margin> Truly, this privilege of the division of action, or the defense from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian, also applies even if one of the sureties was appointed unconditionally <note>Latin: "purè"</note>, and another under a condition, or for a future date. For he who was appointed unconditionally can object so that he is compelled to pay only his own part, and the other part later when the condition has been met—or if the condition is not later met, or if that surety is found to be insolvent after the condition is met, then he who was appointed unconditionally is compelled to pay the increase of the debt. Thus it is held in the Law *If many* at the beginning, in the Digest, *on suretyship*. The same benefit belongs to the heirs and successors of sureties, even against the heirs or successors of co-sureties. Thus it is held in the cited Law *If many*, paragraph 1 and following.

<column-break/>

This benefit also belongs to the surety and his heirs even against the treasury <note>original: "fiſcum"</note>, if the treasury stands as the successor to a co-surety whose goods have been confiscated. In the same way, the same benefit belongs to the treasury against the co-surety of the person whom the treasury succeeded, and against the heirs of such a co-surety. Thus it is held in the Law *Between them*, final paragraph, Digest, *on suretyship*, and the Law *Not rightly*, Code, in the same title. However, many heirs of a single surety are considered as one person with the deceased whom they represent in this matter. But if a surety is given to one of the sureties <note>A "back-up" guarantor</note>, he is also considered as one with that person in this matter; indeed, his goods, along with the goods of the first surety, are to be calculated together to understand whether that surety is insolvent, so that others must pay his portion. Thus it is held in the Law *If many*, the paragraph *Moreover*, and the final paragraph, Digest, *on suretyship*.

<margin>3</margin> This benefit, and the defense from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian, is considered anomalous among **dilatory** <term>dilatory: a legal defense intended to delay the proceedings rather than end the case</term> and **peremptory** <term>peremptory: a legal defense that completely destroys the plaintiff's claim</term> defenses, by the Gloss on the paragraph *If many* at the word *parts*, in the Institutes, *on suretyship*, and by the final Gloss on the Law *Surety*, Code, in the same title; although it is much more peremptory regarding that for which it is given. Truly, that former Gloss says it can only be opposed before the "contest of the lawsuit" <note>original: "litem conteſtatam", the formal start of a trial</note>; yet the later Gloss says better, according to the text there and the common opinion—which Antonio Gómez relates and follows in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 15—asserting that it can be opposed before the final definitive sentence. Hence, if an appeal has been made from a sentence, it can be opposed at the stage of appeal; because an appeal extinguishes the judgment and restores the matter to the state in which it was before the sentence, as Antonio Gómez affirms in the same place with Bartolus and the common opinion, according to various laws which he cites. I, however, would understand that it can be opposed before the final definitive sentence has been mandated for complete execution—that is, before full payment is made—as if, in the meantime, while the surety who is sued for the whole amount has not paid in full, he can oppose it. For in law, after such a surety has paid, since he could have chosen not to pay by using the benefit of the Letter of the Divine Hadrian, they seem to deny him that benefit, establishing that he who paid when he was not bound to pay has himself to blame. The Law *If sureties*, the paragraph *The same responds*, in the Digest, *on suretyship*, concurs. Angelus, related there by Antonio Gómez, used to assert that if sureties were bound in a **guaranteed instrument** <term>guaranteed instrument (guarentigium): a notarized document that allows for immediate debt collection without a full trial</term>, they would not enjoy this benefit and defense, because it is assumed that once the guaranteed instrument has been executed, they are considered condemned by a judgment. Deservedly, however, Antonio Gómez refutes this in the same place, because that is not a true and proper definitive sentence; only when such a sentence is given does negligence intervene, and the surety is considered to have tacitly renounced the defense. And we said something similar following Gregorio López against the same Angelus in the preceding dispute. Add that, as we were just saying, that defense is available until the execution of the sentence is complete, and much more so is it available until the execution of a guaranteed instrument is entirely complete; but it is otherwise after that execution has been entirely completed, even if a formal definitive sentence has not intervened.

<margin>4</margin> This defense † does not belong to a surety after he has paid, whereas the **Velleian defense** <note>The *Senatus Consultum Velleianum* was a Roman law protecting women from being held liable for the debts of others</note> belongs to a woman even after she has paid, as...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether a surety (guarantor) can be forced to pay a whole debt or if they can demand the debt be split among all co-sureties. It moves from general Roman civil law to the specific statutes of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

### Discussion 540
As was said, the gloss on the Law *Fideiussor*, Code, *on suretyship* <note>original: "C. de fideiuss."</note> leans toward this view, and the gloss on the paragraph *Among many* <note>original: "§. in plures"</note> at the word *parts* at the end of the Institutes, *on suretyship*, rightly affirms it. This is also the opinion of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists</note> and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> mentions and follows in the cited number 15. Antonio Gomez, along with Bartolus, gives this reason: although that defense is favorable (just like the **Velleianum defense** <term>Velleianum defense (Velleiani exceptio): a Roman law protection that prevented women from being held liable for the debts of others</term>), it is nonetheless not perpetual. This is because it does not apply if the other surety is not solvent. 

However, this reason is perhaps not solid, because the Velleianum defense also does not apply if a woman stands as a surety for someone’s freedom, or for a dowry, and in other cases reported in discussion 540. Unless you argue that in cases where a woman enjoys that defense, she enjoys it independently of anyone else, and thus perpetually; whereas in the matter proposed, a surety never enjoys that defense except depending on whether the other surety is solvent, and thus it is not perpetual. 

I would say that since this kind of defense is irregular or anomalous, and the laws express that it can be raised right up until a judgment is fully ordered for execution (as has been said), they even add that if one surety pays the whole debt—whether a judgment has been delivered or not—then the entire loss belongs to the one who paid. This is because he could have raised the defense before payment but failed to do so. It does not concern the other co-sureties, as held in the Institutes, *on suretyship*, paragraph *if many*, at the end, and the Law *as a surety*, Digest, *same title*. Certainly, by the very disposition of the law, it has no place after payment as a recovery; and therefore, a defense is granted to a surety against a creditor, or that action is available to him against a co-surety, only if the creditor assigns the action to him either at the time of payment or immediately afterward, and not after an interval of time. This is held in the cited Law *as a surety*, and the Law *with him*, and the Law *if sureties*, in the paragraph *the same must be answered*, Digest, *on suretyship*. From what has been said, it is clear that by the very fact that one of the sureties pays the whole debt to the creditor, the remaining co-sureties remain released from their obligation to the creditor; this is held in **Law 8, Title 12, Part 5** <note>This refers to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish law code</note>.

5 † Observe this: if a surety who is sued **for the whole amount** by a creditor raises the defense at the appropriate time when the other surety is solvent, even if that co-surety later becomes insolvent, the loss belongs to the creditor and not to the surety who raised the defense at the proper time. This is because the creditor was not deceived by him. So it is held in the Law *between them*, paragraph *when between*, Digest, *on suretyship*. 
6 Furthermore, if the time for payment arrives and one of the sureties is solvent then but is drifting toward poverty, the other can require the creditor to demand payment and divide the action between himself and that other surety. If the creditor does not do this and the other becomes insolvent, the one who raised the defense conveniently at that time will enjoy it, so that he is not forced to pay more than **his proportional share** <term>proportional share (virilem portionem): literally "a man's portion," meaning an equal split among the group</term>. This is how I understand the Law *if they contend*, joined with the gloss and summary there, Digest, *on suretyship*. Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century commentator on the *Siete Partidas*</note> agrees on Law 8, Title 12, Part 5, at the words *that the debt is demanded*. 

However, when a surety raises the defense at the appropriate time and the creditor doubts whether the other surety or sureties are solvent, if the surety being sued for the whole amount provides security (a guarantee) that he will pay the expenses and the action is attempted against the others at his own risk, he must be heard—provided that the others who are solvent 

<column-break/>

are available or present. See the Law *if it is doubted*, in the beginning, Digest, *on suretyship*.

7 † In the following cases, however, which the gloss records at the word *parts*, paragraph *if many*, Institutes, *on suretyship*, the defense is not available to the surety: 
**First**, if, for example, two guardians are given to a minor, and they provide two sureties for an undivided amount to ensure the minor’s property is safe. In that case, if one of the guardians is sued for the whole amount, he is entitled to the defense against the minor so that the actions are divided between him and his co-guardian (if both are solvent), as held in Law 1, paragraph *now let us discuss*, Digest, *on guardianship*. But if one of the sureties is sued for the whole amount, he does not enjoy the benefit and defense of the **Letter of the Divine Hadrian** <note>A Roman decree that allowed co-sureties to split a debt</note> to divide the action between himself and the co-surety, even if the co-surety is solvent; rather, he can be sued for the whole amount. The minor, however, is bound to assign the action to him so that he can sue his co-surety to pay him the proportional part that the co-surety was supposed to pay. I believe the same applies when there is one guardian who has provided two sureties for himself. So it is held in the last law, Digest, *that the minor's property shall be safe*.

**Second**, when a surety who is sued for the whole amount denies that he is a surety; then, because of his lie, he is punished by not enjoying that benefit, but can be forced to pay the entire debt. So it is held in the Law *if it is doubted*, paragraph *only then*, Digest, *on suretyship*. The remaining cases which the gloss lists there have already been explained by us.

**Third**, we can add: when the sureties have renounced that benefit and privilege. Since it was introduced only for their favor, if they renounce it, they do not enjoy it, based on the argument of the Law *if anyone in writing*, Code, *on pacts*, and the Law *because favor*, Code, *on laws*. Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors affirm this, which Antonio Gomez mentions and follows in the cited number 15.

Regarding the law of **this Kingdom of Castile**, however, this matter was decreed differently 
8 in **Law 8, Title 12, Part 5**. Namely, when † many sureties are given for an undivided portion of the same debt, and it was not expressed that each should be held for the whole, they are only liable and can only be sued for their **proportional shares**, and not for the whole. This is provided, however, that if any of them is not solvent, the others are bound to pay—again, according to their proportional shares—even that which this person could not pay. 

Therefore, Gregorio Lopez rightly says there, at the words *each one of them*, following Bartolus, that because of the danger that one of them might be found unable to pay his full proportional share, the advice is that the creditor should seek his entire debt against each and against all, by the contribution of all, protesting that he will be satisfied with a single full payment. 

However, when it was explicitly stated that each should be held **for the whole amount**, then the creditor can seek the entire debt from each one, or from several, or from all, as he prefers, provided the protest is made that if he seeks it for the whole from many, he will be satisfied with a single payment. Hence, as Gregorio Lopez well notes there, the benefit and defense of the **Letter of the Divine Hadrian** has no place in this Kingdom, and therefore there is no need to renounce it. This is because, to avoid those ambiguities...

Gregorius Lopez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> teaches, specifically in the first of those points cited from Law 8, that the common law is not corrected. However, I do approve of what he adds at number 18: namely, that Law 1, title 16, book 5 of the *New Collection* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación* (1567), a major compilation of Spanish law</note> should be understood to apply both to those obligated as principals and those obligated as accessories. Therefore, today in this Kingdom of Castile, if any sureties are obligated for a debt and it is not explicitly stated that each is obligated for the whole <term>for the whole (in solidum): a legal term meaning each person is responsible for the entire amount of the debt, not just a portion</term>, it must be judged that each is obligated only for their proportional shares. Consequently, each can only be sued for their own proportional share, even if the others are insolvent. In this regard, that first law corrects Law 8 of the cited *Partidas* <note>The *Siete Partidas*, the foundational medieval law code of Castile</note>. However, when it was sufficiently expressed that each surety was obligated for the whole, that first law agrees with the reports from the cited Law 8 of the *Partidas*.

In Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, the benefit and defense arising from the Letter of the Divine Hadrian <note>A Roman legal rule allowing a surety to demand that the debt be split among all solvent co-sureties</note> does not have a place, nor is there a need to renounce it. Instead, whenever multiple sureties are given for an undivided debt, whether it is expressed that each is held for the whole or not, all are held for the whole. The entire debt can be demanded from each individual or from everyone, as the creditor prefers. It is also commanded that notaries <note>original: "tabelliones"</note> should not include renunciations in the legal instruments made regarding this matter, because they are not necessary for each person to be held for the whole without defense. This is held in book 4 of the *Ordinances*, title 46, at the beginning.

<column-break/>

**10. How a surety must prove he made payment to the creditor in order to act against co-sureties based on assigned rights.**

**W**hen one of the sureties for the whole of a debt pays the entire amount, a distinction must be made. For he either pays it in the name of the debtor, or in his own name as a surety obligated to that debt; or he pays it absolutely, without expressing whether he pays it in the name of the debtor or in his own name as a surety.

<margin>1</margin> In the first case—namely, when he pays in the name of the debtor, taking his place and fulfilling the debtor's obligation and not his own obligation as a surety—the entire debt and every obligation regarding the creditor is extinguished by that very act, both for the principal debtor and for his sureties. This is no different than if the principal debtor had paid the debt himself. Consequently, no room remains for the creditor to assign to such a surety the legal rights <note>original: "actiones"</note> he had against the co-sureties and against the debtor. Therefore, he cannot act against the co-sureties to make them contribute and pay him what they were held to pay the creditor along with him in place of the debtor. Nor, on that basis, can he recover from the principal debtor by having the creditor assign rights against him, since he paid in the name and place of the debtor. Instead, he can only seek recovery from him through a claim of mandate <term>mandate (mandatum): a contract where one person performs a service for another at their request</term> or management of affairs <term>management of affairs (negotiorum gestorum): a legal claim where someone manages another's business or pays their debt without an express contract, but for their benefit</term>, to the extent that he usefully managed the debtor's business in that regard and was presumed to have a mandate to pay, especially since he stood as a surety from the beginning by the debtor's mandate. These points are held in Law 1, title 12, part 5; they are affirmed by the final gloss on the Law *Papinianus* <note>original: "l. Papinian."</note> in the Digest, *on mandate*, and Azo in his *Summa* on the Code, *on suretyship*, and the doctors generally.

<margin>2</margin> In the second case, however—when one of the sureties for the whole pays the entire debt to the creditor in his own name—that is, as a surety of the principal debtor fulfilling his own suretyship obligation, as usually happens—one cannot act against co-sureties to make them contribute and pay what they were held to pay the creditor in place of the debtor unless the creditor first assigns the rights to him that were available against them. This is established in the Law *As a surety* <note>original: "l. ut fideiussor."</note> in the Digest and the Law *With the other* <note>original: "l. cum alter."</note> in the Code under the same title. However, if the creditor does assign the rights to him against both the co-sureties and the principal debtor (which the Spaniards call "granting a letter of reimbursement" <term>letter of reimbursement (carta de lasto): a formal document where a creditor transfers his rights to a surety who has paid the debt</term>), as he is required to do (even if the creditor is unwilling, as held in Law *With the other* in the Code), provided the surety requests it, he can be compelled by the office of the judge to assign them. This is what Gregorius Lopez says on Law 1, title 1, chapter 12, part 5. For the surety could even withhold the payment if the creditor refuses to assign the rights, or recover it as "not owed" if the creditor refuses to assign the rights after payment is made, as the final gloss on the Law *When he* <note>original: "l. cum is"</note> in the Digest says. If, I say, the creditor assigns those rights to such a surety as he is required to do, then that surety can act indiscriminately against either the co-sureties or the principal debtor...

# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...sureties, so that they may contribute and pay their respective portions to him <note>original: "fideiuſſores, ut contribuant, & ſoluant ſibi portiones ſuas"</note>, according to the law on sureties <note>original: "l. fideiuſſoribus... de fideiuſ."</note> and Law 11, Title 12 of the 5th *Partida*. Furthermore, he can demand from the principal debtor that he pay the remaining part that pertains to the surety himself, as cited in Law 11. Alternatively, he can sue the principal debtor to pay the whole amount that he, as the surety, paid, as stated in the cited Law *Cum is* and Law *Cum alter* in the Code on sureties. 

<margin>2</margin> Indeed, he will be able to compel the creditor not only to transfer (cede) all personal actions <term>personal actions: legal rights to sue a specific person for a debt</term> that were available against the debtor and the other sureties, but also all "real" actions <term>real actions: legal rights over physical property, such as the right to seize a house or land used as collateral</term> involving pledges or mortgages, if any were held regarding that same debt. This applies as long as those same properties were not already pledged to the same creditor for some other debt that had not yet been paid. 

However, if the creditor, through his own fault, cannot transfer these rights to the surety—or to another person who is bound as an accessory to the debt (such as someone who authorized a loan to the debtor)—specifically because the creditor sued the principal debtor and lost, then the accessory debtor can block the creditor. He can do this by using a legal exception <note>A "defense" in a lawsuit</note> stating that the creditor cannot transfer the rights, or by citing the "matter already judged" <term>res iudicata: a principle that a matter already decided by a court cannot be relitigated</term> if the creditor already sued the principal debtor and failed. This is affirmed by Gregorius Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> in Law 11. 

In this section, observe that a surety who is forced to pay a debt is not limited to the rights the creditor transfers to him. Even if no rights are transferred, he can still sue the principal debtor using an "action of mandate" <term>action of mandate (actio mandati): a lawsuit based on the fact that the surety acted on the debtor's request or authority</term>. This allows him to recover what he paid on the debtor's behalf and to be compensated for any damages he suffered because the debtor did not pay on time. The surety, after all, stepped forward at the debtor's request, and therefore the debtor is bound by the rules of mandate to cover all these costs.

<margin>3</margin> There are several points to observe regarding this. First: when a surety explicitly pays in his own name to fulfill his obligation as a guarantor, he can ask for the transfer of the creditor’s rights against the other co-sureties and the debtor. He can do this not only if he agreed to it before or at the time of payment, or immediately after, but even after a significant interval of time <note>original: "ex interuallo, quocunq; tpe"</note>, even if nothing was specified in the initial agreement. 

The reasoning is that because he pays in his own name based on an accessory obligation—such as a guarantee or a request to lend money to another—the payment is viewed as having a "tacit agreement" that the rights should be transferred to him. Therefore, he can demand that transfer at any time. This follows the final gloss on Law *Papinianus* and Law *Si quid poſſeſſor* in the Digest.

<column-break/>

This is also clearly gathered from Law 11, Title 12 of the 5th *Partida* if you compare the beginning and the end of that law. Gregorius Lopez affirms this, following the jurist Azzo. 

<margin>4</margin> However, there is the Law of Modestinus <note>A famous Roman jurist of the 3rd century</note> in the Digest regarding payments. It teaches that rights *cannot* be transferred by a creditor after an interval of time has passed since the payment, if it wasn't agreed upon beforehand or requested immediately. This is because, in such cases, the debt is viewed as having been simply "paid" and extinguished, rather than "purchased" as a right to be transferred. Once a debt is paid absolutely or in the name of the principal debtor, all parties are completely released from the burden they owed to the creditor. 

I say that this Law of Modestinus should be understood to apply to "co-debtors" <term>correi debendi: people who are equally responsible for the whole debt as primary borrowers</term>, where each is primarily responsible for the debt. It also applies when an accessory debtor (like a surety) does not specify that he is paying in his own name, but pays without saying whether it is for himself or for the debtor. According to the 5th *Partida*, if the surety asks for the transfer of rights immediately <note>original: "incontinenti"</note> after paying, he is presumed to have paid in his own name. If he does not ask immediately, he is presumed to have paid in the name of the debtor, and thus the rights are considered to have expired and cannot be transferred later. Whether this opinion should be followed outside the Kingdom of Castile will be discussed below.

<margin>5</margin> Observe also the case of "co-guardians" <term>contutores: multiple people appointed to manage the affairs of a minor</term> who are all responsible to the ward. If one is sued for the whole amount, he can demand that the claim be split among the other solvent guardians. Even if the ward does not formally transfer the rights to him, he still has a "useful action" <note>An equitable legal claim</note> against the other guardian on whose behalf he paid.

<margin>6</margin> Observe also: if a co-debtor is sued for the whole and pays what another was supposed to pay, even if rights are not transferred by the creditor, he still has a claim for "management of affairs" <term>negotiorum gestorum: a legal claim arising when one person manages the business or debts of another without a formal contract</term> to recover what he paid on the other's behalf.

<margin>7</margin> The second point: When there are, for example, four sureties for the whole amount <note>original: "fideiuſſores in ſolidum"</note> and one is sued and pays the entire debt, I believe—along with Bartolus and the final gloss on Law *Modeſtinus*—that the creditor can transfer the rights to him so that he can sue each of the others for the whole amount in that same way.

## Second Treatise, Disputation 544. Page 773

...so that they might come forward, just as the creditor himself could have sued them; except for that portion which the surety himself, having been so sued, was bound to pay <gloss>q̃: which</gloss>, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 542 in a similar question regarding two co-debtors. However, if any of the remaining three co-sureties is insolvent <note>original: "soluẽdo non sit" — literally "is not for paying"</note>, the portion belonging to that person should be divided equally between the surety who was sued and the others, so that everyone shares the loss equally, as Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note> rightly says. Nevertheless, the cited Law 11 seems to affirm the contrary: namely, that a surety who pays the debt in full can only sue the others individually for their own pro-rata shares <term>pro-rata shares: equal portions divided among the number of people involved</term>. Thus, if one of them is insolvent, the paying surety can only receive a formal promise <note>original: "cautionem"</note> from him to pay if he eventually comes into a greater fortune. From this, it implies that nothing of that insolvent person's share can be demanded from the others. Gregorius Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist who commented on the *Siete Partidas*</note> attempts to interpret this law so that it does not disagree with Bartolus, as reported below. I suspect, however, that the same Gregorius Lopez contradicts himself in the preceding gloss. As for the laws he cites in that preceding gloss, the final gloss on the law of Modestinus <note>Herennius Modestinus, a 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> correctly understands them as only applying to co-guardians of the same orphan. Co-guardians are not permitted to sue their fellow guardians for the full amount based on rights transferred from the orphan, but only for their pro-rata shares. This is because the legal actions available to an orphan against them are divided among the co-guardians, as was said in the preceding discussion <gloss>q̃: which</gloss>. Each co-guardian has a "beneficial action" <term>beneficial action: a legal right granted by a judge based on equity rather than the strict letter of the law</term> against the others and against anyone else whose place he took when paying the orphan, even if no legal rights were formally transferred by the orphan to him, as was said a little earlier.

<margin>6</margin> The third point is this: These things that have been said—regarding the transfer of legal actions from a creditor to a co-debtor who pays in full, or to a surety who likewise pays in full, both against co-sureties and against the principal debtor—and generally everything said about the transfer of actions from a creditor against a principal debtor to anyone bound to him as an accessory (whether that accessory be a surety, or a "mandator" <note>one who formally authorizes a creditor to lend to another</note>, or anyone else); these things, I say, which have been said about such transfers of actions, were devised and introduced by legislators for a specific purpose. This was so that those who paid the creditor in place of others <gloss>p̃t: as/insofar as</gloss> would have a legal basis to recover what they paid from those whose place they took. This applies whether or not they already had a right to sue based on other grounds, such as a "mandate" <term>mandate: a contract where one person asks another to do something on their behalf</term> or "management of affairs" <term>management of affairs: a legal concept where one person looks after another's interests without a formal contract</term>. Indeed, it is difficult to find a legal basis why co-sureties should be held liable for the full amount to one of their own who paid the entire debt for which they were all individually bound—unless you say that the payer was "managing their affairs" when he released them from the obligation they owed the creditor through that very payment. Because of the fact that once full payment is made to the creditor—whether by the principal debtor, a surety, a mandator, or one of the co-debtors or co-sureties—everyone who was bound for that debt (whether primarily or accessorily) is entirely released from the obligation. Consequently, all the legal actions the creditor held 

<column-break/>

against them expire along with the debt itself, as is clearly seen in the *Institutes* <note>The *Institutes* of Justinian, a foundational Roman law textbook</note> in the chapters on how obligations are dissolved, and on sureties, and on co-debtors, as well as in the Digest. Certainly, so that such legal actions might remain with the creditor to be transmitted to those who satisfy the debt in the place of others, these same legislators introduced a legal fiction: that the satisfaction of the debt should not be treated as a "payment," but as if it were a **purchase of the legal actions** <gloss>q̃: which</gloss> belonged to the creditor, whether against the principal debtor, the co-debtors, or the co-sureties. This happens through an agreement, either formal or implied, to transfer the actions upon receiving satisfaction. Thus, the actions remain with the creditor even after satisfaction is received, not so that he himself can sue the debtor, co-debtor, or co-surety (since these debtors would have a legal "exception" or defense against him, stating he had already received full satisfaction), as the final gloss on Law *Papinianus* says, but so that he could transfer them to the one who satisfied the debt in place of the others. This is done either by an actual exchange of the payment for the transfer of actions, or simply by implication, such as <gloss>qñ: when</gloss> the payment is handed over without any other agreement and the payer immediately asks for the transfer of actions. It is clear from the laws on sureties and the law of Modestinus that this was introduced by legislators for the reason stated above, and that the disposition of the law stands this way.

Truly, it would have been much better if it had been decreed that, by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> and without any formal transfer, the creditor's actions would automatically pass to those who truly pay in the place of others. Civil law, out of great equity, should grant these rights to them directly, rather than using so many subtleties and evasions of the **pagan jurists** <note>Molina is criticizing the complex Roman legal system created by non-Christian authors like Ulpian and Papinian</note>. These jurists impose a burden without cause on people, requiring them to include a "transfer of actions" clause in their agreement when they pay, or to ask for them immediately and not after a delay; otherwise, the rights are treated as if they were already extinguished and cannot be transferred. This serves no other purpose than to multiply lawsuits. It ensures that simple people, who are less experienced and skilled in these legal subtleties, are deprived of the proper help for recovering what they were forced to pay on behalf of others. It also causes legal business before notaries, advocates, and judges to multiply and leads to great expenses. Add to this that so many laws have been multiplied and inserted into the body of Civil Law because of these evasions and subtleties, containing the decrees and opinions of **Modestinus, Julianus, Ulpian, Papinian,** and other pagan jurists. This makes the law excessively long, obscure, and difficult—both to understand each part and especially to make them all agree, reconcile them, and keep them in one's memory. If you then add the inferences, explanations, and the variety of opinions multiplied by the numerous legal experts writing on civil law, you will find an inextricable chaos and a nursery for lawsuits. Therefore, it would be in the best interest of the commonwealth if Christian princes would replace these and similar things with brief and concise laws...

# Luis Molina on Contracts
### Page 774

...completely cut them back. For the whole title concerning sureties <term>sureties: people who guarantee the debt of another</term> can be easily understood through very few and clear laws, and the same is true for many other titles.

From that subtlety of the jurists—namely, that in such dissolutions of debt the debt is not simply satisfied, but rather the legal actions that the creditor holds against the remaining debtors are "purchased"—a question arises: whether a tax is owed on these payments. In this Kingdom of Castile, this tax is called the *alcabala*, and in Portugal, it is called the *sisa*. <margin>9</margin> This tax is established to be paid on all purchases, sales, and exchanges, with a few privileged exceptions. Is this type of "purchase and sale" of the transfer of legal actions <note>original: "cessionis actionum"</note> among those exceptions? Angelus Perusinus <note>A famous 14th-century Italian jurist</note>, as cited by Lassarte in *On the Tenth of a Sale*, question 9, number 2, answers in the affirmative. However, Lassarte rightly asserts the contrary in the same work from number 32 onward. He is guided by this reasoning: that an incorporeal right to receive a certain sum once—which right is counted among movable rather than immovable property—is considered to be of the same nature as the sum of money itself to which the right pertains. Therefore, since the *alcabala* tax is not owed on the exchange of one sum of money for another (as was stated in Disputation 397), then surely the *alcabala* will not be owed on that payment of money by which a legal action is "bought" to recover the same amount of money. I would assert the same thing based on this other foundation: because, specifically, that is not properly a purchase or an exchange, but a true payment, even if it is regarded *as if* it were a purchase for the effect of transferring the legal actions. Furthermore, it has never been accepted by custom, nor ever heard of, that the *alcabala* be paid on such payments and transfers of actions. Nor, by *epikeia* <term>epikeia: a principle of legal interpretation that looks to the "spirit" or "equity" of the law rather than its strict literal wording</term>, should it be thought that those who imposed the tax intended to extend it to this, as that would be unreasonable. Laws, especially those concerning taxes, must not be extended further than they have been accepted by custom and than *epikeia*, the interpreter of laws, suggests they should be extended.

In the third scenario proposed at the beginning of this disputation—namely, when one of the sureties pays the whole debt in full <term>in solidum: for the whole amount, not just a portion</term> absolutely, without specifying whether he pays in his own name as a surety or in the name of the debtor—the last gloss on the law *Papinianus* (Digest, *On Mandates*), as said above, along with Azo <note>A highly influential 13-century jurist at Bologna</note>, considers that if he immediately asks the creditor to transfer the legal actions against the co-sureties and the principal debtor to him, it is to be presumed he paid in his own name, and the actions must therefore be transferred to him. But if he does not ask for this immediately, it is presumed he paid in the name of the debtor, and therefore the actions should not be transferred to him, even if he asks for them later after an interval. Instead, he would only be entitled to an "action of mandate" or an "action for management of affairs" <note>original: "actionem mandati, aut negotiorum gestorum"</note> against the principal debtor to recover what he paid in his place. These points are today enacted, following that gloss and Azo, at the end of Law 11, Title 12, Part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational law code of Castile</note>; and this is therefore to be observed in this Kingdom of Castile. However, Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a giant of medieval law</note> affirms the contrary in the law *Modestinus* (Digest, *On Payments*), as does the common opinion of the doctors, as Gregorius Lopez reports in his citation of Law 11, last gloss. Namely, when one of the sureties pays the whole debt absolutely without specifying in whose name he pays, it must always be presumed he paid in his own name to fulfill his obligation as a surety, rather than in the

<column-break/>

debtor’s name; and therefore, even if he asks for the transfer of actions after an interval, they must be transferred to him. This opinion is the one I approve of, staying within the Common Law. For it must always be presumed that he pays as a surety and not in the name of the debtor, unless the contrary is expressed.

It should also be observed that if someone, by the mandate of a third party, becomes a surety for someone who is absent, then: if the suretyship did not result in the benefit of the person for whom it was made, nor was it reasonably made for him, and the surety pays something for him, that surety indeed has an "action of mandate" against that third-party mandator to compensate him for what he paid, but he has no action against the person for whom he acted as surety. If, however, the suretyship was usefully made for the absent person, the surety can sue indifferently, either against the mandator by the "action of mandate," or against the person for whom he was surety by the "action for management of affairs." But if the person for whom he was surety was present when the third party ordered the suretyship and did not object, then the surety can sue either of them indifferently by the "action of mandate." These points are held in the law *Qui fide iuncta* (Digest, *On Mandates*) and Law 13, Title 12, Part 5. Read what was said in Disputation 539.

Finally, there is a doubt: when a surety pays for a debtor and has a legal claim against him and the other co-sureties, is it enough for the creditor to confess that he received payment from him so that the surety can sue them and force them to pay? Or is it necessary to prove the payment in some other way than the creditor's confession? Bartolus, in the section *If to sureties* (Digest, *On Oaths*), denies that the creditor's confession is sufficient, and certain others embrace that opinion. Nevertheless, the contrary must be affirmed: namely, that the creditor's confession is sufficient, as Bartolus himself says in Law 60, following the common opinion of the doctors received in practice, which Gutierrez <note>Juan Gutiérrez, a prominent Spanish jurist</note> and Antonius Gomez report and follow. The reason is that through that confession, the debtor and the other sureties remain free from the creditor’s claims.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 545.

**10 In which cases a surety of indemnity can raise the exception of the principal debtor’s discussion, even after the joinder of issue.**
*And of how many types, see number 13.*
**11 A surety can renounce the exception of the principal debtor’s discussion.**
*This is clarified, however, at number 12.*

*Understand this, however, and the clarification at number 15.*

<margin>1</margin>
In the past, not only under the law of the Digest but also the Code, it was permitted for a creditor to demand payment from a surety <term>surety: a guarantor</term> while bypassing the principal debtor, if the creditor so wished. This is established in Law 3, final paragraph, of the Digest *On Two Defendants* <note>original: "l. 3. §. vlt. ff. de duob. reis"</note> and in the Code under the laws *Not Rightly* and *By Our Law*. Today, however, under the law of the *Authentics* <note>The "Authentics" refers to the Novels of Justinian, a later layer of Roman law</note>, a creditor is not permitted to demand anything from a surety, or from a mandatory <note>someone who instructs another to lend</note>, or from any other intercessor <note>a general term for anyone stepping into a debt for another</note>, unless a "discussion" <term>discussion: the legal process of exhausting a debtor's assets before turning to the guarantor</term> has first been performed on the assets of the principal debtor. It must be proven that the principal debtor is unable to pay; only then can the debt be demanded from the surety, or their sureties, or any other intercessor. If the sureties or other intercessors are sued before that discussion takes place, they have the right to an "exception" <note>a legal defense</note> based on the laws to be cited, insisting that the discussion of the debtor's assets happen first. This is well-stated in the *Authentic* under the Code *On Sureties*, and more copiously in the title from which Law 9, Title 12, Part 5 [of the *Partidas*] was taken, as well as Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusit. ord."</note>, Title 46, paragraph 1. The common opinion of the doctors of law agrees with this. Nor does Law 3, Title 18, Book 3 of the *Fuero Real* <note>original: "fori"</note> matter, which Gutierrez mentions in *On the Confirmation of Law*, Part 1, Chapter 23, number 7, as stating the contrary according to ancient law. For, as the same Gutierrez, and there Gregorio López <note>A famous 16th-century commentator on Spanish law</note> on Law 8, Title 12, Part 5, at the word "each one of them," and others rightly assert: that law has not been accepted into practice insofar as it goes against the laws of the *Partidas* <note>The Siete Partidas, the primary law code of Castile</note> when those have been accepted into practice.

<margin>2</margin>
However, this requirement—that the discussion of the principal debtor's assets must occur before the sureties or other intercessors are forced to pay—is to be understood only if the principal debtor is present. For if he is absent, the sureties or intercessors can be sued while bypassing the discussion of the debtor's assets, as held in the cited laws. If, however, the sureties request a deadline to bring the principal debtor so that he may be sued first, it should be granted to them, with the time to be determined at the judge's discretion. Once this time has passed, if they do not bring him, the debt can be demanded from them without the discussion of the principal debtor’s assets having been performed; the cre-

<column-break/>

-ditor, however, must cede to them all the legal actions <note>original: "actiones"</note> he has against the principal debtor, as was said in the preceding disputation. All these things are explicitly contained in the cited laws. I believe, however, that if the debtor were very far away, such that it would be quite burdensome for the creditor to wait that long, the debt could be demanded immediately from the sureties or intercessors. This is because, in a just and appropriate time for bringing the principal debtor from such a distant place, the cited laws intended to consult the interests of the intercessors or sureties only so far as it would not result in a notable burden or detriment to the creditor.

The *Gloss* on the *Authentic* regarding sureties, at the word "present," says that a debtor should be considered absent for the purpose of this rule when he is neither in the town nor in the territory of that jurisdiction, such that he cannot conveniently be summoned. This is what the doctors of law commonly affirm, and it is established in Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 46, paragraph 1. Law 9, Title 12, Part 5 [of the *Partidas*], however, says he is to be considered present when he is in the town, making no mention of the territory of jurisdiction. And although Gregorio López there, and Gutierrez in *On the Confirmation of Law*, Part 1, Chapter 23, number 2, suspect those laws might conflict, they eventually agree that the cited *Gloss* and common opinion can be understood in a way that aligns with that law—which is most equitable—treating the mention of "town" in that law as including its territory. I have no doubt that the law should be understood this way, as Antonio Gómez seems to understand it in Volume 2 of his *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 13, number 14.

I am pleased by what is said, in agreement with Salicetus and others cited by Gutierrez in the same place at number 3: Namely, if the debtor is "absent" in the manner explained, but has a home and assets in the town or territory where execution can be carried out without needing to summon the person of the debtor, then the sureties or other intercessors cannot be sued until the discussion or execution is performed on those assets. If, after those assets are exhausted and the price handed to the creditor, some of the debt remains to be paid, then that remainder can be demanded from the sureties or other intercessors for that debt.

<margin>4</margin>
This doctrine currently holds in this Kingdom of Castile when the obligation of such a debtor allows for "ready execution" <note>original: "paratam habet exequutionem"; a summary process for debt collection</note>, according to what was said regarding Law 1 and the following in Title 21, Book 4 of the *New Collection* <note>original: "nouæ collect."</note>, Disputation 538, in the section "But Today." As reported there from Law 19 of the same title, it is not necessary to summon the debtor for such an execution to take place, except only after the public announcements prescribed for selling off his goods "for the final sale" <note>original: "para el remate"</note>, as it is called there. And then, if he is not present, it is enough to summon him at his house, notifying his family or the nearest neighbors to his house, as is held there.

<margin>5</margin>
I also approve of what the same Gutierrez adds, along with Gregorio López on the cited Law 9, Rodrigo Suárez, and others in the same place at number 4. Namely: if the principal debtor is present and has some assets in the territory and others outside the territory and jurisdiction, the discussion must indeed be performed on the assets he has within the territory before the sureties are sued and forced to pay. But this does not apply to assets he has outside the territory, when those he has inside the territory are insufficient for...

# Louis Molina, On Contracts.

...paying the full debt, and it would be troublesome for the creditor to seek execution against those others. Therefore, at that time, with the increase of the debt, it may be agreed that the sureties, having been granted those legal actions against the principal debtor, may themselves compel him to satisfy them.

<margin>5</margin>
This is also proven to us by what is added there in numbers 5 and 6 by others: namely, if the principal debtor is absent and has property in the territory, and the obligation of the debtor is such that to perform execution on those goods it is necessary to first sue and thus summon him, then a distinction must be made. For either he is so absent that he can neither be conveniently called nor is it hoped he will return soon—such as if he is held captive by enemies, or is across the sea in India <note>Molina, writing in the 16th century, uses "India" to denote any extremely distant colony or land across the ocean</note> or in another distant region from which a quick return is not expected, or is similarly elsewhere outside the province in a very distant place, or is a vagabond and his location is unknown—or he is in a place from which he can be conveniently called, or is expected to return soon. In that first case, since a <term>curator bonis: a court-appointed administrator for the property of an absent person</term> can and should be granted for the goods he has in the territory to take up the actions of the absent person, execution can validly be made against the goods for the debt. This follows the law *ab hostibus* <note>original: "l. ab hostibus"</note> along with the gloss on the word "if" <note>original: "si"</note> (which gloss says, for example, "if he is across the sea," although the text extends to many other examples) in the Digest *On what grounds majors...* <note>original: "ff. ex quib. caus. maiores"</note> and the law *The same privilege* <note>original: "l. idem priuilegium"</note> along with the final gloss there, in the Digest *On the privileges of creditors* <note>original: "ff. de priuil. cred."</note>, and Law 2 of the Digest *On granting a curator for goods* <note>original: "ff. de curat. bon. dando"</note>, and Law 12, title 3, part 3, along with Gregorio López’s first gloss on the same.

Since, I say, a curator can then be given for those goods, the <term>discussion: the legal process of exhausting a debtor's assets</term> must certainly be made against those goods before the sureties are compelled to pay the same debt. In the latter case, however, because a curator cannot be given for the goods, the debtor himself must be waited for so that he may be summoned and sued before execution is made against them. This is noted by the additions in the margin of the gloss on the law *The same privilege* in the Digest *On privileges*, according to the second to last law in the Digest *On embassies* <note>original: "l. penult. ff. de legationibus"</note> and the law *To be ignorant* in the Code *On the restitution of soldiers* <note>original: "leg. ignorare. C. de rest. milit."</note>. Gregorio López, as cited above with Baldus and others, and Gutierrez at number 6, agree that the sureties can be compelled to pay the debt immediately.

Furthermore, although the laws cited speak of those absent for the sake of the republic, and seem to speak even if they are not expected to return soon, and therefore do not sufficiently prove the point; and although it literally seems, regarding the first case mentioned, that execution cannot be made on his goods even if a proxy is appointed for those goods—nevertheless, one should not depart from the opinion of these doctors and the common view, with no one objecting, which certainly carries great equity.

<margin>†</margin>
Furthermore, what has been said—that the discussion of the principal debtor's goods must be made before the sureties are sued and compelled to pay—is to be understood unless it is notorious that he can pay nothing, or how much he cannot pay, or unless it is sufficiently proven. Just as it must also be proven regarding the preceding limitation, unless it is notorious that the debtor is absent. This is the opinion of Bartolus and the common view of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez relates and follows in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 14, limitation 1; and Gregorio López on Law 9, title 12, part 5, gloss 2.

<column-break/>

And Gutierrez, where cited above at number 13, based on the argument in the text of the final law at the beginning of the Digest *If a certain thing is sought* <note>original: "l. vlt, in prin. ff. si cer. pet."</note> and the law *The buyer* in the Digest *On actions for purchase* <note>original: "l. emptorem. ff. de act. emp."</note>. The final gloss on the law *Having stipulated ten* in the Digest *On verbal obligations* <note>original: "l. decem stipulatus. ff. de verb. oblig."</note> affirms this. Gregorio López says the same, as cited above with Imola; and let him prove that the principal debtor is litigious and extremely difficult to sue, as more fully explained by Antonio Gómez in the same place, limitation 5. Provided, however, that the principal debtor did not already have that quality at the time the contract was made, which the creditor was not then ignorant of; for if he knew it, he should blame himself for making the contract with him without securing himself otherwise.

<margin>6</margin>
The exception † that a discussion of the debtor's goods has not been made, and should be made first, if not raised by the sureties sued for the debt, does not invalidate the proceedings. Instead, the judgment is valid, and the sureties are lawfully condemned to pay the debt. This is held by Bartolus, Alexander, and others, as well as Gregorio López on the cited Law 9 at the word "first," and Antonio Gómez in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 14, limitation 3. Indeed,

<margin>7</margin>
such an exception †, since it is not <term>peremptory: a defense that permanently kills a claim</term> but <term>dilatory: a defense that merely delays a claim</term>, cannot be raised except before the <term>joinder of issue: the moment the legal issues are formally defined for trial</term> <note>original: "litem contestatam"</note>; after the issue is joined, it has no place. This is held by Bartolus, based on the argument of many laws and the common opinion of the doctors, including Antonio Gómez in the same place, Gregorio López on Law 14, title 13, part 5, at the word "first," limitation 5 (though he treats another matter there), and Gutierrez in *On Confirmed Rights*, chapter 23, number 14. Rightly, however, the same Gutierrez in number 13 of that work rebukes certain people who said that in this Kingdom of Castile, according to Law 1, title 5, book 4 of the *New Compilation* <note>original: "nouæ collect." refers to the Nueva Recopilación, a 1567 code of Spanish law</note>, it could be raised within twenty days of the joinder of issue. For in that place, the discussion is only about peremptory exceptions, as is clearly evident to anyone looking at that law. At its beginning, it speaks of dilatory exceptions, stating they must be raised before the joinder of issue, within the nine days given for joining the issue, counted from the term in which the defendant was cited to appear in court.

<margin>8</margin>
If † goods should come to the principal debtor after the joinder of issue with the sureties, then, after the issue has been so joined, the exception can be raised that a discussion be made first in those goods before progress is made in the lawsuit and before they are compelled to pay. For a dilatory exception can be raised after the joinder of issue when it arises after that joinder, as is clearly evident from the chapter *Insinuante* in *On the office of the delegated judge* <note>original: "ca. insinuante de off. iud. deleg."</note>. Covarruvias delivers this with the common opinion of the doctors in *On Practical Questions*, chapter 26, number 2. So too Gregorio López on Law 14, title 13, part 5, at the word "first," and Gutierrez where cited above at number 17, and others whom they cite.

<margin>9</margin>
A surety † of indemnity is one who, after sureties have been given for the principal debtor, promises that the creditor will be held harmless. He declares that those sureties have sufficient goods from which the debt may be paid to him in full; otherwise, he binds himself formally or by virtue of his promise that if they are found not to have sufficient goods, he himself will pay what is lacking. For this reason, he is customarily called an *abonador* in Spanish <note>original: "abonador Hispanè"</note>. Someone can also be a surety of indemnity for a debtor without any other sureties being given by the principal debtor, if such a surety merely affirms to the creditor that the debtor has sufficient goods to pay from, and in the same way binds himself to pay in his place whatever the principal debtor is found unable to pay. Sometimes, also, many constitute themselves as sureties for someone, but in such a way that one...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the "benefit of discussion" (excussio). On the previous page, he addressed the rights of sureties when a debtor is absent. # Second Treatise. Disputation 545.

...of his own will, he wishes to be a guarantor along with others, provided that the others guarantee his own protection from loss, a separate pact having been entered into with them for this purpose. Sometimes someone even establishes himself as the principal debtor, as a Canon in this city of Cuenca <note>Cuenca is a city in central Spain; Molina often uses local Spanish examples to illustrate Roman-Canonical law</note> is accustomed to do when he takes upon himself a "stewardship" <note>original: "mayordomia"</note>, substituting a layman in his place as the actual debtor to manage the entire business. I have understood that sometimes the Canon demands from this substitute sureties for both of them, who bind themselves to keep the Canon himself harmless. Thus, although everyone remains obligated to the Church—namely, the Canon, the substituted layman, and the provided sureties—nevertheless, the sureties and the substitute bind themselves by another specific pact to keep that Canon entirely harmless. The result is that if the Canon is ever compelled to pay anything, the substitute and the sureties are held to pay it in his place, each for the whole amount <note>original: "in solidum"; a legal term meaning any one of them can be held liable for the total debt</note>.

<margin>10</margin>
This having been established in light of what is to be said, something must be added to the matter we were just discussing. A "surety of indemnity" <note>A guarantor who only agrees to pay whatever balance remains after the creditor has successfully sued the primary debtor and sold their assets</note>—under the first two methods explained—can raise a legal objection <note>original: "exceptionem"</note> even after a lawsuit has been contested against him to pay in the place of the principal debtor or his sureties. He may demand that a full <term>discussion: the legal process of "excussio," where a creditor must first exhaust all legal means to collect from the primary debtor's assets</term> be made first against the assets of all those others. This is because such a requirement is in the very nature of being a surety of indemnity; it is not merely a privilege granted by law, but the very thing he agreed to in his contract. No one can be compelled to pay more than he obligated himself to pay, nor in a different manner than he agreed. If a creditor oversteps these limits, the defendant can always object that the creditor is exceeding his rights and that he is not bound to it. I have said this following Baldus, Hippolytus, and Gutierrez (cited above, number 19) regarding the first two methods; for in the latter two methods, those obligated to the creditor do not have the status of a surety of indemnity in relation to him, regardless of any private obligations made between themselves. Therefore, that objection does not hold ground against the principal creditor.

Following Bartolus, Alexander, and many others (number 20), Gutierrez adds: When sureties or a third-party possessor of mortgaged property have legitimately objected that a "discussion" should first be made of the principal debtor's assets, and the creditor wishes to attempt it, he must summon the sureties or that third-party possessor so they can see that the process is done fully and properly. This is clearly consistent with reason and equity.

<margin>11</margin>
If sureties renounce the rights that allow them to object and demand a prior discussion of the principal debtor's assets, then they do not enjoy that privilege, as it was granted solely for their benefit (based on the laws *C. de pactis* and *C. de legibus*). Consequently, they cannot raise that objection but can be compelled to pay the debt without any discussion of the principal debtor's assets. This is the gloss on the *Authentica* regarding sureties and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13) and Gutierrez (number 21) follow. It is also decreed in the *Institutes of the Ordinances*, Book 4, Title 46.

However, one must observe, following Gama (Decision 

<column-break/>

379), Gutierrez (number 22), Antonio Gomez, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors: 
<margin>12</margin> Even if a surety of indemnity renounces "all privileges of creditors," he is not considered to have renounced the right to a prior discussion of the assets of those for whom he stands as surety. Why? Because it is the very essence of the obligation of a surety of indemnity that he binds himself to nothing other than that which is found to be missing after the assets of the primary debtors are exhausted. Therefore, if he were to bind himself to pay *without* a prior discussion, it would be a contradiction in terms <note>original: "implicaret in adiecto"</note>. It would be contradictory to say he is a "surety of indemnity" while also saying he can be forced to pay before the loss is actually determined. Such a renunciation would essentially turn the agreement into a different kind of guarantee altogether. Thus, if it is expressly agreed that he is a surety of indemnity, even if a clause is added saying he "renounces every privilege of sureties and all other help of the laws," one should not judge—despite what some say—that he has renounced the "benefit of discussion." To do so would utterly destroy the nature of a surety of indemnity. One should judge instead that such a clause was added out of custom, or perhaps the drowsiness <note>original: "oscitantia"</note> and unskillfulness of the notary <note>original: "tabellionis"</note>, rather than the actual intent of the parties. This type of surety is discussed in various laws of the *Digest* and *Code*.

One must also observe—according to Salycetis and others cited by Gutierrez (number 23)—
<margin>13</margin> that if someone stands as a surety for a magistrate or other public official regarding the administration of his office, such a surety cannot be compelled to pay anything in a judgment against that official until a discussion of the official's assets has been made. The legal authorities consider such a person to be a "surety of indemnity" by the very disposition of the law itself.

This is certainly true, considering that this was established even before the laws of the *Authentica* introduced the general privilege of discussion for all sureties. However, it should be noted that there is a great difference between a surety of indemnity created by legal privilege and one created by private agreement. The legal surety is not prohibited from choosing to be a different kind of guarantor if he wishes. Therefore, he can perfectly well renounce that legal privilege and move, by his own will and pact, into a stricter type of guarantee. He is considered to have done this if he establishes himself as a surety for a public official and renounces all privileges of sureties and all other support of the law. Indeed, I believe the same applies if he renounces either just the privileges or just the legal support; by using either clause while becoming a surety for a public official, he sufficiently renounces the legal protection and the privilege...

<summary>This page analyzes the "surety of indemnity," arguing that their right to have the primary debtor's assets seized first is essential to their contract and cannot be waived by general boilerplate language. Molina also distinguishes between sureties who have this protection by private contract versus public officials' sureties who have it by law.</summary>
