# Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...the privilege granted to the guarantors of public officials is considered to pass not only into the general category of common guarantors, but also into a renunciation of the privilege of discussion <note>The right to be sued only after the primary debtor</note>, and any other right granted by law to common guarantors. This is something that Gutierrez and others whom he cites do not sufficiently attend to. However, a guarantor of indemnity <note>one who only covers the final loss</note>, by his own agreement and pact—even if a general renunciation is added—ought not to be thought to destroy the nature of his own specific agreement, nor to depart from it to transition into another type of agreement or guarantee.

<margin>14</margin> When a guarantor † binds himself together with the principal debtor in the same document as both a guarantor and a principal debtor—or by making the debt of the principal debtor his own, as is commonly said—then it is not required that a "discussion" <note>a legal seizure and sale</note> of the principal debtor's goods take place first. Instead, he can be sued immediately and compelled to pay, because in that case, the guarantor and the principal debtor are considered two principal parties responsible for that creditor's debt. This is the view of Alexander and others cited by Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous Spanish jurist who annotated the *Siete Partidas*</note>, and Gutierrez. However, they say the matter is different when the guarantor binds himself as both guarantor and principal debtor in a *separate* document. In that case, they claim he is considered only a guarantor; therefore, even if he binds himself as a principal debtor, it is still necessary that a discussion of the principal debtor's goods happens first.

¶ And † in this latter scenario, all these doctors understand the gloss on the word "guarantor" at the end of the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Roman laws by Justinian</note> concerning guarantors, which states absolutely that when there is no "novation" <note>the replacement of an old debt with a new one</note> of the obligation—even if the guarantor binds himself as a principal debtor—it is necessary to first conduct a discussion of the principal debtor's assets. But the aforementioned authors limit this, saying it does not apply when the guarantor binds himself in the same document as the principal debtor. Truly, I would say that whether it is in the same document or later in another, if the guarantor binds himself as a principal debtor, he can be sued by the creditor without any prior discussion of the principal debtor's goods. This is because, by that very act, he is seen to sufficiently renounce the *Authenticum* concerning guarantors. And whoever renounces that law can be sued without a prior discussion, as was said a little earlier. A renunciation is valid, whether formal or by the force of the act, whether it occurs in the same document or later in another. The Portuguese Law <note>original: "lex Lusit." refers to the *Ordenações Filipinas* or earlier codes of Portugal</note> agrees, stating absolutely that when a guarantor binds himself as a principal debtor, he can be sued and forced to pay without a prior discussion. Because when a guarantor is bound as a principal debtor, he takes on the status of a co-debtor along with the principal. From what was said in Disputation 542, it will be easily understood when, under common law or the law of Castile or Portugal, he is held only for his portion or for the whole amount (*in solidum*), without a prior discussion of the co-debtor's assets. This is especially true 

<column-break/>

when the *Authenticum* concerning "two debtors" <note>original: "authentico de duobus reis"</note> was simultaneously renounced, and he was bound for the whole amount as a principal debtor, as happens every day.

<margin>16</margin> Likewise, if a guarantor † who is sued for a debt for which he stood as surety denies that he is the guarantor for that debt, he loses the privileges that belong to him as a guarantor. Consequently, he can be compelled to pay without any prior discussion of the principal debtor's goods. This is held in the Portuguese Ordinances and is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez follows, based on the argument that he who denies in court the very thing for which a benefit or privilege was granted to him, by that very act loses it.

<margin>Question</margin>
<margin>17</margin> The question is: if a guarantor confirms the contract of guarantee or his obligation with an oath, can he then be sued without a prior discussion of the principal debtor's goods? We are speaking of cases where he otherwise could not be sued without such a discussion. For if, even without an oath, he could be sued based on any of the points explained so far, he can certainly be sued all the more when the force and obligation of an oath are added—unless the contract is rendered void by the very act of adding an oath without Royal permission in Castile or Portugal, according to what was said at the end of Disputation 146.

Gutierrez discusses this matter more copiously, citing doctors for both sides. Most of them believe that whether he is a guarantor of indemnity or a common guarantor, if he confirms the contract with an oath, he can be sued and forced to pay the debt without a prior discussion of the principal debtor's assets. But Gutierrez himself rightly judges the opposite in the first case, when the guarantor is one of indemnity. This is because an oath confirms nothing other than what is in the contract of obligation upon which it is placed. A guarantor of indemnity only binds himself to that which, after a discussion is made, the principal debtor is found unable to pay. That is the nature and essence of an indemnity guarantee. Therefore, even if it is confirmed by an oath, the obligation extends to nothing further. However, when it is a common guarantor, he agrees with the opinion reported above: that the person can be sued without a prior discussion, although he considers the opposite opinion not improbable.

These doctors confirm their opinion from the legal chapter *Ex Rescripto* concerning oaths, where guarantors who had bound themselves by oath are compelled to fulfill what they swore to do when the principal is unwilling to fulfill the contract.

Gutierrez also confirms this because if a woman confirms her guarantee with an oath, she does not enjoy the exception and privilege of the *Velleianum* <note>A Roman law protection that prevented women from being held liable for the debts of others</note>, as was seen in Disputation 540. Therefore, similarly, if anyone confirms their guarantee...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal conditions under which a guarantor loses the "benefit of discussion," focusing on cases where the guarantor signs as a principal debtor or adds a religious oath to the contract. He emphasizes that while oaths reinforce obligations, they do not fundamentally change the nature of "indemnity" contracts.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 545

...[that if someone] confirms a guarantee obligation with an oath, they shall not enjoy the privilege and defense of a prior seizure <note>original: "excussio"; the right to demand the creditor sue the debtor first</note> of the debtor’s assets.

We must embrace the opposite opinion, along with many others cited in the same place by Gutierrez, and followed by Covarruvias (Chapter *Quamvis pactum*, part 1, § 4, number 4) and Antonio Gomez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 14, limitation 6). Namely: even if a guarantee obligation is confirmed by law, provided that the oath does not specifically add or intend to bind the person to *not* raise the defense of prior seizure, but rather the person simply confirms with an oath that they will fulfill their obligation as a guarantor, they can still demand that a seizure be made first against the assets of the principal debtor. The reason for this is that a confirmatory oath—as established in the final law of the Code *concerning non-numbered money* <note>a reference to Roman Law: *Codex Justinianus*, de non numerata pecunia</note> and is clear enough in itself—does not extend further than the obligation or promise upon which it rests. Indeed, a guarantee obligation is understood by the very disposition of the law to be made *only after* a seizure of the principal debtor’s assets has occurred, and not otherwise. Therefore, the confirmation of that same obligation by oath does not exclude this kind of defense.

To the first argument of the others, Covarruvias responds (following Bartolus in the place cited above) regarding the words of the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>. When the Pope says: "Therefore we command that you take care to warn both the principal and the guarantors that, as they have sworn, they cause the same agreement to be fulfilled; otherwise, they shall be compelled by the prescribed censures until worthy satisfaction is made," this must be understood as maintaining the proper order of legal compulsion. That is, the execution should first take place against those principal monks, and only then should the guarantors be compelled. The final Gloss <note>standard legal commentary</note> on that passage says that those guarantors are only compelled to ensure, as much as lies within them, that those monks stand by the agreement; because they only bound themselves to that under oath. This is consistent with the words of the text: "as they have sworn, they cause the same agreement to be fulfilled." Indeed, I would say (as the words of the text clearly sound) that the Abbot mentioned there had made a certain agreement which he swore to fulfill. For greater security of fulfillment, he gave some of his monks as hostages <note>original: "obsides"</note>, and furthermore provided guarantors who bound themselves by oath. In the event that the Abbot did not wish to stand by that agreement, they would effectively see to it that he did, or if he refused, they would pay the damages. This is not being a guarantor for that Abbot in the ordinary way, but in an extraordinary one—so that if the Abbot, despite their persuasion, refused to stand by the agreement, they themselves would pay the interest without waiting for any prior seizure via a judge against that stubborn and powerful Abbot. Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff commanded there that everyone be forced to fulfill the oath in the manner in which each had bound himself. Thus, the ruling of that text in no way contradicts our opinion.

Regarding Gutierrez’s second argument, even if the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied. There is indeed a different logic regarding the Velleianum defense <note>the *Senatus Consultum Velleianum*, a Roman law that prohibited women from acting as guarantors for others</note> and the defense of prior seizure of the debtor’s assets. For the Velleianum defense arises from the fact that a woman's guarantee is void by the privilege of the Velleianum law for the purpose of binding her. However, by the very fact that 

<column-break/>

the guarantee is confirmed by an oath, it assumes legal force, and consequently begins to bind her effectively. In this case, the prior nullity of the act upon which the oath falls—caused by the Velleianum privilege—does not stand in the way. Therefore, as soon as that guarantee assumes the power of obligation through the oath, the Velleianum defense (which relied on the flaw of nullity in that act) ceases. However, the defense of prior seizure did not rely on the nullity of the guarantee, but on a privilege and disposition of the law: that a guarantee and obligation, valid in itself, is understood to apply only if a seizure is first made of the principal debtor's assets. A subsequent oath does not prevent this legal disposition and understanding of the obligation; rather, it affects and reinforces that obligation in the form that the law has established it.

<margin>18</margin> Gutierrez disputes (in the place cited above from number 30) whether a guarantor of indemnity <note>one who guarantees to pay only the final loss after all assets are exhausted</note> who renounces the prior seizure of the debtor’s assets under oath, while binding himself to the guarantee under the same oath, † still enjoys the privilege of seizure. It should be stated briefly. In that case, as said above, he contradicts himself in that contract, and the agreement transitions into a contract of common guarantee with a sworn renunciation of the prior seizure. Since such a contract, thus confirmed by oath, contains nothing unjust, it certainly binds in conscience and in the external court, and it is not then lawful for such a guarantor to raise the defense of prior seizure. However, if a guarantor of indemnity had confirmed such a contract under oath and had renounced all privileges of guarantors and the protection of all laws with a general clause, then unless he specifically intended to include the defense of prior seizure under that generality, it should not be judged that he intended to include something that is against the nature and essence of such a contract. Consequently, in both the external court and the court of conscience, he could still raise that defense.

In the same place (number 31), following Menchaca, Gutierrez adds that when a guarantor of indemnity has previously bound himself under oath *not* to renounce the prior seizure, if he later renounces that defense under oath, the second oath does not bind, as it concerns a "bad thing" <note>an illicit or contradictory act</note> because of the previous contrary oath. Therefore, with the second oath posing no obstacle, he can raise the defense of seizure. However, when the first oath was not taken in favor of some third person, but only had the character of an oath taken to God—like a vow confirmed by an oath—since it did not concern a "greater good," it would not bind at all, according to what was said in Dispute 149. Consequently, with the first oath posing no obstacle, the second oath taken to the creditor would bind, and thus such a guarantor could not raise the defense of prior seizure. Read what was said extensively against the same author in Dispute 540, even if in another similar situation, and according to those points, you may also define this case.

<margin>19</margin> Finally, the same Gutierrez (in the same place, number 32), along with many others whom he cites, observes that if the principal † debtor mortgaged <note>original: "hypothecavit"</note> his assets to the creditor for the debt, and added the "clause of constitutum" <note>a legal fiction where a person stops possessing something in their own name and begins possessing it in the name of another, often used to secure a debt</note> frequently used in contracts, by which he professed that he possessed all those assets in the name of the creditor...

<summary>Molina argues that an oath confirming a guarantee does not waive the "benefit of discussion" unless explicitly stated, as oaths reinforce obligations in their natural legal state. He also distinguishes between different types of legal protections, such as those for women and guarantors of indemnity, regarding how oaths affect their validity.</summary>

Molina is concluding a point about how legal fictions regarding possession affect a creditor's right to seize property without prior legal "exhaustion" of the debtor's other goods.</meta>

...[the right to] surrender. In that case, since possession of those items was transferred to the creditor through that fictitious act <note>A "fictitious act" in law refers to a legal procedure that treats a situation as if something has happened (like a physical transfer of goods) to achieve a legal effect</note>, it is sufficient for the kind of possession required for a <term>strict pledge</term> <note>original: "pignoris presse sumpti"; a pledge where the creditor has direct legal control over the item</note>, according to what was said in Dispute 534. Therefore, through that possession, these items are no longer held as a mere <term>naked mortgage</term> <note>original: "nudæ hypothecæ"; a claim on property where the owner keeps possession</note>, but as a true strict pledge. Consequently, even if the debtor should sell any of those things to someone else, the creditor can reclaim possession from that person through a legal claim <note>original: "condictione ex leg. vltim. C. de acq. poſſ."</note> so that they may receive what is owed from that item, without needing to first seize the rest of the debtor's property. This would not be the case if it were a naked mortgage, where possession (at least through a fictitious act) did not belong to the creditor; in that instance, a third-party possessor could object, demanding that the debtor’s and the legal backers’ other assets be seized first, as was shown in that same dispute.

# When a guarantee ends. And when a guarantor can compel the debtor to release them from the guarantee obligation: or to pay back what was paid on their behalf. And how far the guarantor is bound to defend the case, or the debtor.

## DISPUTE 546.

### SUMMARY.

1. A guarantee is not ended by the death of the guarantor, but passes to the heirs.
2. The various ways a guarantee obligation is extinguished, and in numbers 4 and 5.
3. Whether a guarantor is released from the obligation in a case of <term>eviction</term> <note>The legal loss of property to a third party who has a better claim</note> regarding what was paid by the debtor, or something similar.
> Also, in a case where the creditor extends the deadline set for the debtor’s payment. number 6.
> A guarantor cannot sue the principal debtor using an <term>action of mandate</term> <note>A legal claim used to recover costs incurred while carrying out a task for another</note> or an action for business managed, to be released from the guarantee obligation. However, this fails in many cases or events, as in number 8 and following.
> And concerning the law of Castile in the first event. Ibid.
13. How much a creditor’s negligence in demanding the debt from the principal debtor benefits the guarantor toward their release.
14. A guarantor who pays while ignoring the legal defenses or arguments that could have been raised: what kind of action of mandate they can bring against the principal debtor to reclaim what they paid for them.
> And what if the omitted defense was <term>peremptory</term> <note>A defense that completely destroys the legal grounds of the claim</note>; whether it will harm them, and when. number 15.
16. A peremptory defense knowingly omitted by the guarantor harms that same guarantor, and not the debtor. This is limited and explained there.

1. All these matters must be explained together for the most part. First, however, the guarantee obligation does not end because the guarantor departs from this life;

<column-break/>

rather, it passes to his heirs, along with all the rights and defenses that were available to the guarantor. This is held in the title "On Guarantors" in the Institutes, the Digest, and the Code, as well as the <term>Siete Partidas</term> <note>The 13th-century Spanish statutory code; Molina refers to Law 16, Title 12, Part 5</note>.

2. When the debt is paid—whether by the principal debtor, his heirs, the guarantors, or anyone else—or if the debt is canceled by the creditor, the guarantee obligation expires entirely, as is established in the Institutes regarding how obligations are removed. This is clear enough from what was said previously: because of the payment, the debt upon which the guarantee obligation rests simply ceases to exist in the eyes of the creditor.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
3. If the principal debtor gave something as payment, and it was later <term>evicted</term> <note>Legally taken away because the debtor didn't actually own it</note>, the doubt is whether the guarantor remains released, or whether—if the debtor later becomes unable to pay or the guarantor waived the right to prior seizure—the guarantor can be forced to pay. It must be said, following the <term>Speculator</term> <note>William Durand, a famous 13th-century jurist</note> and <margin>Decision</margin> Antonio Gomez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13, number 20), that the guarantor does not remain released but can be forced to pay. This is because the debtor and guarantor are not released except by a true and valid payment of the debt, which that was not, according to the arguments in the Digest.

If, however, the guarantor or his heirs pay the debt—whether forced or voluntarily outside of court—in an event where the debt was clear and no legitimate defense existed, the guarantor (or heirs) who pays has an <term>action of mandate</term> against the principal debtor. Indeed, they also have the legal actions that the creditor had against that same debtor (if the creditor assigns those rights to them, as he is bound to do, according to Dispute 544), so that they may recover from the debtor what they paid in his place. However, if the debt was only due on a certain day or under a certain condition, and the guarantor pays before that day or before the condition is met, then they have no action of mandate or any other claim against the debtor to recover it until that day arrives or the condition is fulfilled. This is held in the Digest under the title "On Mandate" and the aforementioned law 16. A guarantor may, however, pay the creditor at the appropriate time using the principal debtor’s goods to free himself from the burden of the guarantee; in that case, he commits neither theft nor violence, because there is no malice or fraud, but rather he does it for a just cause. This is held in the Digest and affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez cites.

<margin>4</margin>
4. Likewise, a guarantee obligation expires if a <term>novation</term> <note>The replacement of an old contract with a new one</note> of the principal obligation is made between the debtor and creditor, and the guarantor does not consent to it or become a guarantor for the new debt. This is held in the Code and the Digest. In these latter legal sources, it is held that a pledge and a mortgage are released by a novation of the obligation; the same reasoning applies to guarantors given for the security of that same obligation.

<summary>This page discusses the termination of guarantee obligations, noting that they survive the guarantor's death through their heirs but are extinguished by valid payment or contract novation. It also details the guarantor's right to seek reimbursement from the debtor, provided the payment was legally sound and made at the proper time.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 546. 731

...is a **novation** <note>original: "nouatio"; the legal act of replacing an existing obligation with a new one</note>, and this is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez refers to and follows in the cited number 20. What exactly a novation is will be discussed later in its proper place.

<margin>5</margin> Likewise, a **guarantee obligation** <note>original: "fideiufforia obligatio"</note> expires when the guarantor succeeds the principal debtor, or conversely, when the principal debtor succeeds the guarantor. This is because, when both obligations are joined in the same person, the principal obligation—namely that of the debtor—prevails, and the less important, accessory obligation of the guarantor expires. This is according to the law *generaliter* and the law *cum reus* in the Digest regarding guarantors. The reason is that one must always prioritize the principal and stronger obligation, since the other adds nothing new, nor any extension to anything else, based on the arguments of others which Antonio Gómez cites above. However, when someone has stood as a guarantor for another who was bound only by a **natural obligation** <note>An obligation that is morally binding but not traditionally enforceable by a civil lawsuit</note> and not a **civil** one, then—because the guarantor is bound civilly, as explained in Disputation 539—whether the guarantor succeeds the principal debtor or vice versa, such a successor is bound by both obligations. This is because each serves the creditor and has its own particular strength and some effect beyond the other. This is expressly stated in the law *hēres à debitore*, section *quod si hic*, in the Digest on guarantors. By this same reasoning, if a guarantor becomes the heir to the principal debtor and creates an **inventory** <note>A legal list of assets and liabilities to limit the heir's personal liability for the deceased's debts</note>, even though as an heir (and thus as the principal debtor) he is not liable beyond the value of the inheritance (as discussed in Disputation 210), he is nonetheless liable as a guarantor from his own person and assets for whatever is lacking in the deceased's estate. Therefore, because in this event some special force remains from the guarantee obligation in such an heir for that specific effect, the guarantee obligation does not expire entirely but remains joined with the principal one. This follows Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, and Antonio Gómez as cited above. But I wish that the law would cut away that **subtlety** (and other similar ones) of the pagan <note>original: "ethnicorum"</note> jurists regarding the expiration of an accessory obligation when joined in the same person with a principal one. It would be better to say that both remain, as there is no legitimate reason why one should vanish. Nevertheless, when the accessory obligation has no new power or effect beyond the principal one, prudent reason prescribes that the creditor should act based on the principal rather than the accessory obligation. If this very true doctrine were handed down and accepted, that other firm but barely true notion would cease, and with it the difficulties, the complexity of difficult laws, and new fuel for lawsuits would vanish. For this reason, I do not follow the other limitations which Antonio Gómez provides above, since they should be similarly evaluated according to the doctrine I have just delivered.

<margin>Question</margin> Furthermore, if the creditor extends the **deadline** <margin>6</margin> fixed for payment to the debtor, are the guarantors released from their obligation? Speculator and others cited by Antonio Gómez in chapter 13, number 21, answered in the affirmative. They were led by the idea that when the payment deadline is extended, it is considered a novation of the debt. However, the contrary must be said, following Antonio Gómez and the common opinion of the doctors he refers to. For today, as held in the final law of the Code regarding novations, by an extension of the deadline

<column-break/>

or any other variation made in the obligation, a novation is not considered to have occurred unless the contracting parties expressly state that they are withdrawing from the prior obligation and substituting and embracing the second in its place.

<margin>7</margin> A guarantor **cannot sue** by an action of **mandate** <note>original: "mandati"; a lawsuit based on a contract where one person performs a service for another</note> or an action for **business managed** <note>original: "negotiorum gestorum"; a lawsuit where someone acted for another's benefit without a prior contract</note> against the principal debtor to force them to release him from the guarantee obligation he undertook for him or his predecessor, except in the events I will list below. This is according to the law *si pro ea* in the Code, the law *Lucius* in the Digest, and Law 14, Title 12 of the fifth *Partida*. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors which, besides Gregorio López, is referred to and followed by Antonio Gómez and Alvaro Valasco.

<margin>8</margin> The first case in which a guarantor can act against the principal debtor and compel him to release him from the guarantee is if he has stood as a guarantor for **a long time**. This is found in the law *Lucius* and the final chapter on guarantors, and in Law 24, Title 12 of the fifth *Partida*. Furthermore, as to when one should be considered to have been in that obligation for "a long time": although some have said if he was in it for two years he should be called "long," and others say ten years, the cited law *Lucius* clearly teaches that this should be left to the **judge’s discretion**. The judge must weigh the quality of the debtor, what was agreed between the parties, and other concurrent circumstances; this is affirmed by the gloss there and the common opinion of the doctors, and it is enacted in the cited Law 14. Although Antonio Gómez says this is limited and moderated today by Law 8, Title 18, Book 3 of the *Fuero* <note>A local or municipal code of laws in Spain</note>—which stipulates that if no term was prescribed, the guarantor can compel the debtor to release him after one year has passed—Gregorio López rightly says on the cited Law 14 that we should nonetheless stand by the disposition of Law 14 of the *Partidas*. This is because that *Fuero* law is not accepted in practice, and in the **Kingdom of Castile** specifically, the laws of the *Fuero* do not override the laws of the *Partidas* unless it is proven they have been accepted by custom, as has often been said. It must be observed regarding this event we are discussing that if a deadline was fixed by which the debtor was supposed to fulfill the obligation for which the guarantor was given, the guarantor **cannot** compel the debtor to release him before that deadline arrives, nor before the principal debtor is in **default** <term>mora</term> <note>A legal state of delay or failure to perform an obligation on time</note> in performing what he bound himself to do, even if he has been in that guarantee for a long time. Likewise, if someone had subjected one of their properties to a **pledge** or **mortgage** <note>original: "pignori, aut hypothecæ"</note> as security for the same debt for a debtor, they could not, before that deadline and default, compel the debtor to release the property from that burden (for the law *Lucius* speaks of both matters). Similarly, if it is clear from the nature of the contract that someone intended to serve as a guarantor for a very long time or forever—for example, if a guarantor stood with a mortgage for a seller to guarantee that the item sold would not be **evicted** <note>original: "euinceretur"; a legal term for when a buyer loses a property because someone else has a better legal title to it</note>—the guarantor's obligation remains as long as the item is not evicted. The guarantor cannot compel the seller to release him from that obligation, but must blame himself for having voluntarily taken on that burden...

<summary>This page discusses when a guarantee obligation is legally terminated, particularly through inheritance or "novation," and examines when a guarantor has the right to force a debtor to release them from their commitment, emphasizing the role of judicial discretion and Spanish customary law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 546 of the second treatise, examining the specific legal "events" or scenarios under which a guarantor (fideiussor) has the right to compel the principal debtor to release them from their obligation, even before the debt has been fully settled with the creditor.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

...he wished to undergo the burden, by binding himself to it. And this is indeed what the law *Lucius* <note>A specific law in the Roman Digest (D. 17.1.38)</note> means when it leaves it to the judge's discretion to decide when he ought to compel the debtor to free another's property from the burden of a mortgage, or to free a guarantor from a **guarantee obligation** <note>original: "fideiussoria obligatione"</note>, after weighing what was agreed between the contracting parties and other concurrent circumstances. This is the same point that Antonio Gómez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> makes in the cited number 10, when he infers that a guarantor providing security that a thing will not be **evicted** <note>original: "euincetur"; the legal loss of property to a third party with a better claim</note> cannot, while it is not being evicted, ask to be freed from the guarantee obligation, even if it is never evicted in perpetuity. Likewise, he infers that a guarantor for a **tutor or curator** <note>Legal guardians for minors or those unable to manage their own affairs</note> cannot ask to be released before the guardianship or curatorship ends.

Therefore, a **default** <note>original: "mora"; a legal delay</note> in payment on the part of the debtor is required according to the form of the contract so that the guarantor can compel him to free him from the guarantee obligation. This is because the debtor was already able and ought to have paid according to that form—for instance, because the deadline set for the debtor’s satisfaction has already passed. Or, even if a certain deadline was not fixed (as when he received a loan with a guarantor without a set date for repayment, but it was left to the creditor's will to demand it whenever he wished), the creditor has now demanded it, or equity demanded that the debtor should have already paid it. In similar events, it is left to the judge's discretion to define whether the guarantor has remained in the guarantee obligation so long that he can now compel the debtor to free him from that burden. This is surely what Alvarez Valasco <note>A contemporary legal consultant</note> seems to mean in his cited consultation 36, number 1, when he explains this first scenario in these words: "when the debtor has ceased to pay the debt for a long time." Indeed, this is clearly what the law *Lucius* and the final chapter *On Guarantors* <note>original: "ca. vlti. de fideius."; a reference to Canon Law</note> mean, handing down the same scenario in the same words.

However, I approve of what the same Alvarez Valasco adds in the same consultation: namely, when two **debtors** <note>original: "rei debendi"</note> are bound **jointly and severally** <note>original: "in solidum"; where each person is responsible for the entire debt</note>, either for some debt or some contract, and reason demands that the co-debtor should now pay or that the contract should end, one of them can compel the co-debtor to free him from that burden as he desires. For the same reason, it similarly pertains to the judge to decide whether, considering the concurrent circumstances, a co-debtor or co-debtors ought to free the one demanding it from the obligation by which he is held for them.

9 **The second scenario is:** When the guarantor has been condemned in court to pay part or all of the principal debt. For he can immediately act against the debtor to free him from the guarantee, by paying the creditor or by another means, even before he is forced to pay it himself. This is held in law *Lucius*, joined with the final gloss there in the Digest *on mandates*; the law *if a guarantor for a seller* in the Digest *on guarantors*; the law *if for her* in the Code *on mandates*; the final chapter *on guarantors*; and law 14, title 12, part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish law code</note>. The same applies if **execution** <note>The legal process of seizing assets</note> is already being carried out against the guarantor based on a **guaranty instrument** <note>original: "instrumento guarentigio"; a notarized document allowing for immediate debt enforcement</note>, as Gregorio López <note>A famous commentator on the *Siete Partidas*</note> rightly affirms along with others whom he cites. However, it is otherwise before execution is made against him from that instrument, as Antonio Gómez rightly affirms against certain others at the end of his cited number 10.

10 **The third:** If the principal debtor begins to **squander his assets** <note>original: "dilapidare bona sua"</note>, so that there is a danger that at the time of

<column-break/>

payment he will not be **solvent** <note>original: "soluendo"; having enough money to pay</note>. This is held in law *Lucius*, the law *if for her*, the final chapter, and law 14, cited above. Gregorio López, in the same place in the final gloss, says with Alberico that if someone were a guarantor for two co-debtors, and one of them begins to squander his assets in the aforementioned way, he can act against both to free himself from the guarantee. I believe this is true when some danger to himself would be imminent from it.

11 **The fourth:** If the guarantor—upon the arrival of the deadline set for payment—offers payment due to fear of some penalty or for another reason, and either the creditor does not wish to receive it, or, even if he did wish to, because he is a **minor** <note>original: "minor"; a person under the age of 25 in Roman law</note> and the guarantor fears that if he hands it over, it might later be reclaimed from him by the benefit of **total restitution** <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum"; a legal remedy for minors to undo disadvantageous transactions</note>, he deposits it in a sacred place, or another place deputed for that purpose, or with a public or other suitable depository. For then, even if the guarantor has not been condemned to pay, nor has actually paid the creditor in any other way, he can act against the debtor to free him from the guarantee burden, or have the debtor pay him what he thus offered and deposited in his place. This is held in the law *a guarantor who to a minor* in the Digest *on guarantors*; the law *who a loan*, section *guarantor* in the Digest *on mandates*; and the cited law 14.

12 **The fifth:** When the guarantor entered into a **pact** <note>original: "pactum"; an agreement</note> with the debtor that after a certain time, the debtor would be bound to release him from the guarantee, or whenever the guarantor should ask for it. For then, upon the arrival of that term or upon the guarantor asking for it—even if nothing of what has been said so far has intervened, nor has the creditor been satisfied—he can act against the debtor to free him from the guarantee. This is held in the law *for her* in the Code *on mandates* and the cited law 14.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
13 **A doubt arises:** If, when the time arrived in which the debt was to be paid to the creditor, the creditor was negligent in seeking or receiving it, and later the debtor became insolvent, is the guarantor then freed from the burden of paying the creditor in place of the debtor that which the debtor was later found unable to pay? Antonio Gómez, in volume 2 of *Various Resolutions*, 13, number 9, distinguishes this very well. Either the guarantor was only for **indemnity** <note>A guarantee only against the loss itself, rather than a guarantee of the debt's performance</note>, according to what was said in the preceding Disputation 17, or he was an ordinary or common guarantor.

<margin>Decision</margin>
In the first case, he says: the guarantor is freed from the burden of paying by the very fact that the debtor later became incapable of paying—not only if the creditor was requested by such a guarantor to demand his debt and compel the debtor to pay then, but even if he was not requested by him. The reason is that he only guaranteed that the creditor would be **indemnified** <note>kept free from loss</note> at the time of payment, and he truly would have been indemnified then if he had demanded the debt; let him blame himself that he did not demand it then and that he was not made free from loss. And this very point is proven by the law *if guarantors for that* (otherwise law *guarantors if*) in the Digest *on guarantors*, joined with the gloss there on the word "useful"; and the gloss on the law *if a guarantor to a creditor* in the same title asserts the same. This is also the opinion of Bartolus <note>The most influential medieval jurist</note> and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez refers to in cited number 9. And indeed, regarding a dowry, if someone had only guaranteed that the debtor had sufficient goods from which to pay, and in the event that it was found the matter was not so, he would pay what was missing; then, if it happened by a **fortuitous event** <note>an accident or act of God</note> that before the time destined for payment, the debtor lost...
<meta>catchword: lost (teret)</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 546.

...he might lose his goods, or destroy them through his own wickedness, when nevertheless, had that not happened, he would have been found to have a good conscience at the time of payment. In such a case, this **guarantor of indemnity** <note>original: "indemnitatis fideiussor"; a specific type of guarantor who only covers the loss if the debtor's assets are insufficient</note> would be held to nothing: because he did not obligate himself to anything else than that the debtor would have sufficient goods from which to pay. Since that was true at the time of the agreement, he did not obligate himself for what might happen afterward.

In the second scenario, however—namely, when the guarantor was a "common" or ordinary guarantor—Antonio Gómez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> says that the guarantor is held liable, at least according to the ancient law of the **Digest** and the **Code** <note>The primary components of the Corpus Iuris Civilis, the body of Roman Law</note>. This is because the obligation of a guarantor was absolute and simple, and it was entirely within the creditor’s power to compel the guarantor to pay without first seizing the goods of the principal debtor, bypassing the principal debtor entirely. This is expressly stated in the law *Si fideiussor creditori* in the Digest, under the title "On Guarantors" <note>original: "ff. de fideiuss."; ff. is the standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest</note>, even if the guarantor warned the creditor to sue the debtor and force him to pay. 

However, after the laws of the **Authentica** <note>A collection of Justinian’s later laws (Novels) that modified the earlier Roman legal codes</note>, which introduced the "exception of prior seizure" <term>beneficium excussionis; the right of a guarantor to demand that the creditor first attempt to collect the debt from the principal debtor’s assets before coming to the guarantor</term>, Antonio Gómez correctly states that the same old law applies if the guarantor renounced that right. By renouncing it, the parties agree to abide by the ancient law within that contract. 

But if the guarantor did *not* renounce his rights under the *Authentica*, and if, when the time for payment arrives, he requests the creditor to sue the debtor and seize his goods, and the creditor neglects to do so out of negligence, and the debtor subsequently becomes unable to pay, the guarantor shall be released from that amount which the debtor later could not pay. This is based on the argument in the law *Si fideiussores* and the present *Authentica* in the Code under the same title. 

Yet, if the guarantor does not request the creditor to compel the debtor to pay at the time the debt is due, then even if the creditor is slow to act and the debtor later becomes insolvent, the guarantor is not excused. He must pay in the debtor's place for whatever is found to be unpayable. The reason is that just as a guarantor would be legally compelled to pay if the creditor sued him immediately and the guarantor failed to raise the "exception of prior seizure," so too—and with much greater reason—if the guarantor fails to demand the creditor pursue the debtor, he will not be excused from paying the whole debt later if the debtor becomes unable to pay. This is the view held by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canonist</note> and many others cited by Antonio Gómez at number 9.

### 14. 
When a guarantor, having been sued <insert>†</insert> for the debt of a principal debtor, pays the debt while neglecting to use the legal exceptions or defenses that could have been raised, the question arises: does he then have an **action of mandate** <term>actio mandati; a legal claim to be reimbursed by the person on whose behalf you acted</term> against the principal debtor to recover what he paid? We must make a distinction. 

The exception he could have raised might have been merely "declinatory of the judgment" <note>an objection to the court's jurisdiction</note> or in some other way "dilatory" <note>an objection that merely delays the proceedings without ending the claim</note> rather than "peremptory" <note>a defense that permanently kills the legal claim</note>, even considering the guarantor alone. In that 

<column-break/>

event, even if the guarantor knowingly and prudently omits the defense and pays, he still has the right to an action of mandate against the principal debtor to be paid back. 

**Exception:** If the dilatory exception was based on the fact that the time for payment had not yet arrived, or because a condition for the debt had not yet been fulfilled, and the guarantor pays anyway despite omitting that defense, he does have an action of mandate to be satisfied by the debtor—but *only* after the time for payment has passed or the condition has been met. This is discussed below regarding the law *Si mandauerit tibi pro me in die* <note>original: "If he mandated to you for me on [a certain] day"</note> in the Digest under the title "On Mandate." 

In this scenario, I believe the final gloss on the law *Si pro ea* in the Code is correct. It distinguishes a declinatory exception from other dilatory ones. It agrees with us that if the exception is merely dilatory regarding the payment, the guarantor may not sue before the day of payment arrives. This does not apply to the scenario we explained earlier, which is the only thing that law refers to. 

Regarding other exceptions that would only delay the litigation, and thereby accidentally delay payment: those would not block the guarantor's claim. Since the principal debtor truly owes the debt at that time, if the guarantor pays it to free both himself and the debtor from an obligation that was truly due, he can use the action of mandate to force the debtor to pay him back. 

That a guarantor who pays while omitting dilatory exceptions has a claim against the debtor is shown in the law *Si fideiussor* § *quaedam* in the Digest. An example is given there of a guarantor who pays the creditor’s agent without objecting that the agent was not legally qualified (for instance, because the agent was a soldier, a woman, or excommunicated), even if the guarantor knew about the objection. 

This does not contradict the law *Inter causas* § *mandato* in the Digest. There it says that if I became a guarantor for you and paid the creditor’s agent, I can immediately sue you to get my money back *if* he was a true agent. But if he was not a true agent, but merely lied and pretended to be one, I cannot sue you; I must instead recover the money from the false agent. This rule does not conflict with our teaching. In that paragraph, the action of mandate is denied not because the guarantor failed to object to the agent’s status, but because he did not actually pay the creditor or any authorized person. Therefore, the payment did not release the guarantor or the debtor from the original debt. Thus, the guarantor is rightly denied an action of mandate against the 
<meta>catchword: debtor,</meta>

# Louis Molina: On Contracts

...the matter, but only the recovery of what he paid, from the one who is retired, that he is the representative <note>original: "procuratorem"</note> of the debtor, as if to him it were truly not owed, but owed only to the creditor, or to a person truly substituted in the place of the creditor. If, therefore, the Gloss on the cited paragraph *quædam*, Gregorio López <note>A prominent Spanish jurist, 1496–1560</note> on Law 15, Title 12, Part 5 at the word *remate*, Azo, and others whom Gregorio López cites, seem to oppose our teaching—as if, in the paragraph *mandato*, the action of mandate <term>actio mandati; the legal right of a guarantor to sue the debtor for reimbursement</term> is denied to a guarantor paying in that manner because he did not object that he was not the debtor's representative, and as if a dilatory defense <term>exceptio dilatoria; a temporary legal delay</term> is given which, if not opposed, hinders the action of mandate by itself, as he seems to suggest, and not rather from the head explained by us—certainly their opinion is not approved by us. Rather, the contrary opinion of Baldus, along with Jacobus de Belloviso (whom the same Gregorio López cites), is preferred, provided these authors conceded that to one paying in this way, the action of mandate is denied based on the principle we explained, as is clearly denied to him in the cited paragraph *mandato*.

<margin>15</margin>
But if the defense <note>original: "exceptio"</note> which the guarantor <note>original: "fideiussor"</note> failed to raise was peremptory <term>exceptio peremptoria; a defense that permanently kills the creditor's claim</term>, a distinction must again be made. For it was either available to the person of the guarantor as well as the debtor—as regularly, a defense available to the debtor is also available to the guarantor by reason of him (as in the law *De exceptionibus* and other rights)—or it was available only to the guarantor, or only to the debtor. If it was available to both—such as the defense that the money was never actually counted out <note>original: "non numeratæ fuisse pecuniam"; a defense used when a loan was promised but the cash never actually handed over</note> to the debtor for whom the guarantor was given, or that the debt had already been paid by the debtor, or had been forgiven by the creditor, or a pact had intervened that the creditor would not seek it from the debtor, or that he would seek it from neither the debtor nor the guarantor (it is otherwise, however, if a pact only intervened between the creditor and the guarantor, where the creditor promised the guarantor he would not seek the debt from him, because then that peremptory defense would belong only to the guarantor if the debt were sought from him, but would not belong to the debtor if the creditor sought it from him, as Gregorio López well notes on the cited Law 15 at the word *a el fiador*) and as there are other similar cases: then either the guarantor, knowing and prudent, omitted raising that peremptory defense, or he did so while ignorant. This ignorance is not "gross negligence" <note>original: "lata culpa"</note>, which is compared to fraud and thus to knowledge in this part (as expressly stated in Law 6 *fideiussor* at the beginning, in the Digest *Mandati*), but a fault lighter than gross negligence. If the guarantor, being ignorant of that defense by a fault lighter than gross, omitted raising it, then the ignorance was either of law or of fact. If he omitted it through ignorance of the law, then the action of mandate against the debtor is not available to him, as in the cited law *si fideiussor*, paragraph *non malè*, and as the Gloss affirms there. However, if he paid what was not owed for that reason, he has a claim for recovery <term>repetitio; the right to demand money back</term> against the creditor, unless perhaps the creditor protects himself with the defense of a "judged matter" <note>original: "rei iudicatæ"; a final court judgment that cannot be reopened</note>, as in the cited law *si fideiussor*, paragraph *in omnibus*. In this, however, one must be careful: if the creditor knowingly accepts what is not owed, he is charged with the crime of swindling <term>stellionatus; a category of fraud in Roman law involving dishonest dealings</term>, as is added in the same place. See also in the Gloss at the word *cessat*; when it cannot be recovered from him by a claim for the return of un-owed money <note>original: "condictione indebiti"</note>, it might nonetheless be recovered by other actions. If, however, the guarantor omitted raising it through ignorance of fact, then the action

<column-break/>

of mandate against the debtor is available to him, even if the defense was that the debtor had already paid the same debt: because the debtor was bound to warn the guarantor of that payment. So it is in the cited law *si fideiussor* at the beginning and the following paragraphs, and in the law *si procuratorem*, paragraph *si ignoranter*, in the Digest under the same title. In that case, either the debtor will recover from the creditor via a claim for un-owed money what was paid to him a second time by the guarantor, or the guarantor himself will recover the same from him by the same claim, as he is able. If, however, the guarantor pays before the debtor, and then the debtor pays again, then if the guarantor could have conveniently warned the debtor but did not, the action of mandate against the debtor is not given to him; instead, the debtor is only bound to cede his action against the creditor to him, so that he may recover it as un-owed, since it was paid to him a second time. But if he could not conveniently warn the debtor, or did warn him and the debtor, having forgotten, paid again, then the action of mandate against the debtor is available to the guarantor. All these things are contained in the cited law *si fideiussor*, paragraph *hoc idem*.

<margin>16.</margin>
If the guarantor, knowingly or through gross negligence, failed to raise such a peremptory defense, then the action of mandate against the debtor is not available to him. Instead, if any action is available to him, it is for recovering from the creditor what he paid him, unless, as has been said, the defense of a "judged matter" stands in the way. So it is in the cited law *si fideiussor* at the beginning, joined with the paragraph *in omnibus*, and Law 6 *procuratorem*, paragraph *si ignoranter* in the Digest *Mandati*, and Law *si pro ea* at the end of the Code under the same title, and Law 15, Title 12, Part 5; and the two cited Glosses affirm this. The reason is the same if the guarantor could and should have appealed from a sentence by which he was ordered to pay, or by which he was ordered to pay more than was owed, and he did not appeal: for then the action of mandate against the debtor is not available to him. An exception is made unless he had warned the principal debtor to appeal himself and bear the expenses, if the debtor judged it expedient, or unless because of his own poverty he did not dare to appeal. This is held in Law 6 *procuratorem*, paragraph *si ignoranter*, at the end, in the Digest *Mandati*. As to how far the guarantor can raise a defense that was available to the principal debtor, even against that debtor's will; and that the debtor ought to hand over to him the instruments and other things necessary to prove it; and that he is bound to provide the expenses to him even while the lawsuit is pending to prosecute the case—because the business of the debtor is being conducted in that part—read Gregorio López on the cited Law 15 at the words *tambien a el*.

When a peremptory defense is available only to the guarantor and not to the debtor—as the Velleian defense <term>exceptio Velleiani; a legal protection based on the Senatus Consultum Velleianum which allowed women to void contracts where they acted as guarantors</term> is available to a female guarantor—then, even if the guarantor, knowing and prudent, omits it and pays the debt, the action of mandate against the debtor is available to her, so that he may return to her what she paid in his place. The reason, however, is that the debtor truly owed it, and it was paid in his place; and the guarantor kept the faith, even though she was not bound to keep it, but could have defended herself with that exception. This is held in the law *si fideiussor*, last paragraph, in the Digest *Mandati*, and the second to last law and the last law, paragraph *si mulier*, in the Digest *ad Velleianum*, and Law 15, Title 12, Part 5. Nor does it matter that in the law *idemque*, in the paragraph *et generaliter* in the Digest *Mandati*, mention is only made when the defense would be base or shameful for the guarantor if he raised it: because, as the Gloss explains there, it is to be understood especially...

...in such a way that even if the defense is not shameful to him <note>original: "foeda illi non sit"</note>, and he does not raise it, the action of mandate <term>actio mandati; the right to sue the debtor for reimbursement</term> nonetheless belongs to the guarantor.

Finally, when a peremptory defense <term>exceptio peremptoria; a defense that permanently cancels a debt</term> is available only to the debtor and not to his guarantor—such as the one enjoyed by partners regarding the shared poverty of other partners <note>This refers to the "benefit of competence," where a debtor cannot be stripped of their basic means of survival</note>, and many others which we explained in Disputation 413 and thereafter in the progress of this work: those who, when sued by certain creditors, enjoy a privilege in comparison to them, so that they are not held liable for more than they can conveniently pay, so as not to be in want. When, I say, a peremptory defense is available only to the debtor in the manner explained, then even if the guarantor does not raise it, the action of mandate is available to him against the debtor for whom he paid. An exception is made unless, knowing that the defense was available to the debtor and being able to warn him so that he might defend himself in person or through a representative, the guarantor neglected to warn him; for then the action of mandate is not available to him against the debtor, which I understand to apply to the extent that the debtor could have protected himself from that debt through that defense. This is held in the cited paragraph *Generaliter*. At the end of Disputation 413, we explained two ways in which a guarantor, even if he does not enjoy the defense the debtor enjoys, can nevertheless protect himself so that execution is not made against him for more than what leaves the principal debtor with enough to live. But the cited law says that even if the guarantor does not protect himself in those ways when he could, he still has the action of mandate against the principal debtor; and this is what Gregorio López <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> intends and teaches in his penultimate gloss there. I understand this, however, provided that, according to the cited paragraph *Generaliter*, he warns the debtor to defend himself if he wishes, if it can be conveniently done.

### On guarantors in court.

#### DISPUTATION 542.
#### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> 1. A guarantor in court is given in both civil and criminal cases.
<margin>2</margin> 2. What kind of guarantors a judge ought to accept in court, lest he himself face risk.
<margin>3</margin> 3. A guarantor for a defendant accused of a crime cannot be bound to a corporal penalty, but only a monetary one for producing him in court. This is declared and limited, as noted there.
<margin>4</margin> 4. When a defendant promising to appear in court at a certain time is excluded from the "cleansing of delay" <term>purgatio morae; a legal excuse for being late</term>. And what holds regarding the law of Castile.

<column-break/>

<margin>5</margin> 5. When a guarantor for a defendant appearing in court within a certain time falls under a penalty if he does not produce him within that time. And what holds regarding the laws of Castile and Portugal.
<margin>6</margin> 6. A caution for judges when they accept a guarantor under a specific penalty for producing a defendant in court within a certain time.
<margin>7</margin> 7. When a guarantor under a specific penalty for producing a defendant in court within a fixed time has the choice of defending him after that time has elapsed.
And what if the defendant dies—when he is understood to be freed from the penalty. Number 8.
And also, if no penalty is established, what penalty he can be punished with by the judge because of the delay. Number 9.
Likewise, if no time is established for the appearance, how he can be punished.

At the end of Disputation 539, we promised this disputation as a complement to those things said there regarding guarantors of this kind.
<margin>1</margin> A guarantor in court is sometimes given in a civil case—in which that distinction mainly applies between a guarantor for paying the judgment <note>original: "fideiussoris iudicati solui"</note>, whom they call in Spanish a *fiador de saneamiento* <note>A guarantor who ensures the settlement or "cleansing" of the debt</note>, and a guarantor only for appearing in court <note>original: "fideiussoris iudicio sisti solum"</note>, whom they call a *fiador de la haz* <note>Literally a "guarantor of the face," ensuring the defendant shows up in person</note>; regarding this distinction, it was spoken of in the cited Disputation 539. Sometimes, however, he is given in a criminal case for a defendant accused of a crime, if he is in court, so that by that means the defendant may be released from prison. And sometimes a defendant is removed from public prison, and a certain house is granted to him, or even a town as a "prison," once guarantors have been given that he will keep to that prison and appear in court when he is required; this is passed down by Giulio Claro <note>Italian jurist, 1525–1575</note> in his *Sentences*, book 5, final section, question 46, number 11.
<margin>2</margin> In number 12, he adds how a judge † ought to accept suitable <note>original: "idoneos"</note> guarantors, lest he later face personal risk. And in numbers 14 and 15, he adds when a sworn security <note>original: "iuratoria cautio"</note> from the defendant suffices for him to be released from chains.

---

<margin>3</margin> A guarantor for a defendant † accused of a crime, when a corporal penalty hangs over such a defendant—such as death, mutilation, whipping, or another—cannot be bound to undergo that penalty, or any other corporal penalty for him. This is because a guarantor is not the master of his own limbs so as to subject them to punishment without his own fault; nor does equity allow him to be punished in his body without his own fault, because that would be against the fourth commandment of the Decalogue <note>In the numbering Molina uses, this likely refers to the sanctity of life or the limits of human authority over the body. Scholastic law generally held that one cannot contract away their physical person.</note>. Thus the gloss on the chapter *Cum homo*, at the word *supplicium* <note>Gratian's Decretum, Case 23, Question 5</note>, accepted by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, 1386–1445</note> under the title "On Guarantors," and by the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias <note>Spanish jurist, 1512–1577</note> and Giulio Claro cite and follow; and the law *Si quis reum* <note>Digest 48.3.4</note> agrees. But if the guarantor were at fault for the defendant’s flight—for instance, because he deceitfully took him into his trust so that he might flee and escape punishment—then indeed, because of this fault of his, he could be punished by the judge with an arbitrary penalty, even a corporal one, if the guarantor were worthy of such a great punishment, as the cited gloss, Panormitanus, and others rightly affirm, and as is held in the cited law *Si quis reum*. Because, therefore, a guarantor cannot be bound to a corporal penalty for a defendant, certainly when it is likely that a corporal penalty is to be inflicted on the defendant, he is not usually removed from chains even if guarantors are given to ensure he does not flee and escape corporal punishment, but he is instead usually detained in chains. Thus says Giulio Claro in the cited question 46, and others whom he cites.

<summary>This page discusses the legal limitations and obligations of guarantors in both civil and criminal contexts, establishing that a guarantor cannot be physically punished for a defendant's crime, as one does not have legal "mastery" over their own limbs to pledge them as collateral.</summary>

### Luis Molina On Contracts

...brings. Regarding a purely monetary penalty, a guarantor <term>fideiussor; a person who takes responsibility for another's debt or appearance</term> can bind himself on behalf of a defendant <term>reus; the party being sued or charged</term> to ensure that the defendant stands trial—whether the case is civil concerning a debt (to prevent the defendant from being thrown into prison or to release him from it) or criminal. In criminal matters, this applies when the defendant is only to be punished with a fine, or even if he might face corporal punishment if the crime were proven, yet it remains likely that he is innocent or the evidence is not sufficient to warrant corporal punishment, as Julius Clarus states in the place cited above, number 10. In that same passage, he adds that such a defendant—the one just mentioned—is typically placed in chains at the time of sentencing so that he hears the judgment while held in custody. And not only in these circumstances can a guarantor bind himself to a monetary penalty (either a fixed amount or an uncertain amount to be determined by the court) to ensure the defendant pays, but he may even agree to be placed in chains himself until the full penalty is paid. This is because one can subject oneself even to the hardship of imprisonment on behalf of one’s neighbor. Observe, however, that even though this is called a "penalty" in relation to the guarantor, it does not strictly have the nature of a punishment for him; rather, it is merely a just loss <note>original: "iusti duntaxat detrimenti"</note> endured for his neighbor if the defendant flees and the guarantor cannot produce him in court. For nothing can strictly be considered a punishment unless it is imposed for one's own true fault.

4 When the defendant himself has promised to appear in court at a certain time or when summoned, under a specific penalty, and he fails to keep his promise and thus incurs the penalty, he is permitted to "purge the delay" <term>purgare moram; to rectify a legal default by performing the duty late</term> within two, three, five, or more days to avoid the penalty. This is allowed unless the delay has harmed the plaintiff’s case—for instance, if witnesses have died during that time who would have proven his case, or if a statute of limitations <term>praescriptio; a period after which a legal claim expires</term> ended during that interval, or if the case was worsened in any other way. In such cases, purging the delay is not permitted under common law. However, it is different under the law of Castile; there, one can purge the delay, but the plaintiff’s rights are preserved exactly as if those extra days had not passed. Therefore, those days will not be counted toward the statute of limitations in this Kingdom. This is held in Law 8, "if after three" in the Digest *On giving security* <note>original: "l. 8. si post tres ff. si quis cautionibus"</note>, and Law 36, Title 11, Part 5. But when the harm to the plaintiff resulting from the delay cannot be repaired (as when witnesses have died), then in this Kingdom, the delay would not be purged at that time for the purpose of the defendant avoiding the penalty. So says Gregorio López in his penultimate gloss there. Regarding the fact that a delay can be purged in more than five days to avoid a penalty, the first gloss on Law 8 says they should not be many days, but few, and it should be left to the judge's discretion how many there should be, considering the circumstances. Bartolus affirms the same thing regarding Law "continuous," paragraph "when so," and the paragraph "likewise he who an island" in the Digest *On verbal obligations* <note>original: "l. continuus §. cum ita, & §. item qui insulam ff. de verb. oblig."</note>, and it is sanctioned in the cited Law 36. That same Law 36 extends this to the guarantor (which Gregorio López interprets there as referring to the guarantor of a defendant in a civil suit), though the law "if after three" speaks only of the defendant. Regarding the guarantor, something else is sanctioned under common law, as I will add immediately.

<column-break/>

5 When someone acts as a guarantor for another, whether in a civil or criminal case, promising that he will produce the person in court within a certain time or otherwise pay a certain penalty: if he does not produce him within that time, he immediately incurs the penalty. However, he is not immediately forced to pay it. Instead, if the time within which he was supposed to produce the defendant was six months or less, he should be given the same amount of time again as was given at the beginning. In this extra time, he can purge the delay so that if he produces the defendant within that period, he avoids the penalty. But if at the start it was decided that he should produce the person within a space of time longer than six months, then, once that time has passed, he should only have six months to purge the delay in the manner explained. This is found in the law "we sanction," in the Code *On guarantors* <note>original: "l. sancimus, C. de fideiuss."</note>, and Law 17, Title 12, Part 5. This is the common opinion of the doctors, as Gregorio López confirms in his first gloss, following the common law. However, the cited Law 17 seems to speak only when someone is a guarantor for another in a criminal case, although that is not entirely certain, as Gregorio López weighs and interprets that law and Law 36, Title 11, Part 5 in various ways. <margin>Law of Castile.</margin> Read those. But observe that under the law of Castile, if the aforementioned penalty is not demanded from the guarantor within a year from the day he incurred it, it expires by prescription and can no longer be demanded from him. This is held in Law 3, Title 10, Book 5 of the *Ordinances*, which is Law 10, Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Collection*.

<margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> Under Portuguese law, in the third book of the *Ordinances*, Title 70: once the time in which the guarantor was supposed to produce the defendant in court under penalty has ended (whether that was six months or more or less), only one month is granted to him and his heirs to purge the delay in the explained manner and avoid the penalty. Once that month has passed, the penalty is immediately sent for execution.

6 Julius Clarus, in the cited Question 46, number 23, mentions Angelus <note>Angelus de Ubaldis, a famous 14th-century jurist</note> advising judges that when they accept a guarantor who is to produce a defendant within a certain time under penalty, they should make him renounce the law "we sanction" <note>original: "legi sancimus"</note> regarding that extra time for purging the delay. This ensures that as soon as the time expires in which he was bound to produce the defendant, the penalty is immediately executed. Since this law was introduced for the benefit of the guarantors, such a renunciation is valid according to the law "if anyone in writing" in the Code *On pacts* and the law "what by favor" in the Code *On laws*. He adds that in Milan, it is not customary to accept a guarantor who produces a defendant within a fixed time, but rather one who produces him under a certain penalty (either to pay the judgment or some other penalty) whenever and as often as he is required. Therefore, he says, all these issues cease to apply, because we are outside the case of the law "we sanction." In this same way, such guarantors have frequently been accepted in this Kingdom of Castile. I do not doubt, however, that just as defendants can, so too can such guarantors purge the delay even in this event within two, three, five, or a few other days at the discretion of the judge, according to the law "if after" in the Digest. Azo agrees with this, whom the gloss on the cited law "we sanction" mentions and follows on the words "to do this," and perhaps this was the intent of Law 36, Title 11, Part 5.

...it is certain that the guarantor must present the defendant in court. If the initial time has elapsed, a second period is granted to clear the delay <note>original: "purgandum moram"; a legal term for making up for a failure to meet a deadline</note> by presenting the defendant in court. If the guarantor chooses to defend the defendant during this second period, they may do so effectively, provided they did not waive this right of defense from the beginning. If they did waive it, they cannot defend him. Furthermore, if this second period passes and the guarantor has not chosen to defend the defendant, they are no longer permitted to offer a defense, even if they had not waived the right; instead, they are compelled to pay the penalty.

However, when the guarantor chooses to defend the defendant during the second period, they cannot abandon the case until the final sentence is passed, even if the defendant passes away during that time. Likewise, while the second period is still active, the guarantor is not permitted to simply present the defendant in court and thereby escape the penalty <note>The law implies that once the grace period begins, the guarantor has committed to a specific path of action</note>. This is established in the law "We command" (*iubemus*), in the section "But if" (*sin autem*), in the Code on Guarantors, and in Law 18, Title 12 of the Fifth *Partida* <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the primary legal code of Castile</note>.

In the explanation of the cited Law 18, it is added: If, after taking up the defense, a judgment is rendered in favor of the defendant, the guarantor is entirely freed from the penalty—despite not presenting the defendant at the appointed time or clearing the delay. However, if the judgment goes against the defendant, the one who took up the defense (in a criminal case) is bound, in the defendant's absence, to pay the penalty and all damages that the plaintiff suffered due to the crime, just as the defendant himself would have paid. I would add that they are also liable for the legal costs if the defender is also condemned to pay them.

To whom should the penalty be awarded? The cited Law 18 seems to say it should be awarded to the opposing party. Gregorio López <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> says this should be understood according to Bartolus's commentary on the law "If anyone [accuses] a defendant" regarding the custody of defendants. In that place, Bartolus states it is the custom for the penalty to be applied to the treasury <term>fiscus; the state or royal treasury</term>, unless the plaintiff or their representative stipulates it for themselves with the judge's consent. Julius Clarus confirms this same custom of applying it to the treasury in his 46th question. 

Law 18 adds that if the case was civil and the defendant is condemned, the guarantor is bound to pay the total amount for which the defendant was sued, and all subsequent damages (interpreted in the manner explained just above). However, they are not bound to pay the specific penalty they had restricted themselves to for failing to present the defendant; this is because they have already defended him, stood in his place during the trial, and paid everything the defendant would have paid had he appeared.

8. When a guarantor has bound themselves under a † fixed penalty to present someone in court within a certain time, if that defendant dies within that time, the guarantor remains free from the penalty. But if the defendant dies after that time has elapsed, during the extra time given to the guarantor to clear the delay, then that death does not free the guarantor; they are still bound to pay. This is held in the law "We decree" (*sancimus*), in the penultimate and final sections of the Code on Guarantors, and Law 19, Title 12 of the Fifth *Partida*. There, Gregorio López and others conclude that a hurdle arising during the grace period does not exempt one from a penalty already incurred.

9. When a guarantor † binds themselves to present someone in court by a certain day, but no 

<column-break/>

specific penalty was established, then, if they do not present him within that time, they ought to be punished by the judge with a discretionary fine—either larger or smaller, depending on the circumstances. The judge should increase it if the failure was caused by the guarantor's fault or deceit. This is according to the law "If anyone [accuses] a defendant" regarding the custody of defendants, and Law 19, Title 12 of the Fifth *Partida*. Believe, however, that in this event, the guarantor (like the defendant) can clear the delay within two, three, five, or a few other days at the judge's discretion, and this is primarily what Law 36, Title 13 of the Fifth *Partida* intended.

10. If someone † acts as a guarantor for another's appearance in court, and no time was set for when they should present him, we must distinguish how much time must pass before the guarantor is no longer bound. If no public document was made of this guarantee, and the cause is not a "public" one (such as one pertaining to the Prince or a town community), then if the guarantor is not required to present the defendant within two months, they are thereafter free from the obligation. 

This applies when the guarantor was provided before the "joinder of issue" <term>lis contestata; the formal start of a trial when the parties agree on the matter to be litigated</term>. If the guarantor was provided after the trial began, or if the trial began within those two months, then the guarantor's obligation does not expire in that way. Instead, they are bound to present him until the final judgment, unless they only obligated themselves to present him a single time. This follows the law "In Greek" (*græce*), and the commentaries of Bartolus and Alexander. If, however, a public document was drawn up, or the cause was a public one, the guarantor's obligation does not expire before three years have passed.

Julius Clarus, in his 46th question, advises that when a guarantor is taken for a defendant's appearance "whenever requested," a clause should be added stating they are bound even in the case of an appeal. Otherwise, they say, the guarantee expires once the final sentence is given in the first instance.
