<meta>This page continues Dispute 551 within the Second Treatise, focusing on the legal obligations and liabilities of a "manager of affairs" (negotiorum gestor)—someone who steps in to handle another person’s business without a formal contract. It specifically addresses who can sue whom and the different degrees of negligence for which a manager might be held responsible.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Dispute 551

<margin>5</margin> To the tutor <note>original: "tutori"; referring to a specific law in the Code of Justinian</note> under the title "On Management of Affairs." Indeed, a manager of affairs cannot bring a legal action belonging to the person whose business they are managing, because they lack the necessary mandate <term>mandate: a formal legal authorization or contract of agency</term> and authority to do so. For this reason, if they attempt to bring such an action, they will be blocked by an "exception" <note>a legal defense</note> stating that the matter does not pertain to them, as held in the cited law "To the tutor" and the law "If a ward's" in the section "let us see" <note>original: "l. si pupilli. §. videamus"</note> under the same title in the Digest.

However, when the care of someone else’s property was incumbent upon a person—whether as a mandatary, a proxy, a tutor, a curator, or by any other right—and a third party manages those goods in the absence of the person responsible for them (either with that person present but unaware, or in their absence), a "direct action for management of affairs" <note>original: "actio directa negotiorum gestorum"; the right of an owner to sue a manager for an accounting of their work</note> may be brought against this third-party manager by both the owner of the goods and the person who was responsible for their care. This is because the manager has effectively performed a service for both parties. 

Conversely, this third-party manager is entitled to a "contrary action for management of affairs" <note>original: "actio contraria negotiorum gestorum"; a claim by the manager to be reimbursed for expenses</note> if they spent money usefully <note>original: "utiliter expendit"</note>. This claim can be made indifferently against either the owner of the goods or the person who was responsible for them. This is gathered from the law "If a mandate" in the Code, and several sections of the Digest. Although some laws suggest that for these actions to apply, the third party must have *known* and *intended* to act for both parties—a point asserted by Joannes as cited by Accursius <note>Accursius (c. 1182–1263) was a famous Italian jurist known for his "Great Gloss" on Roman law</note>—Accursius himself argues the opposite. He asserts it is enough that the business was truly managed for both, even if the manager did not know or intend to serve both. This is a sufficiently equitable opinion, which seems to be embraced by Law 27 of the Fifth Partida <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>.

<margin>6</margin> Regarding the degree of fault <note>original: "culpa"</note> for which a manager of affairs is held liable if some loss occurs to the person whose business they are managing, we must make a distinction. If the affairs were abandoned and no one else was going to manage them, then the manager is liable only for fraud <note>original: "dolo"</note> and "gross negligence" <note>original: "lata culpa"; a level of neglect so great it is treated almost like intentional fraud</note>. This is held in the Digest and in Law 30, Title 12, Partida 5, as noted by Gregorio López <note>a prominent 16th-century Spanish commentator on the Partidas</note>. 

However, if the affairs were not abandoned, but were such that anyone else could have easily managed them, we must further distinguish. If no "most diligent person" <note>original: "diligentissimus"</note> was offering to manage them, then the manager is liable even for "ordinary negligence" <note>original: "levis culpa"</note>, just as in similar contracts that benefit both parties. But if a most diligent person was offering to act, but was prevented from doing so because this manager took up the task, then the manager is liable even for "slightest negligence" <note>original: "levissima culpa"</note>.

<column-break/>

This is consistent with the law "If a ward's" in the section "let us see" and the common opinion of the doctors of law. The same is affirmed by the glosses and by Paulus Castrensis <note>a famous 15th-century jurist</note> and Gregorio López, when the person whose business was managed was himself a most diligent individual. Nevertheless, I do not see how a manager who acts without a mandate for a most diligent person should be held liable for the "slightest negligence" if the affairs were entirely abandoned; in that case, he should only be liable for fraud and gross negligence, even if the owner would have executed them with the utmost diligence had he been present.

<margin>7</margin> As for a fortuitous event <term>fortuitous event: an accident or "act of God" that could not be foreseen or prevented, such as a fire or storm</term>, the manager of affairs is regularly not held liable, as is well known from the Code and the Digest. I say "regularly," because if the owner of the business warned the manager not to act in his absence except on the condition that he be liable for accidents, then the manager is indeed liable. 

Likewise, if the manager was at fault for the loss—for example, if he was responsible for the fire that destroyed the property—he is liable for that outcome. Similarly, he is liable for a fortuitous event if the property perished after a "culpable delay" <note>original: "mora"; a legal term for failure to perform an obligation on time</note> in returning it, provided it would not have perished otherwise. Furthermore, if the manager undertook some unusual business in another's name—something the owner was not accustomed to doing and would not have done if present—and the property is lost by accident, the loss falls on the manager, not the owner. For example, if he buys slaves or horses in this manner and they die of disease, the manager bears the loss unless the profit from other transactions compensates for it. Two other scenarios mentioned in the glosses will be discussed in the following two disputes.

<margin>8</margin> If someone has many properties to be administered or many affairs to be managed, and a person manages one of them but omits the rest (which no one else manages), is he liable for the ones he did not touch? We must say that, regularly, he is not liable. 

As stated above, there is a distinction between a manager of affairs who handles another's business of his own accord, and a tutor, curator, or mandatary who is bound by office or contract to manage a ward's or another's business. A manager of affairs may apply himself to whichever tasks he wishes and not care about others. However, a tutor, curator, or anyone else bound by duty or a chosen mandate cannot omit any of the tasks that fall under their responsibility. Thus, the manager of affairs is not generally liable for what he chooses not to manage, unless...

# Louis Molina, On Contracts

...of the absent person, and because he chose to manage certain things himself, that other person chose to manage nothing; certainly, if he was aware that by managing some things he was an obstacle that prevented all things from being managed, he is held liable for those not managed, according to the law *If a ward's*, section *let us see* <note>original: "l. si pupilli. §. videamus. ff. de neg. gestor." Referring to the Digest of Justinian.</note> and in harmony with law 34, title 12, part 5 <note>referring to the Siete Partidas, the Spanish legal code</note>. I would say the same, for the same reason, if he omitted something new that happened later, when there was hope from the beginning that something new would happen, and another person was ready who also wished to manage the future affairs, but this man, by undertaking the administration, was an obstacle so that the other did not manage the future matters. And in this outcome, I believe the opinion of Bartolus and Albericus is true, which Gregorius Lopez refers to in the cited law 34; although he himself believes the opposite to be truer along with Azo, whom he also references. When someone who managed affairs intended from the beginning to manage everything—referring to the addition to the gloss on the law *To the tutor* <note>original: "l. tutori. C. de neg. gest."</note> under the words *his own will*—Bartolus says he is held liable if he omits managing any of them, according to the law *Pomponius 2* joined with the following law. However, I do not see that this is sufficiently gathered from those laws. And certainly, when his manifestation of intent was not an obstacle to others managing everything, I do not see why he should be held liable for those things he omitted to manage, when they were not connected to or dependent on the things he did manage; and this is affirmed by
<margin>9</margin> the cited gloss to which that addition is applied. When, † however, someone begins a certain business and, before it is completed, desists from it, then he is held liable for the damage following from that cause: because a "quasi-contract" <term>quasi-contract: a legal obligation that is treated as if a contract exists, even though no formal agreement was made</term> is considered to have begun between the manager of affairs and the one whose business it is, concerning the doing and completing of it, as in the law *In loans*, section *As if* <note>original: "l. in cōmoda to. §. ficut. ff. commod."</note> and as the addition to the cited gloss affirms. Just as a partnership expires upon the death of one of the partners regarding business not yet started, but differently regarding those things already started, which instead must be completed (as was said in Dispute 514): so, if someone intending to act in all or many of someone's affairs finds that the person to whom they belong departs from this life, the manager of affairs is held to complete what he began; but he is not held to undertake what he had not yet started. So it is held in the law *For even Neratius*, section *If only* <note>original: "l. nā & Neratius §. fi vnico ff. de neg. gest."</note>.
<margin>10</margin> When someone, thinking he is acting in the business of one person, manages the business of another; because that matter pertained to someone else and not to the one with whom he thought he was dealing; there nevertheless results from that management an "action for management of affairs" <note>original: "actio negotiorum gestorum"</note> between the one whose property it was and the manager, regarding those things said in this dispute and what will be said in the following dispute: not differently than it would result between the manager and the one for whose sake it was managed, if the property had pertained to him. So it is held in the law *If when I thought* and the law *To the freedman*, section 1 <note>original: "l. si cum putaui. l. liberto §. 1. ff. de neg. gest."</note> and law 31, title 12, part 5. Likewise, in the law *If when I thought*, it is held that if I thought you had given me a mandate <term>mandate: a formal contract of agency or authorization</term> to act in your business and I did so, when in fact you had mandated no such thing, there arises between me and you an action for management of affairs, but not an action of mandate.
<margin>11</margin> Likewise, if someone † receives something in the name of another, whether it was owed to the person in whose name it was received or not, if the person in whose name it was received ratifies it after knowing of the matter, there arises between the receiver and the person in whose name it was received an action for management of affairs, so that the one in whose name it was received pays the expenses, if any were reasonably made in that

<column-break/>

receiving, or in bringing it to him, and so that he returns to the other what he received in his name, with expenses deducted. So it is in the law *If a ward's*, section *Likewise it is asked* <note>original: "l. si pupilli. §. item quæritur. ff. de neg. gest."</note> and law 32, title 12, part 5. Likewise, if someone pays a debt to another that a third party owes him, by that very act the debtor is freed from the old obligation of the debt, even if the payment was not made by the mandate of the original debtor. Indeed, an action for management of affairs arises between the one who paid and the one for whom he paid, so that the latter pays the former what he thus paid for him; no differently than an action would arise if he had made the payment by the debtor's mandate. So it is held in the law *To be paid* <note>original: "l. soluenda. ff. de neg. gest."</note> and the cited law 32: where Gregorius Lopez asks whether, if the one who thus paid for another offered payment to the creditor and the creditor refused to receive it, the debtor would be freed from a penalty, if any penalty had been established in the event that he did not pay within a certain term. And with Bartolus and Albericus, he says he is freed, according to the law *One who after the postliminium* <note>original: "l. qui post liminiū. C. de capt."; postliminium refers to the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity</note> and the law *The same who*, section 1 <note>original: "leg. qui idem. §. 1. ff. de solut."</note>; and the same is clearly implied in law 1 of the Digest title "On management of affairs."

### DISPUTE 554

#### SUMMARY

1 *A manager of affairs, after a prohibition has been made to him, has no legal action regarding those things he managed after the prohibition; otherwise regarding those things he managed and spent before.*
2 *This fails, however, unless public favor is involved, number 2.*
3 *Useful expenses made in managing a business are owed to the manager of affairs where no prohibition intervened.*
*Indeed, it even suffices that they were useful from the beginning.*
*And what if the manager was deceived, believing he was acting as a servant.*

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "management of affairs" (negotiorum gestio), focusing on when a manager can claim reimbursement for expenses and when their actions are considered a gift or a liability.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 55, Section 4.

<margin>13</margin> **A stepfather spending for his stepson is not presumed to be making a gift; therefore, he has a legal claim for the management of affairs.**
<margin>14</margin> **When a master spends for a servant, it is presumed to have been spent for the sake of piety.**
<margin>15</margin> **How a manager of affairs differs from a procurator <note>a formal legal representative</note> and a mandatory <note>one acting under a specific contract of mandate</note>.**

<margin>1</margin> If someone has expressly signaled to another that they should not manage a certain business or their affairs, and after such an express prohibition the person still acts and spends something—even if they spent it usefully—they do not have an action for management of affairs <note>original: "actio negotiorum gestorum"</note> against the person whose business they managed and for whose benefit they spent the money. Instead, they lose that money entirely. It is otherwise if they spent anything before that prohibition, for they may recover that through the action for management of affairs. This is held in the Code, title *On the management of affairs* <note>original: "l. vl. .C. de nego. gest."</note>, the Digest <note>original: "l. si ex duobus ff. eod. titul."</note>, and the *Siete Partidas* <note>original: "l. 12. in fine tit. 12. p. 5."</note>. There, Gregorius Lopez <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note>, in the final gloss, following Bartolus and others whom he cites, makes an exception

<margin>2</margin> unless the public interest <note>original: "favor publicus"</note> is involved in those expenses. For example, if the expenses are made to free a person from death, mutilation, grave illness, or prison, or for the marriage of a woman, or if public interest is otherwise involved in making them. In these cases, the manager recovers the costs even if the person whose business is being managed contradicted and prohibited the actions before they were done. In other events, however, the manager loses the expenses, at least as a penalty by the disposition of the law. Furthermore, even if the person for whose benefit the costs were incurred has been made wealthier by them, I believe that even in the forum of conscience <note>the moral or religious judgment of a person's soul</note>, they are not bound to pay them—although it is fitting that they should pay insofar as they were made wealthier.

<margin>3</margin> When no prohibition occurred on the part of the person whose business was managed, it is necessary that the business was "usefully managed" <note>original: "utiliter gestum"</note> for the expenses to be owed to the manager. For this, it is enough if the business began to be useful to the owner from the start, even if later, by a chance accident <note>original: "casu fortuito"</note> or some other reason, the utility did not achieve its effect. For example, if someone usefully repaired the house of an absent person that was threatening to collapse, and by chance or the malice of another it was later burned down; or if he provided medical care for a slave’s illness—this was useful to the master, even if the slave died. If, however, the business was not usefully managed from the start (for instance, because someone incurred greater costs in a matter than the utility that could be hoped for), then the owner of the business is not held to those costs, except according to the value of the resulting utility. Truly, when someone believed they were usefully managing another's business, and yet was deceived because in truth it was not useful for that business to be managed (and prudent men would not have done it), then the owner is not held to the manager for the expenses incurred. This is found in the Digest and the *Siete Partidas*, as Gregorius Lopez affirms.

<margin>4</margin> When someone manages another's business for the sake of plunder <note>original: "deprædandi causa"</note> or for some similar reason for their own advantage, and this is sufficiently established, then they are held by the action of management of affairs to everything that other managers are held to (as explained in the preceding dispute). Indeed, if by occasion of how they managed another's business something should perish by chance accident <column-break/> while they are administering it, they are held liable for that accident, as the gloss affirms and the laws cited suggest. However, the owner of that business is not held to pay that person's expenses, except insofar as the owner was made wealthier by those expenses. This is held in the Digest <note>original: "l. si pupilli. §. si quis negotia. ff. de neg. gest."</note> and the *Siete Partidas*. Which, however,

<margin>5</margin> clearly suggests that for the owner to be held to the expenses, it is not enough if they were made wealthier simply within the scope of the expenses themselves, but there is a need that, beyond the scope of the expenses, they retain some utility. Yet, the section from which that law was taken requires no such thing, as Gregorius Lopez notes on the same law, saying this point should be kept in mind.

<margin>6</margin> For which conjectures sufficiently prove that someone managed another's business with the intent of plundering, read Gregorius Lopez in the same place.

<margin>7</margin> When someone has undertaken unusual business <note>original: "negotia insolita"</note> in the name of another, which the owner themselves would not have undertaken—for example, if he bought slaves or horses for a trade that the owner would not have bought them for—and they perish, then the loss and the entire transaction belong to the manager of affairs (as explained in the preceding dispute) and not to the one in whose name the trade was conducted. However, the owner can ratify the transaction, and then, just as with the profit, the entire loss belongs to him, and he is held to pay all expenses if he chooses to ratify the trade and wishes to share in the profit.

<margin>8</margin> When, however, many business matters were managed by the same person in the owner's name, the owner cannot ratify some in which profit is seen and not ratify others in which loss is found, throwing the loss of those back onto the manager. Rather, he is held either to ratify all of them or none. This is held in the Digest and the *Siete Partidas*.

<margin>9</margin> When someone managing another's affairs has made superfluous expenses, the owner is not held to pay the superfluous amount, but only what was equitable for him to spend.

<margin>10</margin> When someone spends something for another's benefit for free and with a liberal mind, whether out of piety (as when a mother or grandmother provides support <note>original: "alimenta"</note> to a son or grandson), or out of domestic affection (as when a master cures a sick servant at his own expense for free, or provides other necessary costs), or finally for any other reason with an eye toward God and charity, or out of friendship, or any other motive for doing something for free: he cannot change his mind after such business has been liberally managed for the good of the other and seek those expenses through an action for management of affairs. This is held in various laws of the Code and Digest and the *Siete Partidas*.

<margin>11</margin> To understand when something is presumed to be done out of piety (so that in an external court the action for management of affairs is denied for seeking what was spent, especially regarding support for someone), one must first keep before one's eyes how far support is owed to descendants by ancestors if the descendants need it and do not have assets from which it may be provided, and...

It establishes that while useful expenses are generally recoverable, those made against an express prohibition or out of pure "piety" (charity) cannot be billed to the owner later.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts

again, the extent to which maintenance is owed by ancestors <note>parents, grandparents, etc.</note> to descendants when they do not have sufficient support from elsewhere; likewise, the extent to which a brother is bound to provide maintenance to another brother, and especially to a sister from the same mother <note>original: "sorori vterinæ"</note>, when she has no support from elsewhere. This matter was discussed extensively in Dispute 168 and Dispute 224 under the section on legitimate causes, and most especially in Dispute 228 regarding the effects of paternal power. In those cases where maintenance is owed because they have no other means, the support cannot be provided with the intention of later offsetting <note>original: "compensandi"</note> the cost if they eventually acquire property; rather, it must be provided for free. Thus, the difficulty of whether the support was given out of piety <note>natural family affection</note> or out of liberality <note>generosity</note> ceases to be an issue, and compensation cannot later be sought through an action for management of affairs <note>original: "actione negotiorum gestorum"</note>. This is observed in the gloss on the law *Nesenius* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de neg. gest."</note>, and is clear enough from the locations cited.

However, when children have assets elsewhere from which maintenance could be provided, a distinction must be made. If a mother or grandmother provides maintenance to a son or grandson, and that child has assets held by the mother or grandmother from which maintenance could be provided—perhaps because the mother or grandmother owes him something—then in a case of doubt, it is presumed that the mother or grandmother intended to provide maintenance from the child's own assets which she held. Consequently, she can later offset those maintenance costs from those assets. This is defined in the law *Nesenius* in the Digest and in Law 36, Title 12, Part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas, the Spanish legal code</note>. The same is to be said if any ancestor in the male line holds the assets of a son or grandson to whom he provides maintenance, or if a brother holds the assets of another brother to whom he provides maintenance. In doubt, all these people are considered to be providing maintenance from the assets of those receiving it, rather than for free from their own personal property; this agrees with what was said in Dispute 239 and elsewhere. 

But when a mother or grandmother provides maintenance to a son or grandson who indeed had assets from which support could be provided, but did not have those assets in the possession of the mother or grandmother, then, in doubt, the mother or grandmother is considered to have provided the maintenance for free out of paternal piety. For that reason, the action for management of affairs to reclaim those maintenance costs is denied to her, unless she made a protest <note>a formal declaration</note> that she was providing it with the intention of reclaiming it, or unless that intention is clear from an account book started at the beginning when she began to provide maintenance, because she immediately began to record what she was spending on maintenance. This is what is defined in the law *Alimenta* in the Code <note>original: "C. de neg. gesto"</note> and the cited Law 36; the law *Nesenius* in the Digest also agrees. The Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "Lusitanæ ord."</note>, Book 4, Title 68, also agree: there it is held that if a mother or grandmother are guardians <note>original: "tutrices, aut curatrices"</note> of the children and spend something of their own on the children, they can demand it from the children even if they made no protest, provided the children have assets to pay it. It is otherwise, however, if they neither manage the children's assets nor protest for reimbursement, for then they are considered to be making a gift—unless the children are rich and the women themselves are poor, and what they spent was a notable quantity which they spent due to the condition and strength of the children's patrimony; in that case, they can reclaim it even if no protest preceded it. These things were said in the cited Dispute 228, and I do not doubt that this last point should similarly

<column-break/>

be affirmed according to common law alone, and thus even outside that Kingdom <note>Portugal</note>. This is because there is then a clear conjecture that the mother or grandmother did not intend to donate that amount to such children. Furthermore, when a mother or grandmother spends something on other necessary things for children or grandchildren that are not maintenance, then in doubt, they are not considered to have spent them with the intention of donating them, but of reclaiming them, as is defined in the same law *Alimenta* along with the gloss there. For there is not as great a presumption that expenses made on other things were done with the intention of donating out of paternal piety as there is regarding expenses made on maintenance; and maintenance is held in greater favor than other things. These same points have even greater force regarding a father or grandfather. Understand these things when the mind and intention of the one making the expenses is not clear. For if it were clear what was intended—at least from conjectures, considering the smallness of the expenses, the abundance of the parents' assets, their generosity of spirit, and their affection for the child or grandchild—one must stand by what is entirely presumed from likely and pressing conjectures.

<margin>12</margin> When a son spends something on his father beyond the maintenance owed to him, the law *Filius* in the Code <note>original: "C. de neg. gest."</note> seems to suggest sufficiently that unless the liberal intention of the son were clear—by which he intended to spend it for free—such an intention is not to be presumed. Therefore, an action for management of affairs is available to both the son and his heirs to reclaim those expenses. The same is suggested even more clearly in the laws *Sive pro fratre* and *Si negotium* in the Code <note>original: "C. de neg. gest."</note> regarding when someone has made expenses for a brother or sister.

<margin>13</margin> Regarding what is spent on stepchildren <note>original: "priuignis"</note>, unless it is clear it was spent with a liberal intention, certainly—whether spent on maintenance or other things—the action for management of affairs is granted to reclaim it. For a generous intention is not to be presumed in a stepfather <note>original: "vitrico"</note> unless it is clear and proven from conjectures of some liberal mind. The final gloss on the law *Si paterno* in the Code <note>original: "C. de neg. gest."</note>, Bartolus, and the common opinion of the doctors affirm this in accordance with the text there. For that law only denies the action if the expenses were made with "paternal affection"; however, it does not affirm or say that they should be presumed to have been made with paternal affection. And certainly, when a stepfather is the guardian of stepchildren and manages their property, I do not doubt that a generous intention is not to be presumed, just as it is not presumed in a mother or grandmother who are guardians and administrators of the property of children and grandchildren. Therefore, even if no protest from the stepfather preceded it, he could offset those expenses from the stepchildren's property. But when someone else is the guardian and administrator of the stepchildren's property, and the stepfather feeds them without any protest, then Law 36, Title 12, Part 5 might apply, which states that unless the stepfather protests that he is not providing maintenance to the stepchildren for free (add: or unless it is otherwise clear he did not provide it for free, such as if he wrote down what he spent on them in an account book from the beginning), the action for management of affairs is not granted to him to obtain those expenses. It states otherwise if useful expenses were made on other assets of the stepchildren, for the stepfather may reclaim those even if he made no protest. In that same place,

# Second Treatise, Dispute 555.

with the cited gloss, it is added that if a stepson serves his stepfather—even if the stepfather protests to the contrary—the stepfather cannot reclaim the costs spent on the stepson's maintenance. Understand this, however, provided that the service is deemed by a judge’s judgment to be worthy of such compensation. But if the service is worth more than the maintenance, then the stepfather is bound to pay the difference to the stepson. The same should be said if a minor <note>a child under the age of 25</note> truly served any other person who was acting as his guardian.

<margin>14</margin>
If † a head of household <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> incurred expenses for a sick servant which were appropriate to the wealth, generosity, charity, and nobility of such a master, and it was fitting for them to be paid for by the household, there is then a strong presumption that he intended to provide them out of liberality and domestic affection. Consequently, such a head of household would not be granted an action for management of affairs <term>actio negotiorum gestorum; a legal claim to recover costs incurred while looking after someone else's business without their prior request</term> to reclaim them. At the very least, a servant is never liable for "superfluous" expenses that go beyond what is appropriate for a person of his status.

Observe this: in all events where it is said to be doubtful whether an act was done with a generous heart and for free, the action for management of affairs is granted. In these and similar cases, the person against whom the claim is made can compel the claimant to first affirm under oath that he made those expenditures with the intention of recovering them from others.

<margin>15</margin>
Finally, observe † that this is the difference between a manager of affairs <note>someone acting without a formal mandate</note> and an agent <note>original: "procuratorem"</note>, or one who has a mandate <note>a formal legal instruction</note> for the task. An unauthorized manager of affairs acquires neither ownership nor possession for the person whose business he manages; rather, that depends on the ratification and acceptance of the person for whose sake he acted, because he was never appointed to act in that person's place. An agent, however—and generally anyone holding a mandate—can acquire possession and ownership for the principal, since he was appointed to the task by the will of the person whose business he manages. So says Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> on the chapter *Accedens*, regarding prebends.

### On other quasi-contracts.

### DISPUTE 555.

### SUMMARY.

1. *For which matters the action for management of affairs is given, both for a guardian against a ward and for the ward against the guardian.*
2. *For which expenses a ward is held liable to a guardian by the action for management of affairs.*
3. *Improper contracts, called "quasi-contracts"; various other examples from which the action for management of affairs arises.*

<margin>1 2</margin>
The Institutes <note>a fundamental textbook of Roman Law</note>, in the section "On obligations arising from quasi-contract" <note>original: "Inst. de obligationibus, quæ ex quasi contractu"</note> at the paragraph *tutores*, provides an example of a quasi-contract in the obligation that results between a guardian <term>tutor; a legal protector of a child</term> and a ward <term>pupillus; a child under the age of puberty under guardianship</term>. Since no actual contract preceded their relationship—the office of guardian having been established by the state for the common good—the guardian is bound to the ward by a "direct action" based on quasi-contract. As we said in Dispute 453 regarding a manager of affairs, the guardian is held liable for "slight negligence" <note>original: "culpa levis"; the failure to show the care an average person would take</note> and for all the ward's business matters where an omission would result in harm

<column-break/>

to the ward, as stated in the cited dispute and found in the law *Tutori* in the Code <note>original: "C. de negot. gestor."</note>. Conversely, † the ward is bound to the guardian by a "contrary action" for the **necessary expenses** the guardian incurred in the ward's business. By "necessary expenses," I mean those he was bound to make by virtue of his office, and those which were clearly intended from the start for the ward's greater benefit, even if the result was hindered by a "fortuitous event" <note>original: "casu fortuito"</note> like a fire or something similar.

As for other expenses which the guardian was not officially bound to make—even if they seemed useful and reasonable at the time they were started—the ward is only liable to the extent that he was **made wealthier** <note>original: "locupletior"; the legal principle that one shouldn't profit at another's expense</note> by them, and no further. Thus, if a third party manages business concerning a ward's property that a guardian was administering, and incurs necessary expenses in the manner explained, both the ward and the guardian are liable to pay him via an action for management of affairs; this is because he acted for the benefit of both, as stated in Dispute 543. However, if he incurred expenses that initially only *seemed* useful and reasonable, the guardian is liable for the full amount, while the ward is only liable to the extent he was made wealthier by them. This is held in the law *Si pupilli* at the beginning, joined with the final gloss there, in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de neg. gest."</note>, and other cited laws in the Code and the *Siete Partidas* <note>original: "l. 28. tit. 12. par. 5."; a major Castilian law code</note>.

Furthermore, at the time the legal proceedings begin <note>original: "tpe litis contestatæ"</note>, one must consider whether the minor is then wealthier from this second kind of expense to understand how far he is or is not bound to pay for them. Such a privilege—that a ward is only liable for "useful" expenses to the extent of his enrichment—is not found in the law to be granted to minors over the age of puberty <note>those between 14 and 25</note>. Thus the gloss on Law 2, Albericus, and others do not extend this to older minors (though some disagree). The cited glosses and Albericus are clearly supported by Law 28 of the *Partidas*.

Indeed, I consider this rule to be rather unfair: that a ward is not held liable for those "useful" expenses whether they were made by a guardian or a third party for the minor's benefit. And I consider it much less fair that when they are made by a third party, the guardian—who ordered no such thing—is held liable for the full amount while the ward is not. Whether this privilege applies to the **Church** <note>original: "Ecclesiæ"</note> is affirmed by Gregorio López and others. However, I do not see that the Church has a greater privilege than minors; for that reason, I would not dare extend a privilege to the Church that I judge to be "odious" <note>legally unfavorable or restrictive</note> and less than reasonable, which was granted only to wards. Regarding this privilege, the gloss also says the rule fails: that a manager of affairs is not liable for fortuitous events. For if a guardian or third party makes "useful" expenses for a ward and they are lost by accident or become useless, the ward is not liable for them, as has been said.

<margin>3</margin>
Another example † of a quasi-contract is provided in the Institutes at the cited section, paragraph *item si inter*, regarding when people who are not in a formal partnership <note>original: "societate"</note> hold some property in common, as if...

# Louis de Molina on Contracts

legacies or gifts have been given to both of them. For if one of them gathers the fruits <note>the profits or produce, such as crops or rent</note> from that property, he is bound to the other by a direct action for half of the value, after deducting expenses. This obligation does not arise from a contract, since no contract preceded it between them, but rather from a **quasi-contract** <term>quasi ex contractu; a legal obligation created by law as if a contract existed, even though the parties never made a formal agreement</term>. Similarly, if one person incurs necessary or useful expenses on real property, the other is bound to him for half of those costs by a "contrary action." The same principle applies if one person gathers fruits from an inheritance held in common with others before it is divided, or if he incurs expenses on it. In these and similar events—such as if a brother administered property held in common with his other brothers, or if one of the sons administered property while the father was still living—the one who administered the property is bound to provide an accounting of his administration. 

As Gregorio López <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> says (in Law 26, Title 12, Part 5, final gloss, along with others he cites), an account must be given of everything in whatever way is possible, considering the concurrent circumstances. Witnesses cannot be brought for every single small thing; instead, in modest matters, one relies on the oath of the person who administered the property. Indeed, this may sometimes apply even to large matters, provided that the status of the person, the plausibility of the matter, and the judge's assessment all agree. However, in rendering an account for the administration of a guardianship or the care of a minor, a more exacting standard and greater proof are required.

In the cited location of Justinian’s *Institutes*, in the paragraph "the heir also" <note>original: "§. hæres quoque"</note>, an example of a quasi-contract is added regarding heirs. By the very fact that an heir enters into an inheritance, he is bound to the legatees <note>those receiving specific gifts in a will</note> for their legacies and to the creditors for the debts of the deceased. This is not by contract, as no contract existed between the heir and the legatees or creditors beforehand, but by quasi-contract. By the disposition of the law, the act of accepting the inheritance results in an obligation to pay the legacies and the debts of the deceased, at least to the extent of the inheritance's value, as if the heir were representing the person of the deceased.

In the same place, in the paragraph "also he" <note>original: "§. itē is"</note>, another example of a quasi-contract is added concerning one who pays what they did not owe by mistake. In cases where the law allows for a "recovery" <note>original: "condictio, seu repetitio"</note> of that payment as something not owed, the person has a right of action. This is not from a contract, because no agreement took place between the payer and the receiver; rather, the person paying the debt intended a "dissolution" <note>original: "distractum"</note>—that is, the ending of an obligation from a previous contract or some other source. Instead, the right of action arises from a quasi-contract.

**ALTHOUGH** a settlement is a type of contract—and for that reason it should have been discussed before quasi-contracts—nevertheless, because a settlement serves to resolve lawsuits and doubts arising from contracts, quasi-contracts, or any other matter, we have deferred the discussion of settlements to this place.

Following Panormitanus <note>a famous canon lawyer</note> and others, and in accordance with various laws, we can define a settlement as follows: It is a **non-gratuitous agreement** <note>meaning something is given or promised by both sides</note> regarding a doubtful matter, a lawsuit, or a controversy already begun. It is called a settlement (*transactio*), as Bartolus and others (cited by Padilla and Gutierrez) follow, as if it were a *transfer of action* (*transitio actionis*). This is because the person who settles—who is more properly the plaintiff than the defendant, though both agree to the settlement—*transfers*, which is to say, withdraws from the legal action that was available to him. 

The definition says "regarding a doubtful matter" because if, at the time of the settlement, it were clear to one of the parties that the matter in dispute belonged entirely to the other, the settlement would be invalid. This is most obvious in the **court of conscience**, because there would be no just title by which one could receive something to withdraw from an action (if he were the plaintiff) or by which he could retain the thing in question or receive something to leave it to the person it belonged to (if he were the defendant).

<margin>Question</margin> 3 Whether a settlement made regarding a matter about

sentence is, at least materially, unjust; nor does it 
entirely appear that the person for whom the sentence was passed has a 
generous mind wanting to grant what he

Indeed, if a generous mind were present, truly

Since in both cases there is exactly the same reason. 
Therefore, just as a promise of interest, or of not seeking its 
return, if either of these is confirmed by an oath, 
obligates the promisor in the forum of conscience 
not to go against the oath unless he first obtains a release 
from it (because the fulfillment of that promise is 
not evil on the part of the promisor); nevertheless it 
does not have strength from the oath such that the usurer 
can in good conscience keep the interest, or so that he 
who promised or paid it cannot seek and obtain a 
release from the oath—and, having obtained that release, 
not pay the interest or seek the return of what was paid—as 
is easily clear from what was said in Dispute 149. So in the 
matter proposed: he who confirmed that settlement with an oath 
is indeed bound in the forum of conscience not to 
go against the oath unless he first obtains a release 
from it, because that is not an evil thing; yet he can 
seek and obtain a release from the oath, 
and having obtained it, he is bound to stand by the settlement 
neither in the forum of conscience nor in the 
external forum. And he with whom the settlement was made 
can retain what he obtained from the 
settlement neither in conscience nor in the 
external forum, even before the other party 
obtains a release from the oath. This is because that 
settlement, being invalid in itself without the oath, was 
confirmed involuntarily; therefore, even by the force of the oath, 
it could not transfer any right to the other, just as 
a promise of interest confirmed by an oath has no 
strength to transfer a right to the usurer.

<meta>This page continues Molina's discussion on the legal definitions of settlements and agreements. The previous page established that a settlement requires a genuine dispute and mutual concession; here, Molina distinguishes between a legal settlement (transactio) and a composition (compositio), specifically regarding ecclesiastical and tax law.</meta>

...the thing, or the right which he can claim regarding it, it would not be a **settlement** <term>transactio; a legal agreement to end a dispute through mutual concessions</term>, but a **composition** <term>compositio; a broader term for an arrangement or remission of a debt or obligation</term>, or a pardon, or a pact, taking the word in its broad sense. Therefore, when the Supreme Pontiff, in the **Crusade Bull** <note>original: "bulla cruciatae"; a papal decree granting spiritual benefits and legal remissions to those contributing to the defense of the faith</note>, grants to one who contributes a single unit in support of the war against infidels a remission of a much larger sum concerning those things owed to **uncertain persons** <note>money that must be restored where the rightful owner cannot be identified, usually given to the poor</note>, and which he is bound to restore to the poor, it is not said to be a settlement, but a composition. This is because what the Supreme Pontiff thus pardons and remits under that condition, he remits truly for free; for the remainder, which is paid in aid of the war against infidels or for another pious end, is also a debt and subject to restitution; hence that bull is called a "composition." The same is true of other compositions made by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff concerning the ill-gotten revenues of **benefices** <term>beneficium; an ecclesiastical office that provides an income</term> and other similar matters.

<margin>5</margin> Observe in this place that "composition" is broader in scope than "settlement," and thus contains the latter within its reach. For we can divide "composition" into that which concerns a matter about which there is no controversy or doubt (such as that which was just explained), and that which concerns a matter over which there is a controversy or doubt as to whom it belongs or to whom it ought to belong in the future. This latter is again subdivided into that by which one of the contending parties gives something, as if for a price, to the other so that he may withdraw from the lawsuit and pardon the right he was claiming regarding that matter—whether what he gives is part of the thing in question, or a right he claimed in it, or something else. And this is the "settlement" defined by us, which we are now discussing; it has no place in spiritual matters, such as in a lawsuit or controversy over an ecclesiastical benefice or other similar thing, as will be said elsewhere. However, that which is included under "composition" in its broad sense is rightly sometimes called a composition. It is further divided into that by which a lawsuit and controversy is settled amicably by the judgment of a wise man, by dividing the thing or the profit expected from it between those who are disputing over it, or by compensating for it from elsewhere according to the quantity and quality of the **doubtful right** <note>a claim that is not legally certain</note> which each of them pretends, so that by this reasoning all lawsuits may be prevented or an end put to those already moved, and peace preserved. This is not, however, as if something were given there as a price, or as if for a price, for the right to a spiritual thing which the other was holding out. And such a composition, which is not truly a settlement, has a place regarding spiritual things, as will be said in another place.

From the definition of a settlement explained thus far, and from what was said in Dispute 252 (where the nature of a contract in general was copiously explained), it is easily established that a settlement is a contract, and not a free one, <margin>6</margin> but an **onerous** one <note>a contract involving a mutual exchange of value rather than a gift</note>. The same must be said of an **arbitration agreement** <term>compromissum; a contract by which parties agree to submit their dispute to a private judge</term> by which some, by mutual consent, refer a controversy to be settled by the opinion of an arbiter or arbitrator, promising that they will stand by and obey it; about which matter there will be more extensive talk in Treatise 5. Indeed, such an arbitration agreement, especially after it has been **homologated** <term>emologatum; legally confirmed or ratified</term>—that is, after a decision or arbitral award has been rendered by mutual consent and accepted—takes on the character of a settlement in the broader sense of the 

<column-break/>

word "settlement," as **Molina** affirms in book 3, *on primogeniture*, chapter 9, number 1, following **Bartolus and most others**, and **Azevedo** in book 4, title 21, of the *New Collection*. For through such an arbitration agreement, not only do both sides withdraw from the lawsuit or controversy, but each of the litigants submits the right he claims in that matter to the judgment of him or those to whom the arbitration is committed, so that the other may similarly submit his claimed right to their judgment.

<margin>7</margin> However, settlements and arbitration agreements are **innominate contracts** <note>original: "contractus innominati"; in Roman law, these were contracts that did not have a specific name (like Sale or Hire) but were enforceable once one party performed their side</note>, specifically of the types: "I do that you may do" or "I give that you may do." That is: "I withdraw from the lawsuit and commit my right to the judgment of such a person or persons, so that you may do the same" (which is seen in an arbitration agreement); or "I give you so much, or such a part of the thing over which we have a controversy, so that you may withdraw from the lawsuit and consequently cede to me the right you claim in that matter" (which is seen in a "settlement" in the strict sense). From this it follows that, because in a settlement one withdraws from a lawsuit by ceding the right that the other party claimed, if the one who cedes it was truly the owner of that thing, he by that very act transfers ownership to the one to whom he delivers it by title of settlement, or to the one who previously possessed it with him and to whom he leaves it by title of settlement. Thus **Laffarte**, *on the sale of tithes*, chapter 17, number 51, affirms with **Baldus**, arguing from the law *ex causa transactionis*, Codex, *on usucaption for a buyer*, and the law *si per errorem*, Digest, same title. Moreover, that a settlement, and likewise an arbitration agreement, are innominate contracts having a similarity with **leasing** <term>locatio</term> and are to be regulated according to it, is affirmed by **Gregorio Lopez** and **Laffarte**, citing **Bartolus and others**, and the laws to be cited in the following paragraph agree. From this, Laffarte infers in both places that a settlement is not subject to the tax which in Castile they call the **alcavala** <term>alcaualla; a high percentage sales tax</term> and in Portugal the **sisa** <term>sisa; a consumption or transfer tax</term>, even if money is given in the settlement to one of the parties so that he withdraws from the lawsuit. For in these Kingdoms, that tax is only owed from buying and selling, and from exchange; but a settlement is a very different contract, even if money is involved in it. **Azevedo** affirms the same with **Padilla** above at number 11. However, if fraud were present—because a settlement was being faked when the contracting parties knew at the time that the thing was truly his who delivered or left it to the other for money or another thing—then it would be a true sale and purchase, or an exchange, and therefore that tax would be owed, as **Laffarte, Padilla, and Azevedo** correctly observe.

<margin>8</margin> An innominate contract, or any other **bare pact** <term>pactum nudum; an agreement that originally lacked a formal legal name or action to enforce it</term>, if a certain form of words is used, such as a **stipulation** or an **acceptilation** <term>acceptilatio; a formal verbal release from a debt</term>, passes into the "named" contract of stipulation or acceptilation, and from that itself a civil obligation arises and an action is granted, as was said in Disputes 253 and 255. <margin>9</margin> From this it is concluded that although a settlement is an innominate contract, if the settlement is celebrated with a stipulation intervening, it passes into a named contract. Therefore, not only a **natural obligation** <note>an obligation binding in conscience or fairness but not necessarily by law</note> but also a **civil obligation** arises, and there is an entitlement from it not only to a legal defense (exception) but also an action to compel the other to fulfill it and stand by it. As is held in law 2, Digest, *on settlements*, and other laws, it has a place in this [con-]tract...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal nature of settlements (transactio). While the previous page distinguished settlements from "compositions" or pardons, this page delves into the formal legal mechanisms used to make a settlement binding in court, specifically the Roman "Aquilian Stipulation," and contrasts this with the more straightforward laws of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 556.

The **Aquilian stipulation** <term>stipulatio Aquiliana; a formal oral contract used in Roman law to consolidate various obligations into one, allowing them to be easily settled or cancelled</term> was introduced by Gallus Aquilius, from whom it takes its name. Its form is handed down in the **Institutes** <note>original: "inst. quib. mod. toll. oblig. §. est autem"; referring to Justinian’s legal textbook, Book 3, Title 29</note>. For example, if one person seeks a hundred from another, claiming it is owed, and the other denies owing anything, and a settlement is made between them to pay only fifty, that settlement is fortified by the Aquilian stipulation. It thereby passes into a **named contract** <term>contractus nominatus; a contract specifically recognized and categorized by law with its own set of rules and actions</term>. 

This happens if the one who claimed the hundred was owed says: "Do you promise to **novate** <term>novatio; the act of replacing an old obligation with a new one</term> the ancient obligation for whatever you owe me beyond fifty?" and the other responds, "I promise." Then, the first person says again: "For whatever I owe you beyond fifty, do you consider those things as received?" and the other responds, "I do." Then, through that stipulation and **release** <term>acceptilatio; a formal verbal acknowledgment that an obligation has been satisfied</term>, the settlement remains fortified by the Aquilian stipulation, which consists of those two parts: the promise and the release.

However, if a settlement is made but not fortified by such a stipulation, then—although an obligation to stand by that contract and fulfill it on both sides arises in the **forum of conscience** <note>the "internal forum" or the moral realm of the soul, as opposed to the public courtroom</note>, as is clear enough from Disputation 257—nevertheless, in the **external forum** <note>the public civil or ecclesiastical courts</note>, a different rule applies. If the person to whom something was promised (in exchange for dropping a lawsuit) has not fulfilled any part of their own side—such as by handing over the document containing their rights or doing something similar—they are not granted a legal action to demand what was promised. Instead, they can only pursue their previous lawsuit or start it anew if it had not yet been attempted. 

But if the other party objects or "excepts" that a settlement took place, the court can then demand that they fulfill their part of the contract by paying what was promised in the settlement, or else they must drop their objection and allow the litigation to proceed. Conversely, the one who promised something so that the other would drop a lawsuit can always raise the "exception of settlement" against the person who tries to continue the lawsuit. This also applies to a **confirmed compromise** <term>compromissum omologatum; an out-of-court agreement ratified by a judge</term>. By this exception, they can repel the other from starting or continuing the suit, even if the person raising the exception has not yet fulfilled their part of the settlement, provided they are ready to fulfill it. 

This type of exception is highly privileged in law for the purpose of extinguishing lawsuits, as is evident from the law "Causas" and the law "Non minorem" in the **Code regarding settlements** <note>the *Codex Justinianus*, the collection of Roman imperial laws</note>. **Molina** <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600), the influential Spanish Jesuit jurist and theologian</note> understands this to mean that this exception blocks the formal "contestation of the suit" <term>litis contestatio; the stage in a trial where the issues are formally defined</term> when the exception is obvious and does not require deep investigation. If it does require deeper investigation, the suit is formally contested, and the exception is examined during the progress of the case. He reports that it has become the custom among many in this **Kingdom of Castile** that such exceptions, which by right should block the contestation of a suit, do not actually block it. He rightly warns that the opposite should happen when such exceptions are clear and do not require long inquiry. 

If a person has fulfilled their part of the contract, they will then be free to either reclaim what they gave (if the other person is allowed to continue the suit), or to raise the exception of the past settlement to block the adversary. The adversary will not be heard unless they fully restore what they received, according to the law "Si diversa" and its words: "the money being returned." 

<column-break/>

This is affirmed by the common opinion and by **Molina** in his fourth book on **primogeniture** <note>the legal right of the firstborn child to inherit the entire estate</note>. These points are established both from Disputation 255—where these matters are explained concerning **unnamed contracts** <term>contractus innominatus; an agreement that does not fall into a specific legal category but is enforceable if one party has performed their part</term> in general and **naked pacts** <term>pactum nudum; an informal agreement that Roman law historically did not enforce with a legal action</term>—and from various laws in the Digest and the Code. These rules hold true even if the settlement was made without a written document. 

However, these subtleties do not have a place in this **Kingdom of Castile**. <margin>Law of Castile.</margin> Here, a civil obligation arises from an "unnamed contract" and a "naked pact," and a legal action is granted, even if it is not fortified or "clothed" by a stipulation or any other formal act. This is established by the laws of the **New Collection** <note>original: "nouae collect."; referring to the *Nueva Recopilación* (1567), a major compilation of Spanish laws</note>. Consequently, even if a "naked" settlement is celebrated between parties in this Kingdom, either party can compel the other to stand by the settlement and fulfill their part. 

The same is true in **Canon Law** and in the **Ecclesiastical Court**, as was said in Disputation 257. <margin>Portuguese Law.</margin> I truly wish that in the **common civil law** <term>ius commune; the Roman-canonical legal system used across much of Europe</term>, those subtleties, formal ceremonies, and distinctions between "named" and "unnamed" contracts, or "naked" and "clothed" pacts, would be abolished! They were introduced by **ethical men** <note>likely referring here to the ancient Roman jurists</note> with the intent of reducing lawsuits, but they serve instead to multiply lawsuits and make them inextricable. They make the civil law obscure and excessively long, and they serve to circumvent **simple men** <note>ordinary people who are not trained in legal technicalities</note> who are least practiced in such subtleties and legal ceremonies.

Whenever a settlement is made under a certain penalty for whoever refuses to stand by it or contravenes it, then the one who does not abide by the settlement can be compelled either to stand by it or to pay the penalty. However, they cannot be compelled to do both. According to the law, the choice belongs to the one who wishes to stand by the settlement: they can force the other either to fulfill the deal or to pay the penalty. 

I do not believe that **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a seminal medieval jurist</note> or the common opinion affirm the contrary in the case of a settlement (which is a **burdensome contract** <term>contractus onerosus; a contract where both parties give and receive something of value</term>), but only in the case of "gratuitous" penal stipulations. If you consult what **Gregorio López** <note>the 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*</note> teaches, he defines this for all promises universally. In my judgment, he is correct, especially after the law in the Code regarding **novations**, which states that by stipulating a penalty, the prior obligation is not considered to have been replaced (novated). This is observed by Gregorio López: in gratuitous obligations, if a penalty is added for non-compliance, the one who is obligated...

## Louis Molina, On Contracts

...if he does not wish to abide by the obligation, he can only be compelled to pay the penalty, but not to fulfill the obligation itself. I do not know if Gutierrez <note>Juan Gutiérrez (1535–1611), a famous Spanish jurist</note> sufficiently considered this in his *On Confirmed Rights*, part 1, chapter 60. However, we will return to these rights in Disputation 559. 

But if a clause is added to a settlement—in which a penalty is applied to the one refusing to abide by it or contravening it—stating "**the agreement nonetheless remaining valid**" <note>original Latin: "rato nihilominus manente pacto"</note>, then the violator can be forced to both pay the penalty and still abide by the terms of the settlement. This is done by blocking him with a legal exception or even, under Canon Law and the laws of Castile <note>The Kingdom of Castile, part of modern Spain</note>, by a legal action compelling him to observe the settlement, as was said in the preceding section. 

That the violator can be compelled to both pay and abide when that clause is present is supported by the law *Qui fidem* in the Digest <note>Digest 2.15.16</note>, the law *Cum proponas* in the Code, and Law 34, Title 11, Partida 5 <note>The *Siete Partidas* was the primary law code of medieval and early modern Spain</note>. This legal principle applies generally to every contract and pact to which a conventional penalty is attached, provided that clause is included. Just as in a settlement without that clause the violator cannot be forced to do both, but only one or the other, so too in other contracts where a conventional penalty is applied, the matter stands similarly, as is clear from the law *Praedia* in the Digest and is affirmed by Padilla and others, as well as Gutierrez in the place cited above. 

However, if one sues for the penalty and it was of greater **interest** <term>interesse; the legal term for "damages" or the financial difference between the contract being fulfilled or not</term> that the contract be kept, one can additionally sue for the increase of that interest beyond the penalty. This is held in the cited law *Praedia*. Furthermore, if the conventional penalty was from the start assigned to a **pious cause** <note>such as a charity, hospital, or church</note> or to someone else, the person to whom faith was not kept can still sue for damages, as affirmed by Alexander, Gregorio López, and Gutierrez.

<margin>14</margin> It must be observed, however, that the clause "the agreement remaining valid" does not mean the agreement is preserved and the penalty is exacted *every* single time it is violated. Rather, it means the penalty is exacted only once—that is, the first time—based on the argument of the law *Boues* in the Digest. This is the case unless the clause "**as many times as**" <note>original: "toties quoties"</note> is added. For then the penalty can be exacted beyond the first time, as the last gloss on the law *Qui fidem* affirms, following Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors. 

In this situation, jurists like Romanus and Padilla add that when the "as many times as" clause is included, the penalty can be exacted only twice, to avoid an infinite cycle of penalties. Truly, as the gloss there asserts, the clause "as many times as" does not literally mean "twice," nor is that gathered from the law. Therefore, I believe that as often as he violates it, he who paid the penalty can be made to pay it again. On all these matters, read Gregorio López on the cited Law 34, last gloss.

<margin>Doubt</margin> Now, a **doubt** arises: when a penalty has been attached for contravening a settlement, if one of the parties says they do not wish to abide by the settlement, but then—before the matter is brought to court and the **joinder of issue** <term>lis contestata; the formal starting point of a trial in Roman-canonical law</term> occurs—they repent and say they *do* wish to abide by it: does such repentance purge the fault and avoid the penalty? 

The last gloss on the law *Qui fidem* and the law *Si quis maior* in the Code respond in the affirmative when the parties simply said they would not seek a claim. This is because
<margin>15</margin>
<margin>Decision</margin>

<column-break/>

it is understood to apply to the court proceedings once the issue is joined. Gutierrez affirms this is true even if the clause "the agreement remaining valid" was added. 

However, the aforementioned glosses say the matter is different if the penalty was attached specifically to "contravening the settlement" or "in any way seeking or disturbing the other party." In that case, the penalty is not purged nor avoided by repentance before the joinder of issue. 

Although the clause "the agreement remaining valid" and the attached penalty are common to both parties at the start, if one of them contravenes the settlement, the other may immediately, without punishment and lawfully, refuse to abide by the same settlement—even if the first party repents and wants to abide again. This is because, even if the settlement was confirmed by both sides with an **oath**, such agreements have a **tacit condition** <term>conditio tacita; an implied requirement</term> that faith is kept by the other party. This is according to Bartolus, Padilla, and the common opinion of the doctors, with which Gregorio López agrees.

<margin>16</margin> When a settlement has been confirmed by an oath and a penalty has simultaneously been attached for contravening it, then both can be sought: that the settlement be fulfilled *and* that the penalty be paid, even if the clause "the agreement remaining valid" was not explicitly added. 

The reason is that, first, the penalty can be sought, and by virtue of the oath, the violator is bound to absolutely abide by the settlement. In civil law, an action is granted based on that oath so that the violator is compelled to keep the informal pact or the **innominate contract** <term>contractus innominatus; a contract that doesn't fall into standard categories like "sale" or "hire" but is still binding if performed by one side</term> of the settlement. Therefore, both can be sought. An oath attached to a settlement, or to any other pact, has the same force as the clause "the agreement remaining valid." 

For this reason, if a penalty is attached for failing to stand by any other pact confirmed by oath, both can similarly be sought: namely, that the penalty be paid and that the pact be fulfilled. This is established in the law *Si quis maior* in the Code, where it is held that he who contravenes a settlement confirmed by oath incurs the penalty of **infamy** <term>infamia; a legal status resulting in the loss of many civil rights and social standing</term> for perjury, pays the penalty if any was attached, returns what he had received to drop the lawsuit, and loses his legal right to the claim. He is repelled from that action as if deprived of it by the very act. This is the common opinion of the doctors. 

Furthermore, if any other pact is confirmed by oath and a penalty is attached, the violator is bound to pay the penalty and is compelled to keep the pact, and similarly falls into the penalty of infamy. One incurs the penalty of infamy under both Civil and Canon Law whenever one violates a **promissory oath** <note>an oath regarding future conduct</note> when the person to whom it is made gains a right from it.

<margin>17</margin> When a settlement was not indeed confirmed by an oath, but was nevertheless secured by the **Aquilian stipulation**...

<page-num>809</page-num>
<header>Second Treatise, Disputation 556.</header>

...stipulation, if a penalty was further applied to the one who violates it, then the penalty can be demanded from the violator at the same time he is compelled to restore anything he received to drop the lawsuit, and he is barred from attempting or pursuing any further legal action. This is the rule in the law *Ubi pactum* in the Code <note>original: "l. vbi pactum. C. de transf." — a reference to the Code of Justinian, title on settlements</note> according to the interpretation of Bartolus, Azo, and the common understanding, as the Gloss affirms there. For this reason, Orozco and Gutierrez (cited above, number 9) say that if a settlement is fortified by an Aquilian stipulation <note>A formal verbal contract in Roman law used to convert informal obligations into a single, binding formal debt</note> and a penalty is applied to the violator—to be incurred as often as he violates it, while the agreement remains always valid—and it is further confirmed by an oath, it possesses the absolute fullest strength, such that no greater power can be added to it. Would that all this strength, by the disposition of the law, were granted to a settlement celebrated as a simple informal agreement <note>original: "pacto nudo" — a "naked pact" or informal agreement that traditionally lacked a cause of action in Roman law</note> with an applied penalty and confirmed by oath. If a simple agreement had all that same strength—save for the force of the penalty and the oath, which could be added at the pleasure of the parties—then the path would be blocked for many lawsuits, and many difficult laws could and should be rescinded, both to make them easier to understand and to reconcile them.

<margin>18</margin>
As we began to say above, a settlement concerning a matter that was doubtful between the parties at the time it was made is valid, both in conscience <note>The "internal forum" or moral standing</note> and in the legal court <note>The "exterior forum" or public law</note>, even if later it becomes clearly evident through some public writing or other source that the thing truly belonged to the other person. In such a case, the person who obtained it through the settlement is not bound to restore it to the person it truly belonged to. Likewise, a person who received something in order to relinquish a right they were claiming in the matter through a settlement is not bound to restore what they received, even if it is later discovered that the right did not belong to them, but to the other person to whom they left it for that price. The reason is that in such a settlement there occurs a kind of sale and exchange of a doubtful right, as it was under that doubt at the time, for the thing given in exchange—regardless of what the truth of the matter was in reality or what might become clear in the course of time. Therefore, whatever might later be proven to the contrary, that settlement is considered valid in both conscience and the legal court. This is found in the law *Lucius*, combined with the Gloss there, in the Digest <note>Digest 36.1.80 (78)</note>, which explains the matter excellently, and in the law *Sub praetextu* 1 and 2 in the Code.

<margin>19</margin>
It must also be observed that for such a contract to be just, it is necessary that equality be maintained between the contracting parties according to the judgment of a prudent person. That is to say, the amount given for the withdrawal from the action or the surrender of the right must be equal to what that right was worth in the estimation of men, as it stood under that state of doubt. If the value of other things that belong to a possessor without any doubt does not consist in a single precise point but has a certain range within the limits of justice, then with much greater reason the value of an uncertain right—which must be determined by lawsuits and expenses—does not consist in a precise point. Rather, it will have a great range within the limits of justice, and for that reason, it is very difficult to condemn any settlement as unjust. However, when it is certain, by the judgment of a prudent person, that equality was not maintained, then the one who did not maintain it would be bound in the forum of conscience

<column-break/>

to bring that settlement contract back to equality.

<margin>20</margin>
<margin>† Question</margin>
Hence the doctors <note>Legal scholars and theologians</note> doubt whether, when one of the parties in a settlement is deceived beyond or below half of the just value <note>The concept of "laesio enormis" or enormous loss, where a contract can be rescinded if the price is less than half the value</note>—not indeed by comparison to what was later discovered through some writing or other source, but by comparison to the value that the doubtful right had as it was under that doubt at the time the settlement was celebrated. This is affirmed by Bartolus and others cited by Gama (decision 110, num. 15), Aires Pinel (on the Code, *de rescindenda venditione*, part 1, ch. 4, num. 12), and Molina (book 4, *de primogeniis*, ch. 9, num. 34). The question, I say, is whether a legal action is then granted in the legal court to the one so deceived, in the same way it is granted to a buyer or seller similarly deceived (as explained in Disputation 349), so that either the contract is reduced to equality or rescinded, as the other contracting party who was not deceived prefers. On this matter, there are so many doctors on both sides (whom Aires Pinel cites copiously from number 12) that it is difficult to judge which opinion is more common. Padilla, toward whose opinion Gutierrez leans (*On Confirmed Rights*, part 3, ch. 2, num. 24), embraces the negative side, which Gregório Lopez (law 34, title 14, Partida 5) thinks is defined there. To me, however, the opinion of the Gloss on the law *Lucius*, final section, Bartolus, Panormitanus, Navarrus, and many others cited and followed by Aires Pinel, is more approved. Namely, that a legal action is granted in the legal court to the one so deceived; this could happen especially to a peasant or a woman <note>Groups traditionally granted extra legal protections against being cheated due to presumed lack of education</note>. And this opinion is especially to be embraced in Portugal, where, as held in Book 4 of the *Ordinances* (title 30, § 3), that action is granted not only in buying and selling and leasing, but also **in any agreement** <note>original Portuguese: "em qualquer auença"</note>. Add that in that Kingdom, when there is no text, custom, or common opinion to the contrary, one must stand by the opinions of Accursius and Bartolus. Molina (cited above), along with many others he cites, approves more of a certain middle opinion between the two extremes mentioned. Namely, that it should be admitted if the harm is enormous—beyond or below half the just value—but denied if it is beyond or below half the just value but not by a great excess. However, I do not approve of that opinion.

<margin>21</margin>
A settlement is not only rescinded and rendered null when one of the parties, at the time the contract was celebrated, knew the thing belonged to the other (as was said above), but also when someone is forced to settle through violence or fear that would affect a steadfast man <note>original: "metum cadentem in constantem virum" — a standard legal test for whether a person was truly coerced</note> (law *Interpositas*, Code, title on settlements).

Regarding how much time one has to bring an action based on this and the preceding chapter to rescind a settlement or an agreement to arbitrate (even one that has been confirmed), this was discussed in Disputation 71. Note, however, especially regarding this latter point, that it can easily happen that there is no good faith on the part of the one possessing by title of a settlement made in that way. In such a case, at any time, while that bad faith persists, ownership cannot be acquired by prescription <note>Gaining legal ownership through the passage of time</note>. Nor do I much approve of what Molina teaches to the contrary in the place cited above, number 38.

<margin>22</margin>
Furthermore, it is rescinded if it was made with a minor, and the minor later finds himself notably harmed, because...
