<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of settlements (transactions). The previous page discussed the strength of settlements when reinforced by penalties and oaths. This page moves into the specific protections afforded to minors and the Church, and the legal consequences when the property involved in a settlement is later claimed by a third party.</meta>

<page-num>810</page-num>
<header>810. Luis de Molina on Contracts</header>

...because (namely, looking at the value of the right which he surrendered and which he released through the settlement, considering the value of that right as it was under that doubt at the time the settlement was celebrated), notably less was given to him for it than it was worth then under that doubt, or he gave notably more for the right of the other party than it was then worth. In this event, however, the settlement is rescinded through the benefit of **restitution in full** <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum" — a legal remedy where a contract is canceled and parties are restored to their original state, usually because one party was a minor or was defrauded</note>, which is granted to a minor during the entire time he is a minor, and for four years thereafter. Then the case returns—both on the part of the minor and on the part of the one who had settled with him—to the state in which it was before the settlement. This is well-established in laws 1 and 2 of the Code, *If against a settlement* <note>original: "l. 1. & 2. C. si aduers. transf."</note> and other laws in the Code regarding settlements. In this place, observe that in this event, and in that other case where a settlement was made through force or fear that would affect a steadfast man, the one who violates the settlement incurs no penalty, even if the settlement had been confirmed by an oath, as held in the law *If any person of age* <note>original: "l. fi quis maior. C. de transf."</note>. However, both a minor and one who was forced to settle by force or fear are bound, under the lethal guilt of **perjury**, to seek and obtain a relaxation of their oath before they act to rescind the settlement—unless in Portugal the oath was taken without the King’s faculty, according to what was said in Disputation 149. I also judge, according to what was said in the cited disputation, that a relaxation of the oath cannot be granted to a minor except solely so that the settlement may be reduced to the limits of a just value; just as the other contracting party is bound to reduce it, even if the oath is not relaxed for the minor. Observe also that what has been said in this section regarding a minor applies similarly to the **Church**, if it finds itself harmed by a settlement in the same way; and that the benefit of restitution in full similarly applies to it, as held in chapter 1, *On restitution in full*. The same must be said of any adult to whom the benefit of restitution in full applies. However, restitution in full is only granted to the Church or any other adult within four years from the celebration of the contract, as held in the final law of the Code, *On the times for restitution in full*, and as will be discussed below.

<margin>23</margin> In Disputation 380, shortly after the beginning, it was said and shown that if the thing in question (and regarding which a settlement was made) is **evicted** <note>original: "euincatur" — Eviction here refers to a legal process where a third party proves they have a superior title to the property, causing the current holder to lose it</note>, then the one who received something to drop the lawsuit is neither bound to return it nor held liable for the eviction. I understand this to be the case whether he himself possessed the thing regarding which the settlement was made and handed it over through the settlement to the one who gave him something to drop the suit, or whether that other person possessed it and gave him something so that he would leave it to him and withdraw from the suit. On the contrary, it was said that if that which was handed over to him so that he would drop the suit is evicted (provided it was not part of the matter in controversy that was left free to him so that he would leave the rest free), then the one who handed it over to him is held liable for the eviction. We provided the reason for both assertions there: because he who withdraws from a lawsuit receives compensation in some thing to drop the suit and leave the thing in controversy to the other; he did not receive that thing in compensation for the *property* itself, but in compensation for the **doubtful right** which he claimed in it, whether he truly had that right or not; and for that

<column-break/>

reason, even if that thing is evicted, he is not held liable for the eviction. But because he received what was given to him as if it were the price of that doubtful right, certainly, if it is evicted, the one who gave it as a "price" for that right is held liable for the eviction. And both points are rightly and very clearly defined, according to the legitimate sense which does no violence to the text, in the law *If in the deep* <note>original: "l. si profundo. C. de transf."</note> cited by us there. The doctors of law agree that when someone begins to possess by title of settlement—either because something was handed to someone to drop a lawsuit regarding a thing another possessed, or because part of the thing in controversy was handed to him so he would leave the rest free in the hands of the former possessor, or finally because the one who possessed the thing in controversy handed it over to the other (who said it belonged to him) after receiving some other benefit in compensation for the doubtful right he claimed in it—the doctors agree, I say, that all these people who begin to possess something that was not truly theirs by title of settlement in any of these ways, acquire the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of it if the ownership belonged to the former possessor; otherwise, they acquire a title for **prescribing** <note>original: "praescribendum" — Prescription or usucapion is a legal method of acquiring ownership by possessing something in good faith for a legally required period of time</note> it in the time necessary for prescription with a title. And this is clearly held in the penultimate law of the Code, *On usucapion for a buyer* <note>original: "l. penult. C. de vsucap. pro empt."</note>, the words of which are: *Those having a just cause of possession from the cause of a settlement can acquire by usucapion.* However, when someone was in long-standing possession of the thing in controversy and regarding which a settlement is made, and the other person withdraws from the suit and leaves it free to him in exchange for something else received in compensation, the doctors make a sub-distinction: Because if the one who thus left it free through the settlement says that he yields his right and transfers the whole right he had in it to the possessor, then he truly transfers the ownership of it to him if he himself was the owner; otherwise, he transfers a title sufficient for prescription, provided the possessor holds it in **good faith** for the entire time required to prescribe it with a title. But if he does not say he yields his right and transfers it all to him, but only that he desists from the lawsuit for that which he receives in compensation, permitting the thing to remain with the former possessor, then they say he does not transfer ownership to the possessor (even if the one withdrawing from the suit was the owner), nor is that settlement a sufficient title for such a possessor in good faith to prescribe it in the time necessary with a title. So affirm the Gloss on the aforementioned penultimate law, Bartolus, and the common opinion, which Antonio Gómez (on the Laws of Toro, 45, numbers 71, 72, and 73) records and follows, gathering this as if by an argument from the contrary sense of the cited penultimate law. However, it seems to me it should be said absolutely: by the very fact that a settlement is made regarding a thing that remains in the power of the former possessor, the latter acquires ownership of it if the ownership belonged to the other party who settled with him; otherwise, he acquires a title sufficient for prescription, provided he possesses it in good faith, judging that the thing, at least after that settlement, belongs to him without any doubt. This is affirmed by Cumanus, as cited by Antonio Gómez at the end of number 73. Nor did Antonio Gómez [think] this opinion improbable...

It also analyzes whether a legal settlement grants full ownership or merely a title for long-term possession (prescription), especially when a third party later claims the property.</summary>

He considers [this]; nevertheless, he adds that one should not depart from the contrary common opinion. The reason, however, by which I am led to this, is this: Because it was always the mind of those making a settlement—and the nature of a settlement is such—that in exchange for the benefit given to the other party, one yields their right (if they had any in that matter) and concedes it to the other to whom the thing is left. Hence, even if it later appears from a public instrument that the thing belonged to that other person, there is no obligation to restore it, neither in conscience nor in the external court, as has been said. This would not be true unless such had been the intention of the parties, and the settlement had that effect of itself. In the event, however, that one party yields to the other (in whose hands the thing remains) their own right, everyone confesses that a sufficient title is acquired for **usucapion** <note>original: "vsucapionē" — the legal process by which ownership is gained through long-term possession</note>, the argument from the contrary sense of the cited law *penol.* being no obstacle. Indeed, that is not truly gathered from that law; for by asserting that when someone begins to possess in good faith by title of settlement, he can acquire by that title and possession, it does not deny that if he possessed it before, and a controversy regarding possession and property began to be moved against him, he can acquire it if the controversy ceases and is settled by the transaction.

Regarding settlements concerning crimes, when they can be made and when not, it will be discussed in the third treatise. Now, however, it must be explained when they cannot be made in civil matters, and by whom. Likewise, that a proper settlement has no place in spiritual matters, or matters annexed to the spiritual, yet an **amicable composition** <note>original: "amicabilis cōpositio" — a friendly settlement facilitated by a third party, often used in canon law to avoid the strictures of a formal "transactio"</note>

has a place in them, as will be said in the material on simony and benefits.

<margin>1</margin> He who cannot **alienate** <note>original: "alienare" — to sell, give away, or otherwise transfer ownership of property</note> certain goods cannot settle or compromise regarding them. For that reason, he to whom **entailed goods** <note>original: "bona vinculata" — property tied to a specific line of succession, such as a primogeniture</note> have come cannot settle or compromise regarding them. In a similar way, a **vassal** <note>original: "feudatarius"</note> cannot settle or compromise regarding feudal matters. Nor likewise can an heir burdened to restore something to another settle or compromise regarding it. And likewise, a **prelate** <note>a high-ranking church official</note> cannot settle or compromise regarding Church property which he cannot alienate. For that reason, whatever cause and formality is necessary for alienating Church property (according to what was said in disputes 465 and 468, combined with the preceding and following disputes), the same is required for settling or compromising regarding those goods. In the same way, moreover, just as a minor himself, or a **tutor** or **curator** <note>types of legal guardians for minors or the incapacitated</note>, cannot alienate the immovable property of a minor without a judge's decree, or those precious movable goods which can be preserved by keeping them (as explained in dispute 224), so they cannot settle or compromise regarding them without that same judge's decree. This is gathered from the law *non solum* in the Code, *concerning the estates of minors*, which, because of the reason given (common to all the aforesaid), holds thus: *Not only by sale are the estates of a ward or youth prohibited from being alienated, but neither by settlement, nor in any other way, can they be transferred without a decree from their owner.* Therefore, you too, if you gave a field to your brothers through a settlement, you can reclaim it. The same is gathered from the chapter *cum tempore*, *concerning arbitrators*, where a similar thing is defined regarding a compromise with an arbitrator, because of the same reason common to all the aforesaid. For the reason is the same for a compromise and a settlement, as was said in the preceding dispute; and if a compromise and settlement were valid regarding a thing prohibited from being alienated, it would easily happen by that route that they would be alienated altogether. The common opinion of the doctors agrees in all these things, which Panormitanus, Antonio Gómez, Gregorio López, Julio Claro, Arias Piñel, and Molina (in his book on primogeniture) relate and follow.

The law *cum hæreditas* in the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, does not stand in the way, where it is held: If an heir burdened to restore an inheritance enters into a compromise regarding some hereditary thing, the **beneficiary of the trust** <note>original: "fideicommissarium"</note>, before the inheritance is restored to him, is held to provide security to that heir that he will keep him harmless if he is condemned; from which some have gathered that a burdened heir can compromise regarding hereditary things. # Luis de Molina: On Contracts

...existence, it would have been done usefully and by the judgment of a prudent man, so that at least by an **action for business managed** <note>original: "actione negotiorum gestorum" — a legal claim where one person acts for another without an express agreement, allowing for the recovery of expenses</note> the **beneficiary of the trust** <note>original: "fideicommissarius" — the person who ultimately receives property held in trust</note> would be held liable to the heir in that matter.

<margin>3</margin> Likewise, the law *before restitution* <note>original: "l. ante restitutam ff. de solut."</note> does not stand in the way, where it is held that releases of debt granted by a **burdened heir** <note>original: "hærede grauato" — an heir who is legally required to eventually pass the inheritance to another (a trust)</note> to the estate's debtors before the inheritance is restored are valid. From this, some conclude that a settlement made by the heir at that time is also valid. However, as Molina says above at number 17, following Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, this must be understood as referring to releases that were necessary at that time, in accordance with payments and the proper administration of the inheritance.

<margin>4</margin> In my judgment, the final law <note>original: "l. vltim. §. vltim. ff. de tranf."</note> carries more weight. It states that a settlement made by an heir so burdened with a debtor of the estate is valid if the debtor was ignorant that the inheritance was subject to a future restoration; in such a case, the debtor has a valid defense both against the heir and against the beneficiary of the trust. However, it must be said that this text actually supports our side. For from it—by arguing from the opposite sense—it is clearly gathered that such a settlement is *invalid* if the debtor knew the inheritance was subject to restoration. When the debtor was ignorant of this, it is rightly established out of a certain equity that the settlement be valid even against the beneficiary, insofar as it was made with the heir who was the true administrator of the estate at that time. However, I understand this law to apply when the settlement concerns a debt of movable goods, but not when it concerns immovable property <note>such as land or buildings</note>. And in the first case, the beneficiary would have the same legal action against the burdened heir regarding that debt as they would have had against the debtor if the heir had not made the settlement, as the final gloss notes there. Therefore, if that settlement brought loss to the beneficiary because it was not made usefully or prudently, the heir would be bound to make up for that loss to the beneficiary.

<margin>5</margin> Furthermore, the chapter *Raynaldus* and the first law regarding pacts <note>original: "c. Raynaldus... l. 1. C. de pact."</note> are not obstacles, where a burdened heir made an arbitration or settlement regarding the inheritance: for he did those things with the beneficiary himself, without prejudice to any third party who might be called to that inheritance, which is permitted. Here, however, we are debating whether an arbitration or settlement by the heir with some *third party*, regarding property subject to restoration and to the detriment of the beneficiary, is valid; this is a far different matter. Hence Afflictus and other **feudalists** <note>legal scholars specializing in the law of fiefs and land tenure</note>, as cited by Molina above at number 18, assert that when a controversy over a **fief** <note>original: "feudo" — land held under a feudal lord in exchange for service</note> is only between the lord and the **vassal** <note>the person holding the land</note>, an arbitration or settlement is valid; this must be understood so long as it does not result in a loss to the **agnates** <note>male-line relatives</note> who are called to and have a right to that fief: for then, to their prejudice, it would be invalid.

Similarly, the first chapter [if a vassal] <note>original: "c. 1. §. ſi vaſallus"</note> does not stand in the way, where it is expressly held that a vassal, once a controversy has arisen, can settle with some third 

<column-break/>

party; and the same is held in the first chapter on controversies between a vassal and another, and the first chapter of the laws of Conrad, which holds that one can enter into arbitration.

<margin>6</margin> These, I say, do not stand in the way: because they were either later corrected by the Imperial chapter on the prohibition of alienating fiefs, or they must be understood as referring to a settlement or arbitration where the fief remains with the old possessor, while some money or other free property is granted to settle the controversy. In this way, no prejudice comes to the lord of the fief or the relatives called to it from that settlement or arbitration. This is the view held with Giulio Claro, Baldus, and others, cited by Molina at number 18.

<margin>7</margin> Certain cases are excepted in which settlements and arbitrations are valid regarding **entailed estates** <note>original: "maioratuum" — property legally tied to a family line that cannot be sold or divided</note> and other things prohibited from being alienated. The first is when these are made or confirmed by the authority of a supreme prince for a reasonable cause, to avoid lawsuits, hatreds, and heavy losses. In the name of a prince, the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>the Pope</note> is also understood in those matters which pertain to the Church or his jurisdiction. This is clearly gathered from the first chapter on settlements, where the Pope wills that a certain settlement, even if it might otherwise be invalid, should obtain strength from his confirmation and authority. The same is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Molina and Aties Pinellus cite and follow. For this power must not be denied to a supreme prince for the common good, even regarding the property of those entailed estates that were established without his specific permission. By this same reasoning, settlements and arbitrations made between two supreme princes regarding a matter—each contending it belongs to the crown of his Kingdom—are valid. For this must not be denied to them for the sake of peace and the public good for a reasonable cause.

<margin>8</margin> The second exception is when the settlement agreement contains a provision that the property remains with the one who cannot alienate it, by giving the other party money or something else that can be lawfully alienated. Thus say the gloss and Bartolus, Panormitanus, Molina, and many others whom they cite. However, when the possessor of an entailed estate settles in this manner, he would be bound to pay that money or other alienable thing from his own pocket; he could not burden his successors in the estate to pay it. Unless, perhaps, the money was a modest amount and the settlement was highly necessary for the preservation of the estate: for then he might perhaps be able to seek and obtain, through an **action for business managed**, that something be taken from the fruits of the estate over time until that full sum is paid back to his heirs in parts, with him also contributing some portion from those same revenues. Read Molina at number 25. In the same way, a burdened heir could not settle without the consent of the beneficiary regarding a thing subject to restoration by burdening the beneficiary to pay later what the heir gave to the other party in compensation so that the property would remain in the inheritance. It is, however, to be observed

### Second Treatise, Disputation 557. 813

Regarding this second outcome, as Bartolus and others rightly observe—along with Molina (at number 28 as cited above) and Arias Piñel (number 46, cited in the section "but with Baldus")—this does not apply when someone who claims property belonging to a **maioratus** <note>An entailed estate that must pass to specific heirs and cannot be sold or broken up.</note> claims it not as their own free property, but as property similarly subject to the bond of the entail. If they obtain it, it must pass down to their successors still under that bond. In such a case, a **settlement** <note>original: "transactio" — a legal compromise to end a dispute</note> made for money or other unburdened property would be entirely void. This is because it would be to the prejudice of the successors of the person claiming the property as their own; therefore, those successors could claim it in the same way, and the settlement could not hinder them, as it could not prejudice their rights. Hence, along with Bartolus and others, they rightly say: just as a settlement concerning immovable property possessed by a minor is invalid unless that property remains with the minor, so a settlement concerning immovable property that a minor claims (while someone else possesses it) is invalid unless the property is handed over to the minor. In the same way, when property is entailed—whether it remains with the current possessor or passes to the claimant—a settlement for property that is not entailed is invalid on neither side, and much less so for other entailed property, or for a portion of the property under dispute.

<margin>9</margin>
The third case is when a settlement or an **arbitration** <note>original: "compromissum" — an agreement to submit a dispute to an arbitrator</note> is necessary because it was commanded by a statute or a judicial sentence, especially with the addition of a Prince's order, to avoid evils and scandals in some arduous and difficult case. The reason is that when the **alienation** <note>The transfer of ownership</note> of certain goods is prohibited, this is understood to mean voluntary alienation, not necessary alienation, which the person administering the goods is forced to perform. This is the opinion of Bartolus and the common consensus of the doctors, which Molina refers to and follows at number 28 and the two following. Deservedly, however, the same author, with Bartolus and others, adds that when a statute commands one to settle or arbitrate in a certain event, it should be understood to apply when the persons are not otherwise prohibited from alienating—such as those we are currently discussing. For that reason, such a statute should not be extended to these persons unless it is clearly expressed.

<margin>10</margin>
The fourth case is when, in a settlement or arbitration, everyone consents in whose favor the prohibition of alienation was made (to ensure they were not prejudiced), provided the due solemnities are observed if the goods belong to minors or the Church. For example, if all the **trust beneficiaries** <note>original: "fideicommissarij" — those entitled to receive property held in trust at a later date</note> to whom the property is eventually to be derived consent to a settlement or arbitration of the inherited goods along with the **burdened heir** <note>The heir currently holding the property but required to pass it on later</note>, that settlement or arbitration is valid. This is gathered from the law *Quoties ab omnibus* (Code, *De fideicommissis*), and the matter is clear in itself. However, in the case of **maioratus** goods, where the future successors to whom the goods are to be derived cannot all consent at once because they do not yet exist, this outcome does not apply. So says Molina at number 31.

Indeed, Molina says at number 32, following the common opinion and various laws he cites: even against these settlements and arbitrations, when they are made by the authority of the Prince, it is lawful to raise the same objections mentioned in the preceding disputation that can be raised against other settlements;

<column-break/>

and arbitrations, so that they may be rescinded—namely, that one of the settling parties was harmed **beyond or below half of the fair value** <note>original: "vltra, aut infra dimidiū iusti valoris" — the legal doctrine of 'laesio enormis,' allowing a contract to be canceled if the price is off by more than 50%</note>, or was forced to settle by force or fear. <margin>11</margin> Indeed, at number 38, he adds that the same time limit for the prescription of these actions mentioned in the preceding disputation is sufficient to prescribe them regarding *maioratus* goods when the settlements were made by the authority of the Prince. Because once the faculty to make a settlement or arbitration concerning those goods is granted, they can therefore be alienated under that title as if they were not entailed at all. No more time is required to prescribe the actions to contend that they should be restored to the *maioratus* than if they had never been entailed. Read his work.

<margin>12</margin> Regarding matters contained in a will, a settlement is invalid unless the parties first know what is contained in that will (Laws *De ijs* and *Non est ferendus*, Digest, *De transactionibus*). This holds true even if the disposition being settled was made in an oral will or a **codicil** <note>An addition or supplement to a will</note>, as is clear from the cited law *Non est ferendus*. However, someone who settles generally regarding all contents of a will cannot later be excused by saying they only understood it to mean a specific part of it. Nevertheless, if codicils made later should come to light, which were not mentioned in the will, the settlement is not extended to the contents of those codicils of which there was no knowledge or mention. It is sufficient to have knowledge of the contents of the will or other last testament through the truthful report of others for a settlement made concerning them to be valid. Such knowledge is presumed in an heir who **enters into the inheritance** <note>The formal act of accepting the rights and duties of an heir</note>, whether they be an outsider or a direct heir. For no one is presumed to enter an inheritance without sufficient knowledge of the contents of the will—even if they are a direct heir, since today by praetorian law a direct heir is allowed to abstain from the inheritance, as was said in the section on wills. From the fact that an heir enters the inheritance, knowledge of the contents of codicils is *not* presumed when those codicils were not mentioned in the will. I said above that knowledge from the truthful report of others is sufficient; for if it is established that a false report was made and one of the settling parties was deceived—whether an heir, a legatee, or a trust beneficiary—the settlement will then be invalid, as it was made without true notice of what was contained in that last will. This is the view of Gutierrez (Part 3, Chapter 2, Number 3), Gregorio Lopez (on the 6th Partida), and many others whom he cites. In a similar way, a gratuitous pact regarding the contents of a last will is not valid if the contents are unknown. This is found in the first law cited, and the same was affirmed by the glosses on the law *De ijs* and by Bartolus and others whom Gregorio Lopez refers to. Although Gutierrez affirms the contrary at the end of the last number, <margin>A Doubt</margin> I do not approve of his opinion. However, a sentence <margin>13</margin> passed without knowing the contents of a last will...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 557. 814

->**Ludovicus Molina on Contracts**<-

...if it is found to be void after the last will has been opened, from which a contrary judgment should have been made. The doctors of law vary on this, as cited by *Gutierrez* (final note) and *Gregorio López* (in the penultimate gloss cited above). I agree with *Gregorio López* that while the settlement might be technically valid, it ought to be rescinded through **restoration to the original state** <note>original: "restitutio in integrum" — a legal remedy where a contract is cancelled and parties are returned to their positions before the agreement.</note> based on a "just error" that was revealed later.

<margin>Decision 14</margin> However, is a settlement made with a debtor of the estate valid if the contents of the deceased’s last will are unknown? *Gregorio López* and *Gutierrez* (chapter 2, number 18) answer in the affirmative, along with others they cite.

<margin>Question</margin> Although a settlement made concerning matters that depend on a last will is void if the contents of that will are unknown (as has been stated);
<margin>15</margin> there is nonetheless a doubt as to whether it is valid if it is made with a **renunciation** <note>A formal rejection of a legal right.</note> of the rights that would otherwise declare it invalid. The *Gloss* on the law *de iis* answers in the affirmative, based on the principle that the law was introduced for the benefit of the person who suffers the loss; and anyone can renounce a right introduced for their own benefit, according to the law *si quis in conscribendis* (regarding pacts) and other laws we have frequently cited.

<margin>Decision</margin> Nevertheless, the common opinion is contrary to that *Gloss*, as held by *Bartolus* and others, and followed by *Gutierrez* (number 19) and *Alvaro Valasco* (consultation 39, number 13). The reason is that this law was established for the common good—to avoid fraud and deception and to ensure that the wishes of testators are fulfilled. Therefore, a renunciation of that right is invalid, no less than a renunciation of the right that forbids the sale of **dotal land** <note>Land belonging to a woman's dowry, which was legally protected from being sold by the husband.</note> or the sale of immovable property or valuable movable goods by a minor without a judge's decree.

<margin>Question</margin> A much greater doubt arises, and one far more controversial: what if that settlement is confirmed by an oath? Such a
<margin>16 †</margin> confirmation carries much more weight than a simple renunciation of rights—whether or not those rights are renounced alongside the oath, either explicitly or through a general clause. The question is whether it is then rendered valid or not.

<margin>Decision</margin> Setting aside a long dispute and the citation of many authors (whom one may read in *Gutierrez* at number 20), the matter can be stated briefly. If the person who was harmed by the settlement was deceived—because they were told the will contained something different than what it actually did—then the settlement confirmed by oath is invalid regarding the "excess" amount they were cheated of and which they did not intend to give up. This is proven because there was no true **consent** <note>Legal and moral agreement.</note> regarding that excess, nor an intention to promise it. Since an oath requires consent to be binding, and cannot extend further than the consent it confirms, it follows that the settlement is entirely invalid regarding that excess. In such a case, there is no need to seek a release from the oath for that portion. Indeed, by taking direct action to punish the crime of such unfair deception, one could seek to have the oath for the remainder released as a just penalty for the crime, making the whole settlement invalid, or seek further punishment for the deceiver. However, if the person was harmed but not deceived by another,

<column-break/>

but rather acted out of their own haste <note>original: "levitate" — lightness of mind or lack of due consideration.</note>, and because they did not expect the deceased to leave them so much, and thus settled and confirmed the settlement with an oath—something they would not have done had they known how much prejudice the settlement would cause them—then a distinction must be made. If neither of the contracting parties knew what was contained in the last will (for example, if one was told they were the heir and the other was told they were left a legacy, without specifying how much; or if one was clearly the heir, like a son, and the other was a beloved friend of the deceased, and it was likely the deceased left them something but the amount was unknown), and they settled under that uncertainty, agreeing to a specific amount regardless of what the outcome proved to be, and confirmed the settlement with an oath; then that settlement is entirely valid. Even if a great loss is later found on one side, it would be wrong to release the injured party from the oath. This is because doing so would cause an unjust injury and loss to the other party, who acquired a true right through that settlement confirmed by oath, according to the arguments explained at length in Disputation 149. The reason is that, given the uncertainty, the settlement was an **equal contract**; both parties exposed themselves equally to gain or loss, and for that reason, it was just and valid in itself, unless it was made void by a provision of civil law. Therefore, since an oath gives strength to a contract that is not in itself unjust or prohibited, but only void by human law (as explained in the cited disputation and the two following), it follows that the settlement was entirely valid, and the other party acquired a true right through it. If, however, the party who was not harmed but gained a benefit *did* know what was in the last will, while the other was ignorant and had no intention of forgiving the excess—and would have refused to settle or would have wanted the settlement to be void if they had known the truth—then I believe that even if they confirmed it with an oath, it is invalid, and no release from the oath is necessary. I am led to this because they did not truly intend to settle in that event, nor did they give consent except under a **virtual condition** <note>An implied condition that is not stated but is understood to exist for the agreement to be valid.</note>: namely, that the other person was not acting with secret knowledge but was also exposing themselves to risk, so that the contract was truly equal regarding a matter uncertain to both. Just as a man who has sworn an oath to marry a woman he did not know was "corrupted" is not bound to marry her if he later finds she is not a virgin—and needs no release from his oath because the promise had a virtual and tacit condition ("if she is a virgin"), even if he did not think of it at the time—so too it is in this case.

<summary>Molina discusses whether settlements (transactions) regarding an inheritance are valid when the parties are ignorant of the deceased's last will. He concludes that while such agreements are generally voidable, an oath may validate a settlement if both parties were equally uncertain, though deception by one party renders the oath non-binding due to a lack of true consent.</summary>

the proposal: because in both cases a full and absolute consensus is lacking, and it is only conditional—under a tacit and virtual condition which does not truly exist. Therefore, that strictly conditional oath does not bind when the condition is not met. Let no one object to us that if someone, while under an oath, promises a hundred to a usurer or a highwayman <note>original: "grassatori" — a bandit or mugger</note> so that he might not be killed, he is bound to pay those sums or obtain a **relaxation of the oath** <note>A formal release from a religious promise, usually granted by a church authority.</note>. For these are absolute oaths, even if they involve a "mixed" will <note>A legal term for a choice made under duress—it is still a choice, but a constrained one.</note>; or, if they have an attached condition (namely, "if you give me a loan" or "if you do not kill me"), the condition is met, otherwise the oath would not bind. Finally, if someone who confirmed a settlement to his own detriment with an oath had a true intention of surrendering whatever might belong to him from the last will, then the settlement would be entirely valid, and the oath could not be relaxed for the one making the settlement, according to what was explained extensively in Disputation 149.

<margin>17</margin>
Regarding **maintenance** <note>original: "alimenta" — the legal right to food, clothing, and shelter, usually provided for in a will.</note> left to someone from a last will or from a gift in anticipation of death, if it is to be provided in the future, a settlement or any other agreement regarding it is invalid without a judge’s authority, an investigation of the case, and the observance of other requirements mentioned in the law cited next. An exception is made unless the settlement results in a greater benefit for the person to whom the maintenance is owed—for instance, if maintenance that was to be paid at the end of the year is agreed to be paid in monthly installments, or in some other way more convenient for the one being supported. In such a case, the settlement or agreement is valid even without a judge’s authority. Note that we said "left from a last will": for if maintenance is owed on some other ground, such as from a contract or elsewhere, a settlement or agreement made concerning it without a judge’s authority will be valid. We also added "if it is to be provided in the future": because a settlement or agreement made without a judge's authority is valid concerning maintenance that should have been provided in the past, or which must be provided in the present and is already fully owed. All these points are found expressly in the law *Cum hi* throughout the entire law in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff." — a standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law.</note> *on settlements*, and the law *on maintenance* in the **Code** <note>original: "C." — the Code of Justinian.</note> under the same title. The common opinion of the doctors agrees with this, which *Gutierrez* (Part 3, Chapter 3) among others reports and follows. The reason for this most wholesome sanction was **public utility** and the common good: so that those to whom maintenance is left for the future by testators—being enticed by a small amount of present money in exchange for future support—would not surrender their rights for it and subsequently live in extreme misery, thereby defrauding the will and intent of the testators. Therefore, because this was decreed not so much as a personal privilege for those to whom maintenance is left, but for the common good, the common opinion of the doctors rightly affirms that a settlement or agreement regarding future maintenance is invalid without a judge’s authority, even if the agreement is made with an express renunciation of that right.

<margin>18</margin>
The doubt remains, however, whether such a settlement or agreement is valid if it is **confirmed by an oath**. Although *Bartolus* (on the cited law *Cum hi*), *Fulgosus*, and *Baldus* asserted it is invalid, the 

<column-break/>

common opinion—along with the same *Bartolus* where he contradicts himself in the law *Si quis pro eo* in the Digest *on sureties* <note>original: "de fideiuf." — de fideiussoribus.</note>, which *Covarrubias* (chapter *Quamvis pactum*, part 2, § last, number 6) and *Gutierrez* (cited above, number 4) report and follow—rightly asserts that it is valid. The reason is that although by the highest right <note>original: "iure optimo"</note>, for the reason given, a pact or sale of the right to future maintenance left by a last will is rendered null and void without a judge’s authority, nevertheless, setting aside that disposition of civil law, the sale of that right or its exchange for another thing is not inherently evil; just as the sale, exchange, or surrender of any other thing bequeathed to the same person is not evil. Therefore, if it is confirmed by an oath, it will be entirely valid in **conscience** and in the external court. Indeed, if no fraud or injustice occurred on the part of the other contracting party—because the contract was equal and just in itself—the oath cannot be relaxed. If, however, injustice occurred, it can only be relaxed to the effect that the contract is reduced to equity. Remember, however, regarding this and the preceding question, that a contract is null by **Portuguese Law** <note>original: "iure Lusitano"</note> by the very fact that it is confirmed by an oath, unless it was performed with the King's permission, as was stated in Disputation 149.

*Covarrubias* (as cited above) and *Gutierrez* (cited chapter 3, number 6), with others they reference, believe this common and true opinion should be limited: provided that because he made a pact under oath regarding future maintenance without a judge’s decree, he does not later fall into **extreme necessity** <note>A state of life-threatening poverty.</note>. For then (as many of them say), after first seeking and obtaining a relaxation of the oath, he could sue for that maintenance to be provided to him, despite having disposed of it under oath without a judge's decree.

I believe this opinion is false. For once he has validly disposed of those rights without a judge's decree, the one who lawfully and validly entered into the pact with him in that manner is no more bound to provide him maintenance in extreme necessity than anyone else would be, or than if he had lawfully bought something else from him and the seller later fell into extreme necessity. Therefore, if the one who has fallen into extreme necessity has an ascendant or descendant <note>Parents or children.</note> who is bound to provide him maintenance, not only in extreme but also in grave necessity (according to what has been said more than once in this second treatise), surely that relative is to be compelled, and not that other party, to provide him maintenance. If, however, he has no such relative, certainly the person who bought the maintenance due to him in the future is no more compelled than anyone else; rather, all can be compelled to contribute to rescuing their neighbor from that extreme necessity, according to what we have said in the matter of **almsgiving**.

Indeed, if in the event of extreme necessity, the one who bought that maintenance could be compelled to return it, there would be no need for a relaxation of the oath to seek it. This is because a sale or settlement regarding those things confirmed by an oath would not be understood to cover such a supervening event; for if the parties to the settlement understood it to apply even in that event, such an agreement would be wicked and evil on the part of both, as intending to bind one to sin, and thus the oath...

<summary>This page discusses the legal and moral validity of settlements involving future maintenance (alimenta) left in wills, emphasizing that while civil law requires judicial oversight to prevent exploitation, a religious oath may render such deals binding unless they violate specific regional laws like those of Portugal.</summary>

# Ludwig Molina On Contracts

that it is void, and therefore no **release of the oath** <note>A formal ecclesiastical dispensation from a religious promise.</note> would be necessary. However, if someone were to sell those rights or otherwise alienate the right to them while facing extreme necessity for food on the part of the one to whom they are owed, then the contract would be invalid; and if it is confirmed by an oath, it is void because it concerns an illicit and bad matter to be fulfilled, and is rendered ineffective by civil law. Therefore, a release of the oath would not be necessary in that case.

In accordance with what has been said so far, Gigas (in *On Pensions*, question 45, from number 9, and question 53, from number 21) and after him Gutierrez (where cited above, number 5) along with others, have asserted that when a **pension** <note>A fixed payment, often from church revenues, assigned for a person's support.</note> for maintenance is assigned to someone from an **ecclesiastical benefit** <note>A church office, like a parish or canonry, that provides an income.</note>, a remission of that pension is not valid without the authority of a superior; whereas without that authority it would be valid if it were not assigned for maintenance. They add, however, that it is valid if the remission is confirmed by an oath, as the common opinion affirms regarding a settlement or agreement concerning future maintenance. And from this doctrine, Gutierrez says, emanated the rule of the **Chancery of Pius V** <note>Pope Pius V (r. 1566–1572) issued many administrative reforms for the Church; the Chancery was the office handling these legal rules.</note>, by which a resignation or renunciation of an ecclesiastical benefit made freely is not admitted without mention of competent maintenance, unless it is established that another benefit remains for the one renouncing it, from which he can be competently supported. I believe, however, that the first assertion of these authors is false. For, as has been said, and as is clearly evident from the law *cum hi* in the **Digest** <note>original: "ff. de trans." — refers to the Digest of Justinian, the primary source of Roman civil law.</note> on settlements, a settlement or pact regarding future maintenance is only void without a judge's authority when the maintenance was left through a **last will** <note>A testament or inheritance.</note>, but not when it is owed to someone from another source. Since such laws, which dispose of things that would otherwise belong to someone by nature in the absence of such laws, are not to be extended further than their wording and disposition sound; and since a pension for maintenance does not have its origin in a last will (as is very well known); it follows certainly that the disposition of the law *cum hi* is not to be extended to a pension granted for maintenance, nor can an effective argument for proving that be drawn from that law. Therefore, since the cited doctors are led by no other argument, their opinion on this matter is undoubtedly false. That rule of the Chancery did not originate from there, since it extends to any benefits whatsoever, even if not granted for maintenance; rather, it is because the Supreme Pontiff rightly did not want to admit resignations of benefits unless the beneficiaries retained competent ecclesiastical revenues from which they could live without disgrace or destitution.

<margin>39</margin> A **procurator** <note>A legal representative or agent authorized to act on behalf of another.</note> appointed to act and defend someone cannot settle or submit to arbitration unless he has a **special mandate** <note>Specific, written permission for high-stakes actions, as opposed to a general power of attorney.</note> for that purpose, according to the law on settlements in the Code and the chapter *qui ad agendum* on procurators in the Sixth Book. Indeed, even if someone is appointed as a procurator with a general clause stating that he can carry out everything that requires a special mandate, he cannot by virtue of such a clause carry out those things that require a special mandate; and therefore, he can neither settle nor submit to arbitration. If, however, it is granted to him in particular to do something that would require a special mandate, and a universal clause were added that he could also carry out everything that requires a special mandate, then he could carry out other things not expressed which require a special mandate, and thus could settle and submit to arbitration. This is held expressly in the cited chapter *qui ad agendum*—

<column-break/>

—to Covarrubias (Book 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 5, number 8). Along with the common opinion, which he cites, he says that if a general clause is included in the procurator's instrument in the aforementioned manner, and something is excepted in particular, or some things requiring a special mandate are excepted which he is denied the power to perform, then he can perform the remaining things that require a special mandate, even if no such thing is expressed in particular as being granted to him. Likewise, if someone is appointed as a procurator in some cause, or regarding all the goods of the person for whom he is appointed, with a clause stating that he is the procurator regarding that cause or all the goods with **free administration and disposition** <note>Broad legal authority to manage property as if the agent were the owner.</note>, just as the person for whom he is appointed could do, then he can settle and do other things that require a special mandate. This is found here in the cited chapter *qui ad agendum*. The common opinion agrees in these matters, which Covarrubias (Book 1, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 6, number 3) reports and follows. Provided, however, as Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading canon lawyer.</note> adds (where he speaks excellently on the restoration of the whole, number 5), that from the matter which requires a special mandate, no notable detriment is likely to follow for any third party; for then a specific expression of that matter is required. Regarding this matter, we speak in Disputation 573. Likewise, he who is appointed as a "procurator in his own matter"—for instance, because a creditor granted him the debt or the entire right which he has regarding the matter in question—can then settle regarding it and do anything else regarding it which would otherwise require a special mandate. This is stated in the last gloss of the cited chapter. But we deal with this more extensively in Treatise 5.

For instance, it is the same to seek the "goods which you managed" or "which belonged to the deceased Peter" as it is to seek "all the goods which you managed" or "which belonged to the deceased Peter."

In the same way in settlements, it is the same to settle regarding certain goods indefinitely as it is to settle regarding them universally. The result is that by the name of a universal petition or settlement, even a petition...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 558

...the petition, or settlement, is understood indefinitely.
This being established, the proposed question must be satisfied by the following conclusions. The first is:

<margin>1</margin> Whether the **legal claim** <note>Latin: *petitio*</note> and the pursuit of the lawsuit were universal or particular—for instance, if a specific thing was sought, such as a certain house or something similar—if a **particular settlement** <note>Latin: *transactio*; a legal compromise where both parties make concessions to end a dispute.</note> follows afterward, such as when a settlement is made regarding a specific thing or specific things expressed in the agreement, then that settlement is not extended to other things. Instead, the right remains intact to bring an action for any other things against the same person with whom the settlement was made, but certainly not regarding those specific things. This is very well known and is established from the law *Age* in the **Codex** <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, part of the body of Roman civil law.</note> under the title *On Settlements*. There, for example, when a debtor owed two hundred, if the plaintiff sought one hundred and a settlement was made for fifty, such a settlement regarding the hundred sought does not impede an action regarding the other hundred, but only regarding those for which the settlement was made. The same is found in the law *Si unus*, in the section *Ante omnia* (otherwise the section *In summa*) in the **Digest** <note>The *Digesta*, another primary part of Roman civil law.</note> under the title *On Pacts*. Nevertheless, the final gloss on the cited law *Ante omnia*, and the final gloss on the law *Si cum tibi*—according to the text there and its summaries—as well as Padilla (on the law *Si de certa*, number 5, in the Codex), Alvaro Valasco (consultation 39, number 5), and others whom he cites, rightly observe that such a settlement is nonetheless extended to things that are **dependent and connected** to the thing or things for which that special particular settlement was made.

<margin>2</margin> The second conclusion: When a settlement was particular regarding a thing, if it was universal regarding **actions** <note>The legal right to sue or the specific power to enforce a claim.</note>—because it was stated that one of the parties yielding to the other remits whatever right they could have regarding that thing under any **title** <note>The legal basis or cause for a claim, such as a contract, inheritance, or gift.</note>—then that thing cannot be sought from them for any other cause or title by which it is newly discovered to have belonged to them. However, if it was particular regarding the action—because it was specifically expressed that they withdraw from such an action and yield to whatever right the thing could pertain to them for that cause or title—then they will be able to seek it again on any other ground or title. But if none of these were expressed in the settlement, and it was only said that they withdraw from the action regarding that thing and yield the right they could have in it, then, if a claim for that thing based on some particular cause and title preceded it, the settlement is only deemed to have been made for that title and cause; therefore, they will be able to seek the same thing based on another title and cause. If, however, a claim for that thing preceded it by stating in general that the thing belonged to them, without expressing the cause or title from which it pertained to them, then the settlement is deemed made regarding that thing from every title and cause. Therefore, they will not be able to seek that thing again from any cause or title preceding that settlement. This is the opinion of **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> on the law *Si de certa* in the Codex, and with him **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> on Chapter 1 of the same title at the end, by the argument of the chapter *Abbate* regarding sentences and res judicata in Book 6, and the law *Si ita quis*, the final section, in the Digest *On Verbal Obligations*.

<margin>3</margin> The third conclusion: If the claim and the pursuit of the lawsuit were general, and a general settlement also followed, then the settlement must be understood generally, even regarding unknown things and those that were not then occurring to the mind. Therefore, whoever has settled in this way is afterward barred from a claim for any thing comprised by those general words. Thus

<column-break/>

it is stated in the law *Sub praetextu*, 2, in the Codex under the title *On Settlements*. This is affirmed by Bartolus and Panormitanus where cited above, Padilla in the cited place number 2, Alvaro Valasco in consultation 39, number 6, and others whom he cites. For a settlement to be valid regarding things unknown in particular but contained under that generality, it is enough that the generality was considered and settled without an exception being made for them. This is what Alvaro Valasco (cited above, number 7) says along with Bartolus and others: that they are **known in the universal**. There is no need for any other explanation in this part of the proposed third conclusion, which Alvaro Valasco and others multiply. 

<margin>4</margin> But an exception is made to the true conclusion proposed: if, by the **fraud** <note>Latin: *dolus*; intentional deception or bad faith.</note> of one of the parties settling, some things comprised under that universality (about which the settlement was made) were hidden or not manifested. For example, if some brothers succeeded their father in his goods, and while they settled universally regarding their entire inheritance, one of them hid or did not manifest certain things which he knew belonged to the inheritance; in that case, the settlement is not extended to those things hidden by fraud. Thus says the law *Tres fratres* in the Digest *On Pacts*, and along with Bartolus and Panormitanus, this is the common opinion which Alvaro Valasco (cited above, number 12) reports and follows. An exception is also made to the conclusion when unknown things were owed by a **last will** <note>A testament or legacy.</note>, and a universal settlement was made that would comprise those things before that last will was shown and known; for then the settlement is invalid by the law itself, as was seen in the preceding disputation.

<margin>5</margin> The fourth conclusion: When the claim was particular and a general settlement followed, a distinction must be made. For if the general settlement can be restricted, while preserving the proper meaning of the speech, to only the particular thing or things about which there was a claim, then it is not understood to cover other things, because subsequent words are understood according to those that preceded them when nothing stands in the way. This is supported by the law *Si de certa re* in the Codex *On Settlements* and the law *Qui cum tutoribus* at the beginning, in the Digest under the same title. This is affirmed by Bartolus and Panormitanus as cited above, Padilla on the cited law *Si de certa re*, and Alvaro Valasco in consultation 39. 

If, however, the general settlement cannot be restricted to the specific thing or things of the claim while preserving the proper meaning of the speech—for example, because the plaintiff, while settling, said they withdraw from actions and renounce the right they had both regarding the thing claimed and regarding **any other things whatsoever**—then the settlement is extended to all things, even if the plaintiff did not think of them in particular. It is enough that they knew of them in the universal and in a confused way (in the manner explained in the preceding conclusion) and that they intended to remit the whole, which is presumed from such general words of settlement. 

They should blame themselves for not being cautious and for using such profuse language. So says Panormitanus where cited above, Bartolus on the law *Emptor*, section *Lucius*, in the Digest *On Settlements*, and others whom Alvaro Valasco (cited above, number 3) reports and follows. There, along with Jacobinus and others, he adds: That if Peter owes John ten from a loan and twenty from another cause—say, from a sale—and John makes a pact with Peter not to seek those ten, even if he were to add these words to that pact or release: "and generally concerning everything that I could seek from you up to the present day," the remission of the other twenty is not deemed to have been made, which...

## On novation and delegation.
### DISPUTATION 559.
->SUMMARY<-

1 From where "novation" is named, and what it is.
2 When and in what ways novation occurs. Also number 3.
And when, and in what cases it is considered made, or not: numbers 4, 12, 13, 14.
5 What "to delegate" means.
6 What is required for a delegation to be valid.
7 Delegation, like novation, ought to be made by **stipulation** <note>Latin: *stipulatio*; a formal verbal contract in Roman law involving a specific question and answer.</note>.
8 Whether novation is considered made through delegation, even if it is not expressed that it is done with the **intent to novate** <note>Latin: *animus novandi*; the specific legal intention to replace an old obligation with a new one.</note>.
And what the law of Castile says: number 9.
Likewise, whether it is considered made by the addition of a penalty, or another penal pact: number 10.
And what of cases where a new law is repugnant to the old, whether it is considered made at least by the help of an exception: number 11.
15 How a penalty is usually applied to someone not standing by a contract.
16 A woman can strike down a novation by the **Velleian benefit** <note>Latin: *beneficium Velleiani*; a Roman legal protection (Senatus Consultum Velleianum) that prohibited women from standing as a guarantor or taking on the debts of others.</note>.
17 Whether a delegated debtor is considered bound to the creditor of the delegating debtor, even if it is later found that he was not a debtor to the delegator.
18 Whether **Alcabala** <note>A Spanish sales tax common in the early modern period.</note>, or a tribute, is owed from a novation.

We must now speak of the fulfillment of contracts, or the dissolution of an obligation arising from them or contracted elsewhere. This indeed happens most especially either by the remission of the obligation made by the creditor, or by the **payment** <note>Latin: *solutio*; the performance or fulfillment of whatever is owed.</note> of that which someone owes by contract or otherwise. Because a "virtual payment" is both the changing of one obligation into another, by which the prior one is extinguished and the later one succeeds in its place and is **subrogated** <note>To substitute one person or thing for another in a legal claim or debt.</note>, and this occurs through no-

<column-break/>

vation and delegation; then also by the **compensation** <note>The balancing of mutual debts between two parties so they cancel each other out.</note> of one debt and obligation with another debt and obligation; and finally by certain other ways. Before we speak of the payments of debts, in this and the two following disputations, we must deal with novation, delegation, compensation, and certain other ways by which a liberation from an obligation occurs, or a payment is considered to have been made.

<margin>1</margin> **Novation** <note>The legal act of replacing an existing obligation with a new one.</note>, according to the author Ulpian in the first law of the Digest *On Novations*, is named from the word "new" <note>Latin: *novo*</note>, and from a "new obligation" which succeeds in the place of the prior one. Whence, by the same author Ulpian in the same place, it is thus defined: *It is the transfusion and transfer of a prior debt or obligation into another obligation, whether civil or natural, so that the prior one is destroyed.* Nor does it matter, says Ulpian, what kind of obligation preceded it, whether purely **natural** <note>An obligation binding in conscience or fairness but not necessarily enforceable in a court of law.</note> or **civil** <note>An obligation fully enforceable by law.</note>, and whether contracted by words, by a thing, or by consent; for it can be novated by words in any way, namely by **stipulation** <note>A formal verbal agreement.</note>, as said there and in the second following law. However, according to the **Law of Castile** <note>Spanish law; Molina often contrasts Roman law with the contemporary laws of the Spanish Empire.</note>, it is valid even if celebrated without a stipulation by a **bare pact** <note>Latin: *nudo pacto*; an agreement made without the formalities of Roman law but still considered binding in later legal systems.</note> according to Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, provided that the following obligation, into which it is transferred and changed, is valid, at least naturally. For example, if a **ward** <note>Latin: *pupillus*; a child under legal guardianship.</note> past infancy were to promise by novating without the authority of a guardian; then, although he would not be bound civilly, he would nonetheless remain bound naturally. Although even that obligation could later be struck down by the benefit of **restitution to the original state** <note>Latin: *restitutionis in integrum*; a legal remedy where a contract is canceled and parties are returned to their original positions.</note>, as discussed in Disputation 224 (from which all these things are said), the novation would be valid, and the prior obligation would be extinguished, as seen in the laws to be cited and Law 18, Title 14, Part 5. But if the following obligation were civilly and naturally—and thus entirely—invalid, then novation would not occur, but the prior obligation would remain whole and unhurt. Thus it is cited here and in the section *Præterea* of the Institutes *By what ways an obligation is ended*, joined with the gloss there. An example is provided in the cited section *Præterea* and Law 17, Title 14, Part 5, regarding a slave who attempted to take upon himself the obligation of another. For because he would remain bound neither civilly nor naturally, there would certainly be no novation, nor would the prior obligation expire. If, however, he had the free administration of some **peculium** <note>Property or funds that a slave or son was permitted by the head of the household to manage as his own.</note>, either he himself or a son under paternal power could novate regarding the matters of the peculium, provided it was not by way of a gift; so it is held in the cited Law 17, joined with the gloss of Gregorio López there, and the final law at the beginning of the Digest *On Novations*.

<margin>3</margin> Novation occurs either by a changed person in the second obligation (as if another is established as the debtor for the same amount, whether he was a debtor to the prior debtor or not); or by adding or releasing a guarantor; or by accepting or releasing a pledge; or by an increase or decrease in the quantity owed; or by a varied term established in the prior obligation; or by a condition applied in the later obligation when the prior obligation had been made **unconditionally** <note>Latin: *purè*; without any attached conditions.</note>; or conversely, by a later obligation being made unconditionally when the prior one was made under a condition. Finally, through these or other variations, provided there is an **intent to novate**, novation occurs. However, when a condition is applied in the later obligation while the prior was unconditional, and this is done with the intent to novate, the novation is only considered made if the condition is fulfilled; for if it fails, then the prior obligation remains, and thus no novation is considered to have occurred. Likewise, if the prior obligation was under a condition...

It outlines how changes to parties, terms, or conditions can trigger a novation, provided there is a clear intent to replace the original obligation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Disputation 559 regarding the legal mechanisms of novation (replacing an old debt with a new one) and delegation (assigning a new person to fulfill a debt). It specifically addresses the role of conditions in these contracts and the requirement of explicit intent under modern law.</meta>

Second Treatise, Disputation 559. 819

...condition, and the second is pure <note>Latin: *pura*; in legal terms, an unconditional obligation.</note>, a novation is not considered to have occurred until the condition of the first obligation is fulfilled. For if the condition fails, the second obligation vanishes, unless it was expressly stated in the agreement that the second pact should remain valid regardless of the failure of the first condition, as held in Law 16, Title 14, Part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational medieval Spanish law code.</note>. The same applies if, before the condition is fulfilled, the second debtor falls so far from their status that they no longer have the legal standing to appear in court. This last point regarding the condition, besides the cited Law 16, is found in the laws *quoties* joined with *si Stichum*, paragraph 1, of the Digest *On Novations* <note>Latin: *ff. de noua.*; 'ff' is the standard abbreviation for the Digest of Justinian.</note>, and the Institutes *By what modes an obligation is dissolved*, and Law 15 at the end, joined with the final gloss of Gregorio López there in Part 5. The remaining points are found in the cited paragraph *praeterea*, and Law 2 and following in the Digest *On Novations*.

<margin>4</margin>
Regarding the † disposition and interpretation of the law, many of the variations explained previously led to a presumption that a novation had been made; for they were presumed to be made with the **intent of novating** <note>Latin: *animo nouandi*; the specific legal intention to extinguish an old obligation by creating a new one.</note>, of extinguishing the prior obligation, and of changing it into the later one. This is held in the cited paragraph *praeterea* at the word *sed cum hoc quidem*, and the final law in the section of the Code *On Novations*, and is evident from Law 2 and following in the Digest of the same title. However, today, by the final law of the Code *On Novations* and the paragraph *praeterea* at the word *ideo nostra* in the Institutes *By what modes an obligation is dissolved*, it has been decreed that whatever variation is made in the second obligation, a novation is **not** considered to have occurred—and thus the prior obligation is not considered extinguished—unless the contracting parties explicitly state that they are creating the second obligation with the **intent to novate**. Otherwise, the second obligation remains alongside the first. Therefore, from the perspective of the creditor, a dual obligation or instrument results. Nevertheless, if it is expressed in the later obligation or pact that something is to be subtracted from the prior obligation, the prior creditor will no longer be entitled to that portion. Likewise, in matters where those obligations overlap as the same thing owed to the creditor, if payment is made once, all those obligations expire regarding that amount, and all those who were bound to pay it under the same obligation are set free.

<margin>5</margin>
To delegate, according to the authority of Ulpian in the law *delegare* in the Digest *On Novations*, is to give another debtor to the creditor in one's own place, or to whomever the creditor commands. The first gloss on the law *quamvis* in the Digest *On the Velleian Decree* and the first gloss on the law *si Titus* in the Digest *On Novations* assert that, by

<margin>6</margin>
reason of delegation, † it is necessary that the person being delegated is already a debtor of the person delegating. This opinion is embraced by Paulus Castrensis <note>A famous 15th-century Italian jurist.</note>, whose summary is found in the cited law *delegare*, and it is embraced by others mentioned by Gregorio López in Law 13, Title 14, Part 5, at the word *abiertamente*, and by Gutierrez in *On the Confirmation of Rights*, part 1, chapter 63, number 5. However, the **common opinion** <note>Latin: *communis sententia*; the prevailing view among legal scholars of the time.</note>, along with Azo and Aretinus, which Gutierrez also records there, affirms the contrary: namely, that for a delegation it is sufficient that the person being delegated, by the mandate of the delegator, constitutes themselves as the debtor to the delegator's creditor. This means they take upon themselves the debt of the delegator, even if they were not previously a debtor to the delegator. Indeed, I approve of this common opinion: first, because the act of delegating someone to constitute themselves as a debtor in the place and stead of the delegator clearly encompasses both—substituting one who was previously a debtor, and substituting one who was not. Furthermore, the definition of delegation provided by Ulpian in the law *delegare* certainly applies to both types of debtors in the place and stead of the delegator.

<column-break/>

Finally, whatever the gloss on the cited law *si Titus* may suggest, the discussion there concerns a delegation in which someone is delegated who was not a debtor of the delegator; rather, by the title of a gift <note>Latin: *donationis*; a voluntary transfer without payment.</note>, they took the delegator's debt upon themselves, binding themselves to pay it from their own resources to the delegator's creditor as a gift to the delegator.

<margin>7</margin>
Delegation, which † is a sub-category of novation, ought to be made by a **stipulation** <note>Latin: *stipulatio*; a formal Roman legal contract consisting of a question and an answer.</note> performed by the delegator's creditor, as Alexander says (cited by Gregorio López in the aforementioned gloss). This requires the consent and promise of the one being delegated in order for it to be a true delegation, as was also said above regarding novation. However, Gregorio López rightly adds there that in the Kingdom of Castile, following Law 2, Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Compilation*, it is sufficient if it is done without a formal stipulation by a **naked pact** <note>Latin: *pacto nudo*; an informal agreement that, under older Roman law, did not necessarily grant a right of action, but was recognized in later Spanish law.</note>, as was also stated above regarding novation. From Law 1 and the law *nec creditoris* in the Code *On Novations*, we learn that even though what someone owes to a delegator can be sold by that delegator to someone else without the debtor's knowledge, and the delegator can transfer the right and action they have against that debtor to another without the debtor's knowledge, a delegation cannot be completed or perfected except with the consent of that debtor. The debtor must promise the delegator's creditor, at the creditor's request, that they will pay the debt in the delegator's place. Likewise, in Law 2 and following, we learn that if a delegation is made with the **intent to novate**, by which a delegator assigns their debtor to their creditor, the delegator is immediately and entirely freed from the obligation they held toward the creditor. The delegator can no longer act against that debtor; only the delegator's creditor, to whom the debtor alone remains bound, can take action against them. However, if a creditor merely **cedes** a debt and the right of action to another person, the debtor is not freed from the original creditor by that cession alone. Rather, if nothing prevents it, that original creditor can still take action against the debtor to recover the debt, except in three instances: First, if the person to whom the action was ceded has already joined issue in a lawsuit <note>Latin: *litis contestatio*; a formal stage in a trial where the issues are joined.</note> against that debtor. Second, if they have already received part of the debt. Third, if they have notified the debtor not to pay the original creditor because the debt and action have been ceded. This is held in the cited Law 3.

<margin>8 Question</margin>
These things being established, the doubt is: If someone delegates another to their creditor, and the delegation is perfected by the consent of the delegated party given to the delegator's creditor (whether through formal stipulation or a naked pact celebrated in this Kingdom), does this count as a novation if it is **not** explicitly stated to be done with the "intent to novate"? That is, does the obligation of the delegator expire entirely so that only the obligation of the delegated party remains? Consequently, if the delegated party does not pay—either due to poverty or any other reason—is the person who delegated them no longer held liable for anything? The more common opinion of Bartolus and many others, opposing the final gloss on this law in the Code *On Novations* (cited by Gregorio López and Gutierrez), affirms that according to common law, a novation **is** considered to have been made, and thus the delegator's obligation has entirely expired. Matthaeus de Afflictis and Alciatus, also cited by Gutierrez, assert that this opinion is accepted in practice. Nevertheless, those who argue that it is not a proper and true obligation...

It also defines delegation as substituting one debtor for another and debates whether the new debtor must have a prior relationship with the original one.</summary>

Consequently, they believe that a **novation** <note>The legal act of replacing an old contract with a new one, thereby extinguishing the original debt.</note> occurs and the original debtor's obligation is extinguished only when the person delegated was already a debtor of the delegator. However, they believe this is not the case when the person was not a debtor, unless it is further explicitly stated that the act is done with the **intent of novating** <note>original: *animo nouandi*; the specific legal intention required to replace a debt rather than simply adding a second person to it.</note>. Nevertheless, Baldus and Alexander (who often contradicts himself), as cited by Gregorio López in Law 1, Title 5, under the words "in his place" and "openly," assert that if someone says to Titius's creditor, "I promise to you, in place of Titius, what he owes you," and the creditor accepts this, a novation is considered to have occurred. Thus, Titius remains entirely freed from his debt by that very act. This is the view of the final gloss on Law 2 of the Code *On Novations*, and many others cited by Giovanni Battista in his *Common Opinions*, letter N, number 44 and following, who affirms this as the common opinion. However, if it is true that the contrary view is actually the more common opinion, they think that even if a debtor is delegated, if nothing else is expressed to indicate an intent to novate, the novation is not considered made. Therefore, the obligation by which the delegator was bound to his creditor does not expire through
<margin>9</margin>
<margin>Law of
Castile.</margin>

<margin>Decision.</margin>
