Consequently, the original obligation of the delegator is not abolished unless it is clearly expressed that the delegation is made so that the delegator remains free from the debt. I believe this opinion is undoubtedly true, even standing solely on the **common law** <note>original: *iure communi*; the shared legal tradition of Europe based on Roman law.</note>, and should be embraced even outside the Kingdom of Castile, provided that a contrary custom has not been so accepted as to override the common law. I am led to this because, although Laws 2 and 3 of the Code *On Novations* and other laws imply that a novation is assumed by delegation, that was a matter of legal presumption and interpretation, as found in the final law of the Code *On Novations* and the paragraph *praeterea* in the Institutes. For whenever a new person was substituted—even if they substituted themselves without the original debtor delegating them—it was considered a novation under the **ancient law** <note>Refers to Roman law prior to the reforms of Emperor Justinian.</note>. Thus, under that old law, the opinion of Alexander and Baldus was undoubtedly true. But later, in the final law of the Code and the cited paragraph of the Institutes, it was established that in such events—whether by change of person or any other reason—where previous laws presumed a novation, it should no longer be assumed unless the contracting parties explicitly state that it is done with the intent to novate and abolish the prior obligation. I am also led to this because a different debtor can be delegated and accepted not with the intent of freeing the original debtor, but so that if the new person pays, both are freed; for this purpose, it is irrelevant whether the person was already a debtor or someone else. Therefore, since the Code has decreed that a change of debtor does not assume

<column-break/>

a novation and the release of the prior obligation unless expressed, it follows that delegation alone—which can be done with a very different intent, at least by the creditor—is not considered a novation today unless the parties sufficiently express otherwise.
<margin>10</margin>
The next doubt is whether, if an agreement regarding a matter exists and a penalty is later added (or another penal pact) for not standing by the first agreement, a † novation is considered made. Is the prior obligation abolished by the addition of that penalty, as if it were done with the intent to novate? Under ancient law, a novation was considered made by legal presumption and interpretation, as is clear in the Digest *On Actions and Obligations*. However, the Gloss there says the matter is different after the final law of the Code *On Novations*. The same is affirmed by the Gloss on the Digest *On Pacts* and the Digest *On Verbal Obligations*. On the contrary, following Bartolus, Gregorio López affirms this in Law 34 and 35 of the *Partidas*. This is also the common opinion followed by Gutierrez, that when a pact was made without a penalty and a subsequent penal pact follows, it replaces the first. I, however, much more approve the opinion of those glosses, which the final law of the Code openly suggests. There is no likely argument to prove that an exception should be made from such a general decree, especially since it is not clearly evident from an added penal pact that the parties intended to withdraw from the prior pact. Rather, if we set aside the specific rulings of law, the presumption is that the penalty was added for the **greater firmness** <note>original: *ad maiorem firmitatem*; to make the original contract more secure rather than replacing it.</note> of the prior pact. I would say that Laws 34 and 35, and other laws cited there, speak of when a penalty is added to corroborate the prior pact; they explain when the party who stood by the pact can sue the transgressor for the penalty, or for the fulfillment of the pact, or for damages, or both at once. These laws do not speak of novation, nor are their decisions decided by the rules of novation, as will be quite clear to anyone looking at those laws and their decisions.
<margin>11</margin>
<margin>Question.</margin>
In those events where novation was once presumed by law but is now forbidden by the Code unless expressly stated, could a † novation today be introduced at least **by way of exception**? <note>original: *ope exceptionis*; a legal defense used in court to block a claim.</note> The Gloss on the Digest *On Novations* and the final law of the Code, approved by Bartolus and a few others, affirm this. However, the contrary view—that a novation is not introduced even by way of exception in these events—is to be embraced. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Gregorio López and Gutierrez; the contrary opinion does not rest on any solid foundation.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of novation from page 820, specifically addressing cases where a new agreement is made without explicit language of replacement, the legal protections for women in such contracts, and the consequences of debts taken on by mistake.</meta>

821 Second Treatise, Disputation 559.

...parties, in a second agreement regarding the same matter, do not explicitly state that they wish to make a **novation** <note>original: *nouationem*; the substitution of a new contract for an old one</note> and extinguish the prior obligation using these or other equivalent words; if, however, it is clear from the manner and quality of the second agreement, or from other evidence, and there is no doubt that they intended to create a novation and withdraw from the prior obligation, then a novation is considered to have been made. This is the common opinion which, among others, Gregorio López mentions and follows in his commentary on Law 1, Title 5, under the words "by manner," as does Gutierrez in the passage cited above at number 8; the matter is quite clear in itself. An example is found at the beginning of the cited Law 1, Title 5, which supports this opinion. For if someone sells a hundred gold coins to another, and they later agree between themselves that the buyer should henceforth owe the seller the price as a **loan** <note>original: *mutuo*; a specific type of loan for consumption where the same amount and quality must be returned</note>, then by this second contract—in which the seller grants those hundred gold coins to the buyer as a loan—a novation of the prior obligation from the sale is clearly considered to have occurred. Thus, with the first obligation extinguished, it passes into an obligation from a loan; for the obligation to pay the same money from a sale and from a loan are incompatible. The same would apply if the seller, before the money was even handed over, used it to buy an **annual rent** <note>original: *censum annuum*; a financial arrangement where one party pays a lump sum in exchange for a yearly return, often secured against property</note> from the buyer on some of the buyer’s property. A novation of the prior obligation from the sale would be considered made, turning it into an obligation from a rental contract to pay an annual return. Therefore, if that prior buyer—now no longer a debtor from the sale but from a new contract of loan or rent—were to become insolvent, even if he had sold the thing he first bought, the seller could not reclaim it from the hand of the current possessor on the grounds that the price he sold it for had not been paid. Yet, he could have reclaimed it on that basis if the novation had not occurred, because ownership of a sold item does not leave the seller until the price is paid to him, or he accepts something else as payment, as was proved in Disputation 338 and Disputation 536 regarding the matter of buying and selling and the matter of pledges.

<margin>13</margin> Likewise, a **novation** is considered made if someone obligates themselves to a creditor on behalf of a debtor under the condition that, from that moment on, the original debtor remains free from the obligation. Likewise, a **novation** 

<margin>14</margin> would be considered made if a debtor handed over to the creditor an obligation—by which another person was bound to that same debtor—**in satisfaction of the debt** <note>original: *in solutum*; a legal term for giving something other than money to fulfill a debt</note>, and the creditor accepted it as such. This is the common opinion, which Gregorio López in the cited gloss and Gutierrez at number 9 report and follow. It is otherwise if he handed over that obligation as a **pledge** <note>original: *pignus*</note>, or if he promised some other obligation or property as a backup in the event that he did not pay within a certain time, for the greater security of the creditor. In that case, it would be entirely up to the creditor either to compel the debtor to fulfill the prior obligation or to demand what was promised as a backup if the prior obligation was not fulfilled within the fixed term, as the cited doctors, along with Decio, rightly affirm.

<margin>15</margin> And indeed, when a **penalty** is attached because one party failed to uphold a status, it is regularly added in this way as a backup for greater security and in favor of the other party who stood by the contract. Therefore, when nothing else was expressed, or in some particular event no other legal provision is found, this doctrine must be followed. This is what is provided by Laws 34 and 35, Title 11, Part 5 <note>referring to *Las Siete Partidas*, the foundational Spanish legal code</note> and other laws discussed in Disputation 556. Nor do those provisions 

<column-break/>

rely on the rules of novations, where a novation is considered made by the addition of a penalty.

<margin>16</margin> Although any **woman** may make a novation by taking upon herself the debt of someone to whom she previously owed nothing, she can nevertheless strike down the novation by using the benefit of the **Velleian Decree** <note>original: *Velleiani*; the *Senatusconsultum Velleianum* was a Roman law protecting women by making their guarantees or assumptions of others' debts voidable</note>, as discussed in Disputation 546. By doing so, she renders her subsequent obligation null, according to Law 1.1 of the Senate's decree, the law "If a paternal," and the law "If a woman [pays] another's debt" in the Code *On the Velleian Decree*, and Law 19, Title 14, Part 5. There, Gregorio López adds that if a woman strikes down her subsequent obligation by using that benefit, then the prior debtor remains obligated to the creditor, based on the argument in the law "Whichever," paragraph "Marcellus," at the words "if a woman" in the Digest *On the Velleian Decree*.

<margin>17</margin> When someone, thinking himself to be a debtor to another who was himself a debtor to a certain creditor, took that person's debt upon himself and bound himself to pay that debt to the creditor in his place—a novation of the prior debt having been made between himself and the creditor—then that prior debtor remains entirely freed in relation to that creditor. This second person remains the only one truly bound to the creditor, even if it is later discovered for certain that he owed nothing to that prior debtor. Nor can this person, in relation to the creditor to whom he bound himself in place of the prior debtor, use the **legal defense** <note>original: *exceptio*</note> that he would have had against the prior debtor. Instead, he would be entirely bound to pay the creditor, even if the creditor, at the time this man bound himself, knew that he owed nothing to that prior debtor—provided, however, that the creditor did not induce him through deceit or fraud to so obligate himself in another's place. On the contrary, if he who obligated himself to the creditor in place of the prior debtor knew at the time he so obligated himself that he had some defense against the prior debtor, and nevertheless obligated himself at that person's command or as his delegate, he is considered to have waived and forgiven that defense, as held in the law "If anyone should delegate" and the law "Of malicious deceit" in the Digest *On Novations*. As to when he should be considered to have known or been ignorant of that defense, see the gloss on the cited law "If anyone should delegate." It should be observed, however, that when it is later found that the one who thought himself a debtor to someone and bound himself to that person's creditor actually owed him nothing, then before he pays the creditor, he has an action against that debtor to release him from the obligation by which he bound himself in his place—either by satisfying the creditor or by some other means. This, however, does not prevent him from being held and compelled to pay the creditor if the prior debtor does not get ahead of him with the payment. But if he who was not truly a debtor to the other person pays the creditor, then he has an action to recover from the prior debtor what he paid in his place, even if he obligated himself to it and paid it without a direct command, provided that the other person truly owed it and could have been compelled to pay it. This is held in the law "If anyone should delegate," the law "If not a debtor," and the law "Of malicious deceit" in the Digest *On Novations*, and Law 19, Title 14, Part 5.

If someone was truly a debtor to another, and thinking this creditor of his owed something to a third party, made a novation with that third party by binding himself to pay him what he thought his creditor owed, then—nothing in that contract of novation preventing it—he is not bound to pay him anything. Rather, he can and should protect himself with the defense that his creditor owed nothing to that person. But if, persisting in ignorance, he had paid...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal effects of novation and begins Disputation 560 regarding the legal principle of set-off (compensatio) in civil law.</meta>

822 Ludovicus Molina | On Contracts

**Left Column**

...if he had bound himself to pay in place of his creditor, then if he bound himself by the command of his creditor, he remains free from his original creditor for the amount he thus paid on his behalf. The creditor then has the right to reclaim that payment as "undue" <note>original: *indebiti*; a legal claim to recover money paid by mistake when it was not actually owed</note> if it was paid in his place. If, however, he bound himself and paid without the command of his creditor, then he remains liable to his own creditor just as if he had paid nothing in his place; nevertheless, he has the right to reclaim the payment as "undue" from the person to whom he paid it. This is held in Law 19 as cited, and is consistent with Law *Julianus* in the Digest regarding the exception for fraud.

<margin>Question</margin>
The question is whether that tax, which is called *alcabala* in Castile <note>A significant sales tax in historical Spain</note> and *sisa* in Portugal <note>A similar consumption tax or excise tax</note>, and which is owed upon a sale or exchange, is also owed upon a **novation** <note>original: *nouatione*; the substitution of a new contract for an old one</note> where a debt in money (or an obligation to pay money) is changed into an obligation to pay wheat, oil, or something similar. Or, conversely, when an obligation to pay wheat or oil is changed into an obligation to pay money, or when an obligation to pay oil is changed into an obligation to pay wheat.

<margin>Decision</margin>
Briefly, it must be said, following Lassarte in his work on the tenth of a sale, chapter 7, numbers 3 and 4, that it is not owed. This is because, as is clear from the definition of novation handed down from Ulpian, in a novation where an obligation to pay wheat is substituted for an obligation to pay money or oil, the physical thing that falls under one obligation is not exchanged or transferred into the thing that falls under the other. Rather, one obligation—which is an incorporeal thing—is transferred into another obligation, with the first one expiring and only the second one remaining. This, as is evident in itself, is not a purchase, a sale, or an exchange, which are the only contracts for which that tax is owed.

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

18 *When someone defending an absent person without a mandate can raise a set-off.*
19 *When a debt due on a certain day or under a condition can be set off against a simple debt.*
20 *When a prior court judgment prevents a set-off from being raised.*

Below, when we speak of theft, we will discuss set-offs in the **forum of conscience** <note>original: *foro conscientiæ*; the internal moral realm/confessional</note>; but for now, we must discuss to what extent set-offs have a place in the **external forum** <note>original: *exteriori foro*; the public legal courts</note>.

1 **Set-off** <note>original: *Compensatio*; a legal mechanism where mutual debts cancel each other out</note> (according to Modestinus in Law 1 of the Digest on set-offs) is the mutual contribution of debt and credit between parties. This is the bringing together of amounts in which two people are simultaneously debtors and creditors to each other, so that what the plaintiff owes the defendant is subtracted from what the defendant owes, and that amount is no longer considered a debt, nor is it pronounced as such. In Spanish we say, *discounting one debt from the other* <note>original: *descontar la vna deuda de la otra*</note>, as found in Law 20, Title 14, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 56.

2 In the beginning, set-off was rightly introduced into civil law because, as Pomponius says in Law 3 of the Digest on set-offs (and as held in the Portuguese Ordinances cited above), it is more in our interest not to pay what we do not owe—if we wish for a set-off to occur because the plaintiff owes us just as much in return—than to have to sue to recover what was already paid. Because anyone who raises a set-off and requests it in those circumstances where it applies (according to what will be said), or (as Navarro says in his commentary on usury, numbers 124 and 125) whoever signifies and protests to the creditor outside of court that he wishes to use it, immediately achieves it **by operation of law** <note>original: *ipso iure*; automatically by the law itself</note> before it is even granted by a judge. Therefore, he is immediately freed by law from the amount of the debt he seeks to set off. This is held in the law beginning *si constat*, together with the gloss there, and the final law in the Code on set-offs. This is affirmed by the doctors whom Navarro cites and follows in the passage above.

3 Indeed, in cases of wrongdoing, and for the purpose of ensuring that interest on a debt does not increase further, as soon as a second debt exists that can be set off against the first, the set-off is considered to have been made by law, even if it is not requested and no protest of set-off is made. This is held in the laws *si constat* and *etiam si* in the Code on set-offs, and laws *si ambo*, *cum alter*, and *idem iussis* in the Digest under the same title. Because these things are so, it follows that the person setting off the debt is considered to have paid the amount he sets off—not only because he is thereby freed from that debt and obligation, but also because anyone freed from an obligation is considered to have paid. This is clear from Law 4, paragraph *soluisse*, in the Digest on court judgments, which says: "We should accept as 'having paid' not only the one who physically paid, but everyone who is freed from an obligation by any means." Furthermore, in the laws *si debitor* and *dediffe*, and Law 10, Title 14, Part 5, it is expressly stated that a set-off is a type of payment, and the one who sets off a debt is to be judged as having paid that which he sets off.

### Second Treatise, Disputation 560

And thus, along with Bartolus and the common opinion of the legal scholars, this is affirmed by Gregorio López in his commentary on Law 20, the first gloss; by Navarro and Covarruvias in the places cited above; and by Gutiérrez in chapter 6, numbers 1 and 2.

Navarro, in the passage cited above, makes an excellent observation: for example, when John has sold a redeemable annuity <note>original: *censum redimibilem*; a type of financial arrangement where one party pays a lump sum for a right to annual income, which the other party can later "buy back" or redeem</note> to Peter for four hundred gold pieces at an equal price, even if Peter later owes John the same amount or more in gold pieces, a "set-off" <note>original: *compensationem*; a legal balancing where mutual debts cancel each other out</note> is not considered to have occurred. Nor is that redeemable annuity considered extinguished until John notifies Peter that he wishes to redeem the annuity with that equivalent debt, and Peter accepts it as payment from that moment. Consequently, for the entire time that John does not notify Peter of this, he owes Peter the returns <note>original: *reditus*; the annual payments or interest</note> on that annuity. The reason is that those returns are not "interest" on the four hundred gold pieces Peter used to buy the annuity from John, but are the returns of the purchased annuity itself—which is a distinct thing from the four hundred gold pieces used to buy it. Furthermore, the annuity is not considered redeemed until the debt or the money is handed over to Peter for that purpose; for John might not wish to use it for that purpose, but might want to reserve it for a completely different use. Finally, the balancing of one debt against another is a far different thing from the redemption (or re-purchase) of that annuity for an equal price. For such a redemption, a new contract or a distinct act of will celebrated by John is required. It is not considered celebrated by operation of law <note>original: *ipso iure*; automatically by the law itself</note> without some other externally expressed consent—whereas a set-off is sometimes considered to occur by operation of law, without a new externally expressed consent or protest, to the effect that interest is no longer owed on the prior debt, as was said shortly before.

<margin>4</margin> It should be observed that when two people are mutually debtors and creditors to each other, if one sues the other in court for what is owed to him, the other has two very different remedies available against him. One is the **counterclaim** <note>original: *reconuentionis*; a cross-suit where the defendant sues the plaintiff back in the same trial</note>, about which we shall speak in Treatise 5. In this, by bringing a similar action against the plaintiff, he counter-sues him so that he may also pay what he himself owes. This remedy is broader than set-off; for in many situations where set-off does not apply (according to what will be said), a counterclaim still has force.

<margin>5</margin> The other remedy is **set-off**, which is the subject of the present dispute. This is ultimately not an "action" <note>a proactive lawsuit</note>, but a **defense** <note>original: *exceptio*; a legal "exception" or plea used to block a claim</note>. By this defense, the person who is being sued for a debt objects and opposes the claim by stating that the plaintiff owes him the same amount, or more, or a portion of it. He declares that he wishes to balance one debt against the other, and therefore the plaintiff can only seek whatever remains after the set-off is made. Therefore, set-off must be raised as a defense and not as an action, as is established in Law 2 and following in the Digest *On Set-offs*, and as noted in Law 20, Title 14, Part 5 [of the *Siete Partidas*], where Gregorio López notes this on the words "that were quit" <note>original: *que fuefen quitos*</note>. He adds, along with Baldus, that he who raises the defense of set-off is seen to be confessing the debt <note>meaning: by asking to cancel it out with another debt, you admit the original debt exists</note>.

<margin>6</margin> The defense of set-off takes place even when that which the plaintiff owes to the defendant is a **natural debt** and not a **civil debt** <note>A "natural debt" is an obligation based on fairness or morality that cannot be enforced by a lawsuit, whereas a "civil debt" is fully enforceable in court</note>. For the plaintiff is bound to balance that against the civil and natural debt he is demanding, as per the Law *Etiam* in the Digest *On Set-offs*. This is affirmed by Maranta in *On the Order of Judgments*, part 4, dist. 6, number 2. For although an "action" is not granted for a purely natural debt,

<column-break/>

a "defense" is nonetheless granted from it, and consequently so is set-off. And in this event, only set-off will have a place, not a counterclaim; this is because an action is not granted for a purely natural debt, and a counterclaim is, by nature, an action.

<margin>7</margin> Likewise, the defense of set-off has force against the execution of a judgment <note>original: *in rem transit iudicatam*; a matter already decided by a judge</note> while the condemned person is being forced by that execution to pay what was judged. For by the very fact that the defense of set-off is raised in those events where it applies, it has the force of law. It frees the person raising it from the obligation of paying the creditor an amount equal to the other debt being sought, as is clear from the laws cited above and the common opinion of the scholars. Law 4, § *Soluisse*, in the Digest *On the Matter Judged*, states: "We ought to accept as 'having paid' not only him who actually paid, but everyone who has been freed from the obligation arising from the judgment." On this basis, Covarruvias (along with Felinus in the place cited) and Gutiérrez (in chapter 6, number 2, along with Matteo de Afflictis and others cited by Afflictis) affirm this. 

From this (as it seems to me to be the correct view, though contrary to the opinion of Bartolus on Law *Aufertur*, § *Qui compensatione* in the Digest *On the Law of the Fisc*), Bartolus asserts that when no time has been given to the condemned person to pay, he cannot raise a set-off even if he offers to prove the debt immediately. This opinion of Bartolus is commonly held as accepted and seems to be proven by sticking to the common law <note>original: *ius commune*; the general Roman-canonical legal system of Europe</note> by Gregorio López and Gutiérrez (who seems to me to contradict himself there). However, sticking to the common law, I instead approve the contrary opinion with Baldus—whom Gregorio López mentions as rejecting Bartolus's opinion—as well as Felinus, Covarruvias, Matteo de Afflictis, and Gutiérrez, as just noted. 

For the same reason, it must be said that when a **guaranty instrument** <note>original: *instrumentum guarentigium*; a notarized document that allows for immediate debt collection without a full trial</note> is sent for execution, a set-off of a clear and undisputed debt <note>original: *debiti liquidi*; a "liquid" debt is one whose amount is certain and proven</note> that can be proven on the spot has a place against that execution, as Baldus (cited there by Gregorio López) rightly asserts. Furthermore, regarding the law of this Kingdom of Castile, Gregorio López and Gutiérrez rightly affirm (along with many others they cite) that both against the execution of a judgment and against the execution of a guaranty instrument, the defense of a set-off of a liquid debt has a place—provided that within the ten days given by Law 20, Title 14, Part 5 to prove the debt for which set-off is sought, and within the ten days given by Law 19, Title 21, Book 4 of the *New Collection* <note>original: *nouæ collect.*; the *Nueva Recopilación* of Spanish laws</note> for proving defenses raised against the execution of judgments and guaranty instruments (of which much was said in Disputation 538), such a debt is sufficiently proven by the defense of set-off.

<margin>8</margin> <margin>Doubt</margin> However, if someone renounces the right to set-off and promises that he will pay a certain debt or satisfy an obligation without using the set-off of another debt, is that renunciation valid? And does set-off then have no place? Gutiérrez, in the cited chapter 6, number 2, raises this doubt and refers to the sayings...

### Louis Molina: On Contracts

the statements of Afflictis on both sides, nor does he settle the matter. However, I do not see why someone cannot validly renounce that right of theirs in favor of the creditor, thereby making the creditor secure on that point. This is especially true since, as we shall see, the law sometimes decrees in favor of certain parties that a set-off <note>original: *compensatio*; the legal balancing of mutual debts to cancel each other out</note> should not take place. Furthermore, the debtor remains entirely free to pursue a counterclaim <note>original: *reconuentio*; a separate legal action brought by a defendant against a plaintiff</note> for the same debt for which they otherwise could have sought a set-off against their creditor, or to bring another action against them to obtain it. Indeed, if it were promised under oath not to use the exception of a set-off, the oath would be binding: for it is not an evil thing to refrain from using it, and the debtor can still countersue their creditor or otherwise demand payment if something is owed to them.

<margin>9</margin>
However, a greater doubt arises: if someone has bound themselves under oath to pay a certain debt or to satisfy some obligation, can they nevertheless use the exception of a set-off? Would they have been able to use it lawfully in that event if they had not confirmed under oath that they would pay that debt or satisfy that obligation? The more common opinion of the doctors, embraced by the vast majority of interpreters of Canon Law—whom Covarruvias cites in *chapter "quamuis pactum," part 1, § 4, number 9*, and whom Gutierrez cites more extensively and follows in *On the Confirmation of Oaths, part 3, chapter 6, from number 3*, and toward which Gregorio López leans in the cited *Law 20, gloss 1*—is this: In such a case, a set-off does not take place. They argue that a person would be a perjurer if, by wishing to use a set-off, they did not intend to actually pay the whole amount they promised to pay under oath.

These authors are led by several reasons. First, and most importantly, the chapter *Ad nostram 1* concerning oaths. In that case, a certain man had lent a sum of money to several people, receiving certain possessions and their income as a pledge <note>original: *pignus*; security for a loan</note>. The borrowers promised under oath that they would cause him no trouble regarding those possessions and income until they had paid back the borrowed money. However, before the lender had received the full principal—that is, the full value of the money lent—from the income of those possessions (after deducting expenses), the Archbishop of Rouen excommunicated him, and the borrowers seized the pledged possessions and income. When the lender complained to the Supreme Pontiff, the Pope commanded: First, after receiving sufficient security from the lender that he would abide by the Archbishop's future mandate and definition, he should be absolved from excommunication. Second, the Pope ordered that the borrowers—who, contrary to their oath, had seized the possessions and income—be compelled by ecclesiastical censures to restore them to the lender. He was not to allow any harassment regarding those items until the borrowed money was fully paid. Finally, he commanded that after the money was paid to the lender according to the oath, the lender should be warned to restore to the borrowers whatever was found to have been received beyond the principal (after expenses). If the lender refused, he should again be bound by excommunication until he complied. The authors of this opinion assert that this is an ex-

<column-break/>

press text showing that when someone has sworn to pay something, a set-off has no place. For these borrowers, who had bound themselves by oath to pay the money lent to them, are not granted a set-off from the income of the pledges, even though that income is owed to them and must be restored, as is defined in this same chapter and elsewhere, and was discussed in Disputation 320.

Second, they are led by the logic that although a set-off is "regarded" as a payment, it is not a *true* payment but a *fictional* one <note>original: *ficta solutio*; a legal construction where no money actually changes hands, but the debt is cleared by balancing it against another</note> that is held in place of a payment. An oath, however, must be kept in its own proper form, fulfilling exactly what was promised under the oath, rather than something else equivalent in its place.

This is confirmed by the chapter *Debitores* concerning oaths. There, a person who promised to pay usury <note>original: *usuras*; interest on a loan, which was often restricted or prohibited in medieval law</note> is bound to pay it so as not to call God as a false witness. This holds even though the usurer is forbidden from accepting it and is bound to restore it after receiving it, and even though the person who promised and gave it could later "set it off" against some other debt. Because the oath must be kept in its proper form, the person is bound to pay the usury they promised under oath, even if they do not truly owe it and could later reclaim it via set-off.

Third, they argue from the case of a deposit <note>original: *deposito*; items left in someone's care</note>, where a set-off has no place because of the "good faith" that must be maintained for the common good, as seen in Disputation 526. Therefore, since faith must be kept much more strictly out of reverence for God when something is promised under oath, it follows that a set-off has no place when the payment of something has been promised by oath.

Gregorio López and Gutierrez (in the cited chapter 6, number 8) believe this opinion should be limited, following Afflictis and others, to when the debtor is solvent. If the debtor cannot pay, they say a judgment should be given that a set-off is allowed. For in that case, the oath does not bind because no one is bound to the impossible in the "court of conscience" <note>original: *conscientia foro*; a person's moral standing before God</note>, even if they are otherwise bound by an oath. Where there is no power to perform something, all guilt for not performing it ceases entirely. However, if the first opinion of these authors were true, a set-off would certainly not take place as long as the person could pay in some way, even if with great difficulty. Indeed, if they later came into a "fat fortune" <note>original: *pinguem fortunam*; significant wealth</note>, they would be bound to fulfill the oath.

The contrary opinion, however—namely, that a set-off still takes place without any danger of perjury—is asserted by Bartolus, Panormitanus, and many others whom Covarruvias cites and follows. This opinion is the one I approve of, understood in the way that John Medina understands and proves it. Namely: in the court of conscience, if the person who promised under oath intends to pay or fulfill the obligation specifically *without* using a set-off, then a set-off has no place. The same must be said in the external court <note>original: *foro exteriori*; the public legal system</note> when either the confession of the one who swore or the surrounding circumstances provide sufficient conjecture to persuade that such was the mind of the person swearing. But when that was not the mind of the swearer, but rather the contrary, or if they only intended to bind themselves...

## Second Treatise, Disputation 557.

This is also true in the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to public church or civil courts, as opposed to the "internal forum" of private conscience</note>, when there are no clear indications of the person's mind or intention to waive the use of set-off or to yield their right to it. I understand this to be the case not only if the debt to be set off was contracted after the obligation was confirmed by oath, but also if it was contracted before that obligation. The first of these—namely, that in the first scenario explained, there is room for set-off—is clear enough in itself and is established from what was said in the preceding doubt; and if anything proves it, the legal chapter *Ad nostram* <note>A specific decree in Canon Law (X 5.19.12) concerning a lender and an Archbishop</note> certainly proves only that. However, I am persuaded of the second point along with the cited authors. This is because, in common usage and according to the disposition and interpretation of the law, to use a legitimate set-off is to pay and fulfill an obligation, as is clear from what has been said so far. Anyone who had bound themselves without an oath to pay or fulfill something would undoubtedly be considered to have paid or fulfilled it by using a legitimate set-off. Therefore, although an oath binds more strictly, it does not bind to anything other than what the promise it confirms contains and signifies in common speech, and according to the disposition and interpretation of the law, by which contracts, promises, and obligations are judged to have been made. It follows, then, that when the intention to bind oneself to pay without using set-off is not evident, set-off has its place, with the oath presenting no obstacle.

But the chapter *Ad nostram*, upon which the doctors of the contrary opinion chiefly rely, confirms our opinion rather than the opposite, if it is correctly weighed. Therefore, I have related the contents of that chapter clearly and at length in the first argument for the contrary opinion, so that the legitimate exposition of that chapter might be understood—one that does no violence to it and confirms our opinion. Setting aside <margin>10</margin> three interpretations of that chapter which Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop</note> relates and attacks in the place cited above, number 10, and also setting aside a fourth which he adds himself (which certainly should not be approved and is least satisfactory), one must first observe, along with Covarruvias, the following: When it is said in that chapter that a lender received certain possessions and revenues as a pledge <note>original: *pignus*; property held as security for a debt</note>, by the term "revenues" <note>original: *reditus*</note> one should not understand the fruits or crops of those possessions (which are movable things), but certain rights to annual income, which are counted as immovable things. For example, if, together with those possessions, there were also given as a pledge annuities placed on the goods of others, or the taxes of some town, or some other similar right to annual income. This is established, first, because when certain possessions are given as a pledge, it is not customary to say that the fruits to be gathered from them were also handed over as a pledge. Furthermore, in the case proposed, if the fruits to be gathered from the possessions given as a pledge had also been given as a pledge along with the possessions themselves, there would certainly be no suspicion of usury, nor would there have been any color of a reason for the borrowers to ask that Archbishop to despoil the lender of the possessions and the fruits already received, on the grounds that he was a usurer, before he had received from the fruits of those possessions the full value of the money lent.

<column-break/>

nor for the Archbishop to order this and put it into execution, as the chapter relates was requested and executed. Second, because it says in that text: "although he had not yet received the principal <note>original: *sors*; the capital sum of the loan</note> from those possessions and revenues, after deducting expenses," which is the same as if it had said: "although the lender, after deducting expenses, had not yet received the principal from the fruits of both the possessions and the revenues." But "fruits of revenues" are not given unless "revenues" are taken to mean rights to annual income, and not the fruits of possessions. Third, because, as the *gloss* <note>The standard medieval commentary on the legal text</note> observes on that text, that lender was contumacious <note>stubbornly disobedient to a court order</note> and had not appealed from the sentence of excommunication, but had recourse by complaint to the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, and for that reason the Supreme Pontiff ordered him to be absolved. However, it is not likely that the fruits already received from the possessions, already turned into money and consumed, were taken away from a contumacious person; rather, he was only violently ejected, by order of that Archbishop, from the possession of the aforesaid things and the rights to annual income handed over to him as a pledge. Nor would he have remained entangled in excommunication if the fruits of the pledges, along with the pledges themselves, had been taken from him, so that he retained neither his loan nor anything else from the pledges and their fruits. Therefore, by the name of "revenues," which the chapter says the borrowers withdrew from him against their sworn oath until the Supreme Pontiff ordered them to be restored to him along with the possessions, and that he not be molested in them until the loan was paid to him, one does not understand the movable fruits of the possessions delivered to him as a pledge, but the rights to annual income. Now, see how that text either supports us or certainly contains nothing that opposes us. The Supreme Pontiff disapproves of the sentence of that Archbishop for this reason (as is clear from the text itself): because although the lender had not yet received the principal from the fruits of the possessions and revenues given to him in pledge, after deducting expenses, the Archbishop had entangled him in the bond of excommunication and the possessions and revenues had been taken from him, contrary to the oath sworn not to molest him regarding those pledges until his loan was paid to him. Therefore, by an argument from the opposite sense, see what is gathered from that text: that if he had received the full principal from the fruits of those possessions and revenues, with expenses deducted, the Supreme Pontiff would not have disapproved of the Archbishop's sentence, nor that the pledges had been taken from the lender, who had already received his full loan from the fruits. If, therefore, an oath of those borrowers preceded, both regarding the payment of the borrowed money to him and also regarding no grievance being inflicted on him concerning the possessions and revenues until the loan was fully paid to him, that text certainly confirms our opinion openly. For in that chapter—with the oath to pay him his debt in full presenting no obstacle—a set-off <note>original: *compensatio*</note> of that entire debt from an equal or greater value received by the same lender from the fruits of those possessions and revenues is openly permitted and approved by an argument from the opposite sense. # 826 Ludovicus Molina on Contracts

<column-break/>

since the same reasoning applies to the set-off <note>original: *compensatione*; the legal procedure where two people who owe each other money cancel out their mutual debts</note> of the whole debt of equal value from the profits <note>original: *fructibus*; income or products derived from a property, such as rent or crops</note> of those pledges, after deducting expenses, as it does to the set-off of a part of that debt from an equal part of the value likewise received from those same profits. Indeed, the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> neither disapproves of this, nor is there anything in that text from which it may be gathered that the Pope disapproves of a set-off of a part based on equal value—which would without any doubt be established as having been received from those profits, expenses having been deducted. 

Thus, if an increase in money were offered to that lender up to the complete payment of the entire loan, he could be compelled to return the pledges and to give an account to the borrowers as to whether he had received anything extra from the profits, and to return that to them. In case of doubt, however, as to whether he had received the full value of the loan when the money was offered to him, no grievance <note>original: *grauamen*; a legal injury or burden</note> could be brought against him concerning those pledges by taking them away from him or demanding them from him, because of the oath he had taken that no grievance would be brought against him regarding them until the entire loan had been paid to him. 

And for this reason, the Supreme Pontiff commands in that chapter that his entire debt first be paid to him, whether from the profits or from additional money, so that it is absolutely certain that he has been paid in full; only then should he return the pledges and be compelled, moreover, to return anything he received beyond the principal <note>original: *sortem*; the original amount of the loan excluding interest</note> by any means. I said above that our opinion is gathered by an "argument from the contrary sense" <note>original: *argumento à contrario sensu*; a method of interpretation where one concludes that because a rule applies to one set of facts, the opposite rule applies to the opposite facts</note> from that text, once clearly explained: if the oath of those borrowers proceeded both regarding the payment of the money accepted as a loan (as the doctors <note>Legal and theological scholars</note> commonly interpret that chapter) and also regarding no grievance being brought against him concerning the possessions and revenues until the loan was paid in full. 

For if you read the whole chapter carefully, you will find that no mention is made in it of an oath that the money given as a loan should be paid to him, but only that no grievance should be brought against him regarding the pledges before the loan was paid in full. Do not be moved by those words toward the end of the text: *when, however, they have paid him the money, as they swore*; for the meaning of those words is: when they have paid him the money without any grievance brought against the pledges before it was fully paid, just as they swore to bring no grievance against him. But if you wish to gather from those words that an oath was also taken to pay the money accepted as a loan in full, as the doctors commonly understand that chapter, then that chapter certainly confirms our opinion openly by an argument from the contrary sense, as has been clearly explained. 

Note two things in addition. The first is: No pact intervened between that lender and those borrowers that he should receive the profits of the pledges to be counted toward the principal, nor likewise that he should receive them *not* to be counted toward the principal. For if that first pact had intervened, the contract would have been openly usurious <note>involving usury, or illegal interest</note>, and after first seeking a relaxation of the oath from that Archbishop, one could best proceed to punish him as a usurer, to pronounce that the contract was null, and to snatch the pledges from him—the now-relaxed oath being no impediment. And the Supreme Pontiff himself would not have protected that lender, nor would he have disapproved of the actions taken against him, but would rather have

<column-break/>

rejected and punished him as a usurer. Furthermore, the Supreme Pontiff would not have uttered those words which, in the complaint and petition offered to the Supreme Pontiff by the lender, appear to be added: *Although from those possessions and revenues he had not yet received the principal, after expenses were deducted.* But if a second express pact <note>an agreement that profits would not count toward the debt</note> had intervened, then let the proponents of the contrary opinion observe that no doubt remains that, despite the oath or oaths taken by the borrowers in the lender’s favor, a set-off should have been made in the value of the profits: because that would have been expressly stated in the pact. 

The second point is this: even if it were recounted in that chapter that an oath had been taken to pay the loaned money in full, and to bring no grievance against the lender regarding the pledges until the money itself—reckoned as money distinct from the value of the profits of the pledges—was paid in full; and even if it were decided in that chapter that set-off of the value of the profits against the debt of the loan had no place in that event (the contrary of which has nonetheless been clearly shown), that chapter would not conflict with our opinion at all, as we state it. For in that case, the right and benefit of set-off would have been clearly renounced; in which event we do not say that, once the oath is taken, there is room for set-off. From this, the first argument proposed for the contrary opinion remains sufficiently answered.

To the second argument, it must be said—as has already been stated and shown—that set-off, in common usage and by the very disposition and interpretation of the law, is understood and included under the name of "payment" and "satisfaction." Therefore, an oath by which it was promised that something would be paid or fulfilled is sufficiently observed in its specific and proper form when, a legitimate set-off having been made, it is paid and fulfilled. Nor is it then truly said to be paid or fulfilled through an "equivalent" <note>original: *æquipollens*; something of equal power or value but not the exact thing promised</note>, rather than through that which is contained in the promise itself, as signified by common usage and the disposition and interpretation of the law. 

Whence, regarding the argument in form, the "major premise" <note>the first part of a logical syllogism</note> must be granted if it is understood as payment in the strict sense, as distinguished from set-off and from other proper satisfactions. When the major premise is taken in this way, it does not serve to prove the point. However, it must be denied if it is understood as payment in the broad sense, which is how it is used in common speech and legal interpretation.

Regarding the confirmation, once that entire preceding point is granted, the conclusion intended to be drawn from it must be denied. For when usuries <note>interest payments</note> are promised under oath, in common usage nothing else is understood or intended to be promised except the usuries themselves—unless perhaps the lender owes something else to the borrower, in which a set-off can be made. For then, with the oath promising the payment of usury being no impediment, a set-off can be made in that debt for the usuries promised under oath. In the common usage of speakers, the promised usuries are considered paid if their debt is set off by another legitimate debt which the lender owes to the borrower.

To the third argument, it must be said that it is only by the disposition of human law that this privilege is granted...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "deposi-", likely referring to a "depositum" (deposit) or similar legal term on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Molina argues that using the profits from a pledged property to pay down a debt (set-off) is legally and morally equivalent to direct payment, even when an oath to pay the full debt exists. He clarifies that unless a person specifically renounces the right to a set-off, it remains a valid form of satisfying a sworn obligation without violating the oath.</summary>

# 827 Second Treatise, Disputation 560.

...deposit, so that the debt of the deposit cannot be paid, against the will of the depositor, through the set-off <note>original: *compensatione*; a legal mechanism where two parties cancel out mutual debts</note> of another debt. This rule exists so that people, fearing lawsuits and these types of set-offs, are not discouraged from placing their property with public depositories <note>early forms of banks or bonded warehouses</note>, which would harm the common good. For this reason, many scholars say that "good faith" <note>original: *bonam fidem*</note>—a common good—must be strictly maintained regarding deposits. However, if we put aside this specific regulation of human law, set-off would naturally apply to debts from a deposit just as much as to debts arising from any other source or cause. 

Therefore, since it has been shown that set-off naturally applies to promises confirmed by an oath, and since human law does not grant those sworn promises a special privilege like the one granted to deposits, and since there is no similar reason to grant such a privilege, it follows logically: simply because "faith" <note>the moral obligation to keep one's word</note> must be kept far more strictly by the very nature of the thing when a promise is made under oath than when something is deposited without an oath, it does not mean that set-off is forbidden in sworn debts just because it is forbidden in deposits.

<margin>11</margin> The exception of set-off <note>a legal defense claiming the plaintiff owes the defendant money</note> can be raised not only before an ordinary judge, but also before a delegated judge, as **Gregorius Lopez** affirms along with **Baldus** in his commentary on the law regarding *the judge* <note>original: *el juzgador* (Spanish)</note>. However, regarding an arbitrator, he says (following **Baldus**) that it cannot be raised if the counter-debt arises from an outside cause unrelated to the matter being arbitrated; it is a different story, however, if it arises from an internal or connected cause.

<margin>12</margin> When the person being sued does not admit to the debt that the defendant wants to use as a set-off, the exception is not allowed unless that debt is "liquid" <note>original: *liquidum*; a debt that is clear, fixed in amount, and undisputed</note> and can be proved easily and promptly. If it requires a long and extensive investigation—either because witnesses or documents needed for proof are in a distant place, or for any other reason—the exception is not admitted. Instead, that debt must be claimed and proved in a separate trial. Judges are instructed not to be too lenient or "soft-hearted" in admitting such exceptions, but rather to use strict law in admitting them when they see a long investigation is needed. This is found in the Code <note>original: *C. de compensat.*</note> and the chapter on good faith regarding deposits. 

As for when an investigation should be considered "not long," the *Final Gloss* on the chapter "Good Faith" and the **Gloss of Accursius** <note>a famous 13th-century legal commentator</note> say it is if the debt can be proven within two months. The **Gloss of Accursius** adds that this should be left to the judge's discretion. This is the second point: following common law, the doctors <note>legal scholars</note> along with **Bartolus**, **Innocent**, and others cited by **Gregorius Lopez**, generally support this. However, according to the law of Portugal <note>original: *Lusitano*</note>, the person raising the set-off is bound to prove the debt within nine days; otherwise, the set-off is not admitted. Under the law of this Kingdom of Castile, one is bound to prove it within ten days.

<margin>13</margin> A set-off can be made between any debts whatsoever, regardless of the type of legal action used to claim them. This means it applies whether both parties have a personal action <note>a claim against a specific person</note>, or if one has a "real action" <note>original: *realis actio*; a claim to recover a specific physical thing</note>—such as an action to recover property <note>original: *rei vendicatio*</note>—and the other has only a personal action, or if

<column-break/>

both have a real action; provided, however, that the other requirements (both those already mentioned and those to be mentioned) are met so that there is a place for set-off. This is found in the Code and the Ordinances of Portugal. When, however, the debt of one party would be a legitimate reason why it should not be paid (or why it should not yet be paid), then it cannot be set off against another, as is clear in itself and held in the Digest <note>original: *ff. de compens.*</note>.

<margin>14</margin> Set-off takes place when both parties owe something that consists of weight, number, or measure <note>fungible goods like grain, oil, or coins</note>, and both owe things of the same nature and species, of equal quality and value. This applies whether the debt is for an "unspecified thing" <note>original: *res indeterminata in indiuiduo*; e.g., "ten bushels of wheat" rather than "those specific ten bushels of wheat in that bin"</note>, such as a certain quantity of money or wheat, or whether both owe things of the same species that are specifically identified. It even applies if one party owes a specifically identified thing and the other owes something of the same species and quality that is not specifically identified. 

This is indeed what is affirmed by **Gregorius Lopez** and the Portuguese Ordinances. **Panormitanus** <note>a famous canon lawyer</note> provides a general rule: set-off is allowed when the things owed by both parties are interchangeable <note>original: *functionem suscipiunt*; they can perform the same function or serve as substitutes</note>, because one can be substituted and paid in place of the other since they are of the same nature, species, and equal value and quality. 

If, however, one person owed wheat in a place where it is worth much more, and the other owed it in a place where it is worth much less, then a set-off of equal measures would not be allowed. Instead, one could "retain" the debt until the other debt of equal value is paid. The same applies to other things measured by weight, number, or measure if one is better or of higher value than the other. When one party owes a thing of one species (like wheat) and the other owes a thing of another species (like barley, or wine versus oil), a set-off of one for the other is not allowed because they are not of the same nature or species, and thus not of the same value. 

However, if one party owed money and the other owed something else that ultimately had to be paid according to its monetary valuation—either because the thing no longer exists or for some other reason—then, because both debts at the time of payment are to be paid in money (which is of the same nature regarding value), a set-off of one debt with the other would be allowed. For this reason, there can be a set-off of a debt in money against a debt in wheat, or any other thing, and vice versa. This is held in the Portuguese Ordinances and affirmed by the glosses and **Gregorius Lopez**. When both parties owe things of the same species that are not measured by weight, number, or measure, but are unspecified...

<summary>This page discusses the legal requirements for "set-off" (compensatio), explaining that while it is restricted in deposits to protect the banking system, it generally applies to mutual debts that are "liquid" (easily proven) and involve interchangeable goods of equal value. The author also notes specific procedural time limits for proving such debts in the laws of Portugal and Castile.</summary>

# 828 Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts.

...divided, then a set-off <note>original: *compensatio*; the legal cancellation of mutual debts</note> would take place. For example, if one person owed another eight sheep specified as individuals <note>original: *in individuo*; specific, unique animals rather than just "eight sheep" in general</note>, and the other owed him the same number of sheep similarly specified as individuals, or owed more or fewer, there would be grounds for a set-off. The same applies if two people mutually owe each other a horse or a slave not specifically identified <note>original: *indeterminatum in individuo*</note>, and so on for other things of the same kind. The reason is that one is not bound to pay the other better or more precious sheep, or other such things, than the other is bound to pay him; therefore, there is room for set-off. This is stated here in the cited Law 21, and in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 56, penultimate paragraph. It is also affirmed by the first gloss on the last law regarding set-offs, according to various legal authorities cited by Azo, whom Gregorius Lopez <note>A famous Spanish jurist (1496–1560) known for his commentary on the Siete Partidas</note> refers to and follows in his commentary on Law 21. However, when the items are of distinct value—either because they must be paid in different places where one is worth more than the other, or for some other reason—then set-off does not take place, as was said regarding things that consist of weight, number, or measure. For the same reason—namely, that they are not of the same value—there is generally no set-off between debts involving different kinds of things. Finally, regarding things that do not consist of weight, number, or measure: if a specific individual thing is owed by one side, but the other side owes something non-specific, set-off does not occur. This is because the things are not of the same value, and therefore one cannot perform the function of the other, such that one could be paid in place of the other against the creditor's will. An exception exists if money were owed on one side, and on the other, the debt was ultimately to be settled by a monetary valuation; in that case, generally, because the debts are ultimately pecuniary <note>monetary</note>, set-off would apply, as has been said. This is found in the cited Law 21, joined with the gloss of Gregorius Lopez, and the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 56, final paragraph. Whether set-off has a place in a "loan for use" <note>original: *commodato*; a gratuitous loan where the specific item must be returned</note> was discussed extensively at the end of Disputation 297. Observe regarding this entire section: when debts are "liquid" <note>original: *liquida*; debts where the amount is certain and undisputed</note> on both sides, even if they are of the type where set-off does not apply according to what was said, one still has the right of "retention" <note>original: *retentio*; the right to physically hold onto an item</note> of the debt until the other is paid. This follows the law "If not the sum" <note>original: *l. si non sortem*</note> in the section "if a hundred," regarding the recovery of undue payments, with the words: "the field, however, shall be retained until the money owed is paid." From this text, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a major 15th-century canon lawyer</note> affirms that if someone else’s property comes into my possession, I can retain it until they pay me what they clearly owe me. If property was given as a pledge for a debt that was turned to the owner's benefit—even if it was done without the owner's knowledge, consent, or ratification—it takes on the nature of a pledge. The owner must restore and pay what is owed because it was used for their benefit; the owner claiming the property is blocked by the legal exception <note>defense</note> that they must first pay what is owed.

<margin>15</margin> Regarding the degree of fault for which partners are liable to one another, this was discussed in Disputation 413. When any partner owes something to the partnership because of a loss resulting from their own fault, it has already been said above that by the law itself <note>original: *ipso iure*</note>, even before it is formally requested, set-off 

<column-break/>

takes place against another debt. This applies even if the other partner owes something to the partnership, either because their own fault caused a different loss, or because some benefit belonging to the partnership came to them, and they wish to set that off against the debt of the other partner arising from the loss caused by that partner's fault. This is held in the law "Both" <note>original: *l. ambo*</note> regarding set-offs and Law 22, Title 14, Part 5 <note>of the Siete Partidas</note>. That law adds that if a partner caused a loss to the partnership through fault on one hand, but brought a benefit to it on the other, the two should be set off against each other. However, this truly seems unreasonable. All benefits and profits coming to the partnership from any of the partners belong to everyone collectively by the very nature of the partnership contract. Losses, however, that occur through the fault of one of them are personal to that individual, and he alone is bound to pay for them. This is the common opinion of the doctors of law based on the *ius commune* <note>the "common law" of Europe based on Roman and Canon law</note>, as Gregorius Lopez admits, though he labors anxiously to explain that law. I do not think the arrangement of that law should be approved in this part unless it is understood as a benefit that comes to the partnership through business beyond what the partner was required to do. In that case, the profit from his extra diligence would set off the debt from the negligence where he failed in his duties. Furthermore, when one partner causes loss to the partnership through fraud <note>original: *dolo*; intentional deceit or malice</note> and another does the same, set-off takes place between those debts. The same applies if a loss occurs through the fraud of one partner in one matter, and the fault of another partner in another. However, if a loss occurs regarding the same item through the fault of one and the fraud of the other, there is no set-off; the one who acted with fraud is solely liable for the loss, and the one who was merely negligent without fraud is not held liable. For example, if one partner was transporting partnership property through dangerous places without proper caution, or did not lock and guard it as he should have, and the other partner stole it or caused it to be stolen. This is gathered from the law "Likewise" <note>original: *l. item*</note> regarding the Aquilian Law <note>a Roman law regarding property damage and negligence</note>. All these points are found in the law "If both" <note>original: *l. si ambo*</note>, together with the second gloss, and the cited Law 23, which adds that the contents of this whole section apply not only to a partnership contract but also whenever people hold any property in common in some way.

<margin>16</margin> A guarantor <note>original: *fideiussor*; someone who promises to pay a debt if the principal debtor fails</note> for someone, if compelled to pay for the person he stood for, can set off anything the creditor owed to the person for whom he was a guarantor. This is because the legal defense available to the principal debtor against the creditor is also available to the guarantor. Furthermore, he can set off anything the creditor owes to the guarantor himself. Both points should be understood to apply in situations where set-off is legally permitted. This is found in the laws "True" and "If anything" regarding set-offs and Law 24, Title 14, Part 5. Likewise, the proxy <note>original: *procurator*; a legal agent or representative</note> of a debtor or guarantor, when the debtor 

<margin>17</margin> or guarantor is condemned and ordered to pay, can set off what the creditor owes them and what they could have asked to be set off. However, this is provided that such a proxy of the guarantor provides a guarantee that the parties they represent will ratify the agreement. This is found in the cited Law 24, and agrees with the law "After" regarding set-offs; this last point is also proven by the argument in the law "When a son of a family," in the final section.

Second Treatise. Dispute 560. 829

...where it is held that if a son under paternal authority <note>original: *filiusfamilias*; a son still legally subject to his father's power</note> owes something and is compelled to pay it, he can request that it be set off <note>original: *compensetur*; a legal balancing of mutual debts</note> against another debt which that same creditor owes to the son's father. This is allowed provided the son provides guarantors <note>original: *fideiussores*</note> that his father will ratify the arrangement. For instance, if John were the legal representative <note>original: *procurator*</note> of Peter against Francis, he could not, without Peter’s consent, set off a debt that he himself owes to Francis against a debt that Francis owes to Peter. This is how the cited Law 24 is interpreted. Indeed, Francis could not be compelled by Peter to set off the debt that Francis owes Peter against a debt that John owes him, as is expressly stated in the law *in rem* <note>original: *l. in rem*; a specific reference to the Digest of Roman Law</note> in the final section concerning set-offs. However, if Peter had assigned <note>original: *cessisset*; transferred the rights of</note> the debt that Francis owed him to John, and had therefore appointed John as a representative in his own cause regarding that debt against Francis, and this had been contested by John against Francis, or if Francis had already paid John part of the debt, or if John had notified Francis not to pay the debt to Peter because it had already been assigned to him; then, because Peter (according to Law 3 of the Code on Novation and what was said in the preceding dispute) could not revoke the assignment, John could set off that debt against another for which he himself was liable to Francis. This is held in the law *in rem* at the beginning, regarding set-offs, along with the gloss there on the word "after litigation," and is affirmed by Gregorius Lopez <note>A prominent Spanish jurist (1496–1560)</note> in his final gloss on the cited Law 24.

<margin>18</margin>
Although no one can initiate an action belonging to another without that person's mandate, and if they attempt it, they will be rejected by the exception that they lack a mandate for it or that the action does not belong to them (as was said in Dispute 553, and for that reason no one can be a "manager of affairs" <note>original: *negotiorum gestor*; someone acting on behalf of another without being asked</note> for another in that regard), nevertheless, not only can a son defend an absent father in court without a mandate, but so can anyone else when they see a legal proceeding being carried out to condemn the absent person or some execution being carried out against them. This is allowed as long as they provide security <note>original: *caueat*</note>, which will be discussed in Treatise 5. This is held in the law *exigendi* of the Code regarding legal representatives. Therefore, whoever † defends an absent person in this way—whether it be the son of the absent person or anyone else—can raise an objection and request that a set-off be made of the debt the absent person is ordered or forced to pay against another debt that the person receiving payment owes to that absent person. However, the one requesting the set-off in place of the absent person must provide guarantors that the absent person will ratify it. This is held in Law 25, Title 14, Part 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish legal code</note>, and it agrees with the final section of the law "if with a son" regarding set-offs. From this, Gregorius Lopez, in his commentary on the cited Law 25, concludes that although a son cannot demand the actual payment of a debt owed to his father from a contract entered into with the father separately from the son, he can nevertheless request a set-off of a debt that the father owes to someone against another debt that the same creditor owes the father in turn, provided he gives security for ratification.

<margin>19</margin>
When something is owed † on a future date or under a condition, a set-off does not take place for that debt before the arrival of that day or before the condition is fulfilled against another debt that is already due for payment now. This is according to the law "that which is on a day" at the beginning, and the final section of the law "if with a soldier" regarding set-offs. If, however, 

<column-break/>

something is already owed, yet by the disposition and mercy of the law it is granted that before execution takes place, the debtor is allowed some time, then a set-off can and must be made with that debt which is already owed to the same debtor by the same creditor and is to be paid immediately. This is held in the final section cited above.

<margin>20</margin>
Although † the exception of a "judged matter" <note>original: *exceptio rei iudicatae*; the principle that a case already decided cannot be relitigated</note> does not prevent another debt from being set off against one that is owed by a judgment that has passed into a decided matter (as was said above and is held in the final section of the law "that which is on a day" regarding set-offs), if, however, the exception of set-off was raised in that trial and the judge rejected it because the debt was not "liquid" <note>original: *liquidum*; clear and undisputed</note>, or it required a longer investigation, or for some other similar reason, then the exception of a judged matter does stand in the way if the set-off is raised during the execution of the sentence. This is held in the final section cited above.

<margin>21</margin>
In the following instances, set-off does not take place. First, † if something is owed to the Treasury <note>original: *fisco*</note>, either as a penalty or for any other reason, or to the Prince, or to the community, a set-off may take place with another clear debt that the Treasury, the Prince, the republic, or the town community owes to that same debtor in turn, as is held in the law *in ea* joined with Law 1 of the Code regarding set-offs. However, when something is owed to them that is designated for the repair or construction of walls, fountains, bridges, and similar things, or for fortifications, food supplies, soldiers' wages, and other matters of war, or for any tribute whatsoever, or if a trust <note>original: *fideicommissum*</note> or other thing is left to eventually come to the Prince or the town community, then a set-off does not take place against another debt that the Treasury, the Prince, the community, the republic, or the town owes to that same debtor. This is held in the law *in ea*, with the glosses there, and the law *ob negotium* regarding set-offs, Law 26 of Title 14, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: *Lusit. ord.*; the laws of Portugal</note>, Title 56, Section 5. There, this privilege seems to be extended to every debt in general owed to the King, the Chamber, or his Treasury; for only when something is owed to the community of a city or a town is an exception made in that section, so that a set-off may be made in instances where it was permitted by common law <note>original: *iure communi*</note> to be done with debts that those same communities owe to their debtors in turn. Likewise, although when someone sells something, the buyer can set off from the price what the seller owes him from another source, if it is the Treasury that is selling something, the buyer cannot set off from that price what the Treasury owes him in turn from another heading. This is held in the law "if from a sale" in the Code regarding set-offs.

Second, when someone is condemned to return something to another because of violence, theft, or another wrongdoing <note>original: *maleficium*</note>: for in that which he must restore on that account—whether it be the stolen thing itself, its valuation, or a penalty imposed on top of it—a set-off does not take place with another debt that the person to whom restoration must be made owes to this person in turn; and this is out of hatred for the crime committed. This is held in the final law at the end, with the final gloss there, in the Code regarding set-offs, Law 27 of Title 14, Part 5, and Book 4 of the Portuguese Ordinances, Title 56, Section 2. An exception is made unless the debt arose from a similar wrongdoing: for then a set-off would take place.

This is because it is neither a sale nor an exchange of one thing for another, but a remission <note>a cancellation</note> and extinction of debt on both sides up to the matching amount. If more debt were remitted on one side than the other, then as far as the excess is concerned, it would be a gift or a free remission of such excess.
