## On other ways by which release from the obligation to pay occurs.

### DISPUTATION 561.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 When an obligation is said to be fulfilled if the specific item owed is destroyed without fault or delay by the debtor.
2 An obligation is also released by an oath administered to the debtor when proof is lacking. With a declaration, as noted there.
3 Whether and when an obligation is released, even in the court of conscience <note>original: *in conscientia foro*; the internal moral judgment rather than a public court</note>, by a legal sentence.
4 Likewise, an obligation is released by prescription <note>original: *praescriptionem*; the loss of a right or obligation over a long period of time</note>. Also by remission of debt, if the obligation is natural; otherwise, if it is civil, it is struck down by an "exception" <note>a legal defense</note>. Number 5. And regarding the law of Castile.

We must now speak specifically about payments. But first, we must explain certain other ways by which someone is released from the obligation to pay something and is considered to have paid it—taking the word "payment" in a broad sense, which also includes "novation" <note>replacing an old debt with a new one</note>, "delegation" <note>assigning a debt to a third party</note>, and "set-off," which were discussed in the two preceding disputations.

<margin>1</margin> The first way is when some specific, unique item is owed <note>original: *res determinata in individuo*; a specific object like a particular horse, rather than a generic quantity like wheat</note>, or one of several specific items, and it perishes without fault or delay <note>original: *mora*; a legal term for a failure to perform an obligation on time</note>

<column-break/>

on the part of the debtor in delivering it. For then the loss falls on the creditor and not the debtor; and thus, it naturally frees the debtor from the burden of paying it. This applies whether the thing is owed through a "gratuitous" contract <note>where only one side benefits</note>, such as a gift, a loan for use <note>original: *commodati*</note>, or a deposit, or through an "onerous" contract <note>where both sides benefit</note>, such as buying and selling. This has been discussed at length in Disputations 269, 296, and the two following, as well as 366, 367, 527, and elsewhere; there it was also explained what degree of fault the debtor is held responsible for in each of these contracts if the thing perishes through their fault. There is no reason to say anything further on that matter here.

<margin>2</margin> The second way is handed down for when someone demands a certain debt from another who denies owing it. If, due to a lack of sufficient proof, the creditor demands in court that the debtor swear whether they owe it, and the debtor denies such a debt under oath—then by that oath, which is called "decisory" <note>original: *decisorium*</note> in law because the lawsuit is decided and ended by it, the debtor remains free from the payment of that debt just as if they had paid it. This is held in laws 1 and 2, and also the law *iurandum* <note>on oaths</note> in the title on oaths in the Digest; and in the law *Stichum*, section *naturalis* <note>regarding natural obligations</note> in the title on payments; and in Law 9, Title 14, Partida 5.

Observe, however, that through a mere oath, even one taken in court, if a judge's sentence of release does not follow by virtue of that oath and the plaintiff's lack of proof, only an "exception" <note>a defense</note> arises against the civil obligation and the legal action that might be attempted again regarding that same debt. This is clearly held in the section *aeque* in the Institutes of Roman Law on exceptions. For if the law *Stichum*, section *naturalis* is correctly weighed, it certainly grants no more power to an oath than to a "naked pact" <note>an informal agreement</note> to remit a debt or not to seek payment. From such a pact, as from a mere oath without a sentence, the section *naturalis* says the corresponding "natural obligation" is extinguished, yet it says nothing about the "civil obligation"—in fact, it clearly implies the opposite. Regarding the civil obligation and the action that can be brought from it, the Institutes on exceptions (sections *praeterea* and *aeque*) say that from a naked pact not to sue and from a decisory oath without a sentence, an "exception" equally arises and is granted; however, the civil obligation is not extinguished by the law itself, and therefore the action is not denied, even if it is defeated by the help of the exception if the suit is brought.

Nevertheless, Law 9 of the *Partidas* <note>the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> cited above seems to establish that even the civil obligation is extinguished, just as if the debtor had paid. Unless, however, you understand it (to avoid a conflict of laws) as requiring a following sentence of release from a judge, as Gregorius Lopez <note>a prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist</note> finally explains that law in his commentary. In that law, it is added: "but not instituted for that purpose" (as it seems), but rather to say that the debtor is freed by that oath just as if they had paid the debt and as if they were freed by a judge's sentence. Would that so many legal tangles <note>original: *tricae*</note> were cut away from the law, and that a "naked pact" were made equal to a "clothed" <note>formalized</note> one! This was achieved in this Kingdom of Castile by the later laws of the *Partidas*, according to which, just as the civil obligation of a debt is removed by the law itself through a naked pact not to sue, and the action to seek it is denied, so I believe the same should be said regarding the decisory oath...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ways obligations are extinguished, moving from set-offs to the "decisory oath," judicial sentences, the statute of limitations, and the formal remission of debt. It concludes by beginning a new Disputation on the nature of "payment" itself.</meta>

831 Treatise 2, Disputations 5 & 21.

...concerning the refusal to seek a debt is considered equal in law. Observe this: the decisory oath <note>An oath taken by one party to a lawsuit that, by agreement or court order, settles the matter decisively.</note> in the external court alone does not release the debtor from paying the debt in the manner explained. However, in the forum of conscience <note>The internal "court" of moral and religious responsibility before God.</note>, if he was previously bound to pay the debt, he remains bound even after the oath. This is true whether he committed perjury or acted with malice by denying the debt he knew he owed, or even if he was ignorant and believed he did not owe it when he swore the oath, but later discovered that he did indeed owe it.

<margin>3</margin> The third way is when a debtor is freed by a judge’s sentence. However, this method—even if it frees the debtor in the forum of conscience in a doubtful matter—only applies when the debtor attempted to test his right without fraud or deceit and a sentence was carried out in his favor. If, however, it was clear to him that he was the debtor, or if it becomes clear to him after the sentence is passed (before the debt is formally recorded as a judgment), it does not free him in the forum of conscience. This is because a sentence does not grant a right, but merely declares where the right belongs; it only has force in the forum of conscience if the reality of the matter matches what the sentence pronounces. This subject must be discussed in Treatise 5.

<margin>4</margin> The fourth way is by the title of legitimate prescription <term>Prescription: A legal mechanism where a right or obligation is gained or lost due to the passage of time, similar to a statute of limitations.</term>, as is very well known in itself and is clear from what was said in the section on prescription. Indeed, if someone pays the debt of another and the creditor legitimately prescribes it, the debtor remains freed from the debt, if done with the intent of payment.

<margin>5</margin> The fifth way is when a debt is forgiven for the debtor by one who has the power to do so, whether this happens through a formal release <note>original: *acceptilatio*; a formal verbal acknowledgment in Roman law that a debt has been satisfied.</note> or by any other "clothed" agreement <note>original: *pacto vestito*; an agreement that meets specific legal requirements to make it enforceable in court.</note>. In this event, under common law <note>original: *ius commune*; the shared legal system of Roman and Canon law across Europe.</note>, the obligation is extinguished by the law itself, both natural and civil, according to what was said in Disputations 5, 24, and following. Even if it is forgiven through a "naked pact" <note>original: *pacto nudo*; an informal agreement that was historically not enforceable by a lawsuit in Roman law.</note>—for example, by saying, "I forgive you this debt," or "I promise you I will never seek this debt from you"—the entire natural obligation of that debt is extinguished under common law. However, the civil obligation is not extinguished, but rather it is blocked by an "exception" <note>a legal defense</note> based on that agreement, according to the Institutes regarding exceptions cited above. However, according to the law of this Kingdom of Castile (Law 3, Title 8, Book 3 of the Ordinance, which is Law 2, Title 6, Book 5 of the New Collection), the civil obligation is extinguished even by an informal agreement, and a legal action is completely denied.

If a creditor were to hand over the document of debt to the debtor, or break it, or cancel it, then he would be judged to have forgiven the debt. It would fall to him, and not to the debtor, to prove that he did not hand it over or break it with that intention. I believe that in such an act—especially the handing over—the agreement is "clothed," and therefore the civil obligation is extinguished even under civil law; this is clearly stated in Law 9, Title 14, Part 5. If, however, the creditor proves that he handed it over because of force or fear, or that it was taken from his power by theft, or that he handed it over for a reason other than forgiving the debt (for instance, he gave it for safekeeping, or broke it not realizing it was the debt document), then the debt is not considered forgiven. The same should be said if there were signs and conjectures that it was taken by theft or snatched by someone else. Thus it is held—

<column-break/>

—in the law of Labeo, joined with the following law in the Digest <note>original: *ff.*; the standard abbreviation for the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman Law.</note> on agreements; and the law on handwriting, joined with the gloss there; the Digest on proofs, law 9; and Law 11, Title 19, Part 3; and Law 40, Title 13, Part 5. Read the opinions in Gregorio Lopez on Law 11, which concern this matter based on common law, and others that could be said about this matter.

# What payment is strictly. And whether one who is bound to an act satisfies it by paying interest. And by what method payment should be safely made to a minor.

## DISPUTATION 522.

### SUMMARY.

1. What payment is.
2. Payment, even taken in a broad sense, frees one from an obligation, including accessory ones.
3. How many types of payments there are.
4. Payment of interest frees one from an obligation of performance: and what is included under the name of "interest." <note>original: *interesse*; in this context, it refers to damages or the value of the non-performed act, not just bank interest.</note>
5. Whether, and when, one bound to an act is freed by paying interest.
6. In what way payment to a minor ought to be made.

<margin>1</margin> Payment <note>original: *solutio*</note>, strictly speaking, is the delivery of that which is owed, or of another thing in its place when the original thing cannot be paid, or by the will of the creditor. For one thing cannot be paid for another against the creditor's will (Law 2, paragraph 2, Digest: *if a certain thing is sought*; and the law *he from whom*, Code: *on payments*, and other laws). Likewise, a debtor cannot be forced to pay one thing for another when the original can be paid (Gloss on *is owed*, law *of the master*, and the gloss there, Code: *on farmers and tax*, book 11). However, by the mutual consent of the debtor and creditor, one thing can be paid for another (Law *manifest*, Code: *on payments*, and Law 3, Title 14, Part 5). When one thing is to be paid for another because what is owed cannot be paid, or for some other reason, and if the debtor and creditor do not agree, the judge ought to decide what should be paid (cited Law 3, and doctors note this in the authentic *this except*, Code: *on payments*).

<margin>2</margin> Once payment is made, not only the debtor himself and his heirs are freed from the obligation and debt, but also the pledges <note>collateral</note> and the guarantors <note>original: *fideiussores*</note>, and finally whoever was bound accessorily along with the debtor. This similarly takes place in any payment, taking the word "payment" in its broad sense, such as those discussed in the three preceding disputations. For once the principal obligation is extinguished, in whatever way it is extinguished, the accessory obligations also remain extinguished. This is held in the Institutes, *by what modes an obligation is dissolved*, at the beginning and the following paragraphs; the law *when the principal*, Digest: *on rules of law*, law 1; and Law 14, Part 5; and other laws. This also takes place even if the debt is paid to the creditor by someone other than the debtor, whether the debtor is unaware of it or knows it, provided it is paid in the name of the debtor. For immediately, both the debtor himself and those accessorily bound for him for that debt are freed from the obligation and the debt remains [satisfied]. Law *manifest*, Code: *on payments*, and *I promise*, Digest: same title; and it was discussed in Disputation 15, where other sworn...

<meta>Catchword: ...we free [mus]</meta>

It also begins defining "payment" (solutio), noting that while creditors usually must receive exactly what was owed, mutual agreement or judicial arbitration can allow for alternative forms of satisfaction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on who is authorized to receive a payment on behalf of a creditor, specifically focusing on administrators like tutors and curators, before beginning a new disputation on payments made to third parties.</meta>

...authority, and the law titled *Solutam* at the beginning of the Digest regarding payments <note>original: "l. solutam in prin. ff. de solu."</note> agrees. The reason, moreover, is that just as an administrator of a minor's goods is established by public authority, so too is he the receiver of those things owed to the minor. And since the tutor or curator is then held liable to the minor for the debt correctly paid to him in the minor's place, the person who paid him is not held liable. Law 4, title 14, part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note> seems to suggest that for a payment to a tutor or curator to be safe, the authority of a judge is necessary. That, however, would be irrational, nor is it observed by custom. Gregorio Lopez, in his summary of that law, explains it as follows: it is sufficient for payment to be made to them, and the authority of a judge is only necessary when the payment is made directly to the minor himself. Furthermore, what has been said and cited in this disputation likewise applies to the insane person and the spendthrift to whom a curator has been assigned, as held in the cited Law 4.

# Whether a payment made to someone other than the creditor frees the debtor from the obligation of the debt, and when it does not.

## DISPUTATION 563.

### S V M M A R Y

1. A payment of a **specific individual thing** made to someone other than the creditor frees the debtor if the thing is lost before it reaches the creditor. This is qualified as stated therein.
2. Whether a payment of a **non-specific thing** made to someone deputized by the creditor frees the debtor if it is lost, and when.
3. And what if it is paid to the creditor’s own proxy? (Number 3).
4. When a payment made to a son or a servant assigned to some business frees the debtor.
5. A payment made to one who is not even a tacit proxy, even if he managed the creditor's affairs, does not free the debtor.
6. When a payment made by the creditor's mandate to someone whose authority was later revoked frees the debtor.
7. Who an "added party" <term>Adiectus: A third party specifically named in a contract as being authorized to receive payment.</term> is, and when a payment made to him frees the debtor.
8. When a payment made to the principal creditor does not free the debtor, such as if the creditor is accused of a crime for which his goods are to be confiscated.
9. Payment cannot be made to a legal proxy <term>Procurator ad litem: An agent authorized only to represent a person in court, not to manage their finances.</term>, even if he wins the case.
10. A legal proxy cannot make a settlement or any other remission of debt unless he has a special mandate for that purpose.

<margin>1</margin> The things stated in the second part of Disputation 296 will free us from a great burden in this place. When what is owed is a **specific individual thing**, or something from among specific individual things—which, if it perishes without the fault of the debtor, is a loss to the creditor and not the debtor (according to what was said in Disputation 561 and other disputations cited there)—then, if it is delivered to another to be carried to the creditor, whether or not that person was designated by the creditor to receive it, and it is lost or perishes before it reaches the creditor, the loss falls on the creditor. The debtor remains free from the obligation of paying

<column-break/>

it. Exception: unless the debtor, in so delivering it, was at fault, for which the creditor may hold him liable according to the quality of the contract from which the debt arose; or unless he had obligated himself for slight negligence or even for "fortuitous events" <note>Accidents or "acts of God" beyond human control.</note> until the thing reached the creditor, and the thing so delivered perished due to that slight negligence of the debtor or by such an accident. In that case, the debtor would be bound to pay it again. All these points are extensively proven in the cited Disputation 296.

<margin>2</margin> When that which is owed is entirely **non-specific** <note>original: "indeterminatum in indiuiduo." This refers to "fungible" goods like cash or grain, where one unit is as good as another.</note>, such as a certain quantity of money, or a certain number of measures of wheat, wine, oil, or anything else non-specific, then if it is delivered to the person the creditor designated to receive it (whether that person was a creditor of the creditor or anyone else, or if the creditor ratified the payment after learning it was delivered), the debtor remains entirely free from that debt. Even if the thing later perishes or disappears and never reaches the creditor, the loss is the creditor's and not the debtor's. The reason is that by that very act, it is deemed delivered or paid to the creditor himself through the person he deputized (or whose receipt he ratified) to receive it in his place. Therefore, from that moment, it disappears or perishes for the creditor and not the debtor. We showed this in Disputation 296, and it is held in the law *Solutam* at the beginning of the Digest regarding payments, and Law 5, title 14, Partida 5.

<margin>3</margin> The same applies if payment is made to a proxy <term>Procurator: An agent or representative acting with power of attorney.</term> having a mandate from the creditor to receive it, or to receive his debts, or to one having the administration of all the creditor’s goods, or of some business to which that payment pertains. This is held in the law *Vero procuratori* in the Digest. It is sufficient for this if he has the administration of the creditor’s goods, even if "free administration" <note>Unrestricted power to dispose of assets as one sees fit.</note> was not granted to him, as the gloss on the law *Vero procuratori* notes regarding the word *administratio*.

<margin>4</margin> From this it follows that if a creditor has a son, a servant, or a slave assigned to some administration or business, or to the demanding or receiving of debts, and payment is made to him, the debtor remains free from that debt even if the thing paid perishes or does not reach the creditor. This is held in the laws *Solutam* and *Solutum*. At this point, observe: if he to whom payment was made was truly established by the creditor at that time to receive it in his name and place (in the ways explained), the debtor is freed from the debt even if he doubted whether the person had a mandate (tacit or express), or if he did not pay attention to it, or even if he believed the person did not have it. The reason is that because the person actually had the mandate and accepted it in the name of the creditor, the creditor actually acquired ownership of it. Therefore, if it later perishes, or through the wickedness of the receiver it does not reach the creditor, the loss is the creditor's. This is discussed by the glosses and by Gregorio Lopez on the cited Law 5, at the word *recebirlo*...

<summary>This page discusses the legal validity of payments made to third parties rather than the creditor directly. It establishes that debtors are generally freed from obligation if they pay an authorized agent, administrator, or designated representative, shifting the risk of loss to the creditor once the transfer occurs.</summary>

# Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts

<margin>5</margin>
...to the contrary seems to be asserted, it is true only to the extent that the debtor, if they doubt the mandate given to the receiver, is not bound to make the payment. It is not, however, as if they make the payment to him, and he truly had a mandate, that they would not be entirely freed from such debt—even in an external court <note>The "external court" refers to a secular or public legal setting, as opposed to the "internal court" of conscience or confession.</note>—if it is established in that court that the receiver truly had a tacit or express mandate from the creditor. Regarding what Gregorio Lopez adds in the same place—stating that Joannes Andreas <note>A famous 14th-century canon lawyer.</note> disputes both sides, namely: if someone pays a sick person who has a mandate from the creditor to receive it, even if the sick person dies and the money disappears and never reaches the creditor, the debtor is freed from that debt—I do not see why anyone could reasonably doubt this. If, however, <insert>†</insert> someone pays one who lied about being the creditor's proxy, or claimed to have a mandate from him to receive payment; and universally, if someone pays one who did not have a tacit or express mandate to receive it, even if that person were managing the creditor's affairs without his mandate, they are not freed from the debt unless the creditor later ratifies it. This is gathered from the law beginning *Vero procuratori*, in the first section, by an argument from the opposite sense <note>original: "argumento à contrario sensu"</note>, and the gloss affirms this on the word *administratio* regarding a mere manager of affairs; it is also found in the last paragraph of the Digest regarding payments <note>original: "§. vlti. ff. de solu." Referring to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman law.</note>, and the matter is clear enough in itself.

<margin>6</margin>
When <insert>†</insert> a creditor has commanded his debtor to pay another what was owed to him, if before the debtor carries this out, the creditor revokes the mandate by word, messenger, or letter, and notice of that revocation reaches him before the payment, then the payment made by the debtor to that other person (after the notice of revocation of such mandate reached him) would not free him from the debt. Instead, he would be bound to pay the same debt again to the creditor. It would be otherwise, however, if he had paid the other person before the notice of the revocation of the mandate reached the one paying; for then it would free him, even if it were done after the mandate had been revoked. This is found in Law 6, Title 14, Part 5 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the Spanish legal code.</note>, and the law *Si vero procuratori* in the Digest regarding payments, and is gathered from the law *Qui hominem*, section *Si Titium*, in the same title. This will be clear from what is about to be said: for it is the same to mandate someone to receive a payment from a debtor, and to command a debtor to pay him, and vice versa. Since one of these is inherently joined with the other, as held in the cited section *Si Titium*, where Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist.</note> and others note this; therefore, what is about to be said regarding the revocation of a mandate given to one appointed to receive payments should be understood similarly regarding the revocation of a mandate given to a debtor not to pay someone or certain people. If, however, the creditor revokes the mandate and the power of receiving payments in his place from a proxy established for that purpose—such as an administrator of all his goods, or someone appointed in any other way to administration or business, and consequently to receiving certain payments—then, if the debtor pays him after notice of that revocation reaches him, he is not freed by that payment from that debt, but would be bound to pay it again to the creditor. If, however, he pays him before notice of that revocation reaches him, he is

<column-break/>

entirely freed from the debt, even if, without him knowing it, the mandate had already been revoked. This is held in the cited section *Si Titium*, and the law *Vero procuratori*, section *Sed et si quis*, in the Digest regarding payments.

<margin>7</margin>
When someone, in a stipulation, or another promise or contract, binds themselves to pay either the person who contracts with them, or a certain designated third party—which <insert>†</insert> third party is called an "added person for payment" <note>original: "adiectus ad solutionem". An *adiectus* is a person named in a contract who has the legal authority to receive the payment but is not the actual creditor.</note> in law, when they do not form two primary creditors with the principal creditor—then whether the payment is made to the principal or to the added person, the debtor is freed from that debt. This is clear in itself and is held in the law *Vero procuratori*, at the beginning, and the law *Si ita stipulatus* in the Digest regarding payments, and Law 3, Title 14, and Law 7, Title 11, Part 5. A payment can indeed be made to the added person, but not to another in their place; for example, if the added person dies, payment cannot be made to their heirs unless that was expressed in the contract. Or, if the added person was the slave of a third party, payment cannot be made to the master of that slave, but only to the slave himself, as held in the law *Si ita stipulatus* at the beginning. Likewise, payment cannot be made to the added person in any place other than the place designated for it, according to the law *Non utique*, section *Idem Iulianus*. Furthermore, the added person cannot free the debtor from the debt, nor "novate" it <note>original: "nouare". Novation is a legal act that replaces an old obligation with a new one.</note> with him, nor even seek payment from him in court; he can only receive it if it is paid to him. Even if he is a minor, he does not need the authority of a tutor or curator for the payment to him to be safe, because he receives that payment in the name and place of the principal creditor, and according to his written instruction. This is held in the law *Quod stipulatus*, joined with the following law in the Digest. The principal creditor later has a cause of action against the added person—as if by mandate or management of affairs—to restore the received payment to him, as the last gloss on the law *Vero procuratori* suggests.

But if an "undue" payment <note>A payment made by mistake that was not actually owed.</note> is made to the added person, then the one paying has a "claim for the return of an undue payment" <note>original: "conditio indebiti"</note> against the principal creditor, because it is considered paid to him rather than to the added person, as held in the law *Si ita stipulatus*. Even if the principal creditor forbids the payment to be made to the added person, if it is nevertheless made, the debtor is freed from the debt by that payment. This is held in the law *Vero creditori*, the second to last section, and Law 5, Title 14, Part 5. An exception is made unless the principal creditor seeks the debt from the debtor in court; for after the "joinder of issue" <note>original: "post litem enim cum eo contestatam". This is the formal start of a trial.</note> with him, he cannot pay the added person. If he does pay, he is bound to pay the principal creditor again; but the debtor can recover from the added person what he paid him, as if it were not owed to him. This is held in the law *Si quis stipulatus fuerit decem in mille*, and the cited Law 5, which seems to assert that beyond the joinder of issue, a prohibition is necessary for the payment to the added person to be invalid. The doctors <note>Legal scholars or theologians.</note>, however, affirm the contrary by standing on common law. Read Gregorio Lopez in the same place at the word *defendimiento*. A payment can indeed be made to the added person, provided however that they remain in the same status they were in when they were established as the added person. For if they change their status <note>Status change (capitis deminutio) in Roman law could mean losing citizenship, freedom, or family standing, which affected legal capacity.</note>, payment cannot be made to them; otherwise, the debtor will be forced to pay the principal creditor again (Except unless the debtor paid him while ignorant that his status had changed).

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding to whom a debt may be legally paid. It specifically examines how a change in the legal status of an "added recipient" (adiectus) or the criminal status of a creditor affects the validity of a payment.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 558.

...since, by the argument of *the law 'If anyone to a slave' in the Digest, Title on Payments* <note>original: "l. si quis seruo. ff. de solut."</note>) if a person who was previously added to a contract as a recipient was free, and then becomes a slave, or enters a religious order, or suffers a "maximal" or "middle" reduction of legal status <note>The Roman concept of "capitis diminutio" involved losing liberty (maximal), citizenship (middle), or family position (minimal).</note> (concerning which we spoke in *Disputation 9*), or even the "minimal" reduction, payment can no longer be made to them. This is evident because the law speaks of a change of status without any restriction. Examples are provided: if the added recipient is banished or emancipated—two examples which pertain to the "minimal" reduction of status, as is established in the *Institutes, on the reduction of status.* That payment cannot be made to an added recipient who has changed their status is found in *the law 'When someone' at the beginning, in the Digest, Title on Payments, and Law 5, Title 14, Part 5* <note>This refers to the Siete Partidas, the famous 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note>. Note, however, that although this is the general rule, if the change in status of the added recipient does not, in the judgment of a prudent person, result in a worse position for the principal creditor (considering all concurrent circumstances), then payment can indeed be made to the added recipient. Hence, Gregorio Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist who wrote a definitive commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> says in his commentary on the aforementioned *Law 5* that if the added recipient was a slave of the creditor and becomes free, payment cannot be made to him, because that status is not "better" in comparison to the principal creditor's interest, even if it is better for the recipient himself. If, however, the recipient was the slave of a third party and becomes free, payment can be made; for in that event, the status of freedom is not worse for the principal debtor than the status of slavery was. Because an added recipient changing status from a "son under paternal power" <note>term: <term>filiusfamilias</term> (a son legally subject to his father's authority)</note> to an emancipated person is not generally worse for the father who appointed him, it follows that *the law 'He who thus' in the section 'Who for himself' in the Digest, Title on Verbal Obligations, and the cited Law 5*, define that this does not prevent a payment made to the now-emancipated son from being valid. This is true even though the contrary seems to be held in *the law 'When someone' at the beginning, in the Digest, Title on Payments*, which must be understood to apply when, from concurrent circumstances, it is less safe or expedient for the principal creditor that payment be made to the emancipated son than to the son under paternal power. This can happen today in the Kingdoms of Castile and Portugal when sons leave their father’s power through a marriage contract, if the son previously managed the father's goods or was set up in business by him, but afterwards the son acquires wealth and trades only for himself. I wish indeed that so many tangles and contradictions were cut away from the law!

<margin>8</margin>
A payment made † to the principal creditor is valid, even if he is accused of a crime for which his goods ought to be confiscated, as seen in *the law 'To the defendant' in the Digest, Title on Payments, and Law 5, Title 14, Part 5*, and other laws cited in the gloss of the aforementioned *law 'To the defendant.'* An exception is made if he is accused of the crime of High Treason <note>original: "læsæ maiestatis humanæ" — literally 'injured human majesty,' i.e., treason against the state or sovereign.</note>; for here, by the very fact that he commits such a crime, he loses by law not only all his goods but also the administration of them. Thus, a payment made to him is invalid, and consequently, it would also be invalid if made to an added recipient appointed by him, since a payment to an added recipient is considered a payment to the principal creditor. This is stated in the cited law. Salycetus <note>Bartholomaeus Salycetus, a 14th-century Italian jurist.</note> and Gregorio Lopez (at the cited *Law 5, final gloss*) make an exception when the debtor pays such an accused person or his proxy while being ignorant of the crime; for then he is freed by that payment, just as one is freed who pays a proxy without knowing that the proxy’s power or mandate has been revoked. These same rules apply, with far greater reason, in the crime of heresy, which is High Treason against God <note>original: "crimine hæreseos lesær maiestatis diuinæ"</note>. Furthermore, from that doctrine

<column-break/>

that payment to a creditor accused of other crimes is valid (even if his goods are to be confiscated), an exception is made if those goods have already been "annotated"—that is, sequestered because of that crime, because he fled, or for some other reason. In that case, payment made to him is invalid, as the gloss on the cited *law 'To the defendant'* affirms, in agreement with *the law 'The last,' final section, in the Digest, Title on Requiring Defendants*, and as Gregorio Lopez affirms in the cited *Law 5, penultimate gloss.*

<margin>9</margin>
Payment † cannot be made to one who is appointed as a legal proxy <note>term: <term>procurator ad litem</term> (an attorney or agent appointed specifically to represent a party in a lawsuit)</note> to pursue a specific lawsuit, even if he wins, in a way that would free the debtor; rather, payment must be made to the creditor who appointed the proxy for that suit. This is established in *the law 'By this law' in the Digest, Title on Payments; the law 'But if only' in the Digest, Title on Pacts; and Law 7, Title 14, Part 5.* However, if someone were a "proxy in their own interest" <note>original: "procurator in rem suam" — an agent who has been granted the right to keep the proceeds for themselves.</note>, payment could and should be made to him, and consequently, he could settle and make other agreements regarding the matter, as per the cited *law 'But if only'*; this is affirmed by the final gloss on the also cited *law 'By this law,'* and it is self-evident. Likewise, if a proxy for a cause that is entirely someone else's is not paid for the expenses incurred in that case because the owner of the case is unable to pay, then, just as he can ensure the judgment is executed and his expenses and salary are paid (as held in *the law 'Of the plaintiff' in the Digest, Title on Proxies*), so too a payment made to him up to that amount is valid and frees the debtor to that same extent, as the cited gloss affirms. Furthermore, if a proxy for another’s cause is given the power not only to pursue the case but also to receive payment, he can receive the payment, and the debtor is freed by it; this is very well known, because he then holds a mandate for that purpose, as is clear from *the law 'Truly' at the beginning*, and from *the law 'By this law' in the section on Payments*, from *the law 'If a proxy' in the Digest, on Proxies*, and from the cited *Law 7.* If a proxy is given power to "demand" or to "act and demand," Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> judges in *the law 'By this law,'* and Gregorio Lopez agrees in the cited *Law 7, gloss 2*, that he is considered to have a mandate to receive payment, and therefore payment made to him then frees the debtor—even though Angelus <note>Angelus de Ubaldis, another prominent medieval jurist.</note> objects.

<margin>10</margin>
A proxy † for pursuing another’s lawsuit cannot make a settlement <note>term: <term>transactionem</term> (a compromise or legal settlement to end a dispute)</note> with the debtor, nor remit any part of the debt to him, as per *the law 'Of settlement' in the Code, Title on Settlements; the law 'But if only' in the Digest, Title on Pacts; and the cited Law 7.* Indeed, not even one to whom general administration has been committed can do these things, as per *the law 'By mandate' and the law 'The proxy of tutors' in the Digest, Title on Proxies.* However, if a proxy for a lawsuit were specifically given a mandate for any of these things, he could certainly do them, because he would have a specific mandate for it. Likewise, if a clause were added granting "full" or "general power" and the faculty of acting or disposing concerning the matter, then he could receive payment, settle, "novate" <note>term: <term>nouare</term> (to replace an old obligation with a new one)</note>, and remit part of the debt through settlement, according to *the law 'A proxy to whom generally' in the Digest, Title on Proxies, and the cited Law 7.* He cannot, however, give it away as a gift, as per *the law 'Against the law,' final section, in the Digest, Title on Pacts, and the law 'A son under paternal power' in the Digest, Title on Donations.* Gregorio Lopez affirms this along with Baldus and Alexander in the cited *Law 7, on the word 'librellenero'*; there, in the penultimate gloss, he adds that for all the aforesaid, it suffices either that "free power" be granted, or that the power be granted to do "everything that the owner could do if he were present," since a single...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of obligations and payments from the previous disputation. While the prior page focused on the identity of the recipient of a payment, this page transitions to the timing of payment and the legal consequences of being late (mora).</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts.

### When payment must be made, and to what extent the "purgation of delay" is permitted.
<note>The "purgation of delay" (purgatio morae) is a legal concept where a debtor who is late in paying can "cleanse" their lateness—and thus avoid penalties—by offering the payment before a formal legal demand is made or within a certain window.</note>

### DISPUTATION 564.

### SUMMARY

1. *How time itself makes a demand for the creditor against the debtor, so that the delay cannot be cleansed. This is clarified in no. 2.*
2. *Whether the purgation of delay is always admitted by canonical equity.*
3. *A specific day or a certain term prescribed for payment puts the debtor in a state of "delay" immediately after it has passed, without any hope of purgation. Clarified in no. 6.*
4. *A debtor who effectively offers payment to the creditor is freed from the penalty and damages.*
5. *Even a specific hour appointed for payment makes a demand on behalf of the creditor.*
6. *A time for payment appointed by a judge makes the debtor liable for interest and damages once it has passed.*
7. *When a promise to do or pay something without a fixed term or penalty obligates the promisor to a penalty and damages.*
8. *When the purgation of delay can be made regarding the presentation of someone in court to avoid a penalty.*

---

When a certain day or a certain thing has been determined, and a period was established within which something should be done or paid, then that certain day or the end of that determined term "interpellates" <note>original: "interpellat"; a legal term meaning the date itself serves as a formal demand for payment, so the creditor does not need to ask.</note> for the creditor against the debtor so that he may perform or pay; nor is it necessary for him to be required or warned by the creditor. This is according to *the law 'Magnam' in the Code, Title on Contracts and Committed Stipulations* and *Law 8, Title 14, Part 5* <note>The "Partidas," the 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note>. Hence, in such a case, no opportunity is granted for the debtor to "cleanse the delay" once that day or term has passed. Instead, he is held liable for interest and damages, according to the nature of the contract. Or, if a penalty was attached, he is held to that penalty—either as an alternative to the payment or completion of the contract and satisfaction of damages, or for the payment of interest alone, at the choice of the creditor. This applies if the penalty was added for the support and firmness of the contract, according to what was said in *Disputation 559*, and if a clause "the contract remaining valid" was not added (per *Disputation 556*). Or, he is held to both if that clause was added; or he is held to the penalty alone if it was added with the intent of "novation" <note>A legal term for replacing an old obligation with a new one.</note>, under the condition that the contract was not fulfilled. No purgation is admitted to avoid the penalty or to avoid the payment of interest and damages. This is the sense of the cited *law 'Magnam'*, and *the law 'Traiecticia' in the Digest, Title on Actions and Obligations*, and *the law 'Pecuniae'*, and *Law 3, Title 11, Part 5*. These things hold true whether the contract is "onerous" (for profit) or "lucrative" (a gift), and whether it

<column-break/>

is a contract of "good faith" (*bonae fidei*) or "strict law" (*stricti iuris*), as Gregorio Lopez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> well observes in his commentary on the cited *Law 3*: because the cited laws speak without distinction. Hence, the same Gregorio Lopez (on *Law 8, Title 14, Part 5*) and more copiously Alvarus Valascus (on *The Law of Emphyteusis, Question 9*) rightly reject—along with the common opinion of the doctors which they cite—the opinion of Baldus. Baldus asserted that in good faith contracts, even if a certain day and penalty are attached, there is a place for the purgation of delay, and that the proposed rule only holds in contracts of strict law. Those same authors, Covarrubias and Alvarus Valascus, also rightly criticize Baldus for asserting that in Canon Law <note>The law of the Catholic Church, which often influenced civil legal practice.</note>, the difference between good faith and strict law contracts was abolished, and that all contracts which are "strict law" in Civil Law are "good faith" in Canon Law. Following Baldus’s opinion, purgation of delay would be granted in all contracts under Canon Law, even if a certain day and penalty were attached. This is argued because in Canon Law, as he says, no mention is made of the distinction between good faith and strict law contracts. This opinion of Baldus is rightly criticized by the cited doctors. Firstly, because it is enough that this distinction was not rejected by Canon Law through some contrary disposition; thus it should stand in Canon Law. Secondly, because an express mention of that distinction is found in the chapter *'Cum venerabilis' in the Title on Exceptions.*

<margin>2</margin> Except from the proposed rule those cases where the law, for some specific reason, grants the purgation of delay in a certain event. An example is "Ecclesiastical Emphyteusis" <note>A type of long-term land lease owned by the Church.</note>, if the rent is not paid within two years, according to what was said in *Disputation 453*; for although the rent was to be paid every year on a certain fixed day, the penalty of forfeiture is not triggered unless the rent remains unpaid for two full years. Also, in the secular laws of Castile, purgation of delay is granted within ten days if the rent has not been paid within three years. These things, which are specifically sanctioned and granted in law, are exceptions to the proposed rule. One should not take an argument from them either to attack the rule or to extend the exception to other cases—though many do not pay enough attention to this.

<margin>3</margin> Gregorio Lopez (on *Law 8, Title 14, Part 5*) says that by "canonical equity," delay can always be cleansed, even if a certain day and penalty are attached. This is argued, first, because in the chapter *'Potuit' in the Title on Leases*, purgation of delay is admitted regarding Ecclesiastical Emphyteusis. Second, because the chapter *'Suam' on Penalties* establishes that when a part was paid and not the whole, the full penalty should not take place, but only a part. Gutierrez agrees with Gregorio Lopez on this point. In confirmation, he cites certain commentaries that carry very little or no weight. From this opinion, Gregorio Lopez infers that since in this Kingdom of Castile it is not expressly provided in the laws of the *Partidas* that there is no place for purgation when a day and penalty are set, and since the Kingdom's own law is deficient in this, one should rather recur to Canon Law than to the Civil Laws of the Emperors...

<summary>This page discusses the legal principle that when a contract specifies a deadline for payment, the passing of that date serves as a formal demand, making the debtor liable for penalties without further notice. Molina analyzes the debates between jurists like Baldus and Gregorio Lopez regarding whether "canonical equity" allows debtors to pay late and avoid penalties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of when a debtor is considered "in delay" (in mora) and whether they can avoid penalties by paying late. It specifically contrasts the views of other jurists like Gutierrez and Palacios Rubias with the laws of the Kingdom of Castile.</meta>

# Second Tractate, Disputation 564. 837

On donations between husband and wife, number 5, the passage "it likewise seems to me it should be said"; it follows that in this Kingdom of Castile, the cleansing of delay <note>original: "morae purgatio"; the legal ability to fulfill an obligation late to avoid a penalty.</note> takes place, even if a specific day and a penalty were attached to the contract. Gutierrez also subscribes to this opinion in chapter 17, cited at numbers 8 and 9.

I, however, think that neither opinion is true. Regarding the first, it only holds place in canonical equity <note>Equity refers to fairness or mercy in the law, as opposed to strict technical rules.</note>; and it is proven by the chapter *suam de poenis*, that when a payment is divisible and no notable loss follows to the party because of the delay—if part of the debt was paid within the term—the full penalty should not take place for the remaining part which was not paid within the three-year period. This applies among ecclesiastical persons <note>Clergy or church officials.</note>, in whom any appearance of greed and avarice is unbecoming, as is the desire to be enriched by another's loss; they should be content with only a portion of the penalty described there as paid, and no more is gathered from that text. Furthermore, regarding the chapter *potuit de locato*, it was said a little earlier that the delay of an omission beyond two years in paying the pension for an ecclesiastical emphyteusis <note>A long-term land lease where the tenant improves the land.</note> can be cleansed; but one cannot take from this an effective argument to prove that the same applies in other events where a specific day and a penalty have been attached. It is likewise false what the aforementioned authors infer from their prior opinion regarding what should be said in this Kingdom of Castile. First, because the law is express in the *Partidas* <note>The "Siete Partidas," the foundational medieval law code of Castile.</note>, Book 5, Title 11, Law 35, which establishes the same thing decreed by Roman Law <note>original: "iure Caesareo"</note> when a specific day and penalty have been attached. Second, because it is false that in Canon Law there is room for the cleansing of delay in that event. Third, because it is false—and insufficiently proven by Palacios Rubias—that in this Kingdom of Castile one must stand by the disposition of Canon Law rather than Civil Law when the matter defined does not concern a matter of sin, faith, or religion, but deals with a purely civil matter; especially when something is established by Canon Law for clerics alone because it suits their status, such as what is found in the chapter *suam de poenis*.

<margin>4</margin>
When a specific day or † term was prescribed for payment, once it has passed, the creditor acting against the debtor has an established claim, as is clear in itself and affirmed by Gregorio López on the cited Law 8, gloss 2, at the beginning. And then, whether a penalty was set or not, if the legal instrument is ready for execution without a judge's sentence, there is no room for the cleansing of delay, as Gutierrez affirms in chapter 17, number 3, and Gregorio López agrees in the same cited gloss. There, with the gloss on the law *stipulatus*, at the word "on a certain day" (*certo die*) in the Digest on verbal obligations, and with the additions of Angelo <note>Angelo de Ubaldis (1328–1400), a famous Italian jurist.</note>, he adds: even if a penalty is attached, if it was agreed between the parties that the creditor should nevertheless notify the debtor or demand the debt from him, then such a day or term does not "interpellate" <note>original: "interpellat"; a legal term meaning the date itself acts as a formal demand for payment.</note> for the creditor so as to prevent the delay from being cleansed; at least when the specific term attached in that event has a tacit condition—that is, if the debt is requested by the creditor. Therefore, before that condition is fulfilled, it does not put the debtor in a state of delay. Hence, with the same Angelo, he concludes that if a specific term is set in an instrument ready for execution, but it is added that the creditor must nevertheless notify the debtor or demand the debt from him, execution cannot be carried out against the debtor before that condition is fulfilled.

<column-break/>

<margin>5</margin>
If the debtor, at the † fitting time and place, effectively offers payment to the creditor by showing it to him, and the creditor refuses to accept it, then if this were established, the debtor would be free from the penalty and damages, according to the law *soluturus* in the Digest and the law *oblatione* in the Code. The same applies if he offers a clear <note>original: "liquidam"; a debt whose amount is certain and undisputed.</note> part of the debt and provides suitable sureties for the part yet to be cleared, as the glosses on the cited law *obsignatione*, Gregorio López, and others cited on Law 8 at the word *affrenta* say. Likewise, if the creditor were absent and left no one to receive the payment in his place and name, the debtor would be free from the penalty, interest, and resulting damages for the fact that payment was not made within the prescribed term. In all these events, since the failure did not lie with the debtor but with the creditor, the interest for the following time would cease. But if the debtor, when the failure is not his but the creditor's, furthermore deposits the money in a safe place or with a trustworthy depositary to be handed to the creditor, then he is considered in reality, as in law, to have paid him; and therefore he would be entirely free from the debt. Furthermore, if the thing so paid were to perish then, it would perish for the creditor and not the debtor. This is held in the law *soluturus*, the law *oblatione*, the law *acceptam*, and Law 8, Title 14, Partida 5. Read Gregorio López there in the last three glosses.

<margin>6</margin>
When the day or † term fixed for payment is not certain, then the day does not "interpellate" for the creditor; rather, for the debtor to be placed in a state of delay, it is necessary that the debt be demanded from him after the appropriate time has arrived. This is clearly gathered from the law *magnam*, the law *traiectitia*, and Law 8, Partida 5. This is affirmed by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential legal commentator.</note> and the common opinion, which Gregorio López refers to and follows. Hence, with Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a student of Bartolus.</note>, Gregorio López maintains that if something is promised to be paid to someone when they reach legal age, a formal demand is necessary to put the debtor in delay and for him to incur a penalty if he obligated himself under one. Likewise, with Bartolus and Jason <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), another famous jurist.</note>, whose opinion he testifies is common, he maintains that if something is promised under a condition, the day the condition is fulfilled does not interpellate for the creditor, but it is necessary that the debt be requested. If, however, the day is tacitly introduced by law but is nonetheless certain, it *does* interpellate for the creditor—such as when an emphyteusis pension is paid annually, and other similar cases. For then the day on which the year is completed interpellates for the creditor, as was said regarding emphyteusis in Disputation 453. He also says the day interpellates, along with many others he cites, when something is owed on Easter day, even if the creditor promised he would not

<margin>7</margin>
demand it before that day. He also says, with Baldus, that a specific † hour established for payment interpellates for the creditor, according to the law *Titio*. Read that.

<margin>8</margin>
When † something has been promised under a certain penalty, but a time had not been established or determined in which, or within which, it should be done or paid...

<meta>This page continues Molina's discussion on the "cleansing of delay" (purgatio morae). It moves from the specific context of ecclesiastical leases discussed on the previous page to the general rules governing all contracts, specifically how judicial discretion and the start of a lawsuit affect a debtor's liability.</meta>

# Luis Molina: On Contracts
### Page 838

...ought to be performed, then, if the time has passed within which it should have been done according to the judgment of a prudent judge, and the creditor asks the debtor in a suitable place and time to fulfill the work, and the debtor is unwilling—or, when the judge had already taxed the time within which the debtor should perform, and he did not do it within that time—he is held liable for the penalty, the <term>interest</term> <note>original: "interesse"; in legal terms, this refers to the "difference" or the loss suffered and the profit lost due to the delay.</note>, and damages. This follows the methods explained at the beginning of this dispute, just as when a certain day and a penalty were attached from the start of the contract. This is supported by the law *mora* at the beginning of the section on <term>usury</term> <note>referring to Digest 22.1, the Roman law section on interest and delay.</note>, law 35, joined with law 13, and other laws cited there by Gregorio Lopez in Title 11, Part 5.

<margin>9</margin>
But if something was promised to be done or paid without a set day or time being established, and without a penalty attached, then once enough time has passed in which it could and should have best been done, and it was omitted through the debtor’s negligence, the creditor can demand what was owed along with all damages resulting from the fact it was not completed in a timely manner. However, if the debtor, before a lawsuit is <term>contested</term> <note>original: "lis contestetur"; the formal start of a legal trial where the issues are joined.</note> against him by the creditor, begins the promised work and follows through to complete it, he thereby "cleanses" the delay and is not liable for subsequent damages. So holds the law *si insulam* regarding verbal obligations and law 35, title 11, part 5. There, Gregorio Lopez in the second-to-last <term>gloss</term> <note>A marginal commentary on legal texts.</note> says this remains true even if a long time passed before the lawsuit began, and he asserts this is the common opinion of the doctors of law, against the view of Bartolus. Observe, however, that the second gloss on the law *si insulam*, which is commonly accepted, limits that law unless the creditor has a specific interest in the work being completed on time, according to the law *si ita quis*, section *Seya*. In that case, someone promised he would pay a woman named Seya a certain price by a certain day for some gardens to be delivered to him. He paid part, and after the day had passed, he wanted to pay the remainder a short time later. Seya did not want to stand by the contract because the buyer had not paid the full price on the appointed day. But the jurist Scaevola responded there that if the buyer wanted to pay the rest of the price after a short time, and Seya suffered no loss other than the delay itself by it not being paid on the set date—both of which are left to the judge's discretion to decide—then Seya must be forced to uphold the contract. Bartolus understands the limitation of that gloss to apply when the creditor’s interest exceeded the estimated value of the act. Yet, Gregorio Lopez rightfully judges that the last gloss of law 35 should be rejected, along with Bartolus's understanding, not only because of law 35 itself, which clearly states the opposite, but also according to common law. For the cited section *Seya* clearly speaks of when a certain day was fixed for payment; it is not dealing there with the cleansing of delay up to the start of the lawsuit, nor even with the cleansing of delay itself, but rather it establishes out of <term>equity</term> <note>fairness and mercy in legal interpretation.</note> that when the rest of the price is offered within a short time and without any loss to the seller, the seller should be forced to stand by the contract. This is far different from the rule in the law *si insulam*. Additionally, in the rule of law *si insulam*, the discussion concerns when damages and losses had followed for the creditor because the debtor did not pay or perform the promised task at a suitable time. Therefore, if it is to be limited so that

<column-break/>

the cleansing of delay up to the start of the lawsuit (as decreed in that law) does not take place when the creditor has an interest in the thing being done at a suitable time, then the rule of that law would never have a place. It would always be destroyed and rendered of no effect by the rule of the section *Seya*. Bartolus’s interpretation is plainly a matter of guesswork and does not agree with either of those laws.

From the cited section *Seya*, a lawsuit should have been decided which Gama mentions in decision 211. For when a certain man had sold 100 <term>cotia</term> <note>A type of commodity or measure, likely related to cloth or trade goods in a Portuguese/Spanish context.</note> to another, and had not delivered them from the many he held in a certain public house, having accepted part of the price immediately and with a pact that the buyer would deliver the remaining part to the seller on that very day, the buyer did not deliver it that day, but brought it to the seller the following morning. The seller, however, did not want to accept it, but said he was neither bound by nor willing to stand by the contract, because the buyer had not delivered the price at the appointed time. This matter was debated, and various contrary sentences were handed down. Finally, however, it was pronounced that the seller should be forced to uphold the contract. Although no mention was made of the cited section *Seya* in that case, it should nevertheless have been decided according to it. For since the rest of the price was offered a little while later—that is, the following morning—surely, if it did not matter much to the seller that the part of the price be paid to him on that very day, he should have been forced to stand by the contract, according to the express definition of the section *Seya*. It would be otherwise if it mattered greatly to the seller to have been paid on that exact day. Gutierrez, in his work on confirmed rights, part 3, chapter 17, number 1, says without distinction that in contracts, delay can be cleansed up to the start of the lawsuit, but not after, citing the law *si insulam* and law 35 at the end of title 11, part 5. Yet in these laws, as has been explained, the discussion only concerns when no penalty was attached and no certain deadline was prefixed for completion. However, at number 2, the same author adds that if the contract was confirmed by an oath, the debtor is held to fulfill it at the promised deadline and cannot cleanse the delay afterward; he pursues this and tries to prove it in the following numbers. I, however, think that although he who confirmed a contract with an oath should follow through (unless he fulfills it as best he can according to the form of the contract and the mind of the one swearing), the oath nevertheless cannot prevent the ability to cleanse the delay when it could have been cleansed even if no oath had been applied. And because this, along with many other points, was said against the same author in Dispute 453 regarding the contract of <term>emphyteusis</term> <note>a long-term land lease.</note>, I will not add more on this matter here. When a creditor accepts a debt after a delay, saying nothing about the penalty or the damages resulting from the delay, he is considered to have waived the damages and the penalty, if he makes no protest, according to the law *Celsus* and other laws cited in the gloss on the words "not after" in the section on the reception of arbitrators, and law 13, title 11, part 5.

<margin>10</margin>
Finally, it must be observed that the reasoning is far different regarding the cleansing of delay in presenting someone in court to avoid a penalty, a topic discussed at length in Dispute 547. Nor should the cleansing of delay in contracts be measured by the rules established for cleansing delay when something was not paid that an arbitrator ordered to be paid; that type of cleansing is discussed in the section on the reception of arbitrators, law *si cum dies*, and the two following.

<summary>This page analyzes the conditions under which a debtor can "cleanse" their delay (purgatio morae) by performing their obligation late. Molina argues that if no specific penalty or deadline is set, or if the delay is minimal and causes no harm, the contract remains valid, even if one party attempts to cancel it.</summary>

...and will be discussed in Treatise 15. However, that which Gutierrez reports in the cited chapter 17, final number, as having been judged in the Senate of Valladolid <note>original: "Pinciano senatu"; referring to the Royal Chancery of Valladolid, the highest court in the Crown of Castile.</note> regarding the cleansing of delay by certain <term>sureties</term> <note>original: "fideiussorum"; people who guarantee the debt of another.</note>, indeed agrees with what we said in the cited Dispute 47. For within an equal amount of time, that delay could be cleansed, as was seen in the cited dispute. ## When the same debtor has contracted various debts toward the same creditor, if he pays him something, for which debt it should be considered paid. And universally concerning the order to be observed in payments.

->DISPUTE LXV.<-

->SUMMARY.<-

<margin>1</margin> If a debtor has several debts with a creditor, which one is he presumed to have paid first?
<margin>2</margin> A debt paid from a more urgent cause, and which weighs more heavily on the debtor, is presumed first. <margin>no. 3.</margin>
<margin>Declare however and limit. no. 3.</margin>
<margin>4</margin> A debt with a surety is considered paid before one without a surety.
<margin>5</margin> Likewise, the older debt, where debts weigh equally on the debtor. no. 5.
<margin>6</margin> Debts arising from a crime are counted alongside personal debts.

<margin>1</margin> **I**n the matter proposed, if the debtor—either before, or when he pays, or immediately on the spot before departing from the place in which he paid—expressed for which debt or debts he was paying, it must be judged that payment was made for that debt or those debts. This is because a debtor can establish the law for his own property <note>i.e., the debtor has the right to decide how his money is allocated.</note>, choosing for which debt he wishes to pay it; the creditor's right remains to demand from the debtor if anything else is owed. If, however, the creditor contradicts this and does not wish to accept the payment for that specific debt, and the debtor <term>consigns</term> <note>original: "deponat"; a formal legal process of depositing money with a third party or court when a creditor refuses payment.</note> it as payment for that debt in the manner explained in the preceding dispute, the payment is considered made for that debt, and by law itself he is entirely freed from it, as was shown there according to various laws. These are found in the law joined with the general gloss of the Code on this title, the law *si usuras* <note>original: "l. si usuras. C. de usur."; Code of Justinian 4.32.1.</note>, and law 20, title 14.

If, however, that debtor pays something and does not express for which debt he pays it, but the creditor—either beforehand, or while the payment is being made, or immediately before they turn to other business—says he accepts it for such or such a debt, and the debtor remains silent, the payment is considered made for that debt. But if the debtor immediately contradicts this before departing from that place, it must be accepted for the debt for which he said he was paying it, or it must be

<column-break/>

returned to him. Furthermore, if the debtor, in the manner just explained, consigns and deposits it for that debt, he will be entirely free from such a debt, as has been said. Thus it is held in the law joined with the general gloss there, and in the two following: Digest on payments, law 1 of the Code on the same title, and law 10, title 14, part 5.

<margin>2</margin> When neither the debtor nor the creditor has expressed for which debt it should be paid, then: if the deadline set for the payment of one of the debts has already arrived and other debts are due on a future day, or under a condition still pending in the future, the payment is considered made for the debt or debts whose deadline has already arrived; not indeed for those whose deadline is still pending in the future. Thus it is held in the law *caeterum*, Digest on payments. Likewise, if the debtor owes the creditor something in his own name, and something as a surety for another, the payment made is considered for what he owes in his own name (law *magis*, and law *cum ex pluribus*, Digest on the same title). Likewise, when one debt is <term>liquid</term> <note>original: "liquidum"; a debt that is certain in its amount and due date, rather than contested or vague.</note> and another is not, the payment is considered made for the liquid debt and not for the non-liquid one (law 1, Digest on the same title). 

When none of these differences are seen among the debts, then, if one of them weighs more heavily on the debtor than another—because if he delays payment, he will incur a penalty, or pay <term>usury</term> <note>original: "vsuras"; interest.</note>, or suffer other detriment that does not similarly threaten from the delay of payment of the other debts—the payment is considered made for that debt from which more detriment threatens the debtor if he delays its payment, than would threaten from the delay of the others. Thus it is held in law *caeterum*, and the two following, Digest on the same title, and law 30, title 14, part 5. By this same reasoning, if one debt is owed from a cause from which <term>infamy</term> <note>original: "infamia"; a legal status of disgrace involving the loss of certain civil rights, often resulting from crimes or specific civil judgments.</note> threatens if a condemnation follows—such as from theft, or from a breach of <term>guardianship</term> <note>original: "tutela"; the duty to manage the affairs of a minor or ward.</note>, and indeed from the Aquilian law <note>The Lex Aquilia was a Roman law governing compensation for damage to property.</note>—and another is from a not-so-infamous or urgent cause, the payment is considered made for that more urgent cause. Likewise, if something is owed because of a judgment to be paid [iudicatum solui], and another is not, nor from any other more urgent cause, it is considered paid toward the extinction of the debt from the cause of the judgment. These are held in the law *si quid ex famosa*, and the law *cum ex pluribus*, Digest on payments.

<margin>3</margin> From the rule that in doubt something is considered paid for the debt from a more urgent cause and for the debt which weighs more heavily on the debtor, there is an exception: when something is owed with usury in the interim while it is not paid. For when usury and other things are owed from the <term>principal</term> <note>original: "sorte"; the capital or principal sum of a debt.</note> or main debt, and something is paid, then the payment is considered made first for the usury already due; if anything remains, only then is it considered paid toward the principal. This is so even if it would be far easier for the debtor if that payment were understood to be for the principal—because the future usury would cease in proportion to the principal paid—rather than being understood for the usury already due. Thus it is held in law 1, Code on payments, and law *vsuras*, Code on usury. 

The reason, however, is that when the principal and the usury are owed from the same root and debt, while the principal remains, the usury is paid as the "fruit" of the principal debt. This applies in cases where usury can be taken today, such as by reason of <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucri cessantis"; a legal justification for charging interest based on the profit the lender could have made elsewhere.</note> to one lending under usury, or from a <term>census contract</term> <note>A type of annuity or ground rent common in early modern finance.</note> with a pact of buy-back, or from a contract of partnership and insurance entered into with the same merchant. For this reason, it was rightly decreed in the two cited laws—in a manner adapted to practice and to what the nature of the matter itself requires—with that other rule (otherwise universal in payments) not standing in the way.

An important exception is noted where payments are applied to interest (usury) before the principal sum.</summary>
