840 Ludovico Molina on Contracts

<margin>4</margin> Furthermore, when something is owed with <term>sureties</term> <note>original: "fideiussoribus"; individuals who guarantee a debt</note> and another thing without sureties, the payment is considered to have been made for the debt with sureties rather than the debt without sureties. This is either because it was ordained in favor of the sureties, or because such a debt truly burdens the principal debtor more—since he sees himself and others bound on his account—than the debt without sureties, in which he alone is bound. This is stated in the Law *Magis* and the Law *In his* <note>original: "l. magis, & l. in his. ff. de solut."; references to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of civil law</note>. An exception is made when sureties are given for one part of a single debt and a <term>pledge</term> <note>original: "pignus"; physical collateral</note> for the remainder. For example, if someone contracts a debt of 30 gold coins, provides sureties for twenty of them, and delivers a pledge for the other ten; then, if the debtor does not pay and the pledge is sold to satisfy the debt, the money coming to the creditor is considered first accepted for those ten out of the thirty for which the pledge was liable. If any surplus remains, it is considered paid toward the twenty owed with sureties. This is found in the Law *Triginta* <note>original: "l. triginta, alias incipit ubi ob triginta, ff. de solu."</note>. Likewise, if something is owed under a pledge or <term>mortgage</term> <note>original: "hypotheca"</note> and another without these, all else being equal, the payment is considered made for the debt under pledge or mortgage rather than the one without. This is held in the Law *Cum ex pluribus* <note>original: "l. cum ex pluribus, ff. eod. tit."</note>. However, I believe that if one debt were owed under a pledge or mortgage and another with sureties, the payment should rather be considered made to release the surety than to redeem one's own pledge or mortgage.

<margin>5</margin> According to common law, when none of these factors are present, or the debts burden the debtor equally, if one debt is older than the other and nothing is explicitly stated, the payment is considered made for the older debt. <note>Citing Law *In iis*, Law *Ubi fideiussor*, etc.</note> A debt is considered "older" not because it stems from a contract celebrated earlier, but because it was due to be paid before the other debt. This goes so far that if two debts are of the same nature regarding their root burden—for example, if interest is owed on both—even if the less-ancient debt carries a higher interest rate than the older one, the payment is considered made for the older one. This is expressly stated in the Law *Si ex pluribus* <note>original: "l. si ex pluribus. §. vlt. ff. de solut."</note>. Finally, according to the same common law, when debts are equal in age because they were due to the same creditor on the same day (even if from different roots) and one does not burden the debtor more than the other, then if something is paid without mentioning which debt it is for, it is considered paid for all of them by a certain proportion. Thus, whatever the proportion of the sum of one debt is to the sum of the other, the payment is divided in that same proportion. This is held in the Law *Illud non* <note>original: "l. illud non. ff. de solu."</note>. Nor is this contradicted by the Law *Si in duab.* <note>original: "l. si in duab. ff. de reg. iur."</note>, for there it is only held that when debts are equal in the ways explained, the fact that more is owed on one debt than another does not mean the payment is considered made for one rather than the other; rather, it is to be divided among them proportionally.

Law 10, title 14, part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish legal code</note>, making no mention that,

<column-break/>

where other things are equal, a payment is understood to be for the older debt as explained above; it only establishes that when debts are such that one does not burden the debtor more than the other, then whatever is paid without mentioning the debt shall be considered paid for all equally—understanding this to mean by a certain proportion. Villalobos, in his *Antinomy* <note>a legal work resolving contradictions in law</note> under the letter S, number 19, refers to this law as if it corrected the common law on this point, although he adds that Gregorio Lopez <note>a famous commentator on Spanish law</note> wishes for that law to agree with the common law. Indeed, although Gregorio Lopez admits that the law was written according to the words of Azo <note>a 13th-century jurist</note>, he adds that it must be understood according to common law—namely, that it does not apply when one debt is older than another. Since that law does not imply a correction of the common law, it can be interpreted perfectly in accordance with it; and this opinion does not displease me.

<margin>6</margin> But observe this: when the debtor pays nothing, but the personal creditors demand their debts—if the debtor is unable to pay everyone in full, or if after his death sufficient goods do not remain to pay everyone in full—then, if no one has a <term>privilege of preference</term> <note>a legal right to be paid before others</note> over the rest, the goods of the deceased are to be divided equally among them by a certain proportion, according to the ratio and quantity of the sum owed to each. This was stated in Dispute 536, where we dealt extensively with the order to be observed in making payments regarding all creditors universally. Also observe that debts arising from a crime—such as theft, robbery, damage caused, and others—are to be reckoned with personal debts when the stolen property no longer exists (such that its ownership would remain with its original owner). Consequently, such creditors have the same standing as other personal creditors who lack special privileges; this is held in Law 13, title 14, part 5.

### Whether when one thing is paid for another, the tax that is called *alcabala* in Castile and *sisa* in Portugal is owed.

---

## DISPUTE DLXVI.

->SUMMARY.<-

1 *Whether the tax or <term>alcabala</term> <note>a historical Spanish sales tax</note> is owed when one debt is paid for another without <term>novation</term> <note>the replacement of an old contract with a new one</note>.*
2 *If the debtor's goods mortgaged to a creditor are sold, whether the tax is owed if their price is not enough to pay the creditor.*

**F**or it was said above that this tax is not owed in cases of novation and <term>compensation</term> <note>balancing mutual debts</note>, and likewise not in a <term>transaction</term> <note>a settlement of a dispute</note>. Our discussion in this place, however, is when one thing is paid for another without novation. Setting aside the long dispute on this matter which may be read in Lassarte <note>a legal authority on taxes</note> regarding the tenth of a sale, chapter 7, let us speak briefly with the same author...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the fulfillment of obligations, specifically focusing on the tax implications (the *alcabala* or sales tax) when a debtor pays a debt using a different asset than originally agreed, and the legal remedies for recovering mistaken payments.</meta>

841 Second Treatise, Dispute 567.

It must be said that if, with no pressing necessity but by the free will of both the creditor and debtor, one thing is paid in place of another—since the specific thing owed could have been paid, but the debtor preferred to pay something else and the creditor accepted it—then that tax is owed. Indeed, if what was owed was money, and the debtor pays another thing in its place, such as an ox, it is considered a sale of that ox for the debt money; therefore, the debtor who sells it is bound to pay that tax in this Kingdom of Castile. If, however, an ox was owed and they agree that the debtor shall pay a certain quantity of money for it, it is the creditor who is considered to be selling the ox, and thus he himself is bound to pay that tax in this Kingdom. In Portugal, however, in either event, the debtor is bound to pay half of that tax and the creditor the other half, because in that Kingdom the seller pays half of the tax and the buyer the other half. But if an ox was owed and the agreement is that the debtor pays several measures of wheat in its place, then it is an exchange of an ox for wheat, and that tax is owed twice, as has often been said in the preceding sections: in exchanges, that tax must be paid double. The reason for this assertion is that since this occurs without pressing necessity but entirely spontaneously and by mutual consent, it is not considered merely a release and extraction of the prior obligation and debt (from which that tax was not owed), but a true contract of exchange of one thing for another celebrated by mutual consent. From this, a single tax is owed if a thing that is money is exchanged for a thing that is not money, because it becomes a purchase and sale, as is established in the law *si praedium* <note>original: "l. si prædiū. C. de euict."; reference to the Code of Justinian on evictions</note>, where it is held that a contract of this kind takes the place of a sale; see also the law *eleganter* <note>original: "l. eleganter in prin. ff. de pignorat. act."; reference to the Digest on pledge actions</note>. If, however, a thing that is not money is exchanged for another thing that is also not money, it is a barter <term>permutation</term> <note>original: "permutatio"; a non-monetary exchange of goods</note>, for which that tax is owed double, as Lassarte affirms here with others in chapter 7, cited from number 1, and on justice from number 44, especially from number 49. If, however, one thing is paid for another not by the common consent of the creditor and debtor, but contrary to their common intent and will—either because the debtor does not have the thing owed to pay, or because some good of the debtor is adjudicated to the creditor as payment—then, since in those events nothing else is being done in itself than the debt being paid and extinguished, certainly no tax is owed for that payment of one debt for another. <margin>no. 54.</margin> And for this reason, in the same place at number 54, he says with others that the practice arose in this Kingdom of Castile that the tax is not exacted from things adjudicated to a creditor as payment.

He rightly advises, however, that if, while execution is made upon the debtor’s goods, something is sold in a public auction <term>subhastatione</term> <note>original: "subhastatione"; a sale "under the spear," or a court-ordered auction</note>, then—whether it is bought by the creditor or by someone else—that tax is owed from that sale, because it is a true purchase and sale. <margin>*</margin> Yet, if according to the prescription of the law the thing is held as purchased but must be returned to the debtor in the event that the debtor pays the debt to the creditor within a certain time, then if the debtor pays the debt within that time, the tax is not owed; instead, it must be returned by the tax collector <term>gabellario</term> <note>original: "gabellario"; an official or private contractor who collected the "gabelle" or sales tax</note> if he has already received it. This is because that purchase and sale, by the very disposition of the law, was

<column-break/>

conditional, provided that the debtor does not pay the debt within such time; when the condition fails, it was rendered null by the law itself, no differently than if it had never been celebrated.

Lassarte raises a fine question in the same place at <margin>no. 59.</margin> number 59: If the goods of a debtor were subject to a pledge or mortgage to a creditor (especially to the treasury), and when sold their price is not sufficient to pay the debt in full, nor are there other goods of the debtor from which it may be paid in full, is that tax owed from such a price to the tax collector who has it under lease? Or is it not, and instead the creditor (who is prior in time and has a right to the thing in comparison to the goods of such a debtor) should be preferred for the whole price? He rightly responds that it is owed: just as other expenses must be paid from there to the crier and other public officials who performed their service in that matter up to the point of the goods being sold. The reason is that the royal law, which imposed that tax on all sales and exchanges (with few exceptions), is understood to apply to all sales universally, by whatever means they occur; it therefore affects and works upon them all by the very fact that wherever a sale occurs, it is affected by that tax. No more is considered to remain from the price—either for the debtor himself or even for his creditors—than what is left over after the payment of that tax to the King.

1 *One who pays by error a debt that is owed neither naturally nor civilly recovers it through a claim for recovery of a non-debt.*

8 *A debt under a condition pending in the future, paid by error, can be recovered.*

Several other matters are joined with the material on payments, which are to be explained consequently. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of financial obligations, shifting from the taxes owed on substitute payments to the "condictio indebiti"—the legal action used to recover a payment made by mistake when no debt actually existed.</meta>

### Ludovicus Molina on Contracts
ij 3

<column-break/>

...is called a debt. This is held in Rule 1 and following of the Digest <note>original: "ff." refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> *On the recovery of a mistaken payment* <note>original: "de condictione indebiti"</note>, and in Rule 28, Title 14, Part 5 <note>The *Siete Partidas*, the medieval Spanish law code</note>. The cited Rule 28 provides an example: when a debtor, unaware that his agent or steward had already paid his creditor what he owed him, pays the same amount to him a second time. Likewise, if a creditor had forgiven a debt in his will, and the debtor, unaware of this, paid the creditor's heir. In the same place, Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist and commentator</note> adds examples: if a father or some deceased person had paid a certain debt, and his heir, being ignorant of this (which is presumed by the rule *He who succeeds to the rights of another* in the Digest *On the rules of law*), paid the same debt again. Likewise, if someone paid something because they were led to do so by a forged document: indeed, in that case, even if a final judgment had been rendered based on the forged document—which would normally have become a settled matter <term>res iudicata: a matter already judged that cannot be reopened</term>—and he had been condemned and forced to pay, the sentence would be rescinded through a "restoration to the original state" <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"</note> and the paid debt would be reclaimed, as held in the rule *Those things acknowledged* in the Digest *On exceptions*, and as will be discussed in the following dispute. In the cases explained here, and in any others similar to them where something not owed is paid entirely due to the error of the payer, the recovery of that payment is granted, whether the payment was made out of an error of law <note>original: "errore iuris," a misunderstanding of legal requirements</note> or an error of fact <note>original: "errore facti," a misunderstanding of the circumstances</note>. For this distinction—whether something was paid by an error of law or fact—only applies when the debt was not owed under civil law but was still owed by "natural law," as we shall add below. Furthermore, the action for recovery of a mistaken payment arises not from a contract, but from a "quasi-contract," as explained at the end of Dispute 55.

<margin>2</margin> When someone seeks something back as having been paid by them when it was not owed, the burden of proof lies with them to show it was not owed; for no one is presumed to pay what they do not owe. An exception is made if the person who paid was a minor, a woman, a soldier, or a simple farmer <note>In the legal tradition of this time, these groups were considered "privileged" or "simple" and thus granted extra protection against being taken advantage of</note>: in those cases, the burden falls on the one who received the payment to prove that it was indeed owed to him. If he does not prove it, he will lose the case and be compelled to return it. Although no one is presumed to pay what is not owed, because it would not be difficult for a creditor to prove a debt was owed to him if it actually was, it is no wonder that the law—in favor of those who usually do not have much experience in affairs or the skill to prove things—shifts the burden of proof onto the creditor to show it was his debt, otherwise he must fail and be forced to return it. However, this exception does not apply when such a minor, woman, soldier, or simple farmer contends that not *all* they paid was owed, but only a part (seeking the rest back), or when they confess it was once a debt but claim it was already paid before, or that they had a legal defense <note>original: "exceptionem"</note> not to pay it which they neglected to raise. In all these specific events, the burden of proof lies with the minor, woman, soldier, or farmer to prove that what they are reclaiming was not owed; otherwise, they will lose. This is held in the rule *When concerning a debt*, section *But if for a part*, in the Digest *On proofs*. Moreover, when someone is sued for something as a payment not owed to them, regardless of who is sued, if they deny that it was paid to them at all, and the other party sufficiently proves it was paid (either by witnesses, writing, or other means), then by that very act the receiver is rendered suspect. For that reason, the burden

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> subsequently falls on him to prove it was owed to him; otherwise, he is compelled to return it unless he proves it was a debt. All these points are found in the cited rule *When concerning a debt* and Rule 29, Title 14, Part 5. However, when something is reclaimed as a mistaken payment, and the one who received it denied receiving any such thing, if it is later proved that he did receive it—but only by the confession of that same receiver, whether under oath or not—then, because that proof does not come from the one who gave it and contends it was not owed, but from the one who denied receiving it, it ought not to harm him such that the burden of proof (that it was a debt) is shifted to him, since otherwise it would belong to the other to prove it was not owed. This is the view of the Gloss on the cited rule *When concerning a debt*, and of Joannes Andreas, Imola, and Vincentius <note>Prominent medieval canonists and legal commentators</note>, and Gregorio Lopez on the cited Rule 29, based on the argument in the rule *Him who*, in the Digest *On oaths*.

He who, knowing he does not owe something, pays it anyway, is presumed to be giving it as a gift; for that reason, he cannot reclaim it later, according to the rule *Not owed* in the Code *On the recovery of mistaken payments*, Rule 1 of the Digest of the same title, the rule *Whose by error* in the Digest *On the rules of law*, and Rule 36, Title 14, Part 5. Gregorio Lopez, on the cited Rule 30, along with Jason <note>Jason de Mayno, a famous Italian jurist</note> and others, limit this to when the receiver also accepted it *as* a gift. For if he receives it as if it were a debt, or under some other title than a gift, he does not acquire ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of it until he accepts it as a gift. This is because there is no "meeting of the minds" <note>original: "non consentiant in unum"</note> or shared understanding between the giver and the receiver, which is required to celebrate any contract, even a gift; nor has that gift yet been accepted by the receiver. This is gathered from the said rule *He who* in the Digest *If a certain thing is sought*.

<margin>2</margin> Where an exception is granted to the receiver—when he knew it was a gift—on the grounds that it was consumed according to the giver's will, or was accepted and retained according to the giver's will, as the Gloss says in that place. But certainly, regarding gifts, I would judge that law to be reconsidered, as it contains nothing other than an opinion of Ulpian <note>One of the great Roman jurists</note> taken from Julian. I would rather hold that when something is delivered with the intention of giving <note>original: "donandi animo"</note>, that is sufficient to transfer ownership. Therefore, not only should the receiver have the legal defense that the law grants him, but the giver should also be denied the right to reclaim it if he had the intention to give. There is no reason why this right of reclamation should be granted to the giver by law while simultaneously granting a defense to the receiver. For if ownership was not transferred by that delivery with the intent to give, and the gift is not considered accepted by that habitual mindset of the receiver (who wishes to receive a thing in the way that is best for him), then surely, if the receiver is certain of the giver's intent before the giver revokes the gift, and the receiver accepts the gift, he thereby acquires ownership of it, and the giver has no right to reclaim it. But if the giver revokes the gift before it is accepted by the receiver—which he is considered to do by the very fact that he seeks the thing back—I do not see how the receiver can have that legal defense which Ulpian (citing Julian) grants him in that law. Otherwise, following Jason and others, this same point is limited to be understood only when there is no counter-presumption from the circumstances...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the recovery of mistaken payments (condictio indebiti). It specifically examines the intention behind payments, the rights of protected classes of people, and how informal wills or conditional debts affect the ability to reclaim money.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 558.
### Page 843

...given or paid with another intent: for if, from any heading, another intention can be presumed, it is not to be presumed as a gift <note>original: "donatio"</note>, based on the argument in the law *If with the authority* <note>original: "l. si cum auto"</note> in the Digest *On payments*. Likewise, a minor under twenty-five years of age, even if he pays a non-existent debt knowingly and prudently, can reclaim it through the benefit of "restoration to the original state" <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that cancels a contract or act to return the parties to their previous position</term>; say the same of a spendthrift <note>original: "prodigo"</note> in the law *Sometimes* <note>original: "l. interdum"</note> in the Code *On the recovery of a mistaken payment*, and the final gloss on the first law of the Digest *On the recovery of a mistaken payment*.

<margin>6</margin> Furthermore, if someone pays while in any way doubting whether he truly owes what he is paying, and it is later discovered or he is able to prove that he did not owe it, recovery is granted, just as if he had paid entirely by mistake. This is held in the final law of the Code *On the recovery of a mistaken payment* and the cited law 30. From this it follows that, in the matter proposed, paying by mistake is the same as paying while in any state of doubt. Understand this provided that, given the doubt, there was no intent to make a gift—which is paid out on the chance that it might not be owed—an intent which is not presumed in the external court <note>original: "foro exteriori," meaning the public legal system as opposed to the internal court of conscience</note>, but rather the contrary is presumed.

<margin>7</margin> Regarding legacies <term>legata: specific gifts left in a will</term> or trusts <term>fideicommissa: property held by one person for the benefit of another as requested in a will</term> left in a "less solemn" <note>original: "minus solemni," referring to a will that lacks certain legal formalities like the required number of witnesses</note> testament: although under Civil Law no legal action is granted to the beneficiaries to demand or obtain these from the heirs of the person who left them in such an informal will (as explained extensively in Dispute 85), the Civil Law nevertheless does not prevent these from being naturally owed if that was the testator's will. The lack of full formality in that final will does not stand in the way, as was said in that same place. From this it follows that if the heir of the deceased, or the heir's heir, pays those things to the beneficiaries, they are not granted recovery of what was paid as if it were a non-existent debt. This is true even if they paid out of ignorance of the law—specifically, that they were not bound in the external court to pay those things based on that informal testament—as was also stated in the cited dispute. An exception is made unless the person who paid out of ignorance of the law was a soldier, a woman, a minor, or a farmer; for to these people recovery would be granted, as held in the law *The Rule* <note>original: "l. regula"</note> in the Digest *On ignorance of law and fact*, and law 31, title 14, part 5 <note>of the Spanish *Siete Partidas*</note>. However, if it is left to their oath to say whether they knew it was the testator's will, and they confess they have no doubt that it was, they will not only be blocked from recovering the payment, but they will even be compelled to pay the legacies if they have not yet paid them, as explained in the cited dispute. But if the heir of the deceased (whether he belonged to one of those four types of privileged persons or not) had paid those legacies or trusts out of an ignorance of the *facts*, rather than ignorance of the *law*, then recovery would be granted to him for what he paid. Yet, if he similarly confessed it was the testator's will, he would not only be denied recovery of what he paid, but also compelled to pay what he had not yet paid, as stated in the cited dispute. Likewise, if an heir had the right to deduct the "Falcidian portion" <term>falcidia: a Roman law right allowing an heir to keep at least one-fourth of the estate, reducing legacies if necessary</term> from the legacies, and he did not deduct it—either knowingly or out of ignorance of the law—recovery is not granted to him. However, it would be granted if he failed to deduct it out of ignorance of the facts, as discussed in Dispute 213 in the eighth scenario, and in the question added at the end of that dispute.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, this does not derive its force from the idea that full legacies are owed to beneficiaries without the Falcidian deduction in cases where the law allows it to be deducted; rather, it is because the law does not allow it to be deducted once the full amounts have been paid, whether knowingly or out of ignorance of the law. Since all these matters have been extensively explained in those two disputes, I will not add more on this subject here. I would only advise that law 31, title 14, part 5, which is taken from the heart of Imperial Law <note>original: "iuris Cæsarei," referring to Roman Law</note>, should be added to the laws of Castile <note>original: "iuribus Castellæ," Spanish law</note> cited in support of our opinion. This confirms what was said there regarding Imperial and Castilian law: namely, that a testament being "less solemn" does not prevent the things disposed in it from being naturally owed, even though Imperial law does not grant a legal action based on that testament.

<margin>8</margin> When something is owed under a condition pending in the future—which consequently might not happen—it is not simply owed before the condition is fulfilled. If the condition fails, it is not owed at all. In either case, if it is paid by mistake before the condition is fulfilled, it can be reclaimed as a mistaken payment, because it was not yet a debt. This is held in the laws *Under a condition* <note>original: "l. sub conditione"</note> and *Let it suffice* <note>original: "l. sufficiat"</note> in the Digest *On the recovery of a mistaken payment*, and law 32, title 14, part 5, and was stated in Dispute 284. In the cited law *It suffices*, it is added that if something is owed outright, but later an agreement was made that such a debt would not be sought except under a certain condition (which might not be fulfilled), then if it is paid by mistake before that condition is met, a recovery of the payment as if it were not owed is available to the payer. However, when something is owed on a "certain day" <note>original: "in diem certum"</note> that will definitely come—whether the exact time is uncertain, such as the day of someone’s death, or certain, such as the upcoming feast of Easter or St. John—if it is paid before that day arrives, recovery is not granted. This is because it is already truly owed at that time, even if it was not to be paid until that day. For the same reason, the rule is the same if something is owed under a condition that is absolutely certain to happen, such as "if the sun rises" or "if there is an eclipse on such a day." This is held in the laws *On a day* <note>original: "l. in diem"</note> and *For even when* <note>original: "l. nam & cum"</note>, joined with the following law, and the law *It suffices* in the Digest *On the recovery of a mistaken payment*, and the cited law 32, as was said in Dispute 284. But when something is owed on an "uncertain day" regarding whether it will ever happen—such as someone's wedding day, which may or may not occur—then it is considered a debt under a pending future condition. Consequently, if it were paid by mistake before that day arrived or the condition was met, it could be reclaimed. This is held in the law *Under a condition* in the Digest *On the recovery of a mistaken payment*. However, if what is owed under a pending future condition were paid knowingly before the condition was met, then it could not be reclaimed before the condition was met, because it is deemed to have been "forgiven" <note>original: "condonatum"</note> so that the payment would be made early. Much less could it be reclaimed once the condition is actually met. But if the condition were to fail, it could be reclaimed: for by the mere act of payment before the condition is met, it is not deemed to be forgiven such that a conditional debt becomes an outright one, with nothing depending on the condition, unless this is expressed or sufficiently gathered from other factors. Both are present...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of recovering mistaken payments (condictio indebiti). While the previous page focused on payments made in error or doubt, this page examines the strict legal boundaries of payments made following a court’s final decision, known as a "matter already judged" (res iudicata).</meta>

The gloss <note>original: "glos." refers to the standard legal commentary on the Corpus Iuris Civilis</note> affirms that one who says they owe something should be able to recover it under the title "on the recovery of what is given for a cause" <note>original: "condicere. ff. de cond. cau. dar."</note>. This is also affirmed by the legal scholars Jason de Mayno and Angelus de Ubaldis, as well as Gregorio Lopez in his commentary on the cited first law, based on the argument of the law "under condition" <note>original: "l. sub conditione"</note> in the Digest regarding payments.

# Payments not owed. Regarding the force of a judgment that has become final, and to what extent it can or cannot be recovered.

## DISPUTE 568.

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> A payment made by virtue of a sentence that has become a final judgment <note>original: "res iudicata"</note> cannot be recovered as "not owed," nor is proof admitted that it was not owed. This fails to apply if the sentence was based on false allegations or evidence. (Number 2).
<margin>3</margin> The same applies if the sentence was delivered against an absent person or a minor.
<margin>4</margin> It also fails to apply to the state treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>, a minor, or the Church; they are granted restoration based on new documents against a final judgment, but not based on new witnesses.
<margin>5</margin> A criminal sentence that has become final cannot be retracted by new evidence; instead, one must appeal to the Prince <note>the sovereign or ruler</note> for its moderation or rescission.
<margin>6</margin> The same applies to a civil sentence, even if there were the clearest proofs; it must be rescinded through the benefit of "restoration to the original state" <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that cancels a contract or act to return the parties to their previous position</term>.
<margin>7</margin> In which events a judge can rescind a final judgment through the benefit of restoration without recourse to the Prince.
<margin>8</margin> In which cases an action for recovery without cause is applicable.
<margin>9</margin> A payment made following a sentence based on a "decisive oath" <note>an oath taken by one party to settle a matter when evidence is lacking</note> can be recovered if legitimate proof to the contrary is found later.
<margin>10</margin> One who pays knowingly after a judgment of acquittal cannot recover the payment.

<margin>1</margin> When something has been paid by the force of a sentence that has become a final judgment <note>original: "res iudicata"</note>, even if the person did not truly owe what was paid, recovery is not granted as if it were not owed. Nor is proof admitted that it was not owed; this is due to the authority of the court and to "close the door to litigation" <note>original: "vt litibus ostium præcludatur"</note>, so that a state of certainty is established by a sentence that becomes final. This is supported by the Code, the Digest, and the Siete Partidas <note>a major Castilian law code</note>.

<margin>2</margin> An exception is made to this rule when the sentence was delivered based on false allegations, false witnesses, or false documents. Proof is admitted to show it was delivered in that manner, and that the judge delivered it relying on those false allegations or documents, and would not have delivered it otherwise. Once both are sufficiently proven—for the first part alone is not enough—the person condemned is restored to their original state and recovers whatever was paid by force of that judgment. Furthermore, those who were at fault for this happening are severely punished.

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> This is found in the Code <note>original: "C. si ex falsis instrum."</note> and the Siete Partidas. And, if a sentence was delivered in that manner against an absent person, it is void by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>. The same applies if it was delivered against a minor.

<margin>4</margin> Although <insert>on account of</insert> the fact that new documents have been found proving a defendant should not have been condemned, "restoration" <note>reversing the judgment</note> cannot regularly be granted against a final judgment—and consequently recovery of what was paid cannot be granted—nonetheless, when the cause is a public one, concerning the state treasury <term>fisco: the public or royal treasury</term>, the King’s chamber, or the commonwealth, it can and should be granted. The same applies if the case concerns a minor or the Church, as the standard glosses commonly affirm. However, the discovery of new witnesses does not allow for the rescinding of a final judgment, even in comparison to the state treasury, as noted by Gregorio Lopez, Padilla, and others.

<margin>5</margin> These rules similarly apply in criminal matters if someone is condemned by a final judgment. For when someone was not condemned through forged or deceitful evidence, even if witnesses or something else are found later to prove their innocence, the sentence cannot be rescinded. One must instead appeal to the Prince, whose role in such an event is to moderate or entirely rescind the sentence. Gutierrez adds, along with Padilla and Gregorio Lopez, that in this Kingdom of Castile, if a judge becomes certain of someone's innocence through other means after a criminal sentence has been passed, they can liberate them from death or another punishment by moderating or rescinding the sentence they themselves passed, without recourse to the Prince. This is based on a law stating that execution should be stayed in such an event. However, as Gregorio Lopez observes, that law follows the Digest regarding someone who confessed a crime under torture and was condemned based on that confession. Both laws command the judge, if they later find the condemned person is innocent, to stay the execution and free the defendant. It is immediately added that when this is discovered, one must write to the Prince, for the condemned should be freed and the sentence rescinded by the Prince's authority, not by the authority of the judge who passed it, even if he presided over the province. This is how Bartolus understands it. Yet, because custom is the best interpreter of laws, if this is the custom in any part...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the finality of court judgments and the specific circumstances under which a case can be reopened or a payment recovered after a "final judgment" (res iudicata) has been reached. It transitions from general principles to specific exceptions involving newly discovered evidence.</meta>

partially received in this Kingdom, I judge that in criminal matters one must stand by that custom, since it is both equitable and consistent with the cited law.

<margin>6</margin>
When, however, in civil matters, after a sentence has been passed which has become a **final judgment** <note>original: "rem iudicatam"; a matter already decided by a court that cannot be appealed under normal circumstances</note>, clear **legal documents** <note>original: "instrumenta"</note> appear, or witnesses who are above all suspicion and whose integrity is not at all to be doubted, from which it clearly appears that what was judged is not owed at all and that the judgment should have been far different—then, even if the sentence had been sent for execution, the condemned person or their heir must wait to appeal to the **Prince** <note>the sovereign or high ruler</note>. They must ask him to have the matter re-examined. It will belong to the Prince, having considered the quality of the matter and the clarity of the proofs, to grant that the matter be brought back to judgment again. If it is established as "more certain than certain" that the thing was not owed and that the judgment would have been different if those proofs had been available then—and provided no malice or negligence was present on the part of the condemned party in offering these at the appropriate time—the sentence may be rescinded through the **benefit of restoration to the original state** <note>original: "beneficium restitutionis in integrum"; a legal remedy that cancels the effects of a judgment and returns the parties to their prior legal positions</note>.

<margin>7</margin>
In the following outcomes, however, many say that the judge himself, without recourse to the Prince, can grant the rescission of the sentence through the benefit of restoration. The first is if it clearly appears that through the malice and knowledge of the winner, it was brought about that those documents or witnesses which appeared later did not appear then, and the condemned person could not use them. In this event, having understood the **gloss** <note>the standard legal commentary</note> which asserts this in the law *si fideiussor* in the section *in omnibus* regarding mandates, Gutierrez approves it in the place cited above at number 7, and with Alexander affirms that it is the more common opinion of the doctors.

The second is when the loser asked for time to be given to him to bring forward proofs—because the witnesses were captives, or he had documents elsewhere, or the witnesses were not then in control of themselves <note>original: "compotes sui"; perhaps due to illness or mental state</note>, and it was not within his power then to bring forward competent proofs—and this was not granted to him, but he was condemned. In that case, if he later has an abundance of such proofs which are entirely clear and remove all doubt, the rescission of the sentence through restoration should be granted to him, as well as the **recovery** <note>original: "repetitio"</note> of what he paid unduly by force of such a sentence. So say Innocent, Bartolus, and Panormitanus, and Gregorio Lopez on law 33, title 14, part 5, under the word *razonadores*. Indeed, the same Gregorio Lopez in the same place under the word *alegaciones*, and the common opinion which Gutierrez refers to and follows above at number 8, affirm that even if the condemned person (whether they be the defendant or the plaintiff) asked for no such thing, provided that at the time of the litigation they were not at fault or negligent in seeking and offering the clear proofs which did not then occur to them, if they later appear, the sentence must be rescinded. Thus, he reports from Padilla that this was done in a certain cause of the citizens of **Segovia**. The same must be said, they assert, when a debt already paid once by someone is demanded again from the same person, and because they did not remember or did not offer the document of payment, they were condemned to pay it again. For if the document appears later and they offer it, by that evidence of the fact, the sentence is rescinded through restoration, and the debt is recovered which was paid a second time by force of a sentence founded on a false

<column-break/>

presumption.

<margin>8</margin>
This last example, and many others, can be reduced to the **condition of a gift without cause** <note>original: "conditione dati sine causa"; a legal action to recover something given for a reason that was false or failed</note>, because the cause for which it was given was reduced to a "non-cause" by what happened later or was discovered, according to what is held in the law *si fullo* in the Digest regarding recovery without cause. For as is held in these laws, and affirmed by Bartolus and others whom Gregorio Lopez and Alvaro Valasco follow, if clothes are handed over to a **fuller** <note>a person who cleans and thickens cloth</note> to be washed, and because they disappeared, he is condemned to pay their value; if they later appear and come entirely into the power of the owner who handed them over to be washed, the fuller is granted a recovery of the price paid for them to the owner, as a "recovery without cause." This is because, although he paid the price because of the loss, that cause, once the clothes are restored to their proper owner, returns to being a "non-cause," since the loss was abolished by the restoration of the clothes. Hence, in the matter proposed, one does not act for the rescission of a sentence that was passed deservedly and justly, but one acts for the recovery of the value of the clothes, which is now retained without just cause (which existed before, or was presumed at the time of the sentence, and in consideration of which the sentence was passed). By this reasoning, since it is clear from the offering of the document of payment that the cause upon which the sentence rested does not exist—because the debt which was believed to be owed from the contract truly no longer was, because it had been resolved by payment—surely, with nothing hindering the sentence (which is not attacked nor sought to be rescinded), the payment is recovered as truly paid without cause. By the same reasoning, Alvaro Valasco argues that when someone had received only one hundred as a loan, but in a public document had confessed to the creditor that they received one hundred and twenty, and by force of that document was condemned to pay one hundred and twenty, and it was later sufficiently proved that the twenty paid above the hundred were paid as **usury** <note>interest charged on a loan, often restricted by religious or civil law</note> on the remaining hundred received, they can—nothing hindering the sentence—recover those twenty as paid without cause and title. Just as one who binds himself by oath to pay usury can, after they are paid and the oath fulfilled, recover them as paid without cause, that is, without just title. However, the things said in this dispute so far belong more broadly to the fifth treatise.

<margin>9</margin>
When a judgment has been terminated by a **decisory oath** <note>original: "iuramento decisorio"; an oath taken by one party to decide the case when other evidence is lacking</note>, granted because of the lack of proofs of the other contender: then by that very fact, if legitimate and clear proofs were later found to the contrary, recovery would be granted. This is because legitimate proofs found later have greater force against that false oath and the judgment terminated by it, than against a sentence otherwise legitimately passed which has become a final judgment. Remember, however, in **Portugal** <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, since not just any proofs create trust in court regarding contracts and their dissolution (as was said in Dispute 360), just any other proofs are not sufficient to rescind a judgment terminated by a decisory oath in that Kingdom.

<margin>10</margin>
When someone was truly a debtor for some debt, even if they are acquitted by a judge’s sentence, if they pay it after that sentence is delivered, they cannot claim it back. This is because the "exception of natural debt" <note>original: "exceptio, quod nihilominus naturaliter illud debeat"; a legal defense stating that even if a debt isn't legally enforceable, a moral or "natural" obligation remains</note> stands in their way. Indeed, if they pay while knowing and being aware that they were acquitted, they are presumed to be paying it as a natural debt nonetheless, or certainly wishing to grant it as a gift. That they cannot claim it back is held in the laws *iudex*, *Iulianus*, and *unus debitorem* in the Digest <note>Roman law collections</note> regarding the recovery of what is not owed, as well as in the *Partidas* <note>Spanish medieval law code</note>.

# Several cases are weighed as to whether the recovery of a payment not owed has a place in them. And to what extent the thing not owed, and its fruits, must be restored.

## DISPUTATION 569.

### SUMMARY.

1. In which cases the **recovery of payment not owed** <term>condictio indebiti: a legal action to get back money paid by mistake</term> does not have a place, and the following numbers.
2. When **alimony** <note>original: "Alimenta"; maintenance or support for living</note> provided out of a sense of piety can be reclaimed.
3. When a **good-faith possessor** of an inheritance, who pays the deceased's creditors, can reclaim that payment.
4. When a person receiving a payment not owed is bound to restore the thing along with the **fruits** <note>original: "fructibus"; the profits or produce generated by a property, like rent or crops</note> collected, and those that could have been collected.
5. What is considered a debt when something is owed **alternatively or disjunctively** <note>e.g., a contract to give "either a horse or 100 gold pieces"</note>.
6. If a debtor performs an action and later realizes they were not bound to do it, they can reclaim the estimated value of what they did.
7. When a **putative heir** <note>someone who believes they are the heir but is not</note> who pays the deceased's debts from the inheritance can reclaim those payments.
8. Whether someone who renounces the recovery of payment not owed, and all legal aid, can still reclaim it. And what if they renounced with an oath? (Number 9).

<margin>1</margin>
Several cases remain to be weighed as to whether the recovery of payment not owed has a place in them. When something is given as a **dowry** to a woman, or for a wedding to a man, because of some believed reason that does not actually exist—for example, because they were believed to be a blood relative when they were not, or for some other similar believed but non-existent reason—the laws decree that even if the giver later discovers that the reason did not exist as they believed, they cannot reclaim it. For they say that it was given for a **pious cause** <note>original: "piam causam"; a socially or morally beneficial purpose, such as supporting a marriage</note>, and even if the "motivating cause" for which it was given (such as the belief they were a relative) did not exist, the pious cause itself for which it was given (namely, that the person was joined in marriage by that gift) did exist, which is a pious thing. This is held in the Digest and the *Partidas*. We can further support this because the gift was given for an "onerous cause" <note>a legal exchange involving a burden or obligation</note> in relation to the other spouse,

<column-break/>

from whom it cannot be taken away, nor from the children born of that marriage, when that spouse was not aware that the gift was moved by that false reason. For in this case, the spouse is not considered to accept it under any hidden condition, but simply and absolutely; nor, if the giver had expressed that condition, would the other spouse have accepted it. Therefore, in comparison to this spouse—in whose order the giving is not free but burdensome—one should not care about what motivating reason it was given for. Rather, the one who gave it ought to have looked out for themselves to see whether the reason they were led to give was true or not. For just as if that same person, for the same motivating reason, gave money to buy something for that woman, the seller of the thing is not bound to restore that money to the giver, even if it later became clear that the reason for giving was false; so it is in this proposal.

However, although this is so, I nevertheless think that if we are discussing the woman to whom it was given as a dowry and who later remained a widow, especially without children from that marriage, those laws are based on a **presumption** that the giver (in that pious cause of dowry and marriage) did not have a "habitual intent" that if the other reason (which motivated the gift) were not true, the gift would be void. Instead, the gift would remain valid, even if perhaps they would not have given it had they known the reason was false before the gift; especially since the laws, in doubtful matters, lean in favor of a pious cause and marriage.

Thus, in Disputation 209, we said that many other laws (which we cited there and which define certain final dispositions made for a similar cause) remain valid based on presumption. In the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the internal moral judgment of the individual before God</note>, however, as we said in the same place, these things are to be judged according to the rules handed down there and in the following disputation. Indeed, even in the **external court** <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public legal system</note>, when it is clear from obvious clues that the opposite of what the civil law presumes is true, the same must undoubtedly be said in this proposal. For this whole matter, both in conscience and in the external court, must be attended to according to the doctrine handed down in those two disputations, even if in doubt one should lean toward and judge according to the presumption of civil law. 

For what if someone had lied, saying they were the son of someone who had been absent from his father’s house for a long time? And by that lie and deceit, he had obtained from the deceived father a marriage to some rich and noble woman, with the father giving many thousands of gold coins for those nuptials? Surely, if the fraud were discovered later, and that motivating reason for giving were found to be entirely false, wouldn't those many thousands of gold coins be snatched from his power, even in the external court? And this despite the loss and detriment to his wife and the children born of that marriage—all of which would have happened through the deceit and fault of that man, who should be severely punished for that reason. Certainly, that would be the case. The cited laws, truly, are only to be understood when someone has deceived themselves by some motivating reason they believed to be true, but not when...

Molina contrasts civil law's preference for maintaining marriages with the moral requirements of the "court of conscience" in cases of active fraud.</summary>

It focuses on specific scenarios: payments made for marriages that did not occur, the reimbursement for raising abandoned children, and debts paid by someone who mistakenly believed they were an heir.</meta>

...and by the fraud of the one who had accepted that marriage, he had been deceived. These things are to be understood when there are no clear indications to the contrary, and a pious cause for the marriage having been established, they show that the giver was in a habitual state of mind when he gave it, such that he would wish the gift to be void if the motivating cause were false. Certainly, if Julianus (from whom the law *cum is* is cited) had intended otherwise, his opinion would not stand. But he sufficiently implies that he speaks only from a presumption when circumstances are not present to show the contrary. This is based on the reason he gave: namely, once the false opinion is removed, the cause of piety remains, from which a repayment cannot be sought. In this place, observe that this matter pertains not so much to the recovery of what is not owed, but rather to the recovery of something given for a specific cause, when that cause does not exist. <note>original: "condictionem dati ob causam, causa non subsistente"; a legal claim used when someone gives something for a future purpose, like a dowry, but that purpose never happens.</note>

<margin>2</margin> In Disputation 554, it was said that when **alimony** <note>original: "alimenta"; here referring to the basic costs of food, clothing, and shelter</note> is provided to someone for free out of regard for God and piety, it cannot later be reclaimed for its value through an "action for business managed." <note>original: "actione negotiorum gestorum"; a legal claim used to recover expenses incurred while looking after someone else’s interests without being asked.</note> Read the section in the Code *on marriages*, which states that if a father has abandoned his daughter and another has raised her and provided her maintenance out of piety, and later wishes to join her in marriage with his own son, but the girl’s father refuses, the nurturer can demand from him the value of the maintenance provided to the daughter. Law 3, title 14, Part 5 of the *Siete Partidas* <note>The famous 13th-century Spanish legal code</note> establishes this same thing, without making any mention of whether she was abandoned by her father. It also establishes this whether the one who raised her wants to marry her himself, or wants to join her with one of his sons. Likewise, it establishes that if the girl's father, or the girl herself, refuses, the nurturer can demand the value of that maintenance from the one who refused. Gregory Lopez <note>A prominent 16th-century commentator on Spanish law</note>, in that same place, makes an exception: unless the nurturer wants to marry her himself and is of a very different age than her, so that the marriage would not be at all beneficial for the girl. For in that case, by refusing, she or her father would not incur the penalty for ingratitude. Truly, this provision should not be extended further, nor does it have any more place than what has been defined by law. And perhaps that law is not equitable and should be revoked: both because of the **freedom of marriage**, and also because there is no fault in a woman not wanting the nurturer or his son as a husband. Therefore, she (or her father) cannot justly be punished by being forced to pay for what had once been given for free out of regard for God and piety, and which in reality was not owed.

<margin>3</margin> If a <term>† good-faith possessor</term> <note>original: "possessor bonæ fidei"; someone who holds property believing they are the rightful owner, even if they are not.</note> of some inheritance—because they believed it was left to them by a will or belonged to them through intestacy <note>dying without a legal will</note>, even though someone else was the legitimate heir—paid certain debts to the creditors of the deceased while possessing it in good faith, a distinction must be made. Either they paid those debts from their own funds in the name of the inheritance and in place of the deceased (which is presumed in case of doubt, as Bartolus and others whom Gregory Lopez cites and follows affirm, even though Jason disagrees); or they paid them in their own name as if they were the heir of the deceased, to whom it therefore fell to pay them. If they paid in the name of the inheritance and in place of the deceased, and not in their own name, then they cannot reclaim it from the creditors to whom it was paid; and by that very act, the legitimate successor to the inheritance remains free from that debt. However, the possessor can keep from the inheritance as much as they paid from their own funds in the name and place of the heir; or they can reclaim it from the legitimate

<column-break/>

successor through an "action for business managed," according to the law *qui utiliter* in the Digest regarding the management of affairs. These points are found in the law *de hereditate* in the Code, and Law 36, title 14, Part 5. If, however, they paid those debts in their own name as the heir, then—because they were not truly the heir and did not owe it, but paid the creditors of the deceased led by an error—they can reclaim those payments from the creditors to whom they were paid through a <term>recovery of payment not owed</term> <note>original: "condictione indebiti"</note>, or even from the legitimate successor through an "action for business managed," because the successor truly owed those debts by reason of the inheritance. These points are held in the law *si poena*, section 1, together with the gloss there, and in the laws *quae a patre* and *si quid possessor*. These are the commonly accepted views.

<margin>4</margin> When <term>† anything is reclaimed through the recovery of a payment not owed</term>, then, if the person who received it was always a good-faith possessor, they are bound to return it along with all the **fruits** <note>original: "fructibus"; profits or products generated by an asset, such as rent, interest, or crops.</note> gathered from it, after deducting expenses. This even includes the offspring of female slaves, if the slaves are being reclaimed. But if the thing or the fruits no longer exist, the receiver is bound to return only as much as they have become "more enriched" <note>original: "locupletior"; a legal concept meaning the person only pays back the actual benefit they retained.</note> by the thing and its fruits. For that reason, if they consumed the thing or the fruits, they are only bound to return what they spent less of from their other goods because of it. By the same logic, if they sold the thing or the fruits, they are bound to return the price. They are not held to the choice of returning the sold thing even if it still exists, nor can the one reclaiming it take it back from the buyer or the final possessor. This is because the one who possessed and sold it in good faith is held liable for **eviction** <note>original: "evictione"; a seller's legal responsibility to a buyer if the item sold is later reclaimed by a third party with a better title.</note>, and thus would suffer a loss through no fault of their own. Hence the laws, especially Law 37 to be cited, establish that the one from whom the thing is reclaimed is bound to return the price to the claimant, but they do not grant the right to reclaim that thing from the buyer. This is found at the end of the law *idem est*, and Law 37 of Part 5. However, when the person who received the unowed payment did so in bad faith, knowing it was not owed to them—or, even if they received it in good faith initially, they later consumed, sold, or otherwise disposed of it in bad faith—they are bound to restore it. This includes the fruits which they could have reasonably gathered after they became a bad-faith possessor but failed to gather through negligence. The one reclaiming it can take it back from the power of whoever it is found with, to whom the seller will then be liable for eviction. And finally, they will be held to whatever a person who took the thing by theft is held to, except for the criminal penalty. For although this person is not a thief (unless they pretended to be a creditor, as the addition to the final gloss of the law *indebiti* notes with Bartolus), they are nonetheless equated to a thief regarding the restoration of the thing and the fruits, even if they did not become "more enriched" by it. This is because that is common to a thief and any other bad-faith possessor. These points are clear enough in themselves and are partly found and partly gathered from the laws *in summa* and Law 37.
Read the law *in summa*, section *sed si servum*, and Law 38, title 14, Part 5. According to that, it is established that if someone has paid another a slave who was not at all owed...

<meta>This page continues Molina’s discussion on the recovery of payments made in error. Having previously discussed payments for non-existent marriages and the support of children, he now addresses the legal consequences when a slave given as payment is subsequently freed by the recipient, and then transitions into a complex discussion of "alternative obligations" (where a debtor owes one of two things).</meta>

...whom the person paying could therefore reclaim. If the person who received the slave has since performed a **manumission** <note>The legal act of a master freeing a slave.</note>, that manumission is considered valid. If, however, the manumission was performed in bad faith, the one who freed the slave is held liable for the slave's value. But if it was done in good faith, they are held to nothing more than surrendering to the true owner all the rights of a **patron** <note>A former master who retained certain legal rights and claims over a freed slave.</note> which they acquired over the slave by reason of the freeing. Truly, such an arrangement seems unjust to me, insofar as it holds the manumission to be valid—whether done in good or bad faith—when the slave belonged to someone else and the ownership truly remained with the person who made the mistaken payment. I believe we should not follow that ruling or the opinion of the **jurist** <term>iurisconsulti; an expert in Roman law</term> Paul—specifically the section beginning "He who clearly erred"—which defines the matter to the contrary. Instead, we should follow the nature of the thing itself and **natural law** <note>Universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, often contrasted with man-made "civil law."</note>. In this matter, one should stand more with the judgment of the Theologians than with that of that pagan moral philosopher, who provided no reasoning whatsoever for his erroneous definition.

In order for the following difficulty to be more easily cleared up, we must first explain what is considered "owed" or what falls under an obligation when things are owed **alternatively** (as the legal experts call it) or **disjunctively** (as the logicians, philosophers, and theologians call it). For example, if a legacy leaves someone "Stichus or Pamphilus" <note>Stichus and Pamphilus were standard placeholder names used in Roman legal examples, similar to "John Doe."</note>, or if the legacy is "Pamphilus or a hundred coins," or if by contract one is owed "a horse or eighty coins," or other similar things under a choice: we must ask what is actually owed and what falls under such debts and obligations. Likewise, it must be explained what falls under an obligation when something is owed **in general** (as the legal experts say) or **in species** but "undetermined as an individual" (as the theologians say). For instance, when a horse is owed indefinitely (not a specific individual horse), or a certain amount of wheat, oil, or wine is owed, we must ask what falls under those debts and obligations.

<margin>1</margin>
Regarding the first of these, many have written long disputes, including Lassarte in *On the Tenth of a Sale*, chapter 7, from number 9. Setting aside other opinions, including Lassarte’s opinion (which I least approve of), it must be said that both of those things are owed or fall under the obligation, but they do so "disjunctively." This is a "diminishing term," because both are not owed **conjunctively** <note>original: "copulatiue"; meaning both things must be delivered together.</note> and simply, but rather "either one" or "both," with this added diminishing condition: disjunctively or alternatively. As the legal experts say, the choice lies either with the debtor (which of them he wishes to pay) or with the creditor (which he wishes to demand), depending on to whom the choice was granted or assigned. When nothing was said to indicate who has the choice, it belongs to the debtor. Since he owes either one or the other disjunctively, by paying whichever one he chooses, he has satisfied the debt according to the proper and strict meaning of the language, and is therefore freed from the obligation. However, when the choice is granted to the creditor, then the debtor does not satisfy the debt unless he pays what the creditor has chosen or permitted. Furthermore, by paying the one thing the creditor chose, he is freed from that alternative obligation which encompassed both things under a disjunction at the creditor's choice. Moreover, in such alternative debts and obligations, that which is thus owed alternatively

<column-break/>

is owed purely and absolutely, and not under a condition. This is true even if the choice of which item will satisfy the debt and free the debtor from the obligation undoubtedly belongs to the debtor (and sometimes to the creditor, as explained). Because in such obligations, it is not just one item—determined specifically—that is owed from that choice, but rather both, yet under a disjunction based on the choice of the creditor or debtor. In the manner explained—namely, that a "disjunctive" is owed, or both parts are owed under a disjunction—certain laws rightly affirm that "both" are owed; yet they mean "under a disjunction." This does not mean there are two obligations for different objects, but only one obligation for that disjunction, or for both parts under a disjunction. Because both are not owed "conjunctively" (and thus, simply speaking, both are not owed, but only with that diminishing addition of the disjunction), other laws rightly deny that "both" are owed, and affirm that only "one" is owed. However, they mean this "indeterminately," which is to say that either one is owed, or both are owed under a disjunction. In this way, the laws—which otherwise seem contrary to one another—are easily reconciled. These things are said based on the proper and strict meaning of the words, drawn from the very principles and heart of **logic** <note>original: "dialectice"; the art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logic.</note>. Since legal experts are not at all skilled in this, it is no wonder if they are blind in the middle of the light and turn toward various strange and far from true opinions, erring frequently in definitions that depend on these principles.

Regarding the second point, in true logic, an "infinite proposition"—a debt or obligation for an "infinite thing" (that is, a thing in its class or "species," but undetermined as an individual, or a thing "in its genus" as the legal experts call it)—is equivalent to an "alternative proposition." It is a proposition concerning a "disjunctive extreme," containing under a disjunction all individuals of that species, not only present ones but also future and possible ones, provided they are such that the debt or obligation can be satisfied by any one of them by reason of the alternative. I say this because when something is owed "indefinitely," the debt is not satisfied by paying something low and worthless of that species, even if the choice is with the debtor; rather, at least something of **average quality** <note>original: "mediocre"; in a legal sense, this means a standard or mid-grade quality, rather than the very best or very worst.</note> must be paid, unless something else was agreed upon in the contract. Likewise, when wheat, wine, or something similar that consists of weight, number, or measure is given as a loan, although the debt is satisfied by returning the same amount of the same species, they must nevertheless be of equal goodness to the thing given in the loan; otherwise, the debt is not satisfied. Therefore, the obligation to pay a horse indefinitely, a sheep, or so many measures of wheat—whether it arises from a legacy, a contract, or elsewhere—is equivalent to this alternative: "you shall pay either this horse, or that one, or any other from the number of those possible under the species of horse," provided it is at least of average quality. The same applies to the obligation to pay a sheep indefinitely, or so many measures of wheat. The result is that in an obligation to pay a thing of a certain species indefinitely, all individuals of that species that are not worthless or low-quality fall under the obligation, yet under a disjunction in the manner explained. This is correctly affirmed by Antonio Gómez in the second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 11, number 49, and by Charles Dumoulin <note>A French jurist often referred to by his Latinized name, Carolus Molinaeus.</note> as cited by Lassarte; and falsely [here...]

<meta>This page continues Molina’s legal analysis of alternative obligations—situations where a debtor is bound to provide one of several possible things. Having previously discussed the recovery of mistaken payments, he now examines whether the specific item chosen for payment is retroactively considered the "sole" object of the debt and the tax implications thereof.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 5, Section 69.

Let there be other opinions, which Antonio Gómez and Lassarte <note>Antonio Gómez (1501–1572) and Iñigo Lasso de Oropesa (Lassarte) were prominent Spanish jurists who commented on Roman and Castilian law.</note> cite in the places mentioned above. Among these, the common opinion held by Bartolus is entirely false, as is the extent to which Lassarte embraces it: namely, that only the specific individual item that was paid falls under the obligation, and that the debtor is subsequently freed from the debt because, once payment is made, it is pulled back by a **legal fiction** <term>fictio iuris; a legal assumption that something is true even if it may not be, to achieve an equitable result</term> so that the contract is treated as if only that item had been in the obligation from the start.

Certainly, this opinion is not gathered from the law "When an uncertain" in the **Digest** <note>original: "l. cum incertus, ff. de leg. 1"; refers to the Digest of Justinian, Book 30, Title 1, Law 75.</note>, where Papinian, following Neratius, says: "When an uncertain slave was bequeathed to you, the heir delivered the slave Stichus to his own servant. Neratius replied that if he delivered him by the will of the master, or if the master later ratified this, he is freed just as if Stichus had been the one bequeathed." These are his words. From these words, it is not concluded that only Stichus, who was paid, was in the obligation once the payment accepted by the legatee followed; rather, it concludes only that the heir is freed from the obligation by which he was held to the legatee just as if Stichus alone had been bequeathed. Thus, he is freed just as if Stichus alone had been in the obligation. 

On the contrary, the opposite is gathered from this: just as Stichus alone was not bequeathed, but rather he was bequeathed under a **disjunction** <note>An "either-or" choice (e.g., Slave A or Slave B).</note> with other slaves who could be paid indifferently by the heir, so too he was not alone in that obligation, but was there with the others under a disjunction. However, by the very fact that he was paid in particular and accepted by the legatee—at least as an average slave among the group—the heir was freed from the legacy and from that indefinite obligation of a slave, just as if it were not an indefinite obligation, but one for Stichus specifically; which is most true.

From what has been said, you will easily understand that when a disjunction was in the obligation and debt, or something was owed indefinitely, by paying something from that disjunction or one of those indefinite items, it is not as if one thing is paid for another (as if the thing paid were not contained in the obligation). Rather, the thing paid is contained under the obligation. Consequently, that long dispute of Lassarte (mentioned above) ceases: whether from such a payment the **alcabala** <term>a heavy Spanish sales tax</term> is owed in Castile, or the **sisa** <term>a Portuguese excise tax on food and goods</term> is owed in Portugal. Since nothing different is paid from what was contained in the obligation and debt, but rather the obligation and debt are dissolved by the payment of that which was owed, certainly that tax is not owed from that payment, as Lassarte himself rightly affirms, even if he does not agree with us regarding the nature of the obligation.

Observe this also with Antonio Gómez in the place cited above: although the debtor remains entirely free from the debt if all parts of the disjunction perish without the debtor’s fault (such as the slaves Stichus and Pamphilus), because everything contained under that obligation has perished and the debtor was held to nothing else. However, in that case, all possible individual items under a certain **species** <note>In legal terms, a "species" is a specific, unique item, while a "genus" is a general category of goods.</note> cannot perish, because it belongs to Divine Providence to have so disposed and preserved the world that no species should perish entirely. From this it follows that jurists rightly say that the **category never perishes** <note>original: "genus non perire"; a legal maxim meaning that if you owe a general thing (like "a horse") rather than a specific one (like "this horse"), you are not freed from the debt if one horse dies, as you can find another.</note>, and the destruction of individuals never frees anyone from an obligation of a category, or one that is indeterminate as to the individual.

These things being so established: when someone was a debtor by disjunction (such as for Stichus or Pamphilus, or for Stichus or eighty coins) such that the choice was with the debtor as to which he wished to pay, if by error he 

<column-break/>

pays both, then, if both survive, he can **reclaim** <term>condicere; to bring a legal action for the return of something</term> whichever of them he prefers as a **payment not owed** <term>indebitum; something paid by mistake that was not actually due</term>. Just as the choice was his as to which he preferred to pay, so the choice should be his as to which he wishes to recover. For in truth, he paid the one he prefers to recover in addition to what he was bound to pay, and therefore he can reclaim it as not owed. Thus, against Ulpian, Marcellus, and Celsus (who granted the choice to the creditor after payment), Justinian defined the matter with Papinian and Julian in the law "If anyone a slave" <note>Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 5, Law 10.</note>, quite appropriately to the nature of the thing.

Julian, in the law "When he" at the beginning <note>Digest 12.6.32.</note>, says: if someone owes two things under a disjunction in the manner explained, and by error, believing himself to owe both cumulatively, pays both—then, whether both have perished or only one, he can reclaim nothing, because the one that remains, remains as the payment. The same is found in Law 39, Title 14, Partida 5 <note>Reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the famous 13th-century Spanish law code.</note>. However, this definition is very doubtful to me. On the contrary, I believe it does not reach the true nature of the matter, but rather arose from that other false opinion: that after both things are paid by error, the choice belongs to the creditor as to which he wishes to retain as payment. Justinian later defined the opposite of this, along with Papinian and that same Julian.

I am led to this because he who paid both things certainly paid more than he owed. He should be able to reclaim whichever of those two he wishes, since the choice is his—both before the payment (as to which he wishes to pay) and after the payment (as to which he wishes to recover), as Justinian defined with Papinian, fittingly to the nature of the thing. Therefore, when the creditor has enjoyed the fruits of the other thing that perished during the entire time it existed, and truly received it as payment, it follows indeed that the debtor not only can recover the other one which survives, but can even recover its fruits, or the value of its use. For example, if it is a slave, he can recover the value of that slave's labor for the entire time the creditor enjoyed it. 

And certainly, even standing by that false opinion of Julian—that the creditor can retain the thing that survives as payment—it should not be doubted that he is bound to restore at least all the fruits and profits he perceived from the thing that perished; for he has been satisfied for everything owed to him by the other thing which survives. Certainly, when a creditor in **bad faith** <note>Knowing that he was not legally entitled to what he was receiving.</note> accepted the payment of both things, knowing that only one (whichever the debtor chose) was owed to him, and he enjoyed both things until one of them perished, there is no doubt that the debtor can recover the one that remains. For besides the fact that he paid it beyond what he owed—on which grounds the debtor could recover it as an undue payment even if the creditor had accepted both in **good faith**—no equity allows that possessor in bad faith to enjoy both things and finally possess the one that did not perish as payment, ultimately reporting a profit from his own bad faith at such a loss to the debtor, who paid out of ignorance, when he was bound to pay only one (whichever he preferred). Therefore, both in conscience and in the external court, I believe one should not stand by that definition of Julian in the law "When someone"...
