<meta>This page continues Molina’s critique of Roman legal interpretations regarding the recovery of mistaken payments (the *condictio indebiti*). He specifically focuses on "alternative obligations," where a debtor owes one of two things but pays a specific one by mistake. He argues that natural justice should allow the debtor to correct such an error, contrary to some strict interpretations by ancient jurists like Celsus.</meta>

# Ludovico Molina On Contracts
### Page 850

...at the beginning of the Digest <note>original: "ff."; a standard abbreviation for the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Justinian's civil law corpus.</note> regarding the recovery of a payment not owed, and in Law 39, which was passed in accordance with that other law. For these laws do not intend to hand down positive law <term>ius positivum; man-made laws enacted by a government, as opposed to natural law</term> against the very nature of the matter; nor, if they did so intend, would they be just laws. Rather, they only intend to define what the nature of the matter holds: in explaining this clearly, both laws erred, as is evident from what has been said.

The jurist Julian, in the law "When he who," in the final section, rightly and appropriately to the nature of the matter, defines that if someone who was an indefinite debtor—either for two things as a choice or for an unspecified item—pays a specific individual thing by error, or pays one part of the choice specifically because he believed he was bound only to that, he can reclaim that thing. This is because it was not owed in that specific detail. He may then pay the other part of the choice, or another average individual item of the same kind, to which alone he was bound according to his own option. This is clear from the nature of alternative and indefinite obligations, as Lassarte <note>Iñigo Lasso de Oropesa (Lassarte), a 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> affirms in chapter 7, number 26. If, however, someone who is knowing and prudent pays something specifically, aware that he is not bound to it in that specific way, then he cannot later reclaim what he paid to offer something else which he could have legitimately paid before that payment. The reason is that through that payment, made with such knowledge, he chose what he would pay; and once a choice is made among things that are within someone's power to pay as an alternative, it is not thereafter in his power to retract it. However, when it is not certain in the external court <term>exteriori foro; the public legal system, as opposed to the "court of conscience"</term> whether someone paid something specific by error, he is presumed to have chosen it; and therefore, in that court, he is not permitted to retract the choice and the payment in that event.

Against Julian's definition, another definition by Celsus <note>Publius Iuventius Celsus, an influential Roman jurist of the 2nd century AD.</note> stands in strong opposition in the law "If he to whom," in the Digest regarding legacies. There, Celsus says: "If a slave, either Stichus or Pamphilus <note>Stichus and Pamphilus are traditional placeholder names used for slaves in Roman legal examples, much like 'John Doe' today.</note>, is bequeathed to someone according to his own preference, and by error, thinking only Stichus was bequeathed to him, he seeks and receives him, he cannot later sue for Pamphilus by offering Stichus back." Similarly, if an heir is ordered to deliver either Stichus or Pamphilus, whichever the heir prefers, and by error he pays Stichus thinking he was ordered to deliver only him, he cannot reclaim him by offering Pamphilus. Various authors offer various interpretations of this law, including Lassarte, which I certainly do not approve of. I believe it should be said that Celsus's definition is either the same as, or connected to, that other definition of his which Justinian, along with Papinian, rejected in the law "If anyone a slave" in the Code <note>original: "C. de condict. indeb."; refers to the *Codex Justinianus*.</note> regarding the recovery of a payment not owed. Therefore, it is not to be cared for, because it defines that in the first instance, that legatee sought and received less by error than was civilly and naturally owed to him; thus he can reclaim what was owed to him by offering Stichus and seeking Pamphilus. In the latter instance, the heir paid more by error than he owed civilly and naturally, and for that reason, he can reclaim Stichus by offering Pamphilus. Therefore, we should not approve of what Lassarte says above—namely, that although Celsus's definition has no place in other legacies, it still holds in pious legacies <term>legatis pijs; bequests left for religious or charitable purposes</term>. This is partly because the nature of the matter holds the contrary, and therefore

<column-break/>

it is not to be admitted even in pious legacies; and also because the first part of his definition would be contrary to the favor shown to such legacies, for according to it, the legacy would be satisfied by paying him less than was otherwise owed.

6. Whenever someone, thinking they are bound to perform something for someone else, performs a different service for them, and it is later found that they were not bound to it, they can reclaim the valuation of what they did—specifically, the amount the recipient would have had to pay another person to perform that same work. See the law "If not the sum," section "the freedman," toward the end, in the Digest; and Law 40, Title 14, Part 5 <note>referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Castilian statutory code.</note>.

7. If any items from a deceased person's estate are paid to some people by error—whether by the executor of the will, or by someone who was believed to be the heir but was not truly the heir, or even by a true heir (for instance, if he paid legacies and later debts of the deceased appeared which had to be paid from those funds)—then, if it later becomes clearly established to whom those items belong as the legitimate successor, that person may reclaim them as things paid when not owed, even if they did not pay them themselves but another did. For that makes no difference. If, however, they were received and consumed in good faith, then the receiver is only held liable to the extent that they were made wealthier by those goods, according to what was said above. This is held in the Digest, Law 2, Section 1, and the three following laws, as well as the *Siete Partidas*, Law 42, Title 14, Part 5.

<margin>Decision on a Doubt</margin>
The question is: if someone renounces the right to reclaim a mistaken payment, or the right to reclaim something given for a cause that did not follow, and renounces all help of the laws, can they nevertheless reclaim it if they later discover they paid what was not owed? It should be answered, according to Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors (which Covarrubias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish canonist and jurist.</note>, Gutierrez, and Padilla cite and follow), that they can reclaim it. The reason is that it must be presumed that no one, believing they are paying a debt, would pay it and simultaneously renounce the right to reclaim it if it were not owed; for otherwise, that would be a gift, not a payment of a debt. Furthermore, it must be presumed that such a renunciation was made out of a belief that it was truly owed, or out of lightheartedness, or ignorance, or rather that the renunciation was added by the custom of the notaries without the consent or awareness of the person renouncing. If, however, someone were to say they renounce the right to reclaim a mistaken payment because, in the event it turns out they did not owe it, they intend to give it as a gift, then there would be no room for reclaiming the payment.

<margin>Decision on a Doubt</margin>
8. A greater doubt arises: if the person paying in the first instance renounces the right to reclaim the mistaken payment with an oath, can they still reclaim it? Gutierrez, cited above, affirms this along with others. I would make a distinction. If the renunciation was made with some knowledge of the matter, for whatever reason the one swearing was led to renounce and confirm it with an oath—purely because they entirely believed they owed it, or out of lightheartedness—then I judge they cannot reclaim it, unless they first seek and obtain a relaxation of the oath <term>relaxatione iuramentis; a formal release from a religious or legal vow</term>. This can and should be granted when the person renouncing did not intend to donate what was not owed. I am moved to this because there was sufficient consent for the oath to be binding, since it concerns a matter that is not illicit on the part of the one swearing. If, however, the renunciation was not made with any notice of it...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "renun-", indicating the next page continues the discussion on renunciations.</meta>

<summary>Molina discusses the legal right to reclaim payments made by mistake, specifically in complex cases involving choices between two items or inheritances. He argues that even if a person renounces their right to reclaim a payment, they may still do so if the renunciation was made under the false belief that the debt was genuine.</summary>

## Given for a cause, when the cause did not follow: to what extent it must be restored. And regarding things received for a shameful cause.

### D I S P V T A T I O N  DLXX.

->S V M M A R Y.<-

1. When the recovery of something given for a purpose <note>original: "Condictio ob causam"</note> takes place.
2. Which action or remedy is available if something is given so that another thing might be done or given, and it is not fulfilled.
3. Whether and when travel expenses given for a journey can be reclaimed.
4. When an action for fraud <note>original: "Actio de dolo"</note> for an appraisal is available against an irreparable act, and when for payment.
5. What remedy is available if something is given to someone to accomplish a task, and it was not done.

<margin>1</margin>When a certain debt or obligation is released to someone because of something <gloss>on the basis of doing something here</gloss> or because they promised to give something in return, then, if the person who promised the recompense does not fulfill it, the person who released the debt or obligation has an option. They may either compel the person through an "action in prescribed words" <term>actio praescriptis verbis; a flexible legal remedy used for contracts that did not fit into standard categories like "sale" or "hire"</term> to pay or do what was promised, or they may demand the original debt or obligation back through a "recovery for a cause not followed" <term>condictio causa data causa non secuta; a legal claim to get back what was given if the reason for giving it failed</term>, as if it were a release given for a purpose where the purpose did not materialize. This is found in Law "if anyone accepted" <note>original: "l. si quis acceptum tulerit"</note> and Law "if a woman" <note>original: "l. si mulier"</note> in the Digest under the title *on recovery of a cause given*, joined with the Law "on account of that cause" in the title *on prescribed words*. Both are also found in Law 41, Title 14, of the Fifth Partida <note>The *Siete Partidas* was a major 13th-century Spanish statutory code.</note>. On this point, the jurist Gregorio López, in his second gloss, notes an exception following Bartolus: when an action, once released, is of such a nature that it cannot be revived by the agreement or consent of the parties—such as a complaint against an undutiful will or an action for injuries—then the person who released such an action for a promised benefit can only sue using the "action in prescribed words" to ensure the promise is fulfilled.

<margin>2</margin>When something is given so that something else might be done or given, such that it is neither a purchase and sale, nor a lease and hire, but an "unnamed contract" <term>contractus innominatus; a contract that does not have a specific Roman legal name but is binding because one side has performed</term>, according to what was said in Disputation 253 and following; even if money is given for an act that is not "hired"—for instance, if money is given so that a slave may be manumitted (freed), which is also called an unnamed contract—as found in Law "natural," in the section "he says she gives" <note>original: "l. naturalis . §. ait eam do."</note> in the title *on prescribed words* and other laws. When, I say, something is given so that another thing may be done or given, if this other thing is not fulfilled, the person who gave it has an action either to compel the other to perform or provide what was promised (if the matter can still be carried out), or, if it can no longer be carried out, or even if it can but the giver prefers otherwise, they have the right to a recovery or reclaiming of what was given, as something given for a purpose where the cause did not follow. Or, if they prefer,

<column-break/>

they may sue for "interest" <note>In legal terms, "interest" refers to the financial difference between the person's current position and where they would have been had the contract been fulfilled.</note>, so that they are satisfied to the extent of their interest in having the work completed. This is found in Law "natural," section "but when he gives" <note>original: "l. naturalis. §. at cũ do."</note> in the title *on prescribed words*; Law "I have given," section "the same" <note>original: "l. dedi. §. idẽ."</note> in the title *on recovery of a cause given*; Law "if a free man" <note>original: "l. si liber"</note> in the Code under the same title; and in the Fifth Partida, Law 5, Title 6, and Law 43, Title 14. These laws seem to teach that one can reclaim what was given *and* additionally sue for interest; however, Gregorio López rightly explains that this should be interpreted so as not to differ from other laws—a matter we also discussed in Disputation 255 regarding unnamed contracts. Read what was said there. However, when something is *done* so that something else might be done under an unnamed contract of the type "I do so that you may do" <note>original: "facio vt facias"</note>, then an action would only be available to compel the other party to fulfill their side of the contract, or for interest; this is because a "deed" <note>An act already performed, as opposed to a physical object.</note> cannot be recovered or reclaimed in the same way property can.

<margin>3</margin>However, when someone hands something over to another for expenses to prepare for a journey upon which they decided to send them, having reached an agreement on that point or something else; yet not by hiring them for a wage (for then it would be a contract of hiring and leasing, where there would be no room for "repentance" <term>poenitentia; the legal right to withdraw from a contract before performance has begun</term> and the rules of that contract would apply); but rather by an unnamed contract, where they handed something to someone who was not accustomed to hiring themselves out for such a thing. If it is the giver's fault that the other does not carry it out—because the giver "repented" or changed their mind, as one is permitted to do in civil law while the matter is still "whole" <note>i.e., before the other party has started performing.</note> such that the other has spent nothing of their own and suffers no loss—even though the person who accepted the money cannot change their mind, it is always permissible for the giver to withdraw from the agreement in the courts of civil law, canon law, and conscience. This is provided they compensate the other for any damages. As custom testifies, there seems to be a "tacit law" in such agreements that the giver may withdraw, provided they pay for the other's labor and effort already applied, and for any damages that might follow (perhaps because the person gave up another business or useful agreement for this one). If, I say, it is the giver's fault that the task is not executed because they changed their mind, or it is due to some intervening "fortuitous event" <term>casus fortuitus; an accident or 'act of God' like a sudden illness</term> that prevented the recipient from carrying it out, then the person who gave the money or thing cannot reclaim what was legitimately spent, even if the purpose for which it was given did not follow. Rather, they are bound to pay the other an appraisal of their labor and industry already applied. However, the giver may reclaim anything that was bought with the money they gave (if it still exists) and whatever part of the money or thing has not yet been spent. But if the task is not carried out due to the change of mind or wickedness of the *recipient*, then the giver can compel them to complete the work or reclaim the payment...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal rights to recover payments or property when a contract's purpose is not fulfilled, specifically within the framework of "innominate contracts." He distinguishes between cases where a party changes their mind in good faith versus when non-performance is due to negligence or malice.</summary>

[Page 852]

**Ludovico Molina on Contracts**

...will return everything he gave, as if given for a cause where the cause did not follow due to the fault of the other party; or he will be able to compel them to pay interest according to what was said shortly before regarding a similar outcome. This is held in the law *si pecunia* in the beginning, along with the glosses there, in the Digest *on the recovery of a thing given for a cause* <note>original: "ff. de condict. caus. data"</note>, and Law 44, Title 14, Part 5, along with what Gregorio López notes there.

<margin>4</margin>
When someone does something so that something may be given to them, in the contract "I do that you may give" <note>original: "facio vt des"</note>, especially if the act performed is irreparable—such as if someone sets a slave free <term>manumission; the legal act of releasing a slave from bondage</term> so that something may be given to them—and afterward that thing is not given: in such a case, the manumission remains valid out of favor for liberty, even if the contract is not fulfilled by the other party. Then, an action for fraud <note>original: "actio de dolo"</note> is available against the one not standing by the contract, so that they may pay the appraised value of the slave, and in addition pay for the damages resulting from the fact that they did not pay at the proper time what was promised in compensation for the freeing of the slave. The person who fulfilled their part of the contract is permitted to swear an oath in court as to how much they value the slave and the resulting damages from the delay, although this is subject to the judge’s prior assessment. In other types of acts, however, an action for fraud is granted to compel the other to pay what was promised and the resulting damages for not paying at the proper time. This is held in the law *naturalis*, section *quod si faciam*, in the Digest *on the action in prescribed words* <note>original: "ff. de præscrip. verb."</note>, and the law *cum proponas* in the Code *on fraud* <note>original: "C. de dolo"</note>, as well as Law 5, Title 6, and Law 45, Title 14, Part 5. These last two laws explain more expressly than the two other common laws to whom that action for fraud extends, as Gregorio López observes in the cited Law 45. In Disputation 255, we said it is difficult for legal experts to give a reason why, in the contract "I do that you may give," this action for fraud is given rather than an action in prescribed words, as in other unnamed contracts. I truly wish that all these variations and subtleties devised by pagan men <note>referring to ancient Roman jurists</note> were cut away from civil law.

<margin>5</margin>
When something is given to someone with the aim that they accomplish something, a distinction must be made. For either it is sufficiently expressed that it is given as a pact and recompense so that they accomplish it; or it is not expressed, but is only given to them as a motivating and final cause on the part of the giver, by which the recipient may be led to accomplish what the giver intends. In this way, gifts are usually sent to a woman, not as a formal pact to consent to shameful behavior, but as things by which she might be softened, affected, and disposed toward consenting. Similarly, gifts are usually sent to those with abundant money so they might be inclined to give a loan in a time of necessity, and they are sent to many others to win over their wills so that they finally accomplish what the sender intends. When something is given in the first way, and that for which it was given does not happen, it is considered given for a cause—or under the condition of a cause—for which it was given; since the cause did not follow, a recovery <term>condictio; a legal claim for the return of property or money</term> or a demand for its return is available, as held in Law 1 and throughout the title in the Digest *on the recovery of a thing given for a cause* and Law 46, Title 14, Part 5. But when something is given in the second way, because it is not given under a condition or pact of the cause that impelled the giver to give, but only in the hope that they might obtain it by that path, then, even if the final and motivating cause for which it was given does not follow, and even if the giver would not have given it had they known they would not obtain it that way, there is no place for recovery. Indeed, even if the recipient knew it was given for that end, neither

<column-break/>

in conscience nor in the external court is he bound to restore what he thus received, or to accomplish that which the gift was intended to induce. And in the external court, if the giver did not sufficiently express that they were giving as a pact and under the condition of the cause for which they were giving, it is considered given in this second way and not the first; therefore, recovery is not granted, whatever the giver may say to the contrary afterward. This is found in the law *si repetendi* in the Code *on recovery for a cause*, and the law *dedi*, section *si quis quasi*, at the end, in the Digest, as well as the cited Law 46; the statements in Disputations 88 and 108, and elsewhere often, agree.

Regarding things given and received for a shameful cause, this has been discussed extensively from Disputation 62, and especially in Disputation 94, and is dealt with from Law 47 to 54, Title 14, Part 5.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding the enforcement of contracts and debt. It specifically transitions into Disputation 57, which examines the legal conditions under which a debtor may be imprisoned and the procedural requirements for seizing assets in the kingdoms of Castile and Portugal.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 57, Section 1

...prison, until he is condemned and a sentence is pronounced by a judge. One should know that the debt must be a matter already settled by a final judgment <note>original: "in rem transeat iudicatam"</note>, or the debtor must have confessed the debt in court and been ordered to pay it. Even then, the judge does not have the power to immediately thrust him into prison. Instead, execution must first be carried out against his goods, by selling them in a public auction <term>subhastatione; a sale of goods to the highest bidder, often conducted under a spear in Roman tradition</term>. Only when it is found that he does not have sufficient assets to pay that debt should he be thrust into prison for it, provided the creditor or creditors request it from the judge, until the debt is paid in full.

Regarding how, in what order, and at what time the execution against the debtor's goods should occur after a final judgment or a court confession—according to common Roman law, Canon law, and the laws of Castile and Portugal—we have explained this extensively in Disputation 538, starting from the section "hitherto we have said" <note>original: "hactenus diximus"</note>, etc. That a debtor cannot be imprisoned for such a debt before these steps are taken is gathered from Code Law 1, *on those who can surrender their goods* <note>original: "C. qui bonis cedere poss."</note>, and Law 4, Title 15, Part 5, along with the first gloss of Gregorio López. It is stated even more expressly in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 52, in the beginning and §1. This is also supported by the Digest, Law 3, § *tutores*, at the word "chains" <note>original: "vinculis"</note>, which states that a debtor should not be thrown into chains for a debt until his poverty and inability to pay are established. This is affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which is cited and followed by Gregorio López (cited above), Covarrubias (in *Various Resolutions*, Book 2, Chapter 1, Number 2), and Antonio Gómez (in *Various Resolutions*, Volume 2, Chapter 11, Number 51). Other laws cited by Covarrubias also agree. He adds that when execution is made against the debtor's assets, if there is no one willing to buy them unless guarantors are provided to protect against legal claims <term>eviction; the loss of property due to a third party's superior legal claim</term>, the debtor is required to provide them. Otherwise, he is to be thrown into prison until the debt is fully paid from those goods or from elsewhere.

<margin>2</margin>
An exception is made to the rule provided † if the defendant is suspected of fleeing. In that case, if he does not have other sufficient assets from which the debt could be paid, then either the thing in question or another equal asset belonging to the debtor should be placed by the judge into deposit or sequestration until a sentence is delivered. Alternatively, the debtor should be compelled to provide sufficient pledges or guarantors. Otherwise, he should be thrown into chains before the sentence, provided that the judge is summarily convinced of the debt. However, if at the time the contract was made the creditor was aware of the debtor's character and his lack of assets, he must blame himself for entering the contract. In such a case, the debtor cannot be thrown into chains before a final sentence and execution against his goods, nor is he required to provide new security, whether through pledges, guarantors, or any other means. This is held in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 52 and Book 3, Title 20.

<margin>3</margin>
Another exception to the same rule † occurs if the debtor specifically bound himself to pay the creditor within a certain time, agreeing that if he did not pay, he would be thrown into chains. In that case, once the time has passed without payment, he can be immediately thrown into chains without first executing against his goods. However, the creditor cannot, by his own authority, thrust

<column-break/>

him into prison, even if the debtor had given him the power to do so. Instead, he is required to carry this out through a public official.

<margin>4</margin>
An exception exists unless † he finds the debtor in flight and no public official is present to seize him and lead him immediately to the public prison. In that case, he may seize the debtor himself and lead him immediately to the public prison. This is held in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 52, §2 and 3, for the contract must be upheld. Regarding the penalties established in this Kingdom of Castile for those who, by their own authority, seize and imprison their debtors or seize pledges from them on their own authority, see Laws 5 and 6 of Book 4 of the *New Collection*, and Laws 2 and 10, Title 17, Book 5. However, Law 1 (cited above) grants power to a creditor to seize his debtor when the debtor granted him that faculty in the contract. Law 5 (cited above) makes a creditor entirely immune if he seizes the debtor by the authority of a judge. Covarrubias notes in *Various Resolutions*, Book 2, Chapter 1, Number 1, along with others he cites, that the sanctions of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law (c. 450 BC), known for its harsh treatment of debtors</note> and other ancient laws—which allowed creditors to seize debtors and execute cruel acts upon those who did not pay on time—have been abolished.

Today, as was said in Disputation 538, according to the law of this Kingdom of Castile (Law 1 and following, especially Law 19, Title 21, Book 4 of the *New Collection*), it is decreed that not only a judgment of debt that has become final, or a confession of debt in court, but also a debt arising from a public instrument—or even a private instrument once acknowledged by the debtor in court—shall have "ready execution" <term>paratam exequutionem; a legal status allowing immediate enforcement without a full trial</term>. This execution against the debt is to be carried out immediately against his movable goods <note>personal property</note>, and in default of movables, against his immovable goods <note>real estate</note>, without needing to summon the debtor. At the same time, the debtor must provide a "security of title" <note>original: "fideiussorem de saneamiento"</note> as they call it; otherwise, the debtor may be thrown into prison at the start of the execution until he pays the debt in full, unless he is among those debtors who, by the law of this Kingdom, cannot be thrust into prison for debts. Read what was said there, in which the Spanish doctors agree. Which goods are privileged—so that execution cannot be made upon them for debts from a contract or quasi-contract, or can only be made in the absence of other goods—under both Common Law and the laws of Castile and Portugal, was explained extensively in Disputation 530.

<margin>5</margin>
Likewise, † when something is owed to the Prince or the Treasury <term>fiscus; the state or royal treasury</term>, the debtor can be thrust into prison as soon as the execution is repeated, until he pays the debt in full. This is gathered from the Digest, Law 20, *on the Julian law regarding embezzlement* <note>original: "ff. ad legem Iuliam pecul."</note>, and the Code, Law *nemo*, *on collections* <note>original: "C. de collect."</note>. It is held that if a debtor of a tax <note>original: "tributi"</note> is stubborn in his payment, he should then be sent to prison and execution made against his goods. Covarrubias (Book 2, *Var. Res.*, Chapter 1, Number 4) and Gregorio López (on this Title 15, Part 5) affirm this along with Johannes de Platea and others. It is also decreed in the Portuguese Ordinances, Book 4, Title 52, §4.

<margin>6</margin> <note>Note: The original margin label repeats "5" but follows the sequence for section 6</note>
A woman, provided † she does not live dishonestly, cannot be thrust into prison for a civil debt arising from a contract or quasi-contract, even if she is a debtor to the King's Treasury. Instead, execution is only made against her goods, if she has any. This is held in the *Authentica* or the New Law (otherwise known today as the New Law) of the Code.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of imprisonment for debt, specifically focusing on the exemptions and privileges granted to certain classes of people—women, soldiers, and the Spanish nobility—under both common Roman law and the specific statutes of the Kingdoms of Spain and Portugal.</meta>

<page-num>854</page-num>
<header>Ludovicus Molina on Contracts</header>

concerning the custody of defendants <note>original: "de cust. reor."</note> and in the authentic text, "that to none of the judges" <note>original: "vt nulli iudicum"</note>, the section "necessary" <note>original: "§. necessarium"</note>, Law 1, and the authentic text joined there, in the Code on the office of civil judges <note>original: "C. de offic. ciu. iud."</note>, and Law 1, Title 14, Part 5 of the Extraordinary Laws of Portugal, and Law 62 of Toro, which is Law 10, Title 3, Book 5 of the *New Compilation* <note>The *Nueva Recopilación*, a major 16th-century collection of Spanish laws</note>, and Law 8 of the same title, it is expressed that one cannot be cast into prison even for a debt of tribute or any other debt owed to the Prince. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the learned doctors, which Antonio Gomez follows in the cited Law 62, as does Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, Book 2, Chapter 1, Number 3, and in the chapter "although a pact" <note>original: "c. qua uis pactum"</note>, Part 2, at the beginning of Number 7.

<margin>7</margin> However, a † woman who lives publicly and dishonestly does not enjoy this privilege; this is stated in the cited Law 62, and Antonio Gomez says the same thing, following Baldus, based on common law and the argument of the final section in the authentic text on restitution and those who give birth in the eleventh month, although that is not sufficiently gathered from there. Furthermore, when a woman's debt arises from a crime <note>original: "ex delicto"</note>, the cited Law 62 expressly states that a woman can be cast into prison for that reason. If Gutierrez speaks concerning the same law of Castile in *On the Confirmation of Rights*, Chapter 16, Part 1, Number 35, where he equates a woman in that regard to the nobleman whom they call an <term>hidalgo; a member of the lower Spanish nobility who enjoyed certain legal exemptions</term> in that Kingdom (of whom we will speak shortly), the matter contains no doubt, nor was there any reason for him to leave that matter to the judgment of the wiser to be corrected. But if he speaks according to common law, the cited laws clearly intend that a woman cannot be cast into prison even for a debt arising from a crime; and so Villalobos affirms, following Baldus, in the *Antinomia* under the letter M.

<margin>Question</margin> There is a doubt: if a woman is the guardian <note>original: "tutrix, aut curatrix"</note> of her children or grandchildren and has renounced, as she is instructed, the <term>Velleian privilege; a Roman law (Senatus Consultum Velleianum) that prohibited women from taking on the debts of others</term> and other privileges † granted to women by law, and she is later held as a debtor for that guardianship or care, can she be thrust into prison for it if there are no other assets of that woman from which she might pay? Bartolus and others, followed by Antonio Gomez (cited Law 62, Number 3) and Villalobos (Number 28), answer in the affirmative according to common law. However, Villalobos, along with Rodrigo Juarez, asserts the contrary to be the law of Castile, given the generality of the cited Law 62. This reasoning is not proved to me, for the privilege granted to women in this regard by common law is no less broad—indeed, it is far more so—than that granted by Law 62, as is easily established from what was just said. Therefore, if that renunciation of privileges made by a woman derogates from the privileges of common law, it will also derogate from the privilege of the cited Law 62. I prefer that we say with Covarruvias:

<margin>Decision</margin> in *Various Resolutions*, Book 2, Chapter 1, Number 3, and in the chapter "although a pact," Part 2, at the beginning, Number 7, and others whom he cites, that for that reason a mother or grandmother cannot be thrust into prison for that debt. This is because, as Bartolus himself affirms, notwithstanding that renunciation, a mother and grandmother enjoy that privilege in comparison to their descendants, so that they are not held to them for more than they can conveniently do <note>original: "quam commode facere possint"</note>. This is because of the reverence that descendants are bound to show to their ancestors, which they would certainly not be preserving if, when the mother or grandmother lacks assets to pay the debt, they cast them into prison until they paid it. Universally, as we shall submit, one who is only bound to a debt to the extent that they can conveniently do so

<column-break/>

cannot be thrust into prison for that debt. Read also Law 1, Title 15, Part 5; here, both ancestors in comparison to descendants, and descendants in comparison to ancestors, enjoy this privilege. Right reason teaches that even if ancestors renounce the privileges granted to them in general, they are not deemed to have renounced this privilege in particular—especially to the effect that they might be thrust into chains for a debt they cannot then conveniently satisfy. Indeed, as Covarruvias rightly observes in the cited Number 7, even if ancestors specifically renounce the privilege of not being jailed by their descendants for debt, they still cannot be jailed, because it conflicts with the piety and reverence that descendants owe to their ancestors by natural law.

<margin>9</margin> A soldier who is † engaged in military service enjoys this privilege: he cannot be sued for debts beyond what he can conveniently do, as seen in the law "a soldier" at the beginning, and the law "likewise a soldier" in the Digest *on judged matters* <note>original: "ff. de re iud."</note>. What this actually means is copiously explained in Disputation 413. He who is only bound to pay as much as he can conveniently do so that he does not fall into need, certainly cannot be cast into prison for that debt; nor can execution be carried out against his goods for that debt any further than by leaving him enough of his own goods so that he does not fall into need, explained in the manner of the cited disputation. Otherwise, he would be pressed more, and bound to more, than he could conveniently do, which is contrary to the reason of his privilege.

<margin>10</margin> Those nobles who are called <term>hidalgos</term> in the Kingdom of Castile, although they are not † soldiers and therefore do not enjoy the privilege on that ground (the privilege of only being sued for what they can conveniently do, which is not found granted to them in the cited laws or elsewhere), nevertheless, among other privileges granted to them by Castilian law, they enjoy the right that they cannot be thrust into prison for civil debts—that is, those not arising from a crime. Instead, execution can only be made against their goods, while leaving them their own horse or mule, the proper armor for their body, and the specific houses in which they live, if they have these. See Laws 3, 4, 5, and 6, Title 2, Book 6 of the *New Compilation*. Indeed, the cited Law 6 is Law 79 of Toro. This is affirmed by Covarruvias, Gutierrez, Antonio Gomez, Villalobos, and other Spanish doctors. By Law 9, Title 1 of the same Book 6, it is forbidden to carry out execution for any debt whatsoever—not only on the horse and arms of these nobles, but also those of the men they call <term>caballeros armados; "armed knights" or men-at-arms</term>, and any others who possess a horse and arms. However, an exception is made if the debt is owed to the King, for then execution can be made even on the horse and arms; though I do not understand this to apply to the horse and arms of those called <term>hidalgos</term>.

If, however, a noble who is called an <term>hidalgo</term> should be a contractor of the King's revenues or takes up the office of collector of those same revenues, then for a debt arising from that service to the King, he does not enjoy the aforementioned privilege but can be cast into prison. So it is held in the cited Law 4, Title 2, Book 6 of the *New Compilation*, which gives this reason: *because in such a case he himself breaks his own liberty* <note>original Spanish: "porque en tal caso el mismo se quebranta su libertad"</note>, namely by undertaking a duty that does not fit his nobility at all. Likewise,

# Second Treatise. Disputation 571.

<page-num>855</page-num>

If the debt of a nobleman arises from a crime <note>original: "ex delicto"</note> or a quasi-delict <note>a legal term for a wrong caused by negligence rather than intent</note>, then he can be cast into prison for it just as if he were not a nobleman. This is held in Law 79 of Toro, which is Law 6, Title 2, Book 6 of the *New Compilation*. In these events, however, and in any others, a selected prison—either distinct from the main prison or a separate part of the prison where commoners <note>original: "viles"</note> and people of the lowest class are held—must be granted to such noblemen and other honored persons who are endowed with learning or other qualities. Given the concurrent circumstances of both the degree of nobility and honor, as well as the quality of the crime and other factors, they should be given a distinct prison, either public or outside the public one, with guards or without them, according to Law 4, Title 29, Part 7 and Law 11, Title 2, Book 6 of the *New Compilation*. Sometimes, their own home, a city, or a town can be assigned to them as a prison. Read, among others, Gregorio López on the cited Law 4, and Gutierrez in the place cited above, number 3.

If the nobility, which is called <term>hidalguia</term> <note>a specific rank of lower Spanish nobility, often exempt from taxes and certain punishments</note>, is notorious <note>well-known or undisputed in the community</note>, such a nobleman should not be thrown into prison for a civil debt. If he was thrown in by error, he must be released immediately. But if his status is in doubt, he is cast into and detained in prison until it is proven. And although it pertains only to the judges called <term>Alcaldes de los hidalgos</term> <note>Judges of the Hidalgos who presided over cases regarding noble status in the Royal Chanceries</note> in the Royal Courts to take cognizance of such nobility—specifically for the purpose of him enjoying that status absolutely and being immune from those Royal taxes from which nobles of that quality are exempt—nevertheless, when the matter is raised incidentally to another different cause (such as for paying a civil debt or punishing some crime), and the defendant alleges he is a <term>fidalgo</term> <note>Portuguese/Old Spanish variant of hidalgo</note> and for that reason cannot be cast into chains for a civil debt or be tortured due to suspicion of some crime, it belongs to the ordinary judge who hears the principal case to take cognizance and judge whether he enjoys that nobility for those particular and incidental effects. Furthermore, to pronounce that he enjoys nobility for those effects alone, it is not necessary to have such complete and legitimate proof as is required in the Royal Courts to pronounce that he enjoys that nobility absolutely; it is enough if it is proven that he is in "possession" or "quasi-possession" of that nobility. It is also customary to add in such sentences that this brings no prejudice to the King’s treasury regarding the actual ownership and possession of the said nobility. This is the view held with Padilla, Otalora, and others by Gutierrez in the place cited above from number 6, and in *Practical Questions*, Book 1, Question 25; and Azevedo in the final law of Title 21, Book 4 of the *New Compilation*, numbers 68 and 69.

Gutierrez in the cited chapter 16, from number 14, and with him Azevedo in the place cited above, number 70, and others whom they cite, affirm that just as someone who "surrenders his goods" <note>the legal process of *cessio bonorum*, similar to bankruptcy</note> is bound to manifest all his assets so they may be handed over to creditors (otherwise, if he hides anything, he does not enjoy the privilege of surrendering goods granted to him by law, as will be discussed in the following disputation), so too a nobleman, when execution is made against his assets, is bound to manifest everything faithfully so that payment may be made to the creditor. Otherwise, if he knowingly hides anything, he commits a crime, and therefore can be cast into prison for that debt, as if it now arose from a crime or were supported and aided by one. This is confirmed: First, because by that concealment he commits deceit and fraud against the creditors; and fraud and deceit constitute a crime, as is proven. Second, because although an heir

<column-break/>

today can, by Praetorian law, abstain from a paternal inheritance and repudiate it (as was discussed extensively in Disputation 180), if he nevertheless removes or conceals anything from the inheritance, he loses that privilege by that very act, as held in Law *si servum*, the section *praetor ait*, and following, in the Digest *on the acquisition of inheritance*, and Law 12, Title 6, Part 6. Third, because in the law *on benefits* in the Digest regarding the *Falcidian Law* <note>a Roman law ensuring an heir received at least one-quarter of an estate</note>, a person is seen as unworthy of the benefit of the Falcidian Law if he acts so that a <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>a legal trust or bequest</note> fails—that is, as the gloss explains there, if the heir cancels a trust from the will, he loses the benefit of the Falcidian Law. Therefore, in the same way, if such a nobleman hides his assets so that debts fail or are not paid, he loses the privilege that he cannot be sent to prison for such a debt. This is confirmed because, as is held in the authentic text regarding heirs and the Falcidian Law, the section "here for us," at the words "we sanction" and "if truly not," and as was said in Disputation 213, an heir who subtracts or conceals anything from an inheritance loses the privilege of subtracting the Falcidian portion. Therefore, it will be the same in the matter proposed. Fourth, because Law 4, Title 19, Book 5 of the *New Compilation* states:

> We command that from now on no merchant who absconds <note>to "abscond" here refers to declaring bankruptcy or fleeing from creditors with assets</note> may enjoy, nor shall enjoy, the privilege of nobility [*hidalguia*], to excuse himself from the penalty of the said crime, nor for any other case or thing. And we command the same to be observed and fulfilled against the collectors and stewards of the councils, or any other persons who abscond.

Therefore, the same must be said regarding the effect of losing the privilege of not being cast into prison for one who has hidden his assets so that creditors are not satisfied therefrom; for he truly commits a crime to protect himself and abuses that privilege. Fifth, a partner who was at fault through deceit so that he could not pay a debt to other partners loses the privilege of not being sued by the other partners beyond what he can conveniently pay, and consequently loses the privilege of not being cast into prison for that debt, as held in the Law *verum* at the beginning and the section *ipsi autem* in the Digest *on partnerships*, and affirmed by the gloss on the section *if concerning a dowry* in the Institutes *on actions*, and discussed in Disputation 413. Likewise, although a husband, in paying the dowry of a wife, cannot be compelled to pay more than he can conveniently afford, and thus cannot be cast into prison for the debt of the wife's dowry; yet if he deceitfully diminishes his substance, he loses that privilege, as all these things were discussed in Disputation 442. Therefore, if the nobleman of whom we speak deceitfully hides assets so that the debt is not fully paid to the creditor, he similarly loses the privilege that he cannot be cast into prison for such a debt. Most of these points with which we have confirmed this so far at least prove that concealment is a crime; otherwise, in the similar cases explained, those penalties we cited would not have been established. Wherefore, since by that very fact the debt of such a nobleman descends from or is fostered by his crime, he can be cast into prison for that debt, as Law 79 sanctions. It follows certainly that by the very fact that he hid assets, he can be cast into prison. Finally, it is confirmed because, as reported at number 29, when a certain nobleman was cast into prison for a certain debt because he had hidden his assets, and he appealed to the Court of Valladolid <note>original: "Pincianu ptoriu", referring to the Royal Chancery of Valladolid</note>, it was approved that he had been deservedly cast into prison. And first it was ordered that he be released from prison upon giving sureties for indemnity <note>original: "saneamiento"</note>; but later, that he be released only upon giving sureties "of the peace" <note>original: "de la baz"</note>; whom he would not have needed to provide if he were enjoying his privilege.

# Luis Molina on Contracts

### On the Privileges of Nobility

Similarly, from the same foundation, it follows that if a nobleman, while entering into a contract with someone and knowing himself to be a noble, denied his status, he can be cast into prison for a debt arising from that contract if the other party was unaware of his status. This is because he contracted the debt through his own crime <note>original: "proprio delicto"</note>, having deceived the creditor regarding the nature of the debt's security. Because the debt originates from fraud and wrongdoing <note>original: "ex dolo, & delicto"</note>, the nobleman loses his privilege. This is the view of Antonio Gomez (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 11, numbers 54 and 179) and Gutierrez (as cited above, number 25). They confirm this through various laws which, in similar events, deny similar privileges. Both authors affirm, however, that if the nobleman denied being a noble because he was ignorant of his own status, or if the creditor knew at the time of the contract that he was a noble, he does not lose the privilege. In the first case, the debt does not descend from the noble’s wrongdoing; in the second, the creditor was not deceived, as he knew the man was a noble and enjoyed that privilege. By the same reasoning, if a nobleman prepared to flee with his goods, or even without them, he could be seized and cast into prison, since by such flight and wrongdoing he would make the recovery of the debt more difficult—at least if he later came into a more substantial fortune. So says Gutierrez (number 3), citing Balbus and others.

<margin>Question 11</margin> There is a doubtful and highly controversial question: if the nobleman we are discussing renounces <note>to "renounce" here means to voluntarily waive a legal right or protection</note> his privilege so that he cannot be cast into prison for a civil debt, can he then be imprisoned just as if he were not a nobleman? Antonio Gomez and Gutierrez (at numbers 47 through 61) have argued that such a renunciation is invalid. Therefore, even with such a waiver, the nobleman cannot be cast into prison for the debt. Gomez adds that even if the renunciation was confirmed by an oath, it remains invalid; however, Gutierrez (at number 62) says that in the case of an oath, it is valid.

These authors are chiefly led by the argument from the text in the chapter *Si diligenti* regarding competent courts, where it is held that a renunciation by which a cleric waives his "privilege of the forum" <note>the right of clergy to be tried only in ecclesiastical/church courts rather than secular ones</note> is null, even if he confirms it with an oath. The reason given there is:

> *Since this benefit is not personal, such that one might be able to renounce it, but is rather granted publicly to the entire ecclesiastical body, it cannot be set aside by the private agreement of individuals.* <note>original: "Cum non sit beneficium hoc personale... cui privatorum pacto derogari non potest."</note>

By this same reasoning, a cleric cannot renounce that other privilege of the canon <note>a law protecting clergy from physical violence</note> which excommunicates anyone who strikes a cleric. Even if the cleric renounces that privilege before being struck, the striker is still excommunicated. Indeed, even if a cleric lethally strikes himself, he is excommunicated, as we shall see in the third treatise.

From this, they argue that a nobleman’s renunciation of the privilege against imprisonment for civil debt is null (some add even if confirmed by oath) because that privilege was similarly granted to the community of nobles and not to individuals in particular. Many other arguments of lesser weight which lead these authors can be read in Gutierrez and Covarruvias, the latter of whom also

<column-break/>

attempts to satisfy many of the arguments of others.

<margin>Decision</margin> However, the contrary opinion pleases me: namely, that the renunciation is valid, even if it is not confirmed by an oath. Consequently, if such a renunciation has been made, the nobleman can be cast into prison for a civil debt. I agree with Covarruvias, who says this was the judgment in the high court of Granada, as well as Gregorio López and others cited by Gutierrez. I am led to this by several points which can be read in the cited authors. 

First, this privilege—that such nobles should not be incarcerated for civil debt—is not a "right of blood" <note>a right inherent in one's biological lineage that cannot be separated from the person</note> in the same way that kinship or the right of a son to receive support from his father are. Rather, it was a merit-based grant from the Kings of Spain to the specific warriors who, at their own risk and expense, helped the Kings recover Spain from the power of the Moors. They were granted this status of <term>hidalguía</term> <note>the status of an hidalgo, the lowest rank of Spanish nobility</note> so that they might enjoy it and pass it down through the male line to all their legitimate descendants. This status had certain privileges attached: exemption from certain taxes, immunity from torture for crimes, and immunity from prison for civil debts. This does not prevent any of them, when making a contract, from waiving the privilege so that if they do not pay at the appointed time, they can be imprisoned. Indeed, anyone can normally renounce a privilege granted for their own benefit. Furthermore, this does not harm other nobles, and it can sometimes be useful or even necessary for a noble to renounce it; otherwise, he might find no one willing to enter into a contract with him that is highly beneficial or necessary for him. 

Second, these nobles are not prohibited by this privilege from yielding or allowing themselves to be imprisoned for a civil debt (a point some overlook); rather, it is the *judges* who are prohibited from imprisoning them while they enjoy that privilege and raise it as an objection. 

Third, this privilege does not arise from the natural reverence and respect that other men are bound to show these nobles by the very nature of things. This is unlike the privilege parents enjoy in relation to their children (where they cannot be sued for more than they can comfortably pay, and thus cannot be jailed); that obligation of reverence remains in the children regardless of whether the parents renounce it, making such a renunciation invalid. In the case of nobles, other men are not bound by the nature of things to refrain from jailing them for unpaid debts; the nobles have this only by a privilege granted by kings in gratitude for the services rendered to the Spanish state by their ancestors. 

Fourth, it is not as if the clergy, who constitute a distinct and exempt community and state...

<summary>Molina argues that while noblemen are generally immune from prison for civil debt, this privilege can be legally waived in contracts to ensure the noble's ability to conduct business, distinguishing this from the non-waivable privileges of the clergy.</summary>

## Treatise Two, Dispute 5, Page 857

...from the secular republic under their own proper Ecclesiastical judges and one supreme head, the Supreme Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ. It results in harm to the republic if Ecclesiastics are subjected to the secular judgment of laypeople. For this reason, Ecclesiastical persons are rightly prohibited by their own republic, under heavy penalties, from allowing themselves to be brought before a secular tribunal. They must not answer there in any way as a defendant, nor call other Ecclesiastics there as plaintiffs <note>The author uses "actor" here in the legal sense of a plaintiff or the party bringing a suit.</note>, as this is unbecoming for the clergy and would produce many evils for their own sacred republic, which is dedicated to God, and would even result in harm to the laypeople. All these matters have been explained copiously in Dispute 31, and it is established from the canon *Si diligenti*, regarding the competent forum. 

I say that Ecclesiastics form a distinct republic, exempt from the lay one, and it is vital that their subjects are in no way subjected to a secular tribunal; for that reason, it is prohibited to them. However, the situation is different for nobles. They form one single republic together with the commoners <note>original: "ignobilibus"</note>. Their privileges are granted to them by the supreme head of that republic, and an individual may waive those privileges in a particular event without any harm or prejudice to others. 

Indeed, nobles do not form their own distinct community any more than all women do. Women are granted the Velleian privilege <note>original: "priuilegiū Velleiani". This refers to the *Senatus Consultum Velleianum*, a Roman law that protected women by making it illegal for them to take on the debts of others as a guarantor or surety.</note> by the republic for a specific reason. According to the law of Castile and the common opinion of many regarding common law, individual women can validly renounce this privilege. And although I have said elsewhere (Dispute 540) that, following the more common and true opinion, such a renunciation is invalid under common law, I did not rely on the foundation that it would harm their community or prejudice others. Rather, I relied on the principle of equity <note>original: "epicheiam"</note>, by which we must judge the intention of the lawmakers who granted the privilege to help their "fragility" <note>original: "fragilitati". In early modern law, "fragilitas" or "infirmitas sexus" was a standard legal term used to justify protective laws for women.</note>. Otherwise, their fragility would not have been sufficiently protected; for they might renounce the Velleian privilege at the request of others with the same ease with which they would take on an obligation for them—especially since creditors would not otherwise be willing to accept them as guarantors.

Fifth, regarding the harm to the community in the case of the privilege of the forum granted to Ecclesiastics: even if such a person commits fraud <note>original: "fraudem committat"</note> by pretending not to be an Ecclesiastic when contracting, or by some other means, he does not lose that privilege. This remains true unless the Ecclesiastical republic itself, to which he belongs, takes it away from him as a punishment in a particular instance. Therefore, an Ecclesiastic who pretends to be a layman when making a contract must still be brought before an Ecclesiastical judge, both regarding the debt and the fraud committed—and in no way before a secular one. 

However, the matter is not the same regarding the privilege of nobles which we are discussing. According to the opinion of the doctors with whom we are debating, they admit that if a nobleman pretended to be a commoner at the time a contract was made, or if he hid any of his goods at the time of execution, he can lose that privilege and consequently be thrust into prison for that debt. 

Finally, 

<column-break/>

regarding the privilege granted to nobles: the head of the republic, just as he granted it, can for a reasonable cause take it away or restrict it. For example, he can ensure it has no force if the debt arises from a crime, or if it is a debt owed to the King because the person managed royal revenues or took on the duty of collecting them. But the privilege of exemption from their own tribunal, once granted by secular princes and given to the Ecclesiastical republic, cannot thereafter be taken away or restricted by those same princes, as was said in Dispute 31.

The primary foundation relied upon by the authors of the contrary opinion is now easily answered: though the premise is granted, the conclusion must be denied. Regarding the privilege of the forum, it was explained that it was granted to the distinct Ecclesiastical republic, and we see how the public favor of that republic is involved, even to the benefit of laypeople. Likewise, it is rightly prohibited by the Ecclesiastical republic, under heavy Ecclesiastical penalties, for persons to renounce it or contravene it in any way. For this reason, even if they renounce it with an oath and promise to answer before a secular judge, the whole act is void and useless, because such a promise and oath concern an illicit thing prohibited to Ecclesiastics. This is all contained in the canon *Si diligenti* regarding the competent forum, upon which these foundations chiefly rest. 

The privilege that a nobleman cannot be thrust into prison for a civil debt, however, was not granted to a distinct republic, nor is the public favor of the republic or any community at stake in it. Furthermore, nobles are not prohibited from renouncing it. Therefore, the reasoning for one privilege is far different from the other. 

Regarding the "privilege of the canon" <note>original: "priuilegiū canonis". This refers to the protection against physical violence toward clergy, historically tied to the canon *Si quis suadente*.</note>: the excommunication issued against those who lay violent hands on Ecclesiastical persons with lethal sin (or at the "instigation of the devil," as that canon says) does indeed result in the good of Ecclesiastics. In that sense, it could be called their privilege. Yet, it is not something granted to them, but a just penalty imposed by the legislator for the security of Ecclesiastics, who are entirely unarmed ministers of God for whom self-defense is unbecoming. Therefore, this penalty depends not on them, but on the legislator, and they cannot renounce it. But the privilege granted to nobles—that they cannot be imprisoned for civil debt—is something granted to them to use if they wish; thus, they can yield and renounce that privilege.

<margin>12</margin> A cleric also has a privilege: he can only be sued for as much as he is "conveniently" able to pay <note>original: "quantum commodè facere possit"</note>. Thus, for debts which he cannot conveniently pay, he cannot be cast into prison, even if he does not surrender his assets <note>original: "esto bonis non cedat". This refers to *cessio bonorum*, the legal surrender of property to creditors to avoid imprisonment.</note>. This is the view of the Gloss and Bartolus on the law *Miles* (at the beginning, *Digest* on *res iudicata*); Panormitanus on the canon *Odoardus* regarding payments; Covarruvias (Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 1, number 9); Gigas on pensions (question 3, number 8); Gutierrez on confirmed law (chapter 16, number 32, and more fully in chapter 17, from number 1); Gregorius Lopez on Law 26, title 6, part 1, on the words "from cleric to another" <note>original: "en clerigo a otro"</note>; and others whom they cite. It is clearly gathered from the cited canon *Odoardus*, where a cleric unable to pay neither surrendered his goods nor was cast into prison; rather, it was ordered that, due to his inability to pay, his excommunication be relaxed upon providing a debt security (at least a sworn one), if another...

<summary>This page distinguishes between clerical "privilege of the forum" and the civil privileges of nobility, arguing that while noble privileges can be waived or lost through fraud, clerical exemptions are jurisdictional and cannot be surrendered. It also details the specific protections for clerics facing debt, noting they should not be imprisoned if they lack the means to pay.</summary>

## Louis de Molina, On Contracts

(if he has no other means) until he comes to **more favorable circumstances**, he shall pay. <note>original: "pinguiorem fortunam", literally "fatter fortune."</note> The reason is—as both the cited gloss, Bartolus, and others say—he is a **soldier of Christ** <note>original: "Christi miles"</note>, and therefore ought to enjoy the privilege of a secular soldier. Furthermore, it is especially not fitting for a minister of Christ to live in a lowly state or be thrust into prison for a civil debt; rather, enough should be left to him to live sparingly, and the remainder is to be handed over to the creditor. 

If a cleric who has ecclesiastical revenues is weighed down by debt that he cannot immediately satisfy in full, the **Ecclesiastical judge**—leaving him enough from both his own inheritance and those revenues to live sparingly—ought to award the remaining goods and revenues to the creditor until the debt is paid in full. As Covarruvias (at the cited number 9) and others rightly state, this is based on the argument of the canon *pervenit*, regarding sureties. However, for a cleric to enjoy this explained privilege, he must first acknowledge the debt, as the canon *Odoardus* <note>A famous decree in canon law protecting clerics who are unable to pay their debts from harsh penalties.</note> clearly states, and provide security. Just as one who "surrenders his goods" <term>cessio bonorum: a legal process where a debtor gives up their assets to creditors to avoid imprisonment</term> must first acknowledge the debts he is to pay if he reaches better circumstances, as will be said in the following dispute, and as Gutierrez affirms (at chapter 17, number 2) following Panormitanus and others.

<margin>13</margin> Although Lapus and many others (whom Gutierrez mentions at chapter 17, number 11) wished to extend this privilege to any clerics of the **first tonsure** <note>The first step toward ordination, involving a ritual cutting of hair to signify clerical status.</note>, whether they are married or not, Covarruvias and Gutierrez (from number 10) rightly judge that—especially today after the **Council of Trent** (Session 23, Chapter 6 on Reform)—it applies only to those who, according to that decree, enjoy the **privilege of the forum** <term>privilegium fori: the right of clergy to be tried in church courts rather than secular ones</term>. It does not apply to others who were rightly excluded from that privilege by the same decree due to their great number, especially in Spain, and because they did not ascend to that rank to be ministers of the Church, but so they could not be punished for their crimes in the secular court. 

In the same place, Gutierrez, along with Montalvo, contends that even before the Council of Trent, this privilege was not extended to married clerics in **minor orders**. This was enacted in the single chapter "On Married Clerics" in Book 6, which states that married clerics (with one wife and she a virgin) who wear the habit and tonsure may indeed enjoy the **privilege of the canon** <note>The "privilege of the canon" (privilegium canonis) protected clerics from physical violence; anyone striking them was automatically excommunicated.</note> if someone—at the devil's persuasion—[attacks them], and likewise the privilege of the forum, but only so far as they cannot be punished by secular judges for their crimes, whether criminally or civilly. But the text adds: *in other matters, however, we do not wish them to enjoy the clerical privilege.* Hence, just as according to that text they are held to pay the taxes that other laypeople are held to (as the gloss and common opinion explain), and they must answer in secular court in purely civil cases, so too they can be thrust into prison for debts. They do not enjoy the privilege of being sued only for as much as they can conveniently pay. 

From this, you will understand that if a married cleric today wears the habit and tonsure and is appointed by the bishop to the service of some church, he enjoys the privilege of the forum (so he cannot be sued for a crime before a secular judge), but not the privilege of avoiding prison for a civil debt, since he did not enjoy this privilege before the Council of Trent, nor did the Council grant it to him anew. The Law 1, Title 4, Book 1 of the New Collection <note>The "Nueva Recopilación", a 16th-century compilation of Spanish royal laws.</note> agrees with this entire doctrine.

<column-break/>

Read also the preceding and following laws in that title.

<margin>14</margin> If a cleric, at the time of the contract, **feigned** not being a cleric (the other party being ignorant of it), or hid his goods so the debt would not be paid to the creditor, or if the debt arises from a crime, then by reason of the crime he committed, he can be thrust into prison for the debt. This is the same as was said above regarding a nobleman, and is affirmed by Gutierrez and others, because clerical crimes (nothing in the canon *Odoardus* hindering this) can be punished by imprisonment. For such crimes, a cleric rightly loses the privilege granted to him there and elsewhere. I judge, however, that the more serious and foul the crime, the more he should be punished by the loss of that privilege; yet regard must always be had for the **clerical state**, so that something is left to him so he does not live sordidly and abjectly. For we are not speaking here of the crime of high treason against God <note>original: "læsæ maiestatis diuinæ", referring to heresy or other extreme religious crimes</note>, or any other grave crime for which he should be punished even in the honor and decency of his status.

Neither a cleric nor a layman can be **excommunicated** for a debt that he is entirely unable to pay. This is because excommunication is only incurred for **disobedience** to the Church when the penalty is attached to a command. He who is entirely unable to fulfill what is commanded is not disobedient; his inability excuses him from fault and disobedience, and consequently from the penalty of excommunication imposed for that fault. Indeed, if it were evident and notorious that he was entirely unable to pay, and he were excommunicated because he did not pay, the excommunication would contain an "intolerable error" and would be not only unjust but null, as Panormitanus correctly affirms regarding the canon *Odoardus*.

<margin>15</margin> If a cleric debtor is **suspected of flight**, he could be thrust into prison until he pays in full or provides sufficient pledge or surety. However, he cannot be seized by the creditor himself unless the debtor is actually attempting flight and no public official is present to seize him; in that case, he must be brought immediately to his own judge and the public prison, as was said regarding a nobleman attempting flight. So says Gutierrez, Covarruvias, Gregorio Lopez, and others.

Covarruvias and Gutierrez rightly affirm against Gomez that even if a cleric has been condemned by **three sentences** <note>In the legal systems of the time, three consistent judgments were often required to finalize a civil case and proceed to full execution of the penalty.</note> to pay a creditor, he still enjoys the privilege of the chapter *Odoardus*, meaning he cannot be compelled to pay more than he conveniently can, and therefore cannot be thrust into prison for that debt. There is no suitable reason why he should not enjoy that privilege, even if he appealed from two sentences and is waiting for a third. For although an exception of nullity is not admitted against the execution of three conforming sentences—due to the strong suspicion of deceit—the exception based on the canon *Odoardus* (that a debtor is not compelled to pay more than he can) is not against the sentence itself...

<summary>This page discusses the legal protections for clergy against imprisonment for civil debts, emphasizing that they must be left enough to live with dignity. It also details how these privileges were restricted by the Council of Trent, especially for married clerics, and how fraud or crime can lead to the loss of these protections.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding the "Odoardus" privilege, which protects clergy from being imprisoned for debt or stripped of the basic means of survival. It specifically addresses whether a cleric can waive this right through a legal oath.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 57, Page 859

...nor should it therefore be mandated for execution; rather, such an exception assumes an admission of the debt, as has been said, and consequently carries the weight of a legal judgment.

<margin>Question</margin>
A greater doubt arises: if a cleric renounces the **privilege of the chapter Odoardus** <note>original: "priuilegio capitis Odoardus." This refers to a specific decree in Canon Law (X 3.23.3) that protects clergy from harsh debt collection.</note>, especially with an **oath**—as notaries frequently include such renunciations even without an oath—

<margin>16</margin>
or if a cleric binds himself by oath to pay the debt, can he then, and should he, be thrown into prison until he pays the debt in full? Is he treated just like those who enjoy no such privilege and are forced to pay?

<margin>Decision</margin>
This doubt must be satisfied by the following conclusions. **First:** Even if a cleric renounces that privilege without an oath, he nonetheless enjoys it. He cannot be thrown into prison, nor can he be forced to pay more than what leaves him enough to avoid destitution. Gutierrez asserts this (cited above, number 34) based on the foundation that this privilege is granted to the entire community of the clergy, just like the **privilege of the court** <term>privilegium fori: the right of clerics to be tried in ecclesiastical rather than secular courts</term>. However, there is a broad distinction between the privilege of the court and this one. A violation of the former would harm the Church's legal standing more than a violation of the debt privilege. The legitimate reason for this rule is that the privilege is granted to clerics not so much for the benefit of the individual person, but for the **honor of God** and the good and decency of the **Christian commonwealth**. It is fitting that clerics be treated with reverence as ministers of God; they should not be cast into prison for a civil debt or oppressed so much that they live in a sordid and abject manner. Therefore, because the same indecency remains even if they renounce the privilege, and the reasons for its granting remain valid, it follows that their renunciation is void. They enjoy the privilege just as if they had not renounced it.

**Second:** If they renounce that privilege with an oath, since they bind themselves by that very oath not to invoke its use or execution, and since such an act is not inherently evil on their part, I believe they **sin mortally** if they invoke the privilege without first obtaining a release from that oath. In that case, they would be bound to endure prison and the loss of all their goods as if the privilege had not been granted to them. However, **Ecclesiastical judges**, despite that renunciation and oath, are neither bound nor permitted to cast them into prison or strip them of goods to the point where they have nothing to live on. Likewise, the clerics themselves can seek a release from the oath, and it can and should be granted. Once obtained, they may invoke the privilege. The first part is clear enough from what has been said, and Gutierrez agrees with us (number 35). The second part regarding the judges is also clear: an oath by which a cleric renounces his privilege does not bind the judges or prevent them from maintaining the privilege, the splendor, 

<column-break/>

and the decency of the ministers of God and the Christian commonwealth. If they can lawfully uphold the use of this privilege, they are certainly bound to do so by virtue of their office. The final part is evident because there is a legitimate cause for the creditor to be compelled to release the debtor from an oath that was introduced against the decency and good of the Christian commonwealth; as the superior of that creditor, the judge can release it.

When no renunciation of the privilege occurs (with or without an oath), but the cleric has simply bound himself by oath to pay the creditor the debt, Gomez (cited by Covarruvias at number 9 and reported by Gutierrez) says that the cleric then cannot use or enjoy the privilege of *Odoardus*. Covarruvias, however, affirms the contrary in the same passage. He argues that the oath must be understood according to the promise it confirms; if a cleric binds himself to pay without an oath, he is only understood to be bound to pay as much as he **conveniently can**. Gutierrez (at number 36) says that if a cleric specifically swore to pay the debt "in full" or "without fail," he cannot invoke the *Odoardus* privilege, and thus Gomez’s opinion is true in that event. But if he only swore absolutely to pay the debt, he can still invoke the privilege, making Covarruvias’s opinion true. Certainly, whoever binds himself by oath or otherwise to pay a debt binds himself to pay the *whole* debt, not just a part, so this distinction seems less fitting.

**Our third conclusion is:** A cleric who binds himself by oath to pay a debt (or the whole of a debt) is covered by Covarruvias’s opinion if he did not explicitly state that he would pay even if it meant destitution, or if he did not specifically intend to obligate himself to that extent. But if he *did* express this or intended to so obligate himself—since this is not inherently evil for the cleric—he is indeed bound to fulfill it as much as he can, just as he would be if he did not enjoy the *Odoardus* privilege. Nevertheless, he can seek and obtain a release from such an oath for the reasons stated in the previous conclusion. The Ecclesiastical judge, notwithstanding that oath, is neither bound nor ought to throw him into prison, for the reasons also stated above. This entire conclusion requires no further proof.

<margin>17</margin>
The same privilege—that one cannot be sued for more than one can conveniently pay <note>original: "vltra quod cómode facere poſſit"</note> and thus cannot be imprisoned for a civil debt—is also granted by the Gloss on the law *Miles* <note>original: "l. miles, ff. de re iud." Referring to Digest 42.1.6, regarding soldiers.</note>. Many others grant it to **advocates** (lawyers) by the same logic. Likewise, they grant the same privilege to **doctors** <note>In this context, "doctors" refers to those holding the highest academic degrees, usually in law or theology.</note>. Gutierrez and Azquedo follow these authors. However, that specific law in the Code does not speak of advocates universally.

<summary>This page analyzes whether members of the clergy can waive their legal protections against debt-related imprisonment through oaths, concluding that while an individual might be morally bound by a specific oath, the Church's judges must still uphold the cleric's dignity and basic needs for the public good.</summary>
<keywords>Odoardus privilege, clerical immunity, debt collection, oaths, renunciation of rights, ecclesiastical judges, legal advocates, academic doctors, Christian commonwealth</keywords>
