Under Portuguese law (Book 5, Title 67), neither those who are called **noblemen** <note>original: "fidalgos"</note> in that Kingdom, nor those called **knights** <note>original: "caualeros"</note>, nor 
18 † senators, nor doctors of law or medicine who have received a degree from any university after a prior examination, nor the wives of any of these (even if they are widows, provided they live honorably), can be thrown into prison, except for a crime for which they deserve natural or civil death. Therefore, they cannot be thrust into prison for a civil debt. ### To what extent the surrender of assets is permitted, and how far it frees a debtor from the payment of debt.

### DISPUTE 572.

#### SUMMARY.
1 A debtor can surrender assets in all cases where they could be thrust into prison for a civil debt.
2 Whether a person surrendering assets for a debt—for which they have a privilege not to be sued beyond what they can afford—loses that privilege.
3 Any debtor can surrender assets, either by themselves or through a proxy, and either by word alone or through writing.
4 Indeed, one can surrender assets even before being sent to prison, number 4.
5 What ought to precede the surrender of assets before it happens.
6 What "surrendering assets" <note>original: "Cedere bonis"</note> means.
7 What a debtor is bound to do when they surrender assets.
8 The ownership of the assets of a debtor who has surrendered them remains with the debtor themselves until they are sold off.
9 A debtor gains two advantages from the surrender of assets.
10 The exception of surrender only benefits the debtor who surrendered assets, not their guarantor.
11 What delays a debtor who wants to surrender assets can seek for payment.
12 A majority of the creditors of a deceased debtor can forgive part of the debt to the prejudice of other creditors, even privileged ones.
13 And what is observed concerning the law of Castile, number 13.
14 Whether the wife of a debtor who has surrendered assets can take her husband's goods for the payment of her dowry and **extradotal property** <term>paraphernalia: property belonging to a married woman beyond her dowry</term> to the prejudice of her husband's other creditors, especially when she proves her husband has squandered her goods.
15 A monetary debt can arise from a crime in two ways.
16 In which cases a monetary penalty is to be converted into physical punishment.

<column-break/>

<margin>
17 Whether the surrender of assets takes place for a debt originating from a crime.
18 And what regarding the law of Castile and Portugal.
19 Whether someone who renounces the surrender of assets with an oath can still surrender assets in events permitted by law.
</margin>

In those events in which—according to what was said in the preceding dispute—it is permitted for a debtor to be thrust into prison for a civil debt, the law has granted for the common good that they may **surrender their assets** <note>original: "cedere bonis"</note>. This means to relinquish and hand over all their assets, rights, debts owed to them, and any property belonging to them to the creditors to be divided, so that payment may be made to them as far as those assets suffice. The remainder is to be paid by the debtor if they should come into **better fortune** <note>original: "pinguem fortunam"</note>, and thus they are freed from prison. This is held in the Code (on those who can surrender assets) and the remaining laws of that title, and the Digest (on the surrender of assets). The same is held in the Siete Partidas (Part 5, Title 15) and the Portuguese Ordinances (Book 3, Title 89). This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Covarruvias, Antonio Gómez, and Gutierrez. The form of the entire process of surrendering assets (which the laws of Spain also call **renouncing the chain** <note>original: "renunciar la cadena"</note>) is handed down by Monterroso in his *Practica*. Since this privilege of surrendering assets was sanctioned by law for the common good—lest debtors be kept in prison forever and perish there without any benefit to the creditors (indeed, to their loss)—and since those who enter into contracts know that debtors enjoy this privilege and enter their contracts with that presupposition, the use of this privilege certainly has no less force in conscience than in the external court.

<margin>Decision.</margin>
Whoever enjoys a privilege such that they cannot be cast into prison for a civil debt—whether this arises because they cannot be sued for that debt except for as much as they are comfortably able to pay, or for another reason—has no need to surrender assets; they cannot be thrust into prison even without any surrender. However, if one who enjoys the privilege of not being sued beyond what they can afford surrenders their assets for a debt in which they enjoy that privilege, can they then be stripped of absolutely all their assets? This is the same way someone who does *not* enjoy that privilege is stripped when they surrender assets. Matthew of Afflictis (whom Gutierrez refers to and does not reject) and Imola and Petrus (cited by Gregorio López) affirm this. Therefore they respond: Afflictis warns that a cleric who is insolvent, when sued for a debt, should protect himself with the exception from the chapter *Odoardus* (on payments), because he enjoys the privilege of not being sued beyond what he can comfortably afford. He should not surrender his assets, lest by that very act he be stripped of all his goods and they be handed over to the creditor. However, the first law cited rightly establishes the opposite, as Gregorio López also notes in the cited gloss. For there is no fitting reason why the surrender of assets should block that other privilege for the one who enjoys it.

Any † debtor can surrender his assets, either by himself—even by word alone, by which he expresses that this is his will—or through his...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "cessio bonorum" (surrender of assets), specifically comparing the procedural requirements and the timing of imprisonment between the laws of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of Portugal.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Dispute 572. (Continued)

through a proxy, or through a written document, as held in the last law of the Digest <note>original: "ff. de cess. bon."</note> on the surrender of assets, joined with the law "In omni" in the Code <note>original: "C. qui bon. ced. poss."</note> regarding those who can surrender assets; this is also found in Law 1, Title 15, Part 5 <note>The "Partidas" was a major Castilian law code from the 13th century.</note>. The last law cited states that the surrender can be made not only in court, but also out of court. However, the first law cited says it ought to be done before a judge. Gregorio Lopez reconciles these cases by stating that although the legal instrument of surrender can be made out of court, for the surrender to be perfected, the instrument must be brought and presented before a judge. Today, however, in Portugal—according to the order prescribed in Book 3, Title 89, paragraphs 1 and the third to last—and much more so in this Kingdom of Castile, according to what we shall report as decreed for surrender in that event, it must be done before a judge. The judge himself then delivers and pronounces the sentence, detailing the order and the timeframe in which the person surrendering their assets must serve their creditors.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding the established rule in common law, I believe a debtor can surrender their assets before they are sent to prison, in order to avoid arrest and imprisonment; Antonio Gómez clearly suggests this in his second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 11, number 52. Portuguese law agrees in the cited Title 89, paragraph 5, where it is established that if any creditor asks for the person who says they wish to surrender assets to be sent to prison, they must be sent to prison immediately. This implies that if such a request is not made, the surrender of assets can be petitioned and completed without the debtor being thrust into prison. Regularly, however, especially in this Kingdom of Castile (according to what we will submit regarding the surrender of assets there), the surrender is petitioned and completed after the debtor has been sent to prison. Covarrubias, in the cited number 5, along with others he references, affirms that the surrender cannot be made unless the debtor was sent to prison at the request of the creditors. He adds that it is sufficient for the debtor to be thrown into prison at the request of just one creditor, and it is not necessary for the others to be summoned; the surrender made then creates a legal precedent for the other creditors. In this Kingdom of Castile, however, before it is finalized, the other creditors must be summoned—including those who are unknown via public proclamation—so it may be pronounced in what order the one surrendering assets must serve them, and which creditor should be preferred over another in that regard. This is the practice in the form of the legal process which Monterroso transmits on this matter above. Likewise, in Portuguese law, Title 89, paragraph 1, it is commanded that whoever must surrender assets must first declare all their debts and confess them, and the instrument of that confession must be brought to the judge. Also, before the surrender is finalized, all creditors to whom the debtor has confessed owing money must be summoned.

<margin>5</margin> Before $\dagger$ the surrender of assets is made or granted, the debts must be established, either through a sentence that has become a final judgment <term>res judicata: a matter already judged that cannot be appealed</term>, or through a confession of those debts made by the debtor themselves, so that by virtue of such a confession, the creditors may seek payment at any time, leaving no room for the debtor to stall. This is held in the second to last law of the Digest on the surrender of assets, and Law 1, Title 15, Part 5, and the Portuguese Ordinance, paragraph 1. It is also gathered from the chapter "Odoardus" on payments and affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Covarrubias and Gutierrez follow. Nevertheless, with the consent of the creditor, a debtor can be admitted to the surrender of assets even if they do not confess the debt, but leave it

<column-break/>

to be settled afterward, as the gloss on the second to last law of the Digest says, along with Azo and Gregorio Lopez.

<margin>6</margin> For someone to surrender assets <term>cessio bonorum: the legal act of a debtor giving up all property to creditors to avoid prison</term> is nothing other than to profess that they are not solvent for all their debts, and therefore they surrender all their goods and hand them over to be divided, so that the debts may be satisfied as far as possible. They can retain absolutely nothing of their goods or the rights that belong to them, nor are the creditors bound to leave them anything, except for cheap clothes to cover themselves. Law 1, Title 15, Part 5 says: "except for linen cloths" <note>original: "si no los pannos de lino"</note>, and many doctors speak in agreement with that law. However, Portuguese law in the cited Title 89, the third to last paragraph, better commands that only the clothes they were wearing at the time of the surrender should be left to them, provided they are not of great value—which that law rightly leaves to the judge's discretion. And so I believe the custom is observed in this Kingdom of Castile, that the clothes they are wearing, or their daily clothes (as Covarrubias says), are not taken from them unless they are precious; in which case they can be exchanged for other mediocre ones. Juan Medina says the tools of their trade should be left to them if they are an artisan. However, Covarrubias and others rightly affirm that this would not be admitted in the secular court <note>original: "exteriori foro"</note>. Indeed, regarding the form of making the surrender of assets, the doctors observe that one must recur to the statutes and customs of each place. In common law, and regularly in private Kingdoms, it is not usually done with shameful words <note>Historically, some regions forced debtors to perform humiliating public acts to surrender assets; Molina notes this is not the standard here.</note>, as the same doctors affirm.

<margin>7</margin> The debtor is bound, when $\dagger$ surrendering assets, to manifest and hand over all their goods so they may be sold and the debts satisfied, hiding nothing at all, as the commonly accepted gloss affirms. This is also held in the Portuguese Ordinances, where it is commanded that the one surrendering assets must create a catalog signed with their own hand of all their goods, or have it made by a public notary, in which they simultaneously declare everything owed to them and what they owe others. This must be presented in court. It is established that if it is ever discovered that the debtor concealed any goods in that catalog, they shall not enjoy the privilege of surrender but shall be thrown into prison until they pay the debt in full. This is decreed according to common law and agrees with Law 4 at the end of Title 15, Part 5. For by that very act, the debt descends from a crime <note>Meaning the debt is now treated as resulting from the "crime" of fraud/theft.</note>, and that privilege has no place regarding it. Just as a debtor who purposefully squandered or alienated their goods so they would not have the means to pay does not enjoy the privilege of surrender. We have said the same regarding a nobleman hiding part of his goods during a prior dispute, showing that he does not enjoy the privilege, and thus can be thrown into prison for that debt.

<margin>8</margin> In the meantime, $\dagger$ while the goods of the debtor who surrendered them have not yet been sold, the ownership of them remains with the debtor...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the legal process for "cessio bonorum" (the surrender of assets) by a debtor. ### Ludovicus Molina, On Contracts
#### Page 862

It pertains to the debtor himself; therefore, if he wishes to defend himself and pay his creditors, he must be heard, and his goods must be returned to him. This is held in Law 3 of the Digest <note>original: "l. 3. ff. de cess. bonor."</note> on the surrender of assets, Law 2 of the Code <note>original: "l. 2. C. qui bon. ced. poss."</note>, and Law 2, Title 15, Part 5. Today, in this Kingdom of Castile, if the debt has been confessed or if the creditors otherwise have a ready execution of judgment, the debtor will not be heard unless he provides a guarantor for **saneamiento** <term>saneamiento: a legal guarantee or warranty that the obligation will be fulfilled</term>, as it is called—meaning a guarantee that the debts will be paid in full. Otherwise, he will not be heard, his goods will be sold off, and he himself will be detained in prison until he pays the debts in full.

<margin>9</margin> Although someone who has surrendered their assets does not remain entirely free from their creditors, but is obligated to pay the debts in full if they eventually become solvent or come into a "fatter fortune" <note>original: "pinguiemve fortunam," meaning significantly improved financial circumstances</note>, and can be compelled to do so by them in the external court <note>The "exteriori foro" refers to public, secular legal proceedings as opposed to the internal "court of conscience."</note>, two specific advantages are obtained from the surrender. First, the debtor is released from prison, and as long as they do not become solvent, they cannot be harassed; rather, they can defend themselves with the "exception of surrender" against creditors so effectively that a lawsuit cannot even be contested against them. This is supported by Law 4, paragraph *Sabinus* of the Digest <note>original: "ff. de cess. bon."</note>, Law 3, Title 15, Part 5 of the *Partidas*, the commentary of Gregorio Lopez, Covarruvias, and the common opinion of the doctors they cite. The second advantage is that when the debtor acquires some goods or reaches a "fatter fortune," they cannot be stripped of all acquired assets (as they were when they first surrendered everything). Instead, they must always be left with what, in the judgment of a prudent judge, is sufficient for their modest and suitable sustenance. Only the remainder can they be compelled to hand over for the payment of debts. Therefore, they are only bound to pay as much as they can "conveniently" do. This is found in Law 4 and the two following in the Digest, Law *ex contractu* in the Code, the Institutes <note>original: "§. vltim. inst. de act."</note>, and the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "lib. 3. Lusit. ord. tit. 89."</note>. This rule also holds in the court of conscience, as Covarruvias rightly says, regardless of what Hadrian and others cited by Covarruvias may have said to the contrary. Since this privilege is granted by civil law, and contracts were celebrated and debts contracted under that assumption, the debtor—while living after the surrender—is only bound in the court of conscience to pay the debts insofar as they can conveniently do so in the manner explained. Domingo de Soto agrees with this, though he does not distinguish between the time of surrender and the time after surrender when new assets are acquired.

<margin>10</margin> Furthermore, from the fact that a principal debtor has surrendered his assets, his guarantors are not released from the burden of paying the debts in full in his place. They can be compelled to pay just as if the principal debtor had not surrendered his assets. The legal exception for surrender <note>original: "exceptio cessionis"</note> applies only to the person of the debtor, not to the guarantors, who are precisely brought in so that if the principal debtor is insolvent, they themselves pay in his place.

<margin>11</margin> A person who wishes to surrender their assets can ask the creditor or creditors to grant him a grace period of five years <term>quinquennium: a five-year period</term>

<column-break/>

to pay, so that he does not have to surrender his assets. If there is only one creditor and he grants it, or if there are many and they grant it (according to what follows), then once that five-year period has passed, the debtor cannot surrender his assets, nor can he do so within the five years. But if, after the five years, he does not pay the debt, he can be thrown into prison until he pays in full. This is the common opinion of the doctors, followed by Gregorio Lopez and defined in the Portuguese Ordinances. When there are many creditors, all must be asked if they wish to grant this grace period. The majority can call the minority to meet in one place to deliberate on the matter, and this will prejudice the minority if they do not agree; it is enough to summon those who are absent. If the creditors to whom the majority of the total debt is owed consent to the five-year grace period, then even if they are fewer in number than the others—even if it is only one person against many, and even if the others have mortgages and priority in payment—the debtor obtains the grace period for all debts. However, if the sum of debt is equal between those who want to grant the grace period and those who do not, then the side that prevails in the *number* of creditors wins, even if the others have priority. How creditors are counted in this event (whether as one or many) is held in the law *si plures* of the Digest. If the creditors on both sides are equal in number and the sum of the debt is also equal, the side that grants the grace period prevails, as it is considered "more pious" <note>original: "tanquam magis pia," meaning the more merciful or charitable legal path.</note>. This is sanctioned in the Code and the Portuguese Ordinances. Those same ordinances state that if all creditors agree that the debtor should take a five-year grace period rather than surrendering assets, the debtor is bound to accept it and cannot choose to surrender; they say this choice belongs by right to the creditors. However, Gregorio Lopez affirms that the common opinion of the doctors—and rightly so—is that although the choice belongs to the creditors in the manner explained, this assumes the debtor *asks* for and *wants* the grace period. Since this was introduced for the favor of the debtor and not the creditors, if the debtor does not want the grace period but prefers to surrender his assets, he should be heard. Law 5 of the *Partidas* suggests that a grace period longer than five years can be requested, and if the majority of creditors agree, the minority must stand by that concession. However, according to common and Portuguese law, the majority cannot prejudice the minority in granting a grace period *beyond* five years, because the law only speaks of that specific timeframe.

<summary>This page discusses the legal protections for debtors who surrender their assets, specifically their right to keep enough for basic survival and the procedures for requesting a five-year grace period from creditors. It highlights the differences between Castilian and Portuguese law regarding when a debtor can be imprisoned and how creditor disputes over payment extensions are settled.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 57, Part 2
#### Chapter II

<margin>12</margin>
Under **common law** <note>original: "de iure communi," referring to the combined Roman and Canon law tradition</note>—specifically the Law "And his own heir" <note>original: "l. & suum hæredem," a reference to the Digest of Justinian</note> and the three laws following it regarding agreements—when there are many creditors of a deceased debtor, and the majority of them (either by the total amount of the debt or by the number of creditors, if the amounts are equal) agree that a portion of the debt should be remitted to the heir so that the remainder may be paid, that remission is valid. This holds even to the prejudice of the minority who refused to consent or those who were absent, provided they were properly summoned <note>The text cites Bartolus and Gregorius Lopez to confirm that a majority can bind a minority in debt settlements to ensure the estate is settled.</note>.

However, if some creditors hold a **privilege of preference** <term>privilegium praelationis: a legal right to be paid before other creditors</term>—provided they do not already have a specific pledge or a **mortgage** <term>hypotheca: a legal claim or lien against property used as security</term>, whether implied or expressed, on the deceased's goods—the remission made without their consent would be invalid regarding the value of the goods specifically pledged to them. 

While common law established these rules for heirs to encourage someone to accept an inheritance for the benefit of creditors, the legal expert **Gregorius Lopez** notes that this should not necessarily be extended to a **living debtor**. Nevertheless, Law 6 of the *Nueva Recopilación* <note>The "New Collection" of Spanish laws compiled in 1567</note> does extend this to living debtors, as it is similarly beneficial for creditors to reach an agreement. Where the law does not explicitly state this, I do not believe it should be extended, as the power to diminish another's legal right and debt against their will should not be granted lightly.

According to Law 2, Title 19, Book 5 of the *New Collection*, it is rightly decreed that merchants, money-changers, or their agents (known as "factors") who **abscond with merchandise or the goods of others** <note>original Spanish: "que se alcan con mercaderias o biens agenos"</note> are to be punished as thieves. No settlement, agreement, or remission made with them shall have any validity to the detriment of those whose goods they hold, and other heavy penalties are imposed upon them.

<margin>13</margin>
At this point, before we proceed further, we must include the specific regulations established in this **Kingdom of Castile** regarding the surrender of assets. In Law 4 and the five following laws (Title 16, Book 5 of the *New Collection*), it is ordained that the debtor must serve his creditors in an order to be explained below until the debts are satisfied through his service. The debtor must be handed over to them wearing an **iron collar** a finger's width in thickness <note>original: "torque ferreo" / "argollo de hierro de grosura de un dedo"</note>. He is required to wear this collar openly; if he is caught without it or hiding it under his clothes, he loses the privilege of having surrendered his assets and shall be cast into prison until the debts are paid in full. Furthermore, any creditor who catches him without the collar and has him imprisoned shall be preferred over all other creditors—even those with older claims—in receiving payment from the debtor's assets or labor. Law 6 and 7 add that if someone held in prison for debt

<column-break/>

does not pay within six months from the moment the debt was made clear, they are treated as if they had surrendered their assets under that law, even if they did not do so voluntarily. From that point, the aforementioned rules regarding the iron collar and being handed over to creditors for service are executed against them.

Law 8 adds that if a debtor who has surrendered his assets has many creditors, the one who has the legal right to be served first must request and have the collar placed on the debtor’s neck within six days of being notified. If he fails to do so, the judge must hand the debtor over to the next creditor in line, and so on, until all are processed. Law 9 follows, stating that when someone has been condemned for theft and has served their criminal penalty, they may still surrender their assets for the remaining civil debts owed to those from whom they stole; the fact that the debt arose from a crime does not prevent the surrender of assets.

The order to be followed in paying debts—which creditors are to be preferred, and how personal creditors with no special rights should be paid proportionally according to the size of their debt—was explained extensively in Disputation 536. Therefore, the price of the goods of one who surrenders his assets should be distributed according to that order. However, in this Kingdom of Castile, for the remaining debts, the debtor must be handed over to creditors for service in the same order: **mortgage creditors** are preferred over others, and among them, those with older or more privileged mortgages. Among personal creditors, those with a right of preference are first. Regarding other personal creditors, I believe the one who is prior in time should be preferred to be served first, followed by others in chronological order. This is because service is rendered successively; there is not a single mass of goods to be distributed simultaneously (in which case everyone would receive a proportional share).

<margin>Dubium 14</margin>
From what has just been said, a **doubt** <note>A "Dubium" is a formal legal or theological question for debate.</note> arises: Since a wife has an implied mortgage on all her husband's goods for her dowry and her **paraphernal goods** <term>paraphernalia: property owned by a married woman that is not part of her dowry</term>, and is usually preferred over his other creditors, if she proves that her husband squandered her dowry or other goods, can she oppose the other creditors and demand that he be handed over to **her** first, to serve her until the debt is compensated? 

Some deny this, arguing that the husband is the head of the wife and it is not fitting for him to serve her. Furthermore, a husband is only bound to his wife for as much as he can comfortably provide, and thus cannot be forced to serve her for a debt. However, the legal authority **Antonius Gomez** affirms the opposite in the second volume of his *Various Resolutions*.

It also raises the legal question of whether a wife can claim her husband's labor as a priority creditor for a lost dowry.</summary>

# Ludovici Molinæ / On Contracts

...chapter 11, number 53. Gutierrez, *On Confirmed Law* <note>original: "de iur. confir."</note>, part 1, chapter 18, number 7. He states that he has already prevailed in a case of this kind. Along with Bacca (whom Gutierrez cites) and Monterroso, he discusses the method for drafting a sentence and the order in which a person who has surrendered his assets <note>original: "cessit bonis," the legal act of giving up all property to creditors to avoid prison</note> must serve his creditors. He argues that it should be decreed that the debtor serve his wife first. Furthermore, during the time he serves her to earn the repayment of his debt, he should not be forced to wear an **iron collar** <note>original: "torquem ferreum"; a public mark of shame for insolvent debtors in 16th-century Spain</note>. This is out of favor for the wife, as it is unbecoming for him to serve her in such an ignominious manner.

I approve of this opinion. In the repayment of her debt, a wife should not be in a worse condition than other creditors. By removing the indecency of the service, he serves her as a husband and is useful to her, rather than serving as if to a mistress. This is what the wife requires, and it will be useful to the husband, as he is meanwhile freed from a harsher and more shameful servitude to others. Although a husband is only bound to his wife to the extent that he can conveniently pay <note>original: "nisi in quantum comode facere potuerit"</note>, this is understood to apply when the matter is solely between him and his wife, and the husband does not wish to pay more. It is different, however, when the husband—to be freed from greater shame and harsher creditors—does not refuse to pay his wife in this manner for his own and his wife's benefit, provided she wishes and requests it.

To resolve the following doubt, observe that a **monetary debt** <note>original: "debitum pecuniarium"</note>, or a debt of some other external thing, can arise from a **wrong** <note>original: "ex delicto," referring to a crime or tort</note> in two ways:

First, as a loss caused to a plaintiff by the fault of the defendant—for example, because the defendant stole something from the plaintiff, burned his crops, or caused some other damage. The debt for these things (or their appraised value) stems from the wrong and is owed to the plaintiff both in the **civil court** and in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "in exteriori, atque in conscientię foro"; meaning both legal and moral obligations</note>, even without waiting for a sentence, as it constitutes the plaintiff's own interest and property. We can also include in this type of debt those which, although arising from a contract (such as a deposit or similar), were later mixed with a "wrong"—for example, when the debt began to be unjustly denied to the plaintiff.

The second way something is owed from a wrong is as a **penalty** <note>original: "poena"</note> justly imposed for the crime. This penalty is sometimes applied to the **treasury** <note>original: "fisco"</note> and sometimes to the offended party. For instance, when theft is punished by a double or quadruple penalty to be paid to the party; in that case, the "simple" amount (the value of the item) included in the total penalty is the plaintiff's interest (the first type of debt), while the additional increase is a debt of this second type. Or, when someone who has insulted another by word or deed is punished with a monetary fine. If this fine is, in part, compensation for damage to honor or reputation (which in my judgment remains with the affected party), it shares the nature of the first type of debt. The remainder, imposed by reason of the crime and guilt, belongs to the second type.

Observe next that the laws decree that when a monetary penalty (or other external good) is imposed on someone, if the defendant has no means to pay, the judge must convert it into **corporal punishment** <note>original: "poenam corporalem"</note>. This includes the penalty of exile and similar punishments used to afflict and punish the defendant, even if no external good 

<column-break/>

thereby reaches the treasury or the injured party. That a monetary fine must be converted into physical punishment when the defendant cannot pay is expressly stated in Law 1, final paragraph of the Digest *On Punishments* <note>original: "l. 1. §. vlt. ff. de pœn."</note>; Law "If anyone that which" of the Digest *On the Jurisdiction of all Judges*; the final law of the Digest *On Summoning to Court*; and the final law at the end of the Code *On Violating Sepulchers*. This is affirmed by Bartolus, Panormitanus, and the common opinion of the doctors, which is followed by Covarruvias, Gutierrez, and Gregorius Lopez. 

These laws speak not only of when the penalty is applied to the treasury (on which all doctors agree), but also when it is applied to the private party. Indeed, the chapter "An end to litigation" <note>original: "c. finem litibus"</note> seems to suggest this applies even to the first type of debt (compensation). However, this must be understood to apply only if the plaintiff consents. Otherwise, as the doctors commonly agree, that chapter must be interpreted as referring to a "pure penalty" (the second type of debt), as Covarruvias explains in his 8th note. 

In note 6, Covarruvias rightly rejects the opinion of those who claim that when a formal, shameful surrender of assets occurs according to local customs and statutes, the debtor is no longer bound to the debts in either the civil or the moral court—as if the debts were "exchanged" for that mark of shame. No equity allows unjust creditors to be deprived of their right to their debts merely because of that ignominy. Rather, that shame is inflicted by public authority on those who surrender their assets (while preserving the creditors' rights) so that debtors might fear falling into such a state, which is ruinous to others. 

The doctors do not agree, however, whether a monetary penalty applied to a private party can be converted into corporal punishment without the consent of the plaintiff when the debtor is insolvent. Panormitanus and others deny this, saying one must wait until the debtor comes into a **greater fortune** <term>pinguem fortunam: a legal term for when a previously insolvent debtor acquires enough wealth to pay their old debts</term> and then pays the party.

Others affirm it. However, I believe we must say the following: regarding that which is strictly a penalty (the second type of debt), it can be converted into corporal punishment even against the will of the party to whom it was to be applied. The laws teach this clearly, and although laws might generally establish a monetary fine out of equity to benefit the offended party, they can establish the opposite—especially when the defendant's poverty prevents payment—so that crimes do not go unpunished and defendants may be more quickly released from prison. 

But regarding that which is included in the penalty as **compensation for damage** (the first type of debt), I believe that against the will of the party, it neither should nor can be converted into corporal punishment. Instead, the defendants should then be handed over to serve either the plaintiffs or others until the debt is compensated. 

Therefore, I do not approve of the judgment of certain judges (which Covarruvias mentions at the end of his 8th note) who condemn those imprisoned for private debts arising from a wrong to serve as **rowers in the galleys** <note>original: "remigandum... in triremibus"</note> for a time, so that there...

<summary>Molina discusses the legal treatment of insolvent debtors, arguing that while public penalties can be converted to physical punishment, private debts for compensation should be settled through labor rather than corporal punishment or galley slavery.</summary>
<keywords>cessio bonorum, surrender of assets, debt, corporal punishment, restitution, wife's dowry, iron collar, galley slavery, Covarruvias, Gutierrez, legal liability</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the surrender of assets (cessio bonorum). The previous page ended discussing how a husband might serve his wife to repay a debt without the indignity of a public iron collar. This page shifts to whether this legal relief applies to debts arising from crimes (delicts) versus private contracts, and examines specific royal ordinances in Castile and Portugal.</meta>

...so that they may earn their wages: unless those wages are applied to the creditors, and they are simultaneously and justly punished with that penalty for the fault of their crime, separate from the damage caused to others.

<margin>17</margin> Having established these points, it is debated whether the **surrender of assets** <note>Latin: *cessio bonorum*; a legal process where an insolvent debtor avoids prison by giving all their property to creditors.</note> takes place for a debt arising from a crime. Gregorio Lopez <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> states that if the debt is the civil damages <note>Latin: *interesse*; the financial compensation for loss or injury.</note> owed to the injured party, the surrender of assets is permitted. He incorrectly cites Panormitanus and others for this opinion. Although these authors affirm that such civil damages should not be converted into corporal punishment if the defendant is insolvent, they do not affirm that the surrender of assets applies to that debt. Covarrubias and Gutierrez seem to embrace Lopez’s opinion, similarly attributing it to Panormitanus and others. Consequently, Lopez, Covarrubias, and Gutierrez affirm that if a cleric owes these same civil damages from a crime, the decree of the chapter **Odoardus** <note>A canon law rule protecting clerics from being sued for more than they can afford to pay, ensuring they don't fall into beggary.</note> applies: he should only be sued for as much as he can conveniently pay, after deducting what is necessary for his own support.

However, I believe it must be said that, according to common law, if a debt arises from a crime—even if it is the civil damages owed to the party—the surrender of assets does not apply. In the case of a cleric who owes this, the decree of *Odoardus* does not apply; rather, he can be sued for more than he can conveniently pay, without leaving him a **basic living allowance** <note>Latin: *competentia alimenta*.</note>. This is affirmed by Panormitanus, Jason, and Faber, and is the common opinion of the doctors. This is also the law in the Ordinances of Portugal, where it is explicitly stated that this applies even to a debt that began as a contract but involved a crime in its execution. Common laws grant these privileges only to debtors in purely civil matters, not to debtors who have mixed a crime into the matter. 

In the Kingdom of Castile, however, it has been rightly decreed that even if the debt arises from a crime, if it is strictly the civil damages owed to the party, the surrender of assets is permitted. This is treated as an exception to the common law. This law does not extend to the penalty or fine applied to the injured party because of the crime itself. Covarrubias reports that this was decreed long ago in the Kingdom of France. Perhaps, since the surrender of assets has been extended in these two kingdoms to debts from crimes regarding civil damages, clerics in those kingdoms will also enjoy the privilege of the chapter *Odoardus* regarding those same debts.

<margin>18</margin> In this Kingdom of Castile, it is decreed that tax farmers <note>Latin: *conductores redituum regiorum*; individuals who "rented" the right to collect royal taxes.</note>, their guarantors, and those they call **endorsers** <note>Spanish: *abonadores*; those who vouch for the financial stability of another.</note> cannot surrender their assets for debts related to their tax collection contracts. They must swear they will not surrender their assets for those debts nor seek a release from that oath; any such surrender is considered void even if they perform it.

In Portugal, if something is owed to the King, even if it is a purely civil debt, there is no place for the surrender of assets. Furthermore, if a debtor hides in the houses of noblemen to avoid being sued for a purely civil debt or to avoid responding to citations, he is not permitted to surrender his assets for that debt. In the same kingdom, to prevent fraud,

<column-break/>

it is decreed that no debtor by contract can surrender assets unless he first proves that at the time of the contract, he possessed enough assets to safely pay the creditor, but that afterward, by misfortune and without his own fault, he became unable to pay. Alternatively, he must prove that at the time of the contract, he disclosed the smallness of his assets and the existing obligations upon them to the creditors.

<margin>19</margin> Finally, there is a question of whether one who renounces the right to surrender assets—at least when accompanied by an oath—can nonetheless surrender assets in cases permitted by law. The common opinion, which Covarrubias mentions and Gutierrez follows, asserts that one who renounces the surrender of assets without an oath can still surrender them. I incline toward this view, not because the contrary would obligate a person to perpetual prison (which conflicts with human liberty), for it does not follow that if one cannot surrender assets, they must stay in prison forever; they might eventually pay or be freed some other way. 

The legitimate reason is that this privilege was granted for the **common good** and the benefit of the state: so that men would not be held in prison forever with little or no gain for the creditors. It should be judged through **equity** <note>Latin: *epicheia*; the principle of interpreting a law according to its spirit when a literal application would be unjust.</note> that the privilege was not granted in such a way as to allow it to be renounced; for if it were renounced, the privilege would be as if it had never been granted. It would be an equal indecency if a debtor, having renounced the privilege, were held perpetually in prison, just as it would be if the privilege did not exist at all. 

Furthermore, even if someone had bound himself by an oath to pay the debt, he would not be hindered from seeking a surrender of assets if he were truly unable to pay. By that surrender, the debtor would actually become more capable of eventually paying the debt rather than less, and therefore the surrender is not an obstacle to payment. However, if someone renounced the surrender of assets *with an oath*, binding himself not to seek it, then since it is not inherently evil, he could not seek it unless his life were at risk. Nevertheless, in the Kingdom of Castile, after six months in prison following a liquid debt, the judge is required by law to grant and execute the surrender even if the debtor does not ask for it. This is because the renunciation and the oath of the debtor do not block the force of that law, which originates not from the debtor's will, but from the Prince, who established it for the common good even against the debtor's resistance.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal remedies for financial losses. While the previous page focused on the "surrender of assets" (cessio bonorum) for insolvent debtors and its application to crimes, this page shifts to the specific legal protections afforded to minors, particularly the remedy of "restoration to original status" (restitutio in integrum) when they are harmed by contracts made before age 25.</meta>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts #

3 *The benefit of **restoration to original status** <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy where a court cancels a contract and returns both parties to their state before the deal was made</note> is granted to minors even within the four-year period after they have completed their twenty-fifth year.*
4 *Anyone who obtains a **pardon of age** <note>original: "aetatis veniam"; a royal decree allowing a minor to be treated as a legal adult before age 25</note> before their twenty-fifth year loses the benefit of restoration to original status.*
5 *A minor finding themselves harmed even by the actions of a **tutor** <note>original: "tutor"; a guardian for younger children</note> or another person administering their goods, has the right to restoration to original status; or they may even sue for damages against that same tutor or **curator** <note>original: "curator"; a guardian for older minors</note>.*
6 *Restoration to original status is not granted for a contract that is naturally or legally void; instead, the case concerns the nullity of the contract itself.*
7 *A minor finding themselves harmed by the acceptance of a harmful inheritance, or the rejection of a profitable one, is restored to their original status once the harm is proven.*
8 *An adopted or **arrogated** <note>original: "arrogatus"; a specific form of Roman adoption where an adult or independent person was adopted</note> minor has the same benefit of restoration as a legitimate and natural minor.*
9 *In which cases restoration to original status is not granted to a minor. See also number 17.*
10 *Any slight harm is not sufficient for a minor to obtain the benefit of restoration; the harm must be significant.*
11 *A minor is granted restoration even if the harm consists in **lost profit** <note>original: "lucro cessante"; money they failed to make because of the contract</note>.*
12 *The harm must be proven by the minor for restoration to be granted.*
13 *How a minor harmed in an **onerous contract** <note>original: "contractu oneroso"; a contract where both parties give and receive something of value</note> is to be restored.*
14 *The case in which a minor is not restored to original status after making a donation.*
15 *A minor receiving a loan and finding themselves harmed has the right to restoration, but with the burden of paying back as much of that money as actually made them wealthier.*
16 *A minor harmed in the renunciation or exchange of an **ecclesiastical benefice** <note>original: "beneficij ecclesiastici"; a church office with an attached income</note> has the right to restoration, even if the matter is no longer intact.*
18 *The benefit of restoration to original status also passes to the heirs of the minor.*
19 *Whether the benefit of restoration is given to a minor even against a third-party possessor.*
20 *The **Alcuala** <note>original: "Alcuala"; a Spanish sales tax</note> is not refunded, even if the contract is rescinded through the benefit of restoration.*
21 *A guarantor for a minor is not released by the rescission of a contract through the benefit of restoration.*
22 *In what ways the benefit of restoration can be sought, and before which judge. See also number 23.*
24 *Before which judge restoration may be sought: whether in the place of the contract or the place of residence.*
25 *Before which judge a Church harmed by a contract made with a layperson may seek restoration.*
26 *A tutor and others having legal administration may seek restoration on behalf of those whose goods they manage, even without a specific mandate. This fails in other cases unless they have a special mandate. See number 27 and understand this as explained in number 29.*
28 *Only a father can seek restoration without a mandate; other relatives cannot.*
30 *A general mandate is sufficient for defending against someone seeking restoration, but a special mandate is required to seek it.*
31 *The benefit of restoration belonging to a minor does not profit an adult if the matter in question is **divisible**,*

<column-break/>

*even if it belongs to both as an undivided whole. But what if the thing is **indivisible**, such as a servitude? See number 32.*
33 *If a minor, having become an adult, ratifies what they did in their minority, they lose the benefit of restoration. The same applies if the minor confirmed the contract with an oath. See number 34.*

It remains for us to speak about **restoration to original status** regarding contracts or quasi-contracts, which alone pertains to our present subject. Regarding restoration in matters of judicial proceedings, it will be discussed more conveniently in the fifth treatise, where the order of legal trials will be addressed.

<margin>1</margin> **Restoration to original status** is a remedy by which a minor who has been harmed is, out of equity, restored to their former state and rights, along with others to whom the law is found to have granted this, following the minor's example. And this benefit, from its primary origin, is granted to anyone of either sex—whether they are still under parental authority <note>original: "filius familias"</note> or not—who finds themselves notably harmed by a contract or quasi-contract validly celebrated (according to what was said at length in discussions 224 and 261) during the time of their minority. This applies whether the contract was made by the minor themselves, or by their parent, tutor, or curator, and whether it was made with a judge’s decree or without it. So it is held in the first law and following in the Digest on *restoration to original status*; in the first law and following in the Digest on *minors*; in the first law and following in title 19 of the sixth *Partida*; and in the sixth law regarding *one having a curator*, and those preceding and following in the Code on *restoration to original status*. See also the second law, the law beginning *liquidè*, joined with the first law of the Code on *the property of minors*, and the final law of the Code on *the guarantors of minors*. In these laws, the discussion concerns the sale of property by judicial decree, and restoration is granted to the harmed minor. See also the law *even if in part* at the beginning of the Digest on *minors*, and the decree on *restoration to original status*, where the discussion concerns a sale made by a father with the consent of his minor children. It is commanded that if the sale was made without the required legal formalities because no judge's decree intervened, it should be declared null; if, however, it was made with the required formalities, and it is proved that the minors were harmed, they should be restored to their original status. The same is held in other laws and was stated in the two cited discussions, and the common opinion of the doctors of law agrees. All these things, however, must be explained more fully and clearly.

<margin>2</margin> And so, to begin with minority: the time of minority, for this purpose and for the appointment of a tutor or curator, is the period up to the completion of the twenty-fifth year. This is held in the first law, final paragraph, of the Digest on *minors*, and more expressly in the third law, the paragraph beginning *minorem*, of the same title, where it is held that this time must be calculated from the moment of birth until the very moment in which the twenty-fifth year is completed on the final day. Furthermore, **leap years** <note>original: "bis sextiles annos"</note> are to be calculated with the extra day they have compared to other years. If, however, someone is born on either of the two days which in a leap year are called the "sixth day before the Calends of March" <note>The Romans added the leap day by doubling the 24th of February, the *sextus Kalendas Martii*. Thus, a leap year was a "bis-sextile" year.</note>, then, since both days are counted as one, the year is completed on the sixth day before the Calends of March of the following year, at the same hour and moment corresponding to the day and moment in which they were born. All these rules are similarly to be observed in calculating the year of profession for religious orders, and in calculating the years by which contracts end, or the deadlines in which something must be paid according to a contract. But if the twenty-fifth year of someone’s age is completed on the sixth day before the Calends of March in a leap year, then it is judged to be completed on the second day, which is the sixth before the Calends...

<summary>This page introduces the legal remedy of 'restitutio in integrum,' which allows minors under 25 to cancel harmful contracts. It details the specific conditions for this relief and the precise method for calculating a person's age, including adjustments for leap years.</summary>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 573 ###

The calculation of the year is said to fall on the Calends of March <note>The first day of March. In leap years, Roman law treated the two "sixth" days of February as a single day for legal purposes</note>, at the exact point of the hour corresponding to the hour of the day of the year in which the person was born. The reason for this is that both days are considered as one; and because the second day completes the four preceding years, which were lacking for the completion of the Sun's full circle through the zodiac. This same rule must be observed in other computations of full years.

<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, this remedy <note>The "restoration to original status" (restitutio in integrum), which voids a contract to protect a vulnerable party</note>, although it applies only to minors for contracts or quasi-contracts entered into during their minority—if they find themselves harmed in the manner already explained and to be explained further—and not for contracts made after they have left their minority, as stated in the Code of Justinian <note>original: "l. si minorem. C. de in integ. rest."</note> and the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. 2. tit. 19. par. 6."; the primary law code of medieval Spain</note>. This matter is clear enough in itself, as this is why it is called the "remedy of minors." Nevertheless, they can implore this remedy, and it ought to be granted to them, not only during the entire time they are minors, but also for a **four-year period** afterward; namely, until they have completed the twenty-ninth year of their age. This is affirmed by the Code <note>original: "l. vlt. C. de tēp. in integ. rest."</note>, the Partidas, and the common opinion cited by Antonio Gómez. Moreover, if it is doubtful whether a contract was celebrated within the time of minority, the burden of proof lies with the one seeking restoration; but if it is doubtful whether the four-year grace period has already passed, the burden of proof lies with the opponent to show that the time has expired. In such a case, this four-year period is considered "useful time" <note>original: "tempus utile"; a legal term for time that only counts days when the court is open and the person is able to act</note>. Thus, if due to the opponent's fraud, violence, or deceit, or due to the minor's absence or another just impediment, the restoration could not be sought during that time, that impediment is not counted against them, and the time must be filled up to a full four years of unimpeded opportunity. The same is understood for the four-year period granted to the Church and others for seeking restoration.

<margin>4</margin> When someone has obtained a **pardon of age** <note>original: "veniam ætatis"; a legal grant from the sovereign allowing a minor to be treated as an adult before age 25</note> before their twenty-fifth year, as explained in Disputation 224, then the benefit of restoration to original status is not granted to them for a contract or quasi-contract made *after* obtaining that pardon. From that point on, regarding this benefit, they are considered as if they were an adult. And although they cannot alienate <note>To sell, gift, or transfer ownership</note> immovable property <note>Real estate or land</note> until they have completed their twenty-fifth year without a judge’s decree, if they do alienate it with a judge’s decree after obtaining the pardon, they do not enjoy the privilege of restoration for that sale. If, however, they alienate it *without* a judge's decree, the contract is void by the law itself, and they do not even need the remedy of restoration.

<column-break/>

But if, before obtaining the pardon of age, they had entered into a contract or quasi-contract by which they were harmed, and the benefit of restoration would have been available to rescind it, then the four-year period given to minors to seek restoration starts to run from the moment the pardon of age was obtained. This is shown in Disputation 224 and is consistent with the Code and the Ordinances of Portugal <note>original: "Lusit. ord. tit. 67. §. cauendo"</note>.

Even if a **tutor** <note>A guardian for children under puberty</note> or another who has the administration of a minor’s goods sells something belonging to the minor out of necessity and without fault, in good faith, or otherwise disposes of it—if, nevertheless, the minor <margin>5</margin> finds themselves harmed by that sale or disposition, the restoration to original status is granted. This is held in the Digest <note>original: "l. tutor vergentibus in princ. ff. de minoribus"</note>. However, when the harm to the minor in that alienation resulted from the fault of the tutor or **curator** <note>A guardian for those between puberty and age 25</note>, then the choice lies with the minor: they may sue the tutor or curator for damages, or they may seek restoration to original status against the person to whom the property was sold. By choosing one path, they are not prohibited from attempting the other. However, if the minor obtains what is owed to them through one path, they cannot seek it from the other, as the Gloss rightly notes regarding a Church harmed by the fault of its prelate or administrator. Yet, if the Church recovered its property from the possessor through restoration, it could still sue the administrator for a penalty, though not for damages. Gregorio López <note>A famous Spanish jurist (1496–1560) known for his commentary on the Siete Partidas</note> says that if a minor sued their guardian for damages, the guardian's right to seek restoration against the possessor could be ceded to them, provided the guardian was only at fault and not acting with deceit. If a minor acted through a **proxy** <note>original: "procuratorem"; a legal agent</note> and was harmed, they do not receive restoration unless they first sue the proxy for damages and the proxy is found to be insolvent. This same rule applies to the Church: if it finds itself harmed by the administration of its prelate or another, it can sue them or their heirs for damages, or it can act against the one to whom the property was alienated.

It also clarifies the minor's right to seek redress when a guardian's actions result in financial loss, drawing parallels to the legal protections afforded to the Church.</summary>

# Luis de Molina, On Contracts #

The petition for restoration to original status <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy that voids a contract and returns parties to their original positions</note> follows the same rule. Along with Joannes de Platea, Gregorio López affirms this in the same place regarding the state treasury, a city, or any other community of a town who find themselves harmed by the sale of property or by another contract involving the administration of their communal goods. Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> agrees in the cited Chapter 1. For these communities, as we shall see, also enjoy the privilege of restoration to original status. Gregorio López, in the cited second gloss, agrees with all the points in this section.

<margin>6</margin>
It was stated above that this benefit is granted to anyone who finds themselves harmed by a contract or "quasi-contract" <note>An obligation that arises from an act that is not a formal contract but is treated like one by the law</note> that was validly executed during their minority. However, if that contract or quasi-contract was executed invalidly and is therefore null and void from the start, the person does not need this benefit, nor is it granted to them. Instead, they take action based on the nullity of the contract, or by a claim to recover the property, or for damages. Or, if they have provided nothing on their part, they protect themselves by an exception <note>A legal defense</note> asserting that the contract was null, so that they are not forced to execute it. This applies, for example, if a contract to sell immovable property was made without a judge's decree, or if a minor who has a guardian celebrated a contract without that guardian's authority, or in other instances where a minor's contract is null by law. This is held in the Code <note>original: "l. 3. C. de in integ. rest. l. 2. C. de præd. minor."</note> and the Portuguese Ordinances <note>original: "lib. 3. Lusit. ord. tit. 86. §. 2."</note>, as discussed in Disputation 224.

<margin>7</margin>
It was also mentioned that this applies to a "quasi-contract." This occurs if a minor finds themselves harmed by accepting a damaging inheritance <note>One where the debts exceed the value of the assets</note>, in which a quasi-contractual relationship with the creditors and legatees of the deceased is perceived (as explained at the end of Disputation 553). It also applies if they have rejected an inheritance that would have been useful and profitable, even if they did so with the authority of a guardian; they are restored to their original status. This is supported by the Digest <note>original: "l. ait Prætor. §. non solum. 1. ver. sed etsi. l. & si sine. §. restitutus. l. quod si minor. §. Sceuola, ff. de minor."</note> and the Code <note>original: "leg. 2. C. si minor ab hæredi se abstinuert"</note>, and the Siete Partidas <note>original: "l. 7. tit. 19. par. 6."</note>, as well as other laws cited by Antonio Gómez. Nevertheless, the harm to the minor must be proven, and the creditors of the deceased must be summoned when the case involves abandoning an inheritance already accepted. If all or some of them are absent, they must be summoned by public proclamation and given a three-month waiting period. In the meantime, the judge must appoint a curator for the inheritance to look after it and prepare an inventory. This is held in the Code and the works of Maranta and Baldus. The gloss on the cited law says that legatees <note>People named in a will to receive specific gifts, rather than the whole estate</note> must also be summoned. If any part of the inheritance was lost through the "imbecility" <note>In this context, meaning the natural lack of judgment or business experience expected of a youth</note> of the minor, such that they were not made wealthier by it, the restored minor is not held liable for that loss; rather, the loss falls upon the inheritance. The minor is similarly restored if they reject a profitable legacy. Likewise, if a minor has the right to choose between several things—whether by a will or some other reason—and they choose the worse option through lack of foresight, choosing what a prudent person would not have chosen, 

<column-break/>

restoration to original status is granted to them. It is otherwise if prudent people would have chosen that option (or at least been indifferent) at the time, but it was later discovered that another option would have been more useful and better, as will be more evident from what follows. This is held in the Digest and the Partidas. Antonio Gómez rightly notes, following Baldus, that the same applies if others are dividing property with a minor and let the minor choose which part they want; if the minor finds themselves harmed in the manner explained, restoration is granted. However, if the parts are assigned by drawing lots in good faith, even if the minor happens to get the worse part, restoration is not granted. This is because the minor was not harmed in the agreement or the consent to use lots, but it later happened by chance that they received the worse share, just as they might have received the better one.

<margin>8</margin>
Even a minor who has been adopted or "arrogated" <note>original: "arrogatus"; a form of adoption in Roman law where the person being adopted was previously legally independent</note> may seek and obtain restoration if they later find themselves harmed by that status—perhaps because their property is being poorly managed, or they are being imbued with "bad morals," or for some other reason. This is supported by the Digest and the Partidas. However, if a minor between twenty and twenty-five years of age sells themselves into slavery in order to share in the price, restoration is not granted, because they lose their entire legal status by losing their liberty.

<margin>9</margin>
Regarding a minor entering a religious order <note>original: "ingressu... in religionem"</note>: because the minor is not considered "harmed" by this, restoration is not granted, as Panormitanus and Gregorio López have noted. Furthermore, restoration does not take place in marriage, because once a marriage is celebrated, it is indissoluble by its very nature. This is the view of Covarruvias, Antonio Gómez, and others they cite. However, regarding harm concerning a promised dowry or other financial matters connected to the marriage, restoration to original status does take place, as these same doctors rightly affirm.

<margin>10</margin>
It was also stated above that restoration is granted for a contract validly celebrated during minority if the minor finds themselves "notably harmed." To grant restoration, "enormous harm" <note>original: "enormis læsio"; typically defined as losing more than half the value</note> is not required; it does not have to exceed half of the just price or value. It is enough for the harm to be much less, as Emmanuel Acosta rightly weighs and proves. Nevertheless, any tiny loss is not sufficient; rather, in the judgment of a prudent judge, the harm must be "notable." This means that, considering the matter at hand, it should not be considered as nothing or almost nothing. The larger the total sum of the contract, the wider the range of what might be considered "nothing." For example, if a contract involves property worth a thousand gold coins, a loss of four, six, eight, ten, fifteen, or twenty coins will be considered as nothing. However, a loss of ten coins would be sufficient to seek restoration if the contract involved property worth only one hundred gold coins. This is held in the Digest...

# Second Treatise, Disputation 57, Part 3 #

regarding restoration to original status; this is affirmed by Panormitanus <note>Nicholas de Tudeschis, a major 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in Chapter 1, "On restoration to original status," number 8; and by Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, Book 1, Chapter 3, number 11, where he weighs the matter learnedly and prudently. Observe, however, that in some particular outcomes, for restoration to original status to be granted, it is required that the harm <note>original: "laesio"</note> not only be something that is not considered as nothing (or almost nothing) in the manner explained, but also that "great harm" be required according to the judgment of a prudent man. 

Specifically, when a minor’s judicial pledge <note>Property seized by court order to guarantee payment</note> is to be sold by public authority to pay that which the minor was condemned to pay: although the minor may later be restored against the sentence and the money paid must be returned to him, the minor is not restored to his original status against the sale itself unless a great loss resulted to the minor from the sale of the pledge. This is found in the law *Si ex causa*, at the beginning, joined with the final gloss there which says that this is a unique feature of that outcome. <note>Digest, Title: "On Minors"</note> The same applies if the property of a minor is sold for any other necessary cause by the authority of the law, as found in the penultimate law of the same title in the Digest; Covarruvias (cited above) and others affirm that this is unique to those outcomes.

This † must also be observed: that restoration to original status is granted to a minor harmed in the explained manner not only if the harm consists in an actual loss <term>damno emergente; financial loss actually incurred</term> arising for the minor himself, but also if it consists in a lost profit. <term>lucro cessante; profit that was expected but not realized</term> This is held in the law *Ait praetor*, the final paragraph. <note>Digest, Title: "On Minors"</note> where Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> says: 
> *Today we use a certain law, so that minors are helped even regarding lost profit.* 

The same is found in the law *Non omnia* of the same title; it is gathered clearly from the Chapter *Constitutus*, "On restoration to original status," and affirmed by Bartolus and the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez reports and follows in *Various Resolutions*, Volume 2, Chapter 14, number 1. Learnedly, Emmanuel Acosta (Part 2, from number 49, especially from number 57) observes that the restoration for that harm consisting of actual loss is more privileged than that consisting of lost profit. For that reason, whether or not the matter concerning which the minor is to be restored remains intact, restoration to original status is granted to him when the harm consists in actual loss. However, when it consists in lost profit, restoration is not granted if the matter is not intact (as far as what has been sold or disposed of, even if money or something else was obtained from it, as Panormitanus affirms in the place cited immediately). Instead, he is only restored if the matter is intact. 

And in this way, Emmanuel Acosta understands and learnedly explains, reconciling it with other laws, the law *Quod si minor*, paragraph *Scaevola*. <note>Digest, Title: "On Minors"</note> There, the discussion concerns the harm to a minor from lost profit, and he is barred from restoration to original status if the inheritance which he refused (and which for that reason passed to a substitute heir) is not intact, but has been sold off by the substitute who sold many things and obtained money from it. For that which is no longer intact, he is not restored. Panormitanus had previously handed down this doctrine in Chapter *Ex parte*, number 15, "On the restoration of stolen goods," as Emmanuel Acosta noted in the same place at number 62, and Covarruvias follows it in *Various Resolutions*, Book 1, Chapter 5, number 2.

<margin>12</margin> For him † who seeks restoration on the grounds that he was harmed while he was a minor, it belongs to him to prove both that he was a minor at the time he was harmed, and also the harm itself; otherwise, restoration is not granted to him. <note>Citing multiple laws from the Digest and Code: *Ait praetor*, *Non solum*, *Verisimile*, etc.</note> 

<column-break/>

This is joined with the law *Minoribus* in the Code, title "On restoration to original status," and Laws 2 and 6 at the end of Title 19, Part 6 <note>Referring to the Siete Partidas, the Spanish legal code</note>. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gómez (cited above at the end of number 5) reports and follows. However, proving the exception—that the four-year period granted beyond the age of minority for seeking restoration has passed—belongs to the adversary who raises that objection, as is held in the cited law *Si minorem*, and as was said above.

<margin>13</margin> If a minor was harmed by a contract of sale, exchange, lease, or any other burdensome <note>original: "oneroso"; a contract where both parties have obligations</note> agreement, a distinction must be made. For † if the harm was placed in the fact that it was not expedient to sell, exchange, or lease the property, etc., and this is proven, then restoration to original status is available and granted to rescind <note>To void or cancel</note> the contract, to reclaim the property, and to restore the minor to the state in which he was in that regard before the contract was celebrated, provided the minor's property still exists. Or, if he was given something that was not expedient for him to have, he returns what he received and the price is restored to him. 

But if the harm was only placed in the price or value, and it is proven that he was harmed in the price, even if the harm was not beyond or below half of the just price <note>original: "dimidium iusti pretij"; referring to the legal doctrine of *laesio enormis* where a contract can be rescinded if the price is off by more than 50%</note>—provided it was not so small that it should be ignored according to what was said above—then the minor is restored to the full value up to the range of the lowest just price. Or, if he gave more for the price than the thing was worth, the increase is returned to him up to the limits of what is just. 

The reason for both assertions is that restoration to original status only repairs the total harm, but not that in which the one being restored was not harmed. Both assertions are clear from the law *Si res*, paragraph 1, of the Digest, title "On the right of dowries." And both are affirmed by the final gloss on the law *Si quidem* in the Code, title "On the property of minors," and with it Bartolus in that place, and Panormitanus in the Chapter *Constitutus*, "On restoration to original status," at the final number. They say that when restoration is only to the amount of the price—because the minor or the Church was only harmed in the amount of the price—then the choice belongs to the buyer: either to increase the price up to the limits of what is just, or to return the property and receive back the price, rescinding the contract entirely. This is because perhaps the buyer would not have wanted to buy the thing at such a high price from the beginning; this is the same way it is arranged when someone buys a thing for less than half the just price, as was said in that place. 

Antonio Gómez also reports and follows the common opinion of the doctors on this matter in Volume 2, *Various Resolutions*, Chapter 14, number 1, corollary 1. Covarruvias also agrees with these in *Various Resolutions*, Book 1, Chapter 3, number 14, in the latest edition. In this place, observe: if a minor is simultaneously harmed in that he sold or exchanged the property at all, and also in that he sold or exchanged it for less than half the just price, he can then act indifferently either by the remedy of Law 2 of the Code ("On rescinding a sale") or by the remedy of restoration to original status. However, if he acts by the remedy of Law 2, it will be in the power of the buyer either to increase the price or to rescind the contract, as the buyer himself prefers. But if he acts by the remedy of restoration to original status, he himself may act indifferently to rescind the contract and compel the buyer to do so, or act to have the price increased. If, however, he acts for this second option, it will be in the power of the buyer (as was said) to refuse to increase the price and instead choose to rescind the contract.

If a minor donated something, he is considered harmed by that very donation, and therefore he can seek
