# Ludovico Molina on Contracts #

14 **restoration to original status.** <note>original: "restitutionem in integrum"; this was a legal remedy allowing a minor to undo a contract that had harmed them financially.</note> An exception is made unless the minor † gave the gift for a just, rational, or useful cause: for instance, if the gift is remunerative <note>A gift given to repay a favor or service.</note> and proportionate to the services and benefits received, or if it is a moderate betrothal gift, considering the quality of the person, the size of the estate, and the custom of the region. Indeed, from these and similar gifts, a minor is not considered "harmed," and therefore restoration to original status is not granted to him, as held in Law 1 of the Code, *If against a gift* <note>Codex 2.30.1</note>, and Law *When several*, section *When a tutor*, in the Digest, *On the administration of tutors*. <note>Digest 26.7.12.3</note> This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish jurist.</note> records and follows in the cited corollary 2, number 1.
   When something has been paid to a minor without the authority of a guardian and a judge, or when it was done with only the guardian's authority, or with both the guardian and the judge's authority, the conditions under which restoration to original status is or is not granted to the minor were discussed in Disputation 224, from the section *from what has been said so far*.

15 If a minor † accepted a loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a simple loan of fungible goods like money.</note> and finds himself harmed by it—because through his own lack of judgment or fault that money was lost or badly spent—he can seek and will obtain restoration to his original status by paying back only that portion of the money by which he was "made wealthier" <note>original: "locupletior"; meaning the amount that actually benefited his estate rather than being wasted.</note> from it. But if he accepted that loan from a usurer, it is up to the usurer to prove how much the minor was made wealthier by that loan, and he can only recover that amount from him. If, however, he accepted the loan from someone else, then the burden falls on the minor to prove that he was not made wealthier but remained harmed, according to the general rule delivered above; and therefore, if he does not prove the harm, he shall be compelled to pay the whole amount. Likewise Law 1 and 2 of the Code, *If against a creditor*, joined with the glosses there, and Law *To the father*, section 1, of the Digest, *On minors*. This is affirmed by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> and the common opinion, which Antonio Gomez records and follows in the same place as above, number 2, corollary 5, and it was mentioned at the end of Disputation 300.

<margin>Question</margin>
16 Whether, moreover, if a minor † finds himself notably harmed in a resignation or an exchange of an **ecclesiastical benefice** <note>A church office that provided a living or income to the holder.</note> made while he was a minor, restoration to original status should be granted to him—especially if the matter is no longer "intact" <note>original: "res iam non sit integra"; meaning the situation has changed, e.g., the office has already been given to someone else.</note> but the benefice has been conferred upon another. Many deny this, whom Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, a leading Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> records in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 5, number 1. However, Covarruvias himself in the same place, number 3, and Emmanuel Acosta, in section *And what if only*, part 2, number 63, and others whom they cite, nevertheless think it should be granted. For there is no reason why this harm to a minor should be excluded from the general rule of the laws. And because a minor so harmed is not acting regarding harm in "lost profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; potential income that was never realized.</note>—which therefore ought not be repaired when the matter is no longer intact—but regarding the harm of "accrued loss" <note>original: "damnum emergens"; an actual loss of existing property.</note> arising from the fact that by his own lack of judgment and levity, he deprived himself of a benefice that was already his, by making that resignation or exchange harmful to himself. And I lean toward this opinion. Truly, Covarruvias rightly asserts in the same place, last number, that in such unequal exchanges regarding the value of the benefices' revenues, the benefit of Law 2 of the Code, *On rescinding a sale* <note>Codex 4.44.2; the famous "laesio enormis" rule allowing a seller to rescind if the price was less than half the value.</note> does not apply. Since revenues and temporal goods, as they are emoluments <note>Profits or salaries.</note> attached to benefices, share the nature of spiritual things <note>original: "rationé fortiuntur spiritualium"</note> because they are attached to them; spiritual things cannot be sold, and in their exchange and sale, insofar as they are so attached, **simony** <note>The illegal buying or selling of spiritual things or church offices.</note> takes place.

17 Finally, † it was said above that restoration to original status is granted to a minor from a contract or quasi-contract validly celebrated during the time of minority, if he finds himself notably harmed at the time

<column-break/>

it was celebrated. For if, when it was celebrated, it was done usefully and prudently—considering the circumstances then occurring—in the way any prudent adult would celebrate it, or would certainly advise a minor then to celebrate it, then even if the outcome later proves harmful or is discovered to be so, restoration to original status is not granted to the minor. This is because at the time it was celebrated, he was not harmed by the contract or quasi-contract. This is expressly held in Law *The truth*, section *It should be known*, and section *Whence Marcellus*, in the Digest, *On minors*. There it is stated that if a minor buys a slave necessary or useful to him, and the slave dies or runs away, restoration to original status is not granted to him, because the harm was not from the contract or at the time of the contract, but from a subsequent accident. Likewise, it is said that if he entered into a wealthy inheritance, and the estates perished by a chance accident, or the slaves and herds died, the minor is not granted the right to later renounce that inheritance through the benefit of restoration; because he was not harmed by entering into it, or at the time of the addition, but afterward by chance. Law 6 at the end, title 19, part 6 <note>Referring to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational Castilian law code.</note> agrees with this. But observe in this place: when something is paid to a minor or given as a loan, because by that very payment or loan he is exposed to harm and loss due to his lack of skill, inexperience, and minor age, any harm coming to the minor afterward—whether by his own lack of judgment, imprudence, and lazy guarding, or by the wickedness of others—is considered as having its cause in that very payment made to the minor or loan given to him. Therefore, restoration to original status is rightly granted to him for that harm. Thus, the difficulty raised on this matter by the Gloss <note>The Standard medieval commentary on the Roman law.</note> on the word "likewise he is restored" in the cited section *It should be known* is resolved.

18 The benefit † of restoration to original status not only applies against the heirs of the person against whom the restoration is granted—as is very well known—but also passes to the heirs of the person to whom that benefit belonged. That is to say, within the whole time in which that person, if he were living, could seek it, his heirs or universal successors can also seek the benefit, even if they are beneficiaries of a trust <note>original: "fideicommissarij".</note>. For that benefit is not merely personal, but because it was granted to certain persons due to harm, it passes to their heirs, even if they do not have the qualities <note>i.e., being minors themselves.</note> because of which it belonged to the deceased. This is held in Law *Not only* in the Digest, *On restoration to original status*; Law *A minor or a magistrate*, the last section, in the Digest, *On minors*; and Law 8 in title 19, part 6. This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez records and follows above at number 6. Indeed, if the heir of the one to whom that benefit belonged is also a minor, or has another legitimate impediment, such as absence in the military or otherwise for the sake of the republic, for which the benefit of restoration to original status would similarly be granted to him, he is entitled—beyond this whole time in which he is a minor or legitimately hindered—to the entire time that belonged to the deceased to seek the same benefit of restoration that belonged to the deceased. This is held in Laws 1, 2, 3, and 4, and throughout the Code, *On the time for restoration to original status*.
   Whether, moreover, restoration to original status is granted against a **third-party possessor**—as when a minor sold or otherwise validly alienated something and finds himself notably harmed, and the person who [acquired] the thing from the minor...

<summary>Molina discusses the limits of legal restoration for minors, explaining that while minors are protected from bad loans and poor judgment, they cannot undo prudent contracts ruined by later accidents, nor can they treat spiritual revenues like common merchandise.</summary>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 573 #

...receives from the minor, and transfers it to another third possessor by sale or some other title, whether
<margin>19</margin> then the minor is entitled to the benefit of **restoration to original status** against that third possessor. This doubt must be resolved by a distinction. For either the minor finds himself harmed only in the amount of the price, or in the thing itself—because it was advantageous to him not to alienate it, and for that reason he seeks to rescind the contract and have the thing restored to him. In this latter event, the benefit of restoration is available to him against whatever possessor the thing is found with. In the former case, however—when the possessor received it being unaware that it had been bought or accepted by another title from a minor—restoration to original status is not granted against him, except in support <note>Latin: "in subsidium"; meaning as a secondary recourse if the primary party cannot pay.</note> of the first person who received it from the minor. This is because, clearly, neither that first person nor his heirs are able to pay what is lacking for the full value of the item; for when either that first person or his heirs can pay, restoration is granted to the minor only against them. However, when the final possessor received the thing knowing it was bought or accepted by another title from a minor, then the minor or his heirs can indifferently seek restoration to original status against either the third possessor or the first who received the thing from the minor, or against his heirs. These points are covered extensively in the Digest, *On minors*, Law 1, section *Sometimes*, and section *Pomponius*, and the following law. <note>original: "ff. de minor. l. 1. § interdum, & § Pomp. ac. l. seq."</note> Nevertheless, it is added in the Law *But where* <note>original: "l. sed ubi"; Digest 4.4.15</note> under the same title, that if the minor seeks and obtains restoration from the last possessor, the latter can sue the predecessor for eviction <note>A legal claim for compensation when a buyer loses property because the seller did not have clear title.</note> regarding his interest, and so on in a certain order back to the first who received it from the minor. This same thing is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez refers to and follows at the cited number 6, and Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarruvias, a famous Spanish jurist.</note> agrees in *Various Resolutions*, chapter 17, number 7. However, he adds that in the event where the minor can sue for the thing itself, if it does not matter much to him to have the thing rather than its valuation, the third possessor who bought the thing should not be forced to hand it over; instead, the price should be returned to the minor by the first possessor. This is derived from the Law *If from a cause* at the beginning, in the Digest, *On minors*. <note>Digest 4.4.47</note> Furthermore, as was said above, that law speaks specifically of judicial pledges <note>original: "pignotib. iudicialib."; property seized by court order to pay a debt.</note> of a minor sold by public authority, and it establishes that in such an event, if the minor is restored against the judgment, he must be content with the price of the pledges, unless it is of great interest to him to have the pledges themselves; and this is to be observed with Lastarte, *On the tithe of sale*, chapter 14, from number 48 to 54. When a minor has sold something and finds himself harmed such that the contract must be rescinded, then certainly—since the contract of sale was valid in the beginning—the tax collector
<margin>20</margin> who has once perfectly acquired the right to the **alcabala** <note>A Spanish sales tax, historically very important.</note> is not bound to return what was paid to him, even if the contract is later rescinded through restoration to original status. And since then both contracting parties must be restored to their original state, and in the Kingdom of Castile it belongs to the seller to pay the alcabala, surely the minor is bound to return to the buyer the full price he gave him for the thing bought; thus the minor will receive his thing back but will remain alone with the loss of the alcabala paid. In Portugal, however, since the buyer pays half of that tribute (which in that Kingdom is called the **sisa**) and the seller the other half, certainly both contracting parties will remain with the loss of half

<column-break/>

of that tribute. However, when the minor recovers his property from the last possessor through the benefit of restoration to original status, after it had passed through many intermediate purchases and sales, then—since the previous seller is always bound to the one who bought from him for the full interest of eviction—certainly the loss of all such tributes from all those sales, both in Portugal and in Castile, will fall upon the first seller who first began selling to others the thing derived from the minor, as Lastarte recently resolved at the cited number 54.
<margin>21</margin> From the fact that restoration to original status is granted to a minor, if he employed a **guarantor** † for the security of the contract, the guarantor is not thereby freed; rather, he is bound in place of the minor for that which is restored to the minor, or for the interest of the creditor. The reason is that restoration to original status has no place unless the contract was valid and an obligation had arisen from it, which is struck down by the help of the restoration. The guarantor, however, obligated himself in place of the minor so that the obligation would remain firm and the contract would be upheld; otherwise, he himself would pay in place of the minor. But indeed, restoration to original status is a personal privilege of the minor, available to him and his universal successors in his place and name, but not to the guarantor. Nor is the minor bound to the guarantor for what he paid in his place by an action of mandate; because he is similarly restored to the original status against that obligation by which he was bound to him from the mandate, because he was similarly harmed by that mandate. Thus, from these foundations, see Law *In the cause* 1 at the beginning, in the Digest, *On minors*; Law 2 of the Code, *On the guarantors of minors*; and Law 5 at the end, title 19, part 6. <note>References to the Digest (4.4.13), the Codex (2.23.2), and the Siete Partidas (the medieval Spanish legal code).</note> This is affirmed by the common opinion of the doctors, which Antonio Gomez refers to and follows above at number 9.
To what extent prescription <note>The loss of a legal right or title due to the passage of time; similar to a statute of limitations.</note> holds against a minor, or does not, was discussed in Disputations 78 and 79. Also, to what extent restoration to original status holds against a prescription completed during the time of minority, or completed against the Church and those who enjoy the privilege of a minor, and likewise to what extent restoration to original status is granted to adults for a just and reasonable cause, was explained copiously in Disputation 80; therefore, there is no reason for us to speak of these matters again in this place.
<margin>22</margin> The benefit of **restoration to original status** can be sought: First, directly, by demanding it from a judge and proving those things mentioned above that must be proved, having summoned the party against whom the benefit is sought. Second, it can also be sought incidentally by way of an exception <note>A legal defense used to delay or defeat a claim.</note>. For instance, if someone sues a minor based on some contract in which he was harmed, he may plead that he was harmed by that contract during the time of his minority and seek restoration to original status. However, this exception cannot be raised after a longer time than restoration can be sought directly according to what was said above. For an exception is only perpetual when it does not arise from an action that one can only bring within a certain time; this exception, however, arises from and is joined with the right to seek restoration to original status, and therefore lasts no longer than four years after minority, which is the only time in which restoration to original status can be sought. Thus Antonio Gomez, at the cited chapter 14, number 8.

### Ludovicus Molina: On Contracts ###

...with the common opinion of the legal experts, which he cites.
<margin>Question</margin>
23 You will ask, however, before which judge **restoration to original status** must be sought. Law 2 of the Code, *Where and before whom the investigation of restoration to original status [is held]*, etc., defines that it must be sought before the judge of the person against whom it is sought. This is because the one seeking it is the plaintiff, and the one against whom it is sought is the defendant; thus, according to the general rule, the plaintiff must follow the "forum of the defendant" <note>Latin: "forum rei"; the legal principle that a lawsuit must be brought in the jurisdiction where the defendant resides.</note>. *Law 8, Title 19* says it must be sought "before the ordinary judge of the place" <note>original Spanish: "delante del iuzgador ordinario del lugar"</note>, where Gregorius Lopez <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist famous for his commentary on the Siete Partidas.</note> explains this is understood to mean the judge of the defendant, and not the plaintiff, according to the cited Law 2. He immediately asks, however, whether in the place where the contract was made, when the defendant does not have a home there, a minor who was harmed regarding that 24 contract can seek † **restoration to original status** before the judge of that place, if the defendant against whom it is sought happens to be found there. Together with Baldus, Guilelmus de Cuneo, and Paulus Castrensis, he answers in the negative: because although one can be sued in the place of a contract even if they do not live there, this only applies to taking action *based* on that contract, not for *rescinding* the contract. Jason and Decius affirm the same, cited by Covarrubias in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 4, 
<margin>Decision</margin>
number 1. However, Covarrubias affirms the opposite there, along with Bartolus and others whom he cites. For that judge is the "ordinary judge," and more truly the judge of that contract; no suitable reason can be given why he should be the ordinary judge for a lawsuit arising from that contract, but not for someone harmed by it to seek restoration, since they have a right to seek it. The cited Law 2, if it sends the minor to seek restoration before the ordinary judge of the defendant's territory, teaches what ought to be done ordinarily; it does not speak of when the contract was celebrated in another place and the person against whom restoration is sought is found with the plaintiff in the place where the contract occurred.

Gregorius Lopez adds that a case for restoration to original status can be specifically delegated by the Prince or by the ordinary judge of the defendant’s residence. He also adds that restoration can be sought before a judge delegated for a "totality of causes" <note>Latin: "vniuersitatem causarum"; a judge appointed to handle all types of cases rather than a specific one.</note> by the ordinary judge of the defendant's residence. Likewise, before a judge delegated for only one specific case, restoration can be sought "incidentally" if the person seeking it is harmed in some act regarding that case; this is because seeking it incidentally is permitted, as he affirms with Paulus Castrensis, and all these things are sanctioned by the final law of the Code, *Where and before whom the investigation...*. Regarding ordinary judges who do not have a fixed territory of jurisdiction—such as the judges of the Scholastic Universities <note>Special courts for students and faculty in medieval/Renaissance universities.</note> and ordinary judges granted to certain religious orders—Gregorius Lopez says, with Paulus Castrensis, that they cannot grant restoration to original status, according to the final law cited. However, if that law is examined closely, it certainly does not deny such judges the power to restore; it only denies it to those they delegate. Likewise, arbitrators cannot grant restoration, as held in the same law; although a gloss there says it can be submitted to them to judge whether restoration *ought* to be granted, which Bartolus, Salicetus, and others approve, though Baldus rejects it. Also, "pedanean" judges <note>Latin: "iudices pedanei"; minor or inferior judges who handled small claims "at the foot" of the higher tribunal.</note>—such as the vicars of Bishops in particular places, and judges of specific towns where no high tribunal is sent—cannot grant restoration to original status, as held in the same law.
<margin>Question</margin>
25 The question is: if the Church finds itself harmed by a contract celebrated with a layman, can it seek 

<column-break/>

restoration to original status before an Ecclesiastical judge, or only before a secular lay judge, following the general rule of the "forum of the defendant"? Innocent, Panormitanus, Maranta, Gregorius Lopez, and the common opinion cited by Covarrubias, all assert that the Church can then seek restoration even before an Ecclesiastical judge belonging to the Church that is seeking it, and that this is a "peculiar privilege" of the Church. In the same way, they say the Church can sue before an Ecclesiastical judge regarding the nullity of a contract it made with a layman. This is suggested by Chapter 1, *On restoration*, and proved much more clearly by the penultimate chapter of *On Church property not to be alienated*. There, when a certain monastery was enormously harmed by a contract with a layman, restoration was ordered through an Ecclesiastical judge. Covarrubias held that this was consistent with the common opinion, saying it could be argued the Ecclesiastical judge in that chapter was also the judge of that layman because that province was subject to the temporal lordship of the Church—though he adds that one might easily be "guessing." I do not think we should depart from the common opinion confirmed by the use of those two chapters. However, I approve of what Covarrubias adds: namely, that this privilege is not to be extended to the private property of Ecclesiastical persons, nor to contracts which clergy celebrate regarding property belonging to themselves. In those contracts, if they are minors and seek restoration, they must follow the forum of the defendant. This privilege only takes place regarding the property belonging to the Churches themselves, which was the subject of the two chapters cited.

Regarding whether one person can seek restoration to original status for another: It must be said that a tutor, 
<margin>Doubt</margin>
26 curator, prelate, † administrator of a hospital, or similar official, and universally all those who have legitimate 
<margin>Decision</margin>
administration of another's property, can seek restoration for those whose property they manage without a specific mandate <note>A specific legal authorization or power of attorney.</note>, because this is part of their own duty. Among these, I count a father administering his son's "adventitious" goods <note>Property the son acquired from someone other than the father (e.g., an inheritance from a mother or uncle).</note>. This is the view of Innocent and Panormitanus, and Covarrubias, based on the law where a minor's representative can appeal a sentence without a special mandate; by the same logic, they can seek restoration, since a mandate is no more required for one than for the other. The same applies to others who have the administration of another’s affairs. This is confirmed because all these people, without a special mandate, can take the "oath of calumny" <note>Latin: "iurāt de calumnia"; an oath that the party is acting in good faith and not bringing a frivolous or malicious suit.</note> for those whose goods they manage. The same opinion is gathered, or rather is openly evident, from the final law of Title 19, Part 6, where it speaks of "those who have in their power" <note>original Spanish: "onde los que an en poder"</note>.

27 When someone is not a legitimate administrator of the property of a person entitled to restoration, they cannot seek restoration for them unless they have a *special* mandate for that purpose; a general mandate for all their causes and business is not sufficient. This is held in the law *Illud*, the final section, in the Digest, *On minors*.

He also clarifies that legal guardians and administrators may petition for this relief on behalf of their charges without a special mandate.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding who is authorized to petition for "restoration to original status" (restitutio in integrum) on behalf of another, specifically focusing on whether a representative needs a general or a special power of attorney.</meta>

### Second Treatise, Disputation 573. ###

This holds true even if a **general mandate** <note>Latin: *mandatum generale*; a broad power of attorney to act in all legal matters.</note> is given for all of one’s causes and business, even if a clause is added stating it applies "even if the matters require a **special mandate**," <note>Latin: *mandatum speciale*; a specific authorization required for high-stakes legal actions that fall outside a general representative's typical powers.</note> as found in the chapters *Qui ad agendum* and *Quia generale* regarding representatives in the *Sixth Book of Decretals*. Regarding which clauses, when added, are deemed to grant a special mandate—even if no mention was made specifically of **restoration to original status**—refer to what was said in Disputation 557, final paragraph, concerning the power to reach a settlement (which also requires a special mandate). 

However, Covarrubias rightly advises in the cited Chapter 6, number 2, along with Bartolus, Innocent, and Panormitanus on the chapter *Coram* regarding restorations, where he speaks excellently: according to the common opinion of the doctors of law, for a representative to seek **restoration to original status** in any particular cause or business of the principal, it is sufficient if he has a mandate from him in general to seek restoration in his place. It is not necessary for him to specify the cause or business individually, nor the persons against whom the restoration must be sought. 

The reasoning is not the same as a father’s mandate to a son to enter into an inheritance. For that, lest the son suffer harm from the entry, it is necessary that the father acknowledge the inheritance specifically and give the son a specific mandate regarding it. Panormitanus says the same above: universally, when a special mandate is required for something, and harm is imminent because the matter is not specifically expressed, this is understood to apply to a third party. However, from a **restoration to original status**, harm rarely or never befalls the one for whom it is sought. 

Similarly, the reasoning is not the same as the "oath of calumny" <note>An oath taken by parties in a lawsuit asserting they are acting in good faith and not for the purpose of harassment or deception.</note> which a representative must take in the principal's place; for this, the representative must receive a mandate for that specific case, otherwise perjury could easily occur in the principal's name. This risk is not seen in a general mandate to seek restoration in the principal's place. Covarrubias, following Cassiodorus, argues that if someone has a mandate "to act, to defend, and to petition," he can be admitted to seek **restoration to original status** on behalf of the principal; because, he says, it is sufficient if a special mandate is implied within a general series of words. 

Cassiodorus and Covarrubias seem to believe that the word "to petition" <note>Latin: *ad supplicandum*.</note> implies a special mandate for restoration; for under the other words, "to act" and "to defend," it is clearly held in the chapter *Qui ad agendum* that restoration is neither included nor implied. I, however, am not certain of this. Therefore, in such an event—it being a doubtful matter whether the representative is deemed to have a special mandate—he could be admitted to seek the restoration provided he offers a **guarantee of ratification** <note>Latin: *cautio de rato*; a legal promise or bond ensuring that the principal will uphold the representative's actions.</note> that the principal will approve it. This is the prescribed course in doubtful cases, according to the law *Quod si* in the section on minors, and noted by Panormitanus and Covarrubias. 

However, simply because a representative is given a general mandate with a clause "to ratify whatever he shall do," he is not deemed to have been granted the power for those things that require a special mandate, as affirmed by the gloss of Accursius and the common opinion of the doctors. For that clause only functions to ensure the representative is not required to provide security for the payment of the judgment, even if he would otherwise be bound to provide such security.

<column-break/>

Although relatives up to the fourth degree, having provided a guarantee of ratification, may act in those matters for an absent relative for which a general mandate suffices, <margin>28</margin> nevertheless, only a father can seek **restoration to original status** for a son. Other relatives cannot, as is expressly held in the law *Patri pro filio* regarding minors, unless the minor were a spendthrift <note>term: *prodigus*; a person legally disqualified from managing their own affairs due to wasteful spending.</note> or insane, and the relatives were his legal guardians. In that case, they could seek restoration in his place, as is manifest from what was said above. So says Covarrubias with the common opinion, which asserts this should generally be understood for other matters requiring a special mandate. 

The chapter *Constitutus* does not contradict this, where a brother was admitted to obtain restoration for another brother. Setting aside other responses by Covarrubias and others which are quite unsatisfactory, the legitimate explanation is this: in that case, the brother was not only a partner in the litigation, but was also seeking restoration for himself, because he himself had been harmed by that contract during the time of his own minority. Therefore, since he was pleading his own cause—which was inseparable from his brother's cause—and was seeking a benefit common to both in the same matter, he certainly had to be admitted. Surely the cited laws do not intend the contrary in such an event. And perhaps he even had a special mandate from his brother to handle their common cause in that manner.

29 † What has been said about the necessity of a special mandate to seek restoration for another is to be understood when it is sought as the **principal claim**. It is different, however, when it is sought **incidentally** <note>As a secondary issue arising within a larger, ongoing court case.</note> regarding the cause or things occurring within a cause for which someone already has a mandate. For he who has a mandate for a certain cause is deemed by that very fact to have it for the incidental matters within it. 

Just as a judge who cannot directly and principally hear a case for **restoration to original status** can nevertheless hear and grant restoration regarding incidental matters in a case committed to him, as was said above. This is according to the chapter *Suscitata* and the common opinion. Furthermore, whatever some may have said to the contrary, while the principal case is being pursued, such a representative can seek restoration regarding **interlocutory sentences** <note>term: *sententia interlocutoria*; a provisional or intermediate ruling made before the final decision.</note> that have passed into "judged matter" <note>Latin: *rem iudicatam*; a final ruling that can no longer be appealed.</note> because they were not appealed in time. This is because he is still deemed to have a mandate for all things pertaining to that cause. However, regarding the **definitive sentence** of the principal cause, he can only seek restoration while the time granted for appealing it still lasts; once that time has elapsed, the cause for which he held a mandate is deemed finished, and he cannot seek restoration without a new, particular mandate for that purpose.

30 Although a special mandate is required to seek and pursue restoration, a **general mandate** is sufficient to **defend** the person against whom the restoration is sought, as Panormitanus notes on the cited chapter *Suscitata*.

It distinguishes between general and special powers of attorney, the rights of family members to intervene, and the difference between seeking restoration as a main claim versus an incidental procedural move.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Molina's legal analysis of "restoration to original status" (restitutio in integrum), a legal remedy allowing a person to undo a contract or legal action that was unfair. He is specifically examining how this remedy applies when property is shared between a minor and an adult.</meta>

[Page 874]

cited by others, and whom Covarrubias refers to and follows in the final number of the section cited above, the answer is quite clear in itself.

<margin>31</margin> When two or more people hold a thing or a right in common, one of whom is an adult and the other a minor (the same applies whenever one party is entitled to <term>restoration to original status</term><note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*; a legal remedy that voids a contract or decision to return the parties to their original legal positions, usually granted to minors or those cheated.</note> for some other reason and the other is not), then, if restoration is granted to the minor and the matter in question is divisible, that restoration does not benefit the other person, even if they held the property jointly. This is expressly stated in the Code, in the law *si in communi eademque causa*. Read other laws cited by Gama in Decision 263, number 1. However, when the matter is indivisible, such as an <term>easement</term><note>Latin: *servitus*; a legal right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way.</note> on another’s estate, the final gloss of the cited law, and with it Paulus Castrensis, argued that the restoration granted to the minor also benefits the adult, based on the principle found in the Digest (*quemadmodum servitutes amittuntur*).

<margin>32</margin> There it is held that if an easement is shared by someone with a ward, it cannot be lost through <term>prescription</term><note>The loss of a legal right because it was not exercised for a specific period of time.</note> against the ward, because as long as he is a ward, prescription has no place against him; nor is the easement lost through non-use against the other party. This is also based on the law *si fundus* in the Digest. There it is stated that if a field to which an easement is owed belongs to several people, each one has the right to a full legal action regarding that easement. However, Antonio Gomez (in his second volume of *Various Resolutions*, chapter 14, number 10) asserts the opposite, following Bartolus and the common opinion. He says that although a minor who shared an easement with others on a certain estate and gave it up along with them may be restored to his original status, and the whole easement restored to him, the others who gave it up are still barred from using it. 

I would say that we must consider whether the thing to which the minor is restored depends so much on his consent that without it, the entire grant or contract would be void. In that case, the minor’s restoration against his own consent or contract benefits the others, because the remaining consents alone could achieve nothing. It is for this reason that in Book 3 of the **Portuguese Ordinances**, Title 87, § 4, it is defined that in contracts which are void under Portuguese law unless both spouses consent, if one is an adult and the other a minor, and the contract was celebrated with the consent of both, and the minor spouse is restored against that contract by reason of their age, that restoration benefits the other spouse. This is because without the consent of the one who is restored, the entire contract collapses and holds no validity. This agrees with the law *per fundum*, which states that because the right of easement on lands shared by many depends on the grant of all of them—even if many of them grant it—the easement is not established as long as any one of them does not grant it. The final consent confirms all previous consents and gives them force; without the final one, the others are insufficient. From this it is clear that if all had consented and one was restored against his consent, the easement would cease entirely, even in comparison to the others. Their consent depended on his to have any force, and thus his restoration benefits the others. Therefore, if there were many owners of a single estate, even if that estate owed an easement to another...

<column-break/>

...if the owners of the estate to which the easement was owed had given it up, either for free or for a price, and one of them was later restored against that renunciation, a distinction must be made. Because if the estate they owned was in some way divisible, then, even if they possessed it jointly, that estate ought to be divided into as many parts as there were owners. The full easement would then be owed only to the part belonging to the person who was restored, but not to the remaining parts, as Bartolus, Antonio Gomez, and others affirm; therefore, that restoration does not benefit the others. If, however, it was entirely indivisible, then that restoration benefits everyone, though they will be bound to return the price if they received any for giving up that easement. Nothing in the law *si communem* contradicts our opinion: for there the discussion concerns the prescription of an indivisible easement common to two people, which, if it is not lost against one of them but remains safe, is not lost against the other. For the use by either of those two would be sufficient to interrupt the prescription. Nor does the law *si fundus* contradict this: for although each of them has a legal action for that easement because it is indivisible, it is added there that the *interest* in it is divisible.

<margin>33</margin> If a minor, after becoming an adult, confirms what he had done during his minority (for which he was entitled to the benefit of restoration), he thereafter loses that benefit. This is because from the time of that confirmation or ratification, the act is deemed to have been done by an adult, and has indeed now been performed by an adult. For the same reason, if a minor’s <term>immovable property</term><note>Real estate, such as land or buildings.</note> was sold without a judge’s decree, and thus the contract was invalid, and after becoming an adult he confirms or ratifies that sale, it becomes valid from then on. Except in either case if fraud was involved, and the adult was ignorant of the fraud while ratifying the contract. This is found in the Code (*si maior factus ratum habuerit*) and is affirmed by the common opinion, which Antonio Gomez follows. However, if there were <term>lesion</term><note>A legal term for financial loss or being cheated in a contract, specifically when the price is far below the true value.</note> beyond half of the fair price, the remedy provided to adults under the law would still be available, as Antonio Gomez rightly adds.

<margin>34</margin> If a minor confirmed a sale or contract by **oath**, then even if immovable property was sold without a judge’s decree, the sale or contract is valid, and there is no room for restoration to original status, unless there was injustice in the harm suffered. In that case, having first obtained a relaxation of the oath specifically for this purpose, the contract may be reduced to the limits of what is fair, according to what was said in Disputation 149 and the two following.

# Second Treatise, Disputation 57, Part 4.

<margin>
This protection is extended also to hospitals and other pious places, which are included under the name of the "Church." Number 2.
However, it fails in some events, so that even beyond the four-year limit, one may have the benefit of restoration. Number 3.
The same applies to the state, the military, and others similar, as in numbers 4 and 5.
</margin>

<margin>1</margin> The Church, <term>like a minor</term><note>Latin: *instar minoris*. In Roman and Canon law, the Church was legally categorized as a minor because it required administrators (clergy) to act on its behalf, much like a child requires a guardian.</note>, enjoys the privilege of <term>restoration to original status</term><note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*; a legal remedy that voids a contract to return parties to their original positions.</note>. However, because the Church is not actually a minor—since it remains perpetually in the same legal state—it only enjoys this privilege for a <term>four-year period</term><note>Latin: *quadriennium*.</note> from the time the contract was made, the quasi-contract was formed, or the injury was sustained. This is the same way a minor enjoys the privilege for four years after reaching the age of twenty-five (that is, until their twenty-ninth year). This "useful four-year period" regarding the Church is explained in the preceding disputation in the same way as it applies to minors. The same is to be understood for others who are eligible for the benefit of restoration, as stated there and established in the final law of the Code, *Regarding the time for restoration to original status*. That the Church enjoys this privilege for those four years is established in Chapter 1 of the same title, joined with the aforementioned law of the Code, and expressly in Chapters 1 and 2 of the Sext, as well as the unique Clementine decree under the same title, and the final law of Title 19, Part 6; the common opinion of the doctors agrees.

<margin>2</margin> Under the name of the "Church" in this context, we also include hospitals and other similar pious places; for all the privileges of the Church are extended to these, as per the law *Omnia* in the Code *Regarding the Most Sacred Churches*. Panormitanus agrees on Chapter 1, as does Johannes Andreae, whom he cites, and others referred to and followed by Gregorio López on the final law cited above, and Maranta in *Regarding Judicial Order*. However, this restoration is granted when the Church itself is injured in its own rights or property, but not when ecclesiastical persons are injured in things that come to them from the Church or from their own ecclesiastical dignity. Hence, if the <term>chapter</term><note>The governing body of a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> of a certain church is injured in the rights or goods of the chapter—which remain the property of the chapter and the community—restoration is granted. But if the injury concerns the distribution of revenues among individuals because someone managed them poorly, restoration is not granted. In the same way, if a <term>benefice-holder</term><note>Latin: *beneficiatus*; a cleric who holds a church office that provides an income (a benefice).</note> acts regarding the right of the benefice itself as it belongs to that Church, and an injury to the Church occurs, restoration is granted. But if he contends with someone else over whether that benefice belongs to him or to the other person, or if he leases the revenues of the benefice for a lower price, then because the injury regards himself and not the Church, restoration is not granted. This is the view of Panormitanus, Gregorio López, and Maranta, as cited above, and the common opinion, which is quite manifest in itself.

<margin>3</margin> In Chapter 1 of the Sext, *Regarding restoration to original status*, it is held that although the benefit of restoration should not regularly be granted to the Church beyond the four-year limit, it *can* nevertheless be granted if the injury was caused by fraud or deceit and this is proven, or if some other reasonable cause exists that ought to move a superior to grant restoration beyond four years. The final gloss there, and with it Panormitanus, commemorate two such causes. First, if the prelate who injured the Church by making a contract in the Church's name lived through the entire four-year period in which restoration should have been sought. Second, if the Church was <term>most enormously injured</term><note>Latin: *enormissime laesae*. In medieval law, "enormous injury" (laesio enormis) usually referred to being cheated out of more than half the fair value of an item.</note>; for on account of an "enormous injury," restoration was granted to the Church after the four-year limit in the chapter *Ad nostram* (which is the second to last) *Regarding the non-alienation of Church property*.

<column-break/>

This is affirmed by Panormitanus and the common opinion, which Covarrubias, Emmanuel Acosta, and others refer to and follow. The final law of Title 19, Part 6, requires that for this extraordinary restoration to be granted to an injured Church or state after the four-year limit has passed, the injury must be so enormous that it exceeds half of the just value. In such cases, it decrees that restoration may be granted for up to thirty years, but not beyond. Rodrigo Suárez, as cited by Emmanuel Acosta and Covarrubias, says that under <term>common law</term><note>Latin: *ius commune*; the combined Roman and Canon law system used in Europe.</note>, restoration for enormous injury is only granted for an additional four-year period, such that the total window is eight years from the contract. Emmanuel Acosta and Covarrubias rightly criticize this. First, because as Hostiensis affirms, restoration was granted after ten years in the cited chapter *Ad nostram*. Furthermore, if restoration is granted beyond four years by the judge's office, that office ought to be perpetual (following the logic of the law *Videamus*), and the action should be available for thirty years, according to the law and the gloss on the word "persecution" regarding the prescription of 30 or 40 years. Therefore, they think that the final law of Title 19, Part 6, was brought into agreement with the common law on this point. Emmanuel Acosta thinks that in said final law—which grants restoration for up to 30 years to the Church and the state when injured beyond half the just value—it is not speaking of the "restoration to original status" we are discussing, but rather the remedy of Law 2 of the Code, *Regarding the rescission of a sale*. However, Covarrubias rightly rejects this, because as is clear from the preceding parts of that law and its entire course, it speaks of "restoration to original status" as a distinct thing from the remedy of Law 2, and Gregorio López and other Spanish interpreters agree on this. Covarrubias believes that restoration beyond four years for enormous injury applies to minors, the Church, and the state. But Emmanuel Acosta says it was never heard of that minors were restored after the four-year period (from age 25 to 29) due to enormous injury. He argues it does not apply to them after that period, but it *does* apply to the Church, and he gives the reason why it is denied to a minor but granted to the Church. He says that if minors do not seek restoration in the four years after turning twenty-five, they are deemed to have tacitly ratified and confirmed what was done during their minority. But because the Church is *always* in the same state (equivalent to a minor) and enjoys a minor's privilege, it was rightly granted that although it normally has four years, if it is enormously injured or another reasonable cause occurs, the benefit of extraordinary restoration is granted to it even beyond four years. Note here that this reasoning applies to both the state and the Church, which was perhaps the reason why the cited law extended restoration beyond four years for enormous injury to the state and Church, making no mention of the minor. As Covarrubias says...

# DISPUTATION 575.

## SUMMARY.

1. Whether <term>fruits</term><note>Latin: *fructus*. In legal terms, this includes any yield or profit from property, such as crops, rents, or interest.</note> regarding a sold item are included in restoration to original status.
2. Interpretation of the chapter *To Our [Inquiry]* on the non-

<column-break/>

alienation of church property, and number 3.
4. Interpretation of the law *But if a minor*, paragraph *Restoration*, and the law *Of the Father*, paragraph *If money*, in the Digest, *On Minors*.
5. Whether restoration is granted to a minor against a completed sale when another buyer is later found who offers a higher price.

<margin>Question</margin>
Regarding the first of these: Covarruvias in *Various Resolutions*, book 1, chapter 3, number 1 (whose opinion Emmanuel Acosta approves, noting it was approved by the Portuguese Senate in Decision 212) and others whom they cite, affirm that when restoration to original status occurs, the property must be returned with the fruits collected from it. <margin>1</margin> They prove this from the law *But if a minor*, paragraph *Restoration*, in the Digest, *On Minors*. There, the jurist Paulus says: *Restoration is to be made in such a way that everyone receives their original right. Therefore, if someone who was cheated in the sale of a plot of land is restored, the praetor should order the buyer to return the land with its fruits and receive back the price.* The jurist adds: *Unless the buyer gave the price to the minor at a time when it was likely to be believed that the minor would squander or lose it; for then he is only to be restored that portion of the price which remains, or by which the minor was made wealthier from it. This is no different than if he had given that money to him as a loan; the minor would only be held to return what remained of the loan, or the amount by which the minor was made wealthier by that loan, as was said in Disputation 573.* However, because he who buys necessarily pays a price in exchange for the thing bought, whereas one who gives something as a loan does not have such a necessity but can abstain entirely from giving a loan to a minor, he adds that one should not act as severely in this part with a buyer as with a lender. For that reason, a lender should indistinctly be returned only what remains of the loan or that which made the minor wealthier; but a buyer should be returned his entire price, unless he paid it to the minor at a time when it was to be believed he would squander or lose it; for only then is he to be returned from that price what remains or that which made the minor wealthier. Thus far Paulus. The jurist Gaius agrees in the law *Of the Father*, paragraph *If money*, in the Digest, *On Minors*, where he adds: if a minor bought a farm with his own money for more than was proper, the seller should be ordered to return the price with the interest he perceived from it or could have perceived, and receive back the farm with the fruits perceived from it, insofar as the minor was made wealthier by them. If, however, the minor sold a farm for a lower price than was proper, the buyer is held to return it with the fruits perceived from it (the gloss adds: and those he could have perceived, as was said just before regarding interest) and he shall receive the price only insofar as the minor was made wealthier by it. Thus far Gaius. Covarruvias confirms the same from the law *The Farm*, in the Digest, *On the farms of minors*. However, the discussion there concerns a case where the contract was void by the law itself, and the minor did not lose ownership of the sold farm because it was sold without a judicial decree; for that reason, it is rightly ordered that the price be returned to him with the fruits perceived from it, if they exist; otherwise, he can sue for their valuation: provided that...

### Second Treatise, Disputation 575.

...so that, if the <term>minor</term><note>In Roman and Canon law, a "minor" was anyone under age 25, who was granted special legal protections against unfair deals.</note> was made wealthier from the price paid, he should return that amount by which he was enriched, including the usual interest paid from that money, and he must also pay for the costs of any improvements made to the estate. The portion categorized as <term>fruits</term><note>Latin: *fructus*. This refers to any legal profit or natural produce from a property, such as crops, rents, or interest.</note>, even those gathered by a <term>possessor in bad faith</term><note>Latin: *mala fides possessor*. Someone who knows they do not have a valid legal title to the property they hold.</note>, are understood to be what remains after deducting the expenses incurred in collecting them; in these expenses, the value of the labor applied is also calculated, as proved by **Covarrubias** in the citation above, number 3. This has also been stated and proved by us in the place cited below and elsewhere in the preceding sections.

**Covarrubias**, in the cited chapter 3, number 4, excepts those fruits from the established doctrine which the possessor of the liable property had gathered in <term>good faith</term><note>Latin: *bona fides*. Acting with an honest belief that one's claim is legally valid.</note> and had consumed in good faith. For equity does not allow him to be forced to restore these, except to the extent that he was made wealthier by them. Indeed, he is not held liable for what was consumed in good faith—where he was not enriched either by the thing received or by the unjust acceptance—and therefore he is simply not required to restore them. However, an objection is immediately raised against this: that such a possessor should not be judged to have consumed them in good faith in a way that would free him from the burden of returning them. This is because he consumed them with the knowledge that the item had been bought or otherwise received from a minor, and therefore, by the disposition of the law, it was subject to <term>restoration to original status</term><note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*. A legal remedy that cancels a contract and returns both parties to their original positions.</note> along with the fruits gathered from it. This is affirmed by **Imola**, **Felinus**, and others whom he cites, and it seems to be established in the *Digest, book 4, title 4, law 1, section 1, at the end*, and was discussed in Disputation 573. Indeed, the mere knowledge in a third or fourth possessor of that property—that it was originally received from a minor—renders him liable, so that an order for restoration can be executed immediately against him, requiring him to restore the property with its fruits, even if the first possessor (who received it directly from the minor) is solvent. It must be observed that there are two types of <term>bad faith</term>, or "lack of good faith," regarding knowledge, since ignorance excludes it. One type is when someone knows they possess what belongs to another and that they are at fault for not restoring it, or at least they doubt the matter. Such bad faith is not present in the possessor we are discussing; for he possesses what has truly become his own through a transfer made with all the required formalities for the sale to be valid, and he has acquired ownership of the thing. Therefore, he possesses what he retains without any fault, and he can lawfully retain it as long as the restoration is not sought. If it is clear to him that he bought the property for a lower price than was fair, he is indeed bound in his <term>forum of conscience</term><note>The "forum of conscience" refers to a person's moral and religious obligation before God, as opposed to the "external forum" of a public courtroom.</note> to increase the price and restore it to the level of a just price; and regarding the fruits gathered from the thing, he must restore what corresponds to that margin of the price, and in that regard, he has bad faith joined with fault. Nevertheless, in safe conscience, he retains that thing as truly his own, as long as restoration is not legally sought. The other type of bad faith (as it pertains to the present matter) is when someone knows they possess a thing that, by the disposition of the law, is liable to restoration along with all fruits gathered from it, if restoration is requested. This is the case for the possessor we are discussing; this knowledge prevents the <term>prescription</term><note>Prescription is the legal method of acquiring ownership of something by possessing it for a long period of time.</note> of the fruits, even if he possesses them with that knowledge for three whole years. The result is that if he consumes them with that same knowledge, he does not consume them in good faith; he is held liable to restore them and is judged to consume them under the condition that, if restoration is later sought, he is bound to restore them from his other assets.

<column-break/>

**Covarrubias** raises this objection to himself and, according to his own opinion, extricates himself from it with difficulty. For in "extraordinary" restorations—those granted beyond four years by the disposition of the law (which we discussed in the preceding disputation, and among which is the one we discuss here regarding the non-alienation of Church property)—the bad faith we are speaking of persists beyond four years, since by law the thing must be restored even after four years; **Covarrubias** seems to suggest the opposite. Furthermore, according to the same opinion, it would have to be said that a third or fourth possessor, who had bought the property at a just price but knew it belonged to a minor, would be held in both the external court and the forum of conscience to restore to the minor all fruits gathered, sold, and consumed, because they were not consumed in good faith in the manner explained; even though the first possessor would be liable to them for <term>eviction</term><note>Eviction here refers to a legal guarantee where a seller must compensate a buyer if the buyer loses the property due to a prior legal claim.</note>.

**Covarrubias** and **Emmanuel Acosta** also raise an objection against themselves regarding the chapter *Ad nostram* [To ours] on the non-alienation of Church property. In that case, the Supreme Pontiff leaves and awards to the person against whom restoration was granted all the fruits gathered from that property. Yet, as **Covarrubias** and **Emmanuel Acosta** rightly argue against **Panormitanus**, those fruits far exceeded the expenses, labor, and industry in gathering them. As is clear from the text itself, the fruits of a single year equaled the entire price given by the possessor for that property. It would have been quite foolish for someone to buy a property for a price where the fruits did not exceed the value of the expenses, labor, and industry applied to gather them; in such a case, the buyer would be the injured party rather than the seller, and thus restoration would not take place—especially not "extraordinary" restoration based on the injury to the seller, such as that case was. Therefore, it follows that in a restoration granted to a minor or the Church, the fruits gathered from the thing being restored do not have to be returned, whether they still exist or have been consumed; instead, only the thing itself must be restored once the price paid has been received back. To this objection, **Emmanuel Acosta** and **Covarrubias** respond that there is a distinction between a "restoration by grace" and a "restoration by justice." A restoration by grace is like when someone punished for a crime by the loss of their goods has those goods returned by the grace of the Prince. A restoration by justice is like when a minor, the Church, or a Republic is ordinarily restored to their original status when an injury has occurred. In a restoration of grace, the fruits of the things of which the person was deprived are not to be restored, but only the things themselves without the fruits, whether they exist or not. This is argued from the law *The same is true of the Nestorians* in the Code, under the title *On Heretics*. There, if some children of heretics were Catholic and some were heretics, all the parents' goods went to the Catholics alone; if the heretic children later converted to the faith, their portions were restored to them by grace, but without accounting for the fruits and administration, because the gathered fruits belonged to the Catholic children who had managed those portions until then. However, in a "restoration of justice," the things must be restored along with the fruits gathered from them, as is clear from the laws cited at the beginning of this disputation. Because, as these authors say, in the "extraordinary" restoration discussed in the cited chapter *Ad nostram*, much of "grace" is mixed in, because that restoration is granted beyond the four-year limit...

### Ludovico Molina, On Contracts

### Page 878

it is granted, it was rightly decreed that the **fruits**<note>Latin: *fructus*. In legal terms, this refers to any income, crops, or profits derived from a property.</note> should not be restored, but should remain entirely with the person against whom the restoration is granted. Therefore, from the doctrine and definition of that chapter, it does not follow that the same must be said for **ordinary restorations of justice**, which are sought and granted within the ordinary **four-year period**<note>Latin: *quadriennium*. Under Roman and Canon law, a minor or the Church usually had four years to contest a contract that was unfairly disadvantageous.</note>.

Certainly, I do not approve of this interpretation of the chapter *Ad Nostram*<note>A specific chapter in Canon Law (Decretals of Gregory IX) dealing with the restoration of Church property.</note>, nor the primary opinion of these doctors—namely, that in an ordinary restoration to the original state, the property must be restored with all its fruits, even if those consumed in **good faith**<note>Latin: *bona fides*. Acting with an honest belief that one’s legal title is valid.</note> before the petition for restoration are excepted (provided the possessor was not made wealthier by them). Nor do I see—regarding the fruits gathered from the property of a minor, the Church, or the state, which was transferred by a valid contract to a new possessor who was truly its owner for the entire time the restoration was not sought or granted—why we should depart from the rules we handed down and proved in **Disputation 463** and other disputations cited there. Those rules state that such fruits do not belong to this possessor only up to the point explained there, just as they belong to other similar possessors who were the true owners of those things at that time. I understand the same regarding the rules handed down in 그hat disputation concerning improvements or expenses made on the property while its ownership remained with this new possessor. I do not repeat all those points here because they were explained at length in that section.

<margin><note>original: manicule pointing to the text</note></margin>
And, to begin from the interpretation of the chapter *Ad Nostram*: first, from the law <term>The same applies to Nestorians</term><note>Latin: *idem est de Nestorianis*. A reference to a law in the Code of Justinian regarding the property of heretics, used here as a legal precedent for how property is handled when ownership is revoked.</note>, it is not established that in a **restoration of grace**<note>Latin: *restitutio gratiae*. A special restoration granted as a favor or privilege by a superior (like the Pope), rather than a standard legal right.</note>, existing gathered fruits are never included, nor that they are granted to others. Rather, when a defendant is restored to all his goods and nothing else is specified, it is understood that they are also restored to the fruits of those goods. Therefore, in the cited law, it was decreed in favor of children who were Catholic at the time of their parents' death; to cut off lawsuits and difficulties, it was decided that the fruits gathered from the portions of heretical children (who later convert to the faith) belong to the children who were already Catholic and to whom those portions had been assigned. One cannot sufficiently conclude from this that in all "restorations of grace," no gathered fruits from the goods being restored belong to those who are receiving the restoration. Furthermore, the **ordinary restoration** granted within four years to minors, Churches, and the state is certainly—if you look at other legal decrees common to all—a "grace" and a pure privilege granted to these groups. When a contract was entirely just, and restoration is only granted because it was not expedient for the minor or Church to sell it, that is "pure grace." But when restoration is granted because the minor or Church was defrauded of the **just value** (even by less than half), there is a sense of justice in reducing that contract to equality. This is no less true for a minor than for an adult; however, because restoration is not granted to adults in such cases to avoid a mountain of lawsuits, but is granted only to minors, the Church, and the state, it is a "mere grace." Therefore, just as these doctors believe that because this restoration (though based in justice) mixes in an element of grace (by being granted to minors but not regularly to adults), it is not a reason for the gathered fruits to belong to the possessor rather than the minor (for these authors say they belong to the minor)...

<column-break/>

...so too, the fact that an **extraordinary restoration** mixes in an element of grace (by being granted for a very just cause beyond the four-year limit) should not be the reason why the fruits—which otherwise should belong to the Church—belong to the person against whom the restoration is granted, as these doctors claim. Likewise, it is very strongly proven that their interpretation of that text is not legitimate. For that layman, who by that contract (which was so unequal on his part) had **enormously harmed** the monastery, was bound in justice in the **court of conscience**<note>Latin: *forum conscientiae*. The internal moral standing of a person before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note> to return the contract to equality. He should have paid the increase in price up to the limits of the just price to the monastery; moreover, regarding the fruits gathered annually, he was bound to pay the monastery a portion that was in the same proportion (after deducting expenses) to the fruits he kept as the price he paid was to the price that was missing to reach the just limit (according to what was said in Disputations 349 and 463). Indeed, in the **outer court**<note>Latin: *forum exterior*. A public, legal court of law.</note>, because that purchase was below half the just price, he could be compelled to this without any special favor being shown to the monastery, simply by using the remedy of the law *De rescindenda venditione*<note>Latin: "On rescinding a sale." A law allowing a seller to cancel a sale if they received less than half the fair value (*laesio enormis*).</note>. Or he himself was bound to offer the villa back to the monastery, reclaiming his price and paying for the fruits according to the explained portion—which were of far greater value than the price he gave for the villa. Consequently, he was bound to restore to the monastery the increase in the value of those fruits beyond the price he paid. Therefore, the fact that restoration is granted to the monastery after four years for the very just cause of that "enormous harm"—and to simultaneously clear the conscience of that layman and rescue him from **mortal sin**—is certainly not a sufficient reason why those fruits of such great value should belong to the layman, when they would certainly have belonged to the monastery (according to the opinion of the doctors we are disputing) if the restoration had been sought within the four-year period. In this matter, observe that it pertained to Canon Law and the **Supreme Pontiff**<note>The Pope.</note> in that chapter to settle the matter so that the layman would not remain in mortal sin. Therefore, I judge the legitimate interpretation of that chapter to be this: that the layman, by the nature of the thing (since by that valid contract the villa became his regarding the **useful ownership**<note>Latin: *utile dominium*. A legal distinction where one person has the right to use and profit from property while another may hold the ultimate title.</note> for that price), was owed a portion of the fruits proportionate to the price he paid, and he truly made them his own by virtue of that contract until it was rescinded by the remedy of restoration. However, the monastery and the Supreme Pontiff forgave the rest of the portion of the fruits to that layman so that he would more easily obey, be rescued from his fault, and return the villa to the monastery without bitterness, while also receiving back the price he gave for it. For those reasons, the monastery was able to forgive him that portion of the fruits to preserve peace and charity with the laity (since they themselves should not have entered into such a contract), and the Supreme Pontiff, as the supreme head of the Church who has authority over all the property of particular churches, was able to forgive that same portion for the same reasons; and it was equitable that he should do so.

<summary>Molina discusses the legal and moral obligations regarding "fruits" (profits) when a contract involving Church property is rescinded due to unfairness. He argues that while laws often protect the Church or minors, the Pope may allow a buyer to keep some profits to ensure a peaceful settlement and save the buyer from the sin of theft.</summary>
<keywords>restitution, fruits, Canon Law, just price, laesio enormis, mortal sin, Pope, monastery, contracts, equity</keywords>
