<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion from page 878 regarding the restoration of property (restitutio in integrum). Molina is specifically debating whether a buyer must return the "fruits" (profits or produce) of a property if a contract with a "minor" (a category including the Church and the State) is later rescinded. He is contrasting his views with legal scholars like Emmanuel Acosta and Diego de Covarrubias.</meta>

# Second Treatise, Disputation 57

### Page 879

nor is it unusual for the kindness and charity of the Church. Therefore, concerning the rigor of justice, that increase of **fruits**<note>Latin: *fructuum*. Refers to the income, crops, or profits generated by a property.</note> could be reclaimed from that layman, which had been granted to him; but not the portion that corresponded to the price he gave for the villa. And regarding that portion, that chapter confirms our opinion, which is contrary to those of Emmanuel Acosta and Covarrubias.

Regarding the primary opinion of Emmanuel Acosta and Covarrubias: Acosta himself (in the place cited above, number 73) confesses that **Baldus**<note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential Italian jurist.</note> and many others whom he cites affirmed the opposite, and that the common practice of **Spain**<note>Latin: *Hispaniarum*. Literally "of the Spains," referring to the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula.</note> follows this; he adds that the practice has erred, having been deceived by the old authority of those doctors. I, however, judge that the practice of Spain rests upon an equity and justice so manifest from the very nature of the matter, that even if some opinion of the **jurists**<note>Latin: *iurisconsultorum*. These were the professional legal experts of Roman and medieval law.</note> were openly to the contrary, I would say that the contrary practice and custom had revoked that opinion. Rightly, that practice did not take account of that opinion from the beginning, following instead what the nature of the thing itself holds and demands, rather than that erroneous opinion which is contrary to equity and justice. For those **heathen jurists**<note>Latin: *ethnici illi iurisconsulti*. Molina refers to the original Roman legal experts who lived before the Christianization of the Empire.</note> were men who could err in examining the nature of the thing and in defining what was more expedient; they often did err, asserting and defining things contrary to one another. Indeed, those who, in the time and by the order of the Emperor **Justinian**<note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD), who commissioned the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundation of civil law.</note>, collected so many opinions into the body of civil law from various books of such jurists, inserted some things that were contrary to each other (as Covarrubias affirms in the cited chapter 3, and as is clear enough in itself). They did not insert everything as certain, but some things as "probable," so that from all of them, what was more expedient might be selected and judged.

Therefore, in the body of the law, one must observe when something is established by the princes themselves as **positive law**<note>Law specifically enacted by a human authority, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>; that must be stood by, unless it has been revoked by some later law or a contrary custom. From the other things, however, which contain the opinions and minds of the jurists—whether they are teaching what the nature of the thing holds, or what should be thought and judged given other positive laws—one should not depart easily (indeed, only with great difficulty), unless they have been similarly revoked by a later law or a contrary custom. Nevertheless, one should not cling to them so tenaciously that one does not instead stand by a contrary right that contains more equity, or a reason that rests upon manifest justice and equity.

In the matter proposed, then, we are discussing contracts against which the civil law (with the consent of **canon law**<note>The law of the Catholic Church.</note>) grants to "minors," the Church, and public states the privilege of **restoration to the original state**<note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*. A legal remedy where a contract is cancelled and parties are returned to their original positions.</note>. These contracts are valid in themselves and transfer ownership of the things alienated through them to new possessors, and this is done after receiving compensation for those things. (We are speaking here of **onerous contracts**<note>Contracts where both parties give and receive something of value, like a sale.</note>; for in **gratuitous**<note>Gifts or contracts where one side gives nothing in return.</note> ones, there is no doubt that restoration must be made, just as with the things alienated for free by "minors" or the Church, so too with the fruits received from them, especially if they were not consumed in **good faith**<note>Latin: *bona fide*. The honest belief that one is the rightful owner.</note> and the possessors were made wealthier by them.) Since, I say, such contracts are valid in themselves, and ownership is transferred to the new possessors upon payment of compensation so that they may retain and enjoy them with a clear conscience as truly their own—not only in conscience but also in the **external court**<note>Latin: *exteriori foro*. The public, legal court system as opposed to the "internal" court of a person's conscience.</note>—until that right

<column-break/>

and ownership is struck down by the benefit of "restoration to the original state" and the contract is rescinded, surely no equity or justice allows this: that while the "minors," Churches, and states have enjoyed that compensation for all that time and used it for their necessities, the possessor of the things received in exchange should not likewise enjoy and retain the fruits of all that time—at least in proportion to the **just price**<note>Latin: *iusti pretii*. The fair market value at the time of the contract.</note> they paid for them. It would be unjust if they were bound to restore the property and all fruits (even those they could have received but did not) to the "minors," Churches, or states.

Truly, if that were the privilege of "minors," Churches, and public states, besides being unreasonable and unfair, it would result in the **detriment** of those very "minors" and Churches. For there would be no one who would want to enter into contracts with them; a person would be foolish indeed to take on such a burden and subject themselves to such a risk.

And to press the matter more closely: surely, when a contract was entirely just and equal, but is rescinded later because it proved not to be expedient for the "minor" to alienate that thing, no equity at all allows the buyer to be forced to return the fruits received from the thing bought. It was bought through an entirely just contract and truly made their own for the entire time they possessed it. However, when the contract was **unjust** because the thing was bought below the just price, and the **injury**<note>Latin: *laesio*. An economic loss resulting from an unfair contract price.</note> lay not in the alienation itself but in the amount of the price, it is clear from what was said in Disputation 57 that the "minor" is only granted restoration up to the amount of the just price, and not so that they may reclaim the sold property. In that case, it is clear enough that the buyer is only bound to increase the price to the limits of what is just, and to restore those fruits which correspond to the portion of the price they add to reach that limit. They are bound to both of these in the "court of conscience," even without the benefit of a legal restoration.

<margin>4</margin> Regarding the two laws cited at the beginning of this disputation for the contrary opinion: First, what **Gaius**<note>A famous 2nd-century Roman jurist.</note> says about interest on the price does not generally have a place among Christians, for whom **usury**<note>Charging interest on a loan, which was largely prohibited or strictly regulated by Church law.</note> is not permitted in that way. Second, if there is a restoration solely because of an injury in the price (because the "minor" bought above the just price or sold below it), the restoration serves to bring the contract back to equality. This is done by returning a portion of the price to the "minor" (if they bought too high) or by increasing the price (if they sold too low). Additionally, a portion of the fruits corresponding to that missing price must be returned. However, there is no restoration such that the contract is rescinded and the property is returned with all fruits; for restoration only exists to repair the "minor's" injury, and no further, as was said in Disputation 57 and gathered from the words of the jurist **Paul** cited earlier. Gaius, and even Paul, seem to suggest the opposite. Also, what Gaius adds—that a "minor" is only bound to return the price precisely to the extent that they were made wealthier by it—must be limited and understood only for when the money was given at a time when it was presumed they would waste and lose it; otherwise, they would be bound to return the full price, whether they were made wealthier or not, unless one wishes to contradict the equitable doctrine cited from the jurist Paul.

<summary>This page argues that when a contract involving a protected entity (like the Church or a minor) is rescinded, the buyer should not be forced to return all profits if they paid a fair price. Molina emphasizes that legal rules must align with equity and warns that overly harsh protections for the Church would actually harm it by making people afraid to do business with it.</summary>

--- Page 936 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding the restoration of property (restitutio in integrum). Molina is concluding his argument on whether a buyer must return the "fruits" (profits or produce) of a property when a contract is rescinded, and begins a new question regarding whether a "minor" (including the Church or State) can cancel a finished contract if a better offer is made later.</meta>

# Luis de Molina on Contracts

...concerning the return of the property with its <term>fruits<note>In legal terms, "fruits" (*fructus*) refers to the produce, rents, or profits generated by a property, such as crops from a field or rent from a house.</note></term>, both jurists teach that if they understand it to mean that the fruits collected in the meantime—while the contract was not yet rescinded—must be returned (regardless of whether they were proportionate to the price or other compensation given), they should not be listened to. This is because such a requirement conflicts with equity and justice, as has been explained. However, both parties to a contract are sufficiently restored to their original state if the buyer retains the fruits we are discussing, which were collected while the contract was still in effect. This is because the property he restored was his own by that <term>onerous contract<note>A contract where both parties provide something of value to the other.</note></term>; therefore, he justly retains those fruits by right of the ownership and authority he most justly held over that property during all that time. This concludes the first of the points proposed.

<margin>Question</margin>
Regarding the second point, **Ulpian**<note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), a celebrated Roman jurist whose writings form a large part of the Digest.</note>—in the law *Et si sive*, section *qui situm*, under the title *on minors*—takes the occasion of what was said in Disputation 573: namely, that <term>restitution to the original state<note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*. A legal remedy where a party is placed back in the position they were in before a contract was made.</note></term> is granted to a minor regarding **loss of potential profit**<note>Latin: *lucrum cessans*. A legal concept referring to profits that were expected but not realized due to an event or breach.</note>. He asks whether, if a minor's property is sold, and after the sale is perfectly completed another person comes forward offering a higher price, the minor should be restored to his original state so that the second buyer may be admitted to increase the price and obtain the property, just as if the sale had not been finalized. He answers in the affirmative, noting that **Praetors**<note>Roman judicial officials.</note> commonly restore minors and admit the bidding of a second buyer. The same, for the same reason, must be said regarding the leasing of a minor’s property. Law 5, title 19, part 6 <note>A reference to the *Siete Partidas*, the foundational statutory code of Castile.</note> agrees with this, providing for the same "provided," it says, "that the judge understands **that it is of great benefit to the minor**<note>Original Spanish: *que es gran pro del menor*.</note>." Since the Church, the State, and towns enjoy the same privilege of restitution as minors, they judge the same regarding things sold or leased by the Church, the State, or the supreme Prince (concerning the goods that belong to him as the head of the State). From this, many—including **Gregorio Lopez**<note>A famous Spanish jurist (1496–1560) known for his commentary on the *Siete Partidas*.</note> and **Gutierrez**—infer that if a contract has been entered into and finalized with a town (for example, that a person will sell all the necessary meat or baked bread in that town at a certain price), and another person offers to sell the same for a lower price (which is more useful to the State), the town can be restored to its original state and admit this second person to the contract, rejecting the first, even if the matter is no longer "whole" <note>Meaning the contract has already begun to be executed.</note>. This is allowed provided the second person keeps the first harmless by taking over at the same price the goods the first had prepared to fulfill the contract, and by paying him for the value of his labor and applied industry. For both the one who is restored and the one against whom the restoration is made must be returned, as far as possible, to their pristine state and kept free from loss. This should be understood, however, provided that the first person did not act in fraud—such as buying or preparing things he otherwise would not have—simply to prevent another from bidding or to impose a heavier burden if another were to bid; for no one should be protected by fraud or deceit. They also understand the previous doctrine to mean that if the first buyer or lessee is willing to pay the same price offered by the second, he should be preferred over the second and remain in the contract, following the argument of

<column-break/>

the second-to-last and last laws in the Code, under the title *on the leasing of civic estates*, book 11.

However, I am persuaded by what **Albericus** and the more common opinion (as cited by Gutierrez and Gregorius Lopez above) affirm. Regarding the business: if the required formalities for selling or leasing were not observed, the contract was null, and therefore a second bidder can be admitted without needing "restitution to the original state." But if the due formalities *were* observed, yet the minor (or one who enjoys the privilege of a minor) was harmed—either by **actual loss**<note>Latin: *damnum emergens*. A loss actually incurred, as opposed to a profit missed.</note> because the property was sold or leased below the lowest fair price, or by **loss of potential profit** because the sale or lease was not celebrated at a proper and fitting time, or because of the disordered affection, deceit, or negligence of the sellers or lessors the property was sold for less than it otherwise would have been—then there is room for restitution, and a second bidder can be admitted. These laws should be understood to apply only in these events. Provided, however, as Law 5 (cited above) adds and explains, that what the second bidder adds is, in the judgment of a prudent judge, something "notable"; for restitution is not granted for a measly gain for the minor or the one privileged as a minor, as explained in Disputation 573. However, when none of these factors are present—but the thing was sold or leased at a proper time and place, with the required formalities observed, and at a fair price, just as any prudent adult would have sold or leased it if it were his own—then there is no place for restitution, nor can the contract be rescinded to admit a new bidder. The reason is clear: because the minor was harmed neither by actual loss nor by loss of potential profit, but it simply happened by chance that someone later bid more for the property and thus increased the profit. Restitution only has a place where a true injury of loss or missed profit occurs. This reason is confirmed because, as stated in the law *Verum*, section *Sciendum* (on minors) and Disputation 573, restitution does not occur when a minor (or someone in his place) has administered the matter soberly, just as an adult would have administered it if it were his own, even if an actual loss follows by chance. Therefore, with much greater reason, restitution has no place when a thing was sold or leased justly, circumspectly, and appropriately, even if later, by chance, someone else offers a greater profit. Therefore, when a matter is handled in this way, I do not agree with what Gutierrez affirms: namely, that if someone later bids so that a great benefit would come to the poor and the State, restitution should occur and a new bidder be admitted. Indeed, based on a large or small profit of this kind, which is essentially accidental in the manner explained, this should not be allowed. And these things—to the praise and glory of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as well as the untainted Virgin Mary—are said concerning this entire matter of contracts.

->PRAISE BE TO GOD.<-

<summary>Molina concludes his discussion on contracts by arguing that legal restitution for minors, the Church, or the State should only occur if they were genuinely harmed at the time of the contract, not simply because a better offer appeared by chance later. He emphasizes that if a sale was conducted fairly and prudently, the contract must stand to maintain legal stability.</summary>
